units.la: MAGNIFICA sane & digna regio propheta vox est, viri nobilitate generis virtuteq; clarissimi, qua Psalmo centesimo decimonono exclamat, Quàm dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua super mel ori meo? Et, Bonum mihi Lex oris tui super millia auri & argenti. Vidit enim vir Dei sanctus, nihil in hac fragili atq; caduca vita, vel ad Deum cognoscendum magis necessarium, vel ad bene beateq; viuendum vtilius existere verbo illo cælesti, quod ex sacrosancto Dei ore manans, de voluntate eius hominem facit certiorem, diuinaq; sapientiæ thesauros patefacit.
units.tr: Truly magnificent and worthy of a king is the voice of the prophet, most distinguished men, when in Psalm 119 he cries out: "How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" And: "The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver." For the holy man of God saw that nothing in this frail and fleeting life is more necessary for knowing God, or more useful for living well and blessedly, than that heavenly word which, flowing from the sacred mouth of God, makes man more certain of God's will and opens up the treasures of divine wisdom.

units.la: Est Deus suapte natura inuisibilis, maiestatem eius videre homo mortalis, quàm diu in mortali huius polluti corporis carcere constrictus est animus, nequit. Vnde Dominus Mosi petenti sibi ostendi gloriam Dei, Non poteris, inquit, videre faciem meam: quia non videbit me homo, & viuet: ad salutem tamen quæ cognitu necessaria sunt, ex abdito suo throno per verbi prædicationem cælestis rex reuelauit. Atq; hæc ipsa via ut humano generi innotesceret, verbum literis proditum ad posteritatem transmittere visum est. Ad scripturas igitur sacras Christus, in quo veritas, via, & vita est, cognitionis Dei & vitæ æternæ auidos remittit, in ijsq; et testimonium de sese, & vitam æternam positam esse demonstrat: à mortuis sciscitari veritatem, Deo vero verboq; eius neglecto, multo est indignissimum. Num requiret, inquit Esaias vates, populus à Deo pro viuis à mortuis? Ad legem & ad testimonium, si non dixerint iuxta verbum hoc, quia non est ei aurora.
units.tr: God is by his nature invisible, and mortal man cannot see his majesty for as long as the soul is confined in the mortal prison of this polluted body. Hence the Lord said to Moses, who asked to be shown God's glory: "You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live." Yet the heavenly King has revealed, from his hidden throne, what is necessary to be known for salvation, through the preaching of the word. And so that this way might be made known to the human race, it has seemed good that the word should be committed to writing and handed down to posterity. Christ, in whom is the truth, the way, and the life, therefore sends those who desire the knowledge of God and eternal life to the holy Scriptures, and in them he shows that his testimony about himself and eternal life are contained. To seek the truth from the dead, while neglecting the true God and his word, is most unworthy. "Shall not a people seek unto their God? Shall they seek for the living to the dead? To the law and to the testimony! If they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no morning light for them."

units.la: Ad Mosen & Prophetas diuitis epulonis, ad tartara condemnati, fratres ire, percontariq; de statu mortuorum, & vita electorum, siue beatorum in cœlis iubentur. Hinc memorabile est illud Eunuchi reginæ Candaces, qui, ut acta Apostolica testificantur, Esaiæ vaticinium de Christi morte & resurrectione in itinere euoluens, plenius per Philippum apostolum de mysterijs hisce edoctus est. Est hominis constitutio ita diuinitus comparata, ut pro ætatis conditione vel mollioris, vel solidioris cibi submini-strationem desideret: pari ratione anima verbo fidei ad vitam æternam sustentari habet necesse: ideoq; annis teneris primis elementis veluti lacte salubri enutriri, ætate verò confirmata solidiori cibo mysteriorum diuinorum pasci aliq; opus habet: lacte semper uti velle puerile & ridiculum est, virilíq; ætati inconueniens: primis elementis semper inhærere, neq; ad altiora contendere, id uero longe
units.tr: The brothers of the rich man (Dives) are bidden to go to Moses and the Prophets, and to inquire about the state of the dead in hell and the life of the elect, or the blessed in heaven. Hence the story of the eunuch of Queen Candace is memorable: as the Acts of the Apostles testify, while he was reading on the way Isaiah's prophecy of Christ's death and resurrection, he was taught more fully about these mysteries by the apostle Philip. Human nature is so divinely constituted that, according to the stage of life, it requires the supply of either softer or firmer food. In the same way the soul must be sustained for eternal life by the word of faith. Therefore in its tender early years it must be nourished on the first elements, as on wholesome milk, but once it has grown strong it has need to be fed on the firmer food of the divine mysteries. To want always to use milk is childish and ridiculous and unfitting for mature age; to cling always to the first elements and not to strive after higher things, this indeed is by far

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: Preface.

units.la: longè est turpissimum. Nulla vitæ huius pars est, quæ cibo illo cælesti destituì sine salutis discrimine possit. Non enim solo pane viuit homo, sed verbo, quod ex ore Dei egreditur: uerba Christi Spiritus sunt & vita: unde Petrus Christo semper adhærescere, utpote verba vitæ habenti, expetit: & recte angelus eidem, cæterùq; discipulis ex carcere Hierosolymitano eductis mandat, ut stantes in templo populo loquantur verba vitæ. Cui consentiunt illa ad Philippenses, quos Paulus doctor gentium clarissimus luminaria vocat in mundo, in medio nationis prauæ ac tortuosæ sermonem vitæ prætendentia, de quibus gloriari possit in die Christi, quòd non frustra cucurrerit, nec in vanum laborauerit. Est verbū Dei instar salis, quo si ecclesia Christi in hoc mundo careret, in peccatorum sordibus computrescceret. Neq; alia ratione ferociam hominum coercere Spiritui sancto visum est, quàm gladio sermonis diuini: huius namq; proprium est, mundum de peccato, de iustitia, deq; iudicio arguere. Quocirca & præpotentes hominum filios, eosq; qui in imperio sunt collocati, exhortatur idem Spiritus, ut erudiri per verbum Dei sese sinant, ne per furorem Dei in via cõsumantur. Lucis usuram si quis spernat, in tenebris is palpitet necesse est. Verbum Dei piorum pedibus lucernam præbet, ad cuius fulgorem gressus suos dirigunt: ab hoc qui defleciunt, in superstitiones, errores, hæreses, variosq; offendiculorũ labyrinthos, ex quibus sese difficulter expediunt, impingunt.
units.tr: It is most shameful. There is no part of this life that can be deprived of that heavenly food without danger to salvation. For man does not live by bread alone, but by the word that proceeds from the mouth of God; the words of Christ are spirit and life. Hence Peter desires always to cleave to Christ, since he has the words of eternal life. And rightly the angel commands the same, and the other disciples led out of the Jerusalem prison, to stand in the temple and speak to the people the words of life. To this agree those words to the Philippians, whom Paul, the most famous teacher of the Gentiles, calls lights in the world, holding forth the word of life in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, so that he might boast on the day of Christ that he had not run in vain or laboured in vain. The word of God is like salt: if the Church of Christ lacked it in this world, it would rot in the filth of sins. Nor has the Holy Spirit thought fit to restrain the ferocity of men by any means other than the sword of the divine word, for it is its proper work to convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment. Wherefore the same Spirit also exhorts the mighty sons of men, and those placed in authority, to allow themselves to be instructed by the word of God, lest they be consumed on the way by the wrath of God. If anyone spurns the use of light, he must necessarily grope in darkness. The word of God offers a lamp to the feet of the pious, by whose brightness they direct their steps; those who fall away from it stumble into superstitions, errors, heresies, and the various labyrinths of stumbling-blocks, from which they extricate themselves with difficulty.

units.la: Fecit Deus initio rerum vniuersarum sapientissimus conditor, Luminaria duo magna, Solem videlicet & Lunam, quorum ille diei, hæc verò noctis præsit: lumen horum si contempseris, ipsam conditoris Dei sapientiam offenderis. Eadem ratione in ecclesia duo luminaria magna, legem inquam & euangelium lucere, ijsdemq; hominem ad regnum cælorum viasq; Dei duci voluit. Et, quemadmodum Luna noctem, Sol verò diem illustrat, ita Lex futurorum bonorum vmbris ac typis continet promissiones, & ad Christum veram lucem pædagogi instar deducit: Euangelium verò mysteria illa ab initio mundi abscondita patefacit, noctisq; prætergressa abditos sapientiæ cælestis thesauros aperit, neq; vmbris & inuolucris est contectum, sed rupta macerie etiam ad gentes in tenebris habitantes radios suos extendit, idq; omne complet, quod olim vmbris obscurioribus fuerat præfiguratum. In luce hac omnes gentes ambulant, hac vniuersi credentes fruuntur ad vitam æternam. Suauitas huius semel percepta, incredibilem amorem in animis fidelium excitat.
units.tr: God, the most wise Creator, at the beginning of all things made two great lights, the sun and the moon, of which the one presides over the day and the other over the night. If you despise their light, you offend the very wisdom of God the Creator. In the same way, in the Church two great lights shine, namely the Law and the Gospel, and by these God wished to lead man to the kingdom of heaven and the ways of God. And just as the moon illumines the night and the sun the day, so the Law, by means of shadows and types, contains the promises of future blessings and, like a schoolmaster, leads to Christ, the true light. The Gospel, however, unveils those mysteries hidden from the beginning of the world, and, with the night past, opens the hidden treasures of heavenly wisdom. It is not covered with shadows and veils, but, the wall being broken down, it extends its rays even to the Gentiles who dwell in darkness, and it fulfils all that was formerly foreshadowed by the darker shadows. In this light all nations walk; in it all believers enjoy eternal life. The sweetness of this, once tasted, kindles an incredible love in the hearts of the faithful.

units.la: Descendit imber & nix de cælo, illucq; non reuertitur, sed inebriat terram, & gignere facit eam & germinare, daregq; semen serenti, & panem comedenti: sic Verbum, quod egreditur ex ore Dei, non reuertitur ad eum vacuum, sed facit quod vult, & prosperatur in his, ad quæ mittitur. Semen videlicet bonum in terram bonam cadens non potest existere sterile.
units.tr: Rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there, but water the earth and make it bring forth and bud, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater. So the Word, which proceeds from the mouth of God, does not return to him empty, but accomplishes what he wills and prospers in those things to which it is sent. A good seed, falling on good ground, cannot fail to bear fruit.

units.la: Ad salutem, per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, erudire possunt litteræ sacræ, quippe quæ ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in iustitia, seruire homini queunt. Hinc factum est, ut Spiritus Dei, qui sanè vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad ipsius agnitionem venire, tàm regibus et principibus, quàm subditis & imperitis Verbi diuini auditum meditationemq; tantopere commendarint: Cùm sederit, inquit Dominus ad Mosen (Deuteronom.17.) super solium regni
units.tr: The holy Scriptures are able to instruct us unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus, since they are profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, which serve man. Hence it came about that the Spirit of God, who indeed wishes all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of him, has so highly commended the hearing and meditation of the divine Word both to kings and princes and to subjects and the unlearned. "When he shall have sat," says the Lord to Moses (Deut. 17), "upon the throne of his kingdom

units.la: Matth.4. Ioan.6. Actor.5. Philip.2. Matth.5. Vis verbi Dei. Hebr.4. Ephes.6. Ioan.16. 2.Cor.10. Psal.2. ánoxio. 2.Petri 1. Psal.118. à comparatis Genes.1. Luna legi, Sol Euangelio cófertur. Heb.10. Galat.3. Rom.16. 2.Cor.6. Coloss.2. Legis & Euangelij differentia. Ephes.2. Esa.60. Ab effectu. Esa.55. Luc.8. Matth.13. 2.Timot.3. 1.Tim.2. Ad omnes salvos fieri cupiétes verbū Dei pertinet. Deut.17. regni sui (de rege & magistratu præceptum ponit) scribet sibi literatam legem hanc in libro à conspectu sacerdotum, Leuitarum. Eritq; apud illum, & leget in eo omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, ut discat timere Iehouam Deum suum, ut custodiat omnia Verba legis huius & statuta hæc, ut faciat illa. Hinc illa præclara Dei vox extat Deuter. 31. ubi Iosuam ducem Mosi senio confecto & propediem morituro sufficit Dominus: Congrega populum, inquit Dominus, viros & mulieres, & paruulos, & peregrinos tuos, qui sunt intra portas tuas, ut audiant, & discant, timeantq; Iehouam Deum Vestrum, & custodiant faciendo omnia Verba legis huius. Et filij eorum, qui non nouerunt, audiant, & discant timere Iehouam Deum vestrum, omnibus diebus, quibus viuturi estis super terram. Et paulo post ibidem: Capite librum istum legis, & ponite eum in latere arcæ fœderis Iehouæ Dei Vestri, sitq; ibi contra te in testē.
units.tr: Matth. 4; John 6; Acts 5; Phil. 2; Matth. 5. The power of the Word of God. Heb. 4; Eph. 6; John 16; 2 Cor. 10; Ps. 2; ἀνοξιο; 2 Pet. 1; Ps. 118. From comparisons: Gen. 1, the moon is compared to the Law, the sun to the Gospel. Heb. 10; Gal. 3; Rom. 16; 2 Cor. 6; Col. 2. The difference between Law and Gospel. Eph. 2; Isa. 60. From the effect: Isa. 55; Luke 8; Matth. 13; 2 Tim. 3; 1 Tim. 2. The Word of God pertains to all who desire to be saved. Deut. 17: "of his own kingdom" (he lays down a precept concerning the king and magistrate), "he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book, from the one before the priests, the Levites. And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear Jehovah his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them." Hence that famous word of God stands in Deut. 31, where the Lord appoints Joshua as leader in place of Moses, now worn out with age and soon to die: "Gather the people," says the Lord, "men and women and little ones, and your strangers who are within your gates, that they may hear and learn and fear Jehovah your God, and keep to do all the words of this law. And their children, who have not known it, shall hear and learn to fear Jehovah your God, all the days that you live upon the earth." And a little after, in the same place: "Take this book of the law and put it at the side of the ark of the covenant of Jehovah your God, that it may be there as a witness against you."

units.la: Atq; in hanc ipsam sententiam ipsi quoq; Iosuæ regni administrationem suscipien ti mandat Dominus, Conforta te, dicens, & robora te Valde, ut custodias & facias secundum omnem legem, quam præcepit tibi Moséh seruus meus: ne declines ab eo ad dexteram, aut sinistram, ut prospere agas in omnibus, ad quæ perrexeris. Non recedet liber legis iste ab ore tuo, sed mediteris in eo, die ac nocte, ut custodias & facias secundum omne quod scriptum est in eo, tunc enim secundabis vias tuas, & tunc intelliges.
units.tr: And to this same effect the Lord also commands Joshua, when he takes up the government of the kingdom: "Be strong and very courageous, that you may keep and do according to all the law which Moses my servant commanded you; turn not aside from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may prosper in all that you undertake. This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate in it day and night, that you may keep and do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success."

units.la: Intellexit hoc regius vates, cuius supra memini, quando beatos pronunciat eos, quorum studia dies noctesq; in lectione meditationeq; legis Dei sunt occupata: & in summis votis hoc unum habet, ut sibi in domo Domini versari concedatur omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, videatq; pulchritudinem Iehouæ: & pulsus à filio Absalomo nihil tam dolet, quàm à sacro cætu abesse: imò animam suam ad atria Domini deficere testificatur. Nihil nunc de Iosia rege pijssimo dicam, qui muneris sui esse statuit, idolis euersis, superstitiosisq; cultibus abrogatis, verum Dei cultum religionemq; ad integritatem reuocare, & libro legis, qui diutissime suppressus iacuerat, in lucem restituto, sacerdotibus & populo studium pietatis veraeq; religionis commendare.
units.tr: The royal prophet, whom I mentioned above, understood this, when he pronounces blessed those whose study is occupied day and night in the reading and meditation of the law of God. In his highest prayers he has this one thing: that he be allowed to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of his life and to behold the beauty of Jehovah. And when driven out by his son Absalom, he grieves over nothing so much as being absent from the holy assembly; indeed he testifies that his soul faints for the courts of the Lord. I need say nothing now of the most pious king Josiah, who considered it his duty, the idols overthrown and superstitious worship abolished, to restore the true worship and religion of God to its integrity, and, the book of the law, which had long lain suppressed, being brought back to light, to commend to the priests and people zeal for piety and true religion.

units.la: Ex quo satis perspicuum fieri existimo, ad omnes hominum ordines siue conditiones, tum ad eos, qui inferioris sunt sortis, tum qui in sublimi gradu sunt collocati, Verbi Dei auditum, lectionem, meditationemq; pertinere.
units.tr: From this I think it is sufficiently clear that the hearing, reading, and meditation of the Word of God pertain to all orders and conditions of men, both to those of lower rank and to those placed in high station.

units.la: Impiè autem facere iudicamus, eos, qui superioris conditionis homines, reges videlicet & principes, à verbo Dei, scripturarumq; sacrarum scrutatione arcent, & ad res vanas impiasq; seducunt: cuiusmodi sunt gnathones illi aulici, qui inanis felicitatis pollicitatione deceptos viros principes ad venationes ferarum, ad equorum agitationes, ad carnis delicias, ad subditorum expilationes, ad fastum, ad luxum, ceteraq; seculi huius studia incitant, neq; quid tam seipsos, quàm illos deceat, expedunt.
units.tr: We judge it impious, however, for those who are of superior condition, namely kings and princes, to be kept away from the word of God and from the searching of the holy Scriptures, and to be led into vain and impious things. Such are those flattering courtiers who, deceiving princes with the promise of empty happiness, incite them to the hunting of wild beasts, to horse-riding, to the delights of the flesh, to the plundering of subjects, to pomp, to luxury, and to the other pursuits of this age, and who do not consider what befits themselves and those princes.

units.la: Detestabiles sunt Epicuri omnes de grege porci, & qui Mammonæ seruiunt, cælestiq; conuiuio Christi contempto agriculturæ inhiant, commerciis incumbunt, vel voluptatis regnum sectantur: de quibus grauis Christi summi iudicis sententia est, nō esse regno Dei dignos.
units.tr: Detestable are all the Epicurean herd of swine, and those who serve Mammon, who, having despised the heavenly banquet of Christ, pursue agriculture, devote themselves to commerce, or chase after the kingdom of pleasure. Concerning them is the grave sentence of Christ, the supreme judge: that they are not worthy of the kingdom of God.

units.la: Adiungi debent his Enthusiastæ & Anabaptistæ, qui Verbi Dei voce repudiata, reuelationes spirituales imperito populo venditant: quorum fraudes si commemorare morare omnes Vellemus, multa haberemus, quæ vere de spiritu impostore Satana in angelum lucis se transformante, proferre possemus: at quia impostura istorum & nænia in hoc opere copiose sunt refutatæ, & alibi à viris doctis descriptæ, camarinâ hanc sordidissimam movere desinemus: id pro certo affirmantes, non posse hominem citra Verbum Dei ad cognitionem filij Dei & fidem veram peruenire, neq; aliam præter hanc ad salutem viam deinceps expectandam.
units.tr: The Enthusiasts and Anabaptists must be added to these, who, rejecting the voice of the Word of God, peddle spiritual revelations to the untaught people. If we wished to recount all their frauds, we would have much that could truly be brought forward about the spirit of imposture, Satan transforming himself into an angel of light. But because their imposture and trifles have been copiously refuted in this work and described elsewhere by learned men, we will stop stirring up this most foul sink, affirming this as certain: that man cannot attain to the knowledge of the Son of God and to true faith without the Word of God, and that no other way to salvation is to be expected henceforth besides this one.

units.la: Cæterum, ut Verbo viam vitæ æternæ Deus aperuit, ita ecclesiam nunquam vel in extremis angustijs deseruit, sed fidos semper aliquos prophetas, apostolos, doctores & ministros donauit, quorum vigilijs ac studijs gregem suum pasceret, quiq; spiritu Dei præditi copiosam messem ingressi, multiplices fructus Patrifamilias Deo in horreum referrent.
units.tr: Moreover, just as God opened the way of eternal life through the Word, so He never abandoned the Church, not even in the deepest distress, but always gave it faithful prophets, apostles, teachers and ministers, by whose watchfulness and labours He might feed His flock, and who, endowed with the Spirit of God and entering the abundant harvest, might bring back manifold fruits to the Father of the household, for God's storehouse.

units.la: Conferebatur olim Spiritus Dei artificibus, qui tabernaculum Mosaicum terrenum extruebant: quinetiam Spiritu prudentiæ donati leguntur, qui vestes Aaronis & cultum sacerdotalem conficiebant. Quanto igitur maiori usui fuisse spiritum Dei ijs censebimus, qui ad tabernaculum Dei spirituale, ecclesiam nimirum Christi, ædificandum, manus auxiliares admouere debebant? Vidit hoc Elizæus, qui ab Elia in cœlos emigraturo duplicis mensuræ spiritum in se cadere postulabat: licet difficile, imò impossibile sibi fore Elias fateretur, talem tantamq; rem petenti præstare: sicut & absurdum erat, ea ab homine petere, quæ in solius Dei & filij eius Iesu Christi manu potestateq; erant posita.
units.tr: The Spirit of God was once bestowed on the craftsmen who built the earthly Mosaic tabernacle; indeed, we read that men filled with the spirit of wisdom made the garments of Aaron and the priestly worship. How much greater use, then, shall we judge the Spirit of God to have been to those who were to put their helping hands to building the spiritual tabernacle of God, namely the Church of Christ? Elisha saw this, who, when Elijah was about to depart to heaven, asked that a double portion of his spirit fall upon him. Although Elijah admitted that it would be difficult, indeed impossible, for him to grant such a great thing to one who asked it, it was equally absurd to ask of a man what had been placed solely in the hand and power of God and of His Son Jesus Christ.

units.la: Rectius Petrus Apostolus omnem dicendi facultatem, omneq; donum linguarum & sanationum ad solum Deum refert, eumq; ex Ioelis testimonio Spiritum Sancti (ad declarandam filij sui maiestatem) in filios hominum contulisse asserit. A quo sane spiritu nihil humanum aut temerarium profectum fuit: omnia quæ profert, cælestia sunt & diuina: nō enim loquitur à semetipso, sed quæ audit in sacrosancto Trinitatis consessu, reuelat, & per prophetas & apostolos Dei annunciat.
units.tr: More rightly, the Apostle Peter refers every faculty of speech, and every gift of tongues and of healings, to God alone, and, from the testimony of Joel, asserts that He poured out the Spirit of the Holy One upon the sons of men (to declare the majesty of His Son). From this Spirit certainly nothing human or rash has proceeded: all that it utters is heavenly and divine. For it does not speak of itself, but reveals what it hears in the most holy assembly of the Trinity, and announces it through the prophets and apostles of God.

units.la: In quibus profecto non postremo loco habuit electum illud & sanctum organon Paulum, magnum doctorem gentium, qui tametsi in tertium usq; cælum raptus, abstrusa & recondita mysteria cognouit, quæ loqui fas non est, attamen reuelationibus tantis minimè elatus, cæteris apostolis & cooperarijs se prætulit, infirmioresq; despexit, sed summæ sibi gloriæ duxit, imbecilliorum ratione habita, omnia fieri omnibus, & in vasculis testaceis cœlestem thesaurum ad gentes circumferre, ac denique nulla re, neq; ex præsentibus, neq; futuris ab officio Veritatisq; propagandæ studio sese abduci pati, imò abortiuum se & apostolorum minimum, apostolatuq; indignum confitetur. (1.Corinth.15.) Diuina profecto in huius monumentis & scriptis elucet sapientia: omnia fidei dogmata solidè, & ad Spiritus Sancti normam ab hoc cernis explicata: nihil in hisce imperfectum est, nihil efficiatum, nihil præposterum: pleraque tamen reprobis proprio ipsorum vitio obscura ac perceptu difficilia: ac gentium quidem Apostolus cum esset, gentis tamen Hebræorum salutem summo semper studio desiderioque affectauit, adeò, ut pro his ipsis anathema fieri expetiuerit, modò errantes in viam reducere, perditosq; requirere posset.
units.tr: Among these, surely, the chosen and holy instrument Paul, the great teacher of the Gentiles, did not hold a lowly place. Although he was caught up into the third heaven and learned hidden and secret mysteries which it is not lawful to speak, yet he was by no means puffed up by such great revelations. He preferred himself to the other apostles and co-workers, and despised those who were weaker. Rather, he counted it his highest glory, having regard to the weaker, to become all things to all men and to carry the heavenly treasure to the Gentiles in earthen vessels. Finally, he allowed himself to be diverted from the duty and zeal of spreading the truth by nothing, neither present nor future things; nay, he confesses himself an untimely birth and the least of the apostles, unworthy of the apostleship (1 Cor. 15). Surely divine wisdom shines forth in his monuments and writings: from them you may see that all the doctrines of faith are solidly and according to the rule of the Holy Spirit explained. Nothing in them is imperfect, nothing unfinished, nothing out of order. Yet many things are obscure and difficult to grasp for the reprobate, through their own fault. And although he was the Apostle of the Gentiles, he always strove with the highest zeal and longing for the salvation of the Hebrew nation, so much so that he desired to become accursed for their sake, if only he might lead the erring back into the way and seek out the lost.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Testis huius affectus est epistola hæc, quam ad Hebræos conscripsit: in qua, ut peculiariter populum suum de mysteriis salutis erudit, ita ad hos ipsos pertinere promissiones & regnum Dei ostendit, ac primaria religionis Christianæ capita diligentissimè pertractat, ut nequaquam cæteris eius epistolis hæc sit postponenda.
units.tr: This letter, which he wrote to the Hebrews, bears witness to that concern. In it he instructs his own people in the mysteries of salvation, shows that the promises and the kingdom of God belong to them, and treats the chief heads of the Christian religion with great care, so that this letter must not be placed below any of his other letters.

units.la: Præterquàm enim, quòd validis firmisq; rationibus Christi diuinitatem asserit, legis etiam abrogationem per Euangelij successionem confirmat. Adhæc fide iustificari hominem absq; legis operibus, graviter euincit. Eos vero, qui vel diuinitatem Christo derogabant, vel pro lege Mosaica pugnabant, hominemq; ex operibus legis, non fide sola in Christum iustificari contendebant, doctè graviterq; redarguit.
units.tr: For besides firmly asserting Christ's divinity with strong and solid arguments, he also confirms by the succession of the Gospel that the law has been abrogated. Further, he powerfully proves that man is justified by faith without the works of the law. He learnedly and forcefully refutes those who either denied Christ's divinity or fought for the Mosaic law, and who contended that man is justified by the works of the law and not by faith alone in Christ.

units.la: In prima namq; epistolæ huius parte euidentissimis argumentis Scripturarum euincit, Christum verum Dei filium, verumq; Deum esse ab æterno, ac proinde Euangelium eius reuerenter ampleƈtendum.
units.tr: In the first part of this letter he proves, by the most evident arguments of the Scriptures, that Christ is the true Son of God and true God from eternity, and that therefore his Gospel is to be embraced with reverence.

units.la: Parte secunda legis ceremonialis, sacerdotij item & sacrificiorum abrogationem, Euangelij verò perpetuitatem dignitatemq; firmis rationibus demonstrat, Christiq; summi & æterni pontificis sacerdotium sacrificiumq; depingit. Tum veram iustitiam in fide positam esse, gratisq; donari, pulcherrimis exemplis illustrat.
units.tr: In the second part he demonstrates with firm reasoning the abrogation of the ceremonial law, and likewise of the priesthood and the sacrifices, and the perpetuity and dignity of the Gospel. He portrays the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, the supreme and eternal high priest. Then he illustrates, with most beautiful examples, that true righteousness is founded in faith and is given freely.

units.la: Ac postremò, ne peccatis fenestram aperire putetur, officia & opera fidei describit: ficq; non sui tantùm seculi hæreticis & hostibus Euangelij occurrit, sed nostræ etiam temꝑestatis erroribus repugnat.
units.tr: Finally, lest it be thought that he opens a window to sin, he describes the duties and works of faith. In this way he confronts not only the heretics and enemies of the Gospel of his own age, but also resists the errors of our own times.

units.la: Refutantur his diuinitatis Christi hostes, qui vel ex Iudæis vel gentibus nati, eoq; blasphemiæ prolapsi sunt, ut maiestati & gloriæ Christi contradixerint: quorum alij Christum purum hominem dixerunt, Deum esse negarunt: alij Deum quidem esse concesserunt, at patre inferiorem: alij diuinitatem cū carne & humanitate initium sumpsisse crediderunt: alij creaturam Christum appellarunt: alij animam excellentem diuinitatis loco statuerunt: alij filium Dei adoptiuum nominarunt. Pari ratione & illis os obturatur, qui incarnationis Christi mysterium fœdus opinionibus erroribusq; corruperunt, & ex utriusq; sexus cooperatione Christum factum esse hominem asseruerunt, vel in mundum venille, & passum esse in cruce negarunt: vel corpus phantasticum Christo affinxerunt: vel corpus cælo detulisse, vel ex quatuor elementis conslatum id esse somniarunt. Quibus ij quoq; adiungi debent, qui circa utriusq; naturæ considerationem delirarunt: quorum sane omnium errores commemorare ipsa prohibet fœditas, neq; conuenire institutæ orationi longiorem enarrationem existimo: quippe cum ab Apostolo Paulo, cæterisq; patrib. orthodoxis & ab Hyperio nostro in præsentibus commentarijs, copiosè & graviter sint refutati. Atq; annumerari illis debent pseudoapostoli, qui legis splendore & facie externa capti sacerdotij Aaronici & cultus Leuitici æternitatem sibi pollicebantur, atque etiamnunc Iudaicæ gentis reliquiæ cæca mente terrenū Messiæ regnum frustrà expeƈtant.
units.tr: Here are refuted the enemies of Christ's divinity: those who, whether born of Jews or of Gentiles, fell into blasphemy so as to oppose the majesty and glory of Christ. Some of them called Christ a mere man and denied that he is God; others conceded that he is God, but inferior to the Father; others believed that his divinity began together with the flesh and humanity; others called Christ a creature; others held that an excellent soul took the place of divinity; others named him an adopted Son of God. In the same way, the mouths of those are stopped who corrupted the mystery of Christ's incarnation with foul opinions and errors, and asserted that Christ was made man through the cooperation of both sexes, or denied that he came into the world and suffered on the cross, or attributed to Christ a phantom body, or dreamed that he brought his body down from heaven, or that it was made of the four elements. To these must also be added those who raved about the consideration of the two natures. The very foulness of all their errors forbids me to recount them, and I think a longer account would not suit the purpose of this work, since they have been refuted fully and weightily by the Apostle Paul, by the other orthodox Fathers, and by our Hyperius in these commentaries. Also to be counted among them are the false apostles, who, captivated by the splendour and outward appearance of the law, promised themselves the eternity of the Aaronic priesthood and the Levitical worship, and even now the remnants of the Jewish nation with blind minds vainly await a earthly kingdom of the Messiah.

units.la: Non dicam simios illos purpuratos & pontificis de grege porcos, qui inanium ceremoniarū superstitiosa obseruatione decepti, singulare in his ipsis sanƈtimoniæ opinione collocarunt: à vero tamen cultu et religione sunt alienissimi: id quod dogmata illorū peruersa, ingenia corrupta, & mores improbi, ad condemnationē ipsorū testificatur.
units.tr: I will not speak of those purple-robed apes and swine of the pontiff's herd, who, deceived by the superstitious observance of empty ceremonies, placed a singular holiness in these very things. Yet they are utterly alien to true worship and religion. Their perverse doctrines, corrupt minds and wicked morals bear witness to their condemnation.

units.la: Quòd si hi omnes ad Christi sacerdotium sacrificiumq; probè respicerent, ex tenebris bris Cymmerijs ad lucem Christi ultro redirent: at quia semel veritatem reiecerunt, & Satanæ genua flectere ausi sunt, ventremq; pro Deo habent, Spiritui Sancto resistere, iacturamq; animæ facere malunt, quàm voluptatū & mendaciorum regnū deserere. Quibus si aliqua salutis spes reliqua esset, facile hac doctrina apostolica in lucem revocari se sinerent, & elapsi ex diaboli laqueis, à quo captiui tenentur, ad voluntatem Dei resipiscerent, neq; extremum animæ discrimen incurrerent. Præclara vero eorum & fœlix conditio est, qui summo pontifici Christo seruientes, & imma culata eius victima sanctificati per fidem sancta sanctorum ingrediuntur: Quales sunt illi, qui umbris legalibus derelicti in Euangelij luce ambulant, & per fidem futurorum bonorum promissiones assequuntur. Siquidem indignum est Christiano homine à sole quod aiunt, ad lucernam, siue à luce ad umbras refugere: Id quod tenebriones illi faciunt, qui Euangelica luce abiecta papisticis tenebris sese implicant.
units.tr: If all these people properly regarded Christ's priesthood and sacrifice, they would willingly return from Cimmerian darkness to the light of Christ. But because they have once rejected the truth, dared to bend the knee to Satan, make their belly their god, resist the Holy Spirit, and prefer to suffer the loss of their souls rather than abandon the kingdom of pleasures and lies, if they had any remaining hope of salvation, they would easily allow themselves to be called back into the light by this apostolic doctrine. Freed from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive, they would return to the will of God and would not incur the final peril of their souls. Truly splendid and happy is the condition of those who serve Christ, the supreme high priest, and who, sanctified by his spotless sacrifice, enter through faith into the holy of holies. Such are those who, leaving behind the legal shadows, walk in the light of the Gospel and through faith lay hold of the promises of good things to come. Indeed, it is unworthy of a Christian man to flee from the sun, as they say, to a lamp, or from light to shadows. Yet this is what those shadow-dwellers do, who, having cast off the light of the Gospel, entangle themselves in papistical darkness.

units.la: Adiungi hisce debet ἀληχ, qui Spiritus Sancti est proprius, quo praue opiniones de iustitia, vitaq; æternæ via, refelluntur. Iudæis olim absurdum videbatur, præter legis Mosaicæ obseruationem, quæ præclarissimas promissiones habebat annexas, iustitiæ nomen quærere: Ita Antichristis & Euangelij hostibus nostra tempestate ψευδάδελφοι videtur, in sola fide, remotis legis operibus, iustitiæ fundamentum ponere, & à gratia Dei salutis principia deriuare: ideoq; fidem talem ad iustitiam necessariā requiri putant, quæ meritis propriis extra Christi gratiam sit suffulta, hominiq; præclarum ad iustitiam salutemq; parandam adiumentum adferat. Quæ quidem opinio cum mortis Christi meritum euertat, gratiaq; & gloriæ Dei, etiam impium per fidem iustificantis, repugnet, merito ab Apostolo ut impia & blasphema exploditur, & iam pridem per doctores ecclesiæ orthodoxos est condemnata.
units.tr: To these must be added the [ἀληχ], which is peculiar to the Holy Spirit, by which false opinions about righteousness and the way to eternal life are refuted. It once seemed absurd to the Jews to seek the name of righteousness apart from the observance of the Mosaic law, which had the most splendid promises attached to it. So in our own time it seems to the Antichrists and enemies of the Gospel, the [ψευδάδελφοι], to lay the foundation of righteousness in faith alone, with the works of the law set aside, and to derive the principles of salvation from the grace of God. Therefore they think that such a faith is required for righteousness, one that is supported by its own merits outside the grace of Christ and brings man a notable aid for obtaining righteousness and salvation. This opinion, since it overthrows the merit of Christ's death and opposes the grace and glory of God, who justifies even the ungodly through faith, is rightly rejected by the Apostle as impious and blasphemous, and has long since been condemned by the orthodox teachers of the Church.

units.la: Ac tametsi pseudochristiani isti clamitent, fidei iustificantis doctrina opera bona pietatemq; inter homines labefactari: nequaquam tamen ea Euangelij & fidei est lasciuia, ut peccatis viam sternat, impunitatemq; sceleribus promittat: quin potius ad Vitæ integritatem sanctimoniamq; hominem ex spiritu & aqua renatum vocat, omniaq; reprobat, quæ ex malo profecta gloriæ nominis diuini, & ædificationi ecclesiæ detrahunt. Quapropter & Apostolus huius epistolæ parte quarta diligenter præcipit, quæ officia & mores ciues Christi deceant: Non proiicit sanctum canibus, nec margaritas porcis exponit (nihil enim cani & balneo sacro) nec quosuis sine delectu regni cælorum participes pronunciat. Verùm tales salutis per fidem præter personarum acceptatione capaces esse statuit, qui paci Christianæ studentes, vitæ innocetia excellunt, charitatis officia in peregrinos ac pauperes exercent, coniugium sancte colunt, ab auaritiæ sordibus sunt alieni, ministris Euangelij dicto sunt audientes, doctrinas nouas & peregrinas auersantur, ac deniq; ἀποστάσας sunt ecclesiæ, lucemq; suam in terris ad gloriam patris cælestis lucere faciūt. Hæc, inquam, charitatis studio officiaq; fides vera in Christi filijs & discipulis producit & exerit.
units.tr: And although these pseudo-Christians cry out that the doctrine of justifying faith weakens good works and piety among men, yet this teaching is by no means such a licentiousness of the Gospel and of faith that it paves the way for sins and promises impunity for crimes. Rather, it calls the man born again of water and the Spirit to integrity of life and holiness, and it condemns everything that proceeds from evil and detracts from the glory of the divine name and the edification of the Church. Therefore the Apostle, in the fourth part of this letter, diligently instructs what duties and manners befit the citizens of Christ. He does not cast what is holy to the dogs, nor throw pearls before swine (for nothing holy belongs to a dog or a sacred bath), nor does he declare just anyone without distinction to be partakers of the kingdom of heaven. Rather, he holds that those are capable of salvation through faith, apart from any acceptance of persons, who strive for Christian peace and excel in innocence of life, who exercise the duties of love towards strangers and the poor, who honour marriage in holiness, who are free from the filth of greed, who listen to the ministers of the Gospel, who turn away from new and strange doctrines, and who, finally, have not [ἀποστάσας] from the Church, and who make their light shine on earth to the glory of the heavenly Father. This love and these duties, I say, are what true faith produces and brings forth in the sons and disciples of Christ.

units.la: Quod cum ita sit, impiæ stoliditatis nefariýq; mendacy arguuntur, qui malorum culpam in fidei professionem reijcientes, vitam suam impuram, doctrinamq; superstitiosam & blasphemam callidè dissimulant. Quales profectò sunt ÿ, qui in pontificis Romanensis detestabili regno meretricem Babylonicam venerantur, Baali genua
units.tr: Since this is so, those are convicted of impious stupidity and wicked lying who, shifting the blame for their evil deeds onto their profession of faith, cunningly conceal their impure lives and their superstitious and blasphemous doctrine. Such, certainly, are those who, in the detestable kingdom of the Roman pontiff, worship the Babylonian harlot and bend the knee to Baal.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: nua flectunt, Bileami vias damnatas sectantur, religionem veram mendacijs pol- luunt, nomê Dei in contemptû adducunt, in otio & delicijs crapulando, scortado, va rijsq; libidinib. vitæ suæ tempus perdunt, ventre pro Deo colût, manus sanguine in- noxio inquinatas gerunt, oculos habent plenos adulterij, coniugium ordinationem Dei sanctam prohibent ac profanant, nec non fabulis ineptis, prodigijsq; mendacibus totum terrarum orbem decipiunt, quinetiam gladio & igne in reluctantes ipsorum technis desæuiunt. Hæc, hæc inquam, an non ex diabolicis superstitionum idolorumq; lustris proueniunt? Nónne hi fructus incredulitatis sunt, quos cædis & mendacij pa- ter Satan in filijs tenebrarum, ad voluntatem suam irretitis, profert? Has suas fru- ges facinorosi anathematisæ & fulminaßri examinent: hæc parietes dealbati ob o- culos ponant, ac tandem fateri cogentur, non doctrinam Euangelicam, siue fidei pro- sessionem malorum esse causßam, sed ipsosmet suis traditionibus falsisq; dogmatibus orbem terrarum iam tot seculis turbare: neq; dubium, quin à iusto iudice Christo mer- cedem iniquitatis aliquando sint reportaturi. Sed laruis hisce papistícis prætermissis, ad Christi & apostolorum doctrinam eos remitto, qui Spiritus istiusmodi impostores probare, & dogmata eorum falsa à veritate discernere expetunt. Nihil enim la- boris studijsq; ad lucis diuinæ illustrationem, fabularumq; & tenebrarum discussione, factum est reliquum. Ad maiestatem igitur filij Dei amplificandam, ad sacerdotij sa- crificijq; eius, atq; Euangelij dignitatem exaggerandam, ad vitæ cœlestis viam de- monstrandam, ad fidei item veræ fructus describendos, singularem ac incredibilem vim epistola hæc ad Hebræos habet, quippe quæ à Spiritu Dei dictata, & per apo- stolum organon selectum prodita est.
units.tr: bow their knees to Baal, follow the condemned ways of Balaam, pollute the true religion with lies, bring the name of God into contempt, waste the time of their lives in idleness and pleasures, in gluttony, debauchery and wanton lusts, worship the belly as their god, bear hands stained with innocent blood, have eyes full of adultery, forbid and profane marriage, God's holy ordinance, and deceive the whole world with foolish fables and lying portents, and even rage with sword and fire against those who resist their schemes. I ask, do not these things arise from the diabolical pollutions of superstitions and idols? Are these not the fruits of unbelief, which Satan, the father of murder and lies, produces in the children of darkness whom he has ensnared to his will? Let these criminal anathematisers and thunderers examine their own fruits; let these whitewashed walls set them before their eyes, and at last they will be forced to confess that it is not the Evangelical doctrine or the profession of faith that is the cause of evils, but that they themselves, by their traditions and false dogmas, have been troubling the world for so many centuries. And there is no doubt that from the just judge, Christ, they will one day receive the wages of their iniquity. But, setting aside these Papist masks, I refer to the doctrine of Christ and the apostles those who desire to test such impostor spirits and to distinguish their false dogmas from the truth. For nothing of labour and zeal has been left undone for the illumination of the divine light and the dispelling of fables and darkness. To magnify the majesty of the Son of God, to exalt the dignity of his priesthood, his sacrifice and the Gospel, to demonstrate the way of heavenly life, and likewise to describe the fruits of true faith, this epistle to the Hebrews has a singular and incredible power, since it was dictated by the Spirit of God and delivered through the apostle as a chosen instrument.

units.la: Quamobrem non abs re vir diuinus Andreas Hyperius commentarios in hæc præ cæteris luculentiores conscripsit, ê re nimirum ecclesiæ fore iudicans, ad gloriam item Dei profuturum cernens, pluribus ea persequi, quæ Christi gloriæ, hominumq; saluti expediunt: idq; eo ordine ac methodo, tantaq; industria & artificio, ut doctissimis eius lucubrationibus, nequaquâ hæ sint inferiores. Iudicium hac ipsa de re ecclesiæ Christi, omnibusq; sana doctrina menteq; præditis relinquo: imperitis verò metam pono, ut ne cum sutore ineptò ultra crepidam. Ac sunt tales, quod iam dudum prouidebam, non pauci, quos instar leporum Leoni mortuo insultare, & vati defuncto conuiciari non pudet. Obijcient hi vel lucubrationum harum vetustatem, vel prolixiorem earum tractationem, vel epistolæ quoq; ipsius ad Hebræos, utpote quæ minime ab apostolo Paulo conscripta esse videatur, indignitatem. Quibus certè momis si iusto argumentorum ordine ac refutatione obuiam ire vellem, in nimis longum ac tædiosum volumen hæc mea crescceret epistola. Scio equidem, ingratas nonnullis has fore vigilias, & labores Hyperij posthumos, quippe qui anno ab incarnatione Christi 1544. Aprilis die vicesimoprimo inchoati, & eiusdem mensis die 24. anno quarto post uix absoluti, & ne nunc quidem ab autore ipso recogniti, & prout optarat, elaborati sint. Mors enim, quæ multis mortalium studijs utilissimis finem imponit, & hos, & alios illius labores interrupit. Temporis tamen longinquitate uetustateq; usus eorum & dignitas deleri, aut obscurari nequiuit. Aurum reconditum uetustate, neq; consumitur, neq; imminuitur: quin imò plus desiderij uoluptatusq; conciliat acquirentibus: id quod de ijs liquet, qui thesauros abditos scrutantur, & in eorundem captatione quicquid est facultatum, absumunt. Ita
units.tr: For this reason, not without cause, the divine Andreas Hyperius wrote commentaries on this epistle, more brilliant than the rest, judging it clearly to be for the good of the Church, and seeing that it would also profit the glory of God, to pursue at greater length those matters which serve the glory of Christ and the salvation of men; and he did so in such an order and method, and with such great diligence and skill, that these commentaries are in no way inferior to his most learned works. I leave the judgment on this very matter to the Church of Christ and to all who are endowed with sound doctrine and judgment; but to the unskilled I set a limit, lest, like the clumsy cobbler, they go beyond the sandal. And, as I foresaw long ago, there are not a few such people, who are not ashamed to trample on these as hares trample on a dead lion, and to revile a dead prophet. They will object either to the age of these lectures, or to their overly long treatment, or even to the unworthiness of the epistle to the Hebrews itself, since it does not seem to have been written by the apostle Paul. If I wished to meet these objections with a proper ordering of arguments and refutation, my letter would grow into too long and tedious a volume. I know indeed that these vigils and the posthumous labours of Hyperius will be unwelcome to some, since they were begun on the twenty-first day of April in the year of Christ's incarnation 1544, were barely finished in the fourth year after, on the twenty-fourth day of the same month, and have not even now been revised by the author himself, nor worked up as he wished. For death, which puts an end to many of the most useful undertakings of mortals, interrupted these and his other labours. Nevertheless, neither the length of time nor the age of these works has been able to destroy or obscure their value and dignity. Gold laid away in the earth by age is neither consumed nor diminished; rather, it wins more desire and delight from those who acquire it, as is clear from those who search out hidden treasures and spend whatever resources they have in the pursuit of them. Thus

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Ita nec verbi Dei, quo quidem nihil est antiquius, nihil suauius, nihil ad salutē humani generis accommodatius, vetustate temporis euilescere potest autoritas. Liber olim legis, Josia rege piissimo in Ierusalem regnante, annis nō paucis occultatus & fere suppressus iacuit, in lucem tandem restitutus maiori, quàm ante, in precio est habitus: sic non minus fructus, suauitatis & ponderis libros hosce sacros, in quibus spi-ritus Sancti dogmata sunt explicata, parituros esse viris doctis & bonis, confido.
units.tr: So too the authority of the Word of God, than which nothing is older, nothing sweeter, and nothing better suited to the salvation of mankind, cannot be diminished by the passing of time. The Book of the Law was once hidden away and almost suppressed for many years, while Josiah, the most pious king, reigned in Jerusalem; when it was at last restored to light, it was held in greater esteem than before. In the same way, I trust that these sacred books, in which the doctrines of the Holy Spirit are set out, will yield no less fruit, sweetness and weight to learned and good men.

units.la: Neq; etiam inficior, commentarios hos reliquis Hyperianis, quos quidem in Pau-linas epistolas edidit, esse prolixiores. Nihil tamen uspiam his inęst sterile, nihil inu-tile: desunt λογομαχίαι & βατ-ολογίαι: desunt scommata & quæstiones absurdæ ac cu-riosæ: in singulis singulare religionis promouendæ elucet studium. Est quidem modus in rebus humanis optimus: at verbi Dei nulla piis debet esse satietas, nedum tædium ac nausea obrepere. Quæ breuia sunt, acuta quidem esse solent, at obscura & intelle-ctu difficilia. In prolixitate hac summam cernere est dilucidita-tem, perspicuitatem s earum rerum, quæ hoc opere exponuntur. Summa his inest grauitas, religiosa suauitas, sapientia incredibilis, methodus doctissima. Id quod in iis locis perspicitur, quos de persona Christi, de sacerdotio & sacrificio eiusdem, de abrogatione legalium sacrifi-ciorum & sacerdotij Aaronici, de Euangelij dignitate, de iustitia fidei, & fructu eius, doctè, grauiter, ordinè, ac sapienter explanat.
units.tr: Nor do I deny that these commentaries are longer than the rest of Hyperius's works, which he published on the Pauline epistles. Yet nothing in them is barren or useless anywhere: there are no verbal wrangles [λογομαχίαι] and idle repetitions [βατολογίαι]; there are no jokes and no absurd and curious questions. In each part the single aim of advancing religion shines through. Measure is indeed the best thing in human affairs, but the devout should never be satiated with the Word of God, let alone have weariness and nausea creep in. Brief writings are usually sharp, but obscure and hard to understand. In this fuller treatment one may see the highest clarity and perspicuity regarding the matters that this work expounds. It has gravity, devout sweetness, incredible wisdom and a most learned method. This appears especially in those passages in which he explains, learnedly, weightily, orderly and wisely, the person of Christ, his priesthood and sacrifice, the abrogation of the legal sacrifices and of the Aaronic priesthood, the dignity of the Gospel, and the righteousness of faith and its fruit.

units.la: Porrò eos quod attinet, qui D. Pauli epistolam hanc esse vel dubitant, vel pror-sus negant, ac proinde Hyperianam operam in hac explicanda frustrà collocatā esse existimant, eos ad Hyperiana argumenta remitto, quibus in huius operis initio eum-cit, esse epistolam hanc non Scripturis tantùm propheticis et apostolicis per omnia cō-sentaneam, sed methodum etiam genusq; docēdi prorsus Paulinum, id quod liquidò constabit, si cum iis conferatur, quæ ad Galatas, ad Ephesios, ad Colossenses, aliasq; scripsit. Unde etiam patres orthodoxi pro Paulinis hæc ad Hebræos semper ha-buēre. Scio quidem, scrupum duplicem ex apostoli verbis oriri, alterum ex capite secundo, alterum ex capite sexto & decimo: at vterq; pluribus ab interprete cum sit explicatus, haudquaquàm necessum esse arbitror iis excutiendis tempus terere. Idta-men monitum lectorem piūm volo, ne scripta sacra temerè, vel propter obscuritatē vel sinistra aliorum præiudicia reiiciat, sed sobriè potius sapienterq; in sacrorū my-steriorum meditatione dijudicationeq; versetur. Caro & sanguis reuelare res diui-nas nequit: Spiritus Dei sanctus in veritatem eos deducit, qui studia eius serio am-plectuntur, enixeq; eorum, quæ recondita & obscura sunt, intelligentiam à Deo pa-tre luminum postulant. Quòd si vero ab impiis etiam & pseudoapostolus Scripturā sacram vsurpari, & (quod satanæ est proprium) improbè deprauari videas, nō usq; adeò eo offendaris, ut aliquam inde sinistrè de verbo Dei, doctrinaq; puriori iudicā-di occasionem, arripias.
units.tr: As for those who doubt or altogether deny that this epistle is by St Paul, and therefore think that Hyperius's labour in expounding it has been spent in vain, I refer them to the arguments of Hyperius, which he brings forward at the beginning of this work, to show that this epistle agrees entirely not only with the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, but also with Paul's method and manner of teaching in every respect. This will become quite clear if it is compared with what Paul wrote to the Galatians, the Ephesians, the Colossians and others. For this reason the orthodox Fathers also have always held this epistle to the Hebrews to be Pauline. I know that two difficulties arise from the apostle's words, one from the second chapter and one from the sixth and tenth; but since both have been explained at length by the commentator, I do not think it necessary to waste time in going over them here. I would, however, advise the pious reader not to reject the sacred writings rashly, either on account of their obscurity or because of the unfavourable prejudices of others, but rather to occupy himself soberly and wisely in meditating on and weighing the sacred mysteries. Flesh and blood cannot reveal divine things; the Holy Spirit leads into truth those who earnestly embrace his teaching, and they ask eagerly of God the Father of lights for understanding of what is hidden and obscure. But if you see that Holy Scripture is also used by the impious and by false apostles, and (as is proper to Satan) wickedly distorted, do not be so offended by this as to seize upon it as an occasion to judge the Word of God and purer doctrine unfavourably.

units.la: Non horret Spiritus mendax Scripturarum testimoniis Christum Dei filiū op-pugnare, & in angelū lucis sese trāsmutare: haud igitur mirū, si filij eius, patris vesti-gia secuti, sanā doctrinā fidei corrūpere, & ad impia sua dogmata stabilienda callidè detorquere ausint: id sanè quod iam inde à primorū parentū seductione, & his postre-mis seculis ab instaurata religione per varios hæreticos et sophistas factū esse cerni-mus. Itaq; eos, qui minus dextrū de epistola hac iudiciū conceperunt, diligentius Scri-pturas
units.tr: The lying spirit does not shrink from assailing Christ, the Son of God, with the testimonies of Scripture, and from transforming himself into an angel of light. It is therefore no wonder if his sons, following the footsteps of their father, dare to corrupt sound doctrine of the faith and craftily twist it to establish their impious tenets. We see this indeed having been done, from the seduction of our first parents onwards, and in these latest centuries since the restoration of religion, through various heretics and sophists. Therefore those who have formed a less favourable judgement of this epistle should more diligently [read] the Scriptures

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: piuras sacras euoluere, iudicia temeraria declinare, moderatiusque de Scriptū sacris sentire iubeo. Id uero nostri nunc est propositi, commentarios hosce Hyperianos, eaq; quæ in his ipsis & docte & pie tradita & explicata sunt, ecclesiæ Christianæ commendare: quanquam non dubito, quin quisq; sana mente iudicioq; præditus animaduersurus sit, quam dilucide elaboratæq; singula in his sint pertractata: quo ordine quaq; methodo omnia collocata: quam moderate grauiterq; opiniones impiæ & absurdæ confutatæ: quanto zelo ueritas ipsa propugnata, ac nihil deniq; prætermissum, quod ad Scripturarum sacrarum genuinam interpretationem, solidamq; falsorum dogmatum redargutionem seruiat.
units.tr: ...to read through the sacred Scriptures more diligently, to avoid rash judgments, and to think more moderately about the sacred writings. Our present purpose is to commend these Hyperian commentaries, and the things taught and explained in them both learnedly and piously, to the Christian Church. I do not doubt that anyone of sound mind and judgment will notice how clearly and carefully each point has been treated in them; in what order and by what method everything has been arranged; how temperately and seriously the impious and absurd opinions have been refuted; with what zeal the truth itself has been defended; and, finally, that nothing has been omitted which serves the genuine interpretation of the sacred Scriptures and the solid refutation of false doctrines.

units.la: Quocirca non possum non succensere Momis illis atque Bionibus, qui mortui uiri labores sugillare, & nomen quoq; improbe petulanterq; optime de ecclesia Christi meriti proscindere non dubitant: laruis tamen hisce nolo insultare: video enim asinos ad lyram & mysteria importuno pede contendere. Discent hi rectius sapere, si ad meliorem mentem redierint, quam ego illis donari opto.
units.tr: Therefore I cannot but be angry with those Momuses and Biones who do not hesitate to carp at the labours of a dead man and, shamelessly and wantonly, to tear apart a name that has deserved very well of the Church of Christ. Yet I do not wish to insult these ghosts: I see that donkeys, with clumsy feet, strive after the lyre and the mysteries. These men will learn to think more rightly if they come to a better mind, which I wish for them.

units.la: Reliquum nunc est, uiri nobilissimi, ut, quibus de causis, amplissimis uestris nominibus lucubrationes hasce ascripserim, & uestro potissimum patrocinio commendarim, breuibus exponam. Sunt hæ inter multas alias præcipuæ. Primam religio uestra & pietatis studium sibi uendicat, quod licet omnium bonorum sit proprium, eos tamen maxime decet, qui propter generis nobilitate uirtutisq; splendorem in sublimi aliquo reipublicæ gradu sunt collocati. Hac una uirtute si uita optimatum sit illustrata, nomen gloriosum & uere nobilitatum ad posteros transmittitur. Hac uero desiderata, omnis gloriæ splendor, omnisq; uirtutis ac nobilitatis opinio obscuratur aut penitus extinguitur. Altera causa in uerbi Dei amore & cognitione rerum diuinarum cernitur, sine qua neq; uita hæc præsens regi, neq; futuræ fœlicitas comparari potest. Regibus olim & principibus in manum legis liber est traditus, in quo statuta & testimonia Dei, quibus uita informanda, & ad Dei notitiam uoluntateq; erudienda est, continebantur. Inclarescit enim magnorum uirorum autoritas, si Dei timentes uerbiq; diuini amantes gloriæ eius inseruiant. Honorantes se iterum honorat Dominus, facitq; ut nomen ac proles iustorum floreat æternum. In historijs sacris laus eorum regum prædicatur, qui cultum & uias Dei secuti sunt: eorum uero infelicitas & ignominiosa abiectio deploratur, qui lege Dei reiecta à uero cultu uijsq; Dei recesserunt. Quo uita cuiusq; est illustrior, eo magis contendere ad ea debet, quæ nobilitatis sunt propria. Vera autem nobilitas & gloria ex uirtute & studijs honestis proficiscitur. Unde non raro à uia hac nobilitatis aberrat, qui solo nomine atq; maiorum gloria contenti, canes, equos, & arma impia sectantur, uel in scelerum uias declinant, ex quibus demum in præsentissimum discrimen & animæ & corporis, fortunarum iacturam non dicam, ducuntur. Vestrorum itaq; nominum gloria, quæ ex uirtutis et religionis radicib. enata, pietatisq; studijs confirmata est, ad posteritatem integra & immortalis perdurabit. Abrahamum Deus olim gentem magnam & fortem futurum promisit, quippe qui filijs suis ac domui sit præcepturus, ut custodiant uiam Domini, faciantq; iustitiam & iudicium: Ita & uestris familijs benedicet Deus, cuius uias, iustitiam & iudicia colitis, assiduéq; filijs uestris inculcari curatis, summoq; fauore & beneuolentia Euangelij ministros prosequimini.
units.tr: It remains now, most noble gentlemen, that I briefly set out the reasons why I have dedicated these labours to your most distinguished names and commended them chiefly to your patronage. These are among many others the chief ones. The first is claimed by your piety and zeal for religion, which, although it belongs to all good people, befits especially those who, by the nobility of their birth and the brilliance of their virtue, have been placed in some high rank in the commonwealth. If the life of the nobles is illustrated by this virtue alone, their glorious name, truly ennobled, is handed down to posterity. But if this virtue is lacking, the splendour of all glory and the reputation of all virtue and nobility is obscured or utterly extinguished. The second reason lies in the love of God's Word and the knowledge of divine things, without which neither this present life can be governed nor future happiness obtained. Long ago the book of the law was handed to kings and princes, containing the statutes and testimonies of God, by which life must be shaped and taught the knowledge and will of God. The authority of great men shines forth when they, fearing God and loving the divine Word, serve his glory. The Lord again honours those who honour themselves, and causes the name and offspring of the righteous to flourish forever. In the sacred histories, the praise is proclaimed of those kings who followed the worship and ways of God; but the unhappiness and shameful downfall of those who, rejecting the law of God, departed from true worship and the ways of God, is lamented. The more illustrious a person's life, the more he ought to strive for those things which are proper to nobility. True nobility and glory, however, arise from virtue and honourable pursuits. Hence it is that those who, content with the name alone and the glory of their ancestors, pursue dogs, horses and arms of impiety, or turn aside into the paths of crimes, often stray from this road of nobility, and from these are led at last into the most immediate peril of soul and body, not to mention the loss of fortune. Therefore the glory of your names, which has sprung from the roots of virtue and religion and been confirmed by pursuits of piety, will endure whole and immortal for posterity. God once promised Abraham that he would become a great and strong nation, since he would command his sons and his household to keep the way of the Lord and to do justice and judgment. So too will God bless your families, whose ways, justice and judgments you cultivate, and whom you take care to have constantly impressed upon your sons, and whom you attend upon with the highest favour and goodwill, as ministers of the Gospel.

units.la: Accedit
units.tr: Added to this is...

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Accedit huc singularis vitæ Vestræ integritas, quæ quidem summis virtutum dotibus ita est exornata, ut pulcherrima quadam proportione ac συμμετρία hæ ipsæ inuicem sese complexentur, e quibus est temperantia in victu, iustitia & prudentia in rebus agendis, fides in consiliis & negociis rerumpublicarum, ad quas etiam multarum rerum pertinet experientia, studiaq; literarum, quibus vos ita auxit Deus, ut non principes solum Hassiæ illustrissimi consiliis vestris vtantur, sed vniuersus etiam ordo equestris abbatijs (quæ quidem adhuc reliquæ sunt ad communes usus huius ordini) vos præfecerint, à vestrisq; consiliis & industria multorum res dependeant.
units.tr: Added to this is the singular integrity of your life, which is so adorned with the highest gifts of virtue that these very qualities embrace one another in a most beautiful proportion and symmetry: temperance in diet, justice and prudence in public affairs, and faithfulness in the counsels and business of the commonwealth, to which also belongs a wealth of experience in many matters, and the pursuit of letters, with which God has so enriched you that not only the most illustrious princes of Hesse make use of your counsels, but the whole equestrian order has also set you over the abbeys (which indeed remain for the common use of this order), and the affairs of many depend upon your counsels and diligence.

units.la: His aliisq; virtutibus vera nobilitas paratur gloria, nominisq; celebritas: hinc domus nobilitatæ splendor ad posteros propagatur. Adiungerem hisce alias causas, quas consultò prætereo, cùm ne longius excrescat oratio, tum ne adulari virtutibus ac nominib. vestris, aliorumq; nobilissimorum virorum laudi derogare velle videar.
units.tr: By these and other virtues true nobility obtains glory and renown of name; from this the splendour of a noble house is handed down to posterity. I would add to these other reasons, which I deliberately pass over, both so that my speech may not grow overlong, and so that I may not seem to flatter your virtues and names or to wish to detract from the praise of other most noble men.

units.la: Quanquàm priuata etiam duo illa me impulerunt, ut has lucubrationes nominibus ac patrocinio vestro commendarem, alterum, quòd te, Reinharde nobilissime, ab Hyperio nostro præceptis institutisq; philosophiæ auctum esse, deq; doctore hoc aliquando me præsente, præclarè locutum, & honorificè adhucdum sentire, recorder, tuamq; eloquentiam, eruditionem, iudiciumq; exquisitu, ipse & audiuerim & ab aliis permultis prædicari intellexerim. Alterum, quòd te, Iohannes Clauere, propter religionis & sacrarum literarum (quibus te præter cæteros addictissimum esse scio) amorem, propter moderationem suauitatemq; ingenij sagacissimi, doctrinam non vulgarè, benevolentiam item & humanitatem incredibilè, qua bonos doctosq; omnes prosequeris, & me non meritum, dum ecclesiæ huic Gemundensi præfui, annis fere nouem, tibi tuisq; obstrinxisti, redamè ac reuerear, idq; de te vere asserere possim, esse te nobilitatis Hassiacæ totius magnū lumen & ornamentū, nulliq; te ex ordine equestri secundum relinquere. Vtinam tua fide, consiliis, industria, & pietate pincipibus nostris, Xenodochijs, maioribus (quorum penes te singularis est administratio) totiq; reipublicæ & patriæ quàmdiutissimè frui concedatur. Tametsi non dubitem, quin tu quoq; Iustle & Alexander, paribus virtutibus & studijs patriæ ac bonis omnibus honori & adiumento futuri sitis.
units.tr: Yet there are also two private reasons that have moved me to commend these labours to your names and patronage. The first is that I remember you, most noble Reinhard, were trained in the precepts and teaching of philosophy by our Hyperius, and that when I was present once, he spoke of you with high praise, and still thinks of you with honour; and I myself have heard, and have learned from very many others, how your eloquence, learning and exquisite judgement are commended. The second is that you, John Clauer, on account of your love of religion and of sacred letters (to which, above all others, I know you are most devoted), on account of the moderation and sweetness of your most shrewd mind, your uncommon learning, and likewise the incredible goodwill and humanity with which you cherish all good and learned men, have bound me, who did not deserve it, to yourself and your family, during the nearly nine years in which I presided over this church of Gemünden. I love and revere you in return, and I can truly affirm of you that you are the great light and ornament of the whole Hessian nobility, and that you yield to no one of the equestrian order. May it be granted that for a very long time our princes, the hospitals, the greater houses (over which you have singular administration), and the whole commonwealth and fatherland may enjoy your faithfulness, counsels, diligence and piety. Although I do not doubt that you too, Justus and Alexander, will by equal virtues and zeal be a source of honour and help to your country and to all good men.

units.la: Hæ aliæq; uirtutes vestræ, uiri clarissimi nobilissimiq;, fecerunt, ut lucubrationes hasce Hyperianas, quas anno superiori recognoui, & veritatis propagandæ studio luce donare constitui, tutelæ vestræ patrocinoq; commēdarim, haud diffidens, quin hæc mea qualiscunq; προσφώνησις grata candori vestro sit futura. Deus opt. max. gratiâ sua cœlesti & donis uos vestrasq; familias prosequatur, regat, seruet, augeat, ad nominis sui gloriam, & ecclesiæ patriæq; conseruationem, Amen.
units.tr: These and your other virtues, most distinguished and most noble men, have led me to entrust these Hyperian labours, which I revised last year and have resolved to bring to light out of zeal for spreading the truth, to your protection and patronage; not doubting that this my address, such as it is, will be welcome to your kindness. May God, best and greatest, accompany you and your families with his heavenly grace and gifts, rule, keep and increase you, to the glory of his name and the preservation of the Church and fatherland. Amen.

units.la: Datæ Gemundæ supra Vuohram Hassiæ calendis Iunij anno ab incarnatione Christi 1584, secundum ueterem Christianorum calculum.
units.tr: Given at Gemünden above the Wohra in Hesse, on the Kalends of June, in the year of the incarnation of Christ 1584, according to the old reckoning of the Christians.

units.la: V. A. obseruantissimus Ioannis Mylius Euangelij minister.
units.tr: Your most respectful servant, John Mylius, minister of the Gospel.

units.la: D. ANDREAE HYPERII COMMENTARII IN D. PAVLI EPISTOLAM AD HEBRAEOS.
units.tr: D. ANDREAE HYPERII COMMENTARII IN D. PAVLI EPISTOLAM AD HEBRAEOS.

units.la: Προλεγόμενα.
units.tr: Prolegomena [Προλεγόμενα].

units.la: QVI FVERINT HEBRAEI.
units.tr: WHO THE HEBREWS WERE.

units.la: EBRAEI sunt, qui aliâs Iudæi. Illud autem notatu dignū, Hebræorum appellationem non esse deductam ab Heber, qui fuit abnepos Sem, & pater Peleg, ipsiusq; Abrahæ atauus. Etiamsi Augustinus de Ciuitate Dei libro 16. cap.3. & Retractationum lib.2. cap. 16. multiq; alij eum secuti ita suspicentur: sed ab Abraham. Id quod tum recentio res quidam, tum Ambrosius scribens in tertium caput epistolæ ad Philippenses, admonuerunt, & ex ipsius Augustini libro de quæstionibus veteris ac noui testamenti, quæstione 108. licet colligere. Rationes autem cur ab Abraham potius, quàm ab Heber dicantur appellati Hebræi, sunt hæ. Prima: Cum non Hebrer aut Hebre dicatur, sed Heber, durior videtur translatio seu deriuatio hæc, qua vocā-tur non Heberæi, sed Hebræi: mollius autem deducitur ab Abraham, quasi dicamus Hebraæi, sicut à Iuda non Iudai, sed Iudæi. Atq; apud Latinos citante Ambrosio, pro medidie, dicimus meridie, causa. Altera ratio, quòd in Scripturis non inue-niuntur proximè descendentes ab Heber appellati Hebræi, sed primi ita dicti sunt fi-lij ipsius Abrahæ, vt Genef 39. Ioseph, & fratres eius, Genef. 45. Et ipse Abrahā primus honoris gratia, & quasi autor eius appellationis ita nominatur. Gen.14. Vnus qui eua serat, nunciauit, Abraham Hebræo, de Loth uidelicet capto à regibus. Tertia ratio, quòd ipsi Iudæi appellationem ac genus suum gloriantur se trahere ab Abraham, nō ab Heber: sicut Ioan. 8. Semen Abrahæ sumus, neq; cuiquam seruiuimus unquam, quomodo tu dicis, liberi reddemini? Ibidem: Pater noster Abraham est. Et cum Abraham tum rebus fortiter & præclarè gestis, tū vitæ sanctimonia, tum Dei ipsius manifesto testimonio & promissionibus semper describebatur multò commendatissimus & excellētissimus, ab hoc potius iudicandum est appellationem Hebræorum deriuatam, quàm ab He-ber, qui, si propius inquireretur, potius obscurus, impius, & idololatra inueniretur, quàm secus: Et ab huiusmodi ducere appellationem, non fuisset admodum honorifi-cum, imò potius inhonestum & pudendum. Quarta ratio ab Etymo uocabuli accipi-tur. Nam cum Hebræi suo idiomate uocentur עברים quæ uox significat transeuntes, seu, ut Paulus Burgensis, citante Ludouico Viue in commentarijs lib. 16. cap. 3. de Ci-uitate Dei, peregrinos: conuenit cū uoce Abrám, qui cognominabatur עברי eò quòd ex Mesopotamia transito flumine in terram Chanaan concesisset, ibiq; pere-grinaretur. Atq; inde appellationem Hebræorum, quasi dicamus peregrinantium, posteri eius acceperunt.
units.tr: The Hebrews are those who are otherwise called Jews. It is worth noting, however, that the name "Hebrews" is not derived from Heber, the great-grandson of Shem, father of Peleg and Abraham's great-great-grandfather. Augustine, in De civitate Dei book 16, chapter 3, and Retractationes book 2, chapter 16, and many others who followed him, suspect this, but the name comes from Abraham. Both a more recent writer and Ambrose, writing on the third chapter of the Epistle to the Philippians, have pointed this out, and it can also be gathered from Augustine's own book De quaestionibus veteris ac novi testamenti, question 108. The reasons why they are called Hebrews from Abraham rather than from Heber are these. First, since the word is not "Hebrer" or "Hebre" but "Heber," this derivation, by which the name becomes not "Heberaei" but "Hebraei," sounds harsher; it is more smoothly derived from Abraham, as if we said "Hebraei," just as from Judah we get not "Judai" but "Judaei." And among the Latins, as Ambrose notes, we say "meridie" for "medidie," which is the same kind of thing. The second reason is that in the Scriptures the people called Hebrews are not the immediate descendants of Heber, but the first so called are the sons of Abraham himself, as in Genesis 39, Joseph and his brothers, Genesis 45. And Abraham himself is named in this way, as a mark of honour and as the founder of the name, in Genesis 14: "One who had escaped told Abraham the Hebrew," namely about Lot taken by the kings. The third reason is that the Jews themselves boast that their race and name derive from Abraham, not from Heber, as in John 8: "We are the seed of Abraham and have never been in bondage to anyone; how is it that you say, you shall be made free?" And in the same place: "Our father is Abraham." Since Abraham was always described, both by his brave and splendid deeds, by the holiness of his life, and by God's own clear testimony and promises, as by far the most commended and excellent, it must be judged that the name of the Hebrews was derived from him rather than from Heber, who, if he were examined more closely, would be found obscure, impious and an idolater rather than otherwise. To derive the name from such a man would not have been very honourable, but rather shameful and disgraceful. The fourth reason is taken from the etymology of the word. For since the Hebrews are called in their own language [עברים, Ibrim], a word meaning "those who pass over," or, as Paulus Burgensis says, citing Ludovicus Vives in his commentary on Augustine's De civitate Dei book 16, chapter 3, "foreigners," it agrees with the name Abram, who was called [עברי, Ibri], because, having crossed the river from Mesopotamia, he settled in the land of Canaan and lived there as a stranger. From this, his posterity received the name Hebrews, as if we said "wanderers."

units.la: Cæterùm cùm Hebræi ijdem sint, qui & Iudæi, quare potius dicitur epistola ad Hebræos, quàm ad Iudæos? Sanè blandior & honorificentior semper fuit appellatio Hebræorum, quàm Iudæorum, id quod liquet ex illo 2. Cor.11. Vbi iactantiæ quorun-dam Iudæorum ista obijcit. In quoquunq; audet aliquis, audeo & ego. Hebræi sunt, sum & ego: Israelitæ sunt, sum & ego: Semen Abrahæ sunt, sum & ego. Et Philip. 3. contra iactationes aduersariorū. Si quis quā alius videtur fiduciā habere in carne, ego magis habeo, circūc ifus o-ctauo die, Israel ex genere, tribus Beniamin, Hebræus ex Hebræis, iuxta legē pharisæus, &c. Et erat reuera splēdidior appellatio, quæ à primo & illustrissimo patriarcha ducebatur Abrahamo, quàm quæ à nepote ipsius multo inferiore, nempe Iuda, à quo Iudæorū ductum uocabulum, & una tantum tribus. Quid, quod apud ethnicos quoque Scri-ptores, ut Horatium, Satyricum, Martialem, Iudæorum vocabulum semper contem-ptius & vilius est habitum, atq; eo usi sunt potius, quàm Hebræorū vocabulo, si quā-do gentē eā voluerunt odiosius insectari. Sed hæc de Hebrēorū appellatione satis.
units.tr: But since the Hebrews are the same as the Jews, why is the epistle called "to the Hebrews" rather than "to the Jews"? Certainly the name Hebrews has always been the milder and more honourable, as is clear from 2 Corinthians 11, where Paul throws back at certain boasting Jews these words: "Whatever anyone dares to boast of, I dare too. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I." And Philippians 3, against the boasts of his opponents: "If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, as to the law a Pharisee," and so on. And the name derived from the first and most illustrious patriarch, Abraham, was really the more splendid than the name derived from his far inferior grandson, Judah, from whom the word "Jews" comes, and who was only one tribe. Moreover, among the pagan writers too, such as Horace, the satirist, and Martial, the word "Jews" was always regarded as more contemptible and cheap, and they used it rather than the word "Hebrews" whenever they wanted to attack that nation more odiously. But this is enough about the name of the Hebrews.

units.la: a
units.tr: a

units.la: Quare scripta, siue qua occasio.
units.tr: Why it was written, or what occasion prompted it.

units.la: Iudæorum permulti, cum alibi, tum præcipuè Hierosolymis Christum, eiusq; sanctum euangelium receperunt, vt liquet ex Act.2.5. & 6.
