Sed hos cæteri, qui adhuc obstinatis animis legi Mosaicæ & ceremoniis superstitiosè erant addicti, nitebantur, quibuscunq; possent rationibus, à Christo & Euangelio auocare. Quam ad rem multa partim contra personam Christi, partim contra Euangelium, & in primis doctrinam fidei congerebant, & in uulgus spargebant. Nam de Christo quidem contendebant iniquissimum, simulq; absurdissimum esse, quòd talis pro filio Dei, seu uero Deo, adeoq; pro promisso illo Messia agnosceretur, præsertim cum hic Christus homo etiam miserrimus abiectissimusq; palam fuerit deprehensus: Euangelium autem eneruare uolentes miris modis extollebant dignitatem legis, atq; inprimis sacrarum ceremoniarum ac Sacerdotij, quòd Deus ipse non frustra, sed utilissimè & velut æter num futurum instituerat: ac proinde legem talem esse, quæ per nouum & suspectum euangelium nequaquam debeat abrogari.
units.tr: Many Jews, both elsewhere and especially at Jerusalem, received Christ and his holy gospel, as is clear from Acts 2, 5 and 6. But the rest, who were still devoted to the law of Moses and its ceremonies with obstinate minds and superstitiously, strove by whatever arguments they could to turn people away from Christ and the gospel. To this end they heaped up many objections, partly against the person of Christ, partly against the gospel, and above all against the teaching of faith, and spread them among the common people. For concerning Christ they argued that it was most unjust and at the same time most absurd that such a man should be acknowledged as the Son of God, or as very God, and therefore as that promised Messiah, especially since this Christ had been openly seen to be a most wretched and abject man. But wishing to weaken the gospel, they extolled in wondrous ways the dignity of the law, and especially of the sacred ceremonies and the priesthood, which God himself had instituted not in vain but most usefully and as if for ever; and therefore that the law was of such a kind that it ought by no means to be abrogated by a new and suspect gospel.

units.la: Interea & doctrinæ de iustitia per fidem, quæ propria est euangelij, iamq; toto pene orbe per Apostolos fuerat propagata, opponebant magno fastu magnifica & illustria sanctorum Patrum opera, quasi per hæc, & non per fidem illi iustitiam apud Deum essent promeriti. Atq; his machinis Christum eiusq; euangelium, necnon doctrinam fidei considebant aduersarij se facile subuersuros. Sed præterea fallacibus his ad seducendos pios technis adiungebant inauditam crudelitatē, diripiendo nimirū credentiū facultates (ut legitur huius epist. cap.10. item Actor.8.) & in corpora eorum dē sequiedo, sicut in Stephanū (Act.7.) multosq; alios, qui uel cæsi virgis fuerūt, uel aliis modis profligati, fecisse illos constat. Ne igitur pij credetes uel propter blasphemias in personam Christi, vel propter extenuationē euangelij, & immodicam prædicationem legis: vel propter iactationem magnificorum operum à sanctis peractorū: vel denique propter publicas persecutiones, à Christo eiusq; euangelio deficerent: voluit Apostolus ad pios Hebræos, seu Hierosolymis seu alibi terrarum agentes, epistolam hanc perscribere, & in ea, ad confirmationem consolationemq; illorum, Christi, nec non euangelij ac fidei dignitatem & præstantiam prædicare assereret.
units.tr: Meanwhile, against the teaching of justification by faith, which is the proper character of the gospel and had by now been spread through almost the whole world by the apostles, they proudly set up the magnificent and illustrious works of the holy Fathers, as if by these, and not by faith, they had merited righteousness before God. And with these devices the adversaries thought they could easily overthrow Christ, his gospel and the teaching of faith. But besides these deceptive tricks for seducing the godly, they added unheard-of cruelty, namely plundering the property of believers (as is read in this epistle, chapter 10, and also in Acts 8), and it is well established that they did this to their bodies too, as they did to Stephen (Acts 7) and to many others, who were either beaten with rods or destroyed in other ways. Therefore, lest the godly believers should fall away from Christ and his gospel, either because of blasphemies against the person of Christ, or because of the weakening of the gospel and the immoderate preaching of the law, or because of the boasting about the great works performed by the saints, or finally because of public persecutions, the Apostle wished to write this epistle to the godly Hebrews, whether they were living at Jerusalem or elsewhere in the world, and in it to proclaim, for their confirmation and consolation, the dignity and excellence of Christ, and also of the gospel and of faith.

units.la: Quid contineat, siue quot eius partes.
units.tr: What it contains, or its parts.

units.la: Diuiditur tota epistola in duas partes principales. Quarum prior, quæ continet grauissimas disputationes de Christi diuinitate, de abrogatione legis, euangelijq; præstantia, de iustificatione per fidem, ad dimidium usq; capitis duodecimi protrahitur. Posterior habens doctrinam charitatis siue morum, occupat quicquid reliquū est epistolæ. Ceterum priorem partem quo clarius perspiciatur, quo ordine omnia in ea tractentur, in tres locos docendi ergo secabimus. Primo itaq; loco, quoniā aduersarij ludei contendebant, oreq; blasphemo uociferabantur, Christū simpliciter non esse Deum, neq; ullo pacto pro filio Dei agnoscendum: Apostolus totus in hoc est, ut Christū filiū esse Dei, uerumq; Deū, astruat. Statim igitur omissa epigrapha atque exordio, generalem totius disputationis de diuinitate Christi propositionem hanc instituit, nempe, Christum, per quem euangelium postremis hisce temporibus reuelatum est, uerum esse cœlestis patris filium. Cuius mox addit velut expositionem, qua Christi diuinam potentiam ab officijs & effectis aperit, dum eum paris cum patre substantiæ & naturę, conditorem & conseruatorem rerum omnium, peccatorum nostrorum expiatorem, denique Patri in omni gloria æqualem celebrat. Inde uenitad confirmationem, efficacibus e penu Scripturarum instructam argumentis, quæ Christum non creaturam tantum ac miserum hominem, ut aduersarij clamitabant, sed omnibus etiam excellentissimis creaturis superiorem, ac proinde uerum Deum, conditorem omnium, manifeste comprobant. Ex quibus argumentis commodè infert secundo capite, Christum cùm talis tantusq; sit, religiose audiendum & colendum, infertis aliquot suasorijs rationibus, quæ ad id faciendum impellunt. Quæ deinde sequuntur, Confutationis loco accipi queunt. Quia enim obijcere potuissent aduersarij,
units.tr: The whole epistle is divided into two main parts. The first, which contains the weightiest disputations on Christ's divinity, on the abrogation of the law, on the excellence of the gospel, and on justification by faith, extends to the middle of chapter twelve. The second, which sets out the teaching on charity or morals, occupies whatever remains of the epistle. So that the first part may be seen more clearly, and the order of its topics understood, we will divide it into three heads of teaching. In the first, since the Jewish opponents contended and cried out with blasphemous mouths that Christ was simply not God and in no way to be acknowledged as the Son of God, the Apostle is wholly intent on proving that Christ is the Son of God and true God. Therefore, omitting at once the greeting and the exordium, he lays down this general proposition for the whole disputation on Christ's divinity: that Christ, through whom the gospel has been revealed in these last times, is the true Son of the heavenly Father. He immediately adds, as it were, an explanation of it, by which he sets forth Christ's divine power from his offices and effects, while he celebrates him as equal to the Father in substance and nature, the creator and preserver of all things, the expiator of our sins, and finally equal to the Father in all glory. Then he comes to confirmation, furnished with forceful arguments drawn from the storehouse of the Scriptures, which clearly prove that Christ is not merely a creature and a wretched man, as the opponents kept shouting, but superior even to all the most excellent creatures, and therefore true God, the creator of all. From these arguments he fittingly infers, in the second chapter, that Christ, being so great and of such a kind, is to be heard and worshipped devoutly, and he adds several persuasive reasons that urge us to do so. What follows may be taken as a refutation. For the opponents might have objected...

units.la: Propositio de Christo uero Dei filio, Confirmatio, Tanto præstantior factus angelis, Cap.2, Confutatio, Testatus est autem, &c. sarij, Christo nequaquam competere tantam dignitatem, utpote qui deprehensus sit angelis multo inferior & abiectissimus homo: Ideo per occupationem profert scripturæ locum ex Psal. 8. quo probari extrema ista Christi abiectio videbatur: sed ex eodem artificiosissimè conuincit, Christum, licet aliqua ex parte valde abiectum, nihilominus omnibus adhuc creaturis multo superiorem, ac proinde saluam sem per manere eius dignitatem. Rursus quia alia Obiectio fieri poterat, nondum experimentis cerni, omnia Christo esse subdita. Respondet breuiter, quod, licet ad tempus inferior factus fuerit angelis, præsertim in gustanda pro omnibus morte, tamen certum sit, eum gloria & honore coronatum: sicut præcedenti Scripturæ loco clarè dicebatur. Atq; hinc, ut semel satisfaceret iis, qui negare volentes Christi diuinitatem semper obijciebant, illum purum tantum hominem, transit ad plenius differendum de Christi humanitate, redditq; causas, quare conueniens fuerit & necessarium, ad perficiendum ea, quæ salutis nostræ sunt, Christum Dei filium humanam naturā induere: & hanc nihil ipsius detrahere dignitati, sed potius commendare eius insignem erga nos bonitatem. Ex quibus inter initio cap. 3. nos de bere ad eum uti patronum & intercessorem respicere confugerec. Vbi rursus noua quodammodo occupatione utitur, quia aduersarij negantes diuinitatem Christi, si quid Christo excellentiæ concedebant, hoc tantum concedebant, quòd nimirum esset excellens propheta uerbo & signis, at nullo pacto Mosi æquandus. Ideo Apostolus prudenter instituit collationem Christi cum Mose, colligitq; euidentissimè, Christum Mose multò esse digniorem. Sequitur deinde conclusio totius huius disputationis, qua monet, ut, quando oportunū est Christum eiusq; euangelium amplectantur, adhibita autoritate Scripturæ, ex Psalm. 94. Quæ Scripturæ locum ut ualde accommodum instituto, maximeq; condu-cibilem excitando durę ceruicis populo, deinceps & capitis quarti maxima parte luculentius & fusius exponit, varia argumenta suasoria conclusioni apta inde eliciens. Eodem capite secundum locum siue secundam disputationem, quæ est de abrogatione legis, & euangelij præstantia, Apostolus aggreditur. Quæ ut clarius percipiatur, sciendum est, Iudæos, quoniam per doctrinam euangelij de iustificatione per fidem in Christum absq; operibus Legis iudicabant uniuersam legis, & inprimis sacrarum ceremoniarum, sacrificiorum, ipsiusq; sacerdotij (in quibus diuinus cultus, iustitiæ ratio, totaq; gentis gloria sita putabatur) dignitatem labefactari, voluisse cogere fratres suos credentes, ut aut legem simul cū euangelio obseruarent, aut euangelio in uniuersum ualedicerent. Ceremonias enim haud frustra à Deo ipso institutas, sacrificia item & sacerdotiū debere perpetuò durare: quam ad rem haud dubiè multa probabilia argumenta proferre poterant. Breuiter, nihil æque ac ceremonialia opponebāt euangelio: & quiduis potius facturi & passuri uidebantur, quàm ut illa negligerent. Proinde Apostolus docturus legem, sacrificia, sacerdotium, & omnia illa finem iam accepisse, miro consilio causam hanc peragit. Ante omnia tanquam propositionem generalem, disputationis suę constituens, ait, profitendum nobis esse, quòd Christus ipse sit uerus & magnus Pontifex, cuius typum duntaxat sacerdotes legis gesserint. Ad cuius rei confirmationem seu probationem, cap. 5. omnia competere Christo, quæ ad sacerdotium requiruntur, incipit declarare, docens, eum ideo factum hominem: deinde diuinitus uocatum: præterea pro populo orasse, & salutem immetrasse: denique sacerdote esse, non secundū ordinē Leui, sed Melchisadech, quod & testimonio psalmi 109. confirmat. Sed hic ut uberem & difficilè ingressus materiā, p digressione uoluit reliqua parte huius capitis, & toto sexto, auditorū animos præparare & excitare. Increpans. n. quorundam ignauiam, quòd perpetuò hærerent in ipsis doctrinæ euangelicæ elemētis, ad maiora deinde & sublimiora capescenda hortatur: Aliās enim parum profutura, quę antea didicerint. Addita deinde mitigatione, qua ait se confidere, illos strenuè profecturos, pollicetur, si modo per fidem & patientiam constantes maneant, futurum fauente Deo, ut etiam intra velum posita, id est, altissima & abditissima mysteria percipiant. Capite septimo redit ad institutum. Illud enim, quod ante digressionem postremo loco urse-rat ex Psal.109. quòd videlicet Christus esset sacerdos secundum ordinem Mel-chisedec, probat recte à se dictum, quandoquidem omnia Christo competunt, quæ in Melchisedec visebantur, qui ipsius Christi quasi typus fuit. Amplificat de-inde valde artificiosè dignitatem sacerdotij Melchisedec, ductis argumentis à præstantia personæ Melchisedec, colligitq; illud multò excellentius esse sacer-dotio Aaronico seu Leuitico: ut hinc tandem inferat, ipsius Christi quoq; sacer-dotium (quod erat secundum ordinem Melchisedec) multò esse præstantissimum, eoq; manifestato eo, quòd præstantius est, abrogatum uetus sacerdotium minus præstans: imò translato iam ad Christum sacerdotio, semel translatam abroga-tamq; totam legem, quæ præcipuè ex sacerdotio pendebat. Nam de regno nō erat amplius disputandum, quod palam videbant sibi ademptum.
units.tr: The proposition concerning Christ the true Son of God; the confirmation, "Made so much better than the angels," chapter 2; the refutation, "But one has testified, etc." The opponents would say that such great dignity by no means belongs to Christ, since he was seen to be a man far inferior to the angels and most abject. Therefore, by a preemptive move, he brings forward a passage of Scripture from Psalm 8, by which these extreme abjections of Christ seemed to be proved; but from the same passage he skilfully demonstrates that Christ, though in some respects greatly abased, is nonetheless still far superior to all creatures, and so his dignity remains intact forever. Again, because another objection could be made, that not yet by experience is it seen that all things are subject to Christ, he replies briefly that, although for a time he was made lower than the angels, especially in tasting death for all, nevertheless it is certain that he is crowned with glory and honour, as was clearly said in the preceding passage of Scripture. And from here, so that he might once and for all satisfy those who, wishing to deny Christ's divinity, always objected that he was a mere man, he passes on to discuss more fully the humanity of Christ, and he gives the reasons why it was fitting and necessary for Christ, the Son of God, to put on human nature in order to accomplish the things that pertain to our salvation; and that this takes nothing away from his dignity, but rather commends his remarkable goodness toward us. From these things, at the beginning of chapter 3, we ought to look to him as our patron and intercessor, to whom we flee. Here again he uses a kind of new preemptive move, because the opponents who denied Christ's divinity, if they conceded any excellence to Christ, conceded only this: that he was an excellent prophet in word and signs, but by no means to be equated with Moses. Therefore the Apostle wisely institutes a comparison of Christ with Moses, and he most evidently concludes that Christ is far more worthy than Moses. Then follows the conclusion of this whole disputation, in which he admonishes that, since it is necessary, they should embrace Christ and his gospel, with the authority of Scripture, from Psalm 95. This passage, being very suitable to his purpose and most useful for rousing a stiff-necked people, he afterwards expounds more clearly and fully in most of the fourth chapter, drawing from it various persuasive arguments fitting the conclusion. In the same chapter the Apostle takes up the second place, or second disputation, which concerns the abrogation of the law and the excellence of the gospel. That this may be perceived more clearly, it must be known that the Jews, since through the teaching of the gospel on justification by faith in Christ apart from the works of the Law they judged that the dignity of the whole law, and above all of its sacred ceremonies, sacrifices, and the priesthood itself (in which the divine worship, the rule of righteousness, and the whole glory of the nation were thought to lie), was being undermined, wished to compel their believing brothers either to keep the law together with the gospel or to renounce the gospel altogether. For they maintained that the ceremonies, as well as the sacrifices and priesthood, instituted by God himself not without reason, ought to endure forever; and they could undoubtedly bring forward many plausible arguments for this. In short, they opposed nothing so much as the ceremonial laws to the gospel, and they seemed ready to do or suffer anything rather than neglect those things. Therefore the Apostle, about to teach that the law, the sacrifices, the priesthood, and all those things have now reached their end, conducts this cause with remarkable skill. First of all, laying down as the general proposition of his disputation, he says that we must confess that Christ himself is the true and great High Priest, of whom the priests of the law were only a type. To confirm or prove this, in chapter 5 he begins to declare that all things required for the priesthood belong to Christ, teaching that he was therefore made man, then called by God, moreover that he prayed for the people and obtained salvation; and finally that he is a priest not according to the order of Levi but of Melchizedek, which he also confirms by the testimony of Psalm 110. But here, having entered upon a rich and difficult matter, he wished by digression to prepare and rouse the minds of his hearers through the rest of this chapter and the whole of the sixth. For, rebuking the sluggishness of some who constantly clung to the very rudiments of evangelical doctrine, he exhorts them to take up greater and higher things, since what they had previously learned would otherwise profit them little. Then, adding a softening qualification, in which he says he is confident that they will make vigorous progress, he promises that, if only they remain steadfast through faith and patience, it will come about, with God's favour, that they will also grasp the things placed within the veil, that is, the deepest and most hidden mysteries. In chapter 7 he returns to his subject. For what he had stressed at the end before the digression, from Psalm 110, namely that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, he proves to have been rightly said, since all the things that were seen in Melchizedek, who was as it were a type of Christ himself, belong to Christ. Then he greatly and skilfully magnifies the dignity of Melchizedek's priesthood, drawing arguments from the excellence of Melchizedek's person, and he concludes that it is far more excellent than the Aaronic or Levitical priesthood; so that at last he may infer that the priesthood of Christ also (which was according to the order of Melchizedek) is by far the most excellent. And since this is shown by the fact that the more excellent displaces the less excellent, the old priesthood, being less excellent, has been abrogated; indeed, with the priesthood now transferred to Christ, the whole law, which depended chiefly on the priesthood, has once and for all been transferred and abrogated. For there was no longer any need to dispute about the kingdom, which they plainly saw had been taken from them.

units.la: Rursus propius expendens Apostolus verba Psalmi, quæ sonant, Christi sa-cerdotium, iuramento ipsius Dei confirmatum, æternum esse: præterea persona Christi multò esse excellentissimam. Ab his circumstantijs iterum amplificat Christi sacerdotium, ut nullum neq; ante, neq; post ei æquandum demonstret.
units.tr: Again, weighing more closely the words of the Psalm, which declare that the priesthood of Christ, confirmed by God's own oath, is eternal, the Apostle further shows that the person of Christ is by far the most excellent. From these circumstances he again magnifies the priesthood of Christ, so as to demonstrate that none can be equated with it, either before or after.

units.la: Capite octauo, Ne ludæi multa amplius obijcere possent, ad defendendam di-gnitatem sacerdotij legalis, vel contenderent pertinacius, debere id esse perpe-tuū, ipse adducto loco Exod. 25. manifeste conuincit, sacerdotium legale cum omnibus adiunctis tantum typum fuisse sacerdotij Christi iam manifestati: imò quod maius est, totum uetus testamentum, seu pactum legis adeò non fuisse ra-tum atq; perfectum, quin aliud perfectius commodiusq; debuerit succedere: id quòd ipsius Dei verbis Ieremiæ 31. palàm nouum testamentum promittentis, con-uincit, mox inferens ex ijsdem verbis, nouum hoc testamentum, cùm iam sit ex-hibitum, necessariò sequi, vetus illud esse abrogatum. Capite nono clarius expli-care volens, in sacerdotio legali tantum typum resplenduisse sacerdotij Christi, luculenta oratione docet, per Sacerdotem legalem semel in anno ingredientem sancta sanctorum, & sanguinem offerentem, significatum esse, quòd Christus quoq; semel ingressurus esset in sancta sanctorum, nempe cœlum, & Deo Patri sanguinem suum proprium oblaturus in remissionem nostrorum peccatorum. Atq; ita Christum esse verum & perfectum reconciliatorem seu sacerdotem no-ui testamenti, quod nunc quoq; sanguine & morte illius confirmatum est: sicut hominum testamenta morte solent confirmari, & ipsum uetus testamentum san-guine fuerat confirmatum. Postremo ne quis putet parum aptè respondere typû-rei, quòd in typo singulis annis obtulerit sacerdos. In nouo autem testamento, Christum tantùm semel: prudenter interpretatur per Occupationem, istud quo-que ad dignitatem sacerdotij Christi accedere. Christum enim ideo tantùm semel obtulisse, quòd ipsius unica hostia pro peccatis satisfaceret: In ueteri autem testa-mento, quod tantùm umbra erat noui, (talibus enim verbis istud exponere inci-pit cap.10.) debuisse sæpius iterari sacrificia, quod per ea pro peccatis nequaquam satisfiebat. His ita expositis infert uerbis Psal.39. Sacrificia legalia debere cessa-re, postquam Christus semel seipsum afferendo voluntatem Dei expleuit, nec-non effecit, vt pater, (quemadmodum Ieremiæ 31. ipse loquitur) peccatorum no-strorum nolit amplius recordari. Vbi enim peccata sunt remissa, ibi sacrificijs mi-nimè est opus. Sequitur Conclusio disputationis, qua hortatur eos, ut magnum sacerdotē Christū amplectantur, & fidē in eum statuentes, nec non baptizatiac purificati eius sanguine, bonos fructus per õem uitā ˌpferant. Quod ni faciant, (sic enim populo durę ceruicis gravem addit comminationem) ultionem Dei haud euasuros. Iam ad locum tertium eodem denuò capite, qui partim hortato-rius est, partim didacticus. Quando enim ludei uel maximè offendebantur do-ctrina de iustificatione per fidem, per quam iudicabant legis dignitatem pror-sus eneruari, & ad hanc è piorum animis excutiendam minas & supplicia ofien-debant. debant. Ideo Apostolus hoc tertio loco hortatur credentes ad constanter seren dum quaecunq; pericula, simulq; exquisitis aliquot argumetis, homines fide iustificari, confirmat. Primùm igitur congerit argumenta quaedam suasoria, ad tolerantiam afflictionum commouentia. Mox quasi propositionis loco, ad disputationem de iustitia fidei, profert sententiam ex Abacuc 2. qua diserte exprimitur, homines fide iustificari, & vitam aeternam habere.
units.tr: In chapter 8, so that the Jews might not be able to raise many further objections in defence of the dignity of the legal priesthood, or insist more stubbornly that it must be perpetual, he himself, by adducing the passage from Exodus 25, plainly proves that the legal priesthood, with all its appurtenances, was only a type of the priesthood of Christ now made manifest; and, what is greater, that the whole Old Testament, or covenant of the law, was so far from being valid and perfect that another, more perfect and more suitable covenant ought to succeed it. This he proves from the very words of God in Jeremiah 31, where a new covenant is plainly promised, and he immediately infers from the same words that this new covenant, since it has now been revealed, necessarily means that the old one has been abrogated. In chapter 9, wishing to explain more clearly that the priesthood of Christ shone forth only as a type in the legal priesthood, he teaches in an eloquent discourse that by the legal priest who once a year entered the Holy of Holies and offered blood, it was signified that Christ too would enter once into the holy of holies, namely heaven, and would offer his own blood to God the Father for the remission of our sins. And thus Christ is the true and perfect reconciler, or priest, of the new covenant, which has now also been confirmed by his blood and death, just as human testaments are wont to be confirmed by death, and the old covenant itself had been confirmed by blood. Finally, lest anyone think that the type does not answer well to the thing, because in the type the priest offered every year, while in the new covenant Christ offered only once, he wisely interprets, by way of preemption, that this too adds to the dignity of Christ's priesthood. For Christ offered only once because his single sacrifice satisfies for sins; but in the old covenant, which was only a shadow of the new (for he begins to expound it in such words in chapter 10), the sacrifices had to be repeated often, because by them satisfaction for sins was by no means made. With these things thus set out, he infers, in the words of Psalm 40, that the legal sacrifices ought to cease, since Christ, by offering himself once, has fulfilled the will of God, and has also brought it about that the Father (as he himself says in Jeremiah 31) is unwilling any longer to remember our sins. For where sins have been forgiven, there is no further need of sacrifices. There follows the conclusion of the disputation, in which he exhorts them to embrace Christ as the great High Priest, and, placing their faith in him, and having been baptized and purified by his blood, to bring forth good fruits through their whole life. If they do not do so (for he adds this grave warning to a stiff-necked people), they will not escape the vengeance of God. Now, in the same chapter, we come to the third place, which is partly hortatory and partly didactic. For the Jews were most offended by the doctrine of justification by faith, through which they judged that the dignity of the law was utterly undermined; and to shake this out of the hearts of the faithful they used threats and punishments. Therefore the Apostle, in this third place, exhorts the believers to bear steadfastly whatever dangers may come, and at the same time, by means of several carefully chosen arguments, he confirms that men are justified by faith. First, then, he gathers certain persuasive arguments that move them to endure afflictions. Then, as if by way of a proposition for the disputation on the righteousness of faith, he brings forward a sentence from Habakkuk 2, which plainly expresses that men are justified by faith and have eternal life.

units.la: Inde capite vndecimo fidem definit, necnon multis exemplis fidei effectus, quomodo videlicet per eam Patres omnes Deo accepti fuerint & iustificati, demonstrat: ita explodens, quę superstitiosi aduersarij de iustificatione per opera solida erant tragicè obijcere. Capite duodecimo, (vt finem causae huic imponat & concludat) iterum variis rationibus ad constantiam in perferendis pro pter euangelium periculis hortatur, de utilitate afflictionum praeclara admiscēs. Secunda pars principalis totius epistolae continens doctrinam charitatis siue operum eodem capite incipit, ac primum ad pacem concordiamq; coledam hortatur. A scortatione & omnibus in genere turpibus animum profanantibus deterret, grauissima argumenta suasoria, praecipuè ab oportunitate reuelati euangelij, eiusq; dignitate ad id adducens. Capite decimo tertio charitatem, & inprimis hospitalitatem caeteraque misericordię opera commendat: sanctum coniugium in honore haberi iubet: Auaritiam detestatur: synceros ministros verbi uult honorari ac iuuari: pseudoapostolos autem peregrinasque doctrinas omni studio uitari: Ad benefaciendum egenis excitat: superioribus, ut pareant praecipit: pro se deniq; orari petit. Postremò uti alias quoq; solet, pia comprecatione claudit epistolam.
units.tr: Then in chapter eleven he defines faith and shows, by many examples, the effects of faith: how all the Fathers were through it accepted by God and justified. In this way he explodes the objections which the superstitious adversaries were wont to hurl tragically concerning justification by works. In chapter twelve (to bring the case to an end and conclude it) he again exhorts them, by various arguments, to constancy in enduring dangers for the sake of the gospel, mixing in the notable benefit of afflictions. The second principal part of the whole epistle, containing the doctrine of charity or of works, begins in the same chapter, and first he exhorts them to cultivate peace and concord. He deters them from fornication and from all things in general that defile the mind, bringing to bear very weighty arguments of persuasion, chiefly from the timeliness of the revealed gospel and its dignity. In chapter thirteen he commends charity, and above all hospitality, and the other works of mercy; he orders that holy marriage be held in honour; he detests avarice; he wills that sincere ministers of the Word be honoured and helped, but that false apostles and strange doctrines be avoided with every care; he rouses them to do good to the needy; he commands them to obey their superiors; and lastly he asks that prayers be made for himself. Finally, as he is also wont to do elsewhere, he closes the epistle with a pious prayer.

units.la: Genus causæ.
units.tr: Genus causæ.

units.la: Cùm in hac Epistola tradantur praecipua capita universæ doctrinæ euangelicæ, nimirum, Christum esse uerum Deum: deinde sacerdotium legale, & cum eo ipsam legem abrogatam, per nouum & multò excellentius sacerdotium Christi: ad hęc fide homines iustificari, rectè generis didactici censebitur.
units.tr: Since in this epistle the chief heads of the whole evangelical doctrine are set forth, namely, that Christ is the true God; then the legal priesthood, and with it the law itself, abrogated through the new and far more excellent priesthood of Christ; and, besides these, that men are justified by faith, it will rightly be judged to belong to the didactic kind.

units.la: Status.
units.tr: Status.

units.la: Ob uarios autem locos hic tractatos, non possumus unum aliquem statum seu generalem propositionem totius epistolę constituere. Quanquam ad statū Finitiuum singuli loci commodè referentur. Definitur enim hic, Christum esse natura Deum: praeterea ex definitione sacerdotis demonstratur, eundem esse uerum & consummatum sacerdotem. Postremò, iustitiam per fidem contingere.
units.tr: Because of the various topics treated here, we cannot set up any single status or general proposition for the whole epistle. Still, the individual topics are conveniently referred to the definitive status. For here it is defined that Christ is God by nature; besides, from the definition of priest it is shown that he is the true and perfect priest. Lastly, that righteousness comes through faith.

units.la: Quanta eius vtilitas, siue quàm varij in ea Christianæ doctrinæ loci.
units.tr: How great its usefulness, or how many loci of Christian doctrine it contains.

units.la: Est hęc epistola non minus diues suppellectilis theologicę, quàm alia quęcunq; amplissima. Profectò enim si cui libeat paulò accuratius rimari, exquirereque passim inspersas ei margaritas ac drachmas euangelicas, inueniet quę ad ditandas, imò æternum beandas conscientias sufficiant. Nos porrò paucula, quęq; magis in oculos intuentium sese ingerunt, proferemus, ita inuitantes eos, quibus plus otij est ad hanc rem, & plus etiam spiritualis acuminis, ut preciosiora eruant seligantque. In ipsa autem limine hi loci statim occurrunt.
units.tr: This epistle is no less rich a storehouse of theology than any other most ample one. For indeed, if anyone should like to search a little more carefully, and seek out the gospel pearls and drachmas scattered everywhere in it, he will find enough to enrich, indeed to make eternally blessed, consciences. We shall set forth a few of these, those which thrust themselves more readily upon the eyes of beholders, thus inviting those who have more leisure for this matter, and more spiritual acuteness, to dig out and select the more precious things. Now these topics present themselves at once on the threshold.

units.la: 1. Euangelium esse reuelatum per ipsum filium Dei. Vnde dignitas eius elucescit ad confirmandas conscientias.
units.tr: 1. That the gospel was revealed through the Son of God himself. Hence his dignity shines forth, to confirm consciences.

units.la: 2. Vnum eundemq; esse Deum à quo Lex & à quo euangelium.
units.tr: 2. That the one and same God is the author of both the Law and the gospel.

units.la: 3. Christum esse filium Dei & uerum Deum: contra Iudaeos & omnes negantes diuinitatem Christi.
units.tr: 3. That Christ is the Son of God and true God: against the Jews and all who deny the divinity of Christ.

units.la: 4. Quàm periculosum sit, contemnere uerbum, seu oblatum euangelium: ad terrendos hostes euangelij.
units.tr: 4. How dangerous it is to despise the Word, or the gospel offered: to terrify the enemies of the gospel.

units.la: 5. Euangelicam veritatem certissimis & plurimis testimonijs comprobatam: ad confirmandas conscientias credentium.
units.tr: 5. The evangelical truth is confirmed by most certain and numerous testimonies: to confirm the consciences of believers.

units.la: 6. Christum esse verum hominem, & quare hominem fieri decuerit: cui loco non pauca ad dignitatem Christi, & consolationem nostrā pertinentia sunt inserta: ut, quòd Christus diaboli, peccati, & mortis abolerit imperium: quod frater noster sit: quod factus miserigarum nostrarum conscius & participes: quod-q; propositus misericors pontifex & intercessor. Cap.3. 7. Discrimen inter legem & euangelium huius q; praestantia. 8. Occasionem amplectendi euangelium, & sanam doctrinam, non sinendam avolare. 9. Per incredulitatem excludi homines a participatione Euangelij & regni Dei. Cap.4. 10. E diuerso suscipientes sermonem cum fide, ingredi in requiem, seu accipere promissiones euangelicas. 11. Verbi Dei efficacia ac dignitas. Cap.5. 12. Per solum Christum verum pontificem obtingere misericordiam et gratiam: vbi mox capite qu ntomulta de dignitate Christi sequuntur, in quibus illud amplissimum & mire confi lato rium, quod fuerit causa salutis aeterna. 13. Omnibus semper ad pleniorem cognitionem & profectum in fide enitendum. Cap.6. 14. Lapsos difficulter quidem resurgere, non tamen de eis desperandum. 15. Deum respicere opera ex charitate prodeuntia, praemijs q; afficere. 16. Plena & certa spe perstandum in fide. 17. Confirmandam spem certitudine diuinarum promissionum, & ex iisdem consolationem omni tempore accipiendam. Cap.7. 18. Insignis locus de abrogatione legalis sacerdotij, simul q; totius legis. 19. Legem per se fuisse imbecillem, inutilem, nihil ad ducentem ad perfectionem, & tantum introducentem ad Christum seu euangelium. 20. Christi sacerdotium simul q; euangelium manere aeternum, neq; aliam legem praestantiorem expectandam. Cap.8. 21. Legem tantum fuisse exemplar & umbram euangely, seu noui testamenti, & illud in lege ac prophetis fuisse promissum. 22. Promissiones euangelicas de remissione peccatorum esse, & uniuersales. Cap.10. 23. Sacrificia veteris legis nihil potuisse efficere ad purgationem conscientiarum, seu iustitiam coram Deo, sed id vere effecisse vnicum sacrificium sanguinis Christi, propter cuius efficaciam omnia alia sacrificia cessare debent. 24. Credentes & purgatos sanguine Christi, debere proferre etiam fidei sua fructus. 25. Contemptores euangelij graviter a Deo puniri. 26. Consolationis locus de non abijcienda spe in afflictionibus. 27. Homines fide iustificari, deq; eius effectibus ac dignitate. Cap.11. 28. Quis vsus exemplorum veteris testamenti, & quomodo ea ad euangelicam doctrinam confirmandam accommodari debeant. Cap.12. 29. Pios, permittente Deo, vulniter & salutariter affligi.
units.tr: 6. That Christ is true man, and why it was fitting for him to become man; in this place not a few things pertaining to the dignity of Christ and to our consolation are inserted: that Christ has abolished the empire of the devil, of sin, and of death; that he is our brother; that, made a partaker of our miseries, he knows them; and that he has been set forth as a merciful high priest and intercessor. Chapter 3. 7. The difference between the Law and the gospel, and the excellence of the latter. 8. That the opportunity of embracing the gospel and sound doctrine must not be allowed to slip away. 9. That men are shut out from participation in the gospel and the kingdom of God through unbelief. Chapter 4. 10. On the contrary, that those who receive the word with faith enter into rest, or receive the evangelical promises. 11. The efficacy and dignity of the Word of God. Chapter 5. 12. That through Christ alone, the true high priest, mercy and grace are obtained; where, right after this, in chapter six, many things about the dignity of Christ follow, among which is that most ample and wonderfully confirming point, that he became the cause of eternal salvation. 13. That all must always strive for fuller knowledge and progress in faith. Chapter 6. 14. That the fallen indeed rise again with difficulty, yet they must not be despaired of. 15. That God regards works proceeding from charity, and rewards them. 16. That one must persevere in faith with full and certain hope. 17. That hope is to be strengthened by the certainty of the divine promises, and consolation is to be received from them at all times. Chapter 7. 18. A remarkable place on the abrogation of the legal priesthood, and at the same time of the whole law. 19. That the law in itself was weak, useless, bringing nothing to perfection, and only introducing to Christ or the gospel. 20. That the priesthood of Christ, and at the same time the gospel, remains forever, and that no other law more excellent is to be expected. Chapter 8. 21. That the law was only a pattern and shadow of the gospel, or of the New Testament, and that this was promised in the law and the prophets. 22. That the evangelical promises concerning the forgiveness of sins are universal. Chapter 10. 23. That the sacrifices of the old law could accomplish nothing toward the purgation of consciences, or righteousness before God, but that the one sacrifice of the blood of Christ truly accomplished this, and on account of its efficacy all other sacrifices must cease. 24. That believers, purged by the blood of Christ, ought also to bring forth the fruits of their faith. 25. That despisers of the gospel are severely punished by God. 26. A place of consolation: that hope is not to be cast away in afflictions. 27. That men are justified by faith, and concerning its effects and dignity. Chapter 11. 28. What is the use of the examples of the Old Testament, and how they ought to be adapted to confirm evangelical doctrine. Chapter 12. 29. That the pious, God permitting it, are afflicted both sharply and salutarily.

units.la: Locus vero secundae partis principalis de doctrina charitatis no opus est in numerato ponere, quando a nobis, ubi totius epistolae partes & oeconomiam ostendimus, satis sunt expositi, & per ordinem a nobis enumerati.
units.tr: There is no need to set down in a list the place of the second principal part, on the doctrine of charity, since we have sufficiently explained it in our own account, where we showed the parts and economy of the whole epistle, and enumerated them in order.

units.la: Vtrum D. Paulus epistolam hanc conscripserit.
units.tr: Whether St Paul wrote this epistle.

units.la: Etsi multa, & in speciem valida, argumenta a nonnullis proferantur, ad demonstrandum, hanc epistolam non esse D.Pauli apostoli: tamen quia rursus graviora & efficaciora comperiuntur, quibus probatur, ab eodem Paulo conditam, ideo nos quoque ad hanc potius partem, quam alteram accedimus, eam pro Paulina agnoscentes. Sed quo iudicij nostri ratio omnibus constet, nos primo loco argumenta aliquot pro multis in medium proferemus, quae nos ad ita sentiendum mouent: Deinde ob oculos etiam ponemus argumenta diuersum a nobis sentientium, eaque refellemus.
units.tr: Although some have put forward many arguments, and arguments that look strong, to show that this epistle is not by the apostle Paul, yet, since on the other side weightier and more effective arguments are found proving that it was composed by Paul himself, we too incline to this view rather than the other and acknowledge the epistle as Pauline. So that the grounds for our judgement may be plain to everyone, we will first set before them a number of the many arguments that move us to think so, and then also present the arguments of those who think otherwise and refute them.

units.la: Hoc igitur in primis manifestum est, nihil in ea contineri, quod aliqua in parte a germana sacrae scripturae sententia dissideat, omniaque apostolico spiritu digna, methodo & dispositione partium Paulinam spirat phrasin & ingenium: dictione quidem purior & sublimior, sed id, quia lingua hebraica est conscripta, in qua foeliciör & grandiloquentior facile fuit Apostolus, quam in graeca.
units.tr: First of all, it is clear that nothing is contained in it that in any part disagrees with the genuine sense of Holy Scripture; everything in it is worthy of the apostolic Spirit; and in its method and arrangement of parts it breathes the Pauline style and genius. Its diction is indeed purer and more elevated, but this is because it was written in the Hebrew language, in which the Apostle could easily be more fortunate and more eloquent than in Greek.

units.la: Deinde vetustissimi & doctissimi quiq; patres eam D. Paulo Apostolo attribuunt, & pro Paulina semper agnitam testantur.
units.tr: Next, the most ancient and most learned Fathers ascribe it to the apostle Paul, and they testify that it has always been recognised as Pauline.

units.la: Clemens ipsius Pauli discipulus, & tertius à Petro Romæ pontifex, à quo nonnulli assiruunt ex Hebræo in græcum sermonem conuersam, in epistola quadam sua, epistolæ Pauli ad Hebræos meminit, eiusq; vtitur testimoniis, vti refert Eusebius Cæsariensis ecclesiasticæ historiæ lib. 3. cap. 38.
units.tr: Clement, a disciple of Paul himself and the third bishop of Rome after Peter, from whom some maintain that it was translated from Hebrew into Greek, mentions the epistle of Paul to the Hebrews in a certain letter of his, and uses its testimonies, as Eusebius of Caesarea reports in Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 38.

units.la: Irenæus Episcopus Lugdunensis, & post hunc Clemens Alexandrinus, eodē Eusebio lib. 6. cap. 11. testante, ait, epistolam ad Hebræos manifeste Pauli Apostoli esse, & Hebræo sermone conscriptam, à Luca verò Pauli discipulo græcè reditam; quandoquidem stilus epistolæ cum libro Lucæ de Actis Apostolicis videtur conuenire.
units.tr: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, and after him Clement of Alexandria, as Eusebius also attests in book 6, chapter 11, say that the epistle to the Hebrews is manifestly by the apostle Paul and was written in the Hebrew language, but was translated into Greek by Luke, Paul's disciple; for the style of the epistle seems to agree with the book of Luke on the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: Origines, (ut Idem Eusebius habet lib. 6. cap 18.) libros Canonicos sacræ Scripturæ ex ordine recensens, quatuordecim enumerat canonicas D. Pauli epistolas: Ita hanc ad Hebræos inter Paulinas collocans. Et addit ibidem hæc Origenis verba. Quamuis nonnulli de ea, quæ ad Hebræos scripta est, dubitauerint, pro eo, quòd non videatur in ea seruari eius illa sententia, quàm de se ipse pronunciat, dicens, se imperitū sermone: Sed ego dico, sicut mihi à maioribus traditum est, quia manifestissimè Pauli est, & semper omnes antiqui maiores nostri ita eam vt Pauli epistolam susceperunt. Idē Origenes in Exodum homilia 9. Paulum Apostolum in epistola ad Hebræos quædam de intelligentia tabernaculi prodidisse sublimia.
units.tr: Origen (as Eusebius also records in book 6, chapter 18), when listing the canonical books of Holy Scripture in order, counts fourteen canonical epistles of St Paul, placing this one to the Hebrews among the Pauline ones. And there he adds these words of Origen: "Although some have doubted about the one written to the Hebrews, because the sentiment that he expresses about himself, saying that he is unskilled in speech, does not seem to be preserved in it, nevertheless I say, as has been handed down to me by our forefathers, that it is most manifestly Paul's, and all the ancient ones among our forefathers have always received it as an epistle of Paul." The same Origen, in homily 9 on Exodus, says that the apostle Paul in the epistle to the Hebrews set forth certain lofty things about the meaning of the tabernacle.

units.la: Irenæus Episcopus Lugdunensis, & cuius idē Eusebius mentionē facit, quæq; græcè scripsisse plurimi autumant, in suis dialogis plurima adsert ex epistola ad Hebræos testimonia, vt eam pro Canonica & Paulina agnoscens.
units.tr: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, whom Eusebius also mentions, and who is thought by many to have written in Greek, in his dialogues brings forward very many testimonies from the epistle to the Hebrews, acknowledging it as canonical and Pauline.

units.la: Rursus Eusebius libro 3. cap. 25. enumerans libros noui testamenti, quorū auctoritas aliquando fuerit suspecta, huius ad Hebræos ibi nullam facit mentionem. Quin cap. 3. disertè ait, Pauli quatuordecim sunt epistolæ, quæ in authoritate habentur: licet sciè apud Latinos de epistola, quæ ad Hebræos scribitur, dubitari. Ita quasi contemnens latinorum de ea dubitantium iudicium, hæc adiecit.
units.tr: Again, Eusebius in book 3, chapter 25, listing the books of the New Testament whose authority has at some time been suspected, makes no mention of this one to the Hebrews. Indeed, in chapter 3 he states plainly that there are fourteen epistles of Paul which are held in authority, although he knows that among the Latins doubt is raised about the epistle which is written to the Hebrews. Thus, as if scorning the judgement of the Latins who doubt it, he added these words.

units.la: Cyrillus thesauri lib. 12. cap. 9. plurima testimonia ex epistola Pauli ad Hebræos congerit.
units.tr: Cyril, in book 12, chapter 9 of his Thesaurus, gathers together very many testimonies from Paul's epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: Nazianzenus idem crebrò facit, vt libro quarto Theologiæ, & alibi. Chrysostomus in commentariis in hanc epistolam, licet à morte eius per Constantinum presbiterū Antiochenum ex notis dicant editos, constanter Diuo Paulo vēdicat.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen does the same often, as in book 4 of his Theology and elsewhere. Chrysostom, in his commentaries on this epistle, although some say that they were published after his death from his notes by Constantine, a presbyter of Antioch, consistently ascribes it to the divine Paul.

units.la: Hieronymus in epistola ad Dardanum, de terra promissionis differens. Illud nostris dicendum est, inquit, hanc epistolam quæ inscribitur ad Hebræos, non solùm ab ecclesiis Orientis, sed ab omnibus retrò ecclesiis sermonis scriptoribus, quasi Pauli Apostoli suscipi: licet pleriq; eam vel Barnabæ, vel Clementis arbitrentur: & nihil interesse, cuius sit, cum ecclesiastici viri sit, & quotidie ecclesiarum lectione celebretur. Quæ si eam Latinorum consuetudo non recipit inter scripturas Canonicas, nec Græcorum quidem ecclesiæ Apocalypsin Ioannis eadem libertate suscipiunt: & tamen nos vtraq; suscipimus, nequaquam huius temporis consuetudinem, sed veterum Scriptorum autoritatem sequentes, qui plerunq; vtriusq; vtuntur testimoniis: non vt interdum de apocryphis facere solent, quippe qui & Gentilium literarum non raro vtantur exemplis, sed quasi canonicis & ecclesiasticis. Idem aduersus Iouinianum de Enoch, citat testimonium ex hac epistola, dicens Paulus apostolus in epist. ad Hebræos plenissimè docer, &c. Erasmus hic refutat Fabri argumentū, sed Erasmus iterum reuincitur verbis Hieronymi supra positis.
units.tr: Jerome, discussing the land of promise in his letter to Dardanus, says: "We must say to our people that this epistle, which is entitled 'to the Hebrews', is received as Paul's by not only the churches of the East but by all the writers of the church from earliest times, although most think it is by Barnabas or by Clement; and it does not matter whose it is, since it is the work of a churchman and is read daily in the churches. If the custom of the Latins does not receive it among the canonical Scriptures, neither do the churches of the Greeks receive the Apocalypse of John with the same freedom; yet we receive both, following not the custom of our own time but the authority of the ancient writers, who often use testimonies from both, not as they usually do with apocryphal books, for they not infrequently use examples from Gentile literature, but as from canonical and ecclesiastical books." The same Jerome, against Jovinian, on Enoch, cites a testimony from this epistle, saying, "The apostle Paul teaches most fully in the epistle to the Hebrews, etc." Erasmus here refutes the argument of Faber, but Erasmus is himself refuted again by the words of Jerome quoted above.

units.la: Augustinus licet alicubi obiter dicat, de epistolæ ad Hebræos autoritate dubitari, tamen in expositione inchoata in epistolā ad Romanos eam Paulo ascribit. Clarius autem suam sententiam indicat lib. 1. de peccatorum meritis & remissione, vbi testimonia prolaturus ex ea contra Pelagianos ita ait: Ad Hebræos epistola quāquam nonnullis incerta sit, tamē quoniam legi quosdam huic nostræ de baptismo paruulorū sententię cōtraria sentientes, etiā ipsam quibusdā opinionibus suis testem adhibere voluisse, magisq; me mouet autoritas ecclesiarū orientaliū, quæ hanc etiam in Canonicis habent, quanta pro vobis testimonia contineat aduertendum.
units.tr: Augustine, although somewhere in passing he says that the authority of the epistle to the Hebrews is doubted, nevertheless in his unfinished exposition of the epistle to the Romans ascribes it to Paul. He indicates his view more clearly in book 1 of On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, where, about to bring forward testimonies from it against the Pelagians, he says: "Although the epistle to the Hebrews is uncertain to some, nevertheless, since I have read that some who hold opinions contrary to this view of ours on infant baptism have wished to use it as a witness for their opinions, and since the authority of the Eastern churches, which also count it among the canonical books, moves me more, it should be noted how many testimonies it contains in your favour."

units.la: Ambrosius licet in hac & in cæteras, cōmentarios non ediderit, tamē subinde ex hac vt vere Paulina citat testimonia. Epistola 82. ad Vercellensem ecclesiā: Vnde nos Apostolus Paulus eorū (inquit) vult imitatores esse, qui per fidē & patientiā possederunt promissiones Abrahę. Quę verba habetur Hebr. 9. Et ad Clementianū. Et licet (inquit) ad Hebræos ipse dixerit, quia testamentum non valet, nisi mors intercedat testatoris, &c. Item in libris de fide cōtra Arrianos, libro de pœnitentia, de his qui initiantur. Postremò Theophylactus, initio enarrationis suæ in hanc epistolam audet dicere, eos qui negant hanc esse Pauli, non minus peccare, quàm si negent Paulum Spiritu Christi afflatum.
units.tr: Ambrose, although he did not publish commentaries on this epistle or the others, nevertheless from time to time cites testimonies from it as truly Pauline. In letter 82, to the church of Vercelli: "Whence the apostle Paul (he says) wills us to be imitators of those who through faith and patience obtained the promises of Abraham." These words are in Hebrews 6. And to Clementianus: "And although the apostle himself said to the Hebrews that a testament is not valid unless the death of the testator intervenes, etc." Likewise in his books On the Faith against the Arians, in his book On Repentance, and in On Those Who Are Initiated. Finally, Theophylact, at the beginning of his exposition of this epistle, dares to say that those who deny that it is Paul's sin no less than if they denied that Paul was inspired by the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Itaq; ob magnum ecclesiarum & doctissimorum quorumq; consensum, æquū est epistolam hanc pro Paulina agnoscere.
units.tr: Therefore, because of the great consensus of the churches and of all the most learned men, it is right to acknowledge this epistle as Pauline.

units.la: Subijciemus nunc argumenta eorum, qui putarunt explodendam, eaq; plane & simpliciter diluemus.
units.tr: We shall now set out the arguments of those who thought it should be rejected, and we shall plainly and simply refute them.

units.la: Stilus & dictionis filū non cōuenit, inquiūt, cum stilo aliarū epistolarū Paulinarū. Respondetur, quōd cum constet hanc scriptā ab Apostolo sermone patrio, nempe Hebræo, in quo facile potuit plus præstare, quàm in lingua græca, qua scri ptsit reliquas epistolas, nihil mirum si hæc elegantiorem stilum resipiat. Potest interea ab eo qui ex Hebræo in Græcū tråstulit, nonnihil esse expolita, id quod suo iure interpretes possunt & solet. Quo pertinet verba Origenis citata ab Eusebio historiæ ecclesiasticæ lib. 6. cap 18. Si requiras, inquit, à me, per quem sit sermo eius compositus, pro certo quidem Deus viderit. Hoc dico tamē, opinio, quæ ad nos vsq; peruenit, hæc est. A quibusdam dicebatur, quōd Clemens apostolorum discipulus, & episcopus vrbis Romæ græco sermone, non tamē sensibus expoliuerit. Alij, quōd Lucas, qui euangelium scripsit & Actus Apostolorū. Quibus verbis significari videtur, ab interprete esse sermone expolitam.
units.tr: They say that its style and the texture of its diction do not agree with the style of the other Pauline epistles. The reply is that, since it is certain that it was written by the Apostle in his native language, namely Hebrew, in which he could easily excel more than in Greek, in which he wrote the other epistles, it is no wonder if this one has a more elegant style. Meanwhile, it may be that the one who translated it from Hebrew into Greek polished it somewhat, which translators may and commonly do do by right. To this pertains the words of Origen, cited by Eusebius in Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 18: "If you ask me who composed its discourse, God indeed knows for certain. But this I say: the opinion that has come down to us is this. Some have said that it was Clement, the disciple of the apostles and bishop of the city of Rome, who polished it in Greek, though not in its thoughts; others, that it was Luke, who wrote the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles." By these words it seems to be indicated that it was polished in style by a translator.

units.la: Ac fieri non potest, quin quod in alienā linguā conuersum est, ipsius interpretis stilū ac dictionē magis redoleat, quàm primi eius operis cōditoris. Illud video- or posse addere, ex stilo velle iudicare de autorū scriptis, non vsq; adeo tutū ac certū. Nā si stilū debemus habere indice, videbitur & epistola ad Ephesios ex ordine Paulinarū semoueda, quādoquidē stilo à cęteris epistolis dissonat: Sed aliter scribunt occupati, aliter liberi & soluti omnibus curis, aliter affecti malis, aliter fœlici successu gaudētes, aliter senes, aliter iuuenes, aliter exercitati in scribēdo, aliter inscribēdo imperiti. Ita illa ad Rom. hyperbatis abūdans multū diuersa à cæteris videtur. Materia quoq; ipsa quæ tractāda suscipitur, & personę, ad quas scribitur, imò temporis ratio, nonnunquā aliam dictionis ac dispositionis requirūt faciem. Certè si quis opera quædam Augustini inter sese conferat, vt libros contra Academicos & similes à iuuene conscriptos, cum aliįs cōscriptis à sene & occupato, nemo habita stili ratione eiusdem autoris esse credat.
units.tr: Nor can it be otherwise than that what has been turned into another language smells more of the style and diction of the translator himself than of the original author. I can add this, that to wish to judge the writings of authors from style is not so very safe or certain. For if we must have style as our guide, the epistle to the Ephesians too will seem to be removed from the order of the Pauline epistles, since in style it differs from the other epistles. But men write in one way when busy, in another when free and released from all cares; in one way when afflicted by troubles, in another when rejoicing in happy success; in one way when old, in another when young; in one way when practised in writing, in another when unskilled in composing. Thus the epistle to the Romans, abounding in hyperbata, seems very different from the others. The subject matter that is taken up for treatment, the persons to whom one writes, and indeed the circumstances of the time, sometimes require a different form of diction and arrangement. Certainly, if anyone compares certain works of Augustine with one another, such as the books against the Academics and similar ones written when he was young, with others written when he was old and busy, no one, taking account of style, would believe they were by the same author.

units.la: Quid, quod Paulus vti solitus sit amanuensibus seu notarijs, et sensum potius dictare, quàm orationem & verba contexere? Itaq; cum non semper eodem amanuense seu notario vti potuerit, nihil mirū, si aliqua stili dissimilitudo in quibusdā epistolis inueniatur. Præterea, qd, si cum sciret nomē suum inuisum Iudæis, voluerit stilum proprium arte dissimulare, ne scriptū hoc vt suspectū quasi ab ipso profectū reiceretur? Sed quid opus est adeo intentū esse in stilū, vbi docēdi methodus acrimonia sentētiarū, vis argumentandi, ratio citandi & explicandi scripturas, eadē prorsus cernitur, quæ in illa ad Romanos 10. sicut par sæpè indicabimus. Sed & cūm de interprete vsq; adeo variant, alius enim Clementem, alius Lucam, alius Barnabam suspicatur: qui apostolo hanc adimunt, non habent tamen certum aūtorem, cui eam tribuant. Dum vero ignoratur interpres, non ideo negandū est, eam esse Pauli: non magis, quàm negandum est, euangelium Matthæi esse Matthęi, propterea quōd eius interpres ignoratur.
units.tr: What of the fact that Paul was accustomed to use amanuenses or scribes, and dictated the sense rather than composing the wording and sentences himself? Since he could not always have used the same amanuensis or scribe, it is no wonder that some difference of style appears in certain epistles. Moreover, what if, knowing that his name was hateful to the Jews, he chose to disguise his own style artfully, so that this writing would not be rejected as suspect, as though it came from him? But why be so concerned about style, when the method of teaching, the sharpness of the sentences, the force of the argument, and the manner of citing and explaining the Scriptures are wholly the same as in the epistle to the Romans, chapter 10, as we will often point out? Furthermore, opinions about the translator vary so widely: one suspects Clement, another Luke, another Barnabas. Those who deny the epistle to the apostle do not have a certain author to whom they can assign it. But even when the translator is unknown, we must not deny that it is Paul's, any more than we must deny that the Gospel of Matthew is Matthew's because its translator is unknown.

units.la: Omissum est, inquiunt, nomē & epigrapha: præterea Exordiū, quod Paulus in ceteris epistolis non facit. Sed hāc obiectione omnes vno ore veteres Scriptores diluūt, dicētes, id non metu aut impediēte cōscientia, sed sano & necessario factū consilio, ne Iudei quibus Paulus vt trāsfuga suspectus erat, & inuisus, si cōspiceret in fronte nomen Pauli, statim aut penitus reiceret hæc scripta, nec lectione digna retur: aut si legeret, minimē tamē animo assentiēdi his, q̃ ab inuiso homine propo nebantur. Cētē quę legis à suspectis aut inuisis hominibus profecta, ea nō facile solet placere. Quanquā ideo quoq̄ suppressisse nomen & officij dignitatē creditur Apostolus, quod licet, vt ad Romanos 8. ac 10. ait, omnib. modis semper quę sierit prodesse suis Iudæis: tamen nō fuit proprius illorum Apostolus, sed gentiū, sicut ait ad Galatas: eoq̄ noluit nomen suū ad illos scribēs præfigere, ne præsumptionis argueretur, quasi se Petro aut Iacobo proprijs Iudæorum apostolis anteponeret, aut in alienam messem falcē immittere velle videretur. Sed, dicis, quādo Apostolus scripsit tantūm credentibus, quare metuebat exprimere nomen suū? Respondetur, quod inter ipsos credentes multi erāt, qui legem simul cum cuāge lio putabant seruandam, & hi ipsi Paulum vt aduersariū legis valde habebant suspectum. Deinde fieri potest, vt interpres, qui primus transtulit, aut habuerit exēplar in fronte mutilatum, aut voluerit id omisso exordio & salutatione, quasi non admodum ad rem facientibus; statim principalē caussam aggredi. Primasius hoc addit: Quoniam Apostolus erat hīc nominaturus ipsum Christum apostolum & pontificem, ideo noluit ipse sui apostolatus nomē exprimere, cūm agnosceret, se nullo pacto cum illo conferendum. Atq̄ erat Apostolus prudens artifex, facileq̄ animaduertebat, quid alibi facere vel omittere expediret.
units.tr: "The name and the greeting are omitted," they say, "and besides, there is an introduction, which Paul does not use in his other epistles." But all the ancient writers refute this objection with one voice, saying that this was done not from fear or a troubled conscience, but by a sound and necessary decision. If the name of Paul, whom the Jews regarded as a deserter and hated, had stood at the head of the letter, they would at once have rejected these writings entirely and judged them unworthy of reading; or, if they had read them, they would have been in no mind to assent to what was put forward by a man they hated. For whatever law comes from suspect or hated men is not easily pleasing. Yet the Apostle is also believed to have suppressed his name and the dignity of his office for this reason: although, as he says in Romans 8 and 10, he always sought in every way to benefit his Jews, he was not their own apostle but the apostle of the Gentiles, as he says to the Galatians. Therefore, writing to them, he chose not to put his name at the head, lest he be charged with presumption, as if he were placing himself above Peter or James, the proper apostles of the Jews, or seemed to thrust his sickle into another's harvest. But you say: when the Apostle wrote only to believers, why was he afraid to express his name? The answer is that among the believers themselves there were many who thought that the law was to be kept together with the gospel, and these very people regarded Paul, as an opponent of the law, with great suspicion. Further, it may be that the translator who first rendered it either had a copy with the beginning torn off, or chose to omit the introduction and greeting, as not very pertinent, and to come straight to the main point. Primasius adds this: since the Apostle was here going to name Christ himself as Apostle and High Priest, he chose not to express the title of his own apostleship, recognising that he could in no way be compared with him. And the Apostle was a prudent craftsman, and easily saw what it was expedient to do or omit elsewhere.

units.la: Illud causati sunt aliqui, quod præter morem Pauli testimonia è veteri testamē to petita, aliter hic citantur, quàm in Hebræo habentur. Sed istud quoq̄ facile dis luitur. Interpres enim græcus citauit testimonia, vt apud septuaginta habentur, quorum versio à græcis hominibus legebatur, & à Paulo græcè scribēte subinde vsurpata est. Et si Lucam interprete esse volumus huius epistolæ, egerit hic istud suo more, qui & in euangelio suo septuaginta interpretū versione semper vtitur.
units.tr: Some have alleged this: contrary to Paul's usual practice, the testimonies taken from the Old Testament are cited here differently from how they stand in the Hebrew. But this too is easily resolved. The Greek translator cited the testimonies as they are found in the Septuagint, whose version was read by Greek people and was often used by Paul when he wrote in Greek. And if we want Luke to be the translator of this epistle, he will have done this in his usual way, since he too always uses the Septuagint version in his Gospel.

units.la: Quartò: Rursus obijcient, à græcis receptam eò lubentius, quòd contineret quędam testimonia aduersus Arrianos.
units.tr: Fourth: Again they will object that it was received by the Greeks more readily, because it contained certain testimonies against the Arians.

units.la: Friuola autē est & hęc ratio. Nam longè ante nomen Arrianorum auditum, de ea iudiciū suū & ecclesiarū retulerunt Clemens Pauli discipulus, Irenæus, Clemēs Alexādrinus, Origenes, alijq̄ Vetustissimi, qui Arrianorum tēpora præcesserūt.
units.tr: But this argument too is trivial. For long before the name of the Arians was heard, Clement, a disciple of Paul, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and other very ancient writers, who preceded the time of the Arians, expressed their judgement of it and of the churches.

units.la: Quinto: Latini homines tardius receperunt. Diluitur istud verbis Hieronymi, dicentis: propterea non imminui eius autoritatem sicut nec Apocalypseos libro quicquam detractum volumus, quòd eum græci tardius receperint. Quan-quam quo tempore primùm receperint, non est facile commonstrare. Sed magis verisimile, semper quidem habitam in precio: sed aliquanto post à quibusdam cæptum de ea dubitari: id quod primum fecisse apparet Gaium quendam disputantem aduersus proculum Montani sectatorem, sub Antonino Seueri filio: in cuius vita hoc quoq̄ Hieronymus memorat (pro re, vt apparet tūm noua, & an tea inaudita) quòd tredecim tantum Pauli Epistolas numeraret, & Epistolam ad Hebræos Pauli non esse assereret. Postea verò videntur aliqui arripuisse pleniorem occasionem reiciendi eam, quod Nouatianorum dogmati videretur patrocinari: qua de re mox dicemus. Cæterū non magni momenti sunt hæ cõsequētiæ. Tertulianus contra Marcionē scribens libro 5. cum ex omnibus epistolis Pauli-nis testimonia proferat, tamē nō profert aliqua ex hac ad Hebræos: Ergo nō est Paulina: quemadmodum si dicas, non vsus est testimonio Ionæ prophetæ, ergo Ionas non est propheta. Si enim non potest haberi liber pro Canonico, nisi statim apud quemuis autorem ecclesiasticum inueniatur citatum ex eo testimonium, tūm nos ipsos pluribus sacris libris spoliauerimus. Sic, quòd dicunt, Ambrosius non scripsit in hanc commentarios, qui tamen scripsit in alias epistolas: Ergo hæc non est Paulina. Non valet consequentia. Et conuincitur, Ambrosio
units.tr: Fifth: the Latins received it more slowly. This is answered by the words of Jerome, who says that its authority is not diminished, just as we do not wish anything to be taken away from the book of the Apocalypse because the Greeks received it more slowly. Yet it is not easy to show when they first received it. It is more probable that it was always held in esteem, but that a little later some began to doubt it. This appears first to have been done by a certain Gaius, disputing against Proclus, a follower of Montanus, under Antoninus, son of Severus. In his life Jerome also records this (as a matter then evidently new and perhaps not yet heard of): that he counted only thirteen epistles of Paul and asserted that the epistle to the Hebrews was not Paul's. Afterwards, however, some seem to have seized a fuller opportunity to reject it, because it seemed to support the doctrine of the Novatians, on which we shall speak shortly. But these consequences are of little weight. Tertullian, writing against Marcion in book 5, although he brings forward testimonies from all the Pauline epistles, does not bring any from this one to the Hebrews. Therefore it is not Pauline? This is like saying: he did not use the testimony of the prophet Jonah, therefore Jonah is not a prophet. For if a book could not be held canonical unless a testimony from it were at once found cited by every ecclesiastical author, we would have stripped ourselves of many sacred books. Likewise, that Ambrose did not write commentaries on this epistle, though he wrote on the others, does not prove that it is not Paul's. The inference does not hold. And it is refuted by the fact that Ambrose...

units.la: 1. Obiectio, omissio Epigraphæ.
units.tr: 1st objection: the omission of the title.

units.la: Alia Obiectio. Nomē nō præfixum. Solutio.
units.tr: Another objection: the name is not prefixed. Solution.

units.la: 3. Obiectio. Varietas citationis locorū. Hieronymus super 6. caput Esaiæ.
units.tr: 3rd objection: variation in the citation of passages. Jerome on chapter 6 of Isaiah.

units.la: 4. Obiectio. cōtra Arrianos. Responsio.
units.tr: 4th objection: against the Arians. Response.

units.la: 5. Obiectio. Serò recepta à Latinis.
units.tr: 5th objection: received late by the Latins.

units.la: 6. Obiectio. Sic argumentatur Beatus Rhenanus in argumēto lib. 5. aduersus Marcionem. Ambrosio probatam, qui alias ipsius tanquam Pauline testimonio est vsus, sicut supra indicauimus. Sunt huiusmodi argumenta tantum coniecturalia, & probabilia in speciem: ac proinde minus efficacia ad aliquid ferio affirmandum. Satis est his opponere, quod, qui nō minoris sunt autoritatis in ecclesia Scriptores, hanc pro Paulina omni tempore agnouerint.
units.tr: 6th objection: Beatus Rhenanus argues thus in the argument to book 5 against Marcion. Ambrose approved it, though he elsewhere used it as a Pauline testimony, as we indicated above. Arguments of this kind are merely conjectural and probable in appearance, and therefore less effective for affirming anything firmly. It is enough to set against them that writers of no less authority in the Church have always acknowledged this epistle as Paul's.

units.la: Sexto: Hinc volūt colligere, hāc non esse Pauli Apostoli, quod huius autor capite secundo fateatur, se ab alijs, qui audierant, edoctū & confirmatū in doctrina euangelica, id quod Paulus alibi ad Galat. 1. Constantissime de se negat. Sed hic cauillus plurimis rationibus euertitur. Primum cum dicit, Quæ cū primum enarrari cœperit per ipsum Dominū, ab ijs qui audierāt, in nos cōfirmata fuit, attestāte Deo et signis. Hæc verba non tātum de Pauli persona accipiēda sunt, sed in genere de omnibus credētibus, illisq; inprimis Iudeis, ad quos verba faciebat, quib. per Apostolos veritas euāgelica fuerat annunciata, quiq; cōfirmati fuerāt in ea videdo miracula, & accipiendo Spiritū sanctū. Quē in modū ipse Paulus licet immediate à Domino vocatus & edoctus, tamē per impositionē manuū Ananiæ accepit etiam Spiritū sanctū, vt sic externo etiā signo apostolico cętui insereretur. Si quis obstrepit ad huc, interpretari licet, ab his qui audierāt, idē quod post eos, q audierāt, vt sit sententia: Paulū post alios apostolos, etiā salutē accepisse, & in euāgelica veritate edoctū. Sic enim græcis voces ἔρχηη & ἔρχαι mutuò sese respiciūt, & ordine significat, sicut latinis ea voces, primū & secundū. Et sępe apud latinos dicimus, ab his, pro eo, quod est, post hos: Plinius, præcipuū, inquit, est stercus columbarū, proximū caprarū, ab hoc ouium. His addatur licet, Apostolo, cum scriberet ad eos, quorū non erat proprius Apostolus, & quos voluit nomen suum latere, non opus fuisse multa de se, quōd Apostolus esset immediate à Deo vocatus, & diuinitus edoctus, differere. Quod nec alibi erat facturus, nisi aduersariorū iniquitas & malitia eum apud getes, quarum erat proprius Apostolus, coegisset Apostolatum suum & diuinam institutionem asserere.
units.tr: Sixth: From this they want to conclude that this epistle is not by the Apostle Paul, because its author admits in the second chapter that he was taught and confirmed in the evangelical doctrine by others who had heard the Lord, which Paul elsewhere, in Galatians 1, flatly denies about himself. But this quibble is overturned by many arguments. First, when he says which, having first been declared through the Lord himself, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, God also bearing witness with signs, these words must be understood not only of Paul's person but generally of all believers, and especially of the Jews, to whom he was speaking, to whom the evangelical truth had been announced through the Apostles, and who had been confirmed in it by seeing miracles and receiving the Holy Spirit. In this way Paul himself, though called and taught immediately by the Lord, nevertheless also received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of Ananias's hands, so that he might be joined to the apostolic body also by an outward sign. If anyone still objects, it is permitted to interpret "by those who heard" as the same as "after those who heard," so that the sense is: Paul too received salvation and was taught in the evangelical truth after the other apostles. For in Greek the words [ἔρχηη and ἔρχαι] refer to each other reciprocally and signify order, just as the Latin words primum and secundum do. And among Latin writers we often say "by" for "after": Pliny says, "The most excellent is pigeon dung, next to it goat dung, after this sheep's." To this may be added that when the Apostle wrote to those for whom he was not the proper apostle, and whose notice he wished to escape, he had no need to say much about himself, that he was called immediately by God and taught divinely. Nor would he have done so elsewhere, had not the injustice and malice of his opponents among the Gentiles, of whom he was the proper apostle, forced him to assert his apostleship and divine appointment.

units.la: Septimo: Ob hanc quoq; caussam reijcere ausi sunt nonnulli, quōd in ea videntur loci aliquot cōfirmare dogma Nouatianorum seu Catharorum, negantiū ijs, qui semel lapsi essent post baptismum, locum resurgendi seu consequedi veniam. Huc enim facere videntur illa capite sexto: Fieri non potest, vt qui semel fuerint illumi nati, gustauerintq; donum cœleste, et participes facti fuerint spiritus sancti, prolabantur, denuò renouentur per pœnitentiam, ab integro crucifigentes sibimetipsis filium Dei, & ludibrio exponētes. Iterum capite 10. Nam si voletes peccauerimus post acceptam cognitionem veritatis, nō vlirā pro peccatis reliqua est hostia: sed formidabilis quaedā expectatio iudicij, & ignis vehementia, qui deuoraturus est aduersarios. Propter hos, inquam, locos, velut qui clarissime videntur confirmare impium dogma Nouati, multi etiam magni viri ad ea tempora moti fuerunt, vt de hac epistola minus, quàm antea, honorifice sentirent, atqz eo potissimum tempore cęperunt Latini, apud quos exortum fuit dogma Nouati, de huius epistolæ autoritate dubitare. Cæterum si propterea reiciendus erit liber, quia ex eo sumpserunt stabiliendi erroris sui instrumenta haeretici: iam euangelium Ioannis, ex quo præcipuē materiam erroris sui hauserunt Arriani, imò vix vlli præterea libri noui testamenti suam dignitatem poterunt retinere. Tota Scriptura instar optimi prati est pulcherrimis flosculis & herbis redolentis, è quibus aliud animalculum mel colligit, aliud vero venenum. Ex Scripturis enim recte intellectis pij excerpunt ea, quibus se in fana doctrina confirment: mali vero ex perperam intellectis colligunt, quibus & se, & alios in errorem abducant. Itaq; quod Nouatianorum dogma in hac epistola quibusdam confirmatum putatur, id non est aliud, quam quod verba Apostoli nō recte intellexerint.
units.tr: Seventh: Some have also dared to reject this epistle for this reason, that in it several passages seem to confirm the dogma of the Novatians or Cathari, who deny that those who have fallen again after baptism can be restored or obtain pardon. For the following words of chapter 6 seem to favour this: It is impossible that those who have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have fallen away, should be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again to themselves the Son of God, and putting him to open shame. Again in chapter 10: For if we sin wilfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a fiery indignation which shall devour the adversaries. On account of these passages, I say, which seem most clearly to confirm the impious dogma of Novatus, many great men of those times were moved to think less highly of this epistle than they had before; and it was especially at that time that the Latins, among whom the dogma of Novatus had arisen, began to doubt the authority of this epistle. But if the book is to be rejected because the heretics drew from it the instruments for establishing their error, then the Gospel of John, from which the Arians chiefly drew the material of their error, and indeed hardly any other book of the New Testament, could retain its dignity. All of Scripture is like an excellent meadow, full of the loveliest flowers and fragrant herbs; from these one little creature gathers honey, another gathers poison. For the godly pick out from Scripture rightly understood those things by which they are confirmed in sound doctrine; but the wicked gather from it wrongly understood those things by which they lead both themselves and others into error. Therefore, that the dogma of the Novatians is thought to be confirmed in this epistle is nothing other than that they have not rightly understood the words of the Apostle.

units.la: 8. Obiectio de dogmate Nouatianorum. Ex Scriptura sacra etiā impijuenenū & falsa dogmata haurire queat.
units.tr: 8. Objection concerning the dogma of the Novatians. Even from holy Scripture an impious and false dogma may be drawn.

units.la: Quod quia non potest nisi pluribus explicari, ideo nos de hac re iam supersedebimus, exposituri omnia exactius & diligentius, vbi ad illorum enarrationem peruenerimus.
units.tr: Since this cannot be explained except at some length, we shall therefore postpone the matter here, intending to set out everything more exactly and carefully when we come to their exposition.

units.la: PRIOR PARS EPISTOLAE, IN QVA PRIMO LOCO DOCET, CHRISTVM ESSE DEI FILIVM, VERVMque Deum: ac proinde eum, eiusq; euangelium amplectendum.
units.tr: THE FIRST PART OF THE EPISTLE, IN WHICH HE TEACHES FIRST THAT CHRIST IS THE SON OF GOD AND TRULY GOD, AND THEREFORE THAT HE AND HIS GOSPEL ARE TO BE EMBRACED.

units.la: CAPVT PRIMVM: PROPOSITIO.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE: THE PROPOSITION.

units.la: Deus olim multifariam multisq; modis locutus patribus per prophetas: extremis diebus hisce locutus est nobis per filium.
units.tr: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.
