units.la: ÆC est pars epistolæ prima, in qua præterquàm quòd sententiæ ipsæ, & excellens materia totius huius epistolæ manifestissimè declarant, hanc epistolam Diui Pauli Apostoli pectus, spiritum, & doctrinam respicere. In quo enim clarius eluceat Pauli excelsus spiritus, quàm in expositione præcipuorum capitum totius religionis Christianæ, videlicet de Christi diuinitate, de abrogatione legis, de iustificatione per fidem? Aut quis grauius absolutiusq; ea tractet, quàm hic sunt tractata? Tum verò ipsa œconomia seu dispositio partium, docendiq; methodus, quæ tota hac epistola conspicitur, planè cum methodo in reliquis epistolis obseruata conuenit. Paulino enim prorsus more distinguunt epistolam in duas partes principales, ita vt priore ea tradat, quæ pertinent ad doctrinam fidei, ad instructionem conscientiarum, & interni ac spiritualis hominis: posteriore verò, quæ pertinent ad doctrinam charitatis siue operum, ad instructionem morum, et externi seu carnalis hominis. Quam diuisionem in singulis epistolis, quas hactenus enarrauimus, obseruatam, quantum conueniebat, indicauimus. Rursus autem Paulino more hoc fit, quòd prior pars in certos locos seu capita, aut, si mauis, disputationes, pro, vt eorum ad quos scribebat, causa & status postulabat, diuiditur. Ad Iudæos namque hanc scribens, è quibus qui euangelio aduersabantur, & credentes conabantur ab euangelio abducere: quoniam hæc tria potissimum negabant, & pertinacissimè impugnabant, nimirum Christum esse Deum verumque Messiam: legem Mosaicam abrogatam, atq; euangelio debere cedere: deinde iustificari homines fide absq; operibus legis: ideo de his tribus locis grauissimè & copiosissimè in hac epistola disputat, & quidem tanta acrimonia, tam aptè colligens, tam concinniter concludens, vt nullus alius Apostolus ita disputare ueniatur: nec verosimile sit quenquam præter ipsum Paulum ita orationem vniuersam dispositurum.
units.tr: This is the first part of the epistle. Apart from the sentences themselves and the excellent subject matter of the whole epistle, which clearly show it, this epistle reflects the heart, spirit and teaching of the divine Apostle Paul. For where would Paul's lofty spirit shine more clearly than in the exposition of the chief heads of the whole Christian religion: namely the divinity of Christ, the abrogation of the law, and justification by faith? Or who could treat them more weightily and thoroughly than they are treated here? Indeed the very economy, or arrangement of the parts, and the method of teaching, which is seen throughout this epistle, agree plainly with the method observed in his other epistles. For in the Pauline manner they divide the epistle into two principal parts: in the first he sets out what pertains to the doctrine of faith, to the instruction of consciences, and of the inner and spiritual man; in the second, what pertains to the doctrine of love or of works, to the instruction of morals, and of the outer or carnal man. We have pointed out this division, as far as it was fitting, in the individual epistles which we have expounded so far. Again, in the Pauline manner, the first part is divided into certain places or heads, or, if you prefer, disputations, according to the cause and condition of those to whom he was writing. For writing to the Jews, of whom some were opposed to the gospel and others, believers, tried to draw away from the gospel, since they especially denied and most stubbornly attacked three things, namely that Christ is God and the true Messiah; that the Mosaic law has been abrogated and must give way to the gospel; and that men are justified by faith without the works of the law; therefore he disputes most weightily and copiously in this epistle about these three places, and indeed with such keenness, so aptly gathering and so neatly concluding, that no other apostle is found to argue in this way, nor is it likely that anyone but Paul himself would arrange the whole discourse thus.

units.la: Sic verò & in alijs epistolis cernitur prior pars principalis in suos locos ad doctrinam fidei pertinentes, & euangelij proprios diuisa. Epistolæ ad Romanos prior pars in tres locos potissimum secatur: quorum primo docet, homines non operibus, sed fide in Christum, etiam absque operibus legis, iustificari. Secundo disserit de peccato, gratia, & lege, eaque inter se ita confert, vt concludat, gratiam multò esse peccato ac lege superiorem, & homines non lege aut operibus, sed tantùm gratia seruari. Tertiò docet, beneficia euangelica per Christum allata etiam ad Gentiles pertinere, non tantùm ad Iudæos, vt ipsi obganiebāt: ita gentiles ad amplectendum Christum excitās, & eos qui eum susceperant, in fide confirmans. Inde venit ad alteram partem principalem de doctrina charitatis siue operum.
units.tr: In the other epistles too, the first principal part is seen divided into its places, which pertain to the doctrine of faith and are proper to the gospel. The first part of the epistle to the Romans is cut mainly into three places. In the first he teaches that men are justified not by works but by faith in Christ, even apart from the works of the law. In the second he discourses about sin, grace and the law, and compares them with one another so as to conclude that grace is far superior to sin and to the law, and that men are saved not by law or works but by grace alone. Thirdly he teaches that the benefits of the gospel brought through Christ pertain also to the Gentiles, not only to the Jews, as they were grumbling; thus he stirs up the Gentiles to embrace Christ and confirms in faith those who had received him. From there he comes to the second principal part, on the doctrine of love or works.

units.la: Sic iterum epistola ad Galatas in duas partes principales secatur, cuius prior etiam pars distinctis locis constat. Primo enim contra aduersarios, contendentes ipsum non verum fuisse Apostolum, sibi diuinitùs commissam fun-ctionem apostolicam conuincit. Altero loco elegantissima methodo de iustificatione per fidem absque operibus legis disputat. Hinc aggreditur secundâ parte principalè de doctrina charitatis. Itidé epistola ad ad Ephesios duas partes principales habet, & priore rursus in suos locos distributa. Primo enim docet, quòd Deus per suâ potentiâ nos gratis per fidem in Christo viuificet seu iustificet. Secundò, quod Deus etiâ Gentiles voluerit euangelicarum promissionum participes facere. Quibus absolutis ad tradendam do-ctrinam Charitatis descendit. Pari modo in epistola ad Colossenses, quæ est velut Epitome eius ad Ephesios: docet prima parte, quòd Deus pater reconciliatos habeat, seu iustificet per Christum omnes, qui in fide stabiles permanserint: Secunda parte exponit doctrinam charitatis. Sed quid opus foret in cæteris epistolis hac methodû & in docendo progressum demonstrare, diutiusque hic occupari? Proinde etiâsi quedâ videretur obstare, quo minus hanc epistolâ pro Paulina agnosceremus: tamen rerum in ea expositarum sublimitas, ipsa item docend ratio & methodus nos merito vrgeat ad tribuendum eam Diuo Paulo Apostolo. Sed vt tandem ad Apostolum propius accedamus, Sex causæ sunt, ob quas omissa videtur in hac epistola salutatio, seu epigrapha & exordium, ac proinde cur non explodenda. Prima, quia illis inuisus fuit & suspectus. Sed dicas, Scripsit tantùm credentibus. Respondetur, quòd inter hostamen multi erant, qui adhuc putabant legem seruandam, & tales offendebantur nominePauli, tanquàm publici hostis legis Mosaicæ. Tertiò, Quia non fuit proprius Iudæorum A-postolus, sed gentium, habebantque illi Petrum, Iacobum, &c. Argui itaque potuisset Pauluspræsumptionis. Quartò, Humilitatis caussa, ne se alijs apostolis proprijs videretur antepo-nere, vel vt Primasius habet, quia vocat postea Christum Apostolum, cui videretur se æqua-re, si se quoque apostolum nuncuparet. Quintò, forte interpres, qui græcè reddit, nastusfuit exemplum mutilum, aut auiditate cognoscendi statim à causa principali incepit, omissaepigrapha & exordio, quasi non multum ad rem facientibus. Sextò, non est nouum exem-plum, quòd nomen vel exordium libro non præfigatur. Haud igitur metu ac dolo, sed certoconsilio, iustissimisque de causis factum est, quòd nomẽ, epigraphen, ac salutatione nullampræmisit. Neq; vero id satis est, ad arripiendâ inde calumniam, quando etiâ nequaquam no-uo exemplo ab apostolo id factum est, vtiam diximus. Nam neq; Moses suum nomen præ-figit à se conscripto Pentateucho, propterea autẽ opus illud velle reijcere, vel alteri cuipiamascribere, quis non intelligat extremæ esse dementiæ? Nec primi duo libri regũ, qui Samue-lis inscribũtur, habent nomen Samuelis, vel alterius cuiuspiã nomen præfixum. Sed & inte-prophetas cum omnium libris pręfixũ sit ex more prophetę nomen, interdum etiam genus, vel conditio: tamen Danielis libro nomen nullũ præfigitur, sed statim à Narratione sumitur exordiũ: neq; propterea quisquâ de reij ciedo eo vnquâ cogitauit. Quid, quòd in nouo testa-mento Matthæus, Marcus, Ioannes, nec nomina, nec præfationem vllam adhibent? neque quicquam vsquam inserunt, vnde à se scriptos eos libros satis possit colligi? etiamsi suarum personarum Matthæus & Ioannes mentionem faciant. Præterea priori epistolæ Ioannis nullum nomen præfigitur. Quare his omissis Apostoli verba aggrediamur.
units.tr: Thus again the epistle to the Galatians is cut into two principal parts, the first of which also consists of distinct places. First, against adversaries who contended that he was not a true apostle, he proves that the apostolic office was committed to him by God. In the second place, with a most elegant method, he disputes about justification by faith apart from the works of the law. Hence he proceeds to the second principal part, on the doctrine of love. The epistle to the Ephesians likewise has two principal parts, and the first is again distributed into its places. For first he teaches that God, by his power, freely quickens or justifies us through faith in Christ. Secondly, that God willed to make the Gentiles also partakers of the gospel promises. When these matters are finished, he descends to deliver the doctrine of love. In the same way, in the epistle to the Colossians, which is as it were an epitome of that to the Ephesians, he teaches in the first part that God the Father has reconciled, or justifies, through Christ, all who have remained steadfast in faith; in the second part he sets out the doctrine of love. But why should I need to demonstrate this method and progress of teaching in the other epistles, and dwell on it longer here? Therefore, even if something seemed to stand in the way of our acknowledging this epistle as Pauline, nevertheless the sublimity of the matters set out in it, and likewise the manner and method of teaching, rightly urge us to ascribe it to the divine Apostle Paul. But that we may at last come closer to the Apostle: there are six reasons for which the salutation, the superscription and the introduction seem to be omitted in this epistle, and therefore why its omission is not to be rejected. First, because he was hated and suspected by them. But you may say: he wrote only to believers. The answer is that among them there were many who still thought the law was to be kept, and such people were offended by the name of Paul, as a public enemy of the Mosaic law. Thirdly, because he was not the particular apostle of the Jews but of the Gentiles, and they had Peter, James and others. Paul could thus have been charged with presumption. Fourthly, out of humility, lest he seem to put himself before the other apostles; or, as Primasius has it, because he afterwards calls Christ an apostle, and he would seem to be equal to him if he also called himself an apostle. Fifthly, perhaps the translator who rendered it into Greek had an incomplete example; or, out of eagerness to know, he began at once from the principal matter, omitting the superscription and introduction as not bearing greatly on the subject. Sixthly, it is not a new practice that a name or an introduction is not prefixed to a book. Therefore it was done not from fear or deceit, but by settled plan and for most just reasons, that he prefixed no name, superscription or greeting. Nor is it enough, in order to seize on this as a calumny, since the apostle did this by no means for the first time, as we have said. For Moses does not prefix his name to the Pentateuch written by himself; yet who would not understand it to be extreme madness, on that account, to wish to reject that work or to ascribe it to someone else? Nor do the first two books of Kings, which are entitled of Samuel, have the name of Samuel or of anyone else prefixed. And although among the prophets the name of the prophet, and sometimes also his family or condition, is prefixed to the books of all, yet no name is prefixed to the book of Daniel, but the introduction is taken straight from the narrative; nor has anyone on that account ever thought of rejecting it. What of the fact that in the New Testament Matthew, Mark and John use neither names nor any preface, nor insert anywhere anything from which it can sufficiently be gathered that they wrote those books, even though Matthew and John mention their own persons? Moreover, no name is prefixed to the former epistle of John. Therefore, with these matters set aside, let us approach the words of the Apostle.

units.la: Deus olim multifariam multisq; modis locutus patribus per prophetas, extremis diebus hisce locutus est nobis per filium.
units.tr: God, who at various times and in various ways spoke in the past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by the Son.

units.la: Repetenda breuiter caussa huius disputationis: vide argumentum, & præterea initium collationis Christi cum Mose. Sed, quare constituit Apostolus hanc disputationem primo loco? Respondetur: Sicut Iudæi hoc loco posito, quòd Christus non esset Deus, facilè po-tuissent euertere etiam uniuersum Euangelium, & omnem doctrinam de iustitia per fidem in Christum: Ita erat hæc causa primo loco stabilienda, vt postea ad reliquas confirmandas fundamentum esset iactum. Fundamentum enim afferendi dignitatem Euangelij, & iustifi-cationis per fidem in Christum ex eo pendet, quòd Christus Deus sit. Quod non ignorantes Iudæi semper primo loco cupiebant tollere Christi diuinitatem & omnem dignitatem. O-missa igitur epigrapha, statim aggreditur Apostolus primum locum seu primam disputatio-nem, in qua contra aduersarios Iudæos, qui Christum pro Deo nolebant agnoscere, manifestissimè astruit, Christum esse Dei filium ac verum Deum. Totius proinde disputationis hæc est propositio: Christus, per quem Euangelium postremis hisce temporibus reuelatum est, verus est Dei filius, ac verus Deus. Apostolus autem non simpliciter eam extulit, sed voluit quadam contentionis forma illustriorem reddere, inferendo, longè benignius honorificen-tiusq; Deum patrem egisse nobiscum, quàm cum superioris seculi sanctis patribus vnquam egerit. Qua ratione in ipso vestibulo insinuat, quòd, vt persona, per quam euangelium alla-tũ est, longè est præstantior, ita ipsum quoq; euangelium multò fit lege præstantius, necnon quòd nos, qui euangelium suscepimus, feliciore agamus conditione quàm patres. Ita conti-net hæc propositio aliquid altius & præclarius in sese, quàm si simpliciter dictum fuisset: Christus est verus Dei filius. Ac videtur mihi eo pacto locus attentionis in ipsa propositione aliquo modo paratus. Vbi enim significat, excellentius quiddam nobis contigisse, quàm vt quam contigerit patribus, mox omnium animi ad attente audiendum hîc excitantur. Estigi-tur ipsa contentionis forma in hac propositione diligenter consideranda: suntq; mẽbra mem-bris conferenda, & singula accurate expêdenda. Est autem sententia: Olim quidem Deus lo-cutus est patribus, & quidem multifariam sæpè multisque modis, sed tantùm per prophe-tas: At nunc Deus locutus est etiam nobis, & quidè semel vnoq; modo, sed per vnicum suum filium Iesum Christum.
units.tr: The cause of this disputation should be briefly recalled: see the argument, and also the beginning of the comparison of Christ with Moses. But why did the Apostle place this disputation first? The answer is this. If the Jews could overturn this point, that Christ is not God, they could easily overturn the whole Gospel and all the teaching about justification by faith in Christ. So this cause had to be established first, so that the foundation would be laid for confirming the rest. For the argument that the Gospel and justification by faith in Christ are worthy depends on the fact that Christ is God. The Jews, who were not unaware of this, always wanted to remove first of all Christ's divinity and all his dignity. So, having omitted the inscription, the Apostle at once takes up the first point, or first disputation, in which, against the Jewish opponents who would not acknowledge Christ as God, he most clearly asserts that Christ is the Son of God and true God. Therefore the proposition of the whole disputation is this: Christ, through whom the Gospel has been revealed in these last times, is the true Son of God and true God. The Apostle, however, did not state it simply, but wished to make it more striking by a certain form of contrast, by pointing out that God the Father has dealt with us far more kindly and honourably than he ever dealt with the holy fathers of the former age. By this method he hints at the very threshold that, as the person through whom the Gospel was brought is far superior, so the Gospel itself is far superior to the law, and that we who have received the Gospel are in a happier condition than the fathers. Thus this proposition contains within itself something higher and more distinguished than if it had simply been said: Christ is the true Son of God. And it seems to me that in this way a place for attention is in some measure prepared in the proposition itself. For when it signifies that something more excellent has befallen us than what befell the fathers, the minds of all are at once aroused to listen attentively. The form of the contrast must therefore be carefully considered in this proposition: the clauses are to be set against one another and each part examined with care. The sense is this: Once God indeed spoke to the fathers, and that often, in many ways and by many means, but only through the prophets. But now God has spoken to us too, and indeed once and in one way, but through his only Son Jesus Christ.

units.la: Locutus est Deus: Sæpè in Scripturis tribuitur Deo locutio seu loquela: Sed cùm Deus incor-poreus sit, neq; ei competat loquêdi ratio, sicut nobis, videndum, quid ea phrasi in Scripturis significetur. Itaq; loqui dicitur Deus, quàdo occulta inspiratione, seu afflatu voluntate suam alicui aperit. Atq; hoc pacto saepè loquitur Deus suis sanctis, & mutabiles voces sine sono vllo ac strepitu in piorum pectoribus edit. Quo pertinet illud Psal. 85: Audiá quid loquatur Deus Iehoua, quoniam loquetur pacé ad populum suum, &c. Itè Deus dicitur loqui, quando facta aliqua seu opera edit, ex quibus voluntas ipsius aequè clara intelligitur, atq; voluntas hominum percipitur ex eorum verbis. Quomodo etiam ipsa opera loqui dicuntur, vt in Psalmo 19. Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum. Est etiam quaedam locutio Dei ipsa eius bona voluntas & potentia, qua, quicquid ei placet, statim perficit. De hac locutionis forma sunt illa: Dixit Deus, fiat Lux, & facta est Lux. Non enim voce aliqua externa, audibiliq; aliquid est locutus, sed tantum voluit, &, ut sic loquar, animo concaepit, statimq; effectum est, quod ei placuit. Postremo loqui Deo tribuitur, quando per creaturas subiectas, siue res creaturis naturaliter conuenientes, hominib. aliquid patefacit: quomodo per angelos humana induetos specie, per somnia immissa, per visiones & imagines propositas saepè multa hominum generi reuelauit, de quibus modis pualò pòst dicemus, Atq; hoc pacto praesenti loco accipiendum est, Deum locutum, quando hic statim additur, multifariam locutus, maximeq; per prophetas.
units.tr: God has spoken. In the Scriptures speech or utterance is often ascribed to God. But since God is incorporeal and the manner of speaking does not belong to him as it does to us, we must consider what is signified by this phrase in the Scriptures. God is said to speak when he reveals his will to someone by a hidden inspiration or breath. In this way God often speaks to his saints and produces changing voices, without any sound or noise, in the hearts of the godly. To this belongs the saying in Psalm 85: "I will hear what the LORD God will say, for he will speak peace to his people," etc. Likewise God is said to speak when he produces some deeds or works from which his will is understood just as clearly as the will of men is perceived from their words. In the same way the works themselves are said to speak, as in Psalm 19: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows his handiwork." There is also a certain speaking of God, namely his good will and power, by which whatever pleases him he at once accomplishes. Of this form of speech are the words: "God said, Let there be light, and there was light." For he spoke not by any external or audible voice, but only willed, and, so to speak, conceived it in his mind, and at once what pleased him was done. Lastly, God is said to speak when, through subject creatures, or things naturally suited to creatures, he makes something known to men. In this way, through angels who took on human form, through sent dreams, through visions and proposed images, he often revealed much to the human race. We shall speak of these modes a little later. In this way, in the present passage, God's speaking must be understood, since it is immediately added: "having spoken many times and in many ways, and especially through the prophets."

units.la: Olim: comprehendit uniuersum temptus, quod intercesit à primo lapsu Adami, tàm ante legem, quàm post legem, ad tempora vsq; Christi & euangelij reuelati. Quod tempus ideo per tot secula protrahi conueniebat, quia ptopter hominum indignitatem, caecitatem, malitiá non nisi lento successu potuerunt omnia de Christo uenturo atq; hominum salute per eundem restauranda praenunciari atq; adumbrari.
units.tr: In the past: this covers the whole time that lay between the first fall of Adam, both before the law and after the law, down to the times of Christ and the revealed Gospel. This period had to be drawn out over so many ages because, on account of human unworthiness, blindness and malice, all the things about the coming Christ and the salvation of men to be restored through him could be foretold and foreshadowed only with slow progress.

units.la: Multifariá multisq; modis: πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως. Prior vox sonat, quasi dicas per varias partes: alia significat variis modijs. πολύτροπον homo variis dotibus & mira dexteritate praeditus, qui in omnem partem & ad omnia possit se componere: qua appellatione Homerus honestauit Vlyssem, proinde sic nonnulli distinguunt duas voces hic positas, ut per priorè signari putet temporum frequentiam: per posteriorem diuersos modos: quandoquidem Deus & valde crebrò, & diuersis modis voluntate suam manifestauit: crebrò quidé & distinctis temporib. Nam à prima mundi conditione ad ipsum Adamum, ad Noah, ad Abrahamum, Dauidem, aliosq; sanctos patres ordine sibi succedentes, de Christo venturo sermo habitus est, & promissiones exhibitae: saepè etiam alijs de rebus, & alijs hominibus Deus voluntatem suam manifestauit. Ita enim Deus nūquá deserují humanū genus, sed omni tempore testimonia extare voluit de bona sua erga homines voluntate. Idq; quo inexcusabiles essent, suaq; voluntate intelligerentur damnati, qui aut noluerint audire, aut, si audierint noluerint obedire. Quo pertinet illud Roman.1. Deus illis patefecit, &c. Ita ut sint inexcusabiles. Nec ita sinet mundum erroribus in uolui, quin semper reluceant aliqua pietatis vestigia, & inter impios pauci saltem pij semper supererunt: cuius rei exemplum est tempore Eliae, 1. Reg. 19.
units.tr: Many times and in many ways: polymeros kai polytropos [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]. The first word sounds as if you said "in various parts"; the other signifies "in various manners." A man of many turns [polytropon] is one endowed with varied gifts and wonderful skill, who can adapt himself in every direction and to every situation; Homer honoured Ulysses with this epithet. Accordingly some distinguish the two words used here, so that the former is taken to signify frequency of times, and the latter diverse manners. For God manifested his will both very often and in diverse ways, often indeed and at distinct times. For from the first creation of the world, to Adam himself, to Noah, to Abraham, David and the other holy fathers succeeding one another in order, there was discourse about the coming Christ and promises were given. Often also God made his will known about other matters and to other men. For in this way God never deserted the human race, but willed that at all times there should be testimonies of his good will towards men, so that those who either would not hear or, if they heard, would not obey, might be inexcusable and be condemned by their own will being understood. To this belongs the saying in Romans 1: "God has shown it to them," etc., "so that they are without excuse." Nor did he allow the world to be so enveloped in errors that some traces of piety did not always shine forth, and among the wicked there always remained at least a few godly men. An example of this is in the time of Elijah, 1 Kings 19.

units.la: Porrò quòd varijs modis Deus per subiectas creaturas sit locutus, promptum est è sacris literis colligere. Apparuit & locutus est Abrahae per angelos humana figura indutos. sub quercu Mambre: Mosi in rubo & igni: alias in nube: sicut & in Euangelio vox è nube audita est, Hic est filius meus dilectus: In imagine militis locutus est cum Iosua. Alijs, ut prophetis, praebuit visendas rerum diuersarum species, quarum significationem interno afflatu illis notam fecit: Unde & prophetae videntes appellati: Et initio sermonum solet praemitti, visio Esaiae: deinde, Haec dicit Dominus. Nonnunquam immisit somnia, ut Samueli, alijsq; rerum futurarum praesagis: Item operibus & facinoribus diuersis, quibus Christus praefiguratus est: iuxta illud 1. Corinth 10. Omnia in figura contingebant illis. Deniq; alijs idgenus modis de voluntate sua sanctos viros edocuit, quibus tanquàm instrumentis usus est ad propalandū etiam reliquis, quod facto uel cognitu opus erat. Imò & per ea, quae inidonea putaremus instrumenta, illE subinde locutus est: ut per asinā Balaā, per ipsum Caiapham impiū sacerdoté. Adeò nihil refert, per quos veriras proponatur, modò constet, à Domino ad nos proficisci. Quacunq; occasione Christum annunciari expedit: Philip. 1. Et per hos alia obscurè, ut per parabolas, per gestus, & actiones quasdá umbraticas sunt propositaalia clare & manifeste verbis & rebus ipsis. Sic enim conueniebat multifariá & multis modis ista fieri, quia captus nostèr aliter diuina mysteria assequi non poterat. Sicut itaq; praeceptores interdum unam eandemq; rem varijs modis declarat explicantq;, ut rudes animi intelligant: ita Deus quoq; cum Patribus multifariam multisq; modis egit. Sed certissima & frequentissima testimonia de voluntate Dei in vetere lege, exhibita sunt per prophetas, ut hic ipse ait.
units.tr: Moreover, that God has spoken in various ways through subject creatures is easy to gather from the sacred letters. He appeared to and spoke with Abraham through angels clothed in human form under the oak of Mamre; to Moses in the bush and in the fire; at other times in a cloud, just as in the Gospel a voice was heard from the cloud, "This is my beloved Son." He spoke with Joshua in the image of a soldier. To others, such as the prophets, he showed visible forms of various things, the meaning of which he made known to them by an inner inspiration; hence the prophets are also called seers, and at the beginning of their discourses it is customary to put "the vision of Isaiah," and then "Thus says the Lord." Sometimes he sent dreams, as to Samuel and to others who foretold future things. Likewise he taught holy men about his will through works and various deeds by which Christ was prefigured, according to 1 Corinthians 10: "All these things happened to them in figure." Finally, by other kinds of means he instructed holy men about his will, and used them as instruments to make known to others also what needed to be done or known. Indeed he also at times spoke through those instruments which we would think unfit, as through the ass of Balaam, and through the wicked high priest Caiaphas. So little does it matter through whom the truth is put forward, provided it is clear that it comes from the Lord to us. Christ is to be proclaimed on whatever occasion is useful, Philippians 1. And some things were set forth obscurely, as through parables, gestures and shadowy actions; others clearly and plainly in words and in the things themselves. For it was fitting that these things be done in many parts and in many ways, because our capacity could not otherwise grasp divine mysteries. Just as teachers sometimes explain and declare one and the same thing in various ways, so that untrained minds may understand, so God also dealt with the fathers in many parts and in many ways. But the most certain and most frequent testimonies of God's will under the old law were given through the prophets, as the text itself says here.

units.la: Per prophetas: Obiter notandum, graecè haberi, ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, hebraica loquendi forma in prophetis, atq; etiam in filio: Sed quod etiam Chrysostomus annotauit, in pro per posito est. Prophetas autem accipimus in genere, quibus praeceteris hominibus Deus voluntatem suam aperuit. alijs per eosdem exponendam: Ita ipsum Enoch, Noah, Abrahamum, inter pro phetas collocabimus. Etiamsi plerunq; illis competit appellatio prophetarum, qui diuinorū
units.tr: Through the prophets: It should be noted in passing that the Greek reads in the prophets [ἐν τοῖς προφήταις], a Hebrew form of expression, and likewise in the Son. But, as Chrysostom also observed, the preposition here stands for "through." We take the term "prophets" in a general sense, for those to whom God made known his will above other men, so that they might set it forth to others. In this way we shall count Enoch, Noah and Abraham among the prophets, although the title of prophet usually belongs to those who stood out among the people by interpreting the divine oracles. Of such prophets there were also schools, as in 1 Kings 10 at Bethel and elsewhere.

units.la: oraculorum interpretatione ad populū præeminebant, qualium prophetarū instituebantur etiam collegia, 1. Reg. 10. in Bethel &c. Inter quos semper erant aliqui insignes, spiritu divino afflati, per quos Deus populum suum electum certum de voluntate sua faceret. Neq; unquam fuit populus Iudaicus talibus in totum destitutus, ita ut hac maxime gloria semper superbiret, quòd præ omnibus aliis nationibus viros habuerit, quibus oracula Dei essent concredita: quibus præterea facultas prædicendi futura esset concessa. Sic commemorantur & in Novo Testamento prophetæ quidam, ut Agabus, & filiæ Philippi, Actor. 21. Item Paulus, item Ioānes autor libri Apocalypseos. Sed tamē hoc peculiare fuit Iudæis, ut omni tempore aliquos & insignes haberent, aut si quando terra sine propheta existens, deploratur, ut Psal. 73. Daniel. 9. Ibi ita dicitur, vel ad significandum iram Dei, qua vellet illis Prophetas adimere: vel de cessatione prophetiæ post revelatum euangelium est vaticinium. Itaq; ex prophetis Iudæi magnam gloriam sibi captabant, & semper aliquos Deus dedit illi populo, quia nunquam voluit omittere, quod ad illorum salutem expediens iudicaret. Hoc erat ergo egregiū bonitatis diuinæ testimonium, quòd prophetas omni tempore ad populum suum mitteret. Et tot testiū taliumq; dignitas ad confirmandam religionē Iudęorum, imò nostram hodie, de qua omnes illi prophetarunt, non parū facit. Nam ipsi de euangelio vaticinati sunt omnia. Vnde Rom. 1. dicitur illud à Deo patre promissum fuisse per Prophetas. Et de Christo Act. 10. Huic omnes prophetæ testimonium ferunt. Et Christus hic expo-suit ex lege & prophetis omnia de se testimonia.
units.tr: Among these there were always some outstanding men, inspired by the divine Spirit, through whom God would give his chosen people certain knowledge of his will. The Jewish people was never wholly without such men, so that it could always boast of this above all, that it had been given men to whom the oracles of God were entrusted, before all other nations, and to whom the power of foretelling the future had been granted. So in the New Testament too certain prophets are mentioned, such as Agabus and the daughters of Philip (Acts 21), and also Paul, and John the author of the Apocalypse. But it was peculiar to the Jews that they always had some outstanding men, and when the land was lamented as existing without a prophet, as in Psalm 74 and Daniel 9, this either signifies the wrath of God, by which he willed to take the prophets from them, or it is a prophecy of the cessation of prophecy after the gospel was revealed. So the Jews prided themselves greatly on their prophets, and God always gave them such men, because he never willed to omit what he judged useful for their salvation. This was therefore a remarkable testimony of divine goodness, that he sent prophets to his people at all times. And the dignity of such witnesses contributes no little to confirming the religion of the Jews, and indeed our own today, of which all those prophets spoke. For they prophesied of the gospel in every detail. Hence Romans 1 says that this was promised by God the Father through the prophets. And of Christ, Acts 10: to him all the prophets bear witness. And Christ himself set forth from the law and the prophets all the testimonies concerning himself.

units.la: Patribus) patres uno nomine non tantum patriarchas illos, Abrahamum, Isaacum, Iacobū, quorū solet Iudæi se filios gloriari, vt habetur in euangelio: sed omnes, qui tempora reuelati euangelij antecesserunt, quibus datum fuit prophetas audire concionantes, & de Christo aliis rebus vaticinantes. Vnde illud Actor. 13. Annūciamus, quod eam repromissionem, quæ ad patres facta est, Deus adimpleuit filijs illorum, nimirum vobis. Luc. 1. Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, &c. Apparet autem singulari prudentia ab Apostolo esse factum, quòd statim voluerit patrum & prophetarū mentionem facere. Cum his enim maximè semper gloriati sint Iudæi, redditi sunt hoc pacto attentiores, & præterea æquiores aliquomodo ad audiendū, quid Apostolus instituat. Quamuis ita fit eorū mentio, ut collatione facta ostendatur Christi atq; euangelij præ illis & lege excellentia.
units.tr: To the fathers: By the one name "fathers" are meant not only those patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, of whom the Jews are wont to boast themselves sons, as the gospel relates, but all who came before the time of the revealed gospel, to whom it was given to hear the prophets preaching and prophesying of Christ and other things. Hence Acts 13: "We announce to you that the promise made to the fathers, God has fulfilled to their children, that is, to you." Luke 1: "As he spoke to our fathers," and so on. It is plain that the Apostle acted with singular prudence in mentioning the fathers and the prophets at once. For the Jews had always boasted most of these, and so they were made more attentive and in some measure more willing to hear what the Apostle would set forth. Yet their mention is made in such a way that, by comparison, the excellence of Christ and of the gospel above them and the law is shown.

units.la: Extremis hisce diebus) Quibus videlicet euangelium iam revelatum est, neq; alia doctrina vel lege præstantior expectari debet, quibus omnia consummata sunt, quæ Sancti vates de Christi aduentu in mundū cecinēre. De quibus locutus est Esaias cap. 2. Erit in nouissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini in uertice montium reuelabitur super colles, & fluent ad eum omnes gentes, &c. Apostolus ad Galat. 4. vocat nouissimos dies plenitudine temporis, siue tempus adimpletū. Itaq; extremi hi dies opponuntur particulæ: Olim, significantq; tempus reuelati euangelij. Ne quis hic garriendum sibi putet de extremo die Domini, quo venturus est ad iudicandū. Chrysostomus, & eum secutus Theophylactus notant, consolatorium hoc esse, & gratum auribus, quòd vocat nouissimos dies. Qui enim tum grauiter affligebantur, penèq; tædium vitæ conceperant, ij audiendo ad extremum & finem iam peruentum, & respirare, & vires resumere poterant. Vel nouissimis diebus, id est, cum nihil restaret spei de auxilio, vel emendatione, cum iam conclamata & desperata viderentur omnia, nos consolationem præter spē accepimus.
units.tr: In these last days: that is, in which the gospel has now been revealed, and no doctrine or law more excellent should be expected, in which all things have been accomplished that the holy seers sang concerning the coming of Christ into the world. Of these Isaiah spoke in chapter 2: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it," and so on. The Apostle in Galatians 4 calls these the last days the fullness of time, or the time fulfilled. So these last days are set against the word "of old," and signify the time of the revealed gospel. Let no one think he must here prattle about the last day of the Lord, on which he will come to judge. Chrysostom, and Theophylact following him, note that this is consoling and pleasant to the ear, because he says "last days." For those who were then grievously afflicted, and had almost conceived weariness of life, could on hearing this breathe again and recover their strength, since the end and limit had now been reached. Either "in the last days" means that when no hope of help or amendment remained, and all things seemed given up and desperate, we received consolation beyond hope.

units.la: Locutus est nobis) cùm nos dicit, se quoq; reliquis pijs humilitate animi annumerat, omnes credentes sibi æquos et pares constitues: cum tamē ad Apostolos proprie Christus locutus fit: apostoli deinde ad reliquos verba Christi protulerunt. Sed id consolatorium est, quòd omnibus nobis Christum locutum dicit, siue Deum patrem.
units.tr: He has spoken to us: In saying "us," he also counts himself among the other godly, in humility of mind, making all believers equal and alike to himself. Yet it was properly to the Apostles that Christ spoke, and the Apostles afterwards delivered the words of Christ to the rest. But this is consoling, that he says Christ, or God the Father, has spoken to all of us.

units.la: Per filium) Quare non dicit simpliciter, nouissimis diebus hisce locutus est nobis ipse filius, sicut & simplex enunciatio propositionis videbatur poscere, sed dicit, Deum locutū nobis per filiū. Respondet Chrysostomus, quòd quia tenerę erant adhuc aures, & infirmi animi Iudæorum, nec satis ferebant, quæ de Christo apertius dicebantur, eòq; prudenti modestia temperat orationem, ac dicit, Deum locutum per filium. Est autem quædam Antonomasia in uoce filij, ita ut tamen si non addatur, suum, tamen manifestè intelligi conueniat, de filio Dei vocem filij accipiendā, Ioan. 1. vnigenitus qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarrauit. Quinetiā appellatione filij oportet Deum, seu diuinam naturam, secundam quam filius patri consubstantialis est, & per omnia æqualis intelligere, id quod ipse etiā valde prudeter docet verbis sequentibus. Locutus est quidem pater per filium humana natura indutum tanquam per instrumentū, sicut etiam locutus est per prophetas: Sed hic filius non tantum fuit instrumentū sicut prophetæ, sed præterea verus Deus. Neq; alias proprie filius Dei diceretur, nisi eiusdem esset cum patre naturæ: Id quod ipsi quoq; Iudæi satis intelligebant, qui hoc pro maximo crimine ausi sunt obijcere, quòd Christus dixisset se filiū Dei. Est itaq; hæc propositio totius disputationis, quòd Christus, per quem extremis hisce diebus reuelatum est euangelium, sit filius Dei, & verus Deus: sed per contentionem illustrior multò reddita: atq; id, ut euangelij prestantia præ lege, ac nostra fœlicitas præ coditione patrũ clarius elucesceret. Nos, inquit Chrysostomus in hoc superiores existimus, & multò amplius fumus consecuti, quòd nobis quidem locutus est ipse Dominus, illis autem tantùm serui & conserui, nempe prophetæ vel angeli. Ac multum facit ad authoritatem parandam Sermoni ipsius loquentis dignitas. Quis dixit hoc? Istud dixit seruus, illud verò ipse Dominus. Ergo hunc potius audiemus, quàm illum. Sic igitur euangelium legi debet anteponi.
units.tr: Through the Son: Why does he not simply say, "in these last days the Son himself has spoken to us," as the plain structure of the sentence seemed to require, but says that God spoke to us through the Son? Chrysostom answers that, because the ears of the Jews were still tender and their minds weak, and they could not well bear what was said more plainly about Christ, he therefore tempers his speech with prudent moderation, and says that God spoke through the Son. Now there is a certain antonomasia in the word "Son," so that, although the word "his" is not added, it is nonetheless plainly to be understood, and the word "Son" is to be taken of the Son of God, as in John 1: "The only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared." Indeed, by the appellation of Son we must understand God, or the divine nature, according to which the Son is consubstantial with the Father and equal in all things, which he himself also teaches most wisely in the following words. The Father indeed spoke through the Son, clothed in human nature, as through an instrument, just as he also spoke through the prophets. But this Son was not merely an instrument like the prophets, but moreover true God. Otherwise he would not properly be called the Son of God unless he were of the same nature as the Father, which the Jews themselves also understood well enough, who dared to object as the greatest crime that Christ had said he was the Son of God. So this is the proposition of the whole discussion: that Christ, through whom the gospel has been revealed in these last days, is the Son of God and true God. This is made much clearer by contrast, and the aim is that the excellence of the gospel above the law, and our happiness above the condition of the fathers, may shine more clearly. "We," says Chrysostom, "are superior in this, and have obtained far more, because the Lord himself has spoken to us, but to them only servants and fellow-servants, that is, prophets or angels." And the dignity of the speaker contributes much to giving authority to the sermon. "Who said this? A servant said that, but the Lord himself said this. Therefore we should rather hear him than that one." So the gospel ought to be set above the law in this way.

units.la: Cæterùm habemus in Scripturis locos aliquot, quibus fere eadem quæ hic, dicuntur. Quòd Deus olim multifariam multisq; modis locutus sit patribus. Osea 12. Locutus sum super prophetas, & ego visionem multiplicaui, & in manu prophetarum assimilatus sum. Sic Ieremiæ 7. Et misi ad vos omnes seruos meos prophetas, per diem, consurgens diluculo, & mittens: & non audierunt me. Item Matth. 20. de operarijs misisis per diuersas horas in vineam æquale præmium recipientibus. Locutū autem nobis nunc per filium: Ioan. 1. vnigenitus, qui est in sinu patris ipse enarrauit. Sed expressissimè hæc redduntur omnia in parabola Matth. 21. vbi pater familias post missos diuersos seruos ad cultores vineæ, tandem misit proprium filium, qui tamen ab eis interfectus est.
units.tr: Moreover, we have in the Scriptures several passages in which nearly the same things are said as here: that God formerly spoke to the fathers in many parts and in many ways. Hosea 12: "I have spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and by the hand of the prophets I have been likened." So Jeremiah 7: "And I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending daily, but they did not hear me." Likewise Matthew 20, of the workers sent at different hours into the vineyard, who all receive the same reward. But that he has now spoken to us through the Son is stated in John 1: "The only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared." Yet all these things are set forth most clearly in the parable of Matthew 21, where the householder, after sending various servants to the vinedressers, at last sent his own son, who nevertheless was killed by them.

units.la: Iam verò eliciendum est nobis hinc, si quid ad consolationem vel doctrinam conscientiarum pertinens, sit in his verbis inclusum. Primùm itaq; illud valde consolatorium est, & diuinæ erga nos bonitatis testimonium amplissimum, quòd Deus loqui dignatus sit nobis per suum filium. Multum erat, quod Iudæi habuerunt prophetas, qui, sicut 1.Pet. 1. dicitur, Spiritu sancto afflati fuerunt, & Dei voluntatem manifestarunt hominib. Sed cum illi ipsi Deũ nunquá viderint, fumus nos multò illis fœliciores, qui in Christo Deum vidimus, & multò perfectissimè agnouimus. Imò cùm Christus semper sit nobiscũ, & manebit etiam usq; ad consummationẽ seculi: Christus adhuc in sacro euangelio, quoties id legimus vel audimus, etiam per occultas & internas inspirationes nobis loquitur. Quo fit etiam, ut quando patres, qui solos habebant prophetas, nihilominus crediderint loquenti per prophetas, multò iustius est nos credamus loquenti per filium unigenitum. Illi habuerunt ministros loquentes, nos autem ipsum filium: Quid si illi audire potuissent ipsum filium? Væ igitur nobis, si fidem Christo non adhibeamus. Facit & istud ad ostendendũ dignitatem euangelij præ lege, & ad confirmandos animos, ut euangelio credant. Quantò enim præstantius est & certius, quod quis audit ab ipso summo præceptore, quàm quod traditur ab eius discipulis: & quantò magis ratum est, quod filius facit in familia, quàm quod seruus: tantò etiam certior est & pluris æstimada doctrina, quam attulit ipse Christus, quàm quod Moses, vel ulli deniq; prophetæ unquá prodiderunt.
units.tr: Now we may draw from these words whatever they contain that pertains to the comfort and instruction of consciences. First, it is very comforting and a most ample witness of God's goodness toward us that God has deigned to speak to us through his Son. The Jews had much in having prophets, who, as 1 Peter 1 says, were moved by the Holy Spirit and made the will of God known to men. But since they themselves never saw God, we are far more fortunate than they, for we have seen God in Christ and have come to know him far more fully. Indeed, since Christ is always with us and will remain even to the end of the age, Christ still speaks to us in the holy gospel, through hidden and inward inspirations, whenever we read or hear it. It follows that if the fathers, who had only the prophets, nevertheless believed the one speaking through the prophets, we ought with much greater justice to believe the one speaking through the only-begotten Son. They had ministers who spoke; we have the Son himself. What if they had been able to hear the Son himself? Woe to us, then, if we do not give faith to Christ. This also serves to show the dignity of the gospel above the law, and to strengthen minds to believe the gospel. For the more excellent and certain it is that someone hears from the highest teacher himself than what is handed down by his disciples, and the more firmly established what the son does in the household than what the servant does, so much more certain and worth esteeming is the teaching that Christ himself brought than anything Moses or any prophet at all ever set forth.

units.la: Tertiò, hoc habemus præsenti loco, tempus reuelati euangelij nouissimũ esse tépus, neq; esse amplius, ut Iudæi infœlices sperant, Mesiam per prophetas patrib. promissum expectandum, neq; etiam expectandum, ut aliud euangelium doceatur, quàm hactenus per vnigenitũ patris Christum ipsum nobis est reuelatum. Falsum enim est, quòd quidà tempus præcedens euangelium ita tribuerunt patri, tempus euangelij filio, quasi tertiũ restaret tempus expectandum, in quo manifestaretur præcipuè potestas spiritus Sancti, quomodo Montanus & Priscilla, (ut habet Augustinus libro contra Faustum) dixerunt, Apostolos nondum accepisse spiritum Sanctum, sed se primos accepisse spiritũ Sanctũ, & tum adfuisse tertium tempus succedens euangelio. Quos confutare non admodum difficile est, tum ex verbis, quibus Christus promisit, post paucos dies à discessu suo mittendũ Spiritum sanctũ, iussitq; ideo manere simul: tum ex his, quæ habetur in Actis Apostolicis, non solùm de Spiritus Sancti missione, sed etiam de signis & præclaris operibus, quæ Apostoli spiritus Sancti virtute perfecerunt.
units.tr: Third, in this passage we have that the time of the revealed gospel is the last time, and that it is no longer to be awaited, as the unhappy Jews hope, that the Messiah promised to the fathers through the prophets will come, nor is it to be awaited that some other gospel will be taught, beyond what has hitherto been revealed to us by Christ himself, the only-begotten of the Father. For it is false that some have assigned the time before the gospel to the Father, and the time of the gospel to the Son, as if a third time remained to be expected, in which the power of the Holy Spirit would be manifested especially. So Montanus and Priscilla said (as Augustine has it in his book against Faustus), that the apostles had not yet received the Holy Spirit, but that they themselves were the first to receive the Holy Spirit, and that then the third time, succeeding the gospel, had arrived. These are not very difficult to refute, both from the words in which Christ promised that the Holy Spirit would be sent a few days after his departure, and therefore bade them remain together, and from what is found in the Acts of the Apostles, not only about the sending of the Holy Spirit but also about the signs and remarkable works that the apostles performed by the power of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Et Mahometes hac ratione decepit orbẽ, quòd diceret, suâ legẽ esse tertiâ & postremâ & consummatissimam, & æternam, per quam abrogaretur Euangelium Christi, sicut peristud abrogata esset lex Mosi.
units.tr: Mahomet also deceived the world by this reasoning, that his law was the third, the last and most perfect, and eternal, by which the gospel of Christ would be abrogated, just as the law of Moses had been abrogated by it.

units.la: Quartò habemus, quòd tam vetus testamentum, quàm nouum ab eodem Deo sit profectum, licet per diuersas personas manifestatum. Qua de re contra Manichæos copiosè disputat Augustinus, quem vide libro de vera Religione cap. 17. Item contra ad uersarium legis & prophetarum, item Antinomos, libro primo. Sed & Ephes. 2. Quoniâ perillum aditum habemus utrique in uno Spiritu ad patrem. Roman. 3. An Iudeorum Deus tantùm? Nõne & gentium? Et huius epistolæ cap. 8. pater promittit nouum testamentum. Ipse Deus semper idem & immutabilis est: Et vetus testamentum typus fuit & figura noui: Et in vtroq; Christus notus, (Ioan. 8. Abraham vidit diem meum) sed in nouo
units.tr: Fourth, we have that the Old Testament as well as the New has proceeded from the same God, although made known through different persons. Augustine disputes at length on this point against the Manichaeans, which you may see in his book on True Religion, chapter 17. Likewise against the adversary of the law and the prophets, and likewise against the Antinomians, in the first book. See also Ephesians 2: "For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father." Romans 3: "Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles?" And in chapter 8 of this epistle the Father promises a new covenant. God himself is always the same and unchangeable; and the Old Testament was a type and figure of the New; and in both Christ is known (John 8: "Abraham saw my day"), but in the New more clearly.

units.la: Nouum testamentum. Deus unus vtriusq; testamenti autor.
units.tr: The New Testament. God is the one author of both testaments.

units.la: nouo clarius. Alia autem præcepta data, non quòd Deus mutet sententiam, sed quòd hominum conditio requirebat mutationem: sicut pro conditione ægrotorum, diuersa medicamina præscribit, & præbet vnus idemq; medicus.
units.tr: more clearly in the New. Other precepts were given, not because God changes his judgment, but because the condition of men required a change; just as one and the same physician prescribes different remedies according to the condition of the sick, and yet remains the same physician.

units.la: Quem constituit hæredem omnium, per quem etiam secula condidit, qui cùm sit splendor gloriæ, & expressa imago substantiæ illius, moderaturq; omni verbo potentiæ suæ, per semetipsum purgatione facta peccatorum nostrorum, consedit in dextera maiestatis in excelsis.
units.tr: Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds; who, being the brightness of his glory and the express image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.

units.la: Expositio imò & expositio propositionis, in qua statim per cogeriem ea enumerat, è quibus Christum esse natura Deum, & per omnia Patri æqualem, clarissimè potest intelligi. Sicut ex signis & miraculis mouebantur homines ad dicendum: Nisi hic homo esset à Deo, no posset hæc signa facere: Et, verè filius Dei erat iste. Ita quæ hic attribuuntur, palàm arguunt, Christū filium esse Dei. Nam effectus & ea, quæ diuinæ tantùm potentiæ sunt propria, colligit, ut tantundem significet, ac si simpliciter diceretur, Christum filium esse Dei, & verum naturā Deum. Voluit autem pluribus verbis, & maximarum rerum commemoratione istud explicare, non solùm quia in more ei est, quoties occasio incidit, Christum amplis titulis celebrare: sed quia præsentis disputationis (in qua, Christum esse verum Deum, probare instituit) exordio iudicabat maximè conuenire. Quare non est quòd quisquam ista putet parui momenti esse, quia videlicet statim ipsi propositioni sunt annexa, quasi loco minus apto: deinde quia nullis adhuc sacræ Scripturæ locis sunt apud auditores probata. Sanè responsum volumus huiusmodi cauillum mouenti, valde oportunè hæc in exordio esse ita proposita, non solùm ut admiratione tantarum rerum redderentur omnes attentiores, sed ut forti & animosa assertione mouerentur eo magis ad assentiendum: nec non ut expectatione argumentorum quæ ad illa comprobanda adferri debebant, tota reliqua oratione redderentur magis attenti. Atq; erant haud dubiè omnia hæc de dignitate Christi sæpius proposita apud eos ac disputata, & pijs abunde nota. Deinde eadem in confirmatione sequenti non obscurè probantur, quando validissimis Sacrarum literarum argumentis, diuinitatem Christo competere, declaratur. Qua enim opera quis probat, esse Deum, eadem confirmat & hæc omnia Christo competere: sicut qui hæc Christo tribuit, idem Christum esse Deum profitetur. Quanquam nos etiam hoc loco in expositione partium, testimonia Scripturarum proferre haud grauabimur, quibus palàm fiet, omnia, quæ hic dicuntur, Christo recte tribui.
units.tr: The exposition, indeed, the exposition of the proposition, in which at once, through the enumeration of the things he lists, it can be most clearly understood that Christ is God by nature and equal to the Father in all things. Just as from the signs and miracles men were moved to say: "Unless this man were from God, he could not do these signs," and "Truly this man was the Son of God." So the things attributed here plainly prove that Christ is the Son of God. For he gathers together the effects and the things that belong to divine power alone, so as to signify as much as if it were said simply that Christ is the Son of God and truly God by nature. He chose, however, to explain this in more words and by recounting the greatest things, not only because it is his custom, whenever the occasion arises, to celebrate Christ with ample titles, but because he judged it most fitting for the beginning of the present disputation, in which he has undertaken to prove that Christ is true God. Wherefore no one should think these things of little weight because they are attached at once to the proposition itself, as if in an unsuitable place, and then because they are not yet proved to the hearers by any passages of Holy Scripture. Indeed, we wish to answer one who raises such a quibble that it was very fitting to set these things forth thus at the beginning, not only so that all would be more attentive through admiration of such great matters, but so that they would be moved all the more to assent by a bold and spirited assertion, and so that the whole remaining discourse would make them more attentive in expectation of the arguments that had to be brought to confirm those things. And undoubtedly all these things about the dignity of Christ had been often set forth and disputed among them, and were abundantly known to the godly. Then in the following confirmation the same things are not obscurely proved, when by the most powerful arguments of the Sacred Scriptures it is declared that divinity belongs to Christ. For whoever proves by works that someone is God, by the same confirms that all these things belong to Christ; just as whoever ascribes these things to Christ professes at the same time that Christ is God. Nevertheless, in this place too, in the exposition of the parts, we will not be reluctant to bring forward testimonies of Scripture, by which it will be made plain that all the things said here are rightly ascribed to Christ.

units.la: Quem constituit hæredem omnium) Dixerat Christum filium Dei. Ne ergo putetur eo tantum pacto filius Dei, quo cæteri quoq; homines voluntatem Dei facientes, id est, credentes dicuntur generatim filij Dei: attexit iam diuersas particulas, quæ dare significant, eum esse natura filium Dei, patri per omnia parem & æqualem. Alia enim ratione Christus filius Dei est, nempe natura: alia verò ratione nos sumus filij Dei, nempe adoptione tantū, qua de re Roman.8. Quicūq; spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filij Dei: non enim accepistis Spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba pater. Idé spiritus testatur unà cum spiritu nostro, quod sumus filij Dei. Prima autem ratio, qua significat Christum esse natura Deum, hæc est. Quem constituit hæredem omnium: Fluit hæc ratio ex præcedenti appellatione filij, estq; petita ex iure humano naturali & diuino. filius enim succedit patri, & hæreditatem accipit plerunq; ius in omnia bona paterna: qua de re apud Iureconsultos plurima. Vnde & Apostolus ad Galat. 4. hac argumentandi forma utitur. Itaq; iam non est seruus, sed filius: Si filius, ergo & hæres per Christum. Itaq; qua ratione Christus dicitur filius Dei, eadem dicitur & hæres Dei. Nomineq; hæredis clarè significatur, quòd Christus in omnia illa habeat potestatem, in quæ potestatem habet pater: sicut filius vnicus hæres succedit secundum ius ciuile, in omnib. bonis paternis, & dominus fit rerum omnium, quarum dominus fuit ipse pater. Non quidem prorsus, ut in rebus humanis fit, filius succedit cum detrimento patris, & morte patris: sed hic æterno patri coæternus et coæqualis filius: sicut naturâ ac diuinitatem habet cum patre communem, & unam: ita gloriam, potentiam, honorem, dignitatem, opera, electos, & omnia huiusmodi cum patre habet paria. Nec patri decedit: nec filio quicquā nouì in tempore accedit. Et sicut Christus alia ratione est filius Dei, quàm nos dicimus filij Dei: ita alia ratione & alio iure accipit ille hæreditatem Dei patris, quàm nos. Ipse enim superat nos, quia naturalis filius, & quia primogenitus. Sic Roma.8.ipse dicitur primogenitus ex multis fratribus: & Colossens. 1. primogenitus ex mortuis: Et Matth.21. in parabola euangelica, hic est, inquiunt latrones, hæres, occidamus eum. Ius igitur primogeniturae illi debetur à natura, ubi nos tantū per gratiā accipimus adoptionem in filios. Ideoq; significatur, & cum emphasi etiam additum est, hærede esse omnium, ut simpliciter intelligatur, nihil esse usquam in potestate patris, quod non item sit in potestate filij. Omnium videlicet hæres est, non tantùm habens Iudæos pro suis, sicut antea soli Iudæi erant populus Dei, sed omnes habens tàm gentiles, quàm Iudæos. Vel omnium, cœli, inquam, & terræ, seculorum, & quicquid unquam fuit conditum. Itidem significanter dicitur, Quem constituit. Notatur enim, ipsius patris voluntate factum esse omnium rerum dominum, ita ut patri nihil decedat ex dignitate Christi, neq; is iniuste quicquam acceperit. Philippens. 1. cum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam arbitratus est, ut esset æqualis Deo, sed semetipsum inaniuit, forma serui accepta, &c. Quapropter & Deus illum in summa extulit sublimi-tatem. Absolon quidem volebat succedere in regnû Patris violenter, non expectans, ut ipse à patre hæres constitueretur & ordinaretur: ac fuit tandem cōstitutus rex à Dauide modestus & pacificus Solomon. Ita Christus quoq; non occupauit regnû, patre non ita ordinante, sicut sibi vendicare volunt summam potestatem & regnum multi pseudo-Christi: sed ipse à Deo patre est constitutus hæres omnium, legitimè ac iustè habens omnium potestatem. A Patre ergo constitutus est, non à se ipso, vel à nobis: ac proinde, cùm vo-luntas patris fit, nos eum pro tali debemus agnoscere. Oecolàpadius. Quem constituit id est, præfiniuit etiam ante rerum initia. Iam uerò testimonia, quæ confirmant, Christû esse hæredem omnium, & parem per omnia cum patre habere potestatem, passim in Scripturis sunt obuia. Daniel. 7. Dedit ei potestatem, & honorem, & regnum, & omnes populi, tribus, & linguæ seruiet ei, potestas eius potestas æterna est, quæ non auferetur, & regnum eius, quod non corrumpetur. Agit de antiquo dierum, cui oblatus erat filius hominis, quo nomine appellatur etiam Christus. Psal. 2. Postula à me, & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terræ. Matth 28. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Matth. 10. Omnia mihi tradita sunt à patre meo. Ioan. 17. Et mea omnia tua sunt, & tua mea sunt, & glorificatus sum in eis. Ex quibus sanè locis par filij potestas cum potestate patris, contra Arrianos & Nestorianos manifeste colligitur. Cæterùm cùm hoc pacto Christus hæres omnium prædicatur, intelligendum est, etiam secundum humanam naturam dignitate hanc ei competere, quam etiam Deus dignatus est hoc honore, propterea quod diuinitati coniuncta fit. Cùm enim Christo secundum diuinitatem omnis gloria & potestas semper competiuerit, tum verò eidem ut homini eadem accessit & donata est. Nam de eo ut homine dictum est illud Psal. 8. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Et ipse de se ut homine etiam post deuictam mortem & diabolum & mundum, ait, sibi datam omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra. Rursus Iudicium dedit ei facere, quia filius hominis est. Hic agetur de communicatione Idiomatum, &c.
units.tr: Whom he appointed heir of all things) He had said that Christ is the Son of God. So that no one thinks he is Son of God only in the way that all other men who do God's will, that is, who believe, are generally called sons of God, he now adds several phrases that show he is by nature the Son of God, equal and co-equal with the Father in all things. Christ is the Son of God in one way, namely by nature; we are sons of God in another way, namely by adoption alone, as Romans 8 says: "As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but ye have received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit beareth witness with our spirit that we are the sons of God." The first reason, showing that Christ is God by nature, is this: "whom he appointed heir of all things." This reason flows from the preceding title of Son and is drawn from natural and divine law as well as human law. For a son succeeds his father as heir and generally receives the right to all his father's goods, a matter treated at length by the jurists. Hence the Apostle also uses this form of argument in Galatians 4: "So then thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir through Christ." So in the same way that Christ is called Son of God, he is called heir of God. By the word heir it is clearly signified that Christ has power over all those things over which the Father has power, just as the only son succeeds by civil law to all his father's goods and becomes lord of all the things of which the father himself was lord. Not, of course, altogether as happens in human affairs, where the son succeeds to the loss and death of the father; rather, the Son is co-eternal and co-equal with the eternal Father, and just as he has with the Father one common and single nature and divinity, so he has with the Father equal glory, power, honour, dignity, works, elect, and all such things. Nothing passes away from the Father, and nothing new comes to the Son in time. And just as Christ is Son of God in a different way from how we are called sons of God, so he receives the inheritance of God the Father by a different way and a different right from us. For he surpasses us, because he is the natural Son, and because he is the firstborn. So Romans 8 calls him the firstborn among many brethren, and Colossians 1 the firstborn from the dead, and in the parable of Matthew 21 the wicked husbandmen say, "This is the heir; come, let us kill him." The right of firstborn is therefore owed to him by nature, whereas we receive adoption as sons only through grace. Therefore it is signified, and with emphasis it is added, that he is heir of all things, so that it is simply understood that nothing anywhere is in the Father's power which is not likewise in the Son's power. He is heir of all, that is, not only holding the Jews as his own, as before the Jews alone were the people of God, but holding Gentiles as well as Jews. Or of all things: of heaven and earth, I say, of the ages, and of whatever has ever been created. Likewise the phrase "whom he appointed" is significant. For it is noted that he became lord of all things by the will of the Father himself, so that nothing of Christ's dignity is taken from the Father, nor has he unjustly received anything. Philippians 2: "Being in the form of God, he did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him." Absalom indeed wanted to succeed to his father's kingdom by violence, not waiting for his father to appoint and ordain him heir; in the end, however, Solomon, meek and peaceful, was made king by David. So Christ too did not seize the kingdom while the Father was not appointing him, as many pseudo-Christs want to claim for themselves supreme power and kingdom; rather he was appointed heir of all things by God the Father, lawfully and justly possessing the power of all things. He was therefore appointed by the Father, not by himself or by us; and so, since it is the will of the Father, we ought to acknowledge him as such. Oecolampadius: "Whom he appointed," that is, he also predestined before the beginning of things. Now the testimonies which confirm that Christ is heir of all and has power equal in all respects to the Father's are found everywhere in the Scriptures. Daniel 7: "He gave him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, and all people, nations, and languages shall serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed." This speaks of the Ancient of days, before whom the Son of man was brought, a name by which Christ too is called. Psalm 2: "Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession." Matthew 28: "All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth." Matthew 11: "All things are delivered unto me of my Father." John 17: "And all mine are thine, and thine are mine, and I am glorified in them." From these passages the equal power of the Son with the power of the Father is plainly deduced, against the Arians and Nestorians. Moreover, since Christ is proclaimed heir of all in this way, it must be understood that this dignity belongs to him also according to his human nature, which God has deigned to bestow upon him with this honour, because it is joined to his divinity. For since all glory and power have always belonged to Christ according to his divinity, so also the same has come to him and been given to him as man. For of him as man Psalm 8 says, "Thou hast put all things under his feet." And he himself, speaking of himself as man, even after overcoming death, the devil, and the world, says that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him. Again, "He hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man." Here there will be discussion of the communication of properties, etc.

units.la: Per quem etiam secula condidit) Alia ratio, qua exprimit, Christû natura Deum, ab eo, quòd non fit creatura, sed creator. Estq; sententia: Christû eiusdé esse potestatis, & semper fuisse cum Patre: non esse creatum, sed creantem, & per se & in se subsistere: ac proinde non nouam iam primùm potestatem accipere, quando constitutus est hæres omnium, sed ab æterno etiam habuisse communem in prima rerum conditione.
units.tr: Through whom also he made the worlds) Another reason which expresses that Christ is God by nature, drawn from the fact that he is not a creature but the Creator. The sense is this: Christ has the same power and has always been with the Father; he was not created but is the creator, and subsists both through himself and in himself; and therefore he did not then for the first time receive a new power when he was appointed heir of all things, but had from eternity a common power in the first creation of things.

units.la: Per quem) Emphasis. Nam patrem cõdidisse omnia, id certò constabat, & ab omnibus concedebatur: sed quòd is per filium, quasi collegam aut cooperantem, fecisset, id verò nò proinde erat perspicuum. Itaq; dicitur, non qui pater, non item qui filius condiderit, sed quod pater per filium condiderit omnia: atq; ita manet patri sua dignitas, quòd uidelicet omnia cõdiderit: & nihilominus accedit eadé dignitas ipsi filio, quòd pater per eū omnia condiderit. Qua locutionis forma personæ discretæ euidenter ostenduntur, & nihilominus essentiæ vnitas, par natura & potestas. Alius qui facit, alius per quem quid fit, & nihilominus aliud non sunt, et actio est communis. Pater Deus est, et Christus Deus est, ideoq; unum sunt: agit pater, agitq; filius: nec ille quidem per hunc quasi inferiorem, aut quasi instrumentum, sed velut sine hoc non facturus. Quibus eadem volūtas, eadé potestas, atq; adeò quidé par & æqualis, ut actio uniius sine actione alterius perfici non intelligatur. Hoc igitur pacto pater per filium agit, non quasi per inferiorem, sed sicut sæpè etiam inter homines, consul agit per aliû consulem sibi parè, cùm alter si-ne altero quodámodo nihil posset, & utriusq; par auctoritas habetur, & utriusq; volûtas & auctoritas ad statuendû aliquid requiritur. Neq; enim homines tàtûm agere dicuntur per inferiores, sed etiam per pares, nonnunquàm & per superiores: sicut quis per magistratû coercet suum aduersarium. Excerpi quidem potest ex hac forma loquedi, filium à Patre procedere, non tamen filium patre inferiorem, quasi ministerillius esset, aut tantùm pro tempore substitutus.
units.tr: Through whom) An emphasis. For it was certainly established, and conceded by all, that the Father made all things; but that he made them through the Son, as through a colleague or co-worker, was not therefore evident. Hence it is said not that the Father made all things, and likewise not that the Son made them, but that the Father made all things through the Son. Thus the Father keeps his own dignity, namely that he made all things, and yet the same dignity is likewise added to the Son himself, because the Father made all things through him. By this form of expression the persons are clearly shown to be distinct, and yet the unity of essence, equal nature and power are shown as well. One is the one who makes, another is that through whom something is made, and yet they are not different things, and the action is common. The Father is God and Christ is God, and therefore they are one: the Father acts, and the Son acts; nor does the one act through the other as through an inferior, or as an instrument, but as one who would not act without him. Between them there is the same will, the same power, and indeed equal and co-equal, so that the action of the one is not understood to be accomplished without the action of the other. In this way the Father acts through the Son, not as through an inferior, but just as often among men a consul acts through another consul equal to himself, when neither could in some sense do anything without the other, and an equal authority is held by each, and the will and authority of both are required to decide something. For men are said to act not only through inferiors, but also through equals, and sometimes through superiors, as when someone restrains his adversary through a magistrate. Indeed, from this form of speech one may gather that the Son proceeds from the Father, yet not that the Son is inferior to the Father, as if he were his minister or merely substituted for a time.

units.la: Condidit) Non iam condit, sed iamdiu, ab æterno, ante susceptum præcedente omnium hæreditatem, imò, ut habetur Ephes. 1. antequàm iacerentur fundamenta mundi. Eoq; dicit, condidit secula: non dicit, condidit cœlû & terram, sed secula, quod multò amplius est significat enim, si quid omninò fuerit etiá antequàm extitit cœlû vel terra, id ipsum per inferiorem. per Christum fuisse conditum. Adeoq; nullum tempus, ac ne minimum quidem instas unquam fuisse, aut futurum, quod à Christo duratione & existendi potestatem non accipiat. Nam cum condita dicit secula, intelligi convenit praesentia praeterita, & futura. Ex his iam sequitur, si ipsum tempus atq; omne tempus per Christum est conditum: Ergo omnia quoq; quae in tempore existunt, per Christum sunt condita. Sed ideo quoq; multo aptissimè ait Apostolus secula per Christum esse codita, ut clare significat, Christum ab aeterno etiam ante ullam durationem temporis constitutam, fuisse, & patri coaeternum, ac per omnia aequalem.
units.tr: He created) He did not create just now but long ago, from eternity, before the inheritance was handed to the Son, who was to be heir of all things. Indeed, as Ephesians 1 says, it was before the foundations of the world were laid. So he says that he created the ages, not that he created heaven and earth. "Ages" is the larger term: it signifies that if anything at all existed even before heaven or earth came into being, that too was created through Christ. Therefore no time, not even the smallest instant, has ever been or will ever be which does not receive its duration and power of existing from Christ. For when he says that the ages were created, we must understand the present, the past and the future. From this it follows that if time itself, and all time, was created through Christ, then all things that exist in time were also created through Christ. The Apostle also says very fittingly that the ages were created through Christ, which clearly signifies that Christ existed from eternity, even before any duration of time was established, that he is co-eternal with the Father, and equal to him in all things.

units.la: Confirmatur aut, quae hic dicuntur, a Paulo etiam aliis multis Scripturae locis, velut Ioan.1. In principio erat verbum, & omnia per ipsum sunt. Coloss.1. Rom.11. Ex ipso, per ipsum, in ipso sunt omnia. Praeterea quibus locis pater describitur condidisse omnia verbo suo, ibi per verbum intelligitur ipse filius Christus. ut Psal. 32, Dixit, & facta sunt, ipse mandavit & creata sunt. Porro convenit haec dignitas & facultas creationis Christo, secundum ipsius divinam naturam. In quantum enim Deus ipse est, ante secula, & omnia condidit: sed homo esse in tempore coepit, tempore, inquam, quod a Deo patre erat praefinitum, Solius Dei, & divinam naturam habentis est creare.
units.tr: What is said here is confirmed by Paul, and by many other passages of Scripture, such as John 1: "In the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through him"; Colossians 1; Romans 11: "from him, through him and in him are all things." Moreover, in those passages where the Father is described as having created all things by his word, the word is understood to be the Son Christ himself, as in Psalm 33: "He spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it was created." Further, this dignity and power of creating belongs to Christ according to his divine nature. Insofar as he is God, he existed before the ages and made all things. But as man he began to exist in time, in time, I say, which had been appointed by God the Father. It belongs only to God, and to one who has the divine nature, to create.

units.la: Qui cum sit splendor gloriae) Alia particula exprimes divinitatem Christi. Ne quis suspicetur patrem per filium omnia condidisse, quasi per inferiorem, & eo modo cooperante, quo creaturae etiam dicuntur Deo cooperari & subserviure: ideo nunc addit, eandem prorsus gloriam convenire Christo, quae convenit Deo patri. Estq; obseruada in singulis membris incrementi ratio: Quo enim longius progrederis, eo animaduertis sublimiora esse & excellentiora, quae Christo hic tribuuntur. Graece habetur ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, atq; ἀπαύγασμα significat relucentiam, resplendetiam, ex alio refulgentem, etiam Solis radium. Proinde metaphora subest, ac tantundem significatur, quòd videlicet in Christo resplendeat universa Dei patris gloria, nullaq; sit in Deo patre res praeclara, quae gloriam meretur, quae non itidem in Christo clarissime reluceat & conspiciatur. Breuiter & crasse, quomodo communi more loquendi dicimus, conspecto generoso puero aliquo, in eius vultu ac moribus relucere omnem indolem & ingenium paternum, (sicut milites dicebant in Annibale viuum sibi redditum Amilcarem) eaq; forma loquendi significatur, omnes virtutes & qualitates patris competere ipsi filio: ita puto de Christi hic tantundem dici, quòd videlicet ipsi competit omnis virtus, dignitas, potetia, gloria, quae Deo patri competit.
units.tr: "Who, being the brightness of glory": another phrase expresses the divinity of Christ. Lest anyone suspect that the Father created all things through the Son as through an inferior, cooperating in the way that creatures too are said to cooperate with God and serve him, he now adds that exactly the same glory belongs to Christ as belongs to God the Father. And in each member of the sentence we must observe a progression: the further you go, the more you notice that the things attributed to Christ here are higher and more excellent. In Greek it is "apaugasma tēs doxēs" [ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης], and apaugasma means a reflected brightness or radiance, shining back from another, like a ray of the sun. So there is a metaphor, and it means this: the whole glory of God the Father shines forth in Christ, and there is nothing illustrious in God the Father that deserves glory which does not likewise shine out and become visible most clearly in Christ.
