To put it roughly and simply, as we commonly say: when we see some noble boy, all the natural disposition and talent of his father shine out in his face and manners (as the soldiers said of Hannibal, that Hamilcar had been returned to them alive). By this manner of speaking it is meant that all the virtues and qualities of the Father belong to the Son himself. So I think that the same is said here of Christ: that all virtue, dignity, power and glory which belong to God the Father belong to him too.

units.la: Est autem magna gratia in uoce ἀπαύγασμα: Latet enim significatio, quòd Christus a patre procedat siue emanet, eodem propemodum pacto, quo a lumine aliquo procedit splendos siue fulgor, siue, ut Sole procedit lux & splendor, & radius illustrans circumpositae. Quo factum, quòd pater in scripturis sit lux appellatus, & inhabitans lucem inaccessibilem(1 Timoth. 6.) Item filius similiter lux, ut Ioan. 1. Ipse erat lux vera illuminans omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. unde & patres dixerunt, Christum ex patre procedere, Deum uerum de Deo uero, sicut lumen procedit de lumine. Quae ratio etiam valde apta est, non solum ad explicandum aliquo modo rationem processionis a patre, sed etiam ad ostendendum distinctionem personarum, & praeterea equalitate potentiae substantiaeq; Sicut a Sole seu corpore lucido procedit splendor, ita a patre procedit filius. Et sicut distinguitur corpus ipsum lucidum a splendore qui inde deriuatur: ita alia est persona patris, alia filij. Rursus autem sicut corpus lucidum non est sine aliquo splendore, neq; splendor sine corpore lucido: ac necessario sunt ista coniuncta in separabiliaq;, sicut & calor ab igne, atq; omnia reddunt luminosa & conspicua: ita pater non est sine filio, nec filius sine patre, sed semper simil extiterunt, & pari potentia illustres communem habet operationem. Quibus rationibus etiam Ambrosius utitur lib.4. de fide contra Arrianos disputans. Itaq; Christus est splendor gloriae, quia in eo, & per eum omnis gloria paterna elucet et illustratur. Augustinus libro primo de Incarnatione verbi cap.11. breuiter mihi expresisse videtur sententia huius loci: Deus, inquit, lux est. Splendor ergo lucis est vni genitus filius, ex ipso insepar abiliter, uelut splendor ex luce procedens, & illuminans vniuersam creaturam. Addit, Christum dici splendorem, quomodo uia dicitur, quia videlicet ducit ad patrem: vel quomodo verbum dicitur, quia arcana sapientiae diuinae interpretatur & exponit nobis: uel quo modo dicitur uia, veritas, resurrectio, quia uide licet ad ista nos adducit, & nobis ista parat. Hoc igitur pacto & splendor appellatur, quia per ipsum, quid sit summa lux, videlicet pater, cognoscitur & sentitur. Neq; est quod cauilletur Marcellus aut Photinus quispiam, splendore non esse quiddam per se existens sed aliunde habere ut sit. Sane cauillu hunc impedire voles Apostolus, addidit proxime sequentib. uerbis, Christum esse expressam imaginem substantiae paternae. Haec de uoce ἀπαύγασμα,
units.tr: The word apaugasma has a great charm. It implies that Christ proceeds, or flows forth, from the Father, in much the same way as light proceeds from a source: splendour or brilliance comes from a lamp, as sunlight and brightness come from the sun, and a ray lights up the things around it. Hence the Father is called light in Scripture, and one who dwells in unapproachable light (1 Timothy 6). Likewise the Son is light, as in John 1: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man who comes into this world." Hence the Fathers also said that Christ proceeds from the Father, true God from true God, as light proceeds from light. This explanation is also very apt, not only for explaining in some way the manner of the procession from the Father, but also for showing the distinction of persons, and besides, the equality of power and substance. As brightness proceeds from the sun or from a luminous body, so the Son proceeds from the Father. And as the luminous body itself is distinguished from the splendour that comes from it, so the person of the Father is other than the person of the Son. Again, as a luminous body is never without some brightness, nor brightness without a luminous body, and these are necessarily joined and inseparable, just as heat comes from fire, and things make luminous and visible: so the Father is never without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, but they have always existed together, and, equally illustrious in power, they have a common operation. Ambrose too uses these arguments in Book 4 of his work On the Faith, when he disputes against the Arians. Thus Christ is the brightness of glory, because in him and through him all the glory of the Father shines and is made manifest. Augustine, in Book 1 of On the Incarnation of the Word, chapter 11, seems to me to have briefly expressed the meaning of this passage: "God," he says, "is light. The splendour of the light, therefore, is the only-begotten Son, proceeding inseparably from him, as splendour proceeds from light, and illuminating the whole creation." He adds that Christ is called splendour in the same way that he is called the way, because he leads to the Father; or as he is called the Word, because he interprets and explains to us the hidden things of divine wisdom; or as he is called way, truth and resurrection, because he, of course, brings us to these things and prepares them for us. In this way he is also called splendour, because through him we know and perceive what the supreme light is, namely the Father. Nor is there any reason for Marcellus or some Photinus to cavil that splendour is not something existing in itself but has its being from elsewhere. Indeed, the Apostle, wishing to prevent this quibble, added in the next words that Christ is the express image of the Father's substance. So much for the word apaugasma.

units.la: Nomine aute gloriae summa dignitas, potentia, excellentia intelligitur, adeoq; omnia illa, propter quæ & per quæ gloria siue laus alicui solet tribui: quæ quidem in Deo vberrimè & copiosissimè resplendent, ita vt metonymia huic uoci videatur subesse. Nam effectus pro causa, siue consequens pro antecedenti ponitur. Atq; ita demonstratur, parem Christo esse potentiā agendi quæuis, ex quibus possit gloria parari, quemadmodū in patre. Quæ interpretatio valde quadrat instituto præsenti. Sunt uero etiā sancti aliquo modo illustrates gloriā Dei, & resplendet in eis Dei gloria, sed nō ea ratione, qua in filio. Gloria Dei homo scrutari nequit. Qui scrutatur maiestatem, opprimetur à gloria, Proueib. 25.
units.tr: By the name of glory is understood supreme dignity, power and excellence, and so all those things on account of which, and through which, glory or praise is usually ascribed to anyone. These shine forth in God most richly and abundantly, so that the expression seems to contain a metonymy: the effect is put for the cause, or the consequent for the antecedent. Thus it is shown that Christ has the same power of doing whatever might bring glory, as the Father does. This interpretation fits the present purpose very well. Indeed, the saints too in some way illuminate the glory of God, and the glory of God shines in them, but not in the same manner as in the Son. "Man cannot search out the glory of God. He who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory" (Proverbs 25).

units.la: Iam sunt loci in Scripturis, quibus istud quoq; de Christo confirmatur, quòd videlicet sit splendor & lux gloriæ paternæ. Ioan. 1. Ipse est lux uera, quæ illuminat omne hominē uenientem in hunc mundum. Et Ioan. 8. Ego sum lux mundi. Huc referendum etiā illud Sapientis: Vapor est enim uirtutis Dei, & emanatio quædam est claritatis omnipotentis Dei syncera, & ideo nihil inquinatum in eam incurrit. Splendor est enim lucis æternæ, & speculum sine macula Dei maiestatis, & imago bonitatis illius. Et cùm sit una, omnia potest, & in se permanēs omnia innouat. Item Abacuc 3. operuit cœlos gloria eius, & laudis eius plena est terra. Splendor eius ut lux erit, cornua in manibus eius. Ibi abscondita est fortitudo eius, ante faciem eius ibit mors. Esa. 62. egrediatur, ut splendor iustus eius. Psal. 36. Apud te est fons uitæ, & in lumine tuo uidebimus lumen. Ioan. 17. pater glorifica me, ea gloria, quam habui apud te, antequàm mundus fieret. Conuenit autē hæc appellatio Christo iuxta naturam diuinam & humanam coniunctim. Nam in eo non solū, ut Deo respondet gloria & maiestas Dei Patris, sed etiā ut homine. Nam Christus homo erat uere lux illuminans omnem hominem: de eo ut homine uaticiniū illud Abacuc accipiendum est. Deniq; ut homo manifestauit & resplendere fecit gloriam Patris sui cœlestis, & per eum etiam hominem adducti sumus in agnitionem Patris.
units.tr: There are passages in Scripture which confirm this also about Christ, namely that he is the splendour and light of the Father's glory. John 1: "He is the true light, which enlightens every man who comes into the world." And John 8: "I am the light of the world." To this also belongs the saying of the Wise Man: "For she is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled finds its way into her. For she is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of God's majesty, and an image of his goodness. Though she is one, she can do all things, and while remaining in herself she renews all things." Likewise Habakkuk 3: "His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. His brightness shall be as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand; there his power was hidden. Before his face went pestilence." Isaiah 62: "until her righteousness goes forth as brightness." Psalm 36: "With you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light." John 17: "Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was made." This name belongs to Christ according to his divine and human natures together. For in him the glory and majesty of God the Father corresponds not only as to God, but also as to man. For Christ as man was truly the light enlightening every man, and that prophecy of Habakkuk must be understood of him as man. Finally, as man he manifested and made to shine forth the glory of his heavenly Father, and through him, as man, we too have been led to the knowledge of the Father.

units.la: Est expressa imago substantiæ illius. Rursus, ne quę hactenus tributa sunt Christo, aliquo modo raperentur ad imminuendam eius dignitatem, quasi duntaxat per participationem aut similem quendam modum illi competerent: nunc nouo incremento addit, omnia illa Christo competere secundum suam naturam: esse enim eum eiusdem cum patre natu-ræ & substantiæ. Sciendum autem, multa interdum, quæ Christi Dei tātum sunt propria, per participationem etiam tribui sanctis: ut quòd Deus iudicabit mundum, siue quòd pater omne iudicium dedit filio: tamen Christus in Euangelio dicit, Apostolos iudicaturos duodecim tribus Israelis. Et 1. Corinth. 6. dicitur, An nescitis, quòd sancti mundum iudicabunt? Sic Christus dicitur proprie hæres Dei, & tamen multis in locis etiam sancti uocantur hæredes, & hæreditatem Dei accipientes. Præterea Christus uocat se lucem mundi: Vos estis lux mundi. Ne itaq; quisquam putaret, hoc pacto Christum dictum hæredem omnium, uel splendorem & lucē gloriæ patris, prudenter addit iam, quomodo Christus sit eiusdem cum Deo patre naturæ.
units.tr: "He is the express image of his substance." Again, lest the things hitherto attributed to Christ be somehow snatched away to diminish his dignity, as if they belonged to him only by participation or some similar manner, he now adds a new increment: all these things belong to Christ according to his own nature, for he is of the same nature and substance as the Father. It must be noted, however, that many things which belong to Christ alone as God are sometimes also ascribed to the saints by participation. For example, God will judge the world, or the Father has given all judgment to the Son; yet Christ says in the Gospel that the Apostles will judge the twelve tribes of Israel. And 1 Cor. 6: "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" So Christ is properly called the heir of God, and yet in many places the saints too are called heirs and receive the inheritance of God. Moreover, Christ calls himself the light of the world, and you are the light of the world. Therefore, lest anyone suppose that Christ is called heir of all things, or the brightness and radiance of the Father's glory, in this same way, the Apostle wisely adds how Christ is of the same nature as God the Father.

units.la: Visus est aūt Apostolus uerbis appositissimis, dicens, Christum esse imaginem substantiæ paternæ. Vbi autē interpres dixit, imaginem expressam, græce est uox χαρακτήρ, quæ significat formam expressam ex alio, siue notam rei cuipiā impressam, à uerbo χαράσσω, quod est insculpo siue notam imprimo. Multoq; significantius est, quòd uocat Characterem, quàm si diceret, Imaginem. Nam & in speculo apparet imago rei cuiusplam, at nequaquàm Character. Neq; unquàm aliquid certius euidentiusq; repræsentatus, quàm si uelut in ceral aut argilla imprimatur: ueluti si quis scite absoluteq; uelit ostendere qualitates omnes suæ manus, imprimat eam cerę, & animaduertet etiam minutissimos ductus linearum adeoq; minimorum punctorum. Iam ὑπόστασις significat substantiā, uel, ut nonnulli uertūt, subsistentiam, quæ quidem differt ab οὐσία, siue essentia. Nam substantia proprie dicitur, quia per se subsistit, & omnib. aliis tanquā fulcris substat οὐσία, quia simpliciter existit. substantia hic proprijsimè significat οὐσίαν per se subsistentem. Et apparet, Apostolū conatum hac voce aliquo modo exprimere nomē illud נתן, quod ductū est Hebraeis à נתן, id est, existere: uide Bucerū ad Rom. pag. 57. Etiāsi οὐσίαν verterunt & substantiā, & usurparūt pro ὑποστάσει, sicuti nostri ὑπόστασιν persoā appellāt. Ac dixerūt patres vnā substantiā (οὐσίαν) esse diuinitatis & tres personas, seu ὑποστάσεις. Græci adhuc paulò aliter accipiūt ὑπόστασιν, quam nos substantiā. Nā ipsi dicūt tres esse ὑποστάσεις, vbi nos nō dicimus tres substātias, sed tres personas. vbi verò nos dicimus vnā substantiā, ipsi usurpant οὐσίαν, non ὑπόστασιν: etiāsi ipsi quoq;, teste Naziāzeno, aliquādo cœperint dicere πρόσωπα, p personis. Significat aūt persona substantiā indiuiduam: Pater quamuis sua proprietate sit à filio distinctus, sic tamen se totum in Christo filio expressit, ut hypostasis illius, totaq; essentia ac natura in hoc refulgeat: sicut si fiat aureæ imaginis aurea imago, ut altera alteri per omnia sit æqualis, ęgreq; vnā ab altera possis discernere, vna recte dicetur imago alterius, secundū materiā, formā, & omnia deniq; siue propria siue accidentia: ita filius est viua imago viui patris, eiusdem substantiæ, naturæ, dignitatis, potentiæ.
units.tr: The Apostle seems to have chosen very apt words in saying that Christ is the image of the Father's substance. Where the translator has rendered "the express image," the Greek word is χαρακτήρ [charaktēr], which signifies a form expressed from another, or a mark impressed on something, from the verb χαράσσω [charassō], to engrave or to stamp a mark. It is much more expressive that he calls him a character than if he had said image. For an image also appears in a mirror, but never a character. Nothing is ever represented more certainly and clearly than when it is, as it were, impressed on wax or clay. Thus, if someone wishes to show neatly and exactly all the features of his hand, he presses it into wax, and he will notice even the smallest strokes of the lines and the tiniest points. Now ὑπόστασις [hypostasis] signifies substance, or, as some translate, subsistence, which indeed differs from οὐσία [ousia], or essence. For substance is properly so called because it subsists through itself and stands under all other things as supports; οὐσία is so called because it simply exists. Here ὑπόστασις properly signifies an οὐσία subsisting through itself. And it appears that the Apostle has in some way tried to express by this word the Hebrew word nathan, which is derived from the Hebrew verb meaning to exist; see Bucer on Romans, p. 57. Although the Greeks translated οὐσία as substantia and used it for ὑπόστασις, just as ours call ὑπόστασις persona. And the Fathers said that there is one substance (οὐσία) of the Godhead and three persons, or ὑπόστασεις. The Greeks still understand ὑπόστασις somewhat differently from how we understand substantia. For they say there are three ὑπόστασεις, where we do not say three substances but three persons. Where we say one substance, they use οὐσία, not ὑπόστασις, although they too, as Nazianzen testifies, at some time began to say πρόσωπα [prosōpa], that is, persons. Now persona signifies an individual substance. The Father, although he is distinguished from the Son by his own property, has nevertheless so expressed himself wholly in the Son, the Son, that his hypostasis, and his whole essence and nature, shine forth in him. Just as if a golden image were made from a golden image, so that one is in every respect equal to the other, and you could hardly distinguish one from the other, one would rightly be called the image of the other, in matter, form, and finally in all things, whether proper or accidental. So the Son is the living image of the living Father, of the same substance, nature, dignity, and power.

units.la: Filius imago Patris.
units.tr: The Son is the image of the Father.

units.la: Proinde hęc mihi videtur simplex esse horum verborum sententia. Quicquid ad substantiam Dei patris & naturam eius pertinet, hoc vniuersum in se habet & exprimit nobis ipse filius. Non vna tantum particula eorum, quæ patri sunt propria cōspicitur in filio, sed reuera tota Patris substantia. Ac proinde quicquid Patri conuenit, siue sapientia, siue potestas, bonitas, gloria, id omne quoq; cōuenit filio, qui est ipsissimus Character paternæ substantiæ. Eamq; ob rem Christus vocatur potentia patris, sapientia patris, iustitia patris, &c. Quæ res etiam mouit Sanctos patres ad confitendum, quòd persone distinctæ siue tres ὑποστάσεις, sint inter se ὁμοούσιοι, id est, eandem habetes essentiam, & naturam, & ut vno verbo nostri reddiderunt, consubstantiales. Pro qua voce licet constat acriter digladiatos veteres, tamen minimè explodenda est, quæ excogitata est ad exprimendum genuinam scripturæ sententiam. Longum autem foret, adferre patrum interpretationes, quibus exponunt, quomodo filius eiusdem sit cum patre substantiæ: nos aliqua tamen ad præsentis loci expositionem conferentia adducemus. Nazianzenus lib.3. & 4. Theologiæ suæ multa habet ad docendum, Christum esse eiusdem cū patre naturæ: sed posteriore libro respiciens ad præsentem locum Apostoli, ait, Christum purum esse patris sui sigillum, & characterem certissimum. Imaginem verò, qui fit eiusdem essentiæ, & quòd hic ab illo, non etiam ab hoc pater. Hæc enim est imaginis natura, ut princeps exemplar, vnde ducatur figura sua, referat. Tametsi plusculū hic reperimus. In cæteris enim rebus, mobilis rei, immobilis est imago. Hic verò viuentis viua quoq; imago. Sanè maior hic similitudo quàm fuerit in Seth ipsius Adam, quamq; in quauis prole sui sit genitoris. Talis enim simplicium rerum natura, non partim quidem eas similes esse, partim verò dissimiles, sed totam totius esse formam. Cyrillus Thesauri lib.2. Filium patri consubstantialem multis modis probat. Et lib.4. cap.2. explicat, quòd, quæ in Scripturis dicuntur de similitudine Christi ad Patrem, intelligenda sint de similitudine essentiali.
units.tr: Accordingly, the simple meaning of these words seems to me to be this: whatever pertains to the substance and nature of God the Father, the Son himself has entirely in himself and expresses to us. Not merely one part of those things which are proper to the Father is seen in the Son, but in truth the whole substance of the Father. And therefore whatever belongs to the Father, whether wisdom, power, goodness, or glory, all of it belongs also to the Son, who is the very Character of the Father's substance. For this reason Christ is called the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Father, the righteousness of the Father, and so on. This matter also moved the holy Fathers to confess that the distinct persons, or three ὑποστάσεις, are ὁμοούσιοι [homoousioi] among themselves, that is, have the same essence and nature, and, as our people rendered it in one word, consubstantial. Although it is well known that the ancients fought bitterly over this word, it is by no means to be rejected, since it was devised to express the genuine sense of Scripture. It would be long to bring forward the interpretations of the Fathers, by which they explain how the Son is of the same substance as the Father. Yet we shall adduce some which bear on the exposition of the present passage. Nazianzen, in books 3 and 4 of his Theology, has much to teach that Christ is of the same nature as the Father. But in the later book, looking to this passage of the Apostle, he says that Christ is the pure seal of his Father and the most certain character. The image, however, which is of the same essence, is not only from the Father but also the Father is in it. For this is the nature of an image: it reproduces the original exemplar from which its form is drawn. Yet here we find a little more. In other things a moving thing has an immovable image; here the living has a living image too. Certainly the likeness here is greater than that of Seth to Adam himself, or than that of any offspring to its parent. For such is the nature of simple things: not partly similar and partly dissimilar, but the whole form of the whole. Cyril, in book 2 of his Thesaurus, proves in many ways that the Son is consubstantial with the Father; and in book 4, chapter 2, he explains that what is said in the Scriptures about the likeness of Christ to the Father must be understood of an essential likeness.

units.la: Hylarius lib.4. de Trinitate, & lib. de Synodis eadem de re copiosè disputat.
units.tr: Hilary in book 4 of On the Trinity, and in his book On the Synods, disputes copiously on the same matter.

units.la: Item Augustinus de Trinitate lib.5. cap.8. vbi ostendit, quòd quicquid de Deo absolutè dicitur, idem de singulis personis dici possit. Sed qui velit plura tum ex ijsdem autoribus, tum ex aliis, huc conferre poterit. Hoc satis sit Paulum his verbis expressisse, Christū esse eiusdem substantiæ cum Deo patre, & nihilominus distinctam à Deo patre persona, nomine characteris indicari. Character quippe, ut Chrysostomus ait, alter est ab eo. Sicut enim forma serui nihil aliud significat, quàm homine proprie, sic & forma Dei nihil aliud manifestat, quàm Deum, cuius enunciat formam. Alter autem non in omnibus sed secundum substantiam. Nam hic character similitudinis omnimodæ habet indicium, ad illud, cuius character ostenditur, & suspicionem vel paruæ dissimilitudinis omninò non recipit. Dicitur quidem & homo imago Dei, sed alia ratione quàm filius. Est enim imago Dei homo, vel ob id, quòd homo videtur esse in terris, quod Deus in cœlo: sicut Deus dominatur omnibus etiam cœlestibus, ita homo dominatur terrestribus. Sed verū est, inquā, hominem esse imaginem Dei secundum principatum, at nō secundum naturam. Ideoq; Christus exprimitur Character substantiæ Dei. Homo autem non est dictus character, non est appellatus forma Dei, quæ voces declarant essentiam vel similitudinem, quæ secundum proprietatem constat essentiæ. Aliqui interpretantur phrasin hebraicam & dici character rem substantiæ, pro eo quod est character substantia subsistēs, & ipsemet Deus. Sicut pauperes sanctorum, pro pauperes sancti, & virtus Dei, pro virtus Deus.
units.tr: Likewise Augustine, On the Trinity, book 5, chapter 8, where he shows that whatever is said of God absolutely can be said of each of the persons. But whoever wishes to bring more here, both from these same authors and from others, will be able to do so. Let it suffice that Paul expressed, in these words, that Christ is of the same substance as God the Father, and yet is a person distinct from God the Father, which is indicated by the name character. For a character, as Chrysostom says, is other than that of which it is the character. For just as the form of a servant signifies nothing other than a man properly, so also the form of God manifests nothing other than God, whose form it declares. But it is other not in all respects but in substance. For this character of likeness has the sign of complete similarity to that whose character it shows, and admits no suspicion of even slight dissimilarity. Indeed, man is also called the image of God, but for a different reason than the Son. For man is the image of God either because man appears on earth as God is in heaven, or because as God rules over all, even the heavenly things, so man rules over the earthly things. But it is true, I say, that man is the image of God according to dominion, but not according to nature. Therefore Christ is expressed as the Character of God's substance. Man, however, is not called a character, nor is he named the form of God; these words declare essence or likeness, which consists in the proper nature of the essence. Some interpret the Hebrew idiom so that the phrase "the character of the substance" is taken as "the character which is a subsisting substance," and God himself, just as "the poor of the saints" means "the poor saints," and "the power of God" means "the power, God."

units.la: Nunc adijciemus testimonia aliquot Scripturarū, quibus ἀπαύγασμα patris in Christo refulgere & cognosci demōstratur. Colos.1. Qui est imago Dei inconspicui, primogenitus vniuersæ creaturæ. Ioan.10. Ego & pater vnum sumus: ibidem, si mihi non creditis, operibus credite, ut cognoscatis, quòd paterin me est, & ego in eo.
units.tr: Now we will add some testimonies of Scripture, by which it is shown that the radiance [ἀπαύγασμα] of the Father shines forth and is recognized in Christ. Col. 1. "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature." John 10. "I and the Father are one." And in the same place: "If you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know that the Father is in me and I in him."

units.la: Ioan.14. Si cognouissetis me, & patrem meum utiq; cognouissetis: Ibid. Philippe qui vidět me, uidet & patrem: & quomodo tu dicis, ostende nobis patrem? Non credis, quòd ego in patre, & pater in me est? Præterea loci, qui docent Christum eadem omnia facere, quæ cognoscuntur patri Deo propria, passim in Scripturis occurrūt. Ioan.5. Quæcunq; il le fecerit, hæc itidem & filius facit. Ibid. Sicut pater suscitat mortuos & viuificat, sic & filius quos vult viuificat. Intelligendus autem est Christus χαρακτὴρ substantiæ paternæ, secundum naturā diuinam. Neq; enim natura humana seorsim considerata, potest diuinam naturam ita ad viuum exprimere.
units.tr: John 14. "If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father." And in the same place: "Philip, he who sees me sees the Father also. How do you say, Show us the Father? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me?" Moreover, passages that teach that Christ does all the same things that are known to be proper to God the Father occur everywhere in Scripture. John 5. "Whatever he does, the Son also does in like manner." And in the same place: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills." Christ must be understood as the character [χαρακτήρ] of the Father's substance according to the divine nature. For the human nature, considered apart, could not express the divine nature so lively.

units.la: Moderetur q; omnia verbo potentiæ suæ) Sicut ante semel asseruit diuinitate Christi, tribuendo ei, quòd per ipsum omnia sint condita: ita nunc rursus idem facit, adijciendo per incrementū, quòd omnia etiam moderetur, seruet, sustentet, quod non minoris est potentiæ quàm res primùm condere.
units.tr: "...and sustains all things by the word of his power." As before he asserted the divinity of Christ by ascribing to him that all things were created through him, so now again he does the same, adding, by way of progression, that he also governs, preserves and upholds all things. This requires no less power than to create things in the first place.

units.la: Atq; ita in Christo potentia & bonitas par demonstratur cum potentia & bonitate patris. tris.Græcè habetur,φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τ Ἰησοῦ αὐτῆς. Chrysostomus cùm dicit,per quem moderatur omnia,sicut antè dixit,per quem condidit & secula. Id autem, ne videatur pater per Christum agere,quasi per instrumentum aut substitutum vicarium. Hic enim tribuit ipsi Christo totam gubernationem & conseruationem omnium rerum conditarum.Neq; verò cùm filio ista tribuuntur,patri aliqua in parte derogatur. Si enim, ut sic loquamur,caussa filij pater est, secundum quod pater, multo magis eorum omnium caussa est, quæ per filium facta declarantur. Et cùm dicitur Christus solo verbo potenti omnia moderari,significatur, quàm facilè, quamq; sine molestia mundum totum gubernet.Sicut nihil fit facilius,quàm quod fit solo verbo: ita quàm facilimum est Christo omnia condita conseruare & regere. Quinetiam cùm dicit non simpliciter verbo, sed addit potenti,molem creaturæ magnitudinemq; tanti muneris Christi significat. Neque enim sine summa potentia mundus regi conseruariq; queat. φέρων autem non tantum significat portans,ferens, baiulans, sicut quidam reddiderunt: sed agens potius siue mouens ac moderans. Nam φερόμενα dicuntur græcis quæ impetu quodam aguntur: vnde & φορὰν impetum vocant: Et ἁγεμονικὴ φέρειν dicitur,qui suo arbitratu moderatur aliquid. Itaque de moderatione & gubernatione intelligemus potius, ut quæ etiam honorificentior & ad potentiam exprimendam aptior est. Quanquàm si quis ferendi seu portandi verbum ita accipiat,ut metaphora ea intelligatur,Christus omnia velut humeris suis portare & gestare re:ut Herculem vel Athlâtem intelligunt poetæ cœlum gestare humeris, non erit etiam prorsus absurda sententia:Christus enim omnia sustentat,conseruat, retinet in sua dignitate,ne concidant ac dissoluantur. Nam alibi quoq; in Scripturis portare pro sustentare, conseruare, gubernare accipitur: Ac verosimile est vocem hebraicam portandi à Paulo fuisse usurpatam. Exod.15.Dux fuisti in misericordia tua populo,quem redemisti,& portasti eum in fortitudine tua ad habitaculum sanctum tuum. Esaiæ 46.Ego feci & ego feră, ego portabo & saluabo. Ibidem: Audite me domus Israel,& omne reliduū domus Israel quæ portamini à meo utero.
units.tr: Thus in Christ power and goodness are shown to be equal to the power and goodness of the Father. In Greek it reads: "bearing all things by the word of his power" [φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ]. Chrysostom, when he says "through whom he governs all things," is repeating what he said before, "through whom he also made the ages." He does this so that it may not seem that the Father acts through Christ as through an instrument or a substitute deputy. For here he attributes to Christ himself the whole governing and preserving of all created things. Nor, when these things are ascribed to the Son, is anything taken away from the Father. For if, so to speak, the Father is the cause of the Son insofar as he is Father, much more is he the cause of all those things which are declared to have been made through the Son. And when it is said that Christ governs all things by the mere word of his power, it is signified how easily, and without effort, he governs the whole world. Just as nothing is done more easily than what is done by a mere word, so it is most easy for Christ to preserve and rule all created things. Moreover, when he says not simply "by the word" but adds "of power," he indicates the massive weight of creation and the magnitude of so great an office of Christ. For the world cannot be governed and preserved without the highest power. The Greek [φέρων] signifies not merely "bearing," "carrying," or "lifting," as some have rendered it, but rather "driving" or "moving and governing." For things that are driven by some impetus are called φερόμενα by the Greeks, whence they also call impetus φορά; and ἁγεμονικὴ φέρειν is said of one who governs something at his own discretion. Therefore we shall rather understand it of governing and directing, which is also the more honourable sense and better suited to express power. Yet if someone takes the word "to bear" or "to carry" in such a way that it is understood as a metaphor, namely that Christ bears and carries all things as on his shoulders, just as the poets imagine Hercules or Atlas bearing the heavens on their shoulders, the sense will not be altogether absurd. For Christ sustains, preserves and holds all things in their dignity, lest they fall and dissolve. Elsewhere in Scripture too, "to bear" is used for "to sustain," "to preserve," "to govern," and it is likely that Paul used the Hebrew word for "bearing." Exod. 15. "You led in your mercy the people whom you redeemed, and you bore them in your strength to your holy habitation." Isa. 46. "I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and I will save." And in the same place: "Hear me, O house of Israel, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, who are carried from my womb."

units.la: Verbo potentiæ)dixit per hebraismum, pro potenti verbo, id est, nutu, iussu, voluntate, imperio: Sicut qui potestate habet in alios, verbo solent exprimere, quid factum uelint, idq; quod dixerint, volunt statim perfici: ita Christus etiâ suo nutu & voluntate omnia conseruat. De patre dicitur proprie,quod verbo suo omnia crearit & feruet, ut psalm.33. Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt,& spiritu oris eius omnis uirtus eorum. De filio itidem accipiendum est,quòd suo uerbo,nutu, & voluntate omnia crearit & feruet, atq; ita par eius cum patre potestas intelligitur. Quanquàm paulò aliter intelligedum uenit, cùm pater dicitur verbo omnia condere & seruare, atque cùm filius hic dicitur omnia verbo suo seruare. Per patris verbum solent accipere personam filij: per verbum autem filij potentiam, nutum & imperiū, vnde & hic posita est vox ῥῆμα, cùm in alijs locis de patre poni soleat uox λόγος, quæ significat personâ. Etiâsi Basilius interpretatur,verbo potetiæ filij accipitur. Verbum pro actione. Christus paria semp operatur cum Patre. Quidam verbum hic positum exi-stimant pro facto seu actione: quomodo Lucæ 2. pastores dicunt, videamus verbum hoc quod factum est ad nos. unde verbum potentiæ factum vertunt. Proinde clara & perspicua est sententia, Christum, sicut scitur paria fecisse cum patre in creatione rerum, ita paria semper facere in rerum omnium sustentatione, gubernatione, conseruatione. Etita summa potestas filij in hoc officio exprimitur. Quàm magnū enim est gubernare mundum? Sic ex ipsa mundi gubernatione iudicauerūt gentiles,esse Deum, certè cum audimus hic munus istud tributum Christo,debemus in Christo diuinam naturam & & potentia agnoscere. Huciam plures loci Scripturæ pertinent idè clarè affirmantes. Nam quæ Pater agit,eadem agit filius: Sicut Ioan.5.ipse ait,Pater meus ad hoc usq; temporis operatur,&ego operor: Quę uerba de coseruatione omniū & procuratione nostræ salutis intelligenda sunt. Item Psal.18. & 23. habentur, quæ de Christo conseruante & gubernante omnia non obscurè sonant.Coloss.1.Omnia in eo constistunt. Sapient.8. Sapientia dominatur à fine usq; ad finem fortiter, & disponit omnia suauiter. Conuenit autem moderari, conseruare omnia Christo maximè secundum diuinâ naturâ, secundū quam conuenit & creare. Hic autem conuincuntur omnes,qui negant dei prouidentiâ contenduntq;, Deo res has inferiores non esse curæ, quasi otiosus esset deus, aut aliis creaturis inferioribus ceu Dijs quibusdam rerum humanarum curam demandaret. Similiter conuincuntur illi Pagani,qui, Chrysostomo referente,dicebant, Dei potestatem & prouidentiam tantum circa illa occupari, quæ sunt supra orbem Lunæ, cærera uerò inferiora ab alijs gubernari.
units.tr: "By the word of his power": he speaks in Hebraism for "by a powerful word," that is, by nod, command, will and authority. Those who have power over others customarily express by a word what they wish to be done, and they want what they have said to be performed at once; so Christ also preserves all things by his nod and will. Properly speaking, it is said of the Father that he created all things by his word and sustains them, as in Psalm 33: "By the word of the Lord were the heavens made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth." The same must be understood of the Son, that by his word, nod and will he created and sustains all things, and so his equal power with the Father is understood. Yet it must be understood somewhat differently when the Father is said to create and preserve all things by his word, and when the Son is here said to preserve all things by his word. By "the word of the Father" people are accustomed to understand the person of the Son; but by "the word of the Son" they understand his power, nod and authority. Hence the word here used is ῥῆμα, whereas in other places the word λόγος, which signifies the person, is customarily used of the Father. Even though Basil explains it, "the word of power" is taken as the power of the Son. "Word" for action: Christ always works the same things as the Father. Some think that the word here means a deed or action, as in Luke 2, where the shepherds say, "Let us see this word that has come to pass" [verbum hoc quod factum est]; hence they translate "the word of power" as "the deed of power." Accordingly the meaning is clear and plain: just as Christ is known to have done the same things as the Father in the creation of things, so he always does the same things in the upholding, governing and preservation of all things. And thus the supreme power of the Son is expressed in this office. For how great is it to govern the world! Thus even the Gentiles, from the very governing of the world, judged that there is a God; certainly, when we hear that this office is ascribed to Christ, we ought to acknowledge in Christ the divine nature and power. Many more passages of Scripture pertain here, clearly affirming the same. For what the Father does, the Son does too, as John 5 says: "My Father works until now, and I work." These words are to be understood of the preservation of all things and of the care of our salvation. Likewise Psalms 18 and 23 contain things which, concerning Christ preserving and governing all things, sound not obscurely. Col. 1. "In him all things consist." Wisdom 8. "Wisdom reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly." Now it is fitting that Christ should govern and preserve all things, especially according to the divine nature, according to which it is also fitting that he should create. Here are refuted all who deny the providence of God and contend that God does not care for these lower things, as if he were idle, or had committed the care of human affairs to some lesser creatures, as to certain gods. Likewise refuted are those Pagans who, as Chrysostom reports, said that the power and providence of God are occupied only with those things that are above the orb of the Moon, while the things below are governed by others.

units.la: Per semetipsum purgatione facta peccatorum nostrorum.
units.tr: By himself, when he had made purification of our sins.

units.la: Adhuc ad afferendam Christi diuinitate, addit de singulari eius erga nos beneficio, quod tale comemorat, ut nō nisi ab eo, qui diuina natura & potetia sit praeditus, coferri posit. Quandoquidē purgare seu remittere peccata solius Dei proprium est, id quod Marci 2. etiā Scribę fatebātur, dicentes: Quis potest remittere peccata nisi solus Deus? Ab hac ergo facultate remittędi peccata, Christus debet pro Deo agnosci, id quod arguūt etiā, quae ibi dicuntur à Christo adduntur, sic enim habetur: Vbi cognouisset Iesus spiritu suo, quòd sic cogitaret intra sese, dicit illis: Quid ita cogitatis in cordib. vestris? Vtrū est facilius, dicere paralytico, Remittūtur tibi peccata? an dicere, Surge & tolle grabbatum tuū, & ambula? Vt autē sciatis, quòd filius hominis habet potestatem in terra remittendi peccata, ait Paralytico, Tibi dico surge, &c. Proderat autem hanc particulam de beneficio Christi erga nos inferre huic descriptioni dignitatis Christi, non solùm quia mire conducit ad promovendam Christi diuinitatem, sed quòd etiam excitare queat omnium animos ad magni faciendum & amplectendum ipsum Christum, qui, cùm in forma Dei esset, dignatus est tamen nostra causa formam serui induere, ut pro peccatis nostris per acerbā suam mortem satisfaceret. Mouere illud poterat animos, quod supra dixit, patrem locutum nobis per suum filium: sed quod nunc addit, per eundem filium remissa esse nobis etiam peccata, istud verò quem non afficiat, quem non rapiat ad filium hunc exosculandum? Et ex nullis quae hic comemorantur de dignitate Christi, tanta vtilitas ad nos emanat, quāta ex hac vna re. Nam Christum condidisse omnia: patri esse parem, &c. parum nos iuuerit, nisi per Christum peccata essent ablata, & sic via ad vitam aeternam aperta & parata.
units.tr: Still further, to establish the divinity of Christ, he adds a note about his singular benefit toward us, which he recounts in such a way that it could be conferred only by one who is endowed with the divine nature and power. For since to purge or remit sins belongs to God alone, the scribes themselves acknowledged this in Mark 2, saying: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" From this power of forgiving sins, therefore, Christ must be recognized as God. What is said by Christ afterwards also proves this; for it is written: "When Jesus perceived in his spirit that they thought thus within themselves, he said to them: Why do you think these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Arise, take up your bed, and walk? But that you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, he said to the paralytic, I say to you, arise, etc." It is useful, moreover, to bring this particular point about Christ's benefit toward us into this description of the dignity of Christ, not only because it greatly serves to advance the divinity of Christ, but also because it can stir the minds of all to esteem highly and embrace Christ himself, who, though he was in the form of God, deigned nevertheless for our sake to put on the form of a servant, that he might make satisfaction for our sins by his bitter death. What he said above, that the Father spoke to us through his Son, could move minds; but what he now adds, that sins too have been remitted to us through this same Son, who would not be stirred by this, who would not be drawn to embrace this Son? And from none of the things recounted here about the dignity of Christ does so great a usefulness flow to us as from this one thing. For that Christ made all things, that he is equal to the Father, and so on, would profit us little, unless through Christ our sins had been taken away, and so the way to eternal life had been opened and prepared.

units.la: Quin ideo quoque appositè inserta est haec particula, quòd Euangelio maximè sit propria, & totum Euangelium de ea concionetur, videlicet de remissione peccatorum propter Christum: de qua etiam saepius & multis agetur in hac epistola. Itaq; cùm in reliquis quae hic de diuinitate Christi dicta sunt, tum praecipuè in hanc particulam de eius erga nos beneficio, decet nos intueri, vtpote quae maximè ad nos pertineat.
units.tr: Moreover, this particle is rightly inserted here, because it is most proper to the Gospel, and the whole Gospel preaches about it, namely the forgiveness of sins for Christ's sake. This will also be discussed often and at length in this epistle. Therefore, while we should look at the other things said here about the divinity of Christ, we should look especially at this particle about his benefit toward us, since it pertains most closely to us.

units.la: Habent autē singula verba quasi emphasin, διʼ ἑαυτῆς καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, per semetipsum: Id dupliciter exponi potest: primò, ut summa etiam potentia ostendatur per semetipsum: id est, proprijs suis viribus, nullis nostris meritis cooperantibus: neq; eriā usus ope angelorum, aut ullius deniq; rei adiutus auxilio. Pater quidem ordinauit & constituit per filium istud faciendum: sed filius per semetipsum omnia adimpleuit, suaq; virtute omnia perfecit: Sponte sua oblatus est, quia ipse voluit, obediens factus patri usq; ad mortem, Philippen. 2.
units.tr: Each word carries a kind of emphasis: having made purification of our sins through himself [διʼ ἑαυτῆς καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]. The phrase "through himself" can be explained in two ways. First, it shows his supreme power: that is, by his own strength, with none of our merits cooperating, and not even aided by the help of angels or of any other thing. The Father indeed ordained and appointed that this be done through the Son, but the Son accomplished everything through himself and brought it all to completion by his own power. He offered himself of his own accord, because he willed it, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death (Philippians 2).

units.la: Vel, ut summa illius erga nos charitas ostendatur: per semetipsum: id est, proprium offeredo ad mortem suum corpus, animam propriam nostri causa ponendo, sanguinem suum, non alienum, non taurorum aut hircorum effundendo in ara crucis. Eoq; ampliorē debet charitas haec intelligi, quòd beneficium remissionis peccatorum Christus vniuersale esse voluerit, quantum ad ipsum pertinet. Nam quòd non omnes uniuersaliter participes fiunt, id imputari ipsorum debet incredulitati & malitiae, ut Chrysostomus hoclo adnotauit.
units.tr: Or, "through himself" shows his supreme love toward us: that is, by offering his own body to death, laying down his own soul for our sake, and pouring out his own blood, not another's, not the blood of bulls or goats, on the altar of the cross. This love must be understood as all the greater because Christ, as far as he himself is concerned, willed the benefit of the forgiveness of sins to be universal. That not all become partakers of it universally must be imputed to their own unbelief and malice, as Chrysostom has noted here.

units.la: Vtraq; interpretatio accōmoda est, & multis Scripturæ locis cofirmata. Itaq; magna emphasi dictum est, per semetipsum: & simul potentia Christi summa, & simul charitas eius amplissima in hoc verbo emicat. Vsus est praeterea verbo purgationis, καθαρισμὸς & κάθαρσις significat purgationem, expiationem, ac lustrationem: quemadmodum olim purgabantur certis rebus in sacrificijs: vnde καθαρσια dicta sunt sacra quaedam, in quibus loca publica purgabantur seu purificabantur. Itaq; videtur hac voce alludere Apostolus ad illa, quae in lege Mosaica fiebant ad purificationem externam, de quibus passim multa in Leuitico & alibi. Tanquam si hic innueret, quod in veteri quidem lege multa instituta erant, quasi ad purificandos homines & ad auferenda peccata idonea: sed nullā reuera ibi erat ad hanc efficax: vera namq; per solum Christū nunc perācta est, per hunc solum expiatio facta est nostrorum peccatorum. Hoc, inquam, modo tacitè videtur Apostolus respexisse & allusisse ad veteres ceremonias pro purgatione facienda instituta. Quanquam Primasius & Theophylactus colligere videntur, subindicari hac voce mysterium Baptismi, quod ad tollenda peccata & purgandum diuinitus est institutum, & lotione sua purificationem inducit: vnde & lauacrū regenerationis, quo purificamur appellatur. Huc pertinet, quod in Apocalypsi & alibi Christus dicitur nos sanguine suo lauisse siue expurgasse.
units.tr: Both interpretations fit well and are confirmed by many passages of Scripture. Thus the words "through himself" are spoken with great emphasis, and in them shines both the supreme power of Christ and his most abundant love. Moreover, he used the word for purging: purgation [καθαρισμὸς and κάθαρσις] signifies purging, expiation, and lustration, just as things were once purged with certain rites in sacrifices. Hence the purifications [καθαρσια] were called certain sacred rites in which public places were cleansed or purified. The Apostle therefore seems by this word to allude to those things which were done under the Mosaic law for external purification, concerning which there is much throughout Leviticus and elsewhere. It is as if he were hinting that in the old law many institutions were set up, as if suitable for cleansing men and taking away sins, yet in truth none of them was effective for this; for the true purification has now been accomplished through Christ alone, and through him alone the expiation of our sins has been made. In this way, I say, the Apostle seems tacitly to have looked back at and alluded to the old ceremonies instituted for making purification. Although Primasius and Theophylact seem to gather that the mystery of Baptism is hinted at by this word, which was divinely instituted to take away sins and to cleanse, and which brings about purification by its washing; hence it is also called the laver of regeneration, by which we are purified. To this belongs what is said in the Apocalypse and elsewhere, that Christ has washed or cleansed us with his blood.

units.la: Peccata nostra) Neq; enim Christus pro peccatis suis aliquid luit, qñ nulla unquā admisit. i. Pet. 2. Qui peccatū non fecit, nec inuentus est dolus in ore eius. Proprie nostra dicuntur, quia ut in peccatis nati & concepti, ita in uita semper ad peccandū ferimur, & peccata nobis adhaerent. Quin etiā nostra, qui videlicet iam viuimus, & in eum credimus, peccata p Christum expiata debemus intelligere, atq; in consolationem omni tempore accipere. Dico autem qui credimus: quia non nisi credentibus beneficium istud Christi impendi-tur. Quod enim ex nostra parte requiritur, id fides est: Sicut & Petrus Actorum 15. ait, Fide purificantur corda.
units.tr: Our sins. For Christ did not atone for any sins of his own, since he committed none (1 Peter 2): "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth." They are called ours properly, because, just as we are born and conceived in sins, so in life we are always carried toward sinning, and sins cling to us. Indeed, we ought also to understand them as our sins, that is, of us who now live and believe in him, and to receive them, expiated through Christ, for our consolation at all times. I say "who believe," because this benefit of Christ is bestowed only on believers. For what is required on our part is faith; as Peter also says in Acts 15: "Their hearts are purified by faith."

units.la: Et peccata per se sunt tam magna, & tàm potentia ad nos damnandum, ut nulla re expugnari potuerimus, nisi sanguine ipsius Christi: multum abest, ut nos aliquid hic puerimus, qui nihil aliud, quàm per omnem vitam peccata peccatis accumulamus.
units.tr: Sins in themselves are so great and so powerful to condemn us that we could not be overcome by anything except the blood of Christ himself. Far from it that we should have accomplished anything here, we who do nothing but heap sin upon sin throughout our whole life.

units.la: Proinde satis perspicua est Pauli sententia, qua hic divinitatem Christi asserit. Quod enim solius Dei proprium est, id Christo ait competere & à Christo perfici: atq; ea verborum forma, ut illum non tantùm Deum esse, sed nobis quoq; Deum esse clare intelligamus. Iam multis Scripturæ locis idem de Christo praedicatur. Esaiæ 53. Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolorem nostrum ipse portavit. Malachiæ 3. Ipse enim quasi ignis conflans, & quasi herba fullonum, & sedebit conflans & emundans argentum, & purgabit filios Levi. Matth. 1. Vocabitur nomen eius Iesus, is enim saluum faciet populum suum à peccatis suis. 1. Petri 2. Ipse enim peccata nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, quo peccatis mortui iustitiae viveremus, cuius eiusdem vibice sanati fuistis. Deniq; alias creditur, illum pro nobis sanguinem suum dedisse, & efficacem fuisse mortem ipsius ad delenda seu purganda peccata ostenditur.
units.tr: Therefore Paul's statement, by which he asserts the divinity of Christ here, is quite plain. For what belongs to God alone, this he says belongs to Christ and is accomplished by Christ, and in such a form of words that we clearly understand him to be not only God but also God for us. Now the same is proclaimed of Christ in many passages of Scripture. Isaiah 53: "Surely he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows." Malachi 3: "For he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap, and he shall sit refining and purifying silver, and shall purify the sons of Levi." Matthew 1: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins." 1 Peter 2: "For he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed." Finally, in other places it is believed that he gave his blood for us, and his death is shown to be effective for blotting out or cleansing sins.

units.la: Conuenit autem istud Christo secundum diuinam naturam & humanum. Nam quòd sanguinem fuderit, mortem obierit, id humanitatis est. Quod autem mors illa efficaciter satisfaciat pro peccatis, seu diluat omnia peccata, id propter diuinâ naturâ coniunctam humanæ. Liquet istud ex illo Marci 2. Ut sciatis, quòd filius hominis habet potestatem in terra remittendi peccata, ait paralytico, Dico tibi Surge, ac tolle grabbatum tuum, & abi in domum tuam. Remittere peccata, Dei est: filium hominis esse, hominis. Quare hic est Communicatio idiomatum consideranda. Etiamsi peccati remittendi facultas Christo, ut homini non absurdè posit tribui, quando eandem facultatem communem fecerit & Apostolis, qui potestate verbi soluunt & ligant.
units.tr: Yet this belongs to Christ according to both his divine and his human nature. For that he shed blood and died belongs to his humanity; but that this death makes satisfaction effectively for sins, or washes away all sins, belongs to him on account of the divine nature united with the human. This is clear from Mark 2, where, that you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, he says to the paralytic, "I say to you, arise, take up your bed, and go home." To forgive sins is God's; to be the Son of man is man's. Hence the communication of properties (idiomatum) must be considered here. And although the power of forgiving sins can not absurdly be attributed to Christ as man, since he has also made the same power common to the Apostles, who loose and bind by the power of the word.

units.la: Consedit in dextera maiestatis in excelsis:
units.tr: He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high:

units.la: Septima particula, qua Christo diuinitatè asserit. Christus, inquit, consedit ad dexteram Dei patris, qd sane ei nō cōtingeret, nisi patri esset æqualis, & verus Deus: ergo est Deus. Qua ratione etiam Christus, declarare volens se Deum, usus est Matth. 22. vbi ait, se non tantum filium Dauid, id est, hominem, sed etiam dominum ipsius Dauid, id est, Deum: utpote de quo & patre ipse Dauid dixisset, Dixit Dominus, videlicet pater, Domino meo, nempe Christo, Sede à dextris meis.
units.tr: The seventh point, by which the deity of Christ is asserted. Christ, it says, sat down at the right hand of God the Father. This would certainly not happen to him unless he were equal to the Father and true God; therefore he is God. By this reasoning Christ also, wishing to declare that he is God, used Matt. 22, where he says that he is not only the son of David, that is, a man, but also the lord of David himself, that is, God. David himself, of course, said of the Father: The Lord said, namely the Father, to my Lord, namely Christ, Sit at my right hand.

units.la: Vbi duplex argumentum diuinitatis Christi habetur, & æqualitatis eius cum patre: alterum quia dominus: alterum, quia Sedens ad dexteram Dei describitur.
units.tr: Here there are two arguments for the deity of Christ and for his equality with the Father: the one because he is Lord, the other because he is described as sitting at the right hand of God.

units.la: Ideo verò ultimo loco & statim postquàm egit de Christo humiliato, istud argumentum collocauit, tum quia post humiliationem Christi contingit, tum quia maxima gloria Christi hic declaratur, qua maior non potest euenire, & quæ æternum est duratura.
units.tr: He placed this argument last, and immediately after speaking of Christ in his humiliation, both because it follows Christ's humiliation and because the greatest glory of Christ is declared here, a glory greater than which cannot come about and which will last for ever.

units.la: Neq; quicquam posset aptius dici, ad summam dignitatem significandam: ideoq; ut præstantissimum & efficacissimû, quodq; omnium animis quasi infixum hærere debet, postremo loco adijcitur.
units.tr: Nothing could be said more aptly to signify the highest dignity. Therefore it is added in the final place, as the most excellent and most effective point, which ought to cling to all minds as if fixed in them.

units.la: καθίσας ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς vox ἐκάθισεν ambigua est: unde quidam reddiderunt, Sedere fecit, constituit, quasi patri tribueretur id: Sed rectius consedit, propterea, quod statim sequitur participium γενόμενος, factus melior angelis. Quare ad filium referendum est verbum ἐκάθισεν, ut filius dicatur consedisse. Quae interpretatio etiam commodior est, ad refellendum Arrianos, qui Christum consedisse quidem fatentur, sed tantùm iussu patris, ut superioris. Quanquàijdem hic satis refelluntur, quod Christus dicitur Sedere non ad sinistram, ut inferior, sed ad dexteram, ut par, & propemodum ut superior.
units.tr: The word ἐκάθισεν [sat down] in καθίσας ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς [having sat down at the right hand of the majesty on high] is ambiguous, and so some have rendered it "made to sit" or "appointed", as if this were attributed to the Father. But "sat down" is more correct, because there follows at once the participle γενόμενος [having become], "having become better than the angels." Therefore the verb ἐκάθισεν must be referred to the Son, so that the Son is said to have sat down. This interpretation is also more suitable for refuting the Arians, who admit that Christ sat down, but only by the command of the Father, as one who is inferior. Yet the point is sufficiently refuted here as well, since Christ is said to sit not at the left, as an inferior would, but at the right, as an equal, and almost as a superior.

units.la: Porrò considere ad dexteram, significat, Christum idem habere & æquale per omnia ius ac potestatem, eiusdem esse dignitatis, parem obtinere in omnibus gloriam. Metaphorica locutio est, sumpta à more hominum, qui, cum alicui summum honorem deferre volunt, solent locum ad dexteram concedere, & ex assidendi ratione solet communiter de dignitate personarum iudicari.
units.tr: Moreover, to sit at the right hand signifies that Christ has the same and in all respects equal right and power, that he is of the same dignity, and that he holds equal glory in all things. It is a metaphorical expression, taken from the custom of men, who, when they wish to give someone the highest honour, usually grant him the place at the right hand; and from the manner of sitting, dignity of persons is commonly judged.

units.la: Dextera Dei in Scripturis, pro potentia, & potestate agendi, gubernandi, seruandi: ut Psal. 117. Dextera Domini fecit virtutem, dextera Domini, &c. forma loquendi ab eo sumpta, quòd præcipua virtus agendi quippiam hominibus in dextera manu sita est. Simili modo brachium tribuitur Deo.
units.tr: In the Scriptures the right hand of God stands for the power and authority of acting, governing and saving: as in Ps. 117: The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord, etc. This is a form of speech taken from the fact that the principal power of doing anything lies among men in the right hand. In a similar way an arm is attributed to God.

units.la: Et sedere quidem per se iudicatur admodum honorificum esse. Nam reges, iudices,
units.tr: Indeed, sitting in itself is judged to be very honourable. For we say that kings, judges,

units.la: magistratus, & publica negotia tractantes sedere praecipuè dicimus. At vero sedere ad dextram, id summum honorem ac dignitatem significat, maximeq; respectu aliorum adsidentium. Hinc quoq; factum, quòd Matth. 20. mater filiorum Zebedaei hoc conata fuerit impetrare filijs suis, ut alter sederet ad dextram Christi, alter ad sinistram. Quibus verbis illa significabat, se petere, ut proximi Christo fierent, & summa potestas rerum proximè Christo illis cederet. Ad significandum igitur, summam esse Christi dignitatē, utitur scriptura hac forma loquendi, quod videlicet Christus ad dexteram Dei sedeat. Alias enim cum Deus in corporeus sit, satis constat, illi dextram aut sinistram non posse attribui. Unde etiam sessionem localem Christo ibi tribuere, non ita est promptum: Sed ut pios dicimus Deo esse propinquos, impios vero à Deo remotos, locorum situm considerantes, sed dignitatem seu acceptationem personarum apud Deum: Ita Christum dicimus adsidere proximum patri, dignitate videlicet magis, quàm loci situ.
units.tr: magistrates and those who manage public affairs sit in particular. But to sit at the right hand signifies the highest honour and dignity, especially in comparison with the others who sit beside. Hence it also happened that in Matt. 20 the mother of the sons of Zebedee tried to obtain this for her sons, that one should sit at the right hand of Christ and the other at the left. By these words she was indicating that she sought that they might be nearest to Christ, and that supreme power over affairs would pass to them next to Christ. To signify, therefore, that the dignity of Christ is supreme, Scripture uses this form of speech, namely that Christ sits at the right hand of God. For since God is incorporeal, it is quite clear that a right or left hand cannot be attributed to him. Hence it is not easy to ascribe a local sitting to Christ there either. But just as we say that the godly are near to God and the impious far from God, considering not the position of places but the dignity or acceptance of persons before God, so we say that Christ sits beside the Father, near by dignity rather than by position in space.

units.la: Vtitur deinde voce maiestatis. In aliis locis, ut Actor. 7. Colos. 3. & huius epistolae cap. decimo dicit, ad dexteram Dei hic verò maiestatis. Voluit, ut apparet, summam dignitatem vocabulo maiestatis (quod per se augustum & excellentissimum quiddam sonat) exprimere. Ac nescio quid splendidius concipiunt animi, cum audiunt vocabulum maiestatis quàm si alias personae qualitas simpliciter exprimatur. Amplius enim quiddam videtur audiri, cum dicitur, regia maiestas voluit, quam si tantum dicatur, Rex voluit. Quod ideo fit, quia vocabulum maiestatis sua natura maximum quiddam significat, & summam potentiam ac dignitatem: veluti cum dicitur Matth. 25. cum venerit filius hominis in maiestate sua. Quamobrem cum Deo patri summa competat dignitas, nomen maiestatis quasi Antonomasia quadam ei frequenter in Scripturis tribuitur. Unde & Psal. 28. Deus maiestatis, seu maiestate plenus appellatur. Et proverb. 25. per maiestate divina omnis potestas & natura clarè significatur, cū dicitur: Qui scrutator est maiestatis, opprimetur a gloria. Itaq; mirificè extollitur hac voce Christi dignitas, quando, cùm patri competat summa maiestas, ad huius tamen maiestatis dexteram sedere describitur. Pari delectuac iudicio factum, quod dixerit, in excelsis. Voce namq; ipsa miram sublimitatem indicat, ita ut nihil altius vel sublimius illi possit tribui. omnia plane magnifica sunt, & ad modū excellentia, mireq; apta ad afferendam Christi diuinam naturam, & parem cum patre potentiā & gloriam. Licet aliquantò quàm hic illustrius istud de confessione Christiin excelsis exprimatur ad Ephes. 1. ubi addit, amplificandi ergò, de principatib. potestatib. dominijs &c: supra quae omnia Christum ait constitutum: Sed haec omnia nomine caelestium intelligi hoc loco convenit. Neq; verò localis sublimitas intelligenda est, sed honoris significatio, uti antè admonuimus.
units.tr: Next he uses the expression "of majesty". In other places, as in Acts 7, Col. 3 and in chapter ten of this epistle, it says "at the right hand of God" only; but here "of the majesty". He wished, as is evident, to express the highest dignity by the word majesty, which of itself sounds something august and most excellent. And minds conceive something more splendid when they hear the word majesty than if the quality of a person were simply stated otherwise. For more seems to be heard when one says "the royal majesty willed", than if one merely said "the king willed". This happens because the word majesty by its nature signifies something very great, and supreme power and dignity, as when Matt. 25 says: When the Son of Man comes in his majesty. Therefore, since supreme dignity belongs to God the Father, the name majesty is frequently attributed to him in the Scriptures, as it were by antonomasia. Hence also in Ps. 28 God is called the God of majesty, or full of majesty. And in Prov. 25 all divine power and nature is clearly signified by majesty, when it says: He who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. Thus the dignity of Christ is wonderfully exalted by this word, since, although supreme majesty belongs to the Father, Christ is described as sitting at the right hand of this majesty. With the same discernment he added "on high". For the word itself indicates a wondrous sublimity, so that nothing higher or more lofty can be attributed to him. All these things are plainly magnificent and in a way excellent, and wonderfully fitted to assert the divine nature of Christ and his power and glory equal to the Father's. Although this confession of Christ is expressed somewhat more clearly, as "on high", in Eph. 1, where he adds, for the sake of amplification, "above principalities, powers, dominions, etc.", over all of which he says Christ is set. But it is fitting to understand all these things here by the name of the heavenly places. Nor is a local height to be understood, but a signification of honour, as we have already warned.

units.la: In summa autem, iterum dicere lubet, plenisimè & sanctissimè summam Christi dignitatem, qua par est per omnia Deo patri, hic descriptam. Ac res quidem ipsa, nempe Christi excellentia omninò maior est, quàm verbis exprimi queat: sed apostolus, sicut prophetae, & alij Spiritu sancto afflati homines, adhibuit verba, quae captui nostro convenirent, quaeq; humano iudicio significarent, quod summum atq; excellentissimum volunt intelligi. Atque hic lubet cum Chrysostomo illud animo voluere, quòd, quae de Deo rectè ac iure dici convenit, nullis verbis aptis possimus exprimere, imò nec mens possit intellectu apprehendere. Multa autem de Deo intelligimus, quae eloqui penitùs non valemus. Multa item loquimur, & ea intelligere non fumus idonei. Verbi gratia. Quòd ubiq; Deus est, scimus: quomodo autem ubiq; fit, intellectu non capimus. Item, Quòd fit in corporea quaedam uirtus, quae omnibus est causa bonorum, scimus: quomodo autem, uel quae ista fit, penitùs ignoramus. Item Deum esse sine principio, Deum genuisse filium ex seipso, ista, inquam, dico, sed intellectu non possum assequi. Rursus autem quaedam intelligimus, sed uerbis exprimere haud valemus. Intelligit mens, sed non valet eloqui, ita ut ipse Paulus quoque interdum arcana quae attingit, oratione non prosequatur. Sic & hoc loco intelligere quidem possumus, Christum Deo Patri pet omnia parem, sed aptis verbis id nequit exprimi, non magis, quàm natura Patris potest verbis explicari. Intelligimus amplissima de Deo, sed verbis afferre ea haud valemus: cum nec ipsum nomen, Deus, aliquo modo essentiam diuinam nobis repraesentet: imò nec nomen, Angelus, exprimit angeli essentiam. Et, ut ad humilius quiddam descendatur, nec animae quidem appellatio apta est ad declarandum ipsius rei, quae anima est, dignitatem. Ergo necessitas quaedam, nempe humani captus imbecillitas, cogit Spiritum sanctum verbis minus proprijs indicare quaedam de diuina natura: ideoque hoc loco, quando ait, sedere Christum ad dexteram & quidem maiestatis diuinae, id similitudine quadam significare voluit, quod reuera nullis uerbis posset explicare.
units.tr: In sum, I again wish to say that the supreme dignity of Christ, which is equal in all things to God the Father, is here described most fully and most holily. The thing itself, namely the excellence of Christ, is indeed far greater than can be expressed in words. But the apostle, like the prophets and other men inspired by the Holy Spirit, employed words which would suit our understanding and which would signify by human judgement what they wish to be understood as supreme and most excellent. And here it is pleasing to bear in mind with Chrysostom that what may rightly and properly be said of God cannot be expressed in any fitting words, nor can the mind even grasp it by understanding. Yet we understand many things about God which we are wholly unable to speak. Likewise we speak many things, and we are not fit to understand them. For example, we know that God is everywhere; but how he is everywhere we do not grasp by understanding. Likewise we know that a certain corporeal power exists which is the cause of all good things; but how, or what this power is, we utterly do not know. Likewise I say, and I cannot grasp by understanding, that God is without beginning, and that God begot a son from himself. Again, on the other hand, we understand certain things, but are not able to express them in words. The mind understands, but cannot speak; so that Paul himself sometimes does not set out in speech the hidden things he touches on. So also here we are indeed able to understand that Christ is equal to God the Father in all things, but this cannot be expressed in fitting words, no more than the nature of the Father can be explained in words. We understand the greatest things about God, but we are not able to put them into words, since not even the name God in any way presents the divine essence to us; nor does the name angel express the essence of an angel. And, to descend to something lowlier, even the appellation soul is not fitting for declaring the dignity of that thing which the soul is. Therefore a certain necessity, namely the weakness of human understanding, compels the Holy Spirit to indicate certain things about the divine nature by words less proper. And so here, when he says that Christ sits at the right hand, and indeed of the divine majesty, he wished to signify by a certain likeness what in truth could not be explained in any words.

units.la: Quare admonemur huiusmodi phrases Scripturæ diligenter obseruare, & cùm occurrerint, religiosa pietate in eas intueri, & quando forte humilius sonant, quàm quod diuinæ naturæ competit, tùm cogitantes, ampliora significari, quàm verbis exprimi, Deum eò magis gloriabimus, extollemus, vtpote qui talis tantusque sit, vt & intellectum hominis longè transcendat, & omnes cogitandi dicentíque vires superet: iuxta illud primo Corinthiorum secundo: Oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, & in cor hominis non ascenderunt, quæ præparauit Deus diligentibus se. Quòd verò hoc pacto subuectus sit Christus in cœlum, & ad dextram Dei sedeat, multis locis Scripturæ confirmabitur, sed apertisimè Psalmo 110. Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede à dextris meis. Et Christus Matthæi vigesimo sexto: Amodo videbitis filium hominis sedentem à dextris virtutis, & venientem in nubibus cœli; Marci 16. Dominus postquàm locutus fuisset eis, receptus est in cœlum, & consedit à dextris Dei. Actor. 7. Stephanus vidit Iesum stantem à dextris Dei. Ephes. 1. Item Coloss. 3. additur, nos quoque cum Christo eadem gloria donandos.
units.tr: Hence we are reminded to observe such phrases of Scripture carefully, and when they occur to regard them with religious reverence. When they sound rather humble compared with what befits the divine nature, we should think that more is signified than the words express, and so we shall glorify and exalt God all the more, since he is so great that he far surpasses the understanding of man and exceeds all powers of thought and speech. This accords with 1 Corinthians 2: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him." That Christ was thus taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God will be confirmed in many places of Scripture, but most plainly in Psalm 110: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand. And Christ in Matthew 26: "Hereafter you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven." Mark 16: "After the Lord had spoken to them, he was received into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God." Acts 7: Stephen saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Ephesians 1. Likewise Colossians 3 adds that we too are to be given the same glory with Christ.

units.la: Conuenit autem istud Christo etiam secundum humanam naturam, quam pater volunt propter maximam humiliationem & obedientiam ad summam dignitatem exaltari: vt clarè dicitur Ephes. primo, & Philippens. secundo. Verè enim illo ipso corpore in cœlum subuectus est, cuius ex Maria virgine sumpsit materiam, sed iam illustrato, & vt loquuntur, glorificato, id est, incorruptibili, immortali iam facto, quemadmodum statim se habuit à resurrectione, & qualia describit corpora resurgentium Diuus Paulus prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto, quo corpore palam est visus cœlum ascendere.
units.tr: This applies to Christ also according to his human nature, which the fathers say was exalted to the highest dignity because of his greatest humiliation and obedience, as is clearly said in Ephesians 1 and Philippians 2. For he was truly taken up into heaven in that very body from which he took his matter from the Virgin Mary, but now made bright and, as they say, glorified, that is, made incorruptible and immortal, just as he was from the resurrection onward, and such as the divine Paul describes the bodies of the risen to be in 1 Corinthians 15. It is plain that he was seen ascending into heaven in that body.

units.la: Errorcs refutati) Cæterùm cum adeò præclara & magnifica sint, quæ de Christo hîc statim in ipso exordio enunciantur, & quidem adeo appositis verbis tamque decenti ordine, vt melius prædicari Christi diuinitas non posset, & præterea vt graues errores, & varij eorum qui dignitatem Christi conati sunt imminuere, refellantur: Equidem non video, cur epistolam hanc velut nequaquam profectam ab Apostolorum principe Diuo Paulo suspectam haberi velint. Neque enim verosimile est, ab alio, quàm ipso Paulo, tàm sublimia argumenta, tantaque mysteria, in tanta breuitate, adeo accurate potuisse pertractari. Vbi enim filius omnium hæres constituitur, manifestum fit parem eum habere cum Patre in omnibus potestatem, contra Arrium eiusque omnes sequaces. Cùm verò dicitur, patrem condidisse per eum secula, conuincitur Samosatenus, qui contendebat, Christum in tempore coepisse. Conuincuntur, quos non pudet dicere, Christum esse creaturam. Conuincitur item Manichæus, qui duos ponens Deos seu principia, quorum alter res externas, & secula, seu temporalia: alter res spirituales & æternas condidisset. Conuincitur denique & Samosatenus cum Serueto, qui λόγον non esse personam, antequam induit humanam naturam, nisi sunt demonstrare. Conuincuntur denique omnes quicunque Christum distinctam esse à patre personam recusant profiteri: vel ita vnum concedunt esse Deum, vt discriminen reijciant personarum. Postremò conuincuntur dicentes, Christum esse eundem, qui pater est, vt Priscillianistae. Cùm appellatur Christus splendor gloriæ, & expressa imago substantiæ, refellentur, qui Christo diuinam naturam adimunt, vel aliqua in parte inæqualem Patri, seu minorem Christum esse contendunt, sicut Arrius & Eunomius, Donatus: vel diuersam ponentes in patre & filio substantiam, vt Sabellius. Cùm describitur Christus omnia moderans verbo potentiæ suæ confutantur, qui putant, ita patrem curare omnia, quasi filius esset otiosus, aut nullum haberet amplius neque ius neque officium. Sed multò clarissimè conuincuntur Epicurei, negantes Deum res istas inferiores curare. Cùm iterum audimus, per Christum factam esse purgationem nostrorum peccatorum, habemus argumentum ad conuincendos eos, qui purgari peccata nostra putant vllis sacrificijs, vel nostris operibus, commentitijs religionibus, cultibus, mandatisque hominum: qui pro remissione peccatorum obtinenda alios intercessores seu mediatores, quàm Christum quærunt: deniq; ij, qui legis sacrificia ceremoniasve, aut etiam quascunque eiusmodi obseruationes putant ad tollenda peccata prodesse. Postremò cùm audimus, Christum sedere ad dextram Patris, iterum æqualis dignitas Christi cum patre contra Arrium & similes confirmatur. Præterea Seleuciani reuincuntur, qui asserebant, Christum non sedere in carne ad dexteram Patris, sed eam exuisse, atque in Sole posuisse, sumpta occasione è psalmo 18. In sole posuit tabernaculum suum. Quando igitur tot tamque portentosi errores (& multi alij procul dubio, quos non commemorauimus) refelluntur hisce paucis verbis, quis dubiter epistolam hanc
units.tr: Refutation of errors) Moreover, since the things said about Christ here at the very beginning are so splendid and magnificent, and indeed so apt in their wording and so fitting in their order that Christ's divinity could not be preached better, and since serious errors are refuted, and the various errors of those who have tried to diminish the dignity of Christ, I certainly do not see why they wish this letter to be regarded with suspicion as not having come from the prince of the apostles, the divine Paul. For it is not likely that such sublime arguments and such great mysteries could have been treated so accurately in such brevity by anyone other than Paul himself. Where the Son is established as heir of all, it is made clear that he has equal power with the Father in all things, against Arius and all his followers. When it is said that the Father made the ages through him, Samosatenus is refuted, who contended that Christ began in time. Those are refuted who are not ashamed to say that Christ is a creature. Manichaeus is refuted too, who posited two gods or principles, one of which made external things and the ages, or temporal things, and the other made spiritual and eternal things. Finally Samosatenus and Servetus are refuted, who could not show that the Word was a person before he put on human nature. Lastly, all are refuted who refuse to profess that Christ is a person distinct from the Father, or who concede one God in such a way that they reject the distinction of persons. Finally, those are refuted who say that Christ is the same as the Father, like the Priscillianists. When Christ is called the brightness of glory and the express image of substance, those are refuted who deny Christ the divine nature, or who contend that Christ is in some part unequal or lesser than the Father, like Arius, Eunomius and Donatus, or who posit a different substance in Father and Son, like Sabellius. When Christ is described as governing all things by the word of his power, those are refuted who think that the Father cares for all things as if the Son were idle, or had no further right or office. But much more clearly are the Epicureans refuted, who deny that God cares for these lower things.
