When we again hear that purification of our sins was made through Christ, we have an argument against those who think our sins are cleansed by any sacrifices, or by our own works, invented religions, worships and commands of men; against those who seek other intercessors or mediators than Christ to obtain remission of sins; and finally against those who think the sacrifices or ceremonies of the law, or indeed any such observances, avail to take away sins. Lastly, when we hear that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, the equal dignity of Christ with the Father is again confirmed against Arius and his like. Besides, the Seleucians are refuted, who asserted that Christ does not sit in the flesh at the right hand of the Father, but had laid aside the flesh and placed it in the sun, taking occasion from Psalm 18: In the sun he has placed his tabernacle. When so many and such monstrous errors (and doubtless many others which we have not mentioned) are refuted by these few words, who could doubt that this letter

units.la: 6 hanc D. Paulo apostolorum columini tribuendam? aut, cui potius quàm Paulo eam vendicabimus?
units.tr: 6 this letter is to be ascribed to Paul, the pillar of the apostles? Or to whom should we rather claim it than to Paul?

units.la: Doctrina) Iam verò res postulat, vt ex ampla & insigni hac Christi Dei descriptione nulla ad doctrinam, confirmationem, & consolationem conscientiarum excerpamus.
units.tr: Teaching) Now the matter requires that from this ample and remarkable description of Christ God we draw nothing for teaching, confirmation and the consolation of consciences.

units.la: Primùm igitur, cum hæc omnia eò tendunt, vt Christum natura esse Deum, & æquali cum patre præditum esse potestate intelligatur: Illud generaliter pro se vnusquiq; secum statuet, Christum pro vero Deo esse agnoscendum, & quidem pro nostro, id est, tali, qui nos quoq; velit sua potentia gubernare, tueri ab omnibus aduersitatibus: denique ad suam gloriam nos in pietatis & religionis officijs retinere & promouere.
units.tr: First, then, since all these things tend to this, that Christ is understood to be God by nature and endowed with equal power with the Father, each person should settle this in general for himself: that Christ is to be acknowledged as true God, and indeed as our God, that is, one who wishes to govern us by his power, to protect us from all adversities, and finally to keep us and advance us in the duties of piety and religion for his own glory.

units.la: Ex eo, quod proponitur hæres omnium, ingens oboritur hinc animis nostris consolatio, statuemus quoq;, quod nobis quoq; hæreditatem cœlestē ille apud se parauerit, vt ipse non solus sit hæres, sed nos quoq; cohæredes ad se perttrahat: qua de re Romanorum, Galat.3.
units.tr: From the fact that he is set forth as heir of all, a great consolation arises for our minds. We shall also judge that he has prepared a heavenly inheritance for himself, so that he is not the sole heir, but draws us also to himself as co-heirs. On this matter see Romans, Galat. 3.

units.la: Cùm audiuimus omnia per illum esse condita, eundem modorari omnia potenti suo verbo, cogimur hinc summam potentiam in illo agnoscere, atque eum vnà cum patre venerari, colere, timere, orare. Sed multò magis admonemur apud nos expendere, quanta sit nostra fœlicitas, quos ille creauit & prædestinauit, vt lumine veritatis suæ illustraret, vt sit mus in laudem gloriæ ipsius, quemadmodum dicitur Ephes.1. Præterea admonemur asside orare, vt quemadmodum cætera omnia, ita nos atq; actiones omnes nostras suo Spiritu moderetur, iuuet, prosperet.
units.tr: When we hear that all things were made through him, and he governs all things by his powerful word, we are compelled to acknowledge in him the highest power, and to venerate, worship, fear and pray to him together with the Father. But we are much more reminded to weigh how great our happiness is, we whom he created and predestined to be illumined by the light of his truth, so that we may be to the praise of his glory, as is said in Ephesians 1. Moreover, we are reminded to pray diligently that, just as he governs, aids and prospers all other things, so he would govern, aid and prosper us and all our actions by his Spirit.

units.la: Cùm audimus, Christum esse splendorem paternæ gloriæ, & expressam imaginem substantiæ illius, orabimus, vt suo fulgore mentes nostras illuminet, vt ad plenam cognitionem patris cœlestis nos perducat, nec non in hac vita consequamur, quicquid ad salutem nostram scitu est necessarium.
units.tr: When we hear that Christ is the brightness of the Father's glory, and the express image of his substance, we shall pray that he illumine our minds with his radiance, lead us to full knowledge of the heavenly Father, and grant that even in this life we may obtain whatever is necessary to know for our salvation.

units.la: Cùm audimus, per ipsum factam esse purgationem peccatorum nostrorum, valde multa hinc nobis sunt consideranda, & ad consolationem atque doctrinam arripienda. Primùm autem expendere crebrò, & altissima mente nos decet, quantum beneficium sit purgari à peccatis, siue obtinere remissionem peccatorum: tatum enim est, vt sine hoc salus nostra constare haud potuerit. Oportet expendere, quanta fuerit eius in nos charitas, qui huius rei perficiendæ gratia non sit grauatus etiam morte subire: vt nos quoq; indeexeplum sumamus bene merendi de proximo. Adhæc consolatio ingens afflictis conscientijs hinc nascitur. Si quando enim Sathanas vel caro nostra perterret nos peccatorum nostrorum magnitudine aut multitudine, ac proinde ad desperandum fere adigimur: tum conueniet, animum nostrum huius beneficij contemplatione erigere, cogitareq; nos nequaquam damnandos, quorum dominus Iesus Christus peccata purgauit, suo sanguine pro eis satisfaciendo. Ipse enim est immaculatus agnus qui tollit peccata nostra, & omnes nostras abstergit maculas. Deniq; ex his verbis arripere debemus occasionem, peccata deinceps vitādi. Si enim animaduertimus peccata nostra semel esse per Christū purgata, valde inde eorum erit, si nos ipsos iterum nouis peccatis contaminemus, cuius rei in enarratione huius loci meminit Chrysostomus.
units.tr: When we hear that through him the purging of our sins was made, very many things are to be considered here and taken up for consolation and teaching. First, however, we ought often to weigh, with the highest mind, how great a benefit it is to be purged from sins, or to obtain remission of sins; it is so great that without it our salvation could not stand. We must weigh how great was his love toward us, who did not shrink from undergoing even death to accomplish this, so that we too may take from him an example of doing good to our neighbour. Besides, great consolation for afflicted consciences arises from this. For if at any time Satan or our flesh terrifies us with the greatness or multitude of our sins, and so almost drives us to despair, then it will be fitting to lift up our spirit by contemplating this benefit, and to think that those are by no means to be condemned whose sins the Lord Jesus Christ has purged, satisfying for them with his blood. For he is the spotless Lamb who takes away our sins and wipes away all our stains. Finally, from these words we ought to seize the occasion to avoid sins henceforth. For if we realise that our sins have once been purged through Christ, it will be very wicked of us if we again defile ourselves with new sins; Chrysostom mentions this in his exposition of this passage.

units.la: Postremò, cùm describitur Christus sedens ad dextram maiestatis in excelsis, intelligere debemus, nobis quoq; propter eundem Christum sedem ibi esse paratam, vt habetur Ephes.1. & nos cum illo iudicaturos orbem, vt 1. Cor.6. Debemus nos consideratione eiusdem gnitatis Christi confirmare in periculis, sicut confirmabatur Stephanus, Actor. 7. Deniq; admonemur illum iudicem nobis placatum auidè expectare.
units.tr: Finally, when Christ is described as "sitting at the right hand of majesty on high," we must understand that a place there has also been prepared for us because of that same Christ, as is stated in Ephesians 1, and that we will judge the world with him, as in 1 Corinthians 6. By considering the same dignity of Christ we ought to be strengthened in dangers, just as Stephen was strengthened (Acts 7). Finally, we are reminded to look eagerly for that Judge, who is reconciled to us.

units.la: Locus de communicatione Idiomatum.
units.tr: Locus de communicatione Idiomatum.

units.la: Quia verò inter enarrandum aliquoties indicauimus, quomodo quædam conueniat Christo, secundum diuinam naturam tantùm: quædam tantùm secundum humanam, quædam secundum vtramq;: nec non obiter mentionem fecimus communicationis idiomatum, visum est quedam huc pertinentia, breuiter adnotare. Vt autem locos de Christo in Scripturis obuios expeditius possimus interpretari, aduertendum est, quòd quemadmodum homo constat duabus substantijs anima & corpore, & nihilominus vnus tantùm manet homo: Ita Christus constat duabus naturis, diuina & humana, & tamen vna tantùm est persona, siue vnus tantùm Christus. Vnde Augustinus in Enchiridio ad Laurentium, capite 34. Quemadmodum est vna persona quilibet homo, anima scilicet rationalis & caro: Ita sit Christus vna persona, verbum & caro. Et Athanasius in Symbolo: Sicut anima rationalis & caro vnus est homo: Ita Deus & homo vnus est Christus. Ad hæc sicut vtraque substantia in homine, sic suam retinet proprietatem, vt altera alteri non permisceatur, (neque enim anima est corpus, neque neq; corpus est anima) Ita vtraq; natura in Christo sic retinet suâ proprietatē, vt inter se nequaquâ confundantur. Iam verò vt quædâ de homine dicuntur, quæ dun taxat cŏue niunt ei secundū animam, vt intelligere, ratiocinari, dolere, gaudere: quædâ verò, dūta- xat conueniunt secundū corpus, vt frigere, sudare, currere, stare, vulnerari: & dicimus, homo mo intelligit, homo est vulneratus, ibi de anima, hic de corpore. Ita in Scripturis quæ- dam de Christo proferuntur, quæ ei non competunt nisi secūdum diuinitatem: vt quòd erat in principio, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi: quòd per ipsum condita sint secula: quòd sit primogenitus vniuersæ creaturæ: denique omnia illa, quibus ostenditur Patri æqualis. Quædam verò, quæ ei non competunt, nisi secundum humanam natu- ram: vt, vbi formam serui habens, nostrarum miseriarum particeps, esuriens, flens, fugi- ens pericula, formidàs mortem, exclamans, moriens, deniq;, quocunq; modo patre in- ferior describitur. Itaque ad explicandos hos locos, tenenda est regula, quam Augustinus habet lib. 1. de Trinitate cap. 15. Cùm de Christo loquimur, quid, secundum quid, & propter quid dicatur, prudens & pius lector intelligere debet. Et eodem libro capi- te 11. Distinguendum, quid sonet secundùm formam Dei, id qua æqualis est patri, & quid secundùm formam serui, in qua minor est patre.
units.tr: Since in the course of our exposition we have several times pointed out how certain things belong to Christ according to the divine nature alone, certain things according to the human nature alone, and certain things according to both, and since we have also touched in passing on the communication of idioms, it seemed good to note briefly some points that pertain here. So that we may more readily interpret the passages about Christ that occur in the Scriptures, we must observe that just as a man consists of two substances, soul and body, and yet remains only one man, so Christ consists of two natures, divine and human, and yet is only one person, or one Christ. Hence Augustine in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 34: "As every man is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, Word and flesh." And Athanasius in the Creed: "As rational soul and flesh is one man, so God and man is one Christ." Moreover, just as in a man each substance keeps its own property, so that the one is not mingled with the other (for the soul is not the body, nor the body the soul), so in Christ each nature keeps its own property, so that they are by no means confused with each other. Now, just as some things are said of a man that belong to him only according to the soul, such as to understand, to reason, to grieve, to rejoice; and other things belong to him only according to the body, such as to grow cold, to sweat, to run, to stand, to be wounded; and we say, "the man understands" (of the soul here) and "the man is wounded" (of the body there), so in the Scriptures some things are said of Christ that belong to him only according to his divinity: that he was in the beginning before the foundations of the world were laid; that the ages were made through him; that he is the firstborn of all creation; and finally all those things by which he is shown to be equal to the Father. But some things belong to him only according to his human nature: as when, "having the form of a servant," sharing in our miseries, hungry, weeping, fleeing dangers, fearing death, crying out, dying, and finally, in whatever way, he is described as inferior to the Father. Therefore, to explain these passages we must hold to the rule which Augustine gives in book 1 of On the Trinity, chapter 15: "When we speak of Christ, the prudent and pious reader ought to understand what is said, in respect of what, and on account of what." And in the same book, chapter 11: "We must distinguish what is said according to the form of God, by which he is equal to the Father, and what according to the form of a servant, in which he is less than the Father."

units.la: Rursus, vt quædam dicuntur de homine, quæ neque de corpore, neque de anima sef- orsim considerata rectè possunt accipi, atq; interdū quę propria sunt animæ, transferun- tur ad corpus: atque è diuerso quæ propria sunt corporis, ad animam: quasi hæ subftan- tiæ sibi inuicem suas proprietates accommodarent: ac tùm quidem opus est eiusmodi locutionum formulas de toto homine explicari. Ita in Scripturis quoque de Christo nonnulla dicuntur, quæ neque de diuina natura, neque de humana seorsim considerata recte exponi queant: sed nonnunquam quæ diuinitatis sunt, tribuuntur humanitati, & è contrario quæ humanitatis sunt, tribuunt diuinitati, tanquam si naturæ sibi inuicem suas proprietates communicarent. Quod vbi euenit, decet eos locos de tota Christi persona exponere. Huc pertinent illa 1. ad Corinthios 2. vbi dicitur, Dominum gloriæ crucifixum. Item Actorum vigesimo, Attendite grægi ecclesiæ Dei, quam acquisiuit suo sanguine. Item 1. Ioan. 3. per hoc cognouimus charitatem Dei, quoniam ille animam suam pro nobis posuit. Qui loci quoniam non possunt de altera tantùm natura accipi, quandoquidem in subiecto sunt, quæ diuinitatem sonant, in prædicato verò quæ humanitatem, adeoque quæ humanitati propria sunt, tribuuntur diuinitati, quali naturæ permiscerentur: sunt exponendi de tota Christi persona, in hunc modum. Persona illa, quæ est Deus atque etiam homo, hæc, inquam persona, mortem crucis sufbijt, ecclesiam acquisiuit suo sanguine, animam suam siue corpus pro nobis posuit. Sic etiam alias eius generis propositiones exponemus, nequaquam confundentes naturas: sed eas potius in vna natura vnitas intelligemus, propositiones verò ipsas integras ad vnam referamus personam. Atque in huiusmodi propositionibus, ob id, quòd naturæ videntur permisceri, & quę vni naturæ propria sunt, tribuuntur seu communicantur alteri, tropus ille est, quem passim vocant <bl>κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων</bl>, communicationem proprietatum, qui diligenter obseruandus est ad explicandos eos locos, qui de Christo sonant, atque spinositatis aliquid obscuritatisq; habent. De quo plura apud Augustinum lib. 1. & alios: de Trinitate. Item epistola 57. ad Dardanum. Item lib. 2. ad Simplicianum, quæstione secunda. Præterea apud Damascenum lib. 3. Theologiæ. Chrysostomus item expo nens illud, quod paulò post sequitur, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, ait Christum filium Dei dici, non tantùm vt est ante secula genitus, sed etiam vt secundum carnem in seculo est natus. Etenim caro, inquit, communicat altioribus, sicut & diuinitas humilioribus communicare dignata est. Qui enim non est homo fieri dedignatus, & qui rem ipsam non abnuit, quomodo ipsa repudiaturus est verba? Ita Chrysostomus.
units.tr: Again, just as some things are said of a man that cannot rightly be understood of the body or of the soul considered separately, and sometimes what is proper to the soul is transferred to the body, and conversely what is proper to the body to the soul, as if these substances accommodated their properties to one another; so in such cases the expressions must be explained of the whole man. Likewise in the Scriptures some things are said of Christ which cannot rightly be explained of the divine nature or of the human nature considered separately; but sometimes what belongs to the divinity is attributed to the humanity, and conversely what belongs to the humanity is attributed to the divinity, as if the natures communicated their properties to one another. When this occurs, those passages ought to be explained of the whole person of Christ. To this belong those words of 1 Corinthians 2, where it is said that the Lord of glory was crucified; likewise Acts 20: "Attend to the flock of God, which he acquired with his own blood"; likewise 1 John 3: "By this we have known the love of God, because he laid down his life for us." Since these passages cannot be understood of only one nature, inasmuch as the subject terms signify the divinity while the predicate terms signify the humanity, and what is proper to the humanity is attributed to the divinity as though the natures were mixed, they must be explained of the whole person of Christ in this way: that person who is God and also man, this person, I say, suffered the death of the cross, acquired the Church with his own blood, laid down his soul or body for us. In this way we will also explain other propositions of this kind, by no means confusing the natures; rather we will understand them as united in one nature, and refer the propositions themselves, entire, to one person. And in propositions of this sort, because the natures seem to be mixed, and what is proper to one nature is attributed or communicated to the other, that figure of speech which they commonly call <bl>κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων</bl> [communicatio idiomatum], the communication of properties, is used. It must be carefully observed in explaining those passages about Christ which sound harsh and have some obscurity. More on this may be found in Augustine, On the Trinity, book 1, and elsewhere; likewise in letter 57 to Dardanus; likewise book 2 to Simplicianus, question 2; besides in Damascene, Theology, book 3. Chrysostom too, expounding what follows shortly, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you," says that Christ is called Son of God not only as he was begotten before the ages, but also as he was born in time according to the flesh. For, he says, the flesh shares in the higher things, just as the divinity has deigned to share in the lowly things. For he who did not disdain to become man, and did not refuse the thing itself, how will he reject the words? So Chrysostom.

units.la: Harum duarum regularum inscitia factum est, vt multi errores in ecclesiam irrepserint. Nestorius naturas non distinguens, sed distrahens, duplicem Christum commini- scebatur, & vnitatem personæ auferebat. E contra Eutyches, dum voluit vnitatem perso- ne seruare, vtramque naturam sustulit. Alij diuinitate Christo ademerunt, dum in ea tan- tùm respiciunt, quæ humanæ naturæ in Christo conueniunt. Alij rursus humanitatem sustulerunt, ea tantùm considerantes, quæ Christum Deum constituunt. Sed grauissi- mi & fœdissimi hi errores facile confutantur, ab eo, qui duas regulas traditas rectè intel- lexerit.
units.tr: From ignorance of these two rules many errors have crept into the Church. Nestorius, not distinguishing but dividing the natures, devised a double Christ and took away the unity of the person. On the other hand Eutyches, while wishing to preserve the unity of the person, removed both natures. Others took away the divinity from Christ, while regarding only those things that belong to the human nature in Christ. Others again abolished the humanity, considering only those things that constitute Christ as God. But these most serious and foul errors are easily refuted by one who has rightly understood the two rules that have been handed down.

units.la: Augustinus in Enchiridio ad Laurentium cap. 36. ait, Christum, vt Deus est & homo, vnitis licet non confusis naturis constans, dominū nostrum vnumq; Dei filium esse etiam secundum humanitatem, et si non ratione humanitatis.
units.tr: Augustine in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 36, says that Christ, who consists of the two natures, united yet not confused, as God and man, is our one Lord and the one Son of God also according to the humanity, even though not by reason of the humanity.

units.la: Natura non communicatur aut confundantur. Quid Christo secundum diuinitatem competat. Quid Christo secundum humanitatem tribuatur. Prima regula Augustini lib. 1. de Trinitat. cap. 15. Communicatio proprietatum qualis sit. Simile ab anima et corpore. Quaenam toti personae Christi tribuantur. 2 regula de communicatione idiomatum. Tropus ἀντιδοσις varius. Infelicia peperit errores. Nestorij error. Eutiches. Augustinus.
units.tr: The natures are not communicated or confused. What belongs to Christ according to the divinity. What is attributed to Christ according to the humanity. The first rule of Augustine, On the Trinity, book 1, chapter 15. What the communication of properties is like. A likeness from soul and body. What things are attributed to the whole person of Christ. The second rule concerning the communication of idioms. The trope antidosis, various. Unfortunate ones produced errors. The error of Nestorius. Eutyches. Augustine.

units.la: CONFIRMATIO.
units.tr: CONFIRMATION.

units.la: Tanto praestantior factus angelis, quanto excellentius prae illis sortitus est nomen. Nam cui dixit unquam angelorum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Ac rursum: Ego ero ei pater, & ille erit mihi filius. Rursum autem, &c.
units.tr: So much better than the angels has he become, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son, today I have begotten you? And again: I will be his father, and he will be my son. And again, etc.

units.la: Sequitur confirmatio, in qua varia congerit argumenta, quibus probatur Christum esse Dei filium verumq; Deum. Sed hac confirmatione nequaquam vsitato confirmandi more, sed quadam potius forma collationis instituit: quod qui fiat, perfacile intelligemus, si ad quos scripserit aduertamus. Scripsit aute ad Hebraeos, homines supra quam dici posset, infensos & infestos Christiano nomini & vniuerso euangelio, qui nunquam ò adducti poterant, vt Christum esse Deum confiteretur. Nam qui vel modestissimi erant inter illos, & de Christo prae caeteris sentiebant honorificentius, hoc solum concedebat, nimirum, Christum insignem quidem & admodum excellente virtum, praeclaris donis supra communem hominum sorte illustratum, ac tale prorsus, qui aut pro angelo diuinitus missus, aut pro eximio propheta, qualis erat Moses, agnosci posset: (ita enim cum angelis aut Mose haud grauatim conferebant) at vero eundem esse Deum, quiduis potius quam istud erant admissuri. Propter horum igitur hominum peruicaciam, & iniquissimum de Christo iudicium, apostolus argumenta sua non ita in ordine redigit, vt nude tantum exponat, perpetuo decursu & vsitata confirmationum formula, Christum esse Deum; sed, quia videbatur ita poscere, collatione instituit, in qua valde artificiose Christum cum angelis & Mose confert: sed ita semper concludens, vt efficacissimis & clarissimis Scripturae testimonijs coiungat, Christum non modo illi superiorem esse, sed plane Deum ac Dei filium. Qua ratione non solum probat confirmatq;, quod in confirmatione maxime agi decebat, videlicet Christum esse Deum: sed praeterea singulis argumentis aperte refellit iniquas aduersariorum de Christo opiniones.
units.tr: Next comes the confirmation, in which he gathers various arguments to prove that Christ is the Son of God and true God. But he does not set out this confirmation in the usual manner of confirming. He arranges it rather in the form of a comparison. We will easily understand why, if we notice to whom he is writing. He wrote to the Hebrews, men more hostile than can be said to the Christian name and to the whole gospel, who could never be brought to confess that Christ is God. Even the most moderate of them, who thought more highly of Christ than the rest, granted only this: that Christ was an outstanding man of very great virtue, adorned with excellent gifts beyond the common lot of men, and that he was such that he could be recognised as either an angel sent from God or an extraordinary prophet like Moses. (They did not hesitate to compare him with angels or Moses in this way.) But that he was God, they would admit anything rather than that. Because of the obstinacy of these men and their most unjust judgment about Christ, the apostle does not arrange his arguments so as simply to set forth, in one continuous course and in the usual formula of confirmations, that Christ is God. Instead, since the situation seemed to demand it, he constructs a comparison, in which he very skilfully compares Christ with the angels and Moses. But he always concludes in such a way as to join the most effective and clearest testimonies of Scripture, showing that Christ is not only superior to them but plainly God and the Son of God. By this method he not only proves and confirms what a confirmation ought chiefly to do, namely that Christ is God, but also, with each argument, openly refutes the unjust opinions of the opponents about Christ.

units.la: Sane Apostolus, vt erat summus in scribendis epistolis gravibus & sublimibus artifex, probe sciebat, quomodo oratio esset attemperanda eorum, ad quos scribebat ingenijs, & quid status ecclesiarum posceret, prudeter animaduertebat, id quod ex alijs epistolis licet colligere. Nam in epistola ad Romanos & Galatas, apud quos contra eos, qui legem conabatur ceu ad salutem necessariam euangelio permiscere, neruosas habet confirmationes, in quibus nuda argumenta probantia iustificationem per fidem absq; operibus Legis, ordinatissime collocat.
units.tr: Certainly the apostle, being a supreme craftsman in writing weighty and lofty epistles, knew well how the style should be adapted to the minds of those to whom he wrote, and he wisely noted what the condition of the churches required, as may be gathered from his other epistles. For in the epistles to the Romans and the Galatians, where he was opposing those who tried to mix the law with the gospel as if it were necessary for salvation, he has vigorous confirmations, in which he most orderly arranges bare arguments proving justification through faith without the works of the law.

units.la: Scribens ad Ephesios foeliciter in doctrina religionis edoctos, nullam adhibet confirmationem, sed satis esse putat, breuiter & clare praecipua capita doctrinae euangelicae de iustitia per fidem in Christum, recensere, & reuocare in memoriam, quae illi antea recte acceperant. Epistola ad Colossenses, etiamsi velut Epitome sit illius ad Ephesios, tamen quia non idem prorsus erat ecclesiae Colossensium status, qui Ephesiorum, habet primo simplice expositione doctrinae Christianae de reconciliatione propter solam Christum. Sed additur deinde confirmatio, neq; haec constans argumentis didacticis, qualia erant in epistola ad Romanos & Galatas. Sed tantum suasoris, quibus ad perstandum in doctrina semel accepta eos animat.
units.tr: Writing to the Ephesians, who had been happily instructed in the doctrine of religion, he adds no confirmation. He thinks it enough to recall briefly and clearly the chief heads of the evangelical doctrine concerning righteousness through faith in Christ, and to bring back to memory what they had already rightly received. The epistle to the Colossians, although it is in a way an epitome of that to the Ephesians, nevertheless, because the condition of the church of the Colossians was not altogether the same as that of the Ephesians, begins with a simple exposition of Christian doctrine concerning reconciliation through Christ alone. But then a confirmation is added, and this does not consist of didactic arguments such as those in the epistle to the Romans and Galatians, but only of exhortations, by which he encourages them to persevere in the doctrine once received.

units.la: Quin adiecit & cofutatione, propter eos, qui partim legem Mosaicam, partim superstitiosos ritus gentilium, volebant euangelio permiscere. Par igitur prudentia & consilio apostolus explorata habens Iudaeorum ingenia, & scies, quam siniistre de Christo iudicarent, vtpote quem vix cum angelis aut Mose conferebant conferendum: voluit quidem in confirmatione sua, id quod praecipue spectandum erat, probare, Christum videlicet verum esse Deum, ac Dei filium: sed eadem opera retundere ineptam & improbam Christi cum angelis vel Mose collationem. Sic igitur confirmationem hanc auspicatur.
units.tr: Indeed he also added a refutation, on account of those who wished to mix partly the Mosaic law and partly the superstitious rites of the Gentiles with the gospel. Therefore the apostle, having equal prudence and counsel, and knowing the mentality of the Jews and how perversely they judged about Christ, since they scarcely compared him with anything but angels or Moses, wished in his confirmation to prove what was chiefly to be attended to, namely that Christ is truly God and the Son of God. At the same time, however, he wished to refute the absurd and wicked comparison of Christ with angels or Moses. Thus he begins this confirmation.

units.la: Tanto praestantior factus angelis, quanto excellentius prae illis sortitus est nomen.
units.tr: So much better than the angels has he become, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.

units.la: Initium est collationis Christi cum angelis, quam per totam fere confirmationem prosequitur. Est q; sententia: Quoufq; tandem vos negatis Christum esse Deum, & contenditis, eum esse duntaxat, vel angelum inter homines versatum, vel hominem angelis aequari dignum? Ego vero affero & luculenter probabo, eum esse omnibus etiam angelis praestantiorem, ac tanto quidem praestantiorem, quanto is prae illis excellentius nomen, potentiam, gloriam, dignitatem, est sortitus. Haec mihi videtur simplex & germana esse sententia. Etiamsi me non fugiat, ita adhuc posse haec verba explicari, vt non solum habeantur pro collationis instituendae initio: sed contineant in se validum argumentum, duo tum ab ipsa nominum Christi, & angelorum ratione, quasi diceretur: Ipsum nomen, quod est Iesus, indicat multo excellentiorem esse eum, quam sint angeli. Nam Iesus significat seruatorem, sicut Matthaeus clare dicitur per angelum, Vocabis nomen eius Iesum, ipse enim saluum faciet populum suum à peccatis.Sed tale nomen nunquam fuit inditum angelorum,qui dantaxat sunt misi siue nuncij,si nomen eorum spectemus. Ergo Christus est angelis multò praestantior. Vis argumenti aptè sumpta videtur ex ipsa nominum ratione, sicut Rhetores etiam docent, argumenta ex proprietate nominum,& vi verbi colligere.Et tritum est illud, Conueniunt rebus nomina saepè suis. Putarunt veteres, ipsis nominibus respondere hominum ingenia,mores,fortunam.In hunc modum fortasis non male explicetur verba Pauli:Sed quia ad finem huius capitis idem fere habetur argumentū, de appellatione videlicet & officio angelorū, vbi dicitur, omnes eos esse administratorios spiritus,haud scio,an hoc loco commeniat simile argumentum instituere.Graece est,τοσούτῳ κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων, ὅσῳ διαφορώτερον ὤνομα κεκληρονόμηκεν: Dicitur Christus γενόμενος, id est, factus, pro eo, quod est, agnitus habitus, suscep-tus:quod ita exponit Chrysostomus,itè Primasius:ne videlicet ex eo,quòd diceretur factus, animo conciperet quispiam, quod Christi dignitati minus conueniret, qui potius genitus secundum diuinitatem dicitur,quàm factus. Et vt factus, siue in tempore natus, secundum humanam naturam non videtur angelis esse superior:qua tamen de re paulo post dicemus clarius, vbi secundum quam naturam Christus angelis sit superior, declarabimus. Etiamsi de diuinitate, Factum esse, dici posse videatur. Nam Ioan. 1. Baptista de Christo ait,ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν,qui ante me factus est, vt nonnulli vertere maluerunt. Quod visum est obiter adijcere, ne quis suspicetur parum aptas voces huic loco adhibitas. Διαφορώτερον verterunt excellentius. Nam licet διαφέρειν significet & differre & praeeminere, tamen hoc loco de praeeminentia accipiendum est. Nomen verò hic positum existimo non simpliciter pro certa aliqua voce,qua Christus quasi proprio nomine appellatur, cuiusmodi est nomen Iesu, aut Christi, &c. Sed vt multis aliis locis Scripturae,pro potentia,dignitate,gloria,maiestate,quae ei propter diuinitatem competit. Sic Psal. 9. Exaudiat te Dominus in die tribulationis, protegat te nomen Dei Iacob,id est, virtus,potentia Dei. Psalmo 8. Domine Dominus noster,quàm admirabile est nomen tuum in vniuersa terra? Actor. 9. de Paulo, Organum electum est mihi iste, vt portet nomen meum coram gentibus & regibus,ac filijs Israel. Vbi portare nomen, significat propagare euangelium,celebrare & illustrem reddere apud homines Dei bonitatem, potentiam, maiestatem , quia ille dignatus est nos saluos facere,ac virtutem Dei notam vbique reddere. Et cùm dicitur Actor. 4. Non est aliud nomen sub caelo datum inter homines,in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri,significatur, non alterius virtute, potentia,posse nos saluos fieri,quàm virtute Christi. Et respicit haec vox ad id, quòd suprà Christus dicitur filius constitutus haeres omnium.Itaque haec perspicua erit Apostoli sententia praesenti loco, Christum videlicet tantò excellentiorem debere agnosci omnibus angelis,quantò reuera amplior est eius potestas,virtus, dignitas,gloria, quae ille non per gratiam accepit,sed velut iure haereditario. Quanquam non desunt,qui de nominibus, quibus Christus appellatur, accipiant, quae nomina variam & multiplicem eius potestatem ac dignitatem exprimunt. Atque huiusmodi nomina plura hoc vno capite recensentur (11. vel 12.) quae singula mirabilem dignitatem Christi declarant. Nam filius Dei statim hic appellatur: deinde primogenitus: tum creator angelorum: hinc thronum habens communem cum Deo, & virgam seu sceptrum gerens : unctus à Deo:fundamenta iaciens terrae,fabricator coeli:idè permanens,incommutabilis,& nunquam deficiens : sedens à dextris Dei: victor & triumphator,pedibus substratos habens omnes aduersarios. Quae sanè nomina Christi sunt multò praeclarissima, atque omnibus titulis regum,principum,addam angelorum,multo splendidiora, ac prorsus significant,longè ampliora competere Christo, quàm competere possent angelis,quibus eadem nomina nusquam in Scripturis tribuuntur. Sed prior interpretatio, quam reddimus,simplicior est & purior. Porrò vbi interpres reddidit Sortitus est,quia graecè habetur κεκληρονόμηκεν, & κληρονομέω proprie significat haereditatem accipio, sonantius erit & aptius ad exprimendam Christi dignitatem, si dicamus, Christum haereditate accepisse praestantius nomen. Haereditas enim subindicat, quòdiure quodam contingat Christo tanta dignitas,euidentius q; exprimit,Christum esse Dei filium naturalem , cui veluti haereditario iure competat etiam dignitas Dei patris:sicut secundum humanas leges filij naturales succedunt haereditario iure in bona paterna,longè alia ratione, quàm filij adoptati accipiunt reliquorum bonorum portionem.
units.tr: This is the beginning of the comparison of Christ with the angels, which he pursues through almost the whole confirmation. The sense is this: How long will you deny that Christ is God, and contend that he is only an angel who has lived among men, or a man worthy to be equated with the angels? I, however, affirm and will clearly prove that he is more excellent than all the angels, and indeed by as much as he has inherited a more excellent name, power, glory and dignity than they. This seems to me to be the simple and genuine meaning. Yet I do not overlook that these words can also be explained so that they are not only regarded as the opening of the comparison to be made, but also contain within them a strong argument, drawn both from the meaning of the name of Christ and from the nature of the angels, as if it were said: the very name, which is Jesus, shows that he is far more excellent than the angels. For Jesus means Saviour, as Matthew clearly says of the angel: You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1). But such a name was never given to the angels, who, if we consider their name, are only sent or messengers. Therefore Christ is far more excellent than the angels. The force of this argument seems to be rightly taken from the very meaning of the names, as the rhetoricians also teach, that arguments may be drawn from the property of names and the force of words. And that saying is common: names often correspond to things. The ancients thought that men's natures, morals and fortunes correspond to their very names. In this way perhaps the words of Paul may not badly be explained. But since at the end of this chapter there is nearly the same argument, namely concerning the title and office of the angels, where it is said that they are all ministering spirits, I do not know whether it is fitting in this place to set up a similar argument. The Greek is τοσούτῳ κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων, ὅσῳ διαφορώτερον ὤνομα κεκληρονόμηκεν. Christ is said γενόμενος, that is, "having become", for "having been acknowledged, held, received"; Chrysostom so explains it, and so too Primasius, lest anyone, from the word "became", should conceive that it was less fitting to the dignity of Christ, who is said to be begotten rather than made according to his divinity. And that he "became", or was born in time, according to human nature, does not seem to make him superior to the angels; but we will say more clearly, a little later, in respect of what nature Christ is superior to the angels. Although it may seem that "having become" can be said even of his divinity. For in John 1 the Baptist says of Christ: ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν, "he who comes after me has become before me", as some have preferred to translate. I have thought it worth adding this in passing, so that no one may suspect that words have been used here that are not fitting. Διαφορώτερον they have translated "more excellent". For although διαφέρειν means both to differ and to surpass, here it must be taken in the sense of surpassing. I think the word "name" is used here not simply for some particular term by which Christ is called as by a proper name, such as the name Jesus or Christ, and so on, but, as in many other places of Scripture, for the power, dignity, glory and majesty that belong to him on account of his divinity. So in Psalm 9: May the Lord hear you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you, that is, the power and might of God. Psalm 8: O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth! Acts 9, of Paul: This man is a chosen vessel to me, to bear my name before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel, where to bear the name means to spread the gospel, and to celebrate and make known among men the goodness, power and majesty of God, because he has deigned to save us and to make the power of God known everywhere. And when it is said in Acts 4: There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, it is signified that we can be saved by no other virtue or power than the virtue of Christ. And this word refers to what was said above, that Christ was appointed heir of all things. Thus this will be the clear meaning of the apostle in the present passage: Christ must be acknowledged as far more excellent than all the angels, by as much as his power, virtue, dignity and glory are truly greater, which he has received not by grace but as it were by hereditary right. Yet there are some who take the words to refer to the names by which Christ is called, which express his manifold power and dignity. And several such names are listed in this one chapter (eleven or twelve), each of which declares the wonderful dignity of Christ. For he is immediately called the Son of God; then the firstborn; then the creator of the angels; then, having a throne in common with God and bearing a rod or sceptre; anointed by God; laying the foundations of the earth, the maker of heaven; therefore remaining, unchangeable and never failing; sitting at the right hand of God; victor and triumphant, having all his adversaries placed under his feet. These names of Christ are indeed most illustrious, and far more splendid than all the titles of kings and princes, and I would add of angels; and they plainly signify that these things belong to Christ far more widely than they could belong to the angels, to whom these same names are nowhere in Scripture attributed. But the former interpretation, which we give, is simpler and purer. Furthermore, where the translator has rendered "has obtained", because the Greek has κεκληρονόμηκεν, and κληρονομέω properly means to receive an inheritance, it will sound more fittingly and better express the dignity of Christ if we say that Christ has received by inheritance a more excellent name. For "inheritance" implies that such dignity falls to Christ by a certain right, and it more clearly expresses that Christ is the natural Son of God, to whom the dignity of the Father belongs by hereditary right, just as, according to human laws, natural sons succeed by hereditary right to their father's goods, in a very different way from adopted sons, who receive only a portion of the remaining goods.

units.la: Caeterum in eandem sententiam alibi quoque dicitur Christo excellentissimum esse datum nomen, vt Philippensi. 2. Deus illum extulit in summam sublimitatem, ac donauit illi nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, vt in nomine Iesu omne genu se flectat, caelestium... cœlestium ac terrestrium, & infernorum, omnisq; lingua confiteatur, quòd Dominus noster Iesus Christus ad gloriam Dei patris. Huc item pertinet Ephesiorum primo, vbi dicitur, Christum sedere ad dexteram patris in cœlestibus, supra omnem principatum ac potestatem, & virtutem, & dominium, & omne nomen, quod nominatur, non solùm in seculo hoc, verùm etiam in futuro. Vbi tantundem significatur, ac si diceretur, Christum multò excellentiorem omnibus angelis. Item illud, quod supra retulimus ex Actorum quarto.
units.tr: Moreover, the same idea is stated elsewhere, that the most excellent name has been given to Christ, as in Philippians 2: "God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is to the glory of God the Father." To the same effect belongs Ephesians 1, where Christ is said to sit at the right hand of the Father in the heavenly places, above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. Here the meaning is the same as if it were said that Christ is far more excellent than all angels. Likewise, the passage we cited above from Acts 4.

units.la: Competit autem hæc excellentia Christo præ angelis, non tantùm secundum diuinam naturam, secundum quam eum præstantiorem esse omnibus creaturis, non est dubium: sed etiam secundum humanam naturam: quòd quidam colligunt exeo, quòd hic dicitur Christus γενόμενος, id est, factus, quippe qui factus dici non possit, nisi secundum humanam naturam. Sed magis illud hic nos mouebit, quòd Christus etiam secundum humanam naturam sedeat ad dexteram Dei in excelsis, & donatus sit, vt Philippensibus dicitur, nomine, quod est supra omne nomen. Vnde & Primasius recte ait: Ipse quoq; homo in hoc est maior omnibus angelis, omni creatura, quia potestas, quæ erat in omni à verbo ante omnia secula, requieuit in illo homine assumpto verbo, ex tempore conceptionis. Quòd si obiiciatur illud, quod alibi psalm. 8. dicitur de Christo, quòd paulò minor factus sit angelis, qui locus etiam sequenti capite ad imminuendam Christi dignitatem videtur in persona aduersariorum citatus: Responderet, in Christo vt homine, duo considerari: nempe infirmitatem carnis, qua ille doluit, tristatus est, esuriuit, fleuit, mortuus est: & secundum hanc certum est angelis factum inferiorem. Sed rursus fuit in illo donorum amplissimorum multitudo, de quo est illud Ioan. primo: Et sermo ille caro factus est, & habitauit in nobis, & conspeximus gloriam eius, gloriam velut vnigeniti à patre, plenus gratia & veritate. Itaque secundum hanc plenitudinem & gloriam, Christus vt homo, recte dicitur etiam angelis superior. Quò pertinet, quod Chrysostomus hoc loco pluribus verbis ait: Hic iam de eo, inquit, qui secundum carnem est, disputat. Illa enim essentia, quæ patris consubstantialis agnoscitur, non est facta, sed genita. Carnalis autem substantia facta est. Sed ad argumenta quibus probatur, Christum esse angelis superiorem ac verum Deum, progrediamur.
units.tr: This excellence belongs to Christ above the angels not only according to the divine nature, according to which there is no doubt that he is more excellent than all creatures, but also according to the human nature. Some infer this from the fact that here Christ is said to have become [γενόμενος], that is, "made," which could not be said of him except according to the human nature. But what will move us more here is that Christ, also according to the human nature, sits at the right hand of God on high and has been given, as the Philippians passage says, the name that is above every name. Hence Primasius also rightly says: "Even as man, he is greater than all the angels and every creature, because the power which was in the Word from before all ages rested in that man whom the Word assumed, from the time of his conception." But if it is objected that what is said of Christ in Psalm 8, that he was made a little lower than the angels, which passage in the next chapter also appears to be cited by our opponents to diminish Christ's dignity, we answer: in Christ as man two things are to be considered, namely the weakness of the flesh, by which he suffered, was saddened, hungered, wept, and died; and according to this it is certain that he was made lower than the angels. But in him there was again a great multitude of most ample gifts, of which that is written in John 1: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." Therefore, according to this fullness and glory, Christ as man is rightly said to be even superior to the angels. To this pertains what Chrysostom says on this passage at greater length: "Here he is now speaking," he says, "of him who is according to the flesh. For that essence which is acknowledged as consubstantial with the Father was not made but begotten; but the carnal substance was made." But let us proceed to the arguments by which it is proved that Christ is superior to the angels and is the true God.

units.la: Nam cui dixit vnquam angelorum: filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te?
units.tr: For to which of the angels did he ever say: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you"?

units.la: Primum argumentum è psalmo secundo, quo probat, Christum angelis esse præstantiorem.
units.tr: The first argument is from the second Psalm, by which he proves that Christ is more excellent than the angels.

units.la: Maior est, qui vocatur filius, quàm qui vocatur tātùm minister, vel alio simili nomine.
units.tr: He who is called Son is greater than he who is called only a minister, or by some other similar name.

units.la: Atqui in Scriptura, psalmo secundo, Christus vocatur filius, angeli autem non ita, sed tantùm ministri, vel simili nomine.
units.tr: But in Scripture, in Psalm 2, Christ is called Son, whereas the angels are not so called, but only ministers or by a similar name.

units.la: Igitur Christus est angelis multò maior.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is far greater than the angels.

units.la: Quod argumentum ita formatum est ab apostolo, vt non solùm concludat simpliciter Christum esse maiorem angelis, sed clarè & apertè conuincit, filium esse Dei, & quidem naturalem. Ac vide hic mirabilem Pauli prudentiam. Non putauit satis fore, si tantùm probaret, Christum angelis superiorem, id quod haud dubiè multis aliis modis facere potuisset, nimirum, aut enarrando res à Christo virtute diuina peractas, quales ab angelis nunquam factæ sunt: aut explicando insignem Christi doctrinam, qualis nunquam per angelos fuit tradita: aut alia eiusmodi præclara proferendo: sed singulari consilio & prudentia ea delegit, & quidem è medijs Scripturis testimonia, quæ palàm declarant, Christum esse Dei filium ac verum Deum. Atque ita non tantùm conuellit absurdum iudicium aduersariorum, qui Christum duntaxat conferebant, & æquabant angelis: sed statim quoque probat, Christum esse Dei filium ac verum Deum: id quod debuisset adhuc probare postea, si prius seorsim confutasset absurdam illam Christi cum angelis collationem. Statim ergo id agit, quod ad scopum principalem totius disputationis pertinet, dum primis verbis probat, Christum esse Dei filium verumque Deum.
units.tr: This argument is so framed by the apostle that it not only simply concludes that Christ is greater than the angels, but clearly and openly proves that he is the Son of God, and indeed the natural Son. And here observe Paul's remarkable prudence. He did not think it enough merely to prove that Christ is superior to the angels, which he could doubtless have done in many other ways: namely, by recounting the things Christ performed by divine power, which the angels never did; or by explaining Christ's remarkable teaching, such as was never delivered through angels; or by bringing forward other such outstanding things. Instead, with singular judgment and wisdom he chose testimonies from the midst of the Scriptures, which plainly declare that Christ is the Son of God and true God. And so he not only overturns the absurd judgment of the opponents, who compared Christ merely with the angels and made him equal to them, but at once also proves that Christ is the Son of God and true God, which he would still have had to prove afterwards if he had first separately refuted that absurd comparison of Christ with the angels. He therefore at once does what pertains to the principal aim of the whole discussion, while in the first words he proves that Christ is the Son of God and true God.

units.la: Sed & hoc valde prudenter factum est, quòd mauult Scripturæ testimonijs hanc causam agere, quàm alijs rationibus. Nam ad probandum, Christum superiorem esse angelis, & filium Dei, potuisset adferre, si cut supra dixi, miracula, signa, excellentem doctrinam Christi, quibus plurimi mouebātur ad fatendū, quòd Christus esset filius Dei, sicut Matt. 14. qui erant in naui, postquàm vidissent Christum ambulante super aquas, & Petrum, ne mergeretur, ereptum, accesserunt & adorauerunt, dicentes: Verè Dei filius es. Et Marci qui spiritui immundo erat obnoxius, prouolutus clamabat: Quid mihi tecum est Iesu fili Dei altissimi? Rursus Marci 15. Cùm vidisset autem Centurio, qui astabat ex aduerso illi, quòd sic emisso clamore expirasset, dixit: Verè homo hic filius erat Dei. Et Petrus etiam ante acceptum spiritum sanctum, Matth. 16. Tu es Christus ille filius Dei viuentis. Idem Ioan. 6. cùm multi discipulorum desecuissent à Christo, & Dominus interrogaret suos, num ipsi quoq; vellent abire, respondit Petrus: Domine ad quem ibimus? Verba vitæ æternæ habes, & nos credimus, & cognouimus, quòd tu es Christus filius Dei vi-ui. Item vox patris, Matth. 3. & 17. audita ad Iordanem & in monte Thabor, etc. Ioan. 1. Nathanael ait, Rabi, tu es ille filius Dei, tu es ille rex Israel. Et Ioan. 7. multi de turba dicebant: Hic est uerè propheta: Alij dicebant, hic est Christus, &c. Et Rom. 1. Qui declaratus fuit filius Dei, cum potentia, secundum spiritum sanctificationis, ex eo, quòd resurrexit è mortuis Iesus Christus dominus noster. His, inquam, varijs rationibus & argumentis ductis ab excellenti doctrina, à potentia miraculorum, à collatione Spiritus sancti, à resurrectione, potuisset Paulus demonstrare, Christum esse filium Dei: sed maluit contra duræ ceruicis homines proferre Scripturas, propterea quòd in omni disputatione de rebus diuinis certiora & efficaciora argumenta produci nequeant, quàm ex ipso Dei verbo. Vnde & nos quoq;, quoties de reb. diuinis sermo instituitur, discamus, firmamē taeorum, quæ afferre volumus, ex ipso Dei uerbo scripto potius petere, non ex huma-na philosophia, vel ex hominum decretis. Pudeat, pudeat eos, qui stentorea voce occla-mant nobis vel canones, canones, vel concilia, concilia, uel decreta, decreta: ubi tamen Scripturam sacram non habent eadem confirmantem. Illis liceat obijcere: quando vn-quam tale dictum est Scriptura? Sicut apostolus hic obijcit Iudæis: ita ut efficax hinc argumentum trahere possimus: Scriptura non ita loquitur: Ergo non est ita. Sed & hoc quoque singulari prudentia factum est, quòd disputaturus de diuinitate Christi apostolus aduersus Iudæos, non aliunde profert testimonia, quàm ex veteri testamento, quod solum illi recipiebant. Alias quidem si patribus, vel nobis nunc sit disputandum cum alijs, qui euangelium ex parte agnoscunt, etiam ex euangelicis literis disputationem contexemus.
units.tr: But it was also very wisely done that he preferred to argue this cause by the testimonies of Scripture rather than by other reasons. For to prove that Christ is superior to the angels and the Son of God, he could have adduced, as I said above, miracles, signs, the excellent teaching of Christ, by which very many were moved to confess that Christ was the Son of God. So in Matthew 14, those who were in the boat, after they had seen Christ walking on the waters and Peter, snatched up lest he sink, came and worshipped, saying: "Truly you are the Son of God." And in Mark, the man subject to an unclean spirit, falling prostrate, cried out: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the most high God?" Again, Mark 15: when the centurion who stood opposite him saw that he had breathed out his last with such a cry, he said: "Truly this man was the Son of God." And Peter, even before he received the Holy Spirit, says in Matthew 16: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Likewise in John 6, when many of the disciples had fallen away from Christ and the Lord asked his own whether they too wished to go away, Peter answered: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Likewise the voice of the Father, heard at the Jordan and on Mount Tabor, Matthew 3 and 17, etc. In John 1, Nathanael says: "Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel." And in John 7 many of the crowd were saying: "This is truly the Prophet," others said: "This is the Christ," etc. And in Romans 1: "who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord." These arguments, I say, drawn from his excellent teaching, from the power of his miracles, from the gift of the Holy Spirit, and from the resurrection, Paul could have used to demonstrate that Christ is the Son of God; but he preferred to bring forward Scriptures against stiff-necked men, because in every discussion of divine things, more certain and more effective arguments cannot be produced than from the very Word of God. Hence we too, whenever discussion of divine matters is undertaken, should learn to seek the confirmation of what we wish to advance from the written Word of God itself, not from human philosophy or the decrees of men. Let them be ashamed, let them be ashamed, who shout at us with stentorian voices, "canons, canons," or "councils, councils," or "decrees, decrees," when they have no Holy Scripture confirming the same. Let it be permitted to us to object to them: when was such a thing ever said in Scripture? As the apostle here objects to the Jews, so that we may draw an effective argument from this: Scripture does not speak thus; therefore it is not so. But this too was done with singular prudence, that the apostle, about to dispute with the Jews concerning the divinity of Christ, brings forward testimonies from no other source than the Old Testament, which alone they accepted. Otherwise, if we or the Fathers were now to dispute with others who acknowledge the gospel in part, we would also weave the argument from the evangelical writings.

units.la: Nunc verò quàm efficacia argumenta, & quàm aptè citata sint scripturarum testimo-nia, restat, explicemus. Est igitur hoc primum testimonium atq; argumentum, quo pro-bare uult, Christum esse filium Dei: quòd de Christo, non de homine aliquo aut angelo, sit accipiendum illud è psalmo secundo, tanquam à Deo patre ad Christum dictum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te.
units.tr: Now let us set out how forceful the arguments are and how aptly the testimonies of Scripture are cited. The first testimony and argument, by which he wants to prove that Christ is the Son of God, is this: the words of the second psalm, spoken by God the Father to Christ, You are my Son; today I have begotten you, must be understood of Christ, not of any man or angel.

units.la: Sed istud testimonium Iudæi uolentes etiam in hunc diem infringere, negant sim-pliciter de Christo sermonem eo psalmo fieri, sed omnia accipienda de Dauide rege, qui tum eum considerat, cùm post susceptum diadema à Philistæis & finitimis gentibus grauiter est oppugnatus, nihilominus animo confirmatus est, sibi successum in regno non defuturum, imò & de aduersarijs se reportaturum claras victorias. Atq; hoc ipsum quidem, nempe de Dauide, & caussa Dauidis, in psalmo hoc agi, nos non negamus. Sed tamen si animaduertimus, sanctos illos patres, qualis erat Dauid, afflatos spiritu Sancto, per quem, cùm de rebus suis aliquid canerent aut dicerent, simul moti sunt ad dicendū loquendumque de Christo: sicut multa passim licet uidere, præsertim in psalmis Dauidicis de Christo luculenta vaticinia: præterea si animaduertimus, patribus omnia, ut dicitur 1. Corinth. 10. in figura contigisse, & res per patres gestas ut plurimum typum fuisse & exemplar rerum gerendarum per Christum: intelligemus, non minus certò, imò multo certius aciustius eum psalmum accipiendum de Christo, quàm de Dauide: praeser-tim cùm huius psalmi bonam partem ipse spiritus Sanctus per apostolos de Christo sit interpretatus, ut licet videre Actor. 4. Certum est, spiritus, qui locutus per os Dauidis, psalmum hunc primum canentis, idem locutus est per Petrum hunc psalmum de Christo exponentem: quòd testimonium, quod hoc loco citatur, Actor. 13. à Paulo ipso citatur, ad probandum, Christum esse filium Dei, fit, ut eò lubentius hanc epistolam pro Paulina a gnoscam. Sic autem ibi legitur: Nos vobis annunciamus, quòd ea re promissionem, quæ ad patres facta est, Deus adimpleuerit filijs illorum, nimirum nobis, resuscitato Iesu, sicut & in psalmo secundo scriptum est: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Imò multi Iudæorū ipsi fatentur, psal. hunc de Mesiah vaticinari: sicut Rabi Dauid Kimhi clarè dicit: Sunt, inquit, qui psalmum hunc expo-nunt de Gog & Magog, & de rege Meschiah, quemadmodum interpretati sunt Ra-bini nostri.
units.tr: But the Jews, wishing even to this day to overturn this testimony, simply deny that the psalm speaks of Christ, and say that everything must be taken of King David. They say he composed it when, after receiving the crown, he was severely attacked by the Philistines and the neighbouring nations; nevertheless he was strengthened in spirit, confident that success in his kingdom would not fail him, and that he would even win clear victories over his enemies. We do not deny that this very thing, namely David and David's cause, is treated in this psalm. But if we consider that those holy fathers, such as David was, were inspired by the Holy Spirit, through whom, when they sang or spoke of their own affairs, they were at the same time moved to speak of Christ (as many things can be seen everywhere, especially in the Davidic psalms, which contain clear prophecies of Christ); and further, if we consider that, as is said in 1 Corinthians 10, everything happened to the fathers in figure, and that the deeds done by the fathers were for the most part types and examples of the deeds done by Christ, we shall understand that this psalm must be taken of Christ no less certainly, indeed far more certainly and more accurately, than of David. This is especially so since the Holy Spirit himself, through the apostles, has interpreted a large part of this psalm of Christ, as can be seen in Acts 4. It is certain that the Spirit who spoke through the mouth of David, the first singer of this psalm, also spoke through Peter, expounding this psalm of Christ. And because the testimony cited here is cited by Paul himself in Acts 13 to prove that Christ is the Son of God, I am the more willing to acknowledge this epistle as Pauline. There it reads: "We bring you the good news that God has fulfilled the promise made to the fathers, to their children, namely to us, by raising up Jesus, as also it is written in the second psalm: You are my Son; today I have begotten you." Indeed, many of the Jews themselves admit that this psalm prophesies of the Messiah, as Rabbi David Kimhi clearly says: "There are," he says, "those who expound this psalm of Gog and Magog and of the king Messiah, as our rabbis have interpreted it."

units.la: Idem Rabi Salomon, & Rabi Ezra. Itaq; hoc nos agemus, primùm breuiter aperie-mus, quatenus, quæ hoc psal. habentur, in Dauide copetant: deinde uerò, quòd omnia multò
units.tr: Likewise Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi Ezra. Therefore we shall do this: first we shall briefly set out in what respects the things contained in this psalm fit David, and then we shall show that they must be understood much more fully and justly of Christ.

units.la: {1} Ex verbo Dei efficacissima argumenta de rebus diuinis proferuntur. multò plenius & iustius de Christo sint accipienda, ostendemus. Proinde psalm. sic habet
units.tr: {1} Efficacious arguments about divine things are drawn from the Word of God. Therefore the psalm reads thus:

units.la: Quare fremuerunt gentes, et populi meditati sunt inania? Adstiterunt reges terrae, & principes conuenerunt in unum, aduersus Dominum, & aduersus Christum eius.
units.tr: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the princes take counsel together, against the Lord and against his Anointed.

units.la: Propositio est, seu breuis Narratio de Philistaeis & finitimis Iudaeae populis, quaerentibus nouum regem Dauid perdere: sicut & 2. Regum 5. scribitur. Et audiuerunt Philistaei, quòd unxissent Dauid in regem super Israel, & ascenderunt omnes Philistaei, ut quaerent Dauid.
units.tr: This is the proposition, or brief narrative, about the Philistines and the neighbouring peoples of Judea, who sought to destroy the new king David, as also written in 2 Samuel 5: And the Philistines heard that they had anointed David king over Israel, and all the Philistines went up to seek David.

units.la: Dirumpamus vincula eorum, & proiiciamus a nobis iugum ipsorum) Sunt verba aduersariorum, quae secum meditabantur, & in consultationibus magno cum affectu loquebantur, quasdam Mimesi recitata.
units.tr: "Let us break their bonds asunder and cast off their yoke from us." These are the words of the adversaries, which they were thinking among themselves and speaking with great feeling in their councils, recited in the manner of mimesis.

units.la: Qui habitat in excelsis, irridebit eos & Dominus subsannabit eos: Tunc loquetur ad eos in ira sua, & in furore suo conturbabit eos. Ego autem constitutus sum rex ab eo super Zion montem sanctum eius.
units.tr: He who sits in the heavens will laugh; the Lord will scoff at them. Then he will speak to them in his anger and terrify them in his wrath. But I have been set up as king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.

units.la: Sic iam loquitur ipse rex & propheta Dauid, confidens, auxilio Dei aduersarios omnes prosternendos, omnesque conatus eorum frustrandos: Se vero, quoniam diuinitus esset constitutus rex, & verbi Dei ac synceri cultus diligens obseruator, in dignitate & regno conseruandum. Etiam si postrema verba sic a nonnullis reddantur: Ego constituit gem meum super Sion montem sanctum meum: quasi sint verba ipsius Dei iam quodammodo irridentis stulta consilia & conatus aduersariorum populi Dei, & promittentis, se seruaturum eum regem, quem ipse secundum cor suum virum inuentum, in Zion praefecerat: Deinde sequitur:
units.tr: Here the king and prophet David himself speaks, confident that by God's help all his adversaries would be overthrown and all their attempts frustrated, and that he himself, since he had been made king by divine appointment and was a diligent guardian of the word of God and of pure worship, would be preserved in his dignity and kingdom. Even if some render the last words thus: "I have set my king upon Zion, my holy mountain," as if they were the words of God himself, already in a way mocking the foolish counsels and attempts of the adversaries of God's people, and promising that he will preserve the king whom he himself had found, a man after his own heart, and set over Zion. Then it follows:

units.la: Praedicabo de praecepto, dominus dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te.
units.tr: I will declare the decree: the Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you.

units.la: Haec iterum Dauidi tribuuntur, qui praedicare vult & gloriari, se diuinitus esse regem constitutum, & diuinis promissionibus de successu regni confirmat, illud subinde magno animo iactans, se a Deo esse electum quasi in filium, se a Deo tanquam patre adiuuandum, promouendum, defendendum. Atq; hic interpretantur, Dauid filium Dei dici, qua ratione omnes in genere vocantur filij Dei, qui Deum audiunt, & ei ex animo seruiunt, sicut filij ex animo obtemperant parentibus, quemadmodum & Deut.14. ad omnes dicitur: Filij estis Domini Dei vestri. Item Genes.6. psal.89. Matth.5.1. Ioan.3. pij vocantur filij Dei, sicut & quotidie dicimus ad Deum, Pater noster. Quod vero dicitur, Hodie genitum, intelligi volunt, de eo ipso die, quo Dauid fuit in regem unctus: quo referunt illud 1. Samuel.16. Vbi Dominus dixit Samueli: Surge & unge eum, quia ipse est. Et tulit Samuel cornu olei, & unxit eum in medio fratrum eius, & mansit spiritus Iehouae super Dauidem a die illa: & deinceps: Eo itaq; die genitus intelligitur Dauid, qui in regem est unctus, & spiritu Domini illustratus.
units.tr: These words are again attributed to David, who wishes to proclaim and boast that he has been appointed king by God, and who confirms by divine promises the success of his kingdom, declaring at times with great courage that he has been chosen by God as a son, and that he is to be helped, advanced and defended by God as by a father. Here they interpret that David is called son of God in the way that all in general are called sons of God who hear God and serve him wholeheartedly, just as sons obey their parents from the heart. So Deuteronomy 14 says to all: "You are the sons of the Lord your God." Likewise Genesis 6, Psalm 89, Matthew 5 and John 3: the godly are called sons of God, just as we also daily say to God, "Our Father." But as for the words "today I have begotten," they want them understood of the very day on which David was anointed king, to which they refer that passage of 1 Samuel 16, where the Lord said to Samuel: "Arise and anoint him, for this is he." And Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers, and the Spirit of Jehovah rested upon David from that day forward. Therefore David is understood to have been begotten on that day, when he was anointed king and enlightened by the Spirit of the Lord.

units.la: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam & possessionem tuam terminos terrae. Reges eos in virga ferrea, & tanquam vas figuli confringes eos.
units.tr: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.

units.la: Adhuc verba Dei ad Dauidem, cui Deus pollicetur, si modo ipse postulet, contra aduersarios omnes foelice victoria. Sic quoq; locutus fuerat dominus ad Dauid, ut dicebat Abner ad seniores Israel, 2. Sam.3. in manu serui mei Dauid seruabo populu meum Israel de manu Philistim, & omnium inimicorum eius. Atq; has ipsas promissiones de subactis gentibus & terminis terrae, adimpletas aiunt, quandoquidem 2. Reg.7. dicitur, quòd Dominus dedit requie Dauid undiq; ab uniuersis inimicis suis. Ibidem: Interfeci uniuersos inimicos tuos a facie tua, feciq; tibi nomen grande iuxta nomen magnorum, qui sunt in terra. Mox eiusdem libri cap.8. Dauid describitur triumphasse de Philistaeis, item de Moabitis, quibus & tributa impositum, de Syria superata & tributaria facta, de Idumaeis, Amonitis, Amalecytis, de Adadezere rega Soba. Sequitur:
units.tr: Again these are God's words to David, to whom God promises, if only he asks, a happy victory over all adversaries. The Lord had spoken to David in the same way, as Abner said to the elders of Israel in 2 Samuel 3: "By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and of all their enemies." And these very promises about subdued nations and the ends of the earth they say were fulfilled, since 2 Samuel 7 says that the Lord gave David rest from all his enemies round about. There it is written: "I have destroyed all your enemies before your face, and made you a great name, like the name of the great men who are on the earth." Soon after, in chapter 8 of the same book, David is described as having triumphed over the Philistines, likewise over the Moabites, on whom tribute was imposed; Syria was conquered and made tributary, and he triumphed over the Edomites, Ammonites and Amalekites, and over Hadadezer, king of Zobah.

units.la: Et nunc reges intelligite, erudimini, qui iudicatis terram, seruite Domino in timore, & exultate ei cum tremore. Apprehendite disciplinam (uel osculamini filium) ne quando irascatur Dominus, & pereatis de uia iusta, cum exarserit in breui ira eius.
units.tr: And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Take hold of discipline (or kiss the Son), lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way, when his wrath is suddenly kindled.

units.la: Exhortatur Dauid, (partim etiā cōminatur) per Apostrophen, reges & principes finitimarū gentiū, quae meditantur ipsi negotiū facessere, ut in tempore resipiscant, Deum uerū, omissis impiis cultibus, timeant & adorent: Deinde, ut & se tanquam Dei filium, id est, regem a Deo constitutum, & in tutelam susceptum agnoscant. Quòd ni faciant, sciant, se ultionem Dei nequaquam euasuros, & breui tempore perdendos.
units.tr: By apostrophe David exhorts (and partly also threatens) the kings and princes of the neighbouring nations, who plan to make trouble for him, that in time they should repent, set aside their impious cults, and fear and worship the true God. Then they should acknowledge him as the Son of God, that is, as the king appointed by God and taken into his protection. If they do not do so, let them know that they will by no means escape God's vengeance and will be destroyed in a short time.

units.la: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo) Epiphonema pro conclusione: significatq; & se beatū, qui auxilio diuino, non proprijs uiribus innitantur, atq; eodem modo oēs alios quoq; beatos fore, qui in Dominū fide solent collocare. In hūc igitur modū de Dauide regnū ineunte, & bella asperrima aduersus finitimas gētes suscepturo, deq; ijs triūphaturo hic psalmus exponitur. Sed nūc videamus, quomodo multò clarius eadē omnia exponātur de Christo, & quomodo aptius quadret, certiusq; omnia adimpleta sint, cū de Christo accipitur psalmus
units.tr: "Blessed are all who put their trust in him": this is an epiphonema, a closing exclamation. It signifies that he is blessed who relies on divine help rather than his own strength, and that in the same way all others will be blessed who are accustomed to place their trust in the Lord. In this way the psalm is expounded as concerning David, when he was beginning his reign and was about to undertake very harsh wars against the neighbouring nations and to triumph over them. But now let us see how all these things are expounded much more clearly of Christ, and how much more aptly they fit and how much more certainly they were fulfilled, when the psalm is taken of Christ than if it were taken only of David.

units.la: {?} Running head and marginal notes are as printed; the marginal note positions are approximate. psalmus ille, quàm si tantùm de Dauide. Sic enim temperabat spiritus sanctus linguam Dauidis & aliorum prophetarum, vt quoties psalmos canerent, vel aliàs concionaretur de rebus suo peractis seculo, semper tamen aliquid admixtum esset, quod nequaquam per omnia competeret illis, de quibus sermonem faciebant: sed ut plurimum aliqua alius assurgebant, quæ de Christo, (cui soli ea competunt, quæ uerè magna sunt, & supra Dauidis, aut aliorum hominum sortem ac potestatem) venturo erant accipienda. Nam ut supra dixi, omnia in figura contingebant illis. Et quibuscunque de rebus prophetæ concionabantur seu uaticinabantur, semper admiscebant vaticinia de Christo, aut ea, quæ Christum aliqua similitudine seu typo adumbrarent. Itaque spiritus sanctus quando Dauidem afflauit ad canendum ista de seipso ad Dei gloriam, simul mouit eum ad interserendum ea, quæ Christum aliquo modo delinearent. Proinde ad hunc modum breuiter de Christo totum psalmum licet exponere.
units.tr: For the Holy Spirit so governed the tongue of David and of the other prophets that, whenever they sang psalms or otherwise preached about matters belonging to their own age, something was always mixed in that did not fully apply to those about whom they were speaking. Rather, for the most part, something rose up that had to be understood of Christ, the one to whom alone those things belong which are truly great and surpass the lot and power of David or of any other man, and who was yet to come. For, as I said above, all things happened to them in figure. And whatever matters the prophets were preaching or prophesying about, they always mingled in prophecies about Christ, or things that foreshadowed Christ by some likeness or type. Thus, when the Holy Spirit inspired David to sing these things about himself to the glory of God, He at the same time moved him to insert things that in some way sketched out Christ. Accordingly, in this manner, the whole psalm may be briefly expounded of Christ.

units.la: Quare fremuerunt gentes, & populi terræ meditati sunt inania? Adstiterunt reges terræ & principes conuenerunt in unum, aduersus Dominum, & aduersus Christum eius.
units.tr: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Anointed.

units.la: Hoc est: Cùm Christi regnum iam esset propagandum, ac multi iam doctrinam eius ampleƈterentur, semperq; alij atq; alij se ei adiungerent: conuenerunt aduersum sanctum filium Dei Iesum Christum, ut Actor. quarto interpretatur ipse Spiritus sanctus per apostolos, Herodes simul & Pontius Pilatus, cum gentibus & populis Israel, ad impediendum, quo minus euangelium, per quod regnare Christus debebat, & in quo regnù Christi situm est, per apostolos dilataretur, minas, flagra, imò & mortem Christi ministris intentantes, id quod historia Act. ibidem, & in omnib. quæ sequuntur, nõ obscurè docet.
units.tr: That is: when the kingdom of Christ was already to be spread abroad, and many were already embracing his teaching, and always others and others were joining themselves to him, they gathered together against the holy Son of God, Jesus Christ. As the Holy Spirit himself interprets through the apostles in Acts 4, Herod together with Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, threatened the ministers of the gospel with threats, scourges, and even the death of Christ, in order to prevent the gospel, through which Christ was to reign and in which the kingdom of Christ consists, from being spread by the apostles. The history in Acts in that place, and in all that follows, teaches this plainly.

units.la: Dirumpamus vincula eorum, & proijciamus à nobis iugum ipsorum.) Sic loquebantur aduersarij Christi, qui aperte cùm apud Pilatum accusarent eum, uociferabantur, se non passuros, ut Christus regnum apud eos obtineret, dicentes: Nolumus hûc regnare super nos: qui à Pilato impetrarunt custodes, quasi possent regium facinus, videlicet resurrectionem Christi impedire, & cù istud non potuissent, pecunijs corruperunt, ut furto sublatù men tirentur. Quorù principes & seniores, & pontifices sæpe uaria habuerunt comitia & cõ silia, nec non crudelitatis omne genus excogitarunt, crudelia edicta promulgarunt, diripuerunt piorũ facultates, quosdam morte affecerunt, (in quibus Stephanus) & hæc omnia, ne suaue & lene iugum regni Christi, quod per apostolos annunciabatur, ferrent.
units.tr: Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us. The adversaries of Christ spoke in this way, for when they openly accused him before Pilate they shouted that they would not allow Christ to obtain a kingdom among them, saying: "We will not have this man to reign over us." They obtained guards from Pilate, as if they could prevent the royal deed, namely the resurrection of Christ; and when they could not do this, they bribed men with money to lie that the body had been stolen. Their leaders, elders, and high priests often held assemblies and councils, devised every kind of cruelty, published cruel edicts, plundered the goods of the pious, put some to death (among them Stephen), and did all these things so that they would not have to bear the sweet and gentle yoke of the kingdom of Christ, which was proclaimed through the apostles.

units.la: Qui habitat in cœlis, irridebit eos, & Dominus subsannabit eos. Tunc loquetur ad eos in ira sua, & in furore suo conturbabit eos.
units.tr: He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and will trouble them in his fury.

units.la: Istud ita se habere res ipsa comprobauit: quandoquidem neq; ne Herodes, neq; Pilatus, neq; Pontifices, neq; ulli deniq; quamlibet potentes & feroces in obscurando seu minuendo regno Christi uotorum suorum effeƈti sunt compotes: Sed potius è diuerso, quo ipsi diligentius sunt aduersati, eò maioribus incrementis euangelium est illustratù. Nam quod à Deo est, non potest dissolui, id quod ipsi quoq; afferente ita Gamaliele, omnes ingenuè fassi sunt, ut habetur Actor. 4.
units.tr: The event itself has shown that this is so.
