For neither Herod, nor Pilate, nor the high priests, nor any of the mighty and fierce men at all, succeeded in their wishes of obscuring or diminishing the kingdom of Christ. Rather, on the contrary, the more diligently they opposed it, the more the gospel was made illustrious by greater increases. For what is from God cannot be dissolved. All men frankly confessed this, Gamaliel having said it, as is recorded in Acts 4.

units.la: Ego autem constitutus sum rex ab eo, super Sion montem sanctum eius.
units.tr: But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.

units.la: Verba Christi asserentis sibi regnum, potestatem omnem, omne iudicium datum, in sancta ecclesia, quæ est uera Sion. Vel, ut alij uertunt: Ego constitui regem meum super Sion montem Sanctum meum: Verba sunt patris, qui Christum voluit regem constituere: Et quidem in Sion, id est, ecclesia, quæ tam latè patet, quàm ulli inueniuntur toto orbe dispersi, quibus euangelium Christi est annunciatum & susceptum. Ita per Sion conuenit accipere significatam ecclesiam: & per regnum Christi, nõ regnum aliquod temporale, armorù & diuitiarum splendore visendum, ad aliquot annos duraturum, (quale regnum etiam Iudæi, qui locum hunc de Messiah interpretantur, ei tribuunt, atq; eo nomine negant, nostro Christo ista competere, quòd temporaliter regnasse haud uisus sit) sed regnum spirituale, situm in piorum cordibus, in euangelij propagatione, quod tantò præstatius est quouis temporali, quantò pluris debent fieri, quæ ad animæ salutem faciunt, quàm quæ ad corpus conducunt: tam latè patet, quàm latè est annunciatum, (exiuit autem in omnem terram sonus apostolorû prædicantium euangeliũ, & in fines orbis terræ uerba eorũ) & tam diu est duraturũ, quamdiu euangeliũ regni prædicabitur, hoc est, ad finẽ usq; mundi, sicutiam à modo mille & quingentis annis: quod sanè longè aliter est regnare, quàm Dauid vnquam regnauit.
units.tr: These are the words of Christ asserting that he has been given kingship, all power and all judgment, in the holy Church, which is the true Zion. Or, as others translate: "I have set my king over Zion, my holy mountain." These are the words of the Father, who wished Christ to be set up as king. And indeed it is in Zion, that is, in the Church, which extends as widely as any people are found dispersed throughout the whole world to whom the gospel of Christ has been announced and received. Thus it is fitting to understand by Zion the Church that is signified, and by the kingdom of Christ not some temporal kingdom, to be seen in the splendour of arms and riches, lasting for a few years (such a kingdom the Jews also attribute to him, who interpret this place of the Messiah, and on that ground deny that these things apply to our Christ, because he is not seen to have reigned temporally). Rather it is a spiritual kingdom, situated in the hearts of the pious and in the propagation of the gospel, which is as much more excellent than any temporal kingdom as those things that serve the salvation of the soul are to be valued more than those that serve the body. It extends as widely as it has been proclaimed (indeed "their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world"), and it will last as long as the gospel of the kingdom is preached, that is, to the end of the world, as it has done now for about fifteen hundred years. Certainly this is a very different thing from reigning as David ever reigned.

units.la: Alias verò quòd Christus siue Messias deberet tenere regnum temporale, in Zion, angusto loco, uti Dauid tantùm regnauit, aut Salomon, hoc sanè exiguum erat futurum adamplifsmam dignitatem, quam oracula prophetarum Messiæ promittunt. Cæterùm regnum Christi siue Messiæ non temporale futurum,ut Iudæi somniant,sed spirituale,hoc nos multis testimonijs possumus comprobare . Nam Zachariæ nono dicitur,Ecce rex tuus venit tibi iustus & saluator,ipse pauper,sedens super asinam. Ofeæ, Saluabo eos in Domino Deo suo , & non saluabo eos in arcu & bello,neq; in facientibus prælium cum equis & equitibus.Ioan.18. Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo: Si ex hoc mundo esset regnû meû,ministri mei vtiq; decertarent, ne traderer Iudæis,etc.
units.tr: Otherwise, if the Christ or Messiah were to hold a temporal kingdom in Zion, in a narrow place, as David alone reigned, or Solomon, this would surely have been too small for the very great dignity which the oracles of the prophets promise to the Messiah. But that the kingdom of Christ or the Messiah would not be temporal, as the Jews dream, but spiritual, we can prove by many testimonies. For in Zechariah 9 it is said: "Behold, your king comes to you, just and a saviour, himself poor, sitting upon an ass." In Hosea: "I will save them in the Lord their God, and I will not save them by bow and sword, nor by those making war with horses and horsemen." John 18: "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would surely fight, that I should not be handed over to the Jews," etc.

units.la: Itaque Christus hoc pacto spirituale regnum tenet in ecclesia,quæ est quouis imperio temporali multò amplior,potentior,durabilior:& in ea dominatur per verbû euangelij, quod potentius est omnibus armis aut diuitijs,quo etiam subegit sibi toto terrarum orbe omnium nationum homines . Id quod etiam colligi potest multò clarius ex verbis sequentibus.
units.tr: Thus Christ holds a spiritual kingdom in this way in the Church, which is far larger, more powerful, and more lasting than any temporal empire. And he rules in it through the word of the gospel, which is more powerful than all arms or riches, and by which he has also subjected to himself men of all nations throughout the whole orb of the earth. This can also be gathered much more clearly from the words that follow.

units.la: Prædicabo de præcepto)quasi dicat:In hoc sum constitutus Rex, ut annunciem hominibus voluntatem Dei patris:siue,vt Christus, cùm Pilatus intulisset ex verbis supra citatis:Ergo Rex es tu? clarè respondit:Tu dicis,quod rex sum ego.Ego in hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum,ut testimonium feram veritati.En quomodo regnum istud,quod hoc psalmo describitur,multò magis conueniat Christo humili docenti veritatem & per se, & per suos apostolos ac ministros,quàm Dauidi temporaliter regnanti, & per se, suosq; fundenti sanguinem,atq; armis rem gerenti.Sed adhuc quę sequuntur, Christum planius sonat, quàm Dauidem.
units.tr: "I will proclaim the decree": as if he said: "I have been appointed king for this, that I should announce to men the will of God the Father"; or, as Christ, when Pilate had brought forward from the words cited above, "So you are a king?", answered plainly: "You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth." See how this kingdom, which is described in this psalm, belongs far more to Christ teaching the truth in humility, both by himself and by his apostles and ministers, than to David reigning temporally, both by himself and by his followers shedding blood and waging war with arms. But what follows speaks of Christ more plainly than of David.

units.la: Dominus dixit ad me,filius meus es tu,ego hodie genui te.) Certè Christum longè alia ratione esse filium Dei,quàm fuerit Dauid,vel alij pij,id res ipsa,id est,doctrina ipsius,potentia miraculorum,resurrectio,missio spiritus sancti,atq; id genus qualia suprà commemoramus,ob quæ & populus palàm fatebatur,eum esse filium Dei, manifestè loquitur. Et Matthæi tertio, Vox patris de cœlis audita est: Hic est filius meus dilectus ,in quo mihi bene complacitum est. Et Paulus Actorum decimotertio, vti semel admonuimus, hæc ipsa verba psalmi de Christo enunciauit. Itaque ut Dauid aliquo modo dicatur filius Dei,at nequaquâ eo modo,quo Christus,qui proprius, & naturalis et unigenitus,& per Antonomasiam filius Dei dicitur:imò nec angelus aliquis potest hac ratione dici filius Dei,sicut verba apostoli clarè sonant,nulli unquam angelorum hanc vocem esse dictam. Quo pertinet illud psal.88. Quis similis erit Deo in filijs Dei? Quasi diceret:Vt multi sint filii Dei,tamen vnus est filius,qui omnes superat, & cui nemo potest æquari.Facit huc,quòd,qui genitus dicitur,naturam exprimit gignentis. Porrò cùm Dauid naturam Dei,à quo genitus dicitur, nequaquam referat , liquet, multò rectius Christo,quàm Dauidi verba ista accommodari. Et alij pij gignuntur per verbum, vel aliam mediam causam.Sic Paulus dicit se genuisse, & iterum parturire Galatas in Christo:sed hic filius ab ipso Deo immediatè est genitus:Ego,ego, inquit,genui te.
units.tr: "The Lord has said to me, You are my son; today I have begotten you." Certainly the thing itself, that is, his teaching, the power of his miracles, his resurrection, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the like things we have mentioned above, on account of which the people openly confessed that he was the Son of God, clearly shows that Christ is the Son of God in a far different way than David or other pious men were. And in Matthew 3 the voice of the Father was heard from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And Paul in Acts 13, as we have once noted, applied these very words of the psalm to Christ. So David may in some way be called a son of God, but in no way in the manner in which Christ is, who is called the proper, natural, and only-begotten Son of God, and, by way of pre-eminence, the Son of God. Indeed no angel can be called a son of God in this sense, as the words of the apostle clearly sound, since no one of the angels was ever told this word. To this pertains that verse in Psalm 89: "Who will be like God among the sons of God?" As if he said: although there are many sons of God, yet there is one Son who surpasses all, and to whom no one can be equal. It is relevant that "begotten" expresses the nature of the one who begets. Moreover, since David does not relate to the nature of God, by whom he is said to be begotten, it is clear that these words apply much more rightly to Christ than to David. Other pious men are begotten through the word or some other intermediate cause. Thus Paul says that he begot the Galatians and again labours in birth for them in Christ; but this Son was begotten immediately by God himself: "I, I," he says, "have begotten you."

units.la: Vox aut Hodie,significat tempus reuelati euangelij seu Christi manifestati: quando nimirum paterna uoce, & spiritus sancti corporali quadà specie testimonium de eo palàm datum, quòd filius Dei esset: quomodo etiam huius epist. cap.4. vox hodie exponitur.
units.tr: The word "Today" (Hodie) signifies the time when the gospel was revealed and Christ was made manifest, when the Father's voice and the Holy Spirit in a bodily form gave public testimony that he was the Son of God. This is how the word "today" is explained in chapter 4 of this Epistle.

units.la: Hodie gignere,hoc est,uno aliquo die generare,concipere,& producere,nulla creatura potest:quare hic mirabilis admodum generatio Christi ex parte notatur.
units.tr: No creature can beget, conceive and bring forth in a single day, which is what "to beget today" means. Here the wonderful manner of Christ's generation is therefore noted.

units.la: Postula à me,& dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terræ,Reges eos in virga ferrea, & tanquam vas figuli confringes eos.
units.tr: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.

units.la: Quòd Christo tribuatur postulare, id non est inconueniens ei secundum humanam naturam:quanquam si bene animaduertimus , quando hæc verba sunt patris ad Christum,sic sunt usurpata ad declarandam singularem Dei patris erga Christum beneuolentiam,& parem in omnibus voluntatem. Cùm enim ait, Postula à me,& dabo tibi, tantundem fere significat,ac si diceret:Quicquid tu volueris,idem ego uolo efficere. Datas uero Christo gentes,& terminos terræ in hæreditatem & possessionem , id manifestum est.Nam quando euangelium eius prædicatum est toto terrarum orbe, ac gentes potissimum per id ad Deum sunt uocatæ,quæ idem alacribus animis receperunt: sanè Christus per euangelium in illis uerè regnat,in hunc usq; diem, & accipit gentes in hæreditatem & possessionem,quia populus Dei peculiaris effectæ sunt. Antea quidem hæreditas & populus acquisitionis erant soli Iudæi: at postquàm Christus uenit, is pro hæreditate accepit gentes:qua de re Roman.9.10.Ephes.2. 1. Petri 2. Qui quondam eratis non populus,nunc populus Dei facti estis,&c.
units.tr: That the asking is attributed to Christ is not unfitting for him according to his human nature. Yet if we consider carefully, when these are the Father's words to Christ, they are used to declare the Father's singular goodwill toward Christ and his perfect agreement with him in all things. For when he says, "Ask of me, and I will give you," it means almost the same as saying: "Whatever you wish, I wish to accomplish as well." That the nations and the ends of the earth were given to Christ as inheritance and possession is plain. For when his gospel has been preached throughout the whole world, and nations in particular have been called to God through it and have gladly received it, then Christ truly reigns in them through the gospel, to this day, and he takes the nations as his inheritance and possession, because they have been made a peculiar people of God. Formerly, indeed, the inheritance and the people of acquisition belonged only to the Jews; but since Christ came, he has received the nations as his inheritance. For this reason see Romans 9 and 10, Ephesians 2, and 1 Peter 2: "Who once were not a people, but are now the people of God," and so on.

units.la: Et regit Christus omnes in uirga ferrea , quando tanta uerbi eius sententur potentia, vt omnes eo regantur melius , quàm ferro aut armis regi ulli possent: nec non aduersarij euangelij facilius eò debellantur,quà gladijs. Huc pertinet q, Christus alibi ait, se gladium uenisse mittere in terram,& ignem. Per gladium uiuificum suum uerbum, pe
units.tr: Christ also rules with a rod of iron, since his word is so powerful that all are ruled by it better than any could be ruled by iron or arms. Likewise the adversaries of the gospel are more easily overcome by it than by swords. To this belongs what Christ says elsewhere, that he came to send a sword and fire upon the earth. By the life-giving sword he means his word, ...

units.la: Christi officiu. Ioan.18.
units.tr: Christ's office. John 18.

units.la: Christus rex veritatis.
units.tr: Christ the king of truth.

units.la: Christus alia ratione filius Dei est, quàm Dauid & cæteri pij.
units.tr: Christ is the Son of God in a different way from David and the other godly.

units.la: Christum esse Dei filium, cõstat ex testimonijs diuinis.
units.tr: That Christ is the Son of God is established from divine testimonies.

units.la: Angeli nõ possunt dici filij Dei, sicut Christus.
units.tr: Angels cannot be called sons of God as Christ is.

units.la: Christus patris filius unigenitus.
units.tr: Christ is the only-begotten Son of the Father.

units.la: Filij Dei per verbum gignuntur.
units.tr: The sons of God are begotten through the word.

units.la: HODIE, tempus reuelati euangelij & manifestati Christi significat.
units.tr: HODIE signifies the time of the revealed gospel and of the manifested Christ.

units.la: Per euangelium gentes Christo donantur.
units.tr: Through the gospel the Gentiles are given to Christ.

units.la: Christus per euangelium regnat.
units.tr: Christ reigns through the gospel.

units.la: Christus regit uirga ferrea uidelicet potentia uerbi. perignem Spiritum sanctum intelligens. Cæterùm Dauid etiam si gentes aliquot finitimas bello superarit: at non tam multas, ut Christus. Deinde non accepit in possesionem, multò minus in hæreditatem. Certè legitimum & hæreditarium imperium ultrà Judæam non extendens.
units.tr: Christ rules with a rod of iron, that is, by the power of the word, the fire being understood as the Holy Spirit. Moreover, even if David defeated some neighbouring nations in war, he did not defeat so many as Christ did. Further, he did not take them into possession, much less as an inheritance, since he did not extend his lawful and hereditary rule beyond Judea.

units.la: Et nunc reges intelligite, erudimini, qui iudicatis terram: seruite Domino in timore, & exultate ei cum tremore. Apprehendite disciplinam (ne forte irascatur Dominus, & pereatis de via iusta: cum exarserit in breui ira eius.
units.tr: And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Take hold of discipline, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the just way, when his anger shall suddenly blaze up.

units.la: Verba sunt Dauidis, prophetico spiritu adhortantis omnes reges, ut patiantur, se vere Dei edoceri, quò vero Deo ac Domino vero timore & læta conscientia seruire quea- ant. Inprimis autem ut osculentur, id est, amplectantur, honorent filium, nempe Iesum Christum, in quo solo patri complacitum est, quem quoq; eo vult audiri præ omnibus. Si qui autem hunc filium contempserint, vltionem Dei in se experientur. In quem sen- sum etiam illud huius epistolæ capite tertio exponitur: Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obturare corda vestra: & quæ sequuntur. Profectò si de se tantùm hoc modo venerando dixisset ista Dauid, videri potuissent dicta arrogantiùs & fastuosius. Se itaque sic honorandum dixit, ut præcipuum tamen honorem vellet ad Deum & Dei filium Christum redire. Epiphonema verò, quod subjicitur, plane euangelij & regni Christi summam continet. Quid enim aliud est, Beati omnes, qui confidunt in eum, quàm illud, quod toto euangelio & apostolicis scriptis inculcatur, nempe salutem siue iustitiam coram Deo, ijs obtingere, qui fidem suam in Christum collocarint. Ita enim istud proprie ad filium referetur, quem proximis verbis dixit osculandum. Qui plura videre auent de expositione psalmi huius ad gloriam Christi, legant Augustinum, alios q; seu vetustos, seu recentes scriptores, qui clariùs, copiosius, splendidius, explicarunt totum psalmum de Christo, quàm nos possemus.
units.tr: These are the words of David, who with prophetic spirit exhorts all kings to allow themselves to be truly taught by God, so that they may serve the true God and Lord with true fear and a joyful conscience. Above all, they are to kiss, that is, embrace and honour the Son, namely Jesus Christ, in whom alone the Father is well pleased, and whom he also wills to be heard above all. But if anyone despises this Son, they will experience the vengeance of God upon themselves. In this same sense, this Epistle's third chapter also expounds it: "Today if you will hear his voice, harden not your hearts," and what follows. Certainly, if David had spoken these things only about himself in this manner of honouring, they might have seemed arrogant and haughty. He therefore said that he was to be honoured in such a way that, nevertheless, the chief honour should return to God and to God's Son Christ. The epiphonema that is added clearly contains the sum of the gospel and of Christ's kingdom. For what else is "Blessed are all who trust in him" but what is urged throughout the gospel and the apostolic writings, namely that salvation, or righteousness before God, is granted to those who have placed their faith in Christ? For thus it is properly referred to the Son, whom he said in the preceding words was to be kissed. Those who wish to see more about the exposition of this psalm for the glory of Christ should read Augustine, and others, ancient or recent writers, who have explained the whole psalm concerning Christ more clearly, fully and splendidly than we could.

units.la: Porrò refellere, quæ Dauid Kimhi, in medium profert ad docendum, nullo pacto psalmum hunc de Christo accipiendum, non puto esse opus, cum inter exponendum nos taciteaaliquot & præcipuas rationes eius refutauerimus. Ait, non rectè nos interpretari, qui dicamus Deo patri esse suum filium, cui dicat: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Nam diuinitati, inquit, non competit paternitas & filiatio: cùm illa scilicet sit inseparabilis & indiuisibilis: cùm non sit corpus, sed vnus Deus omni modo vnitatis, cui nihil accedat, neque decedat, neque sub diuisionem cadat. Sed ista & nos de Diuinitate, quòd vnà indiuisibilisq; sit, concedimus: & tamen distinctionem personarum in eadem diuinitate, ex multis Scripturæ locis possumus comprobare.
units.tr: Furthermore, I do not think it necessary to refute what David Kimhi brings forward to teach that this psalm by no means should be taken of Christ, since in the exposition we have silently refuted some of his principal arguments. He says that we do not interpret rightly when we say that God the Father has his Son, to whom he says: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." For, he says, paternity and filiation do not belong to the divinity, since that is inseparable and indivisible, being not a body but one God in every mode of unity, to which nothing is added, from which nothing is taken, and which is not subject to division. But we also concede these things about the Deity, that it is one and indivisible; and yet we can prove from many passages of Scripture the distinction of persons within the same Deity.

units.la: Rursus, quando ait, patrem naturaliter præcedere filium tempore, & qui gignit, prio rem esse genito. Breuiter respondemus: In diuinis nō ita se habere omnia, ut in humanis. Nàm etiamsi distinguamus personas, ut unam gignentem, alteram genitam dicamus, tamen in illis nihil prius, nec posterius, sed inuicem sunt coæternæ & coæquales. Nec pater sine filio, nec pater & filius sine spiritu sancto intelligi in Trinitate & vnitate potest.
units.tr: Again, when he says that the father naturally precedes the son in time, and that he who begets is prior to the one begotten, we briefly reply: in divine things it is not all the same as in human things. For even if we distinguish the persons, so that we call one the begetter and the other the begotten, yet in them nothing is prior or posterior, but they are mutually coeternal and coequal. Nor can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Father and Son without the Holy Spirit, in the Trinity and unity.

units.la: Iam alia ratione Christum dici filium Dei, quàm Dauidem, vel alios pios, (quod ille negat) in enarratione ostendimus. Similiter quomodo conueniat Christo filio Dei, & æquali ipsi patri, postulare, ex suprà dictis cognosci potest. Diximus enim, secundum humanam naturam id ei tribui, & significari, patrem eiusdem esse voluntatis cum filio.
units.tr: Now, in the commentary we have shown in what way Christ is called the Son of God differently from David or other godly people, which he denies. From what has been said above, it can likewise be recognised how it fits Christ, the Son of God and equal to the Father, to ask. For we have said that this is attributed to him according to his human nature, and that it signifies that the Father is of the same will as the Son.

units.la: Sed, quando ille addit, filio secundum humanam naturam non esse datas gentes in possessionem: quandoquidem nusquam regnum obtinuerit: diluitur id eo, quod suprà diximus de regno Christi spirituali. Et rursus, quando negat, hoc regnum Christi spirituale ad terminos orbis terræ propagatum: multos enim adhuc passim tam Iudæos, quàm Ismaelitas, qui fidem in Christum non receperint, reperiri: responderi potest, quòd, licet quidam non crediderint, nō tamen propterea euacuatam esse Dei promissionem, sicut Romanorum tertio de Iudæis dicitur. Certè ubique terrarum fuit euangelium annunciatum, & ubiq; multi sunt id amplexati, in quibus Christus regnum suum tenet. Qui non amplexati sunt, sua culpa & cæcitate seipsos à regno Christi excludunt. Est diuina ordinatione constitutum est, ut semper aliqui sint, qui regno Christi aduersentur, in primis Iudæi & similes: qua de re copiosius disputatur Romanorum nono & decimo, &c.
units.tr: But when he adds that the nations were not given to the Son as a possession according to his human nature, since he nowhere obtained a kingdom, this is answered by what we said above about Christ's spiritual kingdom. And again, when he denies that this spiritual kingdom of Christ has been extended to the ends of the earth, since many Jews as well as Ishmaelites, who have not received faith in Christ, are still found everywhere, it can be replied that although some have not believed, God's promise has not on that account been made void, as is said of the Jews in Romans 3. Certainly the gospel has been proclaimed in every part of the earth, and everywhere many have embraced it, and in them Christ holds his kingdom. Those who have not embraced it exclude themselves from Christ's kingdom by their own fault and blindness. By divine ordinance it has been established that there always be some who oppose Christ's kingdom, above all the Jews and those like them; on this matter Romans 9 and 10 dispute more fully, and so on.

units.la: Iam uero affines locos, quibus plenius probetur persona Christi in diuinitate: item secundum quam naturam Christus dicatur Dei filius, paulò post explicabimus.
units.tr: Now, the related passages by which the person of Christ in his divinity is more fully proved, and also according to which nature Christ is called the Son of God, we shall explain shortly.

units.la: Hoc tantum admonendum, ut filium, cuius regnum hoc psalm, describitur, osculemur, hoc est, debitum ei honorem, laudem, gloriam, tribuamus: nos illi ex animo submittamus fidem in eum conijciamus: ne, si hac in parte fuerimus negligentes, ira Dei in nos exardeat & æternum damnemur. Sic enim scriptum nobis est: Qui non credit in filium, iam iudicatus est. Orabimus deinde Deum patrem, ut propter Christū nos quoq; velit in filios recipere, hoc est, ut filios tueri, defendere, aduersus quæcunq; pericula, nec non ad cœlestem hæreditatem, credentibus promissam, promouere.
units.tr: This only needs to be added: that we kiss the Son whose kingdom this Psalm describes, that is, that we give him the honour, praise and glory due to him, and that we heartily submit ourselves to him and place our faith in him. If we are negligent in this respect, the wrath of God will blaze up against us and we will be damned for ever. For this is written to us: He who does not believe in the Son is already judged. Then we shall pray to God the Father that, for Christ's sake, he would also be pleased to receive us as sons, that is, to keep us, defend us against all dangers, and advance us to the heavenly inheritance promised to believers.

units.la: Ac rursum: Ego ero ei pater & ille erit mihi filius.
units.tr: And again: "I will be his father, and he will be my son."

units.la: Secundum argumentum, quo Christum esse filium Dei confirmatur, sumptum exse cundi libri Regum capite septimo: ubi Propheta Nathan iubetur à Deo annunciare Dauidi, domum Dei nequaquam ædificandam ab eo: sed expectandum ipsi filium, per quem illa extruatur: sic autem habent verba: cumq; completi fuerint dies tui, & dormieris cum patribus tuis, suscitabo semen tuum post te, quod egredietur de utero tuo, & firmabo regnum eius. Ipse ædificabit domū nomini meo, & stabilita thronum regni eius usq; in sempiternū. Ego ero ei in patrem, & ipse erit mihi in filium. Qui si inique aliquid gesserit, arguam eum in uirga virorum, & in plagis filiorum hominum: & misericordiam meam non auferam ab eo, sicut abstuli à Saul, quem amoui à facie mea: & fidelis erit domus tua, & regnum tuum usq; in æternum ante faciem meam. Quæ verba licet secundum historiam de Solomone videantur prolata, tamen si propius intueamur, inueniūtur multo clarius competere ipsi Christo: ac, licet Solomon ibi typus fuit Christi, tamen simul cum Solomone promissum ipsum Christum: sicut & præcedenti argumento, quæ de Dauide erāt dicta, ostendimus accipienda simul de Christo. Et Solomonem in multis Christi typum fuisse, extra controuersiam est, cum Christus etiā alibi, ut in Canticis, & Matth. 12. plus quam Solomon describatur: quandoquidem Christus uerus pacificus, uerus conciliator, & pacis autor inter Deum & homines existit. Sed istud iterum pluribus verbis nos est faciendum.
units.tr: The second argument, by which it is confirmed that Christ is the Son of God, is taken from the seventh chapter of the second book of Kings, where the prophet Nathan is commanded by God to announce to David that the house of God was not to be built by him, but that a son was to be awaited, through whom it would be erected. The words are these: And when thy days shall be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will raise up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men: but my mercy shall not depart away from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away before thee. And thy house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee. Although these words seem to have been spoken about Solomon according to the history, yet if we look more closely, they are found to apply much more clearly to Christ himself. And although Solomon was there a type of Christ, the Christ himself was nevertheless promised together with Solomon, just as in the previous argument we showed that what was said of David should be understood at the same time of Christ. That Solomon was a type of Christ in many respects is beyond controversy, since Christ is also described elsewhere, as in the Canticles and in Matthew 12, as greater than Solomon, inasmuch as Christ is the true peacemaker, the true reconciler, and the author of peace between God and men. But this we must now set out again in more words.

units.la: Primò itaque verum est, sicut promissio sonat, datum Dauidi filium Solomonē, qui succederit in regno, & domum multò magnificentissimam domino ædificarit, quem etiam Deus pater gubernauit, adiuuit, euexit, defendit, non aliter quàm pater quispiam solet charum filiū regere, seruare, tueri. Et de Solomone proprie illud accipiendum est, quòd si inique aliquid gereret, in uirga virorum foret puniendus. At vero quando promissio sonat de quodam, qui suscitaretur ex semine Dauidis, postquā Dauid dormiret cum patribus, quando additur eius thronum stabiliendum usq; in sempiternum: quando dicitur item fidelis futura domus & regnum in æternum: apparet aliquem aliumibi intelligendum, ideoq; alteriorem sensum quæramus oportet, quærendaq; alia persona, cui ista competant. Itaq; egressus de semine Dauid, post mortem Dauidis, est ipse Christus, qui Dauidi fuit promissus, & pasim filius Dauid appellatur. De Solomone quidem non possunt simpliciter verba illa accipi, utpote quem non solum genitum sibi uidit Dauid, sed præterea ad regium fastigium se uiuo euectum. Ac proinde interpretari de Christo promissio verba illa ipsa uerbotum simplex & nuda significatio nos compellit. Quod verò Christus ædificauerit domum Deo, istud multò est certius, quàm de Solomone.
units.tr: First, then, it is true that, as the promise sounds, a son, Solomon, was given to David, who would succeed him in the kingdom and build a house to the Lord far more magnificent, and whom God the Father also guided, helped, exalted and defended, just as a father is accustomed to rule, keep and protect a dear son. And of Solomon it must be understood in the proper sense that, if he committed iniquity, he would be punished with the rod of men. But when the promise speaks of someone who would be raised up from the seed of David after David had slept with his fathers, when it is added that his throne would be established for ever, when it is likewise said that the house and kingdom would be faithful for ever, it appears that someone else must be understood here, and so we must seek a higher sense and look for another person to whom these things belong. Therefore the one who came forth from the seed of David after David's death is Christ himself, who was promised to David and is everywhere called the son of David. Those words cannot simply be taken of Solomon, since David saw him not only begotten for himself but also raised, while he was still living, to the royal dignity. Accordingly, the plain and bare meaning of the words compels us to interpret that promise of Christ. That Christ built a house for God is far more certain than in the case of Solomon.

units.la: Nam Christus collegit & erexit Deo patri, non ædificium aliquod corporale uel temporale: sed spirituale & perpetuò duraturum, videlicet ipsam ecclesiam, credentium sanctam congregationem: quæ duo templa si quis inter se conferat, inueniet, illud Solomonis prorsus nullam esse, præ isto templo Christi. Nam templum Solomonis diruū est, nec vnquam pristinæ dignitati restitutum, ac nunc ne reliquiae quidem ullæ supersunt.
units.tr: For Christ gathered and raised up for God the Father not some corporeal or temporal building, but a spiritual one that will last for ever, namely the Church itself, the holy congregation of believers. If anyone compares these two temples with each other, he will find that the temple of Solomon is utterly nothing compared with this temple of Christ. For the temple of Solomon was destroyed, was never restored to its former dignity, and now not even any remnant of it survives.

units.la: Quod uero ad thronum & regnum sempiternum attinet, id nullo modo Solomoni competit. Nam ipse ab hostibus est uexatus, & Israelem sensit rebellantem: præterea se viuo intellexit regnum diuidendum, & vnam tantum tribum filio suo cessuram, ut clare describitur 3. Reg. 11. Sed & in vniuersum ademptum omne ius regni posteris Dauidis, a toti genti Iudaicæ, constat, quo tempore per Romanos rex alienigena ipsis præfectus est, nempe Herodes, sub quo Christus natus est, qui tum cœpit regnum in domo Dauid restaurare, sed spirituale & quod æternū durare debeat: sicut hodie durare agnoscitur: nec dubium quin iuxta promissionem Dei æternum duraturum sit. Huc pertinent, quæ de Christi regno in expositione præcedentis argumenti semel commemorauimus. Sed ex his etiam constat, non prorsus competere Solomoni aut posteris eius, quod in uerbis Nathan prophetæ additur, videlicet, quòd Dominus non auferret misericordiam a domo Dauid, quòd domus eius fidelis esset permansura. Nam hæc profectò de Solomone, aut filijs eius confirmari nequeunt. Nam tegni diuisionem ipse suo tempore intellexit: Deinde, ipse non mansit fidelis Deo, utpote qui in manifestam idololatriam lapsus, prolapsus,
units.tr: As for the throne and the everlasting kingdom, this in no way fits Solomon. For he himself was harassed by enemies and perceived Israel rebelling; moreover, while he was still alive, he understood that the kingdom would be divided and that only one tribe would pass to his son, as is clearly described in 1 Kings 11. Furthermore, it is well known that the whole right of the kingdom was taken away from the posterity of David and from the whole Jewish nation, at the time when a foreign king was set over them by the Romans, namely Herod, under whom Christ was born. Then Christ began to restore the kingdom in the house of David, but a spiritual kingdom, one which ought to last for ever, as it is recognised to last today; and there is no doubt that, according to the promise of God, it will endure for ever. To this belong the things we mentioned once in the exposition of the previous argument concerning the kingdom of Christ. But from these things it is also clear that what is added in the words of the prophet Nathan does not fit Solomon or his posterity at all, namely that the Lord would not take away his mercy from the house of David, and that his house would remain faithful. For these things cannot be confirmed of Solomon or his sons. For Solomon himself perceived the division of the kingdom in his own time. Then, he himself did not remain faithful to God, since he fell into manifest idolatry and, having fallen, was utterly turned away from God; therefore the Lord was angry with him and did not deem him worthy of mercy, as is clearly stated in 1 Kings 11.

units.la: {3} Solomonis regnum diuisum: Solomon infidelis & idololatra Deū sensit iratum. prolapsus, & à Deo prorsus auersus, eoq; Dominus illi iratus est, & misericordia nō est dignatus, sicut clarè dicitur 3.Reg.11.Sed si respiciamus ad Christū, inueniemus omnia illa uni Christo quadrare. Christus enim uere fidelis permansit, & innumeros alios patri suo fideles per doctrinā suā & uirtute spiritus S.parauit, & quotidie adhuc parat: Et patrem placatū ac misericordē erga omnes reddidit. Quinetiam huic regno Christi maxime conuenit, quòd dicatur stabiliri ante faciem Domini. Nam coram hominibus quidem despectum est & humile, quia non est de hoc mundo: at coram Deo uere floret, uereq; augustū est, utpote quod spirituale sit & cœleste. Sed si essemus tam oculati, quàm Paulus ipse fuit, possemus haud dubiè alia argumenta inuenire, quibus probari posset, totam promissionem illam multò luculentius de Christo, quā de Solomone loqui. Nos tamen ex aliquot membris videmur clarè satis collegisse, quòd videlicet rectè de Christo praesens testimonium sit citatum, quòdq; ex eo aptè inferatur, Christum esse uerum Dei filium, verumq; Deum: ac proinde etiam angelis omnibus esse multò praestantiorē. Profectò si Iudaei negare vellent, illa promissa Dei per Christum esse adimpleta, ea ratione, qua sumus interpretati, non est quod sperētur, alia ratione adimplenda. Nam de semine Dauid nulli amplius secundum carnem posteri ostendi possunt, cum sub Domitiano Imperatore vniuersam progeniem Dauid extinctam historiae memorent.
units.tr: {3} The kingdom of Solomon divided: Solomon, unfaithful and an idolater, felt God to be angry. But if we look to Christ, we shall find that all those things fit Christ alone. For Christ truly remained faithful, and by his teaching and by the power of the Holy Spirit he has prepared, and still daily prepares, countless others who are faithful to his Father, and he has rendered the Father placated and merciful towards all. Moreover, it is especially fitting for this kingdom of Christ that it is said to be established before the face of the Lord. For before men it is indeed despised and lowly, because it is not of this world; but before God it truly flourishes, and it is truly majestic, since it is spiritual and heavenly. But if we were as sharp-sighted as Paul himself was, we could undoubtedly find other arguments by which it could be proved that that whole promise speaks far more clearly of Christ than of Solomon. Yet from some points we seem to have gathered quite clearly enough that this present testimony is rightly cited of Christ, and that it rightly infers from this that Christ is the true Son of God and true God, and therefore also far superior to all angels. Certainly, if the Jews wished to deny that those promises of God have been fulfilled through Christ, by the interpretation we have given there is no reason to hope for them to be fulfilled in some other way. For no further posterity of David according to the flesh can be shown, since the historians record that the whole family of David was wiped out under the emperor Domitian.

units.la: Sunt verò alij loci in Scripturis, quibus Christus vocatur filius Dei, siue in quibus per filium Dei significatur Christus, ut clarè, Christum esse Deum, nec non distinctam in diuinitate personam à patre posse colligi. Sed ea de re agemus paulò plenius, vbi ad finem argumentorum huius confirmationis peruentum fuerit. Vnus nunc succurrit ex prouerb.28. Quis ascendit in coelum atq; descendit? Quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis? Quis colligauit aquas quasi in uestimento? Quis suscitauit omnes terminos terrae? Quod nomen eius & nomen filij eius si nosti? Vbi indicatur, sapientiam sanctorum esse, ista nosse, quae hic describuntur, nempe nosse, quis ascendit in coelum, quis item descendit: deinde nosse filium Dei. Esa.9. Filius datus est nobis. Et illud Osee 11. Ex Aegypto uocaui filium meum. Quod non tantum de Israelitico populo, ut Iudaei contendunt, sed de Christo accipi debet, sicut Matthaeus ipse indicat. psalm.88. Ipse inuocauit me, pater meus es tu, Deus meus, & susceptor salutis meae: Et ego primogenitum ponam illum, excelsum prae regibus terrae.
units.tr: There are, however, other passages in the Scriptures in which Christ is called the Son of God, or in which Christ is signified through the Son of God, from which it can be clearly gathered that Christ is God, and that in the divinity he is a person distinct from the Father. But we shall treat this matter somewhat more fully when we have come to the end of the arguments of this confirmation. One now comes to mind, from Proverbs 30: "Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? Who hath gathered the wind in his fists? Who hath bound the waters in a garment? Who hath established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?" Here it is indicated that it belongs to the wisdom of the saints to know these things which are described here, namely to know who has ascended into heaven and who likewise has descended, and then to know the Son of God. Isaiah 9: "A son is given to us." And that of Hosea 11: "Out of Egypt have I called my son." This must be understood not only of the Israelite people, as the Jews contend, but of Christ, as Matthew himself indicates. Psalm 89: "He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation. Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."

units.la: Proinde Christus dicitur his argumentis, Filius Dei, & quidē naturalis, eiusdem essen tiē, substantiae, Deus de Deo genitus ante secula, ac proinde maximē filius Dei secundū diuinam naturam. Potest tamen, ut annotauit Chrysostomus, etiam secundum humanam naturam ita appellari, idq; per communicationem idiomatum. Etenim, ut idem Chrysostomus eleganter ait, caro communicat altioribus, sicut & diuinitas humilibus communicare dignata est. Qui enim non est homo fieri dedignatus, & qui rem ipsam non abnuit, quomodo ipsa repudiaturus est verba?
units.tr: Christ is therefore called, on these grounds, the Son of God, and indeed the natural Son, of the same essence and substance, God begotten of God before all ages, and so most of all the Son of God according to the divine nature. Yet, as Chrysostom observed, he can also be so called according to the human nature, and this through the communication of properties. For, as the same Chrysostom neatly puts it, the flesh shares in the higher things, just as the divinity has deigned to share in the lowly things. For he who did not disdain to become man, and did not refuse the thing itself, how will he reject the words?

units.la: Rursum autem cum inducit primogenitum in orbem terrarum, dicit: Et adorent eum omnes angeli Dei.
units.tr: Again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: "And let all the angels of God worship him."

units.la: Tertium argumentum iterum valde acute ex psalmo 96.collectum, utpote in quo simul ostendit Christum angelis superiore, simulq; verū Deū. Nā cū adorandū eum dicit, plane arguit, diuinū honore ei cōpetere: cū uerò adorandū ab angelis declarat, eū multò esse angelis superiorem. Nam adorare inferiorū est, adorari superioris. Ne uerò quis reijceret istud testimonium, ceu minus aptè citatum de filio, voluit ipse vno uerbo indicare, de Christo filio id accipiendum, & prophetam de Christo inducendo in orbē terrarū adiudicandū, vaticinatū. Cū inducit, inquit, primogenitū in orbē terrarū. Nos verò plenius etiā explicabimus, rectè de Christo ea uerba exponi: si tñ prius quaedā minutiora discusseri-mus. Graecè quidem sic legitur, ὅταν δὲ πάλιν εἰσαγάγῃ τὸν πρωτότοκον εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην, λέγει, καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι θεοῦ.
units.tr: The third argument, again very skilfully drawn from Psalm 96, shows at the same time that Christ is superior to the angels and is also true God. For when he says that Christ is to be worshipped, he plainly argues that divine honour belongs to him; and when he declares that he is worshipped by the angels, he shows that he is far superior to them, for to worship is for the inferior, to be worshipped is for the superior. Lest anyone should reject this testimony as cited rather inaptly about the Son, he wished to indicate in one word that this must be understood of Christ the Son, and that the prophet, prophesying of Christ, is to be taken as bringing him into the world: "When he brings in," he says, "the firstborn into the world." We will explain more fully that these words are rightly expounded of Christ, provided that we first discuss some smaller points. In Greek it is read thus: "And again, when he brings in the firstborn into the world, he says, 'And let all the angels of God worship him'" [ὅταν δὲ πάλιν εἰσαγάγῃ τὸν πρωτότοκον εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην, λέγει, καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι θεοῦ].

units.la: Verbum εἰσαγαγεῖν, referunt nonnulli ad prophetam, qui subinde aliam atq; aliam introducit in psalmis suis personam: aliqui potius referunt ad Deum patrem, qui filium intro ducturus sit in mundum cum maxima gloria, ut eum iudicet. Atq; ex eo, quod dicitur πάλιν εἰσαγαγεῖν, quidam colligunt, duplicem Christi in mundum introductionem notari. Cùm enim rursus introducendus dicitur, tacitè significatur, eum semel ante fuisse intro ductum. Fuit ergo primi Christi introductio, cùm ipse à patre ex coelis in mūdum uenit, & carnem induit, inter homines uersans, & omnia tentans, ut doctrina & gratuitae misericordiae oblatione omnes in gratiam cum Deo patre reduceret, atq; illa introductio erat humilitatis & mansuetudinis. Iam altera introductio facta est, cùm Christus à resurrectione & misso spiritu sancto toti mundo est manifestatus per praedicationem euangelij.
units.tr: Some refer the verb "to bring in" (εἰσαγαγεῖν) to the prophet, who from time to time introduces one person after another in his psalms; others refer it rather to God the Father, who is about to bring the Son into the world with the greatest glory, in order to judge it. And from the fact that it says "to bring in again" (πάλιν εἰσαγαγεῖν), some gather that a twofold introduction of Christ into the world is noted. For when he is said to be brought in again, it is tacitly signified that he was brought in once before. There was therefore a first introduction of Christ, when he came from heaven into the world from the Father, put on flesh, lived among men and was tried in all things, so that by his teaching and by the offer of free mercy he might bring all back into grace with God the Father; and that introduction was one of humility and gentleness. Now a second introduction has taken place, when Christ, after his resurrection and the sending of the Holy Spirit, has been made manifest to the whole world through the preaching of the gospel,

units.la: d gelij, nec non regnum atq; imperium spirituale in mentibus hominum occupat. Quòd regnum Christi spirituale toto pfalm.96. à quo præsens argumentum Apostolus depro-pliit, magnificentissimè describitur. Nisi malimus secundam introductionem interpre-tari de secundo aduentu Christi ad iudicium, in quo uere regiâ potestatem palàm demo-strabit, & exercebit potenter, præmia collaturus pijs, & seueriter animaduersurus in im-pios: de quo aduentu cū maiestate, & gloria, & virtute magna, Matth.25. Marci 13. Luc.21. 1. Thessal.4.5. etc. Notat autem Chrysostomus, metaphoram subesse verbo introducen-di, sumptam à more introducendi aliquos in possessionem seu hæreditatem, ut testimo-nium publicum habeatur, eos iure occupare ea bona. Quæ interpretatio etiam ualdè con-uenit institutoi: ita enim significatur, Christo quasi iure hereditario potestatem orbis ob-uenire: sicut supra Christus vocatus est constitutus à Deo patre hæres, & quod in euan-gelio ait, datam sibi omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra.
units.tr: and takes possession of the kingdom and spiritual rule in the minds of men. Psalm 96, from which the Apostle drew the present argument, describes this spiritual kingdom of Christ over the whole world most magnificently. Unless we prefer to interpret the second introduction as referring to the second coming of Christ to judgment, in which he will openly display and powerfully exercise his royal power, bestowing rewards on the godly and punishing the impious severely; of this coming with majesty and glory and great power, see Matt. 25; Mark 13; Luke 21; 1 Thess. 4 and 5, etc. Chrysostom notes that there lies a metaphor in the verb "to introduce," taken from the custom of introducing someone into the possession or inheritance of something, so that there is public witness that they rightly take possession of those goods. This interpretation also fits the present purpose very well, for it signifies that power over the world falls to Christ as by hereditary right, just as above Christ was called the heir appointed by God the Father, and as he says in the gospel that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him.

units.la: Porrò uocat Christum hic πρωτότοκον primogenitum, quomodò Colos 1. πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως, id est, primogenitus uniuersæ creaturæ dicitur: Et Ioan.1. vocatur μονογενὴς unigenitus. Ois unigenitus potest dici primogenitus, at non è diuerso. Vtraq; tamen appel-latio Christo competit. Nam unigenitus quidem est maximè secundum diuinitatem: sed uni-genitus quoq; secundum humanitatem: quando quidem beata virgo alios nullos genuit. Pri-mogenitus quoq; dicitur patris secundum diuinitatem: quia ante omnia, & præ omnib. Christus ab illo est genitus, utpote ipsi patri etiam coætaneus, sicut & sapientia nomine Filij apud Solomonem loquitur: Ego Sapientia ex ore altissimi prodij, primogenita ante omne crea-turam. Secundum humanitatem verò dicitur primogenitus virginis, non quòd alios post eum genuerit, ut cauillari uolebat Heluidius: sed quòd ante eum nullum genuerit. Semper autem apud Hebræos nomen primogeniti significat dignitatem & præeminen-tiam præ cæteris. Vnde ipse populus Israel Exod.4. vocatur filius primogenitus. Acius primogenituræ summam adferebat dignitatem, cuicunq; illud cessisset, siue ei, qui ante alios esset natus, siue post alium. Quod uidere licet in Iacobo, qui iunior erat, & tamen emerat ab Esau ius primogenituræ. Itaq; conuenit intelligamus, Christum ideò vocari primogenitum, ut significetur summa ipsius dignitas: atq; ipsi conuenire gloriam, potes-tiam, quæ nulli alteri filiorum Dei (quoniam tantum sunt filij per adoptionem, cùm ipse sit filius naturalis) posset tribui. Cùm Christo tribuitur, dignitatis & præeminentiæ est nomen, non ordinis genituræ. Atq; hac ratione Roman.8. dicitur de excellentia Christi præ cæteris: quos prædestinarat, eosdem & prædefiniuit conformes imaginis filij sui, ut ipse sit primogenitus inter multos fratres.
units.tr: Moreover, here he calls Christ πρωτότοκον, firstborn, just as in Colossians 1 he is called πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως, that is, firstborn of every creature; and in John 1 he is called μονογενὴς, only begotten. Whatever is only begotten may be called firstborn, but not conversely. Yet both titles belong to Christ. For he is only begotten chiefly according to the divinity, but also only begotten according to the humanity, since the blessed virgin bore no others. He is also called firstborn of the Father according to the divinity, because Christ was begotten by him before all things and above all things, being co-eternal with the Father himself; just as Wisdom speaks in Solomon in the name of the Son: "I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature." According to the humanity, however, he is called firstborn of the virgin, not because she bore others after him, as Helvidius wished to scoff, but because she bore no one before him. Among the Hebrews, moreover, the name of firstborn always signifies dignity and pre-eminence above the rest. Hence the people of Israel itself is called the firstborn son in Exodus 4. And the right of the firstborn carried the highest dignity, and it passed to whoever obtained it, whether he had been born before the others or after another. This may be seen in Jacob, who was the younger and yet had bought the birthright from Esau. It is therefore fitting to understand that Christ is called firstborn so that his supreme dignity may be signified, and that glory and power belong to him which could not be attributed to any other son of God (since they are sons only by adoption, while he is the natural Son). When this name is given to Christ, it is a name of dignity and pre-eminence, not of the order of birth. In this sense Romans 8 speaks of the excellence of Christ above the rest: those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.

units.la: Pariigitur modo Apostolus præsenti loco uolens Christum depingere, honorificum & excellentiæ plenū nomen voluit ei tribuere, per quod intelligeretur uerus Dei filius, patri coæternus, & ante omnia à patre genitus. Atq; his quidem uerbis voluit quasi præ-fari, & docere, quòd, quæ citare uellet è Scripturis, de primogenito illo, nempe Christo, forent accipienda. Iam ergo ad ipsum argumeutum explicandum ueniamus. Sicigi-tur habet argumetū: Et adorent eū omnes angeli eius: sumpta sunt uerba ex 72. interpretibus, apud quos ita legitur: προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι: sed habetur hebraicè pro uoce an-gelorum אלהים quæ uox non tantùm angelos, sed etiam Deos, magistratus, iudices, significat: unde apparet, in argumentis his, quæ fiunt per collationē, hoc est, in quibus confertur cum angelis, commodissimè sumptam esse sententiam 72 interpretum, quæ exprimit appellationem angelorum. Proinde Elohim, siue angeli, iubentur adorare Chri-stum: Igitur Christus est angelis multò superior, imò & Deus: Quandoquidem adorari debet solus Deus: sicut & Deuteron.6. Dominum Deum tuū adorabis, & illi soli seruies. Certum est, Apostolus ualdè acute intuebatur singula huius loci uerba, & uolebat bre-uissimo hoc testimonio manifestè concludere, non solùm quòd Christus esset angelis superior: contra eos, qui uidebantur cōcessuri de Christo, quòd esset eximius angelus, uel eximius propheta, sed insuper quòd Christus esset uerus Deus.
units.tr: Thus the Apostle, wishing in this passage to portray Christ, wanted to give him an honourable name full of excellence, by which it would be understood that he is the true Son of God, co-eternal with the Father, and begotten of the Father before all things. With these words he wished, as it were, to preface and to teach that the passages he intended to cite from the Scriptures were to be understood of that firstborn, namely Christ. Now let us come to the argument itself. The argument stands thus: "And let all his angels worship him." The words are taken from the Seventy, among whom it is read thus: [προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι]. But in Hebrew, in place of the word "angels" stands [אלהים], a word which signifies not only angels but also gods, magistrates and judges. Whence it appears that in these arguments which proceed by comparison, that is, in which Christ is compared with the angels, the sense given by the Seventy, which expresses the name of angels, has been most aptly taken. Accordingly, the Elohim, or angels, are bidden to worship Christ; therefore Christ is far superior to the angels, indeed also God, since God alone ought to be worshipped, as also in Deuteronomy 6: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone." It is certain that the Apostle looked very keenly at each word of this passage, and wished to conclude clearly from this very brief testimony not only that Christ is superior to the angels, against those who seemed ready to concede that Christ was an outstanding angel or an outstanding prophet, but moreover that Christ is true God.

units.la: Primò itaq; ex ipso uerbo adorandi colligi uolebat, Christum esse Deum. Nā adorare hoc loco nō significat tantùm gestum externum honoris, puta genuflexionem, aut simi-le quiddam: quomodo etiam in Scripturis leguntur quidā adorasse reges, principes, aut uiros sanctos: sed significat cultum impendere, aut cū religione honore diuinū tribuere: sicut in ueteri & nouo testamento scribuntur aliqui ascendisse Hierosolymam ut adora-rent: & veri adoratores dicuntur patrem adorare in spiritu & veritate: qualem honorem exigebat diabolus à Christo in deserto, & Christus ei denegauit, dicens, secundum illud ex Deuter. tribuendum tale honore soli Deo. Eodé modo adorare statuā recusabant illi in Babylone: sic Mardochæus nolebat adorare superbū Hamā. Ergo diuinum honore vulg
units.tr: First, then, he wished to gather from the very word "to worship" that Christ is God. For to worship in this place does not signify merely an outward gesture of honour, such as kneeling or something similar, as we read that some worshipped kings, princes or holy men in the Scriptures; it signifies rather to render worship, or to give divine honour with religious reverence. So in the Old and New Testaments some are written to have gone up to Jerusalem to worship, and true worshippers are said to worship the Father in spirit and in truth. It was such honour that the devil demanded of Christ in the wilderness, and Christ refused it, saying, according to what is written in Deuteronomy, that such honour is due to God alone. In the same way those in Babylon refused to worship the statue, and Mordecai would not worship the proud Haman. Therefore divine honour

units.la: Loan.4. Matth.4. Deut.6. Colos.1. Ioan.1. vult impendi primogenito, ac proinde eundem pro Deo agnosci & coli. Sed talem honorem ait debere impendi per angelos, ut euidentissimè hinc colligi debeat, adorationem hic intelligendam, quæ debetur Deo: nam homines sanè ab angelis adorati non leguntur: deinde ipsis angelos multò esse præstabiliores, natura, qualitates, & accidentia alia quamplurima testificantur. Oportet igitur esse Deum, què ipsi angeli adorabūt. Angelos enim Christo non solùm inferiores esse necesse est, sed ipsum quoq; diuinitate præditum esse, qui à tam præclaris ac nobilibus creaturis adoratur. Neq; emphasi caret particula uniuersalis omnes. Si enim omnes angeli debent illud facere: ergo ipse Christus nō est aliquis ex præstantioribus angelis, sicut aduersarij, qui modestissimi erant, concedebant: sed plane supra omnes angelos, quamlibet excellentes vel potentes. Videtur aut additum Dei, ad insinuandum. Itaq; Apostolus singula uerba exactè prouidit, & aptissimè suo accommodauit instituto.
units.tr: Loan.4. Matth.4. Deut.6. Colos.1. Ioan.1. is to be paid to the firstborn, and therefore he is to be acknowledged and worshipped as God. But the apostle says that this honour is to be paid by the angels, so it can be most clearly inferred that the adoration meant here is the adoration owed to God. For men are certainly not read of as being worshipped by angels. Moreover, many other things testify that the angels are far superior in nature, qualities and many other attributes. It must therefore be God whom the angels themselves worship. For it is necessary that the angels be not only inferior to Christ, but that he himself be endowed with divinity, since he is worshipped by such excellent and noble creatures. Nor is the universal particle all without emphasis. For if all the angels ought to do this, then Christ himself is not one of the more outstanding angels, as our opponents, who were quite modest, conceded, but clearly above all angels, however excellent or powerful. The word of God seems to have been added to make this plain. So the apostle weighed each word exactly and fitted it most aptly to his purpose.

units.la: Nunc tamen videamus, qua de causa in psalmo 96. hæc uerba sint posita: quibus de rebus psalmus ille concionetur, quod eius præcipuum sit argumentum & scopus. Deinde uerò inuestigemus breuiter, quomodo ea, quæ in psalmo dicuntur, de Christo rectè exponantur. Inuenio in quibusdam exemplaribus hunc titulum seu potius argumentum præsentis psalmi. Psalmus ipsi Dauid, quando terra restituta est ei: vero simile q; est, hunc à Dauide tunc decantatum, cùm post superatos Ammonitas aliasq; finitimas gentes, regnum ipsius florere maximè videbatur, unde uictoriam & fœlicitatem acceptā ferens, uni Deo ita canit: Dominus regnauit, exultet terra, lætentur insulæ multæ: Addit laudem eius à tremendæ maiestatis excellentia, præcipuè autem à iustitia & potentia eius, per quas duas uirtutes Deus potissimum regnum continet, quæq; reges maximè decent atq; ornant.
units.tr: Let us now see, however, for what reason these words are placed in Psalm 96, what the psalm is about, and what its chief argument and aim is. Then we shall briefly investigate how the things said in the psalm are rightly explained of Christ. I find in some copies this title, or rather argument, of the present psalm: A psalm of David, when the land was restored to him. It is likely that David sang it at the time when, after subduing the Ammonites and other neighbouring nations, his kingdom seemed to be flourishing most of all. Bearing the victory and happiness thus gained, he sings to the one God: The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice, let the many islands be glad. He adds praise drawn from the excellence of his awesome majesty, but especially from his justice and power. By these two virtues God chiefly upholds his kingdom, and these are what most befit and adorn kings.

units.la: Nubes & caligo in circuitu eius, iustitia & iudicium correctio sedis eius. Ignis ante ipsum præcedet, & inflammabit in circuitu inimicos eius. Alluxerunt fulgura eius orbi terræ, uidit & commota est terra. Montes sicut cera fluxerunt à facie Domini, à facie Domini omnis terra.
units.tr: Clouds and darkness are round about him; righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne. A fire goes before him and burns up his enemies round about. His lightnings lit up the world; the earth saw and trembled. The mountains melted like wax at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth.

units.la: Ita valde appositis uerbis exprimit mirabilem æquitatem seu iustitiam, & incredibilem Dei potentiam, unde summatim infert: Annunciauerunt cœli iustitiam eius, et uiderunt omnes populi gloriam eius: quasi diceret: Satis superq; notum est tum in cœlo, tum in terra, quanta sit eius dignitas, quàm sit ille iustus, & potens, quæ duo sunt præcipuè in rege spectanda.
units.tr: In these very apt words he expresses his wondrous equity or justice and his incredible power, and from this he briefly concludes: The heavens declared his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory. It is as if he were saying: it is known well enough and more than enough, both in heaven and on earth, how great his dignity is and how just and powerful he is, which are the two qualities chiefly to be looked for in a king.

units.la: Cùm uerò usq; nota est veri Dei summa iustitia & potentia, hinc per Apostrophen conuertit se ad gentes, atq; hortatur magno affectu eas, ut neglectis suis idolis, quibus ne minima quidem ex parte tale quiddam inest, ad uerum Deum se conuertant. Confundantur omnes, qui adorant sculptilia, & qui gloriantur in simulachris suis. Tum generaliter ad omnes electos, siue angelos, principes, & quoscunq; pios: Adorate eum omnes angeli eius: propter iustitiā uidelicet, & summam eius potentiam. Subijcit, quanto gaudio populum Dei decceat lætari, propter tantam Domini gloriam, ne sibi, sed uni Domino acceptos ferant regni fœlices successus, & habitas præclaras victorias.
units.tr: But since the supreme justice and power of the true God is so well known, he turns by an apostrophe to the nations and earnestly exhorts them to put aside their idols, which have not the least part of such qualities, and to turn to the true God. Let all be confounded who worship graven images and who glory in their idols. Then he addresses in general all the elect, whether angels, princes, or any godly people: Worship him, all you his angels, namely on account of his justice and his supreme power. He adds with how much joy the people of God ought to rejoice on account of so great a glory of the Lord, and not attribute to themselves but to the Lord alone the happy outcomes of their reign and the splendid victories they have won.

units.la: Audiuit, & lætata est Sion: et exultauerunt filiæ Iudæ propter iudicia tua Domine. Quoniam tu dominus altissimus super omnem terram, nimis exaltatus es super oēs Deos.
units.tr: Zion heard and was glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments, O Lord. For you, Lord, are the Most High over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods.

units.la: Postremò generalem addit exhortationem ad omnes pios, ut ipsi quoq; iustitiam propter Deum adeò iustum & potentem, colant: nec dubium quin ille sit eos semper à periculis liberaturus, & è medijs tenebris reducturus ad lucem.
units.tr: Lastly he adds a general exhortation to all the godly, that they too should worship justice on account of God, who is so just and powerful. There is no doubt that he will always deliver them from dangers and lead them out of the midst of darkness into the light.

units.la: Qui diligitis Dominum, odite malum, custodit Dominus animas sanctorum suorum, de manu peccatoris liberabit eos: Lux orta est iusto, & rectis corde lætitia. Lætamini iusti in Domino, & confitemini memoriæ sanctificationis eius.
units.tr: You who love the Lord, hate evil. The Lord guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of the sinner. Light is sprung up for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness.

units.la: Itá quidem Dauid de iustitia & potentia Dei cecinit, postquam per eum adiutus superatis aduersarijs regnum in pace teneret, soli Deo, non suis uiribus, aut humanę prudentiæ acceptos feres fœlices successus. Sed quis nūc nō uidet, id quod & Iudæi etiā aliqui concedunt, hic uaticinatū esse de regno ipsius Christi, quod in uniuersam terrā, & per In sulas innumeras longè lateq; extenditur: quod de regno Dauidico tū dici non poterat. Deinde, regnū Christi maximè situ est in iustitia & potentia: Nā Christus summè iustus, summè potens proprie aperuit nobis, quomodo iusti esse possimus apud Deū per fidē: & ipsum euangeliū uere est, ut habetur Rom. 1. summa potentia (summa uis ignis & spiritus) qua oēs aduersarij & hostes, qui per montes significantur, Dei sunt superati, & ad agnoscendū Deū pro summo rege ac seruatore perrēcti. Quod nullis humanæ sapientiæ præsidijs, nullis armis potuisset effici, id per stultitiā prædicationis euangelij effectū est, 1. Cor. 1. Et hanc iustitiā Christi cœli annunciarūt, (id est, apostoli) quando diuinis oraculis
units.tr: Thus David sang of the righteousness and power of God, after, aided by him, he had overcome his adversaries and held his kingdom in peace, and he ascribed his happy successes to God alone, not to his own strength or human wisdom. But who now does not see what even some Jews concede, that here he prophesied about the kingdom of Christ himself, which extends over the whole earth and through countless islands, far and wide; this could not be said of the Davidic kingdom at that time. Further, the kingdom of Christ consists chiefly in righteousness and power, for Christ, most righteous and most powerful, plainly revealed to us how we may be righteous before God through faith; and the gospel itself is truly, as stated in Rom. 1., the greatest power (the mighty force of fire and of the Spirit), by which all the adversaries and enemies, signified by the mountains, have been overcome by God and brought to acknowledge God as supreme king and Saviour. What could not have been accomplished by any aids of human wisdom or by any arms, has been brought about through "the foolishness of the preaching of the gospel," 1 Cor. 1. And the heavens announced this righteousness of Christ (that is, the apostles), when it had been promised to the world many times before by divine oracles.

units.la: d i culis antea fuit mundo saepius promissa: deinde uiua uoce patris palā comprobata, cū ad Iordanē audita est uox patris: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacitum est, ipsum audite. Et gloria Christi uiderūt omnes populi, quādo euangelium regni praedicatū est apud oēs gentes. Interea & confusi sunt oēs idololatrae, cū successus ipse docuerit, oēs falsas religiones ethnicorū toto orbe per euangelium tandē subuersas & extinctas, homines ad ductos ad agnitionē suorū errorū & uanitatis. Et propterea Christus ab angelis, id est, à sanctis, à regibus, principib. angelis, omnibus deniq; creaturis est adoratus. Certè q ad ipsos angelos attinet, angeli ei ministrasse leguntur, cuiq; praedicasse, cū primū annuncia rent eius natiuitatē pastorib. cū ministraret uictoriā de diabolo in deserto reportarit: cùm testati sunt eius resurrectionē, ite ascensionē ad coelos: cū deniq; in nomine eius omne genū coelestiū & terrestriū & infernorū flectendū, atq; ipsum supra oēs potestates, principatus, dominia, thronos, subuectū, & ab omnib. creaturis unā cū patre ppetuò colendū adorandūq; pasim inculcetur. Quia uerò gloria Christi adeò innotuit, & palā facta est, ideò laetata est Sion, id est, sancta ecclesia, tota piorū congregatio, & gauisa est, q; Christus agnitus est Dominus altissimus, & exaltatus super oēs Deos. Inde & pij studiosè cauent, ne, quod malum est, perpetrent, & fidem in Christum conijciunt, quòd propter eū à potestate peccati, mortis, Satanae, liberabuntur. Agunt Deo gratias, quòd è tenebris gē tium uocati sunt, & translati in admirabile lumen euangelij & regni Christi: propterea semel iustificati semper laetantur in Domino, & nunquam desinunt celebrare maiestatē illius, per quem se iustificatos seu sanctificatos norunt. En ergo, quā praeclarè de regno Christi rex & propheta Dauid fit concionatus, & quā omnia quadret Christo: ut cuius perspicuum esse possit, testimonium siue argumentum, quod apostolus ex hoc psalmo deprompsit ad confirmandam Christi diuinitatem & excellentiam prae angelis, ualde appositè producatam in medium, & uires non paruas habere. Quòd si fortasis morosus Iudaeus aliquis contendat, nihil ibi ad Christū pertinere, sed omnia referenda esse ad unum Deum, uidelicet patrem, qui semper agnitus est mundum regens & gubernans: obij ci poterunt, ad confirmandam interpretationem nostram, & sanctorum patrum, iā breuiter redditam, alij scripturae loci, qui palā significant, Mesiam siue Christum in mū dum uenturum, & plenum ius regni accepturum: inde & iudicaturum more regio uni uersum terrarum orbem: actum facile erit demonstrare, vniuersum psalmum de regno Christi uerè concionari. Sunt autem eiusmodi loci passim obuij. Esaiae. 11. Iudicabit in iu stitia pauperes & arguet in aequitate mansuetos terrae, & percutiet terram uirga oris sui. Daniel. 7. Videbam in uisione noctis, & ecce cum nubibus coeli quasi filius hominis veniebat, & usq; ad antiquum dierum peruenit, & coram eo obtulerunt illum, & dedit ei potestatem, & honorem, & regnum, & omnes populi & linguae ei seruient. Alibi alia occurrunt, & in euangelio saepius istud explicatur, quomodo Christus regnum debeat obtinere, non autem temporale, ut Iudaei somniant, sed spirituale. Potestatem autem me re regiam ille exercebit, cùm ad iudicium est venturus: tunc igne perdet montes, id est, potentissimos aduersarios, & Sion, & iusti omnes perpetuò laeti agent. Haec de praesenti argumento satis. Huc aut pertinet illud Apocal. 7. Ecce turba multa, quàm dinumerare nemo poterat, ex omnibus gentibus, & tribubus, & populis, & linguis, stantes ante thronū, & in cospectu agni, amicti stolis albis, & palmae in manibus eorū, & clamabant uoce magna dicentes: Salus ei, qui sedet super thronum Dei nostri, & agno. Et omnes angeli stabāt in circuitu throni & seniorum, & quatuor animalium, & procubuerunt in conspectu throni in facies suas, & adorauerunt Deum. Adorandū aut Christum ab angelis etiam secundum carnem, non est dubium, ut Chrysostomus rectè annotauit.
units.tr: for ages before, and then openly confirmed by the living voice of the Father, when at the Jordan the voice of the Father was heard: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him. And all peoples saw the glory of Christ when the gospel of the kingdom was preached among all nations. Meanwhile all idolaters were also confounded, since the outcome itself has shown that all the false religions of the heathen throughout the world have at last been overthrown and extinguished by the gospel, and men have been led to acknowledge their errors and vanity. And for this reason Christ is adored by the angels, that is, by the saints, by kings, by princes, by angels, and finally by all creatures. Indeed, as regards the angels themselves, we read that they ministered to him and served him, when they first announced his birth to the shepherds, when he gained the victory over the devil in the desert, when they bore witness to his resurrection and his ascension into heaven; and finally, that in his name every knee of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth should bow, and that he, exalted above all powers, principalities, dominions and thrones, is to be perpetually worshipped and adored together with the Father by all creatures, is everywhere inculcated. Since the glory of Christ has become so well known and so openly displayed, Zion, that is, the holy Church, the whole assembly of the faithful, has rejoiced and been glad that Christ has been acknowledged as the most high Lord and exalted above all gods. Hence the godly also carefully take heed not to commit what is evil, and they place their faith in Christ, because through him they will be delivered from the power of sin, of death and of Satan. They give thanks to God that they have been called out of the darkness of the nations and transferred into the marvellous light of the gospel and of the kingdom of Christ; therefore, having once been justified, they always rejoice in the Lord, and never cease to celebrate the majesty of him through whom they know themselves justified or sanctified. Behold, then, how splendidly King and prophet David preached concerning the kingdom of Christ, and how everything fits Christ. The testimony or argument which the apostle drew from this psalm to confirm the divinity and excellence of Christ above the angels can thus be clearly seen to have been very aptly brought forward, and it has no small force. But if some obstinate Jew should contend that nothing there pertains to Christ, but that everything must be referred to the one God, namely the Father, who has always been acknowledged as ruling and governing the world, then, to confirm our interpretation and that of the holy Fathers, which has now been briefly given, other passages of Scripture may be cited, which plainly signify that the Messiah or Christ is to come into the world and will receive full kingly authority, and thence will judge the whole orb of the earth in royal manner; it will easily be shown that the whole psalm truly speaks of the kingdom of Christ. Such passages occur everywhere. Isaiah 11: "He shall judge the poor in righteousness, and reprove with equity the meek of the earth, and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth." Daniel 7: "I saw in the night visions, and behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all peoples and nations and languages should serve him." Elsewhere other passages occur, and in the gospel this is often explained, how Christ ought to obtain the kingdom, not a temporal one, as the Jews dream, but a spiritual one. He will, however, exercise kingly power in fact when he comes to judgment; then he will destroy the mountains, that is, the most powerful adversaries, with fire, and Zion and all the righteous will rejoice perpetually. So much on the present argument. To this pertains also that passage of Apocalypse 7: "Behold, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands, and they cried with a loud voice, saying: Salvation to him who sits upon the throne of our God and to the Lamb." And all the angels stood round about the throne and the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell before the throne on their faces and worshipped God. That Christ is to be worshipped by the angels even according to the flesh is beyond doubt, as Chrysostom rightly observed.

units.la: Et ad angelos quidè dicit: Qui creat angelos suos spiritus, & ministros suos ignis flamā. Quartū argumentum, quo probat Christū excellētiore angelis, ac proinde verū deū: quod sumit non à persona Christi, ut in praecedentibus actū est: sed à persona angelorū. Vnde hic habēda est ratio collationis, quā supra diximus ab apostolo in hac cōfirmatione institutā, eruntq; omnia perspicua. Respice igitur ad ea, quae hactenus dicta sunt. Primò ait, Christum tanto praestantiorē esse angelis, quanto haberet magnificentius nomē. Ea erat propositio. Inde exposuit aliquot argumentis, quātū nomē Christus fit adeptus, nēpe filij Dei: unde in singulis argumentis & postremò posuit primogenitū. Nūc ergo ratione collationis adijcit de angelis, eos nō appellatos filios, sed tantū ministros, ut hu iusmodi consequentia recte comprehendi cuncta queant. Excellentior est in domo quā filius, quā minister. Atqui Christus est uerus Dei filius, angeli aut tātū sunt ministri. Ergo Christus est angelis multò excellētior. Maior per se est nota. Quod ad minoré attinet, Christū esse filiū, aliquot scripturę locis probatū est. Angelos uerò tātū esse ministros probatur testimonio psal.103.Simili forma argumetationis probat cap.3.Christũ superio re esse Mose.Nec dubiũ,quin Apostolus eo iudicio hũc locũ elegerit citandũ,q; tacitè vo- luerit alia argumenta ad dignitatẽ Christi illustranda conducetia, ex his uerbis colligi. Nã si propius intuemur,cũ dicitur,Qui creat angelos, manifestè significaturibi,angelos esse duntaxat creaturas,sicut aliæ creaturę,quę à Deo sunt in tépore conditę.Proinde cũ ha- benda sit ratio collationis in tota hac confirmatione,& in collatione plurimũ momenti habeant anthiteta,(præsertim in qua res impares conferuntur) erit iã per contrariũ infe rédũ,quòd cũ angeli sint creaturę,Christus sit creator,ac proinde illis superior. Nã alias cũ angeli sint creaturæ omniũ præstantissimæ,id quod nemo nõ concedit, cui modò ullum sit in rebus sacris iudicium : Christus non erit angelis superior,nisi creator confti- tuatur.En ergo primum argumentum ex prima voce,creationis videlicet collectum.Se- cundò cũ dicitur,angelos esse spiritus, hic rursus aliud habemus argumentum,ad asse rendam Christi diuinitatem.Nam si conferendus est Christus cũ angelis,ostendendusq; superior,sanè cũ angeli ipsi sint spiritus,oportetitidem,Christum spiritum esse,intelli- gamus.Sed quando iterum necessum est,Christum alia ratione & sublimiori dignitate spiritum faciamus,quàm angelos: hoc erit proximum discrimen & in promptu expo- situm,quòd angeli sint spiritus creati,Christus autem spiritus creas . Iam verò ex hoc in- fertur,Christus est spiritus creas: Ergo est Deus.
