Tertiò cũ dicitur,angelos esse ministros, hic aliud se prodit ex ratione antithetorum argumentum, ad afferendũ Christi diuinita- tem & summam potentiam.Recte enim colligemus:Angeli sunt tantũ ministri, Ergo Christus,ut maior angelis intelligatur,est Dominus. Atq; ita Christus collatus ad ange- los,se habet sicut dominus ad seruos. Nec dissimili modo liceret colligere dignitatẽ Chri sti,ex ipso vocabulo seu etymologia angelorum. Angelus enim nomen officij est, non naturæ,& significat nũciũ siue missũ. Quare cũ Christus debeat angelis superior consti- tui,si angelus se habet ut missus & obedies:Ergo necessum est,Christus se habeat ut mit tens & imperans.Atq; hoc,inquam,pacto ex ratione antithetorum,quæ diligenter sunt in cõparatione,præsertim qua res inter se conferuntur non ũsquequaq; pares, cõsideră da,ex singulis penè uerbis,quæ humilem conditionem angelorum exprimunt, singula argumenta ad extollendam dignitatem Christi,excerpi quount.Visum est ista paucis in- dicare,ut cæteris,qui oculatiores sunt & fœliciores in aucupandis argumentis occultis & latentibus,occasione demus plura & certiora,in hoc & cõsimilib. locis inuestigādi. Nunc uideamus,ãn citra difficultatem, & proprie hæc uerba sint præsenti instituto, ad probandũ uidelicet inferiore eã conditione angelorũ,quâ sit cõditio Christi,accõmoda- ta.Deinde,qualis angelorũ natura his paucis uerbis describitur. Sumpta igitur sunt hæc nerba ex psal.103.in quo propheta diuino afflatus Spiritu agès Deo pro omnibus bonis gratias,celebrat Dei inexhaustã potentiã,ob rerũ omniũ creatione,nec nõ amplissimam eiusdẽ bonitate & prouidétiã,qua cũcta moderatur,fouet,feruat. Itaq; mira uarietate to- tus ille psal.respersus est,dum res creatę,& præclara opera Dei innumera,in eo ex ordi- ne recensentur. Ac valde facilis est intelleƈtu,ut minimè opus sit,eũ pluribus uerbis explicare. Sic autem habet:
units.tr: And to the angels indeed he says: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire. This is the fourth argument, by which he proves that Christ is more excellent than the angels, and therefore true God. He takes it not from the person of Christ, as was done in the preceding arguments, but from the person of the angels. Here the rule of comparison must be kept, which we said above the apostle set up in this confirmation, and then everything will be clear. Look back, therefore, at what has been said so far. First he says that Christ is as much superior to the angels as he has a more excellent name. That was the proposition. Then he showed, by several arguments, how far Christ has obtained that name, namely Son of God, and so in each argument, and finally, he put "firstborn." Now, by way of comparison, he adds that of the angels it is not said that they are called sons, but only ministers. By this kind of inference, all the points can be rightly grasped. The one who is in the house is greater than the servant, the son than the minister. But Christ is the true Son of God, while the angels are only ministers. Therefore Christ is far more excellent than the angels. The major premise is evident in itself. As for the minor, that Christ is the Son has been proved by several passages of Scripture, and that the angels are only ministers is proved by the testimony of Psalm 103. By a similar form of argument, in chapter 3 he proves that Christ is above Moses. Nor is there any doubt that the Apostle chose this passage to be cited for that reason, since he silently wished that arguments serving to illustrate the dignity of Christ should be drawn from these words. For if we look more closely, when it is said "who makes the angels," it is clearly signified that the angels are merely creatures, like the other creatures which were created by God in time. Therefore, since the rule of comparison must be applied throughout this whole confirmation, and antitheses carry the greatest weight in comparison (especially where unequal things are compared), it will follow by the contrary that, since angels are creatures, Christ is the Creator and therefore superior to them. For otherwise, since angels are the most excellent of all creatures, which no one with any judgment in sacred matters would deny, Christ will not be superior to angels unless he is established as Creator. Here, then, is the first argument, drawn from the first word, namely creation. Secondly, when it is said that the angels are spirits, we have here another argument for asserting the divinity of Christ. For if Christ is to be compared with the angels and shown to be superior, and the angels themselves are spirits, we must understand that Christ is also a spirit. But since it is again necessary to make Christ a spirit in another way, and with a higher dignity than the angels, this will be the next difference, and it is easily set out: the angels are created spirits, but Christ is an uncreated spirit. From this it is inferred: Christ is an uncreated spirit; therefore he is God. Thirdly, when it is said that the angels are ministers, another argument emerges from the reasoning of antitheses, for asserting the divinity and supreme power of Christ. For we will rightly conclude: the angels are only ministers; therefore Christ, to be understood as greater than the angels, is Lord. And so Christ, compared with the angels, stands to them as a lord to servants. In a similar way one could also infer the dignity of Christ from the very word or etymology of "angel." For "angel" is a name of office, not of nature, and signifies a messenger or one sent. Therefore, since Christ must be established as superior to the angels, and an angel stands as one who is sent and obeys, it is necessary that Christ stands as one who sends and commands. And in this way, I say, from the reasoning of antitheses, which must be carefully considered in comparison (especially where things not at all equal are compared), almost each word that expresses the humble condition of the angels may yield a separate argument for exalting the dignity of Christ. It has seemed good to indicate these things briefly, so that we may leave it to others, who are sharper and more fortunate in finding hidden and latent arguments, to investigate more and surer ones in this and similar passages. Now let us see whether these words are, without difficulty and properly, suited to the present purpose, namely to prove that the condition of the angels is inferior, to match the condition of Christ. Then let us see what the nature of the angels is, as described in these few words. These words are taken from Psalm 103, in which the prophet, inspired by the divine Spirit, gives thanks to God for all good things and celebrates the inexhaustible power of God in the creation of all things, as well as his most ample goodness and providence, by which he governs, cherishes and preserves all things. That whole psalm is therefore marked by a wonderful variety, since created things and God's countless excellent works are recounted in it in order. It is very easy to understand, so there is hardly any need to explain it at length. It runs thus:

units.la: Benedic anima mea Domino, Domine deus meus magnificatus es vehementer, confessionem & decorẽ induisti. Amictus lumine sicut vestimento, extendes cœlum sicut pellem. Qui tegis aquis superiora eius, qui ponis nubem ascensum tuũ, qui ambulas super pennas ventorum. Qui facis angelos tuos spiritus & ministros tuos ignē vren- tē. Qui fundasti terram super stabilitatem suam,non inclinabitur in seculũ seculi,etc:
units.tr: Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, you are exceedingly magnified; you have clothed yourself with confession and beauty. You are wrapped in light as with a garment, you stretch out the heavens like a skin. You cover his upper chambers with waters, you make the clouds your chariot, you walk upon the wings of the winds. You make your angels spirits and your ministers a burning fire. You founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for ever and ever, etc.

units.la: Ex his uidere est,qua occasione verba præsentis argumenti psal.inserta sint:neq; scru- pus ullus oriri potest de hoc testimonio ceu tortũ foret,aut longius petitum. Tantũm hoc forafsis aliquis roget,an ad patrem tantũm,an etiã ad filiũ facultas ista creandi an- gelos sit in hoc psalmo relatar Certè si patri tantũ tribnas hîc potestate & gloriã omnẽ, hetid non inepte.Nã in hoc præcipuè adductũ est argumentũ, ut doceatur, angelos ap- pellatos esse ministros,ac proinde Christo esse inferiores,qui in Scripturis appellat filius ac Deus. Quòd si quis malit munus creandi tribuere etiam Christo, ut ita augeatur eius dignitas,atq; eo nomine intelligatur angelis superior, quòd angeli tantũ sint creaturæ, Christus uerò creator:sicut supra ex vocabulo creandi argumentum eiusmodi sumus ue nati:erit & hæc interpretatio ualde accõmoda,nec poterit à quoquâ reijci.Constat.n.pa tri & filio pare potestate ac facultate esse:& crebrò admodũ in Scripturis dicũtur res crea tæ per verbũ,sapientiã, virtute patris,quæ voces filium repræsentant, sicut supra admo nuimus,ubi dicebat Apostolus,per filiũ condita etiã seculaut psalm.32. Verbo Domini cœli
units.tr: From this one can see on what occasion the words of the psalm used in this argument were inserted, and no scruple can arise about this testimony as if it were twisted or fetched from too far away. Only perhaps someone may ask whether this power of creating angels in this psalm is referred to the Father alone, or also to the Son. Certainly, if you attribute to the Father alone the power and all the glory here, that would not be inept. For this passage is cited chiefly for this argument, that it may be taught that the angels are called ministers, and therefore are inferior to Christ, who is called Son and God in the Scriptures. But if someone prefers to ascribe the office of creating to Christ also, so that his dignity is increased and he is understood to be superior to the angels on the ground that the angels are only creatures while Christ is the Creator (as above we drew such an argument from the word "create"), then this interpretation too will be very suitable, and no one will be able to reject it. For it is agreed that the Father and the Son have equal power and ability, and in the Scriptures created things are very often said to be made through the Word, the wisdom, and the virtue of the Father, which words represent the Son, as we noted above, where the Apostle says that the ages were also made through the Son. Psalm 32: "By the word of the Lord were the heavens made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth." And in the same place: "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created," etc. So you may rightly also interpret of the Son that the angels were made or created through him.

units.la: Note: the bottom line of the page reads "cœli" aster the last verse marker; a printed reference "d" and "ʒ" appear at the foot. cœli firmati sunt, & spiritu oris eius omnis virtus eorum. Ibidem: Ipse dixit, & facta sunt, ipse mandauit, & creata sunt, &c. Itaq; recte etiā de filio interpretaberis, per ipsum angelos esse conditos seu creatos. Iam uero sententiam ipsam & vim verborum explicemus. Nam interpretes, qui in psalm. hunc scripserunt, varie interpretati sunt, idq; eo magis, cp vocabula qdā hic sint polysima & multiplicis significationis. Itaq; vocabulorū etiam singulorum in primis habenda ratio est, ut certam sententiam nostro conuenientem instituto excerpamus. Primum igitur de uocabulis: ἀγγέλους ... Et ad angelos qdē dicit: Nō quidē ad angelos uerba hæc pronunciata sunt, sed potius ad Deū, ac de angelis. Ad pro depositū, ut notat Primasius: vel ratione antitheseos ita locutus est, cū mox subijciatur: Ad filium autem, etc.
units.tr: Now let us explain the sense itself and the force of the words. For the interpreters who wrote on this psalm have explained it in various ways, and the more so because some of its words are very ambiguous and have many meanings. Therefore the individual words must above all be considered, so that we may extract a definite sense suited to our purpose. First, then, concerning the words: ἀγγέλους [angels] ... "And to the angels indeed he says": these words were not pronounced to the angels, but rather to God, and concerning the angels. "To" is used in the sense of "concerning," as Primasius notes; or he spoke in this way by way of antithesis, since immediately afterwards it is added: "But to the Son, etc."

units.la: Qui creat) Non dicit qui creauit, sed qui creat, ut sub creationis nomine comprehendatur & conseruatio in præsens tempus: quemadmodum etiam Ioan. 5. Christus ait: pater meus ad hoc usq; temporis operatur, & ego operor. Pariter enim operatur, potentiamq; exerit Deus, dum conseruat res conditas, atq; cum primum condit.
units.tr: "Who makes": he does not say "who made," but "who makes," so that under the name of creation preservation up to the present time is also included, just as in John 5 Christ says: "My Father works until now, and I work." For God works equally and exerts his power while he preserves the things created and at the same time creates them.

units.la: Cæterum cum hic dicitur, creatos angelos, ac proinde eos Christo inferiores, nō est quod obijciatur, etiam Christum dici in Scriptura creatum: siquidem Ecclesiastici 24. dicit Sapientia, per quam intelligitur filius: tunc præcepit & dixit mihi creator omnium, & qui creauit me, requieuit in tabernaculo meo. Chrysostomus quidem ita diluit hanc obiectionem, dicens: verba hæc non de Deo uero accipienda, sed de eo, qui est secundū carnem, & in tempore genitus. Satius autem est, ex eodem capite proferamus aliud verbum, quo Sapientia ibidem de se testatur, & præcedentium uerborum agit uelut interpretem: Ego ex ore altissimi prodij, primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Quo uerbo manifestum fit, Christum nullo pacto pro creatura censendum, cùm palàm dicatur, genitum à patre ante omnem creaturam: ut genitus quidem dici queat, (quemadmodum & supra in illis verbis, Ego hodie genui te) at nequaquam creatus. Relinquitur ergo, angelos esse creatos, Christum autem nullo modo creatum.
units.tr: Since it is said here that the angels were created, and therefore are inferior to Christ, no one should object that Christ too is called "created" in Scripture. In Ecclesiasticus 24 Wisdom says, and it is understood of the Son: "Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me, and he who created me rested in my tabernacle." Chrysostom answers this objection by saying that these words are not to be taken of the true God, but of him who is according to the flesh and was begotten in time. It is better, however, to bring forward another word from the same chapter, in which Wisdom bears witness concerning herself and, as it were, interprets the preceding words: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature." By this word it is made plain that Christ in no way is to be counted among the creatures, since it is plainly said that he was begotten of the Father before every creature. So he may indeed be said to be begotten (as also above, in the words "Today I have begotten you"), but by no means created. It remains, therefore, that the angels were created, but Christ in no way was created.

units.la: Angelus uero) Si spectemus uocabuli etymon, nuncium significat & legatum, à uerbo ἀγγέλλω, nuncio. Itaq; vocabulum est generale, & competit simul omnibus, qui mandata Dei proferunt, seu annunciant Dei uoluntatem, siue doctores, siue prophetæ sint, siue apostoli, siue spiritus cœlestes. Hinc Christus ipse Esaiæ 9. hoc nomen accipit, vbi dicitur: et vocabitur nomen eius, magni consilij angelus. Malachiæ 2. Sacerdotes uocantur angeli. Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & ex ore eius requirent legem, quia Angelus Domini exercituum est. Similiter Ioannes Baptista nuncius & præcursor Domini, angelus dictus est. Ita enim Marcus de eo citat illud Malachiæ 3. Ecce ego mittam angelum meum, & præparabit uiam ante faciem meam. Alias uero usitatissimè pro spiritibus cœlestibus accipitur, quibus Deus vtitur quasi ministris, per eos apud homines peragēs, quæcunq; ipsi visum est: ita, ut per eos doceat, moneat, puniat, à periculis eripiat: denique omnem vitam nostram moderetur ac gubernet: quomodo tota hac disputatione angeli nomen accipitur, & hoc loco accipiendum esse, mox declarabo. Iam & vox spiritus hic πνεῦμα, pro qua Hebræis est רוח plura significat. Aliquando flatum siue uentum: ut Baruch 6. Et spiritus in omni regione spirat, & nubes, cum imperatum fuerit à Deo, perabulant uniuersum orbem. Et Ecclesiastici 11. Quomodo ignoras, quæ sit uia spiritus, & qua ratione compinguntut ossa in uentre prægnantis: sic nescio opera Dei, qui fabricator est omnium. Aliquando Spiritus significat mentem seu animum hominis & impetum animi, 1. Cor. 2. Quis hominum nouit ea, quæ sunt hominis, nisi Spiritus hominis, qui est in eo. Aliquando significat habitum & spirationem, ut apud Iobum cap. 27. quam diu erit spiritus in me. Nonnunquam & pro spiritu Sancto accipitur, ut est distincta persona a patre & filio: quod fere fit, ut annotauit Didymus, quoties apud græcos articulos voci πνεῦμα præponitur. Sed multò frequentissimè pro spirituali & incorporea substantia, quomodo Deus ipse spiritus dicitur: Et rursus spiritus creati sunt alij boni, alij mali, quorum ualde crebrò in Scripturis fit mentio.
units.tr: "Angel": if we look at the etymology of the word, it signifies a messenger or envoy, from the verb ἀγγέλλω [angellō], I announce. So it is a general word, and it applies equally to all who deliver God's commands or announce his will, whether they are teachers, prophets, apostles or heavenly spirits. Hence Christ himself receives this name in Isaiah 9, where it is said: "and his name shall be called the angel of great counsel." In Malachi 2 priests are called angels: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and men shall seek the law at his mouth, because he is the angel of the LORD of hosts." Likewise John the Baptist, the messenger and forerunner of the Lord, is called an angel; for Mark so cites Malachi 3 concerning him: "Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face." But elsewhere the word is most commonly taken for heavenly spirits, whom God uses as ministers, carrying out through them among men whatever seems good to him: so that through them he teaches, admonishes, punishes, rescues from dangers, and in the end governs and guides our whole life. In this way the name angel is taken throughout this discussion, and I will soon show that it must be understood so in this place. Now the word spirit, here πνεῦμα [pneuma], for which the Hebrews have רוח [ruach], also signifies several things. Sometimes it means breath or wind, as in Baruch 6: "The spirit blows in every region, and the clouds, when commanded by God, pass over the whole world." And Ecclesiasticus 11: "As you do not know what is the way of the spirit, and how the bones are knit together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all." Sometimes spirit means the mind or soul of a man and the impulse of the mind, as in 1 Corinthians 2: "Who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him?" Sometimes it means condition and breath, as in Job 27: "as long as the spirit is in me." Sometimes it is taken for the Holy Spirit as a person distinct from the Father and the Son, which, as Didymus observed, generally happens whenever the article is placed before the word πνεῦμα among the Greeks. But by far most frequently it means a spiritual and incorporeal substance, in the way that God himself is called spirit; and again there are created spirits, some good and some evil, of whom mention is very often made in Scripture.

units.la: Sed rursus vocabulū ignis præterquam quòd significat id, quod communi sensu igne appellamus, qui nimirum caloris ui præeminet, fuaq; ui quaeuis penetrat, consumit, diruit. Tum per metaphoram celeritatem in agendo, subtilitatem in substantia significat. Sic & per Metonymiam pro ira Dei, pro impiorum damnatione sæpe ponitur. Nonnunquam pro persecutione & omnis generis calamitate, ut psalmo 38. 1. Corinth. 3. Alias pro verbo Dei, ut Ieremiæ 23. Verba mea quasi ignis. Nonnunquam pro Spiritu sancto, qui linguis igneis apparuit. Aut pro donis Spiritus sancti, potissimum q; charitate: quò pertinet illud, ignem veni mittere in terram. Alicubi summam Dei potentiam in agendo, fue ardente, ut ita dicamus, zelu. Deuter. 4. Deus noster ignis consumens est. Et Exod. 19. Mons
units.tr: "Fire," again: besides signifying what in common speech we call fire, which by the power of its heat surpasses all else and by its force penetrates, consumes and destroys whatever it touches, it also signifies, by metaphor, speed in acting and subtlety of substance. So too by metonymy it often stands for the wrath of God and for the damnation of the wicked; sometimes for persecution and every kind of calamity, as in Psalm 38 and 1 Corinthians 3. Elsewhere it stands for the word of God, as in Jeremiah 23: "My words are like fire." Sometimes it stands for the Holy Spirit, who appeared with tongues of fire, or for the gifts of the Holy Spirit, especially love; to this belongs the saying, "I came to cast fire upon the earth." In some places it signifies God's supreme power in acting, as with a burning, so to speak, zeal. Deuteronomy 4: "Our God is a consuming fire." And Exodus 19: Mount

units.la: Verba psalmi polysima. Mons Sinai fumabat, eō quòd Dominus descenderat super eum in igne: Ibidem 14. Erat autē species gloriæ Dei quasi ignis ardēs. Cū ergo tā variē accipiātur in Scripturis hæ voces angelus, spiritus, ignis, factū est, vt variē quoq; expositus sit præsens locus Psalmi 103. Qui creat angelos suos spiritus, et ministros suos ignis flāmam: & variē redditę sint sententiæ. Quidā enim hoc pacto verterūt: Flatibus vtitur pro nuncijs, & pro ministris igne conflagrāte: accipien tes nimirū flatū pro vento impetuoso & vehementi: ignem autē pro eiusmodi igne, qualis aliquando, cùm magna intēperies est, cernitur per aerem volitare, aut etiam decidere, & dāna terris inferre. Vt fit sententia: Deū vti tempestuosis & procellosis ventis pro nūcijs suę irę & indignationis. Similiter vti igne pro ministro & executore vltionis ac supplicij: quomodo 4. Reg. 2. cùm leuare vellet Dominus Heliā per turbinē in cœlum. Iob 27. Diuitem apprehēdet inopia quasi aqua, nocte opprimet eum tempestas, tollet eū entus vrens, & auferet, & velut turbo rapiet eum de loco suo. Item, Iob 1. Véto vehementi concussa desfcribitur domus, in qua filij Iob erant comedētes & bibentes. En quomodo vento quasi nūcio Dominus vtitur ad demonstrandam voluntatē suam erga pios ac impios. Similiter autem de igne, quomodo Dominus ad diuersas res eius ministerio vtatur, multis in locis manifestū fit. Nam iterum Iob 1. Ignis de cœlo descendisse memoratur, & cunctas oues pueros q; cōsumpsisse, Genes. 19. Dominus pluit super Sodomam & Gomorrhā sulphur & ignem. Num. 11. Igne cōsumpti sunt murmuratores. Et igneo curru Helias in cœlū subuectus est, 4. Reg. 2. & 4. Reg. 6. Mōs plenus currū & equorū igneorū visus est Gehasi ad defendendū Helisæū, & ciuitatē Dothan, contra exercitū regis Syriæ. Verūm hæc interpretatio nequaquā probāda est, neq; instituto nostro aliqua ex parte cōuenit, imò nec ad mentē prophetæ attinet. Quid enim attinet hoc loco vocē רוח seu πνεῦμα p flatu seu vento accipere, cùm propheta prius de aquis, nubibus, ventis, satis egerit, dicēs: Qui ambulas super pēnas ventorum. Et nimirum sapit hęc interpretatio Iudaismum. Solent enim Iudęi & illos locos Scripturę, quibus nitimur probare, Spiritum sanctum tertiā in diuinitate persona, hoc pacto eludere, interpretādo videlicet, spiritū esse flatū seu ventū Ita illud Genes. 1. Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas, statim euertūt, dicendo, aquas agitatas veto, &c. Rectius ergo sermone hīc esse de angelis dicemus, atq; angelos quidē ita intel ligēdos, vt vox angelorū Spiritus quosdā cœlestes creatos significet, quib. Deus vtitur, sicut aliis creaturis, ad suum ministerium. Quanquam ex his, qui de angelis locum hunc accipiūt, vocabula spiritus & ignis adhuc nonnulli ita interpretātur, vt metaphoricē hic posita iudicent, ad explicādum ipsorū angelorū in officijs suis promptitudinē ac diligentiam. Spiritus enim voce significari celeritatem & facultatē citò expediendi quęcūq; negotia, vt instar ventorum aut fulminis ocysimè quóuis ad explendū mandata Dei feran tur: id quod & signi ficatū est eò, quòd angelis videntur in Scripturis & pictūris alæ attribui. Ignis autem voce significari feruorem atq; ardens studiū, seu agendi efficaciam, cùm ignii insit maxima agendi & penetrandi vis. Quò pertinet, quòd angeli leguntur interdū in specie ignis apparuisse: vt in monte Sina, in rubo, cùm vt Stephanus interpretatur Actor. 7. angeli vice Dei in toto negotio Mosaico functi sunt: nimirum externo habitu ministerij sui modum declarantes. Neq; hæc interpretatio est reijcienda. Sed magis arridet magis q; ad sententiam & mente Prophetæ, etiam apostoli, spectare videtur interpretatio eorū, qui dicunt, his verbis describi plane angelorū naturam, nempe substantiā non corporeā, sed spirituale, inuisibile, quæq; omnē corpoream superet, & ignitā, hoc est, viuam, subtile, mouentē, agentē, & maximē spiritualis indolis hīc significari. Et cùm hoc pacto confertur Christus cum excellentissimis creaturis, nimirū quę ipsæ quoq; sunt spiritus, sicut & Deus spiritus est, vt habetur Ioan. 4. & ignitę naturę, sicut Deus quoq; ignis cōsumes appellatur. Tantū abest, vt suspicemur, paru aptā esse ratione, qua videtur angeli quasi pares cum Christo constitui, cùm potius iudicare debeamus, multò aptissimā esse collatione, & mirum in modū ex ea Christi crescere dignitatē, vtpote in qua cū Christus excellentissimis creaturis ostenditur adhuc superior, eò q; ipse vocetur filius, sicut prius demonstratū est: angeli tamē vocātur dūtaxat ministri, sicut præsens locus testatur. Nam vt supra admonuimus, in voce ministri, quæ opponitur appellationi filij, vis argumenti præsentis sita est. Porrò spiritum hic significare natura & substantiā, non qualitatē officij, author est mihi Augustinus, qui enarrās hunc psalmū ita ait: Angelus officij nomē est, nō naturæ, quæris nomē huius naturæ, Spiritus est: quæris officiū, angelus est. Vide illud in homine: nomē natureę, homo: officij, miles: nomē naturę, vir: officij, præco. Et ex recentioribus Pomeranus, Angelos suos Deus facit, inquit, inuisibiles, non carnis & sanguinis partitcipes creaturas, hoc est, facit eos spiritus, & eosdem flammā ignis, id est, ignęæ naturæ siue spiritualis. Et paulò pòst, Angelos in principio creaturarum creatos hīc Augustinus de natura non de qualitate hic interpretatur nomē spiritus. Pomeranus.
units.tr: The words of the psalm have many meanings. "Mount Sinai was smoking, because the LORD had descended upon it in fire." Ibid. 14: "The appearance of the glory of God was like a blazing fire." Since the words angel, spirit, fire are taken in such varied ways in Scripture, the present passage of Psalm 103 has been expounded in various ways too, and its sentences have been rendered variously. For some have translated it thus: "He uses winds as messengers, and a blazing fire as minister," taking spirit as a violent and vehement wind, and fire as that kind of fire which, when there is great bad weather, is sometimes seen flying through the air or even falling and bringing harm to the lands. The sense is: God uses stormy and tempestuous winds as messengers of his anger and indignation, and similarly uses fire as minister and executor of vengeance and punishment, as in 2 Kings 2, when the Lord wished to take Elijah up into heaven by a whirlwind. Job 27: "Poverty will seize the rich man like water; a tempest will overwhelm him by night; the scorching wind will carry him off, and like a whirlwind it will snatch him from his place." Likewise Job 1: the house in which Job's sons were eating and drinking was shaken by a mighty wind and collapsed. See how the Lord uses the wind, as it were a messenger, to show his will towards the godly and the wicked. Similarly, how the Lord uses fire through its ministry for various purposes is made plain in many places. For again Job 1 records that fire came down from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants; Genesis 19: the Lord rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah; Numbers 11: the murmurers were consumed by fire; Elijah was carried up into heaven in a fiery chariot, 2 Kings 2; and 2 Kings 6: Gehazi saw a mountain full of chariots and fiery horses to defend Elisha and the city of Dothan against the army of the king of Syria. But this interpretation is by no means to be approved, nor does it agree in any way with our purpose; indeed it does not even fit the mind of the prophet. For what is the point here in taking the word רוח [ruach], or πνεῦμα [pneuma], as breath or wind, when the prophet has already dealt sufficiently with waters, clouds and winds, saying: "who walks upon the wings of the winds"? This interpretation certainly savours of Judaism. For the Jews are accustomed to evade in this way those passages of Scripture on which we rely to prove that the Holy Spirit is the third person in the Godhead, namely by interpreting spirit as breath or wind. So they at once overturn that text of Genesis 1, "the Spirit of God was moving over the waters," by saying that the waters were stirred by the wind. Rather, we will say that the passage is rightly about angels, and that the angels are to be understood in such a way that the word angels and spirits denotes certain created heavenly beings, whom God uses for his service, as he uses other creatures. Yet some of those who take this passage of the angels still interpret the words spirit and fire as metaphorical, to explain the readiness and diligence of the angels themselves in their duties. For by the word spirit is signified speed and the ability to carry out any business quickly, so that like winds or lightning they are borne with the utmost swiftness anywhere to fulfil God's commands; this is also indicated by the fact that wings are attributed to angels in Scripture and in pictures. By the word fire is signified fervour and burning zeal, or efficacy in acting, since fire has the greatest power to act and to penetrate. To this belongs the fact that angels are sometimes read to have appeared in the form of fire, as on Mount Sinai and in the bush; as Stephen interprets in Acts 7, angels, in God's place, performed the whole Mosaic business, declaring by their outward appearance the manner of their ministry. Nor is this interpretation to be rejected. But the interpretation of those who say that these words describe plainly the nature of the angels seems more pleasing and to look more to the sense and mind of the prophet, and even of the apostles: namely, a substance not corporeal but spiritual, invisible, surpassing every bodily thing, and fiery, that is, living, subtle, moving, acting; and that what is signified here is a most spiritual character. And when Christ is compared in this way with the most excellent creatures, namely those which are themselves spirits, just as God is spirit (as is found in John 4), and of a fiery nature, just as God too is called a consuming fire, we are so far from suspecting that the manner in which the angels seem to be set up as equals with Christ is ill suited, that we ought rather to judge this comparison to be far more apt; and in a wonderful way Christ's dignity grows from it, since in it Christ is shown to be still superior even to the most excellent creatures, the more so because he is called Son, as was demonstrated before, whereas the angels are called only ministers, as this passage bears witness. For, as we noted above, the force of the present argument lies in the word minister, which is set against the title Son. Moreover, that the word spirit here denotes nature and substance, not the quality of an office, I have as my authority Augustine, who, expounding this psalm, says: "Angel is the name of an office, not of a nature; you ask the name of the nature: it is spirit; you ask of the office: it is angel. See this in man: the name of the nature is man, of the office soldier; the name of the nature is man, of the office herald." And among more recent writers, Pomeranus: God makes his angels, he says, invisible, creatures not partaking of flesh and blood, that is, he makes them spirits, and the same a flame of fire, that is, of a fiery or spiritual nature. And a little later: "Augustine here interprets the name spirit as referring to the nature, not the quality, of the angels, who were created at the beginning of creation. Pomeranus."

units.la: hic indicatur. Sic deniq; plures alij exponunt, & reuera sententia prophetæ postulat Est ergo hic potius descriptio quædam naturæ Angelorum secundum substantiam, quàm qualitatem seu officium.
units.tr: here it is indicated. Thus, in the end, many others also explain it, and indeed the sense of the prophet requires it. This passage is therefore rather a certain description of the nature of angels according to their substance than of their quality or office.

units.la: Necesse est autem, vt constet argumentum Apostoli, interpretari verba hęc, Spiritū & igne, non de flatu seu vento, aut de fulgure igneq; deciduo, quibus Deus interdū vtitur quasi ministris, ad significandum aliquid de sua erga homines voluntate: sed de angelis, qui sunt spiritus cœlestes, vt vocabulo spiritus & ignis natura angelorum hic describi intelligatur, nimirum quòd angeli sint substantiæ non corporeæ aut visibiles, sed spirituales, inuisibiles: deinde igneæ naturæ, hoc est, viuę, subtiles, & singulari vi agendi præditæ. Atque hoc pacto interpretatur Augustinus, aliíque plures tàm veteres, quàm recentiores.
units.tr: For the argument of the Apostle to stand, these words, "who makes his angels spirits and a flame of fire," must be understood not of wind or breath, nor of lightning or falling fire, which God sometimes uses as servants to signify something of his will toward human beings, but of angels, who are heavenly spirits. So by the words "spirit" and "fire" the nature of angels is understood to be described here: namely, that angels are substances that are not corporeal or visible but spiritual and invisible, and then of a fiery nature, that is, living, subtle, and endowed with a singular power of acting. Augustine, and many others both ancient and recent, interpret it in this way.

units.la: Quia aūt talis hic habetur angelorū descriptio, qualis vix alibi occurrit, quæ videlicet natura eorū ita exprimat, videmur operę facturi pretiū, si paulò plenius de natura angelorum disputemus: propterea quòd hic locus valde vtilis est, & ad intelligendos varios Scripturæ locos necessarius, & à paucis tractatus.
units.tr: Since such a description of angels is given here as hardly occurs elsewhere, one that expresses their nature in this way, we seem to be undertaking a worthwhile task if we discuss the nature of angels somewhat more fully. This passage is very useful and necessary for understanding various passages of Scripture, and it is seldom treated.

units.la: Primò itaq; generalis definitio angelorū ex præsenti loco colligitur de natura eorum ac substantia, in hunc modū: Angeli sunt creaturæ spirituales, incorporeæ, inuisibiles, atq; igneæ naturæ, hoc est, uiuæ, agiles, subtiles, & singulari ui agendi præditæ. Tantum mihi videntur verba præsentis argumentis sonare. Sunt haud dubiè ea, quæ de natura angelorū dicendæ forent, longè supra hominū captū posita: sicut longè excellentior est angelorū conditio, (quantum ad naturā in quā) quàm hominum. Quare si quid de illis volumus cognoscere, adeundā nobis audiedaq; est magistra Scriptura, quę in sua schola & bibliotheca multa nobis ponit, & quantū scire expedit, vel necessu est: Et tamē sic ea ipsa à nobis cernūtur, vt pleraq; satis assequi haud valeamus. Quid ergo dicemus de ijs, qui etiam, in Scriptura non attingūtur: tamen audēt statuere de angelis, ac definire, nō aliter quàm si nuper cœlo delapsi narrarent, quæ aliquot annorum familiari contubernio, & in angelorum republica dici vel fieri vidissent atq; audij ssent: quasi ipsi vel plura scirent, quàm Spiritus sanctus in Scriptura prodere voluit: aut melius Spiritu sancto nosset, quid & quantum sciri nobis conduceret. Tutissimum ergo intra limites, quos Scriptura præfigit, nos contineamus, existimemusq; valde magnum, vel ea, quæ in Scriptura proponuntur, vtcunq; assequi. Porrò, quomodo crasius aut clarius redderem definitionem aliquam, non video.
units.tr: First, then, a general definition of angels is gathered from the present passage concerning their nature and substance, in this way: Angels are spiritual, incorporeal, invisible creatures of a fiery nature, that is, living, nimble, subtle, and endowed with a singular power of acting. These seem to me to be the only things the words of this passage express. Doubtless what might be said about the nature of angels lies far above human comprehension, just as the condition of angels is far more excellent than that of human beings, as far as their nature goes. Therefore, if we wish to know anything about them, we must approach and hear Scripture as our teacher, which in its school and library sets before us many things, and as much as it is expedient or necessary for us to know. And yet even these things are so perceived by us that we are hardly able to grasp most of them. What then shall we say of those who venture to lay down and define things about angels that are not touched on in Scripture at all, speaking as if they had just come down from heaven and were recounting what they had seen and heard said or done in the commonwealth of angels over a long familiar companionship? As if they knew more than the Holy Spirit wished to reveal in Scripture, or knew better than the Holy Spirit what and how much it is useful for us to know. Therefore it is safest to keep ourselves within the limits that Scripture sets, and to think it a very great achievement to grasp in any way the things that are set forth in Scripture. Moreover, I do not see how I could render any definition more coarsely or more clearly.

units.la: Creaturas esse angelos, hoc est, in tempore à Deo formatos more aliarū creaturarū, manifeste sonat illud verbum: Qui erat: Atq; ita longo interuallo à creatoris, Dei videlicet dignitate distinguuntur, vt nullo modo Deo æquari possint. Quod etiā Theophylactus hunc locū enarras adnotat. Quamobrē hic confutantur, qui dixerunt, in Scripturis non exprimi, quòd angeli sint à Deo creati. Quare & illa concidit impia quorundā opinio, qua angelis creandi munus ausi sunt tribuere, quasi per angelos mundus hic esset creatus. Quomodo ipsi creauerint mundū, cùm ipsi sint in tempore creati, et creaturę appellentur, non creatores? Et cùm cœlū ac terra à Deo cōdita sint in principio, vt loquitur Scriptura, hoc est, antequam tempus vel æuum vllum præexisteret, quomodo intelligemus, angelos ante principium, & antequam cœlum & terrę fieret, exitisse? Simul ergo cum reliquis creaturis maximè cœlestibus, angelos esse creatos, intelligi par est. Facessant inte rea quęstiones illę de tempore & loco, quo angeli fuerint primùm conditi, & de Empyræo cœlo angelis repleto, &c. Sentent.lib.2. distinct. 2.
units.tr: That angels are creatures, that is, formed by God in time like the other creatures, is clearly stated by the words "who was": and so they are distinguished by a long interval from the dignity of the Creator, that is, of God, so that they can in no way be made equal to God. Theophylact also notes this in his commentary on the passage. Hence those are refuted who have said that Scripture does not state that angels were created by God. Likewise that impious opinion of some falls, which dared to assign to angels the office of creating, as if the world here had been created through angels. How could they have created the world, when they themselves were created in time and are called creatures, not creators? And since heaven and earth were created by God in the beginning, as Scripture says, that is, before any time or age existed, how shall we understand that angels existed before the beginning, and before heaven and earth were made? It is therefore fitting to understand that angels were created together with the other creatures, most of all the heavenly ones. Let those questions about the time and place where the angels were first created be set aside, and the question about the Empyrean heaven filled with angels, etc. Sentences, book 2, distinction 2.

units.la: Iam esse creaturas spirituales, satis declarat vox Spiritus, quæ hoc loco opponitur ei, quòd corporeum est, visibile, contrectabile, & sensibus expositum, corruptibile, mortale, quodq; vllo pondere, impedimentis, pasiionibus, sit grauatum: vt palàm hinc fiat, angelos esse incorporeas substantias, inuisibiles, immortales, impassibiles, &c. Quòd pertinet, quòd Christus in euangelio Marci 12. dicit, animas post resurrectionem fore, sicut angelos Dei. Vnde quæ de animarum statu sentire possimus, eadem magna ex parte & de angelis licet constituere. Qua voce summa dignitas angelorum, propinquitas cum Deo, & præeminentia præ reliquis creaturis corporeis & visibilibus ostenditur. Quòd autem speciem corporum induant, nempe humanam, vel igneam, vel huiusmodi, id diuina dispensatione fit, vt apriores sint ad agendum inter homines, quę ipsis à Deo sunt iniuncta. Aliàs quidem ipsos secundum suam naturā nemo poterit cernere, sicut nec Deū aliquis vnquàm vidit, vt ait Ioannes. At secūdum corpora, quę pro tepore assumūt, & iterū deponūt, fiunt oculis cōspicui, audibiles, cōtrectabiles, sicut angelus luctās cū Iacob, Raphael in historia Tobię. Quare corpora illis tribuere qlibet tenuia ac subtilia, admodū abhac definitione Scripturæ alienŭ est:cùm angeli spiritus clarè dicantur, sicut & Deus spiritus est:Spiritus autem nihil corporeŭ est. Cæterùm inquirere quomodo corporum species assumant,an ex rebus elementalibus & corporeis corpora sibi vera formant, satius est,humiliter & reuerenter præterire,quàm scrupulosè inquirere:id quod etiam Augustinus lib.3.de Trinitat.cap.1. iubet,vbi disputat,quomodo Deus,(vel loco Dei ipsi an geli) corporalibus formis apparuerit. Illud autem,quòd angeli dicûtur flámaignis,non possum crassius,quàm feci,reddere.Neq; enim reuera sunt flámæ corporeæ & visibiles, vel sensibiles: sed ea particula puto id, quod ad spiritualem substantiam attinet, aliquo modo plenius declarari,vt nimirŭ igneam indolem quandâ habere intelligantur, id est, instar ignis,puri,lucidi,splendidi,sublimes,agiles, celeres vehementer feruidi & potétes in agendô,nihil ponderis,nihil crassitudinis,nihil impedimenti in se habentes. Quò per tinet,quòd in specie ignis & cum fulgore sepę apparuerint,itė appellatio illa סרפים,id est, ardentes. Tàm mirabilis est natura angelorum, vt nullis verbis propriè describi possit: quodq; de eis scire nos conuenit,aut intelle&us humanus possit capere, Spiritus san&us non putauit aptius posse explicari, quàm duabus hisce vocibus, nempe Spiritus & ignis. Quare plura addere ad explicádum naturam angelorŭ,puto nequaquá esse tutum.
units.tr: That angels are spiritual creatures is sufficiently declared by the word "spirit," which in this passage is set against what is corporeal, visible, tangible, exposed to the senses, corruptible, mortal, and weighed down by any burden, hindrances, or passions; so that it is plain from this that angels are incorporeal, invisible, immortal, impassible substances, etc. As for the fact that Christ says in the Gospel of Mark 12 that souls after the resurrection will be like the angels of God, from this we may largely form the same judgments about angels as we can about the state of souls. By this word the high dignity of angels, their nearness to God, and their preeminence above the other corporeal and visible creatures is shown. That they put on the form of bodies, namely human, or fiery, or of some such kind, is done by divine dispensation, so that they may be more apt to act among human beings in the things enjoined on them by God. Otherwise, indeed, no one can see them according to their own nature, just as no one has ever seen God, as John says. But according to the bodies that they take on for a time and then lay aside again, they become visible to the eyes, audible, and tangible, as the angel wrestling with Jacob, or Raphael in the history of Tobit. Therefore to attribute to them any bodies, however thin and subtle, is far removed from this definition of Scripture, since angels are plainly called spirits, just as God is spirit, and spirit is nothing corporeal. Moreover, to inquire how they assume the forms of bodies, whether they form true bodies for themselves from elemental and corporeal things, is better passed over humbly and reverently than examined scrupulously; Augustine also enjoins this in book 3 of On the Trinity, chapter 1, where he discusses how God (or the angels in God's place) appeared in bodily forms. But that angels are called a flame of fire, I cannot render more coarsely than I have done. For they are not really bodily and visible or sensible flames. But I think that by this particle what pertains to their spiritual substance is declared somewhat more fully, so that they are understood to have a certain fiery quality, that is, to be like fire: pure, bright, splendid, lofty, nimble, swift, very ardent in acting, and powerful, having nothing of weight, nothing of thickness, nothing of hindrance in themselves. To this belongs the fact that they have often appeared in the form of fire and with brightness, and likewise that name seraphim [סרפים], that is, burning ones. The nature of angels is so wonderful that it cannot be properly described in any words; and the Holy Spirit did not think that what it is fitting for us to know about them, or what human understanding can grasp, could be explained more aptly than by these two words, namely spirit and fire. Therefore I think it is by no means safe to add more in explaining the nature of angels.

units.la: Omnes sibi inuicé esse pares,quod ad naturá attinet, satis arguit generalis hæc definitio,quæ de omnibus generaliter accipi potelt: si quæ discrimina adferuntur, ea ab officijs proueniunt.
units.tr: That all angels are equal to one another as regards nature is sufficiently shown by this general definition, which can be taken generally of all of them: if any differences are adduced, they arise from their offices.

units.la: Vtrû rectè dicantur angeli ratiocinari,sicut patres quidâ definiunt, angelû esse ϕωςφορον, haud scio,an affirmari possit,eos more hominŭ colligere & ratiocinari. Iudiciŭ tamé seu intelle&ŭ, voluntatem,liberum arbitriŭ, adimere illis nequaquam licet, cùm cóstet, alios se conuertisse,vt in veritate persisteret,alios à veritate defecisse, sicut Petrus & Iudas in epistolis suis satis clarè docet,ac proinde electione,liberum arbitriŭ eos habuisse. Qua de re plenius, vbi de natura malorum angelorum disseremus. Hæc de angelis in genere. Nunc constituendæ sunt nobis duæ, quas habemus ex Scripturis, angelorum species. Leguntur enim angeli boni,alij verò angeli mali. De his ordine dicamus,ac primùm de bonis.
units.tr: Whether angels may rightly be said to reason, as some of the Fathers define them to be "light-bearing" [φωσφόρον], I do not know whether it can be affirmed that they gather and reason in the manner of human beings. Yet it is by no means permitted to take away from them judgment or understanding, will, and free choice, since it is established that some of them turned themselves so as to persist in the truth, and others fell away from the truth, as Peter and Jude teach quite clearly in their epistles; and therefore they had free choice by election. We shall discuss this more fully when we treat the nature of the evil angels. These things concern angels in general. Now we must set forth the two kinds of angels that we have from Scripture. For good angels are read of, and other angels, evil ones. Let us speak of these in order, and first of the good.

units.la: Angelos bonos licèt definire,adijciendo ad id, quòd generaliter de natura omnium iam dictum est,quòd in ministerium emittuntur propter eos,qui hæredes erunt salutis: quæ verba habentur ad finem huius primi capitis ad Hebræos,eorumq; hæc est sententia:quòd boni angeli sint spiritus ministrantes & obsequentes Deo,qui emittuntur,cùm illi visum est, adiuuandum, docendum, defendendum, feruandum pios credentes.
units.tr: Good angels may be defined by adding to what has been said in general about the nature of all of them, that they are sent into ministry for the sake of those who will be heirs of salvation. These words occur at the end of the first chapter of Hebrews, and their meaning is this: that good angels are spirits ministering to and obeying God, who are sent, when it seems good to him, to help, teach, defend, and keep the faithful who believe.

units.la: Quæ definitio sumpta est ab illorum officijs erga Deum & erga homines, per quæ propriè à malis angelis rebellibus,immorigeris & quæretibus semper incómodare mortaliŭ generi, discernuntur. Atq; ipsa vocabuli ratio,tum etiam quæ per angelos legitur, &iussu Dei facta,huius definitionis certitudinem approbant. Sed priusquam de officijs actionibus angelorŭ bonorum plenius disputem,refutanda est mihi quorúdam opinio, qui angelos negarunt esse Spiritus naturæ subsistentis,seu veras esse res:sed tantùm motus quosdam animorum seu affectiones in nobis,qui tacitè subinde irrepunt. Ac bonos quidem esse angelos cùm de bona re sunt,& ad benè agendŭ excitant:malos verò angelos,qui de rebus malis,& ad male agendum nos sollicitant,impelluntur. Hæc fuit impia opinio Saducęorum & quorundam sequacium,quorum vereor ne alibi supersint adhuc reliquiæ.Proinde doceamus,angelos veros esse spiritus, & supposita quædam per se in sua natura subsistentia. Si non essent naturæ subsistentes & veræ substantię, sed tantum motus animorum, quid opus fuisset externis & corporeis figuris illos apparere,sicut creberrimè apparuisse passim in veteri testamento legimus? Nam & legem data re,tabulis lapideis insculptam,& alia id genus facere,non est,nisi certa natura per se subsistentium.Item,quòd Daniel cap.7.tribuit numerum angelis,ac dicit myriadas angelorum,& plures sibi subsidio à Patre cœlitus mitti posse,nisi calix esset exhauriendus, & Scriptura adimplenda. Sic angeli dicûtur excipi hospitio,prædicare futura, defendere pios, atque etiam pugnare pro eis, hostes fugare, morbos curare, gaudere super vno peccatore resipiscente:gestare Lazarum in sinum Abrahæ, videre patris faciem in cœlo,venturi cum Christo ad iudicium: hæc omnia cùm angelis tribuantur, clarum est,eos esse substantias quasdam, &supposita in sua natura subsistentia. Sed quid multis opus? quomodo intelligerenur illa. Ephef.1. vbi dicitur, Christum sedere ad dexteram patris in cœlestibus, supra omnen potestatem, virtutem, &dominium. Et Colossens. primo, dicuntur per illum creata visibilia, & inuisibilia, siue throni, siue dominationes, siue
units.tr: This definition is drawn from their offices toward God and toward human beings, by which good angels are properly distinguished from the evil angels, who are rebellious, unruly, and always seeking to trouble the human race. The very meaning of the word, and also what is read of angels as doing things at God's command, confirm the certainty of this definition. But before I discuss the offices and actions of good angels more fully, I must refute the opinion of some people who have denied that angels are spirits of a subsisting nature, or real beings, and have claimed that they are only certain movements or affections of our minds, which creep into us unnoticed from time to time. On this view, angels are good when they concern good matters and stir us to do well, and evil when they concern evil matters and urge us to do evil. This was the impious opinion of the Sadducees and of certain followers, and I fear that remnants of it survive elsewhere. Therefore let us teach that angels are real spirits, and substances subsisting in their own nature. If they were not beings of a subsisting nature and true substances, but only movements of the mind, what need would there have been for them to appear in external and bodily forms, as we read that they very often appeared throughout the Old Testament? For the giving of the law on tablets of stone, and other things of that kind, were not done except by beings of a fixed nature that subsist in themselves. Likewise, Daniel 7 assigns a number to the angels, and speaks of myriads of angels, and of more that the Father could send from heaven to help him, unless the cup had to be drunk and the Scripture fulfilled. Angels are said to be received as guests, to foretell the future, to defend the godly, and even to fight for them, to put enemies to flight, to heal diseases, to rejoice over one sinner who repents, to carry Lazarus into Abraham's bosom, to see the face of the Father in heaven, and to come with Christ to judgment. Since all these things are attributed to angels, it is clear that they are certain substances and beings subsisting in their own nature. But why say more? Consider how those things could be understood as Ephesians 1 says, that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavenly places, above every power, virtue, and dominion. And Colossians 1 says that visible and invisible things were created through him, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers.

units.la: Ioan.4. Vnde Angeli corpora assumant. siue principatus,siue potestates. Præterea, quòd Christus confertur hac epistola cum angelis:ostenditurq; angelis superior:hæc,in quam,quomodo intelligerentur, aut quid faceret ad laudé Christi,si angeli essent tantùm inspirationes aut motus animorû,& non res veræ ac substātię,per se excellétes ac præclaræ? Quid item esset animas à resurrectio-ne similes fore angelis?præterea animas sanctorû cum angelis acturas in regno Dei:si an geli non essent substātię,quibus talia possent cōpetere?Satis ergo liquet,valde absurda, & omni ex parte pugnante cum veritate illam persuasione,quòd videlicet angeli sint tan-tum qualitates, inspirationes vel motus,quos Deus inspirat seu immittit hominum ani-mis. Et quemadmodum de bonis angelis satis constitutū est, eos esse substantias, & res quasdā spirituales subsistētes: ita de malis quoq; angelis est sentiendum: quādoquidem mali angeli sua voluntate peccasse,ac deinde iusto Dei iudicio deiecti describûtur:&dia-bolo atque angelis eius ignis æternus dicitur præparatus, ac pœna imminere:quæ nul-lo pacto possent intelligi,si non essent res subsistentes,& spiritus,qui instar animarū sint capaces doloris ac pœnarū.Iam quales sint bonorum angelorū actiones, quæue ossi-cia, exijs,quæ per illos facta narrātur in Scripturis,facile est colligere. Omnes sunt genera-liter administratorij Spiritus,qui in ministerium emittuntur,propter eos,qui hæredes erũt salutis. Genef.16.missus angelus ad Agar,qui eam afflictam solaretur,& moneret redire ad domina,nec non prædiceret natiuitate Ismaelis.Genef.19.Angeli,qui Abrahamo sub quercu Mãbre apparuerant, Lothũ educunt è Sodomitarū excidio.Angelus Domini A-brahamũ reuocat à mactatione filij Isaaci.Genef.24.Abrahã Eliezerũ confirmat munere legationis fũcturũ promissione angeli comitis ac ducis itineris. Genef. 28. Iacob videt angelos ascendetes & descendentes do cœlo:audituq; voce Dei promittetis saluũ iter, & incolumé reditum. Nec fallit opinio: rediens enim ex Harãn videt se circumseptũ ange-lorum legionibus:quare & locum vocat Manahaim, propter exercitus angelorũ, quiil-lic castra locarint in præsidium Iacobi: Genef.32. Labano socero nequam angelus Do-mini cauet,ne vel durius compellet Iacobum,nedum vlla afficiat molestia.Angelus Do-mini luctatus integram nõ stem cum Iacobo,Israelis nomen ei imponit, benedictionéq; diuinam impertit. Vnde non abs re Genef. 48. in benedictione Ephraim & Manasse, angelus ille,inquit, qui eripuit me ab omni malo, benedicat pueris illis, &c. Exod.14. Angelus dicitur præcessisse castra Israelitarum. Exod. 23. Dominus pollicetur,se missu-rum angelum ante faciem ipsorum, qui præcessurus & ductururus ipsos sit in terram Cha-naan.Numeror. 22. Angelus Dei resistit Bileamo, ne maledicat Israelitis. 1. Reg. 19. An-gelus Domini pascit & ducit Eliam fugientem furorem Iezabelis. Tob. 5.Raphael ange-lus mittitur,qui Tobiam ducat & tueatur inter peregrinos.Psalm.34. Angeli Domini ca-str ametari dicuntur,& excubias agere pro electis Dei. Psal. 91. Deus dicitur mandare an-gelis,vt piorum curam gerant,ne pedem offendant ad lapidem. Matth. 4. Christo mini-strant angeli tentato à Satana. Elizæum circumdant exeuntem ex Dothan ; ne Syriei noceant Zachariæ ʒ. Josuę promittit Dominus tutores & custodes, qui ipsi assistebant à dextris.Matth.2.Angelus curam gerit Josephi, Mariæ, & infantis Christi. Actor. 12. An-gelus Petrum educit ex vinculis. Matth. 26.28. Angelus Christum orantem corroborat lapidem sepulchro amouet:resurrectione annunciat. Matth. 18. puerorum angeli vident faciem Dei quotidie in cœlis. Non dicam nunc de singulari angelorũ subsidio, quo pios semper muniunt,iisq; in medijs periculis,fornacibus,& inter leones quoq; sunt præstò, faciũtq;, vt ne pilus quidem de capite ipsorum decidat, præter cœlestis patris voluntate. Imò hostes ecclesiæ bellū faciētes interimūt, (Esa.36.)singulo rūq; fideliū diligentissimā semper curam gerunt.Atq; hinc factū, vt constituerent pleriq; singulis hominibus cre-dētibus,singulos angelos designatos,qui ipsos doceat,confirment,gubernet,defendat: id quod Origenes homilia 71.Et Hieronymus scribens in Matthæum:collegerut exillo, quod Matth.18.de pueris non offendedis dicitur:Dico enim uobis,quod angeli eorum in cœlis sem-per uidẽt faciem patris mei,qui in cœlis est: vbi Hieronymus, Magna dignitas animarum, vt v-naquæq; habeat ab ortu natiuitatis in custodiam sui angelum deputatū. Et hanc opinio-nem fuisse receptā apud Iudæos etiam sanioris mentis. Liquet ex eo,quod Actorum 11. discipuli,cùm Petrus è carcere de insperato liberatus ad eos rediisset,pulsans, existiman-tes ipsum Petrũ reuera non adesse,dicebant esse ipsius angelum. At illud etiá rectè asseri queat,non tātum vnum angelũ, sed plures simul de vnius pij salute esse solicitos. Nam Lucæ 15.dicitur de pluribus,imò generaliter de omnibus angelis, quòd gaudeant super vno peccatore resipiscēte. Et Luc 16. de pluribus angelis dicitur, quòd per angelos trăs-latus sit Lazarus in sinum Abrahæ.Psal.19.Angelis suis mandauit de te,&c. Quin & re-gionibus siue populis angelos esse præsectos custodes ac defensores Scriptura indicat. Nam DiNam Daniel. 10. Angelus princeps Persarum introducitur, resistens angelo principi graecorum. Et 4.Regum 19. angelus mittitur, qui pugnet pro gente Iudaica contra Assyrios, atq; occidit in castris hostium vna nocte centum octoginta quinq; millia.
units.tr: John 4. Whence angels assume bodies. Moreover, Christ is compared in this epistle with the angels, and is shown to be superior to them. How could this be understood, or what would it contribute to the praise of Christ, if angels were only inspirations or movements of the mind, and not real and substantial things, excellent and distinguished in themselves? Likewise, what would it mean that souls after the resurrection will be like the angels, and that the souls of the saints will act with the angels in the kingdom of God, if angels were not substances to which such things could belong? It is therefore sufficiently clear that the persuasion that angels are merely qualities, inspirations, or movements, which God inspires or sends into human minds, is very absurd and in every respect contrary to the truth. And just as it has been established that good angels are substances, and real spiritual beings subsisting in themselves, so we must think the same of evil angels, since evil angels are described as having sinned by their own will and then cast down by the just judgment of God; and eternal fire is said to have been prepared for the devil and his angels, and punishment to hang over them. None of this could be understood if they were not subsisting beings and spirits, capable of pain and punishments like souls. Now it is easy to gather what the actions and offices of good angels are, from those things which are recorded in the Scriptures as done by them. They are all in general ministering spirits, sent to minister for the sake of those who will be heirs of salvation. Genesis 16: an angel was sent to Hagar, to comfort her in her affliction, to advise her to return to her mistress, and also to foretell the birth of Ishmael. Genesis 19: the angels who had appeared to Abraham under the oak of Mamre lead Lot out of the destruction of Sodom. The angel of the Lord calls Abraham back from sacrificing Isaac. Genesis 24: Abraham assures Eliezer that his mission will succeed, by the promise of an angel accompanying him as guide of the journey. Genesis 28: Jacob sees angels ascending and descending from heaven, and hears the voice of God promising him a safe journey and a secure return. Nor did the expectation fail him: returning from Haran, he sees himself surrounded by legions of angels, and therefore he calls the place Mahanaim, because of the armies of angels who had encamped there to guard Jacob. Genesis 32: the angel of the Lord restrains the wicked Laban, his father-in-law, lest he treat Jacob more harshly, let alone do him any harm. The angel of the Lord wrestled with Jacob the whole night, gave him the name Israel, and bestowed the divine blessing. Hence, not without reason, in Genesis 48, in blessing Ephraim and Manasseh, that angel, it says, who has rescued me from every evil, bless these boys, and so on. Exodus 14: an angel is said to have gone before the camp of the Israelites. Exodus 23: the Lord promises that he will send an angel before their face, who will go before them and lead them into the land of Canaan. Numbers 22: the angel of God opposes Balaam, lest he curse the Israelites. 1 Kings 19: the angel of the Lord feeds and leads Elijah, fleeing the rage of Jezebel. Tobit 5: the angel Raphael is sent to lead and protect Tobias among strangers. Psalm 34: the angels of the Lord are said to encamp around and keep watch for the elect of God. Psalm 91: God is said to command angels to take care of the godly, so that they do not strike their foot against a stone. Matthew 4: angels minister to Christ when he is tempted by Satan. Angels surround Elisha as he leaves Dothan, lest the Syrians harm him. Zech. 3: the Lord promises Joshua guardians and keepers, who stand at his right hand. Matthew 2: an angel takes care of Joseph, Mary, and the infant Christ. Acts 12: an angel leads Peter out of his chains. Matthew 26 and 28: an angel strengthens Christ while he prays, rolls away the stone from the sepulchre, and announces the resurrection. Matthew 18: the angels of children see the face of God every day in heaven. I will not now speak of the particular help of angels, by which they always protect the godly, and are present with them even in the midst of dangers, in furnaces and among lions, and cause not even a hair of their head to fall, except by the will of the heavenly Father. Indeed, they destroy the enemies who wage war against the Church (Isaiah 36), and they always take the most careful care of each of the faithful. Hence it happened that many people thought that each believer had a particular angel assigned to him, to teach, strengthen, guide, and defend him. Origen, in Homily 71, and Jerome, writing on Matthew, gathered this from what is said in Matthew 18 about the children who must not be offended: "For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." There Jerome says: "Great is the dignity of souls, that each has from the moment of birth an angel assigned to keep him." And that this opinion was received even among the more sensible Jews is clear from Acts 11, where the disciples, when Peter had returned to them after being unexpectedly freed from prison, knocked, and thinking that Peter himself was really not there, said that it was his angel. But it can also rightly be asserted that not only one angel, but several together, are concerned for the salvation of a single godly person. For Luke 15 speaks of several, indeed of all the angels in general, rejoicing over one sinner who repents. And Luke 16 speaks of several angels, by whom Lazarus was carried into Abraham's bosom. Psalm 91 (Psalm 19 in the Latin numbering): "He has commanded his angels concerning you," and so on. Indeed, Scripture indicates that angels have been set as guardians and defenders over regions or peoples. For Daniel 10 introduces the angel of the Persians, resisting the angel prince of the Greeks. And in 2 Kings 19 an angel is sent to fight for the Jewish people against the Assyrians, and in one night he killed in the enemy camp one hundred and eighty-five thousand men.

units.la: An vero sicut vnicuiq; angelus, bonus praeses datus est, ita vnicuiq; oppositus sit malus angelus, quod Gregorius putat, ad exercitium, non est procliue definire. Videtur potius ea opinio fluxisse ex philosophia gentilium, maxime Aegyptiorum, quibus id persuasum fuit, vnicuique mortalium bonum quedam genium datum, & item malum, quorum alter ad commodum nostrum, alter ad perniciem intentus esset. Empedoclem eiusdem fuisse opinionis refert Plutarchus, & in vita M. Antonij refert exemplum. Illud vero simile videtur posse statui, sicut plures angelos bonos pro piis esse solicitos, ita plures malos insidiari piis, & modo hos, modo illos struere piis technas, quatenus & quando Deus permittit, sicut videre est in illo, qui infestabat Iob: item qui mentiebatur in ore prophetarum Baal: item qui in euangelio, qui obsidebatur a legione, & Magdalena quaedam a septem daemonijs vexata.
units.tr: Whether, as each person is given a good guardian angel, so each is opposed by an evil angel, as Gregory thinks, for the sake of testing, is not easy to settle. That opinion seems rather to have flowed from the philosophy of the Gentiles, especially the Egyptians, among whom it was held that each mortal is given a certain good spirit and likewise an evil one, of which the one is intent on our advantage and the other on our ruin. Plutarch reports that Empedocles held the same opinion, and in the Life of Mark Antony he gives an example. But it seems likely that one may hold that, just as several good angels are concerned for the pious, so several evil ones lie in wait for the pious, and now this one, now that one, devises snares for them, insofar as and whenever God permits, as can be seen in the case of him who afflicted Job; likewise the spirit who lied in the mouth of the prophets of Baal; likewise in the Gospel, the one by whom a man was besieged by a legion, and a certain Mary Magdalene who was vexed by seven demons.

units.la: Quod ad numerum angelorum vel ordines eorum attinet, non potest certi aliquid decerni. Multas myriadas angelorum Daniel, Legiones Christus, item legionem daemoniorum in vno homine euangelica historia commemorat. Ordines vero, quos quidam conantur astruere, quasi alij alijs forent superiores aut praestantiores, sicut in humana politia videntur alij homines alios dignitate, sapientia, potentia, anteire: ex sacris literis haud possunt confirmari. Nam etiamsi Michael princeps magnus vocetur Daniel. 10. et idem in epistola Iudae vocetur Archangelus: & 1. Thessalon. 4. dicatur, Archangelum in extremo die tuba debere canere, ac tum mortuos resurrecturos: praeterea licet thronorum, dominationum, potestatum, nomina illis tribui videantur Ephes. 1. & Colossens. 1. Deinde vt lucifer Esaiae 14. videatur quasi caput & princeps omnium sanctorum angelorum constitutus: tamen hinc non sequitur, tales ordines politicos inter angelos seruari. Illud vero similius est, & tutius vt retineatur: angelos secundum naturam suam omnes esse pares, eiusdem speciei, eiusdem dignitatis: omnes in hoc esse occupatos, vt Deum semper laudent, praedicet, omnes in hac parte eiusdem esse studij & voluntatis. Verum cum diuersa iniungutur illis officia, tunc suscipere eos alia atq; aliam pro tempore conditionis dignitatem, ei muneri, quod obire debent, conuenientem. Et cum in genere valde praestantes sint secundum suam naturam, deinde officia suscipiant multo amplissima, hinc fit quod insignibus & praeclaris titulis appellantur. Inter homines sane imperfectos & corruptos opus est ordines quosdam distingui, alios ordinari praefectos & superiores, alios vero subditos, vt per sublimiores ordines ceteri inferiores legum seueritate cohibeantur. At vero inter angelos, qui perfecti sunt, nullis q; prauis affectibus ad malam intenti, quid opus est talibus politicis ordinibus? Aut inter malos etiam angelos, de quorum resipiscentia non est spes, qui obedire, aut ordinate quicquam facere nesciunt, quae ordinu ratio potest constitui? Sunt ergo magnifica illa nomina, quae in Scripturis tributa cernimus angelis, magis significatia dignitate conueniente officio, quod pro tempore ipsis iniugitur, & simul excellentia substantiae eorum, quam aliquod discriminis ordinis, quo caeteris angelis praeminere aut subiacere intelligerentur. Itaq; de nominibus seu appellationibus angelorum, quae in Scripturis occurrunt, aliquid in medium proferemus. Angeli generaliter vocantur, eo quod omnes omni tempore, vt mittantur, sint parati.
units.tr: As for the number of angels or their orders, nothing certain can be decided. Daniel mentions many myriads of angels, Christ mentions legions, and the Gospel story mentions a legion of demons in one man. But the orders that some try to establish, as if some angels were superior or more excellent than others, just as in human government some men surpass others in rank, wisdom or power, cannot be confirmed from the sacred writings. For although Michael is called "the great prince" in Daniel 10, and the same Michael is called "archangel" in the Epistle of Jude, and 1 Thessalonians 4 says that the archangel will sound the trumpet on the last day and the dead will then rise, and although the names of thrones, dominions and powers are given to them in Ephesians 1 and Colossians 1, and although Lucifer in Isaiah 14 seems to be set up as the head and prince of all the holy angels, still it does not follow from this that such political orders are kept among the angels. What is more likely, and safer to hold, is this: by their nature all angels are equal, of the same kind and the same dignity; all are occupied in this, that they always praise and proclaim God; and in this respect all have the same zeal and will. But since different duties are laid on them, they take on, according to the circumstances of the time, a different rank and dignity suited to the office they must discharge. And since they are very excellent in kind by their nature, and then undertake very great offices, it follows that they are called by distinguished and illustrious titles. Among men, who are imperfect and corrupted, it is necessary that certain ranks be distinguished, some appointed as rulers and superiors, others as subjects, so that the lower are restrained by the severity of the laws through the higher ranks. But among the angels, who are perfect and not inclined to any depraved affections, what need is there for such political orders? Or among the evil angels also, whose repentance is not to be hoped for, who know not how to obey or to do anything in an orderly way, what order could be established? Therefore those magnificent names which we see given to the angels in the Scriptures signify rather the dignity suited to the office laid on them for the time, and at the same time the excellence of their substance, than any distinction of rank by which they might be understood to stand above or below the other angels. So we shall now set forth something about the names or appellations of the angels that occur in the Scriptures. Angels are called in general "angels," because they are all always ready to be sent.

units.la: Archangeli, quando ad sublime & arduum aliquod munus obeundum emittuntur: sicut aliquem etiam homini pro tempore imponitur persona publici legati, qui praestat pro eo tem pore ratione officij ceteris nuncijs mitti solitis.
units.tr: Archangels are so called when they are sent to undertake some lofty and arduous charge, just as a man is sometimes given the character of a public envoy for a time, who, for that time, by virtue of his office, excels the other messengers who are usually sent.

units.la: Seraphim significat ardetes, a שרף arsit, qua appellatione notatur studiu & feruor Spirituum in perfectionem ijs, quae Deus ipsis iniuxerit, simulq; aliquid naturae & substantiae eorum exprimitur, quod uidelicet ignitae sint naturae.
units.tr: Seraphim means "burning ones," from the Hebrew verb [שרף], "he burned." By this name is denoted the zeal and fervour of the spirits in carrying out what God has enjoined on them, and at the same time something of their nature and substance is expressed, namely that they are of a fiery nature.

units.la: Cherubim, dicuntur aues seu volates: ita ostenditur celeritas & agilitas, ac mura facultas expediendi negotia iniuncta.
units.tr: Cherubim are said to be birds or fliers. Thus their swiftness and agility are shown, and their ready ability to dispatch the business laid on them.

units.la: Michael, quis vt Deus, vel, quis est ille dominator.
units.tr: Michael: "Who is like God?" or "Who is that ruler?"

units.la: Gabriel, virtus Dei, vel fortitudo Dei, vel, con fortauit me Deus.
units.tr: Gabriel: "The strength of God," or "the might of God," or "God has strengthened me."

units.la: Raphael, sanatio, vel Medicina Dei, רפא.
units.tr: Raphael: "Healing," or "the medicine of God" [רפא].

units.la: Multa alia nomina habent, tracta a similitudine rerum humanarum, quibus praecellentia, dignitas, potentia, robur significatur.
units.tr: They have many other names, taken from the likeness of human things, by which pre-eminence, dignity, power and strength are signified.

units.la: Exercitus vocatur & militia, eo quod sua multitudine exercitu videntur repraesentare, & circumstant omni tempore laudantes Deum, & ad obeunda munera parati, sicut milites solent circumdare suum imperatorem, ad iussa illius omni tempore parati. Throni appellantur propterea, quòd in illis gloria Dei quodammodo resideat, sicque inter illos gloria Dei elucescat, vt nullius regis maiestas splendidior sit in vllo throno.
units.tr: They are called a host and a militia, because by their multitude they seem to represent an army, and they stand around, always praising God and ready to perform their duties, just as soldiers are accustomed to surround their commander, always ready at his orders. They are called thrones for this reason: that the glory of God in some way resides in them, and so the glory of God shines forth among them, so that the majesty of no king is more splendid on any throne.

units.la: Virtutes nominantur, quòd Dominus virtutem suam & potentiam per illos mirabiliter patefaciat.
units.tr: They are called powers, because the Lord through them wonderfully displays his power and might.

units.la: Sic principatus, potestates, dominationes appellantur, simul vt significetur summa ipsorum angelorum dignitas, simul quòd per eos Deus principes, regna, prouincias, regit, gubernat, moderatur, tuetur, quomodo angelus quidam ob huiusmodi munus princeps vocatur apud Danielem. Simili deniq; de causa etiam Dij in Scripturis appellantur, quòd videlicet Deo sint quàm proximi, & diuina potentia ac bonitas in eis clarissimè elucescat, & diuinitatem aliquo modo repræsentent. Eadem de causa, videlicet ad declarandum muneris pro tempore iniuncti dignitatem, fit, quòd diuersis for-mis angeli apparuerint, alij instar militis, alij instar ignis, al j instar peregrè proficiscentium, &c. Iam verò propter tantam dignitatem angelorum, & propter tàm præclara eorum erga nos officia & beneficia, quidam adducti sunt, vt putarint, angelos quasi Deos tutelares habendos & inuocandos, ac diuinis honoribus afficiendos: sicut gentiles suos genios celebrant. Sed de hac re habemus apertam sententiam Apocalyps. 19, Vbi Ioannes coram angelo se prostrauit adoraturus: sed id angelus ipse vetuit, dicens: Vide ne feceris, conseruus tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum habentium testimonium Iesu: Deum adora. Et cùm in definitione apostolica primo loco à nobis posita clare dicatur, angelos esse creaturas, satis constat, eis nequaquam imponendum illum honorem, qui proprie soli debetur creatori. Prodest autem doctrinam hanc de angelis bonis diligenter tenere: idque eò potissimum: Primùm, vt Dei amor & potentia erga electos, qui in terris adhuc versantur, & malorum angelorum insultibus, tum & mundi furoribus sunt expositi, fiat manifestior. Mirificè enim hac consideratione in periculis recreatur afflicti pii, quas tatuunt, Deum angelis suis ipsorum salutem commendare, qui ipsos tueantur aduersus angelos malos. Secundò discent hinc pij, quàm se deceat caste sanctè; in oculis & conspectu angelorum vitam hanc traducere, quamq; turpe ac periculosum sit, tantis custodibus & comitibus vita scelerata sese priuare, ac sic in retia Satanae se præcipitare.
units.tr: So too they are called principalities, powers and dominions, both to signify the highest dignity of the angels themselves and because through them God rules, governs, directs and protects princes, kingdoms and provinces, as a certain angel is called a prince by Daniel because of this kind of office. Finally, for a similar reason, they are also called gods in the Scriptures, namely because they are very near to God, and the divine power and goodness shine most clearly in them, and they in some way represent the divinity. For the same reason, namely to show the dignity of the office laid on them for the time, it happens that the angels have appeared in various forms: some like soldiers, some like fire, some like travellers setting out, and so on. Now indeed, on account of the great dignity of the angels and their very noble offices and benefits toward us, some have been led to think that angels should be held and invoked as tutelary gods and honoured with divine honours, just as the Gentiles celebrate their genii. But on this matter we have a clear statement in Revelation 19, where John threw himself down before the angel to worship him, but the angel himself forbade it, saying: "See that you do not do it; I am your fellow servant and of your brethren who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." And since in the apostolic definition, which we have set down first, it is clearly said that angels are creatures, it is quite clear that the honour which belongs properly to the Creator alone must by no means be attributed to them. It is useful, moreover, to hold this doctrine about the good angels carefully, and especially for these reasons. First, so that the love and power of God toward the elect, who still live on earth and are exposed to the assaults of the evil angels and to the furies of the world, may be made more manifest. For by this consideration the afflicted godly are wonderfully refreshed in dangers, when they realise that God has committed their salvation to his angels, who guard them against the evil angels. Second, the godly learn from this how fitting it is to live this life chastely and holily, in the sight and presence of the angels, and how shameful and dangerous it is to deprive oneself of so great guardians and companions by a wicked life, and so to throw oneself into the nets of Satan.
