units.la: Tertiò, discemus hinc, semper Deum orare, vt suis angelis de nobis mandet, noftrāq; salutem & vitam modis omnibus protegat, sanctè gubernet, & in vijs suis conseruet, & tandem angelis similes reddat.
units.tr: Third, we learn from this always to pray to God that he will command his angels concerning us, and will protect our salvation and life in every way, govern us holily, keep us in his ways, and at last make us like the angels.

units.la: Sequitur nunc, vt de altero angelorum genere dicamus, quos Scriptura in malis ponit: non quòd tales Deus condiderit, sed quòd sua ipsorum culpa à vijs Dei defiectendo in malitiam & exitium incurrerint. Deus enim, qui boni omnis est autor ac conditor, nihil nisi bonum ac sanctum condere & creare vult & potest: iuxta illud, Vidit Dominus, quæ fecerat, & ecce, erant omnia valde bona. Vt igitur sua & serpentis culpa homo peccator factus est: qui iuxta imaginem Dei erat factus: ita angeli mali sancti quidem & boni fuerunt initio secundum creationem diuinam: à sanctitate verò hac & perfectione desciuerunt. Vnde Christus Ioan. 8. de diabolo dicit, quòd, cùm mendacium loquitur, ex proprijs loquatur, quia in veritate non steterit. In veritate itaque aliquando fuisse necessum est. Sic 2. Petri 2. Angelos malos propter peccatum catenis noctis in tartarum præcipitatos: & iudicio seruari, Spiritus sanctus testatur. Esa. 14. cœlo cecidisse dicitur Lucifer. Modus verò, siue forma peccati Diaboli siue malorum angelorum in Scripturis non exprimitur. Deindeid quoq; notandum est, varias appellationes angelis malis assignari, non propter naturam, sed propter studia & opera mala. Diaboli, id est, calumniatores vocantur pasim: διάβολοι, nequam, maligni, Matt. 6. Ephes. 6. Tentatores: Matt. 4. 1. Thess. 3. Actor. 5. Item Dracones, propter crudelitatem: Psal. 74. 104. Serpentes, propter astutiam, Genes. 2. Apocal. 12, Dæmonia propter naturæ, in qua conditi olim fuerunt, excellentiam: ἀκάθαρτα enim numen & diuinitatem significat: ἀκάθαρτον idem est, quod fœlix diuinus, Deo similis. In Scripturis verò vox ista propter insignem illorum malitiam in partem deteriorem vsurpatur. Tertiò, & hoc de angelis malis, siue diabolis notandum est, semper eos ad malum ferri, ac nunquam ad bene agendum, posteaquam semel lapsi sunt, posse adduci. Desideria diaboli, teste Christo Ioan. 8. semper praua sunt, ac singulis horis dies noctesq; leonis instar rugientis circumit, quærens quem deuoret. Atq; idem primis dat operam, vt gloriæ & regno Dei modis omnibus aduersetur: veritatem meridacijs oppugnat: nomen Dei blasphemijs & sceleribus obscurare infamesq; facere fidet: In angelum lucis callidè se transfigurat: pseudoprophetas & falsos apostolos, in quorum
units.tr: Now it follows that we should speak of the other kind of angels, whom Scripture places among the evil ones: not because God created them such, but because by their own fault, by turning away from the ways of God, they fell into wickedness and ruin. For God, who is the author and creator of all good, wills and is able to create and make nothing but what is good and holy, according to that saying: "The Lord saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good." Therefore, just as man became a sinner through his own fault and the serpent's, though he had been made in the image of God, so the evil angels were indeed holy and good at the beginning, according to the divine creation, but they fell away from this holiness and perfection. Hence Christ says in John 8 of the devil that when he speaks a lie he speaks from his own resources, because he did not stand in the truth. It must therefore be that at some time he was in the truth. So too 2 Peter 2 testifies that the Holy Spirit has cast the evil angels down into hell, bound with chains of darkness, and that they are kept for judgement, on account of sin. Isaiah 14 says that Lucifer fell from heaven. But the manner or form of the sin of the devil or of the evil angels is not expressed in the Scriptures. Next, this too must be noted: various appellations are assigned to the evil angels, not on account of their nature but on account of their evil pursuits and works. They are called devils [διάβολοι], that is, slanderers, everywhere; wicked, malicious [πονηροί], Matthew 6, Ephesians 6; tempters, Matthew 4, 1 Thessalonians 3, Acts 5. Likewise dragons, on account of their cruelty: Psalm 74, 104. Serpents, on account of their cunning: Genesis 2, Revelation 12. Demons [δαιμόνια], on account of the excellence of the nature in which they were once created: for the word [ἀκάθαρτα, unclean] signifies a divinity or divine power, and [ἀκάθαρτον] is the same as "happy, divine, like God." But in the Scriptures this word is used in a worse sense on account of their remarkable wickedness. Third, and this is to be noted about the evil angels, or devils: that they are always carried toward evil, and can never be brought to do good, once they have fallen. The desires of the devil, as Christ testifies in John 8, are always depraved; and day and night, like a roaring lion, he goes about seeking whom he may devour. And he devotes himself above all to opposing the glory and kingdom of God in every way, to attacking the truth with lies, to obscuring and defaming the name of God with blasphemies and crimes; he disguises himself cleverly as an angel of light, and he stirs up false prophets and false apostles, through whose tongues the work of a deceitful spirit is carried on, against the word of God.

units.la: 1. Petri 5. 2. Corinth. 11. quorum linguis fallacis Spiritus munus subit, aduersus verbum Dei excitat. Matth. 4. Christum filium Dei technis suis adoritur, & à fide, officio, cultuque Dei abstrahere conatur. Zachariae 3. Iosuę sacerdoti instauranti templum Hierosolymitanum à dextris obstit Satan. Idem adhuc dum facit, hostes excitando, quibus cursum Euangelij impediat, & pios, qui Christi sunt membra, perseq̈uatur. Cainum instigat, vt Abelem fratrem è medio tollat. Saulem furore crudeli irritat aduersus Dauidem & sacerdotes Nobenses. Iudam inuadit, sicque conatus & consilia eius regit, vt Christum accepto precio triginta argenteorum prodat, ac tandem semetipsum strangulet. Pari ratione nunquam ab ingenio & malitia sua non discedit Satan, quin imò nunquam non regnum & nomen Dei sa crosanctum oppugnat & proscindere studet.
units.tr: 1 Peter 5; 2 Corinthians 11: through the tongues of false teachers, in whom the lying spirit takes up residence, he stirs up opposition to the Word of God. Matthew 4: he assails Christ the Son of God with his tricks and tries to draw him away from the faith, duty and worship of God. Zechariah 3: when Joshua the priest was restoring the temple of Jerusalem, Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. He still does the same today, stirring up enemies to block the course of the gospel and persecuting the godly, who are the members of Christ. He incited Cain to remove his brother Abel from the midst. He provoked Saul with cruel rage against David and the priests of Nob. He invaded Judas, and so directed his attempts and plans that he betrayed Christ for thirty pieces of silver and at last strangled himself. In the same way Satan never departs from his nature and malice; indeed, he never ceases to attack and to try to tear down the holy kingdom and name of God.

units.la: Quòd sPvero non horret Spiritus prauus & nequam Deo creatori & summo magistratui aduersari, eidemq; modis sese opponere, quid non aut tentet, aut efficiat aduersus homines & electos Dei sanctos? A sancto studio euangelij propagādi reuocauit ac retardauit Apostolum Paulum, eiqúe obstitit, ne Philippenses, quemadmodum constituerat, inuiseret: Christo, duce Petro, persuadere nititur, ne Hierosolymam proficiscatur, & crucis morti cruciatibusque sese subijciat. Apostolos Christi vt cribrare liceat, à Deo expetit, pro quibus Christus orat, ne fide deficiant. 1. Petri 5. Leonis rugientis instar hominibus insidiari dicitur. Piorum corpora, fortunas, & animos tentat atque affligit: id quod ex historia Iobi, & Euangelijs passim constat. Matthæi decimotertio, Seminat zizania inter triticum, malosque, vt ante dixi, regno Dei opponit. Achabum decipit falsa persuasione, vt in aciem contra Syros exeat, sciens, eum in pugna casurum. Dauidi suasor est, vt populum numeret: vnde pestem à Deo irato infligendam noverat. Ephesiorum secundo, In filijs contumacibus dicitur agere, qui in concupiscentijs carnis suæ versantur. 2. Corinthior. 4. Deus huius seculi excæcauit sensus incredulorum, ne illucescere illis lumen Euangelij.
units.tr: But that evil and wicked spirit does not shrink from opposing God the Creator and the supreme magistrate, and from setting himself against them in every way. What does he not attempt or accomplish against men and the holy elect of God? He called back and delayed the Apostle Paul from his holy zeal for spreading the gospel, and stood in his way so that he could not visit the Philippians as he had planned. He tries to persuade Christ, through Peter as his leader, not to go up to Jerusalem and submit himself to death on the cross and to its torments. He asks God for permission to sift the apostles of Christ, for whom Christ prayed that their faith would not fail (1 Peter 5). He is said to lie in wait for men like a roaring lion. He tempts and afflicts the bodies, fortunes and minds of the godly; this is clear from the history of Job and from the Gospels throughout. In Matthew 13 he sows tares among the wheat, and, as I said before, he sets himself against the kingdom of God. He deceived Ahab with a false persuasion so that he went out to battle against the Syrians, knowing that he would fall in the fight. He was the instigator who urged David to number the people, since he knew that this would bring down a plague from the angry God. In Ephesians 2 he is said to work in the sons of disobedience, who live in the lusts of their flesh. 2 Corinthians 4: the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel should not shine on them.

units.la: Adhæc in creaturas etiam quascunque furit. Sic Iobi domum euertit, armenta, & homines simul ligne cœlo delapso perdit. In gregem porcorum sæuit, & in aquas præcipitat: Matthæi octauo, Apocalyps. septimo, Angeli quibus id concessum erat, nocent mari, terræ, arboribus. Consilia & conatus Satanæ non possunt satis describi. An verò Diabolus aliquid propria potestate & virtute efficere queat, facile est iudicare, nihil omnino illum habere potestatis, neque angelis malis quicquam virium superesse, nisi à Deo id permittatur. Achabum decipit per falsos prophetas, sed id non potest ante, quàm deus ipsi faciat potestatem (1. Reg. 22.) Iobo non potest nocere, priusquam à Deo facultatis aliquid in ipsius domum, liberos, armenta, ac ipsum denique corpus, tradatur: animæ tamen & vitæ Iobi nequaquam nocere valet. In porcos Gerasænorum non potest suire, nisi Christo concedente (Lucæ octauo) Quinetiam (Marci quinto) Iesum orat diabolus ille legionarius, ne ante tempus ipsum cruciet aut affligat. Curigitur, inquies, Deus illis permittit, vt noceant hominibus, & regnū Dei oppugnent? Habet sane ratio nes suas Deus, qui prorsus nihil sine causa & graui consilio facere consueuit. Prima est: vt earatione suæ potentiæ declararet atq; imperiū, quod in Spiritus & creaturas omnes, sive bone eæ sint, sive malę, habet. Deinde ad prudetiā & sobrietatē hortari vult homines, quos in spirituali hoc & tam periculoso certamine semper decet armatos excubare, ne à tantis hostibus incauti opprimantur. Ephes. 6. 1. Petri 5.
units.tr: Moreover, he rages against all creatures whatsoever. Thus he overturned Job's house and destroyed his oxen and his men together by fire falling from heaven. He raged against the herd of swine and hurled them into the water (Matthew 8). In Revelation 7 the angels to whom this was granted harm the sea, the land and the trees. The plans and attempts of Satan cannot be fully described. But whether the devil can accomplish anything by his own power and strength is easy to judge: he has no power at all, and the evil angels have no strength left except what God permits. He deceives Ahab through false prophets, but he cannot do so before God gives him the power (1 Kings 22). He cannot harm Job until God hands over to him some of his household, children, oxen and finally his body; yet he could by no means harm Job's soul or life. He cannot drive the swine of the Gadarenes into the sea unless Christ allows it (Luke 8). Indeed, that devil of the legion (Mark 5) begs Jesus not to torment or afflict him before the appointed time. Why then, you will ask, does God permit them to harm men and attack the kingdom of God? God certainly has his reasons, since he is accustomed to do nothing without a cause and a weighty purpose. The first is that he may thereby show forth the rule of his power, which he holds over all spirits and creatures, whether good or evil. Secondly, he wants to urge men to prudence and watchfulness, who in this spiritual and so dangerous struggle ought always to stand armed and on guard, lest they be overwhelmed through carelessness by such great enemies (Ephesians 6; 1 Peter 5).

units.la: Tertiò: prodest etiam pijs interdum vexatio Satanæ, vt videlicet ad adorandum, Deoque fidendum, fiant alacriores: peccata item fugiant, à laqueis Satanæ diligenter sibi caueant: atque in hoc omni, quantum roboris Spiritus sanctus per verbum fidei præstet, experiantur: ac tandem victo Satana cum Christo capite summo victore triumphare discant.
units.tr: Thirdly, Satan's harassment sometimes also benefits the godly: so that they may become more eager to pray and to trust in God, that they may flee from sin and carefully guard themselves against Satan's snares, and that in all this they may experience how much strength the Holy Spirit gives through the word of faith, and at last learn to triumph with Christ, the supreme head and victor, once Satan has been conquered.

units.la: Accedit huc, quòd Deus impios & reprobos per diabolum punit: vt in Saule, Iuda, aliisque videre est: Contrà Dei charitas & amor erga pios, in defensione hac, mirifice commendatur. Ac tandem exercitiis hisce diaboli malitia ecclesiæ innotescit, & pudefactatus Goliath in conflictu Christianorum: Deiq; iustitia in iudicio eius aliquando fiet manifestissima. De hisce vide Augustinum de Trinitate lib. 2. cap. 6. de Genesi contra Manichæos lib. 2. cap. 18. de Genesi ad literam lib. 11. cap. 1. Item Chrysostomus de prouidetia Dei.
units.tr: In addition, God punishes the impious and reprobate through the devil, as can be seen in Saul, Judas and others. On the other hand, God's love and affection towards the godly is wonderfully commended in this defence. And at last, through these exercises, the malice of the devil becomes known to the Church, and Goliath is put to shame in the conflict with the Christians; and the justice of God will at some time become most manifest in his judgment. On these matters see Augustine, On the Trinity, book 2, chapter 6; On Genesis against the Manichaeans, book 2, chapter 18; On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapter 1. Likewise Chrysostom, On the Providence of God.

units.la: Quintò, quæri etiam potest, an distincti sint ordines & officia dæmonum. Idque ea potissimum de causa, quia in scripturis diabolus princeps mundi dicitur, & 2. Corinthiorum 4. Deus huius seculi: Ephesior. 6. vocantur potestates domini mundi, principatus, rectores tenebrarum huius seculi. Luc. 11. Beelzebub princeps dicitur dæmoniorū. Obiectio. Alibi dicitur Belial, id est, apostata, prævaricator, absque iugo: Iob. 40. & Leuiathan, id est, Ioan. 17. additamentum, propter amplam potentiam. Esaiae 27. Et Marci quinto legionem se dicit, quasi legionem Spirituum malorum sub se contineat. Nequaquam tamen ex hisce sequitur, distinctos daemonum esse ordines, non magis, quam diversae appellationes angelorum bonorum numerum & ordinum discrimina inter illos constituunt. Ac vocesi-lae Ephes. 6. vsurpantur potentiae declarandae causa magis quam ordinum ostendendo-rum gratia. Omnes daemones ex aequo ad malum faciendum & inferendum semper sunt instructi: verum, cum non plus possint, quam Deus concedit, sequitur, tuncres aliquas per daemones quosdam confici, quando, & per quos Deo visum est ordinare ac permit-tere. Multa de effectis dicuntur spirituum malorum, quae de officijs nequaquam accipi debent, ut Zach. 13. Osee 4. 1. Tim. 4. Omnes enim omnibus pereque nocere studet. Getiles dines fas diversis daemonib. actiones adscripserunt, in aere, in aquis, in fyluis, in diversis creaturis: sed omnia falsa. Qua de re vide D. Hieronymum in 6. caput ad Ephesios, & D. Augustinum de diuinationibus daemonum.
units.tr: Fifthly, it may also be asked whether the orders and offices of demons are distinct. This is asked chiefly for this reason: in the Scriptures the devil is called the prince of this world, and in 2 Corinthians 4 the god of this age; in Ephesians 6 the powers, the rulers of the world, the principalities and the world-rulers of this darkness are mentioned; in Luke 11 Beelzebub is called the prince of the demons. Objection: elsewhere he is called Belial, that is, the apostate, the transgressor, without a yoke (Job 40), and Leviathan, that is, an addition, on account of his great power (Isaiah 27). And in Mark 5 he calls himself a legion, as though he contained a legion of evil spirits under himself. Yet it by no means follows from these things that the orders of demons are distinct, any more than the various names of the good angels establish the number and the distinctions of ranks among them. And those words in Ephesians 6 are used to declare power rather than to show orders. All demons are always equally equipped to do and inflict evil; but since they can do no more than God permits, it follows that some things are accomplished through certain demons only when and through whom it has pleased God to ordain and permit. Many things are said about the effects of evil spirits which must by no means be understood as their offices, as in Zechariah 13, Hosea 4 and 1 Timothy 4. For each one strives equally to harm everyone. The Gentiles assigned different actions to different demons, in the air, in the waters, in the woods, in various creatures; but all of it is false. On this matter see St Jerome on chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, and St Augustine, On the Divinations of Demons.

units.la: Sexto: quaeri etiam potest, an daemones aliquando sint saluandi: Certe Origenes, qui clarius extitit in schola Alexandrina, de hoc Augustinus lib. de haeresib. cap. 41. assent, quod senserit, reprobos, & tandem daemones saluados: qua de re etiam Origenistae quaftiones moverunt: & hoc tempore quida Libertini hallucinantur. At Christi verba Matth. 25. aeternam daemonum damnationem afferunt: vbi ait, Discedite a me maledicti, in igne aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Ignis aeternus autem damnatione aeternam significat. Genes. 3. Maledictio diabolo infligitur ad perpetuitate. Luc. 16. Dives epulo non liberatur a cruciatibus, multo minus Satan & angeli eius. Vide hac de re Augustinum ad Orosium contra Priscillianistas & Origenistas cap. 5. plura hac de re qui requisierit, legat Methodi nostrae li. 2. vbi copiosius de hisce egimus. Prodest autem huius loci cognitio ad intelligendos multos Scripturarum locos, de angelis.
units.tr: Sixthly, it may also be asked whether the demons will at some time be saved. Certainly Origen, who was the most famous figure in the Alexandrian school, is said by Augustine (On Heresies, chapter 41) to have held that the reprobate and at last the demons would be saved; on this question the Origenists also raised doubts, and in our own time some Libertines wander in error. But the words of Christ in Matthew 25 declare the eternal damnation of the demons, where he says: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels." Eternal fire, moreover, signifies eternal damnation. Genesis 3: the curse is laid on the devil for ever. Luke 16: the rich man in Hades is not freed from torments, much less Satan and his angels. On this matter see Augustine's letter to Orosius against the Priscillianists and Origenists, chapter 5. Whoever wishes to inquire further on this point should read book 2 of our Methodus, where we have treated these things more fully. The knowledge of this passage is useful for understanding many passages of Scripture concerning the angels.

units.la: Deinde, ad reddendos cautos aduersus diaboli insidias.
units.tr: Next, to make us wary of the snares of the devil.

units.la: Tertio, ad admonendum, vt sobrie & pie iusteq; vitam hanc transigamus.
units.tr: Thirdly, to admonish us to live this life soberly, piously and righteously.

units.la: Quarto, ad examinandos spiritus, num ex Deo sint.
units.tr: Fourthly, to test the spirits, whether they are from God.

units.la: Quinto, ad potentiam Dei cognoscendam, qui Spiritus hosce creauit, & pro suamisericordia ad tempus furere finit.
units.tr: Fifthly, to know the power of God, who created these spirits and, in his mercy, allows them to rage for a time.

units.la: Sexto, ad galeam fidei & scutum veritatis apprehendendum, quo tela daemonum excipi & retorqueri debet. Exercitium hoc continuum, milites Christi prudenter & caute agere cogit.
units.tr: Sixthly, to take up the helmet of faith and the shield of truth, by which the darts of the demons must be received and turned back. This constant exercise compels the soldiers of Christ to act prudently and cautiously.

units.la: In Dei Spiritu vincedi, & vbi gloriae corona obtingit, Deo primitiae & gloria omnis deferri debent: iuxta illud in oratione dominica, libera nos a malo: quia tuum est regnum, & potentia, & gloria, in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: To conquer by the Spirit of God, and where the crown of glory is obtained, the firstfruits and all the glory must be ascribed to God, according to that petition in the Lord's Prayer: "Deliver us from evil: for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever and ever. Amen."

units.la: Visum autem fuit ista non abs re adijcere. Nam cognitis his de natura hac angelorum praesertim quod ministri tantum sint, dignitas Christi clarius cognosci potest.
units.tr: It seemed good, however, to add these things, and not without reason. For once these things are known about the nature of angels, especially that they are only ministers, the dignity of Christ can be recognised more clearly.

units.la: Ad filium autem: Thronus tuus Deus in seculum seculi, virga rectitudinis, virga regni tui: Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti iniquitatem: propterea vnxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo exultationis vltra consortes tuos.
units.tr: "But unto the Son: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of thy kingdom is a sceptre of righteousness. Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."

units.la: Quintum argumentum ad probandum diuinitatem Christi, sumptum ex psalmo quadragesimo quarto, vbi non tantum filius Dei, aut aliqua ratione angelis superior demonstratur, sed simpliciter & aperte vocatur, Deus, idque bis. Imo vero si diligenter animadvertimus, duo sunt in vno hoc testimonio argumenta, diuinitate Christi non obscure prodentia. Alterum est ex eo, quod Christus bis appellatur Deus: Thronus tuus o Deus, inquit. Deinde, propterea vnxit te qui es Deus, Deus tuus. Alterum, quod dicitur, thronus ipsius siue regnum duraturum in seculum seculi atq; in aeternum, quod sane haud potest homini competere, sed soli Christo natura Deo, de cuius aeterno regno, multis aliis locis Scriptura concionatur. Non possum autem, quin hic commendem librum Psalmorum, quitot tamq; valida argumenta suppeditat, ad confirmanda praecipua religionis Christianae, hoc est, Euangelij capita. Hoc reuera de Psalmorum libro dici potest, quod sit Epitome omnium sacrarum Scripturarum, quod in eo omnia mysteria euangelij plenissime contineantur. Deniq; quod thesaurus incoparabilis, inexhaustus omnis diuinae philosophiae in eo lateat, quodq; de quauis re exempla, argumenta, sententiae, ex eo, tanquam ditissimo instru-mento depromi queant. Et videre est Paulum in epistolis omnibus, denique Christum plurimum vsum testimonijs psalmorum, qui omnibus Iudaeis erant notissimi: (vtpote qui & publice canebantur in sacris Synagogis, & haud dubie etiam priuatim ab omnibus studiose legebantur:) & propter mysteriorum altitudinem ac frequentiam, in maxima habebantur autoritate, & inter omnes libros sacros illi facerrimi semper sunt iudicati. Eam ob causam Christus ita partitus est libros veteris testamenti, in legem, prophetas, & phetas, & psalmos. Lucæ vltimo, vbi ait: Hæc sunt verba quæ locutus sum ad vos, cùm adhuc essem vobiscū, quòd necessesum foret impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege Mosi, & prophetis, & psalmis de me. Itaq; omnes admonitos velim, vt in psalmorū tractatione vnusquisq; diligenter se exerceat: idq; audeo polliceri, quòd qui psalmorum sensum fuerit assecutus, is quoscunq; alios sacræ Scripturæ libros citra negotium intelliget.
units.tr: This is the fifth argument for proving the divinity of Christ, taken from Psalm 44, where the Son of God is not merely shown to be superior to the angels in some respect, but is plainly and openly called God, and that twice. Indeed, if we attend carefully, there are two arguments in this one testimony, which reveal the divinity of Christ clearly. The first is from the fact that Christ is twice called God: "Thy throne, O God," it says, and then, "therefore God, even thy God, has anointed thee." The second is that his throne, that is, his kingdom, is said to last for ever and ever, which can certainly not belong to a man, but only to Christ, who is God by nature, and of whose eternal kingdom Scripture speaks in many other places. I cannot refrain from commending here the book of Psalms, which supplies so many and such strong arguments for confirming the chief heads of the Christian religion, that is, the chief points of the Gospel. This can truly be said of the book of Psalms: that it is an epitome of all the Holy Scriptures, since in it all the mysteries of the Gospel are most fully contained; and finally, that an incomparable and inexhaustible treasure of all divine wisdom lies hidden in it, and that examples, arguments and sayings on any subject can be drawn from it as from the richest storehouse. And one may see that Paul in all his epistles, and finally Christ himself, made much use of the testimonies of the Psalms, which were best known to all the Jews (since they were sung publicly in the holy synagogues, and were no doubt also read diligently in private by all), and which on account of the depth and frequency of their mysteries were held in the highest authority, and have always been judged by all to be the most excellent of the sacred books. For this reason Christ divided the books of the Old Testament into the law, the prophets, and the psalms. In the last chapter of Luke he says: "These are the words which I spoke unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me." Therefore I would have everyone admonished to exercise himself diligently in the study of the Psalms; and I dare promise this, that whoever has grasped the sense of the Psalms will understand the other books of Holy Scripture without difficulty.

units.la: Iam autem res postulat, vt locum hunc ex psalmo 44. recte de Christo esse expositum oste ndamus, nihilq; tortum aut inuolutum in eo latere. Proinde omissa expositione tuli, qui psalmo præfigitur, qui habet, decantatum à filijs Choræ: hoc extra omnem controuersiam est, psalmum hunc primum decantatum pro epithalamio quodam, id est, carmine nuptiali Regi Solomoni, in quo hunc laudant & celebrant, ob quasc unq; virtutes, quæ in rege, præsertim nuptias celebrante & familiam regaliter instituente, atque omni gloria & potentia magnificè ornato prædicare possent. Neq; possunt eludere hoc argumentū Iudæi, interpretantes, Solomonè ipsum appellari Deū, sicut aliquādo in Scripturis principes seu reges eo nomine honestātur: & Moses Exod. 7. Deus Pharaonis ab ipso Domino constituitur. Nā vt omnia agant ad tribuendū ista Solomoni, tamen non possunt ei tribuere thronū seu regnū æternū, cùm constet, ne filio quidē eius integrū regnū obtigisse: imò ipsius Solomonis, dū viueret, gloria obscurata & potentia non mediocriter labefactata. Veteres tamē Iudæi confitetur, Solomone typū gerere Christi, omnia, quæ hic dicūtur, vaticinia, esse de regno Mesiæ intelligēda. Itaq; delibabimus aliquā psalmi partē, ad eū locū, quē hic video ab Apostolo citatū; atq; ea omnia cum de Solomone sint prædicata, tū verò & de Christo multo cōmodisimè accipi ostēdemus. Sic aut habet psalm.
units.tr: Now the matter requires that we show that this passage from Psalm 44 is rightly expounded of Christ, and that nothing twisted or hidden lies within it. Therefore, setting aside the title prefixed to the psalm, which says it was sung by the sons of Korah, this is beyond all controversy: that this psalm was first sung as a kind of epithalamium, that is, a nuptial song, for King Solomon, in which they praise and celebrate him for whatever virtues could be proclaimed in a king, especially one celebrating his marriage and establishing his household in royal fashion, and magnificently adorned with all glory and power. Nor can the Jews evade this argument by interpreting that Solomon himself is called God, as sometimes in the Scriptures princes or kings are honoured with that name; and Moses says (Exod. 7) that Pharaoh was made God by the Lord himself. For even if they do all they can to ascribe these things to Solomon, they cannot ascribe to him an eternal throne or kingdom, since it is clear that not even his son obtained the whole kingdom; indeed, while Solomon himself lived, his glory was obscured and his power not a little weakened. Yet the ancient Jews confess that Solomon bears the type of Christ, and that all the prophecies stated here are to be understood of the kingdom of the Messiah. Therefore we shall touch upon some part of the psalm, up to the passage which I see is cited here by the Apostle; and we shall show that all these things, although they were said of Solomon, apply much more fittingly to Christ as well. The psalm reads thus:

units.la: Eructauit cor meum verbum bonum, dico ego opera mea regi: Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis.
units.tr: "My heart is inditing a good matter; I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer."

units.la: Exordium est ab affectu. Declarat enim vates, se magno affectu quasi rapi ad canendū aliquid ad regis laudem, & gloriam, & linguam suam ita ad hanc rem esse compositam expeditamq;, vt nullius scribę, vel amanuensis manus sic cōposi a esse queat, expeditaq; ad excipiedum seu scribendū ea, quę in laudem regis vult canere. Simili verò animi æstu atq; ardore decet eos esse accensos, qui volunt Christi laudes seriò prædicare. Sequūtur quæ ad laudem regis pertinent, siue panegyricus regi dicatus, qui præclaras regis virtutes canit.
units.tr: The opening is from feeling. For the poet declares that he is, as it were, carried away by a great emotion to sing something in praise and glory of the king, and that his tongue is so composed and ready for this task that no scribe's or amanuensis's hand could be better prepared or more ready to take down or write what he wishes to sing in praise of the king. Truly, those who wish to proclaim the praises of Christ in earnest ought to be kindled with a similar ardour of mind. There follows what pertains to the praise of the king, or a panegyric dedicated to the king, which sings his excellent virtues.

units.la: Speciosus forma præ filijs hominum, diffusa est gratia in labijs tuis, propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum.
units.tr: "Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God has blessed thee for ever."

units.la: Prima laus est à bonis corporis, nēpe à forma & pulchritudine. Sic solent etiā apud poetas à forma & præstantia corporis heroes & principes viri laudari, vt Achilles, Paris, Hector, alijq;: & à Sexto Aurelio toto corpore pulcher describitur Octauius Augustus. Nec dubiū, quin hac dote cōspicuus fuerit Solomō præ cęteris. Sed de Christo quid dicemus? cum Scriptura hūc sic prædicet ob pulchritudinē (præcipuè tamen spirituale) vt quemadmodū i. Petri 1. dicitur, angeli desiderent in eum conspicere: & quæ in Canticis canticorum de pulchritudine Sponsi dicuntur, ea omnia Christo veniūt attribuenda. Secundò laudatur rex à suauiloquentia seu admirabili gratia in dicendo: qualē in Solomone fuisse cōn stat, quando memorantur etiam à remotissimis regionibus venisse in Iudæam, vt de rebus sublimibus differentem audirent, vt regina Saba, alijq;. Atqui Christus quoq; hac virtute longè excelluit quemvis Solomonem: quando vidimus eum plenum gratia & veritate, vt Ioan. 1. quando docuit, vt autoritatem habens, & verba vitæ æternæ proponens: vt multo verius nos de eo, quàm Græci de Pericle dicere posse imus, q; fulminarit, tonuerit, deniq; cœlum terræ miscuerit. Longeq; alia vis spiritus, qua omnium animos ad se trahebat Christus, quàm cathena illa aurea, ex ore demissa, qua omnes homines ad se pertrahebat Hercules ille Gallicus. Christus enim non solùm sermone potes, sed quod neq; de Solomone, neque de alio quocunq; dici potest, etiam opere. Lucæ 24. Tertiò laudatur rex ab eo, quòd præter illas virtutes etiā alias amplissimas ipsi Deus contulerit, per quas fælicè successum deinceps in omnibus obtineret. Et certè magnis successibus vsus est Solomō, si quis alius in toto orbe rex aut princeps, sicut liber 1. Reg. cap. 9. & alijs locis testatur: Sed tamē benedictū esse in æternū, id quomodo homini conueniat Iudæi viderint. Solomone turpiter lapsum & pro benedictione reportasse, potius maledictione, & gloria eius etiā cùm viueret, miris modis obscurata, Scriptura nō dissimulat. Quare in solum Christū (de quo pater dixit, quòd in ipso benè ei esset complacitū, quem etiam turbæ laudarunt benedictū, qui veniret in nomine Domini: qui deniq; post morte suam glorificatus est, & benedictione æternam in cœlis accepit) quadrat, quòd sit in æternum benedictus. Sequitur;
units.tr: The first praise is from the goods of the body, namely from form and beauty. Thus among the poets heroes and princes are commonly praised for the form and excellence of their body, as Achilles, Paris, Hector and others; and by Sextus Aurelius, Octavius Augustus is described as beautiful in his whole body. Nor is there doubt that Solomon was conspicuous above others for this gift. But what shall we say of Christ? Since Scripture so proclaims him for beauty (yet chiefly spiritual beauty), that, as it is said in 1 Peter 1, the angels desire to look into him; and whatever is said in the Song of Songs about the beauty of the Bridegroom must all be attributed to Christ. Secondly, the king is praised for the sweetness of his speech, or his admirable grace in speaking; such as Solomon is known to have had, when it is recorded that people even from the most distant regions came into Judea to hear him discourse on lofty matters, like the queen of Sheba and others. Yet Christ also excelled any Solomon by this virtue, since we have seen him full of grace and truth, as in John 1; when he taught as one having authority, and set forth the words of eternal life. Thus we may say of him much more truly than the Greeks could say of Pericles that he lightened and thundered and finally shook heaven and earth together. And the power of his Spirit, by which Christ drew the minds of all to himself, was far different from that golden chain let down from the mouth by which the Gallic Hercules drew all men to himself. For Christ was powerful not only in word, but, which can be said of neither Solomon nor anyone else, also in deed (Luke 24). Thirdly, the king is praised because God bestowed upon him, beyond those virtues, other very great gifts, through which he would obtain success in all things thereafter. And certainly Solomon enjoyed great successes, if any other king or prince in the whole world did, as 1 Kings chapter 9 and other places attest. But how it can apply to a man that he is blessed for ever, the Jews may consider. Scripture does not conceal that Solomon fell shamefully and brought upon himself a curse rather than a blessing, and that his glory, even while he lived, was obscured in wonderful ways. Therefore it fits only Christ (of whom the Father said that in him he was well pleased, whom also the crowds praised as blessed, who comes in the name of the Lord; who finally after his death was glorified and received eternal blessing in heaven) that he is blessed for ever. The text continues:

units.la: Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum, potentissime, specie tua & pulchritudine tua intende.
units.tr: Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one, and in your splendour and your beauty press on.

units.la: Adhortatio est, seu coprecatio, qua optat, regē tot tantisq; donis à Deo ornatū, magno animo res arduas aggredi, vt etiā virtute bellica, quæ in principib. requiri & spectari, vel primo loco solet, dotes quas habet, augeat & illustret. Ita enim demum nomē & famam, deniq; omnes virtutes in illo posse augeri, & cōspectiores reddendas, si potentia suam in rebus bellicis exerat. Neq; hæc gloria potest Salomoni detrahi, vt q latissime imperari, & formidini fuerit omnibus vicinis gētibus, nec non tributa à quamplurimis regibus & populis acceperit. At noster Dominus multò amplissimā sibi hac ex re parauit gloriā. Accinctus enim gladio, qui est verbū Dei, toto orbe terrarū innumeros populos subiugauit, & spiritualis sui regni pomeria tam late extedit, quam mudus patet. Ipsius enim euangelii potentia est Dei, ad salutē omni credeti, Roman. 1. Et huius epistolæ capite quarto, verbum Dei describitur penetratius quovis gladio utrinq; incidere, quod pertingat usq; ad diuisionē animæ simul ac spiritus. Hoc aut gladio plus effecit intra breue spatiū per Apostolos, quam ullis armis & numerosis exercitibus, vel Solomon, vel coniuncti quicunque reges efficere potuissent.
units.tr: This is an exhortation, or prayer, by which the writer wishes that the king, endowed by God with so many and such great gifts, may tackle difficult undertakings with a great spirit, so that by his martial courage, which is usually required and looked for in princes and often comes first, he may increase and brighten the gifts he has. For in this way, and only in this way, can his name, his fame and finally all his virtues be increased and made more conspicuous, if he puts his power to use in warfare. Nor can this glory be taken away from Solomon, who extended his rule very widely, became a terror to all the neighbouring nations, and received tribute from very many kings and peoples. Yet our Lord has won for himself a far greater glory from this source. For girded with the sword, which is the word of God, he has subdued countless peoples across the whole earth, and has extended the boundaries of his spiritual kingdom as far as the world stretches. For the gospel itself is "the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes" (Rom. 1). And in chapter four of this letter the word of God is described as piercing more keenly than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 4). Yet within a short space of time, through the apostles, this sword accomplished more than Solomon, or any kings combined, could have achieved with any arms or large armies.

units.la: Prospere procede & regna. Propter veritatē & mansuetudinem, & iustitiam, & deducet te mirabiliter dextera tua. Sagittæ tuæ acutæ, populi sub te cadent, in corda inimicorum regis.
units.tr: Prosper, go forth and reign, because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and your right hand shall teach you terrible things. Your arrows are sharp; the peoples shall fall under you, in the hearts of the king's enemies.

units.la: Optat adhuc regnū Solomonis ampliari, indiesq; augustius fieri. Sed inserit, quaratione potisimū debeat fœlices successus, & gloriā amplissimā in regno sperare. Curet se celebrari ob veritatē, mansuetudinem, & iustitiā, has virtutes studios è excolat, nec dubiū, quin Deus omnes ipsius conatus sit fortunaturus, si harū virtutum munimentis regnum suū stabiliat: tum sentiet dexterā suam in omnibus præualere: tum poterit apparatu bellico, (qui per sagittas significatur) omnes aduersarios suos debellare & prosternere. Porro in regno Christi hæc omnia multò manifestius sunt impleta, quàm in regno Solomonis. Nam regnū Christi quod spirituale est, maximè in veritate ac mansuetudine, & iustitia sitū est, atq; vniuersum euangeliū de his potissimū virtutibus concionatur. Christus ipse via, vita, & veritas, & via Dei in veritate docet: ipse mitis & humilis corde, se omnibus pro exemplo mansuetudinis proponēs: Ipse est ille, cuius iustitia manet in seculū seculi, cuius nomē est, vt Hiere. 33. dicitur, dominus iustificator noster, & vt dicitur 1. Cor. 1. fa ctus est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redēptio. Et verè dextera ac potentia illius sic deducta est constituta q;, per prædicationem euangelij, vt omnes sint ei subiecti per auditum verbi, vt potentia & sapientia mundi vniuersa, sagittis euangelicæ prædicationis sint deuicti, & ad credendū corde, & cōfitendū ore coacti: sicut iterū 1. Cor. 1. scriptū est, Ex Esaiæ 29. perdā sapientiā sapientū, & intelligentiā intelligentiū reijciā. Et paulo post: Quæ stulta erant mūdi, delegit Deus, vt pudefaceret sapientes: & quæ erant imbecillia in mūdo, vt pudefaceret ea, quæ sunt robusta, &c. Talia deniq; visa sunt arma Christi, eius q; sagittæ, vt innumeri principes ac tyranni longo ordine inuicem succeden tes, nūquam potuerint propagationem regni Christi impedire. Iam verò sequitur, quod maximè ad rem nostram pertinet:
units.tr: The psalmist still wishes the kingdom of Solomon to be enlarged and to grow more splendid day by day. But he adds by what means he ought above all to hope for happy successes and the greatest glory in his kingdom. Let him make himself famous for truth, meekness and righteousness; let him cultivate and practise these virtues. And there is no doubt that God will prosper all his undertakings, if he establishes his kingdom with the bulwarks of these virtues. Then he will feel that God's right hand prevails in all things, and he will be able to overcome and cast down all his adversaries with a warlike equipment, which is signified by the arrows. Moreover, in the kingdom of Christ all these things have been fulfilled far more plainly than in the kingdom of Solomon. For the kingdom of Christ, which is spiritual, rests chiefly on truth, meekness and righteousness, and the whole gospel preaches mainly about these virtues. Christ himself is the way, the life and the truth, and teaches the way of God in truth; he himself is meek and lowly in heart, setting himself before all as an example of meekness. He is the one whose righteousness endures for ever and ever, whose name, as Jeremiah 33 says, is "the Lord our righteousness"; and as 1 Corinthians 1 says, he "became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption." And truly his right hand and power have been so guided and established, through the preaching of the gospel, that all are made subject to him through the hearing of the word; so that all the power and wisdom of the world are overcome by the arrows of evangelical preaching and compelled to believe with the heart and confess with the mouth. Likewise it is written in 1 Corinthians 1: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will reject the understanding of the understanding" (Isa. 29). And a little later: "God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might shame the wise; and the weak things of the world, that he might shame the strong," and so on. Such, finally, were the weapons of Christ, and such his arrows, that countless princes and tyrants, succeeding one another in a long line, have never been able to hinder the spread of Christ's kingdom. Now there follows what pertains most of all to our purpose:

units.la: Thronus tuus Deus in seculum seculi, virga rectitudinis, virga regni tui. Dilexisti iustitiā, & odisti iniquitatem. Propterea vnxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo exultationis, vltra consortes tuos.
units.tr: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of your kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.

units.la: De Solomone & regni eius successu ista dici cōcedendū, quādo videlicet spes erat, regnū ipsius sic stabiliendū, vt nunquām cōcideret, maximè cùm regnū administraret virgā rectitudinis summa videlicet æquitate & recti obseruatione, quæ sita est in diligēdo iusti tiam, & odio habēdo iniquitatē. Atq; ob has virtutes et iustitiæ cultū, Deus ornauit illum præclaris donis, atq; etiā regia dignitate, præ fratribus, quibus vt senioribus regnū debitū videbatur, quēadmodū Adoniā debere succedere, optimates etiā iudicabāt, vt 1. Reg. 1. dicitur. Verū, vt ita res se habeat, tamen S. sanctus hic se exeruit, & voluit per os Pro- phetę ea aspergere, his carminibus, quæ omnes clarè intelligerent potius alteri cuipiam, quàm Solomoni cōpetere. Nam quendā hic celebrari regem, qui vocetur Deus: deinde cuius regnū sit duraturū in æternū: hoc alterius negotij est: atq; omnes velint nolint, cōgutur cōcedere, de aliquo alio, quàm de Solomone, cuius regnum, sicut & cætera regna mundi etiā multò augustiora, (qualia fuerunt Assyriorū, Persarū, Medorū) collapsum cetnitur, hæc verba accipienda. Itaq; propter hæc verba omnes Iudæi magno cōsensu receperūt hunc psalmū, de regno æterno Messiæ vaticinari, & omnes interpretes veteres Iudæorum dæorum ita statuūt: nec dubiū quin vel ante ipsius Pauli tépora hæc sentētia de hoc Psalmo fuerit pasim in omnibus Synagogis decātata. Quamobré nihil proficiét posteriores Judæi, qui, quádo non possunt negare, aut dissimulare, clarissima verba præsentis loci depingere regnū ac dignitatē Christi: odio Christi & nostro, quia nihil aliud possunt, vim faciunt Spiritus sanéti verbis, atq; aliter, quàm verba simpliciter sonát, conantur interpretari. Vnde quidá sic exponūt: Thronus tuus, qui idē Dei est, stabit in seculū. Rursus aliter Saadiag: Thronū tuū Deus firmabit in seculū: Sed vt omne hic moueant lapidé, vt quantum ad vocē Dei attinet, paululū varient sententiā: at frustra adhuc faciūt omnia, quādo nullo modo cōsistere id potest, quòd Solomonis regnū sit æternū. Aut Deus promissis non stat, quādo nō curauit regnū téporale Solomonis in ęternū confirmari, aut promissio hæc de alio & alterius regno quàm de Solomonis regno sumi debet. Iuxtà leue & vanum est: quòd quidam non immutantes verba Spiritus sanċti, interpretantur ipsum Solomone vocari אלהים Deū, quádo hoc nomine reges & principes in Scripturis aliquādo appellātur, quomodo & Moses Exod. 7. vbi Dominus ad eū ait: Costitui te אלהים, id est Deum Pharaonis. Nam iterum obijcimus illud, quod prius diximus, vt hic vocem Dei cuiát deprauare, eradere, aut exscalpere, adhuc restat, vt de alio regno, quàm Solomonis, sententiá hanc accipiamus, quando reipsa compertum est, Solomonis regnum non durasse in seculū seculi, cùm statim à morte Solomonis miserè fuerit dissipatū, reliĉtis stirpi eius duabus tantùm tribubus, ac tandé in potestatem Romanorum venerint Iudæi, qui regem alienigenam, Herodem videlicet, ipsis præfecerunt, vt nimirum ad præparationē regni Christi æterni, quod iam erat coram mundo illustrádum, impleretur, quod ab ipso Iacob Patriarcha erat prædictum, Genes. 49. Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, & dux de femore eius, donec veniat, qui mittendus est, & ipse erit expectatio gentiū. Itaq; frustra ringuntur & litigant hic Iudæi, nec non spiritui Sanćto sunt valde iniurij, qui dū non habent, quò confugiant, Scripturas peruertere moliuntur. Et quid confidant miseri se prosesturos, quando idem iste psalmus alia habet testimonia, quæ non obscurè regnū Christi describunt? Nā quod post pauca subijcitur, Regem dominū esse reginæ & ab ea suppliciter adorandum, de Christo honorādo ab ecclesia est accipiendū: Sed illud, quod postremo loco additur, Pro patribus tuis nascentur tibi filij, cōstitues eos principes super omnem terrā, falsum est, si de Solomone eius q; filijs successoribus velis interpretari: Sed de Apostolis Christi discipulis & veris terrarū principibus in regno Christi spirituali recte illa accipiantur. Sed hæc satis esse puto ad declarandum, testimonium hoc pro asserenda Christi diuinitate, rectè ab Apostolo esse productum in medium, neq; à Iudæis quoquo modo euerti posse.
units.tr: These things may be granted to be said of Solomon and the success of his kingdom, at least as far as there was hope that his kingdom would be so established that it would never fall, especially since he ruled it with a sceptre of uprightness, that is, with the greatest equity and the observance of what is right, which consists in loving righteousness and hating wickedness. And for these virtues and his cultivation of righteousness, God adorned him with excellent gifts and even with royal dignity, above his brothers, to whom the kingdom seemed due as to the elder, just as the nobles also judged that Adonijah ought to succeed, as 1 Kings 1 says. Yet, however the matter stands, the Holy Spirit here put himself forward and willed, through the mouth of the prophet, to sprinkle these things in verses which everyone would clearly understand to belong rather to someone else than to Solomon. For that a king is here celebrated who is called God, and that his kingdom is to endure for ever: this belongs to another matter entirely, and whether they will or not, all are compelled to concede that these words must be taken of someone other than Solomon, whose kingdom, like the other kingdoms of the world, even much more splendid ones (such as those of the Assyrians, Persians and Medes), is seen to have fallen. Therefore, on account of these words, all the Jews with great unanimity have received this psalm as prophesying of the eternal kingdom of the Messiah, and all the older Jewish interpreters so judge. Nor is there any doubt that this interpretation of the psalm had been sung everywhere in all the synagogues, even before the time of Paul himself. Accordingly, the later Jews gain nothing, since they cannot deny or conceal that the most clear words of this passage describe the kingdom and dignity of Christ; out of hatred for Christ and for us, because they have nothing else they can do, they do violence to the words of the Holy Spirit and try to interpret them otherwise than the words plainly sound. Hence some expound it thus: "Your throne, which is also God's, shall stand for ever." Again, Saadia renders it differently: "God will establish your throne for ever." But to move every stone here, they vary the sense only slightly as far as the word "God" is concerned; yet all their efforts are in vain, since it cannot in any way stand that Solomon's kingdom was eternal. Either God does not keep his promises, since he did not take care that the temporal kingdom of Solomon should be confirmed for ever, or this promise must be taken of another, and of a kingdom other than Solomon's. Equally vain and frivolous is the view of certain men who, without changing the words of the Holy Spirit, interpret that Solomon himself is called Elohim [אלהים], God, since in Scripture kings and princes are sometimes called by this name, as Moses is in Exodus 7, where the Lord says to him: "I have made you Elohim [אלהים], that is, God to Pharaoh." For again we object what we said before: even if one wished to corrupt, erase or chisel out the voice of God here, there would still remain the need to take this sentence of some other kingdom than Solomon's, since it has in fact been established that Solomon's kingdom did not last for ever and ever, for immediately after Solomon's death it was miserably scattered, two tribes alone being left to his line; and at last the Jews came under the power of the Romans, who set over them a foreign king, Herod, so that, to be sure, the preparation of the eternal kingdom of Christ, which was now to be made manifest before the world, might be fulfilled, as Jacob the patriarch himself had foretold in Genesis 49: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from between his feet, until he comes whose it is to be, and he shall be the expectation of the nations." So these Jews struggle and contend in vain here, and they are also deeply unjust to the Holy Spirit, since, having nowhere to take refuge, they labour to pervert the Scriptures. And what do these wretched men hope to achieve, when this same psalm has other testimonies which describe the kingdom of Christ no less plainly? For what is added a little later, that the king, the Lord, is to be the queen's lord and is to be worshipped by her with supplication, is to be understood of the honouring of Christ by the Church; but what is added last, "In place of your fathers sons shall be born to you; you shall make them princes over all the earth," is false if you wish it to be interpreted of Solomon and his successors; rather, it is rightly understood of the apostles, the disciples of Christ, and the true princes of the earth in the spiritual kingdom of Christ. But I think this is enough to show that this testimony was rightly brought forward by the Apostle to establish the divinity of Christ, and that it cannot in any way be overturned by the Jews.

units.la: Lubet nunc singula verba seu partes huius testimonij accuratius expendere, vt eo clarius fiat, omnia in Christum mirum in modum quadrare.
units.tr: Let us now weigh the individual words or parts of this testimony more carefully, so that it becomes clearer that everything fits Christ in a remarkable way.

units.la: Ad filium autem, Thronus tuus Deus in seculum seculi: Ita præmittit hunc locū, quem citare vult de Christo esse accipiendum. ἀρὼν, solium, sedem, sellam significat, & præcipuè eius, qui in summa aliquà dignitate est cōstitutus: Quare per Metonymiā significat regiam dignitatem: sicut aliquando eadem significatur per sceptrum: Simili modo accipitur ea vox Esaiæ 9. vti mox citabo. Habet vero singularem emphasin, quòd dicatur, ὁ θεός, pro qua hebraicè legitur אלהים, vt cùm vsitatissimè in scripturis, tali forma hæ voces tribuuntur vnico Deo, moueri debeant omnes, ad interpretandum ista de Deo, videlicet Christo.
units.tr: But of the Son: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever." This is how he introduces the passage he wants to be understood of Christ. The Greek [θρόνος] signifies a throne, seat, chair, especially of one who has been set in some high dignity. By metonymy it therefore signifies royal dignity, just as the sceptre sometimes signifies the same thing. The word is used in the same way in Isaiah 9, as I will cite shortly. The phrase has a singular emphasis in that it says [ὁ θεός], for which the Hebrew reads [אלהים]. Since these words are most commonly applied in Scripture to the one God in this form, everyone should be moved to interpret these things of God, that is, of Christ.

units.la: In seculum seculi: Phrasis est Scripturę vsurpata, ad significandum ęternitatem, quasi tēpus finitum poneretur pro infinito. Hebraica vox hoc loco posita עולם secundum Abenezra, tempus duarum generationum plerunq; complectitur, hoc est, cētum annos, sicut latinis vox seculi, sed pro longissimo tempore adeoq; pro æternitate ponitur. Itaq; clarè hic significatur, Christum esse Deum, atq; eidem regnum æternum tribuitur, quod spirituale esse oportet, cùm alias, si nimirū téporale & externū sit, ęternū esse nequeat: Quicquid enim téporale est, id simul cū tépore cōcidat necessum est. Neq; Christus voluit vnquā regnū téporale sibi vēdicare: Nam quādo eligere eumturba voluit in regē, fugā inijt, vt habetur Ioan. 6. Et diserte dixit ad Pilatū, regnū suum non esse de hoc mundo, agnoscēs quidē se regē, sed nequaquā tale, quales sunt reges & principes huius mūdi. Itaq; regnū Christo tribuitur, sed spirituale, quod administratur per verbū Euangelij, quodq; locū habet in piorū cordibus. Et cùm spirituale sit, nihil mirū, si æternum duret. Quæ enim spiritualia sunt, nō ita pereūt, aut cōsumuntur, vti téporalia. Ac de eiusmodi regno oportet intelligere quoscūq; alios locos in Scriptura obuios, qui Christo regnū, & quidē æternū tribuūt. Si Iudæi possent agnoscere, regnū Christi esse spirituale, & nequaquam téporale, vt ipsi somniant, facilè ab omni errore liberarentur, & ad credēdum Christo adduci possent.
units.tr: "For ever and ever" is a phrase taken up in Scripture to signify eternity, as if a finite time were put for an infinite one. The Hebrew word used here, [עולם], according to Abenezra, usually embraces the span of two generations, that is, a hundred years, as the Latin word seculum does; but it is also used for a very long time, and so for eternity. Therefore it is clearly signified here that Christ is God, and an eternal kingdom is ascribed to him. This kingdom must be spiritual, since if it were temporal and external it could not be eternal. For whatever is temporal must necessarily perish together with time. Nor did Christ ever want to claim for himself a temporal kingdom. For when the crowd wanted to make him king, he fled, as is recorded in John 6. And he plainly said to Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world, acknowledging indeed that he is a king, but in no way of the kind that the kings and princes of this world are. So a kingdom is ascribed to Christ, but a spiritual one, which is administered through the Word of the gospel and has its place in the hearts of the godly. Since it is spiritual, it is no wonder that it lasts for ever. For spiritual things do not perish or waste away as temporal things do. It is necessary to understand in this sense of kingdom all the other passages in Scripture that present themselves, which ascribe a kingdom to Christ, and indeed an eternal one. If the Jews could recognise that the kingdom of Christ is spiritual and in no way temporal, as they dream it to be, they would easily be freed from every error and could be brought to believe in Christ.

units.la: Sed res postulat pergamus;
units.tr: But the matter requires that we go on.

units.la: Virga rectitudinis, virga regni tui) Laus est regni Christi ab optima administratione sumAE maque recti & æqui obseruantia. Virga enim præsertim recta, significat rectam administrationem, & virga siue sceptrum, Symbolum est iuris & potestatis, quam habet magistratus ad coercendos legum transgressores: quemadmodum ipse Paulus Rom.13. interpretatur, de gladio magistratus differens. Quod si feceris id quod malum est, time: Non enim frustra gladium gestat: nam Dei minister est, vltor ad iram ei, qui quod malum est, fecerit. Sic igitur Christo, videlicet vero regi, datur in manus virga, quo agnoscatur ab omnibus is esse, cui pater dederit omne iudicium, cuiq; tradita sit omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Atque ei præ omnibus conuenit virga rectitudinis, id est, virga recta & recti custos: (est enim ibi hebraismus) quandoquidem ipse est, qui citra personarum acceptionem iudicat, cuius rectas esse semitas Ioannes præcursor eius palàm concinabatur, (cuius euangelium omnem rectitudinem & æquitatem docet, sicut Esaiæ 11. dicitur: Iudicabit in iustitia pauperes, & arguet in æquitate mansuetos terræ, non secundum auditum aurium, aut visionem oculorum, &c.) Matthæi tertio, Qui & in nouissimo die ijs, qui bona egerunt, conferet vitam æternam, illis verò qui mala egerunt, ignem æternum. Interea videtur & illud facere ad declarandum regnum Christi, in mansuetudine & iustitia, & in spiritualibus rebus esse situm, quòd Christo potius virga, quàm gladius tribuitur. Gladius metum omnium animis incutit, & tyrannicum nescio quid videtur præ se ferre: at virga etiam humilibus & modestis datur pastoribus ouiculas modesta animalia regetibus: unde illud Micheæ 7. Pasce populum tuum in virga tua. Virga ergo Christo spiritualiter, & in modestia, & in humilitate regnati aptissimè in manus datur. Huc pertinet illud Matth. 11. Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo vos. Tollite iugum meum super vos, & discite à me, quòd mitis sim & humilis corde, & inuenietis requiem animabus vestris. Iugum enim meum commodum est, & onus meum leue. Ecce mansuetum regem, & verum pastorem populorum, <bl>Chr</bl> Esaiæ 16. præparabitur in misericordia folium, & sedebit super id in veritate. Zachariæ 9. Ecce rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, sedens super pullum asinæ, &c.
units.tr: "The sceptre of uprightness, the sceptre of your kingdom." This is praise of the kingdom of Christ, drawn from its excellent administration and from the observance of what is right and just. For a sceptre, especially a straight one, signifies upright administration, and the rod or sceptre is the symbol of the right and power which the magistrate has to restrain the transgressors of the laws, as Paul himself interprets in Romans 13, speaking of the sword of the magistrate: "But if you do what is evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God's minister, an avenger to wrath against the one who does evil." So a rod is put into the hands of Christ, the true king, so that he may be recognised by all as the one to whom the Father has given all judgment and to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been handed over. And the sceptre of uprightness, that is, a straight sceptre and the guardian of what is right (for there is a Hebraism here), suits him above all others, since he is the one who judges without respect of persons, and whose straight paths his forerunner John openly proclaimed. (His gospel teaches all uprightness and equity, as it is said in Isaiah 11: "He shall judge the poor in righteousness, and reprove with equity the meek of the earth, not after the hearing of the ears, or the seeing of the eyes," etc.) In Matthew 3: "He will also, on the last day, give eternal life to those who have done good, but eternal fire to those who have done evil." Meanwhile it seems also to serve to show that the kingdom of Christ rests in meekness and righteousness and in spiritual things, in that a rod rather than a sword is ascribed to Christ. The sword strikes fear into everyone's minds and seems to display something tyrannical; but a rod is given even to humble and modest shepherds for guiding their gentle little sheep. Hence Micah 7: "Feed your people with your rod." So a rod is most fittingly put into the hands of Christ, who reigns spiritually, in modesty and humility. To this belongs Matthew 11: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, that I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light." Behold the meek king and true shepherd of the peoples. Isaiah 16: "A throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth." Zechariah 9: "Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon a colt, the foal of an ass," etc.

units.la: Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti iniquitatem) Est veluti probatio, quòd virga regni Christi, sit virga recta. Nam in hoc conspicitur recta administratio, si diligatur iustitia, & odio habeatur iniquitas, id est, si præmia conferantur benè agentibus, & pœnis afficiantur mali. Cum verò Christus in hoc totus fuerit, ut doceret homines iustitiam, atque eam inprimis quæ vera est iustitia, non tantùm coram mundo, sed etiam coram Deo. Deinde cùm omnes conciones illius huc conuederint, ut ab iniquitate & malè agedo homines alienarentur, ipse verè ostendit, se cultorem iustitiæ & oforem esse iniquitatis. Quando semper auersatus est superbos, & amarulentos hypocritas pharisæos, impios pontifices, ostendit seinii quitatis & iniustitiæ hostè: quando verò humiles & mansuetos, & pauperes lubeterad ad se recepit & commendauit, ostendit se iustitiæ vere dilexisse. Istud ergo, nepe diligere iustitiam & odisse iniquitatem, maxime proprium est Christo. Neq; certum est, utrum homini, velut Solomoni aut alteri cuipiam liceat istud tribuere. Nam, ut Solomon fuerit mantissimus æqui, & reuera tàm prudenter, tamq; graviter sententias de negotijs ciuibus tulisse legatur, quàm nemo vnquam rex alius: attamen non perinde potest de eo dici, quòd ofor fuerit iniquitatis, vtpote cùm ipse (natura nimirum hominis semper procliui existente in malum) in peccata, & quidem multò crassissima, ut externam idololatriam, fit prolapsus, & contra legis diuinæ præcepta, alienigenas mulieres quamplurimas sibi adiunxerit. Sed sequitur:
units.tr: "You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity." This is as it were a proof that the sceptre of the kingdom of Christ is a straight sceptre. For upright administration is seen in this, if righteousness is loved and iniquity is hated, that is, if rewards are conferred on those who act well and punishments are inflicted on the wicked. Now Christ was wholly intent on this, to teach men righteousness, and above all that righteousness which is true, not only before the world but also before God. Then, since all his sermons tended to this, that men should be turned away from iniquity and from doing evil, he truly showed that he was a lover of righteousness and an enemy of iniquity. Whenever he turned away from the proud and the bitter hypocrites, the Pharisees and the impious high priests, he showed himself an enemy of unrighteousness and injustice; but when he received and commended the humble, the meek and the poor, he showed that he truly loved righteousness. Therefore this, namely to love righteousness and to hate iniquity, is especially proper to Christ. Nor is it certain whether this may be ascribed to a man, such as Solomon or any other. For although Solomon was the most excellent judge of equity, and indeed he is read to have pronounced sentences on civil affairs as wisely and gravely as any other king ever did, yet it cannot in the same way be said of him that he hated iniquity, since he himself (the nature of man being always inclined to evil) fell into sins, and indeed very gross ones, such as open idolatry, and against the precepts of the divine law took very many foreign women to himself. But it follows:

units.la: Propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo exultationis præ consortibus tuis. En præmium, & quasi mercedes sic cultæ iustitiæ & regni benè administrati, quasi diceret: Sicut, ô Christe, præ omnibus alijs rectissimè sanctissimeq; tuū regnū administras: Ita Deus voluit te præ omnibus alijs amplissimis donis honestare & honorare. Aut potius causa regni benè administrati vt sit sententia: ideo quidè tàm sapienter & fœliciter administratu regnu, quia Deus vnxit & illustrauit te clarissimis donis præ cæteris. Nā vbi nos habemus, propterea, hebræus legit, quod rectius reddiderimus, propterea quòd, vt causę sit redditio, sicut nonnulli interpretatur. Quanquam græcus reddidit, vt istud sequi propter præcedentia vi-deatur. Vtroq; tamen modo à nonnullis hæc sunt reddita, neq; pugnat interpretationes cum veritate. Etenim benè administratibus, Deus largiter sua dona suppeditat, sicut nullū bonum finit irremuneratū: & rursus, quibus Deus sua dona iam cotulerit, ijs demū facultas adest benè administrādi, quādo sine Dei auxilio recte agere nil queamus. Te, inquit, quies Deus, unxit te Deus tuus, oleo exultationis. En manifeste Christū vocat Deum, atq; à Deo patre ait huc esse vnctū, ita vt clarissime diuinā naturā in Christo exprimat, similiter & in patre distinctas q; personas constituat. Hebræus legit ... Neq;
units.tr: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." Here is the reward, and as it were the wages, for such cultivated righteousness and a well-administered kingdom, as if he said: "Just as you, O Christ, administer your kingdom most uprightly and most holily above all others, so God has willed to honour and glorify you with more ample gifts than all others." Or rather, the sense may be that the kingdom is well administered for this cause: that it is administered so wisely and happily because God has anointed and enlightened you with the brightest gifts above the rest. For where we have "therefore," the Hebrew reads [על כן], which we would have rendered more correctly "because," so that the statement gives the reason, as some interpret it. Although the Greek has rendered it in a way that seems to follow from what precedes. Yet by either rendering these words have been translated by some, and the interpretations do not conflict with the truth. For God abundantly supplies his gifts to those who administer well, just as he lets no good go unrewarded; and conversely, to those to whom God has already conferred his gifts, the ability to administer well is granted, since without God's help we can do nothing rightly. "You," he says, "because God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness." Behold, he plainly calls Christ God, and says that he was anointed here by God the Father, so that he most clearly expresses the divine nature in Christ, and likewise constitutes distinct persons in the Father. The Hebrew reads ... Nor

units.la: Virga iustitiæ et æquitatis in regno Christi. Neq; alienum est à Scripturis, quo d ita simul coniungantur hæ voces, Deus, Deus, ad o- ftendendam distinctionem patris & filij, & utriufq; diuinitatem: Gen.19. Dominus pluit super Sodomam & Gomorram sulphur & igne à Domino de cœlo. En Dominus à Domino, nimirū filius à patre distinctus. Et Zach.3. Dixit Dominus ad Sathan, Increpet Dominus te Sathan. En iterum dominus de domino alia persona loquitur. Et psalm.68. De patre, currus Dei, viginti millia, millia Angelorum: Dominus inter eos, sicut in Sinai in sanctitate: mox ad filium: Ascendisti in altum, captiuam duxisti captiuitatem, accepisti dona in hominibus: & etiam rebelles, ut inhabitent in tabernaculo Iáh Dei. Neq; hoc detrahit Christi æ qualitati, quam habet cum patre secundum diuinam naturam, quòd dicatur vnctus à patre tanquam superiore, cùm ungi sit quodammodo inferioris, vngere uerò superioris. Nam istud, vngi videlicet & ornari donis, conuenit Christo secundum humanam naturam, secundum quâ patre inferior agnoscitur, & secundum quâ pater Deus Christi in Scripturis appellatur. Sic enim Christus ipse ait: Deus, Deus meus cur me dereliquisti? Et à resurrectione sua, Ioan.20. Ascendo ad patrem meum, & patrem uestrum, & Deum meum, & Deum vestrum. Proinde hîc non tantùm de diuinitate Christi, verùm etiam de humanitate Christi, id est, de vtraq; natura habemus testimonia: de diuinitate Christi, quòd uocetur deus, quodq; habeat regnum æternum: de humanitate verò, quòd ungatur à patre, seu donis ornetur: deinde quòd tribuantur ei consortes. Nùc quomodo Christus unctus sit, & qua li oleo, videamus. In ueteri lege externa nota inaugurationis & ordinationis, ad amplissima munia obeunda in republica uel ecclesia erat unctio publica, & per eos, qui mandatum à Deo habebát: unde reges vngebantur: sicut Saul & Dauid à Samuele, & Solomô à Nathan uncti sunt. Vngebantur item sacerdotes, sicut Aaró & filij eius uncti sunt iuxta Dei à Mose. Præterea vngebantur prophetæ, sicut unctus est Helisæus ab Helia, cui Dominus ita imperauerat, dicens: vnges Helisæum prophetá pro te. Ad hunc igitur modum & Christus (qui reuera uerus est rex, sacerdos, & propheta) à Deo est unctus & uerus rex regni spiritualis declaratus: id cùm aliàs sæpe per doctrinam insignem, & miracu la, tum tamen præcipuè, quando pater uoce sua testatus est dicens: Hic est filius meus, &c.
units.tr: The branch of righteousness and equity in the kingdom of Christ. Nor is it foreign to Scripture that these words, God, God, are joined together in this way, to show the distinction of Father and Son and the divinity of each. Gen. 19: "The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven." Here is the Lord from the Lord, that is, the Son distinguished from the Father. And Zech. 3: "The Lord said to Satan, The Lord rebuke you, Satan." Here again one Lord speaks of another Lord, a different person. And Psalm 68: of the Father, "the chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels; the Lord is among them, as at Sinai, in holiness." Then, turning to the Son: "You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts among men, and also the rebellious, that they may dwell in the tabernacle of Iah God." Nor does it detract from the equality of Christ, which he has with the Father according to the divine nature, that he is said to be anointed by the Father as by a superior. For to be anointed is in some sense proper to the inferior, and to anoint to the superior. That is, to be anointed and adorned with gifts belongs to Christ according to the human nature, according to which he is acknowledged as inferior to the Father, and according to which the Father is called the God of Christ in the Scriptures. Thus Christ himself says: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" And after his resurrection, John 20: "I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God." Therefore here we have testimonies not only concerning the divinity of Christ but also concerning his humanity, that is, concerning both natures: concerning the divinity of Christ, that he is called God and that he has an eternal kingdom; concerning the humanity, that he is anointed by the Father, or adorned with gifts; and then that companions are assigned to him. Now let us see how Christ was anointed, and with what oil. In the old law, the external sign of inauguration and ordination, for the discharge of the highest offices in the commonwealth or the Church, was a public anointing, performed by those who had a command from God. Hence kings were anointed, as Saul and David were anointed by Samuel, and Solomon by Nathan. Priests were anointed likewise, as Aaron and his sons were anointed according to God's command through Moses. Moreover, prophets were anointed, as Elisha was anointed by Elijah, to whom the Lord had so commanded, saying: "You shall anoint Elisha the prophet in your place." In this manner, then, Christ too (who is truly king, priest, and prophet) was anointed by God and declared the true king of the spiritual kingdom. This was shown both at other times by his remarkable teaching and miracles, and yet especially when the Father bore witness by his own voice, saying: "This is my beloved Son, etc."

units.la: Vnctus autem est Christus oleo, non uulgari, sed oleo exultationis. Quod est istud oleum exultationis? Illud nimirum, de quo propheta Esaias canit capit.61. & Christus Lucæ 4. de se exponit: Spiritus Domini super me, propterea quòd unxit me, ut sanem contritos corde, & prædicem captiuis remissionem, & cæcis uisum, ut emittam confractos per remissionem, ut prædicem annum Domini acceptum. Iterum Esaiæ 11. Requiescet super eum spiritus Domini, spiritus Sapientiæ & intellectûs, spiritus consilij & fortitudinis, &c. Et fructus spiritus, Galat.5. sunt, gaudium, exultatio, &c. Romanorum decimoquarto, Non est regnum Dei cibus & potus, sed iustitia, pax, & gaudium in spiritu S.
units.tr: Christ was anointed with oil, not with common oil, but with the oil of gladness. What is that oil of gladness? Surely it is that of which the prophet Isaiah sings in chapter 61, and which Christ explains concerning himself in Luke 4: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to heal the brokenhearted, and to preach liberty to the captives, and sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord." Again, Isaiah 11: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength," etc. And the fruit of the Spirit, Gal. 5, is joy, exultation, etc. Rom. 14: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit."

units.la: En causam exultationis & lætitiæ, omnibus de illa unctione audientibus, ut propterea, quòd gaudium & salus ad alios perueniat ex illa unctione Christi, oleum illud re ête dicatur oleum exultationis: quam ob causam & euangelii nomen à læto nuncio deriuatur. Deque hac ipsa unctione Christi testatus est Ioannes, dicens, quòd spiritum vidisset descendentem in Christum, & in eo manentem. Atq; huc etiam pertinet, quod de Christo sæpe dicitur, quòd sit plenus gratia & spiritu sancto. Ioan.1. Luc.4. quia omnia uberrime in Christum sunt transfusa. Hac de causa Christus quoq; dicitur unctus præ consortibus suis, hoc est, præ omnibus hominibus, siue regibus, siue sacerdotibus, siue prophetis, siue alijs quibuscunq;, qui unquam uncti sunt, siue exterius, siue interius. Nam cùm Christus humanam naturam induit, dignatus est homines ut consortes suos agnoscere: quâ ob causâ dicti sunt homines eius fratres, sicut cap.2. huius epistolæ uidere est: & ipse alibi uocatur primogenitus in multis fratribus. Quò etiam pertinet, quòd in genere omnes sancti etiam Christi appellantur, sicut Dominus apud prophetam ait, Nolite tangere Christos meos. A Christo dicitur Christiani, id est, ab vncto vncti. Et 1. Ioan.2. Vos unctionem habetis à sancto, & nosti omnia. Item 2. Corinth.1. Qui confirmat nos vnà vobiscum in Christum, & qui vnxit nos, Deus est. Ioel.2. Effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem. Proinde Christus præ omnibus accepit amplissima dona, quia cū cæteri ad mensuram fidei dona acceperint: ut Roman.12. & Ephes.4. Christus tamen habuit omnem plenitudinem. Ioan.3. Non enim huic ad mensuram dat Deus. Colos.1. Quoniam in illo complacitum est patri, uniuersam plenitudinem inhabitare. Denique sic accipit ille omnem plenitudinem, ut omnes alij ab illo, tanquam fonte debeant donorum parte accipere: sicut Ioan.1. dicitur, de plenitudine eius nos omnes accepimus. En ergo quomodo Christus unctus sit oleo exultationis præ omnib. consortibus suis.
units.tr: Here is the cause of gladness and joy for all who hear of that anointing: because joy and salvation come to others from that anointing of Christ, that oil is rightly called the oil of gladness. For this reason also the name of the gospel is derived from a joyful message. And concerning this very anointing of Christ, John testified, saying that he had seen the Spirit descending upon Christ and remaining on him. To this also pertains what is often said of Christ, that he is full of grace and of the Holy Spirit (John 1; Luke 4), because all things have been poured into Christ most abundantly. For this reason Christ is also said to be anointed above his companions, that is, above all men, whether kings, or priests, or prophets, or any others whatever who have ever been anointed, whether outwardly or inwardly. For when Christ put on human nature, he deigned to acknowledge men as his companions; for this reason they are called his brothers, as may be seen in chapter 2 of this epistle; and he himself is elsewhere called the firstborn among many brothers. To this also pertains that all the saints in general are called Christs, as the Lord says through the prophet: "Do not touch my Christs." They are called Christians from Christ, that is, the anointed from the Anointed One. And 1 John 2: "You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things." Likewise 2 Cor. 1: "He who establishes us together with you in Christ, and who has anointed us, is God." Joel 2: "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh."
