Therefore Christ received the most ample gifts above all, because while the rest have received gifts according to the measure of faith (as in Rom. 12 and Eph. 4), Christ nevertheless had all fullness. John 3: "For God does not give the Spirit to him by measure." Col. 1: "For it pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell." Finally, he so receives all fullness that all others must receive a part of the gifts from him, as from a fountain; as John 1 says, "Of his fullness we have all received." Behold, then, how Christ was anointed with the oil of gladness above all his companions.

units.la: Cæterum, quia illud hîc præcipuè urgetur, quòd Christo tribuatur regnum, & quidem æternum, ideo uisum est quædam alia testimonia de regno Christi ȼterno, adijcere. Primùm Esaiæ 9. Paruulus natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis, &c. mox sequitur: Super solium Dauid, & super regnum eius sedebit, ut confirmet illud & corroboret in iudicio & iustitia à modo & usque in sempiternum. Vbi vides idem uere dici ijsdé uerbis, quod hoc loco habemus ex psalmo, nempe de solio siue throno. Cui respondet illud Lucæ 1. vbi Angelus ad Mariam, Paries filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum. Is e-rit magnus, & filius altissimi vocabitur, & dabit illi Dominus sedé Dauid patris ipsius, regnabitq; super domum Iacob in æternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Hucitem perti-nent illa Esaiæ 11. Egredietur virga de radice Iesse. Non secundum visionem oculorum iudicabit, neque secundum auditum aurium arguet: sed iudicabit in iustitia pauperes. Ibidem: In die illa radix Iesse, qui stat in signum populorum, ipsum gentes deprecabun-tur. Rursus Esaiæ 16 præparabitur in misericordia solium, & sedebit super illud in veri-tate, in tabernaculo Dauid iudicans, & quærens iudicium, & velociter reddens quod iu-stum est. Daniel. 7. Potestas eius potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur, & regnum eius, quod non corrumpetur. Ex his proinde locis regnum Christi æternum esse & spirituale, satis manifeste colligitur. Vide plura de regno Christi in locis nostris communibus.
units.tr: Moreover, since the point stressed here is chiefly that a kingdom is given to Christ, and indeed an eternal one, I have thought fit to add certain other testimonies concerning the eternal kingdom of Christ. First, Isaiah 9: "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us," etc. Then it follows: "Upon the throne of David, and over his kingdom, he shall sit, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and in justice, from now and forever." Here you see that the same things are truly said in the same words as we have here from the psalm, namely of the throne or seat. This is answered by Luke 1, where the angel says to Mary: "You shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He shall be great, and he shall be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." To this also pertain Isaiah 11: "A shoot shall come forth from the stem of Jesse. He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of his ears, but he shall judge the poor in righteousness." And in the same place: "In that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples, the Gentiles shall seek." Again, Isaiah 16: "A throne shall be prepared in mercy, and he shall sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and speedily rendering what is just." Daniel 7: "His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom, which shall not be destroyed." From these passages, therefore, it is sufficiently clearly gathered that the kingdom of Christ is eternal and spiritual. See more about the kingdom of Christ in our Common Places.

units.la: Interea & hoc notandum est, quod admonuit Chrysostomus, diuersos hic errores hæ-reticorum refelli. Primùm enim conuincuntur tum Iudæi, tum Arriani, tum Carpocra-tiani, qui negant Christum esse Deum, cùm hic bis Deus appelletur. Conuincuntur item Marcellus, item Sabellius & Noetiani, cum coniunctis, qui dicebant, Christum non esse distinctam à Deo patre personam, cùm hic describatur Deus filius, à Deo patre vngen-dus: vt distinctæ personæ manifestissimè intelligantur. Præterea conuincuntur hic, qui negant Christi humanitatem. Nam audiuimus hic, Christum ut hominem ungi, & donis ornari à Deo patre, & eundem habere consortes, nempe homines, qui sunt eiusdem cum eo naturæ, si carnem per se consideremus. Nam hic Christum esse Deum, distinctam personam à patre, item Christum esse hominem, luculentissimè exprimitur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, this also is to be noted, which Chrysostom pointed out: that various errors of heretics are refuted here. For first, the Jews are convicted, and the Arians, and the Carpocratians, who deny that Christ is God, since here he is called God twice. Marcellus is likewise convicted, and Sabellius and the Noetians, together with their followers, who said that Christ is not a person distinct from God the Father, since here the Son of God is described as anointed by God the Father, so that distinct persons may be most clearly understood. Moreover, those who deny the humanity of Christ are convicted here. For we have heard here that Christ as man was anointed and adorned with gifts by God the Father, and that he has the same companions, namely men, who are of the same nature as he, if we consider the flesh by itself. For here it is most brilliantly expressed that Christ is God, a person distinct from the Father, and likewise that Christ is man.

units.la: Nec uacat interea hic locus egregijs documentis, quorum decebat vnumquemque hic esse saltem admonitum. Primùm discimus, Christum pro tali, qualis hic describitur, agnoscendum, hoc est, pro nostro Deo, rege, & conseruatore, nec non orare, beneq; per fidem operado eniti, ut inter subditos & cives suos ipse vicissim nos agnoscat, de qui-bus dictum est, Ephes. 2. Iam non estis hospites & incolæ, sed concives sanctorum ac domestici Dei. Extra huius regnum, quæ est ecclesia, non est salus: & ideo edocti sumus à Christo quotidie orare patrem: dicentes: Adueniat regnum tuum: quo nimirum illud peti-mus, vt regnum ipsius apud nos illustretur, ac nos ei inseramur.
units.tr: Nor is this passage without its excellent lessons, of which each of us ought at least to be reminded here. First, we learn that Christ must be acknowledged as He is described here, that is, as our God, king and preserver, and that we should pray and strive by faith to do good works, so that in turn He may acknowledge us among his subjects and citizens. Of these it is said in Ephesians 2: "So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God." Outside this kingdom, which is the Church, there is no salvation. Therefore we have been taught by Christ to pray daily to the Father, saying, "Thy kingdom come," by which we surely seek that his kingdom may be made glorious among us and that we may be grafted into it.

units.la: Secundò, habemus hic doctrinam de administrandis regnis, rebus publicis, seu qui-cunque hominum societatibus, quòd videlicet administranda sint uirga rectitudi-nis, cultu atq; obseruatione iustitiæ, cum honore seu remuneratione bonorum, nec non detestatione vel punitione malorum.
units.tr: Second, we have here the teaching about governing kingdoms, commonwealths, or whatever human societies there are: namely, that they must be governed with the rod of uprightness, with the cultivation and observance of justice, with honour and reward for good men, and with condemnation and punishment of evil men.

units.la: Tertiò, debemus intueri, quàm incomparabilis sit credentium dignitas, quòd consor-tes sint Christi, & fratres, quodq; participes sint donorum Christi. Contra tentationes & pericula desperationis, quasi pharmacum liceat istud opponere: neque enim despe-rare de donis Dei siue extrema beatitudine possunt, qui animaduertunt, se Christi esse consortes, & oleum exultationis propter Christum, & à Christo esse paratum. Ac sunt eius indolis Dei dona, ut quò quis largius ea expendit & insumit ad Dei honorem, eò ipsa in sese magis augeantur.
units.tr: Third, we ought to consider how incomparable is the dignity of believers, in that they are fellow heirs and brothers of Christ and share in the gifts of Christ. Against temptations and the dangers of despair, we may, as it were, set this up as a remedy. For those who perceive that they are companions of Christ, anointed with the oil of exultation through Christ and prepared by Christ, cannot despair of God's gifts or of ultimate blessedness. And God's gifts are of such a nature that the more largely a person spends and uses them for God's honour, the more they increase in him.

units.la: Et tu initio domine terræ fundamenta iecisti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cæ-li: ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes, & omnes ut vestimentum veterascent, acuelut amictum circumuolues eos, & immutabuntur: tu autem idem es, & anni tui non deficient.
units.tr: And you, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all wax old like a garment, and like a mantle you will roll them up, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail.

units.la: Sextum argumentum ad probandam Christi diuinitatem, quo Christus vocatur Domi-nus, & creator totius mundi: quæ sanè appellationes ei soli competunt, qui natura Deus sit.
units.tr: The sixth argument for proving Christ's divinity, by which Christ is called Lord and creator of the whole world: names which surely belong only to one who is God by nature.

units.la: Sumptum est autem ex psalmo 101. in quo non minus, quàm in proximè citato, aliqua de regno Christi habentur uaticinia. Quæ ratio videtur Apostolu mouisse, ut istud argu-mentum sine ullis uerbis interpositis, præcedenti artissimè connecteret. Quanquá ui-dere potest Apostolus respexisse etiá ad illud, quòd, cū superius enumeraret diuersa ossi-cia Christi, dixit, uidelicet per Christū cōdita esse secula, cuius hic habetur clarissima pro-batio, mirè ad Christi diuinitatē omnéq; dignitatē illustrandā accomoda. Sed sunt præ-terea terea plures rationes praesenti testimonio insertae, quae cum ea exprimant, quae sunt diuinitatis propria, accipi possunt singulae, quasi pro singulis argumentis diuinitatem Christi comprobantibus. Nam, ut breuissime expediam, cum dicitur, Tu domine ab initio, declarant ea verba Christum semper extitisse, atq; ante omnem creaturam, acproinde uerum aeternumq; esse Deum: sicut & Ioan. 1. Christi probatur diuinitas atq; aeternitas, cum dicitur, in principio fuisse uerbum, & per illud creata fuisse omnia.
units.tr: The passage is taken from Psalm 101, in which, no less than in the one just cited, there are some prophecies about the kingdom of Christ. This seems to be what moved the Apostle to link this argument so closely to the preceding one, without any words in between. Yet the Apostle may also be seen to have had in mind that, when he listed the various offices of Christ above, he said that the worlds were made through Christ, and here is a very clear proof of this, admirably suited to illustrate Christ's divinity and all his dignity. Moreover, several reasons are inserted in the present testimony, which express what is proper to divinity, and each of them can be taken separately, as if for separate arguments confirming Christ's divinity. For, to explain very briefly: when it says, "Thou, Lord, from the beginning," those words declare that Christ has always existed, and before every creature, and therefore is the true and eternal God, just as John 1 proves the divinity and eternity of Christ when it says that the Word was in the beginning and that all things were made through it.

units.la: Deinde, cum dicitur, terrae fundamenta iecisti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt caeli, sequitur hinc Christum non esse creaturam, sed creatorem: ideoq; & verum Deum.
units.tr: Next, when it says, "Thou hast laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands," it follows that Christ is not a creature but the creator, and therefore the true God.

units.la: Tertio, cum additur, ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes, docetur, Christum, sicut nec initium habuit, ita nec habiturum finem: quare aeternum esse, semperq; existentem, quod & vere diuinum est.
units.tr: Third, when it is added, "They shall perish, but thou remainest," it is taught that Christ, just as he had no beginning, will have no end. Wherefore he is eternal and always existing, which is truly divine.

units.la: Quarto, Illa denique uerba, omnes ut vestimentum veterascent, ac velut amictum circumuolues eos, & mutabuntur, tu autem idem es: clare sonant, Christum incommutabilem, id quod ad solius Dei quoq; naturam pertinet. Postrema particula, & anni tui non deficient, Christo aeternitatem asserit. Haec conueniebat nequaquam praeterire.
units.tr: Fourth, finally, those words, "all of them shall wax old like a garment, and like a mantle thou wilt roll them up, and they shall be changed, but thou art the same," clearly sound that Christ is unchangeable, which pertains to the nature of God alone. The last clause, "and thy years shall not fail," asserts eternity for Christ. It was by no means fitting to pass these over.

units.la: Explicandum nunc est, quod apostolus recte usus sit hoc testimonio, id de persona Christi allegando. Constat in primis, psalmum hunc (ut plurimi & doctissimi quiq; asserunt) continere grauem querelam populi, multis calamitatibus presi & uexati ab aduer sariis, quo tempore e Babylone reuersus conabatur, fauente Cyro & Dario, urbem & templum reparare. Deinde precationem, ut Dominus dignetur afflictorum miserereri, concederet murorum Sion ac Hierusalem templiq; instaurationem. Plenius cognosci potest huius psalmi decantati tempus & occasio ex libris Esdrae & Nehemiae. Dum autem inspersa sunt multa de spe regni foeliciter restaurandi, spiritus Sanctus ita moderatus est linguam, & ita temperauit uerba canentis prophetae (quisquis autor huius psalmi fuerit) ut clarissima pulcherrimaq; reluceant uaticinia de regno Christi, in quibus praesentis argumenti uerba suum habent locum. Proinde omissis omnibus illis, quae ad querelam per pios factam pertinent, quoniam prolixa sunt, & non usque adeo tractatu necessaria, ea tantum subijciemus explicabimusq;, quae de regno Christi accipenda ueniunt: Sic autem habent:
units.tr: It must now be explained why the apostle rightly used this testimony, adducing it concerning the person of Christ. It is agreed first of all that this psalm (as very many and very learned men assert) contains a grave complaint of the people, oppressed and harassed by many calamities at the hands of their adversaries, at the time when, returning from Babylon with the favour of Cyrus and Darius, they tried to rebuild the city and temple. Then comes a prayer that the Lord would deign to have mercy on the afflicted and grant the walls of Zion and Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple. The time and occasion of this psalm, which was sung, can be learned more fully from the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. But since many things about the hope of the kingdom being happily restored are mixed in, the Holy Spirit so governed the tongue and so tempered the words of the singing prophet (whoever the author of this psalm was) that the clearest and most beautiful prophecies about the kingdom of Christ shine forth, and in them the words of the present argument have their place. Therefore, leaving aside all those things which pertain to the complaint made by the pious, since they are lengthy and not so necessary to our discussion, we shall set out and explain only those which concern the kingdom of Christ. They read as follows:

units.la: Tu exurgens misereberis Sion, quoniam tempus, ut miserearis eius, quoniam uenit tempus: quoniam placuerunt serviis tuis lapides eius, & terrae eius miserebuntur. Et timebunt gentes nomen tuum Domine, & omnes reges terrae gloriam tuam. Quia aedificauit Dominus Sion & videbitur in gloria sua. Respexit ad orationem humilium, & non despexit orationem eorum: scribentur haec in generatione nouissima, & populus qui creabitur, laudabit Dominum. Quia prospexit de excelso sancto suo Dominus, de caelo in terram respexit, ut audiret gemitus compeditorum, ut solueret filios interemptorum: ut annuncient in Sion nomen Domini, & laudem eius in Hierusalem. Dum conuenient populi in unum & reges, ut seruiant Domino. Afflixit in itinere virtutem meam, abbreuiauit dies meos: Dicam, Deus meus, ne perimas me in dimidio dierum meorum, in generatione generationum anni tui.
units.tr: Thou shalt arise and have mercy on Zion, for the time to have mercy on her has come, for her stones have pleased thy servants, and they shall have pity on her dust. And the nations shall fear thy name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth thy glory. For the Lord has built up Zion, and he shall be seen in his glory. He has looked upon the prayer of the humble and has not despised their petition. Let these things be written for the last generation, and the people who shall be created shall praise the Lord. For the Lord has looked down from his holy height; from heaven he has looked upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to loose the sons of the slain; that they may declare the name of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem, when the peoples and the kings gather together to serve the Lord. He has weakened my strength on the way; he has shortened my days. I will say, O my God, do not take me away in the midst of my days; thy years endure from generation to generation.

units.la: Iam sequitur:
units.tr: Now there follows:

units.la: Initio tu Domine terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt caeli. Ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes, & omnes sicut vestimentum veterascent, & sicut vestimentum mutabis eos, & mutabuntur: tu autem idem ipse es, & anni tui non deficient. Filij seruorum tuorum habitabunt, & semen eorum in seculum dirigetur.
units.tr: In the beginning, thou, Lord, didst found the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands. They shall perish, but thou remainest; and all of them shall wax old like a garment, and like a vesture thou wilt change them, and they shall be changed; but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail. The sons of thy servants shall dwell, and their seed shall be established for ever.

units.la: Haec quidem ab afflictis, & anxie cupientibus uidere reaedificatam ciuitatem ac templum, nec non restauratam rempublicam & ecclesiam, recte dicuntur: sed tamen de regno Christi & ecclesiae instauratione per euangelium, necesse est omnia insuper intelligamus, cum nonnulla sint eius generis, quae de regno & ecclesia temporali Iudeorum, non recte exponas, nec uera esse deprehendantur, nisi de regno Christi & ecclesia exponas. Quod quo conspectius & manifestius fiat, nos breuiter percurremus.
units.tr: These things are rightly said of the afflicted, who eagerly desired to see the city and temple rebuilt and the commonwealth and Church restored. Nevertheless, we must understand all these things in addition as concerning the kingdom of Christ and the restoration of the Church through the gospel, since some things of this kind cannot be rightly expounded, nor found to be true, unless you expound them of the kingdom of Christ and the Church. That this may become clearer and more manifest, we shall run briefly through them.

units.la: Tu, inquit, exurgens misereberis Sion, quoniam tempus ut miserearis eius, quoniam uenit tempus.
units.tr: "Thou," he says, "shalt arise and have mercy on Zion, for the time to have mercy on her has come, for the time has come."

units.la: Recte quidem de temporali & externa Sion restituenda suo veteri decori. Sed quis non videt hic, clarissime peti misericordiam illam vniuersalem, quae per Christum ftum exhibenda promissa fuerat? Annón istud valde conuenit cum illo, quod habetur Esaiæ 26. de Christo, Emitte agnum Domine, dominatorem terræ de petra deserti ad mortem filię Sion? Et de temporis plenitudine est illud Galat. 4. At ubi venit plenitudo temporis, emisit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere. Quod sequitur, Quoniam placuerunt seruis tuis lapides eius, et terræ eius miserebuntur: de lapidibus & puluere cementoq; collectis ad aedificandum exponunt: interea tamen per seruos rectissimè intelligimus Apostolos operarios Dei & architectos: sicut Apostolus 1. Corinth. 3. Etenim Dei sumus cooperarij, inquit: Et ibidem: Vt sapiens architectus fundamentum posui, alius autem super illud ædificat. Lapides autem sunt pij credentes, quibus aedificium spirituale ciuitatis sanctæ, id est, ecclesiæ Dei, cōstat. 1. Petri 2. Ipsi quoq; ueluti uiui lapides ædificemini, domus spiritualis, &c. Ephes. Estis concives sanctorum ac domestici Dei, superstructi super fundamentum apostolorum ac prophetarum, summo angulari lapide Christo Iesu. En ergo alia & splendidior ædificatio, alij serui, alij lapides, de quibus spiritus Sanctus haud dubie locutus est. Cementum est fides seu charitas, qua inuicem conglutinantur credentes. De uerbo etiam Dei potest intelligi, quo tanquam cibo spirituali recreantur & aluntur homines, vocanturq; ad consortium hæreditatis sanctorum.
units.tr: Rightly indeed, this speaks of the restoration of Zion in its temporal and external form to its old beauty. But who does not see here that that universal mercy is most clearly sought which had been promised to be shown through Christ? Does not this agree very well with what is found in Isaiah 26 concerning Christ: "Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mount of the daughter of Zion"? And concerning the fullness of time there is that passage in Galatians 4: "But when the fullness of time came, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." As for what follows, "for her stones have pleased thy servants, and they shall have pity on her dust," commentators expound it of stones and dust and mortar gathered for building; yet we rightly understand the servants here as the Apostles, the workers and architects of God, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 3: "For we are God's fellow workers," he says; and in the same place: "According to the grace of God given to me, like a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it." The stones, however, are the godly believers, out of whom the spiritual building of the holy city, that is, the Church of God, is constructed (1 Peter 2): "You also, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house," and so on. Ephesians: "You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone." Therefore there is another and more splendid building, with other servants and other stones, of which the Holy Spirit without doubt spoke. The mortar is faith or love, by which believers are bound together. It can also be understood of the Word of God, by which men are refreshed and nourished as with spiritual food, and are called to share in the inheritance of the saints.

units.la: Et timebunt gentes nomen tuum, Domine, & omnes reges terræ gloriam tuam. Quia aedificauit Dominus Sion, & videbitur in gloria sua.
units.tr: And the nations shall fear thy name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth thy glory. Because the Lord hath built up Sion, and he shall be seen in his glory.

units.la: Iistud an uerum sit de tempore reaedificationis Hierusalem, an etiam postea comple-tum de temporali Sion, quòd uidelicet omnes gentes, & omnes reges terræ propter me-tum eius adducti sint ad timendum, uel confitendum Deū, uiderint Iudæi: cū eorū regnū temporale nunquam acceperit eam dignitatem, quā antea habuerat: neq; regibus vllis admodum fuerit formidabile. Quare de regno Christi spirituali proprie debet uerba hæc accipi. Et sane ubi fuit aedificatum regnū Christi, propagato videlicet per apostolos ser-uos Dei euangelio in omnes partes orbis terrarum, & plenissimè iam manifestata glo-ria Dei per ipsum Christum apud omnes homines, uere impletum est, quòd gentes ti-muerint nomen Domini, & omnes reges terræ coeperint gloriam, potentiam, maiesta-te Dei agnoscere ac reuereri. Non opus est citare multa testimonia, quando successus rerum in hunc usq; diem clarissimè id loquitur. Est itaq; manifestissimum, spiritum San-ctum hic loqui de gentium uocatione, quę temporibus Christi adimpleta est.
units.tr: Whether this is true of the time when Jerusalem was rebuilt, or whether it was later fulfilled in the case of the temporal Sion, namely that all nations and all kings of the earth, drawn by fear of him, came to fear or confess God, the Jews may judge. Their temporal kingdom never regained the dignity it had before, nor was it at all formidable to any kings. These words should therefore be understood properly of the spiritual kingdom of Christ. Indeed, where the kingdom of Christ was built, that is, once the gospel had been spread by the apostles, the servants of God, into every part of the world, and the glory of God had been fully manifested through Christ himself among all men, it was truly fulfilled that the nations feared the name of the Lord and that all the kings of the earth began to acknowledge and revere the glory, power and majesty of God. There is no need to cite many testimonies, since the course of events speaks most clearly of this even to the present day. It is therefore most evident that the Holy Spirit here speaks of the calling of the Gentiles, which was accomplished in the times of Christ.

units.la: Respexit ad orationem humilium, & non despexit orationem eorum.
units.tr: He hath regarded the prayer of the humble, and hath not despised their prayer.

units.la: Sancti & humiles patres diu ac multum optarunt tempus aduentus Christi: & tan-dem Deus illorum pijs votis satisfecit.
units.tr: The holy and humble fathers long and earnestly desired the time of the coming of Christ, and at last God granted their pious wishes.

units.la: Scribentur haec in generatione nouissima, & populus, qui creabitur, laudabit Dominum. Quam obsecro dicemus generationem nouissimam, nisi gentes, quæ postremis tempo-ribus genitæ sunt & regeneratæ Christo, & per Christum? Quis populus, qui creabitur, nisi populus gentilis, qui ex non populo factus est populus? Rom. 9. ex Ose. 2. Vocabo populum, qui meus non erat, populum meum. Atq; hic populus recens creatus, recens receptus in populū, iugiter laudat Dominū, dum sancto Christi euangelium confitetur, & cōstater ei adhæret. Sequitur ratio, quare populus nouus tato pere laudabit Dominū.
units.tr: These things shall be written for the generation to come, and the people which shall be created shall praise the Lord. What generation, I ask, shall we call the latest, unless it is the Gentiles, who were born and regenerated in Christ and through Christ in the last times? What people shall be created, unless it is the Gentile people, which was made a people out of not-a-people? Rom. 9 from Hos. 2: I will call that my people which was not my people. This newly created people, newly received into the people of God, continually praises the Lord as it confesses the holy gospel of Christ and cleaves steadfastly to him. There follows the reason why the new people will praise the Lord so greatly.

units.la: Quia prospexit de excelso sancto suo Dominus, de cœlo in terram respexit, vt audi-ret gemitus compeditorum, ut soluerET filios interemptorum: ut annuncient in Sion no-men Domini, & laudem eius in Hierusalem, Dum conuenient populi in vnum, & re-ges, ut ser tant Domino.
units.tr: For he hath looked down from the height of his sanctuary; from heaven did the Lord behold the earth; to hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death; that they may declare the name of the Lord in Sion, and his praise in Jerusalem; when the people are gathered together, and the kings, to serve the Lord.

units.la: Sunt iustissimæ causæ, ob quas laudandus Deus, nimirum quòd tandem misertus fue-rit Iudæorum captiuorum, & voluerit illos reducere in terram Zion, ubi ipsum laudaret & celebrarent. Atqui dum additur, conuenire debere multos populos in vnum, & præ-terea reges etiam diuersos, ad seruiendum Domino: palā fit, quādo id nunquā apud Iu-dæos completum est, ista accipienda iterum de vocatione gentium, & omnia sonare bo-nitatem Dei erga nos propter missum Christum. Nam mitto Christo, vere dici potest, quòd Dominus misertus totius generis humani prospexerit de excelso sancto suo, & de cœlo in terram respexerit. Pater in excelso constitutus misertus est, videns nostram miseriam. Deinde uero ipse filius ille propius respexit, quando è cœlo in terram ad nos descendit. Et quomodo descenderit ipse, latius explicat Ioan. 6. Et Ephes. 4. Qui descen-dit idem ille est, qui ascendit etiam supra omnes cœlos, vt impleret omnia. Illud autem de causa aduentus Christi additum: Vt audiret gemitus compeditorum, ut saluaret filios interemptorum, ut annuncient in Sion nomen Domini, & laudem eius in Hierusalem, nonne aprisime quadrat, quod Zacharias pater Baptistæ de Christo cecinit: Per uiscera misericordiæ Dei nostræ, quibus quibus uisitauit nos oriens ex alto: ut illucesceret his, qui in tenebris & in umbra mortis sedebant, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in uiam pacis. Imo uero totum illud canticum huc pertinet. Nam statim initio canit, Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui uisitauit & fecit redemptionem plebis suæ, &c. Quod uero sequitur, conuenire debere populos in unum, & reges, ut seruiant Domino, simpliciter non potest nisi de gentibus coadunatis in ecclesia Dei intelligi, de qua coadunatione eleganter Ephes. 2. Ipse Christus est pax nostra, qui fecit ex utrisque unum, & interstitium maceriæ diruit, simultatem, per carnem suam, legem mandatorum in decretis sitam abrogans, ut duos conderet in semetipso, in unum nouum hominem, faciens pacem, & ut reconciliaret ambos in uno corpore, Deo, per crucem, perempta inimicitia, per eam, & veniens euangelizauit pacem vobis, qui procul aberratis, & his qui prope. De eadem coadunatione populorum in unum, nempe & Gentilium, & Judæorum, est etiam illud Simeonis: Viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum, quod parasti ante faciem omnium populorum, lumen ad reuelationem gentium, & gloriam plebis tuæ Israel. Sequitur:
units.tr: There are most righteous causes for which God is to be praised: namely, that at last he took pity on the captive Jews and willed to bring them back to the land of Zion, where they might praise and celebrate him. Yet since it is added that many peoples and also various kings are to be gathered together into one to serve the Lord, it is plain that, since this was never fulfilled among the Jews, these words must be understood again of the calling of the Gentiles, and that all of them proclaim the goodness of God towards us on account of the sending of Christ. For, to pass over the sending of Christ, it can truly be said that the Lord, in his mercy towards the whole human race, looked down from his holy height and beheld the earth from heaven. The Father, seated on high, had mercy, seeing our misery. Then indeed the Son himself looked upon us more nearly, when he came down from heaven to earth to us. How he came down is explained more fully in John 6 and Eph. 4: He who descended is the same who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. But that which is added concerning the cause of Christ's coming, that he might hear the groaning of the prisoners, that he might save the children of the slain, that they may declare the name of the Lord in Sion and his praise in Jerusalem, does it not fit most exactly what Zechariah, the father of the Baptist, sang concerning Christ: Through the tender mercy of our God, whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us; to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace? Indeed the whole of that canticle pertains here. For at the very beginning it sings, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who hath visited and wrought redemption for his people, etc. What follows, that the peoples and kings are to be gathered together into one to serve the Lord, can only be understood simply of the Gentiles gathered into the Church of God. Of this gathering into one Eph. 2 speaks elegantly: Christ himself is our peace, who has made both one and has broken down the dividing wall of hostility, abolishing in his flesh the law of commandments contained in ordinances, so that he might create in himself the two into one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, having slain the enmity by it; and coming he preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near. Of the same gathering of peoples into one, both Gentiles and Jews, is also that saying of Simeon: Mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples, a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. There follows:

units.la: Afflixit in itinere virtutem meam, abbreuiauit dies meos. Dicam: Deus meus, ne perimas me in dimidio dierum meorum.
units.tr: He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days. I said: O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days.

units.la: Sunt verba populi consequentis se iam diu grauiter, permittente Deo, & insultantibus hostibus, afflictum, & multis vexatum malis. Sed interea audet adhuc sperare, & Deum orare, ut annuat videre tepus, quo electa ecclesia & sancta respub. melius se sit habitura. Dicam, inquit, Deus meus, ne perimas me in dimidio dierum meorum. Sic magno affectu & ardore loquitur, ut sciens, tempus non procul abesse, quo uenire ille, qui redempturus esset Israel. Hinc vero postquam tam multa dicta sunt de restituendo uero regno Israel, & spirituali, in quo gentes & reges innumeri coadunati, unu Deu colerent, habentur enim ibi non pauca de vocatione getiu, oratione conuertit S. sanctus per os prophetæ, ad illu ipsu uerū Messia, verū rege, instauratore Sion, ab omnibus populis honorandum, tribuens eiomnia, quæ diuinitatis sunt propria, & verum Deum eundem esse significans: atq; ait:
units.tr: These are the words of a people which has long been grievously afflicted, with God permitting it and the enemies insulting it, and which has been troubled by many evils. Yet meanwhile it still dares to hope and to pray to God that he will grant it to see the time when the elect Church and the holy commonwealth will be better off. I said, O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days. It speaks with such great feeling and ardour because it knows that the time is not far off when he who is to redeem Israel will come. Here, indeed, after so much has been said about the restoration of the true kingdom of Israel, a spiritual one, in which countless nations and kings, gathered together, would worship the one God (for there is not a little here about the calling of the Gentiles), the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of the prophet, turns the prayer to that very Messiah, the true king and restorer of Zion, to be honoured by all peoples, attributing to him all that is proper to deity and signifying that he is the same true God. And he says:

units.la: In generatione generationu anni tui. Et tu initio Domine, terra fundamenta iecisti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli: ipsi peribunt, tu aut permanes, & omnes, ut vestimentum ueterascent, ac velut amictum circumuolues eos, & mutabuntur: tu autem idem es, & anni tui non deficient.
units.tr: Thy years are throughout all generations. Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands. They shall perish, but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed; but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail.

units.la: Ergo per Apostrophen hæc uerba ad Christum uerum instauratorem Zion, ac Hierusalem, ecclesiæ, quæ est mater nostra, referri debent, eiusq; diuinitatem clare describunt. Neq; habent Judæi, quod obijciant, hæc simpliciter de Deo, id est, de persona patris accipienda, non de filio. Nam uaticinia illa de regno & ecclesia, in qua coadunaretur omnes populi, & reges, ut seruiant Domino, non possun taccipi nisi de regno spirituali Christi, cum alias non liceat animaduertere, quomodo illa in temporali regno Judæorum sit completa, vel completa, sicut satis fuse demonstrauimus. Liquet ergo testimoniu hoc de Christo recte allegari. Ia singulas partes nostro more explicabimus. Varia sunt hic membra & illustria, diuina natura in Christo probantia, quare no sunt ofcitanter inspicieda.
units.tr: Therefore these words, by apostrophe, must be referred to Christ, the true restorer of Zion and Jerusalem, that is, of the Church, which is our mother, and they clearly describe his divinity. Nor have the Jews anything to object, that these things are to be taken simply of God, that is, of the person of the Father, and not of the Son. For those prophecies about the kingdom and the Church, in which peoples and kings would be gathered together to serve the Lord, cannot be understood except of the spiritual kingdom of Christ, since otherwise it cannot be seen how they were fulfilled in the temporal kingdom of the Jews, or were fulfilled at all, as we have sufficiently shown at length. It is therefore clear that this testimony is rightly alleged concerning Christ. Now we shall explain the individual parts in our manner. The members of this passage are various and illustrious, proving the divine nature in Christ, so they are not to be looked at carelessly.

units.la: Et tu in initio Domine) Quid opus fuisset spiritui sancto, tot verbis hic prædicare æterni tatem Dei, si tantum de persona patris loqui uoluisset? Et quomodo quasi ex abrupto in media oratione ista tam copiose agerentur? Non est igitur dubium, quin magno animi ardore, & per apostrophen, hæc ad personam filij sint dicta, de cuius regno magna pars psalmi concionatur. Et comodisime post regni descriptionem ipse etiam rex describitur. Hinc vero magna emphasis ait: et tu in initio Domine: ut plane hic idem sit, quod de Christo ait Ioannes: In principio erat uerbum. Nam significatur, Christum esse ab æterno, id quod soli Deo proprium est: vnde Dominus apud Mosen se uocat, Qui est, quia nulla temporis ratio in Deo consideran potest, sed æternitas, initio & fine, atq; omni temporis dimensione carens. Hac ratione Christus Ioan. 8. se dicit, antequam Abraham nasceretur, esse. Antequam Abraham esset, ego sum. Sed præterquam quod his uerbis significatur, Christum esse ab æterno, tum additur, in principio conditos per Christū cœlos & terram. Terræ fundamenta iecisti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli: simili forma dictum est Gen. 1. In principio creauit Deus cœlum & terram. Quo loco etiam Christo tribuitur munus creandi cum patre commune: id quod multis argumentis probari solet: ut quod pluraliter dicatur creauit: ité q, per uerbū patris intelligatur filius: ité quod dictū fit, Faciamus hominē ad imaginē nostrā: & quę nō opus est nūc recitari.
units.tr: And thou, Lord, in the beginning. What need would there have been for the Holy Spirit to proclaim here the eternity of God in so many words, if he had wished to speak only of the person of the Father? And how could these things be so copiously set forth, as it were abruptly, in the middle of a prayer? There is therefore no doubt that these words were spoken with great ardour of spirit, and by apostrophe, to the person of the Son, of whose kingdom the greater part of the psalm speaks. And very fittingly, after the description of the kingdom, the king himself is also described. Hence the words and thou, Lord, in the beginning carry great emphasis, so that here it is plainly the same as what John says of Christ: In the beginning was the Word. For it signifies that Christ is from eternity, which belongs to God alone; whence the Lord calls himself, in Moses, "He who is", because no reckoning of time can be considered in God, but only eternity, without beginning or end, and free from every measure of time. On this ground Christ in John 8 says that he was before Abraham was born: Before Abraham was, I am. But apart from the fact that these words signify that Christ is from eternity, it is also added that the heavens and the earth were founded through Christ in the beginning: Thou hast laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands. It is said in a similar form in Gen. 1: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. In that place also to Christ is attributed the office of creating, common with the Father, which is usually proved by many arguments: such as that it is said in the plural, "created"; that by the word of the Father is understood the Son; and that it is said, Let us make man in our image; and other things which need not be recited now.

units.la: Verum hoc loco ad illustrandam Christi potentiam ac dignitatem, splendidiotibus uerbis usus est. Nop simpliciter dicit, Tu creasti cœlum ac terram: Sed adhibitis metaphoris, ære ædificatoria, & ab operibus, quæ manuum ductu artificiose fiunt; ait, Christum iecisse.
units.tr: Yet in this passage, to illustrate the power and dignity of Christ, he uses more splendid words. He does not simply say, You created the heavens and the earth. Instead, using metaphors drawn from building and from works that are skilfully made by the hand, he says that Christ laid the foundations.

units.la: Ecclesia est coetus gentium & Judæorum. iecisse fundamenta terræ, in quibus iaciendis summa architecti sapientia requiritur, quia fundamenta nisi collocata bene sint, stabile non erit reliquum ædificiu. Nó quòd terra fundamentis ullis, aut substratæ materiæ innitatur (nam & philosophi ipsi definiuerunt pendentem esse, nec habere vacuum circumpositum, in quod recidat) sed per se, & in se subsistit: sicut psalmo 103. eleganter dicitur: Qui fundauit terrā super stabilitatem suam. Deinde cœlos tanquam tectum amplissimi ædificij ait Christum suis manibus fabricasse. Vbi ἀνθρωποποιΐα est, dum Christo ut conditori mundi manus tribuitur: quod tamen facit ad significandam artificij diuini excellentiam, & præterea operandi potentiam: sic enim Scriptura, cum potentiam & promptitudinem agendi in Deo uult ostendere, brachium, manus, digitos ei tribuit: Vt, in brachio excelso, & manu potenti: in digito Dei eijcio dæmonia: Luc. 11.
units.tr: The Church is the assembly of Gentiles and Jews. He says that Christ laid the foundations of the earth, and in laying foundations the highest skill of the architect is required, since unless the foundations are well set, the rest of the building will not stand. Not that the earth rests on any foundations or on some underlying matter (for the philosophers themselves have defined it as hanging, with no void around it into which it might fall), but it stands by itself and in itself, as Psalm 103 elegantly says: "Who laid the earth's foundations, that it should not be moved." Then he says that Christ fashioned the heavens with his own hands, as the roof of a very vast building. Here there is an anthropopathy, since hands are attributed to Christ as the Creator of the world. Yet this is done to signify the excellence of divine workmanship and, besides, the power of acting. For Scripture, when it wishes to show the power and readiness of God to act, attributes to him an arm, hands and fingers, as in "with a stretched-out arm and a mighty hand" and "I cast out demons by the finger of God" (Luke 11).

units.la: Sed est etiam elegans partitio, & ad illustrandum amplificandum q; apta, quòd ubi verbo dici potuisset, à Christo conditum vniuersum mudum, maluit dicere, cöditos pe eum cœlos ac terram. Neq; est, cur disputemus, cœli ne an terra prius fuerit condita, ob id, quòd hic ordine alio atq; in genesi, dicitur, primum terram fundatam, deinde formatos cœlos. Homines pro suo captu debent, qua possunt, ratione ea exprimere, quæ tam per se tam sublimia ac tam miranda sunt, ut exprimi certis uerbis nequeant: satis est intelligere, utraque facta à Deo: quo vero ordine, non decet nos scrupulose inquirere.
units.tr: But there is also an elegant division here, and one well suited to illustrate and amplify the matter: where he could have said in a word that the whole world was created by Christ, he preferred to say that the heavens and the earth were created through him. Nor is there any reason for us to dispute whether the heavens or the earth were made first, because here the order is different from Genesis, where the earth is said to have been founded first and then the heavens formed. Men must express, as far as their understanding allows and by whatever reasoning they can, things that are so lofty and so wonderful in themselves that they cannot be expressed in fixed words. It is enough to understand that both were made by God. As to the order in which they were made, we ought not to inquire over-scrupulously.

units.la: Ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes) Perire & permanere longissimo interuallo distant: tantum ergo discriminis est inter Christum & creaturas. Ac vide rursus, quàm prudenter verba prophetæ sint collocata. Voluit exprimere, Deum esse æternum, & absq; fine. Sed illud nō fecit simpliciter dicēdo, Tu es Deus immortalis, finē nō habens: sed quadam collatione illustrius tantundē significauit, q.d. Cœli quidē sunt excellentissimi inter omnia, q; sunt creata, & tñ his multò excellentior est Christus. Nā cœli quidē pereūt, immutantur: at vero Christus permanet in æternum: quare necessariò intelligi debet Deus. Hoc enim soli Deo proprium est, ut per naturam sit immortalis, & finis ac principij expers: unde 1. Tim. 1. Regi seculorum immortali, inuisibili, soli sapienti Deo honor & gloria: Et 1. Tim. 6. Solus princeps, & rex regnantium, & dominus dominantium, qui solus habet immortalitatem, lucem habitans inaccessam. Etsi autem angelos quoq; statuamus esse immortales, at nequaquam per naturam, sed per gratiam. Quicquid enim creatum est & compositum, id necessum est corruptibile esse, & finem habere. Solus autem Deus est increatus, natura simplex, & neque ex materia & forma, neq; ex actu & potentia compositus, ac proinde nec finem habens. Huc pertinet, quod Iudæi Ioan. 12. confitentur: Nos audiuimus ex lege, quòd Christus manet in æternum, & quomodo tu dicis, oportet exaltari filium hominis? Qua quæstione etiamnum hodie sese fatigant Iudæi, quia Christum ad tempus humiliatum, secundum humanam naturam, ut exaltaretur in æternum, secundum utramq; naturam, non possunt intelligere.
units.tr: "They will perish, but you remain." To perish and to remain are separated by the greatest distance; so great, then, is the difference between Christ and the creatures. And notice again how wisely the prophet's words are arranged. He meant to express that God is eternal and without end. But he did not do this by simply saying, "You are the immortal God, having no end," but by a certain comparison he signified the same thing more clearly, as if to say: "The heavens are indeed the most excellent of all created things, and yet Christ is far more excellent than they. For the heavens indeed perish and change, but Christ remains forever; therefore God must necessarily be understood." For this belongs to God alone, that by nature he is immortal and free of beginning and end. Hence 1 Timothy 1: "To the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory." And 1 Timothy 6: "The only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, dwelling in light unapproachable." Although we hold that the angels too are immortal, they are so not by nature but by grace. For whatever is created and composed must necessarily be corruptible and have an end. God alone is uncreated, simple in nature, not composed of matter and form, nor of act and potency, and therefore has no end. To this belongs what the Jews confess in John 12: "We have heard out of the law that Christ abides forever, and how can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up?" Even today the Jews wear themselves out with this same question, because they cannot understand that Christ was humbled for a time according to his human nature, so that he might be exalted forever according to both natures.

units.la: Lex aut de Christo memorat 1. Par. 17. de æterno regno Christi: Statuā eū in domo mea, & in regno meo, usq; in sempiternū, & thronus eius erit firmissimus in perpetuū. Esa. 9. Super solium Dauid & regnū eius sedebit, ut confirmet illud & corroboret in iudicio & iustitia, amodo & usq; in sempiternum. Deniq; omnes loci huc pertinent, qui de regno Christi æterno mentionē faciunt. Christus ipse ait, de uerbis suis nihil posse intercidere: quare multò minus ipse intercidet. Marc. 13. Cœlum & terra præteribūt uerba aut mea nō præteribunt. Ergo quomodo Christus manet in æternum. Qomodo vero cœli pereāt, siue consumātur, paulo post explicabimus. Nec hoc prætereundum est, quòd Græcè legatur, αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, id est, pereunt, præsenti videlicet tempore, ut significetur, eam esse fragilis & momentanei huius mundi conditionem, ut etiam quotidie aliquid dignitati eius decedat: quemadmodum 1. Cor. 7 dicitur: Præterit habitus huius mundi. Cuius rei consideratione uult moueri nos Apostolus ad contemnendum ea, quæ in hoc seculo pulchra & suauiaducuntur, & ad agnoscendam nostram ipsorum miseriam & indignitatem. Sequitur:
units.tr: The law also speaks of Christ's eternal kingdom in 1 Chronicles 17: "I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be most firm for ever." Isaiah 9: "He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it with judgement and righteousness, from henceforth even for ever." In short, all the passages that speak of the eternal kingdom of Christ belong here. Christ himself says that nothing of his words can perish, and so much less can he himself perish: Mark 13, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." Therefore Christ remains forever. How the heavens perish, or are consumed, we will explain shortly. Nor should this be passed over: in the Greek it reads [αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται], that is, "they perish," in the present tense, clearly to signify that such is the condition of this fragile and momentary world, that something of its dignity departs every day, as 1 Corinthians 7 says: "The fashion of this world passes away." It is by considering this that the Apostle wishes to move us to despise the things in this age that are pleasing and attractive, and to recognise our own wretchedness and unworthiness. The text continues:

units.la: Et omnes vt vestimentum veterascent, ac velut amictum circumuolues eos & mutabuntur: tu autem idem es, & anni tui non deficient.
units.tr: And all shall wax old as doth a garment, and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail.

units.la: Alia descriptio dignitatis Christi, diuinitatem eius arguens, nempe quòd neq; tempore quicquam ei decedat, neq; ulla unquam in parte mutetur. Perfistit autem adhuc in collatione, dicens: Cœlum quidem ueterascere & mutari, at Christum nequaquam. Et sunt insertæ elegantes similitudines siue εἰκόνες, id est, imagines, quæ orationem non parum ornant. Ait cœlum veterascere, sicut vestimentum. Constat, vestimentum usu ac tempore atteri. Sic vero innuit, eum tempore cœlum ipsum quasi ad senium accedere, in quo continget eius immutatio. Neq; enim partes aliquæ cœlorum decidunt minulli nuunturúe ex perpetuo illo attritu inter mouendum(quemadmodum Philosophi non- nulli somniarút, dicentes, decidere à cœlo quasi fragmenta,quę sint rerum omniũ hîc in terris quasi semina: ut refert Plinius lib.2. cap.3.) sed significatur immutatio cœli in propinquo esse, & finis, ut ita loquar: sicut vestis quæ attrita est, non amplius usui priori adhibetur,sed immutatur,aut aliis usibus accommodatur.
units.tr: This is another description of the dignity of Christ, proving his divinity: namely, that nothing departs from him with time, and that he is never changed in any part. The comparison continues, saying that the heavens indeed grow old and are changed, but Christ by no means. Elegant similitudes, or eikones (that is, images), are inserted, which adorn the speech not a little. He says the heavens wax old, as a garment does. It is plain that a garment is worn away by use and time. So he implies that with time the heavens themselves approach old age, in which their change will come. For it is not that some parts of the heavens fall off and are diminished by that constant wearing as they move (as some philosophers dreamed, saying that fragments fall from heaven, which are the seeds of all things here on earth, as Pliny reports in book 2, chapter 3). Rather, the change of the heavens is signified as near, and their end, so to speak: just as a garment that is worn out is no longer used for its former purpose, but is changed or adapted to other uses.

units.la: Altera similitudo siue imago est, uelut amictum circumuolues eos, & mutabuntur: quasi dicat: sicut aliquis potest vestem conuoluere seu contrahere & complicare pro suo nutu, atqʒ eam necessum est tùm mutari:ita tu Christe potes pro tuo nutu cœlum mouere,voluere, idq; pro arbitrio tuo protinus mutatur. Tu autem semper manes idem & immutabilis. Qua similitudine non tantùm immutabilitas Christi, sed summa insuper eius potentia in cœlos, & omnes res creatas declaratur. Christus idé habet iius in cœlos, quod aliquis habet in suas vestes, &c. Porrò Deum (ac proinde etiam Christum) esse immutabilem, liquet ex Malach.3. Ego Deus, & non mutor. Et Iacob.1. Omnis donatio bona,& omne donum perfectum,è superni est,descendens à patre luminum,apud quem non est transmutatio,aut conuersionis obumbratio. Cœlum autem immutabitur, non quidem quòd esse desinet aut corrumpetur: sed quòd ab hac specie transfibit ad meliorem, ab hac densitate ad subtilitatem & claritate longè maiorē: substatia non mutabitur cœlum, sed quibusdam qualitatibus: sicut corpora humana suo modo corrumpentur, ut maiorē gloriam ac dignitatem in se recipiant à resurrectione: qua de re est 1. Corinth. 15. & mox plenius de ea nos dicemus.
units.tr: The second similitude or image is: and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed. It is as if he said: just as someone can fold or roll up a garment at his pleasure, and it must then be changed, so you, O Christ, can move the heavens at your pleasure, roll them up, and at your will they are at once changed; but you always remain the same and unchangeable. By this comparison is declared not only the immutability of Christ but also his supreme power over the heavens and all created things. Christ has over the heavens the same power that a man has over his clothes, and so on. Moreover, that God (and therefore also Christ) is unchangeable is clear from Malachi 3: "I am the Lord, and I change not." And James 1: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning." But the heavens will be changed, not in the sense that they will cease to be or be corrupted, but in that they will pass from this form to a better one, from this density to a far greater subtlety and brightness. The heavens will not be changed in substance but in certain qualities, just as human bodies in their own way will be corrupted so that they may receive greater glory and dignity at the resurrection. On this see 1 Corinthians 15, and we shall speak of it more fully soon.

units.la: Notat autem Primasius cœlum vestimento seu amictui recte cōparari. Nam ut vestis vndiq; cingit ac tegit hominem: ita cœlum omni exparte tegit terram: vnde & pelli alio loco comparatur, Psalmo 103. Extendens cœlum sicut pellem. Pellis autem perinde ut vestis quæcunq;, extenditur, contrahitur, conuoluitur.
units.tr: Primasius rightly notes that heaven is fittingly compared to a garment or cloak. As a garment wraps and covers a man on every side, so heaven covers the earth on every side. Hence it is also compared to a skin elsewhere, in Psalm 103: "stretching out the heavens like a skin." A skin, like any garment, is stretched out, drawn together, and rolled up.

units.la: Postrema particula, & anni tui non deficient: æternitate Christi iterum declarat. Tribuuntur autem Deo anni,per ἀιῶνες, hoc est,similitudine quadam,quomodo hominibus tribuuntur. In Deo duratio temporis non spectatur, multò minus ulla temporis distinctio. Nec præteritum nec futurū: sed omnis Dei duratio se habet, ut tempus præsens: quandoquidē semp existet,& semper sui est similis. Vnde Psal.89. dicitur,Quoniā mille anni ante oculos eins,sicut dies hesterna,quæ præterijt. Et Iob.36. Ecce Deus magnus vinces scientiā nostrā, numerus annorum eius inæstimabilis. 2.Petri 3. Vnus dies apud Dominum perinde est,ut mille anni, et mille anni ut dies unus. Ergo improprie attribuuntur Deo anni: sed id facit Scriptura propter hebetudinē intelle&tus nostri, ut ea locutionis forma quodammodo durationem et perpetuā existentiam Dei intelligamus,quo modo multa alia humano more Deo attribuuntur. Habemus proinde in hoc testimonio uarias diuinitatē Christi exprimentes rationes. Nam quòd ab initio siue ab æterno fuerit: quòd cœlos ac terram ipse creauerit: ac proinde creator sit, non creatura: quòdītem semper maneat, nec finē sit habiturus: deniq; quòd nulla ex parte mutabilis: hæc inquā omnia luculentis verbis de eo hic exponuntur,& nos etiam enarrauimus locos Scripturarum diuersos, qui eò pertinebant, citantes, ut nequaquàm opus, plureslocos affines iam in medium producere..
units.tr: The last clause, "and your years shall not fail," again declares the eternity of Christ. Years are ascribed to God through the Greek ages [ἀιῶνες], that is, by a certain likeness, in the way they are ascribed to men. In God the duration of time is not regarded, much less any distinction of times: neither past nor future, but all of God's duration stands as the present, since he always exists and is always like himself. Hence Psalm 89: "For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed." And Job 36: "Behold, God is great, and we cannot know him; the number of his years is unsearchable." 2 Peter 3: "One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Therefore years are improperly attributed to God, but Scripture does this because of the dullness of our understanding, so that by this form of speech we may grasp in some measure the duration and perpetual existence of God, just as many other things are attributed to God in human manner. In this testimony, then, we have various reasons expressing the divinity of Christ. That he was from the beginning, or from eternity; that he himself created heaven and earth, and so is the Creator, not a creature; that he always remains and will have no end; and finally, that he is changeable in no respect: all these things, I say, are set out here concerning him in clear words. We have also explained the diverse passages of Scripture that bear on these points, citing them, so there is no need now to bring forward several related passages.

units.la: Hoc lubet breuiter adnotare, grauissimos errores & plures his paucis uerbis refelli. Conuincuntur inprimis Paulini quidam qui contendebant,Christum non semper fuisse, sed initium sumpsisse ex Maria,cum hic clarè dicatur, Christum fuisse ab initio. Seruetus item hic damnatur,qui persuadere nisus est, λόγον non fuisse personā ante quam humanā naturā induereŧ,non videns hic eum esse, qui initio egens cœlum ac terram condiderit. Deniq; redarguuntur qui Christum putarunt creaturam,et non creatore:sicut Origenistę quidam suspicati sunt. Item qui Christo adimunt, quæ diuinitatis sunt propria, cum hic multa eiusmodi Christo tribuantur. Habemus interea doctrinam etiam valde utilem in hoc testimonio propositam. Primùm cùm cœlum describitur periturum,veterascens,ad monemur nostram quoq; fragilitatem & miseriam agnoscere,& non supra, quàm decet efferri,res huius mundi caducas non multum admirari,aut auidè appetere,ijs quæ parauerimus nō multū fidere. Cùm verò audimus mutationē fore cœlorū,et quidē, ut Scripturā alibi interpretatur, in melius, (nā Rom. 8. dicitur, quòd vanitati creatura subiacet, non volens,sed propter eum,qui subiecit illam in spe :quoniam et ipsa creatura liberabitur seruitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei) consolationem hic accipere debemus,præsertim qui afflígimur in hoc mūdo,non fore æternas istas molestias, sed conuertendas aliquando in gaudiū,sicut & Christus suis promisit Apostolis, Ioan.16. Et cum Christus describatur æternus, sperare debemus, nos quoq; propter illum fore æternitatis participes.
units.tr: It is worth noting briefly that very grave errors, and more than a few, are refuted in these few words. First, certain Paulinists are convicted, who contended that Christ did not always exist but began from Mary, since here it is plainly said that Christ was from the beginning. Servetus is also condemned here, who strove to persuade that the Word [λόγος] was not a person before he put on human nature, not seeing that here it is he who, existing in the beginning, founded heaven and earth. Finally, those are refuted who thought Christ a creature and not the Creator, as certain Origenists suspected. Likewise those who take from Christ what belongs properly to divinity, when many such things are attributed to him here. Meanwhile we have also a very useful teaching set forth in this testimony. First, when heaven is described as perishing and growing old, we are reminded to acknowledge our own frailty and misery, not to admire the fleeting things of this world beyond what is fitting, nor to desire them eagerly, nor to trust too much in what we have acquired. When, however, we hear that heaven will be changed, and indeed, as Scripture elsewhere explains, for the better (for Romans 8 says that the creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it in hope, since the creature itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God), we ought to take comfort here, especially we who are afflicted in this world: these troubles will not be eternal, but will at some time be turned into joy, as Christ also promised his apostles, John 16. And since Christ is described as eternal, we ought to hope that we too, through him, will be partakers of eternity.

units.la: ƒ
units.tr: ƒ

units.la: Quid sentiendum de mundi excidio, seu quomodo intelligendum, quod mundus dicitur perituros.
units.tr: What is to be thought about the destruction of the world, or how it is to be understood that the world is said to perish.

units.la: Quia hic dicitur, quod cœli peribunt: deinde, quod ut vestimentum veterascunt ac mutantur: visum est, ut horum verborum sana & solida habeatur interpretatio, inquirere, utrum revera cœlum periturum sit: &, si non est periturû, sicut quotidie res innumeræ perire cernuntur, quomodo accipiendum, quod mutatur.
units.tr: Because here it is said that the heavens will perish, and then that they grow old like a garment and are changed, it seemed good to inquire, so that a sound and solid interpretation of these words may be had, whether heaven will truly perish; and, if it will not perish, although countless things are seen perishing every day, how that which is changed is to be understood.

units.la: Priorem quæstionem eò existimaui acriori studio tractandam, quod de mundi fine etiam apud philosophos graues conflictationes extiterint, & in sacris literis quædam occurrunt, quæ efficere videntur, ut merito dubitari ea de re possit. Nos igitur breuiter proferemus in medium, tum ex philosophia, tum ex sacris literis, quæ dubitandi causam præbere videntur. Deinde certam sententiam, de tota ea quæstione quid sentiendum sit, explicantem, e sacris literis, quantum fieri dabitur, eruemus: ut habeamus religiosi animi, quid de perplexa quæstione pronuncient.
units.tr: I have thought the former question should be treated with more keen study, because even among the philosophers serious disputes have arisen about the end of the world, and certain passages in the sacred writings seem to make the matter rightly doubtful. So we shall briefly set forth, both from philosophy and from the sacred writings, the things which seem to furnish cause for doubt. Then we shall draw out from the sacred writings, as far as it will be given, a definite opinion explaining what is to be thought about the whole question, so that a devout mind may have something to hold on this perplexing question.

units.la: Plato, & qui eum secuti sunt, mundum quidem dixerunt esse genitum & initium habuisse (credo ita edoctus e sacris libris, quos à Platone lectos, constans opinio est) sed incorruptibilem, immortalem, & nunquam interiturum. Sed hanc sententiam non ferens Aristoteles, idq; hac ratione potissimum permotus, quod, quæcunq; in tempore genita sunt, necessum est, ea cum tempore concidere: quando quidem genitum & corruptibile inuicem sese consequuntur, ut ipse exponit de cœlo & mundo libro 1. cap. 10. & 12. aliter hac de re pronunciauit, dicens, mundum siue cœlum (nam nomine cœli, sicut alias scriptores crebro faciunt, pro tota mundi machina utimur) neq; factum, neq; corrumpendum, sed æternum, principio & fine carens. Habetur hæc assertio de cœlo & mundo lib. 2. cap. 1 cui quamplurimi sese adiunxerunt philosophantium. Unde & Plin. lib. 2. cap. 1. Mundum, inquit, & quod alio nomine cœlum appellari libuit, numen esse credi par est, æternum, immensum, neq; genitum, neq; interiturum unquam. Alij pariter prodiderunt. Argumenta autem producere, quibus sententiam suam nisi sunt confirmare, nostri non est instituti. Hoc satis est breuiter indicasse, quod tàm Platonici, quàm Peripatetici affirmant, cœlum nunquam periturum. Huc etiam facere videtur, quod Ecclesiastæ 1. dicitur, Generatio præterit, & generatio aduenit, terra autem in æternum stat.
units.tr: Plato and those who followed him said indeed that the world was begotten and had a beginning (I believe he was taught this from the sacred books, which, as is the constant opinion, Plato read), but that it is incorruptible, immortal, and will never perish. Aristotle, however, did not accept this view, and was moved chiefly by this reasoning: whatever has been begotten in time must of necessity perish with time, since what is begotten and what is corruptible follow one another. As he himself explains in On the Heavens book 1, chapters 10 and 12, he pronounced otherwise on this matter, saying that the world or heaven (for by the name of heaven, as other writers often do, we mean the whole machine of the world) is neither made nor to be destroyed, but eternal, without beginning or end. This assertion is found in On the Heavens book 2, chapter 1, and very many of the philosophers attached themselves to it. Hence also Pliny, book 2, chapter 1: "The world," he says, "and what it has pleased some to call by another name, heaven, is rightly believed to be a divine power, eternal, immense, neither begotten nor ever to perish." Others likewise have handed this down. But to produce the arguments by which they sought to confirm their opinion is not part of my purpose. It is enough to have briefly indicated that Platonists as much as Peripatetics affirm that heaven will never perish. This also seems to favour that in Ecclesiastes 1 it is said: "One generation passes and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever."

units.la: Sed rursus ex altera parte fuerunt non pauciores, qui cœlum suo tempore periturum contenderent. Democritus namque, teste Aristotele, mundi uti factum, ita interiturum quoq; opinatus est. Similiter Empedocles & Heraclitus Ephesius, & factum, & interitu rum: sed præterea iterum, contra ac Demosthenes senserat, reparandum, imò crebris vicibus mundum ita interire, & denuò procreari.
units.tr: But on the other side there were no fewer who contended that heaven would perish in its time. For Democritus, according to Aristotle, thought the world would perish just as it was made. Similarly Empedocles and Heraclitus of Ephesus held that it was both made and would perish; and moreover, contrary to what Demosthenes had thought, that it would be restored again, indeed that the world perishes and is created anew in repeated cycles.

units.la: Vetustissimi insuper philosophi duplex mundi excidium distinxerunt, atque alterum quidem aquis, quod tùm quidem perfectum, quando memorabilis ναζαπλύσω, seu diluuium totum mundum semel obruit: alterum vero olim igne perficiendum. Quò pertinet magnus ille annus, Platonicus à nonnullis appellatus, cuius hyems exacta est per cataclysmum, æstas vero succedet per ecpyrosin, seu generalem mundi conflagrationem. Quorum duorum excidiorum mundi, etiam certa tempora Berosus ausus est assignare, dicens, cataclysmum debuisse euenire, cùm sydera omnia ad Capricornum conuenerant: ecpyrosin vero futuram, concurrentibus ijsdem ad Cancrum. Atq; vniuersalis conflagrationis expectandæ plurimi Scriptores meminerunt, veluti sententiam hanc de mundi interitu approbantes.
units.tr: Moreover, the most ancient philosophers distinguished a twofold destruction of the world: one by water, which was then complete when the memorable flood once overwhelmed the whole world; the other, they held, was to be accomplished at some time by fire. To this belongs that great year, called by some the Platonic year, whose winter is completed by the cataclysm, but whose summer will follow by the ecpyrosis, or general conflagration of the world. Berosus ventured to assign definite times to these two destructions of the world, saying that the cataclysm had to occur when all the stars had come together at Capricorn, but the ecpyrosis would come when the same stars gathered at Cancer. Very many writers mention that a universal conflagration is to be awaited, thereby approving this opinion about the world's end.

units.la: Nam Cicero lib. 2. de Natura Deorum, ubi de ignis potentia disserit, tum Ouidius lib. Metamorphos. 1. Censorinus item de die natali, &c. Et Origenes contra Celsum lib. 4. & 5. refert, philosophos de mundi conflagratione disseruisse. Videtur autem & Scriptura, hoc iudicium de mundi interitu confirmare. Nam, præterquàm quòd præsenti loco dicitur clarè, quòd cœli peribunt, tum vero Christus Marci 13. idem suo ore asseruit: Cœlum & terra, inquit præteribunt, verba autem mea non præteribunt. 1. Corinth. 7. Qui utuntur mundo hoc, tanquàm non utantur: præterit enim habitus huius mundi. 1. Ioan. 2. Mundus transit, & concupiscentia eius. Quòd verò igne sint peritvri cœli, verba Petri non obscure sonat: sic enim legitur 2. Petri 3. Veniet dies Domini, sicut fur in nocte, quo cœli praecellæ in morem transibunt, elementa verò æstuantia dissoluentur, terraq;, & quæ in ea sunt opera exurentur. Et addit: cùm igitur hæc omnia soluantur, quales oportet esse nos in sanctis conuersationibus ac pietatibus, expectantes, & accelerantes aduentum diei Dei, per quem cœli incensi soluentur, & elementa æstuantia liquescent? Item Psalm. 49. Deus manifestè veniet, Deus noster, & non silebit. Ignis in conspectu eius ardebit, & in circuitu eius tempestas valida. Aduocabit cœlum sursum, & terram, ut iudicet populum suum. En igitur argumenta, quæ luculenter affirmant, mundum periturum, & quidem igne, qui reuera ad perdendum consumendumq; maximè est idoneus.
units.tr: For Cicero, in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, where he discusses the power of fire; then Ovid, Metamorphoses book 1; Censorinus likewise, in On the Birthday, and others. And Origen, Against Celsus books 4 and 5, reports that the philosophers discoursed about the conflagration of the world. Scripture also appears to confirm this judgment about the world's destruction. For, besides the fact that in the present passage it is plainly said that the heavens will perish, Christ himself in Mark 13 asserted the same with his own mouth: "Heaven and earth," he said, "will pass away, but my words will not pass away." 1 Corinthians 7: "Those who use this world, as if they did not use it; for the form of this world passes away." 1 John 2: "The world passes away, and its lust." But that the heavens will perish by fire, Peter's words sound not obscurely; for thus it is read in 2 Peter 3: "The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, on which the heavens will pass away with a rushing noise, and the elements, burning, will be dissolved, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up." And he adds: "Since therefore all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, awaiting and hastening the coming of the day of God, through which the heavens, set on fire, will be dissolved, and the burning elements will melt?" Likewise Psalm 49: "Our God will manifestly come, and will not keep silence. A fire will burn before him, and around him a mighty tempest. He will call the heaven above, and the earth, to judge his people." Here, then, are the arguments which plainly affirm that the world will perish, and indeed by fire, which is truly most suited to destroying and consuming.

units.la: Quando igitur in hunc modum proposita cernuntur argumenta, quæ partim non periturum mudum, partim periturū, videntnr euincere, quid statuendum? Respondere licet, ut paucis verbis, & citra ambages rem expediamus, cœlum quidé dici in scripturis periturum: non quòd simpliciter peribit, uel esse desinet, secundum suam naturam vel substantiam, sed secundum quasdam tantùm qualitates: ut immutatio uel renouatio mundi potius dici debeat, quàm consumptio: quomodo & hoc loco uerba prophetæ sonant, cœlos uelut amictum conuoluendos & mutandos. Clarius autem hæc sententia expressa est ab ipso Petro, qui iubet nos intueri in mundi excidium, quod antecessit per diluuium tempore Noæ, ut discamus, sicut mundus per diluuiū purgatus & immutatus est uerius, quàm consumptus: ita per ignem quoq; immutandum & innouandū uerius quàm perdendū. Sic autem ait secūdæ epistolæ capite tertio de irridentib. expectatione iudicij Domini: Illud volentes nesciunt, quod cœli iam olim fuerint, ac terra ex aqua, & per aquam con sistens Dei sermone, per quæ is, qui tum erat mundus, aqua inundatus perijt. At qui nunc sunt cœli & terra, eiusdem sermone repositi sunt, & seruātur igni in diem iudicij: et perditionis impiorū hominū. mox adijcit Veniet autem dies Domini, sicut fur in nocte, quo cœli procellæ in morem transibunt, elementa uero æstuantia soluentur, terraq; & quæ in ea sunt opera, exurentur.
units.tr: When arguments are put forward in this way, some seeming to prove that the world will not perish and others that it will, what are we to conclude? We may answer briefly and plainly, to settle the matter without circumlocution: the heavens are indeed said in Scripture to perish, not because they will simply perish or cease to exist in their nature or substance, but only with respect to certain qualities. So the change or renewal of the world should rather be called its passing away than its destruction. The words of the prophet also sound this way here, where the heavens are to be rolled up like a garment and changed. Peter expresses this view more clearly. He bids us look at the destruction of the world that went before by the flood in the time of Noah, so that we may learn that just as the world was purged and changed by the flood rather than consumed, so it is to be changed and renewed by fire rather than destroyed. In the third chapter of his second epistle, speaking of the scoffers and the expectation of the Lord's judgment, he says: "They are willingly ignorant of this, that the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and through the water by the word of God; by which the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But the heavens and the earth which are now are by the same word stored up, reserved for fire against the day of judgment and the perdition of ungodly men." He then adds: "But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will melt with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up."

units.la: Vbi quandoquidé dicitur mundum per diluuium periisse, & tamen periisse eum simpliciter nemo dixerit, sed tantùm per aquas purgatum & immutatū: Ita quoq; statuedū mundum non simpliciter periturum, sed tantùm igne purgandum et immutandū. Quòd verò ita iudicandum sit, confirmatur quoq; verbis Christi Matth. 24. ubi Christus in consummatione mundi ait, subitò futurū iudiciū, sicut in diebus Noæ. Sic quoq; sentiendū collegit Augustinus, qui libro 20. de ciuitate Dei, cap. 14. ita loquitur: Mutatione rerum, non omninò interitu transibit hic mundus: Adijciens ibidem illud Apostoli, præterit figura huius mundi, volo uos sine solicitudine esse, sic ratiocinatur: figura præterit, ergo non natura. Rursus eiusdem libri cap. 24. iubet nos respicere ad has phrases scripturæ, quibus mundus præterire dicitur Marci 13, 1. Corinth. 7. Item dicitur transire 1. Ioan. 2. 2. Petri 3. quæ voces (præterire, inquam, & transire) omninò mitius quiddam significant, quàm perire: ut iterum rectè inferri ex illis possit, mundum quidem transire, seu transmutari in aliam speciem: at simpliciter perire intercidereq; nequaquàm. Quin adhuc multò explicatius de hac re disserit eiusdem libri cap. 16. Iudicatis quippe his, qui scripti non sunt in libro uitæ, & in æternum ignem missis (qui ignis cuiusmodi, & in qua mūdi vel rerum parte futurus sit, hominem scire arbitror neminē, nisi forte cui spiritus diuinus ostendit) tunc figura huius mundi, mundanorū ignium conflagratione præteribit, sicut factum est mundanarum aquarum inundatione diluuij. Illa itaq;, ut dixi, conflagratione mundana, elementorum corruptibiliū qualitates, quæ corporibus nostris corruptibilib. congruebant, ardendo penitus interibunt: atq; ipsa substantia eas qualitates habebit, quæ corporibus immortalibus mirabili mutatione conueniant, ut scilicet mundus in melius innouatus aptè accommodetur hominibus, etiam carne in melius innouatis. Haætenus ille.
units.tr: Since it is said that the world perished by the flood, and yet no one has said that it simply perished, but only that it was purged and changed by water, so we must likewise hold that the world is not simply to perish, but only to be purged and changed by fire. That this is the right judgment is also confirmed by the words of Christ in Matthew 24, where Christ, speaking of the end of the world, says that the judgment will come suddenly, as in the days of Noah. Augustine also gathered that this must be understood in this way. In the twentieth book of The City of God, chapter 14, he speaks thus: "This world will pass away by a change of things, not by utter destruction." Adding there the words of the Apostle, "the figure of this world passes away, I want you to be without care," he reasons: the figure passes away, therefore not the nature. Again, in chapter 24 of the same book, he bids us consider those phrases of Scripture by which the world is said to pass away: Mark 13; 1 Corinthians 7; likewise it is said to pass away in 1 John 2 and 2 Peter 3. These words, "to pass away" and "to pass over," mean something far milder than "to perish." So it can rightly be inferred from them that the world indeed passes over, or is transformed into another appearance, but by no means simply perishes or is utterly lost.
