Indeed, he discusses this matter even more fully in chapter 16 of the same book: "When those who are not written in the book of life are judged and sent into eternal fire (what kind of fire this will be, and in what part of the world or of things it will be, I think no man knows, unless perhaps one to whom the divine Spirit shows it), then the figure of this world will pass away by the conflagration of worldly fires, just as the figure of the world was passed by the inundation of the flood. Therefore, in that worldly conflagration, as I said, the qualities of the corruptible elements, which suited our corruptible bodies, will wholly perish by burning; and the substance itself will have those qualities which agree with immortal bodies by a wonderful change, so that the world, renewed for the better, may be suitably adapted to men, who are also renewed for the better in the flesh." Thus far he.

units.la: Vides autem, quomodo qualitates quasdam interituras dicat, non substantiā, et illarū loco meliores præstantioresq; qualitates successuras. Ac tacitè suggerit nobis, ut cogitemus, talem propemodum fore sortem mundi post conflagrationem, qualis erit corporū à resurrectione. Sicut homines erunt etiam carne innouati, ita mudus innouabitur. De hominum autem resuscitatorum conditione & qualitatibus, 1. Corinth. 15. dicitur, quòd eanente angelo mortui resurgent incorruptibiles, & in pun-cto temporis immutabuntur: & quod seminatum fuit in corruptione, resurget in incorruptibilitate: quod seminatum fuit in ignominia, resurget in gloria: quod seminatum fuit in infirmitate, resurget in potentia: quòd fuit corpus animale, resurget spirituale. Hunc igitur in modū & de mundo rectè statuemus, quod per ignem illum, tantum abest, ut dicatur periturus, ut potius dici debeat renouatus, & præstantioribus qualitatibus ornatus.
units.tr: You see how he says that certain qualities will perish, not the substance, and that better and more excellent qualities will take their place. He also hints to us that we should consider the state of the world after the conflagration to be almost the same as the state of bodies after the resurrection. Just as men will be renewed even in the flesh, so the world will be renewed. Concerning the condition and qualities of the raised dead, 1 Corinthians 15 says that at the sounding of the angel the dead will rise incorruptible, and will be changed in a moment of time; and what was sown in corruption will rise in incorruption; what was sown in dishonour will rise in glory; what was sown in weakness will rise in power; what was a natural body will rise a spiritual body. In this way, then, we shall rightly also conclude about the world: that by that fire it is so far from being said to perish that it should rather be said to be renewed and adorned with more excellent qualities.

units.la: Neq; periodis ullis temporis, uel conuersionibus astrorum, cataclysmus uel conflagratio est asscribenda, sicut putarunt philosophi, sed diuinæ uoluntati, tempus & modū ordinanti, quam nemo mortalium potest intelligere: vide Origenem contra Celsum libro quarto.
units.tr: Neither to any periods of time, nor to the revolutions of the stars, is the cataclysm or conflagration to be ascribed, as the philosophers thought; rather it is to be ascribed to the divine will, which orders the time and manner, and which no mortal can understand. See Origen, Against Celsus, book 4.

units.la: Atq; ista mundi immutatio & renouatio in melius, aliis scripturæ locis confirmatur. Nam Petrus iterū 2. epist. suæ cap. 3. postquàm disseruisset de cœlis soluendis, et elementis liquefaciendis per ignem, statim subiecit: sed nouos cœlos ac terram nouam iuxta promissum illius expectamus, in quibus iustitia inhabitat. Esaiæ 65. de eadem in nouatione
units.tr: This change and renewal of the world for the better is confirmed by other passages of Scripture. For Peter again, in the third chapter of his second epistle, after speaking of the heavens being dissolved and the elements melted by fire, immediately adds: "But we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, in which righteousness dwells." Isaiah 65 prophesies of the same renewal:

units.la: {f} s est vaticinium. Ecce enim ego creo cœlos nouos, & terram nouam: et non erunt in memoria. Rursus cap. 66. de aduentu Domini, ac iudicio in igne, tū de cœlis nouis, ac terra noua iterum vaticinatur. Apocalyp. 21. vidi cœlum nouum, & terram nouam. Primum enim cœlum, & prima terra abijt, & mare iam non est.
units.tr: "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and they shall not be remembered." Again, in chapter 66, concerning the coming of the Lord and judgment by fire, he prophesies again of new heavens and a new earth. Revelation 21: "I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and there is no longer any sea."

units.la: De eadem innouatione accipiendum est illud Roman.8. Etenim solicita creaturæ expectatio expectat, ut palàm fiant filij Dei. Quippe vanitati creatura subiacet, non volens, sed propter eum, qui subiecit illam sub spe. Quoniam & ipsa creatura liberabitur a seruitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei. Scimus enim, quòd omnis creatura congemiscit, simulq; nobiscum parturit, usq; ad hoc tempus. Vbi Apostolus per prosopopœiam creaturæ hoc tribuit, quòd valde auidè desideret illud tempus suæ renouationis. Quare satis constare arbitror, & abundè demonstratum ex ipsis Sacræ scripturæ fontibus, quid de mundi fine excidioq; sentiendum sit, idq; quod semel diximus, manifestè ex omnibus colligi: nimirum, cœlum quidem non simpliciter periturum, vel desiturū secundum suam naturam seu substantiam, sed secundum quasdam duntaxat qualitates, ut mutatio ac renouatio potius dicenda sit, quàm consumptio. Iam verò qualis futurus sit ille ignis, & an per omnia elementa vagabitur: præterea, an omnes res creatæ simul innouabuntur: & quales futuræ sint nouæ qualitates noui mundi, scrupulosè vellein quirere, equidem ad pietatem nihil conducere existimo. Id solùm de omnibus his tutò decerni potest, quòd Scripturæ verba sonant. Ignem, quo mundus ardebit, opponit Petrus aquis diluuij: vnde per collationem liceat forte colligere, quòd, sicut aquæ diluuij erant eiusdem speciei cum aqua, quam nos cernimus: ita ignis futurus est eiusdem speciei cum igne, quo nos vtimur. Qua ratione factum videtur, quòd Augustinus dixerit, mundanis ignibus, mundum conflagraturum: in additionibus quæst. 74. ar.
units.tr: To the same renewal must be referred that passage of Romans 8: "For the earnest expectation of the creature waits for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who subjected it in hope, because the creature itself also will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and labours together with us until now." Here the Apostle, by a personification, attributes to the creature that it eagerly desires that time of its renewal. Therefore I think it is sufficiently clear, and abundantly shown from the very sources of Holy Scripture, what should be thought about the end and destruction of the world, and that what we have said once is evident from all of them: namely, that the heavens are not simply to perish or cease to exist according to their nature or substance, but only according to certain qualities, so that it should rather be called change and renewal than consumption. But as for what sort of fire that will be, and whether it will spread through all the elements; further, whether all created things will be renewed together; and what the new qualities of the new world will be, I think it does nothing to advance piety to inquire into these matters with anxious care. Only this can safely be decided about all these things, that the words of Scripture sound. Peter sets the fire by which the world will burn against the waters of the flood. Hence, by comparison, one may perhaps conclude that just as the waters of the flood were of the same kind as the water we see, so the fire to come will be of the same kind as the fire we use. For this reason it seems that Augustine said that the world will be consumed by worldly fires, in the Additions to Question 74, article ...

units.la: Quod ad elementa attinet, Petrus enumerat cœlos ac terram: tum generaliter effert, elementa soluentur: quid igitur opus est inquirere, quot, vel quæ elementa debeant igne illo purgari? In Apocalypsi etiam mare exprimitur: quidni ergo de omnibus elementis & partibus mundi visibilis verba Petri accipiantur? Quales autem futuræ sint mundi nouæ qualitates per conflagrationem illam, non puto commodius explicari posse, quà illo, quod habetur Roman.8 quòd creatura liberabitur a seruitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei. Exquo equidem puto non absurdè statui posse, quòd, sicut terra, & cum hac vniuersus visibilis hic mundus, propter lapsū & peccatū primi hominis multum de dignitate prima & splendore amisit (sicut Genes. 3. dicitur, propter peccatū hominis maledictā) quem prima sua conditione habuit: ita restituto homine, post resurrectionem primæ suæ dignitati, terra quoq; pristinam suam dignitatem recuperabit. Sicut homo tunc à corruptibilitate liberabitur, & accipiet gloriam, quæ est à Deo parata filijs eius: ita omnis quoq; creatura ab imperfectione corruptibilitatis liberabitur, & nouam gloriā cum pijs hominib. accipiet. Erunt homines tūc sicut angeli Dei, ut Christus ait. Sic & mundus dici posset futurus, quasi Dei paradisus, siue talis, qualis ante lapsum fuit primi hominis. Esa.30. Erit lux Lunæ, sicut Lux solis. Apocal.21.
units.tr: As for the elements, Peter lists the heavens and the earth, and then speaks generally of the elements being dissolved. What need is there, then, to inquire how many, or which, elements must be purged by that fire? In Revelation the sea is also named. Why, then, should Peter's words not be taken to apply to all the elements and parts of the visible world? As for what the new qualities of the world will be after that conflagration, I do not think it can be explained more fittingly than by that passage in Romans 8, that the creature will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. From this I think it may not absurdly be held that just as the earth, and with it the whole visible world, lost much of its first dignity and splendour through the fall and sin of the first man (as Genesis 3 says, the ground was cursed because of man's sin), so, when man is restored after the resurrection to his first dignity, the earth too will recover its former dignity. Just as man will then be freed from corruptibility and will receive the glory that God has prepared for his children, so every creature too will be freed from the imperfection of corruptibility and will receive a new glory together with the godly. Men will then be like the angels of God, as Christ says. So the world too could be said to become like the paradise of God, or such as it was before the fall of the first man. Isaiah 30: "The light of the moon will be as the light of the sun." Revelation 21.

units.la: Vtrùm verò omnes creaturæ restaurabuntur & renouabuntur, veluti animantia, plantæ, &c. curiosè magis quàm vtiliter quæritur: & cum Scriptura hac de re nusquam expresse loquatur: neq; etiam horum usus futurus sit hominibus, in quorum gratiam omnia eiusmodi sunt codita, quid nos cōfidamus rectè expressuros? Quare satis multa puto à nobis hic dicta.
units.tr: Whether all creatures will be restored and renewed, such as animals, plants, and so on, is a question asked more out of curiosity than for any benefit. Scripture nowhere speaks of this expressly, and it is not clear that such creatures will be of any use to men, for whose sake all of them were created. What confidence could we have of saying anything correct about it? I think enough has been said here on the subject.

units.la: Erit autem hic usus huius disputationis, primùm publicè in ecclesia, ut citra molestiā intelligantur ij Scripturæ loci, qui quasi variè loquerentur de fine mundi, vel de nouis cœlis, & noua terra, scrupos & perplexitatem pariunt.
units.tr: This discussion will be useful, first, publicly in the church, so that those passages of Scripture which seem to speak variously about the end of the world, or about new heavens and a new earth, can be understood without trouble and do not cause doubts and perplexity.

units.la: Præterea confutare ex hac disputatione absurdas philosophastrorum, & quorundam hæreticorum de fine mūdi, deq; nouis seu pluribus mundis, opiniones: qua de re apud Augustinum nonnulla inueniuntur. Deniq; proderit & priuatim conscientijs hæc cognitio quòd ex hac mundi renouatione, & in melius restitutione, vnusquisq; in conscientia consolationem aliquam accipiet, nec non spem de renouatione, & reparatione etiam sui corporis, secundum quam ad Dei gloriā æterna et incorrupta corpora coseruabūtur. Atq; illud Rom.8. Solicita creaturæ expectatio expectat, ut palàm fiant filij Dei, quippe vanitati creatura subiacet, non volens, sed propter eum, qui subiecit illam sub spe, si crebrò in animum reuocetur, possit incitare ad expetendum illud renouationis tepus, & ad superandas mundi huius carnisq; molestias.
units.tr: Besides, from this discussion one can refute the absurd opinions of certain philosophasters and of some heretics about the end of the world and about new or additional worlds, a matter on which some things are found in Augustine. Finally, this knowledge will also benefit individual consciences, since from this renewal of the world and its restoration to something better, each person will receive some consolation in conscience, and also hope for the renewal and restoration of their own body, according to which eternal and incorruptible bodies will be preserved to the glory of God. And the words of Romans 8, "The anxious expectation of the creature waits for the sons of God to be revealed, for the creature was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope," if often called to mind, may stir us to long for that time of renewal and to overcome the troubles of this world and of the flesh.

units.la: Ad quem autem Angelorū dixit unquam: sede à dextris meis, donec posuero inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum?
units.tr: To which of the angels did he ever say: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet?

units.la: Septimum argumentum, quo probatur Christi præ angelis excellentia, pariterq; eius diuinitas,
units.tr: The seventh argument, by which the excellence of Christ above the angels, and likewise his divinity, is proved.

units.la: Prosopopœia. diuinitas.Quòd angelis quidem excellentior sit, sic enunciat: Christo dictum est id,quod summæ dignitatis est,videlicet:Sede à dextris meis. Sed hoc nulli unquàm dictum est Angelorum. Ergo Christus est angelis excellentior.
units.tr: Prosopopoeia. Divinity. That he is more excellent than the angels he states thus: to Christ has been said what belongs to the highest dignity, namely, "Sit at my right hand." But this was never said of any of the angels. Therefore Christ is more excellent than the angels.

units.la: Ita perstat in collatione Christi cum Angelis, quâ initio cofirmationis instituit. Quòd autem Christus sit Deus, in hunc modum declarat:sedere ad dexteram non est, nisi superioris aut saltè paris. Atqui Christo dicit Pater, ut sedeat ad ipsius dexterâ. Ergo Christus est Deo patri, etsi non superior, at saltem par.
units.tr: He persists in this way in the comparison of Christ with the angels, which he set up at the beginning of the confirmation. That Christ is God, he shows in this manner: to sit at the right hand belongs to no one but a superior, or at least an equal. But the Father says to Christ that he should sit at his right hand. Therefore Christ is equal to God the Father, if not superior, at least equal.

units.la: Sumptus est autem locus hic ex Psalmo 109. atq; accipi potest etiam pro probatione eius,quod inter alia de dignitatibus Christi ante confirmationem dixit Apostolus,nepe, Christū consedisse in dextera maiestatis in excelsis. Videturq; eam ob causam postremo loco argumentum istud positum, quòd Christi dignitatem maximè exornet: quando-quidem selectis verbis constat,& ad exprimendam amplissimam maiestatem ac gloriâ valdeidoneis. Ecquid enim splendidius vel honorificentius dici queat, quàm Christum ad dexteram Dei sedere?
units.tr: This passage is taken from Psalm 110, and it can also be taken as proof of what the Apostle said among other things about the dignities of Christ before the confirmation, namely, that Christ sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. And it seems that for this reason this argument was placed last, because it especially adorns the dignity of Christ, since it is clear from the chosen words that they are very well suited to express his most ample majesty and glory. For what could be said more splendid or more honorable than that Christ sits at the right hand of God?

units.la: Neq; verò possùt Iudæi, vel quicûq; aduersarij negare, eum Psalmû proprie & simpliciter de Christo loqui: quod equidem duabus potissimum rationibus manifestum redditur.
units.tr: Nor can the Jews, or any adversaries whatever, deny that the Psalm speaks properly and simply of Christ. This is made clear chiefly for two reasons.

units.la: Prior est, quòd cum Christus Matthæi 22. his ipsis verbis usus esset ad confirmandum, se esse ut filium Dauid, ita verum Deum: nemo potuit respondere, aut docere de alio, quàm de Christo eum Psalmum esse scriptum.
units.tr: The first is that when Christ, in Matthew 22, used these very words to confirm that he is the Son of David and also the true God, no one could reply or teach that the Psalm was written about anyone other than Christ.

units.la: Nec dubium,quin ad id tempus communis fuerint omnium Iudæorum opinio, ipsi etiam vulgo decantata,de regno Christi contineri hoc toto psalmo vaticinia.
units.tr: And there is no doubt that up to that time it was the common opinion of all the Jews, also sung abroad among the people, that the prophecies of Christ's kingdom are contained in this whole Psalm.

units.la: Altera ratio,quòd Actorum 2. Petrus ostendit,non de Dauide hæc verba esse accipienda, sed hunc Dominum sedêre iussum ad dexteram, esse ipsum Christum crucifixum.
units.tr: The second reason is that in Acts 2 Peter shows that these words are not to be understood of David, but that the Lord who was bidden to sit at the right hand is Christ himself, who was crucified.

units.la: Tertia ratio est, quòd occurant nonnulla in hoc Psalmo, quæ de Dauide interpretari nullo modo queas: nam,ut omittam hanc particulam, de sedendo addextram Dei,sanè illud ad personam Dauidis nemo rectè accommodarit, quod paulò post dicitur, Tu es sacerdos in æternum,secundum ordinem Melchisedeck: Quomodo obsecro Dauidi ista conferas, qui (sicut nec alij reges) sacerdotij munere nõ est funãtus,nec fungi potuit. Nâ 2. paralip.26. Ozias ausus temerariè adolêre incensum, grauiter reprehensus à sacerdotib. & à Deo percu ssus est lepra. Quomodo itê Dauid dicetur sacerdos secûdû ordinê Melchisedeck, cûm eo tempore solus ordo Aaronicus fuerit agnitus, ut eodê libro paralipom. cap. 26. clarè significatur? Quomodo deniq; Dauid sacerdos in æternum? At verò quòd Christo conueniat illud sacerdotium æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedeck, copiose nec minus luculenter demõstratur huius Epistolę capite septimo. Quare etiamsi rumpantur aduersarij,de Christo proprie hic Psalmus intelligetur. Sed quò de tota causa expeditius certiusq; iudicare unusquisq; possit,nos Psalmum ipsum, quoniam non adeò prolixus est, breuiter, quatenus proprie de Christo, aut etiam de Dauide ut typo loquatur, explicabimus.
units.tr: The third reason is that there are some things in this Psalm which you could in no way interpret of David. For, to pass over this phrase about sitting at the right hand of God, surely no one could rightly apply to the person of David what is said shortly afterwards: "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." How, I ask you, could you compare these things with David, who (like the other kings) was not invested with the office of priest and could not exercise it? For in 2 Chronicles 26, Uzziah, who presumptuously dared to burn incense, was severely rebuked by the priests and struck with leprosy by God. How, moreover, could David be called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, when at that time only the Aaronic order was recognized, as is clearly stated in the same book of Chronicles, chapter 26? And finally, how could David be a priest forever? But that the eternal priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek belongs to Christ is demonstrated at length and no less clearly in chapter seven of this Epistle. Therefore, even if the adversaries burst, this Psalm will be understood properly of Christ. But so that each person may judge the whole matter more quickly and more surely, we shall briefly explain the Psalm itself, since it is not very long, as far as it speaks properly of Christ, or also of David as a type.

units.la: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, sede à dextris meis: donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum:
units.tr: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.

units.la: Quæ verba de Christo ita sunt accipienda, ut sit sententia, Dominum Deum patrem, dedisse Domino Deo filio communem & parem per omnia secum potestate, ius regnâdi super omnia, ut ab omnibus pro Deo & Domino agnoscatur & colatur. Tantundem enim significatur ea phrasi, Sede à dextris meis. In hanc sententiam Christus ait in euãgelio, datam sibi à Deo patre omnē potestatem in cœlo & in terra. Additur, quod ad confirmationem regni Christi faciet, debere subijci omnes ipsius inimicos, non aliter, quàm Scabellum supponitur alicuius pedibus. Nam hæc quoque locutionis forma habet metaphoram.
units.tr: These words are to be understood of Christ in such a way that the meaning is this: the Lord God the Father has given to the Lord God the Son a power common to him and equal in all things with himself, a right to reign over all things, so that he may be acknowledged and worshipped by all as God and Lord. For the phrase Sit at my right hand signifies just this much. To this effect Christ says in the Gospel that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him by God the Father. It is added, which serves to confirm the kingdom of Christ, that all his enemies must be made subject, just as a footstool is placed under someone's feet. For this form of expression also contains a metaphor.

units.la: Idem autem de subijciendis inimicis Christi, peccato, lege, diabolo, & morte, cum omnibus istorum subditis, passim in euangelio & apostolicis scriptis declaratur. Sic enim Christus à resurrectione sua, Ioannis decimosexto, confidite,ego vici mundum. Colossens. secundo, Expoliatus principatus ac potestates ostentauit,palàm triumphàs deillis per semetipsum.Clarius loquitur prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto. Mox finis cûm tradiderit regnum Deo & patri,cûm aboleuerit omnem principatum, & omnem potestatem ac virtutem. Nam oportet eum regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. Nouissimus hõstis aboletur mors. Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes illius. In hunc verò modum explicanda esse hæc de regno ac dignitate Christi, qui in cœlos ascendit, & ibi obtinet parem cum Deo Patre gloriam, liquet ex verbis Petri Actorum 2. Non enim Dauid ascendit in cœlos, inquit, sed dicit ipse: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, sede à dextris mihi, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Vbi addit: certò sciat tota domus Israel, quòd Dominum & Christum fecerit Deus hunc Iesum, quem vos crucifixistis. Rursus liquet idem ex interpretatione ipsius Christi Matthaei 22. qui diserte ait, ipsum Dauidem cecinisse hunc Psalmum de Christo. Quamuis ibi aliud argumentum colligit Christus, quàm quod hoc loco habetur, nimirum ex eo, quòd Dauid vocarit Christum Dominum, sequi quòd Christus sit Deus: ita ut his paucis verbis duplex insit argumentum, quo probari queat, Christum esse Deum: alterum, quòd Christus vocatur Dominus: alterum, quòd sedeat ad dexteram Dei: id quod antea semel admonuimus. Iam de Dauide ut typo explicari ista sic possunt: Dominus Deus constituit atq; ordinavit Dauidem ad summam dignitatem euehere, ac planè talem, qualis nulli regum contigit. Praeterea vero omnes hostes circumpositos, ut Ammonitas, Moabitas, & reliquos ab ipso superandos. Sed quàm conueniat Dauidi, sedere ad dexteram Dei, valde est obscurum. Quomodo vero ob hanc causam Iudaei aliter conati sint haec de Dauide reddere, dicam paulò post.
units.tr: That the same is said of the subjection of Christ's enemies, sin, the law, the devil, and death, together with all their subjects, is declared throughout the Gospel and the apostolic writings. Thus Christ, from his resurrection, says in John 16, "Take heart, I have overcome the world." In Colossians 2, "Having disarmed the principalities and powers, he made a public show of them, triumphing over them by himself." It speaks more clearly in 1 Corinthians 15: "Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death. For he put all things under his feet." That these things are to be explained in this way, concerning the kingdom and dignity of Christ, who ascended into the heavens and there holds glory equal with God the Father, is clear from the words of Peter in Acts 2: "For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." Where he adds: "Let all the house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ." Again, the same is clear from Christ's own interpretation in Matthew 22, where he plainly says that David himself sang this Psalm about Christ. Although there Christ draws a different argument from the one given in this passage, namely, from the fact that David calls Christ Lord, it follows that Christ is God, so that in these few words there is a twofold argument by which it can be proved that Christ is God: the one, that Christ is called Lord; the other, that he sits at the right hand of God, which we have already noted once before. Now, concerning David as a type, these things can be explained thus: the Lord God established and ordained David to be raised to the highest dignity, and in a manner altogether such as no king had attained. Moreover, he would subdue all the enemies round about, such as the Ammonites, the Moabites, and the rest. But how it befits David to sit at the right hand of God is very obscure. How the Jews have tried in other ways, for this reason, to refer these things to David, I shall say a little later.

units.la: Virgam virtutis tuae emittet Dominus ex Zion, dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum.
units.tr: The Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength out of Zion: rule in the midst of your enemies.

units.la: Describit & locum, unde Christus regni sui potentiam exerere inciperet, nimirum è Sion: qua de re plurima extat vaticinia, quae ipse rei euentus docuit omnia esse adimpleta. Nam Psalmo secundo in persona Christi dicitur: Ego autem constitutus sum rex super Zion montem sanctum eius. Esaiae 2. De Zion exibit lex, et verbum Domini de Hierusalem, & iudicabit gentes, & arguet populos multos. Ioelis 3. Dominus de Zion rugiet, & de Hierusalem dabit vocem suam. Atq; ibi coepit dominari in medio inimicorum, quando, inuitis & reluctantibus omnibus impiis, euangelium ita coeptum est illustrari & propagari, ut nullis consilijs, nullis minis aut terroribus potuerint Apostoli & credentes impediri: id quod plenissimè testantur acta apostolica, atq; vniuersi deinde euangelicae doctrinae, quae est virga regni Christi, successus in ecclesia, aduersus quam, nec portae inferorum possunt praevalere. Sed de Dauide, ut typo Christi, haec quoq; dici recte possunt. Nam is in Sion arcem habuit, & in medio hostium prosperis successibus diu usus est, multis & potentibus hostibus fortiter debellatis & repressis, quod ex libris Regum licet plenius colligere.
units.tr: He also describes the place from which Christ would begin to exercise the power of his kingdom, namely Zion. There are many prophecies on this matter, and the outcome itself has shown that all of them were fulfilled. In Psalm 2 it is said in the person of Christ: "But I have been set as king over Zion, my holy mountain." Isaiah 2: "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples." Joel 3: "The Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he shall give forth his voice." And there he began to rule in the midst of his enemies, when, though all the impious resisted and struggled against it, the gospel began to be so illuminated and propagated that neither counsels, nor threats, nor terrors could hinder the apostles and believers. The Acts of the Apostles bears full witness to this, and so does the whole later success of evangelical doctrine in the Church, which is the rod of Christ's kingdom, against which "the gates of hell shall not prevail." But these things can also rightly be said of David as a type of Christ. For he had a stronghold in Zion, and for a long time used prosperous successes in the midst of his enemies, many powerful foes having been bravely overcome and checked, as one may gather more fully from the books of Kings.

units.la: Tecum principium in die virtutis tuae in splendoribus sanctorum, ex utero ante luciferum genui te.
units.tr: Your people shall be a willing people in the day of your power, in the splendours of the saints; from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you.

units.la: Alij reddunt, tecum principatus: Alij, populus tuus aderit voluntarius: quae versio propius accedit ad hebraicam veritatem. Et rursus, ubi habemus, ex vtero ante luciferum genui te: aliqui reddunt: ut ros matutinus aderit ab vtero iuuentus tua. Quomodocunq; accipiamus, postquam propheta cecinit de loco, unde regni Christi ducenda forent principia, iam addit, quomodo id perficeretur: est q; sententia: tu, ô Christe, cum propagandum erit tuum regnum, habebis populum voluntarium & promptum, nempe Apostolos, velut duces negotij, & eos qui euangelium statim ampletentur, vti in Actis cap. 2. legimus, primo die statim accesisse circiter ter mille homines. deinde cap. 4. factus est numerus virorum circiter quinq; millia. Atq; hi quidem omnes tam voluntarij, tamq; prompti fuerunt, ut nulla pericula subire pro dignitate regis Christi tueda detrectarint. Omnes quoq; in splendoribus Sanctorum, quia sanctimonia conspicui, non inhiantes sanguini aut praedae, sicut caeterorum principum duces aut milites solent.
units.tr: Others render it: "With you is the principality"; others: "Your people shall be willing." This version comes closer to the Hebrew truth. And again, where we have "from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you," some render it: "Like the morning dew, your youth shall come forth from the womb." However we take it, after the prophet has sung of the place from which the beginnings of Christ's kingdom were to be drawn, he now adds how this would be accomplished. The sense is this: "You, O Christ, when your kingdom is to be spread abroad, shall have a willing and ready people, namely the apostles, as leaders of the enterprise, and those who would at once embrace the gospel." As we read in Acts 2, on the first day about three thousand men were added at once; then in chapter 4 the number of men came to about five thousand. All these were so willing and so ready that they shrank from no dangers in undertaking the defence of the dignity of the King Christ. All were also "in the splendours of the saints," because they were conspicuous for holiness, not longing for blood or plunder, as the leaders or soldiers of other princes are wont to do.

units.la: Praeterea Christo illud conuenit, ut ros matutinus aderit ab utero iuuentus tua: nam quos ipse sibi parat & acquirit credentes, qui in ipso renascuntur per baptismum, ij vberum, densim, & magno numero exoriuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, this also belongs to Christ: "Like the morning dew your youth shall come forth." For the believers whom he prepares and wins for himself, who are born again in him through baptism, arise abundantly, thickly, and in great number.

units.la: Similitudo est, quòd, quemadmodum res mirabiliter & dese prouenit: ita credentium mirabiliter nascetur & augebitur numerus. Dauidi autem istud tribuì potest, quia videlicet habuit delectum militem, & regnum suum magno successu auxit illustrauitq; : sed tamen quam voluntarium populum, cum multos habuerit per omne tempus aduersarios, etiam domesticos: deinde quam conspicuum sanctimonia (nisi dicamus sanctu, propterea quod in loco sancto & ciuitate sancta habitarent) difficile est iudicatu. Sequitur:
units.tr: The comparison is that, just as the dew comes forth wonderfully and abundantly, so the number of believers will be born and increased wonderfully. This can indeed be attributed to David, since he had a chosen soldiery and enlarged and illustrated his kingdom with great success. Yet how willing a people he had, since throughout the whole time he had many adversaries, even domestic ones, and how conspicuous they were for holiness (unless we say "holy" because they dwelt in a holy place and a holy city), is hard to judge. The text continues:

units.la: Iurauit Dominus, & non poenitebit eum, Tu es sacerdos in aeternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedeck.
units.tr: The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: "You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek."

units.la: Haec verba sic Christo conueniunt, ut nulli alteri personae accommodari recte queant. ant. Significant enim, Christum, uti rex est, ita verum quoque esse sacerdotem: quia ipse solus habuit ius placandi Deum patrem, & offerendi, quo pro peccatis humani generis satisfieret, quod & ipse praestitit, quando seipsum in ara crucis obtulit. Sunt autem singulae particulae magno pondere expressae. Primùm dicitur, Christum institutum esse sacerdotem, ab ipso Deo, non à Mose, vel villis hominibus. Deinde confirmatum sacerdotium eius iuramento Dei, quod humanis viribus imminui aut obscurari nullo modo potest. Adhaec Christum esse sacerdotem in aeternum, quò intelligatur, nec regnum, nec sacerdotium eius esse temporale. Deniq; sacerdotium illud esse secundū ordinem Melchisedeck, nempe novum, ac diversum ab ordine Aaronico: quia etiam lex cum suo sacerdotio Aaronico abrogari, et euangelii novumq; testamentum cum aeterno sacerdotio Christi, succedere debuit. Qua de re copiosius huius Epistolae capite septimo. Quomodo autem Davidi ista attribui possint, non video, etiam si quidam torquere ad eum verba haec moliantur.
units.tr: These words fit Christ so exactly that they can rightly be applied to no other person. For they signify that Christ, as he is king, so is he also a true priest, because he alone had the right to appease God the Father and to offer that by which satisfaction would be made for the sins of the human race; and he himself accomplished this when he offered himself on the altar of the cross. Each part is expressed with great weight. First, it is said that Christ was appointed priest by God himself, not by Moses or by any men. Next, his priesthood is confirmed by the oath of God, which can in no way be diminished or obscured by human powers. Further, that Christ is a priest for ever, so that it may be understood that neither his kingdom nor his priesthood is temporal. Lastly, that this priesthood is according to the order of Melchizedek, namely new and different from the Aaronic order, since the law with its Aaronic priesthood had to be abrogated, and the gospel and the new covenant had to succeed with the eternal priesthood of Christ. On this matter more fully in chapter 7 of this Epistle. But how these things can be attributed to David I do not see, even though some attempt to twist these words to refer to him.

units.la: Dominus à dextris tuis confringet in die irae suae reges: Iudicabit in nationibus, implebit ruinas, conquassabit capita in terra multorum.
units.tr: The Lord at your right hand shall crush kings in the day of his wrath; he shall judge among the nations, fill them with ruins, and shatter the heads over the wide earth.

units.la: Describit potentiam regni Christi, quòd videlicet id praevalebit adversus omnes reges terrae, quòd omnes nationes praesertim gentium illi se submittent, & capita omnium impiarum sectarum, ubicunq; gentium fuerint, atteret conculcabitq; . Quanquàm vaticinari propheta videtur etiam de extremo ac generali iudicio per Christum exercedo. Davidi si tribuamus, poterit id fieri propter insignes victorias diversas, praecipuè autem propter illam contra Ammonitas, quorum etiam regem debellavit, ut 2. Regum 12. legitur, item Adadezer regem Soba, 2. Regum 8. Sed tamen hic nondum Reges plures confracti sunt, sicut de Christo dici potest.
units.tr: It describes the power of Christ's kingdom: that it will prevail against all the kings of the earth, that all nations, especially the Gentiles, will submit to him, and that he will crush and trample the heads of all the impious sects, wherever they are among the nations. Although the prophet seems also to prophesy of the final and general judgment to be exercised through Christ, if we attribute it to David it can be fulfilled by his remarkable and varied victories, especially that against the Ammonites, whose king he also defeated, as is read in 2 Samuel 12, likewise Hadadezer king of Zobah, 2 Samuel 8. Yet here not yet several kings were broken, as can be said of Christ.

units.la: De torrente in via bibet, propterea exaltabit caput.
units.tr: He shall drink of the brook in the way; therefore shall he lift up the head.

units.la: Extrema clausula est, qua summa regis Christi potentia exprimitur. Post stragem hostium factam, & quidem tantam, ut aquae etiam tingendae sint sanguine, ille tùm bibet de torrente infecto sanguine, accipiet signum superatorum & caesorum hostium, ac propterea erit gloriosus & sublimis in aeternum. Sic enim de torrente bibere, esse idem, quod in signum victoriae bibere sanguinem effusum in torrente, quidam exponunt, respicientes ad illud, quod Numer. 23. Balaam dixit de Israelitis: Ecce populus ut leena consurget, & quasi Leo erigetur. Non accubabit, donec devoret praedam & occisorum sanguinem bibat. Qua forma loquendi significatur victoriarum excellentia. Quidam malunt interpretari, vaticinium subesse his verbis de Christo in cruce humiliando, & postea itorum mirabiliter glorificando.
units.tr: This is the final clause, in which the supreme power of the reigning Christ is expressed. After the slaughter of the enemies has been carried out, and on so great a scale that even the waters must be stained with blood, he will then drink from the brook stained with blood. He will receive the sign of the defeated and slain enemies, and for that reason he will be glorious and exalted for ever. Some explain that to drink from the brook is the same as to drink, as a sign of victory, the blood poured out in the stream, looking to what Balaam said of the Israelites in Numbers 23: "Behold, the people shall rise up as a lioness, and as a lion shall it lift itself up. It shall not lie down until it devours the prey and drinks the blood of the slain." By this manner of speaking the excellence of the victories is signified. Others prefer to interpret the words as containing a prophecy about Christ humbled on the cross and afterwards wonderfully glorified.

units.la: Nam de torrente in via bibere, humiliationem maximam significat, metaphora ducta à pauperibus, qui in via solent manu aquam haurire è puteis, aut torrentibus obuijs, & sic tenuiter se reficere.
units.tr: For to drink from the brook in the way signifies the deepest humiliation, a metaphor taken from poor travellers, who on the road commonly scoop water by hand from wells or from streams they meet, and so refresh themselves meagrely.

units.la: Et Christus in Euangelio dixit, bibere calicem, pro eo, quod est pati, & subire pericu lum mortis: apparet proverbialem fuisse Hebraeis locutionem. Utraque autem interpretatio de Christo rectè sumi potest. Ac de Davide viro sanguinum appellato, vel etiam in fuga sua à Saule, sive ab Absalone humiliato, dici ista possent. Sed si quis consideret totius Psalmi ordinem & progressum, intelliget reuera, ubi simpliciter & citra ambages explicatur clarissimè de regno Christi, nec non eiusdem sacerdotio concionari.
units.tr: And Christ said in the Gospel that he would drink the cup, meaning to suffer and to undergo the peril of death; it appears that this was a proverbial expression among the Hebrews. Either interpretation can rightly be applied to Christ. And these words could also be said of David, the man of blood, or of his flight from Saul, or of his humiliation by Absalom. But if anyone considers the order and progress of the whole Psalm, he will understand that it truly preaches, where it is set out plainly and without circumlocution, most clearly of the kingdom of Christ and likewise of his priesthood.

units.la: Ac puto vnumquemq; posse citra negotium deprehendere, vanissima esse commenta Iudaeorum, quorum aliqui, ut de Davide interpretentur, dicunt, conditum esse Psalmum hunc à quodam cantore, sententiamque esse, quòd Dominus Deus dixerit Domino ipsius regi Davidi, ut sederet ad dexteram: Istud verò impletum, quando David habitationem suam habuit ea civitatis parte, qua ad dexteram templi, quòd erat domus Dei, quasi ad dexteram Dei visus est sedere. Sacerdotem verò eum vocatum, quòd more sacerdotum vnctus esset, & à Deo electus, ac confirmatus, vel quòd generali & honorifica appellatione ipsi filij Davidi dicuntur sacerdotes fuisse, 2. Regum 8. quia nimirum rebus sacris addicti erant. Sed haec nihil ad sacerdotium aeternum, & ad ordinem Melchisedeck.
units.tr: And I think that anyone can recognise without difficulty that the Jewish fictions are most vain. Some of them, in order to interpret it of David, say that this Psalm was composed by a certain singer, and that its sense is that the Lord God said to the Lord, his king David, that he should sit at the right hand. This, they say, was fulfilled when David had his dwelling in that part of the city which lay on the right of the temple, which was the house of God, so that he seemed to sit as at the right hand of God. They say he was called a priest because he was anointed in the manner of priests and was chosen and confirmed by God; or because the sons of David are in general and honourable terms called priests, 2 Samuel 8, since they were of course devoted to sacred things. But these matters have nothing to do with the eternal priesthood and the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Nec minus vanum, quod alij interpretari volunt hunc Psalmum de Abrahamo, qui dominus fuerit, etiam cùm viveret, appellatus, ac sedens ad dexteram Dei, quàdo videlicet licet habuit dexteram Dei sibi fortiter auxiliantem, praesertim contra inimicos, quos plu-rimos debellauit & uicit, quia fratrem ipsius, nimirum Loth cum omni substantia sua ceperant, ut dicitur Genes. 14. & sic auxiliante Deo, dominatus est in medio inimicorum suorum. Habuit secum populum voluntarium, videlicet 318. expeditos vernaculos, cum quibus persecutus est hostes usq; in Dan.
units.tr: No less empty is the view of others, who wish this Psalm to be interpreted of Abraham, who, while he was still living, was called lord, and who sat at the right hand of God, namely when he had the right hand of God strongly helping him, especially against enemies, whom he defeated and conquered in great numbers, because they had taken his brother Lot with all his goods, as Genesis 14 says. And so, with God helping, he ruled in the midst of his enemies. He had with him a willing people, namely 318 trained men born in his household, with whom he pursued the enemy as far as Dan.

units.la: Idem porro sacerdos, quia benedictus a Domino, secundum quod ipse Melchisedek ad eum dixerat: Benedictus Abraham Deo excelso, qui creauit coelum et terram. Quin de Abraham illud aptissime dici, quod in die irae suae confregerit reges, cum historia contineat, quatuor reges ab eo caesos. Sed quis no videt, haec durius ita reddita, et logius sane petita? Quare non opus est refellendis his diu occupari. Nunc ad partes explicandas descendamus.
units.tr: Moreover, the same man was a priest because he was blessed by the Lord, according to what Melchizedek himself had said to him: Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth. Indeed, it is said that it may very aptly be said of Abraham that in the day of his wrath he broke kings, since the history records that he slew four kings. But who does not see that these things are rendered too harshly and sought far too remotely? Therefore there is no need to occupy ourselves long with refuting them. Now let us go down to explaining the parts.

units.la: Quod autem ad haec verba attinet: sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum: quid sit, sedere Christum a dextris Dei, supra ante confirmationem satis a nobis expositum est. Hoc tantum de voce donec notandum est, non ita debere accipi eam, quasi, postquam subiecti fuerint Christo omnes hostes, tunc ipse non amplius regnum tenebit, sive sederet ad dexteram: sed significatur, quod ad id usq; tempus, & in omne sequens sedebit. Ita enim vox donec in scripturis passim accipitur: Genes. 8. de coruo emisso, qui egrediebatur & non reuertebatur, donec siccaretur terra: vbi significatur, non quod coruus postea, sed quod nunquam redierit. Sic psal. 122. Oculi nostri ad Dominum, donec misereatur nostri. Matth. 1. Non cognouit eam, donec peperit filium suum primogenitum.
units.tr: As for these words, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet: what it means for Christ to sit at the right hand of God has been sufficiently expounded by us above, before the confirmation. Only this should be noted about the word until: it should not be taken as if, once all enemies have been made subject to Christ, he would then no longer hold the kingdom, or no longer sit at the right hand. Rather, it signifies that he will sit up to that time and for all the time that follows. For the word until is so used throughout the Scriptures: Genesis 8, of the raven that was sent out, which went out and did not return until the earth was dried up. There it signifies not that the raven returned afterwards, but that it never did. So Psalm 122: "Our eyes look to the Lord until he has mercy on us." Matthew 1: "He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son."

units.la: Scabellum autem metaphorice usurpauit, ad denotandum summam subiectionem: ea quippe voce notatur, ita subiiciendos subiugandosq; aduersarios Christi, ut pedibus cuiusque at Scabellum: 1. Pariter extrema subiectio hostium, & summa Christi potestas.
units.tr: But he used the word footstool metaphorically, to denote the utmost subjection. For by that word is indicated that the adversaries of Christ are to be brought under and subdued so completely that they are placed beneath his feet as a footstool. Likewise, the extreme subjection of enemies and the supreme power of Christ.

units.la: Porro loci affines, quibus haec dignitas Christi comprobatur, cum supra a nobis sint producti ante confirmationem, non opus est, eos denuo hic recitari.
units.tr: Furthermore, the related passages by which this dignity of Christ is proved have been brought forward by us above, before the confirmation, so there is no need to recite them again here.

units.la: Quod idem Christo conueniat sedere ad dexteram, etiam secundum humanam naturam, per quam ut humiliatus fuit Christus, ita secundum eandem denuo eum exaltari, ibidem dictum est. Notandum autem & hoc, quod hic habemus distinctionem personarum, patris, inquam, & filii.
units.tr: That it likewise belongs to Christ to sit at the right hand, even according to his human nature, through which Christ was humbled and according to the same nature exalted again, has been said in the same place. But this too should be noted: here we have the distinction of the persons, I mean of the Father and the Son.

units.la: Accipiemus interea consolationem ingentem, ex eo, quod Christus ad dextram Dei sedet, quodq; ipsius hostes omnes debeant subiugari. Sicut Christus obtinet apud Deum patrem tantam gloriam: ita certum esse debet, nos tantae gloriae fore participes, iuxta illud Ephes. 2. Cum essemus mortui per delicta, conuiuificauit nos una cum Christo, simulq; cum eo resuscitauit, & simul cum eo sedere fecit inter coelestes, in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Meanwhile we shall receive a great consolation from the fact that Christ sits at the right hand of God, and that all his enemies must be subdued. Just as Christ obtains such great glory with God the Father, so we ought to be certain that we shall be partakers of such glory, according to Ephesians 2: "When we were dead through our sins, he quickened us together with Christ, and raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him among the heavenly ones, in Christ Jesus."

units.la: Victoria autem Christi, spem victoriae & nobis praebet, contra omnes hostes nostros spirituales, qui nos ad peccatum aut mortem solicitant. Nam ipse ait, se vicisse mundum, ac proinde nos quoq; confidere debere, a nobis itidem mundum vincendum.
units.tr: The victory of Christ also gives us hope of victory against all our spiritual enemies, who urge us toward sin or death. For he himself says that he has overcome the world, and therefore we too ought to be confident that we shall likewise overcome the world.

units.la: Nonne omnes sunt administratorij spiritus, qui in ministerium emittuntur propter eos, qui haeredes erunt salutis?
units.tr: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?

units.la: Collectis argumentis, quibus summa dignitas, ipsaq; adeo diuinitas Christi efficacis-sime est probata: nunc absoluere volens collationem Christi cum angelis, quam initio confirmationis instituerat, atq; hactenus prosecutus est: subiicit breuiter summam dignitatis Angelorum. Est q; sententia: satis copiose probatum est, quanta sit Christi dignitas, quod sit Angelis longe superior. Nam eum esse filium Dei: deinde adorandum etiam ab ipsis angelis: tum Deum, cuius regnum maneat in aeternum: Qui & praeomnibus hominibus sit multiplicibus donis exornatus: praeterea creatorem totius mundi, aeterno existentem, incommutabilem, finem nescientem: deniq; sedentem ad dextram Dei patris: Haec inquam, omnia de Christo recte dici, e Scripturis ostendimus. At vero de angelis nihil tale praedicari potest. Id vnum, & quasi amplissimum de ipsis dici potest, quod sint administratorij spiritus, qui in ministerium emittuntur, propter eos, qui haeredes erunt salutis. Satis ergo & his liquet, angelos nullo modo esse cum Christo conferendos, & Christum esse verum Dei filium, ac verum naturam Deum. Hoc igitur pacto vides hic institutae collationis, ac proinde totius confirmationis aptam conclusionem, sunt autem haec verba desumpta ex eo potissimum loco, quem supra de dignitate angelorum citauit e Psalmo 103. Qui creat angelos suos spiritus, & ministros suos ignis flammam. Id quod ex graeco manifestius fit. Nam cum ibi scriptura vocat angelos πνεύματα, deinde λειτουργός, ipse hic vocat eos λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα. Exprimitur autem hic angelorum natura, quia vocantur πνεύματα, uti supra exposuimus: deinde etiam officiu, quod uide-licet administrent siue emittantur in ministerium. Qualia vero argumenta, de angelorum conditione longe infra dignitatem Christi posita, sumi ex his posint, supra a nobis itidem expositum est.
units.tr: Having gathered the arguments by which Christ's supreme dignity, and indeed his divinity, has been most effectively proved, the author now wishes to complete the comparison of Christ with the angels that he set out at the beginning of the confirmation and has pursued so far. He sums up briefly the dignity of the angels. His meaning is this: it has been proved at sufficient length how great Christ's dignity is, that he is far superior to the angels. For we have shown from the Scriptures that these things are rightly said of Christ: that he is the Son of God; that he is to be worshipped even by the angels themselves; that he is God, whose kingdom endures for ever; that he is adorned with manifold gifts beyond all men; further, that he is the creator of the whole world, existing from eternity, unchangeable, without end; and finally that he sits at the right hand of God the Father. But nothing of this kind can be said of the angels. The one thing that can be said of them, and it is their greatest praise, is that they are ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation. So it is clear enough from this too that the angels are in no way to be compared with Christ, and that Christ is the true Son of God and truly God by nature. You see, then, the fitting conclusion of the comparison that was set up here, and therefore of the whole confirmation. These words are taken chiefly from that passage which he cited above concerning the dignity of the angels, from Psalm 103: "who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire." This is made clearer from the Greek. For where Scripture calls the angels πνεύματα [pneumata] and then λειτουργοί [leitourgoi], the author here calls them λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα [leitourgika pneumata]. The nature of the angels is expressed here by the fact that they are called spirits, as we explained above; and then also their office, namely that they serve or are sent out to minister. What arguments about the condition of the angels, placed far below the dignity of Christ, may be drawn from these words, we have likewise set out above.

units.la: Vnum hic additur de causa finali ministerij eorum, quod rursus humiliorem eorum conditionem videtur arguere, nempe, emitti angelos, propter eos, qui haeredes erunt salutis: quo verbo significatur, angelos esse veluti ministros electorum, & quodammodo infra horum conditionem positos. Et latet hic argumentum: angeli emittuntur in ministerium, etiam propter homines: quomodo ergo non essent inferiores Christo? Illud vero maxime facit ad minuendam illorum dignitatem, quod generaliter dicit, omnes administratorios esse spiritus, & emitti in ministerium. Non habent hic locum, quae Dionysius & quidam alij sic disputant de Angelis, quasi quidam duntaxat mitterentur, quidam vero tantum assisterent ipsi Deo, ut otiosi rerum diuinarum speculatores. Ac producuntilud Daniel. Millia millium ministrabant ei, & decies centena millia assistebant ei: Distinguunt eos, qui ministrant seu emittuntur, ab illis, qui assistunt. Quasi vero qui assistunt, aliam ob causam assistant, quam ut quaecunque iusserit Deus, ipsi celerrime pareant & perficiant. Nam assistere est etiam adesse expectare, mandata, si quae fuerint peragenda. Et quomodocunque distinguant illi ordines angelorum, e quibus alios summos constituunt, alios vero infimos, omnes tamen mitti in Scripturis dicuntur. Nam archangeli Gabriel & Michael missi leguntur: ut videre est apud Danielem & in Euangelio: Itemque vnus de Seraphim missus ad Esaiam, qui calculo purgaret eius labia, Esaiae 6. Perspicuum est ergo, omnes etiam summos mitti, cum omnes ministri generaliter appellentur: quomodo & alio loco de eis dicitur Psalmo 102.
units.tr: One more point is added here about the final purpose of their ministry, which again seems to show their humbler condition: namely, that the angels are sent out for the sake of those who will inherit salvation. By these words it is signified that the angels are, as it were, ministers of the elect and in some way placed below their condition. And an argument lies hidden here: angels are sent out to minister also for the sake of men; how then would they not be inferior to Christ? But what contributes most to diminishing their dignity is that he says generally that all of them are ministering spirits and are sent out to serve. What Dionysius and certain others argue about the angels has no place here, namely that some were merely sent while others only stood before God himself, as idle observers of divine things. They also cite that passage of Daniel: "Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him." They distinguish those who minister or are sent out from those who stand before God. As if those who stand before him stood for any other reason than that they might most swiftly obey and carry out whatever God commands. For to stand before someone also means to be present and wait for orders, if any are to be carried out. And however they distinguish those orders of angels, of which they set some as highest and others as lowest, yet all are said in Scripture to be sent. For the archangels Gabriel and Michael are read of as sent, as can be seen in Daniel and in the Gospel; and likewise one of the Seraphim was sent to Isaiah to purify his lips with a live coal (Isaiah 6). It is plain, then, that even the highest are sent, since all are generally called ministers. So also elsewhere it is said of them in Psalm 102:

units.la: Benedicite Domino omnes virtutes eius, ministri eius, qui facitis voluntatem eius. Et Didymus Alexandrinus in libro de Spiritu sancto, ut refert Primasius, ita sentit.
units.tr: Bless the Lord, all you his powers, his ministers, you who do his will. And Didymus of Alexandria, in his book on the Holy Spirit, as Primasius reports, holds this same view.

units.la: Quod si quis dicat, etiam filium esse missum, atque hunc se gessisse, ut ministrum & forma serui, non ut dominum: ergo angelis non esse superiorem. Respondetur, alia ratione missum filium, quam mittuntur angeli: Missus est Christus, ut filius vnigenitus, tum ut minister angelus, vel Propheta: qua de re in parabola Matthaei 20. Humiliatus est autem, non quia id debebat ex officio, vel natura, sicut angeli: sed quia sponte voluit, factus obediens patri, in omnibus, &c.
units.tr: But if someone says that the Son too was sent, and that he acted as a minister and in the form of a servant, not as lord, therefore he is not superior to the angels: the answer is that the Son was sent in a different way from the angels. Christ was sent as the only-begotten Son, and also as an angel or prophet-like minister; on this matter see the parable in Matthew 20. But he humbled himself not because he owed it by office or nature, as the angels do, but because he willingly chose to, becoming obedient to the Father in all things, and so on.

units.la: Iam quod emittantur angeli in ministerium) propter eos, qui haeredes erunt salutis, hoc quoque aliis Scripturae locis confirmatur: Nam Psalm.91. Angelis suis Deus mandauit de te, ut custodiant te in omnibus vijs tuis. Rursus Psalmo 33. Immittet angelus Domini in circuitu timentium eum, & eripiet eos. Et historiae sacrae passim testantur, quam multa & quam praeclara fuerint angelorum erga homines officia ac ministeria. Aliqui missi ad docendum homines ea, quae de voluntate Dei scire eos conueniebat: ut ad Esaiam missus vnus de Seraphim, & in Apocalypsi ad Ioannem, in Actis ad Cornelium Centurionem: Item angeli missi ad pastores, ut certos facerent de Christi natiuitate: Item cum Christus a morte resurrexisset: Item cum in coelum ascendisset, angeli testimonium tulerunt. Aliqui emissi ad educendum pios e periculis, ad defendendum contra aduersarios: ut qui eduxit Loth ex Sodomis: in Actis apostolum Petrum e carcere: qui occidit tempore Ezechiae Assyrios obsidentes Hierosolymam. Alij denique alia munera, quae ipsis a Deo iniunguntur, obeunt: neque opus pluribus istam causam agere, cum supra de angelis eorumque officijs copiose disseruerimus. Mittuntur vero angeli non tantum ad bonos, sed etiam ad malos, ut videlicet adhortentur eos ad resipiscentiam, vel ut eos pro diuino arbitrio puniant: sicut angelus missus est ad Labanum, ad Bileamum, item ad Herodem qui ipsum percuteret, Actor.12.
units.tr: That the angels are sent out to minister for the sake of those who will inherit salvation, this is also confirmed by other passages of Scripture. For in Psalm 91: "God has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways." Again, in Psalm 33: "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and rescues them." And the sacred histories bear witness everywhere how many and how splendid were the services and ministries of the angels towards men. Some were sent to teach men what they needed to know of God's will: as one of the Seraphim was sent to Isaiah, and in the Apocalypse to John, and in Acts to Cornelius the centurion. Likewise angels were sent to the shepherds to assure them of Christ's birth; and when Christ had risen from death; and when he had ascended into heaven, angels bore witness. Some were sent to lead the godly out of dangers and to defend them against adversaries: as the angel who led Lot out of Sodom; in Acts, the apostle Peter out of prison; and the one who in the time of Hezekiah struck down the Assyrians besieging Jerusalem. Others, finally, perform other duties which are laid on them by God. There is no need to press this point further, since we have discussed the angels and their offices at length above. Angels are sent not only to the good but also to the bad, namely to urge them to repentance, or to punish them according to God's judgment; as an angel was sent to Laban, to Balaam, and also to Herod, to strike him down (Acts 12).

units.la: Interea discemus, & sedulo apud nos expendemus, mirabilem esse Dei erga nos bonitatem, qui adeo est de salute nostra solicitus, ut angelos quoque nobis designet custodes & auxiliares, & ministros: interdum etiam plures simul. Quam ob causam ad gratias illi agendas decet nos excitari, nec non orare, ut animos nostros flectat, efficiatque dictis illorum audietes, nec non auxilium suum, quod per illos praestari potest, nunquam nobis subtrahat.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us learn, and carefully consider among ourselves, how wonderful is God's goodness towards us, who is so concerned for our salvation that he appoints angels also to be our guardians, helpers and ministers, sometimes even several at once. For this reason we ought to be stirred to give him thanks, and also to pray that he may bend our minds, make us listen to their words, and never withdraw from us the help that he can give through them.

units.la: Deinde, ut Chrysostomus quoq; hic admonet, iubemur agnoscere ex eadem bonitate Dei, nostram dignitatem: ut verissimum sit, quod Paulus ait, Omnia esse nostra, siue vita, siue mors, siue praesentia, siue futura: omnia, inquam nostra, nos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei.
units.tr: Next, as Chrysostom also reminds us here, we are bidden to recognise from the same goodness of God our own dignity, so that what Paul says is most true: "All things are yours, whether life or death, whether present or future: all things, I say, are yours; and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's."

units.la: Tertiò: magna consolatio in quibuscunque tentationibus seu aduersitatibus tam externis, quam internis, quod angelos habemus, qui nos erigere, defendere, & tueri venient ac debeant. Diabolus non tam diligenter circuit quaerens quomodo nos deuoret, quin boni angeli multò diligentius circumeant, ut Psalm.33.canit, timentes Deum libe-rare ipsos à periculis cupientes: Hic decet nos intueri, quòd Christo, postquàm tentatus fuisset, statim angeli adfuerunt ministrantes, Matth.4.
units.tr: Third: there is great comfort in whatever temptations or adversities, external as well as internal, that we have angels who will come and ought to come to raise us up, defend us and keep us safe. The devil does not prowl so diligently seeking how he may devour us, but the good angels go about far more diligently, as Psalm 33 sings, desiring to deliver from dangers those who fear God. Here we should note that after Christ had been tempted, angels at once came and ministered to him (Matthew 4).

units.la: Quartò habemus hic incitamentum, ad modestiam & decorum seruandum, in omni-bus nostris actionibus. Si enim cogitemus subinde, angelos nobis astare omni tempo-re, qui conspiciunt nostras actiones, haud dubiè sic afficiemur, ut ne in abditissimis qui-dè latibulis, aliquid indecorè fimus perpetraturi. Tradit Seneca ad Lucilium lib. 3. cap 25. Epicurum solitum dicere: sic fac omnia, tanquàm aliquis spectet. Rectè quidem & val-dè salubriter statuit, semper imaginandam esse boni alicuius viri præsentiam.
units.tr: Fourth: here we have an incentive to keep modesty and decorum in all our actions. For if we often think that angels stand by us at every time, who watch our actions, we will certainly be so disposed that we shall not commit anything unseemly even in the most hidden hiding-places. Seneca, in his letter to Lucilius (book 3, letter 25), reports that Epicurus used to say: "Act in everything as if someone were watching." He rightly and very wholesomely laid down that the presence of some good man should always be imagined.

units.la: At quanto magis excitabimur ad virtutem, atq; à malo deterrebimur, si imaginemur, adesse nobis semper spectatorem bonum angelum, qui ad Deum seuerum etiam cogita-tionum iudicem, omnia nostra facta, dicta, & cogitata, ut sic loquar, perferat?
units.tr: But how much more we would be stirred to virtue and turned back from evil, if we imagined that a good angel is always present with us as a watcher, who carries to God, the strict judge even of our thoughts, all our deeds, words and thoughts, so to speak!

units.la: Hucusq; igitur protracta est disputatio, qua Christi diuinitas asseritur: & septem argu-mentis valdè efficacibus ac selectis confirmatio hæc subnixa est, quæ sanè adeò crassei nobis sunt expositæ, ut credam, vel puerum posse ea citra negotium assequi, explicareq;. Nam hic scopus noster semper, ut quàm crassissimè proposita scripturæ mysteria expli-cemus. Iam verò addemus quædam alia testimonia è veteri testamento, quæ hic ab A-postolo non sunt citata, & tamē de Christo siue Messia proprie & simpliciter sunt dicta, nec non diuinitatem ei manifestè tribuunt: per quæ etiam rectius & clarius intelligetur, tota hæc de dignitate ac diuinitate Christi disputatio.
units.tr: So far, then, this disputation by which the divinity of Christ is asserted has been carried forward, and this confirmation is supported by seven very effective and carefully chosen arguments. These have been set out so plainly that I believe even a boy could grasp and explain them without difficulty. For our aim here has always been to explain the mysteries proposed in Scripture as plainly as possible. Now we shall add certain other testimonies from the Old Testament, which the Apostle has not cited here, yet which speak properly and simply of Christ or the Messiah, and also ascribe divinity to him plainly. Through these the whole of this disputation about the dignity and divinity of Christ will be understood more rightly and clearly.

units.la: Colligam autem tantùm ex veteri testamento, quasi cum Iudæis nobis fit conflictatio. Quòd si quis velit ex nouo testamento, tanquàm certamen initurus cum Arrio, Euno-mio, Aetio, Paulo Samosatesi, licet colligere ex Nazianzeno, sed plurima suppeditat Cy-rillus in Thesauro.
units.tr: I shall gather them only from the Old Testament, as if we were engaged in a contest with the Jews. If anyone wishes to gather them from the New Testament, as one about to contend with Arius, Eunomius, Aetius and Paul of Samosata, he may draw on Nazianzen, but Cyril in his Thesaurus supplies very many.

units.la: Primùm ex illa promissione ad Abrahamum facta Genes.12. & 17. qua dicitur: In Semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes: Quòd vocatur semen Abrahæ, humana natura suscipieda prę-dicitur: quòd verò in eo, siue per eum benedicendæ sint omnes gentes, id non nisi à di-uina potentia proficisci potest.
units.tr: First, from that promise made to Abraham in Genesis 12 and 17, in which it is said: In your seed all the nations shall be blessed. That he is called the seed of Abraham foretells that he is to take on human nature; but that in him, or through him, all the nations are to be blessed, this can proceed from nothing but divine power.

units.la: Genes.49. Non deficiet princeps à Iuda, neq; dux à lumbis eius, donec veniat, qui mit-tendus est, & ipse erit expectatio gentium. Vbi expectatio significat spem, fiduciamq; sa-lutis in eum collocandam: sed fiduciam non conuenit collocare, nisi in Deum: Ergo Chri-stus est Deus.
units.tr: Genesis 49: The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations. Here expectation signifies hope and trust of salvation to be placed in him. But trust is fitting to place only in God. Therefore Christ is God.

units.la: Psalm.24. Attollite portas principes vestras, & eleuamini portæ æternales, & introi-bit rex gloriæ. Quis est iste rex gloriæ? Dominus fortis & potens, Dominus potens in prælio. Attollite portas principes vestras, & eleuamini portæ æternales, & introibit rex gloriæ. Quis est iste rex gloriæ? Dominus virtutum, ipse est rex gloriæ. Hic Christus ap-pellatur dominus virtutum, quæ appellatio Dei propria est.
units.tr: Psalm 24: Lift up your heads, O gates; and be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, O gates; and be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. Here Christ is called the Lord of hosts, which is a title proper to God.

units.la: Psalmo 33. Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt, & spiritu oris eius omnis virtus eorū. Vbi per verbum intelligitur filius: per eum verò firmari cœlum, siue creari omnia, ut alio Psal-mo dicitur, id non nisi diuinæ potentiæ est.
units.tr: Psalm 33: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. Here by the word is understood the Son; that through him the heavens are established, or all things are created, as another psalm says, this belongs to divine power alone.

units.la: Psalmo 89. Quis similis erit Deo in filijs Deorum: cuius loci hic est sensus: vt multi sunt filij Dei, per participationem videlicet, siue adoptionem, tamen unus est proprius et naturalis filius Dei, cui nemo potest æquari: id autem, quia is habet diuinam naturam. Vbi etiam distinctio persona filij, à persona patris, clarè notatur: quo modo etiam Pro-uerb.38. Quis ascendit in cœlum atque descendit? Quis continuit spiritum in manib. suis? Quis colligauit aquas, quasi in vestimento? Quis sustentauit omnes terminos ter-ræ? Quod nomen eius, & nomen filij eius, si nosti? Descensum hunc & ascensum de solo filio Dei intelligi debere, docetur Ioan. 3. & Ephes. 4. aliisq; locis Scripturæ.
units.tr: Psalm 89: Who among the sons of God is like unto God? The sense of this passage is that, although there are many sons of God by participation, namely by adoption, yet there is one proper and natural Son of God, to whom no one can be equated; and this is because he has the divine nature. Here also the distinction of the person of the Son from the person of the Father is clearly marked. In the same way Proverbs 30: Who has ascended into heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name, if you know? That this descent and ascent must be understood of the Son of God alone is taught in John 3, Ephesians 4 and other places of Scripture.

units.la: Esaiæ 9. Puer natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis, & vocabitur magni consilij an-gelus, admirabilis, consiliarius, Deus fortis, potens, princeps pacis, pater futuri seculi, (vel vitæ perpetuæ) ubi Christus vocatur Deus fortis, & pater siue autor vitæ æ-ternæ.
units.tr: Isaiah 9: A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and his name shall be called: Wonderful, Counsellor, the Angel of great counsel, Mighty God, Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come (or of eternal life). Here Christ is called the Mighty God, and the Father, that is the author, of eternal life.

units.la: Esaiæ 7. Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabit nomen eius, Emanuel, id est, nobiscum Deus. In utroque testimonio, pariter humanitas & diuinitas Christi com-probatur.
units.tr: Isaiah 7: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Emmanuel, that is, God with us. In both testimonies the humanity and the divinity of Christ are equally proved.

units.la: Esaiæ 11. Egredietur virga de radice Iesse, & flos de radice eius ascendet, & requiescet super eum spiritus Domini, &c. Sequitur: Non secundum visionem oculorum iudicabit, neque secundum auditum aurium audiet. Istud quidem non est, nisi Dei.
units.tr: Isaiah 11: A shoot shall come forth from the stem of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, etc. It follows: He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of his ears. This certainly belongs to God alone.

units.la: Itidem Esaiæ eodem capite, vndecimo scilicet: In die illo radix Iesse, quæ stat in signum populorum, ipsum gentes deprecabuntur, & erit sepulchrum eius gloriosum. sum. Deprecabuntur, inquit, ideò, quia Deus.Et per sepulchrum mors siue humanitas Christi notatur.
units.tr: Likewise in Isaiah, in the same chapter, the eleventh that is: In that day the root of Jesse, who stands for a sign to the peoples, the Gentiles shall seek him, and his sepulchre shall be glorious. They shall seek him, he says, because he is God. And by the sepulchre is signified his death, or his humanity.

units.la: Capite 35. Deus ipse veniet, & saluabit nos. Tunc aperientur oculi caecorum, & aures surdorum patebunt: tunc saliet sicut cervus, claudus, & aperta erit lingua mutorum. Vbi propheta de aduentu Christi va-ticinatur, ei tribuens eam potestatem, quae soli Deo propria est: sicut & in euangelio colligunt homines ex signis ac miraculis, Christum esse Deum, & Dei filium.
units.tr: Chapter 35: God himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb shall be loosed. Here the prophet foretells the coming of Christ, ascribing to him that power which belongs to God alone; just as in the Gospel men gather from the signs and miracles that Christ is God and the Son of God.

units.la: Capite 40. verba quae Ioannes Baptista de se usurpauit. Ioan.1. Luc.3. vox clamantis in deserto: parate viam Domini, rectas facite in solitudine semitas Dei vestri: omnis vallis exaltabitur, & omnis mons & collis humiliabitur, & erunt prava in directa, & aspera in vias planas. Et revelabitur gloria Domini, & videbit omnis caro, quod os Domini locutum est, id est, ipsum verbum Dei, videlicet filius, qui est ὁ λόγος, &c.
units.tr: Chapter 40: the words which John the Baptist applied to himself, John 1, Luke 3: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert the paths of our God; every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain. And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken, that is, the Word of God itself, namely the Son, who is ὁ λόγος [the Word], etc.

units.la: Esaiae 41. & 42. plurima habentur de Christo eius q; regno vaticinia, in quibus, Deum esse ipsum ostenditur. Esaiae 45. Rorate coeli desuper, & nubes pluant iustum, aperiatur terra, & germinet Saluatorem, et iustitia oriatur simul. Ego Dominus creaui eum. Vbi distinctio personae, filij a persona patris: ite humanitas, quia creatus dicitur, et praeterea diuinitas, quia iustus & saluator. Ibidem: congregamini & accedite simul, qui saluati estis ex gentibus.
units.tr: Isaiah 41 and 42 contain very many prophecies about Christ and his kingdom, in which it is shown that he himself is God. Isaiah 45: Drop down, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the righteous one; let the earth open, and bring forth a Saviour, and let righteousness spring up together. I the Lord have created him. Here there is a distinction of person, of the Son from the person of the Father: the humanity, because he is said to be created; and besides, the divinity, because he is righteous and a Saviour. In the same place: Gather yourselves and come together, you who have been saved from among the nations.

units.la: Capite 53. propter scelus populi mei percusi eum: dabit impios pro sepultura, & diuites pro morte sua, eò quod iniquitatem non fecit, neq; dolus fuerit in ore eius, & Dominus voluerit conterere eum in infirmitate. Si posuerit pro peccato animā suā, videbit semen longaeuum, & voluntas Domini in manu eius dirigetur: pro eo, quòd laborauit anima eius, uidebit & saturabitur. In scientia sua iustificabit ipse iustus seruus meos multos, & iniquitates eorum ipse portabit. Vbi iterum distinctio personarū, humanitas & diuinitas Christi, mors & satisfactio pro peccatis, facultas iustificandi, &c.
units.tr: Chapter 53: For the transgression of my people was he stricken; he shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he had done no iniquity, nor was there guile in his mouth, and the Lord was pleased to bruise him in weakness. If he shall lay down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed by his hand: because his soul has laboured, he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities. Here again there is a distinction of persons, the humanity and divinity of Christ, his death and satisfaction for sins, his power to justify, etc.

units.la: Esaiae cap.59. Veniet ex Sion, qui eripiat, & auertat impietatem à Iacob. & citatur Roman.11.
units.tr: Isaiah 59: A redeemer shall come out of Zion, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob. And it is cited in Romans 11.

units.la: Esaiae 61. 63. 64. 65. de aduentu Christi, morte ipsius, & liberatione nostra per eam, plena sunt omnia, & plurima occurrunt diuinitatem Christi approbantia.
units.tr: Isaiah 61, 63, 64 and 65 are full of the coming of Christ, his death, and our deliverance through it, and very many passages occur which confirm the divinity of Christ.

units.la: Ieremiae 32. Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, & suscitabo Dauid germen iustum, & regnabit rex, & sapiens erit, & faciet iudicium & iustitiā in terra. In diebus illis saluabitur Iuda, & Israel habitabit confidenter. Et hoc est nomen, quòd vocabunt eum, Dominus iustus noster: paulò post dicetur: viuit Dominus, qui eduxit semē domus Israel, de terra Aquilonis. Idem repetitur capite 33.
units.tr: Jeremiah 32: Behold, the days come, says the Lord, and I will raise up to David a righteous branch, and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.
