In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely. And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness. Shortly after it is said: As the Lord lives, who brought up the seed of the house of Israel out of the land of the north. The same is repeated in chapter 33.

units.la: Daniel. 9. Sanctus Sanctorum vocatur Christus, per quem delenda sit iniquitas.
units.tr: Daniel 9: Christ is called the Holy of Holies, through whom iniquity is to be blotted out.

units.la: Ioelis 3. Dominus de Sion rugiet, & de Hierusalem dabit vocem suam. Et mouebuntur coeli & terra, & Dominus spes populi sui, et fortitudo filiorum Israel. Et scietis, quod ego Dominus Deus vester habitans in Sion, in monte sancto meo.
units.tr: Joel 3: The Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he shall give his voice. And the heavens and the earth shall shake, and the Lord will be the hope of his people and the strength of the sons of Israel. And you shall know that I the Lord your God dwell in Zion, in my holy mountain.

units.la: Michaeas cap. 4. de aduentu Christi, & vocatione gentium multa habet. Sed capite 5. istud additur: & tu Bethlehem Ephrata paruulus es in millib. Iuda. Ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel, & egressus eius ab initio à diebus aeternitatis.
units.tr: Micah, chapter 4, has much about the coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles. But in chapter 5 this is added: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me the one who is to be ruler in Israel; and his going forth is from of old, from the days of eternity."

units.la: Deniq;, huc faciunt omnia testimonia de regno Christi aeterno. Sic enim describitur passim, regnaturus Christus in aeternum: Ergo ipse aeternus esse debet. Si autem ipse aeternus: Ergo Deus. Nam aeternum esse soli Deo competit.
units.tr: Finally, all the testimonies about the eternal kingdom of Christ bear on this point. For it is described everywhere in this way: Christ will reign for ever. Therefore he himself must be eternal. But if he is eternal, then he is God, for to be eternal belongs to God alone.

units.la: Interea notandum illud Esaiae 53. GenerationE eius quis enarrabit? nihil facere ad probandam Christi generationē ex patre ab aeterno ante condita secula, sicut Hyeronymus interpretatur in euangelio Matthaei. Nam propheta non de ea ibi loquitur, sed de multitudine credentium in Christum, qui Christo inposterum nascerētur, quorum numerus non magis intelligi posset, quàm arenae maris. Similiter illud ex Psal.110. Ex utero ante luciferum genui te, pari modo inidoneum est ad eandem rem comprobandam. Nam suprà expositum est, ad hebraicam veritatem ita redditum esse: vt, os matutinus aderit ab utero iuuetus tua: quae verba rursus de illis, qui ubertim & largiter, miraq; fertilitate instar roris generarentur Christo, sonat. Visum est ista admonere, ne quis temere putet, statim quaeuis assumenda esse testimonia, quae videt à quibusuis in medium produci.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the words of Isaiah 53, "Who shall declare his generation?", should be noted: they have nothing to do with proving the generation of Christ from the Father from eternity, before the ages were made, as Jerome interprets it in his commentary on Matthew. For the prophet is not speaking there of that generation, but of the multitude of believers in Christ, who would be born to Christ in time to come, whose number could not be grasped any more than the sand of the sea. Likewise, the passage from Psalm 110, "From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you," is equally unsuitable for establishing the same point. For it was explained above that, according to the Hebrew truth, it is rendered thus: "Your youth will be with you from the womb, like the morning dew," and these words again refer to those who would be born to Christ abundantly and plentifully, with a wonderful fruitfulness, like dew. I thought it worth giving this warning, lest anyone rashly suppose that whatever testimonies are seen to be brought forward by anyone at all must straightway be adopted.

units.la: Caeterū alia disputare hoc loco, quomodo videlicet pater genuerit filium, & id genus alia, subtilia magis quàm pia, quàm scitu necessaria, quàm scripturis confirmata, non est nostri instituti, neq; enarrationis munus, quod solùm nos suscepimus, istud fert aut postulat.
units.tr: As for discussing other matters in this place, how the Father begat the Son and other things of that kind, which are more subtle than godly, and which are neither necessary to know nor confirmed by Scripture, this is not part of our purpose, nor is it the task of exposition, which alone we have undertaken; this neither bears nor requires it.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM.
units.tr: Chapter Two.

units.la: Propterea oportet nos vehementius attendere his, quæ dicta sunt, ne quando perfluamus. Etenim si is qui per angelos dictus fuerat, sermo, fuit firmus, & omnis transgressio et inobedientia iustam præmij repensationem accepit, quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem? quæ cum primum enarrari cœperit per ipsum Dominum, ab his qui audierât in nos confirmata fuit, attestante Deo, & signis, & prodigijs simul, varijs q; virtutibus, & spiritus sancti distributionibus, iuxta ipsius voluntatem.
units.tr: Therefore we ought to give more earnest heed to the things that have been said, lest at any time we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? This salvation, having first begun to be declared through the Lord himself, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, God also bearing witness with them by signs and wonders and various miracles, and by distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will.

units.la: Actenus disputatu est. Iam oportune infert, et hortatur Hebræos, ut Christum talem ac tantum agnoscant, veneren-tur, colant, nec non eius doctrinam religiose audiant observetq; : sed istud hic admodum succincte, propterea quod quædam adhuc ad ipsam disputationem pertinentia, nempe de natura in Christo, debet mox adijci: quibus absolutis, multo pleniorem conclusionem attexit, quæ iterum grauissimâ continens adhortatione ad recipiendum Christum eiusq; euangelium, toti primæ parti huius epistolæ finem imponit. Quâquam præsens exhortatiuncula argumentis suasorijs, quæ & aculeu infigere animis posint, nequaquam est destituta. Sic igitur paucis hortatur:
units.tr: So far the argument has been set out. Now he opportunely draws the inference and urges the Hebrews to acknowledge Christ as such and so great, to revere and honour him, and to listen to his teaching religiously and keep it. But he does this here very briefly, because certain matters still belonging to the argument itself, namely concerning the nature of Christ, must be added shortly. When these are finished, he appends a much fuller conclusion, which, again containing a most weighty exhortation to receive Christ and his gospel, brings the whole first part of this epistle to an end. Yet this present short exhortation is by no means lacking in persuasive arguments, which can also drive a sting into minds. So he exhorts briefly in these words:

units.la: Propterea oportet nos uehementius attendere) Διὰ τοῦτο δεῖ περισσοτέρως ἡμᾶς προσέχειν τοῖς ἀκουσθεῖσι. Quasi diceret: Quando tot argumentis probatum est, Christum esse Deum, sane æquum est & necessarium, ipsum veneremur, & multo attentissimè ea, quæ per ipsum & de ipso dicta nobis sunt, audiamus.
units.tr: Therefore we ought to give more earnest heed [Διὰ τοῦτο δεῖ περισσοτέρως ἡμᾶς προσέχειν τοῖς ἀκουσθεῖσι]. It is as if he said: since it has been proved by so many arguments that Christ is God, it is surely fair and necessary that we venerate him and listen with the closest attention to what has been said to us through him and about him.

units.la: Verbum Διὰ & conuenit significat, & necessitatem. Hoc autem loco apte necessitate indicabit. Vult enim Apostolus vehementer urgere & pungere omnium animos, & persuadere, plane necessarium esse ad salute, ut Hebræi Christum audiant. Hanc necessitatem hic significari satis arguunt, quæ mox de periculis & pernicie non audientiū sequuntur.
units.tr: The word [Διὰ] signifies both cause and necessity, and in this place it aptly indicates necessity. For the Apostle wishes to press strongly and prick the minds of all, and to persuade them that it is plainly necessary for salvation that the Hebrews hear Christ. That this necessity is meant here is sufficiently shown by what follows soon after about the dangers and destruction of those who do not listen.

units.la: προσέχειν significat, animum cum diligentia & studio alicui rei intedere: ut hic reuera non tantum dictu fit, benigne audienda excipienda q;, quæ de Christo fuerant propositæ: sed animo ardenti suscipienda, & corde credenda: sicut in scripturis vocabulum audiedi crebrò ponitur, non solum pro eo, quod est audire & auribus percipere: sed pro credere, obtemperare, & obseruare: quemadmodum Ioan. 9. dicit cæcus, Dixi vobis iam, nec audistis, cur iterū vultis audire? Nec audiuistis, inquit, id est noluistis credere. Ioan. 10. Alias oues habeo, & uocem meam audient, et fiet unum ouile, & unus pastor. Rursus alio loco: Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, & custodiunt illud. Vbi posterius fere est interpretatio prioris. Sic igitur attendere hoc loco plus, quam simpliciter audire excipere q; significat id quod ex eo quoq; licet intelligere, quòd additur, περισσοτέρως, id est, vehementius, præstantius, abundantius. Nam περισσόω abundo, supero est: unde περισσὸς abundàs, superfluus, præstans. Ac uidetur hic comparatiuus respicere ad aliquid aliud, quòd itidem fuerit diligenter audiendum, sed non ita diligenter, ut id, de quo nunc sermo est. Quare Chrysostomus ait, abundantius seu vehementius dixisse Apostolum, quòd respexerit ad legem, quæ quidem erat studiosè audienda obseruandaq; : at quæ nunc dicta sunt, per Christum, & de Christo, debet audiri obseruariq; multò studiosius. Fuerunt quidem a Deo profecta, quæ dicta sunt in lege, non minus, quàm hæc ipsa, quæ dicuntur in euangelio: sed est quoddam discrimen: illa enim non erat dicta, ut perpetuò manerent, & semper haberent vim, sed suo tempore abolerentur. Euangelica autem dicta sunt, ut semper maneant, & nunquàm aboleantur. Atq; ob hanc causam vehementius his extendendum. Ergo maximi faciendum est euangelium, et legi præferendum multis interuallis. Qua de re Apostolus adhuc non vult agere apertius, ne in ipso vestibulo epistolæ nimium offendat animos Iudæorum: sed secunda parte huius epistolæ, causa hæc copiosè agitur.
units.tr: [προσέχειν] signifies to direct the mind to something with diligence and zeal. Here it is indeed not merely a matter of listening kindly and receiving what has been set forth about Christ, but of taking it up with an ardent mind and believing it in the heart. So in Scripture the word for hearing is often used not only for hearing and perceiving with the ears, but for believing, obeying and observing. Thus in John 9 the blind man says: "I have told you already, and you did not hear; why do you want to hear again?" "And you did not hear," he says, that is, you were unwilling to believe. John 10: "I have other sheep, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd." And elsewhere: "Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it," where the second clause is nearly an explanation of the first. So to attend here means more than simply to hear and receive, as the words that follow also show: [περισσοτέρως], that is, more earnestly, more excellently, more abundantly. For [περισσόω] means to abound or excel, whence [περισσὸς] means abundant, superfluous, excellent. This comparative seems to refer to something else which was likewise to be heard diligently, but not as diligently as the matter now under discussion. Hence Chrysostom says that the Apostle spoke more abundantly or more earnestly because he had in view the law, which indeed was to be heard and observed with care; but what is now said through Christ and about Christ must be heard and observed much more zealously. The things said in the law did indeed proceed from God, no less than these things which are said in the gospel; but there is a difference. Those were not spoken to remain for ever and always have force, but were to be abolished in their time. The gospel sayings, however, were spoken to remain always and never be abolished. For this reason we must extend ourselves more earnestly to them. Therefore the gospel is to be held in the highest regard and placed far above the law. The Apostle does not yet wish to treat this matter more openly, lest at the very threshold of the epistle he offend the minds of the Jews too much; but in the second part of this epistle the cause is treated at length.

units.la: τοῖς ἀκουσθεῖσι, interpres reddidit, quæ dicta sunt nobis: cum potius sit, quæ audita sunt nobis. Sententia interim est eadem. Quæ enim audiuntur, eadem dici necessum est. Quanquam uidentur hac voce magis urgeri omnes, minusq; posse excusari à suscipiendo euangelio, quòd ipsi illud audierint, & annunciatum ipsis fuerit. Qui non audierunt, excusari possent, & peccare non iudicaretur, id quod Rom. 10. indicatur. An non audierunt? Atqui in omne terram exiuit sonus eorum et in fines orbis terræ verba eorum. Et Ioan. 15. Si non venissem, & locutus fuissem eis, peccatū non haberent. Nunc autem non habent quod prætexant peccato suo. Non dissimile est, quod de gentilibus dicitur Romanos quòd inexcusabiles sint. Et proprie de Christo dicitur, quod sit audiendus, sicut Deuter. 18. de eo vaticinatus est Moses: Prophetā de gēte tua & de fratribus tuis, sicut me, suscitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus,ipsum audietis. Et paulò pòst Deus ibidem loquitur de eodē. Qui autem verba eius,quæ loquitur in nomine meo,audire noluerit,ego ultor existam. Quæ verba plane conueniunt præsenti loco.Et pater de Christo : Hic est filius meus dilectus,in quo mihi complacitum est,ipsum audite. Huc ergo videtur respexisse Apostolus,quando ait,attendendum esse diligenter his,quæ audita sunt nobis. Et Rom. 10. Fides est ex auditu,auditus autem per verbum Dei. Valde igitur apposita sunt vocabula, & mirè ad rem facientia,si quis exactius consideret. Quæ verò fuerunt illa audita? Sunt sanè eadem omnia ex his, quæ in euangelio & apostolicis literis sunt proposita,quæ tùm uiua uoce etiam passim omnibus Iudæis quotidie proponebantur, ut ea suscipe-rent & ample sterentur,tanquam ad salutem necessaria.
units.tr: The translator rendered [τοῖς ἀκουσθεῖσι] as "what has been said to us", whereas it should rather be "what has been heard by us". The sense is nevertheless the same, for what is heard must necessarily be said. Yet by this word all seem to be pressed more strongly, and less able to excuse themselves from receiving the gospel, since they themselves heard it and it was announced to them. Those who have not heard might be excused, and would not be judged to sin, as Romans 10 indicates: "Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." And John 15: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin." Similar is what is said of the Gentiles, that the Romans are without excuse. And it is said properly of Christ that he is to be heard, as Moses prophesied of him in Deuteronomy 18: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your own people and from your brothers, like me; you shall hear him." And a little later God speaks there of the same: "Whoever will not hear my words which he speaks in my name, I myself will be the avenger." These words agree plainly with this passage. And the Father says of Christ: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." It seems, then, that the Apostle had this in mind when he says that we must diligently attend to what has been heard by us. And Romans 10: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." The words are therefore very fittingly chosen and wonderfully suited to the matter, if one considers them more exactly. But what were those things that were heard? They are certainly the same as those set forth in the gospel and the apostolic letters, which were also proposed daily, by living voice, to all the Jews everywhere, so that they would receive them and be persuaded of them as necessary for salvation.

units.la: Ne quando persluamus) Ratio à periculoso: oportet nos multò diligentius attendere his, quæ audita sunt:quia,nisi id faciamus,periculum est, ne perfluamus , Chrysostomus interpretatur,ne pereamus , ne forsitan excidamus, putatq; allusum ad illud Prouerb.3. Fili mi ne effluant hæc ab oculis tuis : vbi græcè eadem vox usurpatur. Quidam sic interpretantur,quasi metaphora esset à papyro perfluida, quæ literas, quæ atramento inprimuntur,non retinet distinctas & perspicuas,sed quasi effluere sinit figu-ras,ut postea legi non facilè queant:& sic nos essemus similes tali papyro,sineremus q; uerba audita excidere,& tanquam infundibula,nihil liquoris uerbi diuini retineremus. Sed rectius retulerimus ad nostras personas,quòd uidelicet periculū sit, ne nos effluamus,id est,ne pereamus,in nihilū redigamur,absumamur.Ac metaphora sumpta est vel ab aquis celerrimè elabentibus,& præterfluentibus,siue in genere ab illis rebus,quę liquantur,& fluèdo cõsumũtur & euanescũt.Estq; ea similitudo etiá Scripturis usurpata: ut psal 67. Sicut fluit cera à facie ignis , sic pereunt peccatores à facie Dei . Et psal.57. sicut cera, quæ fluit,auferentur.Et ea vox aptissima est ad significandum subitum & facilem interitum,& sine omni recuperationis spe,qua significatur,nihil residui esse, quasi non fuerit.Et hæc significatio colligi debet ex his,quæ proximè sequenti argumento dicuntur de puniendis transgressoribus.Cæterũ quã uariè pereant siue profluant, & miserè consiciantur ij,qui nolunt ea,quæ dicta sunt per Christū, & de Christo per Apostolos credere, multis testimonijs scripturæ posset demõstrari. Nã alij fame, alij peste, alij ab immanib. bestijs,alij deniq;,alijs modis absumpti sunt:qua de re in cõclufione principa Ii huius primæ partis,agemus fusius. Satis fuerit,vno uerbo nuncadmonere, quemadmodum,cuius corpus cibo potuq; ad tempus priuatur,necesse est,eum lente consumi, tandemq; extinguitur:ita qui uerbum Dei,præcipueq; euangelium(quod est solidissimus cibus animæ)non recipit,fieri non potest,quin breui perfluat concidatq;.
units.tr: Lest at any time we drift away: this is an argument from danger. We ought to attend much more diligently to what has been heard, because, unless we do so, there is danger that we drift away. Chrysostom interprets it as "lest we perish", lest we perhaps fall away, and he thinks there is an allusion to Proverbs 3, "My son, let these things not slip from your eyes", where the same word is used in Greek. Some interpret it as if it were a metaphor from paper that lets moisture through, which does not keep the letters printed in ink distinct and clear, but lets the shapes run out, so that they cannot easily be read afterwards; and so we would be like such paper, allowing the words heard to escape, and, like funnels, we would retain nothing of the liquid of the divine word. But it is better to refer it to ourselves, namely that there is danger that we drift away, that is, that we perish, are reduced to nothing, and are consumed. The metaphor is taken either from waters swiftly gliding away and flowing past, or generally from things that melt and by flowing are consumed and vanish. This likeness is also used in Scripture, as in Psalm 68 (67): "As wax melts before the face of fire, so the wicked perish before the face of God", and Psalm 57: "like wax that melts, let them be taken away." This word is most apt for signifying a sudden and easy destruction, with no hope of recovery, by which it is meant that nothing remains, as if it had never been. This meaning ought to be gathered from what is said in the argument that immediately follows about the punishment of transgressors. Moreover, how variously those perish or drift away, and how miserably they are wasted, who are unwilling to believe what has been said through Christ and about Christ by the Apostles, could be shown by many testimonies of Scripture. For some have been consumed by famine, others by plague, others by savage beasts, and others finally by other means. On this matter we shall speak at greater length in the conclusion of the principal parts of this first part. It will suffice here to make a single point in a word: as one whose body is deprived of food and drink for a time must necessarily be slowly consumed and at last extinguished, so one who does not receive the word of God, and especially the gospel (which is the most solid food of the soul), cannot help but drift away and collapse in a short time.

units.la: Etenim si is qui per angelos dictus fuerat,sermo fuit firmus, & omnis transgressio & inobedientia,iustam præmij repensationem accepit:quo modo nos effugiemus,si tã-tam neglexerimus salutem?
units.tr: For if the word spoken through angels was firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we have neglected so great a salvation?

units.la: Comprobatio præcedentis rationis,à minore ad maius,in hunc modum: Lex quæ duntaxat per angelos data erat,fuit firma,& quicunque eam ausi sunt transgredi,vel cõtemnere,grauiter sunt puniti.Ergo multò magis euangeliũ,quod per ipsum Christum allatum est,erit firmũ,& quicunq; audebunt transgredi,vel contemnere,gravissimè punientur.Est Enthymema:sed quod nos crassius reddidimus, Apostolus elegantiori orationis figura,& uerbis magis idoneis expressit. Nam non dicit uno uerbo legem,sed ornatus gratia per periphrafin,sermonem, qui per angelos dictus est, ut hac locutionis forma admoneat quoq; considerare, euangelij esse tantò ampliorem dignitatem,quod id allatum sit per ipsum Christum . Et hic rursus respicit ad collationẽ Christi cum angelis,& argumenta,quibus probatum est,Christum esse maiorem Angelis. Deinde non nudè effert uocem euangelij,sed id intelligit nomine salutis, nimirum auxesi quadam euangelium uocans,non salutiferum modo,sed ipsam quoq; salutem, quã amplificare volés uocat etiam cum admiratione quadam, tantam salutem,quasi dicat, mul tò maximam & memorabilem.Et non dicit,si contempserimus,sed si neglexerimus,no tans,etiamsi tantùm supinitate quadam negligatur euangelium, nullo adhuc contemptu accedente,tamen negligentiam etiam haud fore impunitam . Nec sine caussa interserit,legem fuisse firmam:ea enim particula euangelij dignitatem tacitè illustrat.Vide ob secro;quàm grauiter ubiq; argumentetur Apostolus,& quàm concinniter singula membra argumentorum,imò uero & dictiones componat. Sed iam rationem omnium exactiorem reddemus.
units.tr: This is a proof of the preceding argument from the less to the greater, and runs as follows. The law, which was given only through angels, was firm, and those who dared to transgress or despise it were severely punished. Therefore the gospel, which was brought by Christ himself, will be much more firm, and those who dare to transgress or despise it will be punished most severely. This is an enthymeme. But where we have stated it rather crudely, the Apostle has expressed it in a more elegant figure of speech and with more fitting words. For he does not simply say "the law" in one word. Instead, for the sake of ornament, he uses a periphrasis, "the word spoken through angels," so that this form of expression also prompts us to consider that the dignity of the gospel is far greater, because it was brought through Christ himself. Here again he looks back to the comparison of Christ with the angels, and to the arguments by which it was proved that Christ is greater than the angels. Next, he does not bare the word "gospel" but understands it under the name of salvation, calling the gospel, by a kind of amplification, not only "salvific" but salvation itself. Wishing to magnify this, he says "so great a salvation," with a certain admiration, as if to say, "a most great and memorable one." And he does not say "if we have despised," but "if we have neglected." This is because even if the gospel is neglected through a kind of indolence, with no contempt yet added, negligence is nonetheless not to go unpunished. Nor without reason does he insert that the law was firm, for by that particle he tacitly sets off the dignity of the gospel. See, I beg you, how gravely the Apostle argues everywhere, and how neatly he arranges the individual members of his arguments, indeed even his individual words. But now we shall set out the whole reasoning more exactly.

units.la: Etenim si is,qui per angelos dictus fuerat sermio) Non omninò quidem malè accipiamus hæc verba generaliter de quibuscunq; uerbis seu dictis angelorũ à Deo missorum : sic enimg ChrysoChryfoftomus & alij eum secuti interpretantur. Nâ hoc quoq; constat, quòd, quæcũq; angeli locuti sunt, iussu Dei legati, ea omnia sunt adimpleta: sicut angeli Gen. 19. dixerũt ad Loth, fe missos, ut delerent urbe Sodomorum, & ita actum est. Item Gen. 18. angelus promisit Sarę filium, atq; ita quoq; completum, Gen. 21. describitur. Sic ad annunciandā natiuitatem Christi Mariæ uirgini, item pastoribus, missi angeli: & semper compertum est, ita euenisse, sicut dixerunt. Similiter constat, eos, qui sermonem ipsorum contemserunt, nunquam fuisse impunitos. Nam ut alios plures omittam, Zacharias, quia non credidit uoci angeli, (in re alias fecundum naturam difficili & impossibili) ad tempus loquendi potestatem amisit. Sed plures sunt rationes, & iustæ, quæ nos mouent ad accipiendum hæc uerba, pro periphrasi legis. Prima est, quòd oporteat hic respicere adid, q; proximè dixit: diligentius attendendũ his, quæ dicta sunt nobis: per dicta illa nihil aliud intelligens, quàm ea omnia, quæ ad id tempus de Christo, eius q; doctrina erant totimo do, atque ipsis Hebræis quoq; in euangelio proposita, ut susciperentur obseruaretur. Altera, quòd lex dicitur in Scripturis per angelos proprie tradita, & nomine sermonis παρ' ἀγγέλων, crebrò lex intelligitur. Quòd per angelos tradita fit, ad Galat. 3. Ordinata per angelos in manu intercessoris. Et Actor. 7. de Mose, Hic est, qui fuit in congregatione, in solitudine, cum angelo, qui loquebatur ei in monte Sina, & cum patribus nostris, qui accepit sermonem uiuum, ut daret nobis. Atq; in hoc ipso loco vides legem appellari sermonem. Et pfal. 118. Declaratio sermonum tuorum illuminat, & intellectum dat paruulis. Et capite sequenti: At nō profuit illis audiffe sermonem, quòd is non effet cum fide coniunctus ijs, qui audierant. Vbi sermo legem & promissiones significat.
units.tr: For if the word spoken through angels (sermo) — we need not wrongly take these words in a general sense, of any words or utterances of angels sent by God. So Chrysostom and others who followed him interpret them. For it is also certain that whatever the angels spoke as envoys of God, all of it was fulfilled by God's command. Thus the angels told Lot in Genesis 19 that they had been sent to destroy the city of Sodom, and so it was done. Likewise in Genesis 18 an angel promised Sarah a son, and in Genesis 21 it is described as having been fulfilled. So angels were sent to announce the birth of Christ to the virgin Mary, and likewise to the shepherds; and it has always been found that things turned out just as they said. Similarly, it is certain that those who despised their word were never unpunished. For, to omit many others, Zacharias, because he did not believe the voice of the angel (in a matter otherwise difficult and impossible by nature), lost the power of speech for a time. But there are several good and just reasons that move us to take these words as a periphrasis for the law. The first is that we must look here to what he has just said: "We must pay the closer attention to the things that have been said to us," understanding by those things nothing other than all that had been set forth in the gospel about Christ and his teaching, and to the Hebrews too, so that it might be received and observed. The second is that in the Scriptures the law is said to have been delivered properly through angels, and by the phrase "through angels" [παρ' ἀγγέλων] the law is often understood. That it was delivered through angels is stated in Galatians 3: "ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator." And in Acts 7, concerning Moses: "This is he who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living words to give to us." And in this very passage you see the law called "the word." Also Psalm 118: "The declaration of your words gives light and gives understanding to the simple." And in the following chapter: "But the hearing of the word did not profit them, because it was not joined with faith in those who heard." Here "word" signifies the law and the promises.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd de lege accipienda sint hæc uerba, liquet ex illis, quæ mox sequuntur in conclusione principali huius primæ partis, capite tertio, ubi clarius dicitur, legis contemptores in deserto graviter punitos. His igitur de causis rectè interpretabimur, per sermonem dictum ab angelis, legem significari. Quòd si quis roget: Si Apostolus ita voluit, quare ergo non expressit simpliciter uocè legis? Respondetur, id non fine graui & iusto consilio esse factum. Primò noluit adhuc in initio epistolæ offendere Iudæos, qui si audiuissent, legem apertius prædicari, minus prompti fuissent ad audiendum cætera, quæ restant. Et de abrogatione legis simul cũ sacerdotio, plenius & oportunius agit in secunda epistolæ parte. Præterea ualde conueniebat, huiusmodi periphrasi legem significare. Nâ ea facit, ut ratione antitheseos illustretur dignitas euangelij, ac statuamus protinus, euangelium hoc nomine esse præstantius lege, quòd illud nō per angelos, sed peripsum Christum sit allatum. Iâ uerò ualde prudenter addit, sermone per angelos datum fuisse firmum. Hinc statim oritur hæc ratiocinatio. Si lex fuit firma, rata, certa, stabilis: Ergo euangelium multò magis tale erit. Ita ex illa particula, noua collatio Euangelij cum lege nascitur. Dicitur autem lex firma, tum ratione autoris, quia Deus instituit; necessum est id firmum maneat, (sicut Gamaliel fatebatur, Actor. 5.) tum ratione signorum & miraculorum, quibus approbabatur: (fulgura enim, & tonitrua, & multa alia signa edebantur) tũ quia compleri oportet omnia, quæ in ea scripta sunt, seu præsignificata: iuxta illud Matth. 5. Iota unum aut unus apex non præteriet ex lege, quoad omnia facta fuerint. Item ad Gal. 4. Simili modo & euangelium firmum esse debet, quia ab eodem Deo patre profectum: sicut prima propositio habet præsentis epistolæ: Nouissimis hisce temporibus locutus est, inquit, nobis per filium. Præterea confirmatum signis & prodigijs: qua de re Apostolus ipse mox loquitur. Deinde omnia in eo proposita adimpleri debent: sicut adimpleta est spiritus Sancti missio, regni Christi spiritualis propagatio, peccatorũ remissio, deniq; alia innumera, quæ in euangelio facienda & perficienda proponuntur. Effectus ipsi & fructus euangelij satis docent, quanto illud sit confirmatius & potentius ipsa lege. Potentia enim Dei est in salutem omni credenti.
units.tr: Thirdly, that these words are to be taken of the law is clear from what immediately follows in the main conclusion of this first part, in the third chapter, where it is said more plainly that the despisers of the law were severely punished in the wilderness. For these reasons, then, we rightly interpret "the word spoken by angels" as signifying the law. But if someone asks: if the Apostle meant this, why did he not simply express the word "law"? The answer is that this was done for a weighty and just purpose. First, he did not wish, at the very beginning of the letter, to offend the Jews, who, if they had heard the law preached more openly, would have been less ready to hear the rest that remains. He treats of the abrogation of the law, together with the priesthood, more fully and more opportunely in the second part of the letter. Moreover, it was very fitting to signify the law by such a periphrasis. For it makes the dignity of the gospel shine out by way of antithesis, and we immediately conclude that the gospel is more excellent than the law in this respect, that it was brought not through angels but through Christ himself. Then, very wisely, he adds that the word given through angels was firm. From this there immediately arises the following reasoning: if the law was firm, valid, certain and stable, then the gospel will be much more so. Thus from that particle a new comparison of the gospel with the law arises. The law is called firm, moreover, partly on account of its author, because God instituted it, and it must necessarily remain firm (as Gamaliel acknowledged in Acts 5); partly on account of the signs and miracles by which it was confirmed (for lightnings, thunders and many other signs were displayed); and partly because all that was written in it, or foreshadowed in it, must be fulfilled, according to the saying in Matthew 5: "One jot or one tittle shall not pass from the law until all things have been done." Likewise Galatians 4. In the same way the gospel too ought to be firm, because it proceeded from the same God the Father, as the opening proposition of this letter has it: "In these last times he has spoken to us through the Son." Furthermore, it was confirmed by signs and wonders, a point the Apostle himself takes up immediately after. Then, all the things set forth in it must be fulfilled, as the sending of the Holy Spirit has been fulfilled, the spiritual propagation of the kingdom of Christ, the forgiveness of sins, and countless other things that the gospel proposes to be done and accomplished. The effects and fruits of the gospel itself teach sufficiently how much more confirmed and powerful it is than the law itself. For "the power of God is for salvation to everyone who believes."

units.la: Et omnis transgressio & inobedientia iustam præmij repensationem accepit:
units.tr: And every transgression and disobedience has received a just recompense of reward:

units.la: Potuissen t duo Enthymemata consarcinari: alterũ ex præcedēti uerbo: Lex fuit firma: ergo euangeliũ multò magis debet esse firmũ. Deinde alterũ ex præsentib. uerbis: Omnis trangresfio & inobedientia erga legem fuit punita: Ergo multò magis punietur transgressio euangelij. Sed maluimus breuitatis caussa totam sententiam in vnum Enthymema contrahere. Prudenter uerò extulit ista uniuersaliter: et omnis: Nam in hac breui adhortatione, plane urget & impellit Hebreos ad honorandum Christum & euangelium, & significat hac locutionis forma, prorsus neminem euasurum, qui euangelium contemnet. Ac prodest ita uniuersaliter efferri, quæ ad comminationes erga malos, vel promissiones erga bonos pertinent: sicut licet hoc in scripturis obseruare: Deuteron. 27. Execrabilis omnis, qui nō manserit in omnib. quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea. Ioel 2. Et erit, omnis quicunque inuocauerit
units.tr: Two enthymemes could have been put together: one from the preceding words, "the law was firm, therefore the gospel must be much more firm"; and another from the present words, "every transgression and disobedience against the law was punished, therefore the transgression of the gospel will be punished much more." But for the sake of brevity I preferred to compress the whole sentiment into a single enthymeme. The author wisely stated these things universally, and every. For in this short exhortation he plainly urges and impels the Hebrews to honour Christ and the gospel, and this form of expression signifies that no one will escape who despises the gospel. It is useful to state in this universal way what pertains to threats against the wicked or promises to the good, as one may observe in Scripture: Deut. 27. Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them. Joel 2. And it shall be, that everyone who calls

units.la: Rom. 1. ; Luc. 1. ; Periphrasis legis, 1. ratio; 2. Lex per angelos tradita; 3. Legis contemptores puniti in deserto; Obiectio. Solutio. 1. 2. Euangelium lege firmius. Cur lex firma dicatur. 1. ratio ab autore Dei. 2. ratione signorum. 3. ratione compleiionis. uocauerit nomen Domini, saluus erit. Ratio autem est: quia Deus iudicat sine respectu personarum.
units.tr: Rom. 1.; Luke 1.; Periphrasis of the law: first reason; second, the law delivered through angels; third, the despisers of the law punished in the wilderness. Objection. Answer. (1) and (2) The gospel is firmer than the law. Why the law is called firm: first reason, from its author, God; second, from the signs; third, from its completeness. on the name of the Lord shall be saved. The reason is that God judges without respect of persons.

units.la: Caeterùm vbi interpres habet transgressio & inobedientia, graece legitur, ἡ πᾶσα παραβασις ἡ παράκουσις: aliqua tamen exemplaria variant: quaedam enim habent παράφασις, quae vox significat detrectationem vel responsationem, qualis est hominum inuitè & non nisi coacte agentium aliquid, quo malo plerunque laborant serui. Sed si legamus per β, παραβασις, recte uertitur transgressio. Utraque vox quadrat instituto, ideoque usum fuit, saltem admonere uarię lectionis: nos tamen interpretis lectionem retinebimus. Transgressio igitur & inobedientia, duo sunt grauissima uitia, quaeq; damnationem filijs contumacibus adferunt, dum transgrediuntur ac praetereunt ea, quae sunt uetita: aut nolunt facere ex animo ea, quae sunt demandata.
units.tr: But where the translator has transgression and disobedience, the Greek reads ἡ πᾶσα παραβασις ἡ παράκουσις [he pasa parabasis he parakousis]. Some copies vary, however: some have παράφασις [paraphasis], a word which signifies refusal or evasion, such as that of men who do something unwillingly and only under compulsion, a fault to which slaves are very often prone. But if we read it with β, παραβασις [parabasis] is rightly rendered transgression. Both words suit the purpose, and so it has been useful at least to point out the variant reading; yet we shall retain the translator's reading. Transgression and disobedience are therefore two most grievous sins, which bring damnation upon stubborn children, when they transgress and pass over the things that are forbidden, or are unwilling to do from the heart the things that are commanded.

units.la: Ita enim transgressio ad uetita recte referri videtur, obedientia uero ad iussa. Neq; enim solùm peccatur transgrediendo prohibita, & faciendo male, sed etiam non faciendo bene. Atque ideo Scriptura aliquoties ita inculcat, Declina à malo, & fac bonum, inquire veritatem & prosequere eam. Non sufficit, non esse transgressorem: sed requiritur praeterea, ut simus obedientes ad promptè agendum bona.
units.tr: For transgression seems rightly to refer to what is forbidden, and obedience to what is commanded. For we sin not only by transgressing prohibitions and doing evil, but also by not doing good. And so Scripture often presses this: Turn away from evil, and do good; seek truth and follow after it. It is not enough not to be a transgressor; it is required besides that we be obedient, ready to do good works.

units.la: Iustam praemij repensationem) δίκαιον μισθαποδοσίαν, δίκαιον, quod lege est decretum: sicut lex quoque fert uarijs in locis horribiles sententias in omnes transgressores: Anima quae peccauerit, ipsa morietur. Et Deuteronom. capite uicesimo septimo & uicesimo octauo, plena sunt omnia execrationibus & maledictionibus in legis transgressores. Atque opus est in lege tanta seueritate, quia aliàs mali nō possent coerceri. Aduertendumque, quòd temporales illae execrationes includunt etiam damnationem aeternam, suntq; huius praenunciae & significationes: quare omninò maius quiddam hic oportet concipere animo, quàm simpliciter uerba sonant: neque duntaxat respicere, quomodo patres ceciderint in deserto, aut alijs locis, propter neglectam seu contemptam legem: sed multò magis, quomodo aeternum sint damnati: quae grauitas supplicij omnes ad suscipiendū euangelium debet inuitare, imò compellere. Quò etiam ualde conuenit, quòd dixerit: quomodo nos effugiemus? Significat enim haec uox, ualde horribilem esse, metuendamque iram Dei, & omnes, si qua possent rimula, lubenter effugere euadereq; uelle. Sed adeò proculextendi Dei manum, ut effugere nulla arte, nullis consilijs vlli possint. Pertinet huc, quòd impij Ecclesiastici 23. & psalm. 93. consilia ineunt, & confidunt, quòd Dominus nō videat eos. Matth 3. Ioannes concionabatur, ut fugerent à uentura ira, quoniam securis ad radicem posita erat. Fugiunt autem, qui sapiunt, & boni sunt, dum resipiscunt, & in uiam redeunt. Si neglexerimus, ἀμελήσαντες. Quare dicit, si neglexerimus? Et non si contempserimus, uel huiusmodi? Quia indicare uult non tantum damnari contemptum, siue occultum, siue manifestum: sed etiam simplicem negligentiam, & ad credendum tarditatem. Atq; ita multò maximè urget omnes, ut euangelium suscipiant, & serió amplectantur. Non magna res uidetur, esse negligentem, & tamen ob hoc tantillū malum imminet damnatio. Propterea reprehendit Christus discipulos, vocans eos stultos & tardos corde ad credendum, Lucae 24. Rursus Lucę 18. in parabola, Seruus sciens uoluntatem Domini sui, & non praeparans se, nec faciens secundum uoluntatem eius, plagis uapulabit multis. Hierem. 43. Maledictus, qui facit opus suum negligenter. Ex his liquet, non solū damnationem paratam esse ijs, qui, cū euangelium ipsis annunciatur, & offertur, reijciunt, uel contemnunt, siue aperte, siue clàm: sed illis quoq;, qui, cū neq; contemnant, neq; reijciant, tamen non seriò & ex toto corde se illi addicunt. Sed multò magis urget & impellit omnium animos, ad euangelium magnificiendum & religiosè obseruādum, quòd id uocat, tanta salutem: in utraq; uoce mirabilis emphasis & auxesis est. Certè nusquam lex adeò honorifico nomine illustratur. Lex enim non adduxit ad perfectionem seu salutem: sed id facit solum euangelium, ac propterea salus appellatur, & quidem tanta, id est, ualde magna, quanta nunquam alibi fuit proposita uel exhibita. Rom. 1. Euangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Luc. 1. Praebis ante faciem Domini, ad parandum uias eius, ad dandum scientiam salutis populo ipsius, per remissionem peccatorum eius. En euangelium uocatur scientia salutis, quia praedicat remissionem peccatorum. Actor. 13. Vobis Iudaeis sermo salutis missus est. Rectè ergo euangelium salus appellatur, & quidem ualde magna: quandoquidem, si bonorum genus intuemur, adfertur in eo salus spiritualis, animarum, omnibus expos-ita, aeterna, & coelestis, quibus quid amplius bonorum optari queat? In summa, adnotat Chryosomus, hoc argumentum prudentissimè esse & propositum, & tractatum. Eo enim sic conuinci & percuti omnes, qui detrectant euangelium recipere, ut eos fere cogat contra seipsos damnadamnationis ferre sententiam, ni illud recipiant. Quomodo & Nathan parabola proposita arguit convincitq; Dauidem: itern Christus parabola proposita de eo, qui miserat filium ad vinitores, quem & occiderunt, quid, inquit, faciat in eos Dominus vineæ? Quo verbo Iudæos crucifixores Christi compellit ad fatendum suum crimen. Plurimum virium habent huiusmodi argumenta, tam in disputationibus, quàm deliberationibus.
units.tr: The just recompense of reward: δίκαιον μισθαποδοσίαν [dikaion misthapodosian], a just recompense, which has been decreed by the law. So the law too in various places pronounces dreadful sentences on all transgressors: The soul that sins, it shall die. And in Deuteronomy chapters 27 and 28 everything is full of curses and maledictions against the transgressors of the law. And the law must be so severe, because otherwise the wicked could not be restrained. It must be noted that those temporal curses also include eternal damnation and are its foreshadowings and signs; so we must conceive in our minds something greater than the words simply sound, and not only consider how the fathers fell in the wilderness or elsewhere on account of neglected or despised law, but much more how they were eternally condemned. The gravity of this punishment ought to invite all, indeed compel them, to receive the gospel. It also fits very well that he said: how shall we escape? For this word signifies that the wrath of God is very terrible and to be feared, and that all would gladly flee and wish to escape it, if any chink were open. But the hand of God extends so far that no one can escape by any art or any counsel. To this pertains what the impious do in Ecclesiasticus 23 and Psalm 93: they form plans and trust that the Lord does not see them. Matt. 3. John preached that they should flee from the coming wrath, since the axe was laid to the root of the tree. Those who are wise and good flee, when they repent and return to the way. If we neglect, ἀμελήσαντες [amelesantes]. Why does he say, if we neglect? And not, if we despise, or something of the kind? Because he wishes to indicate that not only contempt is condemned, whether hidden or open, but also simple negligence and slowness to believe. And so he urges all the more strongly that all should receive the gospel and embrace it earnestly. Being negligent seems no great matter, and yet damnation hangs over even such a small evil. For this reason Christ rebukes the disciples, calling them foolish and slow of heart to believe (Luke 24). Again, Luke 18, in the parable: the servant who knew his master's will, and did not prepare himself nor act according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. Jer. 48 (43): Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently. From these things it is clear that damnation is prepared not only for those who, when the gospel is announced and offered to them, reject or despise it, openly or secretly, but also for those who, though they neither despise nor reject it, nevertheless do not devote themselves to it earnestly and with their whole heart. But even more strongly does it urge and impel the minds of all to magnify the gospel and observe it reverently, in that it calls it so great salvation: there is a wonderful emphasis and amplification in both words. Certainly nowhere is the law honoured with such a noble name. For the law did not bring to perfection or to salvation; the gospel alone does this, and therefore it is called salvation, and indeed so great, that is, very great, as was never set forth or exhibited elsewhere. Rom. 1.: The gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Luke 1.: You shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people, through the remission of their sins. Behold, the gospel is called the knowledge of salvation, because it proclaims the remission of sins. Acts 13.: To you Jews the word of salvation has been sent. Rightly, then, the gospel is called salvation, and indeed very great salvation: since, if we consider the kinds of good things, there is brought in it a spiritual salvation of souls, offered to all, eternal and heavenly; what more of good things could be wished for? In sum, Chrysostom observes that this argument is most wisely both set forth and treated. For by it all those who refuse to receive the gospel are so convicted and struck that it almost compels them to pronounce sentence of damnation against themselves, unless they receive it. So also Nathan, by a proposed parable, convicted and refuted David; and likewise Christ, by a parable proposed about the man who sent his son to the vinedressers, whom they also killed: what, he says, will the lord of the vineyard do to them? By this word he compels the Jews, the crucifiers of Christ, to acknowledge their crime. Arguments of this kind have great force, both in disputations and in deliberations.

units.la: Cæterùm habemus hic etiam variam doctrinam. Primò enim quando euangelium describitur à Christo ipso allatum, à Deo patre per signa & uaria dona Spiritus confirmatum: quando item uocatur salus: habemus hic mirabilem excellentiam euangelij, omnesque valde excitari debemus ad id toto animo amplectendum, honorandum, defendendum.
units.tr: Moreover, we have here also a varied teaching. First, when the gospel is described as brought by Christ himself, confirmed by God the Father through signs and various gifts of the Spirit; and likewise when it is called salvation: here we have a wonderful excellence of the gospel, and we ought all to be greatly stirred to embrace, honour and defend it with our whole soul.

units.la: Deinde, quando generaliter hic effertur, omnem transgresionem & inobedientiâ grauissimè à Deo puniri, discant hinc mali & duri homines metuere iram Dei, si ipsi euangelio, quando synceriter traditur seu proponitur, quacunque ratione conantur resistere.
units.tr: Next, when it is stated here in general that every transgression and disobedience is most gravely punished by God, let wicked and hard-hearted men learn from this to fear the wrath of God, if they try in any way to resist the gospel itself, when it is sincerely delivered or set forth.

units.la: Tertiò, quia ex eo, quod dicitur, etiam negligentiam puniendam, & non solùm contemptum apertum uel occultum, materiam arripere debent segnes & tardi homines, ad excitandum seipsos, ut alacriores sint ad res diuinas, in quibus tota salus animarum sita est.
units.tr: Thirdly, because it is said that even negligence is to be punished, and not only open or secret contempt, lazy and sluggish people should take this as a reason to rouse themselves to be more eager for divine matters, on which the whole salvation of souls depends.

units.la: Quæ cum primùm enarrari cœperit per ipsum Dominum, ab his, qui audierant, in nos confirmata fuit, attestante Deo & signis & prodigijs simul, uarijsq; virtutibus, & spiritus sancti distributionibus, iuxta ipsius voluntatem.
units.tr: Which, having at the first begun to be spoken through the Lord himself, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, God also bearing witness both with signs and wonders, and with various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will.

units.la: Aliæ rationes comprobantes, quod euangelium sit suscipiendum, constanterque retinendum, ab ipsius præstantia & maiestate, quam ex duabus rebus uult colligi: nempe quòd euangelium sit per ipsum Deum, uidelicet Christum, allatum & publicè enarratum: deinde multis modis ab ipso Deo confirmatum. Atque ita tam excellens, tam certum, tam firmum ostenditur, ut de eius autoritate & fide, dubitari nullo pacto queat, sed tantum & ardentissimis uotis apprehendi debeat. Modos autem, quibus id confirmatum sit, enumerat signa & prodigia: deinde varias uirtutes, & spiritus Sancti distributiones. Hæc breuiter ab Apostolo quasi punctis quibusdam indicantur. Sed eadem mirificè amplificant euangelij dignitatem, & argumentorum suppellex non parua arripi indepossit. Nunc partes explicemus.
units.tr: There are other reasons proving that the gospel is to be received and steadfastly held, drawn from its excellence and majesty, which the author wants inferred from two things: namely, that the gospel was brought and publicly declared by God himself, that is, Christ, and then was confirmed in many ways by God himself. And so it is shown to be so excellent, so certain, and so firm that there can be no doubt at all about its authority and trustworthiness, but it ought to be grasped with the most ardent prayers. He lists the signs and wonders as the means by which it was confirmed, and then the various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle indicates these briefly, as it were by certain points. But these same things greatly enlarge the dignity of the gospel, and no small store of arguments may be drawn from them. Now let us explain the parts.

units.la: Quæ cum primùm enarrari cœperit per ipsum Dominum) Hæc est magna dignitas euangelij, quòd id non sit enarratum, siue in lucem productum, per homines aliquos, sicut multa per philosophos & acutos homines, primùm sunt in mundo inuenta, & sicut cum autoribus suis nata, ita simul cum ijsdem collapsa: non item per angelos, per quos omnia in ueteri testamento, quæ ad uoluntatem Dei aperiendam hominibus pertinebant, sunt perfacta, sed per ipsum Dominum, uidelicet Christum Iesum, qui proprie ad id à Deo patre in terram missus fuerat. Atque hic habenda ratio antitheseos, hoc est, consideranda quomodo lex nullo pacto euangelio æquari posit, utpote, quæ duntaxat lata sit per angelos ministros: istud uerò per ipsum Dominum. Ita enim vox Domini, opponitur ministris, qui sunt ministri, sicut in argumentis præcedentibus non obscurè demonstrauimus.
units.tr: Which, having at the first begun to be spoken through the Lord himself. This is the great dignity of the gospel, that it was not declared, or brought into the light, through any men, as many things were first discovered in the world through philosophers and clever men, and, just as they were born together with their authors, so they fell together with them. Nor was it done through angels, through whom everything in the Old Testament that pertained to revealing the will of God to men was carried out, but through the Lord himself, namely Christ Jesus, who had been sent into the earth by God the Father expressly for this purpose. Here the contrast must be taken into account, that is, we should consider how the law can in no way be made equal to the gospel, since the law was only given through angels as ministers, but the gospel through the Lord himself. For the word "Lord" is set over against the ministers, who are servants, as we have clearly shown in the preceding arguments.

units.la: Et consultò usus est Apostolus hac voce Dominus: non enim ratione antitheseos tantùm, sed etiam ad exprimendam Christi diuinitatem: si dixisset, per Iesum Christum, magnum quidem id fuisset, quando eundem esse Deum, iam satis est probatum: sed quando uocat illum simpliciter Dominum, statim diuinam maiestatem, omnium audientiû animis ingerit: atque omnes mouentur ad tantò honorificentius sentiendum de euangelio, quod audiunt, illud per ipsum Dominum esse in mundum allatum. Non caret emphasi pronomen ipsum, monet enim, vocabulum Domini non de alio, quàm de Christo ut Deo accipiendum. Unde & creberrimè vocatur in scripturis, Euangelium Dei, alias euangelium Iesu Christi, nimirum, quia à Deo patre est constitutum, & per Christum Deum propalatum, & quomodocunque accipiamus, soli Deo ut autori & manifestatori acceptum ferendum. Sed nec sine iudicio factum, quòd dixerit, enarrari: significat enim uox hæc, clarè & perspicuè propositum esse euangelium, atque omnibus manifestatum, ut excusari ab eis cognitione & suscèptione, nulli possint. Euangelium non occultè aut fraudulenter inductum est, sicut solent ab impijs clanculum spargi impia dogmata: sed palàm, in tectis (sic enim Matth.10. Christus ait: Quod dico uobis in tenebris, dicite in luce, & quod in aurem audistis, prædicate in tectis) coram omnibus barbaris & Græcis, sapientibus & insipientibus, Iudæis & gentibus, magnis & paruis. De euangelio omni sana doctrina illud rectissimè dici potest:Veritas non quærit angulum: Videtur autem re spexisse ad illud, quòd Ioan. primo habetur, Deum nemo uidit unquam, unigenitus filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrauit. Quanquam est apud Ioannem, ἐξηγήσατο, hoc autem loco est λαλεῖσθαι: quòd uerbum licet plerunque significet, temerè & inconsideratè garrire, tamen hoc loco, & interdum aliis significat apertè & palàm loqui.
units.tr: The Apostle used this word "Lord" deliberately: not only for the sake of the contrast, but also to express the divinity of Christ. If he had said "through Jesus Christ," it would indeed have been a great thing, since it has already been sufficiently proved that he is God. But when he calls him simply "Lord," he at once impresses the divine majesty on the minds of all who hear, and all are moved to think far more honourably of the gospel they hear, that it was brought into the world through the Lord himself. The pronoun "himself" is not without emphasis, for it warns that the word "Lord" must be understood of no one but Christ as God. Hence also in the Scriptures he is very often called "the gospel of God," and elsewhere "the gospel of Jesus Christ," doubtless because it was established by God the Father, and declared through Christ God, and however we take it, must be credited to God alone as its author and revealer. Nor was it without reason that he said "declared." For this word signifies that the gospel has been set forth clearly and plainly and made manifest to all, so that no one can excuse himself from knowing and accepting it. The gospel was not brought in secretly or deceitfully, as impious doctrines are usually spread stealthily by the wicked; but openly, "in the housetops" (for so Christ says in Matt. 10: "What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light, and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops"), before all, barbarians and Greeks, wise and foolish, Jews and Gentiles, great and small. Of the gospel, as of all sound doctrine, this may most rightly be said: Truth does not seek a corner. He seems to have had in view what is written in John 1: No one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him. Although in John the word is exēgēsato [ἐξηγήσατο], here it is lalēsthai [λαλεῖσθαι]. Although this verb usually means to chatter rashly and thoughtlessly, in this place, and sometimes elsewhere, it means to speak openly and plainly.

units.la: Quòd autem ait, cùm primùm enarrari cœpit, per uocem primùm notatur præfinitum illud tempus, quo euangelium cœptum est publicè per ipsum Christum annunciari in terris, sicut euangelistæ omnes narrant, quòd postquam tentatus fuisset, cœperit prædicare euangelium, & dicere: Resipiscite, inflat enim regnum cœlorum: Matthæi quarto, & Marci primo. Aliàs enim euangelium ab æterno fuit constitutum à Deo patre, sicut Ephesior. primo dicitur, Patefacto nobis arcano uoluntatis suæ, iuxta beneplacitum suum, quod proposuerat in seipso, usque ad dispensationem plenitudinis temporum, ut summatim instaurare t omnia per Christum. Et fuit idem promissum statim ipsi Adamo, quando dictum est, Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis: deinde Abrahamo, qui audiuit, in semine suo benedicendas omnes gentes: tum Dauidi alijsque, ac deinceps sæpe per diuersos prophetas in scripturis promissum, Romanorum primo. sed semel tandem per ipsum Christum palàm enarratum, & toti mundo expositum. Est autem & hæc dignitas euangelij mirabilis, quòd sit æternum, ab æterno uidelicet à Deo patre ordinatum: deinde, nunc sic stabilitum & propagatum, ut nulla alia doctrina excelentior ei succedere, neque unquam aboleri aut abrogari possit.
units.tr: When he says at the first begun to be declared, the word "first" marks the set time at which the gospel began to be publicly proclaimed on earth by Christ himself, as all the evangelists relate: that after he had been tempted, he began to preach the gospel and say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matt. 4 and Mark 1). For otherwise the gospel had been established from eternity by God the Father, as is said in Ephesians 1: Having made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he had purposed in himself, unto the dispensation of the fullness of times, that he might gather together all things in Christ. And the same promise was given at once to Adam himself, when it was said: The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent; then to Abraham, who heard that in his seed all nations would be blessed; then to David and others, and afterwards often promised through various prophets in the Scriptures (Rom. 1), but at last once for all declared openly through Christ himself and set forth to the whole world. This dignity of the gospel is also remarkable: that it is eternal, ordained from eternity by God the Father; and then that it is now so established and spread that no other doctrine more excellent could succeed it, nor could it ever be abolished or repealed.

units.la: Ab his, qui audierant, in nos confirmata fuit Hæc uerba uariè explicantur. Primùm, sic nonnulli accipiunt, ut sit sententia, quod autor epistolæ huius fatetur, doctrinam euangelicam in se quoque confirmatam esse, ab illis, qui Christum ipsum audierant, hoc est, se edoctum & confirmatum in euangelio ab apostolis.
units.tr: Confirmed to us by those who heard him. These words are explained in various ways. First, some take them to mean that the author of this letter confesses that the evangelical doctrine was also confirmed in himself by those who had heard Christ himself, that is, that he himself was taught and confirmed in the gospel by the apostles.

units.la: Atque ita colligere hinc uolunt, epistolam hanc non esse Pauli Apostoli, sed alterius cuiuspiam: quando Paulus nullo modo fateri uult ad Galatas primo, se ab homine, uel ab Apostolis ipsis quicquam didicisse. Sed ut comprobetur, hanc epistolam esse ipsius Pauli, aliter hunc locum, & minimè torte uel oblique exponunt. Vno modo, ut significetur, apostolum dicere, quòd doctrina euangelica sit primùm annunciata à Christo: deinde ab Apostolis: postremò in ipsum quoque confirmata: unde ab his, qui audierant, perinde, ac si diceret, post illos, qui Christum uiua uoce concionantem audierant, & similiter cum illo vixerant. Quem in modum alibi quoque ait, se post cæteros apostolos ad munus apostolatus diuinitùs uocatum & confirmatum. Quod uerò, ab his, significet, post hos, latinis auribus non est inusitatum. Plinius ait, præcipuum stercus columbarum, proximum caprarum, ab hoc ouium. Et apud Græcos ἀρχὴν, & τέλος, hæ uoces mutuò se respiciunt, & ordinem significant, sicut apud Latinos primum & secundum.
units.tr: From this they wish to infer that this letter is not by the Apostle Paul but by someone else, since Paul in Galatians 1 in no way wants to admit that he learned anything from a man, or even from the apostles themselves. But in order to prove that this letter is by Paul himself, they explain this passage otherwise, and not at all in a forced or indirect way. In one way, so that it is understood that the apostle means that the evangelical doctrine was first announced by Christ, then by the apostles, and finally confirmed in himself too; so that "by those who heard" is as if he said "after those who had heard Christ preaching with the living voice and had lived with him in the same way." In the same manner he says elsewhere that he himself was called and confirmed by God to the office of apostle after the other apostles. That "by these" means "after these" is not unusual to Latin ears. Pliny says the chief dung is that of doves, next that of goats, and after this that of sheep. And among the Greeks archēn [ἀρχὴν] and telos [τέλος] look to each other and signify order, just as among the Latins "first" and "second" do.

units.la: Sententia ergo est: Euangelium primum enarratum esse ab ipso Christo: deinde ab apostolis, qui ipsum audierant: post hos uerò idem factum ab ipso Paulo. Theophylactus autem uidetur non simpliciter reijcere, quòd apostolus hic diceret, se ab alijs in doctrina euangelica confirmatum. Nam licet alibi Apostolus studiosè docuerit, se ab apostolis nequaquam edoctum: id quidem ita res poscebat, apud eos, qui de eius apostolatu dubitabant, quibusque per aduersarios persuasum erat, ipsum non fuisse legitimum apostolum, sed tantùm apostolorum discipulum. Verùm hoc apud eos, qui de apostolatu eius non dubitabant, non multum referebat, si se quodammodo ab alijs confirmatum fateretur. Potest etiam ita reddi, ut accipiamus, Apostolum dicere, doctrinam euangelicam, quam ipse iussu & imitatione Christi annunciabat, confirmatam & approbatam esse ut ueram, ab omnibus illis, qui eandem ex ipso Christo audierant, atque nihil aliud, quàm ab aliorum apostolorum testimonio & suffragio suam doctrinam obiter commendaret.
units.tr: The sense therefore is: the gospel was first declared by Christ himself; then by the apostles, who had heard him; and after these, the same was done by Paul himself. Theophylact, however, does not seem simply to reject the idea that the apostle here says he was confirmed in the evangelical doctrine by others. For although elsewhere the Apostle carefully taught that he had by no means been taught by the apostles, this was indeed required by the situation among those who doubted his apostleship, and who had been persuaded by his adversaries that he was not a true apostle but only a disciple of the apostles. But among those who did not doubt his apostleship, it would not matter much if he admitted that he was in some sense confirmed by others. It can also be rendered so that we understand the Apostle to say that the evangelical doctrine, which he himself announced by the command and example of Christ, was confirmed and approved as true by all those who had heard it from Christ himself, and that he was simply, in passing, commending his own doctrine by the testimony and support of the other apostles.

units.la: Aliter uerò exponunt hunc locum, non de persona Pauli, sed generaliter de omnibus qui euangelium amplexi fuissent ad id usque tempus: quasi diceretur, Doctrina euangelica postquam semel annunciari cœpit per ipsum Christum, statim ab omnibus, qui audierunt, confirmata, id est, credita, approbata, & suscepta est, atque etiam in nos, id est, ad nos usque & nostra tempora. Idque eò magis, quòd Deus etiam testimonium ferretilli doctrinæ per signa & miracula, ut nullus reijcere eam aut dubitare de eius excellentia & maiestate potuerit. Sic uerò Apostolus cùm dicit nos, non tantùm suam personam intelligit, sed omnes simul credentes: & humilitatis causa se alijs etiam peccatoribus crebrò annumerat. Atque hæc ominum simplicissima uidetur interpretatio, Chrysostomo accepta, & à Primasio quoque expressa. Tametsi confirmatam etiam interpretantur. tantur solidam, perfectam, ratam, & æternam, quemadmodum suprà dictum est, quòd sermo per angelos dictus fuit βεβαιος, id est, firmus: ac propterea statui debet, multò firmius esse euangelium. Vnde interpres Chrysostomi, Quid est, confirmata est? Credita atq; perfecta est? Pignus, inquit, habemus, hoc est, non extincta, non diminuta est salus, quæ nobis attribuit, sed permanet & præualet in æternum. Est autem magna dignitas euangelij, quòd ita firma & perfecta sit, ut infirmari nulla potentia diaboli aut mundi possit.
units.tr: Others explain this passage differently: not of Paul's own person, but generally of all who had embraced the gospel up to that time. It is as if it were said: "The gospel doctrine, once it began to be announced through Christ himself, was at once confirmed by all who heard it, that is, believed, approved and received, and so it was also confirmed among us, that is, down to us and our own times. This was all the more so because God also bore witness to that doctrine through signs and miracles, so that no one could reject it or doubt its excellence and majesty." When the Apostle says "us," he understands not only himself but all believers together, and out of humility he often counts himself among other sinners. This seems to be the simplest interpretation of all, and it was accepted by Chrysostom and also expressed by Primasius. Some also interpret "confirmed" as "solid, perfect, fixed and eternal," just as above it was said that the word spoken through angels was [βεβαιος], that is, firm; and so it must be held that the gospel is far firmer. Hence the interpreter of Chrysostom asks: "What is 'confirmed'? Believed and perfected? We have," he says, "a pledge; that is, the salvation given to us is not extinguished or diminished, but remains and prevails forever." The dignity of the gospel is great, in that it is so firm and perfect that no power of the devil or the world can weaken it.

units.la: Attestante Deo) En altera ratio dignitatis euangelij, quòd videlicet Deus multis modis illud comprobarit. Sic autem Deus semper verbo suo addidit alia externa testimonia, quibus verbum suum comprobaret: vt, cum Abrahamo promitteretur semen, cum Mosen vocaret ad libe-randum populum, cum legem daret: sic deniq; alias creberrimè, & in euangelica historia Christus quoq;, postquam præclarè docuit, semper subiunxit protinus miraculum.
units.tr: "God bearing witness": here is another reason for the dignity of the gospel, namely that God confirmed it in many ways. For God always added to his word other external testimonies by which he would confirm it: as when the seed was promised to Abraham, when he called Moses to free the people, when he gave the law. So too, very often in the gospel history, Christ, after teaching brilliantly, always immediately added a miracle.

units.la: Id autem ita, duabus potissimum de causis. Primò, quia humana infirmitas, quæ difficulter vult credere, debet signis externis induci ad credendum, & ita confirmari. Secundò, quia ipse ita vult probare suâ potentiâ, ac certù facere, quòd reuera possit ea præstare, quæ ipse loquitur. Vnde signa omnia semper superant naturæ facultatem, & amplissimâ Dei potestate declarât. Atq; hic generaliter adhuc uoco signa, quæcunq; exterius percipiuntur supra naturæ ordinem posita, & ad confirmationem verbi Dei, siue doctrina adiecta atq; edita: cuiusmodi signa præcipua in nouo testamento fuerunt miracula & dona spiritus sancti: nam ta hęc, quæ illa pariter ad confirmandum, & ad mouendos hominum animos sunt idonea. Et sicut utraq; aptissima sunt ad declarandam Dei potentiam, & confirmandum eius dicta, tu utraq; utilitate hominib. maximâ adferunt.
units.tr: This was done chiefly for two reasons. First, because human weakness, which finds it hard to believe, must be led to belief by external signs and so be confirmed. Second, because he himself wishes thereby to prove his power and to make certain that he really can do what he says. Hence all signs surpass the capacity of nature and declare the most ample power of God. Here I use the word "signs" generally, for whatever is perceived externally, placed above the order of nature, and serving to confirm the word of God, or the doctrine added and set forth. The principal such signs in the New Testament were miracles and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, for both are equally suited to confirm and to move men's minds. Just as both are most apt for declaring God's power and confirming his words, so both bring the greatest benefit to men.

units.la: Vnde sequitur: Et signis & prodigijs simul, uarijsq; uirtutibus, & spiritus Sancti distributionibus: Hiis videlicet rebus Deus Christi & euangelij dignitatem attestatus est. Alibi quoq; crebrius hæc eadem numerantur, quasi instrumenta, quibus homines ad amplectendum euangelium sunt adducti: Actor. 2. Obortus est autem omni animæ timor, multaq; prodigia & signa per Apostolos edebantur. Act. 4. Da seruis tuis, vt cum omni fiducia loquamur sermonem tuum, manum tuam porrigendo, in hoc, ut sanatio, & signa, & prodigia edan-tur per nomen sancti filij tui Iesu. Et paulò post: Virtute magna reddebant Apostoli testi-monium resurrectionis Domini Iesu, & gratia magna erat super omnes illos. Actor. 5. Per manus autem apostolorum edebantur signa ac prodigia multa in populo. Actor. 6. Stepha-nus plenus fide ac fortitudine edebat signa & prodigia magna in populo. Et multis aliis locis eadem occurrunt. Sic autem fuerat Christus pollicitus, quemadmodum Mar. ult. dicit: porrò signa eos, qui crediderint, hæc sequentur, per nomen meum dæmonia eijcient, linguis loquentur nouis, serpentes tollent, & si quid lethale biberint, non nocebit eis: su-per ægrotos manus imponent, & bene habebunt. Illi uero egressi prædicauerunt ubiq; domino operante, & sermonem confirmante per signa subsequentia. 1. Cor. 12. Signis & prodi-gijs dicit comprobatum suum apostolatum & doctrinam. Notandum aut est harum vocum discrimen.
units.tr: Hence it follows: "both with signs and wonders, and with various powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit." By these things God attested the dignity of Christ and the gospel. Elsewhere too these same things are listed more often, as instruments by which men were led to embrace the gospel. Acts 2: "And fear came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles." Acts 4: "Grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all confidence, stretching out your hand, so that healings, signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Son Jesus." And a little later: "With great power the apostles gave witness to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all." Acts 5: "Through the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people." Acts 6: "Stephen, full of faith and power, did great signs and wonders among the people." The same occur in many other places. Christ had promised this, as Mark says at the end: "And these signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues, they will take up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover." And they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed. 1 Cor. 12: he says that his apostleship and doctrine were attested by signs and wonders. But the difference between these words must be noted.

units.la: σημεῖον, signum, generale vocabulum est, significas omne illud, quod aptè assumi potest ad co-probandum aliquid vel refutandum: quomodo etiam rhetores tradunt, argumenta quædam si-gnis duci: quomodo ite homines in contractibus & multis negotijs solent confirmandi ergo signum aliquod inuicè porrigere: cuiusmodi etiam est arrha, annulus, chirographum. Atq; hoc pacto in Scripturis passim sumitur. Sic Gen. 9. Arcus in nubibus constituitur in signum fœderis inter Deum atq; homines: Sic ite signum datum est Gedeoni in uellere, Iu-dicum 6. Ite 4. Reg. 20. Ezechias ad Esaiam, Quod est signum, quòd Dominus me sanabit, & quia ascensurus sum die tertia templum Domini? Et subijcitur, quòd ad preces Esaiæ ducta sit umbra per lineas, quibus iam descenderat in horologio decem gradibus. Et in no-uo testamento Matth. 12. Generatio praua & adultera signum quærit, & signum nō dabitur ili-ni, nisi signum Ionæ prophetæ. 1. Cor. 1. Iudæi signum petunt, Græci sapientiam. Vides ergo in scripturis signa generaliter dici quæcunq; ad confirmandum aliquid de uoluntate Dei erga homines fiunt. Sic ad confirmanda diuinitatem suam Christus pro signo haberi uult suam re-surrectionem, quando loquitur de signo Ionæ. Signum fœderis & beneuolentiæ erga genus humanum erat arcus in cœlo. Eodem modo & miracula, & sanationes, & linguæ, & dona S.S. erant generaliter signa confirmatia dignitatem Christi, & eius doctrinam: quo pasim descri-bitur Christus post doctrinam præclaram semper ferè adiecisse signa miraculorum aliqua, per quę doctrina ipsa confirmaretur. Et Mar. 16. generaliter multa nomine signorum suntcöpta hensa.
units.tr: [σημεῖον], "sign," is a general term: it signifies anything that can aptly be used to prove or refute something. As the rhetoricians also teach, certain arguments are drawn from signs. So men, in contracts and many transactions, are accustomed to offer some sign to one another to confirm a bargain, such as an earnest-money, a ring, or a written bond. In this way the word is used throughout the Scriptures. Thus Gen. 9: "The bow is set in the clouds as a sign of the covenant between God and men." So too a sign was given to Gideon in the fleece, Judg. 6. Also 4 Kings 20: Hezekiah to Isaiah: "What is the sign that the Lord will heal me, and that I shall go up to the temple of the Lord on the third day?" And it is added that, at Isaiah's prayer, the shadow was made to go back along the lines by which it had already descended ten steps on the dial. In the New Testament, Matt. 12: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah." 1 Cor. 1: "Jews ask for a sign, Greeks seek wisdom." You see, then, that in Scripture whatever is done to confirm something of God's will toward men is generally called a sign. Thus, to confirm his divinity, Christ wishes his resurrection to be regarded as a sign when he speaks of the sign of Jonah. The sign of the covenant and of God's goodwill toward the human race was the bow in the sky. In the same way, miracles, healings, tongues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit were generally signs confirming the dignity of Christ and his doctrine. Everywhere it is recorded that Christ, after brilliant teaching, almost always added some miraculous signs by which that very doctrine would be confirmed. And in Mark 16 many things are generally comprehended under the name of signs.

units.la: Prodigiū q, græcè τέρας dictū, nonnulli uolunt quasi porro agendū, uel prædi-cium, quod semper mali aliquid prædicat siue præsagiat. Aliqui dicunt prodigia esse deo-rum iras uel minas. Hoc pacto igitur prodigia ea potissimum diceret, quæ Deus edidit ad puniendum peccatores, & ad declarandam suam erga eos ira. Hoc pacto prodigiuessel, quòd Ananias cum Saphira vxore sua collapsus ad pedes Petri expirauit, Actorum quinto. Item quòd Herodes percussus ab Angelo, & erosus à vermibus expirauit, Actorum duodecimo. Et cæcitate percussus Elymas magus doctrinam euangelicam impugnans, Actorum decimotertio. Sed quia crebrò occurrit vox prodigium, vbi tamen huiusmodi signorum non fit mentio, sed potius eorum, per quę misericordia Dei declarabatur: ideò rectè etiam accipiemus eam vocem, pro omnibus in genere, quæ præter communem naturæ more fiunt: cuiusmodi sunt resuscitatio mortuorum, curatio morborum, & id genus, quæ sola virtute Dei, & verbo ipsius fieri poterant, & ad confirmandam Dei potentiam atq; euangelicam doctrinam, eduntur.
units.tr: A prodigy, called [τέρας] in Greek, some want to derive from something like "to be driven forward," or a foretelling, because it always predicts or presages something evil. Others say that prodigies are the anger or threats of the gods. In this way, then, prodigies would be especially those things which God produced to punish sinners and to declare his anger against them. On this view it would be a prodigy that Ananias, collapsing together with his wife Sapphira, expired at Peter's feet, Acts 5; likewise that Herod, struck by an angel and eaten by worms, expired, Acts 12; and that Elymas the magician, who opposed the gospel doctrine, was struck with blindness, Acts 13. But since the word "prodigy" often occurs where no mention is made of such punishments, but rather of those things through which the mercy of God was declared, we shall rightly take the word in a general sense for all things which happen beyond the common course of nature: such as the raising of the dead, the cure of diseases, and the like, which could be done by the power of God alone and by his word, and which are produced to confirm God's power and the evangelical doctrine.

units.la: Virtutes autem, cùm græcè habeatur vox δυνάμεις, omnia illa accipiemus, quæ mirabilem potentiam spiritualem declarant, ostenduntque, potenter agere sanctos, vt resistii ipsis nulla ratione queat.
