Sic magna virtute reddebant apostoli testimonium resurrectionis Iesu Christi, id est, magni animi constantia, argumentis supra modum efficacibus, facultate mouendi animos, reprimendi aduersarios, maiestate & summa auctoritate, ac gratia in dicendo, occulta Spiritus sancti vi & potentia. Quomodo etiam Apostolus 1. Corinth. 2. ait, Sermo meus & prædicatio mea non erat in persuasorijs humanæ sapientiæ verbis: sed in ostensione spiritus ac potentiæ, vt fides vestra non sit in sapientia hominū, sed in potentia Dei. Omnia quæ adiuncta fuerunt Paulo apostolo ad efficaciter docendum, hic in genere vocantur δυνάμεις: Simili modo accipitur Matt. 13. vbi de Christo dicebant: vnde huic sapientia hæc, & virtutes? Et ibidem: vnde igitur huic hæc omnia?
units.tr: "Powers" (virtutes): since the Greek has [δυνάμεις], we shall take this to mean all those things which declare a wonderful spiritual power and show that the saints act so mightily that no one can resist them in any way. Thus "with great power the apostles gave witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ" means with great constancy of spirit, with arguments exceedingly effective, with the ability to move minds and restrain adversaries, with majesty, supreme authority and grace in speaking, and by the hidden strength and power of the Holy Spirit. So the Apostle also says, 1 Cor. 2: "My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith may rest not in the wisdom of men but in the power of God." Everything that was joined to the apostle Paul for teaching effectively is here called, in general, [δυνάμεις]. It is used in a similar way in Matt. 13, where people said of Christ: "Where did this man get this wisdom and these powers?" And again there: "Where then did this man get all these things?"

units.la: Quamuis in eodē capite, statim ponitur vox virtutū pro miraculis: Non edidit illic vir tutes multas propter incredulitate illorum. Sed hoc loco latius omnino patet, quàm vt ad miraculorum significationē restringamus, præsertim cùm hic habeantur voces Signorū & prodigiorū, sub quibus miracula etiā comprehenduntur. In summa, hæ voces per congeriē collatæ, generales sunt, multas res magnas & præclaras sub se comprehendentes: ita vt omnia & præcipua instrumenta, quibus Deus vsus est ad propagationē euangelij, hīc intelligantur, quæ sane multa sunt, & longū foret ea enumerare. Quare ne adhuc plura enumeraret, addidit, quo summatim omnia continentur, quodque omnium latissimè patet, de Spiritus sancti distributionibus: quasi diceret: in summa, ne diutius occupet enumerando omnia, per quæ Deus attestatus est dignitatem Christi, & Euangelij, varia & multiplicia dona Spiritus sancti, Deus sanctis distribuit, per quę Christi diuinitas & euangelij veritas comprobata est, vt omnes per ea commoueantur ad Christū eius q; Euangeliū suscipiendū, amplectendū, colendū. Quæ autem sint, & quales distributione Spiritus, Apostolus explanat, 1. Corinth. 12. Vnicuique datur, inquit, manifestatio spiritus, ad id, quod expedit. Nam huic quidem per Spiritum datur sermone sapientiæ: alij vero sermo scientiæ, secundum eundem Spiritum: alij vero fides per eundem Spiritum: alij vero dona sanationum: alij efficaciæ potentiarum: alij vero prophetia: alij vero discretiones spirituum: alij vero genera linguarum: alij vero interpretatio linguarum. Sed hæc omnia efficit vnus ille & idem spiritus, diuidens peculiariter vnicuiq;, sicuti vult. Vides autem, signa, prodigia, virtutes, spiritus Sancti distributiones, plurali numero efferri. Ac distributiones vocat, propter largam, liberalem, spontaneam, & citra respectum personarum, donorum collationem.
units.tr: Although in the same chapter the word "powers" is used straight away for miracles ("He did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief"), here it extends far more widely, and it should not be restricted to the meaning of miracles, especially since the words "signs and wonders" also appear, under which miracles too are included. In short, these terms, taken together in a series, are general and comprise many great and excellent things, so that all the principal instruments by which God used to spread the gospel are understood here. These are indeed many, and it would take too long to list them. So, lest he should go on listing more, he added a term that sums up everything and extends most widely: the distributions of the Holy Spirit. As if he were saying: in short, rather than spend longer enumerating everything through which God attested the dignity of Christ and the Gospel, God distributed to the saints the various and manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which the divinity of Christ and the truth of the gospel were proved, so that everyone might be moved by them to receive, embrace and cherish Christ and his Gospel. The Apostle explains what these distributions of the Spirit are and what kind they are, in 1 Corinthians 12: "But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues: but all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will." You see, moreover, that signs, wonders, powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit are all named in the plural. He calls them distributions because of the generous, liberal, voluntary bestowal of the gifts, without regard to persons.

units.la: Iuxta ipsius voluntatem) Causa, cur tàm varia dona adhibita. Distribuit enim illa seu spiritus, seu Deus pater, prout vult. Vel potius causa, quare & in nos fit confirmata veritas ac salus euangelica. Deus siquidem non participes facit salutis euangelicæ, non propter nostra merita, aut vota nostra: sed iuxta suam voluntatem, & gratuitam misericordiam: quemadmodum ad Ephesios primo, selectis verbis tantundem significatur. Iuxta diuitias gratiæ suæ, de qua vbertim nobis impartiuit, in omni sapientia & prudentia, patefacto nobis arcano voluntatis suæ, iuxta beneplacitum suum, quod proposuerat in se ipso. Ibidem: In fortem asciti sumus, et prædestinati secundū propositū ipsius. In summa, hac particula ostenditur, reuelatione Euangelij, cognitione eius nobis data, confirmatione ite eius per signa & miracula, soli bonitati & potentiæ Dei accepta feredam: ac proinde nos gratias illi debere omni tempore agere.
units.tr: "According to his own will": this states the cause why such varied gifts were applied. For he distributes them, whether it is the Spirit or God the Father, as he wills. Or rather, this is the reason why the truth and salvation of the gospel are also confirmed in us. For God does not make us partakers of the gospel's salvation on account of our merits or our vows, but according to his own will and free mercy. Paul says the same thing with carefully chosen words in Ephesians 1: "According to the riches of his grace, which he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence; having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself." And again in the same chapter: "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him." In sum, this phrase shows that the revelation of the Gospel, the knowledge of it given to us, and its confirmation through signs and miracles, must be credited solely to the goodness and power of God; and therefore we ought to give him thanks at all times.

units.la: Discimus autem, magnam esse dignitatem Euangelij, quod, cùm à Christo ipso vero Deo sit ad nos allatum, tum etiam variis & multiplicibus signis, & Spiritus Sancti donis, coram toto mundo est confirmatum, oportet esse multò maximum, propter quod Deus voluit tot potentiæ suæ signa edere. Et sunt in his paucis verbis grauisimæ res propositæ, quæ nos ad constanter adhærendum euangelio debent permouere. Setam, quæ ab insigni & præstantissimo philosopho sit profecta, homines mundi huius magnifaciunt, & se haud grauatim illi totos astringunt, eam tuentur defenduntque contra
units.tr: We learn also that the Gospel is of great dignity: since it was brought to us by Christ himself, the true God, and has been confirmed before the whole world both by various and manifold signs and by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, it must be far greater, on account of which God willed to show so many signs of his power. In these few words, most weighty matters are set forth, which ought to move us to cling constantly to the gospel. A sect that has come from some famous and outstanding philosopher is held in high esteem by the men of this world, and they readily bind themselves wholly to it, defend it and guard it against all, and think they must not depart from its doctrines by so much as a finger's breadth.

units.la: Virtutes ἀωμεως quid? contra omnes, ab eius dogmatibus putant sibi ne latum quidem digitum discedendum.
units.tr: What of the virtues [ἀωμεως]? Against all, and think they must not depart from its doctrines by so much as a finger's breadth.

units.la: Quanto igitur decet nos constantius & pertinacius adhærere euangelio, quod allatum est, non per philosophos, aut oratores, aut principes aliquos, neque item per angelos, qui hominibus omnibus sunt in cognitione bonorum præstantiores: sed per ipsum Deum, qui est omnis boni fons & origo, cuius iudicium & doctrina, non potest aliquid falsi, aut dubij habere admixtum? Deinde, si populus multus aliquando vel vnius miraculi (licet alias falsi & a spiritu impostore editi) cospectu est adductus subinde ad recipiendum vel falsam doctrinam vel veram, a qua forte desciuerat (sicut tempore Heliæ contigerat) multo æquius est, nos adhærere ei doctrinæ, quæ tot signis & prodigijs toto orbe fuit confirmata: & quæ hodie etiam, cum ipsa restituì nostro tempore tandem cœpit, totSpiritus Sancti donis quotidie illustratur, latius propagatur, & confirmatur. Vides sane, vides clarissime, quomodo hæ rationes vnumquemq; quasi irretitum & captiuum teneant, vt cogatur vel inuitus concedere Euangelio suam dignitatem, & illi honorem desere. Hanc breuem exhortationem Apostoli deceret nos, præsertim hoc tempore, quo, aboletis multis falsis dogmatibus & superstitionibus, cœpit euangelica veritas iterum munido patefieri, omni tempore in animo circumferre, & pectus nostrum quasi clypeo contra omnes tentationes & potentiam mundi, qua nos ab euangelica veritate conatur abducere, munire & confirmare. Et hodie quoq; signa non desunt, licet nos nequaquam consideremus.
units.tr: How much more fittingly, then, ought we to cling more steadfastly and firmly to the gospel, which was brought not by philosophers, orators or any princes, nor likewise by angels, who surpass all men in knowledge of good things, but by God himself, who is the fount and origin of all good, whose judgment and teaching cannot contain anything false or doubtful? Next, if a great crowd has at some time been drawn, by the sight of a single miracle (even one that was otherwise false and wrought by a deceiving spirit), to receive either a false doctrine or a true one from which it had perhaps fallen away (as happened in the time of Elijah), it is far more right that we should cling to that doctrine which has been confirmed throughout the whole world by so many signs and wonders, and which today too, now that it has at last begun to be restored in our time, is daily made more illustrious by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, spreads more widely, and is confirmed. You see indeed, you see most clearly, how these reasons hold each person as if ensnared and captive, so that he is compelled, even against his will, to grant the Gospel its dignity and to yield it honour. The Apostle's brief exhortation should lead us, especially in this time, when, with many false doctrines and superstitions abolished, evangelical truth has again begun to be revealed more openly, to carry it in our minds at all times, and to arm and fortify our breast, as with a shield, against all temptations and against the power of the world, which seeks to draw us away from evangelical truth. And today too, signs are not lacking, though we do not take notice of them at all.

units.la: DE MIRACVLIS, QVAE VERA, QVAE FALSA, ET QVATENVS AD CONFIRMANDAM DOCTRINAM VALEANT.
units.tr: On Miracles: Which Are True, Which False, and How Far They Serve to Confirm Doctrine.

units.la: Vdiuimus, euangelicā doctrinā approbatā esse à Domino, & confirmatā apud homines signis & prodigijs, vt p hæc homines ad suscipiendū euangeliū adducerent. Sed quia multiplicia & varia sunt miracula, nec statim quelibet doctrina recipieda, quę miraculis videt coprobari: sicut nec reijcieda, cui miracula nō accedunt: ideo operæ facturi videmur pretiū, si de natura miraculorū paulo fusius differamus.
units.tr: We have heard that evangelical doctrine has been approved by the Lord and confirmed among men by signs and wonders, so that men might be led by them to accept the Gospel. But since miracles are manifold and varied, we should not at once receive every doctrine that appears to be supported by miracles, just as we should not reject a doctrine to which no miracles attach. Therefore we think it worth our effort to discuss the nature of miracles somewhat more fully.

units.la: Quando ergo dicitur, euangelicam doctrinam esse confirmatam & roboratamin-nimis hominum per miracula, scire oportet, quæ proprie & vere miracula huic rei conuenientia appellari deceat. Miracula igitur, quibus euangelica veritas, aut denique etiam in veteri testamento, vel doctrina, vel promissiones, vel potentia Dei est confirmata: sunt externa opera, siue facta in admiratione apud homines habita, & talia reuera existunt, qualia apparet, diuina tantum virtute, non arte, aut naturalibus viribus, nec magica ope, vel dæmonum ingenio, & ad testandam veritatem fidei, illustrandamque Dei gloriam, edita. Huiusmodi esse oportet miracula, per quæ euangelium comprobetur, & quæ nomen veterum miraculorum mereantur. Profecto enim quæcunque, quamlibet alias admiranda & suspicienda, alio modo constiterint, pro veris miraculis censerinenquaquam debent. Id quod per singula membra eundo plenius explicabimus.
units.tr: When it is said, then, that evangelical doctrine is confirmed and strengthened among men through miracles, we must know which things can properly and truly be called miracles fitting for this purpose. The miracles by which evangelical truth, or indeed even in the Old Testament doctrine, promises, or the power of God, has been confirmed are external works or deeds that are held in admiration among men, and which really exist just as they appear. They are wrought by divine power alone, not by art, natural forces, magical operation, or the cleverness of demons, and they are performed to attest the truth of the faith and to illustrate the glory of God. Miracles by which the Gospel is proved must be of this kind, and only such deserve the name of the miracles of old. For whatever else, however admirable and wonderful, has come about in some other way, must by no means be counted as true miracles. We shall explain this more fully by going through the parts one by one.

units.la: Primum dixi miracula, de quibus hic loquimur, esse externa opera siue facta. Nam sunt sine dubio etiam miranda opera Dei omni tempore producta, occulte, clam, inuisibiliter: sed ea quia foris non videntur, pro miraculis apud homines no agnoscuntur.
units.tr: First, I said that the miracles of which we speak here are external works or deeds. For there are without doubt also God's wonderful works produced at all times in secret, hidden and invisibly; but because these are not seen outwardly, they are not recognised among men as miracles.

units.la: Huiusmodi miracula sunt, quòd Deus peccatores occulto spiritus sancti suo motu excitat ad resipiscentiā, quòd ex incredulis facit credentes, quòd ob omnem vitā turpiter anteacta damnationis reos, subito & in extremo vitę iustificat. Quæ sane in exhaustam Dei potentiam arguunt, quod nullus vnquam sanctorum talia possit efficere: & tam præclara sunt, vt an geli propter ea omni tempore in cœlis Deum laudent. Miraculū omnes esse concedunt, a corporali morte reuocare ad corporalē vitam breui tempore duraturam. Quanto igitur illustrius miraculum, reuocare aliquem à morte spirituali ad vitam spiritualem, quæ durabit æternum?
units.tr: Of this kind are the following miracles: that God by the secret impulse of his Holy Spirit stirs sinners to repentance; that he makes believers out of unbelievers; that he justifies those who, guilty of damnation because of a shamefully spent life, are suddenly justified at the end of life. These truly argue an inexhaustible power of God, since no saint could ever bring such things about; and they are so glorious that the angels praise God in heaven for them at all times. All concede that it is a miracle to recall someone from bodily death to bodily life, which will last only a short time. How much more illustrious, then, is the miracle of recalling someone from spiritual death to spiritual life, which will last for ever?

units.la: Deinde hæc miracula, quibus coprobatur fidei veritas, oportet eiusmodi esse, vt apud homines in admiratione, & quidè summa, habeantur. Nam nisi hęc quoq; ratio accedat, pro miraculis non habentur, etiam si reuera miracula sint multo amplissima, & hominū captum superantia. Innumera autē huius generis quotidie miracula visuntur: sed quia quotidiana sunt, & passim obuia, miraculorum videntur gratiam amittere. Ecquid magis mirabile, quàm inter tot homines toto orbe terrarum dispersos, tamen non inueniri vel alterum alteri similem? Natura quidem si suo iure posset agere, semper ad similitudinem in omnibus exprimendam elaboraret. At uero Deus mirabili sua potentia facit, vt dissimiles homines tū corporibus, tum animis conspiciātur. Quæ tamen res adeo à miraculi ratione discessit, vt duos aliquos vtcunque similes magis admiremur, quàm tot homines dissimiles. Præterea, quòd Deus omni tempore ex vno grano tritici, magnam aristâ cum spica & multis granis producat, & sic pascat totum orbem: annón ѓquè magnû, atq; ex paucis panibus simul saturare aliquot hominum millia? Interea tamen dum illud mirifice factum extollimus, illud, quod multò maius est, negligimus. Possem de creatione hominis in vtero, deque alijs similibus multis dicere: sed cùm ea naturæ ascribuntur (quę nihil aliud est, quàm Deus ipse in defessè operans) pro miraculis diuina potentia editis, non numerantur. Adhæc quæ miracula appellabuntur, talia debent reuera esse, quia apparent. Vbi enim præstigiæ adhibentur & ludificantur hominum oculi, vt id se videre arbitrentur, quod tamen reuera ita non est, miraculi dignitas amittitur. Neque ignotum est, dæmones atque homines etiam dæmonum arte adiutos, posse efficere per præstigias (referente ita Augustino libro de ciuitate Dei 18. capite 18.) vt secundum phantasma & imaginationem hominis, aliquid veluti corporatum in alicuius animalis effigie appareat sensibus alienis, talisque etiam sibi homo esse videatur, sicut talis sibi videri posset in somnis, & onera portare. Quæ onera, si vera sunt corpora, portantur à dæmonibus, vt illudatur hominibus, partim verò corpora onerum, partim iumentorum falsa cernentibus: Quomodo patricius quidam de patre suo retulerat, nempe sumpto veneno in caseo, dormiuisse eum per multos dies, nec potuisse excitari. Postea verò experrectum narrasse, quasi id ita somniasset, se factum fuisse Ca-ballum, annonam inter alia iumenta baiulasse militibus. Ita autem & compertum fuisse, sicut ille se somniasse existimarat.
units.tr: Next, the miracles by which the truth of the faith is proved must be of such a kind that they are regarded among men with admiration, and indeed with the greatest admiration. For unless this further condition is present, they are not counted as miracles, even if they really are miracles of far greater magnitude and surpassing human understanding. Countless miracles of this kind are seen every day; but because they are everyday occurrences and met with everywhere, they seem to lose the grace of miracles. What is more wonderful than that, among so many men scattered over the whole world, not even one is found who is wholly like another? Nature, indeed, if it could act by its own right, would always labour to express likeness in all things. But God by his wonderful power makes it that men, both in bodies and in souls, appear unlike one another. Yet this fact has so departed from the reason of a miracle that we admire two persons, however alike, more than so many dissimilar men. Moreover, that God at all times from one grain of wheat produces a great ear with a spike and many grains, and so feeds the whole world: is this not equally great, and is it not a marvel to satisfy several thousand men at once from a few loaves? Yet while we extol that as wonderfully done, we neglect this, which is far greater. I could say many things of the same kind about the formation of a human being in the womb and about many other similar things; but since these are ascribed to nature (which is nothing other than God himself working unceasingly), they are not counted as miracles wrought by divine power. Besides, what are called miracles must really be such, because they appear to be so. For where illusions are employed and men's eyes are deceived, so that they think they see what in fact is not so, the dignity of a miracle is lost. Nor is it unknown that demons, and men aided by the art of demons, can by illusions (as Augustine reports in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 18) bring it about that, according to the fancy and imagination of a man, something appears embodied, as it were, in the likeness of some animal to the senses of others, and that the man himself seems to himself to be such, just as he might seem to be such in dreams, and to carry burdens. If these burdens are real bodies, they are carried by demons in order to mock men; but partly they are bodies of burdens, partly false beasts of burden, to those who look on. In the same way a certain patrician had reported about his father: that, having taken poison in cheese, he slept for many days and could not be roused; and afterwards, when he woke, he told how he had been made a horse, as if he had dreamed it, and had carried provisions for the soldiers among the other beasts of burden. And this was also found to be so, just as that man had supposed he had dreamed it.

units.la: Aliquando etiam sublatis veris corporibus, hominum videlicet aut similium, alia verò subitò substitui, brutorum videlicet, & idgenus, quomodo pro Iphigenia Agamemnonis filia supposita fuit cerua, quod ex eo liquet, quòd Iphigenia postea iterum viua reperta est. Atque hoc errore transformationes plures ab hominibus stultè creditæ sunt, apparentibus nimirum subitò nouis figuris, atque etiam sæpè veris corporibus, & prioribus subitò sublatis, nec amplius comparentibus. Sic igitur vbi id nequaquàm veréest, quòd esse decepti hominum sensus falsò suspicantur, ibi miraculum verum dici nequit.
units.tr: Sometimes, too, when the real bodies of men or of similar creatures have been taken away, other bodies are suddenly substituted in their place, namely those of beasts and the like; as a deer was put in place of Iphigenia, the daughter of Agamemnon, which is clear from the fact that Iphigenia was afterwards found alive again. And by this error many transformations have been foolishly believed by men, when new shapes suddenly appear, and often even real bodies, while the earlier ones are suddenly removed and no longer appear. Thus, wherever it is not in fact the case that men's senses are deceived, which people wrongly suspect, a true miracle cannot be said to have occurred there.

units.la: Quartò, vt vera dicantur miracula aliqua, oportet ea tantùm diuina virtute, non arte seu naturalibus viribus, non magica ope, non item dæmonum industria fieri. Constat au temid, quod & Augustinus subindicat de ciuitate Dei lib. 21. cap. 6. trifariam posse edi miracula, diuina ope nequaquam concurrente. Primùm arte humana, ab iis, qui naturas lapidum, herbarum, aliarumq; rerum callent, multa quæ homines valdè mirentur, & su pra naturæ communem constitutionem posita esse putent, confici possunt. Quomodo in quodam templo ferream imaginem in sublimi sine sustentaculis pendentem, pro numine suspectam & honoratam, cùm interim à magnetibus ex omni parte ædificij iusta proportione dispositis, facilè retineri ibi pensilis imago ea potuerit. Sic in fano quodam Veneris lampadem seruatam, quæ nunquam extingueretur, pro miraculo incomparabili habuēre, cùm tamen fieri id potuerit, adhibito nimirum lapide Asbesto, qui in Arcadia reperitur, eiusque est naturæ, vt semel accensus, nunquam extinguatur. Quocirca & illud puto admonendum, non dicenda simpliciter omnia esse miracula, quæ præter communem naturæ cursum fiunt. Habet sine dubio & ipsa natura, sua in se miracula. Et quæ Deus (qui est natura naturans, vt loqui solent) sic temperat, ex naturalibus causis producantur, etiamsi homines aliter hæc se habere cernant, quàm in naturalibus causis ipsi sunt experti, vt plurimum euenire: non tamen contra naturam, aut supra naturam facta debent iudicari. Vnde & monstra, quæ à demonstrando, quòd aliquid significando demonstrent: & ostenta ab ostendendo, & portenta, à portendendo, id est, præ ostendendo: & prodigia, quòd porrò dicant, id est, futura prædicant, sic creduntur appellata, non simpliciter pro miraculis agnoscuntur: (vide Augustinum de ciuitate Dei libro vigesimoprimo, capite octauo) quandoquì demplerunque ex causis proueniunt à natura non alienis: cuius generis sunt permulta quæ in aere & aquis, terra conspiciuntur: quorum causas indagare & exponere, philosophi ausi sunt. Secundò, fiunt miracula arte magica, qua homines auxilio dæmonum, quos euocat & alliciunt, res inusitatas producunt: quomodo Exodi septimo, magi multa egerunt suis incantationibus, quæ Moses diuina ope peregerat. Nam virgas conuerterunt in dracones, aquas fluminum in sanguinem, ranas itidem produxerunt innumeras. Possent multa alia de magia hic explicari & disputari: Sed locus præsens non requirit.
units.tr: Fourthly, for certain things to be called true miracles, they must be wrought by divine power alone, and not by art or natural forces, nor by magical operation, nor likewise by the industry of demons. It is established, as Augustine also hints in The City of God, book 21, chapter 6, that miracles can be performed in three ways without the concurrence of divine aid. First, by human art: by those who know well the natures of stones, herbs and other things, many things can be accomplished which men greatly marvel at and think to lie beyond the common order of nature. Thus in a certain temple an iron image hanging in mid-air without supports was suspected and honoured as a divinity, although in fact that hanging image could easily be held there by magnets set in every part of the building in due proportion. So too in a certain temple of Venus they regarded as an incomparable miracle a lamp kept burning that was never extinguished, although this could have been done, namely by using asbestos, the stone found in Arcadia, which is of such a nature that once it is lit it is never put out. Hence I think it should also be pointed out that not everything which happens beyond the common course of nature is to be called a miracle simply. Nature itself has, without doubt, its own miracles. And those things which God (who is, as they are accustomed to say, 'nature creating') so orders that they are produced from natural causes, even if men see these things to be otherwise than they themselves have experienced from natural causes, which happens for the most part, ought not on that account to be judged contrary to nature or above nature. Hence monsters, which are so named from demonstrating, because by signifying something they point it out; portents, from showing forth; omens, from showing before; and prodigies, because they foretell things, that is, predict future things, are called so, but are not simply recognised as miracles (see Augustine, The City of God, book 21, chapter 8). For the most part they arise from causes not foreign to nature, and of this kind are very many things that are seen in the air, in the waters and on the earth; philosophers have dared to investigate and explain their causes. Secondly, miracles are performed by magical art, by which men, with the help of demons whom they summon and entice, produce unusual things. Thus in Exodus chapter 7 the magicians did many things by their incantations which Moses had accomplished by divine help. For they turned rods into serpents, the waters of the rivers into blood, and likewise produced countless frogs. Many other things about magic could be explained and discussed here, but the present place does not require it.

units.tr: Thirdly, signs:

units.la: {a} Tertiò, signa

units.la: Tertiò, fiunt miracula per ipsos dæmones, qui cùm rerum naturalium vires optimè norint, possunt multa efficere, ipsi quoq; varias formas induere, se subinde trásmutare, corpora subire possunt, vt mille modis fallant, & in errorem homines abducant. Quàde re multa videre est in historijs, præsertim gentilium, apud quos omnia falsorum Deorum miracula à dæmonibus ipsis sunt edita, vt homines in cæcitate & idololatria, aliisque affinibus peccatis retinerentur. Quæcunque igitur ab hominibus arte humana, vel magica, vel per ipsos dæmones fiunt, ea Deo quidem permittente, at nequaquam promouente, eduntur: quare & pro veris miraculis, qualia adhibita sunt ad confirmationem euangelij, haberi non debent.
units.tr: Thirdly, miracles are performed by the demons themselves. Since they know the powers of natural things very well, they can accomplish many things. They can also take on various forms, change their shape from time to time, and enter into bodies, so that they deceive people in a thousand ways and lead them into error. Many examples of this can be found in histories, especially those of the Gentiles, among whom all the miracles of the false gods were performed by the demons themselves, so that men would be kept in blindness, idolatry and other related sins. Therefore, whatever is done by men through human art, or magic, or through the demons themselves, is brought about with God's permission but by no means with his help. For this reason, such things should not be regarded as true miracles, of the kind that were given to confirm the gospel.

units.la: Causa efficiens (id enim diligenter in hac tractatione notandum est) verorum miraculorum est verbum Dei. Matthæi octauo, & eiecit spiritus verbo, omnesque malehabentes sanauit. Matthæi 10. Datur potestas à Deo discipulis. Lucæ 10. In nomine meo dæmonia eijcient. Petrus Actorum tertio, dicit claudo, In nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni surge, & ambula. Item Matthæi 17. Si fidem habueritis vt granum Sinapis, &c. Christus item non edidit miracula virtute magica, sicut quidam impij dixerunt, sed propria virtute diuina, & virtute sui verbi: Matthæi 8. & eijciebat dæmonia verbo, & omnes male habentes sanabat. Contra quos Augustinus de consensu Euangelistarum lib. 1. cap. 11.
units.tr: The efficient cause of true miracles (for this must be carefully noted in this discussion) is the Word of God. Matthew 8: "He cast out the spirits by a word and healed all who were sick." Matthew 10: power is given by God to the disciples. Luke 10: "In my name they will cast out demons." Peter, Acts 3, says to the lame man: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk." Likewise Matthew 17: "If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed," etc. Christ also did not perform miracles by magical power, as some impious men have said, but by his own divine power and by the power of his word: Matthew 8: "he cast out demons by a word and healed all who were sick." Against those men Augustine, On the Harmony of the Evangelists, book 1, chapter 11.

units.la: Postremò, vt miracula aliqua dicantur vera, illud quoque requiritur, vt ad compro-bandam veritatem, illustrandamque Dei gloriam parati sint: id quod Marci vltimo, & præsenti loco Apostoli satis clarè dicitur. Hic finis & scopus omnium verorum miraculorum existit. Magi quidem miracula ediderunt aliquando ad impugnandam veritatem, vt illi apud Pharaonem, vel etiam quæstus & parandæ inanis gloriæ causa, Dæmones verò ad obscurandam Dei gloriam, & sibi diuinitatis laudem vedicandam: Quare vera miracula dici non debent, vtpote quæ recto fine miraculorum sint destituta.
units.tr: Finally, for any miracles to be called true, it is also required that they be given to prove the truth and to illustrate the glory of God. This is stated quite clearly in Mark's last chapter and in the present passage by the apostles. This is the purpose and goal of all true miracles. Magicians indeed have performed miracles at times to attack the truth, as those did before Pharaoh, or also for profit and to obtain empty glory. Demons, however, do so to obscure the glory of God and to claim divine praise for themselves. Therefore these should not be called true miracles, since they lack the right purpose of miracles.

units.la: Proinde ex his non obscurè intelligitur, quænam vera sint miracula, quæ item falsa: & de qualibus potissimum miraculis statuendum sit, quòd per ea veritas euangelica sit confirmata. Nam per hæc duntaxat id fit, quæ exterius exhibentur admiratione digna, & verè talia existunt, qualia cernuntur, nec non diuina tantùm virtute, ad Dei gloriam illustrandam parantur. Voluit ergo Deus pater eiusmodi miracula permulta in veteri testamento, per seipsum, per angelos, & per homines edere, (longum foret, neque etiam opus est exempla & miracula omnia recensere) sed multo plura in nouo testamento per Christum Iesum dilectum suum filium, & per apostolos. Christus autem vt miracula edidit longè præclariora, quàm edita fuerunt per angelos, vel sanctos homines: ita etiam diuersa admodum ratione. Nam sancti omnes precando & inuocando Deum, seu nomen Dei. Christus verò imperando, & vt potestatem habens. Sanctiin nomine Dei miracula ediderunt, Christus in nomine suo. Vnde sæpè etiam vsus est verbis imperatiui modi, Surge & ambula, aperire, Lazare veni foras. Quòd aliquando vsus precatione legitur, id fecit, vt gloriam à se reijciens, & ad patrem eam transferens: deinde vt sanctis exemplum inuocandi patris præbens. Sanctos verò semper inuocantes, aut in nomine Iesu præcipientes cernimus: aut certè precationis forma quadam vtentes. Vnde & illud Iosuæ decimo, Sol, contra Gabaon ne mouea־ris: optantis seu precantis vox, non imperantis, agnosci debet. Et Christus facultatem edendi miracula apostolis ipsis contulit, Marci 16.
units.tr: From these points it is therefore not obscurely understood which miracles are true and which false, and which kinds of miracles especially must be judged to confirm the evangelical truth. For this happens only through those things which are outwardly displayed as worthy of wonder, which truly are such as they appear, and which are brought about by divine power alone, to illustrate the glory of God. God the Father therefore willed to perform very many such miracles in the Old Testament, through himself, through angels, and through men (it would be lengthy, and there is no need, to recount all the examples and miracles), but far more in the New Testament, through Christ Jesus his beloved Son, and through the apostles. Christ performed miracles that were far more excellent than those performed through angels or holy men, and also in a quite different manner. For all the saints performed their miracles by praying and calling upon God, or upon the name of God. Christ, however, performed them by commanding, as one having power. The saints performed miracles in the name of God; Christ performed them in his own name. Hence he often used imperative words: "Rise and walk," "Open," "Lazarus, come out." That he is sometimes read to have used prayer, he did so in order to refuse glory for himself and transfer it to the Father, and also to give the saints an example of calling upon the Father. We see the saints always calling upon God, or commanding in the name of Jesus, or certainly using some form of prayer. Hence also that passage in Joshua 10: "Sun, do not move against Gibeon": the voice of one wishing or praying, not commanding, must be recognized. And Christ conferred the power of performing miracles on the apostles themselves, Mark 16.

units.la: Sed ex omnibus, quæ de veritate miraculorum dicta sunt, illud præcipuè considerandum venit, quod de fine seu vero vsu miraculorum annotauimus, propter quem præcipuè moti sumus ad copiosius de miraculis differendum.
units.tr: But of all that has been said about the truth of miracles, the point especially to be considered is what we have noted about the end, or true use, of miracles. For the sake of this we were especially moved to discuss miracles more fully.

units.la: Ostenditur passim in Scripturis, in hunc finem, & ob hanc vtilitatem, edita esse tàm in veteri testamento, quàm in nouo, miracula, vt homines duri & increduli atque etiam infirmi ad fidelem in uerbo Dei, quæ propositæ erat, adduceretur: deinde ad laudandum Deum agendas q; ei gratias excitarentur. Ac generaliter hoc de omnibus miraculis in Scriptura de scriptis statuendum, quòd qua ratione vnum creditur, eadem credi decet omnia: & quo magis uidentur fidem superare, eò sunt magis credenda. Nam ea est miraculorum natura, ut captum humanæ mentis superent, & quo magis superant, eò magis sunt pro miraculis habenda. Quare qui unum è miraculis sacræ Scripturæ reijcit, perinde peccat, ac si reijciat omnia. Qui verò reijcit illa miracula, is reijcit Dei uerbum. Nam miracula sunt ipsum Dei uerbum: uerbo Dei fiunt, sunt uerbum agens siue uiuens, sunt uerbū non tantùm audibile, sed uisibile, contrectabile. Sicut enim Deus loquitur uerbo, & uerbo confirmat suorum animos: ita (cùm miracula edit) Deus loquitur factis, & operibus confirmat suorum animos. Sediam hic quæstio oritur, Si in hoc data sunt miracula potissimum, vt per ea confirmetur sana doctrina, & doctrina euangelica per miracula inprimis est confirmata: an igitur omnis doctrina statim erit suscipienda pro sana, quam viderimus per miracula probari? Respondetur, quòd non. Etratio est, Deus permittit etiam per malos & impios, & falsos doctores edi miracula, Exod.7. Magi & malefici apud Pharaonem suis artibus signa ediderunt, sicut Moses. Matthæi 7. Christus inducit quosdam dicentes in die iudicij, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo dæmonia eiecimus? quibus tamen dicetur, nescio vos. Matthæi vigesimoquarto, Surgent pseudochristi & pseudoprophetæ, & dabunt signa magna, & prodigia, ita vt in errorem inducantur, si fieri possit, etiam electi, secunda Thessalon. sect. do, Aduentus Antichristi describitur secundùm operationem Satanæ, cum omni potentia, & signis, & prodigijs mendacibus, & cum omni deceptione iniustitiæ, in his, qui pereunt, pro eo quòd dilectionem veritatis non habuerint. Nec dubium, quin Deus etiam peccatores exaudiat aliquando, (sicut exaudiuit publicanum) & sinat per malos edi miraculà: sed non propter personam ipsorum, sed propter invocationem sui nominis, quam illi adhibent: vel propter personas circumstantes, quas Deus per miracula, aut vult in sana doctrina confirmari, aut permittit ab ea abduci. Actorum decimonono, Iudæi quidam exorcistæ nomen Iesu, quem Paulus prædicabat, invocabant, super eos, qui habebant spiritus malos. Et dæmones sæpè permittuntur edere miracula. Clarum itaq; est, etiam per malos atque falsa docentes edi miracula, ac proinde non necessarium, vt doctrinæ talium fides statim adhibeatur.
units.tr: It is shown throughout the Scriptures that miracles were performed, both in the Old Testament and in the New, for this end and for this usefulness: so that hard, unbelieving and even weak people would be brought to faith in the word of God that was set before them, and then stirred to praise God and give him thanks. Generally, this should be decided about all the miracles in Scripture, that for whatever reason one is believed, all should be believed in the same way; and the more they seem to surpass faith, the more they are to be believed. For it is the nature of miracles to surpass the grasp of the human mind, and the more they surpass it, the more they are to be regarded as miracles. Therefore whoever rejects one of the miracles of Holy Scripture sins just as if he rejected all of them. Whoever rejects those miracles rejects the word of God. For miracles are the word of God itself: they are done by the word of God; they are a word that acts or lives; they are a word not only audible but visible and tangible. For just as God speaks by a word and confirms the minds of his people by a word, so (when he performs miracles) God speaks by deeds and confirms the minds of his people by works. But here a question arises. If miracles were given chiefly for this purpose, that sound doctrine might be confirmed by them, and especially if the evangelical doctrine has been confirmed by miracles, will every doctrine that we see proved by miracles at once be accepted as sound? The answer is no. And the reason is this: God permits miracles to be performed also through wicked, impious and false teachers. Exodus 7: the magicians and sorcerers before Pharaoh performed signs by their arts, just as Moses did. Matthew 7: Christ introduces some who say on the day of judgment, "Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name?" Yet to them it will be said, "I never knew you." Matthew 24: "False christs and false prophets will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error." 2 Thessalonians 2: the coming of Antichrist is described as according to the working of Satan, with all power, and with lying signs and wonders, and with all deception of wickedness, among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth. Nor is there doubt that God sometimes also hears sinners (as he heard the tax collector), and allows miracles to be performed through evil men; but not on account of their person, rather on account of the invocation of his name which they use, or on account of the people present, whom God wishes to be confirmed in sound doctrine by miracles, or permits to be drawn away from it. Acts 19: certain Jewish exorcists tried to invoke the name of Jesus, whom Paul preached, over those who had evil spirits. And demons are often permitted to perform miracles. It is therefore clear that miracles are also performed through wicked men and false teachers, and consequently it is not necessary that faith be given at once to the doctrine of such men.

units.la: Sed obijciat aliquis, Impij etiam inuocant nomen Dei: Igitur habent Christum, seu verbum autorem suorum miraculorum. Respondetur, negando consequens: Si enim ita esset, Christus impijs hypocritis non dixisset Matthæi septimo, Nunquam noui vos: discedite à me omnes qui operamini iniquitatem, id est, qui prætextu nominis seu verbi mei facitis miracula, sine fide & cum impietate. Quam igitur causam habent hypocritæ suorum miraculorum? Repsondemus: Diabolum, quia prætextu nominis Dei, & sub pallio verbi Dei prætexunt diabolum, cui seruiunt. Cur ergo Deus permittit ab illis fieri miracula, interposito suo nomine? Respondetur, eadem ratione permittit, vt hypocritæ glorientur, se habere verbum Dei, sacramenta, &c. Vtuntur igitur vere nomine seu verbo Dei, quando edunt miracula? Respondemus, vtuntur vere sed non recte: abutũ tur enim: sicut videmus ariolos, incantatores, ad sua maleficia etiam adhibere verbũ, seu nomen Dei. Quid ergo erit faciendum? Primò, quod ad miracula illorum attinet, sciedum est, nõ esse miracula vera, sed, sicut de Antichristo dicitur ad 1 Thessalonicenses, mendacia. Sunt autem mendacia, vel quia reuera non ita se habent, sicut putantur, & sicut oculis fascinatis apparet: vel, si res ipsæ verè sint, sicut à magis Pharaonis veras ranas, veros dracones, concedùt nonnulli conditos: tamen nondum erant vera miracula, quando non fiebat virtute diuina: sed virtute rerum naturaliũ & magica: quando item non fiebant ad comprobandam veritatem, seu illustrandam Dei gloriam, sed ad fines contrarios. Qui spiritu Dei sunt præditi, semper aliquod lumen habent, & oculos fidei, per quos præstigias, & dolos falsorum doctorum possint deprehendere: sicut de Machario refertur, quòd is puellam, quam parentes arte magica mutatam existimarunt in vaccam, vidit humana specie subsistentem, quia oculi eius falli non poterant. Et semper illud accidit, vt virga seu serpens Mosis devorat virgas & serpentes maleficorum: & magi suis artibus fraudantur, vt præ vlceribus coram Mose non potuerint diu consistere. Ac credi par est, per eos, qui falsam doctrinam adferunt, vera miracula ad talis doctrinæ confirmationem edi non posse: aut, si tamen vera edant, non doctrinæ stabiliendæ causa Deus permittit: sed potius propter sui nominis invocationem: propter quod nomen omnia fiunt, etiam ad votum malorum & indignorum ministrorum: sicut Matthæi septimo ostenditur, Item Actorum decimonono. Sed si quis plenius cognoscere auet, quomodo aliter sancti edant miracula, aliter magi, aliter verò pseudoprophetæ, videat Augustinum libro octogesimotertio quæstionum, quæstione septuagesimanona, vbi copiosè hac de re agitur.
units.tr: But someone may object: impious men also invoke the name of God; therefore they have Christ, or the Word, as the author of their miracles. The answer is to deny the consequence. For if this were so, Christ would not have said to the impious hypocrites in Matthew 7, "I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity," that is, who under the pretext of my name or word perform miracles without faith and with impiety. What reason, then, do the hypocrites have for their miracles? We answer: the devil. For under the pretext of the name of God, and under the cloak of the word of God, they conceal the devil whom they serve. Why then does God permit miracles to be performed by them when his name is put forward? The answer is that by the same reasoning he permits hypocrites to boast that they have the word of God, the sacraments, and so on. Do they then truly use the name or word of God when they perform miracles? We answer: they use it truly, but not rightly; for they abuse it. Just as we see sorcerers and enchanters also employ the word or name of God for their evil practices. What then is to be done? First, as far as their miracles are concerned, it must be known that they are not true miracles, but, as is said of Antichrist in 1 Thessalonians, lies. They are lies either because the things are not really as they are thought to be, and as they appear to bewitched eyes; or, if the things themselves are real, as some concede were the real frogs and real serpents produced by Pharaoh's magicians, they were still not true miracles, since they were not done by divine power but by the power of natural things and by magic; and also because they were not done to prove the truth or to illustrate the glory of God, but for contrary ends. Those who are endowed with the Spirit of God always have some light and the eyes of faith, by which they can detect the tricks and deceptions of false teachers. So it is related of Macarius that he saw a girl, whom her parents believed had been changed into a cow by magical art, standing there in human form, because his eyes could not be deceived. And it always happens that the rod or serpent of Moses devours the rods and serpents of the sorcerers, and the magicians are defeated by their own arts, so that, because of their sores, they could not stand before Moses for long. And it is right to believe that through those who bring false doctrine, true miracles cannot be performed to confirm such doctrine; or, if they do perform true miracles, God permits this not for the sake of establishing the doctrine, but rather on account of the invocation of his name, because of which all things are done, even according to the wish of evil and unworthy ministers. This is shown in Matthew 7, and likewise in Acts 19. But if anyone wishes to know more fully how the saints perform miracles, how the magicians do so differently, and how the false prophets do so otherwise, let him see Augustine, book 83 of the Questions, question 79, where this matter is discussed at length.

units.la: Verum, quia difficilius est iudicare de miraculorum veritate & falsitate, num vi- delicet verè ita se habeant, sicut apparent, nec ne: num item virtute diuina, ad nor mam verbi Dei, & gloriam eiusdem fiant: ideo tutissimum est respicere ad doctrinam, & hanc, vera ne, an falsa sit, examinare: quod consilium paratum & expositum habemus Deuteronomij decimotertio. Si surrexerit in medio tui propheta, aut qui somnium vidisse se dicat, & prædixerit signum atq; portentum, & euenerit, quod locutus est, & dixerit tibi: Eamus & sequamur Deos alienos, quos ignoras, & seruiamus eis: non audies uerba prophetæ illius aut somniatoris: quia tenquia tentat uos Dominus Deus uestros, ut palàm fiat utrum diligatis eum, annón, in toto corde, & in tota anima uestra. Dominum Deum uestrum sequimini, et ipsum timete, mandata illius custodite, & audite uocem eius: ipsi scruietis, & ipsi adhærebitis. En quando dubitas de doctrina propositå, non ex miraculis iudicium colliges, sed ex lege & voce Dei, id est, ex verbo Dei. Confer doctrinam propositam cum verbo Dei, cum lege, Prophetis, euangelio: & si illam inueneris, conuenire cum hoc, & nequaquam pugnare, audacter amplectere, & venerare. Sin autem diuersa fuerit à verbo Dei, ut pestem fugito. Sic Actor. 17. Thessalonicenses versabantur in Scripturis, explorantes, num ita se haberent. Et Christus Ioan. 5. remittit Iudæos ad Scripturarum scrutationem. Esaiæ 8. ad legem & ad testimonium. Item Christus Luc. 16. ad diuitem in inferno, & petentem, ut Lazarus mitteretur ad fratres ipsius, Moysen habet, & prophetas. Matth. 12. Generatio prava signum quærit, &c. Certè ubi non inuenitur conuenire cum doctrina sacra, præcipueq; euangelica, quæ interpretatur, et comprehendit in se legem & prophetas: siue angelus fuerit, siue Paulus, qui eam è cœlo dicat se adferre, anathema sit, ut Galat. 1. clarè dicitur. Sunt autem variæ causæ, quare Deus permittat, per falsos doctores, & per magos edi miracula. Non possunt quidem aliquid efficere, nisi quatenus Deus permittit, sicut necipsi dæmones quicquam aliter possunt. Unde magi apud Pharaonem cyniphes, quæ sunt muscarum species, producere non potuere, fasciq; sunt, Moysen digito, seu virtute Dei agere. Permittitur autem etiam malis facultas ededi miracula: primò vt & ipsi, qui edunt miracula, & omnes qui eos suspiciunt seducantur, & in errorem mittantur, & in cæcitate sua retineantur. Sic enim disponsat Deus, vt qui ita sibi fuisq; peruersi opinionibus innituntur, omnia sentiat sibi pro voto succedere, quo in impietate sua confirmentur: atq; ita finit eos etiam miraculorum potentia valere, quando alioqui non est spes, eos ab impietate abduci posse, ac ne potentioribus quidem miraculis adhibitis: sicut Pharao qualibet stupenda signa per Moysen ederetur, non potuit tamen à semel coepta impietate dimoueri. Obijcitur autem, cum mali æquè edant miracula atq; boni, certè nullum videtur discrimen inter miracula vtrorumq;. Respondetur: piorum miracula causam habent peculiarem, potestatem diuinam, sicut Apostoli à Christo habuerunt. Matth. 10. Verbum, fides, & orationem, causas habent. Impij non itidem, sicut videre licet Matth. 7. 24. Item in forma est diuersitas. Vtuntur mali opera diaboli, vel superstitiosis ritibus: vel non proprius vera sunt miracula. Item in fine, ad obscurandum gloriam Dei, ad fallendum simplices, ad quæstum faciendum, &c. Sæpè etiam impediuntur mali, quo minus præstent quod cupiunt: Actorum decimonono Iesum scio, & Paulum noui, vos autem qui estis? Secundò, propter personas circumstantes, ac primò propter malos. 2. Thess. 2. Tertiò concessa est malis potestas miraculorum, ad exercendam probandamq; piorum patientiam & constantiam. Sic Deuteron. 13. dicitur, quòd Deus per falsum prophetam vera prædicentem, & signa edentem, suos tentet: qua ratione sæpè magi contra sanctos permissi sunt, signa edere, vt magi contra Moysen, & de Simone mago narratur, quòd multa gesserit contra Petrum. Et Antichristus hac de causa signis erit conspicuus. Quartò, permittitur malis potestas miraculorum, ne sancti, quibus eadem potestas data est, immodicè efferrentur, neue homines cæteri sanctitatem metirentur ex miraculis, & homini-bus diuinitatem tribuerent, quod non sine iniuria Dei fieret: quomodo Actorum. 14. Lycaones propter restitutum claudum sanitati, voluerunt apostolis diuinum honorem impendere.
units.tr: Yet because it is harder to judge whether miracles are true or false, that is, whether they really are what they appear to be, and whether they are done by divine power, to confirm the word of God and to his glory, it is safest to look to the teaching and test whether it is true or false. We have this counsel set out and explained in Deuteronomy 13: If there arise in the midst of you a prophet, or one who says he has seen a dream, and he foretells a sign or wonder, and it comes to pass, of which he spoke, and he says to you, "Let us go and follow other gods, whom you have not known, and serve them," you shall not hear the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God tests you, to make it plain whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul. You shall follow the Lord your God, fear him, keep his commandments, and obey his voice; you shall serve him and cleave to him. So when you doubt a proposed doctrine, you should not draw your judgement from miracles, but from the law and voice of God, that is, from the word of God. Compare the proposed doctrine with the word of God, with the law, the Prophets and the gospel; and if you find that it agrees with these and in no way conflicts with them, embrace and reverence it boldly. But if it differs from the word of God, flee from it as from a plague. So in Acts 17 the Thessalonians searched the Scriptures to see whether these things were so. And Christ in John 5 sends the Jews to the searching of the Scriptures; Isaiah 8 sends us to the law and to the testimony; and Christ in Luke 16, speaking to the rich man in hell who asked that Lazarus be sent to his brothers, says they have Moses and the prophets. In Matthew 12, "An evil generation seeks a sign," etc. Certainly, where a doctrine is not found to agree with sacred teaching, especially the gospel, which interprets and comprehends the law and the Prophets within itself, then whether it be an angel or Paul who says he brings it from heaven, let him be accursed, as is plainly said in Galatians 1. There are, however, various reasons why God permits miracles to be wrought through false teachers and magicians. They can indeed accomplish nothing except insofar as God permits, just as the demons themselves can do nothing otherwise. Hence the magicians of Pharaoh could not produce gnats, which are a kind of fly, and were overcome, confessing that Moses acted by the finger, that is, the power, of God. But the power to work miracles is also granted to the wicked: first, so that both those who work the miracles and all who admire them may be led astray, fall into error, and be kept in their blindness. For God so arranges things that those who lean so perversely on their own opinions think that everything succeeds according to their wish, and so they are confirmed in their impiety; and he thus allows them to prevail even by the power of miracles when there is otherwise no hope of drawing them away from impiety, even when more powerful miracles are brought forward; just as Pharaoh, though all manner of astonishing signs were wrought through Moses, could not be turned from the impiety he had once begun. It is objected, however, that since the wicked work miracles just as the good do, there seems to be no difference at all between the miracles of either. The answer is that the miracles of the pious have a peculiar cause, the divine power, just as the Apostles had it from Christ (Matt. 10). They have as their causes the word, faith and prayer. The wicked do not have these, as may be seen in Matthew 7 and 24. There is also a difference in form: the wicked use the works of the devil or superstitious rites, or else their miracles are not truly miracles. Likewise there is a difference in the end: to obscure the glory of God, to deceive the simple, to make gain, and so on. Often too the wicked are hindered from achieving what they desire, as in Acts 19: "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?" Secondly, the power is granted on account of the persons present, and first on account of the wicked (2 Thess. 2). Thirdly, the power of miracles is granted to the wicked to exercise and prove the patience and constancy of the pious. So Deuteronomy 13 says that God tests his people through a false prophet who foretells true things and works signs; and for this reason magicians have often been permitted to work signs against the saints, as the magicians did against Moses, and it is told of Simon Magus that he did many things against Peter. And for this reason Antichrist will be conspicuous for signs. Fourthly, the power of miracles is granted to the wicked so that the saints, to whom the same power has been given, should not be immoderately exalted, and so that other men should not measure holiness by miracles and attribute divinity to men, which would not happen without injury to God; as in Acts 14, when the Lycaonians, because of the lame man restored to health, wished to pay divine honour to the apostles.

units.la: Quintò, ne hoc donum videretur magnoperè affectandum, & ne statim in omnibus fides haberetur ijs, qui miracula videntur edere: sic Deus sapienter disponit omnia, & nouit donis suis ad multas simul vti, & permittit malos ijsdem inter-dum abuti: sicut alij abutuntur dono linguarum, alij dono sapientiæ: ita mali abuntur dono miraculorum, si tamen diuina ope contingat eos miracula edere, & non potius ope diaboli. Et diabolus valde curiosus est, & omni tempore laborat, vt diuina operâ videatur edere: unde Deus etiam illi ad cumulum damnationis suæ & aliorum, aliquando permittit. Hinc vero licet intueri, quàm rectè faciant, qui doctrinam quamlibet sacris Scripturis consentaneam & comprobatam, tamen poscunt miraculis comprobari. Constat miracula non semper esse vera, constat multa fieri arte, dolo, fraude, cuiusmodi etiam multa deprehensa sunt per monachos & sacrificulos, conficta & excogitata, quæstus gratia: vt de virgine, imò meretrice illa in Anglia, Dauid Gedarith, & hæretici, de quibus Epiphanius: constat à dæmonibus & hypocritis, falsis doctoribus, posse edi: ideo non temerè est postulandum, vt doctrina aliqua miraculis comprobetur: quando aliàs possumus de doctrinæ præstantia, & synceritate, iudicium petere ex ipsis sacris literis, quas Deus voluit nobis esse propositas, tanquam omnium aliarum doctrinarum iudices. Et Deus non abstulit ab ecclesia donū illud, discretione spirituū, donum prophetiæ, aliaq; dona, per quæ de doctrinis posset iudicari. Et quanquam illi ipsi, qui falsam doctrinā afferunt, ex ijsdē solent petere sua firmamenta: tamen non est vsq; adeò difficile dispicere, an recte & appositè ipsi firmamentis illius vtantur. Ipsa Scriptura sui interprete agit, & si quando de aliquo in ea loco dubitatur, inquirendi sunt alij loci, qui eundem apertiorem reddunt. Quòd si huiusmodi loci desunt, quòd si item quæ allata sunt à falso doctore, conuinci possunt, non eum habere sensum, quem ipse vult, & significationem, (id quod facilè potest fieri, si acutè intueamur præcedentia & sequentia ad illos locos, quos ipse citat) magno animo doctrina ipsius reijcietur, neq; erit opus miracula adhibere: aut vt maximè adhibeantur, fides tamen doctrinæ non dabitur. Quò factū, quòd pleriq; sanctorū de miraculis edendis non fuerint admodū soliciti: & non adeò multa legūtur mira cula per Paulū edita, qui etiā cùm alibi glorietur, se plus omnibus laborasse, se Apostolū constitutū immediatè ab ipso Deo, nusquā tamē de miraculis gloriatur. Itaq; cùm verbū Dei sit multò certius perpendiculū ad explorandū doctrinā, quàm miracula: cum itē alijs modis possit examinari doctrina, quàm miraculis: cū item petere miracula, fit dubitantiū duntaxat & incredulorū: liquet, eos incredulitatis notā non effugere, qui doctrinam, (præsertim quæ per Scripturā satis luculenter potest cōprobari) cupiūt per miracula cōfirmari. Hinc reprehēdit Christus Iudæos Matth. 12. Natio prava & adultera, inquit, signū quærit, & signū nō dabit ei, nisi signū Ionę prophetę. Itē Marc. 8. Christus ingemuit spiritu suo, & indignatus est, q; generatio illa signū peteret. Et 1. Cor. 1. pro argumento increduli tatis & duriciei obijcit Apostolus, qp Iudæi signū peteret, græci verò sapientiā. Ioan. 4. ad regulū, Nisi signa & pdigia videritis, non credetis. Luc. 22. Herodes notatur vanę curiosi tatis, quòd sperarat signū aliquod à Christo edendū videre, qui tamē ob multa alia signa audita nō credebat. Sed iā rursus dicit aliquis: Si nō adeò magna res est donū miraculorū, cur ergo Deus voluit eo potissimū adduci homines ad fide in primitiua ecclesia? Et, si nūc miracula maximè fuerūt necessaria, quare etiā nūc non perinde sunt in vsu? Respōdetur, miracula in primitiua ecclesia habita pro aptissimo instrumēto, quo doctrina euangelica cōfirmaretur, vt ita plures adducerētur, & in fide alerētur. Et cōueniebat ita fieri, tūm ratione doctrinę, quandoquidē ea noua erat, suspecta & inuisa omnibus, (Eiusmodi etiā erat hæc doctrina, quæ rationibus humanis credi aut cōfirmari non poterat, quandoquidem rationi videtur maximè aduersari) & in speciem legi Mosaicę, cuius maxima erat au toritas, contraria: tum ratione hominū infirmorū & in superstitionibus induratorū: si omnes faciles & flexibiles se præbuissent, & si verbū per se potuisset statim efficax esse in omnium pectoribus, nihil opus fuisset miraculis. Et si solis persuasorijs verbis res fuisset a acta, habita fuisset tota doctrina pro eiusmodi, qualis fuit philosophorum & pharisæorū, & Saducæorū, qui defectis rationibus sua poterant in specie reddere probabilia, sed nō miraculis. At verò q; nūc non opus sanā doctrinā euangelicā ita miraculis externis cōfirmare, plures sunt rationes. Non q; manus Domini abbreviata nūc fit, aut ecclesia sit destituta donis spiritus, quæ ad conseruationē & illustrationē ipsius sunt necessaria: sed quòd doctrina Euāgelica, nūc non est noua, aut suspecta, sicut erat tēporibus apostolorū, sed veritas eius & dignitas satis iam nota est, ac per innumera miracula, inprimis per resurrectionem Christi, per missionē Spiritus sancti, per obedientiam totius mundi erga euangelium, abundē confirmata, ita, vt qui propter ista non credit, nec propter alia miracula fit crediturus. Et propterea voluit Deus nunc cessare potestatem miracu lorum, sicut tempore reuelati euangelij cessauit prophetia: quia, quæ antea fuerant per prophetas prædicenda, non erant adimpleta. Et tamen sicut post reuelatum euāgelium adhuc aliqui extiterunt prophetæ, vt Agabus, quatuor filiæ Philippi, Paulus, Ioannes euangelista seu Theologus: ita etiam nunc haud dubiè multis in locis per sanctos edun tur miracula: sed eorū notitia non ad omnes ita peruenit, sicut illorum, quæ sacræ literæ narrant edita per Christum & apostolos. Et si rariora sunt miracula externa, sunt tamen frequentia miracula interna, prouenientia ex virtute verbi in cordibus hominū. Potest et iā causa esse, cur pauciora miracula fiant nunc, quàm olim, partim q; nūc pauci, vel nulli sint, qtali fide sint prædicti, per quā miracula edi possunt: partim, q; populus indignus est propter quę edantur miracula, & tāta duricie, vt, quādo respuūt Scripturas, nec miraculis crediturī sint: sicut di ctū est diuiti, cupieti, vt mitteret aliquis ex mortuis ad fratres ipsius, cui dictū est, quòd haberet Mosen & prophetas, quibus si non crederet, nec alicui ex mortuis essent crediturī: & qui petunt, non propter gloria Dei petūt, sed quadā curiositate, & ex ce ca malitia, quibus Christus noluit dare signū, nisi Ionę prophetę. Deinde, ne in abusum veniant miracula: ne, qui potestate haberet, abuteretur ad gloria suā, & obscuratio nem glo- & indignitas. něgloriæ Dei:ne,qui viderent,aliquid supra hominem illis tribueret: & constat, magnū fuisse miraculorum abusum apud corpora mortuorū,& apud statuas,etiā nostris tepo-ribus:in Anglia, Mesenis, Quirinus,&c. Quare qui nunc petunt,doctrinā euangelicā,cūm syncerita-ti proponitur cōfirmari miraculis,ij resurrectioni Christi, missioni S.S. &c.sunt iniurij,& ostendūt,se pro nihilo illa omnia habere, quę Scriptura nobis palàm memorat.
units.tr: Fifthly, so that this gift should not seem to be sought after too eagerly, and so that people should not give immediate credence to everyone who appears to work miracles, God orders all things wisely. He knows how to use his gifts for many purposes at once, and he sometimes allows the wicked to misuse them, as others misuse the gift of tongues or the gift of wisdom. So the wicked misuse the gift of miracles, provided they work miracles by divine power and not rather by the power of the devil. The devil is very inquisitive and always strives to appear to act by divine power, and God sometimes allows him to do so, to add to his own damnation and that of others. From this we may see how wrongly they act who, though a doctrine agrees with the Holy Scriptures and has been approved by them, still demand that it be confirmed by miracles. It is certain that miracles are not always genuine. It is certain that many are performed by skill, trickery and fraud. Many such have been exposed among monks and minor priests, invented and devised for the sake of gain, as with the virgin, or rather harlot, in England, David Gedarith, and the heretics of whom Epiphanius writes. It is certain too that miracles can be worked by demons and hypocrites and false teachers. Therefore it is not rashly to be demanded that any doctrine be confirmed by miracles, since we can in any case seek judgement about the excellence and purity of a doctrine from the Holy Scriptures themselves, which God wished to be set before us as the judges of all other doctrines. God has not taken away from the Church that gift of discerning of spirits, the gift of prophecy and the other gifts by which doctrines can be judged. And although those who bring forward false doctrine usually seek their supports from the same Scriptures, it is not so very difficult to see whether they use those supports rightly and appropriately. Scripture is its own interpreter. If ever there is doubt about some passage in it, other passages are to be sought which make the same thing clearer. But if such passages are lacking, or if what a false teacher has brought forward can be shown not to have the meaning and sense he himself claims (which can easily be done if we attentively consider the context before and after those passages which he cites), his doctrine will be rejected without difficulty, and there will be no need to bring in miracles. Or, even if miracles are brought in as much as possible, belief in the doctrine will still not be given. This is why many of the saints were not very anxious to work miracles, and we do not read of very many miracles performed by Paul. Although he elsewhere boasts that he laboured more than all the others, and that he was made an apostle immediately by God himself, nowhere does he boast of miracles. Therefore, since the Word of God is a far surer plumb-line for testing doctrine than miracles, and since doctrine can be examined in other ways than by miracles, and since to demand miracles belongs only to the doubtful and unbelieving, it is clear that those who wish a doctrine (especially one that can be sufficiently and plainly proved from Scripture) to be confirmed by miracles do not escape the mark of unbelief. For this reason Christ rebukes the Jews in Matt. 12: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah." Likewise in Mark 8, Christ "sighed in his spirit and was indignant that that generation sought a sign." And in 1 Cor. 1, the Apostle offers as a proof of unbelief and hardness that the Jews ask for a sign and the Greeks seek wisdom. In John 4, to the nobleman: "Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe." In Luke 22, Herod is marked by vain curiosity, because he hoped to see some sign performed by Christ, though he did not believe even after hearing of many other signs. But someone will again say: "If the gift of miracles is not so great a thing, why then did God wish men to be brought to faith especially by this means in the primitive Church? And if miracles were then most necessary, why are they not equally in use now?" The answer is that in the primitive Church miracles were regarded as the most suitable instrument by which the evangelical doctrine was confirmed, so that more might be brought in and nourished in the faith. And it was fitting that this should be so, both because of the nature of the doctrine, since it was new, suspect and hateful to all (such was this doctrine, which could not be believed or confirmed by human reasons, since it seems chiefly to oppose reason), and because it was contrary to the Law of Moses, whose authority was very great; and both because of the weakness of men, who were hardened in superstitions. If all had shown themselves easy and pliant, and if the Word could at once have been effective in the hearts of all of them by its own power, there would have been no need of miracles. And if the matter had been carried on by persuasive words alone, the whole doctrine would have been held to be of the same kind as the doctrine of the philosophers, the Pharisees and the Sadducees, who, when their reasons failed, could still make their positions appear probable, but not by miracles. But as to why there is now no need to confirm sound evangelical doctrine in this way by outward miracles, there are several reasons. It is not that the hand of the Lord has been shortened now, or that the Church has been left without the gifts of the Spirit, which are necessary for its preservation and enlightenment. Rather, the evangelical doctrine is now not new or suspect, as it was in the time of the apostles. Its truth and dignity are already sufficiently known, and it has been abundantly confirmed by countless miracles, above all by the resurrection of Christ, by the sending of the Holy Spirit, and by the obedience of the whole world to the gospel. So whoever does not believe on account of these things will not be brought to belief by other miracles either. For this reason God willed that the power of miracles should now cease, just as prophecy ceased at the time the gospel was revealed, because those things which had previously been foretold by the prophets were not yet fulfilled. Yet just as after the gospel was revealed there still arose some prophets, such as Agabus, the four daughters of Philip, Paul, and John the evangelist or theologian, so also now, without doubt, miracles are performed by the saints in many places. But the knowledge of them does not reach everyone in the way that the knowledge of those which the sacred writings relate as performed by Christ and the apostles does. And although outward miracles are rarer, inward miracles are frequent, arising from the power of the Word in the hearts of men. There may also be another cause why fewer miracles are performed now than formerly: partly because there are now few or none endowed with such faith as can work miracles, and partly because the people are unworthy of the miracles that would be performed, and are so hardened that, when they reject the Scriptures, they will not believe even miracles. This is like what was said to the rich man who desired that someone be sent from the dead to his brothers, and to whom it was answered that they had Moses and the prophets, and that if they did not believe these, they would not believe even someone risen from the dead. And those who ask for miracles do not ask for the glory of God, but out of a certain curiosity and from that same wickedness, to which Christ did not wish to give a sign except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Furthermore, miracles must not come into abuse: lest one who had the power should misuse it for his own glory, to the obscuring and dishonouring of God's glory; lest those who saw such things should attribute something beyond man to them. And it is clear that there was great abuse of miracles in connection with the bodies of the dead and with statues, even in our own times: in England, at Mesenis, at Quirinus, and so on. Therefore those who now ask that evangelical doctrine, when it is set forth in sincerity, be confirmed by miracles, as if the resurrection of Christ, the mission of the Holy Spirit, and so on, were not enough, do injury to these things, and show that they hold all those things for nothing which Scripture plainly sets before us.

units.la: An mali possint vera edere miracula) Cęterū,à malis verè vera miracula non edi,hisce ratio-nibus demonstrari quodammodo posse videtur. Primùm. Miracula impetrantur oratione. Atqui peccatores Deus non audit. Ioan.9. Scimus,quòd peccatores Deus non exaudit, Et Prouerb.28. Qui declinat aures suas,ne audiat legé,oratio eius erit execrabilis. Respon-detur: Oratio ad impetrandū non in nititur merito & dignitati orātis, sed misericordiędi uinę,quæ etiā ad malos se extendit. Itaq; etiā qui peccator est,interdū exauditur,idq; vel ad salutē suā,vel alterius,vel ad Dei gloriā. Sic exauditus est publicanus peccator Luc.18.
units.tr: Whether evil men can work true miracles. Moreover, it may be shown in some measure by the following reasons that true miracles are not wrought by evil men. First: miracles are obtained by prayer. But God does not hear sinners. John 9. We know that God does not hear sinners. And Proverbs 28: He who turns away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer will be abominable. The answer is that prayer for obtaining something rests not on the merit and dignity of the one who prays, but on the mercy of God, which extends even to the wicked. So even a sinner is sometimes heard, and that either for his own salvation, or for another's, or for the glory of God. Thus the sinful publican was heard, Luke 18.

units.la: Deinde obijcitur: Miracula attribuuntur fidei: Matt.17. Si habueritis fidem, vt granū Sina-pis,&c. Fides autē sine operibus mortua est: igitur mali,quiq; non habēt bona opera,nō possunt miracula edere. Respondemus: Etiāsi impius sit mortuus spiritualiter,tamē nihil prohibet,quin res viua vtatur instrumēto mortuo,sicut homo vtitur baculo: atq; hocpa-ëto Deus operatur per fidem hominis peccatoris instrumentaliter.
units.tr: Next it is objected: miracles are ascribed to faith. Matt. 17. If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, etc. But faith without works is dead; therefore the wicked, who have no good works, cannot work miracles. We reply: even if the impious man is spiritually dead, nothing prevents a living thing from using a dead instrument, as a man uses a staff. In this way God works through the faith of a sinful man as an instrument.

units.la: Tertiò: Miracula sunt quædam diuina testimonia. Hebr.2. Contestante Deo signis & portētis,&c. Sed Deus non potest esse testis falsitatis: igitur mali homines miracula ede-re non possunt. Respondetur: Miracula sunt,vera testimonia eius, ob quod inducuntur. Vnde à malis,qui falsam doctrinam enunciant,nunquam fiunt vera miracula ad confir-mationē suę doctrinę, quamuis quandoq; fieri possint ad cōmendationē nominis Chri-sti,quod inuocant,& virtute Sacramentorū,quæ exhibent. Ab his autē qui verā doctrinā annūciant,fiunt quādoq; vera miracula ad confirmationē doctrinæ,non autē ad testifica-tionē sanctitatis. Vnde August.lib.83.quæst.quęstione 79. Aliter magi faciūt miracula, aliter boni Christiani,aliter mali magi per priuatos contractus cū dæmonibus: boni Christiani p publicā iustitiā,mali Christiani per signa publicę iustitię. In eodē libro Augustin. ait, quædā miracula etiā sceleratos homines facere,qualia sancti facere nō possunt: vt pseu-doprophetæ,de quibus Matt.24. Et Luc.17. Apostoli nō poterāt expellere dæmones. Nō tamē ideo mali Deo sunt acceptiores: sicut nec magi magis placuerūt Deo quàm Moses.
units.tr: Thirdly: miracles are certain divine testimonies. Heb. 2. God also bearing witness with signs and wonders, etc. But God cannot be a witness to falsehood; therefore evil men cannot work miracles. The answer is that miracles are true testimonies of God for whatever cause they are brought forward. Hence, by evil men who proclaim false doctrine, true miracles are never done to confirm their doctrine, although they can sometimes be done for the commendation of the name of Christ, which they invoke, and by the power of the sacraments which they administer. But by those who announce true doctrine, true miracles are sometimes done to confirm the doctrine, though not to attest holiness. Hence Augustine, Questions, book 83, question 79: Magicians work miracles in one way, good Christians in another, and evil magicians through private contracts with demons; good Christians through public justice, evil Christians through the signs of public justice. In the same book Augustine says that some miracles are also done by wicked men, of a kind the saints cannot do, such as the false prophets of whom Matt. 24 speaks, and Luke 17 tells how the apostles could not cast out demons. Yet the wicked are not on that account more acceptable to God, just as the magicians did not please God more than Moses did.

units.la: Quartò: Boni sunt Deo magis coiuncti,quàm mali: Sed non omnes boni faciūt mira-cula: igitur multò minus mali. Respondemus, vt Augustin.ait eodē lib.83.quęstionū: Idēo non omnibus sanctis ista attribuūtur,ne periculosissimo errore decipiātur infirmi,æsti-mantes,in talibus factis esse maiora dona,quàm in operibus iustitiæ, quibus vita æterna comparatur. Ad summā,fiunt miracula quædā ad comprobationē veritatis: quędā ad de-monstrationē sanctitatis alicuius, quam Deus vult hominibus proponi ad exemplum. Prioris generis miracula edūt quiuis. Posterioris soli boni. Sic sanctitas Pauli cōprobata est Actorum,19. quādo etiam sudaria eius posita super infirmos iuuabant. Ex Augustino lib.83.quæstionū,quæstione 79. Sancti habentes donum miraculorum secundū publicā & quodāmodo imperiale legē,id est,summi Dei potestatem, imperant infimis potestati-bus,ad quædā visibilia miracula facienda: in illis enim Deus ipse imperat, cuius templum sunt & quem cōtempta sua priuata potestate ardētissimè diligunt. In magicis autem im-perationibus præstant potestates illę inferiores aliquid se honorātibus,idq; priuato quo-dam iure. Videntur quoq; interdū mali cōminari Spiritibus: id verò fit ad ludificatione circūstantium. Satanas non expellit Satanā: verum est: aut enim non verè discedit Sa-tanas,sed simulat: aut,si discedit,facit id,vt magis decipiat. Colludunt enim inter se dæ-mones,vt facilius malum perficiant,& cùm egreditur corpus alicuius,tùm ingreditur nimiam eius. Luc.10. Nolite in hoc gaudere quòd spiritus vobis subijciuntur,sed gaudete, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis.
