Et apud eundē cap.11. negat Christus, adhibitis firmissimis rationibus, Satanam à Satana posse expelli: Imò pulsum dæmonem peram-bulare loca arida,in quibus si requietem non reperiat,redire ad domum suā, ex quaiam ante egressus fuerat,eamq;,assumptis septem spiritibus se peioribus,ita occupare, vt ex-trema hominis illius primis fiant peiora,&c. Hæc de miraculis per digressionem com-memorāsse satis fit, progrediemur nunc ad verba autoris,à quibus nonnihil discēssisse vi-demur, confutationem ea enim in se continent.
units.tr: Fourthly: the good are more closely joined to God than the wicked. But not all the good work miracles; therefore much less do the wicked. We reply, as Augustine says in the same book of Questions: for this reason these things are not attributed to all the saints, lest the weak be deceived by a most dangerous error, thinking that in such deeds there are greater gifts than in the works of righteousness by which eternal life is obtained. In sum, some miracles are done to confirm the truth, others to demonstrate the holiness of some person, which God wills to be set before men as an example. Miracles of the former kind anyone may work; only the good work those of the latter kind. Thus the holiness of Paul was attested in Acts 19, when even his handkerchiefs laid upon the sick helped them. From Augustine, Questions, book 83, question 79: Saints who have the gift of miracles, by a public and, as it were, imperial law, that is, by the power of the supreme God, command the lower powers to perform certain visible miracles. For in such commands God himself commands, whom they, having despised their own private power, love most ardently. In magical incantations, however, those lower powers serve whoever honours them, and that by a certain private right. Also, evil men sometimes seem to command spirits, but this is done to mock the bystanders. Satan does not cast out Satan: that is true. For either Satan does not truly depart but feigns, or, if he does depart, he does so in order to deceive all the more. The demons collude with one another so that they may more easily bring about evil, and when one departs from a body, he returns to it with greater force. Luke 10: Do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven. And in the same place, chapter 11, Christ, using very firm arguments, denies that Satan can be cast out by Satan. Indeed, when the expelled demon wanders through dry places and finds no rest there, he returns to the house he had left, and taking seven spirits worse than himself, occupies it so that the last state of that man becomes worse than the first, etc. It is enough to have recalled these things about miracles by way of digression. We now proceed to the words of the author, from which we seem to have departed somewhat, for they contain the refutation.

units.la: CONFVTATIO.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: Non enim angelis subiecit orbem terræ futurū, de quo loquimur. Testatus est autem alicubi quidam, dicens: Quid est homo, quòd memor es eius? aut filius hominis, quòd inuisis illū? Fecisti eum paulisper inferiore angelis, gloria & honore coronasti eū, et cō-stituisti stituisti eum super opera manuū tuarū. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. In hoc enim quòd ei subiecit omnia, nihil omisit illi non subiectum, &c.
units.tr: For he did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak. But someone has testified somewhere, saying: What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet. For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him, etc.

units.la: Hic confutationē huius primę partis epistolæ, in qua de diuinitate Christi disputatur, recte constituemus, adferūtur enim nunc ea, quę Christū non solùm non esse Deum, sed etiam angelis ipsis inferiore videntur probare, eadēq; reprehenduntur. Erat aūt illud va- lidissimum, & quòd semper moriosissimè obijciebāt Iudęi, ad euertendā diuinitatē Chri-sti, quòd videlicet Christus esset homo. Quam vnam rationē, (quādoquidē impossile & absurdū esse videtur, vt vna eadēq; persona & Dei dignitatem, & hominis vilitatē in se sustineat) sufficientem iudicabant ad concludendū, Christū non esse Deum, vel angelis superiore. Verùm apostolus hac ratione nihil deterritus, non negat quidē, Christū fuisse hominem, at docet interim, regnū illud spirituale, & plenā in omnia potestatem, Christo etiam homini cōuenire, & eundē vt homine esse angelis multò superiore: ac ,pinde merito etiā pro Deo agnoscendū. Hinc mox descēdit ad reddendū rationē, quare Christum, quē supra probatū est, Deū esse ab æterno, nec nō cœli terræq; cōditore, Deo patri per omnia æquale, assumere in tēpore humanā naturā decuerit, quādoquidē hīc solus restabat scrupus, quomodo videlicet factū, vt qui ab æterno fuisset Deus, factus esset homo. Quæ ,psestò omnia tàm prudenter, tàm cōcinniter ab apostolo sunt disposita, vt nulli rhetores vel dialectici splēdidius id possent, vel acutius. Cęterū videtur cōtextus verborū, ob breuitatem, nōnihil obscuritatis habere, & paulò esse intricatior: sed confido, me claram & perspicuā redditurū Apostoli sententiam.
units.tr: Here we shall rightly set out the refutation of this first part of the epistle, in which the divinity of Christ is disputed. For now there are brought forward arguments which seem to prove that Christ is not only not God but even inferior to the angels, and these are rebutted. This was a very strong objection, and one the Jews always most stubbornly raised to overturn the divinity of Christ: namely, that Christ was a man. They judged this one argument sufficient to conclude that Christ is not God, or superior to the angels, since it seems impossible and absurd that one and the same person should bear both the dignity of God and the lowliness of man. But the apostle, undeterred by this argument, does not deny that Christ was a man, but teaches that that spiritual kingdom and full power over all things belong also to Christ as man, and that the same one, as man, is far superior to the angels, and therefore is rightly to be acknowledged even as God. Hence he goes on at once to give the reason why it was fitting for Christ, who has been proved above to be God from eternity and the creator of heaven and earth, equal in all things to God the Father, to assume human nature in time, since the only scruple left was how it came about that he who had been God from eternity became man. All these things the apostle has arranged so prudently and so harmoniously that no rhetoricians or dialecticians could do so more splendidly or more acutely. Yet the context of the words, owing to its brevity, seems to have some obscurity and to be rather intricate; but I trust that I shall make the apostle's meaning clear and perspicuous.

units.la: Nō enim angelis, inquit, subiecit orbē terræ futurū, de quo loquimur: repetit initio summā & caput totius disputationis, qd̄ aptè fit, quoniā ea debet in tota disputatione versari ob oculos. Estq; sententia: Constāter adhuc assero, Christū esse angelis multò superiorem, ac proinde Deū. Nā non legitur, quòd orbis futurus, id est, omnia quæ in cœlis & in terra sunt, in futurū subijci debeat angelis, sicut Scriptura aperte dicit, omnia subijcieda Christo, eūq; in æternū regnaturū. Sic nimirū aptè & magno animo præfatur, quasi nihil formidās argumēta aliqua in diuersum proferenda, quæ ipse non sit facilimè dissoluturus. Sumpta aūt sunt hæc verba ex his, quæ mox sequūtur, vbi dicitur, omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius: atq; ipse inferet & cōcludet: Christo etiam vt homini omnia subijcieda. Inde ,pducit argumentū & primum & principale aduersariorum, quod & statim clarissimè diluit: sic autē illi argu- mētabantur. Christus, quē tu contendis angelis esse superiore, ac ,pinde Deū, manifestè deprehēsus est verus homo. Sed homo est inferior angelis: sicut Scriptura palàm dicit Psal. 8. Quid est homo, quòd memor es, &c. Ergo Christus non solū non est Deus, sed etiam angelis inferior. Atque hoc paēto, habita ratione collationis Christi cum angelis, quam institutam fuisse in initio confirmationis diximus, videtur efficacissimè concludi, Christum non esse Deum, imò ipsis quoque angelis multò inferiorem. Apparet, aduersarios pro argumenti sui probatione tantùm citaresolitos priora illa verba, quibus generaliter significatur, hominem esse angelis inferiorem. Proinde apostolus valdè argutè refellit istam obiectionē, ac perspicuè ostendit ex eodem loco, Christum, etiamsi verus homo sit angelis, nihilominus superiorem; ideoque verum Deum, & orbem terræ futurum illi, vt homini debere subdi. Sic enim respondet. Concedo quidem Christum esse hominem, sed tamen docebo, id non obstare, quò minus angelis sit superior. Nam eodem loco Scriptura habet, Gloria et honore coronasti eum, et constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum: omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Ex his sic colligo: Omnia sunt subiecta pedibus hominis. Sed qui dicit, omnia, nihil excludit: Ergo etiam angeli Christo vt homini sunt subiecti. Quare salua manet Christi dignitas, quam asserui. Christus adhuc superior angelis agnosci debet: imò quia super opera manuū Dei, id est, super creaturas constitutus, etiam creator, sine Deus, cum de creatura nō possit simpliciter dici, quòd sit supra omnes creaturas. Hæc est, meo iudicio, clara & perspicua sententia Apostoli, neq; quicquā durius reddidimus, nihil à sim plici ac germano sensu detorsimus, & Scripturæ verba ad amussim huic interpretationi quadrant. Iam partes nostro more explicabimus. Non enim angelis subiecit orbem terræ futurū, de quo loquimur: Quomodo hæc verba locum hic habeant, & an præcedentia respiciant, an ad sequentia, aliqui non satis expendunt. Quidam connectunt præcedentibus, ac respicere ea volunt ad id, quod supra ante exhortatione proximā pater dixit ad filium: Sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum: item ad cætera, quibus Christo thronus & regnū æternū tribuebatur. Quidā verò ita addita putant hęc, verba vt sint veluti probatio eius, quòd in proxima exhortatione Christus appellatus est Dominus, quā do dictum est, euangelium allatum esse per ipsum Dominum. Rectè appellatum Domi- num, his verbis probaretur. Nam ipsi Christo vt Domino proprie omnia sunt subiecta, non autem angelis, qui propterea domini non possunt appellari, sed tantùm ministri, sicut supra dictum est, eos esse ministratorios spiritus, qui in ministerium emittuntur. Sed multò rectius ea referimus ad sequentia, sicut & clare ex sequetibus sumpta sunt. Nam mox subijcitur, omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius: quae verba arripit Apostolus pro testimonio, ad probandum, quòd Christo etiam homine angeli sint inferiores. Itaq; iam quasi à modo absoluisset argumentum illud, magno feruore primo loco enunciat, quod intendit concludere, quemadmodum solent aliquando rhetores conclusionem primo loco constituere. Et perspicuum est cuiuis, haec verba, Non enim angelis subiecit orbem terrae futurum, plane sumpta esse ex illis, quae sequuntur, Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Facit huc quòd quidam in voce loquimur, dictunt, enallagen esse temporis, & praesens positum esse pro futuro: quasi diceret: loquemur. Proinde non haec verba ita posita esse existimamus, ✱ sit veluti repetita propositio, & summa totius disputationis, in qua probatum est, Christum esse angelis superiorem, ac proinde verum Deum: quam solent etiam Rhetores subinde studio repetere, quia perpetuò ob oculos versari debet, cauedumq;, ne ab ea oratione digrediatur. Sicut Cicero pro Roscio, ante confutationem ita proponit: Occidisse patrem Sextus Roscius arguitur. Itaq; cùm hic venturus esset Apostolus ad confutationem, commodè repetit disputationis generalem propositionem. Quinetiam mos est Scripturae interdum primo loco enunciare, & summatim completi, ex quibus alia, quae praeire debebat, possint intelligi. Iosuae 2. Quia Dominus dedit in manum nostram omnem terram. Vbi non conuenit, istud fuisse principium sermonis eorum. Nam dictio, id est, quia rationem reddit eius quod ante dictum intelligitur. Verum completitur Scriptura finem sermonis eorum, ex quo principium eius intelligere potes. Haec propter particulam enim: Non enim angelis, etc. Eam verò conflat ex verbis, quae proximè sequuntur, è quibus iterum colleturus est, Christum angelis esse multò excellentiorem. Proinde quòd nos hic confutationem constituamus, puto, omnes id rectè à nobis fieri iudicaturos, si animaduertant, ea, quae iam proferuntur de humanitate Christi, maximè semper obijci solita à Iudaeis, ad infirmandam Christi diuinitatem. Et cùm Apostolus clarè doceat, humanitate Christi non obesse, quo minus idem omnia (etiam angelos) subiecta habeat, pariterq;, redddat, causas, cur decuerit Christum, qui ab aeterno Deus est, in tempore fieri hominem: facile animaduertit quibus, hic grauissimè & aptissimè dilui ea, quae ab aduersarijs ad euertendam Christi dignitatem proferebantur. Sed sit satis hoc pacto cōsilij nostri rationem reddidisse. Videndū iam, quid Apostolus hic vocet ????? ??? ????? orbem terrarū futurum. ????? quidam interpretantur orbem terrarum, quidam terram habitabilem. Ac videtur Apostolus respexisse ad initium Psalmi octaui, ex quo sequens testimonium desumptum est, quo dicitur, Domine Dominus noster, quàm admirabile est nomen tuum in universa terra. Sed non male videbimur per orbem terrarum, ????????? intelligere coelum ac terram, adeoq; omnes res creatas, quomodo etiam vocabulum mundi apud Scriptores saepè pro coelo ac terra vsurpatur. Atq; ita hic tantundem significabit, quantum verbis sequentibus, vbi dicitur, Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius: In quam sententiam etiam Christus Matth. 28. dicit, Data sibi omne potestate in coelo & in terra. Et Ioan. 13. Omnia dedit mihi pater in manus. Ephes. 1. describitur Christus sedens ad dexteram patris, & constitutus supra omnem principatū ac potestatem, & virtute, & dominiū, & omne nomen, quod nominatur non solū in hoc seculo, verumetiā in futuro: & addit, omnia subiecta sub pedes illius. Quòd ergo in his locis effertur per distributionem, de omnibus in coelo & terra subditis Christo, quodq; itarum summatim vno verbo dicitur, Omnia subiecta sub pedes Christi, idem hic significari puto, cum dicitur, Christo subiectum orbem terrarum. Vocat autem orbem terrae futurum, non quòd alius orbis ab eo, qui nunc est, condendus sit, & Christo subijciendus, aut quòd Christus in eo, qui nunc est, regnum non obtineat, & solus diabolus, qui in Euangelicis literis vocatur princeps mundi huius, habeat in eo potestatem: sed quadā ratione collationis Christi cum mundo. Si enim animaduertimus, Christū semper fuisse, esse, & fore: mundū verò coepisse in tempore, rectè hic respectu Christi, qui erat ab aeterno, dicitur futurus: Quomodo etiam Esaiae 9. Christus vocatur pater futuri seculi, id est, conditor & creator orbis, nō quod seculum, quod tèpus illud antecesserat, non condidisset, & aliud in posterum esset conditurus, quando generaliter ipse omnium seculorum sit conditor, sicut initio huius epistolę dictum est: Sed ratione collationis Christi cum mundo. Nam hic in tempore incipiens esse respectu Christi ab aeterno agentis, futurus appellatur. Non dissimili modo Rom. 5. Christus homo factus in tempore, & aliquot retrò seculis, post primum parentè nostrum Adamū, collatus cum hoc vocatur Adam futurus. Regnauit, inquit, mors ab Adā vsq; ad Mosen, in eos quoq;, qui non peccauerat ad similitudinem transgressionis Adā, quityʼ
units.tr: "For he has not subjected to angels the world to come, of which we speak," he says. He repeats at the outset the summary and head of the whole argument, which is fitting, since it ought to stay before our eyes throughout the discussion. The meaning is this: I still maintain firmly that Christ is far superior to the angels and therefore is God. For it is nowhere written that the world to come, that is, all things that are in heaven and on earth, must be made subject to angels in the future, whereas Scripture plainly says that all things are to be subjected to Christ, and that he will reign forever. He introduces the matter in this way, appropriately and with a bold spirit, as if he feared no arguments that might be brought against him which he would not easily dissolve. These words are taken from what immediately follows, where it is said, "You have put all things under his feet," and the apostle himself will go on to conclude that all things are to be subjected to Christ even as man. From there he brings forward the first and chief argument of the opponents, which he also refutes at once. The opponents argued as follows: "Christ, whom you contend is superior to the angels and therefore God, has clearly been shown to be a true man. But man is inferior to the angels, as Scripture plainly says in Psalm 8: 'What is man, that you are mindful of him,' and so on. Therefore Christ is not only not God, but is even inferior to the angels." And by this reasoning, having taken into account the comparison of Christ with the angels, which we said was set up at the beginning of the proof, it seems to follow most effectively that Christ is not God, but is far inferior even to the angels themselves. It is evident that the opponents, in proving their argument, were accustomed to cite only those earlier words by which it is stated in general that man is inferior to the angels. Accordingly the apostle very skilfully refutes this objection, and shows clearly from the same passage that Christ, even though he is a true man, is nevertheless superior to the angels, and therefore is the true God, and that the world to come ought to be subjected to him, as to a man. For he answers thus: "I grant indeed that Christ is a man, but I will show that this does not stand in the way of his being superior to the angels. For in the same passage Scripture says: 'You crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet.' From this I conclude as follows: all things are subject to the feet of this man. But he who says 'all things' excludes nothing. Therefore the angels too are subject to Christ as man. Thus the dignity of Christ which I have asserted remains safe: Christ must still be acknowledged as superior to the angels, indeed, because he is set over the works of God's hands, that is, over creatures, he is also creator and God, since it cannot simply be said of a creature that it is above all creatures." This, in my judgment, is the clear and plain meaning of the apostle, and we have not made anything harsher, nor have we twisted anything away from the simple and genuine sense, and the words of Scripture fit this interpretation exactly. Now we shall explain the parts in our usual way. "For he has not subjected to angels the world to come, of which we speak": how these words fit here, and whether they look back to what precedes or forward to what follows, some do not weigh sufficiently. Some connect them with what goes before, and want them to refer to what the Father said to the Son in the preceding exhortation, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet," and likewise to the other passages by which a throne and an eternal kingdom are attributed to Christ. Others think these words are added as a proof of the fact that in the preceding exhortation Christ was called Lord, when it was said that the gospel was brought by the Lord himself. Calling him Lord was rightly proved by these words, for all things are properly subject to Christ himself as Lord, but not to the angels, who for that reason cannot be called lords, but only ministers, as was said above, that the angels are ministering spirits sent out for service. But we refer these words much more rightly to what follows, as is also clear from the sequel. For immediately it is added, "You have put all things under his feet," which words the apostle seizes upon as testimony, to prove that the angels are inferior to Christ even as man. And so, as if he had already finished that argument, he states with great fervor at the start what he intends to conclude, just as orators sometimes put their conclusion first. And it is plain to anyone that these words, "For he has not subjected to angels the world to come," are plainly taken from what follows, "You have put all things under his feet." To this point belongs what some say about the word "we speak," namely that there is an enallage of tense, and the present is used for the future, as if he were to say "we shall speak." Accordingly we do not think these words were put in this way as a repeated proposition and summary of the whole discussion, in which it has been proved that Christ is superior to the angels and therefore the true God. Orators too are accustomed to repeat such a summary deliberately from time to time, because it ought to be kept constantly before the eyes, and care must be taken that the speech does not stray from it. Thus Cicero, in the speech for Roscius, before the refutation, sets out his case in this way: "Sextus Roscius is accused of having killed his father." So, since the apostle was about to come to the refutation, he appropriately repeats the general proposition of the discussion. Moreover, it is the custom of Scripture at times to state at the beginning, in brief, the things from which other things that ought to precede may be understood. Joshua 2: "For the Lord has given us all the land into our hands." Here it does not fit that this was the beginning of their speech. For the word "for" (quia) gives the reason for what was said before, which is understood. But Scripture completes the end of their speech, from which you can understand its beginning. Here the particle "for" (enim) in "For he has not subjected," and so on, is joined to the words that immediately follow, from which the apostle will again conclude that Christ is far more excellent than the angels. Therefore, since we here set up a refutation, I think everyone will judge that we are right to do so, if they notice that the things now brought forward about the humanity of Christ were always most often objected by the Jews, to weaken the divinity of Christ. And since the apostle clearly teaches that the humanity of Christ does not hinder him from having all things, even the angels, subjected to him, and at the same time gives the reasons why it was fitting that Christ, who is God from eternity, should become man in time, one easily perceives how most severely and most aptly he has here dissolved those things which were put forward by the adversaries to overthrow the dignity of Christ. But let it be enough to have given the reasoning of our plan in this way. Now we must see what the apostle means here by the word [οἰκουμένην] "the world to come." Some interpret it as the world, others as the inhabited earth. And the apostle seems to have looked back to the beginning of Psalm 8, from which the following testimony is taken, where it is said, "O Lord our Lord, how excellent is your name in all the earth." But we shall not be wrong to understand by "the world" [οἰκουμένην] heaven and earth, and so all created things, just as the word "world" among writers is often used for heaven and earth. And so here it will signify just as much as the following words, where it is said, "You have put all things under his feet." To this same sense Christ also says in Matthew 28: "All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth." And in John 13: "The Father has given all things into my hands." In Ephesians 1 Christ is described as sitting at the right hand of the Father, and set above every principality and power and virtue and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this age but also in that to come; and it adds that all things are subjected under his feet. Therefore, since in these passages it is expressed by enumeration, that all things in heaven and on earth are subject to Christ, and since this is said briefly in one word, "all things are put under the feet of Christ," I think the same is meant here when it is said that the world is subjected to Christ. But he calls it "the world to come," not because another world, different from the one that now exists, is to be created and subjected to Christ, nor because Christ does not hold kingship in the world that now exists, while the devil alone, who in the Gospel writings is called the prince of this world, has power in it; but by a certain comparison of Christ with the world. For if we consider that Christ always was, is, and will be, but the world began in time, it is rightly called "to come" here with respect to Christ, who was from eternity. Similarly in Isaiah 9 Christ is called the "Father of the future age," that is, the founder and creator of the world, not because the age or time that preceded him had not been founded by him, and because he would found another in the future, since he is generally the founder of all ages, as was said at the beginning of this epistle, but by comparison of Christ with the world. For here, since he begins to be in time with respect to Christ who acts from eternity, he is called "future." In a not dissimilar way, in Romans 5, Christ, made man in time and some centuries after our first parent Adam, when compared with him, is called the "future Adam." "Death reigned," it says, "from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a figure of the one to come." Therefore the figure of that future one is...

units.la: Ideo disputationis semper respiciendā. quitypum geritillius futuri. Coloss.2.cibus,potus,nouilunia vocantur vmbra futurorū. Et hæcinterpretatio maximè conuenit cum eo, quòd prius diximus,nomine orbis intelligere nos omnia,quæ funtin cœlo &in terra,videturq; apostolicæ menti propius accedere. Quod verò ad testimoniū Scripturæ ex Psal.8.adductū attinet, constat, eo psalmo non malè illud vsurpari ab aduersarijs,ad probandū,Christū,quoniā homo erat,esse infe riorem angelis : Sed multò rectissimè etiā Apostolus ex eode loco obiectione dissoluit; colligens,quòd,tametsi Christus fuerit homo, tamen ob hoc nequaquā angelis sit infe-rior.Ex eo enim,quòd omnia homini sunt subiecta,sequitur,etiā angelos homini, &in-primis Christo esse subiectos . Quamuis longè alia ratione,&alio iure tribuendam esse hanc dignitatem Christo,quàm cæteris homnibus,extra controuersiam est.
units.tr: Therefore the argument must always be referred back to that future reality, which the type bears. In Colossians 2 food, drink and new moons are called a shadow of things to come. This interpretation agrees best with what we said earlier, that by "world" we understand all things that are in heaven and on earth, and it seems to come closer to the mind of the apostle. As for the testimony of Scripture from Psalm 8, it is agreed that the adversaries use that psalm not without reason to prove that Christ, since he was a man, is inferior to the angels. But the Apostle answers the objection from the same passage much more correctly, concluding that although Christ was a man, he is by no means for that reason inferior to the angels. For since all things are subjected to man, it follows that the angels too, and above all Christ, are subjected to him. It is beyond dispute, however, that this dignity belongs to Christ by a very different reason and right than it does to all other men.

units.la: Alij propterea, quòd orbis subijciendus Christo vocetur futurus,accipiūt nomine or-bis futuri, vniuersum tepus quod deinceps ad fine vsq; mundi succedet, ab illo,quo euā-gelium Christi cœptum est primùm annunciari &propagari. Hoc nimirum toto tepore futuro Christus potestate omnium accipiet,&dominus omniū constituetur.Orbis prę-teritus habuit legē, quàdiu illa suas vires habere debuit, &Moses habitus fuit in precio. Atnobis futurus,qui nouus erit per spirituale regenerationē,habiturus est euangelium perpetuò duraturū,&eū orbē Christus habebit sibi subditū,solus Christus ab eo pro Do mino agnoscetur. De Chiliastis nihil attinet dicere,qui fortasis ex hoc loco aliquod ar-gumentum confirmando suo dogmati hauserunt; quo de vide Lactantium &D. Augu-stinum. In resurrectione omnes erunt sicut angeli,&peracto iudicio, alij statim erunt in regno, alij in ignem æternum mittentur. 1. Corinth.15. &4.
units.tr: Others, because the world to be subjected to Christ is called future, understand by "the future world" the whole time that will follow from then until the end of the world, from the point at which the gospel of Christ was first begun to be announced and spread. Certainly throughout all that future time Christ will receive power over all things and will be established as Lord of all. The past world had its law for as long as that law was bound to have its force, and Moses was held in honour. But for us, the future world, which will be new through spiritual regeneration, will have the gospel, which will last forever, and Christ will have that world subject to himself; Christ alone will be acknowledged by it as Lord. There is no need to say anything about the Chiliasts, who perhaps drew some argument from this passage to confirm their doctrine; on this see Lactantius and St Augustine. In the resurrection all will be like the angels, and when judgment is over, some will at once be in the kingdom, while others will be sent into eternal fire. 1 Corinthians 15 and 4.

units.la: Alij rursus per orbē terrę futurū intelligūt tépus futuri seculi,in quo regnū Christi ple-nè cōsummabitur.Nam nunc quidé nondū videtur Christus habere plena omniū rerum potestate,cùm diabolus adhuc suū regnum in mūdo habeat,item peccatū, mors, adhuc retinet latū imperiū . At verò post extremū iudiciū, cùm renouata erit terra, &renouati cœli,tunc regnū Christi, qd' nunc dūtaxat cœptū est illustrari,&quotidie quibusdá au-ctibus roboratur, prorsus erit cōsummatum:quéadmodū 1.Cor.15.dicitur: Primitiuæ resurgen-tium Christus:deinde ij, qui sunt Christi in aduētu ipsius,mox finis,cùm tradiderit regnum Deo,&patri,cùm aboleuerit omnem principatū &omnē potestatem,ac virtutē . Nam oportet eū regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. Nouissimus hostis aboletur mors.Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes illius. Tūc ergo orbis futurus post cōsum-mationem seculi Christo erit subditus:Christi regnum tūc erit integrū, nec vllis amplius patebit hostium insultibus, sed ibi erit solus ipse rex regū &Dominus dominantiū . Sed rectius tribuerimus Christo etiam nunc potestatem in totum terrarum orbem, nam nūc potentiam,&sicut ipse quoq; statim à resurrectione sua testatus est Matt.28.sibi data esse omnem potestatem in cœlo &in terra:&Ephes.1.2.item Philippes.2. dicituriam nunc su per omnia cōstitutus.Id quod ex eo quoq; colligitur,quòd statim subijcit aliud argumē-tum aduersariorum,obijcientium.quòd nondum videamus illi omnia subiecta : Quam certè obiectionem Apostolus haud opponerer, si non vellet, clarè intelligi, quòd etiam nunc præsens orbis,&omnia,quæ in eo sunt, Christo sint subiecta.
units.tr: Others again understand by the future world of the earth the time of the coming age, in which the kingdom of Christ will be fully completed. For now Christ does not yet seem to hold full power over all things, since the devil still has his kingdom in the world, and sin and death still retain their wide dominion. But after the final judgment, when the earth and the heavens have been renewed, then the kingdom of Christ, which has now only begun to shine forth and is daily strengthened by certain increases, will be utterly completed; as 1 Corinthians 15 says: "Christ the firstfruits; then those who are Christ's at his coming; then the end, when he has delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has put all things under his feet." Then, therefore, the future world, after the consummation of the age, will be subject to Christ; the kingdom of Christ will then be whole, and no longer open to the assaults of enemies, but there he alone will be King of kings and Lord of lords. But we may more rightly attribute to Christ even now power over the whole circle of the earth; for now he has power, and as he himself testified immediately after his resurrection, Matthew 28, all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him; and Ephesians 1 and 2, likewise Philippians 2, says that he is now exalted above all things. This is also gathered from the fact that he immediately adds another argument of the adversaries, who object that we do not yet see all things subjected to him. Certainly the Apostle would not have raised this objection if he did not want it to be clearly understood that even now the present world and all that is in it are subject to Christ.

units.la: Testatus est autem alicubi quidā dicens: Quid est homo, quòd memor es eius, aut filius hominis, quòd inuisis illum? Fecisti eum paulisper inferiorem angelis.
units.tr: Someone has testified somewhere, saying: "What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You have made him a little lower than the angels."

units.la: En quæ ad argumentū aduersariorū pertinet. Verosimile est, hæc sola in hunc modum citata ab aduersarijs,ad probandū,quòd Christus, quoniā homo fit, inferior esset Ange-lis.Neq; verò ex contemptu aliquo dicit,quendā ita testatū:sed sic loquitur,suppresso auto-ris &operis nomine,quia testimoniū profert,quod omnibus erat valde notū,quéadmo-dum antea semel diximus , psalmos, quoniam decantabantur &recitabantur ferè sem-perin omnibus synagogis, multò notisimos fuisse omni etiam vulgo Iudæorum: Et cum locupletisima in psalmis contineatur rerum diuinarum suppellex, plurimaq;, oc-currant in illis de Christo &Euangelio vaticinia, Apostolus lubenter ex illis testimonia depropsit.Poterit etiam dixisse,quendā testatum,et alicubi:propterea,quòd de autore Psalmi, nūvidelicet Dauidis is fuerit,an Asaph,an aliquis filiorum Chorę,an alius quispiā hunc cōfecerit:deinde quotus ordine fuerit hic Psalmus,non venerit tūc in mentē. Neq; verò semper opus est, librū &caput citare,quando,quod citamus,in sacris literis ita haberi cō-stat.Superstitiosorū est &de scripturæ doctorū·q; autoritate dubitantiū, aut certè in Scri-pturis nō versatorū.Hinc videre est,veteres Scriptores etiā in grauissimis disputationib. raròeomemorasse librorū, è quibus sua proferebant argumenta,titulos siue nomina,ca-pita verò nunc̄,cùm verosimile fit,ad illa tépora libros in capita nondū fuisse,vt nūc eer-nimus,distinctos. Nō sit ergo nobis tāta solicitudo,vt in disputādo, docēdo,scribēdoue citemus
units.tr: Here is what pertains to the adversaries' argument. It is likely that these words, cited in this form, are the only ones the adversaries used to prove that Christ, since he is a man, was inferior to the angels. Nor does he speak in this way out of any contempt when he says "someone has testified"; rather he speaks thus, leaving out the name of the author and the work, because he is bringing forward a testimony that was very well known to all, as we said once before: the psalms, since they were sung and recited almost everywhere in all the synagogues, were very well known even to the whole common crowd of the Jews. And since the psalms contain a most abundant store of divine things, and many prophecies about Christ and the gospel occur in them, the Apostle gladly drew testimonies from them. He could also have said "someone has testified somewhere", because it did not come to mind at that point who the author of the psalm was, whether David, or Asaph, or one of the sons of Korah, or some other person who composed it, nor how far down in order this psalm stood. Nor is it always necessary to cite book and chapter when what we cite is agreed to be so in the sacred letters. It is the mark of superstitious people, and of those who doubt the authority of the teachers of Scripture, or who are certainly not versed in the Scriptures, to do so. From this we may see that the ancient writers, even in the most serious disputations, rarely mentioned the titles or names of the books from which they brought forward their arguments, and still less the chapters; for it is likely that in those times the books had not yet been divided into chapters as we now see them. Let us not, then, be so anxious that in disputing, teaching or writing we cite

units.la: h § citemus libros & capita: sed in hoc aduigilemus, vt proprie, appositè, & ad rem testimonia coferamus. Vt autem de Psalmi huius argumeto & materia, paululū differamus: passim in exemplaribus tàm hebreis, quàm aliis, tribuitur ipsi Dauidi. Quod verò in Hebreis habetur <bl>למנצח על הגתית</bl> id est, Vinceti in Githith, ac quasi sensus sit decatatum ad gloriam Dei, instrumento appellato Githith: vel <bl>[illegible, ~10 letters]</bl> super torcularia: quasi post peractam vindemiam, & expressa torcularibus vina, sit decantatus, id non est opus nunc explicare, aut plenius discutere: satis sit praesenti loco adnotare, hoc Psalmo magno animi affectu laudari Deum & celebrari, quòd potentiam & gloriam suam in toto orbe illustrem reddat, & cum aliis rebus, tum hac potissimum, omnibus etiam abiectissimis & contemptissimis hominibus tantam cognitionem sui det, vt aduersus superbissimos hostes pietatis posint praevalere. Quod cùm per se longè maximum, tamen accedit aliud beneficiū multò amplius, quòd videlicet homo per Deū omnibus quoque creaturis sit praepositus: pro qua re celebrari Deus nunquam satis queat. Et quia non admodum prolixus est Psalmus, neq; etiam opus est uaria & multiplici expositione, per allegoriam aut <bl>[illegible, ~5 letters]</bl>, nos breuiter ab initio percurremus.
units.tr: books and chapters; but let us take care that we bring together testimonies that are apt, suitable and to the point. But to defer for a little while the subject and matter of this psalm: everywhere in copies, both Hebrew and others, it is attributed to David himself. As for what is found in the Hebrew, lamnatstsēach ʿal haggitit [למנצח על הגתית], that is, "To the victor, upon the Gittith", and as if the sense were that it was sung to the glory of God on an instrument called Gittith, or "upon the winepresses", as if it were sung after the vintage was over and the wines pressed out in the presses, there is no need to explain or discuss this more fully now. It is enough to note at this point that in this psalm God is praised and celebrated with great warmth of feeling, because he makes his power and glory famous throughout the whole world, and above all, among other things, gives such knowledge of himself even to the most abject and despised men that they can prevail against the most arrogant enemies of piety. Although this is by itself by far the greatest, there is added another benefit much greater still, namely that man, through God, has been set over all creatures; for this reason God can never be celebrated enough. And since the psalm is not very long, and there is no need for varied and manifold exposition, by allegory or [illegible], we shall run through it briefly from the beginning.

units.la: Domine Dominus noster, quàm admirabile est nomen tuum in uniuersa terra.) Propositio est qua magno affectu & animi stupore exclamat Propheta, gloriā Dei & potentia, (hęc enim per nomen intelligitur) multò esse amplissimam, nec sermone posse explicari. Iam sequuntur rationes, quibus admirabilem esse Dei potentiam comprobatur.
units.tr: "O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth." This is a proposition with which the prophet cries out with great feeling and wonder of spirit: the glory and power of God (for this is what is understood by the name) is far more ample and cannot be explained in words. Now follow the reasons by which the power of God is shown to be admirable.

units.la: Quoniā elevata est magnificetia tua super cœlos. Prima ratio, ab eo, quòd quae in coelis apparet, vt primò sydera, deinde eorundē perpetui & ordinati motus, tot deniq; alia his agnata, & ab his proueniētia, mirificè arguūt Dei potentiā & gloriā. Qua de re videre est, preclarè & excellenter dicta esse multa per ipsos gentiles philosophos, qui ex rerum coelestium contemplatione permoti sunt, ad fatendum, vnum esse Deum, qui cuncta optimè sapientissimeq; moderetur & gubernet.
units.tr: "For your majesty is raised above the heavens." The first reason is drawn from the fact that the things that appear in the heavens, first the stars, then their perpetual and ordered motions, and finally so many other things joined to these and arising from them, wonderfully demonstrate the power and glory of God. On this matter one may see that many things have been said finely and excellently even by the heathen philosophers themselves, who, moved by the contemplation of heavenly things, were led to confess that there is one God who governs and steers all things most wisely and well.

units.la: Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudē, propter inimicos tuos, ut destruas inimicum ultorē.) Alia ratio, per quā multò indicat efficacius Dei potentiā & bonitatē illustratā, quasi dicat: Valdè quidē exerit sese potetia & maiestas tua in rebus coelestibus: sed in hac tamē re multò magis quòd paruulos, abiectos, ac rudes aliquos homines donaueris maximarū rerū diuinarū cognitione, ac tanta quidē, vt omnes aduersarios, qualibet potetes & instructos, celsitudinis & veritatis tuæ hostes posint facilimè superare. Istud verò magnū & mirabile, quod, quos Deus spiritu suo illuminat, & cognitione rerū diuinarū auget, ij quáuis iuxta mūdum ineptissimi, omnes sapientes mūdi philosophos, reges, principes, possunt sapientia sua spirituali superare. Id quod deprehensum est esse verum, maximè in pauperculis & illiteratis apostolis, qui mundū vniuersum sua doctrina spirituali ad Christū perttraxe runt: quòd neq; armis, neq; vllis humanis consilijs, aut viribus potuisset perfici. Videa- postolum 1.Cor.1. & 2. Item Matth.11. Abscondisti ea à sapientibus, & reuelasti paruulis.
units.tr: "Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise, because of your enemies, that you might destroy the avenging enemy." This is another reason, by which he shows the power and goodness of God far more effectively, as if he were saying: Your power and majesty indeed display themselves very strongly in heavenly things; but in this matter much more, that you have endowed little ones, lowly and untutored men, with knowledge of the greatest divine things, and so great that they can very easily overcome all adversaries, however powerful and well equipped, who are enemies of your loftiness and truth. This is a great and wonderful thing: those whom God illumines by his Spirit and increases in the knowledge of divine things, though by the world's reckoning most unskilled, can by their spiritual wisdom surpass all the philosophers, kings and princes of the world. This has been shown to be true, above all in the poor and unlettered apostles, who by their spiritual teaching drew the whole world to Christ, which could not have been accomplished by arms, by any human counsels, or by any strength. See the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 1 and 2. Likewise Matthew 11: "You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones."

units.la: Quoniā uidebo cœlos tuos, opera digitorū tuorum, Lunam & stellas, quae tu fundasti: Quid est homo, quòd memor es eius? aut filius hominis, quòd visitas eū?) Amplificat hominis dignitatē quadā collatione eius cum rebus coelestibus, atq; infert rursus, multò magis bonitate & potentia Deidee-clarata in homine, quàm in rebus coelestibus. Est& sententia: quādo conteplor coelos tàm mirabiliter dispositos & ornatos: quādo intueor sydera, atq; inprimis duo illa clarissima mundi lumina, quòd à te condita sunt & coseruantur, vt tepora nobis constituat ac discet nàt: quòd itē actionibus multiuarijs suis, terrā & omnia inferiora haec vegetet, foueátq;: cogor equidē valdè admirari tuā bonitate & potentiā. Sed quando rursus me conuerto ad cōsiderationē hominis, non possum animo cōcipere, quid causę esse possit, cur illū adeò per se abiectum & vilem, tot tamq; amplis velis beneficijs ornare & onerare. In hoc vno ornando & locupletando, tu tuam potentiam & bonitatem plenisimè ostentas.
units.tr: When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him? (The psalmist enlarges on the dignity of man by comparing him with the heavenly things, and then concludes that God's goodness and power shine more brightly in man than in the heavenly things. The sense is this: when I contemplate the heavens so wonderfully arranged and adorned, when I look at the stars, and above all at those two brightest lights of the world, which were created and are preserved by you so that they may mark out the seasons and days for us, and which by their many varied movements also quicken and cherish the earth and all these lower things, I am compelled to marvel greatly at your goodness and power. But when I turn again to consider man, I cannot grasp what reason there can be why you should adorn and burden with so many and such great benefits one who is in himself so abject and worthless. In adorning and enriching this one creature you display your power and goodness most fully.)

units.la: Minuisti eum paulò minus ab angelis, gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius, oues & boues uniuersas, in super & pecora campi, volucres coeli, & pisces maris, qui perambulant semitas maris.) Iam exponit, quęnā sint illa amplissima & plurima beneficia Dei in homine, è quibus potetia & bonitas ipsius luculentius cognosci queat, quàm ex rebus coelestibus. Tu illū, inquit, talē reddidisti, vt angelis (qui sunt omniū creaturarū excelletisimi) sit pene par: si quid ad verā laudē aut gloriā ptinet, id vniuersū valde largiter in homine cōtulisti: deniq; omnibus creaturis illū quasi dominū præposuisti, vt secundum te, homine nihil maius excellentiusue conspiciatur. Vsus est breuiter illis verbis propheta, quibus posset res maximas, & omnes dotes tàm spirituales & internas quàm externas significare: quas omnes oportet hic animo comprehendi, si velimus hunc locum recte intelligere. Sed vt plenius animaduerteretur, summa hominis digni-tas, voluit enumeratione seu çongerie quadam çreaturarum, quibus homo dominatur, hominis dignitatem illustriorem reddere. Enumerantur siquidem quæ in terra, & quæ in aquis, & quæ in aere degunt, hac partitione volens omnes creaturas complecti: ut ostendat, hominem semel omnium creaturarum esse dominum: quæ potestas etiam homini statim, ut conditus fuit, collata à Deo est, Gen. 1. Postremò, quasi qui præ magno affectu & stupore animi non possit orationem logius deducere, iterum exclamat ijsdem verbis, quibus exorsus fuerat:
units.tr: You have made him a little less than the angels, you have crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet: sheep and oxen, all of them, and the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the seas. (Now he sets out what those very great and numerous benefits of God toward man are, from which his power and goodness may be known more clearly than from the heavenly things. "You," he says, "have made him such that he is nearly equal to the angels, who are the most excellent of all creatures; whatever pertains to true praise and glory, you have bestowed on man very largely; finally, you have set him over all creatures as their lord, so that, in your sight, nothing greater or more excellent than man is seen." The prophet has used these few words, by which he could signify very great things and all gifts, both spiritual and inward as well as outward. All of these we must take into our minds if we wish to understand this passage rightly. But so that the supreme dignity of man might be noticed more fully, he chose to make man's dignity more illustrious by a kind of enumeration or list of the creatures over which man rules. For he lists those that live on the land, those in the waters, and those in the air, wishing in this division to embrace all creatures, so as to show that man is at once lord of all creatures. This power was conferred on man by God as soon as he was made, Gen. 1. Lastly, as one who, out of great feeling and amazement of mind, cannot carry on his speech any further, he again exclaims in the same words with which he had begun.)

units.la: Domine Dominus noster, quàm admirabile est nomen tuum in universa terra?) Hæc est simplex & germana interpretatio huius psalmi, & videre est nihil aliud, quàm cani laudes Deo, ob eximiâ potentiâ & bonitate, qua homine innumeris donis ornauit, atq; omnib. creaturis secit præeminere. Quo etiam Hebræi omnes, & tam græcorũ, quàm latinorũ plurimi exponût. Et quauis nonnulli per Catagogam exponant eũ de Christo, & vaticinium hic contineri de humiliatione Christi & morte, rursus q; de eiusdé exaltatione & regno spirituali, ac plena potestate in omnia: tamé nulla necessitas nos hic ad eiusmodi interpretationé impellit: & dũ retinetur simplex illa interpretatio, quæ nos reddidimus, argumentũ aduersariorũ in specie valet, & eius dissolutio rursus p apostolũ facta satis quadrat. Nã clarè adhuc sequit, q; Christus, licet fuerit homo, ob hoc tñ nequaquam sit angelis inferior: sicut apostolus rectè infert: in hoc, quòd ei subiecit omnia, nihil omisit illi nõ subiectũ. Quòd si quis dicat, dũ hoc modo exponimus psalmũ, posse eadé ratione inferri, de quolibet homine, quòd angelis sit superior, atq; ita nihil excellentiæ tribui Christo præ cæteris hominib. Respondeo, mihi nõ esse religionè, cõcedere de homine, qui cognitione Dei fuerit illustratus. Nã, ut præcedenti capite dictũ est, angeli emittuntur propter homines: & ministeria per angelos erga homines exhibita passim in Scripturis leguntur: & hominibus præsertim ministris verbi appellatio angelorum subinde tribuitur. Matt. 22. dicitur, q; in resurrectione homines erũt sicut angeli Dei in cœlo, Apocal. 22. angelus ab homine adorari renuit, vocans se cõseruũ Ioannis, & prophetarũ, & omniũ piorũ fratrũ. 1. Cor. 6. An nescitis, q; angelos iudicabimus? Itaq; non absurdè dici queat de quouis homine donis Dei illustrato, q; angelis sit superior. Quod tñ hæc dignitas alia ratione & alio iure cõueniat Christo, q̃ cæteris hominibus, istud quis neget? Quod n. credentibus contingat illa dignitas, ipsius Christi beneficio contingit. Quemadmodũ ius suũ & præeminentiâ in omnia creata amisit homo per lapsum Adæ: ita vbi per Christum est restitutus, recipit illud vetus ius atq; excellentiâ propter Christũ. Etiâ dæmones per homines sanctos comprimitur & coercentur: deniq; & homo omnib. creaturis imperat, nõ tantũ ijs quæ hic à propheta enumerantur: sed Christus iure habet hanc potestatẽ, homo autem duntaxat per gratiam & per participationem. Huc pertinet, quod Ephes. 2. dicitur, Nos simul cum eo sedere fecit inter cœlestes cũ Christo Iesu, vt ostenderet in seculis superuenientibus eminentem opulentiam gratiæ suæ, benignitate erga nos per Christum Iesum. Sed iam breuiter singula verba præsentis testimonij excutiamus.
units.tr: O LORD our Lord, how excellent is your name in all the earth! This is the simple and genuine interpretation of this psalm, and it is evident that it is nothing other than a song of praise to God for his remarkable power and goodness, by which he has adorned man with countless gifts and made him pre-eminent over all creatures. All the Hebrews, and most of the Greeks and Latins, also explain it this way. And although some explain it by way of anagoge, and maintain that it is about Christ, and that a prophecy about the humiliation and death of Christ, and again about his exaltation, his spiritual kingdom and his full power over all things, is contained here, yet there is no necessity that drives us to such an interpretation. And while that simple interpretation, which we have given, is retained, the argument of our opponents has some force in appearance, and its refutation, again made by the apostle, fits well enough. For it still clearly follows that Christ, although he was man, is nonetheless in no way inferior to the angels, just as the apostle rightly infers: in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing unsubjected to him. But if someone says that, while we explain the psalm in this way, it could by the same reasoning be inferred of any man that he is superior to the angels, and so no excellence would be attributed to Christ above other men, I answer that I see no scruple in conceding this of a man who has been illuminated by the knowledge of God. For, as was said in the preceding chapter, angels are sent forth on account of men, and ministries performed by angels toward men are read everywhere in the Scriptures, and the name of angels is often given to men, especially to ministers of the Word. Matt. 22 says that in the resurrection men will be as the angels of God in heaven; Apoc. 22 the angel refused to be worshipped by a man, calling himself the fellow servant of John, and of the prophets, and of all pious brothers; 1 Cor. 6: Do you not know that we shall judge angels? Therefore it can not absurdly be said of any man illuminated by the gifts of God that he is superior to the angels. But who would deny that this dignity belongs to Christ by another reason and another right than to other men? For what dignity happens to believers, happens through the benefit of Christ himself. Just as man lost his right and pre-eminence over all created things through the fall of Adam, so when he has been restored through Christ, he receives that old right and excellence again on account of Christ. Even demons are restrained and held in check by holy men; finally, man rules over all creatures, not only over those listed here by the prophet; but Christ has this power by right, while man has it only by grace and by participation. To this belongs what is said in Eph. 2: He made us sit together with him among the heavenly ones in Christ Jesus, so that he might show in the ages to come the surpassing riches of his grace, in kindness toward us through Christ Jesus. But now let us briefly examine the individual words of the present testimony.)

units.la: Quid est homo, quòd memor es eius, aut filius hominis, quòd inuisis illum) Optimè hæc exprimunt magnam admirationem. Et repetitio sententiæ, quando uidelicet idé bis dicitur, licet uerbis immutatis, magnâ habet apud Hebræos, præsertim in affectibus augendis, gratiam: sicut & Dauid Kimhi & hoc loco adnotat, & illud psalm 2. Dirúpamus vincula eorũ, & proiciamus à nobis iugũ ipsorũ: Quid est homo, inquit? quasi diceret: Homo est per se quidé abiectissima creatura, & omniũ animantiũ ςrumnosissima, suo creatori inobediens, & propterea innumeris miserijs & calamitatib. expositus est: si spectes ortũ huius, limus est: si spectes finë, esca uermiũ: si cætera spectes, in hac uita omniũ miseriarũ, calamitatũ, ægritudinũ, deniq; omniũ malorũ quedã theca: & totus hic mũdus qd aliud, q̃ apertũ theatrũ, in quo perpetua ludibria humanæ miseriæ exhibetur. Et tñ ut adeò abiectus sit homo, atq; adeò videatur uel minimis animalculis multò inferior, Deus mirificè illi fauet & incoparabilibus exornat beneficijs. Sed mirè quadrat in statuto uoces hebrææ hic positæ ad exprimendũ conditionis humanæ uilitatẽ. Nã אנוש hominé significat, sed ut deriuatur videtur ab אנש q, idé est, ac doluit, infirmatus est, & אנושlaborans, grauiter ægrotas: quare illa appellatio statim admonet nos, ad agnoscendâ propria infirmitate. Nec minus aptũ est, q, secundo loco ubi interpres reddidit, filius hominis, hebraicè habet בן אדם q.d. filius Adæ, quomodocũq; uertas, certè conditio uilitatis humanæ & miseria ualde appositè exprimitur: si animaduertamus, nos hominũ miserorũ tantũ esse filios: aut, si ad primũ parentẽ nostrũ Adamũ, autorẽ omniũ ærũnarũ per suũ lapsum, quid poterimus de nobis magnificè polliceri? Rursus מִבָּקֵר inuisis, à uerbo פקד id est visitauit, recordatus est in parte bona & mala accipit, quia dominus vtroq; modo visitat homines: tñ hoc loco in bonâ parte. Dicere. n. vult, q, Dominus magnâ gerit hominis cura, & uarijs modis studet eũ promouere, & beneficijs occupletare: nõ derelinqt hominem in sordib. suis putrescẽte. Itaq;
units.tr: What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? These words express great amazement very well. And the repetition of a statement, when the same thing is said twice, though with the words changed, has great grace among the Hebrews, especially in intensifying feelings; as David Kimchi also notes at this place, and as in Psalm 2: Let us break their bonds, and cast away their yoke from us. "What is man," he says? As if he were saying: man is in himself indeed the most abject creature, and the most wretched of all living things, disobedient to his creator, and therefore exposed to countless miseries and calamities. If you look at his origin, he is mud; if you look at his end, he is food for worms; if you look at the rest, in this life he is a kind of case for all miseries, calamities, sicknesses, and finally all evils; and this whole world is nothing else but an open theatre in which the perpetual mockeries of human misery are displayed. And yet, however abject man is, and however much he seems far inferior even to the smallest animalcules, God wonderfully favours him and adorns him with incomparable benefits. The Hebrew words used here to express the lowliness of the human condition fit remarkably well into the sense. For enosh [אנוש] means man, but it seems to be derived from anash [אנש], which means to be pained, to be weakened, and anush [אנוש] means labouring, grievously sick; so that this name at once reminds us to acknowledge our own weakness. Nor is it less apt that in the second place, where the translator has rendered "son of man," the Hebrew has ben adam [בן אדם], that is, son of Adam. However you translate it, the condition of human lowliness and misery is very aptly expressed, if we consider that we are only sons of wretched men; or, if we look to our first parent Adam, the author of all troubles through his fall, what magnificent things can we promise ourselves? Again, mibbaqqer, "visit," comes from the verb paqad [פקד], that is, to visit, to remember; it takes both a good and a bad sense, because the Lord visits men in both ways; here, however, it is in the good sense. For he means to say that the Lord takes great care of man, and by various means strives to advance him and enrich him with benefits; he does not leave man to rot in his own filth. And so

units.la: Hominis fragilitas. Itaq;, sicut utilitas hominis summa, ita e contrario summa etiam Dei de hominis salute cura luculensisimè hic describitur. Non admodū dissimilia his leguntur, Iob.7. parce mihi Domine: nihil est homo, quia magnificas eum. Ad quid apponis ergā eum cortuū? Visitas eum diluculo, & subitò probas illum. sed quid intelligendum sit per uisitationem Dei, facile est ex sequentibus colligere.
units.tr: The frailty of man. Therefore, just as the greatest benefit to man is described here, so too, conversely, is God's supreme care for man's salvation described here most clearly. Passages not very different from these are read in Job 7: "Spare me, Lord; man is nothing, that you magnify him. Why do you set your heart on him? You visit him in the morning and test him suddenly." But what is meant by God's visitation is easy to gather from what follows.

units.la: Fecisti eum paulo'sper inferiorem angelis, gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius.
units.tr: You have made him a little lower than the angels, and have crowned him with glory and honour, and have set him over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet.

units.la: En, quomodo Dominus visitarit hominem, & ad quantam dignitatem eum euexerit. Consideranda est in singulis membris incrementi ratio. Primò fecisti eum paulisper inferiorem angelis. Interpretes hic dissentiunt. Nā cùm hebraicè habeatur אלהים , atque אלהים Deum significet, seu Deos, non angelos, qui dicuntur אלהים: quidam ita martiunt uertere: Fecisti eum paulo inferiorem à Deo, (ut Hieronymus, & Felix Pratensis, item Bucerus à Dijs, Et Cāpensis, Fecisti eū tantū nō Deum. Sed quando non nouum est uocem אלהים significari non tantum Deum, sed frequentissimè vsurpari eam pro angelis, pro principibus, iudicibus, quid opus est hic cauillari? Aben Ezra putat tantum dici אלהים propter angelos, quòd ipsorum ministerio utatur ad sua opera perficienda. Et septuaginta reddiderunt hoc loco, vocem angelorum. Et paraphrasis Chaldaica exponit hunc locum de angelis. Ité Dauid Kimhi secutus haud dubiè praestantissimos quosq; Rabinos, de angelis sermonem hic fieri ait. Et omnes reliqui interpretes nostri de angelis enarrant.
units.tr: See how the Lord has visited man and raised him to such great dignity. The reasoning of the individual clauses must be considered. First: "You have made him a little lower than the angels." The interpreters disagree here. For although the Hebrew has elohim [אלהים], which means God or gods, not angels, some want to translate it "a little lower than God" (as Jerome does, and Felix Pratensis; likewise Bucer, "than the gods"; and Campensis, "you have made him only not God"). But since it is well known that the word elohim signifies not only God but is very often used for angels, for princes and for judges, why bother to quibble here? Aben Ezra thinks the word is applied to angels only because God uses them in carrying out his works. The Seventy translated this passage with the word "angels," and the Chaldee paraphrast also explains the passage as referring to angels. David Kimhi, following without doubt the most distinguished rabbis, likewise says that the discourse here concerns angels. And all our other interpreters also expound it of angels.

units.la: Postremò quando, vti iam saepius admonuimus, in tota hac disputatione de dignitate Christi oportet rationem habere collationis institutae Christi cum angelis, nō poterit amplius hoc loco reddi vox אלהים quā per uocem angelorum. Est ergo haec primo loco posita, & multò maxima dignitas hominis, quòd sit paulisper inferior angelis, id est, angelis propemodum aequalis. βραχύτι, paululū quiddā, & ad tempus hęc particula, modicè, referenda est, quia nimirū Christus pro tempore humanitatē induit, & in ea certo tempore eoq; exiguo (dū videlicet cruciaretur, morte ut mox exponetur) angelis inferior apparuit, modicè tantum distans à dignitate angelorum. Nā hoc erat omninò receptissimū Iudaeis, quòd angeli essent excellentissimae cuiusdā naturę, & Deo per omnia proximi & similimi: itaq; ad significandā summā dignitate hominis, dicitur, eū angelis propemodū esse parē. Vnde saepe in Scripturis, quando significare volūt, aliquē valde excellentē & insignē esse supra cōmunē hominū morē, & propē diuinis dotibus ornatū, dicunt, eū quasi angelum Dei esse, aut similē angelis, ut 1. Sam. 29. Achis ait ad Dauid: Bonus es tu in oculis meis, sicut angelus Dei: sed principes Philistinorum dixerunt: nō ascendet nobiscū in prælium. 2. Sam. 14. Mulier Thecoitis ad Dauid: Sicut angelus Domini, sic est Dominus meus rex, ut necbe nedictione nec maledictione moueatur. Act. 6. de Stephano, Intuentes eum omnes, qui sedebant in concilio, viderunt faciem eius, tanquam faciem angeli. Ecce, ubi aliquid supra humanam conditionem in homine uolunt significare, utuntur similitudine angeli, & dicunt, eum similem angelo, quia nimirum angelos praestantioris conditionis esse, quàm homines sint, communi iudicio receptum erat. Sunt enim spirituales creaturae, sicut & Deus est substantia spiritualis: item perstat, boni inquam in sua dignitate & perfectione, qua primùm fuerunt conditi, immortales, expertes nostrarum miseriarum, incorruptibiles.
units.tr: Finally, since, as we have often noted already, throughout this whole discussion of the dignity of Christ we must take account of the comparison Christ draws with the angels, the word elohim cannot here be rendered by anything but "angels." This statement is therefore placed first, and the greatest dignity of man is that he is a little lower than the angels, that is, almost equal to the angels. The particle "a little" [βραχύ τι] (a little something, and for a time) should be referred to the modest and temporary state, because Christ, for the time being, put on humanity, and in it, for a certain brief time (namely while he was suffering, unto death, as will be explained shortly), he appeared lower than the angels, differing only slightly from the dignity of the angels. For it was entirely accepted among the Jews that angels were of an excellent kind of nature, and most near to God and most like him in every respect; so to signify the highest dignity of man, it is said that he is almost equal to the angels. Hence, when the Scriptures wish to signify that someone is very outstanding and remarkable, above the common manner of men, and adorned with almost divine gifts, they say that he is as an angel of God, or like the angels, as in 1 Samuel 29, where Achish says to David: "You are good in my eyes, as an angel of God; but the princes of the Philistines have said, he shall not go up with us to the battle." In 2 Samuel 14 the Tekoite woman says to David: "My lord the king is like the angel of the Lord, so that he cannot be moved either by blessing or by cursing." In Acts 6, of Stephen: "All who sat in the council, looking at him, saw his face as the face of an angel." Here, then, where they wish to signify something above the human condition in a man, they use the likeness of an angel, and say that he is like an angel, because it was a commonly accepted judgment that angels are of a more excellent condition than men. For they are spiritual creatures, just as God is a spiritual substance; and, moreover, they remain good, I say, in their dignity and perfection, in which they were first created, immortal, free from our miseries, and incorruptible.

units.la: Huc pertinet, quod Rabi Dauid Kimhi hoc loco ait, de angelis hic sermonem fieri, & in hoc pare esse homine angelis, quòd anima hominis fit incorporea & spiritualis, sicut ipsi angeli quoq; incorporei sunt & spirituales: differre hominem ab angelis, & inferiorem esse in hoc, quòd homo habeat corpus, angeli nequaquam. Sed alias dignitate angelorum expositum, ut nequaquam opus sit diutius his immorari. Sequitur:
units.tr: To this belongs what Rabbi David Kimhi says here, that the discourse concerns angels, and that man is equal to angels in this respect, that the soul of man is incorporeal and spiritual, just as the angels themselves are also incorporeal and spiritual; and that man differs from the angels and is inferior in this, that man has a body, while angels by no means do. But these matters have been explained elsewhere in terms of the dignity of the angels, so there is no need to dwell on them longer. The text continues:

units.la: Gloria & honore coronasti eum) Sunt & haec verba valde apta ad exprimendum augustam quandam dignitatem & maiestatem. Coronasti eum, inquit: ita regiam quandam maiestatē, cui corona & sceptrum conuenit, hac voce delineat. Sic Petrus credentes vocat regale genus.
units.tr: "Crowned him with glory and honour." These words too are very apt for expressing a certain majestic dignity and sovereignty. "Crowned him," it says: with this word it sketches a kind of royal majesty, to which a crown and a sceptre belong. So Peter calls believers a royal race.

units.la: Per gloriam autem & honorem, intelligere conuenit omne genus dotes, internas & externas, spirituales & corporales, quibus deus homines, & praesertim pios atq; electos suos ornat, in quibus vel minima virtus à Deo ipsis collata, in primis quae spiritualis sit, & ad animae salutem conducens, omnino maior est, quàm ut ei ullae diuitiae, ulla pompa aut triumphi huius mundi calamitosissimi comparari queant. Ecquid enim praeclarius, quà saltem nosse Deum, & Iesum Christum, per quam cognitionem, vt Christus diserte ait, vita aeterna paratur? Possem alia eiusmodi dona spiritualia enumerare, in quibus vera & spiritualis gloria amplissima sita est. Huc pertinet illud Hier.9. Nō glorietur sapiens in sapietia sua, & nō glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua, & nō glorietur diues in diuitijs suis, sed in hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire & nosse me, quia ego sum Dominus, qui facio misericordiam & iudiciū, & iustitiā in terra. Psalmo 31. Lætemini in Domino, & exultate iusti, & gloriamini omnes recti cor de. Rom.5. Gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum Dei. 1.Cor.1. Factus est nobis Christus sapiē-tia à Deo, iustitiaq;, & sanctificatio, & redemptio, ut, quemadmodum scriptum est, qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Sed de gloria in altera uita, Deus bone, quàm multa restarent nobis dicenda. Satis ergo uides, quàm uerum sit, quòd Deus hominem uera gloria & honore coronauerit.
units.tr: By "glory and honour" it is fitting to understand every kind of gift, inward and outward, spiritual and bodily, with which God adorns men, and especially his pious and elect people; among these, even the least virtue conferred on them by God, above all what is spiritual and conduces to the salvation of the soul, is so much greater than any riches or pomp or triumph of this most wretched world that nothing can be compared to it. For what is more splendid than at least to know God and Jesus Christ, through which knowledge, as Christ plainly says, eternal life is prepared? I could list other such spiritual gifts, in which true and spiritual glory is found in the greatest measure. To this belongs that passage of Jeremiah 9: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he knows and understands me, that I am the Lord who does mercy and judgment and justice in the earth." Psalm 31: "Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you righteous, and glory, all you upright in heart." Romans 5: "We glory in the hope of the glory of the sons of God." 1 Corinthians 1: "Christ has been made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, he who glories, let him glory in the Lord." But, good God, how many more things would remain for us to say about the glory in the other life! So you see well enough how true it is that God has crowned man with true glory and honour.

units.la: Et constituisti Deum super opera manuum tuarum) Iterum noua & amplior dignitas. Postquā homo à Deo est coronatus insignibus plusquam regalibus, iam etiam regnum ei in manus traditur & inauguratio, Iam Dominus constituitur omnium operum, quę Deus manibus suis (anthropopathia est passim obuia) condidit. Quid maius, quid amplius dici posset, quā nō angelos quidem, sed hominem esse constitutum super omnia? Nam hominis causa Deus omnia condidit, homini Deus omnia ad usum concedit: quomodo 1. Cor.3. Omnia namq; uestra sunt, siue Paulus, siue Apollos, siue Cephas, siue mundus, siue uita, siue mors, siue præsentia, siue futura: omnia inquam, vestra sunt, vos autē Christi, Christus verò Dei. At videtur propheta hic respexisse ad id, quod Genf.1. Dominus dicit, Crescite & multiplicamini, & replete terram, & subijcite eam, & dominamini piscibus maris, & volatilibus cœli, & uniuersis animantibus, quæ mouentur super terram: & in sequetibus, vbi diuidit res creatas, respexit ad hæc verba. Quæ potestas iterū collata est hominibus post diluuiū, ne quis putet, primam illam potestatem per peccata prorsus fuisse sublatam: quanquam auctam per Christum, & propter Christum, eam potestatem, hoc extra controuersiam est. Porrò, vt summatim semel explicaret, summam esse hominis in omnia potestatem, addidit breuiter, omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius: omnia, inquit, nihil excludens, quod non sit illi subiectum, quod verum quoq; est: quandoquidem homo super omnia per Christū, & propter Christum euehetur, maximeq; ubi gloriam cœlestem & æternam accipiet. Et forma illa verborum, sub pedibus, extremam subiectionem, per metaphoram significat: sicut illa, Ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum.
units.tr: "And have set him over the works of your hands." Again a new and greater dignity. After man has been crowned by God with insignia more than royal, now also a kingdom is put into his hands and he is installed; now the Lord is set over all the works that God made with his hands (an anthropopathy, found everywhere). What greater or fuller thing could be said than that not angels indeed, but man, has been set over all things? For God created all things for the sake of man, and God grants all things to man for his use: as in 1 Corinthians 3: "For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come: all are yours; and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." But the prophet here seems to have looked back to what the Lord says in Genesis 1: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over all living things that move upon the earth"; and in what follows, where he divides up the created things, he looked back to these words. This power was again given to men after the flood, lest anyone think that the first power had been wholly taken away by sins; although it is beyond controversy that this power was increased through Christ and on account of Christ. Moreover, so that he might explain in brief, once for all, that man's power over all things is supreme, he added briefly, you have put all things under his feet. All things, he says, excluding nothing that is not subject to him; which is also true, since man will be raised above all things through Christ and on account of Christ, and especially when he receives the heavenly and eternal glory. And that form of words, under his feet, signifies by metaphor the utmost subjection, as in that other, I will make your enemies the footstool of your feet.

units.la: Proinde ex his postremis verbis Apostolus solutionem argumenti sic colligit, dicēs: in hoc enim, quòd ei subiecit omnia, nihil omisit illi non subiectum: Ratiocinatur à toto ad quantam eius partem, siue ab uniuersali ad particularem, affirmatiuè, ac clarè docet, Christum et iam ut hominem angelis multò esse superiorem: sicut supra satis puto à nobis declaratū. Et si tanta dignitas competit cuiuis homini, sicut prius ostendimus, quantò magis ea cōueniet ipsi Christo?
units.tr: Therefore, from these last words, the Apostle draws his solution to the argument, saying: For in that he put all things under him, he left nothing that was not subject to him. He reasons from the whole to one of its parts, that is, from the universal to the particular, affirmatively, and he clearly teaches that Christ, even as man, is far superior to the angels, as I think I have sufficiently declared above. And if such dignity belongs to any man, as we showed earlier, how much more will it belong to Christ himself?

units.la: Decet autem dignitatem hanc Christi interpretari de eo, ut, quia aliàs superiorem esse angelis, ut Deum, non est quod in dubium uocetur. Christus sicut per humanitatē suā fuit maximè humiliatus: ita rursus in eadem est maximè exaltatus, id quod plenius ad Philip.2. dicitur. Qui cum esset in forma Dei, non rapinā arbitratus est, ut esset æqualis Deo, sed semetipsū exinaniuit, formā serui sumpta, in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus ut homo, humilē præbuit semetipsum, factus obediens usq; ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Quapropter & Deus illū in summā exaltauit sublimitatem ac donauit illi nomen, quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Iesu omne genu se flectat cœlestiū, ac terrestriū, & infernorū, omnisq; lingua confiteatur, quòd Dominus sit Iesus Christus, ad gloriā dei patris. Restat, ut breuiter attexamus, quæ do ctrinā nobis arripere ex his uerbis debeamus. Primò, hoc habemus ex his uerbis præclarum, & nobis ualde utile, quod Deus nos quā libet abiectos, tamen visitat, habet nostri curam, & non solùm prospicit nobis uitæ necessaria, quod tamen ualde magnum est: sed præterea amplissimis bonis locupletat, & dotibus incredibilibus exornat. Consideranda est etiā hic maxima nostra dignitas, qua angelis propemodum pares dominium & potestatem habentes describuntur. Hinc primò charitatem Dei in nos ingentem debemus agnoscere, qui nos tanto honore dignatus est, quòd nos per natura miserrimos & calamitosissimos voluerit per gratiam constituere dignissimos & potentissimos. Quare hac consideratione nostræ dignitatis decet nos ad gratiarum actionem excitari.
units.tr: This dignity of Christ should be understood as referring to him in such a way that there is no room for doubt that he is also superior to the angels in his divine nature. Christ, who was most greatly humbled in his humanity, was in the same humanity most greatly exalted, as is said more fully in Philippians 2: "Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself and became obedient to death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." It remains for us to add briefly what doctrine we ought to draw from these words. First, we have from these words this excellent truth, which is very useful to us: that God, however lowly we are, nevertheless visits us, cares for us, and not only provides for the necessities of life, which is indeed very great, but moreover enriches us with the greatest blessings and adorns us with incredible gifts. Here also our great dignity must be considered, by which we are described as almost equal to the angels, having dominion and power. From this we must first acknowledge God's great love toward us, who has deigned to honour us so highly that he has willed to make us, who by nature were most wretched and miserable, most worthy and most powerful through grace. Therefore, by this consideration of our dignity, we ought to be stirred up to give thanks.

units.la: Deinde hinc debemus magnā consolationem accipere in omnibus tentationibus. Si enim mundus, vel Satanas, uel quæcunq; tandem malorum agmina aliquid cōtra nos moliantur, erit hæc præsentissima consolatio, quòd Dominus nos dominos omnium rerum constituerit, effecerit q;, ut, si modò in fide constantes perstiterimus, ne portæ quidē inferorū aduersum nos queant præualere.
units.tr: Second, from this we ought to receive great consolation in all temptations. For if the world, or Satan, or whatever host of evils, should plot anything against us, this will be a most present consolation: that the Lord has made us lords of all things, and has brought it about that, if only we persevere steadfast in faith, the gates of hell itself cannot prevail against us.

units.la: At nondum videmus, illi omnia esse subiecta. Eum uerò, qui paulisper diminutus fuerat infra angelos, cernimus Iesum, propter crucidtum mortis, gloria & honore co-ronatum, vt per gratiam Dei pro omnibus gustaret mortem.
