units.tr: Yet we do not yet see all things subjected to him. But we see Jesus, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. (Hebrews 2:9)

units.la: Alia obiectio aduersariorum. Hi enim cùm audirêt, tantopere prædicari Christi dignitatem, ac potestatem in totum orbem terrarum, atq; in ipsos adeò angelos: ubi non haberent amplius quòd opponerent: tandem magno contemptu, & propemodum cum irrisione obijciebant, quòd vanum videretur, usq; adeò prædicare Christi potentiam, quasi omnia deberent ei subijci, cùm talis potentia experimentis nequaquam deprehenderetur, sed tantùm imaginaria & confiĉta appareret. Existimabant autem cæci aduersarij, quæ dicebantur de potestate Christi, ea accipienda de potestate externa & temporali, quemadmodum adhuc hodie Iudæi tale regnum Messiæ futurum expectant. Atq; hac ratione putabant se omnia, quæ de præeminetia & potestate Christi præferebatur, facile euersuros. Sed hanc obiectione paucis verbis diluit Apostolus, & velut respiciês adhuc ad præcedens argumetû, concedit quidem aliqua ex parte videri Christũ inferio rem angelis: at rursus docere uult, eum alia ex parte superiorem: inferiorem quidem concedit hac in parte, quòd, cùm angeli sint immortales, ipse morte pertulerit. At nihilominus eundem alia in parte conspectum esse palam gloria & honore coronatum, ac proinde angelis superiorem. Quomodo uerò talis tantus q; sit conspectus, ipse non declarat, (for tasis contemnens ratione aduersariorû, ceu infirmam & indignâ, cui pluribus uerbis respondeatur) sed intelligit hauddubie gloriam & potentiam Christi abundè manifestatâ in ipsius resurrectione, & in cœlũ ascensione: quomodo alibi sæpius ipse Christus in euangelio se à morte per resurrectione glorificandum, & ad gloriam patris euehendũ sæpè dixit: ut Ioan. 17. ubi orat patre, ut ipsũ glorificet. Atq; ex hoc clarisimo argumeto potentiæ Christi, quasi ex signo intelligi uult, hoc quoq; necessariò adimpledum, quòd omnia ei subijciêtur. Qui enim sua uirtute resurrexit, & mortem ipsam sibi subiecit, prætereaiı cœlum ascendit, uti manifeste uisum fuit, an alienum, quòd ei subijcientur omnia? Sed ne aduersarij arriperent exilla humiliatione Christi ansam constituendi eum infra angelos, duas grauissimas rationes addit, quibus insinuat, per illam Christi ad mortem usque humiliationem nihil detractum eius dignitati, nullaq; in parte gloriam eius obscurata. Altera est à caussa efficiente, nimirum bona uoluntate Dei patris sic misericorditer ponente: Pergratiam Dei, inquit, quasi dicat: Quòd Christus ita fuerit humiliatus, hoc non cedit ad obscurandam ipsius dignitatem, sed potius ad illustrandam Dei erga nos clemtiam & misericordiam. Altera ratio est à caussa finali, siue ab effectu, quando ait: Ut pro-mni degustaret mortem: est. n. sententia: Quando hic amplisimus effectus secutus est exhumiliatione Christi, quòd per mortem ipsius temporalem omnes credentes liberati sunt à morte æterna: quomodo illam humiliationem non accipiemus potius cedere ad augustiorem gloriam Christi, quàm ad eius imminutionem. Atq; his rationibus sic obiter subiectis & indicatis verius, quàm expositis, viam sibi parat ad plenius explicadum causas susceptæ à Christo humanitatis & omnis eius humiliationis. Scio quidem, aliter totû hunc locum ab alijs explicari: & quia obscurus est, non grauabor, bona fide, breuiter aliorum interpretationes recitare: ut liberum sit cuiuis, quòd habebit, probare & sequi. Chrysostomus sic accipit, quasi à pijs afflictis, & anhelantibus uidere Christum in summa potestate constitutũ, hæc obijceretur, qui conqueri potuissent, ualde absurdè dici, quòd Christo Domino omnia subijceretur, atq; ipsi interea ab aduersarijs grauissimas cogerentur ferre iniurias. Addidit ergo Apostolus consolationis loco, quòd, cùm Christus miris modis fuerit humiliatus, & nihilominus pòstea gloria & honore coronatus, ipsi quoq; æquanimiter deberent ad tempus ferre molestias, & constanter expectare gloriam & honore, molestijs successurum. Quòd uerò dicitur, omnia Christo subiecta, id uaticinium esse, & in futurum expectandum, & reuera successu temporis adimplendum. Potentiam enim Christi quotidie in mundo augeri & illustrari, sed plenam & consummatam nequaquam conspiciendam ante extremum diem, quo venturus est ipse cũ gloria & maiestate ad iudicandum uiuos & mortuos. Quidam sic distinguunt, ut uerba illa, omnia subiecisti sub pedes eius, accipienda putent, de uniuersali quadam subiectione, qua omnes creaturæ subiectæ esse debent suo creatori, atq; ita Christo uere omnia subiecta. Præsentis autem loci uerba: at nondum uidemus illi omnia subiecta, sonare subiectione voluntaria, qua quilibet per fidem in Christum se illi submittit, illumq; pro Domino agnoscit: atq; hoc pacto uerum quoq; esse, quòd nondum omnia sint Christo subiecta. Nam peccatores & increduli nondum sunt ei subiecti, ac ne prædestinati quidem omnes, iam sunt ei subiecti, quippe nondum nati, & ad finem usq; mundi alij alijs successuri.
units.tr: Another objection of the adversaries. For when they heard the dignity and power of Christ so greatly proclaimed over the whole world, and indeed over the angels themselves, and had nothing more to set against it, they finally objected with great contempt, and almost with mockery, that it seemed vain to proclaim the power of Christ so extravagantly, as though all things ought to be subjected to him, when such power was nowhere perceived in experience, but appeared to be merely imaginary and feigned. The blind adversaries, however, thought that what was said about the power of Christ should be understood of an external and temporal power, just as the Jews even today expect such a kingdom of the Messiah to come. And by this reasoning they thought they could easily overturn everything that was asserted about the pre-eminence and power of Christ. But the Apostle dismisses this objection in a few words, and, as if still looking back at the preceding argument, he grants that in some respect Christ may seem inferior to the angels, but he wishes to teach that in another respect he is superior. He concedes that in this respect he is inferior, because, although the angels are immortal, he endured death. Yet nevertheless, in another respect, he is plainly seen to be crowned with glory and honour, and therefore superior to the angels. But how such a great sight came about he does not himself explain, scorning the reasoning of the adversaries as weak and unworthy of a lengthy reply. Rather, he undoubtedly understands the glory and power of Christ to have been abundantly manifested in his resurrection and ascension into heaven. Elsewhere, Christ himself often said in the Gospel that he would be glorified from death through the resurrection and raised up to the glory of the Father, as in John 17, where he prays to the Father that he may glorify him. And from this most clear argument of Christ's power, he wishes us to understand, as if from a sign, that this also must necessarily be fulfilled: that all things will be subjected to him. For if he rose again by his own power, and subjected death itself to himself, and then ascended into heaven, as was plainly seen, why would it be strange that all things should be subjected to him? But so that the adversaries might not seize upon that humiliation of Christ as an occasion to place him below the angels, he adds two very weighty reasons, by which he hints that nothing was taken from his dignity through that humiliation of Christ, even to the point of death, and that in no respect was his glory obscured. The first is from the efficient cause, namely the good will of God the Father, who in his mercy so ordained it: "by the grace of God," he says, as if to say: that Christ was so humbled does not diminish his dignity, but rather serves to illustrate God's kindness and mercy toward us. The second reason is from the final cause, or from the effect, when he says: "that he might taste death for everyone." For the sense is this: since the most ample effect followed from the humiliation of Christ, namely that through his temporal death all believers are freed from eternal death, why should we not rather take that humiliation as contributing to the greater glory of Christ, than to its diminution? Having thus briefly put forward and indicated these reasons, rather than expounded them, he prepares the way for himself to explain more fully the causes of Christ's assumption of humanity and of all his humiliation. I know indeed that this whole passage is explained otherwise by others, and since it is obscure, I shall not hesitate, in good faith, to briefly recite the interpretations of others, so that each may freely judge and follow what he finds acceptable. Chrysostom takes it thus: that this objection might have been raised by pious people who were afflicted and longing to see Christ placed in supreme power, and who might have complained that it was utterly absurd to say that all things were subjected to the Lord Christ, while they themselves were meanwhile compelled by the adversaries to bear the most grievous injuries. So the Apostle added, by way of consolation, that since Christ was humbled in wonderful ways and yet afterwards crowned with glory and honour, they too ought to bear their troubles calmly for a time and steadfastly await glory and honour, which would follow their troubles. As for the statement that all things are subjected to Christ, this is a prophecy, to be awaited in the future, and truly to be fulfilled in the course of time. For the power of Christ is daily increasing and becoming more manifest in the world, but it will not be seen in its full and complete form before the last day, when he will come with glory and majesty to judge the living and the dead. Some distinguish in this way: they think that the words "you have put all things under his feet" should be understood of a certain universal subjection, by which all creatures ought to be subject to their Creator, and thus all things are truly subject to Christ. But the words of the present passage, "yet we do not yet see all things subjected to him," they take to mean voluntary subjection, by which each person, through faith in Christ, submits himself to him and acknowledges him as Lord; and in this way it is also true that not all things are yet subjected to Christ. For sinners and unbelievers are not yet subject to him, and not even all the predestined are yet subject to him, since they are not yet born, and others will succeed others until the end of the world.

units.la: Alij propius accedunt & interpretantur omnia subiecta esse Christo, imò & cuiuis pio in spiritu videlicet: quia omnes creaturæ seruiunt pijs ad salutem, oues, boues, pisces, ati-dès
units.tr: Others come closer and interpret that all things are subject to Christ, indeed to every godly person in spirit, because all creatures serve the godly for their salvation: sheep, oxen, fish, birds. Besides these, sin, death and hell (are subject to him).

units.la: Obiectio de morte Christi. aues: praeterea peccatum, mors, inferi. Quādo uerò iam obijcitur, nondum videri, quòd omnia sint Christo subiecta: id verum esse, quòd caro non possit videre istam Christi in omnia potestatem: quia potestas haec non est sita in rebus externis & temporalibus: sed internis & spiritualibus: quae quidem solis oculis mentis potest considerari, & locum habet solummodo in piorum mentibus. Palàm autem conspiciendam hanc potestatem Christi plenam in omnia, cùm videlicet extremo tempore, mors, diabolus, infernum, pedibus Christi subijcietur. Atq; haec sententia pluribus probatur. Nos autem exposuimus, vti existimauimus causae, quae agitur, & menti apostolicae maximè conuenire, crassius & rudius. Nunc partes explicabimus.
units.tr: Objection concerning the death of Christ. When it is objected that it is not yet seen that all things are subject to Christ, this is true in the sense that the flesh cannot see this power of Christ over all things. For this power does not lie in external and temporal things but in internal and spiritual ones. It can be considered only by the eyes of the mind, and it holds sway only in the minds of the godly. Yet this full power of Christ over all things will be plainly seen when, at the last time, death, the devil and hell are placed under the feet of Christ. Many people prove this view. We, however, have set out the matter more crudely and roughly, as we judged best suited to the case in hand and to the mind of the apostle. Now we shall explain the parts.

units.la: At nondum uidemus, illi omnia esse subiecta) Sic introducit aduersarios loquentes, quomodo Rhetores etiam solent mimesi quadam id facere, verba aduersariorum & gestus exprimentes, maximeq; ubi infirmum est argumentum, & causae non usque adeò accommodatum: ut ita aduersarios in contemptum adducant. Sequuntur verba Apostoli, seu objectionis solutio.
units.tr: But we do not yet see that all things are subject to him. The apostle introduces the opponents speaking in this way, as the rhetoricians also often do, by a kind of mimicry, expressing the opponents' words and gestures, especially where the argument is weak and not very well suited to the cause, so that they may thereby bring the opponents into contempt. What follows are the words of the apostle, or the answer to the objection.

units.la: Eum uero, qui paulisper diminutus fuerat infra angelos, cernimus Iesum, propter cruciatum mortis gloria & honore coronatum) Habet non nihil obscuritatis sententia haec, propter particulam illam infertam propter cruciatum mortis, ἀντὶ τοῦ παθήματος τῆς θανάτου. Non directè soluit, sed nihil aliud quā simpliciter dicit oppositā, nulla adhibita declaratione vel probatione. Vbi n. aduersarij dicebant: Nos nō videmus omnia illi subiecta. Respondet Apostolus, At nos cernimus, (βλέπομεν) eum gloria & honore coronatum, vt, omnia illi subijcienda, sit nobis multò certissimum: & distinguendae sunt diligenter illae voces, ὁρῶμεν & βλέπομεν.
units.tr: But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death. This sentence has some obscurity, because of the phrase added here, because of the suffering of death, [ἀντὶ τοῦ παθήματος τῆς θανάτου, that is, on account of the suffering of death]. He does not answer directly, but simply states the opposite without any explanation or proof. For where the opponents said, "We do not see all things subject to him," the apostle replies, but we see [βλέπομεν] him crowned with glory and honour, so that it is for us far more certain that all things shall be subjected to him. The words [ὁρῶμεν] and [βλέπομεν] must be carefully distinguished.

units.la: Potest particula haec referri & ad illud, quod dicit, Christum diminutum ab Angelis, vt sit sententia, Iesum, propter, siue per cruciatum mortis, diminutum esse paulisper ab angelis, id est, inferiorem esse angelis, propterea quod mortem subierit. Rursus autem potest referri, ad illa uerba, gloria & honore coronatum: vt sit sententia: idep Christum gloria & honore coronatum, quia antea per mortis cruciatum fuit maximè humiliatus. In quā sententiam Philip. 2. Christus, cùm esset in forma Dei, & aequalis Deo, semetipsum inaniuit, forma serui sumpta, in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus ut homo, humilem praebuit semetipsum, factus obediens vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Quapropter & Deus illum in summam extulit sublimitatem, ac donauit illi nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, &c. Nos autem, ratione argumenti praecedetis, prioris modo expositum, vt habeatur veluti declaratio, quomodo intelligendū, quòd Christus sit angelis inferior. Iterum uere dicit paulisper diminutum, βραχύ τι ἠλαττωμένον. Vox βραχύ breuitatem temporis notat, quia uidelicet pro tempore duntaxat Christus fuit humiliatus, & inferior angelis, eo nimirum, quo ipse mortem pertulit. Nam toto eo tempore, quo homo inter homines uersatus est, dicere eum inferiorem angelis, non admodum conuenit: quando quiuis homo illustratus donis Dei, angelis non sit apud Deum inferior: multò minus Christus, cui angeli saepe leguntur ministrasse, ut, agenti in deserto, & alibi. Sed in morte reuera Christus, & ministerio angelorum, & auxilio Dei est destitutus, vt naturam humanam tunc solam sibi relictam appareat. Vnde & Christus ipse dixit, se à Deo derelictum, & angelos, qui pro ipso depugnarent, noluisse impetrare. Ergo de tempore mortis praecipuè humiliatio haec accipitur, idq; eò magis, quòd hic difer te dicatur, Christum per mortem esse diminutum ab angelis. Si quis aliter uelit illud, paulisper, explicare, de dignitate uidelicet & qualitatibus, quibus humana natura in genere distat ab angelica, non refert. A sensu enim nihil discedituř. Nam mors ipsa ab humana natura provenit, & morte potissimum differunt sancti ab angelis. Certè Chrysostomus, paulisper, referrat illud breue tempus, triduanum videlicet, quo Christus mortuus est, & descendit ad infernum. Neq; abs re dixit Apostolus, cruciatum mortis: ita enim veros dolores, veram mortem Christi voluit exprimere. Atq; ita manifestum reddidit, quo maximè distet Christus ab angelis, qui corporeorum dolorum & mortis sunt expertes. Nemo suspicetur siue cum Manichaeis, siue cum Apollinaristis, siue cum Archoticis, siue Basilidianis, Christum non uere passum, quasi aut non habuisset uerum corpus, aut figuram suā corpoream in alium transtulisset, qui pro ipso in crucem fuisset raptus. Hi errores adeò crassi sunt & foedi, nec nō à Scripturis adeò manifestè refutati, ut mirum sit, inueniri aliquādo potuisse, qui paterentur sibi tā absurda persuaderi. Sed hanc Christi humiliatione, & ueros cruciatus ac morte Esaias luculenter expresit cap. 53. Non est species ei, neq; decor, & uidimus eum, & non erat aspectus, & desiderauimus eum despectum & nouissimum uirorum, virum dolorum & scientem infirmitatem, & quasi abconditus vultus eius & despectus, unde nec reputauimus eum. Verè languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portauit, & nos putauimus eũ quasi leprosum & percussum à Deo, & humiliatum. Ipse autem uulneratus est propter infirmitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra, &c. Sunt passim multi alij loci apud prophetas, & plurimi in scriptis apostolicis: sed hic unus, quoniam ualde illustris est, & mirè conuenit præsenti loco, pro multis sit.
units.tr: This phrase may refer to what he says about Christ being made lower than the angels, so that the sense is: Jesus, because of, or through, the suffering of death, was made a little lower than the angels, that is, he was inferior to the angels because he underwent death. On the other hand, it may refer to the words crowned with glory and honour, so that the sense is: the same Christ was crowned with glory and honour because before, through the suffering of death, he had been most greatly humbled. To this sense agrees Philippians 2: Christ, being in the form of God and equal to God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man; he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also highly exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name, etc. We, however, according to the nature of the argument, have set out the matter in the former way, so that it may be seen as an explanation of how it is to be understood that Christ is lower than the angels. Again, he rightly says "a little lower," [βραχύ τι ἠλαττωμένον]. The word [βραχύ] denotes the shortness of time, because Christ was humbled only for a time, and was inferior to the angels only so long as he endured death. For during the whole time that he lived among men, it is not very fitting to call him inferior to the angels, since any man endowed with God's gifts is not inferior to the angels before God, much less Christ, whom the angels are often read to have ministered to, as when he was in the desert, and elsewhere. But in death itself Christ was deprived both of the ministry of the angels and of the help of God, so that then only his human nature appeared to be left to him. Hence Christ himself said that he was forsaken by God, and that he had not wished to call upon the angels, who would have fought for him. Therefore this humiliation is chiefly understood of the time of death, and all the more so because here it is said that Christ was made lower than the angels through death. If anyone wishes to explain the word "a little" otherwise, of the dignity and qualities by which human nature in general differs from angelic nature, it does not matter, for the sense is not departed from at all, since death itself comes from human nature, and the saints differ from the angels chiefly by death. Certainly Chrysostom refers "a little" to that brief time, namely the three days, in which Christ was dead and descended into hell. Nor did the apostle speak without reason of the suffering of death, for in this way he wished to express the true sorrows and the true death of Christ. And so he made plain how far Christ is distant from the angels, who are free from bodily pains and death. Let no one suspect, whether with the Manichaeans, the Apollinarians, the Archontics or the Basilidians, that Christ did not truly suffer, as if he had not had a true body, or had transferred his bodily form to another who had been caught up to the cross in his place. These errors are so gross and foul, and so plainly refuted by the Scriptures, that it is a wonder that anyone could ever be found who would allow himself to be persuaded of such absurdities. But Isaiah set forth this humiliation of Christ and his true torments and death brilliantly in chapter 53: "He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He is despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief; and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows; yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities," etc. Many other passages occur here and there in the prophets, and very many in the apostolic writings, but this one, since it is most illustrious and agrees wonderfully with the present place, may stand for many.

units.la: Cùm deinde dicit, gloria & honore coronatum, sunt uerba sumpta quidem ex præcedenti testimonio, è psalmo octauo, sed tantundem sibi uolunt, ac si simpliciter ad argumentũ aduersariorum diceretur, omnia Christo esse subiecta. Ex his enim uerbis hoc ipsum uult colligi, sicut & in psalmo etiam statim tantundem sequitur. Et mos est Scripturæ, unum aliquod interdum exprimere, ex quo intelligi conuenit cætera: & sæpe exprimitur, quod primum est in oratione, ut inde intelligantur sequentia: sæpe item quod ultimum est, ut inde intelligantur præcedentia. Verbi caussa, Josuæ 2. exploratores reuersi dixerunt: Quia dedit Dominus in manum nostram omnem terram. Haud dubiè præferunt alia uerba eorum, (id quod maximè liquet ex rationali coniunctione, quia, כי) sed qualia ea fuerint, potest ex illis paucis facilè coniectari. Item Luc.24. O stulti & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus, quæ locuti sunt prophetæ: Non ne hæc oportuit pati Christum, & intrare in gloriam suam? Vbi plurima subintelliguntur, quæ Christus ex prophetis de se exposuerat, sicut uerbis sequentibus indicatur. Et exorsus à Mose & omnib. prophetis, interpretabatur illis in omnibus scripturis, quæ de ipso erant. Et eodem capite: Tunc aperuit illorum mentem, ut intelligerent Scripturas, & dixit eis, Sic scriptum est, & sic oportebat Christũ pati, & resurgere à mortuis tertio die, & prædicare in nomine eius pœnitentiâ & remissione peccatorum in omnes gentes. En pauca uerba, ex quibus tamen multa & sequentia & antecedentia debent intelligi. Sic etiam hoc loco, quando apostolus ait, cernimus eum gloria & honore coronatum, ualde multa oportet ex his verbis intelligi. Nec dubium, quin pij multa potuerint animo comprehendere his auditis, maximè cum intuerentur in ea, quæ de dignitate Christi prius dicta sunt, & secum repeterent, quomodo Christus mirabili potétia resurrexisset, atq; in cœlos ascendisset: quomodo misisset spiritum Sanctũ cum innumeris & amplissimis donis: quomodo intra breue tempus per paucos & infimæ sortis homines propagasset euangelium toto orbe: hæc, inquam, pijs omnibus erant notissima, atq; ex his iudicabant, Christum uerè gloria & honore coronatum, Christo diabolum, peccatum, mortem, infernum, denique omnia debere esse subdita.
units.tr: When he then says crowned with glory and honour, these words are indeed taken from the preceding testimony, from Psalm 8, but they mean the same as if it were simply said in answer to the opponents' argument, all things are subject to Christ. For from these words it is meant that this very thing should be inferred, as in the psalm too the same follows immediately. It is the custom of Scripture sometimes to express one thing from which the rest ought to be understood, and often what comes first in a passage is expressed, so that what follows may be understood from it, and often likewise what comes last, so that what precedes may be understood from it. For example, Joshua 2: the spies, returning, said, "Surely the LORD hath delivered into our hands all the land" [כי]. Doubtless they used other words too (which is most clear from the causal conjunction, [כי] "for"), but what those words were can easily be conjectured from these few. Likewise Luke 24: "O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?" Here much is to be understood that Christ had expounded about himself from the prophets, as the following words indicate. And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. And in the same chapter: "Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise again from the dead the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations." Behold, a few words, from which yet much that follows and precedes must be understood. So also in this place, when the apostle says, we see him crowned with glory and honour, a great deal must be understood from these words. Nor is there any doubt that the godly could have grasped much in their minds on hearing these things, especially when they considered what had been said before about the dignity of Christ, and recalled to themselves how Christ had risen again by his wonderful power and ascended into the heavens, how he had sent the Holy Spirit with innumerable and very great gifts, and how within a short time he had spread the gospel through the whole world by a few men of the lowest rank. These things, I say, were all most well known to all the godly, and from them they judged that Christ was truly crowned with glory and honour, and that to Christ the devil, sin, death and hell, and finally all things, ought to be made subject.

units.la: Hacigitur de caussa apostolus non demonstrauit, non probauit hic in pluribus uerbis, quomodo Christus esset gloria & honore coronatus, seu quomodo omnia ei esset subiecta. Et certè vbi aduersariorum argumenta sunt absurda, & à principali negotio valde aliena, sapientis hominis est, potius ea contemnere & reijcere, quàm directè respondere. Stulto responde iuxta stultitiam suam, inquit sapiens, Prouerb.26. Quando ergo tam crassè obiecerunt, intelligentes de potétia quadam externa & temporali, quæ apud pios accipiebantur de potentia Christi interna & spirituali, ualde aliena ab institu-to erat illorum obiectio.
units.tr: Therefore the apostle, for this reason, did not demonstrate or prove at length here how Christ was crowned with glory and honour, or how all things were made subject to him. And indeed, where the arguments of opponents are absurd and far removed from the main business, it is the mark of a wise man to despise and reject them rather than answer them directly. "Answer a fool according to his folly," says the wise man (Prov. 26). Since they objected so crudely, taking the power in question as some external and temporal power, whereas the godly understood it as Christ's inner and spiritual power, their objection was altogether foreign to the subject.

units.la: Simili autem modo Apostolus Rom.3. absurdas & impias obiectiones quorundam cum contemptu reijcit, non diluit. Quidam enim audientes, quòd per iniustitiam nostram iustitia Dei commendaretur, inferebant, iniustum ergo uideri Deum, qui propter peccata nos puniret, & addebant: ergo peccandum nobis, ut iustitia & bonitas Dei (quàdo remittet peccatum) occasione peccati nostri illustretur. Non dignatus est Apostolus blasphemas obiectiones alia dilutione, quàm quòd talia dicentium iusta sit damnatio. Satis igitur perspicuum est, quare Apostolus ad obiectionem aduersariorum aliter non responderit. Sequitur:
units.tr: In a similar way, the apostle in Rom. 3 rejects, with contempt, the absurd and impious objections of certain people rather than refuting them. For some, hearing that through our unrighteousness the righteousness of God is commended, inferred: then God is unjust who punishes us on account of our sins; and they added: then let us sin, so that the righteousness and goodness of God (in forgiving sin) may be made more illustrious by the occasion of our sin. The apostle did not deign to answer these blasphemous objections in any other way than by saying that the condemnation of those who speak thus is just. It is therefore quite clear why the apostle did not answer the objections of his opponents otherwise. It follows:

units.la: Vt per gratiam Dei) Hoc est, per gratuitam misericordiam Dei patris. Is enim est fauor & beneuolentia Dei patris erga genus humanum, siue, vt Ioan.3. inquit Christus, sic dilexit Deus mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum daret. Hæc, inquam, dilectio & charitas Dei, per gratiam hic significatur, quomodo passim per gratiam Dei patris, per diuitias gratiæ ipsius seruati dicimur.
units.tr: "By the grace of God": that is, by the free mercy of God the Father. For this is the favour and goodwill of God the Father toward the human race, or, as Christ says in John 3, "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son." This love and charity of God is here signified by grace, just as we are everywhere said to be saved by the grace of God the Father, by the riches of his grace (Eph. 2).

units.la: Ephef.2.
units.tr: Eph. 2.

units.la: Pro omni gustaret mortem) Id est, ut sua morte temporali & momentanea liberaret omnes à morte æterna: ut pro omnium peccatis sua morte quasi uictima oblata, aut precio redemptionis satisfaceret. Et hic notanda est uocum proprietas. Pro omni, supple homine: quomodo aliàs quoque in scripturis ea locutionis forma occurrit. Ioan. 4. Omnis, qui bibit ex aqua hac, sitiet iterum. Rom.10. Esaiæ 28. Omnis, qui fidit illi, non pudebit. Vel, potest dici, in huiusmodi locis singularem numerum poni pro plurali: ut pro omni intellitantundem sit, ac si diceretur pro omnibus. Atque aliqui interpretantur, per omnes, intelligendos electos tantum. Sed sciendum, quòd quoties Scriptura beneficium mor tis Christi, vel misericordiam Dei patris, vel simile quiddam ad salutem hominum per tinens, commemorat, passim usurpat notas universales: id autem ad amplificandam & illustrandam Dei bonitatē, & effectum mortis Christi; ut beneficia Dei non ad paucos tantum, sed vniuersaliter ad omnes pertinere intelligantur. Verissimum enim est illud, & maxime ex sententia Dei pronunciatum, Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri: Verum, tametsi illa sit voluntas ipsius Dei, tamen, quoniam ad salutem nostram aliquid requiritur etiam ex parte nostra, nimirum ut credamus, & salutem apprehendamus propter Christum: (qua de re plenius disputatur Rom. 9. ac 10. vbi causae explicantur reiectionis Iudaeorū) hinc fit, quòd non omnes salui fiant: hinc fit, quòd effectus mortis Christi non omnibus æquabiliter accommodetur. Ergo Christus pro omnibus quidem mortuus est, & sua morte pro omnium peccatis abunde satisfecit: sed quò minus omnes consequantur, quod ille promeritus est, ipsi sibi causa sunt, qui nolunt credere, & per fidem in Christū salutem accipere.
units.tr: "That he should taste death for every man": that is, that by his temporal and momentary death he might free all from eternal death, so that, his death being offered as a victim for the sins of all, or as a price of redemption, he might make satisfaction. Here the proper sense of the words must be noted. "For every man," supply "man": the same form of expression occurs elsewhere in the Scriptures (John 4: "Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again"; Rom. 10; Isa. 28: "Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame"). Or it may be said that in such passages the singular is put for the plural, so that "every one" means the same as "all." And some interpret "all" to mean the elect only. But it should be understood that whenever Scripture recounts the benefit of Christ's death, or the mercy of God the Father, or something similar pertaining to the salvation of men, it everywhere uses universal terms; and this is to magnify and illustrate the goodness of God and the effect of Christ's death, so that the benefits of God are understood to pertain not only to a few but universally to all. For that saying is most true, and pronounced especially in accordance with the will of God: "God wills that all men be saved." Yet although this is the very will of God, nevertheless, since something is also required on our part for our salvation, namely that we believe and lay hold of salvation on account of Christ (on which matter Rom. 9 and 10 dispute more fully, where the causes of the rejection of the Jews are explained), it comes about that not all are saved; it comes about that the effect of Christ's death is not applied equally to all. Therefore Christ indeed died for all, and by his death fully satisfied for the sins of all; but that not all obtain what he has merited is their own fault, those who are unwilling to believe and to receive salvation through faith in Christ.

units.la: Quemadmodum si medicina parata sit, quam certum sit omnibus laborantibus para- lysi, aut alio morbo, succurrere: sane si qui recusant accipere, quòd tales nō recipiant sa- nitatē, nō medicinæ vel medico, sed illis ipsis ægrotis debet imputari. Interea multò ap- positissima vox est gustandi, quando ait, Christū gustasse mortem. Nam ea vox & satis- significat, Christum mortis vim in se expertum, si mulq; significat, morti non potuisse ma nere obnoxium. Gustare enim est nō penitus exhaurire & devorare, sed tantùm leuiter attingere, ita tamen, ut de sapore alijsq; qualitatibus perinde iudicare posit, qui paululū gustat, atq; qui totum absorbet. Ita Christus quoq; uere sensit mortem, sed nō ita, ut qui toti à morte absorbentur, & perpetuò ab ea detinentur: sed ipse tantùm ad breue momē tum sensit, siquidem ipsemet fuit mors mortis, & absorpsit morte per victoriā, 1. Cor. 15: Itaq; ipse nihil aliud, quàm eam gustauit, à qua captiuus teneri non potuit. Scitè hic Chry sostomus: quemadmodum medicus non habens necessitatem, quæ præparantur ægro- to, gustare: sed illi consulens primus ex illius cibo degustat, ut persuadeat ægroto prom ptius illos cibos accipere: sic & Dominus, quoniam omnes homines mortem timebat, & ipse nullam habens necessitatem, mortem gustauit, ita persuadens eis, suo exemplo, ut fiducialiter ad mortem accederent.
units.tr: It is as if a medicine were prepared which surely would help all who suffer from paralysis or some other disease: if some refuse to take it and so do not recover their health, the blame must be laid not on the medicine or the physician but on the sick themselves. Meanwhile the word "to taste" is very apt when he says that Christ tasted death. For that word signifies that Christ experienced the force of death, yet signifies also that he could not remain subject to death. For to taste is not to drain and devour completely, but only to touch lightly, yet in such a way that one who tastes a little can judge of the flavour and other qualities just as well as one who swallows the whole. So Christ also truly felt death, but not in such a way as those who are wholly swallowed up by death and held by it forever; he himself felt it only for a brief moment, since he himself was the death of death, and swallowed up death in victory (1 Cor. 15). Therefore he did nothing other than taste it, by which he could not be held captive. Chrysostom says well here: just as a physician, who has no need of the food prepared for the sick man, nevertheless tastes it first for the sake of the sick man, in order to persuade him to take that food more readily, so also the Lord, since all men feared death, and he himself having no necessity, tasted death, persuading them by his example to approach death with confidence.

units.la: Ergo habemus hîc hanc doctrinā de præparatione ad morte, & non formidanda mor te: quòd si enim Christus nostra causa non detrectauit gustare mortem, & quidem adeò acerbam, cùm tamen ipse nulla necessitate mortis, (utpote qui nunquam peccasset) pre- meretur: nec nos debemus multum angi, si morte, cùm voluerit Dominus, subeamus, qui nostris peccatis ei obnoxij sumus atq; eam promeriti. Si cōsideremus peccatorū no strorum magnitudinem & multitudinem, contrà, quàm Christus innocens fuerit & à peccato alienus, nequaquam nobis graue erit mori. Sed tum quidem multò adhuc mi- nus molestum erit, si consideremus, illum nostri causa esse mortuum: si deniq; confida- mus per illius mortem temporalem liberandos nos à morte secunda & æterna. Quę cō fideratio valde utilis est, & consolatoria contra oēs tentationes, quę imminente mortis truculentia possunt euenire. Certè si tūc cogitet quispiam, ecce Christus humiliatus est, sic volente Deo patre, ut pro omni gustaret morte: hauddubiè & gustauit pro me. Ipse pro peccatis meis per morte suâ dependit ac satisfecit. Qui hoc pacto, inquam, secum cogitat, is nullis diaboli tentantis insultibus ad desperandum adigetur, is deo gratâ red- detanimam. Sed præterea ex alijs uerbis alia documenta licet colligere. Cùm enim Chri- stus describitur usq; adeò humiliatus, ut iam non infra angelos modò, sed infra abiectif- simos & vilissimos homines positus videatur: commendatur hîc nobis humilitas, & reprehenditur nostra superbia. Christus, qui natura Deus erat, factus est vermis, & non homo, opprobrium hominum, & abiectio plebis, ut psal. 22. ipse loquitur. Nos uerò, qui natura sumus indignissimi vermiculi, quid tantum superbimus? quid nostris uiribus fi- dimus? quid inflati sumus in nostris sordibus? quid deniq; in tanta uilitate constituti al- ter alterum conamur deprimere, imperium & potestatem in fratres nostros exer- cere ambientes.
units.tr: Therefore we have here this teaching concerning preparation for death, and that death is not to be dreaded. For if Christ for our sake did not refuse to taste death, and that so bitter a death, when he, having no necessity of death (as one who had never sinned), was nevertheless pressed by it, then neither ought we to be greatly distressed if we undergo death when the Lord wills, we who are liable to it on account of our sins and have deserved it. If we consider the magnitude and multitude of our sins, and on the other hand how innocent Christ was and free from sin, it will by no means be grievous for us to die. But it will be much less troublesome still if we consider that he died for our sake, and finally if we trust that through his temporal death we shall be delivered from the second and eternal death. This consideration is very useful and consoling against all the temptations that can arise from the fierceness of impending death. Certainly, if someone at that time reflects: "Behold, Christ was humbled, so that by the will of God the Father he might taste death for every man"; without doubt he tasted it for me too; he himself paid and satisfied for my sins by his death. Whoever thinks in this way, I say, will not be driven to despair by any assaults of the tempting devil, and will yield up his soul pleasing to God. But besides, other lessons may be gathered from other words. For when Christ is described as so humbled that he seems placed not only below the angels but below the most abject and vilest of men, humility is commended to us here, and our pride is rebuked. Christ, who was by nature God, was made a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people, as he himself says in Psalm 22. But we, who by nature are most unworthy little worms, why are we so proud? Why do we trust in our own strength? Why are we puffed up in our filth? Why, finally, placed in such lowliness, do we try to depress one another, seeking to exercise dominion and power over our brothers?

units.la: Præterea, quando cruciatus mortis in Christo describitur, admonemur & nos ad to- lerantiam & patientiam quarumcunq; aduersitatum. Cùm verò additur, Christū, licet sic affectum, nihilominus gloria & honore coronatum: hinc magnam consolationem in ad uersis debemus concipere, ac statuere, quòd sicut Christus post humiliationem illam est glorificatus, ita nos quoq; post tentationes & pericula à malis liberandos:
units.tr: Moreover, when the torments of death are described in Christ, we are also admonished to endure and be patient in whatever adversities befall us. But when it is added that Christ, though so afflicted, was nevertheless crowned with glory and honour, we ought to conceive from this great consolation in adversity, and to hold that, just as Christ was glorified after that humiliation, so we too shall be delivered from evils after temptations and dangers:

units.la: I. Postre-
units.tr: I. Final-

units.la: Postremò, quando audimus, Christum per gratiam siue bonam uoluntatem Dei patris sic humiliatum, qui videns nostram miseriam & damnationem voluit nos recipere in gratiam, & quidem gratis (nam omnia ista debent in animum uenire, cū dicitur, gratia dei) excitari debemus hic ad contemplandam immensam dei bonitatem, qua ille deno stra salute semper est solicitus, & misericordiam suam in reos, & nihil nisi damnatione commeritos vult exercere, & neglecta ratione nostrorum meritorum ex sola Dei bonitate lubenter toti pendebimus. Certè, si haec animo reuoluamus, mirabilem consolatio nem ex his in omni vita accipiemus: sed nostra rursus interest, vt gratias ei pro tanta erga nos beneuolentia habeamus.
units.tr: Finally, when we hear that Christ was thus humbled through the grace, that is, the good will, of God the Father, who, seeing our misery and damnation, willed to receive us into favour, and that freely (for all these things should come to mind when we hear the words "the grace of God"), we ought to be stirred up here to contemplate the immense goodness of God, by which he is always concerned for our salvation, and wills to show his mercy towards guilty people who deserve nothing but damnation. Setting aside any reckoning of our merits, we will gladly hang wholly on God's goodness alone. Certainly, if we turn these things over in our minds, we will gain from them a wonderful consolation in every part of life. But it is also our duty again to give him thanks for such great kindness towards us.

units.la: Decebat enim cum, propter quem sunt omnia, et per quem sunt omnia, ut multis filijs in gloriam adductis, principem salutis illorum per afflictiones perfectum redderet.) Admonent quidem interpretes, Apostolum hic iam differere de natura humana Christi, sicut supra disseruit de natura diuina. Sed, qua occasione, quo consilio, non attingunt. Nos, ut clarius intelligatur, quomodo cohaereant haec cum praecedentibus, & quomodo ex illis sequantur, habita diligentira tione totius disputationis ab initio instituta, qua occasione ad differendum de humanitate Christi, descenderit Apostolus, utcunq; indicabimus.
units.tr: For it became him, for whom are all things and by whom are all things, that, when he was bringing many sons to glory, he should make perfect through afflictions the captain of their salvation. Indeed, the interpreters point out that the Apostle is now speaking of the human nature of Christ, just as above he spoke of his divine nature. But they do not touch on the occasion or the purpose of this. So that it may be understood more clearly how these things cohere with what precedes and how they follow from it, we shall indicate, with careful attention to the whole course of the argument from the beginning, what occasion led the Apostle to speak of the humanity of Christ.

units.la: Oportet considerare ecclesiae omnem statum, quales fuerint aduersarij, quae principalis disputatio, quae argumeta in utramque partem potuerint fieri: atque ita omnia expendere, quasi coram sis, atq; ibi in ipsis difficultatibus versferis. Constanter quidem hactenus asseruit Apostolus Christi diuinitatem ac dignitatem, & proximis verbis ostendit, humiliationem eius in assumpta humana natura & morte, dignitati ac gloriae ipsius nihil obesse. Sed nondum ita satisfactum est aduersarijs. Restabat enim adhuc nouus scrupus, qui omnes etiam non adeo iniquos caussae Christi, ad dubitandum de ipsius diuinitate atq; excellentia potuisset adducere. Sic enim aduersarij dicere adhuc poterant: Vos contenditis, Christum Deum esse, illam vero humiliationem contigisse per gratiam & bonam voluntatem Dei patris, ut homines per mortem Christi temporanea a morte aeterna liberarentur. Bene quidem, quando ita vultis: sed tamen, si Christus erat Deus, vt vos praedicatis, quid opus erat illum hominem fieri, & acerbos mortis cruciatus subeundo non solu infra angelos, sed etiam infra abiectissimos homines deiici: quado potuisset sola sua diuina uirtute, imo vel solo uerbo humanum genus a morte aeternalibe rare, & ad salutem perducere? Et certè vehemens & valde pungens apparebat haec ratio, quae hauddubie eo etiam plus ponderis habebat apud omnes, quod valde pugnans cum ratione & absurdum videretur, eum, qui Deus erat, fieri homine, & praeterea mortem guitare. Atq; haec sine dubio fiebat obiectio ab aduersarijs: sed Apostolus ea, quod non abesset a blasphemia, non nude exprimit. Vt ergo hanc quoq; obiectionem tacitam tamen & reuera grauem atq; molestam diluerat Apostolus, & nihil amplius supereresset, quod ad imminuendam Christi dignitatem obijceretur: nunc per occupationem copiosius & clarius exponit, quibus de causis Christum ab aeterno Deum, in tempore fieri homine decuerit, nec non quare eundem decuerit & mortem subire. Quibus expositis omnis scrupus ab omnium animis eximetur. Proinde haec est propositio, qua simpliciter asserit, sic decuisse & constitutum fuisse a Deo patre, vt Christus princeps & autor salutis omnium ad aeternam salutem vocandorum, primùm per afflictiones in humana natura humiliaretur, ac deinde ad summam perfectionem seu dignitatem & gloriam exaltaretur: vt plane idem hic dicatur, quod Christus diuersis in locis de se dixit, oportuit pati Christu, & sic intrare in gloria sua. Luc.24.24. Mar.8.10. Habet aut haec verba aliquid obscuritatis: quàdoquidem haec verba, decebat eum, propter quem sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia, alij ad patrem, alij ad filium transferunt, cum graece habeatur, διὰ ὃν τὰ πάντα καὶ δι᾽ οὗ τὰ πάντα, πολλοὺς υἱοὺς εἰς δόξαν ἀγαγόντα, τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας αὐτῶν διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι. Vbi illa, δι᾽ ὃν, & δι᾽ οὗ, fere semper de filio dicitur, ac pinde pro periphrasi, qua pater significaretur, nolunt accipi. Perfectum autem reddere principem salutis de filio dici non potest, sed de patre, cuius bona voluntate filius humiliatus est, ac postea exaltatus.
units.tr: One must consider the whole condition of the Church: who the adversaries were, what the principal dispute was, and what arguments could be made on each side. One must weigh everything as if one were present and were standing in those very difficulties. Up to this point the Apostle has steadfastly asserted the divinity and dignity of Christ, and in the preceding words he has shown that his humiliation in the assumed human nature and his death do nothing to diminish his dignity and glory. But the adversaries were not yet satisfied. For a new scruple remained, which could have led even those not wholly hostile to the cause of Christ to doubt his divinity and excellence. The adversaries could still say: "You contend that Christ is God, yet that humiliation came about through the grace and good will of God the Father, so that by the death of Christ men might be freed from eternal death in exchange for temporal death. Very well, if you say so. But if Christ was God, as you preach, why was there any need for him to become a man, and by undergoing the bitter torments of death to be cast down not only below the angels but even below the most abject men, when he could have freed the human race from eternal death, and brought it to salvation, by his divine power alone, or indeed by a single word?" This objection certainly seemed sharp and very cutting, and it undoubtedly carried all the more weight with everyone because it seemed strongly at odds with reason and absurd that he who was God should become a man and, besides, should suffer death. Without doubt this objection was being made by the adversaries, but the Apostle does not state it bluntly, because it verged on blasphemy. So, in order to answer this objection as well, which was unspoken yet in reality serious and troubling, and so that nothing further would remain to be raised against the dignity of Christ, he now anticipates and sets out more fully and clearly the reasons why it was fitting for Christ, who is God from eternity, to become man in time, and also why it was fitting for him to undergo death. Once these things are set out, every scruple will be removed from the minds of all. Therefore this is the proposition, by which he simply asserts that it was so fitting and so decreed by God the Father that Christ, the prince and author of salvation for all who are called to eternal salvation, should first be humbled through afflictions in human nature and then be exalted to supreme perfection or dignity and glory. So the same thing is plainly said here as Christ said of himself in various places: "It behoved Christ to suffer and so to enter into his glory" (Luke 24:26; Mark 8:31). Yet these words have some obscurity, since some refer the words "it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things" to the Father, others to the Son, although in the Greek the text reads: "διὰ ὃν τὰ πάντα καὶ δι᾽ οὗ τὰ πάντα, πολλοὺς υἱοὺς εἰς δόξαν ἀγαγόντα, τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας αὐτῶν διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι." There, the phrases "δι᾽ ὃν" and "δι᾽ οὗ" almost always refer to the Son, and so they are unwilling to take them as a periphrasis meaning the Father. But to make the captain of salvation perfect cannot be said of the Son, but of the Father, by whose good will the Son was humbled and afterwards exalted.

units.la: Quare per illa verba, δι᾽ ὃν, & δι᾽ οὗ, patrem πεφιφαγωγον voluntintelligi. Sed non opus est multis verbis, & citra negotium scrupus omnis tollitur. Verba illa, propter quem sunt omnia, et per quem sunt omnia, recte filio accommodabuntur. Illud autem, decebat eum, ut relatiuum eum respiciat ad id, quod prius dictum est, per gratiam Dei. Estque sententia: Decebat enim Deum patrem, (qui per gratiam & misericordiam sua amplissima constituerat, utiam dictu est, Christu pro omnibus gustare morte) ut Christū, propter quem sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia, postq; multos alios filios adduxisset in gloria, tanq; principem, autorem salutis omnium illorum per afflictiones & propter afflictiones tantas perse-ctum redderet, & ad summam gloriam eueheret. Rationes autem, cur in hunc modum reddam Apostoli sententiam, & prius illud, Decebat eum, ad patrem referam, cae-tera autem, propter quem{a}sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia, plures me mouet. Primùm, decebat eum, rectè refertur ad Deum patrem, de cuius gratia sermo proximè praecesserat, cui ista per particulam rationalem γὰρ sunt connectenda, & ibi admonuimus, viam paratam ad ea quae nunc dicuntur. Haec verò, propter quem sunt omnia, & per què sunt omnia, tribuimus Christo. Primò, quia alias saepius illae formulę loquendi de Christo ἀπρὶ exponuntur: ut 1. Cor. 8. Vnus est Deus, qui est pater ille, ex quo omnia, & nos in illū, & vnus Dominus Iesus Christus, per quē omnia, & nos per illum. Ioan. 1. Omnia per illum facta sunt. Sic Rom. 11. vbi dicitur: Quoniam ex illo, & per illum, & in illum omnia. Priorem particulam de patre solent exponere, alteram frequenter de filio. Eph. 1. vt summatim instauraret omnia per Christum, & quae in coelis sunt, & quae in terra, per eundē, per quē & in fortem adsciti sumus. Coloss. 1. Primogenitus vniuersae creaturae, quòd per illum creata sint omnia, quae in coelis sunt, & quae in terra. Ibidem: Omnia per illum & in illum creata sunt, & ipse est ante omnia, & omnia per illum consistunt. Postremò, & huius epistolae cap. 1. Per quem condidit & secula. Quibus omnibus locis illud ἀὶ οὗ, de filio proprie sonat, quod pater licet agat quidem, tamen per filium, quasi adiutorem & cooperarium, & fere semper particula illa, per, filij memoriam nobis ingerit. Alia ratio est, quòd, quoniam hic agitur de humiliatione Christi, conuenit ea interserere, quae dignitatem ipsius adhuc declarent. Vnde cum de afflictionibus ipsius sermo habetur, aptè additur, ad ostendendum, quòd per eas nihil detrahatur ipsius dignitati, ipsum esse, propter quem sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia.
units.tr: Therefore by the words "δι᾽ ὃν" and "δι᾽ οὗ" some understand the Father, and they are wrong to do so. But there is no need for many words, and the scruple is removed without any trouble. The words "for whom are all things, and by whom are all things" will rightly be applied to the Son. As for "it became him," the relative "him" looks back to what was said before, "by the grace of God." And the sense is this: "For it became God the Father (who, by his grace and most abundant mercy, had decreed, as has been said, that Christ should taste death for all) that Christ, for whom are all things and by whom are all things, after he had brought many other sons into glory, should make perfect, as the prince and author of salvation for all of them, through afflictions and because of such great afflictions, and should raise him to the highest glory." I refer the Apostle's sentence in this way, and I refer the first clause, "it became him," to the Father, for several reasons. First, "it became him" is rightly referred to God the Father, of whose grace the discussion had just spoken, and to whom these things are to be linked by the reasoning particle "for" (γάρ). There we have already pointed out the way prepared for what is now being said. But "for whom are all things, and by whom are all things" we attribute to Christ. First, because elsewhere these formulas of speech about Christ are commonly explained of the Father, as in 1 Cor. 8: "There is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him." John 1: "All things were made by him." So Rom. 11: "For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things." The first part of these phrases they usually explain of the Father, and the second often of the Son. Eph. 1: "that he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth, even in him, in whom also we have obtained an inheritance." Col. 1: "the firstborn of every creature, for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth." Likewise: "All things were created by him and for him, and he is before all things, and by him all things consist." Lastly, in chapter 1 of this epistle: "by whom also he made the worlds." In all these places the phrase "by whom" (δι᾽ οὗ) properly refers to the Son, since the Father, although he acts, does so through the Son as his helper and co-worker, and the particle "by" almost always brings the Son to our memory. There is another reason: since the humiliation of Christ is the subject here, it is fitting to insert words that still declare his dignity. Hence, when his afflictions are being spoken of, it is aptly added, to show that his dignity is not diminished by them, that he is the one for whom all things are and by whom all things are.

units.la: Atq; ita etiam clarius fit, quomodo per gratiā Dei factum est, quòd sic ita humiliatus, qui tantae semper est dignitatis. Tertiò, conuenit Christo tribuere illa verba, ne ex eo, cp hic subijcitur, eum perfectum reddendum, intelligatur Christo noua dignitas conferenda, quam antea non habuisset. Ne ergo tale quiddam aliquis de Christo conciperet animo, quòd videlicet hactenus non fuisset perfectus, sed nunc primùm perfectus redderetur: rectè inseritur de Christo, quòd propter eum, & per eum sunt omnia. Nam secundū diuinam naturam habuit summam gloriam apud patrem etiam antequam mundus fieret, (sic enim ait Ioan. 17. Et nunc glorifica me tu pater apud temetipsum gloria, quā habui priusquam hic mundus esset apud te) sed secundum humanitatem verum quidem est auctā illius gloriam, nempe per humanam naturam, quam assumpserat, exaltatam, quae facta est voluntate patris, vt nos quoq; in eadem natura exaltaremur.
units.tr: And so it also becomes clearer how, by the grace of God, he who is always of such great dignity was humbled in this way. Thirdly, those words must be attributed to Christ with care, lest from what is added here, that he was made perfect, someone should understand that a new dignity was being conferred on Christ, one he had not possessed before. So that no one should form such a notion about Christ, namely that he had not been perfect until then and was only now first made perfect, it is rightly inserted that all things are for him and through him. For according to his divine nature he had the highest glory with the Father even before the world was made (for he says in John 17, "And now, Father, glorify me with your own self, with the glory which I had with you before the world was"). But according to his humanity it is true that his glory was increased, namely through the human nature he had assumed, which was exalted by the will of the Father, so that we too might be exalted in that same nature.

units.la: Propter has igitur causas, de Christo particulas illas, propter quem & per quem omnia, putamus hoc loco explicandas. Sunt autem omnia verba valde appositā & conuenientia instituto. Primùm ait, Decebat eum: Non dubium, quin Deus, quandoquidem omnipotes est, potuisset alia ratione saluti humani generis prospicere (quid enim non potuisset efficere in redimendo, qui solo uerbo effecit omnia in creando?) Sed alius modus conuenientior haud potuisset inueniri, quàm vt humana natura per hominem restauraretur: & qui mortem peccando promeriti erant, per mortem alicuius redimerentur: & cùm agen da causa esset inter Deum & homines, nec sufficeret mors puri hominis, conueniebat eum, qui satisfaceret & pacaret, utriusq; naturæ, diuinæ inquam & humanæ esse partici peni, ac talis personae mortem aptam constituere: qua de re Augustinus de Trinitate li-bro 13. cap. 10. copiosius agit, & nos in sequentibus easdem rationes explicabimus. Propterhanc igitur causam appositissimè dictum est, Decebat.
units.tr: For these reasons, then, we think those words, "for whom and through whom are all things," should be explained in this place. All the words are very apt and suited to the purpose. First he says, "It became him." There is no doubt that God, since he is omnipotent, could have provided for the salvation of the human race by some other means (for what could he not have done in redeeming, he who by his word alone made all things in creating?). But no more fitting method could have been found than that human nature should be restored through a man; and since those who had merited death by sinning had to be redeemed by the death of someone, and since there had to be a settlement between God and men, and the death of a mere man would not suffice, it was fitting that one who would make satisfaction and reconcile should be a partaker of both natures, divine and human, and that the death of such a person should be made fitting. Augustine treats this matter more fully in On the Trinity, book 13, chapter 10, and in what follows we will explain the same reasons. For this cause, therefore, the word "it became" is most aptly used.

units.la: Propter quem sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia) Valde apta & haec ad significandam Christi diuinitatem. Nam solus Deus potest intelligi, quòd omnia condiderit, quòd omnia ser uet, quòd omnia ad se tanquā sua, suo iure pertrahat: quomodo cap. 1. probatus est deus, exeo, quòd pater per ipsum condidisset & secula. Et quando hoc pacto ei, qui describitur hic per afflictiones perficiendus, tribuitur, quòd propter eum, & per eum, sint omnia, clarum fit, diuinitatē semper humanitati fuisse adiunctam, neq; Christū propter humani tatem in tempore susceptā, aliquid amisisse diuinę suae potestatis, quā habuerat ab æterno.
units.tr: "For whom are all things, and through whom are all things." These words are also very apt for signifying the divinity of Christ. For only God can be understood to have created all things, to sustain all things, and to draw all things to himself as his own by his own right. As was shown in chapter 1, God is proved to have made the ages through him, because the Father made the worlds through him. And when, in this way, it is ascribed to him who is described here as being made perfect through afflictions, that all things are for him and through him, it becomes clear that divinity was always joined to humanity, and that Christ did not, because of the humanity taken up in time, lose anything of his divine power, which he had from eternity.

units.la: Vt multis filijs in gloriam adductis:) Ecce quomodo rursus humiliationem Christi tempora-neam ab iniuria & contemptu asserit, à causa finali, siue ab effectu eius humiliationis, quasi diceret: Quid? putatis vos obscurari dignitatem Christi, ex eo, quòd sit ad mortem humiliatus? Imò verò hęc humiliatio potius ad gloriam ipsi debet cedere. Ideò enim sic ad tempus inglorius factus est & humiliatus, vt alios ad gloriā æternam perduceret. Vo-cat autem eos, qui ad gloriam adducendi sunt, filios nimirum Dei, vt ea appella-tione ostendat amplissimam Dei erga homines beneuolentiam & bonitatem, qua ipse uehit. dignatus est eos, qui hostes erat, non modò recipere in gratiã, ut amicos: sed, quod maius est, recipere pro filijs, & affectum paternũ erga eos in omnibus ostendere, & iá quasi hæredes cœlestis regni constituere. Quomodo autem alij efficiantur filij Dei, siue qui propriè filij Dei sint appellandi, habemus Ioa.1. Quotquot receperunt eũ, dedit eis, ut liceret filios Dei fieri, videlicet his, qui crediderunt in nomine ipsius. Et quomodo generentur Deo hi filij ad huc explicatur Ioan.3. Vbi Christus ait ad Nicodemum, Amen, amen dico tibi, nisi quis natus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Quomodo uerò agnoscantur hi filij, & quomodo discernantur ab vnigenito filio Christo, quanta item bona ipsis sint expectanda, clarius Rom.8. Quòd si spiritu facta corporis mortificetis, viuetis. Etenim quicunq; spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filij Dei. Non enim accepistis spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba pater: Idem spiritus testatur vnà cum spiritu nostro, quòd sumus filij Dei. Quòd si filii, igitur & hæredes: hæredes quidem Dei, cohęredes autem Christi. Satis perspicua sunt hęc uerba, & clarissimè ex his intelligi potest, quales filij ad gloriam adducantur per unigenitum illum filium Iesum Christum. Quare dicit multos? Quia illustratur & hac uoce gloria & dignitas Christi, quòd non paucos quosdam, quasi personarum acceptor, aut quasi non potes plures seruare, ad salutem adduxerit, sed multos. Tum etiam, quia non omnes. Nam omnibus quidem propositum est uerbum & salus, sed non omnes apprehenderunt: iuxta parabolam Matt.22.Luc.14. de homine qui fecerat cœnam magnam, & vocauit multos. Sed ex multis vocatis pauci erant electi. Huc item pertinet illud Matth.8. Dico uobis, non inue ni tantam fidem in Israel. Dico autem vobis, quòd multi uenient ab Oriente & Occidente, & accumbent cum Abraham, Isaac, & Iacob in regno cœlorum, filij autem regni eijcienturin tenebras exteriores. Et ad finem usq; mundi restant adhuc multi adducendi.
units.tr: "In bringing many sons to glory." Here again he asserts that the temporal humiliation of Christ is free from insult and contempt, by its final cause, or by the effect of that humiliation, as if he were saying: "What? Do you think the dignity of Christ is obscured because he was humbled to death? Rather, this humiliation ought to add to his glory. For he was made thus inglorious and humbled for a time so that he might lead others to eternal glory." He calls those who are to be brought to glory sons of God, so that by this title he may show the very great benevolence and goodness of God toward men, by which he has deigned to receive those who were enemies not only into grace, as friends, but, what is greater, to receive them as sons, to show a fatherly affection toward them in all things, and already to appoint them as heirs of the heavenly kingdom. Now how others become sons of God, or who are properly to be called sons of God, we have in John 1: "As many as received him, to them he gave the power to become the sons of God," namely to those who believed in his name. And how these sons are begotten to God is further explained in John 3, where Christ says to Nicodemus, "Verily, verily, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." But how these sons are recognised, and how they are distinguished from the only-begotten Son Christ, and likewise what good things are to be expected for them, is made clearer in Romans 8: "If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you will live. For whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit bears witness together with our spirit that we are the sons of God. But if sons, then also heirs: heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ." These words are quite plain, and from them it can be understood most clearly what sort of sons are brought to glory through that only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ. Why does he say "many"? Because the glory and dignity of Christ is also illustrated by this word: that he did not bring to salvation a few, as though he were a respecter of persons, or as though he could not save more, but many. Also, because not all. For the word and salvation are offered to all, but not all have laid hold of them, in accordance with the parable in Matthew 22 and Luke 14 of the man who made a great supper and called many. But out of the many called, few were chosen. To this also belongs that saying in Matthew 8: "I tell you, I have not found so great faith in Israel. But I tell you that many will come from east and west and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the sons of the kingdom will be cast into outer darkness." And until the end of the world many still remain to be brought in.

units.la: Gloriam posuit pro vita æterna, & pro omni fœlicitate ac beatitudine, quę post hanc vitam propter Christum succedet: quomodo iterum Rom.8. Non reputo esse pares afflictiones præsentis temporis ad gloriam, quæ reuelabitur erga nos. Et 2. Cor.4. Nam momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostræ mirè supra modum æternum pondus gloriæ parit nobis, dum non spectamus ea, quæ videntur, sed ea, quæ non videtur. Ephes.1. vt sciatis, quæ spes, ad quam ille vocauit, & quàm opulenta gloria hæreditatis illius in Sanctis. In summa, gloria filiorum fere idem sonat, quod Christi perfectio & consummatio, de qua hic quoq; agitur, quæ alibi in Scripturis glorificatio, & gloria appellatur. Sed elegantèr etiam hæc gloria filiorum opponitur afflictionibus Christi, ut ita indignitas hominum & summa beneficetia Dei clarius consideretur. Quà enim admirandæ bonitatis est, filium Dei extremè affligi, atq; abijci, ut tu exalteris: nec minus aptè vsurpauit voce adducendi: græcè habetur, ἀγάγετε, a verbo ἄγω, quod significat ducere. Quod rectè dicitur de credentibus. Nam credere non est nisi volentium, adeò ut Deus, qui credentes trahit: iuxta illud Galat.5. εἰ δὲ πνεύματι ἄγεσθε, si spiritu ducimini, non estis sub lege. Quanquam Ioan.6. pij etiam trahi dicitur. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Sed trahi interpretantur quidam nondum credentes, eos verò, quiiam credunt, duci. Certè, cùm uia ad salutem nobis sit ignota: cùm deinde omnes tanquam cæci simus, in ijs, quæ ad salutem pertinent: neq; nostris viribus possumus eò prorepere vel contendere: oportet nos & duci, &, si segniores simus, etiam trahi, iuxta illud Matt. vigesimo secundo, compelle intrare: quomodò Paulus, quomodo multi gentiles tracti & compulsi sunt.
units.tr: He put "glory" for eternal life, and for all the happiness and blessedness which follows after this life because of Christ, as again in Romans 8: "I reckon that the afflictions of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." And in 2 Corinthians 4: "For our momentary light affliction produces for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things which are seen but at the things which are not seen." Ephesians 1: "that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, and how rich is the glory of his inheritance in the saints." In sum, "the glory of the sons" means almost the same as the perfection and consummation of Christ, which is also here the subject, and which elsewhere in Scripture is called glorification and glory. But the glory of the sons is also elegantly set over against the afflictions of Christ, so that both the unworthiness of men and the supreme beneficence of God may be considered more clearly. For how wonderful the goodness that the Son of God should be utterly afflicted and cast off so that you might be exalted! No less aptly does he use the word "to bring": in Greek it is [ἀγάγετε], from the verb [ἄγω], which means to lead. This is rightly said of believers. For believing is only of those who are willing, so much so that God, who draws believers, [is said to lead them] according to that saying in Galatians 5: [εἰ δὲ πνεύματι ἄγεσθε], "if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law." Although in John 6 even the godly are said to be drawn: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." But some interpret "draw" as referring to those not yet believing, and "lead" to those who already believe. Certainly, since the way to salvation is unknown to us, and since then we are all blind in the things that pertain to salvation, and cannot by our own strength creep or strive toward it, it is necessary for us to be led, and, if we are rather slothful, even to be drawn, according to that word in Matthew 22: "compel them to come in," as Paul was drawn and compelled, and as many Gentiles were.

units.la: Principem salutis illorum: ἀρχηγὸν, principem, regem, imperatorem, ducem significat, quare mirificè exornatur hoc titulo Christus, & humiliatio laudi vertitur: qui etiam Iesus appellatus est, id est, seruator, quia, ut angelus dixerat, ipse saluauit populum suum à peccatis eorum. Ipse vnus est salutis princeps & autor, dux noster ad salutem, & imperator, sine quo nihil possumus consequi, sine ipso nihil possumus facere in his, quæ salutis nostræ sunt. Et propter hanc particulam valde coueniebat, verba illa, propter quē, & per quem sunt omnia, de Christo exponere. Nam tacitè in illis ratio redditur, cur hic titulus Christo tribui posisit aut debeat. Si quis enim roget, quomodo Christus sic humilatus posiit esse autor salutis omnium? Si illi proponatur ob oculos, quòd Christus sit, propter quem, & per quem omnia, id est, verus natura Deus, tum facilè assentit, Christum esse salutis autorem.
units.tr: "The prince of their salvation" [ἀρχηγὸν] means prince, leader, commander, or captain. Christ is thereby splendidly adorned with this title, and his humiliation turns to praise. He is also called Jesus, that is, Saviour, because, as the angel had said, he saves his people from their sins. He alone is the prince and author of salvation, our leader to salvation and our commander, and without him we can achieve nothing; without him we can do nothing in the matters that concern our salvation. Because of this phrase it was very fitting to explain the words "for whom and through whom are all things" as referring to Christ. For in them the reason is tacitly given why this title can and ought to be ascribed to Christ. If someone asks how Christ, so humbled, could be the author of salvation for all, the answer is clear once it is set before his eyes that Christ is "the one for whom and through whom all things are," that is, true God by nature. Then he will readily agree that Christ is the author of salvation.

units.la: Per afflictiones: διὰ παθημάτων: Intelligit tum miserias humanæ conditionis, quas omnes, dempto peccato, Christus in se recepit: sed præcipuè cruciatum mortis, de quo prius dixit.
units.tr: "Through afflictions" [διὰ παθημάτων]: he means both the miseries of the human condition, which Christ took upon himself (apart from sin), and especially the torment of death, of which he spoke earlier.

units.la: Perfectum reddere) τελειῶσαι; aliqui verterunt consummare, nonnulli, sanctificare seu confirmare. fecrare: propterea quòd sequitur de sanctificandis & sanctificante. Sed quia alijs verbis utitur Apostolus in sequentibus, nihil opus est hac interpretatione, praesertim quando hic significatur per perfectionem Christi, non potestas sanctificandi, ante mortem seu in morte conferenda, sed summa dignitas, gloria, potestas omnium conferenda à morte seu post humiliationem, qualis dignitas Ephes.1. Philippens. 2. describitur. Hac enim gloria accepta Christus perfectus redditur, quando videlicet humanitas ipsius etiá glorificata est, & perinde secundum humanitatem ac diuinitate gloriosius factus est, ad dextera Dei patris in coelo sedens. De qua accesiua dignitate ob glorificatâ humanitatem, aliàs sermone fecimus. Atq; hanc gloriâ seu perfectione decebat Christo addi per patrē. Caeterum habemus in his paucis verbis multiplicem instructionem. Primò, quòd oportet eos, qui ad salutem peruenient, esse filios Dei: & cùm filij Dei efficiantur credendo in Christū, sicut Ioan.1. & 3. exponitur, decet omnes fidem in Christum suscipere, utpote quae sola ex parte nostra ad salutem sit efficax. Inde commendare debemus nos Deo, & orare, ut ille dignetur pectora nostra mouere, trahere, ducere, regere, gubernare, ne vnquam à fide excidamus. Nisi enim ille nos ducat in viam salutis, & gubernet, fieri non potest, quin aberremus ac tandem pereamus.
units.tr: "To make perfect" [τελειῶσαι]: some have rendered it "to consummate," others "to sanctify or confirm." Some say "to consecrate," because what follows speaks of those who are sanctified and of the one who sanctifies. But since the Apostle uses other words in what follows, there is no need for this interpretation, especially since the perfection of Christ here signifies not the power of sanctifying, to be conferred before or in death, but the highest dignity, glory, and power of all, conferred by God after death and humiliation, the kind of dignity described in Ephesians 1 and Philippians 2. For by receiving this glory Christ is made perfect, namely when his humanity is also glorified, and so he is made more glorious according to his humanity as well as his divinity, sitting in heaven at the right hand of God the Father. We have spoken elsewhere about this added dignity arising from the glorified humanity. And it was fitting that this glory or perfection should be added to Christ by the Father. Moreover, in these few words we have a manifold instruction. First, those who come to salvation must be sons of God; and since they become sons of God by believing in Christ, as is explained in John 1 and 3, all should take up faith in Christ, since faith alone is effective for salvation on our part. Hence we ought to commend ourselves to God and pray that he would deign to move, draw, lead, rule, and govern our hearts, so that we never fall away from faith. For unless he leads us into the way of salvation and governs us, it cannot be that we do not go astray and at last perish.

units.la: Secundò, quando vocatur Christus princeps salutis, liquet, per solum Christum salu- tem contingere, ut nequaquam possimus alios mediatores vel seruatores constituere, multò minus nostris viribus, meritis, vel bonis operibus ascribere. Non est aliud nomē sub coelo datum inter homines, in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri, Actor. 4.
units.tr: Second, when Christ is called the prince of salvation, it is clear that salvation comes through Christ alone, so that we can by no means set up other mediators or saviours, much less ascribe salvation to our own strength, merits, or good works. "There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4).

units.la: Tertiò, cùm dicitur, Christum propter afflictionem perfectum redditū, discimus hinc ad consolationem in omnibus aduersitatibus, quòd afflictiones sunt velut media ad gloriam. Quò pertinet illud Act.14. Cofirmabant apostoli animas discipulorū, exhortates, ut perseuerarent in fide, & quòd per multas afflictiones oportet intrare in regnū Dei. Quoniam ergo per illas afflictiones venitur ad gloriam, & perfectio acquiritur, sicut in Christo exemplum perfectionis post humiliationem nobis est propositū, ferenda sunt momentanea in commodia, pro percipiendis commodis aeternis.
units.tr: Third, when it is said that Christ was made perfect through affliction, we learn from this, for consolation in all adversities, that afflictions are as it were means to glory. To this pertains Acts 14: "The apostles confirmed the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God." Since, then, glory is reached through those afflictions, and perfection is acquired, and since in Christ the example of perfection after humiliation has been set before us, we must bear momentary inconveniences in order to obtain eternal benefits.

units.la: Porrò, quia obiter fecimus mentionem eius quaestionis, quae agitare solet, vtrū uideli- cet in morte Christi diuinitas separata ab humanitate, visum est nonnulla attingere. Alii qui ex uerbis Chrysostomi colligere uolunt, quòd fuerit separata, propterea quòd Chry- sostomus, ut supra indicauimus, in illo uerbo, paulisper diminutus ab angelis, ait, Christum ad breue tempus, nempe triduum, quo in inferno fuit, infra angelos constitutū, col liguntq; id non ob aliud, quàm quòd diuinitas ad id tempus fuerit separata.
units.tr: Furthermore, since in passing we have mentioned the question that is commonly debated, namely whether in the death of Christ his divinity was separated from his humanity, it seemed good to touch on some points.
