Some who wish to gather from the words of Chrysostom that it was separated, because Chrysostom, as we noted above, on the words "a little lower than the angels," says that Christ was placed below the angels for a short time, namely three days, during which he was in hell, gather this for no other reason than that his divinity was separated for that time.

units.la: Pręterea Theophylactus in illud, ut gratia Dei pro omni gustaret mortem. Nestoriani, inquit, Scripturam hanc Pauli depraυantes, non gratia dicunt, sed sine Deo, id est, sine diuinitate, pro omnibus mortem gustaret, ut, quod ipsi pessimè sentiunt, Christo scilicet cruci affixo diuinitatem astruant, non adfuisse, utpote quae non substantialiter illi inesset, sed effectione quadam vnita.
units.tr: Moreover, Theophylact, on the words "that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone," says: the Nestorians, corrupting this text of Paul, do not say "by grace" but "without God," that is, without divinity, that he tasted death for all; so that, what they themselves hold most wickedly, they may assert that divinity was not present when Christ was fixed to the cross, as though it did not dwell in him substantially but was united to him by some kind of effect.

units.la: Nazianzenus in epistola quadam ad Nectarium episcopum Constantinopolitanum, inter alia Apollinarij haeretici falsa dogmata, hoc quoq; addit. Sed & hoc omnium grauissimū, inquit, quòd ipsum unigenitū Deū, iudice omniū, autore uitę, mortis destructo rem, mortalem esse facit, ac propria eius diuinitate pasionem suscepisse, & in triduana illa mortificatione corporis diuinitatem quoq; vnà cum corpore occubuisse.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, in a certain letter to Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, among other false dogmas of the heretic Apollinaris, also adds this: "But this too is the gravest of all, that he makes the only-begotten God, the judge of all, the author of life and the destroyer of death, mortal, and that by his own divinity he underwent suffering, and that in that three-day death of the body the divinity also lay down together with the body."

units.la: Iterum Theophylactus 2.cap.ad Colos.super illo uerbo, in ipso inhabitat plenitudo diuinitatis, dicit, quòd Christo in sepulchro posito diuinitas nò aberat, neq; similiter aberat, quando Christus descenditad inferos, &c.
units.tr: Again, Theophylact, on Colossians 2, on the words "in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead," says that when Christ was placed in the sepulchre his divinity was not absent, nor likewise was it absent when Christ descended into the underworld, and so on.

units.la: Quandoquidem & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificatur, ex uno sunt omnes. ) Prima ratio, quare decuerit Christum hominem fieri, sumpta à conditione eorum, qui erant à morte aeterna liberandi, siue, ut ipse splendidius elegantiusq; exprimit, sanctificandi: quā sic crasius li cet reddere. Conuenit, eum, qui sanctificat, eiusdem conditionis esse, cuius sunt sanctifi- candi. Sed sanctificandi sunt homines: ergo eū, qui hos sanctificaturus erat, decebat ho- minē fieri. Scio plerosq; interpretes haec uerba accipere, quasi probatione contineret, q; Christus uere pati & affligi potuerit, ut postea perduceretur ad gloriā: quando quide ex eodem videlicet primo parente Adamo humanā natura (quae per se aerumnis, afflictioni bus, & morti est obnoxia) contraxit siue accepit, ex quo nos. Aliqui fortasis diceret, hic significari, quemadmodū Christus primū afflictus est, deinde perfectus redditus: ita nos quoq; debere eodē modo primū affligi, deinde perfectos reddi: idq; eò magis, q, & nos & Christus ex uno sumus. Sed huiusmodi interpretatio non videtur satis explicare Apo- stoli sententiam. Nam quòd Christus esset homo, & quidem pasibilis, nec non afflictio- hibus expositus, nemo probari poscebat, erat id abunde notum : imò aduersarij obijcie- bant;
units.tr: "For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one." The first reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man is taken from the condition of those who were to be freed from eternal death, or, as he expresses it more elegantly and fittingly, those to be sanctified; this can be put more crudely as follows: it is fitting that the one who sanctifies be of the same condition as those who are to be sanctified. But men are to be sanctified; therefore the one who was going to sanctify them had to become a man. I know that most interpreters take these words as if they contained a proof that Christ could truly suffer and be afflicted, so that afterwards he might be brought to glory, since he had received, or contracted, human nature (which in itself is liable to troubles, afflictions, and death) from the same first parent, Adam, from whom we come. Perhaps someone would say that what is meant is that just as Christ was first afflicted and then made perfect, so we too ought in the same way first be afflicted and then made perfect, all the more so because we and Christ are of one. But this interpretation does not seem to explain the Apostle's meaning adequately. For that Christ was a man, and indeed subject to suffering and exposed to afflictions, no one needed proof; it was abundantly well known. Indeed, opponents objected

units.la: 1 3 bant, velut probri loco, afflictiones & morte Christi, ad extenuandu & evertendu omnia quæ de ipsius diuinitate pferebantur. Deinde testimonia, quæ proximè sequuntur, ad horum verborum confirmationem, nō eò potissimū sunt adducta, ut demonstrent, Christū fuisse pasibilem seu mortalem: sed potius ad declarandum, quòd Christū decuerit propter homines hominem fieri, quodq; diuina prouidentia, longè ante, quâ Christus nasceretur, ita ordinasset. Proinde nos oculum intendentes, & ad ea, quæ sequuntur, & quæ præcedunt, item ad principalem causam totius disputationis, interpretamur, his verbis simpliciter rationem reddi, quare Christum hominem fieri decuerit. Liberum vnicuique esse debet, quod uelit sentire: ac proinde arbitror, nos quoq; non offensuros, si quod maxime putamus ad mentem Apostoli explicandam pertinere, ingenuè proferimus.
units.tr: (the Apostle's point being that) the afflictions and death of Christ were objected as a reproach, in order to diminish and overturn everything that was said of his divinity. Next, the testimonies that closely follow are adduced in confirmation of these words not chiefly to demonstrate that Christ was capable of suffering or mortal, but rather to declare that it was fitting for Christ to become man for the sake of men, and that divine providence had so ordained it long before Christ was born. Accordingly, keeping our eyes both on what follows and what precedes, and on the principal cause of the whole discussion, we interpret that these words simply give the reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man. Each person must be free to hold whatever view he wishes; and so I think we shall not give offence if we openly set forth what we most believe pertains to explaining the Apostle's mind.

units.la: Cæterum valde concisè loquitur Apostolus, ut & superius in omnibus egit argumentis, & tota hac disputatione: quæ res in causa est, cur diligentius oporteat veram sententiam venari, & quam eruerimus, illustrius explicare. Excutiedum vero nobis est aliquanto diligentius, quid sit sanctificare & sanctificari, siue ἁγιάζειν: nam hoc loco habetur duo participia ἁγιάζων, ἁγιαζόμενος. Sanctificandi verbum diuersis modis accipitur. Sæpe de diuersis rebus uel inanimatis, vel ratione carentibus dicitur, quòd sanctificetur Domino, vel quòd sanctificentur simpliciter. Porrò sanctificari eas Domino nihil aliud est, quàm ad vsus sacros accommodari, Deo offerri, & consecrari: quo pacto hostiæ in veteri testamento, imò & omnia vasa seu instrumenta, quorum vsus erat in loco sacro, dicebantur sancta esse & sanctificata Domino, quia ad vsus sacros electa & accommodata, neq; in alios vsus transferenda erant. Hoc verò pacto etiam homines postea cœperunt dici sanctificati, qui videlicet diuino cultui erant destinati, & in eo occupati, & ad certum tempus ab omni genere negotiorum externorum, quæ pro prophanis habebantur, alieni: sic primogenitos suos homines Deo ac diuino cultui debebant nuncupare, & quasi ad rerum diuinarum tractationem destinare. Hoc item pacto sacerdotes ipsi (adhibitis ceremonijs, quæ internum & spirituale quiddam adumbrarent, & exterius quoque factum testatum facerent) sanctificabantur, & Domino consecrabantur. Sed in omnibus his sanctificatio fiebat per homines, quare nihil magni ea sanctificatio nobis repræsentat. Nam licet non fuerit contemnenda, utpote à Deo instituta & præcepta, & Deus etiam suum verbum interposuerit, quomodo Deus 2. Paral. 7. dicitur sanctificasse templum, vt esset ibi nomé ipsius: tamen parui momenti esse iudicatur, quando duntaxat in rebus externis sita est, & significans seu adumbrans potius aliquid spirituale, quàm illud in se continens. At verò quibus locis proprie homo dicitur sanctificari, & ipsum sanctificandi munus tribuitur soli Deo: sanè oportet altius quiddam per sanctificationem intelligere. In huiusmodi ergo locis, & maximè qui occurrunt in nouo testamento, sanctificari significat purgari, mundari, intus in spiritu, in conscientia, hoc est, immunem à peccato & omni immunditie spirituali reddi, Deo gratu effici, ex iniusto iustu fieri, nouis ornari donis ac beneficijs, ut noua vita, noui fructus spirituales, deniq; post hanc vitâ æterna gloria succedat, & cū Deo noua cōiunctio atq; æterna. Et planè idé sibi uult uerbū sanctificandi, q; iustificādi, beatificādi, Rō. 4. & alijs locis. Sic Christus Ioan. 17. petit sanctificari suos discipulos: sanctifica eos per veritatē tuā: sermo tuus veritas est. Et quasi explicās, quid per sanctificationē intelligi velit, addit: ut ipsi in nobis unū sint; ut credat mundus, quòd tu me misisti, & ego gloriā, quā dedisti mihi, dedi eis, ut sint unū, sicut & nos unū sumus, ego in eis, & tu in me, ut sint cōsummati in unū, & ut cognoscat mundus, quòd tu me misisti, & dilexisti eos, sicut & me dilexisti. Pater, quos dedisti mihi, uolo ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum, ut uideant gloriā meā, quā dedisti mihi. Clarius est, q. habetur Ephes. 5. Christus exposuit semetipsum pro ecclesia, ut illā sanctificaret, mundatā lauacro aquæ per uerbū, ut exhiberet eā sibi ipsi gloriosam, ecclesiam non habentē maculā aut rugā, aut quicquā eiusmodi, sed ut esset sancta & irreprehensibilis. En hic clarissimè & modus & effectus sanctificationis describitur. Iterum 1. Thessal. 5. Ipse autem Deus pacis sanctificet vos totos. Et integer vester spiritus, & anima, & corpus, ita ut in nullo posnitis culpari, in aduentu Domini nostri Iesu Christi seruetur. 1. Cor. 1. Christus factus est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemptio, vt, quemadmodū scriptū est, qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Iterū 1. Cor. 6. Postquam dixisset, adulteros, scortatores, &c. non accepturos regni Dei hæreditatē, subiecit: Atq; hæc eratis quidam, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis, per nomen Domini Iesu, & per spiritum Dei nostri. Sed non opus est pluribus testimonijs. Satis ex his constare debet, quid per vocē sanctificandi hoc loco intelligi coueniat, & q. lōgè maximæ res spirituales & æternæ per sanctificationē notentur: & tale sanctificationē in veteri testamento nequaq; expressam. Potest quidē Apostolus uoce sanctificādi alludere ad ritū & morē sanctificandi veteris testamenti: sed re sine dubio longè excellentiore intelligit, nēpe idipsum, q. priores illæ sanctificationes tantum adumbrabant & præfigurabant.
units.tr: The Apostle speaks very concisely here, as he has done throughout the earlier arguments and in this whole discussion. That is the reason we must seek the true meaning more carefully and then explain what we have found more clearly. We must examine somewhat more closely what it is to sanctify and to be sanctified [ἁγιάζειν], for this passage contains the two participles [ἁγιάζων] and [ἁγιαζόμενος]. The verb to sanctify is used in different ways. Often it is applied to various things, whether inanimate or without reason, to say that they are sanctified to the Lord, or simply that they are sanctified. Now to be sanctified to the Lord means nothing other than to be set apart for sacred uses, offered to God and consecrated. In this way the sacrifices under the Old Testament, and indeed all the vessels and instruments that were used in the holy place, were called holy and sanctified to the Lord, because they were chosen and set apart for sacred uses and were not to be transferred to other uses. In this same sense people too came later to be called sanctified, namely those who were destined for divine worship, occupied with it, and for a set time kept free from every kind of external business that was regarded as profane. So they were to dedicate their firstborn sons to God and to divine worship, and as it were appoint them to handle holy things. In the same way the priests themselves were sanctified and consecrated to the Lord, with ceremonies added that foreshadowed something inward and spiritual and also showed by an outward act what was being done. But in all these cases the sanctification was carried out through men, and so this sanctification represents nothing great to us. For although it is not to be despised, since it was instituted and commanded by God, and since God also added his own word (as God is said in 2 Chronicles 7 to have sanctified the temple, so that his name might be there), nevertheless it is judged to be of little moment, since it lies only in external things and signifies or rather foreshadows something spiritual rather than containing it. But in those passages where a man is properly said to be sanctified, and the office of sanctifying is ascribed to God alone, we must surely understand something deeper by sanctification. In passages of this kind, and especially those that occur in the New Testament, to be sanctified means to be cleansed and purified inwardly, in spirit and in conscience; that is, to be made free from sin and from every spiritual uncleanness, to be made acceptable to God, to be made righteous out of unrighteous, to be adorned with new gifts and benefits, so that there follow a new life and new spiritual fruits, and finally, after this life, eternal glory and a new and eternal union with God. And plainly the word to sanctify has the same meaning as to justify, to make blessed, as in Romans 4 and other places. So Christ in John 17 asks that his disciples be sanctified: "Sanctify them through your truth; your word is truth." And as if explaining what he wishes to be understood by sanctification, he adds: "That they may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me, and I have given them the glory that you gave me, that they may be one, just as we are one, I in them and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, and that the world may know that you sent me and have loved them, just as you have loved me. Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory, which you have given me." What is found in Ephesians 5 is clearer still: Christ gave himself up for the church, that he might sanctify it, cleansing it by the washing of water through the word, that he might present it to himself as a glorious church, having no spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but that it might be holy and blameless. Here, very clearly, both the manner and the effect of sanctification are described. Again, in 1 Thessalonians 5: "May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly; and may your whole spirit, soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." In 1 Corinthians 1: "Christ has been made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, he who glories may glory in the Lord." Again in 1 Corinthians 6, after he had said that adulterers, fornicators, and so on, will not inherit the kingdom of God, he adds: "And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God." But more testimonies are not needed. From these it should be sufficiently clear what is rightly to be understood here by the word sanctify, and how far the greatest spiritual and eternal realities are signified by sanctification; and that such sanctification was by no means expressed in the Old Testament. The Apostle may indeed allude by the word sanctify to the rite and custom of sanctifying in the Old Testament, but he undoubtedly means by it a thing far more excellent, namely the very thing that those earlier sanctifications only shadowed and prefigured.

units.la: Singulari igitur prudentia & consilio Apostolus hac voce vsus est, ad significandum res maximas eam delegit. Ac vide, quomodo Apostolus gaudet diuersis modis exprimere causas suscepte à Christo humanæ naturæ. Paulò ante dixerat, Christum humiliatum, vt pergratiam Dei pro omni morte gustaret: proximè dixit, vt multos adduceret in gloriam. Nunc verò quasi per incrementum ait, ut omnes sanctificarent: Quæ tria inuicem sibi in hac causa agnata sunt, sed singula valde illustria & apposita. Et tantum de vocis significatione. Sed & singulari consilio factum, quòd Apostolus ita locutus sit, & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur: potuisset dicere: decebat Christum, vt homines sanctificaret, hominem fieri: sed maluit quasi antithesi quadam illustrius rem efferre, quasi diceret: Decebat eum, qui sanctifi caret, homine fieri, sicut homines erat qui sanctificari egebât. Tacitè videt suggerere quâdam collatione Christi, & personarum sanctificandarum, vt ita beneficij Christi amplitudo magis illucesceret, et mysterium incarnationis accuratius expederet. Age, breuiter collatio nè faciamus. Homines inprimis sunt, quoniam impuri sunt, peccatis vitiati, æternæ mortis rei, egent sanctificatione, reparatione, restauratione. Sed quo sanctificabutur? Proprijs meritis, vel nouis operib. bonis? Nō. Nam haud possùt hæc per se, vt talia sint apud Deum, præstare. Sed neq; vllis externis sacrificijs, hircorū, &c. Si per se suaq; bona opera homo non potest sanctificari, multò minus per sanguinem hircorum, per opera aliena, &c. Quæreda ergo est persona, quæ id faciat. Atqui quæ id posit, nō potest esse, nisi quæ primùm sancta sit: dein de, quæ potestate habeat etiā conferedi sanctitatem alijs: & tamè expediret eiusdē esse natu ræ, cuius suntipsi sanctificandi. Istud verò cùm de nullo homine dici aut mente concipi queat, opus est, ipsum Deum hanc partem ad se recipere. Nam sanctificandi potestas, soli Deo potest competere. Ergo vt humana natura illius sanctificationis foret capax & particeps, Christus habes potestate sanctificādi, homo fieri est dignatus, vt primùm in se, deinde in alijs humanam naturā sanctificaret. Ecce inquā quare Apostolus repetiuit idem verbum, & distinxit sanctificantem & sanctificandos. Christus est qui sanctificat: homines & nos miseri peccatores sumus sanctificandi. Egregia iam hic posset institui collatio, si te pus ferret. Hoc interim adhuc notandum est, quod Apostolus, vbi hic agit de humiliatione Christi, tamen semper interserit, quæ humiliatione Christi ab iniuria vindicent, atq; ei qualibet deiecto & afflicto, diuinitate afferant. Huiusmodi enim est verbū sanctificādi, quo plane diuina potētia Christo attribuitur. Oportet illum sanctū esse præ omnibus, & diuinam habere potestatem, qui alios sanctificabit. Atque ipse est reuera sanctificatio nostrasi, cut 1 Corinth. 1. clarè dicitur. Iam particula illa, Ex uno sunt omnes, à nonnullis exponi tur, quasi sententia esset, & eos, qui sanctificantur, & eum qui sanctificat ex vno esse, vi-delicet Deo, qui communis est & Christi, & omnium nostrum pater, licet nos alia ratione filij eius sumus quàm Christus: & tamè Deum patrem velle nos omnes ex æquo, exemplo Christi, post afflictiones perfectos reddet. Sed ex his, quæ prius diximus, satis appa-ret, ad præsentem disputationē non pertinere huiusmodi interpretationē. Quare rectius reddidimus, ex vno, videlicet, primo parēte humanæ naturæ propagatore, ex quo & Christus originē trahere voluit, sicut nos, vt sic per omnia (depto peccato) nobis similis fieret, &, vt sequitur, nos suos fratres eiusdē naturę participes appellaret. Simili modo Actor. 17. de Deo dicitur, dat omnibus vitam & halitum per omnia, fecitq; ex vno sanguine omne genus hominum, vt inhabitaret super vniuersam faciem terræ. Enibi Adam vnus sanguis siue homo vocatur. Et Rom. 5. Propterea, quèadmodum per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introijt, & per peccatum mors: & sic in omnes homines mors peruasit, quatenus omnes peccauimus. Ergo ex vno, scilicet homine, rectè intelligemus. Huc pertinet, quòd Lucas Christi generatione ad Adam vsq; deducit. Vbi clarè vides, Christum habuisse verum corpus, per omnia simile corporibus nostris, quod est cōtra Valetinianos, & nostri tempo-ris quosdam Anabaptistas, qui dicunt, Christū attulisse suum corpus è cœlo, nihilq; sumpsisse ex Maria Virgine: qua de re nos paulò post copiosius disseremus.
units.tr: By singular prudence and design the Apostle used this word and chose it to signify very great things. And see how the Apostle delights to express in various ways the causes for which Christ undertook human nature. A little before he had said that Christ was humbled so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all; shortly after he said that he might bring many into glory. Now, as if by way of increase, he says that he might sanctify all. These three things are bound together in this cause, but each is very striking and fitting. And so much for the meaning of the word. But it was also by a singular design that the Apostle spoke as he did, he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified. He could have said: it was fitting that Christ, who was to sanctify men, should become man. But he preferred, by a kind of antithesis, to set the matter forth more clearly, as if he were saying: it was fitting that he who sanctifies should become a man, just as those were men who needed to be sanctified. He tacitly suggests by a certain comparison between Christ and the persons to be sanctified, so that the greatness of Christ's benefit might shine forth more brightly and the mystery of the incarnation be more exactly unfolded. Come, let us make the comparison briefly. Men are first of all impure, since they are defiled by sins, liable to eternal death, and in need of sanctification, restoration and renewal. But by what means are they to be sanctified? By their own merits, or by new good works? No. For these by themselves cannot make them such as to be acceptable before God. Nor by any external sacrifices, of goats and so on. If a man cannot be sanctified through his own good works, much less through the blood of goats, or through the works of others, and so on. Therefore a person must be sought who can do this. But one who could do it cannot be anyone unless he is first holy; and further, he must have the power to confer holiness on others too; and it would be advantageous for him to be of the same nature as those who are to be sanctified. But since this cannot be said or conceived of any man, it is necessary that God himself take this part upon himself. For the power of sanctifying can belong to God alone. Therefore, so that human nature might be capable of and share in that sanctification, Christ, who had the power of sanctifying, condescended to become man, so that he might first sanctify human nature in himself and then in others. See, I say, why the Apostle repeated the same word and distinguished the one who sanctifies from those who are to be sanctified. Christ is the one who sanctifies; men, and we miserable sinners, are those who are to be sanctified. A fine comparison could now be set out here, if time allowed. Meanwhile this should still be noted, that the Apostle, when here he treats of the humiliation of Christ, nevertheless always adds things that vindicate Christ from disgrace and bring divinity to him, however lowly and afflicted he may be. For of this kind is the word to sanctify, by which divine power is plainly ascribed to Christ. He who is going to sanctify others must needs be holy above all and have divine power. And he himself is truly our sanctification, as is plainly said in 1 Corinthians 1. Now that phrase, All are from one, is explained by some as if the sense were that both those who are sanctified and he who sanctifies are from one, namely God, who is the common Father both of Christ and of all of us, although we are his sons in a different way from Christ; and that God the Father, after afflictions, will make us all equally perfect, as he did Christ. But from what we said before it is sufficiently clear that such an interpretation does not pertain to the present discussion. Therefore we have rendered it more correctly, from one, that is, from the first parent and propagator of human nature, from whom Christ also chose to derive his origin, just as we do, so that in all things (sin excepted) he might become like us, and, as follows, might call us his brothers, sharers in the same nature. In a similar way in Acts 17 it is said of God: "He gives to all life and breath and all things," and "he made from one blood every nation of men, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." There Adam is called one blood, or one man. And in Romans 5: "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death spread to all men, inasmuch as all have sinned." So we shall rightly understand from one, namely from the one man. To this belongs the fact that Luke traces Christ's genealogy back to Adam. Here you clearly see that Christ had a true body, in all things like our bodies; this is against the Valentinians and certain Anabaptists of our own time, who say that Christ brought his body from heaven and took nothing from the Virgin Mary; on this matter we shall speak more fully a little later.

units.la: Dicit verò, omnes, & nō vtriq;, quia plenius & illustrius exprimit conformitate naturæ, quasi diceret: Christū nobis omnibus per omnia simile, quatum ad naturā ex vno Adamo contractam, dempto peccato. Et quod ad voces attinet, omnes, &, uno, apte opponuntur.
units.tr: Moreover he says all, and not both, because this expresses the likeness of nature more fully and more clearly, as if he said: Christ is like us in all things, as far as nature drawn from the one Adam is concerned, apart from sin. And the words all and one are rightly set over against each other.

units.la: Porrò duplicē hic habemus doctrinā, nempe quòd solus Christus sit sanctificans, & omnis sanctitatis in nobis autor. Ipse est agnus immaculatus, tollens peccata mundi. Nec est, quod ab vllis aliis quamlibet sanctis & magnis expectemus nos sanctificādos. Quoniam non est sanctus, vt est Dominus.
units.tr: Here we have a twofold teaching: that Christ alone is the sanctifier, and the author of all holiness in us. He is the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. We must not expect to be sanctified by any other persons, however holy and great. For none is holy as the Lord is.

units.la: Deinde cp nos simus sanctificandi, idque non solùm quo tempore in crasis versamur peccatis, sed tùm etiā, cùm nos sanctos putamus. Nam nunquā ita sanctificamur in hoc mūdo agentes, quin adhæreat nobis nostræ carnis corruptio, seu ad malum procliuitas, quæ impedit, quò minus plenè sanctificemus, & subinde facit, vt à sanctificatione nostra
units.tr: Next, we are to be sanctified, and this not only at the time when we live in sins, but also when we think ourselves holy. For we are never so sanctified while living in this world that the corruption of our flesh, or the proneness to evil, does not cling to us. This hinders us from sanctifying ourselves fully, and from time to time causes us to fall away from our sanctification

units.la: ad tem ad tepus excidamus: quomodo Dauid licet vir secundū cor Dei, & electus, tamē aliquan do relictus sibi & desertus à Deo in grauissima peccata lapsus est. Et nunquā etiam siccō tingit nos sanctificari, quin incrementa & auctus sanctificationis posint adijci.
units.tr: for a time. So David, though a man after God's own heart and chosen, was yet at times left to himself and forsaken by God, and fell into most grievous sins. Nor are we ever so sanctified that increases and growth in sanctification cannot still be added.

units.la: Sed hic quæri potest: quare hic dicatur tantum homines sanctificandi, & non angeli, cùm tamen angeli lapsi perinde sanctificatione egeāt, atq; homines? Vide Primasium in illud verbum, Unde debuit per omnia similis fratribus reddi: Item, alios hac causam pertractantes.
units.tr: But here one may ask: why is it said only that men are to be sanctified, and not angels, since fallen angels need sanctification just as men do? See Primasius on the words Unde debuit per omnia similis fratribus reddi, and others who treat this question.

units.la: Quam ob causam non erubescit fratres illos vocare, dicens: Annunciabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in medio ecclesiæ laudabo te.
units.tr: For this cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren, saying: I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing thy praise.

units.la: Ne verò rationes, quibus declarare vult, Christū necessarijs de causis factū hominem, minus haberent ponderis, ac pro absurdis haberentur, (valde enim absurdum videtur, quòd, qui Deus sit, idè intelligatur miser homo) confirmat eas Scripturæ testimonijs, quæ palàm faciūt, quòd Christus humanam naturam induēret, atq; ita maximè humiliaretur, à Deo patre multis antè seculis fuisse prœordinatum & decretum, ac propterea neminem offendi debere, quòd audiret, Deum Christum filium hominem. Citat autē varia testimonia humanitatem exprimentia, (quemadmodum suprà quoq; varia testimonia adduxit, ad probandam Christi diuinitatem) è quibus primum est huiusmodi ex Psalmo vicesimo secundo. Propheta in persona Christi longè post venturi ita loquitur: Annunciabo nomē tuum fratribus meis: Vbi, cùm Christus homines vocat suos fratres, perspicuè significatū est, quòd homo deberet fieri, quod aliàs fratres recte eos appellare non posset. Iterū repe tendū est, non eò hæc dici, vt probetur, Christū fuisse hominē: nam de ea re satis cōstabat omnibus: sed vt probetur ita decuisse fieri, & sic à Deo patre fuisse constitutū. Videndum aūt, quā appositis verbis testimoniū istud primū suo aptet instituto. Quā ob causam, inquit, Διὰ ἡμ αἰτίαν: Referenda est hæc rationalis particula ad id, quod proximè dixit: Nos ex Christū ex uno primo parente Adamo esse omnes: quasi diceret: Et quia nos omnes ex vno parente su- mus, eandem habentes humanam naturam, hanc ob causam Christus non erubescit nos homines appellare suos fratres.
units.tr: Lest the reasons by which he wishes to show that Christ was made man for necessary causes should seem less weighty, and be thought absurd (for it seems very absurd that he who is God should be understood to be a wretched man), he confirms them by testimonies of Scripture, which plainly show that Christ put on human nature, and so was most humbled, and that this had been foreordained and decreed by God the Father many ages before. Therefore no one should be offended to hear that God is the Son of man. He cites various testimonies expressing the humanity, just as above he also adduced various testimonies to prove the divinity of Christ. The first of these is taken from Psalm twenty-two. The prophet, speaking long before the coming of Christ in the person of Christ, says: I will declare thy name unto my brethren. Here, since Christ calls men his brethren, it is clearly signified that he had to become man, for otherwise he could not rightly call them brethren. Again, it must be repeated that these things are not said in order to prove that Christ was a man, for that was sufficiently certain to all; but to prove that it was fitting for this to happen, and that it was so appointed by God the Father. We must consider with what apt words this first testimony fits his purpose. For this cause, he says, [Διὰ τοῦτο]: this rational particle is to be referred to what he said just before: that we are all from the one first parent, Adam. As if he said: since we all come from one parent, and have the same human nature, for this cause Christ is not ashamed to call us men his brethren.

units.la: Nō erubescit fratres illos appellare:) Valde elegater dixit, Nō erubescit. Nā ea voce simul indicat maximā Christi dignitatē, quia ille secundū diuinā naturam omnibus hominibus est præstatior, & simul admirabilē illius humilitatē & bonitatē, quā nō dedignatus est eos, q multis inueruallis in ipso sunt inferiores, quasi pares agnoscere. Videt sumpta hęc locutionis forma, à more illorum hominū, qui, cùm ab humili loco euecti fuerint ad augustiore dignitatē, suos veteres amicos & cōsanguineos nolūt amplius agnoscere, pudet illos suorū parentū, suorū amicorū omniū, putantq; indignos esse suos, quos ƥ suis deinceps agnoscat: quomodo etiā Prouerb. 19. dicit: Omnes fratres hominis pauperis odcrūt eū, insuper et amici recesserū procul ab eo. At verò Christus quis p se semp maior & potētior, quàm vt vllo modo aliquā creatura ad se admitteret, nō erubuit nos viles homines, & peccatores, æternę dānationis reos, nothos, & degeneres, appellare suos fratres. Itaq; valde illustrat hac voce Christi bonitas & humilitas. Similis ƥ pemodū forma locutionis occurrit Philippēsi: Qui cùm esset in forma Dei, nō rapinā arbitratus est, vt esset æqualis Deo, sed semetipsū inaniuit, forma serui sumpta, in similitudine hominū cōstitutus: Vbi sicut dicit, nō prapi nam, id est, nulla iniuria in Deū facta, sed optimo iure Christū esse Deū, sumpta loquendi forma ab his, qui mendacijs & furtim se amplis & illustribus familijs inferere volunt, de quibus integrū caput habetur apud Valerium Maximū lib. 9. cap. 16. Ita è diuerso hic dicit, Christū nō erubescere, se factū esse hominem, sumpta forma loquendi ab ijs, qui euecti ad honores, non amplius agnoscere volunt veteres amicos seu cōsanguineos. Quid, quòd hac ipsa voce Non erubescit, retūduntur etiam morosi aduersarij, qui ƥ bri loco obijciebant Christi humiliationē. Nam hac voce ostenditur, Christi dignitate nihil imminutā ex eo, quòd humanam naturam induerit, neq; vllo modo pudendum, confiteri, quòd Christus, quem Deū prædicamus, homo esse cōceditur. Quòd verò voce Fratrū recte significet naturæ æqualitas, pòst explicabimus. Quòd verò aptè hoc testimoniū de Christo fit citatū, nūc oftedamus. Quantū argumentū Psalmi attinet, vt cōcedatur, à Dauide cōpositū, quo tēpore à Saule multis variisq; insidijs quærebat ad mortē, & quodāmodo desperaret de regno in posterū obtinēdo: tamē manifestissimū est, Dauidē typū gessisse Christi, & licet hæc de se quidē cecinerit, nihilominus etiā de Christo intellexisse, vt erat spiritu Dei affla tus, q primū ipsius instar foret humiliādus, deinde verò exaltādus, & regno spirituali stet noq; præficiedus. Nec desūt argumēta & loci Scripturę, quib. de Christo accipiendū hūc psalmū cōfirmet. Nā Christus ipse, vt referūt euāgelistę, initiū huius psalmi sibi, cū in cru ce pēderet, accōmodauit, dicēs hebraicē, Eli, Eli, Lama sabachthani (Syriacū est, ƥ eo, qđ diceret azaphthani; dereliqsti me) Hoc est, Deus meus, quare dereliquisti me: & plurima verba, quę sequūtur in hoc psalmo, illi loco euangelistę cōueniūt Matt.27. Iterū Ioan.ca.19. narrás, quō milites nolētes scindere veste Christi inconsutilem, forte iecerint, cui ea cederet, addit ita factū ordinatione diuina, ut nimirū Scriptura impleret, dicēs: partiti sunt vestimenta mea sibi, & in vestē meam miserunt sorte. Quod oraculū etiā ex hoc Psalmo, vt proprie historiam humiliationis Christi continentem, euangelista desumpsit. Tertiò, continet idem Psalmus multò plura testimonia, quæ nō nisi de Christo recte exponi possunt. Sed quo tota res clarius elucescat, nos breuiter Psalmum de Christo exponemus.
units.tr: Is not ashamed to call them brethren. He said very elegantly, is not ashamed. For by this word he indicates at once the very great dignity of Christ, since he according to his divine nature is far superior to all men, and also his wonderful humility and goodness, in that he did not disdain to acknowledge as equals those who in many respects are inferior to him. This form of expression is taken from the custom of those men who, when they have been raised from a humble station to a more august dignity, no longer want to acknowledge their old friends and relatives. They are ashamed of all their parents and friends, and think them unworthy to be called their own, so that they no longer acknowledge them. So also Proverbs 19 says: All the brethren of the poor man hate him; moreover his friends go far away from him. But Christ, who is always greater and more powerful in himself than that any creature could be admitted to him in any way, was not ashamed to call us, vile men and sinners, guilty of eternal damnation, bastards and degenerate, his brethren. So this word greatly illustrates the goodness and humility of Christ. A similar form of expression occurs in Philippians: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men. There, as he says, it was not robbery, that is, no wrong was done to God, but Christ rightly was God; the form of speech is taken from those who by lies and stealth want to insert themselves into great and illustrious families, about which an entire chapter is found in Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 16. So conversely, here he says that Christ was not ashamed to be made man, using a form of speech taken from those who, once raised to honours, no longer wish to acknowledge their old friends or relatives. Moreover, by this very word is not ashamed, the troublesome adversaries are also refuted, who used the humiliation of Christ as a reproach. For by this word it is shown that the dignity of Christ is diminished in no way by his having put on human nature, and that there is nothing shameful in confessing that Christ, whom we proclaim as God, is granted to be man. That the word brethren rightly signifies equality of nature, we shall explain later. That this testimony is aptly cited concerning Christ, let us now show. As far as the argument of the Psalm is concerned, granted that it was composed by David at the time when he was sought to death by Saul with many and various snares, and in some way despaired of obtaining the kingdom in the future, it is nonetheless most evident that David bore the type of Christ, and although he sang these things of himself, nevertheless he also understood them of Christ, as he was inspired by the Spirit of God, who was first to be humbled in his likeness, and then exalted, and set over a spiritual kingdom. Nor are there lacking arguments and passages of Scripture by which this psalm is confirmed as to be understood of Christ. For Christ himself, as the evangelists report, applied to himself the beginning of this psalm when he hung on the cross, saying in Hebrew, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani (in Syriac, as the evangelist reports, azaphthani; thou hast forsaken me), that is, My God, why hast thou forsaken me? And most of the words that follow in this psalm agree with that passage of the evangelist, Matthew 27. Again, John 19 relates how the soldiers, unwilling to tear Christ's seamless coat, cast lots for whom it should fall to; he adds that this was done by divine ordering, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, saying: They parted my garments among them, and for my vesture they cast lots. The evangelist took this oracle also from this Psalm, as one properly containing the history of the humiliation of Christ. Thirdly, the same Psalm contains many more testimonies which can rightly be expounded only of Christ. But so that the whole matter may shine more clearly, we shall briefly expound the Psalm concerning Christ.

units.la: Deus, Deus meus respice in me, quare me dereliquisti?) Omnia plena sunt affectibus, qui animum mire afflictū deiectūq; exprimunt. Et quāuis Dauid sępè periclitās, & grauiter cōmotus, aptissimè in sua causa potuerit huiusmodi affectus exprimere: sed tamē ostedemus inter explicandū, plurima hic cōtineri, quæ multò certius, iustius, verius de Christo, quàm de Dauide accipi debeāt, secundū simplicem & historicum sensum. Primò itaq; hæc verba Christo iam morituro & morte acerbam gustaturo maximè cōueniunt, vtpote quæ ipse in cruce pendens pro se, & tanquam de se scripta vsurpauit, sicut ante admonuimus.
units.tr: O God, my God, look upon me; why hast thou forsaken me? Everything is full of emotions which express a mind wonderfully afflicted and cast down. And although David, often in danger and gravely disturbed, could most aptly have expressed such emotions in his own cause, nevertheless we shall show as we expound that much is contained here which ought to be understood far more certainly, justly and truly of Christ than of David, according to the plain and historical sense. First, therefore, these words most fittingly suit Christ, who was about to die and to taste bitter death, since he himself, hanging on the cross, took them up for himself and as if written about himself, as we noted before.

units.la: Longè à salute mea verba delictorum meorum: vel verba rugitus mei habet fælix. Estq; sententia, verba seu clamor rugitus mei salutē mihi parare non possunt. Vel, verba seu facta delictorū meorū efficiunt, vt procul sim à labore. Sic verò Christus, qui cùm peccatum nullū nosset, tamē pro nobis peccatoribus factus peccatū, & peccata nostra ad se recipiēs, rectè dicere potuit. Gesìt enim in illa humiliatione nostram personā, non suā, & nos è contrario ornati sumus persona ipsius, induti ipsius iustitia: id quod 2. Corin. 5. Apostolus indicauit, dicens: Eum qui non nouit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum.
units.tr: Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions; or, the words of my roaring are happy. The sense is: the words or cry of my roaring cannot bring me salvation. Or: the words or deeds of my transgressions bring it about that I am far from relief. Christ, who knew no sin yet was made sin for us sinners and took our sins upon himself, could rightly say this. For in that humiliation he bore our person, not his own, and conversely we are clothed with his person and put on his righteousness. The Apostle indicated this in 2 Cor. 5: He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

units.la: Deus meus clamabo per diem, & non exaudies: & nocte, & c.) Hæc itidē magnū affectū exprimūt, & planè talem, qualis fuit Christi orantis, ac dicentis: Pater, si fieri potest, transeat à me calix iste. Et non ad insipientiam mundi) quasi diceret: Quòd ita clamem omni tempore, & tamen non exaudiar, non reputabitur mihi ad stultitiā, nequaquam vitio verti poterit. Sic enim constantiam in oratione commendat, quam tamen caro non intelligit vtile & necessariam esse, sed velut stultam & superuacaneam despicit. Sed Christus sæpè & cum lachrymis orabat patrem, vt, si fieri posset, calix supplicij ab ipso transiret.
units.tr: O my God, I cry by day, and you do not hear; and by night, and so on. These words likewise express great emotion, exactly the kind Christ showed when he prayed and said: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. And the phrase "not to the folly of the world" means: that I cry out at all times and yet am not heard will not be counted to me as folly, and can never be held against me. For the psalm commends perseverance in prayer, which the flesh does not understand to be useful and necessary, but despises as foolish and superfluous. Yet Christ often prayed to the Father with tears that, if it were possible, the cup of suffering might pass from him.

units.la: Tu autem in sancto habitas, laus Israel) His verbis Dei bonitatē & æquitatē prædicat, omnia ipsius relinquens voluntati ac iudicio: quomodo Christus etiam dixit: Veruntamen non mea voluntas, sed tua voluntas fiat.
units.tr: But you dwell in the holy place, O praise of Israel. By these words he proclaims God's goodness and justice, leaving all things to his will and judgment, just as Christ also said: Nevertheless not my will, but yours, be done.

units.la: In te sperauerunt patres nostri, sperauerunt & liberasti eos: Ad te clamauerunt, & salui facti sunt, in te speraverunt, & non sunt confusi.
units.tr: In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were saved; in you they hoped, and were not put to shame.

units.la: Sic pia mens se solatur & confirmat ab exemplis sanctorum patrum, quos vt scit, post-quam otarunt, liberatos à malis: ita statuit, se quoq; ab angustijs liberandā. Tantundē significavit Christus, cùm toties diceret, se per humiliationē, quæ instabat, glorificandum: certus quippe erat, se post humiliationem liberandum.
units.tr: So the devout mind comforts and strengthens itself by the examples of the holy fathers, whom, as it knows, God freed from evils after they had prayed; so it resolves that it too shall be freed from its distresses. Christ signified the same thing when he so often said that he would be glorified through the humiliation that was at hand; for he was certain that after the humiliation he would be delivered.

units.la: Ego autem sum vermis & non homo, opprobrium hominum & abiectio plebis. Omnes videntes me, deriserunt me, locuti sunt labijs, et mouerunt caput: Speravit in Domino, eripiat eum, saluum faciat eum, quoniam vult eum.
units.tr: But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. All who see me have mocked me; they have spoken with their lips and shaken their heads: He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he delights in him.

units.la: Quis non videat ista Christo extremè humiliato, maximè conuenire? Et planè eadem esse cum illis, quæ habetur Marci 15. Impleta est Scriptura, quę dicit, (Esaię 53.) Et cum iniquis deputatus est. Et qui præteribant conuitiabātur illi, mouentes capita sua, ac dicētes: Vāh qui demoliris templum, & in tribus diebus extruis, serua teipsum, & descende de cruce. Similiter & summi Sacerdotes, illudētes cum Scribis, dicebāt: Alios seruauit, seipsum seruare non potest. Christus ille rex Israel descēdat nūc de cruce, vt videamus & credamus.
units.tr: Who does not see that these things apply most fitly to Christ when he was utterly humiliated? And they are plainly the same as what is found in Mark 15. The Scripture was fulfilled which says (Isa. 53): And he was numbered with the wicked. And those who passed by reviled him, shaking their heads and saying: Aha, you who would destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself and come down from the cross. Likewise the chief priests, mocking with the scribes, said: He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let that Christ, the king of Israel, come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe.

units.la: Quoniam tu es, qui extraxisti me de ventre, spes mea ab vberibus matris meæ, in te proiectus sum ex vtero de ventre matris meæ, Deus meus es tu, ne discesseris à me.
units.tr: For you are he who drew me out of the womb; my hope from my mother's breasts. I was cast upon you from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my God; do not depart from me.

units.la: Quoniam tribulatio proxima est, & non est qui adiuuet.
units.tr: For trouble is near, and there is none to help.

units.la: Ita Christus, vt extremè deiiciatur, tamen nunquam desperat, sed certus de liberatione sua Dei patris expectat auxilium.
units.tr: Thus Christ, though he was brought down to the utmost depths, never despairs, but, certain of his deliverance, waits for the help of God the Father.

units.la: Circumderunt me vituli multi, & tauri pingues obsederunt me: Aperuerunt super me os suum, sicut Leo rapiens & rugiens:
units.tr: Many young bulls have surrounded me; fat bulls have besieged me. They have opened their mouth against me, like a lion ravening and roaring.

units.la: Amplificatio afflictionum, à potentia, multitudine hostium, eorundem q; crudelitate, quam elegantibus similitudinibus graphicè depingit.
units.tr: An amplification of afflictions, from the power and number of the enemies and their cruelty, which he depicts vividly with apt comparisons.

units.la: Sicut aqua effusus sum, & dispersa sunt omnia ossa mea, factum est cor meum tanquam cera liquescens in medio ventris mei. Aruit tanquam testa virtus mea, & lingua & lingua mea adhæsit faucibus meis, & in pulverem mortis deduxisti me.
units.tr: I am poured out like water, and all my bones are scattered; my heart has become like wax melting in the midst of my belly. My strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue cleaves to my jaws, and you have brought me into the dust of death.

units.la: Tot elegantes Similitudines & metaphoræ ad explicandum extremum dolorem, hoc vnum mihi videntur sonare, quod Christus, iam morte imminente, dixit, Tristis est anima mea vsq; ad mortem.
units.tr: So many apt similitudes and metaphors to express extreme pain seem to me to sound only this one thing, which Christ said, with death now imminent: My soul is sorrowful even unto death.

units.la: Quoniam circumdederunt me canes multi, consilium malignantium obsedit me. Foderunt manus meas, & pedes meos, dinumerauerunt omnia ossa mea. Ipsi vero consideraverunt, & inspexerunt me, diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea, & super vestem meam miserunt sortem.
units.tr: For many dogs have surrounded me; a council of evildoers has beset me. They have pierced my hands and my feet; they have counted all my bones. But they looked on and gazed at me; they divided my garments among them, and cast lots for my clothing.

units.la: Quis non intelligit ista simpliciter, &, vt ad verbum sonant, omnia impleta esse in Christo, & multo verius de Christo, quàm de Dauide (cui certè contigisse ista non leguntur) accipienda? Vtpote cùm Christus sic fuerit confossus & vulneratus in cruce, cùm super vestem eius milites sortem pro ea miserint.
units.tr: Who does not understand these things plainly, and as the words sound, that all of them were fulfilled in Christ, and that they are to be understood far more truly of Christ than of David (of whom it is certainly not read that these things happened to him)? Certainly Christ was so pierced and wounded on the cross, when the soldiers cast lots for his garment.

units.la: Tu autem Domine ne elongaveris auxilium tuum à me, ad defensionem meam conspice. Erue à framea Deus animam meam, & de manu canis vnicam meam. Salua me ex ore Leonis, & à cornibus vnicornium humilitatem meam.
units.tr: But you, O Lord, do not remove your help from me; look upon me for my defence. Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog. Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns.

units.la: Hæc adhuc pro precatione Christi, postulantis à se transferri calicem, aut si id fieri non possit, cupientis tandem ab imperio mortis, diaboli, inferni, liberari, possunt accipi. Elegantes sunt admixtæ metaphoræ acerbitatem mortis & tormentorum omnium significantes. Atq; hactenus quidem Christus humiliatus descriptus est: Iam sequuntur, quæ ad glorificationem eius pertinent, quæq; secutura sint illam eius humiliationem.
units.tr: These words may still be taken as the prayer of Christ, asking that the cup be taken from him, or, if that cannot be, desiring at last to be freed from the power of death, the devil and hell. The metaphors mixed in are elegant, signifying the bitterness of death and of all torments. So far Christ humiliated has been described; now follow the things that pertain to his glorification and that were to follow that humiliation.

units.la: Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in medio ecclesiæ laudabo te.) Quod Christo glorificato iam maximè conuenit, quoniam potentiam Dei patris post resurrectionem multis modis manifestauit, atq; euangelium iam iussit propagari in omnes fines terræ, dicens discipulis suis: Acci pite Spiritum sanctum, &c. Euntes prædicate euangelium omni creaturæ, &c. Ac licet toto tempore, quo in terris egit, nomen Dei manifestasset hominibus, (sicut ipse Ioan. 17. diserte ad patrem ait) tamen nunquam illud plenius & magnificetius egit, quàm post humiliationem. Atq; istud munus proprium Christi munus est, quod Dauidi non perinde potest tribui.
units.tr: I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you. This applies most of all to Christ glorified, since after the resurrection he showed the power of God the Father in many ways, and now commanded the gospel to be spread to all the ends of the earth, saying to his disciples: Receive the Holy Spirit, etc.; go and preach the gospel to every creature, etc. And although during the whole time he spent on earth he had made the name of God known to men (as he himself says plainly to the Father in John 17), yet he never did this more fully and more gloriously than after his humiliation. And this is the proper office of Christ, which cannot be attributed to David in the same way.

units.la: Qui timetis Dominum, laudate eum, vniuersum semen Iacob glorificate eum. Timeat eum omne semen Israel, quoniam non spreuit, neq; despexit deprecationem pauperis: Nec auertit faciem suam à me, & cum clamarem ad eum, exaudiuit me.
units.tr: You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him. Let all the seed of Israel fear him, because he has not despised or scorned the supplication of the poor; nor has he turned his face from me, and when I cried to him, he heard me.

units.la: Inuitantur omnes ad agendum Deo gratias, & laudandum eum, pro liberatione Christi, cuius liberatio nostra quoq; liberatio & salus est.
units.tr: All are invited to give thanks to God and to praise him for the deliverance of Christ, whose deliverance is also our deliverance and salvation.

units.la: Apud te laus mea in ecclesia magna, vota mea reddam in conspectu timentium eum.) Promittit Christus se celebraturum & magis illustre redditurum nomen Dei patris, in noua & vere magna ecclesia, collecta nimirum non solùm ex multis gentibus, verùm etiam ex gentibus, de quarum conuersione sequitur vaticinium.
units.tr: My praise is in the great church; I will pay my vows in the sight of those who fear him. Christ promises that he will celebrate and make more illustrious the name of God the Father in the new and truly great church, gathered, that is, not only from many nations but also from the nations whose conversion the prophecy that follows concerns.

units.la: Edent pauperes, & saturabuntur, & laudabunt Dominum, qui requirunt eum, vivet corda eorum in seculum seculi. Reminiscentur, & convertentur ad Dominum vniuersi fines terræ. Et adorabunt in conspectu eius vniuersæ familiæ gentium.
units.tr: The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their heart shall live for ever and ever. All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord; and all the families of the nations shall worship before him.

units.la: Annon hic audimus de regno Christi æterno, de vocatione gentium clarissima vaticinia, quæ nullo pacto Dauidi possunt accommodari? Sequitur:
units.tr: Do we not hear here the most clear prophecies concerning the eternal kingdom of Christ and the calling of the nations, which can in no way be applied to David? The psalm goes on:

units.la: Manducauerunt & adorauerunt omnes pingues terræ, in conspectu eius cadet omnes, qui descendunt in terram. Et anima mea illi viuet, & semen meum seruiet ipsi. Annunciabitur Domino generatio uentura, annunciabunt cœli iustitiam eius, populo qui nascetur, quem fecit Dominus.
units.tr: All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshipped; before him shall fall all who go down into the earth. And my soul shall live to him, and my seed shall serve him. It shall be declared to the Lord a coming generation; the heavens shall declare his righteousness to a people yet to be born, whom the Lord has made.

units.la: Hæc itidem omnia de Euangelio prædicando gentibus, de iustitia per Christum parta clarè loquuntur, nec causæ Dauidis satis conueniunt. Hactenus obiter de psalmi materia & argumento, & tota dispositione, quantum satis esse arbitror. Ac videre hic licet, quàm absurdum sit Iudæi quidam totum hunc Psalmum interpretari volunt, canere eum de sui populi postrema, qua nunc premuntur, captiuitate, in qua cùm maximè sint humiliati ac deiecti, confidutam adhuc liberandos, & temporaliter toto orbe regnaturos, sicut Rabbini Ezra & Kimhi somniant. Nunc paulò plenius testimonium hoc loco citatum ex eo enarrabimus. Proinde aptissimè tribui Christo, qui annunciaturus sit nomen Dei suis fratribus, in medio ecclesiæ Deum laudabit, nō difficile est demonstrare. Nam Christus fere fuit nuncius & præco Dei in terris, longè aliter, quàm Dauid, qui regè ageret, & multis de causis, ea crebrò liberabatur à gravissimis periculis, prædicabat gloriam Dei apud omnes. Nō tamen eadem ratione & eodem modo. Christus enim proprie, & ex officio agebat euangelistâ in terris, prædicauit voluntatem suæ patris, ecclesiá collegit et in stituit, nihil aliud agés toto tépore, quo in terris egit, et omnia sua ad hunc fine referens. Quare hic latet quedâ grauissima ratio, q uare decuerit Christũ homine fieri. Significat enim, ideò quo q; Christũ mittendũ fuisse, vt homines erudiret ac doceret voluntate Patris, restauraret & propagaret verâ cognitione Dei, quę apud Iudeos iam collapsa erat, apud exteros penitus extincta: de quo officio suo & missionis causa ipse palsim cocionatur. Erant quidé antea sæpè Prophetæ & diuini homines plurimi misi: sed cùm illi parum proficerent, nec possent etiam ostendere modum reparandæ salutis, multò minus ipsi salutem parare, opus erat & Christum mitti, qui vnus omnia perficeret, sicut ipse solus erat idoneus, & ab æterno ad hoc munus à Deo patre desti- natus. Hųc pertinet illud Matthæi 11. Nemo nouit Patrem nisi filius, & cui filius volu erit reuelare. Itaque ad adducendos homines ad cognitionem Dei Patris, propriè mittendus erat Christus.
units.tr: These things likewise all speak clearly of the Gospel to be preached to the nations, of the righteousness won through Christ, and they hardly fit the cause of David. So far, in passing, on the subject and argument of the Psalm and its whole arrangement, as much as I think is enough. Here one may see how absurd it is that certain Jews want this whole Psalm to be interpreted as a song about their people's final captivity, in which they are now oppressed. In that captivity, when they are most humbled and cast down, they are still confident that they will be freed and will reign temporally over the whole world, as the rabbis Ezra and Kimhi dream. Now we shall explain the testimony cited here a little more fully. It is not difficult to show that it is rightly applied to Christ, who was to announce the name of God to his brothers and in the midst of the Church would praise God. For Christ was almost the messenger and herald of God on earth, in a very different way from David, who was a king, and who, though often delivered from the gravest dangers for many reasons, proclaimed the glory of God before all. Yet not by the same reasoning or in the same manner. For Christ, properly and by his office, acted as the evangelist on earth. He preached the will of his Father, gathered and established the Church, and did nothing else during the whole time he spent on earth, referring all his works to this end. Hence there lies here a very weighty reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man. It signifies that Christ too had to be sent so that he might instruct and teach men about the will of the Father, and restore and spread the true knowledge of God, which had already collapsed among the Jews and was utterly extinct among foreigners. He himself preaches openly about this his office and the cause of his mission. There were indeed many earlier prophets and very many godly men who were sent, but since they made little progress and could not even show the way of restoring salvation, much less produce salvation themselves, it was necessary that Christ be sent, who alone would accomplish everything, since he alone was fit for it and from eternity had been appointed by God the Father to this task. To this pertains that saying of Matthew 11: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him." Therefore, in order to bring men to the knowledge of God the Father, Christ properly had to be sent.

units.la: Porrò per nomen Dei, hoc loco intellige potentiam & bonitatem Dei, qua voluit humano generi salutem reddere, adeoque bonam Dei erga homines voluntatem, qua signi ficatione Christus vsurpauit Ioan. 17. quando ait, Manifestaui nomen tuū hominibus, quos dedisti mi- hi de mundo. Similiter Actorum nono, Organon electum est mihi iste, vt portet nomen meum coram gentibus, & regibus, ac filijs Israel.
units.tr: Furthermore, by the name of God in this place understand the power and goodness of God, by which he willed to restore salvation to the human race, and so God's good will toward men. Christ used the word in this sense in John 17, when he says: I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. Likewise in Acts 9: "This man is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the sons of Israel."

units.la: Quòd ad vocem fratrũ attinet, nonnulli hic per fratres intelligi volunt, præcipuè apostolos & discipulos, ac deinde quotquot credentes in eum, Dei patris voluntatem student perficere. In quam sententiam Christus Ioannes cap. 20. ad Mariam plorantem ait: Vade ad fratres meos, & dic eis: Ascendo ad patrem meū, & patre uestrum, Deum meum, & Deum uestrum. Et Matthæi duodecimo, Protensa manu in discipulos, dixit: Ecce mater mea, ecce fratres mei. Quisquis enim fecerit uoluntatē patris mei, qui in cœlis est, ipse est frater meus, etc. Al as omnes homines generaliter dicuntur fratres, quoniam vnum communem Patrem habent in cœlis: quo- modo Malachiæ 2. Nunquid non pater vnus omnium nostrūm? Et Matthæi vigesimo- tertio, Patrem nolite vocare vobis in terra, vnus est enim pater vester, qui in cœlis est. Iterum Ephesiorum tertio, fleċto genua ad patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ex quo o- mnis à communi patre cognatio in cœlis, & in terra nominatur. Et quoniam Christus missus est in mundum, vt generaliter annunciaret Euangelium & voluntatem patris o- mnibus hominibus, & nō tantum paucis quibusdam, potius hoc pacto de omnibus ho- minibus accipietur hic vox fratrum, quàm de solis credentibus. Imò dictus est quidem Christus à Mose peculiariter frater Iudæorum, vtpote originem ducens secundum carnem ex Abraham & patribus Iudæorum: Deuteron. 18. (vbi sic legitur, Prophetam suscitabo eis de medio fratrum suorum, & ponam verba mea in ore eius:) Sed quoniam hîc adducuntur ista ad confirmandam summam æqualitatem Christi cum cæteris hominibus, secundum humanam naturam, ideò commodissimè hoc loco, per fratres intelligemus omnes in vniuersum homines humana natura præditos, secundum quam reuera omnes, qui ab vno primo parente Adamo trahunt originem, sicut & Christus secundum carnem, fratres inter se sunt: quomodo & supra dictum est, tàm Christum sanctificantem quàm cæteros sanctificandos ex vno primo parente Adamo omnes esse. Et certè, vt nulli iudicantur sic inter se conuenire natura, habitudine corporum, ingenio, moribus, deniq; omnibus rebus, atq; qui secundum carnem sunt fratres ex vno patre carnali geniti: Ita ad significandum summam æqualitatem (quantum ad naturam humanam) Christi cum cæteris hominibus, non posset aptior vox adhiberi. Ergo fratres dixit Propheta, pro omnibus in genere hominibus, quibus secundum humana natura Christus per omnia similis inuetus est: tametsi dū oēs homines fratres dicimus Christi, ppter cōmuné natura, & cō munem parentē Adamū: non tamen dubium est, quin pios potissimum pro fratribus a- gnoscat, qui ex vno patre spirituali trahunt originē, & ad eundem omnes iterum tēdunt. Cēterum, mirabilis consolatio in omnibus aduersitatibus ex hoc nasci nobis debet, q stissanē & coheredes.
units.tr: As for the word "brothers," some want it understood here to mean chiefly the apostles and disciples, and then all who believe in him and strive to fulfil the will of God the Father. To this sense Christ, in John 20, says to the weeping Mary: Go to my brothers and say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. And in Matthew 12, stretching out his hand toward the disciples, he said: Behold my mother, behold my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, etc. But all men in general are called brothers, since they have one common Father in heaven, as in Malachi 2: "Has not one Father of us all?" And in Matthew 23: "Do not call anyone on earth your father, for one is your Father, who is in heaven." Again, Ephesians 3: "I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named." And since Christ was sent into the world to proclaim the Gospel and the Father's will generally to all men, and not only to a few, the word "brothers" will be taken here of all men rather than of believers alone. Indeed Christ was called by Moses in particular the brother of the Jews, as one who by descent according to the flesh came from Abraham and the fathers of the Jews: Deuteronomy 18 (where it is read thus: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, and will put my words in his mouth"). But since these words are here cited to confirm the full equality of Christ with other men according to human nature, we shall therefore understand here by "brothers" all men in general endowed with human nature, according to which indeed all who trace their origin from the one first parent Adam are brothers among themselves, just as Christ is according to the flesh. In the same way, as was said above, both Christ who sanctifies and the others who are to be sanctified all come from the one first parent Adam. And certainly, just as those are judged to agree among themselves in nature, bodily constitution, temperament, manners, and in short in all things, who are brothers according to the flesh, born of one carnal father, so no more apt word could be used to signify the full equality of Christ with other men (as far as human nature goes). Therefore the Prophet called them brothers, meaning all men in general, to whom Christ according to human nature has been found similar in all things. Although we call all men brothers of Christ on account of their common nature and their common parent Adam, there is no doubt that he chiefly acknowledges as brothers the godly, who trace their origin from one spiritual Father and all tend to the same goal. Moreover, a wonderful consolation in all adversities ought to arise for us from this.

units.la: Christi fratres appellamur & sumus, si eius fratres sumus, igit & cohæredes: vti Rom. 8. clarè dicitur. Atq; hinc statuere certò debemus, q pater cœlestis nostri cura gerat, & nunquā sit nos deserturus, maximè si nos ita geramus, vt p germanis fratribus Christi agnoscipossimus: qd nimirū facimus, quādo præcepta Dei obseruādo voluntate patris perficimus. Pręterea habemus hoc loco, quod facit ad dignitatē Euangelij, nimirū per ipsum Christū Dei filium annūciatum, (sicut & Ioan. 1. dicitur, vnigenitus, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrauit) & quidem non clàm vel occulta fraude, sicut solet furtim falsa dogmata noctu seminare hæretici ministri diaboli: sed palàm & in medio ecclesiæ.
units.tr: We are and are called brothers of Christ, if we are his brothers, and so also heirs, as Romans 8 plainly says. From this we ought surely to conclude that our heavenly Father takes care of us and will never forsake us, especially if we so conduct ourselves that we may be recognised as true brothers of Christ. We do this indeed when, by observing God's precepts, we fulfil the will of the Father. Besides, we have here something that contributes to the dignity of the Gospel, namely that it has been announced through Christ himself, the Son of God (as John 1 also says: the only begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared it), and that not secretly or by hidden fraud, as heretics, the ministers of the devil, are wont to sow false doctrines furtively at night, but openly and in the midst of the Church.

units.la: Et rursum: & ego ero fides in illo) Secūdū testimoniū, quo cōfirmat, Christū hominem debuisse fieri à Deo patre præordinatū, & à Prophetis prædictū. Christus apud Prophetam ait: Ego ero fides in illo. Sed fidere in Deo nō potest Christo cōuenire, nisi secundū humanitatē. Ergo decuit Christum homine fieri, & vere homo factus agnosci debet: neq; est, quod quisquam pro ridiculo aut absurdo habeat, quod Christus, qui erat Deus ab æterno, factus sit in tempore homo. Constat autem, quod fidere in alium, sit inferioris. Deum enim fidere Deo, cuius obsecro aures tam absurdum ferant locutionem? Christus vero inferior patre non potest intelligi, nisi secundum humanitatem. Siue autem hæc verba sumantur ex Esaiæ 12. siue ex Psalmo 17. (nam duobus hisce locis occurrunt) non difficile est demonstrare, ea de Christo recte accipi. Apud Esaiam sic legitur: Ecce Deus salvator meus, fiducialiter agam, & non timebo: quia fortitudo & laus mea Dominus, & factus est mihi in salutem. Psalmo vero 17. sic habetur: Diligam te Domine, fortitudo mea, Dominus firmamentum meum, et refugium meum, & liberator meus: Deus meus, adiutor meus, & sperabo in eum. Sed nos utrumque locum plenius explicabimus, & de Christo recte accipi docebimus.
units.tr: And again: "And I will be trust in him." This is the second testimony, by which he confirms that Christ had to be made man, preordained by God the Father and foretold by the Prophets. Christ says through the Prophet: I will be trust in him. But to trust in God cannot belong to Christ except according to his humanity. Therefore it was fitting that Christ be made man, and having truly become man he ought to be acknowledged as such. Nor should anyone regard it as ridiculous or absurd that Christ, who was God from eternity, became man in time. It is plain that to trust in another belongs to one who is inferior. For would God trust God? Whose ears, I beg you, could bear so absurd an expression? But Christ cannot be understood as inferior to the Father except according to his humanity. Whether these words are taken from Isaiah 12 or from Psalm 17 (for they occur in these two places), it is not difficult to show that they are rightly understood of Christ. In Isaiah it is read thus: Behold, God is my saviour; I will act with confidence and will not fear, for the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation. In Psalm 17 it is found thus: I will love you, Lord, my strength. The Lord is my firmament and my refuge and my deliverer. My God, my helper, and I will hope in him. But we shall explain both passages more fully, and teach that they are rightly understood of Christ.

units.la: Primum apud Esaiam verba illa convenire Christo, vel ex eo satis liquet, quod, ut mos est Prophetarum, post reprehensionem peccatorum, & comminationem iræ divinæ, adere consolationem, & præcipue à misericordia propter Messiam seu Christum expectanda: ita Esaias postquam capite 9. ac 10. reprehendit gravissima quædam suæ gentis vitia, nec non prænunciauit eius propter peccata dispersionem, (similiter & excidium regni Sennacherib) statim capite 11. consolari suos iterum cupiens, vaticinatur de adventu Christi, eius q; florentissimo regno, præterea de immensis bonis, quæ pij in eo regno consequentur, id quod ad Roman. 15. & Actorum 13. citata ex eodem capite testimonia, lucu-lenter arguunt. Inueni, inquit, Dauid, filium Iesse, virum secundum cor meum, qui faciet omnes voluntates meas. Huius e semine Deus ita, ut promiserat, adduxit Israelem Seruatorem Iesum. Inde vero capite 12. subijcit generalem, nomine totius ecclesiæ, pro tantis beneficijs Dei per Messiam siue Christum conferendis, gratiarum actionem. Cum autem ecclesiæ caput sit Christus, non est obscurum, omnia quæ ibi habentur, sicut toti ecclesiæ, ita capiti eius Christo competere. Porrò, quo clarius istud percipiatur, nos nonnulla ex Esaia, quoniam non admodum prolixa sunt, ascribemus. Post enarrata ergo capite undecimo, beneficia Dei erga homines per Christum, nempe de adventu Christi in carnem, de regno ipsius & potentia, beneficijs ipsius aduetum secuturis, de vocatione gentium, de recipiendis Iudæis in gratiam post diuturnam dispersionem: tandem capite 13. ita subijcit:
units.tr: That these words of Isaiah apply to Christ is clear enough from the fact that, as is the custom of the prophets, after rebuking sins and threatening the wrath of God, they add consolation, especially consolation to be expected from mercy through the Messiah or Christ. So Isaiah, after rebuking in chapters 9 and 10 some very serious vices of his nation, and foretelling their dispersion for sin (and likewise the destruction of Sennacherib's kingdom), immediately in chapter 11 desires to comfort his people again and prophesies the coming of Christ and his most flourishing kingdom, and also the immense blessings which the godly will obtain in that kingdom. The testimonies cited from this same chapter in Romans 15 and Acts 13 clearly prove this. "I have found," he says, "David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will. From his seed God, as he had promised, brought to Israel a Saviour, Jesus." Then in chapter 12 he adds a general thanksgiving, in the name of the whole Church, for such great benefits of God to be conferred through the Messiah or Christ. Since Christ is the head of the Church, it is not obscure that everything found there belongs to the whole Church and likewise to its head, Christ. Moreover, so that this may be perceived more clearly, we will set out some passages from Isaiah, since they are not very long. So, after chapter 11 has recounted the benefits of God towards men through Christ, namely the coming of Christ in the flesh, his kingdom and power, the benefits that will follow his coming, the calling of the Gentiles, and the reception of the Jews into grace after their long dispersion, at last in chapter 13 he continues thus:

units.la: Et dicas in die illa: Confitebor tibi Domine, quoniam iratus es mihi, conuersus est furor tuus, & consolatus es me. Ecce Deus saluator meus, fiducialiter agam, & non timebo: Quia fortitudo et laus mea Dominus, & factus est mihi in salutem. Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Saluatoris: & dicetis in die illa: Confitemini Domino, & invocate nomen eius. Notas facite in populis adinuentiones eius, mementote, quoniam excelsum est nomen eius. Cantate Domino, quoniam magnifice fecit, annuntiate hoc in universa terra. Exulta & lauda habitatio Sion, quia magnus in medio tui sanctus Israel. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: And thou shalt say in that day: I will praise thee, O Lord; for though thou wast angry with me, thy anger is turned away, and thou hast comforted me. Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not fear: for the Lord God is my strength and my song, and he is become my salvation. With joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation. And in that day shall ye say: Praise the Lord, and call upon his name. Make known his doings among the people; remember that his name is exalted. Sing unto the Lord, for he hath done excellent things; this is known in all the earth. Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion, for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee. Thus far there.

units.la: Porrò interpres Epistolæ huius reddidit ex septuaginta, apud quos sic legitur <bl>ιδου ο θεος μου ο σωτηρ μου, πεποιθως εσομαι και ουκ φοβηθησομαι</bl>. Ecce Deus meus, seruator meus, ero fidens in illo. Si ad hebræa respiciamus, potius sic sonabit: Ecce Deus salus mea, confidam, & non timebo: sic enim legitur הנה אל ישועתי אבטח ולא אפחד. Itaq; sententia plane est eadem. Et hæc omnia toti ecclesiæ, cuius caput est Christus, recte attribuuntur, & Christus simul cum ceteris membris ita canit. Eadem q; ratione dicitur Christus fidere in Deum, qui ipse exclamauit in cruce pendens, Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me deseruisti? secundum humanitatem eius, satis conueniut. Cæterum, quia hoc loco habetur, <bl>ιδου εσομαι πεποιθως εν αυτω</bl>, valde verosimile est, Apostolum ex Esaia sua verba mutuatum. Nihilominus, quod etiam conueniant, si quis è Psalmo sumpta esse malit, breuiter explicabimus.
units.tr: Moreover, the translator of this Epistle rendered it from the Seventy, where it reads thus: "Behold, my God, my saviour; I shall be trusting, and I shall not fear" [ἰδοὺ ὁ θεὸς μου ὁ σωτήρ μου, πεποιθὼς ἔσομαι καὶ οὐ φοβηθήσομαι]. If we look to the Hebrew, it will rather sound thus: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and I will not fear" [הנה אל ישועתי אבטח ולא אפחד]. So the meaning is plainly the same. All these things are rightly attributed to the whole Church, whose head is Christ, and Christ sings them together with the other members. For the same reason it is said that Christ trusted in God, who himself cried out while hanging on the cross, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" These things agree well enough with his humanity. Furthermore, since in this passage there is "Behold, I shall be trusting in him" [ἰδοὺ ἔσομαι πεποιθὼς ἐν αὐτῷ], it is very probable that the Apostle borrowed his words from Isaiah. Nevertheless, in case anyone prefers that they were taken from a Psalm, we will briefly explain that they also agree.

units.la: Si ergo ex Psalmo 17. placet hoc testimonium desumptum, citra negotium ostendi posse, eum Christo recte attribui. Nam tametsi titulus apud Hebræos loquatur, epinicion esse seu gratiarum actionem, decantatam à Dauide, postquam ab omnium aduersariorum, & inprimis Saulis eiusque familiæ insidijs esset liberatus: tamen, cum negari non possit, Dauidem tam cum humiliaretur, quam cum nouam consequeretur gloriam, gestisse in multis typum Christi, & subinde inter agendum de proprio regno vaticinatum, de regno Christi, consentaneum quoque erit, concedere ea, quæ Dauid de se in sua causa pro tempore cecinit, etiam Christo seu humiliato, seu glorificato competere, & vaticinia de regno Christi ab eodem Dauide plurima esse edita. Facit insuper huc, quod Roman. 15. ex hocipso Psalmo testimonium de vocatione gentium ad regnum Christi proferatur, hisce verbis:Propter hoc confitebor tibi in gentibus, & nomini tuo canam.Et certum est, Apostolum non ita fuisse vsurum hoc testimonio, nisi edoctus fuisset & a spiritu Sancto, & a maioribus,eum Psalmum de Christo eiusque regno concionari. Præterea inspersa sunt non pauca eidem Psalmo,quę de regno & potentia Dauidis non satis aptè exponas,Christo autè mirè conueniunt, cuiusmodi sunt illa:Eripies me de contradictionibus populi,constitues me in caput gentium:populus,quē non cognoui,seruiuit mihi,in auditu auris obediuit mihi. Quibus sanè verbis clarissimè describitur vocatio gentium,quæ auditu verbi ad obedientiam fidei adducerentur. Sed & miracula pluribus versibus descripta,nempe vbi dicitur,commota est,& contremuit terra, fundamenta montium conturbata sunt, quoniam iratus est eis, & quæ octauo aut nono deinceps versibus continentur,haud scio,an de Dauide posint explicari, cùm talia in ipsius gratiam facta Scriptura non memoret: Sed Christo, in cuius morte talia signa in terra & cœlo sunt conspecta, rectè aptantur.
