Quæ rationes efficiunt, vt de Christo tum psalmum illum non abs re interpretemur, & quæ Dauid tanquam de se cecinerit, eadem Christi causam præfigurasse. Ac nisi psalmus adeo esset prolixus, nos ista omnia fusius aperiremus. Proinde verba psalmi hoc loco citata,Christus ad patrem loquens tempore acerbæ suæ afflictionis,vsurpat in hunc modum:
units.tr: If, then, it pleases us to think this testimony was taken from Psalm 17, it can be shown without difficulty that it is rightly attributed to Christ. For although the title in Hebrew speaks of an epinicion, that is a song of thanksgiving, sung by David after he had been freed from the snares of all his adversaries, and especially of Saul and his household, yet, since it cannot be denied that David, both when he was humbled and when he obtained new glory, was in many respects a type of Christ, and at times while acting prophesied of his own kingdom and of the kingdom of Christ, it will also be fitting to concede that what David sang of himself in his own cause at the time applies to Christ, whether humbled or glorified, and that many prophecies about the kingdom of Christ were uttered by this same David. It also bears on this point that Romans 15 quotes from this very Psalm a testimony about the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of Christ, in these words: "Therefore I will confess to thee among the Gentiles, and sing to thy name." And it is certain that the Apostle would not have used this testimony in this way unless he had been taught both by the Holy Spirit and by the elders that this Psalm speaks of Christ and his kingdom. Moreover, there are not a few things scattered through the same Psalm which cannot be explained very aptly of David's kingdom and power, but fit Christ wonderfully, such as these: "Thou wilt deliver me from the contradictions of the people; thou wilt make me the head of the nations; a people whom I have not known has served me; at the hearing of the ear it has obeyed me." These words describe most clearly the calling of the Gentiles, who by hearing the word were to be brought to the obedience of faith. But also the miracles described in several verses, namely where it says, "The earth shook and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were disturbed, because he was angry with them," and what is contained in the eighth or ninth verses following, I do not know whether they can be explained of David, since Scripture does not record such things done in David's favour; but they are rightly applied to Christ, in whose death such signs were seen in earth and heaven. These reasons mean that we interpret that Psalm not without cause of Christ, and that what David sang as of himself foreshadowed the cause of Christ. And if the Psalm were not so long, we would set out all these things more fully. Therefore Christ, speaking to the Father at the time of his bitter affliction, uses the words of the Psalm cited here in this way:

units.la: Diligam te Domine fortitudo mea, Dominus firmamentum meum, & refugium meum,& liberator meus. Deus meus, adiutor meus,& sperabo in eum,protector meus,& cornu salutis meæ,& susceptor meus.
units.tr: I will love thee, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my firmament, and my refuge, and my deliverer. My God, my helper, and I will hope in him, my protector, and the horn of my salvation, and my supporter.

units.la: Sunt omnia magno cum affectu enunciata. Hic verò dicitur: Et sperabo in eum, pro eo: quod in Esaia est, Et ero fidens in illo, vel, confidam: quod Christus suo iure potuit dicere, vt pote qui certus erat,se ab afflictione illa liberandum,& ad amplissimam gloriam prouehendum. Vide lib. tertium,sententiarum,distinctione vigesimatertia, (quæritur vtrùm in Christo fuerit fides & spes) distinctione vigesimasexta, ad finem, respondetur quæstioni longè alia ratione, quàm nos speramus siue credimus. Nam Christus non quasi in ænigmate aut speculo, vti nos videmus per fidem:sed iam clarissima cognitione & perspicuè videbat ea,quæ credebat. Atque ipse etiam in illa extrema necessitate solus perstitit, fidens in Deum, cùm cæteri omnes Apostoli offendiculum passi ex tanta humiliatione Christi fugerent:sicut ipse quoque illis prædixerat Matthæi capite vigesimo sexto, Omnes vos offendiculum patiemini mea causa in nocte hac: Scriptum est enim: Percutiam pastorem,& dispergentur oues gregis.
units.tr: All these things are uttered with great feeling. But here it says, "And I will hope in him," in place of what is in Isaiah, "And I will be trusting in him," or "I will trust," which Christ could rightly say of himself, as one who was certain that he would be delivered from that affliction and raised to the most ample glory. See book three of the Sentences, distinction 23 (where it is asked whether there was faith and hope in Christ), and distinction 26 at the end, where the question is answered in a quite different way from how we hope or believe. For Christ did not see those things he believed as in an enigma or a mirror, as we see through faith; he saw them with the clearest knowledge and plainly. And in that extreme necessity he alone persisted, trusting in God, when all the other Apostles, stumbling at the offence of Christ's great humiliation, fled; as he himself had also foretold them in Matthew 26: "You will all be offended because of me this night; for it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered."

units.la: Neque verò est diuersitas vlla, quod ad sententiam attinet, quando vno loco dicitur, Confidam in illum, altero, Sperabo in eum: sicut etiam hic in hebræo,licet diuersa sunt vocabula,in Esaia & in psalmo. Nam fides & spes sic sunt agnata sibi inuicem, vt separari ægrè queant, & pro eodem sæpè accipiantur,id quod ex illa descriptione fidei, quæ habetur Hebræorum vndecimo,potest colligi:qua dicitur, Fides est earum rerum, quæ sperantur, substantia & argumentum eorum,quæ non videntur: Vbi fides per spem definitur.
units.tr: Nor is there any difference as to the sense when in one place it says, "I will trust in him," and in another, "I will hope in him," just as here in the Hebrew, though the words are different, in Isaiah and in the Psalm. For faith and hope are so closely bound together that they can hardly be separated, and are often taken for the same thing, which can be gathered from that description of faith found in Hebrews 11: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen," where faith is defined by hope.

units.la: Proinde nihil aliud significatur, quàm Christum omnem fidem seu fiduciam, aut spem, si velis,coniecisse in Deum patrem, & pro certo habuisse, secuturam post extremam illam deiectionem longè maiorem glorificationem. Hoc autem pacto sperare & confidere in Deum,humanam conditionem in Christo palàm arguit, qua solaipse Deo patre inferior est, & sperare seu credere dici potest. Cæterùm ex hac fide & constantia Christi,nos quoq; discere debemus. Doctrina hæc breuiter excerpi hinc potest:quòd omnes debemus in Deum fidere,toti ex illo pendere. Et si Christus ita describitur fidens in Deum,qui tamen diuina sua virtute nunquam fuit destitutus, multò magis nos miseros & calamitosos,qui nihil ex nobis possumus,id facere decet,modò in aduersis constistere & inuicti permanere concupiscimus.
units.tr: Therefore nothing else is signified than that Christ placed all his faith, or trust (if you prefer, hope), in God the Father, and held for certain that after that extreme abasement a far greater glorification would follow. Yet to hope and trust in God in this way plainly shows the human condition in Christ, in which alone he is inferior to God the Father, and can be said to hope or to believe. Moreover, we too ought to learn from this faith and steadfastness of Christ. This doctrine may be briefly drawn from it: that all of us ought to trust in God and depend wholly on him. And if Christ is described as trusting in God, though he was never forsaken by his own divine power, how much more fitting it is for us, wretched and miserable as we are, who can do nothing of ourselves, to do the same, if we wish to stand firm in adversity and remain unconquered.

units.la: Et iterum : Ecce ego & pueri, quos mihi dedit Deus.
units.tr: And again: Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.

units.la: Tertium testimonium, in quo Christus se pueris seu discipulis suis æquat, quos & a Deo patre tanquam superiore se accepisse fatetur. Atqui istud non conuenit de Christo accipi,nisi secundum humanam naturam,quia sola potest esse discipulis æqualis & patre inferior. Ergo Christus licet sit Deus,tamen etiam homo esse intelligitur: & hominem cum futurum fuerat diuinitus præordinatum,atque à Prophetis prædictum: & minimè pro absurdo habendum, quòd, quem Deum ab æterno dicimus, in tempore homo factus sit. Habentur autem hæc verba Esaiæ capite octauo, ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἃ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ θεός, חנה אנכי והילדים אשר נתן לי יהוה. De Christo autem accipienda esse partim ex eo,quòd illo capite diuersa, eaque manifestissima de Christo continentur vaticinia: partim,quòd quæ ibi proximè præcedunt,in nouo testamento non vno loco citantur, &
units.tr: This is the third testimony, in which Christ puts himself on a level with the children, or disciples, whom he confesses he has received from God the Father as his superior: Behold, I and the children whom God has given me [ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἃ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ θεός], Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me [חנה אנכי והילדים אשר נתן לי יהוה]. But this cannot be taken of Christ except according to his human nature, since only that nature can be equal to the disciples and inferior to the Father. Therefore Christ, although he is God, is also understood to be man; and it is not absurd that he who we say is God from eternity was made man in time, since this was divinely foreordained and foretold by the prophets. That these words of Isaiah in chapter eight are to be taken of Christ is shown partly by the fact that this chapter contains various and very plain prophecies about Christ, and partly by the fact that the passages immediately preceding it are cited in many places in the New Testament and are explained of Christ. The prophet reads thus:

units.la: k de Christo explicantur. Sic vero legitur apud Prophetam: Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate, & ipse pavor vester, & ipse terror vester, & erit vobis in sanctificationem, in lapidem autem offensionis & petram scandali duabus domibus Israel, & in laqueum, & in ruinam habitantibus Hierusalem: & offendent ex eis plurimi, & cadent, & conterentur, & irretientur, & capientur. Liga testimonium, signa legem in discipulis meis, expectabo Dominum, qui abscondit faciem suam a domo Iacob, & praestolabor eum. Ecce ego & pueri mei, quos dedit mihi Dominus in signum, & in portentum Israel a Domino exercituum, qui habitat in monte Sion.
units.tr: Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself, and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the two houses of Israel, and for a gin and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken. Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples. I will wait for the LORD, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him. Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me for signs and wonders in Israel, from the LORD of hosts, who dwells in Mount Zion.

units.la: Vbi cum illa priora, quod videlicet is, qui erit in sanctificatione, futurus sit ipsis etiam in lapidem offensionis, & petram scandali domibus Israel, & in ruinam habitantibus Hierusalem, exponuntur de Christo, tum Lucae 2. a Simeone, tum ad Roman. 9. a Paulo: tum a Petro prioris epistolae capite secundo: (etiamsi Simeon respexisse videtur ad illa, quae in eandem sententiam habentur Zachariae 14. Paulus vero ad similia verba Esaiae 28) aequo est sentire, & praesentis loci verba, quae statim subiiciuntur, de Christo esse accipienda. Quod si qui contendat, haec verba, Ego & pueri mei: Prophetae esse, non Christi, non possunt tamen inficias ire. Prophetam subinde in persona Christi loqui, & typum Christi gerere. Quare vel hac ratione verba illa Christo recte attribuentur. Quod eo iustius est concedendum, quod diversis in locis novi testamenti tantundem significantia de Christo dicta occurrunt. Quantum enim ad primum membrum attinet, quo ait, datos sibi pueros a Deo patre, conveniunt haec cum illis, quae habentur Ioan. 17. Manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi de mundo. Tui erat, & mihi dedisti eos, & sermonem tuum servaverunt. Ibidem: Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his, quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt. Ibidem: Quos dedisti mihi, custodivi, & nemo ex eis periit, nisi filius perditionis: & alia, quae sequuntur. Huc item referri poterit illud Ioan. 6. Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Vbi autem discipulos suos vocet pueros, locus est Ioan. 21, ubi stans in littore & non agnitus a discipulis, ait illis: Pueri, num quid obsonij habetis? De qua appellatione mox iterum dicemus. Quantum vero ad alterum membrum attinet, quo ait, se & pueros esse in signum & portentum Israel, quibus verbis notat, se cum suis irrideri, ludibrio haberi, contemni, & oppugnari. Haec mire conveniunt cum eo, quod Simeon ait de Christo. Ecce positus est hic in ruinam, & in resurrectionem multorum in Israel: Item cum illo Ioannis septimo, Me odit mundus, quia ego testimonium fero de illo, quod opera eius mala sint. Et Ioannis decimo quinto, Si mundus vos odit, scitis quod me prius, quam vos, odio habuerit, &c. Quia de mundo non estis. Sed ego selegi vos de mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Item 1. Cor. 4. Arbitror, quod Deus nos, qui sumus Apostoli postremi, ostenderit tanquam morti addictos: quoniam spectaculum facti sumus mundo, & angelis & hominibus. Nos stulti propter Christum, vos autem prudentes per Christum. Et mox subiicit: veluti excrementa mundi facti sumus, omnium rei ectamentum ad hunc usque diem. Ex his igitur videre est, quam valde apposite verba illa psalmi Christi accommodent.
units.tr: Where those earlier words, that he who shall be for sanctification shall also be to the houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem a ruin, are explained of Christ, both by Simeon in Luke 2 and by Paul in Romans 9, and by Peter in the second chapter of his first epistle (although Simeon seems to have had in view those things that stand to the same effect in Zechariah 14, and Paul the similar words of Isaiah 28), it is equally right to understand the words of the present passage, which immediately follow, as being about Christ as well. And if anyone contends that these words, I and my children, belong to the prophet and not to Christ, they cannot nonetheless deny that the prophet at times speaks in the person of Christ and bears the type of Christ. Therefore these words may rightly be attributed to Christ even on this ground, and this is the more justly conceded because in various places of the New Testament there occur sayings about Christ which signify the same thing. As far as the first member is concerned, where he says that the children were given to him by God the Father, these agree with what is found in John 17: "I have manifested thy name unto the men whom thou gavest me out of the world; thine they were, and thou gavest them me, and they have kept thy word." And again: "I pray not for the world, but for them whom thou hast given me, for they are thine." And again: "Those whom thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition." And other things that follow. To this may also be referred that passage of John 6: "No man can come to me, except the Father which sent me draw him." But where he calls his disciples children is in John 21, where, standing on the shore and not recognised by the disciples, he says to them: "Children, have ye any meat?" We shall speak again of this form of address shortly. As far as the second member is concerned, where he says that he and the children are for a sign and a wonder in Israel, by these words he indicates that he and his people are mocked, held in derision, despised, and assailed. These agree wonderfully with what Simeon says of Christ: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel." Likewise with that in John 7: "The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil." And John 15: "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you... Because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you." Also 1 Cor. 4: "I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death; for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men. We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ." And soon after he adds: "We are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day." From these things, therefore, one can see how very aptly those words of the psalm fit Christ.

units.la: Si quis autem illud Esaiae 8. capite plenius & oculatius inspexerit, in ueniet praeclara ibi, sicut praecedentibus & sequentibus capitibus, de Christo vaticinia. Nam statim initio capitis propheta iubetur scribere nomen pueri nati ex insigni prophetissa, (qua intelligere convenit beatam virginem, de qua & capite 7. dixit, Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabis nomen eius Immanuel) haec imponitur puero nomina מהר שלל חש בז, id est, festina praedicari, & חש בז, id est, accelera direptione: additurque, quod is, priusquam posset vocare patrem suum, aut matrem suam, tolleret fortitudinem Damasci, & spolia Samariae coram rege Assyriorum. Quod sane non nisi de Christo potest accipi, qui vere spoliavit diabolum & omnes eius copias (quae significatae sunt per regem Assyriorum) qui & Lucae 11. describitur fortis ille armatus superveniens, & vincens alterum, & universa eius arma auferens, & spolia distribuens: & per quem, ut habetur Ioan. 12. & 16. princeps mundi huius eiectus est foras. Coloss 2. Expoliatos principatus ac potestates ostentavit palam triumphans de illis per semetipsum. Ephes. 4. Ascendens in altum captivam duxit captivitatem, & dedit dona hominibus. Deinde per Apostrophen ad hostes, quod tamen non potuerint praevalere: Congregamini populi, & vincemini: & audite universae procul terrae: confortamini, & vincemini, accingite vos, & vincemini: inite consilium, & disipabitur: loquimini verbum, & non fiet, quia nobiscum Deus, vel, (ut hebraice habetur, Immanuel. Praeterea bis habetur hoc capite venerandum illud nomen עמנו אל, primo sic, Et erit extensis alarum eius (scilicet regis Assyriorum cum omnibus adiunctis populis qui veniunt ad vastandam Iudaeam) implens latitudinem terrae tuae o Immanuel. Quod Christi proprium esse satis indicatur Matthaei primo, ubi ita dicit Angelus ad Ioseph, pariet autem filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum. Is enim salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis suis. Porro totum hoc factum est, ut perficeretur id, quod dictum fuerat a Domino per prophetam ita loquentem: Ecce hic Ecce uirgo crit prægnans, & pariet filium, & uocabunt nomen eius Immanuel, quod si quis interpretatur, sonat nobiscum Deus. Quem locum & euangelista citat ex Esaiæ capite septimo. Proinde hæc visum fuit indicare, ut quando adeo manifestè Esaias illo capite octauo de Christo vaticinatur, eo clarius intelligatur & certius, verba præsenti loco citata Christo conuenire.
units.tr: If anyone examines that eighth chapter of Isaiah more fully and attentively, he will find there, as in the preceding and following chapters, remarkable prophecies about Christ. For at the very beginning of the chapter the prophet is commanded to write the name of a son born of a notable prophetess (whom it is fitting to understand as the blessed Virgin, of whom also in chapter 7 he said, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel"). To this child are given the names Maher-shalal-hash-baz [מהר שלל חש בז], that is, "Hasten to the spoil, accelerate the prey," and it is added that before he could call his father or mother he would carry off the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria before the king of Assyria. This can truly be understood only of Christ, who truly despoiled the devil and all his forces (which are signified by the king of Assyria), who in Luke 11 is described as the strong man armed coming upon the other, overcoming him, taking away all his armour, and distributing his spoils; and through whom, as we read in John 12 and 16, the prince of this world was cast out. Colossians 2: "Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in himself." Ephesians 4: "When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men." Then, by an address to the enemies, that yet they shall not prevail: "Gather yourselves together, O peoples, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and give ear, all ye of far countries; gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces; take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand, for God is with us," or, as it is in the Hebrew, Immanuel [עמנו אל]. Moreover, this venerable name Immanuel [עמנו אל] occurs twice in this chapter: first thus, "And the stretching out of his wings (namely of the king of Assyria with all the peoples joined to him who come to lay waste Judah) shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel." That this is proper to Christ is sufficiently indicated in Matthew 1, where the angel speaks thus to Joseph: "She shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus; for he shall save his people from their sins." Indeed, all this came to pass that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." The evangelist cites this passage from Isaiah chapter 7. Therefore I thought it worth pointing out these things, so that since Isaiah so plainly prophesies of Christ in that eighth chapter, the words cited in the present passage may be understood more clearly and certainly to agree with Christ.

units.la: Cæterùm, quod ad voces attinet: nan Ecce, vox est Emphatica, certitudinem & obedientiam ac promptitudinem indicans: sicut reuera Christus patri fuit obedientissimus: tantum reddenda ratio est vocis Puerorum. Hæc autem vox sæpè apud græcos, vti & apud Latinos, pro famulis & ministris siue seruis accipitur, licet non apud Hebræos, quibus ילד puerum vel filium significat: vide ילדים vt 1. Regum 21. Si mundi sunt pueri, maximè à mulieribus, manducent. Vbi sanè non de pueris ætate sermo est, sed de ministris & famulis illis, qui Dauidem in fuga comitabatur, & defendere ac pugnare pro eo erant parati. Verùm hoc loco accipitur pro discipulis, & in genere pro omnibus adhærentibus Christo, & credentibus in eum, quos pater ei dedit, tradidit, commisit: quomodo Christum quoq; appellasse suos discipulos suprà meminimus, ex capite Ioannis vltimo: quomodo item Actor. 4. Dauid vocatur puer in oratione apostolorum dicentium: Domine tu es Deus, qui fecisti cœlum ac terram, mare & omnia, quæ in eis sunt, qui per os Dauid pueri tui dixisti: Quare fremuerunt gentes? &c. Quamuis hic puer pro ministro, famulo, seruo non malè sumatur: præsenti tamen loco ita accipienda est vox puerorum, vt etiam humana indoles, natura, & substantia, per eam significetur: atq; ita declaratur, Christum esse æqualem, quantum ad naturam humanam attinet, cæteris hominibus, sic enim argumenti ratio postulat. Atque huc facit, quod ipse Apostolus mox interpretatione subiicit: Posteaquam igitur pueri commertium habent cum carne & sanguine, & ipse similiter particeps factus est eorundem.
units.tr: Furthermore, as to the words: "Ecce" (behold) is an emphatic word, indicating certainty, obedience and readiness, just as Christ was in truth most obedient to the Father. Only the reason for the word Puerorum ("of the children") must be given. This word is often taken among the Greeks, as among the Latins, for servants, attendants or slaves, though not among the Hebrews, for whom ילד [yeled] means a child or son; see ילדים [yeladim], as in 1 Kings 21: "If the young men are clean, especially from women, let them eat." There, certainly, the talk is not of children by age, but of those servants who accompanied David in his flight and were ready to defend him and fight for him. In this place, however, the word is taken for disciples, and generally for all who cling to Christ and believe in him, whom the Father gave, delivered and committed to him. So we noted above that Christ called his disciples this in the last chapter of John; likewise in Acts 4 David is called "servant" in the prayer of the apostles, who say: "Lord, you are the God who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, who through the mouth of David your servant said: Why did the nations rage? etc." Although this "child" is not badly taken for minister, attendant or slave, in the present place the word "children" must be understood so that it also signifies human nature, condition and substance; and thus it is declared that Christ, as far as human nature is concerned, is equal to other men, for the logic of the argument demands this. And to this the Apostle himself points by the explanation he adds straight after: Since therefore the children have fellowship in flesh and blood, he himself likewise was made partaker of the same.

units.la: Quomodo verò Deus pater dicatur aliquos dare filio, id perspicuum fit ex locis suprà citatis, qui satis ostendunt, illos proprie à Deo patre dari filio, quos ipse sua diuina potentia & spiritu mouet occulte, excitatq; ad audiendum & sequendum Iesum suum filium. Omnes hoc pacto diuinitus provocati & excitati, sunt Christo à Deo patre dati. Nam ad Christum venire, eiq; toto corde adhærere, non est volentis, neq; currentis, vt Romano 9. rectè dicitur, sed Dei miserentis. Deus pater volens ostendere iram & potentiam suam, vt ibidem dicitur, fert multa animi lenitate vasa iræ apparata in interitum, atq; ita, sicut Roman. 1. loquitur Apostolus, tradit illos in sensum reprobum. Rursus autem volens notas facere diuitias gloriæ suæ erga uasa misericordiæ, quæ præparauerat in gloriam, tradit eos Christo, gregi Christi inserit, vult ad suum ouile pertinere.
units.tr: How God the Father is said to give some to the Son is made plain from the passages cited above, which sufficiently show that those are properly given by God the Father to the Son whom he secretly moves by his divine power and Spirit, and stirs up to hear and follow Jesus his Son. All who are thus divinely called and stirred up are given to Christ by God the Father. For to come to Christ and cleave to him with the whole heart is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, as is rightly said in Romans 9, but of God who has mercy. God the Father, wishing to show his wrath and power, as it says there, endures with great patience the vessels of wrath made ready for destruction, and so, as the Apostle says in Romans 1, he gives them up to a reprobate mind. But again, wishing to make known the riches of his glory towards the vessels of mercy, which he had prepared for glory, he gives them to Christ, inserts them into the flock of Christ, and wills that they belong to his own fold.

units.la: Cæterùm, hanc habemus hoc loco doctrinam, quòd omnes, qui Christo adhæremus, euangeliumq; eius amplectimur, ei sumus quodammodo pares, & ab illo pro conseruis, socijs, & cohæredibus agnoscimur, maximeq; cùm exemplo illius à mundo contemnimur, irridemur, diuexamur, sicut apud Esaiam loquitur. Quare in gentem consolatio- nem hinc possumus in tanto, qui nunc est contemptu ministrorum verbi, accipere, si in hanc dignitatem nostram intueamur. 1. Cor. 3. appellantur ministri verbi cooperarij Dei, & ministri Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei: sicut pueri seu ministri habent sua officia in magna aliqua familia. Discimus & hoc, quòd nos ita viuere deceat, vt agnosci possimus palam pro pueris Christi: deinde, quòd gratias agere debeamus Deo, qui nos nullis nostris meritis præeuntibus, vel sequentibus, dignatus est in puerorum Christi numerum cooptare. Quandoquidè, vt dicitur Ephes. 1. elegit, prædestinauit nos, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, antequam quicquam boni aut mali egissemus (sicut Roman. 9. dicitur de Iacob & Esau) vt essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles coram illo, vt simus in laudem gloriæ ipsius. Sed quando intueor huiusmodi testimonia ab Apostolo hic cita, subit animum admiratio, qui factum sit, quòd Apostolus hæc potius, quàm alia volue- rit citare, cùm passim multa occurrant, quæ quodammodo clarius & efficacius humanitatem Christi exprimunt: quale est illud Esaiæ 7. Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Immanuel, butyrum & mel comedet, vt sciat reprobare malum, & eligere bonum. Hæc verba multò manifestissimè humanam naturam exprimunt. Et quærenti eiusmodi innumera obuenirent, & nos, volente Deo, ad finem huius disputationis plura in medium proferemus. Sed huic dubitationi facilè est respondere. Satis fuit Apostolo pauca proferre testimonia: quandoquidem ipse semper est breuiloquus, & satis est in disputando vnum aut alterum efficax firmamentum nostrarum rationum proferre. Hæc autem voluit Apostolus eligere primò, quia euidentissimè in illis æquatur Christus cæteris hominibus, & naturæ eorum per omnia particeps ostenditur. Cùm enim reliquos homines vocat suos fratres, cùm se æquat cæteris pueris, nonne hæc clarissimè indicant æqualitatem naturæ?
units.tr: Moreover, we have in this place the doctrine that all of us who cleave to Christ and embrace his gospel are in a sense equal to him, and are acknowledged by him as fellow-servants, companions and co-heirs; and especially when, after his example, we are despised, mocked and harassed by the world, as he speaks of it in Isaiah. Hence we may draw consolation for the great contempt now shown to the ministers of the Word, if we look upon this our dignity. In 1 Corinthians 3 the ministers of the Word are called fellow-workers of God, ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, just as children or servants have their duties in some great household. We learn also that we ought to live in such a way that we may be recognised openly as children of Christ; and then that we ought to give thanks to God, who, with no merits of ours going before or following, has deigned to enrol us in the number of the children of Christ. For, as it says in Ephesians 1, he chose us and predestined us before the foundations of the world were laid, before we had done anything good or evil (as is said of Jacob and Esau in Romans 9), that we should be holy and blameless before him, to the praise of his glory. But when I consider such testimonies as the Apostle cites here, wonder comes over me why the Apostle preferred to cite these rather than others, since many everywhere occur which express the humanity of Christ in a somewhat clearer and more effective way, such as that of Isaiah 7: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Immanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good." These words express the human nature far more plainly. And if one were looking for such things, countless ones would come to hand, and we, God willing, will bring forward more of them towards the end of this discussion. But this doubt is easily answered. It was enough for the Apostle to offer a few testimonies, since he himself is always brief in speech, and in disputing it is enough to bring forward one or two effective props for our arguments. The Apostle chose these, however, first because in them Christ is most plainly made equal to other men, and is shown to share their nature in all things. For when he calls the rest of men his brothers, when he puts himself on a level with the other children, do not these things most clearly indicate equality of nature?

units.la: Secundò, maluit fortasis illa eligere, quia etiam officium Christi, quantum ad euangelij propagationem, materiam, successum, aliquo modo declarant. Nam in primo testimonio significatur, Christum esse factum hominem, vt euangelium mundo afferret. In secundo, præterquam quòd Christum esse inferiorem Deo patre arguitur, tum fides in Deum commendatur: quo verbo summa & caput doctrinæ euangelicæ comprehenditur. In tertio vocatio hominum ad Euangelium, & iudicij mundi de eodem tacitè indicatur. Hinc ergo apparet factum, quòd ista potius, quàm alia testimonia ad confirmandum propositum elegerit. Potest & hæc addi ratio, quòd his testimonijs Dei bonitas erga homines illustratur, & nostra dignitas, magis quàm vllis alijs testimonijs. Bonitas Dei, quia nomesuum voluit nobis manifestari per proprium filium, quia item dedit nos Christo, & nos dummodò fidamus, seruare, tueri. Dignitas nostra, quòd fratres Christi, quòd pueri Christi, appellamur. Quanquam & ideo factum istud ab Apostolo dici potest, quòd fortassis ista testimonia in eiusmodi disputationibus de vtraque natura Christi, & inprimis humana, fuerint passim fere q; à vulgo vsurpata, & à quibusdam Rabinis aliquando de Mesia venturo expositta.
units.tr: Secondly, he perhaps preferred to choose those because they also set out in some measure the office of Christ, as regards the spread of the gospel, its subject-matter and its success. For in the first testimony it is signified that Christ was made man in order to bring the gospel to the world. In the second, besides showing that Christ is inferior to God the Father, faith in God is commended, a word in which the sum and head of evangelical doctrine is comprehended. In the third the calling of men to the gospel and the judgement of the world concerning it are tacitly indicated. Hence it is evident why he chose these testimonies rather than others to confirm his point. This reason may also be added: that by these testimonies the goodness of God towards men is illustrated, and our dignity, more than by any other testimonies. The goodness of God, because he willed to make his name known to us through his own Son, and because he has given us to Christ and, provided we trust in him, keeps and guards us. Our dignity, because we are called brothers of Christ, children of Christ. Yet this may also be the reason the Apostle said this: perhaps these testimonies were in such disputations about the two natures of Christ, and especially the human, commonly used almost everywhere by the people, and at times expounded by some rabbis as referring to the Messiah to come.

units.la: Posteaquam igitur pueri commertium habent cum carne & sanguine, & ipse similiter particeps factus est eorundem.
units.tr: Since therefore the children have fellowship in flesh and blood, he himself likewise was made partaker of the same.

units.la: Illatio est, perficiens ex proximis verbis Enthymema seu Syllogismum: quasi diceret, in hoc testimonio Christus se componit cum pueris, vt per omnia parè & æqualem: sed illi pueri sunt veri homines, constantes carne & sanguine. Ergo & Christus est verus homo, constans carne & sanguine. Quemadmodum autem hic infert ex proximo testimonio: ita ex duobus prioribus rectè inferri posset, nempe, quòd, quoniâ fratres, & quicunq; fidentes in Deû, sunt veri homines, constantes carne & sanguine, Christus quoq; verus homo constans carne & sanguine debet intelligi. Atq; ita abundè satis confirmatû esse vult hisce testimonijs, quòd Christum secundû dispensationem Dei patris decuerit humanam naturam assumere, minimeq; pro absurdo habendum, quòd qui Deus erat ab æterno, in tempore homo factus dicatur.
units.tr: This is an inference, completing from the preceding words an enthymeme or syllogism: as if he were saying, in this testimony Christ puts himself on a level with the children, so as to be equal to them in all things; but those children are true men, consisting of flesh and blood. Therefore Christ too is a true man, consisting of flesh and blood. Just as he here infers from the nearer testimony, so from the two earlier ones one could rightly infer that, since brothers, and all who trust in God, are true men consisting of flesh and blood, Christ too must be understood as a true man consisting of flesh and blood. And so he wishes it to be sufficiently confirmed by these testimonies that it was fitting, according to the dispensation of God the Father, for Christ to assume human nature, and that it is by no means to be held absurd that he who was God from eternity should be said to have been made man in time.

units.la: Hoc verò hoc loco tantùm annotadum, quid nomine carnis & sanguinis intelligatur. Proinde caro & sanguis, hæc duo coniuncta, eodê fere modo accipiuntur subinde, quo vox Caro sola & seorsim posita. Aliquando enim caro & sanguis, sola posita, significat non solûm naturam humanam, sed præterea vitia & malitiam illi congenitam, adeoque ipsos affectus peruersi ingenij, libere agentis pro suo nutu: & spiritus Sancti auxilio destituti. Roman. 8. Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. Ibidé, si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Et cû hoc pacto accipitur caro, ei plerûq; opponitur Spiritus, vtriusq; fructus seu effectus aptè describûtur Gal. 5. Simili significatione videtur dictum 1. Cor. 15. Hoc autem dico fratres, quòd caro & sanguis regni Dei hæreditatem consequi non possunt. Neq; enim corruptio incorruptibilitatis hæreditatem accipit. Vbi non significatur, quòd corpora ista, quæ constant carne & sanguine, sint excludêda à gloria: sed potius, vt vitio & peccato sunt obnoxia, vt primum hominem terrenum referunt naturæ malitia. Nam corpora quidem eadem materia gloriam à resurrectione accipient, sed reuera valdè immutata, & solûm non ita immutata, vt mori amplius non possint, sed vt nec peccare amplius possint, quandoquidem referent secundum hominem cœlestè, Christum vide licet: erunt omnes sicut angeli Dei æternis laudibus Dei occupati. Alias verò caro, siue caro & sanguis, significat simpliciter humanam naturam, siue homines, prout carne & sanguine constat, veluti materia, fragilitatem tamen & miseriam humanam pariter indicando, sed nô ita, vti prioribus locis vitiatâ & peccatis obnoxiam malitiâ. Sic Matt. 26. Christus de natura humana, qualem ipse in se sentiebat: Spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma. Ioan. 3. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est: quod natû est ex spiritu, spiritus est. Similiter Matth. 16. ad Petrû, postquam confessus fuit Christi diuinitatê: Beatus es Simon Bar Iona, quia caro & sanguis nô reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus, qui est in cœlis. Vbi caro & sanguis idê, quòd homo vel humana natura. Eodem modo Galat. 1. Ast vbi Deo visum est, vt prædicarem ipsum inter gentes, continuò non contuli cum carne & sanguine, id est, cum vllo homine, neq; redij Hierosolymâ ad eos, qui ante me fuerât apostoli: sed ab ij in Arabiam, &c. In hunc igitur modum hoc loco accipitur caro & sanguis, vt videlicet significet tantùm humanam naturam, fragilem & infirmâ: eiusq; particeps factus dicitur Christus, qui reuera naturam humanam in se recepit, prorsus eodem modo, quo nos, excepta illa malitia ingenita & impellente ad peccandum, quia ille caruit, quia aliter, quàm nos, conceptus. Quòd peccatum non nouerit: 2. Corinth. 5. Eum qui non nouit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos iustitia efficeremur per illum, 1. Petri 2. Christus afflictus est pro nobis, relinquens
units.tr: Here, however, it need only be noted what is meant by the name of flesh and blood. Flesh and blood, these two joined together, are taken at times in much the same way as the word flesh alone and by itself. For sometimes flesh and blood, used alone, signifies not only human nature but also the vices and malice innate in it, and so the very affections of a perverse mind, acting freely at its own will and destitute of the help of the Holy Spirit. Romans 8: "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God." And there: "If you live according to the flesh, you will die." And when flesh is taken in this way, Spirit is usually set against it, and the fruits or effects of each are aptly described in Galatians 5. In a similar sense it seems to be said in 1 Corinthians 15: "Now this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; nor does corruption inherit incorruptibility." Here it is not signified that these bodies, which consist of flesh and blood, are to be excluded from glory; but rather, insofar as they are subject to vice and sin, insofar as the malice of nature brings back the first earthly man. For the same material bodies will indeed receive glory at the resurrection, but truly greatly changed; and not only so changed that they can no longer die, but so that they can no longer sin either, since they will bear the image of the heavenly man, namely Christ; all will be like the angels of God, occupied with eternal praises of God. Elsewhere, however, flesh, or flesh and blood, simply signifies human nature, or men insofar as they consist of flesh and blood as their matter, while equally indicating human frailty and misery, but not in the way that in the earlier passages it signifies what is corrupted and liable to sin through malice. So in Matthew 26 Christ speaks of human nature as he himself felt it: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." John 3: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." Similarly Matthew 16, to Peter, after he confessed the divinity of Christ: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." Here flesh and blood means the same as man or human nature. In the same way Galatians 1: "But when it pleased God to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not confer with flesh and blood, that is, with any man, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but went away into Arabia, etc." In this way, then, flesh and blood is taken in this place, to signify only human nature, frail and weak; and Christ is said to have partaken of it, who truly took human nature upon himself in exactly the same way as we do, except that malice inborn and driving to sin, since he was free from it, because he was conceived otherwise than we are. That he knew no sin: 2 Corinthians 5: "He who knew no sin he made to be sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." 1 Peter 2: "Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow in his steps; he who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth."

units.la: Christus homo factus carnem et sanguinem assumpsit. Christus expers peccati. ques nobis exemplum, vt in sequere mini vestigia ipsius, qui peccatum non fecerat, nec inuentus est dolus in ore illius. Quod de Christo totidem verbis praedixit Esaias capite quinquagesimotertio, propterea Rom.8. dicitur. Quod lex praestare non poterat, ea parte, qua imbecillis erat per carne, hoc Deus &pprio filio misso sub specie carnis peccato obnoxiae praestitit, ac de peccato condenauit peccatu per carnem. En nō carne peccato obnoxia, sed sub specie carnis obnoxiae peccato. Vnde & Christus Ioan. 8. potuit dicere: Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? Ergo, vt finem faciamus, Caro & sanguis hic significat plane naturam humanam, fragilitatem omnem & miseriam nostram, sed citra peccati vitium consideratam: & summatim idem quod caro, Ioan.1. Vbi dicitur, Verbum caro factum est. Sic igitur Christus per omnia particeps factus est nostrae conditionis, omnes miserias accepit, quae in omnes homines naturaliter cadunt, demptis illis, quae peccato sunt coniunctae, & plenitudini gratiae eius detrahunt. Nam semper fatendum est, plenum gratiae & veritate eum visum: unde ignorantia & similia contraria gratiae, item peccatum in eo locum non habuerunt: caetera autem, vt mors, fames, sitis, lassi tudo, tristitia, & eiusmodi, quae ordinate in omnes cadunt, etiam in Christo conspecta sunt. Et propter hac causam usus est verbo μετέχω. Nam μετέχω idem est, quod particeps sum, participo, κοινωνέω, μεταλαμβάνω. Latini non habent proprium, quo reddant, nisi participare. Itaq; non omnia, quae sunt nostrae naturae assumpsit Christus, quia nequaquam vitia. Sed partem accepit. Nobiscum habuit carnem & sanguinem.
units.tr: Christ, made man, took on flesh and blood. Christ was free from sin, and he has become an example for us, so that we should follow in his steps, since he had committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. Isaiah foretold this of Christ in almost the same words in chapter fifty-three, and so Romans 8 says: what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and he condemned sin in the flesh. Notice: not flesh that is subject to sin, but in the likeness of flesh that is subject to sin. Hence Christ in John 8 could say: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" To sum up: flesh here plainly means human nature, all frailty and our misery, but considered apart from the taint of sin. In short it means the same as flesh in John 1, where it is said: "The Word became flesh." Thus Christ was made in every respect a partaker of our condition. He took on all the miseries that naturally fall upon all men, except those that are joined to sin and detract from the fullness of his grace. For we must always confess that he was seen as full of grace and truth; so ignorance and similar things contrary to grace, and likewise sin, had no place in him. But the other things, such as death, hunger, thirst, weariness, sadness and the like, which fall upon all men as a matter of course, were also seen in Christ. And for this reason he used the verb "partake" (μετέχω). For μετέχω means the same as "I am a partaker, I share in," (κοινωνέω, μεταλαμβάνω). The Latins have no word of their own to render it except "participate." Therefore Christ did not take on everything that belongs to our nature, since by no means did he take on its vices; but he took a part. He had flesh and blood in common with us.

units.la: Caeterum ex ipsis vocibus carnis & sanguinis admonemur nostrę vilitatis, fragilitatis, miseriae, & ad humilitatem debemus excitari. Recte dixit Iob capite septimo, Induta est caro mea putredine, & sordibus pulueris cutis mea, prima epistola Petri primo. Omnis caro gramen, & omnis gloria hominis quasi flos graminis. Exaruit gramen, & flos decidit: at verbum Domini manet in aeternum.
units.tr: Moreover, from the very words "flesh and blood" we are reminded of our baseness, frailty and misery, and we ought to be stirred to humility. Job rightly said in chapter seven: "My flesh is clothed with corruption and the dust and filth of my skin." And in the first chapter of the first epistle of Peter: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord abides for ever."

units.la: Quod si satis vellemus intueri, haud dubie multas peccatorum occasiones vitaremus, & huius mundi pompam, opes, factum non ita auide appeteremus. Praeterea hic habemus exemplum humilitatis in Christo, qui cum in forma Dei esset, semetipsum exinanivit, & nostrae salutis causa se humiliauit ad omnes miserias nostras in se recipiendum: atque adeo, vt carnem seu naturam nostram tam vilem ipse ad summam dignitatemueheret: quae dignitas propter eundem Christum a resurrectione omnibus sanctis dabitur, & sicut Christus participauit nobiscum in vilitate seu indignitate, ita nos cum illo participabimus in gloria.
units.tr: If we were willing to consider this carefully, we would undoubtedly avoid many occasions of sin, and would not so greedily seek after the pomp, wealth and deeds of this world. Besides, here we have an example of humility in Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself and, for the sake of our salvation, humbled himself so as to take upon himself all our miseries; and so he raised our flesh, or our nature, so vile, to the highest dignity. This dignity will be given to all the saints through the same Christ from the resurrection onward; and just as Christ shared with us in vileness or unworthiness, so we shall share with him in glory.

units.la: Porrò, & his vocibus carnis & sanguinis refellitur Marcion, qui negauit Christum habuisse verum corpus, sed tantum phantasticum. Certe cum particeps nostri dicitur effectus, habendo vnà nobiscum carnem & sanguinem, manifestum fit, eum carne & sanguinem habuisse, vti nos habemus. Huc etiam pertinet, quòd dicitur verbum caro factum, & quòd Christus aiebat, Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere, palpate, & videte, &c. Item Christus passim se vocat filium hominis.
units.tr: Furthermore, Marcion is also refuted by these words "flesh and blood," since he denied that Christ had a true body, but only an apparent one. Certainly when he is said to have become a partaker of us, having flesh and blood in common with us, it is clear that he had flesh and blood just as we have them. To this also belongs the statement that "the Word became flesh," and Christ's saying: "A spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have them; touch me and see," etc. Likewise, Christ everywhere calls himself the Son of Man.

units.la: Vt per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est diabolum, & libros redderet eos, quicunque metu mortis per omnem vitam obnoxij erant seruituti.
units.tr: That through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might free those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

units.la: Secunda ratio, quare decuerit Christum hominem fieri, sumpta a modo sanctificandi homines. Vt hac voce respiciamus ad primam illam rationem, qua dictum est, & eum qui sanctificat, et eos qui sanctificatur, ex vno esse. Est autem haec praesentis rationis sententia: Homines, quoniam, per peccatum obnoxij erant facti aeternae morti, debebant per mortem alicuius sanctificari seu liberari. Sed mori non potuisset Christus, nisi fieret homo. Ergo ob hanc causam decuit Christum homine fieri. Quae ratio necessario erat attexenda, quia nō profuisset humano generi, Christū nasci, nisi idem etiam fuisset mortuus, et sua morte humanam genus a morte aeterna asseruisset. Adhaerent autem verba haec praecedenti conclusioni, ut diuellenda non videantur. Sed sic saepe solet Apostolus etiam quae distincta & diuersa sunt, alijs illigare, ut nisi quis paulo oculatius intedat, distinctas esse rationes vix fit animaduersurus. Neq; erat admodum opus disiungere. Nam alias iterum decuisset repeti, Christum hominem factum, induisse carnem & sanguinem, aut aliquid huiusmodi, ac deinde prosequendum, ut per mortem aboleret eum, &c.
units.tr: The second reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man is taken from the manner of sanctifying men. By this phrase we look back to the first reason that was stated, namely that he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one. The sense of the present reason is this: men, because through sin they had become liable to eternal death, had to be sanctified, that is, freed, through the death of someone. But Christ could not have died unless he became man. Therefore for this reason it was fitting for Christ to become man. This reason had necessarily to be added, because it would not have profited the human race for Christ to be born unless he had also died and by his death had rescued the human race from eternal death. These words, however, are so joined to the preceding conclusion that they seem not to be separable from it. But the Apostle often does this, binding together things that are distinct and different, so that unless someone looks more closely he will hardly notice that the reasons are distinct. Nor was there any need to separate them. For otherwise it would have been necessary to repeat that Christ, made man, put on flesh and blood, or something of that sort, and then to continue, "that through death he might destroy him," etc.

units.la: Caeterum, Apostolus mirè aptis verbis expressit hanc causam, & ea inseruit, quae simul humanitatem Christi, & humanitatis suscepta causam, simul etiam diuinitate summaq; potentiam euidenter declarant.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle expressed this cause most aptly in words that bring together both the humanity of Christ and the cause of his assumption of humanity, and at the same time clearly declare his divinity and supreme power.

units.la: Vt per mortem, inquit, aboleret: vox abolendi amplificat effectum mortis Christi. Significat enim, non solum vtcunq; imminutam potestatem diaboli per mortem Christi, sed plane
units.tr: "That through death," he says, "he might destroy." The word "destroy" magnifies the effect of Christ's death. For it signifies not only that the power of the devil was in some measure diminished through the death of Christ, but that it was plainly

units.la: {k} ἀναχρύσ planè euacuatam & annihilatam. Itaque valdè magnum est beneficium mortis Christi, quando per eam potestas diaboli fracta & euersa est. Per mortem: ita mors Christi erat medium aptissimum iudicatum, quo homines à morte æterna, quam per peccatum incurrerant, liberarentur. Non quòd alia ratione non potuissent homines ab illa morte liberari, sed Deus apud se constituit nullam rationem magis idoneam. Unde Ephesiorum secundo, Deus qui dives est in misericordia, propter multam charitatē suam qua dilexit nos, etiā cùm essemus mortui per delicta, conuiuificauit nos vnà cum Christo. Quò perti-net, quòd Christus ait Lucæ capite vigesimo secundo. Filius quidem hominis secundum quòd definitum est, vadit, veruntamen vç homini illi, per quem proditur Ioan. 12. Pater sç ua me ex hora hac, sed propterea veni in horam hanc. Pater illustra nomen tuum. Unde & prophetç de morte Christi vaticinati sunt, Deo illis suam voluntatem & consilium reuelante. Id quod Christus quoq; Lucæ vltimo declarat hisce verbis: Hæc sunt uerba, quæ locutus sum ad uos, cùm adhuc essem uobiscū, quòd necesse foret impleri omnia, quæ scripta sunt, in lege Mosi, et prophetis, & psalmis de me. Tunc aperuit illorum mentem, ut intelligerent scripturas: & dixit eis: Sic scriptū est, & sic oportebat Christum pati, &c. Et Ioannis capite tertio, ipse de mortis suæ genere: Sicut Moses exaltauit serpentem in deserto, ita exaltari oportet filium hominis. Fuit ergo mors Christi à Deo patre præordinata, & à prophetis prænunciata, ut aptissima ratio, per quam humanum genus à morte æterna liberaretur. Alias causas inquirere, quare decuerit Christum mori, vanum est. Proinde qua ratione constituit pater, humanum genus seruare per mortem Christi, eadem ratione constituit Christum hominem fieri, quando non per angelicam, sed tantum per humanam naturam, mortem obire potuerit. Quare valdè grauis & præcipua ratio hæc est, quare decuerit Christum hominem fieri.
units.tr: wholly emptied and annulled [καταργέω]. Therefore the benefit of Christ's death is very great, since through it the power of the devil has been broken and overthrown. Through death: so the death of Christ was judged to be the most suitable means by which men might be freed from the eternal death that they had incurred through sin. Not that men could not have been freed from that death by another way, but God decided within himself that there was no more fitting way. Hence Ephesians 2: "God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ." To this belongs what Christ says in Luke 22: "The Son of Man indeed goes as it has been determined; but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed." John 12: "Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name." Hence also the prophets prophesied about the death of Christ, God revealing to them his will and counsel. Christ himself also declares this in the last chapter of Luke in these words: "These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms concerning me." Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and said to them: "Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer," etc. And in John 3 he himself speaks of the manner of his death: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." The death of Christ was therefore foreordained by God the Father and foretold by the prophets, as the most fitting means by which the human race would be freed from eternal death. To seek other causes why it was fitting for Christ to die is vain. Therefore, by the same plan by which the Father determined to save the human race through the death of Christ, he also determined that Christ should become man, since he could die only through a human nature and not through an angelic one. Therefore this is a very weighty and principal reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man.

units.la: Eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, diabolum) Simplex sententia est, Christum debuisse per suam mortem liberare homines à morte. Sed Apostolus voluit splendidius efferre, & ad amplificandum effectum mortis Christi, dixit non solùm morte abolitum per mortem Christi, sed ipsum quoq; diabolū, q mortis habebat imperiū: & cū diabolo simul peccatū quoq; extinctū intelligi conuenit, quod ipse sua inuidia homini suggesisit. Ofeæ 13. De manu mortis liberabo eos, & de morte redimā eos: Ero mors tua, ô mors. Sic verò de morte per Christum superata, 1. Cor. 15. Cùm corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, et mortale hoc induerit immortalitatē, tùc fiet sermo qui scriptus est: Absorpta est mors in victoriā. Vbi tuus mors aculeus? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Itè Rom. 6. Autoramenta peccati mors: donū autem Dei vita æterna, per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum. De diabolo autem per Christū superato, Ioan. 12. Nunc iudicium est mundi huius, nunc princeps mundi huius eijcietur foras. Ephes. 4. Expoliatos principatus ac potestates ostentauit, palam triumphans de illis per semetipsum. Sic etiam de mundo superato: Ioan. 16. Confidite, ego vici mundum. Itaq; amplissimi esse ctus mortis Christi hic demonstratur, quādo non solùm à morte, sed etiam à potestate diaboli sumus per mortem vnius Christi liberati. Porrò quomodo simpliciter intelligendū, quomodo seu quatenus à morte & potestate diaboli simus liberati, cùm tamen & mors & diabolus videatur adhuc multū in nos posse, paulò pòst plenius explicabimus. Interea notādum, de diabolo dici, quòd habet imperiū mortis non eadem ratione, qua Deus, qui solus habet potestatē mortificādi & viuificandi, vt habetur Deut. 32. & 1 Sam. 2. qui & mortem pro pœna comminatus est, statim in Paradyso, Genes. 2. Quocunq; die comederitis ex eo, morte moriemini: Sed dicit diabolus habere imperiū mortis quoniā homines ad peccandum impellit, atque ita per peccatū detrudit in mortis, vincula, seu conijcit homines in mortē, et mortis imperiū auget pro viribus et illustrat. Huc pertinet illud Sapientiæ secundo, Inuidia diaboli peccatum introiuit in orbem terrarum: & Roman. 5. additur quòd per peccatum mors, &c. Unde, quia diabolus sic in mundum inuexit peccatum, idq; semper promouet, & per peccatum vires habuit mors, (prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto, aculeus mortis peccatum:) hinc ipse quasi imperium habens, & causa omnium malorū, etiam in morte dicitur habere imperiū. Deus quidē habet potestatē in morte sicut iudex, qui legitimè infert morte in transgressores: diabolus verò tantum sicut latro & homicida illicitē vendicans sibi potestatem alios occidendi, unde & homicidia abinitio appellatur. Proinde hunc, qui hoc pacto visus est habere potestatem & imperium in morte, Christus per mortē suam penitus aboleuit. Valdè mirum diabolus per mortem maximè valebat & exercebat in genus humanū suam sæuitiam: sed quando voluit attentare, vt Christū quoq; per morte perderet, sicut alios omnes perdidit, factū est, vt & ipse, & mors simul p Christū morientē sint debellati et superati: et quodammodo ,pprijs armis diabol» cōfossus est, nō aliter q blasphemus Goliath suo ipsius gladio à Dauide est obtrū catus. Quia in Christū, qui peccati omnis fuit expers, voluit morte immittere, sicut immi sit in alios, qui per peccatū iam venerant in ipsius potestate, ideo ipse iā mortis amisit imperium.
units.tr: Him who had the power of death, that is, the devil) The plain sense is that Christ had to free men from death by his own death. But the Apostle wished to express this more splendidly, and to magnify the effect of Christ's death, so he said that not only death was abolished through the death of Christ, but also the devil himself, who held the power of death; and it is fitting that sin, which he suggested to man out of his envy, is understood to be extinguished along with the devil. Hosea 13: "I will ransom them from the power of the grave, and redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plague." Likewise, concerning death overcome through Christ, 1 Cor. 15: "When this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" Likewise Rom. 6: "The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Concerning the devil overcome through Christ, John 12: "Now is the judgment of this world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out." Eph. 4: "Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in himself." So too concerning the world overcome: John 16: "Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." Thus the very great effect of Christ's death is shown here, since we have been freed not only from death but also from the power of the devil through the death of Christ alone. How, or in what sense, we are freed from death and the power of the devil, since both death and the devil still seem to have much power over us, we will explain more fully a little later. Meanwhile it should be noted that the devil is said to have the power of death not in the same way that God does, who alone has the power to kill and to make alive, as is held in Deut. 32 and 1 Sam. 2, and who threatened death as a punishment already in Paradise, Gen. 2: "In the day that ye eat thereof, ye shall surely die." But the devil is said to have the power of death because he drives men to sin, and so by sin thrusts them into the bonds of death, or casts men into death, and increases and extends the power of death as far as he can. To this belongs that saying of Wisdom 2: "Through the envy of the devil sin entered into the world"; and Rom. 5 adds that through sin came death, etc. Hence, because the devil thus brought sin into the world, and always promotes it, and because death has its strength through sin (1 Cor. 15: "The sting of death is sin"), he is said, as one who holds a kind of rule and is the cause of all evils, to have power even in death. God indeed has power over death as judge, who lawfully inflicts death on transgressors; but the devil only as a robber and murderer, who unlawfully claims for himself the power of killing others, for which reason he is called a murderer from the beginning. Therefore Christ, through his death, utterly abolished him who in this way seemed to have power and rule over death. Truly it is remarkable that the devil through death was most powerful and exercised his cruelty against the human race; but when he tried to destroy Christ also by death, as he had destroyed all the others, it came about that both he and death were conquered and overthrown together through Christ dying; and in a way he was pierced with his own weapons, just as the blasphemer Goliath was struck down by David with his own sword. Because he wished to inflict death on Christ, who was free from all sin, as he had inflicted it on others who had already fallen into his power through sin, therefore he has now lost the power of death.

units.la: Diabolus imperium mortis habere, quomodo dicatur. Diabolus in peccatum ducens domum mortem introducit. Sapient. 2. Peccati origo. Deus iudex. Diabolus & latro & homicida. Ioan. 8. Proprijs sire armis satan confoditur. Goliath. 1. Samuel 17. perium, ut in immerentem & innocentem volens exercere suam tyrannidem. Ioan. 15. Christus ait: Venit princeps mundi huius, & in me non habet quicquā. Immisit diabolus in cor Iudae, vt traderet Christum: deinde in cor Iudaeorum, vt peterent illum crucifigi & occidi quasi reum, &c. Sed quia Christo hęc vis illata est iniustè, procurante diabolo, ideò diabolus imperium suū, quod in mortem habebat, & per mortē exercebat, amisit.
units.tr: That the devil is said to have the power of death. The devil, leading into sin, introduces death into the house. Wisdom 2. The origin of sin. God is judge. The devil is both robber and murderer. John 8. Satan is pierced with his own weapons. Goliath. 1 Samuel 17. He wished to exercise his tyranny over one who did not deserve it and was innocent. John 15: Christ says: "The prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me." The devil put it into the heart of Judas to betray Christ; then into the hearts of the Jews, that they should seek to have him crucified and killed as a criminal, etc. But because this violence was done to Christ unjustly, through the devil's contrivance, therefore the devil lost his power, which he had over death and exercised through death.

units.la: Et liberos redderet eos, qui cunq; metu mortis obnoxij erant seruituti) Per interpretationem expo-nit effectum mortis Christi sequutum ex abolitione diaboli, nimirū quòd homines, qui propter mortē, siue metu mortis sibi à diabolo infligendae obnoxij erant seruituti ipsius diaboli, & per omnia cogebantur ipsius imperata facere, & tyrannidē perpeti, nunc sint facti prorsus liberi. Quae interpretatio valde iterum amplificat beneficium mortis Christi. Et sunt verba etiam valde appositā. Vt liberos, inquit, redderet: siquidem libertate nihil amabilius, nihil magis optabile: vnde beneficium Christi huiusmodi locutionū formulis valde illustratur. Quid enim maius dici posset, quàm q; e seruis facti sumus liberi? Et videtur Apostolus habuisse, illustrandi causa, ratione antithesis, vbi seruitute oppositum libertati. Et non simpliciter dicit, qui erant serui, sed qui ἐνοχοι, id est, obnoxij, obligati erant seruituti: infaelicitatem hominum, & asperitatem seruitutis eo pacto exaggerans, pari-terq; significans, quòd nullo pacto, postquam se semel dediderunt diabolo in seruitutē, possint se ab ea extricare vel eximere. Obligatos enim fuisse non aliter, quàm qui dato chirographo se alteri obstrinxerint. Huc pertinet illud Rom. 6. An nescitis, quòd cui accommodatis vosipsos seruos ad obediendum, eius serui estis cui obeditis, siue peccati ad mortem, siue obedientiae ad iustitiam? Vide ibidem plura. Ioan. 8. Omnis, qui facit peccatum seruus est peccati. Ibidem mox additur de libertate per Christum paranda: Si vos filius liberos reddiderit, verè liberi estis. Et alijs locis, quomodo per Christi mortem simus à peccato, morte, diabolo, liberati, frequenter ostenditur.
units.tr: And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage) By way of explanation he sets out, as an interpretation, the effect of Christ's death that follows from the abolition of the devil, namely that men who, on account of death, or fear of the death the devil inflicted on them, were held in bondage to the devil himself, and were compelled in every way to do his bidding and to endure his tyranny, have now become entirely free. This interpretation again greatly magnifies the benefit of Christ's death. The words are also very apt. "To set free," he says: for nothing is more lovable than liberty, nothing more desirable; hence the benefit of Christ is greatly illustrated by expressions of this kind. For what greater thing could be said than that we have been made free from slaves? And the Apostle seems to have used, for the sake of illustration, the antithesis by which slavery is set against liberty. And he does not simply say "who were slaves," but who were ἐνοχοι [enochoi], that is, bound and obligated to bondage, thereby magnifying the unhappiness of men and the harshness of servitude, and at the same time signifying that in no way, once they had given themselves over to the devil in servitude, could they disentangle or free themselves from it. For they were bound in no other way than those who, having signed a bond, have pledged themselves to another. To this belongs Rom. 6: "Know ye not that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey, whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?" See there for more. John 8: "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." Immediately afterwards in the same place is added concerning the liberty to be obtained through Christ: "If the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." And in other places it is frequently shown how we are freed from sin, death and the devil through the death of Christ.

units.la: Metu mortis) Hoc pacto exprimit causam, cur homines obnoxij fuerint seruituti diaboli. Cum enim diabolus dictus sit habere imperium mortis, & omni tempore hominibus exitium & mortem minetur, rectè dicit, huius metu homines in seruitute ipsius detineri. Constat autem, homines vel amore ac spe boni, vel metu mali obnoxios detineri: sed metus cogit quosuis, & tyrannis etiam saepe optimos opprimit. Itaq; metu mortis, qua nihil magis auersantur aut formidant homines, utpote ad cuius vel memoriam omnes toto animo exhorrescunt, sicut & Christus ipse coepit ea imminente tædio ac pauore affici. Et timor mortis corporalis eo est grauior, praesertim in impijs, quòd formident etiam mortem alteram. Sed Christus liberauit à morte, imò & à metu mortis, ita ut impij mortem amplius non formident, postquam se Deo per amorem subdiderunt: unde cum Apostolo magno animo dicunt: neq; mors, neq; uita possunt nos à dilectione Dei separare: Rom. 8. Postremò, particula illa, per omnem uitam, sicut infaelicitatem humanā aggerat, ita beneficium Christi mirificè illustrat & amplificat. Si in tota uita non licuit à metu mortis vel respirare, sanè miserrima erat conditio eorum, quorū dorso flagellum diaboli mors semper insidebat: & oportet amplissimum agnoscere beneficium, à tanto malo esse liberatos.
units.tr: Through fear of death) By this he expresses the cause why men were held in bondage to the devil. For since the devil is said to have the power of death, and at all times threatens men with destruction and death, he rightly says that men are kept in his servitude by fear of this. It is certain that men are held bound either by love and hope of good, or by fear of evil; but fear constrains all, and tyranny often oppresses even the best. Therefore by fear of death, than which men shrink from or dread nothing more, since all at the very mention of it shudder with their whole soul, just as Christ himself began to be seized with dread and terror when it drew near. And the fear of bodily death is the more grievous, especially in the wicked, because they also dread the second death. But Christ has freed us from death, indeed even from the fear of death, so that the wicked no longer dread death, once they have submitted themselves to God through love; whence with the Apostle they say with great courage: "Neither death nor life can separate us from the love of God," Rom. 8. Lastly, the phrase "all their lifetime," while it heaps up human unhappiness, also wonderfully illustrates and magnifies the benefit of Christ. If during their whole life they were not allowed even to breathe free of fear of death, then surely the condition of those on whose back the scourge of the devil, death, always sat was most wretched; and we must acknowledge the very great benefit of having been freed from so great an evil.

units.la: Cæterum, quando tam præclari effectus mortis Christi praedicantur, nimirum liberatio à peccato, liberatio à morte, quæ propter peccatum infligitur, deniq; liberatio à potestate diaboli, qui nos per peccatum & mortem, sub suo detinet imperio. Qui fit, dicet aliquis, quòd, licet per baptismū participes facti sumus mortis Christi, & semel à peccatis, ac proinde ab his, quae peccatum consequuntur, liberati: tamen adhuc sentiamus, quā diu viuimus, mirabiles peccati vires in nobis, item mortem, deniq; & diabolum multis modis in nos saevientem? Certè Rom. 6. dicitur. An ignoratis, quòd quicunq; baptizati sumus in Christum Iesum, in mortem eius baptizati sumus? Sepulti igitur sumus unà cū illo per baptismum in mortem, vt quemadmodū excitatus est Christus ex mortuis per gloriā patris, ita & nos in nouitate vitae ambulemus. Et paulò post. Vetus ille noster homo cum illo crucifixus est, vt aboleretur corpus peccati, vt posthac non seruiamus peccato. Etenim qui mortuus est, iustificatus est à peccato. En ibi dicit, per mortē Christi, & nostram spiritualem, in baptismo, aboletum esse uniuersum corpus peccati. Praeterea Rom. 5. pluribus uerbis ostenditur, loco peccati & mortis, quae per primum hominem inducta fuerant, succesisse per Christum gratiam & vitam aeternam. Et praesenti loco à morte & diabolo dicimur liberati, id quod & alijs locis plurimis inculcatur. Qui fit tamen, quòd, cùm ista praedicantur, tanquam bona per Christum collata, & tanquam effectus mortis Christi, hos effectus aliter non percipiamus? Nam uidemus nos adhuc semper peccare, semper mori, à diabolo grauiter uexari, atq; etiam subinde opprimi? An effectus mortis Christi nulli sunt, sicut haud dubiē aduersarij soliti sunt Christianis obijcere?
units.tr: Moreover, when such outstanding effects of Christ's death are proclaimed, namely liberation from sin, liberation from death, which is inflicted on account of sin, and finally liberation from the power of the devil, who holds us under his dominion through sin and death. Someone will say: how does it happen that, although through baptism we have been made partakers of Christ's death and have once been freed from sins, and therefore from the things that sin brings in its train, we still feel, as long as we live, the remarkable power of sin within us, and likewise death, and finally the devil raging against us in many ways? Certainly Romans 6 says: "Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life." And a little later: "Our old self was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer be enslaved to sin. For whoever has died has been freed from sin." Here he says that through the death of Christ, and our own spiritual death in baptism, the whole body of sin has been destroyed. Moreover, Romans 5 shows at length that in place of the sin and death that came through the first man, grace and eternal life have succeeded through Christ. And in the present passage we are said to be freed from death and the devil, which is also urged in very many other places. Yet how does it happen that, while these things are proclaimed as blessings conferred through Christ and as effects of his death, we do not perceive these effects in any other way? For we see that we still always sin, always die, are grievously troubled by the devil, and are even at times overwhelmed by him. Or are there no effects of Christ's death, as our adversaries have commonly objected to Christians?

units.la: Quæstio.
units.tr: Question.

units.la: Huic quæstioni breuiter respondebimus, quantum in præsenti succurrit. Certū ergo esse dicimus, hos effectus mortis Christi, videlicet liberationē à peccato, morte, diabolo, à credentibus in Christū & fide apprehendentibus misericordiā propter Christū, etiam in hac vita percipi, licet cōsummati & omni ex parte plenì nō nisi post hāc vitā obtinenda uentant: sicut & Rom.8. Ipsi, qui primitias spiritus habemus, in nobis ipsis gemimus, adoptione expectātes, redemptione corporis nostri: si quidē spe seruati sumus. Itē Rom.5. Iustificati igitur ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem & accessum habemus ... nobis, ut perducemur in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus, & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Itaq; post hanc vitam oēs illi effectus plenissimè percipientur, adeoq; fructus illorum effectuum tūc apparebunt. Sed interea hoc quoq; concedendū est, q̃ in hac vita effectuū illorū nō paruam portionē sentiamus: q̃, quomodo intelligi debeat, explicabimus: & primo, quo in hac uita liberati sumus à peccato: deinde, quomodo à morte: tertiò, quomodo à diabolo. Quod igitur ad primū attinet, omnes qui credentes in Christū baptizantur, à peccato liberantur, & originali, qui huic tantū sunt obnoxij, ut paruuli: & actuali, qui per ætatem & iudicium prouectiores actualia perpetrarūt: atq; omnia summatim peccata ipsis propter mortem Christi sunt remissa. Atq; hoc pacto intelligendi sunt omnes loci, qui peccatorum expiationem per mortem Christi fieri testantur. Cæterum, quòd, quibus hoc pacto semel remissa sunt omnia peccata, tamen adhuc maneat adhærens concupiscētia, neq; ea prorsus extinguitur, sed subinde impellit eos ad peccandū: nō propterea sequit, mortem Christi minus esse efficace, siue illos nequaq̃ à potestate peccati liberatos. Nā vt adhuc adhæreat illis concupiscentia, tñ ea nequaquā sic est efficax in illis, ut in cæteris, qui gratia Dei non sunt consecuti: deinde, ut etiā peccata nonnulla admittant: sicut & sancti omnes fatentur se esse peccatores, (iuxta illud psalmi 142. Non intres in iudicium cū seruo tuo Domine, quoniam non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis uiuens. Et Psalm.32. Dixi, confitebor aduersum me præuaricationes meas Domino, & tu remisisti impietatem cordis mei, propter hoc orabit ad te omnis sanctus. Et 1.Ioan.1. Si dixerimus, quòd peccatum non habemus, nosmetipsos seducimus. Itē Rom.7. video aliā legē in mēbris meis, rebellantē legi mentis meæ, & captiuū me reddentē legi peccati:) tñ sunt adhuc liberi à peccato, quia tantus est effectus mortis Christi erga illos, ut peccatū ipsis non imputetur. Deinde, ut non possit in ipsorū corporibus regnare, sicut in aliorum infidelium regnat corporibus. Qui effectus reuera magni sunt. eosq; pij per spiritum S. confirmati egregiè sentiunt in suis conscientijs: Huc pertinet illud Rom.8. Nulla igitur nunc est condemnatio his, qui insiti sunt Christo Iesu, qui non iuxta carnem versantur, sed iuxta spiritū. Nam lex spiritus vitæ per Christū Iesum, liberum me reddidit à iure peccati & mortis. Rom.6. Ne regnet peccatum in mortali vestro corpore, vt obediatis illi per cupiditates eius. Et de spiritu Sancto confirmante pectora nostra. Rom.8. Non accepistis spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timore, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus Abba pater. Idem spiritus testatur vnà cum spiritu nostro, quòd sumus filij Dei.
units.tr: We shall answer this question briefly, as far as occurs to us at present.
