We say, therefore, that it is certain that these effects of Christ's death, namely liberation from sin, from death, and from the devil, are received in this life by those who believe in Christ and by faith lay hold on God's mercy on account of Christ, even though they are not obtained in their completeness and fullness in every respect until after this life, as Romans 8 also says: "We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body; for we were saved by hope." Likewise Romans 5: "Therefore, justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have access ... that we may be brought into this grace in which we stand, and boast in the hope of the glory of God." Therefore after this life all those effects will be received most fully, and the fruit of those effects will then appear. But meanwhile this too must be conceded, that in this life we perceive no small portion of those effects. How this is to be understood we shall explain: first, how we have been freed from sin in this life; then, how from death; third, how from the devil. As to the first, all who are baptized as believers in Christ are freed from sin, both original sin, which binds only those who are as yet little children, and actual sin, which those who are older by age and judgment commit; and in sum, all sins have been forgiven them on account of Christ's death. And in this way must all the passages be understood which testify that the expiation of sins takes place through the death of Christ. But that, although for these people all sins have once been forgiven in this way, the clinging concupiscence still remains, and is not wholly extinguished, but from time to time drives them to sin, does not mean that the death of Christ is less effective, or that they are not at all freed from the power of sin. For although concupiscence still clings to them, it is not so effective in them as in others who have not obtained the grace of God; and further, they still admit some sins, as all the saints also confess that they are sinners (according to Psalm 143: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no one living will be justified in your sight"; and Psalm 32: "I said, I will confess my transgressions to the Lord against myself, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart; for this every saint shall pray to you"; and 1 John 1: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves"; likewise Romans 7: "I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin"). Yet they are still free from sin, because the effect of Christ's death toward them is so great that sin is not imputed to them. Further, sin cannot reign in their bodies as it reigns in the bodies of other unbelievers. These effects are indeed great, and the godly, confirmed by the Holy Spirit, feel them clearly in their consciences. To this belongs Romans 8: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death." Romans 6: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its lusts." And about the Holy Spirit confirming our hearts: Romans 8: "You did not receive a spirit of slavery to fear again, but you received a spirit of adoption, through which we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God."

units.la: Itaq; liberi sancti etiam in hac uita à peccato, non quidē quòd amplius peccare non possint, aut ab omni prorsus peccato sint immunes: sed ut id nō possit in ipsos regnare: deinde, ut ad damnationem ipsis non imputetur. Sicut & liberati à lege, nonne ea, quæ legis sunt, non amplius faciant, sed quòd, vt etiam non faciant, damnari propterea non possint. Rom.7. Nunc autem liberati sumus à lege, mortui ei, in qua detinebamur, ut seruiamus per nouitatem spiritus, & non per uetustatem literæ. Et Rom.6. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur. Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Augustinus lib.1. de nuptijs & concupiscentia, cap.25. Non substantialiter manet concupiscentia, sicut aliquod corpus aut spiritus, sed affectio est quædam malæ qualitatis, sicut languor paulò post quotidie minuitur in proficientibus. cap.26. & 27. ostendit, quòd, sicut peccatum tranßit actu, manet tamē reatu: ita è diuerso potest fieri, ut peccatum maneat actu, prætereat reatu. Et non facit, qui non consentit concupiscentiæ. Sed iterum dices fortasis: si tantus est effectus mortis Christi, ut peccata non amplius imputentur, quare non simul auferatur tota illa uis concupiscentiæ, ut prorsus etiam fine peccato sancti hic uiuant? Respondetur, ad utilitatem ipsorum hominum fieri, quòd diuina prouidentia relin qui in sanctis velit peccati quasdam reliquias. Hac enim ratione ad bona opera magis excitabuntur, carnem suam studebunt crucifigere cum concupiscentijs suis. Habebūt cum quo quasi hoste se exerceant, ne velut securi efficiantur torpidi, & negligetes, id quod Augustinus indicat libro primo de peccatorum meritis & remissione, capite 39. Atq; per hanc fragilitatem homo in humilitate retinetur, ne de se nimis altum sapiat. Cogitur itē implorare opem Dei, & aliis modis fidem suam exercere ac roborare.
units.tr: Therefore the saints are free from sin even in this life, not in the sense that they can no longer sin, or are wholly immune from all sin, but so that it cannot reign over them, and so that it is not imputed to them for condemnation. Just as those who are freed from the law, do they not no longer do the things of the law, yet they cannot be condemned for them even though they do not do them? Romans 7: "But now we have been released from the law, having died to that by which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter." And Romans 6: "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace." Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 1, chapter 25: "Concupiscence does not remain as a substance, like some body or spirit, but is a certain affection of bad quality, like a sickness which is gradually diminished day by day in those who are making progress." Chapters 26 and 27 show that, just as sin passes in act but remains in guilt, so conversely it can happen that sin remains in act but passes in guilt; and he does not commit sin who does not consent to concupiscence. But perhaps you will say again: if the effect of Christ's death is so great that sins are no longer imputed, why is not that whole force of concupiscence also removed at once, so that the saints might live here altogether without sin? The answer is that it is for the benefit of these men themselves that divine providence wills to leave some remnants of sin in the saints. For in this way they will be more stirred up to good works, and they will strive to crucify their flesh with its lusts. They will have, as it were, an enemy with whom to exercise themselves, lest they become careless and sluggish as if they were secure; which Augustine points out in book 1 of On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, chapter 39. And through this frailty a person is kept in humility, lest he think too highly of himself. He is also compelled to implore God's help, and in other ways to exercise and strengthen his faith.

units.la: Deinde ostenditur hinc, quòd gratia Dei homini per omnem vitam opus sit, & quod gloria æterna per gratiam non per merita conferatur. Huiusmodi exercitia, confessiones, deprecationes Scriptura in sanctis passim proponit spectandas, quibus plena ab omni sensu peccati liberatio non nisi in altera vita continget.
units.tr: Next, it is shown from this that the grace of God is needed by a person throughout his whole life, and that eternal glory is conferred through grace, not through merits. Scripture sets these exercises, confessions and prayers of the saints before us everywhere to be observed, and a full deliverance from every sense of sin will not come until the next life.

units.la: Nunc de liberatione nostra à morte. Quomodo intelligendum est, nos per mortem Christi liberari à morte, cùm tamen re ipsa comperiamus, eos, qui credunt, perinde mori, ut cæteros incredulos? Quomodo iudicabimus credentibus illos effectus mortis Christi obtingere? Respondetur, duplicem esse mortem, corporis videlicet & animæ. Proinde ab utraq; sunt credentes per mortem Christi liberati. A morte corporis quidem, non quasi illud non debeat semel mori, (quando enim peccati meritum in se gerit, manet conditionis mortis obstrictu) sed quod, postquam semel fuerit mortuum, iterum reuiuiscit propter Christum ad gloriam. Non liberantur corpora nostra ita, ut non sint mortalia, sed ut non sint morti obnoxia. Huc pertinet illud Roman.8. Porrò si Christus in uobis est, corpus quidem mortuum est, propter peccatum, scilicet corporaliter, ut D. Augustinus interpretatur, spiritus autem vita est propter iustificationem. Quòd si spiritus eius, qui excitauit Iesum à mortuis, habitat in uobis, is qui excitauit Christum à mortuis, viuificabit & mortalia corpora vestra, propter ipsius spiritum inhabitantem in vobis. Et 1.Cor.15. Postquam enim per hominem mors, etiam per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Ergo homines per Christum etiam à morte corporali liberati sunt: non quidem quòd non moriantur temporaliter, sed quòd à morte iterum resurgant ad gloriam, & regno mortis (quæ, ut Rom.5. habetur, regnauit ab Adam usq; ad Molen) non sunt subiecti, ut cæteri increduli. Nam Christi gratia regnum mortis destruit. Addi potest & hoc, consecutos esse pios credentes, ut mortem non formident, sed magis optent, eam nimirum, pro malo non amplius æstimantes. Hinc illud Philipp.1. Cupio dissolui & esse cum Christo. Sed iterum obiiciet aliquis: si peccatum est remissum etiam in hac uita, & mors non sequitur, nisi ex peccato, videtur quòd omnino non debebant pij mori. Respondetur, quòd quia ab origine omnes contraxerunt peccatum, ideo etiam omnes debent mortem gustare: iuxta illud Rom.5. Quemadmodum per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introijt, & per peccatum mors: & sic in omnes homines mors peruasit, quatenus omnes peccauimus. Quanquam non est dubium, quin preciosa sit in conspectu Domini mors sanctorum, ac longè alia, quàm impiorum. Unde sancti dormire dicuntur, & minore haud dubie molestia mortem subeunt, quàm cæteri. Salutariter autem & sapienter Deus voluit, ut etiam credentes in Christum morerentur. Primò, ut pij expectatione mortis temporalis semper sese præpararent, & in officio continerent. Deinde, ut fortitudine, vires, gratiam sibi à Deo datam in perferenda morte & quibuscunq; miseriis clarius experiretur. Sic primi parentes iuste uiuendo, & per Dominum hauddubiè à peccatis liberati, non meruerunt in paradisum reuocari. Sic & caro peccatrix, etiasi remissis peccatis homo in ea iuste vixerit, nō cōtinuò meretur eā morte nō perpeti, quæ traxit de pagine peccati.
units.tr: Now concerning our deliverance from death. How are we to understand that we are delivered from death through the death of Christ, when in fact we see that those who believe die just as the other unbelievers do? How shall we judge that these effects of Christ's death come to believers? The answer is that death is twofold, namely of the body and of the soul. Accordingly, believers are delivered by the death of Christ from both. From the death of the body, not as if the body need not die once (for as long as it bears the desert of sin, it remains bound by the condition of death), but because, once it has died, it lives again for Christ unto glory. Our bodies are not delivered so that they are no longer mortal, but so that they are no longer subject to death. To this belongs that passage in Romans 8: "And if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin," that is, bodily, as Augustine explains, "but the spirit is life because of justification. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit who dwells in you." And 1 Corinthians 15: "For since by a man came death, by a man also came the resurrection of the dead." Therefore men have also been delivered from bodily death through Christ. Not indeed that they do not die in time, but that they rise again from death unto glory, and they are not subject to the reign of death (which, as Romans 5 says, reigned from Adam to Moses) as the other unbelievers are. For the grace of Christ destroys the reign of death. This may also be added: godly believers have attained this, that they do not fear death but rather desire it, no longer counting it an evil. Hence that word of Philippians 1: "I desire to depart and be with Christ." But someone will object again: if sin is forgiven even in this life, and death follows only from sin, it seems that the godly ought not to die at all. The answer is that, since all have contracted sin from their origin, therefore all must also taste death, according to Romans 5: "As through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, so death passed upon all men, inasmuch as all have sinned." Yet there is no doubt that the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, and quite different from that of the wicked. Hence the saints are said to sleep, and they undergo death with undoubtedly less distress than others. God, however, has willed, wisely and for our good, that even believers in Christ should die. First, that the godly might always prepare themselves in expectation of temporal death and keep to their duty. Then, that they might experience more clearly the strength and the grace given them by God in bearing death and all kinds of miseries. So our first parents, living righteously and undoubtedly delivered from sins through the Lord, did not deserve to be recalled into paradise. So also the sinful flesh, even if a man has lived righteously in it with his sins forgiven, does not at once deserve not to undergo that death which it has drawn from the guilt of sin.

units.la: Si item non morerentur credentes, carni quidem fœlicitas adderetur, minueretur autem fidei fortitudo. Sic enim homines mortem istam timent, ut non ob aliud fœlices dicerent esse Christianos, nisi quòd mori omnino nō possent. Ac per hoc nemo propter illam vitam, quæ post istam mortem beata futura est, per uirtutem etiam contemnendæ ipsius mortis ad Christi gratiam festinaret, sed propter remouendam mortis molestiam in Christum crederetur. Plus ergo gratiæ præstitit, plus fidelibus sine dubitatione donauit. Quid enim magnum erat videndo non mori eos, qui crederent, credere, se nō mori turum? Quanto est maius, quanto fortius, quanto laudabilius, ita credere, ut se speret moriturus sine fine victurum? An verò optabile foret, hic manere: si alio commigrandū, quomodo id melius, quàm per morte fieret, qua omnis corruptio hic relinquitur? Hæc de effectu mortis Christi, videlicet liberatione nostra à morte, etiam temporali. At verò de liberatione credentium à morte spirituali, quæ aliàs mors secunda & æterna dicitur, perspicuum magis est, quà ut probationibus id declarari debeat, cùm passim in scriptis propheticis & apostolicis id inculcetur.
units.tr: Likewise, if believers did not die, happiness would be added to the flesh, but the strength of faith would be diminished. For men fear that death so much that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all. And so no one would hasten to the grace of Christ for the sake of that life which is to be blessed after this death, by the power of despising death itself, but men would believe in Christ for the sake of removing the distress of death. He therefore bestowed more grace and gave more to the faithful beyond doubt. For what great thing would it be, if believers were seen not to die, to believe that they would not die? How much greater, how much stronger, how much more praiseworthy it is to believe in such a way that one who is about to die hopes to live without end! Indeed, would it be desirable to remain here? If we must migrate elsewhere, how could this be done better than through death, by which all corruption is left behind here? These things concern the effect of Christ's death, namely our deliverance from death, even temporal death. But concerning the deliverance of believers from spiritual death, which is elsewhere called the second and eternal death, it is more evident than that it needs to be declared by proofs, since it is everywhere inculcated in the prophetic and apostolic writings.

units.la: Restat vt explicemus, quomodo à potestate diaboli simus per mortem Christi liberati, cùm tamen eius insidias & mirabilem tyrānidem adhuc cogamur sentire? nā ipsi quoque Sancti, qui S.S. unà cū multis donis receperūt, experti sunt mirabiles diaboli insultus, & sepe etiā in desperatione, deinde dānatione æterna per diabolū pertracti. Certè Paul.2.Cor.12. fatetur sibi, ut humiliaretur, datū stimulū per carnē, nuncii Satanæ, qui ipsum colaphis cæderet. Itē 1.Thessal.2. ait, se impeditū à satana, quo minus Thessalonicenses inuiserit. Et Petrus 1.epistolæ capite 5. monet pios, ut sobrij sint & uigiles, propterea quòd ptcr futuram gloriam et fœlicitatem. 5. Si alio commigrandum, quomodo id melius, quàm per morte fieret, quia omnis corruptio hic relinquitur. Liberatio à morte secunda 3. Liberatio à potestate diaboli. Satanæ uis. quòd diabolus omni tempore obambulet tanquam leo rugiens & quærens quem de-uoret. Si ergo Diabolus hoc pacto nullum facit nos persequendi finem neq; modû, cer-tè videtur, quòd per mortem Christi nequaquam simus à potestate diaboli liberati. Re-spondetur ergo, quòd, etiamsi diabolus nos subinde adhuc molestet, nihilominus verû fit, quòd effectus mortis Christi sint multò amplisimi, & per eam simus à potestate dia-boli liberati. Nàm hoc obtinent credentes ex morte Christi, quòd diabolus non amplius ita potest ius & potestatem in eos obtinere, sicut antea obtinuit. Nam antea mirabilem habuit in incredulos potestatem, id quod liquet Ephef.2. Vos cûm essetis mortui deliĉtis ac pec-catis, in quibus aliquando ambulastis iuxta seculum huius mundi, iuxta principem, cui potestas est aeris, qui est spiritus nunc agens in filijs contumacibus.
units.tr: It remains for us to explain how we have been delivered from the power of the devil through the death of Christ, when nevertheless we are still compelled to feel his snares and his remarkable tyranny. For the saints themselves, who received the Holy Spirit together with many gifts, have experienced the remarkable assaults of the devil, and often have been dragged by him into despair and then into eternal damnation. Certainly Paul in 2 Corinthians 12 confesses that a goad in the flesh, a messenger of Satan who would buffet him, was given to him so that he might be humbled. Likewise, in 1 Thessalonians 2 he says that he was hindered by Satan from visiting the Thessalonians. And Peter in the first chapter of his epistle, chapter 5, warns the godly to be sober and watchful, because the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. If, then, the devil in this way makes no end or measure of persecuting us, it certainly seems that through the death of Christ we are by no means delivered from the power of the devil. The answer, then, is that even if the devil still troubles us from time to time, it is nonetheless true that the effects of Christ's death are far greater, and that through it we have been delivered from the power of the devil. For believers obtain this from the death of Christ: the devil can no longer get right and power over them as he formerly did. For formerly he had a remarkable power over unbelievers, as is clear from Ephesians 2: "You, when you were dead in trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience."

units.la: Deinde, non potest diabolus credentes tentare supra quàm possunt ipsi ferre, & deus illi promittit, imò tentatio cedit pijs ad commodum & gloriam, diabolo verò adigno-miniâ. Vnde 1.Cor.10. Fidelis est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari supra id quod potestis: imò faciet unà cû tentatione euentû, quo possitis sufferre. Tû, ut contingat pios tentari, tamê hic etiâ est effectus mortis Christi, & hoc modo sunt à potestate diaboli liberati, quòd possunt resistere diabolo, id q; Petus indicat, quando addit, pios debere ei per fide resistere. Et 2. Pet.2. Nouit Dominus pios è tétatione eripere. Et Paul. etiâ ad Ephef.6. oste-dit, quali armatura pij resistere possint rectoribus tenebrarû seculi huius & spiritualibus astutijs, ad diaboli satellitiû peinentibus. Sic ergo credentes sunt à potestate diaboli per morte Christi liberati, quatenus diabolus nō amplius potest in eos præualere: ad cuius ef-sectus cofirmatione etiâ externû hoc signû & donû collatû est ecclesię, ut pij in nomine Christi dæmonia è locis quę occupât, eijciât. Quòd si qui ex credetiû numero visi sunta-liquando à diabolo superati, sicut Iudas & quidâ alij, id non cõtingit, q; mors Christi fue-rit inefficax, sed q; ipsi vel nō recte crediderint, vel in se potestate diabolo fecerint. In-terea aût Deus ob diuersas causas pmittit diabolo, ut pios tétet subinde ac molestet. Pri-mò ut sancti sic per oem vitâ probentur & exerceantur, non efferantur, non torpescant, ob securitatê, sed excitetur ad orandû quotidie, Ne inducas nos in tétationê. Deinde, ut post te-tationem & victoriâ obtentâ in fide confirmetur, Deiq; beneficia agnoscant. Nâ cû San-cti liberantur, ne succumbant, tunc quoq; potentia Dei illustratur. Hac de caussa & Chri-stus ipse à diabolo tentatus est. Tertiò permittit Deus nônihil diabolo, ut mali metu dia-boli, qui est velut tortor & carnifex Dei, coerceantur: propter quam caussam Deus vo-luit in ecclesia manere potestatem tradêdi immorigeros Satanæ. Adhæc permittit deus diabolum sæuire in sanctos, ut ipse sibi maiorem damnationis paret cumulum.
units.tr: Next, the devil cannot tempt believers beyond what they are able to bear, and God promises him this; indeed, temptation turns out for the godly to their advantage and glory, but for the devil to his shame. Hence 1 Corinthians 10: "God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able; but with the temptation he will also make a way of escape, so that you may be able to bear it." Yet although it happens that the godly are tempted, this too is an effect of Christ's death, and in this way they have been delivered from the power of the devil, in that they are able to resist the devil. Peter indicates this when he adds that the godly must resist him by faith. And 2 Peter 2: "The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation." And Paul too, in Ephesians 6, shows with what armour the godly can resist the rulers of the darkness of this age and the spiritual wickedness that belongs to the devil's underlings. So believers are delivered from the power of the devil through the death of Christ, in that the devil can no longer prevail over them. And to confirm this effect, this external sign and gift was also given to the Church, so that the godly, in the name of Christ, might cast out demons from the places they occupy. But if some from the number of believers have at times been seen to be overcome by the devil, as Judas and some others were, this does not happen because the death of Christ was ineffective, but because they either did not believe rightly or made themselves subject to the devil's power. Meanwhile, God for various causes permits the devil to tempt and trouble the godly from time to time. First, so that the saints may be proved and exercised in this way throughout their whole life, so that they are not puffed up or grow sluggish through security, but are stirred up to pray daily, "Lead us not into temptation." Then, so that after temptation and victory obtained they may be confirmed in faith and acknowledge God's benefits. For when the saints are delivered so that they do not succumb, the power of God is then also made manifest. For this reason Christ himself was tempted by the devil. Thirdly, God permits the devil some freedom so that the wicked may be restrained by fear of the devil, who is, as it were, the torturer and executioner of God; for this reason God willed that in the Church there should remain the power of handing over the disobedient to Satan. Moreover, God permits the devil to rage against the saints so that he may heap up for himself a greater measure of damnation.

units.la: Ex his igitur cōstat, quòd vere à potestate diaboli per mortem Christi simus liberati, fractis nimirum diaboli viribus, adempto iure, quod antea in nos habebat: deinde colla-ta nobis potestate eum superandi. Atq; hęc cû precedentibus puto equidem non me-diocriter prodesse ad intelle-ctum, effectus mortis Christi uerè à pijs etiâ in hac vita per-cipi, & liberatione à peccato, morte, diabolo, manifestam ex morte Christi contingere. Et habet magnam vtilitatê hæc doctrina, utpote quæ effecit, vt certę sint conscientiæ de effectibus mortis Christi, neq; dubitêt, se, si in fide persistât, eos percepturos. Deinde, vt interea non torpescant, non diffluant, quasi prorsus securæ: non item efferantur, sedcõ-tineantur in obedientia, humilitate, & omnibus officijs, quæ per ipsos sunt præstanda. Verba aût Apostoli hoc loco posita, amplissimâ in se continent consolationê & doctri-nâ. Qui à diaboli imperio audit se liberatû per morte Christi, quid iâ amplius formidet illius insultus uel machinationes? Et qui bene expendit dignitatê & potentiâ personæ Christi, non poterit de tantis effectibus dubitare. Neq; tantum unquâ potest diabolus, quin Christus possit longè maiora. Collatio partium rem omnê satis declarat. Deinde, addiscimus hic, mortem nequaquâ esse formidandâ pijs, utpote quàm qui verè fidunt Christo, neq; tam acerbam possunt sentire, ut increduli, quibus nihil hac caduca & mise-ra uita potest esse suauius siue maius: neq; præterea possunt sentire eius imperium post hanc uitam: quandoquidem vitam æternam occupant, à morte secunda prorsus liberi. Mors Christi, eiusdemq; reuiuiscentia, nobis fregit mortis tyrannidem, & vitam æter-nam parauit. In summa, in omnibus tentationibus & aduersitatibus consolationem ma-ximam concipiet, quicunq; secum reputarit, à quanta seruitute, ad quantam libertatem per Christum sit restitutus.
units.tr: From this it is plain that by the death of Christ we are truly freed from the power of the devil, since the devil's strength is broken and the right he once had over us is taken away, and then the power to overcome him is given to us. I think this, together with what has gone before, contributes no little to understanding that the effects of Christ's death are truly perceived by the godly even in this life, and that deliverance from sin, death and the devil comes plainly from the death of Christ. This doctrine is also of great use, since it makes consciences certain of the effects of Christ's death and leaves them in no doubt that, if they persevere in faith, they will receive those effects. Further, it keeps believers from becoming sluggish and careless, as if they were altogether safe, and equally from becoming puffed up; rather, it keeps them in obedience, humility and all the duties that they must perform. The words of the Apostle in this place contain the greatest consolation and teaching. Whoever hears that he has been freed from the rule of the devil by the death of Christ, why should he fear the devil's assaults or schemes any more? And whoever weighs carefully the dignity and power of the person of Christ cannot doubt such great effects. The devil can never be so strong that Christ cannot be far stronger; the comparison of the parties makes the whole matter sufficiently clear. Further, we learn here that death is by no means to be dreaded by the godly, who truly trust in Christ, and who cannot feel it as bitterly as unbelievers do, for whom nothing in this fleeting and wretched life can be sweeter or greater. Nor can they feel its dominion beyond this life, since they possess eternal life and are wholly free from the second death. The death of Christ and his rising again have broken the tyranny of death for us and have prepared eternal life. In sum, whoever considers from how great a bondage he has been restored through Christ, to how great a freedom, will conceive the greatest consolation in all temptations and adversities.

units.la: Non enim uidelicet angelos assumit, sed semen Abrahæ assumit. Quia verò proxima ratio declarat, Christum debuisse eâ naturam assumere, qua posset pro salute hominum morte obire, commodè subijcit quadam occupationis forma, hinc quoq; factum, quòd naturam hu-manam & non angelicá afsumpserit. Apparet autem aduersarios, qui negabant, Christû esse Deum, angelisq; superiorem, obiecisse aliquando in hunc modum: si Christus erat Deus,
units.tr: For he does not take hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Since the nearer reason shows that Christ had to take on that nature by which he could die for the salvation of men, the Apostle appropriately adds, in a certain form of transition, that this too is why he took on human nature and not angelic nature. It appears that the opponents who denied that Christ is God and superior to the angels once raised this objection: if Christ was God...

units.la: Piorum sobrie-tas et vigilia. Responsio, cur Satan homine molestet. 1. Diaboli potestas fracta morte Christi. 2. Satan non potest credentes tentare ultra quàm deus permittit. 3. Pij possunt diabolo resistere per fidem. Portæ inferorum, i.e. satani non possunt prævalere al-iversus electos. Fides hypocritarum fallax et vitæ à diabol. Cur deus permittat Diabolum pios tétare. 1. credentium exercitium. 2. Fidei confirmatio et agnitio potentiæ Dei. 3. mali metu diaboli coercentur. 4. diaboli damnatio. Vtilitas doctrinæ. 1. Conscientiarum recreatio. 2. Securitas fugienda. 3. Consolatio piorum. 4. Christus fortior et potentior est diabol. 5. mors pijs non pertimescenda. Pij feliciter vitâ caducam commutant cum æterna. Cur Christus humanam potius quàm angelicam naturam assumpserit. Deus, ac debuit definito tempore humiliari, quare potius non angelicam naturam assumpsit, quae praestantior est, & ad diuinam magis accedens, quàm humanam, secundum quam non videtur posse fieri superior. Nec dubium, quin habuerit varias & minimè leues causas adita obijciendum. Magis enim competebat diuinae maiestati, fieri angelu, quàm hominem. Deinde olim Deus per angelos plurima erga homines effecit. Huic obiectioni satisfaciunt rationes praecedentes, praecipuè posterior, qua dicitur, ideò Christum factum hominem, quòd sanctificatio seu liberatio hominū debuerit fieri per mortem: quam sanè gustare Christus secundum angelicam naturam haud potuisset: quandoquidem angelos constat esse immortales. Haec proinde est causa, quare Christus nō angelos, sed semē Abrahae, id est, veram & perfectam naturam humanam ex posteritate Abrahae contractam.
units.tr: The sobriety and watchfulness of the godly. Answer: why Satan harasses man. (1) The power of the devil broken by the death of Christ. (2) Satan cannot tempt believers beyond what God permits. (3) The godly can resist the devil through faith. The gates of hell, that is, Satan, cannot prevail against the elect. The faith of hypocrites is deceptive, and they are led astray by the devil. Why God permits the devil to tempt the godly: (1) to exercise believers; (2) to confirm faith and the recognition of God's power; (3) the devil is restrained by fear of evil; (4) the devil's damnation. The usefulness of the doctrine: (1) the refreshing of consciences; (2) security is to be avoided; (3) consolation of the godly; (4) Christ is stronger and more powerful than the devil; (5) death is not to be dreaded by the godly. The godly happily exchange this fleeting life for eternal life. Why Christ took on human rather than angelic nature. God, and indeed it was fitting, that at a set time he should be humbled. Why he did not rather take on the angelic nature, which is the more excellent and comes closer to the divine, rather than human nature, by which he does not seem able to become greater. There is no doubt that he had various and by no means slight reasons for this, which must be brought forward in answer to the objection. For it was more fitting for the divine majesty to become an angel than a man. Further, God formerly accomplished very many things toward men through angels. The preceding reasons satisfy this objection, especially the latter one, which says that Christ became man because the sanctification or deliverance of men had to be accomplished through death; and Christ could certainly not have tasted death according to his angelic nature, since it is agreed that angels are immortal. This, then, is the cause why Christ took hold not of angels but of the seed of Abraham, that is, true and perfect human nature descended from the posterity of Abraham.

units.la: Ergo praesentibus verbis Apostolus nihil aliud sibi vult, quàm ex praecedenti ratione de morte per Christum subeunda, perspicuum quoq; euadere, cur Christum potius hominem, quàm angelum fieri decuerit. Ait igitur Apostolos, Non angelos videlicet assumit: οὐ γὰρ ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται. Vox ἆρα interdum interrogatiua est, nunquid: & interdum locum notat, & idem significat, quod alicubi: unde οὐ ἆρα, id est, nusquam, nullibi: essetque tum sententia, Christum nusquam assumere angelicam naturam, sed semen Abrahae: quasi diceretur: Nusquā legi in Scripturis, q; Christus assumere deberet angelicā naturam: at hoc legi, quòd assumerer semen Abrahae. Sed quoniam creberrimè est particula afseueradi, & veritur, utiq;, videlicet, certè, nimirū, rectè meo iudicio hoc hoco interpres reddidit, ut ad asseuerandum faciat. Similiter verbum ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι saepe idem est, quod apprehendo: ut 1. Tim. 6. libenter communicantes, ut apprehendant vitam aeternam: sed saepe etiam assumo: atq; hic ea significatione accipiendum satis arguit sententiae ratio. Hic enim dicitur, quòd Christus assumpserit humanam naturam, quae formalo quendi multò est in hac disputatione usitatissima. Quanquam nec inepte adnotatum est à Chrysostomo, apprehendendi potius significatione accipiendum: Metaphoram nāq; subesse verbo ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι, ductam ab ijs, qui alium praecurrentem & fugientem persequuntur, conanturque retinere, ac tandem manu praehendunt. Qua metaphora hic mira Dei erga humanum genus beneuolentia & charitas declaratur. Nam ille nos, qui longè eramus, & ad nostrum exitium quasi cursu rapiebamur, insecutus est, tandem arripuit, retinuit, & ad salutem reduxit. Atque ita cura, solicitudo, labor, festinatio, pro salute generis humani ea una voce significatur.
units.tr: Therefore in these words the Apostle means nothing other than that, from the preceding reasoning about the death to be undergone through Christ, it also becomes clear why it was fitting for Christ to become man rather than angel. The Apostle therefore says: he does not indeed take hold of angels [οὐ γὰρ ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται]. The word ἆρα [ara] is sometimes interrogative, "whether, then?", and sometimes denotes a place, and means the same as "somewhere"; hence οὐ ἆρα [ou ara], that is, nowhere, nowhere at all. The sense would then be that Christ nowhere takes on the angelic nature but the seed of Abraham, as if it were said: nowhere in the Scriptures is it read that Christ ought to take on the angelic nature, but it is read that he took hold of the seed of Abraham. But since the particle is very often an asseverative, and is rendered "indeed", "surely", "certainly", "truly", I judge that the interpreter has rightly rendered it here so as to serve as an asseveration. Likewise the verb ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι [epilambanesthai] often means the same as "to apprehend", as in 1 Tim. 6: "willingly sharing, that they may lay hold on eternal life" [ἐπιλάβωνται τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς]; but it often also means "to assume", and the sense of the passage sufficiently shows that it must be taken in this meaning here. For it is said that Christ assumed human nature, which is a very common manner of speaking in this discussion. Yet Chrysostom has noted, not unfittingly, that it should be taken rather in the sense of "to seize": there lies in the word ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι a metaphor drawn from those who pursue another who is running ahead and fleeing, trying to hold him back, and at last seize him with their hand. By this metaphor the wonderful goodwill and love of God toward the human race is here declared. For he pursued us, who were far off and were being carried headlong as if in a race to our destruction, and at last seized us, held us, and brought us back to salvation. Thus care, solicitude, labour and haste for the salvation of the human race are signified in that one word.

units.la: Angelos, posuit pro angelica natura, id quod ex ratione sententiae satis potest euidenter colligi.
units.tr: He put "angels" for the angelic nature, which can be quite clearly gathered from the reason of the sentence.

units.la: Simili modo Semen Abrahae dixit, pro natura humana: sed non est dubiū, quin iudicio & certis de causis maluerit ea verborum forma enunciare animi sensa, quàm verbis aliis. Dicendo enim semen Abrahae, simul suggerit omnium animis memoriam promissionis ad Abraham factae de Christo, humanam carnem ex posteritate ipsius susceperturo: sì mul apertissimè docet, Christum non modò verum habuisse corpus, id quod & supra significauit verbis carnis & sanguinis: sed praeterea corpus illud non allatum è coelo, ut Valentinus suspicatus est, aut compositum ex mundi elementis, ut Appelles contendit: sed reuera ex humana carne nimirum beatissimae virginis susceptum. Quare multò aptissima est haec locutionis formula ad confirmandam ueram Christi humanitatem. Ut non dicam, tacitam in ea latere adhortationem ad Iudaeos, ut Christum ex ipsorum sanctissimo patriarcha genus ducentem eò lubentius amplectantur. Nam se quoque filios esse Abrahae miris modis gloriabātur: & vel ex eo nomine adduci debuissent ad Christum magnificiendum. Sed videmur non abs re facturi, si paulò plenius, quomodo Christus ex semine Abrahae carnem induerit, & quomodo hic refellatur Valentinus, & cum eo quidam nostri temporis Anabaptistae, explicemus.
units.tr: In a similar way he said "seed of Abraham" for human nature; but there is no doubt that, by judgment and for definite reasons, he chose to express his meaning in this form of words rather than in others. For by saying "seed of Abraham" he at once brings to the minds of all the memory of the promise made to Abraham concerning Christ, who would take on human flesh from his posterity; and at the same time he most clearly teaches that Christ had not only a true body, as he also indicated above by the words "flesh and blood", but moreover that this body was not brought from heaven, as Valentinus suspected, nor composed of the elements of the world, as Apelles contended, but was truly taken from human flesh, namely of the most blessed virgin. Therefore this manner of speaking is far more apt for confirming the true humanity of Christ. Not to mention that there lies hidden in it a silent exhortation to the Jews, that they might the more gladly embrace Christ, who derives his descent from their most holy patriarch. For they too gloried in a wonderful way that they were sons of Abraham, and on that very title they ought to have been led to magnify Christ. But we shall seem to be acting not without reason if we explain somewhat more fully how Christ clothed himself with flesh from the seed of Abraham, and how Valentinus is refuted here, and with him certain Anabaptists of our own time.

units.la: Promissionem factam ad Abrahamum constat ex Gen. 22. vbi postquam Abraham patratus fuit offerre vnicum suum filium, audiuit ab angelo: Per memetipsum iuraui, dicit dominus: quia fecisti hanc rem, & non pepercisti filio tuo unigenito, benedicam tibi, & multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas coeli, & velut arenam maris. Possidebit semen tuum portas inimicorum suorum, & benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terrae. Quae promissio adeo celebris & magnifica est, tāin veteri testamento, quàm in nouo, ut nulla magis. Nàm in veteri testamento oēs prophetae de Christo vaticinantes ad illam respexerunt, illamq; pro suo habuerunt fundamento. Deniq; oēs prophetię ex illa tanquā fonte profluxerunt, & per semē illud personā Christi indubitatò respexerūt. In nouo autē testamento Act. 3. Gal. 3. ité praesenti loco, ex illis ipsis verbis salute propter Christū obtinendā, eāq; tā gentib. & Iudaeis cōmuniter esse paratam: deinde fide
units.tr: The promise made to Abraham is found in Gen. 22, where, after Abraham was ready to offer his only son, he heard from the angel: "By myself have I sworn, saith the Lord, because thou hast done this thing and hast not spared thy son, thine only son, that in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the sea shore. Thy seed shall possess the gates of his enemies; and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." This promise is so famous and magnificent, both in the Old Testament and in the New, that none is more so. For in the Old Testament all the prophets prophesying of Christ looked to it and held it as their foundation. Indeed all the prophecies flowed out from it as from a fountain, and through that seed they unquestionably looked to the person of Christ. In the New Testament, in Acts 3 and Gal. 3, and also in the present passage, from those very words it is taught that salvation is to be obtained on account of Christ, and that it is prepared in common for Gentiles and Jews alike; then by faith...

units.la: Vide ad Gal. 3. fide in Christum contingere illam, non vllis legis operibus: adhæc Christum verum esse hominem, & ex stirpe Abrahæ suam habere originem: hæc inquam tam præclara & præcipua vniuersæ doctrinæ euangelicæ capita ex adeo paucis uerbis colliguntur.
units.tr: See on Gal. 3 that this faith in Christ is obtained not by any works of the law. Further, Christ is true man and has his origin from the stock of Abraham. These, I say, are the very notable and principal heads of the whole evangelical doctrine, gathered from so few words.

units.la: Propter illam ergo insignem & memoratissimam promissionem ad Abrahamum factam, dicitur hoc loco Christus semen Abrahæ assumpsisse: quomodo & euangelista Matthæus capite primo genealogiam Christi texere volens, eam ad Abraham usq; ceu primum quendam, & valde illustrem auum deducit: vbi etiam propter similem promissionem ad Dauidem factam etiam filius Dauid, sicut & Roman. 1. ex femine Dauid natus describitur. Et Luc. 1. Is erit magnus, & filius altissimi vocabitur, & dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem Dauid patris ipsius, regnabit in æternum, & regnei us non erit finis. Et sæpe à populo & aliis vocatus est Christus filius Dauid. Quibus appellationibus illustris ac nobilis secundum carnem ex Regum stirpe descendens Christus celebratur. Sed quia multò celeberrima fuit promissio facta ad Abraham, & ab eodem omnes Iudæi se descendere gloriabantur: præsertim quando sub eodem Abraham suscipiente circumcisionem coepit distinctio manifesta haberi Iudæorum à cæteris populis: hinc ad significandum, ex ipsorum Iudæorum carne & sanguine Christum trahere suam originem, siue humanam naturam assumpsisse, dixit Apostolus, Christum semen Abrahæ apprehendisse. In quam sententiam & Rom. 9. dicit: Optarim ego ipse anathema esse à Christo, pro fratribus meis, cognatis meis secundum carnem. Et mox sequitur: quorum sunt patres, & hi, ex quibus est Christus, quantum attinet ad carnem, qui est in omnibus Deus laudandus in secula.
units.tr: Therefore, on account of that remarkable and most famous promise made to Abraham, Christ is said in this place to have taken up the seed of Abraham. So the evangelist Matthew, wishing to trace the genealogy of Christ in chapter 1, leads it back to Abraham as to a first and very illustrious grandfather. There, on account of the similar promise made to David, he is also described as son of David, just as in Rom. 1 he is described as born of the seed of David. Luke 1: "He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Highest, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father. He will reign for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." Often by the people and others Christ was called Son of David. By these appellations Christ, descending according to the flesh from the stock of kings, is celebrated as illustrious and noble. But because the promise made to Abraham was far more famous, and all Jews gloried that they descended from him, especially since under this same Abraham, when he received circumcision, a clear distinction of the Jews from the other peoples began to be held, the Apostle said, to signify that Christ drew his origin from the very flesh and blood of the Jews, or that he assumed human nature, that Christ took hold of the seed of Abraham. To this effect Rom. 9 also says: "I could wish myself to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh." And soon follows: "whose are the fathers, and of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever."

units.la: Tantum, quomodo Christus dicatur filius Abrahæ, siue ex femine Abrahæ. Iam uerò ipsa vox semmis plurimum momenti habet ad refellendum & Valentinum, qui ausus est afferere, Christum nihil de beata uirgine assumpsisse, sed spirituale seu cœleste corpus secum attulisse, idque per eam, quasi rimam aut fistulam, in mundo editum: quem erorem quidam hac tempestate nisi sunt reuocare. Sed quàm vane id conentur, & quàm luculenter e Scripturis refellantur, breuiter declarabimus.
units.tr: So much for how Christ is said to be son of Abraham, or from the seed of Abraham. Now the very word "seed" has great weight for refuting Valentinus too, who dared to assert that Christ took nothing from the blessed virgin, but brought a spiritual or heavenly body with him, and that he was put forth into the world through her as through a channel or pipe. Some in this age have not been able to recall this error. But how vainly they attempt this, and how clearly it is refuted from the Scriptures, we shall briefly declare.

units.la: Certè argumenta si quæ habeant, illud validissimum fortasis iudicari posset, quod & Manichæus usurpauit ad tribuendum Christo corpus aerium, prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto.
units.tr: Certainly, if they have arguments, the most powerful of them might perhaps be judged to be the one which Manichaeus also used to attribute to Christ an aerial body: 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: Factus est primus homo Adam in anima viuente, extremus Adam in spiritum vivifi cantem: mox additur: Primus homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo ipse Dominus de cœlo. Ex his uerbis euinci uidetur, corpus Christi & spirituale & è cœlo allatum. Sed si quis animaduertat, quid ibi agat Apostolus, aliud sentiet. Docet autem nos, sicut secundum carnem, & lapsum in ea referimus primum parentem nostrum Adamum: itaà resurrectione referemus quoque Christum, prorsus tales tum futuri, qualis à resurrectione fuit ipse Christus. Neque ibi discernit naturam corporis nostri à natura corporis Christi, sed ab exemplo Christi confirmat resurrectionis, & per eam immutationis nostræ modum. Imò sequentibus verbis æquat nostra corpora corpori ipsius Christi, quando ait: Qualis terrenus, tales & hi, qui terreni sunt: & qualis ille cœlestis, tales & hi, qui cœlestes sunt. Et quemadmodum gestauimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus & imaginem cœlestis. Et in tota illa disputatione inepta ducerentur argumenta ad confirmandam resurrectionem nostram ac exemplo Christi, nisi par esset corporum nostrorum & corporis Christi ratio.
units.tr: "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit." Soon it is added: "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven." From these words it seems to be proved that the body of Christ is both spiritual and brought from heaven. But if anyone considers what the Apostle is doing there, he will think otherwise. He teaches us that, just as we refer our first parent Adam to the flesh and to the fall in it, so by the resurrection we refer Christ too, since we shall be altogether such as Christ himself was from the resurrection. Nor does he there distinguish the nature of our body from the nature of the body of Christ. Rather, from the example of Christ he confirms the resurrection, and through it the manner of our change. Indeed, in the following words he makes our bodies equal to the body of Christ himself, when he says: As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly. In that whole disputation the arguments for confirming our resurrection from the example of Christ would be pointless, unless the nature of our bodies and the nature of the body of Christ were alike.

units.la: Aliud argumentum mutuantur ex Ioan. 8. vbi Christus ait, vos ab infernis estis, ego de supernis sum: vos de mundo hoc estis, ego non sum de hoc mundo. Ex quibus verbis Manichæus quidè Christū attulisse corpus ex mundo altero inuisibili, (nā duos ille constituebat mundos, sicut duo principia: & inuisibilem mundum conditum à bono principio, visibilem verò hunc ab altero principio) & Valentinus corpus Christi è cœlo defluxisse in terras opinabatur. Sed adhoc quoq; argumetum facile est respondere. Esse de supernis, & non esse de hoc mundo, nihil ibi significat de substantia corporis, sed potius qualitates quasdam animæ eæ phrases significat: nempe esse immunem à peccatis, & nequaquam esse rebus huius mundi deditum: id quod ex contextu uerborum sequentium liquet colligere: nam statim sequitur: Dixi ergo uobis, quòd moriemini in peccatis uestris: quia nimirum ipsi de infernis erant, & de mundo hoc, id est, peccatis dediti, carnalibus rebus occupati, à rebus diuinis, cœlestibus, & spiritualibus toto animo alieni & abhorrentes. Similiter modo Ioan. 15. dicit et discipulos suos non esse de mundo. Quia de mundo non estis, & ego elegi uos de mundo, propterea odit uos mundus. Quod & repetit Ioan. 17. Mundus eos odio habuit, quia non sunt de mundo, sicut & ego non sum de mundo. Quinetiā cœlestis homo dicitur, qui 1. Cor. 2. spiritualis, spiritum ex Deo habens, & omnia dijudicans, & huius epistolæ cap. 3. credentes vocantur fratres sancti, uocationis cœlestis participes.
units.tr: They borrow another argument from John 8, where Christ says: "You are from beneath, I am from above; you are of this world, I am not of this world." From these words Manichaeus supposed that Christ brought a body from another, invisible world (for he posited two worlds, as two principles: the invisible world created by the good principle, and this visible one by the other principle), and Valentinus thought that the body of Christ flowed down from heaven to the earth. But this argument too is easily answered. To be from above, and not to be of this world, signifies nothing there about the substance of the body, but rather expresses certain qualities of the soul: namely, to be free from sins and in no way given over to the things of this world. This is clear from the context of the following words, for immediately it follows: I said therefore to you, that you will die in your sins. Obviously they were from beneath and of this world, that is, given over to sins, occupied with carnal things, and wholly alien to and abhorrent of divine, heavenly and spiritual things in their whole mind. Similarly, in John 15 he says that his disciples are not of the world: Because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. He repeats this in John 17: The world has hated them, because they are not of the world, as I also am not of the world. Moreover, a heavenly man is called one who is spiritual, having the Spirit from God and judging all things (1 Cor. 2). And in chapter 3 of this epistle believers are called holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling.

units.la: Quanquam
units.tr: Although

units.la: Quanquàm quòd Christus ait Ioan.8.se de supernis esse, & nequaquam de hoc mun- do, potest ad diuinitatem eius referri, secundum qu am dicitur de hoc mundo non esse, sed mundum cõdidisse, & in mundum venijsse. Et simili modo accipitur illud Ioan.3. Qui è supernis venit, supra omnes est. Qui è terra profectus est, terrenus est, & è terra loqui- tur. Qui è cœlo venit, supra omnes est, & quod vidit & audiuit, hoc testatur, & testimo- nium eius nemo accipit. Sed satis hæc sint ad soluenda argumenta, non solùm quæ iam protulimus, sed alia quoq;, quæ ab illis ad stabiliendum impium dogma proferri possent.
units.tr: Although the statement of Christ in John 8 that he is from above and not at all of this world can be referred to his divinity, according to which he is said not to be of this world but to have made the world and come into it. In a similar way that saying of John 3 is understood: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth is earthly, and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all; what he has seen and heard, of this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony." But these things are enough to solve the arguments, not only those we have now put forward but also others which could be brought forward from these sources to establish the impious dogma.

units.la: Nunc videamus, quàm validis testimonijs Scripturæ, Christū habuisse verum corpus simile corporibus nostris, & ex humana carne, illibatæ nimirum virginis suam traxisse carnem, comprobetur. Primùm hoc loco vacabulū feminis manifestissimè arguit, veram carnem ex humana carne contraxisse: id quod in omnibus locis Scripturæ, vbi locutio eiusmodi occurrit, omnes ita accipiunt, vt Genes.3. vbi ad serpentem Dominus ait: Inimicitias ponam inter te & mulierem, & semen tuum & semen ipsius. Ipsum conteret caput tuum, & tu insidiaberis calcaneo eius. Vbi notandū, non rectè legi in vulgata editione, ipsa conteret: cùm relatiuum non ad mulierem, sed ad semen referri debeat. Nam Hebræis ibi זרע relatiuum est masculini generis, & refert זרע semē. Rectè autem dixit Augustinus sermone 5. de Trinitate. Cùm dicit Apostolus Galat. 4 Christum filium Dei missum & factum ex muliere, hac particula, ex muliere, substantiam veri hominis expressit: ut hæc sit natura facti hominis, quæ fuit ipsius, vnde factus est, id est, vt ea creditur esse natura Christi, qui est factus ex virgine, quæ fuit natura virginis, ex qua Christus formatus & natus est. Inde est, quod alibi idè Apostolus de Dei filio dici: qui factus est ei ex semine Dauid secundum carnem. Nam etsi non intercessit semen hominis in conceptione virginis, tamen quia ex carne Christus formatus est, quæ constat ex semine, dicitur factus ex semine. Quemadmodum ergo secundum diuinitatem vna est patris & filij natura: ita etiam iuxta humanitatem eadem est matris & filij, id est, Mariæ Christiq; natura. Tantum Augustinus, duo testimonia nostro instituto conuenientia exponens. Huc etiam pertinet, quod suprà citauimus ex Roman.9. Expatrib. est Christus secundū carnem. Et Psalmo 132. ad Dauidem promissio facta: iurauit Dominus Dauid veritatem, & non frustrabitur eum, de fructu uentris tui ponam super sedem tuam. Esaiæ 7. Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filiū, & vocabit nomē eius Immanuel. Quibus verbis angelus etiam vsus est Lucę 1. Et Elizabetha ad Mariam, Benedictus fructus ventris tui. Eadè de causa se filium homi nis passim appellare gaudet. Quibus locis, fructus ventris, cōcipere, parere, satis arguūt, Christum ex beata virgine carnem assumpsisse. Hæc visum est, quia tēporis huius ratio aliquo modo videbatur postulare, paulò fusius exponere. Quomodo verò hic Valenti nus, ita & Appelles reuincitur, qui Christi corpus ex elementis mundi conflatū asseruit, idq; à morte iterum resolutum in elementare materiam, & Christū sine carne in cœlos ascendisse. Contra quod etiam est, quòd Christus palàm ostenderit, se à resurrectione carnem & ossa adhuc habuisse, & palàm visus sit, cum eodem corpore ascendisse.
units.tr: Now let us see by how strong testimonies of Scripture it is proved that Christ had a true body like our bodies, and that he drew his flesh from human flesh, namely from the undefiled virgin. First, this word "seed" most plainly shows that he took true flesh from human flesh. All who meet such an expression in any place of Scripture understand it in this way, as in Gen. 3, where the Lord says to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he shall bruise your head, and you shall lie in wait for his heel." Here it should be noted that the Vulgate edition is not rightly read with the feminine pronoun, "she shall bruise", since the relative ought to refer not to the woman but to the seed. For there the Hebrew word [זרע] is a relative of masculine gender, and refers to the seed. Augustine rightly said in sermon 5 on the Trinity: when the Apostle says in Gal. 4 that Christ the Son of God was sent and made of a woman, by this phrase "of a woman" he expressed the substance of a true man. So this is the nature of the made man which was of her from whom he was made; that is, it is believed that this is the nature of Christ, who was made of the virgin, which was the nature of the virgin from whom Christ was formed and born. Hence the Apostle elsewhere says of the Son of God that he was made to him of the seed of David according to the flesh. For although no seed of a man intervened in the conception of the virgin, yet because Christ was formed from flesh, which consists of seed, he is said to be made of seed. Just as, therefore, according to divinity there is one nature of Father and Son, so also according to humanity the nature of mother and son is the same, that is, of Mary and Christ. So far Augustine, expounding two testimonies agreeing with our purpose. To this also pertains what we cited above from Rom. 9: "of whose fathers Christ is according to the flesh." And there is the promise made to David in Ps. 132: "The Lord swore to David in truth, and will not frustrate him: of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne." Isa. 7: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." The angel also used these words in Luke 1, and Elizabeth to Mary: "Blessed is the fruit of your womb." For the same reason he everywhere delights to call himself Son of man. By these passages, "fruit of the womb", "conceive", "bear", it is sufficiently proved that Christ assumed flesh from the blessed virgin. This seemed fitting to set out somewhat more fully, because the reason of this time seemed in some way to demand it. But just as Valentinus is refuted here, so too is Apelles, who asserted that the body of Christ was compounded from the elements of the world, and that this body, dissolved again at death into elemental matter, and Christ ascended into the heavens without flesh. Against this also is the fact that Christ plainly showed that after the resurrection he still had flesh and bones, and was plainly seen to have ascended with the same body.

units.la: Cæterùm, vt etiam doctrinam aliquam excerpamus ex eo, quòd Christus dicitur semen Abrahæ potius asumpsisse, quàm angelos, maximam hinc colligimus naturæ humanæ dignitatem, quam Deus etiam angelis hac in parte præferre voluerit. Vnde & hoc loco Chrysostomus, reuera magnum est, & admirabile, & stupore plenum est, carnem nostram supra sedere, & adorari ab angelis & Archangelis. Hoc sæpius ego mente versans excessu patior, & multò maxima de genere humano concipio. Sed rursus hic quæritur: si ex semine seu carne viginis caro Christi assūpta & formata est: quomodo dicitur Christus conceptus è spiritu Sanƈto? De hac quæstione elegantem vide responsionem in Caluino folio 147. Item Bucerum Roman.cap. 11.sol.59. Ad verba autoris.
units.tr: Moreover, to draw some teaching from the fact that Christ is said to have taken on the seed of Abraham rather than angels, we gather from this the very great dignity of human nature, which God chose to prefer even to the angels in this respect. Hence Chrysostom, in this place too: it is truly great and admirable and full of wonder that our flesh sits above and is adored by the angels and archangels. I often turn this over in my mind and am overwhelmed, and I conceive very great things about the human race. But here again a question arises: if the flesh of Christ was taken and formed from the seed, or the flesh, of the virgin, how is Christ said to have been conceived of the Holy Spirit? On this question see the elegant answer in Calvin, folio 147, and likewise Bucer on Romans, chapter 11, page 59. On the words of the author.

units.la: Vnde debuit per omnia fratribus similis reddi, vt misericors esset & fidelis pontifex, in his quæ apud Deum forent agenda, ad expiandum peccata populi. Nam ex hoc, quod ipsi contigit tentatum esse, potest & his, qui tentantur, succurrere.
units.tr: Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in the things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For since he himself has suffered and been tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.

units.la: Conclusio totius huius loci, in qua paulò plurib. verbis, quia id poscebat aduersariorum improbitas, cur Christum oportuerit hominem fieri, causas duas grauissimas reddit. Artificiosè autē, & singulari prudentia inserit nonnulla de Christi officijs, quæ etiā aliquo modo declarant, cur Christum decuerit humanam naturam assumere, certè præcedentes causas principales confirmant & illustrant, vt mox indicabimus.
units.tr: The conclusion of this whole passage, in which, at somewhat greater length, because the impudence of the adversaries demanded it, he gives two most weighty reasons why Christ had to become man. He skilfully and with singular prudence inserts some points about Christ's offices, which also in some way show why it was fitting for Christ to assume human nature; they certainly confirm and illustrate the principal causes given above, as we shall point out shortly.

units.la: Est autem multò aptissimum conclusioni, quod ait: unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis reddi, quasi diceret: propter has causas iam enumeratas decebat Christum verum hominem eiusdem naturæ, cuius sunt cæteri homines, fieri ὡφαλ, inquit, id est, debuit, significans ea voce non simpliciter & absolutè necessitatem: quandoquidē non est dubium, quin Deus alia ratione, si voluisset, potuisset humanam genus saluum facere: sed conue-nientiam atq; ordinatum aptisimumq; modum, qua ratione superius dixit, Decebat enim cum, per quem sunt omnia, etc.
units.tr: The phrase "unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis reddi" fits very well with the conclusion, as if he were saying: for the reasons already listed, it was fitting for Christ to become a true man of the same nature as the rest of men. He says "it was necessary" [ὤφειλε], that is, "he ought", meaning by that word not simple and absolute necessity, since there is no doubt that God could have saved the human race by another method had he wished; rather, a suitable and orderly manner, which is why he said above: "For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom are all things, etc."

units.la: Fratres vero accipit in genere pro quibuscunq; hominibus, in quibus humana natura resplendet, secundum quam Christus omnium hominū frater est: quando quidē omnes ex uno, videlicet primo parente Adamo trahunt originem. Quo sensu accipi vocabulū fratrum expositum supra in illo testimonio ex Psalmo 22. Annunciabo nomen tuum fratribus meis: ad quod testimonium haud dubie respexit Apostolus, quando hac forma verborum, similis reddi debuit fratribus, voluit absolutam & perfectam naturam humanam in Christo explicare. Et cum utitur verbo ὁμοιωθῆναι, id est, assimilari, similem fieri, non tantum significat similitudinem qualemcunq;, quomodo inanimata tabula similitudinem refert rei animatae, sed omnimodam similitudinem & aequalitatem secundum substantiam, naturam, & vires praecipuas: quomodo in initio huius epistolae, vocabulū imaginis siue χαρακτὴρ sumitur, vbi dicebatur Christus χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρός.
units.tr: He takes "brothers" in a general sense, for all men in whom human nature shines, according to which Christ is the brother of all men, since all draw their origin from one, namely the first parent Adam. In this sense the word "brothers" was explained above in that testimony from Psalm 22: "I will declare your name to my brothers." The Apostle clearly had this testimony in view when, with the words "he ought to be made like his brothers," he wished to set forth a complete and perfect human nature in Christ. And when he uses the verb ὁμοιωθῆναι [homoiōthēnai], that is, to be made like or to become similar, he does not mean any sort of resemblance, as a lifeless picture resembles a living thing, but complete likeness and equality in substance, nature and principal powers. So at the beginning of this letter the word "image" or χαρακτὴρ [charaktēr] is used, where Christ was called "the stamp of the substance of the Father" [χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρός].

units.la: Quare Marcion hic nihil potest ex voce ὁμοιωθῆναι pro se arripere, ut dicat Christum non utiq; verum corpus habuisse, sed tantum simile nostris corporibus, id est, phantasma & similitudinem corporis: sicut putabat etiā idē colligere ex illis locis, Rom. 8. vbi dicitur, filium missum sub specie carnis peccato obnoxiae: & Philippen. 2. Cum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam arbitratus est, ut esset aequalis Deo, sed semetipsum inaniuit, forma serui sumpta, in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus ut homo, humilē praebuit semetipsum.
units.tr: Hence Marcion can grasp nothing here from the word ὁμοιωθῆναι [homoiōthēnai] in his own favour, so as to say that Christ did not have a true body but only one similar to our bodies, that is, a phantom and an likeness of a body. He also thought he could gather the same from those passages in Romans 8, where it is said that the Son was sent "in the likeness of sinful flesh," and from Philippians 2: "Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in human appearance, he humbled himself."

units.la: Ex his, inquam, locis nihil potest Martion pro se arripere, non solū quia supra quoq; dictum est satis clare, Christum participem esse factum carnis & sanguinis, & proximē, assumpsisse eum semen Ahrahae: sed quia vox similitudinis non significat qualecunq; similitudinem, sed omnimodam similitudinem & aequalitatem secundum substantiam: id quod multo euadit maninefestius ex eo, quod hic additur, per omnia: quae particula magnam habet Emphasim, ad demonstrandum, Christum esse verum hominem, verumcae nem suscepisse, anima rationali, & carne, caeterisq; sensibus, ut nos, praeditum, etiam communibus miseriis, (intelligo eas, quae nihil detrahunt plenitudini gratiae, quamin eo semper oportet agno scere) obnoxium. Qui enim dicit, per omnia nostri similem, quid videtur spectare in nobis, quod non item velit spectari in illo? Ita ut dicendo, Similis per omnia nobis factus est, tantundem videatur dixisse, natus est, ut nos miseri homines, lactatus, educatus, esuriuit, sitiuit, alsit, friguit, profecit aetate & sapientia, doluit, fleuit, commotus est spiritu, contristatus est, tentatus est, dolores & miserias multas expertus est, deniq; et mortuus est, in summa, omnia huiusmodi quae in nobis miseris mortalibus cernimus & sentimus, eadem in illo quoq; uisa sunt, & ipse in se sensit: & sic vere per omnia nobis miseris & calamitosis suis fratribus similis factus est. Licet autē semel exposuerimus, quomodo Christus & sanguine nostrum cū his, quae aggenita his sunt, suscepit, tamen non possum, quin idem hic aliquando explicatius aperiam.
units.tr: From these passages, I say, Marcion can grasp nothing in his own favour, not only because it has already been said clearly enough above that Christ has been made a partaker of flesh and blood, and, closer to the point, that he took the seed of Abraham; but because the word "likeness" does not signify any sort of likeness, but complete likeness and equality in substance. This becomes much more evident from what is added here, "in all things." This phrase has great emphasis, to show that Christ is a true man, that he took on a true body and a rational soul, and was endowed with the other senses as we are, and was also subject to common miseries (I mean those which detract nothing from the fullness of grace, which in him must always be acknowledged). For when he says "made like us in every respect," what does he seem to look for in us that he does not likewise wish to be found in him? So by saying "he was made like us in every respect," he seems to have said exactly this: he was born as we miserable men are, nursed, brought up, he hungered, thirsted, grew cold, felt the cold, advanced in age and wisdom, grieved, wept, was moved in spirit, was saddened, was tempted, suffered many pains and miseries, and finally died. In short, all such things as we miserable mortals see and feel in ourselves were also seen in him, and he felt them in himself; and so he truly was made like his miserable and afflicted brothers in every respect. Although we have already explained once how Christ took on our flesh with those things that are born with it, nevertheless I cannot refrain from setting it out here again, at some point more fully.

units.la: Hoc inprimis tenendum, Christum corpore & anima constare, sicuti nos, (abfitut diuinitatem loco animae illi adfuisse suspiceremur, & a verbo assumptam carnem, tantū sine anima, quemadmodum Arrius & quidam alij imaginati sunt) proinde cum tam ex parte, animae, quam corporis sint in nobis multiplices miseriae & calamitates, videndū quae ex his Christo coueniant, itē quę non. Quod ad miserias corporis attinet, quaereuera multae sunt et variae: quamuis ea sint immissae propter peccatū, et sint peccati poena, adeoq; multa, & omnes homines, quoniam peccatores sunt, debent eas in se sentire: (id quod liquet ex illo ad Roman. 5. per peccatum mors, & sic in omnes homines mors peruasit, quatenus omnes peccauimus) Christus autem, qui nullum admisit peccatum, merito debuisset esse immunis ab omnibus miseriis: utpote ubi causa non est, ibi quoq; abesse debet effectus, & vbi culpa non est, non debet intelligi poena: tamen voluit nihil ominus miserias communes in se recipere, & sic per omnia fratribus similis fieri, idq; trib. de causis. Prima ratio ex praesenti loco sumitur, Christum ideo suscepisse humanas miserias, ut misericors fieret, ut tentatis eo lubentius subueniret. Secunda est, ut ita doceret, se verum esse hominem, & naturae nostrae per omnia participem, & non tantū habuisse corpus phantasticum aut impassibile, sicut quidam falsò sunt opinati. Tertia causa est, decuit id ita fieri, propterea, quod pro peccatis nostris venit satisfacturus: licet ipse non peccarit, ac proinde merito debuisset expers manere nostrarum miseriarum: tamen quia propter nostra peccata expianda venit in terras, voluit miserias in se experiri, perinde ac si ipse peccatum perpetrasset: quomodo aliās dicitur ipse, qui non fecit peccatum, factus pro nobis peccatum, & languores nostros vere portasse describitur. Quarta ratio addi potest, cum subijsse nostras miserias, ut exemplum ab eo haberemus, & consolationem in miseris nostris, quas nos nostro merito patimur, æquanimiter tolerandis. Quò pertinet, quòd de perferendis miserijs propter peccatum tenaciter inhærens dicitur initio capitis duodecimi huius epistolæ: deposito onere omni, & tenaciter inhærete peccato per tolerantiam curramus in proposito nobis certamine, respicientes ad fidei ducem, & consummatorem Iesum, &c. Ob has, inquam, causas conueniebat, Christū per omnia fratribus similem fieri, & miserias nostras in se recipere. Iam ergo quod ad corporis miserias attinet, ut expediamus, num omnes Christus in se receperit: sciendū est, duplices esse miserias corporales. Quæda sunt naturales, quæ à nullo homine inueniuntur abesse & communiter in omnibus, in quantum homines sunt, cernuntur, & per eas intelligun tur vere esse homines: ut fames, sitis, &c. Huiusmodi ergo miserias omnes Christus, ut se verum esse hominem ostenderet, in se expertus est. Sunt aliæ miseriæ, quæ non communiter in omnibus cernuntur, aut accidentariò eueniunt, & interdum culpa ipsorum hominum, alijsq; peculiaribus causis, ut ex immoderato viͤtu, nimia libidine, &c. Huiusmodi autem miseriæ in Christo non habuerunt locum: quandoquidem causæ etiam in eo non fuerunt. Qui enim erat plenus gratia & veritate, non poterat aliquid cō mittere, vnde id genus miseriæ prouenirent.
units.tr: First of all it must be held that Christ consists of body and soul, as we do (far be it that we should suspect that the divinity was present in him in place of a soul, and that the flesh was assumed by the Word only without a soul, as Arius and certain others imagined). Therefore, since there are many miseries and calamities in us, both in the soul and in the body, we must consider which of these apply to Christ and which do not. As for the miseries of the body, indeed there are many and various; although they were sent because of sin and are the punishment of sin, and so many of them, and all men, since they are sinners, ought to feel them in themselves (as is clear from Romans 5: "through sin death came, and so death spread to all men, inasmuch as all have sinned"). Christ, however, who committed no sin, rightly ought to have been free from all miseries: where there is no cause, there the effect too ought to be absent, and where there is no fault, punishment should not be understood. Nevertheless he willed to receive into himself the common miseries, and so to be made like his brothers in every respect, and this for three reasons. The first reason is taken from the present passage: Christ therefore took on human miseries so that he might become merciful, and might more willingly help those who are tempted. The second is that he might teach that he is a true man, and a partaker of all our nature, and not merely that he had a phantom or impassible body, as some have falsely supposed. The third reason is that it was fitting for it to happen thus, because he came to make satisfaction for our sins; although he himself did not sin, and so rightly ought to have remained free of our miseries, nevertheless, since he came to earth to make atonement for our sins, he willed to experience miseries in himself, just as if he had committed sin himself; in the same way it is said elsewhere that he who did not know sin was made sin for us, and is described as having truly borne our infirmities. A fourth reason may be added: that he underwent our miseries so that we might have an example from him and consolation in our miseries, which we suffer by our own merit, to be endured with equanimity. To this belongs what is said at the beginning of the twelfth chapter of this letter, about enduring the miseries that come on account of sin, clinging firmly: "laying aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the leader and perfecter of faith," and so on. For these reasons, I say, it was fitting that Christ should be made like his brothers in every respect and take our miseries upon himself. Now, then, as far as the miseries of the body are concerned, to clarify whether Christ took on all of them, it must be known that there are two kinds of bodily miseries. Some are natural, which are found in no man to be absent, and are seen commonly in all, insofar as they are men, and through them we understand that they are truly men: such as hunger, thirst, and so on. Christ therefore experienced all such miseries in himself, to show that he is truly man. There are other miseries, which are not seen commonly in all, or happen by chance, and sometimes through the fault of men themselves or other particular causes, such as from immoderate living, excessive lust, and so on. Such miseries had no place in Christ, since the causes of them were not in him either. For he, who was full of grace and truth, could not commit anything from which miseries of that kind might arise.

units.la: Nunc, quod ad miserias animæ proprias attinet, sciendum, eas quoq; duplices posse cōsiderari: alias, quæ damnationem in nobis pariunt, & gratiæ Dei prorsus aduersantur, ut peccatum cum omnibus adiunctis: alias verò, quæ nequaquam sunt huiusmodi: ut tristitia, dolor, ira, timor, admiratio, &c. quas plerunq; vocant animæ affectiones, seu passiones. Itaq; breuiter responderi potest, quòd quoniam Christus fuit, ut habetur Ioan. 1. plenus gratia & veritate, adeò ut de plenitudine eius omnes acceperint, primi generis miseriæ in eo locum habere non possunt, hoc est, neq; peccatum, neq; propensio ad peccatū, neq; quicquam his affine, vel ex his proueniens: quo pertinet illa Esaiæ 53. Ioan. 8. Quis ex vobis arguet me peccati? 2. Corinth. 5. Eum, qui peccatum non nouit, fecit pro nobis peccatum. 1. Petri 2. Qui peccatum non fecit, &c. Alterius verò generis miseriæ, quatenus peccato non sunt adiuncte, & ex peccato nō prouenium in eo cōspectæ sunt, sic tamē, ut in vitium non abirent, & rationi nequaquam dominarentur: vnde Matth. 26. coepit affici dolore & mœstitudine. Tunc ait illis Iesus: mœsta est anima mea usq; ad mortem. En dolor & mœstitudo. Marci 14. coepitq; expauescere & angi. En pauor & metus. Matth. 8. tribuitur Christo admiratio secundum humanitatem. Hæc autem cum audisset Iesus, admiratus est, & ait sequentibus se, Amen dico vobis, ne in Israel quidem tantum fidei reperi. Ioan. 11. Iesus ut vidit Mariam plorantem mortuum Lazarum, infremuit, & turbauit semetipsum. Ioan. 2. Iratus & commotus eiecit vendentes & ementes. Et subijcitur: Recordati sunt discipuli eius quod scriptum est: Zelus domus tuæ exedit me. Psalmo 86. En ira, fremitus, indignatio, aliæq; passiones in Christo: sed quatenus communes omnibus hominibus per naturam, & quatenus à peccato alienæ. Ex his igitur palàm fit, particulam hanc, per omnia, magnam quidem habere Emphasin, & rectissimè vsurpatam ab Apostolo, ad exprimendum, quòd Christus verus fuerit homo, veram carnem susceperit, anima rationali & carne, nec non sensibus, ut nos, præditus: deniq; omnibus miserijs tàm corporis, quàm animæ obnoxius, quæ naturales censentur, & in omnibus hominibus conspiciuntur. Ita tamen, ut intelligamus eas in Christo locum nō habere, quæ vel in corpore prouenuntaccidentariò, ex particularibus causis, in quibus culpa inest seu vitium: vel in anima sunt, ad damnationem parandam idoneæ, vel aliàs quocunq; modo gratiæ Dei (qua Christum fuisse plenum, necesse est iuxta Ioannis testimonium concedamus) repugnantes. Quare cùm Christus per omnia similis fratribus id est, omnibus natura humana præditis, describitur, significatur quidem, illum expertū esse in se communes miserias corporales, nempe famen, sitim, algorem, æstum, fatigatio nem, &c. at vérò ægritudines ex immoderato viͤtu, vel huiusmodi ærumnas nequaquā.
