Deinde significatur, sensisse eum miserias siue affectiones animæ, quatenus peccato non sunt adiuncte, & à recto non aberrantes: ut, dolorem, mœstitiam, Matth. 26. pauorem siue metum, Marci 14. fremitum & animi commotionem Ioan. 11. indignationem siue zelum, Ioan. 2. At vérò peccatum, aut aliquid peccato affine, vel ad peccatum inducens, aut ex peccato oriens, nequaquam: id quod liquet Ioan. 8. 2. Corinth. 5. 1. Petri 2. Esaiæ 53. vbi ab omni peccato immunis ostenditur. Igitur quando dicitur, an Christus per omnia generaliter sit fratribus factus similis, prudeter distinguendum est. Interea hac particula omnes errores, negantium veram Christi humanitatem, confutantur. Vide Aquensem in illud Ioannis, verbum caro factum est, &c.
units.tr: Now, as far as the miseries proper to the soul are concerned, it should be noted that these too can be considered in two kinds. Some produce damnation in us and are wholly opposed to the grace of God, such as sin with all its attendants. Others are not of this sort at all, such as sadness, grief, anger, fear, wonder, and so on, which are commonly called affections or passions of the soul. So it can be briefly answered that, since Christ was, as is stated in John 1, full of grace and truth, so that all have received from his fullness, the first kind of misery cannot have a place in him. That is, there was in him neither sin, nor any propensity to sin, nor anything akin to these or arising from them. To this belong Isaiah 53, John 8, "Which of you convicts me of sin?", 2 Corinthians 5, "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us," and 1 Peter 2, "who committed no sin," and so on. But the second kind of misery, insofar as it is not joined to sin and was not seen in him as arising from sin, did occur in him, yet in such a way that it did not pass into vice and never ruled over reason. Hence Matthew 26 says he began to be seized with grief and heaviness. "Then Jesus said to them, my soul is sorrowful even unto death." Behold grief and heaviness. Mark 14: he began to be troubled and distressed. Behold fear and dread. In Matthew 8, wonder is ascribed to Christ according to his humanity: "When Jesus heard these things, he marvelled, and said to those who followed him, Truly I say to you, I have not found such faith even in Israel." John 11: when Jesus saw Mary weeping and the dead Lazarus, he groaned and troubled himself. John 2: angered and moved, he drove out those who sold and bought. And it is added: "His disciples remembered that it was written, zeal for your house has consumed me." Psalm 86. Behold anger, groaning, indignation, and other passions in Christ, but insofar as they are common to all men by nature, and insofar as they are free from sin. From these things it is therefore plain that this little particle, in every respect, has great emphasis, and was most rightly used by the Apostle to express that Christ was a true man, that he assumed true flesh, endowed with a rational soul and flesh, and also with senses like ours, and finally that he was subject to all the miseries of body and soul that are counted natural and are seen in all men. Yet we must understand that those miseries which arise in the body by accident, from particular causes in which there is fault or vice, or which are in the soul and are fit to prepare damnation, or which in any other way are opposed to the grace of God (which, according to John's testimony, we must concede Christ was full of), have no place in him. Therefore, when Christ is described as in every respect generally made like his brothers, that is, to all who are endowed with human nature, it is indeed signified that he experienced in himself the common bodily miseries, namely hunger, thirst, cold, heat, weariness, and so on, but by no means sicknesses arising from immoderate living or such hardships. Next, it is signified that he felt the miseries or affections of the soul insofar as they were not joined to sin and did not go astray from what is right: such as grief and sadness (Matthew 26), fear or dread (Mark 14), groaning and agitation of spirit (John 11), indignation or zeal (John 2). But sin, or anything akin to sin, or leading to sin, or arising from sin, by no means. This is clear from John 8, 2 Corinthians 5, 1 Peter 2, and Isaiah 53, where he is shown to be free from all sin. Therefore, when it is asked whether Christ was made in every respect generally like his brothers, one must make a careful distinction. Meanwhile, this particle refutes all the errors of those who deny the true humanity of Christ. See the Aquensis on the words of John, "the Word was made flesh," and so on.

units.la: Et mirabilis humiliatio Christi hic describitur. Quòd enim ille secundum diuinam naturam Deo patri per omnia æqualis est, regnans in cœlo, summa dignitate & gloriaiL: lustris, dignatus est non modò se in terras demittere, aut simpliciter humanam carnem induere, sed præterea cum ipsa carne simul assumere carni congenitas miserias, & sic per omnia fratribus similis reddi, nonne valde admiráda est in Christo tâta humiliatio, tanta ipsius exinanitio, & extrema deiectio? Quid ergo nos iniquè ferimus & deploramus nostræ conditionis vilitatem, quam ipse Christus non dedignatus est ad se totam recipere? Aut è diuerso, quid nos superbimus, quando cernimus Christum per se potentissimum & dignissimum tamen usq; adeò nostri causa humiliatum? Nostri causa dico, quia nos nostro merito humiliamur, & miserias patimur, propter peccatum enim omnis miseria: at Christus, qui peccatum non fecit, nullo iure debebat miserias nostras in se sentire.
units.tr: Here also the wonderful humiliation of Christ is described. For since he, according to his divine nature, is in every respect equal to God the Father, reigning in heaven, endowed with the highest dignity and glory, he deigned not only to come down to earth, or simply to put on human flesh, but furthermore to take up together with the flesh the miseries connate with flesh, and so to be made like his brothers in every respect. Is not such great humiliation in Christ, such great self-emptying and extreme abasement, truly admirable? Why then do we wrongly bear and lament the lowliness of our condition, which Christ himself did not disdain to take wholly upon himself? Or conversely, why do we pride ourselves, when we see Christ, who is most powerful and most worthy in himself, nevertheless humbled so far for our sake? For our sake, I say, because we are humbled and suffer miseries by our own merit: for all misery is on account of sin. But Christ, who committed no sin, had by no right to feel our miseries in himself.

units.la: Ut misericors esset) Ratio, quare debuerit Christus fratribus per omnia similis reddi, siue experiri in se communes fratrum miserias, sumpta ab ipsius officio. Est quàs sententia: Christus missus est, ut misericordiam Dei erga homines notam redderet, siue ut misericordia erga nos exerceret. Quando autem nulla ratione magis commoveri poterat ad præstandam misericordiam, quàm perfecta cognitione nostrarum miseriarum, conueniens fuit, illum omnes quoq; nostras miserias in se sentire. Cognitio enim & sensus nostrarum miseriarum, promptiorem illum ad miserendum erat redditurus. Quomodo etiam homines tum demum sentiunt, quid sit miserorum hominum inopia, necessitas, calamitas, cum ipsi calamitatibus aliquibus obruuntur. Atq; hæc ratio non parum illustrat superiores causas, ob quas dictum est, Christum debuisse humanam naturam suscipere. Nam sanctificatio hominum, eorundemq; liberatio à morte æterna, & potestate diaboli, per mortem Christi temporaneam, nonne incomparabilis misericordiæ & bonitatis Christi sunt opera?
units.tr: That he might be merciful. This is the reason why Christ ought to have been made in every respect like his brothers, or to experience in himself the miseries common to his brothers, taken from his office. The sense is this: Christ was sent that he might make the mercy of God towards men known, or that he might exercise mercy towards us. Now, when he could be moved to show mercy by no means more than by a perfect knowledge of our miseries, it was fitting that he should feel in himself all our miseries too. For the knowledge and feeling of our miseries would make him readier to pity. So also men only then feel what the want, need, and calamity of wretched men are, when they themselves are overwhelmed by some calamities. And this reasoning greatly illustrates the earlier causes for which it was said that Christ ought to take on human nature. For is not the sanctification of men, and their deliverance from eternal death and the power of the devil, through the temporal death of Christ, works of incomparable mercy and goodness in Christ?

units.la: Misericors, dicitur à miseria, & proprie est is, qui aliena mouetur miseria, adeò, ut miser ricors esse non possit, nisi qui alterius miseriam respicit: quomodo Christus Matth.15. recte dixit, Miseret me turbæ, propterea quòd iam triduum perseuerant apud me, & non habent quod edant. En respicies eorum miseriam & inopiam, misericordia motus est. Sic inclamans ad Christum cæcus, Luc. 18. dicit, Miserere mei. Item diues in inferno ad Abraham, & alij simili modo implorantes opem, quid aliud sibi volunt, quàm si aliter dicerent: Respice in meas miserias, & me ab illis libera? Sic item Pater cœleslis proprie dicitur misericors, (Luc.6. Estote misericordes, sicut pater vester misericors est) quia facile mouetur nostris miseriis, & semper videt, quibus indigeamus, ut habetur Luc.11. Roma.8. dicitur, coclusit Deus omnes sub incredulitatem, ut omnium misereatur: quod perinde sonat, ac si diceretur, Deus voluit omnes esse miseros, infœlices, perditos, ut cōsideratis omniū miseriis, ipse ampliorem haberet occasionem exercendi in eos misericordiam. Recte ergo dicitur, Christum debuisse per omnia similem reddi fratribus, hoc est, miseriarum omnium fieri participem, ut misericors fieret, & agnitis nostris miseriis, ad misericordiam citius moueretur. Atq; in hoc quoq; ipse in terras missus est, nimirum, ut misericordiam exerceret, & misericordiam Dei Patris toti orbi notam faceret. Unde ad Titum 3. At postquàm bonitas, & erga homines amor apparuit seruatoris nostri Dei, non ex operibus, quæ sunt in iusticia, quæ faciebamus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam saluos nos fecit, per lauacrum regenerationis, ac renouationis spiritus sancti, quæ effudit in nos opulente, per Iesum Christum seruatorem nostrum, ut iustificati illius gratia, hæredes efficeremur iuxta spem vitæ æternæ. Lucæ 1. Zacharias sic canit: & tu puer Propheta altissimi vocaberis: præibis enim ante faciem Domini, ad parandum vias eius, ad dandam scientiam salutis populo ipsius, per remissionem peccatorum eius: per viscera misericordiæ Dei nostri, quibus visitauit nos oriens ex alto. Et Matth.9. cum Pharisæi murmurarent, quòd cibum sumeret cum publicanis & peccatoribus Iesus, vbi id audiuit, dixit: non opus habetis, qui validi sunt, medico, sed qui male habent. Quin potius ite, & discite, quid sit illud: Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium. Non enim veniad vocandum iustos, sed peccatores ad pœnitentiam.
units.tr: "Merciful" is derived from "misery," and properly he is merciful who is moved by another's misery, so that one cannot be merciful unless he regards the misery of another. Thus Christ rightly said in Matthew 15, "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me three days and have nothing to eat." Behold, he regarded their misery and want, and was moved with mercy. So the blind man crying out to Christ in Luke 18 says, "Have mercy on me." Likewise the rich man in hell to Abraham, and others who implore help in a similar way, what else do they mean than if they said: Look upon my miseries, and free me from them? So too the heavenly Father is properly called merciful (Luke 6: "Be merciful, as your Father is merciful"), because he is easily moved by our miseries and always sees what we lack, as is stated in Luke 11. Romans 8 says, "God has shut up all under unbelief, that he might have mercy on all," which means just as much as if it were said: God willed that all should be wretched, unhappy, and lost, so that, having considered the miseries of all, he might have a greater occasion of exercising mercy towards them. Rightly, then, it is said that Christ ought to have been made in every respect like his brothers, that is, made a sharer in all their miseries, so that he might be merciful, and, having recognised our miseries, might be more quickly moved to mercy. And in this also he was sent into the world, namely that he might exercise mercy, and make the mercy of God the Father known to the whole world. Hence Titus 3: "But after the kindness and love of God our Saviour towards men appeared, not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life." Luke 1: Zechariah sings thus: "And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, through the tender mercy of our God, by which the dawn from on high has visited us." And in Matthew 9, when the Pharisees murmured that Jesus ate with publicans and sinners, he heard this and said: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. But go and learn what it means: I desire mercy and not sacrifice. For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."

units.la: Proinde cùm audimus, Christum ideo missum, ut misericordia exerceat, & ideo factus esse participem miseriarum nostrarum, ut misericors fieret: magnam hinc debemus consolationem arripere, & quotiescunq; magnitudine & multitudine nostrarum miseriarum, quibus cùm corpore, tum anima obruimur, efficimur consternati, quasiq; ad desperationem adigimur, opponamus nostris miseriis Christi misericordiam.
units.tr: Therefore, when we hear that Christ was sent so that he might exercise mercy, and was made a partaker of our miseries so that he might become merciful, we ought to take great comfort from this. Whenever we are dismayed by the greatness and number of our miseries, with which we are overwhelmed both in body and in soul, and are driven, as it were, toward despair, let us set Christ's mercy against our miseries.

units.la: Et fidelis pontifex, in his, quæ apud Deum forent agenda, ad expiandu peccata populi.
units.tr: And a faithful high priest, in those things which pertain to God, to make expiation for the sins of the people.

units.la: Alia ratio similiter explicans, cur Christum decuerit per omnia similem nobis reddi, & rursus ducta ab eius officio. Debuit Christus fieri pontifex, inquit, id est, sicut ipse per interpreinterpretationem adijcit, mediator & intercessor, in his quæ forent inter Deum & homines pro reconciliatione utriusq; partis peragenda.
units.tr: Another reason, similarly explaining why it was fitting for Christ to be made like us in all things, is drawn again from his office. Christ, he says, had to be made a high priest, that is, as the author himself explains by the word that follows, a mediator and intercessor in those things which must be done between God and men for the reconciliation of both parties.

units.la: Sed quia hoc munus commodè & fideliter non videbatur posse peragare, nisi etiam naturæ humanæ fieret particeps, perinde atq; particeps erat naturæ diuinæ, (alias enim alteram duntaxat habens naturam credi potuisset in eandem plus æquo propensior) ob hanc inquam causam decuit illum hominem fieri, & per omnia similem nobis reddi.
units.tr: But since this office did not seem to be able to be carried out suitably and faithfully unless he also became a partaker of human nature, just as he was a partaker of the divine nature (for if he had only one nature, he could have been thought to be more inclined than was fitting toward that one), for this reason, I say, it was fitting that he should become a man and be made like us in all things.

units.la: Confirmat autem hæc ratio & illustrat illam secundam causam principalem, qua dicebatur, homines per mortem Christi (in qua ipse & pontificem egit, & simul fuit hostia) à peccatis liberandos.
units.tr: This reason also confirms and illustrates the second principal cause, which was stated: that men are freed from sins through the death of Christ, in which he both acted as high priest and at the same time was the victim.

units.la: Est autem nobis paulò oculatius huic rationi intendedū, propterea quòd valde excellenter officium Christi hic describitur, quo ille agit pontificem et intercessorem inter nos & Deum, ut expientur, purgentur, remittantur nostra peccata. Præsupponit autem hęc ratio, Christum non posse fideliter agere munus pontificis, id est, intercessoris & placatoris, pro hominibus apud Deum, nisi & ipse homo fieret, atq; ita sciret, qualia hominib. deberet, postularet, & moueretur ad causam hominum agendam diligentius. In quam sententiam etiam infrà capite quinto dicitur: Omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus constituitur, in his, quæ apud Deū aguntur, ut offerat donaria & uictimas pro peccatis, qui placabiles esse possit ignorantibus & errantibus, quandoquidem & ipse circumdatus est infirmitate. En hic dicitur, circumdatum esse sacerdotem infirmitate, ut ipse infirmis & peccantibus sit placabilis. Sic etiam de Christo est hoc loco accipiendum, quòd videlicet, ut magis moueretur ad fideliter agendū causam infirmorū fratrū apud Deum, decebat eum fratribus per omnia similem reddi. Poteritiştud similitudine commodius explicari. Dives quispiam & potes, si intercedere debeat apud regem vel principem, non pari cura & diligentia intercedit pro pauperibus, qua pro diuitibus: sed inferioris conditionis intercessor pro pauperib. sui similibus intercedit multò diligentissimè. Eodem propemodum pacto præsumitur, Christum (exemplo ducto ab humano more) non eadem fide acturum causas miserorū hominum, si tantum diuinam naturam retinuisset, & non assumpsisset etiam humanam, qua miseris fratrib. per omnia similis redderet. Manifesta ergo est hęc ratio, Christū ideo factum esse fratrib. per omnia similem, ut fieret fidelis pontifex, in his, quę apud Deum forent agenda, ad expiandum peccata populi. Interea dum hoc loco commemorat hoc Christi officium, obiter viam parat, ad secundum locum principalem huius epistolæ, in quo de novo sacerdotio & pontificatu Christi, nec non veteris sacerdotij Leuitici (& cum hoc etiam legis) abrogatione luculentissimè disputat. Ait igitur:
units.tr: We must, however, give somewhat closer attention to this reason, because the office of Christ is here described very excellently, by which he acts as high priest and intercessor between us and God, so that our sins may be expiated, cleansed and forgiven. This reason presupposes that Christ could not faithfully perform the office of a high priest, that is, of an intercessor and appeaser, for men before God, unless he himself also became a man, and so knew what things men needed, asked for them, and was moved more diligently to plead the cause of men. To this effect it is also said later in chapter five: Every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed for men in those things which pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, who can have compassion on the ignorant and the erring, since he himself also is compassed with infirmity. Here it is said that the priest is compassed with infirmity, so that he may be able to have compassion on the weak and the sinning. So also must this passage be understood of Christ: that, in order to be more moved to plead faithfully the cause of his weak brothers before God, it was fitting that he should be made like his brothers in all things. This can be explained more fittingly by a comparison. Some rich and powerful man, if he must intercede with a king or prince, does not intercede for the poor with the same care and diligence as for the rich; but an intercessor of lower rank pleads for those of his own condition with much greater diligence. In much the same way it may be supposed (by an example taken from human custom) that Christ would not plead the causes of wretched men with the same faithfulness if he had retained only the divine nature and had not also assumed the human nature, by which he would be made like his wretched brothers in all things. This reason, then, is clear: Christ was made like his brothers in all things so that he might become a faithful high priest, in those things which must be done before God, to make expiation for the sins of the people. Meanwhile, in mentioning this office of Christ at this point, the author also paves the way, in passing, to the second principal topic of this letter, in which he argues most clearly about the new priesthood and high priesthood of Christ, and about the abrogation of the old Levitical priesthood (and with it also the law). He says, therefore:

units.la: Et fidelis pontifex) Græce est ἀρχιερεύς, quasi dicas, summum sacrorum præsidem, aut summum sacerdotem. Latinis placuit & pontificem appellare eum, qui rebus sacris præesset: & cùm plures essent apud veteres, vnum qui omnibus præerat, maximum pontificem dixerunt. Vnde verò deductum nomé pontificis, non satis constat. Q. Mutius Scęuola à posse & facere appellatos existimat pontifices: at M. Varro à ponte & facio maluit, eò quòd ab his primùm pons sublitius factus, ac sæpè restitutus esse perhibeatur, ut refert Fenestella lib. 1. de Romanorū magistratibus: cuius rei non meminissem, nisi etiam Primasius hunc locum enarrans ita Christo appellationem pontificis accommodaret, dicens, quòd Christus nobis pontem & viam fecerit præeundo nobis per bona exempla quæ sequeremur, & præterea viam ad Patrem cœlestem aperiendo. Quanquàm leuiculumistud censeri posset. Verè autè competit Christo appellatio sacerdotis & pontificis maximi, quoniam ipse verè est mediator inter Deum & homines, & sacrificium tale obtulit, quo Deus pater placatus est generi mortalium, & offensam remisit. Quod licet sequenti disputatione copiosius & fusius explicetur, tamè aliunde quoq; testimonia citabimus, quibus idem officium eademq; dignitas Christo tribuitur. 1. Petri 2. vocatur pastor & Episcopus animarum nostrarum. Certè Roman. 5. describitur reconciliator noster. Si, cùm inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem filij eius, multò magis reconciliati seruabimur per vitam ipsius. Rom. 8. Christus est, qui mortuus est, imò qui & suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dexteram Dei, qui & intercedit pro nobis. Ephes. 5. Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem ac victimam Deo, in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ. Propterea etiam Esaiæ 53. dicitur ipse oblatus, quia voluit: pontifex simul fuit & hostia. 1. Ioan. 2. Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud Patrem, Iesum Christum iustum. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: non pro nostris autem tantùm, sed etiam pro totius mundi. Proinde cùm Christus ita sit reconciliator, intercessor, advocatus inter nos & Deum, & victimam præterea offerat, nempe se ipsum: qua victima nihil maius, nihil præstantius efficaciusq; posset offerri, rectè ipse pontifex noster appellatur. Iam quare dicitur fidelis? Sine dubio satis fuisset quodammodo dicere, Christum pontificem
units.tr: And a faithful high priest. The Greek is ἀρχιερεύς [archiereus], as if you were to say chief president of sacred things, or chief priest. The Latins have been pleased to call pontiff the one who presided over sacred things, and since there were many among the ancients, they called the one who was over all of them the chief pontiff (pontifex maximus). Where the name pontiff is derived from, however, is not entirely clear. Q. Mucius Scaevola thinks pontiffs were so called from posse and facere (to be able and to make), but M. Varro preferred from pons and facio, because it is said that the first sublician bridge was made by them and often repaired, as Fenestella reports in book 1 of On the Magistrates of the Romans. I would not have remembered this matter, except that Primasius, expounding this passage, applied the title of pontiff to Christ in this way, saying that Christ made a bridge and a way for us by going before us through the good examples we should follow, and besides by opening the way to the heavenly Father. Yet that could be regarded as rather trifling. Truly the title of priest and chief pontiff fits Christ, since he is truly the mediator between God and men, and offered such a sacrifice that God the Father was appeased toward the human race and remitted the offence. Although this will be explained more fully and at length in the following discussion, we shall also cite testimonies from elsewhere by which the same office and the same dignity are ascribed to Christ. In 1 Pet. 2 he is called the shepherd and bishop of our souls. In Rom. 5 he is described as our reconciler: "If, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more shall we be saved by his life." In Rom. 8 Christ is the one who died, or rather who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, and who also intercedes for us. In Eph. 5 Christ loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odour of sweet smell. Therefore also in Isa. 53 he is said to have been offered because he willed it: he was at once priest and victim. In 1 John 2: If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Therefore, since Christ is thus reconciler, intercessor and advocate between us and God, and moreover offers a victim, namely himself, than which nothing greater, nothing more excellent or more effective could be offered, he is rightly called our high priest. Now why is he called faithful? Without doubt it would have been sufficient, in a way, to say that Christ had to be made a pontiff.

units.la: 1 3 pontificem debuisse fieri: Sed quia id maxime erat necessarium, ut Christus bona fide & accuratè partes nostras tueretur: Ideo addidit nō fine Emphasi, fidelis. Et hoc maximè requiritur in quibuscunq; intercessoribus,aduocatis,mediatoribus, ut fideles sint,bonaq; fide ac synceriter agant,quæ ipsis sunt concredita, siue quæ ab ipsis expectantur.Itaq; ut ostendatur,Christum esse verum pontificem, qui synceriter agat suum officium, addita est vox πιστὸς: quæ appellatio sic proprie competit uni Christo,ut cæteris pontificibus per participationem possit accommodari. Nam ut etiam conati sint intercedere inter Deū & populum, & placare Deum, tamen quando ipsi ne pro se quidem id satis potuerunt (unde & pro se priuatim debebant offerre hostias, & eas semper iterum offerre, quia nūquam satis faciebant) non possunt vere fideles appellari, & bona fide aliorum causam apud Deum agere.
units.tr: But because it was most necessary that Christ should guard our interests with good faith and diligence, he added the word faithful, not without emphasis. This is especially required in all intercessors, advocates and mediators: that they be faithful, and act in good faith and sincerely in the matters entrusted to them or expected of them. Therefore, to show that Christ is the true priest who discharges his office sincerely, the word πιστὸς [pistos] was added. This title belongs properly to Christ alone, while it can be applied to the other priests only by participation. For although they tried to intercede between God and the people and to appease God, yet since they could not even do this sufficiently for themselves (whence they had to offer sacrifices privately for themselves as well, and always offer them again, because they never made satisfaction enough), they cannot truly be called faithful, nor act in good faith in the cause of others before God.

units.la: Sed solus Christus istud vere peregit,& propterea proprie fidelis pōtifex appellatur. Notandum interea, hac ipsa voce etiam viam parari ad collationem Christi cum Mose, quæ capite mox sequenti breuiter absoluitur, in qua fidelis pontifex Christus ostenditur fideli Mose multo esse excellentior.
units.tr: But Christ alone accomplished this truly, and therefore he is properly called the faithful pontiff. Meanwhile it should be noted that by this very word the way is also prepared for the comparison of Christ with Moses, which is briefly completed in the next chapter, where Christ the faithful high priest is shown to be far more excellent than Moses, who was faithful.

units.la: In his quæ apud Deum forent agenda, ad expiandum peccata populi.
units.tr: In those things which were to be done before God, to make expiation for the sins of the people.

units.la: Hæc per interpretationem ad explicandum, quod sit officium pontificis, & maximè Christi, sunt addita. Græcè habetur πιστὸς ἀρχιερεὺς, τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν: quæ græcismū interpres quo par fuit,modo reddidit. Hac particula,apud Deum, nō solum proprie discernitur munus pontificis: quando quidem is pro salute hominum agere debet, non apud homines, iudices,principes, vel huiusmodi,sed apud Deum: & actiones eius non sunt ciuiles, sed spirituales: verum insuper Christi beneficia amplificantur,quando ea valent apud ipsum Deum,quando ipse placat Deum,quem nulli homines, nulla humana iustitia potuissent placare. ὡς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ. ἱλάσκομαι vertut subinde expio,placo,recōcilio, propitium reddo: & maximè conuenit illi placationi seu reconciliationi, quæ fit inter Deū & homines offerendo sacrificium seu hostiam ad obtinēdam peccati remissionem, quemodo sæpius in Leuitico usurpatur hoc vocabulū, ut Leuitici 5. Sacerdos cremabit hostiam super altare,in monumentum eius, qui obtulerit, rogans pro illo & expians: & statim ibi sequitur de remissione peccatorum obtinenda. Sic quoq; Latinis vocabulum expiandi usurpatur,ut apud Horatium,Syluanū,lacte piabant,id est,placabant sacrificio Lactis ,purgabat se à peccatis. Hoc igitur pacto Christus est ille sacerdos,qui solus potuit expiare peccata nostra, Deum placatum reddere,& reconciliare, offerendo nimirum nō lac,non vitulos,non arietes,sed semetipsum. Atq; hinc quoq; ipse apud Ioannē vocatur ἱλασμὸς,id est,expiatio,placatio,siue,ut interpres ibi reddidit,propitiatio.Sic enim habetur 1.Ioan.2. Ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris,nō pro nostris autem tantum,sed etiam pro totius mundi. Rursus eiusdem epistolæ capite quarto,in hoc est charitas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum,sed quod ipse dilexerit nos,& miserit filium suum propitiatione pro peccatis nostris. Vtrobiq; autem habetur ἱλασμὸς.item Rom.4.vocatur ἱλαστήριον,sed interpres reddit reconciliatorem.Iustificantur,in quit,gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu,quem proposuit Deus reconciliatorem per fidem, interueniente ipsius sanguine. En ergo quomodo Christus proprie reconciliator & expiator,ac proinde verus pōtifex, peccata nostra delens seu pro peccatis Deo Patri satis offenso satisfaciens. Sed & quādo Christus proprie designatur expiator peccatorū, argumētū est,beneficia Christi non esse temporalia & externa,sed spiritualia,interna,& æterna: deinde peccati vim omninò maiorem esse, quàm ut homo aliquis pro peccato possit satisfacere: tantum abest, ut vel arietibus,vel hircis,vel alijs deniq; oblationibus potuerit pro peccato satisfieri. Nam sacrificia illa veteris testamenti nequaquam instituta fuerunt,quasi vires haberent ad ause- renda peccata hominum, sed tantum signa fuerunt, vnicum istud sacrificium, quod per Christum pontificem offerretur,efficax ad expiandum omnia peccata omnium hominum adumbrantia & prænunciantia.Cuius rei id argumentum euidentissimum est,quòd oblato per Christum sacrificio expiationis omnia illa iam cessarunt. Atq; huc valde quadrare mihi videtur, quod legitur Leuitici 16. de festo expiationis: mense septimo decima die mensis affligetis animas vestras, nullum q; opus facietis siue indigena, siue aduena, qui peregrinatur inter vos. In hac die expiatio erit vestri atque mundatio, ab omnibus peccatis vestris coram Domino mundabimini. Sabbatum enim ad requiescendum est, & affligetis animas vestras religione perpetua. Expiabit autem sacerdos, qui unctus fuerit & cuius manus initiatæ sunt,ut sacerdotio fungatur pro patre suo: induetur q; stola linea & vestibus sanctis, & expiabit sanctuarium & tabernaculum testimonij, atq; altare, sacerdotes quoq; & uniuersum populum. Eritq; vobis hoc legitimum sempiternum, ut oretis pro filijs Israel,& pro cunctis peccatis eorum, semel in anno.
units.tr: These words have been added by way of interpretation, to explain what the office of a priest is, and especially of Christ. The Greek reads ta pros ton theon [τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν], which the translator rendered as well as he could, with a Greek idiom. The phrase before God does not only distinguish the priestly office properly. The priest must act for the salvation of men, not before men, judges, princes or the like, but before God, and his actions are not civil but spiritual. Moreover, Christ's benefits are magnified, since they avail before God himself, and since he appeases God, whom no men and no human righteousness could have appeased. The Greek hōs to hilaskesthai tas hamartias tou laou [ὡς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ], to make propitiation for the sins of the people. Hilaskomai [ἱλάσκομαι] is sometimes rendered expio, placo, reconcilio, propitium reddo, and it fits especially that appeasement or reconciliation which takes place between God and men by offering a sacrifice or victim to obtain forgiveness of sin. This word is used often in Leviticus, as in Leviticus 5: "The priest shall burn the victim upon the altar, as a memorial of him who offered it, praying for him and making expiation." Immediately there follows the obtaining of forgiveness of sins. So too the Latin word expiandi is used, as in Horace, where Silvanus lacte piabant, that is, they appeased Silvanus with a sacrifice of milk, that is, they purged themselves from sins. In this way Christ is that priest who alone could expiate our sins, make God propitious and reconcile him, offering, of course, not milk, not calves, not rams, but himself. Hence also in John he is called hilasmos [ἱλασμός], that is, expiation, appeasement, or, as the translator there rendered it, propitiation. For thus it is written in 1 John 2: "He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." Again in the fourth chapter of the same epistle: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." In both places the word is hilasmos. Likewise in Romans 3 he is called hilasterion [ἱλαστήριον], but the translator renders it "reconciler": "They are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a reconciler through faith, through his blood." Behold, then, how Christ is properly the reconciler and expiator, and therefore the true priest, blotting out our sins, or satisfying God the Father, who was offended by sins. And when Christ is properly designated as the expiator of sins, this is an argument that Christ's benefits are not temporal and external, but spiritual, inward and eternal. Further, the power of sin is far greater than that any man could satisfy for sin; so far is it from being possible that sin could be satisfied by rams, goats or other offerings of any kind. For those sacrifices of the Old Testament were by no means instituted as though they had power to take away the sins of men; they were only signs, and that one sacrifice which was to be offered by Christ the priest was effective for expiating all the sins of all men, which those sacrifices foreshadowed and foretold. The clearest proof of this is that, once the sacrifice of expiation was offered through Christ, all those sacrifices ceased. And what is read in Leviticus 16 about the feast of expiation seems to me to fit this very well: "On the tenth day of the seventh month you shall afflict your souls, and you shall do no work, whether native or stranger who sojourns among you. On this day expiation shall be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before the Lord. For it is a sabbath of rest, and you shall afflict your souls by a perpetual ordinance. And the priest who is anointed, and whose hands are consecrated to serve as priest in place of his father, shall make expiation; he shall put on the linen tunic and the holy garments, and he shall make expiation for the holy place and the tabernacle of meeting and the altar, and for the priests and all the people. And this shall be a statute to you for ever, that you make atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year."

units.la: Quo loco præsentia verba per typum admodum eleganter explicantur. Nam pontifex ille unctus expians sanctuarium & tabernaculum testimonij atq; altare, sacerdotes quoq; & vniuersum populum: est ipse Christus, per quem ecclesia atq; etiam ipsi sacerdotes sanctificantur.
units.tr: In this passage the present words are explained very elegantly through a type. For that anointed priest who makes expiation for the sanctuary, the tabernacle of meeting, the altar, the priests and all the people, is Christ himself, through whom the Church and the priests themselves are sanctified.

units.la: Quemadmodum & eodem capite hircus portans omnes iniquitates hominum in si-militudine Christi typum gessit, qui peccata nostra & omnes languores nostros ipse tulit, sicut Esaias capite 53. interpretatur. Cæterum ex hoc ipso loco videtur etiam colligi posse, cur Apostolus hic dixerit, peccata populi, & non, hominum siue mundi, sicut Ioannes in epistola sua ait. Apparet, eum respexisse ad verba illa ex Leuitico citata, quibus dicitur, quod expiabit vniuersum populum.
units.tr: In the same chapter the goat that bears all the iniquities of men likewise bore the type of Christ, who himself bore our sins and our infirmities, as Isaiah interprets in chapter 53. Moreover, from this very passage it seems possible to gather why the Apostle here said the sins of the people, and not of men or of the world, as John says in his epistle. It appears that he had regard to those words from Leviticus which are cited, where it is said that he shall make expiation for the whole people.

units.la: Quanquàm Chrysostomo placet, Apostolum nomen populi usurpasse ad significandum, quod Christus præcipuè venerit propter Iudæos, qui proprie dicti sunt populus Dei: atque hac appellatione non solum præclarum genus Hebræorum extollit, sed etiam nititur animos eorum flectere, ut Christum eò lubentius suscipiant, benigniusq; audiant, quæ de Christo prædicantur.
units.tr: Yet Chrysostom thinks that the Apostle used the name people to signify that Christ came chiefly on account of the Jews, who are properly called the people of God. By this appellation he not only extols the excellent race of the Hebrews, but also strives to bend their minds, so that they may more willingly receive Christ and more kindly hear what is preached about Christ.

units.la: Quod verò Iudæi nomine populi significentur, & quòd propter eos potissimum sit missus, diuersis locis probatur. Matth.1. Angelus ad Ioseph: Pariet autem filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum: is enim saluum faciet populum suum à peccatis suis. Et de electione populi Iudaici Exod.19. In quorum locum successit nouus populus, videlicet credentes: qua de re Roman.9. Tit.2.1. Petri 2. vbi credetes in genere nouus populus & nouum peculium Dei appellantur. De missione ad Iudæos ipse Christus ait Matth.15. mulieri Cananææ, Non sum missus, nisi ad oues perditas domus Israelitica. Et Matth.10. Iussit discipulos, non ire in viam gentium, sed potius ad oues perditas domus Israel. Act.13. Paulus ac Barnabas ad Iudæos: Vobis oportebat primum loqui sermonem Dei, sed quoniam repellitis illum, & indignos vos iudicatis æterna vita, ecce conuertimur ad gentes.
units.tr: That the Jews are signified by the name of people, and that he was sent chiefly on their account, is proved in various places. Matthew 1: the angel to Joseph: "She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins." And concerning the election of the Jewish people, Exodus 19. In their place there succeeded a new people, namely believers; on this matter see Romans 9, Titus 2, and 1 Peter 2, where believers in general are called a new people and a peculiar people of God. Concerning his mission to the Jews, Christ himself says in Matthew 15 to the Canaanite woman: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." And in Matthew 10 he commanded the disciples not to go into the way of the Gentiles, but rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Acts 13: Paul and Barnabas to the Jews: "It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles."

units.la: Tametsi nomine populi, intelligi omnes homines, quandoquidem salus per Christum vniuersaliter omnibus est proposita, & credentes, siue gentiles sint, siue Iudæi, nomine populi Dei censentur, meo iudicio fuerit commodius: quo sensu etiam capite 5. sequenti dicitur, Christum, cùm obtulisset precationes & supplicationes apud Deum, omnib. qui ipsi obedierant, fuisse causam salutis æternæ. Cæterùm hæc ipsa ratio plurimum habet in se consolationis. Si quando enim animus perterreatur magnitudine ac multitudine peccatorum, at non est quod propterea desperemus.
units.tr: Yet it would, in my judgment, be more fitting to understand by the name people all men, since salvation through Christ is offered universally to all, and believers, whether Gentiles or Jews, are counted among the people of God. In this sense also in the fifth chapter that follows it is said that Christ, when he had offered prayers and supplications before God, was the cause of eternal salvation for all who obeyed him. Moreover, this very reasoning contains much comfort. For if at any time the mind is terrified by the greatness and multitude of sins, yet there is no reason for us on that account to despair.

units.la: Si magna & multa sunt nostra peccata, at multo amplior & præclarior est Dei bonitas & misericordia. Poscentibus ille paratus est ignoscere. Tunc autem potissimum, ubi Christus pontifex noster & expiator inuocatus à nobis interceßerit, qui, sicut promptissimus est ad orandum pro nobis, ita à Deo patre citò exauditur. Notandum insuper, quòd dixerit, peccata, plurali numero, non tantùm peccatum. Quia non solum actualia peccata per Christum auferri debebant, sed etiam originale.
units.tr: If our sins are great and many, yet God's goodness and mercy are far greater and more glorious. He is ready to forgive those who ask. And this is especially so when Christ, our priest and expiator, invoked by us, intercedes, who, as he is most ready to pray for us, so is he quickly heard by God the Father. It is to be noted further that he said sins, in the plural, not only sin. For not only actual sins had to be taken away through Christ, but also original sin.

units.la: Nam ex hoc, quod ipsi contigit tentatum esse, potest & his, qui tentantur, succurrere.
units.tr: For from the fact that he himself was tempted, he is also able to help those who are tempted.

units.la: Probatio seu confirmatio eius, quòd suprà dixit, Christum suscipere debuisse in se humanas miserias, ut misericors redderetur. Vbi enim inquit, ipse sensit, quid sit tentari, & humanis ærumnis exponi, hinc habebit occasionem maiorem ad dolendum hominum vicem, quos nouit eodem pacto tentari, & ad in tempore succurrendum ijsdem.
units.tr: This is the proof or confirmation of what he said above, that Christ had to take upon himself human miseries so that he might become merciful. For when he says that he himself has felt what it is to be tempted and exposed to human hardships, he will thereby have a greater occasion to feel compassion for the lot of men, whom he knows are tempted in the same way, and to help them in their time of need.

units.la: Fluit hæc ratio ex eo, quòd homines nunquam magis mouentur ad opitulandum laborantibus siue oppressis, quàm cùm ipsi prius experti sunt, quid sit laborare siue opprimi. Græcè quidem sic legitur, ςυ ... πεπονθεν ... Vbi initio videtur quædam obscuritas, propter inusitatam locutionem, qua coniunguntur ista duo πεπονθεν πειραζόμενος. Quidam interpretati sunt, participium passiuum loco verbi infinitiui, quasi diceretur: Alij participium reddiderunt per nomen verbale, hoc pacto: In quo enim contigit illi tentatio. Alij prius verbum etiam per participium reddiderunt in hunc modum: In quo enim passus est ipse & tentatus: qui addiderunt copulatiuam, Et. At quomodocunq; vertamus, & ut dicamus par participium poni pro infinitiuo, siue pro nomine, tamen quod ad sententiam attinet, nulla est ambiguitas. Clarè enim significatur, Christum tentationes esse expertum, hoc est, omnes miserias sensisse, quæ fragilem nostram carnem (dempto, inquam, peccato) comitari solent. Prudenter verò utitur Apostolus verbo tentationis.
units.tr: This reasoning arises from the fact that people are never more moved to help those who labour or are oppressed than when they have themselves first experienced what it is to labour or be oppressed. The Greek reads thus: in which he himself has suffered, being tempted [ἐν ᾧ αὐτὸς πέπονθεν πειρασθείς]. Here at first there seems to be some obscurity, on account of the unusual construction by which these two words, πεπονθεν and πειραζόμενος, are joined. Some have translated the passive participle in place of an infinitive verb, as if it were said: in which he has been tempted. Others have rendered the participle by a verbal noun, thus: in which the temptation befell him. Others again have rendered the first verb too by a participle, in this manner: in which he himself suffered and was tempted, adding the conjunction "and". However we translate it, and whether we say that a participle is put for an infinitive or for a noun, there is no ambiguity so far as the sense is concerned. For it is plainly signified that Christ has experienced temptations, that is, that he has felt all the miseries which usually accompany our frail flesh (sin excepted, I say). The Apostle uses the word "temptation" wisely.

units.la: Hac enim voce non solùm illud suggerit, quomodo videlicet Christus tentatus fuerit à diabolo in deserto, ut scribitur Matth.4. quæ quidem tentatio non dubium, quin val de moverit Christum ad rectius prouidendum, quanta sit nostra miseria, quantisq; periculis simus expositi, quoties à diabolo solicitamur ad superbiam, auaritiá, vel huiusmodi: sed animis nostris proponit in genere omnia pericula, quæ nobis solent euenire ex ipsa naturæ humanæ necessitate, cuiusmodi sunt dolere propter aduersa, flere, ingemiscere, tædio affici, pauere, mala auersari, &c. quæ sanè Christus etiam in se est expertus, & tentationum nomine comprehendit: sicut ipse diserte ait Lucæ 22. Vos estis, qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis: Et non parum mouere possunt Christum adintuendum in nostram fragilitatem nobis ingenitam, quæ graui pondere peccati pressa longè alia, & magis commiseratione digna est in nobis, quàm in Christo esse potuit, utpote cui peccatum perinde ut nobis non fuit ingenitum.
units.tr: For by this word he suggests not only that temptation by which Christ was tempted by the devil in the wilderness, as is written in Matthew 4, a temptation which undoubtedly moved Christ to consider more carefully how great our misery is and how many dangers we are exposed to whenever the devil tempts us to pride, avarice, or things of that kind. He also sets before our minds, in general terms, all the dangers which commonly befall us from the very necessity of human nature: to grieve over adversities, to weep, to groan, to be weighed down with weariness, to fear, to shrink from evils, and so on. Christ himself certainly experienced these too, and he includes them under the name of temptations, just as he himself plainly says in Luke 22: "You are those who have continued with me in my temptations" (Luke 22:28). And these things can move us no little to consider Christ's regard for our frailty, which is innate in us. Weighed down by the heavy burden of sin, this frailty is in us far different from, and more worthy of compassion than, what it could be in Christ, to whom sin was not innate in the way it is in us.

units.la: Magna sine dubio tentatio siue miseria naturæ erat Christo, cùm fleret mortuum Lazarum, cùm fleret excæcationem Iudæorum, & Hierosolymæ euersionem: maior etiam, cùm se tristem usq; ad mortem diceret, & auerti à se calicem peteret, cùm fateretur, spiritum quidem promptum, carnem autem infirmam.
units.tr: Without doubt Christ was subject to a great temptation or misery of nature when he wept over the dead Lazarus, when he wept over the blindness of the Jews and the overthrow of Jerusalem. Greater still was it when he said that he was sorrowful even unto death, and asked that the cup be taken from him, when he confessed that the spirit indeed was ready but the flesh weak.

units.la: Quare si tantam tentationem ipse, qui nec peccare, nec vinci à peccato, vel satana potErat, in se sensit, sine dubio poterit iudicare, quales sint tentationes, quæ per naturam ad malum feruntur. Vnde capite sequenti quarto: Non enim habemus pontificem, quinò posset affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum per omnia, iuxta similitudinem, absq; peccato.
units.tr: Therefore, if he who could neither sin nor be overcome by sin or by Satan felt such a great temptation in himself, he will undoubtedly be able to judge what kind of temptations are those which are carried by nature towards evil. Hence in the following chapter, the fourth, it is said: "For we have not a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but who was tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin" (Heb. 4:15).

units.la: Quamobrem ubi tantùm discrimen est inter tentationes nostras, & tentationes Christi, puto consultò esse factum, quod Apostolus de Christo quidem dixerit, quòd passus sit se tentari, siue, quòd contigerit ipsum tentari. De nobis verò loquens, simpliciter vocat nos πειρασμοῖς.
units.tr: Since there is so great a difference between our temptations and the temptations of Christ, I think it was deliberately done that the Apostle said of Christ that he suffered himself to be tempted, or that it happened to him to be tempted. But when speaking of us he simply calls us tempted [πειρασμοῖς].

units.la: Nam reuera Christus tentari accidentariò tantùm potuit: vnde inducente spiritu Sancto, dicitur tentationi diaboli fuisse expositus.
units.tr: For in truth Christ could be tempted only by accident; hence, by the leading of the Holy Spirit, he is said to have been exposed to the temptation of the devil.

units.la: Deinde tentatio non accidit ex propria ipsius fragilitate propensione, ad malum, seu ex propria concupiscentia, sed ipsius satanæ importunis & vanis conatibus, magisq; ea facta est, ut diabolus vinceretur, & nos exemplo perferendi tentationes & vincendi haberemus, quàm ut persona Christi periculis peccati expositá foret: reliquæ item tentationes etiamsi propter alios, tamen sine peccati contagio fuere. At nos reuera sumus illi, qui ad tentationum miserias videmur, & nati, & facti, ac per totam vitam assiduis tentationibus versamur obnoxij, & totus hic mundus (in quo quicquid est, aut est concupiscentia carnis, aut concupiscentia oculorum, aut superbia vitæ, ut recte inquit Ioannes prioris epistolæ capite secundo) nihil aliud, quàm πειρασμὸν est, in quo nunquàm possumus conquiescere: ut multò iustissimè dixerit Iob, vitam hominis propterea esse militiam super terram, & Christus nos quotidie iusserit orare patrem coelestem, ne nos in tentationem labi permittat. Est autem tentationis genus triplex.
units.tr: Moreover, the temptation did not arise from his own frail propensity towards evil, or from his own concupiscence, but from the importunate and vain attempts of Satan himself. It was rather made so that the devil might be overcome, and that we might have in his example both the means of enduring temptations and of conquering them, than that the person of Christ might be exposed to the dangers of sin. The remaining temptations too, even if they were on account of others, were nonetheless without the contagion of sin. But we are truly those who seem to have been both born and made for the miseries of temptation, and who throughout our whole life are subject to constant temptations. And this whole world (in which whatever there is, is either the lust of the flesh, or the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life, as John rightly says in the second chapter of his first epistle, 1 John 2:16) is nothing other than a temptation [πειρασμόν], in which we can never find rest. Hence Job very justly said that the life of man is a warfare upon the earth (Job 7:1), and Christ has daily commanded us to pray to our heavenly Father that he would not allow us to fall into temptation. There are three kinds of temptation.

units.la: Primum à Carne seu propria concupiscentia, cùm caro cöcupiscit aduersus spiritum: & hoc genus tentationis Christus non sensit. Secundò tentamur à diabolo. Tertiò, à mundo. Et utrunq; expertus est Christus. Tentant autem diabolus & mundus, vel alliciendo blanditiis, vel terrendo aduersis. Blanditiis tentauit eum diabolus Matth.4. Minis verò & insidijs mundus, ut scribæ, Pharisæi.
units.tr: The first comes from the flesh, or from one's own concupiscence, when the flesh lusts against the Spirit; and Christ did not experience this kind of temptation. Secondly, we are tempted by the devil. Thirdly, by the world. Christ experienced both of these. The devil and the world tempt either by enticing with flatteries or by frightening with adversities. The devil tempted him with flatteries in Matthew 4. The world, however, tempts with threats and snares, as the scribes and Pharisees did.

units.la: Sic ergo Christus est ille, quem tentari quodammodo & ad tempus contigit: nos verò sumus, qui per omnem vitam tentationibus inuoluimur. Atq; ille quidem sine periculo peccati: nos verò semper cum peccati & damnationis periculo. Sed tamen qualescunq; fuerint Christi tentationes, omninò eiusmodi fuerunt, per quas ille ad intelligendum, quales sint nostræ, qui illo sumus longè inferiores, tentationes, satis moueretur, atq; ex earum cognitione ad succurrendum nobis induci posset. Sed & multò appositissimè usus est voce illa βοηθῆσαι. Cùm enim βοηθέω dicatur, quasi οὐ βοῇ θέῳ, hoc est, ad vocem (periclitantis & quiritantis videlicet) accurro: notatur ea voce, & eos quidem, qui tentatur, debere Deum inuocare atq; auxilium petere: Christum verò ut intelligentem, quid agatur, & quàm graue periculum immineat ei, qui ipsum inuocat, statim & sine morafene suppetias.
units.tr: Thus Christ is one who, in a certain manner and for a time, was accustomed to be tempted; but we are those who are entangled in temptations throughout our whole life. And he indeed was without danger of sin, while we are always in danger of sin and damnation. Yet, whatever Christ's temptations were, they were certainly of such a kind that through them he was sufficiently moved to understand what ours are (ours being far inferior to his), and from knowing them could be led to help us. But he also used the word to help [βοηθῆσαι] most aptly. For since to help [βοηθέω] is said as if from to run at a cry [οὐ βοῇ θέῳ], that is, to run to the voice (namely, of one in danger and crying out), this word signifies that the one who is tempted ought to call upon God and seek aid, while Christ, understanding what is being done and how grave the danger is that threatens him who calls upon him, at once and without delay brings aid.

units.la: Sicut mater, ad vehementem clamorem tenelli infantis, quem scit oriri, quia aliquo indiget, vel dolet, vel alias periclitatur, statim toto animo accurrit, ut subueniat: Ita Christus, ubi nos clamauerimus, quandoquidem nouit nostras miserias, statim paratus est ad opem ferendam.
units.tr: As a mother, at the loud cry of a tender infant, which she knows arises because it needs something, or is in pain, or is otherwise in danger, runs at once with her whole heart to help, so Christ, when we have cried out, since he knows our miseries, is at once ready to bring help.

units.la: Proinde quando Christus hic describitur tentatus, ut tentatis eo promptius succurrat, magna hic consolatio proponitur omnibus, qui affliguntur, seu quocunque modo tentantur. Respiciant tantùm in Christum, & huius opem imploret, nec dubium, quin propter hunc, & ab hoc auxilium sint percepturi: & sicut Christus in tentationibus vicit, ita nos per eum vincemus. Et quamuis non statim id contingat, tamen id fit haud dubiè nostro bono. Deus enim nos sinit interdum grauius periclitari, ut postea tantò conspe- &ius sit illius auxilium: 1.Corinth.10.Fidelis est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari supra id, quod potestis: imò faciet vnà cum tentatione euentum, quo possitis sufferre. Iacob 1. pro summo gaudio ducite fratres mei, quoties in tentationes incideritis varias. Ibidem: Beatus vir qui suffert tentationem. Item 1. Petri 1. Etiam cum gaudio affligi nos oportet in variis experimentis, si opus sit, quo exploratio fidei nostrae reperiatur in laudem & gloriā &honorem.
units.tr: Therefore, when Christ is here described as tempted, so that he may the more readily help those who are tempted, a great consolation is set before all who are afflicted or in any way tempted. Let them only look to Christ and implore his help, and there is no doubt that they will receive help because of him and from him. And just as Christ conquered in temptations, so we shall conquer through him. And although this does not happen at once, yet it undoubtedly happens for our good. For God sometimes allows us to be in greater danger, so that his help may afterwards be the more evident: "God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that you may be able to bear it" (1 Cor. 10:13). "My brethren, count it all joy when you fall into diverse temptations" (James 1:2). "Blessed is the man who endures temptation" (James 1:12, in the same place). Likewise 1 Peter 1: "Wherefore we must also rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, we are in heaviness through manifold temptations, that the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory" (1 Pet. 1:6–7).

units.la: Præterea addiscimus hic, quòd cùm omnes ex æquo, quotquot sumus homines, sumus tentationibus & periculis obnoxij, & semper ipsi egemus tum hominum, tum Dei auxilio, fratres nostros, quos videmus subinde in tentationes incidere, & aliquādo succumbere, non contemnamus: sed potius ijs condoleamus, & quantum res fert, seu docendo, seu admonendo, seu alia quacunq; ratione opem feramus, sicut optamus Deum succurrere nobis. Si Deum volumus nobis in tentationibus succurrere, oportet & nos fratribus tentatis & afflictis succurramus.
units.tr: Furthermore, we learn here that since all of us who are human beings alike are subject to temptations and dangers, and always need the help of both men and God, we should not despise our brothers whom we see falling into temptations from time to time and sometimes giving way. Rather, we should sympathise with them and, as far as the situation allows, bring them help, whether by teaching, by admonishing, or in some other way. As we hope God will come to our aid, so we should come to the aid of tempted and afflicted brothers, if we want God to help us in our temptations.

units.la: Atq; his paucis Apostolus satisfactum vult aduersarijs, qui valde importunè obijcie-bant, Christum, si Deus erat, uti in confirmatione afferebatur, nequaquàm debuisse humanam naturam assumere: quandoquidem per diuinam potentiam, vel solo verbo, sine ulla sui ipsius humiliatione homines saluos poterat facere. Docuit autem, equisimis de causis à Deo patre constitutum, ut Christus, qui semper erat Deus, homo in tempore fieret. Quas ut confirmaret (uti nihil fere solet proferre in medium, quòd non protinus muniat, stabiliatq; scripturarum præsidijs) etiam testimonia è veteri testamento nonnulla adiecit, sed pauca & magno iudicio selecta, id quod inter explicandum ea ostendimus.
units.tr: With these few words the Apostle wishes to satisfy the opponents, who very insistently objected that Christ, if he was God (as was asserted in the confirmation), by no means ought to have assumed human nature, since by divine power, or by a word alone, without any humbling of himself, he could have saved men. The Apostle taught, however, that for the most just reasons God the Father decreed that Christ, who was always God, should in time become man. To confirm these reasons (for he seldom brings anything forward that he does not at once fortify and establish with the support of the Scriptures), he also added some testimonies from the Old Testament, few in number but chosen with great judgment, as we showed in explaining them.

units.la: nos verò, non quasi non esset abundè per Apostolum satisfactum, sed ut eandem disputationem de causis suscepta humanitatis à Christo apertiore reddamus, volumus quaedam adhuc proferre ex scripturis selecta oracula, quae Christum carnis nostrae naturam subiturum pronunciarunt: quemadmodum etiam finita confirmatione, de diuinitate Christi quaedam adiecimus, diuinitatem Christi comprobantia. Haec autem non profere mus ex euangelica historia, in qua innumera continentur humanitatem Christi comprobantia: sed ex ipsa veteri lege: qualia verosimile est Iudæis de aduentu Messiae plurima fuisse nota & decantata. Nam nobis sic agendum, tanquam si cum Iudæis res foret.
units.tr: We, however, not as though the Apostle had not satisfied the matter fully, but so as to make the same discussion about the causes for which Christ took on humanity clearer, wish to bring forward some further oracles chosen from the Scriptures, which declared that Christ would undergo the nature of our flesh. Just as, after the confirmation was finished, we also added some points confirming the divinity of Christ, so here too we do this. We do not draw these from the gospel history, in which countless passages confirming the humanity of Christ are contained, but from the Old Law itself. It is likely that many such passages were well known and sung about among the Jews concerning the coming of the Messiah. For we must proceed as though we were dealing with the Jews.

units.la: Principio igitur omnes illæ sententiæ in veteri Testamento, quæ vel usurpatæ sunt à patribus, prophetis, regibus, Christi typum gerentibus, vel de illis dictæ ad significandum aliquid de persona Christi, quandoquidem ipsi homines erant, & eorum actiones humanę, præfigurabant utique & Christum hominem futurum, & quòd deceret Christum, ad perficiendum verè illa, quæ ipsi egerunt in typo, hominem fieri.
units.tr: First, then, all those sayings in the Old Testament which either were used by the fathers, prophets and kings, who bore the type of Christ, or were spoken about them to signify something concerning the person of Christ, since they themselves were men and their human actions prefigured that Christ would be a man, and that it was fitting for Christ to become man in order truly to accomplish those things which they did as types.

units.la: Adhæc promissiones factæ ad patres, inprimis illa Genef. 3. ad ipsum Adamum, de Semine, quod comminueret caput serpentis: tum Genef. 22. ad Abrahamum, Iacobum, (Genef. 28.) aliosq;, de semine, in quo benedicerentur omnes gentes: item ad Dauidem de fructu vetris & successore ex familia eius, cuius regnum foret æternum: (de qua promissione Psalmo 131. item Esaiæ 11. Hierem. 23. & alibi sæpius) omnes, inquam, huiusmodi promissiones de expectando Messia ex gente Iudaica, clarè, Christum debuisse fieri hominem, pronunciant.
units.tr: Besides these, the promises made to the fathers, above all that one in Genesis 3 made to Adam himself, concerning the Seed who would crush the head of the serpent; then in Genesis 22 to Abraham, to Jacob (Genesis 28) and others, concerning the seed in whom all the nations would be blessed; likewise to David, concerning the fruit of his womb and a successor from his family whose kingdom would be eternal (on which promise see Psalm 131, also Isaiah 11, Jeremiah 23 and elsewhere very often): all such promises, I say, clearly declare, concerning the expected Messiah from the Jewish nation, that Christ had to become a man.

units.la: Quid quòd omnes loci apud prophetas, qui Messiae tribuunt regnū, quod Iudæi falsò credunt fore temporale, omnes sanè tales loci Christum debuisse hominem fieri, non obscurè insinuabant?
units.tr: And what of the fact that all the passages in the prophets which ascribe a kingdom to the Messiah (which the Jews wrongly believe will be temporal) did not obscurely hint that Christ had to become man?

units.la: Item quæ citantur in nouo testamento ex lege & prophetis, ad comprobandum ea, quæ per Christum facta sunt, siue quæ in Christo visebantur: quemadmodum Ioan. 1. Phi lippus ait ad Nathanaelem: De quo scripsit Moses in lege, & prophetæ, inuenimus Iesum filium Iosephi: ad humanitatem Christi non minus quàm diuinitatem comprobandum: sunt à spiritu sancto prodita. Et haud dubiè Philippus ita loquens, veramq; humanitatem in eo cōfitens, dum vocat filium Iosephi, præclara & etiam vulgo nota vaticinia de humanitate Christi animo versabat, cuiusmodi erant illa apud populum Israeliticum passim decantata, de promissionibus ad patres eorū factis, & alia id genus, è quibus pauca subijciemus.
units.tr: Likewise, the passages cited in the New Testament from the law and the prophets to confirm what was done by Christ, or what was seen in Christ, were brought forth by the Holy Spirit to prove his humanity no less than his divinity. Thus in John 1 Philip says to Nathanael: "We have found him of whom Moses in the law and the prophets did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph." Undoubtedly Philip, speaking thus and acknowledging in him a true humanity when he calls him the son of Joseph, had in mind the notable and even commonly known prophecies about the humanity of Christ, of the kind that were sung about everywhere among the Israelite people, concerning the promises made to their fathers, and others of that sort, from which we shall set out a few.

units.la: Genef. 49. vaticinium Iacob de Iuda, Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, & dux de femore eius, donec veniat, qui mittedus est, & ipse erit expectatio gentiū, ligās ad vineā pullū iuum, suum, & ad vitem, ô fili mi, asinam suam. Lauabit invino stolam suam, & in sanguine vuæ pallium suum. Pulchriores sunt oculi eius vino, & dentes eius laãte candidiores.
units.tr: Genesis 49: Jacob's prophecy about Judah: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from between his feet, until he come who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations, binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's colt, my son, to the choice vine. He shall wash his garment in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes. His eyes shall be redder than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk."

units.la: Vbi etiam de morte Christi, ac proinde de humanitate, vaticinium comprehenditur. Item Deuteronom. 18. Prophetam de gente tua, & de fratribus tuis, sicut me, suscitabitur Dominus Deus tuus, ipsum audies. Et paulò pòst: Qui autem verba eius, quæ loquentur in nomine meo, audire noluerit, ego vltor existam. Quod testimonium etiam citatur Actor. 7. & 3 Esaiæ 7. Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Immanuel: Butyrum & mel comedet, ut sciat reprobare malum, & eligere bonum. Quæ verba etiam citantur Matth. 1. ab angelo apud Mariam Lucæ 1. & humanitatem Christi coprobat. Ite Esaiæ 9. Paruulus natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis, & factus est principatus super humeru eius: et vocabitur nomen eius admirabilis, consiliarius, &c. paulò pòst: super solium Dauid & super regnum eius sedebit. Hæc clarè etiam humanitate Christi sonant: & posteriora verba propemodum citantur Lucæ 1. ab angelo: licet etiam de prompta videri queant ex Michææ quarto. Hæc inquam testimonia, et alia multò plura Apostolus apud se voluebat animo, quæ fine dubio erat omni populo notissima pro calrissimis vaticiniis de aduentu Mesiæ, & omnia humanitatem manifeste illi tribuunt. Sed adhuc alia quædam alibi de Christo citantur quibus humanitas ipsius suculenter describitur, in memoriam nos ea reuocabimus. Galat. 3. citatur de Christo illud Deuteron. 21. Maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno. Pendere autem in ligno, hominis est. Actorum 2. attinguntur duo vaticinia Dauid, alterum ex psalmo 15. Iurauit Dominus Dauid veritatem, & non frustrabitur eum, de fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam: alterum ex Psalmo 15. Quoniam non derelinques animam meam in inferno, nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, & Petrus ibi interpretatur, quod caro eius (quæ sola est corruptibilis) non viderit corruptionem: ita confirmans carnis Christi resuscitationem: sed in vtroq; humanitas Christi clarissime comprobatur. Esaiæ 11. Egredietur radix de Iesse, & flos de radice eius ascendet. Citatur Rom. 15. & Actor. 13. vbi origo secundum carnem ex Iesse ac Dauid describitur. Esaiæ 42. Ecce puer meus, quem elegi dilectus meus, in quo sibi complacuit anima mea. Citatur Matth. 12. Quanquam hic locus ad confirmandam Christi diuinitate magis conducet. Esaiæ 53. Plura habentur de humiliatione Christi vaticinia, nempe, languores nostros ipse vere tulit, & infirmitates nostras accepit: item, quod tanquam ouis ductus ad occisionem: item, quod peccata nostra in corpore suo portauerit: quæ sane singula humanitate in Christo explicat: vnde & primum illud citatur Matth. 8. secundum Actorum 8. postremum 1. Petri 2.
units.tr: Here too a prophecy about the death of Christ, and therefore about his humanity, is contained. Likewise Deuteronomy 18: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall hear him." And a little later: "But whoever will not hear his words, which he speaks in my name, I myself will be the avenger." This testimony is also cited in Acts 7. And Isaiah 7: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Immanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good." These words are also cited in Matthew 1, and by the angel to Mary in Luke 1, and they confirm the humanity of Christ. Likewise Isaiah 9: "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and dominion is laid upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor," etc. A little later: "He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom." These words clearly sound of the humanity of Christ too, and the last words are almost cited by the angel in Luke 1; though they may also seem to be taken from Micah 4. These testimonies, and many more besides, the Apostle turned over in his mind, which were without doubt most well known to every people as most clear prophecies of the coming of the Messiah, and all of them manifestly ascribe humanity to him. But certain other things are cited elsewhere about Christ, by which his humanity is richly described; we shall recall these to memory. Galatians 3 cites concerning Christ that passage from Deuteronomy 21: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." But to hang on a tree belongs to a man. Acts 2 touches on two prophecies of David, one from Psalm 15 (Psalm 131 in the Vulgate numbering): "The Lord has sworn to David in truth, and he will not break it: I will set the fruit of your womb upon your throne," and the other from Psalm 15: "For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you suffer your Holy One to see corruption." And Peter there interprets that his flesh (which alone is corruptible) did not see corruption, thus confirming the resurrection of Christ's flesh; but in both passages the humanity of Christ is most clearly attested. Isaiah 11: "A shoot shall come forth from the stock of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root." This is cited in Romans 15 and Acts 13, where the origin according to the flesh from Jesse and David is described. Isaiah 42: "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased." This is cited in Matthew 12, although this passage would serve more to confirm the divinity of Christ. Isaiah 53 contains further prophecies about the humiliation of Christ, namely: "He truly bore our infirmities, and took upon himself our sicknesses"; also, that "as a sheep he was led to the slaughter"; also, that "he bore our sins in his body." Each of these clearly explains the humanity in Christ; hence the first of them is cited in Matthew 8, the second in Acts 8, and the last in 1 Peter 2.

units.la: In summa, cùm omnia, quæ per Christū acta sunt, etiam per prophetas pronunciata sunt, plurima liceret adferre ex illis testimonia, quæ clarissime humanitate ipsius testantur: qualia sunt passim obuia de humiliatione & morte Christi, Esaiæ capitibus 61, 63, 64, 65.
units.tr: In sum, since all that was done by Christ was also foretold by the prophets, we could bring forward very many testimonies from them which most clearly attest his humanity, such as those everywhere found concerning the humiliation and death of Christ in Isaiah chapters 61, 63, 64 and 65.

units.la: Ioannes Chrysostomus in libello quodā cōtra Gentiles, quo demonstrat, quod Christus sit Deus, non pauca huic loco idonea congesit: in quibus est illud Baruch 3. sicut diuinitatem, ita humanitatem Christi clarissime comprobans. Hic est Deus noster, & non æstimabitur alius aduersus eum. Hic adinuenit omnem viam disciplinæ, & tradidit illa Iacob puero suo & Israel dilecto suo. Post hæc in terris visus est, & etiam hominib. conuersatus est. Sic deinceps testimonia Prophetarum adfert, quibus prædictum fuit, quo modo, quo loco, quo tempore, Christus nasciturus, ac deinde cætera quæ in Christo, & maximè secundum humanam naturam visa sunt: qui volet, poterit ex illo colligere. Nā omnia eiusmodi testimonia ex veteris testamenti libris proferre ordine, quis sufficiat?
units.tr: John Chrysostom, in a little book against the Gentiles in which he shows that Christ is God, gathered not a few passages suited to this point, among them the one from Baruch 3, which proves Christ's humanity as clearly as his divinity: "This is our God, and no other will be counted against him. He found every way of understanding and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterwards he was seen on earth and lived among men." He then goes on to cite the prophets' testimonies, in which it was foretold how, where and when Christ would be born, and then the other things seen in Christ, especially according to his human nature. Anyone who wishes may gather the rest from that work. For who could be equal to setting out in order all such testimonies from the books of the Old Testament?

units.la: Proinde hic est finis totius confutationis, in qua luculentissimè dissoluta sunt præcipua & validissima quæq; argumenta, quæ ad euertendum ea, quæ prius de Christi diuinitate sunt disputata, ab aduersarijs obijciebantur.
units.tr: Therefore this is the end of the whole refutation, in which the chief and strongest arguments that the adversaries raised against the earlier disputation on Christ's divinity are most clearly dissolved.

units.la: Sequitur de usu totius disputationis, ac deinde paraphrasis: vel ponatur priore loco paraphrasis, tum usus totius disputationis.
units.tr: Next comes the use of the whole disputation, and then the paraphrase; or the paraphrase may be placed first, and the use of the whole disputation after it.

units.la: Iam quo plenius cognoscatur totius disputationis huius de vtraq; natura in Christo ordo & oeconomia, et tam confirmationis, in qua assertum est, Christum esse natura Deum quam confutationis, in qua diluta sunt, quæ ad euertendam diuinitatem Christi obijciebantur de eius humanitate: simulq; redditæ sunt causæ, quare decuerit Christum hominem fieri, argumenta omnia clarius intelligantur: visum est iterum ab initio totam disputationem percurrere, & partium dispositionem, singulorumq; argumentorum formis breuiter repetere: idq; eo modo & facilitate, ut quilibet possit statim & percipere, & eadem reddere, seu alteri explicare. Proinde si quis vestrū interrogetur, quid huius Epistolæ prima parte doceatur: Respon debit, pulcherrimam hic contineri disputationem de utraq; in Christo natura, et clarissi-mè hic doceri, quòd Christus sit Deus: necnō, quare, cū Deus sit, ꝟecuerit ipsum humanam naturam induere.
units.tr: Now, so that the order and plan of this whole disputation, both of the two natures in Christ, and of both the confirmation, in which it is asserted that Christ is God by nature, and the refutation, in which the objections brought against Christ's divinity from his humanity are answered, and the reasons why it was fitting for Christ to become man are also given, may be understood more clearly, I have thought it right to run through the whole disputation again from the beginning, and briefly to repeat the arrangement of its parts and the form of each argument, in a way and with an ease that anyone may grasp at once and restate or explain to another. So if anyone among you is asked what is taught in the first part of this Epistle, he should answer that a most beautiful disputation on the two natures in Christ is contained here, and that it is most clearly taught here that Christ is God, and also why, since he is God, it was fitting for him to put on human nature.

units.la: Sed qua occasione Apostolus suscepit hanc disputationem ita tractandam? Respondetur: Iudæos siue Hebræos, ad quos scripta est hæc, nunquàm ferè adduci potuisse ut Christū esse Deū agnoscerent, imò infensissimis animis pleriq; omnia, quæ de Christo adferebantur, reijciebant, nec de euangelio ferre quicquā poterant. Et qui vel modestis-simi erant inter Iudæos, & de Christo paulò honorificentius sentiebant, hi hoc solum concedebant, quòd nimirū Christus esset valdè excellens vir, & admirandis donis præ-cæteris hominibus præditus, & plane tanquā angelus è cœlo missus inter homines versans, aut eximius propheta, propemodum similis illi Prohpetarū phœnic Mosi. At verò quòd Christus esset Deus, hoc nulli erant admissuri. Proinde ut illos argueret, qui omnia de Christo simpliciter reijciebant, & illos doceret, qui tantū angelis vel Mosi æquâ-dum concedebant, voluit Apostolus docere, quòd Christus esset & Angelis & Mose multò superior, ac reuera Deus Deiq; filius. Atq; ita instituit statim primo loco docere, quòd Christus esset verus Deus.
units.tr: But on what occasion did the Apostle undertake this disputation to be handled in this way? The answer: the Jews, or Hebrews, to whom this letter was written, could almost never be brought to acknowledge that Christ is God. Indeed, most of them, with the bitterest minds, rejected everything that was said about Christ and could take nothing from the gospel. Even those who were the most moderate among the Jews, and thought somewhat more honourably of Christ, conceded only this: that Christ was a truly excellent man, endowed beyond other men with wonderful gifts, moving among men as if he were an angel sent from heaven, or an outstanding prophet, rather like Moses, the chief of the prophets.
