But that Christ was God, they would not admit at all. Therefore, in order to refute those who rejected everything about Christ outright, and to teach those who granted him only equality with the angels or Moses, the Apostle wished to show that Christ was far superior both to the angels and to Moses, and indeed was God, the Son of God. And so he set out to teach, straight away in the first place, that Christ is the true God.

units.la: Sed quia insuper obijciebât aduersarij, multa de Christi cōperta humanitate, per quā putabant se euersuros omnia, quæ dicebantur de Christi diuinitate: ideò deinde in con-sutatione dixit de Christi humanitate, simulq; ostendit, quare decuerit eum, qui natura Deus erat, in tempore hominem fieri. Hæc igitur est susceptæ huius disputationis, & in ei ordinis seu œconomiæ causa. Quomodo igitur incipit Apostolus? Respondetur: Deus olim multifariam, &c.) Propositio est, qua omissa epigrapha & exordio, statim asserit, Christum esse Dei filium ac verum Deum. Est enim sententia: Christus, per quem euan-gelium postremis hisce temporibus mundo patefactum est, est verus Dei filius, ac verus Deus. Sed siue attentionis parandæ causa, siue ad ostendendum, quantò præstantius sit euangelium lege, extulit propositionem hanc quadam forma collationis, dicens, Deus olim, &c.
units.tr: But because the adversaries also objected many things about the humanity of Christ, by which they thought they would overthrow everything said of Christ's divinity, therefore afterwards, in the refutation, he spoke of Christ's humanity, and at the same time showed why it was fitting that he who was God by nature should become man in time. This, then, is the reason for undertaking this disputation and for its order or plan. How, then, does the Apostle begin? The answer: God, who in the past spoke to the fathers in many portions and in many ways, etc. This is the proposition, in which, leaving aside the inscription and the exordium, he at once asserts that Christ is the Son of God and true God. The sense is: Christ, through whom the gospel has been revealed to the world in these last times, is the true Son of God and true God. But whether to prepare attention, or to show how much more excellent the gospel is than the law, he set out this proposition in a certain form of comparison, saying, God, in times past, etc.

units.la: Quid sibi voluntillatâm multa adiecta: quem constituit, &c.? Respondetur: satis quidē fuisset simpliciter dicere: locutus est nobis per filium suum verum Deum: sed placuit Apostolo ex-polire propositione, & per congeriem enumerare diuersos effectus & proprietates di-uinæ potentiæ, ut ex his omnibus quasi certissimis signis colligeretur & perciperetur, Christum natura esse Deum. Nam tantundem ista omnia quasi per periphrasin enuncia-ta & inserta significant. Et valdè conuenit hæc expolitio ipsi exordio, & statim mirificè illustrat Christi dignitate. Sunt autem septem particulæ, singulæ ad diuinitatem in Chri-sto declarãda valde idoneę, atq; ita collocatæ, ut incrementi ratio in eis obseruari debeat.
units.tr: What did he mean by adding so much afterwards: whom he appointed, etc.? The answer: it would certainly have been enough simply to say: has spoken to us by his Son, the true God. But the Apostle chose to elaborate the proposition, and to enumerate by an accumulation the various effects and properties of divine power, so that from all these, as from most certain signs, it might be gathered and perceived that Christ is God by nature. For all these things, set out and inserted as if by periphrasis, signify just as much. This elaboration fits the exordium very well and at once illustrates the dignity of Christ wonderfully. There are seven clauses, each very suitable for declaring the divinity of Christ, and they are so arranged that the order of growth ought to be observed in them.

units.la: Exponę igitur eas breuiter, & succinctè. Respondetur. Quem constituit hæredē omnium: fluit hæc ratio ex præcedenti appellatione filij. Si enim filius est Dei, ergo & hæres om-nium, quæ Dei sunt. Vim habet ex eo, quòd more humano, imò & naturali ac diuino filius plenum ius accipit in omnia bona paterna. Per quem etiam secula condidit: creator est, ergo Deus, & nequaquam creatura.
units.tr: I shall therefore explain them briefly and succinctly. The answer: whom he appointed heir of all things: this reason flows from the preceding title of Son. For if he is the Son of God, then he is also heir of all that belongs to God. It has force from the fact that, after the manner of men, indeed also naturally and divinely, a son receives full right to all his father's goods. Through whom also he made the worlds: he is the Creator, therefore God, and in no way a creature.

units.la: Qui cum sit splendor gloriæ) ἀπαύγασμα. In Christo relucet eadem gloria, quæ est ipsius Pa-tris. Sed hoc non posset fieri, nisi esset Deus.
units.tr: Who being the brightness of his glory [ἀπαύγασμα]. In Christ shines the same glory which belongs to the Father himself. But this could not be unless he were God.

units.la: Et expressa imago substantiæ illius: χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. Id est, eiusdē est cum patre naturæ & substantiæ, ne quis putet, ea, quæ hactenus tributa Christo sunt, duntaxat competere illi per participationem aut similem modum.
units.tr: And the express image of his substance [χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ]. That is, he has the same nature and substance as the Father, so that no one may think that the things hitherto attributed to Christ belong to him only by participation or in some similar manner.

units.la: Moderetur q; omnia verbo potentiæ suæ: ab officio diuinæ prouidentiæ. Non solùm condidit omnia, sed sua prouidētia moderatur, feruat, sustētat omnia. Et sic prouidētia, bonitas, potentia Dei ipsi tribuitur.
units.tr: And upholding all things by the word of his power: from the office of divine providence. He not only created all things, but by his providence governs, preserves and sustains them all. And so providence, goodness and power are attributed to him as to God.

units.la: Per semetipsum purgatione fa-cta peccatorum nostrorum: à facultate remittendi peccata, quæ soli Deo competit, ut dicitur Marci 2. Estq; insignis cōmemoratio beneficij Christi erga nos.
units.tr: When he had by himself purged our sins: from the power of forgiving sins, which belongs to God alone, as is said in Mark 2. And it is a remarkable reminder of Christ's benefit towards us.

units.la: Consedit in dextra maiestatis in excelsis: forma locutionis, ad parem dignitatem significandā Christi cum patre, sumpta à more hominum, quo cum cuipiam summum honorem tri-buere volunt, locum ei concedunt ad latus dexterum.
units.tr: Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high: a form of speech, taken from human custom, to signify Christ's equal dignity with the Father. When men wish to give someone the highest honour, they give him a place at their right side.

units.la: Etsi autē hæ particulæ non habeant adiectas probationes suas, (vnde & aliquis forte putaret posse reijci) tamen satis constabit earum veritas ex sequenti confirmatione, in qua, Christum esse Deum, & patri per omnia æqualem, comprobabitur.
units.tr: Although these clauses do not have their proofs added (so that someone might perhaps think they could be rejected), nevertheless their truth will be sufficiently established by the following confirmation, in which it will be proved that Christ is God and in all things equal to the Father.

units.la: Quid deinde sequitur? Respondendum. confirmatio: tantò præstantior factus angelis, &c.
units.tr: What follows next? The answer must be given: confirmation: having become so much better than the angels, etc.

units.la: Quare sic auspicatur eam, & non potius simpliciter dicit: Quia Christus sit Deus,
units.tr: Why does he begin it in this way, and not rather simply say: Because Christ is God,

units.la: multis argumentis probabimus? Respondendum propter aduersarios, qui Christum duntaxat æquabant angelis, aut pro angelo venerandum putarunt, instituit totam hanc confirmationem, non nudè quidem, sed quadam forma collationis: ut ita simul refellat impias opiniones de Christo conceptas, simulq; afferat, Christum esse natura Deum. Qua in re consilium & prudentiam suam singularem Apostolus testatam facit.
units.tr: we shall prove by many arguments? The answer: on account of the adversaries, who only put Christ on a level with the angels, or thought he was to be honoured as an angel. He arranged this whole confirmation not simply, but in a certain form of comparison, so that at the same time he might refute the impious opinions conceived about Christ and assert that Christ is God by nature. In this matter the Apostle shows his singular counsel and prudence.

units.la: Nomen hic ponitur pro potentia, dignitate, gloria, maiestate, ut Psalmo 8. Domine Dominus noster, quàm admirabile est nomen tuum, &c.
units.tr: Here "name" is used for power, dignity, glory and majesty, as in Psalm 8: O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name, etc.

units.la: Proferiam argumenta cófirmationis. Respondetur. En primum argumentum ex psalmo sumpt. Hoc probat, Christum non solum angelis superiorem, sed reuera filium Dei. Maior est, qui vocatur filius, quàm qui vocatur tantum minister, vel alio simili nomine. Atqui in Scriptura Christus vocatur filius, angeli autem non ita, sed tantum spiritus ministratorij. Igitur Christus est angelis maior: quandoquidem filius & quidem Dei est: Quare Christus etiam Deus. Ac vide prudentiam Apostoli, quòd non sufficeperit primò declarandum, quòd Christus esset maior angelis, quòd posset facere, proferendo vel admiranda quædam opera, vel alia huiusmodi: ac deinde debuisset seorsim probare, Christum esse filium Dei, ac verum Deum: sed voluit statim probare Christum esse filium Dei, ac verum Deum: atq; ita eadem opera couellit illos, qui habebant Christum duntaxat pro eo, qui esset par angelis. Deinde illud considerandum, quod non vult probare, Christum esse Deum, ex potentia miraculorum, aut similibus causis, sed testimonijs Scripturæ, & Prophetarum vaticinijs.
units.tr: I shall set out the arguments of the confirmation. The answer: here is the first argument, taken from the Psalm. It proves that Christ is not only superior to the angels, but truly the Son of God. He who is called Son is greater than he who is called only minister, or by some similar name. But in Scripture Christ is called Son, whereas the angels are not so called, but only ministering spirits. Therefore Christ is greater than the angels, since he is indeed the Son, and of God. Hence Christ is also God. And note the Apostle's prudence: it was not enough first to declare that Christ was greater than the angels, by showing that he could do certain wonderful works, or other things of this kind; and then to prove separately that Christ is the Son of God and true God. He wished at once to prove that Christ is the Son of God and true God, and so by the same stroke he overturned those who held Christ only to be one who was equal to the angels. Further, it should be noted that he does not wish to prove that Christ is God from the power of miracles or similar causes, but from the testimonies of Scripture and the prophetic utterances.

units.la: Recte autem citatum esse præsens testimonium, quatuor aut quinq; rationib. nos supra ostendimus. Dic secundum argumentum. Respondetur.
units.tr: I have already shown above, on four or five grounds, that the present testimony is rightly cited. Say the second argument. Answer.

units.la: Ac rursum: Ego ero ei pater, & ille erit mihi filius. Secundum argumentum sumptum ex 2. Samuel. 7. Vbi propheta Nathan iubetur à Deo annunciare Dauidi, domū Dei nequaquam ædificandam ab ipso, sed ab alio quodam filio eius successuro. In quibus tamen vel bis vaticinium de Christo ex familia Dauid prodituro, & domum Dei, id est, veram ecclesiam ædificaturo continetur: id quod iam supra satis fusè exposuimus.
units.tr: "And again: I will be his father, and he shall be my son." The second argument is taken from 2 Samuel 7, where the prophet Nathan is commanded by God to tell David that the house of God is not to be built by David himself but by another son who will succeed him. Yet this contains a twofold prophecy: of Christ, who would come from the family of David, and who would build the house of God, that is, the true Church. We have already set this out at sufficient length above.

units.la: Da tertium argumentum. Respondetur.
units.tr: Give the third argument. Answer.

units.la: Rursum autem cum inducit primogenitum, &c. Tertium argumentum ex Psalm. 96. quo & Christum angelis superiorem, & verum Deum declarat. Christus adorandus est: Ergo Deus est. Angeli vero adorabunt eum. Ergo angeli sunt inferiores eo. Nam adorare inferiorum est, adorari superioris & proprie Dei.
units.tr: "Again, when he brings in the firstborn, etc." The third argument is from Psalm 96, by which he declares Christ to be superior to the angels and true God. Christ is to be worshipped; therefore he is God. Yet the angels will worship him; therefore the angels are inferior to him. For to worship belongs to an inferior, and to be worshipped belongs to a superior, and properly to God.

units.la: Recte autem citatum esse, ipse suis verbis, quæ præmittit declarat, & nos etiam sufficiens ostendimus.
units.tr: That this is rightly cited, the words which he sets before it make clear, and we have also shown this sufficiently.

units.la: Dic quartum argumentum. Et ad angelos quidem dicit: Qui creat angelos. Quartum argumentum ex Psalmo 103. quo probat, Christum angelis superiorem, ac proinde verum Deum. Quod sumit non à persona Christi, ut in præcedentibus, sed à persona angelorum. Habendaq; est ratio hic collationis institutæ, qua Christus confertur cum angelis, respiciendumq; ad ea, quæ hactenus dicta sunt. Primò dixit, Christum tanto præstantiorem angelis, quanto præstantius adeptus est nomen. Inde exposuit aliquot argumentis, quantum nomen Christus adeptus fuerit, nempe filij Dei. Nunc ergo ratione collationis adijcit de angelis, eos non appellatos filios, sed tantùm ministros, ut huiusmodi consequentia comprehendi cuncta possint. Excellentior est in domo filius, quàm minister. Atqui Christus est filius, angeli vero ministri: Ergo Christus angelis est excellentior. Maior est nota. Minor ex præcedentibus argumentis probata est. Angelos vero tantum ministros esse, probatur præsenti testimonio. Recte esse citatum, ostendimus supra.
units.tr: Give the fourth argument. "And of the angels indeed he says: who makes his angels." The fourth argument is from Psalm 104 (103), by which he proves that Christ is superior to the angels, and therefore true God. He takes it not from the person of Christ, as in the preceding arguments, but from the person of the angels. The comparison here instituted, by which Christ is compared with the angels, must be kept in mind, and we must look back to what has been said so far. First he said that Christ is as much more excellent than the angels as the name he has obtained is more excellent. Then he showed by several arguments how great a name Christ obtained, namely that of Son of God. Now, by way of comparison, he adds concerning the angels that they are not called sons but only ministers, so that all things can be comprehended in this kind of inference: The son in the house is more excellent than the servant. But Christ is the Son, and the angels are ministers; therefore Christ is more excellent than the angels. The major premise is well known. The minor has been proved by the preceding arguments. That the angels are only ministers is proved by the present testimony, and that it is rightly cited we have shown above.

units.la: Ad filium autem: Thronus tuus Deus in seculum. Quintum argumentum ex Psalm. 44. In quo aperte bis vocatur Deus. Imò duo argumenta Christi diuinitatem probantia hic latent. Alterum, quòd bis vocatur Deus: Thronus tuus, ò Deus, inquit: Item, propterea vnxit te, ò Deus, Deus tuus. Alterum, quòd dicitur thronus, siue regnum ipsius duraturum in seculum seculi, atq; in æternum: quod non potest, nisi de Christo Deo competere, de cuius spirituali & æterno regno etiam alias Scriptura concionatur. Recte autem tribui Christo, phrafes ipsæ satis testantur.
units.tr: "But to the Son: your throne, O God, is for ever." The fifth argument is from Psalm 45, in which he is openly called God twice. Indeed two arguments proving Christ's divinity lie hidden here. One is that he is called God twice: "Your throne, O God," he says; likewise, "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you." The other is that his throne, or kingdom, is said to endure for ever and ever, and to eternity, which can belong only to Christ who is God, of whose spiritual and eternal kingdom Scripture elsewhere also speaks. That these words are rightly applied to Christ the phrases themselves sufficiently testify.

units.la: Et tu in initio Domine terræ fundamenta iecisti, &c. Sextum argumentum ex Psalmo 101. quo Christus vocatur creator totius mundi, ac proinde Deus. Imò plura inseruntur, quæ diuinitatis sunt propria, & quasi singula argumenta constituunt. Annectit hoc præcedenti argumento sine verbis interpositis, siue quia nequaquam semper opus est ostendere, nouum esse argumentum: siue quia ex parte affinis est præcedenti, quia hic etiam de regno Christi nonnulla continentur. Argumenta autem hæc possunt colligi.
units.tr: "And you, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundations of the earth, etc." The sixth argument is from Psalm 102 (101), by which Christ is called the creator of the whole world and therefore God. Indeed several further points are introduced which belong to divinity, and they make up, as it were, separate arguments. He joins this to the preceding argument without any intervening words, either because it is not always necessary to show that an argument is new, or because it is in part related to the preceding one, since here too some things about the kingdom of Christ are contained. These arguments may be gathered as follows.

units.la: Tu Domine ab initio: Ergo ab æterno extitit, & ante omnem creaturam: Terræ fundamenta iecisti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli)Ergo creator est, ac proinde Deus. Tu autem permanes)Ergo nec finem est habiturus, & manet in æternum.
units.tr: "You, Lord, from the beginning": therefore he has existed from eternity and before every creature. "You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands": therefore he is the creator, and consequently God. "But you remain": therefore he will also have no end, and he remains for ever.

units.la: Tu autem idem es) Ergo incommutabilis est. Rursus: Anni tui non deficient: Ergo æternùm manet. Quæ omnia diuinitatem in Christo arguunt. Recte autem de Christi persona hæc accipi, nos supra ostendimus.
units.tr: "But you are the same": therefore he is unchangeable. Again: "your years will not fail": therefore he remains for ever. All these things prove the divinity of Christ. That these words rightly apply to the person of Christ we have shown above.

units.la: Ad quem autem angelorum dixit unquam, sede à dextris, &c.) Septimū argumentum ex psal.110. quo simul superior angelis, simul Deus probatur. Christo dictum est, quod summæ est dignitatis, uidelicet, sede à dextris meis. Sed hoc nulli unquam dictum est angelorū. Ergo Christus est angelis excellentior.
units.tr: "But to which of the angels did he ever say: sit at my right hand, etc.?" The seventh argument is from Psalm 110, by which he proves at once that Christ is superior to the angels and that he is God. To Christ has been said what belongs to the highest dignity, namely: sit at my right hand. But this was never said to any of the angels. Therefore Christ is more excellent than the angels.

units.la: Ita perstat in collatione Christi cum angelis. Simul hic probatur, Christum esse Deū, in hunc modum. Sedere ad dextram non est nisi superioris, aut paris. Sed pater dicit Christo, sede à dextris, &c. Ergo Christus est Deo patre, si non superior, at saltem par.
units.tr: Thus he persists in the comparison of Christ with the angels. At the same time it is proved here, in this way, that Christ is God. To sit at the right hand belongs only to a superior or an equal. But the Father says to Christ: "sit at my right hand, etc." Therefore Christ is equal to God the Father, if not superior, at least equal.

units.la: Postremo loco positum videtur argumentum, quia maximè dignitatem Christi, & probare etiam videtur, quod postremo loco positum fuerat in expolitione propositionis. Aptum esse hoc argumentum, probatur Matth. 22. Actor. 2. &c.
units.tr: The argument seems to be placed last because it chiefly concerns the dignity of Christ, and it also seems to prove what was placed last in the exposition of the proposition. That this argument is apt is proved by Matthew 22 and Acts 2, etc.

units.la: Nonne omnes sunt administratorij spiritus, qui in ministerium emittuntur, propter eos, &c.
units.tr: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who, etc.?"

units.la: Collectis argumentis probantibus dignitatem & diuinitatem Christi, breuiter subijcit summam dignitatis angelorum, ex psal.103. Estq; sententia. Satis copiosè probatum est, quanta sit Christi dignitas, quòd verus Deus sit, & multis interuallis angelis præstatior. At verò de angelis talia ne quaquam dici possunt, qualia de Christo sunt pronunciata. Hoc vnum, & quasi summum de eis dici potest, quòd sint administratorij spiritus, &c. Quæ quidem dignitas non parua est: sed si conferatur cum dignitate Christi, propemodum nulla aut certè multò inferior. Atq; ita finis imponitur toti confirmationi, in qua Christus per collationem comprobatus est non solùm angelis superior, sed insuper verus Deus. Quid deinde sequitur? Respondetur.
units.tr: Having gathered the arguments which prove the dignity and divinity of Christ, he briefly adds the sum of the dignity of the angels, from Psalm 104 (103). The sense is this: It has been proved quite fully how great the dignity of Christ is, that he is true God and far superior to the angels by many degrees. But such things cannot in any way be said of the angels as have been declared of Christ. This one thing, and as it were the highest thing, can be said of them, that they are ministering spirits, and so on. This dignity is certainly not small, but if it is compared with the dignity of Christ it is almost nothing, or at any rate much inferior. And so an end is put to the whole confirmation, in which Christ, by comparison, has been shown to be not only superior to the angels but moreover true God. What follows from this? Answer.

units.la: Propterea oportet nos uehementius attendere his, quæ dicta sunt nobis) Confirmationi subijcit brevem exhortationem ad Hebræos, ut Christum talem ac tantum agnoscant & uenerentur, eiusque euangelium non contemnant: sicut solent rhetores post argumenta fidem facientia addere nonnulla ad mouendos affectus, & ad pertrahendum auditores in suam sententiam. Sic verò & hæc conclusio habet inspersa aliqua ad mouendos affectus valde idonea, id quod licet paucis animaduertere.
units.tr: "Therefore we ought to attend more earnestly to the things which have been said to us." To the confirmation he adds a brief exhortation to the Hebrews, that they should acknowledge and reverence Christ as such and so great, and not despise his gospel. Just as the rhetoricians are accustomed, after arguments that create belief, to add some things to move the emotions and to draw hearers to their opinion, so this conclusion too has here and there some matters very suitable for moving the emotions, as may be noticed briefly.

units.la: Ne quando profanus) Ratio est à periculoso.
units.tr: "Lest at any time we drift away." The reason is drawn from danger.

units.la: Etenim si qui per angelos) Comprobatio à minore ad maius. Lex quæ duntaxat per angelos fuit data, fuit firma, & transgressores eius, seu contemptores eius fuerunt puniti. Ergo multò magis euangelium, quod per Christum allatum est, debet firmum esse; & transgressores seu contemptores eius punientur.
units.tr: "For if the word spoken through angels...": a proof from the lesser to the greater. The law which was given through angels alone was firm, and its transgressors or despisers were punished. Therefore much more the gospel, which was brought through Christ, ought to be firm, and its transgressors or despisers will be punished.

units.la: Quæ cum primùm enarrari cœpit per ipsum Dominum) Aliæ rationes suasoriæ ab euangelij præstatia, quam uult colligi ex duabus rebus, nempe, ab eo, quòd euangelium enarratum sit ab ipso Domino: (non sine causa uocat Christum Dominum) deinde, quòd multis modis confirmatum: unde sequitur: attestante Deo, & signis & prodigijs simul, &c. Quæ sanè rationes plurimum ponderis habere deberent ad commouendum omnes, ut Christum eiusque euangelium suscipiant.
units.tr: "Which, when it was first begun to be spoken by the Lord himself...": other persuasive reasons, drawn from the excellence of the gospel, which he wishes to be inferred from two things: first, that the gospel was declared by the Lord himself (not without reason he calls Christ the Lord); and second, that it was confirmed in many ways, whence it follows: "God also bearing witness with signs and wonders at the same time, etc." These reasons ought certainly to carry great weight in moving all men to receive Christ and his gospel.

units.la: CONFVTATIO.
units.tr: Confutation

units.la: Non enim angelis subiecit orbem terræ futurum, de quo loquimur. Testatus est autè alicubi quidam, dicens: Quid est homo, quòd memor es eius? aut filius hominis, quòd inuisis illum? Fecisti eum paulisper inferiorem angelis. Gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. In hoc enim quòd ei subiecit omnia, nihil omisit illi non subiectum.
units.tr: For he did not subject the world to come, of which we speak, to the angels. But one has testified somewhere, saying: What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet. For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.

units.la: Confutatio huius disputationis de diuinitate Christi. Nunc enim confutantur ea, quæ aduersarij ad euertendam diuinitatem Christi adferebant. Obijciebant autem præcipuè Christum compertum esse hominem, ac proinde non solùm non esse Deum, sed nec angelis superiorem. Ac reuera uidebatur absurdissimum, quòd una eademque persona & dignitatem Dei, & vilitatatem hominis in se haberet. Quare valde efficaces putarunt Iudæi suas de humanitate Christi obiectiones. Sed Apostolus ualde prudenter illis satisfacit, & mox graviores aliquot obiectiones rectissimè diluit.
units.tr: This is a refutation of the argument concerning the divinity of Christ. For now are refuted the objections that the opponents brought forward to overthrow the divinity of Christ. They chiefly objected that Christ was found to be a man, and therefore not only was not God but was not even superior to the angels. And indeed it seemed most absurd that one and the same person should have both the dignity of God and the lowliness of man. Therefore the Jews thought their objections based on the humanity of Christ very effective. But the Apostle answers them most wisely, and soon refutes with great accuracy several more serious objections.

units.la: Prima aute illa verba(Non enim angelis, &c.) sunt velut repetita propositio, & summa totius disputationis, in qua probatum est, Christum esse angelis superiorem ac verum deum. Quem in modum solent etiam Rhetores ante confutationem repetere propositionem principalem. Sed hinc obscuritas quaedam est hoc loco, 𝓟 verba propositionis sumpta sunt ex argumento statim sequenti, quo colligit, Christo etiam ut homini omnia fore subiecta.
units.tr: Those first words (For he did not subject, etc.) are like a repeated proposition, and the sum of the whole argument, in which it has been proved that Christ is superior to the angels and is true God. Orators also commonly repeat the principal proposition before a refutation. But here there is some obscurity, since the words of the proposition are taken from the argument that immediately follows, by which he infers that all things will be subjected to Christ also as man.

units.la: Testatus est autem alicubi quidam, dicens: Quid est homo? En prima aduersariorum obiectio, quos apparet sic argumentatos. Christus, quem tu contendis angelis superiorem, ac verum Deum, manifeste deprehensus est verus homo. Sed homo est inferior angelis, sicut Scriptura palam dicit, psalmo 8. Quid est homo? &c. Ergo Christus non solum non est Deus, sed etiam angelis inferior. Atq; hoc pacto semper ieruata collatione illa Christi cum angelis, quam initio confirmationis diximus fuisse institutam, videtur efficacissime concludi, Christum non esse Deum, imo ipsis quoq; angelis multo inferiorem. Apparet autem, aduersarios tantum priora illa uerba citare solitos pro argumenti sui probatione, quibus generaliter dicitur, hominem esse angelis inferiorem.
units.tr: "But one has testified somewhere, saying: What is man?" Here is the first objection of the opponents, who evidently argued thus: Christ, whom you contend to be superior to the angels and true God, is plainly shown to be a true man. But man is inferior to the angels, as Scripture plainly says in Psalm 8: What is man, etc. Therefore Christ is not only not God, but is even inferior to the angels. And in this way, keeping that comparison of Christ with the angels which we said at the beginning of the argument had been set up, it seems most effectively to be concluded that Christ is not God, indeed is much inferior even to the angels themselves. It appears, moreover, that the opponents were accustomed to cite only those first words, in which it is said in general that man is inferior to the angels, as proof of their argument.

units.la: Sed Apostolus valde argute refellit istam obiectionem, ac perspicue offendit ex verbis eodem loco sequentibus, Christum, etiamsi verus homo sit, angelis nihilominus superiorem, & omnia illi debere subiici, etiam angelos: ac proinde Deum esse, & saluam manere eius dignitatem. Sic enim respondet: Concedo quidem, Christum esse hominem, sed docebo, id non obstare, quo minus angelis superior sit. Nam eodem loco Scriptura habet: Gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Ex quibus sic colligo: Omnia sunt subiecta pedibus hominis. Sed, qui dicit, omnia, nihil excludit. Ergo etiam angeli Christo ut homini sunt subiecti. Quare salua manet Christi dignitas, quam asserui: Christus adhuc superior angelis agnosci debet.
units.tr: But the Apostle very shrewdly refutes this objection, and clearly shows from the words that follow in the same place that Christ, even though he is a true man, is nonetheless superior to the angels, and that all things ought to be subjected to him, the angels too; and therefore that he is God and his dignity remains intact. For he answers thus: I grant indeed that Christ is a man, but I will show that this does not prevent him from being superior to the angels. For in the same place Scripture says: You crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet. From these words I argue thus: All things are subjected to the feet of man. But he who says "all things" excludes nothing. Therefore the angels too are subject to Christ as man. Wherefore the dignity of Christ that I asserted remains intact: Christ ought still to be acknowledged as superior to the angels.

units.la: At nondum uidemus illi omnia subiecta) Alia obiectio, contra praecedentem dilutionem. Cum enim pij valde praedicarent summam potestatem Christi in omnia, atque adeo in ipsos angelos, cum non haberent amplius quod opponerent, tandem cum quodam contemptu, & velut irridentes obijciebant, quod vanum videretur, tantopere praedicare Christi potentiam, quasi omnia deberent ei subijci, cum talis potentia nusquam experimentis deprehenderetur, sicque tantum confecta & imaginaria appareret. Existimabant autem caeci aduersarij, quae dicebantur de potestate Christi, accipienda de potestate externa & temporali, quemadmodum adhuc hodie Iudaei tale regnum expetunt. Proinde vna hac obiectione putarunt, se omnia, quae de potestate Christi praedicabantur, destruere.
units.tr: "But we do not yet see all things subjected to him." This is another objection, against the preceding answer. For when the godly loudly proclaimed the supreme power of Christ over all things, and so over the angels themselves, and had no more to oppose, the opponents finally objected with a certain scorn, and as if mocking, that it seemed vain to proclaim so greatly the power of Christ, as if all things ought to be subjected to him, when such power was nowhere perceived in experience, and so appeared to be merely invented and imaginary. The blind opponents, moreover, thought that the things said about the power of Christ were to be understood of an external and temporal power, as the Jews even today still seek such a kingdom. Therefore by this one objection they thought they destroyed everything that was preached about the power of Christ.

units.la: Respondet Apostolus: (Eum uero, qui paulisper diminutus) velut concedens quidem, Christum aliqua in parte, qua videlicet pertulit cruciatum mortis, visum esse inferiorem angelis, ac potestate illa amplissima exutum. At vero alia in parte palam cerni, praesertim a pijs, gloria & honore coronatum, hoc est, omnia habere sibi subiecta. Quomodo vero cernatur Christus omnia habere in sua potestate, ipse non declarat, fortasis contemnes rationem aduersariorum, ceu nimis crassam, infirmam & indignam, cui pluribus verbis respondeatur. Sed intelligit haud dubie gloriam & potentiam Christi abunde manifestam in ipsius resurrectione, & in coelum ascensione, quomodo alibi ipse Christus per resurrectionem glorificandum se, & ad gloriam patris cuehedum saepe dixit: ut Ioan. 17. vbi orat patrem, ut ipsum glorificet.
units.tr: The Apostle replies: "But him who was made a little lower" (as if conceding that Christ, in some respect, namely in that he suffered the agony of death, was seen to be inferior to the angels and stripped of that most ample power). But in another respect, he says, he is plainly seen, especially by the godly, to be crowned with glory and honour, that is, to have all things subject to him. But how Christ is seen to have all things in his power, he himself does not explain, perhaps because he disdains the argument of the opponents as too crude, weak and unworthy to be answered at length. But he undoubtedly means the glory and power of Christ abundantly manifest in his resurrection and ascension into heaven, just as Christ himself elsewhere often said that he was to be glorified through the resurrection and to be restored to the glory of the Father; as in John 17, where he prays the Father that he would glorify him.

units.la: Proinde ex his manifestis argumentis potentiae Christi, quasi ex signis intelligi, ac pro certo statui vult Apostolus, hoc quoq; necessario adimplendum, quod omnia ei subiciantur. Qui enim sua virtute resurrexit, & mortem sibi subiecit, qui item palam visus est in coelum ascendere, an alienum, quod ei subijciantur omnia? Ne vero aduersarij adhuc arriperent ex illa humiliatione Christi ansam constituendi eum infra angelos, aut lias quocunq; modo eleuandi dignitatem Christi: addit duas grauissimas rationes, quibus insinuat, per humiliationem illam Christi ad mortem usq; nihil detractum ipsius dignitati, nulla q; in parte gloria eius obscuratam. Prior ratio est a causa efficiente, nimirum bona voluntate Dei patris sic misericorditer disponente.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle wills that from these manifest proofs of the power of Christ, as if from signs, it be understood and firmly held as certain that this also must necessarily be fulfilled, that all things are subjected to him. For he who rose again by his own power, and subdued death to himself, and who was also seen plainly to ascend into heaven, why should it seem strange that all things are subjected to him? Lest the opponents should still seize upon that humiliation of Christ as an occasion for placing him below the angels, or for lowering in any other way the dignity of Christ, he adds two very weighty reasons, by which he hints that through that humiliation of Christ, even unto death, nothing was taken from his dignity, and his glory was in no part obscured. The first reason is from the efficient cause, namely the good will of God the Father, who thus disposed it in mercy.

units.la: Per gratiam Dei, inquit: quasi diceret: Non humanis meritis id obtinentibus, sed gratia & beneuolentia Dei sic administrante. Altera ratio a causa finali siue effectu. Vt pro omni gustaret mortem: Est q; sententia. Quando hic secutus amplissimus effectus ex illa humiliatione Christi, &c.
units.tr: "By the grace of God," he says, as if he were saying: Not by human merits obtaining this, but by the grace and benevolence of God so administering it. The second reason is from the final cause or effect: "that he might taste death for everyone." The sense is this: the most ample effect follows from that humiliation of Christ, etc.

units.la: Decebat enim eum, propter quem sunt omnia) Habebant aduersarij adhuc quod obijcerent. Quoniam enim ita constanter hactenus defensa est Christi dignitas, ac demonstratum, quod humiliatio eius ad mortem non obfuerit eius potentiae vel dignitati samea. tamen hic nouus scrupus exortus est. Dicere enim rursus potuerunt aduersarij. Vos contenditis, Christum esse Deum, omnia habere sibi subiecta: humiliatum vero eum per gratiam & bonam voluntatem Dei patris, nec non ut omnes nos per suam mortem temporaneam à morte æterna liberaret. Sed istud est valde absurdum, quòd, qui Deus erat, & poterat vel solo verbo humanum genus à morte æterna liberare, voluerit tamen fieri homo, & quidem nō infra angelos modò, sed omnes etiam homines deiectus. Quid opus erat, fieri hominem, & acutos cruciatus mortis perpeti, quādo eadem potuisset efficere, solam diuinam naturam retinendo? Et certè istud argumentum in speciem vehemens et potuisset vel addictissimos Christo ad dubitandum de eius dignitate, vel etiam de prouidentia Dei adducere. Hæc sine dubio fiebat obiectio ab aduersarijs: sed Apostolus, quia ea non abest à blasphemia Dei, non voluit nudè exponere.
units.tr: "For it became him, for whom are all things..." The opponents still had something to object. For since the dignity of Christ has been so steadfastly defended up to now, and it has been shown that his humiliation unto death did not detract from his power or his dignity, nevertheless a new scruple arose here. For the opponents could again say: You contend that Christ is God, having all things subject to him; but that he was humbled through the grace and good will of God the Father, and also that by his temporal death he might free all of us from eternal death. But this is very absurd: that he who was God, and could free the human race from eternal death by a single word, nevertheless willed to become man, and indeed to be cast down not only below the angels but below all men. Why was it necessary for him to become a man and to suffer the bitter agonies of death, when he could have accomplished the same by retaining the divine nature alone? And indeed this argument, in appearance quite forceful, could have led even those most devoted to Christ to doubt either his dignity or the providence of God. This objection was doubtless being made by the opponents; but the Apostle, because it is not far from blasphemy against God, did not wish to set it out plainly.

units.la: Diluit autem multò sapientissimè, exponendo paulò copiosius, quibus de causis de cuerit Christum, qui ab æterno erat Deus, in tempore hominem fieri, & mortem hominum causa subire. Proinde hæc verba sunt loco propositionis accipienda. Simpliciter enim asserit, sic decuisse & conueniens fuisse, ut Christus princeps & autor salutis omnium ad æternam gloriam vocandorum, primùm per afflictiones in humana natura humiliatur, deinde ad summam perfectionem ac gloriam exaltaretur.
units.tr: He answers it most wisely, however, by explaining at somewhat greater length for what reasons it was fitting that Christ, who was God from eternity, should in time become man and undergo death for the sake of men. Therefore these words are to be taken in place of the proposition. For he simply asserts that it was fitting and suitable that Christ, the prince and author of the salvation of all who are called to eternal glory, should first be humbled in human nature through afflictions, and then be exalted to the highest perfection and glory.

units.la: Quandoquidem & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes) Prima ratio, quare decuerit Christum hominem fieri, sumpta à conditione eorum, qui erant à morte æterna liberandi, siue sanctificandi. Conuenit, eum qui sanctificat, eiusdem esse conditionis, cuius sunt sanctificandi. Sed sanctificādi sunt homines. Ergo eum, qui hos sanctificaturus erat, decebat hominem fieri.
units.tr: Since both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one. This is the first reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man, drawn from the condition of those who were to be freed from eternal death, or sanctified. It is fitting that he who sanctifies should be of the same condition as those who are to be sanctified. But men are the ones to be sanctified. Therefore it was fitting that he who was to sanctify them should become a man.

units.la: Quum ob causam non erubescit fratres illos uocare, dicens: Annunciabo nomen tuum fratribus meis.) Confirmat rationem præcedentem aliquot Scripturæ testimonijs, ex quibus manifestum fit, constitutum ita fuisse longe ante ab ipso Patre, quòd Christus deberet humanam naturam induere. Istud autem testimonium sumptum ex psal. 22. vbi propheta in persona Christi ficloquitur. Vis autem argumenti est in uoce fratrum.
units.tr: Therefore he is not ashamed to call them brethren, saying: I will declare thy name unto my brethren. He confirms the preceding reasoning by several testimonies of Scripture, from which it is clear that it had been determined by the Father himself long before that Christ should put on human nature. This testimony is taken from Psalm 22, where the prophet speaks in the person of Christ. The force of the argument lies in the word brethren.

units.la: Et rursum: Et ego ero fidens in illo) Secundū testimoniū ex Esaiæ 12. vel psalm. 17. Christus apud prophetam dicit, Ego ero fidens in illo: sed fidere in Deo non potest Christo conuenire, nisi secundum humanitatem. Ergo decuit Christum hominem fieri: & uerè homo fatus agnoscì debet. Constat autem, quòd fidere in alio, sit inferioris. Christus verò inferior patre non potest intelligi, nisi secundum humanitatem.
units.tr: And again: I will put my trust in him. The second testimony is from Isaiah 12 or Psalm 17. Christ says through the prophet, I will put my trust in him. But to trust in God cannot belong to Christ except according to his humanity. Therefore it was fitting that Christ should become man, and he must truly be acknowledged as man. It is certain that to trust in another belongs to one who is inferior. But Christ cannot be understood as inferior to the Father except according to his humanity.

units.la: Et iterum: Ecce ego et pueri mei, quos mihi dedit Deus) Tertium testimoniū ex Esaiæ 8. In quo se pueris seu discipulis suis æquat, quos & à Deo patre tanquam superiore fatetur se accepisse.
units.tr: And again: Behold I and the children whom God hath given me. The third testimony is from Isaiah 8. In it he makes himself equal to the children, or his disciples, whom he confesses to have received from God the Father as from his superior.

units.la: Posteaquā igitur pueri cōmertiū habent cū carne et sanguine, et ipse similiter particeps factus est eorundē) Illatio est perficiens ex proximis uerbis enthymema seu syllogismum. Et simili modo ad singula testimonia illatio subijci poterat. Quare hæc testimonia potius quàm alia elegerit, vide suprà.
units.tr: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same. This is an inference completing, from the preceding words, an enthymeme or syllogism. In the same way an inference could be added to each of the individual testimonies. As to why he chose these testimonies rather than others, see above.

units.la: Viper morte aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, &c.) Secunda ratio: quare decuerit Christum hominem fieri, sumpta à modo sanctificandi homines, ut respiciamus hac uoce ad primam rationem, in qua sanctificationis uerbum vsurpauit. Ecтque sententia. Homines, quoniam per peccatum obnoxij erant facti æternæ morti, debebant per mortem alicuius sanctificari seu liberari. Sed mori non potuisset Christus, nisi fieret homo. Ergo ob hanc causam decuit Christum hominem fieri. Sunt inspersæ elegantes rationes, beneficium Christi non parum amplificantes.
units.tr: That through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, etc. The second reason why it was fitting for Christ to become man, drawn from the manner of sanctifying men, so that we may refer this word to the first reason, in which he used the word sanctification. The sense is this: since men, through sin, had become liable to eternal death, they had to be sanctified or freed through the death of someone. But Christ could not have died unless he became man. Therefore for this reason it was fitting for Christ to become man. Elegant reasons are woven in here, which greatly magnify the benefit of Christ.

units.la: Non enim uidelicet angelos assumit, sed semen Abrahæ assumit) Apparet etiam aliam obiectionem adhuc factam ab aduersarijs, in hunc modum. Si omnino oportuit Christum, qui Deus erat, humiliari, quare non potius angelicam naturam assumpsit, quàm humanam? Nec dubium, quin habuerint rationes, quæ videbantur ostendere, quòd potius debuisset angelicam naturam induere, quàm humanam. Proinde Apostolus satisfacere omnibus cupiens, ex ratione præcedenti manifestum fieri vult, cur Christum potius homine fieri oportuerit, quàm angelum. Cùm enim morte debuerit satisfacere, & mortem non potuisset obire, si factus fuisset angelus, hæc, inquit, est causa, cur semen Abrahæ potius apprehenderit, quàm angelos.
units.tr: For verily he took not on him the nature of angels, but he took on him the seed of Abraham. There also appears another objection, raised by the opponents, in this manner: If it was altogether necessary for Christ, who was God, to be humbled, why did he take on the angelic nature rather than the human? Doubtless they had reasons which seemed to show that he ought rather to have put on the angelic nature than the human. Therefore the Apostle, wishing to satisfy everyone, wants it made clear from the preceding reason why it was necessary for Christ to become a man rather than an angel. For since he had to satisfy by death, and could not have undergone death had he become an angel, this, he says, is the reason why he took hold of the seed of Abraham rather than the angels.

units.la: Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis reddi.) Conclusio, qua infert, necessarium fuisse propter duas causas præcedentes, Christum hominem fieri. Inferuntur nonnulla de Christi officio: ut, quòd misericors esse deberet, & fieri pontifex: quæ declarant, cur per omnia similis nobis debuerit effici, & præcedentes causas illustrant.
units.tr: Wherefore it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren. This is the conclusion, by which he infers that, on account of the two preceding causes, it was necessary for Christ to become man. Some things are inferred concerning Christ's office, namely, that he ought to be merciful and become a high priest; these show why he had to be made in all things like us, and they illustrate the preceding causes.

units.la: Hoc pacto repetiuisse totam disputationem puto nequaquam pœnitendum fore, & non mediocriter prodesse ad confirmandum in memoria, ea, quae hactenus à nobis tradita sunt.
units.tr: I think that repeating the whole discussion in this way will by no means be regretted, and that it will not a little help to fix in the memory what has hitherto been delivered by us.

units.la: Quia uero hæc cognitio de duabus naturis in Christo, maximè est necessaria in vniuersa doctrina euangelica, & hic articulus inter primos fidei articulos numeratur: deinde cùm hæc tractatio reuera scrupulosa sit, & facilimè in ea labamur, adeò, ut vel parum apta loquendi formula hæresin pariat: ideò putaui facturum me operæprecium, si nonnulla paulò altius ex patrum scriptis repetita, de formulis loquendi in hac causa usitatis adijcerem, ut tyrones theologi discant, siue quibus animus est disputare in scholis, siue qui ueterum scripta euoluere cupiunt, habeant, quò prudenter de sublimi mysterio duarum in Christo naturarum & ipsi loquantur, & aliorum dicta examinent.
units.tr: But since this knowledge of the two natures in Christ is especially necessary in the whole evangelical doctrine, and this article is counted among the first articles of faith; and since this treatment is really delicate, and we very easily slip in it, so that even a slightly unsuitable form of speech gives rise to heresy, I have thought it would be worthwhile to add some things, taken up a little more deeply from the writings of the Fathers, concerning the forms of speech customarily used in this matter, so that young theologians may learn, whether they intend to dispute in the schools or wish to read through the writings of the ancients, to speak prudently themselves about the sublime mystery of the two natures in Christ, and to examine the sayings of others.

units.la: Proinde analogæ fidei & à sanctis patribus usurpatæ loquendi formæ in hoc argumento sunt hæ. In Christo prout est distincta persona à patre & spiritu sancto, sunt duæ naturæ: Item duæ naturæ in vna persona sunt unitæ: Item Christus assumpsit humanam naturam: & id genus. Vt autem hæ & similes, quo decet, sensu ab omnibus accipiantur, quid hic nomine personæ & naturæ, præterea verbis uniendi & assumendi, sibi uelint, breuiter explicabimus.
units.tr: Therefore the forms of speech in this subject, agreeing with the faith and used by the holy Fathers, are these: In Christ, as the person is distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit, there are two natures; likewise the two natures in one person are united; likewise Christ assumed human nature; and things of that kind. Now we shall briefly explain what these words, and similar ones, mean, namely the words "person" and "nature", and besides them the words "uniting" and "assuming", so that they may be received by all in the sense that is fitting.

units.la: Persona hic sumunt, quomodo alias quoque, cùm de trinitate disputatio est, pro substantia in diuidua, quo modo dicunt, aliam personam esse patris, aliam filij, aliam Spiritus sancti. Vbi non ita distinguuntur personæ ut inter homines, (quandoquidem nullæ appellationes rerum humanarum satis aptæ sunt ad exprimendum res diuinas) Sed quòd pater, filius, spiritus Sanctus discernuntur proprietatibus & officijs, cùm natura ac diuinitate unum sint, ut eleganter Augustinus sermone primo de trinitate. Et Athanasius: Alia est, inquit, persona patris, alia filij, alia spiritus Sancti: sed patris, & filij, & spiritus Sancti una est diuinitas, æqualis gloria, & coæterna maiestas. Et prima Ioannis quinto. Tres sunt, qui testimonium dant in cœlo, Pater, Verbum, & Spiritus sanctus, & hi tres unum sunt.
units.tr: Persona is taken here, as elsewhere too when there is discussion of the Trinity, for an individual substance, in the way they say that one person is the Father, another the Son, another the Holy Spirit. Here the persons are not distinguished as among men (since no names of human things are apt enough to express divine things), but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished by properties and offices, while they are one in nature and divinity, as Augustine elegantly says in his first sermon on the Trinity. And Athanasius: "The person of the Father," he says, "is one, the person of the Son another, the person of the Holy Spirit another; but of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is one divinity, equal glory, and co-eternal majesty." And in the first epistle of John, chapter five: "There are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one."

units.la: Natura autem hoc loco non est principium generationis, vel causa motus & quietis, ut definitur ab Aristotele libro secundo de physico auditu: neque præterea accipitur hic, vt dicunt vnam naturam omnium hominum: sed significat essentiam siue οὐσίαν, specie distinctam ab alia, adeò, ut, cùm dicitur, vni personæ Christi duas inesse naturas, perinde id sit, ac si diceretur, Christum habere duplicem essentiam, alteram ab altera specie distinctam, cuiusmodi reuera sunt diuinitas & humanitas.
units.tr: But nature here is not the principle of generation, or the cause of motion and rest, as Aristotle defines it in the second book of the Physics; nor is it taken here, as some say, for the one nature of all men; but it signifies essence, or ousia [οὐσίαν], specifically distinct from another, so that when it is said that two natures are in the one person of Christ, it is just as if it were said that Christ has a double essence, one specifically distinct from the other, such as in truth are divinity and humanity.

units.la: A voce naturæ non admodum distat substantia: quare & substantia pro natura in hac disputatione subinde vsurpatur.
units.tr: Substance does not differ much from the word nature; therefore substance is also repeatedly used for nature in this discussion.

units.la: Consideratis ergo harum uocum proprijs significationibus, non difficile est, discernere, quomodo de duabus naturis in una persona prudenter loquendum sit. Recte dicetur in una persona cerni duas naturas, siue (quomodo Hieronymus locutus est ponens articulos fidei) duas substantias: & personam assumpsisse naturam.
units.tr: Therefore, once the proper meanings of these words have been considered, it is not difficult to see how one ought to speak prudently about two natures in one person. It will rightly be said that two natures, or (as Jerome spoke when setting out the articles of faith) two substances, are seen in one person, and that the person assumed the nature.

units.la: At uero personam assumpsisse personam (uidelicet hominis) vel naturam assumpsisse naturam, nequaquam dicetur. Nisi fortasis in postrema hac formula nomen naturæ priore loco pro persona ponatur, & non simpliciter pro tota diuina essentia, citra distinctionem alicuius personæ: aut significet quidem diuinam naturam, sed prout in persona Christi assumens dicitur respectu humanæ naturæ, quæ proprie assumpta dicitur: qua de re mox iterum sermo fiet.
units.tr: But that a person assumed a person (namely of a man), or that a nature assumed a nature, will by no means be said. Unless perhaps in this last formula the word nature is put in the first place for person, and not simply for the whole divine essence without distinction of any person; or it signifies indeed the divine nature, but as it is said in the person of Christ to assume, with respect to the human nature, which is properly said to be assumed; on this matter we shall speak again shortly.

units.la: Adhæc pro persona accipiendo vocabulum ὑπόστασις, quemadmodum & Græci dicunt, in diuinitate vnam esse οὐσίαν, tres uero ὑποστάσεις, aptè dicetur, duas naturas spectari in vna ὑποστάσει: si uero sumamus ὑπόστασιν pro substantia seu natura, quo sensu Hebraeorum primo, Christus vocatur χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως patris, & ueteres sic aliquando vsurparunt ὑπόστασιν pro οὐσίᾳ: tùm etiam non male videmur dicturi, in Christo duas esse hypostases, id est, duas substantias seu naturas: si modo pari gratia vocabulum ὑποστάσεως humanæ naturæ accommodari queat, qua accommodatur diuinæ. At dicere, in Christo duas hypostases, id est personas, id plane absurdum est, qua de re Synodus Ephesina definiuit.
units.tr: Moreover, taking the word hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] for person, as the Greeks also say that in the Godhead there is one ousia [οὐσία], but three hypostases [ὑποστάσεις], it will be rightly said that two natures are regarded in one hypostasis. But if we take hypostasis for substance or nature, in which sense the Hebrews, in the first chapter, call Christ the character [χαρακτὴρ] of the hypostasis of the Father, and the ancients sometimes used hypostasis for ousia, then we shall also seem to be rightly saying that in Christ there are two hypostases, that is, two substances or natures, provided that the word hypostasis can be applied to human nature with the same justification with which it is applied to the divine. But to say that in Christ there are two hypostases, that is, persons, is plainly absurd, and this the Council of Ephesus defined.

units.la: Iam quod attinet ad voces vnionis & assumptionis, sunt hæ quoque prudenter distinguendæ. Vnio ostendit collationem vnius naturæ ad alteram, & coniunctionem earum iam in vno aliquo perfectam, nulla habita ratione inæqualitatis. Assumptio uero insinuat actionem quandam, in qua altera pars se habeat uelut superior & assumens, altera velut inferior & in tempore assumpta. Hinc fit, quod recte dicitur in Christo, in persona, in hypostasi Christi vnitas esse duas naturas: item humanam naturam vnitam diuinæ, atqj e diuerso, diuinam vnitam humanæ. Contrà autem in Christo siue à Christo assumptas duas naturas, haud recte dixeris. Diuina quippe natura assumpta non est, quia ab æterno ea Christo adfuit. Item humanam naturam assumptam à persona, siue à natura diuina, satis aptè: diuinam uerò naturam assumptam ab humana, nullo modo.
units.tr: Now, as far as the words "union" and "assumption" are concerned, these too must be carefully distinguished. Union signifies the joining of one nature to another and their conjunction, already complete in some one thing, with no account taken of inequality. Assumption, however, implies a certain action in which one part stands as superior and assuming, and the other as inferior and assumed in time. Hence it is rightly said that in Christ, in the person or hypostasis of Christ, there is a union of two natures; likewise the human nature is united to the divine, and conversely the divine to the human. On the other hand, you would not be right to say that the two natures were assumed in Christ or by Christ. For the divine nature was not assumed, since it has been with Christ from eternity. But that the human nature was assumed by the person, or by the divine nature, is fairly apt; that the divine nature was assumed by the human is in no way true.

units.la: Etenim diuina natura in Christo est velut superior & assumens, humana autem inferior est & assumpta. Vnde etiam constare potest, quo sensu dici queat, quod supra retulimus, naturam à natura assumptam. Nec hoc omittendum, quòd in hoc genere disputationum diuinitas seu diuina natura significat essentiam Dei, & quicquid Dei proprium est: Humanitas verò seu humana natura, totum hominem, quantus est, cum anima & corpore, seu cum anima carne, & omnibus sensibus, (demptis tantum, quæ vitiosa sunt, vel peccato affinia) vt perinde vera diuinitas atque vera humanitas Christo tribuatur.
units.tr: For in Christ the divine nature is, as it were, the superior and assuming one, while the human nature is inferior and assumed. From this it can also be seen in what sense we may speak of one nature being assumed by another, as we mentioned above. Nor should it be left out that in this kind of disputation, divinity or the divine nature signifies the essence of God and whatever belongs to God alone; while humanity or the human nature signifies the whole man, as he is, with soul and body, or with soul, flesh and all the senses (excepting only those that are faulty or akin to sin), so that true divinity and true humanity are equally attributed to Christ.

units.la: Has proinde loquendi formulas ex diuersis congestas autoribus, visum est in gratiam tyronum adnotare, quas & similes, in legendis scriptis patrum & in disputationibus accuratè obseruare debent: propterea, quòd modica immutatione, vel deflexione, aut nouata aliqua phrasi, procliue est in fœdum errorem labi. Apostolus verò vsurpauit uerbum assumendi, dicens: Dixit ex vno esse Christum, ex quo nos.
units.tr: These forms of speech, then, gathered from various authors, I have thought it worth noting for the benefit of beginners. They ought to observe these and similar phrases carefully both in reading the writings of the Fathers and in disputations, because with a slight change, or a twisting, or some novel expression, it is easy to slide into a grave error. The Apostle indeed used the word "assume," saying: "Christ has said to be of one, from whom we are."

units.la: Ex quibus locis patres verbum assumendi & vniendi videntur deprompsisse. Dixit participem esse carnis & sanguinis, vbi carnem & sanguinem pro humanitate dixit. Dixit, Christum debuisse per omnia fratribus similem reddi. Quæ phrases valde sunt in tota hac disputatione annotandæ, & in disputationibus vsurpandæ.
units.tr: From these passages the Fathers seem to have drawn their language of assuming and uniting. He said that he was a partaker of flesh and blood, where he spoke of flesh and blood for humanity. He said that Christ had to be made like his brothers in all things. These phrases are to be carefully noted throughout this whole discussion, and to be used in disputations.

units.la: Iam verò si quis penitius vult scrutari, quomodo facta fit ista vnio duarum naturarum in Christo, sanè istud supra humanum captum situm est. Vnus locus Ioannis Verbum caro factum est, clarissimè exprimit, quicquid de modo vnionis scitu est necessarium. Vbi verbum (id est, filius, diuina natura præditus) dicitur factum caro, siue, vt quidem loqui gaudent, incarnatum, hoc est, suscepisse humanam naturam, quæ carne constat & sanguine. Id autem non ita quidem caro factum, quod conuersum sit in carnem, quasi diuina natura esset mutata (cùm constet eam esse immutabilem) non item quòd diuina natura confusè permixta sit humanæ, & quodammodo in unam coaluerint: sed quod utraque natura retinens suas proprietates, & distinctæ manentes ab inuicem, sunt in una persona (quæ iam tum erat Christus) unitæ, & sibi inuicem coniunctæ. Dicam adhuc crasius. Vna erat persona Christus, seu filius Dei ab æterno, eidem diuina natura adfuit ab æterno: sed in tempore à Deo patre defi- nito, hæc ipsa persona in uterum sacræ virginis se recepit, atque ibi congesta assumpta- que carnis materia, animaque carni indita, hanc totam & integram naturam humanam ita conflatam sibi adiunxit: sic nimirum conseruans suam dignitatem, ut id, quod erat, permanserit, & nihilominus, quod non erat, factus sit.
units.tr: But if anyone wishes to inquire more deeply how this union of the two natures in Christ came about, that certainly lies beyond human understanding. One passage of John, "The Word was made flesh," expresses most clearly whatever it is necessary to know about the manner of the union. Here the Word (that is, the Son, endowed with the divine nature) is said to have been made flesh, or, as they like to put it, to have been incarnate, that is, to have taken up the human nature, which consists of flesh and blood. Yet he was not made flesh in the sense that he was changed into flesh, as though the divine nature had been altered (since it is agreed that it is unchangeable); nor in the sense that the divine nature was confusedly mixed with the human and somehow fused into one. Rather, each nature retains its own properties and, remaining distinct from the other, they are united and joined to one another in one person (who was already then Christ). I will put it more coarsely still. Christ was one person, the Son of God from eternity, to whom the divine nature was present from eternity. But at the time appointed by God the Father, this same person received himself into the womb of the holy virgin, and there, having gathered matter of flesh and infused a soul into the flesh, he joined to himself this whole and entire human nature so formed. Thus, of course, he preserved his dignity, so that what he was he remained, and nevertheless became what he was not.

units.la: Hoc igitur pacto in una persona duæ naturæ vnitæ seu coniunctæ sunt. Et quemadmodum vnum esse hominem dicimus, qui tamen constat anima & corpore, quæ res reuera sunt inter se distinctæ: ita Christus filius Dei vna persona est, habens diuinā naturam & humanam, quæ perinde distinctæ sunt inter se, vt anima & corpus: quandoquidem anima diuinum quiddam refert, corpus humanum quiddam siue terrenum. Quò factum etiam (quemadmodum alias admonuimus, cùm ageremus de communicatione idiomatum) quòd multa in scripturis proposita sunt de Christo, quorum alia de altera tantum natura, alia de utraque coniunctim, ac tota persona Christi decet accipere: ut nimirum diuersitas naturarum, & personæ vnitas ita comprobetur, & ne naturas confundamus, aut vna posita tollamus alteram, aut personas multiplicemus. Quòd si quis adhuc crasius velit sibi explicari vnionis duarum naturarum in Christo modum: fateor me non posse aliud adferre, nisi quod angelus ipse Lucæ primo: Beatæ virgini de eodem negotio admiranti & scisciitanti respondit. Illa enim admirans, quomodo fieret (quia uirtute fieret, non quo modo) quòd conciperet & pareret, quæ nullum cum viro habuerat commercium, audiuit: Spiritus sanctus superueniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Quapropter & quod nascetur sanctum, vocabitur filius Dei.
units.tr: In this way, then, two natures are united or conjoined in one person. And just as we say that a man is one, though he consists of soul and body, which are really distinct from each other, so Christ the Son of God is one person, having the divine nature and the human, which are as distinct from one another as soul and body; for the soul bears something divine, the body something human or earthly. Hence also (as we have noted elsewhere, when we dealt with the communication of properties) many things are set forth in the Scriptures about Christ, some of which must be understood of one nature only, others of both together and of the whole person of Christ. Thus the diversity of the natures and the unity of the person are confirmed, and so that we neither confuse the natures, nor, by positing one, remove the other, nor multiply the persons. But if anyone still wishes the manner of the union of the two natures in Christ to be explained to him more coarsely, I confess I can offer nothing other than what the angel himself said in Luke 1, to the blessed virgin, when she marvelled and asked about this matter. For she, marvelling how it would happen (since it would come about by power, not by what manner), that she should conceive and bear, having had no intercourse with a man, heard: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also that which is to be born will be called holy, the Son of God."

units.la: Ecce spiritus Sanctus in hoc negotio mirabiliter cooperatus est, atque ubi ipse aduenit, ibi nihil difficile, nihil impossibile. Hic facilè potuit præparare corpusculum virginis, ut, quod in aliis mulieribus ad generandum suppeditat auxilium viri, id in utero virginis efficeret virtus altissimi. Ergo spiritu Sancto superueniente, & corpus uirginis. ginis præparante, filius quoque illapsus est, ibique materiam formandi corporis sui simul selegit, simulque animam addidit, sicque hominis completam naturam assumpsit.
units.tr: Behold, the Holy Spirit wonderfully co-operated in this matter, and where he comes, nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. Here he could easily prepare the little body of the virgin, so that what in other women supplies the help of a man for generation, that the power of the Most High should accomplish in the virgin's womb. So, with the Holy Spirit coming upon her and preparing the body of the virgin, the Son also slipped in, and there at the same time chose the matter for forming his own body, and at the same time added a soul, and so assumed the complete nature of man.

units.la: Quò pertinet, quod Augustinus in libro de fide ad Petrum capite decimo octauo ait: Non carnem Christi sine diuinitate conceptam in utero virginis, priusquam suscipere-tur à verbo: sed ipsum verbum Deum suæ carnis acceptione conceptum, ipsamque carnem verbi incarnatione conceptam. Idem libro de Trinitate: Non esset Dei hominum-que mediator, nisi esset idem Deus, idem homo, in utroque unus & verus, quam seruilem formam à solo filio suscepta m, tota trinitas, cuius una est voluntas & operatio, fecit. Non autem in utero virginis prius caro suscepta est, & postmodum diuinitas venit in carnem: neque etiam seorsum assumpta caro, & paulo post anima: sed mox ut verbum venit in vterum, seruata veritate propriæ naturæ, factum est caro & perfectus homo, & in veritate carnis, & animæ natus est. Sed nolumus plura, ne curiosius mysterium hoc, quàm par est, inuestigando, citius eremus, quâ aliquid certius inueniamus.
units.tr: To this belongs what Augustine says in his book On Faith to Peter, chapter eighteen: "The flesh of Christ was not conceived in the womb of the virgin without divinity, before it was taken up by the Word; but the Word itself, God, was conceived by the reception of his flesh, and the flesh itself was conceived by the incarnation of the Word." And in his book On the Trinity: "There would not be a mediator between God and men unless he were the same God and the same man, one and true in both; the whole Trinity, whose will and operation is one, made that servile form which the Son alone assumed." Nor did the flesh first get assumed in the virgin's womb, and afterwards divinity come into the flesh; nor was the flesh assumed separately and a soul a little later; but as soon as the Word came into the womb, the flesh was made, with the truth of its own nature preserved, and a perfect man, born in the truth of flesh and soul. But we do not wish to say more, lest by investigating this mystery more curiously than is fitting we should weary ourselves before we find anything more certain.

units.la: Quanquam hoc ipsum puto profuturum nonnihil, si & errores, qui diuersi diuersis temporibus in ecclesiam irrepserunt, in medium protulero. Nam in obscuris & perplexis quæstionibus, præsertim de natura Dei, & rebus diuinis, tam prodest sciri, quid non sit tenendum, quàm quid tenendum. Ingenij nostri ea imbecillitas est, ut, ubi de rebus diuinis solicitè aliquid inquirit, quia quid sint, non poterit assequi, confugere debet ad videndum, quid non sint. Et semper procliuius est dicere, quid non sint, quàm quid sint. Ergo per ipsos errores etiam in veritatis cognitionem adduci poterimus. Et trita est sententia, Contraria iuxta inuicem posita magis elucescere. Vnde, qui uult scire calamitates belli, videat, quantæ sint vtilitates pacis. Et vt de amaro melius iudices, gusta id quod dulce est. Eodem pacto ut in tantis mysterijs de duabus naturis in Christo pro-pius cognoscamus, quid sit pro certo tenendum, videbimus etiam, quid non sit tenendum. Atque hac de causa hauddubiè passa est prouidentia diuina multos & graues errores in ecclesiam prorepere, vt nimirum paucorum quorundam lapsu quàm plurimi alij in sana doctrina stabilirentur, & ut enatis scrupis ac dubitationibus pij homines tanto magis mouerentur ad veri indagationem. Vnde etiam factum, vt nunquam obortæ sint aliquæ hæreses, quin eodem tempore emerserint simul quàm plurimi doctissimi viri, veritatem explorantes & defensantes.
units.tr: Yet I think that this very thing will profit somewhat if I bring forward the errors which, at different times, crept into the Church in different forms. For in obscure and perplexing questions, especially concerning the nature of God and divine things, it is as useful to know what must not be held as what must be held. Our mind is so weak that, when it anxiously inquires about divine things and cannot grasp what they are, it must take refuge in seeing what they are not. And it is always easier to say what a thing is not than what it is. Thus, even through the errors themselves we may be led to the knowledge of the truth. And the saying is well worn, that contraries set side by side shine out the more. Hence whoever wishes to know the calamities of war, let him see how great the benefits of peace are. And, to judge rightly about the bitter, taste what is sweet. In the same way, that in such great mysteries we may know more closely concerning the two natures in Christ what must be held for certain, we shall also see what must not be held. And for this reason, undoubtedly, divine providence has permitted many grave errors to creep into the Church, so that by the fall of a few the greater number might be established in sound doctrine, and so that, once doubts and scruples have sprung up, godly people might be moved all the more to the search for the truth. Hence it has also come about that no heresies have ever arisen without very many most learned men emerging at the same time, testing and defending the truth.

units.la: Age igitur, licet antea sæpius mentionem fecerimus, quoties oportunum fuerit, diuersorum errorum circa humanitatem ac diuinitatem Christi, tamen ut certius edoceamur de duabus in Christo naturis, deque modo vnionis earum naturarum, errores, ordine recensebimus, ac primum eos, qui de diuina natura Christi oborti sunt: deinde, qui de natura humana: tertiò, qui de modo vnionis earundem, seu de utraque coniunctim.
units.tr: Come now, although we have mentioned the errors about the humanity and divinity of Christ often before, whenever it was fitting, nevertheless, so that we may be more certainly taught about the two natures in Christ and about the mode of their union, we will recount the errors in order: first those that arose concerning the divine nature of Christ, then those concerning the human nature, and third those concerning the mode of their union, or concerning both together.

units.la: Errores de diuinitate Christi.
units.tr: Errors concerning the divinity of Christ.

units.la: Certè valde mirandum est, quòd Christus totiniurijs affectus fuerit à malis hominibus, etiam à sua glorificatione. Sed diabolus nunquam non laborat ad obscurandam Christi gloriam: & Deus permittit diabolum & ministros eius operari, ad exercitationem bonorum, vt excitentur ad inquirendam veritatem: sicut iam diximus.
units.tr: It is indeed very remarkable that Christ was treated with every kind of injury by wicked men, even concerning his glorification. But the devil never ceases to labour to obscure the glory of Christ, and God permits the devil and his ministers to act, for the exercise of good people, so that they may be stirred to seek the truth, as we have already said.

units.la: Proinde ex his, qui diuinitatem Christi impetiuerunt, primus fere fuit Ebion Hebræus & Cerinthus, qui dixerunt, Christum fuisse purum hominem, ac iustum quidé: at Deum esse negarunt. Propter quos creditur, Ioannem euangelistam permotum fuisse ad scribendum euangelicam historiam, in qua luculentissimè asserit Christi diuinitatem, sicut & in hac epistola multis agit Apostolus. Et facilè crediderim, propter eos, qui perillos seducti fuerant, scripta fuisse hanc epistolam, quantum ad primam eius partem attinet.
units.tr: Accordingly, of those who attacked the divinity of Christ, the first were almost Ebion the Hebrew and Cerinthus, who said that Christ was a mere man, indeed a just one, but denied that he was God. On account of them it is believed that the evangelist John was moved to write the evangelical history, in which he most clearly asserts the divinity of Christ, as the Apostle also does in many places in this epistle. And I would readily believe that this epistle was written, as far as its first part is concerned, on account of those who had been seduced by them.

units.la: Nonnulli concesserunt, Christū esse Deū, sed eundem plane, qui alias vocetur pater, alias spiritus Sanctus, qui dum vnitatem voluerunt statuere, concesserunt quoque nominum diuersam appellationem, sed euerterunt distinctionem personarum, aut potius personas confuderunt: id quod fecisse aiunt Sabellium, item Noetium.
units.tr: Some conceded that Christ was God, but said he was plainly the same one who is at one time called the Father and at another the Holy Spirit. In wanting to establish unity, they also conceded a different application of the names, but overthrew the distinction of persons, or rather confused the persons. This, they say, was done by Sabellius, and likewise by Noetus.

units.la: Sed in hac epistola habuimus plura testimonia, quibus hic error confutatur. Vt stamen initio, vbi pater dicitur nobis locutus per filium: item per eundem condidisse secula, & imago substantiæ patris: item illa ex scripturis citata: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: Ego cro illi in patrem, propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo exultationis. Item illa patris uerba ad filium, Sede à dextris meis. Qui loci clarissimè docent filium esse distinctam personam à patre & spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: But in this epistle we have many testimonies by which this error is refuted. Namely, at the beginning, where the Father is said to have spoken to us through the Son, and likewise that through him he made the worlds, and is "the image of his substance"; and likewise those passages cited from the Scriptures: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you"; "I will be to him a Father"; "therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness." Likewise those words of the Father to the Son: "Sit at my right hand." These passages most clearly teach that the Son is a person distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Alij concesserunt esse deū, sed patre inferiore, & minore, & quodammodo seruiente: quèadmodū apud homines filius minor & inferior patre est. In qua opinione fuerunt, Dionysius quidà: deinde Arrius, Eunomius, Aetius, Donatus: quorum diuersis temporibus & locis in hoc
units.tr: Others conceded that he is God, but inferior to the Father, and less, and in some way subordinate, just as among men a son is less than and inferior to his father. Those who held this opinion were a certain Dionysius, then Arius, Eunomius, Aetius and Donatus. In their various times and places they strove for this, namely to say that Christ was not equal to the Father,

units.la: Lib.3. sententiarum distinct. 2. in hoc contenderunt, vt dicerent, Christum non esse parem patri, licet alij alijs rationibus id molirentur astruere. Neque enim vt definirent, quomodo esset inferior patre, ipsi inter se conuenerunt. Sed hos omnes videmus etiam redargui, ex illis primis verbis annexis primae propositioni huius epistolae: vbi ea, quae propria sunt patris, secundum naturam diuinam, omnia ex aequo tribuuntur Christo, nempe creatio, seculorum moderatio, seu gubernatio omnium rerum conditarum, quam etiam Christo tribui ostenditur ex Psalmo centesimoprimo, quo dicitur: Initio tu Domine terram fundasti, &c. Denique confessio ad dextram patris, quae confessio (cum etiam ex Psalmo 109 Christo tribuatur) palam facit, Christum patri per omnia parem & aequalem.
