units.tr: (Lib. 3 Sententiarum, dist. 2), although they tried to establish it by different arguments. For they did not agree among themselves on how he is inferior to the Father. But we see all of these also refuted by those first words attached to the first proposition of this epistle, where the things that belong to the Father according to the divine nature are all equally attributed to Christ: namely creation, the governance of the ages, or the ruling of all created things, which is also shown to be attributed to Christ from Psalm 101, where it is said: "In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth," etc. Finally, the confession of his seating at the right hand of the Father, which confession (since it is also attributed to Christ in Psalm 109) plainly shows that Christ is in all things equal to the Father.

units.la: Alij concesserunt item, Christum fuisse Deum, sed tum primum, cum homo in mundo natus est, ac tum quidem nascendo suscepisse beneficio Dei patris, diuinam naturam, sicut ex matre accepit naturam humanam. Qua in opinione fuerunt, Arthemon, Berillus, & Marcellius, & nostra tempestate non multum ab his diuersum sensisse videtur Seruetus, contendens, λόγον non prius fuisse distinctam a patre personam, quam humanam naturam induceret. Atque alij quidam concesserunt quidem Christum semper fuisse, sed non semper filium, quod nomen acceperit primum, cum in mundo natus est. Sed videant, Christum dici filium, per eundem condita secula, terrae fundamenta iacta, esse χαρακτῆρα patris substantiae & intelligere ex his poterunt, filium etiam, antequam mundus conderetur, esse Deum, ac deinde personam a patre distinctam.
units.tr: Others likewise conceded that Christ was God, but only from the time when he was born as a man in the world, and that then, at his birth, he received the divine nature by the benefit of God the Father, just as he received human nature from his mother. Those who held this opinion were Artemon, Beryllus and Marcellus; and in our own time Servetus seems to have thought not much differently from these, contending that the Logos [λόγον] was not a distinct person from the Father before he took on human nature. Certain others conceded that Christ always existed, but was not always the Son, a name he first received when he was born in the world. But let them consider that Christ is called the Son through whom the worlds were made and the foundations of the earth laid, and that he is the express image [χαρακτῆρα] of the Father's substance. From these things they will be able to understand that the Son, even before the world was made, was God, and then a person distinct from the Father.

units.la: Postremo, fuerunt iterum, qui omnem honorem diuinum Christo volentes detrahere, dixerunt Christum creaturam, vt nonnulli Origeniani, a quo tamen Origene incertum. Samosatensis etiam dixit, Christum ex Maria sumpsisse initio. Bonosiani, Christum filium Dei, sed adoptiuum, vt nos sumus. Alij, vt Photiniani, simpliciter purum hominem, & ex vtroq; sexu natum: sed anima (quod addiderunt Carpocratiani) praeditum fuisse admodum excellenti, qua res supernas & diuinas intelligeret. Hos quoque hic superatos habemus, quando Christus describitur filius patris ab aeterno, & conditor coeli ac terrae, ac proinde creator, non creatura. Ex vtroque vero parente non esse natum, aliunde petendum est, quomodo confutetur maxime ex illo Lucae primo. Quomodo fiet istud, quoniam virum non cognosco? & Angelus, Spiritus Sanctus superuenient in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Quapropter & quod nascetur sanctum, vocabitur filius Dei, &c. Alibi plura suppetunt argumenta hoc ipsum comprobantia.
units.tr: Finally, there were again those who, wishing to take away all divine honour from Christ, said that Christ was a creature, as some Origenists did, though it is uncertain whether they really were followers of Origen. Samosatenus also said that Christ took his beginning from Mary. The Bonosians said that Christ was the Son of God, but adoptive, as we are. Others, like the Photinians, said simply that he was a mere man, born of both sexes; but, as the Carpocratians added, endowed with a most excellent soul by which he understood heavenly and divine things. We also have these refuted here, since Christ is described as the Son of the Father from eternity, and the founder of heaven and earth, and therefore creator, not creature. That he was not born of both parents must be sought elsewhere, and it is best refuted from the first chapter of Luke: "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" And the angel: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also that which shall be born holy will be called the Son of God," etc. Elsewhere many arguments confirm this same point.

units.la: Errores de humanitate Christi. Ad errores de humanitate adiungi inprimis potest & illę, quę proxime recensuimus de diuinitate, nempe Photinianorum, asserentiu Christum factu hominem, sed ex vtriusq; sexus cooperatione: quod etiam asseruit Ebion. Sed praecedenti loco confutatus est hic error ex Lucae 1.
units.tr: Errors concerning the humanity of Christ. To the errors concerning the humanity can especially be added those we have just recounted concerning the divinity, namely those of the Photinians, who asserted that Christ was made man, but by the cooperation of both sexes; Ebion also asserted this. But this error was refuted in the preceding passage, from Luke 1.

units.la: Simoniani quidam, a Simone mago, negarunt Christum venisse in mundum, vt filium Dei, & a Iudaeis quicquam pertulisse: Sed asserebant, Simone temporibus Tiberij Caesaris in persona filij putatiue venisse. Sed crassior est hic error, quam vt confutatus videatur. Etta-mehabemus clarissime in exordio huius epistolae, Deum nobis locutum per filium. Deinde capite secundo, eundem cruciatus mortis pertulisse, & pro omnibus gustasse mortem, & ad expianda peccata, peragendaq; ea: quae inter Deu & homines erant facienda, factum hominem.
units.tr: Certain Simonians, followers of Simon Magus, denied that Christ came into the world as the Son of God, and that he suffered anything from the Jews. They asserted instead that in the time of Tiberius Caesar Simon had come in the person of a son, in appearance only. But this error is too crude to seem worth refuting. Yet we have it very clearly refuted at the opening of this epistle, where God is said to have spoken to us through the Son; then in the second chapter, where he is said to have suffered the pains of death, to have tasted death for all, and to have been made man to expiate sins and to accomplish those things that had to be done between God and men.

units.la: Fuerunt Archontici quidam ausi dicere, Christum non esse natum ex foemina: neq; habuisse carnem, neq; vere mortuum fuisse, vel quicquam passum: sed omnia in illo tatum apparentia fuisse, & mortem simulatam. Sed quando hic clare dicitur, Christum & nos ex vno primo parente esse omnes, eundem participem esse carnis & sanguinis, semen Abrahae apprehendisse, per omnia fratribus factum similem: deinde, cruciatus mortis sensisse, gustasse mortem pro omnibus, per mortem aboleuisse eum, qui mortis habebat imperium: quiuis intelligit tanti erroris foeditatem. Eisdem rationibus conuincitur Manichaei, item Marcion, qui dixerunt, Christum habuisse duntaxat phantasticum corpus: cui sane aduersatur corpus Christi constans carne & sanguine.
units.tr: Some Archontics dared to say that Christ was not born of a woman, nor had flesh, nor truly died, nor suffered anything, but that everything in him was merely apparent and his death was feigned. But since it is clearly said here that Christ and we are all from one first parent, that he is a partaker of flesh and blood, took hold of the seed of Abraham, and was made like his brothers in all things; then that he felt the pains of death, tasted death for all, and through death destroyed him who had the power of death, anyone can understand the foulness of so great an error. The Manichaeans are refuted by the same arguments, and likewise Marcion, who said that Christ had only a phantasmal body; to which the body of Christ, consisting of flesh and blood, is clearly opposed.

units.la: Valentinus vero, & cum eo quidam nostri temporis, verum corpus non negauit, sed negauit assumptum ex carne virginis, atque allatum corpus dixit e coelo. Quem errorem confutauimus, plenius exponentes illud, vbi dicebatur, Christum assumpsisse semen Abrahae.
units.tr: Valentinus, however, and with him certain men of our own time, did not deny a true body, but denied that it was taken from the flesh of the virgin, and said that the body was brought from heaven. We have refuted this error, explaining more fully the passage where it is said that Christ took on the seed of Abraham.

units.la: Apollinarius idem dixit, referente Nazianzeno in epistola ad Nectarium episcopum Constantinopolitanum.
units.tr: Apollinaris said the same, as reported by Gregory Nazianzen in his letter to Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople.

units.la: Ab hoc autē differentiens Apelles, non attulisse Christum suam carnē è cœlo, neq; item à Maria accepisse: sed conflasse sibi corpus ex quatuor elementis mundi, in quam materiam rursus illud corpus sità morte ipsius resolutum. Refutatur, qua ratione præcedens error confutatus est: & præterea, quòd palàm visus sit corpus contrectabili, palpabili, in cœlum ascendens. Arrius corpus assumptum à Christo concedebat, sed non animam, cuius loco ipsam ait fuisse diuinitatem: cui aduersatur, quòd hic dicitur in epistola, Christum per omnia similem fratribus debuisse fieri, vt misericors esset, atq; alias etiam affectiones animæ humanæ in se sentiret.
units.tr: Apelles, differing from him, said that Christ brought his flesh neither from heaven nor likewise from Mary, but fashioned a body for himself from the four elements of the world, into which material that body was again resolved by his death. This is refuted by the same argument by which the preceding error was refuted, and moreover because he was seen to have a body that could be touched and handled, ascending into heaven. Arius conceded that Christ assumed a body, but not a soul; in its place he said the divinity itself was present. This is opposed by the statement in the epistle that Christ had to be made like his brothers in all things, so that he might be merciful and also feel the other affections of the human soul in himself.

units.la: Apollinaris animā concessit, sed sensitiuam tantùm, non intellectiuam, cuius vicem gereret ipsa diuinitas. Refutatur eodem is argumento, quo Arrius.
units.tr: Apollinaris conceded a soul, but only a sensitive soul, not a rational one, and in its place he set the divinity itself. He is refuted by the same argument as Arius.

units.la: Erant & Basilidiani, qui negarent, Christum passum, quomodo & patripassiani, ficap-pellati, quòd patrem tantùm passum asserarent, non autem filium: quasi verò non hæc fuerit principalis causa, cur oportuerit Christum hominē fieri, nimirùm, vt per mortem suam semel liberaret nos à morte æterna. Plura vide contra hos Psal. 22. Matth. 17. Ioan. 5. Hebr. 2, & alibi passim.
units.tr: There were also the Basilidians, who denied that Christ suffered. The patripassians, so called, were similar: they asserted that the Father alone suffered and not the Son. But surely this was the main reason why Christ had to become man, namely, that by his death he might once for all deliver us from eternal death. For more on these men see Ps. 22; Matt. 17; John 5; Heb. 2, and passim elsewhere.

units.la: In summa, producatur quæcunq; hæreses contra diuinitatē vel humanitatem Christi, & certè licet affirmare, omnes ex hac disputatione præsentis epistolæ posse clarissimè confutari.
units.tr: In short, let whatever heresies there are against the divinity or the humanity of Christ be brought forward. Certainly it may be affirmed that all of them can be most clearly refuted from the argument of this epistle.

units.la: Errores de duabus naturis coniunctim. Sed restat adhuc quidam errores exponendi circa duas naturas in Christo, & modum vnionis earundem.
units.tr: Errors concerning the two natures taken together. But there remain some errors to be set forth concerning the two natures in Christ and the manner of their union.

units.la: Plures sanè negarunt duas naturas in Christo. Nam Acephali quidam, præterea, Gionitæ, item Theodosiani, vnam solam naturā tribuerunt Christo. Eutyches certè solam naturam diuinā concessit. Qui purū tantùm hominē dixerunt, sōlam humanā eidem dixerunt. Sed hi simul omnes conuincuntur hac disputatione, in qua duplex natura Christo asseritur, diuina, in quam, & humana.
units.tr: Indeed several have denied that there are two natures in Christ. For certain Acephali, also the Gionites, and likewise the Theodosians, ascribed only one nature to Christ. Eutyches certainly conceded only the divine nature. Those who said he was merely a man ascribed to him only the human nature. But all of these are refuted together by this discussion, in which a twofold nature is asserted for Christ, the divine and the human.

units.la: Sed & circa modum vnionis duarum naturam quidam fœdissimè lapsi sunt.
units.tr: But some have also fallen most foully concerning the manner of union of the two natures.

units.la: Quidam senserunt, verbum ita factum carnē, siue ita vnitas esse duas naturas, quasi aliquid ipsius verbi, seu diuinæ naturæ esset in carnem conuersum, veluti cùm farina fitpanis: id quod Eutychen fecisse aiunt.
units.tr: Some have thought that the Word was so made flesh, or that the union was such, that something of the Word itself, or of the divine nature, was turned into flesh, as when flour becomes bread. They say Eutyches did this.

units.la: Quidam, vt Timotheus, à quo Timotheani, præterea Apollinaris, commixtas esse putarunt naturas in vnum, sicut vinū aqua commixtum dicitur: quasi vna natura peralterā esset corrupta, ac de sua proprietate aliquid amisisset. Sed quæ à nobis expositæ sunt, de vtraq; natura integra, & distincta in Christo: quomodo videlicet Christus vtramq; naturam integram in se habuerit, atq; ita, vt per humanam nihil detractum sit diuinæ: & diuina rursus non obstiterit, quò minus omnia in Christo fuerint pertinetia ad humanam naturā (dempto peccato) facilè est errore illum refutare, maximè colligendo seorsim testimonia, quæ & veram humanitatem Christo tribuunt, & rursus veram diuinitatem: qualia testimonia nos iam sæpè repetiuimus.
units.tr: Others, like Timotheus, from whom the Timotheans take their name, and also Apollinaris, thought the natures were mixed into one, as wine is said to be mixed with water, as if one nature were corrupted by the other and had lost something of its own property. But what we have set forth concerning each nature being whole and distinct in Christ (namely, how Christ had both natures whole in himself, so that nothing of the divine was taken away by the human, and the divine in turn did not prevent everything in Christ from pertaining to the human nature, sin excepted) can easily refute that error, especially by gathering together separately the testimonies which ascribe to Christ both a true humanity and again a true divinity. We have already repeated such testimonies often.

units.la: Arrius quidem, atque etiam Eunomius, concessit, Verbum assumpsisse carnem pro integritate humanæ, sed sine anima cuius loco fuerit diuinitas, vti semel meminimus. Verum, quomodo is concedet, Christum verum esse hominem factum, qui animam illi adimit, solamq; tribuit carnem, cùm verus homo & humanitas, seu humana natura sola cat ne constare non posset?
units.tr: Arius indeed, and Eunomius too, conceded that the Word took on flesh for the completeness of humanity, but without a soul, in whose place there was the divinity, as we mentioned once before. But how would he concede that Christ was made a true man, when he takes away his soul and gives him only flesh? For a true man and humanity, or a human nature, could not consist of flesh alone.

units.la: Apollinaris verò, præter carnē etiam animam assumptam concessit, sed absq; ratione, absq; sensu, loco quorum esset diuinitas.
units.tr: Apollinaris, however, conceded that a soul as well as flesh was assumed, but without reason, without sense, and in place of these there was the divinity.

units.la: Nestorius verò quando voluit accuratè distinguere naturas, in eum incidit errorem, vt in Christo constituerit duas personas, & duos filios, atque alium filium virginis, alium filium Dei. Neque enim virginem dicendam esse matrem. Quod si esset, reuera non recte diceretur, Verbum caro factum, siue filium Dei factum esse participem carnis & sanguinis.
units.tr: When Nestorius wished to distinguish the natures precisely, he fell into the error of positing two persons in Christ and two sons, one the son of the virgin and another the Son of God. For he denied that the virgin should be called mother. But if that were so, it would not be rightly said that the Word was made flesh, or that the Son of God became a partaker of flesh and blood.

units.la: Quæ formulæ locutionum clarissimè sonant, in vna persona duas naturas, non autem distinctas personas considerandas. Impossibile est diuersitatem personarum in aliquo vno comprehendi. Item impossibile est, quòd duorum singularium, quorum diuersa sunt suppositā seu indiuidua, vnum prædicetur de alio. Vnde, si alia sit persona verbi, & rursus, alia persona carnis, non recte dixerit euangelista, verbum esse factum carnem.
units.tr: These forms of expression sound most clearly that in one person there are two natures to be considered, and not distinct persons. It is impossible for a diversity of persons to be contained in one thing. Likewise it is impossible that one of two individual things, which have different supposits or individual natures, should be predicated of the other. Hence, if the person of the Word were one and the person of the flesh another, the evangelist would not rightly have said that the Word was made flesh.

units.la: Ex his iam declaratis, promptum est vnicuique videre, quid de duabus naturis in Christo sentiendum sit, & quæ opiniones vitandæ. Proinde certam confessionem de vtraque natura in Christo, adeoque de tota Christi dignitate, lubet promi exhis,quæ iam exposuimus, partim ex disputationis apostolicæ verbis colligere, ac subnectere.
units.tr: From what has now been set out, it is easy for anyone to see what is to be thought concerning the two natures in Christ, and which opinions are to be avoided. Therefore we wish to set forth, from what we have now expounded and partly by gathering and adding the words of the apostolic discourse, a definite confession concerning each nature in Christ, and so concerning the whole dignity of Christ.

units.la: Credimus ergo,& confitemur,Iesum Christum,per quem euangeliū & voluntas Dei patris non uisimis temporibus mundo est manifestata, verum esse eiusdem Dei patris filium, distinctam personam ab eodem patre & spiritu Sancto, plenam habentem in omnia potestate, sicut habet pater, & sicut hæredes accipiunt plenū ius & potestate bonorū à parentibus. Adhæc non esse creaturam, aut in tempore cœpisse Deum fieri: sed ab æterno, vnà cum ipso patre simul diuinitate præditum: nec patre prius tépore extitisse, aut prius fuisse Deum, quàm hunc filiū: imò per eundē iuxta atq; per patrem, etiā secula, antequá mundus, vel quicquá in mundo existeret, cōdita esse & creata: Ac proinde patre nulla in parte inferiorem aut minorem, (tātum abest, vt angelis aliquo modo inferior existimetur:) sed per omnia æqualem: & sicut in lumine lumen, ita in hoc filio cerni omnem splendorem, dignitatem & claritudinem ipsius patris: nec non totam substātiam & naturam patris plenissimè euidentissimeq; in eo expressam, ita, vt quicquid, quantum ad naturam diuinitatis attinet, de patre, idé & de filio recté dici queat. Sicut enim æternus, increatus, immensus, incommutabilis, Deus, Dominus, creator, & conseruator, seu moderator omnium est pater: ita æternus, increatus, immensus, incommutabilis, Deus, Dominus & creator & cōseruator, seu moderator omniū, est filius, potenti suo verbo ac nutu diuino, etiam nunc omnibus dans esse, omnia moderās & gubernans. Deniq;, quò plenius intelligatur vniuersa Christi, par cū patre dignitas, quodq; nulla in parte patre sit factus, vel futurus vnquā inferior, ipse etiam, post humiliatione suā in terris factam, ad summū gloriæ locum exaltatus est, atque ad dexteram Dei patris, par & æqualis agnoscendus, ab ipso patre est constitutus, vt ab angelis & hominibus pro vero Deo agnoscatur & colatur: nec non cum eadem maiestate ad iudicium viuorum & mortuorum venturus, vbi visum erit, expectetur, atque alijs vitam æternam ex gratia conferat, alios pro meritis suis in ignem æternum præcipitandos iubeat. Atque hanc æqualitatem filij cum patre, summamq́ue filij dignitatem, ab initio manifeste patribus & prophetis à Deo expositam: deinde per hos in Scripturis expressam, vt à primis vsque temporibus ad nostra vsq; extaret, semper omnipotentiæ & diuinitatis eius cognitio, vt salutem ex eo, & per eum omnes expectarent. Vnde diuersa passim inspersa cernuntur sacris literis testimonia, in quibus omnia, quæ de diuinitate Christi hic cōsitemur & prædicamus, clarissimè tradita sunt: qualia non nulla ab Apostolo nobis hoc loco sunt commedata. Quibus qui credere nolunt, aut qui doctrinam euangelicam per ipsum manifestatam nolunt recipere, iram Dei effugere non posse, certum est.
units.tr: We therefore believe and confess that Jesus Christ, through whom the gospel and the will of God the Father has been made manifest to the world in these last times, is the true Son of the same God the Father, a person distinct from the same Father and the Holy Spirit, having full power in all things, just as the Father has, and just as heirs receive from their parents full right and power over the goods. Moreover, he is not a creature, nor did God begin to be in time; rather, he was endowed with divinity from eternity together with the Father himself. Nor did the Father exist before him in time, nor was the Father God before this Son was: indeed, through him as well as through the Father, even the ages, before the world or anything in the world existed, were founded and created. Accordingly, he is in no part inferior or less than the Father (so far is he from being thought in any way inferior to the angels), but equal in all things. And just as light is seen in light, so in this Son is seen all the splendour, dignity and brightness of the Father himself, and the whole substance and nature of the Father is expressed in him most fully and most evidently, so that whatever can rightly be said of the Father as regards the nature of the divinity can also be said of the Son. For just as the Father is the eternal, uncreated, immeasurable, unchangeable God, Lord, creator, preserver, or governor of all, so the Son is the eternal, uncreated, immeasurable, unchangeable God, Lord, creator, preserver, or governor of all, giving being to all things even now by his powerful word and divine nod, governing and directing all. Finally, so that the whole equal dignity of Christ with the Father may be understood more fully, and that he was made, or will ever be, in no part inferior to the Father, he himself, after his humiliation on earth, was exalted to the highest place of glory, and was appointed by the Father himself to be acknowledged at the right hand of God as equal and like, so that he may be acknowledged and worshipped as true God by angels and men. And he will come with the same majesty to judge the living and the dead, and he is to be awaited when it seems good; he will bestow eternal life by grace on some, and will command others to be cast into eternal fire according to their deserts. Moreover, this equality of the Son with the Father and the highest dignity of the Son were clearly set forth by God from the beginning to the fathers and prophets, and then were expressed through these in the Scriptures, so that from the earliest times down to our own the knowledge of his omnipotence and divinity has always stood, that all might expect salvation from him and through him. Hence diverse testimonies are seen scattered everywhere in the sacred letters, in which all the things we here confess and proclaim concerning the divinity of Christ are most clearly delivered; some of these the Apostle has commended to us in this passage. It is certain that those who are unwilling to believe these things, or who are unwilling to receive the gospel doctrine made manifest through him, cannot escape the wrath of God.

units.la: Sed credimus & confitemur insuper, eundem Iesum Christum ab æterno Deum, non aliam personam in plenitudine temporis, quod pater ab æterno præsinierat, in mundū esse missum, & humanam naturam assumpsisse, vt perferendo cruciatus mortis omnes, nos à morte seu damnatione æterna liberaret.
units.tr: But we also believe and confess, moreover, that this same Jesus Christ, God from eternity, was sent into the world, not as another person, in the fullness of time, which the Father had foreordained from eternity, and assumed human nature, so that by enduring the torments of death he might deliver all of us from death or eternal damnation.

units.la: Contraxisse autem eum humanam naturam, cum omnibus, quæ ei agnatæ sunt, & perpetuò cohærentes, miserijs, (demptò peccato & vitiosis affectibus, siue malis ex peccato prouenientibus) vt reuera ipse sanctificans omnes, ex eodem primo parente, ex quo nos, suam ducere originem, manifeste visus sit. Vnde perfectè in se habens nostram naturam, nos pro fratribus agnoscere, nos in suos pueros recipere, non est dedignatus: præsertim carne & sanguine, vt nos eadem materia, iisdem partibus, quibus nos, constans, denique per omnia nostrae naturae particeps factus. Neque enim phantasticum corpus habuit, sed verum, visibile, contrectabile, palpabile, doloribus & cruciatibus obnoxium. Neque illud allatum è cœlo, vel formatum ex elementis, sed sumptum ex semine Abrahæ, id est, ex corpore & carne sanctissimæ Virginis, quæ ab Abraham & Dauid, cæterisq́ue sanctis patribus suam traxit originem.
units.tr: Now he took upon himself human nature with all the miseries that belong to it and cling to it perpetually (sin and sinful affections, or evils arising from sin, excepted), so that he was truly seen to sanctify all, drawing his origin from the same first parent from whom we draw ours. Hence, having our nature perfectly in himself, he did not disdain to acknowledge us as brothers and to receive us as his children, especially since he was made a partaker of our nature in all things, consisting of the same matter, flesh and blood, and in the same parts as we do. For he did not have a phantom body, but a true, visible body, which could be touched and handled, and was liable to pains and torments. Nor was it brought down from heaven or formed from the elements, but taken from the seed of Abraham, that is, from the body and flesh of the most holy Virgin, who drew her origin from Abraham and David and the other holy fathers.

units.la: Neque etiam solam carnem assumpsit, neglecta anima, eius loco habens solam diuinitatem: prius carne, quàm animā: neq; etiam solam animā sensitiuam: sed præterea intellectiuam, & quicquid ad perficiendum hominem pertinet, ipse ad se recepit, vt perfectus homo, nobis fratribus suis per omnia similis, ad perficiendam hominum salutem idoneus inueniretur.
units.tr: Nor did he assume only flesh, neglecting the soul and putting the Godhead in its place, so that flesh came before soul. Nor did he take only the sensitive soul, but he also took the intellectual soul, and he received into himself whatever pertains to completing a man, so that he might be found a perfect man, in all things like us his brothers, and fit to accomplish the salvation of men.

units.la: Atque ita, quando Christus erat is constitutus, per quem deberent perfici, quæcunque pro hominum salute apud Deum forent agenda, duas naturas in eo confitemur, diuinam, quam habuit ab æterno: humanam, quam assumpsit in tempore: nequaquam tamen duas personas, aut duos filios, quasi alter Dei esset, alter hominis, constituentes. Vnus enim Christus, vna persona, & est, & fuit, & semper manet, licet secundum veritatem vnius naturæ natus sit ex Deo, Dei filius; itidem secundum alterius naturæ veritatem natus ex homine, (non tamen per hominem) hominis filius: sed ita duas naturas in vna persona vnitas, vt integra vnaquęq; permaneat, neq;, cùm vniretur, diuina conuersa sit in humanā, neq; eæ inuicē inordinatè cōfusę sint aut permixtæ. Atq; ita in summa, vnus idēq; verus Deus, verus item homo Christus Iesus, mediator Dei & hominū cōstitutus est, sua morte, quæ in cæteris hominibus peccati poena est, pro peccatis omnium hominum satisfaciens, ob quod in terras missus est, & à prophetis omnia facturus prænunciatus.
units.tr: And so, since Christ was the one appointed through whom all things to be done before God for the salvation of men should be accomplished, we confess two natures in him: the divine, which he had from eternity, and the human, which he assumed in time. Yet we by no means posit two persons or two sons, as if one were God's son and another man's. For one Christ, one person, both is, and was, and always remains. According to the truth of one nature he was born of God, the Son of God; and likewise, according to the truth of the other nature, he was born of a man (yet not through a man), the Son of man. The two natures are so united in one person that each remains whole. When they were united, the divine was not changed into the human, nor are they confusedly or disorderly mingled or mixed together. And so, in sum, one and the same true God, and likewise true man, Christ Jesus, has been constituted mediator between God and men, satisfying for the sins of all men by his death, which in other men is the penalty of sin. For this he was sent into the world, and was foretold by the prophets as one who would do all things.

units.la: Hæc est nostra de duabus naturis in Christo, ac modo vnionis earundem, confessio, quam orthodoxam, & analogiæ fidei consentientem ducimus.
units.tr: This is our confession concerning the two natures in Christ and the manner of their union, which we hold to be orthodox and in agreement with the analogy of faith.

units.la: Restat, vt quanta sit totius huius disputationis de vtraque natura in Christo, cùm publicè in ecclesia, tum priuatim ecclesijs, vtilitas, expendamus. Proinde huius disputationis ab Apostolo habitæ, hæc est maxima in ecclesia vtilitas, quòd, nisi ea in ecclesia cognosceretur, planè fides in vniuersum subuerteretur. Hæc enim disputatio totius euangelij fundamentū est, cui omnia, quæ de Christo nouimus & credimus, innituntur. Si enim Christus non est Deus, inanis est fides nostra, frustrà iustificationem & salutem ab eo expectamus: deniq; nihil efficax, nihil ratum abillo factum est, falsæ et omnis doctrina, quā traditur, propter eum, & per eum nos adductos ad vitā æternam. Rursus, si hominem esse non intelligimus, pro vanis narrationibus & fabulis omnia, quæ in euangelio de natiuitate eius, doctrina, miraculis, morte, resurrectione, in cœlos ascensione, proponuntur, haberi possunt. Quia ergo salutem nostram per Christum peractā non potest intelligi, & falsa videtur vniuersa doctrina euangelica, nisi hæc cognitio de vtraq; natura teneatur, nemo non intelligit, hanc disputationem Pauli maximum fructum ecclesiæ allaturam. Huc pertinet, quòd in confessione fidei & Symbolo omnes ita loquuntur, & ecclesia semper ita confitetur: Credo in Iesum Christum filium Dei naturā unicum, Dominum nostrum, qui conceptus est de spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria virgine.
units.tr: It remains for us to weigh how great is the usefulness of this whole disputation concerning both natures in Christ, both publicly in the Church and privately in the congregations. Accordingly, of this disputation held by the Apostle, this is the greatest usefulness in the Church: unless it were known in the Church, faith in general would be utterly overthrown. For this disputation is the foundation of the whole gospel, on which all that we know and believe about Christ rests. If Christ is not God, our faith is empty and we expect justification and salvation from him in vain. In short, nothing efficacious and nothing valid has been done by him, and all the doctrine taught because of him and through him, leading us to eternal life, is false. Again, if we do not understand that he is man, all the things set forth in the gospel about his nativity, teaching, miracles, death, resurrection and ascension into heaven may be regarded as empty stories and fables. Since, therefore, our salvation accomplished through Christ cannot be understood, and the whole evangelical doctrine seems false, unless this knowledge of both natures is held, everyone understands that this disputation of Paul will bring the greatest fruit to the Church. To this pertains the fact that in the confession of faith and in the Creed everyone speaks thus, and the Church has always so confessed: I believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, his only begotten by nature, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.

units.la: Secundò, prodest toti ecclesiæ hæc disputatio, quòd sine ea Scripturæ veteris instrumenti, quæ vtramque naturam aperte Christo tribuunt: item promissiones de Christo factæ ad patres, de nascituro ex semine eorum, per quem benedicerentur omnes gentes præterea vaticinia de ijs, quæ per Christum in terris forent peragenda: hæc, inquam, non possent intelligi, neq; fuissent adimpleta, Christus naturam humanam in tempore à Deo patre præfinito, non suscepisset. Tertiò, hanc ecclesia ex præsenti disputatione vtilitatem consequitur, quòd certa de vtraq; natura in Christo habeatur sententia, quomodo videlicet in Christo integra fuerit natura diuina, & secundum eam patri per omnia æqualis: rursus, quomodo in eodem etiam integra fuerit natura humana, quemadmodum in nobis, exceptâ naturali illa nostra corruptione, quæ nobis agnata est, in ipso verò locum non habuit: Item quomodo hæ duæ naturæ fuerint vnitæ in vna persona. Item, quare decuerit à Christo humanam naturam assumi, cùm tamen per solam diuinam potuisset humanum genus saluum facere. Quas res qui non potuerunt assequi, vtiā hac disputatione sunt expositæ & probatæ, hi à fide sana turpiter aberrarunt, & in monstrosas de Christo opiniones sunt prolapsi.
units.tr: Secondly, this disputation benefits the whole Church. Without it, those passages of the Old Testament which clearly attribute both natures to Christ could not be understood, nor could the promises made to the fathers about one to be born of their seed, through whom all nations would be blessed, nor the prophecies about what was to be accomplished through Christ on earth. These things, I say, could not be understood, nor would they have been fulfilled, if Christ had not taken on human nature in time, as appointed by God the Father. Thirdly, the Church gains this usefulness from the present disputation: there is a firm opinion concerning both natures in Christ. Namely, how in Christ the divine nature was whole and, according to it, equal to the Father in all things; again, how in the same one the human nature also was whole, as in us, except that natural corruption which is innate in us, which had no place in him; likewise how these two natures were united in one person. Likewise, why it was fitting for Christ to assume human nature, when yet the human race could have been saved by the divine nature alone. Those who have not been able to grasp these matters, which have now been set out and proved in this disputation, have shamefully strayed from sound faith and fallen into monstrous opinions about Christ.

units.la: Quamobrē & hæc utilitas quarto loco capietur ex disputatione habita, quòd aduersus venena hæreticorum, qui impiè de duabus naturis in Christo senserunt, quales fuisse plurimos supra ostendimus, remedia & quasi pharmaca hinc colligetur: siquidem hic omne genus argumentorum congestum est, ad errores omnes refutandos.
units.tr: Wherefore this usefulness will also be drawn, in the fourth place, from the disputation held: against the poisons of heretics who have impiously thought concerning the two natures in Christ (as we showed above, there were very many of them), remedies and, as it were, medicines will be gathered from here. For here every kind of argument has been brought together to refute all errors.

units.la: Priuatim verò prodest vnicuiq; hæc disputatio in cōscientijs: primùm, quòd certa & solida habebunt de tota hac re, quę caput est euangelij, & fundamentū fidei, cognitione. Nec parui faciēda est hæc cognitio, sine qua cætera, quæ ad salutē sunt necessaria, cognosci nequeunt: & cuius inscitia permulti in graues & fœdos errores sunt prolapsi. Philosophiæ Christianæ magnam se tenere portionem sciat, qui huius disputationis summam tenuerit.
units.tr: This disputation is also useful to each person privately, in conscience. First, because they will have certain and solid knowledge of this whole matter, which is the head of the gospel and the foundation of faith. This knowledge is not to be valued lightly, for without it the other things necessary for salvation cannot be known, and through ignorance of it very many have fallen into grave and foul errors. Let him know that he holds a great portion of Christian philosophy who has grasped the sum of this disputation.

units.la: Deinde, in huius mysterij contemplatione piæ conscientię, si se subinde exerceant, mirabilem consolationem accipient, & contra omnia pericula in fide confirmabuntur. Primùm enim aduertent, Christum propter salutem ipsorum factum esse hominem, sibi factum & datum paruulum, & humiliatum, vt ipsi dij fiant, & magni, & ad summam gloriam exaltentur. Gaudium magnum in conscientijs concipient cum pastoribus, (de quibus Lucæ capite secundo) quia natus est ipsis saluator mundi, quia datus est, in quo benedicuntur omnes gentes: quia prodijt illud semen, per quod caput serpentis aduersarij nostri debet comminui, & nostra carnalis natiuitas in spiritualem reparari. Quæ vtique litates incarnationis Christi passim in Scripturis declarantur.
units.tr: Next, in the contemplation of this mystery, pious consciences, if they exercise themselves in it from time to time, will receive a wonderful consolation and will be strengthened in faith against all dangers. For first they will notice that Christ was made man for their salvation, given to them and made a little child, and humbled, so that they themselves may become gods, great, and be exalted to the highest glory. They will conceive great joy in their consciences, together with the shepherds (of whom we read in Luke, chapter 2), because the Saviour of the world is born for them, because he is given, in whom all nations are blessed, because that seed has come forth through whom the head of the serpent, our adversary, must be crushed, and our carnal birth restored into a spiritual one. These benefits of the incarnation of Christ are indeed declared everywhere in the Scriptures.

units.la: In summa, hæc humiliatio Christi, qua ille dignatus est nostra causa, cùm Deus esset, homo fieri, vt nos à morte æterna liberaret, incitamentum esse debet etiam nobis, humilitatis, mansuetudinis, charitatis in Deum, & homines: denique quarumcunq; virtutum, quarum omnium exemplar in vno Christo lucidissimè resplenduit. Huc pertinent illa Philippens. 2. Is affectus sit in vobis, qui fuit in Christo Iesu, qui cùm esset in forma Dei, non rapinam arbitratus est, vt esset æqualis Deo, sed semetipsum inaniuit, formam serui sumpta, in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus vt homo, humilem præbuit semetipsum, factus obediens vsq; ad mortem. Item ad Titum 1. Illuxit gratia Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, vt abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatis sobriè, & iustè, & piè viuamus in præsenti seculo, expectantes beatam illam spem, & apparitionem gloriæ magni Dei, & Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi, qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, vt redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, sectatorem bonorum operum.
units.tr: In sum, this humbling of Christ, by which he deigned, for our sake, though he was God, to become man, so that he might free us from eternal death, ought also to be an incitement to us to humility, gentleness, and love towards God and men, and finally to all virtues, of which the pattern shone most brightly in Christ alone. To this pertain those words of Philippians 2: "Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death." Likewise Titus 1: "The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age, looking for that blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works."

units.la: Hæc habui, quæ quasi ad disputatione de duabus naturis in Christo, cum primis vtilia, & vnicuiq; Christiano scitu necessaria in præsenti adijcerem. Nunc ad Apostoli Pauli verba regrediamur. Subijciemus nunc paraphrasin, eaq; parabitur ex repetitione artificij, perpetua oratione, &c.
units.tr: I have added these things, which are especially useful as a supplement to the disputation concerning the two natures in Christ, and which every Christian needs to know at present. Now let us return to the words of the Apostle Paul. We shall now add a paraphrase, which will be prepared by the repetition of the method, in continuous discourse, etc.

units.la: BREVIS COLLATIO CHRISTI CVM MOSE ANNEXA, IN QVA CHRISTVM MOSE præstantiorem, clarissimè cuincitur. CAPVT TERTIVM.
units.tr: A SHORT COMPARISON OF CHRIST WITH MOSES, IN WHICH CHRIST IS CLEARLY SHOWN TO BE SUPERIOR TO MOSES. CHAPTER THREE.

units.la: Vnde fratres Sancti, vocationis cœlestis participes, considerate apostolum & pontificem confessionis nostræ, Christum Iesum, quòd fidelis sit ei qui ipsum constituit, quemadmodum, & Moses in tota domo ipsius. Tanto namq; maiore gloria, quàm Moyses, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Christ Jesus, who is faithful to him who appointed him, as Moses also was in all his house. For he has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, etc.

units.la: Inita disputatione de vtraque natura in Christo, quæ instituta potissimùm erat, ad asserendā Christi diuinitatem, subijcienda nunc erat conclusio principalis totius huius primæ partis. Sed priusquā id faciat Apostolus, vult adhuc de dignitate Christi, propter alios quosdam aduersarios, nonnulla subnectere. Erant enim permulti apud Iudæos, qui nihil magnificentius de Christo poterant sentire, quàm quòd esset eximius propheta: quales antea non pauci diuersis temporibus apud gentem Iudaicam, vita iuxtà ac doctrina, miraculorum item facultate, aliisq; donis Spiritus conspicui extiterunt, in quibus Helias, Hieremias, & principes omnium Moses. Quæ opinio etiam sparsa fuit Christo superstite, vt liquet Matth. 16. Sed ma gis recepta & confirmata, postquam emicante paulatim euangelio per vniuersum orbem, aliij aperte cœperunt confiteri, Christum esse Deum, alij eundem vt perditū & facinoro- sum prorsus damnarunt. Hoc inquam tepore, qui sibi visi sunt præ cæteris sapere, quasi mediam viam ingredi cupientes, statuerunt, Christū neq; Deum esse, neq; flagitiosum hominem, sed valde insignem prophetam, sicut etiam in Iosephi libris licet videre. Propter hos ergo, quoniam Christo gloriam, quanta debetur, nondum tribuebant, paucis docere iam vult Apostolus, Christum etiam omnibus prophetis superiorem. Peragit verò hanc causam iterum quadam collationis forma, quomodo superiore tractauit. Et cófert Christum cum ipso Moyse, quàm cum alio quopiā propheta, idque quàtum iudicare possum, sue quia Christum sic agnoscebant quidem prophetam, vt tamen infra Moysen colloca tent: siue, quia vbi demonstrarit Christum superiorem Moyse, perspicuum inde fiet, eundem omnibus reliquis prophetis præeminere, quorum nemo vnquam Moysi par est iudicatus. Nec sine prudenti consilio Apostolus hanc partim breuiter, & remoto omni argumentorum apparatu absoluit. Quid enim opus fuisset diutius occupari in demonstrando, quòd Christus sit prophetis præstantior, quando ex præcedenti disputatione in qua luculenter probatum est, Christum esse Deum, idem clarè intelligi poterat? Deum enim esse, qui cognoscit, quomodo non videbit etiam eminentiorem esse omnibus prophetis, qui tantùm homines fuere? Adhæc præclara doctrina, invsitata & creberrima miracula non obscurè testata fuerant, Christum amplitudine ac celebritate virtutum & miraculorum multo interuallo Mosen anteire. Præterea expediebat, compendio rem agere, ob morositatem Iudæorum, qui, vt est genus hominum supra modum irritabile, tragœdias maximas erant excitaturi, si contra Moysen rositi ipsorum.
units.tr: Having begun the discussion of the two natures in Christ, which was undertaken chiefly to establish the divinity of Christ, the principal conclusion of this whole first part now had to be added. But before the Apostle does so, he wishes first to add some points about the dignity of Christ, because of certain other opponents. For there were very many among the Jews who could think of Christ in no more exalted way than as an outstanding prophet. Earlier, at various times, not a few such men had stood out among the Jewish nation, in life and teaching alike, and likewise in the power of miracles and other gifts of the Spirit: among them Elijah, Jeremiah, and above all Moses. This opinion was also current while Christ was still living, as is clear from Matt. 16. But it became more widely held and confirmed once the gospel gradually shone forth through the whole world. Some began openly to confess that Christ is God, while others condemned him outright as a lost and wicked man. At this time, those who seemed to themselves wiser than others, wishing to take a middle path, decided that Christ was neither God nor a wicked man, but a very remarkable prophet, as can also be seen in the books of Josephus. Because these men did not yet give Christ the glory that is due to him, the Apostle now wishes to teach in a few words that Christ is also superior to all the prophets. He carries out this argument again by a form of comparison, as he treated it before. He compares Christ with Moses himself rather than with any other prophet. As far as I can judge, this is either because they acknowledged Christ as a prophet but still placed him below Moses, or because, once he has shown Christ to be superior to Moses, it will be plain that he surpasses all the other prophets, none of whom has ever been judged equal to Moses. The Apostle did not finish this matter, partly briefly and without any display of arguments, without wise purpose. For why would it have been necessary to spend longer proving that Christ is superior to the prophets, when from the preceding discussion, in which it had been clearly proved that Christ is God, the same could be clearly understood? For he who knows that Christ is God, how will he not also see that he is far above all the prophets, who were only men? Moreover, the excellent teaching, the unusual and very frequent miracles had not obscurely shown that Christ far surpasses Moses in the magnitude and fame of his virtues and miracles. Besides, it was expedient to deal with the matter in brief, on account of the obstinacy of the Jews, who, being a people exceedingly quick to take offence, would have stirred up great tragedies if any of them had spoken rather boldly against Moses. (The sign of this is that even if they had confessed Christ to be Elijah or Jeremiah, yet no mention is made of Moses, and that would have been plainly a sacrilege.) The Apostle, however, like all men, wanted to win the Jews over above all rather than provoke them. For these reasons he aimed at brevity.

units.la: Christus pro phetis etiam superior. Collatio Christi & Moysis. 1. 2. Christus Mose superior. Causæ breuitatis. 1. Christi diuinitas constat ex præcedentibus. Deus maior prophetis. 2. Christi doctrina et miracula. 3. Iudæorum mo rositas. ipsorum quisquâ paulò audacius loqueretur, (indicio,id est,quòd vulgus Matt. 16. etiam si Christum confessi sint,Heliam vel Hieremiam, de quando tamen eum Mosi nulla fit mentio,fuissetq; id planè piaculum) Apostolus verò sicut omnes homines,ita Iudeos inprimis conciliare magis cupiebat, quàm irritare. His igitur de causis breuitati studuit.
units.tr: Christ is superior even to the prophets. Comparison of Christ and Moses. (1) Christ is superior to Moses. Reasons for brevity: (1) Christ's divinity is established from what precedes. God is greater than the prophets. (2) Christ's teaching and miracles. (3) The obstinacy of the Jews. Any of them who spoke a little too boldly would have been in danger, and the Apostle, like all men, wished to conciliate the Jews above all rather than irritate them. For these reasons he aimed at brevity.

units.la: Cæterum transit Apostolus ad hanc partem quadam breui exhortatiuncula necessario annectenda præcedentibus,ex ijsdemq; desumpta,ita tamen composita, vt propositionem sequentis collationis Christi cum Mose, inseparabiliter adiunctam contineat, & nullo pacto,si orationis integrum seruare contextum volumus,ab inuicem eas quea-mus diuellere: Sic enim ait:
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle passes to this part with a short exhortation that must necessarily be attached to what precedes, and taken from the same material, yet so composed that it contains the proposition of the following comparison of Christ with Moses, inseparably joined to it. In no way, if we wish to keep the continuous context of the discourse, can we separate these from one another. For he says:

units.la: Vnde fratres sanctli, vocationis cœlestis participes, considerate, apostolum & pontifi-cem confessionis nostræ Christum Iesum, quòd fidelis sit ei, qui ipsum constituit, quem-admodum & Moyses in tota domo ipsius.
units.tr: Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Christ Jesus, who is faithful to him who appointed him, as Moses also was in all his house.

units.la: Ex quibus illa: Vnde fratres sanctli, &c. proprie pertinent ad exhortationem. Hæc verò, Quòd fidelis sit, &c. Propositionis loco sunt sumenda. Et sicut ex præcedentibus cognosci potest excellentia Christi præ Moyse, resteq; ex præcedentibus infertur:ita collatio sequens re-stè etiam indiuulsè annectitur præcedentibus.
units.tr: Of these, the words Therefore, holy brothers, etc. properly belong to the exhortation. But who is faithful, etc. is to be taken in the place of a proposition. And just as the excellence of Christ above Moses can be known from what precedes, and the conclusion follows from what precedes, so the following comparison is joined to what precedes as a conclusion, without any break.

units.la: Et monet me nonnihil hic modus transeundi ab vna causa ad aliam,vt eo lubentius hanc epistolam pro Paulina agnoscam. Nam Paulo istud perquàm familiare est, vtag-gressurus nouam caussam,verbis talibus cõiungat alteram alteri,vt, quomodo & quolo co secernen-dę sint ab inuicem,non statim quiuis possit animaduertere.
units.tr: This manner of passing from one topic to another also makes me think a little that this epistle is rightly acknowledged as Pauline. For this is very characteristic of Paul: when about to begin a new topic, he links one to another with such words that it is not immediately obvious to anyone how or where they are to be separated.

units.la: Qua de re nos alias sæpè diximus,tum in epistola ad Romanos, tum ad Galatas se-cundo. Vbi, postquam dixisset: Natura Iudæi, & non ex gentibus, peccatores quoniam scimus,iustificari homine ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi: & nos in Christû credimus,vt iustificaremur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Hinc transit ad secû-dam partę epistolæ didactica,in qua confirmat iustificari homines tantum per fidem:sic incipiés: propterea quòd non iustificabitur ex operibus legis omnis caro. Quæ verba sic sunt posita,vt ratione reddant præcedentiû, & nihilominus accipi etiam debeant pro propositione di-sputationis sequentis. Et in eadè epistola cap. 5. Vide quomodo veniat ad tertiâ partē,quę parænetica est, dicendo: Tantùm ne libertatem in occasionem detis carni. Item in epistola ad Ephesios capite secundo, vbi postquam egisset de admirabili Dei potentia ac bonitate per quam gratis propter Christum nos vnà cum Christo spiritualiter resuscitat & viuificat,transit ad dicendum de vocatione, quam illis quoque cognitam in exordio optabat. Incipit autem hanc secundam partem,dicens: Quapropter mementote,quòd vos quon-dam gentes in carne uocabamini præputium, ab ea,quæ uocatur circumcisio. Similiter in epistola ad Co-lossenses prima pars epistolæ,qua docetur, quòd Deus pater habeat omnes reconcilia-tos propter Christum, qui in fide stabiles permáserint:incipit in primo capite, ibi, Gratias agentes Patri, qui idoneos nos fecit: vbi nouam propositionem non possis animaduertere. Con-firmatio deinde sequitur eodem capite: Nec dimouemini à spe euangelij: Quæ verba etiam à præcedentibus videntur diuelli non posse. Confutatio capite secundo: Videte,ne quis sit,qui vos deprædetur: Secunda pars principalis de doctrina operum, postquam dictum fuisset, emortuos esse debere cum Christo,in Deo:ibi sequitur,cùm dicitur: Mortificate igitur mèbra vestra terrestria. Sed,quid ego tàm multus sum in his repetendis? Hoc tamen puto nonni-hil facere ad comprobandum,quòd epistola hæc ab apostolo Paulo profecta videatur.
units.tr: We have often remarked on this elsewhere, both in the epistle to the Romans and in the second chapter of Galatians. There, after he had said: "We who are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles, know that a man is justified not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ; and we have believed in Christ, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law," he passes from this to the second part of the epistle, which is doctrinal, in which he confirms that men are justified only through faith, beginning thus: because by the works of the law no flesh will be justified. These words are so placed that they give the reason for what precedes, and yet they ought also to be taken as the proposition of the following discussion. And in the same epistle, chapter 5, see how he comes to the third part, which is hortatory, by saying: Only do not use your liberty as an occasion for the flesh. Likewise in the epistle to the Ephesians, chapter two, where, after he has spoken of God's wonderful power and goodness, by which he raises us up and makes us alive together with Christ spiritually, freely, on account of Christ, he passes to speak of the calling, which he wished them to know already at the beginning. He begins this second part by saying: Therefore remember that you, once Gentiles in the flesh, were called "the uncircumcision" by those who are called "the circumcision." Similarly, in the epistle to the Colossians, the first part of the epistle, in which it is taught that God the Father has all who are reconciled through Christ, those who have remained steadfast in faith, begins in the first chapter with the words Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit, where you cannot notice a new proposition. Confirmation then follows in the same chapter: nor are you moved from the hope of the gospel. These words also seem unable to be separated from what precedes. Refutation in chapter two: See that no one plunders you. The second principal part, concerning the doctrine of works, after it has been said that they must be dead with Christ in God, follows there, where it says: Mortify therefore your earthly members. But why am I so long in repeating these things? Yet I think this helps somewhat to prove that this epistle seems to have come from the apostle Paul.

units.la: Ad explicandam exhortationem accedamus: Vnde fratres sancti,uocationis cœlestis participes, considerate apostolum & pontificem confessionis nostræ Christum Iesum.
units.tr: Let us proceed to explain the exhortation: Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Christ Jesus.

units.la: Breuis est & arguta exhortatio,nec sine iustis causis addita. Ita enim declarat, præce-dentis disputationis adesse finem,ac nisi alia quædam de dignitate Christi necessariò suis-sent attexenda,hîc habituri eramus conclusionem principalem. Eadeḿq; est causa,cuŕ tàm breuis sit,quia nimirû adhuc alia sunt adijcienda. Præterea sic decet,nec non ita faci-endum docent Rhetores,vt post argumenta quibus fides fit,subijciantur nonnulla con-uenientia mouendis animis. Quod & ante confutationem fecit,verbis,vti par erat, pau-lò pluribus, & nunc hîc iterum tàm eleganter facit,vt nullus rhetor posset in tanta breui-tate elegantius. Quàm enim selecta verba,& quàm acriter pungetia,nemo verbis queat explicare. Pauca sanè sunt verba (fratres,sancti,vocationis,cœlestis,&c.) sed mirabilem vim in se habent.Nos vtcúq; explicare conabimur. Vnde fratres sanctli: ἀδελφοι particula illatio-nibus apta,vnde,quare, quocirca. Blandissima autem,& admouędos affectus aptissima est vox Fratrum. Qui sic se appellari audiunt, quomodò non benigno animo loquentem audiant?
units.tr: The exhortation is short and sharp, and it is added not without good reasons. For it so declares that the preceding discussion is coming to an end, and that, unless some other matters concerning the dignity of Christ had to be necessarily added, we would have arrived here at the principal conclusion. This is also the reason why it is so brief: namely, that other things are yet to be added. Besides, this is fitting, and rhetoricians teach that it should be done in this way: after the arguments by which faith is produced, some points suited to moving the minds should be added. He did this also before the refutation, with words somewhat more numerous, as was proper, and now here again he does it so elegantly that no rhetorician could do more elegantly in such brevity. No one can explain in words how carefully chosen the words are, and how sharply they pierce. The words are few indeed (brothers, holy, calling, heavenly, etc.), yet they have a wonderful force in themselves. We will try to explain them in some way. Therefore, holy brothers [ἀδελφοί]: the particle is suited to inferences: therefore, wherefore, for which reason. But the word brothers is most affectionate and most apt to move the feelings. Those who hear themselves so addressed, how could they not listen to the speaker with a kindly mind?

units.la: Vocat autem h̃: Iudæos fratres, non ea ratione, qua omnes illi propter eximios pa-triarchas,à quibus genus se ducere gloriabantur, vel propter communia instituta legis
units.tr: He calls the Jews brothers, not in the sense in which they all used to greet one another as brothers, because of their illustrious patriarchs from whom they boasted descent, or because of the common institutions of the Mosaic law,

units.la: Mosaicæ, soliti sunt se inuicem fratres salutare: sed propter fidei, & euangelicæ doctrinæ consortium. Nam hæc non ad omnes Iudæos in genere, verùm ad pios tantùm referun tur. Quod ex eo licet colligere, quòd hoc loco vocat fratres sanctos & cœlestis vocatio- nis participes. Sed ad Roman. 9. loquens de omnibus in genere, vocat fratres & cognatos secundum carnem. Distinguuntur ergo fratres secundum carnem, & fratres secundum Spiritum, siue sancti. Quando verò & hoc pacto vocat eos sanctos, annon æquum, si suo nomini respondere velint, placidè audiant iusta monentem? Nonne præterea præclaræ hæ appellationes, quas solius Christi beneficio obtinebant, valde mouere debebant ad Christum amplectendum & honorandum?
units.tr: but because of their shared faith and the gospel teaching. For these words refer not to all Jews in general, but only to the godly. This can be gathered from the fact that in this place he calls them holy brothers and partakers of the heavenly calling. But in Romans 9, speaking of all people in general, he calls them brothers and kinsmen according to the flesh. Brothers according to the flesh and brothers according to the Spirit, that is, holy ones, are therefore distinguished. Since he also calls them holy in this way, would it not be fair that, if they wish to live up to their name, they listen calmly to one who admonishes them justly? Moreover, should not these excellent titles, which they obtained solely through the benefit of Christ, greatly move them to embrace and honour Christ?

units.la: Proinde vocantur omnes credentes etiamnū dum in terris agunt, sancti, propterea, qp sanguine Christi sanctificati, purgati, ex immundis mundi, ex iniustis iusti sunt redditi: quomodo Christus capite præcedenti appellatus est sanctificans. ἁγιάζων, & qui per eum erant à peccatis liberandi & ad salutem adducendi, vocati sunt sanctificandi, οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι. Vbi plenius expositimus, quid sanctificationis nomine intelligi conueniat, & inter alia testimonia, illud quoq; produximus ex 1. Corinthior. 6. Vbi Apostolus, postquam dixisset, adulteros, scortatores, &c. non accepturos regni Dei hæreditatem, adiecit: Atque hæc quidam fuistis, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis, per nomen Domini Iesu, & per spiritum Dei nostri. Ex quo loco clarissimè intelligi potest, quomodo credentes, qui per fidem liberati & abluti sunt à peccatorum sordibus, quiq; spiritum sanctificantem & purificantem cordae acceperunt, sancti appellentur. Porrò hiuc quo magis moueat eorum, ad quos scribit, animos, siue quo plenius illustret credentium dignitatem, appellat eos adhuc Vocationis cœlestis participes.
units.tr: Therefore all believers, while they still live on earth, are called holy, because they have been sanctified, cleansed by the blood of Christ, and from unclean have been made clean, from unrighteous have been made righteous; just as Christ is called in the preceding chapter the one who sanctifies [ἁγιάζων], and those who were to be freed from sins through him and brought to salvation are called those being sanctified [οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι]. There we have set out more fully what ought to be understood by the name of sanctification, and among other testimonies we also cited that from 1 Corinthians 6. There the Apostle, after saying that adulterers, fornicators, etc. will not inherit the kingdom of God, added: "And such were some of you, but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified, but you have been justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God." From this passage it can be understood most clearly how believers, who through faith have been freed and washed from the filth of sins, and who have received the Spirit that sanctifies and purifies the heart, are called holy. Furthermore, so that he might move the minds of those to whom he writes more strongly, or illustrate more fully the dignity of believers, he calls them still partakers of the heavenly calling.

units.la: Vox fratrum multum mouere poterat, magis etiam appellatio sanctorum. At hæc voces quandoquidem clarissimè ingerunt omnium animis gratuitam misericordiam Dei & beneficia spiritualia, cœlestia & æterna, longè maius apud omnes pondus habere debent. Tantundem enim hæc sibi volunt, ac si diceretur: Vos estis iam per Christum liberati & abluti à peccatis, ex iniustis iusti, ex miseris felices, à morte æterna redditi vitæ æternæ: & hoc quidem non vestris meritis, sed solius Dei vocantis vos & eligentis beneficio, aciam per illum cooptati & idonei redditi ad possidendum, non quidem terrena, & cum tempore peritura, sed cœlestia & æterna bona. Cùm ergo vos hoc modo fitis à Deo affecti amplissima dignitate, æquum est, Christum, per quem hæc etiam obtinerunt, magno in honore habeatis. Participes, inquit, estis vocationis. Hoc est, inter alios multos qui vocati sunt, vos quoque vocati estis. Magnum est, habere hoc modo partem in regno Dei, & inter electos connumerari. Nam ita hic vocationis facit mentionem, vt de electione simul loquatur intelligatque. Nam cum multi sint vocati ad nuptias summi patrisfamilias, pauci tamen electi, vt vix videatur profuturum quicquam, esse vocatum, nisi per misericordiam suam Deus nos eligat. Quocirca paulo post in hoc capite, Christi participes facti sumus, si sane initium substantiæ usq; ad finem firmum tenuerimus. Non omnes, qui vocantur, participes sunt cœnæ, quam Dominus suis instruit, sicut parabola illa Matthei vigesimo secundo, & Lucæ decimoquarto satis clarè ostenduntur. Cæterum, nulla ratio plus momenti habere potest ad commouendos animos, quā vocationis commemoratio. Præterquam enim quòd vocatio admonet omnes gratuitæ misericordiæ, (iuxta illud Romanorum nono, Secundum electionem Dei propositum manet, non ex operibus, sed vocante, &c.) tùm etiam omnes audita mentione suę vocationis, ad officium præstandum inuitantur.
units.tr: The word "brothers" could move them greatly, and the title "saints" even more. Since these words plainly place before everyone's mind the free mercy of God and spiritual, heavenly and eternal benefits, they ought to carry far greater weight with all. For they mean just the same as if it were said: "You are now, through Christ, freed and washed from sins, from unrighteous made righteous, from wretched made happy, restored from eternal death to eternal life; and this not by your merits, but by the sole benefit of God who calls and chooses you, and through him you have been enlisted and made fit to possess, not earthly goods that perish with time, but heavenly and eternal goods." Since you have been endowed by God with such a most ample dignity, it is right that you hold Christ, through whom you have obtained these things, in great honour. "You are partakers," he says, "of the calling." That is, among the many others who have been called, you too have been called. It is a great thing to have a share in the kingdom of God in this way and to be counted among the elect. For here he speaks of the calling in such a way that he also understands and speaks of election at the same time. For although many are called to the wedding of the supreme householder, few are chosen, so that being called would seem to profit nothing unless God chooses us through his mercy. Hence shortly afterwards in this chapter: "We have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our substance firm to the end." Not all who are called are partakers of the supper which the Lord prepares for his own, as those parables in Matthew 22 and Luke 14 show quite clearly. Moreover, no consideration can have more weight in moving minds than the recollection of the calling. For besides the fact that the calling reminds all of free mercy (according to that of Romans 9: "The purpose of God according to election remains, not from works, but from him who calls," etc.), all are also invited, when they hear mention of their calling, to perform their duty.

units.la: Vocati enim sumus in laudem gloriæ eius, qui nos vocauit, vt simus sancti & irreprehensibiles coram illo. Ephesiorum primo, & secunda Thessalonicensium secundo, secunda Petri primo. Cœlestis autem dicitur vocatio credentium, non tantùm quia è cœlo vocamur, siue à patre cœlesti: quandoquidem nemo venit ad filium, nisi pater traxerit eum: Sed quia ad res cœlestes obtinendas, sicut Apostolus prima Thessalonicensium secundo indicat, dicens: Obtestantes, ut ambuletis digne Deo, qui vocasset vos in suum regnum & gloriam. Vnde Philippensium tertio, appellat vocationem supernam: Insequor, inquit, ad palmam supernæ vocationis. Eleganter Chrysostomus: Nihil hic quæratis; illuc vocati estis. Illic est merces; illic est retributio. Quando igitur per Christum, & propter Christum, nullis nostris meritis vocamur, & adoptamur ad possidendum regnum cœleste, & gloriam æternam, non posset maius bonum ob oculos proponi. Quare tàm efficax ratio hic latet ab vtili seu commodo, vt nulla aptior posset excogitari.
units.tr: For we have been called to the praise of the glory of him who called us, that we may be holy and blameless before him: Ephesians 1, 2 Thessalonians 2, 2 Peter 1. The calling of believers is called heavenly, not only because we are called from heaven, that is, by the heavenly Father, since no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him, but because it leads to obtaining heavenly things, as the Apostle indicates in 1 Thessalonians 2, saying: "Charging you to walk worthily of God, who has called you into his own kingdom and glory." Hence in Philippians 3 he calls it the upward calling: "I press on," he says, "toward the prize of the upward calling." Chrysostom well says: "Do not seek anything here; you have been called there. There is the reward; there is the recompense." Therefore, since through Christ and for Christ's sake we are called, without any merit of our own, and adopted to possess the heavenly kingdom and eternal glory, nothing greater could be set before our eyes. Hence so effective an argument lies hidden here, drawn from what is useful or advantageous, that none more fitting could be devised.

units.la: Consideratè apostolum & pontificem confessionis nostræ Christum Iesum. κατανοέω non est simpliciter respicio vel intueor, sed magno studio & tota mente in aliquid intendo: vnde & κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν solerter & prudenter excogitatum remedium alicubi dicitur Aristoteli, vt notat Budaeus in commentarijs. Quamobrem hoc loco sic accipiendum est verbum considerandi, tanquàm si diceretur: mentes animosque vestros magno studio in Christum conuertite, illi omnem honorem, omnem gloriam tribuite, in illum fidem vestram conijcite, sit ille scopus vnicus, ad quem omnia referatis. Quo fere sensu etiam dicitur huius epistolae capite duodecimo: Per tolerantiam curramus in propositum nobis certamine, respicientes (ἀφορῶντες) ad fidei ducem, & consummatorem Iesum. Quo etiam loco Christum appellat ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν τῆς πίστεως, sicut hic vocat Apostolum & pontificem nostrae confessionis. Proinde non est dubium, quin voce considerandi tacitè multò plura hic insinuentur, quàm ipsa simpliciter per se significat. Dicendo Christum Iesum, duas voces simul voluit exprimere, per quas animis omnium suggeret ea, quae hactenus praedicauit, nimirum, quòd esset verus pontifex vnctus à Deo patre, ad peragendam expiationem nostrorum peccatorum: item quòd esset verus seruator, liberans nos populum suum à peccatis, ei vel ex nominibus competere. Sed quo dilucidius exprimeret omnem hanc Christi dignitatem, appellat eum apostolum & pontificem. Et reuera Christus, quando quidem apostolos dimittendos, & illi saepe orarunt Deum, vt semel mitteretur. Genesis quadragesimonono, Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, & dux de femore eius, donec veniat, qui mittendus est. Et ipse se misit seu legatum appellat Ioannis capite sexto, Haec est voluntas eius, qui misit me patris, ne quid perdam ex omnibus, quae dedit mihi: sed resuscitem illam in nouissimo die. Haec est voluntas eius, qui misit me, vt omnis, qui videt filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam. Ioannis capite vigesimo, Sicut misit me pater, ita & ego mitto vos, quasi diceret: sicut ego sum Apostolus factus à patre, ita ego vos creo apostolos. Vnde & ibidem statim, flando in eos, dedit eis spiritum Sanctum. Et alibi passim Actorum tertio, Romanorum octauo, Galatarum quarto. Filius Dei missus in mundum describitur, additis officijs ipsius, siue causis, propter quas missus est.
units.tr: "Consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Christ Jesus" [κατανοέω]. To consider is not simply to look at or gaze upon, but to direct oneself to something with great zeal and the whole mind; hence also a remedy devised skilfully and wisely is said, by analogy [κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν], to belong to Aristotle, as Budaeus notes in his commentaries. Therefore in this place the verb "consider" must be taken as if he said: turn your minds and souls with great zeal to Christ, ascribe to him all honour and all glory, cast your faith upon him, let him be the one goal to which you refer everything. In much the same sense it is also said in chapter twelve of this letter: "Let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking [ἀφορῶντες] to Jesus, the leader and perfecter of faith." In this passage too he calls Christ "the author [ἀρχηγὸν] and perfecter [τελειωτὴν] of faith," just as here he calls him the Apostle and High Priest of our confession. Therefore there is no doubt that by the word "consider" far more is tacitly suggested here than the word itself simply signifies. By saying "Christ Jesus" he wished to express two names together, through which he brings to the minds of all those things which he has hitherto preached: namely, that he is the true high priest anointed by God the Father to accomplish the expiation of our sins; likewise that he is the true Saviour, freeing his people from their sins, which belong to him by these names. But so that he might express this whole dignity of Christ more clearly, he calls him "Apostle and High Priest." And indeed Christ, since he is the Apostle, is the one sent by God; for the Jews often prayed God that the one who was to be sent might come once. Genesis 49: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from between his feet, until he comes who is to be sent." And he himself, in John 6, speaks of himself as sent, calling himself the one sent: "This is the will of him who sent me, the Father, that I lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day. This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life." In John 20: "As the Father has sent me, so I also send you," as if he said: as I am made apostle by the Father, so I make you apostles. Hence immediately there, breathing on them, he gave them the Holy Spirit. And elsewhere everywhere: Acts 3, Romans 8, Galatians 4. The Son of God sent into the world is described, with his offices, or the causes for which he was sent, added.

units.la: Simili modo vocatur Christus quod potifex, intercessor, reconciliator noster fit, facies ea, sicut supra dictum, quae apud Deum agenda sunt, ad expiandū peccata nostra. Quò pertinet illud 1. Timoth. 2. Vnus enim Deus, vnus etiam conciliator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit semetipsum precium redemptionis pro omnibus. Ea paucis veri pontificis siue sacerdotis officium à Christo peractum. Petrus prioris epistolae capite secundo, vocat Christum ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν. Sed praecedeti capite aliquid de pontificatu Christi diximus: vbi admonuimus, ea voce stratam viam ad haec ipsa, quae nunc tractamus: atque hic indicat ista vox ἀρχιερεύς, hanc exhortationem ad praecedentia referendam.
units.tr: In a similar way Christ is called high priest, intercessor and reconciler for us, since he does the things that, as said above, must be done before God to atone for our sins. To this belongs 1 Timothy 2: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all." In a few words, this sums up the office of the true high priest or priest as performed by Christ. In the second chapter of his first letter, Peter calls Christ the shepherd and bishop of your souls [ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν]. But in the preceding chapter we said something about the priesthood of Christ, where we noted that this word paved the way to the very matters we are now treating; and here the word high priest [ἀρχιερεύς] shows that this exhortation is to be referred to what has gone before.

units.la: Quidā quadā antithesis apostolū dici Christū putant, vt sic opponatur Moysi: Pontifice vero, vt opponat Aaroni. In summa autem, his appellationibus inclusam vult omnē dignitatē & officiū, quod in praecedetibus Christo est tributū. Cęterum cōfessionis nostrae apostolū & pontifice dicit, propterea quòd eum solū, & vt talē confessio nostra debet sonare. Estque sententia: haec debet esse communis & indubitata nostra confessio, quam decet & ad mortem vsque retinere, quòd Christus sit noster apostolus & pontifex, id est, à Deo patre in terras missus, vt perficeret ea, quae sunt agenda apud Deum, pro expiatione nostrorum peccatorum. Haec debet esse summa & caput nostrae confessionis, si quis confessionem nostrae fidei à nobis exigat. Huc pertinent illa Matthaei capite decimo. Omnis qui confitebitur me coram hominibus, confitebor & ego illum coram patre meo, qui est in coelis. Porrò quisquis negauerit me coram hominibus, negabo eum & ego coram patre meo, qui est in coelis. Romanorum capite octauo, Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Prima epistola Ioannis capite quarto, Quisquis confessus fuerit, quòd Iesus est filius Dei, Deus in eo manet, & ipse in Deo. En ergo, quare Christus dicatur apostolus & pontifex nostrae confessionis. Atque haec de breui elegantique exhortatiuncula: cuius haec est summaria sententia. Quando igitur Christus est verus apostolus, verus pontifex, id est, sicut supra declaratum est, intercessor, mediator, consideIrate eum, &c. Interea habemus in hac ipsa praeclaram doctrinam, quam arripere omnes inde debent. Primò discimus exemplum modestiae apostolicae, in adhortationibus praesertim quae ad rudes vel infirmos sunt faciendae. Videmus enim hic, quanto artificio, & quàm blandè Apostolus Iudæos ad amplectedum honorandumq; Christum inuitet. Et Paulus reuera in hoc artificio omnes excelluit.
units.tr: Some think that Christ is called apostle by way of antithesis, so as to be set against Moses, and high priest so as to be set against Aaron. In sum, however, the writer means that all the dignity and office ascribed to Christ in what precedes is contained in these titles. Moreover, he says apostle and high priest of our confession because our confession must sound of him alone and as such. The meaning is this: our common and undoubted confession should be that Christ is our apostle and high priest, that is, sent into the world by God the Father to accomplish those things that must be done before God for the expiation of our sins; and this confession we ought to hold fast even to death. This should be the sum and head of our confession, if anyone demands an account of our faith from us. To this belong the words of Matthew 10: "Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him also before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I will deny him also before my Father who is in heaven." Romans 10 (chapter 8 in this edition) says: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." And 1 John 4: "Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God." Here, then, is why Christ is called the apostle and high priest of our confession. This is the summary of this brief and elegant exhortation. Since Christ is therefore the true apostle and the true high priest, that is, as has been explained above, intercessor and mediator, consider him, and so on. Meanwhile we have in this passage an excellent teaching, which everyone should take from it. First, we learn an example of apostolic moderation, especially in exhortations that must be addressed to the untaught or the weak.
