For we see here with what skill and how winningly the Apostle invites the Jews to embrace and honour Christ. And Paul in truth excelled all others in this skill.

units.la: Secundo, addiscimus, quanta nostra sit dignitas. An enim paruum est, eos, qui credunt, vocari sanctos, deinde participes vocationis cœlestis, vocari ad hæreditatem cœlestem cum Christo percipiendam. Vtinam autem dum hanc dignitatem nobis per Christum paratam intelligimus, sic vitam instituamus, ne eam amittamus, & nos excludamus a regno cœlorum per nostra peccata, ad quod vocauit nos Deus per suam misericordiam.
units.tr: Second, we learn how great our dignity is. Is it a small thing that those who believe are called saints, and then partakers of the heavenly calling, called to receive the heavenly inheritance with Christ? Would that, while we understand this dignity prepared for us through Christ, we might so order our lives as not to lose it and shut ourselves out from the kingdom of heaven through our sins, to which God has called us by his mercy.

units.la: Tertio, discimus qualis debeat esse nostra confessio de Christo, quòd nimirum sit non ser Apostolus, nostra causa missus, (quod etiam est valde consolatorium) quodq; pontificatu pro nobis fungatur, id est, Deum patrem omni tempore mitiget & placet pro nobis. Atq; hæc confessio per omnem vitam est tenenda, quia talis est, vt ne inferorum quidem portæ possint aduersus eam præualere, sicut Christus ait Petro ita confitenti, Matthæi capite decimosexto: Huc refer exhortationem Apostoli, prima Timothei sexto, Certa bonum certamen fidei, apprehende vitam æternam, ad quam & vocatus es, & professus es bonam professionem coram multis testibus. Quæ verba sic accipi decet, tanquam ad nos proprie dicta. Nunc ad ea verba, quæ propositionis loco posita diximus.
units.tr: Third, we learn what our confession about Christ ought to be: namely, that he is the apostle sent on our account (which is also very comforting), and that he discharges the priestly office for us, that is, that he always appeases and pleases God the Father on our behalf. This confession must be held throughout our whole life, because it is such that not even the gates of hell can prevail against it, as Christ said to Peter when he so confessed, Matthew 16. To this refer the Apostle's exhortation in 1 Timothy 6: "Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life, to which you were called, and of which you made the good confession before many witnesses." These words should be taken as addressed properly to us. Now we turn to the words that we said were placed as the proposition.

units.la: Quod fidelis sit ei qui ipsum constituit, quemadmodum & Moses in tota domo ipsius.
units.tr: That he is faithful to him who appointed him, as Moses also was in all his house.

units.la: Valde artificiose collaturus Christum cum Mose, statim primo loco commendat Mosen à fidelitate potius, quàm ab aliis virtutibus. Nam hæc reuera in Mose clarissime emicuit, testante ipso Domino, Numerorum 12. (nec dubium, quin Apostolus ad hunc locum respexerit) vbi sic loquitur ad Mariam & Aaronem contra Mosen murmurantes; Audite sermones meos: si quis fuerit inter vos propheta Domini, in visione apparebo ei, vel per somnium loquar ad illum. At non talis seruus meus Moses, qui in omni domo mea fidelissimus est. Ore enim ad os loquor ei palam, & non per ænigmata & figuras Deum videt. Quare ergo non timuistis detrahere seruo meo Mosi? Ex quo ipsius Dei testimonio certum est, Iudæos occasionem arripuisse, extollendi suum Mosen, & præferendi omnibus aliis prophetis, maximeque quòd præ omnibus esset fidelis iudicatus.
units.tr: Intending to compare Christ with Moses very skilfully, he first commends Moses for his faithfulness rather than for his other virtues. For this virtue truly shone most clearly in Moses, as the Lord himself testifies in Numbers 12 (and there is no doubt the Apostle had this passage in mind), where he speaks thus to Miriam and Aaron, who murmured against Moses: "Hear my words: if there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in a dream. But not so my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. With him I speak mouth to mouth, plainly, and not in riddles and figures does he behold the Lord. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" From this testimony of God himself it is certain that the Jews seized the opportunity to exalt their Moses and to prefer him to all the other prophets, especially because he was judged faithful above all.

units.la: Proinde Apostolus istud non ignorans, cum iam collationem vellet instituere, lubenter id, quod ad amplissimas laudes Mosi faciebat, producit in medium, vt, vbi in progressu breuiter & argutè, nihilominus manifeste, demonstrauerit, Christum esse Mose multò præstantiorem & fideliorem, euidens nunc hinc fiat, etiam quæ maxima sunt in Mose, exigua tamen esse & prope nulla, quando dignitati Christi opponuntur. Quare iudicandum est, apostolum tanto artificio hanc causam agere, quanto nullus clarissimorum rhetorum posset. Quid? quòd in tota collatione mirabili prudentia breuiter absolhit collationis membra, & breuissimè ea, quæ dignitatem Christi complectuntur, quæ tamè putaret aliquis merito debuisse amplificationibus miris ornari & locupletari? Sed sic voluit Apostolus, habita ratione ingeniorum Iudaicorum, quàm modestissimè se gerere, ne aduersarios irritaret, potius quàm placaret, qui alias vbi oportunum censet, acer & vehemens esse solet.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle, not ignorant of this, when he was about to institute the comparison, willingly brings forward into the open what contributed to the very high praises of Moses, so that, having shown briefly and acutely, yet clearly, in the course of the argument, that Christ is far more excellent and more faithful than Moses, it might now be evident that even the greatest things in Moses are small, and almost nothing, when they are set against the dignity of Christ. Hence it must be judged that the Apostle conducts this case with a skill that none of the most famous rhetoricians could match. Moreover, throughout the whole comparison he dispatches the members of the comparison with remarkable prudence, and very briefly sets forth those things that embrace the dignity of Christ, though one might think they ought rightly to have been adorned and enriched with wonderful amplifications. But the Apostle wished it so: having regard for the Jewish temperament, he conducted himself with the greatest moderation, lest he provoke his opponents rather than conciliate them; he who, elsewhere, when he judges it opportune, is wont to be sharp and vehement.

units.la: Vocatur autem Christus ab Apostolo fidelis sicut Moses: quia ijsdem de causis spectan da est in Christo fidelitas, quas spectata fuit in Mose, qui Christi veri liberatoris nostri à spirituali seruitute Pharaonis, id est, diaboli, peccati & mortis, typum gessit. Porrò fidelitas maximè requiritur in ijs, qui publicè administrant, præsertim in spiritualibus.
units.tr: Christ is called faithful by the Apostle, as Moses was, because faithfulness is to be regarded in Christ for the same reasons for which it was regarded in Moses, who bore the type of Christ, the true deliverer from spiritual bondage to Pharaoh, that is, to the devil, sin and death. Moreover, faithfulness is chiefly required of those who administer publicly, especially in spiritual matters.

units.la: Vnde vir Dei missus ad Heli; & significans, quòd ex domo ipsius nemo successurus esset in sacerdotio, ait nomine Dei: Suscitabo mihi sacerdotem fidelem, qui iuxta cor meum & animam meam faciet. Item prima Corinthiorum quarto, Sic nos æstimet homo, vt ministros Christi & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Quod superest autem, illud requiritur in dispensatoribus, vt fidus aliquis reperiatur. Et sæpè Apostolus diuersos ministros commendat, sed eo potissimum nomine, quòd sint fideles. Sic ibidem prima Corinthiorum quarto, commendat Timotheum, quòd sit fidelis in Domino. Ephesiorum sexto, Tychicum vocat fidum ministrum in Domino. Et Matthæi vigesimo quarto, describitur fidelis seruus & prudens, quem præfecit dominus familiitio suo, vt det illis cibum in tempore additurque Beatus seruus ille, quem cùm venerit dominus eius, inuenerit sic facientem. Itaque & Moses & Christus, velut præcipui dispensatores seu Oeconomi in domo Domini, hoc nomine conferuntur & prædicantur, quòd fuerint maximè fideles. (Atque ita videtur hic fidelitas prædicari, vt eius nomine, omnes præclaræ virtutes sint intelligendæ, quæ in ministris spectari debent: sicut subinde nomine iustitiæ apud philosophos olim virtutum chorus notatur.) De Mose quidem quòd fuerit fidelis, satis constat ex testimonio Dei, & rebus per eum gestis. Quòd verò Christus fuerit fidelis imò fidelior Mose, res etiam actæ satis superque comprobant, & vox patris, dicens: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacitum est: Item Christi sermo ad patrem Ioannis capite decimoseptimo, per totum caput, quo veluti ratione Christus patri suæ fidei & diligentiæ reddit, satis clare testatur: Item, quando dixit, consummatum est. Non multis probat Apostolus: sed hoc tamen indicat insequentibus argumentis. Dum enim in altero ait, Christum se habere tanquam conditorem ac dominum domus, in altero tanquam filium. Et constat omnibus, diligentiores fidelioresque esse in domo: fos dominos seu patresfamilias & filios, quàm substitutos seruos: manifestum inde eua dere vult, quòd Christus fuerit fidelior Mose, qui tantùm fuit substitutus minister, licet reuera inter omnes ministros primus. Iam, cui fuit Christus fidelis? Ei, qui ipsum constituit: nempe Deo patri, qui ipsum miseratin mundum ad apostolatum & pontificatum subeundum. Cui & Moses fuerat fidelis, cui item omnes ministri diuersis temporibus missi, fideles esse debebant. Deus pater est ille paterfamilias & dominus, qui diuersis temporibus misit diuersos ministros, qui hominibus voluntatem ipsius aperirent, quique ostenderent, quomodo salutem nancisci possent. Cæterùm, quia græcè habetur τῷ ποιήσαντι αὐτὸν, quidam verterunt qui fecit vel condidit illum, quod etiam non male dicitur, licet creatura esse Christum colligi inde nequaquam debeat. Nam secundum humanitatem, secundum quam, ut Chrysostomus quoque annotauit, describitur Christus fidelis Apostolus & pontifex, Christus etiam factus dicitur. Galat. quarto, Misit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere. Item Ioan. 1. Sermo ille caro factus est. Secundum diuinitatem verò nec factus, nec creatus, sed genitus, ut inquit Athanasius.
units.tr: Hence the man of God sent to Eli, signifying that no one from his house would succeed in the priesthood, said in the name of God: "I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do according to my heart and my soul" (1 Samuel 2). Likewise, 1 Corinthians 4: "Let a man so regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." What remains is that faithfulness is required of stewards, that someone be found trustworthy. And often the Apostle commends various ministers, but chiefly on this ground, that they are faithful. Thus in the same place, 1 Corinthians 4, he commends Timothy because he is faithful in the Lord. Ephesians 6 calls Tychicus a faithful minister in the Lord. And Matthew 24 describes the faithful and wise servant whom the lord set over his household to give them food in due season; and "Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds so doing." So Moses and Christ, as the chief stewards or managers in the house of the Lord, are compared and proclaimed under this name, because they were most faithful. (And so faithfulness seems here to be proclaimed in such a way that under its name all the excellent virtues are to be understood which ought to be seen in ministers; just as, in the same way, under the name of justice the philosophers of old marked the whole company of virtues.) That Moses was faithful is sufficiently established from the testimony of God and from the deeds done through him. That Christ was faithful, indeed more faithful than Moses, the deeds themselves also sufficiently and more than sufficiently prove, and so does the voice of the Father saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"; likewise Christ's address to the Father in John 17, throughout the whole chapter, in which, as it were, Christ gives an account to the Father of his faithfulness and diligence, testifies clearly enough; likewise when he said, "It is finished." The Apostle proves this with few words, but nevertheless indicates it by the arguments that follow. For in the one he says that Christ has the place of the builder and lord of the house, and in the other that of a son. And it is agreed by all that those who are masters or heads of the household and sons are more diligent and faithful in the house than hired servants who are substitutes. It is clear from this that he wants to show that Christ was more faithful than Moses, who was only a substitute minister, although in truth the first of all ministers. Now, to whom was Christ faithful? To him who appointed him, namely God the Father, who sent him into the world to undertake the apostleship and the high priesthood. To him Moses also had been faithful, and to him likewise all the ministers sent at various times ought to be faithful. God the Father is that householder and lord, who at various times sent various ministers, who should make known his will to men and show how they might obtain salvation. But since in Greek it stands τῷ ποιήσαντι αὐτὸν [to him who made him], some have rendered it who made or founded him, which is also not badly said, although it must in no way be inferred from this that Christ is a creature. For according to his humanity, in respect of which, as Chrysostom also noted, Christ is described as the faithful apostle and high priest, Christ is also said to be made. Galatians 4: "God sent his Son, made of a woman." Likewise John 1: "That Word was made flesh." But according to his divinity he was neither made nor created, but begotten, as Athanasius says.

units.la: Tota, inquit, quia reuera tota illis hic in terris concredita. Amplificatur ergo & Christi & Mosis dignitas, hac voce significante, quòd non exiguum aliquod munus gesserint, aut in parte aliqua publicorum munerum fuerint versati, sed quòd totam domum gubernarint. Per domum autem hanc intelligere conuenit ecclesiam, seu congregationem credentium, tàm illorum, qui ante reuelatum euangelium fuerunt, quàm qui pòst. Sicut enim vnus idemq; Deus semper est ac dominus: ita eadem prorsus domus. Et omnium credentium, tàm patrum, quàm nostra, eadem fuit fides, eadem spes: sed tamen Oeconomia & oeconomi fuerunt à Deo patre diuersi constituti. Olim quidem oeconomus præfectus est Moses, & is administrauit secundum legem, secundum quam tota domus debuit regi, & gubernari. Post verò præfectus est Christus, & is administrauit secundum euangelium, secundum quod tota domus bene habet. Semper vna veritas, vna via ad salutem ducens, Abraham vidit diem meum, & gauisus est. Pertinuit Abraham ad hanc domum, in qua administrarunt Christus & Moses, etiam si ipse ante vtrumque extiterit. Per vnum Christum omnes salutem sunt consecuti, omnes patres baptizati sunt, sicut & nos, 1. Corinthiorum 5. item 10. Omnes nos quoque circumcisi, sicut illi, Colossenses 2. Denique omnia, quæ ad nos & Deum simul pertinent, & ad principalem causam nostræ salutis, sunt paria: licet in iis, quæ ad nos tantùm pertinent, nempe quæ de formanda vita nostra externa sunt præcepta, multa sunt diuersa & immutata, poscente nimirum id nostra fœlicitate. Itaq; vna domus, vnus populus, eodem modo habentes sunt omnes incolæ. Quae de re nos iterum paulò pòst, vbi Apostolus ipse interpretatur, credentes esse hanc domum. Sed & in veteri testamento ipsa congregatio credentium nomine domus appellatur: Item in nouo testamento domus ac templum, vt Psalmo octogesimo tertio, Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine in secula seculorum laudabunt te, Prima epistola Petri capite secundo, Ipsi quoque veluti viui lapides aedificemini, domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias, &c. Prima Timoth. tertio, Hæc tibi scribo, vt noris, quomodo oporteat in domo Dei versari, quæ est ecclesia Dei viuentis, columna & stabilimentum veritatis. Prima Corinthiorum tertio, An nescitis, quòd templum Dei estis, & spiritus Dei habitat in vobis? Si quis templum Dei profanat, hunc perdet Deus. Nam templum Dei sanctum est, quod vos estis.
units.tr: "All," he says, "because in truth the whole house was entrusted to them here on earth." The dignity of both Christ and Moses is thereby magnified by this word, signifying that they did not carry out some small office or take part in only some portion of public duties, but that they governed the whole house. By this house we should understand the Church, or the congregation of believers, both of those who lived before the gospel was revealed and of those who came after. For just as one and the same God is always God and Lord, so the house is entirely the same. The faith and hope of all believers, of the fathers as of us, was the same; yet the economy and the stewards were appointed differently by God the Father. Formerly Moses was set over the house as steward, and he administered it according to the law, by which the whole house was to be ruled and governed. Afterwards Christ was set over it, and he administers according to the gospel, by which the whole house now fares well. There is always one truth, one way leading to salvation: "Abraham saw my day and rejoiced" (John 8:56). Abraham belonged to this house, in which Christ and Moses administered, even though he lived before both. Through the one Christ all have obtained salvation; all the fathers were baptized, as we are (1 Corinthians 10). We too were all circumcised, as they were (Colossians 2). Finally, all things that pertain both to us and to God, and to the principal cause of our salvation, are alike; although in those things that pertain only to us, namely the precepts that shape our outward life, there are many differences and changes, as our happiness surely requires. So there is one house, one people, and all its inhabitants are in the same position. We will return to this matter a little later, where the Apostle himself explains that this house is the believers. But also in the Old Testament the congregation of believers is called by the name of house, and in the New Testament likewise house and temple, as in Psalm 83 (84): "Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you for ever and ever." In 1 Peter 2: "You also, like living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices," etc. In 1 Timothy 3: "I write these things to you so that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth." In 1 Corinthians 3: "Do you not know that you are God's temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. For God's temple is holy, and that is what you are."

units.la: Idem affert ie secunda Corinthiorum sexto, adducto testimonio est Leuitici vigesimo sexto, Vos, inquit, templum estis Dei viuentis, quemadmodum dixit Deus: Inhabitabo in illis, & inambulabo: & ero illorum Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. De gentilibus verò & Iudæis pertinentibus ad eandem domum, passim occurrunt multa, vt Ephes. 2. & alibi. Quae de re plenius suo loco dicemus.
units.tr: The same is stated in 2 Corinthians 6, where the testimony of Leviticus 26 is adduced: "You," he says, "are the temple of the living God, just as God said: 'I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.'" That Gentiles and Jews belong to the same house occurs frequently in many places, as in Ephesians 2 and elsewhere. We will speak of this matter more fully in its own place.

units.la: Satis sit hoc loco annotare, omnibus administrantibus, præsertim in ecclesia, propositum esse exemplum fidelitatis, quæ in Christo & Mose, denique & in omnibus pijs ministris ecclesiæ maximè laudata est. Certum est, qui in paruo fuerint fideles, ij à Domino mino constituentur super multa, & accipient suæ fidei ac diligentiæ amplissima præ- mia. Nec dubium, quin, vbi fideles & synceri sunt ministri, ibidem quoq; futuri sint fi-deles auditores, qui in domo Domini, vti par est, sancte & pie per omnem vitam versa-buntur.
units.tr: It is enough to note here that the example of faithfulness, which has been most highly praised in Christ and Moses, and finally in all godly ministers of the Church, is proposed to all who administer, especially in the Church. It is certain that those who have been faithful in little will be set by the Lord over many things, and they will receive the greatest rewards for their faith and diligence. Nor is there any doubt that where the ministers are faithful and sincere, there will also be faithful hearers, who will conduct themselves holily and piously throughout their whole life in the house of the Lord, as is fitting.

units.la: Quanquam Deus nunquam reliquit ecclesiam suam sine fidelibus ministris, licet pauci fuerint, & non semper à mundo cognoscatur, imò mundus se potius illis opponit, sicut se oppositi Mosi & Christo.
units.tr: Yet God has never left his Church without faithful ministers, although they may be few, and it is not always recognized by the world; indeed, the world rather sets itself against them, just as it set itself against Moses and Christ.

units.la: Tanto namq; maiore gloria, quàm Moses, hic dignus est habitus, quanto maiorem habet honorem is, qui construxit domum, quàm ipsa domus. Omnis enim domus con-struitur ab aliquo. Porrò qui condidit omnia, Deus est.
units.tr: For he has been counted worthy of so much greater glory than Moses, as the one who built the house has greater honour than the house itself. For every house is built by someone. But he who built all things is God.

units.la: En primum argumentum collationis, quo docet, Christum esse fideliorem & præstantiorem Mose, aptissimè ductum ex proportione. Sicut se habet pars domus ad conditorem siue dominum: ita se habet Moses ad Christum.
units.tr: Here is the first argument of the comparison, by which he teaches that Christ is more faithful and more excellent than Moses, very aptly drawn from proportion: as a part of the house stands to its builder or lord, so Moses stands to Christ.

units.la: Sed conditor siue dominus haud dubiè multò excellentior est, quàm aliqua domus pars, imò quàm tota domus. Ergo Christus est multò excellentior Mose.
units.tr: But the builder or lord is without doubt far more excellent than any part of the house, indeed than the whole house. Therefore Christ is far more excellent than Moses.

units.la: Minor est per se nota. Maioris altera partem, quòd videlicet Christus sit conditor, siue dominus, breuiter, licet paulò conuolutius, probat in hunc modum:
units.tr: The minor premise is self-evident. The major premise, namely that Christ is the builder or lord, he proves briefly, though somewhat more involved, in this way:

units.la: Cùm omnis domus ab aliquo construatur, hæc domus, in qua Moses fideliter sese gerit, cuiusq; ipse quædam fuit pars, constructa est à Deo, sicut reuera & omnia à Deo sunt condita.
units.tr: Since every house is built by someone, this house, in which Moses conducts himself faithfully and of which he himself was a part, was built by God, just as indeed all things were created by God.

units.la: Sed Christus est Deus. Ergo domus illa constructa est à Christo. Quare manifestum euadit, quòd Christus se habeat vt ædificans domum, & vt dominus. Moses verò tantùm vt pars domus à Christo ædificatæ. Iam ex hoc colligendum est, Christum esse fideliorem & præstantiorem Mose: quòd semper dominus seu conditor domus multò sit fidelior, diligentior, & per omnia excellentior, quàm quiuis alius qui in domo tantùm subit iniun ctum aliquod sibi munus.
units.tr: But Christ is God. Therefore that house was built by Christ. Hence it becomes clear that Christ stands as the builder of the house and as its lord, while Moses stands only as a part of the house built by Christ. From this we must now conclude that Christ is more faithful and more excellent than Moses: because the lord or builder of the house is always far more faithful, more diligent, and in every way more excellent than any other who in the house undertakes only some assigned office.

units.la: Hæc omnia sine dubio Apostolus paucis hisce verbis sibi voluit, sed prolixius crasi-uè non expositum, ne morosius videretur Mosi vel Iudæis insultare. Christum verò esse Deum, nequaquà exprimit, sed subintelligi vult vtpote quod in præcedenti disputatione satis superq; fit declaratum.
units.tr: Without doubt the Apostle wished all these things to be understood from these few words, but he did not expound them at greater length or more diffusely, lest he should seem to be insulting Moses or the Jews more than necessary. That Christ is God he does not express at all, but wishes it to be understood, since it has been sufficiently and more than sufficiently declared in the preceding argument.

units.la: Iam ergo aperte Christo gloriam præ Mose tribuit, nec amplius tantùm æqualem dicit: & magno animo Christi suam laudem vendicat. Ac licet verborum adsit pompa, & amplificationum apparatus, tamen reuera in tanta parcimonia orationis plurimùm effi-cit. Eoque iudicandus est id maiori arte facere, quo felicius artem dissimulat.
units.tr: Now therefore he openly ascribes glory to Christ above Moses, and no longer says merely "equal"; and with a great spirit he claims his praise for Christ. And although there is a display of words and an apparatus of amplifications, yet in reality he accomplishes very much with such restraint of speech. Therefore he is to be judged to do this with the greater art the more successfully he conceals his art.

units.la: Dicit igitur, Christum maiori dignum gloria, quàm Mosen. Gloriæ vox ponitur pro honore, excellentia, laude, dignitate, quomodo ijs, qui res bene gesserunt, dicimus gloriam & honorem deferendum, & eos qui de republica bene meriti sunt, multam gloriam consecutos, multa gloria & honore dignos. Psalmo vigesimo octauo, Afferte Domino gloriam & honorem, afferte domino gloriā nomini eius, id est, tribuite Deo laudem excellentiam, honorem. Romanorum secundo. Gloria verò & honor & pax omni operanti bonum. Ita namq; est gloria quædam Deo, quædā verò hominibus præstantibus debita, nec non apud Deum & apud homines gloria, laus, honor, paratur, licet, aliter atq; aliter: quemadmodum aliter quoq; iudicat Deus, aliter homines. Et sæpè in hac significatione, gloria & honor coniunguntur in Scripturis, & hoc loco vtrumq; habetur, δόξα & τιμή, atq; vna vox alteram explanat. Proinde Mosi concedit suam gloriam, quæ sanè magna fuit, sicut Deus ipse suo ore est testatus. At verò Christi gloriam ait longè maiorem, imò tantam, vt gloria Mosis vix fit comparanda gloriæ Christi: quemadmodum nec pars domus comparanda est cum ipso domino. Huc mirè quadrat, quod dicitur secunda Corinthiorum tertio, Quòd si administratio mortis in literis deformata in saxis fuit in gloria, adeò, vt non possent oculos intendere filij Israel in faciem Mosis, propter gloriam vultus eius, quæ aboletur: cur non potius administratio spiritus erit in gloria? Nam si administratio condemnationis gloria, multò magis excellit administratio iustitiæ in gloria. Quàdoquidem ne glorificatum quidem fuit, quòd glorificatum est in hac parte, propter eminentem gloriam. Etenim si quod aboletur, fuit in gloria, multò magis id quod manet, est in gloria. Respicit autem Apostolus ad illud, quod Exodi 34. de Mose scribitur, quòd cornuta fuerit facies eius ex consortio sermonis Domini. Videntes autem Aaron & filij Israel cornutam Mosis faciem, timuerunt propè accedere. Vnde illi coactus est velum obducere faciei, quando ad illos loquebatur. Ex his igitur colligit ibi Apostolus, quòd gloria illa vultus Mo-
units.tr: He says, therefore, that Christ is worthy of greater glory than Moses. The word glory is used for honour, excellence, praise, dignity, just as we say that glory and honour are to be given to those who have done well in affairs, and that those who have deserved well of the commonwealth have obtained great glory, are worthy of much glory and honour. Psalm 28: "Ascribe to the Lord glory and honour; ascribe to the Lord the glory due his name," that is, give to God praise, excellence, honour. Romans 2: "But glory and honour and peace to everyone who works good." Thus there is a certain glory due to God, and a certain glory due to excellent men; and glory, praise and honour are procured both before God and before men, though in different ways, just as God also judges differently from men. And often in this sense glory and honour are joined together in the Scriptures, and here both are found: glory [δόξα] and honour [τιμή], and one word explains the other. Accordingly he grants to Moses his glory, which was indeed great, as God himself testified with his own mouth. But he says that the glory of Christ is far greater, indeed so great that the glory of Moses can scarcely be compared with the glory of Christ, just as a part of the house cannot be compared with the lord of the house himself. This agrees remarkably with what is said in 2 Corinthians 3: "For if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, came with glory, so that the children of Israel could not look steadily at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which was fading away, how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation had glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. Indeed, what was glorified in this respect was not glorified at all, on account of the surpassing glory. For if what is being abolished was in glory, much more is what remains in glory." The Apostle has in mind what is written of Moses in Exodus 34, that his face was horned from converse with the Lord. And when Aaron and the children of Israel saw Moses' horned face, they were afraid to come near. Hence he was compelled to cover his face with a veil whenever he spoke to them. From these things therefore the Apostle there concludes that that glory of the countenance of Moses,

units.la: Exod. 34. Mosis facies cornuta sine splendens descens. tus Mosaici, in quam intendere oculos Israelitæ non poterant, vix fit appellanda gloria, præeminente gloria ipsius Christi. Tanto enim gloriam Christi splendidiorem esse gloria Mosis, quantum excellit vita mortem, spiritus literam, iustitia condemnationem, res permanens & æterna rem caducam & effluentem. His enim antithetis ipse valde appositè vtitur. Et Christus non obscurum præbuit eius dignitatis suæ specimen, quando etiam excellentiorem splendorem, qualis est Solis, in vultu visendum præbuit discipulis selectis, totam ecclesiam repræsentantibus in monte Thabor: vbi præterea viua voce Dei patris dignitas eius est comprobata, longè alio modo, quàm confirmata fuit dignitas Mosi. Matthæi decimoseptimo, Refer huc item illud Ioannis cap. 1, Et conspeximus gloriam eius, gloria velut vnigeniti à patre, plenus gratia & veritate. Et paulo post collatio Christi & Mosis: Lex per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum exorta est. Cæterum non caret Emphasi, quod dicit ἀξιωτὰς, dignus est habitus: Significat enim ea vox, tantam gloriam non tribui Christo sola æstimatione veluti hominum, sicut & sæpè, vbi homines falluntur, præter ius ac meritum alicui tribuuntur, supra quàm par est: Sed, quòd ipsius merito tanta dignitas ei debeatur actribuitur. Homines sæpè indignis & immerentibus deferunt honorem. Christo autem omnis honor debetur vt digno & optimè merito. Quo sensu significantissimè dicitur Apocal. 4. Dignus es Domine accipere gloriam & honorem & virtutem, quia tu creasti omnia, & propter voluntatem tuam sunt, & creata sunt.
units.tr: Exod. 34. Moses' face was horned, that is, shining as he came down from the mountain. The glory of the Mosaic countenance, on which the Israelites could not fix their eyes, can scarcely be called glory, since the glory of Christ himself far surpasses it. For Christ's glory is as much more brilliant than the glory of Moses as life excels death, the Spirit the letter, righteousness condemnation, and what remains and is eternal what is fleeting and passing away. The Apostle uses these antitheses very aptly. Christ also gave no obscure proof of his dignity when, on Mount Tabor, he showed a more excellent splendour, like that of the sun, in his face to the chosen disciples, who represented the whole Church. There, moreover, his dignity was confirmed by the living voice of God the Father, in a very different way from how the dignity of Moses was confirmed. Compare Matthew 17. Refer here also to John 1: "And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." Shortly after comes the comparison of Christ and Moses: "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." Moreover, the word ἀξιοῦται [axioutai], "he is counted worthy", is not without emphasis. It signifies that such great glory is not given to Christ merely by the estimate of men, as often happens when men are deceived and bestow on someone more than his right and merit warrant, beyond what is fitting; rather, such dignity is owed to him and ascribed to him on account of his own merit. Men often pay honour to the unworthy and undeserving, but all honour is due to Christ as to one who is worthy and has best deserved it. In this sense it is very significantly said in Revelation 4: "You are worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power, for you created all things, and by your will they are and were created."

units.la: Is qui constrvxit domum) ὁ κατασκευάσας αὐτὸν κατασκευάζω, paro, fabrico, instruo, & proprie est artificis, κατασκευάζομαι vero potius locatoris, qui opus impensis suis faciundum curat. Latinæ voces, ædifico, siue constrvo, de artifice & de locante ex æquo dicuntur. Proin de hic proprie sermo est de ipso artifice, significaturque, Christum esse illum, qui suo mate suaque propria opera domum spiritualem fabricarit, quod sanè amplius est & admonipotentiam Christi declarandam magis idoneum, quàm si ita tribueretur Christo potestas eius domus, quasi per alios esset extructa: sicut quidam aliquando opinati sunt, munidum & omnia externa per angelorum ministeria esse condita.
units.tr: "Is who built the house" [ὁ κατασκευάσας αὐτὸν, ho kataskeuasas auton]. The verb κατασκευάζω [kataskeuazō] means to prepare, fabricate, equip, and properly belongs to the craftsman, while κατασκευάζομαι [kataskeuazomai] belongs rather to the contractor, who has a work done at his own expense. The Latin words aedifico or construo are used alike of the craftsman and of the one who contracts the work. Here, therefore, the discourse is properly about the craftsman himself, and it is signified that Christ is the one who fabricated the spiritual house by his own power and by his own proper work. This is certainly more fitting for declaring the power of Christ and more to the point than if the power over his house were ascribed to Christ as though it had been built through others, as some have at times supposed, that the world and all external things were created through the ministry of angels.

units.la: Quàm ipsa domus) Quare dicit, Christum maiore honore dignum esse, quàm ipsa domus, & non potius, quàm pars domus, cùm revera Moses tantum fuerit pars amplissimæ domus domini, id est, totius congregationis credentium?
units.tr: "Than the house itself." Why does he say that Christ is worthy of greater honour than the house itself, and not rather than a part of the house, since in truth Moses was only a part of the most ample house of the Lord, that is, of the whole congregation of believers?

units.la: Respondetur, non sine consilio factum, quòd totam domum maluit exprimere potius, quàm partem domus. Magna enim hic vis latet ad amplificandam Christi dignitatem. Significatur namque aliquid amplius, quàm simpliciter instituta argumenti forma fuisset illatura: Siquidem vbi inferendum fuisset, Christum præstantiorem Moyse, qui tantum erat pars domus, hic iam clare dicitur, Christum præstantiorem etiam totapsa domo, quod sanè multo est amplissimum. Et tantundem sibi voluntatis verba, acsi diceretur: Quid vultis conferre Mosen cum Christo? Moses erat duntaxat pars quædam in domo: Christus autem non pars, sed Dominus & conditor.
units.tr: The answer is that it was not done without purpose that he chose to speak of the whole house rather than a part of the house. For a great force lies hidden here for magnifying the dignity of Christ. Something more is signified than the plain form of the argument as it had been set out would have carried. For where it ought to have been inferred that Christ is more excellent than Moses, who was only a part of the house, it is now clearly said that Christ is more excellent even than the whole house itself, which is certainly a very great claim. The words have just as much force as if it were said: "What do you want to compare Moses with Christ? Moses was merely a certain part in the house; Christ, however, is not a part but the Lord and builder."

units.la: Quare non tantùm Mose vestro præstantior est, sed etiam tota domo, tota sanctorum congregatione. Itaq; vides Apostolum magno certè artificio longè ampliora de Christo insinuare, quàm nuda videntur sonare verba: & sic collationem hanc instituere, vt quodammodo declaret, Mosen non magis esse cum Christo comparandum, quàm exigua particula domus cum ipso totius domus domino. Qua præfecto ratione mirum in modum amplificat & illustrat Christi gloriam, longisimisque interualis Mosi præponit. Huc pertinet, quòd Christus diuersis in locis describitur tota domo siue tota ecclesia excellentior: vt Ephesiorum primo, Omnia subiecit sub pedes illius, & eum dedit caput super omnia ipsi ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus illius, complementum eius, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet. Eiusdem epistolæ capite quinto, Vir est caput vxoris, quemadmodum & Christus est caput ecclesiæ. Colossens. primo, Omnia per illum & in illum creata sunt, & ipse est ante omnia, & omnia per illum consistunt, & ipse est caput corporis ecclesiæ. Atqui ita perspicuum fit, Christum esse maiore gloria dignum, quàm totam domum.
units.tr: Therefore he is more excellent not only than your Moses but also than the whole house, the whole congregation of the saints. So you see that the Apostle, with great skill, suggests things about Christ far greater than the bare words seem to sound, and sets up the comparison in such a way as to show, in a sense, that Moses is no more to be compared with Christ than a tiny part of the house with the Lord of the whole house. By this method he magnifies and illustrates the glory of Christ in a remarkable way, and places it far above Moses by the greatest interval. To this belongs the fact that Christ is described in various places as more excellent than the whole house or the whole Church: as in Ephesians 1, "He subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all." In the fifth chapter of the same letter: "The husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the Church." Colossians 1: "All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things consist through him, and he is the head of the body, the Church." Surely it is thus made plain that Christ is worthy of greater glory than the whole house.

units.la: Omnis enim domus construitur ab aliquo, porrò qui condidit omnia, Deus est.
units.tr: For every house is built by someone, but he who built all things is God.

units.la: Hæc quomodo ad probandum, quòd Christus sit conditor illius domus, subiecta sint, satis est indicatum. Et verbum κατασκευάζω bis hic positum est, nihilque à significatione priori discessum est.
units.tr: How these things are set down to prove that Christ is the builder of that house is sufficiently indicated. The verb κατασκευάζω is used twice here, and nothing has departed from its earlier meaning.

units.la: Hoc notandum, quòd non dicit, Porrò qui condidit domum, Deus est, sed, qui condidit omnia. Quod rursus factum est amplificandæ dignitatis Christi gratia. Ait enim, non tantùm domum illam à Christo esse conditam, sed revera simul omnia, hoc nia, hoc est, mundum cum omnibus, quæ in eo continentur. Quo sanè dignitas Christi mirabilis & immensa declaratur. Imò ostenditur, tantum distare Mosen à Chri- sto, quátū distat creatura à creatore: quandoquidē ipse Moses à Christo est cōditus sicut tota domus. Et cùm dicitur, omnia ab eo condita, satis intelligitur, etiam domum ab eo conditam. Qui enim dicit, omnia, nihil excludit, & sub vniuersali comprehenduntur singularia eiusdem generis.
units.tr: It should be noted that he does not say, "But he who built the house is God," but "he who built all things." This was done again for the sake of magnifying the dignity of Christ. For he says that not only that house was built by Christ, but in truth all things at once, that is, the world with all the things contained in it. By this the wonderful and immeasurable dignity of Christ is clearly declared. Indeed, it is shown that Moses is as far from Christ as a creature is from the Creator, since Moses himself was created by Christ, just like the whole house. And when it is said that all things were created by him, it is sufficiently understood that the house too was created by him. For he who says "all things" excludes nothing, and the singular things of the same kind are included under the universal.

units.la: Porrò quòd omnia per Christum sint condita, nihil opus erat declarare, sicut neque quòd Deus sit. Nam utrumque abundè expositum est disputatione præcedenti, vbi dictum est de Christo, quòd per eum pater condiderit secula: item, quòd angelos creauerit Spiritus: quòd in initio terræ fundamenta iecerit, & opera manuum ipsius sint cœli, &c. Ad quæ sine dubio Apostolus hîc nos voluit respicere. Quòd autem Christus condiderit siue collegerit sibi ecclesiam, diuersis locis Scriptura docet. Psalmo 101. Timebunt gentes nomen tuum Domine, & omnes reges terræ gloriam tuam. Quia ædificauit Dominus Sion, & videbitur in gloria sua. Proverb. 9. Sapientia ædificauit sibi domum, & excidit columnas septem, immolauit victimas suas, miscuit vinum, & proposuit mensam suam. Misit ancillas suas, vt vocarent ad arcem & ad mœnia ciuitatis: Si quis est paruulus, veniat ad me. Matth. 16. Super hanc petram (fidei confessionem videlicet) ædificabo ecclesiam meam. Quibus locis certum est spiritum Sanctum de collectione fidelium per Christum uerba facere. Et quanta diligentia collegerit Christus credentes, sæpius ipse apud euangelistas memorat. In summa, quando quidem omnes credentes per Christum sunt conditi & collecti, rectè dicitur, quòd ipse domum spiritualē, quæ est ecclesia, condiderit.
units.tr: Moreover, that all things were created through Christ there was no need to declare, just as there was no need to declare that God exists. Both have been sufficiently set out in the preceding discussion, where it was said of Christ that through him the Father made the ages; likewise that he created the angels by the Spirit; that he laid the foundations of the earth in the beginning, and that the heavens are the works of his hands, and so on. Without doubt the Apostle wished us here to look back to these things. That Christ built, or gathered for himself, the Church, Scripture teaches in various places. Psalm 101 [102]: "The nations shall fear your name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory. For the Lord has built Zion, and he shall be seen in his glory." Proverbs 9: "Wisdom has built herself a house, and has hewn out her seven pillars, has slain her victims, mixed her wine, and set out her table. She has sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and the walls of the city: If anyone is a little one, let him come to me." Matthew 16: "Upon this rock (that is, the confession of faith) I will build my Church." In these places it is certain that the Holy Spirit speaks of the gathering of the faithful through Christ. And how diligently Christ gathered believers, he himself often mentions in the Evangelists. In sum, since indeed all believers are created and gathered through Christ, it is rightly said that he built the spiritual house, which is the Church.

units.la: Atq; hoc est, quod, quantum ad doctrinam attinet, hîc potissimum est notandum, videlicet, quòd Christus vniuersam ecclesiam, quæ ab initio mundi fuit in hunc usque diem, condiderit, eius sit autor, institutor, gubernator. Sicut vnus est Deus patrum & noster, veteris testamenti & noui: ita vna est ecclesia veterum & nostra, vna fides, vna per Christum salus, vna omnium communis de dignitate Christi confessio. Constat enim, Adamo primo parenti promissionem factam de Christo, per quem deberet cōminui ca put serpentis hostis nostri Sathanæ, & ex ea accepisse consolationem de salute recupe-randa.
units.tr: And this is what must be especially noted here, as far as doctrine is concerned: that Christ, who built the whole Church, which has existed from the beginning of the world until this day, is its author, founder, and governor. Just as there is one God of the fathers and of us, of the Old Testament and of the New, so there is one Church of the ancients and of us, one faith, one salvation through Christ, one common confession of all concerning the dignity of Christ. For it is established that the promise concerning Christ was made to Adam, our first parent, through whom the head of the serpent, our enemy Satan, was to be crushed, and that from it he received consolation about the recovery of salvation.

units.la: Constat similiter, omnes patres, qui eum deinde sunt secuti, eidem promissioni innixos, cùm eadem sit crebrò uoce Dei apud ipsos repetita, nec non per prophetas subinde inculcata & luculenter exposita. Quare non obscurū est, veterem illā ecclesiam plane eandem esse, quæ nunc est, neq; euangelicam distinguendam ab illa primitiua. Omnes enim credentes quocunq; tempore, loco, conditione, siue Iudæi, siue gentes fuerint, uel sint futuri, ad euangelium pertinent, eiusdem ecclesiæ facti sunt membra, eundem Christum pro suo capite agnouerunt, licet alij ut venturum, alij ut qui iam aduenerit. Et quicquid nos per Christum, ad parandam salutem humani generis, confitemur & agnoscimus iam peractum, id illi agnouerunt & confessi sunt per Christum perficiédū, certoque de ijs tum prophetarum concionibus, tum illustrium uirorum, qui Christi typum in multis gerebant actionibus, fuerunt plenissimè edocti: qua de re Ephes. 2. Ipse est pax nostra, qui fecit ex utrisq; vnum, & interstitium maceriæ diruit, simultatem per carnem suam, legem mandatorum in decretis sitam abrogans, ut duos conderet in se-metipso in vnū nouū hominē, faciens pacē, & ut reconciliaret ambos in vno corpore, Deo per crucem, perempta inimicitia per eam, & veniens euangelizauit pacem vobis, qui procul aberatis, & his qui prope. Quoniam autem per illum habemus aditum vtriq; in uno spiritu ad Patrem, &c.
units.tr: It is likewise clear that all the fathers who followed Adam relied on the same promise, since God's voice repeated it often among them, and the prophets pressed it again and again and set it out plainly. It is therefore not obscure that the ancient Church is entirely the same as the one that exists now, and that the gospel church must not be distinguished from the primitive one. For all believers, at whatever time, in whatever place, and in whatever condition, whether Jews or Gentiles, who have been or will be, belong to the gospel, have become members of the same Church, and have acknowledged the same Christ as their head, though some acknowledge him as one who is to come and others as one who has already come. And whatever we confess and acknowledge as already accomplished through Christ, to prepare salvation for the human race, they acknowledged and confessed as to be accomplished through Christ. They were thoroughly taught about this both by the sermons of the prophets and by the illustrious men who bore the type of Christ in many of their actions. On this point Ephesians 2: "He is our peace, who has made the two one and has broken down the dividing wall of hostility, abolishing in his flesh the law of commandments contained in ordinances, so that he might create in himself one new man out of the two, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, having put enmity to death by it. And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father," and so on.

units.la: Et Moses quidem fidelis fuit in tota domo illius, ueluti minister, in testimonium eorum, quæ post dicenda erant: At Christus tanquam filius administrauit domum ipsius) Argumentum secundum itidem ex proportione satis clarè propositum. Sicut, inquit, seruus in domo se habet ad filium: ita se habet Moyses ad Christum. Sed constat, filium multo esse fideliorem & excellentiorē seruo. Ergo Christus agnosci debet multo fidelior & excellentior Moyse.
units.tr: "And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken afterwards; but Christ as a son over his own house." This is a second argument, likewise set out fairly clearly by way of comparison. "As a servant," it says, "stands in the house in relation to the son, so Moses stands in relation to Christ." But it is agreed that the son is far more faithful and excellent than the servant. Therefore Christ ought to be acknowledged as far more faithful and excellent than Moses.

units.la: Cæterum Christum esse filium, Mosen uerò tantùm seruum, ipse non probat, reputās utrumque satis fuisse notum. Illud enim ex præcedenti disputatione, in qua (capite primo) Scripturę testimonijs (præsertim ex illo Psal. 2. Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: & ex 2. Samuelis septimo. Ego ero ei pater, & ille erit mihi filius) cōprobatum est, Christum esse Dei filium, ac uerum natura Deum, potest intelligi. Istud verò præsupponit manifestum ex uerbis ipsius Dei Numeror. 12. vbi, sicut & alibi crebrò, Dominus vocat Mosen suum seruum. Neque etiam ipsi Iudæi aliter de Moyse statuebant, quàm fuisse eum eximium Dei ministrum.
units.tr: Moreover, the apostle does not himself prove that Christ is the Son and Moses only a servant, since he regards both as sufficiently well known. That Christ is the Son of God, and truly God by nature, can be understood from the previous argument, in which this was established by the testimonies of Scripture (especially Psalm 2, "You are my son, today I have begotten you," and 2 Samuel 7, "I will be his father, and he will be my son"). Moreover, the apostle presupposes that Moses was a servant, which is clear from the words of God himself in Numbers 12, where, as often elsewhere, the Lord calls Moses his servant. Nor did the Jews themselves think otherwise of Moses than that he was an outstanding minister of God.

units.la: Atque hic iterum cernis, quomodo ex cognitione precedentis disputationis pręsens causa expediri queat. Sita est igitur vis argumenti in collatione serui & filij, quæ voces distinctam & valde diuersam conditionem, ciuili more loquendo, significant: neq; quicquam est in uocibus obscuritatis.
units.tr: And here again you see how the present question can be settled from knowledge of the preceding argument. The force of the argument therefore lies in the comparison of servant and son, words which, speaking in the civil manner, signify a distinct and very different status. Nor is there anything obscure in the words.

units.la: Vocat Apostolus Mosen θεράπωντα, quasi dicas fidelem ac diligentem obseruatorem: θεράπων enim non significat qualemcunq; ministrum, siue domesticum, sicut vox οἰκέτης, sed famulum frugis & utilem, cum θεραπεύειν sit obsequiose colere, seq; alicui totum adicere. Itaque concedit quidem, quod Moyses fuerit fidelis, diligens, obsequiosus minister Dei: sed ut omnia amplissima de illo dicantur, tn non poterit alio loco constitui, quia loco famuli. Christus autem est verus summi patrisfamilias, Dei inquam, filius. Quare multis parasangis præferri eum Mosi necessum est. Quantum vero præemi-neat filius seruo, certe ius naturæ ac iura ciuilia satis arguunt: neque in Scripturis id dissimulatur. Lex enim Mosaica non pauca hac de re habet. Et Genes. vicesimoprimo, vt etiam recitatur Galat. 4. Filius ancillæ prohibetur hereditatem adire cum filio liberæ, Marci duodecimo paterfamilias postquam misisset diuersos seruos ad agricolas, qui eos occiderunt, tandem misit dilectum filium suum, dicens: Reuerebuntur filium meum. Item Ioan. octauo, Seruus non manet in domo in æternum: Filius manet in æternum. Si ergo vos filius liberos reddiderit, vere liberi eritis, &c.
units.tr: The Apostle calls Moses therapon [θεράπων], as if to say a faithful and diligent observer. For therapon [θεράπων] does not signify any sort of minister, whether a household servant, as the word oiketes [οἰκέτης] does, but a serviceable and useful attendant, since therapeuein [θεραπεύειν] means to serve dutifully and to devote oneself wholly to someone. So the apostle grants that Moses was a faithful, diligent and obedient minister of God. But however much is said of him in the highest terms, he cannot be placed in any other position than that of a servant. Christ, however, is the true son of the great master of the household, of God, I say. Therefore he must be preferred to Moses by many parasangs. How far the son surpasses the servant, the law of nature and the civil laws clearly show, and the Scriptures do not conceal it. For the Mosaic law has not a few provisions on this matter. And in Genesis 21, as is also recited in Galatians 4, the son of the slave woman is forbidden to inherit with the son of the free woman. In Mark 12, after the householder had sent various servants to the tenants, who killed them, he at last sent his beloved son, saying, "They will respect my son." Likewise in John 8: "A servant does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. If therefore the son shall make you free, you will be truly free," and so on.

units.la: Proinde satis liquet, Christum qui domum Dei, id est, ecclesiam administrat vt filius, hæres, ius habens & plenam potestatem, esse multo diligentiorem, & omnibus modis excellentiorem Mose, qui oeconomum egit duntaxat ut seruus, a Deo patre ad tempus substitutus. Verum est quidem, si conferatur Moyses cum cæteris ministris, qui diuersis temporibus in eadem domo sunt fideliter versati, inuenietur profecto maximus: at collatus cum filio, quem, sicut supra dictum est capite primo, pater constituit hæredem vniuersorum, plane nullus est. Non opus est pluribus hac de re agamus. Cæterum, non abs re inseruit, Mosen esse ministrum.
units.tr: Therefore it is quite clear that Christ, who as son administers the house of God, that is the Church, as heir, with right and full power, is far more diligent and in every way more excellent than Moses, who served as steward only as a servant, appointed by God the Father for a time. It is true, indeed, that if Moses is compared with the other ministers who served faithfully in the same house at different times, he will certainly be found the greatest. But when compared with the son, whom the Father, as said above in the first chapter, appointed heir of all things, he is plainly nothing. There is no need to say more on this matter. However, it was not out of place to insert that Moses was a minister.

units.la: In testimonium eorum, quæ post dicenda erunt) Obiter enim hisce verbis exponit, quod fuerit officium Mosi in domo Domini, siue, circa quæ ministerium eius potissimum fuerit occupatum. Ait, ministerium eius hoc fuisse, ut testimonium ferret de ijs, quæ in posterum erant dicenda faciendaque, videlicet per Christum salutis humanæ instauratorem. Descriptio hæc officij Mosaici non parum facit ad prædicandam Christi præ Mose excellentiam.
units.tr: "For a testimony of those things which were to be spoken afterwards." For in these words the apostle briefly explains what the office of Moses in the house of the Lord was, or rather, with what matters his ministry was chiefly occupied. He says that his ministry was this: to bear witness to those things which were to be said and done in the future, namely through Christ, the restorer of human salvation. This description of the Mosaic office contributes not a little to proclaiming the excellence of Christ over Moses.

units.la: Arguunt verba illa, Moysen nihil aliud, quam veluti humilem præcursorem missum a Deo, ad annunciandum nonnulla, quæ per Christum post venturum & superiorem forent peragenda: quo modo solent principes, si quando ciuitatem aliquam suntingref suri, quosdam ministros, qui hospitia & sumptus necessarios parent, præmittere. Atque itarem se habere, quod nimirum ob hanc tantum causam missus fuerit Moyses, diuersis Scripturæ locis comprobatur. Hinc enim fit, quod Galat. 3. dicitur, Legem fuisse paedagogum nostrum ad Christum: quia reuera Moyses docuit, quomodo adeundus excipiendus que foret Christus. Item Ioannis primo, Lex per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum. Sic saepius vmbra tribuitur legi & Mosi, Christo vero res ipsa seu veritas. Et Deuteronom 18. quæ citantur a Petro Actor. 3. de Christo clare vaticinatus est: Prophetam de gente tua, & de fratribus tuis, sic me suscitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus ipsum audies. Et paulo post alia verba Dei addit: Qui uerba eius, quæ loquetur in nomine meo, audirenoluerit, ego ultor existam.
units.tr: Those words show that Moses was sent by God as nothing more than a humble forerunner, to announce certain things which were to be accomplished afterwards through Christ, who was to come and be greater. Princes do likewise, when they are about to visit some city, send ahead certain servants who prepare lodgings and necessary provisions. That this is indeed the case, namely that Moses was sent for this reason alone, is confirmed by various passages of Scripture. Hence it is said in Galatians 3 that the law was our schoolmaster leading us to Christ, because Moses truly taught how Christ was to be approached and received. Likewise in John 1: "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." So the shadow is often attributed to the law and to Moses, but the reality itself, or truth, to Christ. And in Deuteronomy 18, which Peter cites in Acts 3, Moses clearly prophesied about Christ: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall hear him." And a little later he adds another word of God: "Whoever will not hear his words, which he speaks in my name, I myself will be the avenger."

units.la: Sed & idem Moyses in institutione esus agni paschalis, in liberatione populi e seruitute & tyrannide Pharaonis, in transitu maris rubri, in erectione serpentis in deserto, denique in multis aliis, quid aliud quam testimonium tulit de ijs, quæ postea per Christum forent ad implenda.
units.tr: But also Moses himself, in the institution of the paschal lamb's eating, in the liberation of the people from slavery and the tyranny of Pharaoh, in the passage through the Red Sea, in the raising of the serpent in the desert, and finally in many other things, what else did he do but bear witness to those things which were afterwards to be fulfilled through Christ?

units.la: Huc iam pertinent illa Ioann. 1. verba Nathanaelis: De quo scripsit Moyses in lege, & prophetæ, inuenimus Iesum Filium Ioseph Nazarenum. Item Ioan 3. Nolite putare, quod ego accusaturus sim uos apud Patrem, est qui accusat vos Moyses, in quo vos speratis. Si enim credidissetis Moysi, credidissetis utiq; mihi: de me enim ille scripsit. Luc. 24. apud duos discipulos exorsus a Mose & omnibus prophetis, interpretabatur illis in omnibus Scripturis, quæ de ipso erant.
units.tr: To this belong the words of Nathanael in John 1: "We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets: Jesus, the son of Joseph of Nazareth." Likewise John 3: "Do not think that I shall accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope. For if you had believed Moses, you would certainly have believed me; for he wrote about me." Luke 24: beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he explained to the two disciples what was written about himself in all the Scriptures.

units.la: Ibidem apud reliquos discipulos vndecim, Hæc sunt uerba quæ locutus sum ad vos, cum adhuc essem uobiscum, quod necesse foret impleri omnia, quæ scripta sunt in lege Mosis, & prophetis & psalmis de me. Et Petrus Actor. 3. profert testimonium Mosis de Christo, additque, omnes alios deinceps prophetas annunciasse dies istos. Item Stephanus Actorum septimo. In summa, passim inculcatur, Moses, prophetas, & quotquot deniq; verè functi sunt suo munere, in domo Dei, quæ est ecclesia, testimonium tulisse & prænunciasse ea, quæ per Christum forent agenda.
units.tr: In the same chapter, to the other eleven disciples: "These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms concerning me." Peter also, in Acts 3, cites the testimony of Moses about Christ, and adds that all the prophets from Samuel onward have foretold these days. Likewise Stephen in Acts 7. In short, it is everywhere insisted that Moses, the prophets, and all who have truly discharged their office in the house of God, which is the Church, have borne witness to and foretold what was to be done through Christ.

units.la: Hinc quoq; factum, quòd prophetę & apostoli passim in Scripturis vocantur testes, & officium eorum testimonium. In primis Christus ipse Esaiæ 55. Ecce testem populis dedi te, ducem ac præceptorem gentibus, ecce gentem, quam nesciebas, vocabis, & gentes, quæ te non cognoverunt, ad te current, propter Dominum Deum tuum sanctum Israel, quia glorificavit te. Luc. 24. Vos autem testes estis horum, ad apostolos & discipulos inquit Christus. Actor. 1. Accipietis virtutem, postea quam spiritus Sanctus advenerit super vos, & eritis mihi testes non solum Hierosolymis, verum etiam in universa Iudæa, Samaria, & usque ad extrema terræ. Actor. 2. Petrus ait: Hunc Iesum suscitavit Deus, cuius omnes nos sumus testes. Actor. 10. Hunc Deus suscitavit tertio die, & exhibuit eum, ut manifestus fieret, non toti populo, sed testibus prius ad hoc delectis à Deo, nimirum nobis, qui comedimus & bibimus vna cum illo, postea quam resurrexit à mortuis, & præcepit nobis, ut prædicaremus populo, ac testificaremur, quòd ipse sit ille, qui constitutus erat à Deo iudex viuorum & mortuorum. Actor. 26. Christus ad Paulum: Adhoc apparui tibi, ut constituam te ministrum ac testem eorum, quæ uidisti. Actor. 23. Oportet te & Romæ testificari. 2. Tim. 1. Ne te pudeat testimonij Domini nostri, &c.
units.tr: Hence also it is that the prophets and apostles are everywhere in the Scriptures called witnesses, and their office is called testimony. First of all Christ himself, in Isaiah 55: "Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you will call a nation you did not know, and nations that did not know you will run to you, because of the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you." Luke 24: "But you are witnesses of these things," Christ says to the apostles and disciples. Acts 1: "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses not only in Jerusalem, but also in all Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." Acts 2: Peter says, "God raised up this Jesus, of whom we are all witnesses." Acts 10: "God raised him on the third day and caused him to be seen, not by all the people, but by witnesses chosen beforehand by God, that is, by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead, and he commanded us to preach to the people and testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead." Acts 26: Christ says to Paul, "For this I have appeared to you, to appoint you as a minister and a witness of the things you have seen." Acts 23: "You must bear witness also at Rome." 2 Tim. 1: "Do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord," etc.

units.la: Hocigitur pacto Moyses minister constitutus est, & testis eorū, quæ post foret dicenda. Sed, quare ait, dicenda, potius quàm agenda? Fortasis, vel quia in uaticinio Moysis Deu teron. decimo octauo, ita Deus de Christo loquitur: Ponā uerba mea in ore eius, loquetur̄q; ad eos omnia, quæ præcipio illi. Fieri potest, uti Apostolus ad hæc uerba respexerit. Vel, quòd sæpe apud Hebræos verbum pro re seu facto ponatur: ut Lucæ primo, per omnia montana vulgabantur verba hæc. Item Lucæ secundo, Videamus hoc uerbum, quod factum est ad nos, id est, inquiramus rem ipsam seu factum. Item Angelus ad Mariam, Apud Deum non est impossibile omne verbū. Itaque & dicere, siue loqui, accipitur Hebræis subinde pro eo, quod est facere: præsertim quando Deus aliquid dicitur loqui siue dicere. Dei enim dicere plane idem est, quod operari. Id quod illæ formulæ satis indicant, Dixit Deus, Fiat lux, & facta est lux: ipse dixit, & facta sunt, ipse mandauit, & creata sunt. Ite psalmo secundo, loquetur ad eos in ira tua, & in furore suo conturbabit eos.
units.tr: Thus Moses was appointed a minister and a witness of the things that were to be spoken afterwards. But why does he say "to be spoken" rather than "to be done"? Perhaps because in Moses's prophecy, Deuteronomy 18, God speaks of Christ thus: I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. It is possible that the Apostle had these words in view. Or because among the Hebrews a word is often put for a thing or a deed: as in Luke 1, "all these words were noised abroad throughout the hill country." Likewise Luke 2: "Let us see this word which has come to pass," that is, let us examine the thing itself or the deed. Likewise the angel to Mary: "With God nothing will be impossible in word." So also to say or to speak is taken by the Hebrews, from time to time, for to do, especially when God is said to speak or to say something. For God's saying is plainly the same as his working. The formulas make this clear enough: God said, Let there be light, and there was light; he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. Likewise Psalm 2: "He will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will trouble them."

units.la: Proinde hæc est excellentia Christi præ Mose, quòd vbi Moyses tantum fuit missus ad testandum de futuris & faciendis per Christum: Christus verò ad alias res & sublimiores missus est.
units.tr: Accordingly, this is the excellence of Christ above Moses: whereas Moses was sent only to bear witness to the things to be done through Christ in the future, Christ was sent to other and more exalted matters.

units.la: Cæterum, ex eo, quod dicitur, Moses factum ministrum, in testimonium eorum, quę post erant dicenda, oštenditur, ministerium in ecclesia esse testimonium de ijs, quæ per Christum partim perącta sunt, partim peragenda. Circa hæc enim omnis ecclesiarum doctrina uersari debet, nepe in exponendo, quæ per Christum acta sunt, quæq; propter eundem nobis adhuc expectanda, videlicet, ut mundum iudicet, Antichristum spiritu oris sui destruat, ut gloriam & uitam æternam nobis largiatur.
units.tr: Furthermore, from the statement that Moses was made a minister, in testimony to the things that were to be spoken afterwards, it is shown that the ministry in the Church is a testimony concerning those things which have in part been accomplished through Christ and in part are yet to be accomplished. For all the teaching of the churches ought to be occupied with these matters, namely, in expounding what has been done through Christ, and what is still to be expected on account of the same Christ: that he will judge the world, destroy Antichrist with the breath of his mouth, and bestow on us glory and eternal life.

units.la: Secundò, commendatur hic euangelij veritas, quodq; non tanquam noua suspecta haberi debeat, sed à Mose ipso, omnibusq; sanctis patribus sit prænunciata.
units.tr: Secondly, the truth of the gospel is commended here: it ought not to be regarded as something new and suspect, but as foretold by Moses himself and by all the holy fathers.

units.la: Tertiò: Doctrinam euangelicam non esse iudicandam ex qualitate ministrorum, cùm ij non sint eius autores, sed tantùm testes, quæ sit bona Dei voluntas erga homines, ho minibus nunciantes.
units.tr: Thirdly: the evangelical doctrine is not to be judged by the character of its ministers, since they are not its authors but only its witnesses, announcing to men what is God's good will towards them.

units.la: Possēt thema istud de collatione Christi & Moysis plenius tractari, esset⁠que dignum thema, in quo quis vires dicendi exerceret.
units.tr: This theme, the comparison of Christ and Moses, could be treated more fully, and it is a worthy theme on which a man might exercise his powers of speaking.

units.la: Cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & gloriationem spei, ad finem usq; firmam tenuerimus.
units.tr: Whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of hope firm to the end.

units.la: Perinterpretationem subijcit, quanam sit illa domus Dei, quam prius Moyses, deinde Christus administrarunt: atq;, domum illam constare piis credentibus. Neque enim de tabernaculo ullo aut templo materiali, quod homines fabricarunt, sermo est in hac collatione, sed de spirituali quadam domo, quam extruxit ipse Deus. Ea est fidelium omnium qui sunt, fuerunt, vel erunt, congregatio; quorum pectora Deus inhabitat & inambulat, sicut ostenditur plenius prima Corinthiorum tertio. Secunda Corinthiorum sexto. Leuitici vicesimo sexto. Prima Timoth. tertio. Prima Petri secundo. Vt nequaquam opus sit istud hoc loco pluribus verbis explicare. Et Apostolus etiam sciebat, satis propemodum intelligi, in præcedentibus argumentis, quid per domum sibi uellet: ideoque postremo loco eam adijcit: nec forte erat adiecturus, nisi hac interpretatione cum latacitè voluisset pios animare, & ad constantiam exhortari.
units.tr: He then adds an explanation of what that house of God is, which Moses first and then Christ administered; and that this house consists of believing and pious people. For this comparison is not about any tabernacle or temple of material construction, which men built, but about a certain spiritual house, which God himself erected. It is the congregation of all the faithful who are, have been, or will be, whose hearts God inhabits and walks in, as is shown more fully in 1 Corinthians 3, 2 Corinthians 6, Leviticus 26, 1 Timothy 3, and 1 Peter 2. So there is no need to explain this at greater length here. The Apostle also knew that, from the preceding arguments, it was almost sufficiently understood what he meant by the house; and so he adds it at the end, and perhaps he would not have added it, had he not wished, by this interpretation, to encourage the pious tacitly and to exhort them to steadfastness.

units.la: Recte
units.tr: Rightly.

units.la: Rectè verò addit hanc descriptionem domus Dei seu ecclesiæ, posteriori membro de Christo: quia ecclesia vniuersa tam patrum ab initio mundi, quàm posteriorum omnium ad hæc vsque tempora, ad Christum propriè pertinet, vnum Christum habet pro capite & præcipuo administratore, imò & pro Domino. Nam & illa sub Mose ecclesia in Christum respexit quasi Dominum, ab uno Christo docebatur salutem petere, & per eundem futura bona expectare.
units.tr: Rightly indeed he adds this description of the house of God, or the Church, in the latter clause, concerning Christ, because the whole Church, both of the fathers from the beginning of the world and of all those since, down to the present times, belongs properly to Christ; it has one Christ as its head and chief administrator, indeed also as its Lord. For that Church under Moses also looked to Christ as Lord; it was taught to seek salvation from Christ alone, and through him to expect the good things to come.

units.la: Cæterùm, quamuis descriptio hæc videatur de illis potissimum accipienda credentibus, qui ad illud tempus uiuebant, quia ait, cuius domus sumus nos: non tamen est dubium, quin omnes omnium ætatum credentes comprehendat, id quod uel propositio huius collationis satis indicat, in qua citra distinctionem temporum vel personarum dicitur, & Mosen, & Christum in domo Dei fidelem fuisse. Sed placuit Apostolo, quasi de illius temporis hominibus, descriptionem hoc pacto formare, ut eos, qui tum viuebant, partim ad expendendum suam dignitatem ac fœlicitatem, quòd domus Dei essent membra: partim ad diligenter cauendum, ne propter insultationes aduersariorum à fide deficerent, atq; ita sese ab hac domo Dei excluderent, acrius incitaret. Animaduertere enim quiuis facilè potest, vocem, nos, magnam habere emphasin: deinde hæc uerba, Si fiduciam & gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam tenuerimus, grauem exhortationem in se complecti, & magnum reuera calcar ad constantiam in fide addere.
units.tr: Moreover, although this description seems to refer chiefly to those believers who were living at that time, since he says whose house we are, yet there is no doubt that it embraces all the believers of all ages. This the very statement of this comparison makes sufficiently clear, in which, without distinction of times or persons, it is said that both Moses and Christ were faithful in the house of God. But it pleased the Apostle to frame the description in this way, as though it concerned the men of that time, so that he might sharpen the exhortation: partly so that those who were then living might weigh their dignity and happiness, that they were members of the house of God; partly so that they might take careful heed lest, because of the taunts of their adversaries, they should fall from the faith, and so shut themselves out from this house of God. For anyone can easily see that the word we carries great emphasis; and then these words, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of hope firm to the end, contain a weighty exhortation and truly add a great spur to steadfastness in the faith.

units.la: Quamobrem sunt exactius singulæ voces considerandæ: quandoquidem clarissimè docent, qui ad domum Dei, quæ est ecclesia, iudicandi sint, pertinere. Primo igitur loco ponitur fiducia, παῤῥησία, quæ significat audaciam magno animo confitendi Christum, eiusq; veritatem. Quam audaciam qui non habet, non est quod inter ecclesiæ sana membra numeretur.
units.tr: Therefore each of the words is to be considered more exactly, since they very clearly teach who are to be counted as belonging to the house of God, which is the Church. In the first place, then, is set confidence [παῤῥησία], which signifies the boldness to confess Christ and his truth with a great spirit. A man who does not have this boldness has no reason to be numbered among the sound members of the Church.

units.la: Atq; hæc merito prima collocatur, quandoquidem, ubi homines audito uerbo credunt, per ueram, minimeque fictam confessionem ipsi ecclesiæ inseruntur, seque in ciuium Dei societatem recipi velle declarant. Hoc est, quod dicitur Rom.10. Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Ideoque Actorum quarto, apostoli illud petebant sibi in primis dari, dicentes: Et nunc Domine aspice in minas eorum, & da seruis tuis, ut cum omni fiducia (μετὰ παῤῥησίας πάσης) loquantur sermonem tuum. Apostolus quoque Ephes.6. petit & pro se orari, ut ipsi detur sermo in apertione oris seu cum libertate, (ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ) ut notum faciat mysterium euangelij. 1. Thessal.2. Ipsi nostis fratres introitum nostrum ad uos, quòd non fuerit inanis, sed quòd ante malis afflicti & contumelijs affecti: quemadmodum scitis Philippis, audacter egerimus (ἐπαῤῥησιασάμεθα) in Deo nostro, ad loquendum apud uos euangelium Dei in multo certamine. Etin alijs locis ipse precatur credentibus hanc fiduciam: quomodo etiam hortatur Ioannes prioris epistolæ capite secundo: Et nunc filioli manete in eo, ut, cùm apparuerit, habeamus fiduciam, & non pudefiamus ab eo in aduentu eius.
units.tr: And this is rightly placed first, since when people hear the word and believe, they are grafted into the Church itself through a true and by no means feigned confession, and declare that they wish to be received into the fellowship of God's citizens. This is what is said in Rom. 10: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." And so in Acts 4 the apostles asked above all that this be given them, saying: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your servants that with all boldness [μετὰ παῤῥησίας πάσης] they may speak your word." The apostle also asks in Eph. 6 that prayer be made for him too, that speech may be given him in the opening of his mouth, or with freedom [ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ], so that he may make known the mystery of the gospel. In 1 Thess. 2: "You yourselves know, brethren, that our coming to you was not in vain, but though we had before suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness [ἐπαῤῥησιασάμεθα] in our God to speak to you the gospel of God amid much conflict." In other places too he prays for this confidence in believers; so John also exhorts in the second chapter of his first epistle: "And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not be ashamed before him at his coming."

units.la: Qui verò fiduciam hanc libere & intrepidè confitendi nomè Christi & doctrina eius non habent, quia metuunt excludi à Synagogis (quales describuntur quidam principes Ioan.12.) tales ad ecclesiam non pertinent, etiamsi veram cognitionem habeant, quos Christus etiam non confitebitur coram patre suo, ut habetur Matth.10. Contra conscientiam enim hærent in synagoga, ubi antea fuerunt. Quapropter ipsi sese, reos statuunt omne enim quod contra conscientiam fit, peccatum est: Rom.14. 1. Corinth.8. Quanquam cùm multi nunc pasim sunt, qui ualde dolent abusus in ecclesijs; apud quos agunt, & tenent interea, quænam sit sana doctrina, an hi debeant statim erumpere, & errantibus se palàm opponere, hoc non definio. Certè oportunitas expectanda omni tempore est: & non semper priuati est publicè proponere innouandum, quod per ipsos magistratus innouari proprie debet, præsertim ubi uerosimile est, magistratus ipsos intelligere satis, quæ sint vitia in ecclesia, & quomodo ea possint corrigi.
units.tr: But those who do not have this confidence of confessing freely and fearlessly the name of Christ and his doctrine, because they fear being cast out of the synagogues (like the rulers described in John 12), do not belong to the Church, even if they have true knowledge; Christ will not confess them before his Father, as is said in Matt. 10. For they remain in the synagogue against their conscience, where they were before. Therefore they make themselves guilty, for whatever is done against conscience is sin: Rom. 14; 1 Cor. 8. Yet since there are now many everywhere who grieve deeply over the abuses in the churches among whom they live, and who meanwhile hold what sound doctrine is, I do not decide whether these ought to break out at once and openly oppose those who err.
