Certainly the opportunity must be awaited at all times; and it is not always the place of a private person to propose publicly what ought properly to be reformed by the magistrates themselves, especially where it is likely that the magistrates understand well enough what the faults in the Church are and how they can be corrected.

units.la: Et charitas iubet habere rationem fratrum infirmorum, ne quos offendamus. Quare ideo visum est nobis mentionem facere, ne, cùm dicimus, eos non pertinere ad ecclesiam qui non habent fiduciam seu παῤῥησίαν, videamur statim damnare omnes, qui synceram doctrinam norunt, & toto animo ample tuntur, & tamen ubi habitant, non audent palàm confiteri. Notum est ex actis Apostolicis, ipsos apostolos alicubi (in Asia, Phrygia, Galatica regione) loqui uetitos à spiritu, quia forte peccata incolarum merebantur: & Christus non ubique voluit signa edere: & ad tempus prohibuit Apostolis ire in uiam gentium: & apud ingratos iusit apostolos excutere puluerem pedum, & abire. Et Deus solus videt, ubi, & quando opportunum fit, sanam doctrinam promoueri, & fructus euangelicos produci. Sed de hac re satis. Sequitur.
units.tr: And charity bids us have regard for weak brethren, lest we give offence. For this reason it seemed right to us to mention this, so that when we say that those who lack confidence, or παῤῥησία, do not belong to the Church, we may not seem at once to condemn all who know sound doctrine, hold to it with their whole heart, and yet, where they live, do not dare to confess it openly. It is known from the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles themselves were at one time forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia and in the region of Phrygia and Galatia, perhaps because the inhabitants had deserved it by their sins; and Christ did not wish to work signs everywhere; and for a time he forbade the apostles to go into the way of the Gentiles; and among the ungrateful he bade the apostles shake off the dust from their feet and depart. And God alone sees where and when it is fitting for sound doctrine to be advanced and gospel fruits to be produced. But enough on this matter. Next follows.

units.la: Et glorianEt gloriationem spei. τὸ καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος. καυχώμαι glorior, magno animo iacto. Secundo loco opus est, ut, qui velit ecclesiae membrum agnoscI, firmam & inexpugnabilem habeat spem. Spes est, qua expectamus per patientiam futura bona post hanc vitam propter Christum promissa. Unde saepe in Scripturis describitur, spes gloriae, & aliquando pro re sperata, id est, pro ipsa gloria, & pro aeternis illis bonis coelestibus accipitur. Neq; aliter etiam potest intelligi, nisi quadam relatione ad res speratas in futurum accipiendas. Romanorum octauo. Spe seruati sumus. Porrò spes si videatur, non est spes. Quod enim quis cernit, cur idem speret? Si uero quod non videmus speramus, id per patientiam expectamus. Quando quidem bona in hac vita non percipiuntur, nisi spe, qua sola animae nostrae recreantur, mens in fide confirmatur, contra tentationes quascunq; munitur. Magis quadrat huic loco, quod dicitur 2. Corinth. 3. Etenim, si quod aboletur, fuit in gloria, multo magis id, quod manet, est in gloria. Itaque cum habeamus huiusmodi spem, multa libertate utamur. Vbi vides, libertatem seu fiduciam cum spe coniunctam Tit. 3. Paulus seruus Iesu Christi, iuxta fidem electorum Dei, & agnitionem veritatis, quae est secundum pietatem in spe vitae aeternae. Quo loco fidei & spei agnatio pulchrè declaratur. Ergo spes iuxta ac fides est ad salutem necessaria, neq; ecclesiae venit annumerandus, qui spem non habet, qui de promissionibus Dei dubitat, & inconcussa spe eas non expectat. Verù Apostolus, ut ostenderet, qualis spes nostra esse debeat, dixit, requirii in no bis non simpliciter spem, sed gloriationem spei, hoc est, tam firmam, tam solidam, tam inexpugnabilem spem, ut etiam deo gloriari audeamus apud eos, qui nos irrident, vel contemnunt, quasi vana spe laetaremur. Quam ratione spei expresit Apostolus Rom. 5. Iustificati ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem & contigit nobis, ut fide perduceremur in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus, & gloriamur sub spe gloriae Dei. Vbi vides & spem gloriae, & gloriationem spei coniunctam 2. Corinth. 1. vocat spem firmam, sicut & hoc loco βεβαίαν: Spes nostra, inquit, firma est pro vobis, cum sciamus, quod, quemadmodum participes estis afflictionum, sic futuri sitis & consolationis. Colos. 1. Reconciliauit vos in corpore carnis suae per mortem, ut exhiberet vos sanctos & irreprehensibiles & inculpatos in conspectu suo, siquidem permanetis in fide fundati ac stabiles, nec dimouemini a spe euangelij, quod audistis. Et infrà capite sexto, vocat spem anchorà firmà. En, quantum ad intelligendum, quae sit gloriatio spei, seu firma spes, satis est. Additiam tertium membrum: Ad finem usque: Haec particula maximè est necessaria. Quid enim prosit, ad tempus audire verbum, credere, sperare, si postea imminente persecutione, vel propter abundantiam bonorum temporalium, vel propter quascunq; alias tentationes, à fide deficias? Qui perseuerauerit in finem, saluus erit, Matth. 10. inquit Dominus. Alias certè si quis tenet voluntatem Domini, & postea resilit, tanquam canis ad vomitum, satius esset nunquam nouisse. 2. Petr. 2.
units.tr: And the boasting of hope [τὸ καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος]. To boast [καυχώμαι] is to glory, with a bold and high spirit. Secondly, it is necessary that whoever wishes to be acknowledged as a member of the Church should have a firm and unconquerable hope. Hope is that by which we await through patience the future good things promised for the sake of Christ after this life. Hence in the Scriptures it is often described as the hope of glory, and sometimes it is taken for the thing hoped for, that is, for glory itself and for those eternal heavenly goods. Nor can it be understood otherwise than by a certain reference to the things hoped for, to be received in the future. Rom. 8: "We were saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope; for why does anyone hope for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience." For good things are not received in this life except by hope, by which alone our souls are refreshed, the mind is confirmed in faith, and is fortified against all temptations. What fits this place better is what is said in 2 Cor. 3: "For if that which was passing away was glorious, much more is that which remains in glory." Therefore, since we have such hope, we use great freedom. Here you see that freedom or confidence is joined with hope. Tit. 3: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, in the hope of eternal life." In this place the kinship of faith and hope is beautifully declared. So hope, just as much as faith, is necessary for salvation, and he who has no hope, who doubts the promises of God and does not await them with unshaken hope, is not to be counted among the Church. But the apostle, to show what sort of hope ours ought to be, said that there is required in us not simply hope but a boasting of hope, that is, a hope so firm, so solid, so unconquerable, that we dare even to glory in God before those who mock us or despise us, as if we rejoiced in a vain hope. Paul expressed this by the reasoning of hope in Rom. 5: "Justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God." Here you see both the hope of glory and the boasting of hope joined. In 2 Cor. 1 he calls it a firm hope, as here βεβαίαν: "Our hope for you is firm, since we know that as you share in the sufferings, so you will share also in the comfort." Col. 1: "He has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and blameless and irreproachable before him, if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast, and are not moved from the hope of the gospel that you heard." And in chapter 6 below he calls hope a firm anchor. Behold, this is enough to understand what the boasting of hope, or firm hope, is. Let me add the third member: "to the end." This particle is especially necessary. For what good is it to hear the word, believe, and hope for a time, if afterwards, when persecution threatens, or because of an abundance of temporal goods, or because of any other temptations, you fall away from the faith? "He who endures to the end will be saved," says the Lord in Matt. 10. Otherwise, certainly, if someone has held the will of the Lord and afterwards turns back, like a dog to its vomit, it would have been better never to have known it. 2 Pet. 2.

units.la: Proinde haec habemus nobis ex his verbis documenta. Primò magna consolatio & felicitas hic nobis proponitur consideranda, quando dicitur, nos, qui credimus, esse membra eius domus, quam Deus inhabitat. Cùm extra ecclesiam non sit salus, esse in ecclesia, id perinde est, atq; de salute certum esse. Quare haec conditio magni à nobis debet fieri, multumq; adferre solatium, quoties tentationes aliquae nos fatigant, quasi à Deo essemus derelicti. Caput hauddubiè sentit, quoties lęduntur membra: sic & Christus sem per succurrit, quoties nos, qui sumus membra corporis ipsius, quod est ecclesia, iniuste affligimur, vel bona Dei voluntate tentamur.
units.tr: Therefore we have these lessons from these words. First, great consolation and happiness is set before us to consider here, when it is said that we who believe are members of his house, which God inhabits. Since there is no salvation outside the Church, to be in the Church is just the same as to be certain of salvation. Therefore we ought to make much of this condition, and it brings great solace whenever any temptations weary us, as if we had been forsaken by God. The head surely feels whenever the members are hurt; so Christ too always comes to our aid whenever we, who are members of his body, which is the Church, are unjustly afflicted, or are tested by God's good will.

units.la: Adhaec discimus hic, quomodo ecclesiae Dei possimus inseri, siue per quas res agno scere debeamus, utrum ad ecclesiam Dei pertineamus, & inter membra Christi numeremur. Si Christum eiusque doctrinam confiteri non erubescimus: si certam & firmam spem retinemus obtinendi promissa nobis per Christum bona: & si decretum est, in hac fiducia & spe perseuerare: Christus hauddubiè nos pro suis agnoscet, & de salute nostra cum tota ecclesia, hoc est, omnibus sanctis, certi erimus.
units.tr: Furthermore, we learn here how we may be grafted into the Church of God, or by what marks we may recognise whether we belong to the Church of God and are counted among the members of Christ. If we are not ashamed to confess Christ and his doctrine; if we hold a certain and firm hope of obtaining the blessings promised us through Christ; and if we have resolved to persevere in this confidence and hope: Christ will undoubtedly acknowledge us as his own, and we shall be certain of our salvation together with the whole Church, that is, with all the saints.

units.la: Certè Chrysostomus multò copiosissimè, necnon elegantissimè hic docet, quanta o porteat nos fortitudine & constantia in fide esse praeditos ad finem usque, si salutem consequi optamus.
units.tr: Certainly Chrysostom teaches this here most copiously and most elegantly: how much fortitude and constancy in the faith we ought to possess, right up to the end, if we desire to attain salvation.

units.la: EANDEM ESSE ECCLESIAM, QVAM ADMINISTRAVIT Moses & Christus: & quo conueniant lex & euangelium, quo item differant, &c.
units.tr: THAT IT IS THE SAME CHURCH WHICH MOSES AND CHRIST ADMINISTERED: and how law and gospel agree, and how they likewise differ, etc.

units.la: Quoniam propositio huius collationis Christi cum Mose continebat, & Christum & Mosen fideles fuisse in domo Dei, ibique interpretati sumus, vnam eandemque sem perfuisse Dei domum, id est, ecclesiam. Praeterea, quia, cum hic confertur Christus cum Mose, intelligere debemus, eadem opera conferri legem cum euangelio, nec non concludi, euangelium esse præstantius lege. Ideo visum est, hoc loco copiosius ista explicare,
units.tr: Since the proposition of this comparison of Christ with Moses contained the point that both Christ and Moses were faithful in the house of God, and since we there explained that the house of God, that is, the Church, has always been one and the same, moreover, because when Christ is compared with Moses we must understand that law is at the same time being compared with gospel, and that it is concluded that the gospel is superior to the law, it has seemed good to explain these matters more fully at this point.

units.la: Quod ad primum igitur, eandem esse omnium temporum ecclesiam, id hac una ratione demonstrari potest. Quorum est idem scopus ac meta & spes bonorum post hanc vitam obtinendorum, quorum item vita ijsdem præceptis fidei & charitatis instituitur, & regitur: quorum deniq; hæc est communis fides & cognitio, quòd per Christum, & propter Christum, ex sola misericordia, consequantur salutem: eos omnes pertinere ad eandem ecclesiam, necesse est iudicemus. Sed in his omnibus conueniunt tam illi sancti patres, qui ante manifestatum toti mundi euangelio fuerunt, quàm qui post. Ergo oes quoq; ad eandem ecclesiam pertinent. Consequetia nihil habet obscuritatis. Minor est à nobis copiosius explicanda. Ac primùm, quæ conueniant ijs, qui post manifestatum toti orbi euangelium: deinde eadem etiam communia patribus fuisse, ostendemus.
units.tr: As to the first point, then, that the Church of all times is one and the same, this can be demonstrated by one reason alone. Those whose aim, goal and hope of blessings to be obtained after this life are the same, whose life is likewise formed and governed by the same precepts of faith and love, and finally whose common faith and knowledge is that they obtain salvation through Christ, on account of Christ, from mercy alone: we must judge that all of these belong to the same Church. But in all these things agree both those holy fathers who lived before the gospel was made manifest to the whole world and those who came after. Therefore all of them also belong to the same Church. The consequence is perfectly clear. The minor premise must be explained more fully by us. First we will show what things agree among those who came after the gospel was made manifest to the whole world; then we will show that these same things were also held in common with the fathers.

units.la: Primùm ergo piorum sub euangelio credentium scopus, meta, & spes est de bonis spiritualibus & æternis post hanc vitam expectandis. Vnde in confessione dicunt quotidie, se credere, sperare, & expectare carnis resurrectionem & vitam æternam. Sic enim edocti sunt à Christo, dicente: Matth. 25. Ibunt hi (de malis loquitur) in supplicium æternum, iusti autem in uitam æternam. Ioan. 17. Pater venit hora, glorifica filium tuum, ut & filius tuus glorificet te, sicut dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis, ut, quotquot dedisti ei, det eis vitam æternam. Ioan. 5. Amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in condemnationem non veniet, sed transiit à morte in vitam. Amen Amen dico vobis, quòd veniet hora, & nunc est, quando mortui audient vocem filij Dei, & qui audierint, viuent. Sicut enim pater habet uitam in semetipso, sic dedit & filio vitam habere in semetipso, & potestatem dedit ei iudicandi quoque, quia filius hominis est. Nolite mirari hoc, quia veniet hora, in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem eius, & prodibunt, qui bona fecerunt, in resurrectionem vitæ, qui verò mala egerunt, in resurrectionem condemnationis. Passim occurrunt in scriptis euangelicis huiusmodi de resurrectione & vita æterna, deq; participatione gloriæ cum Christo, testimonia.
units.tr: First, then, the aim, goal and hope of the pious who believe under the gospel is concerning spiritual and eternal blessings to be expected after this life. Hence in the confession they say daily that they believe, hope, and look for the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life. For they were so taught by Christ, who said: Matth. 25. "These shall go away into everlasting punishment" (he speaks of the wicked), "but the righteous into eternal life." John 17. "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you, as you have given him power over all flesh, so that to all whom you have given him he may give eternal life." John 5. "Truly I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself, and has given him authority to judge too, because he is the Son of man. Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of condemnation." Testimonies of this kind about the resurrection and eternal life, and about participation in glory with Christ, occur everywhere in the evangelical writings.

units.la: Porrò patres quoq; in Christum incarnatum eandem spem de bonis æternis post hanc vitam habuerunt, id quod non difficile est demonstrare. Certum est, promissiones temporales de terra promissa & Canaan, illis aliquid altius præsignasse, nimirum terram attypus uitæ futuræ. Hebr. 11. Promissiones de bonis æternis & spiritualibus. Psalmus 105. Esaiæ 51. Ezechiel. 37. Esaiæ 16. Hierosolymam & omnia bona cœlestia, quæ post hanc vitam deberent contingere: id quod huius epistolæ capite undecimo declaratur, vbi dicitur, patres fide mortuos esse, cùnò accepissent promissiones, sed procul eas vidissent & credidissent, salutasse que & confessi fuissent, se hospites atq; aduenas esse in terra. Nam hæc qui dicunt, declarant, se patriam inquirere. Itaque ipsi innumeris miserijs, & calamitatibus semper presi iudicare debuissent magnificas promissiones Dei vanas atq; irritas, si non dea-lijs bonis, quàm temporalibus eas accepissent. Sed semper, quo propior fuit aduentus Christi, eò clarior extitit sanctorum patrum de æternis bonis confessio. Hinc Dauid psalmo 116. Preciosa est in conspectu Domini mors sanctorum eius. Quod etiam habetur proverb. 10. vbi additur, mortem peccatorum pessimam. Esaiæ 51. Cœli, inquit Dominus, sicut fumus liquescent, terra sicut uestimentum atteretur, & habitatores eius, sicut hæc interibunt: salus autem mea in æternum erit, & iustitia mea non deficiet. Item adhuc in psalmis: Custodit Dominus animas sanctorum suorum, & de manu peccatoris liberabit eos. Lux orta est iusto, & rectis corde lætitia. Item: Iustitia pij manet in seculum seculi, cornu eius exaltabitur in gloria. Item: In memoria æterna erit iustus, ab auditione mala non timebit. 1. Reg. 2. Dominus pedes sanctorum seruabit, & impij in tenebris conticescent. Et de resurrectione confessio patrum non obscura est. Iob. 19. Scio, quòd redemptor meus uiuit, & in nouissimo die de terra surrecturus sum, & in carne mea videbo Deum saluatorem meum. Repositta est hæc spes in sinu meo. Ezechiel. 37. Hæc dicit Dominus Deus: Ecce ego aperiam tumulos uestros, & educa vos de sepulchris vestris populo meus, & educam uos in terram uestram Israel, & scietis, quia ego Dominus, cum aperuero sepulchra uestra, & eduxero uos de tumulis vestris populo meus, & dedero spiritum meum in uobis, & vixeritis. Esaiæ 26. Viuent mortui tui, interfecti mei resurgent. Expergiscimini & laudate qui habitatis in puluere, quia ros lucis ros tuus, & terram gigantum detrahes in ruinam. Vade populo meus, intra in cubicula tua, claude ostia tua super te, abscondere modicum ad monumentum, donec pertranseat indignatio mea. Ecce enim Dominus egredietur de loco suo, ut uisitet iniquitatem habitatoris terrae contra eum, & reuelabit terra sanguinem suum, nec operiet diutius interfectos suos. Esaiæ vltimo, sicut cœli noui & terra noua, quæ ego facio stare coram me, dicit Dominus Deus, sic stabit semé vestrum, & nomen vestrum, & erit mensis ex mense, & Sabbathum ex Sabbatho. Veniet omnis caro, ut adoret coram facie mea, dicit Dominus: & egredien-tur, videbuntq; cadauera virorū, qui præuaricati sunt in me. Vermis eorū nō morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, eruntq; opprobrium omni carni. Danielis 12. Et tunc saluabitur populus tuus omnis, qui inuentus fuerit scriptus in libro: & multi de his, qui dormiunt in terræ puluere, euigilabunt, alij in vitam æternam, alij in opprobrium sempiternum. En, quàm clarè Scriptura docet, patribus eundem scopum, & metam, ac spem fuisse promissionum spiritualium & æternarum, quæ est eorum, qui post manifestatum Christum crediderunt. Fuitque hæc pars paulò plenius nobis explicanda, propter eos, qui sic iudicarūt de patribus, quasi duntaxat in temporales promissiones fides eorum fuisset inteta, neq; altius, quàm ad res terrenas animus eorū fuisset erectus.
units.tr: Moreover, the fathers too, living before Christ was incarnate, had the same hope of eternal blessings after this life, and this is not difficult to demonstrate. It is certain that the temporal promises concerning the promised land and Canaan foreshadowed something higher for them, namely the land as a type of future life. Heb. 11. Promises of eternal and spiritual blessings: Psalm 105. Isa. 51. Ezek. 37. Isa. 16: Jerusalem and all the heavenly goods which were to befall them after this life. This is declared in the eleventh chapter of this epistle, where it is said that the fathers died in faith, not having received the promises but having seen them from afar and believed, and having greeted them and confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth. For those who say such things declare that they are seeking a homeland. Therefore they, always oppressed by innumerable miseries and calamities, would have had to judge God's magnificent promises vain and void, if they had received them only as temporal rather than eternal goods. But always, the nearer the coming of Christ, the clearer became the confession of the holy fathers concerning eternal goods. Hence David, Psalm 116: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." This is also found in Prov. 10, where it is added: "the death of the wicked is the worst." Isa. 51: "The heavens," says the Lord, "shall melt away like smoke, the earth shall wear out like a garment, and its inhabitants shall perish likewise; but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail." Likewise in the Psalms: "The Lord keeps the souls of his saints, and will deliver them from the hand of the sinner. Light has risen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart." Also: "The righteousness of the pious endures for ever and ever; his horn shall be exalted in glory." Also: "The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil tidings." 1 Kings 2: "The Lord will keep the feet of his saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness." And the confession of the fathers concerning the resurrection is not obscure. Job 19: "I know that my redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God my saviour. This hope is laid up in my bosom." Ezek. 37: "Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up from your sepulchres, O my people, and bring you into the land of Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have opened your sepulchres and brought you up from your tombs, O my people, and put my Spirit in you, and you shall live." Isa. 26: "Your dead shall live, my slain shall rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is the dew of light, and you will bring the land of the giants down to ruin. Go, my people, enter your chambers, shut your doors behind you, hide yourselves for a little while until my indignation has passed. For behold, the Lord will come out of his place to punish the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him, and the earth will reveal its blood and no longer cover its slain." Isa. last chapter: "As the new heavens and the new earth, which I make to stand before me, says the Lord God, so shall your seed and your name stand; and it shall be from month to month, and from Sabbath to Sabbath. All flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord; and they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh." Dan. 12: "And then your people shall be saved, everyone who is found written in the book; and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, others to everlasting shame." See how clearly Scripture teaches that the fathers had the same aim, goal and hope as those who believed after Christ was made manifest: spiritual and eternal promises. This part had to be explained somewhat more fully by us, on account of those who have judged about the fathers as if their faith had been directed only at temporal promises, and their minds had not been raised higher than earthly things.

units.la: Iam secundò probandum est, quòd & patres, & qui sub euangelio sunt pij, ijsdem præceptis fidei & charitatis vitam suam formauerint. Lex enim tota in hoc erat, ut fides & charitas exerceretur. Nam prima tabula doctrinam fidei, secunda charitatis, imò vtraq; charitatem, illa Dei, hæc proximi, complectitur: sicut Christus ipse Matth. 22. interpretatur: in his duobus mandatis tota lex & prophetæ pendent. Roman. 13. consummatio legis est dilectio. Et Christus non tulit noua viuendi præcepta, neq; damnauit vetera: sed apud omnes rata esse voluit quæcunque viuendi præcepta, quæ ad charitatem declarandam conducerent: vnde Matthæi 5. Ne existimetis, quòd venerim ad destruendam legem, aut prophetas, imò non veni, ut destruam, sed ut compleam. Additque: quisquis igitur soluerit unum ex mandatis hisce minimis, & docuerit sic homines, minimus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Atque ibi Christus non condit nouam legem, sed tantum veterem interpretatur. Et Matthæi 19, si vis ad vitā ingredi, serua mādata. Galat. 5. Tota lex in vno verbo completur, nempe hoc, diliges proximū tuum vt te ipsum. In summa quando eisdem præceptis vitam suam informarunt, & qui post reuelatum euangelium vixerunt, & ante illud tempus pij patres, manifestum est, nullum ex hac parte discrimen inter eos ponendum, & eidem ecclesiæ Dei accersendos. Dixi autem de præceptis pertinentibus ad fidem & charitatem. Nam horum præcipuè habenda est ratio apud pios. Ceremonialia autem ad hanc rem non adeò pertinuerunt, utpote quæ, dum significaret res quasdam spirituales & æternas, de Christo, de futura gloria, & rudimenta quædam fuerunt fidei, quorū loco alia successerunt, licet pauciora, multò tamen efficaciora: quam quàm manifestata clara luce vmbris minus opus est.
units.tr: Second, it must be shown that both the Fathers and those who live under the gospel have shaped their lives by the same precepts of faith and charity. For the whole law was aimed at this, that faith and charity should be exercised. The first table teaches the doctrine of faith, the second that of charity; indeed both tables embrace charity, the first toward God and the second toward neighbour. Christ himself explains this in Matt. 22: "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." Rom. 13: "Love is the fulfilling of the law." Christ did not bring new precepts for living, nor did he condemn the old ones; he wished every precept that serves to display charity to remain in force for all. Hence Matt. 5: "Do not think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets; I did not come to destroy but to fulfil." He adds: "Whoever therefore breaks one of these least commandments, and teaches men so, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven." There Christ does not establish a new law but only interprets the old one. Matt. 19: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." Gal. 5: "The whole law is fulfilled in one word, namely this: you shall love your neighbour as yourself." In sum, since both those who lived after the gospel was revealed and the godly Fathers before that time have ordered their lives by these same precepts, it is clear that no distinction in this respect should be drawn between them, and both are to be counted as belonging to the same Church of God. I have spoken, however, of the precepts that pertain to faith and charity, for these are chiefly to be considered by the godly. The ceremonial precepts did not pertain to this matter so much: since they signified certain spiritual and eternal things, concerning Christ and future glory, they were the rudiments of faith, and other precepts, fewer but far more effective, have taken their place. Once the clear light has been revealed, shadows are less needed.

units.la: Restat probādū tertiū, videlicet quòd patres habuerint fidē & cognitionē de Christo, quòd propter eum misericordiam consequerentur, sicut & illi, qui sunt sub euangelio. Hoc etiam constare potest ex eo, quòd statim post lapsum primorum parētum Christus, qui conteret caput serpentis, sit promissus, ac deinde sæpè patribus succedētibus varijs modis promissus & præsignatus: ut ad Abrahamum, Isaacum, Dauidem, alios q; : eéque promissiones populo per prophetas omni tempore inculcabantur: & semper plura ac clariora per eosdem de Christo vaticinia sunt edita, quæ lōgum foret recésere, in quibus & singula etiam Christi opera prædicta fuerunt. Nec dubium, quin multò clarius fuerit illi populo cognitus Christus, quàm Scriptura videtur commemorare, etiamsi commemoret et clarissimè. Hinc illa confessio Zachariæ Lucæ 1. Laudandus Dominus Deus Israel quia visitauit, & fecit redemptionem populo suo. Et erexit cornu salutis nobis in domo Dauid pueri sui: sicut locutus est per os sanctorum, qui à seculo sunt, prophetarum eius, &c. Item Beatæ Virginis ibidem: suscepit Israel puerum suum, ut memor esset misericordiæ, sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, nimirum Abrahamo & semini eius in æuum. Item Simonis Lucæ 2. Huc pertinet, quod Christus ait Ioannis 8. Abraham exultauit, ut videret diem meum, & vidit & gauisus est. Item quod ad signa externa attinet, quibus oportuit homines fide de Christo profiteri, 1. Corinth. 10. Patres nostri omnes sub nube erant, & omnes per mare transierunt, & omnes in Mosen baptizati sunt in nube, & in mari, & omnes eandem escam spiritualem comedebāt, & omnes eundem potum spirituale bibebāt. Bibebant enim de spirituali, quæ illos comitabatur petra: petra autem fuit Christus. En, in illis baptismum & manducationem spiritualem ad testandam fidem de Christo, sicut in nobis. Et sicut nobis baptismus est signaculum iustitiæ fidei: ita erat illis circumcisio: Roman. 4. E diuerso, Colossens. 2. nobis tribuit circumcisionem spiritualem, sicut & Roman. 2. Et Christus ipse euidēter docuit, omnia tām nobis, quàm Patribus esse communia, quæ ad salutem pertinet: ut Matthæi 8. Vbi credentes post tempus reuelati euangelij constituit cum Abraham: multi, inquit, ab oriente & occidēte venturi sunt, & accumbet cum Abraham, & Isaac, & Iacob in regno cœlorum.
units.tr: The third point remaining to be proved is that the Fathers had faith and knowledge of Christ, and that through him they obtained mercy, just as those who are under the gospel do. This can also be established from the fact that immediately after the fall of our first parents Christ, who would crush the serpent's head, was promised, and then, as the fathers succeeded one another, was often promised and foreshadowed in various ways: to Abraham, Isaac, David and others. These promises were constantly impressed upon the people through the prophets at every period, and always through these same prophets more and clearer prophecies about Christ were published, in which even the individual works of Christ were foretold. It is beyond doubt that Christ was known to that people far more clearly than Scripture seems to record, even though it records him very clearly. Hence the song of Zechariah in Luke 1: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old." Likewise the Blessed Virgin in the same place: "He has helped Israel his servant, that he might remember his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his seed for ever." Likewise Simeon in Luke 2. To this belongs what Christ says in John 8: "Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad." As for the external signs by which people were bound to profess faith in Christ, 1 Cor. 10: "Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." See, in them there was a spiritual baptism and a spiritual eating, to attest faith in Christ, just as in us. And as baptism is for us the seal of the righteousness of faith, so circumcision was for them (Rom. 4). On the other hand, Col. 2 attributes to us a spiritual circumcision, as also Rom. 2. Christ himself plainly taught that all things that pertain to salvation are common to us and to the Fathers alike, as in Matt. 8, where, after the time of the revealed gospel, he counts believers together with Abraham: "Many, he says, will come from east and west, and will recline with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven."

units.la: o Petrus Actorum secundo, Deum Abraham, Isaac, & Iacob, Deum patrum ipsorum ait glorificasse filium suum Iesum: & huic omnes prophetas, Moses, Samuelem, & quotquot secuti sunt, tulisse testimonium, & illum esse, quem Deus promiserit patribus, atque omnes per illum benedicendos. In summa, omnium unus Deus, eadem spes patribus de vita aeterna, eadem viuendi regula secundum legem fidei & charitatis, par item cognitio Christi & cofessio de salute propter Christum obtinenda, solus Christus omnibus oftiu ad vitam aeternam: denique omnia, quae principalia sunt & maxime requisita ad salutem, illis & nobis inueniuntur communia: quare aequum est intelligere, omnes ad eandem ecclesiam pertinere, omnes vnius capitis Christi esse membra, omnes in eodem spiritu accessum habere ad patrem. Iudaei tempore reuelati euangelij viuentes, beneficia illa se accepisse confitebantur, quae erant patribus eorum promissa, in fide patrum suorum per fuerunt, eiusdem erant ecclesiae, (loquor de Iudaeis credentibus, qui non tantum secundum carnem erant filij Abrahae) cuius erant ipsorum patres. Deinde euangelio propagato ad gentes, hae eundem spiritu acceperunt, eandem fidem, quam habebant illi Iudaei: licut eleganter Ephes. 2. declaratur. Ergo manifestum est, & gentes, qui prius crediderunt, & qui hodie adhuc credunt, & Iudaeos, qui cum annunciaretur euangelium, viuentes, & patres illorum, qui ante crediderunt, omnes simul vnam tantum ecclesiam constituere, & ad eandem domum Dei pertinere, in qua primum Moses, post vero Christus administrauit.
units.tr: Peter in Acts 2 says that the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of their fathers, glorified his Son Jesus; and that all the prophets, Moses, Samuel and all who followed, bore witness to him, and that he is the one whom God promised to the fathers, and through whom all are to be blessed. In sum, there is one God of all; the Fathers had the same hope of eternal life, the same rule of living according to the law of faith and charity, likewise the same knowledge of Christ and the same confession that salvation is obtained on account of Christ; Christ alone is the door to eternal life for all. Finally, all things that are principal and most required for salvation are found to be common to them and to us. Wherefore it is right to understand that all belong to the same Church, that all are members of the one head, Christ, and that all have access to the Father in the same Spirit. The Jews living at the time of the revealed gospel confessed that they had received those benefits which had been promised to their fathers, and they were in the faith of their fathers; they belonged to the same Church (I am speaking of believing Jews, who were not merely children of Abraham according to the flesh), of which their fathers were members. Then, when the gospel was spread to the Gentiles, these received the same Spirit and the same faith that those Jews had, as is elegantly declared in Eph. 2. Therefore it is clear that the Gentiles who believed earlier, and those who still believe today, and the Jews who lived when the gospel was proclaimed, and their fathers who believed before them, all together constitute only one Church and belong to the same house of God, in which first Moses and then Christ served.

units.la: Sed ex his iam sequi videtur, quando videlicet omnia paria constituuntur inter patres & nos, nullum esse inter legem & euangelium discrimen, cum tamen multis in locis apostolicae literae euangelium clare discernant a lege, & praecedenti collatione demonstratum est, Christum esse Mose praestantiorem: unde id quoq; colligendum est, quod euangelium sit praestantius lege. Quoniam haec ratio, quod Euangelium sit lege praestantius, apte sequi videtur ex praecedenti collatione: & quia nosse discrimen legis & euangelij, nonnihil etiam proderit ad disputationem sequentem, ideo visum est de hac re paulo pluribus agere. Itaque primum id de quaestione oblata vniuersaliter respondemus, quod cum ecclesia eadem sit patrum & nostra, euangelium & lex etiam reuera secundum substantiam, & quantum ad ea, quae principalia sunt ad salutem nostram, item quantum ad ea, quae bonam Dei voluntatem declarant erga homines, nihil inter se differunt. Semper eadem voluntas patris, idem consilium de restaurando humano genere: eadem salvandi per Christum ratio: eadem praecepta de officijs fidei & charitatis: eadem bona promissa omnibus propositia: eadem via, vita, veritas: eadem ecclesia, eadem domus: idem dominus & paterfamilias.
units.tr: But from these things it now seems to follow, namely when all things are established as equal between the fathers and us, that there is no difference between law and gospel; yet in many places the apostolic letters clearly distinguish the gospel from the law, and it has been shown in the preceding comparison that Christ is superior to Moses. Hence this also must be inferred: that the gospel is superior to the law. Indeed this argument, that the gospel is superior to the law, seems fittingly to follow from the preceding comparison; and since knowing the difference between law and gospel will also be of some help for the following discussion, it has seemed good to treat this matter at somewhat greater length. Accordingly, first, we answer the question raised in general terms: since the Church is the same for the Fathers and for us, the gospel and the law, in substance and as far as concerns the things that are principal for our salvation, and likewise as far as they declare God's good will toward men, in fact do not differ from one another. The will of the Father is always the same, the same plan for restoring the human race, the same manner of saving through Christ, the same precepts concerning the duties of faith and charity, the same good things promised and offered to all, the same way, life and truth, the same Church, the same house, the same Lord and master of the household.

units.la: Sed quod ad administrationem attinet, fatemur nonnihil esse discriminis, actale quidem, ut euangelium inde intelligi possit lege multo esse praestantius, sicut inter personas ministrantes, vna est altera praestantior. Neque haec varietas contigit, quod Deus ipse eo filium vel voluntatem aliquo tempore mutarit: sed quod ipsorum credentium status & conditio ita postulat: sicut in magna domo aliter ministratur, & praebentur quaedam pueris, aliter proueditioribus: & aliter oeconomia administratur tempore hyemali, aliter tempore aestiuo: & sic deinceps aliae circumstantiae alia quaedam innouari cogunt, nihilominus manet eadem domus, idem dominus & paterfamilias, eadem publicae utilitatis consideratur ratio: ita in ecclesia & multitudine credentium oportuit fieri. Proinde, quae diuersitas inter euangelium & legem sit consideranda, nos breuiter explicabimus, & ostendemus, in illo discrimine, semper euangelium legi praeeminere.
units.tr: But as far as administration is concerned, we admit there is some difference, so that the gospel can be understood to be far more excellent than the law, just as among ministering persons one is more excellent than another. Nor has this variety come about because God himself changed his Son or his will at some point. It is because the status and condition of the believers themselves demand it. In a large household, things are administered differently: some things are given to children and others to the more mature, and the household economy is managed one way in winter and another in summer. So too, other circumstances compel other things to be renewed. Nevertheless the house remains the same, with the same lord and householder and the same consideration of public benefit. So it had to be in the Church and the multitude of believers. Therefore we shall briefly explain what difference between the gospel and the law is to be considered, and show that in this difference the gospel always excels the law.

units.la: Primum discrimen hoc est, quod in lege Deus ad bona aeterna & spiritualia apprehendenda excitabat illos, proponendo etiam terrena & temporalia bona, vt sic a terrenis ad coelestia paulatim adduceretur. In euangelio autem omissis promissionibus illis de terrenis bonis, sola spiritualia proponuntur expetenda, atque etiam exhibentur. Atque illa ratio conueniebat illi aetati, tanquam pueritiae: sicut pueros solent propositis paruis praemijs, pomis atque esculentis ad virtutem excitare. Quo pertinet quod apostolus Galat. 4. facit eos, qui sub lege erant, similes pueris, eos vero, qui sub euangelio sunt, similes adultis. Itaque lex paedagogia erat piorum hominum, & propositis, praeter aeterna & spiritualia praemia, etiam praemijs temporalibus, eos inofficio cotinebat. Non quod illi non iuberentur erigere animos potissimum in aeterna & spiritualia, sed quod temporalibus bonis quasi signis essent in spe spiritualium confirmandi, ac fides eorum vtriusque generis promissionibus debebant acui & exerceri.
units.tr: The first difference is this: in the law God stirred them to lay hold of eternal and spiritual goods, while also setting before them earthly and temporal goods, so that they might gradually be led from earthly things to heavenly ones. In the gospel, however, those promises of earthly goods are set aside, and only spiritual things are proposed to be desired and are also offered. That method suited that age, which was like childhood, just as children are usually stirred to virtue by small rewards set before them, such as apples and sweets. To this pertains what the apostle does in Gal. 4, making those who were under the law like children, and those who are under the gospel like adults. Thus the law was a schoolmaster of pious men, and, besides eternal and spiritual rewards, it kept them in their duty by setting before them temporal rewards as well. Not that they were not commanded to lift their minds chiefly to eternal and spiritual things, but temporal goods were, as it were, signs by which they were to be confirmed in hope of spiritual things, and their faith was to be sharpened and exercised by promises of both kinds.

units.la: Qua etiam de causa de aeternis poenis docere volens Deus, tunc multiplicauit, & crebro inflixit poenas corporales: quia per corporalia erant adducendi ad spiritualia. Ac revera eodem tendunt omnia tam veteris, quam noui testamenti, & ad spiritualia aeterna bona.
units.tr: For this reason too, God, wishing to teach about eternal punishments, then multiplied and frequently inflicted bodily punishments, because through bodily things they were to be led to spiritual things. And indeed all things of both the Old and the New Testament tend to the same end, namely spiritual and eternal good.

units.la: Augustinus libro 3. ad Bonifacium similia habet. Communitas salutis omnium credentium.
units.tr: Augustine, in book 3 to Boniface, has similar things. The communion of salvation of all believers.

units.la: Quaestio. An nullum sit Euangelij & legis discrimen. Responsio. Ecclesia patrum eadem, quae nostra. Euangelium et lex secundum substantiam et primipalia, non differunt. In quibus lex & Euangelium conueniant. Discrimen in administratione. Vnde varietas administrationis, etc. Ratio credetium poscit diuersitate, etc.
units.tr: Question: whether there is no difference between gospel and law. Answer: the Church of the fathers was the same as ours. The gospel and the law do not differ in substance and in principal matters. In what respects law and gospel agree. The difference lies in administration. Whence the variety of administration, etc. The condition of believers demands diversity, etc.

units.la: 1. discrimen legis et euangelij. Lex continet bona temporalia promissa euangelium spiritualia. Pueris dat crustula blandis. Lex paedagogia piorum. Poenae corporales indicia sunt aeternarum. bona, proficiscuntur promissiones factæ ad patres, sicut illæ, quæ factæ sunt per Christũ in euangelio: ut reuera discrimen admodum paruum, quantum ad hanc rem in veniatur. Porrò quanto præstantius est iam, directè et immediatè accipere spiritualia, quàm ad ea peruenire primum ductu temporalium, & quanto præstantior est ætas virilis, quàm puerilis: tantò excellentius est euangelium lege.
units.tr: (1) The difference between law and gospel. The law contains temporal goods as promises; the gospel, spiritual ones. It gives children sweets with caresses. The law is the schoolmaster of the pious. Bodily punishments are signs of eternal ones. The promises made to the fathers proceed, like those made through Christ in the gospel, so that in truth the difference is very small as far as this matter is concerned. Moreover, how much more excellent it is to receive spiritual things directly and immediately, rather than first to come to them by the guidance of temporal things, and how much more excellent manhood is than childhood, by so much is the gospel more excellent than the law.

units.la: Secundum discrimen est, quòd in veteri testamento figurę & vmbrę proponebantur: In euangelio res, veritas, & corpora exhibentur. 1. Corinth.10. omnia figurę contigerūt illis. 2. Corinth.3. Velamen Mosi in lectione veteris testamenti. Vide ibi collationem, vbi lex vocatur litera deformata in tabulis lapideis, prædicatio mortis, damnationis, euacuanda. Euangelium verò spiritus, scriptum in cordibus, prædicatio vitæ, iustitiæ, permanens. Christus Matthæi 11. A' diebus Ioannis baptistæ usque ad hûc diem regnum cœlorum vim patitur, & violenti rapiunt illud. Nam omnes prophetæ & ipsa lex usque ad Ioannem prophetauerunt. Ideoque ipse adimplens omnia, quæ præfigurata fuerunt, dixit: consummatum est: & diuersis locis figuras veteris testamenti ipse de se exposuit: ut de manna in deserto, de serpente erecto, de Iona in ventre ceti, &c. Huc item pertinet illud Matthæi 13. Multi reges & prophetæ desiderarunt videre, quæ vos videtis, & non viderunt, et audire, quę vos auditis, et non audierunt, &c. Beati ergo oculi vestri, quia vident, & aures vestræ, quia audiunt, &c. De reuelata nimirum gratia & veritate per Christum, euangelium ubique loquitur, quia Christus in lege solum erat promissus & adumbratus. Cæterùm cùm præstantior sit veritas & corpus, quàm imago siue vmbra, & præsentia exhibita præstant promissis, liquet etiam, euangelium lege esse eminentius. Illudque notandum, quòd, ubi huiusmodi collationes legis cum euangelio occurrunt, inquibus lex vocatur ministra mortis, &c. Non ita sunt hæc accipienda, quasi lex ideò foret inutilis, aut penitùs damnanda: sed itaper collationem dicuntur, ad ostendendam dignitatem euangelij. Vnde non tantùm faciunt discrimen, quantum primo aspectu apparet. Et vbi idem intelligitur esse tàm veteris, quàm noui testamenti obiectum videlicet Christus, certè, quantum ad principale, quod in vtroque agitur, discrimem prorsus nullum est.
units.tr: The second difference is that in the Old Testament figures and shadows were set forth, while in the gospel the reality, the truth and the bodies are exhibited. 1 Cor. 10: all these things happened to them as figures. 2 Cor. 3: the veil of Moses in the reading of the Old Testament. See there the comparison, where the law is called the letter engraved on tablets of stone, a preaching of death and condemnation, to be abolished; but the gospel is the Spirit, written in hearts, a preaching of life, righteousness and permanence. Christ, Matt. 11: "From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. For all the prophets and the law itself prophesied until John." Therefore he himself, fulfilling all that had been foreshadowed, said: "It is finished," and in various places he himself expounded the figures of the Old Testament concerning himself, as of the manna in the desert, of the serpent lifted up, of Jonah in the belly of the whale, etc. To this also pertains Matt. 13: "Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it, etc. Blessed, then, are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear, etc." Indeed the gospel everywhere speaks of grace and truth revealed through Christ, because in the law Christ was only promised and foreshadowed. Moreover, since truth and body are more excellent than image or shadow, and present reality surpasses promises, it is also clear that the gospel is more eminent than the law. And this is to be noted: where such comparisons of law and gospel occur, in which the law is called the minister of death, etc., these are not to be taken as if the law were therefore useless or wholly to be condemned. They are made by way of comparison, to show the dignity of the gospel. Hence they make not as great a difference as appears at first sight. And where it is understood that the object of both the Old and the New Testament is the same, namely Christ, then, as far as the principal matter treated in both is concerned, there is no difference at all.

units.la: Tertium discrimen. Vetus testamentum ad seruitutem quodammodo adigebat, & timorem incutiebat: euangelium autem adfert spiritualem libertatem, & reddit conscientias tranquillas. Hoc discrimen collectum est ex illo Roman. 8. Non accepistis spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus Abba, pater. Idem confirmat Apostolus Galat. 4. vbi per allegoriam de duobus filijs Abrahæ, omnes ex Agar ancilla, quę significat montem Sina, in qua data est lex, natos seruos esse ait: eos verò, qui nati sunt ex Sara, quæ significat cœlestem Hierusalem, vnde prodijt euangelium, liberos esse. Quòd si qui ex patribus dicuntur eodem spiritu libertatis fuisse prædidi, quem accepimus sub euangelio, id non contigit illis nisi per Christum, in quem salutis suæ spem collocabant, & cuius iam tùm gustum aliquem percipiebant.
units.tr: The third difference. The Old Testament in some sense bound men to servitude and instilled fear, but the gospel brings spiritual liberty and makes consciences calm. This difference is gathered from Rom. 8: "You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, through whom we cry, Abba, Father." The apostle confirms the same in Gal. 4, where, through an allegory about the two sons of Abraham, he says that all born of Hagar the slave woman, who signifies Mount Sinai, where the law was given, are born slaves; but those born of Sarah, who signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, whence the gospel came forth, are free. But if some of the fathers are said to have been endowed with the same spirit of liberty that we have received under the gospel, this did not happen to them except through Christ, in whom they placed the hope of their salvation, and of whom they already then perceived some taste.

units.la: Porrò cùm patres contigerit etiam spirituali libertate gaudere, sicut de Abrahã ait Christus Ioan.8. & rursus eos, qui sub euangelio etiamnum hoc tempore sunt, oportet terrore & duritia legis humiliari, atque ita ad pœnitentiam adduci, priusquàm fructus euangelij percipiant: sanè manifestum est, eundem spiritum & libertatis & seruitutis utroq; tempore suum habuisse, & habere locum: ac proinde discrimen istud perexiguum esse. Interea temporis cùm aliter non possit constitui, quàm spiritum libertatis propriũ esse euangelio: & libertatem cŏstet multis interuallis præire seruitutem, iudicare vnus quisque potest, quantum legi præemineat euangelium.
units.tr: Moreover, since it also happened to the fathers to rejoice in spiritual liberty, as Christ says of Abraham in John 8, and conversely, those who are under the gospel even now at this time must be humbled by the terror and hardness of the law and thus brought to repentance before they receive the fruits of the gospel, it is clear that the same Spirit, of both liberty and bondage, had and has its place in both periods; and therefore that difference is very slight. Meanwhile, since it cannot be established otherwise than that the spirit of liberty is proper to the gospel, and since liberty by its nature requires that bondage go before it over many intervals, each one can judge how much the gospel excels the law.

units.la: Quartũ discrimen est, quòd veritatis cognitio et lex olim ad vnam tantũ gentem pertinuit, ut Deuteronomij 10. Psalm.78. Deuteron.32. & aliis locis multis ostenditur. Euangelium verò ad omnes homines toto orbe terrarum dispersos pertinet. Per Christum enim vocatæ sunt etiam gentes, & omnes adeò creaturæ. Qua de re Marci vltimo, Roman.9. Ephes.2. 1.Petri 2. vbi de vocatione gentium. Quia placuit Deo, cognitionem sui latius diffundere, & dona spiritus largius distribuere: hoc solùm, quantum ad hanc partem attinet, est inter legem & euangelium discrimen, quòd profectò non magnum est, sed ad euangelij præstantiam commendandam valde idoneum.
units.tr: The fourth difference is that the knowledge of the truth and the law formerly pertained to one nation only, as is shown in Deut. 10, Ps. 78, Deut. 32, and many other places. But the gospel pertains to all men scattered throughout the whole world. For through Christ even the Gentiles have been called, and indeed all creatures. On this matter see Mark, last chapter, Rom. 9, Eph. 2, and 1 Pet. 2, where the calling of the Gentiles is discussed. Because it has pleased God to spread the knowledge of himself more widely and to distribute the gifts of the Spirit more abundantly, this alone, as far as this part is concerned, is the difference between law and gospel. It is certainly not a great one, but it is very suitable for commending the excellence of the gospel.

units.la: Sed iam dicis, Si adeò modicum est discrimen, cur ergo sic discernuntur appellatione, vt euangelium vocetur testamentum nouum, Lex autem testamentum vetus: notum autem est quantum distent inter se vetus & nouum. Et hæc differentia expressa est Hieremiæ 31. & citatur huius epistolæ capite octauo, Ecce dies veniet, dicit Dominus, & consummabo super domum Israel, et super domum Iuda testamentum (vel fœdes) nouum, non iuxta testamentum quod feci cum patribus illorũ, in die cum apprehenderē manũ illorum,
units.tr: But you will say: if the difference is so slight, why are the two so distinguished by name that the gospel is called the New Testament and the Law the Old Testament? It is well known how far the old and the new differ. This difference is expressed in Jeremiah 31 and is quoted in chapter eight of this epistle: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord."

units.la: ο ι illorum, ut educerem vos ex Ægypto, quoniam ipsi non perstiterūt in testamento meo, & ego neglectui eos habui, dicit Dominus. Et Christus Matth. 26. accepto populo, gratijs actis, dedit illis, dicens: Bibite ex hoc omnes. Hic est enim sanguis meus, qui est noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Idem habetur Marci 14. Lucæ 22. 1. Corinth. 11, Proinde dicendum est: tam vetus, quam nouum testamentum reuera vnū idemque esse & fuisse, quod ad substantiam attinet, verū certo tempore appellatione noui id accepisse, propter nouam, & alio modo factam tradendi formam, confirmationem & obsignationem. Nam antea quidem id obsignatum erat etiam sanguine, Exodi 12. & ceremonijs diuersis: postea verò, vbi Christus aduenit, is obsignauit & confirmauit id proprio suo sanguine, & ceremoniæ cænæ institutione, quam inde dominicam appellamus. Et per hanc posteriorē obsignationē omnia, quæ prioris obsignationis erant, vtpote iam supervacanea, & respectu posterioris, nullius mométi euincutur. Similitudine istud posset commodius explicari. Si quis semel condidit testamentum præsentibus testibus, & satis rite pro more: postea verò idem testamentum exhibet Senatui, vt is cognitionem habeat, & præterea sua autoritate reddat confirmatius validiusq; huiusmodi, in quam, testamentum erit vnum idemq; testamentum, & tamen respectu confirmationis apud Senatum factæ nouum vel renouatum dicetur, cuius respectu prior obsignatio vetus dicetur, ac iam vires suas amittit, & quodammodo aboletur. Sed de his satis, vt, quomodo in eadem domo Dei & Christus & Moses administrarint, cognosci possit.
units.tr: And Christ, in Matthew 26, when he had taken the cup and given thanks, gave it to them, saying: "Drink ye all of it. For this is my blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins." The same is found in Mark 14, Luke 22 and 1 Corinthians 11. Therefore it must be said that the old covenant and the new are really one and the same in substance, as far as their substance goes, but at a certain time the covenant received the name of new, on account of the new form of delivering it, which was made in another way, and on account of its confirmation and sealing. For before, indeed, it had been sealed also with blood (Exodus 12) and with various ceremonies; but afterwards, when Christ came, he sealed and confirmed it with his own blood and by the institution of the supper, which we therefore call the Lord's. And by this later sealing, all that belonged to the earlier sealing are proved to be of no account, since they are now superfluous and, in comparison with the later, count for nothing. This could be explained more fittingly by a comparison. Suppose someone once drew up a will in the presence of witnesses, and quite properly and according to custom; afterwards he presents the same will to the Senate, so that it may be known there, and besides, by its authority, it is made more firm and more valid. The will will still be one and the same will, and yet, with respect to the confirmation made before the Senate, it will be called new or renewed, and with respect to this the earlier sealing will be called old, and it now loses its force and is in some measure abolished. But enough of these things, so that it may be known how both Christ and Moses served in the same house of God.

units.la: Addenda hic breuis repetitio totius collationis Christi cum Mose.
units.tr: Here a brief recapitulation of the whole comparison of Christ with Moses should be added.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: QV apropter sicut dicit spiritus ille Sanctus. Hodie si uocem eius audieritis, ne obdurelis corda vestra, sicut in exacerbatione, in die tentationis in deserto, vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri, probauerunt me, & viderunt opera mea quadraginta annis. Quapropter infensus eram generationi illi, & dicebā: Semper errant corde, ipsi vero non cognouerunt vias meas, sicut iuraui in ira mea, si ingressuri sunt in requiem meam. Videte fratres, &c.
units.tr: Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: "Today if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was grieved with that generation, and said: They always err in their heart, and they have not known my ways. So I swore in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest." Take heed, brethren, etc.

units.la: Hæc est totius primæ partis Conclusio, inquā, quandoquidē hactenus satis diffusè & luculenter probatum est, Christum esse natura Deum, ac proinde (contra atque aduersarij cōtendebant) superiore angelis: deinde ipso etiam Mose præstantiorem, iam recte infert, & hortatur, ut Christum talem tātumque, nec non eius doctrinam placidè suscipiant atque amplectantur: quod nisi dum oportunum est, faciant, iram Dei nequaquam euasurus.
units.tr: This is the conclusion of the whole first part. I say this because it has now been sufficiently and clearly proved at length that Christ is God by nature, and therefore (contrary to what the adversaries contended) superior to the angels, and even more excellent than Moses himself. The apostle now rightly infers and exhorts that they should receive and embrace Christ, so great and so exalted, and his doctrine too, calmly. Unless they do so while there is still opportunity, they will by no means escape the wrath of God.

units.la: Hæc conclusionis, quam prolixam & elegantem plenamq; affectib. instituit, summa est. Respicit autem hæc exhortatio clare ad propositionem disputationis, qua dicebatur eum nobis hodie, id est, nouissimis hisce diebus locutum per filium. Ac videtur plane Apostolus, quod ad sententiam attinet, mente defixus fuisse in illud vaticinium Mosis de Christo Deuteronomij 18. Qui autem verba eius, quæ loquetur in nomine meo, audire noluerit, ego ultor existam. Etiamsi verborum istorum mentionem nequaquam faciat. Fortasis ideo nō usus est hoc testimonio Mosis, vel quòd ab Apostolis alias creberrimè & propemodum ad tædium usque efsetinculcatū, nihilque eò haberetur tritius, ut liquet Actorum tertio & septimo: vel, quòd Iudæi eo supra modum commoueri offendique solerent.
units.tr: This is the summary of the conclusion, which he composed at length, elegantly, and full of feeling. This exhortation clearly looks back to the proposition of the argument, where it was said that God has spoken to us "today," that is, in these last days, through the Son. The apostle, as far as the sense goes, seems plainly to have had in mind that prophecy of Moses about Christ in Deuteronomy 18: "Whoever will not hear my words, which he shall speak in my name, I myself will be the avenger." Yet he makes no mention of those words. Perhaps he did not use this testimony of Moses either because the apostles had elsewhere very often pressed it, almost to the point of tedium, and nothing was more familiar, as is clear from Acts 3 and 7; or because the Jews were wont to be stirred and offended beyond measure by it.

units.la: Quomodocunque res se habeat, mirabili profectò consilio, alijs verbis, alio item assumpto aptissimo testimonio, eandem exprimit sententiā, & maiori artificio, quàm explicari à nobis vnquàm posit. Probè enim consideranst, Iudæos ad quos scribebat, morosos, duræ ceruicis homines esse, quique minis impelli potius quàm blanditijs duci deberent, ita instituit adhortationem, ut primò non suis verbis eam texat, sed eximij prophetæ: ex quo deinde testimonium eiusmodi eligit, quo non queat aliud ad causam commodius excogitari, utpotè, quod graues minas contra credere nolentes continet, quòd propter exemplum patrum in eo ob oculos positum, valde omnes moueat pungatque. Denique ex quo varia, & admodum efficacia argumenta ad excitandos illorum animos excerpi posfiat. Vnde paulò fusius & accuratius excutiendo quasi singulas eius testimonij particulas, suasoria argumenta ex illis non pauca elicit, atque ita insignem conclusionē absoluit. Addit itaq;: Quapropter sicut dicit spiritus ille Sanctus: nō sine causa ait, à spiritu Sancto ista dici potius, quàm à Dauide, cùm tamen ab hoc pronunciata constet. Ita enim nō solùm attentiores reddit omnium animos, verùm etiam ab autoritate diuina grauissimū addit suæ exhortationi pondus, ut qui vel Apostolum, si suis tantùm verbis loqueretur, vel Dauidem etiam auderent contemnere, vel verba Dauidis aliter interpretari, à mente Spiritus sancti ea deflectendo, scirent tamen, sibi audiendum spiritum Sanctum, qui revera per os prophetarum loquitur (testante id Petro posterioris epistolæ suæ capite primo) & cuius verba nemo impunè contemnit. Sic ergo ab Hebræis vult exhortationem istam excipi, tanquàm si spiritum Sanctum, id est, Deum ipsum concionantem hic audirent. Notum autem est, inter testimonia primum locum diuina oracula obtinere: qua de re etiam Rhetores recte tradiderunt. Facile itaque quiuis cernit, prudentissimè hanc conclusionem institui, sicque incipere: Quapropter sicut dicit spiritus ille sanctus: Hodie particula illationibus & conclusionibus apta. Infert enim hic, perinde ac si diceretur: Hactenus satis demonstratum est, Christum esse Deum ac proinde angelis ac Mose multò excellentiorem. Quapropter hoc iam restat, ut eum præ Mose amplectamini & celatis.
units.tr: However the matter stands, with remarkable judgement he expresses the same sentiment in other words, adducing another most apt testimony, and with greater skill than we can ever explain. For he considers well that the Jews to whom he was writing were stubborn, hard-necked people, who ought to be moved by threats rather than drawn by flattery. So he framed his exhortation not by weaving it first from his own words, but from those of an eminent prophet. From him he then chooses a testimony of such a kind that no other could be devised more suitable to the cause, since it contains grave threats against those unwilling to believe, and because of the example of the fathers set before their eyes in it, it strongly moves and pricks them all. Finally, from it can be drawn various and very effective arguments for stirring their minds. Hence, by examining more fully and carefully, as it were, each part of this testimony, he elicits from it not a few persuasive arguments, and so completes a striking conclusion. He adds therefore: Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today. He says not without cause that these things are spoken by the Holy Spirit rather than by David, although it is established that they were uttered by David. For in this way he not only makes the minds of all more attentive, but also adds the greatest weight of divine authority to his exhortation. Those who would dare to despise the Apostle if he spoke only in his own words, or even to despise David, or to interpret David's words otherwise, turning them away from the mind of the Holy Spirit, would nevertheless know that they must listen to the Holy Spirit, who truly speaks through the mouths of the prophets (as Peter testifies in the first chapter of his second epistle), and whose words no one despises with impunity. So he wants this exhortation received by the Hebrews as if they were hearing the Holy Spirit, that is, God himself preaching here. Now it is well known that among testimonies the divine oracles hold the first place, and the rhetoricians have rightly taught this too. Anyone can easily see, therefore, that this conclusion is very wisely constructed and begins thus: Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, the particle being suited to inferences and conclusions. For it infers here, as if it were said: It has been sufficiently demonstrated so far that Christ is God, and therefore far more excellent than the angels and than Moses. What remains, therefore, is that you embrace him before Moses and hold him dear.

units.la: Spiritus ille Sanctus) non caret emphasi articulus τὸ. Significat enim, se spiritum illum intelligere, qui Deus est, distinctaque persona à patre & filio: Sic verò solent græci, præsertim interpretes, subinde notare, articulum plurimum habere momenti ad personarum discretionem. Itaque spiritus Sancti, id est, Dei, adfert testimonium, quo illos, ad quos scribebat, acrius urget. Fortassis etiam ideò, ut doceat, quòd, quemadmodum pater testimonium tulit de filio, id quod in disputatione de diuina natura Christi declaratum est: ita spiritus Sanctus quoque de Christo tulerit testimonium. Cuius testimonium magni debebat fieri, sicut Ioannes Baptista Ioannis primo, diserte ait: Vidi spiritum descendentem specie columbæ de cœlo, & mansit super eum, & ego non noueram eum: sed, qui misit me, ut baptizarem aqua, is mihi dixit: super quem videris spiritum descendentem, ac manentè super eum, hic est, qui baptizat spiritu Sancto. Et ego vidi & testificatus sum, hunc esse filium Dei. A quo non admodum diuersum est illud Lucæ 4. Cùm Christus veniffetin Synagogam, & surrexisset ut legeret, traditus est ei liber Esaiæ prophetæ, & ut explicuit librum, inuenit locum, vbi scriptum erat: Spiritus Domini super me, propterea quod unxit me, &c. Et Roman. 1. dicitur Christus declaratus filius Dei cum potentia, secundum spiritum sanctificationis. Hoc igitur pacto Christo fert testimonium de diuinitate, etiá spiritus Sanctus, cuius testimonium magni ab omnibus debet fieri. Sed dicat aliquis: Quorsum adducat Apostolus testimonium spiritus Sancti; cùm Iudæi eum non agnouerint? Imò, videtur quòd hoc nomine potius reiecturi fuissent Iudæi istud testimonium, quàm suscepturi, præsertim cùm distinctas personas filij & Spiritus sancti in diuinitate non agnouerint? Respondetur: si ad ipsos credentes Apostolus verba facit, sicut reuera facit, nihil offendit. Dubium enim non est, quin hi de mysterio Trinitatis edocti fuerint, & sicut filium, ita quoque Spiritum sanctum distinctas personas intellexerint. Quod verò ad aduersarios attinet, non erat quòd hac forma loquendi offenderentur. Nam etiá si Spiritum sanctum distinctam personam in diuinitate, uti nos, non crediderint, tamen aliquo modo diuinam virtutem, ipsumque Deum ea forma locutionis intelligebant. In Scripturis enim veteris instrumenti sæpè de Spiritu sancto, de Spiritu Domini, vel Dei, fit mentio, & per homines, etiam hominib. Spiritus Dei agere describitur: ut Geneseos 41. Pharao ad ministros suos: Num inuenire poterimus talem virum, qui Spiritu Dei plenus sit? Exodi 31. Locutus est Deus ad Mosen, dicens: Ecce vocaui de nomine Bezalel filiu Vri filij Hur e tribu Iuda: replevi eum Spiritu Dei, sapientia, & intelligentia, & scientia, & omni arte, ad excogitandum quicquid fabre fieri potest ex auro & argento & ære: & in arte lignaria, ut operetur in omni opere, &c. Exodi. 11. Quis tribuat, ut omnis populus propheter, & det eius Dominus Spiritum suum?
units.tr: The Holy Spirit) the article [τὸ] is not without emphasis. For it signifies that he means the Spirit who is God, and a person distinct from the Father and the Son. The Greeks, especially the translators, often note that the article has great weight for distinguishing the persons. Thus he brings forward the testimony of the Holy Spirit, that is, of God, by which he urges more sharply those to whom he was writing. Perhaps also this is done so that he may teach that, just as the Father bore witness concerning the Son (which was declared in the discussion of the divine nature of Christ), so the Holy Spirit too has borne witness concerning Christ. This testimony ought to be greatly valued, as John the Baptist plainly says in John chapter 1: "I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him, and I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. And I saw and testified that this is the Son of God." Not very different from this is Luke 4: when Christ had come into the synagogue and stood up to read, the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him, and when he had unrolled the book he found the place where it was written: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me, etc. And in Romans 1 Christ is said to be declared the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of sanctification. In this way the Holy Spirit too bears witness to Christ concerning his divinity, and his testimony ought to be greatly valued by all. But someone may say: why does the Apostle adduce the testimony of the Holy Spirit, since the Jews did not acknowledge him? Indeed, it seems that the Jews would rather have rejected this testimony under this name than accepted it, especially since they did not acknowledge the distinct persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit in the divinity. The answer is: if the Apostle is speaking to the believers themselves, as in fact he is, he gives no offence. For there is no doubt that these had been taught about the mystery of the Trinity, and understood the Holy Spirit as a distinct person just as they did the Son. As for the adversaries, there was no reason for them to be offended by this manner of speaking. For even if they did not believe the Holy Spirit to be a distinct person in the divinity, as we do, nevertheless in some way they understood by this form of speech the divine power, and God himself. For in the Scriptures of the Old Testament there is frequent mention of the Holy Spirit, of the Spirit of the Lord or of God, and it is described that the Spirit of God acts through men, even upon men: as in Genesis 41, Pharaoh says to his servants: "Can we find such a man as this, in whom the Spirit of God is?" In Exodus 31 God spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and every skill to devise whatever can be made skilfully from gold, silver and bronze, and in carving wood, to work in every craft, etc. In Exodus 11: "Would that all the people were prophets, and that the Lord would give his Spirit upon them!"

units.la: Et passim de sanctis viris dicitur, quòd irruit in eos spiritus Domini, & prophetarunt, spiritus Domini induit eos, &c. ut de Simsone Iudicum 14. Item Dauid psalmo 50. Ne proijcias me à facie tua: Spiritum sanctum tuum ne auferas à me. Quibus in locis spiritus non aliter potest accipi, quàm quo nos quoque modo accipimus, quoties de spiritu sancto pro ut distincta persona est in diuinitate, eiusq; donis loquimur. Nam de donis eius spiritus vbique sermo est, cuiusmodi dona describit Apostolus 1. Corinth. 12. sicut & ante eum dona diuersa enumerarat, Esaias capite vndecimo.
units.tr: And in many places it is said of holy men that the Spirit of the Lord came upon them and they prophesied, or the Spirit of the Lord clothed them, etc., as of Samson in Judges 14. Likewise David in Psalm 50: "Cast me not away from your face, and take not your Holy Spirit from me." In these places the Spirit cannot be understood otherwise than in the way we also understand it whenever we speak of the Holy Spirit as he is a distinct person in the divinity, and of his gifts. For throughout there is discussion of his gifts, of the kind the Apostle describes in 1 Corinthians 12, just as Isaiah before him had listed various gifts in chapter 11.

units.la: Proinde, quia adeo clara testimonia de spiritu Dei occurrunt, multi etiam Iudæi coacti sunt fateri, vocem רוּחַ, quæ ipsis significat ventum, flatum, spirationem, anhelitum, non semper his significationibus accipiendam, præsertim quando adiuctam habet vocem אֱלֹהִים vel יְהֹוָה: sed sæpè ipsi interpretati sunt רוּחַ, significare spiritum, mentem diuinam, voluntatem & consilium, quo Deus res admirandas peragit. Sic inquam veteres Iudæi hominum significationes sunt interpretati, planè idem, quod nos, sentientes ea in parte: nisi quòd distinctas personas nostro more non sunt confessi.
units.tr: Therefore, since such clear testimonies about the Spirit of God occur, many Jews have also been compelled to admit that the word רוּחַ [ruach], which for them means wind, breath, blowing, or breathing, is not always to be taken in these senses, especially when it is joined with the name אֱלֹהִים [Elohim] or יְהֹוָה [Jehovah]. Often they have themselves explained רוּחַ to mean the divine Spirit, the divine mind, the will and counsel by which God accomplishes wonderful works. I say that the ancient Jews interpreted the word in this way, and in this respect they judged just as we do, except that they did not confess distinct persons in our manner.

units.la: ò s
units.tr: (The line is illegible in the scan.)

units.la: Recentiores autem Iudęi semper Spiritū significatione flatus, venti, anhelitus, vel aliquo modo voluntatis Dei exponunt: at ea significatione, qua nos accipimus, nunquam: idque ne videantur Trinitatem personarum in vnitate essentiæ nobiscum approbare. Attamen quia hoc nō ignorabant, nec dissimulare poterant, quòd spiritu Dei afflati seu imbuti locuti sint sancti prophetæ, apta erat hæc apud ipsos quoque aduersarios locutio, quòd Spiritus sanctus ista diceret, quæ propheta prius enunciarat. Et hoc idem ex phrasibus scripturæ edocti erant, quod nobis tradidit Petrus prioris epistolæ capite primo, dicens: Non enim uoluntate hominis allata est olim prophetia, sed à spiritu Sancto impulsi locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Vbi Petrus præmittit, quod hoc loco nobis notandum erat, nempe, quanta sit propheticorum dictorum vtilitas, & quanta æstimatio eorundem apud nos esse debeat. Et habemus, inquit, firmiorem sermonem propheticū, cui dum attenditis ceu lucernæ apparentem obscuro loco, recte facitis, donec dies illucescat, et lucifer exoriatur in cordib. vestris.
units.tr: But more recent Jews always explain Spirit in the sense of blowing, wind, or breath, or in some way as the will of God, but never in the sense in which we take it. They do this so that they may not seem to approve with us the Trinity of persons in the unity of essence. Yet, since they did not ignore this and could not deny that the holy prophets spoke when moved or filled by the Spirit of God, this way of speaking was also acceptable even to their opponents: that the Holy Spirit said those things which the prophet had earlier declared. They had been taught this same point from the phrases of Scripture, as Peter handed it down to us in the first chapter of his first epistle, saying: "For the prophecy came not by the will of man at any time, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit." Here Peter first sets out what we ought to note at this point, namely how great the usefulness of the prophetic sayings is, and how highly we ought to esteem them. "And we have a more sure prophetic word," he says, "to which you do well to take heed, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star arises in your hearts."

units.la: Pulchrè confert propheticū sermonem lucernæ ardenti in obscuro: quia reuera prophetarum sermonibus quasi prælucentibus redis erant Iudæi ad agnitionem euangelij adducendi.
