Atque hinc est (ut hoc obiter admoneamus) quòd Apostoli & Euangelistæ diuersum scribendi morem habeant, quàm prophetæ, nimirum quòd prophetæ suas conciones proferebat, præmittedo simpliciter, hæc dicit Dominus: vel alia huiusmodi. Apostoli autem non ita: sed confirmando omnia sua dictis prophetarum: id autem tum quia hæc semper fuit, sicut & esse debet, propheticorum sermonum existimatio, ut recta doctrina non posit ab illis dissentire: tum quia Iudæi suorum prophetarum testimonia erant conuincendi, demonstrandumque, in euangelio non diuersa, sed plane eadem, quæ illi exposuerunt, contineri. Sed, ne quid amplius dicamus, satis ex his constat, recte, imò non sine grauissimis causis dictum ab Apostolo, verba prophetæ esse spiritus Sancti, id est, ipsius Dei verba. Et hanc debemus ex hac locutionis formula doctrinam colligere, quòd doctrina prophetarum & Apostolorum, est doctrina spiritus Sancti, ac proinde religiosissimè colenda, omnibusque doctrinis humanis longè præferenda. Sed ad ipsum testimonium, quod Apostolus citauit, veniamus:
units.tr: Peter aptly compares the prophetic word to a burning lamp in a dark place, because in truth the Jews were to be led to the knowledge of the gospel by the words of the prophets, which shone before them like lamps. From this (so that we may note this in passing) comes the difference in the manner of writing between the Apostles and Evangelists and the prophets. The prophets introduced their sermons simply by saying Thus says the Lord, or something of this kind. The Apostles did not do so, but confirmed all their teaching by the sayings of the prophets. They did this both because this has always been, and must be, the esteem for the prophetic words, so that sound doctrine cannot dissent from them, and because the Jews had to be convicted by the testimonies of their own prophets, and it had to be shown that the gospel contains not different things but plainly the very same things which the prophets set forth. But, to say no more, it is clear enough from these points that the Apostle rightly, and indeed not without the weightiest reasons, called the words of the prophet the words of the Holy Spirit, that is, the very words of God. And from this form of speech we ought to draw this teaching: that the doctrine of the prophets and Apostles is the doctrine of the Holy Spirit, and therefore is to be honoured most religiously and preferred far above all human doctrines. But let us come to the testimony itself which the Apostle cited:

units.la: Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, ne obduretis corda vestra, sicut in exacerbatione, in die tentationis in deserto, vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri, probauerunt me, & viderunt opera mea quadraginta annis. Quapropter infensus eram generationi illi, & dicebam: semper errant corde, ipsi uero non cognouerunt uias meas, sicut iuraui in ira mea, si ingressuri sunt in requiem meam.
units.tr: Today if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works forty years. Wherefore I was grieved with that generation, and said: they always err in heart, but they have not known my ways; as I swore in my wrath, that they shall not enter into my rest.

units.la: Sumptum est testimonium hoc ex Psalmo 94. qui reuera quantus est, potuisset huic argumento rectissimè accommodari.
units.tr: This testimony is taken from Psalm 94, which, great as it is, could have been applied most fittingly to this argument.

units.la: Clarissimè enim in eo omnes inuitamur ad honorandum, colendum, adorandumque Deum, & ad agendum ei gratias, idque cum omni tempore, quia videlicet ipse nos, sicut & omnia condidit, præterea adhuc seruat ac tuetur, habens nos semper pro peculiari suo populo: tum verò præcipuè hodie, id est, tempore reuelati euangelij, quo vocem eius audiimus, per Christum videlicet, qui existens verbum patris factus est caro, & habitauit in nobis.
units.tr: For in it we are all most clearly invited to honour, worship, and adore God, and to give him thanks, and this at all times, since he indeed made us, as he made all things, and moreover still preserves and guards us, always holding us as his peculiar people. Above all, however, he invites us today, that is, in the time of the revealed gospel, in which we hear his voice, namely through Christ, who, being the Word of the Father, became flesh and dwelt among us.

units.la: Ac nisi vocem eius euangelicam benignè audiamus, metuendum, ne miserè eamus perditum, atque à spirituali, cœlesti, & æterna requie excludamur, sicut perierunt, prohibitiqúe sunt requiem terræ promissæ ingredi omnes illi patres, qui in deserto, indurantes corda sua, audire vocem Dei noluerunt.
units.tr: And unless we kindly hear his gospel voice, there is reason to fear that we shall wretchedly perish and be shut out from the spiritual, heavenly, and eternal rest, just as all those fathers perished and were forbidden to enter the rest of the promised land, who in the wilderness, hardening their hearts, were unwilling to hear the voice of God.

units.la: Hoc igitur cum sit eius Psalmi argumentum, cumque apertissimè vaticinetur de tempore reuelati euangelij, & pios, qui id amplexati fuerint, ad gratiarum actionem prouocet: impijs verò, qui id auersantur, adhibito exemplo patrum, ob incredulitatem in defectu pereuntium, comminetur exitium: quiuis intelligit testimonium hoc præsenti loco admodum conuenire. Sed quo facilius istud ab omnibus percipiatur, nos breuiter Psalmū totum percurremus.
units.tr: Since this is therefore the argument of that Psalm, and since it prophesies most plainly about the time of the revealed gospel, calling the pious who have embraced it to thanksgiving, and threatening the impious who reject it with ruin, citing the example of the fathers who perished for unbelief and in default, anyone can see that this testimony fits the present passage very well. But so that this may be grasped more easily by all, we will briefly run through the whole Psalm.

units.la: Satis apparet, eum certo aliquo die magno affectu & lætitia cani solitum, quo populus Israeliticus partim ob beneficia antea accepta, laudabat & agebat gratias: partim etiā confitebatur, se alia ampliora expectare, maximeque auditionem diuinæ vocis, quando ardendissimo affectu illud additur: hodie si uocem eius audieritis, ne obduretis corda uestra, etc. ergo ait:
units.tr: It is clear enough that it was a song customarily sung on some set day with great feeling and joy, in which the people of Israel both praised God and gave thanks, partly for benefits received before, and partly also confessed that they expected greater things, and above all the hearing of the divine voice, when with the most ardent feeling it is added: Today if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts, etc. Therefore it says:

units.la: Venite, exultemus Domino, iubilemus Deo saluatori nostro. Præoccupemus faciem eius in confessione, et in Psalmis iubilemus ei. His verbis primùm inuitantur pij ad laudes & gratiarum actiones.
units.tr: Come, let us exult in the Lord, let us rejoice in God our saviour. Let us come before his face in confession, and let us rejoice in him with psalms. By these words the pious are first invited to praises and thanksgivings.

units.la: Quoniam Deus magnus Dominus, et rex magnus super omnes Deos. Hæc non habentur neque in Hebræo, neq; in Græco. (quoniam non repellet Dominus plebem suam) Quia in manu eius
units.tr: For God is a great Lord, and a great king above all gods. These words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek. (For the Lord will not reject his people.) In whose hand

units.la: Iudæi negant Trinitatem, etc. eius sunt omnes fines terræ, & altitudines montium ipsius sunt. Quoniam ipsius est mare, & ipse fecit illud, & aridam manus eius formauerunt.
units.tr: The Jews deny the Trinity, etc. are all the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his. For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.

units.la: Ratio, quare laudandus & celebrandus Deus, à potentia & bonitate ipsius elucente in creatione vniuersi.
units.tr: The reason why God is to be praised and celebrated: from his power and goodness shining forth in the creation of the universe.

units.la: Venite adoremus, & procidamus, & ploremus ante Dominum, qui fecit nos: quia ipse est Dominus Deus noster, & nos populus eius, & oues manus eius.
units.tr: Come, let us worship and bow down, and weep before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.

units.la: Per affectum, ut acrius incitentur omnes ad laudandū Deum, repetit inuitationis sententiam, adiecta insuper alia ratione particulari, sumpta ab eo, quòd Deus ipsos elegisset in peculiarem populum (hoc enim erat singulare beneficiū, ob quod populus ille maximē debebat Deo gratias omni tempore agere,) & non minori cura prospiceret illorum saluti, quàm bonus & fidus pastor prospicit suis ouibus. Huc pertinet, quòd Christus Ioannis decimo, bonum pastorem se nominat, & esse confirmat. Quanquàm Deus pater quoque pastor est, omnes nos, imò & volucres cœli, & abiectissima quæq; animalcula sua bonitate pascens, ut Matthæi sexto ostenditur. Iam sequitur:
units.tr: Out of feeling, so that all may be the more keenly stirred to praise God, he repeats the sentence of invitation, adding besides another, particular reason, taken from the fact that God had chosen them as his peculiar people (for this was the singular benefit for which that people ought most of all to give thanks to God at all times), and that he cared for their salvation no less than a good and faithful shepherd cares for his sheep. To this belongs the fact that Christ, in John 10, calls himself the good shepherd and affirms that he is one. Yet God the Father is also a shepherd, feeding all of us, and indeed the birds of heaven and the lowliest little creatures, by his goodness, as is shown in Matthew 6. Next follows:

units.la: Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra, sicut in exacerbatione secundum diem tentationis in deserto, vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri, probauerunt & viderunt opera mea. Quadraginta annis offensus fui generationi illi, & dixi, semper hi errant corde. Et isti non cognouerunt vias meas, & iurauí in ira mea, si introibunt in requiem meam.
units.tr: Today if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works. For forty years I was offended with that generation, and said: these always err in heart. And they have not known my ways, and I swore in my wrath that they shall not enter into my rest.

units.la: Iam inuitantur omnes, ut vocem Domini, id est, Euangelium, in quo auditus est loquens ipse Deus, videlicet Christus filius Dei, in quo pater nouissimis diebus locutus est, quando illum manifestari cōtingeret (nam Iudæi omnes sic edocti à patribus & prophetis, ad quos promissiones erant factæ, auidissimè expectabant tempus, quo illa se mel audirentur) lubenter & gratis animis amplecterentur, atq; animos nequaquam obdurarent. Ita enim spiritus Sanctus per os prophetę loquebatur, pręuidens, quòd quàmplurimi forent Iudæi, qui, cùm vox illa diuina in terris audiretur, se illi pertinacissimè opponerent, sicut euentus ipse docuit, & in hunc usque diem comprobat.
units.tr: Now all are invited to hear the voice of the Lord, that is, the gospel, in which God himself, namely Christ the Son of God, is heard speaking, in whom the Father spoke in the last days, when it should come about that he was made manifest (for all the Jews, taught thus by the fathers and prophets, to whom the promises were made, were most eagerly awaiting the time in which those promises were to be heard), and they are to embrace it gladly and willingly, and by no means harden their hearts. For thus the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouth of the prophet, foreseeing that there would be very many Jews who, when that divine voice was heard on earth, would most obstinately set themselves against it, as the event itself has taught and as it confirms down to this very day.

units.la: Sequitur deinde ratio, quare non essent obdurandi animi, à periculosso. Commemorat enim, quanta mala perpessi sint patres eorum, qui olim in deserto vocem Dei contempserunt. Quam rationem pluribus verbis, & non sine amplificatione duriciei & malitiæ illorum pertractat, idq; ut eò magis omnium animos permoueat, & ab incredulitate auocet. En vides, quomodo etiam totus ille psalmus aptissimè præsenti causæ possit accommodari. Sed Apostolo satis fuisset seligere, quòd magis erat idoneum, nempè postremam istam psalmi partem, in qua de voce Domini manifestanda agitur, & duri animi illam contemnentes perterrentur.
units.tr: There follows next the reason why hearts should not be hardened, from the danger involved. For he recalls how many evils the fathers of those who once despised the voice of God in the wilderness suffered. He treats this reason at greater length, and not without amplifying the hardness and malice of those men, and he does so in order to move the minds of all the more and to turn them away from unbelief. See how that whole psalm can be most aptly adapted to the present case. But it would have been enough for the Apostle to select what was more suitable, namely that last part of the psalm, in which the manifestation of the voice of the Lord is treated, and hard hearts that scorn it are terrified.

units.la: Videbat Apostolus grauem istam comminationem magno usui sibi fore, ad agendum cum pertinacibus Iudæis, qui minis cogi semper malunt, quàm blandis promissionibus allici, quiq; se redargui, & incredulitatem suam damnari ægerrimè ferunt, nullisq; rationibus conuinci facilius possunt, quàm exemplis suorum patrum, ob incredulitatem à Deo damnatorum, propositis. Nullis fere alijs argumentis ora eorum possunt obstrui. Vnde & videmus subinde, vbi Christus, vel Apostoli aliquid cupiunt, vel reprehendere, vel è diuerso commendare, semper adducunt exempla seu testimonia patrum ipsorum. Hinc toties commemoratæ promissiones, de venturo semine ad patres factæ, iustitia, & præclara opera patrum passim prædicta & obiecta impiè viuentibus Iudæis: sic deniq; vbiq; patres Iudæis conuincendis opponuntur, & proponuntur.
units.tr: The Apostle saw that this grave warning would be of great use to him in dealing with stubborn Jews, who always prefer to be driven by threats rather than enticed by kind promises, and who take it very badly to be rebuked and to have their unbelief condemned, and who can be convinced more easily by no arguments than by the examples of their fathers, set before them as men condemned by God for unbelief. Their mouths can almost be stopped by no other arguments. Hence we see again and again that whenever Christ or the Apostles wish either to rebuke or, on the contrary, to commend something, they always bring forward the examples or testimonies of their fathers. Hence the promises, so often recalled, made to the fathers about the coming seed, and the righteousness and famous works of the fathers, are everywhere proclaimed and thrown in the face of the impiously living Jews. In this way, finally, the fathers are everywhere set against the Jews and put forward to convict them.

units.la: Cæterùm, tametsi Apostolus ipse copiosè & artificiosè hanc posteriorem Psalmi partem explicat, dum è singulis quasi membris grauissimas rationes suasorias excerpit, nos tanquam viam paraturi ad intelligenda ea, quæ exponuntur per Apostolum, minutiora nonnulla breuiter annotabimus.
units.tr: Moreover, although the Apostle himself explains this latter part of the Psalm fully and skilfully, while from its individual members, as it were, he draws out the most weighty persuasive reasons, we, as it were preparing a way to understand those things which are set out by the Apostle, will briefly note some smaller points.

units.la: Hodie si vocem eius audieritis) Satis conueniunt, quæ hic habentur, cum hebraica veritate, ut nequaquam opus sit in versionis munere occupari, & si quid animaduersione dignum fuerit, nos in progressu indicabimus. Vox Hodie, hoc loco magnam habet emphasin, significatq; tempus reuelati Euangelij; quod sanè ipsi Iudæi tanta cupiditate expectabant, ut quocunq; die psalmum hunc canerent, reuera manifestādum putarent. Christus quidè secundum diuinitatem est heri & hodie, & in secula, ut rectè dicitur huius epistolæ cap. ii. At verò quia nostri causa humana naturam induere est dignatus in tempore, etiā in tempore, ut hodie, esse dicitur.
units.tr: Today, if you hear his voice) What is said here agrees sufficiently with the Hebrew truth, so that there is no need to be occupied with the task of translation; and if anything worthy of remark arises, we will point it out as we go. The word Today here carries great emphasis and signifies the time of the revealed Gospel, which the Jews themselves indeed awaited with such eagerness that on whatever day they sang this psalm they thought it was truly to be made manifest. Christ, indeed, according to his divinity, is "yesterday and today, and forever", as is rightly said in chapter 2 of this epistle. But because he deigned to take on human nature in time for our sake, he is also said to be in time, as today.

units.la: Certo enim tempore, quod à patre fuerat ante constitutionem mundi præfinitū, ipse inter homines homo versatus est. Simili modo accipi vocem hodie, interpretati sumus dicatur. capite primo, enarrantes eum locum psalmi, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: Qua etiam significatione illud dictum apparet Deuteron.27. à Mose ad populum: Attende & audi Israel: Hodie factus es populus Domini Dei tui, audies vocem eius & facies mandata atque iustitias, quas ego praecipio tibi.
units.tr: For at a certain time, which had been predetermined by the Father before the foundation of the world, he dwelt among men as a man. In a similar way we have explained that the word today is to be taken, in the first chapter, where we expounded that passage of the psalm, You are my son; today I have begotten you. In this same sense, too, that saying of Moses to the people in Deuteronomy 27 appears: Attend and hear, Israel: Today you have become the people of the Lord your God; you shall hear his voice and do the commandments and the righteous statutes which I command you.

units.la: Qui locus ob id, quòd continet de audienda uoce Dei, praesenti loco congruit. Item Zachariae 9. vbi describitur Christi aduentus: Ecce rex tuus veniet tibi iustus & saluator, ipse pauper, & ascendens super asinam, & super pullum filium asinae, & disperget quadrigam ex Ephraim, & equum de Hierusalem, & disipabitur arcus belli, & loquetur pacem gentib. & potestas eius a mari usque ad mare, & a fluminibus usque ad fines terrae. Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti emisisti vinctos tuos, de lacu, in quo non est aqua. Conuertimini ad munitionem vincti spei: hodie quoq; annuncians, duplicia reddam tibi. Vbi & de tempore Euangelij reuelandi, vox hodie sine dubio accipienda est.
units.tr: This passage, because it speaks of hearing the voice of God, agrees with the present place. Likewise Zechariah 9, where the coming of Christ is described: Behold, your king will come to you, just and a saviour, himself poor, and riding on an ass, and on a colt, the foal of an ass; and he will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be broken, and he will speak peace to the nations, and his dominion will be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth. You also, by the blood of the covenant, have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit in which there is no water. Turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope; today also I announce that I will restore to you double. Here too the word today must undoubtedly be taken of the time of the revealing of the Gospel.

units.la: Huc referri & illud Christi potest Lucae 19, cùm fleret super ciuitate Hierusalem: Si cognouisses & tu, & quidem in isto die tuo, quae ad pacem tuam pertinent, curares. Ibidem: Et non relinquent in te lapidem super lapidem, eò quòd non cognoueris tempus visitationis tuae. Hic dicendo, isto die, item tempus visitationis, tantundem quod est hodie, significauit. In summa, non est quod aliam interpretationem quaeramus, quando ipse Apostolus capite sequenti diserte idem docet, dicens: per vocem hodie quendam diem multo tempore post venturum praefiniri. Quamobrem non sunt ferendi Iudaei, qui, ut huiusmodi interpretationem euitent, vel obscurent, vocem hodie aliter ordinant, quàm hic ab Apostolo ordinata est. Aben Ezra constituit vocem hodie cum verbis praecedentibus, in hunc modum: Venite adoremus, & procidamus, & ploremus ante Dominum hodie. Dauid Kimhi in illis: Nos populus eius, & oues manus eius sumus hodie: perstemus nos in sententia Apostolica.
units.tr: To this can also be referred that saying of Christ in Luke 19, when he wept over the city of Jerusalem: If you had known, even you, at least in this your day, the things that belong to your peace. And again: And they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation. Here, by saying this day, and likewise the time of your visitation, he signified just as much as today. In sum, there is no need to seek any other interpretation, since the Apostle himself in the following chapter plainly teaches the same, saying that by the word today a certain day is appointed to come after a long time. Therefore the Jews are not to be tolerated, who, in order to avoid or obscure such an interpretation, arrange the word today otherwise than the Apostle has arranged it here. Aben Ezra joins the word today with the preceding words, in this manner: Come, let us adore and bow down and weep before the Lord today. David Kimhi (joins it) in those words: We are his people and the sheep of his hand today: let us stand in the Apostle's sense.

units.la: Pari studio obscurandi spiritus Sancti sententiam, Vocem Domini, hoc loco interpretantur Iudaei, sonare praecedentem inuitationem: cùm tamen per vocem Domini intelligere conueniat Euangelium, & Dei Patris de Christo manifestato toti mundo testimonium: quomodo Matthaei tertio, cùm Christus baptizaretur, vox Patris de coelo audita est: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacitum est. Iterum in monte Thabor Matthaei decimoseptimo, vox e nube dicens: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacitum est, hunc audite: ob quod testimonium Christum audiendum, etiā Petrus argumentatur, dicens posterioris epistolae capite primo: Acceperat, inquit, à Deo patre honorem & gloriam, voce ad illum delata huiusmodi à magnifica gloria: Hic est ille filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est.
units.tr: With the same zeal for obscuring the meaning of the Holy Spirit, the Jews interpret The voice of the Lord in this place as meaning the preceding invitation; yet by the voice of the Lord it is fitting to understand the Gospel, and the testimony of God the Father concerning Christ made manifest to the whole world: as in Matthew 3, when Christ was baptized, the voice of the Father was heard from heaven: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Again, on the mount Tabor, Matthew 17, a voice from the cloud saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him. Peter argues from this testimony that Christ must be heard, saying in the first chapter of the second epistle: He had received, he says, from God the Father honour and glory, when such a voice was brought to him from the magnificent glory: This is that my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

units.la: Et hanc vocem nos audiuimus à coelo delatam, cùm essemus vnà cum illo in monte sancto. Quin ipsa doctrina Christi voluntate, ac iussu Patris manifestata vox appellatur, Ioan.10. Alias oues habeo, quae non sunt ex hoc ouili, illas quoq; oportet me adducere, & vocem meam audient, & fiet vnum ouile, & vnus pastor. Quo loco Christus dissent de gentilibus Euangelium suscepturis, postquàm Iudaei illud aspernarentur.
units.tr: And we heard this voice brought from heaven when we were together with him on the holy mountain. Indeed, the very teaching of Christ, manifested by the will and command of the Father, is called a voice, John 10: I have other sheep which are not of this fold; those also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd. In this place Christ speaks of the Gentiles who would receive the Gospel, after the Jews had spurned it.

units.la: Itaque vox testimonium patris de Christo, adeóque ipsam doctrinam Christi, & Euangelium significat: vt, hodie audire vocem, perinde sit, atq; agnoscere, amplecti, obtemperare (hoc enim sibi vult vocabulum audiendi) sancto Euangelio, nobis certo & praefini to tempore voce ipsius Dei propositio: sicut & initio epistolae dictum est, Deum locutum esse nobis hisce diebus per filium.
units.tr: Thus the voice signifies the testimony of the Father concerning Christ, and so the very teaching of Christ and the Gospel: so that to hear the voice today is the same as to acknowledge, embrace and obey (for this is what the word to hear means) the holy Gospel, which has been proposed to us at a certain and appointed time by the very voice of God; just as it was said at the beginning of the epistle, that God has spoken to us in these last days by the Son.

units.la: Quibusdam placet, Euangelium dici vocem, ad discrimen legis: quandoquidem lex muta erat, scripta in tabulis: Euangelium viua voce ipsius Dei est editum.
units.tr: Some think that the Gospel is called a voice in contrast to the law, since the law was mute, written on tablets; the Gospel has been published by the living voice of God himself.

units.la: Audire verò est intelligere, mente percipere, cognoscere: Et maximè de verbo externo dicitur, quo homines ad credendum adducuntur: vnde illud Roman.10. Quomodo credent ei, de quo non audierunt? Ibidem: Ergo fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei.
units.tr: To hear, however, is to understand, to perceive with the mind, to know; and it is said especially of the external word, by which men are brought to believe: whence that saying in Romans 10: How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And in the same place: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.

units.la: Ne obduretis corda uestra) Quid est obdurare cor? Est totum adhaerere & obtemperare cordis sui natiuae malitiae.
units.tr: Do not harden your hearts) What is it to harden the heart? It is to cling wholly to and obey the inborn malice of one's own heart.

units.la: Cor hominis ad malum promptum est: huic proinde per omnia assentiri, & reiicere, quic quid proponitur tibi, quo ad bonum adduci posses: deniq; spiritui Sancto ad bonum te incitanti, siue per verbum externum propositum, siue quocunque alio modo, omnibus viribus resistere. Sic interpretatur ipse Stephanus Actorum 7. dicens: Duri ceruice, & incircumcisi corde & auribus, vos semper spiritui Sancto resistitis, sicut patres vestri, ita & vos.
units.tr: The human heart is prone to evil; therefore to assent to it in all things, and to reject whatever is put before you by which you could be led to good; and finally to resist with all your strength the Holy Spirit urging you to good, whether through the external word set forth, or in whatever other way. Thus Stephen himself interprets it in Acts 7, saying: Stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you.

units.la: Quae verba praesenti loco aperiendo, quoniam de patribus mentionem faciunt, valde conueniunt. Item Zachariae 7. Cor suum posuerunt, ut adamantem, ne audirent legem, gem, & verba, quæ misit Dominus exercituum, spiritu suo, per manum prophetarum priorum.
units.tr: These words, since they make mention of the fathers, agree very well with the present passage when it is explained. Likewise Zechariah 7: They set their heart like adamant, lest they should hear the law and the words which the Lord of hosts sent by his Spirit through the former prophets.

units.la: Videtur autem forma loquendi ducta ab eo, quòd, ut materiæ duræ non facilè potest aliquid insculpi vel imprimi: Ita quorum pectori non facilè potest instillari sana doctrina, tales duro corde appellantur.
units.tr: The form of speech seems to be drawn from this: just as nothing can easily be carved or impressed upon hard material, so those in whose breast sound doctrine cannot easily be instilled are called hard of heart.

units.la: Quomodo verò cōtingat hæc induratio, vtrum duntaxat ex nobis, vel etiam ex Deo, & an sola permissione, an etiam impulsione, pòst dicemus. Infumma ergo hæc verba, Hodie, si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra: sunt, uti antè indicaui, accipienda loco propositionis, qua inuitantur omnes, ut hodie, id est, hoc præsinito à Deo patre tempore, quo mundo reuelari Euangelium ille voluit, audiant vocem Dei, hoc est, doctrinam Christi, atq; Euangelio credant: siue Dei patris testimonium, quod is viua voce de Christo tulit, dicens: Hic est filius meus dilectus, &c. gratis animis recipiant, & nequaquàm se huic opponant, sed reuera credant, propter filium se illi placituros. Sequitur deinde ratio, à periculoso seu damnoso: continet enim exemplum patrum ob duriciem cordis & incredulitatem punitorum, atque à requie, quæ promissa erat, exclusorum. Hanc verò rationem pluribus verbis explicat, non sine amplificatione duritiæ & malitiæ illorum, idq; simul ut magnitudo peccati, videlicet incredulitatis, ab omnibus clarius perspiciatur, simul ut omnes ab incredulitate magis deterreantur.
units.tr: How this hardening comes about, whether only from us or also from God, and whether by mere permission or also by impulsion, we shall say later. In sum, then, these words, Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, are, as I indicated before, to be taken in the place of a proposition, by which all are invited: that today, that is, in this time appointed by God the Father, when he willed the Gospel to be revealed to the world, they should hear the voice of God, that is, the teaching of Christ, and believe the Gospel, or the testimony of God the Father which he gave by living voice concerning Christ, saying: This is my beloved Son, etc. They should receive it with willing minds, and by no means set themselves against it, but truly believe that they will please him through the Son. Next follows the argument from danger or harm, for it contains the example of the fathers, who were punished for hardness of heart and unbelief and shut out from the rest that had been promised. He explains this argument at greater length, not without amplifying the hardness and malice of those men, so that the magnitude of the sin, namely unbelief, may be seen more clearly by all, and at the same time so that all may be more deterred from unbelief.

units.la: Sicut in exacerbatione secundum diem tentationis in deserto, vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri) Vbi & hoc notandum est, verba, quæ propositionis loco iam constituimus, esse velut ab ipso propheta pronunciata: hæc verò in persona Dei enunciari: quomodo in prophetijs, & maximè in Psalmis crebræ cernuntur personarum mutationes. Et prudenter propheta ipsum Deum hæc verba introducit loquentem: Multò magis enim omnium animi mouentur, cùm audiunt Deum ipsum graues minas intonantem, & exprobrantem patrum incredulitatem, statuuntq;, certissimè euentura mala, quæ Deus ipse hoc pacto sua uoce euentura prædicit. Dicit ergo: Nolite vos indurare corda vestra, sicut indurarunt corda sua vestri Patres.
units.tr: As in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me) Here too it must be noted that the words which we have now set in place of a proposition are, as it were, pronounced by the prophet himself, but are uttered in the person of God, as frequent changes of persons are seen in the prophecies, and especially in the Psalms. And wisely the prophet introduces God himself speaking these words. For the minds of all are moved much more when they hear God himself thundering grave threats and rebuking the unbelief of the fathers, and they judge that the evils will surely come, which God himself, with his own voice, thus foretells will come. He says therefore: Do not harden your hearts, as your fathers hardened their hearts.

units.la: Et proponit insignem & memorandam indurationem patrum pro exemplo, cùm alijs perpetuum ferè esset Iudæis, induratis erga vocem Dei esse animis, sicut Christus, itemque Stephanus, illis exprobrarunt. Quando ergo contigit memorabilis illa induratio?
units.tr: And he sets forth the notable and memorable hardening of the fathers as an example, since for the rest it was almost constant among the Jews to have minds hardened against the voice of God, as Christ and likewise Stephen rebuked them. When, then, did that memorable hardening occur?

units.la: In exacerbatione, secundum diem tentationis in deserto, vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri) Quasi dicerent: Tunc sanè ostenderunt, se admodum induratos corde, quando me exacerbauerunt, & adiram prouocarunt, illo videlicet tempore, quo me tentabant in deserto, vbi sanè miris modis, & ualde indignè me tentarunt. Ita enim exaggerandi caussa tentandi vox repetita uidetur. Loquitur verò Deus de memorabili illa duritia & incredulitate Iudæorum, quam in illis expertus fuit, in Raphidim, quæ tanta fuit, ut ab ea nomen loco inditum sit Massa Meriba, id est, tentatio iurgij (sicut & Numeror. 11. sepulchra concupiscentiæ) de qua repetenda nobis historia est, quæ habetur Numerorū decimoquarto. Hic enim narratur, quòd, postquàm reuersi essent exploratores è terra Chanaan, narrassentque aliqui, incolas esse robustissimos, ciuitates præterea munitas, & omnia sic instructa, ut de ea obtinenda videretur desperandum, cœpit populus murmurare contra Mosen, optantes se mortuos potius in Ægypto, quàm tali conditione eductos, & cadere in vasta solitudine, imò nouum ducem, per quem denuò in Ægyptum reducerentur, creare constituerunt, quasi Deus non posset illis terram illam tradere, quasi promissis neutiquam vellet stare, aut fallere homines soleret: quòd existimare, quanta sit blasphemia, quis nō videt? Aciam etiam Mosen & Aaronem populus ille lapidibus opprimere volebat. Orantibus ergo Moyse & Aarone coram omni multitudine, tandem dixit Deus: Quousque detrahet mihi populus iste? Quousq; non credent mihi in omnibus signis, quæ feci coram eis? Feriam igitur eos pestilentia, atq; consumam: te autem faciam principem super gentem magnam, & fortiorem, quàm hæc est.
units.tr: In the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me) As if they said: then indeed they showed themselves very hardened of heart, when they provoked me and stirred up my anger, namely at that time when they tempted me in the wilderness, where indeed they tempted me in wondrous ways and most shamefully. For the word "tempt" seems to be repeated for the sake of amplification. God speaks of that memorable hardness and unbelief of the Jews, which he experienced in them at Raphidim, which was so great that the place was given the name Massah Meribah, that is, the temptation of strife (as also at Numbers 11, the graves of lust), and whose story we must recall, which is found in Numbers chapter 14. Here it is narrated that, after the spies had returned from the land of Canaan, and some had reported that the inhabitants were very strong, the cities moreover fortified and everything so arranged that obtaining it seemed hopeless, the people began to murmur against Moses, wishing rather to have died in Egypt than to be led out on such terms and fall in the vast wilderness. They even resolved to create a new leader through whom they might be led back into Egypt, as if God could not give them that land, as if he would in no way stand by his promises or was accustomed to deceive men. Who does not see how great a blasphemy it is to think this? That people also wanted to stone Moses and Aaron. Therefore, while Moses and Aaron prayed before the whole multitude, at last God said: How long will this people detract from me? How long will they not believe me in all the signs which I have done before them? I will therefore strike them with pestilence and consume them, but I will make you prince over a nation greater and stronger than this.

units.la: Cæterùm, dum Moses semper orare & intercedere pergit, nec non petit, propter gloriam Domini inducì populum in terram promissam, & condonari ei grauissimum istud peccatum, tandem audit à Domino: Dimisi iuxta uerbum tuum: sed addidit etiam iuramento interposito: Viuo ego, & implebitur gloria Domini uniuersa terra: attamen omnes homines, qui uiderunt maiestatem meam, & signa, quæ feci in Ægypto, & in solitudine, & tentauerunt pro pane, pro aqua, pro carnibus, me iam per decem vices, nec obedierunt uoci meæ, non videbunt terram, pro qua iurauì patribus eorum, nec quisquam ex illis, qui detraxit mihi, intuebitur eam. Iterum pòst pauca Dominus ad Mosen & Aaronem: Vsquequò multitudo hæc pessima murmurat contra me? Querelas filiorum Israel audiui.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while Moses kept on praying and interceding, and also asked that, for the glory of the Lord, the people be brought into the promised land and that this most grievous sin be pardoned them, at last he heard from the Lord: I have pardoned according to your word. But he added also, with an oath interposed: As I live, and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord; yet all the men who have seen my majesty and the signs which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now ten times, for bread, for water, for flesh, and have not obeyed my voice, shall not see the land about which I swore to their fathers, nor shall any of those who detracted from me look upon it. Again, after a few words, the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: How long does this most wicked multitude murmur against me? I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel.

units.la: Dic ergo eis: Viuo ego, ait Dominus sicut locuti estis audiente me, sic faciam vobis. In sol̄‐tudine hac iacebunt cadauera vestra. Omnes, qui numerati estis a viginti annis, & supra, & murmuraftis contra me, non intrabitis terram, super quam leuaui manum meam, ut habitare vos facerem, praeter Caleb filium Iephone, & Iosua filium Nun. Paruulos autem vestros, de quibus dixistis, quod praede hostibus forent, introducam vt videant terram quae vobis displicuit. Vestra cadauera iacebunt in solitudine: filij vestri erunt vagi in deserto annis quadraginta, & portabunt fornicationem vestram, donec consumantur cadavera patrum in deserto, iuxta numerum quadraginta dierum, quibus desideraftis terram. Annus pro die imputabitur. Et quadraginta annis recipietis iniquitates vestras, & scietis vltionem meam. Quoniam sicut locutus sum, ita faciam omni multitudini huic pesimae, quae surrexit aduersum me. In solitudine hac deficiet & morietur. Atque itaque omnia perfecta sunt, ut solus Caleb et Iosua post tot annos terram promissam ingressi sint, nec quisquam alius illorum, qui ex Aegypto venerant. Proinde de hoc tempore, quo murmurarunt Iudaei, sermo hoc loco est: & hoc tempus vocat hic diem tentationis in deserto. Atque haec historia valde illustrat omnia prophetae verba, omnia fient hic matur, in diebus regum, in diebus Noae: sed tamen hic singulari numero dicitur praesenti loco admodum congruens. Quoties exacerbauerunt eum in deserto, in iram concitauerunt eum in solitudine? Et reuersi sunt, & tentauerunt Deum, & Sanctum Israel limitauerunt. Proinde hic tantum annotandum, quid sit exacerbare Deum, quid item Deum tentare. Nam dies tentationis vocatur, quia ipsi Deum tentarunt, non quod Deus tentasset eos. Exacerbare Deum, est peccando eum ad iram prouocare: quare cum dicitur, sicut in exacerbatione, ὡς ἐν παραπικραμῶ, perinde est, ac si dicatur, sicut in tempore illo, quo Deus fuit ad iram prouocatus & irritatus. παραπικράω, unde παραπικρασμός, idem quod irrito, & ad iram incito, acerbum & amarulentum reddo. Quomodo & Coloffen. 3. vbi dicitur: Viri diligite vxores vestras, καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς: Interpres vertit ne sitis amarulenti aduersus illas. Porro tentare est experimentum de aliquo sumere. Itaque tentare Deum, est velle sumere experimetum de Deo, an possit & velit facere, quod petimus, vel quod expectamus: vbi tamen id nequaquam opus est, nec poscit necesitas quandoquidem alias de bonitate eius & potentia sufficientem habemus cognitionem. Quamobrem signum petere a Deo ad declarandam ipsius potentiam, vel bonitatem, vbi haec alias satis fele prodit, est tentare Deum. Sic Christus interpretabatur, se tentaturum fuisse Deum, si se de pinna templi dedisset praecipitem, atque ita voluisset habere experimentum, an Deus iuxta promissionem, quam allegabat aduersarius, mitteret angelos, qui ipsum seruarent.
units.tr: Say therefore to them: As I live, says the Lord, as you have spoken in my hearing, so will I do to you. In this wilderness your carcasses shall lie. All of you who have been numbered from twenty years old and upward, and have murmured against me, shall not enter the land upon which I lifted up my hand to make you dwell there, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun. But your little ones, of whom you said they would be prey to the enemies, I will bring in, that they may see the land which displeased you. Your carcasses shall lie in the wilderness. Your sons shall be wanderers in the desert for forty years and shall bear your whoredom, until the carcasses of the fathers are consumed in the wilderness, according to the number of the forty days in which you searched the land: a year for a day shall be counted. For forty years you shall bear your iniquities, and you shall know my vengeance. For as I have spoken, so will I do to all this most wicked multitude which has risen against me. In this wilderness they shall fail and die. And so all things were accomplished, so that only Caleb and Joshua entered the promised land after so many years, and none of the others who had come out of Egypt. Therefore the discourse here concerns this time, in which the Jews murmured, and this time he here calls the day of temptation in the wilderness. And this history greatly illuminates all the words of the prophet; all things shall come to pass here in haste, in the days of the kings, in the days of Noah, but nevertheless here the word is in the singular number, and it is very fitting to the present passage. How often did they provoke him in the wilderness, and anger him in the desert? And they turned back and tempted God, and limited the Holy One of Israel. Therefore here it is only to be noted what it is to provoke God and likewise what it is to tempt God. For it is called a day of temptation because they themselves tempted God, not because God tempted them. To provoke God is to incite him to anger by sinning; so when it is said "as in the provocation" [ὡς ἐν παραπικρασμῷ], it is just as if it were said: as in that time when God was provoked and irritated to anger. [παραπικράω], whence [παραπικρασμός], means the same as to irritate and incite to anger, to make bitter and embittered. Just so Colossians 3, where it says: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them [καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς]; the interpreter renders it: do not be embittered against them. Moreover, to tempt is to take the experience of someone. So to tempt God is to wish to take experience of God, whether he can and will do what we ask or expect, where yet there is no need of this at all, nor does necessity require it, since otherwise we have sufficient knowledge of his goodness and power. Wherefore to ask God for a sign to declare his power or goodness, where these are otherwise sufficiently made known, is to tempt God. Thus Christ explained that he would tempt God if he threw himself headlong from the pinnacle of the temple, and so wished to have experience whether God, according to the promise which the adversary alleged, would send angels to keep him safe.

units.la: Sic item tentant Deum, qui nolunt laborare, expectantes ut Dominus otiosis cibum in os sit missurus: quia ipse dicitur pascere volucres coeli, & pullos coruorum, &c. cum alia ratione possint bonitatem Dei sentire, nempe si fideliter laborando victui necessaria comparent, quae quidem nunquam ita parantur, quin bonitati Dei potius, quam nostrae industriae accepta ferri debeant.
units.tr: In the same way, those tempt God who refuse to work and wait for the Lord to put food into their idle mouths, because he is said to feed the birds of the heaven and the young ravens, and so on. Yet they could perceive God's goodness in another way, namely by working faithfully to obtain what is necessary for life. Such things are never so obtained that they ought to be credited to God's goodness rather than to our own industry.

units.la: Sic item Deum tentant, qui cum sciant bonitatem Dei & promissa eius, tamen quia vident exterius obuenire impedimenta, propter quae promissa eius videntur adimplenda, diffidunt de Deo, quasi Deus non posset aut no vellet praestare quae promiserat.
units.tr: Likewise they tempt God who, though they know his goodness and his promises, nevertheless distrust him when they see external obstacles appear, because of which his promises seem unlikely to be fulfilled. They act as if God could not, or would not, perform what he had promised.

units.la: Dixi, vbi opus non est: quia interdum licet etiam signum ad certitudinem aliquam petere, cum videlicet eiusmodi res sit valde ardua & plena periculo, vel necessaria ad salutem totius multitudinis: item cuius exemplum non praecesserit.
units.tr: I said "where there is no need," because sometimes it is also permitted to ask for a sign to gain some certainty: namely, when the matter is very difficult and full of danger, or necessary for the salvation of the whole people; likewise when no example has gone before.

units.la: Sic Gedeon petiuit signum in vellere: Iudicum 6. Helias item ignem de coelo petiuit, qui consumeret carnes oblatas. 1.reg.18. Item Esaias ad Achab, Pete tibi signum a Domino, sed ille, ut contemnens promissionem Dei per prophetam factam, renuit, & suae malitiae hoc velamentum adhibuit, quod no vellet tentare Dominum. Sciebat quippe hoc esse Dominum, videlicet experimentum et signum exigere, quo de voluntate Dei fiamus certi. Proinde cum dubitare & diffidere de Deo, maxime aduersetur fidei, etiam maximum peccatum decet iudicari, ac propter id Deus valde exacerbatur. Sed de his satis. Quod autem dicitur, tentauerunt me patres vestri, exprobrationis speciem habet, & durioris expostulationis, qua moueri possint ad eo diligentius vitandum exemplum patrum suorum. Ac valde solent moueri filij, si quando ipsis obijciatur aliquid à parentibus turpiter perpetratum. Vnde Stephanus Actorum septimo, item Christus Lucæ vndecimo obijcit, quòd patres occidissent prophetas, quodque ipsi patrum facta comprobarent. Sequitur: Probauerunt me, & viderunt opera mea: Exaggeratio est criminis & incredulitatis Patrum. Est enim sententia: Quid opus erat sic murmurare contra me, & diffidere, cùm ipsi antea experti fuissent, & vidissent crebra & magna opera, in gratiam illorum facta. Non solùm promiseram illis, quòd inducerem eos in terram Chanaan, sed insuper tot admiranda signa & opera propter eos edidi, ut me posse & velle perducere eos in terrā promissam, potuerint pro certo cognoscere. Ita nimirum emphasis in voce, opera, esse videtur. Qualia autem opera ediderit, cuiusmodi inprimis fuit transitus maris rubri, manade cœlo, aqua de lapide, &c. longum esset commemorare. In Psalmo 77. repetuntur. Propterea etiā in loco citato ex Numerorum decimoquarto, diserte dicitur: Homines, qui viderunt maiestatem meam, &c.
units.tr: Gideon asked for a sign in the fleece (Judg. 6). Elijah likewise asked for fire from heaven to consume the offered flesh (1 Kings 18). Isaiah said to Ahab, "Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord," but Ahab, as one who despised the promise of God made through the prophet, refused, and used this pretext of his malice, that he would not tempt the Lord. He knew well that this was what the Lord meant: to demand an experiment or sign by which we may be made certain of God's will. Therefore, since to doubt and distrust God is especially opposed to faith, it must be judged a very great sin, and for this reason God is greatly provoked. But enough of these matters. The words "your fathers tempted me" have the appearance of a reproach and a harsher expostulation, by which children may be moved to avoid more diligently the example of their fathers. Children are especially moved when something shamefully committed by their parents is thrown in their faces. Hence Stephen in Acts 7, and Christ in Luke 11, reproach the people that their fathers killed the prophets, and that they themselves approve the deeds of their fathers. It follows: They tested me, and saw my works. This is an amplification of the crime and unbelief of the fathers. The sense is: why was there any need to murmur thus against me and to distrust me, when they had already experienced and seen so many great works done for their sake? I had not only promised them that I would bring them into the land of Canaan; I had also performed so many wonderful signs and works on their behalf that they could know for certain that I was able and willing to lead them into the promised land. This, surely, is the emphasis of the word works. What sort of works he performed, above all the crossing of the Red Sea, manna from heaven, water from the rock, and so on, would take too long to recount. They are repeated in Psalm 77. For this reason, also, in the passage cited from Numbers 14 it is expressly said: "the men who have seen my majesty," and so on.

units.la: Cæterùm particula hæc, Quadraginta annis, hic annectitur præcedentibus, fortasis, quia editio septuaginta sic habet, quorum testimonijs interpres in cæteris epistolis solet uti. Sed apud Hebræos annectitur sequentibus: sicut ipse quoq; mox exponit, dicens: Quibus autem infensus fuit quadraginta annis? Et comminatio illa Dei supra citata, qua ait, Filij vestri erunt vagi in deserto annis quadraginta, ita collocandum satis arguit. Vnde religio mihi non foret, dicere, in septuaginta punctum male collocatum errore librariorum potius, quàm à septuaginta interpretibus. Tametsi, etiam si ita accipiamus, uti primo loco ponitur, videlicet cùm præcedentibus nihil absurdi continetur. Nam erit amplificatio bonitatis Dei, in hanc sententiam, quòd toto illo tempore viderint miranda Dei opera, & experti sint amplissimam eius bonitatem. Externa siquidem beneficia sem per adhuc largiter recipiebant, alimenta illis non defuere, vestes & calcei nunquàm deterebantur. Et reuera etiamsi per quadraginta annos Deus fuerit iratus, tamen illud tepus iræ Dei non fuit illis vacuum à Dei beneficijs. Nam Dominus etiam, cùm percutit, sanat: cùm vulnerat, medetur: cùm occidit, viuificat. Nullum Dei opus, in quo non misericordia & veritas eluceat, & misericordia semper superat iudicium. Et nos quoq; misericorditer à Deo flagellamur nunc, ne post hanc vitam cum mundo damnemur.
units.tr: Moreover, this phrase "forty years" is joined here to what precedes, perhaps because the edition of the Seventy reads it so, and the writer of this letter is accustomed to use their testimonies in his other letters. But among the Hebrews it is joined to what follows, as he himself explains immediately afterwards, saying: "But with whom was he displeased for forty years?" And the threat of God cited above, in which he says, "your children will wander in the desert for forty years," sufficiently shows that it should be placed so. Hence I would not scruple to say that the point is misplaced in the Seventy through the error of copyists rather than by the Seventy translators. Yet even if we take it as it stands in the first place, nothing absurd is contained in the preceding words. For it will be an amplification of God's goodness, to this effect: that throughout that whole time they saw God's wonderful works and experienced his very ample goodness. For external benefits still came to them abundantly all along; food never failed them, and their clothes and shoes never wore out. And indeed, even if God was angry for forty years, that time of God's anger was nonetheless not empty of his benefits to them. For the Lord, even when he strikes, also heals; when he wounds, he also cures; when he kills, he also makes alive. There is no work of God in which mercy and truth do not shine forth, and mercy always prevails over judgement. We too are now chastised by God in mercy, so that we may not be condemned with the world after this life.

units.la: Quapropter infensus eram generationi illi) Hoc est, odio habui, & magna animi moleStia periuli. Græcè enim verbum προσοχθίζω habetur, quod sonat, tædio & moleStia affici ex re quapiam. Vnde hic metaphora est, seu anthropopatheia Deo attributa, ab eo, quòd homines, dum hostes suos coràm vident, dolore & quasi cruciatu afficiantur: qua re summum odium intelligitur: atque ita significatur hac voce, quòd Deus odio summo patres illos sit persecutus. Ad hebraicam veritatem potius ita vertendum erat: Quadraginta annis cum tædio pertuli generatione illam. Nam hebraicè est קוץ. Hieronymus vertit, disp licuit: Munsterus, moleStiam passus fui à generatione hac: vide radicem קוץ. Aptisimè etiam ad exprimendum contemptum & permotionem animi dicitur, Generationi illi: Sic enim cū cōtemptu & generali appellatione solent exprobrationes fieri, ut Matth.12. Christus, Generatio praua & adultera signum quaerit, & signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum Ionæ prophetæ. Idem habetur Matthæi 16. Rursus Matth.17. Oratio incredula & diutorta, quousq; tandem ero vobiscum? Vsquequò patiar vos? Philippens. 2. Omnia facite sine murmurationibus ac disceptationibus, tales sitis, ut nemo de vobis queri possit, sine cri-q;, filij Dei irreprehensibiles, in medio nationis prauæ ac tortuosæ, in quibus lucere, ut luminaria in mundo.
units.tr: Therefore I was displeased with that generation: that is, I held it in hatred, and was afflicted with great vexation of mind. For the Greek word is προσοχθίζω [prosochthizō], which means to be affected with weariness and annoyance by some thing. Hence this is a metaphor, or an anthropopatheia, ascribed to God, taken from the fact that men, when they see their enemies before them, are affected with pain and as it were torment; by which a supreme hatred is understood. Thus the word signifies that God, with supreme hatred, persecuted those fathers. Yet to follow the Hebrew truth it should have been rendered: "For forty years I endured that generation with weariness." For in Hebrew it is קוץ [quts]. Jerome translated "it displeased me"; Münster, "I suffered annoyance from this generation." See the root קוץ. The phrase "that generation" is also very aptly used to express contempt and agitation of mind. For reproaches are usually made in this way, with contempt and a general appellation, as in Matthew 12, where Christ says: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah." The same occurs in Matthew 16. Again, in Matthew 17: "O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you?" Philippians 2: "Do all things without murmurings and disputes, that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without reproach, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world."

units.la: Et dicebam: Semper errant corde) Hæc verba ab animo commoto quidem, sed tamen contolente, & quodammodo expectante, ut aliquādo resipiscant, videtur prophetā: id quod ex eo videtur colligi posse, quòd dicat, eos tantùm errare. Quamuis errare etiam dicuntur, qui graviora crimina perpetrant. Vnde & aberrare à fide 1. Timoth. 6. Radix omnium malorum est studium pecuniæ, quam quidam dum appetunt, aberraverunt à fide, & seipsos implicuerunt doloribus multis. Tit. 3. Nam eramus quondam & nos stulti, inobedientes, errantes, seruientes desiderijs ac voluptatibus, &c. Ait autem, errasse eos corde, non solum autem, quia licet exteriorem iustitiam quidam visi sunt seruare, tamen impuri manserunt corde: sed multò magis, quia cor eorum semper ad errandum propensum ferebatur, & ut populus duræ ceruicis erroribus teneri gaudebat: præterea quia peccatu tentationis Dei, seu incredulitatis, de quo hic agitur, corde potissimum committitur, sicut & corde vera fides exercetur.
units.tr: And I said: They always err in heart: these words, spoken by a mind indeed moved but still patient, and in some way hoping that at some time they will come to their senses, seem to be those of the prophet. This may be gathered from the fact that he says only that they err. Yet those who commit more serious crimes are also said to err; hence also to stray from the faith, 1 Timothy 6: "The root of all evils is the love of money, which some, while they pursue it, have strayed from the faith and have entangled themselves in many sorrows." Titus 3: "For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, erring, serving our desires and pleasures," and so on. He says, moreover, that they erred in heart, not only because some seemed to keep an outward righteousness yet remained impure in heart; but much more because their heart was always inclined to wandering, and like a people of stiff neck, they delighted to be held by errors. Besides, the sin of tempting God, or of unbelief, of which he is speaking here, is committed chiefly in the heart, just as true faith is also exercised in the heart.

units.la: Vnde illa Roman.10. Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Lucæ 14. Tardi corde ad credendum appellantur discipuli. Matthæi 15. De corde exeunt cogitationes prauæ, &c. Non etiam sine causa dicit, Semper. Nam omni tépore recalcitrabat populus durae ceruicis, nec in viam reduci se patiebatur, subinde alijs atque alijs modis Deum tétans, sicut Dominus ipse Numerorum decimo quarto conqueritur, dicens: tentauerunt me iam per decem vices. Vbi denarius numerus, sicut & alijs locis, pro abundanti & multiplici sumi poterit, ut, cum dicitur decies, intelligi conueniat valde crebrò. Finitus numerus pro infinito in Scripturis passim vsurpatur. Deuteronomij 31. Semper cōtentiosè egistis cōtra Dominum. Actorum 7. semper restitistis Spiritui Sancto.
units.tr: Hence the words of Romans 10: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Luke 24 calls the disciples slow of heart to believe. Matthew 15: "Out of the heart come evil thoughts," and so on. Nor is he speaking without cause when he says always. For at all times the stiff-necked people kicked against the goad, and would not allow itself to be brought back into the way, continually tempting God in one way or another, as the Lord himself complains in Numbers 14: "They have tempted me now ten times." Here the number ten, as in other places, may be taken for abundance and multiplicity, so that when it is said "ten times," it is fitting to understand "very often." A finite number is used for an infinite one throughout Scripture: Deuteronomy 31: "You have always been contentious against the Lord." Acts 7: "You have always resisted the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Ipsi uero non cognouerunt vias meas) Hoc est, ipsi semper perrexerunt aberrare, uti cœperant: propemodum interpretatio est verborum praecedentium. Neque enim de ignorantia agitur crassa, &ut vocant, simplici, sed de spontanea & affectata: quando videlicet, vbi eis abundè propositum est, quod ad salutem pertinet, nec tamen volunt agnoscere, sed perduratis animis in caecitate sua perstant, de quibus dicitur in psalmo: noluerunt intelligere ut bene agerent. Vias hebraico more posuit, pro doctrina, lege, praeceptis, institutis Dei. Sunt viae Dei, sunt viae hominum, sed maximè inter se differunt. Esaiae 55. Non cogitationes meae, cogitationes vestrae, nec viae meae viae vestrę: quoniam sicut exaltantur coeli à terra, sic exaltatae sunt viae meae à vijs vestris. Viae Domini spirituales sunt, & misericordia & veritas, iuxta Psalm 24. Viae autem hominum carnales sunt, & impietas, & mendacij, quales passim in Scripturis describuntur.
units.tr: "They have not known my ways": that is, they always went on straying, as they had begun. This is almost a restatement of the preceding words. The ignorance meant is not crude and so-called simple ignorance, but wilful and deliberate ignorance: when the things that pertain to salvation have been set before them in abundance, they nevertheless refuse to acknowledge them, and persist in their blindness with hardened hearts. Of such people the Psalm says, "They would not understand, that they might do well." He uses "ways" in the Hebrew manner, for teaching, law, precepts and ordinances of God. There are the ways of God and there are the ways of men, and they differ greatly. Isaiah 55: "My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways." The ways of the Lord are spiritual, full of mercy and truth, according to Psalm 25. The ways of men, however, are carnal, full of wickedness and falsehood, and are described everywhere in Scripture.

units.la: Sicut uerui in iramea) Hic animi admodum irati, & omninò graviter punire destinantis affectus optimè describitur, quomodo apud poetas quoq; sępe licet tales affectus cum metis aut imprecationib. obseruare. Tribuitur autem Deo in Scripturis iuramentum eo fere modo, quo & ira, hoc est, per anthropopatheian. Neque enim opus est Deum confirmare per iuramentum: quandoquidem fallere ipse nec solet, nec potest, et quod semel ille statuit, necessarium est euenire, nec minus certum est ac ratum, quàm quod maximè videtur iuramento, vel alia quacunq; ratione confirmatum. Sed ad confirmandam fidem hominum, qui, cùm promittuntur grandia & difficilia, aegrè credunt sui similibus mendacibus, & fallere solitis hominibus, Deo etiam iuramentum attribuitur, tanquàm certitudinis quoddam signum. Hoc igitur pacto patribus saepè iurasse describitur, & promissiones iuramento interposito cōfirmasse. vnde Lucae primo Zacharias: ut memor esset testamenti sui sancti, praestaret, iusiurandum, quod iurauit ad Abraham patrem nostrum. Et haec de iuramenti diuini vsitata forma, Viuo ego, apud prophetas crebrò auditur.
units.tr: "As I swore in my wrath": Here the feeling of a man who is very angry and resolved to punish severely is very well described, just as the poets too often express such feelings with threats or curses. In Scripture an oath is ascribed to God in much the same way as anger, that is, by anthropopatheia. There is no need for God to confirm anything by an oath, since he neither commonly nor can deceive, and what he has once decreed must necessarily come to pass, and is no less certain and binding than anything that seems most confirmed by an oath or by any other means. But to confirm the faith of men, who, when great and difficult things are promised, scarcely believe fellow men who are liars and given to deceit, an oath is also attributed to God, as a kind of sign of certainty. In this way it is often described that he swore to the fathers and confirmed his promises by an interposed oath. Hence Zechariah in Luke 1: "that he would perform the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would remember his holy covenant." And this is the common form of a divine oath, "As I live," which is often heard among the prophets.

units.la: Si ingressuri iunt in requiem meam) En iuramentum Dei itidem humano more, & tanquàm perturbato affectu elegantissimè expressum. Est enim hic ἀποείωσιν, quae vehementioribus affectibus, praesertim vbi iuramentum vel imprecationes interueniunt, solet adiberi, quomodo etiam communi more vulgi loqui solemus. Quòd si iustud concesserò, sub auditur, male peream, nunquàm habear pro viro probo, vel huiusmodi. Sic etiam in praesenti forma iuramenti decore aliquid subintelligitur. Hoc autem iuramentum plenius exprimitur Numerorum decimoquarto: viuo ego, ait Dominus, sicut locuti estis audien te me, sic faciam vobis, &c.
units.tr: "If they shall enter into my rest": Behold God's oath, likewise in human fashion and most elegantly expressed as by a disturbed feeling. For here there is an aposiopesis [ἀποσιώπησις], which is usually employed with more vehement feelings, especially where an oath or curses intervene, as we also commonly speak in the usual manner of the crowd. For example, "If I concede this, may I perish badly, and may I never be held an honest man," or something of the kind. So also in the present form of the oath something fitting is understood. This oath, however, is expressed more fully in Numbers 14: "As I live, says the Lord, as you have spoken in my hearing, so will I do to you," and so on.

units.la: Per requie, si respiciamus historiam Patrum, intelligenda venit terra promissa Canaan, in qua tuti & quieti tanquàm in proprio solo Israelitae agere debebant. Sed quia promissiones temporales, & inprimis promissio terrae Canaan, adumbrat bona spiritualia, ideo de requie quadam spirituali verba spiritus Sancti hic accipieda sunt: id quod Apostolus fusius docet in sequentibus, vbi vniuersum istud testimonium Spiritus sancti accommodat causae euangelij & credentium, et nos explicare pro virili conabimur.
units.tr: As to "rest": if we look at the history of the fathers, the promised land of Canaan must be understood, in which the Israelites were to live safe and at peace, as in their own soil. But because temporal promises, and above all the promise of the land of Canaan, foreshadow spiritual goods, the words of the Holy Spirit here must be taken of a certain spiritual rest. This the Apostle teaches more fully in what follows, where he applies this whole testimony of the Holy Spirit to the cause of the gospel and of believers, and we shall try to explain it as best we can.

units.la: Videte fratres, ne quando sit in ullo vestrum cor prauum, obnoxium incredulitati, ut desciscat à Deo viuente: sed exhortemini vos inuicem quotidie, quoad appellatur dies hodiernus, ne quis ex vobis induretur seductione peccati. Christi participes facti sumus, si sane initium substantiae vsque ad finem firmum tenuerimus. In hoc, quod dicitur, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, ne obduretis corda vestra, sicut in exacerbatione.
units.tr: Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God: but exhort one another daily, while it is called Today, lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence steadfast unto the end. While it is said, Today if you will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.

units.la: Haftenus ipsius Prophetae verba, quae grauem sane continent exhortationem, ut omnes auditum euangelium alacriter suscipiant. Ac debuisset exhortatio haec vel sola esse satis: verum partim quia per se foecunda est et vberem augmentorum proventum suppeditans, dignaque, in qua explicanda aliquis diutius occupetur: partim, ne quis parum penderet, reijceretque eam, quasi non huius temporis hominibus, sed illis tantum congrueret, qui, cum propheta afflatus spiritu Sancto, ederet Psalmum, viuebant: nunc excita ducit varia argumenta, & quasi per singulas eundo partes, ostendit omnia plane conuenire praesenti causae, & sic debere Hebraeos credentes ista accipere: tanquàm si propter se, & ad se, & in eodem negotio à propheta dicta & scripta essent.
units.tr: So far the words of the prophet himself, which contain a truly serious exhortation that all who hear the gospel should receive it eagerly. And this exhortation alone should have been enough. But partly because it is in itself fruitful and yields a rich harvest of growth, and is worthy of being explained at length by someone; and partly so that no one should value it lightly and reject it, as if it suited only those people who lived when the prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit, composed the Psalm, and not the people of this time, the Apostle now brings forward various arguments and, going through them part by part, shows that all of them plainly fit the present cause, and that the Hebrew believers ought to receive them as if the prophet had spoken and written them for their own sake, and for themselves, and in this very matter.

units.la: Primùm ergo generalem exhortationem instituit in hunc modum: Videte fratres,ne quando sit in ullo uestrum:quasi dicat:Audistis,quid spiritus Sanctus loquatur, eiusque verba sic decet accipi,vt ad vos proprie pertinentia, sicut & reuera propter vos ita locutus est. Itaque his verbis vos admonemini,etiam atque etiam videatis,ne vos post audi-tam vocem Dei, siue euangelium, obduretis corda uestra, seu habeatis cor praeuum,obnoxium incredulitati. Licet ergo vnicuiq; obseruare, quàm artificiosè & quàm consultè Apostolus omnia faciat. Quomodo obsecrò potuisset aptius,grauius, conclusio tractari? Reliqua ad artificium ac dispositionem pertinentia nos inter discutiendum partes annotabimus.
units.tr: First, then, he sets out a general exhortation in this way: Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you. It is as if he said: You have heard what the Holy Spirit says, and his words ought to be received as pertaining properly to you, just as indeed he has spoken for your sake. Therefore by these words you are admonished, to see again and again that, after hearing the voice of God, or the gospel, you do not harden your hearts, or have an evil heart, liable to unbelief. Anyone may therefore observe how skilfully and how wisely the Apostle does everything. How, I ask, could a conclusion have been handled more fittingly and more weightily? We shall note the remaining points that pertain to his art and arrangement as we go through the parts.

units.la: Videte fratres) Pulchrè in conclusionibus solet Apostolus,ut magis excitet, blandeq; demulceat omnium animos,honorificam appellationem fratrum inserere:quandoquidem ea Christianorum maximè propria est,ad mutuam charitatem inter sese, ad agnitionem & obseruationem vnius communis coelestis patris in coelo solicitans & impellens, diligenter accuratèq; intuemini ac dispicite. Iubet in se descendant, & seipsos examinent. Valde visitatum verbum,quoties adhortamur,vel attentos,cautos,circumspectos auditores esse volumus. Sic 1.Cor.1. Videte vocationem vestram. Iterum Ephes.5. Videte,quomodo caute ambuletis:vtrobique habetur.
units.tr: Take heed, brethren. The Apostle is accustomed, in his conclusions, to insert the honourable name of brethren, very beautifully, so as to stir up and gently soothe the minds of all. This is especially proper to Christians, since it urges and impels them to mutual love and to the acknowledgment and obedience of one common heavenly Father in heaven. Look at it diligently and carefully. He bids them descend into themselves and examine themselves. It is a very common expression whenever we exhort, and wish our hearers to be attentive, cautious and watchful. So in 1 Corinthians 1: "Consider your calling." Again, Ephesians 5: "See that you walk carefully," both of which occur.

units.la: Ne quando sit in ullo uestrum cor prauum) Supra dixit de indurato corde,hic cor prauum manet ponit:sic generaliter licet humanum cor prauum appellare:ut Genef. 6. dicitur, quòd multa sit hominum malitia, & cuncta cogitatio cordis intenta sit ad malum omni tempore. Hieremiae 17. Prauum est cor hominis, & inscrutabile, quis scrutabitur illud? Ego Dominus scrutans renes & corda. Sed non simpliciter dicit hic inspiciendum,an cor sit prauum,sed an prauum sit ἀπιστία, hoc est,per incredulitatem. Hoc enim pacto interpretatur,quid sit habere cor induratum,seu cor prauum. Ait ἀπιστίαν, id est,incredulitate esse,per quam cor redditur maximè prauum: simulq; interpretatur spiritum Sanctum cùm dicit,Nolite obdurare corda uestra,tatundem sibi uelle,ac si diceret: nolite esse increduli. Graecè autem sonat, ἀπιστίαν ..., quasi dicamus, Cor prauum incredulitatis, siue incredulitate, vel potius,cor deprauatum incredulitate. Itaque sermo hic praecipuè est contra incredulitatem,sicut reuera peccatum, ob quod patres in deserto adeò seueriter suerunt puniti,erat incredulitas,ex qua tanquam fonte,murmur,seditiones, tumultus, contra Deum,& contra Mosen oriebantur.
units.tr: Lest there be in any of you an evil heart. Above he spoke of a hardened heart; here he puts an evil heart. Thus the human heart may generally be called evil, as Genesis 6 says that the wickedness of men was great, and every imagination of the thoughts of their heart was only evil continually. Jeremiah 17: "The heart is deceitful and desperately wicked; who can know it? I the Lord search the heart and try the reins." But he does not simply say here that one should look into whether the heart is evil, but whether it is evil through ἀπιστία, that is, through unbelief. For in this way he explains what it is to have a hardened or evil heart. He calls it ἀπιστίαν, that is, unbelief, through which the heart is made most evil; and at the same time he interprets the Holy Spirit when he says, "Do not harden your hearts," meaning exactly the same as if he said: do not be unbelievers. In Greek the phrase reads ἀπιστίαν ..., as if we said: an evil heart of unbelief, or rather a heart corrupted by unbelief. So this speech is chiefly against unbelief, just as the sin for which the fathers were so severely punished in the wilderness was indeed unbelief, from which as from a fountain came murmuring, sedition, tumults against God and against Moses.

units.la: Sicut fides merito prima virtus, & ad salutem maximè necessaria iudicatur,maximeque Deo placens:ita è contrario incredulitas grauissimum peccatum,prima ad damnationem via,& maximè Deo displicens censeri debet. Scitè Chrystomus: Sicut obdurata corpora & dura non obsequuntur manibus medicorum: sic animae obduratae non obsequuntur verbo Dei.
units.tr: As faith is rightly judged the first virtue, most necessary for salvation and most pleasing to God, so on the contrary unbelief must be counted the most grievous sin, the first way to damnation, and most displeasing to God. Chrysostom aptly says: As hardened bodies and hard ones do not yield to the hands of physicians, so hardened souls do not yield to the word of God.

units.la: Hac igitur de causa hortatur Apostolus Hebraeos,ut euangelio manifestato credant, ne sint deinceps increduli, & omnia ferè sequentia argumenta contra incredulitatem dirigit:quemadmodum etiam passim in Scripturis incredulitas tanquam caput malorum omnium reprehenditur,& propter incredulitatem puniti homines describuntur. Vnde Num.20.Moses sic Iudaeos alloquitur: Audite rebelles & increduli,num de petra hac vobis aquam poterimus excutere? Vbi etiam de Aarone dicit Deus,quòd non ingrediatur terram promissam,idq;,quia fuit incredulus. Esaiae 65. Deus de Iudaeis vocatis & audire contemnentibus,Expandi manus meas tota die ad populum incredulum,qui graditur in uia non bona post cogitationes suas. Propterea additur ibi,vocandas gentes. Iterum Hieremiae 5.Populo huic factum est cor incredulum & exasperans: recesserunt & abierunt,& non dixerunt in corde suo: Metuamus Dominum Deum nostrum, &c. Acuerosimile est,Apostolum,cùm totus esset in reprehendeda incredulitate,ad hos prophéticos sermones respexisse,qui iam diu praedixerant,incredulitati fore obnoxios Iudaeos,in quibus etiam semper maximè fuit idem uitium notatum. Ob quam causam Christus Marci 16,etiam suis apostolis incredulitatem vt grauissimum peccatum obiecit: Et Ioannis 16.Spiritus Sanctus promittitur venturus,qui arguat mundum de peccato,& deiustitia,& de iudicio,ac de peccato quidem,quia non credunt in me. Rom.10. Defracti sunt rami,ut ego insererer,bene dicis: per incredulitatem defracti sunt,tu uerò fide constitisti. In summa,quia incredulitas maximum peccatum est,& in Iudaeis maximè conspicuum,ideò contra incredulitatem,sicut & ratio causae poscit,praecipuè disserit, eamq; exaggerat. Ac nos paulo post de ea quaedam adhuc subijciemus.
units.tr: For this reason the Apostle exhorts the Hebrews to believe the manifested gospel, lest they be unbelievers from now on, and he directs almost all the following arguments against unbelief, just as throughout Scripture unbelief is rebuked as the head of all evils, and men are described as punished on account of unbelief. Hence in Numbers 20 Moses thus addresses the Jews: "Hear now, you rebels and unbelievers, shall we bring you water out of this rock?" There too God says of Aaron that he shall not enter the promised land, and this because he was unbelieving. Isaiah 65: God, speaking of the Jews who were called and despised hearing, says: "I have stretched out my hands all day to a faithless people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts." Therefore it is added there that the Gentiles are to be called. Again, Jeremiah 5: "This people has an unbelieving and provoking heart; they have turned aside and gone away, and have not said in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God," and so on. And it is very likely that the Apostle, while wholly engaged in rebuking unbelief, had regard to these prophetic words, which had long before foretold that the Jews would be liable to unbelief, in whom also this same vice had always been most conspicuously marked. For this reason Christ, in Mark 16, also charged his own apostles with unbelief as the most grievous sin. And in John 16 the Holy Spirit is promised as coming to convict the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment; and of sin indeed, because they do not believe in me. Romans 10: "The branches were broken off that I might be grafted in. Well said: they were broken off through unbelief, but you stand by faith." In sum, because unbelief is the greatest sin, and most conspicuous among the Jews, therefore the Apostle chiefly argues against unbelief, as the nature of the case demands, and magnifies it. And we shall add some further remarks on it a little later.

units.la: Vt desciscat à Deo uiuente: Caussa formalis atq; effectus incredulitatis, qui hoc pacto ob oculos positus ualde omnium animos ab incredulitate possit deterrere. Estq; sententia: Quomodo agnoscitur cor deprauatum incredulitate? Respondetur:
units.tr: That he might fall away from the living God. This is the formal cause and the effect of unbelief, which, once set before the eyes in this way, can greatly deter everyone's mind from unbelief. The sense is: how is a heart known to be depraved by unbelief? The answer is given:

units.la: p detur, cùm deficit à Deo, vel in deficiendo à Deo. Ac videtur propemodum hæc descri-ptio incredulitatis hinc posse elici. Incredulitas est, qua quis deficit à Deo, non vult Deo adhærere, ex Deo pendere, salutem & auxilium ab eo expectare, sed in aliis rebus, puta, sapientia humana, proprijs viribus, rebus caducis spem suam collocat: quæ res in om-nibus illis considerantur, qui in Scripturis ob incredulitatem deprehenduntur. Huc per-tinent omnes loci in Scripturis, in quibus Deus conqueritur, quod populus eius ipsum deseruerit, & post Deos alienos abierit, in quibus incredulitatis arguuntur. Hierem. 2. Me dereliquerunt fontem aquæ uiuæ, &c. Et profectò non parua res est à Deo deficere, eundemq; deserere. Si enim nos eum deserimus, ipse vicissim deserit nos. Hoc uerò ubi contigerit, planè de nobis actum est. Quamobrem & valde eleganter dicit, defectum esse à Deo viuente.
