Tacitè enim hac uoce innuit, eum, qui ab hoc desciuerit, vitam non habere, & planè esse mortuū, quo quid miserabilius cogitari queat? Hinc Ioan. 3. de fide in Christum Ioannes Baptista sic testatur: Qui credit filio, habet vitam æternam: qui ue-rò non credit filio, non uidebit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super illum. Et ibidem ipse Chri-stus. Nō misit Deus filium suum, ut condemnet mundū, sed ut seruetur mundus per eū. Qui credit in eum, non condemnatur: qui verò non credit, iam condēnatus est. Rom. 1. Iustus ex fide viuet. Ergo sicut per fidem accedimus ad Deum, & consequimur vitam: ita per incredulitatem mors, & quidem non tantùm temporalis, sed æterna.
units.tr: ...when it falls away from God, or in the very act of falling away from God. This description of unbelief seems almost to follow from this point. Unbelief is that by which a person falls away from God, is unwilling to cling to God, to depend on him, and to look to him for salvation and help, and instead places his hope in other things: human wisdom, his own strength, or fading things. This is what we see in all those in Scripture who are found to be unbelievers. To this belong all the passages in Scripture in which God complains that his people have forsaken him and gone after other gods, and in which they are charged with unbelief. Jeremiah 2: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water," and so on. Indeed, it is no small matter to fall away from God and to desert him. For if we forsake him, he in turn forsakes us, and when that happens, our case is utterly lost. That is why the author very elegantly says that they have fallen away from the living God. By this word he implies that the one who has turned away from him has no life, and is simply dead. What could be more wretched than that? So John the Baptist testifies about faith in Christ, John 3: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him." And Christ himself says in the same chapter: "God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him. He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned." Romans 1: "The righteous shall live by faith." Therefore, just as through faith we draw near to God and obtain life, so through unbelief comes death, and not only temporal death but eternal death.

units.la: Sed exhortemini uos inuicem quotidie, quoad appellatur dies hodiernus, ne quis ex vobis induretur sal-lacione peccati) Dixit, cauendum, ne habeamus cor prauum: addit ergo nunc, quomodo id facere queamus. Ac docet, id hac ratione posse fieri, si crebris exhortationibus nos inui-cem ab incredulitate deterreamus, & ad fidem excitemus. Piæ enim exhortationes, præ-sertim sumptæ ex uerbo Dei, & spiritus Sancti oraculis, cuiusmodi est, quod iamiam ci-tatum est, fidem excitare, alere, & confirmare possunt. Porrò græcè sic legitur, ἀλλὰ παρα-καλεῖτε ἑαυτοὺς: q; nonnulli malùt vertere: sed exhortemini uosipsos: sed hinc nullus in sententia sequitur scrupus, & coniuncta hæc sunt, videlicet exhortari nosipsos, & exhortari alios: id q; mox ostendemus. Cæterū, verbū, παρακαλεῖν, præterquā, q; significat aduocare, co-solari, etiā est adhortari, & diligenter incitare: quo modo Apostolus usurpauit 1. Tim. 6. ταῦτα διδάσκει καὶ παρακάλει, hæc doce & exhortare: & Tit. 1. de officio Episcopi: Oportet esse tenacem eius, qui secundum doctrinam est, fidelis sermonis, ut potens sit etiam exhortari (παρακαλεῖν) per sanam doctrinam.
units.tr: But exhort one another daily, while it is called "today," lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin (Heb. 3.13). He had said that we must take care not to have an evil heart; now he adds how we may do this. He teaches that it can be done in this way: if by frequent exhortations we turn one another away from unbelief and rouse one another to faith. For pious exhortations, especially those drawn from the Word of God and the oracles of the Holy Spirit, such as the one just cited, can arouse, nourish and confirm faith. Moreover, the Greek reads thus: but exhort yourselves [ἀλλὰ παρακαλεῖτε ἑαυτοὺς], which some prefer to render but exhort yourselves. Yet no difficulty arises for the sense here, and the two are joined, namely to exhort ourselves and to exhort others, as we shall show shortly. Besides meaning to summon or to console, the verb parakalein [παρακαλεῖν] also means to exhort and to urge earnestly. In this sense the Apostle used it in 1 Tim. 6: these things teach and exhort [ταῦτα διδάσκει καὶ παρακάλει]; and in Tit. 1, on the office of bishop: It is necessary that he hold firmly to the faithful word which accords with the teaching, so that he may be able also to exhort (παρακαλεῖν) by sound doctrine.

units.la: Quam facultatem exhortandi ideò requirit in Episcopo, quòd pigros & tardos corde ad credendum opus sit assiduè excitare, extimulare, & quodammodo impellere. Quia igitur Hebræorum plurimi erant admodum tardi ad credendum, & periculum semper erat, ne illi ipsi, qui recte credebant, à fide tandem deficerent, seducti ab aliis, vel propriq infirmitate: ideò uult Apostolus exhortationes frequentes adhiberi, per quas in tardis ac duris fides excitetur, in aliis alatur & confirmetur. Et maximam utilitatem adferunt, tam publicè, quàm priuatim factæ piæ exhortationes. Vnde in prima ecclesia formanda confirmandaque Apostolos legimus in exhortando plurimum fuisse occupatos, Actor. 2. de Petro ad Iudæos concionante: alijs què uerbis plurimis testificatus est, & exhorta-tus est eos, dicens: Seruemini à generatione ista prava: Actorum 14. Cumque euangelizassent ciuitatı illi, ac docuissent multos, reuersi sunt Lystram & Iconium, & Antiochiā, denuò confirmantes animos discipulorum, exhortantesque, ut perseuerarent in fide, Actorum 20. Fratres in Macedonia Paulus ubique multo sermone exhortatus dicitur. Etibidem insignis illa adhortatio ad Præsbyteros ecclesiæ Ephesinæ, quos ad se Miletum euoca-rat, describitur. Ergo, ut & Hebræi in fide confirmentur, & ab incredulitate auocentur, monet exhortationes crebras fieri.
units.tr: He requires this ability to exhort in a bishop because the lazy and slow of heart need constant rousing, prodding, and in a sense pushing toward belief. Since very many of the Hebrews were extremely slow to believe, and there was always the danger that even those who believed rightly might at last fall away from faith, either led astray by others or by their own weakness, the Apostle wishes frequent exhortations to be applied, by which faith may be roused in the slow and hard, and nourished and strengthened in others. Pious exhortations, whether given publicly or privately, bring the greatest benefit. Hence we read that in forming and strengthening the first Church the apostles were very much occupied with exhorting. In Acts 2, when Peter preached to the Jews, "with many other words he testified and exhorted them, saying: [Save yourselves from this crooked generation]." Acts 14: "When they had preached the gospel to that city and taught many, they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening again the souls of the disciples and exhorting them to continue in the faith." Acts 20: "Paul is said to have exhorted the brothers in Macedonia everywhere with much speech." And there the notable exhortation to the elders of the church of Ephesus, whom he had summoned to Miletus, is described. Therefore, so that the Hebrews also may be confirmed in faith and turned away from unbelief, he urges that frequent exhortations be made.

units.la: Estque singulare Dei donum in ministris uerbi, si in exhortando valeat. Multi etiamsi didactici sint, tamen non perinde valent facultate docendi.
units.tr: It is a singular gift of God in ministers of the Word if they are able to exhort. Many, even if they are skilled in teaching, do not have the same ability to exhort.

units.la: Vult autem exhortentur sese inuicem, uel seipsos. Coniuncta enim hæc sunt. Prius decet vnumquemque priuatim exhortari seipsum, deinde alios. Neque alios possumus rite adhortari, si ipsi simus frigidi & negligentes. Et præclarum est charitatis opus, alios exhortari.
units.tr: He wishes them to exhort one another, or themselves. For these are joined together. First each person ought to exhort himself privately, and then others. Nor can we properly exhort others if we ourselves are cold and negligent. And to exhort others is an excellent work of love.

units.la: De exhortatione sui ipsius illa uidentur 2. Corinthiorū decimotertio, Vos ipsos ten-tate, num sitis in fide, uos ipsos probate. Annon cognoscitis uosmetipsos, quòd Iesus Christus in uobis est? Nisi sicubi reprobi estis. Galat. 6. Opus suum probet unusquisque in semetipso, & tunc in semetipso tantum gloriationem habebit, & non in alio. De ex-hortādo inuicē plurimi loci passim, &c. Addit uerò quotidie, καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, ut assiduē in adhortando se inuicem sint. Semel atq; iterum adhortari non satis est: sed oportet creberrimè id facere. Vbi semper adsunt pericula, ibi semper adhiberi debent remedia. Quare cùm simul ob nostram fragilitatem, simul ob insidias diaboli semper instet periculum labendi in diffidentiam, non possunt satis frequentes exhortationes adhiberi.
units.tr: Concerning the exhortation of oneself, these passages seem relevant: 2 Corinthians 13: "Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless perhaps you are reprobate." Galatians 6: "Let each one prove his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another." Concerning mutual exhortation there are many passages scattered throughout. He adds daily [καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν], so that they may exhort one another constantly. It is not enough to exhort once or twice; it must be done very often. Where dangers are always present, remedies must always be applied. Therefore, since on the one hand the danger of slipping into distrust always threatens because of our frailty, and on the other because of the snares of the devil, exhortations cannot be applied too frequently.

units.la: Ne quis ex nobis induretur: ἵνα μὴ σκληρυνθῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν) Respicit istud ad illud in testimonio spiritus Sancti, ne obduretis corda vestra: Nam hic habetur σκληρυνθῇ, ibi vero, μὴ σκληρύνητε: Etquo dammodo exponit, quomodo, siue vnde contingat illa induratio, quando addit, Seductione peccati, ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας: quasi dicatur: peccato seducete. Exponit enim, quomodo siue unde contingat illa induratio. Significat quippe, eam esse vim peccati in nobis, (quandoquidem ingenitum est, & à natura inhærens) ut seducere nos possit, & à veritate penitus abducere, vnde fit, ut postea induremur. De qua vi peccati Romanorum 7. sic ait Apostolus: Peccatum occasione accepta per praeceptum decepit me, vel potius, seduxit me (graece enim legitur ἐξηπάτησέ με) & per illud occidit. Ibidem paulò ante. Cùm essemus in carne, affectus peccatorum, qui sunt per legem, vigebant in membris nostris ad fructificandum morti. Deinde, occasione accepta, peccatum per praeceptum genuit in me omnem concupiscentiam: siquidem absque lege peccatum erat mortuum.
units.tr: Lest any of you be hardened [ἵνα μὴ σκληρυνθῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν]. This refers to that passage in the testimony of the Holy Spirit, Do not harden your hearts. For here the text has σκληρυνθῇ [σκληρυνθῇ], there μὴ σκληρύνητε [μὴ σκληρύνητε]. And he explains somewhat how, or from what source, that hardening comes about, when he adds by the deceitfulness of sin [ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας], as if to say: by the seduction of sin. For he explains how or from what source that hardening arises. Clearly he means that sin has this power within us (since it is inborn and clings to our nature), that it can lead us astray and draw us completely away from the truth, and from this it follows that we are afterwards hardened. Concerning this power of sin the Apostle says in Romans 7: "Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me [ἐξηπάτησέ με], or rather seduced me, and through it killed me." Just before this: "When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which are through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death. Then, taking occasion through the commandment, sin produced in me every kind of concupiscence, for apart from the law sin was dead."

units.la: Ob hanc igitur tantam virtutem peccati, quod habitat in nobis, seu in carne nostra, atque impellit aliquo modo etiam sanctos ad ruinam, peccato facultas seducendi hoc loco tribuitur: sicut in aliis locis seducendi potestas diabolo vel serpenti, ita eodem modo hic peccato. Et revera ita est praua nostra voluntas, siue ingenitum peccatum, & corrupta natura, item instigatio Sathanae, causa peccati, praecipueque induarationis sunt. Vnde & multis in locis peccatum diabolo, & nobis imputatur, dicimurque nos metipsos seducere. Huc pertinet illud 2. Corinthiorum 11. Adiunxi vos vni viro, ut virginem castam exhiberetis Christo, sed metuo, ne qua fiat, ut, quemadmodum serpens Euam de cepit uersutia sua, ita corrumpantur sensus vestri à simplicitate, quae erat erga Christum. Galat 6. Si quis sibi videtur aliquid esse, cùm nihil sit, suum ipse fallit animum. 1. Ioan. 1. Si dixerimus, peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. En ergo, quomodo Satanas nos seducat, quomodo nos ipsi, siue peccatum in nobis habitans nos seducat, quantum praesenti loco satis est.
units.tr: Because of this great power of sin, which dwells in us, or in our flesh, and which in some way drives even the saints toward ruin, the power of seducing is here attributed to sin, just as elsewhere the power of seducing is attributed to the devil or the serpent; in the same way it is attributed here to sin. And indeed our evil will, that is, inborn sin and corrupt nature, together with the instigation of Satan, are the cause of sin, and especially of hardening. Hence in many places sin is imputed both to the devil and to us, and we are said to deceive ourselves. To this belongs 2 Corinthians 11: "I have betrothed you to one husband, so that I might present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is toward Christ." Galatians 6: "If anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceives his own mind." 1 John 1: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Behold, then, how Satan seduces us, and how we ourselves, or the sin dwelling in us, seduce us; this is enough for the present passage.

units.la: Quoad appellatur dies hodiernus, ἀξχὴς οὗ τὸ σήμερον καλεῖται) τὸ σήμερον hodie. Respicit haec particula ad vocem hodie, supra positam in testimonio spiritus Sancti, videturque argumentum subesse ab oportunitate temporis: quasi dicat: Oportet vos quotidie exhortari inuicem, ne quis ex vobis induretur, idque maxime hodie, cùm uidelicet manifestatum est euangelium, de quo hodierno die Spiritus Sanctus locutus est, ac proinde oportet vos eius hodierni temporis habere rationem. Quae interpretatio eo magis quadrare videtur, quòd statim subijcitur: In hoc, quod dicitur, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis. In quam sententiam & Roman. 13. dicitur: Praesertim cum sciamus tempus, quod tempestiuum sit, nos iam à somno expergisci. Nunc enim propius adest nobis salus, quam tum, cùm credebamus.
units.tr: "As long as it is called 'today'" [ἄχρις οὗ τὸ σήμερον καλεῖται]: today [τὸ σήμερον]. This particle refers back to the word "today" in the testimony of the Holy Spirit quoted above, and it seems to imply an argument from the opportunity of the time. It is as if he said: you must exhort one another every day, lest any of you be hardened, and especially today, since the gospel has now been made known, the gospel of which the Holy Spirit spoke on this day; therefore you ought to take account of this present time. This interpretation seems all the more fitting because it is immediately added: "In that it is said, Today if you will hear his voice." To the same effect Romans 13 says: "Especially since we know the time, that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed."

units.la: Quòd si hoc loco nō placet τὸ σήμερον accipere de tepore manifestati euangelij, sumatur ergo pro toto tepore nostrae vitae, ut sit sententia, exhortationibus esse confirmandos animos quotidie, quamdiu hic viuimus: quae sententia non male conuenit, praesertim quia sequitur, nos debere ad finem usque firmum retinere initium substantiae. Et vniuersum tempus vitae nostrae recte appellatur, utpote quod reuera nihil aliud, quàm dies vnus est, si eius breuitate bene consideremus: sicut & philosophus quidam totam uitam nomine dieciolae appellauit. Iob. 7. Dies mei velocius transierunt, quàm à texente tela succiditur, & consumpti sunt absque ulla spe. Etiá uniuersum tempus quo Deus nos vocat, & salutis verbum proponi facit, dies noster, seu dies hodiernus appellari potest, id quod supra ex Lucae 19. capite, semel indicauimus, vbi Christus ait: Et quidem in isto die tuo, quae ad pacem tuam pertinent, curares. Chrysostomus hodie interpretatur totum tempus, quo constat mundus.
units.tr: But if in this place you do not like taking today [τὸ σήμερον] of the present season of the gospel's manifestation, then let it be taken for the whole span of our life, so that the sense is: our souls must be strengthened by exhortations every day for as long as we live here. This meaning agrees well enough, especially since it follows that we must hold the beginning of our substance firm to the end. The whole time of our life is rightly called a day, since, if we consider well its brevity, it is really nothing other than one day; so also a certain philosopher called the whole of life by the name of a little day. Job 7: "My days have passed more swiftly than the weaver's shuttle is cut off, and they are spent without any hope." Also the whole time in which God calls us and causes the word of salvation to be set before us can be called our day, or today, as we have already noted above from Luke 19, where Christ says: "If you had known, even you, at least in this your day, the things that belong to your peace." Chrysostom interprets "today" as the whole time during which the world endures.

units.la: Christi participes facti sumus, si sane initium substantiae usque ad finem firmum tenuerimus.
units.tr: We have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our substance firm to the end.

units.la: Ratio obiter interposita, quare debeamus quotidie, & quàdiu hic viuimus, nos ipsos adhortari, quia oportet nos, si Christi participes agnosci volumus, fidem retinere firmā ad finem usque. Quod sanè fieri non potest, nisi crebris exhortationibus eam alamus & roboremus. Ac videtur haec uerba veluti per parenthesin interposita, adeò, ut nisi hoc pacto sumantur, aegrè deprehendi queat, quomodo sequentia cohaereant. Est ergo sententia: ideò opus esse, ut inuicem omni tempore exhortemur, quia eatenus sumus Christi participes, & accipiemus communem cum eo gloriam, quatenus in fide constantes perseuerauerimus.
units.tr: This is a reason inserted in passing, why we ought to exhort ourselves every day and as long as we live here: because, if we want to be acknowledged as partakers of Christ, we must hold the faith firm to the end. This cannot indeed be done unless we nourish and strengthen it by frequent exhortations. These words seem to be inserted as a parenthesis, so that unless they are taken in this way it is hard to see how what follows coheres. The sense, then, is this: there is need for us to exhort one another at all times, because we are partakers of Christ only so far as, and we shall receive a common glory with him only so far as, we persevere steadfast in faith.

units.la: Quoniam participes facti sumus: μετοχοὶ γὰρ γεγόναμεν τῆς χρίστου. Nobis omnia facta sunt communia cum Christo, non quidem nostro aliquo merito, sed illius & Dei patris amplissima bonitate. Ille resurrexit, ut nos quoq; resurgamus: ille ascendit in coelum, viuit æternum, æterna potitur gloria, vt nos quoq; pari modo ascendamus in coelum, viuamus in æternum, æterna gloria potiamur. Deniq;, sicut ipse particeps est per omnia carnis nostræ & sanguinis, ut dictum est capite secundo: ita nos participes efficimur ipsius Spiritus, & uitæ æternæ, seu bonorum spiritualium. Hinc Ioannis primo: De plenitudine eius omnes nos accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia, quia lex per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum exorta est. 1. Corinthiorum 1. Ex eodem autem vos estis in Christo Iesu, qui factus fuit nobis sapientia a Deo, iustitiaque & sanctificatio & redemptio. Ephes. 1. Per quem habemus remissionem peccatorum, iuxta diuitias gratiæ suæ, de qua vbertim nobis impartiuit, in omni sapientia & prudentia, pate facto nobis arcano voluntatis suæ. Ephes. 2. Deus, qui dives est in misericordia, propter multam charitatem suam, qua dilexit nos, etiam cum essemus mortui per delicta, conuiuificauit nos una cum Christo (per gratiam estis seruati) simulque cum eo resuscitauit, & simul cum eo sedere fecit inter coelestes, in Christo Iesu. Item supra fumus appellati consortes Christi, ubi cap. 1. dictum est de Christo: Vnxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo exultationis ultra consortes Christi. Postremo, multis aliis locis describitur, quanta bona cum Christo & per Christum accipimus: quomodo item Dei haeredes, & Christi cohaeredes sumus. Et passim oditur, quod etiam in hac uita participemus cum Christo, (cum uidelicet per fidem illi, ut capiti, agglutinamur, & donis spiritus Sancti ab eo ornamur. per verum usum Sacramentorum corpori ipsius, quod est ecclesia, inferimur, ad haereditatem coelestem vocamur, per fidem in verbum eius peccatorum remissionem consequimur:) verumetiam in altera uita omnia adeoque ipsum regnum cum Christo accipiamus. Quare multum est, hoc pacto participem Christi appellari. Atque hanc foelicitatem accipimus sola Dei bonitate & gratia, sicut Ephes. 1. & 2. clare ostenditur. Quanquam est etiam, quod ex parte nostra requiratur, nempe, Si sane initium substantiae usque ad finem firmum tenuerimus. Hoc est, ut breuiter explicem, si in fide stabiles usque ad finem uitae nostrae perstiterimus: quomodo multis aliis locis perseuerantia per omnem vitam requiritur, quemadmodum supra in fine collationis Christi cum Mose, vbi dicebatur: cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam tenuerimus. Et Christus Matthaei 10. Qui perseuerauerit usque in finem, saluus erit. Colos. 1. Reconciliauit vos in corpore carnis suae per mortem, ut exhiberet uos sanctos & irreprehensibiles & inculpatos in conspectu suo: si quidem permanetis in fide fundati ac stabiles. Hoc tantum in praesentiarum notandum est, quid nimirum sibi uelit Apostolus per initium substantiae. Sane per substantiam rectissime fidem intelligimus: quandoquidem ipsa fides est, per quam subsistimus, per quam Chrysostomus, & post hunc Theophylactus recte interpretatur, diuina & spiritualis essentia efficimur, & in nouas quodamodo substantias & creaturas regeneramur. Quod anima est in uita corporali, id fides est in uita spirituali: unde illud, Iustus ex fide uiuet: Fide igitur dum subsistimus, recte substantia appellatur. Et plane idem per substantiam intelligendum esse, quod Colossen. 1. significat fides, ipsa sententia ratio satis declarat. Quod uero fides recte appelletur substantia, seu ὑπόστασις, liquet ex hius epistolae capite undecimo, ubi fides hoc pacto describitur: ἐστὶ δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπο-στασις πραγμάτων ἐλέγχος οὐ βλεπομένων: id est: Est autem fides earum rerum, quae sperantur, substantia, argumentum eorum, quae non videntur. Quam definitionem hoc loco non opus est ut plenius excutiamus. Quod vero dixerit initium substantiae, notauit per ἀρχήν, quod fidei esse nt in credentibus quaedam initia, ac deinde quaedam incrementa, & ab exiguo initio fidei paulatim ueniendum ac progrediendum ad fidem pleniorem.
units.tr: "For we have become partakers": [μετοχοὶ γὰρ γεγόναμεν τοῦ Χριστοῦ]. All things have been made common to us with Christ, not indeed by any merit of our own, but by the most abundant goodness of him and of God the Father. He rose again, so that we also might rise; he ascended into heaven, lives forever, and possesses eternal glory, so that we also in like manner might ascend into heaven, live forever, and possess eternal glory. Finally, just as he himself became a partaker of all that belongs to our flesh and blood, as was said in the second chapter, so we are made partakers of his very Spirit, of eternal life, or of spiritual goods. Hence John 1: "Of his fulness we have all received, and grace for grace; for the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ." 1 Corinthians 1: "But of him are you in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." Ephesians 1: "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he has lavishly bestowed upon us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will." Ephesians 2: "God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our sins, has made us alive together with Christ (by grace you are saved), and together with him has raised us up, and together with him has made us sit among the heavenly ones in Christ Jesus." Likewise above we were called companions of Christ, where in chapter 1 it was said of Christ: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." Lastly, in many other places it is described how great good things we receive with and through Christ, and how we are likewise heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. And everywhere it is taught that we even in this life participate with Christ (namely, since by faith we are joined to him as to our head, and are adorned by him with the gifts of the Holy Spirit; we are brought into his body, which is the Church, through the true use of the sacraments; we are called to the heavenly inheritance; and through faith in his word we obtain the remission of sins), and moreover that in the other life we shall receive all things, and indeed the kingdom itself, together with Christ. Therefore it is a great thing to be called a partaker of Christ in this way. And we receive this happiness by the goodness and grace of God alone, as is clearly shown in Ephesians 1 and 2. Yet there is also something required on our part, namely: "If indeed we hold the beginning of our substance firm to the end." That is, to explain briefly: if we remain steady in faith to the end of our life. In many other places perseverance throughout the whole of life is required in the same way, as above at the end of the comparison of Christ with Moses, where it was said: "Whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the glorying of hope firm to the end." And Christ in Matthew 10: "He who perseveres to the end will be saved." Colossians 1: "He has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and blameless and unreproachable in his sight, if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast." This only needs to be noted for the present: what the Apostle means by "the beginning of our substance." Surely by substance we most rightly understand faith, since faith itself is that through which we subsist, through which, as Chrysostom, and after him Theophylact, rightly interpret, we are made of a divine and spiritual essence, and are in a manner regenerated into new substances and creatures. As the soul is in bodily life, so faith is in spiritual life; hence the saying, "The just shall live by faith." Therefore, since we subsist by faith, it is rightly called substance. And that substance in Colossians 1 plainly means faith, the sense of the passage itself makes sufficiently clear. That faith is rightly called substance, or hypostasis [ὑπόστασις], is evident from the eleventh chapter of this epistle, where faith is described in this way: "Now faith is the substance [ὑπόστασις] of things hoped for, the evidence [ἔλεγχος] of things not seen." That is: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the argument of things not seen." It is not necessary to examine this definition more fully here. But when he said "the beginning of our substance," he signified by "beginning" [ἀρχήν] that in believers faith has certain beginnings, and then certain increases, and that from a small beginning of faith one must gradually come and advance toward fuller faith.

units.la: Hinc Christus Petrum vocat modicae fidei, & alibi modicam fidem comparat grano sinapi: Apostoli item suam fidem augeri petebant: Et Apostolus Paulus multis in locis precatur, ut in fide proficiant: & alios ait crescere in unitate fidei & agnitionis filii Dei in virum perfectum, alios vero adhuc esse in Christo pueros, imo alios denuo uult parere, donec Christus in eis formetur, Gal. 4. Ob hanc igitur causam Apostolus hac forma loquendi usus est: est q; sententia: Fidei initia & rudimenta, qualia cunq; ea fuerint, firmiter esse retinenda, imo semper in fide ad finem usq; proficiendum, sicut bene coepistis, ita bene progrediamini. Et reuera merito ita locutus est. Nam vbi adhuc tenera & recens planta erat ecclesia, vbi graue periculum erat, ne multi a fide euangelica resilirent, quid aliud, quam initia quaedam fidei habebantur? Potest & hoc addi, quod, ut Apostolus Paulus alias solet antithetis delectari: ita uisus est hic antitheseos gratia, voce τέλος, voluisse ἀρχήν opponere.
units.tr: Hence Christ calls Peter "of little faith," and elsewhere compares little faith to a grain of mustard seed; the apostles likewise asked that their faith be increased; and the Apostle Paul in many places prays that they may make progress in faith, and says that some grow into the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, into a perfect man, while others are still infants in Christ, and indeed he wishes to bring others to birth again until Christ is formed in them (Galatians 4). For this reason, therefore, the Apostle used this form of speech: and the sense is this: the beginnings and rudiments of faith, of whatever kind they may be, must be firmly held, and indeed one must always advance in faith to the end, "as you have begun well, so also go on well." And indeed he rightly spoke thus. For where the Church was still a tender and recent plant, where there was grave danger that many would fall back from the evangelical faith, what else was there but certain beginnings of faith? This may also be added: as the Apostle Paul is elsewhere wont to delight in antitheses, so here he seems, for the sake of antithesis, to have wished to set beginning [ἀρχήν] against the word end [τέλος].

units.la: Ephes. 4. Et sæpe cùm volumus aliquid absolutum, consummatum, & perfectum significare, ab initio ad finem usq; id commendamus: ita ad significandam consummatam & perfectam, & omnibus numeris absolutam fidem, dicit, initium fidei ad finem usq; firmum retineri debere. Sequitur:
units.tr: Ephes. 4. And often, when we want to signify something complete, finished and perfect, we commend it as being so from beginning to end. In the same way, to signify a faith that is consummated, perfect and absolute in every respect, he says that the beginning of faith must be held firm to the end. There follows:

units.la: In hoc quod dicitur, Hodie si uocem eius audieritis, ne obduretis corda uestra, sicut in exacerbatione) Græce est, ἐν τῷ λέγεσθαι, hoc est, in quo dicitur, vel, dicendo. Nam Græci præpositiones sub- inde præponunt in finitiuis, sicut nos gerundijs, & tales loquendi formulas nostri per gerundia sæpe reddunt. Proinde ista verba præcedentibus hoc pacto annecte. Ne quis ex vobis induretur seductione peccati, exhortemini vos ipsos quotidie, in hoc quod dicitur, vel dicendo: Hodie si uocem eius audieritis, &c. ut sit sententia: eos debere sese mutuo exhortari, & ab induratione cordis deterrere, usurpando & sæpe inuicem inculcando dictum illud spiritus Sancti, Hodie, si uocem eius audieritis, &c.
units.tr: The words "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation" are, in Greek, "in what is said" [ἐν τῷ λέγεσθαι], that is, "in which it is said," or "in saying." Greek writers often place prepositions before infinitives, as we do with gerunds, and our translators often render such phrases with gerunds. So join these words to what precedes in this way: "Lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, exhort one another every day, in what is said, or in saying: Today, if you hear his voice, &c." The sense is that they ought to exhort one another and turn each other back from hardening of the heart, by using and often repeating to one another that saying of the Holy Spirit, "Today, if you hear his voice, &c."

units.la: Et vix alia ratione haberi potest perspicua sententia, quàm si ad hunc modum ista superioribus adiungantur: & illa, Christi participes facti sumus, &c. quasi per parenthesin inserta forent, intermittantur. Chrysostomus quidem notat hic hyperbaton esse: sed si coniugimus hæc uerba præcedentibus, eo pacto, quo coniungenda ostendimus, non opus est ad hyperbati rationem confugere, omnisque obscuritas tollitur.
units.tr: The clear sense can hardly be had in any other way than by joining these words to what precedes in this manner, and by setting aside those words, "We have become partakers of Christ, &c.", as if they were inserted by way of parenthesis. Chrysostom indeed notes that there is a hyperbaton here; but if we join these words to what precedes in the way we have shown they should be joined, there is no need to take refuge in a hyperbaton, and all obscurity is removed.

units.la: Cæterum habemus hic præclara documenta, è quibus facile primum est, quomodo maximus sit ad omnia usus sacrarum literarum. Non sine causa dixit Christus Ioan. 5. Scrutamini Scripturas, quia vos videmini vobis in ipsis vitam æternam habere, & illæ sunt, quæ testificantur de me, nec vultis venire ad me, ut vitam habeatis. Et Lucæ 10. quærentes, quid faciendo ad vitam æternam peruenirent, remittit ad Scripturam legis, dicens: In lege quid scriptum est? quomodo legis? Iterum Lucæ 16. petenti diuiti, ut mitteretur Lazarus ad fratres eius, quos de præcauenda damnatione edoceret, ait Christus, quòd habeant Mosen & prophetas, quos audire debeant. Quæ omnia huc tendunt, quòd Scripturarum maxima sit dignitas & utilitas, utpote in quibus clare, quæcunque ad salutem necessaria sunt traduntur. Nā de Christo, per quem solū salus contingit, item de vitæ nostræ omni institutione: deniq; de omnibus, quæ ad uerè beatè agendum etiam post hanc vitam conducunt, plenissimè per eam edocemur.
units.tr: Moreover, we have here excellent lessons, from which it is easy to see first how great is the use of the holy letters for everything. Christ rightly said in John 5: "Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life, and it is they that testify of me; yet you are unwilling to come to me that you may have life." And in Luke 10, when people asked what they should do to attain eternal life, he refers them to the Scripture of the law, saying, "What is written in the law? How do you read it?" Again, in Luke 16, when the rich man asked that Lazarus be sent to his brothers, to teach them how to avoid damnation, Christ answers that they have Moses and the prophets, whom they ought to hear. All these point to this: the Scriptures have the greatest dignity and usefulness, since in them are clearly set down whatever is necessary for salvation. For through them we are most fully taught about Christ, through whom alone salvation comes, about the whole ordering of our life, and finally about everything that leads to living truly and blessedly, even after this life.

units.la: Quare quæcunque in ea continentur, sic accipienda sunt, ut omnium ætatum omnibus hominibus scripta: sicut omnes quoque doceri, & in sana doctrina confirmari egét: sic debemus illa accipere, tanquam ad nos pertinentia. Atque huc pertinet illud Romanorum decimo quinto, Quæcunque scripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam præscripta sunt. Et 1. Corinthiorum 10. Hæc omnia figuræ contigerunt illis: scripta uero sunt, propter admonitionem nostri, in quos termini ætatum inciderunt. 2. Tim. 3. At tu perfistito in his, quæ didicisti, & quæ tibi concredita sunt, sciens à quo didiceris, & quòd à puero sacras literas noueris, quæ te possunt eruditum reddere ad salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in iustitia, ut integer sit Dei homo, ad omne opus bonum apparatus. Quibus sane locis egregiè sacrarum literarum laus & dignitas prædicatur, & præterea, quomodo nos illas ad nostram vtilitatem priuatim debeamus conuertere, ostenditur. Sicut Apostolus conuertit illa verba prophetæ ad utilitatem eorum, quos in fide confirmare cupiebat. Omnia enim quocunque tempore, de quibuscunque, vel ad quascunque personas scripta sunt, tamen ideò, tanquam archiui ecclesiæ, integra sunt tot seculis conseruata, ut nos ex illis excerperemus, quæ in omnem euentum, consolationem, doctrinam, exhortationem nobis possunt suppeditare. Et si putamus, quæ in archiuis ciuitatum continentur, in quibus iudicata & acta de rebus temporalibus sunt, vtiliter & necessariò seruari propter posteros: quanto maiori cum utilitate seruata sunt sacra biblia, in quibus continentur ea, quæ ad res spirituales, cœlestes, & æternas conducunt.
units.tr: Therefore whatever is contained in them must be taken as written for all people of all ages, just as all also need to be taught and confirmed in sound doctrine. So we ought to receive those things as pertaining to us. To this belongs what is said in Romans 15: "Whatever was written was written for our instruction." And 1 Corinthians 10: "All these things happened to them as figures; but they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come." 2 Tim. 3: "But you, continue in the things you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and that from childhood you have known the holy letters, which can make you wise unto salvation through the faith that is in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." In these passages the praise and dignity of the holy letters are proclaimed excellently, and it is also shown how we ought to turn them to our own private profit. Just as the Apostle turned those words of the prophet to the profit of those whom he wished to confirm in faith. For all things, written at whatever time, about whatever matters, or to whatever persons, have nevertheless been kept whole through so many ages, as in the archives of the Church, so that we might select from them those things which can supply us with consolation, teaching and exhortation in every event. And if we think that what is kept in the archives of cities, in which judgments and transactions concerning temporal affairs are recorded, is usefully and necessarily preserved for posterity, how much greater is the usefulness of the holy Bible, which has been preserved and in which are contained those things that lead to spiritual, heavenly and eternal matters.

units.la: Hinc verò iam sequitur, illud testimonium spiritus Sancti, quod Paulus profert ad confirmandos sui temporis homines, accommodandum esse pernos etiam præsenti tempori: quoddque ijdem verbis uti debemus hodie, id est, hoc tempore, quo per gratiam Dei euangelicæ doctrinæ lux cœpit denuò refulgere, & multi per falsos doctores à iustitia fidei, ad falsam iustitiam operum abducuntur, sicut Hebrei, ad quos scribebat Apostolus, per Scribas & Pharisæos abducebantur.
units.tr: Hence it follows that the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which Paul brings forward to confirm the people of his own time, must also be applied to the present time, and that we too ought to use the same words today, that is, in this time, in which by the grace of God the light of evangelical doctrine has begun to shine again, and many are led by false teachers from the righteousness of faith to the false righteousness of works, just as the Hebrews, to whom the Apostle was writing, were led astray by the scribes and Pharisees.

units.la: Et vox, hodie, admonet nos, quotiescunque in Scripturis legendis occupamur, intueri, quid ibi nostris temporibus conueniens occurrat, adeò, ut singulis locis, qui de rebus præsentibus nos erudiunt, commodè ascribi vox illa possit.
units.tr: The word "today" also admonishes us, whenever we are occupied in reading the Scriptures, to look out for what there suits our own times, so that this word can be fittingly applied to individual passages which instruct us about present matters.

units.la: Præterea habemus hic locum de perseuerantia in fide ad finem usque. Eatenus siquidem dem ait nos esse Christi participes, quatenus in fide constantes permanserimus.
units.tr: Besides, we have here a passage about perseverance in faith to the end. For he says that we are partakers of Christ only insofar as we have remained steadfast in faith.

units.la: Denique habemus, quòd incredulitas maximum sit peccatum, ac proinde summo su-gio vitanda. Huius enim uitij sunt illa contra Deum blasphema, Labia nostra apud nos sunt, quis noster Dominus est? Item: Dixit insipiens in corde suo, Non est Deus: corrupti sunt, & abominabiles facti sunt in studijs suis non est timor Dei ante oculos eorum, &c.
units.tr: Finally, we have here that unbelief is the greatest sin, and therefore must be avoided with the utmost care. To this vice belong those blasphemies against God: "Our lips are our own; who is our Lord?" Likewise: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt and have become abominable in their doings; there is no fear of God before their eyes," etc.

units.la: DE INDVRATIONE CORDIS, AN HOMINIS tantum sit, an etiam & Dei? &c.
units.tr: ON THE HARDENING OF THE HEART: whether it belongs only to man, or also to God? etc.

units.la: Cæterùm, quia dicitur hic, Nolite indurare corda vestra: & induratio alicubi tribuitur ipsi Deo, veluti Romanorum 9. dicitur: Cuius vult, miseretur, quem autem vult, indurat: hinc statim subit animum dubitatio, an indurari, vel non indurari, sit in hominum potestate: & quomodo intelligi conueniat, quòd homo dicatur se indurare, quòd item dicatur Deus hominem indurare: quae reuera videntur in speciem pugnare, & quomodocunque statuatur, multos scrupulos in conscientijs parere.
units.tr: But because it is said here, Do not harden your hearts, and hardening is elsewhere ascribed to God himself, as Romans 9 says: He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens, a doubt immediately comes to mind: whether to be hardened or not to be hardened lies in human power, and how it is fitting to understand that man is said to harden himself, and likewise that God is said to harden man. These things seem in appearance to conflict, and however they are settled, they produce many scruples in consciences.

units.la: Sed ad hanc speciem explicandam, opus est nonnulla de humanis viribus, seu libero quod vocant, arbitrio, praelibemus, sine quibus ad quaestionem propositam responderi satis non potest. Dabimus autem operam, ut, quanta fieri potest breuitate, causam hac absoluamus. Proinde ante omnia, quid sit liberum arbitrium: deinde, an homini adscriptum, quantum eo possit, expediemus: atque ita ad quaestionem discutiendam patebit aditus.
units.tr: But to explain this appearance, we must first touch on some matters concerning human powers, or what they call free choice, without which the question proposed cannot be answered adequately. We shall take care to settle the matter as briefly as possible. Accordingly, first, what free choice is; then, what power is ascribed to man and how far it extends; and so the way will be open to discussing the question.

units.la: Liberi arbitrij definitio sumi potest, quòd videlicet sit facultas rationis ad bonum malumue discernendum, voluntatis ad utrumuis eligendum. Sic Origines περὶ ἀρχῶν libro tertio: Item Augustinus diuersis in locis, in eadem definit sententiam, & omnes fere patres, vim liberi arbitrij in ratione & uoluntate sitam esse volunt, & nomine liberi arbitrij intelligunt voluntatem liberam, propriae rationis arbitrium ultro sequentem.
units.tr: The definition of free choice may be taken as follows: it is the faculty of reason to discern good from evil, and of the will to choose either. So Origen in the third book of On First Principles [περὶ ἀρχῶν]. Augustine, in various places, defines it in the same sense, and almost all the Fathers hold that the power of free choice lies in reason and will, and by the name of free choice they understand a free will that willingly follows the judgement of its own reason.

units.la: Iam si quaeritur, an huiusmodi liberum arbitrium insit homini, commodè etiam respondeti potest, iuxta Augustini sententiam, sicut homini concedimus rationem & voluntatem, quae rectam rationem lubenter sequitur: ita liberum ei arbitrium esse conceditur. Id quod non solùm experimur, dum quae recta ratio bona esse colligit, statim animo amplectimur: quae uero mala, fugimus & uitamus: uerumetiam Scriptura manifestè probat, dum in omnibus praeceptis solent proponi praemia iis, qui obseruauerint, & poenis iis, qui transgredientur. Quae quidem ideo proponuntur, ut ratio nostra & voluntas ad persequendum bona & fugiendum mala illiciatur: id quod Augustinus, & patres fere omnes solent eiusmodi locis occurrentibus annotare, nec non multos alios eodem pertinentes in medium producere.
units.tr: Now if it is asked whether such free choice is present in man, one may answer fittingly, following Augustine's view: just as we grant that man has reason and will, which gladly follows right reason, so free choice is granted to him. This is not only what we experience, when we at once embrace what right reason judges to be good, and flee and avoid what it judges to be evil; Scripture also plainly proves it, since in all its precepts rewards are customarily set before those who keep them, and punishments before those who transgress. These are indeed set forth so that our reason and will may be enticed to pursue good and flee evil. Augustine and almost all the Fathers are accustomed to note this whenever such passages occur, and also to bring forward many others that pertain to the same point.

units.la: At vero si iam tertio loco quaeritur, quid possit, seu quantum valeat hoc liberum arbitrium: Respondebimus, aliquot propositiones in medium adferendo, quarum prima est.
units.tr: But if, thirdly, it is asked what this free choice can do, or how much it is worth, we shall answer by setting forth several propositions, of which the first is this.

units.la: Distinguendum est, aliam esse rerum terrenarum & externarum, quae uidelicet ad communem hanc vitam pertinent intelligentiam: aliam vero rerum coelestium, id est, spiritualium, internarum, & ad Deum regnumque eius pertinentium: aliam denique rerum mediarum. Porro si de terrenis & externis rebus loquimur, concedendum quidem est, arbitrium hominis nonnihil hic ualere, & posse pleraque huiusmodi recte probare & amplecti. Hinc enim etiam in gentilibus visa sunt magna & praeclara iudicia, leges sapienter constitutae, artes mirabiliter tractatae, multa non dissimilia diuinis oraculis pronunciata: deinde uita multorum, quantum ad res externas attinet, inculpata & irreprehensibilis. Nec dubitare debemus, quin Deus etiam gentiles suis donis illustrarit, saltem in illis naturam humanam, quamlibet alias corruptam, eximijs donis ornarit: imò cogimur hoc fateri, cùm eiusmodi videamus ab illis praestita, quae sine peculiari dono, & bonitate Dei praestari nunquam possent.
units.tr: One must distinguish between earthly and external things, which pertain to this common life and understanding; heavenly things, that is, spiritual and internal things, which pertain to God and his kingdom; and finally, intermediate things. If we speak of earthly and external things, it must indeed be conceded that human choice has some worth here, and can rightly approve and embrace most such things. For among the Gentiles great and notable judgements have been seen, wisely constituted laws, arts wonderfully practised, and many things pronounced not unlike the divine oracles; further, the life of many, as far as external matters are concerned, has been blameless and irreproachable. Nor should we doubt that God has also enlightened the Gentiles with his gifts, and at least in them adorned human nature, however otherwise corrupted, with exceptional gifts. Indeed we are compelled to confess this, since we see from them accomplishments that could never be achieved without a special gift and the goodness of God.

units.la: Et Deus per quaecunque instrumenta potest agere, per impios aeque atque per pios producit quae pertinent ad illustrandam suam gloriam, iustitiam, potentiam, & bonitatem. Liquet ergo, in rebus terrenis & externis, vires aliquas, seu liberum arbitrium hominis superesse. Quanquam ne iustud quidem negari potest, saepe etiam homines in hisce rebus terrenis & externis valde praepediri. Ratio valde infirma est, ingenita est omnibus naturalis quaedam caecitas, omnes natura ad malum sumus procliuiores, unde fit, ut in eligendo saepe aberrent, & noxia pro utilibus sequenda statuant.
units.tr: And God can work through whatever instruments he pleases; through the impious as well as through the pious he brings about what pertains to displaying his glory, justice, power and goodness. It is clear, therefore, that in earthly and external things some strength, or free choice of man, remains. Yet it cannot be denied that men are often greatly hindered even in these earthly and external matters. Reason is very weak; a certain natural blindness is innate in all; all of us are by nature more inclined to evil, whence it happens that in choosing they often go astray and decide to follow harmful things in place of useful ones.

units.la: Hanc deinde naturalem infirmitatem, diabolus etiam variis modis perturbat, us
units.tr: Moreover, the devil also disturbs this natural weakness in various ways, us

units.la: Rationis infirmitas & caecitas. Liberum arbitrium in externis saepe fallit. vt reuera valdè exiguũ sit, & modica gaudes libertate, etiam in rebus terrenis, arbitrium, & nunquam ab errore liberum.
units.tr: The weakness and blindness of reason. Free choice often fails in external matters, so that its power is truly very small; it has only a modest freedom, even in earthly things, and is never free from error.

units.la: Quòd si iam sermo sit de rebus cœlestibus & Spiritualibus, deq; ijs, quæ pertinent ad vitam coram Deo, id est, ad veram sanctimoniam, qua Deo placeamus, certè hic liberum arbitrium prorsus nihil potest. Nam per rationem & voluntatem propriam nosse Deum intelligere eius erga nos voluntatem, vitam nostram secundum hanc formare, nullo pacto possumus, sed per solùm spiritum sanctũ, (qui renouat nos, & metes nostras imbuit, gubernat, dirigit,) ista assequimur, foliis q; Dei beneficio, non nostris viribus, attribui debet, si quid tale nobis contingere in hac vita animaduertimus. Istud Scriptura nusquam non inculcat. 1. Cor. 2. Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Ioan. 6. Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum. 2. Cor. 3. Nõ sumus idonei ex nobisipsis cogitare quicquam tanquam ex nobis, sed si ad aliquid idonei sumus, id ex Deo est. Quamobrem ipse Augustinus diuersis in locis fatetur, adeò prorsus nullum esse, vt vix nomen & appellatio liberi arbitrij constare possit, qui ob hanc causam ita quoq; definiuit liberũ arbitrium, vt dixerit, esse facultatem rationis & voluntatis, qua bonũ eligitur gratia afsisten-te, malũ ea desistete, aperte significas, ne electionem quidem boni nobis esse integram, si absit Dei gratia.
units.tr: But if the discussion now concerns heavenly and spiritual things, and those that pertain to life before God, that is, to true holiness by which we please God, then here free choice certainly can do absolutely nothing. For we cannot in any way know God through our own reason and will, understand his will toward us, or shape our life according to it; rather, we attain these things only through the Holy Spirit, who renews us, imbues our minds, governs and directs them. Whatever such thing we perceive happening to us in this life must be ascribed to the benefit of God, not to our own powers. Scripture everywhere impresses this. 1 Cor. 2: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. John 6: No one comes to me unless the Father draws him. 2 Cor. 3: We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God. Therefore Augustine, in various places, confesses that free choice is so utterly nothing that the very name and appellation of free choice can scarcely stand. For this reason he also defined free choice in such a way that he said it is the faculty of reason and will by which good is chosen with grace assisting, and evil is rejected when grace is absent. He clearly indicates that even the choice of good is not whole in us if the grace of God is absent.

units.la: De rebus medijs etsi pleriq; in ijs liberam electionem homini fecerint, tamen videtur hoc concedendũ, specialis esse gratię Dei, si vel in his aliquid in mentem recti veniat, & voluntas eò inclinetur, siue ad persequendum bonum, siue ad refugiendum malum. Atque hucse protendit diuinæ prouidentiæ vis, non modò vt rerum euentus succedant, quemadmodum expedire prospexerit: sed vt voluntates quoque hominum eò tendat.
units.tr: Concerning intermediate things, although many have granted man free choice in them, it seems nevertheless that this must be conceded: it is a special grace of God if something of what is right comes into the mind even in these matters, and the will is inclined thereby either to pursue the good or to shun the evil. And to this extends the power of divine providence, not only so that the outcomes of events succeed as it has seen fit to arrange, but also so that the wills of men are directed thither.

units.la: In summa ergo, cõstat, hominis liberum illud arbitrium adeò exiguarum esse virium non solùm in spiritualibus actionibus, in quibus sine spiritu Dei prorsus nihil potest: verumetiã in cæteris actionibus, corporalibus in quam, externis, & medijs, vt ægrè quicquam rectè possit sine Dei benigno auxilio.
units.tr: In sum, then, it is established that man's free choice has such small powers, not only in spiritual actions, in which without the Spirit of God it can do absolutely nothing, but also in other actions, bodily, external and intermediate, that it can scarcely do anything rightly without the kind help of God.

units.la: Tata est naturę nostrę ingenita infirmitas, & libertatis nostrę imbecillitas, atq; hęc ab illa miris modis semper grauatur, imò captiuo detinetur, vt ad bonum commouere se non possit, nedum applicare.
units.tr: So great is the weakness innate in our nature, and the feebleness of our freedom; and this is always weighed down by that nature in wonderful ways, and indeed held captive, so that it cannot move itself toward the good, let alone apply itself to it.

units.la: Cum verò spiritus non adsit à natura, sed à regeneratione, & vt Deus dederit, caro verò adsita natura, eaq; semper moliatur, quod ingen o ipsius conuenit. Est enim affectus carnis, vt Romanorum 8. dicitur, mors: propterea, quòd affectus carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum. Nam legi Dei non subditur, siquidem ne potest quidem. Et Roman. 7. Ego carnalis sum, venditus sub peccatum. Ibidem: Noui, quòd non habitet in me, id est, in carne mea, bonum. Rursus: Video aliam legem in membris meis, rebellantem legi mē tis meæ, & captiuum reddentem me legi peccati, quæ est in membris meis. Cùm hæc inquam fit miseri hominis destituti spiritu Dei miserrima conditio, palàm est, hominem sua natura nihil aliud, quàm ad malum & ad peccatum tendere. Huc pertinet, quod passim in Scripturis prauum & inscrutabile cor hominis describitur, Hieremiæ 17. Sed clarissimè peruersum hoc ingenium, & opera vitiosæ naturæ describit Apostolus Romanorum tertio, Vbi ait, non esse iustum, non esse intelligentem, ne vnum quidem. Omnes declinauerunt, &c. Et passim locis aliis similia occurrunt. Hæc igitur opus erat prælibare de humani arbitrij libertate pariter & infirmitate: vt quomodo homo per se, & suapte voluntate induretur, intelligi clarius possit.
units.tr: For when the Spirit is not present by nature, but comes through regeneration, and as God has given it, while the flesh is present by nature and always strives for what befits its nature: for the affection of the flesh, as Romans 8 says, is death, because the affection of the flesh is enmity against God. For it is not subject to the law of God, since indeed it cannot be. And Romans 7: I am carnal, sold under sin. There too: I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good thing. Again: I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. Since this, I say, is the most wretched condition of miserable man destitute of the Spirit of God, it is plain that man by his nature tends to nothing but evil and sin. To this pertains what is everywhere described in the Scriptures as the perverse and inscrutable heart of man, Jeremiah 17. But the Apostle describes this perverse disposition and the works of corrupt nature most clearly in Romans 3, where he says: There is none just, there is none who understands, no, not one. They have all gone astray, etc. Similar things occur throughout other passages. These matters, then, needed to be touched on beforehand concerning the freedom and the weakness of human choice alike, so that it may be made clearer how man is hardened by himself and of his own will.

units.la: Hocigitur pacto homo destitutus spiritu Dei, quoniam arbitrium habet valde infirmum, naturam verò semper ad malum procliuem, fit paulatim, vt hoc ipsum arbitrium, quod ei inest, indies magis magisque obscuretur, vt tandem quasi ratione & voluntate spoliati, neque intelligant, neque velint amplius, quod cum bono coniunctum sit. Quò cùm peruentum fuerit, necessum est prorsus excæcari: excæcationem verò sequitur præceps in omne vitium ruina, vitij assuetudo denique induratos reddit: Id quod Ephe-siorum quarto, non obscurè declaratur, vbi ait: Ne posthac ambuletis, quemadmodum & reliquæ gentes ambulant in vanitate mentis suæ, dùm mentem habent obtenebratam, abalienati à vita Dei, propter ignorantiam, quæ est in illis, & excæcatio-nem cordis eorum: qui posteaquam peruenerunt eò, vt dolere desierint, semetipsos dediderunt lasciuiæ, ad patrandam immundiciam omnem cum auiditate. Vos autem non sic didicistis Christum. Et eiusdem epistolæ capite secundo: Conuersabamur aliquando in concupiscentijs carnis nostræ, facientes, quæ carni ac menti libebant: & eramus natura filij iræ, quemadmodum & cæteri. Quo sanè loco perfectissime depingitur homo libero suo arbitrio præditus, & spiritu Dei destitutus, cuius miseria etiam plenius cognosci potest ex fœlicitate hominis spiritu Dei per misericordiam illustrati, quæ ibidem mox adijcitur. En ergo, quomodo homo suo arbitrio relictus, quia spiritu Dei nequaquam illuminatur, semper in peccata labitur, ac tandem induratur. Huc pertinent iam illa, quibus exprobrant incredulis, quòd aures obdurarint, & voci Domini ni obedire noluerint. Vt Ieremiæ 17. Hæc gens non audiuit vocem Domini Dei sui, nec recepit disciplinam, ideo proiecta est à Domino, Ierem.32. Quia induraftis cor vestrum, & noluistis obedire Domino, hæc omnia mala euenerunt vobis. Ieremiæ 26. Quia vocavi vos, & non responditis, faciam huic domui, sicut feci Silo. Hieremiæ 5. Percusisti eos & non doluerunt, attriuisti eos, & renuerunt accipere disciplinam: induraverunt facies suas supra petras, & noluerunt reuerti. Similiter Hieremias 7.17.19. contra eos, qui indurarunt ceruices suas, concionatur. Et Christus Matthæi vigesimotertio, Hierusalem, Hierusalem, quæ occidis Prophetas, & lapidas eos, qui ad te missi sunt, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos, & noluistis? Sed alibi quoque passim, vtà Stephano Actorum septimo, & alibi ab alijs obijcitur Iudæis, quòd indurati & excæcati sint, idque propria sua malitia, & libera sua voluntate.
units.tr: So when a man is deprived of the Spirit of God, and since his free will is very weak while his nature is always inclined to evil, it happens little by little that this very will which he has is darkened more and more each day. In the end, as if stripped of reason and will, he neither understands nor wills any longer what is joined with good. Once a man has come to this point, he must necessarily be blinded altogether. Blindness is followed by a headlong fall into every vice, and finally the habit of vice makes men hardened. The fourth chapter of Ephesians, where Paul says, declares this plainly: "Henceforth do not walk as the other Gentiles also walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. Having become past feeling, they have given themselves over to lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness. But you have not so learned Christ." And in the second chapter of the same letter: "We once lived in the lusts of our flesh, doing what the flesh and the mind desired, and we were by nature children of wrath, as the others were." In that passage a man endowed with free choice and deprived of the Spirit of God is depicted most perfectly, and his misery can be known more fully from the happiness of the man illumined by the Spirit of God through mercy, which is added immediately afterwards in the same place. Here, then, is how a man left to his own choice, since he is by no means illumined by the Spirit of God, always slips into sin and at last is hardened. To this belong the passages in which unbelievers are reproached because they have hardened their ears and were unwilling to obey the voice of the Lord: Jeremiah 17: "This nation has not listened to the voice of the Lord its God, nor received discipline; therefore it has been cast off by the Lord." Jeremiah 32: "Because you have hardened your heart and would not obey the Lord, all these evils have come upon you." Jeremiah 26: "Because I called you and you did not answer, I will do to this house as I did to Shiloh." Jeremiah 5: "You struck them and they did not grieve; you wore them down, and they refused to receive discipline; they have made their faces harder than rock and have refused to turn back." Likewise Jeremiah 7, 17 and 19 preaches against those who have made their necks stiff. And Christ in Matthew 23: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I would have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not?" But elsewhere too, as in Stephen in Acts 7, and elsewhere by others, the Jews are charged with being hardened and blinded, and that by their own wickedness and their own free will.

units.la: Vnde hoc quoque notandum est, quòd tametsi homo sic vi peccati habitantis in ipso feratur, & impellatur ad peccandum, vt sese à peccando cohinere nequeat, nihilominus manet voluntas. Neque enim dum in hanc necessitatem peccandi detrusus est homo, spoliatus est voluntate, sed voluntatis sanitate. Semper manet in homine voluntas: sed vt male velit, ex corrupta fit natura: vt autem bene, ex gratia. Et sic intelligi debet illi loci, quibus dicitur, homines bonum noluisse.
units.tr: From this it must also be noted that, although a man is so driven and impelled to sin by the power of the sin that dwells in him that he cannot restrain himself from sinning, the will nevertheless remains. For when a man is thrust into this necessity of sinning, he is not stripped of his will, but of the soundness of his will. The will always remains in man; but to will evil it becomes so from corrupt nature, and to will good it becomes so from grace. And those passages must be understood in this way which say that men have not willed the good.

units.la: Proinde ex his constat, quomodo homines propria sua voluntate peccent, & assiduè peccando, ac resistendo spiritui Sancto, reijciendoque ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, indurentur.
units.tr: Therefore it is clear from these things how men sin by their own will, and how, by sinning continually and resisting the Holy Spirit, and by rejecting what belongs to the Spirit of God, they become hardened.

units.la: Sed iam quid dicemus, quòd alijs multis locis dicitur Deus indurare homines, vt Romanorum nono, generaliter dicitur: Cuius vult, miseretur, quem vult, indurat. Exodi 4.7. 10.11.14. passim inculcatur, quòd Dominus indurauerit cor Pharaonis, & etiam omnium Ægyptiorum. Item Deuteronomij secundo: Et noluit Sihon rex Hesbon dare nobis transitum: Indurauerat enim IehouahDeus tuus spiritum eius, & obfirmauerat cor eius, vt traderetur in manus tuas, sicut nunc vides. Efaiæ 63. Quare errare nos fecisti Domine de vijs tuis, indurasti cor nostrum, ne timeremus te? Ioannis 12. ex Esaiæ sexto: propterea non poterant credere, quia iterum dixit Esaias, Excæcauit oculos eorum, & induravit cor eorum, ne viderent oculis, & ne intelligant corde, & conuertantur, & sanem eos. Sic Romanorum 1. dicitur Deus tradere in reprobum sensum. Alibi dicitur vertere, quocunq; voluerit: alibi inclinare corda: & quotidie precamur, Nec nos inducas in tentationem, &c. Quomodo ergo hi loci veniunt intelligendi?
units.tr: But what shall we say about the many other passages which say that God hardens men? Romans 9 says in general: "Whom he wills he has mercy on, and whom he wills he hardens." Exodus 4, 7, 10, 11 and 14 repeatedly insists that the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and of all the Egyptians too. Likewise Deuteronomy 2: "And Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through; for Jehovah your God had hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, so that he might be delivered into your hands, as you now see." Isaiah 63: "Why, O Lord, have you made us wander from your ways and hardened our heart so that we do not fear you?" John 12, from Isaiah 6: "Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes and understand with their heart and be converted, and I should heal them." So Romans 1 says that God gave them over to a reprobate mind. Elsewhere it says that he turns men wherever he wills, and elsewhere that he inclines hearts; and every day we pray, And lead us not into temptation, etc. How then are these passages to be understood?

units.la: Certè hinc statim videntur sequi grauissima offendicula. Hinc enim apparet inferri posse, quòd, qui hoc pacto indurantur à Deo, non possint aliter, quàm male agere. Deinde, quòd induratio non fit hominibus imputanda, vtpote ad quam quodammodo inuiti, impellente Deo, homines perducantur. Præterea Deum fore autorem peccati & mali. Quid ad ista omnia dicemus?
units.tr: Surely from these things very grave difficulties seem to follow at once. For it appears to follow that those who are hardened in this way by God cannot act otherwise than wickedly. Further, that hardening is not to be imputed to men, since they are led into it, somewhat against their will, by God's impelling. Besides, God would be the author of sin and evil. What shall we say to all these things?

units.la: Propter has rationis humanæ ineptas illationes etiam sancti Patres, ne viderentur reuerenter loqui de admirandis operibus Dei, interpretati sunt hos locos, referendo eos ad Dei præscientiam, ita, vt, quando dicitur Deum indurasse homines, idem sit sensus, ac si diceretur, Deum præuidisse & præscisse indurandos: atque ita cùm prævidere, seu præscire malum, non sit ipsum malum facere, aut ad id impellere, hac interpretatione illationes illæ omnes euertuntur.
units.tr: Because of these foolish inferences of human reason, the holy Fathers, lest they should seem to speak irreverently about the wonderful works of God, interpreted these passages by referring them to God's foreknowledge, so that when it is said that God has hardened men, the meaning is the same as if it were said that God foresaw and foreknew that they would be hardened. And since to foresee or foreknow evil is not to do evil itself or to impel men to it, all those inferences are overturned by this interpretation.

units.la: Alij formulas illas locutionum retulerunt ad permissionem, seu patientiam, dicentes: Deus induravit, id est, permisit indurari, passus est indurari. Et hi defendunt suam interpretationem illis verbis: 1. Corinthiorum 10. Non sinet vos Deus tentari supra id quod poteritis. Item Actorum septimo, permisit Deus gentes errare, &c. Verum quando pasim multæ occurrunt in Scripturis eiusmodi locutionum formulæ in eandem sententiam, nequaquam videtur cõuenire, vt passim tales interpretationes adhibeatur. Proinde nos citra periculum dicere poterimus, has formulas proprie, vt sonant, accipiendas, & Deo indurationem & excæcationem tribui id quod Augustinus ipse contra Iulianum libro quinto, item libro de gratia & libero arbitrio, dicere nõ est veritus, nec propterea sed qui, ipsum contra bonitatem, vel iustitiam agere, vel causam peccati existere.
units.tr: Others referred those forms of speech to permission, or to patience, saying: God hardened, that is, he permitted them to be hardened, he suffered them to be hardened. And these defend their interpretation by these words: 1 Corinthians 10: "God will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear." Likewise Acts 7: God permitted the Gentiles to go astray, etc. But since many forms of such expressions occur throughout the Scriptures with the same sense, it does not seem fitting that such interpretations should be applied everywhere. Therefore we can say without danger that these forms are to be taken properly, as they sound, and that hardening and blinding are ascribed to God, which Augustine himself did not hesitate to say against Julian in book 5, and likewise in his book on grace and free choice; yet this does not mean that God acts against goodness or justice, or that he is the cause of sin.

units.la: De Induratione vide interpretes in caput 9. ad Romanos, sententiarum lib. 1. distinct. 45. & 46. Augustinum libro retractationum 1. capite 11. Item contra Iulianum libro 5. Etin Ioánnem tractatu 85. Et Deum non peccare indurando, August. de ciuitate libro 14. cap. 11. & 17. Item libro sententiarum 2. distinct. 47.
units.tr: On the hardening, see the commentators on Romans chapter 9; the Sentences, book 1, distinctions 45 and 46; Augustine, Retractions, book 1, chapter 11; likewise Against Julian, book 5; and on John, tractate 85. And that God does not sin in hardening, see Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapters 11 and 17; likewise the Sentences, book 2, distinction 47.

units.la: Primò ergo dicitur Deus indurare, & excæcare, dùm secundum iustitiam peccata prio- ora peccatis punit, eosque, qui commeriti sunt per peccata præcedentia, quia oblatam cognitionem respuerunt, eos iusto suo iudicio eò præcipitat, vt resurgere nunquam possint. In quo facto neque contra iustitiam, neque contra bonitatem suam quicquam facit, neque etiam peccati caussa existit. Huc pertinent illa Romanorum 1. vbi dicitur de impijs, quòd, cùm noluissent Deum cognoscere, aut, cùm cognouerint, noluerint honorare, vt par est, tradidit illos Deus per cupiditates cordium suorum, &c. Item secunda Thessalonicensium secundo, Mittet illis Deus efficaciam seductionis, vt crederent mendacio, vt iudicentur omnes, qui non crediderunt veritati, sed approbauerunt iustitiam.
units.tr: First, then, God is said to harden and blind when, according to justice, he punishes earlier sins with later ones, and casts down into such a state, by his just judgment, those who have deserved it through earlier sins, because they have rejected the knowledge offered them, so that they can never rise again. In doing this he does nothing contrary to his justice or his goodness, nor is he the cause of sin. To this belong those words of Romans 1 about the wicked, that, since they were unwilling to know God, or, having known him, were unwilling to honour him as is fitting, God gave them up to the lusts of their hearts, etc. Likewise 2 Thessalonians 2: "God will send them a powerful delusion, so that they will believe a lie, that all who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in unrighteousness may be condemned."

units.la: Secundò, dicitur Deus indurare & excæcare, quando aufert ab hominibus suam gratiam, suumque spiritum, & relinquit illos sibiipsis, vt pro suo ingenio faciant, quod libet, à quo sane non possunt nisi ad malum ferri, ac proinde eos excæcari & indurari necessum est. Neque hic Deus contra iustitiam quicquam facit. Nam illuminare homines, vel aliàs sua dona quocunque modo impendere non tenetur: Solius misericordiæ id est, & immensæ atque gratuitæ bonitatis: cùm nos sane nihil apud illum promereamur: Gratis seruamur, gratis beneficia eius accipimus. Neq; ob hanc causam peccatum in illum potest reijci. Nam nostra voluntate, quæ libera nobis permittitur, non adimitur, ad malum, sublato illo spiritu, currimus. Huc pertinet illa Iob. 12. Comutans labium veracium, & doctrinam suam auferens. Ibidem: Qui immutat cor principum populi terræ, & decipit eos, vt frustra incedant per inuium. Item Roman. 11. ex Esaiæ sexto: Dedit eis Deus spiritum compunctionis, oculos, vt non videant, & aures, vt non audiant, vsque ad hodiernum diem. Quo etiam vtitur Matthæi 11. Et sæpè dicit Christus qui aures habet audiendi, audiat, qui potest capere capiat: & abscondita dicuntur mysteria à sapientibus, reuelata autem paruulis.
units.tr: Second, God is said to harden and blind when he takes away from men his grace and his Spirit, and leaves them to themselves, so that they do whatever they like according to their own nature; and they cannot but be carried toward evil, so that it is necessary for them to be blinded and hardened. Nor does God do anything against justice here. For he is not bound to illuminate men or to bestow his gifts in any other way; this belongs only to his mercy, his immense and free goodness, since we deserve nothing from him. We are saved freely, and we receive his benefits freely. Nor for this reason can sin be imputed to him. For when the Spirit is taken away, we run to evil by our own will, which is still left to us as free. To this belongs Job 12: "He changes the lips of the trustworthy and takes away their understanding." In the same place: "He changes the heart of the princes of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste." Likewise Romans 11 from Isaiah 6: "God has given them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, to this very day." Matthew 11 also uses this, and Christ often says, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," "He who is able to receive, let him receive"; and the mysteries are said to be hidden from the wise and revealed to little children.

units.la: Tertiò, dicitur Deus excæcare & indurare, quia reuera vult quosdam insigniter malos esse, vt ex eorum malitia illustrior reddatur ipsius iustitia & potentia, vel in perdendo illos postea, vel in affligendo per illos tanquam instrumenta, alios. Hoc enim licet certò statuere, quòd, sicut Dominus sanctos suos etiam in vtero, & priusquam nascatur, format, parat, sanctificat ad præclaram aliquod munus, sicut de Hieremia, Ioanne baptista, item de Iacob legitur: Ita quoque format & parat quosdam ad alia opera, per quos vult suam gloriam & potentiam exercere, & illustriorem reddere, illorumque postea confiliaper ministrum Satanam ad malum destinat, & voluntates excitat, & ad perficiendum corroborat. Nouit enim Deus etiam malis vti, tanquam instrumentis, ab bonum tamen finem. Atque hoc pacto induratus fuit Pharao, siue hac de causa: vt clarè dicitur Romanor. 9. vbi ad id citatur ex Exodo nono: In hoc ipsum excitaui te, vt ostendam in te potentiam meam, & vt annunciatur nomen meum in tota terra. Et ante Exodi 7. palàm dicitur Dominus, quòd induraret cor Pharaonis, ita vt stupenda signa nihil tamen moueretur. Id verò ideo, vt postea potentiam suam, liberando ex manu adeò duri tyranni suum populum, notam faceret, id quod multis locis ibidem declaratur. Ibique palàm dicitur, quòd Dominus aggrauarit cor illius, ita vt manifestè significetur, voluntatem Pharaonis destinato motam ad id quod Dominus ita volebat per illum fieri.
units.tr: Thirdly, God is said to blind and harden, because he really does want certain people to be notably wicked, so that his justice and power may appear more illustrious from their wickedness, either by destroying them afterwards or by using them as instruments to afflict others. For we may safely hold that, just as the Lord forms, prepares and sanctifies his saints even in the womb, before they are born, for some outstanding office (as we read of Jeremiah, John the Baptist and Jacob), so he likewise forms and prepares some men for other works, through whom he wills to exercise and display his glory and power more fully. Afterwards he directs their counsels to evil through Satan his minister, stirs up their wills, and strengthens them to carry the evil through. For God knows how to use even evil men as instruments, yet to a good end. In this way Pharaoh was hardened, whether for this reason alone or for others, as is plainly stated in Romans 9, where Exodus 9 is cited for this: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth." Also, before Exodus 7, the Lord is plainly said to harden Pharaoh's heart, so that he was not moved by the wonderful signs. This was so that afterwards he might make known his power by delivering his people from the hand of so hard a tyrant, as is declared in many places in that same account. There too it is plainly said that the Lord hardened his heart, so that it is clearly indicated that Pharaoh's will was moved, by a fixed purpose, to do what the Lord so willed to be done through him.

units.la: Et neq; ob id, Deus venit iniustitiæ, vel omissæ bonitatis insimulandus: tum, quia potest artifex instrumentis, seu rebus fabricatis à se, vti ad quamcunq; rem velit: tum quia facit ita, ad finem maioris boni, (sicut lapsus Iudæorum ad salutem gentium, Romanor. 11.) tum, quia etiam non tenetur aliter facere, quàm hominem malum, quo meretur, detrudere.
units.tr: Nor on that account is God to be charged with injustice, or with neglecting goodness. First, because an artificer may use his instruments, or the things he has made, for whatever purpose he wishes. Secondly, because he acts thus for the sake of a greater good (as the fall of the Jews became the salvation of the Gentiles, Romans 11). Thirdly, because he is not bound to act otherwise than by thrusting down the wicked man to the place he deserves.

units.la: Hocipsum etiam Rom. 9. ostenditur: vbi talis fit obiectio: Quid adhuc conqueritur? Nam voluntati eius quis resistit? (sequitur responsio) Atqui ô homo, tu quis es, qui exadversus respondes Deo? Num dicet figmentum ei, qui finxit: Quare me finxisti ad hunc modum?
