Annon habet potestatem figulus luti, vt ex eadem massa fingat aliud quidem vas in honorem, aliud verò in ignominiam? Quòd si Deus voles ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiâ suam, tulit multa animi lenitate vasa irae, apparata in interitum, & vt notas faceret diuitias gloriæ, erga vasa misericordiæ, quæ præparauerat in gloriam. Hæc igitur est ratio, quam Apostolus vult adhiberi ad retundendum ora illorum, qui Deum vellent hic omissæ bonitatis insimulare, vel suum peccatum in Deum reijcere. Non est vlterius inquirendum, quare, vel quaratione Deus ista faciat, vt hoc pacto aliqui inducentur, vt veritatem & cognitionem auditam respuant. Dicamus potius, quádo huc peruentum uentum fuerit, cum Apostolo, Roman. 11. ô profunditatem diuitiarum & sapientiæ & cognitionis Dei, quàm inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius, & imperuestigabiles viæ eius? Quis enim cognouit mentem Domini? aut, quis illi fuit à consilijs?
units.tr: This same point is also shown in Romans 9, where the objection is raised: "Why does he still complain? For who resists his will?" (the answer follows): "But indeed, O man, who are you, that you answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, 'Why have you made me thus?' Does not the potter have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour? But if God, willing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory toward vessels of mercy, which he had prepared for glory." This, then, is the argument the Apostle wishes to be used to silence the mouths of those who would charge God with neglecting goodness here, or who would cast their own sin upon God. We should not inquire further why or by what means God does these things, so that by this method some are led to reject the truth and the knowledge that they have heard. Rather, when we have come this far, let us say with the Apostle, Romans 11: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?"

units.la: Constat ergo, quòd homines à Deo variis de causis indurentur, & tamen ob id culpa peccati vel damnationis eorum Deo imputari non debeat. Nam etsi excæcatio opus Dei sit, tamè causa peccati non aliunde quæretur, quàm à voluntate hominis, ob quam peccatum illi imputatur, & damnatio iuste infligitur. Quomodo etiam peccata dicuntur opera Satanæ, & tamen ea certum est hominis tantùm voluntate committi, & voluntati imputari. Imò ipse Satanas quoque dicitur excæcare: vt 2. Corinthior. 4. Deus huius seculi excæcauit sensus incredulorum, ne illucesceret illis lumen euangelij gloriæ Christi. Et Ephes. 2. Ambulastis in peccatis iuxta principem, cui potestas est aeris, qui est spiritus nunc agens in filijs cõtumacibus. Quæ quidē non sic decipiuntur, quasi inuitos & reluctates posse Satan impellere & cogere, sed quòd homines partim naturæ prauitate corrupti, partim dolis Satanę seducti, se totos sponte illius suggestionibus accommodant.
units.tr: It is therefore established that men are hardened by God for various reasons, and yet on that account the guilt of their sin or condemnation ought not to be imputed to God. For although blinding is the work of God, the cause of sin is nowhere else to be sought than in the will of man, on account of which sin is imputed to him and condemnation is justly inflicted. So also sins are called the works of Satan, and yet it is certain that they are committed by the will of man alone and are imputed to that will. Indeed, Satan himself is also said to blind: as in 2 Corinthians 4, "the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them." And Ephesians 2: "You walked in sins according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience." Yet these men are not so deceived as if Satan could drive and compel unwilling and resisting people, but because men, partly corrupted by the perversity of their nature and partly seduced by the wiles of Satan, freely give themselves wholly to his suggestions.

units.la: Neque absurdum est, dicere, Dei, & Satanæ, & hominis actiones ad idem opus conuenire: simulque indurationem tribuere Deo, Satanæ, & homini. Potest id exemplo demonstrari. Aptissimum verò sumetur ex historia Iob. Ad huius afflictiones voluntas Domini intercessit, Satanæ studium & conatus, malorum item hominum violentia. Hic igitur erant primò Chaldæi, qui insigni animi malitia & crudelitate pastores Iob interemerunt, greges abegerunt, &c. Ad quæ haud dubiè voluntas illorum currebat, & grauiter peccasse, extra controuersiam est. Interea diabolus hic strenuè laborabat, imò omnium malorum autor erat, & homines incitabat, & per se damnagra-uissima intulit. Neque abfuit ab hoc opere Deus, cùm constet, hunc diabolo potestatem fecisse, vt habetur Iob primo: Dixit Dominus ad Satan, Ecce, vniuersa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt, tantùm in eum ne extendas manum tuam. Et iterum ibidem ipse Iob vni Deo accepta fert omnia, dicens, Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est, sit nomen Domini benedictum.
units.tr: Nor is it absurd to say that the actions of God, of Satan and of man converge on the same work, and that hardening is at once ascribed to God, to Satan and to man. This can be shown by an example, and the most apt is taken from the history of Job. The will of the Lord intervened in Job's afflictions, and so did the zeal and efforts of Satan, and likewise the violence of wicked men. First, then, there were the Chaldeans, who with remarkable malice and cruelty slew Job's shepherds, drove off his flocks, and so on. Undoubtedly their will was running towards these acts, and that they sinned gravely is beyond dispute. Meanwhile the devil laboured vigorously here; indeed, he was the author of all these evils, and he stirred up men and inflicted the gravest losses through them. Nor was God absent from this work, since it is clear that he gave the devil power, as we have in Job 1: "The Lord said to Satan, 'Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.'" And again in the same place Job himself ascribes everything to God alone, saying: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass; blessed be the name of the Lord."

units.la: Deinde secundo capite, cùm Satanas eum percussisset vlcere pessimo in corpore: Si bona suscepimus, inquit, de manu Domini, mala cur non sustineamus? Et passim | de-inceps Domino accepta fert omnia. Hic igitur licet videre, ad afflictionem Iob, pariter Dei, Satanæ, & hominum opus intercedere. Et Chaldæos quodámodo à Deo etiam excitatos ad damna inferenda sancto Iob. Et tamen Deo propterea peccatum Chaldæorum non magis, quàm malitia Satanæ imputari debet. Id quod ex eo licet intelligere, quòd alio fine atque alia ratione Deus hic, & in similibus actionibus agit, quàm Satanas vel homines. Deus enim inprimis iustè facit, vt potè habens potestatem in omnes res à se conditas, sicut figulus, quæ per gratiam dat, ipse cùm vult, iustè aufert: iustè peccatum quæ cutit eum, qui quomodocunq; agat, semper coram ipso reus est. De diabolo & homine non est idem dicendum. Neque habentius in alios, nisi quatenus pro tempore, & in certis rebus, ipsis à Deo permittitur.
units.tr: Then in the second chapter, when Satan had struck him with a most grievous ulcer in his body, Job said: "If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?" And throughout what follows he ascribes everything to the Lord. Here, then, one may see that the work of God, of Satan and of men concurred in Job's affliction. The Chaldeans were in some sense also stirred up by God to inflict harm on the holy Job. And yet the sin of the Chaldeans is not to be imputed to God any more than the malice of Satan is. This can be understood from the fact that God acts here, and in similar actions, with a different end and in a different manner from Satan or from men. For God, first of all, acts justly, since he has power over all things he has created, like the potter; what he gives by grace, he takes away justly when he wills; and he justly punishes sin, for whoever acts in whatever way is always accountable before him. The same cannot be said of the devil and of man. Nor do they have any right over others, except insofar as it is permitted them by God for a time and in certain matters.

units.la: Deinde, cùm Dominus etiá malos incitat, vel indurat, vel emittit, utitur illis tanquam instrumentis, facitq; illos seruire suæ iustitiæ, & vtitur ad explenda sua consilia, quæ necessariò semper ad bonum tendunt. Nam, quæ huiusmodi facit, eo fine facit, vt postea illustret suam gloriam, potentiam, quam quacunque ratione illustrari semper iustum & necessarium est, vt pro malis rependat duplicata bona, sicut in Iob quoq; fecit. Atvero diabolus, siue homo, ad huiusmodi finem non respiciunt, sed pro ingenita sua malitia quærunt nocere, & perdere, & pro viribus, quantum possunt, lædunt. Itaq; patet, quòd licet ad idem opus conuenire actio Dei, actio Satanæ, & actio hominis, tamen Dei iustitia non possit in his culpari: Satanæ verò seu hominum malitia non possit excusari.
units.tr: Next, when the Lord also stirs up, hardens or sends forth wicked men, he uses them as instruments, and makes them serve his justice, and uses them to carry out his purposes, which always necessarily tend to the good. For whatever he does of this kind, he does with the end that he may afterwards display his glory and power, which it is always just and necessary to display in whatever way, so that he may repay good things twofold for evil, as he also did in Job's case. But the devil, or man, does not look to such an end; rather, from his innate malice he seeks to harm and destroy, and injures as far as he can. Thus it is plain that, although the action of God, the action of Satan and the action of man may converge on the same work, yet the justice of God cannot be blamed in these matters, while the malice of Satan or of men cannot be excused.

units.la: Proinde, ex his constabit, quomodo contingat homines indurari suapte culpa, & quomodo, etiamsi Deus multis in locis Scripturæ dicatur indurare & excæcare, ipsita-men culpa hominum, seu peccatum non possit imputari. Necessariò hucres redit, vt homo, quandoquidem voluntate sua non est prorsus spoliatus, & habet sibi abunde proposita, quæ ad veritatis cognitionem possent inducere, & tamen magis eligit, & naturas propensus fertur ad ea, quæ sunt mala, suapte culpa indurari dicitur. Deus autor peccati dici non potest, sed homo peruersæ suæ voluntati obtemperans, quæ suggestionibus diaboli, semper quoq; ad malum impelletis, lubenter assentitur. Huc pertinent Scripturæ loci, qui docet peccatum homini & diabolo acceptum ferendum. Ioan. 8. Vos ex patre diabolo estis, & desideriis patris vestri vultis obsequi. Ille homicida erat ab initio, & in veritate non stetit...
units.tr: From these things it will be clear how men become hardened through their own fault, and how the guilt or sin of men cannot be imputed to God, even though in many places Scripture says that God hardens and blinds. It follows necessarily that man, since he is not wholly stripped of his will, and since abundant means are set before him that could lead him to knowledge of the truth, yet prefers what is evil and is carried by his nature toward it, is said to be hardened through his own fault. God cannot be called the author of sin. Rather, man, obeying his perverse will, which always and willingly assents to the suggestions of the devil urging him on to evil, is responsible. To this belongs the passage of Scripture that teaches that sin is to be ascribed to man and to the devil. John 8: "You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth..."

units.la: Dei iustitia si ne peccato. Satan et homo malitiosi & rei. Homines sua ipsorum culpa indurantur et excæcatur. Peccatum ex homine & diabolo. veritate non stetit, quia non est veritas in eo: cùm loquitur mendacium, ex propriis loquitur, quia mendax est, atque eius rei pater. Ephes. 2. Potestas diaboli & voluntas hominis clarè ostenditur. Et vos cùm effetis mortui delictis ac peccatis, in quibus aliquando ambulastis iuxta seculum mundi huius, iuxta principem, cui potestas est aeris, qui & Spiritus nunc agens in filijs contumacibus. 1. Ioannis 3. Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est, quoniam ab initio peccat. Lucae vigesimo secundo, Intrauit Satanas in Iudam, abijtq; & locutus est cum principibus Sacerdotum, ac magistratibus, quem admodum illum traderet eis. Actorum 5. Anania, cur impleuit Satanas cor tuum, vt mentireris spiritui Sancto? Ibidem: Quare posuisti in corde tuo rem istam? Ita passim & homini, & Satanae coniu nctim peccatum tribuitur. Iacobi 1. Ne quis, cùm tentatur, dicat, se à Deo tentari. Nam Deus, vt malis tentari non potest, ita necipse quenquam tentat. Imò vnusquisque tentatur, dum à propria conscientia abstrahitur et inescatur. Deinde, concupiscentia postquam concepit, parit peccatum, peccatum verò perfectum gignit mortem.
units.tr: The justice of God is without sin. Satan and man are malicious and guilty. Men are hardened and blinded through their own fault. Sin comes from man and from the devil. "...did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and the father of it." Ephesians 2: the power of the devil and the will of man are clearly shown: "And you, when you were dead through your offences and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince who has power over the air, the spirit now working in the sons of disobedience." 1 John 3: "He who commits sin is of the devil, for the devil has sinned from the beginning." Luke 22: "Satan entered into Judas, and he went away and spoke with the chief priests and the magistrates about how he might betray him to them." Acts 5: "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?" Likewise: "Why have you conceived this thing in your heart?" Thus sin is attributed everywhere both to man and to Satan together. James 1: "Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God. For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. Rather, each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own conscience. Then desire, once it has conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is full grown, brings forth death."

units.la: Nam quidam cùm audissent, exacerbauerunt, at non omnes, qui profecti fuerant ex Aegypto per Mosen. Quibus autem infensus fuit quadraginta annis? Nónne ijs qui peccauerant, quorum membra conciderunt in deserto? Quibus autem iurauit, non ingressuros in requiem suam, nisi ijs, qui non obedierant? Et videmus, quòd non potuerunt ingredi propter incredulitatem.
units.tr: For some, when they had heard, provoked him; yet not all who had come out of Egypt through Moses did so. But with whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who had sinned, whose bodies fell in the desert? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, except to those who had not obeyed? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.

units.la: Incipit excutere quasdam testimonij allegati partes, atque argumenta inde ducere. Quoniam autem scopus eius in hac conclusione est, auocare seu deterrere eos ab incredulitate: ideo vult in testimonio illo ante omnia attentissimè considerari, quae ad genus criminis, & grauitatem punitionis spectant, colligitq;, incredulitatem potissimum adeò graviter in patribus punitam. Haec igitur membra testimonij huius excutiuntur: exacerbauerunt, siue, tentauerunt & probauerunt, item, errant corde, non cognouerunt vias meas: quae hic notantur alijs verbis, videlicet peccandi, non obediendi, & incredulitatis: & haec omnia ad genus criminis pertinent. Deinde, hae particulae, Infensus fui quadraginta annis, iurauî in ira mea, si introibunt in requiem: quae pertinent ad genus supplicij. Ex his verò omnibus manifestum conficitur argumentum, ductum à grauitate diuinae vltionis in incredulitatem. Est enim omnium horum haec sententia: in illo testimonio spiritus Sancti, quod iam citaui, vos audistis, quòd Deus per quosdam sit exacerbatus: audistis, quòd quibusdam fuerit infensus per quadraginta annos: audistis, quòd iurauerit quibusdam, quòd nunquam ingrederentur in promissam requiem: Quae sanè verba magnum habere debent pondus, sicut reuera grauem admodum & horrendam vltionem significant. Sed si bene consideramus, adeò horrendam vltionem Deus exercuit, in eos potissimùm, qui ipsum exacerbauerunt per incredulitatem, dum promissionibus eius de inducendo ipsos in terram Canaan fidem non adhibuerunt. Ergo vobis quoq;, si per incredulitatem eum exacerbaueritis, & promissiones ad vos factas de ingressu in requiem spiritualem neglexeritis, eodem modo metuendum est, ne infensum habeatis Deum, & excludamini, a requie optata frustremini.
units.tr: He begins to examine certain parts of the testimony cited and to draw arguments from it. Since his aim in this conclusion is to call them back from unbelief and to deter them from it, he wishes first of all that the things in that testimony which relate to the kind of crime and the gravity of the punishment be carefully weighed. He concludes that unbelief in particular was punished so severely in the fathers. So these parts of the testimony are examined: they provoked, or tempted and tested; likewise, they err in heart, they have not known my ways. These are noted here in other words, namely sinning, not obeying, and unbelief, and all of these pertain to the kind of crime. Then these clauses: I was angry with that generation for forty years; I swore in my wrath that they would not enter into my rest, pertain to the kind of punishment. From all of these a clear argument is drawn, from the gravity of divine vengeance against unbelief. For the sense of all of them is this: in that testimony of the Holy Spirit which I have already cited, you have heard that God was provoked by some; you have heard that he was angry with some for forty years; you have heard that he swore to some that they would never enter the promised rest. These words certainly ought to carry great weight, since they really signify a very grave and dreadful vengeance. But if we consider well, God exercised so dreadful a vengeance especially on those who provoked him through unbelief, when they did not give credence to his promises of bringing them into the land of Canaan. Therefore, if you too provoke him through unbelief and neglect the promises made to you of entering into the spiritual rest, in the same way you must fear lest God be angry with you and you be shut out and cheated of the rest desired.

units.la: Haec est simplex & perspicua sententia, debentque omnia haec: Nam quidam, cùm audissent, &c. ad eum vsque locum: Etenim nobis annunciatum est, &c. coniungi, vt perfecta argumentatio habeatur. Nam verba illa initio capitis quarti posita, Metuamus igitur, &c. complexionem seu conclusionem constituunt, ex praecedentibus manantem. Hinc autem apparet, inesse his nonnihil obscuritatis, quòd Apostolus, partim vehementiae, partim euidentioris demonstrationis causa, orationem adhibet figuratam, & interrogationibus subiectionibusque illustratam more rhetorico. Quod enim dixit: Quibus autem infensus fuit quadraginta annis? Nónne ijs, qui peccauerant, quorum membra conciderunt in deserto? Quibus autè iurauit, nō ingressuros in requiem suam, nisi ijs, qui non obedierant? Hoc, inquam, pacto ista enunciata, multo plus habent acrimoniae, nec non maiori luce & criminis qualitatem, & supplicij acerbitatem exprimunt, quàm si simpliciter dixisset, quod summatim ex illis colligens mox subiicit: Et uidemus, quòd non ob aliam causam prohibiti sunt ingredi, quàm propter incredulitatem.
units.tr: This is the plain and clear sense, and all of these things, from "For some, when they had heard," down to that place, "For the gospel has been preached to us," should be joined together so that a complete argument is had. For those words placed at the beginning of chapter four, "Let us fear therefore," etc., form the conclusion, flowing from what precedes. From this it appears that there is some obscurity in these things, because the Apostle, partly for the sake of vehemence and partly for the sake of a clearer demonstration, uses a figured speech, illustrated by questions and subjoined clauses in the rhetorical manner. For what he said, "But with whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who had sinned, whose bodies fell in the desert? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, except to those who had not obeyed?" These statements, I say, put in this way, have much more force, and express with greater clarity both the quality of the crime and the bitterness of the punishment, than if he had simply said what he immediately subjoins, summarising it from those things: And we see that they were prohibited from entering for no other cause than unbelief.

units.la: Igitur potissimum membra testimonij hic excutiuntur, exacerbauerunt, siue tentauerunt me, probauerūt, & viderūt opera mea: praeterea illa: Infensus fui quadraginta annis, iurauî in ira mea, si ingredientur in requiem meam. Tantum de dispositione principalis argumenti. Cætera obseruatu digna inter explicandum partes annotabimus. Ait ergo: Nam quidam, cùm audissent, exacerbauerunt, &c. τινὲς δὲ ἀπίσαυϛε ωαςεπίπχαναν·ἀλλ᾿ ὁ wαὶτιὰ ἐξελ&ὁνῖ&s ἐξ ἀιγύπτης Διὰ μωσέωσ particula γὰρ connectit ista praecedentibus, & ad explicationem viam sternit. Quasi dicat: Rectè ait, In exacerbatione, notandaque est illa particula, non minus quàm caeterae quae sequuntur. Nam ita reuera accidit, quidam, cùm audissent vocem Domini, exacerbauerunt, at non omnes, qui profecti fuerant ex Aegypto, per Mosen: Hic autem ipse clare exponit, de qua exacerbatione, ac punitione spiritus Sanctus per Psalmographum loquatur, nimirum de ea, quae contigit sub Mose, quae describitur Numerorum decimoquarto, ut suprà declarauimus. Quod etiam satis colligi potest ex verbis Spiritus sancti, quibus addit, exacerbationem factam in deserto, vbi tentauerunt Deum patres, &c. Sed, quare dicit, quidam, praeterea, non omnes? Non solum, quia nonnulli ab exacerbando Deum sibi temperarunt, sicut historia ipsa testatur: sed multo magis, vt acerbitatem supplicij ad certos peccatores, & ad certum crimen, nempe incredulitatem pertinere doceat. Etenim vbi aliquis forte dixisset, ob alia quaedam crimina adeo atroces poenas in fictas populo, quemadmodum propter adoratum vitulum Exodi trigesimo secundo, caesi sunt fere triginta tria millia hominum: item propter petitas carnes fata plaga magna, cùm datae eae essent, Numerorum 11. Item propter excitatum schisma, Numerorum 16. à terra absorbentur ducenti quinquaginta, qui cum Corah incensum offerunt in rebellione. Item propter fornicationem cum filiabus Moab, Numerorum 25, caesa viginti quatuor millia hominum. Refellit & excludit Apostolus haec omnia, nec non clare docet infertque ob solam incredulitatem, (quae describitur Numerorum 14, vbi, cùm iam ad limites terrae promissae peruenissent, & tam diu in tam multis negotiis experti fuissent Dei potentiam, & amplissimam bonitatem, credere tamen noluerunt, quòd Deus posset & vellet eos in illam inducere:) patres adeò graviter punitos. Itaque prudenter & valde eleganter dicit, quosdam exacerbasse Dominum, non tamen omnes: vt intelligatur, punitionem, quae hic grauissima describitur, non vniuersalem, & in quosuis, aut propter quoduis crimen, irrogatam: sed particularem, & in eos potissimum, qui fuerunt increduli, atque ita incredulitatem adeò seueriter à Deo punitam. Quod tamen hic non statim exprimit, sed commodius putauit maiori acrimonia declarare: unde et interrogationes mox subijcit, quibus illud manifestum facit. Nam vt vniuscuiusque mens, cùm audit, quosdam tantùm fuisse, statim monetur ad inquirendum: si quidam fuerunt, qui hoc pacto exacerbauerunt, & adeò seueriter sunt puniti, quales ergo fuerunt illi, in quos visum est Deo ita saeuire? Quibus autem infensus fuit? &c.
units.tr: Therefore the principal parts of the testimony are examined here: "they provoked," or "they tempted me," "they tested," "and saw my works"; besides those: "I was angry with that generation for forty years; I swore in my wrath that they would not enter into my rest." So much for the arrangement of the main argument. We will note the other things worth observing in explaining the parts. He says, then: "For some, when they had heard, provoked, etc." [τινὲς γὰρ ἀκούσαντες παρεπίκραναν· ἀλλ' οὐ πάντες οἱ ἐξελθόντες ἐξ Αἰγύπτου διὰ Μωσέως]. The particle "for" connects these things with what precedes and prepares the way for the explanation, as if he were saying: "He rightly says, 'in provocation,'" and that particle is to be noted no less than the others that follow. For thus it truly happened: some, when they had heard the voice of the Lord, provoked him; yet not all who had come out of Egypt through Moses did so. Here he himself clearly explains which provocation and punishment the Holy Spirit speaks of through the psalmist, namely the one that happened under Moses, which is described in Numbers 14, as we declared above. This can also be sufficiently gathered from the words of the Holy Spirit, in which he adds that the provocation happened in the desert, where the fathers tempted God, etc. But why does he say "some," and "not all"? Not only because some refrained from provoking God, as the history itself testifies, but much more so that he may teach that the bitterness of the punishment pertains to certain sinners and to a certain crime, namely unbelief. For if someone perhaps had said that for other crimes such dreadful punishments were inflicted on the people, as for the worship of the calf in Exodus 32, when about thirty-three thousand men were slain; likewise for the craving for meat, when a great plague struck them after the quail had been given, Numbers 11; likewise for the stirred-up schism, Numbers 16, when two hundred fifty were swallowed up by the earth, who offered incense with Korah in rebellion; likewise for fornication with the daughters of Moab, Numbers 25, when twenty-four thousand men were slain, the Apostle refutes and excludes all of these things, and also clearly teaches and infers that the fathers were punished so severely for unbelief alone. (This is described in Numbers 14, where, although they had now arrived at the borders of the promised land, and had so long experienced God's power and very ample goodness in so many matters, they nevertheless were unwilling to believe that God could and would bring them into it.) Thus he prudently and very elegantly says that some provoked the Lord, but not all, so that it may be understood that the punishment described here as most grievous was not universal, nor inflicted on anyone whomsoever, or for any crime whatsoever, but particular, and inflicted especially on those who were unbelieving; and thus that unbelief was punished by God so severely. This, however, he does not state at once, but thought it more fitting to declare it with greater force. Hence he immediately subjoins questions by which he makes this plain. For, so that the mind of each one, when it hears that only some were such, is at once prompted to inquire: if there were some who provoked in this way and were punished so severely, what sort were they on whom God was pleased to rage so fiercely? "But with whom was he angry?" etc.

units.la: Constat autem ex historia, quòd non omnes fuerint increduli in illo memorabili die tentationis in deserto. Nam Numerorum decimotertio dicitur, quòd licet explorarores detraherent terrae, mouerentque populum ad desperandum de ea obtinenda, tamen Caleb, qui etiam fuerat explorator, compescebat murmur populi, dicens: Ascendamus, & possideamus terram, quoniam poterimus obtinere eam. Et capite decimoquarto, Iosua & Caleb simul multis verbis hortati sunt populum, ne dissiderent, Dominum posse virēs hostium disipare, & suos, quò vellet, inducere. Nec dubium, quin aliqui alij ex multitudine horum persuasionibus adducti in fide perstiterint, & sic Deum ad id tempus non offenderint. Quanquam postea ex omnibus illis, qui Aegyptum egressi sunt (memorantur autem in deserto Synai sexcenta millia) duo isti soli ingressi sunt terram promissam, vt habetur Numerorum 26. ipso Mose quoque, & ante eum Aarone in deserto mortuis. Ex alijs verò ingressi terram promissam dicuntur Numeror. 26. sexcenta millia, & mille, septingenti, triginta, quibus terra erat diuidenda. His itaq; animaduersis citra negotium caetera intelligentur. Hoc enim solum agit Apostolus, per interrogationes subsequentes vult ostendere, ob solam incredulitatem patres adeò graviter punitos, ideoque incredulitatem maximè nobis vitandam. Non dissimili modo 1. Corinthiorum 10. docet, quòd non debeant concupiscere, quòd non debeant simulachra colere, quòd non debeant stuprиc in quinari, quòd non debeant Deum tentare, quòd non debeant murmurare: argumentum ducens à grauitate animaduersionis, qua in illa crimina vsus est Deus in deserto. Vbi etiam Apostolus, vt hoc loco, vtitur formulis loquendi, quidam eorum murmurarunt, &c. Vt hinc quoque ex phrasi liceat colligere, hanc epistolam esse Pauli Apostoli.
units.tr: It is clear from the history that not all were unbelieving on that memorable day of testing in the wilderness. In Numbers 13 we read that, although the spies disparaged the land and moved the people to despair of obtaining it, Caleb, who had also been one of the spies, quieted the people's murmuring, saying: "Let us go up and possess the land, for we shall surely be able to obtain it." And in chapter 14, Joshua and Caleb together earnestly exhorted the people with many words not to rebel, since the Lord could overthrow the strength of the enemy and bring his own people in where he wished. There is no doubt that some others from the multitude, persuaded by these exhortations, persevered in faith and so did not offend God up to that time. Yet afterwards, of all those who had come out of Egypt (six hundred thousand men are recorded in the wilderness of Sinai), only those two entered the promised land, as we find in Numbers 26, since Moses himself and Aaron before him died in the wilderness. Of the others, Numbers 26 says that six hundred thousand and one thousand seven hundred and thirty entered the promised land, to whom the land was to be divided. With these things noted, the rest will be understood without difficulty. For the Apostle is doing only this: by the questions that follow he wishes to show that the fathers were so severely punished for unbelief alone, and therefore that we must above all avoid unbelief. In a similar way, in 1 Corinthians 10 he teaches that they must not lust, must not worship idols, must not commit fornication, must not tempt God, must not murmur, drawing his argument from the severity of the punishment with which God visited those sins in the wilderness. There the Apostle also uses, as here, the form of speech "some of them murmured," and so from this phrasing too one may gather that this letter is by the Apostle Paul.

units.la: Proinde, quia scopus Apostoli est, in hac conclusione auocare omnes ab incredulitate, huc tendunt omnia ista verba, vt doceat, incredulitatem potissimum esse adeò graviter punitam. Atque hinc fit, quòd pluribus verbis genus criminis vult signare: sicut pluribus verbis signatur grauitas supplicij. Ait itaq;:
units.tr: Therefore, since the Apostle's aim in this conclusion is to call everyone away from unbelief, all these words tend to this end: to teach that unbelief is above all things punished so severely. And hence it comes about that he marks the kind of offence with many words, just as the severity of the punishment is marked with many words. So he says:

units.la: Quibus autem infensus fuit quadraginta annis? Nónne ijs qui peccauerant, quorum membra conciderunt in deserto?
units.tr: But with whom was he displeased for forty years? Was it not with those who had sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?

units.la: Hic valde appositè adiungit particulam illam, quadraginta annis, illis verbis, infensus fuit, vt ita supplicij grauitas clarius exprimatur. An enim leue fuit, ob incredulitatem & neglectum promissionum diuinarum puniri totam multitudinem per tot annos? Cùm in historiis profanis scribitur, decem annis obsidione pressos Troianos, eosdem superatos annis ite rum decem, (id quòd de Græcis etiam, inprimis q; vlysse memoratur,) aut amplius oberrasse. Certè ista annorum multitudine calamitas illorum mirum in modum augetur, & quæuis ad cõmiserationem permoueat. At verò audire, hoc pacto punitos per annos quadraginta: deinde tantâ multitudinem, & ob vnum peccatum incredulitatis in deserto cõcidisse, multò est miserrimum. Quare verò deceat coniungi has particulas, suprà à me alia quoque reddita ratio est. Exprimit deinde, quinam fuerint illi, quibus Dominus vsque adeò fuit infensus: ijs, inquit, qui peccauerant. Videtur Apostolus quasi per gradus quosdam ad manifestandum peccatum in incredulitatis voluisse progredi. Primò enim ait, Qui peccauerant: qua voce in genere graviter peccasse eos significat. Secundò dicit, Qui non obedierant: qua voce accedit adhuc propius. Tertiò autem loco incredulitatem aperte nominat. Quæ progrediendi ratio cùm incrementi speciem habeat, ad exaggerandum valde est idonea: ac verosimile est, Apostolum his tot verbis voluisse exaggerare genus criminis: quemadmodum etiam pluribus verbis spiritus Sancti, quibus dicitur, Deum exacerbatum, infensum fuisse annis quadraginta, prostrauisse membra in deserto, prohibuisse ingredi in requiem, eleganter supplicij atrocitas amplificatur. Rectè ergo primo loco ait, Deum illis iratum fuisse, qui peccauerant. Ita ante omnia iustè inflictas poenas notatur. Peccantibus enim Deus iustè irascitur: qui præcepta Dei transgredi, vocemque Dei contemnere audent, iustum est, eos à Deo puniri, iuxta illam vniuersalem legem Exodi vigesimoprimo, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam & quartam generationem, eorum, qui oderunt me. Quam etiam Moses citabat apud Deum, Numerorum decimoquarto, vbi peccatum istud & punitio describitur. Quanquam potest illud quoque dici, peccare per Antonomasiam idem valere, quod esse incredulum: & peccatum pro incredulitate ponitur Ioannis capite decimosexto: Cùm venerit, ille arguet mundū de peccato, & de iustitia & de iudicio. De peccato quidem, quia non credunt in me.
units.tr: Here he very fittingly adds the phrase for forty years to the words was displeased, so that the severity of the punishment may be expressed more clearly. For was it a light thing for the whole multitude to be punished for so many years because of unbelief and neglect of the divine promises? In profane histories it is written that the Trojans, besieged for ten years, were conquered in the same way after another ten years (as is also recorded of the Greeks, and especially of Ulysses), or that they wandered for longer. Certainly the number of years makes their calamity wonderfully greater and is able to move anyone to pity. But to hear that they were punished in this way for forty years, and that so great a multitude fell in the wilderness for the one sin of unbelief, is far more wretched. Why these phrases ought to be joined, I have already given a reason above. Next he states who those were with whom the Lord was so displeased: those, he says, who had sinned. The Apostle seems to have wished to advance, as it were by steps, in disclosing the sin of unbelief. For first he says who had sinned, by which word he signifies that they had sinned grievously in general. Second he says who had not obeyed, by which word he comes closer still. In the third place he names unbelief openly. Since this manner of progressing has the appearance of an increase, it is very well suited to amplifying, and it is likely that the Apostle wished by these many words to magnify the kind of offence, just as, by the many words of the Holy Spirit by which it is said that God was provoked and displeased for forty years, that he struck down their bodies in the wilderness, and that he forbade them to enter his rest, the atrocity of the punishment is elegantly enlarged. Rightly, then, he says first that God was angry with those who had sinned. Thus, before all else, the punishments that were justly inflicted are noted. For God is justly angry with sinners: since it is right that those who dare to transgress God's commands and despise his voice be punished by God, according to that universal law in Exodus 21: I am the Lord your God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation, of those who hate me. Moses also cited this law before God in Numbers 14, where this sin and its punishment are described. Yet it may also be said that, by antonomasia, to sin means the same as to be unbelieving; and sin is put for unbelief in John 16: "When he comes, he will convict the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment. Of sin, indeed, because they do not believe in me."

units.la: Quorum membra conciderunt in deserto) Comprobat, peccasse eos, à signo diuinæ vltionis, quasi dicat: Hoc erat signum, quòd valde peccauerant, & quòd Deus valde infensus fuerit, nam ipsi prostrati iunt in deserto. Interpretatur Apostolus, quomodo Deus propter peccatum infensus illis fuerit, poenæ grauitatem explicando. Inseruit autem Apostolus hæc verba, respiciens ad id, quòd sæpius ista inculcantur Numerorum decimoquarto: Viuo ego dicit Dominus, sicut locuti estis audiente me, sic faciam vobis: In solitudine hac iacebunt corpora vestra. Et iterum: paruulos autem vestros, de quibus dixistis, quòd præde hostibus forent, introducam, vt videant terram, quæ vobis displicuit: Filij vestri erunt vagi in deserto annis quadraginta, & portabunt fornicationem vestram, donec consumantur cadauera patrum in deserto, iuxta numerum quadraginta dierum, quibus consideraftis terram: Annus pro die imputabitur. Iterum: sicut locutus sum, ita faciam multitudine huic pessimæ, quæ consurrexit aduersum me, in solitudine hac deficiet & morietur. Ad hæc, inquam, verba toties ingeminata ad exprimendam magnitudinem iræ Dei, & grauitatem suplicij respiciens Apostolus, inseruit ista, Quorum membra conciderunt in deserto. Apostolus autem non dixit cadauera, sed τὰ νῶλα, id est, membra atque etiam ossa, seu ossium multitudo. Quod quidem non solùm eleganter fit quadam Synecdoche, vt partes ponantur pro totis hominibus, sed potius eleganti ὑποτυπώσει, vt quodammodo oculis subijciat spectàda membra, atq; ossa hinc inde sparsa, eorum, qui diuinitus cæsi erant, non aliter, quàm in bello, vbi magna strages facta est, videtur hinc capita, inde tibiæ, hinc brachia, hinc manus, inde pedes, aliaq; membra iacere. Atq; huiusmodi hypotyposis mirè conuenit amplificando supplicio, nec nō commouendis omnium animis, vt velint ab incredulitate sibi cauēre. Sequitur:
units.tr: Whose bodies fell in the wilderness. He proves that they had sinned by the sign of divine vengeance, as if to say: this was the sign that they had sinned greatly and that God had been greatly displeased, for they were struck down in the wilderness. The Apostle explains how God was displeased with them because of sin, by setting out the gravity of the punishment. He inserted these words, moreover, with regard to the fact that these things are repeated so often in Numbers 14: "As I live, says the Lord, as you have spoken in my hearing, so will I do to you: in this wilderness your bodies shall lie. And again: your little ones, of whom you said that they would become prey to the enemy, I will bring in, that they may see the land which you despised. Your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years and bear your fornication, until the carcasses of your fathers are consumed in the wilderness, according to the number of the forty days in which you searched the land: a year shall be counted for a day. Again: as I have spoken, so will I do to this wicked multitude which has risen against me; in this wilderness they shall be consumed and die." Looking back to these words, I say, which are so often repeated to express the greatness of God's wrath and the severity of the punishment, the Apostle inserted this: whose bodies fell in the wilderness. The Apostle did not say cadavera (corpses), but [τὰ μέλη], that is, the limbs, and even the bones, or the multitude of bones. This is done not only elegantly by a certain synecdoche, so that parts are put for whole persons, but rather by an elegant [ὑποτυπώσει] (vivid description), so that he sets before our eyes limbs and bones scattered here and there of those who had been slain by divine judgment. It is as in war, where a great slaughter has been made: here one sees heads, there shins, here arms, there hands and feet, and other limbs lying about. Such a vivid description agrees wonderfully with amplifying the punishment, and also with moving the minds of all to take care to guard themselves against unbelief. It follows:

units.la: Quibus autem iurauit, non ingressuros in requiem suam, nisi ijs, qui non obedierant?
units.tr: Those to whom he swore that they would not enter into his rest, except those who had not obeyed?

units.la: Iam propius accedit ad exprimendam incredulitatem. Sunt autem & hæc verba sumpta ex Numerorum decimoquarto, vbi dicitur: Et quia tentauerunt me iam per decem vices, nec obedierunt voci meæ, non videbunt terram, pro qua iuraui patribus eo, rum
units.tr: Now he comes closer to expressing the unbelief. These words too are taken from Numbers 14, where it says: "And because they have tempted me now ten times, and have not obeyed my voice, they shall not see the land for which I swore to their fathers."

units.la: Q rum. Quid autem per inobedientiam recte notetur, non est difficile demonstrare. Est enim ipsissima incredulitas, cum vocem Dei audieris, & praesertim, quae promissiones habet adiunctas, & tamen obedire non vis. Si enim vere credideres verbis Dei, haud dubie obedires. Huc pertinent illa 1. Samuelis 15. verba Samuelis ad Saulem, qui non percusit Amalech, nec demolitus est universa eius, sicut iussus fuerat. Nunquid vult Dominus holocausta & victimas, & non potius ut obediatur voci Domini? Melius est obedientia, quam victimae, & auscultare magis, quam offerre adipem arietum: quoniam quasi peccatum ariolandi, est repugnare, & quasi scelus idololatriae, nolle acquiescere: pro eo, quod abiecisti sermonem Domini, abiecit te Dominus, ne sis rex.
units.tr: It is not difficult to show what is rightly meant by disobedience. For it is unbelief itself when you have heard the voice of God, especially one that attaches promises, and yet you are unwilling to obey. For if you truly believed God's words, you would undoubtedly obey. To this belong those words of Samuel to Saul in 1 Samuel 15, who did not strike Amalek nor utterly destroy all that belonged to him, as he had been commanded: "Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that the voice of the Lord be obeyed? Obedience is better than sacrifice, and hearing better than offering the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusing to submit is like the crime of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, that you should not be king."

units.la: Sic vero & Israelitae in deserto, si credidissent verbo Domini, sane obedijssent, & authorem fuissent inuadere terram hostium, sperassentque de ijs victoriam. Quanto igitur inobedientes vocat Apostolus, incredulos satis aperte notat. Siquidem inobedientia eorum manifestissimum erat incredulitatis signum. Hinc illae quoque locutiones Romanorum primo, Per quem accepimus gratiam, ac muneris Apostolici functionem, ut obediatur fidei inter omnes gentes. Romanorum decimo, At non omnes obedierunt Euangelio, id est, crediderunt. Romanorum decimo sexto, Ei, qui potens est vos confirmare secundum euangelium meum, & praeconium Iesu Christi, iuxta revelationem mysterij temporibus aeternis taciti, manifestati vero nunc, & per Scripturas propheticas, iuxta delegationem aeterni Dei, in obedientiam fidei. Galat. 5. Currebatis bene, quis vos impediuit, ut non crederetis veritati? Vbi habetur, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι: quare potius reddendum erat, ut non obedires, sicut aliqui etiam verterunt. 2. Thessalon. 1. Cum revelabitur Dominus Iesus de caelo, cum angelis potentiae suae, cum incendio flammae, qui infligit ultionem his, qui non noverunt Deum, & qui non obediunt euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quibus in locis verbum obediendi accipitur pro voce credendi. Quamobrem, & hoc loco per inobedientiam incredulitas apte notatur. Sed tamen voluit ipse crassius idem explicare, quando velut summatim colligens, & semel enunciare volens, id quod principaliter est in causa spectandum, dicit:
units.tr: Thus indeed the Israelites in the wilderness, if they had believed the word of the Lord, would surely have obeyed, and would have been the ones to invade the land of their enemies, and would have hoped for victory over them. Therefore, when the Apostle calls them disobedient, he quite plainly marks them as unbelieving, for their disobedience was a most manifest sign of unbelief. Hence also those expressions in Romans 1: "Through whom we have received grace and the office of apostleship, to bring about the obedience of faith among all nations." Romans 10: "But not all have obeyed the gospel," that is, have believed. Romans 16: "To him who is able to establish you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times but now made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, according to the command of the eternal God, unto the obedience of faith." Galatians 5: "You were running well; who hindered you, that you should not believe the truth?" Where it has not to be persuaded by the truth [τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι]; so it ought rather to be rendered "that you should not obey," as some have also translated it. 2 Thessalonians 1: "When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ." In these places the word for obeying is taken for the word for believing. Wherefore here too unbelief is aptly signified by disobedience. Nevertheless, he wished to explain the same more plainly, when, as it were summing up briefly and wishing to state once what is chiefly to be considered in the matter, he says:

units.la: Et uidemus, quod non potuerint ingredi propter incredulitatem) Tanquam si diceretur: Si dispiciamus, quaenam fuerit principalis causa, ob quam adeo graviter puniti sunt patres in deserto, & ita prohibiti ingredi terram promissam, in qua requiescerent, invenimus fuisse crimen incredulitatis. Et revera murmuratio populi contra Mosen, pusillanimitas, & diffidentia de obtinenda terra, conspiratio de creando novo duce, qui reduceret ipsos in Aegyptum, haec omnia ad incredulitatem tanquam caput suntrefrenda, & ab incredulitate tanquam fonte emanarunt. Notant autem nonnulli hic, τοί, habere vim illatiuam, quasi poneretur pro ergo, vel sic, sicut alias quoque: ut prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto, Postea quam enim per hominem mors, & per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Quinetiam vox, uidemus, certitudinem & euidentiam notat, quod videlicet clarissime id colligatur, tanquam si oculis coram omnia cernerentur.
units.tr: And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief. As if one were to say: If we examine what was the principal cause for which the fathers in the wilderness were so severely punished, and so prohibited from entering the promised land, in which they would rest, we find that the crime was unbelief. And indeed the murmuring of the people against Moses, their faintheartedness and distrust about obtaining the land, and the conspiracy to appoint a new leader who would lead them back into Egypt, all these are to be traced back to unbelief as to their head, and have flowed from unbelief as from a fountain. Some note here that the particle toi [τοί] has an inferential force, as if it were put for "therefore" or "thus," as elsewhere too, as in 1 Corinthians 15: "For since by man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead." Moreover, the word we see denotes certainty and evidence, namely that this is inferred most clearly, as if everything were being seen with our own eyes.

units.la: CAPVT QVARTVM
units.tr: CHAPTER 4

units.la: Metuamus igitur, ne quando derelicta promissione introeundi in requiem tiun, videatur aliquis ex vobis fuisse frustratus.
units.tr: Let us therefore fear, lest, while a promise of entering into his rest is still left open, any of you should seem to have come too late.

units.la: Haec est, ut supra diximus, conclusio seu complexio argumentationis. Fuisset autem Apostolo crassius & nostro more loquendo, dicendum: Metuamus igitur & nos, ne similiter simul increduli, & ob incredulitatem parimodo puniamur: ut verba praecedentium propositionum in conclusione retinentur: sed maluit ipse elegantia quadam oratoria, eandem sententiam alijs verbis exprimere.
units.tr: This is, as I said above, the conclusion or summing-up of the argument. In plainer language the Apostle would have said: "Let us too fear, lest in the same way we, being likewise unbelieving, are punished alike for unbelief." That would have kept the words of the preceding propositions in the conclusion. But he preferred, with a certain rhetorical elegance, to express the same sense in other words.

units.la: Pro incredulitate posuit, derelictam promissionem introeundi in requiem, per periphrasin & Synecdochen, qua saepe prius ponitur pro posteriori, & e diverso, ut concutere muros, pro oppugnare, &c. Et pro punitione posuit fructratum esse. Quam vero apposite & eleganter singula sint dispositia, plenius excutiemus.
units.tr: For unbelief he put "a promise left unclaimed of entering into rest", by periphrasis and synecdoche, a figure by which the consequence is often put for the cause and the reverse, as "to shake the walls" is put for "to attack", and so on. For punishment he put "to come too late." We shall examine more fully how aptly and elegantly each part is arranged.

units.la: Metuamus igitur, inquit, Non dicit simpliciter, igitur Deus nos quoque puniet, si fuerimus increduli: sed metuamus: qua voce melius ponit gravitatem supplicij ob oculos, nec non animos omnium vehementius concutit. Atque eos, qui durioris sunt animi, quales Iudaei omnes propemodum natura sunt, maxime decet poenarum metu coercere, & ad virtutem quasi compellere: Ac prodest conscientijs. scientijs timorem huiusmodi inculcare, sicut ante decalogum Deus ipse timorem poenarum inculcat. Et vere ad resipiscendum primus gradus est, timere: Initium Sapientiæ timor Domini. Item Prouerb.28. Beatus homo, qui semper est pauidus. Item Psal. 127. 112. Beatus homo, qui timet Dominum. Vnde passim Prophetæ ad timendum Deum, illos, qui peccarant, primo loco excitant: quia, vt beata virgo canit Lucæ primo, Miseri-cordia Domini parata est in progeniem & progeniem, timentibus eum. Huc item pertinet prima concio euangelica, à Ioanne facta Matthæi tertio, Poenitentiam agite vitæ prioris, in propinquo est enim regnum cœlorum. Et Actorum secundo, Petrus ad compunctos corde, & rogantes, quid facerent, poenitentiam delictorum agite, & baptizetur vnusquisque vestrum in nomine Domini Iesu Christi, &c. Ita enim decet à timore & poenitentia initium salutis facere.
units.tr: "Let us therefore fear," he says. He does not simply say, "Therefore God will punish us too, if we are unbelieving," but "let us fear." By this word he sets the severity of the punishment before our eyes more effectively, and shakes the minds of all more forcibly. Those of harder mind, as nearly all Jews are by nature, ought above all to be restrained by fear of punishment and, as it were, compelled toward virtue. It also profits consciences to instil fear of this kind, just as God himself instils fear of punishment before the Decalogue. Indeed, fear is truly the first step toward repentance: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Prov. 1). Likewise Prov. 28: "Blessed is the man who is always fearful." Likewise Ps. 127 [112]: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord." Hence the Prophets everywhere, first of all, stir up those who have sinned to fear God, because, as the blessed Virgin sings in Luke 1, "the mercy of the Lord is upon those who fear him from generation to generation." To this belongs also the first evangelical sermon, preached by John in Matthew 3: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." And in Acts 2 Peter says to those pricked in heart who asked what they should do: "Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ," and so on. For thus it is fitting to begin the way of salvation from fear and repentance.

units.la: Ne quando derelicta promissione) Valde eleganter in credulitatis naturam exprimit. Prius enim quàm quis credat, vel non credat, propositæ sunt ei à Deo promissiones de rebus spiritualibus, vel temporalibus, quæ certè res spirituales adumbrant, quæ eum illici ant ad amplectendum & sequendum. Has ergo si confidit ad implendas, & earum obtinendarum spe cætera omnia posthabet, dicitur credere: Sin verò parui facit, neglegit vel con temnit, & aliis rebus intendit, dicitur non credere, siue esse incredulus.
units.tr: Lest while a promise is left unclaimed: He expresses the nature of unbelief very elegantly. For before anyone believes or does not believe, God sets before him promises concerning spiritual or temporal things, which indeed foreshadow spiritual things, and these draw him on to embrace and follow them. If, then, he trusts these promises to be fulfilled, and for the hope of obtaining them he sets aside all other things, he is said to believe. But if he makes little of them, neglects or despises them, and devotes himself to other things, he is said not to believe, or to be unbelieving.

units.la: Itaque derelinquere promissionem rectè dixit, pro eo, quod est, non credere. Sed plaecuit Apostolo, ipsam promissionem, siue obiectum fidei addere, dicendo: introeundi in requiem eius: vt ita animi tacitè incitaretur ad contemplandam rerum promissarum excellentiam, pariterq; ad apprehendendam promissionem de tantis bonis magis moverentur. Fides enim excitatur, alitur, & augetur frequenti bonorum promissorum consideratione. Hinc nusquam non inculcantur & repetuntur promissiones, & quidem in veteri testamento de bonis temporalibus, per quę adumbrabantur spiritualia & æterna: in nouo autem de vita æterna & regno cœlorum. Et multò appositissimè hic dicit, promissione fuisse de introeundo in requiem. Neq; enim id tantùm, quia in testimonio spiritus Sancti supra citato, ex quo ducuntur hic argumenta omnia, à requie sunt prohibiti: sed quòd ipsa vox requiei mirificè omnes mouere posset, ad amplectandam eiusmodi promissionem, cùm omnes homines naturaliter requiem valdè desiderent, nihilq; ducant maius aut suauius, quàm aliquando quietè viuere. Quicunq; ergo hic audiunt, promissionem esse de introeundo in requiem, statim mouebuntur ad eiusmodi promissionem amplectendam, atq; omnibus modis studebunt, ne ab illa excludantur.
units.tr: So he rightly said "to leave a promise" for "not to believe." But the Apostle chose to add the promise itself, or the object of faith, saying "of entering into his rest," so that the mind might be quietly stirred to consider the excellence of the promised things, and be moved all the more to lay hold of a promise of such great goods. For faith is awakened, nourished and increased by frequent consideration of the promised good things. Hence the promises are everywhere inculcated and repeated: in the Old Testament concerning temporal goods, through which spiritual and eternal things were foreshadowed; in the New concerning eternal life and the kingdom of heaven. And most fittingly he says here that the promise was of entering into rest. This is not only because, in the testimony of the Holy Spirit cited above, from which all the arguments here are drawn, they were forbidden to enter rest; but because the very word "rest" can move everyone wonderfully to embrace such a promise, since all men by nature greatly desire rest and think nothing greater or sweeter than to live quietly at some time. Therefore, whoever here hears that the promise is of entering into rest will at once be moved to embrace such a promise, and will strive by every means not to be shut out from it.

units.la: Atque oportet accipere Apostolum hic iam de alia requie, quàm de temporali, quæ patribus fuit promissa in terra Canaan, quæ etiam requies diuersis in locis Scripturæ appellatur, vt Deuteronom. 25. Iosuæ 1. sentire: id quod colligendum est ex particula, tius, quæ habet magnam emphasin, vtpote quæ significat ingressum in requiem ipsius Dei, hoc est, non carnalem, vel temporalem, sed spiritualem & æternam, qualis est requies ipsius Dei, quam Deus in testimonio spiritus Sancti supra citato vocat suam, dicens: Si introibunt in requiem meam. Qua de re Apostolus mox aget plenius: non dubium tamen, quin da eadem requie spirituali iam à modo in conclusione loquatur.
units.tr: And we must understand the Apostle here to be speaking now of another rest, not the temporal rest that was promised to the Fathers in the land of Canaan, which is also called rest in various places of Scripture, as in Deut. 25 and Joshua 1. This is to be gathered from the particle "thus" [tius], which carries great emphasis, since it signifies entering into the rest of God himself, that is, not a carnal or temporal rest but a spiritual and eternal one, such as is the rest of God himself, which God in the testimony of the Holy Spirit cited above calls his own, saying: "If they shall enter into my rest." The Apostle will treat this more fully presently. Nevertheless there is no doubt that here, in the conclusion, he already speaks of this same spiritual rest.

units.la: Videatur aliquis ex vobis fuisse fructratus) Cùm dicit, aliquis ex vobis, indicat, se maxima cura salutis omnium teneri, vehementerq; dolere, si vel vnus aliquis ex omnibus illis peniret, atque à requie spirituali excluderetur. Pariter benè se de illis sperare ostendit, & confidere, quòd vix pauci ex illis promissionem diuinam deserant.
units.tr: Lest any of you should seem to have come too late: When he says "any of you," he shows that he is bound by the greatest care for the salvation of all, and grieves intensely if even one of them should fall away and be shut out from spiritual rest. Likewise he shows that he hopes well of them and is confident that scarcely any of them will abandon the divine promise.

units.la: Porrò, vbi interpres reddidit fuisse fructratus: græcè est ὑστερηκέναι, quod significat damnum pati, deficere, proprie autem tardius venire, & postremum adesse: vt hic metaphora esse videatur ab iis, qui, quò tempestiuius venire debebant, comparent tardius, atque ob id præmia vel bona, quæ diuiduntur, non accipiunt: quo respiciens interpres non male vertit, fructratus esse. Itaque sententia est: Metuendum, ne si non credimus promissionibus Dei, nos quasi tardius, & quod dicitur, post festum venientes, optata requie fructremur. Et valde quadrat metaphora hæc, ob id, quod præcesset de introeundo. Huc pertinet parabola Matthæi vicesimoquinto, de virginibus fatuis tarde venientibus, & ideo exclusis. Item illud Lucæ 13. Ait illi quidam, Domine, an pauci sunt, qui salutem consequuntur? Ille verò dixit ad illos: Contendite intrare per angustam portam, quia multi, dico vobis, quærent intrare & non poterunt, &c. 1. Corinthior. 9. Sic currite, vt comprehendatis. Omnes deniq; illi loci, qui monent, in tepore, siue, dum tempus est, bene agere, huc quadrat. Cæterum in hoc Syllogysmo multiplex & varia doctrina nobis est proposita.
units.tr: Moreover, where the translator has rendered to have come too late, the Greek is ὑστερηκέναι [hysterekenai], which means to suffer loss, to fall short; properly, to arrive later and to be behind at the end. So the metaphor seems to be taken from those who, when they ought to come in good time, arrive late and therefore do not receive the prizes or goods that are being distributed. The translator, looking to this, rightly rendered it "to have come too late." The sense is therefore: we must fear that, if we do not believe God's promises, we shall, as if arriving late and, as the saying goes, after the feast, miss the rest we desire. And this metaphor fits well, because the preceding words were about entering. To this belongs the parable of the foolish virgins who came late and were therefore shut out (Matt. 25). Also Luke 13: "Someone said to him, Lord, are there few who are saved? But he said to them, Strive to enter through the narrow gate, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able to," and so on. 1 Cor. 9: "So run that you may obtain." Finally, all those passages which admonish us to do good in the time of favour, or while there is time, fit here. But in this syllogism a manifold and varied teaching is set before us.

units.la: Primò, cùm dicit, quòd quidam duntaxat exacerbauerint Dominum, non omnes, discimus, quòd Deus nunquam finit totam ecclesiam cadere, sed semper aliquos in fide constantes seruat: vt omnibus murmurantibus & diffidentibus Iosue, Caleb, Moses, & pauci
units.tr: First, when he says that some only provoked the Lord, not all, we learn that God never allows the whole Church to fall, but always preserves some who remain steadfast in faith, just as, when all were murmuring and distrustful, Joshua, Caleb, Moses and a few

units.la: Exod. 19. Timor Dei primus ad refipiscentiam. & pauci quidam alij in fide perstiterunt. Tempore diluuij Noe cum suis in fide perstiterunt. Tempore Heliæ Dominus adhuc seruauerat septem millia virorum, qui non curuauerant genua ante Baal. Dominus semper pusillum aliquem gregem, licet abditum, & mūdo ignotum, seruat pro suo peculio. Et vnusquisq; pius certa fide statuere apud se debet, se reuera huius gregis esse membrum.
units.tr: Exod. 19: The fear of God is the first step to repentance. and a few others persevered in faith. In the time of the flood Noah with his household persevered in faith. In the time of Elijah the Lord had preserved seven thousand men who had not bowed the knee to Baal. The Lord always preserves some small flock, though hidden and unknown to the world, as his own possession. And each godly person ought to be certain, by firm faith, that he is in truth a member of this flock.

units.la: Secundò, cùm ait, membra illorum incredulorum concidisse in deserto, expendendum nobis est, quàm grauiter Deus puniat peccata etiam in hac vita, postquam punitionem iterum punit post hanc vitam: sicut sine dubio omnes illi patres post mortem temporalem etiam æternam mortem subire sunt coacti. Et licet huiusmodi punitiones externæ & corporales non semper manifestæ sint, sicut erant in veteri testamento: tamen sine dubio semper sequuntur aliquæ, etiam vbi nos propter cæcitatem & duritiam cordis non animaduertimus. Deus punit inferedo etiam mala spiritualia, vt cæcitate cordis, &c. item concedendo prosperum successum in mundo, qui exitij causa & instrumentum esse possit: deniq; in liberos & proles vindictam occultis vel manifestis modis exercendo. In summa, certissimum esse debet, cum cætera peccata, tum præcipue incredulitatem, nunquam manere impunitam.
units.tr: Secondly, when he says that the bodies of those unbelievers fell in the desert, we must weigh how grievously God punishes sins even in this life, and afterwards punishes again after this life. Undoubtedly all those Fathers, after their temporal death, were also forced to undergo eternal death. And although such external and bodily punishments are not always manifest, as they were in the Old Testament, yet without doubt some punishments always follow, even where we do not notice them because of our blindness and hardness of heart. God punishes also by inflicting spiritual evils, such as blindness of heart, and so on; likewise by granting prosperous success in the world, which can be a cause and instrument of ruin; finally by exercising vengeance upon children and descendants in hidden or manifest ways. In sum, it must be most certain that other sins, but above all unbelief, never remain unpunished.

units.la: Tertiò, cum exprimit, incredulitatem præcipuam esse causam, cur adeo seueriter puniti sint Patres, admonemur, vt sedulò intueamur, quàm graue peccatum sit increde-ulitas, & quanto studio id euitare debeamus: contra quod & tota hæc exhortatio instituta est.
units.tr: Thirdly, when he says that unbelief is the chief cause why the Fathers were punished so severely, we are reminded to consider carefully how grave a sin unbelief is, and with what diligence we ought to avoid it. The whole of this exhortation is directed against it.

units.la: Quartò, cùm dicit Apostolus, Metuamus igitur, discendum nobis hic est, timore Dei, hil esse salubrius, & quasi pharmacum contra omnem incredulitatem, indurationem, & similia vitia capitalia, Deum timere. Itaque ministri verbi summa cura debent huncin docēdo vrgere & inculcare. Nunc certe alicubi frigidius de hoc agitur, non sine gravissima spiritualium fructuum, qui ex vero timore oriri solent. Iudicium Domini, præsertim vniuersale illud extremis diebus futurum, si animo sæpè meditentur, haud dubie ad virtutes calcar habebunt, & à vitijs abstcrrebuntur. Eò autem magis hic timor nunc est necessarius, quò certius est, aduentum Domini ad iudicium foribus nostris propius instare.
units.tr: Fourthly, when the Apostle says, Let us therefore fear, we are taught here that nothing is more wholesome than the fear of God, and that it is, as it were, a remedy against all unbelief, hardening, and similar capital vices. Therefore the ministers of the Word ought with the greatest care to press and impress this upon their hearers in their teaching. Indeed, this subject is now treated somewhat coldly in some places, to the great loss of those spiritual fruits which usually arise from true fear. If people often meditate in their hearts on the judgment of the Lord, especially that universal judgment which is to come in the last days, it will undoubtedly spur them on to virtues and turn them away from vices. And this fear is all the more necessary now, since it is more certain that the coming of the Lord to judgment is drawing near to our doors.

units.la: Quintò, quia ait, exclusos à requie spirituali, ob derelictam seu neglectam promissionem, admonemur, crebrò & intentis animis in promissiones Dei, quæ in Euangelio nobis sunt propositæ intueri, animum nostrum illis tanquam pabulo saluberrimo pascere, fidem erigere in tentationibus, cósolationem petere, in aduersis patientiam firmare, deniq; quamplurimos fructus spirituales ex illis colligere.
units.tr: Fifthly, because he says that they were shut out from spiritual rest on account of an abandoned or neglected promise, we are reminded to look often and with attentive minds upon the promises of God set before us in the Gospel, to feed our minds on them as on the most wholesome food, to raise up faith in temptations, to seek comfort, to strengthen patience in adversity, and finally to gather from them very many spiritual fruits.

units.la: Etenim nobis annunciatum est, quemadmodum & illis. At non profuit illis audisse sermonem, quod is non effect cum fide coniunctus iis qui audierant.
units.tr: For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

units.la: Aliud argumentum, quo respiciens ad particulam illam, Si uocem eius audieritis, colligit seu asserit, eam nobis quoque competere. Reuelato enim euangelio, nos vocem Domini audisse, & promissiones ad nos factas, non minus, quàm ad patres. Sed præterea infert, nihil profuturum, quòd audierimus, nisi auditis credamus: sicut nec patribus profuit audisse vocem Domini, quando credere noluerunt. Atque ita rursus exemplum patrum vrgens, ab incredulitate eos auocat. Sic autem argumentatur:
units.tr: He draws another argument, looking back to that clause, If ye will hear his voice, from which he infers or asserts that it belongs to us also. For since the Gospel has been revealed, we have heard the voice of the Lord, and the promises made to us no less than to the fathers. But he further infers that hearing will profit us nothing unless we believe what we have heard, just as hearing the voice of the Lord did not profit the fathers when they were unwilling to believe. And so, again urging the example of the fathers, he turns us away from unbelief. He argues thus:

units.la: Nunc reuolato euangelio, nos quoq; vocem Dei audiuimus, perinde atq; olim patres. At non profuit illis audisse sermonem, quòd ij, qui audierant, fidem sermoni non adhibuerunt.
units.tr: Now that the Gospel has been revealed, we too have heard the voice of God, just as the fathers did. But hearing the word did not profit them, because those who heard did not add faith to the word.

units.la: Ergo nec nobis proderit audisse vocem Domini in euangelio, nisi fidem adhibeamus, seu credamus.
units.tr: Therefore hearing the voice of the Lord in the Gospel will not profit us either, unless we add faith, that is, believe.

units.la: Maiorem non probat, satis notam existimans ex ipso successu, id est, prædicatione euangelij: præterea ex his, quæ scripta sunt: vt in Exordio epistolæ, vbi dicebatur, Deum locutum per filium: Item ex tota disputatione superiore, in qua diuersis locis beneficia per Christum collata explicantur.
units.tr: He does not prove the major premise, thinking it sufficiently known from the very outcome, that is, from the preaching of the Gospel; and besides, from what has been written, as in the opening of the epistle, where it is said that God spoke through the Son; and also from the whole preceding discussion, in which the benefits conferred through Christ are explained in various places.

units.la: Minor Manifesta euadit ex argumento præcedenti, & ipso testimonio Spiritus Sancti. Ita verò conexa hæc sunt præcedentibus, vt præcedentium videantur reddere rationem. Quod ad versionem attinet, sciendum græcè haberi, ἀκούσωσι quod ad verbum ita sonat: Etenim sumus euangelizati, quemadmodum & illi. Eẜque sententia: Patres quidem audierunt vocem Dei, habuerunt insignes & admirandas promissiones, quòd inducerentur in terram bonam, in qua daretur eis quiescere: sed certè nos etiam per euangelium vocem Dei audimus, & promissiones deeque multò fœliciore accepimus. Habet hanc vim & emphasin, meo iudicio, vox ἀκηκόαμεν.
units.tr: The minor premise becomes clear from the preceding argument and from the testimony of the Holy Spirit himself. These statements are so linked to what precedes that they seem to give the reason for what has gone before. As for the translation, it should be known that the Greek has akousōsi [ἀκούσωσι], which word for word reads: "For we have been evangelized, just as they were." And the sense is this: the fathers indeed heard the voice of God and had remarkable and admirable promises, that they would be led into a good land in which rest would be given them; but we too hear the voice of God through the Gospel, and have received promises of a much happier rest. In my judgment, the word akēkoamen [ἀκηκόαμεν] has this force and emphasis.

units.la: Euangelium fœliciore requiē quàm lex, pro mittit. λεγόμενον, quòd significat, longè alia ratione nobis auditam vocem Dei, quàm patribus, & longè excellentiora bona nobis promissa & proposita, vt videatur hoc discrimen latere, quòd patres quidem audierint vocem Domini quocunque modo, & acceperint promissiones de rebus quidem temporalibus: at nos audimus euangelium, quod est vox ipsius Dei, & accepimus promissiones de rebus spiritualibus.
units.tr: The Gospel promises a happier rest than the law. The word legomenon [λεγόμενον] signifies that the voice of God has been heard by us in a far different manner than by the fathers, and that far more excellent goods have been promised and set before us, so that this difference seems to lie in this: the fathers indeed heard the voice of the Lord in whatever manner, and received promises concerning temporal things; but we hear the Gospel, which is the voice of God himself, and have received promises concerning spiritual things.

units.la: Vocabulum εὐαγγελισμένοι notat excellentiam euangelij præ lege, ac proinde omnia nobis excellentiora contigisse, quàm patribus, qui sub lege erant. Quæ emphasis etiam Matthæi 11. videtur indicari, vbi Christus iubet renunciari Ioanni, dicens: Ite, & renunciate Ioanni ea quæ auditis & videtis: cæci visum recipiunt, claudi ambulant, leprosi mundantur, surdi audiunt, mortui excitantur, πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται, id est, pauperes lætum accipiunt euangelij nuncium. Quod interpres ita reddidit, retinendo vocem euangelij, propterea quòd aliquid singulare & valde sublime ea voce significatur: vnde & inter admiranda illa, quibus Christus diuinitatem suam, & se redemptorè esse, à Ioanne intelligi voluit, postremo loco quasi dignissimum collocatur. Ergo sententia est, quòd nos etiam multò excellentius audimus vocem Dei, quàm patres: vt inde etiam colligamus, nos graviùs puniendos, quàm patres si ijs, quæ in euangelio audimus non credimus. Etiamsi paulò post etiam patres dicantur εὐαγγελισθέντες: sed id propterea, quòd de euangelio post futuro aliquid acceperunt: atque ita exaggeratur crimen eorum. Quod autem illud ita se habeat, vt omittamus illa quibus posset ostendi euangelij præ lege eminentia, satis arguit Christus Matthæi decimo tertio: Amen dico vobis, quòd multi prophetæ, & iusti desiderauerunt videre, quæ videtis, & non viderunt, & audire, quæ auditis, & non audierunt. Liquet autem ex his, quòd appositè testimonium illud rebus præsentibus accommodetur: quando non posset ibi quicquam accipi ita dictum de patribus, quin multò conuenientius conueniat ijs, qui sunt sub euangelio. Vnde & vaticinium conterit de euangelio, nos suprà, cùm exponeremus ipsum testimonium, declarauimus. Et quæ patres gesserunt in deserto, omniaque, quæ illis contigerunt, typus fuerunt rerum euangelicarum.
units.tr: The word euangelisthentes [εὐαγγελισθέντες] denotes the excellence of the Gospel over the law, and therefore that we have received all things more excellent than the fathers, who were under the law. This emphasis seems also to be indicated in Matthew 11, where Christ bids that word be carried back to John: "Go and show John again those things which ye do hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, to the poor the gospel is preached" [πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται], that is, the poor receive the joyful message of the Gospel. The translator rendered this by retaining the word gospel, because something singular and very sublime is signified by that word. Hence it is placed, as most worthy, last among those wonderful things by which Christ wished John to understand that he was himself the Messiah and Redeemer. So the sense is that we too hear the voice of God far more excellently than the fathers did, and from this we also gather that we will be punished more severely than the fathers if we do not believe what we hear in the Gospel. Yet a little later the fathers too are called [euangelisthentes — εὐαγγελισθέντες], but this is because they received something about the Gospel later on, and so their guilt is magnified. That this is so, leaving aside the many things by which the pre-eminence of the Gospel over the law could be shown, Christ sufficiently proves in Matthew 13: "Verily I say unto you, that many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which ye hear, and have not heard them." It is clear from this that the testimony fits present circumstances aptly, since nothing said there of the fathers could be taken in a way that would not fit much more suitably those who live under the Gospel. Hence the prophecy also bears on the Gospel, as we showed above when we expounded that very testimony. And what the fathers did in the wilderness, and everything that happened to them, were types of the evangelical realities.

units.la: Et promissiones patribus factæ de rebus temporalibus, adumbrant promissiones euangelicas de rebus spiritualibus, etiamsi ipsi apertas promissiones euangelicas acceperunt, & cum temporalibus promissionibus animo concipiebant pariter spirituales: qua de re Romanorum quarto, vbi Apostolus ex illis verbis, Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad iustitiam, colligit pulcherrima argumenta negotio euangelico necessaria, ac tandem disertè subiicit: Non scriptum est autem propter illum tantùm, imputatum fuisse illi, sed etiam propter nos, quibus imputabitur credentibus in eum, qui excitauit Dominum Iesum à mortuis, &c. Roman. 15. Quæcunq; præscripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam præscripta sunt, 1. Corinth. 10.
units.tr: And the promises made to the fathers concerning temporal things foreshadow the evangelical promises concerning spiritual things, even though they themselves received the explicit evangelical promises and in their minds conceived spiritual promises along with the temporal ones. On this matter, in Romans 4, the Apostle, from those words, "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness," draws most beautiful arguments necessary to the evangelical business, and at last expressly adds: "Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; but for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead," etc. (Romans 15): "Whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning" (1 Corinthians 10).

units.la: Hæc autem omnia figuræ contigerunt illis: scripta verò sunt propter admonitionem nostri. Et paulò ante: Hæc autem figuræ nostri fuerunt, ne nos simus concupiscentes rerum malarum, quemadmodum & illi concupierunt. 2. Corinthiorum 4. Cùm habeamus eundem spiritum fidei, iuxta illud quod scriptum est (Psalmo centesimo decimo quinto) Credidi, & ideò locutus sum: & nos credimus, quapropter & loquimur, scientes, quod qui suscitauit Dominum Iesum, nos quoq; per Iesum suscitabit, & constituet vobiscum. Galat. 4. Duos filios Abrahæ interpretatur typum fuisse Legis & euangelij. Christus in euangelio de se exponit historiam Ionæ, serpentis æneí, mannæ in deserto. Præterea, tempus iudicij cum tempore diluuij, reginam Saba cum gentilibus, item viduam Sarephthanam cum ijsdem. Euangelista agnum paschalem cùm Christo: Os non comminuetis ex eo, &c. Simili ergo ratione ait, nobis quoq; conuenire illa, quæ contigerunt, vel dicta sunt de patribus, & nos quoque audisse vocem Domini, perinde, imò multò certius & efficacius, atq; audiuerunt patres.
units.tr: Now all these things happened to them as figures, and they were written for our admonition.
