And a little before: "Now these things were our examples, to the intent that we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted" (2 Corinthians 4): "Having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak; knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you" (Galatians 4). He interprets the two sons of Abraham as a type of the law and the Gospel. In the Gospel Christ expounds of himself the history of Jonah, the brazen serpent, and the manna in the wilderness. Besides, the time of judgment with the time of the flood, the queen of Sheba with the Gentiles, and likewise the widow of Sarepta with the same. The Evangelist (John) compares the paschal lamb with Christ: "A bone of him shall not be broken," etc. In a similar way, then, he says that those things which happened to the fathers, or were said of them, also belong to us, and that we too have heard the voice of the Lord just as the fathers did, indeed far more surely and effectively than they.

units.la: At non profuit illis audiisse sermonem) Hic sermonem vocat generaliter, quæ audita fuerunt à Deo, & nomine Dei proposita, & tàm ea intelligi conuenit nomine sermonis, quàm quæ ad legem pertinent, quàm quæ ad euangelium: quomodo etiam vsurpatur nomen vocis in testimonio spiritus Sancti, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis. Sic enim suprà capite secundo, quæ olim patribus fuerunt propositæ per angelos, vocat sermonem, dicens: Etenim si is, qui per angelos dictus fuerat, sermo fuit firmus, & omnis trangresio & inobedientia iustam præmij repensationem accepit, quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem? Et hoc capite præsenti mox subiicitur: Viuus est sermo Dei, & efficax, & penetrantior quouis gladio vtrimque incitente.
units.tr: "But it did not profit them to hear the word": here he calls generally "word" all that was heard from God and proposed in God's name. This word should be understood as including both what pertains to the law and what pertains to the gospel. The term "voice" is used in the same way in the testimony of the Holy Spirit: "Today, if you will hear his voice." So earlier, in the second chapter, he calls "word" what was once proposed to the fathers through angels, saying: "For if the word spoken through angels was steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great salvation?" And later in this present chapter it is added: "The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword."

units.la: Quin ipsum euangelium multis in locis per Antonomasiam sermo Dei appellatur, vt 1. Thessalonic. 3. Orate fratres pro nobis, vt sermo Domini currat, & glorificetur sicut & apud vos. Quibus omnis locis habetur dictio λόγος, cum articulo ὁ, vt manifestum in de fiat, non sine emphasi vocabulum istud accipiendum. Sed praeterea maiorem emphasin illud mihi videtur habere, quod graece legitur ὁ λόγος ἀκοῆς, quasi dicatur, verbum auditionis, vt hebraismus fit, ac significetur, illud verbum maxime esse audiendum, solumque dignum audiri prae omnibus, & ab omnibus. Illud verbum auditionis, maxime audiedum, illis non profuit, in quit. Atq; ita pariter insinuatur illud, quod Rom.10. habetur, Fides est ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei.
units.tr: Indeed, the gospel itself is called in many places, by antonomasia, the word of God, as in 1 Thessalonians 3: "Brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as it is also with you." In all these places the Greek word λόγος is used with the article ὁ, which shows that the term must be taken with emphasis. But it seems to me that the phrase which is read in Greek as ὁ λόγος ἀκοῆς has even greater emphasis. It is as if he said "the word of hearing", a Hebraism, and meant that this word above all is to be heard, and alone is worthy to be heard before all things and by all. "The word of hearing, which above all must be heard, did not profit them," he says. In the same way the passage in Romans 10 is also hinted at: Faith comes from hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

units.la: Non profuit illis: (μὴ συγκεκραμένους τῇ πίστει) Verbum Dei proponitur ad salutem eorum, qui audiunt, vnde verbum salutis & verbum vitae passim appellatur, suaq; natura eiusmodi est, vt, vbi in cor promptum & beneuolum ciciderit, fructum multo amplissimum profert, quemadmodum parabola illa Lucae 8. ostenditur. Quod vero minus sequatur talis effectus verbi, id non contingit imbecillitate verbi, sed indispositione & ineptitudine ipsorum audientium, sicut hic quoque id satis explicatur hisce verbis. Videtur autem Apostolus tanquam elegantiae causa, vsus metaphora, dicendo: μὴ συγκεκραμένους τῇ πίστει: quod est, non admixtus seu contemperatus fidei. (Quaedam exemplaria habent, μὴ συγκεκραμένους: vide Chrysostomum & Theophylactum, qui Basilij interpretationem adfert) Nam συγκεράννυμι, idem est, quod admisceo, tempero, quomodo solet aqua admisceri vino, vel temperari pharmaca. Hinc ergo ducta metaphora, ait, Sed monem non fuisse admixtum fidei illorum, qui audierant, siue illos, qui audierant, fidem suam non admiscuisse sermoni. Ac debet reuera fides coniungi, conglutinari cum sermone audito, non aliter, quam metalla cum metallis conglutinantur in ferruminatione. Ergo audientes sermonem veracem euangelij, debent fidem adhibere, si profectum & commodum ex eo volunt consequi: sicut Roman.10. satis luculenter ostenditur. Atque vbi fides adhibetur, haec non poterit esse otiosa, sed necessario profert fructus longe pulcherrimos, ex quibus palam cognosci poterit, vtiliter & salutariter verbum esse auditum. Id quod apostolus satis arguit, vbi ait 1. Thessalon. 2. Nos gratias agimus Deo indesinenter, quod, cum acciperetis sermonem a nobis, quo Deum discebatis, accepistis non sermonem hominum, sed sicut erat vere, sermonem Dei, qui & agit in vobis credentibus. Vos enim imitatores facti estis, fratres, ecclesiarum Dei, quae sunt in Iudaea. Simili modo Philippensium primo, Gratias ago Deo meo in omni memoria vestri, semper in omni precatione mea pro vobis omnibus, cum gaudio precationem faciens, quod veneritis in communionem euangelij, a primo die vsque ad hoc tempus, persuasum habens hoc ipsum, quod is, qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet vsq; ad diem Iesu Christi.
units.tr: It did not profit them [μὴ συγκεκραμένους τῇ πίστει]: the word of God is set forth for the salvation of those who hear it, which is why it is everywhere called the word of salvation and the word of life. By its nature it is such that, when it falls into a ready and well-disposed heart, it brings forth a much more abundant fruit, as the parable in Luke 8 shows. That this effect of the word does not follow more often is not due to any weakness in the word, but to the unfitness and unpreparedness of the hearers themselves, as is sufficiently explained here by these words. The Apostle seems, as a matter of elegance, to have used a metaphor when he says not mixed with faith [μὴ συγκεκραμένους τῇ πίστει], that is, not blended or tempered with faith. (Some copies have μὴ συγκεκραμένους; see Chrysostom and Theophylact, who gives Basil's interpretation.) For συγκεράννυμι means the same as to mix or temper, as water is usually mixed with wine, or medicines are tempered. From this metaphor he says: the word was not mixed with the faith of those who heard it, or those who heard did not mix their faith with the word. Indeed faith ought to be joined and fused with the word heard, just as metals are fused together in soldering. Therefore those who hear the true word of the gospel must bring faith to it, if they wish to gain progress and benefit from it, as is clearly shown in Romans 10. And where faith is brought, it cannot be idle, but necessarily brings forth very fine fruits, by which it can plainly be known that the word has been heard usefully and savingly. The Apostle argues this well when he says in 1 Thessalonians 2: "We thank God without ceasing, that when you received from us the word of God's teaching, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God, which also works in you who believe. For you became imitators, brethren, of the churches of God which are in Judea." In a similar way in the first chapter of Philippians: "I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all, making my requests with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now, being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ."

units.la: Proinde colligimus breuiter hanc doctrinam, quod non debemus existimare, nos esse vere Christianos, si nihil aliud, quam verbum audimus, interea non adhibemus fidem, & fructus fidei non proferimus. Roman.1. Non enim qui audiunt legem, iusti sunt apud Deum, sed qui legem factis exprimunt, iusti habetur. Iacob.1. Recipite insitum sermone, qui potest saluas reddere animas vestras. Sitis autem effectores sermonis, & non auditores tantum, fallentes vosmetipsos. Idè capite secundo, quod ex factis fides perficitur. Quare, cum audimus verbum, opus est credamus: si autem vere credimus, sunt fructus quoque producendi.
units.tr: Therefore we briefly gather this teaching: we ought not to think that we are truly Christians if we only hear the word and meanwhile do not bring faith and do not produce the fruits of faith. Romans 1: "For it is not the hearers of the law who are just before God, but the doers of the law will be justified." James 1: "Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves." Hence in the second chapter, that faith is made perfect by works. So when we hear the word, we must believe; and if we truly believe, fruits must also be brought forth.

units.la: Introimus enim requiem, nos qui credimus, quemadmodum dixit: Sicut iuraui in ira mea, si ingressuri sint in requiem meam. Et quidem operibus a iactis fundamentis mundi perfectis. Dixit enim quodam in loco de septimo die sic: Et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis. Et in hoc rursum, Si introibunt in requiem meam. Posteaquam igitur illud reliquum est, aliquos introire in eam, & quibus prius annunciatum fuit, non introierunt propter incredulitatem. Rursum quendam praefinit diem, Hodie, in Dauid dicens post tantum temporis, quemadmodum dictum est: Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, ne obduretis corda vestra. Nam si eis Iesus requiem praestitisset, nec quaquam de alio posthac die locutus fuisset. Itaque relinquitur Sabbatismus populo Dei. Nam, qui ingressus est in requiem illius, & ipse requieuit ab operibus suis, quemadmodum a suis Deus.
units.tr: For we who have believed enter into that rest, as he said: As I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter into my rest; although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has spoken in one place about the seventh day in this way: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works. And again in this place: They shall not enter into my rest. Since therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and those to whom it was first preached did not enter because of unbelief, again he sets a certain day, Today, saying in David after so long a time, as has been said: Today, if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. For if Jesus had given them rest, he would not have spoken afterwards of another day. So a sabbath rest remains for the people of God. For he who has entered his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.

units.la: Aliud argumentum, in quo expendit hanc particulam, Si introibunt in requiem meam quam quam putat nobis quoque conuenire,& eos, qui credunt euangelio, requiem illam ingressuros.
units.tr: Another argument, in which he weighs this clause, "If they shall enter into my rest", which he thinks applies also to us, and that those who believe the gospel will enter that rest.

units.la: Istud ergo primùm claris verbis proponit, dicens: Introimus in requiem nos, qui credidimus, quemadmodum dixit: sicut iuraui in ira mea, si ingressuri sint in requiem meam: hoc est, Requies illa, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur, & à qua prohibentur increduli, pertinent ad eos, qui credunt euangelio, etiá nostris hisce temporibus. Hanc propositionem aptissimis mox rationibus & efficacibus argumetis, sed mirabili prudetia & incredibili artificio collectis dispositisque: sicut & hæc pars cæteris difficilior est, & operæ plus requirens. Vnde, quia aduersarij hauddubiè interpretati sunt, in testimonio spiritus Sancti sermonem habitum esse tantùm de requie temporali, quæ patribus fuit promissa in terra Canaan: præterea illam eo quoque tempore contigisse patribus, quo terram Canaan, duce Iosua, fœlicis-ter & magna cum gloria occuparunt: ac proinde verba illa de requie, ad credentes minimè pertinere, neque imaginandam aliam requiem: quàm temporalem, vel aliud insuper tempus eius denuò obtinendæ. Apostolus non ignorans, quòd has potissimùm rationes aduersarij ad peruertendam spiritus Sancti sententiam, possent adferre, hoc ordine suam interpretationem instituit, vt primò doceat, de alia requie, quàm de temporali, verba spiritus Sancti accipienda: secundò, eam alio insuper tempore obtinendam, quam illi volebant, nimirum præsenti, quo euangelium reuelatum est.
units.tr: He first sets this out in clear words, saying: We who have believed enter into that rest, as he said: As I swore in my wrath, If they shall enter into my rest. That is: the rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks, and from which unbelievers are shut out, belongs to those who believe the gospel, even in these our times. He establishes this proposition by very apt arguments, and effective ones, gathered and arranged with wonderful prudence and incredible skill. Therefore this part is more difficult than the rest and requires more labour. Our opponents, undoubtedly interpreting it, claim that the testimony of the Holy Spirit speaks only of the temporal rest promised to the fathers in the land of Canaan; moreover, that this rest came to the fathers at the time when, under the leadership of Joshua, they occupied the land of Canaan happily and with great glory; and that therefore those words about rest do not pertain at all to believers, nor should any other rest be imagined than the temporal one, or some other time for obtaining it again. The Apostle, knowing that the opponents could bring forward these very arguments to pervert the sentence of the Holy Spirit, arranges his interpretation in this order: first he teaches that the words of the Holy Spirit must be understood of a rest other than the temporal one; second, that this rest is to be obtained at another time than they supposed, namely the present time, in which the gospel has been revealed.

units.la: De temporali igitur requie non loqui spiritum Sanctum, volens probare, argumetü trahit, meo iudicio, ex pronomine, meam, atque in hunc ratiocinatur modum: Et quidem operibus à iactis fundamentis mundi perfectis: Dixit enim quodam in loco de septimo die sic: Et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis. Et in hoc rursum: si introibunt in requiem meam. Hoc est, vt nostro more crasius explicemus: in hoc testimonio spiritus Sancti, Deus requiem diserte vocat suam.
units.tr: Wishing to prove that the Holy Spirit does not speak of the temporal rest, he draws an argument, in my judgement, from the pronoun "my", and reasons in this way: And indeed the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has spoken in one place about the seventh day in this way: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works. And again in this place: If they shall enter into my rest. That is, to explain it in our own more plain manner: in this testimony of the Holy Spirit, God expressly calls the rest his own.

units.la: Atqui requies Dei non est temporalis vel terrena, verù eiusmodi, qualis describitur Genes. 2. vbi, postquàm perfecta fuerunt omnia opera à iactis fundamentis mundi, de die septimo dicitur: Et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis: quæ sanè requies spiritualis est & cœlestis. Igitur, quod hîc rursus Deus dicit, Si introibunt in requiem meam, oportet non de temporali, sed spirituali & cœlesti requie ipsius Dei intelligere. Atque ita obseruata significatione pronominis illius, meam, firmum & solidum argumentum conficitur, ad probandum quòd non de temporali aut terrena, sed de spirituali & cœlesti, quæ proprie diuina est, requie accipi spiritus Sancti uerba deceat. Illatio, quæ pòst subijcitur, satis arguit, hoc pacto iudicandum de argumento Apostoli. Parit autem in oratione apostolica obscuritatem nonnullam, familiaris, & quodammodo affectata Hebræis breuitas.
units.tr: Yet God's rest is not temporal or earthly, but of the kind described in Genesis 2, where, after all the works from the foundation of the world were finished, it is said of the seventh day: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works. That rest is certainly spiritual and heavenly. Therefore, when God here says again, If they shall enter into my rest, it must be understood of God's own rest, which is not temporal but spiritual and heavenly. By observing the force of that pronoun, my, a firm and solid argument is constructed to prove that the words of the Holy Spirit should be taken to mean not a temporal or earthly rest but a spiritual and heavenly rest, which is properly divine. The inference that follows sufficiently shows that the apostle's argument should be judged in this way. The apostolic discourse, however, produces some obscurity, through a brevity that is familiar to the Hebrews and somewhat studied.

units.la: Iam alteram partem, quòd videlicet spiritus Sanctus non loquatur de requie temporali, quæ contigisse existimata est temporibus Iosuæ: sed de alia, quæ longè pòst, nempe, tempore reuelati euangelij deberet obtineri, hoc pacto probat: Posteaquà igitur illud reliquum est, aliquos introire in eam, &c. Quasi diceret: Hoc omnino necessarium erat, vt aliqui promissam requiem, de qua loquitur spiritus Sanctus, certo tempore ingrederentur. Sed eam nequaquam sunt ingressi illi patres, eo tempore, quo ipsis fuit annunciatum: quando quidem impediti fuerunt per suam increduIitatem. Ergo relinquitur, quòd quidam alij, & alio quidem tempore eam ingredi debuerint.
units.tr: Now he proves the other point, namely that the Holy Spirit does not speak of the temporal rest that was thought to have come in the time of Joshua, but of another rest, which was to be obtained long afterwards, namely in the time of the revealed gospel. He proves it in this way: Since therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and so on. As if he said: It was altogether necessary that some should enter, at a certain time, the promised rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks. But those fathers by no means entered it at the time when it was announced to them, since they were prevented by their unbelief. Therefore it follows that certain others, and at another time, ought to enter it.

units.la: Est argumentū ab eo, quòd necessariò debeat adimpleri promissio, & quòd antea nò fuerit adimpleta. Verùm quia aduersarij adhuc fortasis pertinaciter contendissent, incredulos quidem à requie illa fuisse exclusos, at patres credentes eam ingressos, duce Iosua. Hanc ob causam Apostolus aliter rursus idem probat, sumpta ratione ex voce, hodie, hoc pacto colligens:
units.tr: This is an argument from the fact that a promise must necessarily be fulfilled, and that it was not fulfilled earlier. But since the opponents might still perhaps stubbornly contend that the unbelievers were indeed excluded from that rest, while the believing fathers entered it under the leadership of Joshua, for this reason the apostle proves the same point again in another way, taking an argument from the word today, and concluding thus:

units.la: Spiritus Sanctus quando longè pòst illorum patrum tempora, per Dauidem dicit, Hodie si uocem eius audieritis: aperte hac uoce, hodie, nouum quoddam tempus præfinit.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit, long after the times of those fathers, says through David: Today, if you hear his voice. Clearly by this word today he marks out a new time.

units.la: Sed ita locutus non fuisset, si patres prisco illo tempore veram requiem, de qua hic sermo est, sub Iesu, seu Iosua, obtinuissent.
units.tr: But he would not have spoken thus if the fathers in that earlier time had obtained, under Jesus (or Joshua), the true rest of which this discourse speaks.

units.la: Igitur oportet aliud tempus, quàm illud pris cum, intelligi, quo requies hæc sit præstanda.
units.tr: Therefore another time than that earlier one must be understood, in which this rest is to be given.

units.la: Hoc uerò tempus, est tempus præsens & hodiernum, quo iterum vox Dei in euangelio toti mundo audita est. Postremò subijcit: Itaq; relinquitur Sabbatismus, &c. Vbi illatio seu complexio est, qua ex præmissis rationibus duo colligit. Primum quidé tempus sabbatismi seu requiei, de qua spiritus Sanctus locutus est, reliquum esse populo Dei: hoc est, nondum contigisse olim patribus, sed adhuc superesse, & nunc primùm recipi à credentibus, euangelio iam reuelato.
units.tr: This time, however, is the present and today's time, in which the voice of God has again been heard by the whole world in the gospel. Finally he adds: So there remains a sabbath rest, and so on. Here is the inference or conclusion, by which he draws two things from the premises. First, that the time of the sabbath rest or repose of which the Holy Spirit spoke remains for the people of God: that is, it had not yet come to the fathers of old, but still remains, and is now first received by believers, since the gospel has been revealed.

units.la: q Secundum, requiem hanc non esse corporalem aut temporalem, sed spiritualē re quiei ipsius Dei similem: qua nimirum sanctis hominibus datur eodem modo quiescere ab operibus suis, quo perfecta vniuersa mundi machina, ab operibus suis requieuit ipse Deus. Cætera, quæ ad artificium pertinentia explicatu digna videbuntur, in progres-su indicabimus.
units.tr: Second, that this rest is not bodily or temporal, but is like the rest of God himself: by which, namely, holy men are given to rest from their works in the same way that God himself rested from his works when the whole machinery of the world was completed. The other matters pertaining to the art that seem worth explaining we will point out in the course of the work.

units.la: Introimus enim in requiem, nos, qui credidimus, quemadmodum dixit: sicut iuraui in ira mea, si ingressuri sint in requiem meam) Quasi dicat: Audistis quidem, quod nos quoque vocem Domini perinde audiuerimus, atque olim patres: sed tamen nihil profuturum nobis, quod audierimus, si non credamus. Estque hæc ratio: Quia aliter non ingrediemur requiem, nisi credamus. Requies enim illa, de qua loquitur spiritus Sanctus, proprie pertinet ad credentes: id quod non difficile est probare. Ita connectit ista præcedentibus Apostolus, per particulam, enim, tanquam si hic esset præcedentium ratio, atque ab inuicem diuelli nequaquam possent. Videtur autem Apostolus hanc propositionem extulisse, habita quodammodo ratione contrariorum, seu antithesiseon. Cum enim in testimonio spiritus Sancti dicatur, non ingressuros in requiem, eos, qui manent increduli, recte hoc statui & inferri videtur, quod requiem illa ingredietur qui credunt. Hac igitur de causa apparet, ab Apostolo propositionem istam in hunc modum esse enunciatam, & non crasso & communi nostro more loquendi. Requies de qua loquitur spiritus Sanctus, pertinet ad eos, qui hoc tempore credunt euangelio. Sed verbis præterea vtitur multo appositissimis.
units.tr: For we who have believed enter into rest, as he said: As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest. As if he said: You have indeed heard that we too have heard the voice of the Lord just as the fathers did, but still, what we have heard will profit us nothing unless we believe. And the reasoning is this: we shall not enter the rest unless we believe. For that rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks properly belongs to believers, which is not difficult to prove. Thus the apostle connects this with what precedes by the particle for, as if this were the reason for what precedes, and they could by no means be separated from each other. The apostle seems to have put forward this proposition by means of a kind of consideration of contraries, or antithesis. For since in the testimony of the Holy Spirit it is said that those who remain unbelieving will not enter into rest, it seems rightly to be stated and inferred that those who believe will enter it. For this reason it is clear that the apostle has stated the proposition in this manner, and not in our crude and common way of speaking. The rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks belongs to those who believe the gospel in this present time. But besides, he uses words most fitting to the purpose.

units.la: Nos qui credidimus: οἱ πιστεύσαντες) Comprehendit hac voce omnes, qui iam tum reuelato euangelio crediderant, licet vniuersaliter complectatur omnes cuiuscunque ætatis seu seculi, quorum fides iam certa ac nota esset. Et prius est credendum, quam requiem sperata ingrediamur. Quare quandam fidei energiam significat & requirit.
units.tr: We who have believed [οἱ πιστεύσαντες]: by this phrase he embraces all who had already believed when the gospel was revealed, although it also universally takes in all, of whatever age or century, whose faith was already certain and known. And believing must come before we enter the hoped-for rest. Wherefore it signifies and requires a certain energy of faith.

units.la: Similiter, quod dicit, introimus, in præsenti, εἰσερχόμεθα, & non in futuro, facit id adindicandam mirabilem certitudinem eius requiei accipiendæ: & sic eam ponit considerandam omnium animis, tanquam si amodo ingrederentur & obtinerent. Loquitur autem sic more prophetico, qui non solum præsenti, verumetiam præterito subinde vtitur pro futuro. Quomodo etiam Christus de credentibus in eandem sententiam pet verbum præsentis temporis, nec non præteriti, loquitur. Ioannis 5. Qui credit in eum non condemnatur. Qui vero non credit, iam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen vnigeniti filij Dei. Ioan. 5. Amen, amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in condemnationem non venit, sed transiuit a morte in vitam.
units.tr: Similarly, in saying we enter [εἰσερχόμεθα] in the present tense, and not the future, he makes it a sign of the wonderful certainty of receiving that rest, and so sets it before the minds of all to be considered as if they were already entering and obtaining it. He speaks in this way after the manner of the prophets, who often use the present, and also the past, tense for the future. So Christ too speaks of believers in the same sense with verbs of the present and also the past tense. John 5: He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. John 5: Verily, verily I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life.

units.la: Et quidem operibus a iactis fundamentis mundi perfectis)Græce est, καὶ τοι τῶν ἔργων ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου γενομένων. Vbi particula καὶ τοι uariè latinis usurpata peperit obscuritatem. Quando enim ea interdū est disiunctiua, valēs: sed, verū, atqui: alias aduersatiua, quomodo latinis, quanquam, tametsi, licet: alias collectiua, tantundem significans, ac proinde, itaque: alias expositiua, assertionibus idonea, quomodo, sane, quidem. Hinc alij uerterunt, quanquam, seu licet, operibus a iactis fundamentis mundi perfectis, quomodo Erasmus sententiam in hunc modum exprimens, quod iurarit Deus, illos non introituros in requiem, licet iamdiu paratam, nempe, perfectis mundi operibus, quibus absolutis, requieuit Deus die septimo.
units.tr: And indeed, from the works finished from the foundation of the world: in Greek it is καὶ τοι τῶν ἔργων ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου γενομένων. Here the particle kai toi, which Latin writers have used in various ways, has produced obscurity. For sometimes it is disjunctive, meaning but, indeed, and yet; at other times adversative, like the Latin although, even though, granted that; at other times collective, meaning the same as and so, therefore; at other times explanatory, suited to assertions, like indeed, certainly, truly. Hence others translated it although or granted that: although the works were finished from the foundation of the world, as Erasmus did, expressing the sense in this way: God swore that they would not enter into rest, although it had long been prepared, namely with the works of the world finished, after which God rested on the seventh day.

units.la: Alij maluerunt uertere, & quidem, & sane: quæ uersio & nobis magis arridet, commodiusque seruit institutio. Cum enim dixisset, requiem, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur pertinere ad credentes, oportune hoc pacto venit ad probationem, in qua magna asseueratione sic ait: Et quidem ab operibus a iactis fundamentis mundi, perfectis. Videtur autem ecliptica esse oratio, quomodo sæpe Hebræi loquuntur, ac desiderari aliquid, nempe id declaratū est, vel præsignificatum: ut hæc sit sententia: Quod autem requies illa, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur, propositā & parata sit credentibus, & sane, siue, & quidem ab initio conditi mundi, id declaratum est. Atq; hæc uerba præmittedo videtur indicare Apostolus, vel valde promptum esse inuenire probationem eius rei, nimirum statim in exordio sacrorum librorum: uel certe ualde diu, & statim a mundo condito, hanc requiem credentibus destinatam, quomodo alias dicuntur pij electi esse a Deo ad vitam æternam a constitutione mundi. Sic enim legimus Ephes. 1. vbi habetur, πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, quemadmodum hic habetur ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου.
units.tr: Others preferred to translate and indeed, and certainly, which rendering also pleases us more and serves the teaching more conveniently. For when he had said that the rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks pertains to believers, he comes opportunely to the proof in this way, in which with great assertion he says: And indeed, from the works finished from the foundation of the world. The speech seems elliptical, as the Hebrews often speak, and something is wanting, namely what has been made clear or previously signified; so that the sense is: That indeed this rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks is set before and prepared for believers, and certainly, from the beginning of the created world, this has been declared. By putting these words first, the apostle seems to indicate either that it is very easy to find proof of this matter, namely at the very beginning of the sacred books; or certainly that this rest was destined for believers very long ago, from the founding of the world, just as the godly elect are elsewhere said to be chosen by God to eternal life from the foundation of the world. For so we read in Ephesians 1, where it says πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [before the foundation of the world], just as here it has ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [from the foundation of the world].

units.la: καταβολή, id est, fundamentum.
units.tr: Katabolē, that is, foundation [καταβολή].

units.la: Significat autem vox καταβολή, fundamentum, molitionem, constitutionem. Quomodo autem probatur illud de requie? Dixit enim quodam in loco de die septimo sic: Et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis: Ecce, inquit, cum perfecta essent omnia opera a iactis fundamentis mundi, dixit, scilicet spiritus Sanctus, in quodam loco, πού, quod satis est ad indicandum, haberi id non sacris literis. Habetur autem Genesios secundo: sed in capita distinguere, & capita citare veteribus visitatum non fuisse quis nescit?
units.tr: The word καταβολή means foundation, laying down, or constitution. But how is the statement about rest proved? For he said somewhere, about the seventh day, in this way: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." Behold, he says, when all works were finished from the foundations of the world laid, the Holy Spirit said in a certain place, πού [somewhere], which is enough to show that it is not found in the Holy Scriptures. It is found, however, in Genesis 2. But who does not know that the ancients did not divide books into chapters or cite chapters?

units.la: Certè librum Genesios, & locum in eo videtur Apostolus indicasse, quando ait: perfectis operibus à iactis fundamentis mundi. Nam neque libros ita citant seu vocant suis titulis Hebrei, vti nos, sed verè appellationes librorum, præsertim legalium, ducunt ex prima voce operis: unde, quem librum nos Genesin imitati græcos appella mus, ipsi בראשית dicunt: Rursus Exodum ואלה שמות & sic deinceps. Deinde vnumquemq; librum distinguendi in partes, pro varietate historiarum, quarum aliæ longiores aliæ breviores sunt, titulos hinc atque inde novos faciunt. Unde in Genesi, quicquid ad sextum vsq; saput continetur, distinguant nomine בראשית Sexto capite titulum facere incipiunt נח quia ibi historia Noah texitur. Capite duodecimo alium titulum faciunt: לך לך quod significat ad verbum vade tibi: Interpretes uerterunt, egredere: quia ibi inicium est historiæ Abraham, & incipit caput: Et dixit Dominus ad Abraham, egredere de terra tua. Hic verò titulus ad decimum septimum caput usque protrahitur, & sic deinceps.
units.tr: Certainly the Apostle seems to have pointed to the book of Genesis and a passage in it when he says: "when the works were finished from the foundation of the world." For the Hebrews do not cite or name books by their titles as we do, but really take the names of the books, especially the legal ones, from the first word of the text. Hence the book we imitate the Greeks in calling Genesis they call בראשית [Bereshit]; again Exodus is ואלה שמות [Ve'elleh Shemot], and so on in order. Then, dividing each book into parts according to the variety of the narratives, some longer and some shorter, they make new headings here and there. So in Genesis, everything contained up to the sixth chapter they mark with the title בראשית; at the sixth chapter they begin a new title, נח [Noah], because the story of Noah is woven there. At the twelfth chapter they make another title, לך לך [Lekh lekha], which literally means "go for yourself"; the translators rendered it "go out," because there begins the history of Abraham, and the chapter starts: "And the Lord said to Abraham, go out from your land." This title, however, extends to the seventeenth chapter, and so on.

units.la: Hac ergo ratione quando Hebraei non solent, sicut nec veteres scriptores, distinguere libros exactius in capita, satis fuit Apostolo dixisse, quod quodam in loco scriptum habetur. Sed maioris certitudinis ergò addidit, De die septimo, περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης. Interpres nosteer addidit vocem diei, quæ in greco non habetur, sed usitato more subintelligitur. Proinde videnda nobis est historia Genesios, quæ de die septimo à creatione mundi tradit, quæ præsenti instituto seruiunt.
units.tr: For this reason, since the Hebrews, like the ancient writers, were not accustomed to divide books into chapters with exactness, it was enough for the Apostle to say that it is written in a certain place. But for greater certainty he added, "about the seventh day," περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης, "concerning the seventh." Our translator added the word "day," which is not in the Greek but is understood by the usual idiom. Accordingly we must now consider the history in Genesis which tells of the seventh day from the creation of the world, which serves our present purpose.

units.la: Sic autem ibi legitur capite primo: Postquam benedixisset Deus homini à se condito, dicens: Crescite & multiplicamini, & replete terram, & subijcite eam, & dominamini piscibus maris, & volatilibus cœli, & vniuersis animantibus, quæ mouentur super terram, &c. Mox additur: vidit quæ Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, & erant valde bona. Et factus est vesperè & mane dies sextus.
units.tr: Now there it is read in the first chapter: "After God had blessed the man he had made, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the heaven, and all living things that move upon the earth," etc. Soon it is added: "God saw all that he had made, and they were very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day."

units.la: Hinc sequitur capite secundo, Igitur perfecti sunt cœli & terra, & omnis ornatus eorum. Compleuitque Deus die septimo opus suum, quod fecerat, & requieuit die septimo ab vniuerso opere, quod perarat. Et benedixit diei septimo, & sanctificauit illum, quia in ipso cessauerat ab omni opere suo, quod creauit Deus ut faceret. En quæ ad explicandum uerba præsentis argumenti sunt scitu necessaria: neque opus est, plura de distinctione dierum, aut de operibus, quæ illis diebus singulis sunt perfecta, vel etiam de mysterio diei septimi, quod uidelicet iam tum præsignabat requiem spiritualem producere.
units.tr: Then follows in the second chapter: "Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their host. And God finished on the seventh day his work which he had made, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God had created to do." Behold what is necessary to know in order to explain the words of the present argument. Nor is there need to say more about the distinction of the days, or about the works which were finished on each of those days, or even about the mystery of the seventh day, which indeed already foreshadowed the production of spiritual rest.

units.la: Tantùm itaque incitabimus, quæ præteriri recte non possunt. Apostolus itaque citat: Et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis. Deinde infert: Et in hoc οὐ τούτῳ supple sensum, iterū dicitur Spiritus S. hoc loco: Si introibunt in requiem meam. Non ob aliud, ut supra ostendimus, citat Apostolus hoc testimonium ex Genesi, quam ad propandum, qualis sit requies, de qua spiritus Sanctus hic loquitur, & quàm ipse ait credetibus esse propositam. Respiciens enim in particulam, meam, quando Deus dicit, in requiem meam, ex Genesi vult docere, qualis sit illa requies Dei, quam Deus diserte vocat suam.
units.tr: Therefore we will only point out what cannot rightly be passed over. The Apostle thus cites: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." Then he infers: "And in this οὐ τούτῳ [in this place] supply the sense: again the Holy Spirit says in this place: 'If they shall enter into my rest.'" The Apostle cites this testimony from Genesis for no other purpose, as we have shown above, than to show what sort of rest is meant by the Holy Spirit here, and what he says is set before believers. For by attending to the particle "my," when God says "into my rest," he wishes to teach from Genesis what that rest of God is like, which God expressly calls his own.

units.la: Genesis autem describit requiem spiritualem, benedictam, sanctam, plenam gloria, & prorsus Deo dignam, sicut tibi aperte dicitur, Benedixit Deus diei septimo, & sanctificauit illum: atque ita satis manifestè declarat, requiem, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur, non esse corporalem seu temporalem, qualis erat umbratica quædam concessa patribus in Canaan: sed spiritualem, æternam, & diuina benedictione stabilitam, & post hanc vitam apud Deum expectandam.
units.tr: Now Genesis describes a spiritual rest, blessed, holy, full of glory, and altogether worthy of God, as is openly said to you: "God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it." And so it declares quite plainly that the rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks is not bodily or temporal, such as was a certain shadowy rest granted to the fathers in Canaan, but spiritual, eternal, established by the divine blessing, and to be awaited with God after this life.

units.la: Certum autem est, potuisset Apostolus aliis quibusdam Scripturæ testimonijs propare, requiem spiritualem pijs & credentibus propositam, sed qui respiciebat in prononmen meam, ideò voluit istum locum producere, in quo requies Dei describitur. Et vbi ostendit, requiem, de qua spiritus loquitur, esse eandem cum requie Dei, multò profectò aptissimè ostendit, spiritualem & cœlestem requiem esse, de qua agitur. Et qui potuisset commodius dignitatem huius requiei demonstrare, quàm docendo, quòd sit requies Dei? Qua ratione magis inflammentur animi credentium, & fortius retundantur aduersarij, quàm hoc pacto explicando testimonium spiritus Sancti de requie Dei?
units.tr: It is certain, however, that the Apostle could have proved from other testimonies of Scripture that a spiritual rest is set before the pious and believers. But since he was looking to the pronoun "my," he chose to bring forward this passage, in which the rest of God is described. And by showing that the rest of which the Spirit speaks is the same as the rest of God, he certainly showed most aptly that the rest under discussion is spiritual and heavenly. And how could he more fittingly demonstrate the dignity of this rest than by teaching that it is the rest of God? In what way are the minds of believers more inflamed, and adversaries more strongly repelled, than by explaining in this way the testimony of the Holy Spirit about the rest of God?

units.la: Cæterùm de requie spirituali, quomodo passim Scriptura adhuc loquatur, & q; fine dubio patres & plurimi Iudæi potuerint intellegere de requie, lubet declarare. Psalmo quarto: In pacem in idipsum dormiam & requiescam, quoniam tu Domine singulariter in spe constituisti me, Esaiæ tricesimo secundo, Et erit opus iustitiæ pax, & cultus iustitiæ silentium & securitas usque in sempiternum. Et sedebit populus meus in pulchritu‐dine pacis, & in tabernaculis fiduciæ, & in requie opulenta. Esaiæ 58. Cùm effuderis esu‐rienti animam tuam, & animam afflictam repleueris, orietur in tenebris lux tua, & tene‐bræ tuæ erunt, sicut meridies: & requiem tibi dabit Dominus Deus tuus semper, & im‐plebit splendoribus animam tuam, & ossa tua liberabit. Esaiæ capite vltimo, Erit Sab‐batum ex sabbato, & calendæ ex calendis. Denique sunt multi alij loci de pace & vita quieta expectanda per Mesiam in prophetis. Præterea permultæ promissiones de quie‐te temporali, huius spiritualis typum gerentes: qui omnes loci huic instituto rectè pos‐sent accommodari.
units.tr: Moreover, it is good to show how Scripture everywhere speaks of spiritual rest, and how the fathers and very many Jews could undoubtedly have understood it as rest. In Psalm 4: "In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you, Lord, alone have established me in hope." Isaiah 32: "And the work of righteousness will be peace, and the service of righteousness quietness and security forever. And my people will sit in a beautiful dwelling of peace, and in tabernacles of confidence, and in rich rest." Isaiah 58: "When you pour out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul, your light will rise in darkness, and your darkness will be as midday; and the Lord your God will give you rest always, and will fill your soul with splendours, and will deliver your bones." Isaiah, last chapter: "There shall be Sabbath after Sabbath, and new moon after new moon." Finally there are many other passages about peace and a quiet life to be expected through the Messiah in the prophets. Besides, very many promises of temporal rest, bearing a type of this spiritual rest, all of which can rightly be applied to this subject.

units.la: Hos igitur & similes locos ex veteri testamento apud prophetas obuios potuisset‐ poftolus adducere, ad demonstrandum, requiem, quę credentibus proposita est, esse spi‐ritualem: & fuissent non solùm commodæ, sed etiam valde efficaces rationes: verùm quia aduersarij semper procliues erant ad reijcienda hæc testimonia, dicendo, quòd in‐telligenda essent de requie temporali, sicut etiamnum hodie quæcunque de bonis spiri‐tualibus sub Christo habendis, item de regno Christi, adducimus, euertunt & reijciunt contendendo, de temporalibus bonis, & de temporali requie omnia intelligenda: ideò Apostolus maluit eligere illud testimonium ex Genesi, quòd, sicut luculentisime oftea dit, qualis sit requies Dei, & spiritualis: ita non potest calumnijs aduersariorum euerti. Promissiones enim illæ ex Esaia, & similes, ostendebant aliquo modo, qualis foretre‐quies, quam Deus vellet dare alijs: at qualis esset requies proprie ipsius Dei, nusquam expresius, quam Genesis secundo declaratur: atq; hæc propter pronomen, meam, ma‐xime erant explicanda. Iam uerò oportet in quiramus, quid sibi velit Scriptura, cùm dicit, Deum requiescere, atque inde qualis sit futura requies credentium, rectius perspi‐cietur. Quiescere Deum, interpretantur nonnulli, quando ille facit, ut nos quiescamus. Sic enim sæpè in Scripturis Deo attribuuntur illa, quæ ipse in nobis operatur, cuique cunque in nobis bona sunt, ipse reuera eadè in nobis agit & perficit: quomodo Gal. 4. Deus dicitur cognoscere, quando nos ipsum cognoscimus. At nunc, inquit, posteaquàm cognouistis Deum, quin potius cogniti estis à Deo.
units.tr: These and similar passages found in the Old Testament among the prophets the Apostle could have adduced to demonstrate that the rest set before believers is spiritual; and these would have been not only suitable but also very effective arguments. But since the adversaries were always prone to reject these testimonies, saying that they must be understood of temporal rest, just as even today, whatever we adduce about the good things to be had spiritually under Christ, and likewise about the kingdom of Christ, they overturn and reject, contending that all such things must be understood of temporal goods and temporal rest, the Apostle preferred to choose that testimony from Genesis, which, as he has most clearly shown, displays what the rest of God is, and that it is spiritual; and so it cannot be overturned by the calumnies of the adversaries. For those promises from Isaiah and similar ones showed in some way what rest God wished to give to others, but what the rest of God himself properly is, is nowhere more clearly declared than in Genesis 2; and this was especially to be explained because of the pronoun "my." Now, indeed, we must consider what Scripture means when it says that God rested, and from that it will be seen more correctly what the future rest of believers will be. Some interpret that God rests when he causes us to rest. For thus in the Scriptures those things which he himself works in us are often attributed to God, and whatever good things are in us, he himself really works and perfects in us; just as in Galatians 4 God is said to know when we know him. "But now," he says, "after you have known God, or rather have been known by God."

units.la: Alij exponunt, Deum quieuisse ab operibus, id est, desijsse res nouas creare. Iam enim sexto die omnia quę mundi sunt, quæq; ad mundi perfectionem & ornatum necessaria sunt, perfecta erant, & quicquid etiam postea rerum extitit, eius materia, vel quocunq; modo appellari placet, illud, ex quo cætera originem trahere debebant, iam tum condi‐tum erat, & ad producendum alias res erat idoneum. Ergo quando illa prima rerum o‐mnium, quæ pòst successerunt, elementa sunt condita, solumq; restitit, ut bene condita conseruarentur, Deus dicitur ab operibus suis die septimo quieuisse. Ab operibus, in‐quam, creandis, non tamen conseruandis moderandisq;. Nam ut illo modo dicatur quiescere ab operibus, tamen hoc modo semper agit atq; operatur: sicut & Christus Ioan. 5. diserte ait, Pater meus ad hoc usq; temporis operatur, & ego operor. Nam quæ ad conseruationem & salutem tum omnium rerum conditarum, tum præcipuè homi‐num pertinent, ille efficere nunquam intermittit. Quare ab Augustino rectè dictum, Deum semper quietum, omnia tamen agere.
units.tr: Others explain that God rested from his works, that is, that he ceased to create new things. For by the sixth day everything in the world, and everything needed for the world's completion and adornment, was already finished. Whatever things came into being afterwards, their matter (or whatever one prefers to call that from which all other things were to derive their origin) had already been created and was fit to produce other things. So when those first elements of all things, which came after, had been created, and only the task remained of preserving and governing what had been well made, God is said to have rested from his works on the seventh day. I say from his works of creation, not from preserving and governing them. For although he is said in this way to rest from his works, yet in another way he always acts and works, as Christ also plainly says in John 5: "My Father works until now, and I work." For he never ceases to bring about whatever pertains to the preservation and salvation both of all created things and especially of human beings. Hence Augustine rightly said that God is always at rest and yet does all things.

units.la: Verùm mihi videtur adhuc aliter posse quies Dei explicari, & ad præsentis loci cau‐sam accommodatius. Deum enim quiescere dici puto eodem pacto, quo dicitur & sedere in folio maiestatis, & in gloria: & quiescere Deum nihil aliud esse, quàm Deum, postquam condidit & perfecit omnia, quæ ad potentiam, bonitatemque ipsius illustrå‐dam faciunt, iam accipere ex operibus illis suam gloriam. Non, quòd ratione operum duntaxat accipiat gloriam, vel ex operibus, sicut solent artifices: sed quòd propter opera necessariò sequatur Deum summa gloria. Vnde non dicitur Deum quiescere ex ope‐ribus, vel, in operibus: sed ab operibus. Quomodo enim qui laborauit, & res ma‐gnas in bello vel pace peregit, uotorumque suorum factus est compos, dicitur postea quiescere ab operibus, maximè ubi gloriam & laudem veluti fructum & præmia sua‐rum virtutum apud suos percipit: ita Deus postquam omnia opera condidit, per quæ potentiam & bonitatem suam notam faceret, postea sua, qua dignus est, potitur in om‐nibus gloria, & ita quodammodo conquiescit.
units.tr: Yet it seems to me that the rest of God can be explained in yet another way, one better suited to the present context. I think God is said to rest in the same way that he is said to sit on the throne of majesty and in glory. To rest, then, is nothing other than for God, after he has created and completed all the things that serve to display his power and goodness, now to receive his glory from those works. This is not because he receives glory merely by reason of his works, or from his works, as craftsmen do, but because great glory necessarily follows God on account of his works. Hence God is not said to rest from his works in the sense of resting in them or by them, but from them. For just as one who has labored and achieved great things in war or in peace, and has obtained the fulfilment of his desires, is afterwards said to rest from his labours, especially when he receives glory and praise among his own people as the fruit and reward of his virtues, so God, after he has created all the works through which he would make known his power and goodness, then takes possession of the glory he deserves from all things, and in this way in some measure comes to rest.

units.la: Sicut Christus postquam peregit omnia, quæ ad salutem humani generis erant fa‐cienda, gloriam suam obtinet apud patrem, & dicitur ibi ad dextram sedere: ita Deus cöditis & absolutis omnibus, per quæ potetia & bonitas ipsius debebat illustrari, dici‐tur quiescere, & suam gloriam obtinere. Sedere enim, & conquiescere haud multum ab inuicem differunt, & quiescere ab eo, quod sedere in gloria, rectè accipi posse existimem.
units.tr: Just as Christ, after he had accomplished all the things that had to be done for the salvation of the human race, obtains his glory with the Father and is said to sit there at the right hand, so God, once all the things through which his power and goodness were to be displayed have been created and completed, is said to rest and to obtain his glory. For to sit and to rest do not differ much from each other, and I think that to rest can rightly be understood as sitting in glory.

units.la: Simili significatione dicitur Apocalypseos decimoquarto, quòd mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur, debent requiescere à laboribus: quod perinde mihi uidetur, ac si dicetur, quòd debent potiri optata & sperata gloria. Iam verò ubi hoc pacto accipimus requiem Dei, vt significet gloriam ac dignitatem Dei, quae ipsi à conditis operibus debet tur, valde praeclarum est, quòd eandem requiem dicuntur credentes acceptuli, & manifestum fit, requiem non esse temporalem seu corporalem, sed aeternam, spiritualem, & coelestem, quae eos manet, ut verè dicantur quiescere: sicut & Deus ipse quiescit ab operibus suis, id quod suis verbis mox pronunciat Apostolus. Ergo omnes loci, qui de futura gloria in nouo testamento, imò & in ueteri, concionantur, qualis nimirum & quanta ea sit futura, ad declarandum, qualis sit haec requies, quae credentibus proposita est, conducunt.
units.tr: In a similar sense it is said in Revelation 14 that the dead who die in the Lord must rest from their labours. This seems to me the same as saying that they must enjoy the glory they desired and hoped for. Now when we understand the rest of God in this way, as signifying the glory and dignity of God which is due to him from the works he has created, it is very remarkable that believers are said to receive the same rest. And it becomes clear that the rest is not temporal or bodily, but eternal, spiritual and heavenly, and it remains for them so that they may truly be said to rest, just as God himself rests from his works, as the Apostle soon declares in his own words. Therefore all the passages which preach of future glory in the New Testament, and indeed in the Old too, concerning what that glory will be and how great, serve to declare what kind of rest this is which is held out to believers.

units.la: Posteaquam igitur illud reliquum est, aliquos introire in eam, &, quibus prius annunciatum fuit, non introierunt, propter incredulitatem.
units.tr: Since therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and those who previously received the good news did not enter because of unbelief.

units.la: Innititur haec ratio ei, quòd necessarium est adimpleri diuinas promissiones. 1.Cor.1 Quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei, per ipsum sunt etiam, & per ipsum Amen, Deo ad gloriam per nos. Psalmo 104. Memor fuit in seculum testamenti sui, verbi quod mandauit in mille generationes, quod disposuit ad Abraham, & iuramenti sui Isaac, &c. deus fallere nō potest, semper verax est, quod promisit, hauddubiè semper praestat. Itaque quando Deus in hoc testimonio promisit per spiritum Sanctum, se daturum requiem credentibus: Ergo necessariò debet adimpleri.
units.tr: This argument rests on the fact that the divine promises must necessarily be fulfilled. 1 Cor. 1: "For all the promises of God are in him yea, and in him Amen, to the glory of God through us." Psalm 104: "He has been mindful of his covenant for ever, of the word he commanded to a thousand generations, which he made with Abraham, and of his oath to Isaac," etc. God cannot deceive; he is always true, and what he has promised he undoubtedly always performs. Therefore, since God in this testimony has promised through the Holy Spirit that he will give rest to believers, it must necessarily be fulfilled.

units.la: Hac igitur hypothesi data, procedit argumentum. Deus promisit, se daturum requiem credentibus: Ergo debet adimpleri in alijs. Patres autem per periphrasin vocat τὸς πρότερον εὐαγγελισθέντας, quasi dicat prius euangelizatos. Quandoquidem nuncium siue promissio facta, ad illos de ingressu in requiem temporalem terrae Canaan, typum gerebat nuntij, seu promissionis de ingressu in requiem spiritualem, de qua concionatur euangelium. Et sicut suprà, ubi dicebatur, quòd simus ευαγγελισμένοι diximus, significatum, quòd excellentius vocem Dei audierimus, quàm patres: ita hic ea forma locutionis exaggeratur patrum crimen, qui ad tantam certitudinem auditae vocis Dei, tamen increduli perstiterint.
units.tr: Granted this hypothesis, the argument proceeds: God has promised that he will give rest to believers; therefore it must be fulfilled in others. The Apostle calls them, by a periphrasis, tous proteron euangelisthentas [τοὺς πρότερον εὐαγγελισθέντας], as if to say, "those who were first evangelised," that is, the good news was first announced to them. For the message or promise made to those people concerning their entry into the temporal rest of the land of Canaan was a type of the promise of entry into the spiritual rest of which the gospel preaches. And just as above, where it was said that we are euangelismenoi [εὐαγγελισμένοι], we noted that we have heard the voice of God more excellently than the fathers, so here this form of speech magnifies the sin of the fathers, who, despite such certainty of the voice of God they had heard, nevertheless persisted in unbelief.

units.la: Non introierunt) videlicet in requiem spiritualem, de qua hic loquitur spiritus Sanctus, quaeque similis est requiei diuinae. Nam requiem temporalem obtinuisse patres, id extra controuersiam est, maximè eos, qui non murmurarunt, siue non peccarunt per incredulitatem.
units.tr: They did not enter: namely into the spiritual rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks here, and which is like the divine rest. For that the fathers obtained the temporal rest is beyond controversy, especially those who did not murmur, or did not sin through unbelief.

units.la: Constat enim, ut habetur Numerorum vicesimo sexto, ingressos terram Canaan ad sexcenta millia, & mille, septingentos, triginta. Exclusi quidem fuerūt increduli, sed credentes sunt admissi, ut habeatur typus, quòd ad spiritualem quoque requiem patebit aditus per fidem: incredulos autem ab ea excludendos.
units.tr: For it is recorded in Numbers 26 that they who entered the land of Canaan numbered six hundred thousand and one thousand, seven hundred and thirty. The unbelievers were indeed excluded, but the believers were admitted, so that there might be a type that access to the spiritual rest would also be open through faith, while unbelievers were to be shut out from it.

units.la: Ac necessarium erat adimpleri promissiones de requie temporali ad patres, etiamsi impij fuerint exclusi. Ita enim Deus semper perficit, quae promisit, erga bonos quidem: erga malos verò, non eodem modo. Vnde 1.Samuel.2. vir Dei ad Heli: Quia honorasti filios tuos magis, quàm Deum, ait Dominus Israel: Loquens locutus sum, ut domus tua, & domus patris tui ministraret in conspectu meo vsque in sempiternum. Nunc autem dicit Dominus: Absit hoc à me, sed quicunque honorificauerit me, glorificabo eum: qui autem contemnunt me, erunt ignobiles. Ecce dies ueniunt, & praecidam brachium tuum, & brachium domus patris tui, vt non sit senex in domo tua in omnibus diebus: verumtamen non auferam penitus virum ex te ab altari meo, sed ut deficiat oculi tui, & tabescat anima tua, & pars magna domus tuae morietur, cùm ad virilem aetatem perue-nerit, &c. Item psalmo 88. In aeternum seruabo illi misericordiam meam, & testamentū meum fidele ipsi. Et ponam in seculum seculi semen eius, & thronum eius, sicut dies coeli: si autem dereliquerint filij legem meam, & in iudicijs meis non ambulauerint, si iustitias meas profanauerint, & mandata mea non custodierint, visitabo in virga iniquitates eorum, & in ueruberibus peccata eorum. Misericordiam autem meam non disperget eo, neque mentiar in veritatem meam: neque profanabo testamentum meum, & quae procedunt de labijs meis, non faciam irrita: semel iurauī in sancto meo, si Dauid mentiar, semen eius in aeternum manebit. Vbi clarè vides, quòd Deus promissiones suas semper implet: sed erga pios & credentes: impios verò iustè & non sine nota in-constantiae vel mutabilitatis excludit: & quando non erga omnes, tamen semper ꝑ aliquos, &si non vno modo corporaliter uidelicet, tamen alio, videlicet spiritualiter. Sic promissiones ad Abraham impletæ sunt, licet non in filijs secundum carnem, tamen in filijs promissionis, Galat.4. Roman.9. Ite promissiones ad Dauid de filijs in æternum regnaturis impletæ sunt, non quidem in regno temporali, sed in regno spirituali, in quo Christus eius filius secundum carnem regnat in æternum. Huc item parabola pertinet Matthei vicesimo secundo, de nuptijs à quibus cum vocati excluderentur, alij sunt in tromisi.
units.tr: And it was necessary that the promises concerning temporal rest made to the fathers be fulfilled, even though the wicked were excluded. For God always carries out what he has promised, with respect to the good indeed; but with respect to the wicked, not in the same way. Hence 1 Samuel 2, the man of God to Eli: "Because you have honoured your sons more than me, says the Lord God of Israel: I spoke indeed that your house and the house of your father should minister before me for ever. But now the Lord says: Far be it from me; but whoever honours me, I will glorify, and those who despise me shall be dishonoured. Behold, the days come when I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house, so that there shall not be an old man in your house for all days; yet I will not utterly cut off a man of yours from my altar, but so that your eyes may fail and your soul be consumed, and a great part of your house shall die when it reaches manhood," etc. Likewise Psalm 88: "For ever I will keep my mercy for him, and my covenant shall stand firm with him. I will establish his seed for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven. If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with stripes. But my mercy I will not take away from him, nor will I lie in my truth; I will not profane my covenant, nor alter the word that has gone out of my lips. Once I have sworn by my holiness; if I lie to David, his seed shall endure for ever." Here you clearly see that God always fulfils his promises, but towards the godly and believing; the impious he justly and not without mark of inconstancy or mutability excludes. And if not towards all, yet always through some, though not in one way, namely bodily, but in another, namely spiritually. Thus the promises made to Abraham were fulfilled, although not in the children according to the flesh, yet in the children of promise (Gal. 4; Rom. 9). The promises to David concerning sons who would reign for ever were fulfilled, not indeed in a temporal kingdom, but in a spiritual kingdom, in which Christ, his son according to the flesh, reigns for ever. To this also pertains the parable in Matthew 22 concerning the wedding, from which, when those who were invited were excluded, others were brought in.

units.la: Hoc igitur pacto & à requie temporali, & à requie spirituali increduli eijciuntur, pij admittuntur, & promissiones Dei necessariò implentur. Et propterea diserte etiam caute addidit, dicens: propter incredulitatem, significans, quòd, sicut olim patres erant exclusi à requie temporali propter incredulitatem, ita excludendi etiam à requie sint spirituali, propter incredulitatem. Et quia contendissent aduersarij, patres credetes videlicet potitos requie, de qua hic loquitur spiritus Sanctus, quando sunt ingressi terram Canaan: ideò rursus probat Apostolus, id non posse ita intelligi, quia hic spiritus Sanctus aliud nouum tempus præfinit:
units.tr: In this way unbelievers are shut out both from the temporal rest and from the spiritual rest, believers are admitted, and God's promises are necessarily fulfilled. Therefore he added carefully and deliberately the words on account of unbelief, signifying that just as the fathers were formerly excluded from the temporal rest on account of unbelief, so unbelievers are to be excluded from the spiritual rest on account of unbelief. And since our opponents had contended that the believing fathers had actually obtained the rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks here, when they entered the land of Canaan, the Apostle therefore proves again that this cannot be understood in that way, because the Holy Spirit here fixes another, new time:

units.la: Rursum, inquit, quendam præfinit diem, hodie, Dauid dicens: post tantum temporis, quemadmodum dictum est: Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, ne obdureris corda vestra.
units.tr: Again, he says, he fixes a certain day, Today, saying through David, after so long a time, as has been said: Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.

units.la: Vbi ex eo, quod Spiritus S. dicit, hodie si voce eius audieritis, vrgens vocabulum hodie, collegit, spiritum Sanctum loqui, non de antea acta aliqua requie, qualem visi sunt accipere patres: sed de noua quadam, & spirituali, quæ adhuc foret expectanda: quomodo & initio conclusionis ostendimus, hunc psalmum continere vaticinium de reuelando euangelio, in quo vox Dei denuò esset audienda, & ab ijs, qui ei crederent, spiritualis requies accipienda. πάλιν τινὰ ἡμέραν σύμφορον. Quando ait, τινὰ ἡμέραν, quendam diem, sic loquitur, tanquam de die expectando, & nondum præsenti palàm sentiat, qui tamen quotidie sit expectandus. Quæ sententia etiam exponitur in particula, Si, cum dicitur: hodie si vocem eius audieritis, notans, aliquando audiendam, at nondum adesse tempus. Tametsi quædam exemplaria vocem τινὰ non habent. Cùm verò dicit, præfinit, summam notat certitudinem eius diei aduenturæ, quodque necessariò præfinito & certo aliquo tempore vox Dei foret audienda.
units.tr: Here, from the fact that the Holy Spirit says today if you hear his voice, and by stressing the word today, he infers that the Spirit is not speaking of some rest already past, such as the fathers seemed to receive, but of a new and spiritual rest which was still to be expected. As we showed at the beginning of the conclusion, this psalm contains a prophecy about the revealing of the gospel, in which the voice of God was to be heard again, and the spiritual rest was to be received by those who believed it. Again a certain day [πάλιν τινὰ ἡμέραν]. When he says a certain day, he speaks as of a day to be awaited, and one that he does not yet plainly perceive as present, though it is to be awaited every day. This sense is also expressed by the particle if in the words today if you hear his voice, marking that the voice is to be heard at some time, but that the time has not yet come. Some copies, however, do not have the word a certain [τινὰ]. When he says he fixes, he indicates the complete certainty that this day would come, and that the voice of God would necessarily have to be heard at some fixed and determined time.

units.la: Quare manifestum fit, per vocem hodie, notari tempus reuelati euangelij, & certo aliquo tempore præfinito à Deo patre debuisse id reuelari. Vnde & illa hinc inde obuia de praefinito tempore. Galat.4. At vbi venit plenitudo temporis, emisit Deus filium suum. Ephes.1. Patefacto nobis arcano voluntatis suæ, iuxta beneplacitum suum, quod proposuerat in seipso, usque ad dispensationem plenitudinis temporum. Ephes.3. appellat euangelium mysterium Christi, quod in alijs ætatibus nobis innotuit, quemadmodum nunc reuelatum est sanctis apostolis eius. Ibidem vocatur mysterium absconditum seculis in Deo, sed notum debuisse fieri ecclesiæ, secundum præfinitionem seculorum, quam fecit in Christo Iesu. Ad Titum 1. Agnitio veritatis, quæ est secundum pietatem in spe vitæ æternæ, quam promisit is, qui mentiri nescit Deus, ante tempora æterna, patefecit autem temporibus suis. Præfinitum igitur & præstitutum à Deo fuit tempus euangelij per totum orbem manifestandi.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that by the word today is meant the time of the revealed gospel, and that it had to be revealed by God the Father at some fixed and predetermined time. Hence also those passages found on every side about a predetermined time: Galatians 4: But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son. Ephesians 1: Having made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he had purposed in himself, for the dispensation of the fullness of times. Ephesians 3 calls the gospel the mystery of Christ, which was made known to us in other ages, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles. In the same place it is called a mystery hidden from the ages in God, but which was to be made known to the Church according to the predetermination of the ages, which he made in Christ Jesus. Titus 1: The knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before the eternal times, but revealed in his own times. Therefore the time of manifesting the gospel throughout the whole world was determined and appointed in advance by God.

units.la: In Dauid) id est, per Dauid, quo spiritus Sanctus tanquam instrumento usus est. Simili modo in propositione totius epistolæ, οὑ pro Δαυὶδ ponebatur, cùm diceretur, Deum locutum esse patribus in prophetis. Liquet autem hinc, psalmi eius autorem indubitatum esse ipsum Dauidem.
units.tr: In David: that is, through David, whom the Holy Spirit used as an instrument. In the same way, at the beginning of the whole epistle, the preposition in stood in place of through, when it was said that God spoke to the fathers in the prophets. It is clear from this that the author of the psalm is beyond doubt David himself.

units.la: Post tantum temporis) Hæc particula magnam habet emphasin, ad significandum, nullo pacto intelligi posse verba spiritus Sancti, de requie temporali, quam patres acceperant visi sunt sub Iosua, quando multis retrò seculis hic de nouo tempore expectando Spiritus sit vaticinatus. Et certè si cui lubeat obseruare temporum rationem, inueniet clarissimè rem ita se habere. Supputes enim à tempore Iosuæ ad tempora usque Dauidis, & consideres spiritum Sanctum per Dauidem denuò locutum, de voce Dei rursus audienda, nec non de requie expectanda, intelliges haud dubiè, promissionem hanc spiritus Sancti nullo modo patribus competere. Sanè ex libris Iudicum & Samuelis pritus, facilè est deprehendere. Mortuo Iosue successit Iudas, qui multo tempore præclaras res gesisit. Inde octo annis seruierunt regi Mesopotamiæ, & successit Othoniel liberator eorum, sub quo terra quieuit quadraginta annis.
units.tr: After so long a time: this phrase carries great emphasis, to show that the words of the Holy Spirit cannot in any way be understood as referring to the temporal rest which the fathers seemed to have received under Joshua, when the Spirit prophesied here, many ages afterwards, about a new time still to be awaited. And indeed, if anyone should wish to observe the chronology, he will find the matter stands very plainly so. For if you reckon from the time of Joshua down to the time of David, and consider that the Holy Spirit spoke again through David about the voice of God to be heard again, and also about the rest to be expected, you will undoubtedly understand that this promise of the Holy Spirit by no means applies to the fathers. This is easily discovered from the books of Judges and of Samuel. After the death of Joshua, Judah succeeded, who for a long time performed outstanding deeds. Then for eight years they served the king of Mesopotamia; and Othniel, their liberator, succeeded, under whom the land had rest for forty years.

units.la: Inde duo uiginti annis seruierunt Eglon regi Moab, à cuius potestate iterum liberati sunt per Ehud seu Aioth. Post Aioth iudicauit Samgar.
units.tr: Then for eighteen years they served Eglon, king of Moab, from whose power they were again freed through Ehud, or Ehud the son of Gera. After Ehud, Shamgar judged.

units.la: Hinc per uiginti annos oppressi sunt Israelitæ à Iabin rege Canaan, liberati rursus per Deborām.
units.tr: Then for twenty years the Israelites were oppressed by Jabin, king of Canaan, and were again liberated through Deborah.

units.la: 8. annis seruiunt regi Mesopotamiæ. 40. Quies. 18. Regi Moab. 20. Iabin rex Canaan. Deboram & Barak: & tunc quieuit iterum terra per quadraginta annos.
units.tr: Eight years they served the king of Mesopotamia; forty years of rest. Eighteen years to the king of Moab; twenty years to Jabin, king of Canaan. Deborah and Barak; and then the land rested again for forty years.

units.la: Rursus per septem annos oppressi sunt à Madianitis, liberati autem per Gedeonem, sub quo iterum terra per quadraginta annos quieuit.
units.tr: Again, they were oppressed for seven years by the Midianites, but were freed through Gideon, under whom the land again rested for forty years.

units.la: Abimelech fraude occupans imperium, tribus annis.
units.tr: Abimelech, seizing the rule by fraud, for three years.

units.la: Hinc Thola iudicauit annis 23.
units.tr: Then Tola judged for twenty-three years.

units.la: Iair annis 22.
units.tr: Jair for twenty-two years.

units.la: Iephthe annis 6.
units.tr: Jephthah for six years.

units.la: Iozan annis 7.
units.tr: Ibzan for seven years.

units.la: Elon annis 7.
units.tr: Elon for ten years.

units.la: Abdon annis 8.
units.tr: Abdon for eight years.

units.la: Deinde per quadraginta annos vexati sunt à Philistæis.
units.tr: Then they were afflicted for forty years by the Philistines.

units.la: Samson annis 20.
units.tr: Samson for twenty years.

units.la: Interregnum, de quo Iudicum 21.
units.tr: An interregnum, of which see Judges 21.

units.la: Heli sacerdos, de quo lib.1. Samuelis iudicauit annis quadraginta.
units.tr: Eli the priest, of whom see the first book of Samuel, judged for forty years.

units.la: Samuel, qui valde diu ad multam senectutem iudicauit, filios substituit. Saulem deinde Regem creauit.
units.tr: Samuel, who judged for a very long time, into great old age, appointed his sons. Then he made Saul king.

units.la: Cui successit Dauid, per quem spiritus Sanctus ita locutus est.
units.tr: David succeeded him, through whom the Holy Spirit spoke in this way.

units.la: Atque inuenire est, si tam non expressa, quàm expressa simul colligantur, annos supra quadringentos intercessisse inter tempora Iosuæ & Dauidis. Quare recte dixit hic Apostolus, post tantum temporis: & clarissimè euincitur, spiritum Sanctum, cùm per Dauidem loqueretur, hodie si uocem eius audieritis, nullo modo sensisse de uoce Dei, quæ iam olim fuisset audita in deserto: sed de ea quæ denuò foret audienda, videlicet in euangelio: & audientibus seu credentibus promissam similiter nouam requiem, à qua increduli excluderentur, prorsus eo modo, quo olim patres in deserto, qui voci auditæ credere noluerunt, sunt à requie temporali exclusi.
units.tr: And it is found, if the things not expressly stated are added together with those expressly stated, that more than four hundred years intervened between the times of Joshua and David. Therefore the Apostle rightly said after so long a time, and it is most clearly shown that the Holy Spirit, when he spoke through David, today if you hear his voice, by no means meant the voice of God which had been heard long before in the wilderness, but the voice which was to be heard again, namely in the gospel; and that to those who hear or believe, a new rest is similarly promised, from which unbelievers will be excluded, exactly in the way that the fathers in the wilderness, who refused to believe the voice that had been heard, were excluded from the temporal rest.

units.la: Sed ipse Apostolus hoc suis verbis adhuc declarat: Nam si eis Iesus requiem præstitisset, nequaquam de alio posthac die locutus fuisset. Perinde ac si dicat: Si hanc requiem, de qua spiritus S. hic loquitur, patres accepissent sub Iosua, nequaquam dixisset, de nouo aliquo die intelligens, hodie si uocem eius audieritis: sed potius dixisset: Si tunc audiuissent uocem Domini, &c. utita respiceret ad tempus, quod per tot sæcula antecesserat. Nominat autem filium Naue, quem alias uulgò Iosue, cuius nomine liber inscribitur, qui eius præclara facta, quomodo videlicet Mosi succedès introduxerit Israelitas in terram Canaan, & distribuerit illis regiones per tribus, continet. Sed rectissimè factum, quòd expresserit illud nomè: quàdoquidem sicut nomine, ita factis quoque Christi Iesu typum gessit. Ac iubemur audita voce Iesu, in Christum Iesum mentis aciem defigere, qui reuera unicus est & solus liberator, introducens nos in ueram requiem spiritualem, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur, & quam patres sub illo Iosue filio Naue consequi haud potuerunt. Atque ut istud per nos fieret, videlicet audita voce Iesu, respiceremus in nostrum Iesum Christum seruatorem, non dubium est, quin data opera Apostolus eam vocem ita expresserit.
units.tr: But the Apostle himself still makes this plain in his own words: For if Jesus had given them rest, he would not afterwards have spoken of another day. It is as if he said: If the fathers had received this rest, of which the Holy Spirit speaks here, under Joshua, he would never have spoken, meaning some new day, of today if you hear his voice; he would rather have said: If they had then heard the voice of the Lord, etc., so that it would refer to a time that had gone before through so many ages. He names the son of Nun, whom elsewhere we commonly call Joshua, in whose name the book is entitled, and which contains his outstanding deeds, namely how, succeeding Moses, he brought the Israelites into the land of Canaan and distributed the regions among the tribes. But it was most rightly done that he expressed that name, since, as by his name, so also by his deeds, he bore the type of Christ Jesus. And we are commanded, when the voice of Jesus is heard, to fix the eye of the mind on Christ Jesus, who is truly the only and sole liberator, leading us into the true spiritual rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks, and which the fathers could not attain under that Joshua, the son of Nun. And that this might be done by us, namely that when the voice of Jesus is heard we might look to our Jesus Christ the Saviour, there is no doubt that the Apostle expressed that voice in this way on purpose.

units.la: Itaque relinquitur sabbatismus populo Dei) Hæc ad conclusionem argumentationis pertinere supra diximus, tantundemque sit, velle, ac quod in ipsa propositione dictum est, quòd videlicet requies spiritualis, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur, pertineat ad credentes. Ita enim populum Dei honorifica appellatione, quæque omnes admonere posset ad ambulandum digne Deo, sic enim loquitur Apostolus Colossens. 1. & 1. Thessalon. 2. appellat credentes: quomodo alias quoque sæpius populus Dei, atque adeò peculiaris vocantur: 1. Petri 2. Vos autem (credentes alloquitur) genus electum, regale, sacerdotiū, gens sancta, populus, qui in lucrum accessit, ut virtutes prædicetis illius, qui è tenebris vos vocauit in admirabilem suam lucem. Et addit ex Osea secundo, Qui quondam non populus, nunc populus Dei: qui quondam non consecuti misericordiam, nunc estis misericordiam consecuti. Qua de re etiam Romanor. 9.
units.tr: Therefore there remains a sabbath rest for the people of God. We said above that this pertains to the conclusion of the argument, and it amounts to the same thing as what was said in the proposition itself, namely that the spiritual rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks belongs to believers.
