For he calls the people of God by an honourable title, one which can admonish all to walk worthily of God; thus the Apostle speaks in Colossians 1, and in 1 Thessalonians 2 he calls believers the people of God, as elsewhere also the people of God, and indeed a peculiar people, are often so called. 1 Peter 2: But you (he addresses believers) are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. And he adds from Hosea 2: Who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; who once had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy. Concerning this matter also see Romans 9.

units.la: Porrò sabbatismus significat simpliciter requiem, cùm Hebræis verbum שבת idem sit, quod quieuit, cessauit, quomodo & in testimonio illo Geneseos secundo supra citato dicitur de Deo שבת. Inde nomen שבתון Exod. 16. Item שבת. Leuitic. 23. & Esaiæ vltimo, quod quietem significat: & aliqui etiam hic requiem latinè reddiderunt.
units.tr: Moreover, sabbatismus simply means rest, since in Hebrew the verb שבת [shabath] is the same as "rested" or "ceased," as the Hebrew of the Genesis 2 testimony cited above also says of God, שבת [shabath]. Hence the noun שבתון [shabbaton] in Exod. 16, and שבת [shabbath] in Lev. 23 and at the end of Isaiah, which signify quiet. Some have also rendered it here in Latin as requies (rest).

units.la: Inde verò interpres græca diductione σαββατισμὸς Voluit autem formare nomen istud interpres à voce Hebræa & quodammodo ipsam Hebræam retinere potius, quàm dicere κατάπαυσιν, uti alias facit, singulari, ut apparet, quodam cōsilio: idque ideò, nì fallor, ut nomine Sabbatismi, quod alias satis notum & vsurpatum est sacris literis, tacitè admoneret omnes ad respiciendū in sabbata legalia, quæ, quoniam ita instituta fuerunt, ut, si nuda verba tantùm spectemus, ab omni opere externo & corporali cessaretur: sed si mysteriū spectare lubet,inueniemus,umbras hauddubiè fuisse spiritualis requiei, quà hic ad credentes dicitur pertinere.Id quod & ex Exodi vicesimo, & Colossensium secundo potest non obscurè demonstrari. Nam Exodi vicesimo hisce verbis iustituitur: Memento vt die Sabbathi sanctifices:sex diebus operaberis, & facies omnia opera tua. Septimo autem die Sabbathum Domini Dei tui est. Non facies omne opus in eo,tu & filius tuus,& filia tua,seruus tuus,& ancilla tua,iumentum tuum,& aduena, qui est intra parietes tuos. Sex enim diebus Deus fecit cœlum & terram,& mare,& omnia, quæ in eis sunt,& requieuit die septimo: idcirco benedixit Dominus Deus diei Sabbathi,& sanctificauit eum.
units.tr: The Greek interpreter formed the word by derivation as σαββατισμὸς [sabbatismos]. The interpreter chose to form this name from the Hebrew word and to keep the Hebrew in some sense, rather than to say κατάπαυσιν [katapausin], as he does elsewhere. He evidently did this by a deliberate plan, and I think it was so that, by the name Sabbatism, which is otherwise well known and used in Holy Scripture, he might tacitly remind everyone to look back to the legal sabbaths. Those were instituted so that, if we look only at the bare words, all external and bodily work should cease. But if we look at the mystery, we will find that those sabbaths were undoubtedly shadows of a spiritual rest, which here is said to pertain to believers. This can be shown clearly from Exodus 20 and from Colossians 2. For Exodus 20 lays it down in these words: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor the stranger that is within thy gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day, and hallowed it."

units.la: Hoc pacto institutum est Sabbathum illud externum: sed tamē multis modis docet hæc institutio,spiritualis requiei id fuisse vmbram,& id non vere obseruasse eos, quiin spiritualem requiem & res spirituales non erant intenti. Quid enim aliud sibi voluntil la verba,primò,quòd Sabbathum dicitur sanctificatum,nisi rebus sacris & spiritualibus id esse dicatum? Deinde,quòd vocatur Sabbathum Domini: quòd prohibetur omne opus externum,id est,corporale, carnale, (opponitur enim illud spiritualibus operibus)in eo fieri:quòd deinde proponitur consideranda requies ipsius Dei post conditū vniuersum mundum.
units.tr: This is how that external Sabbath was instituted. Yet this institution teaches in many ways that it was a shadow of spiritual rest, and that those who were not intent on spiritual rest and spiritual things did not truly keep it. For what else do these words mean? First, that the Sabbath is said to be sanctified, unless it is dedicated to sacred and spiritual things? Next, that it is called the Sabbath of the Lord; that every external work, that is, bodily and carnal work (for this is set against spiritual works), is forbidden on it; and then that the rest of God himself after the whole world was made is proposed for consideration.

units.la: Postremò,quòd iterum additur,Deum benedixisse & sanctificasse eum diem,nonne hæc omnia ad spirituale sabbathum,id est,requiem cœlestem,diuinam,æternam iubent respicere? Et quod de sabbatho dicitur,idem de omnibus aliis feriis iudicandum est,quę omnes in hoc institutae fuerunt,ut rebus diuinis vacaretur. Et propter hanc causam cum aliis legalibus obseruationibus, tū de sabbatho sic locutus est Apostolus, Colossensis: Ne quis vos iudicet in cibo aut potu,aut in parte diei festi, aut nouilunij, aut sabbathorum,quæ sunt vmbra rerum futurarum,corpus autem Christi. Vbi apostolus disertè pro nunciat res illas externas in lege institutas, umbram fuisse rerum futurarum, nempe spiritualium,& præcipuè post hanc vitam propter Christum expectandarum. Id quod Esaias etiam capite vltimo non obscurè testatus est,vbi cum plura dixisset de mittendis, qui vocarant oēs gentes ad agnitionē euangelij,tandē subijcit: sicut cœli noui & terra nova,quę ego facio stare coram me,dicit Dominus deus,sic stabit semen vestrum, & nomen vestrum, & erit mēsis ex mēse,& sabbathū ex sabbatho. Quib. verbis perpetuū, & spirituale sabbathum seu requiem signauit, & sabbatha externa seu corporalia designasse quietē interna,& spirituale postea sub euangelio per Christū accipiendā. Atq; hoc loco obitet lubet admonere, doctrinā nobis hic propositam, quo nostræ quoq; serię,quas oportet aliquas habere propter rudiores homines,& ut ordinatè omnia fiat in ecclesia, certisq; temporibus omnes conueniant ad audiendum verbum Dei, & discendum percipiendumque mysteria euangelij,nobis ita sunt obseruandæ, ut assiduè cogitemus in eis de rebus spiritualibus agendum,& eas adumbrare nobis hac requiem spiritualem, de qua spiritus Sanctus loquitur, quamq; ex euangelio discimus, nobis post hanc vitam apud Christum,& propter Christum expectandam.
units.tr: Finally, when it is added again that God blessed and sanctified that day, do not all these things bid us look to the spiritual Sabbath, that is, the heavenly, divine, and eternal rest? And what is said of the Sabbath must be judged to apply to all the other feast days, all of which were instituted for this purpose, that one should be free for divine things. For this reason the Apostle, in Colossians, speaks of the Sabbath together with the other legal observances in this way: "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ." Here the Apostle plainly declares that those external things instituted in the law were a shadow of things to come, namely spiritual things, to be expected especially after this life, on account of Christ. Isaiah also bore witness to this not obscurely in his last chapter, where, after saying many things about those who would be sent to call all nations to knowledge of the gospel, he finally adds: "For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith the LORD, so shall your seed and your name remain. And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me." In these words he marked a perpetual and spiritual sabbath or rest, and showed that the external or bodily sabbaths designated an inner quiet and spiritual rest to be received afterwards under the gospel through Christ. And here, while we are on the subject, I wish to remind you that the teaching set before us here, namely that our assemblies (which we must have for the sake of the rougher people, and so that all things may be done in order in the Church, and so that at fixed times everyone may come together to hear the Word of God and to learn and receive the mysteries of the gospel) are to be observed by us in such a way that we constantly think that spiritual things are to be done in them, and that they shadow for us that spiritual rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks, and which we learn from the gospel, to be expected by us after this life with and on account of Christ.

units.la: Cæterum constat ex his, quæ hactenus de requie congesimus, de duplici requie,in hac disputatione actum esse. Corporali videlicet, quæ utcunque contigit patribus in terra Canaan,sub duce Iosua:& spirituali,de qua spiritus Sanctus locutus est in testimonio supra citato:quę expectanda erat, & primum accipienda sub euangelio à credentibus,quàm quia Deus suam vocat,iudicare conuenit parem illi requiei, qua Deus ipse dicitur Genesēos secundo requieuisse.
units.tr: Moreover, it is clear from what we have so far gathered about rest that in this discussion there has been treatment of a twofold rest: bodily, namely that which the fathers in the land of Canaan somehow obtained under the leader Joshua; and spiritual, of which the Holy Spirit spoke in the testimony cited above, which was to be expected and first received under the gospel by believers. Since God calls it his own rest, it is fitting to judge that it is like that rest in which God himself is said in Genesis 2 to have rested.

units.la: De requie autem Sabbathi nulla fit mentio, nisi quòd interpres, qui epistolam hanc ex Hebræa in græcam transmutauit,videtur tacitè & obliquè voluisse animis eam suggerere,vocabulum sabbatismi ex hebræo retinendo. Quod ideò uisum est adnotare, propterea quòd videā,omnes fere, & quidē secutos Chrysostomū, distinguere triplicē requiem. Vnam sabbathi,qua Deus requieuit ab operibus suis : secundam in Palestina, quam ingressi sunt Iudæi: tertiam, quæ est reuera requies , hoc est , regnum cœlorum.
units.tr: But there is no mention of the rest of the Sabbath, except that the interpreter who translated this epistle from Hebrew into Greek seems tacitly and obliquely to have wanted to suggest it to our minds by retaining the word sabbatismos from the Hebrew. I thought this worth noting, because I see that almost all, and indeed those who follow Chrysostom, distinguish a threefold rest: one of the Sabbath, in which God rested from his works; a second in Palestine, which the Jews entered; and a third, which is truly rest, that is, the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Ac de prima quidem non loqui hic spiritum Sanctum,neque item de secunda:sed tam tum de tertia. Sed non bene mihi videtur factum, quod tertia hæc requies ita distingue-tur à prima,& dicatur,spiritum Sanctum non loqui de prima,cùm,ut supra ostendimus, Apostolus declarare volens, quòd postrema requies, de qua loquitur spiritus Sanctus, eadem sit cum illla,quia utraque requies Dei appellatur:& illa, videlicet de qua Genesēos secundo,& ista,in quam introducendi sunt credentes. Id quod & verbis Apostoli sequentibus demonstratur.Ita enim addit:
units.tr: Now, the Holy Spirit does not speak here of the first, nor likewise of the second, but only of the third. But it does not seem to me rightly done that this third rest is so distinguished from the first, and that it is said that the Holy Spirit does not speak of the first. For, as we showed above, the Apostle, wishing to declare that the final rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks is the same as that one, since both are called God's rest, namely that of Genesis 2 and that into which believers are to be brought. This is also shown by the words of the Apostle that follow. For he adds:

units.la: Nam qui ingressus est in requiem illius, & ipse requievit ab operibus suis, quemadmodum à suis Deus.
units.tr: For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.

units.la: En hic clarè subijcitur, quòd omnes credentes, qui ingredientur in requiem Dei, eodem modo quiescent, quo quiescit ipse Deus. Et cùm quies Dei alia, quàm spiritualis non possit intelligi, eademq; sit cœlestis & æterna, manifestum est, requiem, quæ propositâ est credentibus, spiritualem quoque esse, & cœlestem, & æternam. Quam requiem etiam promittit Matthæi vndecimo, vocans requiem, non corporum, sed animarum. Discite à me, inquit, quòd mitis sum, & humilis corde, & inuenietis requiem animabus vestris. Item in parabola Matthæi vicesimo quinto, Euge serue bone & fidelis, super pauca fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam, intra in gaudium Domini tui. Item describit eam typo rerum externarum Lucæ vicesimo secundo: Et ego dispono vobis, sicut disposuit mihi pater meus regnum, vt edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo, & sedeatis super thronos, iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel. Item Apocal.14. Audiui vocem de cœlo dicentem mihi, scribe: Beati qui in Domino moriuntur amodò: Etiam dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant à laboribus suis. In summa, si quis possit mente concipere, qualis, quàm beata & præclara sit requies Dei, idem possit intelligere, qualis sit requies credentibus propositâ. Vnde habet magnam emphasin hic pronomen relatiuum αὐτῆς, illius seu ipsius. Vtitur & verbis præteriti temporis, dicens: qui ingressus est, requiescit: eadem de causa ob quam dixit in propositione huius argumentationis, introimus in requiem nos qui credidimus, &c. Annotandum & illud, quòd cùm dicitur, credentes quiescere à operibus, intelligendum de molestijs & periculis, quibus, quamdiu in hoc mundo agunt, semper sunt expositi, tunc autem ab illis prorsus erunt immunes: Non quòd tum quoque erunt quasi otiosæ statuæ, sed rursus quoque operabuntur, (sicut & Deus operatus est etiam post illos sex dies) nimirum in laudibus Dei perpetuò occupati: sicut Apocalyps.7. describuntur magna voce clamantes: Salus ei, qui sedet super thronum Dei nostri, & agno. Et capite quinto, & aliis locis plura eiusmodi traduntur. Sed hæc puto ad præsentis argumentationis explicationem esse satis.
units.tr: Here it is plainly stated that all believers who enter into God's rest will rest in the same way as God himself rests. Since God's rest cannot be understood as anything other than spiritual, and is also heavenly and eternal, it is clear that the rest offered to believers is likewise spiritual, heavenly and eternal. Matthew 11 also promises this rest, which it calls the rest not of bodies but of souls: "Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and ye shall find rest unto your souls." Likewise in the parable of Matthew 25: "Well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things; enter thou into the joy of thy lord." Luke 22 also describes it by means of external things: "And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me, that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." So too Revelation 14: "I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth. Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours." In sum, whoever can conceive in his mind how rich, how blessed and how splendid God's rest is, can understand what rest is offered to believers. Hence the relative pronoun αὐτῆς [of that, of his own] carries great emphasis: "that is, of his own rest." He also uses the past tense, saying qui ingressus est, requiescit [he who has entered, rests], for the same reason that in the premise of this argument he said introimus in requiem nos qui credidimus [we who have believed do enter into rest], and so on. It should also be noted that when it is said that believers rest from their works, this is to be understood of the troubles and dangers to which they are always exposed as long as they live in this world, and from which they will then be wholly free. This does not mean that they will then be like idle statues, but rather that they will work again (as God too worked even after those six days), namely, constantly occupied in praising God, as Revelation 7 describes them crying out with a loud voice: "Salvation to him that sitteth upon the throne of our God, and unto the Lamb." Chapter 5 and other places also record many things of this kind. But I think these remarks are enough to explain the present argument.

units.la: Restat, vt nonnulla ad doctrinam pertinentia hinc colligamus. Primùm ergo cùm hic describatur talis requies propositâ credentibus, qualis est ipsius Dei, deceret nos ma gno spiritu ad contemplationem huius requiei accendi, & per omnem vitam hanc, quæ laboribus & miseriis innumeris semper inuoluitur, de requie illa cogitare, sic sarcinas nostras hic componere, sic negligere & contemnere præsentia terrena, tâquam si quotidie ad cœlestem illam requiem euocemur & gradum aliquem faciamus.
units.tr: It remains to draw from this some points that pertain to doctrine. First, since the rest offered to believers is here described as being of the same kind as God's own rest, we ought to be kindled with a great zeal to contemplate this rest, and throughout this life, which is always wrapped up in countless labours and miseries, to think of that rest; thus we should lay down our burdens here, and thus neglect and despise present earthly things, as if we were called every day to that heavenly rest and were taking a step towards it.

units.la: Sanè requies etiâ terrena & corporalis per se est multò dulcissima, & omnes naturaliter ad eâ aspirant, paratique sunt, quamlibet magnos labores subire spe requiei obtinendæ: quid igitur non decet nos aspirare, & omnia moliri, vt semel perueniamus ad requiem talem, qualis est ipsius Dei? Quòd si possemus vel animo concipere, quanta in se comprehendat illa requies, nos omnia pericula, omnia & bona & mala huius mundi contemneremus, quotiescunque vel cogitatio aliqua eius obreperet. Rectè Apostolus 1. Corinth. 2. de requiei illius amplitudine, Oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, & in cor hominis non ascenderunt, quæ Deus præparauit diligentibus se.
units.tr: Indeed, even earthly and bodily rest is in itself most sweet, and all men by nature aspire to it and are ready to undergo whatever great labours in hope of obtaining it. Why then should we not aspire, and strive by every means, to reach at last that rest which is God's own? If we could even grasp in mind how much that rest contains, we would despise all the dangers and all the goods and evils of this world, whenever any thought of it crept upon us. The Apostle rightly says of the vastness of that rest, in 1 Corinthians 2: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him."

units.la: Secundò, cùm Apostolus hic aperte vocem hodie ait, significare tempus reuelati euangelij, atque id verè & rectè: sic decet nos hanc interpretationem accipere, vt ad nostra quoque tempora, & ad nostras ecclesias concionem hanc accommodemus. Nam nostrum quoque tempus est hodie, & vox Domini quotidie adhuc auditur, Dominus quotidie per euangelium suum in toto orbe terrarum clamat & loquitur, maximeque nunc quando euangelij lux clarior, quàm multis antè seculis, resplenduit. Multis quidem temporibus, sicut Hieremias ait capite nono, deseruimus legem Dei, non audiuimus vocem eius, neque ambulauimus in ea, sed secuti sumus peruersam libidinem cordis nostri, & post Baalim, quos docuerunt nos patres nostri, iuimus: sed tandem placuit Domino Solem verbi sui mundo reddere, & vocem suam euangelicam denuò audiendam exhibere.
units.tr: Second, since the Apostle here expressly says "today" and means by the word the time of the revealed gospel, and this truly and rightly, so we ought to accept this interpretation and apply this sermon to our own times and our own congregations. For our time too is "today," and the voice of the Lord is still heard every day; the Lord every day cries out and speaks through his gospel throughout the whole world, and especially now, when the light of the gospel shines more clearly than in many earlier ages. In many times past, as Jeremiah says in chapter 9, we forsook the law of God, did not hearken to his voice, nor walked in it, but followed the wicked stubbornness of our own heart, and went after the Baals whom our fathers taught us. But at last the Lord was pleased to restore the sun of his word to the world, and to make his gospel voice to be heard again.

units.la: Tertiò, & hoc discimus, quòd, quoniam hic Iesus Naue significatur Christi typum gesisse, ita in legendis sacris versari deceat, vt vigilanter & attente omnia, quantum heri potest, ad Christum referamus, quomodo constat non hunc tantùm, sed alios quosque patres Isaac, Iacob, Iosephum, Mosen, Dauidem, aliosque Christi typum aliquo modo gesisse, & mysteria de rebus euangelicis & de Christo in lege repositia & latentia omni studio inuestigemus, & in hoc, quòd voluerit Deus patribus in figuris rerum corporalium adumbrare res spirituales, ipsius consilium admiremur, nec non oremus, vt nobis semper bis semper oculos aperiat, ut iugiter toto animo in bona spiritualia & cœlestia intendamus, & quæ nunc tantum velut in speculo & sub ænigmate intelligimus, postea reuera & plenissime percipiamus.
units.tr: Third, we learn also from this that, since Joshua the son of Nun is here said to have borne the type of Christ, we ought in reading the sacred books to act so that we refer all things, as far as we can, carefully and attentively, to Christ. Just as it is established that not only he but also other fathers, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David and others, in some way bore the type of Christ, so we should with all zeal search out the mysteries concerning gospel matters and Christ that are laid up and hidden in the law. In this we should admire God's purpose, that he willed to shadow spiritual things to the fathers in figures of bodily things; and we should pray that he would always open our eyes, that we may continually with our whole mind attend to spiritual and heavenly goods, and that what we now understand only as in a mirror and in a riddle, we may afterwards truly and fully perceive.

units.la: Studeamus igitur ingredi in illam requiem, ne quis eodem concidat incredulitatis exemplo. Viuus est enim sermo Dei, & efficax, et penetrantior quouis gladio vtrinq; incidente, & pertingens usq; ad diuisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumq; ac medullarum, & discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis, Nec est ulla creatura quæ non manifesta sit in conspectu illius, sed omnia nuda & resupinata oculis eius, ad quem nobis est sermo. •
units.tr: Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief. For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do. •

units.la: Satis fusè expositum est spiritus Sancti testimonium, clarissimeq; demonstratum, instituto id per omnia conuenire, ductis ex eo multis aptissimis argumentis. Iam, ut vniuersæ conclusioni huius primæ partis finem imponat, breuem subijcit adhortationem, qua monet, ne corda sua ad auditam vocem Domini in euangelio indurent, sed credendo studeant in illam, de qua dictum est, requiem spiritualem, & hoc tempore propositā ingredi. Nec desunt huic argumentationi atgumenta suasoria, quæ per ordinem indicabimus.
units.tr: The testimony of the Holy Spirit has been expounded at sufficient length and most clearly demonstrated, to show that it agrees in every respect with the purpose, and many most apt arguments have been drawn from it. Now, to bring to an end this whole conclusion of the first part, he adds a brief exhortation, in which he warns them not to harden their hearts when they hear the voice of the Lord in the gospel, but to strive by believing to enter into that spiritual rest of which he has spoken, which is now offered in this time. Nor are there lacking in this argument persuasive arguments, which we shall point out in order.

units.la: Studeamus igitur ingredi in illam requiem σπουδάζω, diligenter, cum labore & serió aliquid agO. Itaque ea voce monet, omnibus viribus caueant, ne in incredulitatem prolabantur, per quam à requie illa excluderentur. Notandum autem, huiusmodi exhortationes, quales passim in Scripturis sunt obuiæ, non ita accipiendas, quasi significaretur, in nostris positum esse viribus, quacunque voluerimus ratione, ad Deum tendere, fidem in nobis ipsis per nos promouere, confirmare, alere, conseruare: sed cùm acuunt quidem fidem, quæ est in credentibus, tum verò hoc præcipuè sibi volunt, quòd nimirum admonent, Deum, ut in nobis fidem confirmet, auxilium suum præbeat, implorare. Atq; huc pertinet, quòd, cùm multis locis huiusmodi exhortationes occurrunt, alijs tamen locis docetur, quomodo exhortationes in nobis perficiantur. Sic Actorum 13. Paulus & Barnabas apud Antiochiam exhortati sunt credentes, vt perseuerarent in gratia Dei. Sed, quamodo id posset fieri, tantum ope diuina, ipse alijs locis explicat: vt Ephes. 6. Quod super est, fratres mei, fitis fortes per Dominum, perque potentiam roboris illius. Sic in eadem epistola plura occurrunt in eandem sententiam: ut capite tertio, Peto ne deficiatis ob afflictiones meas. Sed mox addit: Huius rei gratia flecto genua mea ad patre Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ex quo omnis à communi patre cognatio in cœlis & in terra nominatur, ut det nobis iuxta diuitias gloriæ suæ, ut fortitudine corroboremini per spiritum suum. Deinde, capite quarto, Hortor itaque vos ego vinctus in Domino, ut ambuletis ita, ut dignum est vocatione, qua vocati estis. Sed paulò post ait, à Deo vocatos, Deum esse in omnibus, & vnicuique datam esse gratiam iuxta mensuram donationis Christi, &c.
units.tr: Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest [σπουδάζω], that is, to act diligently, with toil and seriousness. By this word he warns them to take care with all their strength that they do not slip into unbelief, through which they would be shut out from that rest. It should be noted, however, that exhortations of this kind, such as are found everywhere in the Scriptures, are not to be taken as meaning that it lies in our own power, by whatever means we like, to press towards God, to advance, confirm, nourish and preserve faith in ourselves by our own efforts. Rather, while they indeed stir up the faith that is in believers, their chief purpose is this: they remind us that we must implore God to confirm faith in us and to give his help. And to this belongs the fact that, although such exhortations occur in many places, in other places it is taught how the exhortations are carried out in us. Thus in Acts 13 Paul and Barnabas at Antioch exhorted the believers to continue in the grace of God. But how this could come about, he himself explains elsewhere, only by divine help: as in Ephesians 6, "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might." So in the same epistle many passages to the same effect occur: as in chapter 3, "I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations." But he immediately adds: "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named, that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit." Then in chapter 4: "I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called." But shortly after he says that they were called by God, that God is in all, and that grace is given to each one according to the measure of the gift of Christ, and so on.

units.la: Quibus verbis non obscurè docet, Dei tantum beneficijs posse omnia in nobis fieri. Item Coloss. 1. 1. Thessalon. 3. 2. Thessalon. 1. Denique in omnibus fere epistolis similes loci occurrunt docentes, quòd, ut studeamus bona facere, constanter in fide perseuerare non possimus, nisi opitulante Deo.
units.tr: By these words he teaches clearly that all things in us can be brought about by the benefits of God alone. Likewise Col. 1; 1 Thess. 3; 2 Thess. 1. Finally, in almost all the epistles, similar passages occur, teaching that we cannot strive to do good or persevere constantly in faith unless God helps us.

units.la: Itaque obseruandum est hoc in Scripturis, quòd quotiescunque exhortationes, vel præcepta obueniunt, fere semper subijcitur aliquid de ope, auxilio, vel de promissionibus Dei sine quo nos nihil possumus efficere: aut vbi non subijcitur expresse, tamen, ut per se notum debet subintelligi, & ex alijs locis colligi. Tametsi sunt pleræque omnes exhortationes eiusmodi ad habentes cognitionem verbi ac Dei, & aliquo modo credentes factæ qui aliquam spiritus Sancti in se acceperunt portiunculam, qua infirmitas ipsorum adiuuatur, confirmatur, & qui satis intelligunt, per se non posse quicquam boni sine ope diuina perfici. Quod ideò placuit admonere, ne quis ex præsenti adhortatiuncula aut similibus, putaret sibi argumentum petendum ad stabiliendam arbitrij ad spirituales res libertatem. Quodque dicimus de exhortationibus, idem de præceptis intelligi cõuenit: quæ quidè eatenus possunt per nos perfici, quatenus Dominus vires suppeditauerit: & fere semper præceptis sunt promissiones, de corroboradis nobis ad perficiendum ea, adiũctæ, aut certè sua gratuitate & difficultate vltrò compellunt nos ad opę diuinam adimpledam. Quò pertinet regula quinta, Tyconij apud Augustinum, qua docet distinguere inter legem & promissiones, siue, ut Augustinus mauult, inter mandata & gratiam: quia ita quidem mandata à Deo dantur, ut tamen non nisi per gratiam eius adimpleantur.
units.tr: Therefore this must be observed in the Scriptures: whenever exhortations or precepts occur, something about God's help, aid, or promises almost always follows, without which we can accomplish nothing. Where it is not expressly added, it must nevertheless be understood as self-evident and gathered from other passages. Yet nearly all such exhortations are addressed to those who have knowledge of the word and of God, and who believe in some way, and who have received some small portion of the Holy Spirit, by which their weakness is aided and strengthened, and who understand well enough that nothing good can be done by themselves without divine help. This is worth noting, lest anyone, from this little exhortation or similar ones, think that an argument is to be drawn for establishing free will in spiritual matters. What we say of exhortations should be understood equally of precepts: these can indeed be fulfilled by us only so far as the Lord supplies strength; and almost always promises are joined to the precepts, to strengthen us to perform them, or else their very gravity and difficulty compel us of their own accord to seek the divine help. To this pertains the fifth rule of Tyconius, reported by Augustine, which teaches us to distinguish between the law and the promises, or, as Augustine prefers, between the commandments and grace: for God gives commandments in such a way that they nonetheless cannot be fulfilled except through his grace.

units.la: In quam sententiam eleganter idem Augustinus ait in Echiridio ad Laurentiũ cap. 16. de gratia & libero arbitrio: iubet Deus, quæ non possumus, ut nouerimus quid ab ipso petere. pętere debeamus. Item homilia 29. in Ioannem, Magna est præceptorum vtilitas, si libero arbitrio tantùm detur, ut gratia Dei amplius honoretur. Item epistola vicesima quarta: Fides impetrat, quod lex imperat: imò ideò lex imperat, ut fides impetret, quod imperatum erat per legem: imò fidem ipsam exigit à nobis Deus, & non inuenit, quod exigat, nisi dederit, quod inueniat. Item, dat Deus, quod iubet, & iubeat, quod velit. Sed veror, ne hæc fortassis nimis multa. Tantundem enim significatur præsentibus verbis, sedulò cauendum, ne in incredulitatem incidant, sed orent Deum, vt ipsis det in fide constantiam, quo in requiem promissam admittantur. Cæterùm, quòd dicit, requiem, illam; magnam habet emphasin, iubetq; respicere præcedentia, quæ de dignitate requiei spiritualis dicta sunt.
units.tr: To this effect Augustine himself says elegantly in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 16, on grace and free will: God commands what we cannot do, so that we may know what we ought to ask of him. Likewise, in homily 29 on John: "The usefulness of the precepts is great, if they are given to free will only so that the grace of God may be honoured more." Likewise in epistle 24: "Faith obtains what the law commands; nay rather, the law commands so that faith may obtain what was commanded by the law; nay, God himself demands faith from us, and he does not find what he demands unless he has first given what he may find." Also: "God gives what he commands, and commands what he wills." But I fear these citations are perhaps too many. For the present words signify the same thing: we must take care lest they fall into unbelief, but let them pray God to give them constancy in faith, so that they may be admitted into the promised rest. Moreover, when he says "that rest," it has a great emphasis and bids us look back to what was said before about the dignity of spiritual rest.

units.la: Ne quis eodem concidat incredulitatis exemplo) Prima ratio à periculoso, siue ab exemplo patrum in deserto propter incredulitatem punitorum. Quam rationem supra pluribus verbis inculcatam ideò repetit, vultq; fixam inhærere Iudæorum pectoribus, quòd sciret ilos, vt admodum durae ceruicis homines, non alia magis ratione, quàm pœnarum atrocitate, & patrum exemplis commouendos. οἱ τῷ αὐτῷ ὑπο δείγματι: quasi dicat, in illo ipso exemplo siue signo, quod supra clarissimè est expositum, vbi concidisse patres in deserto docet, propter inobedientiam, siue propter incredulitatem. Nam ἀπειθεία & incredulitatem & inobedientiam significat, & pro vtroque in eadem sententia vsurpatur, vti su prà capite tertio ostendimus. Et cadere hic non tantùm significat temporalem mortem subire, qualis uisa est patrum: sed magis mortem spiritualem, quæ præcipuè metuenda est, quam simul subierunt illi patres. Nam etsi Deus puniat subinde in hac vita, ad salutem in vita altera, sicut ostenditur 1. Thessalon. 1. ne videlicet postea puniat seuerius, & Dominus quos diligit, corripit: tamen eos, qui cùm antea icti fuerint, multisque modis, tùm blanditijs, tum verberibus prouocati, non resipiscunt; Deus punit tandem & in hac vita, & in altera. Sic autem patres illi, sicut Deus ipse prædixerat & comminatus fuerat, morte mulctati fuerunt & in hac vita, & post hanc vitam: quando quidem in incredulitate morientes seipsos à requie spirituali excludebant. Cæterùm, multò grauius illi peccant, qui, cùm habuerint exempla præeuntia, tamen adhuc nō resipiscunt: id quod Christus quoque indicat Matth. 11. Væ tibi Chorazin, væ tibi Bethsaidan, &c.
units.tr: Lest anyone fall by the same example of unbelief. The first reason is drawn from the danger, or from the example of the fathers in the desert who were punished on account of unbelief. He repeats this reason, which he had pressed above with many words, and wishes it to stick fast in the hearts of the Jews, because he knew that they, as men of very stiff neck, were to be moved by nothing more than by the severity of punishments and the examples of the fathers. [ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ὑποδείγματι]: as if he said, in that very example or sign, which was set out most clearly above, where he teaches that the fathers fell in the desert on account of disobedience, or on account of unbelief. For [ἀπειθεία] signifies both unbelief and disobedience, and is used in the same sense for both, as we showed above in chapter 3. And "to fall" here means not merely to undergo temporal death, such as the fathers suffered, but rather spiritual death, which is especially to be feared, and which those fathers underwent at the same time. For although God sometimes punishes in this life, for salvation in the life to come, as is shown in 1 Thess. 1, lest he afterwards punish more severely, and "the Lord chastens those whom he loves," nevertheless those who, though previously struck and provoked in many ways, both by flatteries and by blows, do not repent, God at last punishes both in this life and in the other. And so those fathers, just as God himself had foretold and threatened, were punished with death both in this life and after this life, since, dying in unbelief, they were shutting themselves out from spiritual rest. Moreover, those sin much more gravely who, though they have preceding examples, still do not repent; which Christ also indicates in Matt. 11: "Woe to you, Chorazin! woe to you, Bethsaida!" and so on.

units.la: Viuus est enim sermo Dei, & efficax, & penetrantior quouis gladio vtrinq; incidente, ac pertingens vsq; ad diuisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumq;, & medullarum, & discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis.
units.tr: For the word of God is living, and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

units.la: Secunda ratio à dignitate; & necessario adimplendis effectibus verbi Dei, inprimis testimonij spiritus Sancti supra citati, quod grauissimam continet, aduersus eos, qui audita extremis hisce diebus voci Dei in euangelio recusant credere, comminationem; nempe, quòd à requie spirituali & cœlesti sint excludendi. Itaque hoc verbum Dei, siue hoc testimonium spiritus Sancti non esse ab ipsis contemnendum, sed maximè debere eos toto animo per illud commoueri; cùm in genere omnis verbi Dei amplissima sit dignitas atq; efficacia. Atq; hæc ratio plurimum ponderis hic habere debet, valdeque prudenti consilio est adhibita: Iudæi namque mirum in modum gloriabantur verbo Dei, lege, oraculis, prophetis, atque omnia contemnebant quæ hinc non erant petita; neque alijs modis, quàm verbo Dei, cuius haberi volebant obseruantissimi, videbantur reuincendi. Quando ergo citauit verbum Dei, & quidem ex ipsis sacris psalmis, quo clarissimè ostenditur, ipsos debere voci Dei denuò auditæ in euangelio credere, &, nî audiant, à requie spirituali excludendos, peraptè hanc rationem de dignitate & efficacia verbi Dei subijcit, qua eos acriter commoueat, & quodammodo inuitos ad credendum verbi impellat. Ita verò hæc adiuncta sunt præcedenti rationi, vt aliquo modo confirmare eam videantur. Periculum enim omnibus, qui non credunt, metuendum, ex eo intelligitur, quòd verbo ipsius Dei proditum sit, eos, qui non credunt, à requie spirituali excludendos.
units.tr: The second reason is drawn from the dignity and the necessarily fulfilled effects of the word of God, especially from the testimony of the Holy Spirit cited above, which contains a most grave threat against those who, having heard the voice of God in the gospel in these last days, refuse to believe: namely, that they are to be shut out from spiritual and heavenly rest. Therefore this word of God, or this testimony of the Holy Spirit, is not to be despised by them, but they ought most of all to be moved by it with their whole heart; since in general every word of God has the greatest dignity and efficacy. And this reason ought to carry great weight here, and it has been introduced with very prudent counsel: for the Jews boasted in a remarkable way of the word of God, the law, the oracles, the prophets, and they despised everything that was not drawn from these; nor could they be refuted by any means other than the word of God, of which they wished to be considered most observant. Therefore, since he cites the word of God, and indeed from the very Psalms, by which it is most clearly shown that they ought to believe the voice of God heard again in the gospel, and, unless they hear, that they are to be excluded from spiritual rest, he aptly subjoins this reason, drawn from the dignity and efficacy of the word of God, by which he may sharply move them and, in some measure, drive them, unwilling as they are, to believe the word. Indeed these things are so joined to the preceding reason that they seem in some way to confirm it. For the danger to be feared by all who do not believe is understood from this: that it has been declared by the very word of God that those who do not believe are to be excluded from spiritual rest.

units.la: Cæterùm, valde eleganter describitur hic verbi Dei præstantia & efficacia: ac dignissimus est hic locus, qui summa diligentia discutiatur, cùm vix similis in libris sacris occurrat: quod & eò nunc faciemus iustius ac lubentius, ne postea feorsim hic locus debeat topiosius à nobis pertractari.
units.tr: Moreover, the excellence and efficacy of the word of God are described here most elegantly; and this passage is most worthy to be examined with the greatest diligence, since hardly any like it occurs in the sacred books. We shall do this now more fittingly and more willingly, so that afterwards this passage need not be treated by us separately and at greater length.

units.la: Viuus est enim sermo Dei: ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος θεοῦ τε θεῖ.) Emphasin aliquam habet græcus articulus ὁ. Item vocabulum Dei, magna quoque emphasi sonandum est, sicut alias, quotiescunq; pronunciatum principis, vel magna autoritate prædicti viri adsertur in medium, omnes statim audita appellatione insignis personæ suspensi tacent, & tectum habent; quod dicitur;
units.tr: "For the word of God is living": [ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ]. The Greek article [ὁ] has a certain emphasis. Likewise the word "God" is to be pronounced with great emphasis, as at other times, whenever a prince or a man endowed with great authority is named in the midst, all at once, on hearing the name of such a distinguished person, fall silent and hold their peace; so that it is said...

units.la: Vocatur autem sermo Dei ante omnia uiuus, quòd ex eo, quomodo uita nostra eterna sit instituenda, addiscamus: unde illud psalmi 118. In quo corrigit adolescentior viam suam in custodiendo sermones tuos. Et sic reuera est, nihil ad bene pieq; viuendum poss et exigi, quod in sacro verbo Dei non sit clarissimè propositum. Aliter verbum Dei viuum dicitur, quòd per illud vitam spiritualem animae nostrae accipiant. Unde illud Matthaei 4. Non in solo pane viuit homo, sed in omni verbo, quod procedit ex ore Dei. Luc. 11. Beati, qui audiunt verbum Dei, & custodiunt illud. Petrus ad Christum Ioan. 6. Domine, verba vitae aeternae habes. Et Luc. 10. Legisperitus interrogabat, quid faciendo vitam aeternam possidebo? Et Christus ad eum, In lege quid scriptum est? quomodo legis? Ille respondit, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex totis viribus tuis, & ex tota mente tua, & proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Dixitque illi, Recte respondisti, hoc fac, & vives.
units.tr: The word of God is called living above all because from it we learn how our eternal life is to be arranged; whence that verse of Psalm 118 (119): "Wherewith shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed to thy words." And indeed it is so: nothing can be required for living well and piously that is not set out most clearly in the sacred word of God. In another sense the word of God is called living because through it our souls receive spiritual life. Whence Matt. 4: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God." Luke 11: "Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it." Peter to Christ, John 6: "Lord, thou hast the words of eternal life." And Luke 10: a lawyer asked, "What shall I do to inherit eternal life?" And Christ said to him, "What is written in the law? How do you read it?" He answered, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbour as yourself." And he said to him, "You have answered rightly; do this, and you shall live."

units.la: Sed magis placet, verbum Dei dici viuum, praesertim hoc loco, à singulari potestate agendi. Nam agere quicquam non dicitur, nisi quatenus viuum est, qua ratione etiam aliàs verbum Dei vocatur Spiritus, quia nimirum spiritu seu anima viuitur. Unde Ioan. 6. Spiritus est, qui viuificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Verba, quae ego loquor vobis, spiritus & vita sunt. Ita enim spiritualis quaedam vis agendi verbo inesse significatur: unde & per interpretationem videtur adiectum, quòd sit etiā efficax, ἐνεργὴς. ἐνεργέα significat efficaciam, & quidem valde euidentem & potentem, ut necessario actiones proueniant & percipiantur: quo pacto etiam fides Galat. 5. vocatur per dilectionem ἐνεργουμένη, id est, efficax siue operans. Hieronymus videtur legisse ἐνεργὴς, quia alibi vertit hic euidens; sed aptius est ἐνεργὴς. Sic autem verbum Dei semper habet suos effectus, nunquam otiosum est, vel sterile, necessario producit ingentes fructus. Unde aliàs solo verbo suo Deus omnia dicitur facere, nihilque ille loquitur, quod non adimpletur. psalmo 32. Ipse dixit, & facta sunt, ipse mandauit, & creata sunt. Esaiae 55. Verbum quod egredietur de ore meo, non reuertetur ad me vacuum, sed faciet quodcunq; uolui. Necessario semper sequuntur effectus uerbi. Tantum dic verbo, inquit, Lucae 7. Centurio ad Christum, & sanabitur puer meus.
units.tr: But it pleases me more to call the word of God "living," especially in this passage, because of its singular power of acting. For nothing is said to act except insofar as it is alive. For this reason the word of God is also elsewhere called spirit, because it is of course quickened by spirit or life. Hence John 6: "It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit and life." In this way a certain spiritual power of acting is signified to be in the word. Whence also, through the interpretation, it seems to have been added that it is also effective, ἐνεργὴς [energēs]. ἐνέργεια [energeia] signifies efficacy, and indeed a very evident and powerful efficacy, so that actions necessarily arise and are perceived. In the same way faith in Galatians 5 is called ἐνεργουμένη [energoumenē] through love, that is, effective or operative. Jerome seems to have read ἐνεργὴς, since elsewhere he renders it "evident," but ἐνεργὴς is the more apt reading. Thus the word of God always has its effects; it is never idle or barren, but necessarily produces great fruits. Hence elsewhere God is said to do all things by his word alone, and he speaks nothing that is not fulfilled. Psalm 32: "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created." Isaiah 55: "The word that goes out of my mouth shall not return to me empty, but shall do what I please." The effects of the word always necessarily follow. "Only say the word," says Luke 7, the centurion to Christ, "and my servant will be healed."

units.la: Cùm itaque tanta vis sit & efficacia verbi, intelligi hinc potest, quàm grauis sit haec ratio, quantumque ponderis habere debeat in praesentiloco. Si verbum Dei habuit olim suos effectus in patribus, & omnes propter incredulitatem ceciderunt miserè in desertò, fieri non potest, quin etiam nunc suos effectus verbum Dei sortiatur, & à requie spirituali, quotquot non credunt, excludantur. Atq; ob hanc causam ait, sermonem Dei semper viuum esse & efficacem. Et possemus quidem, nec non posceret etiam locus, ut pluribus de effectibus seu efficacia Dei ageremus: verum, quia ipse eâ clarissimè adhuc describit, nos supersedebimus. Addit ergo:
units.tr: Since such is the power and efficacy of the word, it can be understood from this how weighty this argument is and how much weight it ought to carry in the present passage. If the word of God once had its effects on the fathers, and all of them, on account of unbelief, miserably fell in the desert, it cannot be that the word of God does not still obtain its effects now, and that all who do not believe are excluded from spiritual rest. For this reason he says that the word of God is always living and effective. We could indeed discuss at greater length the effects or efficacy of God's word, and the passage itself would call for it; but since he describes it most clearly here, we shall forbear. He therefore adds:

units.la: Et penetrantior quouis gladio vtrinq; incidente, ac pertingens vsq; ad diuisionem animae simul ac spiritus, compagumq; & medullarum.
units.tr: And sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow.

units.la: Satis quidem fuisset, dixisse, sermonem Dei viuum esse & efficacem, cōstitisseq; plena ratio: sed siue quia verbum Dei nunquam satis potest praedicari, siue quia iudicauit cōuenire, ut eius authoritate magis ipsorum conscientias permoueret, adiecit illustrem effi-caciae verbi Dei descriptionem, in qua non omnes quidem, sed tantum praecipuos maximeque admirandos effectus eius indicat, dum nimirum comparat illud gladio, insinuans, quòd, quemadmodum gladius mirabiliter agit & concutit intima corporis: ita multò mirabilius verbum agit, penetratque in animas. Quae ratio ad pungendum omnium animos, & ita commouendum, tanquam si se gladio feriri persentiscerent, est apositissima. Primò ergo ait, quòd sermo Dei sit penetrantior quouis gladio, utrinq; incidente. Quod verbum Dei aptè coparetur gladio, non est à Scriptura alienum. Nam & Esaias capite 49. ita loquitur: Audite insulae, & attendite populi de longè. Dominus ab utero vocauit me, de ventre matris meae recordatus est nominis mei, & posuit os meum tanquam gladium acutum. Vbi de uerbo Dei, quod ipse suo ore enunciare debebat, ita loquitur.
units.tr: It would have been enough to say that the word of God is living and effective, and the argument would have been complete. But whether because the word of God can never be praised enough, or because he judged it fitting that by its authority it should more strongly move their consciences, he added a vivid description of the efficacy of the word of God. In it he indicates not all of its effects, but only the chief and most admirable ones, comparing it to a sword. He suggests that, just as a sword works wonderfully and shakes the inner parts of the body, so the word works far more wonderfully and penetrates into souls. This comparison is most apt for pricking the minds of all and so stirring them, as if they felt themselves struck by a sword. First, then, he says that the word of God is sharper than any two-edged sword. That the word of God is fittingly compared to a sword is not foreign to Scripture. For Isaiah in chapter 49 also speaks thus: "Listen, O islands, and attend, O peoples from afar. The Lord called me from the womb, from my mother's belly he remembered my name, and he made my mouth like a sharp sword." There he speaks of the word of God, which he was to utter with his own mouth.

units.la: Ac verosimile est Apostolum eò respexisse. Et certè cùm idem sit usus verbi, qui est gladij, aptissima est comparatio. Sicut enim gladio nos defendimus contra hostiles insultus: & gladio hostem prosternimus: ita in spirituali certamine verbum Dei vice gladij est, & ad prosternendum hostem conducit. Unde Ephesiorum sexto: Verbum Dei gladius spiritus seu spiritualis appellatur, quo possimus nos aduersus spirituales nequitias defendere.
units.tr: And it is likely that the Apostle had this in mind. Since the use of the word is the same as that of a sword, the comparison is most apt. For just as we defend ourselves with a sword against hostile assaults, and with a sword strike down an enemy, so in spiritual combat the word of God takes the place of the sword and serves to overthrow the enemy. Hence in Ephesians 6 the word of God is called the sword of the Spirit, or spiritual sword, by which we can defend ourselves against spiritual wickedness.

units.la: Item Ité Esaiæ vndecimo: Et secunda Thessal. secundo. Antichristus describitur spiritu oris Domini, id est, verbo Dei, tanquā gladio conficiendus. Sicut & Christus eodē gladio verbi Sathanam superauit: vt nos discerem us & consideremus eodem gladio eundem demuincere. Augustinus libro de Ciuitate Dei vigesimo capite vigesimoprimo, Rectè ergo verbum Dei gladio comparatur. Sed quo euidentius vim verbi admirādam exprimeret, ait, id simile esse gladio utrinq; incidenti. Hoc enim ἀμφηκες significat, quasi dicatur, duo habens ora. In Scripturis enim acies gladij vocatur στόμα, os, quòd hac parte mordeat: quomodo etiam Luc. 22. dicitur, ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ῤομφαία: vbi Erasmus reddidit: & cadent acie gladij: vetus interpres, & cadent in ore gladij. Hieronymus autem vertere solet, bicipiti, alij ancipiti: similiter vero appellatur verbum Dei Apocal. 1. Ex ore eius ῥομφαία ἀμφήκης, id est, gladius vtraque parte acutus exibat. Item Apocal. 19. De homine insidente equo albo, vocato fideli, veraci, cuiusq; nomen erat sermo Dei, de quo mox subijcitur: Et ex ore eius procedit gladius ex vtraq; parte acutus, vt eo percutiat gentes, & ipse reget eas in virga ferrea. (Quamuis hic græcè non habetur ἀμφήκης, sed tantùm ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα) Quemadmodum igitur gladius admodum acutam habens aciem, & vtrinq; incidens, facilime quòuis penetrat: Ita verbum mirabiliter & nullo negotio penetrat conscientias audientium. Imò, inquit, est multò penetrantior. Neque enim ita confert verbum gladio, quasi res essent prorsus æquales: sed sumit gladium in exemplum, pro re, quæ maximam habet penetrandi vim: Deinde colligit, verbum Dei multò tamen maiorem habere penetrandi facultatem, eoque vtitur comparatiuo. Proinde licet ex hac prima comparationis huius particula statim animaduertere, valde mirabilem esse verbi Dei vim. Quàm grauiter ictu gladij profundè & violeter iniecti concutiantur, & comoueantur corpora nemo est qui nesciat, præsertim cui vnquam in vita vulnus inflictum fuerit. Quosdam videas ita commoueri, vt etiamsi non eo loco, quo mors inferri posset, vulnerentur, tamen protinus toto corpore expalleant, contremiscant, & tandem velut exanimes concidant.
units.tr: Likewise in Isaiah 11, and in 2 Thessalonians 2, Antichrist is described as to be destroyed by the breath of the Lord's mouth, that is, by the word of God, as by a sword. Christ also overcame Satan with this same sword of the word, so that we might learn to subdue the same enemy with the same sword. Augustine, in the twenty-first chapter of the twentieth book of The City of God, says: "Rightly, then, the word of God is compared to a sword." But in order to express more clearly the admirable power of the word, he says that it is like a sword two-edged. For this signifies ἀμφηκες [amphēkes], as if it were said to have two mouths. In the Scriptures the edge of a sword is called στόμα [stoma], mouth, because it bites on that side. So also Luke 22 says ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ῤομφαία [ek tou stomatos rhomphaia], where Erasmus renders "and they will fall by the edge of the sword"; the old interpreter, "and they will fall by the mouth of the sword." Jerome, however, usually renders it "two-edged," others "double-edged." Similarly the word of God is called in Revelation 1 ῥομφαία ἀμφήκης [rhomphaia amphēkēs], that is, a sword sharp on both sides, issuing from his mouth. Likewise in Revelation 19, concerning the man sitting on a white horse, called Faithful and True, whose name was the Word of God, it is then added: "And from his mouth proceeds a sharp sword on both sides, so that with it he may strike the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod." (Although here in the Greek the word ἀμφήκης is not found, but only ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα [rhomphaia oxeia].) Just as a sword with a very sharp edge, cutting on both sides, penetrates anything with the greatest ease, so the word wonderfully and without difficulty penetrates the consciences of hearers. Indeed, he says, it is much more penetrating. For he does not compare the word to the sword as if the two were wholly equal, but takes the sword as an example, a thing that has the greatest power of penetrating. Then he concludes that the word of God nonetheless has a much greater faculty of penetrating, and he uses the comparative for this. Therefore, from this first part of the comparison one may at once perceive that the power of the word of God is very admirable. Nobody is there who does not know how gravely bodies are shaken and stirred by a blow from a sword driven deep and violently, especially one who has ever received a wound in life. You may see some so moved that, even when they are wounded in a place where death could not be inflicted, they immediately turn pale over their whole body, tremble, and at last collapse as if lifeless.

units.la: Vnde & plerunque, vbi quis gladium bene acutum in se strictum semel consp exerit, statim toto horret corpore, & quiduis potius acturus est, quàm ictum excepturus, omnia denique tentat, quo aciem stricti gladij euadat. Si ergo tanta tamque formidabilis vis gladij agnoscitur, qualem quæso existimabimus vim verbi Dei, quod quidem agit eo vehementius, quòd agit in partem nostri preciosiorem, nempe animam? Sicut corpora mouentur gladio materiali, ita animæ seu conscientiæ permouentur ad auditum verbi Dei. Sed tanta hæc vis verbi plenius declaratur verbis sequentibus.
units.tr: Hence also, generally, when someone has drawn a very sharp sword against himself, he at once shudders over his whole body, would rather do anything than receive the blow, and at last tries every means to escape the edge of the drawn sword. If, then, such and so formidable a power is recognized in a sword, what power, I ask, shall we think the word of God has, which acts all the more vehemently because it acts upon the more precious part of us, namely the soul? As bodies are moved by a material sword, so souls or consciences are moved at the hearing of the word of God. But this great power of the word is more fully declared in the words that follow.

units.la: Ac pertingens vsq; ad diuisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumq; & medullarum.
units.tr: And piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow.

units.la: Hoc est, verbum Dei adeò est efficax, vt totum hominem, quantus quantus est, maximè permoueat & impellat, nec non animam, mentem, omnesque vires, & conscientiam grauissimè concutiat. Aliquid obscuritatis pārere videtur ista hominis in partes principales diuisio.
units.tr: That is, the Word of God is so effective that it powerfully moves and drives the whole man, however great he is, and strongly shakes his soul, mind, all his powers, and his conscience. This division of man into his principal parts seems to bring some obscurity.

units.la: Proinde, quid intelligendum per animam & spiritum, breuiter explicandum. Animam vocant eam facultatem, qua corpus ipsum viuit, sustentatur, mouetur, & quæ per membra diffunditur, suasque vires passim exerit, qua separata, corpus vita & motu carer, iamque emortuum & exanime appellatur. (Aliqui animam & spiritum non discernunt, & simpliciter facultatem viuendi appellant, quòd viuere quispiam dicitur, quamdiu adest ei anima, & quamdiu inest aliquis spiritus seu facultas spirandi: Sed Scriptura aliquid altius considerat in his vocibus.
units.tr: Therefore, what is to be understood by soul and spirit must be briefly explained. They call "soul" that faculty by which the body itself lives, is sustained and moves, which is spread through the limbs and puts forth its powers everywhere, and when it is separated from the body, the body lacks life and motion and is then called dead and lifeless. (Some do not distinguish soul and spirit, and simply call it the faculty of living, because a person is said to live as long as the soul is in him, and as long as some spirit or faculty of breathing is within him. But Scripture considers something higher in these words.)

units.la: Spiritum verò definiunt mentem humanam, nempe intellectum & voluntatem. Ita vt animam quidem statuant nobis conuenire cum brutis, spiritum verò cum substantijs spiritualibus. Gregorius Nissenus, referente Theophylacto in illud 1. Thess. 5. Et integer vester spiritus, & anima, & corpus, in aduētu Domini nostri Iesu Christi seruetur: partitionem hanc exponit, dicens: hominem ex omni specie potentiarum animæ compositum: namin eo esse intellectiuam potentiā, quæ propria hominis est: & sensitiuam, quam communē habet: cum brutis & vegetatiuam, quę inest plātis. Itaq; ibi per Spiritū intelligi debere potētiam animę intellectiuam: per corpus, potentiā vegetatiuā: per animam potentiam sensitiuam. Quod certè vt ab eo, qui versatus multum in philosophia, satis aptè. Grypeus ψυχή est, qua viuitur, nobis etiam cum bestijs cōmunis: animus discipline capax est, quiq; docetur: sic ergo solet distinguere, & spiritū eum posuerunt, quem animū vocant. Sed quia huiusmodi partitiones hominis videmus alijs quoq; locis in Scripturis obuias, conueniet paulò aliter explicare. Sic autē Apostolus 1. Thess. 5. ait: Ipse autem Deus pacis sanctificet vos totos: & integer vester spiritus & anima & corpus, ita vt in nullo possitis culpari,
units.tr: They define "spirit" as the human mind, namely the understanding and the will. So they hold that the soul is what we have in common with the brutes, but the spirit is what we have in common with spiritual substances. Gregory of Nyssa, as Theophylact reports, on the text 1 Thess. 5, "And may your whole spirit, and soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ," explains this division, saying that man is composed of every kind of power of the soul: for in him there is the intellectual power, which is proper to man; and the sensitive power, which he has in common with the brutes; and the vegetative power, which is in plants. Therefore, he says, the spirit there should be understood as the intellectual power of the soul, the body as the vegetative power, and the soul as the sensitive power. This is said rather aptly, as one would expect from a man well versed in philosophy. The soul [ψυχή] is that by which one lives, which we share even with beasts; the mind is capable of discipline and is taught. So he is accustomed to distinguish in this way, and they posited as spirit what they call mind. But since we see such divisions of man in other places of Scripture as well, it will be fitting to explain the matter somewhat differently. Thus the Apostle says in 1 Thess. 5: "May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly; and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless, so that you may not be found at fault, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." Likewise Luke 1: "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour."

units.la: Vis verbi Dei admirabilis. Collatio gladij & verbi. Anima quid? Augustinus de anima & spiritu lib. 4. ad Vincentium Victorem. Spiritus quid? Pontentæ animæ. culpari, in aduentu Domini Iesu Christi seruetur. Item Lucae primo, Magnificat anima mea Dominum, & exultauit spiritus meus in Deo seruatore meo. His ergo & similibus locis consideratis, corpus quidem seorsum statuunt partem hominis abiectissimam, quae instrumentum tantum est, & quasi theca animae & spiritus, quod alias quoque mundum seruari praecipitur, vt Romanorum duodecimo: Obsecro igitur vos fratres per miserationes Dei, vt praebeatis corpora vestra hostiam viuentem, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem cultum vestrum. Item prima Corinthiorum sexto, Omnepeccatum quodcunque fecerit homo, extra corpus est: Sed, qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat. An nescitis, quod corpus vestrum templum est habitantis in vobis spiritus Sancti, quem habetis a Deo? Item prima Corinthiorum nono, Subijcio corpus meum, & in seruitutem redigo, ne quo modo fiat, vt cum aliis praedicarim, ipse reprobus efficiar.
units.tr: The admirable power of God's Word. Comparison of sword and word. What is the soul? Augustine, On the Soul and Its Origin, book 4, to Vincentius Victor. What is the spirit? The powers of the soul. Blameless. At the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise Luke 1: "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour." In light of these and similar passages, they set apart the body as the lowliest part of man, which is only an instrument and, as it were, the case of soul and spirit; this is also commanded to be kept pure in other places, as in Romans 12: "I beseech you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service." Likewise 1 Cor. 6: "Every sin that a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body. Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, whom you have from God?" Likewise 1 Cor. 9: "I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest by any means, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified."

units.la: Iam animam definiunt eam partem hominis, qua corpus inprimis vegetatur, sentit, mouetur, sicut bruta: qua item supra conditionem brutorum intelligit, & vult, eaque persuestigat, quae naturae suae maxime conueniunt, & ad quae ratio seu intellectus suis viribus potest progredi. In hac omnes affectus tam bonos, quam malos, puta amorem, odium, spem, metum, & quicquid est huiusmodi, collocant tanquam in proprio domicilio.
units.tr: Now they define the soul as that part of man by which the body is chiefly vegetated, feels and moves, like the brutes; by which also, above the condition of the brutes, he understands and wills, and pursues those things which best suit his nature, and to which reason or the intellect can advance by its own powers. In this part they place all affections, both good and bad, such as love, hatred, hope, fear, and whatever is of this kind, as in their proper dwelling.

units.la: Quam partem Apostolus alias quoque carnem, alias mentem, alias mentem carnis vocat. 2. Corint. 10. Rogo autem vos, ne praesens audeam ea fiducia, qua exist imor audax fuisse in quosdam, qui putant, nos veluti secundum carnem ambulare: Nam in carne ambulantes non secundum carnem militamus, 2. Timoth. 3. Quemadmodum autem Iannes & Iambres resistebant Mosi: ita & hi resistunt veritati, homines mente corrupti, reprobi circa fidem, sed non proficient amplius. Item Colossen. 2. Ne quis vobis palmam interuertat, data opera per humilitatem & superstitionem angelorum, in his, quae non vidit fastuosus incedens, frustra inflatus a mente carnis suae.
units.tr: This part the Apostle also calls at other times "flesh," at other times "mind," and at other times "mind of the flesh." 2 Cor. 10: "But I beg you, that I may not have to be bold when I am present with that confidence with which I reckon to be bold against some who think that we walk according to the flesh. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh." 2 Tim. 3: "Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth, men of corrupt mind, disqualified concerning the faith; but they will not advance further." Likewise Col. 2: "Let no one rob you of your prize by delighting in humility and the worship of angels, dwelling on things he has not seen, puffed up without cause by the mind of his flesh."

units.la: En ergo, quid per animam, seu carnem, mentem, & metem carnis intelligi conueniat, nimirum eam partem, qua viuimus, mouemur, agimur, raciotinamur, intelligimus, volumus. At vero Spiritus multo excellentius quiddam significat, id videlicet, quo homo res invisibiles, aeternas, & quae spirituales alias appellantur, apprehendit, & supra communem hominum sortem progreditur, ad res diuinas penetrans. In ea parte sedem habent, fides, spes, charitas, & quae proprie res spirituales dicuntur. Atque hoc pacto aliquid excellentius sacrae literae tribuunt homini, quam philosophia: vt pote quae de spiritu & spiritualibus rebus nihil iudicat. In summa, anima capax est bonorum naturalium, seu naturae: Spiritus bona supernaturalia apprehendit: Sicut anima praeminet corpori, its spiritus animae. Anima corpus vegetat, spiritus vero animam. Anima praestat ratione seu naturali iudicio: Spiritus vero debet animam gubernare & moderari, sine spiritu bene habere, nec anima, nec corpus bene habere possunt. Multis autem in locis de spiritu praestantia prae anima agitur, & discernuntur homo spiritualis & homo animalis, item opera spiritus, & opera animae, mentis, seu carnis: Vt Romanorum octauo, Qui carnales sunt, quae carnis sunt curant: at qui spirituales, quae spiritus sunt. Nam affectus carnis mors est: affectus vero Spiritus, vita & pax. Propterea quod affectus carnis inimicitia est apud Deum. Nam legi Dei non subditur, siquidem ne potest quidem. Prima Corinthiorum secundo, Animalis (ψυχικὸς) autem homo non accipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Stultitia siquidem illi sunt, nec potest cognoscere, quod spiritualiter dijudicatur. Hinc ergo constare potest, quid fit, quod ait, verbum Dei pertingere vsque ad diuisionem animae & spiritus. Cum enim verbum Dei sit velut gladius spiritualis, id quoque agit in res incorporeas, &, vt sic loquar, spirituales. Adeo vero agit violenter, vt penetret vsque ad diuisionem animae & spiritus, hoc est, vt diuidat, secet, & omnibus modis permoueat, & animam, hoc est, rationem, intellectum humanum, & spiritum, id est, quicquid praeterea anima ipsius sublimius, vel excellentius in homine considerari potest. Sicut etiam cum beata virgo canit: Magnificat anima mea Dominum, & exultauit spiritus meus in Deo seruatore meo, perinde est, ac si dicat, se tota ratione intellectu, mente, corde, deniq; omnibus viribus Deum velle celebrare. Quomodo & Marci duodecimo, ex Deuteronomij sexto, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota mente tua, & ex totis viribus tuis. Vbi cor, anima, mens, vires, plane idem repraesentant nobis, quod hic anima & spiritus. Descripta est igitur hic ea vis verbi, quod, vbi id auditur, statim totum hominem, & quicquid in eo est, maxime commoueat & concutiat. Vnde & illae voces additae sunt per metaphoram, Compacompagum & medullarum: Sicut homini spiritum & animam, ita compages quoque & medullas tribuit. Non autem quòd in has quoque, quæ sunt res corporales, agat verbum, quod est res spiritualis: sed significatur vis maxima agendi & penetrandi, quam habet præ quocunque gladio materiali. Nam gladius materialis actus in corpora, tamen subinde obtunditur, vbi dura occurrunt, & impeditur, quo minus penetret per compagines, & internodia, & præterea per ossa spisiora: at verbum Dei eam habet vim, vt penetret & cōpages & medullas, hoc est, omnia intima. Itaq; valdè apta metaphora, ad significandum maximam agendi vim, est, qua dicitur, verbum penetrare etiam compages & medullas. Sed quia fortasis non satis possum exprimere hanc vim verbi, nec omnes adhuc assequuntur plane, quâta sit, & quomodo efficiatur, ideò nos aliis modis id declarabimus, nimirum exemplis aliquot propositis.
units.tr: See then what is fitly meant by soul, or flesh, or mind, and mind of the flesh: namely that part by which we live, are moved, are driven, reason, understand and will. But Spirit signifies something much more excellent, namely that by which a man apprehends invisible and eternal things, which are called spiritual, and rises above the common lot of men, penetrating divine things. In this part are seated faith, hope, love, and those things which are properly called spiritual. In this way Holy Scripture ascribes to man something more excellent than philosophy does, since philosophy has no judgment about the spirit and spiritual things. In sum, the soul is capable of natural goods, or of nature; the spirit apprehends supernatural goods. Just as the soul excels the body, so the spirit excels the soul. The soul gives life to the body, but the spirit to the soul. The soul excels in reason or natural judgment; but the spirit ought to guide and govern the soul; without the spirit, neither the soul nor the body can fare well. In many places, moreover, the excellence of the spirit above the soul is discussed, and the spiritual man and the natural man are distinguished, as are the works of the spirit and the works of the soul, mind, or flesh: as in Romans 8: "Those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace. Because the mind of the flesh is hostility toward God; for it does not submit to the law of God, neither indeed can it." 1 Cor. 2: "But the natural [ψυχικὸς] man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned." From this it can be seen what is meant by his saying that the word of God reaches to the division of soul and spirit. For since the word of God is like a spiritual sword, it also works upon things that are incorporeal and, as I may say, spiritual. Indeed it works so forcefully that it penetrates to the division of soul and spirit, that is, it divides, cuts, and moves in every way both the soul, that is, reason and the human understanding, and the spirit, that is, whatever else in the soul can be considered higher or more excellent in man. Just as when the blessed Virgin sings, "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour," it is as if she said that with her whole reason, understanding, mind, heart, and finally all her powers, she wishes to praise God. So also Mark 12, from Deuteronomy 6: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength." Here heart, soul, mind, and powers plainly represent the same thing to us as soul and spirit do here. The power of the word is therefore described here, namely that when it is heard, it immediately moves and shakes the whole man and whatever is in him. Hence those words are added by way of metaphor, compages and marrows: just as he attributes spirit and soul to man, so he also attributes joints and marrows. Not that the word, which is a spiritual thing, acts also upon these, which are corporeal things; but the greatest power of acting and penetrating is signified, which it has beyond any material sword. For a material sword, though it acts upon bodies, is nevertheless at times blunted where hard things meet it, and is hindered from penetrating through the joints and the sinews, and moreover through thicker bones; but the word of God has such power that it penetrates even joints and marrows, that is, all inmost things. Therefore the metaphor is very apt for signifying the greatest power of acting, by which it is said that the word penetrates even joints and marrows. But since perhaps I cannot sufficiently express this power of the word, nor do all yet fully grasp how great it is and how it is effected, therefore we will declare it in other ways, namely by setting forth several examples.

units.la: Verbum Dei cùm auditur, & intenta mente consideratur, sic subinde permouet audientium animos, vt reuera spiritus & anima, id est, tota ratio, intellectus, & præterea si quæ eminentiora sunt, omnia conturbentur, accendantur, & ad agendum, vel intelligendum id quod verbo Dei proponitur, tacitis & occultis quibusdam aculeis incidetur: itavt nonnunquam sequatur subita & admiranda animorum, & morum etiam externorum immutatio, ac videantur ex improbis fieri probi, ex cæcis illuminati, ex impijs pij, ex adulteris & scortatoribus casti, ebriosis sobrij, &c. Sic Matthæus audito verbo Christi, statim relictis omnibus, secutus est Christum, Matthæi capite nono, Sic Ninivitarum rex cum suis permotus est ad conciones Ionæ Prophetæ, secunda Esdræ octauo, cùm Esdras legeret librum legis à mane vsque ad meridiem, populus attentissimè audiebat. Et sequitur: flebat omnis populus, cùm audiret verba legis, secundo Samuelis duodecimo, Dauid audiens verbum Domini ex Nathan, agnouit iuum peccatum, & venia rursus obtinuit. Esaiæ trigesimo octauo. Cùm Esaias iussu Domini nunciasset Ezechiæ regi ægrotanti, vt disponeret domum suam, quia ei esset moriendum: hic statim eo verbo commotus fleuit & orauit, & obtinuit vitam ad quindecim annos prolongari.
units.tr: When the word of God is heard and considered with an attentive mind, it often so moves the minds of the hearers that spirit and soul, that is, the whole reason and understanding, and also whatever is higher in us, are all thrown into confusion and kindled, and are pricked by certain hidden and silent goads to act upon or understand what is proposed in the word of God. Sometimes there follows a sudden and remarkable change, not only of minds but also of outward conduct, so that the wicked seem to become good, the blind enlightened, the impious pious, adulterers and whoremongers chaste, drunkards sober, and so on. Thus Matthew, on hearing the word of Christ, at once left everything and followed Christ (Matthew 9). Thus the king of the Ninevites was moved by the sermons of the prophet Jonah (2 Esdras 8). When Ezra read the book of the law from morning until midday, the people listened most attentively, and it follows: "All the people wept when they heard the words of the law" (2 Samuel 12). David, hearing the word of the Lord from Nathan, acknowledged his sin and again obtained pardon (Isaiah 38). When Isaiah, at the Lord's command, announced to King Hezekiah, who was sick, that he should set his house in order because he was to die, the king at once, moved by that word, wept and prayed, and obtained that his life should be extended by fifteen years.

units.la: Sed multò conuenientissimum exemplum habemus Actorum secundo: Petrus concionabatur de Christo, quòd esset ille promissus Dauidi, de quo & Deus dixerat: Sede à dextris meis, &c. quodque ipsi illum crucifixissent, & subijcitur: His autem auditis compuncti sunt corde, & dixerunt ad Petrum & reliquos Apostolos, Quid faciemus, viri Fratres? Petrus ait ad illos, delictorum pœnitentiam agite, & baptizetur vnusquisque vestrûm in nomine Iesu Christi, paulo post: Accesserunt in die illo animæ circiter ter mille. Hic sine dubio verbum Dei illorum spiritum & animam mirabiliter penetrarat.
units.tr: But we have a most fitting example in Acts 2. Peter was preaching about Christ, that he was the one promised to David, of whom God had also said, "Sit at my right hand," etc., and that they had crucified him. And it follows: "Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, 'What shall we do, men and brethren?' Peter said to them, 'Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.'" A little later: "That day there were added about three thousand souls." Here without doubt the word of God had wonderfully pierced their spirit and soul.

units.la: Actorum vicesimosexto, aliquos motus verbi sentiebat Agrippa, dicens: Modica ex parte persuades mihi, vt fiam Christianus.
