Actorum decimoseptimo, Paulus veniens Berrhæam, intrauit in synagogam Iudæorum, & quidam susceperunt verbum cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas, si hæc ita se haberent: & multi crediderunt ex eis. Sed hæc satis ad declarandam hanc mirabilem, quam Apostolus describit, verbi vim.
units.tr: In Acts 26 Agrippa felt some stirrings of the word, saying, "Almost you persuade me to become a Christian." In Acts 17, when Paul came to Berea, he entered the synagogue of the Jews, and some "received the word with all eagerness, searching the Scriptures daily, whether these things were so, and many of them believed." But these examples are enough to explain this remarkable power of the word, which the Apostle describes.

units.la: Sequitur adhuc de eadem re:
units.tr: He goes on about the same matter:

units.la: Et discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis κριτὴς, iudex, qui iudicare & discernere potest: vnde Critici dicti. Discernit autem verbum cogitationes & intentiones cordis, dùm videlicet maximè permouet omnium animos, & varias cogitationes inducit, alias carnales pugnantes contra spirituales refellit verbum, & damnat cogitationes carnales: Sicut & aptè dicitur prima Corinthiorû decimoquarto, Quòd si omnes prophetetis, ingrediatur autem incredulus aut indoctus, coarguitur ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnibus, & sic occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt, atq; ita procidens in faciem adorabit Deum, renuncians, quòd reuera Deus in vobis sit. Vel, verbum iudicat etiam cogitationes, quia ostendit, cogitationes esse peccata, easq; damnat Esaiæ primo: Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis.
units.tr: And a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart [κριτὴς, a judge, one who can judge and discern]; hence they are called critics. The word discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart when it powerfully moves the minds of all and brings in various thoughts: it refutes some carnal thoughts that fight against spiritual ones and condemns the carnal thoughts. This is aptly said in 1 Corinthians 14: "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an uninstructed person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all, and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so falling on his face he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you." Or, the word judges even thoughts, because it shows that thoughts are sins, and condemns them, as in Isaiah 1: "Take away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes."

units.la: Porrò, quòd quidam interpretantur præcedentia omnia, viuus est sermo Dei; & efficax, de persona Filij, qui etiam verbum siue sermo patris appellatur, non video, quomodo satis quadret ea interpretatio. Quare non putauimus, nobis aliquam de filio expositionem admiscendam.
units.tr: Moreover, that some interpret all the preceding, "the word of God is living and effective," of the person of the Son, who is also called the Word or Speech of the Father, I do not see how that interpretation fits well enough. Therefore I have not thought it right to mix into our exposition any explanation about the Son.

units.la: Nec est vlla creatura, quæ non manifesta sit in conspectu illius: sed omnia nuda & resupinata oculis eius, ad quem nobis est sermo.
units.tr: Nor is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight, but all things are naked and laid open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

units.la: Tertia ratio ab eo, quòd Deus, imò Christus, qui itidem verus Deus est, omnium lustrat corda & iudicat. Quæ ratio vltimo loco posita mirificè omnium animos debet permouere, idque non solùm, quia admodum verenda est diuina maiestas, vbique
units.tr: The third reason rests on the fact that God, or rather Christ, who is likewise true God, searches and judges the hearts of all. This reason, placed last, ought to stir the minds of all wonderfully, and not only because the divine majesty, present everywhere, is greatly to be feared, and judges severely both thoughts and actions,

units.la: Ioan. 3. vbiq; præsens, & tàm cogitationes, quàm actiones seueriter dijudicans: verùm etiam quia tacitè conscientijs redarguuntur hypocritæ, qui eo tempore (quando videlicet tùm passim in pios sæuiebatur) tantùm simulatè, aut certè non ea, qua decebat ratione, crederent. Quos omnes his verbis admonitos vult, vt depositá omni simulatione ac dubitatione seriò synceriterque credant, & aperte fidem suam profiteantur. Nec dubium quin partim propter sæuitiam potentum Iudæorum, partim propter efficaciam inspeciem rationum earum, quas ad oppugnandum euangelium illi proferebant, valdè multi claudicantes in fide fuerint: id quod ex eo potest colligi, quod huius epistolæ capite duodecimo dicitur: Quapropter manus remissas & genua soluta surrigite, & facite, vt recti sint gressus pedibus vestris, ne claudicatio aberret à via, imò sanetur potius. Sed non satis apparet, quomodo ista reuellantur à præcedentibus. Nam cùm nulla aperta nota separentur seu disiungantur, de dignitate verbi videntur adhuc accipienda, & tamen propriè hæc conueniunt ipsi Deo. Quamobrem nonnulli senserunt, hæc promiscuè & de verbo, & de Deo dici. De verbo quidem, quia id discernit etiam cogitationes cordis, sicut dictum est: de Deo autem, quòd istud, nimirum respicere & cognoscere corda, Dei proprium manifeste intelligatur. Sed mihi videntur hæc simpliciter de Christo accipienda, qui quandoquidem Deus est, ἀπαύγασμα merito dicitur. Ac transfit Apostolus, meo iudicio, valde eleganter quadam ἀντανακλάσεως forma, à verbo Dei ad homines dicto seu pronunciato, ad personam filij, qui etiam verbum seu λόγος communi nomine appellatur. Atque eam ob causam non erat opus vocem filij, vel τῆς λόγος hic exprimere, cùm supra nomen λόγος fit positum, & hic satis aptè licet mutata paululum significatione queat subintelligi. Etiamsi dici posset, referenda hæc ad vocabulum Dei, quod initio periodi semel est positum: Et de filio accipienda hæc verba, satis arguit illud, ad quem, seu de quo nobis sermo est: cuius rei pleniorem rationem mox reddemus. Item quòd oculos ponit, qui non sunt tribuédi verbo, quod anteacum gladio contulit. Hoc verò pacto disputationem, quæ ad afferendam diuinitatem Christi fuerat instituta, commemoratione diuinitatis eius scitissimè claudit. Etenim, vbi Christo tribuit, quòd etiam occultissima cordis clarè inspiciat, reuera diuinitatem eius celebrat.
units.tr: John 3. but also because hypocrites are silently rebuked in their consciences, who at that time (when, namely, the persecution of the pious was raging everywhere) believed only feignedly, or at any rate not in the manner that was fitting. The Apostle wants all of them, admonished by these words, to lay aside all pretence and doubt and believe seriously and sincerely, and openly profess their faith. There is no doubt that many were lame in faith, partly because of the savagery of the powerful Jews, and partly because of the apparent force of the arguments which they put forward to attack the gospel. This can be gathered from what is said in chapter twelve of this epistle: "Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be turned out of the way, but rather be healed." But it does not sufficiently appear how these words are connected with what precedes. For since they are not separated or disjoined by any clear mark, they seem still to be understood of the dignity of the word, and yet they properly apply to God himself. Hence some have thought that these things are said indiscriminately both of the word and of God: of the word, indeed, because it also discerns the thoughts of the heart, as has been said; of God, however, because this, namely to behold and know hearts, is clearly understood to be the proper work of God. But to me it seems that these things should be taken simply of Christ, who, since he is God, is rightly called ἀπαύγασμα [radiance]. And the Apostle, in my judgment, passes very elegantly by a certain form of ἀντανακλάσεως [reflection] from the word of God spoken or uttered to men, to the person of the Son, who is also called the Word or λόγος by a common name. For this reason there was no need to express here the word "Son," or "the Word," since the name λόγος was placed above, and here it can be understood well enough, though its meaning is changed a little. Even if it could be said that these words refer to the word "God," which was placed once at the beginning of the sentence, and that these words are to be taken of the Son, the phrase "to whom we have to speak" sufficiently shows it; of this matter we shall give a fuller account shortly. Likewise, that he attributes eyes, which are not to be given to the word, is consistent with what he had earlier compared to a sword. In this way he most skilfully closes the argument, which had been undertaken to establish the divinity of Christ, by recalling his divinity. For when he ascribes to Christ that he clearly sees even the most hidden things of the heart, he truly celebrates his divinity.

units.la: Deo autem propriè dandum, quòd corda scrutetur, pluribus Scripturæ locis demonstratur. Psalmo 7. Consumetur nequitia peccatorum, & diriges iustum, scrutans corda & renes Deus. Psalmo quadragesimo tertio, Nonne Deus requiret ista? Ipse enim novit abscondita cordis. Nunquid vir habitabit in abscondito, & ego non videbo eum? Psalmo 93. Intelligite insipientes in populo, & stulti aliquando sapite. Qui plantauit aurem, non audiet? Et qui finxit oculum, non considerat? Qui corripit gentes, non arguet? Psalmo centesimo trigesimonono, Si ascendero in cœlos, tu illic es: & si iacuero in inferno, ades: Si assumpsero pœnas diluculo, si habitauero in extremis maris, etiam illuc deducet me manus tua, & tenebit me dextera tua. Esaiæ 20. Væ, qui prudentes estis in oculis vestris, vt à Domino abscondatis consilium. Hieremiæ 17. Prauum est cor hominis, & inscrutabile, quis cognoscet illud? Ego Dominus scrutans cor, & probans renes. Romanorum octauo, Ille, qui scrutatur corda, nouit, quis sit sensus spiritus, quoniam secundum Deum intercedit pro sanctis. 2. Corinth. 4. Ne ante tempus quicquam iudicetis, donec venerit Dominus, qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarum, & patefaciet consilia cordium, ac tunc laus erit vnicuique à Deo. Eiusdem epistolæ, capite tertio: Dominus nouit cogitationes sapientum, quòd sint vanæ. Sed quid pluribus opus est? Passim tribuitur istud Deo, & diuinæ naturæ, non autè Dei verbo ad homines enunciato, quare de Christo Deo hæc accipienda recte constituitur. Nunc ad partes explicandas veniamus.
units.tr: That it must be attributed properly to God to search hearts is shown in many places of Scripture. Psalm 7: "The malice of sinners shall be consumed, and you shall direct the just, God who searches hearts and reins." Psalm 43: "Shall not God require these things? For he knows the secrets of the heart. Shall a man hide himself in secret places, and I shall not see him?" Psalm 93: "Understand, you foolish among the people, and you fools, be wise at last. He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? And he who formed the eye, does he not consider? He who chastises nations, shall he not rebuke?" Psalm 139: "If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I lie down in hell, you are present. If I take my wings in the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me." Isaiah 20: "Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, that you may hide the counsel from the Lord." Jeremiah 17: "The heart of man is perverse and unsearchable; who shall know it? I, the Lord, search the heart and try the reins." Romans 8: "He who searches the hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God." 2 Corinthians 4: "Judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts, and then each one shall have praise from God." In the same epistle, chapter 3: "The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." But why need there be more? Everywhere this is attributed to God and to the divine nature, and not to the word of God spoken to men; therefore it is rightly determined that these things are to be understood of Christ as God. Now let us come to the explanation of the parts.

units.la: Nec est ulla creatura, quæ non manifesta sit in conspectu illius) Non tantùm ait, corda hominum explorata esse Deo, sed omnes creaturas. Sint angeli, sit aliud quiduis, quàmuis spirituale & incorporeum, tamen propterea non potest Deum latere. Dum enim vbiquè ille est, vbique etiam omnia contemplatur. Quare hæc ratio valde omnes vrgebat, vt sincerò & deposito omni fuco in caussa fidei & confessionis euangelicæ agerent. Sicut reuera hic minimè est ludendum, aut fingendum. Homines quidem falli & deludipo-sunt, & hypocritæ frequentando cœtus sacros, audiendo verbum Dei, psallendo & orando cum cæteris psalletibus, participando de mensa Domini, deniq; aliis multis externis actionibus fingere possunt, se credere apud homines, cùm tamen haud verè credant. Sed apud Deum fictio non habet aliquem locum: quandoquidem etiam omnes creaturas ille habet exploratas, & cordium etiam inspex est. Et quia hæc ratio adeò est confidenter necessaria, ideo placuit Apostolo luculentissimis verbis eam inculcare. Sed omnia nuda & resupinata oculis eius) Elegantibus vtitur metaphoris ad explicandum, quòd omnia Deo sint manifesta & conspicua. Omnia, inquit, sunt nuda apud Deum. Quæ sub vestibus aut larua abdita sunt, non animaduertuntur ab omnibus: si scabies, si deformitas membrorum sit, ea vestibus tegitur, quo minus possint homines intueri: At apud Deum omnia nuda sunt, detracta est vestis, detracta larua, & denique omne illud, quo fucus, fraus, vitium tegi posset. Sic alias quoque nudum dicitur, quod apertum & manifestum volumus significare: vt de manifesta & aperta veritate dicimus, quòd nudata sit. Et ipsi poetæ nudas Gratias finxerunt, quòd aperta & sine fuco deberet esse gratia & beneuolentia.
units.tr: No creature exists that is not manifest in his sight. He does not say merely that the hearts of men are known to God, but all creatures. Let there be angels, or anything else, however spiritual and incorporeal, yet for that reason it cannot escape God. For since he is everywhere, he also beholds all things everywhere. Hence this reason pressed very strongly on everyone, that they should act sincerely, with all pretence laid aside, in the cause of faith and the evangelical confession. Indeed, here one must truly not play or feign. Men indeed can be deceived and made fools of, and hypocrites can, by frequenting sacred assemblies, hearing the Word of God, singing psalms and praying along with the others, taking part at the table of the Lord, and finally by many other outward actions, pretend before men that they believe, when yet they do not truly believe. But before God pretence has no place at all, since he has all creatures known to him and is also the inspector of hearts. And because this reason is so strongly necessary, the Apostle was pleased to impress it with most brilliant words. But all things are naked and laid open before his eyes) He uses elegant metaphors to explain that all things are manifest and visible to God. All things, he says, are naked before God. Things that are hidden under clothing or a mask are not noticed by everyone: if there is a scab or a deformity of the limbs, it is covered by clothing, so that people cannot look at it. But before God all things are naked; the clothing is removed, the mask is removed, and finally everything by which deceit, fraud or vice could be covered. So too we also call a thing naked when we wish to signify that it is open and manifest, as we say of a manifest and open truth that it has been laid bare. And the poets themselves pictured the Graces as naked, because grace and goodwill ought to be open and without pretence.

units.la: Porrò resupinata vertit interpres, quod græcè legitur τεταχυλισμένα, à verbo ταχυλίζω, quòd plura significat, nempe excorio, pellem à ceruice detraho, item supinum colloco, diuido animal per spinam. Ab his ergo omnibus per elegantem metaphoram Apostolus mutuatur, ductam ab excoriatione animalium, eorumque ventris supinata collocatione, & per mediam spinam incisione. Quod cùm fit, omnia intestina ibi fiunt conspicua.
units.tr: Moreover, the translator renders as "laid open" what is read in Greek as τεταχυλισμένα [τεταχυλισμένα], from the verb ταχυλίζω [ταχυλίζω], which has several meanings: to flay, to strip the skin from the neck, also to lay on the back, to divide an animal along the spine. The Apostle therefore borrows from all these things by an elegant metaphor, drawn from the flaying of animals and their being laid on their backs, and cut open along the middle of the spine. When this is done, all the entrails there become visible.

units.la: Eadem igitur ratione significatur, omnia manifesta & conspicua esse Deo, sicut manifesta & conspicua sunt animalium intima viscera, cum excoriantur, deinde supina collocantur, & per medium dissecantur. Ibi enim omnia explorantur, ac minutissima quæque membra aperiuntur, imò & id quod in medio spinæ abditum erat, nescio quid medullæ simile eruitur. Quare non potuisset, meo iudicio, aptior vox, ad significandum intimarum rerum manifestationem excogitari. Neque videtur mihi vis & gratia metaphoræ vna voce satis potuisse exprimi, etiamsi illud interpres reddidit, quod omnium significantissimum videbatur, & latinis auribus maximè proprium, quemadmodum ipse quoque reddit rationem, citando illud Iuuenalis: Aulam resupinat amici: quod de lustrante & scrutante & omnia scitè dictum est. Iam & per anthropopatheian Deo tribuitur, oculi vt videlicet, captui nostro manifestius explicetur insignis & admiranda illa potestas scrutandi & cognoscendi omnia, quam ipse solus præditus est. Eodem pacto oculus Domini pro cognitione, quam Deus de omnibus rebus habet, creberrimè in Scripturis vsurpatur.
units.tr: Therefore by the same reasoning it is signified that all things are manifest and visible to God, just as the inner organs of animals are manifest and visible when they are flayed, then laid on their backs, and cut in two along the middle. For there everything is examined, and the smallest members are laid open; indeed, even that which lay hidden in the middle of the spine, some marrow-like thing, is drawn out. Hence, in my judgement, a more apt word could not have been devised to signify the manifestation of inmost things. Nor does it seem to me that the force and grace of the metaphor could have been sufficiently expressed by a single word, even though the translator rendered it with what seemed the most significant of all and most proper to Latin ears, as he himself also gives the reason, citing that line of Juvenal: Aulam resupinat amici, which was aptly said of one who searches and scrutinises and examines everything. Furthermore, by anthropopatheia the eyes are attributed to God, so that, evidently, that remarkable and admirable power of searching out and knowing all things, which he alone possesses, may be explained more plainly to our capacity. In the same way, the eye of the Lord is very often used in the Scriptures for the knowledge which God has of all things.

units.la: Ad quem nobis sermo est) Hac particula de persona Christi, de quo disputatum est, & cui vt Deo competit, omnia explorata habere, & corda etiam inspicere, significat. Ac πρὸς pro πρὸς, dixit, per præpositionum enallagen, de quo: quomodo & supra capite primo, Et ad angelos quidem dicit, pro eo, quod est, de angelis quidem: id quod sententiæ ratio postulat, sicut tùm admonuimus. Nonnulli verò hanc particulam in hunc modum interpretantur, vt significetur, nobis reddendam apud Deum rationem, vt λόγον accipiatur pro ratione, quam Deo scrutanti corda aliquando debemus reddere. Nam & Christo omne iudicium à patre esse commissum, præterea eidem reddendam omnium à nobis actorum vel dictorum rationem, satis constat. Siquidem Actorum decimo, Petrus apud Cornelium Centurionem, Præcepit, inquit, nobis vt prædicaremus populo ac testificaremur, quòd ipse sit ille, qui constitutus erat à Deo iudex viuorum ac mortuorum.
units.tr: To whom is our speech) By this particle he signifies Christ, of whom the discussion has been, and to whom, as to God, it belongs to have all things explored and to inspect even the hearts. And he wrote πρὸς [πρὸς] for περὶ [περὶ], by an exchange of prepositions, as above in the first chapter, But to the angels he says [πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ἀγγέλους λέγει], for concerning the angels; which the sense of the passage requires, as we noted then. Some, however, interpret this particle in such a way that it signifies that an account is to be rendered by us before God, taking λόγον [λόγον] as the reckoning which we must at some time give to God who searches hearts. For it is quite certain that all judgement has been committed by the Father to Christ, and moreover that an account of all things done or said by us must be rendered to him. Indeed, in Acts 10 Peter, speaking to the centurion Cornelius, says: "He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one who was appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead."

units.la: Item secunda Corinthiorum quinto, Omnes nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, vt reportet vnusquisque ea, quæ fiunt per corpus, iuxta id, quod fecit siue bonum siue malum. Quæ interpretatio quod ad sententiam attinet, ab instituto non est aliena. Sed prior est simplicior. Interea cuiuis liberum esto, quam maximè velit, sequi sententiam.
units.tr: Likewise, in 2 Corinthians 5: "We must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil." This interpretation, as far as the sense is concerned, is not foreign to the purpose. But the former is simpler. Meanwhile, let anyone follow whichever opinion he most wishes.

units.la: Cæterum breuis hæc adhortatio, qua disputatio tota de duabus in Christo naturis clauditur, sicut diuersas, & valde efficaces rationes suasorias, ita doctrinam excellentem & variam continet. Etenim prima illa ratio à periculoso nos admonet, exempla patrum magnificienda, quodque ea tanquam pro speculo virtutum & vitiorum debeamus in omni vita proponere. Solent etiam profani scriptores exempla profanorum & incredulorum magnificere, quidamque in locos communes quamplurima ex omni historiarum genere congesserunt, nimirum iudicantes, id quod res est, maxima cum vtilitate proponi in illis, quæ in vita expetere vel fugere deceat, & primam eam facultatis partem alienis exemplis edoceri, & sapientem reddi (sic autem videmus Valerium Maximum, & alios quosdam deinde secutos fecisse.) Quare tanto pluris decet nos facere exempla Patrum in sacris literis propositta, quanto hæc sunt magis certa, & magis imitatione digna.
units.tr: Moreover, this brief exhortation, with which the whole discussion of the two natures in Christ is closed, contains, as well as diverse and very effective arguments of persuasion, an excellent and varied teaching. For that first reason warns us of the danger of not magnifying the examples of the Fathers, and that we ought to set them before us in every part of life as a mirror of virtues and vices. Profane writers too are accustomed to magnify the examples of pagans and unbelievers, and some have gathered very many examples of every kind of history into commonplaces, judging, as is the case, that what is to be sought or avoided in life is set forth in them with the greatest usefulness, and that that first part of wisdom is taught by other people's examples and makes one wise (so we see that Valerius Maximus and some others who followed him did). Therefore it is fitting that we should set so much greater store by the examples of the Fathers proposed in the sacred letters, as these are more certain and more worthy of imitation.

units.la: Neq; verò quicquam vnquam traditum est à profanis scriptoribus, quod non item clarius, licet fortasse breuius, in Scripturis tradatur. Adeò omnis doctrinæ suppellex in libris sacris (quos non sine causa ita vocant) locupletissima inuenitur.
units.tr: Nor indeed has anything ever been handed down by profane writers which is not likewise handed down, more clearly though perhaps more briefly, in the Scriptures. So completely is the whole store of doctrine found in the sacred books (which are not without cause so called), in the greatest abundance.

units.la: Secundò, habemus hic insignem locum de dignitate & præstantia verbi Dei: dignam que iudico hanc descriptionem, quæ omnibus pulpitis téplorum aureis literis inscribitur, & ante omnes sacros libros depingatur. Nam, siue confirmandi sint pij in recta deverbo Dei sententia, siue terrendi verbi contemptores, sanè ad omnia est descriptio hęc multò vtilisima. Pij siquidem si vulnerentur gladio huius verbi, vulnerantur ad suam salutem: quandoquidem per verbum aut excitantur, aut admonentur, aut corriguntur, aut docentur, aut consolationem capiunt. Contemptores autem sic subinde audiunt, & feriuntur acie huius gladij, ut intimè commoueantur, & apostema impietatis, quo din corde alunt, scindatur, atque ipsi tandè curentur, mentisque sanitatem percipiant. Alij verò ad internecionē hoc gladio delentur impij, & qui in incredulitate perseuerunt: sicut virtute verbi ceciderunt increduli patres in deserto. Ita namque & pij & impij pariter feriuntur gladio verbi.
units.tr: Secondly, we have here a notable passage on the dignity and excellence of the Word of God. I judge this description worthy to be inscribed in golden letters on all the pulpits of churches, and to be painted before all the sacred books. For whether the godly are to be confirmed in the right opinion of the Word of God, or the despisers of the Word are to be terrified, this description is certainly most useful for all these purposes. For if the godly are wounded by the sword of this Word, they are wounded for their own salvation, since through the Word they are either roused, or admonished, or corrected, or taught, or receive consolation. The despisers, however, are from time to time so heard and struck by the edge of this sword that they are deeply moved, and the abscess of impiety, which they have long nourished in their heart, is lanced, and they themselves are at last healed and receive soundness of mind. But others, the impious and those who persevere in unbelief, are destroyed by this sword to their ruin, just as the unbelieving fathers fell in the desert by the power of the Word. For thus both godly and impious alike are struck by the sword of the Word.

units.la: Et alijs est gladius ad salutem, alijs ad perditionem: quo modo Apostolus quoque de verbo, & verbi ministris deserte loquitur 2. Corinth. 2. Deo autem gratia, qui semper triumphat per nos in Christo, & odorem notitiæ suæ manifestat per nos in omni loco. Quoniam Christi bona fragrantia fumus Deo in his, qui salui fiunt, & in his, qui pereunt: his quidem odor mortis ad mortem: illis verò odor vitæ ad vitam. Quamobrem oportet omnibus, ut verbum Dei ad vitam, non ad mortem audiamus.
units.tr: And the sword is to some for salvation, to others for perdition; as the Apostle also speaks, in 2 Corinthians 2, of the Word and of the ministers of the Word: "But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and makes manifest through us the savour of his knowledge in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God, among those who are saved and among those who perish: to the latter indeed a savour of death unto death, but to the former a savour of life unto life." Wherefore we must all hear the Word of God unto life, not unto death.

units.la: Tertiò, quando hic describitur Deus, ut omnes tàm cogitationes, quàm actiones nostras perpetuò intuens & considerans, habemus quo animos nostros à malis affectibus refrenemus, quantum in viribus est, & cohibeamus saltem, omnique studio caueamus, ne quid per nos committatur, quo scimus illum offendendum. Valde commendabiles sunt illæ sententiæ in Scripturis, quibus inculcatur, sæpè cogitandum de Dei extremo iudicio, quod ille feret etiam in abscondita cordium: iudicaturus haud dubiè sine personarum acceptione. Huius iudicij meditatione nos à peccando haud dubiè cohiberemur. Quid, quòd conscientiæ hic incitantur ad synceriter agendū in rebus omnib. & ad vitandam omnem hypocrisin? Si ista vox, Deus videt, siue bonus vir aliquis videt, (ut apud Senecam rectè Epictetus faciedum monet, imaginandam omni tempore boni viri præsentiam) satis posset imprimi nostris animis, incomparabiles fructus bonorum operum per omnem vitam proferremus.
units.tr: Third, when God is described here as continually watching and considering all our thoughts as well as our actions, we have a reason to restrain our minds from evil desires as far as we can, to check them at least, and to take every care that nothing is done by us that we know will offend him. The sayings in Scripture that urge us to think often of God's final judgment, when he will judge even the hidden things of the heart, without any respect of persons, are very commendable. Meditation on that judgment would certainly keep us from sinning. And does this passage not also urge consciences to act sincerely in all matters and to avoid all hypocrisy? If the words "God sees," or "a good man sees," (as Epictetus rightly advises in Seneca, that the presence of a good man should be imagined at all times) could be impressed deeply on our minds, we would bring forth incomparable fruits of good works throughout our whole lives.

units.la: Postremò, habemus in vniuersa conclusione præsenti, mirabile exemplum tractandi Scripturam, per quod admonemur, quanta diligentia & fide in Scripturis versandis explicandis sq; deceat nos agere, quomodo eas caulsis nostris accommodare, singulas particulas accurate expedere, argumenta efficacia & solida inde excerpere debeamus, adeò ut dicere ausim bonam partem methodi tractationis Scripturarum in hac conclusione demonstrari. Et quia valde prodesset, meo iudicio, hanc rem plenius ab omnibus cognoscì, nec posset paucis explicare, ideo nos conclusionis dispositionem atque argumenta omnia repetemus, uti in confirmatione & confutatione supra egimus, quo videlicet rectius omnes perspiciant Apostoli mentem ac disputationis scopum: sed præterea eadem opera, quæ in eaad methodum tractandi Scripturam pertinentia obseruandaque occurrant, quanta licebit breuitate, annotabimus: ut sic duplicem quodammodo fructum ex hac repetitione percipiatis.
units.tr: Last, in this whole conclusion we have a remarkable example of how to handle Scripture. It teaches us with how much diligence and faithfulness we ought to work in reading and explaining the Scriptures, how we should apply them to our causes, carefully unfold each single part, and draw out from them effective and solid arguments. So much so that I dare say a good part of the method of treating Scripture is demonstrated in this conclusion. And because, in my judgment, it would greatly help everyone to know this matter more fully, and it cannot be explained in a few words, I will repeat the arrangement and all the arguments of the conclusion, as I did above in the confirmation and the refutation, so that everyone may more clearly see the mind of the Apostle and the aim of his discussion. Besides, along the way I will note, as briefly as I can, the points that bear on and must be observed in this method of handling Scripture, so that you may gain a twofold benefit from this repetition.

units.la: Proinde absoluta confirmatione, in qua probauit, Christū esse Deum, ac proinde angelis superiorem: absoluta item confutatione, in qua diluit, quæ de humanitate Christi, ad infirmandam Christi diuinitatem obijciebantur, docuit, quibus de causis Christum hominem fieri decuerit: deinde postquam breuiter ostendit, Christum ipso etiam Mose praestantiorem: Iam subijcit grauem & elegantem & plenam affectib. conclusionem, in qua hortatur, ut quando satis intelligere possunt, Christum natura esse Deum, deinde perficiendæ salutis nostræ causa factum hominem, eum eiusque euangelium lubenter audiant & suscipiant, ait ergo:
units.tr: Therefore, having completed the confirmation, in which he proved that Christ is God and therefore superior to the angels, and having also completed the refutation, in which he dispelled the objections drawn from Christ's humanity against his divinity, and taught for what reasons it was fitting for Christ to become man; and then, after briefly showing that Christ is greater even than Moses himself, he now adds a weighty, elegant conclusion, full of feeling, in which he exhorts them, since they can now understand that Christ is God by nature and was made man for the sake of accomplishing our salvation, to hear and willingly receive him and his gospel. He therefore says:

units.la: Quapropter sicut dicit spiritus ille sanctus: hodie si uocem eius audieritis) vbi statim multa occurrunt obseruanda.
units.tr: "Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says, 'Today if you hear his voice'" [Hebrews 3:7]; where many things immediately present themselves for observation.

units.la: Primò, quòd rectè consideranś, qua de causa instituerit disputationem, ita conclusionem hanc texit, ut pulcherrimè conueniat cum ipsa disputationis propositione. Respicit enim hæc verba, Hodie si uocem eius audieritis, illud quod primo loco dixit, Deum nobis nouissimis hisce diebus locutum per filium. Et sic vltima à primis non dissentiūt. Secundò, prudenter animaduertens, ad quales scribat, nimirum morosos & proteruos Iudæos instituit adhortationem, non suis verbis, sed prophetæ, imò Spiritus sancti: atqui, meo iudicio, valde artificiosè, non solùm attentos reddit, verùm etiam quasi cogit ad audiendum, & ne reijciant vel contemnant, si suis verbis modo locutus fuisset, impedit præcā-
units.tr: First, the Apostle, rightly considering for what reason he began the discussion, has woven this conclusion so that it agrees beautifully with the very proposition of the discussion. For these words, "Today if you hear his voice," look back to what he said first, that God spoke to us in these last days through the Son. And so the last things do not disagree with the first. Second, prudently noting to whom he is writing, namely stubborn and headstrong Jews, he gives the exhortation not in his own words but in the words of the prophet, or rather of the Holy Spirit. And indeed, in my judgment, very skilfully, he not only makes them attentive but almost compels them to listen, and he forestalls any rejection or contempt on their part, which would have arisen if he had spoken merely in his own words.

units.la: Doctrinæ fuppellex locupletes libri sacri. 2. uerbi Dei dignitas. Verbū Dei ut agat in pijs. Verbo Dei uis in impijs. præcauetq;. Porrò locus à pronunciato, siue ab autoritate, quantum pondus habeat, vel pueris notum est.
units.tr: The rich stock of doctrine is in the holy books. (2) The dignity of the Word of God. How the Word of God works in the godly. The power of the Word of God in the ungodly. He forestalls it. Moreover, how much weight a statement or an authority carries is known even to boys.

units.la: Tertiò, hoc obseruandum, quòd habita adhuc ratione personarũ, cùm alia testimonia potuisset in hac causa producere, tamen sciens, qualia etiam ingenia Iudæorũ, eligit eiusmodi testimoniũ, in quo graues minæ continentur: item in quo exemplũ patrũ propter incredulitatem punitorũ proponitur: quibus duabus rebus iudicabat Iudæorũ animos maximè commouendos. Minis enim duræ ceruicis homines sunt vrgendi: præterea, qui patres suos semper iactabant, exemplo patrum terreri debebant.
units.tr: Third, we must observe that, while still taking account of the persons, although he could have brought forward other testimonies in this matter, he nevertheless, knowing the kind of minds the Jews had, chose a testimony that contains grave threats, and also one in which the example of the fathers punished for unbelief is set forth. He judged that the minds of the Jews were to be moved most strongly by these two things. For men of stiff neck must be pressed with threats; and moreover, those who were always boasting of their fathers ought to be frightened by the example of their fathers.

units.la: Quartò, multò appositisimè esse adhibitũ hoc testimoniũ, satis liquet ex eo, quòd plurima & multo efficacisima argumeta ad excitados animos Iudæorũ inde mox excerpat. Cæterum ex his iam colligemus aliquot præcepta, ad methodum tractádi Scripturas & conciones sacras pertinentia: è quibus hoc primum. Si docendi sunt nobis imperiti, si redarguendi aduersarij, si admonendi vel corrigendi tardi seu errantes, si quid tradendum vel præcipiendũ de vera iustitia, ad omnia hæc satius est agamus scripturæ testimoniis & pronunciatis, quàm quibuscunq; aliis. Sicut & hũc proprie esse vsum scripturæz. Timoth.3. aperte dicitur, Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata, & vtilis ad doctrinã, ad redargutionem, ad correctione, ad institutionem, quæ est in iustitia, ut integer fit Dei homo ad omne opus bonum apparatus.
units.tr: Fourth, that this testimony was applied very aptly is clear enough from the fact that he soon draws from it a great many very powerful arguments to stir up the minds of the Jews. Meanwhile, from these things we will now gather some precepts pertaining to the method of treating Scripture and sacred sermons, of which this is the first. If we have to teach the unlearned, refute adversaries, admonish or correct the slow or erring, or hand down or prescribe anything concerning true righteousness, it is better for us to do all these things with testimonies and sayings of Scripture than with any others whatever. Just as this is clearly said to be the proper use of Scripture, 2 Tim. 3.: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work."

units.la: Secúdum. Huic proximũ est & agnatũ, ut ex illis potisimum Scripturis adhibeamus testimonia, quæ sunt, ut loquuntur, de canone, id est, quæ sic rata & comprobata sunt in ecclesijs, ut solida argumenta ad confirmandũ ea, quæ sunt fidei, inde duci possint. Sunt autem de canone omnes libri in sacris biblijs congesti, exceptis, Tobia, Iudith, Baruch, epistola Hieremiæ, Esdræ tertio & quarto libris, Sapientia Salomonis, sapiëtia Iesu filij Syrach: cantico trium Sanctorum puerorum, historia Susannæ, item Draconis Belis interfectione, libro Danielis adijci solitis: item aliquot posterioribus capitibus, nempe, 11.12.13. 14.15.16. Esther, & trib. libris Machabæorũ: qua de re nunc non est nobis plenius agedũ.
units.tr: Second. Closely related to this and akin to it, we should adduce above all those testimonies of Scripture that are, as they say, of the canon, that is, which have been so accepted and approved in the churches that solid arguments for confirming the articles of faith can be drawn from them. The books gathered in the sacred Bibles are all of the canon, except Tobit, Judith, Baruch, the Epistle of Jeremiah, the third and fourth books of Esdras, the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Jesus the son of Sirach; the Song of the Three Holy Children, the story of Susanna, and also the destruction of Bel and the Dragon, which are customarily added to the book of Daniel; likewise some of the later chapters, namely 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 of Esther, and the three books of the Maccabees. We need not treat this matter more fully now.

units.la: Tertium. Delectus habendus eorũ, quæ in mediũ proferre volumus, habendaq; ratio, ut ex multis ea adhibeamus, quæ maximè conueniunt, quæq; rebus, quib. de agimus: itè si fieri queat, personis, quæ docemus, sint accommoda: sicut Apostolum hic fecisse cerni mus. Quartum: vbi aliqua præceßerunt, danda opera, ut quæ citamus, etiam cum illis quadrent, & aptè cohæreat. Quintũ: prodest & hoc, si ita citamus, ut cum decoro podus illis addamus, maiestatéq; earum omnium animis inculcemus, quod Apostolus hic agit, dicens: sicut dicit spiritus Sanctus. Sed ad Apostoli verba redeamus.
units.tr: Third. We must make a selection of what we wish to bring forward, and take account of which of many passages to use: those that agree best and fit the matters we are treating, and, if it can be done, suit the persons we are teaching. We see that the Apostle has done this here. Fourth: where some things have gone before, we must take care that what we cite also fits with them and coheres aptly. Fifth: it is also useful, when we cite in this way, to add with due dignity some weight to the words, and to impress the majesty of them all on the minds of our hearers. This the Apostle does here, saying: "as the Holy Spirit says." But let us return to the words of the Apostle.

units.la: Videte fratres, ne quando sit in ullo uestrum cor prauũ) Exponit Apostolus, illam adhortationẽ spiritus Sancti accommodam esse instituto, ac Iudæos illa commoueri, ut quando nunc audita est ipsis vox Dei in euangelio, nõ debeat corda suâ indurare, seu euangeliũ contenere, sed potius inuicem exhortari per omne tépus, usurpando ista verba: hodie si uocë eius audieritis, nolite indurare corda uestra, &c. Ita plane significat Apostolus, sic accipiendum istud testimonium spiritus Sancti à Iudæis, tâquàm si proprie propter illos, & ad illos, & propter præsentem causam verba illa dicta sint.
units.tr: "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart..." The Apostle explains that this exhortation of the Holy Spirit is suited to his purpose, and that the Jews are moved by it, so that, since the voice of God has now been heard by them in the gospel, they ought not to harden their hearts or resist the gospel, but rather exhort one another every day, using these words: "Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," etc. The Apostle clearly means that this testimony of the Holy Spirit is to be received by the Jews as if these words had been spoken properly for them, and to them, and for the present case.

units.la: Illa verba obiter interposita, quæ & per parethesin legi expediret, Christi participes facti sumus, ratione continent, quare debeamus toto hoc tépore nos ipsos adhortari. Est enim sententia: Nos eatenus esse Christi participes, quatenus fide firmâ ad finé vsq; retinemus. Proinde, si volumus in fide esse constantes, operæ est precium, nos inuicem crebris & assiduis exhortationib. incitemus & confirmemus. Iam quod ad methodũ tractádi scriptu-ras attinet, colligemus hic Sextum præceptũ huiusmodi. Sextò: Quando citamus scripturę testimoniũ aliquod, paucis indicare oportet, quomodo illud in instituto nostro conueniat. Septimò: simulq; ostendendum, quomodo eo rectè vti ad nostram utilitatem debeamus. Nam Apostolus hic ait, quòd testimonio spiritus Sancti debeant se inuicem exhortari. Nam quidam cum audiffent, exacerbauerunt. Incipit excutere quasdã testimonij citati partes, atq; argumenta inde ducere. Primo autem loco colligit, quæ velit potissimũ expendi in illo testimonio, & conclusionis seu adhortationis caput exponit. Quare, quoniam scopus ipsius fuit & caput conclusionis, excitare ad amplectendã fidem, deterrere eos ab incredulitate, ideo statim congerit omnia membra, quibus in illo testimonio notatur genus criminis nimirũ incredulitas: item atrocitas supplicij, quo Deus in incredulitatem animaduertit: atq; ita ex his omnibus constituit argumentum hortatorium ductũ à gravitate diuinæ vltionis in incredulitatem. Sunt autem hæc membra testimonij hic excussa, primò ad genus criminis pertinentia, exacerbauerunt, siue, tentauerunt, & probauerunt, item, errant corde, non cognouerunt uias meas: licet hæc alijs verbis hic notantur, videlicet, peccandi, non obediendi, & incredulitatis. Deinde quæ ad genus supplicij pertinent: Infensus fui quadraginta annis, iuraui in ira mea, si introibūt in requiē meam. Ex his omnibus in hunc argumentatur modum:
units.tr: These words, thrown in along the way, which it would also be useful to read as a parenthesis, "we have become partakers of Christ," give the reason why we ought to exhort one another throughout this whole time. For the meaning is this: we are partakers of Christ only so far as we hold fast to the end with a firm faith. Therefore, if we want to be constant in the faith, it is worth the effort to stir up and strengthen one another by frequent and constant exhortations. Now, as far as the method of handling the Scriptures is concerned, here I will set out a sixth rule of this kind. Sixth: when we cite some testimony of Scripture, we should briefly indicate how it fits our purpose. Seventh: and at the same time we must show how we ought to use it rightly for our own benefit. For the Apostle here says that they ought to exhort one another by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. For some, when they had heard it, were embittered. He begins to examine certain parts of the cited testimony and to draw arguments from them. In the first place, he gathers which points he wishes to be weighed especially in that testimony, and he sets out the heading of his conclusion or exhortation. Because his aim and the head of his conclusion was to rouse them to embrace the faith and to deter them from unbelief, he at once gathers together all the members of the testimony by which the kind of crime is marked, namely unbelief, and likewise the severity of the punishment with which God punishes unbelief. And so from all these he builds a hortatory argument drawn from the gravity of divine vengeance against unbelief. The members of the testimony examined here are these: first, those that pertain to the kind of crime, "they were embittered," or "they tempted and tested," and likewise, "they err in heart, they have not known my ways"; although these are noted here in other words, namely sinning, disobedience, and unbelief. Next, those that pertain to the kind of punishment: "I was grieved with that generation for forty years; I swore in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest." From all these he argues in this manner:

units.la: In hoc testimonio Spiritus Sanƈti, quod iam citaui, audistis, quòd Deus fuerit quibusdā infensus per quadraginta annos, quòd iurauerit quibusdam, quòd nunquàm ingredē-renturin promissam requiem. Sed adeò horrendam vltionē Deus exercuit in eos po-tissimum, qui ipsum exacerbauerunt, tentauerunt, eisque non obedierunt, nimirum non credendo promissionib. eius, quibus pollicitus fuerat, se inducturū eos in terrā Canaan.
units.tr: In this testimony of the Holy Spirit, which I have already cited, you have heard that God was angry with certain people for forty years, and swore to some that they would never enter into his promised rest. Yet God exercised a most dreadful vengeance above all on those who provoked him, tested him, and disobeyed him, namely by not believing his promises, by which he had pledged to bring them into the land of Canaan.

units.la: Ergo vobis quoq;, si eum per incredulitatē exacerbaueritis, & promissiones advos factas in euangelio, de ingressu in requiem spiritualem, contemp seritis, eodem modo metuendum, ne infensum Deum habeatis, & à requie optata excludamini, & sic frustre-mini. Hæc sine dubio est simplex & germana Apostoli sententia: sed Apostolus non tàm crassè expressit. Voluit enim partim vehemētiæ, partim euidentioris demonstratio-nis caussa orationem suam interrogationibus & subiectionibus more Rhetorū illustra-re, imò etiam delectis verbis voluit acrimonia adhibere, ut videlicet genus criminis, & acerbitas supplicij altius omnium animis infigeretur. Et prudenter Apostolus hocargu-mentum primo loco constituit, tum quòd exhortationis ratio istud maximè exigebat, ut videlicet inferret statim id quod caput erat totius negotij: tum, quòd ista ratio de exem-plo patrum ob incredulitatem punitorum, maximū pondus erat habitura apud Iudeos, qui exempla patrum magni faciebant.
units.tr: Therefore, if you too provoke him through unbelief and despise the promises made to you in the gospel, of entering into the spiritual rest, you likewise have reason to fear that you will have God angry with you, be shut out from the rest you desire, and so fall short. This is without doubt the plain and genuine meaning of the Apostle, but the Apostle does not express it so bluntly. For, partly for the sake of vehemence and partly for the sake of a clearer demonstration, he chose to adorn his argument with questions and subjoined clauses in the manner of the rhetoricians, and even to add sharpness through chosen words, so that both the nature of the sin and the severity of the punishment would be fixed more deeply in the minds of all. And the Apostle wisely placed this argument first, both because the purpose of the exhortation especially required that he state at once what was the heart of the whole matter, and because this reasoning from the example of the fathers, punished for their unbelief, was bound to carry the greatest weight with the Jews, who held the examples of the fathers in high esteem.

units.la: Pro methodo autem docendi tractandiq; scripturas, sumemus hinc quoq; aliquotre-gulas. Sit ergo hæc regula octaua. Postquàm testimonij Scripturę citatum ostendimus instituto cōuenire, tū inferre decet id, quod præcipuè ad causam facit, & propter quod citare illud in animum induximus. Argumentum autem nō tantùm nudè & crassè ex-plicabimus, sed etiam simul ut lucem adferamus sententijs, simul ut moueamus audito-rum affectus, quàm licet artificiosissimè ea tractabimus, sicut Apostolum hìc fecisse vide-mus. Operæ precium est, eum qui docere vult, curam impendere, ut suauitate quadam delectet & grauitate etiam permoueat: cuius rei summus artifex fuit noster Paulus. Et Au-gustinus libro quarto de doctrina Christiana multis in locis de hac re præcipit, iubetqué artificium in sacris literis accuratè obseruare, ibiq; cap. 6. 7. de schematibus rhetorum, cæsuris, periodis, annotandis præcipit. Capite vicessimo, de tribus dicendi generibus: capite vicessimoseptimo, de Shematibus & tropis, &c.
units.tr: As for the method of teaching and handling the Scriptures, we shall also take some rules from here. Let this be the eighth rule. After we have shown that the cited testimony of Scripture fits our purpose, we should then draw out what bears most directly on the cause, and for which we had resolved to cite it. We shall explain the argument not only plainly and baldly, but also so as at once to shed light on the sentences and to move the feelings of the hearers, and we shall treat these things as skilfully as possible, as we see the Apostle did here. It is worth the effort for one who wishes to teach to take care to delight his hearers with a certain sweetness and to move them with gravity as well; in this matter our Paul was the supreme craftsman. And Augustine, in the fourth book of On Christian Doctrine, prescribes this in many places, and bids us observe the art carefully in the sacred letters; and there in chapters 6 and 7 he gives precepts about the figures of the rhetoricians, caesurae, and periods, which are to be noted; in chapter 20 on the three kinds of speaking; in chapter 27 on figures and tropes, and so on.

units.la: Etenim nobis annunciatum est, quemadmodum) Aliud argumentum, in quo excutit particulam illàm, si uocem eius audieritis: Apparet autem, simul hìc reddi ratione præcedentiū verborū, quibus dicebatur, metuendū, ne nos à requie excludamur: simul quadam occupatione satisfieri aduersarijs, qui fortassis contedere voluissent, præsentibus rebus testimonium illud haud conuenire. Atq; ita grauiter inculcat, ad nos pertinere illud testimoniū, & no-bis promissam requiem spiritualem, non minus, quàm patribus in deserto fuit promissa requies temporalis. Sed præterea non contentus simplici huius rei assertione, infertiterū urgens exemplum patrum, ut sibi ab incredulitate caueant. Atq; hoc pacto videtur col-locatum argumentū. Nunc reuelata euangelio nos quoq; vocem Dei audiuimus, pe-rinde atq; olim patres. At non profuit illis audisse sermonem, quando ei fidem non ad-hibuerunt. Ergo nec nobis proderit, audisse vocem Domini in euangelio, nisi fidē ad-hibeamus. Maiorem non probat, ut satis notā, tum ex prima propositione totius episto-læ, qua dicebatur, Deum extremis diēb. hisce locutū per filiū: tum ex tota disputatione superiore, in qua diuersis locis beneficia per Christū collata, explicantur. Minor mani-festa euadit ex argumento proximè præcedenti. Cęterūm & hìc aliud præceptum, ad tractationem scripturarum conduces, excerpemus, videlicet:
units.tr: Then comes another argument, in which he examines that particle, "if you hear his voice." It is also clear here that he gives the reason for the preceding words, in which it was said that we must fear lest we be shut out from the rest; and at the same time he meets, by a certain preemptive move, the objections of opponents who might perhaps have wished to contend that the testimony does not fit the present situation. And so he presses home earnestly that this testimony pertains to us, and that the spiritual rest promised to us is no less promised to us than the temporal rest was promised to the fathers in the wilderness. But besides, not content with the simple assertion of this matter, he again urges the example of the fathers, that we may guard ourselves against unbelief. In this way the argument seems to be framed thus: Now that the gospel has been revealed, we too have heard the voice of God, just as the fathers did of old. But hearing the word did not help them, since they did not give it faith. Therefore hearing the voice of the Lord in the gospel will not profit us either, unless we give it faith. He does not prove the major premise, as it is sufficiently well known, both from the first statement of the whole epistle, where it is said that God has spoken in these last days through the Son, and from the whole preceding discussion, in which the benefits conferred through Christ are explained in various places. The minor premise is manifest from the argument immediately preceding. But here too we shall pick out another precept that is useful for handling the Scriptures, namely this:

units.la: Vbi testimoniū aliquod citauimus, & instituto nostro quadrare ostendimus, videndū nū istud possit ab aduersarijs reijci, vel dici tortū parũq; aptè & minus in loco adhibitū. Quòd si istud possit fieri, est nobis breuiter vel prolixius, ut res postulabit, ostendendū, nos vim nullam Scripturæ facere, non torquere, non contra Spiritus Sanƈti mente vsur-pare. Qua in re magna prudētia opus est. Aliquādo opus erit etiā singula verba & circūstā-tias rimari, ut recte à nobis asseri, quod intēdimus, declaremus: qua de re mox dicemus.
units.tr: Where we have cited some testimony and shown that it fits our purpose, we must consider whether the opponents can reject it, or say that it has been twisted, or is only loosely and poorly applied and used in an unsuitable place. If they can do so, we must show briefly, or at greater length as the matter requires, that we do no violence to Scripture, do not distort it, and do not misuse it against the mind of the Holy Spirit. In this matter great prudence is needed. Sometimes it will also be necessary to examine the individual words and circumstances, so that we may declare correctly what we mean to assert; we shall speak of this shortly.

units.la: Introimus enim in requiem nos qui credidimus.
units.tr: For we who have believed enter into rest.

units.la: Aliud argumentū, in quo expendit hanc particulā, si introibunt in requiē meā: quā arguti-s rationibus probat illis proprie cōuenire, qui euangelio recens reuelato crediderant, uel credituri essent. Itaq; primùm claris verbis hàc sententiā effert, dicens: introimus in requiem nos qui credidimus, quemadmodū dixit: sicut iuraui in ira mea: si ingressuri sunt in requiē meā: quasi dicat: requies illa, de qua Spiritus Sanƈtus loquitur dicens, ab ea prohibitos in credulos, pertinet ad illos, qui euangelio iam reuelato credunt, vel credituri sunt. Sed quia istud reuera erat valdē valde difficile probatu, idque eo magis, quòd aduersarij longè alia ratione, & in speciem verosimili, neq; adeò inepta, hæc verba interpretabantur. Contendebát enim hi, in testi monio Spiritus Sancti sermone haberi potissimum de requie temporali, quę patribus pro- missa fuerat in terra Canaan. Præterea, requiem illa eo tempore contigisse patribus in fide perstantibus, quo terram Canaan duce Iosua fœliciter & magna cum gloria occuparunt. Quare verba illa nullo pacto ad credentes euangelio referenda esse, minimeq; imaginada aliam requiem, quàm temporalem, uel aliud tépus, quo ea obtineretur, quâ illud, quod iàm tot seculis elapsum fuerat, quo videlicet temporalis requies patribus in terra Canaă fuit concessa. Quę rationes certe videbatur podus habere, & poterant multis locis scripturę, qui de requie temporali sonant, confirmari: cuiusmodi habentur in promissionib. ad patres factis, et alibi passim Apostolus igitur no ignoras, quòd hoc pacto aduersarij conaretur spiritus Sancti sententia peruertere, mirabili prudetia, incredibiliq; artificio propositione sua probat atq; eo ordine sua probatione instituit, ut primo loco doceat, de alia requie quàm de temporali, verba spiritus Sancti accipienda. Secundò, eam alio insuper tépore quàm aduersarij volebat, obtinendam, nimirum præsenti, quo euangelium reuelatu est, & vox Dei in euangelio audita. Quod ad primum itaq; attinet, ut probet, spiritus Sancti nō loqui de requie temporali, argumentu trahit, meo quidé iudicio, ex emphasi pronominis illius, meam: atq; in hùc ratiocinatur modu: & quidé operibus, &c. Quod nostro more crasius sic licet reddere: In hoc testimonio spiritus Sancti Deus requie promissa diserte vocat suâ, dicens, in requie meâ: atqui requies Dei non est temporalis vel terrena, verù eiuf modi, qualis describitur Geneseos secundo: vbi postquàm perfecta fuerut omnia opera àiactis mūdi fundamētis, de die septimo dicit: et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnib. operib. suis. Quæ sane requies non potest nisi spritualis & cœlestis intelligi. Igitur, quod hic rursus Deus dicit: si introibunt in requiem meam, oportet eodem sensu non de temporali, sed spirituali & cœlesti requie ipsius Dei intelligamus. Atq; ita obseruata significatione pronominis illius, meam, argumentum efformat ad probandu, de requie spirituali & cœlesti, non autem corporali vel terrena spiritu Sancto loqui. Iam altera partem, videlicet requiem istam nō iam olim acceptá à patrib. sub duce Iosua, sed nunc demum, tépore inquá reuelati euan- gelij, à credetib. accipiendu, hoc pacto probat: Posteaqua igitur illud reliquu est, aliquos introire in eá, &c. Quasi dicat, Hoc omninò neceffariu erat, ut aliqui promissa requie, de qua loquitur spiritus Sanctus, ingrederentur. Sed eam nequaquàm ingresi sunt illi Patres, eo tempore, quo ipsis fuit annúciatů: quandoquidé impediti fuerunt per suam incredulitate. Relinquitur ergo, quòd quidà alij, & alio quidé tépore eam ingredi debuerint. Est argumentu ab eo, quòd necessario debeat adimpleri promissio, & quòd antea non fuerit adimpleta. Verùm, quia aduersarij rursus fortassis pertinaciter contendissent, verù quidem esse, quòd increduli à requie illa fuerint exclusi, nihilominus patres credentes & in fide conftátes esse ingressos duce Iosua. Hàc ob causam Apostolus aliter idè probat, sumpta ratione ex voce hodie, hoc pacto colligens: Spiritus Sanctus quàdo longè post illorum patrum tempora per Dauidem dicit: hodie si uocem eius audieritis: aperte hac voce, hodie, nouum quoddam tempus præfinit. Sed ita locutus non fuisset, fi patres prisco illo tempore verà requiem, de qua hic sermo est, sub Iesu seu Iosua obtinuissent. Igitur oportet aliud tempus, quàm illud prifcu, intelligi, quo requies hæc fit præstanda. Hoc verò tempus, est tempns præsens seu hodiernum, quo iterum vox Dei in euangelio toti mūdo audita est. Postremò subijcit: itaq; relinquitur Sabbatismus, &c. vbi illatio seu complexio est, qua ex præmissis rationibus duo colligit: primum quidem, tépus sabbatismi seu requiei, de qua spiritus Sanctus locutus est, reliquum esse populo Dei, hoc est, nondú contigisse olim patribus, sed superesse adhuc, & nunc recipi à credentib. euangelio iam reuelato. Secundum, requiem hanc non esse corporalem aut terrenam, sed spiritualem, requiei ipsius Dei prorsus similem, qua nimirum pijs credetibus dabitur, eodem modo requiescere ab operibus, quo perfecta vniuersa mundi machina ab operib. suis requieuit ipse Deus. Atq; ita illatio hæc ijs, quæ præcesserunt, pulchrè respondet.
units.tr: Then there is another argument, in which he weighs this clause, "if they shall enter into my rest," and by subtle reasoning he proves that it belongs properly to those who believed, or were going to believe, the gospel just revealed. And so first he states this sentence in plain words, saying: "We who have believed enter into rest," just as he said: "as I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest." It is as if he said: that rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks, saying that the unbelieving were shut out from it, belongs to those who now believe, or are about to believe, the gospel already revealed. But because this was indeed very, very hard to prove, and all the more so because the opponents interpreted these words in a quite different way, and in a plausible guise, and not at all foolishly. For they contended that in the testimony of the Holy Spirit the discussion is chiefly about the temporal rest that had been promised to the fathers in the land of Canaan. Moreover, that rest had come to the fathers who remained in faith at the time when, under the leadership of Joshua, they happily and with great glory occupied the land of Canaan. Therefore those words must in no way be referred to those who believe the gospel, and we must not imagine any rest other than the temporal one, or any other time in which it might be obtained, than that which had already passed so many centuries ago, when the temporal rest was granted to the fathers in the land of Canaan. These reasons certainly seemed to have weight, and they could be confirmed by many passages of Scripture that speak of temporal rest, of which kind there are many among the promises made to the fathers, and elsewhere throughout. The Apostle, therefore, knowing that by this method the opponents would try to pervert the meaning of the Holy Spirit, with wonderful prudence and incredible skill proves his proposition, and arranges his proof in such an order that first he teaches that the words of the Holy Spirit must be taken of another rest than the temporal one. Secondly, that this rest is to be obtained at another time than the opponents wanted, namely the present time, in which the gospel has been revealed and the voice of God has been heard in the gospel. As for the first point, then, to prove that the Holy Spirit does not speak of the temporal rest, he draws his argument, in my judgment, from the emphasis of that pronoun, "my"; and he reasons in this way: "for indeed the works..." etc. This can be rendered more crudely, in our manner, thus: In this testimony the Holy Spirit has God expressly call the rest he promised his own, saying "my rest." But the rest of God is not temporal or earthly, but of the kind described in Genesis 2, where, after all the works from the foundation of the world were finished, it says of the seventh day: "and God rested on the seventh day from all his works." This rest can indeed be understood only as spiritual and heavenly. Therefore, when God here says again, "if they shall enter into my rest," we must understand it in the same sense, not of a temporal rest but of the spiritual and heavenly rest of God himself. And so, observing the meaning of that pronoun, "my," he builds his argument to prove that the Holy Spirit speaks of a spiritual and heavenly rest, and not of a bodily or earthly one. Now, as to the other part, namely that this rest is not to be received now, as it was once received by the fathers under the leadership of Joshua, but only now at last, at the time of the gospel revealed, by those who believe, he proves in this way: "Since therefore it remains that some should enter into it," etc. It is as if he said: it was altogether necessary that some should enter the promised rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks. But those fathers by no means entered it at the time when it was announced to them, since they were prevented by their unbelief. It remains, therefore, that certain others, and at another time, ought to enter it. This is an argument from the fact that a promise must necessarily be fulfilled, and that it was not fulfilled earlier. But because the opponents might perhaps have stubbornly contended again that it is true that the unbelievers were excluded from that rest, yet the fathers who believed and stood firm in faith nevertheless entered under Joshua, for this reason the Apostle proves the point in another way as well, taking his reasoning from the word "today." He concludes thus: the Holy Spirit, when long after the times of those fathers he says through David, "Today, if you hear his voice," by this word "today" clearly fixes a new time. But he would not have spoken thus if the fathers had obtained the true rest of which he speaks in that earlier time, under Jesus or Joshua. Therefore another time than that earlier one must be understood, at which this rest is to be given. This time is the present or today's time, in which the voice of God has again been heard throughout the world in the gospel. Finally he adds: "So there remains a sabbath rest, etc." Here there is an inference or conclusion, by which from the premises he draws two things: first, that the time of the sabbath or rest of which the Holy Spirit spoke remains for the people of God, that is, it did not come to the fathers of old, but is still to come, and is now received by those who believe the gospel already revealed. Second, that this rest is not bodily or earthly, but spiritual, altogether like the rest of God himself, which is to be given to pious believers, so that they rest from their works in the same way as God himself rested from his works when the whole machinery of the world was finished. And so this conclusion answers well to what went before.

units.la: Iam de ratione tractandi Scripturas & hanc regulam hinc poterimus excerpere.
units.tr: Now we can draw from this the method of handling the Scriptures and this rule.

units.la: XI. Sæpè, ut certius & euidentius declaremus testimonium, quod citauimus, conue- nire nostræ causæ, atq; tandem eliciamus id, quod causa, quam tractandā suscepimus, postulat: opus est singula membra oculatius introspicere, & examinare, quomodo Apostolus hic pen ficulatè animaduertit in particulâ hodie, itè in pronomè, meam, atq; inde ducit efficacissima argumeta. Atq; eadé diligentia requiritur fere in omniú Scripturarú interpretatione, sed tamen maximè, cùm graujores disputationes instituuntur.
units.tr: XI. Often, in order to declare more certainly and evidently the testimony we have cited, so that it agrees with our cause, and finally to draw out what the cause we have undertaken to treat requires, it is necessary to look more carefully into the individual members and examine how the Apostle here observes, with close attention, the particle "today" and likewise the pronoun "my", and from these draws most effective arguments. And the same diligence is required almost in the interpretation of all the Scriptures, but chiefly when more serious disputations are undertaken.

units.la: Et licet videre, quomodo Paulus etiam in reliquis epistolis hunc moré obferuarit, ut in grauioribus disputationibus argumenta aliquando duxerit, ex singulis propemodum sententiæ alicuius membris seu dictionibus. Sic Roman.4. postquàm probasset authoritate Scripturæ, Abraham iustificatū esse fide, ex eo videlicet, quod habetur Genesεos decimoquinto, Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatū est illi ad iustitiam: statim subijcit argumentum ductum ex voce, imputatum: ostendit enim, id quod velut merces pro opere datur, non rectè dici imputatum, sed imputādi vocem significare gratuitum beneficium: quam rationem mox confirmat addito alio testimonio ex Psalmo tricesimo primo, vbi dicitur: Beatus vir, cui non imputauit Dominus peccatū. Atque ita clarissimè concludit, ex vi verbi imputandi, iustitiam gratis, non propter opera cōtingere: & fidem esse, quæ sola imputetur pro iustitia apud Deum. Simili modo Galat.3. probare volens Apostolus, non iustificari homines ex operibus legis, sed per solum Christū, adfert promissionem illam factam ad Abraham, Genes. 12. 22. Benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes. Non contentus aut hoc testimonio, perlustrauit diligenter singulas in ea voces, & ex eis novorum argumentorū collegit materiā. Primò enim animaduertēs in vocē illam, benedicentur, collegit è contrario: quòd si per illud semen esset benedictio, ergo citra illud semen non haberetur nisi maledictio. Quare infert, omnes esse sub maledictione, etiam eos, qui sunt sub lege. Et quia istud videbatur admodum dure dictum, adducit probādi caussa illud ex Deuteron. 27. Execrabilis omnis, qui non manserit in omnib. quæ scripta sunt, &c. Deinde subijcit, Christū factū execratione, ut declararet, quomodo execratio illa ab omnib. qui etiam sub lege erant, ablata esset. Et Christum factum execrationem, etiam probat ex Deuteronomij 21. Rursus respiciens ad particulam illam, omnes gentes, infert ibidem, sed breuiter, benedictione pertinere quoq; ad gentes. Si autem ad gentes, & gentes nō habebant legem. Ergo non ex lege est iustitia, sed citra legem, per solam fidem. Perrahit enim illud ad probandum, contingere iustitiam ex fide: & nō ex operibus legis, id quod ratio disputationis exigebat.
units.tr: And one may see how Paul, also in his other epistles, observed this custom, so that in more serious disputations he sometimes drew his arguments from almost every single member or word of some sentence. Thus in Romans 4, after he had proved by the authority of Scripture that Abraham was justified by faith, namely from what is written in Genesis 15, "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness", he immediately adds an argument drawn from the word "reckoned". For he shows that what is given as a wage for work is not properly said to be reckoned, but that the word "reckoning" signifies a free benefit; this reasoning he soon confirms by adding another testimony from Psalm 31, where it is said: "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not reckon sin." And so he most clearly concludes that, from the force of the word "reckoning", righteousness comes freely and not on account of works, and that it is faith alone which is reckoned for righteousness before God. In a similar way, in Galatians 3, wishing to prove that men are not justified by the works of the law but through Christ alone, the Apostle brings forward that promise made to Abraham, Genesis 12:3, "In your seed all the nations shall be blessed". Not content with this testimony alone, he carefully went through the individual words in it and gathered from them the material of new arguments. For first, noting the word "shall be blessed", he drew the contrary conclusion: that if there were blessing through that seed, then without that seed there would be nothing but curse. Therefore he infers that all are under the curse, even those who are under the law. And because this seemed a very harsh saying, he adduces in proof Deuteronomy 27: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide in all the things written," etc. Next he adds that Christ was made a curse, to show how that curse, which lay on all who were under the law, was removed; and he also proves that Christ was made a curse from Deuteronomy 21. Again, looking at that particle "all the nations", he infers briefly in the same place that the blessing pertains also to the Gentiles. But if it pertains to the Gentiles, and the Gentiles did not have the law, then righteousness is not from the law but without the law, through faith alone. For he draws that word to prove that righteousness comes from faith and not from the works of the law, which the course of the disputation demanded.

units.la: Tertiò, respiciens in particulam illam, in semine tuo, sic argumentatur: Abrahæ dictæ promissiones & semini eius: nō dicit, & seminibus, tāquām de multis: sed tanquām devno, & in semine tuo, qui est Christus. Postea subijcit argumetum ex vocabulo promissionis: si ex lege est hæreditas, non iam est ex promissione. Atqui Abrahæ per promissionem donauit Deus. Ergo est hæreditas non ex lege, sed ex promissione. Sic deniq; & in alijs locis Apostolus ex vna aliqua voce grauissima ducit argumeta. Satis est ista, exēpli caussa, in medium produxisse. Proinde habemus hic, quòd valde necessariū & volenti tractare sacras literas, aut disputatiōes graviores instituere, singulas particulas accuratè examinare, ac deinde argumeta apta & efficacia inde educere. Studeamus igitur ingredi in illā requiē, etc. Finē totius conclusionis huius primæ partis disputationis volens facere, subijcit breuē exhortationem, qua monet, ut excussa duricie cordis & omni incredulitate, auditæiam in euāgelio voci Dei credant, atq; ita requiem spiritualē, de qua spiritus Sanctus locutus est, ingrediantur. Atq; habet hæc exhortatio, quàmuis breuis, tamen diuersa & aculeata argumeta luasoria admixta: è quibus primum sumptum est à periculoso, siue ab exēplo patrum, qui propter incredulitatem in deserto ceciderunt, idq; veluti vno verbo, tamen valde scitè & quasi graphicè depingit, dicens: Ne quis eodem concidat incredulitatis exemplo: secundum argumentū sumptum est à dignitate verbi Dei, & necessaria eius adimpletione: vt ita secum multò exactius cōsiderent, necessum esse, ut credant voci Dei auditæ, alias certò sciant, se non euasuros graues minas spiritus Sancti, quas necessum est adimpleri, si ipsi nolint euangelium recipere. Valde autem elegantibus similitudinib. & metaphoris vim verbi Dei describit, ut nimirum omnes hac maiestate & potentia verbi tantò magis permouerentur, ad suscipiendum Christi euangelium, quod totum nihil aliud est, quàm verbum Dei, sicut & Christus ipse Dei verbum est.
units.tr: Thirdly, looking at that particle "in your seed", he argues thus: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed; it does not say "and to seeds", as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed", who is Christ. Afterwards he adds an argument from the word "promise": if the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from promise. But God granted it to Abraham by promise. Therefore the inheritance is not from the law but from promise. Thus finally, in other places too, the Apostle draws arguments from a single very weighty word. It is enough to have brought forward these examples for illustration. Accordingly we have here that it is very necessary for one who wishes to treat the sacred letters, or to undertake more serious disputations, to examine each particle carefully and then to draw out fitting and effective arguments from it. Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, etc. Wishing to make the end of the whole conclusion of this first part of the disputation, he adds a brief exhortation, in which he warns that, having shaken off hardness of heart and all unbelief, they should hear and believe the voice of God in the gospel, and so enter the spiritual rest of which the Holy Spirit has spoken. And this exhortation, though brief, nevertheless contains various and piercing arguments mixed with persuasion: of these, the first is taken from danger, or from the example of the fathers, who fell in the desert because of unbelief; and although he depicts this in a single word, he does so very skilfully and almost vividly, saying: "Lest anyone fall by the same example of unbelief." The second argument is taken from the dignity of the word of God and its necessary fulfilment, so that they may consider more exactly that it is necessary to believe the voice of God when heard, and otherwise know for certain that they will not escape the grave threats of the Holy Spirit, which must be fulfilled if they are unwilling to receive the gospel. He describes the power of the word of God with very elegant similitudes and metaphors, so that all might be moved all the more by this majesty and power of the word to embrace the gospel of Christ, which is wholly nothing other than the word of God, just as Christ himself is the Word of God.

units.la: Tertium argumentum ductum est à potentia ipsius Dei, qua omnium etiam corda scrutatur, quando ait: Nec est ulla creatura, quæ non manifesta sit in conspectu ipsius: Qua ratione omnes hypocritæ grauissimè vrgentur, ut depósito omni fuco & simulatione, ingenuè euangelium profiteantur, ipsum solum Deum habentes præ oculis, qui sicut nec fallere, ita neq; falli potest. Quomodo verò, & quàm appositè hæ rationes sint appositæ, nuper expositimus.
units.tr: The third argument is taken from the power of God himself, by which he searches the hearts of all, when he says: "There is no creature that is not manifest in his sight." By this reasoning all hypocrites are most severely pressed to lay aside all deceit and pretence and openly profess the gospel, keeping before their eyes God alone, who, as he cannot deceive, so cannot be deceived. How and how fittingly these arguments are apt, we have explained recently.

units.la: Cæterùm hic vides, quàm eleganter, & quàm artificiosè, præterea, quanta argumentorum frequentia, & soliditate in partibus singulis, prima præsentis epistolæ disputatio, quæ est de diuinitate Christi sit dispositā. Certè qui in hæc diligenter intuetur, non poterit aliter iudicare, quàm epistolam hanc ab summo aliquo apostolo, potissimum verò à Paulo esse conscriptam.
units.tr: Moreover, here you see how elegantly and how skilfully, and besides, with what abundance and solidity of arguments in its individual parts, the first disputation of the present epistle, which concerns the divinity of Christ, has been arranged. Certainly whoever looks at these things diligently will be unable to judge otherwise than that this epistle was written by some highest apostle, and especially by Paul.

units.la: FINIS PRIMAE PARTIS.
units.tr: END OF THE FIRST PART.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS EPISTOLAE D. PAVLI AD Hebræos.
units.tr: The Second Part of the Epistle of St. Paul to the Hebrews.

units.la: § 3 SECVN-
units.tr: § 3 SECUN-

units.la: SECVNDA PARS, SIVE SECVNDVS LOCVS EPISTOLAE, in quo docet, ceremonias omnes legis, id est, sacerdotium & sacrificia esse abrogata, easque cedere debere Euangelio.
units.tr: THE SECOND PART, OR THE SECOND SECTION OF THE EPISTLE, in which he teaches that all the ceremonies of the law, that is, the priesthood and the sacrifices, have been abrogated, and that they must yield to the Gospel.

units.la: PROPOSITIO.
units.tr: PROPOSITION.

units.la: Habentes igitur pontificem magnum, qui penetrauit cælos, Iesum filium Dei, teneamus professionem.
units.tr: Since then we have a great high priest, who has passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession.

units.la: {a}Ac secunda parte continetur disputatio de abrogatione legis. Constituit enim Apostolus, legem, illucescente euangelio, esse abrogatam, id quod satis liquet ex illationibus illis, capite septimo. Translato sacerdotio necesse est, ut legis translatio fiat. Rursus: Abrogatur enim quod præcesserat præceptum propter imbecillitatem & inutilitatem. Item sermo iurisiurandi, qui supra legem fuit, filium constituit in æternum consummatum.
