Præterea capite octauo: Etenim si prius illud tale fuisset, ut nihil in eo posset reprehendi, haudquaquam fuisset secundo quæsitus locus. Iterum: per hoc, quod dicitur nouum, antiquauit prius. Porrò quod antiquatur ac senescit, in propinquo est, ut euanescat. Item capite decimo ex Esaiæ 31. Hoc est testamentum, quod condam ergà illos post dies illos, dicit Dominus, dans leges meas in corda illorum, & in mentib. illorum inscribam eas, & peccatorum atque iniquitatū illorum non recordabor amplius. Porrò vbi horum est remissio, nō est amplius oblatio pro peccato. Qui loci omnes clarè sonant, sublatam legem. Etsi verò hac de re in aliis quoque epistolis actum sit, veluti Roman 6. & 7. Galat. 4. & 5. Hic tamen longè alia ratione, quàm in illis eandem causam peragit: quemadmodum & ecclesiarum, ad quas scribebat, status poscebat. Nam apud gentiles nequaquam opus erat pari cura huic argumento insistere, quando illi suapte sponte legem auersabantur: & satis erat de abrogatione legis ea paucis attingere, quæ tranquillandis cōscientijs illorum, quos pseudoapostoli, legem ceu necessariam ad salutem imponere conantes, perturbauerant, erant conducibilia, magisq; in illis epistolis commendabaturiam accepta de abrogatione legis cognitio, quàm recens abroganda proponebatur vel defendebatur. At nunc vbi ad ipsos scribit Iudæos, quos pariter docere & acriter conuincere oportebat, longè alia via ingreditur, multa, nec non multò efficacissima argumenta in medium proferens. Hinc autem præcipuè probat, legem cum suis ceremonijs, atq; adeò ipso sacerdotio, abrogatā: quòd omnia illa nihil aliud erant, quàm (sicut vno verbo idem effert Colossens. 2. & præsentis epistolæ capite decimo) vmbræ rerum per Christum gerendarum: Sacerdotium enim & sacrificia typos fuisse sacerdotij & sacrificij Christi: quare, hoc adueniente & suo fungente munere, illa ceu superuacanea & inutilia abolita esse: his verò abolitis, simul totam legé suas amisisse vires, seu, ut ipse loquitur, translatam esse. Hæc argumentorum omniumferè summa est.
units.tr: {a}The discussion of the abrogation of the law is contained in this second part. For the Apostle establishes that the law has been abrogated now that the Gospel has dawned, which is quite clear from the inferences he draws in the seventh chapter: "When the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law also." And again: "For there is a setting aside of the former commandment because of its weakness and unprofitableness." Likewise: "The word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, who has been made perfect for evermore." Moreover, in the eighth chapter: "For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion sought for a second." Again: "In that he says, A new covenant, he has made the first obsolete. Now that which is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away." Also in the tenth chapter, from Isaiah 31: "This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their hearts, and write them in their minds, and I will remember their sins and iniquities no more. Now where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin." All these passages speak plainly of the law being taken away. Although this matter is treated in other epistles as well, as in Romans 6 and 7 and Galatians 4 and 5, here he carries out the same cause by a quite different method than there, as the condition of the churches to which he wrote demanded. For among the Gentiles there was no need to dwell with equal care on this argument, since they of their own accord turned away from the law; and it was enough to touch briefly on the abrogation of the law only those things which were useful for calming the consciences of those whom the false apostles, trying to impose the law as necessary for salvation, had disturbed. In those epistles the knowledge of the abrogation of the law was commended more as something already received than as something now being proposed for abrogation or defended. But now, when he writes to the Jews themselves, whom it was equally necessary to teach and to convict sharply, he takes a very different path, bringing forward many and much more effective arguments. Here he proves chiefly that the law, with its ceremonies, and indeed the priesthood itself, has been abrogated, because all those things were nothing but shadows of the things to be accomplished through Christ (as in one word he expresses the same thing in Colossians 2 and in chapter ten of this epistle). For the priesthood and the sacrifices were types of the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. Therefore, when he came and performed his office, those things were abolished as superfluous and useless; and with them abolished, the whole law at the same time lost its force, or, as he himself says, was transferred. This is almost the sum of all the arguments.

units.la: Cæterum, quare Apostolus hac potissimum ratione probare abrogationem legis voluerit, tùm demùm clarè intelligemus, ubi, qualis status ecclesiæ Iudaicæ fuerit, animaduerterimus. Sciendum igitur, cùm primum toto orbe spargeretur euangelium, atque ubiq; per Christi Apostolos inculcaretur magno feruore doctrina de iustificatione per fidem absq; operibus legis, multos Iudæos hinc grauiter offensos, ac iudicasse, (id quod &res erat) ea doctrina labefactari non mediocriter vniuersam legem, inprimis autem ceremonias & sacrificia, in quibus præcipua legis dignitas, atq; etiam sanctimoniæ verèq; iustitiæ ratio consistere videbatur. Vnde eò ventum est, ut (quemadmodum colligere quiuis potest ex Actorum decimoquinto) pertinaciter cōtendere nonnulli illorum coeperint, ad iustitiam nihil profuturam fidem, nisi lex Mosaica, atq; inprimis sacræ ceremoniæ obseruarentur: atq; ita pro ceremonijs legis, pro circumcisione, sacerdotio, sacrificijs, tanquàm pro aris & focis certamina asperrima sunt enata. Neq; sanè abs re videbanturita tumultuari. Nam à Deo institutas fuisse ceremonias, & illas quidem multò pulcherrimas, nécnon, ut ad verum, inuiolabilem, ac nunquàm mutandum cultū pertinentes, erat omnibus persuasissimum. Tantoq; in honore erant hæ ceremoniæ, ut earū gratia aliquando gentes exteræ Hierosolymam cōfluxerint, sicut Ioan. duodecimo dicitur:
units.tr: Furthermore, we will understand clearly why the Apostle chose to prove the abrogation of the law chiefly by this method only when we have noticed what the state of the Jewish church was. We must therefore know that when the Gospel was first spreading through the whole world, and the doctrine of justification by faith without the works of the law was being pressed everywhere with great fervour by the apostles of Christ, many Jews were gravely offended by this and judged (and it was indeed the case) that the whole law, and especially the ceremonies and sacrifices, in which the chief dignity of the law and also the very ground of holiness and true righteousness seemed to consist, would be not a little undermined by that doctrine. Hence it came about that (as anyone may gather from Acts 15) some of them began to contend stubbornly that faith would avail nothing for righteousness unless the Mosaic law, and above all the sacred ceremonies, were observed. And so the most bitter contests arose over the ceremonies of the law, over circumcision, the priesthood and the sacrifices, as if over altars and hearths. Nor indeed were they without reason in being thrown into such an uproar. For it was thoroughly persuaded in everyone's mind that the ceremonies had been instituted by God, and very beautiful ones at that, and that they pertained to the true, inviolable worship which must never be changed. And these ceremonies were held in such honour that at times foreign nations flocked to Jerusalem for their sake, as is said in John 12.

units.la: {a} Propositio. Lex abrogata, manifestata Euangelio. Sacerdotio translato, fit etiam Legis translatio. Cap. 7. Cap 8. Cap. 10. Quare hic diter, quàm alibi agat. Vide cap. 7. in illum locum: Translato sacerdotio, necessum est & legem transferri. 1. 2. 3. Quomodo hic agat. Argumentorum summa: vide capite 8. in illud: Omnis enim pontifex. Sacerdotiū, sacrificiū, & ceremoniæ fuerunt umbræ: ideoq; abrogandæ, per uerum sacerdotiū & sacrificium Christi. Status ecclesiæ Iudaicæ. Offendiculum acceptum. Error Iudæorū de legis obseruatione. 1. à Deo institutæ ceremoniæ. 2. 3.
units.tr: {a} Proposition. The law is abrogated, made manifest by the Gospel. With the priesthood transferred, there also follows a transfer of the law. Chapter 7. Chapter 8. Chapter 10. Why he treats it here differently than elsewhere. See chapter 7 on that place: "With the priesthood transferred, it is necessary that the law also be transferred." 1. 2. 3. How he treats it here. The sum of the arguments: see chapter 8 on the words: "For every high priest." The priesthood, the sacrifices and the ceremonies were shadows; therefore they are to be abrogated through the true priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. The state of the Jewish church. The stumbling block received. The error of the Jews concerning the observance of the law. 1. The ceremonies were instituted by God. 2. 3.

units.la: Erant autem quidam græci ex his, qui ascenderat, ut adorarent in die festo Actorum 8. Vir Æthiops Eunuchus, præfectus Cadaces reginæ Æthiopum venerat adoraturus Hierosolymam. 2. Machabæorum 3. dicitur, quod ipsi reges & principes exteri, locum illum summo in honore habuerint, & dona miserint, ut Seleucus Asiæ rex. Etiamsi Actor. 21. apparet, non potuisse græcos in templum ingredi. Nam hoc pro maximo crimine obijciebant Paulo, quod induxisset græcos in templum, et ita profanasset locum sacrum. (Chrysostomus etiam quodam in loco gentiles fuisse ingressos dicit) Præterea, quando iam pridem regno atque omni potentia ciuili erant exuti Iudæi, constitutis nimirum apud eos per Romanos tetrarchis & præsidibus, ac de regno deinceps recuperando disputare, aut aliquid moliri seditiosum propemodum ceferetur: quid restabat adhuc Iudæis episcopi gloria, præter pauculas ceremonias & sacerdotium? quod si nunc tandem per doctrinam tolleretur, plane de omni gloria gentis actum foret. His inquam de causis adeo grauiter permoti sunt Iudæi, ad disceptandum pro sacerdotio & ceremonijs retinendis. Sic hodie papistæ maximè laborant pro ceremonijs & sacerdotum pompa retinenda, doctrinam autem de iustificatione per fidem cupiunt extinguere, quia eneruatillas ceremonias & pompam externam. De moralibus quidem præceptis non erat disputatio, quia hæc omnibus gentibus erant communia. Forensia verò iam ex parte per Romanos, ius dicetes illis immutata erant: sola ergo restabant ceremonialia, & hæc iam periclitabantur.
units.tr: Now there were certain Greeks among those who had gone up to worship at the feast, as Acts 8 says: an Ethiopian eunuch, an official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, had come to Jerusalem to worship. In 2 Maccabees 3 it is said that the foreign kings and princes themselves held that place in the highest honour and sent gifts, as did Seleucus, king of Asia. Yet Acts 21 shows that Greeks could not enter the temple, for they charged Paul with this as a great crime, that he had brought Greeks into the temple and so profaned the holy place. (Chrysostom also says that in a certain place Gentiles had entered.) Moreover, since the Jews had long since been stripped of kingdom and all civil power, with tetrarchs and governors established among them by the Romans, it would have been almost seditious to dispute about recovering the kingdom or to attempt anything of the kind. What, then, was left to the Jews of the glory of their church, apart from a few ceremonies and the priesthood? If these were now at last taken away by doctrine, all the glory of the nation would have been utterly undone. For these reasons, I say, the Jews were so gravely moved to contend for retaining the priesthood and the ceremonies. So today the Papists labour most strenuously to retain the ceremonies and the pomp of the priests, while they desire to extinguish the doctrine of justification by faith, because it weakens those ceremonies and their external pomp. Now there was no dispute about the moral precepts, because these were common to all nations. The judicial laws had already in part been changed by the Romans, who now pronounced judgment for them; so only the ceremonial laws remained, and these were now in danger.

units.la: Proinde Apostolus considerans, quod hisce potissimum rationibus Iudæi ad stabilien-dam dignitatem legis niterentur, ut probet, legem illucescente iam euangelio abrogatu, summa prudentia, artificio, fide, diligentia docet, Christum esse vnicum seu solum summum sacerdotem, & quidem multò præstantiorem, quàm fuerit aliquis posterorum Aaronis. Præterea, sacrificium per illum oblatum omnibus sacrificijs veteribus præferendum, utpote, quo vno semel fit Deo patri pro peccatis hominum satisfactu. Per hoc autem adeo excellens sacerdotium ac sacrificium Christi, sacerdotium vetus, simulque sacrificia vniuersa (quæ tantùm vmbræ ac typi erant eorum, quæ à Christo persectata sunt) aboleri seu transferri. Translato autem ad eum modum sacerdotio, necessariò & legem transferri: quod totius disputationis caput est. Atque ita satis expositum arbitror, quomodo hac secunda parte de abrogatione legis potissimum agatur: quare item plenius, atque aliter hic ea de re differat Apostolus, quàm in cæteris epistolis: qualibus item potissimum argumentis id, quod vult, efficiat: Denique, quo consilio, quibusue de causis potius à Christi sacerdotio, & sacrificio, quàm aliunde argumenta delegerit, ut legem aboliam euinceret. Sic verò causam hanc aggreditur.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle, considering that the Jews relied chiefly on these arguments to establish the dignity of the law, in order to prove that the law has been abrogated now that the Gospel has dawned, teaches with the greatest prudence, skill, faithfulness and diligence that Christ is the one and only high priest, and indeed far more excellent than any of the posterity of Aaron. Moreover, the sacrifice offered by him is to be preferred to all the old sacrifices, inasmuch as by it alone, once for all, satisfaction is made to God the Father for the sins of men. Through this, the far more excellent priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, the old priesthood and all the sacrifices (which were only shadows and types of those things which have been accomplished by Christ) are abolished or transferred. And when the priesthood has been transferred in this way, the law too must of necessity be transferred; this is the chief point of the whole discussion. And so I think it has been explained sufficiently how in this second part he treats chiefly of the abrogation of the law; hence also he discusses the matter here more fully and differently than in his other epistles, and by what arguments in particular he achieves what he wants. Finally, we must consider by what design, and for what reasons, he chose arguments from the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ rather than from elsewhere, in order to prove the abolition of the law. He takes up this cause in the following way.

units.la: Habentes igitur pontificem magnum, qui penetrauit cœlos, Iesum filium Dei, teneamus professionem. Hæc est totius disputationis propositio, qua, ut post euincat, vetus sacerdotiū, ceremonias, ac proinde legem ipsam abrogatam, primùm asserit Christum verum summum pontificem. Hæc est enim simplex istorum verborum sententia: Christus est verus summus pontifex, omnibus pontificib. veteris testamenti excellentior. Exegisset autem principalis causæ quam hic agi ostendimus, ratio, aliter propositionem instituì, nimirum hoc modo: Lex manifestato iam euangelio abrogata est: uel sacerdotiu, cæremoniæ, ac proinde ipsa adeò lex abrogata est. Verum quia, si ante allata vlla argumenta istud probantia, sic aperte extulisset Apostolus, protinus offensi hauddubiè, atque alienati ab audiedo fuissent Iudæorum animi: placuit ei aliis verbis, sed eo tamen sensu, ex quo tantundem clarissimè sequebatur, enunciare. Sequi namque ex assertione sacerdotij Christi, abrogatam esse legem, ipse capite septimo, diserte docet, ubi ait: si quidem populus per sacerdotium legem acceperat, necesse est, translato sacerdotio, legis quoq; translationem fieri: Quare perspicuum est, verba propositionis, quibus dicitur, Christum esse verum summum pontificem pollere, quod hæc, Lex est illucescente Euangelio abrogata. Hoc syllogismo potest totius huius disputationis summa comprehendi:
units.tr: "Therefore, having a great high priest, who has passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession." This is the proposition of the whole disputation. By means of it the Apostle intends to prove afterwards that the old priesthood, the ceremonies and therefore the law itself have been abrogated. First he asserts that Christ is the true high priest. The plain meaning of these words is: Christ is the true high priest, more excellent than all the priests of the Old Testament. Yet the reasoning of the principal question we are showing to be at issue would have required the proposition to be framed differently, namely: the law has been abrogated now that the gospel has been revealed; or, the priesthood and the ceremonies, and therefore the law itself, have been abrogated. But because, had the Apostle stated this so openly before offering any arguments to prove it, the minds of the Jews would doubtless have taken offence and turned away from hearing him, he chose to express it in other words, though in a sense from which the same conclusion very clearly follows. For that the abrogation of the law follows from the assertion of Christ's priesthood, he himself teaches plainly in chapter seven, where he says: "For if the people received the law through the priesthood, it is necessary that, with the priesthood changed, the law also be changed." It is therefore plain that the words of the proposition, which say that Christ is the true high priest, carry the force of this: the law has been abrogated now that the gospel has dawned. The whole sum of this disputation can be comprehended in this syllogism:

units.la: Per sacerdotium populus acceperat legem, seu, manente sacerdotio incolumis manet Lex.
units.tr: The people received the law through the priesthood; or, while the priesthood remains, the law remains intact.

units.la: Sed nunc per Euangelium abrogatum est sacerdotium. Ergo simul abrogata est etiam Lex.
units.tr: But now the priesthood has been abrogated through the gospel. Therefore the law too has been abrogated at the same time.

units.la: Maiorem relinquit ut manifestam: nam Lex Iudaica per sacerdotium & ceremonias potissimum discernebatur à legibus aliarum gentium.
units.tr: He leaves the major premise as obvious, for the Jewish law was distinguished from the laws of other nations chiefly by the priesthood and the ceremonies.

units.la: Minor est τὸ ἀγενέαλογον, quo de per totam disputationem agitur, quoq; probato, necessario sequitur conclusio.
units.tr: The minor premise is the point about Christ being "without genealogy" [ἀγενεαλόγητον], which is argued throughout the whole disputation; once this is proved, the conclusion follows of necessity.

units.la: Ac verosimile est, cum antea de abrogatione legis sæpius apud Iudæos disputatum esset, hisque semper illud esset postremum refugium, quòd contenderent sacerdotium & ceremonias diuinitùs institutas, debere ad cultum Dei perpetuò retineri: strenuè quidè asserit ab
units.tr: And it is likely that, since the abrogation of the law had often been debated among the Jews, their last refuge had always been this: that the priesthood and the ceremonies, divinely instituted, ought to be retained for the worship of God for ever. The Apostles vigorously assert against this

units.la: Papistæ pro ceremonijs et pompa externa gladiantur. ab Apostolis, Christum esse verum pontificem suo vno sacrificio expiantem, peccata hominum: verum hanc partem nondum satisfuisse efficaciter probatam, & solam restitisse adhuc explicandam. Venturus igitur Apostolus ad eandem disputationem, & fusissime iam demonstraturus, Christum esse verû pontificem, huiusmodi praefigere propositionem commodum censuit. En ergo, meo iudicio, quare Apostolus statim in propositione sacerdotium Christi asserit, disputationisq; initium inde vult sumere, cùm tamè animus ei sit concludere, legem abrogatam.
units.tr: The Papists fight for ceremonies and external pomp. that Christ is the true priest, who by his one sacrifice expiates the sins of men. But this part, they thought, had not yet been effectively proved and was the only one still needing explanation. The Apostle, therefore, about to come to the same disputation and to demonstrate fully that Christ is the true priest, judged it fitting to prefix a proposition of this kind. Here, then, in my judgement, is why the Apostle at once asserts Christ's priesthood in the proposition and wishes to take the beginning of his disputation from there, although his purpose is to conclude that the law has been abrogated.

units.la: Iam est & hoc notandum, quòd Apostolus propositionem hanc non nudam effert, sed quadam forma exhortationis: quò fit, ut hoc loco propositionem constituendam nouae disputationis, non omnes perinde animaduertant. Ac si bene perpedimus, istud sine certo consilio haud factum est. Hoc enim pacto non solùm reddit ad vniuersam hanc nouam disputationem valde attentos, verùm etiam ut altiore mente considerent dignitatem Christi multo amplissimam, & beneficia, quae ex sacerdotio Christi expectare debemus, artificiosè inuitat.
units.tr: It must also be noted that the Apostle does not state this proposition baldly, but in a certain form of exhortation. As a result, not everyone notices at once that here he is laying down the proposition of the new disputation. If we weigh it carefully, this was not done without a definite purpose. In this way he not only makes his hearers very attentive to the whole new disputation, but also skilfully invites them to consider with a higher mind the dignity of Christ, which is far greater, and the benefits we ought to expect from Christ's priesthood.

units.la: Artificium enim est non paruum propositioni admiscere, quae affectum moueant. Et summa est ars artem dissimulare. Quid, quòd verba ipsa mutuatur exijs, quae in fine confutationis, extrema parte secundi capitis, posita erant, ubi causas exponens, cur Christum hominem fieri docuerit, ait, ob hanc quoq; causam Christum debuisse per omnia fratribus similem reddi, ut misericors esset, & fidelis pontifex, in his, quae agenda forent apud Deum, ad expiandum peccata populi? Quo loco admonuimus, Apostolum respexisse aliquo modo ad hanc secundam disputationem principalem de Christi sacerdotio. Quamobrem nunc veluti memor eorundem verborum rectè ea ad propositionem huius disputationis inde texendam adhibet.
units.tr: For it is no small art to mingle with a proposition things that stir the emotions, and the highest art is to conceal art. Moreover, he borrows these very words from those which were set down at the end of the argument, in the final part of the second chapter, where, explaining why he taught that Christ became man, he says: "For this cause also it behoved Christ to be made like unto his brethren in all things, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in those things which pertain to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people." At that place we pointed out that the Apostle looked back in some way to this second principal disputation concerning Christ's priesthood. Therefore now, as if mindful of those same words, he rightly uses them to weave in the proposition of this disputation.

units.la: Caeterum lubet nunc verba singula expendere. Tametsi enim ad finem capitis secundi, quae ad sententiam attinent, de verbis etiam nonnulla sint à nobis expósita: tamen quaedam hic, quandoquidem paulò alia ratione, maioreq; emphasi videntur posita, conueniet breuiter annotare.
units.tr: Otherwise, let us now weigh the individual words. For although, at the end of the second chapter, some things pertaining to the sense were set out by us, and some words were also explained, yet since certain things here seem to be put in a rather different way and with greater emphasis, it will be fitting to note them briefly.

units.la: Habentes igitur pontificem magnum) Particula οὖν, igitur, non est simpliciter illatiua, quasi ista verba deberent accipi tanquam sequentia ex praecedentibus, & tanquam diuelli nō possent: sed saepè ornat, saepè etiam abundat, deinde & principijs accommodatur, quomodo apud Latinos quoq; particula igitur, statim in exordijs narrationum, vel expositionum adhibetur.
units.tr: "Therefore, having a great high priest". The particle οὖν, "therefore", is not simply inferential, as if these words had to be taken as following from what precedes and could not be separated from it. Rather it often adds ornament, often is redundant, and is also suited to beginnings, just as among the Latins the particle "igitur" is used right at the openings of narratives or expositions.

units.la: Quanquàm videtur admonere, ut respiciamus ad illa, quae de pontificatu Christi ad finem capitis secundi dici coepta sunt.
units.tr: Yet it seems to urge us to look back to what began to be said about Christ's priesthood up to the end of the second chapter.

units.la: Habentes igitur) Rectè, quoniam exhortationem parat admiscere, dicit, habentes: significat enim ea vox, Christum esse pontificem, & quidem nostrum: quòd videlicet nos habeamus illum intercedentem & orantem, & sacrificium offerentem pro nobis. Quae ratio valde animare omnes debet, ut Christi sacerdotium magnificaciant, & eius dignitatem bonitatemq; toto animo complectantur.
units.tr: "Having therefore". He rightly says "having", since he prepares to mingle an exhortation: the word signifies that Christ is our priest, and indeed our own, that is, that we have him interceding and praying, and offering sacrifice for us. This consideration ought greatly to stir all to magnify Christ's priesthood and to embrace his dignity and goodness with the whole heart.

units.la: Quomodo autem competat Christo appellatio pontificis, supra expósuimus, & id multò plenissimè in tota oratione sequenti patefiet, vbi officio pontificis, intercessoris, & mediatoris fungi, sacrificiumq; offerre, & omnia agere, quae ad pontificem pertinent, describitur.
units.tr: How the title of high priest fits Christ we have explained above, and this will be made much more fully plain in the whole following discourse, where he is described as discharging the office of priest, intercessor and mediator, offering sacrifice, and doing all the things that belong to a high priest.

units.la: Tantùm hoc notandum, vbicunque ponitur vocabulum pontificis, Graecè habeti vocem ἀρχιερεύς: & cùm ἱερεύς proprie significet sacerdotem, ἀρχιερεύς plane significat summum sacerdotem, omnibus alijs sacerdotibus praeeminentem. Itaque in voce pontificatus, semper summam quandam dignitatem Christi mente decet concipere.
units.tr: This only must be noted: wherever the word "high priest" occurs, the Greek has ἀρχιερεύς [archiereus]; and since ἱερεύς [hiereus] properly means priest, ἀρχιερεύς plainly means the chief priest, preeminent above all other priests. Therefore, in the word "high priesthood", the mind ought always to conceive some supreme dignity of Christ.

units.la: Sed ipse Apostolus aptissimis verbis dignitatem Christi hîc illustrauit: unde statim addidit, Magnum: Suprà quidem dixit Fidelem, quia id commodissimum erat, ubi voluerit describere misericordem, & nostrarum miseriarum conscium.
units.tr: But the Apostle himself illustrated Christ's dignity here in very apt words, and so he at once added "great". Above, indeed, he had said "faithful", because that was most suitable where he wished to describe a merciful one, aware of our miseries.

units.la: At hic dignitatem eius amplissimam expositurus, quàm prae omnibus pontificibus obtinet, meritò magnum eum appellauit.
units.tr: But here, about to set forth his most ample dignity, which he holds above all high priests, he rightly calls him great.

units.la: Quomodo autem Christus sit verè magnus, & maior omnibus alijs, explicat verbis sequentibus: Qui penetrauit coelos:
units.tr: How Christ is truly great, and greater than all others, he explains in the following words: "who has passed into the heavens".

units.la: Haec particula mirificè extollit Christi pontificatum: Significat enim, Christum non solùm ingressum tabernaculum aliquod manu factum, siue sanctâ sanctorum vocata, sedipsos coelos, quò penetrasse caeteros sacerdotes nequaquàm dicitur. Et in hanc formam dicit, capite septimo sequenti, Christum pontificem esse pium, innocentem, impolutum, segregatum à peccatoribus, & sublimiorem coelis factum. Iterum capite nono, Nō enim in manu facta sancta ingressus est Christus, exemplaria verorū, sed in ipsum coelum, ut appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis. Vnde apparet hic tacitè coelos opponi sanctis sanctorum, in quae pontifices semel in anno ingredi erat soliti: uthic fit sententia: sint alij sacerdotes magni, ob id, quòd ingressi sunt sancta sanctorum, sicut Leuitici decimo sexto dicitur. At oportet Christum fateamur multò maximū, qui ingressus sit ipsos coelos. Atque haec Christi in coelos penetratio, declaratur aliis scripturæ locis, vbi describitur Christus sedens ad dexteram Dei patris. Notatur autem hic, pontificatum Christi non esse terrenum vel carnalem, sed coelestem & spiritualem. An verò etiam secundum carnem Christus ex linea sacerdotali natus fuerit, pontificatumque obtinuerit, nunc nolumus addere, sed exponemus capite septimo, vbi dicitur, Christum è tribu Iuda natum, è qua nullus altari astitit. Addit deinde, quod iterum dignitatem Christi valde amplificat, dicens:
units.tr: This phrase greatly exalts Christ's priesthood. For it signifies that Christ has entered not merely some tabernacle made by hand, whether called the holy of holies, but the heavens themselves, into which it is not said the other priests ever penetrated. In this same way he says in the following seventh chapter that Christ is a priest who is holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. Again in chapter nine: "For Christ has not entered into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true, but into heaven itself, to appear now in the presence of God for us." From this it appears that the heavens are here tacitly set against the holy of holies, into which the high priests were accustomed to enter once a year; so the sense is this: other priests are great, because they entered the holy of holies, as is said in Leviticus 16; but we must confess that Christ is far greater, who entered the heavens themselves. And this penetration of Christ into the heavens is declared in other passages of Scripture, where Christ is described as sitting at the right hand of God the Father. It is noted here, moreover, that Christ's priesthood is not earthly or carnal, but heavenly and spiritual. Whether Christ also, according to the flesh, was born of the priestly line and held the priesthood, we do not now wish to add; we shall expound this in chapter seven, where it is said that Christ was born of the tribe of Judah, from which no one has attended the altar. He then adds, which again greatly magnifies Christ's dignity, saying:

units.la: Iesum filium Dei) Primò nomen Iesu exprimit, certitudinis ergò, ne videlicet de aliquo alio sermonem haberi existimemus, quàm de persona Christi, quē hoc pacto nominari, statim in principio conueniebat: intelligeretur, totam disputationem sequente de persona ipsius instituit. Quamuis expresso nomine Iesu, potest intelligi, tacitè respexisse ad aliam quendam Iesum, etiam sacerdote magnum, sed nequaquam cum hoc nostro conferendum. Suprà quoque in conclusione expresit nomen Iesu, videlicet illius, qui filius fuit Naue, subindicans, eum Christi Iesu nostri typum gessisse. Hic verò Iesu nostri nomē ponit, volens itidem hunc illi alteri Iesu sacerdoti praeferre. Porrò de Iesu sacerdote filio Iozedeck Aggaei 1. Itē Zachariæ 3. Ostendit mihi Dominus Iesum sacerdotem magnum, stantem coram angelo Domini. Vbi diem quoque dicitur ἱερεὺς μέγας, sed tamē non talis, qui ut Christus, coelos penetrauerit.
units.tr: "Jesus the Son of God". First he expresses the name Jesus, for the sake of certainty, lest we suppose that any other person is being spoken of than the person of Christ, whom it was fitting to name in this way from the start. By understanding this, he sets out the whole disputation that follows concerning his person. Although by expressly naming Jesus one may understand that he tacitly alludes to some other Jesus, also a great priest, yet he is by no means to be compared with ours. Above, too, in the conclusion he expressed the name Jesus, namely that of him who was the son of Nun, hinting that he bore a type of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here, however, he puts the name of our Jesus, wishing likewise to set this one before that other Jesus, the priest. Further, concerning Jesus the priest, son of Jehozadak, see Haggai 1 and likewise Zechariah 3: "The Lord showed me Jesus the great priest standing before the angel of the Lord." There too the priest is called great, but not such a one as entered the heavens, as Christ did.

units.la: Praeterea non talis qui appellari possit filius Dei. Et videtur Apostolus expressisse Iesum filium Dei, non solùm ad discrimē Iesu filij Iosedeck, vel alterius cuiuspiam, verùm multò magis ad ostendendum excellentiam ipsius prae caeteris omnibus, qui vocatisunt filij Aaronis. Nam de sola stirpe Aaronis ad sacerdotium solebant euocari, sicut capite septimo huius epistolae indicatur, vbi notat Apostolus, praeter veterem ordinationem, Christum dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, & non secundum ordinem Aaron.
units.tr: Moreover, he is not one who could be called the Son of God. The Apostle seems to have stated that Jesus is the Son of God not only to distinguish him from Jesus the son of Jozadak or any other man, but much more to show his excellence above all the others who are called sons of Aaron. For men were ordinarily summoned to the priesthood from the stock of Aaron alone, as is indicated in chapter 7 of this epistle, where the Apostle notes that, apart from the old ordination, Christ is called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to the order of Aaron.

units.la: Praeterea ex tribu Iuda, non autem ex tribu Leui. Et plenius Exodi 28. vbi dicitur, legitimum sempiternum erit Aaron, & semini eius post eum. Item Numeror 16. & 17. vbi, cū caeteri ex tribu Leui in dignabundi murmurarent, quòd Aaron & filij eius viderentur praelati, Dominus grauiter puniuit murmurantes, quod etiā capite nono huius epistolae notatur, & virga Aaronis florente ostendit, se Aaronem prae caeteris elegisse. Et Psal. 117. Omnes sacerdotes ad laudandū Deum inuitantur, nomine domus Aaron. Dicat nunc domus Aaron, quoniam in seculum misericordia eius. Declaratur ergo, Christum pontificem esse longè excellentiorem omnib. aliis, quòd vbi caeteri sunt dūtaxat filij Aaronis, ipse est filius Dei. Cēterùm quomodo Christus Iesus nouus iste sacerdos sit filius Dei, ac verus Deus, notum est ex precedenti disputatione, ut nequaquam opus sit probationes vllas hic adijcere. Proinde talem, tam insignem cū habeamus pōtificem, rectè addit exhortando omnes, teneamus professionem: ὁμολογίας: id est, maneamus constantes in cōfesione Christi & euangelij eius, nec patiamur nos ab eo diuelli ullis aduersariorū molestijs. In hanc sententiam supra capite tertio, vocauit Christum Apostolum & sacerdotem nostrae confessionis, dicens: Vnde frates sancti vocationis coelestis participes considerate Apostolum & pontificem confessionis nostrae, Iesum Christum. Vbi de cōfesione Christi & euangelij plura diximus. Videre ergo vnusquisque potest, quàm appositis verbis Apostolus ad describendam Christi dignitatem vtatur, & quomodo exhortationem instituat, quam etiam prudendissimè persequitur: sed priusquā id declaremus, breuiter annotandū puto, valde & excitari animos ad agnoscendū Christum pro pontifice: praeterea ad accipiendam consolationem ex hoc Christi pontificatu, quòd dicit, nos Christum habere pontificem. Magnum enim quiddam est, Christum ita habere sibi propositum, aduocatum, patronum, intercessorem, vti hic & in sequentibus describitur.
units.tr: Moreover, he is of the tribe of Judah and not of the tribe of Levi. This is set out more fully in Exodus 28, where it is said: "The priesthood shall be a perpetual statute to Aaron and to his seed after him." Likewise in Numbers 16 and 17, where, when the others of the tribe of Levi murmured indignantly because Aaron and his sons seemed to be preferred, the Lord severely punished the murmurers. This is also noted in chapter 9 of this epistle, and by the flowering rod of Aaron he showed that he had chosen Aaron above the rest. And Psalm 117: all priests are invited to praise God under the name of the house of Aaron: "Let the house of Aaron now say, because his mercy endures for ever." It is therefore declared that Christ the high priest is far more excellent than all others: where the others are only sons of Aaron, he is the Son of God. Moreover, that Christ Jesus, this new priest, is the Son of God and true God is known from the preceding discussion, so there is no need to add any proofs here. Therefore, since we have such a great and notable high priest, he rightly adds, exhorting everyone: let us hold fast the profession [ὁμολογίας], that is, let us remain steadfast in the confession of Christ and of his gospel, and not allow ourselves to be torn away from him by any troubles from adversaries. To this same effect, above in chapter 3, he called Christ "the Apostle and high priest of our confession," saying: "Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus Christ." We have said more about the confession of Christ and of the gospel in that place. Each one can therefore see how aptly the Apostle uses his words to describe the dignity of Christ, and how he frames his exhortation, which he also pursues most prudently. But before we explain it, I think it should be briefly noted that minds are greatly stirred to acknowledge Christ as high priest, and also to receive consolation from this priesthood of Christ, in that he says that we have Christ as our high priest. For it is a great thing to have Christ thus set before us as our advocate, patron and intercessor, as is described here and in what follows.

units.la: Non enim habemus pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum per omnia, iuxta similitudinem, absque peccato.
units.tr: "For we have not a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who was tempted in all things according to our likeness, without sin."

units.la: Ratio, cur merito tenenda professio seu confessio Christi atque euangelij, ducta ab vtili, vel potius ab insigni Christi erga nos bonitate, qua nimirum, vt nostrarum miseriarum probè conscius, ad miserendum & intercedendum pro nobis admodum semper promptus est. Repetita autem est fere ex capite secūdo, vbi admonuimus, eam ex hoc fluere, quòd illi plerunque solent præ cæteris moueri ad iuuandum afflictos, qui ipsi multis adversitatibus antea obruti fuerint. Ac valde appositè ratio hæc, humanitatem Christi ponens ob oculos, verbis illis de diuinitate, quibus videlicet, Christus iamiam dictus est cœlos penetrasse, & appellatus filius Dei, subijcitur. Ne enim miser & abiectus aliquis homo, diuini ç maiestatis amplitudine attonitus anxiè metueret, sibi nequaquàm expectandum auxilium ab eo, qui tàto interuallo sit superior, peroportunè simul exhibet Apostolus Christum spectandum hominem per omnia nobis similem, & ad condolendum peccatoribus tentatis obuium expositumque. Atque ita peccatorum, qui propemodū desperabat, insigni bonitate Christi rursum erigit, necnon ad perstandū in confessione corroborat.
units.tr: The reason why the profession or confession of Christ and of the gospel should rightly be held fast is drawn from the usefulness, or rather from the remarkable goodness of Christ towards us: namely, that, being thoroughly aware of our miseries, he is always most ready to show mercy and to intercede for us. This has been taken up again almost from chapter 2, where we pointed out that this follows from the fact that those who have themselves been earlier overwhelmed by many adversities are usually moved more than others to help the afflicted. And this reason, which sets the humanity of Christ before our eyes, is very fittingly joined to those words about his divinity, namely that Christ has just been said to have passed through the heavens and to be called the Son of God. For lest some wretched and downcast man, astonished at the greatness of the divine majesty, should anxiously fear that no help was to be expected from one who is so far above him, the Apostle at the same time very opportunely presents Christ to be regarded as a man in every respect like us, and ready and at hand to sympathise with sinners who are tempted. And so by the remarkable goodness of Christ he raises up again the sinner who was almost despairing, and strengthens him to persevere in the confession.

units.la: Cæterùm, quia pleraque huic loco intelligendo couenientia exposuimus capite secundo, nos hic in explicandis partibus breuiores erimus.
units.tr: But since we have set out in chapter 2 most of what is suitable for understanding this passage, we shall be briefer here in explaining its parts.

units.la: Non enim habemus, inquit, pontificem) Hæc est horum verborum sententia. Tenenda est fidei in Christum confessio. Id autem eò magis, quòd is, licet cœlos penetrauerit, & præterea sit filius Dei, tamen nequaquàm morosus est, vel arrogans nostri contemptor, verum admodum beneuolus, & ad recipiendum nos in gratiam, & ad intercedendum pro nobis paratus. Nā & ipse ideò factus homo est, per omnia nostri similis, infirmitates plurimas in se expertus, vt misericors esset & fidelis pōtifex, in his, quæ apud Deum forent agenda, ad expiandum peccata populi sicut capite secundo dicitur. Quare verò decuerit Christum participem fieri nostrarum miseriarum, item quales ex his, quæ seu corporis, seu animæ sunt, senserit, nos ibi plenius expositimus, nec animus est nunc repetere. Breuiter: Miseriæ corporales quædam omnibus communes & necessario adsunt: quædam non omnibus, sed aliquibus, & accidentariò, & plerunque ipsorum hominum culpa.
units.tr: "For we have not," he says, "a high priest." This is the sense of these words: the confession of faith in Christ is to be held fast. And all the more so because he, although he has passed through the heavens and is moreover the Son of God, is nevertheless by no means peevish or arrogant, a scorner of us, but very kindly and ready both to receive us into favour and to intercede for us. For he himself was made man for this reason, like us in all things, having experienced very many infirmities in himself, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in those things which had to be done before God, to make expiation for the sins of the people, as is said in chapter 2. Why it was fitting for Christ to share in our miseries, and what sort of things he felt, both those which belong to the body and those which belong to the soul, we have explained more fully in that place, and it is not my intention to repeat it now. Briefly: some bodily miseries are common to all and are necessarily present; others are not common to all but affect some, and by accident, and most often through the fault of the men themselves.

units.la: Miseriæ verò animæ aliæ damnatione in nobis pariunt, & gratiæ Dei prorsus aduersantur: aliæ non aduersantur, cuiusmodi sunt affectiones, dolor, tristitia, metus.
units.tr: Miseries of the soul, on the other hand, some produce damnation in us and are wholly opposed to the grace of God; others are not opposed to it, such as the emotions of pain, sorrow and fear.

units.la: Recepit autē Christus miserias nostras: Primùm, vt ipse misericors quoque erga nos fieret. Secundò, vt ita doceret, se verum hominem per omnia nostri similem. Tertiò, quia venit pro peccatis nostris satis facturus, voluit aliquos peccatorum effectus in se recipere.
units.tr: Christ took upon himself our miseries: first, so that he himself might also become merciful towards us; secondly, so that he might show that he was a true man, in all things like us; thirdly, because he came to make satisfaction for our sins, he willed to take upon himself some of the effects of sin.

units.la: Quartò, vt exemplum haberemus & consolationem, ad perferendum æquanimiter nostras miserias, quas propter peccata nostra subimus: qua de re huius epistolae capite duodecimo.
units.tr: Fourthly, so that we might have an example and consolation for bearing calmly the miseries which we undergo on account of our sins. On this matter, see chapter 12 of this epistle.

units.la: Eleganter autem retinet verbum habendi, quia prius dixerat, habentes pontificem, &c. videlicet vbique indicans, nostrum, & nobis proprie propositum esse illum pontificem.
units.tr: He elegantly retains the verb "to have," because earlier he had said "having a high priest," and so on, clearly indicating everywhere that it is our own high priest, and that he has been set before us properly.

units.la: Qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum) Valde significanter exprimitur græce, vna voce, quod interpres reddidit p πεισθεὶς. Græce enim legitur, μὴ δυνάμενον συμπαθῆσαι ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν: quasi dicatur, non potentem compati (si modò hanc vocem delicatæ aures admitterent) infirmitatibus nostris. Græca vox συμπαθῆσαι sonat velut compati, hoc est, affici moueriquesensu alieni mali, cōmodè fortasis vno verbo latinè reddetur, qui non possit cōdolere, plane idem significatur hīc, quod capite secūdo, vbi dixit, ἵνα ἐλεήμων γένηται, vt misericors esset. συμπαθῆσαι & misericordem esse idem sibi volunt. Præclarè autem describitur hic officium Christi, & maximè conuenit ei, qui aget pontificē, seu intercessorem pro alijs, videlicet affici sensu alienarum miseriarum. Et certè nunquàm seriò & fideliter aget alienam causam, quūnon sic eam ad se recipit, quasi propria ipsius esset. Itaque valde confirmat conscientias istud verbum, ut audeant bene de Christo sperare, quando audiunt eum talem esse, qui miserias alienas in se sentiat, & lubenter succurrat.
units.tr: "Who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." This is expressed in Greek in a very significant way, in one word, which the translator rendered by "touched" [πεισθεὶς]. For the Greek reads: "not being able to sympathise [συμπαθῆσαι] with our infirmities [ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν]," as if one were to say "not able to suffer with" (if only delicate ears would tolerate this word) our infirmities. The Greek word συμπαθῆσαι means roughly "to feel with," that is, to be affected and moved by the feeling of another's evil; it might perhaps be fitly rendered in Latin by one word, "to condole with." What is meant here is plainly the same as in chapter 2, where he said "that he might become merciful" [ἵνα ἐλεήμων γένηται], that he might be merciful. Sympathising [συμπαθῆσαι] and being merciful mean the same thing. The office of Christ is here described admirably, and it especially fits him who acts as high priest or intercessor for others, namely to be affected by the feeling of others' miseries. Indeed, no one will ever act seriously and faithfully in another's cause unless he takes it up as if it were his own. Therefore this word greatly strengthens consciences, so that they dare to hope well of Christ, when they hear that he is such a one as feels the miseries of others in himself and gladly gives help.

units.la: Atque hoc ingenium suum Christus etiamnum in terris agens ubique demonstrauit, dum vbicunque occasio esset, egentibus, vel aliàs quocunque modo malè habentibus lubenter succurrit.
units.tr: And Christ, while still living on earth, has shown this disposition of his everywhere, since wherever there was an opportunity he gladly helped the needy, or those who were otherwise in distress in whatever way.

units.la: Valde autem graniter admonentur hic cùm omnes Christi nomē profitentes, tum præcipue qui pontificem cum & sacerdotum vice in ecclesia Christi funguntur, vt hoc exemplum condolendi & iuuandi alios sibi proponant: & reprehenduntur quicunque morosi, rigidi, inexorabiles, qui alienis malis non mouentur, sed potius gaudent, imò laborant etiam contra omne ius, afflictis afflictionem addere.
units.tr: Here all who profess the name of Christ are very seriously admonished, but especially those who act as high priests and in the place of priests in the Church of Christ, to set before themselves this example of sympathy and of helping others. And those are rebuked who are peevish, harsh and inexorable, who are not moved by the evils of others, but rather rejoice, and even labour, against all right, to add affliction to the afflicted.

units.la: Porrò voce ἀσθενείας, id est, infirmitatis, intelligit quascunque miserias, in quas homi-num conditio secum trahit, quales Christus etiam in se fuit expertus: sed in primis illas, quas quæ in animis locum habent: qui ad has præcipuè curandas, & leuådas Christus missus est, & solus potest eas minuere seu auferre. Vnde & peccata, et omnia, quæ ad damnationem pertrahunt, hoc nomine infirmitatum intelliguntur, quæ tamen Christus in se non sensit, sicut mox diserte exceptio peccatorum in Christo ponitur. Sic verò alibi in scripturis peccatum vocatur languor seu infirmitas, & peccatis obnoxij infirmi: vt Esaiæ 53. Non est species ei neque decor, & vidimus eum, & non erat aspectus, & desiderauimus eum despectum, & nouissimum virorum, virum dolorum, & scientem infirmitatem: & quasi abscoditus vultus eius, & despectus: vnde nec reputauimus eum: verè languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portauit. Psalmo 6. Miserere mei Domine, ἐπὶ ἀσθενὴς εἰμί, sana me Domine, quoniam conturbata sunt ossa mea. Vbi de infirmitate spirituali sermonem esse non est dubium.
units.tr: Moreover, by the word ἀσθενείας [ἀσθενείας], that is, infirmity, he means whatever miseries the human condition brings with it, and of which Christ himself also had experience; but above all those that have their place in the mind. Christ was sent to cure and relieve these especially, and he alone can lessen or remove them. Hence sins too, and everything that drags people toward condemnation, are understood under this name of infirmities. Christ did not feel these in himself, as is soon made clear by the explicit exception of sin in Christ. Elsewhere in Scripture sin is indeed called languor or infirmity, and those subject to sin are called weak, as in Isaiah 53: "He has no form or comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows." Psalm 6: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak [ἐπὶ ἀσθενὴς εἰμί]; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled." That the discussion there concerns spiritual infirmity there is no doubt.

units.la: Et propriè homini tribuitur infirmitas ipsi per carne ingenita, quâ spiritus subleuat. Roman. 8. spiritus auxiliatur infirmitatibus nostris, συναντιλαμβάνεται τᾶις ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν. Atque aptissima est hæc vox ad suggerendam animis nostram ipsorum infirmitatem, propter quam Christi pontificis nostri opem implorare cogitur. Sicut primus gradus est ad sanitatem corporalem recuperandam, nolle genus morbi: ita ad sanitatem spirituale primus gradus est, propriam infirmitatem agnoscere. Propter hanc infirmitatem Christus medicum se vocauit, & peccatores infirmos: Matth. 9. & 11.
units.tr: In the proper sense, infirmity is attributed to a man on account of the flesh innate in him, by which the Spirit comes to his aid. Romans 8: "the Spirit helps our infirmities [συναντιλαμβάνεται τᾶις ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν]." This word is most apt for bringing to our minds our own infirmity, on account of which we are compelled to implore the help of Christ our high priest. Just as the first step toward recovering bodily health is to be unwilling to acknowledge the kind of sickness, so the first step toward spiritual health is to recognise one's own infirmity. On account of this infirmity Christ called himself a physician and sinners the sick: Matthew 9 and 11.

units.la: Porrò ad comprobandum, Christū posse condolere nobis, addit, quomodo Christus quoq; dolores in se senserit, cum dicit: sed tentatum per omnia: singulæ voces habent magnā emphasin, vti capite secundo plenius à nobis declaratū est. Notat Erasmus rectius præponi disiunctiuâ, hoc pacto: sed tentatum, & paulò post dici, tentatum autem, & rectè. iuxta similitudinem: καθ' ὁμοιότητα id est, ad similitudinem nostram tentatus est, siue, prorsus eodem modo, quo nos tentamur. Notanda phrasis. Aliqui Hebraismū esse putant, quo summa æqualitas significatur. Significat autem hæc vox similitudinis, non tantùm similitudinem qualemcunque, quomodo id, quod pictum est, simile dicitur illi, quod verum in natura existit: sed plane omnimodam similitudinem & æqualitatem secundum substantiam. Quomodo Exodi 25. Faciesque mihi sanctuarium iuxta omnem similitudinē, quam ostendā tibi, id est, prorsus tale, quale illud, quod ostendo. Philippens. 2. Cum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam arbitratus est, vt esset æqualis Deo, sed semetipsum inaniuit, forma serui sumpta, in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus vt homo, humilem præbuit semetipsum. Roman. 5. Regnauit mors ab Adam vsque ad Mosen, in eos quoq;, qui non peccauerant in similitudinem (id est, eodem modo) transgressionis Adam. Quæ ideò repetimus, vt inhæreat omnium animis, quomodo possint Marcionitis & quibusdam Anabaptistis resistere, contendentibus, ob huiusmodi quasdam loquedi formulas, Christum non habuisse verum corpus, sed tantùm simile nostris corporib. id est, phantasma, & corpus tantùm imaginarium, apparés. Qui error ex multis aliis locis, quales aliquot suprà adnotauimus, refelli potest, præsertim vbi dicitur, Christū perom-nia similem fratribus, & semen Abrahæ apprehendisse, & mortem subijsse, &c.
units.tr: Next, to prove that Christ can sympathise with us, he adds how Christ also felt sorrows in himself, when he says: but tempted in all things. Each word carries great emphasis, as we explained more fully in the second chapter. Erasmus rightly observes that the disjunctive should be placed first, in this way: "but tempted," and shortly afterwards "tempted, however," and correctly so. according to likeness: καθ' ὁμοιότητα [καθ' ὁμοιότητα], that is, he was tempted in our likeness, or, in exactly the same way in which we are tempted. This is a phrase to be noted. Some think it is a Hebraism by which the highest equality is signified. This word of likeness signifies not merely any sort of likeness, such as a painted thing is called like that which really exists in nature, but a plain and complete likeness and equality in substance. So in Exodus 25: "And you shall make me a sanctuary according to all the likeness that I shall show you," that is, altogether such as that which I show. Philippians 2: "Who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself." Romans 5: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness (that is, in the same way) of Adam's transgression." We repeat these things so that they may cling to the minds of all, and so that they may be able to resist the Marcionites and certain Anabaptists, who contend, on account of such forms of speech, that Christ did not have a true body, but only one like our bodies, that is, a phantasm and an merely imaginary body that appeared. This error can be refuted from many other passages, some of which we have noted above, especially where it is said that Christ was in all things like his brethren, and took hold of the seed of Abraham, and underwent death, and so on.

units.la: Absque peccato) Hæc particula per correctionem valdè necessariò additur: ne quis, cùm dicitur, Christum per omnia tentatū, sicut nos tentamur, cogitet, in Christum etiam peccatum potuisse cadere, aut aliquem in eo habere locum. Peccatum autem, & quicquid ad id tendit, vel ex eo emergit, in eo non habuisse locum, alibi, vt Esaiæ 53. Ioan. 8. 1. Corinth. 5. 1. Petri 2. declaratur: nos suprà capite secundo, eadem testimonia citauimus. In secundo capite nō expressit hanc particulam, sed subintelligi voluit: vnde hic necessariò putauit adijciendam.
units.tr: without sin) This particle is added by way of correction, and is very necessary, lest anyone, when it is said that Christ was tempted in all things as we are tempted, should think that sin could have fallen upon Christ, or that it had any place in him. That sin, and whatever tends toward it or arises from it, had no place in him is declared elsewhere, as in Isaiah 53, John 8, 1 Corinthians 5, and 1 Peter 2; we cited these same testimonies above in the second chapter. In the second chapter he did not express this particle, but wished it to be understood; hence he thought it had to be added here.

units.la: Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad thronū gratiæ, vt consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam inueniamus ad opportunum auxilium.
units.tr: Let us therefore come with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace for timely help.

units.la: Christi bonitate erga nos & officio breuiter exposito, subijcit clariorem & pleniorem exhortationem, qua infert & monet omnes, vt alacriter magnaque fiducia ad Christum confugiant, ac per eum, & propter eum misericordiā expectent. Qua exhortatione omnes ad diligenter considerandum agnoscendumque Christi pontificatum excitantur, atque adeò vsus sacerdotij Christi in hac disputatione descripti, pulcherrimè aperitur, eo propemodū pacto, quo, qui in bonis artib. tradere præceptiones aliquas volunt, prius ad illiciendos excitandosque omnium discentium animos, de vsu earum solent non-nihil præliBare. Quamobrem, iudicandus est Apostolus admodum artificiosè propositioni disputationis exhortationem de vero vsu sacerdotij Christi in hunc modum admiscuisse. Describitur autem hic sacerdotium Christi, in disputatione sequenti, ad probandum quidem veteris sacerdotij atque adeò legis abrogationem: sed tamen interea nobis quoq; alius vsus sacerdotij Christi, spiritualis videlicet,& priuatim ad conscientias om- nium confirmandas pertinens, venit considerandus. Hunc verò Apostolus iam paucis verbis insinuat, vt vnusquisq; deinceps altiori animo eum rimetur. Dicit igitur, Christum esse pontificem, & quidem per omnia nostro more tentatum, vt tanto fidelius nostram ageret causam, & misericordia erga nos citius moueretur, ac per eum expectanda mise- ricordiam & gratiam. Talibus propemodum verbis vsus sacerdotij hic exprimitur. Sed quòd ex aliis locis aliis verbis possit plenius explicari, capite secundo supra dictum est. Christum misericordem & fidelem esse pontificem, in his, quæ apud Deum forent agen- da ad expiandum peccata populi. Et capite quinto mox sequenti, omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus constituitur, in his, quæ apud Deum aguntur, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis. Et paulò post subijcitur de Christo, quòd, cùm obtulisset precationes & supplicationes apud Deum, omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis æternæ. Deinde sæpius ibidem inculcatur, quomodo videlicet Christus sua victima, id est, oblatione sui ipsius purgauerit nostras conscientias, æternam redemptionem inuenerit, pro peccatis nostris satisfecerit. Quæ omnia plane idem sibi volunt, quod hic dicitur, videlicet Christum esse datum nobis pontificem, & quidem hominem nostri si- milem, ad miserendum nostri eo magis propensum, vt confidamus, nos per eum, & prop- ter eum, misericordiam ac gratiam consecuturos. Cùm autem valde magnum sit, mise- ricordiam & gratiam apud Deum consequi, peccata nostra deleri, purgari conscientias, intelligere debemus, multò maximum esse sacerdotij Christi vsum, & fructum amplisi- mum inde ad nos redire. Quamobrem primum ex hac doctrina de sacerdotio Christi æquû est, conscientias confirmari in fide, vt certò statuat, sibi propter Christum misericordiam et gratiam esse propositam. Audiunt enim hîc, Christum in hoc propositum esse sacerdo- tem, vt omnes fiduciâ habeant, se propter eum misericordiam & gratiam consecuturos.
units.tr: Having briefly set out Christ's goodness towards us and his office, he adds a clearer and fuller exhortation, by which he urges and bids all to flee to Christ eagerly and with great confidence, and through him and on account of him to look for mercy. By this exhortation all are roused to consider diligently and to acknowledge the priesthood of Christ, and thus the use of Christ's priesthood described in this discussion is most beautifully laid open, much as those who wish to teach some precepts in the liberal arts usually first offer some foretaste of their use, in order to attract and rouse the minds of all the learners. Therefore the Apostle is rightly judged to have very skilfully mingled with the proposition of his discussion an exhortation concerning the true use of Christ's priesthood. The priesthood of Christ is described here, in the following discussion, certainly to prove the abrogation of the old priesthood and so of the law; but meanwhile there also comes to our consideration another use of Christ's priesthood, namely the spiritual use, pertaining especially to the confirmation of the consciences of all. The Apostle now hints at this in a few words, so that each may henceforth search it out with a higher mind. He says, then, that Christ is a high priest, and indeed one tempted in all things after our manner, so that he might plead our cause the more faithfully and be more quickly moved to mercy towards us, and so that mercy and grace may be looked for through him. In such nearly these words the use of the priesthood is expressed here. But that it can be explained more fully from other passages, in other words, was said above in the second chapter: that Christ is a merciful and faithful high priest in those things which are to be done before God for the expiation of the sins of the people. And in the fifth chapter, immediately following, every high priest who is taken from among men is appointed for men in those things which are done before God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. And a little later it is added concerning Christ that, when he had offered prayers and supplications to God, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obeyed him. Then elsewhere in the same place it is repeatedly inculcated how Christ, by his sacrifice, that is, by the offering of himself, purged our consciences, obtained eternal redemption, and satisfied for our sins. All these things plainly mean the same as what is said here, namely that Christ has been given to us as a high priest, and one who is like us in nature, and therefore the more inclined to have mercy on us, so that we may be confident that we shall obtain mercy and grace through him and on account of him. Since it is indeed a very great thing to obtain mercy and grace before God, to have our sins blotted out and our consciences cleansed, we ought to understand that the use of Christ's priesthood is far greater, and that the most abundant fruit of it returns to us. Therefore, first, it is right that from this doctrine of Christ's priesthood the consciences should be confirmed in faith, so that they may firmly determine that mercy and grace are set before them on account of Christ. For they hear here that Christ has been set forth as priest for this purpose, that all may have confidence that they will obtain mercy and grace through him.

units.la: Secundò, admodum consolatoria est hæc cognitio omnibus conscientijs multitudine & magnitudine peccatorum suorum territis, & impulsu Satanæ ad desperationem inclinan- tibus: hic habent, quo mètes erigant, & contra desperationis venenum sibi medeantur. Respiciant in pontificē Christum, & is pro ipsis apud Deum intercedet, vt misericordiam & gratiam consequantur.
units.tr: Secondly, this knowledge is very comforting to every conscience that is terrified by the number and magnitude of its sins and is inclined towards despair under the prompting of Satan. Here they have something by which to lift up their minds and find a remedy against the poison of despair. Let them look to Christ the high priest, and he will intercede with God on their behalf, that they may obtain mercy and grace.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd ex sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi, nos quoq; munus sacerdotij accipia- mus, vt videlicet nos ipsos hostiâ sanctam & viuentem Deo offeramus, (Rom.12.) & nos totos diuinis rebus consecremus: de quo 1. Petri 2. In summa, maximus vsus sacerdotij Christi ex eo poteit colligi, quòd quæ pasim in doctrina euangelij sonât Dei misericor- diam & gratiam, quæ propter Christum contingit, ad sacerdotium Christi referenda sunt, & sacerdotium istud nobis ponunt ob oculos. Igitur paucis hisce verbis Apostolus res maximas & vtilissimas expressit. Sed iamquàm proprijs & elegantibus id effecerit, videamus.
units.tr: Thirdly, from the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ we also receive the office of priesthood, namely that we offer ourselves as a holy and living sacrifice to God (Rom. 12), and consecrate ourselves wholly to divine things; on this see 1 Pet. 2. In sum, the greatest use of Christ's priesthood can be gathered from this: that what the gospel doctrine everywhere proclaims of God's mercy and grace, which comes to us because of Christ, is to be referred to Christ's priesthood, and sets that priesthood before our eyes. So in these few words the Apostle has expressed very great and very useful things. But let us see how skilfully and elegantly he has done it.

units.la: Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ. Quando, inquit, Christus talis tantusque est pontifex, nimirum cœlos penetrans, & filius Dei: deinde, quando adeò misericors est, & ad iuuandum tentatos propensus: accedamus eum, eius opem imploremus, magna cum fiducia, & ne dubitemus, quin misericordiam & gratiam simus ab eo accepturi.
units.tr: Let us therefore draw near with confidence to the throne of grace. Since Christ, he says, is such a great high priest, who has indeed passed through the heavens, and is the Son of God; and since he is so merciful and so ready to help those who are tempted, let us approach him, let us implore his aid with great confidence, and let us not doubt that we shall receive mercy and grace from him.

units.la: Accedamus autem idem est, quod imploremus opem, inuocemus, fidamus. Neque de accessione, quæ fit motu corporis, sed de accessione mentis seu cordis sermo est. Quomodo etiâ capite decimo huius epistolæ dicitur, quæ verba cum his conueniunt: cum ha beamus sacerdotē magnū præfectū domui Dei, accedamus cū vero corde in certitudine fidei. Et capite vndecimo: Nam, qui accedit ad Deum, hūc credere oportet esse Deum, & esse remuneratorem quærentibus se. Sumpta autē est forma loquēdi ab eo, quod principes seu magnates, præsertim si paulò duriores sint & implacabiles, vulgus minus audet accedere, at verò qui comes sunt, & benigni, & facilè conuenire possunt, eas quiuis adire audet. Quò pertinet, quod diserte addidit, cum fiducia, interpretatur audaciâ, qua intrepidè aliquid agimus vel aggredimur, alias etiam libertate, quemadmo dum exposuimus supra capite tertio super illo verbo, Cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & gloriationem spei firmam tenuerimus. Certè hoc loco spem obtinendi petita, & non patiendi repulsam significat, iubetq; ea vox sic confirmatos esse animo omnes, qui per Christū & propter Christum aliquid impetrare volunt, vt statuant pro certo, se id accepturos, nulloq; metu patiendi repulsam debere eos percelli. In quam sententiam Iacobus cap.1. præcipit, vt ij, qui postulare aliquid à Deo volunt, faciant id cum fiducia, nihil hæsitantes. Nam qui hæsitat, is similis est fluctui maris, qui ventis agitur & impetu rapitur. Neque existimet homo ille, se quicquam acceptu-rum à Domino. Vbi valde elegantibus similitu- tinibus
units.tr: Accedamus means the same as imploremus, invocemus, fidamus: let us implore help, call upon him, trust. The word refers not to approaching by bodily movement but to the approach of mind or heart. So also in chapter ten of this epistle it is said, in words that agree with these: "Since we have a high priest set over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart in the assurance of faith." And in chapter eleven: "For he who comes to God must believe that God exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him." The form of speech is taken from the way people approach great men. Princes and magnates, especially if they are rather harsh and implacable, are approached by the common people with little boldness; but those who are affable and kind, and easy to meet, are approached by anyone who dares. To this belongs the phrase he adds, with confidence, which means boldness, by which we act or undertake something fearlessly, and also freedom, as we explained above in chapter three on the words, "whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the glorying of hope." Here, certainly, the word denotes hope of obtaining what is asked, and not fear of being refused. It bids all who wish to obtain something through Christ and for Christ's sake to be so strengthened in mind that they hold it as certain that they will receive it, and that they must not be struck by any fear of being refused. James, in chapter one, enjoins to this same effect that those who wish to ask anything of God should ask in faith, doubting nothing. For the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed about, and that man should not think he will receive anything from the Lord. There, by very elegant comparisons, is described the feeling of those who doubt God's goodness, or tremble lest they be repelled.

units.la: Vsus spiritualis ... fiducia & audaciam suppli cationis diuinæ notat. Fides orantiû. dinibus describitur dubitantium de bonitate Dei, vel trepidantium ne repellantur, affectus: & praeterea quali fiducia oporteat nos Deum invocare.
units.tr: The spiritual use... denotes the boldness and confidence of divine supplication. The faith of those who pray. Besides, it sets forth with what kind of confidence we ought to call upon God.

units.la: Ad throinum) Et hic voce throni per metaphoram mirabilem ostendit Christi dignitate. Depingit enim instar regis, & maximi cuiusdam pontificis sedentem in sublimi throno, (quādoquidem is vere sedet in coelis ad dexteram patris) cuius maiestate omnes reuereri merito debeant, ἐφόν enim vt plurimum regiam sellam significat: vt in libro Iudicum scribitur, Eglon regem Moabitarum surrexisse de throno suo, cum ei loqueretur Ehud. Etiam libris Reg. palsim: 3. Reg. 10. fecit rex Solomon thronum de ebore grandem, & vestiuit eum auro fulvo nimis, qui habebat sex gradus. Quibus omnibus locis vocabulum throni habetur. Iudith 1. Iurauit Nabuchodonosor per thronum & regnum suum, quod defenderet se de omnibus regionibus his. Vbi pro maiestate & potentia per Metonymiam accipitur.
units.tr: Ad thronum: here, by the wonderful metaphor of the word "throne," he shows the dignity of Christ. For he portrays him as a king and a great high priest sitting on a lofty throne (since he truly sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father), whose majesty all rightly ought to revere. For θρόνος [thronos] for the most part signifies a royal seat, as in the book of Judges it is written that Eglon, king of the Moabites, rose from his throne when Ehud spoke to him. Also in the books of Kings, passim; in 3 Kings 10: King Solomon made a great throne of ivory and covered it with very fine gold, which had six steps. In all these places the word "throne" occurs. Judith 1: Nebuchadnezzar swore by his throne and his kingdom that he would avenge himself on all those regions. There the word is taken by metonymy for majesty and power.

units.la: Qua descriptione cum Christi dignitas elegantissime delineetur, tum possent miseri peccatores aliquo modo deterreri, quo minus illum auderent accedere. Sed Apostolus, ne hoc incommodi sequeretur, prudenter vocavit hunc thronum Christi thronum gratiae. Non occupat Christus thronum severitatis vel horrendi iudicij, sed gratiae & misericordiae: Quia gratia & veritas potissimum contingit per Iesum Christum: Ioan. 1. Saepius autem ad explicandam maiestatem Christi in Scripturis, ei thronus tribuitur: vt supra capite primo ex Psalmo 44. Psalmo 83. vbi vaticinium habetur de Christo ex semine David regnaturo: Semel iuravi in sancto meo, si David mentiar, semen eius in aeternum manebit. Et capite octavo praesentis epistolae statim initio. Thronum autem gratiae competere Christo, omnes illi loci testantur, qui docent, per Christum misericordiam, & gratiam mundo allatam. Recte ergo ait, adeundum nobis thronum gratiae, vt consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam inueniamus: Vt consequamur, inquit, misericordiam, & gratiam inueniamus. En quare adeundus thronus gratiae, & quid a tanta maiestate Christi debeamus expectare. Summae maiestati & potentiae summa adiuncta est misericordia. Et per potificatum Christi misericordiam & gratiam accipimus. Appositissime aute expressit hic, gratis, & nullis nostris meritis misericordiam Dei nobis propter solum Christum obtingere. Nam praeterquam quod vocabulum gratiae illud satis arguat, (sic enim Rom. 11. clare argumentatur: Quod si per gratiam, iam non ex operibus: Quandoquidem gratia iam non est gratia, &c.) tum vero vocabulum inueniendi ide satis declarat. Hinc valde vsitata est Scripturis haec phrasis, inuenire gratiam in oculis, pro eo, quod est, praeter meritum sola benevolentia placere. Sic Exodi 33. Dixit Moses ad Dominum: praecipis, vt educam populum istum, & non indicas mihi, quem missurus es mecum, praesertim cum dixeris: Novi te ex nomine, & inuenisti gratiam coram me. Si ergo inueni gratiam in conspectu tuo, ostende mihi faciem tuam, vt sciam te, et inueniam gratiam ante oculos tuos. Respice populum tuum, gentem hanc. Et Luc. 1. Angelus ad Mariam, Ne timeas Maria, nacta es enim gratiam apud Deum: graece, εὗρες χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ. Et nos accipere gratiam, & Deus dare gratiam, eodem fere sensu dicitur. Quae phrases vsitatae sunt Scripturis, ad exprimendam gratuitam Dei erga nos misericordiam contra vlla nostra merita exhibitam. Quanquam est & hoc notandum, quod Scriptura Christo etiam tribuat thronum iudicij & severitatis. Quemadmodum Psalmo 9. Parauit in iudicio thronum suum, & ipse iudicabit orbem terrae in aequitate, & iudicabit populos in iustitia. Et cap. primo huius epistolae ex Psalmo 44. thronus iudicij Christo tribuitur, verum de secundo Christi aduentu haec dignitas & potestas iudicandi accipienda est: vnde ipse ait Matthaei 25. Cum venerit filius hominis in gloria sua, & omnes sancti angeli cum eo, tunc sedebit super sede gloriae suae, & congregabuntur ante eum omnes gentes. Et Lucae 22. Christus disponit apostolis, vt sedeat olim super thronos, iudicates duodecim tribus Israel. Ergo Christo alius est thronus gratiae, alius iudicij. Sed gratiae thronum ipse nunc insidet, vbi ad dexteram Dei patris constitutus, nunc intercedit pro nobis, & pontificatus munere fungitur, sicut postea functurus est munere regis & severi iudicis. Porro de throno gratiae nunc adeundo, antequam ille se transferat ad thronum iudicij, hoc loco sermo est: & quādoita insidet Christus throno gratiae, misericordiam possumus consequi & inuenire gratiam, si cum fiducia eum adeamus & invocemus, sicut sequitur.
units.tr: Since Christ's dignity is most elegantly portrayed by this description, wretched sinners might be in some way deterred from daring to approach him. But the Apostle, lest this inconvenience follow, wisely called this throne the throne of grace. Christ does not occupy the throne of severity or of dreadful judgment, but of grace and mercy, because grace and truth came chiefly through Jesus Christ (John 1). Moreover, a throne is often attributed to Christ in the Scriptures to explain his majesty: as above in chapter 1 from Psalm 44, and Psalm 83, where there is a prophecy about Christ, who was to reign from the seed of David: Once I have sworn by my holiness that I will not lie to David; his seed shall endure for ever. And at the very beginning of chapter 8 of the present letter. That the throne of grace belongs to Christ, all those passages bear witness which teach that mercy and grace have been brought to the world through Christ. Rightly, then, he says that we must approach the throne of grace, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace: so that we may obtain, he says, mercy, and find grace. Here is why the throne of grace is to be approached, and what we ought to expect from the great majesty of Christ. Great mercy is joined to supreme majesty and power. And through Christ's priesthood we receive mercy and grace. Most aptly he has expressed here that God's mercy comes to us freely, without any merits of ours, through Christ alone. For, apart from the fact that the word grace sufficiently proves this (for thus Rom. 11 argues clearly: But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace, etc.), the word find also sufficiently makes it plain. Hence this phrase is very common in the Scriptures: to find grace in the eyes of someone, meaning to please by goodwill alone, apart from merit. So in Exodus 33 Moses said to the Lord: You command me to lead this people, and you do not tell me whom you will send with me, especially since you have said: I know you by name, and you have found grace before me. If then I have found grace in your sight, show me your face, that I may know you and find grace before your eyes. Look upon your people, this nation. And Luke 1, the angel to Mary: Fear not, Mary, for you have found grace with God; in Greek, εὗρες χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ [you have found grace with God]. Also to receive grace and God to give grace are spoken in almost the same sense. These phrases are common in the Scriptures for expressing God's freely given mercy towards us, shown against all our merits. Yet this too is to be noted: the Scripture also attributes to Christ the throne of judgment and severity, as in Psalm 9: He has prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness, and he will judge the peoples in uprightness. And in chapter 1 of this letter, from Psalm 44, the throne of judgment is attributed to Christ; but this dignity and power of judging is to be understood of Christ's second coming, whence he himself says in Matthew 25: When the Son of man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit upon the seat of his glory, and all the nations will be gathered before him. And in Luke 22, Christ appoints for the apostles that they shall sit one day upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. So Christ has one throne of grace and another of judgment.
