But he now sits on the throne of grace, where, placed at the right hand of God the Father, he now intercedes for us and discharges the office of priest, just as he will afterwards discharge the office of king and stern judge. Moreover, the throne of grace which we are now to approach is what is spoken of here, before he transfers himself to the throne of judgment; and while Christ sits on the throne of grace, we can obtain mercy and find grace, if we approach and invoke him with confidence, as follows.

units.la: Ad oportunum auxilium) Hanc particulam video a veteribus sic expositam, vt de opportunitate temporis accipi velint, quasi significaretur, nunc nunc adeundum esse & interpelandum Christum: quandoquidem hoc tempore oportunum est, ab eo auxilium petere & expectare: atque ipse nunc propior est ad subueniendum, quam olim erit, vbi sedebit pro tribunali, seuerum agens iudicem. In quam sententiam &c 2. Corinth. 6. dicitur: In tempore accepto exaudiui te (quod ex Esaiae 49. sumptum est) & in die salutis succurri tibi. Ecce nunc tempus acceptum, ecce nunc dies salutis. Ita fere Chrysostomus & Primasius. Quae quidem interpretatio licet mihi non improbetur, quandoquidem graece habetur,
units.tr: The phrase "for timely help": I see that the older writers explain this particle as referring to the opportuneness of the time, as if it meant that now, at this time, we must draw near to Christ and plead with him, since it is timely now to seek and expect help from him, and he is now nearer to help than he will be later, when he sits on the judgment seat as a stern judge. To this sense belongs 2 Corinthians 6: "In an acceptable time I have heard you" (which is taken from Isaiah 49), "and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." So Chrysostom and Primasius more or less interpret it. Although I do not reject this interpretation, since it is found in Greek,

units.la: Thronus Christi gratiae, non severitatis et iudicij. Chrjstum in gratiam patris restituit omnes credentes. Gratia dei excludit opera sive merita hominum. Thronus iudicij & severitatis impijs et incredulis paratus. Secundus Christi aduentus ad iudicium. Matthaei 19. Quomodo Christus functur munere pontificis, & iudicis. Tempus opportunitas non negligenda. 2. Corinth. 6. Tempus gratiae & salutis sub euangelio nobis manifestatum est. ἀπ' ἀνυκτὸν βούλεσαι, & προ̈ς ad tempus, adeoque articulum temporis proprie refertur: attamen non incommode puto reddiderimus, in oportunum auxilium: & sententiam ad modum seu formam auxilij referemus, perinde ac si dicatur: Etsi variis modis Deus posset nobis prospicere, nosque ad salutem adducere, tamen nullum auxilium commodius magisque oportunum, quam gratia & misericordia. Misericordia & gratia sunt nobis in oportunum auxilium, sicut dicitur aliquid in medicinam esse. Non opera nostra, vel quicquam aliud oportune in auxilium posset adhiberi, sed sola gratia & misericordia nobis prosunt, & oportune pro auxilio a Deo praestantur. In quam sententiam illud Psalmo centesimovigesimonono videtur accipiendum, Si iniquitates observaueris Domine, Domine quis sustinebit? Quia apud te propitiatio est, & propter legem tuam sustinui te Domine: & que ibi sequuntur. Item Psalmo centesimo quadragesimo secundo, Non intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis viuens. Quibus significatur, nulla ratione commodius oportuniusue succurri potuisse humano generi, per gratiam & misericordiam, cum alias, si iustitia operum humanorum fuisse expectanda, vel examinanda, nihil nisi damnationem promererentur. Atque ita gratia & misericordia in oportunum auxilium contingerent, per Iesum Christum pontificem nostrum, gratiae & misericordiae omnis autorem.
units.tr: The throne of Christ is a throne of grace, not of severity and judgment. He restores all believers to the Father's favour in Christ. Grace excludes the works or merits of men. The throne of judgment and severity is prepared for the impious and unbelieving. The second coming of Christ is for judgment. Matthew 19. How Christ functions in the office of priest and judge. Opportunity in time is not to be neglected. 2 Corinthians 6. The time of grace and salvation has been made known to us under the gospel. The preposition [ἀπ' ἀνυκτὸν βούλεσαι], and [πρός] with reference to time, is properly applied to the time-marker itself. Nevertheless, I think it is not unsuitable to render it as timely help, and to relate the sense to the manner or form of the help, as if one said: although God could provide for us in various ways and bring us to salvation, yet no help is more convenient and timely than grace and mercy. Mercy and grace are for us a timely help, just as something is said to be a medicine. Our works, or anything else, could not be applied as timely help, but only grace and mercy profit us, and are rightly granted to us by God as help. In this sense Psalm 129 seems to be understood: "If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand? For there is forgiveness with you, and because of your law I have waited for you, Lord," and what follows there. Likewise Psalm 142: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no living man shall be justified." By these words it is signified that by grace and mercy no more convenient or timely help could have been given to mankind by any means; whereas otherwise, if the righteousness of human works were to be expected or examined, they would merit nothing but damnation. And so grace and mercy come as timely help through Jesus Christ our priest, the author of all grace and mercy.

units.la: Caeterum, nos multiplicem & variam doctrinam ex his paucis debemus nobis excerpere. Ante omnia autem hoc excipiemus pertinens ad docendi methodum, vsurpandumque, quoties grauiorem aliquam disputationem volumus instituere: nimirum, vt de vsu earum rerum, quibus de agimus, nonnulla statim praemittamus: quomodo cernimus Apostolum hic facere, quando monet, in hoc nobis proponi disputatione de Christi sacerdotio, vt certi reddamur de misericordia & gratia propter Christum pontificem accipienda. Et certe, vbi hoc pacto auditores initio disputationis admonentur de vtilitate & fructu negotij tractandi, multo magis accenduntur ad penitus id percipiendum, nec non animum in id intendunt, vt priuatim commodum quantum fieri potest, inde capiant. Ea propter qui artes docent aliquas, solent ante omnia animos discipulorum acuere, agedo de artis, quam tradunt, sine & vsu siue fructu: id quod & apud Dialecticos & apud Rhetores in primis licet obseruare.
units.tr: Moreover, from these few words we ought to draw out various and manifold teaching. Above all, we shall take from this a point pertaining to the method of teaching, to be used whenever we wish to undertake some weightier disputation: namely, that we should first set forth some matters concerning the use of the things we are discussing. We see the Apostle doing this here, when he warns that this disputation about Christ's priesthood is set before us so that we may be assured that mercy and grace are to be received because of Christ our priest. And indeed, when hearers are admonished at the outset of a disputation about the usefulness and fruit of the matter to be treated, they are much more stirred to grasp it thoroughly, and they direct their minds to take from it, as far as possible, some private benefit. Therefore those who teach any arts usually, above all, sharpen the minds of their pupils by speaking first of the use and fruit of the art they are handing on; this can be observed especially among the dialecticians and the rhetoricians.

units.la: Secundo, hic discimus, quis sit vsus sacerdotij Christi tam publice in ecclesia, quam priuatim in conscientijs. Etsi enim instituta sit disputatio de sacerdotio Christi, ad probandum, quod per nouum sacerdotium Christi abrogatum sit vetus sacerdotium Aaronicum, ac proinde simul lex: tamen praemonet, vnicuique priuatim hunc fustum esse propositum, vt in tentationibus consolationem hanc accipiant, quod vidclicet, Christus homo ideo sit sacerdos, & sequester inter Deum & homines, vt per eum misericordiam & gratiam consequamur. Vbi caro, mundus, vel Satanas nos molestant, coguntque, de remissione peccatorum desperare, erigendus est animus, respiciendumque, omissa nostra & dignitate & indignitate, ad pontificem animarum nostrarum Iesum Christum, & pro certo statuendum, quod is misericordiam & gratiam per suum sacrificium, quod in ara crucis pro nobis obtulit, nobis apud patrem caelestem obtinebit. Quare & consolationem accipere nos vult apostolus ex sacerdotio Christi, & praeterea conscientias in fide de peccatorum remissione confirmari. Eamque ob causam vult nos constanter tenere hanc de pontificatu Christi professionem, quando Christus talis est potifex, nimirum miseriarum nostrarum particeps, vt ad miserendum nostri fit propensior.
units.tr: Second, here we learn what the use of Christ's priesthood is, both publicly in the Church and privately in consciences. For although the disputation is set up about Christ's priesthood in order to prove that by the new priesthood of Christ the old Aaronic priesthood, and therefore the law at the same time, has been abrogated, yet it also forewarns that this is set before each person privately so that in temptations they may receive this consolation: that Christ, as man, is therefore priest and mediator between God and men, so that through him we may obtain mercy and grace. Where the flesh, the world, or Satan trouble us and force us to despair of the forgiveness of sins, the spirit must be raised up, and, setting aside both our worthiness and our unworthiness, we must look to Jesus Christ, the priest of our souls, and hold it for certain that he will obtain for us mercy and grace from the heavenly Father through his sacrifice which he offered for us on the altar of the cross. Hence the Apostle wishes us to receive consolation from the priesthood of Christ, and besides, that consciences be confirmed in faith concerning the forgiveness of sins. For this reason he wants us to hold constantly to this confession about the priesthood of Christ, since Christ is such a priest, namely a sharer in our miseries, so that he may be the more inclined to have mercy on us.

units.la: Quin etiam de nostro spirituali sacerdotio, quo per Christi sacerdotium omnes credentes initiantur, vt se ipsos Domino, totos consecrent, hic admonemur. Sed de hoc sacerdotio, nos in sequentibus nonnihil dicemus.
units.tr: Indeed, here we are also reminded of our spiritual priesthood, by which all believers are initiated through the priesthood of Christ, so that they wholly consecrate themselves to the Lord. But we shall say something more about this priesthood in what follows.

units.la: Quarto, quando hic audimus, per solum Christi contingere gratiam & misericordiam, discamus, solum Christum esse verum & ordinarium mediatorem atque aduocatum, non nostra opera vel satisfactiones, vel ἐπιλοβημασίας, multo minus opera sanctorum, praesertim mortuorum. Ille solus propter suam dignitatem Deo patri placet, & exaudi-tur. Hic est filius meus dilectus, inquit, pater, in quo mihi bene complacitum est: & propter illum solum etiam nos, si quando oramus, exaudimur. Ipse est simul sacerdos offerens & intercedens pro nobis: Ipse est simul hostia placens & placans. Nullus sanctorum vel pro proprijs peccatis potest iustae irae Dei satisfacere, multo minus pro peccatis aliorum. Solus autem Christus is est, qui mortuus est, & satisfecit pro peccatis non suis, quae nulla habuit, sed totius mundi, hoc est, nostris & eorum omnium, qui vel ante nos fuerunt, vel post nos erunt. Proinde magnus vsus est huius disputationis de Christi sacerdotio: nec solum ex eo discere debemus, sacerdotium legale, adeoque ipsam legem per sacerdotium tiū Christi abrogatā esse, sed insuper nobis viam ad salutē per id esse patefactā, & Christū in hoc esse factū sacerdotē, vt pro peccatis nostris offerret Deo patri, ac satisfaceret. Valde ergo prudenter & vtiliter Apostolus in initio nouæ huius disputationis ista insinuauit.
units.tr: Fourth, when we hear here that grace and mercy come through Christ alone, let us learn that Christ alone is the true and appointed mediator and advocate, not our works or satisfactions, or [ἐπιλοβημασίας], much less the works of the saints, especially of the dead. He alone, because of his dignity, is pleasing to God the Father and is heard. "This is my beloved Son," says the Father, "in whom I am well pleased;" and for his sake alone we too are heard whenever we pray. He is at once the priest offering and interceding for us; he is at once the victim that pleases and propitiates. No saint, even for his own sins, can satisfy the just wrath of God, much less for the sins of others. Christ alone is he who died and made satisfaction for sins not his own, since he had none, but for the sins of the whole world, that is, for ours and for all those who were before us or will be after us. Therefore this disputation about Christ's priesthood is of great use: from it we ought to learn not only that the legal priesthood, and so the law itself, has been abrogated by the priesthood of Christ, but also that a way to salvation has been opened up through it, and that Christ has been made priest in this respect, to offer and make satisfaction to God the Father for our sins. Very wisely and usefully, therefore, the Apostle at the beginning of this new disputation hinted at these things.

units.la: CAPVT QVINTVM. CONFIRMATIO.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE. CONFIRMATION.

units.la: NAM omnis pōtifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus constituitur, in his quæ apud Deū aguntur, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis, qui placabilis esse possit ignorantibus & errantibus, quandoquidem & ipse circundatus est infirmitate. Et propter hac debet, quēadmodum pro populo, ita & pro seipso immolare pro peccatis. Nemo sibi ipsi vsurpat honorē, sed qui vocatur etiā a Deo, quēadmodum & Aaron. Ita et Christus non semetipsum glorificauit, vt fieret pōtifex, sed is qui dixerat illi: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Sicut & alibi dicit: Tu es sacerdos in æternum, secūdum ordinē Melchisedeck. Qui in diebus carnis suæ, cūm et precationes & supplicationes apud illum, qui poterat ipsum a morte seruare, cum clamore valido et lachrymis obtulisset, et exauditus esset pro reuerentia, tametsi filius erat, tamen didicit ex his, quæ passus est, obedientiam, ac perfectus redditus omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis æternæ, cognominatus a Deo pontifex secundum ordinationem Melchisedeck.
units.tr: For every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed for men in the things that pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; one who can have compassion on the ignorant and erring, since he himself also is surrounded with infirmity. And because of this he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins. And no one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. As he also says elsewhere: You are a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedec. Who, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with strong crying and tears, and was heard for his reverence; though he was a son, yet he learned obedience from the things he suffered, and being made perfect he became to all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation, named by God a high priest according to the order of Melchisedec.

units.la: ONFIRMATIO, in qua Apostolus hoc ordine progreditur, vt ante omnia presenti capite doceat, Christum esse verum legitimumq; pontificē. Deinde, quia non satis erat ostendisse Christum esse sacerdotē, vtpote quo nihil aliud, quàm æquaretur dūtaxat sacerdotibus reliquis, ideò capite septimo (nam quicquid a dimidio huius quinti capitis ad septimū vsque interponitur, ad admixtam digressionē hortatoriam pertinet) declarat argumentis artificiosissimis, pontificatum Christi multò præstatiorem esse pontificatu legali. Hoc vero probato, rectè infert, hunc illi debere cedere, atq; hunc adeoq; ipsam simul legem per Christi pontificatum abrogari: id quod capite octauo Scripturæ testimonijs aptissimè corroborat. Capite vero nono, altera confirmationis pars queat constitui. Nam eo quàm exactissimè docet, Christum pontificatus munere egregiè functum, nec non sacrificium obtulisse, quod omnibus itidem sacrificijs veterum longè præferri mereatur. Ex quo capite decimo infert, etiam sacrificiale galia per sacrificium Christi abolita. Atque ita non tantùm sacerdotium veteris testamenti, verùm etiam sacrificia omnia (pro quibus retinendis, Iudæi fortasis etiam post concessionem abrogati sacerdotij voluissent contendere) per sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi sublata esse, aptissima methodo in hac confirmatione ostedit. Primo igitur loco hīc perspicuè probat, Christum esse verum & legitimum pontificem, idque in hunc fere modum: Colligit breuiter quænam potissimum necessaria sint, vt quis in pontifice ordinetur, & pro pontifice agnoscatur: ea autem omnia Christo competere, & plenissimè in eo conspici, clarè docet: Vnde Christū esse verum pontificem manifestum habere vult. Ac videtur mihi summa argumentorum, quæ hīc ab Apostolo congeruntur, vna hac ratione comprehendi posse.
units.tr: This is the confirmation, in which the Apostle proceeds in the following order. First, in the present chapter, he teaches that Christ is the true and lawful high priest. Then, since it was not enough to have shown that Christ is a priest, for by that alone he would be merely equal to the other priests, therefore in the seventh chapter (for whatever lies between the middle of this fifth chapter and the seventh is an exhortation digressing in between) he declares, by most skilful arguments, that the priesthood of Christ is far more excellent than the legal priesthood. Having proved this, he rightly infers that the latter must give way to the former, and that the law itself is thereby abrogated through the priesthood of Christ. This he confirms very aptly by testimonies of Scripture in the eighth chapter. In the ninth chapter a second part of the confirmation can be marked out, for there he teaches most exactly that Christ discharged the office of priest with distinction and offered a sacrifice which deserves to be preferred far above all the sacrifices of the old covenant. From this, in the tenth chapter, he infers that the sacrificial law too has been abolished through the sacrifice of Christ. And so, by a most apt method in this confirmation, he shows that not only the priesthood of the Old Testament but all the sacrifices (for the retention of which the Jews perhaps would have contended even after the abrogation of the priesthood was conceded) have been taken away through the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. First, therefore, he here clearly proves that Christ is the true and lawful priest, and he does so in roughly this way. He briefly gathers which things are chiefly necessary for someone to be ordained as priest and acknowledged as such, and he clearly teaches that all of these belong to Christ and are seen fully in him. Hence he wants it to be plain that Christ is the true priest. And the sum of the arguments gathered here by the Apostle seems to me to be comprehended under this one line of reasoning.

units.la: Quicunq; habet omnes virtutes seu qualitates veri & legitimi pontificis, æquum est, hunc pro vero pontifice agnoscamus.
units.tr: Whoever has all the virtues or qualities of a true and lawful priest, it is right that we acknowledge him as a true priest.

units.la: Atqui Christus habet omnes eiusmodi virtutes & qualitates. Igitur Christus pro vero pontifice agnoscì debet.
units.tr: But Christ has all such virtues and qualities. Therefore Christ ought to be acknowledged as a true priest.

units.la: Nos autem partium in tyronum gratiam facientes seriem argumentorum, & quæ membra cum quibus sint coniungenda, indicabimus nec non rudius & clarius, vt est in prouerbio, singula explicare enitemur. Debent autem omnia hæc ab initio capitis, Nam omnis pontifex, &c. ad eum vsque locum, de quo nobis forent multa dicenda, &c. coniūgi, & velut in vnam orationem perpetuam colligari quandoquidem vna tantum connexionis nota (vbi videlicet semel dicitur, ita & Christus, &c.) posteriora membra prioribus coaptantur. Porrò è multis virtutibus seu qualitatibus in bono pontifice spectádis, tres aut quatuor potissimum eligit, quas dum in Christo elucere cōmonstrat, totidem efficacibus argumetis inde eductis, Christum esse verum pontificē euincit. Sed est paulò difficilius, argumentorū diuersitatē & collocationē obseruare. Quia enim Apostolus partim breuitatis, partim elegantiæ studio ductus, plura argumeta conatus est pau cis com.
units.tr: But for the benefit of beginners, we will set out the sequence of the arguments and which members are to be joined with which, and we will try to explain each point more plainly and clearly, as the proverb goes. All of these must be joined together from the beginning of the chapter, "For every high priest," etc., up to the place where much would have to be said, etc., and gathered into one continuous speech, since with only one mark of connection (namely where it is said once, "so also Christ," etc.) the later members are fitted to the earlier ones. Moreover, from the many virtues or qualities to be considered in a good priest, he chooses three or four principal ones, and while he shows them shining in Christ, he draws from them as many forceful arguments and so proves that Christ is the true high priest. But it is a little harder to observe the variety and arrangement of the arguments. For since the Apostle, partly led by a desire for brevity and partly by a desire for elegance, tried to comprehend many arguments in few words, he wished meanwhile to express everything in splendid language, with changes of sentence, and thus with a wholly rhetorical loftiness and variety.

units.la: Confirmatio. Christum esse sacerdotem verum. Christus præstatior pontifex Aarone et legalibus sacerdotibus: ideoq; abrogatus per hunc sacerdotē pontificatus legalis. Sacrificium legale per Christi sacrificium abrogatum. Christū esse verum pontificē. A virtutibus veri pontificis. eis comprehendere, interea tamen splendidis verbis sententiarum commutatione, adeoque prorsus rhetorica sublimitate ac varietate omnia exprimere voluit, hinc obscuritas suboritur orationi eius nonnulla videtur, et tyrones assueti dutaxat huius temporis in scholis vi-tato crasso nostro docendi more, quo singula constringuntur in arctos Syllogismos, & membra membris respondetia simpliciter componuntur, hic resistunt, neque certam sententiam possunt elicere. At nosse debent, summam esse artem, artem dissimulare, quod sane fecisse autorem huius epistolae extra controversiam est.
units.tr: Confirmation. That Christ is the true priest. Christ is a more excellent high priest than Aaron and the legal priests; therefore the legal priesthood has been abrogated through this priest. The legal sacrifice has been abrogated through Christ's sacrifice. That Christ is the true high priest. From the virtues of the true high priest. Hence obscurity arises in his discourse, and to some it seems that beginners, accustomed only to the schools of this age, where, avoiding our coarse method of teaching, by which each point is bound into tight syllogisms and members are simply matched one against another, stop here and cannot draw out a definite meaning. But they must know that it is the highest art to conceal art, which the author of this epistle certainly did, beyond all dispute.

units.la: Primum itaque argumentum a causa principali & officio pontificis, adeoque a propria & vsitata pontificis descriptione, atque in hunc modum argumentatur:
units.tr: First, therefore, the argument is drawn from the principal cause and office of the priest, and thus from the proper and customary description of a high priest, and it runs in this manner:

units.la: Omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus constituitur, in his, quae apud Deum aguntur, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis.
units.tr: Every high priest, who is taken from among men, is appointed for men in the things that pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.

units.la: Atqui Christus etiam homo ex hominibus est assumptus, & pro hominibus constitutus, in his, quae apud Deum sunt agenda, atque obtulit insuper donaria & victimas pro peccatis. Igitur Christus est pontifex. Hoc argumentum perspicue positum est, nihilque habet obscuritatis, atque ex Apostoli sententia totum est expressum. Verum ipse minore hanc splendidoribus verbis, & adhibita quodammodo cura illustradi amplificadique dignitate Christi, extulit, dicens: Ita & Christus in diebus carnis suae precationes & supplicationes apud illum qui poterat ipsum a morte seruare, id est, apud Deum patrem, cum clamore valido & lachrymis obtulit, & pro reuerentia exauditus est. Vbi clare vides, hoc membrum respondere, & coniungendo esse illi, quod pro Maiori collocamus, & prorsus eandem esse sententiam, quam in Minore expressimus, sed paululum diuersa verborum forma redditam. Non dissimili modo agit in argumentis reliquis.
units.tr: But Christ also was taken from among men and appointed for men in the things to be done before God, and moreover offered gifts and sacrifices for sins. Therefore Christ is a priest. This argument is plainly put, has no obscurity, and is wholly drawn from the Apostle's statement. Yet in the minor premise he has put it in more splendid words, and with some care to illustrate and magnify the dignity of Christ, saying: So also Christ, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, that is, to God the Father, with strong crying and tears, and was heard for his reverence. Here you clearly see that this member corresponds and is to be joined to what we have placed as the major premise, and that it is exactly the same sentiment as we expressed in the minor, but rendered in a slightly different form of words. He proceeds in much the same way in the other arguments.

units.la: Secundum argumentum ducit a qualitate personae, quae ad pontificatum possit proinoueri. Et sic ratiocinatur: Omnis, qui assumitur in pontificem, debet esse placabilis ignorantibus & errantibus.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from the quality of the person who may be promoted to the priesthood. And he reasons thus: everyone who is taken up as priest ought to be able to have compassion on the ignorant and erring.

units.la: Atqui Christus est placabilis & misericors erga ignorantes & errates. Ergo Christus est pontifex. Et hoc argumentum manifestum est, mentesque Apostoli simpliciter exprimit. Quamquam apud Apostolum Maior habet annexa ratione, quare videlicet deceat pontificem esse placabile: praeterea eius rationis comprobatione, sicut infra plenius ostendemus. Minoris vero sententiam sic extulit: ita Christus, tametsi filius erat, tamen didicit ex his, quae passus est, obedientia, ac perfectus redditus omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis aeternae. Vbi uno verbo dicens Christum passum, notat eum infirmitates & miserias humanae conditionis expertum, vt ita magis misericors erga homines redderetur. Quae addita sunt, ad illustrandam Christi dignitatem faciunt.
units.tr: But Christ is compassionate and merciful towards the ignorant and erring. Therefore Christ is priest. This argument is evident and expresses the Apostle's thought simply. Although in the Apostle the major premise has an attached reason, namely why it is fitting for a priest to be compassionate, and a confirmation of that reason, as we shall show more fully below. But he expressed the sense of the minor thus: so Christ, though he was a son, yet learned obedience from the things he suffered, and being made perfect became to all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation. Here, by the single word "suffered," he indicates that Christ experienced the infirmities and miseries of the human condition, so that he might be rendered more merciful towards men. The things added serve to illustrate Christ's dignity.

units.la: Tertium argumentum sumptum est a modo vocationis ad pontificatum, id sic habet:
units.tr: The third argument is taken from the manner of calling to the priesthood, and it runs thus:

units.la: Pontifex non sibi ipsi vsurpat honorem, sed vocatur a Deo, quemadmodum & Aaron. Atqui Christus non sibi vendicauit honorem, vt fieret pontifex, sed vocatus est ab eo qui dixerat illi: Filius meus es tu, Ego hodie genui te, etc. id est, a Deo patre suo coelesti. Igitur Christus est verus & legitimus pontifex.
units.tr: A priest does not take the honour to himself, but is called by God, just as Aaron was. But Christ did not claim the honour for himself, that he should become priest, but was called by him who said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you, etc., that is, by God his heavenly Father. Therefore Christ is a true and lawful priest.

units.la: Ipse Apostolus hoc argumentum ita ad verbum expressit: sed addit praeterea, ad confirmatione praecedentium argumentorum, testimonium e Scriptura, in quo Christus diserte a Deo patre constituitur & pronunciatur Sacerdos. Sicut (inquit) alibi dicit: Tu es sacerdos, &c. Quod testimonium quo consilio, & quam appositae ad praesentem causam citatum sit, suo loco copiosius exponemus. Nam ex eo tanquam vberrimo fonte adhuc plurima deriuatur argumenta, quibus excellentia pontificatus Christi luculenter demonstratur.
units.tr: The Apostle himself expresses this argument in exactly these words. But he adds, to confirm the preceding arguments, a testimony from Scripture in which Christ is expressly appointed and declared a priest by God the Father: "As he says elsewhere, You are a priest, etc." We will explain later, in its proper place, with what purpose and how aptly this testimony is cited for the present case. For from that most abundant source many further arguments are still drawn, by which the excellence of Christ's priesthood is clearly demonstrated.

units.la: Iam ex hoc testimonio & quartum argumentum Apostolus, licet non adeo aperte, producit, sumptum ab eo, quod pontifices semper secundum aliquem certum ordinem seu ritum instituuntur. Est autem argumentum huiusmodi:
units.tr: From this same testimony the Apostle also produces a fourth argument, though not so openly, taken from the fact that priests are always installed according to some fixed order or rite. The argument runs as follows:

units.la: Omnis pontifex secundum aliquem certum ordine instituitur. Atqui Christus institutus & cognominatus est a Deo pontifex secundum certum ordine, videlicet Melchisedeck.
units.tr: Every priest is installed according to some fixed order. But Christ was installed and named priest by God according to a fixed order, namely that of Melchizedek.

units.la: Igitur Christus est verus ac legitimus pontifex.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is a true and lawful priest.

units.la: Maior latenter continetur in testimonio citato, & alias non est ignota: quadoquidem sub lege omnes instituebantur secundum ordinem Aaronicum, & ex tribu Leui. Minor totidem plane verbis posita est ab Apostolo, in postrema parte.
units.tr: The major premise is tacitly contained in the cited testimony and is otherwise not unknown, since under the law all were installed according to the order of Aaron and from the tribe of Levi. The minor premise is stated by the Apostle in plain words in the last part.

units.la: En vbi hoc pacto comonstratum est, quae membra consequentia quibus respondeant antecedentibus, quemuis existimo facilime assequi, quid Apostolus sibi velit, videreq; quot & qualibus argumetis, Christu esse verum pontifice, euincat. Sed adhuc maioris lu-tis ergo, quoq; expeditius animo comprehendantur argumenta simul omnia, lubet ea in vnum Syllogismum constringere, huc in modum:
units.tr: Here, once this is laid out, I think anyone can very easily see which consequent clauses correspond to which antecedents, and grasp what the Apostle means and with how many and what kinds of arguments he proves that Christ is a true priest. But so that all the arguments may be taken in together, more clearly and more readily, for the sake of greater clarity, it is good to compress them all into one syllogism, in this manner:

units.la: Quicunq; constituitur in his, quae apud Deu pro hominibus sunt agenda, vt offerat dona-ria & ria & victimas pro peccatis: praeterea, qui placabilem & misericordem se praebet erga ignorantes & errantes: adhaec, qui non seipsum ambitiose ingerit, sed diuinitus vocatur: postremo, qui secundum certum ordine sacerdotio praeficitur: talis est verus legitimusq; pontifex agnoscedus. At Christus hoc modo constitutus est, in his, quae apud Deum pro hominibus sunt agenda, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis: praeterea placabilis est et misericors erga ignorates & errantes: adhaec vocatus est ad munus hoc a Deo patre suo coelesti: postremo secundum certum ordinem, videlicet Melchisedech institutus & praefectus: nec deniq; aliquid illi deest, quod in bono pontifice posset desiderari.
units.tr: Whoever is appointed in those matters which are to be performed before God on behalf of men, so as to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; moreover, who shows himself placable and merciful toward the ignorant and the erring; furthermore, who does not thrust himself forward out of ambition but is called by God; lastly, who is set over the priesthood according to a fixed order: such a one is to be acknowledged as a true and lawful priest. But Christ has been appointed in this way, in those matters which are to be performed before God on behalf of men, so as to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; moreover, he is placable and merciful toward the ignorant and the erring; furthermore, he was called to this office by God his heavenly Father; lastly, he was installed and set over the priesthood according to a fixed order, namely that of Melchizedek. Nor is anything lacking in him that could be desired in a good priest.

units.la: Igitur Christus est verus legitimusq; pontifex. Obiter istud adijcia: Prorsus eadem mihi videtur argumenti forma vsus Apostolus, quale habet Cicero in oratione pro lege Manilia, ad probandu, Cn. Pompeiu esse bonu Imperatore, & prae quibuscunq; aliis bello Mithridatico praeficiendu. Sic enim argumentatur: Qui habet scientiam rei militaris, virtutem, autoritatem, foelicitatem, hunc prae caeteris Imperatorem eligi convenit.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is a true and lawful priest. By the way, let me add this: the Apostle seems to use exactly the same form of argument that Cicero uses in his speech for the Manilian law, to prove that Gnaeus Pompey is a good commander and is to be placed in charge of the war against Mithridates before all others. For Cicero argues thus: he who has knowledge of military affairs, virtue, authority and good fortune, it is fitting that he be chosen commander above all others.

units.la: Cn. Pompeius habet scientiam rei militaris, virtutem, autoritatem, foelicitatem.
units.tr: Gnaeus Pompey has knowledge of military affairs, virtue, authority and good fortune.

units.la: Ergo Cn. Pompeius prae caeteris in Imperatorem est eligendus.
units.tr: Therefore Gnaeus Pompey is to be chosen commander above all others.

units.la: Haec summa est eius orationis. Sed Cicero in Minore explicanda, hoc est, in demonstrando, quod Cn. Pompeius talibus virtutibus sit conspicuus, diutius occupatur, singulasq; partes fuse probat, quod nequaquam hic facit Apostolus, vtpote breuitati studens, & paucis suis verbis bona parte probationu includes, & existimas, in re no obscura multam orationem nequaquam requiri: Etiamsi in confirmatione sequeti omnia reuera plenius discutiuntur. Sed de artificio haec sint satis. Nec puto scrupulu aliquem, quantu ad dispositionem attinet, restare. Quare aut Apostolus aliis subinde verbis consequentia, seu minores propositiones expresserit, quae ite admixta sint, siue probationu loco, siue ad amplificandam Christi dignitate, nos in progressu exactius ostendemus. Sed quare Apostolus hoc pacto omnia antecedetia in vnu fasce congerit, priusquam vnu ex consequentibus addat? Respondetur, quia p se singula posita potuisset aliquo pacto in firmari: quare voluit prius simul omnia confirmare, adferedo proprium testimonium Scripturae de Sacerdotio Christi differes, quo semel posito, omnia consequentia obtinebut suum robur. Atq; idcirco omnia antecedetia simul cum testimonio priori loco sunt coniuncta: postea vero simul subiecta consequetia. Ceterum quado intueor, quomodo Apostolus hac causam instituerit, quibusq; argumetis Christu esse pontifice probet, animaduerto singulare in eo prudentia. Nam si bene perpendimus, valde difficile erat, & no vacans periculo, praesertim apud Iudaeos sacerdotio Aaronico immodice gloriates, & id perpetuu esse debere contedentes, Christi pontificatu afferere probareq;. Siquidem Christus, si externas & corporales res spectemus, nihil pontifice dignu gesisse visus est, non magis, quam regiam maiestatem aliquam in re prae se tulit. Quid vero a Christo vnquam actum est, quod vel imaginem aliquam regiae maiestatis poteatisque adumbraret? Soluit censum, sicut caeteri, pauperet tenui supra modum conditione natus, & semper vixit: rex a vulgo in deserto salutatus fugit: semel ludibrij causa, fertum spineum pro diademate capite impositum gesit: arundo pro sceptro in manus data: denique in crucem inter duos latrones probrosissime actus est. En regiam coram mundo maiestatem. Non multo foelicius egit Christus pontificem.
units.tr: This is the substance of that speech. But in explaining the minor premise, that is, in demonstrating that Gnaeus Pompey is distinguished by such virtues, Cicero spends a long time and proves each part at length. The Apostle does nothing of the kind here, since he aims at brevity, and with his few words he includes a large part of the proofs. And he judges that in a matter that is not obscure, much speech is by no means required, although in the confirmation that follows, everything is in fact discussed more fully. But let these remarks on the method suffice. Nor do I think any scruple remains concerning the arrangement. Whether the Apostle sometimes expresses the consequent clauses, or minor propositions, in other words, which are interspersed either as proofs or to amplify the dignity of Christ, we will show more exactly as we go on. But why does the Apostle heap all the antecedents together in one bundle before he adds any of the consequents? The answer is that each of them, taken singly, could have been confirmed in some way on its own. He therefore wished first to confirm them all together, by bringing forward the proper testimony of Scripture concerning the priesthood of Christ, which, once placed, gives all the consequents their force. And for this reason all the antecedents have been joined together, along with the earlier testimony, in the first place, and afterward the consequents are set out together. Moreover, when I consider how the Apostle has set up this cause, and with what arguments he proves that Christ is a priest, I notice in him an singular prudence. For if we weigh it well, it was very difficult, and not free from danger, especially among the Jews, who boasted excessively of the Aaronic priesthood and contended that it must last forever, to assert and prove the priesthood of Christ. For if we look at external and bodily things, Christ seemed to have done nothing worthy of a priest, just as he showed no sign of royal majesty. What indeed did Christ ever do that might even faintly shadow the image of royal majesty and power? He paid the census like others, born in a condition of extreme poverty, and so he always lived. When the common people wanted to make him king in the desert, he fled. Once, for the sake of mockery, a crown of thorns was placed on his head in place of a diadem; a reed was put into his hands for a scepter; and finally he was led to the cross, most shamefully, between two robbers. Behold his royal majesty before the world. Christ did not act as a priest much more happily.

units.la: Ex familia Aaron, vel ex tribu Leui originem non traxit: patre sacerdote non est natus: cum sacerdotibus vel pontificibus nullum ei commertium: imo his maxime infensus, & ab his semper odio est habitus: ab hominibus nunquam ad pontificatum, vel vllum ministerium sacrorum electus: altare nunqua erexit, vitulos vel arietes, vel aliquam huius generis victimam nunquam obtulit. Vbi igitur aliqua obsecro in Christo relucet pontificalis dignitatis species? In Ioanne Baptista, imo in Anna & Caipha, alijsque nonnullis promptius erat inuenire huiusmodi conditiones, quam in Christo.
units.tr: He did not trace his origin from the family of Aaron or from the tribe of Levi; he was not born of a priestly father; he had no dealings with priests or high priests; indeed he was most hostile to them and was always held in hatred by them; he was never chosen by men to the priesthood or to any sacred ministry; he never erected an altar, never offered calves or rams or any victim of that kind. Where then, I beg you, does any appearance of priestly dignity shine forth in Christ? One would more readily find such qualifications in John the Baptist, or indeed in Annas and Caiaphas and some others, than in Christ.

units.la: Nec dubium quin Iudaei, cum audirent, Apostolos inter disputandum velle probare abrogationem sacerdotij legalis, per nouum sacerdotium Christi, irriserint istud, & impossibile iudicauerint.
units.tr: Nor is there any doubt that the Jews, when they heard that the Apostles in their disputation wished to prove the abrogation of the legal priesthood through the new priesthood of Christ, laughed at this and judged it impossible.

units.la: Apostolus ergo animaduertens difficile admodum esse, probare Christum pontificem, maxime apud eos, qui vsque adeo contendebant pro temporali suo sacerdotio, & inter quos ambitiosissime pleriq;, republica & religione ia penitus corruptis & lapsantibus, sacerdotiu captabat, atq; etiam pecunijs redimebat: no laborauit, vt Christi genus ad Aaronē vel tribu Leui referret, vt coprobaret, Christu etiam in Synagoga docuisse, vel huiusmodi, quae videretur aliquo modo accedere ad ostedendu, sacerdotale munus Christo potuisse copetere. Sed, neglectis illis externis & crasis insignib. selegit muneris pontificalis causas potissimas, & inprimis spirituales internas, Deo magis quam mudo probatas, quae
units.tr: The Apostle, therefore, noticing that it was very difficult to prove Christ a high priest, especially among those who so strongly contended for their temporal priesthood, and among whom very many were most ambitiously seeking the priesthood, with the state and religion now wholly corrupt and falling, and even buying it with money: he did not labour to refer Christ's lineage to Aaron or the tribe of Levi, nor to prove that Christ had even taught in the synagogue, or anything of this kind that might seem in some way to show that the priestly office could belong to Christ. But, neglecting those outward and gross insignia, he chose the chief causes of the pontifical office, and above all the spiritual and inner ones, approved by God rather than by the world, which

units.la: Christi regnū Spirituale. quæ omnibus externis insignibus, vestibus, infulis, tinctionibus, pompis, anteferuntur. In summa, tales elegit excutiendas qualitates pontificum, in quibus præcipua pontificalis dignitas & vis sita est, & eas Christo competere euidenter ostendit, addito etiam Scripturæ testimonio, quo luculentissimè omnia comprobantur, adeò vt aduersarij, in quorum mentibus vlla scintilla cognitionis rerum diuinarum resederit, fateri coacti sint, per Christum plenissimè peractum esse, quicquid à bono pontifice requiri posset. Nam constitutum esse mediatorem inter Deum & homines, sacrificium & victimam obtulisse, diuinitus ad munus sacerdotale vocatum, ordinatum item secundum certum ordinem: (quæ quidem præcipuè sunt spectanda, vt quis pro pontifice agnoscatur) hæc inquam omnia luculentissimè in Christo esse demonstratur, & ipsis rebus per Christum actis, nec non prophetæ oraculo comprobantur. Quis hic non videat mirabilem prudentiam adhibitam? & sic temperatam orationem, vt ne hostes quidem arripere possent indignā occasionem, quasi Christo seditiosè contra ius ac fas sacerdotij dignitas cum magna iniuria aliorum attributa foret. Imò sic tractat in sequentibus hanc causam, vt, quæ obij ci potuissent veluti ad euertendum Christi sacerdotium, cuiusmodi sunt, quòd non esset extribu Leui, sed de tribu Iuda: quòd non secundum ordinem Aaronicum esset vocatus: quòd non mactarit pecudes pro victimis, & huiusmodi: ea ipsa arripiat Apostolus ad comprobandam sacerdotij Christi excellentiam præ sacerdotio legali. Quis istam diligentiam & acumen nō miretur? Quis item rhetor tali grauitate sermonis, dictionis puritate, permissis tamen idiotissimis illis proprijs, & appositā ratione dicendi causam hanc sic posset peragere, vt peracta est? Itaq; valde notanda est hæc Apostoli fides ac diligentia, iudicandum que, epistolam hanc non ab alio esse scriptam, quàm ab eo, qui vere fuerit spiritu Dei illustratus.
units.tr: Christ's spiritual kingdom. which are preferred to all outward insignia, vestments, mitres, anointings, and pomps. In sum, he chose for examination such qualities of high priests in which the chief dignity and power of the pontificate lies, and clearly showed that these belong to Christ, adding also the testimony of Scripture, by which all things are most splendidly proved; so that his adversaries, in whose minds any spark of knowledge of divine things has settled, are compelled to confess that whatever could be required of a good high priest has been most fully accomplished through Christ. For that he has been appointed mediator between God and men, offered a sacrifice and victim, called divinely to the priestly office, and likewise ordained according to a certain order (which are the chief things to be considered in order that someone be acknowledged as a priest): all these things, I say, are most clearly shown to be in Christ, and are confirmed by the things themselves done through Christ and by the oracle of the prophet. Who here does not see the wonderful prudence employed, and such a moderated style, that not even enemies could seize an unworthy occasion, as if the dignity of the priesthood had been seditiously attributed to Christ against right and law, with great injury to others? Indeed, he so handles this cause in what follows, that the things which could have been objected, as if to overthrow Christ's priesthood, such as that he was not of the tribe of Levi but of the tribe of Judah, that he was not called according to the Aaronic order, that he did not slaughter beasts for victims, and the like: these very things the Apostle takes up to prove the excellence of Christ's priesthood above the legal priesthood. Who would not admire this diligence and acuteness? Who, as a rhetorician, with such gravity of speech and purity of diction, yet allowing those peculiarly idiomatic expressions, and with fitting method of speaking, could carry through this cause as it was carried through? Therefore this faithfulness and diligence of the Apostle is to be noted well, and it is to be judged that this epistle was written by no one other than him who was truly illumined by the Spirit of God.

units.la: Cæterum foret illud è re nostra, si ea, quæ in lege descripta sunt de sacerdotum seu pontificum institutione & officijs, hic repeteremus, & in summam contraheremus: verum quia hoc longum foret, & multa scripta sunt, quæ nequaquam per omnia conueniūt instituto, ideò nos hoc labore supersedebimus, & in progressu confirmationis argumentorum septimi & octaui capitis, quæ ex veteri testamento de sacerdotio erunt conducetia, fideliter annotabimus, ne quid desideretur. Satis est hoc admonere, Apostolum prudenter admodum in hoc egisse, quòd probaturus, Christum esse pontificem, omnia delegit ex veteri testamento sacerdotum propria & præcipua officia, quibus id, quod vult, efficiat: sicut oportebat apud Iudæos agere, qui lege & prophetarum oraculis erant conuincendi. Ex humana ratione argumentum non trahit: neque etiam leuicula vel obscura ex lege, sed grauia perspicuaque sunt omnia, & proprie ad rem pertinentia: ut in tota disputatione neque redundet quicquam, neque desideretur. Id quod inter explicandum partes, Deo volente, demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Otherwise it would be to our purpose to repeat here what the law prescribes about the institution and duties of the priests or high priests, and to summarise it. But since that would be long, and many things were written that by no means fit our plan in every respect, I will forgo that labour. Instead, as I go through the proofs of the seventh and eighth chapters, which will be drawn from the Old Testament concerning the priesthood, I will faithfully note what is relevant, so that nothing is lacking. It is enough to point out that the Apostle acted very wisely here. Wishing to prove that Christ is the high priest, he chose from the Old Testament all the proper and principal duties of the priests, by which he might establish what he intends. This was necessary when dealing with the Jews, who had to be convinced by the law and the oracles of the prophets. He does not draw his argument from human reasoning, nor from trivial or obscure passages of the law, but everything is weighty, clear and pertinent to the matter, so that nothing superfluous appears in the whole discussion and nothing is missing. We will demonstrate this, God willing, as we explain the parts.

units.la: Porrò partes hoc ordine explicabimus: Antecedentia coniungemus consequentibus, & argumenta singula seorsum integra excutiemus: tum dictiones explicabimus. Primi igitur argumenti verba apud Apostolum sic habent:
units.tr: Next, we will explain the parts in this order: we will join what precedes to what follows, examine each argument separately and in full, and then explain the individual words. The words of the first argument in the Apostle read as follows:

units.la: Nā omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus constituitur, in his, quæ apud Deum aguntur, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis: ita & Christus in diebus carnis suæ, cùm & precationes & supplicationes apud illum, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare, cum clamore valido et lachrymis obtulisset, exauditus est pro reuerentia.
units.tr: For every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed on behalf of men in the things that pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; so also Christ, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with strong crying and tears, was heard because of his reverence.

units.la: Hæc est apta definitio sacerdotis seu pontificis, sumpta à causa finali seu proprio sacerdotis officio, congesta ex diuersis Scripturæ locis, in quibus officium sacerdotum describitur, quòd proprie destinati sint peragendis his, quæ ad Deum & cultum Dei, & sacrificia offerenda pertinent. Nullus dialecticus posset exactius id perficere: neque enim deest ei quicquam, neque redundat. Primùm expendemus quæ ad rem attinent, proximè q ad verba. Pontifex, inquit, ex hominibus assumitur: Hoc est, eū, qui pontificatu fit functus, oportet esse hominem, nimirū, ut hominū partes siue causas maiori fide ac diligentia peragat. Certè angelus pontificis munus obire non potest, utpote à nostra natura alienus, ac proinde non ita fideliter acturus nostras partes.
units.tr: This is an apt definition of the priest or high priest, drawn from the final cause, that is, from the proper office of the priest. It is put together from various places of Scripture, where the office of the priests is described: they are appointed specifically to perform those things which pertain to God, to the worship of God, and to the offering of sacrifices. No dialectician could make this more precise, for nothing is lacking in it and nothing is superfluous. First we will consider the matters, and then the words. He says, "the high priest is taken from among men." That is, the one who has been made high priest must be a man, so that he may perform the part or cause of men with greater faithfulness and diligence. Certainly an angel cannot discharge the office of high priest, since he is alien to our nature and therefore would not act faithfully on our behalf.

units.la: Pro hominib. constituitur) Hac particula notatur, pontifices cæteris hominibus præeminere, & curam salutis hominum gerere: sicut reuera nulla actio magis pro hominibus esse dici potest, quā ea, qua laboratur pro salute animarū. Corpora curare præclara res est, hominum actiones dirigere, & legum moderamine in officio continere: quorum illud medicorum est, istud iurisconsultorum: at uero ea efficere prospicere que, quæ sunt salutis animarum,
units.tr: "Appointed on behalf of men." This phrase notes that high priests excel other men and have care for men's salvation. Indeed no action can rightly be said to be more on behalf of men than that by which labour is spent for the salvation of souls. To cure bodies is an excellent thing, and to direct men's actions and keep them in duty by the governance of laws is also excellent. The first belongs to physicians, the second to jurisconsults. But to bring about and provide for the things that concern the salvation of souls,

units.la: 4 animarum, hoc est, verè pro hominibus & hominum utilitate constitutum esse.
units.tr: 4 to be truly constituted on behalf of men and for the benefit of men, is the work of the priest.

units.la: Frustra succurritur corpori, frustra laboratur ad conseruandas opes seu facultates, si anima periclitatur, sicut in euangelio præclarè dicitur: Quid prodest homini, si vniuer-sum mundum lucretur, animæ verò suæ detrimentum patiatur? Verum, quia hominum curam gerere non tantum pontificum est, verumetiam quorundam aliorum, veluti regum, ducum, & magistratuum, qui etiam ministri Dei sunt, & quidem in bonum & v. tilitatem hominum subditorum, (id quod aperte etiam docet Apostolus Romanor. 13.) iam adijciūtur differentiæ, per quas pontifices à cæteris in dignitate constitutis discer-nuntur. Prior est: in his, quæ apud Deum aguntur. Cæteri magistratus, nempe politici, constitu-ti sunt in his, quæ sunt hominum inter se mutuo, vt pacem & tranquillitatem tuean-tur, dissensiones, iniurias, uim, prohibeant: & ipsi apud homines efficiunt antoritate sua & æquitate legum, vt in bono statu sint omnia. At pontifices in his occupantur, quæ per-tinent ad placandum hominibus Deum, & voluntatis diuinæ apud homines aguntin-terpretes in rebus spiritualibus & spectantibus præcipuè gloriam Dei. Adeò, ut omnia, quæ sunt primæ tabulæ decalogi, ad pontifices pertineant, & per eos conseruentur. Quæ verò secundæ tabulæ sunt, pertinent ad magistratus politicos.
units.tr: Care for the body is in vain, and labour to preserve wealth or property is in vain, if the soul is in peril, as the Gospel rightly says: "What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his own soul?" But since the care of men belongs not only to priests but also to certain others, such as kings, leaders and magistrates, who are also ministers of God, and indeed for the good and benefit of their subjects (as the Apostle clearly teaches in Romans 13), differences are added by which priests are distinguished from others placed in dignity. The first is: in the things that pertain to God. The other magistrates, namely the civil ones, are appointed in those things that concern men's dealings with one another, that they may guard peace and tranquillity, and prevent dissensions, injuries and violence. By their authority and the equity of the laws they bring it about among men that all things are in a good state. But priests are occupied with those things that pertain to appeasing God for men, and to being interpreters of the divine will among men, in spiritual matters that concern chiefly the glory of God. So much so that all the things in the first table of the decalogue belong to the priests and are preserved through them. Those in the second table pertain to the civil magistrates.

units.la: Verum, quo euidentius adhuc perspiciatur, quomodo pontifex à cæteris distingua-tur, addit aliam particulam ab externo officio eius sumptam: ut offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis: Istud certè nullis nisi pontificibus legitimis accommodari potest. Fuerintlicet alij, qui etiam aliquo modo curent ea, quæ ad Dei cultum pertinent, sicut pleriq; omnes Leuitæ & prophetæ faciebant, & quiuis ex quauis tribu docere poterant, sicut Actor. 9. & 13. Paulus è tribu Beniamin docebat in synagoga, item Christus ipse è tribu Iuda quo tidie docebat in synagoga: tamen offerre victimas ad solos pōtifices pertinebat, id quod Dathan & Abyro, qui nō erat vocati diuinitus, suo funesto casu, item Ozias rex, de quo 2. Paral. 26. (& nos postea iterum admonebimus, vbi de vocatione erit agendum) quod quia temerè ausus est offerre incensum, lepra percussus est, edocuerunt. Id autem maxi-mè verum est de sacerdotibus legalibus, qui certis ritibus instituebantur, & ab omni-bus alijs hominibus discernebantur, non tantum hoc officio victimas offerendi pro pec-catis, verum alijs aliquot rationibus. Sed istud insigne præ cæteris erat magis spectan-dum, & inter ea, quæ apud Deum erant agenda, præcipuum. Itaq; propriās notas pon-tificis hic descripsit Apostolus, vt definitio optimè constituta habeatur.
units.tr: But so that it may be seen even more clearly how the priest is distinguished from others, he adds another phrase taken from his external office: that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. This can certainly be applied to no one except lawful priests. There were others who in some way also took care of the things pertaining to the worship of God, as most of the Levites and prophets did, and anyone from any tribe could teach, as in Acts 9 and 13. Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin, taught in the synagogue, and Christ himself, of the tribe of Judah, taught daily in the synagogue. Yet offering sacrifices belonged to the priests alone. This was shown by the fatal fall of Dathan and Abiram, who were not divinely called, and likewise by King Uzziah, of whom we read in 2 Chronicles 26 (and we will again remind you of this later, when we treat of the calling). He, because he rashly presumed to offer incense, was struck with leprosy. This is most true of the legal priests, who were installed with fixed rites and were distinguished from all other men, not only by this office of offering sacrifices for sins but also for several other reasons. But this distinguishing mark was to be regarded above the rest, and was the chief among the things to be done before God. Therefore the Apostle here describes the proper marks of the priest, so that the definition may be regarded as very well framed.

units.la: Hoc porrò officium sacerdotum passim in Scripturis inculcatur. Huc enim pertinet illa Exodi 28. Portabitq; Aaron iniquitates eorum, quæ obtulerunt & sanctificauerunt filij Israel, in cunctis muneribus & donarijs suis. Item Exodi 29. de institutione Aaronis & filiorum eius in sacerdo-tes. Item Leuit 9. Moses & Aaron; Offer holocaustum, & deprecare pro te & pro popu-lo. Leuit. 1. & 4. de ritu offerendi victimas & donaria plura habentur. Item Numeror. 18, de officio sacerdotum ministerioque eorum in tabernaculo, multis verbis disseritur. Β quibus omnibus locis summatim colligi potest, quòd hic in vnam definitionem est con-gestum. Iam verò vniuersum hoc officium pontificale à Christo peractum esse ait, in hunc modum: ita & Christus in diebus carnis suæ, cum & precationes & supplicationes apud illum, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare, cum clamore valido & lachrymis obtulisset: exauditus est pro re-uerentia.
units.tr: Moreover, this office of the priests is inculcated throughout the Scriptures. To this pertains that passage of Exodus 28: Aaron shall bear the iniquities of those things which the sons of Israel have offered and consecrated, in all their gifts and offerings. Likewise Exodus 29 concerns the installation of Aaron and his sons as priests. Also Leviticus 9: "Moses and Aaron: Offer a burnt offering and pray for yourself and for the people." Leviticus 1 and 4 contain many matters about the rite of offering sacrifices and gifts. Likewise Numbers 18 discusses at length the office of the priests and their ministry in the tabernacle. From all these places it can be summarily gathered that what is here gathered into one definition is correct. Now he says that this whole priestly office was carried out by Christ, in this manner: so also Christ, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with strong crying and tears, was heard because of his reverence.

units.la: Placuit Apostolo alijs & magnificentioribus verbis, quàm in antecedente sunt po-sita, hanc partem posteriorem exprimere, ut nimirum ita signisicaret, personę Christi lon-gè iustius competere pontificis appellationem ac dignitatem, quàm vllis alijs. Proinde mirabili artificio vniuersum officium pontificale per Christum peractum esse asserit: quā quam non simpliciter solùm asserit, verumetiam latenter probat. Sic enim ista omnia Christo attribuit, ut eadem opera aliquo modo probet, etiam rectè ei attribui. Aliàs pro-sectò debuisset singularum partium adijcere probationes, (quomodo Ciceronem vide-mus in oratione pro lege Manilia multò copiosissimè probare, virtutes omnes boni Im-peratoris in Cn. Pompeio relucere) sed siue quòd breuitati studeret, siue quòd in re mani-festa duceret non admodum id requiri, præsertim cùm res ipsæ per Christum palàm ge-stæ, præterea testimonium illud ex psalmo 109. grauissimarum probationum vice sint. Primùm, quòd pontificem decet esse homine, ex hominibus assumptū, notat hisce ver-bis: in diebus carnis suæ: significans, Christum, licet esset Deus ab æterno, tamen in tempore humanam naturam siue carnem nostram induisse: atque eo tempore verè esse homine ex hominibus assumptum in pontificem. Quò pertinet, quod supra cap. 1. dictum est, Christum per omnia debuisse similem fratribus reddi, ut misericors & fidelis pontifex esset: cùm alias reuera pontifex fieri haud potuisset.
units.tr: The Apostle chose to express this latter part in other and more elevated words than those in the preceding sentence, so that he might signify that the title and dignity of high priest belong far more justly to the person of Christ than to any others. Accordingly, with remarkable skill he asserts that the whole priestly office has been performed by Christ, and not only asserts it but also proves it implicitly. For he attributes all these things to Christ in such a way that, by the same act, he in some measure proves that they are rightly attributed to him. Otherwise he ought surely to have added proofs for each of the parts (as we see Cicero, in his speech for the Manilian law, proving at great length that all the virtues of a good commander shine forth in Gnaeus Pompey). But whether because he aimed at brevity, or because he judged that it was not very necessary in a matter so evident, especially since the things themselves were openly done by Christ, and moreover that testimony from Psalm 110 stands in place of the weightiest proofs. First, that the high priest should be a man taken from among men, he notes in these words: in the days of his flesh, signifying that Christ, although he was God from eternity, yet in time put on human nature or our flesh, and at that time was truly a man taken from among men to be high priest. To this pertains what was said above in chapter 1, that Christ had to be made like his brethren in all things, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest, since otherwise he could not in truth have become a high priest.

units.la: Qui verò pro hominibus in his, quæ apud Deum forent peragenda, nec non donaria donaria ac victimas obtulisset: vide quàm luculenter in tanta breuitate omnia hæc intelligen- da proponat.
units.tr: Now he who offered gifts and sacrifices on behalf of men in those matters that had to be performed before God: see how clearly, in so few words, he sets out all these things to be understood.

units.la: Precationes et supplicationes ait eum obtulisse pro donarijs & victimis: illas autem intel- ligi uult tantò his præstantiores, quanto pluris æstimanda sunt spiritualia sacrificia Deo oblata, quàm corporalia: cùm ipse Deus, qui spiritus est, spiritu & veritate adorari velit potius, quàm rebus corporalibus. Cùm addit: Apud illum, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare: non solùm hac periphrasi notat paternam maiestatem, cui Christus precationes & supplicationes obtulit, verumetiam tempus, quo oblatio facta est, nempe tempus mortis, quam Christus, vt victima pro peccatis nostris mactata, obiuit nostræ salutis causa, adeoque ipsum Christum in morte non solùm sacerdotem, sed ipsam quoque victimam factum inhuit.
units.tr: He says that Christ offered prayers and supplications along with the gifts and sacrifices. He wants these to be understood as far more excellent than the gifts, just as spiritual sacrifices offered to God are valued far above bodily ones, since God himself, who is Spirit, wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth rather than with bodily things. When he adds before him who was able to save him from death, this periphrasis marks not only the Father's majesty, to whom Christ offered prayers and supplications, but also the time at which the offering was made, namely the time of death. Christ, slain as a victim for our sins, underwent that death for the cause of our salvation. Thus he shows that in death Christ was not only the priest but also the victim itself.

units.la: Illis autem verbis, cum clamore ualido et lachrymis: ardentem affectum fideliter & tota mente pro nobis orantis pontificis eleganter delineat. In sacrificijs legalibus hauddubiè affectus sacerdotis pro populo orantis requirebatur: sed certum est, nunquam eos sic fuisse affectos, ad intercedendum pro aliorum salute, sic affectus fuit Christus: quâdoquidem nemo unquam sic obtulit, vtpote qui animam suam propriam pro salute hominum posuit: vnde Philipp. 2. Is affectus sit in vobis, qui fuit in Christo Iesu, qui, cùm in forma Dei esset, figura repertus est vt homo, humilem præbuit semetipsum, factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Postremò cùm addit:
units.tr: By the words with strong crying and tears, he elegantly portrays the burning affection of the high priest who prayed for us faithfully and with his whole mind. In the legal sacrifices, the priest's affection in praying for the people was certainly required, but it is certain that the priests were never so affected in interceding for the salvation of others as Christ was. No one ever offered in this way, since he laid down his own soul for the salvation of men. Hence Philippians 2: "Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, was found in fashion as a man, humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, the death of the cross." Finally, when he adds:

units.la: Et exauditus est pro reuerentia) hic multò plus de Christo dicitur, quâ de reliquis pontificibus dici posset, planeque certus effectus oblationes Christi consequens describitur. De cæteris namque pontificibus bene dici potest, quòd obtulerint, quòd orarint: at quòd exauditi sint, & quidem pro reuerentia, hoc est, seu ratione cultus, quem exhibuerunt, seu ratione dignitatis suæ, dici nequaquam potest. Itaq; vt in pauca conferamus, palàm est, longè ampliora & excellentiora in hoc consequenti de Christo dici, quòd videlicet præ- clarè pontificatus munere fit functus: quàm de pontificibus generatim dicta sunt in antecedente. Quòd si quis plura desideret de hoc officio per Christum peracto testimonia, ea quoque passim sunt obuia. Quomodo enim Christus victima & propitiatio factus fit, & seipsum obtulerit, nusquam non inculcatur. Esaiæ 53. Oblatus est, quia ipse voluit; & non aperuit os suum: sicut ouis ad occisionem ducetur, & quasi agnus coram tondete se obmutescet. Quo de loco etiam Actor. 8. Philippus apostolus disserit. Hinc ipse Christus à Ioanne Baptista dictus est agnus, qui tollit peccata mundi: quia videlicet offerri pro expiatione peccatorum debebat. Ephes. 5. Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem ac victimam Deo in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ. Alia testimonia citauimus capite secundo, vbi exposuimus illud, quomodo Christus sit fidelis pontifex ad expiandum peccata nostra: neque opus est plura congerere in re manifesta: & inter explicandum minutiores partes, interdum opus erit quædam proferre in medium.
units.tr: And he was heard for his reverence. Here much more is said of Christ than could be said of the other high priests, and the clearly certain effect following Christ's offerings is described. For it can rightly be said of the other priests that they offered and prayed, but that they were heard, and indeed for their reverence, that is, either because of the worship they rendered or because of their dignity, cannot be said at all. So, to compare briefly: it is plain that in this following clause far greater and more excellent things are said of Christ, namely that he discharged the office of high priest with distinction, than were said of priests in general in the preceding clause. If anyone wants more testimonies about this office carried out by Christ, these too are everywhere at hand. For how Christ was made the victim and propitiation, and offered himself, is urged everywhere. Isaiah 53: "He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth; as a sheep is led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is dumb, so he does not open his mouth." Philip the apostle discourses on this passage in Acts 8. Hence Christ himself was called by John the Baptist the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, because he had to be offered for the expiation of sins. Ephesians 5: "Christ loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and a victim to God for a sweet-smelling savour." We cited other testimonies in the second chapter, where we explained how Christ is a faithful high priest to expiate our sins. There is no need to heap up more in a matter that is plain; and in explaining the smaller parts, it will sometimes be necessary to bring certain things forward.

units.la: Nam omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus constituitur) Particula nam, reddit causam propositionis, quæ præcesserat, qua dictum fuit, Christum esse pontificem magnum, qui penetrauit cœlos: valde apta est probationibus attexendis ad propositionem. Omnis pontifex: Vniuersali particula utitur, quandoquidem generalem pontificis definitionem uult conficere: præterea quia argumenti seu Syllogismi ratio id poscit. Syllogismum enim Apostolus format in tertio modo primæ figuræ, id est, Darij: id quod ex argumentorum serie supra à nobis exhibita licet videre. Loquitur autem de pontificibus legalibus, qui ex præscripto Dei fuerant instituti, & cum quibus Christum vult conferre. Quod ideò admonendum puto, ne qui ex hac nota vniuersali arripiant occasionem asserendi, eos etiam, qui nunc in ecclesia agunt pontifices, debere offerre victimas & donaria, instar legalium: ac deinde inferant, missam esse sacrificium siue oblationem pro vivis & mortuis, non secus atque si missa se haberet instar legalis sacrificij. Igitur tantum de legalibus pontificibus seu sacerdotibus sermo est sacrificia & victimas ex præscripto legis quotidie offerentibus. Nam alias apostolus nihil efficeret his argumentis: quandoquidem nec Christus etiam obtulit tales victimas, quales obtulerunt legales sacerdotes. Quare non est, quod hic omnia pertrahantur ad sacerdotes nostri temporis.
units.tr: For every high priest, who is taken from among men, is appointed for men. The particle for gives the reason for the proposition that went before, in which it was said that Christ is the great high priest who has passed through the heavens; it is very apt for attaching proofs to the proposition. Every high priest: he uses a universal particle, since he wants to frame a general definition of the high priest, and also because the logic of the argument or syllogism demands it. The Apostle forms the syllogism in the third mood of the first figure, that is, Darii, as can be seen from the sequence of arguments we set out above. He speaks, however, of the legal high priests, who had been appointed by God's prescription, and with whom he wishes to compare Christ. I think this must be noted, lest anyone seize on this universal mark as an occasion for asserting that those who now act as priests in the Church ought also to offer victims and gifts after the manner of the legal ones, and then infer that the Mass is a sacrifice or offering for the living and the dead, just as if the Mass stood in the place of a legal sacrifice. Therefore the discussion concerns only the legal high priests or priests, who daily offered sacrifices and victims according to the prescription of the law. For otherwise the Apostle would accomplish nothing with these arguments, since Christ himself did not offer such victims as the legal priests offered. Hence there is no reason to drag all these things over to the priests of our own time.

units.la: Qui ex hominibus assumitur) Non solùm ita loquitur, quia hominem esse eum decet, qui ad pontificatū euehetur, qua de re disseruimus capite secundo: verumetiam quia collatio instituitur hominum potificum, ad Christum pontificem, qui Deus est, & Dei filius. Atq; ita tacitè præeminentia Christi præ cæteris pontificibus notatur: tanquam si hæc lateat sententia: pontifices, qui nihil aliud quàm homines sunt, agunt pro hominibus ea, quæ ad Deum pertinent: quid ni igitur eadem dignitas, imò multò maior, competat Christo, qui non nō tantùm homo, verumetiam Deus est? Verbum assumēdi sæpe eo modo, quo hic positum est, in Scripturis usurpatur, videlicet pro eo, quod est vnum è multis ad munus aliquod deligere, designare, vel euocare. Esaiæ 66. de vocatione gentium: Ex eis assumam (λῆϑομαι) sacerdotes & Leuitas. Rom.14. Qui vescitur, non vescentem ne despiciat, & qui non vescitur, vescentem ne iudicet. Deus enim illum assumpsit, προσελάβετο.
units.tr: Who is taken from among men. He does not say this merely because he who is raised to the priesthood must be a man, a point we discussed in the second chapter; but also because the comparison is made between human high priests and Christ the high priest, who is God and the Son of God. And so the pre-eminence of Christ above the other high priests is tacitly marked, as if this thought lay hidden: the priests, who are nothing but men, act for men in those things that pertain to God; why, then, should the same dignity, indeed a much greater one, not belong to Christ, who is not only man but also God? The verb to take is often used in the Scriptures in the sense in which it is used here, namely to choose, appoint or call one out of many for some office. Isaiah 66, concerning the calling of the Gentiles: "I will take [λήψομαι] from them priests and Levites." Romans 14: "Let him who eats not despise him who eats, and let him who eats not judge him who eats; for God has taken him [προσελάβετο]."

units.la: Pro hominibus constituitur) Id est, vt agat causas hominum apud Deū, oret pro populo, po-stulet noxam condonari, & rursus, de voluntate Dei homines certos reddat. Sumptam apparet formam loquendi ab eo, quòd, qui apud magnatem aliquem, vel etiam iudices in foro, causam habet agendam, si diffidunt, se posse, quod cupiunt, efficere, alios adhi-bent patronos seu intercessores, & magno interdum cōducunt, qui eorum partes agāt, quos putant promptius dexteriusque curaturos omnia, & citius audiendos. Sic vero o-lim patresfamiliās pro sua familia Deum orabant, suos docebant, sacrificia offerebant, (sic enim legimus de Iacob cùm iret in Bethel, item de Iob, & nonnullis alijs) qui tamen sacerdotio non fungebantur, sicut ij, qui postea per legem sunt sacerdotes ordinati: sed erant nihilominus pro suis tanquanm digniores & patroni constituti.
units.tr: Is appointed for men. That is, to plead men's cases before God, to pray for the people, to ask that guilt be pardoned, and again to make men sure of the will of God. The form of speech seems to be taken from the case of someone who has a cause to be pleaded before some great man, or even before judges in the court. If he distrusts his own ability to achieve what he wants, he brings in other advocates or intercessors, and sometimes hires for a large fee those whom he thinks more ready and more skilful to manage everything and to be heard more quickly, to act on his behalf. So in former times the heads of households prayed to God for their households, taught their own people, and offered sacrifices (for so we read of Jacob when he went to Bethel, and likewise of Job and some others). Yet these men did not exercise the priesthood as those who were afterwards ordained as priests by the law did; nevertheless they were appointed for their own people as the more worthy and as their advocates.

units.la: Atque ex hac forma locutionis animaduertere licet, pontifices non debere quære-re, quæ sua sunt, non ambitionem, gloriam, opes, &c. sed salutem eorum inprimis, quo-rum partes ipsi apud Deum debent agere: qua de re 2. Corinth. 4.
units.tr: From this form of speech it may be noted that priests ought not to seek their own things, not ambition, glory, wealth, and so on, but above all the salvation of those for whom they must plead before God. On this, see 2 Corinthians 4.

units.la: In his, quae apud Deum aguntur, τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν) Hæc particula valde notanda est: quia vel maximè discernit pontifices àreliquis quibuscunque magistratibus. Apparet autem sumptam ex capite quarto Exodi, vbi Dominus in hunc modum ad Mosen loquitur de Aarone: Ipse loquetur pro te ad populum, & erit os tuum: tu autem eris ei in his, quæ ad Deum pertinent: vbi septuaginta sic habent: τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν. Exodi 18. Iethro ad Mosen: Esto tu pro populo coram Deo, & referres difficiles ad Deum: & doce eos sta-tuta & leges, & indica eis viam, per quam ambulent, & opus, quod faciant, &c. Nec dis-simile est, quod Moses de se ait Deuteron. 5. Ego sequester & medius fui inter Deum & vos, in tempore illo, vt annunciarem vobis verba eius. Quò item pertinere videtur illud 1. Cor. 4. vbi ministri vocantur dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Quia nimirum nihil a-liud, quàm curant ea, quæ Dei sunt, & rebus diuinis ac spiritualibus per omnem vitam intentos eos esse decet: qua de re multò copiosissimè in lege & omnibus sacris scriptis tam apostolicis, quàm propheticis. Itaque hæc particula egregiè admonet omnes mini-stros ecclesiarum sui officij. Neque est, quòd illa verba de Mose dicta suspicetur quis sa-cerdotibus non recte aptari. Nam Moses quoque sacerdos fuit: utpote qui sacrificia ob-tulit, mediatorem egit, ipsum Aaronem cum filijs in sacerdotē ordinauit, deniq; omnia pontificū munia peregit. Vnde & psal. 98. recte dicitur, Moses & Aaron in sacerdotibus eius. Et Nazianzenus: Nec obest, quòd idem dux populi ac iudex simul fuerit. Nam Mel-chisedech & rex & sacerdos erat: itē sacerdotes Domini, ut Heli, Samuel, multiquea-lij Israelem iudicábant: & negotia grauiora ad sacerdotes deferenda præcipitur Deute-ronom. 17.
