Quod obiter visum est admonere plenius ea de re capite septimo.
units.tr: In those things which are done before God [τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν]. This particle is to be especially noted, because it above all distinguishes priests from any other magistrates whatever. It seems to have been taken from the fourth chapter of Exodus, where the Lord speaks in this manner to Moses about Aaron: "He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be a mouth for you; but you shall be to him in those things which pertain to God"; where the Seventy have: [τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν]. Exodus 18, Jethro to Moses: "Be you for the people before God, and bring the difficult matters to God; and teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way in which they should walk, and the work which they should do," etc. What Moses says of himself in Deuteronomy 5 is not unlike: "I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to declare to you his word." To this also seems to pertain 1 Corinthians 4, where ministers are called stewards of the mysteries of God. Clearly they attend to nothing but the things of God, and it is fitting that they should be intent on divine and spiritual matters throughout their whole lives; on this the law and all the sacred writings, both apostolic and prophetic, speak most abundantly. So this particle admirably admonishes all ministers of the churches concerning their office. Nor should anyone suspect that those words said of Moses do not fit priests correctly. For Moses too was a priest: he offered sacrifices, acted as mediator, ordained Aaron himself with his sons as priests, and finally discharged all the duties of the high priests. Hence Psalm 99 (98) rightly says, "Moses and Aaron among his priests." And Nazianzen: "Nor does it matter that the same man was both leader and judge of the people. For Melchizedek was both king and priest; likewise the priests of the Lord, such as Eli and Samuel, judged Israel; and in Deuteronomy 17 the more serious matters are ordered to be referred to the priests." Since this has come up incidentally, it has seemed good to remind the reader of it more fully in the seventh chapter.

units.la: Vt offerat donaria & victimas) Cùm præcipua functio ministerij sit in rebus spiritualibus & internis, tamen externa adhibentur, quæ internorum sint veluti signa rudiores ani-mos admonentia. Nam hic proprius est omnium ceremoniarum usus. Ergo ad significa-dum internum & spirituale quiddam, quomodo fateri nos & dolere peccata, proinde si-de poscere veniam peccatorum à Deo, orareque vt nobis placatus efficiatur, signa adhi-bita externa, quæ hanc nostram pœnitentiam & fidem in Deū declarent. Hæc proinde maximè exerceri debebant per sacerdotes, vt signis hisce populus de interna pœnitētia & fide doceretur: de qua re etiam post erit dicendi locus. Porrò de donarijs & victimis Exod. 25. & 28. & alibi sæpius. Ac volunt nonnulli hoc discrimen esse inter donaria & victimas, vt donaria sint, quæ gratitudinis ergo conferebantur: qualia erant, quæ Exod. 25. sponte conferebat populus ad extruendum tabernaculum, & omnia sacris necessa-ria, vt ceram, &c. Victimæ verò, quæ dabantur cum confessione peccatorum, & veluti pro remissione obtinenda. Dona sanguinolenta non erant, nec uiua, victimæ plerunq; viuæ & cruentatæ, licet nō omnes, de qualibus Exod. 28. Leuitici 1.
units.tr: "To offer gifts and sacrifices": although the chief function of the ministry concerns spiritual and inward matters, outward things are also employed, which serve as signs of the inward realities and remind the cruder minds of them. For this is the proper use of all ceremonies. So outward signs were used to signify something inward and spiritual, such as confessing and grieving for our sins, then seeking pardon for sins from God with faith, and praying that he may be made gracious to us. These outward signs declare our repentance and faith toward God. Such signs were chiefly to be administered through the priests, so that by them the people might be taught about inward repentance and faith. I shall also have a place to speak of this matter later. On gifts and sacrifices, see Exod. 25 and 28, and elsewhere quite often. Some hold this distinction between gifts and sacrifices: gifts were those offered out of gratitude, such as the things the people freely brought in Exod. 25 for building the tabernacle and everything needed for worship, such as wax, and so on. Sacrifices, however, were given with confession of sins and, as it were, to obtain forgiveness. Gifts were not bloody, nor living; sacrifices were usually living and bloodied, though not all of them, as described in Exod. 28 and Lev. 1.

units.la: Pro peccatis) ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν non pro peccato. Nam & pro suo peccato, & pro alienis offer-re debebat: quod copiosè scribitur Leuitici 4. & 5. Non autem, quòd ratione victimarum illarum peccatorum remissio obtineretur (etiamsi passim Scriptura sic sonare videtur, vt Leuit. 4. Pro eis rogabit sacerdos, & pro peccatis eius, & dimittentur ei) sed propter veram uictimam, id est, Christum, cuius omnes illæ victimæ typi erant atque umbræ.
units.tr: "For sins": Greek ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, not "for sin." For the priest had to offer both for his own sin and for the sins of others, which is written at length in Lev. 4 and 5. Yet this does not mean that forgiveness of sins was obtained by reason of those sin-offerings (even though Scripture often seems to sound this way, as in Lev. 4: "The priest shall make atonement for them, and for their sins, and they shall be forgiven"), but on account of the true sacrifice, that is, Christ, of whom all those sacrifices were types and shadows.

units.la: Et fides pœnitentium veniamque poscentium præcipuè respiciebatur, non victima-rum kum qualitas, quæ tantum erat internæ fidei offerentium, & confitentium peccata sua, externum symbolum. Hoc duximus obiter admonendum, ne quis animo conciperet, remissionem peccatorum obtigisse ratione ipsorum sacrificiorum tanquam ex opere operato. Nunc ad verba consequentia.
units.tr: The faith of penitents and of those seeking pardon was chiefly regarded, not the quality of the victims, which was only an outward symbol of the inward faith of those offering them and confessing their sins. I have thought it worth noting in passing, lest anyone conceive in his mind that forgiveness of sins came about by reason of the sacrifices themselves, as though by the work worked. Now to the words that follow.

units.la: Qui in diebus carnis suæ) Hoc est, in tempore, quo hic in terris homo inter homines versatus est. Per hebraismum dies sæpe pro toto vitæ tempore accipiuntur. Sic 1. Regum 3. Dominus ad Solomonem, Quia postulasti verbum hoc, & non petisti tibi dies multos, nec diuitias. Et paulò post: Si ambulaueris in vijs meis, & custodieris præcepta mea, longos faciam dies tuos. Iob. 7. Dies mei velocius transierunt, quàm à texente tela succidit. Atque ita satis fuisset dicere: Qui in diebus suis: quomodo & Christus ad patrem loquitur psalm. 114. Dilexi, quoniam exaudiet Dominus vocem orationis meæ. Quia inclinauit aurem suam mihi, in diebus meis inuocabo. Vnde apparet, Apostolum hanc loquendi formam de Christo mutuatum. Verùm Scriptura etiā sæpe addit aliquid voci diei: vnde illæ phrases: Quot sunt dies annorum vitæ tuæ? Sic enim Gen. 47. Pharao interrogat Iacob, & respondit, Dies peregrinationis vitæ meæ centum triginta annorum sunt, parui & mali. Ec ce dies annorum, dies peregrinationis, dies vitæ. Sed Apostolus quoniam de Christo loquitur, cui secundum diuinam naturam nulla tempora, anni, vel dies possunt attribui; sed tantùm secundum humanam naturam tribui potest tempus, quo ille naturam humanam in eo significaret: ideò diserte usus est alia phrasi, & dixit: Qui in diebus carnis suæ: quasi diceret: eo tempore, quo carne induit, & homo inter homines versatus est: sicut Ioan. 1. dicitur: Verbū caro factū est, & habitauit in nobis. Vt dies carnis significet illud proprie tempus, quo Christus carne nostra fragili circundatus est, & carnis communes miserias (quæ tamen à vitio & peccato abessent) in se sensit. Prudenterque additum videtur pronomen suæ: quandoquidem caro ipsius fuit quidem multis miseriis communibus humanæ conditioni obnoxia, at nequaquam illis, in quibus peccatum est. Quare peculiare quiddam præter communem nostram carnem, caro Christi in se habuit. Neq; verò est, quod quisquam ex eo, quod hic dicitur, in diebus carnis suæ: cauilletur, Christum iam non amplius carnem habere, quasi tantùm habuisset carnem usque ad tempus mortis suæ temporalis. Nequaquam ita est: habet enim, ut ipse ait Lucæ ult. carnem & ossa sicut antea, & non est factus spe-
units.tr: "In the days of his flesh": that is, in the time when he, a man, lived here on earth among men. By a Hebraism, "days" are often taken for the whole time of life. So in 1 Kings 3 the Lord says to Solomon: "Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself many days, nor riches..." And a little later: "If you walk in my ways, and keep my commandments, I will lengthen your days." Job 7: "My days have passed more swiftly than the weaver's shuttle is cut off." And so it would have been enough to say: "who in his days," as Christ too speaks to the Father in Psalm 114: "I loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer. Because he has inclined his ear to me, I will call upon him in my days." Hence it appears that the Apostle borrowed this manner of speaking about Christ. But Scripture also often adds something to the word "day": hence such phrases as "How many are the days of the years of your life?" For in Gen. 47 Pharaoh asks Jacob this, and he answers: "The days of the years of my pilgrimage are a hundred and thirty years, few and evil." Here we have "days of years," "days of pilgrimage," "days of life." But since the Apostle is speaking of Christ, to whom according to his divine nature no times, years, or days can be attributed, time can be attributed to him only according to his human nature, by which he signified the human nature in himself. Therefore he deliberately used another phrase and said: "in the days of his flesh," as if to say: in the time when he put on flesh and lived as a man among men, just as John 1 says: "The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." So "days of the flesh" properly denotes that time when Christ was clothed in our frail flesh and experienced in himself the common miseries of the flesh (which nevertheless were free from vice and sin). And the pronoun "his" seems to have been added wisely, since his flesh was indeed subject to many miseries common to the human condition, but by no means to those in which sin is. So Christ's flesh had something peculiar in it, beyond our common flesh. Nor should anyone, from what is said here, "in the days of his flesh," quibble that Christ no longer has flesh, as if he had had flesh only until the time of his temporal death. By no means is this so: for he has, as he himself says in the last chapter of Luke, flesh and bones just as before, and he has not been made a spirit.

units.la: Nam Αὐχεῖν proprie sunt orationes, quibus petimus à malis liberari: quæ vox mire cō-uenit pontifici oranti, vt homines liberentur à peccatis. ἱκετηρία supplicatione significat, adeoque gestus ipsos magno ardore orantis, veluti manuum extensionem & huiusmo-di. Itaque hæc vox quadrat pontifici, qui in publica oratione gestus etiam decoros ad incitandum circumstantium animos, & suum feruorem declarandũ addit: quos gestus Christus in horto orans, item in cruce extensis brachijs pulcherrimè expresit. Porrò, quando ita Christus describitur orasse & supplicasse, non pro se quidem ista fecit, (sicut sacerdotes legales pro se quoque debebant sacrificia & victimas offerre) sed pro aliorū salute. Id quod ex illo Ioan.17.vbi petit credentes sanctificari, potest cognosci: item ex illo, Pater ignosce illis: quæ non tantùm pro crucifigentibus, sed pro toto humano ge-nere facta sunt: sicut omnia vniuersaliter facta sunt ibi. Ipse enim, qui peccatum non fe-cit, quare pro remissione peccati oraret? Et cùm nunquam fuerit diuina potentia sua de-stitutus, quid debuisset ipse tanquam impotens petere? Illæ autem voces, si fieri potest, transeat me calix iste: item, Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me deseruisti? non sunt peten-tis auxilium, vel poscentis liberari à morte: sed veritatem naturæ humanæ declarant. Cùm alias ille diuinam suam naturam prædicans clarè dicat: Ego potestatem habeo po-nendi animam meam, & iterum accipiendi. Rursus Ioan.2. Soluite templum hoc, & rur-sus post triduum suscitabo illud. Quod eò pertinet, ut melius intelligantur se-quentia.
units.tr: For δεήσεις [deēseis] properly means prayers by which we ask to be delivered from evils, a word which fits remarkably well the priest praying that men may be freed from sins. ἱκετηρίας [hiketērias] signifies supplication, and so also the very gestures of one praying with great fervour, such as the stretching out of the hands and the like. Hence this word suits the priest, who in public prayer also adds becoming gestures to stir the minds of those present and to show his own fervour. Christ praying in the garden, and likewise on the cross with arms outstretched, expressed these gestures most beautifully. Moreover, when Christ is described as having prayed and made supplication in this way, he did not do so for himself (as the legal priests too had to offer sacrifices and victims for themselves), but for the salvation of others. This can be known from that passage in John 17, where he asks that believers be sanctified, and likewise from his words, "Father, forgive them," which were spoken not only for those who crucified him but for the whole human race, just as everything there was done universally. For he who did not commit sin, why would he pray for the remission of sin? And since he was never deprived of his divine power, what ought he to have asked as one powerless? Those words, "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me," and likewise, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" are not the request of one seeking help, or asking to be delivered from death, but they declare the reality of human nature. Elsewhere, when he proclaims his divine nature, he says plainly: "I have power to lay down my life, and to take it up again." Again in John 2: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." This bears on the matter, so that what follows may be better understood.

units.la: Apud illum, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare) Sicut supra dixi, tempus, quo Christus obtule-rit suas orationes & supplicationes, hic notatur, videlicet tempus mortis. Et reuera præ-cipua oratio, & amplissimum sacrificiū Christi in morte peragebatur, quo & orauit pro hominum salute, & semetipsum in hostiam obtulit, adeoq; ipse simul sacerdos, simul vi-ctima hic depingitur. Victimæ enim per mortem & mactationem offerebatur. Et hæc est caussa, cur mortis mentionem inserat. Nam satis fuisset dicere, ad Deum patrem supplicationes oblatas: sed ut tempus exhibitarum supplicationum, & formam ple-nius ostenderet, voluit de morte aliquid inferere. Vnde non est, quod ex his arripiat ali-quis occasionem dicendi, quòd Christus ideò orarit, ut à morte liberaretur. Nam etise-cundum fragilitatem naturæ visus sit ita petere, tamen subiecit etiam verba, quibus do-cebat, se voluntatem paternæ disputationis præponere voluntati carnis suæ. Sic enim ait: Veruntamen non sicut ego uolo, sed sicut tu. Atque erat impossibile, Christum à morte teneri, sicut Actorum 2. dicitur.
units.tr: "Before him who was able to save him from death": as I said above, the time at which Christ offered his prayers and supplications is noted here, namely the time of death. And indeed the chief prayer and the greatest sacrifice of Christ was accomplished in his death, when he both prayed for the salvation of men and offered himself as a victim; thus he is depicted here as at once priest and victim. For victims were offered through death and slaughter. And this is the reason why he inserts mention of death. For it would have been enough to say that supplications were offered to God the Father, but in order to show more fully the time of the supplications and their form, he chose to add something about death. Hence no one should seize on these words as an occasion for saying that Christ prayed so that he might be delivered from death. For although according to the frailty of his nature he seemed to ask thus, nevertheless he added words by which he taught that he set the will of the Father above the will of his flesh. For he says: "Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." And it was impossible for Christ to be held by death, as is said in Acts 2.

units.la: Et certè potuisset Deus per suam potentiam aliter prospicere saluti humani ge-neris, & Christum à morte illa liberare: sed aliter non expediebat, uti supra ostendi-mus capite secundo, vbi caussæ, quare Christum decuerit hominē fieri & mortem ob-ire, sunt expositæ, maximè illo loco, vbi ait Apostolus, Decebat enim eum, propter quem sunt omnia, &c. Per mortē enim Christi temporanea oportuit nos liberari à morte æterna. Igi-tur verbis illis, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare, in primis periphrasticos omnipotentia Dei patris, deinde aliæ quædam circumstantiæ notantur. Hoc uerò hic discendum, quòd so-lum Deum debemus inuocare, utpote qui solus omnipotens, solus nos à morte æterna liberare valens.
units.tr: And certainly God could have provided for the salvation of the human race by his power in another way, and freed Christ from that death; but another way was not expedient, as I showed above in chapter 2, where the reasons why it became Christ to be made man and to die are set out, especially in the place where the Apostle says, "For it became him, for whom are all things," etc. For through the temporal death of Christ it was necessary that we be freed from eternal death. Therefore in the words "who was able to save him from death" the omnipotence of God the Father is named in a periphrasis, and then other circumstances are noted. What is to be learned here is that we ought to call upon God alone, since he alone is almighty and alone able to free us from eternal death.

units.la: Cum clamore ualido & lachrymis) Signa sunt externa, quibus uehemes animi affectus in-terior eleganter significatur. Atque hæc ipsa signa affectuum in euangelio describuntur. De lachrymis enim licet aliàs sæpius, tamen præcipuè ante mortem videtur illud acci-piendum Luc.22. Et correptus angore prolixius orabat. Et erat sudor eius sicut gutt͏ę san-guinis in terram decurrentis. Vbi mirabilis ardor & mirabiles lachrymæ describuntur. De clamore item Luc.23. Et cum clamasset voce magna Iesus, ait, Pater, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum: sanè non tam se, quàm totam ecclesiam, pro qua sacrifica-bat, Deo commendans. Nec posset ullis verbis ingens ardor Christi, quo pro nobis ora-uit, & semetipsum obtulit, satis explicari. Ideò Apostolus saltem his verbis voluit obiter tantundem insinuare. Quanquam de internis lachrymis, per quas charitas, condolentia & commiseratio nostræ miseriæ significatur: item de clamore interno, id est, vehemen-ti affectu accipi hæc posse quis neget? Qui enim aliorum uicem valde dolent, collachry-mantur: sicut Christus fleuit super Lazari mortem, item propter euersionem Hierosolý-morum, quam præuidebat. Et clamor etiam tacitum & latentem affectum significat: Vnde Exodi 14. Dominus ad Mosen prostratum in terra, & ta cite orantem, Quid cla-mas ad me?
units.tr: With strong crying and tears. These are external signs by which the inward, vehement affections of the mind are elegantly signified. And these very signs of the affections are described in the Gospel. Concerning tears, though they are mentioned often elsewhere, this is especially to be understood of the time before death, Luke 22: "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat was as drops of blood falling down upon the ground." Here a wonderful ardour and wonderful tears are described. Likewise concerning the cry, Luke 23: "And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit": surely commending not so much himself as the whole Church, for which he was sacrificing, to God. No words could sufficiently explain the immense ardour of Christ, with which he prayed for us and offered himself. Therefore the Apostle wished, at least by these words, to hint at as much in passing. Yet who would deny that these words can also be taken of inward tears, through which charity, sympathy and compassion for our misery are signified; and of an inward cry, that is, a vehement affection? For those who grieve greatly for the sake of others weep together with them, just as Christ wept over the death of Lazarus, and likewise over the overthrow of Jerusalem, which he foresaw. And a cry also signifies a silent and hidden affection: whence in Exodus 14 the Lord said to Moses, who lay prostrate on the ground and prayed silently, "Why do you cry out to me?"

units.la: Notandum interea, nos hic de modo orandi doceri: magno enim animi feruore o-randum est, tota mente, omnibusque viribus, si à Deo exaudiri volumus.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is to be noted that we are taught here about the manner of praying: for we must pray with great warmth of spirit, with the whole mind and with all our strength, if we wish to be heard by God.

units.la: Et exauditus est pro reuerentia) Et hæc particula arguit, Christum non orasse pro se, ut à morte liberaretur. Quando enim mortem non euasit, dici non posset exauditus. Sed exauditus est: quia, vbi orauit pro salute generis humani, ip se eâ impetrauit. Effectus enim precationum & supplicationum Christi hac voce significatur: Sciebat autem Christus, se à patre exaudiendum: sicut ipse Ioannis vndecimo diserte ait, Ego autem sciebam, quod semper me audis. Et paulo ante Martha ad Iesum: Domine, si fuisses hic, frater meus non fuisset mortuus: sed & nunc scio, quòd, quaecunque popposceris à Deo, daturus sit tibi Deus. Neq; est, quod obijciatur, Christum non esse exauditum pro omnibus, quando plurimi exluderis perditum, & hodie adhuc innumeri ex ijs, qui per baptismum & caenâ Domini cooptati sunt in ciues ecclesiae Dei, pereunt. Nam Christus orauit tantum pro ueris creditur, sicut clare videtur Ioan. 17. Verba quae dedisti mihi, dedi eis, & ipsi acceperunt, & cognouerunt vere, quòd à te exiui, & crediderunt, quòd tu me misisti. Ego pro eis rogo: non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his, quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt. Ibidem: Pater sancte serua eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi. Paulo post: Non pro eis autem rogo tantum, sed & pro ijs, qui crediturisunt per sermonem eorum in me, &c. Ergo fuit exauditus pro omnibus, qui suapte malitia per incredulitatem seipsos non erant à participatione misericordiae Dei excluduri. Quod autem dicit, pro reuerentia, va rie exponitur. Quidam intuentes in constructionem graecam, ita exposuerunt, quasi diceretur, Christum exauditum ab ipsa reuerentia, id est, à Deo patre, qui prae omnibus est maximè reuerendus, adeoque ipsa maiestas & reuerentia. Alij verò, quoniam non tantum reuerentiam significat, sed pietatem, transferunt particulam hanc ad modu precationum & supplicationum Christi, ut sit sententia: Christum exauditum propter singularem suam in supplicando pietatem. Rursus autem etiam significat dignitatem & autoritatem, quae cuipiam ut optime merito defertur, & propter quam placet proburque, quod ab illo fit. Atq; hoc modo sententia est, Christum exauditum propter suâ dignitatem, excellentiam, propter quam Deo patri in eo maximè complacitum est. Et certè propter dignitatem personae ipsius audiendi sunt caeteri, quid ni ipse propter propriam dignitatem audiatur? Iubet autem ac docet ipse, vt à patre in nomine ipsius petamus, & tum certum fore, nos audiendos. Atq; hac ratione illustratur mirum in modum Christi dignitas, & prae veteribus pontificibus excellentia. Nâ de nullis dici potest, quòd propter personae suę dignitatem sint exauditi, nisi de solo Christo, in quo vno ipse pater testatus est sibi bene complacitum. Imò nulla unquâ sacrificia accepta fuerunt, nisi propter Christum, & quatenus fide in Christum erant oblata. Quare haec interpretatio magis arridet: idq; eò magis, quòd consolatoria admodum sit. Si quàdo enim nos oramus, & metuimus, nos propter nostram indignitatem non exaudiendos, respiciamus in dignitatem Christi, & certò statuamus, propter illum omnia nobis à patre concedenda.
units.tr: And he was heard for his reverence. This particle shows that Christ did not pray for himself that he might be freed from death. For since he did not escape death, he could not be said to have been heard. But he was heard, because when he prayed for the salvation of the human race, he obtained it by that very prayer. The effect of Christ's prayers and supplications is signified by this phrase: Christ knew that he would be heard by the Father; just as he himself expressly says in John 11: But I knew that you always hear me. And a little before, Martha said to Jesus: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you. Nor is there any force in the objection that Christ was not heard for all, since very many perish, and even today countless of those who have been admitted through baptism and the Lord's Supper as citizens of the Church of God are perishing. For Christ prayed only for true believers, as is clearly seen in John 17: "The words which you gave me I have given to them, and they have received them and have truly known that I came out from you, and they have believed that you sent me. I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours." Again: "Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me." A little later: "I do not pray for them alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word," etc. Therefore he was heard for all who, by their own wickedness, through unbelief, were not going to exclude themselves from participation in the mercy of God. But what he says, "for his reverence," is variously explained. Some, looking to the Greek construction, have explained it as if it were said that Christ was heard from the very reverence, that is, from God the Father, who above all is most worthy of reverence, and so from majesty and reverence itself. Others, since the word signifies not only reverence but also piety, transfer this particle to the manner of Christ's prayers and supplications, so that the meaning is: Christ was heard on account of his singular piety in supplicating. The word also signifies dignity and authority, which is rightly and deservedly accorded to someone, and on account of which what is done by him is pleasing and approved. In this way the meaning is: Christ was heard on account of his dignity and excellence, for which the Father was especially well pleased with him. And surely, if others are to be heard on account of the dignity of their person, why should not he be heard on account of his own dignity? He himself also bids and teaches us to ask the Father in his name, and then it will be certain that we shall be heard. In this way the marvellous dignity of Christ, and his excellence above the ancient high priests, is illustrated. For it can be said of no one that he was heard on account of the dignity of his person, except of Christ alone, in whom the Father himself testified that he was well pleased. Indeed no sacrifices were ever accepted except on account of Christ, and insofar as they were offered in faith in Christ. Wherefore this interpretation pleases more, and all the more because it is very comforting. For if, when we pray, we fear that we shall not be heard on account of our unworthiness, let us look to the dignity of Christ, and firmly hold that everything is to be granted us by the Father on account of him.

units.la: Hac de causa ecclesia docuit, orationes omnes claudere hac particula, per Christum Dominum nostrum: quandoquidem & ipse Christus docuit in nomine suo petendum, si quid à Deo patre volumus obtinere.
units.tr: For this reason the Church has taught that all prayers be concluded with this phrase, "through Christ our Lord," since Christ himself taught that we must ask in his name if we wish to obtain anything from God the Father.

units.la: Qui placabilis esse possit ignorantibus & errantibus. Quandoquidé & ipse circumdatus est infirmitate: & propter hanc debet quemadmodum pro populo, ita & pro se ipso immolare pro peccatis: ita & Christus, tametsi filius erat, tamen didicit ex his, quae passus est, obedientiam, ac perfectus redditus, omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis aeternae.
units.tr: He can have compassion on the ignorant and on those who go astray, since he himself also is compassed with infirmity; and for this reason he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins. And so Christ, though he was a Son, yet learned obedience from the things which he suffered; and being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him.

units.la: Haec secundi argumenti ratio fluit ex argumento praecedenti. Quando enim pontificis est, donaria & uictimas offerre, ex hoc iam sequitur, placabilem & misericordem erga alios eum esse debere. Quomodo enim serio intercedat pro alijs, nisi eorum uicem doleat, & iuuare ex animo sit paratus? Atq; ut clarius ostendat, qua in re sita sit haec placabilitas, siue, erga quos deceat pontifices esse placabiles, addit:
units.tr: This second line of argument follows from the preceding one. For when it is the office of a high priest to offer gifts and victims, it follows at once that he ought to be placable and merciful toward others. For how could he intercede earnestly for others unless he grieves for them and is ready from the heart to help? And so that he may show more clearly in what this placability consists, or toward whom high priests ought to be placable, he adds:

units.la: Ignorantibus & errantibus) Hi enim maximè commiseratione digni sunt, qui vel per ignorantiam peccant, vel certè per fragilitatem, & non spontaneam malitiam, ut errare, quadam extenuationis forma, potius dicantur quâ peccare. Huiusmodi autem omnes illi sunt, qui, postquâ peccarunt, agnoscunt peccatum suū, & poscunt à Deo veniam, cupiūt per pontificem pro se intercedi, victimas, quae nomine ipsorum offerantur, adducunt. Requiri autem placabilitatem & moderationé affectuum in pontifice, satis arguunt lo ci illi, quibus praecedens definitio est comprobata. Quanquam etiam illud nominatim de Mose praedicatur, Num. 12. Erat Moses vir mitissimus super omnes homines, qui moraban tur in terra. Malachiae 2. inter alia vitia, in quae lapsi fuerunt sacerdotes, illud quoq; obijcitur. Quare despicit vnusquisq; vestrum fratrem suum, violans pactum patrum nostrorum? Ezechiel 34. contra pastores Israel: Gregem autem meu non pascebatis, quo i infirmum fuit, non consolidastis, & quod ægrotum, non sanastis, quod confractum est, non alligastis, & quod abiectum est, non reduxistis, & quod perierat, non quæsistis: sed cum austeritate imperabatis eis, & cum potetia. Luc.10.hoc maximè damnatur in sacerdote & Leuita, quòd eius, qui inciderat in latrones, non fuerant miserti: quia nimirum eorum maximè intererat misereri. Paulus hanc condolentiam & placabilitatem in sepre dicat, 2. Cor.11.dicens: Quis infirmatur, & ego non infirmor? Quis offenditur, & ego non uror? 2. Tim.2.Seruum Domini oportet esse placidum. 1. Petri 3. Spiritus placidus sit & quietus, &c.
units.tr: The ignorant and those who go astray. For those are most worthy of compassion who sin through ignorance, or at least through frailty and not through deliberate malice, so that to err is said, by a kind of softening, rather than to sin. All those are of this sort who, after they have sinned, acknowledge their sin and ask pardon from God, desire that intercession be made for them through the high priest, and bring victims to be offered in their name. That placability and moderation of the affections are required in a high priest, those passages sufficiently prove by which the preceding definition was confirmed. Indeed it is also said expressly of Moses, Num. 12: "Now Moses was a very meek man, above all men who lived on the earth." In Malachi 2, among the other faults into which the priests had fallen, this too is laid against them: "Why does each of you despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers?" Ezekiel 34 speaks against the shepherds of Israel: "But you did not feed my flock; the weak you did not strengthen, the sick you did not heal, the broken you did not bind up, the outcast you did not bring back, the lost you did not seek; but you ruled over them with harshness and with force." In Luke 10 this is most condemned in the priest and the Levite, that they had not had mercy on the man who fell among robbers: because it was especially their business to show mercy. Paul sums up this sympathy and placability in 2 Cor. 11, saying: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" 2 Tim. 2: "The servant of the Lord must be gentle." 1 Pet. 3: "Let the spirit be gentle and quiet," etc.

units.la: Cæterùm ipse Apostolus, quare placabilis esse debeat pontifex, addit rationem: Quàdoquidem & ipse circundatus est infirmitate: Sumpta est hæc ratio ab experientia propriarum miseriarum. Quæ quis in se mala senserit, eadem in alio respiciens, citius ad miserandum movetur. Unde illud vulgò iactatum: tu si hic fies, longè aliter sentias. Qua de re supra capite secundo super illo, Nam ex hoc, quod ipsi contigit, tentatum esse, potest & his, qui tentantur succurrere.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle himself adds the reason why the high priest ought to be compassionate: since he himself also is compassed with infirmity. This reason is drawn from experience of one's own miseries. Whoever has felt evils in himself, and sees them in another, is more quickly moved to pity. Hence the common saying: if you were in his place, you would feel quite differently. On this matter, see above in chapter two, on the words, "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able also to succour them that are tempted."

units.la: Sequitur:
units.tr: It follows:

units.la: Et propter hanc debet, quemadmodum pro populo, ita & pro seipso immolare pro peccatis.
units.tr: And for this reason he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins.

units.la: Probatio rationis præcedentis à signo, quasi dicat: En euidens signum, quòd pontifex sit circundatus infirmitate & peccatis. Nam & ipse debet pro se suisq; peccatis perinde immolare, atque pro alijs, qui infirmitate sunt circundati. Quod sanè, si peccati esset expers, facere haud deberet. Quomodo verò pontifices orare & offerre debeant pro propriis peccatis, habes multis locis Leuit.4. Si sacerdos, qui unctus est, peccauerit, delinquere faciens populum, offeret pro peccato suo vitulũ immaculatū, &c. Leuit.6.Hæc est oblatio Aaron & filiorum eius, quà offerre debet Domino in die unctionis suæ. Decimâ partem Ephi offerent similæ in sacrificio sempiterno, medium eius mane, & medium eius uespera, quæ in sartagine oleo conspersa frigetur. Leuit.9. Moses ad Aaron: Accede ad altare, & immola pro peccato tuo. Offer holocaustum, & deprecare pro te, & pro populo. Mox subditur: Statimque Aaron accedens ad altare immolauit vitulũ pro peccato suo, &c. Sed præterea propter infirmitates & vitia sua etiam valde crassa reprehenduntur pontifices & sacerdotes in prophetis, ut non necessarium videatur, probationes aliquas de re manifesta adferre. Et hoc quiuis potest iudicare, quòd pontifices, qualibet alias conspicui vitæ sanctimonia, tamen semper infirmitate fuerint circundati, & pro peccatis suis orare debuerint & sacrificia offerre. Necessariò illud sequitur: Si fuerunt homines, (licut omnes certè fuerunt) fuerunt & peccatores. Quanquam existimandum non est, Apostolum sine causa probationem istâ de pontificum infirmitate, & oblatione pro propriis peccatis produxisse. Etsi enim de re per se manifesta sit, atque insuper ad collationem, quæ instituta est, non videatur admodum facere, quandoquidem in consequenti membro de Christo eadem (quòd videlicet per infirmitatem peccarit, & pro peccatis suis victimas obtulerit) dici pari modo non poterunt, tamen certum est, studio & singulari prudentia ab apostolo ita factum. Hoc autem mihi videtur eius fuisse consilium. Voluit infirmitate pontificũ hac ratione de oblatione pro peccatis ipsorũ probare, ut nimirum, vbi post asserturus est, Christum itidem infirmitate circundatum, passum multa, & didicisse obedientiam, ac proinde placabilem factum, sicq; potificijs virtutibus egregiè ornatum: illud verò de oblatione pro peccatis propriis addi tamen poterit, (cùm hæc particula Christo omnis peccati experti nequaquam competat) ut Christi gloria ac dignitas hinc magis illustretur, eiusque præ omnibus alijs pontificibus excellentia clarius agnoscatur. Nam vbi Christum dicturus est, more aliorum pontificum, ut facilius condoleat nobis, infirmitate circundatum, quia reuera multa in carne passus est, dum obedies fuit patri usq; ad mortem: atq; hac in parte docebit, omnia communia esse Christo cũ cæteris pontificibus: verùm hanc particulam, quòd videlicet infirmitates ipsius fuerint vitiosæ, vt propter eas deberet orare, & victimas offerre, sicut victimas obtulit pro infirmitatib. & peccatis aliorum: istud, inquam, cùm de Christo addere nō poterat, & hac nota inprimis Christus distat à cæteris pontificibus: quis nō videat istud ad Christi laude amplissimâ facere? Annón magna est excellentia Christi, quòd per omnia similis sit cæteris pontificibus, & omnes virtutes eorum in se habeat, at nulla eorū vitia: omnes infirmitates, dempto peccato. Non igitur otiosè, sed graui de causa & summo planè artificio Apostolus probationem istam de infirmitate pontificum subiecit. Tantum de antecedente: nunc de consequente.
units.tr: This is a proof of the preceding reason from a sign, as if he said: "Here is a clear sign that the high priest is compassed with infirmity and sins. For he must offer for himself and his own sins, just as for others who are compassed with infirmity. Certainly, if he were free from sin, he would not need to do this." Where the Law teaches that high priests must pray and offer for their own sins, you have it in many places in Leviticus 4: "If the priest that is anointed shall sin, to the trespass of the people, then let him bring for his sin a young bullock without blemish," and so on. Leviticus 6: "This is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they shall offer unto the Lord in the day when he is anointed: the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour for a meat offering perpetual, half of it in the morning and half of it at night. In a pan it shall be made with oil." Leviticus 9: Moses said to Aaron, "Go unto the altar, and offer thy sin offering, and thy burnt offering, and make an atonement for thyself, and for the people." Immediately afterwards it is added: "And Aaron went unto the altar, and slew the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself." Moreover, the high priests and priests are rebuked in the prophets even for their infirmities and their very gross faults, so that it seems unnecessary to bring forward proofs for a matter so plain. Anyone can judge that the high priests, however conspicuous for the holiness of their lives, were nevertheless always compassed with infirmity, and ought to have prayed and offered sacrifices for their sins. It necessarily follows: if they were men (as all certainly were), they were also sinners. Yet we must not suppose that the Apostle brought forward this proof, about the infirmity of the high priests and their offering for their own sins, without cause. For although it is plain in itself, and although it does not seem to contribute much to the comparison he has undertaken (since in the following clause the same things cannot be said in the same way of Christ, namely that he sinned through infirmity and offered victims for his own sins), it is certain that the Apostle did this with deliberate and singular prudence. This seems to me to have been his purpose. He wished to prove by this argument, from the infirmity of the priests, that they offered for their sins, so that when he afterwards goes on to say that Christ too was compassed with infirmity, that he suffered much and learned obedience, and thus became compassionate and was adorned with priestly virtues in an outstanding way, he might add, about the offering for his own sins, something that cannot properly apply to Christ, who knew no sin: namely, that the glory and dignity of Christ might be the more illustrated, and his excellence above all other high priests the more clearly acknowledged. For when he is about to say of Christ, in the manner of the other high priests, that he was compassed with infirmity so that he might more readily sympathise with us, because he really suffered many things in the flesh while he was obedient to the Father even unto death, he will teach in this respect that everything is common to Christ and the other high priests. But this particular point, that his infirmities were faulty, so that on account of them he ought to pray and offer victims, just as he offered victims for the infirmities and sins of others, this, I say, he could not add concerning Christ. And by this mark especially Christ differs from the other high priests. Who does not see that this makes for the highest praise of Christ? Is not the excellence of Christ great, that he is in all things like the other high priests, and has all their virtues, yet none of their vices: all their infirmities, except sin? Therefore the Apostle subjoined this proof about the infirmity of the high priests not idly, but for a serious reason and with consummate skill. So much for the antecedent; now for the consequent.

units.la: Ita & Christus, tametsi filius erat, tamen didicit ex his, quæ passus est, obedientiâ, ac perfectus reddit us, omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis æternæ.
units.tr: So also Christ, though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered; and being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him.

units.la: Et istud consequens perinde ac præcedentis argumenti, alijs verbis reddit, quàm po-sita sita fuerant in antecedente, atque vbi simpliciter dicendum fuisset, Christus quoq; fuit placabilis, quoniam & infirmitate circundatus, placuit ei eiusmodi oratione tantundem significare, cuius singulæ particulæ rursus dignitatem Christi supra omnium pontificum dignitatem attollunt: id quod eundo per singulas particulas nō difficulter ostendemus. Primùm particula hæc, tametsi filius erat, præterquam quòd Christum ostendit excellentiorem cæteris sacerdotibus eo nomine, quòd hi quidem tantùm hominum filij sint, ipse verò filius Dei: tum verò bonitatem & placabilitatem eius mirificè prædicat amplificatque, quòd videlicet Christus, cùm tantus sit, tamen, vt patri obediret, humilis fieri, & nitro more omne genus miseriarum in se sentire non sit dedignatus. Quæ sanè res mirabilem ostendit Christi dignitatem præ cæteris pontificibus, qui profectò si potuissent infirmitates & miserias euadere, nullo modo se ad eas perferendas submisissent. Non disimili modo amplificatur Christi bonitas Philippens. 2. Qui, cū esset in forma Dei, nō rapinā arbitratus est, vt esset æqualis Deo, sed semetipsum inaniuit, forma serui sumpta, in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus ut homo, humilem præbuit semetipsum, factus obediens vsque ad mortem. Qui locus valde conuenit præsenti explicando, quandoquidem de obedientia Christi, de qua & hic sermo est, diserte loquitur.
units.tr: This consequent, just as in the preceding argument, expresses in other words what had been stated in the antecedent. Where he might simply have said, "Christ also was compassionate, since he too was compassed with infirmity," it pleased him to signify the same thing by a form of speech, each part of which again raises the dignity of Christ above the dignity of all high priests. We shall not find it difficult to show this by going through the parts one by one. First, the phrase though he was a Son not only shows Christ to be more excellent than the other priests on this ground, that they are only sons of men while he is the Son of God, but also marvellously proclaims and magnifies his goodness and compassion, namely that Christ, though so great, nevertheless did not disdain to become humble, in order to obey the Father, and after our manner to feel every kind of misery in himself. This truly shows the wonderful dignity of Christ above the other high priests, who certainly, if they could have escaped infirmities and miseries, would in no way have submitted themselves to bearing them. The goodness of Christ is magnified in a similar way in Philippians 2: "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death." This passage fits very well in explaining the present matter, since it speaks expressly of the obedience of Christ, which is also what is spoken of here.

units.la: Tamen didicit ex his, quæ passus est, obedientiam) Hæc particula præcipuè spectanda est, utpote qua significare uult, Christum esse placabilem. Vtitur autem quadam Synedoches forma, ponens id, quod prius est, ut ex eo intelligatur posterius, more Scripturæ admodum vsitato. Addit enim, multa passum esse, atque ita obedientiam didicisse, hoc est, vere expertum omne genus miseriarum, quas pater ab æterno constituerat, eum debere experiri. Ex hac porrò miseriarum & infirmitatum experientia sequi, & quemuis intelligere posse, eum factum placabilem.
units.tr: Yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered. This phrase must be considered especially, since it is meant to signify that Christ is compassionate. It uses a certain form of synecdoche, putting what is prior so that the posterior may be understood from it, a manner very common in Scripture. For he adds that he suffered much, and so learned obedience, that is, truly experienced every kind of misery which the Father from eternity had appointed that he should undergo. From this experience of miseries and infirmities it follows, and anyone can understand, that he was made compassionate.

units.la: Sic verò in antecedente dictum est, pontifices debere esse placabiles, eò, quòd ipsi quoque infirmitate sint circundati. Et suprà capite secundo de Christo homine facto. Ex hoc, quòd contigit tentatum esse, potest & his, qui tentantur, succurrere. Item capite quarto: Non habemus pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum per omnia. Ac notanda est valde elegans loquendi forma, qua ait, Christũ didicisse obedientiam. Vt enim significet, Christum reuera admodum graues & multas miserias pertulisse: ac deinde intelligatur etiam, præ cæteris omnibus valde placabilem, sicut semper magis placabiles esse conuenit, qui ipsi plura pertulerint aduersa, ait, proverbiali propemodum figura, siue figurata locutione, Christum exijs, quæ passus est, didicisse obedientiam, hoc est, egregiè, &, ut sic loquar, humano more, fere supra quàm ptabile ei foret, expertũ omnis generis calamitates & miserias. Vulgus ipsum ita loqui solet, si quando significare volunt, quempiam probè nosse & abundè aliquid expertum, præsertim quod durius vel molestius est: veluti si quispiam reuersus è militia narret, & queratur, se multa pertulisse, multò plus expendisse, quàm lucratum, dicent, illum egregiè didicisse militare. Qui item cum vafro & fraudulento homine habens commertium, inuenit se deceptum, dicet, se didicisse, quid sit cum eiusmodi hominibus habere consuetudinem.
units.tr: Thus it was said in the antecedent that the high priests ought to be compassionate, because they too are compassed with infirmity. And above, in chapter two, of Christ made man: "In that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able also to succour them that are tempted." Likewise in chapter four: "We have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but was in all points tempted like as we are." And a very elegant form of speech is to be noted here, in which he says that Christ learned obedience. For to signify that Christ really suffered very grave and many miseries, and that it may then also be understood that he was above all others very compassionate (as those who have suffered more adversity ought always to be more compassionate), he says, by an almost proverbial figure, or figurative expression, that Christ learned obedience from the things which he suffered, that is, that he experienced, in an outstanding way and, so to speak, in human fashion, almost beyond what was fitting for him, every kind of calamity and misery. The common people are wont to speak thus when they wish to signify that someone knows something well and has had ample experience of it, especially if it is harder or more troublesome: for example, if someone returning from military service tells of it and complains that he endured much and spent much more than he gained, they will say that he has learned his soldiering thoroughly. Likewise, one who has dealings with a crafty and deceitful man, and finds himself cheated, will say that he has learned what it is to keep company with such men.

units.la: Sic prouerbialiter dicitur in eandẽ sententiam, meo malo istud didici: utinam non tã edoctus essem hancrem: Quæ nocent, docent: τὰ πεπόνθματα μαθήματα. Ictus sapit piscator. Respublica virum docet. Simili igitur forma ait, Christum ex his, quæ passus est, didicisse obedientiam, id est, egregiè expertum, quid sit patri obedire. Atque erat patris voluntas, vt filius certo tempore homo fieret, omnes humanas miserias subiret, denique & mortem pro salute generis humani perferret. Quæ omnia vbi peregit Christus, vbi omnia quæ præordinauerat pater expleuit, profectò didicit, & egregiè expertus est, quid esset patri obedire, egregiè didicit obedientiam.
units.tr: Thus it is proverbially said to the same effect: I learned that by my own harm; I wish I had not been taught so thoroughly. What harms also teaches: [τὰ πεπόνθματα μαθήματα] (what we suffer teaches us). The sting teaches the fisherman. War teaches the man. So in a similar way the Apostle says that Christ learned obedience from the things he suffered, that is, he thoroughly experienced what it means to obey the Father. It was the Father's will that the Son should become man at a certain time, undergo all human miseries, and finally endure death for the salvation of the human race. When Christ had accomplished all these things, when he had fulfilled everything the Father had ordained beforehand, he certainly learned and thoroughly experienced what it means to obey the Father; he learned obedience thoroughly.

units.la: Et discere etiam propria significatione experiri, sentire, intelligere significat: vnde experimento discere pro ualde certò nosse. In bonam partem, Philippens. 4. Ego didici in quibus sum, his contentus esse. Noui & humilis esse, noui & excellere. Vbique & in omnibus institutus sum, & saturari, & esurire, & abundare, & penuriam pati. In malam partem, Ezechiel. 19. contra principes Israel. Et tu fili hominis assume planctũ super principes Israel, & dices: Quare mater tua leæna inter leones cubauit? In medio leunculorũ enutriuit catulos suos. Et eduxit vnum de leunculis suis, leo factus est, & didicit capere prædam hominemque comedere. Et audierunt de eo gentes, & non absque vulneribus suis ceperunt eum, & adduxerunt eum in cathenis in terram Aegypti. 1. Tim. 1. Nonnulli circa fidem naufragium fecerunt, quorum de numero est Hymenæus & Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ, vt discant non maledicere.
units.tr: In its proper sense, to learn also means to experience, to feel, to understand; hence "to learn by experience" means to know something for certain. In a good sense, Philippians 4: "I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound. In every place and in all things I have been instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need." In a bad sense, Ezekiel 19, against the princes of Israel: "And you, son of man, take up a lament over the princes of Israel, and say: What was your mother, a lioness, doing lying among lions? She nursed her cubs among the young lions. And she brought up one of her young lions; he became a lion, and he learned to seize prey and to devour men. And the nations heard of him, and they took him in their pit, not without wounds, and they brought him in chains into the land of Egypt." 1 Timothy 1: "Some have made shipwreck concerning the faith, of whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme."

units.la: In his locis dicitur, didici contentus esse, esurire, &c. didicit prædam capere: non discant maledicere, penè ea forma, qua dicitur hic Christum didicisse obedire, seu didicisse obedientiâ. Notat igitur Apostolus hac loquendi forma, didicit ex his, quæ passus est, obedientiam, maiorem in Christo conspici posse placabilitatem, quàm in cæteris pontificibus, cùm longè alia ratione expertus sit miserias & infirmitates, quàm cæteri. Ac mul tò significantius est, quod dicit, Christum didicisse obedientiam, ex his, quæ passus fuit, quàm si simpliciter dixisset, Christum fuisse infirmitate circundatum.
units.tr: In these places it is said "I have learned to be content," "to hunger," etc., "he learned to seize prey," "they may learn not to blaspheme," almost in the same form in which it is said here that Christ learned obedience, or learned by obedience. The Apostle therefore indicates by this manner of speaking that he learned obedience from the things he suffered, so that a greater gentleness can be seen in Christ than in the other high priests, since he experienced miseries and infirmities in a very different way from the others. And it is much more emphatic that he says Christ learned obedience from the things he suffered, than if he had simply said that Christ was surrounded by weakness.

units.la: Ac perfectus redditus) Supple, per obedietiam & humiliationem. Idem hic sibi vult, quod cap. 2. dixit: Decebat cum, propter quem sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia, ut multis filijs in gloriam adductis, principem salutis illorum per afflictiones perfectum redderet. Quanquam verosimilius est, hanc particulam, ad extollendam Christi dignitatem præ cæteris pontificibus, esse addi tam. Vbi enim præcedentibus verbis satis declarauit, Christum more aliorum multis infirmitatibus fuisse obnoxium, nunc adijciendum putauit, quo Christus rursus omnes ex cellit, & ab alijs distinguitur, nimirum, quòd infirmitates Christi non tendant ad imperfectionem, vel damnationem, sed potius ad perfectionem, quòd Christus per eas fit perfectus. Atq; ita notat, vitiosas infirmitates in Christo non habere locum, sicut & supradixit, per omnia tentatum, absq; peccato.
units.tr: "And, having been made perfect": supply, through obedience and humiliation. Here he means the same thing he said in chapter 2: "It was fitting that he, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, should make perfect through afflictions the author of their salvation." Yet it is more probable that this particle "indeed" is added to exalt the dignity of Christ above the other high priests. For when, in the preceding words, he had made clear enough that Christ, like others, was subject to many infirmities, he thought it must now be added, so that Christ might again surpass all and be distinguished from the others: namely, that Christ's infirmities do not tend to imperfection or condemnation, but rather to perfection, since Christ is made perfect through them. And so he indicates that vicious infirmities have no place in Christ, just as he said before, "tempted in all things, without sin."

units.la: Omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis æternæ) Et hic, quemadmodum in primi argumenti posteriore parte, effectus sacerdotij seu placabilitatis Christi adijcitur: ex quo iterum quantò sit Christus cæteris pontificibus excellentior, aduerti potest. Estque sententia: Christus ad eum modum perfectus redditus, fuit omnibus obedientibus, id est, euangelium eius amplectentibus & credentibus causa perfectionis seu salutis, & quidè (quod non sine emphasi additur æternæ, cùm cæteri pontifices propria sua virtute nec tempora-neam quidem salutem sibiipsis, multò minus alijs, conferre potuerint. Hic vero patefit, pro quibus Christus orauerit, & fuerit exauditus, nempe pro obedientibus & credentibus. Proinde vides mirabili artificio pariq; prudentia ab Apostolo omnia esse disposita, & omnibus quæ addita sunt, valde dignitatem Christi in cœlum vehi. Nunc de vocibus & minutioribus rebus nonnulla adijciemus.
units.tr: "He became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obeyed him." Here too, as in the latter part of the first argument, the effect of the priesthood, or of Christ's gentleness, is added; from this again it can be noticed how much Christ is more excellent than the other high priests. And the sense is: Christ, made perfect in this way, became the cause of perfection or salvation for all the obedient, that is, for those who embrace and believe his gospel; and indeed (which is added not without emphasis) of eternal salvation, since the other high priests could not confer even temporal salvation on themselves by their own power, much less on others. Here, however, it is revealed for whom Christ prayed and was heard, namely for the obedient and believing. Therefore you see that all things have been arranged by the Apostle with wonderful skill and equal prudence, and that by all the additions the dignity of Christ is raised high to heaven. Now we will add some remarks on the words and smaller matters.

units.la: Qui placabilis esse possit: μετριοπαθεῖν Ἀπαθὲς ἀπάθειαν) Nonnulli reddiderunt: Qui condolere possit, quomodo etiam græcorum nonnulli expositi sunt per συμπαθεῖν, qua voce etiam paulò ante vsus est Apostolus.
units.tr: "Who can be moderately affected" [μετριοπαθεῖν]; "unfeeling, without passion" [Ἀπαθὲς ἀπάθειαν]. Some rendered it: "who can sympathize," as some of the Greeks also explained it by [συμπαθεῖν], a word which the Apostle also used a little earlier.

units.la: Etsi verò hac interpretatione à sensu non discedatur, tamen proprietas vocabuli nondum satis exposita est. Quamobrem Theophylactus nisus est pluribus verbis vim eius reddere dicens: μετριοπαθεῖν idè esse quod συμπαθεῖν, συγκαταβαίνειν, συγγινώσκειν, hoc est, condolere seu compati, condescendere, & sese accommodare, ignoscere. Qui propius accedunt, intuentes in vocis etymon, vertunt, moderatè ferre, quod & alias μέτριον dicitur. μέτριον enim mensura, mediocritas, modus dicitur, unde aduerbium μετρίως, & adiectiuum μετριοπαθής vero affici est. Proinde cùm vim vocis intueor, aliquid amplius mihi videtur hac voce significatum, quàm à quoquam expressum sit, & quàm vna voce latine exprimi queat. Existimo enim voce μετριοπαθεῖν significari, sic moderatam & recuperatam esse debere affectionem pontificis, ut veluti medium semper teneat, neque sic condoleat, ut indulgere videatur, & conniuendo fenestram aperire grauioribus vitijs: neque etiam sic corripiens ea, quæ corripienda sunt, ut exasperet animos delinquentium, & à bene agendo alienet, vel ad desperandum cogat. Qua quidem in re cùm summa opus sit prudentia, nec cuiusuis sit istud præstare, voluit una voce hæc omnia innuere, eoque maluit adhibere vocem hanc μετριοπαθεῖν, quàm eam, qua suprà vsus est, συμπαθεῖν. Et quis nescit pontificis esse, non tantùm condolere, sed etiam monere, corripere, increpare, cùm res poscit? sicut Apostolus diserte docet 2. Tim. 3. Omnis Scriptura, inquit, vtilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in iustitia. Deinde capite quarto, Prædica sermonem, insta tempestiuè, intempestiuè, argue, increpa, exhortare, cum omni lenitate & doctrina.
units.tr: Although by this interpretation the sense is not departed from, nevertheless the proper force of the word has not yet been sufficiently explained. Therefore Theophylact took pains to render its force with more words, saying that [μετριοπαθεῖν] is the same as [συμπαθεῖν], [συγκαταβαίνειν], [συγγινώσκειν], that is, to suffer with or sympathize, to condescend, and to accommodate oneself, to forgive. Those who come closer, looking at the etymology of the word, translate it "to bear moderately," which is also elsewhere called [μέτριον]. For [μέτριον] means measure, moderation, mean; hence the adverb [μετρίως] and the adjective [μετριοπαθής], which means one who is moderately affected. Therefore, when I consider the force of the word, it seems to me that something more is signified by this word than has been expressed by anyone, and than can be expressed in Latin by one word. For I think that by [μετριοπαθεῖν] is signified that the affection of the high priest should be so moderated and controlled that he always keeps, as it were, the middle way, neither sympathizing in such a way as to seem to indulge, and by winking open a window to graver vices, nor again rebuking those things which must be rebuked in such a way as to exasperate the minds of wrongdoers and alienate them from doing well, or drive them to despair. In this matter, since the greatest prudence is required, and it is not for just anyone to achieve it, the writer wished to indicate all these things in one word, and therefore preferred to use this word [μετριοπαθεῖν] rather than that which he used above, [συμπαθεῖν]. And who does not know that it is the task of a high priest not only to sympathize, but also to admonish, to correct, to rebuke, when the matter requires it? As the Apostle plainly teaches in 2 Timothy 3: "All Scripture," he says, "is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." Then in chapter 4: "Preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching."

units.la: Hæc igitur omnia cùm sint magno studio à pontificibus præstanda, sed tamen modera-te, prudenter, & magno cum iudicio, hęc inquam omnia sic peragi debere puto per vocem μετριοπαθεῖν indicari. Ad eum verò modū plenissimè omnia officia sua peragit Christus, ut præ alijs omnibus edoctus sit vere μετριοπαθῶς, docens, exhortans, blandè inuitans, seueriter increpans, vbi opus esse videbat, sed ubique moderatè & cum decoro, modum nusquam excedens. Cæterùm, cùm erga omnes tali moderatione vti deceat, *maximè tamen erga ignorantes & errantes.
units.tr: Since therefore all these things must be performed by the high priests with great zeal, yet moderately, prudently, and with great judgement, I think that all these things, I say, are indicated to be carried out in this manner by the word [μετριοπαθεῖν]. And in this manner Christ fulfilled all his offices most fully, so that, beyond all others, he was truly taught to be [μετριοπαθῶς], teaching, exhorting, gently inviting, sternly rebuking where he saw need, yet everywhere moderately and with decorum, never exceeding the measure. Moreover, although it is fitting to use such moderation toward all, it is most fitting toward the ignorant and the erring.

units.la: Aduerte autè, quòd non simpliciter dixit, peccantes: sed, quadam extenuationis forma, ignorantes & errantes: quia erga hos maximè decet moderatè affici, qui peccant per ignorantiam & tiam & errorem.Constitui enim videtur quidam malorum gradus, è quibus nonnullos decet placidè & omni modestia ad resipiscentiam adduci,sicut 2.Tim.2.dicitur: Seruum Domini non oportet pugnare,sed placidum esse erga omnes, propensum ad docendū, tolerantem malos cum mansuetudine, erudientem eos qui obsistunt, si quando det illis Deus poenitentiam ad agnoscendam veritatem, & resipiscant è diaboli laqueo,capti ab eo ad ipsius voluntatem.Quosdam verò decet auersari:sicut ibidem capite tertio statim plenius ostenditur:Item ad Titum 3. Hominem sectarum autorem post vnā & alteram admonitionem fuge,sciens,quòd euersus sit,qui eiusmodi est, & peccet per se damnatus.Auersabimur ergo eos tantùm, de quorum salute videtur desperandum: caeteros verò, de quibus aliqua superest spes,ut infirmos,ignorantes, & errantes assumemus,& quanta fieri poterit moderatione arguemus,docebimus,hortabimur, & in viam reducemus.
units.tr: Note that he did not simply say "the sinning," but, by a form of softening, "the ignorant and the erring," because it is especially fitting to be moderately disposed toward those who sin through ignorance and error. For there seems to be a certain gradation of evils, and some of them must be brought to repentance gently and with all modesty, as 2 Timothy 2 says: "The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient toward the evil, instructing those who oppose, if perhaps God may give them repentance to know the truth, and they may come to themselves out of the snare of the devil, having been taken captive by him to his will." But some must be avoided, as is shown more fully in the same chapter 3 immediately: likewise Titus 3: "A man who is a factious person, after one or two admonitions, avoid, knowing that such a one is perverted, and sins, being condemned by himself." We will therefore avoid only those of whose salvation there seems to be no hope; but the others, in whom some hope remains, we will take up as weak, ignorant, and erring, and we will rebuke them with as much moderation as possible, teach them, exhort them, and lead them back into the way.

units.la: Porrò ex ignorantia & errore caeteraquoq; peccata tanquam primis fontibus oriuntur. Per ignorantiam autem committuntur, quae non sponte siue ex deliberatione animi fiunt.Vnde Leuit.4. & 5.dicuntur peccata ἀκουσίως,id est,non sponte patrata:vbi vulgata translatio habet,peccata per ignorantiam facta: & quid pro talibus offerendum sit, ibidem describitur.Error autem est,vbi quis mente obtenebratus non videt, quomodo in errorem labatur,& falsa pro veris amplectitur.Sic de idololatria Deuteronom.4. Ne faciatis vobis ullam similitudinem vel imaginem, neque oculis eleuatis ad coelū videas solem & lunam,& omnia astra coeli,& errore deceptus (πλανηθεὶς) adores ea & colas, quae creauit Dominus.2. Tim.3. Porrò mali homines & impostores proficient in peius, dum & in errorem abducunt,& errant ipsi (πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι)Iacob.5.Fratres,si quis inter vos erraverit à veritate,& conuerterit quis eum,sciat,quòd qui couerti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suae,saluam faciet animam à morte,& operiet multitudinem peccatorum.
units.tr: Moreover, other sins also arise from ignorance and error, as from their first sources. Sins are committed through ignorance when they are done not willingly, that is, not from deliberate intention. Hence Leviticus 4 and 5 call such sins ἀκουσίως [akousiōs], that is, committed not willingly, where the Vulgate translation reads "sins committed through ignorance." What must be offered for such sins is described in the same place. Error, however, is when someone, with his mind clouded, does not see how he is slipping into error and embraces falsehoods as truths. So with idolatry, Deuteronomy 4: "Do not make for yourselves any likeness or image, nor, lifting your eyes to heaven, look at the sun and the moon and all the stars of heaven, and be deceived by error (πλανηθεὶς [planētheis]) and worship and serve them, which the Lord created." 2 Tim. 3: "But evil men and impostors will advance to worse, leading others into error and being in error themselves (πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι [planōntes kai planōmenoi])." James 5: "Brothers, if anyone among you has wandered from the truth, and someone turns him back, let him know that whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins."

units.la: Quandoquidem & ipse circundatus est infirmitate) De infirmitate, & quomodo peccatum per eam significetur,supra dictum est.Sed quare dicitur circundatus? Vt sciat,se quoque nulla in parte à peccato esse immunem,sed quantus quantus est,etiam peccatis inuolutari & circundari,non aliter,quàm quis circundatus dicitur veste.Qua metaphora extenuatur sacerdotum dignitas.Natura enim omnes sunt vitiosi.
units.tr: Since he himself too is beset with weakness: Concerning weakness, and how sin is signified by it, we have spoken above. But why is he said to be beset? So that he knows that he himself is immune from sin in no part, but however great he is, he is also enveloped and surrounded by sins, just as someone is said to be surrounded by a garment. By this metaphor the dignity of priests is diminished. For by nature all are sinful.

units.la: Et quamuis efficiat spiritus Sanctus, vt non omnes perinde labantur in crassa peccata,tamen inhaeret omnibus corruptio naturae,sicut Apostolus Romanorum septimo fatetur,dicens:Noui,quòd non habitet in me,hoc est,in carne mea,bonum.Atque etiamsi sancti mente seruiant legi Dei,tamen carne seruiunt legi peccati, sicut ibidem adhuc dicitur.Et propterea placuit Apostolo circudatum dicere infirmitate,vt quasi totum inuolutum peccatis depingeret,atque ita,quanto inferiores essent pontifices legales Christo, indicaret.
units.tr: And although the Holy Spirit brings it about that not all fall alike into gross sins, nevertheless the corruption of nature clings to everyone, as the Apostle confesses in Romans 7, saying: "I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, nothing good dwells." And even if the saints serve the law of God in mind, yet in flesh they serve the law of sin, as is said further in the same place. Therefore the Apostle chose to say "beset with weakness," so as to depict him as wholly wrapped in sins, and thus to show how much inferior the legal high priests were to Christ.

units.la: Et propter hanc debet,quemadmodum pro populo,ita & pro seipso immolare pro peccatis) προσφέρειν offerre.sicut supra positum est,vt offerat,ἵνα προσφέρῃ.
units.tr: And on account of this he ought, just as for the people, so also for himself, to offer sacrifice for sins. προσφέρειν [prospherein], to offer, as stated above, so that he may offer, ἵνα προσφέρῃ [hina prospherē].

units.la: Tametsi filius erat,tamen didicit,ex his,quae passus est,obedientiam) Videtur elegans esse αὐτὰν ἀλλὰ in vocib. illis,ἐμαθὲν ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαθε.Et prouerbialiter dicitur,ἐξ ὧν ἔπαθες, ἐμαθες.Et latinè, Quae nocent,docent.
units.tr: Although he was a son, yet he learned obedience from what he suffered: The phrase seems to carry an elegant point in the words ἔμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαθε [emathen aph' hōn epathe]. And proverbially it is said, ἐξ ὧν ἔπαθες, ἔμαθες [ex hōn epathes, emathes], "from what you suffered, you learned," and in Latin, "what harms, teaches."

units.la: Et perfectus redditus:(καὶ τελειωθεὶς)etiam sanctificatus & initiatus verti potest,τελειῶ,sanctifico, consecro,initio,ratio significat,&c. Supra plenius de hac voce egimus capite 2.
units.tr: And having been made perfect: (καὶ τελειωθεὶς [kai teleiōtheis]) may also be rendered as sanctified and initiated, since τελειῶ means to sanctify, consecrate, initiate; the context shows the meaning. We treated this word more fully above, in chapter 2.

units.la: Omnibus,qui sibi obedierunt,fuit causa salutis aeternae: ἐγένετο τοῖς ὑπακούουσιν αὐτῷ πᾶσιν αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου.Emphasin habet,quod ait omnibus.Notat enim,euangelium esse vniuersale,& omnibus ex aequo id esse propositum,eiusque fructus omnibus contingere,qui modò obediant,& seipsos per incredulitatem non excludant.
units.tr: To all who obeyed him he became the cause of eternal salvation: ἐγένετο τοῖς ὑπακούουσιν αὐτῷ πᾶσιν αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου [egeneto tois hypakouousin autō pasin aitios sōtērias aiōniou]. The word omnibus, "to all," carries emphasis. For it indicates that the gospel is universal, and that it is offered equally to all, and that its fruit comes to all who now obey and do not exclude themselves through unbelief.

units.la: Obedierunt)id est,crediderunt.Nàm obedire saepe pro credere ponitur,ut ad finē capitis tertij ostendimus.Apparet autem,Apostolum delectatum allusione vocum,ὑπακοή,& ὑπακούω,& propterea secundo loco vocem retinuisse.
units.tr: Obeyed: that is, believed. For to obey is often put for to believe, as we showed at the end of chapter 3. It appears that the Apostle, delighting in the wordplay of ὑπακοή [hypakoē] and ὑπακούω [hypakouō], therefore kept the word in second place.

units.la: Sibi)cum emphasi etiam dicitur,sicut & illa,patris uoce,ipsum audite.
units.tr: To himself: this too is said with emphasis, as also in hear him in the Father's voice.

units.la: Fuit causa)Caeteri pontifices non possunt dici causae,licet aliquo modo per intercessionem suam dici queant cooperari:at,quòd ipsorum causa Deus condonet peccata,nullo modo. Sed Christus proprie est causa, propter quam solam obtingit peccatorum remissio. Hinc illę phrases, In nomine Christi,per Christum & propter Christum,exprimunt,Christum esse salutis omnium causam.
units.tr: Was the cause: The other high priests cannot be called causes, although in some way they can be said to cooperate through their intercession; but that God forgives sins for their sake, in no way. Christ alone is properly the cause, on account of whom alone forgiveness of sins is obtained. Hence those phrases, "in the name of Christ," "through Christ and on account of Christ," express that Christ is the cause of salvation for all.

units.la: Postremò magna emphasi adiecit,Salutis aeternae causam esse. Neque enim simpliciter salui fiunt credentes per Christum,pro tempore,vel,ut salutem consequantur tempora lem,sed in aeternum,& ut salutem habeant nunquam impediendam vel finiendam.
units.tr: Finally, with great emphasis he added that he is the cause of eternal salvation. For believers are not saved through Christ merely for a time, or so that they obtain a temporal salvation, but forever, and so that they have a salvation that is never to be hindered or ended.

units.la: Quanti autem referat, adiecisse hanc vocem, ex eo licet intelligere, quod infra capite nono dicet, Christum ingressum semel in sancta non manu facta, sed aeterna redemptione reperta. Item, eundem per spiritum aeternum seipsum obtulisse immaculatum Deo. Et paulo post: Vtij, qui vocati sunt, promissionem accipiant aeternae haereditatis. Itaque nim non de temporali, sed de aeterna salute, & aeternis bonis euangelium proprie concionatur. Et Esaias capit. 45. diserte ait: Israel saluatus est in domino salute aeterna. Ad quem locum apparet, Apostolum dum hac phrasi vteretur, respexisse.
units.tr: How much it matters that this word was added may be understood from the fact that below, in chapter 9, he says that Christ entered once into the holy places, not made with hands, but having obtained eternal redemption. Likewise, that through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without blemish to God. And a little later: that those who are called may receive the promise of eternal inheritance. Thus the gospel properly preaches not of temporal but of eternal salvation and eternal goods. And Isaiah 45 plainly says: "Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation." Here it appears that the Apostle, in using this phrase, had that passage in view.

units.la: Nemo sibi ipsi usurpat honorem, sed qui vocatur etiam a Deo, quemadmodum & Aaron. Ita & Christus non semetipsum glorificauit, vt fieret pontifex, sedis, qui dixerat illi: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Sicut & alibi dicit: tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself, so as to become high priest, but he who said to him: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." As he also says elsewhere: "You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek."

units.la: Tertij argumenti ratio haec vel maxime consideranda est. Nam vt constet de genere officij, de qualitatibus item personae, quae hominum externa tantum intuentium iudicio censetur ad munus publicum idonea, tamen, nisi contingat diuinitus moueri, vocari, atque etiam in ipsa functione regi gubernarique, certum est, nihil cum laude aut fructu a tali persona perficiendum. Tam alte vero haec ratio insculpta est etiam a natura omnium animis, ut nulli vnquam, qui modo aliqua sapientiae scintillula fuerunt praediti, putarint sibi temere ambiendam expetendamue publicam in hominum quacunque societate functionem, nisi tacite sentirent, se quibusdam arcanis impulsibus ad eundum publicum munus excitari: nisi item viam sibi paratam aliquo modo cernerent ad felicirer & cum successu administrandum. Quae de re etiam apud philosophos & poetas extant sententiae & prouerbia, cuiusmodi illa sunt: Maiora ne te quaesieris: alia res sceptrum, alia plectrum: Noli altum sapere, sed time. Asinus ad lyram. Simia in purpura: Induere leonis exuuium. Seruus cum sis, cur comam geris? Tecum habita, vt noris, quam sit tibi curta suppellex. Quibus omnibus solent dehortari ab affectando dignitatem, cui non sis par.
units.tr: The reasoning of this third argument deserves especial consideration. For although it is established what kind of office it is, and likewise what qualities the person has, who in the judgment of outward observers alone is deemed fit for public office, nevertheless, unless it happens that he is moved by God, called, and even in the very discharge of the office ruled and governed, it is certain that nothing will be accomplished by such a person with praise or fruit. This reasoning is so deeply engraved by nature in the minds of all that no one endowed with any spark of wisdom has ever thought that a public function in any human society should be rashly sought or desired, unless they tacitly felt that they were stirred by certain hidden impulses to undertake that public duty; and unless they likewise saw some way somehow prepared for them to administer it happily and with success. There are also opinions and proverbs on this matter among the philosophers and poets, such as these: "Do not seek things greater than you"; "one thing is a sceptre, another a plectrum"; "Do not think highly of yourself, but fear"; "an ass at the lyre"; "an ape in purple"; "to put on the lion's skin"; "since you are a slave, why do you wear long hair?"; "live with yourself, so that you know how scanty your furniture is." By all these they are accustomed to dissuade people from aspiring to a dignity for which they are not equal.

units.la: Similiter nec populus vnquam lubenter aliquem suscepit, nisi quem viderant quodammodo diuinitus aliquibus signis externis, aut certe ipso rerum successu comprobatum: cuius rei exempla passim in historiis licet cernere.
units.tr: Likewise the people never willingly accepted anyone unless they had seen him in some way approved by God through external signs, or at least by the very success of his undertakings; examples of this can be seen everywhere in the histories.

units.la: Merito ergo praesentis argumenti tertij ratio sic accipietur, tanquam magnam habens vim ad confirmandum argumenta praecedentia, quando praecedentes rationes, quod videlicet victimas pro peccatis obtulerit, quod item se placabilem exhibuerit, ignorantibus & errantibus, nondum sufficiunt, ut pro pontifice agnoscatur, nisi praeterea vocatum a Deo ad munus pontificium eum constet.
