Atque haec haudquaquam dubie causa est, cur istud argumentum, sicut plurimum habet ponderis, dignissimumque est, quod omnes accuratius expendant: ita postremo loco collocatur, necnon statim habet annexum suum consequens, contra ac ordine dicendi poscere videbatur, secundum quem quo ordine posita sunt antecedentia, eodem deceret poni & consequentia, ut singula singulis situ responderent.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, the reasoning of this third argument is taken as having great force to confirm the preceding arguments. For the preceding reasons, namely that he offered sacrifices for sins, and that he likewise showed himself placable toward the ignorant and erring, are not yet sufficient for him to be acknowledged as high priest, unless it is further established that he was called by God to the priestly office. And this is certainly the reason why this argument, which has very great weight and is most worthy of being weighed more carefully by all, is placed last, and immediately has its consequence attached to it, contrary to what the order of discourse seemed to require; according to that order, since the preceding points were set out in a certain order, the consequents too ought to be placed in the same order, so that each would correspond to each in position.

units.la: Eadem de causa factum videtur, quod extulerit propositionem hanc vniuersaliter, dicens: Nemo sibi ipsi usurpat honorem, sed qui uocatur etiam a Deo: Prorsus generaliter in omnibus spectandum hoc ait, num qui muneri publico praesunt, a Deo vocati sint, an semet ambitiose ingesserint, e quibus istud si in eis animaduertitur, pro legitimis magistratibus non habendo: cum ij potissimum agnoscendi sint pro veris praefectis, quos Dominus ipse sua voluntate & autoritate praefecerit.
units.tr: For the same reason it seems to have happened that he stated this proposition universally, saying: "No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God." He says that this must be considered quite generally in all cases, whether those who preside over public office have been called by God, or have thrust themselves in ambitiously; if the latter is found in them, they are not to be held as legitimate magistrates, since those are especially to be acknowledged as true rulers whom the Lord himself has set over by his own will and authority.

units.la: Negatio vniuersalis simpliciter omnibus non vocatis honorem denegare videtur. Quid? quod vniuersaliter dicit, honorem, innuit, non tantum in pontificatus munere, verum etiam in quacunque functione, habendam a Deo vocationis rationem.
units.tr: A universal negation seems simply to deny honour to all who have not been called. Moreover, since he says honour universally, he implies that account must be taken of a divine calling not only in the office of the high priesthood, but in any function whatever.

units.la: Quanquam apparet, Apostolum ratione ταῖς ἀντιπροφέρεσθαι huc in modum propositionem hanc efformasse, quasi respexisset ad obiectionem, quae plane his ipsis uerbis per aduersarios fieri poterat. Etenim aduersarij dicere poterant, quod, licet Christus praesumpsisset offerre victimas, item placabilem se exhibuisset erga peccates: denique omnibus virtutibus, quae in pontifice requiruntur, esset spectabilis: ista tamen omnia nihil facere ad probandum eius legitimum pontificatum, nisi certum sit, eum diuinitus vocatum, cum nemo usurpare sibi debeat honorem, nisi qui vocatur a Deo.
units.tr: Although it appears that the Apostle, by way of anticipating an objection (ταῖς ἀντιπροφέρεσθαι [antiprospheresthai] sense), framed this proposition in this manner, as if he had looked ahead to an objection that could plainly be made by adversaries in these very words. For the adversaries could say that, although Christ presumed to offer sacrifices, likewise showed himself placable toward sinners, and finally was admirable in all the virtues required in a high priest, yet all these things contribute nothing to proving his lawful priesthood, unless it is certain that he was called by God, since no one ought to take the honour to himself except he who is called by God.

units.la: Quae obiectio eo magis in promptu erat aduersarijs, quod ad pontificatum non fere alij vocabantur secundum legem, quàm qui erant ex tribu Leui, & ex familia Aa-ron,sicut alias admonuimus: quodque iam tùm quidam incipiebant pretio ac dolo pon tificatum sibi parare, quomodo sub Hircano & Herode factum, Iosephus memorat. Et si hoc pacto Christus parasset sibi pontificatum, non fuisset profectò pro vero & legitimo pontifice habendus. Respondet ergo Apostolus, verum quidem esse, quòd nemo vsur-pat honore, nisi quis sit vocatus à Deo: sed Christũ etiá à Deo esse vocatum, ideoq; pro legitimo pontifice agnoscedum. Propter talem igitur obiectionem, quæ per aduersarios fortasis fiebat, voluit Apostolus in hanc formam antecedens istud efferre.
units.tr: This objection would have been all the more readily available to the opponents because, as we have noted elsewhere, under the law almost none were called to the priesthood except those of the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron. Josephus also records that even then some men were already trying to acquire the priesthood for themselves by bribery and trickery, as happened under Hyrcanus and Herod. If Christ had obtained the priesthood for himself in this way, he could not rightly have been regarded as a true and lawful priest. The Apostle therefore replies that it is indeed true that no one takes this honour unless he is called by God, but that Christ was also called by God, and so must be acknowledged as a lawful priest. It was on account of such an objection, which the opponents perhaps raised, that the Apostle chose to put his antecedent in this form.

units.la: Est etiam aduertendum, & generaliter & illud dici: Qui uocatur à Deo: Variè enim contingit vocari à Deo, sicut rectè Hieronymus notat, enarrans epigraphã epistolę ad Galatas. Quidam vocantur à Deo ad munus apostolicum, siue etiam aliud munus, immediatè, hoc est, ipsius Dei viua voce, nullis hominum suffragijs intercedentibus: quomodo vocatus est olim Moses, Esaias, duodecim apostoli, item Paulus. Alij item vocantur à Deo, sed mediatè, hoc est, intercedentibus hominibus, ius ac potestatem habentibus: quomodo, iubente Deo, per Mosen vocatus est Aaron, item Iosue, praeterea ab apostolo Paulo institutus episcopus Titus, Timotheus, à reliquis vocati septem diaconi: & tales sunt quidem vocati à Deo, sed per hominem. Alij verò accedunt & inuadunt publica munera, ab hominibus quidem vocati, sed non à Deo: sicut qui fauore aut precio obtinent dignitates. Alij verò neq; à Deo, neque per hominem, neque ab hominibus vocantur, sed semetipsos dolosè & violenter ingerunt. Proinde ex illis, qui à Deo vocantur, cum alij mediatè, alij immediatè vocentur, nullum hic discrimen attingitur, sed generaliter dicit, qui à Deo vocantur, vt ostendat, eos, qui pro legitimis pontificibus agnoscendi veniunt, saltem altero modo uocatos esse debere. Quomodo autem Christus vocatus, quomodo verò pontifices legales, post dicemus.
units.tr: It should also be noted that this phrase, he who is called by God, is to be taken in a general sense. People are called by God in different ways, as Jerome rightly observes in his commentary on the inscription of the Epistle to the Galatians. Some are called by God to the apostolic office, or to some other office, immediately, that is, by God's own living voice, without any human vote intervening. So Moses, Isaiah and the twelve apostles were called of old, and likewise Paul. Others are also called by God, but mediately, that is, through the intervention of men who have the right and authority to call: so Aaron was called through Moses at God's command, and likewise Joshua; and Titus and Timothy were appointed bishops by the apostle Paul, and the seven deacons were called by the rest. These men were indeed called by God, but through a human agent. Others, however, push into public offices and seize them; they are called by men, but not by God, as those who obtain dignities by favour or bribery. Still others are called neither by God, nor through a man, nor by men, but thrust themselves in deceitfully and violently. Therefore, among those who are called by God, some are called mediately and some immediately, and no distinction is touched upon here. The Apostle speaks generally of those who are called by God so as to show that those who are to be acknowledged as lawful priests must have been called at least in one of these ways. How Christ was called, and how the legal priests were called, we shall discuss later.

units.la: Quemadmodum & Aaron) Probatio antecedentis ab exemplo: quod licet vnum tantum ponatur, tamen sufficiens est ad probandũ, rem generaliter ita se habere: quomodo vnū pro multorū enumeratione poni Scriptoribus non est insoles, maximè vbi contrariū nō facile potest adduci: quomodo hic contrarium, quòd videlicet, qui nō fit vocatus à Deo, non agnosci debeat pro legitimo, pontificè difficile est demonstrare. Vocatum aūt Aaron nem ad munus pontificatus diuinitùs, liquet ex illo Exodi 28. Accerse ad te Aaron fratrē tuum cum filijs suis de medio filiorũ Israel, vt sacerdotio fungantur mihi, Aaron, Nadab & Abihũ, Eleazar & Ithamàr, filij Aharón. Item Numeror. 16. historia, qua narratur, Dathàn & Abiron cum ducentis quinquaginta viris incensum offerentibus, absumptos igne. Praeterea Numeror. 17. vbi describitur virga Aaron præ cæterorum virgis florens, in signum, quòd familia ipsius præ cæteris à Deo esset electa, satis docetur, quàm non sit temerè vsurpandus honos, ad quem à Deo ipse non vocaris: & quomodo Aaronem præ cæteris pontificem Deus esse voluerit. Nec difficile est similia exempla inuenire tàm in sacerdotijs, quàm in reliquis magistratibus. Quà de re post nonnihil dicemus.
units.tr: Just as Aaron also: this is a proof of the antecedent from an example. Although only one instance is given, it is sufficient to prove that the matter stands in general in this way. It is not unusual for writers to put one example in place of an enumeration of many, especially where the contrary cannot easily be shown; and here it is difficult to demonstrate the contrary, namely that one who has not been called by God ought not to be acknowledged as a lawful priest. That Aaron was called to the priestly office by God is clear from Exodus 28: "Bring near to you Aaron your brother with his sons from among the children of Israel, that they may serve me as priests: Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron." Likewise Numbers 16, the story in which Dathan and Abiram, with two hundred and fifty men offering incense, are consumed by fire. Moreover, Numbers 17, where the rod of Aaron is described as blossoming above the rods of the others, as a sign that his family had been chosen by God above the rest, sufficiently teaches how rashly that honour is not to be seized, to which one is not called by God, and how God willed Aaron to be priest above the others. Nor is it hard to find similar examples in the priesthoods as well as in the other magistracies. We shall say something more about this matter later.

units.la: Ita et Christus non semetipsum glorificauit, vt fieret pontifex, sed ùs, qui dixerat illi, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te.
units.tr: So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you.

units.la: Aduerte rursus, quomodo alia verba, & quę maiori euidentia exprimunt, quomodo, & à quo Christus ad munus pontificium sit vocatus, adhibeat. Simpliciter quidem satis fuisset dicere: Ita Christus vocatus est à Deo. Sed veluti rationem habens Occupationis; quæ latebat in antecedente, præterea dilucidius demonstrare cupiens, Christum vocatum immediatè à Deo patre suo coelesti, eleganter ita ait: Ita & Christus non semetipsum glorificauit, etc. Prioribus sanè verbis sumptis ab illorum more, qui gloriæ auidi sunt, qui seipsos semper quærunt glorificare, quacunque ratione, per fas & nefas, & miro artificio virtutes, aut saltem fucum virtutum ostentat: eleganter amolitur à Christo omnem vel suspicionem arrogantiæ & ambitionis, clarisime que significat, quòd se nunquam ingesserit præterius ad tantum munus, quo Deus pater ipsum fungi voluit. Quomodo ipse quoque alias sæpè testatus est, inprimis Ioannis octauo: Ego dæmonium non habeo, sed honesto patre meum, & vos ignominia affecistis me. Ego autem nō quæro gloriam me am, est qui quærat & iudicet. Ibidem, cùm Iudæi obiecissent illi, Quem teipsum tu facis? Respondit Iesus: Si ego glorifico meipsum, gloria mea nihil est: est pater meus, qui glorificat me, quem vos dicitis Deum vestrum; & tamen non cognouistis eum, ego autem noui eum. Sic ergo depingit Christum ab omni ambitione & studio gloriæ multò alienisimum, atque aliquid amplius dicit, quàm si simpliciter dixisset, Christus non vsurpauit sibi honorem. Sequitur altera particula multò magis Christi dignitatem illustrans: Sed is, qui dixerat illi, Filius meus es tu: Periphrasi quidem persona
units.tr: Notice again how the author uses other words, which express more clearly how and by whom Christ was called to the priestly office. Simply to say, "So Christ was called by God," would have been enough. But, as if to take account of the reasoning that lay hidden in the antecedent, and wishing to show more clearly that Christ was called immediately by God his heavenly Father, he elegantly says: So also Christ did not glorify himself, etc. By the first words, taken from the habit of those who are eager for glory and always seek to glorify themselves by any means, rightly or wrongly, and who display virtues or at least the pretence of virtues with remarkable skill, he elegantly removes from Christ every trace of suspicion of arrogance and ambition, and very clearly signifies that he never thrust himself forward to so great an office, which God the Father wished him to discharge. He himself also bore witness to this often elsewhere, especially in John 8: "I do not have a demon, but I honour my Father, and you have dishonoured me. But I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges." In the same place, when the Jews had said to him, "Whom do you make yourself out to be?", Jesus answered: "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God; and yet you have not known him, but I know him." Thus he portrays Christ as far removed from all ambition and pursuit of glory, and says something more than if he had simply said, "Christ did not assume the honour to himself." There follows a second clause which illustrates Christ's dignity much more: But he who said to him, You are my Son. Here, by a periphrasis, he indicates the person of the Father.

units.la: sonam notat Patris:Sed praeterea, cum ait, illum dixisse ad filium, euidenter declarat, Christum immediatè à Deo ad pontificis munus vocatum, adeoque patrem viua sua voce Christum pontificem ordinasse: quod de Aarone caeterisque legalibus pontificibus dici non potest, qui licet à Deo vocati fuerint, tamen non nisi mediatè, siue per homines.
units.tr: Moreover, when he says that the Father spoke these words to the Son, he clearly declares that Christ was called to the office of priest immediately by God, and so that the Father by his own living voice ordained Christ as priest. This cannot be said of Aaron and the other legal priests, who, although they were called by God, were nevertheless called only mediately, that is, through men.

units.la: Praeterea insinuat Apostolus, Christum constitutum esse pontificem,non vt filium Aaronis, quomodo secundum legem & familia Aaronis ad pontificatum omnes legebantur, sed vt filium Dei. Vt reuera duplici nomine vocatio Christi aliorum vocatione sit excellentior, nimirum quòd vocatus sit immediatè à Deo, deinde, quòd vocatus vt filius Dei, non vt filius Aaronis. Ac videtur sanè singulari prouidentia Dei factum, quòd Aaron non fuerit immediatè à Deo vocatus, vt nimirum hac ratione vocatio Christi aliorum pontificum vocatione excelleret. Eleganter verò ad perficiendam periphrasin adhibet testimonium,quod supra capite primo citatum est, ad comprobandam Christi diuinitatem, vt ita ingerat omnium animis hanc cogitationem, quòd Christus fit Dei filius,& verus natura Deus: ac proinde intelligatur, tanto certius à Deo patre ad pontificatum vocatus. Sumptum est testimonium ex Psalmo secūdo,nec opus est nunc repetere pluribus,quomodo propheta ibi locutus sit in persona patris,ad Christum eiusmodi verba facientis,cum id à nobis capite primo satis sit expositum.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Apostle indicates that Christ was appointed priest not as a son of Aaron, as under the law all were chosen to the priesthood according to the family of Aaron, but as the Son of God. Thus the calling of Christ is in truth more excellent than the calling of others in two respects: first, because he was called immediately by God; and second, because he was called as the Son of God and not as a son of Aaron. It seems certainly to have been by a singular providence of God that Aaron was not called immediately by God, so that in this way the calling of Christ might excel the calling of the other priests. In completing the periphrasis, the author aptly adduces the testimony which was cited above in chapter one to establish the divinity of Christ, so that the thought is impressed upon all minds that Christ is the Son of God and true God by nature; and it is therefore understood that he was called to the priesthood by God the Father all the more surely. The testimony is taken from Psalm 2. Nor is it necessary now to repeat at length how the prophet there speaks in the person of the Father, addressing Christ in such words, since this was sufficiently explained by us in chapter one.

units.la: Caeterum,quod ad minutiores partes seu voces in hoc tertio argumento positas attinet,nihil fere singulare occurrit, nisi de voce vationis. Vocare itaque hoc loco idem est,quod eligere,designare,ordinare, ad certum genus vitae, siue ad certam functionem. Hoc pacto passim in Scripturis Deus dicitur vocare suos,id est,ad certum vitae genus eligere perducereque. Et illa ipsa vitae conditio vocatur uocatio κλήσεως. Huc pertinent illa Romanorum vndecimo. Dona quidem & Vocatio Dei eiusmodi sunt, vt eorum illum poenitere non possit. Prima epistola Corinthiorum septimo, Vnusquisque in eo, in quo vocatus fuit,maneat apud Deum. Apparet autem inde translatam hanc vocem, ad significandum vitae genus seu functionem, quadam similitudine, quòd quemadmodum ministri statim praesto sunt dominis suis vocantibus seu appellantibus: ita nos quoq; oportet promptos esse ad obediedum Domino, ad quamcunq; vocationem illa nos vocarit.
units.tr: As for the smaller parts or words in this third argument, scarcely anything distinctive occurs except the word calling. To call in this place is the same as to choose, designate or ordain for a certain kind of life or a certain function. In this way Scripture everywhere says that God calls his own, that is, chooses and brings them to a certain way of life. That condition of life itself is called a calling [κλήσεως]. To this belong the passages in Romans 11: "The gifts and calling of God are such that he does not repent of them." And 1 Corinthians 7: "Let each one remain with God in that condition in which he was called." It is clear that this word was transferred to signify a way of life or function by a certain likeness: just as servants are at once ready at hand when their masters call or summon them, so we too ought to be prompt to obey the Lord, to whatever calling he summons us.

units.la: Vbi verò interpres dixit,Nemo usurpat: graecè est λαμβάνει, quam initio huius capitis reddidit per vocem assumendi,de qua à nobis dictum est ibi: Nam omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur. Item vox τιμή significans honorem,(sicut etiam Rom. 13. Cui timorem, timorem, cui honorem,honorem) hic verò per metonymiam significat ipsam functionem,propter quam quis honorem promeretur,effectus pro causa,vel posterius pro priore: adhibita est,siue vti supra diximus,ad significandum,sententiam hanc de quacunq; functione vniuersaliter accipiendam,siue,vt per Antonomasiam indicaret, pontificatum,seu ministerium in ecclesia,omnibus aliis dignitatibus seu functionibus praeeminere, nullosque maiori honore reuera dignos,quàm qui sacrum officium rite administrant.
units.tr: Where the interpreter has "Nemo usurpat" (in Greek λαμβάνει [lambanei]), he rendered it at the beginning of this chapter by the word "assumes," which we discussed there: For every high priest, who is taken from among men. Likewise the word τιμή [timē], meaning honour (as also in Rom. 13: "Honour to whom honour is due"), here by metonymy signifies the office itself, for which someone earns honour, the effect standing for the cause, or the later for the earlier. It is used, as we said above, to indicate that this sentence is to be taken universally of every office, or, by antonomasia, to show that the high priesthood, or the ministry in the Church, excels all other dignities or offices, and that none are truly more worthy of honour than those who rightly administer the sacred office.

units.la: Sicut & alibi dicit: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech) Vbi cernitur Christus cognominatus à Deo pontifex secundum ordinationem Melchisedech. Ne verò exi-stimaretur Apostolus abs re asseruisse, Christum à Deo patre vocatum ad munus pontificium, iam subijcit testimonium è Psalmo centesimonono,in quo Propheta luculentissimè ea de re disserit, & perspicuè docet, à quo, secundum quem ordinem Christus sit sacerdos ordinatus. Ex quo, vti supra quoque indicauimus, quartum quoddam argumentum elicitur, quòd videlicet, sicut omnis pontifex debet secundum aliquem certum ordinem instituì,ita & Christus secundum certum ordinem,nempe Melchisedech, sit pontifex institutus, ac proinde pro legitimo pontifice agnoscendus.
units.tr: As he says elsewhere too: "Thou art a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek." Here Christ is seen as named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek. But lest the Apostle be thought to have asserted without cause that Christ was called by God the Father to the priestly office, he now adds the testimony from Psalm 109, in which the prophet speaks most clearly on this matter and plainly teaches by whom, and according to which order, Christ was ordained priest. From this, as we also indicated above, a fourth argument is drawn: namely that, just as every high priest must be instituted according to some fixed order, so Christ too was instituted high priest according to a fixed order, namely that of Melchizedek, and therefore must be acknowledged as a lawful priest.

units.la: Quod argumentum ipse Apostolus omnium mentibus suggerit, quando postremo loco ait,Cognominatus à Deo pontifex secundum ordinationem Melchisedech. Ad quae verba attexenda apparet, permotum fuisse aduersariorum morositate & calumnijs, qui fortasis obiolius insultantes volebant demonstrari,secudum quem ordinem Christus ordinatus esset pontifex,cùm neq; ex tribu Leui, neq; ex familia Aaronis originem traheret: cùm praeterea non esset legali more & ceremonijs diuinitus institutis ordinatus. Nec dubiū, quin eiusmodi obiectionem valde vrserint,qui ceremoniarum et eiusmodi leuiculatum rerum erat admodum curiosi aestimatores,imò & rigidi exactores. Et quòd soli filij Aaron & Leuitę deberent ministrare,non autē extraneus,habetur Numerorum 3.De consecratione item sacerdotum Exodi 28.29. & Leuitici 8. Sed huic interrogationi seu obiectioni vniuersae,breuiter satisfactum vult, dicendo: iuxta verbum citati testimonij,eum hij, eum cognominatum pontificem à Deo secundum ordinationem Melchisedech.
units.tr: The Apostle himself suggests this argument to every mind when he says last, "named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek." In adding these words it appears that he was moved by the obstinacy and calumnies of opponents, who, perhaps mocking, wanted it shown according to which order Christ was ordained priest, since he derived his origin neither from the tribe of Levi nor from the family of Aaron; moreover he was not ordained according to the legal custom and the ceremonies divinely instituted. There is no doubt that those who were very curious appraisers of ceremonies and such trifling matters, and indeed rigid exactors, pressed this objection hard. And that only the sons of Aaron and the Levites should minister, and not an outsider, is found in Numbers 3; likewise on the consecration of priests, Exodus 28, 29 and Leviticus 8. But he wishes this whole question or objection to be answered briefly, saying: according to the word of the cited testimony, "thou art named a priest by God after the order of Melchizedek."

units.la: Vnde satis constat, graui de causa, atq; etiam quadam occupationis forma, hæc verba ab Apostolo esse subiecta. Quamuis ea de re pòst dicetur plenius. Cæterùm adeò solidum & efficax est illud testimonium, vt non tantùm tertium argumetum proximè præcedens, sed & reliqua ante posita eo confirmentur: quæ reuera corruissent omnia, nisi Apostolus hoc pacto è sacris literis, Christum esse pontificem ab ipso Deo institutum, potuisset demonstrare. Atq; hinc factum puto, quòd antecedentia omnia, eo, quo cernis modo, in vnum fascem sunt congesta, priusquam eis cõsequens vllum annecteretur. Expediebat enim potius in medium proferri istud testimonium, ex quo quæ deinceps subijcenda erant cõsequentia, robur & vires acciperèt: quæ certè omnia, si testimonium hoc tam pestiuè non fuisset productum, facilè ceu nullius momenti, reijci potuissent. Sed est praeterea vnum hoc testimonium tàm locuples & fœcundum, vt pro basi & fundamento totius disputationis Apostolus illud elegerit, nec non præcipua argumenta, quibus deinceps probat, Christi sacerdotium excellentius esse sacerdotio Aaronico, ex eo colligat.
units.tr: Hence it is quite clear that these words were added by the Apostle for a serious reason, and by a certain form of pre-emptive move. This will be explained more fully later. But that testimony is so solid and effective that not only the third argument immediately preceding, but also the earlier ones placed before it, are confirmed by it. These would indeed all have collapsed, unless the Apostle could in this way demonstrate from holy letters that Christ is a priest instituted by God himself. And hence, I think, it happened that all the preceding points were, as you see, gathered into one bundle before any consequence was attached to them. For it was more fitting to bring that testimony forward into the open, so that the consequences to be subjoined afterwards might receive strength and force from it. All of these, certainly, if this testimony had not been produced so opportunely, could easily have been rejected as of no weight. But moreover this one testimony is so rich and fruitful that the Apostle chose it as the basis and foundation of the whole disputation, and from it he draws the principal arguments by which he afterwards proves that Christ's priesthood is more excellent than the Aaronic priesthood.

units.la: Quemadmodum in epistola ad Romanos, ad confirmandum iustificari homines fide absque operibus legis, sumit pro fundamento & principali probatione, testimonium illud e Geneseos decimoquinto: Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est illi ad iustitiam: ex eo, tanquam ditissimo penu, diuersorum argumentorum depromit materiam: Rursus in epistola ad Galatas, disputaturus, quòd non per opera legis, sed tantùm per fidem in Iesum Christum iustificatio contingat, adhibet illa promissionis diuinæ verba ex Geneseos 22, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes: & ex ijsdem alia atq; alia subinde texit argumenta instituto conuenientia. Ita sanè hoc loco demonstraturus, Christum esse vnum & solum summum pontificem, cuius pontificatu & oblatione vniuersum legale pontificium cum oblationibus & ceremonijs sit abrogatum, excerpsit è Scripturis vnum hoc testimonium, ex quo totius disputationis præcipua hauriet argumenta, & quod instituit, clarissimè euincet.
units.tr: Just as in the epistle to the Romans, to confirm that men are justified by faith without the works of the law, he takes as the foundation and principal proof that testimony from Genesis 15: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness; from it, as from a very rich storehouse, he draws material for various arguments. Again, in the epistle to the Galatians, intending to argue that justification comes not through the works of the law but only through faith in Jesus Christ, he uses those words of divine promise from Genesis 22: In thy seed shall all the nations be blessed; and from the same words he weaves now one and now another argument suited to his purpose. So too in this place, intending to demonstrate that Christ is the one and only supreme high priest, by whose priesthood and oblation the whole legal priesthood with its offerings and ceremonies has been abrogated, he has selected from the Scriptures this one testimony, from which he draws the chief arguments of the whole disputation and most clearly establishes what he set out to prove.

units.la: Et profectò vel ex hac ratione docendi argumentandiq;e, quam hic parem inuenio cum illa, quæ conspiciturin reliquis Diui Pauli epistolis, valde equidem moueor, ad statuendum, hanc epistolam non esse alterius, quam ipsius Pauli nomine recipiendam.
units.tr: And indeed, from this very method of teaching and arguing, which I find here similar to that seen in the other epistles of the divine Paul, I am greatly moved to conclude that this epistle is to be received as belonging to no one other than Paul himself.

units.la: Porrò recte istud testimonium esse citatum, ad comprobandum, Christum esse pontificem, non opus est nunc pluribus explicemus, quando satis manifestum est, totum illum Psalmum 109. de Christi regno & sacerdotio vaticinari, sicut nos vtcunque often dimus, caput primum enarrantes, illa verba ex eodem sumpta: Sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos scabellum pedum tuorum: & ipse Apostolus capite septimo sequenti singula verba præsentis loci excutit, & quadrare Christo valdè artificiosè ostendit. Intempestiua sunt, quæ nonnulli statim hic adseruunt, annotantes, hic discrimen inter sacerdotium Christi, & sacerdotium Aaronicum exhiberi, his videlicet particulis, in æternum, & secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Christi enim sacerdotium durare æternum, cùm Aaronicum fuerit duntaxat temporale: item æternù dici sacerdotiũ Christi, quia ille semper pro nobis offert seu intercedit: vel, quod multò absurdissimè quidam ausi sunt dicere, quòd per ministros Dei semper offertur. Sinamus Apostolum agere interpretem, & ipsius interpretationem solam audiamus, quam ipse capite septimo ponit.
units.tr: Moreover, that this testimony was rightly cited to prove that Christ is priest need not be explained at length now, since it is quite plain that the whole of Psalm 109 prophesies of Christ's kingdom and priesthood, as we in some measure expounded when explaining the first verse, taking from the same those words: Sit at my right hand, until I make thine enemies a footstool for thy feet. And the Apostle himself, in the following seventh chapter, examines each word of the present place and very skilfully shows that it fits Christ. Those things are out of place which some assert here at once, noting that a distinction between the priesthood of Christ and the Aaronic priesthood is shown here by these particles, for ever, and after the order of Melchizedek. For Christ's priesthood lasts for ever, whereas the Aaronic was only temporary; likewise the priesthood of Christ is called eternal because he always offers or intercedes for us; or—which some have most absurdly dared to say—because it is always offered through the ministers of God. Let us allow the Apostle to act as interpreter, and let us hear his interpretation alone, which he himself gives in chapter seven.

units.la: Similiter discrimen notant ex particula, Secundum ordinem Melchisedech: quòd hoc nomine distet sacerdotium Christi ab Aaronico, quòd in Aaronico offerebantur animalia: In Melchisedecico panis & vinum. Quasi verò Christus nihil aliud, quàm panem & vinum pro nobis obtulisset, & panis & vinum expiarent nostra peccata. Quis sanæ mentis has ferat næuias? Quanto satius, audire ipsum Apostolum in sequentibus interpretantem, quomodo Christus sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech, & quomodo istud sacerdotium sit Aaronico præstantius? Omisis itaque his, illud libet adijcere, me vehementer mirari iudicium, dexteritatem, & solertiam Apostoli in disputando & proferendis Scripturis: & quomodo sic ex vno testimonio statim integram, & illam quidem grauem disputationem instituat.
units.tr: Similarly, they note a distinction from the phrase according to the order of Melchizedek: that by this name Christ's priesthood differs from the Aaronic, in that in the Aaronic animals were offered, but in the Melchizedekian bread and wine. As if Christ had offered nothing else for us than bread and wine, and bread and wine expiated our sins! Who of sound mind can bear these trifles? How much better to hear the Apostle himself in what follows explaining how Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek, and how that priesthood is more excellent than the Aaronic. Setting these aside, then, I want to add that I greatly marvel at the judgment, skill and cleverness of the Apostle in disputing and in citing the Scriptures, and how he thus from a single testimony straightway constructs a whole, and indeed weighty, disputation.

units.la: Legerat Apostolus oculatissimè illum Psalmum, & cùm à spiritu Sancto edoctus intelligeret, totum concionari de Christo, ac palàm diceretur in eo, quòd in posterum deberet constitui sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech: interea autem constaret, sub lege non constitui pontifices, nisi secundum ordinationem Aaronis, ex tribu Leui, ex Aaronis familia, præterea certis ceremoniolis in id adhibitis: hinc statim colligebat Apostolus, Prophetam sensisse ita de Christo longè pòst venturo, & quòd sacerdotium Aaronicum, item ceremoniæ debeťent immutari, atque etiam abrogari: præ-
units.tr: The Apostle had read that Psalm most carefully, and when taught by the Holy Spirit he understood that the whole of it speaks about Christ, and that it was plainly said in it that he should in the future be appointed priest after the order of Melchizedek. Meanwhile it was established that under the law priests were appointed only according to the ordinance of Aaron, from the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron, and moreover with certain small ceremonies added for that purpose. Hence the Apostle immediately concluded that the Prophet had thus thought of Christ, who was to come long afterwards, and that the Aaronic priesthood, and likewise the ceremonies, ought to be changed and indeed abrogated; especially

units.la: Interpretatio inepta.
units.tr: An inept interpretation.

units.la: Papistarum error.
units.tr: The error of the Papists.

units.la: Panis & vinū non expiant peccata.
units.tr: Bread and wine do not expiate sins.

units.la: Sacerdotes ueteris testamenti ex tribu Leui. gari: præsertim cùm durante lege non posset conuenire, vt aliquis diceretur sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Nec posset etiam mente concipi, quòd de aliqua alia persona, quàm de Christo possent ista verba accipi. Quem enim vnquam confessi sunt Iudæi sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech? Et tamen debuisse aliquando compleri illud vaticinium, hoc erat extra controuersiam. Ergo debet necessario istud Christo aptari, & omnia iudicanda sunt in Christo impleta, sicut Apostolus rectissimè interpretatur: & hæc ratio de nouo sacerdotio Christi, accipi debet validissima, ad comprobandam abrogationem veteris sacerdotij Aaronici cum omnibus annexis, perspicuumque est, Apostolum mirabili iudicio vnum hoc testimonium probasse disputationis elegisse. Nec possunt Iudæi interpretationem Apostoli vllo pacto eluderc. Nam vbi volunt exponere Psalmū de Dauide, (sicut supra capite primo indicaui-mus) miris modis sese torquent, nec satis possunt habere, quomodo, quæ eo Psalmo continentur, Dauidi accommodent. Omnium verò minimè possunt ei accommodare ista verba:
units.tr: The priests of the Old Testament were from the tribe of Levi. ...since, while the law endured, it could not fit that anyone be called a priest after the order of Melchizedek. Nor could it even be conceived in mind that these words could be taken of any person other than Christ. For whom have the Jews ever acknowledged as a priest after the order of Melchizedek? And yet that this prophecy would at some time be fulfilled was beyond controversy. Therefore it must necessarily be applied to Christ, and all things are to be judged fulfilled in Christ, as the Apostle most rightly interprets; and this argument about Christ's new priesthood ought to be taken as most valid for proving the abrogation of the old Aaronic priesthood with all that belonged to it. And it is plain that the Apostle, by a wonderful judgment, chose this one testimony to prove his disputation. Nor can the Jews in any way evade the Apostle's interpretation. For when they wish to expound the Psalm of David (as I showed above in chapter one), they twist themselves in wondrous ways, nor can they sufficiently fit what is contained in that Psalm to David. But least of all can they fit to him these words:

units.la: Tu es sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech) Quomodo enim sacerdotem faciant illo tempore, qui neque ex tribu Leui, neque ex familia Aaronis fit ortus? cùm præterea palàm fit, regibus non licuisse sacerdotij munere fungi: quod testatur Ozias le pra, ob id quòd auderet incensum adolere, percussus, 2. Paralipom. 26. Quomodo itèm sacerdos secùdum ordinem Melchisedech, quando ad id tempus solus ordo Aaronicus floruerit, quem infringere vel immutare erat nefas, id quod 2. Paralipomen. 26. clarissimè asseritur? Postremò, quomodo competet Dauidi, vt sacerdos dicatur, in æternum? Omnia verò hæc vni Christo conuenire, Apostolus manifestissimè demonstrabit.
units.tr: Thou art a priest for ever, after the order of Melchisedec) For how could they make him a priest at that time, when he was not born of the tribe of Levi or of the family of Aaron? Moreover, it is plain that kings were not permitted to perform the office of priest. Uzziah the leper bears witness to this: he was struck down because he dared to burn incense (2 Chron. 26). Again, how could he be a priest after the order of Melchisedec, when up to that time only the Aaronic order had flourished, and it was wrong to break or change it, as 2 Chron. 26 clearly asserts? Lastly, how could it fit David to be called a priest for ever? But the Apostle will most clearly demonstrate that all these things agree with Christ alone.

units.la: Discamus autem nos, ex hac Apostoli in legendis scrutandisque Scripturis diligentia & perspicuitate, quomodo nobis quoque summa diligentia in Scripturarum lectione fit versandum, & quanta cura deceat vel minutissima quæque expendere. Animari debemus exemplo tanti Apostoli ad ita legendum, vt germanum sensum, atq; ipsa adeò mysteria posssimus eruere, quod quidé Spiritus ille Scripturarum autor & dictator annuet, si ipsum pro intellectu & successu in diligentia nostra assiduè oremus.
units.tr: Let us learn from this diligence and clarity of the Apostle in reading and searching the Scriptures how we too must apply the greatest diligence in reading Scripture, and with what care it is fitting to weigh even the smallest details. We ought to be encouraged by the example of so great an Apostle to read in such a way that we may draw out the genuine sense and even the mysteries themselves. The Spirit, the author and dictator of Scripture, will surely grant this if we constantly pray to him for understanding and success in our diligence.

units.la: Præterea admonemur hic, cùm cernimus Apostolum duce Spiritu, penetrasse intima Scripturarum, & eruisse mysteria, qualibet abdita, vt honorificè de scriptis apostolicis sentiamus, cogitemusq;, Apostolos vtpote edoctos à spiritu Sancto, quæ nulla humana sofertia possent addisci, probeq; intellexisse Scripturam, & optimè sua tradidisse & confirmasse: sicut hic videmus Apostolum facere.
units.tr: Moreover, we are admonished here. When we see the Apostle, with the Spirit as his guide, penetrating the inner depths of Scripture and drawing out mysteries however hidden, we should think honourably of the apostolic writings. We should consider that the Apostles, taught by the Holy Spirit, understood Scripture well, and transmitted and confirmed their teaching most excellently, things which no human industry could learn. As we see the Apostle doing here.

units.la: Sed iam expositis ita singulis seorsim argumentis, operæ est pretium nonnulla adhuc eligamus, ex illis, quæ ad doctrinam faciunt, quæq; omnibus etiam hoc tempore sint salutaria, excerpenda.
units.tr: But now that the individual arguments have been set out separately, it is worth selecting some others from those which pertain to doctrine and are salutary for everyone even at this time, and drawing them out.

units.la: Ex primo igitur illo argumento, quo dicitur, quòd omnis pontifex pro hominibus constituitur, in his, quæ apud Deum aguntur, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis: admonemur de officio pontificum seu sacerdotum nonnulla colligere. Non est autem quod dicamus, nunc quoque sacerdotum interesse victimas offerre, vel huiusmodi externa facere, quando per Christum illa externa omnia sunt sublata: sicut Apostolus luculeter paulo post docebit. Ergo oportet alia ratione officium nostrorum Sacerdotum explicemus, & aliam doctrinam hinc colligamus.
units.tr: From that first argument, in which it is said that every high priest is appointed for men in the things pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, we are admonished to gather some things about the office of high priests or priests. It is not, however, that we should say that now too it is the business of priests to offer victims or do such external things, since through Christ all those external things have been removed, as the Apostle will teach clearly shortly after. Therefore we must explain the office of our ministers on another principle, and draw another teaching from it.

units.la: Primùm ergo in genere hoc præsenti loco discamus, omnes credentes esse similiter per sacerdotium Christi sacerdotes constitutos, sicut 1. Petri 2. dicitur, Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus qui in lucrum accessit, ut virtutes prædicetis illius, qui e tenebris uos vocauit in admirabilem suam lucem. Vbi & de sacrificio eorum aliquid annotatur, videlicet, quòd Dei virtutes debeant prædicare.
units.tr: First, then, let us learn in general from this passage that all believers are likewise constituted priests through the priesthood of Christ, as 1 Pet. 2 says: "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people acquired as a possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light." Here something is also noted about their sacrifice, namely that they ought to proclaim the virtues of God.

units.la: Non enim corporale quiddam offerunt, sed spiritualia omnia, atque adeò semetipsos totos in odorem suauitatis, vnde ibidem dicitur: Ipsi veluti viui lapides ædificemini, domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias, acceptabiles Deo per Iesum Christum. Et Romanorum capite duodecimo, Obsecro vos fratres per miserationem, vt præbeatis corpora vestra hostiam viuentem, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem cultum vestrum. Ita Christiani omnes sunt sacerdotes, sunt ipsa templa, sunt ipsæ hostiæ & victimæ, sed spirituales. Quam dignitatem per Christi sacerdotium sunt adepti. Vt autem ab vniuersali hoc sacerdotio credentium transeamus ad sacerdotium particulare, hoc est, ad functionem eorum, qui præ cæteris præsunt rebus sacris in ecclesijs, non eadem est ratio euangelicorum sacerdotum, quæ erat Mosaicorum seu legalium: Vbi veterum sacerdotum munus erat offerre sacrificia, victimas;
units.tr: For they offer nothing bodily, but all things spiritual, and indeed themselves wholly, as a sweet-smelling savour. Whence in the same place it is said: "You yourselves, as living stones, are built up into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." And Rom. 12: "I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, your reasonable service." So all Christians are priests; they are the temples themselves, they are the victims and sacrifices themselves, but spiritual ones. They have obtained this dignity through the priesthood of Christ. But to pass from this universal priesthood of believers to the particular priesthood, that is, to the function of those who preside above others over sacred matters in the churches, the principle for evangelical priests is not the same as that for the Mosaic or legal priests, whose office was to offer sacrifices and victims;

units.la: Ratio ualida ad comprobandam sacerdotij Aaronici abrogationem. {a}timas,&c. Nostrorum vero est administrare Sacramenta, & annunciare verbum Dei: quorum vtrumque quauis sacrificiorum oblatione est praestantius. Neque enim in administratione sacramentorum nostri offerunt sacrificium aliquod, sed semel oblati per Christum sacrificij memoriam in illis faciunt, quod Sacramentorum vsus & institutio clare docet. Nam & Baptismus & Sacra coena mortis Domini sunt commemorationes:& in baptismo cum Christo morimur, sepelimur, & resurgimus: Similiter in sacra coena mortem Domini annunciamus, donec veniat. Quanquam docendo ipsi vere sacrificat, & quodammodo tot hostias gratas Deo offerunt, quot ipsi homines ad salutem per verbum adducunt.
units.tr: A strong argument for proving the abrogation of the Aaronic priesthood: ...victims, etc. But the duty of ours is to administer the sacraments and to announce the Word of God, and both of these are more excellent than any offering of sacrifices. For in administering the sacraments our ministers offer no sacrifice at all; rather, they make a memorial of the one sacrifice once offered through Christ, as the use and institution of the sacraments clearly teach. For both Baptism and the Lord's Supper are commemorations: in baptism we die with Christ, are buried, and rise again; similarly, in the Lord's Supper we proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes. Although, by teaching, they truly do sacrifice, and in a way offer as many sacrifices acceptable to God as they bring men to salvation through the Word.

units.la: Nulla siquidem gratior hostia Deo patri potest offerri, quàm pia mens, quae credit, & se totam Deo committit, sicut supra diximus, omnes credentes debere facere.
units.tr: For no more acceptable sacrifice can be offered to God the Father than a pious mind which believes and commits itself wholly to God, as we said above all believers ought to do.

units.la: Ergo hoc officium pontificis est seu sacerdotis euangelici, administrare videlicet sacramenta à Christo in memoriam sui sacrificij vnici instituta, & synceriter docere euangelium: quod officium longè excellit officium sacerdotium legalium. Neque verò est, quod aliqui hinc arripiant occasionem tuendi suas missas, quasi sint sacrificia. Nihil tale vnquam ad sacrificium fuit à Christo institutum, cùm ipse solus vnum semel sacrificium obtulerit, quo omnia sacrificia sunt abolita, quà de re capite nono huius epistolae plenius.
units.tr: Therefore this is the office of the evangelical high priest or priest: namely, to administer the sacraments instituted by Christ in memory of his one sacrifice, and to teach the gospel sincerely. This office far surpasses the office of the legal priests. Nor is there reason for some to seize on this as an occasion to defend their masses, as if they were sacrifices. Nothing of the kind was ever instituted by Christ as a sacrifice, since he alone offered one sacrifice, once, by which all sacrifices have been abolished. On this matter, more fully in chapter nine of this epistle.

units.la: Neque coena Domini, quam sordidi illi sacrificuli Romanenses profanant, sacrificium est, vti à nobis peragitur, sed tantum, vt dixi, sacrificij Christi commemoratio, quomodo Christus ipse vocat sui commemorationem, item annunciationem mortis suae, donec veniat. Et, si apud veteres Scriptores sacrificij vocem invenias vsurpatum, oportet eam pro sacrificij commemoratione per metonymiam accipias. Aut certè gratiarum actiones & laudem Dei nomine sacrificij intelliguntur, quae sunt sacrificia eucharistica appellata. Sacrificium autem propitiatorium, quod proprie sacrificij nomine venit appellandum, vnicum & solitarium est, quod videlicet obtulit in ara crucis Christus Iesus, cuius legalia sacrificia gerebant typum vt de re futura. Quod verò nos agimus, idem repraesentat vt rem praeteritam & anteactam, & de effectibus sacrificij Christi certos nos reddit in conscientijs, fructusque eius impartit. Id autem semel duntaxat oblatum est, sicut Christus semel duntaxat mori potuit: quod ad finem noni capitis huius epistolae, luculenter demonstratur.
units.tr: Nor is the Lord's Supper, which those filthy little Roman sacrificers profane, a sacrifice in the way it is performed by us. Rather, as I said, it is only a commemoration of Christ's sacrifice, just as Christ himself calls it a remembrance of himself, and likewise an announcement of his death until he comes. And if you find the word sacrifice used by the ancient writers, you must take it by metonymy for a commemoration of the sacrifice. Or certainly thanksgivings and praise of God are understood under the name of sacrifice, and these are called eucharistic sacrifices. But the propitiatory sacrifice, which properly is to be called by the name of sacrifice, is unique and solitary: namely, that which Christ Jesus offered on the altar of the cross, of which the legal sacrifices bore the type, as of a future thing. What we do represents the same thing as a past and accomplished one, makes us certain in our consciences of the effects of Christ's sacrifice, and imparts its fruits to us. But it was offered only once, just as Christ could die only once; this is clearly demonstrated at the end of chapter nine of this epistle.

units.la: Ex secundo argumento alia virtus maxima, vel maximè necessaria omnibus ministris verbi addiicenda proponitur: Ea est ars moderandi affectus, qua erga alios blandè, modestè, benignè, erga alios verò seueriter, grauiter, duriter oportet agere, prout variae occurrunt causae, & varia sunt hominum, quibuscum agendum est, ingenia. Opus est columbina simplicitate & prudentia serpentina ei, qui cum fructu animarum salutem vult procurare. Omnes quidem credentes sunt fratres nostri, sed alij duci volunt, alij verò etiam trahi debent. Sicut non omnes morbi curantur eodem pharmaco, nec cuilibet vulneri recte adhibetur quodlibet malagma, cum alteri acredines conueniant, alteri embrochae: ita in multitudine tanta, vbi alij proficti sunt in fide & doctrina, alij infirmi, alij medio quodam modo se habentes, certum est, mirabilem sapientiam requiri in eo, qui omnes suscipit curandos.
units.tr: From the second argument another great virtue, or one most necessary to all ministers of the Word, is set forth. It is the art of moderating the emotions, by which one must act gently, modestly and kindly towards some, and towards others severely, gravely and sternly, as various causes arise and the dispositions of the men one has to deal with are various. There is need of dovelike simplicity and serpentine prudence in one who wishes to secure the salvation of souls with fruit. All believers are indeed our brethren, but some want to be led, and others must even be dragged. Just as not all diseases are cured with the same drug, nor is any plaster rightly applied to every wound, since for one kind caustics are suitable and for another embrocations, so in so great a multitude, where some have advanced in faith and doctrine, some are weak, and some are in an intermediate condition, it is certain that wonderful wisdom is required in the one who undertakes to care for them all.

units.la: Necleue peccatum exiistimandum est, quos potuisses modestia tua & blandis monitis reducere in rectiorem viam, seueritate nimia & vehementia à sana doctrina, adeoque ab omni ecclesia alienare. Deum immortalem, quàm graviter saepè in hanc partem peccant, qui praesunt ecclesijs. Certum est, sicut olim de Tertulliano factum memorant, molestijs, & improuida vehementia sacerdotum etiam magnas & doctos viros detrusos ad factiones & schismata, vel etiam haereses, qui alias, si irritati indigne non fuissent, in ecclesiae castris perstitissent, & fortissimi fuissent ecclesiae propugnatores, cuius facti sunt hostes & impugnatores. Sed nunc non vacat pluribus de hac re agere.
units.tr: Nor should it be thought a light sin to alienate, by excessive severity and vehemence, from sound doctrine and so from the whole Church, those whom your modesty and gentle admonitions could have brought back to the straighter way. Immortal God, how grievously those who preside over churches often sin in this direction! It is certain, as they record was once done in the case of Tertullian, that great and learned men, thrust out by the troubles and imprudent vehemence of priests, have been driven into factions and schisms, or even heresies. Otherwise, had they not been unworthily provoked, they would have remained in the camp of the Church and would have been its most brave defenders, but they became its enemies and assailants. But now there is no time to treat this matter at greater length.

units.la: DE VOCATIONE.
units.tr: On Vocation.

units.la: Iam verò, quia in tertio argumento dicitur: Neminem assumere honorem, nisi qui vocatur à Deo: videmur operae facturi precium, si de vocatione paulò fusius disseramus.
units.tr: Now, since the third argument states that no one should take up an office unless he is called by God, we shall be doing useful work if we discuss vocation at somewhat greater length.

units.la: Primùm est vniuersalis quaedam vocatio omnium, qua videlicet Deus omnes vocat, & ad se pertrahere vult, vt euangelium cognoscant, piè & sanctè viuant in hoc seculo, remissionem peccatorum, nem peccatorū & vitam æternā accipiant. Sic Matthæi 11. vocat Christus omnes homines,dicens:Venite ad me omnes,qui laboratis & onerati estis,& ego reficillabo uos. Tollite iugum meum super uos,& discite à me,quòd mitis sim & humilis corde, & inuenietis requiem animabus uestris.Et cùm omnes laborēt,sint infirmi,& onerati propriis peccatis, certum est,omnes hīc vocari,sicut in alio quoq; loco dicitur,quòd Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri. Sed eius vocationis fructum non ferè alij percipiunt,quàm qui suam infirmitatē intelligunt, & vocatione Dei sentiunt se adiuuandos. Quò pertinet, quod Christus ait Matthæi 9. postquàm vocasset Matthæum publicanum, tandem subijcit: Non veni ad vocandum iustos,sed peccatores ad pœnitentiam. Quibus verbis non significatur,iustos non vocari, cùm vocatio ipsa omnem iustitiam,ipsamq; fidem præeat,imò nostram quoq; natiuitatem,(sicut Ephes.1.dicitur,vocari atq; eligi pios ante cōstitutionem mundi, exsolo proposito & beneuolentia Dei patris) sed eatenus vocari, quatenus se iniustos & peccatores agnoscunt.Atq; hæc vocatio quomodo variè contingat,videlicet per verbum externum,per internos motus spiritus, per exempla bonorum, per punitionem malorū, per fœlices successus immissos, per aduersitates,per miracula,&c. Atq; alius quidem vocatur in iuuentute,alius in senectute, alius per ministros verbi legitimos, alius per aduersarios.
units.tr: First there is a certain universal calling of all people, by which God calls all men and wishes to draw them to himself, so that they may know the gospel, live godly and holy lives in this world, and receive forgiveness of sins and eternal life. So Christ, in Matthew 11, calls all people, saying: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." Since all labour, are weak, and are burdened by their own sins, it is certain that all are called here, just as it is said elsewhere that God wills all men to be saved. Yet few people reap the fruit of this calling, except those who recognise their own weakness and feel through God's calling that they need help. To this belongs what Christ says in Matthew 9, after he had called the tax collector Matthew: "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." These words do not mean that the righteous are not called, since the calling itself precedes all righteousness and faith, and indeed our very birth (as Ephesians 1 says, that the godly are called and chosen before the foundation of the world, from the fixed purpose and goodwill of God the Father). Rather, they mean that people are called only insofar as they acknowledge that they are unrighteous sinners. This calling comes to people in various ways: through the external word, through the inward motions of the Spirit, through the examples of good people, through the punishment of the wicked, through happy successes sent to us, through adversities, through miracles, and so on. Some are called in youth, others in old age; some through lawful ministers of the Word, others through adversaries.

units.la: Quomodo item Dominus quosdam se offerentes reiecerit, alios non offerentes vocauerit. Præterea varij & multiplices sunt fines seu effectus huius vocationis,tàm in præsenti vita,quàm in futura:&, quomodo gnauiter laborandum, vt hanc vocationem nostram testatam faciamus:præterea,quàm graue sit peccatum,huic vocationi non obedire,vel de ea dubitare,longum sanè esset explicare,neq; id nunc est nostri instituti.Est autem alia vocatio,de qua nobis agendum.Ea est particularis,qua videlicet quis post priorem vniuersalem,adhuc vocatur à Deo,seu immediatè,seu mediatè, ad certum vitæ genus & functionem,qua Deo placere,& proximo prodesse queat. De quo genere vocationis illud 1.Corinth.12.Alios quidē posuit Deus in ecclesia Apostolos,deinde prophetas,tertiò doctores,deinde potestates,deinde dona sanationum, subsidia, gubernationes, genera linguarum. Et paulò ante in eodem capite: Diuisiones donorum ,sed idem spiritus,& diuisiones ministeriorum sunt,& idem Dominus & diuisiones operationum sunt,sed idem est Deus efficiens omnia in omnibus. Vnicuiq; verò datur manifestatio spiritus ad id,quod expedit.In eandem sententiam plura dicuntur ad Ephes.4.
units.tr: Likewise, it is shown how the Lord has rejected some who offered themselves and called others who did not offer themselves. Moreover, the ends or effects of this calling are various and manifold, both in the present life and in the future. How diligently we must labour to make our calling sure, and how grave a sin it is to disobey this calling or to doubt it, would take a long time to explain, and that is not now my purpose. There is, however, another calling that we must discuss. It is particular, by which someone, after the earlier universal calling, is still called by God, either immediately or mediately, to a certain way of life and function, by which he may please God and benefit his neighbour. Concerning this kind of calling there is 1 Corinthians 12: "God has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues." And a little before, in the same chapter: "There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all in all. But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is profitable." Many things are said to the same effect in Ephesians 4.

units.la: Quemadmodum verò de diuersis vitæ generibus & functionibus in ecclesia & in republica spiritualibus hæc dicuntur:ita intelligi conuenit & in politia, adeoq; in omni hominum societate,in qua vt ordinatè omnia fiant, debent esse diuersa officia & functiones, quibus qui funguntur,Deo in suo vitæ genere placent, & proximis prosunt. Hinc est, quòd magistratus Rom.13.appellantur ministri Dei,quia nimirum in eo vitæ genere Deo placent,diuinitus ad id vocantur,promouentur,conseruantur,defenduntur.Et 1.Petri 2. Subditi estote cuiuis humanæ creaturæ, propter Dominum, siue regi tanquam præcellenti,siue præsidibus,vt qui per eum mittantur,ad vindictam quidem nocentium,laude verò recte agentium.En ibi ait,mitti præsides per Deum, perinde ac si diceret, vocari & ordinari,quomodo in alio Scripturæ loco dicitur de ministris verbi, Quomodo prædicabūt, nisi mittantur? Quicunq; ergo vnquam à Deo misi sunt ad aliquod munus seu administrationem,tàm in ecclesia,quàm in politia,tales dicuntur vocati. Et ipsa functio seu officium appellatur vocatio.Ac Deus quidem ad se recepit hanc vocandi, ordinandi, instituendi facultatem,vt omnia in hominum societate rectius agerentur.Cùm enim homines omnes sint varij, inconstantes,ambitiosi,ad lædendum inuicem propensi, ne temerè omnia sine ordine fierent,& commiscerentur,voluit diuersa esse vitæ genera, & alios homines ad hoc,alios ad illud promouere,vt sic alij inferiores, alij superiores essent, & inuicem sibi prodessent,inseruirent,coniungerentur,inuicem non despicerent,alter alterius opem implorarent, & opem mutuam ferrent, nemo limites sibi constitutos transgrederetur. Quare statuendum, quocunque in munere quis versatur, diuinitus eum ad id vocatum,propterea habendum eum in suo honore, quem pro ratione muneris,prout prodest humanæ societati,promeretur.
units.tr: But just as these things are said of the various ways of life and functions in the Church and in the spiritual commonwealth, so they should be understood also of the civil polity, and indeed of every human society, in which, so that everything may be done in an orderly way, there must be different offices and functions, and those who discharge them please God in their way of life and benefit their neighbours. Hence magistrates are called "ministers of God" in Romans 13, because in that way of life they please God, are called by God to it, are promoted, preserved and defended. And in 1 Peter 2: "Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors, as sent by him to punish evildoers and to praise those who do well." There he says that governors are sent by God, just as if he said that they are called and appointed, as in another passage of Scripture it is said of the ministers of the Word: How shall they preach, unless they are sent? Therefore, whoever has ever been sent by God to any office or administration, whether in the Church or in the commonwealth, such people are said to be called. And the function or office itself is called a calling. God has taken to himself this power of calling, ordaining and instituting, so that everything in human society may be done more rightly. For since all people are varied, inconstant, ambitious, and prone to harm one another, lest everything be done rashly, without order, and in confusion, he willed that there should be different ways of life, and that some men should be advanced to this and others to that, so that some should be inferior and others superior, and that they should benefit and serve one another, be joined together, not despise one another, implore each other's help and bring mutual aid, and so that no one should transgress the limits set for him. Hence we must hold that whatever office a man holds, he is called to it by God, and therefore he is to be regarded as deserving honour in his office, in proportion to the office and as it benefits human society.

units.la: Cæterùm,quemadmodum diuersa sunt vocationum genera,ita diuersis quoque modis Deus ad vocationes istas adducit. Quosdam ad munus propheticum, ad gubernandam rempublicam, vel ecclesiam vocat immediatè: quomodo vocati Prophetæ plurimi & apostoli,item Moses,& quidam alij. Quosdam vocat per homines, puta quando homines , penes quos ius est, eligunt quempiam ad certam functionem, tuncis à Deo intelligitur vocatus,sed per homines: sicut per Apostolos multi sunt instituti & ordinati episcopi: item per Samuelem constituti reges Saul, Dauid. Per angelum item vocatus ad munus iudicis Gedeon. Et in summa, quoties describitur in Scripturis, quòd Dominus excitarit cor alicuius ad aliquid magni perficiendum, ibi reuera intelligi conue nit, tacitam fuisse illorum ad hoc munus vocationem. Nam si præter vocationem aliqui attentent quippiam, pro certo statuendum est, quòd frustrabuntur successibus, nisi diuinitus sint ad id vocati. Sic licet videre semper frustratos illorum conatus, qui non vocati & non habentes mandatum, ausi sunt res magnas aggredi, puta subire munus sacerdotis, vel principis, &c. Ea propter semper solet comprobari vocatio, præsertim ad publicâ functionem, vel accedentibus illorum suffragijs, quorum interest eligere, vel alijs exterpis signis, & subinde etiam miraculis, quomodo cum multis sanctis actum legimus.
units.tr: Moreover, just as there are different kinds of callings, so God also brings people to these callings in different ways. Some he calls immediately to the prophetic office or to govern the commonwealth or the Church: so were many prophets and apostles called, and Moses, and certain others. Some he calls through men, for example when men who have the right choose someone for a certain function; such a man is understood to be called by God, but through men. So through the apostles many bishops were instituted and ordained; likewise through Samuel Saul and David were set up as kings. Gideon was called by an angel to the office of judge. And in sum, whenever Scripture says that the Lord stirred up someone's heart to accomplish something great, it is truly to be understood that a silent calling to that office had been given to him. For if anyone attempts something apart from a calling, it must be held for certain that he will be frustrated in his successes, unless he has been called to it by God. Thus we may always see the efforts of those frustrated who, not being called and having no commission, have dared to undertake great things, such as taking up the office of priest or prince, and so on. Therefore a calling is usually confirmed, especially to a public function, either by the votes of those whose interest it is to choose, or by other external signs, and sometimes even by miracles, as we read happened with many saints.

units.la: Sed dicat hic aliquis: Quomodo sciam, utrùm Deus me ad eiusmodi munus vocarit, vel non vocarit? Veluti vbi nunc exerceo me in hac arte, vel in hoc genere vitæ, quomodo sciam, vtrùm me Deus sic velit manere, an ad aliam functionem possim aspirare? Respondetur, quòd Deus, quando aliquos vocare vult ad certam functionem, interdum per miracula certos facit de vocatione, sicut certus factus est Gedeon: item Samuel: præterea Moses, & multi alij.
units.tr: But someone here may say: "How shall I know whether God has called me, or has not called me, to such an office? For example, where I now practise in this art or in this way of life, how shall I know whether God wills me to remain thus, or whether I may aspire to another function?" The answer is that when God wishes to call some to a certain function, he sometimes makes them certain of their calling through miracles, as Gideon was made certain, and Samuel, and besides Moses and many others.

units.la: Aliquando verò suggerit & præmittit quasdam notas, è quibus certò cognosci possit, ad quid Deus hominem vocarit. Sicut enim poetis futuris indita est quædam procliuitas, præterea occulta vis & facultas aduersus conficiendos, ac propterea dici solet, poetas nasci debere: & sicut ferè semper vnusquisque quasi à teneris fertur ad ea studia, quæ po stea vir factus amplectitur: Ita reuera statuendum est, Deum indere vires & facultatem vnicuiq; : præterea plerunq; & mirabilem ardorè contendedi eò, quò Dominus ipsum vult vocare, ac tàtum interdum, ut reluctari & animum adducere inde nullo modo possint. Exempli causa: Qui iam versantes in scholis, toto animo intenti sunt cognitioni sacrarum literarum, certum id indicium est, Deum velle eos aliquando vocare, vt ministerium verbi in ecclesia suscipiant.
units.tr: But at other times he suggests and sends beforehand certain marks from which it can be known with certainty to what God has called a man. For just as a certain inclination is implanted in future poets, together with a hidden power and aptitude for composing, and for this reason it is commonly said that poets ought to be born, and just as almost always each person is carried from his tender years to those studies which he afterwards takes up as a man, so in truth we must hold that God implants powers and aptitude in each person, and also usually a remarkable zeal to strive towards that to which the Lord wishes to call him, so strong that in no way can they resist or turn their minds away from it. For example, those who are already in the schools and wholly intent on knowing the sacred letters, this is a sure sign that God wishes at some time to call them to undertake the ministry of the Word in the Church.

units.la: Sic quos videmus pro viribus & magno successu dare operam Iuri, argumento id est, Deum velle olim eos vocare ad causarum patrocinium, vel rerum publicarum administrationem, &c. Et sic de alijs iudicandum. Ac videmus nonnunquam, quòd quidam sic ad hæc studia ferantur, vt, licet vel amicorū blanditijs inde videantur abduci, vel per inopiam diffidere, vel propter studiorum difficultatem debere desperare, vel denique quocunque alio modo propria voluntate illis studijs valedicere: tamen arcano quodam impulsu, & præter expectationem ac voluntatem propriam pergunt, & tandem successus experiuntur. Quod sanè non posset fieri, nisi diuinitus vocarentur, iuuarentur, impelle rentur. Et certè audeo dicere, nisi esset hæc diuina vocatio, & diuinus impulsus, non credo, quòd aliqui studijs incumberent, minimè autem theologicis, præsertim hoc tempore, quo ita cõtemnuntur & literæ, & literati omnes, inprimis Theologi. Quem verò hoc non deterreat ab hisce studijs?
units.tr: So too, when we see people who with all their strength and great success devote themselves to law, this is an argument that God wishes at some time to call them to the advocacy of causes or the administration of public affairs, and so on; and we should judge others in the same way. And we sometimes see that some are so drawn to these studies that, although they seem to be led away by the flattery of friends, or to lose heart through poverty, or ought to despair because of the difficulty of the studies, or finally are minded in whatever other way to bid farewell to those studies by their own will, nevertheless, by a certain hidden impulse, and beyond their expectation and own will, they persist and at last experience success. This certainly could not happen unless they were called, helped and impelled by God. And I certainly dare to say that, unless there were this divine calling and divine impulse, I do not believe that anyone would apply himself to studies, and least of all to theological ones, especially in this time, when letters and all literary men, above all theologians, are so despised. Yet who would not be deterred from these studies by this?

units.la: Si artem manuariam exerces, vel mercatum, intra breue tempus sine multo sumptu potes assequi, ex quo dulcem & multum fructum percipias.
units.tr: If you practise a manual trade or commerce, you can within a short time, and without great expense, attain something from which you may gain sweet and abundant profit.

units.la: Si autem Theologiæ vis dare operam, multos annos, puta decem, vel quatuordecim, debes in magnis miseriis impendere: dum artes & linguas addiscis, vniuersum expendis patrimonium, & post hæc omnia adhuc parum eris consecutus, & inter eximios nõdum numerari poteris. Iam ut etiam aliquid assecutus sis in Theologia, tamen prospicienda librorum ampla suppellex, quærenda conditio, qua te alas, ea non quouis loco, nec statim pro dignitate parata est: quare hic iam ad famem adigeris.
units.tr: But if you wish to devote yourself to theology, you must spend many years, say ten or fourteen, in great hardship. While you learn the arts and languages, you use up your whole patrimony, and after all this you will still have achieved little and will not yet be numbered among the distinguished. Even if you have gained something in theology, you must still procure a large stock of books, and a position by which you can support yourself is not available in every place, nor at once in a manner worthy of you. So here you are driven to hunger.

units.la: At qui nouit artem manuariam, quocunq; venit, vbi vult laborare, inuenit parata instrumenta, potest sumptus necessarios facile lucrari, & taceo, quòd apud vulgus, apud nobiles magna inuidia paratur, si quando quis propter eruditionem promouetur. Vt non dicam, quòd molestias docti homines interdum parant sibi inuicem. Quis ergo non potius quamlibet artem addiscat, quàm det operam studijs, præcipuè theologicis, quæ nunc quidem eo sunt loco, vt quidam cerdones agere mallent, quàm theologos? Vt ad famem, propemodùm dixissem, ad reStim res illis redeat, cùm credebant, se iam iucundum fructum suorum laborum anteactorum, & sumptuum percepturos? Sed hæc non debent alienare ingenia ab his studijs, sed potius confirmare, ut in coepto proposito pergant, quando non dubium est, quin, quiita student, tametsi tot tantaque cernant impedimenta, diuinitus ad sua studia vocentur, & adiuuentur: ac nisi vocatio eorum diuina exisferet, nequaquam in ea possent persistere.
units.tr: But one who knows a manual trade, wherever he goes and wherever he wishes to work, finds ready tools and can easily earn the necessary expenses. I say nothing of the fact that among the common people and the nobles great envy is stirred up when anyone is promoted on account of his learning, not to mention that learned men sometimes make trouble for one another. Who then would not rather learn any craft than devote himself to studies, especially theological ones, which are now in such a state that some cobblers would prefer to act than to be theologians? Must their situation, I almost said, come down to hunger and the rope, when they believed they would now reap the pleasant fruit of their past labours and expenses? But these things ought not to turn talents away from these studies; rather they should confirm them to persevere in the course they have begun. For there is no doubt that those who study in this way, although they see so many and such great obstacles, are called and assisted by God for their studies; and unless their calling were divine, they could never persist in it.

units.la: Cuius rei argumentum è contrario licet sumere. Nam licet aliqui valeant ingenio, habeant amicos impellentes, præterea opes, ætatem, instrumentum, præcepfores, & omnia parata, quæ ad hæc studia excitanda & foueda creduntur necessaria, tamen nihil adhuc proficiunt. Quid in caussa? Nisi, quòd Deus eos nequaquam ad hoc studiorum genus vocat, nec vult eos postea ad publicam functionem, cui seruiunt ea studia, promouere, aut certè non vult illos id facere fœliciter.
units.tr: The argument may be taken from the opposite side. For although some have talent, have friends urging them on, besides wealth, age, equipment, teachers, and everything ready which is believed necessary to stir up and foster these studies, yet they make no progress. What is the cause? Only that God does not call them to this kind of study, nor does He wish to advance them afterwards to the public function which these studies serve, or at least He does not wish them to do so successfully.

units.la: Quamobrē, sicut solet dici, Tu nihil inuita facies dicesue Minerua: Ita multò iustius dici potest: T u nihil facies vel dices, vbi Deus te non vocarit. Cuius rei exemplum occurrit in Paulo, qui cùm pro sua voluntate decerneret persequi sanctos, Dominus vocauit eum, ut Euangelium prædicaret, dictumque est ei: Ne contra stimulum calcitres: sed nolo de hac re plura.
units.tr: Therefore, as is commonly said, You will do nothing against the will of Minerva, so much more justly it can be said: You will do or say nothing where God has not called you. An example of this appears in Paul, who, when he had determined of his own will to persecute the saints, was called by the Lord to preach the Gospel, and it was said to him: Kick not against the goad. But I do not wish to say more on this matter.

units.la: Ex his puto vnumquemque abundè posse intelligere, quomodo vocationem suam, quam Dominus esse voluerit, possit animaduertere. Circumspiciat quilibet dona, quibus præditus est, quibus possit gloriam Dei interea promouere, & iuuare hominum societatem: item ad quod genus functionis sentiat se maximè excitari: nec dubium, quin certa iam ipsi præfixa sit vocationis ratio. Ita enim paratum est, Deus præmittit signa, & confert dona, quibus quis præparatur, & idoneus redditur ad eam functionem, ad quam vult ipsum vocare.
units.tr: From these things I think everyone can understand well enough how he may recognise his own calling, which the Lord has wished him to have. Let each consider the gifts with which he is endowed, by which he may meanwhile promote the glory of God and help human society; likewise to what kind of function he feels himself most strongly drawn. There is no doubt that a definite plan of calling has already been set before him. For thus it is arranged: God sends signs beforehand and bestows gifts by which a person is prepared and made fit for that function to which He wishes to call him.

units.la: Sic Paulus doctus in lege, Timotheus à pueritia instructus sacris literis, Apollo, &c. Item in veteri testamento Moses, Daniel, bene eruditi: prophetæ instituebantur apud seniores, &c. Atq; ita de nobis & nostro statu iudicandum est. Quibus Deus conferdonum scientiæ & cognitionis, quíque toto pectore ad cognitionem sacrarum rerum feruntur, certum est, quòd Deus velit illos aliquando ad publicum ministerium vocare.
units.tr: So Paul, learned in the law; Timothy, instructed from childhood in the holy letters; Apollos, and so on. Likewise in the Old Testament, Moses and Daniel, well educated; the prophets were trained among the elders, and so on. And thus we must judge ourselves and our own state. Those to whom God has given gifts of knowledge and understanding, and who are borne with their whole heart toward the knowledge of sacred things, it is certain that God wishes at some time to call to the public ministry.

units.la: Quamobrem sicut cœperunt, debent pergere, &c, quæcunq; aduersa veniût, forti animo persistere, cùm alias grauissimè peccet, qui vocationem suam fastidiunt, vel deserit qua de re paulò pòst dicemus.
units.tr: Therefore, just as they have begun, they ought to continue, and whatever adversities come, they should persist with a brave spirit. For he sins most gravely who scorns his calling or deserts it, a matter we shall discuss a little later.

units.la: Verùm hic rursus aliquis quæstionem mouet, dicens: Vbi iam satis didicero, vt idoneus videar ad publicam functionem, & interea non vocor, hærebo ne semper in eodem scholarum luto, expectans vocationis tempus, an desperans cœuertam animum ad aliud vitæ genus? præsertim cùm ante vocationem se ingerere ad munus obtinendum non licet, sicut hic dicit Apostolus?
