Respondetur: Verum quidem est, nõ licet ambire munus publicum, videlicet si quis non respiciens, quale, & quàm sublime sit munus, & utrùm sit idoneus, sed tantùm propter opes suas, per arrogantiam & cupiditatem confidit, se propter amicos, vel propter alias similes caussas obtenturum, etiam si reuera non sit idoneus. Sed tamen licet dare significationem, te paratum esse ad suscipiendum munus, si modò ecclesia te approbauerit idoneum, & velit acceptare. Qui hoc pacto petit, suam vi-delicet operam offerens ecclesiæ, & lubenter se submittens ecclesiæ iudicio, quę iudicabit, vtrùm idoneus sit, vel non, neq; ægre ferens, si respuatur, neque quærens inhonesta media, propter quæ contra ius recipi studeat: certè is non peccat, sed potius iudicandus est rectè facere, iuxta illud 1. Timoth. 3. Si quis episcopatum expetit, bonum opus desiderat. Item 1. Corinth. 14. Itaq; & vos, quandoquidem sectatores estis spirituum ad ædificationem ecclesiæ, quærite vt excellatis. Quapropter qui loquitur lingua, oret vt interpretetur, &c. Ibidem: Proinde fratres ad id enitamini, vt prophetetis, & loquilinguis ne vetueritis. Omnia decenter & secundum ordinem fiant.
units.tr: But here again someone raises a question, saying: When I have learned enough to seem fit for public office, and meanwhile am not called, shall I remain forever in the same mud of the schools, waiting for the time of my calling, or, despairing of it, turn my mind to another way of life? Especially since it is not permitted to thrust oneself forward to obtain the office before being called, as the Apostle says here? The answer: It is true that it is not permitted to seek public office by canvassing, namely if someone, not considering what kind of office it is, how exalted, and whether he is fit for it, but relying only on his wealth, through arrogance and greed, trusts that he will obtain it on account of friends or other similar causes, even though he is not truly fit. But nevertheless it is permitted to signify that you are prepared to undertake the office, provided the Church approves you as fit and is willing to accept you. He who seeks in this way, namely offering his labour to the Church and willingly submitting himself to the Church's judgment, which will decide whether he is fit or not, neither taking it badly if he is rejected nor seeking dishonourable means by which he strives to be received contrary to right, certainly does not sin, but is rather to be judged to act rightly, according to that of 1 Timothy 3: "If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work." Likewise 1 Corinthians 14: "So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to excel for the edification of the Church. Therefore let him who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret, and so on." And there: "Therefore, brethren, strive to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. Let all things be done decently and in order."

units.la: Itaq; bonum est hoc pacto episcopatum appetere. Debent pis se offerre, vt innotescat ecclesiæ, & hæc possit scire, quos habeat eligendos.
units.tr: Therefore it is good to seek the episcopate in this way. They ought to offer themselves, so that they may become known to the Church, and so that it may know whom it has to choose.

units.la: Quod prodest fieri, vt cæteri exemplo illorum, quos cernunt eligi, excitentur ad sacra studia excolenda.
units.tr: It is also useful, for others to be stirred by the example of those whom they see chosen, so that they are roused to cultivate sacred studies.

units.la: Nec dicendi sunt ambitiosi, qui hoc pacto petunt promoueri: quandoquidem ipsi se subijciunt iudicio ecclesiæ, non ægrè laturi, si non eligantur.
units.tr: Nor are those to be called ambitious who seek promotion in this way, since they submit themselves to the Church's judgment, not taking it hard if they are not chosen.

units.la: Quamuis semper hoc in eis requiritur, vt, dum petunt, reuera habeant hunc scopum & hoc propositum, dum petunt ministerium publicum: Primùm, quòd seriò, & exanimo ad docendum & viuendum iuxta præscriptum Euangelij, vt ecclesia per ipsos ædificetur, non destruatur, cupiunt munere illo fungi: quòd gloriam Dei quærere, & spiritualēs promissiones magis respicere velint, quàm suam gloriam, vel priuatum suum temporale commodum: Deinde, quòd parati sint reddere rationem Deo pro salute animarum sibi concreditarum. Quem scopum qui in sua petitione habet, is digne petit, & dignus est, qui accipiat. Nec Deus finit tales suis pijs votis frustrari, sed largiter illis ubiq; prospicit, & lætos successus dat. Quòd si qui non hoc scopo, neq; iudicio ecclesiæ vocati, se ingerunt ad publicum munus obtinendum, iij sunt mercenarij, quibus non est cura ouium, sed tantùm sui quæstus: imò ij sunt lupi rapaces, fures & latrones, qui in ouile intrant non per ostium, sed aliunde, & gregem miserè laniant, sicut Christus docet Ioan. 10. In quos etiam inuehitur Ieremias cap. 23. Ezechiel 34.
units.tr: Yet it is always required of them that, when they seek, they really have this aim and purpose in seeking the public ministry: first, that they desire to fill that office seriously and sincerely, to teach and to live according to the prescription of the Gospel, so that the Church may be built up through them and not destroyed; that they wish to seek the glory of God and look more to the spiritual promises than to their own glory or private temporal advantage; and then, that they are ready to render account to God for the salvation of the souls entrusted to them. He who has this aim in his petition petitions worthily, and is worthy to receive. Nor does God allow such men's pious wishes to be frustrated, but abundantly provides for them everywhere and gives them happy success. But if those who are not called with this aim, nor by the Church's judgment, thrust themselves in to obtain public office, they are hirelings, to whom the care of the sheep is no concern, but only their own gain. Indeed they are ravening wolves, thieves and robbers, who enter the sheepfold not by the door but from elsewhere, and miserably tear the flock, as Christ teaches in John 10. Jeremiah also inveighs against them, chapter 23, and Ezekiel, chapter 34.

units.la: Et propterea Paulus 1. Timoth. 3. reijcit neophytum, propter ambitionem & elationem animi. Et violenter ingredientes non habent ecclesiam fauentem: vnde ministerium illorum contemnitur. Iam vbi quis electus est ad certum munus, danda illi opera, ut ea faciat, quae vocationem ipsius decent, nec temere & sine graui peccato potest eam deserere, iuxta illud Roman. 12. Quemadmodum in vno corpore membra multa habemus, membra vero omnia non eundem habent actum: sic multi vnum corpus sumus in Christo, singulatim autem alij aliorum membra, sed tamen dona habetes iuxta gratiam datã nobis varia: siue prophetiam iuxta portionem fidei, siue ministerium in administratione, siue qui docet in doctrina, siue qui exhortatur in exhortatione, qui impertit in simplicita te, qui praeest in diligentia, qui miseretur in hilaritate, &c. Vnusquisque in ea arte se exer ceat, quam didicit, vulgo dicitur. Sic vnusquisque ea peragat, quae suae sunt vocationis, & bene agetur cum rebuspublicis & cum ecclesijs. In ecclesia episcopi, praesbyteri, euangelistae, pastores, doctores, sacramentorum dispensatores, diaconi, pauperum prouisores, Catechistae rudium praeceptores, omnes laborent ad instaurationem sanctorum in aedificationem corporis Christi. Similiter in republica consules, senatores, praetores, tribuni, quaestores, milites, agant (sicut Ioannes Baptista quoque recte praescripsit) suum officium, neminem concutientes, vel quocunque modo iniuste opprimentes, spartam, qua nacti sunt, adornent, & Deo in suo vitae genere placere poterunt.
units.tr: And therefore Paul, 1 Timothy 3, rejects a neophyte because of ambition and arrogance of mind. And those who enter violently do not have the Church favouring them, so their ministry is despised. Now when someone has been chosen to a certain office, he should take care to do those things which befit his calling, and he cannot lightly, and without grave sin, desert it, according to Romans 12: "As in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another; but having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or he who teaches, in teaching; or he who exhorts, in exhortation; he who gives, in simplicity; he who rules, in diligence; he who shows mercy, in cheerfulness," and so on. Let each one exercise himself in the art which he has learned, as the common saying goes. Thus let each carry out those things which belong to his calling, and it will go well both with commonwealths and with churches. In the Church, bishops, elders, evangelists, ministers, teachers, dispensers of the sacraments, deacons, providers for the poor, and catechists, the instructors of the untaught, should all labour for the restoration of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ. Similarly in the commonwealth, consuls, senators, praetors, tribunes, quaestors and soldiers should perform their duty (as John the Baptist also rightly prescribed), harming no one and unjustly oppressing no one in any way, and should adorn the lot which they have received; and in their own way of life they will be able to please God.

units.la: Quicunque vero suam vocationem negligunt, ceu se indignam, vel minus, ut ipsi iudicant, honorifica aut frugifera, ac propterea volunt se ad aliam transferre, quam censent, quaestuosiorem & illustriorem, ij grauissimè peccât: Id quod Christus Matthaei 24. satis ostendit parabola illa de seruo prudente, & faciente officium, quem Dominus cum inuenerit eum sic facientem, super omnia bona constituet. Item Matthaei 25. in parabola Dominus seruum, qui defoderat talentū, neque vsuram aliquā eo fecerat, iubet proijci in tenebras exteriores, nec non tolli ab eo talentum, & dari alteri, qui habebat decem talenta. Quo significatum est, quòd Dominus illis, qui in vocatione nolunt pergere, sua dona adimit, neque foelices successus illis concedit. Et quid aliud est reijcere & respuere vocationem, quàm sperniere Deum vocantem, & reluctari bene volenti Imperatori tuo Deo, qui in hac mundi acie certâ tibi vult designare stationē, nolle obedire? Quomodo quaesio in castris talis miles tractabitur? Eodem igitur modo & de eo sentiendum est, qui vocationem suam contemnit vel deserit.
units.tr: Those who neglect their calling, regarding it as beneath them, or as less honourable or profitable than they judge it to be, and therefore want to move to another which they think more lucrative and distinguished, sin most gravely. Christ shows this well in Matthew 24, in the parable of the faithful and wise servant who does his duty, whom his lord, when he finds him so doing, will set over all his goods. Likewise in Matthew 25, in the parable, the lord orders the servant who buried his talent and made no gain from it to be cast into outer darkness, and the talent to be taken from him and given to the one who had ten talents. This signifies that the Lord takes away his gifts from those who are unwilling to persist in their calling, and grants them no happy success. And what else is it to reject and spurn one's calling than to despise God who calls, and to resist, by refusing to obey, your good Emperor, God, who wishes to assign you a fixed post in this army of the world? How would a soldier who deserted his post in the camp be treated? So we must think the same of the one who despises or abandons his calling.

units.la: Et reuera fere semper licet intueri, eos non habere successus, qui in eo vitae genere, ad quod Deus semel ipsos vocauit, se non continent.
units.tr: And indeed one can almost always observe that those who do not keep to the way of life to which God once called them have no success.

units.la: Sed de hac vocatione satis multa in praesens. Nunc subijcemus ea, ex quibus cognosci queat, quàm necessaria & quàm vtilis sit et publice et priuatim vnicuiq; huius doctrinae de vocatione cognitio.
units.tr: But I have said enough about this calling for now. Next I shall set out the considerations by which it may be understood how necessary and how useful the knowledge of this doctrine of calling is, both publicly and privately, to each person.

units.la: Primùm, si nesciamus, vocationem esse debere à Deo, non possumus certa conscientia vllum vitae genus amplecti. Vbi autem intelligimus, Deum velle nos vocare ad certum genus, in eo nos continebimus, & alacriter illud amplectemur.
units.tr: First, if we do not know that a calling must come from God, we cannot embrace any way of life with a sure conscience. But when we understand that God wishes to call us to a certain kind of life, we shall keep to it and embrace it eagerly.

units.la: Deinde, in actionibus omnibus id primo loco respiciendū, vt bene agamus id, quod agere volumus: (vide quid tuam vocationem deceat. Ad quid venisti) num conueniat nostrae vocationi. Ita vocatio debet omnium actionū nostrarū esse norma, & quasi Lex.
units.tr: Next, in all our actions the first consideration should be that we do well what we want to do: see whether it suits your calling (consider what your calling requires; why have you come?). Thus calling ought to be the rule and, as it were, the law of all our actions.

units.la: Hinc si vocationem nostram intueamur, fiet, ut ea contenti, & in eam solam intenti, aliorum vocationi praesertim superiorum non obstrepamus: nec aliorū munus ad nos conabimur pertrahere. Quòd si ab omnibus fieret, mirabilis quies in tota hominum societate perspiceretur.
units.tr: Hence, if we keep our own calling in view, we shall be content with it and intent on it alone, and we shall not meddle with the calling of others, especially of those above us, nor try to draw the duties of others to ourselves. If everyone did this, a wonderful peace would be seen throughout the whole society of men.

units.la: Praeterea, ut excitemus nos ad diligentiam, & ne infra vocationem nostram nos deijciamus, nullum aptius est calcar, quàm propriae vocationis consideratio. Qui aduertit, ad quid sit vocatus, sine dubio ad praestandū officiū nō mediocriter excitatur & omnia sua ad vocationem quasi ad scopum conferet. Et sic decet nos ratione nostrae vocationis in studijs animari. Adhaec si nobiscū reputemus, quomodo Deus etiā illis, quos vocat, semper suppeditet dona & vires, ut praestent ea, quae vocationi ipsorū conueniunt, erit haec magna consolatio, ne diffidamus nobis aliquid defuturū, quod nobis fit necessariū, ne etiam desperemus de mercede & vitae necessarijs nobis conuenientibus.
units.tr: Moreover, to stir ourselves to diligence, and not to let ourselves sink below our calling, nothing is a sharper spur than the consideration of our own calling. Whoever notices what he has been called to will undoubtedly be roused not a little to perform his duty, and will direct all his efforts towards his calling as towards a goal. And so it is fitting that we be encouraged in our studies by reference to our calling. Furthermore, if we consider how God always supplies gifts and strength to those whom he calls, so that they perform what suits their calling, this will be a great consolation: we shall not distrust that anything necessary for us will be lacking, nor despair of the reward and of the necessities of life fitting for us.

units.la: Rursus, qualiscunque sit nostrae vitae conditio, qua agimus in hoc mundo, boni eam cōsulemus, imò magnam consolationem in summis miserijs accipiemus, si intueamur in vocationem, & cogitemus, diuinitus vocatos ad id genus vitae, quod, sicut & omnia alia vitae genera, semper nonnihil periculorum habet adiunctum. Quò pertinet illud apophthegma 1. Tessalon. 3. Ipsi nostis nos in hunc vsum positos esse, &c.
units.tr: Again, whatever the condition of our life in which we live in this world, we shall accept it willingly; indeed, in the greatest miseries we shall receive great comfort if we look to our calling and reflect that we have been divinely called to this kind of life, which, like all other kinds of life, always has some dangers attached. To this belongs that saying of 1 Thessalonians 3: You yourselves know that we have been appointed to this purpose, etc.

units.la: DIGRESSIO.
units.tr: DIGRESSION.

units.la: De quo nobis multa forent dicenda, ea q. difficilia explicatu, quandoquidem segnes facti estis auribus. Etenim cum debeatis pro temporis ratione doctores esse, rursum opus habetis, ut doceamus vos, quae sint elementa initij eloquiorum Dei, factiq. estis y, quibus lacte fit opus, & non solido cibo. Nam quisquis, &c.
units.tr: Of this we would have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become sluggish in hearing. For though you ought by now to be teachers, given the time, you again need someone to teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and you have become such that you need milk and not solid food. For everyone who, etc.

units.la: Apostolus ingressus disputationem habentem nonnihil obscuritatis ac difficultatis, praeterea non admodum fauorabilem, utpote qua non solùm aduersarios, sed nonnullos quoque è pijs iam credentibus verofimile erat aliqua in parte offendendos, commode per digressionem paulò prolixiorem animos auditorum conciliat reficitque, ut nimirum & alacrius audiant, & æquioribus animis ea, quæ de Christi sacerdotio, legisque perid abrogatione dicenda sunt, accipiant. Sic verò & rethores suadent, vbi obscuru vel alias minus plausibile occurrit tractandum argumentum, interpositis aliquibus rationibus, quæ vel resicant, vel admoneant, vel placent, vel rogent, vel laudent, aut simile quiddā instituto conueniens faciant, leuemus & tædium, & auditorū animos nobis reddamus addictiores. Qua de re Fabius libro 4. cap. 3. & Cicero diuersis in locis.
units.tr: Having entered upon a discussion that has some obscurity and difficulty, and moreover is not very favourable, since it was likely to offend not only opponents but also some of those already believing and pious, the Apostle, by a rather lengthy digression, conveniently wins over and refreshes the minds of his hearers, so that they may listen more eagerly and accept with more equable minds what must be said about the priesthood of Christ and the abrogation of the law. Orators indeed advise this too: when a subject arises that is obscure or otherwise less pleasing, they interpose some arguments which either calm, or warn, or please, or ask, or praise, or do something similar suited to the purpose, so that they may lighten both the tedium and win the minds of their hearers more favourably to themselves. On this matter see Quintilian, book 4, chapter 3, and Cicero in various places.

units.la: Porrò quòd expedierit istud facere hoc loco apud Hebraeos, cuiuis promptum est iudicare. Omnes in eo populo à teneris imbiberant praeclaras opiniones de sacerdotio & ceremonijs, inprimis quòd à Deo ipso essent institutae: deinde quod ipsae ordinationes seu ritus omnes tàm per se videbantur pulchri, ut nihil pulchrius ab omnibus excogitari posse putaretur, sicut reuera nec excogitari poterat, testantib. & confessis id caeteris omnibus nationibus. Plurimum praeterea vtiles ad commouendos affectos, cùm externa illa omnia aliquid internum tacitè omnium animis ingererent.
units.tr: Moreover, that it was expedient to do this here, among the Hebrews, is easy for anyone to judge. From their tender years all of that people had imbibed high opinions of the priesthood and the ceremonies, above all that they had been instituted by God himself; then, that all these ordinances or rites themselves seemed so beautiful that nothing more beautiful could be thought of by anyone, as indeed it could not be thought of, as all other nations testified and admitted. Moreover, they were very useful for stirring the affections, since all those external things silently impressed something inward on the minds of all.

units.la: Vbi ergo de his abolendis agebatur, non dubium, quinetiam optimi quique sint gravissimè commoti: & licet fortassis quidam vi argumentorum apostolicorum convincerentur, tamen verosimile tacitè in animis illos adhuc supra modum probasse legales ceremonias. Sanè si Petrus ipse post acceptum spiritum Sanctum tantopere abhorruit sumere cibos lege interdictos, quid censebimus caeteros pios illi nequaquam pares sensisse de ceremonijs, quae iudicabantur ad cultum Dei petinere? Et quò quis magis ad pietatem sibi videbatur propensus, eò gravius ferebat de abrogantis ceremonijs mentione fieri. Imò pietas videbatur illas tueri ac defendere. Sapiēter itaque Apostolus praemollire cupiens caussam, quam agendam hic suscepit, & animos auditorū studens conciliare hanc digressionem, antequam progrediatur, interserit: sicut Rhetores docent, post Narrationem, aut ante quaestionem, certè ante quàm longius progrediamur, adhibere. Hoc porrò agit in hac tota digressione. Ante omnia praemollire volens caussam, ait, grauem ac tractu difficilem esse hanc quaestionē, quam segnes homines non facilè assequantur. Qua ratione Apostolus eos, quibus displicebat assertio haec sacerdotij Christi, artificiosè cogit se submittere, ne protinus aspernetur, vel temere damnent quod propter sublimitatem nondum satis intelligunt.
units.tr: Therefore, when the abolition of these things was being discussed, there is no doubt that even the best were most gravely moved; and although perhaps some were convinced by the force of the apostolic arguments, it is nevertheless likely that they still tacitly approved the legal ceremonies beyond measure in their hearts. Indeed, if Peter himself, after receiving the Holy Spirit, so greatly shrank from eating foods forbidden by the law, what shall we suppose the other pious men, by no means his equals, thought about the ceremonies which were judged to pertain to the worship of God? And the more anyone seemed inclined to piety, the more heavily he bore any mention of the abrogation of the ceremonies. Indeed, piety seemed to protect and defend them. Wisely, therefore, the Apostle, wishing to soften the cause he has undertaken to handle here, and striving to win over the minds of his hearers, inserts this digression before he proceeds, as the rhetoricians teach that one should do after the narration, or before the question, and certainly before we go further. He does this throughout this whole digression. Wishing above all to soften the cause, he says that this question is weighty and hard to handle, and that sluggish men do not readily grasp it. By this means the Apostle artfully compels those who disliked this assertion of the priesthood of Christ to submit, so that they do not at once reject, or rashly condemn, what on account of its sublimity they do not yet sufficiently understand.

units.la: Inde ut excitet eos, obijcit valde indecorum esse, quòd adhuc haereat in religionis elementis, quos decebat iam ad summū cognitionis gradum conscendisse, proindeipsis ad maiora percipienda enitendū. Ac nisi reuera perstates in doctrina accepta, ad maiora deinceps progrediantur proficiantque, ea quae haētenus perceperunt, ipsis nihil profutura, imò verò, si retrocedant, allatura damnationē. Huius igitur rei gratia se nunc velle sublimiora quaedam tradere, nec diffidere, quin ipsi per gratiam Dei omnia clarè possint assequi. Deum enim iustum esse, & pijs ad plenam fidei ac spei cognitionem aspirantib. lubenter talem ac tantam conferre, qua etiam ad ea, quae intra velum sunt, id est, abditissimas & altissimas res coelestes, penetrent. Sed hęc omnia in progressu orationis clarius explicabimus. Ad summā: excitat digressione hac auditores ad auidius audiendum & discendum, quae de pontificatu Christi restant explicanda, arguitque inprimis illorum segnitiem & inscitiam, in quam solam reijcit, quòd ipsis difficilis & grauis videatur ista de sacerdotio Christi disputatio. Turpe autē, illos semper haerere in elementis, & nunquam ad pleniorem veritatis cognitionem venire. Quamobrem monet, ut omissis minutioribus ad altiora enitantur. Ac sperandum quidē, facilè Deo fauente id posse fieri. Sed quo diligentius in id laborent, addit insuper comminationem, dicens: Quod, si post quàm iam gustarunt bonum Dei verbum, deinceps in cognitione non progrediantur, sed malint retrocedere ac dediscere, grauissimè ipsos peccare, & Christum quodámodo crucifigere ac ludibrio exponere. Idque confirmat similitudine dućta à terra, quae, cùm vberiorem frućtum, quam antea, profert, ampliorem quoque accipit benediċtione: vbi verò illud non facit, maledictionem incurrit.
units.tr: Then, to rouse them, he objects that it is very unseemly that those who ought by now to have climbed to the highest degree of knowledge should still cling to the elements of religion, and therefore should strive to grasp higher things. And unless they persevere in the doctrine received and go on to greater things and make progress, what they have so far perceived will profit them nothing, and indeed, if they draw back, it will bring damnation. For this reason he says that he now wishes to hand down some higher matters, and that he does not doubt that by the grace of God they can all clearly attain them: for God is just, and gladly grants such and so great a gift to the pious who aspire to full knowledge and hope, that they may penetrate even those things which are within the veil, that is, the most hidden and highest heavenly things. But we shall explain all these things more clearly as the discourse proceeds. In sum: by this digression he rouses his hearers to listen and learn more eagerly what remains to be explained about the priesthood of Christ, and he chiefly rebukes their sluggishness and ignorance, which he alone blames for their finding this discussion of the priesthood of Christ difficult and burdensome. It is shameful for them always to cling to the elements and never to come to a fuller knowledge of the truth. Therefore he advises them, leaving aside the smaller matters, to strive for higher things. And it is to be hoped that this can easily be done with God's favour. But so that they may labour at it the more diligently, he adds a warning, saying: if, after they have already tasted the good word of God, they do not then advance in knowledge, but prefer to draw back and unlearn, they sin most gravely and in a way crucify Christ again and expose him to mockery. He confirms this by a comparison drawn from the earth, which, when it bears a richer fruit than before, also receives a greater blessing; but where it does not do so, it incurs a curse.

units.la: Porrò cōminationi huic subiscit, quę mitiget illoꝝ animos, erigátq;: nēpe, nullo paćto se diffidere, quin ipsi strenuè ad altiora velint cotendere, atq; in religione proficere. Spe hanc cofirmat cofideratione iustitiæ Dei, quandoquidé is semper remunerat benefacta, & pios lubenter promouet. Quare concludens iterum monet, imò veluti pia compreca- tione optat, ut studeant deinceps perfectiores in fide & spe euadere, benedictionem magno animo, exemplo sanctorum patrum, inprimis Abrahæ, à Deo expectent, qui dubio procul quæ promittit præstat, maximè vbi iuramento dignatur se obstringere, & serió cupiétes in fide ac spe promoueri, ita promouet & confirmat, ut ad eas, etiá res, quæ intra velum sunt, id est, altissimas & abditissimas, pertingant. Ita veluti paraphrasi totius dispositionis sententiam crassiore nostro modo expresissimus. Sed in progressu singularum partium dispositione clarius explicabimus. Ait igitur multa adhuc superesse, quæ de pontificatu Christi dici debeant: sed ea esse difficilia, nec à quibusuis posse satis intelligi.
units.tr: Next to this threat he adds something to soothe and encourage their spirits: he does not doubt at all that they will strenuously strive toward higher things and make progress in religion. He confirms this hope by considering the justice of God, since God always rewards good deeds and gladly advances the godly. So, concluding, he warns them again, or rather, as with a pious prayer, wishes that they may become more perfect in faith and hope, and that they await the blessing from God with a great spirit, following the example of the holy fathers, above all Abraham, who without doubt performs what he promises, especially when he deigns to bind himself by an oath. Those who earnestly desire to be advanced in faith and hope, he advances and confirms so that they reach even those things which are within the veil, that is, the most lofty and most hidden things. Thus I have expressed, in my own cruder manner, the sense of the whole arrangement as a kind of paraphrase. But in the progress through the individual parts of the arrangement we will explain it more clearly. He says, therefore, that many things still remain to be said about the priesthood of Christ, but that these are difficult and cannot be sufficiently understood by just anyone.

units.la: De quo nobis multa forent dicenda, eaq; difficilia explicatu: Sed addit praeterea: Quandoquidem segnes facti estis auribus: En ratio, quare difficilia. Non sunt quidem ista simpliciter propter sese dif- sicilia, sed propter ipsorum segnitiem & tarditatem. Atque hoc pacto dum causam difficultatis apparentis reijcit in illorum ruditatem, artificios è parat sibi viam ad accusandū eos segnitiei, & ad excitādum ad maiorem diligentiam. Fabius loco supra citato monet, in digressionibus habendam rationem personarum, ad quas nobis sermo est: item vi- dedum accurate, quid, qua occasione, interserendum sit. Neque enim quid- nis, quouis loco habere gratiam. Hoc Apostolus, quando duros Iudæos satis acerbe re- prehendit & arguit, optimè quoque animaduertisse videtur. Iudæi enim etiáfi perpetuò versarentur in Scripturis, tamen respicientes in nudā & crassam litera, & in res externas ac carnales, mysteria Scripturarum & quæ verè spiritualia erant, non poterant eruere.
units.tr: There would be much to say about this, and these things are difficult to explain: But he adds further: since you have become sluggish in your hearing: Here is the reason why they are difficult. They are not difficult in themselves, but because of the sluggishness and dullness of his hearers. In this way, while he puts the cause of the apparent difficulty on their rudeness, he skilfully prepares a way to accuse them of sloth and to stir them to greater diligence. Fabius, in the passage cited above, advises that in digressions one should take account of the persons to whom we speak, and also consider carefully what should be inserted, and on what occasion. Indeed, there is no reason why one should not have regard to grace in any place. The Apostle seems to have understood this very well when he rebukes and reproves the hard-hearted Jews quite sharply. For the Jews, although they were constantly occupied with the Scriptures, looking only at the bare and crude letter and at external and carnal things, could not bring to light the mysteries of the Scriptures, which were truly spiritual.

units.la: Omnium vero minimè ea assequebatur, quæ de dignitate Christi in scripturis propo- sita erat. Vnde illis hoc vitij, quòd uidelicet siue propter hebetudinē ingenij, siue pro- pter malitiam & duritiem cordis nō assequerentur ea, quæ spiritus Dei sunt, crebrò & à Christo & ab Apostolis obiectum est. Ioan. 5.
units.tr: Least of all did they grasp what was set forth in Scripture about the dignity of Christ. Hence the fault was often charged against them, both by Christ and by the apostles, that they did not grasp the things that belong to the Spirit of God, whether because of dullness of mind or because of wickedness and hardness of heart. John 5.

units.la: Qui misit me pater, ipse testificatus est: Neque vocem eius audistis unquam, neque speciē eius vidistis, & sermonē eius non babetis in vobis manente: quia, quem misit ille, huic vos non creditis. Scrutamini scripturas, quia vos videmini vobis in ipsis vitā æter nam habere, & illæ sunt, quæ testificantur de me, nec vultis venire ad me, ut vitam habeatis, &c. Ibidem: Si credidissetis Mosi, credidissetis utiq; mihi, de me enim ille scripsit.
units.tr: "The Father who sent me has himself borne witness: you have never heard his voice nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe him whom he has sent. Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life, and it is they that testify of me; yet you will not come to me that you may have life," etc. In the same place: "If you had believed Moses, you would have believed me, for he wrote of me."

units.la: Ioannis tertio ad Nicodemum, qui erat magister in Israel, si terrena dixi vobis, & non creditis, quomodo si dixero vobis cœlestia, credituri sitis? Ioan. 6. vbi Christus cocionabatur in synagoga in Capernaum, quòd ipse esset panis viuus, qui de cœlo descendit, multi audientes dixerunt: Durus est hic sermo, quis potest eum audire? Ioann. 16. ad discipulos, multa habeo, quæ vobis dicam, sed non poteistis nunc ferre. Christus Lucæ 24. ad duos illos: ô stulti & tardi corde ad credendū, in omnib. quæ locuti sunt prophetæ, &c. Aliàs sæpè cæcitatem, & inscitiam exprobrauit Christus, tàm aduersarijs, quàm suis discipulis. Apostolus Roman. 10. de fratribus suis concedit, quòd studium Dei habeant, sed non secundum scientiam. Et Roman. 11. ex Esaiæ sexto: Dedit eis spiritum compunctionis, oculos, ut non videant: aures, ut non audiant, usq; ad hodiernū diem. 2. Chorinth. 3. Obcæcati sunt sensus illorum. Nam usque in hodiernum diem idem velamen in lectione veteris testamenti manet, &c. Item 1. Corinth. 4. Quòd si adhuc velatum est euangelium nostrum, in his, qui pereunt, velatum est: in quibus Deus huius seculi excæcauit sensus incredulorū, ne illuceferet illis lumē euangelij gloriæ Christi, qui est imago Dei.
units.tr: In John 3 he said to Nicodemus, who was a teacher in Israel: "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?" In John 6, when Christ was teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum that he was the living bread which came down from heaven, many who heard said: "This is a hard saying; who can hear it?" In John 16 he says to the disciples: "I have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now." Christ, in Luke 24, says to those two: "O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken," etc. Elsewhere Christ often upbraided blindness and ignorance, both in his adversaries and in his own disciples. The Apostle, in Romans 10, concedes that his brothers have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. And in Romans 11, from Isaiah 6: "God has given them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, unto this day." 2 Corinthians 3: "Their minds were blinded; for until this day the same veil remains at the reading of the Old Testament," etc. Likewise 1 Corinthians 4: "But if our gospel is still veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine on them."

units.la: Respiciens ergo Apostolus in hanc Iudæorum segnitiem & cæcitatem, propter quam immodicè erant affecti externis illis & carnalibus rebus legis, solisque vmbris delecta bantur, ait, ea, quæ dicenda sunt de pontificatu Christi, difficilia videri. Non quòd reuera ijs, qui modò habeant oculos apertos, essent adeò difficilia: quandoquidem Scriptura clare de sacerdotio Christi disserit, sicut patet ex testimonio Psalmi 109. proximè citato, & capite septimo, ac sequentibus aliquot ipse Apostolus palàm faciet. Sed qui segnes sunt & tardi corde, ij non possunt intelligere. Certè quod animo hebeti vel segni obtruditur, quacunque ratione id fiat, & quamlibet perspicuè traditur, tamē locum in animo non habet.
units.tr: The Apostle, therefore, looking to this sluggishness and blindness of the Jews, on account of which they were excessively attached to those external and carnal things of the law and took delight only in its shadows, says that the things to be said about the priesthood of Christ seem difficult. Not that they would really be so difficult for those who now have their eyes open, since Scripture speaks clearly of the priesthood of Christ, as is evident from the testimony of Psalm 109, cited just above; and in chapter seven and the following chapters the Apostle himself will make this plain. But those who are sluggish and slow of heart cannot understand. Certainly what is forced upon a dull or sluggish mind, by whatever means it is done, and however clearly it is presented, has no place in the mind.

units.la: Atque inter ipsos credentes tales fuisse segnes, non est mirum, cùm altissimè infede- rint animis eorum legalia illa, quæ ab impijs suis atque incredulis patribus acceperunt, & in quibus fuerunt educati. In his autem, quæ propria sunt euangelij, duntaxat præcipua fidei documenta ad salutem necessaria. edocti fuerant, & quotidie plurima occurrebant impedimenta, propter sæuitiam & malitiam aliorum, quo minus ad altiora pertingerent.
units.tr: That such men among the believers themselves were sluggish is no wonder, since those legal things, which they had received from their unbelieving and impious fathers and in which they had been brought up, had sunk deep into their minds. They had indeed been taught the chief articles of faith necessary for salvation, which are proper to the gospel, but every day very many hindrances stood in the way, on account of the savagery and malice of others, so that they could not reach higher things.

units.la: Ideo dicitur Deus pios promouere, quod quoties vocentur, ab eis ...
units.tr: Therefore God is said to advance the godly, because whenever they are called, by them...

units.la: Non omnibus datū est nosse mysteria, inquit Christus. Et sunt gradus quidam cognitionis rerum spiritualium. Vnicuique dat Dominus ad mensuram fidei. Et quis legens de sacerdotio Melchisedec cogitasset, id pertinere ad sacerdotium Christi, ibique typū Christi latuisse? Quanquam admodum etiam consultò videtur, Apostolus difficultatē huius disputationis reiicere in auditorum segnitiem: quòd hac potissimum ratione eos, qui assertionem sacerdotij Christi, siue propter imbecillitatem intellectus, siue propter malitiam & inexpugnabilem affectum erga sacerdotium legale, ferre non poterant, per totā digressionem hanc reprimit. Tacitè enim iubet eos in sese descendere, & propriam potius agnoscere inscitiam, quàm aspernari, vel temerè damnare, quodipsi non intelligūt. Sic autem propensum est hominum ingenium, ut quæ non intelligunt, ea impudenter damnet. Quòd si potius respicerent in suam ipsorū hebetudinem & segnitiem, æquius ferrent, quæ ab alijs rectè & verbo Dei consentanea proferūtur. Exépla licet hodie passim obseruare. Et cetesi respiciamus ad statū ecclesiarum præsentis temporis, multa erūt hic nobis clariora. Habemus aduersarios graues & multos, qui audent damnare doctrinam ex sacris literis, per nos propositam. Sed huc audaciæ mouet eos in primis propria inscitia & segnities. Atq; omnia fere, quæ hac digressione continentur, possunt siue aduersarijs, siue infirmis pijs accommodari: & facta collatione quadam nostrorum temporū, erunt nobis omnia in hac digressione magis peruia. Sed priusquam pergamus, aliquid de vocibus breuiter est annotandum. Græcè quidem sic habetur, ... Simili modo 1. Petri 3. Domini patiētiam salutem arbitremini, quēadmodum & dilectus frater noster Paulus iuxta sibi datam sapientiā scripsit vobis, etiā in omnibus fere epistolis, loquens de his, inter quæ sunt nonnulla difficilia intellectu, quæ indocti parumque firmi detorquent, sicut & cæteras scripturas, ad suam ipsorum perniciem. Quo loco etiam dicitur, quomodo quidam non assequuntur sententiam scripturæ propter suam imperitiam & inscientiam, quod præsenti caussæ seruit.
units.tr: "It is not given to all to know the mysteries," says Christ. There are certain degrees of knowledge of spiritual things. "To each the Lord gives according to the measure of faith." And who, reading about the priesthood of Melchizedek, would have thought that this pertained to the priesthood of Christ, and that a type of Christ lay hidden there? Although the Apostle seems quite deliberately to lay the difficulty of this discussion upon the sluggishness of his hearers, because in this way he restrains throughout this digression those who could not bear the assertion of the priesthood of Christ, whether on account of weakness of understanding or on account of wickedness and an unconquerable attachment to the legal priesthood. For he silently bids them look into themselves and rather acknowledge their own ignorance than despise or rashly condemn what they do not understand. Yet human nature is so inclined that it shamelessly condemns what it does not understand. But if they looked rather at their own dullness and sluggishness, they would bear more fairly what is rightly and in agreement with the word of God set forth by others. Examples may be observed everywhere today. And if we look at the state of the churches of the present time, many things here will be clearer to us. We have many serious adversaries who dare to condemn the doctrine from the holy writings which we set forth. But this audacity is chiefly prompted in them by their own ignorance and sloth. And almost everything contained in this digression can be applied either to adversaries or to weak godly people, and, with a certain comparison to our own times, all these things in this digression will be more open to us. But before we proceed, something must briefly be noted about the words. In Greek it stands thus... Similarly 1 Peter 3: "Regard the patience of the Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, speaking of these things in almost all his epistles, among which there are some hard to understand, which the unlearned and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures." In this place it is also said how some do not grasp the sense of Scripture because of their own inexperience and ignorance, which serves the present cause.

units.la: In hoc, quod dicit, ... facti estis, significat, ut Theophylactus notat, nonnihil illos à priori diligetia refilisse: quare mordacitatis nonnihil subest huic verbo, & quodammodo reprehensionem reddit acerbiorem.
units.tr: In saying "you have become" (... facti estis), he signifies, as Theophylact notes, that they had somewhat fallen away from their earlier diligence. Hence there is a touch of biting reproach in this word, which makes the rebuke somewhat sharper.

units.la: Significanter vero ait, segnes νωθροὶ, tardi, languidi, ignaui, pigri: Auribus, innuit, non libenter audire, & inuitè in aures recipere ista, quæ occinuntur ipsis de pontificio Christi. Lucæ vltimo ad discipulos illos duos ait Christus, ὦ ἀνόητοι καὶ βραδεῖς τῇ καρδίᾳ. Ita in scripturis considerare licet tarditatem cordis, tarditatē aurium, &c. Sicut & Stephanus Act. 7. Iudæos vocat duros ceruice, & incircumcisos corde & auribus, qui spiritui Sancto semper resistunt.
units.tr: He significantly calls them "sluggish [νωθροὶ], slow, languid, lazy, idle" in their ears. He means that they did not gladly listen, and did not willingly receive into their ears those things which are sung to them about the priesthood of Christ. In the last chapter of Luke, Christ says to the two disciples, "O foolish and slow of heart [ὦ ἀνόητοι καὶ βραδεῖς τῇ καρδίᾳ]." So in the Scriptures one may observe slowness of heart, slowness of ears, and so on. Likewise Stephen in Acts 7 calls the Jews stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears, who always resist the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Etenim cū debeatis pro temporis ratione doctores esse, rursum opus habetis, vt doceamus vos, quæ sint elementa initij eloquiorum Dei, factiq; estis ij, quibus lactē sit opus & nō solido cibo. Nam quisquis lactis est particeps, is rudis est sermonis iustitiæ, infans enim est. Porrò perfectorum est solidus cibus, nempe horum, qui propter assuetudinem sensus habent exercitatos, ad discretionem boni pariter ac mali.
units.tr: For when by reason of time you ought to be teachers, you again have need that someone teach you the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God; and you have become such as have need of milk and not of solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the perfect, namely to those who by reason of practice have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.

units.la: Probat, quòd fiat segnes, ab eo, quòd tàm multo tèpore cum didicerint, parum tamē promouerint. Habet paulò plus acrimoniæ hæc probatio, si quadam sarcasmi specie, aut certè cum stomacho ac gestu acriter reprehendentis & subirascentis pronunciata accipiantur. Sic autem pronūciatam colligere licet ex ipsa rerum & verborum dispositione. An enim non uehementer pungunt illa, inprimis quòd segnitiem exaggerat à diuturno tempore quo didicerunt: deinde, quòd iucunda quadam antitheseos forma ait, eos, cùm docere alios debebant, egere adhuc ut doceantur? Postremò, quòd docendi sintipsum initium eloquiorum Dei, imò huius initij elementa. Quis obsecro non videat, hic valde aculeatam subesse reprehensionem, qua omnes ad agnitionem suæ ignauiæ & pudorem permoueantur? Atque huiusmodi affectus digressionib. apti sunt, & Pauli, qui semper vehemens fuit, ingenio, præterea Iudæis, quos decebat durius increpari, hæc conueniunt. Est autem hæc sententia: Dico quidem vestræ segnitiei imputandum esse, quod disputatio hæc de pontificatu Christi videatur vobis difficilis. Id autem iure à me dicitur. Nam reuera estis supra modum segnes, meritoque hac in parte culpādi. An'ne enim euidens hoc est ignauiæ argumentum, quòd, cùm tato tempore audiueritis doctrinā euangelicam, tamē non adeò promouistis in ea, quin, qui debebatis pro tanti temporis ratione esse aliorum doctores, versandum est vobis adhuc in ipsis elementis?
units.tr: He proves that they have become sluggish from the fact that, though they have been learning for so long a time, they have made little progress. This proof has a little more bitterness if it is taken as delivered in a kind of sarcastic manner, or certainly with the feeling and gesture of one who rebukes sharply and is somewhat angry. That it is delivered in this way can be gathered from the very arrangement of the matters and words. Do not those things sting sharply, first because he magnifies their sluggishness by the long time in which they have learned; then because, in a pleasing form of antithesis, he says that they, who ought to be teaching others, still need to be taught; and finally because he says they need to be taught the very beginning of the oracles of God, indeed the elements of this beginning? Who, I beg you, does not see that a very piercing rebuke lies hidden here, by which all are moved to recognise their idleness and to feel shame? And such emotions suit digressions, and this is consistent with Paul's character, which was always vehement, and besides, such rebukes fit the Jews, whom it was fitting to reprove more severely. The sense is this: I say that it is to be imputed to your sluggishness that this discussion about the priesthood of Christ seems difficult to you. And I say this rightly. For you are truly sluggish beyond measure and deservedly blameworthy in this respect. For is not this a clear sign of idleness, that, although you have heard the evangelical teaching for so long a time, you have not advanced in it so far that you, who ought by reason of so long a time to be teachers of others, must still be occupied with the very elements?

units.la: Quod sanè quàm turpe, & indignum vobis sit, quilibet intelligit. Sic verò & alijs in locis, quomodo semper proficere debeamus, inculcatur. Sed multò maximè id erat necessarium inculcare apud Iudæos, quos oportebat multa legalia, & traditiones Seniorum, quibus à teneris assuerant, dedisc ere: quòd in causa haud dubie erat, cur tardiores essent, & ne ita in doctrina Euangelica proficerent.Et licet apostoli,& quidam electi, quos Deus constituit in ecclesia ad docendum, diuinitùs essent & breuissimo spacio edocti, quemadmodum Apostoli,& in primis Paulus in triduo consummatè doctus: tamen id nequaquam generaliter ita de omnibus est accipiendum, quando non omnes ad munus docendi Dominus vocauit: sicut nec omnes statim accipiebant donum linguarum, donum sanationum, &c.
units.tr: How shameful and unworthy this is for you, anyone can understand. In other places too he urges us always to make progress. But it was much more especially necessary to inculcate this among the Jews, who had to unlearn many legal observances and the traditions of the elders, to which they had been accustomed from childhood; and this was undoubtedly a cause why they were slower and did not advance so well in evangelical doctrine. And although the apostles, and certain chosen men whom God set in the Church to teach, were taught divinely and in a very short time, as the apostles were, and Paul above all was fully taught in three days, yet this must by no means be taken in general as applying to all, since the Lord did not call all to the office of teaching; just as not all immediately received the gift of tongues, the gift of healing, and so on.

units.la: Ergo temporis successu, sicut & hodie, proficiebant, & paulatim post plantationem vnius doctoris, post rigationem alterius, incrementum accipiebant à Domino.
units.tr: Therefore, with the passing of time, as also today, they advanced, and gradually, after one teacher had planted and another had watered, they received the increase from the Lord.

units.la: Huc pertinent exhortationes & comprecationes pro piorum profectu in doctrina passim obuiae. Ephes.1. Mentionem vestri facians in precibus meis, ut Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater gloriae det vobis spiritum sapientiae & reuelationis, per agnitionem sui, &c. Ephes.3. Flecto genua ad patrem, Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ex quo omnis à communi patre cognatio in coelis, & in terra nominatur, ut det vobis iuxta diuitias gloriae suae, ut fortitudine corroboremini per spiritum suum in internum hominem, ut inhabitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris, in charitate actis radicibus, & fundamento itato, ut valeatis assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quae sit latitudo, & longitudo, & profunditas, & sublimitas, cognoscere q; praeminentem cognitionis dilectionem Christi, ut impleamini in omnem plenitudinem Dei. Et capite quarto, Non amplius simus pueri, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quouis vento doctrinae per versutiam hominu; per astutiam, qua nos adoriuntur, ut imponant nobis: sed veritatem sectantes in charitate, adolescamus in illu, per omnia, &c. Philippen. 1. Illud oro, ut charitas vestra adhuc magis, ac magis exuberet in agnitione omniq; intelligetia, &c. Coloss.1. Non definimus orare pro vobis, & poscere, ut impleamini agnitione, voluntatis eius in omni sapientia & prudentia spirituali. Sic passim alibi. Item loci, in quibus exprobratur tarditas in discendo, & in credendo, huc pertinent. Sed qua ratione quasi per gradus proficiendum in doctrina, nos postea explicabimus vberius. Nonnulla de partibus adijciemus.
units.tr: To this belong the exhortations and prayers for the progress of the godly in doctrine that are met with everywhere. Ephesians 1: "Making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation, through the knowledge of himself," etc. Ephesians 3: "I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might through his Spirit in the inner man, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, being rooted and grounded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height, and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." And in chapter 4: "Let us no longer be children, tossed to and fro and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by the cunning of men, by the craftiness with which they lie in wait to deceive; but speaking the truth in love, let us grow up in him in all things," etc. Philippians 1: "This I pray, that your love may abound still more and more in knowledge and in all understanding," etc. Colossians 1: "We do not cease to pray for you and to ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding." So also elsewhere in many places. Likewise the passages in which slowness in learning and in believing is reproached belong here. But in what way one must advance in doctrine, as it were by steps, we shall explain more fully afterwards. We shall add some things about the parts.

units.la: Cum debeatis esse doctores, rursum opus habetis, ut doceamus uos) Est antitheseos seu vocum coniugatarum ratio hic consideranda, quòd nonnihil gratiae habeat in sermone, & non parum exaggeret illorum ignauiam. Est autem hoc haud dubie dictum in genere ad omnes, ut recte videatur hic annotatum esse à Chrysostomo, quòd etiam laici debeant docere: sicut Stephanus Actor.7. etiamsi esset tantùm diaconus constitutus ad ministrandum mensis pauperum, tamen etiam docuit, sicut concio ipsius testatur. Et verum est, quod Deus vnicuiq; mandauit de proximo suo, & alter alteri debet, quae ad ædificationem pertinent, commonstrare, patresfamiliàs suis domesticis, parentes liberis, vicini vicinis. At non propterea inferendum est vniusçuiusque interesse publicè docere, seu Scripturarum arcana exponere, & contrà, ac interpretantur publici & legitimi ministri, explicare.
units.tr: Since you ought to be teachers, you again have need that we teach you. The reason of the antithesis, or of the matched words, is to be considered here: it gives a certain grace to the speech and greatly magnifies their idleness. This was undoubtedly said generally to all, so that Chrysostom rightly notes here that even laymen ought to teach. Stephen in Acts 7 likewise, although he had been appointed only as a deacon to serve tables for the poor, nevertheless also taught, as his sermon bears witness. And it is true that God commanded each one concerning his neighbour, and one ought to show another what pertains to edification: heads of households to their household members, parents to children, neighbours to neighbours. But it does not follow from this that it is the concern of every individual to teach publicly, or to expound the hidden things of the Scriptures, and, as the public and lawful ministers do, to explain them.

units.la: Scire atque etiam docere praecipua capita fidei, vniuscuiusq; interest: ferre sententiâ de quibuscunq; perplexis quaestionibus, aut docere, non est vniuscuiusq;. Eam ob rem Deus diuersa dona contulit, & alios constituit doctores, Euangelistas, &c. 1.Corinth.14. Prophetae duo aut tres loquantur & caeteri dijudicent. Porro si alij fuerit reuelatum assidenti, prior taceat. Potestis singulatim omnes prophetare, ut omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accipiant, & spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur. Non enim est confusionis autor Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus congregationibus sanctorum. Et paulo post: Omnia decenter & secundum ordinem fiant. Rursus Rom.9. Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi mittantur? Iacob. cap.3. docet, non temerè suscipiendū docendi munus: Nolite plures magistri fieri fratres mei, scientes, quòd maius iudicium sumpturi sumus.
units.tr: It is the concern of each individual both to know and also to teach the chief articles of faith; but to pronounce judgement on any perplexing questions, or to teach them, is not the concern of everyone. For this reason God bestowed various gifts and appointed some as teachers, evangelists, and so on. 1 Corinthians 14: "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first keep silent. You can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may receive comfort; and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not the author of confusion but of peace, as in all the congregations of the saints." And a little later: "Let all things be done decently and in order." Again Romans 10: "How shall they preach unless they are sent?" James 3 teaches that the office of teaching is not to be undertaken rashly: "Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that we shall receive the greater judgement."

units.la: Quamobrem grauiasime peccant clanculari illi concionatores, qui neq; vocati, neque reuera Spiritum Dei, aut mandatum Dei habentes, spargunt ea, quae neq; publicè audent asserere, neq; possent Scripturis rectè accommodatis approbare. Porrò, quòd Iudaei, qui antea versati fuerant in Scripturis, doctrinam Euangelicam continentibus, etiá iiuuentute: praeterea, qui Apostolos ipsos apud sese habuerant, quàm plurimos item alios donis spiritus Sancti illustratos: imò pleriq; ipsum Christum docentem, & miracula edentem audierant, non altius profecerant, erat valde detestandum, cùm ex ipsis quoque eligi debebant, qui ad gentes mitterentur, & gentium ecclesijs praeficerentur.
units.tr: Wherefore those secret preachers sin most gravely, who, being neither called, nor truly having the Spirit of God or the commission of God, scatter those things which they do not dare to assert publicly, nor could they rightly approve them from the Scriptures suitably applied. Moreover, that the Jews, who had previously been versed in the Scriptures containing the evangelical doctrine, even from youth, and besides, who had had the apostles themselves among them, and very many others likewise illumined by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, indeed most of them had heard Christ himself teaching and performing miracles, had not advanced further, was very much to be detested, since from among them too those were to be chosen who should be sent to the Gentiles and set over the churches of the Gentiles.

units.la: Propter has causas prudenter inseruit particulam, pro temporis ratione: Quibus neque tempus, neque aliud quicquam defuit ad proficiendum, valde turpe est non profecisse. Simili modo Christus exprobrat Philippo, & in Philippo etiam caeteris discipulis Ioannis 14. Tanto tempore vobiscum sum, & non cognouistis me? Philippe, qui videt me, videt & patrem, &c.
units.tr: For these reasons he prudently inserted the particle, according to the circumstances of the time: "They lacked neither the time nor anything else needed to make progress, so it is very shameful that they have not progressed." In the same way Christ rebukes Philip, and through Philip the other disciples as well, in John 14: "I have been with you for so long, and yet you have not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father," and so on.

units.la: Quæ sunt elementa initij eloquiorum Dei) Eloquia Dei, seu λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ, ponuntur pro tota doctrina, quæ nobis voce Dei in sacris Scripturis est propositá, præcipuè autem pro doctrina Euangelica, quæ per vniuersam Scripturam tam veteris, quàm noui Testamenti passim traditur: quomodo ea vox sæpè in utroq; testamento usurpatur. Roman. 3. Vbi interpres reddidit, Oracula, græcè sic habetur, ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ.
units.tr: "The elements of the beginning of the oracles of God." The oracles of God, or λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ [logia tou theou], stand for the whole teaching that is set before us by the voice of God in the sacred Scriptures, and especially for the gospel teaching, which runs throughout the whole of Scripture, of both the Old and the New Testament. The word is often used in this way in both Testaments. In Romans 3 the translator rendered it "oracles," but in Greek the text reads: "because the oracles of God were entrusted to them" [ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ].

units.la: Cæterum horum oraculorum, seu elogiorum Dei, dicit illis tradendum esse initium, τῶν ἀρχῶν: imò ut magis exaggeret illorum ignauiam, τὰ ἀρχῆς τὰ στοιχεῖα, id est, elementa ipsa. Qua voce alludit ad pueros alphabetarios seu elementarios, siue addiscentes prima rudimenta alicuius artis. στοιχεῖα elementa trado, seu prima rudimenta. Vnde quidam suos libellos de primordijs alicuius disciplinæ, Elementa inscripserunt, quomodo apud græcos Euclydes. Simili fere modo usurpauit Apostolus hanc vocem Galat. 4.
units.tr: Moreover, he says that a beginning must be made with these oracles, or declarations, of God, τῶν ἀρχῶν [tōn archōn]. And to make their sluggishness appear greater, he says "the very elements," τὰ ἀρχῆς τὰ στοιχεῖα [ta archēs ta stoicheia], that is, the elements themselves. By this word he alludes to children who learn their letters or are beginning the first rudiments of some art. στοιχεῖα [stoicheia] means elements, or first rudiments. For this reason some men have entitled their little books on the first principles of some discipline "Elements," as Euclid did among the Greeks. The Apostle used this word in almost the same way in Galatians 4.

units.la: Sic & nos cùm essemus pueri, sub elementis mundi eramus in seruitutem adacti, &c.
units.tr: "So also we, when we were children, were held in bondage under the elements of the world, and so on."

units.la: Ibidem: At nunc posteaquàm cognouistis Deum, quin potius cogniti estis à Deo, quomodo conuertimini denuò ad infirma & egena elementa, quibus iterum ab integro seruire vultis? Dies obseruatis, & menses, & tempora, & annos. Vbi clarè ostendit, se per elementa egena intelligere ceremoniolas & traditiones, quibus rudes Iudæi tanquà pueri in religione erant imbuti, &c. Item Colossens. 2. Videte, ne quis vos deprædetur per philosophiam & inanem deceptionem, iuxta constitutionem hominum, iuxta elementa mundi, & non iuxta Christum. Ibidem: Itaq; si mortui estis cùm Christo ab elementis mundi, quid, quasi viuentes in mundo, decretis tenemini? Sed hoc discriminis est in hoc obseruandum, quòd Apostolus, quoniam improbare voluit, quibus Galatæ & Colossenses in hærebant, vocat elementa mundi, non iuxta Christum. Hic autem quæ recta & necessaria concedit, vocat elementa eloquiorum Dei: ut hæc addisci velit, illa verò dedisci. Alia ergo sunt illa elementa mundi, alia ista elementa eloquiorum Dei. Qualia illa desci bit Apostolus illic, vocans obseruationes dierum, temporum, &c. traditionum humanarum. Qualia verò ista sint, mox subijciet, enumerans, pœnitentiam ab operibus mortuis, fidem in Deum, Baptisma, doctrinam, manuum impositionem, resurrectionem mortuorum, iudicium æternum.
units.tr: In the same place: "But now that you have come to know God, or rather have been known by God, how is it that you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you want to be in bondage all over again? You observe days, and months, and seasons, and years." Here he plainly shows that by the beggarly elements he means the ceremonies and traditions in which the rude Jews, like children, had been schooled in religion. Likewise Colossians 2: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ." Again: "If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as if you were living in the world, do you submit to decrees?" But in this matter one must observe a difference: when the Apostle wanted to condemn what the Galatians and Colossians were clinging to, he calls it "the elements of the world, and not according to Christ." Here, however, he grants what is right and necessary and calls it "the elements of the oracles of God," because he wants these to be learned and those to be unlearned. So those elements of the world are one thing, and these elements of the oracles of God are another. The Apostol describes the former there, calling them observances of days, seasons, and so on, which are human traditions. What the latter are he immediately sets out, listing repentance from dead works, faith in God, baptism, teaching, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.

units.la: Factiq; estis if quibus lacte sit opus, & non solido cibo) Per expositionem rursus idem dicit, quod prius. sed adhibita perapta similitudine, quæ segnitiem & ruditatem illorum scitissimè delineat.
units.tr: "And you have come to need milk, and not solid food." By this explanation he says again what he said before, but with a very apt comparison that describes most accurately the sluggishness and rudeness of these people.

units.la: Ea sumpta est ab infantibus, quorum stomachus molle tantùm lactis pabulum fert, solidum omnem cibum reijciens. Atq; eam doctrinam, quam prius intellexit nomine eloquiorum, nunc complectitur voce lactis, quomodo alias quoq; talem doctrinam vocauit lac, & eos, quibus ea propter imbecillitatem proprie conuenit, infantes. Sicenim 1. Corinth. 3 legimus: Ego fratres, non potui loqui vobis, ut spiritualibus, sed loquendum fuit, ut carnalibus, ut infantibus in Christo. Lactis enim potu vos alui, & non cibo. Nondum enim poteratis, imò ne nunc quidem adhuc potestis, nam adhuc carnales estis.
units.tr: This is taken from infants, whose stomachs bear only soft milk-food and reject all solid nourishment. And the teaching which he previously understood under the name of "utterances," he now embraces under the name of milk, just as elsewhere too he called such teaching milk, and those who, because of their weakness, properly fit it, infants. For thus we read in 1 Corinthians 3: "I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but had to speak as to carnal people, as to infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not with solid food. For you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, even now you are still not able, for you are still carnal."

units.la: Quo loco rudes in religione vocat infantes & carnales, doctrinam illis conueniente vocat Lac. Et rectè quidem: nam doctrina verbi Dei se habet generaliter instar cibi, quo pascuntur animæ, quemadmodum Christus ipse ex Deuteronomij octauo citauit Matthæi 4 Non solo pane viuit homo, sed omni verbo, quod egreditur per os Dei. Ioann. 6.
units.tr: In this passage he calls those who are untrained in religion "infants" and "carnal," and he calls the teaching suited to them "milk." And rightly so: for the doctrine of the word of God is in general like food, by which souls are nourished, just as Christ himself cited from Deuteronomy 8 in Matthew 4: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." John 6.

units.la: Verba, quæ ego loquor vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt. Ibidem Petrus: Domine, ad quem ibimus? Verba vitæ æternæ habes. Ob quam causam Apostolus Philippenf. 2. appellat verbum vitæ: Agite, ut filij Dei, irreprehensibiles in medio nationis prauæ ac tortuosæ, inter quos lucete tanquàm luminaria in mundo, sermonem vitæ sustinentes. Item 1. Ioannis 1. Quod perspeximus, & manus nostræ contrectauerunt, de sermone vitæ: & vita manifestata est, & vidimus, & testamur, & annunciamus vobis vitam æternam. Actor. 5. Angelus ad Petrum & Ioannem captiuos: Ite, & stantes loquamini in templo, populo omnia verba vitæ huius. Et hic paulò post subijcit Apostolus metaphoram de gustando verbo.
units.tr: "The words that I speak to you are spirit and life." In the same place Peter says: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." For this reason the Apostle in Philippians 2 calls it the word of life: "Act as children of God, blameless in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life." Likewise 1 John 1: "That which we have seen and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life, and the life was manifested, and we have seen and testify and proclaim to you eternal life." Acts 5: the angel says to Peter and John, when they were in prison: "Go and stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life." And here a little later the Apostle adds the metaphor of tasting the word.

units.la: Itaq; cum verbo Dei vita paretur, conseruetur, Spiritualis inquam vita, & animarum recte verbum generaliter cibus appellatur. Porrò homines, qui debent hoc cibo refici, prout ipsi aliter, atq; aliter in se sunt affecti: ita diuersimodè quoq; hunc cibum accipiunt: atque alij quidem sic sumunt, ut non nisi leuem, & exiguum possint ferre: alij verò plus eius accipiunt, atq; etiam solidum possunt accipere. Hinc igitur istę similitudines, quibus infirmiorum doctrina deprompta ex penu sacri verbi comparatur lacti, proiectiorum verò doctrina comparatur cibo solido.
units.tr: Not that the teaching itself is varied in itself, or that one part of it is more or less perfect than another. For all sacred teaching is equally perfect, equally worthy, and everything in it is linked together; but the variety of human capacity produces this distinction, on account of which some things must be taught first and others later. In Peter, milk signifies the simplicity of manners and innocence, such as is seen in children.

units.la: Non quòd doctrina ipsa in se sit varia, vel altera eius pars altera sit perfectior seu imperfectior: vniuersa enim doctrina sacra æquè est perfecta, æquè digna, & omnia in ea sunt inuicem concatenata: sed varietas humani captus istam distinctionem parit, propter quam opus est alia prius, alia posterius tradere. Apud Petrum lac significat simplicitatem morum & innocentiæ, qualis in pueris cernitur.
units.tr: So the Apostle, by a certain comparison, aptly wanted to signify how rude and unskilled they were in the teaching of religion. He said that they had become such people as need milk, that is, people who still ought to be taught the elements of the oracles of God.

units.la: Aptè ergo significare vole s Apostolus quadam similitudine, quàm essent rudes & imperiti in doctrina religionis, dixit, eos esse factos eiusmodi, quib. lacte opus sit, id est, qui adhuc doceri debeant elementa eloquiorum Dei.
units.tr: It is agreed, moreover, both from the tradition of the natural philosophers, that milk is given to children because it is thin, warming, nourishing, and very quickly converted into bodily substance. Also, because it is more like a drink than food, and since infants have no teeth, they could not chew solid food. I think, too, that this comparison and manner of speaking about milk is taken from Isaiah 55.

units.la: Constat autem vel ex Physicorum traditione, ideo pueris dari lac, quòd tenue sit, cale faciens, nutriens, celerrimè convertibile in substantiam corpoream: Item quòd potus instar se potius habeat, quàm cibi instar, quæ cùm dentes non habeant, non possent manere. Existimo autem hanc similitudinem & formam locutionis de lacte, sumptam ex Esaiæ 55.
units.tr: There the evangelical teaching and gifts seem to be compared to wine and milk. For there it reads: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters, and you who have no money, come, buy and eat; come, buy without money and without any price, wine and milk, and so on."

units.la: Vbi doctrina ac dona euangelica vino ac lacti videntur comparata, Sic enim ibi: Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas, & qui non habetis argentum, properate, emite, & comedite: venite, emite absque argento, & absque ulla commutatione, vinum & lac, &c.
units.tr: Here the evangelical teaching and gifts seem to be compared to wine and milk. For thus it says there: "All you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no money, hurry, buy and eat; come, buy without money and without any exchange, wine and milk," etc.

units.la: Quod addit per contrarium, Et non solùm cibo: Lucis causa fit, sicut solent antitheta sententiam clariorem reddere.
units.tr: What he adds by way of contrast, "and not only solid food," is for the sake of clarity, as antitheses are accustomed to make the sense clearer.

units.la: Possunt autem lacti comparari illa legalia, & in primis ceremonialia, quæ aliàs vocantur pædagogia ad Christum, quibus Iudæi rudes in Euangelio erant immodicè addicti, nec poterant oculos mentis ab umbris illis rerum corporalium, quæ prius diximus elementa esse, ad res ipsas spirituales attollere, quæ se habent instar solidi cibi. Item lactis nomine intellige eadem, quæ mox enumerat, in pertinentibus ad sermonem inchoantem in Christo. Solidi verò cibi dignitatem obtinent, quæ mox de sacerdotio Christi, de abrogatione legis, de nouo cultu spirituali vult tradere, ad quæ sanè percipienda Iudæi multò erant tardissimi. στερεὸν autem vocatur solidum, quomodo etiam geometræ dicunt corpus solidum, quod in longum, latum, profundum extenditur: à verbo στερεῶ, quod est firmo. Quòd igitur proprie corporibus convenit, etiam aliis rebus accommodatur quadam, uti apparet, metaphora: quomodo etiam apud latinos vox soliditatis.
units.tr: Moreover, those legal things can be compared to milk, and especially the ceremonial ones, which are elsewhere called the schoolmaster leading to Christ, to which the Jews, untrained in the Gospel, were excessively attached, and they could not lift the eyes of their minds from those shadows of bodily things, which we said before are elements, up to the spiritual things themselves, which are like solid food. Likewise, by the name of milk understand the same things that he now lists, pertaining to the word beginning in Christ. But the dignity of solid food is held by those things which he now wants to set forth concerning the priesthood of Christ, the abrogation of the law, and the new spiritual worship, which the Jews were very slow to grasp. Now στερεὸν is called solid, just as geometers also speak of a solid body, which extends in length, breadth and depth, from the word στερεῷ, which means firm. What therefore properly belongs to bodies is applied to other things by a certain metaphor, as is evident; just as also among the Latins the word soliditas is used.

units.la: Nam quisquis lactis est particeps, is rudis est sermonis iustitiæ, infans enim est. Porrò perfectorum est solidus cibus, nempe horum qui propter assuetudinem sensus habent exercitatos, ad discretionem boni pariter ac mali.
units.tr: For whoever partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the mature, namely those who, through habit, have their senses trained to discern good and evil alike.

units.la: Similitudinem in medium productam plenius exponit, describendo, & quales sint illi, quibus tantum convenit lac doctrinæ: atque iterum per contrarium quales illi, quibus convenit solidus cibus, haud dubiè hac contrariorum expositione sententiam cupiens multo illustriorem efficere. Propterea autem placuit Apostolo plurib. verbis istud agere, ac diutius immorari descriptioni ignaviæ & ruditatis, ut clarius ob oculos poneret, Hebræis suam ipsorum segnitiem contemplandam, atq; ita ad pudorem confessionem; propriæ infirmitatis pertraheret. Interea verò ut ignauos hic compescit, ne (quod & antea à nobis dictum est) sublimem doctrinam de sacerdotio Christi, quam non intelligut, temerè damnare præsumant. Ita rursus addita descriptione perfectorum valde pruden ter artificioseq; eos, qui in doctrina religionis præ cæteris promouerant, sibi cöciliat, nec non ad percipiendum ea, quæ tradenda restant, alacriores reddit. Neq; verò accipien dü est, ita Apostolum arguere Hebræos, quasi ad vnum omnes essent rudes, cùm certum sit, inter eos multos fuisse valde peritos & prouectos in doctrina, quales Apollo, & quidā alij nominantur. Ita namq; posterius istud membrum nonnullam quodammodo mitigationem reprehensionis paulò acerbioris in se habere videtur. Sunt igitur omnia ordinatissimè disposita, & singula verba suam habent proprietatem & pondus.
units.tr: He sets out the comparison more fully by describing it, and by describing what kind of people are suited to milk-teaching alone; and again, by the contrary, what kind are suited to solid food. Undoubtedly he wishes, by this exposition of contraries, to make the sense much clearer. For this reason the Apostle was pleased to treat the matter at length in many words, and to linger over the description of sloth and crudeness, so that he might set before their eyes more vividly the Hebrews' own sluggishness for contemplation, and so draw them, by shame, to a confession of their own weakness. Meanwhile, he restrains the idle here, so that (as we have said before) they may not presume rashly to condemn the lofty doctrine of the priesthood of Christ, which they do not understand. Likewise, by adding the description of the mature, he very prudently and skilfully wins over those who had advanced further than the rest in the teaching of religion, and makes them more eager to receive what remains to be delivered. Nor should it be understood that the Apostle rebukes the Hebrews as if they were all unskilled, since it is certain that among them there were many who were very learned and advanced in doctrine, such as Apollos and some others are named. For this latter clause seems to contain in itself a certain softening of a rebuke that is somewhat harsh. Everything, then, is arranged most orderly, and each word has its own precise meaning and weight.

units.la: Quisquis, inquit, lactis est particeps, is rudis est sermonis iustitiæ) Videtur hypallage quædā esse, cùm sententia hunc ordinem poscat. Omnis, qui rudis est, lacte eget. Significare enim vult, ruditatem esse causam, cur lac debeat illis propinari. Vel, ita potius construe, ut tanquàm à signo sumatur ratiocinatio. Quisquis lactis est particeps, signum est, eum esse rudem: Vos autem, ait, adhuc lacte vescimini: Ergo estis rudes. Sed ista minutiora sunt. Dicitautem, Quisquis lactis est particeps: pro eo, quod est: Quisquis adhuc cum aliis rudib. lacte vescitur, & in doctrinæ rudimentis semper hæret.
units.tr: "Whoever," he says, "partakes of milk, is unskilled in the word of righteousness." There seems to be a kind of hypallage here, since the sense demands the order: "Everyone who is unskilled needs milk." For he wishes to signify that their crudeness is the cause why milk ought to be poured out for them. Or, better, construe it so that the reasoning is taken as from a sign: whoever partakes of milk is a sign that he is unskilled; but you, he says, still feed on milk; therefore you are unskilled. But these are minor points. He says, "Whoever partakes of milk," for: whoever still feeds on milk along with other unskilled people, and always clings to the rudiments of doctrine.

units.la: Nam aliàs quidem participem esse eiusmodi doctrinæ, improbari nullo modo potest, imò omnes debent eius esse participes, nec tantùm participes esse, sed totam imbibisse, priusquàm ad altiora ascendant. At verò semper hærere in illo lacte, & nunquàm ad solidum cibum capiendum consurgere, hoc sanè euidens est ruditatis & segnitiei argumentum.
units.tr: For otherwise, to be a partaker of such doctrine can by no means be condemned; indeed, all ought to be partakers of it, and not merely partakers, but to have soaked it all in before they ascend to higher things. But to cling always to that milk, and never to rise to take solid food, is clearly a proof of crudeness and sloth.

units.la: Rudis est sermonis iustitiæ, ἄπειρος λόγος δικαιοσύνης) ἄπειρος ide quod inexpertus. παραδομα ex-perior, periculum facio, utor, adipiscor. ἄπειροι, qui dicti.
units.tr: "Unskilled in the word of righteousness" (ἄπειρος λόγος δικαιοσύνης). ἄπειρος is the same as "inexperienced." πείρα: I experience, I try, I make trial, I make use of, I obtain. ἄπειροι: those who are so called.
