units.la: Significat ergo, eum, qui semper haeret in elementis religionis, nihil adhuc expertum esse, nihilq; adeptum in ijs, quae ad perfectionem sunt necessaria. Sed ex sequentibus in proximo membro, vbi videlicet ait, perfectos habere sensus exercitatos ad discretionem boni pariter & mali, intelligitur, qui sint rudes. Ex quibus verbis etiam colligi potest per contrarium, quid intelligi debeat per sermonem iustitiae.
units.tr: Therefore it signifies that the one who always clings to the elements of religion has not yet experienced anything, and has obtained nothing in those things which are necessary for perfection. But from what follows in the next clause, where he says that the mature have senses trained to discern good and evil alike, it is understood who the unskilled are. From these words it can also be gathered, by the contrary, what ought to be understood by the word of righteousness.

units.la: Videtur enim sermo iustitiae significare doctrinam de discretione boni & mali, qui & iniqui. Quamuis non per omnia innitendum huic interpretationi ex contrario. Nam ibi reuera utitur illis verbis, quae plenius explicant eius ingenium, qui ad virilem aetatem iam peruenerit, ut sic per metaphoram, eorum quoq;, qui in religione prae caeteris profecerunt, dignitas magis elucesceat. Hic vero per sermonem iustitiae spirituale quiddam significat, videlicet doctrinam, qua traditur, quomodo ad veram iustitiam perueniatur. Quomodo & 2. Timoth. 3. de sacra Scriptura: Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quae est in iustitia, ut integer sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum apparatus. In quam sententiam Psalmo 119. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lumen semitis meis, iuraui & statui custodire iudicia iustitiae tuae. Proinde cum omnis doctrina proposita nobis verbo Dei in sacris literis huc tendat, ut nos ad veram iustitiam perducamur, recte doctrina illa nomine sermonis iustitiae intelligitur. Quidam dicunt sermonem iustitiae, quasi sermonem iustum, id est, perfectum, integrum, cui nihil deest, &c. Sed haec durior interpretatio est, minusq; vsitata Scripturis. In hac porro doctrina & schola, ut alij plus assecuti sunt, alij minus: ita hi quidem rudes atque inexperti sermonis iustitiae dicuntur, alij vero probe experti.
units.tr: For the word of righteousness seems to signify the doctrine concerning the discernment of good and evil, and of the righteous and the unrighteous. Although this interpretation by contrast should not be relied on in every respect. For there he uses those words which more fully explain the disposition of one who has already reached manly age, so that, by metaphor, the dignity of those also who have progressed beyond the rest in religion may shine forth more clearly. Here, however, by the word of righteousness he signifies something spiritual, namely the doctrine by which it is taught how one comes to true righteousness. So also in 2 Timothy 3, of Holy Scripture: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, which is in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." To the same effect Psalm 119: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths; I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness." Therefore, since all doctrine set before us in the Word of God in the sacred letters tends to this, that we may be brought to true righteousness, that doctrine is rightly understood by the name "word of righteousness." Some say that "word of righteousness" means, as it were, a just word, that is, perfect, whole, lacking nothing, and so on. But this is a harsher interpretation, and less customary in the Scriptures. In this doctrine and school, moreover, some have made more progress and others less; so these are called unskilled and inexperienced in the word of righteousness, while others are called thoroughly experienced.

units.la: Infans enim est: νήπιος γὰρ ἐστι. Pulchra ratio, quare qui semper haeret in lactis pabulo, sit nudis sermonis iustitiae. Se enim habet in doctrina, sicut infans in iudicio boni & mali.
units.tr: "For he is an infant": νήπιος γὰρ ἐστι. A fine reason why the one who always clings to the food of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness. For he stands in doctrine as an infant does in the judgment of good and evil.

units.la: Proprie autem νήπιος dicitur, quasi νη ἔπιος, non loquens, ab ἐπέω, loqui, dicere, & sic ad aetatem infantilem proprie refertur. Sed frequenter, praesertim in sacris literis ad animum & sensum refertur, ut dicantur pueri, qui videlicet ingenio, iudicio, moribus, sunt pueri, non aetate: quomodo Esaiae 65. Puer centum annorum morietur, peccator centum annorum maledictus erit. Hinc & senes proverbialiter pueri appellantur, quando redeunt ad pueriles mores. Hoc igitur loco ad sensum seu iudicium in rebus religionis & spiritualib. refertur, quomodo & Ephes. 4. Non amplius sumus pueri, νήπιοι, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quouis vento doctrinae.
units.tr: Strictly, νήπιος is called as if νη ἔπιος, not speaking, from ἐπέω, to speak, to say, and so it properly refers to infant age. But frequently, especially in the sacred letters, it refers to mind and understanding, so that those are called children who are children in intellect, judgment and morals, not in age: as in Isaiah 65, "The child shall die at a hundred years old, and the sinner at a hundred years shall be accursed." Hence also old men are proverbially called children when they return to childish ways. In this place, therefore, it refers to understanding or judgment in matters of religion and spiritual things, as also in Ephesians 4, "We are no longer children, νήπιοι, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine."

units.la: Et 1. Corinth. 14. Fratres, ne sitis pueri (παιδία) sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis (νηπιάζετε) sensibus vero perfecti sitis: τῇ δὲ φρεσὶ τέλειοι γίνεσθε.
units.tr: And 1 Corinthians 14: "Brothers, do not be children (παιδία) in understanding, but be children (νηπιάζετε) in malice; but in understanding be mature (τέλειοι γίνεσθε)."

units.la: Ergo licet alias imperitum in dicendo significat, ut Hieremiae 1. Vbi propheta excusans se dicit, Ah, ah, Domine, ecce nescio loqui, quia puer ego sum: alias humilem, abiectum, vitae innocentia praeditum, ut Marci 9. vbi Christus vult omnes effici instar puerorum: hoc tamen loco ad cognitionem in rebus spiritualibus transfertur, in qua alij infantes, alij iuuenes, alij puerti dici possunt, prout plus aut minus cognitionis sunt assecuti.
units.tr: Therefore, although elsewhere it signifies one unskilled in speaking, as in Jeremiah 1, where the prophet, excusing himself, says, "Ah, Lord God, behold I cannot speak, for I am a child"; and elsewhere humble, abject, endowed with innocence of life, as in Mark 9, where Christ wishes all to be made like children; yet in this place it is transferred to knowledge in spiritual things, in which some may be called infants, some young men, and some children, according as they have obtained more or less knowledge.

units.la: Porro perfectorum est solidus cibus (τελείων δὲ ἐστιν ἡ στερεὰ τροφή). Ratio similitudinis postulasset nomen, quod aetatem exprimeret, veluti virorum, vel senum, vel adultorum: quomodo Ephes. 4. Vult omnes peruenire in vnitatem fidei, & agnitionem filij Dei, in mensuram aetatis plenae adultę Christi, hoc est, ut ipsi velut adultę aetatis Christum itidem perfectu, & iam velut adultum agnoscant, non autem velut puerum ludibundum ipsi pueriliter venerentur, in elementis semper haerentes: sed Apostolo satis fuit dicere perfectos: quo modo itidem Ephes. 4. ait, perueniamus in virum perfectum. Itaq; perfectos eos intelligit, qui iam gradum fecerunt in doctrina, & assequi possunt solidum cibum, id est, sublimiora & graviora mysteria: quales haud dubie non pauci apud Hebraeos erant, sicut & inter gentiles. De qualibus 1. Corinth. 2. Porro sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos (ἐν τοῖς τελείοις) sapientiam autem non seculi huius, neq; principum seculi huius, qui abolentur. Sed loquimur sapientiam Dei, quae est recondita, quam praefinierat Deus ante secula, in gloriam nostram, quam nemo principum seculi huius cognouit. Et cap. 14. Sensibus sitis perfecti. Et ad Philippens. 3. Quotquot itaq; perfecti (τέλειοι) sumus, hoc sentiamus, & si quid aliter sentitis, hoc quoq; vobis Deus reuelabit. Attamen ad id quod assecuti sumus, eadem procedamus regula, ut simus concordes. Quibus omnibus locis loquitur Apostolus de perfectione illa in maiore cognitione.
units.tr: "But solid food belongs to the mature" (τελείων δὲ ἐστιν ἡ στερεὰ τροφή). The logic of the comparison would have required a name expressing age, such as of men, or of old men, or of adults: as in Ephesians 4, he wishes all to come to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to the measure of the stature of the full-grown Christ; that is, that they might acknowledge Christ as perfect, and now as fully grown, and not, as a playful child, venerate him childishly while always clinging to the elements. But it was enough for the Apostle to say "perfect," just as in Ephesians 4 he says, "we may come to a perfect man." Therefore he understands by the perfect those who have already made progress in doctrine and are able to take solid food, that is, the higher and weightier mysteries; such people were undoubtedly not few among the Hebrews, as also among the Gentiles. Of such 1 Corinthians 2: "Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect (ἐν τοῖς τελείοις), but a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. But we speak the wisdom of God, which is hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age has known." And chapter 14: "Be mature in understanding." And Philippians 3: "As many of us therefore as are perfect (τέλειοι) should think this; and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this to you also. Nevertheless, let us walk by the same rule to which we have attained, so that we may be of one mind." In all these places the Apostle speaks of that perfection in greater knowledge.

units.la: Hanc vero perfectionem tribuunt sanctis, non quod simpliciter perfectio & summa absolutio in cognitione hic possit parari: sed duntaxat quodam respectu, videlicet aliorum, qui nondum eodem peruenerunt, necad eandem mensuram fidei donati acceperunt.
units.tr: This perfection, however, is ascribed to the saints not because perfection and complete attainment in knowledge can be reached in this life without qualification, but only in a certain respect: namely, in comparison with others who have not yet reached the same point and have not been given the same measure of faith.

units.la: Quandoquidem Apostolus diserte dicit 1. Corinth. 13. Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus. Ast vbi venerit id quod perfectū est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Cum essem puer, ut puer loquebar, ut puer sentiebam, ut puer cogitabam: at vbi factus sum vir, aboleui puerilia.
units.tr: Since the Apostle says plainly in 1 Corinthians 13: "For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things."

units.la: Cernimus enim nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc vero cognoscam, quemadmodū & cognitus sum. Sanè quàm diu hic agimus, nihil aliud quàm manemus discipuli, & semper volutamur in eade schola, in eodem puluere, & semper est proficiendi locus. Neque quisquam talia habet dona, quin eadem auctiora in eo posint fieri. Donorum omnium gradus quidam sunt atq; incrementa: Vnde ipse Apostolus, qui, ut ipse refert 2. Corinth. 12. raptus fuit in tertium usq; cœlum, & audiuit arcana verba, quæ fas non sit homini loqui: quem item constat donis illustratum præ omnibus aliis, & præ aliis etiam laborasse: qui item (ut est Galat. 1.) profecerat antea in Iudaismo supra multos æquales in genere suo, cùm vehementer esset studiosus à maioribus suis traditorum institutorum: cuius etiam scripta, in quib. Petrus fatetur multa grauia & difficilia, amplissimam cognitionem testantur: tamen confessus est Philippens. 3. se nondum perfectum. Sic enim ibi ait: Postquam diligentiam & studiū suum in cognoscendo Christo expositiùet: Non quòd apprehenderim, aut iam perfectus sim, sed sector, si etiam apprehendam, quatenus & apprehensus sum à Christo Iesu. Fratres ego meipsum non arbitror assecutum esse.
units.tr: "For now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face: now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known." As long as we live here, we remain nothing but pupils, always turning over the same lessons in the same school, in the same dust, and there is always room to advance. Nor does anyone possess such gifts that they cannot be increased in him. All gifts have their degrees and their growth. Hence the Apostle himself, who (as he reports in 2 Corinthians 12) was caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words that it is not lawful for a man to utter, and who is known to have been distinguished by gifts above all others and to have laboured more than all of them, and who (as in Galatians 1) had made progress in Judaism beyond many of his contemporaries, being very zealous for the traditions of his fathers, and whose writings, in which Peter confesses there are many grave and difficult matters, bear witness to his very wide knowledge: nevertheless he confessed in Philippians 3 that he was not yet perfect. For there, after setting out his diligence and zeal in knowing Christ, he says: "Not that I have already attained, or am already perfect, but I press on, if indeed I may lay hold of that for which I was also laid hold of by Christ Jesus. Brethren, I do not count myself to have attained."

units.la: Quare ita accipiendum est, aliquos dici perfectos, non quidem simpliciter, sed respectu aliorum, qui paria non sunt assecuti. Atq; eam ob causam Apostolus, ne quis perfectos aliter, quàm decet, intelligeret, voluit pleniore interpretatione ostendere, quòsnam perfectos appellet, dicens: Nempe horum, qui propter assuetudinem, sensus habent exercitatos ad discretionem boni pariter & mali.
units.tr: Therefore it must be understood that some are called perfect, not absolutely, but in comparison with others who have not attained the same. And for this reason the Apostle, so that no one should understand "perfect" in a sense other than the right one, wished to show more fully whom he means by the perfect, saying: "Namely, those who, by reason of habit, have their senses exercised to discern good and evil alike."

units.la: En quales vocet perfectos, & quàm aptè his verbis virilis proiectiorque ætas describitur: nimirum non eos, qui possunt mente percipere res magnas & præclaras, vel qui possunt acutè subtiliterque disputare, vel aliàs mirabiliter differere in corona hominū: sed eos in primis, qui possunt discernere bonum à malo, quod reuerea primarium est, & sine quo nemo pro viro agnoscendus est: discernere rem corporeā à spirituali, legem ab euangelio, diuinum præceptum ab humano, iustitiam fidei à iustitia operū. Sed præterea opus est habeant sensus ad id exercitatos (sicut pugiles & quicunque artifices exercitio multum parantur) quod perfectum est & singulare. Postremò, qui habet exercitatos quadā longa & diuturna assuetudine: sicut senes dicūtur habere experientiā. Quæ singula necessum est accuratè expendere, & inueniemus haud dubiè non pauca nomine perfectionis intelligi.
units.tr: Here you see whom he calls perfect, and how aptly by these words a mature and more advanced age is described: certainly not those who can grasp great and famous matters with the mind, or who can argue sharply and subtly, or who otherwise speak wonderfully before a crowd; but above all those who can distinguish good from evil, which is truly the first thing, and without which no one may be recognised as a man: to distinguish the bodily from the spiritual, the law from the gospel, the divine precept from the human, the righteousness of faith from the righteousness of works. Moreover, it is necessary that they have their senses exercised for this (as boxers and all craftsmen are much prepared by practice), which is perfect and distinctive. Finally, they must have been exercised by a long and lasting habit, as the old are said to have experience. Each of these points must be weighed carefully, and we shall undoubtedly find that not a few things are understood under the name of perfection.

units.la: Habitus est alicuius rei sive in animo, sive in corpore à natura concepta, sed usu corroborata & plena perfectio. Vide Ciceronem de Inventione libro primo. Opus est multarum rerum longa & assidua experientia, ut quis perfectus dicatur. Qui multa vidit, multa audiuit, multas est expertus tentationes, pericula, & in omnibus constanter se statu est sanâ doctrinam, potuitque refugere, & damnare falsam, talis potest dici perfectus: quomodo Paulus multis in locis gloriatur, se diu in Euangelij negotio versatum & multa expertum. Item Timotheus, qui ab Apostolo institutus, multa vidit, sæpè etiā ad ecclesiarum res tractandas ab Apostolo missus, ut ad Corinthios, Philippenses, Thessalonicenses, & alios. Nec excludendi sunt alij, qui feliciter iam in discendis, audiendis, docendis sacris fuerant exercitati, quales fuisse sparsos per omnes ecclesias certum est. Ac de eiusmodi sensuū exercitio sunt illa, quæ apostolus præcipit Timotheo, Tito, & alijs omnibus, de profectione in doctrina: ad Timotheum quidem 1. Epistolæ capite quarto: Hæc exerce, in his esto, ut tuus profectus manifestus sit in omnib. Attende tibi ipsi & doctrinæ, perfiste in his. Nā si id feceris, teipsum seruabis, & eos qui te audierint.
units.tr: Perfection is the full and mature state of something conceived by nature, whether in the mind or in the body, but strengthened by use. See Cicero, On Invention, book one. A long and constant experience of many things is needed before someone is called perfect. One who has seen much, heard much, and has been tested by many temptations and dangers, and who has stood firm in all things, has been able to shun false teaching and condemn it, may be called perfect in this way: as Paul boasts in many places that he had long been engaged in the business of the gospel and had experienced much. So too Timothy, who was instructed by the Apostle, saw much and was often sent by the Apostle to deal with the affairs of the churches, as to the Corinthians, Philippians, Thessalonians and others. Nor are others to be excluded who had already been happily exercised in learning, hearing and teaching the sacred things, such as were certainly scattered through all the churches. To this exercise of the senses belong those instructions which the Apostle gives to Timothy, Titus and all others about progress in doctrine: to Timothy indeed in the fourth chapter of the first Epistle: "Practise these things, be in them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Take heed to yourself and to the teaching, persist in these things. For if you do this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you."

units.la: Discernere enim (ut ad superiora redeam) bonum à malo, propria videtur esse nota vitae rilis ætatis, & perfectionis primum indicium: id quod Esaias etiam admonuit cap. 7. ad quem locum apparet Apostolum respexisse: Sic enim de Christo ibi ait: Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Immanuel. Butyrum & mel comedet, ut sciat reprobare malum, & eligere bonum. Huc refer illud 1. Thessal. 5. Omnia probate, quod bonum fuerit, tenete, ab omni specie mala abstinete. Esaias cap. 5. concionatur contra illos, qui abutentes facultate rectè iudicandi sibi donata, dicunt malum bonum, bonum malum: et quia tales impij & hypocritæ semper erigūt caput, ideò valde opus est, ut qui perfectus esse vult, sciat discernere bonum & malum. Et propterea Deus inter alia dona largitus est ecclesiæ discretionem doctrinarum seu spirituum. Sed hæc de partibus sint satis. Nonnulla ad doctrinam pertinentia adijciamus,
units.tr: For to discern (to return to what was said above) good from evil seems to be the proper mark of a mature age and the first sign of perfection; this is what Isaiah also taught in chapter 7, and it is clear that the Apostle had this passage in view. For there he speaks of Christ thus: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Immanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to refuse the evil and choose the good." To this belongs 1 Thessalonians 5: "Test all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every form of evil." Isaiah in chapter 5 preaches against those who, abusing the faculty of right judgement given to them, call evil good and good evil; and because such impious and hypocritical people always lift up their heads, it is very necessary that whoever wishes to be perfect should know how to discern good and evil. And for this reason God, among other gifts, has bestowed on the Church the discernment of doctrines or spirits. But let this be enough on these parts. Let us add some points that pertain to doctrine.

units.la: Ante omnia hæc reprehensio segnitiei in Hebræis, satis admonet nos, ut in propria segnitiem incumbamur.
units.tr: Above all, this rebuke of sloth among the Hebrews is enough to warn us to take pains against our own sloth.

units.la: Reuera autem nunc valde frigidi & pigri sumus, & in discendo, & in exercendo ea, quæ sunt pietatis, ut, nisi Dominus aliter excitet & accedat corda, metuendum sit, ne penitus cognitio omnis & studiū cognoscendi extinguatur. Et hic licet animaduertere, quantū malum sit illa segnities & ruditas. Efficit enim, ut omnia, quæ nobis proponuntur, difficilia appareant. Spiritualia non possumus assequi, quam diu in carnalibus elementis, in traditionibus conquiescimus. Quamobrem opus est excutere pœnas, ab ignauo somno surgere, & vigilanter luci Scripturarum intendere. Orandusque nobis Deus, ut corda nostra promoueat, & opus bonum, quod cœpit in nobis, tandem perficiat. Et reuera nonminus peccatū est, postquam didicisti elementa, non progredi ad altiora, quā sniuersam doctrinam & verbū continere, id quod Apostolus ipse suis verbis paulò post significat, dicens, eos qui retrocedunt, Christum recrucifigere & ludibrio exponere. Cum igitur tantum peccatum est non proficere, valde opus est segnitiem ab animis nostris depelli à Deo petamus. Sicut ridendū se propinat, qui, postquam iecit præclara fundamenta ædificij, non potest superstruere: & sicut valde indecorum, in schola semper manere alphabetarium, & nunquam ad altiorem classem prouehi: sic multò indignisimū est, in religione post cognita rudimenta, non pergere ad sublimiora.
units.tr: Indeed, we are now very cold and lazy, both in learning and in practising the things that belong to godliness, so that, unless the Lord otherwise rouses and touches our hearts, it is to be feared that all knowledge and the zeal for knowing will be utterly extinguished. Here one may notice how great an evil that sloth and dullness is. For it makes everything that is set before us appear difficult. We cannot attain spiritual things so long as we rest in carnal elements and in traditions. Therefore we must shake off our pains, rise from idle sleep, and attend watchfully to the light of the Scriptures. We must also pray to God that he may advance our hearts and at last bring to completion the good work that he has begun in us. And indeed it is no less a sin, after you have learned the elements, not to go on to higher things than to keep to the whole teaching and word only; the Apostle himself signifies this in his own words a little later, saying that those who fall away crucify Christ again and expose him to mockery. Since, then, not to make progress is such a great sin, we should earnestly ask God that sloth be driven from our minds. As one makes himself ridiculous who, having laid splendid foundations of a building, cannot build upon them; and as it is most unseemly to remain always in the school among the alphabet-learners and never be promoted to a higher class: so it is far more shameful in religion, after the rudiments have been learned, not to press on to higher things.

units.la: Interea quoque quando hic describuntur rudes Hebræi, argumentū est, etiam rudes pertinere ad ecclesiam, nec esse contemnendos vel reijciendos. Non potest esse magna societas sine aliquib. infirmis, imperitis, & rudibus, nō magis, quàm possunt esse doctores in ecclesia, nisi sunt qui doceantur. Quare non recte faciunt, qui infirmiores fratres præ se continent, vel comminantur excludendos ab ecclesia, nisi de grauioribus mysterijs sciant differere. Christus sæpè imperitum agricolam, imò meretricē à diuinis rebus alienam, præfert doctis, scribis & pharisæis, qui, cùm habeant clauem scientiæ, ipsi tamen non ingrediuntur, & alios ab ingressu impediunt. Semper oportet esse rudes, priusquam ad altiora tendatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, too, when the rude Hebrews are described here, it is an argument that the rude also belong to the Church, and are not to be despised or rejected. There cannot be a great society without some weak, unskilled and rude members, any more than there can be teachers in the Church unless there are those who are to be taught. Therefore those do not act rightly who keep weaker brothers at a distance, or threaten to exclude them from the Church unless they can discourse on the weightier mysteries. Christ often preferred an unlearned farmer, or even a harlot alien to divine things, to the learned scribes and Pharisees, who, though they have the key of knowledge, do not enter themselves and hinder others from entering. It is always necessary to be rude before one strives toward higher things.

units.la: Vnde etiam constare debet, munus docendi rudes in ecclesia, veluti catechistā agere, non esse sordidum, sicut quidam falsò suspicantur.
units.tr: Hence it should also be clear that the task of teaching beginners in the Church, as in catechising, is not a base one, as some falsely suspect.

units.la: Adhæc illa descriptio perfectorum nobis calcar esse debet ad studium ac diligentiam in perdiscendis rebus spiritualibus, promptosque nos reddere ad labores subeundos.
units.tr: Moreover, that description of the mature ought to be a spur to us for study and diligence in learning spiritual things thoroughly, and it ought to make us ready to undertake labours.

units.la: Neque reuera parua res est, hanc perfectionē in ecclesia consequi, multa requiruntur, oportet variè exerceri, præire certamina, pericula, labores, sudores, experientiam, præcipuè autem literarum sacrarum tractatio ad perfectionem quasi viam sternit. Beatus est qui in lege Domini meditabitur die ac nocte. Propterea scholæ, & in his exercitamenta disputationum, concionum sacrarum instituuntur.
units.tr: Indeed, attaining this maturity in the Church is no small matter. Many things are required: one must be exercised in various ways, go through struggles, dangers, labours, sweat and experience. Above all, the handling of the sacred letters paves the way, as it were, to maturity. "Blessed is the man who will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night" [Ps. 1.]. For this reason schools are established, and in them exercises of disputation and sacred sermons.

units.la: Postremò habemus hîc euidens documentum, quòd aliter docendi sint infirmi, aliter prouecti. Sicut in frequenti conuiuio non omnium palatis omnes cibi ex æquo sapiunt: ita nō cuiusuis credentis captui quælibet doctrina apta est. Cuius rei diliges ratio doctoris ecclesiastico habēda est. Optima apud populum familiaris docendi ratio, qualis conspicitur in doctorum Homilijs, præsertim Chrysostomi: apud eruditos graviores disputationes & sublimior docendi ratio, qualem cernere est in scriptis plurimis Augustini.
units.tr: Lastly, we have here clear evidence that the weak must be taught in one way and the advanced in another. As at a crowded banquet not all foods taste equally good to everyone's palate, so no teaching suits the understanding of every believer indiscriminately. In this matter the teacher of the Church must take account of the reasoning of each. The best method of teaching for the people is the familiar one, such as is seen in the homilies of the teachers, especially Chrysostom's; among the learned, the weightier disputations and a more sublime manner of teaching, such as is to be seen in the many writings of Augustine.

units.la: QVINTI CAPITIS FINIS.
units.tr: The End of the Fifth Chapter.

units.la: CAPVT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: Excitatio ad studium & uigilantiam. Carnalib. elementis in hæretes nō possumus assequi spiritualia. Peccatum torporis et segnitiei. Conceptus pro gressuum Deo exosus. Simile ab architecto impe-rito et ignauo. Progressus pueroru in ludo literario. Rudes ab ecclesia non sunt arcendi. Vbi doctores, ibi & rudes. Christi lenitas & moderatio. Munus catechisticum, magnum & præclarum est in ecclesia. Calcar diligentiae in discēdis mysterijs sacris. Quomodo pueniendum ad perfectionem. Psalm. 1. Scholarum usus. Discrimen & delectus discentium. Simile à cibis. Quomodo, quoq; loco sit docendum.
units.tr: An exhortation to study and vigilance. Those who cling to carnal rudiments cannot attain spiritual things. The sin of sluggishness and laziness. A conceit of having made progress is hateful to God. A simile from an unskilled and idle architect. The progress of boys in the school. The unlearned are not to be shut out of the Church. Where there are teachers, there are also the untaught. The gentleness and moderation of Christ. The office of catechizing is great and excellent in the Church. A spur to diligence in learning the sacred mysteries. How one should press on to perfection. Psalm 1. The use of schools. The distinction and selection of learners. A simile from foods. How and in what place one should teach.

units.la: CAPVT SEXTVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 6.

units.la: Quapropter omissò, qui in Christo rudes inchoat, sermone, ad perfectionem feramur, non rursum fundamentum iacientes pœnitentiæ ab operibus mortuis, et fidei in Deum, baptismatum, doctrinæ, ac manuum impositionis, et resurrectionis mortuorum, & iudicij æterni. Atq; id faciemus, siquidem permiserit Deus.
units.tr: Therefore, leaving aside the teaching that begins the Christian life in the simplest way, let us press on to perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith in God, of baptisms, of doctrine, of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgement. And this we shall do, if God permits.

units.la: Vando satis posuit illis ob oculos tarditatem & segnitiem, addit nunc exhortatione, qua monet, ut omissis initijs doctrinæ Christianæ, in quibus iam diu versati fuerat, ad maiora percipieda enitatur. Nihil est hic obscuritatis, quare breuiter percurremus. Elegāti periphrasi eam doctrinam, quæ initiandis in Christo seu primum instituendis in doctrina Christiana proponitur, uocat sermonem, qui rudes in Christo inchoat, seu, ut græcè habetur τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ λόγον, hoc est, sermonem initij Christi, quasi dicatur, initialem sermonem rerum Christianarum. Adeò, ut si quis prima capita religionis, qualia ipse quoq; hic enumerat, in libellum digereret, inscribere recte posset, hoc pacto: ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀρχῆς τῆς Χριστοῦ: vel, ut supra expressit, τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ λογίου τῆς θεοῦ. Vel, ut mox sequitur, ἐμπέλιον τοῦ λογίου τῆς θεοῦ, id est, fundamentum eloquiorum Dei. Nam hæc tria plane idem sibi volunt. Imò etiam λάλια, id est, lac doctrinæ Christianæ: quandoquidem his omnibus appellationibus ipse hic vtitur. Qui nunc libelli circumferuntur eam doctrinam complectentes, appellantur Catechismi, sumpro nomine ex eo, quòd habetur Galat. 6. Communicet autem qui catechizatur sermone, ei, qui se catechizat, in omnibus bonis: quæ vox κατηχέω etiam habetur apud Lucam.
units.tr: Having already set before them their slowness and sluggishness, he now adds an exhortation, urging them to leave behind the first principles of Christian teaching, in which they had long been occupied, and to strive after greater things. There is nothing obscure here, so we shall run through it briefly. With an elegant periphrasis he calls the teaching that is set before those who are being initiated into Christ, or first instructed in Christian doctrine, "the word that begins the rudiments of Christ", or, as the Greek has it, "ton tes archēs tou Christou logon" [τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ λόγον], that is, the word of the beginning of Christ, as if one said the initial discourse on Christian matters. So that if anyone were to set down the first heads of religion, such as he himself lists here, in a little book, he could rightly entitle it in this way: "ho logos tes archēs tes Christou", or, as he expressed it above, "ta stoicheia tes archēs tou logiou tes theou" [τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ λογίου τῆς θεοῦ]. Or, as he goes on to say, "themelion tou logiou tou theou" [θεμέλιον τοῦ λογίου τοῦ θεοῦ], that is, the foundation of the oracles of God. For these three phrases plainly mean the same thing. Indeed he also uses the word "gala" [γάλα], that is, the milk of Christian teaching, since he employs all these expressions here. The little books now in circulation that contain this teaching are called Catechisms, the name being taken from Galatians 6, "Let him who is taught the word share all good things with him who teaches him" [Gal. 6.], where the word "katechein" [κατηχέω] also occurs, and it is found in Luke as well.

units.la: Hieronymus in libro de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis scribit, Origenè Adamantiū, qui in ecclesia Alexandrina post Clementè docuit, itè Heraclā presbyteros & Catechistas idē munus subiuisse, & opus κατηχήσεων aggressum, cùm antea non nisi viua voce & quasi per manus traderetur, sicut & ipsa vocabuli ratio satis arguit, ἠχέω enim sonare est, sed ad Apostoli sententiam reuertamur.
units.tr: Jerome, in his book on ecclesiastical writers, writes that Origen Adamantius, who taught after Clement in the Alexandrian Church, and likewise Heraclas, presbyters and catechists, undertook this same office and took up the work of catechising, whereas before this it had been handed on only by the living voice and, as it were, from hand to hand, as the very derivation of the word sufficiently shows, for "ēcheō" [ἠχέω] means to sound. But let us return to the Apostle's words.

units.la: Quapropter omissò, in quit, sermone, qui in Christo rudes inchoat.) Omittendum ait sermonem hunc initialem, non quòd prætereundus sit vel negligendus, quasi infrugifer seu minus necessarius: quādoquidem addiscì ab omnibus primo loco debet, & animo semper hærere infixus: sed, quòd iam omittendus, quando grauiora debent addisci.
units.tr: "Therefore, leaving aside," he says, "the word that begins the rudiments of Christ." He says that this initial discourse is to be left aside, not because it is to be passed over or neglected, as if it were unfruitful or less necessary, since it must be learned by all in the first place and always remain fixed in the mind; but because it is to be left behind now, when weightier things must be learned.

units.la: Ordine & per gradus in doctrina progrediendum est, methodus semper seruanda est. Primo loco discenda sunt elementa: inde omissis elemetis itur ad ea, quę proxima sunt, & sic deinceps, donec veluti ad summam classem perueniatur.
units.tr: Teaching must proceed in order and by stages, and method must always be observed. First the elements must be learned; then, the elements having been set aside, one goes on to what comes next, and so on, until one reaches, as it were, the highest class.

units.la: Ad perfectionem feramur) id est, ad ea, quæ perfectos decet, ad solidum cibū & sublimiorē doctrinam. Perfectione cognitionis intelligit, eo modo, quo iam iám dixit perfectos esse, quibus solidus cibus doctrinę competit. In eo, quòd dixit, Feramur, tacitè videtur innuere, nos in profectu spirituali agi potius alicūde, nempe à Deo, quam per nos agere. Quomodo Christus quoq; dixit, neminem venire ad se, nisi pater traxerit eum. Et Roman. 8. Quicunq; spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filij Dei. Et præsenti loco, Siquidem permiserit Deus. Videtur & hoc obseruandum, quod Apostolus in prima persona loquitur, vt nimirum, dum se quoq; illis videtur annumerare, blandiorem affectum spiret oratio, nec non gratiori animo adhortatio hæc ab omnibus accipiatur. Vbi doctor se gerit non tantum vt ducem, sed etiam vt socium & commilitonem, beneuolentiam ea res apud omnes parat.
units.tr: "Let us press on to perfection": that is, to those things which befit the mature, to solid food and a loftier teaching. By perfection he means knowledge, in the sense in which he has just called them mature, for whom solid food of teaching is suitable. In the words "let us press on", he seems tacitly to hint that we are moved forward in spiritual progress from elsewhere, namely by God, rather than doing it ourselves. So Christ also said that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him (John 6). And Romans 8: "Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God." And in this passage, "if God permits." It also seems worth noting that the Apostle speaks in the first person, so that, while he includes himself among them, his speech breathes a more affectionate feeling and this exhortation is received more kindly by all. When a teacher presents himself not merely as a leader but also as a companion and fellow soldier, this wins goodwill from everyone.

units.la: Non rursum fundamentum iacientes pœnitentiæ ab operibus mortuis, & fidei in Deū, baptismatum, doctrinæ, ac manuum impositionis, & resurrectionis mortuorum & iudicij æterni.
units.tr: Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith in God, of baptisms, of doctrine, of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgement.

units.la: Interpretatur clarius, quis ille sit sermo rudes inchoans, quē nunc omitti vult, quemquesupra intellexit nomine elementorum initij eloquiorum Dei, item nomine lactis. Enumerat enim hic præcipua aliquot eius sermonis capita, & quasi summam totius doctrinæ initialis, paucis complectitur. Ac rursus noua similitudine ducta à re ædificatoria, vocat hanc doctrinam initialem, Fundamentum. Quemadmodum enim in ædificio materiali, priusquam parietes vel tectum erigas, opus est ante omnia iacere fundamentum: Ita in ædificio spirituali priusquam sublimior tradatur doctrina, opus est præmittere minutiora quædam, quæ se habent instar fundamenti.
units.tr: He explains more clearly what that initial teaching is, which he now wants to be left aside, and which he previously understood under the name of the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and likewise under the name of milk. For here he lists some of the principal heads of that initial teaching and sums up the whole of the first instruction in a few words. And again, drawing a new comparison from building, he calls this initial teaching a foundation. For just as, in a material building, before you raise walls or a roof, you must above all lay a foundation, so in a spiritual building, before a loftier teaching is delivered, it is necessary to set down certain simpler matters, which serve as the foundation.

units.la: Iterum autem iacerent Hebræi fundamentum, si semper eadem rudimenta religionis repe-
units.tr: Yet the Hebrews would be laying the foundation again if they kept repeating the same rudiments of religion,

units.la: y nis repeterent, nec vnquam ad altiora progressum facerent. Caeterum de aedificio spiri⁠tuali et progressu in eo faciendo, plura habes Ephes.2. item Luc.2. Vbi parabola de iacien⁠te fundamentum supra solidam petram. Item 1.Cor.3. Vt sapiēs architectus fundamentū po⁠sui, alius autem super illud aedificat. Caeterum capita ista, quae se habent veluti fundamen⁠tum in doctrina nostrae religionis, mox fusius ex ordine explicabimus, sicut digna sunt, in quibus plus operae collocetur.
units.tr: and never made progress to higher things. Moreover, you have more about the spiritual building and progress in building it in Ephesians 2, and likewise in Luke 2, where there is the parable of the man laying a foundation upon a solid rock; also in 1 Corinthians 3, "As a wise master builder I have laid the foundation, and another builds upon it." But these heads, which serve as the foundation in the teaching of our religion, we shall shortly explain in order at greater length, as they deserve to receive more labour.

units.la: Atq; id faciemus) Quasi perspectam habens illorum voluntatem & proficiendi desiderium, subijcit veluti illorum nomine magno animo ad perfectionem velle contendere, acde progressu bene sperandum: Sic enim rhetores interdum quasi nomine personarum, ad quas eis sermo est, solent respondere, vel sententiam de re propositā ferre: vt, Non dubi⁠to, quin ista facturi sitis sponte, etiam nulla nostra cohortatione accedente, &c. Ac puto figuram hanc locutionis ad simulationem referri debere, de qua Fabius lib.9. cap.2. Fin⁠git Apostolus, iam paratos esse illos ad progrediendum. Quod si hoc pacto non placet ea verba accipere, habeantur ergo pro verbis Apostoli, suā in docendo, ea, quę perfectionis sunt, operam pollicentis. Sed in hac re non opus est curiosius agere.
units.tr: And this we shall do: as if he had a clear view of their willingness and desire to advance, he adds, as it were in their name, that they are ready with a bold spirit to strive towards perfection, and that good hope may be entertained of their progress. For rhetoricians sometimes respond in this way, as if in the names of the persons to whom they speak, or pronounce an opinion on the matter proposed, as in "I do not doubt that you will do these things of your own accord, even without any exhortation from us," and so on. I think this figure of speech should be referred to simulation, of which Quintilian speaks in Book 9, chapter 2. The Apostle pretends that they are already prepared to go forward. But if it does not please anyone to take the words in this way, let them be regarded as the words of the Apostle, promising his own effort in teaching what pertains to perfection. But in this matter there is no need to be more curious.

units.la: Siquidem permiserit Deus) Opportunē vbi de re ardua, & propemodum (si humanarum vi⁠rium spectetur imbecillitas) desperanda agitur, addit particulam hanc de ope Dei expe⁠standa, perinde ac si vellet significare, tūm maximē expectandum foelicem progressum in doctrina, vbi Deus adspirauerit interea eum pulsandum precibus, & haud dubie pijs conatibus lubenter adfuturum. Quanquam videntur hic etiam obturari ora eorum, qui disputationem de sacerdotio Christi, & similes reijciebant, quod non poterant assequi, quia non erat illis a Deo datum: cùm singulare sit donum Dei in doctrina proficere. Huc pertinent illa Ioan.15. Sine me nihil potestis facere. 2. Corinth.3. Non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis cogitare quicquam tanquam ex nobis ipsis, sed si ad aliquid idonei sumus, id ex Deo est. Philippens.2. Deus est is, qui agit in vobis & vt velitis, & vt efficiatis pro bono animi proposito. Sic Roman.1. & 15. cupit Apostolus volente Deo peruenire ad Romanos, & illos docere. Iacobi 4. Dicere debetis, Si Dominus voluerit, faciemus hoc aut illud. Proinde hanc postremam particulam debemus ad nos pertrahere, atque inde di⁠scere, quod nec nos quoq; serio sperare profectum in sacra doctrina per nostras vires & solertiam debeamus, si Dei non adsit nobis fauor. Hinc videmus multos esse, qui nun⁠quam ad altiora conscendant, quia nimirum Deus illis pleniorem cognitionem non concedit. Singulare itaque Dei donum est, in religione & cognitione sacrarum litera⁠rum proficere: & nemo potest sine praeceptore spiritu Sancto progressum facere. Vnde cognitio & prophetia donum spiritus Sancti in ecclesia appellatur. Ergo si cupimus in sacris studijs proficere, diuinum auxilium omni tempore imploremus, & ante lectionem, conciones, disputationes, spiritus Sancti lumen nobis dari petamus.
units.tr: If God permits: he appropriately adds this particle about waiting for God's help when a difficult matter is being treated, and one that is almost to be despaired of if the weakness of human powers is considered. It is as if he wished to signify that a happy progress in teaching is then especially to be looked for, when God has meanwhile breathed upon it, and that he must be besought with prayers, and that he will undoubtedly and gladly be present with our pious efforts. Although here too the mouths seem to be stopped of those who rejected the discussion of Christ's priesthood and similar matters, because they could not grasp them, since it had not been given them by God, whereas to make progress in teaching is a singular gift of God. To this belong those words of John 15: "Without me you can do nothing." 2 Corinthians 3: "We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but if we are sufficient for anything, it is of God." Philippians 2: "It is God who works in you both to will and to do for his good pleasure." So in Romans 1 and 15 the Apostle desires, God willing, to come to the Romans and teach them. James 4: "You ought to say, If the Lord wills, we shall do this or that." Therefore we ought to draw this last particle to ourselves and learn from it that we too should not seriously hope for progress in sacred teaching through our own powers and skill, if the favour of God is not present with us. Hence we see many who never rise to higher things, because God does not grant them fuller knowledge. Progress in religion and in the knowledge of the sacred letters is therefore a singular gift of God, and no one can make progress without the Holy Spirit as teacher. Hence knowledge and prophecy are called gifts of the Holy Spirit in the Church. So if we desire to advance in sacred studies, let us always implore the divine help, and before reading, sermons and disputations, let us ask that the light of the Holy Spirit be given to us.

units.la: DE CATECHISMO.
units.tr: ON THE CATECHISM.

units.la: Quando quidem praecipua capita, atque adeò breuis summa totius doctrinę Christia⁠nae comprehenditur, visum est plenius apertiusque singula huius enumerationis mem⁠bra, si tamen prius de necessitate & vtilitate Catechismi paucula praefati fuerimus, per⁠currere. Quàm necessaria sit haec doctrina, vel ex eo liquet, quòd Apostolus eam hic vo⁠cat fundamentum. Quemadmodum ad aedificium materiale erigendum ante omniare⁠quiritur fundamentum aliquod, cui reliqua structura innitatur: ita sanè, si quis in spiri⁠tuali aedificio Christi aliquid velit pro sua conditione & propriae animae salute efficere, debet primo loco fundamentum istud Christianae doctrinae tenere. Sed nec est, quod quisquam se salutem post hanc vitam consecuturum speret, nisi qui hęc doctrinae capita didicerit, & ex eis, quo ad vitam aeternam peruenire queat, acceperit. Imò verò nullae actiones humanae rectè instituentur, neq; charitas, neque fides, neque spes exercebitur, nisi prius ex lege, quomodo Deum, quomodo item proximum diligere debeamus: nisi item è symbolo quid credendum, quid non credendum: nisi item ex precatione domi⁠nica & sacramentorum, ex doctrina de resurrectione & extremo iudicio, quid nobis sperandum post hanc vitam sit, perceperimus. Sed hinc iam vtilitas quoque Catechis⁠mi facile potest deprehendi. Quomodo enim non multò vtilissimum censeatur id, quo solo vita rectè instituitur? Quantò homo praestat caeteris animantibus, quia ratio⁠ne est praeditus: tantò etiam homo pius praestat caeteris hominibus, quia imbutus est doctrina catechismi.
units.tr: Since the chief heads, and indeed the brief summary of the whole Christian doctrine, are comprised in this enumeration, it seemed good, after first saying a few things about the necessity and usefulness of the Catechism, to run through each of its members more fully and openly. How necessary this teaching is becomes clear from the fact that the Apostle calls it here a foundation. Just as a material building cannot be erected without some foundation on which the rest of the structure rests, so, if anyone wishes to accomplish anything in Christ's spiritual building, according to his condition and for the salvation of his own soul, he must first hold to this foundation of Christian doctrine. Nor can anyone hope to obtain salvation after this life unless he has learned these heads of doctrine and received from them how he may attain eternal life. Indeed, no human actions will be rightly undertaken, and neither love, faith, nor hope will be exercised, unless we have first learned from the law how we ought to love God and our neighbour; unless we have learned from the creed what is to be believed and what is not; unless we have learned from the Lord's Prayer and the sacraments, and from the doctrine of the resurrection and the last judgment, what we are to hope for after this life. The usefulness of the Catechism can also readily be discerned from this. For how could it not be considered by far the most useful thing, the one thing by which life is rightly ordered? As man excels the other living creatures because he is endowed with reason, so the pious man excels other men because he is steeped in the doctrine of the Catechism.

units.la: Porrò cùm haec docendi ratio, haec methodus doctrinae Christianae diuinitùs fuerit instituta, & ab Apostolis vsurpata, & a patribus deinceps diligenter in ecclesijs observata,
units.tr: Moreover, since this method of teaching, this method of Christian doctrine, was instituted by God and used by the Apostles, and afterwards diligently observed in the churches by the Fathers,

units.la: Catechisticā doctrina funda mētū est cognitionis Dei & religionis. Necessitas & usus doctrinae Catechisticae. Institutio vitae. Diuina institutio Catechismi uata, quandoquidem legimus præstantissimos quos q; è patribus hoc munere tradendi Catechismum functos in ecclesia: merito agendæ sunt Deo patri gratiæ, quòd hæc Catechismi doctrina, quę hactenus aliquot seculis in abdito latuit, ac vix de nomine fuit nota, nostra tempestate sit in lucem revocata; & ad eam methodum, quam ab Apostolo hic attingi cernimus, sit redacta. E diverso autem vix agnosci decet pro ecclesijs, vbi hæc prima religionis nostræ elementa vel obscurata sunt, vel penitùs neglecta iacent.
units.tr: Catechetical doctrine is the foundation of the knowledge of God and of religion. The necessity and use of catechetical doctrine. The training of life. The divine institution of the Catechism. Since we read that the most outstanding men among the Fathers discharged this office of teaching the Catechism in the Church, we rightly owe thanks to God the Father that this doctrine of the Catechism, which for some centuries lay hidden and was scarcely known even by name, has in our own time been brought back into the light and reduced to the method which we see the Apostle touching on here. On the other hand, it hardly becomes churches to be recognised where these first elements of our religion have been obscured or lie wholly neglected.

units.la: Sed iam videamus, quænam sint illa doctrinæ Christianæ capita, & quo ordine sint dispositá.
units.tr: But let us now see what these heads of Christian doctrine are, and in what order they are arranged.

units.la: Primo igitur loco constituit Fundamentum pœnitentiæ ab operibus mortuis: Quid istis sibi vult? Nimirum quòd hoc primo loco illis, qui Christo initiari volebant, proponebatur, vt opera mortua, id est, mortem spiritualem & æternam parantia diligenter contemplarentur: deinde ea toto animo auersarentur, & facta à se se dolerent, hinc autem vitam penitus renouare, id est, aliam & longè sanctiorem instituere meditarentur. Neque enim satis est, dolere admissa crimina, nisi accedat studium emendationis. Sic verò Christus ipse hanc doctrinam instituit Matthæi 4. statim vbi docere inciperet, dicens: Resipiscite, instat enim regnum cœlorum. Et sic faciendum deinceps per Apostolos, & ea doctrina semper auspicandum, præscripsit Christus. Marci 6. Et egressi prædicabant, vt resipiscerent. Luc.24. prædicari in nomine eius pœnitentiam ac remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes iubentur. Petrus item Actorum primo, rogantibus, quid facerent, Delictorum pœnitentiam agite, inquit, & baptizetur vnusquisque vestrum. Actorum 3. Pœniteat vos igitur, & conuertimini, vt deleantur peccata vestra. Actor.11.20. eadem pœnitentia prædicatur. Et Apostolus Paulus passim in suis epistolis pœnitentiam inculcat: vt Rom.2. 2.Corinth.7. Ephes.2. Ergo primus gradus ad salutem est pœnitentia ab operibus mortuis. Sed vnus hic locus de pœnitentia etiam plures alios locos in se comprehendit. Quando enim pœnitentia esse non potest, nisi agnito peccato, agnitio verò peccati contingit per Legem (Roman.7.) Sequitur, ad hunc locum referri debere & legem & peccatum: Ac proinde hic Decalogus primo loco tradendus est in doctrina Christiana, vt ex eo discant pij, quæ sint peccata, quæ item non: & ob quæ dolendum sit, quæ item facienda, quæque omittenda. Hæc enim sine Decalogo intelligi non possunt: quandoquidem Decalogus est magister humanarum actionum erga Deum & erga homines, ac propterea etiam pædagogus ad Christum appellatur. Neq; charitas vera, per quam debent animi quodammodo præparari, aliunde quàm ex Decalogi institutione addiscitur. Vbi enim ex Decalogo noris quæ vitare debeas, eadem opera intelligis, quæ deceat te facere. Proinde primum istud caput de pœnitentia ab operibus mortuis reuera multiplicem doctrinam & varios fructus in se includit.
units.tr: First, then, he sets down the foundation of repentance from dead works. What does this mean? Namely, that this was set before those who wished to be initiated into Christ in the first place, so that they might diligently consider the dead works, that is, those which prepare spiritual and eternal death; then that they should turn away from them with their whole mind and grieve over what they had done; and hence that they should resolve to renew their life entirely, that is, to institute another and far holier one. For it is not enough to grieve over the sins committed unless the zeal for amendment follows. Thus Christ himself instituted this teaching in Matthew 4, immediately when he began to teach, saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. And Christ prescribed that it should be done thus thereafter through the Apostles, and that one should always begin with this teaching. Mark 6: "And going out they preached that men should repent." Luke 24: They are commanded to preach repentance and the remission of sins in his name to all nations. Peter likewise in Acts 2, when they asked what they should do: "Repent of your sins," he said, "and let each of you be baptized." Acts 3: "Repent therefore and turn, that your sins may be blotted out." Acts 11:20: the same repentance is preached. And the Apostle Paul everywhere in his epistles inculcates repentance, as in Romans 2, 2 Corinthians 7, Ephesians 2. Therefore the first step to salvation is repentance from dead works. But this one head on repentance also comprises many other places within itself. For since repentance cannot exist unless sin has been acknowledged, and the acknowledgment of sin comes through the Law (Romans 7), it follows that both the law and sin must be referred to this place. And therefore the Decalogue must be delivered first in Christian doctrine, so that the godly may learn from it what sins are, and what are not, and for what things one ought to grieve, and what things are to be done or omitted. For these cannot be understood without the Decalogue, since the Decalogue is the teacher of human actions towards God and towards men, and for that reason is also called our schoolmaster leading to Christ. Nor is true love, through which minds ought in some measure to be prepared, learned from any source other than the instruction of the Decalogue. For when you know from the Decalogue what you ought to avoid, by the same act you understand what it becomes you to do. Therefore this first head, on repentance from dead works, truly contains within itself a manifold doctrine and various fruits.

units.la: Poenitentia ab operibus mortuis habet hos locos adiúctos Deum & proximum 1. Legem: qua docemur de officijs erga
units.tr: Repentance from dead works has these topics attached to it: 1. the Law, by which we are taught our duties towards God and neighbour;

units.la: 2. Peccatum: Originale & Actuale
units.tr: 2. Sin: original and actual;

units.la: 3. Resipiscentia, cui subsequi tui possunt: Peccati agnitio ac detestatio & Vitæ renouatio in melius.
units.tr: 3. Repentance, which may be followed by: recognition and detestation of sin, and renewal of life for the better;

units.la: 4. Renouationem
units.tr: 4. Renewal.

units.la: Et fidei in Deum) En secundum fundamentum initialis doctrinæ Christianæ. Postea quam homo per legem adductus est ad agnitionem peccati & pœnitentiam, proximum est, vt sciat, quomodo peccatorum remissionem accipiat: post agnitionem sui opus est, incipiat agnoscere Deum. Hæc verò cum fide in Deum accipitur, eòque doctrina fidei in Deum secundum habere locum debet. Et ita Christus instituit, quando post annuntiatam pœnitentiam statim subiecit de peccatorum remissione, de regno cœlorum sicut patet in locis ante citatis. Præterea ex aliis plurimis locis, quibus docetur, accedetem ad Deum debere credere: sine fide impossibile esse, vt quis Deo placeat: per fidem iustificari homines etiam absque operibus Legis: fide purificari corda: Fidei fundamentum requiri, priusquam vera charitas vel vllæ veræ virtutes haberi possint. Porrò cum expri-
units.tr: And faith in God. Here is the second foundation of the initial Christian doctrine. After a person has been brought by the law to the recognition of sin and to repentance, it is next that he should know how he receives forgiveness of sins; after recognising himself, he must begin to recognise God. This is received through faith in God, and therefore the doctrine of faith in God ought to have its place next. And so Christ instituted it, for after proclaiming repentance he immediately added the forgiveness of sins and the kingdom of heaven, as appears in the passages cited above. Besides, from very many other passages, in which it is taught that the one who approaches God must believe; that without faith it is impossible to please God; that men are justified by faith even apart from the works of the Law; that hearts are purified by faith; and that the foundation of faith is required before true love or any true virtues can be had. Moreover, when

units.la: mitur Fides in Deum, sicut reuera in solum Deum, qui solus potest ab omnibus malis seruare, debet fiducia obtinendae misericordiae collocari, aequum est, hoc loco pleniorem de Deo cognitionem adiici, qualis est de Dei vnitate, omnipotentia, bonitate, gratuita misericordia: item de distinctione personarum patris, filij, & Spiritus sancti, quarum personarum officia: quomodo pater nos, & omnia nostri causa creauerit, & disposuerit, vt salui fieremus: quomodo filius humanam naturam assumendo, & semet ipsum in mortem tradendo nos saluos fecerit: quomodo spiritus Sanctus nos omnes sanctificet, gubernet, seruet, in salute per Christum accepta. Et propter hanc causam summarium illud fidei, quod Symbolum apostolicum vocant, secundo loco in ecclesijs traditur.
units.tr: faith in God is expressed, since truly it must be placed in God alone, who alone can preserve from all evils, the trust for obtaining mercy ought to be fixed there. It is fitting, therefore, that a fuller knowledge of God be added at this point, such as concerning the unity of God, his omnipotence, goodness and free mercy; likewise concerning the distinction of the persons of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and their offices: how the Father created us and all things for our sake and ordained that we should be saved; how the Son, by assuming human nature and delivering himself to death, saved us; how the Holy Spirit sanctifies, governs and preserves us all in the salvation received through Christ. And for this reason that summary of faith which they call the Apostles' Creed is delivered second in the churches.

units.la: Baptismatum) En tertium fundamentum. Postquam aliquis adductus est ad poenitentiam vitae antea actae, & propositum corrigendi vitam in melius: postquam item didicit ad Deum fide confugere, & misericordiam implorare, proximum est baptizetur, atque externa baptismi nota poenitentiam & fidem suam in Deum testatam faciat, accipiatque vicissim a Deo peccatorum suorum remissionem. Sic vero Christus instituit, vt ad salutem in primis necessarium. Ioan. 3. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Item caeteris locis, quibus post resurrectionem praecepit discipulis, vt irent in mundum vniuersum, & praedicarent Euangelium omni creaturae, qui crediderint & baptizati fuerint, saluos fore: qui vero non crediderint, condemnandos. Matthaei capite vigesimo octauo, Marci decimosexto, Et Apostoli etiam, vt liquet in actis, statim post poenitentiam & fidem baptismum suscipere docuerunt, & petentibus contulerunt.
units.tr: Baptism. Here is the third foundation. After someone has been brought to repentance for his former life and to the resolve to correct his life for the better; after he has likewise learned to flee to God by faith and to implore mercy, it is next that he should be baptized and, by the outward mark of baptism, bear witness to his repentance and his faith in God, and in turn receive from God the forgiveness of his sins. Christ instituted this as necessary above all for salvation: John 3: "Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." Likewise in other passages, in which after the resurrection he commanded his disciples to go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature: whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned (Matthew 28, Mark 16). And the Apostles too, as is clear in the Acts, taught that baptism should be received immediately after repentance and faith, and conferred it on those who asked.

units.la: Caeterum est hic animaduertendum, quod nonnulli has voces, βαπτισμῶν, διδαχῆς, separant, ac duo diuersa capita faciunt: plerique coniungunt, quemadmodum videre est in scholis graecanicis. Qui coniunctim legunt, sic construunt, vt in genere intelligant, omnem eam doctrinam, quae baptizandis proponi solet, velut cum eis exponitur, quid sibi velit baptismus: quid significet, nos mori cum Christo, & sepeliri, iterumque viuificari: quid item ibi promittamus: qui eius effectus: quantaque bona a Deo per illud accipiamus. Hanc doctrinam vniuersam, doctrinam baptismatum intelligunt. Quidam vero sic coniungunt vocem doctrinae, ad singula deinceps membra iudicent pertinere, & in singulis repetendam, hoc sensu, vt dicatur, doctrinam baptismatum tertium locum habere: quartum vero doctrinam impositionem manuum: quintum doctrinam resurrectionis, &c. Nos vero malumus separatim legere, atque ita quidem, vt pro nouo capite elementorum religionis habeatur, & sic quoque mox seorsim exponemus. Ergo tantum de baptismo, qui sequitur poenitentiam & fidem, particulam hanc accipiamus. Sed hic difficultas nascitur non parua, ex eo, quod Apostolus expresserit plurali numero, βαπτισμῶν, cum tamen vnum tantum sit nobis baptisma, & semel duntaxat conferri possit. Ephesiorum capite quarto, Vnus Deus, vna fides, vnum baptisma.
units.tr: Meanwhile, it should be noted here that some separate the words "of baptisms" [βαπτισμῶν] and "of teaching" [διδαχῆς] and make them two different items, while most join them together, as can be seen in the Greek schools. Those who read them together construe them so that they understand by the whole phrase all the teaching that is usually set before those to be baptized, for example when they are told what baptism means, namely that we die with Christ, are buried, and rise again to life; what we promise there; what its effects are; and how great the blessings are that we receive from God through it. They take this whole teaching to be "the teaching of baptisms." Others join the word "teaching" so that it applies to each of the following members and is repeated for each, in such a way that the teaching about baptisms holds the third place, the teaching about the laying on of hands the fourth, the teaching about the resurrection the fifth, and so on. We, however, prefer to read the words separately, so that they are taken as a new head of the elements of religion, and we shall expound them separately straight away. So let us take this phrase as referring only to baptism, which follows repentance and faith. But here a considerable difficulty arises, because the Apostle has written "baptisms" [βαπτισμῶν] in the plural, although for us there is only one baptism, and it can be conferred only once. Ephesians 4: "One God, one faith, one baptism."

units.la: Chrysostomus ait, plurali numero sic locutum Apostolum, veluti quodam contemptu atque Ironia, quasi exprobraret illis tarditatem, qua semper inhaerebant primus istis elementis, ac iam uidebantur denuo instituendi in baptismo, & quodammodo itera baptizandi: quod si fieret, plane perditi essent & incorrigibiles, deque eorum salute penitus foret desperandum: si semper haerarent in elementis, id perinde absurdum & indignum, ac si saepius baptizarentur. Sicque dum illis exprobrate vult tantam ruditatem, qua videntur egere, vt denuo baptizentur, plurali numero baptismata expressit. Haec mihi videtur Chrysostomi sententia.
units.tr: Chrysostom says that the Apostle spoke in the plural with a certain contempt and irony, as if he were rebuking them for the slowness by which they kept clinging to these elementary things, so that they seemed to need to be instructed afresh in baptism and, in a way, to be baptized again. If that happened, they would be altogether lost and incorrigible, and their salvation would have to be utterly despaired of; if they kept clinging to the elements, that would be just as absurd and unworthy as if they were baptized over and over. Thus, while he wishes to reproach them for such great crudeness, which made it seem they needed to be baptized again, he expressed it in the plural, "baptisms." This seems to me to be Chrysostom's view.

units.la: Alij, inter quos Theophylactus, numero plurali loqui Apostolum putant, propterba ptismatu varias species, quas Hebrei suo quoda more obseruabat: quales partim ex lege habebant, in qua frequentes praecipiuntur lotiones, partim ex traditionibus Seniorum, de quibus Marci capite septimo, & capite nono huius epistolae. Sed cum has lotiones Apostoli neq; obseruarint, neque approbarint, quam conueniat ista interpretatio, alijs relinquamus iudicandum.
units.tr: Others, among whom is Theophylact, think the Apostle speaks in the plural because of the various kinds of washings which the Hebrews observed in a certain manner of their own; some of these they had from the law, in which frequent washings are commanded, and some from the traditions of the elders, of which we read in Mark 7 and in chapter 9 of this letter. But since the Apostle neither observed these washings nor approved of them, let others judge how well this interpretation fits.

units.la: Primasius dixit, baptismata plurali numero efferri, pro varietate accipientium.
units.tr: Primasius said that "baptisms" is put in the plural in view of the variety of those who receive it.

units.la: Oecolampadius fieri potest, inquit, vt pluraliter dixerit baptismi, eo, quod tertio intingi solebant pueri. Quis nouit, an id tum obseruatum fuerit in ecclesia?
units.tr: Oecolampadius says: "It may be that he spoke of baptisms in the plural because children were then customarily dipped three times." Who knows whether this was observed in the Church at that time?

units.la: Alij propter triplicem baptismi speciem putant, quia videlicet distinguitur, baptismus fluminis, baptismus flaminis, baptismus sanguinis: e quibus duae posteriores species valent, cum non adest facultas vtendi prima specie, quam certe semper decet habere in votis. Dicuntur autem diuersa baptismata, sed quantum ad effectum, vnum baptisma. Baptismo sanguinis abluebantur innocentes, martyres, pueri. Flaminis, patres, & omnes recte vtentes, atque adeo reipsa percipientes. Fluminis, omnes qui exterius baptismum suscipiunt. Nec valet hic, (loquendo de effectu) nisi etiam spiritus Sanctus accipiatur: propterea Christus ait, Ex aqua & spiritu Sancto. Ioannis capite tertio.
units.tr: Others, on account of a threefold kind of baptism, think that the plural is used because a distinction is made between baptism of water, baptism of the Spirit, and baptism of blood. Of these, the latter two have force when there is no opportunity of using the first kind, which one should certainly always desire. They are called different baptisms, but as far as their effect goes, there is one baptism. By baptism of blood innocents, martyrs and children are washed; by baptism of the Spirit, the fathers and all who use it rightly, and so in fact receive it; by baptism of water, all who receive the outward baptism. Here it has no force, speaking of the effect, unless the Holy Spirit is also received; therefore Christ says: "Unless one is born of water and the Holy Spirit," John 3. Ex aqua & spiritu Sancto.

units.la: Aliqui baptismata hic accipiunt in genere pro quibuscunque purgationum seu purificationum generibus. Cum enim βαπτίζω idem sit, quod mergo & tingo, & ea, quae mundare volumus seu purgare, solemus lauare ac tingere, hic per Metalepsin baptismus pro emundatione & purgatione accipitur, vt sit sententia: doceri rudes de purgationum generibus, quod videlicet sanguine Christi abundè simus purgati, eaque vna purgatione semel impositus finis omnibus aliis purgationibus. Quid autem, si dicamus, baptismata plurali numero posita pro Sacramentis inter quę cum primum & excellentissimum fit baptisma, huius nomen positum sit plurali numero, ad significandum per Metonymiam, (qua vicinum nomen pro vicino sumitur, vt signum pro significato, sicut fractio panis pro vsu vtriusque speciei accipitur) omnia eodem pertinentia, & eidem cognata: hoc est, & ad significandum baptisma ipsum, & praeterea sacram coenam Domini. Et cum, qui baptizatur, eo ipso idoneus fit ad coenam Domini: imo olim solebat haec simul cum baptismo conferri: non videtur adeo ineptum esse, si coenam Domini quasi alterum baptismum statuamus, cum vtroque mors Domini annuncietur, pariq; significentur, effectus itidem pares accipiantur, pari modo per ea homines purificentur.
units.tr: Some take "baptisms" here in general for whatever kinds of cleansing or purification there are. For since βαπτίζω means the same as to immerse and to dip, and we are accustomed to wash and dip those things which we want to make clean or purge, here by metalepsis "baptism" is taken for cleansing and purging, so that the sense is: the untaught are instructed about the kinds of purification, namely that we have been abundantly purged by the blood of Christ, and that by this one purification, once applied, an end is put to all other purifications. But what if we say that "baptisms," put in the plural, stands for the sacraments, among which baptism is the first and most excellent, and its name is put in the plural to signify by metonymy (by which a neighbouring name is taken for a neighbouring thing, as a sign for what is signified, just as the breaking of bread is taken for the use of both kinds) all the things that pertain to the same thing and are akin to it; that is, to signify baptism itself and, besides, the Lord's Supper? And since the one who is baptized is by that very fact fit for the Lord's Supper, and indeed once it was customary to confer these together with baptism, it does not seem so absurd to regard the Lord's Supper as, as it were, a second baptism, since by both the death of the Lord is proclaimed and signified in the same way, and equal effects are received, and in the same way men are purified by them.

units.la: Ad hunc ergo tertium locum pertinebit tractatio Sacramentorum, quae initiandis tradi debet: & hic docendi sunt rudes de baptismo & coena Domini: Sicut etiam nunc fieri in ecclesijs nostratibus videmus, & a veteribus factum certo scimus. Et Christus eadem ratione praecepit vsum coenae dominicae, qua baptismi. Ioannis capite sexto, Nisi ederitis carnem filij hominis, & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habetis vitam in vobis. Item Matthaei capite vigesimosexto, Marci capite decimoquarto. Lucae vigesimosecundo. Prima Corinthiorum vndecimo. Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Et propter hanc causam recte in Catechismo doctrinae fidei subijcitur doctrina Sacramentorum, quae pro quodam testimonio & exercitio fidei sunt propositá.
units.tr: To this third place, then, belongs the treatment of the sacraments, which must be handed on to those being initiated, and here the untaught are to be instructed about baptism and the Lord's Supper, as we also see being done now in our churches, and as we know for certain was done by the ancients. Christ also commanded the use of the Lord's Supper for the same reason as baptism. John 6: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you." Likewise Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22, 1 Corinthians 11: "Do this in remembrance of me." And for this reason it is rightly placed in the catechism of the teaching of the faith, the doctrine of the sacraments, which have been set forth as a kind of witness and exercise of faith.

units.la: Doctrinæ) Quartum fundamentum, est doctrina, quam conseruari & propagari, & fideliter proponi Deus semper vult, in qua Apostoli omnes labores expendunt. Huc pertinet quod postea dicit, gustauerunt que bonum Dei verbum. Oportet vero baptizatum & sacramentorum participem iam plenius erudiri, & scire, quae sint religionis ipsius propria, quibus rebus ab aliorum religione distinguatur: quae item eum, qui sacramentis initiatus est, facere deceat.
units.tr: Teaching) The fourth foundation is the doctrine which God always wills to be preserved, propagated and faithfully set forth, and on which all the labours of the Apostles are spent. To this belongs what he says afterwards: "they have tasted the good word of God." gustauerunt que bonum Dei verbum. But the one who has been baptized and has shared in the sacraments must be instructed more fully and know what is proper to this religion itself, by which things it is distinguished from the religion of others, and what it befits one who has been initiated by the sacraments to do.

units.la: Ad hunc ergo locum pertinet inprimis sacra Scriptura eiusque autoritas, discrimen euangelij a lege, illiusque excellentia, (sicut in hac disputatione docet Apostolus, & in Corinthijs & Romanis) discrimen Pharisaicae doctrinae a doctrina Dei, Matthaei capite decimosexto, & praeterea alia, quae ad res maiores percipiedas praeparat. Oportet enim baptizatum esse semper discendi auidum, eniti que, vt in melius proficiat, gradumque in cognitione religionis faciat, donec etiam, si fieri queat, ipse alios docere possit. Item huc referri poterit doctrina de oratione, de officijs charitatis erga magistratus, dotores, &c. Item de eleemosyna, de ieiunio, & similibus exercitijs, de vocatione, de contemptu rerum terrenarum, de constantia in aduersis, de cruce ferenda, de quibus rudes erunt diligenter informandi. Et sunt haec prima capita religionis omnibus statim inculcanda. Hinc illa a Christo dicta, Euntes in universum mundum docete omnes gentes. Item omnes praeceptiones & exhortationes in apostolicis literis, quae iubent doceri homines, & in sana doctrina confirmari, maximè ad Titum & Timotheum, quos Apostolus, quomodo docere debeant, & quae doctrina omnibus sit necessaria, instituit.
units.tr: To this place belongs first of all Holy Scripture and its authority; the difference between the gospel and the law, and the excellence of the gospel (as the Apostle teaches in this disputation, and in the letters to the Corinthians and Romans); the difference between Pharisaic doctrine and the doctrine of God, Matthew 16; and besides, other things which prepare one to grasp greater matters. For the one who has been baptized must always be eager to learn, and must strive to advance for the better and to make progress in the knowledge of religion, until, if it can be managed, he himself can teach others. Also to be referred here will be the doctrine of prayer, of the duties of charity towards the magistrates, teachers, and so on; also concerning almsgiving, fasting and similar exercises, concerning calling, contempt of earthly things, constancy in adversity, bearing the cross; on these the untaught must be carefully instructed. These are the first heads of religion, to be impressed on everyone at once. Hence those words spoken by Christ: Euntes in universum mundum docete omnes gentes. Likewise all the precepts and exhortations in the apostolic letters, which command that men be taught and confirmed in sound doctrine, especially those addressed to Titus and Timothy, in which the Apostle instructs them how they ought to teach and what doctrine is necessary for all.

units.la: Impositionis manuum, ἀπὸστασις τε χειρῶν) Quintum fundamentum doctrinae Christianae. Vbi praedicta acceperit tyro Christianus, iam docendus est de ordinatione ecclesiastica eiusque autoritate & potestate. Neque enim de ea impositione manuum sermo est, qua edebantur miracula, de qua Christus ait Marci decimosexto, Super aegros manus impo-nent, & bene habebunt. Et Lucae capite quarto. Sed de impositione manuum, quae fiebat & in confirmatione eorum, qui iam erant baptizati, & recte instituti, vt acciperent spiritum Sanctum, & praeterea in ordinatione publicorum ministrorum verbi. De vtraq; apparet sermonem fieri: quamuis, quia prior magis pro tempore instituta erat, quando conueniebat visibili signo spiritum Sanctum conferri credentibus, de posteriore plura sunt dicenda. De priore Actorum capite octauo, Petrus & Ioannes orauerunt pro credentibus in Samaria, vt acciperent spiritum Sanctum. Nondum enim in quenquam illorum lapsus fuerat, sed baptizati erant tantum in nomine Christi Iesu. Tunc imponebant manus super illos, & accipiebant spiritum Sanctum. Simile habetur Actorum capite decimonono. De posteriore est illud prima Timothei quarto, Ne neglexeris, quod in te est donum, quod datum est tibi per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum, autoritate sacerdotij, id est, seniorum. 2. Timothei 1. Commonefacio te, vt suscites donum Dei, quod est in te per impositionem manuum mearum.
units.tr: Laying on of hands, [ἀπὸστασις τε χειρῶν]) The fifth foundation of Christian doctrine. When the novice in Christianity has received the things mentioned, he must now be taught about ecclesiastical ordination and its authority and power. For this is not a discussion of that laying on of hands by which miracles were wrought, of which Christ says in Mark 16: Super aegros manus impo-nent, & bene habebunt. and in Luke 4. But it concerns the laying on of hands which was used both in the confirmation of those who had already been baptized and rightly instructed, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, and also in the ordination of public ministers of the Word. It is clear that both are spoken of; although, because the former was instituted earlier, when it was fitting for the Holy Spirit to be conferred on believers by a visible sign, more is to be said about the latter.
