Perhaps, by deriving it not so far, he would have said more forcefully to renew in repentance, that is, in baptism, which is the sacrament of repentance, taking εἰς simply for ἐν. But this is of no importance.

units.la: Ab integro crucifigentes sibimetipsis filium Dei, & ludibrio exponentes) Duplici de causa potius dicit, crucifigentes filium Dei, quàm conculcantes, sicut capite decimo, vel simile quiddam. Prior est, ut ita clarius exprimat atrocitatem criminis eorum, qui post lapsum denuò volunt renouari in pœnitentia. Simili modo, ad denotandum graue crimen dicit Petrus, Actor 2. Hunc definito consilio & præscientia Dei traditum, cùm accepistis per manus iniquorum, crucifixum interemistis. Et paulò post: Quem vos crucifixistis. Similiter Actorum 4. atrocitatem criminis illis obijcit, vt ad pœnitentiam adducat. Altera est, quòd in baptismo Christi crucifixio & mors repræsentatur, adeò, vt denuò velle baptizari videatur perinde esse, atque velle ostendere Christum bis mori, quod impossibile est.
units.tr: Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God, and exposing him to mockery. He says "crucifying the Son of God" rather than "trampling underfoot", as in chapter 10, or something similar, for two reasons. The first is so that he may express more clearly the atrocity of the crime of those who after their fall wish to be renewed again through repentance. In the same way, to denote a grave crime, Peter says in Acts 2: "Him, delivered up by the set purpose and foreknowledge of God, you took and by the hands of wicked men you crucified and killed." And a little later: "whom you crucified." Likewise in Acts 4 he charges them with the atrocity of their crime, in order to lead them to repentance. The second is that in the baptism of Christ his crucifixion and death are represented, so that to wish to be baptized again seems to be the same as wishing to show that Christ dies twice, which is impossible.

units.la: Roman. 6. Quicunque baptizati sumus in Christum Iesum, in mortem eius baptizati sumus. Sepulti sumus igitur vna cum illo per baptismum in mortem. Iterum, Insitiij facti sumus illi per similitudinem mortis eius. Et, vetus ille noster homo cū illo crucifixus est, ut aboleretur corpus peccati. Sequitur paulò post: Christus excitatus à mortuis non amplius moritur, mors illi non amplius dominatur, &c. Item Colos. 2. Per quem & circumcisi estis circumcisione, quæ fit sine manibus, dum exuistis corpus peccatorum carnis per circumcisionem Christi, consepulti simul cum illo per baptismum, &c. Itaque crucifigere dicit eos, qui denuò ad baptismum redire volunt, simul vt exaggeret genus criminis, quod æquat peccato illorum, qui Christum crucifixerunt. Nec caret emphasi, quod ait, sibimetipsis: In suam enim perniciem & excidium eos id facere significat. Chrysostomus, Bene dixit, Sibimetipsis: Qui enim hoc facit veluti prioris gratiæ oblitus, & negligenter suam vitam disponens, tanquam si sit secundum baptisma, sic omnia gerit: idcirco animaduertere opus est & cautelam adhibere.
units.tr: Romans 6: "As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death." Again: "We have become united with him by the likeness of his death." And: "our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed." It follows a little later: "Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him," etc. Likewise Colossians 2: "In whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, when you put off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ, buried together with him in baptism," etc. So he says that those who wish to return again to baptism crucify the Son of God, both to exaggerate the kind of crime, which equals the sin of those who crucified Christ. Nor is the emphasis lacking in the words "to themselves": for he means that they do this to their own ruin and destruction. Chrysostom: "He rightly said 'to themselves'. For he who does this, as if forgetful of the earlier grace and carelessly arranging his life, acts in all things as if he had a second baptism; therefore it is necessary to take heed and apply caution."

units.la: Filium Dei) Non quòd natura diuina pati possit, aut premi, aut mori: sed secundum humanam naturam Christus crucifixus est & mortuus. Igitur reuocanda est in memoriam regula de communicatione idiomatum, quam suprà capite primo expositimus, secundum quam huiusmodi propositiones intelligendæ sunt: Maria est mater Dei: Christus Deus seu filius Dei crucifixus est. Quæ forma locutionis etiam habetur 1. Corinth. 2. Si cognouissent, haud quaquam dominum gloriæ crucifixissent.
units.tr: The Son of God) Not that the divine nature can suffer, be oppressed or die; but Christ was crucified and died according to his human nature. Therefore the rule about the communication of properties, which we set out above in the first chapter, must be called back to mind, and according to it propositions of this kind are to be understood: "Mary is the mother of God," "Christ, God or the Son of God, was crucified." This form of speech also occurs in 1 Corinthians 2: "If they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory."

units.la: Et ludibrio exponentes) Circumlocutus est interpres, quod vna voce haud poterat exprimi. Græca enim vox παραδειγματιζοντας, perinde est, quasi exemplificantes & exemplo proponentes. Videtur proprie dici de reis, qui ad infamiā & in exemplum proponuntur publicè spectaculo: vnde interpres noster Matth. 1. vertit eam vocem per infamare: ficenim ibi habetur, Iosephi maritus eius quoniam erat iustus, & nolebat illam infamare (græce est, ... ) voluit clanculum ab ea diuertere. Proinde valde idonea est hæc vox ad exprimendum summam contumeliam Christo illatam.
units.tr: And exposing to mockery) The translator has used a circumlocution, because one word could not express it. The Greek word παραδειγματιζοντας [paradeigmatizontas] amounts to "making an example of" or "putting forward as an example." It seems properly to be said of criminals who are publicly displayed for infamy and as an example. So our translator, in Matthew 1, renders the word by "to expose to infamy," for there it reads: "Joseph her husband, since he was a just man and did not wish to expose her to infamy [Greek: deigmatisai]" (the Greek is ...), "he resolved to put her away secretly." Therefore this word is very apt for expressing the great contumely heaped upon Christ.

units.la: Cæterum, quia duobus potissimum modis expósita sunt hæc à nobis, videlicet denò repetendo baptismo, itemq; de peccato in spiritum Sanctum, poscere videtur occasio, vt & de non repetendo baptismo, & præterea de peccato in spiritum Sanctum nonnulla dicamus. Ac de non rebaptizando quidem cogimur ipsa temporum nostrorum necessitate vrgente, copiosius differere, ut studiosis velut in compendium contraham, quæ ab aliis fusius ea de re sunt pertractata, nostra nonnulla adijciemus. Dabimus tamen operam, vt ad captum omnium ea attemperemus, & quiuis posit, si quando opus erit, eadem de re agere. Huc refer ex volumine nostro maiore, in quo, quæcunque huc necessaria sunt, congesimus in vnum locum. In eodem volumine de peccato in spiritum Sanctum quædam præsenti loco conuenientia annotauimus.
units.tr: But since these matters have been explained by us mainly in two ways, namely by the repetition of baptism and by the sin against the Holy Spirit, the occasion seems to call for us to say something both about not rebaptizing and, in addition, about the sin against the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the very pressing necessity of our own times compels us to discuss at greater length the matter of not rebaptizing; to lay before students, as it were in summary, what others have treated more fully on this subject, and to add some points of our own. Yet we shall take care to adapt these things to the understanding of all, so that anyone may, if ever the need arises, treat the same matter. For this, refer to our larger volume, in which we have gathered together in one place everything necessary here. In that same volume we have noted some things about the sin against the Holy Spirit that fit the present passage.

units.la: Siquidem terra, quæ imbrem sæpius in se veniente combiberit, & progenuerit herbam accommodam eis, opera quorum & colitur, recipit benedictionem à Deo: at quæ produxerit spinas & tribulos, reproba est, & maledictioni confinis, cuius exitus huc tendit, vt exuratur.
units.tr: For the earth which has drunk in the rain that often falls upon it, and brings forth herbs fit for those by whom it is tilled, receives blessing from God; but that which bears thorns and briers is rejected and is near to a curse, whose end is to be burned.

units.la: Probatio seu confirmatio rationis præcedentis, à simili sumpto, à re rustica: in quo eleganter proponit benedictionem Dei, ac præmia, si vlterius in doctrina religionis progrediantur: rursusque per antithesin comminatur iram Dei ac pœnas, si proficere detrectent: ita vt hic graues rationes suasoriæ, ab vtili videlicet ac damnoso, comprehensę sint. Estque sententia: Ideò debetis, posteaquàm iam diu fœliciter iecistis fundamenta religionis, & illuminati estis, &c. progredi & nequaquà prolabi seu retrocedere: quia, sicut terra, quæ imbrem sæpius venientem combiberit, & progenuerit herbam accommodam eis, quorum opera colitur, recipit benedictionem à Deo: at quæ produxerit spinas & tribulos, reproba est, & maledictioni confinis, atque igne exurenda: ita homines, qui quando iam diu ac multum audiuerunt sanam doctrinam, proficiunt semper, præbent· quę que profectus sui specimen ad Dei gloriam, & utilitatem proximorum, accipiunt benedictionem Dei, atq; amplioribus donis ornantur ac illustrantur: e diverso autem qui non proficiunt, sed potius dediscunt, gloria Dei & utilitatem proximi impedientes, non promouetes, tales Deus æternis supplicijs ignis æterni deuouebit. Similitudo bene constat & perspicua est, si terræ comparemus corda hominum, quibus quasi agris & sulcis verbum Dei inseritur: si per imbrem intelligamus cœlestem doctrinam: si per herbam accommodam intelligamus sanæ doctrinæ fructus, nempe assiduum profectum in illustrando gloriam Dei & promouendo utilitatem proximi: si per cultores agrorum intelligamus doctores, qui tu demum interpretantur, se magnum fructu laborum suorum pcipere, quando per auditores cernunt gloriam Dei augeri, fidem & charitatem exerceri: si per benedictionem intelligimus inprimis bona spiritualia, deinde etiam externa & temporalia, quibus Deus pios, & fructum in pietate facientes ornat. Deinde si in altera parte similitudinis per spinas & tribulos intelligamus diuersum a profectu, nempe impedimenta illustrandæ gloriæ Dei & iuuandi proximi: per maledictionem denique seueritatem iudicij Dei, & pœnas æternas. Nec difficile est, hanc collationem rectè esse institutam, è Scripturis probare. Videtur namq; hanc similitudinem deprompsisse fere ex eo, quod habetur Esaiæ 55. Quomodo descendit imber & nix de cœlo, & illuc ultrà non reuertitur, sed inebriat terram & infundit eam, & germinare eam facit, & dat semen serenti, & panem comedenti: sic erit verbum meum, quod egredietur de ore meo. Non reuertetur ad me uacuum, sed faciet, quæcunque volui, & prosperabitur in his, ad quæ misi illud. Quæ ibi dicuntur à propheta ad declarandum, quomodo Dominus per verbum suum, præsertim per euangelium, velit omnes reducere ad salutem, & quomodo necessario, quæ Dominus semel uerbo suo decreuerit, debeant adimpleri. Item huc referenda est parabola Christi, quam legimus Matth. 13. Luc. 8. de seminante, & seminis alia parte cadente in terram bonam, alia in spinas, alia cadente in saxosa.
units.tr: This is the proof or confirmation of the preceding argument, drawn from a similar case taken from farming, in which he elegantly sets forth the blessing of God and the rewards if they advance further in the doctrine of religion; and conversely, by way of contrast, he threatens the wrath of God and punishments if they refuse to make progress. Thus the grave reasons of persuasion are included here, namely from what is useful and from what is harmful. The sense is this: Therefore you ought, since you have now for a long time happily laid the foundations of religion and have been enlightened, etc., to go forward and by no means slip or fall back. For just as the earth which has drunk in the rain that often comes upon it, and brings forth herbs fit for those by whom it is tilled, receives blessing from God, but that which bears thorns and briers is rejected, near to a curse, and to be burned with fire; so men who, having heard sound doctrine for a long time and in abundance, always make progress and show the evidence of their advance for the glory of God and the profit of their neighbours, receive God's blessing and are adorned and illustrated with greater gifts. On the other hand, those who do not make progress but rather unlearn, hindering the glory of God and the profit of their neighbour, not advancing, God will doom such people to eternal punishments of the eternal fire. The likeness is well founded and clear if we compare the hearts of men to the earth, in which the word of God is sown as into fields and furrows; if by rain we understand heavenly doctrine; if by fit herbs we understand the fruits of sound doctrine, namely continual progress in illustrating the glory of God and promoting the profit of our neighbour; if by the tillers of the fields we understand teachers, who, as the interpreters say, perceive a great fruit of their labours when through their hearers they see the glory of God increased and faith and love exercised; if by blessing we understand first of all spiritual goods, and then also external and temporal goods, with which God adorns the godly and those who bear fruit in piety. Then, in the other part of the likeness, if by thorns and briers we understand what is contrary to progress, namely the hindrances to illustrating the glory of God and helping our neighbour; and finally by curse, the severity of God's judgement and eternal punishments. Nor is it difficult to prove from the Scriptures that this comparison is rightly made. For he seems to have drawn this likeness mainly from what is found in Isaiah 55: "As the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there, but water the earth and make it bring forth and bud, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be, which goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish what I please, and it shall prosper in the things for which I sent it." These things are said there by the prophet to declare how the Lord, through his word, especially the gospel, wishes to bring all to salvation, and how necessarily those things which the Lord has once decreed by his word must be fulfilled. Likewise, the parable of Christ that we read in Matthew 13 and Luke 8 about the sower, and of the seed, part of which fell on good ground, part among thorns, and part on rocky places, belongs here.

units.la: Exquibus duobus locis verosimile est, Apostolum præsentis similitudinis arripuisse materiam, cùm res & uerba pleraque cum præsenti similitudine magna ex parte conueniant. Nos proinde per singula membra eundo, & partes cum his alijsq; Scripturę lo cis conferendo, similitudinis elegantiam aptitudinemque explicabimus.
units.tr: From these two passages it is likely that the Apostle took the material of the present likeness, since for the most part the things and the words agree closely with the present comparison. We shall therefore go through the individual parts and explain the elegance and fitness of the likeness, comparing them with other passages of Scripture.

units.la: Siquidem terra, quæ imbrem sæpius uenientem combiberit) Terra recte significat nobis hominem, seu potius cor atq; animā hominis. Id autem non solùm, quia ad hominem dictū est Gen. 1. Terra es, & in terram conuerteris, verumetiam quia, sicut terra se habet ad suscipiendū semen, quod in eam iacitur: ita se habet per omnia cor hominis ad suscipiendum verbum Dei, quod per docto res pala proponitur: sicut Dominus ipse interpretatur in parabola Matth. 13. & Luc. 8. Nam apud Lucam sic clarè dicit: Quod autem in bonam terram, hi sunt, qui in corde honesto ac bono audientes sermonem retinent, & fructum afferunt per patientiam. Item psalm. 142. Cor hominis terræ comparatur: Expandi manus meas ad te, anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi.
units.tr: For the earth which has drunk in the rain that often comes upon it) The earth rightly signifies to us man, or rather the heart and soul of man. This is so not only because it was said to man in Genesis 1, "You are earth, and you shall return to the earth," but also because, just as the earth stands in relation to receiving the seed cast into it, so the heart of man stands in every way in relation to receiving the word of God, which is set forth by the teacher, as the Lord himself explains in the parable of Matthew 13 and Luke 8. For in Luke he says plainly: "But that which fell on good ground: these are they who, hearing the word in an honest and good heart, keep it and bear fruit with patience." Likewise Psalm 143: "The heart of man is compared to the earth: I stretch out my hands to you; my soul is like a land without water for you."

units.la: Imber vitros) quæ vox etiam habetur Esaiæ 55. loco supra citato: alibi quoque sacræ doctrinæ comparatur. Sic enim Esaiæ 5. vbi uaticinatur de deferenda synagoga: Ostendam vobis, quid faciam vineæ meæ: Auferam sepem eius, & erit in direptionem, diruam maceriam eius, & erit in conculcationem, & ponam eam desertam: non putabitur, & non fodietur, & ascendent super eam vepres & spinæ, & nubibus mandabo, ne pluat super eam imbrem. Vbi Dominus per prophetā cōminatur illis, quòd spoliabit eos imbre sanę doctrinę: & apostolos seu doctores (qui Esaiæ 60. cōparantur nubibus volantibus: Qui funtisti, qui ut nubes volant & quasi colubæ, & c) sit ablaturus. Idē propheta cap. 55. doctrinam comparat aquis: Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas, & qui non habetis argentū, properate, emite, & comedite. Et psalm. 64. Visitasti terram, & inebriasti eam, multiplicasti locupletare eam: flumen Dei repletum est aquis, &c. Sed clarissimè imber sacræ doctrinæ comparatur Ioelis 2. Filiæ Zion exultate, & lætamini in Domino Deo vestro, quia dedit vobis doctorem iustitiæ, & descendere faciet ad vos imbrem matutinum & serotinum, sicut in principio. Notandum autem, tunc imbrem proprie vocari, quando molliores & minores cadunt guttæ: sicut pluuiam, cùm ruunt maiores: nimbum siveλαι̃λαι̃ρ, cū multa densitate atq; impetu. Vnde liquet, voce imbris rectius cōuenire iisti tuto, quàm aliam quamcunque. Cæterum non sine causa dicit, Sæpius in se uenientem combiberit: Ea enim particula nonnihil exaggeratHebræorum crimen. Significat quippe, multò creberrimè illis propositam & auditam sanam doctrinā, diuq; in ea versatos, ac propterea magis culpandos, quòd ad altiora non promouerint. Huc pertinet, quod Dominus multò maxima cura voluit docere, & per apostolos doceri primū Iudæos; ut tantò iustius damnarentur, si verbum auditum non reciperent: vide parabolā de missis seruis in vineam, & eis interfectis, Matth. 21. Item Matth. 10. Ne in viam gentium abirent Apostoli, qui & primò diutissime solos Iudæos docuerunt. Et Ioan. 15. Si non venissem, & locutus non fuissem eis, peccatum non haberent: nunc autem non habent, quod præteriant peccato suo.
units.tr: The rain) This word also occurs in Isaiah 55, the passage cited above, and elsewhere sacred doctrine is compared to it. So in Isaiah 5, where the prophet prophesies about the coming removal of the synagogue: "I will show you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trodden down, and I will make it a desert; it shall not be pruned, nor dug, but briars and thorns shall come up on it, and I will command the clouds not to rain on it." Here the Lord threatens them through the prophet that he will deprive them of the rain of sound doctrine, and will take away the apostles or teachers (who in Isaiah 60 are compared to flying clouds: "Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves?"). The same prophet in chapter 55 compares doctrine to waters: "Come, all you who thirst, to the waters, and you who have no money, hurry, buy and eat." And Psalm 65: "You visited the earth and watered it; you greatly enriched it; the river of God is full of water." But most clearly the rain of sacred doctrine is compared in Joel 2: "Rejoice and be glad, O daughters of Zion, in the Lord your God, because he has given you a teacher of righteousness, and he will cause to come down to you the early and the latter rain, as at the beginning." It should be noted that it is properly called rain (imber) when the drops fall softer and smaller, but shower (pluvia) when larger ones pour down, and storm [Greek: lailaps] when there is great density and force. Hence it is plain that the word rain (imber) suits this matter more fittingly than any other. Moreover, he says not without reason "that often comes upon it, and it has drunk in": for that particle somewhat magnifies the sin of the Hebrews. For it signifies that the sound doctrine was set before them and heard very frequently, and that they had been long engaged in it, and therefore are the more to be blamed because they did not advance to higher things. To this belongs what the Lord took great pains to teach, and to have taught through the apostles, that the Jews were to be first; so that they would be condemned all the more justly if they did not receive the word heard: see the parable of the servants sent into the vineyard and killed, Matthew 21. Likewise Matthew 10, that the apostles should not go into the way of the Gentiles, who for a very long time at first taught only the Jews. And John 15: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin."

units.la: Et progenuerit herbam accommodam) Genesis primo, vbi legitur apud nostros, Producat terra herbam, septuaginta habent vocem βοτανίλη, hebraice legitur ΝΨΤ quæ vox, licet teste Kimhi, significet proprie herbam tenerrimam ac recentem, tamen etiam de arboribus dicitur: quare latius patet eius significatum. Quamobrem & nos in similitudine nomine herbæ accipiemus generaliter omnes fructus, qui solent bonam doctrinam consequi, qui sunt fructus spiritus, quales describuntur Galat. 5. charitas, gaudium, pax, lenitas, benignitas, &c. Et omnes virtutes, quæ reuera semper sunt oportunæ & accomodæ, vbi gloria Dei, & vtilitas proximi per eas promouetur.
units.tr: And let it bring forth the herb fit for use. In Genesis 1 our translators read "Let the earth bring forth grass." The Septuagint has the word βοτάνη [βοτάνη], and the Hebrew is [דֶּשֶׁא]. Although, according to Kimchi, this word properly means very tender and fresh herbage, it is also applied to trees, so its meaning is wider. Accordingly, in this figure of the herb, we will understand in general all the fruits that usually follow good teaching, which are the fruits of the Spirit, such as are described in Galatians 5: love, joy, peace, gentleness, goodness, and so on. We will also understand all the virtues, which are always truly fitting and suitable, where the glory of God and the benefit of our neighbour are advanced by them.

units.la: Huc pertinet, quòd in parabola Christi, verbum Dei auditu varie dicitur fructu proferre, apud aliu profert fructu centuplu, apud alium sexagecuplum, trigecuplum. Et verbo Domini non reuertitur ad eum vacuum, semper aliquid efficit: & licet mundus cum maximis suis turbis illud contemnat, tamen semper aliqui, licet pauci, sunt qui fructum faciunt. Et propterea nunquam importune proponitur verbum, quia nunquam id fit sine fructu. Propterea Apostolus supra dixit, sermonem Dei efficacem esse, & penetrantiore quouis gladio utrimque incidente.
units.tr: To this belongs what Christ says in the parable, that the word of God, when heard, is said to bear fruit in different measures: in one it bears a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, in another thirtyfold. And the word of the Lord does not return to him empty; it always accomplishes something. Although the world with all its tumults despises it, there are always some, though few, who bear fruit. For this reason the word is never proclaimed to no purpose, because this never happens without fruit. Therefore the Apostle said above that the word of God is effective and sharper than any two-edged sword.

units.la: Eis, opera quorum & colitur) γεωργέω agricolor, colo terram. Per cultores terræ intelligimus ipsos verbi ministros & doctores: quomodo & Christus ipse patrem suum cœlestem dicit agricolam usque modò operantem, (Ioannis decimoquinto) & plantantem vineam, &c. Apostolus prima Corinthiorum tertio, Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit, Deus incremetum dedit: Dei sumus cooperarij (συνεργοί) Dei agricolatio (θεοῦ γεώργιον) Dei ædificatio estis. Sed quomodo herba siue fructus verbi intelligetur accommodus esse ipsis doctoribus? Maximè quidem fructus verbi seminati redit ad ipsos auditores, quorum pectora verbum lubenter accipiunt: unde & propter fructum auditorum proponitur. Deinde ad gloriam Dei illustrandam proponitur, ita ut uacuum & sine fructu nunquam ad Deum redeat.
units.tr: To them, by whose labour it is also tilled. The Greek [γεωργέω] means to be a farmer, to till the soil. By the tillers of the soil we understand the ministers and teachers of the word themselves. So too Christ himself calls his heavenly Father the husbandman, still working until now (John 15), and planting the vineyard, and so on. The Apostle, 1 Corinthians 3: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. We are God's fellow workers [συνεργοί], you are God's tillage [θεοῦ γεώργιον], God's building." But how is the herb, or fruit, of the word understood to be fitting for the teachers themselves? Chiefly, the fruit of the sown word returns to the hearers themselves, whose hearts gladly receive the word; hence it is also put forward for the sake of the hearers. Then it is put forward to illustrate the glory of God, so that it never returns to God empty and without fruit.

units.la: Sed eatenus dicitur potissimum ad ipsos doctores redire verbi vtilitas, quatenus ipsis nihil potius, nihilque antiquius est, quàm ut ex ipsorum doctrina permoueantur ad bene agendum homines, unde pariter gloria Dei illustrari queat. Adeò quicquid ad Dei cedit gloriam & proximi vtilitatem, ipsi doctores suum commodum & lucrum interpretantur. Verum quidem est, habent doctores & hunc fructum ex ministerio verbi, quòd videlicet vitæ necessaria ab auditoribus accipiunt, id quod pluribus probat Apostolus prima Corinthiorum nono. Sed tamen, quia in hoc lucro non præcipuè debent esse fixi eorum animi, sed scopus principalis esse debet, illustrare gloriam Dei, & homines ad salutem adducere: ideò quando istud perficitur, ipsi quodam modo mirabiles fructus hic se iudicant percipere. Hinc Paulus prima Corinthiorum nono. Cùm liber sim abomnibus, omnibus meipsum seruum feci, quò plures lucrifaciam. Ibidem: Omnibus factus sum omnia, vt omnino aliquos seruos. Philippensi 2. Quouis modo, siue per occasionem, siue per veritatem, Christus tamen annunciatur, & in hoc gaudeo, quinetiam gaudebo: Noui enim, quòd hoc mihi cedet in salutem.
units.tr: But the benefit of the word is said to return especially to the teachers themselves, inasmuch as nothing is more important or dearer to them than that people should be moved by their teaching to do good, whereby the glory of God may equally be made manifest. So whatever contributes to God's glory and the benefit of the neighbour, the teachers themselves count as their own gain and profit. It is true that teachers also have this fruit from the ministry of the word, namely that they receive from the hearers what is necessary for life; the Apostle proves this at length in 1 Corinthians 9. But since their minds ought not to be fixed chiefly on this gain, while the principal aim must be to illustrate the glory of God and to bring people to salvation, therefore, when that is accomplished, they judge that they in a certain way receive wonderful fruit here. Hence Paul, 1 Corinthians 9: "Though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, so that I might gain more." And in the same place: "I have become all things to all, that I might by all means save some." Philippians 2: "In whatever way, whether by occasion or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, yes, and I will rejoice. For I know that this will turn out to my salvation."

units.la: Hic igitur est fructus, quem auditores adferunt doctoribus, nimirum si in cognitione rerum diuinarum & vitæ pietate proficiant. Sed maximum fructum accipiunt ipsi verbi auditores, quos prius diximus terræ fructiferæ comparatos. Vnde sequitur: Recipit benedictionem à Deo: terram esse feracem, id contingit singulari Dei beneficio, magis quàm cultorum opera. Ideoque facultas hæc, siue feracitas rectè benedictionis nomine appellatur: quemadmodum etiam ea res Deuteron. 28. inter primas benedictiones numeratur: Istæ benedictiones uenient super te, si præcepta eius audieris. Benedictus tu in ciuitate, & benedictus in agro: benedictus fructus ventris tui, & fructus tuæ, &c.
units.tr: This, then, is the fruit which the hearers bring to the teachers, namely if they grow in the knowledge of divine things and in the piety of life. But the hearers of the word, whom we said earlier are likened to fruitful soil, receive the greatest fruit. Hence it follows: receives blessing from God. That the earth is fertile comes about by a singular benefit of God, more than by the labour of the tillers. And so this fertility, or productiveness, is rightly called by the name of blessing; just as this thing is also numbered among the first blessings in Deuteronomy 28: "All these blessings shall come upon you, if you hearken to his commandments. Blessed shall you be in the city, and blessed in the field; blessed shall be the fruit of your womb, and the fruit of your ground," and so on.

units.la: Cæterum benedictiones, quæ proueniunt ijs, qui verbum Dei lubenter audiunt, diuersis in locis Scripturæ exponuntur. Lucæ vndecimo, Beati, qui audiunt verbum Dei, & custodiunt illud. Ioannis octauo, Qui sermonem meum seruauerit, mortem non videbit. Nônne egregia benedictio, effici beatum, obtinere vitam æternam? Sed & omnes fructus tam temporales, quàm spirituales, qui ex audito & credito verbo solent consequi, per hanc benedictionem decet intelligi, ut reuera quàm latissimè & ad maximas res benedictio hæc extendatur.
units.tr: Moreover, the blessings that come to those who gladly hear the word of God are explained in various places of Scripture. Luke 11: "Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it." John 8: "Whoever keeps my word shall never see death." Is this not an excellent blessing, to be made blessed, to obtain eternal life? Yet all the fruits, both temporal and spiritual, which usually follow from the word heard and believed, ought to be understood through this blessing, so that this blessing truly extends as widely as possible, even to the greatest things.

units.la: Et rectè addidit particulam, à Deo, siue ad declarandum, eas benedictiones potissimum spectandas, quæ spirituales sunt, & nos recta deducut ad Deum, siue, ut agnoscceremus, nos sine fauore & afflatu numinis nihil profecturos, quamlibet alias asidui simus verbi auditores. Quocirca Iacob.cap.1.monet postulare spiritualem sapientiam a patre luminum: & Christus aiebat, neminem ad se venire, nisi quem pater traxerit, Ioan.6.
units.tr: And he rightly added the particle from God, either to show that the blessings chiefly to be regarded are the spiritual ones, which lead us straight to God, or to make us acknowledge that we shall make no progress without the favour and breath of the divine power, however constantly we hear the word. Therefore James 1 advises us to ask for spiritual wisdom from the Father of lights; and Christ said that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him, John 6.

units.la: At quae produxerit spinas & tribulos, reproba est) Antithesis haec praeterquam quod illustrat praecedentia, tum vero promouendis affectibus valde est accommoda. Reprobam vero esse terram, quae producit spinas & tribulos, liquet ex illo Genes.3. Maledicta terra in opere tuo, spinas & tribulos germinabit tibi. Saepe item alias, vbi Dominus grauiter commi-natur transgressoribus, inter alia illud adjici solet, quod terra eorum tantum spinas & vepres proferet. Vt Esaiae 5. & 7. & alibi saepius. Sed iam eos quoque spinas & tribulos proferre, qui post auditum verbum nihil faciunt, quo gloria Dei illustretur, vel iuuetur proximus, sed potius diuersum agunt, & bona opera impediunt, sicut spinae & tribuli impediunt triticum, non difficile est demonstrare. 2. Reg. 23. Ipsi peccatores cum spinis conferuntur: praeuaricatores, inquit, quasi spinae euellentur vniuersi. Deinde peccata & ingenita malitia, per quae bona opera impediuntur, etiam spinis comparantur Matth.13. vbi dicitur in parabola: Insurrexerunt spinae & suffocauerunt ea. Luc.cap.8. spinas interpretatur sollicitudine, diuitias, voluptates, ijs nominibus omne genus malorum, quo a be ne agendo retrahimur, intelligens. Porro qui hoc pacto vel ipsi sunt spinae, vel producunt spinas, expectare debent, quod hic de sterili & noxia terra dicitur, quod fit, finis, cuius exitus huc tendit, ut exuratur: Haec a more rusticorum, exuretur, quicquid noxiarum est herbarum, de impiorum damnatione in sacris literis usurpantur, Matth.13 zizania tempore messis colligentur vt exurantur. Quam parabolam Christus ipse ibi plenius exponit, dicens: in consummatione seculi omnia offendicula, & eos, qui patrant iniquitatem, mittendos in caminum ignis, vbi erit ploratus stridorque dentium. Luc. 13. Ficus sterilis iubetur succidi & tolli. Sed Matth.24. plenissime & de benedictione bonorum, & maledictione malorum agitur. Et Ioan.15. de palmite ferente fructu, & de sterili fertur sententia, praesenti loco conueniens.
units.tr: But that which brings forth thorns and briers is reprobate. This antithesis, besides illustrating what goes before, is also very well suited to stirring the affections. That the land which produces thorns and briers is reprobate is plain from Genesis 3: "Cursed is the ground for your sake; thorns and briers shall it bring forth to you." Often elsewhere too, when the Lord severely threatens transgressors, it is usually added among other things that their land will produce only thorns and brambles, as in Isaiah 5 and 7, and elsewhere very often. But that those too bring forth thorns and briers who, after hearing the word, do nothing by which the glory of God is illustrated or the neighbour helped, but rather act to the contrary and hinder good works, just as thorns and briers choke wheat, is not difficult to show. 2 Samuel 23: transgressors are compared with thorns: "They shall all be thrust away like thorns, which are not taken with the hand." Next, sins and innate wickedness, by which good works are hindered, are also compared with thorns, Matthew 13, where it is said in the parable: "The thorns sprang up and choked them." Luke 8 interprets the thorns as cares, riches, and pleasures, understanding by these names every kind of evil by which we are drawn back from doing good. Moreover, those who in this way either are thorns themselves or produce thorns ought to expect what is said here of the barren and harmful land, namely that it be burned. The end toward which its outcome tends is that it be burned up. According to the custom of farmers, whatever is harmful among the herbs is burned; and such words are used in Holy Scripture for the condemnation of the wicked. Matthew 13: the tares are gathered at harvest time to be burned. Christ himself explains that parable more fully there, saying: at the close of the age all stumbling-blocks, and those who work iniquity, will be cast into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Luke 13: the barren fig tree is commanded to be cut down and removed. But Matthew 24 deals most fully both with the blessing of the good and the curse of the wicked. And John 15 speaks of the branch bearing fruit, and pronounces sentence on the barren one, which suits this passage.

units.la: Caeterum ex his paucis verbis variam doctrinam accipimus. Primum, maximum esse vsum similitudinum, ac parabolarum in docendo, maximasque vires inesse illis ad mouendos animos auditorum, praesertim rudium: & valere potissimum in caulis suasoriis. Hinc passim cernimus similitudines a prophetis & Christo vsurpatas, & veteres Scriptores lubenter vsi sunt, foelicissime vero omnium Chrysostomus.
units.tr: Otherwise, from these few words we gain various teaching. First, that similitudes and parables are of great use in teaching, and that they have the greatest power to move the minds of hearers, especially the unlearned; and that they are most effective in persuasive matters. Hence we see everywhere similitudes used by the prophets and Christ, and the ancient writers have gladly used them; but of all, Chrysostom has used them most happily.

units.la: Secundo, ex illa particula, cum saepius imbrem in se uenientem combiberit: admonemur nos, qui saepe audimus & legimus verbum Dei, volumus prae caeteris audire pij & euangelici, vt pro assidua meditatione scripturarum fructus cognitione nobis data dignos proferamus. Ne, si negligentes simus, post habitas tot proficiendi occasiones, maledictionem accipiamus a Deo pro benedictione: sicut Luc. 11. graues comminationes proponit Christus illis, qui verbum Dei cum audiant, tamen illud nolunt custodire, aitq; : Niniuitas, Reginam austri, in iudicio condemnaturos eos, quibus verbum Dei clare fuit propositum, & in fructibus producendis pigri perstiterunt.
units.tr: Second, from that phrase since it has often drunk in the rain that comes upon it, we are admonished that we who often hear and read the word of God should above others wish to hear what is godly and evangelical, so that, through constant meditation on the Scriptures, we may bring forth fruit worthy of the knowledge given to us. Lest, if we are negligent, after so many opportunities of progress have been wasted, we receive a curse from God instead of a blessing. Christ too sets forth grave threats in Luke 11 against those who, though they hear the word of God, are unwilling to keep it; and he says that the Ninevites and the Queen of the South will condemn in judgement those to whom the word of God was clearly set forth, and who remained lazy in producing fruit.

units.la: Tertio, habent doctores seu ministri verbi, quales fructus potissimum spectare, & expectare debeant, nempe ut auditores proferant herbam accommodam, id est, omnigenas virtutes, quibus gloria Dei illustratur, & consulitur vtilitati proximorum. Ad huiusmodi fructus spirituales debent doctores verbi primo & vltimo loco aspirare. Quamuis interea, quia spiritualia seminant, aequum est eos metere & carnalia ab auditorum agris, &c.
units.tr: Third, the teachers or ministers of the Word should consider which fruits they ought chiefly to look for and expect, namely that their hearers bring forth the herb that is fit for them, that is, every kind of virtue by which the glory of God is made known and the good of neighbours is served. Teachers of the Word ought to aim at such spiritual fruits first and foremost. Meanwhile, since they sow spiritual things, it is fair that they should reap carnal things from the fields of their hearers, etc.

units.la: Quarto, multum vnicuiq; proderit ad excitandos animos ad diligentiam asidua di uinarum promissionum; itemq; comminationum consideratio. Si enim vnusquisq; secum diligenter reputaret, quantae benedictiones sint propositae bene agentibus: atq; e contrario, quantae maledictiones male agentibus, non dubium, quin multo alacriores esse-mus ad producendos veros fructus, & ad cauendum a spinis & tribulis, &c.
units.tr: Fourth, it will greatly help to rouse minds to constant diligence if people consider the promises of God and likewise his threats. For if each person would carefully reflect how great the blessings are that are set before those who act well, and, on the contrary, how great the curses are for those who act badly, there is no doubt that we would be far more eager to bring forth true fruits and to beware of thorns and thistles, etc.

units.la: Caeterum persuasimus nobis de vobis dilecti, quae his sint meliora, & cum salute coniuncta, tamet si sic loquamur. Non enim iniustus est Deus, ut obliuiscatur operis ve-stri, & laboris ex charitate suscepti, quam exhibuistis erga nomen illius, qui minis-trastis sanctis, & ministratis, &c.
units.tr: But we are persuaded, beloved, of better things concerning you, and things that accompany salvation, though we speak in this way. For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the labour of love which you have shown toward his name, in that you have ministered to the saints and still minister, etc.

units.la: Quoniam reprehensioni & exhortationi praecedenti immixta fuerunt nonnulla pau-lo acerbius & velut cum stomacho dicta, cuiusmodi sunt, quod statim initio digressionis palam illos insimulauit foedae segnitiei, quod obiecit, eos docendos adhuc prima elemen-ta, prorsus rudes esse sermonis iustitiae; semper inhaerentes operibus mortuis poeniten-tiae: deniq; quod proximis verbis visus sit dicere, eos spinas & tribulos potius qua her-ba accommodâ producere, (quae sane verosimile est eo loco accepta, quo nunc accipiut illi.
units.tr: Since some things were mixed into the earlier rebuke and exhortation, said somewhat more harshly and, as it were, with irritation, such as, at the very beginning of the digression, his openly accusing them of shameful sluggishness; what he objected, that they still needed to be taught the first elements and were quite unskilled in the word of righteousness, always clinging to the dead works of repentance; and finally that in the words just before he seemed to say that they were bringing forth thorns and thistles rather than the herb that is fit (which, it is indeed likely, was understood in that place in the sense in which those people now take it.

units.la: z j illi, quos aliquis magno contemptu appellat asinos, stipites, fungos, caudices) atq; his, licet alioquin iustissimè contra eos, qui ad altiora detrectant progredi, dicta essent, exacerbari & ad indignationem excitari facile potuissent praefractorū Iudaeorū animi: ideò Apostolus nunc prudenter miroq; artificio subijcit nonnulla, quibus quae durius sonare visa sunt, mitiget atq; emolliat, necnon auditorū animos demulceat, pariterq; ad diligentiā maiore prouocet. Est autē horū verborū sententia: Tametsi sic loquamur, ac durius plane videantur nonnulla in praecedenti sermone à nobis dicta, quasi incredibili quodam contemptu vestri nos ea protulisse mus, aut, quasi omnino de vestra salute desperaremus, iudicates, vos aliter neq; velle, neq; posse agere: Absit, vt hoc nobis in mente veniat: sed ita loquimur, existimantes, vestros animos ea ratione ad meliora posse excitari: persuasimus enim nobis de vobis meliora, nimirum vos esse illos, qui nolitis amplius segnes haberi, vel diutius inhaerere primis elemetis: sed potius enitaminì ad altiora conscende re, & herbam accommodā producere, & benedictionem Domini multò largissimam accipere. Magnam gratiam habet ad amoliendam contemptus, ac maleuolentiae desperationisq; conceptae suspicionem, correctiuncula illa.
units.tr: Those whom someone with great contempt calls asses, stumps, mushrooms, blockheads. And although these things were said against those who refuse to advance to higher things, and quite justly, the minds of the stubborn Jews could easily have been exasperated and stirred to indignation. Therefore the Apostle now prudently and with wonderful skill adds some words by which he softens and eases what seemed to sound too harsh, soothes the minds of his hearers, and at the same time stirs them to greater diligence. The sense of these words is this: although we speak in this way, and some things said in the preceding discourse seem quite harsh, as if we had said them out of a certain incredible contempt for you, or as if we had altogether despaired of your salvation, judging that you neither wish nor are able to act otherwise: far be it that this should come into our minds. But we speak thus, thinking that your minds can be roused to better things by this method. For we are persuaded of better things concerning you, namely that you are those who no longer wish to be held sluggish, or to cling longer to the first elements, but rather strive to climb to higher things, to bring forth the fit herb, and to receive the blessing of the Lord in far more abundant measure. That little corrective has great force in removing the suspicion of contempt, ill will and despair that had been conceived.

units.la: Tametsi sic loquamur) Clarè enim significat haec correctiuncula, quòd etiamsi verba ipsius durius quiddam viderentur significare, nullo modo tamen accipienda esse, tanquam si ab animo parū amico essent profecta. Et talibus loquendi formulis saepè etiam solent Rhetores, quoties quid incidit scabrosius, vel horridius, ἀπαπάτηλ. Porrò quando ait: Non enim iniustus est Deus: addit rationem, quare meliora de illis speret, sumptam ab ordinaria dispensatione diuinae iustitiae & bonitatis, secundū q̃ nullū benefactū irremuneratū relinquitur, sed semper aut tèporalib. bonis, aut spiritualib. quę potiora sunt, largiter cōpensatur. Ait itaque, se ideò bene sperare de illis, q̃ Deus, ut est iustus remunerator bonorum operum, pro benefactis illorum daturus sit, vt posint proficere, & ad altiora contendere. Interea dum ad hanc rationem explicandam cogitur commorare res aliquas praeclarè ab ipsis gestas, ac celebrat eximiam charitatem, qua erga sanctos vsi fuerant, & adhuc vtebantur, artificiosè hac ipsa laude eos ad virtutē ac diligentiam extimulat: quādoquidē obiter laudando subinde plus efficitur apud quosdā, q̃ grauissimè excitando: id q̃ de poeta ille elegater expressit, qui ait: laudataq; virtus crescit & im mesum gloria calcar habet. Pulchrè etiam conuenit haec ratio cum eo, quod prius dixit, Deum illi terrae, quae profert accommodam herbam, largiri suā benedictione: nec dubiū est, quin Apostolus hic ad illa verba respexerit. Fluūt. n. ista ex illis, ac rectè sequitur: Si Deus terrę pro ferenti uberè herbā impendit suā benedictionē: Ergo à simili Deus ijs, qui bene agunt, praecipueq; qui producunt vberes fructus charitatis, suā benedictionē ac dona spiritualia lubenter impartietur. Vide obsecro, an non valde consentiāt ista, atq; ordinatissimè sibi omnia cohaereant. Sed illud insuper animaduersione dignum, prudentissimè factum ab Apostolo, quòd profectum Iudaeorum in melius non humanae voluntati, aut studio, viribusue tribuat, sed soli diuinae bonitati iustitiaeq;. Ita namque simul ipsorum Iudaeorum animos & alacres reddit, ut in melius proficere desiderent: simul maximè confirmat, quòd, etiamsi illi adeò turpiter fuissent prolapsi, ut, quantum humano iudicio cerni poterit, nulla amplius affulgeret de reditu illorum in rectam viam spes, tamen se non posse aliter, quàm bene de illis sperare, propterea, quòd Dominus lubeter confert dona sua illis, qui semel bene coeperint, atq; in charitatis officijs se exercuerint, & q̃ supra humanas vires positum est, quàm facilimè semper efficit. Sed quàta prudentia, quantoq; artificio Apostolus ista reddiderit, in explicatione partium magis elucebit.
units.tr: Although we speak thus. For this little corrective clearly signifies that even if his words seemed to mean something rather harsh, they are in no way to be taken as if they had proceeded from a mind not well disposed. Rhetoricians also often use such formulas of speech whenever something harsh or grating has fallen in, [ἀπαπάτηλ]. Moreover, when he says: For God is not unjust, he adds the reason why he hopes better things of them, drawn from the ordinary dispensation of divine justice and goodness, according to which no good deed is left unrewarded, but is always generously recompensed either with temporal goods or with spiritual goods, which are the greater. He says, therefore, that he has good hope concerning them because God, as the just rewarder of good works, will give them, in return for their good deeds, the means to make progress and to strive toward higher things. Meanwhile, while he is compelled to linger over the explanation of this reason, he celebrates certain things done by them that are splendid, and praises the outstanding love which they had shown, and still showed, toward the saints; by this very praise he skilfully spurs them on to virtue and diligence. For praise offered in passing often accomplishes more with some people than the most severe exhortation; the elegant poet expressed this when he said: praised virtue grows, and glory has an immense spur. This reasoning also agrees well with what he said before, that God bestows his blessing on that land which brings forth the fit herb; and there is no doubt that the Apostle here had those words in view. For these things flow from those, and it follows rightly: if God gives his blessing to the land that bears fruitful herb, then by like reasoning God will gladly impart his blessing and spiritual gifts to those who act well, and especially to those who bring forth abundant fruits of love. Please see whether these things do not agree very well and whether all of them cohere most orderly. But it is worth noting, moreover, that the Apostle has very prudently done this, in that he attributes the progress of the Jews toward better things not to human will, zeal, or strength, but solely to divine goodness and justice. For in this way he makes the minds of these very Jews both eager and willing to advance toward better things; and at the same time he most strongly confirms that, even if they had fallen so shamefully that, as far as human judgement can discern, no hope of their return to the right way shone any longer, nevertheless he could not hope otherwise than well concerning them, because the Lord gladly bestows his gifts on those who have once begun well and have exercised themselves in offices of love, and what lies beyond human powers he always brings about most easily. But how great the prudence and how great the skill with which the Apostle has framed these things will become clearer in the explanation of the parts.

units.la: Persuasimus nobis de vobis dilecti) Haec mitigatio multò appositissimè subijcitur ijs, quae proximè dicta sunt de terra proferente spinas & tribulos: quę pars si militudinis maximè ignauos Hebraeos perstringere videbatur. Eoq; postquam illos ibi mordacius quodā modo pupugit, peroportunè statim mitigatio ista subijcitur. Postquā. n. eos (Chrysostomi verbis utor) increpauit sufficienter, & terruit, & percussit, curat eos iterū, ne amplius eos deijciat & supinos efficiat. Tardū enim qui percutit, tardiorem efficit. Neq; ergo in omnibus adulatur, ne supiniores efficiat: neq; in omnibus percutit, sed aliquantulū quidem percussoria apponens adfert, quae vehementer curat, per ea, quae subijciūtur. Quid enim dixit: Non veluti culpantes vos haec dicimus, neq; veluti putates vos spinis plenos, sed timentes, ne tales efficiamini. Melius est enim vos terrere, quàm vt rebus ipsis doleatis. Et hoc sapientiae Pauli est, & quidem maximae. Ita Chrysostomus. Videamus autem, quanta cura etiam verba selegerit.
units.tr: Persuaded, beloved, of you. This softening is placed most fittingly after what was just said about the land that brings forth thorns and thistles; that part of the comparison seemed to strike the very sluggish Hebrews. And after he had stung them there somewhat sharply, this softening is most opportunely added at once. For after he has sufficiently rebuked, frightened and struck them (I use the words of Chrysostom), he heals them again, lest he cast them down further and make them listless. For one who strikes slowly makes the stricken slower. Therefore he does not flatter them in everything, lest he make them more listless, nor does he strike them in everything, but applies a little comfort that gently heals by means of what follows. For what did he say? We do not speak these things as blaming you, nor as thinking you full of thorns, but fearing lest you become such. For it is better to frighten you than that you should be grieved by the facts themselves. And this is the wisdom of Paul, and indeed of the greatest kind. Thus Chrysostom. But let us see with what care he has chosen even his words.

units.la: Persuasimus nobis) inquit: Non ait, putamus, vel suspicamur, vel expectamus: sed, persuasimus, vel, ut alij legunt, confidimus: qua uoce omnino certitudo quaedam, quae procul absit à dubitatione, significatur. Atque ita hac voce omnem suspicionem odij, maleuolentiae, ac desperationis conceptae à se amolitur. Sic Galat.5.Ego confido de vobis in Domino, quòd nihil aliud sensuri sitis. Vbi similiter eadem voce vtitur ad mitigandum increpationem ibidem præcedentem, vbi dixerat,currebatis bene, &c.
units.tr: We are persuaded, he says. He does not say we think, or suspect, or expect; but we are persuaded, or, as others read, we are confident. By which word a certain certainty is plainly signified, far removed from doubt. And so by this word he removes from himself any suspicion of hatred, ill will, or conceived despair. Thus Gal. 5: I have confidence in you through the Lord, that you will think nothing otherwise. Where he uses the same word in a similar way to soften the rebuke immediately preceding there, where he had said: you were running well, etc.

units.la: Dilecti,ἀγαπητοί) Vide & hic blandam vocem, ad placandum, & ad exprimendū charitatis affectum, mirè idoneam. Non dissimile huic est illud Galat.4.Filioli mei, quos iterum parturio, donec formetur Christus in vobis.
units.tr: Beloved, [ἀγαπητοί]. See here too an endearing word, wonderfully suited to placate and to express affection of love. Not unlike this is that in Gal. 4: My little children, for whom I labour again in birth until Christ is formed in you.

units.la: Quæ bis sint meliora, & cum salute coniuncta) Græcè sic habetur, τὰ νενεργημένα ... quasi diceret: Meliora, & vicina, vel coniuncta, vel cohærentia (sic enim Augustinus legit ad Crescentium) saluti. Confidimus, inquit, de vobis meliora: supple: quàm, vt præcedentia de vobis dici queant, videlicet, quòd tantùm spinas & tribulos proferatis, &c.
units.tr: The things that are better, and joined with salvation) In Greek this reads "the things that have been done [τὰ νενεργημένα ...]", as if he were saying: better things, and near to or joined with salvation (for so Augustine reads it in his letter to Crescentius). "We are confident," he says, "of better things concerning you," supply "than", so that the things said before about you can be taken as said: namely, that you bring forth only thorns and briars, and so on.

units.la: Sed addit, quadam incrementi, imò amplificationis forma: cum salute coniuncta: Non sim pliciter bono eos esse in statu significat, sed reuera in tali, q sit saluti valde ppinquus. Ita Iudæos, qui iam elementa religionis probè didicerat, neq; exasperat, neq; cogit diffidere, dicendo, eos procul esse à salute: sed potius animat atq; excitat, dicendo, eos esse saluti vicinos. Et poterat quidè multa rectè & benè ab illis fieri, cuiusmodi erat obseruatio plerorúq; legalium: sed tamen illa non erant admodum vicina saluti: Nunc verò significat, se confidere, talia in illis adhuc elucere, per quæ intelligi possint salutì valde vicini: Et iam non infœliciter eos viam salutis ingressos, tantum requiri, vt progrediantur. Dicuntur autem vicini esse saluti, qui studiosi sunt rerum diuinarum, & iam quadantenus profecerút, & paucis tàtùm egent, vt ad consummationem peruenient. Psalmo 118.Longe à peccatoribus salus, quia iustificationes tuas non exquisierunt.
units.tr: But he adds, by way of increase, or rather amplification: joined with salvation. This does not mean simply that they are in a good state, but that they are truly in such a state as is very near to salvation. So he neither exasperates the Jews, who had already learned well the elements of religion, nor forces them to despair by saying that they are far from salvation; he rather encourages and stirs them up by saying that they are near to salvation. Many things were indeed done rightly and well by them, such as the observance of most of the legal duties; but these were not very near to salvation. Now, however, he signifies that he is confident such things are already shining forth in them, by which they may be understood to be very near to salvation, and that, having not unhappily entered the way of salvation, they need only press on. Those are said to be near to salvation who are zealous for divine things, have already made some progress in some measure, and lack only a little to reach completion. Psalm 118: "Salvation is far from the wicked, for they have not sought your statutes."

units.la: Tametsi sic loquamur) Sic supple, durius in specie. Nō semper verba quę durius sonant, ex animo maleuolo pficiscuntur. Bonus pater seuerius filiū, quē diligit, castigat interdū, nec tamen paternū affectū exuit. Huiusmodi fere formula mitigādi habetur 2 Cor.12. Factus sum insipiens gloriando. Vos me coegistis. Sic enim interdū cogūtur amici asperiora quædā dicere, quæ tamen nequaquā animo malo dicūt, quæ ob id debēt gratiora esse, quàm quęcūq; verba adulatorū. Hinc Prouerb. 27. Melior est manifesta correctio, quàm amor abscōditus: & meliora sunt vulnera diligētis, quàm fraudulēta oscula odiētis. Anima satu rata calcabit fauū, & anima esuriēs etiā amarū pro dulci sumet. Huc ergo respiciēs Apostolus prudenter hanc mitigationem subiecit. Iam addit rationē, qua probat, verum esse, quòd ita sentiat, vt loquitur, nempe, quòd persuaserit sibi, & planè ratum habeat, illos ad meliora progressuros, & optata salute minimè frustrandos.
units.tr: Although we speak thus) Supply "thus", that is, rather harshly in appearance. Words that sound harsh do not always proceed from an ill-disposed mind. A good father sometimes chastises more severely the son whom he loves, and yet does not lay aside his paternal affection. A formula of this softening kind occurs in 2 Cor. 12: "I have become foolish in boasting; you have compelled me." For friends are sometimes obliged to say somewhat harsh things, which nevertheless they do not say with an evil mind, and which for that reason ought to be more welcome than the words of flatterers. Hence Prov. 27: "Open rebuke is better than hidden love, and the wounds of a lover are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates. The sated soul will tread on the honeycomb, but the hungry soul will take even bitter things for sweet." Looking to this, the Apostle wisely added this softening. Next he adds the reason by which he proves that what he says is true, namely that he has persuaded himself, and fully holds it as settled, that they will advance to better things and will by no means be disappointed of the salvation they desire.

units.la: Nō enim iniustus est Deus, ut obliuiscatur operis uestri) Nō diceretur autDeus iniustus etiāsi nequaquā largiretur benè agetibus suā benedictionē. Nam quicquid dat, non cōfert quasi debitū, sed per gratuitā misericordiam. Iustè quidē punit, pro meritis infligēs pœnas, sed non simpliciter iustè pedit bona, vtpote quæ nullo pacto possumus promereri. Nā illud ipsum, quod benè fit, iam ipsius Dei beneficio contigit, neq; humanis viribus partū est, vnde Deus superaddere seu repedere non tenetur. Sed loquitur Apostolus communi more loquēdi, & sequēs cōmunē sententiā, qua dicitur, à Deo nullū bonū relinqui irremuneratū: & documentū exhibet iusti iudicij Dei, in hoc, vt digni habeamini regno Dei, p quo & patimini: quomodo 2.Thess.1.dicit: Iustū est apud Deū, reddere his, qui affligunt vos, afflictionē, & vobis, qui affligimini, relaxationem. Cùm alias vt Deus simpliciter iustis diceretur, necesse esset, vnicuiq; pro operū dignitate alij plus, alij minus retribuere: cùm tamē in parabola euangelica describatur ille, qui postremus venit in vineā, parē mer cede accipiēs cum eo, qui primus venit. Id quod valde notādū est, ne quis hic merita humana nimia euehat, & cum Pelagianis contedat, nostris benefactis regnū cœlorum quasi deberi. Eamq; ob causam nonnullis hic placuit interpretari, iustū, dici Deū, quia verax, & & iustū esse idē quod veracē, quia, quēadmodū promisit, se benefacta largiter omni tempore velle cōpensare, ita reuera id præstat. Quomodo verò promiserit Deus, se benè agentibus daturū amplissima præmia, tàm in hac vita, quàm in altera, minimè opus est multis Scripturę testimonijs explicare: quādo etiā gentiles ipsi idè agnouerint & cōfessi sint. Et dicitur Deus iustus hac in parte, non solùm quia præstat promissa, verùm etiam quia quorum opera bona misericorditer acceptat, eos iustos facit & pronunciat.
units.tr: For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work) God would not be called unjust even if he did not bestow his blessing on those who do good. For whatever he gives, he does not confer as a debt, but through free mercy. He punishes justly indeed, inflicting penalties according to merits; but he does not simply bestow good things justly, since we can by no means merit them. For that very good which is done has already come about by the benefit of God himself, and has not been produced by human strength, so God is not bound to add or repay anything further. But the Apostle speaks in the common manner of speaking, following the common opinion by which it is said that no good is left by God unrewarded; and he shows evidence of the just judgment of God in this, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which also you suffer. So he says in 2 Thess. 1: "It is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to you who are afflicted, rest." Otherwise, if God were simply said to be just, it would be necessary that to each one, according to the worth of his works, some would be repaid more and some less; yet in the gospel parable the man who came last into the vineyard is described as receiving the same wage as the one who came first. This must be very carefully noted, lest anyone here exalt human merits excessively and contend with the Pelagians that the kingdom of heaven is, as it were, owed to our good deeds. For this reason some have chosen here to interpret that God is called just because he is true, and to be just is the same as to be truthful: because, as he has promised, so he really does at all times bountifully repay good deeds. How God has promised to give the most ample rewards to those who do good, both in this life and in the next, there is no need to explain at length by many testimonies of Scripture, since even the Gentiles themselves have recognised and confessed this. And God is called just in this respect not only because he performs what he has promised, but also because he mercifully accepts the good works of those whose works they are, and pronounces them and makes them just.

units.la: Vt obliuiscatur operis uestri, et laboris ex charitate suscepti) Græcè habetur, ... quasi diceret: Vt obliuiscat operis vestri et laboris ipsi charitatis, vt fit sententia: Charitate ipsorū fuisse ingenté, atq; per eā multū operis et laboris illos insumsipsse. Videtur hebraismus esse laboris dilectionis, quasi dicat laboris ex charitate. Nec sine em phasi atq; insigni auxesi apposuit voce laboris. Satis quidē fuisset dicere, operis vestri ex charitate suscepti: Sed addit, & laboris: nimirū, vt à magnitudine studij, & difficultate pstādi charitate illorū extolleret. Omne quidē opus bonū suā laude meretur: at verò quod præstitum est multo labore, atq; etiam cum periculo, veluti vbi quis suppeditat afflctis propter euangelium necessaria, recipiendo eos in domum, aut conferendo vitæ necessaria: ob quæ facta discrimen vitæ quàdam aliquando incurrerunt: hoc opus hic labor est: &, sicut à paucis præstatur, ita maximam coram Deo & hominibus gloriam obtinebit.
units.tr: So that he may forget your work and the labour undertaken out of love) In Greek it reads "...", as if he were saying: that he may forget your work and the labour of love itself, so that the sense is: that their love was great, and through it they had expended much work and labour. The phrase "labour of love" seems to be a Hebraism, as if he said "labour from love". Nor without emphasis and a notable heightening did he add the word "labour". It would indeed have been enough to say "work undertaken out of love", but he adds "and labour", namely so as to extol their love from the greatness of their zeal and the difficulty of performing it. Every good work certainly deserves its praise; but what is performed with great labour, and even with danger, as when someone supplies the afflicted for the sake of the gospel with necessities, receiving them into his house or contributing the necessities of life, deeds for which they at times incurred some risk to life: this work is here called labour; and, since it is performed by few, it will obtain the greatest glory before God and men.

units.la: Ex charitate suscepti, seu charitatis) Hæc particula maximopere erat necessaria: quia, quàm libet præclara & admiranda opera fiant, tamen Deo non placent, nisi ex radice charitatis progrediantur. Magna effecerunt plerique gentilium, sed quia non ex charitate Dei & proximi, sed, vel propter gloriam apud homines parandam, vel propter metum, &c. non placuerunt Deo, nec mercedem à Deo, sed, sicut Christus de operibus Pharisæorum ait, mercedem ab hominibus acceperunt. Adeò sola Charitas bonorum operum est suaue condimentum. Hinc illud 1. Corinth. 13. Etsi habeam prophetiam, & nouerim mysteria omnia, omnemque scientiam, & si habeam omnem fidem, adeò vt montes loco dimoueam, &, si insumam in alimoniam omnes facultates meas, & si tradam corpus meum, vt comburar, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum, nihil vtilitatis capiam. Commendantur ergo & hic vehementer opera Hebræorum, quòd ex charitate, non fastu, ambitione, vel metu essent perac-ta. Et charitas, quæ modò sic appellanda venit, non est otiosa, sed necessario erumpit in opus, nullaq; difficultate à bene agendo deterretur: vnde Ioannes 1. epistolæ cap. 3. Filioli mei, ne diligamus verbo, neq; lingua, sed opere & veritate. Fucus omnis procul abesse debet, nec non opera testantia internum affectum requiruntur.
units.tr: Undertaken out of love, or of love) This particle was most necessary, because however splendid and admirable works may be, they do not please God unless they proceed from the root of love. Many of the Gentiles have accomplished great things, but because they were not done out of love for God and neighbour, but either to win glory among men, or from fear, and so on, they did not please God, nor did they receive a reward from God, but, as Christ says of the works of the Pharisees, they received their reward from men. Thus love alone is the sweet seasoning of good works. Hence 1 Cor. 13: "Though I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, and though I spend all my goods on food, and though I give my body to be burned, but have not love, I am nothing, I gain nothing." So the works of the Hebrews are here strongly commended, because they were performed out of love, not out of pride, ambition or fear. And love, which is now to be called by this name, is not idle, but necessarily breaks out into work, and is deterred from doing good by no difficulty; whence John, 1 Epistle, ch. 3: "My little children, let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and truth." All pretence must be far away, and works that bear witness to the inward affection are required.

units.la: Quàm exhibuistis erga nomen illius) Dicturus erat erga sanctos, sed maluit prius dicere, erga nomen illius. Hac enim ratione tum illustrat seu amplificat opera illorum, quòd videlicet non tantum erga proximu facta sint, sed etiá erga Deu: tum certiores illos reddit de recipiedis nouis à Deo beneficijs. Si qui erga Deu fuerint grati, Deus vicissim erga ipsos nō erit ingratus. Hinc vero sumpsit Apostolus hac loquendi formula, quòd, quæcunq; beneficia hominibus impenduntur, Deus ea sic habet, tanquam sibi ipsi impensa, maximè si in nomine seu propter nomen ipsius id fiat. Matthæi 25. Quod fecistis vni de his fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Marci 10. Quisquis ad bibendum dederit vobis calicem aquæ nomine meo, quòd sitis Christi, amen dico vobis, nequaquam perditurus est mercedem suam. Imò quæcunq; opera in nomine Dei & ad gloriam Dei facienda sunt, vt vere bona habeantur. Coloss. 3. Et quicquid egeritis sermone aut facto, omnia in nomine Domini Iesu facite, gratias agentes Deo & patri per illum.
units.tr: Which you have shown toward his name) He was going to say "toward the saints", but preferred first to say "toward his name". For by this he both illustrates or amplifies their works, in that they were done not only toward a neighbour but also toward God; and he makes them more certain of the new benefits to be received from God. If people have been thankful toward God, God in turn will not be ungrateful toward them. But the Apostle took this manner of speaking from the fact that whatever benefits are bestowed on men, God so regards them as if they had been bestowed on himself, especially if this is done in the name or for the sake of his name. Matt. 25: "What you did to one of these my least brethren, you did to me." Mark 10: "Whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you are Christ's, truly I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward." Indeed, whatever works are to be done in the name of God and for the glory of God, if they are to be regarded as truly good. Col. 3: "And whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him."

units.la: Qui ministraftis Sanctis & ministratis) Interpretatur, quodnam sit illud præcipuum opus ex charitate suscep-tum, quod Deus dignabitur largiter compensare, aitq; id esse minis-terium Sanctorum. Quin eadem opera prædicat & amplificat illorum studium ac diligentiam, nec non confirmat eos, vt pro certo expectent Dei beneficia, quòd ait, non solum ante id tempus, sed etiam nunc adhuc charitatem illam exercere. Constantia in virtutibus requiritur. Qui perseuerauerit, is præmium indubitatò accipiet. Et hac ratione clarissimè ostendit, se iustissimè ex animo sperare de illis meliora: quando quidè non ita prolapsi fuerunt, quasi prorsus desiissent bene agere, sed bono adhuc in statu res eorum errant: desiderabatur, vt alacrius ad pleniorem cognitionem rerum euangelicarum conscenderent, & æquis animis ἀκοῆ μαθητεία legis deponerent.
units.tr: Who have ministered to the saints and do minister: he explains what that particular work of love is, which God will deign to reward generously, and he says that it is the ministry to the saints. Indeed, he also commends and magnifies their zeal and diligence, and confirms them so that they may confidently expect God's blessings, when he says that they have exercised that love not only before this time but even still now. Constancy is required in virtues: "He who has persevered will undoubtedly receive the reward." By this reasoning he shows most clearly that he rightly hopes from his heart for better things from them. They have not so fallen away as to have ceased altogether to do good, but their affairs are still in a good state. It was desired that they should press on more eagerly toward a fuller knowledge of the gospel things, and with calm minds lay aside the rudiments of the law, the hearing and learning of it [ἀκοῆ μαθητεία].

units.la: Cæterum ministerium Sanctorum significat officia charitatis & beneuolentiæ in pios quoscunque, maximè verò afflictos propter confessionem verbi, atque ipsos vt bi ministros exhibita, dum illis tectum, mensa, vestis, consilii, & omnis generis auxilii propter Christum impenditur. Lucæ capite octauo, sequebantur Christum mulierculæ, quæ ministrabant ei de facultatibus suis. Romanorum capite decimoquinto. Etenim si spiritualia sua communicauerunt gentibus, debent & hę in carnalibus ministrare illis. Actor. 6. illa distributio facultatum, & officia mutua vocantur ministerium quotidianum. Ortu est murmur græcorum aduersus Hebræos, eò quòd despiceretur in ministerio quotidiano ipsorum viduę, &c. Hoc ipsum ministerium commendat cap 13. huius epistolæ dicens, Beneficentiæ & communicationis ne obliuiscamini.
units.tr: But the ministry of the saints signifies the offices of charity and goodwill toward all the godly, and especially toward those afflicted for the confession of the word; these are shown to them as to ministers of Christ, when house, table, clothing, counsel, and every kind of help are bestowed on them for Christ's sake. In Luke chapter 8, little women followed Christ and ministered to him from their means. Romans chapter 15: "For if they have shared their spiritual things with the Gentiles, they ought also to minister to them in material things." Acts 6: that distribution of goods and these mutual offices are called the daily ministry. "A murmuring of the Greeks arose against the Hebrews, because their widows were overlooked in the daily ministry," etc. This same ministry he commends in chapter 13 of this epistle, saying: "Do not forget beneficence and sharing."

units.la: Discimus porrò ex his, quomodo increpationibus prudenter admiscenda sint, quæ mitigent: ne fortasis animi auditorum exacerbati, omnem deinceps admonitionem aueant. Cogitandum est docenti, in magna multitudine varia esse ingenia, & eos, qui generosiore sunt pectore, duci malle quàm trahi: ita vt semper mansuetudo plus valitura sit etiam apud quoscunq;, quàm acerbior obiurgatio. Asperitate enim boni offenduntur, mali in malitia interdum indurantur, citius quàm molliuntur: blandior verò oratio omnium animis est acceptior, & etiá malos emollit frágitq;. Quanquá hęc quoq; prudentia adhibeda est in oratione mansuetiore, ne ea adulatione resipiat, quę docetis autoritatem minuit, & nuit, & nonnunquam parit auditores ipsius doctrinæ contemptum. Horum præceptorum plurima in Scripturis extant exempla & testimonia.
units.tr: From these things we learn further how reproofs are to be prudently mixed with softening words, lest perhaps the minds of the hearers be exasperated and thereafter they shun all admonition. The teacher must consider that in a large crowd there are various dispositions, and that those of a more generous spirit prefer to be led rather than dragged. So gentleness will always prevail, even among all, more than a harsher rebuke. For by harshness good people are offended, and the wicked are sometimes hardened in their malice more quickly than they are softened; but a gentler speech is more acceptable to all minds, and even softens and breaks the wicked. Yet this prudence must also be applied in gentle speech, lest it lose its savour through flattery, which diminishes the authority of the teacher and sometimes produces in the hearers contempt for the doctrine itself. Very many examples and testimonies of these precepts exist in the Scriptures.

units.la: Secundò, ad extimulandum nos ad bona opera, item ad sperandum omni tempore Dei auxilium valde confert, quod hic traditur de bonorum operum à Deo remuneratione: de qua re passim multa in Scripturis, atq; etiam apud gentiles. Dupliciter autem Deus compensat bona opera, nempe primùm in hac vita: deinde post hanc vitam: sicut Paulus aperte dicit. 1. Timoth. 4. Pietas ad omnia utilis est, vt quæ promissiones habeat vitæ præsentis & futuræ. Marci 10. Nullus est, qui reliquit domũ aut fratres, aut sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut vxorem, aut liberos, aut agros, mea causa, & euangelij, quin recipiat centupla, nunc in tempore hoc, domos, & fratres, & sorores, & matres, & liberos, & agros, cum persecutionibus: ac in seculo venturo vitam æternam.
units.tr: Second, what is taught here about God's rewarding of good works greatly helps to spur us on to good works, and likewise to hope for God's help at all times. On this matter there is much throughout the Scriptures, and also among the Gentiles. God rewards good works in two ways: first in this life, then after this life, as Paul plainly says, 1 Timothy 4: "Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come." Mark 10: "There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my sake and the gospel's, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time: houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields, with persecutions; and in the age to come, eternal life."

units.la: Cæterum in hac vita duplicia percipiuntur præmia: nempe corporalia seu temporalia, vt diuitiæ, honores, proles, &c. & spiritualia, vt, pax, gaudium, &c. De corporalibus Matthæi sexto: Primùm quærite regnum Dei, & hæc omnia adijcientur vobis. De spiritualibus 2. Corinthior. 9. Potens est Deus efficere, vt totum beneficium in vos exuberet, vt in omnibus omnem sufficientiam habentes, exuberetis in omne opus bonum, quemadmodū scriptum est: Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in seculum, & quæ ibi sequuntur. Porrò hæc bonorum operum præmia ita dispensat Deus in hac vita hominibus, vt boni quidem simul accipiant spiritualia præmia cum carnalibus, (atque omnia cedant eis ad maius bonum & ornamentum) frequentius autem spiritualia, quæ illis magis sunt utilia, & quibus rectius possunt & norunt uti. Malis autem dat Deus, sua quoque beneficiorum præmia, sed non fere alia, quàm carnalia & temporalia, quæ illis etiam cedunt subinde ad malum & exitium, veluti cùm diuitijs & lætis successibus abutuntur. Spiritualia autem dona nequaquam dat malis, aut certè si similia sint spiritualibus bonis, qualia cernuntur in pijs: tamen, quia mali non sciunt recte vtiillis, neq; ex spiritu fecerunt opera sua præcedentia, dici, spiritualia præmia non mercentur, sed potius carnalia: cuiusmodi sunt sapientia, intellectus, iustitia, temperantia, fortitudo, &c. quæ in gentilibus & incredulis visa sunt illustria: & sapientia, iustitia, temperantia, fortitudo in illis, similesque virtutes ab Apostolo carnales virtutes appellantur, sicut ipsi carnales homines, Romanorum capite octauo, prima Corinthiorum secundo. Iam post hanc vitam remunerat Deus benefacta, tantum bonis, & qui dem conferendo præmia spiritualia & æterna, eaq; tam in anima, quàm in corpore, quo sua gloria illustrabitur. Mali autem ibi pro bonis operibus nihil accipiunt, sed tantum pro malefactis pœnas ac supplicia æterna.
units.tr: Moreover, in this life two kinds of reward are received: bodily or temporal, such as riches, honours, offspring, etc.; and spiritual, such as peace, joy, etc. Concerning the bodily, Matthew 6: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you." Concerning the spiritual, 2 Corinthians 9: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you, so that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound in every good work, as it is written: He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever," and what follows there.
