Moreover, God so dispenses these rewards of good works in this life that the good receive spiritual rewards together with carnal ones (and all things turn out to their greater good and ornament), but more often the spiritual, which are more useful to them and which they can and know how to use more rightly. To the wicked, God also gives his rewards of benefits, but scarcely any other than carnal and temporal ones, which also at times turn to their evil and ruin, as when they abuse riches and happy successes. Spiritual gifts, however, he never gives to the wicked; or if they are like the spiritual goods seen in the godly, yet because the wicked do not know how to use them rightly, and have not done their former works from the Spirit, they are said not to merit spiritual rewards but rather carnal ones. Of this kind are wisdom, understanding, justice, temperance, fortitude, etc., which have appeared illustrious in Gentiles and unbelievers; and wisdom, justice, temperance, and fortitude in them, and similar virtues, are called carnal virtues by the Apostle, just as carnal men are, Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 2. Now after this life God rewards good deeds only for the good, conferring spiritual and eternal rewards, both in soul and in body, by which his glory will be displayed. But the wicked there receive nothing for good works, but only eternal punishments and torments for their evil deeds.

units.la: Liquet ergo, quomodo semper verum sit, benefacta etiam malis hominibus semper à Deo remunerari, tiinimirum si non post hanc vitam, tamen in hac vita: & si non præmijs spiritualibus, at certè carnalibus & temporalibus. Et tamen interea nequaquam statuen dum, quòd benefacta promereatur eiusmodi præmia, sicut quis pro certo labore diurno certa accipit mercedem: propterea, quòd Deus præmia quæcunq; cõfert ex gratuita miseri cordia, cùm hoc ipsum, quod quisquã boni quippiã agat, ipsius Dei cõtingat beneficio.
units.tr: It is clear, therefore, how it is always true that good deeds done even by wicked men are always rewarded by God: namely, if not after this life, yet in this life; and if not with spiritual rewards, yet certainly with carnal and temporal ones. And yet, meanwhile, we must by no means hold that good deeds merit such rewards, as someone receives a fixed wage for a certain day's labour; because God bestows all rewards out of free mercy, since this very fact, that anyone does any good at all, itself happens through the benefit of God himself.

units.la: Vnde, quoniam præsenti loco dicitur, quòd Deus non obliuiscatur bonorũ operum, hic occurrit breuiter conciliandum, quod habetur Ezechielis 18. Si impius egerit pœnitentiam ab omnibus peccatis suis, quæ operatus est, & custodierit omnia præcepta mea, & fecerit iudicium & iustitiam, vita viuet, & non morietur: omnium iniquitatum, quas operatus est, non recordabor. Mox subijcitur per contrarium: Si autem auerterit se iustus à iustitia sua, & fecerit iniquitate, secundum omnes abominationes, quas operari solet impius, nunquid viuet? Omnes iustitiæ eius, quas fecerat, non recordabuntur. Quomodo igitur hæc verba Ezechielis conueniunt cum verbis Apostoli?
units.tr: Hence, since in the present passage it is said that God does not forget good works, here we must briefly reconcile what is found in Ezekiel 18: "If the wicked man turns from all his sins which he has committed, and keeps all my precepts, and does judgement and justice, he shall live and not die; I will not remember any of the iniquities which he has done." Immediately after, it is added by way of contrast: "But if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and does iniquity, according to all the abominations which the wicked man is wont to do, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds which he has done shall be remembered." How then do these words of Ezekiel agree with the words of the Apostle?

units.la: Respondetur. Verba Apostoli accipienda esse de ordinaria Dei dispensatione secundum misericordiam, qua ille solet bene agentibus semper fauere & benefacere. Verba autem Ezechielis dicta sunt de iudicio seu exacta Dei iustitia, secundum quam pro vno peccato merito potest ac debet omnes dãnare, & non tenetur, quæ bene egerunt, bonis compensare, cum hoc ipsum, q; quicquã boni egerint, misericordiæ ipsius fuerit. Et satis liquet intueri illud caput, Ezechielis sermone illic haberi de exacto Dei iudicio, secundum quod vnusquisq; pro suo peccato mori debet: etiãsi more prophetarũ rursus è contrario de Dei misericordia etiã sermo interseratur. Quia verò misericordia Domini semp superat iudi ciũ, & cùm iratus est, misericordiæ recordatur: sicut dicitur Abacuc 1. Et Deus nõ quærit mortem peccatoris, sed potius vt cõuertatur à vijs suis & viuat, (vt dicitur apud eundē Ezechielem, cap. 18.) rectè dictum est de Deo, secundū magnam misericordiam, quòd bonorum operum semper recordatur; & vera certaq; manet Pauli sententia.
units.tr: The answer: the words of the Apostle are to be understood of God's ordinary dispensation according to mercy, by which he is accustomed always to favour and reward those who do well. But the words of Ezekiel are spoken of judgement, that is, of the strict justice of God, according to which for one sin he can and ought rightly to condemn all, and is not bound to repay with good things those who have done well, since even that they have done any good was itself of his mercy. And it is quite clear, on looking at that chapter of Ezekiel, that the discourse there concerns the strict judgement of God, according to which each one ought to die for his own sin, even though, after the manner of the prophets, a discourse on God's mercy is interwoven in turn on the opposite side. But since the mercy of the Lord always surpasses judgement, and when he is angry he remembers mercy, as it is said in Abacuc 1, and since God does not seek the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn from his ways and live (as is said in the same Ezekiel, chap. 18), it is rightly said of God, according to his great mercy, that he always remembers good works; and Paul's sentence remains true and certain.

units.la: Tertiò hic discimus, ea demum bona opera vere bona censeri, ac Deo placere, remuneratione etq; acceptura, quæ fiūt impulsu charitatis: Charitatis inquam erga proximum; sed quæ oriūtur item ex Charitate Dei. Nam benefaciendum est proximo, sed non propter homines, non propter gloriam vel verecundiam apud homines, at propter Deum, si modò à Deo potius, quàm ab hominibus mercedem volumus accipere.
units.tr: Thirdly, here we learn that only those good works are truly good and pleasing to God, and will receive a reward, which are done from the impulse of love: love, I say, for our neighbour, but also love that arises from the love of God. For we must do good to our neighbour, but not for the sake of men, not for glory or reputation before men, but for God's sake, if indeed we wish to receive our reward from God rather than from men.

units.la: Quartò, ex eo, quòd dicitur exhibita charitatem erga nomen Dei, habemus rationem suasoriā, quæ nos valde moúere debet ad opera charitatis exercēda, quando, quæcunq; facimus bona erga fratres nostros, Deus perinde accepta habet, ac sibiipsi impensa.
units.tr: Fourthly, from the statement that love has been shown toward the name of God, we have a persuasive argument that ought to move us strongly to exercise works of love: whatever good we do toward our brothers, God counts it as done to himself.

units.la: Quintò habemus, quòd inter alia opera charitatis maximè cōmendabile est ministerium sanctorū, id est, eleemosyna, & omne genus officij charitatis erga pios, qui affliguntur propter iustitiam, & erga ministros verbi, quos præcipuè nomine sanctorum Apostolus hic intelligit.
units.tr: Fifthly, we have that among the other works of love, the ministry to the saints, that is, almsgiving and every kind of service of love toward the godly who suffer for righteousness, and toward the ministers of the Word, whom the Apostle here especially understands by the name of saints, is most commendable.

units.la: Cupimus autē, vt vnusquisq; vestrum idem præstet studium ad plenam spei certitudine, vsq; ad perfectionem, ne sitis imbecilles, sed imitatores eorum, qui per fidem acpatientiam, hæreditatem accipiunt promissionis.
units.tr: We desire that each one of you show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you do not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

units.la: Testatus se nihil eorum, quæ durius videbantur dicta, malo dixisse animo: Iam exponit clarius, quare eum in modum sit locutus, imò quem in finem totam hanc digresionem instituerit. Vbi itaque plerique Iudæorum offensi præcedenti obiurgatione, forte rogaturi erant: Quorsum hæc ô Paule? &c, unde commeriti sumus, vt eiusmodi verbis nos lacessas? Prudenter ait: Nos nequaquam morosè vos lacesimus, multò minus aliquid inciuiliter exprobramus: sed in hunc finem nos ita locuti sumus, quòd ar dentisime cupiamus, vt vnusquisq; vestrum idem præstet studium ad plenam spei certitudinem vsque ad perfectionem: vt vestræ consulam saluti, atque ad maiora capessenda extimulem, hæcà me dicta sunt, non vt vos irritem, vel à proficiendo deterream, animisue cogam despondere. Ac dum hoc pacto explicat, quo animo cuncta dixerit, eadem opera generalem profert exhortationem, qua summa & caput totius digresionis comprehenditur: planeq; conueniunt hæc cum ijs, quæ initio huius capitis exhortandi causa sunt posita, vbi ait: Quapropter omisso, qui in Christo rudes inchoat, sermone, ad perfectionem feramur, &c. Vt videas ultima primis, imò singula sibi inuicem pulchrè respondere. Sed his non contentus, siue quò euidentius exprimeret suum erga eos optimum affectū, siue quò magis acueret eos ad progrediendū ad altiora, per expolitionē rhetoricam addit, se in eum fine dixisse hæc omnia, vt nō amplius essent segnes siue imbecilles, sed potius strenuè imitarentur suos patres, qui ad summa progressi per fidem a longanimitatem, diuinas promissiones sint consecuti. Quæ verba itidem peraptè respondent initio digresionis, vbi dixit, eos segnes factos esse auribus. Nam & hic, & illic eadem dictio ῥᾳθυμοι habetur, etiamsi interpres hic maluit reddere imbecilles. Breuiter, hæc est totius digresionis summa, ipsaque conclusio, cùm quæ sequuntur confirmandi illustrandiq; gratia potissimùm sint adiecta. Sed Apostolus hic miro artificio expresit affectus, ac verba ipsa accommodatissima habet ad id, quod cupit, omnium animis instillandum.
units.tr: Having declared that he had spoken none of the harsher things with an ill intent, he now explains more clearly why he spoke in this way, and indeed to what end he set up this whole digression. Many of the Jews, offended by the preceding rebuke, would perhaps ask: "Why this, O Paul? What have we done to deserve that you assail us with such words?" He answers prudently: "We do not assail you out of peevishness, much less do we reproach you uncivilly; but we have spoken thus to this end, that we most ardently desire that each one of you show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope until the end. I say this to consult your salvation and to spur you on to undertake greater things; these things have been said by me not to discourage you, or to turn you from making progress, or to force you to despair." And while he explains in this way with what spirit he spoke all these things, he at the same time gives a general exhortation, in which the sum and head of the whole digression is contained. These things agree plainly with those set down at the beginning of this chapter, for the sake of exhortation, where he says: "Therefore, leaving aside the discourse on the rudiments of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection," and so on. You see that the last things answer beautifully to the first, indeed each thing to the other. But not content with this, whether to express his good feeling toward them more clearly, or to stir them more sharply to advance to higher things, by a rhetorical amplification he adds that he said all these things to this end: that they should no longer be slothful or weak, but should rather strenuously imitate their fathers, who, having advanced to the highest things, obtained the divine promises through faith and long-suffering. These words likewise answer very aptly to the beginning of the digression, where he said that they had become dull of hearing. For both here and there the same word, ῥᾳθυμοι [rathymoi, slothful], occurs, although the translator here preferred to render it "weak." In short, this is the sum of the whole digression and its very conclusion, since what follows was added chiefly for the sake of confirming and illustrating it. But the Apostle here has expressed his feelings with remarkable skill, and he has words most suited to instilling into all their minds what he desires.

units.la: Cupimus autem, ut unusquisque uestrum) ἐπιθυμοῦμεν. Obseruauit Chrysostomus, apposite ad affectum beneuolum prorsusque amicum pertinere, quod non dicit, volumus, aut iubemus, quod sanè imperiosius sonuisset: sed, cupimus, seu desideramus, paternam planè indolem egregiè delineans. Quis autem ita cupienti & quodammodo precanti, licet paulò seuerior increpatio antecesserit, non lubenter auscultet? ἐπιθυμῶ vehementer affecto & concupisco, 1 Thessalonic. 2. Cæterùm nos, fratres, orbati vobis ad spatium temporis, aspectu, non corde, vehementius studuimus videre faciem vestram cum multo desiderio, ἐν πολλῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ.
units.tr: Cupimus autem, ut unusquisque vestrum: ἐπιθυμοῦμεν [epithymoumen, we desire]. Chrysostom observed that it belongs to a kindly and thoroughly friendly feeling that he does not say "we wish" or "we command," which would have sounded more imperious, but "we desire" or "we long for," clearly portraying a paternal disposition. Who would not willingly listen to one who desires in this way, and almost entreats, even though a somewhat severer rebuke has gone before? ἐπιθυμῶ [epithymō] means to be vehemently affected and to long for, as in 1 Thessalonians 2: "But we, brethren, being bereaved of you for a short time, in presence, not in heart, endeavoured more eagerly to see your face with great desire," ἐν πολλῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ [en polle epithymia].

units.la: Vt unusquisq; uestrum idem præstet studium) En, quomodo non adimit illis prorsus omnes virtutes, sed plane tribuit studium aliquod ac diligentiā, eaque agit modestia, quasi dicat, se tantum velle, vt quemadmodum coeperunt, deinceps pergant. Qua sanè in re mirabilem ostendit Apostolus, Chrysostomo teste, prudentiam. Atque ipsa vox, vnusquisque, seu quisq; videtur indicare, quòd, cùm multi perstiterint, & constantes fuerint in fa na doctrina, tamen non in vnoquoq; par studium diligentiamq; potuisse, conspici: se proinde nunc auidè cupere, vt vnusquisque adeoque singuli parem industriam velint adhibere. Et propter tales quosdam rectè vsurpata verba præcedetia. Sed quomodocunq; accipiamus, ingenté certè affectū suum pro vtilitate illorum omnium optimè expresit, & sibi curæ esse omnes tàm paruos, quàm magnos, ostendit. Significat autem ἐπιδείνυμι, manifestum & conspicuum rei specimen siue exemplū præbeo, & veluti cum quadā cupiditate
units.tr: That each one of you show the same diligence: Behold how he does not take away from them all virtues altogether, but plainly attributes to them some zeal and diligence, and speaks with such modesty, as if he were saying that he only wishes them to continue on as they have begun. In this matter the Apostle, as Chrysostom bears witness, shows remarkable prudence. And the very word "each one," or "every one," seems to indicate that, although many had persisted and been constant in sound doctrine, yet the same zeal and diligence could not be seen in every one; therefore he now eagerly desires that each one, and so individually, should apply equal industry. And it is rightly for certain such persons that the preceding words are used. But however we take it, he has most excellently expressed his great affection for the good of all of them, and shows that all, both small and great, are of concern to him. ἐπιδείκνυμι [epideiknymi] means I offer a manifest and conspicuous specimen or example of a thing, and, as it were, with a certain eagerness.

units.la: Apostoli pru-dētia & studiū in excitandis animis audiētium. ἐνδείκνυμι qd. piditate glorię ex re benè gesta. Itaq; valde significanter Apostolus hic loquitur, & clarè significat, vt iudicari possit de profectu aliquorum in religione, opus esse claris & perspicuis demonstrationibus. Hinc 2. Petri 1. Operam date, vt vocationem & electionem vestram firmam efficiatis. Ideoq; alio loco suadetur, probandos esse spiritus, num ex Deo sint: & discretio spirituum inter dona spiritus Sancti numeratur. Oportet enim arripere certa indicia & argumenta, quibus veritas probetur, simulatioq; si qua subsit, detegatur. Ergo Apostolus vult serio & citra simulationem, vnumquemque intentum esse ad proficiendum in pietate.
units.tr: The Apostle's prudence and zeal in stirring the minds of his hearers. ἐνδείκνυμι [endeiknymi] means eagerness for glory from a well-performed deed. So the Apostle speaks very significantly here, and clearly indicates that, so that one may judge of the progress of some in religion, clear and perspicuous demonstrations are needed. Hence 2 Peter 1: "Give diligence to make your calling and election sure." Therefore elsewhere it is urged that spirits are to be tested, whether they are of God, and the discerning of spirits is counted among the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For one must seize upon certain signs and arguments by which the truth may be proved and any pretence, if there is some, may be detected. Therefore the Apostle wills that each one be earnest and without pretence, intent on making progress in piety.

units.la: Huc pertinet, quod ait, studium siue σπουδή, quæ vox laborem conatumque significat: quandoquidem non oscitantibus, sed laborantibus Deus collaborat. Vnde alibi iubemur omni tempore vigilare & circumspectè agere in omnibus, sic item instruere nos tanquam semper ad spiritualem pugnam parati: quia nimirum diligetia, studio, labore, opus est volenti in religione proficere.
units.tr: To this belongs what he says: zeal, or σπουδή [spoudē], a word that signifies labour and effort, since God works together not with the slothful but with those who labour. Hence elsewhere we are commanded to watch at all times and to act circumspectly in all things, and likewise to prepare ourselves as always ready for spiritual warfare; because, of course, diligence, zeal, and labour are needed by one who wishes to make progress in religion.

units.la: Ad plenam fidei certitudinem: πρὸς τὴν πληροφορίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος πληροφορίαν, quæ vox in scriptis apostolicis sæpè recurrit, significat certam & plenam persuasionem, quæ sit argumentis aut re ipsa exhibita, ita ut iam amplius nihil dubitari queat. Spes vero pro rebus sperandis, atq; ijs, quæ ad eas dirigunt tenduntq; per Metonymiam accipitur. Quare sententia horum verborum est: Eos omnes debere concordibus animis summa ope in id eniti, vt plenè persuadeantur, doceantur, de ijs omnibus, quæ ad futurâ vitam pertinet, quæq; scitu necessaria sunt ijs, qui in cognitione doctrinæ euangelicæ cupiunt serio proficere, gradúq; aliquè facere. Alij interpretatur de operibus, videlicet, eos debere operibus testatu facere, quod certa habeant spem futurorum bonorum. Sed malo exponere de profectu in doctrina euangelica, cùm scopus Apostoli in tota hac digressione sit, eos ad pleniorē & exactiorem cognitionē excitare: & nostra interpretatio cum præcedentibus omnibus, & proximè sequētibus magis quadrat. Et quò quis plenius edocetur, eò cōfirmatiore animo apprehendit bona vitæ futuræ: sicut e contrario, qui nequaquam plenè edocti sunt, facilè abilla spe abducuntur: sicut parabola euangelica docet de semine, quod cecidit, vbi radices non fixerat.
units.tr: To the full assurance of hope: πρὸς τὴν πληροφορίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος [pros tēn plērophorian tēs elpidos], a word that often recurs in the apostolic writings, signifies a certain and full persuasion, which is supported by arguments or by the thing itself displayed, so that nothing further can be doubted. But "hope" is taken by metonymy for the things hoped for, and for those things which lead to them and tend toward them. Therefore the sense of these words is: that all of them ought, with united minds, to strive with all their might to be fully persuaded and taught about all those things which pertain to the future life, and which are necessary to know for those who desire earnestly to advance in the knowledge of evangelical doctrine and to make some step forward. Others interpret it of works, namely, that they ought to show by their works that they have a sure hope of future good things. But I prefer to explain it of progress in evangelical doctrine, since the aim of the Apostle in this whole digression is to stir them to a fuller and more exact knowledge; and our interpretation agrees better with all that precedes and with what closely follows. And the more fully one is taught, the more confidently he grasps the good things of the future life; as, on the contrary, those who are not fully taught are easily drawn away from that hope, as the parable of the gospel teaches about the seed that fell where it had not taken root.

units.la: Vsq; ad perfectionem: εἰς τέλειος Id est, donec sitis perfecti & consummati in doctrina, qui hactenus in ea fuistis similes pueris, & tātum elemeta fuistis consecuti. Simili modo suprà initio huius capitis, ἐπὶ τὸν τελειότητα φερώμεθα, ad perfectionē feramur, omisso initiali sermone. Quò apparet interprete respexisse, dùm vocabulū perfectionis hîc retinuit. Et habet cognitio pietatis suos quosdā gradus, non aliter atq; ætas, & profectus in disciplinis humanioribus: qua de re elegater Ephesior 4. Alios dedit Apostolos, alios verò prophetas, alios autem euangelistas, alios autem pastores ac doctores, ad instaurationem sanctorum in opus administrationis, in ædificatione corporis Christi, donec perveniamus omnes in vnitatem fidei, & agnitionis filij Dei, in virum perfectum, in mensuram ætatis plenè adultæ Christi, vt non amplius simus pueri, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quouis vento doctrinæ. En alios in cognitione esse velut pueros, alios verò esse viros perfectos & adultos: id quod etiam indicauimus fusius in digressionis, initio capite quinto. Potest & aliter exponi, ἄχρι τέλους, id est, vsque in finem; seu per omnem vitam: vt sit sententia: aspirandam esse ad pleniorem certioremque rerum diuinarum cognitionem, quàm diu hîc viuitur, quo vniuerso tempore spacium & oportunitas discendi adest. Et nemo sic vnquam proficit, quin semper altius queat proficere, & plenius quidam addiscere: quandoquidem consummata omnibus numeris cognitio non nisi post hanc vitam obtingit, testante id Apostolo prima Corinthiorum decimotertio. Atque hæc quidem ad exhortationem sufficiebant, absoluuntq; sententiam: Sed placuit Apostolo, vt magis eos moueret, siue affectum suum etiam viuidius exprimeret, vt antè dixi-mus, superaddere.
units.tr: Unto perfection: εἰς τέλειον [eis teleion]. That is, until you are perfect and complete in doctrine, you who until now have been like children in it, and have attained only the elements. In a similar way, at the beginning of this chapter, ἐπὶ τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα [epi tēn teleiotēta pherōmetha], let us be carried on to perfection, leaving aside the discourse on the rudiments. By this it appears that the translator had regard to the original, when he retained the word "perfection" here. And the knowledge of godliness has its certain degrees, just as age and progress in the humanities do; on which matter Ephesians 4 speaks elegantly: "And he gave some apostles, and some prophets, and some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, until we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ; that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine." See, some are as children in knowledge, while others are perfect and full-grown men; which we have also pointed out more fully at the beginning of the fifth chapter of the digression. It can also be explained otherwise, ἄχρι τέλους [achri telous], that is, to the end, or throughout the whole of life; so that the sense is: we ought to aspire to a fuller and more certain knowledge of divine things for as long as we live here, during the whole time in which there is space and opportunity for learning. And no one ever advances so far that he cannot still advance higher and learn more fully; since knowledge complete in all respects is not attained except after this life, as the Apostle testifies in 1 Corinthians 13. These things indeed were enough for exhortation and complete the sense. But it pleased the Apostle, in order to move them more, or to express his feeling more vividly, as I said before, to add something further.

units.la: Ne sitis imbecilles) vel potius segnes, quomodo initio digressionis reddidit: Segnitiem enim & tarditatem, quam initio in eis accusauit ac damnauit, voluit præcedenti obiurgatione, imò tota hac digressione ab animis illorum excutere. Hic illi scopus est, hoc illius consilium. Quamobrem de proficiendo in doctrina aptè sumus proximè præcedentia verba interpretati. Concesit quidem Apostolus Hebræis diligentiam, ac laudem operum charitatis: sed profectum in doctrina in eis desiderat, sicut sæpè videre est etiam rudes & imperitos bonis operibus esse intentissimos. Atq; opera quidem satis edocti fuerant ex ipsa lege: sed in doctrina euangelica infantes adhuc erant parumq; promouerant.
units.tr: Do not be weak, or rather sluggish, as he rendered it at the start of the digression. For by the preceding rebuke, and indeed by this whole digression, he wanted to shake out of their minds the sluggishness and slowness that he had blamed and condemned in them at the outset. This is his aim and purpose here. That is why, when we interpreted the immediately preceding words, we rightly discussed advancing in doctrine. The Apostle has already conceded to the Hebrews their diligence and their praise for works of charity, but he finds them lacking in progress in doctrine. We often see that even the untaught and unskilled are very keen on good works. They had indeed been well enough instructed in works from the law itself, but in evangelical doctrine they were still infants and had made little progress.

units.la: Proinde cupit illos nō amplius in discēdo segnes esse, sed bonis operibus adiúgere studiū plenioris cognitionis: doctrinæ operū, q hauserat satis ex lege, coniungere doctrinā fidei, quæ euangelij psopria est. Hæc germana est apostolicorum verborum sententia, Sed imitatores eorum, qui per fidem ac patientiam hæreditatem accipiunt promissionis.
units.tr: Therefore he wants them no longer to be slack in learning, but to devote their zeal to good works and to fuller knowledge, joining to the doctrine of works, which they had learned well enough from the law, the doctrine of faith, which is proper to the gospel. This is the true sense of the apostolic words: But imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promise.

units.la: Addit rationem suasoriam ad tale studium alacrius proficiendi, sumptam ab aliorum præcipueque patrum exemplis, quos constat adeo diligentes fuisse, ficq; in cognitione rerum diuinarum profecisse, vt per fidem ac patientiam hæreditatem promissam à Deo acceperint. Quæ ratio eo artificiosius consultiusque est adhibita, quod Hebraei, quia maximi soliti sunt gloriari patribus, nullo pacto ad fugienda vitia, vel ad persequendas virtutes sic extimulantur, atque si exempla patrum eis ponantur ob oculos, à quibus degenerare filios, multò esse turpissimum, etiam natura omnes docet. Quanta autem fuerit patrum hac in parte excellentia, manifestius est, quàm vt pluribus demonstrari debeat. De ipso Abraham ita Christus Ioan. 8. Abraham pater vester exultauit, vt videret diem meum, & vidit, atque gauisus est. 1. Corinthior. 10 Omnia patribus communia sunt, quæ nobis sub euangelio. Romanor 9. de vniuerso Iudæorum genere: Quorum est adoptio, & gloria, & testamenta, & legis constitutio, & cultus, & promissiones, quorum sunt patres, & hi, ex quibus est Christus, quantum ad carnem attinet.
units.tr: He adds an argument to persuade them to pursue such study more eagerly, drawn from the examples of others, and especially of the Fathers, who were plainly so diligent and so advanced in the knowledge of divine things that through faith and patience they received the promise from God as an inheritance. This argument is employed the more skilfully and effectively because the Hebrews, who were accustomed to boast greatly of their fathers, are not spurred on in any way to flee vices or pursue virtues unless the examples of the fathers are set before their eyes. Nature itself teaches everyone that it is most shameful for sons to degenerate from such fathers. How great the excellence of the fathers was in this respect is too plain to need many proofs. Christ says of Abraham in John 8: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it and was glad. In 1 Corinthians 10: All things were common to the fathers, which are ours under the gospel. In Romans 9, of the whole Jewish race: To whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; of whom are the fathers, and of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came.

units.la: Quid, quòd Prophetæ, & Patriarchæ amplissimis donis fuerunt exornati, ex quibus clarè cerni potest, eos in cognitione rerū diuinarum exactè & plenè fuisse edoctos, eoq; conscendisse, quo altius scandi non potest? Talium igitur Patrum studium, diligentia, & profectus merito debet Hebræos excitare, vt excussa segnitie ad proficiendum vlterius enitantur. Etsi verò tantùm quædam periphrasis hic esse videatur, qua patres eorumq; præcipuae quaedam virtutes, quibus maximè fuere spectabiles, tanquam ante alias primo loco imitandæ commendantur, tamen illis verbis:
units.tr: What of the fact that the prophets and patriarchs were adorned with the richest gifts? From this it can clearly be seen that they were thoroughly and fully instructed in the knowledge of divine things and climbed to where no higher climb is possible. The zeal, diligence, and progress of such fathers should therefore rightly stir the Hebrews, so that, shaking off their sluggishness, they strive to advance further. Although here there seems to be only a kind of periphrasis, by which the fathers and certain of their outstanding virtues, for which they were especially admirable, are commended as things to be imitated above all else in the first place, nevertheless by those words:

units.la: Per fidem & patientiam seu longanimitatem) Occupationem minimè prætereundam subesse suspicor: idque eò magis, quòd vbi obseruando rationem antithesis, postquâ dixerat, non debere esse segnes, subijciendum fuisset, Sed imitatores eorum, quorum diligentia & profectus in cognitione rerum diuinarum passim celebrantur: placuit illi alijs vel bis dicere: sed imitatores eorum, qui per fidem & patientiam hæreditatem adepti sunt promissionis. Id autem hac de causa apparet factum. Segnes illi, quibuscum agit Apostolus, quemadmodum solet id genus hominum multa præterexere suæ ignauiæ, & quæuis causari, ne ad laborem pertrahantur (testante id Solomone, qui Prouerb. 22. scite describit pigrorum ingenium) illud fortasse causaturi erat, quòd profectus & perfectionis in religione nulli aut certè exigui perciperetur in hac vita fructus, atq; ita fœdâ suam segnitiem tueri & extenuare, aut sibi nonnihil indulgendum esse, voluissent obtinere. Proinde Apostolus, vt hunc prætextum talibus eriperet, omnemq; ignauiæ excusationem admeret, paucis graviter tamen, innuit, quòd, libet non statim succedat & percipiantur fructus promissi, at per fidem & longanimitatem eos tandem obtineri, & patres sic olim accepisse, quos ideò conuenit imitari. Eadem q; ratione significat, se vehementer cupere, vt saltè paulatim & temporis progressu enitantur proficere, nec non fide ac longanimitate præcipua esse spiritualis profectus signa atq; exercitamenta, per quæ ad perfectionem veniatur, eosq; iudicados plurimum proficere, in quibus fides & longanimitas clarius resplendere rint. Hæc porrò interpretatio non mediocriter confirmari mihi videtur illis, quæ mox subiiciuntur, videlicet, quòd Abrahâ, cùm patienter expectasset, cõsecutus fit promissum: item q spes velut ancora animæ tum tuta, tum firma, per quâ introimus ad ea vsq;, quæ sunt intra velū, id est, vsq; ad altissima & abstrusissima mysteria. Probat præterea hac sententia, quæ legitur de spe, Rom. 8. Sed & ipsi q primitias spiritus habemus, & nos ipsi in nobis ipsis gemimus adoptione, expectates redemptionem corporis nostri: si quidè spe seruati sumus. Porrò spes si videatur, nō est spes. Quod enim quis cernit, cur idè speret? Si verò quod nō videmus, speramus, id per patientiam expectamus. Vbi Apostolus illis verbis diluit cauillū illorū, qui obijciebat, nihil gloriae nobis per Christū partę in hac vita percipi: ac respondet, nos hic spe tenere, quod posthea obtinebimus re. Eodè igitur pacto nos hic interpretamur, satisfieri illis, qui ignauiâ suam tueri volētes, obijciebat, non apparere hic spiritualis pfectus & perfectionis fructus. Atq;, vt Apostolus semper valde circúspectè loquitur, & omnes remoras seu impedimenta solet tollere, puto sanè hac de causa eum hic de spe & longanimitate adiecisse, suamque hanc esse mentem, in sequentibus aniımaduerti posse. Et Chrysostomus, eumq; secutus Theophylactus, quædam habent non admodum disimilia à nostra interpretatione. Hæc enim fere est eorum sententia: de fide & patientia istâ addi, ne existimarent, se à Deo negligi vel contemni, si non statim promissa acciperent, sed scirent potius, fortes & strenuos viros debere hic varijs exerceri tentationibus, priusquam promissa accipiant, & Deum ipsum magnis & præstantibus viris sic vti solere. Nam si confestim traderet Deus, quod est pollicitus, nequaquam
units.tr: through faith and patience, or long-suffering. I suspect that a point not to be passed over lies hidden here. This is all the more likely because, when observing the form of antithesis, after he had said that they ought not to be sluggish, he should have added, "But imitators of those whose diligence and progress in the knowledge of divine things are celebrated everywhere." Instead he chose to say again, or a second time: "But imitators of those who through faith and patience obtained the promise." It appears that this was done for a reason. Those sluggards with whom the Apostle deals, as this sort of people usually do, make many excuses for their idleness and plead any cause so that they will not be drawn into labour (as Solomon testifies, who in Proverbs 22 neatly describes the nature of the lazy). They would perhaps have pleaded that no progress or perfection in religion was perceived, or only a very small fruit, in this life, and so they wished to defend and excuse their foul sluggishness, or to obtain that they should be allowed to indulge themselves a little. Therefore the Apostle, to snatch this pretext from such men and to remove every excuse for idleness, indicates briefly yet weightily that although the promised fruits do not come at once and are not perceived immediately, nevertheless they are finally obtained through faith and long-suffering, and that the fathers received them in this way of old, and so they ought to be imitated. By the same reasoning he signals that he earnestly desires them at least gradually, and as time goes on, to strive to advance, and that faith and long-suffering are the chief signs and exercises of spiritual progress, through which one comes to perfection; and that those who show faith and long-suffering most clearly are to be judged to be making the greatest progress. Moreover, this interpretation seems to me to be not a little confirmed by what follows immediately: namely, that Abraham, having waited patiently, obtained the promise; likewise that hope is like an anchor of the soul, both sure and firm, by which we enter into those things that are within the veil, that is, into the highest and most hidden mysteries. Furthermore, this sense is supported by what is read about hope in Romans 8: But we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body. For we were saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope; for why does one hope for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. There the Apostle refutes the objection of those who argued that no glory obtained through Christ is perceived in this life, and he answers that we hold to it here by hope, and afterwards we shall obtain it in reality. In the same way, then, we interpret here that an answer is given to those who, wishing to defend their idleness, objected that no spiritual progress or fruit of perfection appears here. And since the Apostle always speaks very cautiously and is accustomed to remove all hindrances and obstacles, I think he has added here the matter of hope and long-suffering for this reason, and that this is his intention, as can be noticed in what follows. Chrysostom, and Theophylact following him, have some things not very different from our interpretation. Their view is roughly this: that this patience and faith are added so that they would not think they were neglected or despised by God if they did not receive the promises at once. Rather, they should know that brave and vigorous men must be tried here by various temptations before they receive the promises, and that God himself usually deals in this way with great and outstanding men. For if God gave immediately what he had promised, it would by no means

units.la: Ratio ab exemplo patrum hortatur ad studium proficiendi.
units.tr: The argument from the example of the fathers urges zeal for advancing.

units.la: Fides Patrum robusta.
units.tr: The robust faith of the fathers.

units.la: Occupatio.
units.tr: Diligence.

units.la: Segnities in fide doctrina est periculosa. Piger leo est in via.
units.tr: Sluggishness in faith and doctrine is dangerous. "The sluggard says, there is a lion in the way."

units.la: Per fidem percipiuntur fructus & successus, etc.
units.tr: Through faith fruits and success are obtained, etc.

units.la: Apostoli uotu. Spe introducunda quæ sunt intra uelum.
units.tr: The Apostle's wish. By hope those things that are within the veil are to be brought in.

units.la: Spe hic tenenda, quæ olim obtinebimus in re.
units.tr: Here we must hold by hope what we shall afterwards obtain in reality.

units.la: Ante perceptione bonorum futuræ uitæ: tentationes huius uitæ perferredæ. quaquam, quanta effet credentium fides, deprehenderetur: quæ tunc quidé manifesta euadit, vbi etiamsi longum tempus intercedat, priusquam promissa præstetur, inconstâs & inconcussa perseuerat, & neque torpore minuitur, neque metu non recipiendi promissa euellitur. Sed de his satis. Quod ad partes attinet, notat Theophylactus, fidem nō abs re præponi patientiæ seu longanimitati(ita enim aliàs solet interpres longanimitatem vertere, & hoc loco puto sententiam id exigere, quando paulò post agit de expectatione per patientiam, item de spe) quando quidé longanimitas ex fide oriri solet, & vbi firma non est fides, ibi non potest quispiam longanimiter Dei promissa expectare. Est verò opus fide & longanimitate ei, qui vult fructus spiritualis profectus & perfectio nis percipere. Sicut in discedis artibus non licet statim peruenire ad summa, sed minutis incrementis ad altiora conscenditur: ita plane in cognitione rerum diuinarum, & spirituali perfectione paulatim duntaxat incrementa percipiuntur. Absoluta autem, & cui nihil deest cognitio, contingit post hanc vitam. Quare homini ad perfectionem contendenti verè magna fide & longanimitate opus est. Cæterum vox κληρονομήσαντος, id est, hæreditario iure accipientium, magnam habet in Scripturis gratiam, amplisimamque Dei bonitate erga homines graphicè depingit: significat enim ita accipere homines à Deo bona promissa, tanquàm si hæreditario iure illis obtingeret, & à Deo haberentur pro filijs, qui ipsi in possessione omnium bonorum succedant, omniaque communia cum ipso habeant, sicut filij carnales habent communia, & participant bona carnalium parentum. Et quia tàm apta est, ad significandam summa Dei bonitatem erga homines, ideò spiritus Sanctus crebrò in Scripturis eam usurpat. Atque eam significatione ac vim vocis exposuit Apostolus Roman. 8. vbit ait: Quicunque spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filij Dei. Non accepistis spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba pater. Idem spiritus testatur vnà cum spiritu nostro, quòd sumus filij Dei. Quòd si filij, igitur & hæredes: hæredes quidé Dei, cohæredes autè Christi. Quæ omnia oportet, mente concipere, quoties de hæreditate promissionum quicquam occurrit.
units.tr: Before the enjoyment of the good things of the future life, the temptations of this life must be endured. be made clear how great the faith of believers was, which is indeed made manifest when, even if a long time passes before the promises are fulfilled, it persists unwavering and unshaken, and is neither weakened by torpor nor torn away by fear of not receiving the promises. But enough of this. As for the words, Theophylact notes that faith is not without reason placed before patience or long-suffering (for elsewhere the translator usually renders long-suffering in this way, and I think the sense here requires it, since a little later he speaks of waiting with patience, and likewise of hope). For long-suffering usually arises from faith, and where faith is not firm, no one can patiently wait for God's promises. Faith and long-suffering are indeed needed by the one who wishes to obtain the fruits of spiritual progress and perfection. Just as in the liberal arts one cannot reach the highest things at once, but one climbs to higher things by small increments, so plainly in the knowledge of divine things and in spiritual perfection, increases are received only gradually. Complete knowledge, lacking nothing, comes only after this life. Therefore the man who strives toward perfection truly needs great faith and long-suffering. Furthermore, the word kleronomēsantōn [κληρονομήσαντος], that is, of those receiving by right of inheritance, has great grace in the Scriptures and vividly depicts the immense goodness of God toward men. For it signifies that men receive the good promised by God as though it came to them by hereditary right, and that they are regarded by God as sons, who succeed to possession of all good things and share everything in common with him, just as natural sons share things in common and partake of the goods of their natural parents. And because this word is so apt for signifying the supreme goodness of God toward men, the Holy Spirit often uses it in the Scriptures. The Apostle set out the meaning and force of this word in Romans 8, where he says: As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, by which we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit bears witness together with our spirit that we are the children of God. And if children, then heirs; heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ. All of these things ought to be kept in mind whenever anything about the inheritance of the promises comes to mind.

units.la: Per promissiones hoc loco intelligi cōuenit in genere quæcúque bona, maximè autè spiritualia, quæ Deus credentibus & longanimiter expectantib. cognoscitur promisisse. Iam videamus, quid hîc nobis discendum propositum sit.
units.tr: By "promises" in this place we should understand, in general, all good things, especially spiritual ones, which God is known to have promised to believers who wait patiently. Now let us see what we are here taught to learn.

units.la: Primum discimus, quo animo obiurgationes & monitiones fieri debeant, nimirum, non ut fratres nostros contemptos reddamus aut despectos, neque ut nostris indulgeamus affectibus, eosque lædamus, qui nos offenderint: neque ut aliquos in desperatione deijciamus, sed ut ad frugē eos reuocemus, & in rectiorem viam reducamus: quomodo Apostolus hic dicit, se cupere illorum profectum & salutem. Omnis quàmlibet seuerae aut durae increpationis origo & finis esse debet charitas, à qua omnes etiam actiones nostras decet sumere initium, & in quam omnes debent desinere.
units.tr: First, we learn with what attitude rebukes and admonitions ought to be given: not to make our brothers contemptible or despised, nor to indulge our own feelings and wound those who have offended us, nor to cast anyone down into despair, but to call them back to a better course and lead them into a more upright way. So the Apostle here says that he desires their progress and salvation. The origin and end of every rebuke, however severe or harsh, ought to be love, which should also be the starting point of all our actions and the goal to which they all return.

units.la: Secundò discimus, quòd non subito & sine laboribus detur in rerum diuinarū cognitione, & in his, quæ sunt pietatis, proficere. Opus est multo magnoque studio, nec eo quidem occulto, sed aperto & manifesto, ut palàm deprehendi queat, utrum gradum in pietate quis faciat. Non vno die aut mense perdiscit aliquis textrinam, ut fabrile, ut sculpturam, ut picturam, aut artes, quas vocat illiberales: sed opus multo tepore & assiduis exercitijs: quantò plus iudicabimus requiri tempus, & experientiam tentationum, ac periculorum, ut quis conscendat ad perfectionem pietatis? Multi, inquit Apostolus ad Titum 1. profitentur, se Deum scire, cæterum factis negant, cùm sint abominabiles, & dicto non audientes, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi. Et 2. Timoth. 2. Multi habentes formam pietatis, sed vim eius abnegates. Quocirca mirādum est illorum iudicium, qui putat statim lectis paucis libellis, fingi absoluique theologus, priusquam nulla sublimiorum rerum theoria, nulla spiritualium rerum praxis illis sit explorata.
units.tr: Second, we learn that growth in the knowledge of divine things, and in those matters that belong to godliness, does not come suddenly or without labour. It requires much effort and great zeal, and not a hidden zeal but an open and visible one, so that it can be plainly seen whether someone is making progress in godliness. No one learns weaving, metalworking, sculpture, painting, or those arts called "illiberal" in a day or a month; they require much time and constant practice. How much more, then, must time and experience of temptations and dangers be needed for anyone to climb to the perfection of godliness? "Many," says the Apostle to Titus (1), "profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him, since they are abominable and disobedient, and unfit for any good work." And in 2 Timothy 2: "Many have the form of godliness, but deny its power." Therefore the judgement of those is to be wondered at who think that a theologian can be formed and perfected as soon as a few small books are read, before any theory of higher things or any practice of spiritual things has been tested in them.

units.la: Tertiò discimus hic, quomodo exempla sanctorum patrum sint diligenter proponenda, & quanti æstimanda. Sunt enim hi veluti typi, ad quorum fidem virtutesque revocanda est posteritas. Sic in epistola ad Romanos cap. 3. & 4. ad exemplum fidei Abrahæ filij credetes accersuntur. Sic Ioannis octauo capite, Christus Iudæos ad fidem & obedientiam Abrahæ reducit, iubetque à desideriis malis & affectibus satanæ, si germani filij Abrahæ & vocari, & esse desiderent. In historijs regum pij successores ad Dauidis vias & integritatem respicere iubentur, laudanturque, si huius vitam et fidem sint secuti: vituperantur contrà, qui ab hisce deflexerunt, & Ieroboamum filium Nebat sunt secuti. De quo plura Psalmo 89. & historia Salomonis ac posterorum.
units.tr: Third, we learn here how the examples of the holy fathers are to be carefully set forth and held in high esteem. For they are, as it were, types, to whose faith and virtues posterity ought to be recalled. So in the Epistle to the Romans, chapters 3 and 4, believers are summoned to the example of the faith of Abraham, the father. So in John chapter 8, Christ leads the Jews back to the faith and obedience of Abraham, and bids them, if they wish to be called and to be true children of Abraham, to abandon evil desires and the affections of Satan. In the histories of the kings, the godly successors are commanded to look back to the ways and integrity of David, and they are praised if they have followed his life and faith; on the contrary, those who turned aside from these and followed Jeroboam the son of Nebat are blamed. More on this may be found in Psalm 89, and in the history of Solomon and his posterity.

units.la: Deus enim pollicitus Abrahæ, cū nō posset per quenquam maiorem iurare, iurauit per seipsum, dicens: Nisi benedicens benedixero tibi, & multiplicans multiplicauero te: atque ita cum patienter expectassef, consecutus est promissum. Nam homines quidem per eum iurant, qui sit maior, atque ipsdem omnis controuersia finis est, si accedat iurisiurandi confirmatio. Qua in re Deus cum eximie vellet haeredibus promissionis ostendere firmitatem constily sui, interposuit iusiurandum, uti per duas res immutabiles, in quibus fieri non posset, ut mentiretur Deus, validam consolationem habeeremus, qui huc confugimus, ut potiamur propositae spe, quam velut ancoram tenemus animae, cum iutam, tum firmam, et introeuntem usque ad ea quae sunt intra velum, vbi praecursor pro nobis est Iesus.
units.tr: For God, when he promised Abraham, since he could swear by no one greater, swore by himself, saying: "Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you." And so, when he had patiently waited, he obtained the promise. For men indeed swear by one who is greater, and for them every dispute finds its end when an oath is added as confirmation. In this matter God, wishing especially to show to the heirs of the promise the firmness of his counsel, interposed an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, we who have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us, which we hold as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which enters into that within the veil, where Jesus has gone before us as a forerunner.

units.la: Haec omnia uti paulo ante dixim us, ad septimum usque caput, confirmandi illustrandi gratia sunt addita. Primo igitur loco addit probationem, quod per fidem & longanimitatem accipiantur fructus promissi, perueniaturque ad perfectionem, ab exemplo ipsius Abrahami, cuius profectus in rebus, diuinis plus, quam aliorum patrum, illustris extitit, cuiusque filij & imitatores agnosci Hebraei maximopere affectabant. Unde vnum hoc exemplum multorum loco, & ad probationem abunde sufficiens. Sic autem argumentatur: Abraham fide & longanimitate consecutus est Dei promissiones.
units.tr: All these things, as we said a little earlier, are added up to the seventh chapter for the sake of confirming and illustrating. In the first place, then, he adds a proof: that through faith and patience the fruits of the promise are received, and perfection is reached, from the example of Abraham himself, whose progress in divine things stood out more than that of the other fathers, and whose children and imitators the Hebrews were especially eager to be recognised as. Hence this one example is enough in place of many, and is amply sufficient as a proof. He argues in this way: Abraham, by faith and patience, obtained the promises of God.

units.la: Ergo & vos, si in fide & longanimitate perstiteritis, fructus promissionis percipietis.
units.tr: Therefore you also, if you persist in faith and patience, will receive the fruit of the promise.

units.la: Hoc Enthymemate summa omnium horum comprehenditur: sed admiscet ac subijcit nonnulla Apostolus ad exponendum expoliendumque accommoda, quod expediens iudicarit pluribus verbis inculcare, quod videlicet fide ac longanimitate ad perfectionem ascendatur, & promissiones obtineantur. Hinc est, quod statim obiter indicat animaduertendum esse, quomodo fides longanimitasque in nobis confirmari queant, nempe ex duabus causis, videlicet ex ipsa promissione, quod, ubi Deus quid promisit, opus sit fide adhibere: Deinde ex promissionis forma: quandoquidem vbi quid iuramento firmatum est, necesse est id perfici. Quas duas causas ipse mox plenius exponit. Hoc enim sibi vult, dum praemonens obseruadam adhibitam iuramenti formam (quando inquam ait, Cum non posset per quenquam maiorem iurare) citat ex Genes. 22. luculentam promissionem, iuramenti forma expressam, quam ita accipi vult, tanquam ad omnes credentes in genere pertinentem: sicut reuera omnes promissiones euangelicae tam in veteri testamento, quam nouo exhibitae, vniuersaliter omnibus a Deo sunt propositae, & ex aequo ad omnes pertinent, ut per eas omnium pariter piorum animi in fide & spe, seu longanimitate confirmentur. Sicut Roman. 4. Non propter Abraham scriptum, &c. Et ipse Apostolus mox declarat, ad nos pertinere, qui ad spem confugimus. Ideo vero delegit hanc promissionem prae quibuscunque aliis ad Abrahamum factis, quod ea ad declarandum, quomodo, qui in fide & longanimitate perstiterint, promissiones accipiant, multo fit aptissima: quandoquidem ea post fidem Abrahae longo tempore, & per multos annos probatam, facta atque adimpleta est. Nam sicut colligitur ex historia Geneseos prima promissio, ut habetur Gen. 12. facta est ad Abrahamum hisce verbis: faciam te in gentem magnam, & benedicam tibi, & magnificabo nomen tuum, erisque benedictus. Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, & maledicam maledicentibus tibi, atque in te benedicetur vniuersae cognationis terrae. Hoc tempore agebat Abraham annum septuagesimum quintum, ac iam fides illius erat hac promissione excitata, ac deinceps exercitanda.
units.tr: The sum of all these things is comprised in this enthymeme; but the Apostle adds and subjoins some matters suited to explaining and clarifying it, since he judged it fitting to press upon them at greater length the point that by faith and patience one ascends to perfection and obtains the promises. Hence he immediately indicates in passing that we must consider how faith and patience can be strengthened in us, namely from two causes: first, from the promise itself, since where God has promised something, faith must be applied to it; and second, from the form of the promise, since where something has been confirmed by an oath, it must necessarily be fulfilled. The Apostle soon explains these two causes more fully. For this is what he means when, first noting the form of oath used (when, I say, he says "since he could swear by no one greater"), he cites from Genesis 22 the clear promise, expressed in the form of an oath, which he wishes to be understood as pertaining to all believers in general. Indeed, all the evangelical promises, both in the Old Testament and in the New, are offered universally by God to all, and pertain equally to all, so that by them the minds of all the godly alike may be confirmed in faith and hope, or patience. Compare Romans 4: "It was not written for Abraham's sake alone," etc. And the Apostle himself soon makes clear that it pertains to us who flee to hope. He chose this promise rather than any others made to Abraham because it is most apt for showing how those who persevere in faith and patience receive the promises; for it was made and fulfilled after Abraham's faith had been tested over a long time, through many years. For, as is gathered from the history of Genesis, the first promise, as found in Genesis 12, was made to Abraham in these words: "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you, and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." At this time Abraham was seventy-five years old, and his faith had already been stirred up by this promise and was thereafter to be exercised.

units.la: Rursus Geneseos decimotertio audiuit hanc promissionem, omnem terram, quam conspicis, tibi dabo, & semini tuo vsque in sempiternum, faciamque semen tuum sicut pulue rem terrae. Geneseos capite decimoquinto petiuit Abraham filios sibi dari, & audiuit a Domino: non erit hic (vernaculus tuus) haeres tuus, sed qui egredietur de vtero tuo, ipsum habebis haeredem: Et paulo post, suspice coelum, & numera stellas, si potes, sic erit semen tuum. Credidit Abraham Deo, & reputatum est illi ad iustitiam. Et eodem capite: in illo die pepigit Dominus foedus cum Abraham, dicens: Semini tuo dabo terram hanc. Sed postquam ne tunc quidem adhuc habuit filium, capite decimosexto refertur, quod volente Sara ingressus sit ad ancillam Agar, quae illi genuit Ismaelem, anno aetatis Abrahae octogesimosexto. Iterum anno nonagesimo nono (Genes. 17.) Abrahae renouatum foedus, repetita promissio, confirmataque institutione circumcisionis, & promissus in annum sequentem nasciturus Isaac ex Sara. Anno igitur centesimo aetatis Abrahae natus est Isaac (Genes. 21.) Cum vero hic iam successisset, & iam in delitiis esset, maximamque spem posteritatis faceret, Deus iusit hunc ipsum filium sibi offerri in holocaustum, quod & Abraham non detrectauit, sed paratus fuit illu, in quo vno spes omnis sita erat posteritatis, quemque totannis petiuerat & expectarat, propria manu interficere & immolare. Genes. 22. Postquam igitur & hoc & multis aliis modis, veluti bellis, peregrinationibus & similibus periculis, per plurimos, a prima promissione facta annos, nempe ad minimum
units.tr: Again, in Genesis chapter 13 he heard this promise: "All the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed for ever, and I will make your seed like the dust of the earth." In Genesis chapter 15 Abraham asked that children be given to him, and he heard from the Lord: "This man (your home-born servant) shall not be your heir, but he who shall come out of your own body, he shall be your heir." And a little later: "Look up to heaven, and number the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be." "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness." And in the same chapter: "On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your seed I will give this land." But since even then he still had no son, it is related in chapter 16 that, at Sarah's wish, he went in to her maidservant Hagar, who bore him Ishmael, when Abraham was eighty-six years old. Again, in his ninety-ninth year (Genesis 17), the covenant with Abraham was renewed, the promise was repeated, the institution of circumcision was confirmed, and Isaac was promised to be born of Sarah in the following year. So in the hundredth year of Abraham's life Isaac was born (Genesis 21). But when this son had now grown up, and was already the object of delight, and was giving the greatest hope of posterity, God commanded that this very son be offered to him as a burnt offering; and Abraham did not refuse, but was ready to slay and sacrifice with his own hand the one in whom alone all hope of posterity lay, whom he had asked for and waited for year after year. (Genesis 22.) Therefore, after this and many other trials, such as wars, wanderings and similar dangers, over very many years, namely at least from the first promise made...

units.la: Probatio: q per fidem & longanimitatem accipiuntur fructus promissi, & pfectio ab exemplo Abrahami. Abraham fide assequitur Dei promissiones. Fides duab. in reb. a nobis aguntur & confirmatur, promissionis videlicet forma, quae iuramentum habet. Promissiones euangelicae sunt uniuersales. Prima promissio extra parentes ad Abrahamum facta. Genes. 12. Abrahami aetas in prima promissione fuit 75. annorum. Genes. 13. Genes. 15. Abraham iustificatur per fidem. Genes. 16. Ismael gignitur ex Agar, anno aetatis Abrahae 86. Genes. 17. Renouatio foederis anno 99. per circumcisionem. 25. anni a prima promissione. Genes. 21. Isaac nascitur anno 100. Genes. 22. Isaac iubetur immolari. mum triginta octo, aut plures, (si Isaac salte tredecim fuerit annorum) Dominus probasset fidem & longanimitatem Abrahæ, tandem volens omnia promissa adimplere, ita per Angelum ad eum locutus est: Per memetipsum iuravi, dicit Dominus, quia fecisti hanc rem, & non pepercisti filio tuo vnigenito, benedicam tibi, & multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum, sicut stellas cœli, & velut arenam, quæ est in littore maris. Possidebit semen tuum portas inimicorum suorum, & benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terræ, quòd obedisti voci meæ. Merito ergo Apostolus hanc promissionem præ quibuscunq; aliis produxit in medium, & recte per omnia probat, quòd, qui in fide & longanimitate expectarint, hæreditatem promissionis sint accepturi.
units.tr: Proof that the promised fruits are received through faith and patience, and the example of Abraham shows this to be perfect. Abraham by faith obtains God's promises. Faith is exercised and confirmed in two respects: namely, the form of the promise, which has an oath. The evangelical promises are universal. The first promise was made to Abraham outside his parents' home. Gen. 12. Abraham's age at the first promise was 75 years. Gen. 13. Gen. 15. Abraham is justified by faith. Gen. 16. Ishmael is born of Hagar, when Abraham was 86. Gen. 17. The covenant is renewed in the 99th year, by circumcision, 25 years after the first promise. Gen. 21. Isaac is born in the 100th year. Gen. 22. Isaac is commanded to be sacrificed. When the Lord had tested the faith and patience of Abraham for thirty-eight years or more (even if Isaac was at least thirteen years old), he at last, wishing to fulfil all his promises, spoke to him through the angel in this way: "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son, I will bless you, and by multiplying I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice." Rightly, therefore, the Apostle brought this promise forward before all others, and he proves in every respect that those who wait in faith and patience shall receive the inheritance of the promise.

units.la: Neque verò aliqua est in verbis Apostoli difficultas: omnia illa: Cum nõ posset per quenquam maiorem iurare: per seipsum iurauit, dicens: Nisi benedicens benedixero tibi, & multiplicans multiplicauero te, interposuit, partim ut subindicaret, quo loco in sacris literis colligatur, quòd Abraham per fidem & longanimitatem fit promissum cosecutus, partim ut intentos redderet animos in promissionem, ac cerneret, iuramento eam confirmatam, ac proinde eiusmodi, per quam vnusquisque priuatim in fide & longanimitate exemplo Ahrahę confirmetur.
units.tr: Nor is there any difficulty in the words of the Apostle. He inserted all those words, "Since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself, saying: Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you," partly to point out in which place of Holy Scripture it is gathered that Abraham obtained the promise through faith and patience, and partly to make minds attentive to the promise and to see that it was confirmed by an oath, and therefore of such a kind that each person, following the example of Abraham, may be strengthened in faith and patience.

units.la: Citata autem sunt verba ex septuaginta interpretib. apud quos sic legitur, ἀ μὴν ἀλογῶν ἀλογήσω σε, καὶ πληθύνων πληθυνῶ τὸ σπέρμα σου, ὡς τὴν ἄμμον τῆς θαλάσσης, &c.
units.tr: The words are quoted from the Septuagint, where they read thus: ἀμὴν ἀλογῶν ἀλογήσω σε, καὶ πληθύνων πληθυνῶ τὸ σπέρμα σου, ὡς τὴν ἄμμον τῆς θαλάσσης, etc.

units.la: Vbi particula ἀμήν adverbium est, iuramentis accommodum, quomodo etiam usurpamus particulam Nisi, quadam apostiopesi, ad maiorem vim exprimendam, veluti cum dicimus, Nisi istud fecero: non quòd ista particula ἀμήν, idem fit, quod ἀμήν, id est, nisi, vel, si non, sed quòd fere idem fit eius vsus. Vnde nonnulli ut declarent, valde, aptam ad confirmandum aliquid, quemadmodum fieri solet in iuramentis, vertunt eam, profectò, sanè, sicut vertit Primasius & ipse Theophylactus, qui etiam adnotat eodem pacto usurpari ad confirmandam veritatem, hanc vocem, ἀμήν, quomodo Christus crebrò vsurpat voce Hebræam אמן Amen, quæ afferendę veritati seruit. Quanquàm in Hebræo hęc particula non habetur אמן אמן, id est, Quoniam benedicendo benedicam tibi, & multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum. Vbi particula הא continuatiua est coniunctio. Tigurini verterunt, certissimè benedicam tibi.
units.tr: Here the particle ἀμήν [amen] is an adverb suited to oaths, just as we also use the particle "Unless," by a kind of aposiopesis, to express greater force, as when we say, "Unless I do that": not that this particle ἀμήν is the same as ἀμήν [amen], that is, "unless" or "if not," but that its use is almost the same. Hence some, to express that it is very apt for confirming something, as is customary in oaths, translate it "truly," "certainly," "surely," as Primasius and Theophylact himself do. Theophylact also notes that in the same way this word ἀμήν is used to confirm the truth, just as Christ often uses the Hebrew word אמן, Amen, which serves to assert truth. Although in the Hebrew this particle is not found, [אמן אמן], that is, "Because by blessing I will bless you, and by multiplying I will multiply your seed." Here the particle הא is a continuative conjunction. The Tigurine translators rendered it, "most certainly I will bless you."

units.la: Interea tamen, etiamsi non respiciatur in eam particulam apud Septuaginta, ἀμήν, tamen rectè dicitur, promissionem eam iuramento firmatam, quandoquidem promittitur in scriptura, Per memetipsum iuravi, dicit Dominus, quia fecisti hac re, &c. In quæ verba Apostolum respexisse verosimilius est, quàm in particulam בי, propterea quòd disertè ait, cum nõ posset per quenquam maiorem iurare, iurauit per seipsum: Quibus verbis notat, promissionem debere esse multò certissimam, quando ea iuramento est confirmata, quo maius præstari non posset. Neque enim aliquid certius vlla ratione potest confirmari, quàm per ipsum Deum, qui est ipsissima veritas, & neq; fallere, neque falli potest. De qua iurandi forma etiam post agemus. Satis hic annotare, Apostolum voluisse oculatè considerari, promissionem eam iuramento confirmari, cuius rei causam ipse mox explanat. Quod autem verba promissionis attinet, sciendum est, eiusmodi formulas loquendi, Benedicendo benedicam, multiplicando multiplicabo, (Rhetores vocant Traductionem, cum eadem vox mutato casu repetitur) venustatem habere in hebræo sermone, & præterea habere singularem Emphasin, ad varios affectus significandum.
units.tr: Meanwhile, even if no word corresponding to that particle ἀμήν is found in the Septuagint, it is still rightly said that the promise is confirmed by an oath, since Scripture says, "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing," etc. It is more likely that the Apostle had regard to these words than to the particle בי, because he expressly says, "Since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself." By these words he shows that a promise ought to be much more certain when it is confirmed by an oath, than which nothing greater could be given. For nothing can be confirmed more certainly in any way than by God himself, who is very truth itself, and can neither deceive nor be deceived. We shall speak later of the form of this oath. It is enough to note here that the Apostle wished us to consider carefully that the promise was confirmed by an oath, the reason for which he explains immediately afterwards. As for the words of the promise, it must be known that such forms of speech, "Blessing I will bless, multiplying I will multiply" (rhetoricians call this traductio, when the same word is repeated with a changed case), have elegance in the Hebrew language, and besides have a special emphasis for expressing various feelings.

units.la: Primò autem ad significandam magnam certitudinem: quomodo &1. Reg. 2. Quacunque die egressus fueris, & transieris torrentem Cedron, sciens scias, quod morte morieris. Alias significat repetitio talis frequentiam & comminationem. vt Geneseos tertio, Multiplicando multiplicabo dolorem tuum, & conceptum tuum: vbi valde multiplicem & continuum dolorem fore significatur.
units.tr: First, indeed, they signify great certainty, as in 1 Kings 2: "On whatever day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall surely die." Otherwise such repetition signifies frequency and a threat, as in Genesis 3: "I will greatly multiply your pain and your conception," where it is signified that the pain will be very manifold and continual.

units.la: Alias verò significat acceleratiorem & cotinuationem, vt Genes. 2. De omni ligno horti comedendo comedes. Et paulo post. Quacunque die comederis ex ea, morte morieris. Vbi prioris exempli geminatio illa significat continuationem, quòd videlicet assiduè & continuè illis vescerentur: Posterioris exempli significatio acceleratione, quòd videlicet statim morerentur, & mortis sentirent imperium.
units.tr: Otherwise it signifies speed and continuance, as in Genesis 2: "Of every tree of the garden you shall eat freely." And a little later: "On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Here the doubling of the first example signifies continuance, namely that they would feed on those things constantly and continually; the meaning of the second example is speed, namely that they would die at once and feel the rule of death.

units.la: Proinde hac promissione, cùm ait, benedicendo benedicam, significatur, quòd certò & valdè citò vellet benedicere. Rursus cùm ait, Multiplicando multiplicabo, idem est, ac si diceret, frequenter & cōtinuè augebo te resque tuas omnes. Itaque magna vis inest verbis promissionis, quam merito obseruemus.
units.tr: Therefore, by this promise, when it says "blessing I will bless," it is signified that he would bless certainly and very quickly. Again, when it says "multiplying I will multiply," it is the same as if it said, "I will increase you and all your possessions frequently and continually." Thus great force lies in the words of the promise, which we should rightly observe.

units.la: Benedicere autem idem est, quod fortunare, fœlicem dare successum, locupletare, & equitur quædam eius vocis interpretatio, quando additur, multiplicádo multiplicabo.
units.tr: To bless, moreover, is the same as to make fortunate, to give a happy outcome, to enrich, and a certain explanation of that word follows when "by multiplying I will multiply" is added.

units.la: Benedictio autem hæc tam in spiritualibus, quàm in temporalibus bonis intelligenda est, sicut vtrumque etiam verbis Dei exprimitur, quando ait, semen ipsius possessurum portas.
units.tr: This blessing, moreover, must be understood both in spiritual and in temporal goods, as both are expressed by the words of God when he says that his seed shall possess the gates.

units.la: Á i portas inimicorū, quod de temporalibus bonis recte accipitur. Præterea, In semine ipsius benedicedas omnes gentes terræ, quod ad spiritualia bona recte refertur, quæ per Christum humano genere sunt collata. Huiusmodi itaque promissione tàm insignem, Abraham post diuturnam expectationem consecutus est, ut omnes quoque debeant promissionibus Dei fidere, & longanimiter promissos fructus expectare.
units.tr: "The gates of its enemies," which is rightly taken of temporal goods. Besides, "In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed," which is rightly referred to spiritual goods, which have been conferred on mankind through Christ. Abraham, therefore, after long expectation, obtained so remarkable a promise of this kind, so that all also ought to trust in the promises of God and patiently await the fruits promised.

units.la: Sed, dicat aliquis, quomodo dicitur, Abraham ū cōsecutum res promissas, cùm tamen terram illam Canaan, quā Deus promiserat illi Genes. 13. nunquā possederit, sicut dicitur Actorum septimo, quòd Deus non dedit illi hæreditatem in ea, ne vestigium quidem pedis.
units.tr: But someone may say: how is it said that Abraham obtained the promised things, when yet he never possessed that land of Canaan which God had promised him in Genesis 13, as it is said in Acts 7, that God gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth?

units.la: Præterea cùm non viderit multiplicationem filiorum, sicut promissio sonabat: Deniq; cùm aperte etiam huius epistolæ capite vndecimo dicatur, quòd Abraham reliqui̇ patres iuxta fidem mortui sint omnes, cùm non accepissent promissiones, sed procul tantum eas vidissent, & credidissent, salutassentque? Respondetur.
units.tr: Besides, since he did not see the multiplication of his descendants, as the promise sounded; and finally, since it is plainly stated in the eleventh chapter of this Epistle that Abraham and the other fathers all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them only from afar, and having believed and greeted them? I reply.

units.la: Sicut duplices promissiones sunt, temporales inquam & spirituales: ita duplici modo patres eas obtinuerunt, quasdam nimirum in re, quasdam in spe.
units.tr: Just as the promises are twofold, temporal, I mean, and spiritual, so the fathers obtained them in a twofold way: some indeed in reality, others in hope.

units.la: Spirituales, quæ potiores sunt, & in quas potissimum intenti fuerunt patres, in spe obtinuerūt, quòd circa eas debebat fides ipsorum per omnem vitam exerceri: atq; ita capite vndecimo huius epistolæ dicitur, in fide mortuos esse, & promissiones, videlicet cœlestes non accepisse, sed tantùm salutasse, &c.
units.tr: The spiritual promises, which are the more important, and on which the fathers were chiefly intent, they obtained in hope, because their faith had to be exercised concerning them throughout their whole life. And so in the eleventh chapter of this Epistle it is said that they died in faith, and did not receive the promises, namely the heavenly ones, but only greeted them from afar, etc.

units.la: Sicut & nos omnes hic etiam post reuelatum euangelium eas in spe accipimus, cùm nunc quidem tantùm per speculum & ænigmaticæs eas contemplemur, 1. Corinth. 13.
units.tr: Just as we all also, even here after the gospel has been revealed, receive them in hope, since now we contemplate them only through a glass and in an enigma, 1 Corinthians 13.

units.la: Quod autem attinet ad carnales promissiones, de terra Canaan possideda, de multiplicatione filiorum, dicitur, quòd, tametsi non ita perfectè cerneret Abraham eas adimpletas, tamen iam vidit præparationem ad implendas eas, & sensim cœpit res succedere, quando illius opes, & potentia, & autoritas, in bellis, in aliis euentib. creuerunt, quando filijs duobus auctus est: ita ut reuera mirabiles fructus benedictionis diuinæ senserit, itaque confirmatus fuerit, tanquàm si omnia coràm vidisset impleta.
units.tr: As for the carnal promises, concerning the possession of the land of Canaan and the multiplication of descendants, it is said that although Abraham did not see them fulfilled so perfectly, yet he already saw the preparation for their fulfilment, and gradually things began to succeed, when his wealth, power and authority grew through wars and other events, when he was blessed with two sons. So he truly perceived the wonderful fruits of divine blessing, and was thus strengthened, as if he had seen everything fulfilled before his eyes.

units.la: Deinde quod in ipso completum non fuit, hoc collatum est eius semini, ad quod communiter promissiones pertinebant: & sic ipse possedit terram, & occupauit omnia in semine, seu in filijs, quomodo Ezechielis tertio dicitur, vnus erat Abraham, & hæreditate possedit terram, id est, possedit in hæredibus & per filios, quos certò sciebat omnia promissa diuina consecuturos.
units.tr: Then, what was not completed in him was bestowed on his seed, to which the promises were commonly referred. So he possessed the land and occupied everything in his seed, or in his sons, as it is said in Ezekiel 3: "Abraham was one, and by inheritance he possessed the land." That is, he possessed it in his heirs and through his sons, whom he knew would certainly obtain all the divine promises.

units.la: Denique omnia illi adimpleta sunt in vno semine, videlicet Christo, cuius diem ipse quoq; vidit & gauisus est: atque ita adimpleri omnia ipse vidit: neque Deus potest vanitatis coargui quasi fidelem Abrahamum aliqua in re fefellisset. Ideoque valde notanda sunt etiam verba Apostoli.
units.tr: Finally, all things were fulfilled for him in the one seed, namely Christ, whose day he also saw and rejoiced (John 8:56). So he saw all things fulfilled. God cannot be convicted of vanity, as if he had deceived his faithful Abraham in any matter. Therefore the words of the Apostle are also to be carefully noted.

units.la: Atque ita cum patienter expectasset, consecutus est promissum) maximè quod ait μακροθυμήσας, id est, longanimiter expectans. Ita enim notat, longanimitatem in illis requiri, qui diuina promissa sunt recepturi.
units.tr: And so, having patiently waited, he obtained the promise: especially what he says, makrothymēsas [μακροθυμήσας], that is, waiting with long patience. For this indicates that long-suffering is required of those who are to receive the divine promises.

units.la: Promittit quidem Deus, nec potest quicquam amplius in eo desiderari: sed ex parte nostra etiā illud requiritur, ut simus longanimes, adeò, ut Chrysostomus nō dubitauerit dicere, nostram longanimitatem non minus necessariam & efficacem in acceptione bonorum spiritualiū, atque ipsam Dei promissionem. Cùm animaduertere liceat, eos promissiones Dei non accipisse, qui longanimes non fuere, quales fuere murmurantes & impatientes, ac queruli illi in deserto, qui quia noluerunt longanimes expectare, promissam terram nunquam ingressi sunt. Ergo valde commendanda est longanimitas, & recte dicitur, Abrahamum consecutum esse promissiones, eò quòd longanimiter expectasset: Sequitur:
units.tr: God indeed promises, and nothing more can be desired on his part. But on our part it is also required that we be long-suffering, so much so that Chrysostom did not hesitate to say that our long-suffering is no less necessary and effective in receiving spiritual goods than God's own promise. It may be observed that those did not receive God's promises who were not long-suffering, such as those murmuring, impatient and complaining people in the desert, who, because they would not wait patiently, never entered the promised land. Therefore long-suffering is to be highly commended, and it is rightly said that Abraham obtained the promises because he waited patiently. The text continues:

units.la: Nam homines quidem per eum iurant, qui sit maior, atque ijs de omnis controuersia finis est, si accedat iurisiurandi confirmatio.
