Qua in re Deus cum eximie vellet haeredibus promissionis ostendere firmitatem consilij sui, interposuit iusiurandum, vt per duas res immutabiles, in quibus fieri non posset, ut mentiretur Deus, validam consolationem haberemus, qui huc confugimus, ut potiamur propositā spe.
units.tr: For men indeed swear by one greater than themselves, and for them an end of every controversy is confirmation by oath. In this matter God, wishing especially to show the heirs of the promise the firmness of his purpose, interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled here to lay hold of the hope set before us might have a strong consolation.

units.la: Quod prius obiter indicauit de obseruando iuramento promissioni diuinæ annexo, iam plenius exponit, vt nimirum hac ratione promissionum diuinarum euincat certitudinem, atque inde inferat, omnes debere in fide & longanimitate confirmari, nec non promissos fructus indubitatò & longanimiter expectare. Sic autem argumentatur à forma & vsu seu causa finali iuramenti apud homines vsitati.
units.tr: What he had earlier touched on in passing, about the oath attached to the divine promise, he now explains more fully. His purpose is to establish by this reasoning the certainty of the divine promises, and thence to infer that everyone ought to be confirmed in faith and long-suffering, and to await the promised fruits without doubt and with patience. He argues in this way from the form and use, or final cause, of the oath as it is customary among men.

units.la: Vbi homines confirmant aliquid iuramento, præsertim per Deum facto, creditur eorum verbis, atque id, quod spondent, firmum ratumque habetur.
units.tr: When men confirm something by an oath, especially one sworn by God, their words are believed, and what they promise is held firm and valid.

units.la: Atqui Deus promissiones suas (inprimis illam ad fidelé ac longanimem Abrahamū) confirmauit iuramento, & quidem per Deum, quo nihil maius,facto.
units.tr: But God confirmed his promises (above all that made to the faithful and long-suffering Abraham) by an oath, and indeed by God, than whom there is nothing greater.

units.la: Ergo nos quoque decet promissionib.diuinis credere,& pro certo habere eas,si modò in fide & longanimitate exemplo Abrahae perstiterimus erga nos adimplendas.
units.tr: Therefore it is fitting for us too to believe the divine promises and hold them as certain, provided that we persevere in faith and long-suffering, after the example of Abraham, until they are fulfilled toward us.

units.la: Ac ducitur plane hoc argumentum à minore ad maius affirmatiué,tanquàm si simpli- citer diceretur: Homines credunt iuranti homini. Igitur multò magis credent iuranti Deo, cui alias iniurato, & tantum promittenti credere omnes iure debét. Omnis homo natura mendax: Deus autem natura verax,nec fallere,nec falli potest: Quare ergo,si ho- mini credimus, non multo magis credamus Deo? Verùm Apostolus aliquanto splendi dius hoc argumentum effert, rhetorum more nonnulla aspergens, quæ rationem quasi succo & colore magis viuida efficiant.Nos ea inter explicandu breuiter annotabimus.
units.tr: This argument is plainly drawn affirmatively from the lesser to the greater, as if it were simply said: men believe a man who swears; therefore much more will they believe God who swears, whom everyone ought to believe by right even when he has not sworn but only promised. Every man is a liar by nature; God is true by nature, and can neither deceive nor be deceived. Why, then, if we believe man, should we not much more believe God? But the Apostle sets this argument forth more splendidly, after the manner of the rhetoricians, sprinkling in some things which make the reasoning, as it were, more vivid in juice and colour. We shall briefly note these as we explain them.

units.la: Nam homines quidem) A rebus humanis quædam producere ad comprobandum res di- uinas aliquando licet, imò nonnunquàm fit valdè appositè, ut hoc loco videre est: præ-sertim ubi ratio aliqua ducitur à minori ad maius affirmatiue. Non tamen id crebrò usur-pandum,præsertim ubi ualde disparia sunt,quæ conferenda ueniunt. Neq; aliàs à rebus humanis necessariæ trahitur consequentiæ, sed tantùm contingetes & probabiles. Ideo magna prudentia hic opus est.
units.tr: For men indeed: it is sometimes permissible, and indeed sometimes very apt, as can be seen here, to bring forward human things to prove divine things, especially where an argument is drawn affirmatively from the lesser to the greater. Yet this should not be used often, especially where things very unlike one another are being compared. Nor do necessary consequences otherwise arise from human things, but only contingent and probable ones. Therefore great prudence is needed here.

units.la: Per eum iurant, qui sit maior) causa formalis iuramenti notatur,ex qua,quàm seriò ac legi- timè factum fit,quantamque vim habeat obligandi, aduerti debet. Etenim cùm iuramē-tum semper in hoc fiat,ut confirmet,seu potius ut obliget,nempe,vel alterum ad præstā-dum,vel alterum ad credendum,conuenit adhiberi iuramento rem præstantiorem quā-piam,cuius veneratione atque excellentia hominum animi permoueantur ad habendū pro certo & rato, quod eius nominis commemoratione significatur.Et cùm nihil sit ex- cellentius magisque venerandum ipso Deo, hinc receptissima iurandi formula est, qua per Deum iuratur. Vnde scriptura Deuteronomij sexto præscribit,per nomen Dei iurá-dum. Dominum Deum tuum timebis,inquit, & ipsi soli seruies, ac per nomen illius iu- rabis. Item Esaiæ 45. & 65. Et illæ formulæ iurandi passim sunt obuiæ : viuit Dominus: Hæc faciat mihi Deus, & hæc addat 2. reg. 3. Item, viuit anima mea: &, testis est mihi Deus Roman.1. &c. Testem Deum inuoco in animam meam. 2. Corinth. 1. Notandumque, quasdam formas obtestationis, & imprecationis accipi simplici quadam attestatione & confirmatione,vti in prioribus illis fit: quasdam verò tàquam per execrationem,utpote quæ sic sonant,tanquàm si dicatur: Ita me Deus bene amet, vel male me perdat, vlciscá-tur in animam meam.
units.tr: By one greater they swear: the formal cause of the oath is noted, and from it one should observe how seriously and lawfully it is made, and what force it has to bind. For since an oath is always made so as to confirm, or rather to bind, either the one to perform a promise or the other to believe it, it is fitting to use for the oath something more excellent, by whose veneration and excellence men's minds are moved to hold as certain and valid what is signified by the mention of its name. And since nothing is more excellent or more worthy of veneration than God himself, the most received formula of swearing is that by which one swears by God. Hence Scripture, in Deuteronomy 6, prescribes swearing by the name of God: "You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him alone, and you shall swear by his name." Likewise Isaiah 45 and 65. Such formulas of swearing are met with everywhere: "As the Lord lives"; "God do so to me, and add this" (2 Reg. 3); likewise "as my soul lives"; and "God is my witness" (Rom. 1), and so on. "I call God as witness against my soul" (2 Cor. 1). It should be noted that some forms of adjuration and imprecation are taken as a simple attestation and confirmation, as in those former examples; but others are taken as by way of execration, such as those which sound as if one said: "So may God love me well, or destroy me badly; may he take vengeance on my soul."

units.la: Iosephgenes.42. iurauit per salutè Pharaonis, nō quòd summo loco haberet Pharaō nem quasi Deum,sed quòd in eo Dei potestas & maiestas eluceret: quandoquidē omnis potestas à Deo est. Atque ita per creaturam iuratur, non simpliciter propter dignitatem creaturæ, sed quia in ipsa ut valde eximia dignitas ac maiestas Dei spendidius elucet. Quanquàm dici rectius potest,Iosephum iurasse per salutem Pharaonis, quadam forma execrationis,quasi diceret:ita Deus tueatur salute Pharaonis,vel ita benefaciet Pharaoni. In summa, videamus quascunque iuramentorum formas,in scripturis extantes,& inue-niemus semper iuramenta, per maiorem fieri, in primis per Deum, & certè per ea, quæ maximo loco sunt,& in quib. Dei potestas resplédet: vt,viuit Deus:Iesus est mihi Deus. Item,viuat anima mea: quid aliud,quàm Deus animæ meæ salutem tueatur: Testem in-uoco Deum in animam meam,id est,Deus malè me perdat,si ita non est,ut dico. Item per salutem Pharaonis,id est,ita Deus benefaciat Pharaoni: vel, per Seruatorem Pharao-nis. Hucpertinet,quòd olim iurantes leuare manum ad cœlum solebant. Tantum de iu-ramentorum formulis.
units.tr: Joseph swore by the health of Pharaoh (Gen. 42), not because he held Pharaoh in the highest place as a god, but because the power and majesty of God shone forth in him, since all power is from God. So one swears by a creature, not simply on account of the creature's dignity, but because in it the exceedingly excellent dignity and majesty of God shines more brilliantly. Although it can be said more correctly that Joseph swore by Pharaoh's health with a kind of formula of execration, as if he said: "So may God keep Pharaoh's health, or so may he do good to Pharaoh." In sum, let us look at whatever forms of oath are found in the Scriptures, and we will always find oaths made by one greater, above all by God, and certainly by those things which hold the highest place and in which the power of God shines: "As God lives"; "Jesus is my God." Likewise "may my soul live": what else is this but "may God keep my soul safe"? "I call God as witness against my soul" means "may God destroy me if it is not as I say." Likewise "by the health of Pharaoh" means "so may God do good to Pharaoh," or "by the Saviour of Pharaoh." To this belongs the custom that those swearing of old used to raise their hand to heaven. So much for the formulas of oaths.

units.la: Atq; ijsdem omnis controuersiæ finis est, si accedat iurisiurandi confirmatio. ) Causa finalis seu vsus,adeoque effectus iuramenti. Nam in hoc adhiberi solet apud Iudices in foro iuramentum quasi extremum,post cætera omnia frustrà tentata, remedium, vt omnis dubitandi litigandiqué tollatur occasio, & de eo, quod in controuersiam venit, aliquid certi statuatur.
units.tr: And the same things make an end of every controversy when confirmation by oath is added. This is the final cause, or use, and so the effect of the oath. For in court before judges an oath is customarily employed in this way, as a last remedy after all other attempts have failed, so that the occasion for all doubt and dispute may be removed, and something certain be settled about what has come into controversy.

units.la: Porrò has duas potissimum causas iuramenti voluit Apostolus spectandas propone-re,omissis aliis,quæ de iuramento commodè dici poterant, quòd utraq; in iuramento Domini annexo promissioni obseruanda veniat. Nam & Deus in iuramento suo for-mam præscriptam retinuit, per maiorem videlicet,id est, per seipsum, quo maius nihil excogitari queat,iurans:præterea in eum finem, ut omnis dubitandi de promissis ipsius occasio tolleretur. Atq; hisce duabus causis principalibus legitimum iuramentum effi- citur,ut impleri necessum sit.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle wished to set forth for consideration chiefly these two causes of the oath, leaving aside the others that could fittingly be said about oaths, because both of these apply to the oath which the Lord annexed to the promise, to be observed. For in his oath God retained the prescribed form, namely swearing by one greater, that is, by himself, than whom nothing greater can be conceived. Furthermore, he did so to the end that every occasion of doubting his promises might be removed. By these two principal causes a lawful oath is made, so that it must necessarily be fulfilled.

units.la: Certè de hac caussa finali iuramenti tum in lege Mosaica,tum in Iure Ciuili Romano-rum rum non pauca extant, quæ tamen recitare non est opus:tum apud gentiles præclarè etiam numerantur exempla de fine & causis iuramenti edita: semperque religiosissimè apud gentes quascunque præstitum fuit, quicquid iuramento promissum fuerat. Sanè Exodi 22. sic legimus:Si quis commendauerit amico pecuniam,vel vas in custodiam,& ab eo, qui susceperit, furto ablata fuerint, si inuenitur fur, duplum reddat: Si latet fur, dominus domus applicabitur ad Deos, & iurabit, quòd non extenderit manum in rem proximi sui, ad perpetrandam fraudem, &c. Ibidem: Si quis cômodauerit proximo suo asinum,bouem,ouem,& omne iumentum ad custodiam, & mortuum fuerit, aut debilitatum vel captum ab hostibus, nullusque hoc viderit, iusiurandum erit in medio, quòd non extenderit manum ad rem proximi sui, suscipietque dominus iuramentum, & ille reddere non cogetur. En quomodo per iuramentū domino redditum confirmata sit rei veritas, unde reus absoluitur, accusatorque nihil amplius potest exigere, & sic finitur controuersia. Veritate confirmata, quò vlterius eatur? Proprie enim iuramenti finis & effectus est confirmare veritatem,qua confirmata,tolluntur controuersiæ. Unde non tantum in iudiciis foresibus præstari soletiuramentū, verū etiam in contractibus, maximè fœderibus & pactis quibuscunque, quæ confirmationem requirunt. Sic Genesis vicesimo quinto iurauit Esau ipsi Iacob, se daturū primogenita. Genes. 26. Iurat sibi mutuo Abimelech & Isaac,quòd alter alteri nō sit nociturus. Genes. 47. Iosephiurat patri, quòd post mortem translaturus sit ossa eius in terram Canaan. 1. Samuel. 20. Dauid & Ionathan fœdus ineunt, idque iuramento confirmant.
units.tr: Certainly concerning this final cause of the oath, both in the Mosaic law and in the civil law of the Romans there are not a few things, which, however, need not be recited. Among the Gentiles also, examples setting out the purpose and causes of the oath are famously recorded; and whatever had been promised by oath was always most religiously performed among all peoples. Indeed Exodus 22 reads thus: "If anyone commits money or goods to his friend for safekeeping, and they are stolen from the one who received them, if the thief is found, he shall restore double; if the thief is not found, the master of the house shall be brought before God, and he shall swear that he has not put his hand to his neighbour's property to commit fraud," and so on. Likewise in the same place: "If anyone lends his neighbour an ass, an ox, a sheep, or any beast for keeping, and it dies, or is injured or taken by enemies, and no one has seen it, an oath shall be made between them, that he has not put his hand to his neighbour's property; and the master shall accept the oath, and the other shall not be compelled to restore it." See how, by an oath given to the master, the truth of the matter is confirmed, whereby the accused is acquitted and the accuser can demand nothing further, and so the controversy ends. Once the truth is confirmed, where can one go further? For the proper end and effect of an oath is to confirm the truth, and once it is confirmed, controversies are removed. Hence an oath is customarily given not only in courts of law but also in contracts, especially covenants and pacts of every kind which require confirmation. So in Genesis 25 Esau swore to Jacob that he would give him his birthright. Gen. 26: Abimelech and Isaac swear to each other that neither will harm the other. Gen. 47: Joseph swears to his father that he will carry his bones to the land of Canaan after his death. 1 Sam. 20: David and Jonathan enter a covenant and confirm it by oath.

units.la: Ea propter solent distinguere iuramentū aliud esse assertorium, quo videlicet de rebus præteritis vel præsentibus veritas simpliciter asseritur, aliud verò promissorium, quo videlicet aliquid futurum asseueratur. Quemcunque verò in finem tendat, perspicuum fit, confirmandæ veritatis,atque ita tollendæ omnis controuersiæ ergò, iuramētum adhiberi. Ideoque contra iusiurandum non licet facere, cùm violentum iuramentum grauissimè à Deo puniatur: cuius exemplum luculentum habemus 2. Samuelis 21. vbi iuramentum à Saule violatum,quo iurauerant Israelitæ,se non nocituros Gabaonitis, fametrium annorum punitur à Deo,nec cessat malum,nisi morte septem filiorum Saul suspensorum ab ipsis Gabaonitis. Sed quomodo obliget iuramentum,quomodo ei veritas,iudicium & iustitia adiuncta esse debeant, & alia quædam eius generis, nos paulo post fusius explicabimus. Item quomodo intelligendi loci,qui videntur iuradi potestatem adimere in Euangelio,&c.
units.tr: Hence they usually distinguish between an assertory oath, by which the truth of past or present matters is simply affirmed, and a promissory oath, by which something future is solemnly promised. Whatever the end it serves, it is clear that an oath is used to confirm the truth and so to remove every controversy. Therefore it is not lawful to act against an oath, since God punishes a violated oath most severely. We have a striking example in 2 Samuel 21, where the oath that the Israelites had sworn, not to harm the Gibeonites, was violated by Saul, and God punished it with a famine of three years. The evil did not cease until seven of Saul's sons were hanged by the Gibeonites themselves. But how an oath binds, how truth, judgement and righteousness ought to be joined to it, and certain other matters of that kind, we will explain more fully a little later. Likewise, how the passages that seem to take away the power of swearing in the Gospel are to be understood, etc.

units.la: Quain re Deus cùm eximiè vellet hæredibus promissionis ostendere firmitatem consilij sui, interposuit iusiurandum.
units.tr: Why God, wishing very much to show the heirs of the promise the firmness of his purpose, interposed an oath.

units.la: Erant præcedentes causæ de forma videlicet, & de fine iuramenti hic repetendæ, ut Minor argumenti simpliciter absoluetur: sed satis duxit inculcare caussam finalem, tū quòd ea vel maximè sit spectāda ad confirmandos in fide & longanimitate animos,tum quòd formalem supra exposuerit,vbi dixit: cùm non posset per maiorem iurare, iurauit per seipsum. Atque vtitur vocibus multo aptissimis.
units.tr: The earlier causes, namely of the form and of the purpose of the oath, were to be repeated here, so that the minor point of the argument might be fully completed. But he thought it enough to press the final cause, both because it is chiefly to be considered for confirming minds in faith and patience, and because he had already set out the formal cause above, where he said: since he could not swear by a greater, he swore by himself. And he uses words most apt for the purpose.

units.la: Cùm vellet, inquit,eximiè ostendere, περισσότερον ἐπιδεῖξαι, ἐπιδείνυμαι & ἐπιδέιγνυμι idem quod euidenter demonstro, & quasi ad ostentationem exhibeo: unde ἐπιδεῖξαι demonstrationes, quales sunt mathematicorum, & ἐπιδεικτικὸν γένος τῆς λόγης, genus orationis demonstratiuum. Itaque sententia est, quòd valde cōspicuam,euidente,& certam voluerit Deus promissionem suam reddere. Sed addidit præterea,περισσότερον: verbum περισσόν significat abundo,supero,& περισσὸς,superfluus,abundans. Quare sententia est, quòd non satis fuerit illi, clarè satis demonstrare certitudinem promissionis, sed prꝫterea clarius id eum fecisse, quàm reuera necesse erat,vel, quàm facere tenebatur. Quādoquidem vbi satis fuisset simpliciter promittere,voluit Deus insuper,quod non opus erat,iuramento se obstringere. Vides ergo quàm appositè expressit summam certitudinem.
units.tr: "Since he wished," he says, "to show very clearly" (περισσότερον ἐπιδεῖξαι [perissoteron epideixai]). ἐπιδεῖξαι, ἐπιδείκνυμαι and ἐπιδείκνυμι mean the same as to demonstrate evidently, and as it were to exhibit for display. Hence ἐπιδείξεις are demonstrations, such as those of the mathematicians, and ἐπιδεικτικὸν γένος τοῦ λόγου [epideiktikon genos tou logou] is the demonstrative kind of speech. So the sense is that God willed to render his promise highly conspicuous, evident and certain. But he added moreover περισσότερον: the word περισσόν means abundant, exceeding, and περισσός means superfluous, abundant. So the sense is that it was not enough for him to demonstrate the certainty of the promise clearly enough; he also did so more clearly than was really necessary, or than he was bound to do. For where it would have been enough simply to promise, God wished in addition, which was not required, to bind himself by an oath. You see, then, how aptly he expressed the highest certainty.

units.la: Sed adhuc magis exprimit eam, dicēs,τὸ ἀμετάθετον,id est,immutabilem,quodq; nullo pacto mutari seu transponi posset: sicut hominum promissa vel etiam summè cōfirmata: tamen mutari ac dissolui subinde cernūtur,quod nullo pacto promissis Dei potest tribui τῆς βεβαίως αὐτῆς. Dicendū erat,promissionis ἐπαγγελίας: Quare autem dicit, consilij? Respondeo: Hac voce significari, quòd Deus nihil faciat sine certo consilio & iustis causis,ac proptera certiores nos esse debere de adimpletione promissionum, quas constat ex sapientissimo consilio trahere originem. Quicquid Dominus semel consultò statuit, necessum est id adimpleri, iuxta illud Esaiæ 46. Consilium meum stabit,& omnis voluntas mea fiet. Et psalmo 32. Dominus reprobat consilia principum. mox sequitur:Consilium autem Domini in æternum manet.
units.tr: But he expresses it still more strongly, saying τὸ ἀμετάθετον [to ametathetion], that is, the immutable, which could in no way be changed or altered, as the promises of men, even when most solemnly confirmed, are nevertheless seen to be changed and dissolved from time to time; whereas this cannot in any way be attributed to the promises of God (τῆς βεβαιώσεως αὐτῆς [tes bebaiosseōs autēs]). It ought to have said "of the promise" (ἐπαγγελίας [epangelias]). Why then does he say "of the counsel"? I answer: this word signifies that God does nothing without a sure counsel and just causes, and therefore we ought to be more certain of the fulfilment of the promises, which clearly derive from his most wise counsel. Whatever the Lord has deliberately decided once, it must necessarily be fulfilled, according to that saying of Isaiah 46: My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done. And Psalm 33: The Lord brings the counsels of the princes to nothing; and soon after follows: But the counsel of the Lord endures for ever.

units.la: Nota
units.tr: Note.

units.la: Non quòd imaginari debeamus, Deum humano more ratiocinantem & deliberantè, quid eligere velit aut reijcere: Sed dicitur cõsilium ipsius immutabilis voluntas, ipsiusq; velle, est simpliciter consulere, vel consultare, quomodo consilium & voluntatem rectè ab Esaia coniuncta cernis. Itaq; ipsum consilium Domini verè dicitur immutabile.
units.tr: Not that we should imagine God, reasoning and deliberating in a human manner, what he wishes to choose or reject. But his counsel is called his immutable will, and to will is simply to take counsel or to deliberate, as you see the counsel and the will rightly joined together by Isaiah. Thus the very counsel of the Lord is truly said to be immutable.

units.la: Quanquàm negari non potest, per prouidentiam Dei quaedam interdum mutari, quæ tamen aliter prius fuerant proposita. Hinc illud Hieremiæ 18. Repente loquar aduersus gentem, & aduersus regnum, ut eradicem & destruam, & disperdam illud: Si poenitentiam egerit gens illa à malo suo, quod locutus sum aduersus eam, agam & ego poenitentiam super malo, quod cogitaui ut facerem ei. Item Esaiae 37. ad Ezechiam, Dispone domui tuæ, quia morieris tu, & non viues. Similiter Ionæ 3. Adhuc quadraginta dies, & Niniue subuertetur. In quibus testimonijs quæ proposita sunt tanquam necessariò propter voluntatem Dei adimplenda, constat ea nequaquam impleta fuisse. Verùm nô ideo dicendum, quòd consilium, vel voluntas Dei inuertatur, aut affectus commutetur: quandoquidem Deus non est, ut homo qui mutetur, vel poenitentia ducatur, sicut ipse Bileam fatetur Numerorum vicesimotertio: Sed dicendum, in eiusmodi propositionibus, etsi simpliciter affirment, tamen latentes conditiones contineri. Apud Hieremiam clarè dicitur, si egerint poenitentiam, mala omnia ab illis auertenda.
units.tr: Yet it cannot be denied that through the providence of God certain things are sometimes changed, which had earlier been proposed otherwise. Hence the saying of Jeremiah 18: Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root up, pull down and destroy it; if that nation turns from its evil, against which I have spoken, I too will repent of the evil which I purposed to do to it. Likewise Isaiah 38 to Hezekiah: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live. Similarly Jonah 3: Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. In these testimonies, the things that were proposed as if they must necessarily be fulfilled because of the will of God are clearly shown not to have been fulfilled at all. Yet we should not therefore say that the counsel or will of God is overturned, or that his purpose is changed, since God is not like a man who changes or is moved to repentance, as Balaam himself confesses in Numbers 23. Rather, it must be said that in propositions of this kind, even if they are affirmed absolutely, hidden conditions are nevertheless contained in them. In Jeremiah it is plainly said: if they repent, all the evils are to be averted from them.

units.la: Ezechias verò sic præmonitus fuit, ut ad orandum excitaretur. Niniuitis comminatus est Deus per Ionam, ut ad poenitentiam similiter se conuerterent, quod ubi fecissent, salutem adepti sunt, id quod Dominus haud dubiè ita futurum prædestinarat & constituerat. Manet igitur semper inuiolabile cõsilium Domini: & sic promissiones ipsius intelligi debent necessariò adimplendæ.
units.tr: Hezekiah, however, was so forewarned in order to be stirred to prayer. God threatened the Ninevites through Jonah, so that they likewise would turn to repentance; when they did so, they obtained salvation, which the Lord had undoubtedly predestined and determined would so come to pass. Therefore the counsel of the Lord always remains inviolable, and so his promises must be understood as necessarily to be fulfilled.

units.la: Τοῖς κληρονόμοις: En hic promissiones factas ad Abraham, transfert ad omnes hæredes, omnes posteros: quandoquidem non tantùm ad personam Abrahæ pertinebant, sed ad vniuersum eius semen. Et cùm semen Abrahæ sint non tantùm qui secundum carnem ex eo sunt nati, sed omnes reuera, qui sequuntur fidem ipsius, quam habuit ille adhuc in præputio agens: (id quod plenius docetur Romanor. 4. & 9. Galat. 4.) sequitur, ad omnes credentes tàm gentiles, quàm Iudæos istas promissiones pertinere. Igitur istud significare volens, dicit generaliter, τοῖς κληρονόμοις, hæreditatem accipientibus, id est, omnibus credentibus. Cùm verò ad omnes credentes pertineant hæ promissiones, æquû est, eos omnes de promissionibus certò adimplendis in fide & spe confirmari. Propterea enim interposuit, inquit, iusiurandum. Vbi fragilitas nostra nos à credendo et spe rando abduceret, debet iusiurandum interpositum animos nostros erigere, & in fide confirmare. Neque tantùm de hac promissione citata accipiendum est, quòd iuramento sit confirmata, sed præterea de multis alijs, quæ extant Deuteron. 7. 11. Lucæ 1. Genef. 26. Iosuæ 21. 1. Samuel. 12. item Dauid, & in omnibus patribus factis. Non puto aptè adnotatum à nonnullis, quòd in hac commemoratione iuramenti respiciat Apostolus ad id, quòd Christus fuerit iuramento confirmatus pontifex secundum ordinem Melchisedec. Nam ea particula pòst suo tempore excutietur.
units.tr: To the heirs [τοῖς κληρονόμοις]: Here he transfers the promises made to Abraham to all the heirs, all the posterity, since they pertained not only to the person of Abraham but to his whole seed. And since the seed of Abraham are not only those who are born of him according to the flesh, but in truth all who follow the faith which he had while still living in uncircumcision (as is taught more fully in Romans 4 and 9, and Galatians 4), it follows that these promises pertain to all believers, Gentiles as well as Jews. Therefore, wishing to signify this, he says generally to the heirs, that is, to those who receive the inheritance, namely all believers. Since these promises pertain to all believers, it is right that all of them be confirmed in faith and hope concerning the promises that are certain to be fulfilled. For this reason, he says, he interposed an oath. Where our frailty would draw us away from believing and hoping, the interposed oath ought to lift up our minds and confirm them in faith. Nor is it to be understood only of this cited promise that it was confirmed by an oath, but also of many others, which are found in Deuteronomy 7 and 11, Luke 1, Genesis 26, Joshua 21, 1 Samuel 12, likewise of David, and in all the fathers' acts. I do not think it has been rightly noted by some that in this mention of the oath the Apostle looks to the fact that Christ was confirmed by an oath as priest according to the order of Melchizedek. For that particle will be examined in its proper place later.

units.la: Vti per duas res immutabiles, in quibus fieri non posset, ut mentiretur Deus, validam consolationem haberemus, qui huc confugimus, ut potiamur propositaspe.
units.tr: That through two immutable things, in which it would be impossible for God to lie, we who have fled here to lay hold of the hope set before us might have a strong consolation.

units.la: Hæc pro conclusione syllogismi accipienda sunt. Plus autem infert, quàm necesse erat, & quàm ex duabus præmissis simpliciter sequebatur. Infert namque, duas ob res, videlicet ob promissionem ipsam, quæ vel sola sufficiens esse debebat: deinde, ob confirmationem eius per iuramentum, tali forma, & in eum finem adhibitum, debere eos merito fideles & longanimes perfistere, sicque magna cum consolatione fructus promissos expectare. Duas autem illas res vocat immutabiles, quia simpliciter, quod promisit Deus, citra conditionem adiunctam debet impleri: multò autem magis debet impleri ipsius iuramentum. Interserit rationem huius immutabilitatis, à natura ipsius Dei, secundum quam necessariò verax est, nec mentiri seu in iurando, seu in promittendo tantùm potest. In quibus inquit, fieri non posset, ut mentiretur Deus. In quibus, scilicet promisso & iuramento.
units.tr: These words are to be taken as the conclusion of the syllogism. But they imply more than was necessary, and more than could simply follow from the two premises. For they imply that, on two grounds, namely the promise itself, which should have been sufficient on its own, and then its confirmation by an oath, employed in such a form and for such a purpose, believers ought rightly to persevere faithfully and patiently, and so with great comfort await the promised blessings. He calls these two things immutable because what God has promised must be fulfilled absolutely, without any added condition; but his oath must be fulfilled far more surely still. He gives the reason for this immutability from the nature of God himself, according to which he is necessarily truthful and cannot lie, either in swearing or in promising. Of these two things, he says, it is impossible that God should lie: that is, of the promise and of the oath.

units.la: Validam consolationem haberemus) ἰσχυρὰν addit validam, vt intelligeretur, non parvam, nec modico tempore duraturam, sed valde amplam planeque inconcussam consolationem & certitudinem omnes debere conspicere ex eo, quòd vident promissiones Dei iuramentis confirmatas. Amplificat ergo vsum promissionum, ex eo, quòd iuramentis sint confirmatæ. An uerò multò amplissimam inexpugnabilemq; consolationem omnes hinc debent accipere, q, omnia bona ipsis Deus ultrò promiserit, & præterea quòd minimè debebat? Sed immèsa est bonitatis ac misericordiæ, lese etiam iuramento obstringere. Valida consolatio opponitur pusillanimitati. Et consolatio erigit confirmatq; , sicut afflictio deijcit ac terret. 1. Thessalon. 5. Consolamini pusillanimes, subleuate infirmos, &c. 2. Corinth. 1. Deus consolatur nos in omni afflictione nostra, in hoc ut possimus consolari eos, qui sunt in quauis afflictione, per consolationem, qua nos ipsos consola-tur Deus.
units.tr: We might have a strong consolation: he adds "strong" [ἰσχυράν], so that it may be understood as not a small consolation, nor one lasting only a short time, but a very great and entirely unshaken consolation and certainty, which all ought to draw from the fact that they see God's promises confirmed by oaths. He therefore magnifies the use of the promises from the fact that they are confirmed by oaths. But should not all draw from this a most ample and unconquerable consolation, that God has freely promised them all good things and, moreover, was under no obligation to do so? Yet it is boundless goodness and mercy to bind himself even by an oath. A strong consolation is opposed to fainthearted despair. Consolation raises up and strengthens, just as affliction casts down and terrifies. 1 Thessalonians 5: "Comfort the fainthearted, support the weak," etc. 2 Corinthians 1: "God comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which God himself comforts us."

units.la: Qui huc confugimus, ut potiantur propositta spe) Declarat, ad quos valida illa consolatio perue-niat, atque, ad eos peruenire, qui toto animo ad coelestia bona in promissionibus propo-sita aspirant: quod pro pemodum perinde est, ac si diceret, consolationem tantam ad eos omnes pertinere, quotquot fideles & longanimes perstiterint. Fide siquidem & spe in propo-sita bona intenditur: Et sine fide ac spe impossibile est mentem aliqua cosolatione refocillari. Quod vero ait, Qui huc confugimus, partim notat pro magna foelicitate, & quo-dammodo pro liberatione à periculis & egregia munitione ducendum, vbi quis spe est insignitus, adeoq; spem esse tanquam refugium asylum, & tutum propugnaculum: par-tim quod suapte sponte ac veluti ipsi ambientes Euangelium susceperint, eoq; agnosce-re velint, se debere promissionibus credere, & in fide ac longanimitate expectare earun-dem impletionem. ηγαπω teneo, capio, apprehendo, rerum potior: quare potentia & dignitas quaedam credentium ea voce notatur. Supra capite quarto: Habentes igitur po-tificem magnum, teneamus professionem, &c.
units.tr: Who have fled here to lay hold of the hope set before us: he explains to whom that strong consolation comes, and that it comes to those who aspire with their whole heart to the heavenly goods set forth in the promises. This is almost the same as saying that this great consolation belongs to all who have been faithful and have persevered patiently. For faith and hope are directed to the goods set before us, and without faith and hope it is impossible for the mind to be refreshed by any consolation. But when he says who have fled here, he partly indicates that it is to be regarded as great happiness, and in a sense as deliverance from dangers and an excellent defence, when someone is endowed with hope, so that hope is like a refuge, a place of asylum and a safe stronghold; and partly that they have received the gospel of their own accord, as it were running towards it, and wish to acknowledge that they ought to believe the promises and, in faith and patience, await their fulfilment. [κρατῶ] means to hold, to seize, to lay hold of, to take possession of things; so a certain power and dignity of believers is marked by this word. Above, in chapter 4: "Since then we have a great high priest, let us hold fast our confession," etc.

units.la: Quam uelut ancoram tenemus animæ, cum tutam, tum firmam, & introeuntem usq; ad ea, quæ sunt intra uelum) Subijcit insignem Spei descriptionem, qua eam commendat ab usu seu effectib. quòd videlicet per eam tutam & confirmati contra omnes diaboli, mundi, carnis, insul-tationes reddimur: Deinde, quòd per eam non solùm cognoscimus affequimurq;, quæ in hac vita ad salutem necessaria percipi possunt, verùm etiam penetramus ad cognitio-nem rerum supernarum & coelestium, quæ post hanc vitam credentibus sunt promissæ. Nec dubium, quin velit Apostolus hæc de usu seu effectibus spei accipi pro grauissimis rationibus suasorijs, quæ omnium animos ad longanimitatem & spem impellant.
units.tr: Which we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and firm, and entering into that which is within the veil: he adds a notable description of hope, by which he commends it from its use and effects, namely that through it we are made secure and confirmed against all the taunts of the devil, the world and the flesh. Then, that through it we not only apprehend and attain what can be received in this life for salvation, but also penetrate to the knowledge of the heavenly and supernal things promised to believers after this life. There is no doubt that the Apostle wishes these words to be taken, concerning the use or effects of hope, as the weightiest reasons of persuasion, which drive the minds of all towards patience and hope.

units.la: Quemadmodum reuera ubi quis audit, spem esse veluti ancoram, cui tuto in omnibus vitæ periculis innitamur, & à qua salus nostra dependeat. præterea talem, qua penetremus & percipiamus et amnum altissima abstrusissimaq; coelestis patriæ gloriæque mysteria: quis non ardentissime affectet laboretq;, quantum in se est, ea muniri & confirmari? Vi-des autem, non otiose sed appositissimè hæc omnia esse adiecta, ad illustrandum confir-mandumq; illud, quod supra dixerat, Non debere cos esse segnes, sed imitatores eorum, qui per fidem ac longanimitatem hæreditatem accipiunt promissionis. Comprehensa enim hic sunt argumenta aliquot suasoria, quæ ad imitationem fidei & longanimitatis sanctorum Hebræos extimulant.
units.tr: Indeed, when someone hears that hope is like an anchor, on which we may rest securely amid all the dangers of life, and on which our salvation depends, and moreover that it is a means by which we penetrate and perceive the most lofty and hidden mysteries of the heavenly fatherland and glory, who would not most ardently desire and strive, as far as in him lies, to be fortified and confirmed in it? You see that all these things have been added not idly but most fittingly, to illustrate and confirm what he had said above, that they ought not to be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promise. For several arguments of persuasion are gathered here, which spur the Hebrews on to imitate the faith and patience of the saints.

units.la: Quidam pronomen, Quam, relatiuum faciunt consolationis, ut sententia sit, consola-tionem esse tanquam ancoram animæ: Sed non video, qui id conueniat, cùm ratio simi-litudinis magis quadret spei, quæ aptius confertur cum ancora, quàm consolatio: cùm item de consolatione non satis commodè accipi queat, quod sequitur de penetrando in coelestia, quod de spe tamen rectissimè dicitur, sicut mox indicabimus: cùm deniq; tota dispositio clarè edoceat, de spe confirmanda sermonem haberi.
units.tr: Some make the pronoun which refer relatively to consolation, so that the sense is that consolation is like an anchor of the soul. But I do not see how this fits, since the likeness agrees better with hope, which is more aptly compared with an anchor than consolation is; and since what follows, about penetrating into the heavenly things, cannot be understood sufficiently well of consolation, although it is most rightly said of hope, as we shall show shortly; and finally, since the whole arrangement clearly teaches that the discussion concerns the strengthening of hope.

units.la: Nihilo rectius faciunt, qui ancoram animæ interpretantur Christum. Nam etsi verum sit, quòd sub eo tuti degimus, & in eo tanquàm in tranquillo portu læti possumus con-quiescere: præterea quòd per eum introimus in coelum: tamen quomodo cohærebit sine vitio aliquo, præsertim προδρομος, quòd subijcitur, Vbi præcursor pro nobis ingressus est Iesus, &c. Quàm porrò conueniat, de spe verba ista accipi, facilè est demonstrare.
units.tr: Those who interpret the anchor of the soul as Christ do no better. For although it is true that under him we live safely, and that in him, as in a calm harbour, we may rest gladly; and moreover that through him we enter heaven; yet how can this be consistent without some fault, especially with the forerunner [πρόδρομος] that follows: "Where the forerunner Jesus has entered for us," etc.? How suitable it is to take these words of hope is easy to demonstrate.

units.la: Primùm spem dicit esse tanquam ancoram, & quidem animæ, id est, spiritualem, non corporalem. Aptissimè autem spes cum ancora confertur. Quemadmodum enim qui in mari nauigant, si quàdo metuunt tempestatem, vel alia pericula, puta errorem, scopulos, hostes, &c. Volunt conquiescere, nauemq; certo loco tranquillam sistere, iaciunt magni ponderis ancoram, quæ tum vi iactus, tum pondere sic in subiectam terram defigitur, ut nauis nec retrocedere, nec fluctibus iactari possit, sed tranquilla, tuta, firma stare cogatur. Ita profectò quoties miseri homines, præsertim pij, in mari magno huius mundi percel-luntur tentationibus siue afflictionibus, persecutionibus, calumniijs diaboli, mundi, car-nis, his maximè opus est, ut spe futurorum bonorum præsentia mala extenuent, ficq; ani-mos suos tranquillent, & ipsi fortes immobilesque persistant.
units.tr: First, he says hope is like an anchor, and indeed of the soul, that is, spiritual, not bodily. And hope is most aptly compared with an anchor. For just as those who sail on the sea, when they fear a storm or other dangers, such as error, rocks, enemies and so on, and wish to rest and bring their ship to a steady halt in a certain place, cast a heavy anchor, which by the force of its throw and by its weight is fixed in the ground beneath, so that the ship can neither drift back nor be tossed by the waves, but is compelled to stand calm, safe and firm; so surely, whenever wretched men, especially the godly, are battered on the great sea of this world by temptations or afflictions, persecutions and the slanders of the devil, the world and the flesh, there is most especially need that by the hope of future goods they may lessen present evils, and so calm their minds, and themselves remain strong and unmoved.

units.la: Ita sola spes est afflictis pijs, quod ancora est nautis: Sola spes quietas & tranquillas reddit conscientias: per solam spem animæ tutæ & firmæ redduntur. Hinc pasim in Scripturis hoc nomine commendatur. Roman. 8. Spe seruati sumus. Romanor. 5. Afflic-tio patientiam parit, patientia probationem, probatio autem spem, porrò spes non pu-defacit. defacit. Psalmo 90. Qui habitat in adiutorio altissimi, in protectione Dei coeli commorabitur: multi & praeclari effectus spei describuntur. Item psalmo 103. Hinc Esai 30. In silentio & spe erit fortitudo vestra. 1. Thes. 5. comparatur galeae, sicut hic ancorae. Sobrij simus, induti thoracê fidei & charitatis, & pro galea spem salutis. 2 Corinth. 1. Spes etiam nostra firma est pro vobis, cum sciamus, quòd quemadmodum participes estis afflictionum, sic futuri sitis & consolationis. Ibidè plura subiiciuntur, & inter alia: In quo spe fixa habemus, quòd etiam posthac erepturus sit, &c. En spem instar ancorae tutâ, firmam, fixam. Philip. 1. Novi, secundum expectationem & spem meam, quòd nulla in re pudefiam. Hoc solum nomine dissimilis est spes ab ancora, quòd ancora in terrâ defigitur, spes in coelum: alias, quod ad firmitatem & tranquillitatem attinet, conveniunt maximè.
units.tr: Thus hope alone is to the afflicted godly what the anchor is to sailors. Hope alone makes consciences quiet and tranquil; through hope alone souls are made secure and firm. Hence throughout the Scriptures it is commended under this name. Romans 8: "By hope we have been saved." Romans 5: "Affliction produces patience, patience proof, and proof hope; and hope does not disappoint." Psalm 90: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven," where many notable effects of hope are described. Likewise Psalm 103. Hence Isaiah 30: "In quietness and in hope shall be your strength." 1 Thessalonians 5 compares hope to a helmet, as here to an anchor: "Let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation." 2 Corinthians 1: "Our hope for you is firm, since we know that as you share in the afflictions, so you will also share in the consolation." In the same place more is added, including: "In whom we have set our hope that he will yet deliver us," etc. See hope as a safe, firm and fixed thing, like an anchor. Philippians 1: "I know that according to my eager expectation and hope I shall in nothing be put to shame." Hope differs from an anchor only in this: an anchor is fixed in the earth, but hope in heaven. In other respects, as regards firmness and tranquillity, they agree most closely.

units.la: Adhaec quòd spe penetrentur coelestia, sive quòd spes proprie tendat ad coelestia, non sique in ea inducat, pluribus locis docetur. Roman. 5. Gloriamur in spe gloriae Dei. Rom. 8. Vanitati creatura subiacet, non volens, sed propter eum, qui subiecit illam sub spe. Quoniam & ipsa creatura liberabitur à servitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei. Ibidè exponit, cur spes sit de futuris bonis: spes enim si videatur, non est spes. Quod enim quis cernit, cur idè speret? Tit. 1. Agnitio pietatis est in spe vitae aeternae, quam promisit is, qui mentiri nescit Deus, ante tempora aeterna. Tit. 2. Sobriè & iustè & piè viuamus in hoc seculo, expectantes beatam illam spem & apparitionem gloriae magni Dei. Ad Tit. 3. Spiritum Sanctum effudit in nos opulenter per Iesum Christum seruatorem nostrum, ut iustificati illius gratia haeredes efficeremur iuxta spem vitae aeternae, &c. Enigitur, quomodo spe introimus ad coelestia vsque mysteria cognoscenda, & quae hic percipere haud possumus re, tamen spe eadem obtinemus. Plura adferte in eundem sensum non esset adeò difficile, cùm saepè etiam spes in Scripturis pro rebus coelestibus speratis accipiatur.
units.tr: Moreover, that heavenly things are reached by hope, or that hope properly extends to heavenly things and does not stop short of them, is taught in many places. Romans 5: "We rejoice in the hope of the glory of God." Romans 8: "The creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope. For the creation itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God." There the Apostle explains why hope concerns future goods: for hope that is seen is not hope, since why would anyone hope for what he sees? Titus 1: "The knowledge of godliness rests on the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before eternal times." Titus 2: "Let us live soberly, righteously and godly in this age, waiting for that blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God." Titus 3: "He poured out the Holy Spirit upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life," and so on. Thus by hope we enter into the heavenly mysteries, to know them, and what we cannot yet perceive in reality here, we nevertheless obtain by that same hope. It would not be very difficult to adduce more passages to the same effect, since hope is often used in Scripture for the heavenly things that are hoped for.

units.la: Porrò hoc periphrasi, quae intra uelum sunt, scite abstrusas & reconditas res, seu mysteria incognita delineat: quandoquidem quae velo aliquo tecta sunt & conclusa, cerni oculis cognosci haud possunt. Quocirca Apostolus 1. Corinth. 3. volens exprimere, quòd Iudaei pro caecitate mentis non possent assequi mysteria spiritualia, ait, cordibus illorum fuisse velamen impositum, idque tollendum, vbi ad Dominum conuersi fuerint. Hic habetur κάλυμμα, quae vox significat tegmen generaliter, & genus quoddam retis. Porrò ad declarandum, de quibus mysteriis ipse loquatur, per interpretationem addidit:
units.tr: Moreover, by this periphrasis, those things which are within the veil, he sketches out things wisely hidden and concealed, or mysteries unknown. For things covered and shut in by some veil cannot be seen or known by the eyes. Hence the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 3, wishing to express that the Jews, because of the blindness of their minds, could not grasp spiritual mysteries, says that a veil had been placed over their hearts, and that it must be taken away when they turned to the Lord. Here we have covering [κάλυμμα], a word that signifies a covering in general, and a kind of net. Moreover, to show which mysteries he is speaking of, he added an explanation:

units.la: Vbi praecursor pro nobis ingressus est Iesus) Quibus verbis iterum προδρομος significat mysteria coelestia & superna, cùm Christus, vti ad Colossenses tertio, & alibi saepius dicitur, sit in coelis, ibi ad dexteram sedens Dei patris. Et quae ibi sunt, quoniam cum spe & revelatione spiritus Sancti à nobis, dùm hic viuimus, percipiuntur, recte intra velum esse dicuntur, iuxta illud 1. Corinthiorum 2. sumptum tamen ex Esaiae 64. Oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, & in cor hominis non ascenderunt, quae praeparauit Deus diligentibus se. Decebat uerò interpretationem hanc per Apostolum adijci, propterea quòd verba illa, quae intra uelum sunt, allegoriam resipiunt: allegoriae autem saepenumerò diuerso sensu explicantur, quodque vnus hoc pacto, alius aliter interpretatur. Sumpta est autem allegoria siue similitudo, ab eo, quòd Dominus, vt legitur Exodi quadragesimo, instituit tabernaculum testimonij (alias sancta sanctorum dictum) in quo arca sisteretur, amplo velo discerni à tabernaculo anteriore, in quo sacrificia offerebantur, neque cuiquam fas erat, praeterquam sacerdoti, idque semel tantum intra annum, (vt habetur Leuitici decimosexto) locum eum ingredi.
units.tr: Where Jesus has entered as forerunner for us. By these words the term forerunner [πρόδρομος] again signifies heavenly and supernal mysteries, since Christ, as is said in Colossians 3 and more often elsewhere, is in heaven, sitting there at the right hand of God the Father. And the things that are there, since they are perceived by us while we live here, through hope and the revelation of the Holy Spirit, are rightly said to be within the veil, according to 1 Corinthians 2, taken however from Isaiah 64: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." The Apostle rightly added this interpretation, because the words which are within the veil have the character of an allegory; and allegories are often explained in different senses, so that one person interprets them in one way and another differently. The allegory or likeness is taken from the fact that the Lord, as we read in Exodus 40, instituted the tabernacle of testimony (otherwise called the holy of holies), in which the ark was placed, separated by a broad veil from the front tabernacle, in which sacrifices were offered; and no one was permitted to enter that place except the priest, and that only once a year (as is found in Leviticus 16).

units.la: Quare ad significandum sacra insignia, & praesertim coelestia mysteria, ea allegoria maximè accommodata est. Certè Apostolus capite nono ac decimo huius epistolae, elegantissimè tabernaculum testimonij, seu sancta sanctorum interpretatur coelum, quòd Christus pontifex dum semel moriens, semel ingressus est, sanguinem non hircorum aut vitulorum, sed proprium offerens pro expiatione peccatorum totius humani generis. Non dubium autem, quin hoc loco ad id respexerit. Proinde haec est ingens commendatio spei, quòd per eam introimus ad abstrusissima coelestis gloriae mysteria, & rerum diuinarum cognitionem, quanta satis est, assequimur: Quare per fidem & spem ad perfectionem eniti debemus, omnemque segnitiem ab animis excutere, & in fide ac spe semper ad altiora progredi. His sententia Apostoli aptè absoluitur & claudITur. Quod ad voces ipsas attinet: quando ait, εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον, quasi diceret, ad id, quod interius est, amplificat dignitatem & effectum spei, ei tribuens, quòd ad interiora etiam penetret, & non tantum velut ad limina coelestium accedat.
units.tr: Therefore, to signify sacred mysteries, and especially heavenly ones, that allegory is most suitable. The Apostle, in chapters nine and ten of this epistle, most elegantly interprets the tabernacle of testimony, or holy of holies, as heaven, because Christ the high priest, dying once and entering once, offered not the blood of goats or calves but his own, to atone for the sins of the whole human race. There is no doubt that in this place he had that in view. This, then, is a great commendation of hope: that through it we enter into the most hidden mysteries of heavenly glory, and attain, so far as is enough, the knowledge of divine things. Therefore we ought to strive for perfection through faith and hope, to shake off all sloth from our minds, and always to advance to higher things in faith and hope. The Apostle's sentence is aptly completed and closed with this. As for the words themselves: when he says into the inner part [εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον], as if to say, into that which is more inward, he magnifies the dignity and effect of hope, attributing to it that it penetrates even to the inner things, and does not merely approach the threshold of heavenly things.

units.la: ἀποκάλυμμα propriè significat quod obtenditur seu obducitur alicui rei, ne conspici possit. Quae uox etiâ habetur Exodi quadragesimo, loco supra à nobis citato, & alibi saepius occurrit. Spei itaq; omnia patefiunt, neq; quicquam obtendi potest, quod cognitionem eius impediat. Christum deinde vocat πρόδρομον, pro nobis præcursorem: quandoquidem ille nobis viam parat ad cœlestia, quòq; nostris viribus non possumus peruenire, illius ductu nos eò peruenimus, & propter illum nobis patefiunt omnia. Hinc ipse ait Ioan nis decimoquarto: Vado paraturus vobis locum: iterum veniam, & assumam vos ad me ipsum, vt vbi sum ego, ibi & vos sitis: & quò ego vado, scitis, & viam scitis. Proinde valde consolatorium illud est, quòd Christus dicitur præcursor pro nobis, valdeq; debemus hac ratione in spe confirmari. Si ille pro nobis præcurrit, & viam aperuit, quid metuemus viam nobis præcludendam? Quando caput eò penetrauit, sequentur haud dubie & membra. Præterea, quomodo non totis viribus conabimur illum insequi? Si enim præcursor est, ergo nos currentes eundem insequamur, & sic curramus, ut non incertum, sed vnà cum Apostolo comprehendamus. Tota hac vita curredum est, & laboriose quidem: sed si perrexerimus constanter, eòdem perueniemus per gratiam, quò Christus noster præ cursor iam peruenit, vbi pater cœlestis nos vnà considere faciet cum Christo inter cœlestes. Nos ambulemus, sicut ille ambulauit, insequamur vestigia eius, nec poterimus aberrare, rectaq; ad metam pertingemus. Et sic ad hunc cursum nos hortatur Apostolus Coloss.3. Si resurrexistis vnà cum Christo, superna quærite, vbi Christus est, ad dexteram Dei sedens: supernà curate, non terrestria: Siquidem emortui estis, & vita abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Quandocunq; Christus manifestatus fuerit, vita nostra, tunc & vos cum illo manifestabimini in gloria.
units.tr: Unveiling [ἀποκάλυμμα] properly signifies what is spread over or drawn across something so that it cannot be seen. This word also occurs in Exodus 40, the passage cited above by us, and elsewhere more often. So all things are opened up by hope, nor can anything be drawn over to hinder its knowledge. Then he calls Christ a forerunner [πρόδρομος] for us: since he prepares the way for us to heavenly things, which we cannot reach by our own strength, by his leading we arrive there, and on account of him all things are opened to us. Hence he himself says in John 14: "I go to prepare a place for you; I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also; and where I go you know, and the way you know." Therefore that saying, that Christ is called our forerunner, is very consoling, and we ought to be greatly strengthened in hope by this reasoning. If he has run ahead for us and opened the way, what shall we fear, that the way will be closed against us? When the head has penetrated there, the members will undoubtedly follow. Moreover, how shall we not strive with all our strength to follow him? For if he is the forerunner, then let us follow him as we run, and so run that we may grasp the prize not uncertainly, but together with the Apostle. The whole of this life must be run, and laboriously indeed; but if we persevere constantly, we shall come by grace to the same place to which Christ our forerunner has already come, where the heavenly Father will make us sit together with Christ among the heavenly ones. Let us walk as he walked, let us follow his footsteps, and we cannot wander, but shall reach the goal straight. And so the Apostle exhorts us to this course in Colossians 3: "If you have risen together with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things above, not on the earthly; for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, is manifested, then you also will be manifested with him in glory."

units.la: Iam ad doctrinam pertinentia quaedam subijciamus. Primùm, omnibus his, quæ addita sunt, in primis proxima de scriptione spei, argumenta aptissima habemus, quæ nos ad amplectendam spem, & longanimitatem incitent. Et certè adeò necessarium est, vt spe nos alamus & confirmemus, præsertim si volumus in spiritualibus & sublimioribus proficere, vt, nisi id faciamus, non possimus in tot malis, quæ nos vndique circumueniunt, subsistere, non magis, quàm nauis potest subsistere in medijs fluctibus, si ei ancora sit adempta. Ea propter Apostolus ubiq; ad spem & longanimitatem credentes hortatur. Debet autem proprie tendere ad ea, quæ sunt intra velum, id est, ad res cœlestes & spirituales. Nam longanimem esse, seu sperare in bona temporalia, vel propter bona temporalia, id non est credentium, sed infidelium, qui dicuntur potius spem non habere, vt in posteriori habetur ad Thessalonicenses. Quomodo enim spem firmam, & qualem decet esse Christianorum, habebunt? vel, quomodo vere erunt longanimes, qui in res temporales & momento perituras respiciunt? Sed inter enarrandum verba Apostoli de spe satis dictum est.
units.tr: Now let us add some points pertaining to doctrine. First, from all these things that have been added, especially those immediately preceding about the description of hope, we have most suitable arguments that stir us to embrace hope and patience. Indeed it is so necessary that we nourish and strengthen ourselves with hope, especially if we want to make progress in spiritual and higher things, that unless we do so we cannot stand against the many evils that surround us on every side, any more than a ship can stay steady in the midst of the waves if its anchor has been taken away. Therefore the Apostle everywhere exhorts believers to hope and patience. But hope ought properly to reach toward those things which are within the veil, that is, toward heavenly and spiritual things. For to be patient, or to hope in temporal goods or on account of temporal goods, is not the mark of believers but of unbelievers, who are rather said not to have hope, as is stated in the later letter to the Thessalonians. For how will they have a firm hope, such as befits Christians? Or how will they truly be patient, who look to temporal things that will perish in a moment? But in expounding the Apostle's words on hope, enough has been said.

units.la: Secundò, hìc iubemur intueri in certitudinem diuinarum promissionum. His nos solari in aduersis, confirmare in prosperis, imò in omnibus casibus debemus. Vbi aduersa imminent, consolabuntur nos promissiones diuinæ, certoq; statuemus, nos non posse perire, quando ille recepit, se velle esse Deum, hoc est, protectorem & adiutorem nostrū. Neque enim fallere nos vult, aut potest, modò ipsi in fide & longanimitate perstemus. Et hic valde prodesset conscientijs omne genus promissionum diuinarum ex sacris literis collectarum in promptu habere. Rursus autem vbi bene nobiscum agitur, cogitemus, non propter nostram dignitatem, vel merita id fieri, sed propter diuinas promissiones, eoq; annitamur Deo agere, pro beneuolētia & fauore, quo nos prosequitur, gratias.
units.tr: Second, here we are bidden to look upon the certainty of the divine promises. We ought to be consoled by them in adversity, strengthened in prosperity, and indeed in every kind of circumstance. When adversities threaten, the divine promises will console us, and we shall firmly determine that we cannot perish, since he has undertaken to be God to us, that is, our protector and helper. For he neither wishes nor is able to deceive us, provided that we ourselves persevere in faith and patience. And here it would greatly profit consciences to have at hand every kind of divine promise gathered from the sacred letters. Again, when things go well with us, let us consider that this comes about not on account of our dignity or merits, but on account of the divine promises; and let us strive to give thanks to God for the goodwill and favour with which he pursues us.

units.la: Si non esset hæc certitudo promissionum, omnis nostra fides & religio euanesceret, neque quicquam possemus de meliori uita animo contemplari. Tantares est diuinarum promissionum certitudo.
units.tr: If there were no such certainty of the promises, all our faith and religion would vanish away, and we could contemplate nothing of the better life with a cheerful mind. So great is the certainty of the divine promises.

units.la: Tertiò, quoniam hic eleganter describitur iuramenti forma, & vsus, res ipsa poscit, de iureiurando plenius differamus, maximeq; quòd hac nostra tempestate de eius vsu exot tæ sunt controuersiæ. Vide de iureiurando in volumine rhapsodiarum diuinarum.
units.tr: Third, since the form and use of an oath is described here with elegance, the matter itself demands that we treat more fully of the oath, especially because in our present age controversies have been stirred up about its use. See on the oath in the volume of Divine Rhapsodies.

units.la: REDITVS.
units.tr: RETURN.

units.la: Iuxta ordinem Melchisedech, pontifex factus in æternum, &c.
units.tr: According to the order of Melchisedec, made a priest for ever, etc.

units.la: Redit ad institutum, hoc est, ad disputationem de Christi sacerdotio, quam ante digressionem exorsus fuerat, planeq; ijsdem id agit verbis, quibus, antequàm digrederetur, si nem dicendi fecerat, & quidem adeò appositè, vt si quis quæ iam sequuntur, uelit, omissa uniuersa digressione, coniungere ijs, quæ ibi extremo loco erant posita, deprehēsurus sit, omnia sibi inuicem pulchrè cohærere, nihilq; aliud agi, quàm deinceps pluribus euidentioribus q; argumentis coprobari, seu potius explicari, quod ibi paucis concludebatur, nempe Christū esse uerū pontificē à Deo constitutū secundū ordinē Melchisedech.
units.tr: He returns to his subject, that is, to the discussion of Christ's priesthood, which he had begun before the digression, and he does so in the very words with which he had closed his discourse before he digressed. He does this so aptly that anyone who, leaving aside the whole digression, joins what now follows to what had been placed at the end before it, will find that everything coheres beautifully, and that nothing else is being done than that what was there concluded briefly is now confirmed, or rather explained, by many clearer arguments: namely, that Christ is the true priest appointed by God according to the order of Melchisedec.

units.la: Etsi verò verba hæc conglutinata sint proximè præcedentibus, ut diuelli inde ægrè queant (Sunt enim participio ἵνα, seu factus, connexa) tamen sciendum est, id Pau-lino lino more fieri, quando eandem rationem progrediendi ab vna orationis parte ad alteram in cæteris epistolis licet obserua e,quam & supra aliquoties indicauimus
units.tr: Although these words are so closely joined to the immediately preceding ones that they can hardly be separated from them (for they are connected by the participle ἵνα, or "made"), nevertheless it must be understood that Paul does this in his usual manner, and that the same method of moving from one part of the discourse to another can be observed in his other epistles, as we have pointed out several times above.

units.la: In Epistola ad Galatas prima pars apologetica est, à qua transit ad secundam didacticam, verbis quæ fluunt ex præcedentibus, & miro modo .nter se comparata sunt. Sic enim ibi capite primo ait: Propterea, quòd non iustificabitur ex operibus legis omnis caro. Quæ verba sic sunt posita, ut rationem reddere videantur præcedentium, & nihilominus propositionis vice sunt ad disputationem ibidem sequentem. Rursus in eadem epistola sic finem facit secundæ partis de doctrina fidei capite quinto: Vtinam abscindantur, qui vos labefactant: Vos enim in libertatem vocati fuistis fratres. Hinc aggreditur alteram partem de doctrina charitatis, indiuulsè adijciendo. Tantum ne libertatem in occasionem detis carni, sed per charitatem seruire vobis inuicem.
units.tr: In the Epistle to the Galatians the first part is apologetic, and from it he passes to the second, didactic part, with words that flow from what precedes and are wonderfully related to it. Thus in the first chapter he says: "Because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified." These words are so placed that they seem to give the reason for what precedes, and yet at the same time they serve as the proposition for the discussion that follows there. Again, in the same epistle he brings to an end the second part, on the doctrine of faith, in chapter five: "Would that those who unsettle you were cut off! For you were called to liberty, brethren." From here he goes on to the other part, on the doctrine of love, adding without any break: "Only do not use liberty as an occasion for the flesh, but through love serve one another."

units.la: Similiter in Epistola ad Ephesios, finito exordio bene longo, grauissimaq; doctrina referto, sic incipit capite secundo, primam partem principalem de excellenti magnitudine potentiæ Dei erga credentes, qua gratis eos per fidem saluos facit. Et vos cùm essetis mortui, &c. Mox alteram partem de spe vocationis, seu de vocatione gentium. Ibidem: Quapropter memento te, quòd vos quondam gentes, &c. Vbi & conclusio subijcitur capite tertio simili connectendi forma: Huius rei gratia flecto genua mea ad patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Similarly, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, after a fairly long introduction, full of most weighty doctrine, he begins chapter two with the principal first part, on the excellent greatness of God's power towards believers, by which he saves them freely through faith: "And you, when you were dead, etc." Soon after comes the second part, on the hope of calling, that is, on the calling of the Gentiles: "Therefore remember that you, once Gentiles, etc." Here also a conclusion is added in chapter three, with the same method of connecting: "For this reason I bow my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: In Epistola ad Colossenses prima pars didactica de gratuita misericordia Dei erga credentes indiuulsè adhæret verbis exordij: Ibi enim incipit pars didactica: Gratias agentes patri, qui idoneos nos fecit, &c. Confirmatio deinde eodem capite: Nec dimouemini à spe Euangelij, quod audistis: Quæ verba rursus nullo modo separari à præcedentibus possunt. Et secunda pars de Charitate seu doctrina operum capite tertio: Mortificate igitur membra vestra, &c. Nec difficile foret, in reliquis epistolis, exempla alia demonstrare. Hoc igitur pacto licet hæc verba, iuxta ordinem Melchisedech pontifex factus in æternum, necessariò coniuncta sint præcedentibus, propter participium γενόμενος, tamen in hoc sunt adiecta, ut ad disputationem semel coeptam parent reditum, viamq; aperiunt ad congerendum noua argumenta.
units.tr: In the Epistle to the Colossians the first, didactic part, on the free mercy of God towards believers, clings inseparably to the words of the introduction; for there the didactic part begins: "Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit," etc. Then follows the confirmation in the same chapter: "Nor are you moved away from the hope of the gospel, which you have heard." These words again cannot in any way be separated from what precedes. And the second part, on charity or the doctrine of works, in chapter three: "Mortify therefore your members," etc. Nor would it be difficult to show other examples of this in the remaining epistles. In this way, although these words, "according to the order of Melchisedec, made a priest for ever," are necessarily joined to what precedes because of the participle γενόμενος, nevertheless they are added here so that they prepare a return to the discussion once begun, and open the way to bringing together new arguments.

units.la: Prudenter autem hac verborum forma petita è testimonio Scripturæ initio disputationis citato reditum istum facit, tum, quòd hæc ratio redeundi ad institutum, qua ea verba, quæ ante digressionem postrema fuere, in memoriam reuocantur, frequentissima sit, & vel vulgo usitata: tum, quòd hoc testimonium Scripturæ, quando quidem veluti basis & fundamentum est, cui tota disputatio innititur, deceat perpetuò versari ob oculos: tum quòd eiusdem testimonij singulas partes accuratè nunc velit discutere, nec non diuersorum argumentorum materiam inde elicere. Quas ob causas etiam paulò post idem testimonium aliquoties repetitur. Quomodo igitur his verbis reditus fiat, quanto q; artificio Apostolus hic, sicut & in cæteris, utatur, equidem satis puto manifestum. Iam ad rem progrediamur.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle prudently makes this return by means of this form of words, taken from the testimony of Scripture cited at the beginning of the discussion. He does so, first, because this way of returning to the subject, by which the words that were last before the digression are recalled to mind, is very frequent and even common in ordinary use; second, because this testimony of Scripture, since it is as it were the base and foundation on which the whole discussion rests, is fitting to be kept constantly before the eyes; third, because he now wishes to examine the individual parts of that same testimony carefully, and also to draw from it the material for various arguments. For these reasons the same testimony is also repeated several times shortly afterwards. How the return is made by these words, and with how much skill the Apostle uses it here, as elsewhere, I think is sufficiently clear. Let us now proceed to the matter itself.

units.la: CAPVT SEPTIMVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN.

units.la: Nam hic erat Melchisedech rex Salē, pontifex Dei altissimi, qui occurrit Abrahæ reuertenti à cæde regum, & benedixit illi, cui & decimas ex omnib. impartitus est Abraham, qui primùm quidem ex interpretatione dicitur rex iustitiæ: deinde verò etiam rex Salem, quod est rex pacis: ignoti patris, ignota matris, ignoti generis, nec initium dierum, neq; vitæ finem habens, sed assimilatus filio Dei manet sacerdos in perpetuum.
units.tr: For this Melchizedek was king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; to him also Abraham gave a tenth of all, who first, by interpretation, is called king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, which is king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever.

units.la: NITIO disputationis diximus, huc tendere omnia, quæ de sacerdotio Christi proferuntur, ut demonstretur, per sacerdotium Christi præstantius atq; excellentius abrogari sacerdotium legale, ac proinde simul abrogari ipsam legem. De huius enim abrogatione omnem fuisse controuersiam. Proinde statim quatuor validis argumentis probauit, Christum esse sacerdotem, idq; adhibito Scripturæ testimonio confirmauit. Sed quia aduersarij Hebræi protinus negaturi erant, illud testimonium de Christo esse accipiendum, ideo nunc campū disputationis latiorem ingrediens, colligit argumentorum copias, atq; illud ipsum testimonium per partes examinat, nec non plurimis argumentis clarè docet, Christo per omnia competere. Hoc autem ordine progreditur. Toto hoc capite 7. docet, Christum legitimè ordinatum esse pontificem secundum ordinem Melchisedec, quemadmodum testimonio citato significatur. Capite vero octauo, eum insuper munere sacerdotali egregiè perfunctum, hoc est, donaria & victimas obtulisse. Quibus duabus rebus ita probatis, Christum verum legitimumq; esse sacerdotem euincitur.Interea autem semper confert sacerdotium Christi,cum facerdo tio legali,sacerdotium Melchisedech cum sacerdotio Aaronico seu Leuitico:omnia tàm quæ ad ordinationem,quàm quæ ad ministerium seu sacrificium utriusq; pertinent,dili-genter expendens:ac dum in collatione manifeste ostendit, facerdotiu Christi seu Mel-chisedechi,longo interuallo eminentib. esse sacerdotio legali seu Aaronico, recte & val-de artificiose infert,iltud,quod minus est,per illud,quod præstatius est,abrogari, ideoq; sacerdotium legale,sacrificia,ceremonias,adeoq; vniuersam legé finem accipere, & per sacerdotium Christi eneruari. Sic igitur priorem partem,qua videlicet docet,Christum le-gitimè ordinatum esse pontificem, & quidem iuxta ordinem Melchisedech,aggreditur.
units.tr: In the statement of the disputation we said that everything that is set forth about the priesthood of Christ tends to this: to show that the Levitical priesthood is abrogated by the more excellent and surpassing priesthood of Christ, and therefore that the law itself is abrogated at the same time. For the whole controversy concerned this abrogation. Accordingly, he first proved by four strong arguments that Christ is a priest, and confirmed this by the testimony of Scripture. But since the Hebrew opponents were about to deny at once that this testimony should be understood of Christ, he now enters a wider field of disputation, gathers his stock of arguments, examines that very testimony part by part, and by many arguments clearly teaches that it applies to Christ in every respect. He proceeds in this order. In this whole seventh chapter he teaches that Christ was legitimately ordained priest according to the order of Melchizedek, as the cited testimony signifies. In the eighth chapter he further shows that Christ has excellently discharged the priestly office, that is, that he offered gifts and victims. With these two things thus proved, Christ is shown to be the true and lawful priest. Meanwhile he constantly compares the priesthood of Christ with the legal priesthood, and the priesthood of Melchizedek with the priesthood of Aaron or the Levites, carefully weighing everything that pertains to the ordination of each, and to its ministry or sacrifice. And while in this comparison he clearly shows that the priesthood of Christ, or of Melchizedek, is far above the legal or Aaronic priesthood, he rightly and very skilfully infers that the lesser is abrogated by the more excellent: therefore the legal priesthood, the sacrifices, the ceremonies, and indeed the whole law come to an end and are weakened through the priesthood of Christ. So he takes up the first part, namely that he teaches that Christ was legitimately ordained priest, and indeed according to the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Nam hic erat Melchisedec rex Salem, pontifex Dei altißimi, qui occurrit Abrahæ reuertenti à cæde regū, & benedixit illi,cui & decimas ex omnibus impartitus est Abraham:
units.tr: For this Melchizedek was king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; to him also Abraham gave a tenth of all.

units.la: Primùm examinare volens illam testimonij citati particulam, Secundum ordinem Melchi-sedec, qualis fuerit ille Melchisedec, qualisq; eius ordo, simplici & plane historica narra-tione exponit,paucis verbis sumptis ex Genefeos capite 14.ubi sic legitur: At verò Mel-chisedec rex Salem proferens panem & vinum (erat autem sacerdos Dei altisimi) bene dixitq; ei,& ait:Benedictus Abraham Deo excelso,qui creauit cœlum & terram, & bene dictus Deus excelsus,quo protegente hostes in manibus tuis sunt. Et dedit ei decimas ex omnibus. Neq; vsquàm alibi, præter quàm Psalmo 109. è quo suprà citatum est testi-monium, & præsenti epistola Melchisedechi fit mentio. Nec opus est,ut pluribus expo-namus,qua occasione verba illa in Genesi sint posita.
units.tr: Wishing first to examine that part of the cited testimony, according to the order of Melchizedek, he sets out, in a simple and plainly historical narrative, who Melchizedek was and what his order was, using a few words taken from Genesis chapter 14, where it is read as follows: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine (now he was priest of the Most High God), and he blessed him and said: Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands. And he gave him a tenth of all." And he is mentioned nowhere else, except in Psalm 110, from which the testimony cited above is taken, and in the present epistle. Nor is there need for us to explain at length the occasion on which those words were set down in Genesis.

units.la: Narratur, Chedor-laòmer regem Elamitarum, adiunctis sibi tribus alijs regibus con-fœderatis, mouisse bellum in regem Sodomorum,regem Gomorrhæorù, alios tres, qui postquàm duodecim annis illis seruij ssent,& tributa pependissent, ab ipso desciuerunt. Proinde in hac pugna fugisse reges Sodomorum, & Gomorrhæorum,& Chedorlaomer ita obtinuisse victoriam magnaq; spolia,& captiuos plurimos abduxisse,in quibus etiam gentilis Abrahæ ipse Loth,filius,inquam,fratris Abrahæ. Huius proinde liberandi ergò, Abraham statim collegit expeditos vernaculos suos 318. & persecutus est regem Che-dorlaomer cum suis vsque in Dan. Et diuisis copijs irruit in eos nocte, percusitq; eos, & persecutus est eos usq; in Hobah,quæ est à sinistra Damasci. Et recuperauit omnem substantiam,sed & Loth fratrem suum,& substantiam illius reduxit,& mulieres atq; po-pulum. Vbi igitur hoc pacto Abraham præclaram reportasset victoriam,redeunti à cæde Chedorlaomer aliorumq; trium regum, egressus est obuius rex Sodomę in valle Sauch (id est,plana quæ est vallis regis. Similiter egressus est obuiam Abrahæ hic Melchisedec rex Salem,de quo in præsentiarum sermo est.
units.tr: It is told that Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, with three other kings allied to him, made war on the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, and three others, who, after they had been subject to him for twelve years and had paid tribute, revolted from him. Accordingly, in this battle the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and Chedorlaomer gained the victory, carried off great spoils and many captives, among whom was Lot, Abraham's kinsman, indeed the son of Abraham's brother. Therefore, to rescue him, Abraham at once gathered his 318 trained servants born in his house and pursued Chedorlaomer and his men as far as Dan. And dividing his forces, he fell upon them by night, struck them down, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which lies to the left of Damascus. And he recovered all the goods, and also his brother Lot, and brought back his goods, and the women and the people.
