When Abraham had thus won a splendid victory, on his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the three other kings, the king of Sodom came out to meet him in the valley of Shaveh (that is, the Plain, which is the King's Valley). Likewise there came out to meet Abraham this Melchizedek, king of Salem, who is the subject of our present discussion.

units.la: Et Iosephus Antiquitatum Iudaicarum lib. 1. cap. 18. eleganter rem omnem explicat. Suscepit eum,inquit,rex Melchisedec, quòd significat rex iustus, & erat utiq; sine dubio talis,ita ut propter hanc causam etiam Dei sacerdos esset Solymorum, quam ciuitatem postea Hierosolymam vocauerunt. Ministrauit autem iste Melchisedec Abraham exerci-tui xenia,& multam abundantiam rerum oportunarum (quæ omnia more hebræo no-mine panis & vini decet intelligi) simul exhibuit,& super epulas eum col-laudare cœpit,& benedicere Deum,qui ei subdiderat inimicos. Abraham verò dante ei-tiam decimas spoliorum, munus accepit, &c. Ex quibus satis manifesta euadit historia. Tantùm adijciendum nonihil de Salem,& quomodo intelligendum,eundem Melchi-sedech,simul regem fuisse & sacerdotem. Dicunt pleriq;,quod & Iosephus ait lib.7.belli Iudaici,hanc Salem esse, quæ postea dicta fuit Hierusalem , conditamq; & Melchisede-cho: quod quidem ad prædicandam antiquitatem vrbis Hierosolymorum accommodè dicitur:& verosimile est, hanc sententiam Iudæis, ut gloriæ studiosis, & antiquitatum suarum iactatoribus placuisse.
units.tr: Josephus, in the first book, chapter 18, of his Jewish Antiquities, explains the whole matter elegantly. "King Melchizedek received him," he says, "which means righteous king; and he was surely such, so that for this reason he was also priest of God to the Solymites, a city which they later called Jerusalem. This Melchizedek provided the army with hospitality and a great abundance of suitable things (all of which, in the Hebrew manner, ought to be understood under the names of bread and wine), and he began to praise him over the feast and to bless God, who had subjected his enemies to him. And Abraham, giving him also a tenth of the spoils, received the gift," etc. From these things the history becomes sufficiently plain. It must only be added that something should be said about Salem, and how it is to be understood that the same Melchizedek was at once king and priest. Most people say, as Josephus also says in the seventh book of the Jewish War, that this Salem is the place which was afterwards called Jerusalem, and that it was founded by Melchizedek. This indeed is said appropriately to proclaim the antiquity of the city of Jerusalem, and it is likely that this opinion pleased the Jews, who were eager for glory and boasted of their antiquities.

units.la: Sed Hieronymus in libro de locis hebraicis, & ad Euagrium scribens, diuersum con-tendit:nec ullo pacto Salem hanc esse,quę post dicta fuerit Hierusalem.In libro de locis Hebraicis ait,Hierosolymam initio tenuisse Adonibezech, cuius primùm fit mentio Io-suæ 10. qui ibi appellatur rex Hierusalem.Inde tenuisse Iebusæos,à quibus Iebus fuit ap-pellata,ut memoratur Iosuæ 18. & 1. Paralipomen. 11. Longo verò post tempore pri-mùm à Dauide Hierosolymam appellatam, 1.Paralip.11. Et ad Euagrium scribens ait,sicut loci non ferre,ut Abrahamo Melchisedec ex Hierosolymis occurreret.
units.tr: But Jerome, in his book on Hebrew places and in his letter to Evagrius, maintains the opposite, and by no means holds that this Salem is the place that was afterwards called Jerusalem. In the book on Hebrew places he says that Jerusalem was at first held by Adonizedek, whose name first occurs in Joshua 10, where he is called king of Jerusalem. Then it was held by the Jebusites, from whom it was called Jebus, as is recorded in Joshua 18 and 1 Chronicles 11. But a long time afterwards it was first called Jerusalem by David, 1 Chronicles 11. And in his letter to Evagrius he says that the place does not allow that Melchizedek should have met Abraham from Jerusalem.

units.la: Proinde Salem aliud esse oppidum iuxta Scythopolim,cuius mentio fit Genefeos tri-cesimo tertio, vbi sic legitur:Reuersus est itaq; illo die Esau itinere, quo venerat, in Seyr: & Iacob venit in suchoth,vbi aedificata domo, & fixis tentorijs,appellauit nomen loci il-lius Sochoth,id est, tabernacula:transiuitq; in Salem urbem Sichimorum, quæ est in terra Canaan,& habitauit juxta oppidum, &c. Etrursus Ioan.3. Baptizabat autem Ioannes in Ænon iuxta Salim, quia aquæ multæ e-rant illic: vbi siue Salim legas, siue Salem, non refert, maximè cùm Hæbraei codices pun-ctavocalia habere non soleant. Taceo, quòd quidam dicere audent, in Salem monstrari regalis palatij Melchisedech quædam vestigia & ruinas, vt refert Primasius. Et tradunt Cosmographiæ periti, oppidum istud Salem Iordanis ripis impositum, similiter & Ænô ad meridialem plagam vrbis Samariæ. Sed de hac re qui plura velit, legat Hieronymum locis supra citatis, & Cosmographos. Iâ verò nequaquâ pro absurdo reputabitur quòd idem Melchisedech simul sacerdos & rex appelletur. Neq; enim nouum fuit priscis seculis, vtijs, quorum probitas, prudentia, vitæq; sanctimonia explorata erat, gubernacularum politicarum & religionis simul committerentur. Moses dux populi fuit, rerum politicarum gerens curam: & nihilominus sacerdotio fungebatur, hostias offerens, alios in sacerdotes vngens. Deinde ex illis quos Scriptura iudices celebrat apud Israelitas, Heli, præterea Samuel, & quidâ alij simul sacerdotio fungebantur. Neq; apud Hebræos tantum, verum apud alios quoq; populos eiusdē rei exempla est reperire. Apud Romanos Numa Pompilius simul reipublicæ & religioni præerat. Et lógo pòst tempore idem qui pontifex erat, etiam consul, vel censor esse poterat, quod contigit Crasso Licinio, qui pontificatum Maximum & consulatum, mox censuram prœturamq; simul gesisit. Et Linum pontificem pro prætore ordinibus præfuisse referunt.
units.tr: Accordingly, Salem is another town near Scythopolis, mentioned in Genesis chapter 33, where it is read as follows: "So Esau returned that day on the road by which he had come, to Seir; and Jacob came to Succoth, and when he had built a house and set up tents, he called the name of that place Succoth, that is, tabernacles; and he passed over to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, and dwelt near the town," etc. And again in John 3: "Now John was baptizing at Aenon, near Salim, because there was much water there." Whether you read Salim or Salem makes no difference, especially since Hebrew manuscripts are not accustomed to have vowel points. I pass over the fact that some dare to say that certain remains and ruins of the royal palace of Melchizedek are shown in Salem, as Primasius reports. And those skilled in geography say that this town Salem lies on the banks of the Jordan, and likewise Aenon lies to the south of the city of Samaria. But whoever wishes to know more about this matter should read Jerome in the places cited above, and the geographers. Indeed, it should not be considered absurd that the same Melchizedek is called both priest and king at once. For in earlier ages it was not unusual that the government of the state and of religion were committed together to those whose uprightness, prudence and holiness of life had been tested. Moses was leader of the people, bearing the care of public affairs, and yet he also discharged the priestly office, offering sacrifices and anointing others as priests. Then among those judges whom Scripture celebrates among the Israelites, Eli, and also Samuel and some others, exercised the priesthood at the same time. And examples of the same thing are found not only among the Hebrews but also among other peoples. Among the Romans, Numa Pompilius presided over the state and religion together. And at a later time the man who was pontiff could also be consul or censor, as happened to Crassus Licinius, who held the chief pontificate and the consulship, and soon after the censorship and the praetorship together. And they report that Linus, the pontiff, presided over the orders as praetor.

units.la: Apud Spartanos reges cùm primùm ad eam dignitatem assumpti erant, Iouis cœlestis & Lacedæmonii sacerdotio fungebantur, vbi porcellos immolabant.
units.tr: Among the Spartans, when their kings were first raised to that dignity, they performed the priesthood of heavenly Jove and of the Lacedaemonians, where they sacrificed little pigs.

units.la: Panthei sacerdotes omnium duces fiebant, ijsdemq; caussarum iudicia, & publicarum rerum arbitria tribuebantur. In Aritia Artemisiæ Dianæ sacerdos etiam rex vocabatur. Eadem erat sacerdotû dignitas in Cappadocia, fano Bellonæ: itè in Comatijs & Zela. Apud Ægyptios mos erat, ex Philosophis sacerdotes, ex sacerdotibus probatissimû in regé eligere. Vnde Mercurius Trismegistus, id est, ter maximus nomen traxit, quòd nimirum philosophus maximus, sacerdos maximus, & rex maximus esset. Et alibi apud Virgilium legimus: Rex Arnus, rex idem hominum phœbiq; sacerdos.
units.tr: The priests of Pan became leaders of all, and judgments in cases and decisions in public affairs were given to them. In Aritia the priest of Artemis Diana was even called king. The same dignity of priests existed in Cappadocia at the temple of Bellona, and likewise in Comatia and Zela. Among the Egyptians it was the custom to choose kings from among the philosophers, and from among the priests the most approved man. Hence Mercurius Trismegistus took his name, that is, thrice greatest, because he was the greatest philosopher, the greatest priest and the greatest king. And elsewhere in Virgil we read: "King Arnus, king of men and priest of Phoebus."

units.la: Cætera explicabuntur in sequentibus, quomodo videlicet Melchisedech benedixerit Abrahæ, quomodo idem decimas spoliorum ab Abraham acceperit. Hoc fortasis no tari potest, ex facto Abraham constare posse, quomodo Christianis liceat bella gerere, & ab hostibus sua legitimo bello repetere. Deinde, quòd afflictis rebuspublicis ac fugientibus etiam regibus desperantibusq;, liceat alterius ordinis principi è coniunctis vel confœderatis, vel etiam è subditis (qualis erat Abraham) rempublicam defendere, & quatenus fieri licitis modis queat, recuperare: ita tamen, vt potitus victoria regnû ad se non recipiat, sed superioribus principibus seu regibus, imò & cuiuis alteri, quod illis debitum est, reddat, quomodo Abrahamum fecisse cernimus, qui reuersus à cæde regum (ita enim loquitur Apostolus, vt significet valde præclaram victoriam & maximè celebrandam) sicut honoratus est à regibus, ita decimas obtulit è spolijs primùm regi Melchisedech, deinde partitus est etiam cum rege Sodomorum, cedens etiam partem reliquis, vt delicet Aner, Escol, & Mambre. Visum est obiter ista admonere.
units.tr: The rest will be explained in what follows, namely how Melchizedek blessed Abraham and how he received tithes of the spoils from Abraham. Perhaps this can be inferred from Abraham's deed: that Christians may lawfully wage war and reclaim their own from enemies by a just war. Further, that when commonwealths are afflicted and kings are fleeing and despairing, it is lawful for a prince of another rank, whether a kinsman or ally, or even a subject (as Abraham was), to defend the commonwealth and, so far as it can be done by lawful means, recover it. Yet he must do so in such a way that, having gained the victory, he does not take the kingdom for himself, but returns it to the superior princes or kings, and indeed to anyone else to whom it is owed, as we see Abraham did. For he, returning from the slaughter of the kings (for so the Apostle speaks, to signify a very splendid victory and one most worthy of celebration), was honoured by the kings, and so first offered tithes of the spoils to King Melchizedek; then he shared them also with the king of Sodom, yielding a part to the rest, namely Aner, Eshcol and Mamre. It seemed worth while to mention these things in passing.

units.la: Qui primùm quidem ex interpretatione dicitur rex iustitia: Deinde verò etiam rex Salem, quod est rex pacis: ignoti patris, ignota matris, ignoti generis, nec initium dierum, neq; vitæ finem habens, sed assimilatus filio Dei manet sacerdos in perpetuum.
units.tr: who is first, by interpretation, called king of righteousness; then also king of Salem, which is king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever.

units.la: Iam quæ de Melchisedech dicta sunt, competere Christo, ac proinde Christum secundum eius ordinem esse sacerdotem, pluribus atq; euidetibus argumentis colligit, è quibus primum sumptû est ab interpretatione nominis siue ab etymologia: quod sic crassius licet reddere.
units.tr: Now, he gathers from several clear arguments that what has been said of Melchizedek applies to Christ, and that therefore Christ is a priest after his order. The first of these is taken from the interpretation of the name, or etymology, which may be rendered roughly as follows.

units.la: Vocabulum Melchisedech idem significat, quod rex iustitiæ.
units.tr: The name Melchizedek means the same as king of righteousness.

units.la: Atqui Christus etiam verè præ omnibus, si quis alius, est rex iustitiæ.
units.tr: But Christ too is truly, above all others, king of righteousness.

units.la: Igitur rectè dicitur de Christo, quæ scripta sunt de Melchisedech, Christûq; sacerdotem esse secundum ordinem Melchisedech bene infertur.
units.tr: Therefore what is written of Melchizedek is rightly said of Christ, and it is rightly inferred that Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Est hoc genus argumentorum valde vsitatum scriptoribus, & tempestiue adhibitum, magnum habet & pondus & gratiam, diligenterq; & Rhetores & Dialectici in scholis de eo præceperunt. Sunt autem plura genera definitionis nominum: Sed hoc genus ab interpretatione nominis facilè primum locum obtinet, censeturque efficacissimum: vulgò vocatur κατ' ἐτυμολογίαν, Aristoteli συμβολον, Ciceroni Nota & Notatio, Quintiliano Originatio. Quod verò attinet ad rationem nominis Melchisedech, propriam eius significationem
units.tr: This kind of argument is very commonly used by writers and is applied opportunely; it carries great weight and force, and both rhetoricians and dialecticians have taught it carefully in the schools. There are several kinds of definition of names, but this kind, from the interpretation of the name, readily holds the first place and is considered the most effective. It is commonly called kata etymologian [κατ' ἐτυμολογίαν]; by Aristotle it is called symbolon, by Cicero nota and notatio, by Quintilian originatio. As for the meaning of the name Melchizedek, its proper signification

units.la: argumentum Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech ab etymologia. Melchisedech rex iustitiæ. Vsus argumentationum ab etymo. cationē Apostolus reddidit. Nam Hebraeis vox מלך idem quod rex, descendens à verbo מלך id est, regnauit, imperauit. Psalmo nonagesimo septimo מלך Dominus regnauit, exultet terra. Deinde צדק idem quod iustitia, à verbo צדק iustus fuit, iuste egit. Unde צדק iustus: inde vero צדקה iustitia.
units.tr: the Apostle set forth as an argument that Christ is priest after the order of Melchizedek, drawn from etymology: Melchizedek is king of righteousness. This is the use of arguments from etymology. For the Hebrew word מלך [melek] is the same as king, deriving from the verb מלך [malak], that is, he reigned, he ruled. In Psalm 97: "The Lord reigned [malak], let the earth rejoice." Then צדק [tsedeq] is the same as righteousness, from the verb צדק [tsadaq], he was just, he acted justly. Hence צדיק [tsaddiq] means just, and from it צדקה [tsedaqah] means righteousness.

units.la: Has autem appellationes conuenire Christo, non est difficile ex propheticis scriptis & apostolicis, praeterea ex rebus per ipsum gestis demonstrare. Ac primùm quidem quòd sit rex, etiamsi id proximo argumento potius videbatur declarandum, vbi describitur rex Salem, tamen si hoc loco exposuerimus, non erit quod ibi repetamus. Inter explicandum caput primum sepè citauimus huiusmodi testimonia. Ex Psalmo 2. Dominus dixit ad me, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: postula à me, & dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terrae. Reges eos in virga ferrea, & tanquam vas figuli confringes eos. Quo Psalmo etiam praecedit: Ego autem constitutus sum rex ab eo, super Sion monte Sanctum eius. Esaiæ 9. Non nobis parvulus natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis, & factus est principatus super humerū eius: paulo post. Multiplicabitur eius imperium, & pacis non erit finis: Super solium Dauid & super regnum eius sedebit, vt confirmet illud & corroboret in iudicio & iustitia, à modo & vsque in sempiternū. Item illud: Ego ero ei pater, & ipse erit mihi filius ex secūdi regum septimo citatur de Christo. Sed ibidem praecedunt haec verba: Stabiliam thronum regni eius vsque in sempiternum.
units.tr: That these appellations apply to Christ is not difficult to demonstrate from the prophetic and apostolic writings and, besides, from the things he has done. First, that he is king. This might seem more properly to be shown in the next argument, where the king of Salem is described; yet if we set it out here, there will be no need to repeat it there. In explaining the first chapter we have often cited testimonies of this kind. From Psalm 2: "The Lord said to me, You are my son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron and break them in pieces like a potter's vessel." The same Psalm also goes before: "But I have been set up as king by him over Zion, his holy mountain." Isaiah 9: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and dominion is laid upon his shoulder." Shortly after: "His rule shall be increased, and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it with judgment and justice, from now and for ever." Likewise that saying, "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Sam. 7), is cited concerning Christ. But in the same place these words precede it: "I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever."

units.la: Iterum quod sequitur ex Psalmo quadragesimoquarto, Thronus tuus Deus in seculum seculi, virga rectitudinis virga regni tui. Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti iniquitatem: propterea vnxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo. Exultationis vltra consortes tuos. Zachariae capite nono, Ecce rex tuus venit tibi iustus & saluator, ipse pauper sedens super asinum, &c. Danielis capite septimo, & aliis locis plurimis regnum Christi luculenter describitur. In nouo autem testamento ecce statim Lucae primo angelus ad Mariam: Filius altissimi vocabitur, & dabit illi Dominus sedē Dauid patris ipsius, regnabit in domum Iacob in aeternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Ioannis decimo octavo Christus apud Pilatum fassus est, se regem, licet non terrenum vel huius mundi. A resurrectione sua regiam suam potestatem declarauit, dicens: sibi datam à patre potestatem omnem in coelo in terra. Et in epistolis passim gloria & potestas eius, qua deuicit diabolum, peccatum, mortem, infernum, quaque iam triumphat in coelis sedens ad dexteram patris, describitur. Ergo, quomodo Christus verus sit rex. Et conueniisset fortasis, plenius explicari regnum Christi ab Apostolo, si per omnia similem eum Melchisedech volebat ostendere: sed supra in initio huius disputationis causam reddidimus, quare de regno Christi Apostoli non soleant disputare.
units.tr: Again, what follows from Psalm 44: "Your throne, O God, endures for ever and ever; the sceptre of your kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." Zechariah 9: "Behold, your king comes to you, just and a saviour, poor, riding upon an ass," and so on. Daniel 7 and many other places describe the kingdom of Christ clearly. In the New Testament, at the very beginning of Luke 1, the angel says to Mary: "He will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord will give him the throne of his father David; he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." In John 18 Christ confessed before Pilate that he is a king, though not an earthly king or of this world. After his resurrection he declared his royal power, saying that all power in heaven and on earth had been given to him by the Father. And throughout the Epistles his glory and power are described, by which he overcame the devil, sin, death and hell, and by which he now triumphs in heaven, sitting at the right hand of the Father. Therefore, how Christ is a true king. It might perhaps have been fitting for the Apostle to explain the kingdom of Christ more fully, if he wished to show him to be altogether like Melchizedek; but at the beginning of this disputation we gave the reason why the Apostles are not accustomed to dispute about the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Nam regnum illius non erat temporale sed Spirituale, situm in piorum cordibus, & constans ipsa multitudine credentium, ideoque non perinde ab omnibus intelligi poterat. Sed quidam forte accepissent, agi de regno temporali: atque ita doctrinam de regno Christi tanquam seditiosam omnibus viribus reiecissent & oppressissent.
units.tr: For his kingdom was not temporal but spiritual, situated in the hearts of the pious and consisting in the very multitude of believers; and so it could not be understood in the same way by everyone. Some, perhaps, would have taken it to be a temporal kingdom, and so would have rejected and suppressed the teaching about the kingdom of Christ with all their might, as seditious.

units.la: Hoc autem loco cùm disputatio instituta sit tantùm de Christi sacerdotio, quid attinuisset multis agere de ipsius regno? Satis est simpliciter dixisse eum regem, quod extimonijs primo capite citatis notum esse poterat. Sed iam quòd Christus sit iustus, imò & rex autor, collator iustitiae, seruator, id etiam per se est manifestum. Certè in testimonijs iamiam addu ctis de regno, etiam declaratur, regnum ipsius situm esse, nō in viribus externis & potentia temporali, sed iniustitia. Vide illud ex Esaiae nono, ex Psalmo quadragesimo quarto, ex Zachariae nono. Item Esaiae capite vndecimo, Egredietur virga de radice Iesse, &c. paulo post: Iudicabit in iustitia pauperes. Esaiae capite decimo sexto, praeparabitur in misericordia solium, & sedebit super illud in veritate, in tabernaculo Dauid, & quaerens iudicium, & velociter reddens, quod iustum est. Rorate coeli desuper & nubes pluant iustum Esaiae 45. Regnabit rex, & sapiens erit, & faciet iudicium & iustitiam in terra. Malachiae 4. Orietur vobis Sol iustitiae. In nouo testamento passim, prima Corinth. cap. primo, & quinto, Factus est nobis sapientia à Deo iustitiaque & sanctificatio & redemptio. Neque tantum rex iustitiae, quia administrat aequo & bono, sed quòd, quemadmodum regnum ipsius est spirituale, ita conferat nobis iustitiam spiritualem, quae valet apud Deum, qui non nisi spiritualibus delectatur: Romanorum cap. 4. 5. 8. Esaiae cap. 53.
units.tr: In this place, since the disputation has been undertaken only concerning the priesthood of Christ, what would it have profited to speak at length of his kingdom? It is enough to have said simply that he is king, which could be known from the testimonies cited at the beginning of the first chapter. But that Christ is just, and indeed the author and bestower of righteousness, a saviour, this too is evident in itself. Certainly in the testimonies about his kingdom just now adduced, it is also made clear that his kingdom is situated not in external forces and temporal power, but in righteousness. See this in Isaiah 9, in Psalm 44 and in Zechariah 9. Likewise Isaiah 11: "A shoot will come out from the root of Jesse," and so on; shortly after: "He will judge the poor in righteousness." Isaiah 16: "A throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, seeking judgment and swiftly rendering what is just." Isaiah 45: "Let the heavens drop down from above and the clouds rain down the just one." Isaiah 45: "A king shall reign and be wise, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth." Malachi 4: "The Sun of righteousness shall rise upon you." Throughout the New Testament, as in 1 Corinthians 1 and 5: "He has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." He is king of righteousness not only because he administers with equity and goodness, but because, just as his kingdom is spiritual, so he bestows on us a spiritual righteousness, which avails before God, who delights only in spiritual things: Romans 4, 5, 8; Isaiah 53.

units.la: Deinde verò etiam rex Salem, quod est rex pacis.
units.tr: Then indeed also Melchizedek was king of Salem, which means king of peace.

units.la: Secundum argumentum sumptum à vitae conditione, hoc est, à publica dignitate seu functione, sic habet:
units.tr: The second argument, taken from the condition of his life, that is, from his public dignity or office, runs as follows:

units.la: Melchi-
units.tr: Melchi-

units.la: Chrisstum esse regem. Melchisedech erat rex Salem, id est, rex pacis.
units.tr: Christ is king. Melchizedek was king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

units.la: Sed Christus etiam est verus rex, & autor, & collocator pacis.
units.tr: But Christ is also the true king, the author, and the bringer of peace.

units.la: Igitur recte dicitur de Christo, quod de Melchisedech, siue Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: Therefore what is said of Melchizedek is rightly said of Christ, or that Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Scriptores artium enumerant varios locos personarum, iubent inter cætera spectari etiam, qua quis agat conditione, id est, magistratúm ne gerat, an sit priuatus: clarus an obscurus: seruus, an liber, &c. Ex his uero argumenta ducuntur ad laudandum vel vituperandum, & personæ cum personis conferuntur: & hoc pacto præsens quoque argumentum collectum est, nimirum à vitæ conditione. Hic quidem pluribus agendum erat de Christi regia dignitate, vt ita clarius Melchisedech æqualis, vel certè superior agnosceretur: sed quare id nequaquam fecerit Apostolus, neque etiam operæ precium sit à nobis fieri, supra caussam reddidimus. Interea regem esse Christum, perinde atque erat Melchisedech, satis notum est, & nos, quantum requirebatur, demonstrauimus.
units.tr: The writers on the arts list various headings for persons, and they direct us to consider, among other things, what condition a person is in: whether he holds a magistracy or is a private man; whether he is famous or obscure; whether he is a slave or free, and so on. From these, arguments are drawn to praise or blame, and persons are compared with persons; in this way the present argument also has been drawn, namely from the condition of life. Here, to be sure, much would have had to be said about Christ's royal dignity, so that Melchizedek might be recognised more clearly as his equal, or rather his superior. But why the Apostle did not do this at all, and why it is not worth our effort to do so, I have explained above. Meanwhile, that Christ is king, just as Melchizedek was, is well enough known, and I have shown this as far as was required.

units.la: Regem autè esse Salem, id est, pacis, rectè ab Apostolo dicitur: Quandoquidem vox שלם hebraeis pacem significat.
units.tr: That he was king of Salem, that is, of peace, is rightly said by the Apostle, since the Hebrew word שלם [shalem] means peace.

units.la: Est quidè Apud Hebraeos verbū, quod ijdem literis consonantibus scriptū, tamen pro variatione punctorum vocalium diuersam habet significationem. Primo enim cum scribitur שלם, idem est quod restituit, retribuit: cum scribitur שלם, significat consummatum est, finem accepit. Cum scribitur שלם, pacificus fuit. Vnde mox שלום & שלם pacificus: deinde שלמים hostia pacifica, votum, placatio. שלום pax masculino genere: quod etiā adiectiuè capitur pro pacifico.
units.tr: There is a Hebrew word which is written with the same consonants, yet, according to the variation of the vowel points, has a different meaning. For when it is written שלם [shalam], it means he restored or repaid; when it is written שלם [shalem], it means it was finished, it reached its end; when it is written שלם [shelem], it means he was peaceable. Hence soon come שלום [shalom] and שלם [shalem], peaceable; then שלמים [shelamim], a peace offering, a vow, a propitiation. שלום [shalom], peace, is masculine in gender, and it is also taken adjectivally for peaceable.

units.la: Porrò & testimonijs prophetarum, & scriptis apostolicis & rebus à Christo gestis, docetur, Christum regem, autorem, & largitorem esse omnis veræ pacis: Sic enim Esaiæ capite nono dicebat, quòd in regno eius pacis non foret finis. Item Esaiæ tricesimo secundo, Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, &c. Psalmo septuagesimo primo, Orietur in diebus eius iustitia & abundantia pacis. Lucæ 1. vt illucescerēt, his qui in tenebris & in vmbra mortis sedent, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis.
units.tr: Moreover, both from the testimonies of the prophets, from the apostolic writings, and from the deeds done by Christ, it is taught that Christ is the king, the author, and the giver of all true peace. Thus Isaiah in chapter nine said that in his kingdom there would be no end of peace. Likewise Isaiah chapter thirty-two: My people shall sit in the beauty of peace, etc. Psalm seventy-one: In his days shall righteousness spring up and abundance of peace. Luke 1: to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

units.la: Romanorum capite 5. Iustificati ex fide, pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Ephesiorum capite secundo, Christus est pax nostra, qui fecit ex vtriusque vnum, vt reconciliaret Iudaeos & gentes in vno corpore, Deo, per crucem. Collossenf. capite primo. Placuit patri in Christo vniuersam plenitudinem inhabitare, & per eum cuncta reconciliare erga se, pacificatis per sanguinem crucis eius, per eundem, siue quæ in terra, siue quæ in cœlis sunt. Et à resurrectione sua pacem discipulis annunciauit, & impartitus est, quam & perpetuam illis esse voluit.
units.tr: Romans chapter 5: Justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Ephesians chapter 2: Christ is our peace, who made the two into one, so that he might reconcile Jews and Gentiles in one body to God through the cross. Colossians chapter 1: It pleased the Father that in Christ all fullness should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross, through him, whether they are on earth or in heaven. And after his resurrection he announced peace to his disciples and bestowed it on them, and he willed that it should be lasting for them.

units.la: I antò autem iustius dicitur Christus rex iustitiæ, item rex pacis, quanto excellentior est tum iustitia, tum pax eius, quàm ea, quæ spectari poterat in Melchisedech. In hoc enim spectari tantùm poterat externa & temporalis iustitia siue pax: In Christo verò spiritualis & æterna. Deinde, Melchisedech non sic iustus aut pacis amans, vt alijs posset iustitiam aut pacem impartiri: At Christus hæc dona alijs est largitus. Quare tantò excellentius hi præclari tituli seu appellationes conueniunt Christo præ Melchisedech, quantò præstantior est veritas typo, & corpus vmbra. Rectissimè ergo Christus sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech dicitur.
units.tr: Christ is therefore rightly called more justly the king of righteousness, and likewise the king of peace, by as much as his righteousness and his peace are more excellent than those which could be seen in Melchizedek. For in him there could be seen only external and temporal righteousness or peace; but in Christ they are spiritual and eternal. Further, Melchizedek was not so righteous or so great a lover of peace that he could impart righteousness or peace to others; but Christ has bestowed these gifts on others. Therefore these illustrious titles and appellations belong to Christ above Melchizedek by as much as the truth is more excellent than the type, and the body than the shadow. Rightly, then, is Christ said to be a priest after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Ignoti patris, ignota matris, ignoti generis, neq; initium dierum, neq; vitæ finē habens, sed assimilatus filio Dei manet sacerdos in perpetuum.
units.tr: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like unto the Son of God, abideth a priest continually.

units.la: Tertium argumentum, quo probat, ea, quæ de Mechisedech dicuntur, Christo cōpetere, atq; ita Christum rectè dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, sumptum ab vtriusq; initio & exitu, in hunc modum:
units.tr: The third argument, by which he proves that the things said of Melchizedek belong to Christ, and that thus Christ is rightly called a priest after the order of Melchizedek, is taken from the beginning and the end of each, and runs thus:

units.la: Melchisedech erat ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neq; initium dierum, neque vitæ finem habens.
units.tr: Melchizedek was ἀπάτωρ [apatōr], ἀμήτωρ [amētōr], ἀγενεαλόγητος [agenealogētos], having neither beginning of days nor end of life.

units.la: Sed Christus itidem ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neq; initium dierum, neq; vitæ finem habens.
units.tr: But Christ likewise is ἀπάτωρ [apatōr], ἀμήτωρ [amētōr], ἀγενεαλόγητος [agenealogētos], having neither beginning of days nor end of life.

units.la: Ergo rectè dicuntur de Christo, quæ de Melchisedech, & Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, rectè colligitur.
units.tr: Therefore, what is said of Melchisedech is rightly said of Christ, and it is rightly concluded that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchisedech.

units.la: Et valdè acutum & subtile hoc argumentum est: Quare autem, & quomodo excogitatum sint, mox plenius explicabimus. Porrò de Minore eius satis constat, maximè si in Christo distinguamus. Quòd enim ἀπάτωρ sit, id est, sine patre, id verum est de eo, quia secundū humanam naturā, secundum quam habuit matrem, nempe beatam virginem, sed non patre. Quod enim in ea natū erat, de spiritu Sancto erat, vt habetur Lucę 1. non do alii quō carnali patre. Iosephus tantum putatiuus fuit pater, virginis intactæ & sancti fœtus ἀμήτωρ. custos à Deo ordinatus. Est item Christus ἀμήτωρ, id est, sine matre, nimirum secundum diuinitatem ex patre genitus est ante secula: sicut Ioannes præclarè ait: In principio erat verbum, &c.
units.tr: This is a very keen and subtle argument, and I shall soon explain more fully why and how it was devised. Meanwhile, the minor premise is quite certain, especially if we distinguish the natures in Christ. That he is ἀπάτωρ, that is, without a father, is true of him in respect of his human nature, according to which he had a mother, namely the blessed Virgin, but no father. For what was born in her was of the Holy Spirit, as is found in Luke 1; there was no earthly father. Joseph was only the putative father, the guardian of the untouched virgin and of the holy offspring, appointed by God. Christ is likewise ἀμήτωρ, that is, without a mother, since according to his divinity he was begotten of the Father before the ages; as John aptly says: "In the beginning was the Word," etc.

units.la: Item Christus ἀγενεαλόγητος, id est, sine genere, & neq; initium dierum, neque finem vitæ habens, secundum diuinā naturā: secundū quam semper patri par, principij & finis omnis expers est: sicut Ioan. 1. copiosè explicat: & de natura Dei non potest aliud mente concipi. Secundum humanitatem quidem genus Christi legitur & à Matthæo, & à Luca descriptum: sed secundum diuinam naturam Ioannes recte ait fuisse ab initio, genealogiam omnem excludes. Sed hæc de minore satis, quæ filio Dei pulchrè copetere ipse Apostolus exprimit, dicens: Melchisedech assimilatu filio Dei. Maior plus habet difficultatis: sumpta est, quòd in sacris literis neq; genus Melchisedech, neq; vita, neq; mors describatur, cùm tamen de illustribus viris, præsertim qui Christi typu gerunt, hæc omnia soleant accurrate discuti, & Iudæi semper fuerint curiosi earum rerum obseruatores: nec dubium interea sit, quin ille certis parentibus sit ortus, mortem quoque communi more & lege cæterorum hominum obierit. Vult autem Apostolus accipi, id ita factum singulari spiritus Sancti prouidentia consilioque, vt nimirum, vt in sacerdote Melchisedech, cuius neque vita, neq; mors commemoratur, eò clarius Christi æternum sacerdotium, qui fuit ab æterno & manet in æternum, eluceret: sicut haud dubiè spiritus Sanctus iam tùm prædestinabat oraculum per Dauidem postea edere de sacerdotio Christi æterno secundum ordinem illius Melchisedech. Itaque Melchisedech hac ratione dicitur ab Apostolo ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neque initium dierum, neq; finem vitæ habens, non quòd reuera patrem vel matrem non habuerit, & instar Veneris apud poetas e spuma maris subito prodierit, vel, vt homines facti ex lapidibus, quos post tergum iecit Deucalion: neque etiam quòd non fuerit mortuus, verùm translatus seu raptus instar Enoch aut Heliæ: sed quòd Scriptura neq; parentes eius, neque genus, præterea neque finem vitæ, seu genus mortis commemorarit. Cuius rei rationem habuisse mihi videtur latinus interpres, qui noluit simpliciter vertere, Sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, sicut græcæ voces significant: Sed vertit ignoti patris, ignotæ matris, ignoti generis. In quam sententiam etiam Chrysostomus exposuit hæc verba, dicens: Non reipsa sic accipienda hæc verba de Melchisedech: sed, quia nos ignoramus, quem patre, vel, quam matrem ille habuerit, quando item natus, vel mortuus. Atq; Apostolus ipse suorum verborum interpretatione prudenter adiicit, quando ne quis verba illa sic acciperet, quasi inde colligi posset, Melchisedech esse filium seu virtutem Dei, sicut historiæ testantur, quosdam aliquando sic opinatos, erroreque turpi deceptos ac damnatos (quos & Melchisedecianos nunc appellatos dicunt) subiecit: Melchisedech ea in parte assimilatum filio Dei, cui soli id proprie & secundum naturam conuenit, vt dicatur ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neque initium dierum, neque vitæ finem habens. Quod verbum haud dubie ideo subiectum fuit ab Apostolo, tum ne quis putaret, eum simpliciter asserere, Melchisedech talem fuisse: tum vt innueret, se animaduertere, in Scripturis singulari spiritus Sancti consilio omissa fuisse illa omnia, vt sic Melchisedech Christum euidentius repræsentaret. Quapropter reijcienda sunt delyria Iudæorum, qui de genere, vita, mortenuæ Melchisedech plura, quàm in Scripturis expressa sunt, audent comminisci.
units.tr: Likewise Christ is ἀγενεαλόγητος, that is, without genealogy, and has neither beginning of days nor end of life, according to his divine nature, in which he is always equal to the Father and free from all beginning and end; as John 1 explains at length, and no other concept of the nature of God can be formed in the mind. According to his humanity, indeed, the lineage of Christ is recorded both by Matthew and by Luke; but according to the divine nature John rightly says he was from the beginning, thereby excluding every genealogy. But this is enough about the minor premise, which the Apostle himself expresses as fitting the Son of God beautifully, saying: "Melchisedech, made like to the Son of God." The major premise has more difficulty: it is taken from the fact that in the sacred letters neither the lineage, nor the life, nor the death of Melchisedech is described, although about illustrious men, especially those who bear the type of Christ, all these things are usually examined carefully, and the Jews have always been curious observers of such things. Meanwhile there is no doubt that he was born of definite parents and died in the common manner and by the law applying to other men. The Apostle, however, wishes it to be understood that this was so done by the singular providence and counsel of the Holy Spirit, namely so that, in the priest Melchisedech, of whom neither life nor death is recorded, the eternal priesthood of Christ, who was from eternity and abides for eternity, might shine forth more clearly; just as the Holy Spirit, without doubt, had already predestined to give later through David the oracle concerning the eternal priesthood of Christ according to the order of that Melchisedech. Thus Melchisedech is called by the Apostle ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, not because he truly had no father or mother and suddenly came forth from the foam of the sea like Venus among the poets, or like the men made from stones which Deucalion threw behind his back, nor again because he did not die, but was translated or carried off like Enoch or Elijah; but because Scripture has not recorded his parents, nor his lineage, nor, moreover, the end of his life or the manner of his death. The Latin translator, it seems to me, took account of this matter, for he did not wish to render simply "without father, without mother, without genealogy," as the Greek words signify, but rendered it "of unknown father, of unknown mother, of unknown lineage." Chrysostom also expounded these words in this sense, saying: "These words are not to be taken in their literal sense about Melchisedech; but because we do not know who his father or mother was, or when he was born or died." And the Apostle himself, prudently adding an explanation of his own words, lest anyone should take those words as if it could be inferred from them that Melchisedech was the Son or power of God, appended the clause: "Melchisedech, in that respect made like to the Son of God, to whom alone this properly and according to nature belongs, that he is called ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, having neither beginning of days nor end of life." Without doubt the Apostle added this phrase both so that no one might think he was simply asserting that Melchisedech was such, and so that he might indicate that he was aware that in the Scriptures all those things had been omitted by the singular counsel of the Holy Spirit, so that Melchisedech might more clearly represent Christ. Therefore the dreams of the Jews are to be rejected, who dare to invent more about the lineage, life and death of Melchisedech than is expressed in the Scriptures.

units.la: Confingunt aliqui Melchisedech esse ipsum Sem primogenitum Noæ: aliqui ex hoc Sem natum, atque eo tempore, quo natus est Abraham, annorum fuisse ducentorum nonaginta duorum. Cùm verò Abraham moreretur, superuixisse Melchisedech adhuc annos trigintaquinque, quare vniuersum tempus vitæ eius fuisse sexingentorum annorum. Nec nimirum, si Abrahæ obuius iuerit, commeatum & victum largiter suppeditans, quando Abrahæ abnepoti suo iure propinquitatis id propemodum debuerit. Valeant hæ nugæ, quæ præter Scripturam, & contra spiritus Sancti mentem obtruduntur. Certum est, si spiritus Sanctus non vidisset expedire, vt descriptio generis, & vitæ, & mortis Melchisedech omitteretur, nequaquam omisisset, vtpote qui semper solet largiter & clarè ascribere, quæcunque ad salutem & mysteriorum significationem cognitu sunt necessaria. Debet pijs animis ea esse religio, vt Scripturæ sanctæ nihil assuant, & vt ceu cognitu necessarium non obtrudant, quod spiritus Sanctus cognoscendum non exposuit. Id si fieret, errores plerique essent iam diu repressi, de quibus adhuc apud curiosulos acrius litigatur. Simus contenti ijs, quæ in Scripturis sunt prodita.
units.tr: Some have invented that Melchisedech was Shem, the firstborn son of Noah, and others that he was born of this Shem and was two hundred and ninety-two years old at the time Abraham was born. And when Abraham died, Melchisedech, they say, was still alive for another thirty-five years, so that the whole span of his life came to six hundred years. Nor, they add, would it be surprising if, when he met Abraham, he supplied him generously with provisions and food, since by right of kinship he almost owed this to his great-grandson. Let these trifles go, since they are foisted on us apart from Scripture and against the mind of the Holy Spirit. It is certain that if the Holy Spirit had not judged it useful to omit a description of the descent, life and death of Melchisedech, He would never have omitted it, since He is accustomed to set forth fully and clearly whatever is necessary to know for salvation and for the meaning of the mysteries. Godly minds ought to observe this piety: not to add anything to Holy Scripture, and not to impose as necessary to know what the Holy Spirit has not set forth to be known. If this were done, most of the errors that are still hotly disputed among the overcurious would have been suppressed long ago. Let us be content with what has been handed down in the Scriptures.

units.la: Vltra hæc ne superstitiose scrutemur: valde atque hac in parte argumentum ab auctoritate etiam negatiue, vt dicatur: Non habetur in Scriptura expressum: Ergo non est credendum. Sic enim Apostolus ipse hoc loco argumentatur: Melchisedech neque initium mitium vitæ, neque finis describitur: Igitur manet sacerdos in æternum. Vnde & sequitur:
units.tr: Let us not, beyond these things, scrutinize superstitiously. In this matter especially, an argument from authority may be used even negatively, so that one says: It is not stated expressly in Scripture; therefore it is not to be believed. For the Apostle himself argues in this way here: Melchisedech is described as having neither beginning of days nor end of life; therefore he remains a priest for ever. And from this there follows:

units.la: Manet sacerdos in æternum) Quartum argumentum è proximè præcedenti fluens, quo quandoquidem præcedentia satis declarauerunt, Christum rectè dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, iam probatur sacerdotium istud Christi esse æternum.
units.tr: He remains a priest for ever. This is the fourth argument, flowing from the immediately preceding one. Since what precedes has sufficiently shown that Christ is rightly called a priest after the order of Melchisedech, it is now proved that this priesthood of Christ is eternal.

units.la: Melchisedech, inquit, manet sacerdos in æternum.
units.tr: Melchisedech, he says, remains a priest for ever.

units.la: Igitur & Christus manet sacerdos in æternum.
units.tr: Therefore Christ also remains a priest for ever.

units.la: Quare palàm fit testimonium illud suprà capite quinto citatum, Tu es sacerdos, secundum ordinem Melchisedech, Christo per omnia conuenire. Vide autem, quàm necessarium fuerit postremum istud argumentum, imò & proximè antecedens (sunt enim, si bene expendimus, coniungenda potius, quàm separanda) adijcere, quamquè prudenter atque artificiosè Apostolus ea constituerit. Aduersarij quidem duobus primis argumentis permoti, fortasis haud grauatim concessuri erant, Christum rectè dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech: Sed obijcere adhuc poterant, cùm testimonium suprà citatum loquatur de sacerdotio, quomodo Christi sacerdotium secundum illum ordinem foret æternum: quòd sanè arbitrati sunt probatu multò difficillimum, quando ne ipsius quidem Melchisedech sacerdotium æternum fuerit, sed finem citò, vt apparet, acceperit, succedente ei sacerdotio Aaronico (in speciem) præstantiore. Propter hanc igitur obiectionem coactus est Apostolus nouas rationes excogitare, quibus aduersariorum cauillis satisfaceret.
units.tr: Hence it is plain that the testimony cited above in chapter five, You are a priest after the order of Melchisedech, agrees with Christ in every respect. Notice how necessary this last argument was, and indeed the one immediately before it (for, if we weigh them well, they ought to be joined rather than separated), and how prudently and skilfully the Apostle arranged them. Indeed, moved by the first two arguments, the opponents might have conceded without much difficulty that Christ is rightly called a priest after the order of Melchisedech. But they could still object: since the testimony cited above speaks of a priesthood, how would Christ's priesthood after that order be eternal? This they judged to be a very difficult thing to prove, since not even the priesthood of Melchisedech himself was eternal, but, as is evident, came quickly to an end, when the Aaronic priesthood, more excellent (in appearance), succeeded it. Because of this objection, therefore, the Apostle was compelled to devise new reasons, by which he might satisfy the quibbles of his opponents.

units.la: Et quamuis satis futurum videbatur, nostra opinione, si in eadem causa versandum nobis esset, si probaretur, Christum esse æternum, id quod ex prima parte huius epistolæ, qua de diuinitate agebatur, manifestum haberi poterat: tamen voluit euidenter probare, etiam ipsius Melchisedech sacerdotium æternum esse, vt inde quoq; apertius concluderet, & Christi sacerdotium æternum esse. Sic igitur, & vt subtiliter, ita grauiter perspicueq; æternitatem sacerdotij Melchisedech asserit.
units.tr: Although, in our judgement, it would have been enough, if we were engaged in the same dispute, to prove that Christ is eternal, which could be seen plainly from the first part of this letter, where his divinity was treated, yet he wished to prove clearly that the priesthood of Melchisedech itself is eternal, so that he might conclude more openly from this that the priesthood of Christ is also eternal. Thus, both subtly and weightily and clearly, he asserts the eternity of Melchisedech's priesthood.

units.la: Non legitur sacerdotium Melchisedech initium vel finem habuisse, quandoquidem de origine, vita, morte, Melchisedech, vel de abrogatione sacerdotij eius nihil est proditu.
units.tr: The priesthood of Melchisedech is not read to have had beginning or end, since nothing is recorded about his origin, life, or death, or about the abrogation of his priesthood.

units.la: Ergo Melchisedech manet sacerdos in æternum.
units.tr: Therefore Melchisedech remains a priest for ever.

units.la: Ex hoc verò iam conficitur:
units.tr: From this, moreover, the following is now inferred:

units.la: Christus est sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech: sicut prius probatum est.
units.tr: Christ is a priest after the order of Melchisedech, as was proved before.

units.la: Igitur & sacerdotium Christi, perinde ac sacerdotium Melchisedech, manet in æternum.
units.tr: Therefore also the priesthood of Christ, just as the priesthood of Melchisedech, remains for ever.

units.la: Atque ita abundè comprobatum relinquitur integrum illud testimonium Scripturæ:
units.tr: And thus, having been abundantly confirmed, that whole testimony of Scripture stands:

units.la: Tu es sacerdos in æternum, secundū ordine Melchisedech, in Christum per omnia copetere, & de solo Christo accipiendum. Præsupponit autem, sicut prius diximus spiritum Sanctum data opera, & consulto suppresisse omnia de origine, vita & exitu Melchisedech, vt typus æterni sacerdotij Christi clarius in eo resplenderet. Quis iam non animaduertit, insigni prudentia & ingenti artificio argumenta hæc esse collecta? Quis Rhetor, quis Dialecticus vel animo conciperet, tali pacto probationes eiusmodi posse confici? Et quis vnquam cogitasset, in tàm paucis, quæ Melchisedech sunt prodita, tantam vim argumentorum fuisse repositam, & tàm sublimia de Christo mysteria latuisse, nisi ipse spiritus Sanctus postea per Dauidem, deinde verò per apostolum Paulum, huius epistolæ citra controuersiam autorem, in apertum protulisset?
units.tr: You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchisedech, applies fully to Christ and is to be understood of Christ alone. But, as we said before, it presupposes that the Holy Spirit deliberately and purposely suppressed everything about the origin, life and departure of Melchisedech, so that the type of Christ's eternal priesthood might shine more clearly in him. Who does not now notice that these arguments have been put together with remarkable wisdom and great skill? What rhetorician or dialectician could even conceive that proofs of this kind could be constructed in such a way? And who would ever have suspected that so great a force of argument lay hidden in the few things that have been handed down about Melchisedech, and that such sublime mysteries of Christ lay concealed, unless the Holy Spirit Himself had later brought them to light, first through David and then through the Apostle Paul, beyond dispute the author of this letter?

units.la: Sed vide præterea quàm appositè singula sint dicta: vt clarius æternitatis naturam exprimat, ait, Melchisedech neque initium, neque finem habuisse, quod proprie est æternum seu ἀνώνυμος esse: neque alia periphrasis, ad significandum continuum, & vnquam intermissum aptior excogitari haudquaquam posset. Deinde, non dixit, est, vel fit sacerdos in æternum: sed quod multò significantius, manet sacerdos in æternum, clarè indicans, nunquam desijsse eum ordinem, sed in præsens quoque perseuerare. Tametsi vero hoc argumentum ab autoritate scripturæ sumptum sit negatiuè, tamen vires debet habere propterea, quòd spiritus Sanctus in sacra Scriptura, sicut nihil otiosè exprimit, ita nihil otiosè omittit. Proinde valde eleganter excussum est illud testimonium Scripturæ: Tu es sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech, clareque in tanta breuitate demonstratum est, id de Christo simpliciter esse accipiendum, & expositum, quis vel qualis ordo ille Melchisedecicus, & quomodo eius ordinis sacerdotium duret æternum.
units.tr: But observe further how aptly each point is stated. To express the nature of eternity more clearly, he says that Melchisedech had neither beginning nor end, which properly means to be eternal or [ἀνώνυμος]. Nor could any more fitting periphrasis be devised to signify what is continuous and never interrupted. Next, he did not say "is" or "becomes a priest for ever", but, what is much more significant, "remains a priest for ever", clearly indicating that this order never ceased, but continues even to the present. Although this argument drawn from the authority of Scripture is negative, it must nonetheless have force, because the Holy Spirit in Holy Scripture, just as He expresses nothing idly, so likewise omits nothing idly. Therefore that testimony of Scripture, You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedech, has been very elegantly examined, and it has been shown clearly, in so brief a space, that it is to be understood simply of Christ, and it has been explained what that Melchisedechian order is and how the priesthood of that order endures for ever.

units.la: Iam ex his doctrinam minimè vulgarem licet colligere. Primùm, ex eo, quòd Christus describitur rex iustitiæ, egregiam & doctrinam & consolationem accipiemus.
units.tr: From these things we may gather a teaching that is by no means common. First, from the fact that Christ is described as the king of righteousness, we receive both an outstanding teaching and an outstanding consolation.

units.la: B Doctrinam quidem, quòd solus Christus sit autor & largitor iustitiæ per quem satisfit pro omnibus nostris peccatis Deo patri, & propter quem nos etiam iusti pronunciamur. Quæ cognitio caput est totius euangelij: &, qui hanc non volunt suscipere, non est quod sperent vnquam interiustos se annumerandos. Qua de re Apostolus in omnibus fere agit epistolis, & Christus ipse passim.
units.tr: B The teaching indeed is this: that Christ alone is the author and bestower of righteousness, through whom satisfaction is made to God the Father for all our sins, and on account of whom we too are pronounced righteous. This knowledge is the chief point of the whole gospel; and those who are unwilling to receive it have no reason to hope that they will ever be counted among the just. For this reason the Apostle deals with it in almost all his letters, and Christ himself does so everywhere.

units.la: Consolatio verò hæc ingens est, quòd, vbi terretur conscientia magnitudine peccatorum, & iniustitiæ nostræ proprię, ac diabolus conatur nos tum in foueam desperationis præcipitare, confugiendum est nobis ad iustitiam Christi ipsius, vt eam nobis impartiat, dicendum q; cum propheta, In iustitia tua libera me.
units.tr: The consolation is great indeed: when conscience is terrified by the greatness of our sins and by our own unrighteousness, and the devil tries to hurl us into the pit of despair, we must flee to the righteousness of Christ himself, that he may impart it to us, and we must say with the prophet, In your righteousness deliver me.

units.la: Secundò, in hoc titulo, quo Christus describitur nobis rex pacis, insignis nobis proponitur consolatio, qua muniemur contra pericula quæcunque, & omne genus tentationum, quæ conscientiam nostram possent inquietare, adeò, vt si toto pectore in hanc particulam intueamur, eaq; fide, qua decet, pacem nobis per Christum partam amplectamur, neq; mors, neq; vita, neq; angeli, neq; principatus, neq; potestates, neq; instantia, neq; futura, neq; altitudo, neque profunditas, neque vlla creatura alia poterit nos sic perturbare, vtà dilectione Dei diuellamur. Certè sunt valde speciosi, & regia maiestate pleni hi tituli, quibus Christus describitur hic rex iustitiæ, præterea rex pacis, item sacerdos Dei altissimi, vt ex illis vere agnosci possit rex regum & Dominus dominantiu. Et sicut qui sub potentissimo aliquo principe agunt, confidunt, se securos fore ab iniurijs, neq; aliquem aduersarium inferiorem posse aduersus regnum potentissimum præualere, ita qui agunt in hoc regno Christi, verè tuti & securi sunt ab omni molestia diaboli, & quorumcunque tyrannorum visibilium & inuisibilium, qui sub Imperatore diaboli militant.
units.tr: Secondly, in this title, by which Christ is described to us as the king of peace, a remarkable consolation is set before us, by which we are fortified against whatever dangers and every kind of temptation that might disturb our conscience. So much so that, if we look upon this part with our whole heart, and embrace with the faith that is fitting the peace won for us through Christ, neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to disturb us so as to tear us away from the love of God. Certainly these titles, by which Christ is here described as king of righteousness, further as king of peace, and likewise as priest of the Most High God, are very splendid and full of royal majesty, so that from them he may truly be recognized as King of kings and Lord of lords. And just as those who serve under some most powerful prince trust that they will be safe from injuries, and that no lesser adversary can prevail against so mighty a kingdom, so those who live in this kingdom of Christ are truly protected and secure from every harassment of the devil, and from all visible and invisible tyrants who serve under the emperor the devil.

units.la: Tertiò, proponitur hic nobis mirabilis modus tractandi Scripturas, quo ad magnam diligentiam & solertiam in eliciendis argumentis, & examinandis minutissimis partibus excitamur. Quis obsecro rogatus explicare, quisnam sit ordo Melchisedech, explicaret eo modo, quod istud fecit Apostolus, maximè verò illam particulam, quòd ordo Melchisedecicus duraret in æternum? Ea propter exhortor vnumquemque, qui sertò aliquando vult rhetoricari, vt magna alacritate animi in Scripturarum perscrutatione versetur, omnibusq; bonis artibus instructus, inprimis pia mente accedat, & quod in bonis artibus, quæ etiam sunt Dei dona, haud quibusfuis obuia, fuerit diminutum, postulet à Deo per spiritum Sanctum sibi adijci. Nam reuera vt prosint bonarum artium disciplinæ, vtpote quæ ancillarum hic fungi debeant munere, tamen spiritus Sanctus est ille magister, qui docet omnem veritatem, monstratq;, quomodo solida & certa argumenta formari constituique posint, aduersus cuius argumenta nulla sophistica potest præualere. Eia ò bone, quis es, qui putas te per Aristotelem edoceri, quomodo explicanda sit sacra Scriptura?
units.tr: Third, here we are shown a remarkable way of handling the Scriptures, which stirs us up to great diligence and skill in drawing out arguments and examining the smallest parts of the text. Who, I ask you, if he were asked to explain what the order of Melchizedek is, could explain it in the way the Apostle did, especially that phrase that the order of Melchizedek lasts forever? For this reason I urge everyone who wishes at some point to become a skilled speaker to devote himself to searching the Scriptures with great eagerness of mind. Let him come first with a pious mind, equipped with all the liberal arts, and if anything has been lacking in those arts, which are also gifts of God and by no means common, let him ask God through the Holy Spirit to add it to him. For although the disciplines of the liberal arts are useful, since they ought to serve here as handmaids, the Holy Spirit is nevertheless the teacher who teaches all truth and shows how solid and certain arguments can be formed and set in place, against which no sophistry can prevail. Ho there, my friend, who are you who think you are taught by Aristotle how sacred Scripture is to be explained?

units.la: Considerate verò, quàtus hic fuerit, cui etiam decimas dederit Abraham patriarcha de spolijs?
units.tr: Consider, then, how great he was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth even of the spoils.

units.la: Hactenus perspicuis aliquot argumentis probauit, Christum recte dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech: Iam incipit conferre ordinem Melchisedech, cum ordine Aaronico seu Leuitico, vt, vbi euicerit, illum isto præstantiorem, mox inferat, per sacerdotium Christi, quod est secundum ordinem Melchisedech, sacerdotium legale, quod est ordinis Leuitici, abrogari. Hac autem ratione probat, ordinem Melchisedech præeminere ordini Aaronico seu Leuitico. Confert in primis personam Melchisedech cum persona Abrahæ: deinde etiam ordinem seu sacerdocium, Melchisedech cum ordine ac sacerdotio Leuitico, ac clarissime euincit Melchisedech esse maiorem ipso Abraham, præterea ordinem Melchisedech excellentiorem ordine Leuitico. Ducit verò argumenta omnia ex breui historia Melchisedech: ac primùm ex ea particula, qua dicitur, quòd Melchisedech acceperit decimas ab Abraham: ex qua sola, (quis cogitasset istud posse fieri?) diuersa argumenta elicit, optimo ordine summoq; artificio contexta. Primum argumentum sic habet:
units.tr: Up to this point the Apostle has shown by several clear arguments that Christ is rightly called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Now he begins to compare the order of Melchizedek with the Aaronic or Levitical order, so that, having proved the former to be superior to the latter, he may straightway infer that through the priesthood of Christ, which is according to the order of Melchizedek, the legal priesthood, which belongs to the Levitical order, is abrogated. He proves this by the following reasoning: that the order of Melchizedek excels the Aaronic or Levitical order. First he compares the person of Melchizedek with the person of Abraham; then also the order or priesthood of Melchizedek with the Levitical order and priesthood; and he most clearly proves that Melchizedek is greater than Abraham himself, and further that the order of Melchizedek is more excellent than the Levitical order. He draws all these arguments from the brief history of Melchizedek, and first from that clause in which it is said that Melchizedek received tithes from Abraham. From this alone (who would have thought it could be done?) he draws out various arguments, woven together in the best order and with the greatest skill. The first argument runs thus:

units.la: Qui decimas accipit, procul dubio maior est eo qui dat.
units.tr: He who receives tithes is without doubt greater than he who gives them.

units.la: Sed Melchisedech est, qui accipit: Abraham autem, qui dat. Ergo Melchisedech præstantior est Abraham.
units.tr: But Melchizedek is the one who receives, and Abraham the one who gives. Therefore Melchizedek is greater than Abraham.

units.la: Maior ex eo manifesta euadit, quòd decimarum oblatio diuinitus instituta sit, ad testandum, tum gratitudinem erga Deum, tum honorem erga Dei ministros sacerdotes. Minor liquet ex historia, Genes. 14.
units.tr: The major premise becomes clear from the fact that the offering of tithes was instituted by God, to attest both gratitude towards God and honour towards God's ministers, the priests. The minor premise is clear from the history in Genesis 14.

units.la: Hoc argumentum breuiter his verbis comprehenditur, etiamsi ad ea, quæ mox sequuntur, quuntur, propositio tantùm videatur referenda. Sed hîc reuera argumentum integrum continetur: in sequentibus autem verbis potius collatio est Melchisedec cum Leuitis, aliudque argumentum ex præsenti deriuatur. Obseruandum autem, quàm eleganter & illustribus verbis hoc argumentum in tanta breuitate efferat. Consideraté, inquit: Dicturus dere, quæ aliàs difficulter videbatur posse probari, quamque fortasis minimè expectas- sent aduersarij, attentiores hanc uoce auditores reddit. ἀκούετε, inquit, quasi dicat, diligenter & arrectis auribus aduertite. ἀκούω idem quod contemplor, speculor, & sæpe rerum sublimium adeoque cœlestium & spiritualium consideratione accomodatur.
units.tr: This argument is briefly summed up in these words, although the proposition seems to refer only to what follows. But here there is in fact the whole argument; in the following words there is rather a comparison of Melchizedek with the Levites, and another argument is derived from the present one. It should be noted how elegantly and with what striking words he sets forth this argument in such brevity. Consider, he says. Because he is about to speak of a matter which otherwise seemed difficult to prove, and which perhaps the adversaries would least expect, he makes his hearers more attentive by this word. [ἀκούετε] "Hear," he says, as if to say: attend diligently and with ears pricked up. [ἀκούω] means the same as to contemplate or to observe, and it is often applied to the consideration of lofty, and indeed heavenly and spiritual, things.

units.la: Cui etiam decimam dederit de spoliis (ἀπὸ δεκάτην) significat decimam partem, & verbum ἀποδεκατόω pendo, vel etiam exigo decimam. Non potest dici, quòd dederit Melchisedec, tanquam comilitoni, sicut duces inter se prædas interdum partiuntur: quia aperte dicitur, quòd Melchisedec Abrahæ iam reuertenti à bello occurrerit. Ergo dedit ut sacerdoti Dei altissimi, & ut superiori. De decimis pendendis, quomodo institutum, quatenus necessarium, & quibus debeatur, nos postea dicemus argumento sequenti. Ait autem, decimas in τῶν ἀκροθινίων, hoc est, si ad verbum reddatur, ex primitiis frugum. ἀκροθίνια enim sunt primitiæ frugum, quæ solent à summo acervo tolli.
units.tr: "To whom he also gave a tenth of the spoils" [ἀπὸ δεκάτην]: the phrase signifies a tenth part, and the verb [ἀποδεκατόω] means to pay, or indeed to exact, a tenth. It cannot be said that Melchizedek gave it as a fellow soldier, as commanders sometimes share out plunder among themselves, because it is plainly said that Melchizedek met Abraham as he was returning from the battle. Therefore he gave it as to a priest of the Most High God, and as to one superior. Concerning the payment of tithes, how it was instituted, how far it is necessary, and to whom it is due, we shall speak later under the next argument. He says, moreover, that the tithes were given out of [τῶν ἀκροθινίων], that is, if rendered word for word, out of the first fruits of the harvest. For [ἀκροθίνια] are the first fruits of the harvest, which are usually taken from the top of the heap.

units.la: Vox composita ab ἄκρος summum, & θίνες acerui frumentorum, proprie quæ mercatores in littore soluebant pro mercibus conseruatis. Itaque ἀκροθίνια sunt è summo acervuo frugum collecta: & ἀκροθινιάζειν summa quæque delibare, primitias consecrare.
units.tr: The word is compounded from [ἄκρος], the top, and [θίνες], heaps of grain, and was properly used of the goods merchants paid on the shore for the wares they had stored there. Thus [ἀκροθίνια] are things gathered from the top of a heap of grain, and [ἀκροθινιάζειν] means to take the best of each thing, to consecrate first fruits.

units.la: Verum hoc loco Apostolus, per Catachresin, usurpauit vocem pro spoliis, siue exuuijs abhoste detractis, propterea quòd historiæ ratio ita poscit: quando quidem à cæde reuersus, & recuperata omni substantia, & ablatis opimis spoliis, Abraham decimas has dedit. Deinde aliàs apud Græcos, ut apud Philostratum, ea vox pro spoliis accipitur. Unde & Chrysostomus in ea significatione hic expositu: quamobrè & interpres rectissimè spolia reddidit. Atque erat veteribus mos, non tantùm primitias frugum, sed etiam spoliahostibus adempta Deo offerre, in primis spoliorum decimas, id quod liquet aliquo modo ex primo Samuelis decimoquinto, vbi Saul dicebat seruatas meliores oues & armenta, ut immolarentur Domino. Apud Gentiles decima prædæ sæpe etiâ voto Iouî ac Dijs nuncupabatur, unde & Iupiter prædator est appellatus. Id maximè apud Gallos receptum fuit. Nam legimus Gallos sub duce Aristontio pugnantes contra Romanos, voto promisisse Martî torquem aureum de præda hostium. Sed Flamminius ut voto vinceret, de torquibus Gallorum Martî trophæum posuit. De Crotoniatis etiam referunt, quòd, cùm pugnarent aduersus Locrenses, decimam prædæ vouerint Apollini: quod vbi audissent Locrenses, ij voto & spe vincendi vouerunt nonam partem. Crebra sunt exempla tam apud poetas, quàm historiographos.
units.tr: But here the Apostle, by catachresis, has used the word for spoils, or booty stripped from an enemy, because the course of the history requires it: since Abraham, returning from the slaughter, had recovered all his property and taken the rich spoils, and then gave these tithes. Elsewhere, too, among the Greeks, as in Philostratus, the word is taken to mean spoils, and Chrysostom expounds it in that sense here; therefore the interpreter has also rendered it most rightly as spoils. And it was the custom of the ancients to offer to God not only the first fruits of the harvest but also the spoils taken from enemies, especially a tenth of the spoils; this is made clear in some measure from the first book of Samuel, chapter fifteen, where Saul said that he had spared the better sheep and oxen so that they might be sacrificed to the Lord. Among the Gentiles the tenth of the booty was often vowed to Jupiter and the gods, and for this reason Jupiter was also called the plunderer. This was especially received among the Gauls. For we read that the Gauls, fighting under their leader Aristontius against the Romans, vowed a golden necklace from the enemy's booty to Mars. But Flaminius, in order to win by a vow, set up a trophy to Mars made of the Gauls' necklaces. They also report of the Crotoniates that, when they were fighting against the Locrians, they vowed a tenth of the booty to Apollo; when the Locrians heard this, they, out of a vow and hope of victory, vowed a ninth part. Examples are abundant both among the poets and among the historians.

units.la: Abraham Patriarcha) Non sine emphasi vox patriarchæ accipienda est. Non solum enim honoris causa eam addidit Apostolus, siue, ut æquanimiores redderet tali appellatione Iudæos, qui semper iactabant, se habere patrem Abraham, sed multò magis causa amplificandæ dignitatis Melchisedec. Vbi tantus prædicatur Abraham, & nihilominus Melchisedec ab eo accepit decimas, oportet hunc Melchisedec longè amplissimo loco esse constitutum.
units.tr: "Abraham the patriarch." The word patriarch must be taken with emphasis. For the Apostle added it not only for the sake of honour, or in order to make the Jews, who always boasted that they had Abraham as their father, more gentle through such a title, but much more for the sake of magnifying the dignity of Melchizedek. Since Abraham is so greatly extolled, and yet Melchizedek received tithes from him, this Melchizedek must be placed in a far more eminent position.

units.la: Vox Patriarchæ tantundem significat, atque sic dicas, summum & principem patrem. 1. Paralipomen. octauo. Hi sunt patriarchæ & cognationum principes, qui habitauerunt in Hierusalem.
units.tr: The word patriarch means as much as if you were to say the chief and principal father. 1 Chronicles 8: "These are the patriarchs and heads of the families who dwelt in Jerusalem."

units.la: Latinè fortasis aborigines dici possit. Hebraica vox & de quibuscunque illustribus viris, quorum valde amplæ extiterunt familiæ, dicitur. Per Antonomasiam aut accommodatur ea appellatio Abrahæ, Isaac, & Iacob, ad quos præ omnibus promissiones factas constat, quòd multarum gentium patres & primates forent.
units.tr: In Latin it might perhaps be called "aborigines." The Hebrew word is also applied to any illustrious men whose families were very large. By antonomasia this title is fitted to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom it is well known the promises were made above all others, because they were to be the fathers and chiefs of many nations.

units.la: Atque ij quidem, qui quòd sint de numero filiorum Leui, sacerdotij functionem suscipiunt, præceptum habent, ut decimas accipiant à populo iuxta legem, hoc est, à fratribus suis, licet egressis ex lumbis Abrahæ: at is, cuius genus non recensetur ex illis, decimas accepit ab Abraham.
units.tr: Now those indeed who, being of the number of the sons of Levi, take up the office of the priesthood, have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brethren, even though they have come out of the loins of Abraham; but he whose lineage is not counted among them received tithes from Abraham.

units.la: Melchisedec esse præstantiorem Abrahamo, probatum est. Alio igitur argumento infertiam, ordinem Melchisedec esse præstantiorem ordine Leuitico: idq; ex collatione personarum, à quibus uterq; ordo accepit decimas. Sic enim ratiocinatur:
units.tr: That Melchizedek is superior to Abraham has been proved. He now therefore establishes by another argument that the order of Melchizedek is superior to the Levitical order, and this from a comparison of the persons from whom each order received tithes. For he reasons thus:

units.la: Leuitæ decimas accipiebant à sibi paribus, nempe suis fratribus & contribulibus, qui omnes perinde atque ipsi ex eodem parente orti fuerant.
units.tr: The Levites received tithes from their equals, namely their brethren and fellow tribesmen, who had all, just like them, sprung from the same parent.

units.la: Ac Mechisedec non accepit à talibus, cùm nequaquam eiusdem fuerit generis: sed ab ipso Abraham, qui omnium illorum, etiam Leuitarum communis extitit parens.
units.tr: But Melchizedek did not receive from such persons, since he was by no means of the same kind; he received from Abraham himself, who was the common parent of all of them, including the Levites.

units.la: Igitur ordo Melchisedec Leuitico longè maior est. Hic verò semper subintelligè Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedec (id quod abundè satis demonstratum est) ideoque per istud excellentius eius sacerdotium abrogari sacerdotium Leuiticum, & cùm hoc ipsam legem. Huc enim tendunt argumenta omnia, sicut Apostolus ipse paulò pòst suis docebit verbis. Cernis autem & istud atgumentum duci ex breui historia Melchisedec, atque ex eadem particula, ex qua ducebatur praecedens. Neque magna est in oratione Apostoli obscuritas: nos breuiter percurremus omnia.
units.tr: Therefore the order of Melchizedek is far greater than the Levitical. Here, however, always understand that Christ is priest according to the order of Melchizedek (which has been sufficiently demonstrated), and that through this more excellent priesthood of his the Levitical priesthood is abrogated, and with it the law itself. For all the arguments tend to this, as the Apostle himself will teach a little later in his own words. You see, moreover, that this argument too is drawn from the brief history of Melchizedek, and from the same clause from which the preceding one was drawn. Nor is there great obscurity in the Apostle's discourse; we shall run through everything briefly.

units.la: Atque ij quidem, qui, quòd sunt de numero filiorum Leui, sacerdotij functione sumunt.
units.tr: Those indeed who, because they are of the number of the sons of Levi, take up the function of the priesthood.

units.la: Interpres noster perspicuitatis causa pluribus verbis sententiâ optimè reddidit, pro ἐκ τῶν ἱερέων λευί vertens, quòd sunt de numero filiorum Leui: & pro τὴν ἱερατείαν, sacerdotij functionem. Caeterum, quomodo apud Israelitas sola tribus Leuitica sacris ministeriis fuerit destinata, atque in hac ij soli, qui ex familia Aaronis, ad sacerdotium promouentur, habes Exodi vicesimo octauo. Applica ad te Aaron cum filijs suis de medio filiorum Israel, ut sacerdotio fungantur mihi. Vbi additur ad finem capitis: Legitimum sempiternum erit Aaron, & semini eius post eum. Idem Numerorum decimooctauo. Reliquarum familiarum Leuitae non fungebantur sacerdotio, sed sacerdotibus ministrabant, & praeterea per ciuitates Iudaeae hinc inde sparsi ea, quae religionis erant & cultus diuini populum docebant. De Leuitis separandis offerendisque Domino, ut seruiant in ministerio, habes Numerorum tertio, item octauo, vbi inter alia illud adijcitur, haec est lex Leuitarum: à uiginti quinque annis, & supra, ingredientur, ut ministrent in tabernaculo foederis, cumque quinquagesimum annum aetatis impleuerint, seruire cessabunt, eruntque ministri fratrum suorum in tabernaculo foederis, vt custodiant, quae sibi fuerint commendata, opera autem ipsa non facient.
units.tr: Our interpreter, for the sake of clarity, rendered the sense very well with more words: for ἐκ τῶν ἱερέων λευί he translated "because they are of the number of the sons of Levi", and for τὴν ἱερατείαν, "the function of the priesthood". Moreover, that among the Israelites the tribe of Levi alone was set apart for the sacred ministries, and that among them only those of the family of Aaron are promoted to the priesthood, you have in Exodus 28: "Bring near to you Aaron with his sons from among the children of Israel, that they may serve as priests to me." There it is added at the end of the chapter: "It shall be a perpetual statute to Aaron and to his seed after him." The same in Numbers 18. The Levites of the other families did not serve as priests, but ministered to the priests; and besides, scattered here and there through the cities of Judea, they taught the people what pertained to religion and the worship of God. Concerning the separating of the Levites and their offering to the Lord, that they might serve in the ministry, you have Numbers 3 and likewise Numbers 8, where among other things this is added: "This is the law of the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall enter to minister in the tabernacle of the covenant; and when they have completed the fiftieth year of their age, they shall cease to serve, and they shall be ministers to their brothers in the tabernacle of the covenant, to keep what has been committed to them, but they shall not do the work itself."

units.la: Sic disponès Leuitas in custodijs suis.
