Non dissimile legitur Deuteron. decimo, Numerorum decimooctauo, De habitatione eorum in diuersis ciuitatibus per omnes tribus Numerorum tricesimoquinto, item Deuteronomij decimooctauo, Moses legebatur per singulas ciuitates, sicut dicitur in Actis capite decimoquinto: Moses ab aetatibus antiquis in singulis ciuitatibus habet, qui ipsum praedicet in synagogis, vbi per omne sabbatum legitur. Quod sine dubio per Leuitas potissimum fiebat. Tantum de Leuitis, & quomodo ex ea sola tribu rebus sacris sint destinati.
units.tr: Thus they arranged the Levites in their duties. A similar thing is read in Deuteronomy 10; in Numbers 18 concerning their dwelling in the various cities throughout all the tribes; in Numbers 35; likewise Deuteronomy 18. Moses was read through the individual cities, as is said in Acts chapter 15: "Moses has had from ancient generations in every city those who preach him in the synagogues, where he is read every sabbath." This without doubt was done chiefly by the Levites. So much concerning the Levites, and how from that tribe alone they were appointed to sacred things.

units.la: Praeceptum habent, ut decimas accipiant à populo, iuxta legem, hoc est, à fratribus suis) Sanè amplificatur dignitas Leuitarum hac ratione, quòd diuinitus praeceptum sit decimas illis tanquam dignioribus pendi. Sed haec ipsa laus Leuitarum illustriorem reddit, & mirum in modum amplificat dignitatem ipsius Melchisedec. porrò praeceptum extat Numerorum decimooctauo in haec verba: Filijs Leui dedi omnes decimas Israel in possessionem, pro ministerio, quo seruiunt mihi in tabernaculo foederis. Paulò pòst: Legitimum sempiternum erit in generationibus vestris. Nihil aliud possidebunt, decimarum oblatione contenti, quas in usus eorum, & necessaria separaui, &c. Ibidem: Comedetis eas in omnibus locis vestris, tam vos, quàm familiae vestrae, quia merces est vobis pro ministerio vestro, quo seruitis in tabernaculo testimonij. Item 2. Paralipom. tricesimoprimo. Caeterum, quare diuinitus ordinatum sit, dare decimas Leuitis, atque, utrum etiam nunc dandae sint ministris verbi, vel etiam magistratibus, quaeque huc pertinent, nos mox plenius explicabimus.
units.tr: They have a command to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers. Certainly the dignity of the Levites is magnified in this way, because it was commanded by God that tithes be paid to them as to the more worthy. But this very praise of the Levites makes their dignity more illustrious, and marvellously enlarges the dignity of Melchisedec himself. Moreover, the command stands in Numbers 18 in these words: "To the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel for a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant." A little later: "It shall be a perpetual statute in your generations. They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their use and needs," etc. In the same place: "You shall eat them in all your places, both you and your households, because it is your reward for your ministry, by which you serve in the tabernacle of testimony." Likewise 2 Chronicles 31. But why it was ordained by God to give tithes to the Levites, and whether they are still to be given now to the ministers of the Word, or also to the magistrates, and what pertains to these matters, we will shortly explain more fully.

units.la: Hoc est, à fratribus suis) Hac interpretatione ostendit summam aequalitatem inter Leuitas accipientes decimas, & personas dantes, vt è diuerso tanto clarius eluceat dignitas Melchisedec accipientis, non à fratribus vel contribulibus, sed ab alienigena, nempe Abraham, quem uerosimile est non daturum fuisse decimas Melchisedec, nisi is valde exi mius, & multis nominibus excellentior fuisset. Et consultò videtur Apostolus addidisse hanc interpretationem, Hoc est à fratribus: quia euidentius exprimit aequalitatem, quàm si tantùm dictum fuisset, à populo: quae forma locutionis videtur quosdam inferiores ac dispares innuere. Quomodo autem fratres vocentur omnes Iudaei, siue propter communem parentem Abrahamum, quem semper omnes iactant: siue propter communem religionem, satis notum est. Scriptura passim obtinet, vt omnes Iudaici generis fratres inter se appellentur, voce ad charitatem ac beneuolentiam omnes incitante.
units.tr: "That is, from their brothers." By this interpretation he shows the great equality between the Levites receiving tithes and the persons giving them; so that, on the other hand, the dignity of Melchisedec receiving them may shine forth all the more clearly, not from brothers or fellow tribesmen, but from a foreigner, namely Abraham, who, it is likely, would not have given tithes to Melchisedec unless he were very much more excellent and superior in many respects. And the Apostle seems to have deliberately added this interpretation, "that is, from their brothers," because it expresses the equality more clearly than if he had said only "from the people"; this form of speech seems to hint at certain inferiors and unequals. Now how all Jews are called brothers, whether on account of the common parent Abraham, whom they all always boast of, or on account of the common religion, is well known. Scripture commonly holds that all of Jewish stock are called brothers among themselves, a word that stirs everyone to love and goodwill.

units.la: Licet egressis ex lumbis Abrahae) Et haec particula ad ostendendam aequalitatem Leuitarum accipientium decimas, cum dantibus, adiecta est. Est autem phrasis hebraica, egredi ex lumbis, vel prodire de ventre, ad significandum id quod nobis est nasci, vel originem trahere. Sic Genes. tricesimoquinto, Non vocaberis ultra Iacob, sed Israel erit nomè tuum. Et appellauit eum Israel, dixitque ei, Ego Deus omnipotes: cresce & multiplicare, gentes & populi nationum ex te erunt, reges de lumbis tuis egredientur, Micheæ 5. Ex te egredietur dux, qui regat populum meum. Et psalmo 131. De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam.
units.tr: "Although they came out of the loins of Abraham." This particle too was added to show the equality of the Levites receiving tithes with those giving them. Now it is a Hebrew phrase, "to come out of the loins," or "to proceed from the belly," to signify what for us is to be born, or to derive one's origin. So in Genesis 35: "You shall no longer be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel. And he called him Israel, and said to him: I am God Almighty; increase and multiply; nations and peoples of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come out of your loins." Micah 5: "Out of you shall come forth a ruler who shall govern my people." And Psalm 132: "Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne."

units.la: At is, cuius genus non recensetur ex illis) Alienigena quippe erat Cananæus inquâ, cū ea regio vb Salem sita erat, à Cananæis tum occupuretur. Aut, si quis velit Salem eandem, quæ post dicta sit Iebus, deinde Hierusalem, certè genere fuit Iebusæus. Quocunque modo sit, hæc pars icula opponitur illi, à suis fratribus, & inæqualitatem magnam inter Melchisedec & Abraham constituit, vt inde constet, Melchisedec, qui alienigena accepit decimas ab Abraham, longè excellentiorem esse, cum ipso Abraham, tum Leuitis omnibus, qui decimas accipiebant tantùm à sibi paribus suis fratribus.
units.tr: "But he whose genealogy is not counted from them." Indeed the land where Salem was situated was then occupied by Canaanites, so he was a Canaanite, a foreigner. Or, if anyone wishes Salem to be the same as the place afterwards called Jebus and then Jerusalem, certainly by descent he was a Jebusite. In whatever way it is, this clause is set against that one, "from their brothers," and establishes a great inequality between Melchisedec and Abraham, so that it is clear that Melchisedec, who received tithes from Abraham though he was a foreigner, is far more excellent than Abraham himself, and than all the Levites, who received tithes only from their equal brothers.

units.la: Immò verò Apostolus, dicendo, Melchisedec non traxisse genus exillis, tacitè suggerit animis cogitandum, id quod supra dictum est, eum videlicet sine patre, sine matre, sine genere extitisse, quod reuera dignitatem Melchisedec, supra quàm dici queat, amplificat.
units.tr: Indeed the Apostle, by saying that Melchisedec did not derive his descent from them, tacitly suggests to the minds of his readers what was said above, namely that he existed without father, without mother, without genealogy; and this truly magnifies the dignity of Melchisedec beyond what can be said.

units.la: Dum verò hoc pacto prædicatur excellentia Melchisedec, eò referri hæc debent omnia, ut intelligamus multò amplissimam dignitatem Christi, cuius typum gesit Melchisedec, utque agnoscamus, sacerdotium Christi, quod est secundum ordinem Melchisedec, multo præstantius esse sacerdotio legali, quod est secundum ordinem Leui: imò ordinem, siue sacerdotium Aaronicum cum omnibus adiunctis, per sacerdotium Christi abrogari. Hic enim disputationis præsentis scopus est, & ad finem hunc tendunt argumenta omnia. Et verè Christus est ipsissimus Melchisedec, qui Abrahamo benedictionem impendit, cuique decimas vicissim Abraham obtulit, adeoque ob cuius gloriam & dignitatem ipsi Leuitæ quoq; decimas à fratribus accipiebant, & cui se totos ipsi confrabant: cui denique & nos debemus omnium, quæ à nobis fiunt, vel habentur, tam primitias, quàm decimas offerre, proferendo ea opera, per quæ gloria ipsius, & Dei patris in terris posit illustrari, quæque maiestati ipsius nouimus esse grata.
units.tr: While the excellence of Melchisedec is proclaimed in this way, all these things ought to be referred to this end: that we may understand the far greater dignity of Christ, whose type Melchisedec bore; and that we may acknowledge that the priesthood of Christ, which is according to the order of Melchisedec, is far more excellent than the legal priesthood, which is according to the order of Levi; nay, that the order, or the Aaronic priesthood with all its appendages, is abrogated by the priesthood of Christ. For this is the aim of the present discussion, and all the arguments tend to this end. And truly Christ is the very Melchisedec, who bestowed a blessing on Abraham, and to whom in turn Abraham offered tithes; and for whose glory and dignity the Levites themselves also received tithes from their brothers, and to whom they devoted themselves entirely; to whom finally we too ought to offer, from all that is done by us or possessed by us, first-fruits as well as tithes, by setting forth those works through which his glory, and that of God the Father, may be made illustrious on earth, and which we know to be pleasing to his majesty.

units.la: DE DECIMIS.
units.tr: ON TITHES.

units.la: Quia verò hoc loco dicitur præceptum esse Leuitis, ut decimas à populo accipiant: ideò res ipsa poscere videtur, ut de decimis paulò fusius disseramus, idq; eò magis, quòd nostra memoria vidimus alicubi cótrouersias & disceptationes de hac re habitas, adeoque quibusdam ausos negare simpliciter esse dandas. Hoc autem progrediamur ordine: Primum, quid in veteri testamento de his sit proditum, qua videlicet occasione introductæ: quare, & quibus pendi solitæ. Deinde, quid in nouo testamento sit de ijs statuendum.
units.tr: Since this passage says that the Levites were commanded to receive tithes from the people, the matter itself seems to call for a rather fuller discussion of tithes. This is all the more needful because in our own time we have seen controversies and disputes about the subject in various places, and some have even dared to deny flatly that tithes are to be given at all. We will proceed in this order. First, what is recorded about tithes in the Old Testament: on what occasion they were introduced, why, and by whom they were customarily paid. Second, what must be decided about them in the New Testament.

units.la: Principiò de ratione nominis nihil attinet dicere, cùm decimas constet esse dictas ab eo, quod ex magno acervo, decretum sit aliquando decimam quamque portionem siue Deo, siue Dei ministris offerre. A numero seu ordine rerum offerendarum, quem homines pro suo arbitrio varium constituerunt, variæ etiam appellationes sunt vsurpatæ, ut aliquando quæ dari iussa sunt, appellata sint, nomine centesimarum, nomine sexagesimarum, quinquagesimarum, vicesimarum, ac tandem etiam decimarum, &c.
units.tr: To begin, there is no need to say anything about the origin of the name, since it is well established that tithes are so called because it was decided that a tenth portion of a great heap should be offered to God or to God's ministers. From the number or the order of the things to be offered, which men have arranged variously as they pleased, various names have also come into use. So what was commanded to be given was sometimes called by the names of hundredths, sixtieths, fiftieths, twentieths, and finally tenths, and so on.

units.la: Constat autem primùm diuinitus inditum animis mortalium, & à primis parentibus reliquos deinde ita edoctos, ut declarandæ gratitudinis ergò erga Deum, partem aliquam, quantam volebant, & frugum, & pecorum Domino offerrent, id quod Geneseos quarto, ab Abel & Cain statim factum legimus. Succedente tempore cum res poscerent, quosdam rebus sacris præfici, quia non omnes ex æquo poterant illis vacare, constituique legitimos magistratibus, constitutum est, etiam ijs, qui sacris præficiebantur, portionem aliquam, siue honoris gratia, siue, ut se familiamque inde pascerent, conferri.
units.tr: It is agreed that the custom was first implanted in the minds of mortals by God, and that the first parents then taught the rest so that, as a sign of gratitude toward God, they would offer to the Lord some part, as large as they wished, of their crops and their flocks. We read in Genesis 4 that this was done at once by Abel and Cain. As time went on, circumstances required that certain men be set over sacred things, since not all could give themselves equally to these duties, and legitimate officers were appointed to the magistracy. It was then established that some portion be conferred on those who were set over sacred things, either as a mark of honour or so that they and their households might be supported.

units.la: Atque etiam iam decima portio cœpta est in vsu haberi, nec tantùm frugum aut pecorum, sed aliorum quoque, quæ obtigerant bonorum. Colligitur istud perspicuè ex eo, quod Apostolus hic citauit ex Genes. 14. quòd videlicet Abraha dederit decimas ex omnibus spoliis Melchisedec sacerdoti Dei altissimi. Item ex eo, quòd Iacob similiter Geneseos vicesimo octauo promittit, se Deo daturum decimas cunctorum bonorum, quæ per misericordiam Dei contingerent. Imò iam tum & regibus decimas pendi, aut certè qualem portionem ex historia Abrahæ apparet: quando quidem ibidem dicitur, Regem Sodomorum partem facultatum quasi iure suo exegisse, ab eo, quem alias honore & mu neribus potius debuisset afficere.
units.tr: Indeed, already at that time a tenth portion began to be in use, not only of crops or flocks but also of other goods that had come to a person. This is clearly gathered from the fact that the Apostle cites here from Genesis 14 that Abraham gave tithes of all the spoils to Melchizedek, priest of God Most High. Likewise, from Genesis 28, Jacob similarly promises that he will give to God tithes of all the goods that came to him by God's mercy. Indeed, even then tithes were paid to kings, or at least some portion of the kind that appears from the history of Abraham; for it is said in the same place that the king of Sodom demanded a part of the possessions as if it were his right, from the man whom he ought rather to have honoured and rewarded.

units.la: Id magis liquet ex eo, quod Genefeos quadragesimo septimo. per Iofeph administrantem rempublicam Aegyptiacam, ius introductum est, ut frumenti non tantùm decima, sed quinta pars regi penderetur: quod ius in multum tempus, certè ad ætatem Mosi usq; ibi seruatum est.
units.tr: This is made clearer by Genesis 47, where, through Joseph who administered the Egyptian commonwealth, a law was introduced that not only a tenth but a fifth part of the grain was to be paid to the king. This law was kept there for a long time, certainly down to the age of Moses.

units.la: Manifestum igitur est, statim ab initio apud omnes homines constitutum & receptū, ut tam iis, qui sacris præerant, quàm regibus, certa portio frugum & pecorum, aliquando & aliarum rerum penderetur. Causas verò plenius explicabimus in sequentibus.
units.tr: It is therefore plain that from the very beginning it was established and accepted among all men that a fixed portion of crops and flocks, and at times of other goods, be paid both to those who presided over sacred things and to kings. We will explain the causes more fully in what follows.

units.la: Cùm verò Dominus peculiarem populum sibi deligeret, legesque huic tam ad religionem, quàm ad politiam pertinentes præscriberet, voluit & decimarum habere rationem, quas ijs inprimis, qui religionis curam gerebant, reddi præcepit. Qua de re Exodi vicesimo secundo, Decimas (more aliarum gentium & patribus eorum iam usitato) & primitias non tardabis offerre. Leuit. 27. Omnes decimæ terræ, siue de pomis arborum, siue de frugibus, Domini sunt, & illi sanctificantur.
units.tr: When the Lord chose for himself a peculiar people and prescribed laws for them that pertained both to religion and to civil government, he also willed that tithes be taken into account, and he commanded that they be given above all to those who had the care of religion. Concerning this, Exodus 22 says: "You shall not delay to offer tithes (as other nations and their fathers already did) and first fruits." Leviticus 27: "All tithes of the land, whether of the fruit of trees or of crops, belong to the Lord, and they are holy to him."

units.la: Si quis autem voluerit redimere decimas suas, addet quintam partem earum. Onium decimarum bouis & ouis, & capræ, quæ sub pastoris virga transeunt, quicquid decimum venerit, sacrificabitur Domino. Numer. decimoctauo, ad Aaronem & Leuitas omnes primitias sanctuarij, quas offerunt filij Israel Domino, tibi dedi, & filijs ac filiabus tuis iure perpetuo. Mox sequitur, Filijs autè Leui dedi omnes decimas Israel in possessionem, pro ministerio, quo seruiunt mihi in tabernaculo fœderis, &c. Ibidem: Nihil aliud possidebunt, decimarum oblatione contenti: quas in usus eorum, & necessaria separaui. Locutusque est Dominus ad Mosen, dicens: Præcipe Leuitis, atque denuncia: cùm acceperitis à filijs Israel decimas, quas dedi vobis, primitias earum offerte Domino, id est, decimam partem decimæ, ut reputetur uobis, in oblationem primitiuorum, tam de areis, quàm de torcularibus, & vniuersis, quarum accipitis primitias, offerte Domino, & date ea Aaroni sacerdoti. Omnia quæ offertis ex decimis, & in donaria Domini, separabitis, optima & electa erunt cuncta. Deuteronom. decimo quarto. Decimam partem separabis de cunctis frugibus tuis, quæ nascuntur in terra per annos singulos, & comedes in conspectu Domini Dei tui, in loco, quem elegerit: ut in eo nomen illius inuocetur. Decimam frumenti tui, & vini, & olei, & primogenita de armentis & ouibus tuis, vt discas timere Dominum Deum tuum in omni tempore.
units.tr: "If anyone wishes to redeem his tithes, he shall add a fifth part of them. Of all the tithes of oxen, sheep, and goats, whatever passes under the shepherd's rod, every tenth animal shall be sacrificed to the Lord." Numbers 18: "To Aaron and all the Levites I have given all the first fruits of the sanctuary, which the children of Israel offer to the Lord; to you and to your sons and daughters by a perpetual right." Soon after follows: "To the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel for a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant," and so on. In the same place: "They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their use and needs." And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "Command the Levites and declare to them: when you have received from the children of Israel the tithes that I have given you, you shall offer their first fruits to the Lord, that is, a tenth part of the tithe, so that it may be reckoned to you as an offering of first fruits, from the threshing floors as well as from the wine presses, and from all whose first fruits you receive; offer them to the Lord and give them to Aaron the priest. You shall set apart for the Lord's gifts from all the tithes you offer, the best and chosen parts of everything." Deuteronomy 14: "You shall set apart a tenth part of all your crops which grow in the earth every year, and you shall eat before the Lord your God, in the place he has chosen, so that his name may be invoked there: the tenth of your grain, and of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God at all times."

units.la: Cùm autem longior fuerit via & locus, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, tibiquè benedixerit, nec potueris ad eum hæc cuncta portare, vendes omnia, & in pretium rediges, portabisque manu tua, & proficisceris ad locum, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, & emes ex eadem pecunia, quicquid tibi placuerit, siue ex armentis, siue ex ouibus, vinum quoque & siceram, & omne quod desiderat anima tua, & comedes coram Domino Deo tuo, & epulaberis tu & domus tua, & Leuita, qui intra portas tuas est. Caue ne derelinquas eum, quia non habet aliam partem in possessione tua.
units.tr: "But if the way is long, and the place which the Lord your God has chosen is far, and he has blessed you, and you cannot carry all these things there, then you shall sell everything and turn it into money, and carry the money in your hand, and go to the place which the Lord your God has chosen, and with that money buy whatever pleases you, whether of herds or of sheep, wine too and strong drink, and whatever your soul desires; and you shall eat before the Lord your God, and you and your household shall feast, and the Levite who is within your gates too. Take care that you do not forsake him, because he has no other portion or possession with you."

units.la: Ibidem: Anno tertio separabis aliam decimam ex omnibus, quæ nascuntur tibi eo tempore, & repones intra ianuas tuas, veniétque Leuites, qui aliam non habet partem, nec possessionem tecum, & peregrinus, ac pupillus, & vidua, qui intra portas tuas sunt, & comedent, & saturabuntur, vt benedicat tibi Dominus Deus tuus in cunctis operibus manuum tuarum, quæ feceris. Sed & Deuteronomij vicesimo sexto de eadem re.
units.tr: "Also: in the third year you shall set apart another tenth of all that is produced for you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates; and the Levite, who has no other portion or possession with you, shall come, and the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates, and they shall eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you do." Deuteronomy 26 also speaks of the same matter.

units.la: Vbi & pro beneficijs acceptis (liberatione scilicet ex Aegypto, donatione terræ fluentis lacte & melle) dari primitias & decimas, quaque verborum forma uti debeant offerentes, stenditur: vbi inter alia sic adijcitur: Quando compleueris decimā cunctarum frugum tuarum anno decimarum tertio, dabis Leuitæ, & aduenæ, & pupillo ac viduæ, ut comedant infra portas tuas & saturentur, loquerisque in conspectu Domini Dei tui: Extuli sanctificatum è domo, & etiam dedi illud Leuitæ, & peregrino, pupillo, & viduæ, secundum omne præceptum tuum, quod præcepisti mihi: &c. tandem subijcitur precatio: Respice de habitaculo sanctitatis tuæ, è cœlo, & benedic populo tuo Israeli, & terræ, quam dedisti nobis, quemadmodum iurasti patribus nostris, terræ fluentis lacte & melle, 2. Paralipomen. 31. præcepit Ezechias rex populo, vt darent partes sacerdotibus & Leuitis, vt possent vacare legi Domini. Quod cùm percrebuisset in auribus multitudinis, plurimas obtulere primitias frumenti, vini, olei, mellis quoque & omnium, quæ gignit humus, decimas obtulerunt. Et cùm multa superessent, quæ non expenderant Leuitæ, dixit Azarias sacerdos ad regem, plurima remansisse, eò, quòd Dominus benedixerit populo suo. Malachiæ tertio, contra eos, qui decimas dare detrectabant, vel fraudulenter eas dabant: in quo confiximus tęin decimis & in primitijs, & in penuria vos maledi&ti. tiestis, & vos mea rapitis, gens toto. Afferte omnes decimas in domum thesauri, ut sit cibus, in domo mea, & probate me in hoc, dicit Iehouah exercituum: Si non aperuero vobis chataractas coeli, & effudero vobis benedictionem, vsque ad abundantiā.
units.tr: There it is shown that first fruits and tithes were to be given in return for benefits received (namely, the deliverance from Egypt and the gift of a land flowing with milk and honey), and in what form of words those who offer them ought to speak. Among other things it is added: "When you have finished paying the tenth of all your crops in the third year, the year of tithes, you shall give it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, so that they may eat within your gates and be satisfied. And you shall speak in the sight of the Lord your God: I have taken the holy things out of the house, and I have also given them to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, according to all your commandment which you commanded me," and so on. At last the prayer is added: "Look down from the habitation of your holiness, from heaven, and bless your people Israel and the land which you have given us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey." 2 Chronicles 31: King Hezekiah commanded the people to give portions to the priests and Levites, so that they might be free to attend to the law of the Lord. When this word spread among the multitude, they offered very many first fruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all that the earth produces; they brought tithes. And when much was left over, which the Levites had not spent, the priest Azariah said to the king that much had remained, because the Lord had blessed his people. Malachi 3, against those who refused to give tithes or gave them fraudulently: "In which you have been cursed with a curse, and you rob me, the whole nation, in tithes and in offerings. Bring all the tithes into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord of hosts: if I do not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out on you a blessing until there is abundance."

units.la: Quid pluribus opus est? Quo iure dandae sint decimae Leuitis, satis est perspicuum: & ex his, quibus de causis, in quem vsum decimas dari solitum sit, quamque multiplices decimae fuerint, promptum est colligere.
units.tr: What more is needed? The right by which tithes are to be given to the Levites is clear enough, and from these points, for what causes and to what use tithes were customarily given, and how many kinds of tithes there were, it is easy to gather.

units.la: Tres siquidem decimarum species licet aduertere. Primi generis erant, quae singulis dabantur annis, de collectis primitijs & frugibus quibuscunque, quae cedebant sacerdotibus & Leuitis, ut inde vescerentur. Secundi generis erant harum decimarum decimae, quas Leuitae ipsi, ut habeant Leuitici vicesimo septimo, Numerorum decimo octauo, Domino offerre debebant. Tertij generis erant decimae, quae tertio quoque anno colligebantur, ad vsum peregrini, pupilli & viduae, quorum ordinum maxima semper Deo cura fuit, & hominibus esse voluit.
units.tr: Indeed, three kinds of tithes may be noted. The first kind were those given every year, from the gathered firstfruits and whatever crops, which fell to the priests and Levites for their food. The second kind were the tithes of these tithes, which the Levites themselves were bound to offer to the Lord, as is found in Leviticus 27 and Numbers 18. The third kind were the tithes gathered every third year, for the use of the stranger, the orphan and the widow, whose welfare was always of the greatest concern to God and whom he wished to be cared for by men.

units.la: Causae vero, ob quas decimae penderentur, atque vsus decimarum multiplices in praedictis locis exprimuntur. Prima quidem quidem causa, cur merito pendendae sint, expressit ur Leuit. vicesimo septimo, Quia Domini sunt, & illi sanctificantur. Si enim Deus nobis sanctificat omnia, & sua benignitate largiter donat, aequum est id agnoscamus, & gratias agamus, illi de omnibus primitias ac decimas offerentes.
units.tr: The causes for which tithes were paid, and the various uses of tithes, are set out in the places mentioned. The first cause, why they are rightly to be paid, is expressed in Leviticus 27: because they are the Lord's, and are made holy to him. For if God sanctifies all things for us and bestows them generously by his goodness, it is fitting that we acknowledge this, and give thanks to him by offering firstfruits and tithes from all things.

units.la: Secunda causa exprimitur Deuteronomij decimo quarto: vt videlicet discas timere Dominum Dominum Deum tuum in omni tempore: hoc est, ut omni tempore Deum iusto honore prosequamur, metuamusque eum offendere, ne iratus nos damnis frugum, pecorum, & aliarum rerum afficiat. Quò pertinet, quae dicuntur Deuteronomij vicesimo sexto, Malachiae tertio, de benedictione terrae, & omnium rerum abundantia per diuinam bonitatem concessa.
units.tr: The second cause is expressed in Deuteronomy 14: namely, that you may learn to fear the Lord your God at all times; that is, that at all times we may render God due honour, and take care not to offend him, lest, angered, he afflict us with losses of crops, cattle and other things. To this pertain the words in Deuteronomy 26 and Malachi 3 concerning the blessing of the land and the abundance of all things granted by divine goodness.

units.la: Tertia ratio saepe exponitur, nimirū vt sacerdotes & Leuitae inde sustententur, qui occupati tractatione rerum diuinarum sibi alia ratione non prospiciunt.
units.tr: The third reason is often set out: that priests and Levites may be sustained from them, since they, occupied with the handling of divine things, cannot otherwise provide for themselves.

units.la: Quarta ratio, vt inde alantur pauperes, praecipuè peregrini, pupilli, viduae quorum pauperum miserrima est conditio. Cùm ergo talibus de causis decimas dari sit à Deo constitutum, quiuis intelligit, omnes ad eas pendendas fuisse obligatos, nec euasuros iram Dei, quicunque pendere detrectarent. Quamobrem studiosè & liberaliter plurimi Iudaei conferebant decimas, non tantum harum aut illarum rerum, sed omnium simul bonorum: & quo quis videre cupiebat sanctior, eo liberalius decimas exoluebat.
units.tr: The fourth reason: that the poor may be fed from them, especially strangers, orphans and widows, whose condition is most wretched. Since, therefore, it has been ordained by God that tithes be given for such causes, anyone can understand that all were bound to pay them, and that whoever refused to pay them would not escape the wrath of God. Wherefore many Jews gave tithes eagerly and generously, not only of these or those things but of all their goods together; and the more holy someone wished to appear, the more liberally he paid tithes.

units.la: Hinc illa gloriatio pharisaei Lucae decimo octauo, Decimas do omnium bonorum, quę posideo. Et Matthaei decimo tertio, de pharisaeis refertur, quòd supererstitiosè decimarent mentham, anethum, & cyminum, alia interea magis necessaria opera charitatis, vt, iudicium & misericordiam, negligentes. Succedentibus vero temporibus etiam iussu Dei regibus decimae & seruitia decreta sunt: Sic enim primo Samuelis octauo, inter alia, sed & segetes vestras, & vinearum redditus addecimabit, ut det eunuchis & famulis suis: greges quoque vestros addecimabit, vosque eritis ei serui. En paucis decimas dandas, & simul quare, siue in quem vsum, ibidem exprimitur. Dicitur enim, quòd constituet sibi equites, tribunos, centuriones, & omnia necessaria ad defendendam rempublicam, & propulsandam uim iniustā. Ita debet iudices constituere, salarijs honestis in officio retinere: praeterea ciuitates, arces munire, conseruare, &c. quae non possunt sine sumptibus magnis fieri. Hac igitur de causa & decimae & vectigalia, & tributa regibus, principibusque sunt diuinitus constituta, & ita, ut publico assensu sunt permissa, soluere omnes debent. Hæc de decimis tam Leuitarum, quàm regum, ex veteri testamento, quantum satis est.
units.tr: Hence that boast of the Pharisee in Luke 18: "I give tithes of all that I possess." And in Matthew 23 it is related of the Pharisees that they tithed mint, dill and cumin too scrupulously, while neglecting in the meantime the weightier works of charity, such as judgement and mercy. In later times, by the command of God, tithes and services were also decreed for kings. Thus in 1 Samuel 8, among other things: "He will take the tenth of your seed and of the revenues of your vineyards, to give to his eunuchs and servants; he will also take the tenth of your flocks, and you will be his servants." Here, in brief, it is set out that tithes are to be given, and at the same time why, that is, for what use. For it is said that he will appoint for himself horsemen, tribunes, centurions, and all things necessary for defending the commonwealth and repelling unjust force. Likewise he must appoint judges and keep them in office with honourable salaries; moreover, to fortify and maintain cities and citadels, and so on, which cannot be done without great expense. For this reason, therefore, both tithes and tolls and taxes were divinely established for kings and princes, and, as they were allowed by public consent, all are bound to pay them. So much, from the Old Testament, concerning the tithes both of the Levites and of the kings, is enough.

units.la: Hactenus quidem de origine decimarum, sacerdotibus, nécnon regibus pendi solitarum, tám ante legem latam, quàm sub lege, & quotuplices in lege fuerint praeceptae: quis denique earum vsus & finis fuerit, tam apud Leuitas, quàm apud reges.
units.tr: Thus far indeed concerning the origin of the tithes customarily paid to priests and likewise to kings, both before the law was given and under the law, and how many kinds were commanded under the law; and finally what their use and purpose was, both among the Levites and among the kings.

units.la: Iam quaeritur, vtrùm agentibus sub euangelio, & felicior conditione agentibus, atque liberatis à lege Mosaica, etiam decimae dandae rectè imponantur. Ac videtur sane, quòd nequaquam id fieri deceat. Primùm, quia nusquam in scriptis euangelicis aliquà extat vel admonitio vel praeceptum, de decimis conferendis seu sacerdotibus, seu regibus.
units.tr: Now it is asked whether tithes may rightly be imposed also upon those living under the gospel, and in a happier condition, and freed from the Mosaic law. And it certainly seems that this ought by no means to be done. First, because nowhere in the evangelical writings is there any admonition or command concerning the paying of tithes, whether to priests or to kings.

units.la: Deinde, cùm non extat praeceptum aliquod expressum, & legalia obseruare etiam cū peccato videatur coniunctum: tantum abest, vt quis ad soluendum impelli debeat, vt vel volens soluere non videatur sine peccato id posse praestare.
units.tr: Second, since there is no express command, and to observe legal prescriptions seems to be bound up even with sin, it is so far from being the case that anyone ought to be compelled to pay, that one who would pay willingly does not seem able to do so without sin.

units.la: Tertiò, multae sunt regiones, in quibus decimae non soluuntur: quare, qua ratione vna regio libera est ab onere decimarum, eadem ratione libera esse debet & altera.
units.tr: Third, there are many regions in which tithes are not paid. Therefore, by the same reasoning by which one region is free from the burden of tithes, another ought to be free too.

units.la: Quartò, ut etiam alicubi sit receptum pendi decimas, tamen, vbi eæ non expenduntur in eos vsus, ob quos primùm sunt concessæ, haudquaquam videntur soluendæ: & qui soliti sunt accipere, videntur ius exigendi amittere.
units.tr: Fourth, even if it is customary somewhere to pay tithes, yet where they are not spent on those uses for which they were first granted, they seem by no means to be owed; and those who were accustomed to receive them seem to lose the right of exacting them.

units.la: Aut certè, si aliquæ sunt soluendæ, indignum tamen & iniquum, suppeditari tam graues, & tam multas, quibus cernimus populum non mediocriter grauari, & quasi opprimi.
units.tr: Or certainly, even if some are owed, it is nevertheless unworthy and unjust to impose such heavy and so many, by which we see the people not moderately burdened and, as it were, oppressed.

units.la: Possent & aliæ rationes his non admodum dissimiles adferri, quales obiectæ sunt sæpius, tum per Rusticos, qui superioribus annis tumultuabantur, tum per nuperos Anabaptistas.
units.tr: Other reasons, not much unlike these, could also be advanced, such as have been often objected, both by the peasants who rioted in recent years and by the recent Anabaptists.

units.la: Vt respondeamus quæstioni, breuiter dicendum, quòd, vt manent eædem causæ decimarum, quæ fuerunt in veteri lege: ita & ius pendendi decimas apud eos, qui semel communibus suffragijs asserunt, integrum adhuc manet. Nec admodum difficile est obiectiones diluere, ei, qui originem siue causam decimarum conferendarum diligenter considerauerit. Proinde, vt quiuis clarè & perspicuè possit decernere, quid in vniuersum de omnibus in hac causa sit sentiendum, nos de omni genere de decimarum nostris temporibus vsitatis plenius differemus. Et cùm quadruplices videamus pendi decimas, nempe, quasdam ecclesijs: quasdam nobilibus siue magistratibus: quasdam minister ijs: quasdam verò priuatis personis: de his ordine agemus, quæ earum origo: quis vsus vel finis: quatenus soluendæ: utrùm propter abusus tollendæ: denique, quomodo abusus, si qui enati sunt, queant corrigi, explicantes: quibus cognitis, perfacile erit quascunque obiectiones maleuolorum dissoluere.
units.tr: To answer the question, it must be said briefly that, just as the same causes of tithes remain that existed under the old law, so too the right of paying tithes remains whole among those who have once affirmed it by common vote. Nor is it very difficult to dissolve the objections for one who has carefully considered the origin or cause of tithes to be paid. Therefore, so that anyone may clearly and plainly decide what is to be thought in general about all these matters, we shall treat more fully of every kind of tithe in use in our times. And since we see that tithes are paid in four ways, namely, some to churches, some to nobles or magistrates, some to ministers, and some to private persons, we shall deal with these in order: what their origin is, what their use or purpose is, how far they are to be paid, whether they are to be abolished on account of abuses, and finally, explaining how abuses, if any have arisen, can be corrected; with these matters known, it will be quite easy to dissolve whatever objections of ill-wishers there are.

units.la: DE DECIMIS ECCLESIARVM.
units.tr: On the Tithes of the Churches.

units.la: Cùm & ante legem, & sub lege, graues causæ & multæ extiterint, ob quas homines permoti sunt ad pendendas decimas sacrorum ministris: certè ubi eædem causæ manent, recte constituitur, decimas eodem iure pendedas. Causas autem has fuisse, ex verbis Domini in lege expresis collegimus, videlicet, ut testemur, nos agnofere, quòd dei beneficio & misericordia ea bona nobis obtigerint: ut in timore Domini perstemus, qui propter peccata nostra potest calamitatem, ut sterilitate per intemperiem, atq; aliis modis inducere, nosq; ita affligere. Deinde, ut habeant ministri verbi, quo se alant, cum aliis rationibus, nempe mercatu aut operibus manuarijs non possint, propter assiduum studium rerum diuinarum, sibi familiaeq; vidum prospicere. Adhæc, ut prospiciatur etiam aliqua ratione peregrinis, pupillis, viduis, aliisq;, quos alias oporteret præ inopia periclitari. Cùm verò hæ causæ omnes maneat, & merito vnumquemque moueant, ut aliquid conferant de suis facultatibus, quo & testetur primum affectum gratitudinis & honoris erga Deum, & iuuent tum ministros ecclesiarum, tum pauperes: æquum fuit, imò necessarium, excogitare, quibus modis ista perficerentur. Et cùm non posset commodius fieri istud, quàm si vnusquisque aliquid è frugibus, è pecoribus, vel ex alijs rebus in commune conferret, communi consensu maiores statim ab initio ordinarunt, alibi oblationes, alibi decimas ecclesijs, in vsus ministrorum & pauperum conferri. Et certè de alendis pauperibus passim extant tum in veteri testamento, tum in nouo, præcepta, promissiones, & exempla, quæ nequaquam opus est recensere. Apostolus Paulus collectam pecuniam deferebat Hierosolymam, discipuli item in commune contulerunt omnia.
units.tr: Both before the law and under the law, there were many weighty reasons that moved people to pay tithes to the ministers of sacred things. Where those same reasons still hold, it is rightly established that tithes should be paid by the same right. We gather from the words of the Lord in the law what these reasons were: first, that we acknowledge that these goods have come to us by the favour and mercy of God, and that we remain in the fear of the Lord, who can bring calamity on account of our sins, through sterility, bad weather, and other means, and so afflict us. Second, that the ministers of the Word should have something on which to support themselves, since they cannot, because of their constant study of divine things, provide for themselves and their households by trade or manual labour. Third, that provision should also be made in some way for strangers, orphans, widows, and others who would otherwise be in danger because of want. Since all these reasons remain, and rightly move each person to contribute something from his resources, both to show first his affection of gratitude and honour towards God, and to help both the ministers of the churches and the poor, it was fitting, indeed necessary, to devise ways of accomplishing this. And since this could not be done more conveniently than if each person contributed something in common from the fruits of the field, from his flocks, or from other goods, our forefathers at once from the beginning arranged by common consent that offerings in some places, and tithes in others, should be given to the churches for the use of the ministers and the poor. Certainly, precepts, promises, and examples concerning the support of the poor are found everywhere, both in the Old Testament and in the New, and there is no need to recount them. The Apostle Paul carried a collection of money to Jerusalem; likewise the disciples shared all things in common.

units.la: Ministris verò ecclesiarum largiendum, quòd honesto & frugali victui est necessarium, docet ac iubet Christus Matth.7. Dignus est operarius mercede sua: id quod Paulus eleganter & copiosè præcipit, 1. Cor.9. Galat.6.1.Tim.5.
units.tr: That what is necessary for a decent and frugal livelihood should be given to the ministers of the churches, Christ teaches and commands in Matth. 7: "The labourer is worthy of his wages." Paul prescribes this elegantly and fully in 1 Cor. 9, Gal. 6, and 1 Tim. 5.

units.la: Quia verò cernebant maiores nostri, decimas in hos vsus pendi solitas sub lege, & vix alia ratio commodior posset excogitari, ideò placuit illis de decimis dandis non tantum exhortationes, sed & leges diuino iuri consentaneas edere. Aut, quibus in locis nō sunt designatæ decimæ, tamen vel oblationes, vel redditus, vel alia id genus sunt in eos vsus tributa. Hæc ergo decimarum origo fuit iusta, pia, necessaria, ex diuino iure deriuata. Neque est quod obijciatur, quia decimæ in lege præceptæ fuerunt, & legalia iam sunt abrogata, ideò eas nunc non amplius pendendas. Etsi enim legalia dicantur abrogata, tamen id intelligendum est potissimum de ceremonialibus, quæ figuræ, typi, & umbræ tantum erant. Cætera verò, quæ ad bonos mores, ad officia exercendę charitatis conducunt, semper in vsu manent, sicut charitas ipsa semper à nobis exigitur.
units.tr: Since our forefathers saw that tithes had been customarily paid for these purposes under the law, and hardly any more convenient plan could be devised, they resolved to issue not only exhortations about giving tithes but also laws consistent with divine right. Or, in places where tithes were not fixed, there were nevertheless offerings, rents, or other such payments assigned to these uses. The origin of tithes was therefore just, pious, and necessary, derived from divine right. Nor is there any force in the objection that, because tithes were commanded in the law, and the legal precepts have now been abrogated, tithes should no longer be paid. For although the legal precepts are said to be abrogated, this must be understood chiefly of the ceremonial ones, which were only figures, types, and shadows. The rest, which pertain to good morals and to the duties of exercising charity, always remain in use, just as charity itself is always required of us.

units.la: Et si bene aduertimus præceptum de pendendis decimis, quatenus habuit aliquid ce-remoniale, puta ut de talibus rebus, ut tali loco, ut in vsum sacrificij, uel huiusmodi pen-derentur, id vniuersum est abrogatum. Quatenus vero habet communitatem cum præ-ceptis moralibus, nimirum ut ministris ecclesiæ, ut pauperibus prospiciatur, sane integrū & inuiolatum manet. Atque hoc pacto seruatur illud ius, non quia Moses iubet, vel quod Judaicos ritus putemus imitandos, sed quia expediens est ad perficiendum opera chari-tatis. Eamque ob causam nequaquam constitutum est, ut vbique apud omnes ecclesias idem ius æquè valeat, cum alibi redditus, alibi oblationes, alibi etiam bona sint assignata, neque etiam ex ijsdem rebus, de quibus lex præcepit. Quomodo enim decimas vini, vel olei, uel caprarum pendat, ubi vinum uel oleum non nascitur, & capræ nullæ aluntur? constitutum tantum est iure diuino, alibi plus, alibi minus, pro ut & locus, & res hominum ferunt, aliquid in eos usus conferri.
units.tr: And if we rightly observe the precept about paying tithes, insofar as it had something ceremonial about it, such as that such things should be paid, in such a place, for the use of sacrifice, or for things of this kind, all of that has been abrogated. Insofar as it has something in common with the moral precepts, namely that provision be made for the ministers of the church and for the poor, it certainly remains whole and inviolate. In this way that right is maintained, not because Moses commands it, or because we think Jewish rites should be imitated, but because it is expedient for carrying out works of charity. For this reason it has by no means been established that the same right should apply equally everywhere among all churches, since in some places rents, in others offerings, and in others goods have been assigned, and not even from the same things that the law prescribed. For how could someone pay tithes of wine, oil, or goats where no wine or oil grows and no goats are kept? It has been established only by divine right that something should be contributed for those uses, more in one place, less in another, according as the place and the circumstances of men allow.

units.la: Iam hinc liquet, quis sit decimarum usus, nimirum, ut inde alantur ministri verbi & pauperes: cuius rei maxima cura habita est apud veteres, ut licet diuersis synodis, cōsilijs, decretis, & scriptis patrum cernere. Earumque facultatum administratio ac dispensatio ad episcopos uel diaconos pertinebat: quomodo scimus Apostolum Paulū collectas ex Achaia, & alijs locis, item septem diaconos apud Hierosolymā, & pauperibus distribuisse acceptas eleemosynas.
units.tr: From this it is now clear what the use of tithes is, namely that the ministers of the Word and the poor may be supported from them. The ancients took the greatest care of this matter, as can be seen in various synods, councils, decrees, and the writings of the Fathers. The administration and distribution of these resources belonged to the bishops or the deacons, as we know that the Apostle Paul distributed the collections from Achaia and other places, and likewise the seven deacons at Jerusalem distributed the alms received to the poor.

units.la: Porrò, cùm talis sit origo atque usus decimarum, quiuis intelligit, iure diuino omnes teneri ad earum solutionem, ubi sic sunt institutæ. Rationes sunt:
units.tr: Furthermore, since such is the origin and use of tithes, anyone can see that all are bound by divine right to pay them where they have been so instituted. The reasons are these:

units.la: Prima, quia propter causas adeò necessarias sunt in stitutæ, ut, si non collatione decima-rum, certè aliarum rerum collatione debeat idem perfici.
units.tr: The first is that they were instituted for causes so necessary that, if not by the contribution of tithes, then certainly by the contribution of other goods, the same purpose ought to be achieved.

units.la: Secunda, quia communi ecclesiæ consensu & promissione sunt institutæ: quæ vero in situta sunt, vel consensu, vel promissione, debent seruari, sicut alia quæcunque pacta.
units.tr: The second is that they were instituted by the common consent and promise of the church. Things instituted either by consent or by promise ought to be kept, just like any other agreements.

units.la: Tertia ratio, quia per magistratus sunt approbatæ: & quæ magistratus sanciunt, quiuis nouit, haud temerè esse contemnenda.
units.tr: The third reason is that they have been approved by the magistrates. Everyone knows that what the magistrates sanction is not to be despised lightly.

units.la: Quarta addi potest, ut tales benedictiones obtineantur, quales in lege à Domino promit-tebantur decimas soluentibus: unde & Georgius Nazianzenus in quadā oratione habita de calamitate per grandinem, imputat calamitatem contingere propter peccata, & inter alia numerat fraudatos decimis sacerdotes & pauperes.
units.tr: A fourth reason may be added: that such blessings may be obtained as the Lord promised in the law to those who paid tithes. Hence Gregory of Nazianzus, in a certain oration delivered about the calamity of hail, attributes the calamity to sins, and among other things counts priests and the poor who have been defrauded of tithes.

units.la: Aliàs certè, si quibus in regionibus neque communi consensu vnquam decretæ sunt, neque magistratuum autoritate concessæ uel confirmatæ, certè ibi neque exigi possunt à populo, neque hi tenentur reddere: quod & fit, ubi alia ratione ministris ecclesiarum & pauperibus prospicitur.
units.tr: Otherwise, certainly, in those regions where tithes have never been decreed by common consent, nor granted or confirmed by the authority of the magistrates, they certainly cannot be exacted from the people, and these are not bound to pay them. This also happens where provision is made for the ministers of the churches and the poor by some other means.

units.la: Dicat aliquis: Si tunc ferebant tempora, ut haud grauatim penderentur decimæ, tamen nunc non est eadem ratio, & consensus maiorum nostrorum non potuit nos in præsens obligare: Sublata enim causa, cessat & effectus.
units.tr: Someone may say: "If the times were such that tithes were paid without much complaint, yet now the situation is not the same, and the consent of our forefathers cannot bind us at present. For when the cause is removed, the effect ceases as well."

units.la: Respondetur, quòd, quamdiu manent causæ, propter quas ius decimarum fuit intro-ductum, fancitum, manet etiam obligatio soluendi. Quòd si alia ratione queat ecclesiæ ministris & pauperibus satis prospici, veluti si redditus conferantur, &c. potest haud dubiè ius decimarum abrogari, quod non est simpliciter abrogari, sed potius in melius commu-tari. Aliàs eadem ratione manet obligatio, quæ in cæteris contractibus.
units.tr: The answer is that, as long as the causes remain for which the right of tithes was introduced and established, the obligation to pay also remains. But if the ministers of the church and the poor can be sufficiently provided for by some other means, as for example if rents are conferred, and so on, then undoubtedly the right of tithes can be abrogated. This is not simply to abolish them, but rather to change them for something better. Otherwise, by the same reasoning, the obligation remains that exists in other contracts.

units.la: Vtrùm qui præest ecclesiæ, & satis diues est ex hæreditate paterna, possit dicimas acci-pere? Respondetur. Cum decimæ debeantur ecclesiæ potius quàm personæ ministrā-ti, idque tum iure diuino, tum iure positiuo, sunt simpliciter pendendæ decimæ, etiam tali diuiti: Primò, quia æquum est etiam laborem ipsius mercede aliqua cōpensari, iuxta verbum Domini Matthei 7. Secundò, quia recipit, non tanquàm in vsum proprium, sed potius in vsum pauperum, quibus ipse debeat eas impędere, & fideliter distribuere, adeò ut, si ipse non acciperet decimas, videretur ea in parte pauperes fraudare, quibus aliter non poteßt prospici. Quare, si non propter ipsum ministrum, tamen propter pauperes ibi pendi debent. Neque quisquam excusatur, nisi fortasis qui præest ecclesiæ, velit cuipiā propter aliquam magnam causam, quo tempore alias satis habet ecclesia, ad tempus re-mittere. Tametsi, an hic, qui alias habet, unde cōmodè viuat, posit adhuc, bona ecclesiæ sibi vsurpare, in certum est. Non defuerunt, qui definiret, à sacrilegij crimine non abesse, si qui, quod pauperum est, in suos vsus transferunt. Ita Hieronymus sensit, & refertur in Decretis 12. quæst. 2. cap. Clericos. Item Augustinus ad Bonifacium 12. quæst.1. Si priuatū. Exiistimarim tamen hic videndum, quomodo expendant vel vtantur: si in honestos vsus non peccare: sin secus, etiam peccare perinde eos, qui non habent patrimonium à pa-rentibus. Atque illa ratione alienarentur, qui honestis nati sunt familijs, ab Ecclesiarum ministerio. Et certum est, in veteri testamento leuitæ etiam cùm parentum bona occu-parent, parent, ut hortos, &c. etiam decimas recepisse: si sua non augent, sed tantum conseruanint ea dignitate, qua acceperunt, nihil peccant.
units.tr: Whether one who presides over a church, and is wealthy enough from a paternal inheritance, may receive tithes? The answer: since tithes are owed to the church rather than to the person who holds the ministry, and this is so both by divine right and by positive right, tithes are to be paid absolutely, even to such a rich man. First, because it is fair that even his labour should be compensated by some wage, according to the word of the Lord in Matthew 7. Second, because he receives them not for his own use, but rather for the use of the poor, to whom he ought to spend them and distribute them faithfully. So much so that, if he did not receive the tithes, he would seem in that respect to defraud the poor, for whom provision could not otherwise be made. Therefore, even if not on account of the minister himself, they must still be paid there on account of the poor. Nor is anyone excused, unless perhaps the one who presides over the church wishes, for some great reason, to remit his share for a time, when the church is otherwise sufficiently supplied. Yet whether one who already has means from which he can live comfortably may still take the goods of the church for himself is certainly doubtful. There have not been lacking those who have determined that it is not free from the crime of sacrilege if anyone transfers to his own uses what belongs to the poor. Jerome thought so, and it is cited in the Decretum, 12 q. 2, ch. "Clericos." Likewise Augustine, to Boniface, 12 q. 1, "Si privatum." I would think, however, that here one must consider how they spend or use them: if for honourable uses, they do not sin; but if otherwise, then they sin just as much as those who have no patrimony from their parents. And by that reasoning, men born into honourable families would be excluded from the ministry of the churches. It is certain that in the Old Testament the Levites, even when they occupied their parents' goods, such as gardens and so on, also received tithes. If they do not increase their own goods, but only preserve them in the dignity in which they received them, they sin in nothing.

units.la: Iam iterum insurgit quispiam. Quando verus usus abolitus est decimarum, non amplius prospicitur pauperibus, sacerdotes omnia ad se recipiunt, nec solum in usus necessarios, verum etiam superfluos & luxu plenos expendunt. Alibi ex facultatibus ecclesiarum filios lasciue & sumptuose alunt: sicut Hieronymus alibi de sui seculi episcopis queritur. Alibi alunt etiam canes, scorta, &c. quorum abusuum exempla utinam nos nunc non haberemus, etiam apud eos, qui iactant se ecclesiae columina: An in tali rerum statu subditi multis aliis grauati exactionibus adhuc decimas pendere debeant? Quid, quod multis in locis, ne ab ecclesiis quidem decimae occupantur, sed priuati quidam homines colligunt, vixq; superest, quo ipsi pastores tenuiter alantur?
units.tr: Now someone rises up again. Since the true use of tithes has been abolished, the poor are no longer provided for; the priests take everything to themselves and spend it not only on necessary needs but also on superfluous things full of luxury. Elsewhere they bring up their sons wantonly and extravagantly out of church revenues, as Jerome complains elsewhere about the bishops of his own age. Elsewhere they even feed dogs, prostitutes, and so on. Would that we did not now have examples of these abuses, even among those who boast of being the pillars of the Church! In such a state of affairs, should subjects, already burdened with many other exactions, still be obliged to pay tithes? And what of the fact that in many places tithes are not even taken up by the churches, but are gathered by certain private individuals, and scarcely anything is left by which the ministers themselves can be meagrely supported?

units.la: Respondetur, quod, etiamsi foedi abusus exorti sint, tamen ius pendendarum decimarum propter primas causas supra expositas, manet integrum.
units.tr: The answer is that, even if foul abuses have arisen, the right of paying tithes nonetheless remains intact, on account of the first causes set out above.

units.la: Danda vero diligens est opera per magistratus atq; episcopos, ut sublatis abusibus, rursus iterum omnia ordinentur, ac nulla consilia omittenda, quae huc conducant. Proinde, si sacerdotes fraudant pauperes, valet hoc consilium, si illi certa portio, quanta satis iudicatur, assignetur, reliqua pars per altos adhibitos & constitutos ad hoc ministerium in pauperes erogetur. Qua de re etiam apud veteres quaedam constitutiones sunt editae: ac diuisi redditus ecclesiarum in quatuor partes: quarum prima assignabatur episcopo & clericis, altera pauperibus, tertia sacris aedibus, & aedificijs ecclesiasticis, quarta peregrinis & extraneus pauperibus, propter quos publice erecta fuerunt Ptochodochia, vel potius Xenodochia. Qua de re extant verba Gelasij 16. quaest. 3. cap. praesulum. & Gregorij 12. quaest. 2. c. Mos est.
units.tr: Diligent effort, however, must be made through the magistrates and bishops that, once the abuses are removed, everything may be set in order again, and that no measures which tend to this end be neglected. Accordingly, if the priests defraud the poor, this measure is useful: that a fixed portion, judged sufficient, be assigned to them, and the remaining part be distributed to the poor through overseers appointed and established for this ministry. Indeed, certain constitutions were issued on this matter among the ancients, and the revenues of the churches were divided into four parts: the first was assigned to the bishop and clergy, the second to the poor, the third to the sacred buildings and church edifices, and the fourth to strangers and foreign poor, for whom hospices, or rather guesthouses, were publicly erected. Words of Gelasius on this subject are extant, Causa 16, question 3, chapter "Praesulum", and of Gregory, Causa 12, question 2, chapter "Mos est".

units.la: Sin luxu perditi sunt, qui viuunt ex decimis sacerdotes, ij redigendi sunt in ordinem, quam fieri potest modis optimis, aut certe, si detrectent, deponendi, ostendendumq; eis, quod non recte praesint, ac propterea non recte etiam accipiant fructus, alendiq; cum ceteris clericis. Quae vero abalienatae sunt decimae, & in potestatem redactae priuatorum, aut alias nequaquam ecclesiasticorum ministrorum, nequaquam violenter debet ab his recipi: sed inquirendum modeste, quo iure eo peruenerint, quibus conditionibus, quibus pactis eas ab ecclesia acceperint. Quod si haec necessitate aliqua coacta pretio vendidit aliquando, rogandi sunt, ut recepta summa, quae ex pretio, vel ex pacto eis debetur, decimas ecclesiae restituant, ut inde pastoribus & pauperibus prospici queat, praesertim quando alias his prospici non possit. Alias nulla vis, nulla machinatio, nullum ius cotentiose est opponendum. Decimae pendi debent talibus personis, quam diu id ius habent, nec potest eripi ius illud, nisi supra dictis conditionibus. Magisq; peccauerunt in hac parte, qui primi decimas vendiderunt, quam ij, qui fortasis rogati emerunt, multamq; pecuniam deprompserunt. Ideoq; valde expediret legibus caueri, ut tam vendetes bona ecclesiarum, quam ementes, grauiter puniren tur. Fraudantur enim hic non tantum illi, qui debebant inde sustentari, sed preterea omnes pij, qui decimas conferunt, quorum mens & voluntas est, ut ex decimis collatis alantur pastor & pauperes. Atq; haec de decimis ecclesiarum. Nunc de decimis nobilium & magistratuum.
units.tr: But if the priests who live from tithes have been ruined by luxury, they are to be brought back into order by the best possible means; or, if they refuse, they are to be deposed, and it is to be shown to them that they do not govern rightly and therefore do not rightly receive the fruits, and they are to be fed along with the other clergy. As for those tithes which have been alienated and brought into the power of private persons, or of others altogether not ministers of the Church, they must by no means be taken from them by violence; rather, it is to be inquired soberly by what right they came into their hands, under what conditions and agreements they received them from the church. But if someone, compelled by some necessity, once sold them for a price, they are to be asked to restore to the church the sum received, which is owed to them from the price or the agreement, so that from it provision can be made for the ministers and the poor, especially when otherwise provision cannot be made for them. Otherwise no force, no trickery, no contentious claim of right is to be brought against them. Tithes ought to be paid to such persons for as long as they have that right, and that right cannot be taken away except under the conditions stated above. Those who first sold the tithes sinned more in this matter than those who perhaps bought them when asked and paid a large sum of money. Therefore it would be very advisable for the laws to provide that both those who sell the goods of the churches and those who buy them be severely punished. For here it is defrauded not only those who ought to be supported from them, but also all the godly who contribute tithes, whose mind and will it is that the minister and the poor be fed from the tithes given. And so much concerning the tithes of the churches. Now concerning the tithes of nobles and magistrates.

units.la: DE DECIMIS NOBILIVM ET MAGISTRATVVM.
units.tr: ON THE TITHES OF THE NOBLES AND MAGISTRATES.

units.la: Svpra ostendimus, & ante legem, Regibus decimas seu tributa aut census pedisequerent & historiae memorat, apud quosuis gentes idem receptum fieri, alibi plus, alibi minus, atque alibi ex his rebus, alibi ex aliis. Apud Indos quarta pars fructuum singulis annis dabatur regibus.
units.tr: Above we have shown, both before the law and from histories, that tithes, tributes or taxes followed kings; history records that the same custom was received among all peoples, more in one place and less in another, and in some places from these things, in others from different ones. Among the Indians a quarter of the produce was given to the kings every year.

units.la: Leptis in Africa singula in dies talenta pendebat Carthaginensibus: Aethiopes tertio quoque anno binos semodios auri rudis Dareo regi dabant, & ducentos fasces Ebeni, qui, nos pueros elephantorum dentes vigenos. Babylon regi Persarum singulis diebus singulas argento plenos artabas soluebat. Vici quidam circa Babyloniam ad praebenda cibaria canibus regum cogebantur, reliquis oneribus exempti. Apud Romanos veteres ex agris & noualibus decima seminum dabatur Romano populo. Alia deinceps tributa vectigalia pro temporum necessitate, & ad tempus sunt imposita, deinde etiam remissa, de quibus historiae consulantur. Proinde, quod tot seculorum, & tot populorum consensu confirmatum est, idem in hunc vsque diem apud nostrae religionis cultores obtinuit, atque regibus, principibus, nobilibus, quibus ipsi locis suum habent imperium, decimae, seu vectigalia, tributa, census, multae, seruitiae, aut quocunque nomine placet appellare, penduntur. Quorum omnium originem ad vetustissima secula referendam, & communem assensum populorum planum est. Quibus autem de causis, fiu e in quos usus ea iam conferantur nobilibus, etiam manifestū ex ijs,quæ suprà diximus, de decimarū usu regib. in veteri testameto concessarum.
units.tr: Leptis in Africa paid the Carthaginians a talent each day; the Ethiopians gave Darius the king two half-measures of raw gold every third year, and two hundred bundles of ebony, and twenty elephant tusks, as they say. Babylon paid the king of the Persians one artaba full of silver every day. Certain villages near Babylon were compelled to provide food for the king's dogs, being exempt from other burdens. Among the ancient Romans a tenth of the seed from fields and newly broken land was given to the Roman people. Other taxes and duties were then imposed, according to the needs of the times and for a time, and afterwards also remitted; on these the histories may be consulted. Therefore, what has been confirmed by the consent of so many ages and so many peoples has held even to this day among the adherents of our religion, and tithes, or duties, taxes, levies, fines, services, or whatever name one likes to give them, are paid to kings, princes and nobles in those places where they hold their own dominion. That the origin of all these is to be traced to the most ancient ages, and to the common assent of the peoples, is plain. For what reasons and to what uses these are now granted to the nobles is also clear from what we said above about the use of tithes granted to kings in the Old Testament.

units.la: Iam verò has decimas seu vectigalia,aut quocunque nomine placet appellari,Christianus homo iure diuino tenetur soluere: quando de ijs expressa in scripturis præcepta habentur. Huc enim pertinet verba Samuelis 1.reg. 8. Hoc est ius regis,&c. Segetes vestras&vinearū redditus addecimabit,ut det eunuchis &famulis suis.Greges quoque vestrosaddecimabit, vosque eritis ei serui. Et Christus sua voce Matthæi vicesimosecundo ro-gatus de hac eadem quæstione,respondit, Reddite,quæ sunt Cęsaris,Cęsari,& quæ Dei, Deo. Qui etiam ipse didrachma pendi solitum apud Capernaum lubenter soluit,miraculoparans pecuniā; qui per inopiā potuisset excusari, Matthæi decimoseptimo. Et PaulusRoman.13. Multò clarissimè: Oportet esse subditos magistratibus,non solum propter iră, verūmetiam propter conscientiam. Propter hoc enim & victigalia soluitis: siquidem mi-nistri Dei sunt in hoc ipsum incumbentes . Reddite igitur omnibus quod debetur, cui tributū, tributum: cui vectigal,vectigal: cui timorem,timore:cui honorem,honorem:En,quomodo propter conscientiam vult esse subditos, & vectigalia seu tributa vocat debita.
units.tr: Now indeed a Christian is bound by divine right to pay these tithes or duties, or whatever name one likes to give them, since precise precepts about them are found in the Scriptures. To this pertains the word of Samuel in 1 Samuel 8: "This is the right of the king, etc. He will tithe your grain and the revenue of your vineyards, that he may give it to his eunuchs and servants. He will also tithe your flocks, and you will be his servants." And Christ, asked about this same question in his words of Matthew 22, answered: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." He himself also willingly paid the didrachma that was customarily paid at Capernaum, providing the money by a miracle, though through poverty he could have been excused: Matthew 17. And Paul, Romans 13, speaks much more clearly: "It is necessary to be subject to the magistrates, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience's sake. For this reason you also pay taxes, since they are ministers of God attending to this very thing. Render therefore to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is owed, customs to whom customs, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour." See how he wishes them to be subject for conscience's sake, and calls taxes or tributes debts.

units.la: An autem licet principi uel nobili subinde nouas exactiones imponere? Respondetur breuiter, stipendijs ordinarijs semel communi omnium subditorum assensu decretis contos esse conuenit, sicut Ioanes Baptista in simili propemodum causa docebat milites. Lucæ 3. Quamuis interea pro imminente noua & improuisa necessitate,veluti bello,autrestaurandis aedificijs noua rursus imponere ad tempus potest, eadem remissurus, vbimalo,quod ingruebat,remedium fuerit oppositum. Sic Moses,sic Esdras à populo collige-runt aurum, argentum, & id genus ad sumptus faciendos sacrorum vasorum. Ioseph exegitab Ægyptijs quintam partem fructuum: Genes. 47. Et ad bellicum apparatum,authimilem euentum pro reipublicæ salute,æquum est subditos præstare omnem quam possunt,operam. Sed de hac re non opus est nunc plura præscribere.
units.tr: But is it lawful for a prince or noble from time to time to impose new exactions? The answer briefly is: it is fitting that ordinary stipends, once decreed, be fixed by the common consent of all subjects, as John the Baptist taught soldiers in a nearly similar matter, Luke 3. Yet meanwhile, in the face of an imminent new and unforeseen necessity, such as war or the rebuilding of buildings, he may for a time impose new levies again, to be remitted again when the evil that threatened has been met with a remedy. So Moses and Ezra gathered gold, silver and the like from the people for making the sacred vessels. Joseph exacted a fifth part of the produce from the Egyptians: Genesis 47. And for military preparation, or for a similar event for the safety of the commonwealth, it is right that subjects furnish every effort they can. But there is no need to prescribe more on this matter now.

units.la: Quòd siiam reges,principes, vel magistratus abutantur illis,quæ hac ratione accipiuntà subditis, veluti faciunt sæpe pompam aulicam, inutile, & noxiam immesis sumptibus instituentes,plurimū expendentes in venationibus & aucupijs,comessationibus,alæ dis fortis,& exoletis adulatoribus,perditisque iuuenibus: certè hic grauiter peccant tales magistratus,rationemque reddituti sunt Domino Deo. Non tamen ob hoc negare ordi-narium ius decimarum vel vectigalium quisquam debet,neque absoluitur:quandoquidè obedientia præcipitur erga magistratus etiam impios, quales omnes erant temporibus Christi & Apostolorum.
units.tr: But if kings, princes or magistrates abuse those things which are received from the subjects in this way, as they often do by keeping up courtly display, establishing useless and harmful expenses with excessive spending, spending heavily on hunting and fowling, drinking parties, banquets, and worthless flatterers and dissolute young men, then such magistrates certainly sin gravely, and they will render an account to the Lord God. Yet on this account no one ought to deny the ordinary right of tithes or duties, nor is he released from them, since obedience is commanded towards magistrates, even impious ones, such as all were in the times of Christ and the Apostles.

units.la: Quomodo verò abusus hi corrigendi sint,admonedique,siue à consiliarijs,siue ab alijs ephoris magistratus, nos pluribus prosecuti sumus in libello de honorandis magistratibus.
units.tr: How these abuses are to be corrected and admonished, whether by counsellors or by other overseers of the magistrate, we have treated at more length in the little book on honouring magistrates.

units.la: DE DECIMIS MONASTERIORVM.
units.tr: ON THE TITHES OF MONASTERIES.

units.la: Vidimus nostra tempestate multis in regionibus monasteria suprà modum opuleta, cum principibus de opibus & de pompa certantia, quæq; non minus, quàm principes,suas decimas,& vectigalia,& censum à populo accipiunt.
units.tr: In our own time we have seen monasteries in many regions grown beyond measure in wealth, vying with princes in riches and display, and they take their tithes, tolls and rents from the people no less than princes do.

units.la: Explicandum igitur primùm, ut ordinem seruemus semel institutum,quæ earum decimarum origo, & quo iure monachi eas acceperint. Deprehendimus autem, quasdam donatas, quasdam arte paratas, quasdam emptas. Quo enim tempore primùm instituebantur monasteria,nihil aliud erant,quàm quidam bonorum & studiosorum coùentus, & scholæ quædam,vbi proueᵭiores quidam docebant iuniores rerum diuinarum cogni-tionem,scribebant, disputabant, denique quàm optimè instituebant suos,ut inde postea eligi possent,qui ecclesijs præessent,episcopatu vel sacerdotio fungerentur,& populum in religione docerent.Sicut Augustinus & alij suis temporibus factum testantur: & in Germania ex monasterio Fuldensi,Hersfeldensi,& similibus,episcopi & præsbyteri diuersis in locis electi ac creati leguntur.
units.tr: First, then, let us explain, to keep the order we have set ourselves, what the origin of these tithes is and by what right the monks received them. We find that some were given as gifts, some were obtained by artifice, and some were bought. For when monasteries were first founded, they were nothing other than gatherings of good and studious men and certain schools, where the more advanced taught the younger ones the knowledge of divine things, wrote, disputed, and, in short, trained their pupils as well as possible, so that from among them men could later be chosen to preside over churches, to serve as bishops or priests, and to teach the people in religion. As Augustine and others attest, this happened in their own times; and in Germany we read that bishops and presbyters were chosen and appointed in various places from the monastery of Fulda, Hersfeld and similar houses.

units.la: Itaque propter pium institutum,partim nobiles, partim episcopi, vel etiam ecclesiæ aliquid contulerunt,unde studiosi, & doctores,& discipuli ibi frugaliter alerentur.
units.tr: Accordingly, on account of this pious purpose, some nobles, some bishops, and even some churches contributed something, so that students, teachers and pupils might be supported there frugally.

units.la: Postea verò quando ijdem etiam hospitalitatem exercebant,& similia pietatis officia, alia deinceps illis sunt adiecta, ut iam decimas & prouentus non contemnendos,monasteria illa reciperet ab ipsis quoque ecclesijs, utpote,apud quos implebatur, videlicet munus docendi iuuentutem ,excipiendi pauperes, quod alicubi fortasis ab episcopis & pastoribus negligi cœperat.
units.tr: Later, when these same monasteries also practised hospitality and similar works of piety, other things were added to them, so that those monasteries then received from the churches themselves tithes and revenues not to be despised, since in them was carried on that office of teaching the young and receiving the poor, which in some places had perhaps begun to be neglected by the bishops and ministers.

units.la: Succedentibus temporibus hæc melior disciplina refriguit, & pro doctrina atq; hospitalitate superstitiosi cultus excogitati sunt,& in monasterijs obseruati,qui admirandam & nouam sanctimoniæ speciem præ se ferebant, nimirum, noua vota, nouas vestes, ac Hypocrisis,
units.tr: As time went on, this better discipline grew cold, and in place of teaching and hospitality, superstitious forms of worship were devised and observed in the monasteries, which put on a wonderful and new appearance of holiness: namely, new vows, new garments, and hypocrisy,

units.la: C a siduas cantiones, missationes, sepulturæ, memoriæ mortuorū, & id genus, in quibus summa religionis posita est. His ergo superstitionibus vires accipientibus, iterum permoti sunt principes, nobiles, & diuites omnes ad dadum monasterijs, ea conditione, ut vel ibi sepe-lirentur, sacellū peculiare extruerent, in quo missa per omne tempus fieret, & in hac mor-tuorum memoria, vt sic precationibus monachorum obtineret regnum æternū in cœlis. Deinde creuerunt superstitiones, pro reliquijs mortuorum, & Diuorum inuocatione, ut miracula quoque edita fuerint, crebrique concursus & peregrinationes religionis ergo facti.
units.tr: constant chanting, masses, burials, remembrances of the dead, and that sort of thing, in which the sum of religion was thought to lie. Since these superstitions gained strength, the princes, nobles and all the rich were again moved to give to the monasteries, on condition that they might be buried there, build a private chapel in which mass would be said at all times, and by this memorial of the dead obtain, through the prayers of the monks, eternal kingdom in heaven. Then the superstitions multiplied: relics of the dead and the invocation of the saints came in, so that miracles were also reported and crowds and pilgrimages were made for the sake of religion.

units.la: Quibus artibus monasteria tandem omne genus oblationum, decimarum, prouentuū, a quibusuis acceperunt, eti am vicos, prædia integra, oppidula tandē occupantes, & cum his postremò ciuilem quoque iurisdictionem, præfecti monasteriorum sunt consecuti. Huiusmodi ergo bona, siue decimas, siue census, siue vectigalia appellentur, dicimus arte parata, nempe hypocrisi, fraude, dolo, astu.
units.tr: By these arts the monasteries at last received every kind of offering, tithe and revenue from whomever, and, seizing villages, whole estates and finally small towns, the heads of the monasteries also obtained civil jurisdiction along with them. Whether such goods are called tithes, rents or tolls, we say they were obtained by artifice, namely by hypocrisy, fraud, deceit and cunning.

units.la: Iam verò sic ditata monasteria, tandem accumularunt opes opibus, & decimas ab ecclesijs, a nobilibus, necessitate aliqua coactis vndique plurimas præsente pecunia coemerunt. Has igitur placet emptas appellare. Atque ita quibus modis, & in quem finem, monasteria decimas acceperint, satis est expositum.
units.tr: Now, monasteries made rich in this way heaped wealth upon wealth, and at last, with ready money, bought up many tithes from churches and from nobles who were forced by some need from every side. We think these should be called purchased tithes. And so, by what means and to what end the monasteries received tithes, enough has been set out.
