units.la: Quis verò vsus harum decimarum ac bonorum omnium collatorum, fuerit & adesse debeat, ex prima institutione monasteriorum cerni potest.
units.tr: What the use of these tithes and of all the goods bestowed on them was, and what it ought to be, can be seen from the first institution of the monasteries.

units.la: Nam quæ postea per illos parta sunt, sicut non recte parta, ita nec in bonos vsus sunt expensa, sed sicut per abusus & superstitiones parata sunt, ita in fœdos abusus sunt consumpta.
units.tr: For what was later acquired by them was not rightly acquired, and it was not spent on good uses either; just as it was obtained through abuses and superstitions, so it was consumed in shameful abuses.

units.la: Vtrum ergo adhuc æquum est, omnes has decimas illis pendere? Respondetur: Quæ primi generis sunt, optimo iure debentur, nec vllo modo sunt detrahendæ, vtpote quæ ob rem maximè piam & ecclesijs necessariam fuerunt collatæ.
units.tr: Is it then still right that all these tithes be paid to them? The answer is: those of the first kind are owed by the best right and must in no way be withdrawn, since they were given for a most pious purpose and one necessary for the churches.

units.la: Quæ secundi generis sunt, debentur illis, quia sunt veluti testamentis legata, ac necessum est maiorum voluntatem perficere, maximè quia etiam scriptis & sententijs magistratuum sunt approbata, sicut ostendere possunt monasteria illa tabulis, quas in suis archiuis seruarunt. Et si ea non penderentur monasterijs, deberent pendi hæredibus illorum, qui illa monasterijs primi contulerunt.
units.tr: Those of the second kind are owed to them, since they are like legacies in wills, and the wishes of those who went before must be carried out; especially since they were also approved by written documents and decisions of the magistrates, as those monasteries can show from the deeds they have kept in their archives. And if they were not paid to the monasteries, they ought to be paid to the heirs of those who first gave them to the monasteries.

units.la: Tertij generis decimas quis neget pendendas, cum quæ pretio empta sunt a quopiam, iure ipse exigit, & iure debent ei reddi, quemadmodum in omnibus contractibus debet fieri?
units.tr: Who would deny that tithes of the third kind should be paid, since whoever has bought something with money rightly claims it, and by right it ought to be returned to him, as must be done in all contracts?

units.la: Sed quâdo monachi iam nihil amplius faciunt eorum, quæ maximè debebât, & propter quæ acceperūt illas decimas, præsertim primi generis, quæ illis omnium iustissimè sunt collatę, neque amplius docet aliquos, neque instituunt, qui posint seruire ecclesijs: neque etiam pauperes excipiunt hospitio, neque quicquam eiusmodi faciunt: sed potius inuerso ordine alunt otiosos ventres, & delicatos sacrificulos: qui alunt equos, canes, ut aucupentur, venentur, vendunt, emunt, potitât, ludunt alea, scortantur, denique alia horrenda faciunt, nihil retinentes, quo distinguatur a perditissimis hominibus, præter vestes, gesticulationes, boatus, missationes, nonne talibus adhuc decimas dabimus?
units.tr: But when the monks no longer do any of those things which they ought most of all to do, and for which they received those tithes, especially those of the first kind, which were given to them most justly of all; when they no longer teach or train anyone who could serve the churches, nor receive the poor in hospitality, nor do anything of this kind, but rather, in an inverted order, feed idle bellies and pampered little priests, who keep horses and dogs for hawking and hunting, buy, sell and trade, gamble with dice, consort with harlots, and in short do other dreadful things, retaining nothing by which they are distinguished from the most abandoned men except their garments, gestures, bellowing and masses: shall we still give such men tithes?

units.la: Respondetur: Deberi illis, iam satis ostendimus. Qui verò nō in rectos vsus expendūt, ipsi reddituri sunt Deo iudici rationem.
units.tr: The answer: that they are owed to them, we have already sufficiently shown. But those who do not spend them on right uses will themselves have to render an account to God the judge.

units.la: Tu interea fac, quod tui est muneris: cui debes tributū, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal dependas. Quod tu bene facis, non cedet tibi in malum, quòd alius beneficio tuo non recte vtatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile you do what belongs to your office: to whom you owe tribute, pay tribute; to whom toll, pay toll. What you do rightly will not turn to your harm because another does not use your benefaction rightly.

units.la: Interea ad magistratū pertinet, tales monachos, sicut alios quoscunque perditos homines, in ordinem redigere, curare, ut prima forma monasteriorum restituatur, hoc est, ut docentur ibi iuuenes, qui postea præsint ecclesijs, atq; in vera religione promoueda vsui esse queant. Pro prouentuum ratione curent plures vel pauciores ibi ali, qui doceant, & qui discant, aut, qui hospitalitatem veteri more exerceant. Sicubi prouentus non suffecerint ad hac rem, potius addendum erit, quàm detrahendum, vbi prius vsus successerit, id quod fieri potest aliquando, ab vno monasterio ad aliud quasdam facultates transrendo. Quæ secundo ordine enumerauimus, in meliores vsus conuertantur, nempe vel pauperibus & Xenodochijs erogentur, vel ecclesijs pauperioribus, quæ vix possunt ministros alere, conferantur. In summa, cura fit, & consilia quæratur, quomodo in meliores vsus conuerti luxuriosæ opes queant. Alias sine crimine in priuatos vsus nemo conuertet. Quæ ab illis inueniuntur empta pretio, quæ tertio loco enumerauimus, redimi ab ecclesijs, vel hæredibus eorum, a quibus primum emerunt, permittantur, precium-que illud reformato monasterio, & iam in scholam restituto reddatur, ad stipendium docentium.
units.tr: Meanwhile it belongs to the magistrate to bring such monks, like all other abandoned men, into order, and to see that the original form of the monasteries is restored, that is, that young men are taught there who may afterwards preside over churches and be of use in promoting true religion. According to the amount of revenue, they should see to it that more or fewer are maintained there to teach and to learn, or to practise hospitality in the old manner. Where the revenues do not suffice for this purpose, they should rather be added to than taken away, once the proper use has been established, which can sometimes be done by transferring certain resources from one monastery to another. What we listed in the second group should be turned to better uses: that is, either distributed to the poor and to hospitals, or given to the poorer churches that can scarcely support their ministers. In short, care should be taken and counsel sought as to how the luxurious wealth may be turned to better uses; otherwise no one will convert it to private uses without crime. Those goods that they are found to have bought with money, which we listed third, should be allowed to be redeemed by the churches or by the heirs of those from whom they were first bought, and the price should be paid back to the reformed monastery, now restored to a school, for the salary of its teachers.

units.la: Xenodochia et ptochodochia erigantur, ecclesiæ instaurentur. Redemptio tentanda. docentium, vel bibliothecam publicam, aut eiusmodi res necessarias parandas. De qua re etiam plures docti viri hac nostra tempestate admonuerunt.
units.tr: Hospitals and almshouses should be set up, churches restored. Redemption should be attempted; teachers should be provided for, or a public library, or other necessary things procured. Several learned men in our own time have also urged this matter.

units.la: DE DECIMIS PRIVATORUM.
units.tr: On the tithes of private persons.

units.la: Nueniuntur multis in locis priuati homines, ut opulenti quidam ciues, qui decimas multas & amplas diuersis in vicis accipiunt, cùm tamen nec reipublicae, nec ecclesiae vlli seruiant, vel quicquam omnino pro illis facere videantur.
units.tr: In many places private individuals are found, such as wealthy citizens, who receive large and substantial tithes in various villages, although they serve neither the commonwealth nor any church, or seem to do anything at all for them.

units.la: Videamus, quae harum origo. Hae sunt duplices, siue duobus modis a talibus hominibus obtinetur: primo iure emptionis. Contigit aliquando ecclesias necesitate aliqua inexpectata grauari, aut etiam viros principes egere magna summa pecuniaria. Itaque vt siue ecclesiae, siue principes illi viri haberent praesentem pecuniam, decimas suas alicui diuiti, qui poterat statim numerare, vel oppignorarunt, vel cedentes omni iure suo venderunt.
units.tr: Let us see what the origin of these is. They are obtained by private persons in two ways. First, by the right of purchase. It has sometimes happened that churches were burdened by some unexpected necessity, or that princes needed a large sum of money. So that they might have ready money, either the churches or the princes pledged their tithes to some rich man who could pay at once, or, ceding all their right, sold them outright.

units.la: Secundo, obtinent alicubi decimas priuati homines, quod ipsis propter rem praeclare domi aut foris gestam, & posteris eorum, principes libera donatione certas decimas contulerunt. His, inquam, duobus modis priuati homines ad occupandas decimas perue-nerunt. De vsu vel abusu harum decimarum non est facieda quaestio: satis est, nosse, quo iure obtineantur, & an solui debeant.
units.tr: Second, in some places private persons hold tithes because princes granted them freely, as a gift, to such men and their descendants, on account of some distinguished deed done at home or abroad. These, I say, are the two ways by which private persons came to seize tithes. Whether these tithes are used or misused is not a question to be raised here. It is enough to know by what right they are held and whether they ought to be paid.

units.la: Quid ergo, soluentur ne hae decimae? Respondetur: Maxime. Quod quis iure emptionis obtinet, quare ei non reddatur? Mutato domino vel possessore no tollitur ius, quod prius fuit, non magis quàm fit in agris, domibus, praedijs, vel quibuscunque similibus.
units.tr: What then? Ought these tithes to be paid? The answer is: certainly. Why should what someone holds by the right of purchase not be returned to him? A change of owner or possessor does not abolish the right that existed before, no more than it does in fields, houses, estates, or any similar property.

units.la: Quod etiam donatum est cuiquam à principe, cur ei denegetur, cùm alias ipsi principi idem pendendum foret, qui & habet ius conferendi, & detrahendi aliquid sibi ipsi, seu impartiendi id, quibus vult? Et recte facit, qui tali donatione aliorum animos ad virtute excitat. Nihil ne hic est immutandum?
units.tr: Likewise, if something has been given to someone by a prince, why should it be refused to him, since otherwise the same thing would be owed to the prince himself, who has the right both to confer and to withdraw something from himself, or to bestow it on whom he wishes? And he acts rightly who by such a gift stirs the minds of others to virtue. Should nothing here be changed?

units.la: Respondetur: Nihil sane, nisi quod, quae tantum impignorata sunt, vsitato iure possunt redimi: aut, quae ab alio empta, si induci eo posit, qui emit, similiter redimi poterunt. De hac re supra nonnihil attigimus.
units.tr: The answer is: certainly nothing, except that those tithes which were only pledged may be redeemed by the customary law, or, if they were bought from another, they may likewise be redeemed if the buyer can be persuaded to it. We touched on this matter somewhat above.

units.la: Haec de decimis puto satis copiosè à nobis exposita, & qui in hac intuebitur, facilè, quaecunque obijci solent à rerum nouandarum studiosis hominibus, diluet.
units.tr: I think I have set out these matters about tithes fully enough. Whoever considers this will easily refute whatever is usually objected by men eager for revolutionary change.

units.la: Et habenti promissiones benedixit. Porrò nemo negat, quin id quod minus est, ab eo, quod maius est, benedictionem accipiat.
units.tr: And blessed him that had the promises. Moreover, no one denies that the lesser is blessed by the greater.

units.la: Tertium argumentum, quo rursus, quemadmodum & primo argumento egerat, euincit, Melchisedech longè praestantiorem ipso Abrahamo: ductumque est ex particula illa historiae, qua dicebatur, quod Melchisedech benedixit Abrahamo. Sic autem ratiocinatur:
units.tr: The third argument, by which he again proves, just as he did with the first argument, that Melchisedec is far superior to Abraham himself, is drawn from that part of the history where it is said that Melchisedec blessed Abraham. He reasons thus:

units.la: Qui dat benedictionem, multo maior est eo, qui accipit. Sed Melchisedech est qui dat, Abraham autem qui accipit. Igitur Melchisedech multo maior est Abrahamo.
units.tr: He who gives the blessing is much greater than he who receives it. But Melchisedec is he who gives, and Abraham is he who receives. Therefore Melchisedec is much greater than Abraham.

units.la: Maiorem vult esse per se notam ex ipso benedicendi vsitato more: vnde ipse diserte ait, neminè, quod ita res habeat, posse negare, siue, ut graecè expresis dicitur, sine omni contradictione. Minoris veritas patet ex historia.
units.tr: He wants the major premise to be known in itself from the customary manner of blessing. Hence he says plainly that no one can deny that this is so, or, as it is expressed in Greek, "without all contradiction." The truth of the minor premise is clear from the history.

units.la: Rursus vero, quemadmodum supra diximus, subintellige, sacerdotium Christi, quod est secundum ordinem Melchisedech, excellentius esse sacerdotio Leuitico, quod ab Abraham deriuatur, ideoque istud per illud abrogari.
units.tr: Again, as we said above, understand that the priesthood of Christ, which is according to the order of Melchisedec, is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood, which is derived from Abraham, and therefore that the latter is abrogated by the former.

units.la: Habet autem gratiam, imo magnam vim ad amplificandu laudes Melchisedech, quod Abraham prorsus insigni elogio hic describitur habes promissiones. Significatur enim, quod, cùm Abraham is fuerit, ad quem prae caeteris patribus plures eaeque eximiae factae sint promissiones, atque eo nomine facile reliquos omnes excellat, longè tamen tanto viro eminentiorem censeri debere nostrum Melchisedech, qui illi benedictionem impedirit. Adeò, quamlibet excellens aestimetur Ahraham, necessum est interim ei praeponere sacerdotem Melchisedech.
units.tr: Moreover, the description of Abraham in this passage, "him that had the promises," has a notable force and serves greatly to magnify the praises of Melchisedec. For it signifies that although Abraham was the one to whom more and more excellent promises were made than to the other patriarchs, and on that account easily surpasses all the rest, our Melchisedec must nevertheless be judged far more eminent than so great a man, since he blessed him. Thus, however excellent Abraham is esteemed, it is necessary meanwhile to set the priest Melchisedec above him.

units.la: Porrò, quanta gloria fuerit Abrahę propter promissiones, & fidem ipsius in eas, oftèn dimus capite sexto, vbi exposita est promissio illa Geneseos vicesimo secundo: Nisi bene dicés benedixero tibi: commemorauimusque ibi, quinque vicibus insignes illas promissio nes, quibus etiam vniuersa posteritas immodice superbiuit, ad Abraham esse factas. Et alijs locis Scripturae passim laus eius inde canitur, psal. 104. Lucae 1. Roman. 4. Galat. 3. & alibi. Quod vero attinet ad illud, quod dicitur minores solitos esse benedici à maioribus, videndum est, quid ea de re in Scripturis fit proditum, & quę origo vsusque benedictionis sacerdotum.
units.tr: Further, how great the glory of Abraham was on account of the promises and his faith in them, we showed in the sixth chapter, where that promise in Genesis 22 was explained: "Surely blessing I will bless thee." There we recalled that those five notable promises, in which the whole posterity also boasted excessively, were made to Abraham. And elsewhere in Scripture his praise is sung on this basis, Psalm 104, Luke 1, Romans 4, Galatians 3, and elsewhere. As for what is said, that the lesser are customarily blessed by the greater, we must consider what Scripture reports on this matter, and what is the origin and custom of the priestly blessing.

units.la: Varia autem sunt exempla, quibus often ditur, maiores impartiri benedictionem mi-noribus. Primùm enim Deus dicitur benedicere hominibus, reuera maior hominib. Ac Deum ita benedicere, nihil aliud est, quàm fortunare, prosperare, omni bonorum genere ornare. Et sicut sunt bona quædã temporalia, quædam spiritualia: ita duplex quoque Dei benedictio celebratur, teporalis inquam, qua nimirum confert credentib. bona tempora-lia: ut honores, victorias, opus, sicut semper solet electis conferre. Deinde spiritualis, qua confert iustitiam, pietatem, fortitudinem animi, tranquillitatem mentis, & vitam æternam. De vtroque genere benedictionum Scriptura passim canit. Iam è diuerso si legantur homines benedicere Deum, hic iam alia significatione vox benedicendi accipitur: significat enim laudare Deum, celebrare, gratias agere: ut, Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus eius in ore meo.
units.tr: There are various examples by which it is shown that the greater impart blessing to the lesser. First, God is said to bless men, who are truly greater than men. To bless men in this way is nothing other than to make fortunate, to prosper, and to adorn with every kind of good. And just as some goods are temporal and some spiritual, so also a twofold blessing of God is celebrated: the temporal, namely, by which he bestows on believers temporal goods, such as honours, victories, and work, as he always customarily grants to the elect; and then the spiritual, by which he bestows righteousness, piety, fortitude of mind, tranquillity of soul, and eternal life. Scripture sings of both kinds of blessing throughout. Conversely, if men are said to bless God, the word "to bless" is then taken in another sense: it signifies to praise God, to celebrate, to give thanks, as in: "I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth."

units.la: Secundò, legitur in Scripturis benedicere homines hominibus, & sæpè maiores iu-nioribus: id autem duplici ratione.
units.tr: Second, in Scripture men are read to bless men, and often the greater bless the younger. This happens for two reasons.

units.la: Primùm, cùm parentes dicûtur benedicere filijs, quorum reuera benedictio ad benedictionem Dei quàm proximè accedit, ita ut, quæ parentes benedicedo bene precati sunt suis filijs, vel etiam male precati, nutu Dei adimpleri obseruatum sit, atque ea in parte voluntas parentum habita sit, pro ipsius Dei voluntate. Exemplo sit, quod legitur Genes. 9. de Noah benedicente filijs suis Sem & Iaphet, ac maledicente Cam.
units.tr: First, when parents are said to bless their children. Their blessing comes very close to the blessing of God, so that what parents have prayed for good or even for evil upon their children has been observed to be fulfilled by the will of God, and in that matter the will of the parents has been regarded as the will of God himself. An example is what we read in Genesis 9 about Noah blessing his sons Shem and Japheth, and cursing Ham.

units.la: Maledictus, inquit, puer Canaan, seruus seruorum erit fratribus suis. Dixitque: benedicat Dominus Deus Sem, sit Canaan seruus eius. Dilatet Deus Iaphet & habitet in tabernaculis Sem, sitque Canaan seruus eius. Et reuera fuit voluntas Noæ hac in parte voluntate Dei impleta, ut Cam totaque posteritas semper vilior contemptiorque maneret. Quod sine dubio Deus statim ab initio mundi ita ordinauit, ut filij erga parentes in obsequio & officio continerentur, & ut minores ea ratione discerent magnificare maiorum suorum iudicium & voluntatem. Quo factum ut tanto studio Rebecca laborarit Genes. 27. ut clarissimus filius Iacob à patre Isaac benedictionem præ Esau acciperet: Sciebat quippe, quòd, qui benedictionem illam paternam, præsertim extremam, & ante diem mortis obtineret, mirabiles successus à Deo quoque esset percepturus.
units.tr: "Cursed," he says, "be Canaan, a servant of servants shall he be to his brethren." And he said: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant. God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." And indeed the will of Noah in this matter was fulfilled by the will of God, so that Ham and his whole posterity would always remain more base and despised. This God undoubtedly ordained from the beginning of the world, so that children would be kept in obedience and duty towards their parents, and so that the younger would learn in this way to magnify the judgment and will of their elders. Hence it came about that Rebekah laboured with such zeal (Genesis 27) so that her favourite son Jacob would receive the blessing of his father Isaac before Esau. For she knew that whoever obtained that paternal blessing, especially the last one, and before the day of death, would also receive wonderful successes from God.

units.la: Vbi &, quâ horrenda sit parentum maledictio, pius Iacob suis verbis testatur, dicens: Quid, si inducat super me maledictione pro benedictione? Sunt autem præclara verba benedictionis Isaac: Ecce, inquit, odor filij mei sicut odor agri pleni, cui benedixit Dominus. Det tibi Deus de rore cœli, & de pinguedine terræ, abundantiam frumenti, vini, & olei, & seruiant tibi populi, & adorent te tribus. Esto dominus fratrum tuorum, ut incurventur ante te filij matris tuæ. Qui maledixerit tibi, sit ille maledictus, & qui benedixerit tibi, benedictionibus repleatur. Quòd verò solitus fuerit Deus confirmare hanc parentum benedictionē liquet ex verbis Isaac sequentibus ad Esau: benedixi ei (scilicet Icaob) & erit benedictus. Ratum enim erat apud Deum, quod senex pater volebat, etiamsi inscius & quodammodo non volens ipsi Iacob benedixisset.
units.tr: Here too, the pious Jacob bears witness in his own words how dreadful the curse of parents is, saying: "What if he bring upon me a curse instead of a blessing?" The words of Isaac's blessing are excellent: "Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the Lord hath blessed. God give thee of the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth, plenty of corn, wine, and oil. Let peoples serve thee, and tribes bow down to thee. Be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother's sons bow down before thee. Cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be he that blesseth thee." That God was accustomed to confirm this blessing of parents is clear from the following words of Isaac to Esau: "I have blessed him (namely Jacob), and he shall be blessed." For what the aged father wished was binding before God, even though he had blessed Jacob unknowingly and in some sense against his will.

units.la: Nec potuit infœlix Esau talè benedictione postea obtinere, sed tantùm illud audiebat, In pinguedine terræ, & in rore cœli desuper erit benedictio tua: viues in gladio, & fratri tuo seruies. En, quàm dispar benedictio: Et benedictionib. vtrisque successus respondit. Huc pertinet, quod Genes. 48. Iacob benedicit filijs Ioseph: itè Genes. 49. morituus singulis filijs suis benedixit proprijs benedictionib. quæq; singulis expectan da forent, prædicens. Unde & Dns, vbi præcepit in lege honorari parentes, adiecit etiā promissiones de vita longæua & fœlicijs, qui præceptum illud strenuè obseruarent. Quamobrem etiam hodie multis in locis manet benedictionis parentum dignitas, & non putant, sibi successus lætos expectandos, quibus parentes benedictionem, præsertim in extremo vitæ die, denegarint. Apud Britannos inprimis sacræ antiquitatis vestigia etiamnum hodie clara in hac parte sunt.
units.tr: Nor could the unhappy Esau afterwards obtain such a blessing. He heard only this: "In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be. You shall live by the sword and serve your brother." Behold how unequal the blessings are, and success corresponded to both. To this belongs what is written in Genesis 48, that Jacob blessed the sons of Joseph, and in Genesis 49, that dying he blessed each of his sons with his own blessing, foretelling what was to be expected for each. Hence also the Lord, when he commanded in the law that parents be honoured, added promises of long and happy life to those who diligently kept that precept. For this reason even today in many places the dignity of a parent's blessing remains, and people do not think they may expect happy outcomes if parents have withheld their blessing, especially on the last day of life. Among the Britons in particular, traces of sacred antiquity are even today clear in this matter.

units.la: Quòd si iam filij aut inferiores alicubi legantur benedicere suis maioribus, certè id nequaquàm pari forma, aut potestate, sed ita, ut potius gratiarum actio, & gratitudinis mutuæ signum sit: quomodo & homines dicuntur benedicere Deum.
units.tr: But if somewhere sons or inferiors are read to bless their elders, this is certainly not done in the same form or with the same authority, but rather so that it is an act of thanksgiving and a sign of mutual gratitude, just as men are also said to bless God.

units.la: Tertiò, inueniuntur etiam sacerdotes benedixisse populo, idque diuina haud dubie ordinatione, sicut de benedictione parentum erga filios diximus: atque haud dubie idè statim ab initio mundi diuinitus ita fuerat constitutum: secundum quem Melchisedech describitur benedixisse Abraham: cuius benedictionis forma Genes. 14. ita exprimitur, Benedictus Abraham Deo excelso, qui creauit cœlum & terrā: & benedictus Deus excelsus, quo protegente hostes in manibus tuis sunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, priests are also found to have blessed the people, and this without doubt by divine ordinance, just as we have said of the blessing of parents towards their children. Without doubt this had been established by God from the very beginning of the world. In accordance with this, Melchizedek is described as having blessed Abraham, and the form of that blessing is expressed in Genesis 14 as follows: "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands."

units.la: Vnde etiam posteā in lege constituum fuit, per sacerdotes, præsertim ad finem sacrorum, benedici vniuersum populum: quemadmodum Leuitici 9. legitur:
units.tr: Hence it was afterwards also established in the law that the whole people be blessed by the priests, especially at the end of the sacred rites, as is read in Leviticus 9:

units.la: Cùm cremati essent adipes super altare, pectora eorum & armos dextros separauit Aaron, eleuans ea coram Domino, sicut praeceperat Moses: & extendens manum ad populum benedixit ei: Sicque completis hostijs pro peccato & holocaustis & pacificis descendit. Sed clarius ea de re Numerorum sexto, dixit Dominus ad Mosen, Loquere Aaron & filijs eius: sic benedicetis filijs Israel, & dicetis eis:
units.tr: "When the fat had been burned upon the altar, Aaron separated the breasts and the right shoulders, lifting them up before the Lord, as Moses had commanded; and stretching out his hand toward the people, he blessed them. And so, the sin offerings, the burnt offerings and the peace offerings being completed, he came down." But more clearly on this matter, in Numbers 6, the Lord said to Moses: "Speak to Aaron and his sons: thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them:"

units.la: Benedicat tibi Dominus, & custodiat te, ostendat Dominus faciem suam tibi, & misereatur tui, convertat Dominus vultum suum ad te, & det tibi pacem.
units.tr: The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you, and be gracious to you; the Lord lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace.

units.la: Inuocabuntque nomen meum super filios Israel, & ego benedicam eis. Vbi & forma & effectus benedictionis sacerdotalis clarè describitur, quòd videlicet Deus ‹am ratam habeat. Populus verò respondebat, Amen, non vicissim benedicebat. E diuerso, de maledictionibus sacerdotis in mulierem adulteram, earundemq; effectibus habes Num. 5. Visus proinde benedictionis sacerdotalis deinceps semper seruatus est, & à synagoga etiam ad nostras Ecclesias deriuatus: id quod ex 1. Corinth. 14. licet colligere, vbi dicitur, idiotam, siue eum, qui implet locum indocti, non posse respondere Amen, ad benedictionem, seu etiam gratiarum actionem, nisi intelligat, quid orans vel benedicens loquatur. Augustinus in epistola ad Paulinum, qui nouem quaestiones ei proposuerat, in dilutione quaestionis quintae, qua quaerebatur, quomodo differrentillae species, 1. Tim. 2. Obsecrationes (Δεήσεις) Orationes (προσευχαί) Interpellationes, gratiarum actiones (ἐντεύξεις) Ibi interpellationes, quae graecis ἐντεύξεις, interpretatur benedictionem sacerdotalem: Interpellationes, inquit, seu postulationes, vt quidam habent, fiunt, cùm populus benedicitur. Tunc enim antistites velut aduocati suscepios suos per manuum impositionem miseri cordissimae offerunt potestati. Quid? Annon benedictionis species est manus impositio, & absolutio, contrà vero maledictionis species ligare aliquem seu tradere Satanae? Nec illud dissimulandum est interea, etiam duces, principes & reges olim vniuersum populum benedicere consueuisse. Sic enim Iosuae 22. Ipse Iehosua postquàm conuocasset, & exhortatus fuisset ad constantiam in obseruanda lege Domini Rubenitas & Gaditas, atq; dimidiam tribum Manasse, benedixit eis, & dimisit eos, qui abierunt in tabernacula sua. 1. Paralipom. 16. Dauid, cùm complessett offerre holocausta & pacifica coram arca Dei, benedixit populo in nomine Domini. 3. Reg. 8. Rex Solomon in domo Domini recens extructa, & cùm primùm arca fuisset inuecta, conuertens faciem suam ad populum benedixit vniuersae congregationi Israel, substitit∙q; tota ecclesia Israel. In summa, ex his omnibus, siue cùm Deus benedicit hominibus, siue cùm parentes filijs, sacerdotes populo, principes aut reges similiter populo, (qua significatione vocabulum benedicendi hic sumitur) manifestum est, benedictionem impendi à maioribus, erga inferiores. Atque ita satis comprobata est argumenti huius maior. Quod ad doctrinam attinet, illud fortasis hic commodum annotari queat, maximam esse sacerdotij dignitatem, quando à sacerdotibus benedictionem nomine Dei recipit vniuersa multitudo piorum, & Deus ipse ratum habet, vultq; perficere, quòd hac in parte illi vt ministri Dei perfectum desiderant.
units.tr: "And they shall invoke my name upon the sons of Israel, and I will bless them." Here both the form and the effect of the priestly blessing are clearly described, namely that God will ratify it, while the people answered "Amen" and did not in turn bless. On the other hand, concerning the curses of the priest upon the adulterous woman and their effects, you have Numbers 5. The custom of the priestly blessing was therefore always observed from then on, and it was derived from the synagogue into our churches as well. This may be gathered from 1 Corinthians 14, where it is said that the layman, or the one who fills the place of the unlearned, cannot answer "Amen" to a blessing or thanksgiving unless he understands what the one praying or blessing is saying. Augustine, in his letter to Paulinus, who had proposed nine questions to him, in resolving the fifth question, which asked how those kinds of things in 1 Timothy 2 differ, namely "supplications" (δεήσεις), "prayers" (προσευχαί), "intercessions," and "thanksgivings" (ἐντεύξεις), there explains that the intercessions, which the Greeks call ἐντεύξεις, are the priestly blessing. "Intercessions," he says, or "petitions," as some have it, are made when the people are blessed. For then the bishops, like advocates, offer their charges by the laying on of hands to the most merciful power. What then? Is the laying on of hands and absolution not a form of blessing, whereas on the contrary binding someone or handing him over to Satan is a form of cursing? Nor should it be passed over in the meantime that dukes, princes and kings also used of old to bless the whole people. Thus in Joshua 22: Joshua himself, after he had summoned and exhorted the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh to constancy in keeping the law of the Lord, blessed them and dismissed them, and they went away to their tents. In 1 Chronicles 16: David, when he had finished offering burnt offerings and peace offerings before the ark of God, blessed the people in the name of the Lord. In 3 Kings 8: King Solomon, in the newly built house of the Lord, and as soon as the ark had been brought in, turning his face to the people, blessed the whole assembly of Israel, and the whole church of Israel stood. In sum, from all these instances, whether God blesses men, or parents their children, or priests the people, or princes or kings likewise the people (which is the sense in which the word "to bless" is used here), it is clear that the blessing is bestowed by superiors upon inferiors. And so the major premise of this argument is sufficiently proven. As for doctrine, it may perhaps be fitting to note here that the dignity of the priesthood is very great, when the whole multitude of the godly receives a blessing from the priests in the name of God, and God himself ratifies it and wishes to bring to completion what the ministers of God in this part desire for them.

units.la: Atq, hic quidem homines qui moriuntur, decimas accipiunt, illic autem is, de quo testatum est, quòd viuat.
units.tr: And here indeed men who die receive tithes, but there one of whom it is witnessed that he lives. (Heb. 7:8)

units.la: Quartum argumentum, in quo, quemadmodum egerat argumento secundo, confert ordinem seu sacerdotium Melchisedech cum ordine seu sacerdotio Leuitico, & ratione personarum in vtroque ministrantium colligit, ordinem Melchisedech multis modis praecellere. Estque hęc argumenti sententia. Hic, nempe in ordine Leuitico, decimas accipiunt homines mortales: at in ordine Melchisedech accipit decimas homo immortalis, siue is, qui, vt supra ostendimus, manet in aeternum.
units.tr: The fourth argument, in which, as he dealt with the second argument, he compares the order or priesthood of Melchizedek with the Levitical order or priesthood, and from the status of the persons ministering in each concludes that the order of Melchizedek surpasses in many ways. The sense of the argument is this: here, that is in the Levitical order, mortal men receive tithes; but in the order of Melchizedek, a man receives tithes who is immortal, namely he who, as we have shown above, remains forever.

units.la: Ergo, quanto praestantius est id, quòd manet in aeternum, eo quod transit, nec diu durat: tanto quoq; censeri debet sacerdotium Melchisedech praestantius sacerdotio Leuitico.
units.tr: Therefore, the more excellent is that which remains forever than that which passes away and does not last long, so much the more must the priesthood of Melchizedek be judged more excellent than the Levitical priesthood.

units.la: Contentionem siue ἀντίθεσιν vocant Rhetores, vbi hoc modo aliquid per contraria declaratur seu amplificatur. Ac perspicuum est argumentum, vbi quis intenderit in illud, quod supra dixit, Melchisedech sine patre, sine matre, ignoti generis, manere sacerdotem in perpetuum.
units.tr: The rhetoricians call this contention or antithesis, where something is declared or amplified by contraries in this manner. And the argument is clear, where one attends to what he said above, that Melchizedek, without father, without mother, of unknown lineage, remains a priest forever.

units.la: Hoc enim est, quod ait, de eo testatum: Non quòd non sit mortuus ipse Melchisedech, sed quòd scriptura tempus, vel genus mortis eius non memoret, quemadmodum supra exposuimus. Leuitarum autem mortem, & aliorum in locum demortuorum successionem crebrò scriptura narrat. Participium illud ἀχεβούμενος participium medium est, vixq; alia ratione reddi queat, quàm qua interpres reddidit, de quo testatum est, vel, testimonium consecutus. Et ut ita loquar, in Abraham decimatus est etiam ipse Leui, qui decimas solet accipere. Nam is adhuc in lumbis patris erat, cum occurreret ei Melchisedech.
units.tr: For this is what he says is witnessed of him: not that Melchizedek himself did not die, but that Scripture does not record the time or manner of his death, as we explained above. Scripture, however, frequently narrates the deaths of the Levites and the succession of others in place of the dead. The participle ἀχεβούμενος is a middle participle, and it cannot be rendered in any other way than the translator rendered it, "of whom it is witnessed" or "having obtained testimony" [μαρτυρούμενος]. And, so to speak, Levi himself, who is accustomed to receive tithes, was himself tithed in Abraham. For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him.

units.la: Quintum argumentum fluens e præcedentibus, potissimumq; e primo argumento, quo iterum probat, Melchisedech, nec non ordinem Melchisedech multo eminentiorē esse ordine Leuitico, ac valde profecto artificiose arguteq;. Sic enim colligit:
units.tr: The fifth argument flows from the preceding ones, and especially from the first argument, by which he again proves that Melchizedek, and also the order of Melchizedek, is far more eminent than the Levitical order, and he does so very skilfully and subtly. For he concludes thus:

units.la: Ipse ordo Leuiticus dedit decimas nostro Melchisedech. Igitur ordo Leuiticus Melchisedecico longè est inferior.
units.tr: The Levitical order itself gave tithes to our Melchizedek. Therefore the Levitical order is far inferior to the Melchizedekian.

units.la: Valet consequentia ab eo, quòd, ut supra dictum est, minor est, qui dat decimas, maior verò qui accipit. Sed quia absurdè dictum videri poterat, ordinem Leuiticum pependisse decimas ipsi Melchisedech, quando ad id tempus ordo Leuiticus nondum fuerit institutus, ideo addit probationem, in hunc modum:
units.tr: The inference holds from the fact that, as was said above, the one who gives tithes is the lesser and the one who receives them the greater. But because it might seem absurd to say that the Levitical order paid tithes to Melchizedek himself, since the Levitical order had not yet been instituted at that time, he therefore adds a proof in this way:

units.la: Quando Abraham dedit decimas Melchisedech, Leui erat in lumbis Abrahæ, & ex hoc debebat ordo Leuiticus nasci ac propagari.
units.tr: When Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek, Levi was in the loins of Abraham, and from him the Levitical order was to be born and propagated.

units.la: Ergo, quando Abraham dedit decimas, simul cum eo intelligendus est decimas dedisse ipse Leui, seu ordo Leuiticus. Quare palàm sequitur, ordinem Melchisedech lògè esse præstantiorem ordine Leuitico. Ducta videtur probatio ex consequentibus, vel certè a comparatis, tanquàm diceretur: Si pater dedit decimas, igitur & filius debet dare. Si rex est subditus Imperatori: igitur & dux, comes, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, when Abraham gave the tithes, the Levites, or the Levitical order, must be understood to have given tithes along with him. From this it plainly follows that the order of Melchizedek is far superior to the Levitical order. The proof seems to be drawn from consequences, or rather from comparisons, as if one were to say: If the father gave tithes, then the son must also give them. If a king is subject to the emperor, then so is a duke, a count, and so on.

units.la: Expressit autem argumentum istud verbis multò appositissimis. Et ut ita loquar, inquit, ὡς ἵπῳ εἰπεῖν, quod nusquam alibi apud Paulum occurrit. Estq; elegans præmollitio, ne videlicet reijciatur hoc argumentum, propterea quòd appareat paulò petitū longius, etiamsi quandam incrementi & exaggerationis vim ea forma locutionis obtineat, quasi diceretur: Et ut aliquid maius dicam, ut, quòd magis miremini proferam, &c. Quod ait etiam ἀτδεκάτωσαι, passiue decimatus est, subiectionem exprimit multò significantius, quàm si tantum dixisset, dedit decimas. Innuit ea locutio, quasi iure quodam Leui comprehensum inter eos, qui decimas dare debebant. Leui, pro ordine Leuitico per Metonymiam, vel potius synecdochen: vel, ut Chrysostomo placet, dixit Leui, potius, quàm Leuitæ, ut intelligatur, ipse etiam pater totius tribus, & à quo ordo accepit appellationem, decimas dedisse, quod ad amplificandum adhuc coducit. Et particula illa, ὁ ἀτδεκάτως λαμβάνων, quasi diceret, ille decimas accipiens, non sine amplificandi gratia est interpolita.
units.tr: He expressed this argument in very apt words. And, so to speak, he says, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, a phrase that occurs nowhere else in Paul. It is an elegant softening, lest the argument be rejected as a rather far-fetched one, even though this form of expression gives it a certain force of amplification and emphasis, as if one were to say: And, to say something greater, something you will marvel at even more, I will add. What he adds, ἀποδεδεκάτωται [the Latin has ἀτδεκάτωσαι], "has been tithed," in the passive, expresses subjection much more forcefully than if he had only said "gave tithes." The expression suggests that the Levites were, as it were by a certain right, included among those who had to pay tithes. "Levi" stands for the Levitical order by metonymy, or rather by synecdoche. Or, as Chrysostom prefers, he said "Levi" rather than "the Levites," so that it is understood that Levi himself, the father of the whole tribe and the one from whom the order received its name, gave tithes, which also serves to amplify the point. And the clause ὁ δεκάτας λαμβάνων [the Latin has ἀτδεκάτως λαμβάνων], as if to say "he who receives tithes," is inserted not without a view to amplification.

units.la: Quamuis enim magna dignitas fuerit Leuitarum, quòd decimas ab aliis acceperint, tamen hoc non obest, quo minus illi quidem decimas pendant ipsi Melchisedech. In eandem sententiam argumento secundo dicebatur, quòd Leuitæ præceptum habebant accipiendi decimas.
units.tr: For although the Levites had great dignity in that they received tithes from others, this does not prevent them from paying tithes to Melchizedek himself. To the same effect, the second argument stated that the Levites had a commandment to receive tithes.

units.la: In lumbis erat) Phrasis hebraica, pro eo, quod nondum erat natus, sed breui nasciturus: sicut egredi ex lumbis, pro eo, quod est nasci. Atq; hac ratione dicitur Leui in lumbis Abrahæ patris, quòd Leui, non quidè ex ipso Abraham, sed ex Abrahæ posteritate esset natus, adeò, ut pater Leui dicatur Abraham, quomodo pater quorumcunq; aliorū ex eo secundum carnem etiam post aliquot secula descendentium. Nam si exactius discutere volumus, ex Abraham natus Isaac, Isaac deinde genuit Iacob, Iacob verò inter alios duodecim numero filios genuit hunc Leui: Abraham reuera fuit ipsius Leui proauus. Fuit autem tertius filius Iacob Leui natus ex Lea, quæ peperit Ruben, Simeon, Leui, Iudà, foro re Rachele adhuc sterili permanente, Genes. 29. Sed ab hoc tempore adhuc aliquot secula, nempe quadringenti fere anni, intercesserunt, priusquà tribus Leuitica ad ministerium sacrorum à Deo eligeretur. Nihilominus quia omnes originem traxerunt ab Abraham tanquam primo parente, rectè dicuntur in Abraham decimati. Ac solet etiam dici, quæ parentibus, vel aliàs primùm inclarescentib. in familia quapiam propria fuere, transfire, veluti iure quodam ad totam familiam ac posteritatem: sicut videmus etiamnum hodie apud nobiles priuilegia, dignitates, officia, in quibusdam familijs summa cura conseruari, & retineri, seu præstari ea, quæ à maioribus ipsorum retinebantur, vel præstabantur. Item si quid præclarè gestu à maioribus, posteri id ad suam pertrahunt gloriam. Rursus, si quid turpiter egerint, ex eo etiam posteris nota infamiæ inuritur. Et in prædijs manet seruitia, manent redditus soluendi, qui antea fuerunt constituti & soluti à maioribus.
units.tr: "Was in the loins": a Hebrew idiom meaning that he was not yet born but was about to be born, just as "to come out of the loins" means "to be born." In this sense Levi is said to have been in the loins of his father Abraham, because Levi was born not directly from Abraham himself but from Abraham's posterity. So Abraham is called the father of Levi, just as he is the father of all others who descend from him according to the flesh after many centuries. For if we want to examine the matter more exactly: Isaac was born of Abraham, Isaac then begot Jacob, and Jacob begot, among his twelve sons, this Levi. Abraham was in truth Levi's great-grandfather. Levi was the third son of Jacob, born of Leah, who bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah, while Rachel remained barren for a time (Gen. 29). But many centuries, roughly four hundred years, passed from that time before the tribe of Levi was chosen by God for the sacred ministry. Nevertheless, since all of them drew their origin from Abraham as the first parent, they are rightly said to have been tithed in Abraham. It is also customary to say that things which belonged to a family through its parents, or earlier distinguished persons, pass on to the whole family and its descendants, as if by a certain right. We see even today that among noble families privileges, dignities and offices are preserved and retained with the greatest care, and that the services and obligations which their ancestors kept or performed are still rendered. Likewise, if the ancestors have done something nobly, the descendants claim it for their own glory. Conversely, if they have behaved shamefully, a mark of infamy is branded on the descendants as well. And on estates, the services and the obligations of payment that were established and discharged by the ancestors remain in force.

units.la: Non dissimili ratione, sicut scribitur Roman. 5. à primo parente peccatum propagatū est in omnes homines, & per peccatum mors, in omnes inquam homines, qui communi nascendi lege, puta per viri & mulieris copulam ex Adam trahunt originem: quæ exceptio adhibenda est, propter Christum, qui ea lege non est natus, sed ex virgine de Spiritu Sancto fœcundata: qua exceptione etiam tollitur cauillus, ne quis ansam arripiat hinc inferendi, eadem ratione posse dici, & Christum decimatum in lumbis Abrahæ, sicut decimatus dicitur in lumbis Abrahæ ipse Leui, maximè cùm Christus etiam appelletur filius Abrahæ perinde ac Leui, Matthæi 1. Atqui Christus in hoc excellit, quòd non eadem ratione ex Abraham trahit originem, qua Leui, vel cæteri, ad Christum usque. Fuit quidem Christus etiam secundum carnem in lumbis Abrahæ, quia tamen non communi lege, id est, secundum concupiscentiam carnis ex eo descendit, non potest dici Christus, ut Leui, in Abraham decimatus.
units.tr: In a not dissimilar way, as it is written in Rom. 5, sin was spread from the first parent to all men, and through sin death, to all men, I say, who by the common law of birth, that is, by the union of man and woman, derive their origin from Adam. This exception must be made on account of Christ, who was not born under that law, but conceived of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin. By this exception also the quibble is removed, lest anyone seize the opportunity to argue that by the same reasoning Christ too could be said to have been tithed in the loins of Abraham, just as Levi himself is said to have been tithed in the loins of Abraham, especially since Christ is also called a son of Abraham just as Levi is (Matt. 1). But Christ excels in this, that he does not trace his origin from Abraham by the same reasoning by which Levi, or all the others down to Christ, do. Christ was indeed also in the loins of Abraham according to the flesh; but since he did not descend from him by the common law, that is, according to the lust of the flesh, Christ cannot be said to have been tithed in Abraham as Levi was.

units.la: Atque ita recte dicitur Leui in Abraham decimatus: neque est, quod ad persona Christi simile detorqueatur, aut cauillari quisquam possit, Christum hac in parte nihilo præstantiorem ipse Leui, quasi qui similiter in Abraham decimas pependisset Melchisedec. Qua de re plura vide apud Augustinum de Genesi ad literam libro 10. cap. 19. & Magistrum sententiarum lib. 3. distinctione 3. Proinde valde artificiose excogitatum est hoc argumentum, & ad confirmandam causam mire appositum.
units.tr: And so it is rightly said that Levi was tithed in Abraham. Nor is there any reason to twist this into a likeness with the person of Christ, or for anyone to cavil that Christ in this respect is in no way superior to Levi, as if he too had paid tithes to Melchizedek in Abraham. On this matter, see more in Augustine, On Genesis according to the Letter, book 10, chapter 19, and the Master of the Sentences, book 3, distinction 3. Accordingly, this argument has been very skilfully devised and wonderfully well suited to confirming the cause.

units.la: Proinde si consummatio per Leuiticum sacerdotium erat (siquidem sub hoc populus legem acceperat) quid præterea fuit opus alium exoriri sacerdotem, qui secundum ordinem Melchisedech, & non secundum ordinem Aaron diceretur? Quandoquidem translato sacerdotio, necesse est, ut legis quoq; translatio fiat.
units.tr: Therefore, if perfection came through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people had received the law), what further need was there for another priest to arise, who would be called after the order of Melchizedek and not after the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that the law also be transferred.

units.la: Satis probauit, Christum esse sacerdotem (initio capitis quinti) & quidem secundum ordinem Melchisedech (statim in principio præsentis capitis septimi:) Deinde huius ordinis sacerdotium multo esse præstantius sacerdotio ordinis Leuitici (hoc enim ordine hucusque est progressus:) Iam venit ad id, quod totius disputationis caput est, atque inferre incipit, per nouum istud sacerdotium Christi secundum ordinem Melchisedech usque adeò excellens abrogari humile & inutile sacerdotium legale ordinis Leuitici: præterea cum sacerdotio simul abrogari ipsam quoq; legem.
units.tr: He has sufficiently proved that Christ is a priest (at the beginning of chapter five), and indeed according to the order of Melchizedek (at the very start of the present seventh chapter). Then he has shown that the priesthood of this order is far superior to the priesthood of the Levitical order (for it is by this order that he has advanced thus far). Now he comes to what is the head of the whole discussion, and begins to infer that through this new priesthood of Christ, according to the order of Melchizedek, which is so far more excellent, the humble and useless legal priesthood of the Levitical order is abrogated; and furthermore that along with the priesthood the law itself is abrogated too.

units.la: Cæterùm non ita crasse Apostolus hanc sententiam suam exprimit, nihilominus tamè orationem talem instituit, quæ tantundem non obscurè significat: idq; in hunc modum, & duobus fere argumentis, quorum prioris hæc est sententia: Constat ex præcedentibus, Christum esse sacerdotem, & quidem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, qui præstantior est ordine Leuitico. Proinde quia Christus, sic iam alius sacerdos exoritur, & quidem secundum multò præstantissimum ordinem Melchisedech, argumentum est, sacerdotium ordinis Leuitici nullarum plane esse virium, & consummationem seu perfectionem nequaquam in se habere (alias enim si hanc haberet, quorsum opus erat spiritum sanctum vaticinari de alio sacerdotio Christi secundum alium & perfectiorem ordinem?)
units.tr: The Apostle does not express his view so crudely, yet he constructs his discourse in such a way that it signifies the same thing clearly enough, and this in the following manner and by roughly two arguments, the first of which has this sense: It is established from what precedes that Christ is a priest, and indeed according to the order of Melchizedek, which is superior to the Levitical order. Therefore, since Christ, another priest, now arises, and indeed according to the far more excellent order of Melchizedek, it follows that the priesthood of the Levitical order has no real power at all, and does not in itself contain consummation or perfection. For otherwise, if it had it, why was it necessary for the Holy Spirit to prophesy of another priesthood of Christ according to another and more perfect order?

units.la: Iam adijciamus, quod consequentiam absoluat. Si igitur per sacerdotium Leuiticum non habetur consummatio, sed ea potius proponitur expectada ab alio sacerdotio Christi alterius ordinis: sequitur, per istud nouum, ac præstantius sacerdotium Christi abrogari imbecille & inutile illud sacerdotium Leuiticum. Ista vero adijcienda esse satis indicant verba illa: Quandoquidem translato sacerdotio, &c. Atque hæc est, meo iudicio, prior Apostoli consequentia, germano sensu reddita, manifesta atque efficax ex eo, quòd, vbi adest præstantius & vtilius, merito omittitur, quod erat imbecille & inutile: quam rationem ipse mox suis verbis aperit, vbi ait, abrogari præceptum quod præcessit, propter imbecillitatem & inutilitatem.
units.tr: Let us now add what completes the inference. If, therefore, consummation is not had through the Levitical priesthood, but is rather held out as something to be expected from another priesthood of Christ of a different order, it follows that through this new and more excellent priesthood of Christ that weak and useless Levitical priesthood is abrogated. That these things must be added is sufficiently indicated by those words: "For when the priesthood is transferred," and so on. And this, in my judgement, is the Apostle's first inference, rendered in its true sense, clear and forceful from the fact that where something more excellent and more useful is present, what was weak and useless is rightly set aside. He himself soon makes this reasoning explicit in his own words, where he says that the commandment which went before is abrogated because of its weakness and uselessness.

units.la: Extulit autem Apostolus consequentiam hanc paulò strictius & per interrogationem, maioris videlicet acrimoniæ caussa, ut nimirum hoc orationis schemate citius obtineat, quasique ab inuitis extorqueat, maximam esse sacerdotij Christi præ sacerdotio Leuitico excellentiam, aliorag; omnes animis concipiant, quàm ipse verbis designat.
units.tr: The Apostle put this inference somewhat more tightly and in the form of a question, for the sake of greater force: by this figure of speech he wants the point to be grasped more quickly and to be drawn, as it were, from unwilling hearers, namely that the excellence of Christ's priesthood over the Levitical priesthood is very great, and that people should conceive of it in their minds even more than he expresses in words.

units.la: Porrò hoc dato, quòd in quam humile sacerdotium legale ordinis Leuitici abrogetur per nouum sacerdotium Christi, aliud condens enthymema, infert: Si translatum est sacerdotium: Igitur simul translata est & lex, hoc est, omnia, quæ sacerdotio adiuncta sunt, veluti ceremoniæ, ritus, obseruationes temporum, ciborum, &c.
units.tr: Granting this, that the lowly legal priesthood of the Levitical order is abrogated through the new priesthood of Christ, he draws another inference by forming an enthymeme: if the priesthood has been transferred, then the law has been transferred at the same time, that is, everything that was joined to the priesthood, such as the ceremonies, rites, observances of times, foods, and so on.

units.la: Ratio seu probatio huius consequentiæ petenda est ex illis per parenthesin appositis: Siquidem per hoc, siue sub hoc, populus legem acceperat: Quorum verborum hic est sensus: Eodem tempore ordinata est simul lex & sacerdotium leuiticum: præterea legis administratio, hoc est, doctrina, ritus, ceremoniæ, obseruationes, quæ per sacerdotes potissimum exercebatur, atque obseruandę procurabantur.
units.tr: The reason or proof of this inference is to be sought in those words placed in parentheses: for under this priesthood the people had received the law. The sense of these words is this: the law and the Levitical priesthood were ordained at the same time; moreover, the administration of the law, that is, its teaching, rites, ceremonies and observances, was carried out chiefly through the priests, who also saw to it that they were kept.

units.la: Quamobrem recte conficitur, ut ubi conciderit sacerdotium, simul concidere debeat ipsa lex. Vbi non amplius erit sacerdos, nec sacrificia conferent, neque alia eiusmodi fient; di fient: quemadmodum vulgo notum est, sublato instrumento, siue medijs ad finem, im-pediri simul ipsum finem seu effectum. Atq; tendit tota disputatio: in hunc scopum om-nia argumenta tàm precedentia, quàm sequentia diriguntur. Partes etiam breuiter ex-plicemus.
units.tr: Therefore it rightly follows that when the priesthood has come to an end, the law itself must come to an end too. Where there is no longer a priest, sacrifices will not avail and no such things will be done, as is commonly known: when the instrument, that is the means to an end, is removed, the end or effect itself is hindered at the same time. The whole argument aims at this goal, and all the arguments, both preceding and following, are directed to it. Let us also briefly explain its parts.

units.la: Proinde si consummatio per Leuiticum sacerdotium erat, quid praterea fuit opus alium exoriri sacerdotem, qui secundum ordinem Melchisedech, & non secundum ordinem Aaron diceretur?
units.tr: Therefore, if perfection was through the Levitical priesthood, what further need was there for another priest to arise, who would be called after the order of Melchizedek and not after the order of Aaron?

units.la: Primùm quidem simpliciter & clare significatur his verbis, nouum sacerdotium Chri-sti secundum ordinem Melchisedech, multò praestantius esse sacerdotio Leuitico: imò, quod maius est, per sacerdotium Christi Melchisedecicum contingere consummatione, perfectionem, & salutem, quæ per Leuiticum non poterat confingere: qua ratione multò plus hic dicitur, quàm dictum est argumentis precedentibus.
units.tr: First, it is stated simply and clearly by these words that the new priesthood of Christ according to the order of Melchizedek is far more excellent than the Levitical priesthood; indeed, what is greater, that through the Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ there comes perfection, consummation and salvation, which could not be attained through the Levitical. In this way much more is said here than was said in the preceding arguments.

units.la: Iam verò quòd ex his inferendum sit, inefficax & inutile sacerdotium Leuiticum ab-rogari per nouum sacerdotium Christi Melchisedecicum, satis docent verba sequentia, maximè ista: Translato sacerdotio, necesse est, ut legis quoq; translatio fiat. Item, Abrogatur, quod præcesserit præceptum, propter imbecillitatem & inutilitatem. Quare existimo, nos ea, quæ pro-prie ad mentem Apostoli pertinent, non male explicuisse. Apostolo autem satis fuit, eadé prius absoluere, & nunc tantum tacitè intelligenda insinuare.
units.tr: Now, that it must be inferred from these things that the ineffective and useless Levitical priesthood is abrogated through the new Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ, the following words teach sufficiently, especially these: When the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that the law also be transferred. Likewise, the commandment that went before is abrogated because of its weakness and uselessness. Therefore I think we have not badly explained those things which properly belong to the mind of the Apostle. But it was enough for the Apostle to have first settled these matters, and now only to hint at what is to be understood tacitly.

units.la: Auferinteirogationis Schema, & videbis claram sententiam, dicasq; hoc pacto: Con-summatio per Leuiticum sacerdotium non erat, & propterea opus alium exoriri sacerdo-tem alterius ordinis. Nonne hæc verba perspicuè sonant, abrogari vetus sacerdotium, & exoriri aliud? præterea illud non habere consummationem, istud verò eam habere? Consummatio) τελείωσις, siue τελειότης, perfectio, & salutis summa est, quà Hebræi valde con-tentiosè tribuebant legi, & inprimis sacerdotio. Hoc enim ad sanctificationem & salute putabant facere, utpote, quod in sacrificijs, ceremonijs, expiationibus, purificationibus, totum occupatur: sed falsi sunt hac in parte sua opinione, cùm vniuersum illud sacerdo-tium tantùm fuerit umbra & typus alterius sacerdotij, nempe Christi, per quod solùm con-tingere potest consummatio & perfecta salus. Huc pertinent illa Roman. 8. Quod lex præstare non poterat ea parte, qua imbecillis erat per carnem, hoc Deus proprio filio mis-so sub specie carnis peccato obnoxiæ præstitit. Galat.3. Lex tantùm pedagogus dicitur ad Christum. Quò etiam pertinet, quòd Moses typus legis terra promissam non est ingres-sus, sed tantùm procul conspexit, Deuteronomij ultimo. Et quod hoc ipso capite statim subijcitur, quòd lex nihil ad perfectionem adduxit, verùm tantùm erat introductio ad spem potiorem.
units.tr: Remove the figure of question, and you will see the clear sense, and you may put it this way: perfection was not through the Levitical priesthood, and for that reason another priest of a different order had to arise. Do not these words plainly sound that the old priesthood is abrogated and another arises? Moreover, that the former does not have perfection, and the latter does have it? Perfection (consummatio) [τελείωσις], or [τελειότης], is the perfection and the sum of salvation, which the Hebrews contended very vigorously should be ascribed to the law, and above all to the priesthood. For they thought that this made for sanctification and salvation, since it is wholly occupied with sacrifices, ceremonies, expiations and purifications. But they are wrong in this opinion of theirs, since that whole priesthood was only a shadow and type of another priesthood, namely Christ's, through which alone perfection and full salvation can be obtained. To this belong those words of Romans 8: what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. Galatians 3: the law is called merely a tutor leading to Christ. To this also belongs the fact that Moses, a type of the law, did not enter the promised land but only saw it from afar, in the last chapter of Deuteronomy. And what is immediately added in this same chapter, that the law brought nothing to perfection but was only an introduction to a better hope.

units.la: Christus deinde talis describitur, qui possit saluos facere ad plenum: & ad finem addi-tur, Christum constitutum esse in æternum consummatum τεθελειωμένον. Ex his igitur sa-lutis constat, quomodo per sacerdotium Leuiticum consummatio, & perfecta salus haberi non potuerit. Quia verò per illud non potuit haberi consummatio, & tamen interereat diuinæ prouidentiæ, ea procurare, per quæ homines semel ad perfectionem adduceren-tur, ideò opus fuit aliud sacerdotium introducere & constituere, per quod homines salu-tem potuissent consequi. Hinc ergo ait, Opus fuit alium exoriri sacerdotem: Valde appositè dicit, alium: ita enim maximum discrimen inter sacerdotium Christi & legale constituit: sicut etiam titulis, seu ordinis appellatione valde distinguuntur: Alius quippe secundum ordi-nem Melchisedech. Igitur alia res Christus, alia res sacerdos legalis: alia res lex, alia res euangelium: utpote quæ non minus, quàm umbra & corpus, imago & res, differunt. Sed & prudenter dicit, exoriri, ἀνίστασθαι, quasi diceret, resurgere, reexcitari. Neque enim dicit, primùm oriri Christum sacerdotem, utpote qui antea semper fuerit, sed nunc exoriri, re-surgere, ac manifestari omnibus. Sicut nec dixit nouum exoriri sacerdotem, sed alium. A-lius enim rectius dicitur Christus sacerdos, quà nouus, quia Christus reuera semper fuit sacerdos, etiam ante sacerdotium Leuiticum: & ij ipsi, qui sub lege agentes cõsecuti sunt salutem, per solum Christum consummatum & consummationis autorem eam adepti sunt. Sed nunc potisimum est manifestatus, & palàm toti orbi declaratus, ac propo-situs sacerdos, ut per eum salutè plenam consequantur, iusfiq; sunt homines in hunc so-lum deinceps intueri, neglectis illis, qui ad tempus erant sacerdotes, neque sibi, neque a-lijs potentes salutem parare. Siquidem per hoc, siue, sub hoc, populus legem acceperat) ὑπὸ hoc modo positum, cùm datiuo ferè significat potestate & arbitrium, ὑπὸ βασιλέα τῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων, id est, in potestate regis sub-ditorum sunt bona. Alias notat causam, & significat propter, vel pro: ἐν ἀγαθῷ ταῦ-τα ἱνοία. Interpres Interpres Chrysostomi & Theophylacti vertit, in hoc.
units.tr: Next Christ is described as one who is able to save completely, and at the end it is added that Christ has been appointed for ever as one made perfect [τεθελειωμένον]. From these words of salvation it is clear how through the Levitical priesthood perfection and full salvation could not be had. And since perfection could not be had through it, and yet it pertained to divine providence to provide the means by which men might once for all be brought to perfection, therefore it was necessary to introduce and establish another priesthood through which men could obtain salvation. Hence he says: it was necessary that another priest should arise. He says very aptly "another": for in this way he sets up the greatest difference between the priesthood of Christ and the legal one; they are also greatly distinguished by their titles or by the name of their order, since the one is "after the order of Melchizedek." Christ is therefore one thing, the legal priest another; the law one thing, the gospel another, since they differ no less than shadow and body, image and reality. He also says wisely arise [ἀνίστασθαι], as if he meant rise again, be raised up. For he does not say that Christ first began to be a priest, since he had always been one, but that he now arises, rises again, and is made manifest to all. Likewise he did not say that a new priest arises, but another. For Christ is more rightly called a priest as "another" than as "new," because Christ truly always was a priest, even before the Levitical priesthood; and those who lived under the law and obtained salvation obtained it through Christ alone, the one who is perfected and the author of perfection. But now he has been manifested above all, openly declared to the whole world, and set forth as priest, so that through him men may obtain full salvation; and men are commanded from now on to look to him alone, neglecting those who were priests for a time and who were able to procure salvation neither for themselves nor for others. For through this, or under this, the people had received the law [ὑπὸ]: this construction with the dative usually signifies power and authority, as in [ὑπὸ βασιλέα τῶν ἀνθρώπων], that is, goods are in the power of the king's subjects. Elsewhere it marks cause and means "on account of" or "for": [ἐν ἀγαθῷ ταῦτα ἱνοία]. The interpreter of Chrysostom and Theophylact renders it in this.

units.la: Potest itaq; parenthesis dupliciter intelligi. Primùm quasi addita, ad probandum, in sa{a}cerdotio debere esse consummationem, perinde ac si diceretur: Maximè quidem videbatur consummatio debere contingere per sacerdotium, quia per hoc, siue sub hoc, populus accipiebat legem, & docebatur in lege, quæ perfectionem visa est promittere, & per quam homines perfici se credebant. Sed quia huiusmodi perfectio per sacerdotium illud non est præstita, ideò necessum fuit, aliud sacerdotium succedere, per quod ea habere posset. Aliter, & maximè si respiciatur in particulam, per hoc, vel sub hoc, aut, ut quidam legunt, in hoc, interposita est ad significandum connexionem legis & sacerdotij inter se, ut sit sententia: Cum sacerdotio, seu, in Sacerdotio, simul eodemq; tépore accepta est lex, planeq; sacerdotium & lex coniuncta sunt inuicem, non aliter, quàm relatiua, ut sacerdos non sit, nisi secundum aliquam legem, ritus, & ceremonias, quarum præscripto agat omnia, seruariq; ea, quæ religionis sunt, procuret: Atq; è contrario non est lex, ritus, ceremoniæ, nisi sit sacerdos executor atq; obseruator. Quamobrem pariter de vtriusque, tam sacerdote inquam, quàm lege serri debet iudicium, statuedumq;, quæ simul inceperint, etiam simul desinere: &, sublato sacerdotio, cõsequi id, ut auferatur quoq; lex. Vtraq; interpretatio habet causas in Scriptura expositas.
units.tr: The parenthesis can therefore be understood in two ways. First, as added to prove that there ought to be perfection in the priesthood, as if one said: perfection seemed most of all bound to come through the priesthood, because through this, or under this, the people received the law and were taught in the law, which seemed to promise perfection and through which men believed they were made perfect. But since such perfection was not supplied through that priesthood, it was necessary for another priesthood to succeed, through which they might have it. Otherwise, and especially if the particle is taken as through this or under this, or, as some read it, in this, it is inserted to signify the connection of law and priesthood with each other, so that the sense is: the law was received together with the priesthood, or in the priesthood, at the same time, and the priesthood and the law are plainly joined together reciprocally, so that a priest exists only according to some law, rites and ceremonies, by whose prescription he does all things and sees to it that the things belonging to religion are kept; and conversely there is no law, rite or ceremony unless there is a priest to carry it out and observe it. Therefore judgement must be passed on both alike, on the priest as much as on the law, and it must be settled that those which began together also cease together, and that when the priesthood is removed, the law is removed too. Both interpretations have their grounds set out in Scripture.

units.la: Perfectionem in lege sitam, & per legem patari Iudæi ambitiosisimè contendebant: sed & cùm lex ipsa per sacerdotes docebatur atq; administrabatur: præterea, cùm inter omnia, quæ legis erant, maximè emineret sacerdotium, ceremonia, sacrificia, purificationes, cum omnibus adiunctis: sanè si qua ex vniuersa lege perfectio erat prouentura, ea sacerdotio accepta ferri debebat. Sed cùm nulla in parte legis sita fuerit perfectio, id quod patet ex aliis locis aliarum epistolarum, ubi de abrogatione legis disputatur: item exijs, quæ mox eadem de re subijciuntur, liquet per sacerdotium cõsummationem neq; quam esse.
units.tr: The Jews eagerly contended that perfection lay in the law and was to be obtained through the law. Moreover, since the law itself was taught and administered through the priests, and since the priesthood stood out above all the other parts of the law, together with the ceremonies, sacrifices, purifications and everything attached to them, any perfection that could come from the whole law ought surely to have been credited to the priesthood. But since no perfection lies in any part of the law, as is clear from other passages of these letters where the abrogation of the law is discussed, and from what is set out immediately below on the same subject, it is plain that perfection is in no way achieved through the priesthood.

units.la: Altera interpretatio itidem per se manifesta est, sacerdotiū & ceremonialia sunt quodammodo correlatiua, quæ semper simul esse necessum est. Huc pertinent illa Deuteronomij decimoseptimo, ubi iubentur in omnibus dubijs causis adire sacerdotes, qui indicabunt iudicij veritatem, quorumq; sententiam sequi oportebit. Et qui superbierit, nolens obedire sacerdotis imperio, qui eo tempore ministrat, ex decreto iudicis morietur homo ille. Deuteron.21. è verbo eorum omne negocium pendére dicitur. Nehemiæ 7. Dixit eis Thirsatha, ne manducarent de sanctitate sanctitatum, donec consurgeret sacerdos, qui portaret Vrim & Thummim. Vbi Hieronymus respiciens ad sensum vertit, doctus & eruditus: sed de ijsdem vocibus ita legitur Exodi 28. Pones quoq; in pectorali iudicij Vrim & Thummim, eruntq; super cor Aaronis, cùm ingreditur coram Domino, & gestabit Aaron iudicium filiorum Israel super cor suum iugiter coram Domino. Vrim claritatem & illustrationem significat: Thummim, innocentiam & integritatem. Hieronymus vertit prius in rationali iudicij doctrinâ & veritatem, id est, τὼ δηλωσιν, καὶ τὼ ἀληθειαν, manifestationem. Vbi septuaginta habent, καὶ ὠπθειαν ὠὴ τὲ λόγιον τὴ ἠσιωτ.
units.tr: The second explanation is equally clear in itself: the priesthood and the ceremonial laws are in a sense correlatives, which must always exist together. To this belong those words of Deuteronomy 17, where in all doubtful cases people are commanded to go to the priests, who will declare the truth of the judgment, and whose sentence they must follow. "And the man who acts presumptuously, refusing to obey the priest who ministers at that time, or the judge's decree, shall die" (Deut. 21). Everything is said to hang upon their word. Nehemiah 7: "Tirshatha said to them that they should not eat of the most holy things until a priest stood up who had the Urim and Thummim." Here Jerome, attending to the sense, translated "learned and erudite." But the same words are read in Exodus 28: "You shall put in the breastpiece of judgment the Urim and Thummim, and they shall be upon Aaron's heart when he goes in before the Lord, and Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart continually before the Lord." Urim signifies clearness and illumination; Thummim, innocence and integrity. Jerome first renders in the breastpiece of judgment "doctrine and truth," that is, [δήλωσιν καὶ ἀλήθειαν] manifestation and truth. Where the Seventy have [λόγιον τῆς κρίσεως] the oracle of judgment...

units.la: Esaias capite 18. contra sacerdotes grauiter concionatur, propter ignorantiam, & quòd docere alios non possent. Quem docebit, inquit, scientiam, & quem intelligere faciet iudicium? Apud eundem ipsi sacerdotes licet impij ita dicunt capite decimooctauo: Non peribit lex à sacerdote, neq; consilium à sapiente, nec sermo à propheta.
units.tr: Isaiah in chapter 18 preaches sternly against the priests, because of their ignorance and because they could not teach others. "Whom," he says, "will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make to understand the message?" In the same book, in chapter 28, the priests themselves, though wicked, speak thus: "The law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet."

units.la: Sed Ezechielis 7. Dominus comminatur, quòd Lex peribit à sacerdote, & consilium à Senioribus. Oseæ quarto, Quia tu scientiam repulisti, expellam te, ne sacerdotio fungaris mihi. Malachiæ secundo, Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem requirent ex ore eius, quia angelus Domini exercituum est. Ex his inquam locis satis liquet, quomodo, si perfectio aliqua ex lege erat habenda, ea sacerdotio, per quod lex doceri debebat, accepta ferri debuisset.
units.tr: But in Ezekiel 7 the Lord threatens that the law shall perish from the priest and counsel from the elders. In Hosea 4: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest to me." In Malachi 2: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and men shall seek the law at his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts." From these passages it is quite clear enough how, if any perfection was to be had from the law, it ought to have been credited to the priesthood, through which the law was to be taught.

units.la: Quandoquidem translato sacerdotio, necesse est, ut legis quoq; translatio fiat) Prudenter, ut in hac illatione, dicit per τεπείνωσιν siue μείωσιν, transferri potius sacerdotium & legem, seu, μετά- eius fieri, quàm simpliciter abrogari vel euerti. Hoc enim pacto æquiores reddit Hebræorum animos, qui forte ægrius tulissent, si protinus aperte diceretur, sacerdotium ac legem abrogatam. Etiam Apostolus mox idem clarè exprimit, dicens, abrogari, seu ἀθέτησις ιμ fieri prioris præcepti. Atque est reuera multò aptisima loquendi forma, qua sacerdotium siue lex transponi dicitur.
units.tr: "Since, when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that the law also be transferred." Wisely, as in this inference, he says that the priesthood and the law are rather transferred by [ταπείνωσιν] humbling or [μείωσιν] diminution, or made into a [μετάθεσιν] transposition, than simply abrogated or overturned. For in this way he makes the minds of the Hebrews more favourable, who might perhaps have borne it with more difficulty if it had been openly said at once that the priesthood and the law were abolished. The Apostle also soon expresses the same thing clearly, saying that there is an [ἀθέτησις] annulment of the former commandment. And indeed this is by far the most apt way of speaking, in which the priesthood or the law is said to be transposed.

units.la: Neque enim simpliciter sacerdotium in totum abrogatur: opus est siquidem, sacerdotium aliquod semper superesse, sed ablata est ea dignitas à tribu Leui, & collata alteri multo præstantiori, magisq; idoneo, videlicet Christo, qui possit perfectionem & salute hominum perficere.
units.tr: For the priesthood is not simply abrogated altogether. There must indeed always remain some priesthood, but that dignity has been taken from the tribe of Levi and conferred upon another, far more excellent and more suitable, namely Christ, who is able to bring to completion the perfection and salvation of men.

units.la: Similitea Similiter lex non simpliciter abrogata est, imò manet: debent enim præcepta bene viuendi semper extare, quibus externa vita, & inprimis homines rudes, instituantur accu-bernentur. sed translata est, ita ut, quæ Moßis Lex dicta fuerat, dicatur Lex Spiritus, & quæ perfectionem non afferebat, & per se inutilis erat, iam demonstratum est, quomodo ui-lis esse queat, & unde perfectio peti debeat. Pædagogus esse definit, tamen doctrina, quærudi & puerili ætate per eam accepimus, debet retineri. Sed, quomodo intelligendum, quòd Lex sit abrogata, mox plenius ostendemus. Interea vocabulo Legis, tamen si in parenthesi præcedenti accipi queat de vniuersa lege, quæ per sacerdotes doceri debebat etiam si non tota ad sacerdotium pertineret, propter iudicialia: tamen in hac illatione intelligimus ritus, sacrificia, obseruationes veltium, temporum, ciborum, genera purificationum, & quicquid est huiusmodi ceremonialium nomine comprehensum. Quæ reuera coniuncta sunt sacerdotio, & quodam relationis modo necessario cohærent, ut simul cum sacerdotio, vel maneant in honore, vel intercidant. Ac pro his conseruandis, nec no pas-sim apud gentes introducendis Iudæi vbiq; laborabant, addentes tandem & hoc, quòd ab his consummationem seu perfectionem expectari oporteret. De horu igitur ceremonialium præceptorum abrogatione Apostolus hic potissimum disputat, non de abroga-tione totius Legis, uti in epistola ad Galatas & Romanos. Actor. 15. seditio exorta describitur propter eos, qui descendentes à Iudæa docebant fratres, Nisi circucidamini secundum morem Moisis, non potestis esse saluì Galat. 3.
