Dies obseruatis & meses, & tempora, & annos, metuo de vobis, ne frustrà laborauerim. Colos 2. Ne quis vos iudicet in cibo aut potu, aut in parte diei festi, aut nouilunij, aut sabbatorum, quæ sunt vmbra rerum futurarum. De his mox copiosius. Porrò illis verbis, opus fuit exoriri alium sacerdotem, egregie aperitur, quantum sit legis & Euangelij discrimen, quemadmodum in explicatione partium admonuimus, neque opus est nos copiosius hic ea de re agere.
units.tr: Similarly the law has not been simply abrogated; rather it remains. For precepts of living well must always stand, by which the outward life, and above all rude people, are trained and brought up. But it has been transferred, so that what was called the Law of Moses is now called the Law of the Spirit; and that which did not bring perfection, and was in itself useless, has already been shown how it can be useless, and whence perfection must be sought. It has ceased to be our schoolmaster, yet the teaching we received through it in our rude and childish age ought to be retained. But how the law is to be understood as abrogated we shall show more fully below. Meanwhile, by the word "law," although in the preceding parenthesis it could be taken of the whole law, which was to be taught through the priests (even though not all of it pertained to the priesthood, on account of the judicial laws), in this inference we understand the rites, sacrifices, observances of garments, times, foods, kinds of purification, and whatever is comprehended under the name of ceremonial matters. These are indeed joined to the priesthood and cohere with it by a kind of necessary relation, so that together with the priesthood they either remain in honour or perish. And in defending these, and in introducing them everywhere among the nations, the Jews laboured on every side, adding finally that perfection and completion were to be expected from them. Therefore the Apostle here chiefly disputes about the abrogation of these ceremonial precepts, not about the abrogation of the whole law, as in the letters to the Galatians and Romans. Acts 15 describes the uproar that arose over those who came down from Judea and taught the brothers: "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." Galatians 3: "You observe days and months, and times, and years; I fear for you, lest I have laboured in vain for you." Colossians 2: "Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival day, or a new moon, or sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come." Of these things more fully soon. Moreover, by those words, "there was need for another priest to arise," it is excellently made plain how great the difference is between the law and the Gospel, as we pointed out in the explanation of the parts; and there is no need for us to treat this matter at greater length here.

units.la: Iam si quis roger, cur nos in illatione hac dicamus, nomine Legis intelligendum esse eam legis partem, quæ ceremonialia complectitur, & non vniuersam legem, cum tamen in epistolis ad Romanos & ad Galatas, ubi de abrogatione legis agitur, definiri soleat, abrogari totam legem? Huic breuiter respondebimus: Et certè mirari aliquis posset, quomodo conueniant hæc, ut, cum tot locis disputetur de abrogatione legis, alibi dicatur, agi de abrogatione legis totius, alibi verò tantum de abrogatione partis ceremonialis. Vt interim non dicamus, multos & magnos viros etiam in epistola ad Romanos & Galatas eximaffe tantum de abrogatione ceremonialis partis sentire Apostolum.
units.tr: Now if someone asks why we say in this inference that by the name of Law is to be understood that part of the law which comprises the ceremonial matters, and not the whole law, since in the letters to the Romans and Galatians, where the abrogation of the law is treated, it is usually defined that the whole law is abrogated, we shall answer briefly. Indeed someone might well wonder how these things agree: that, while the abrogation of the law is discussed in so many places, it is said elsewhere that the abrogation of the whole law is in view, and elsewhere only the abrogation of the ceremonial part. Not to mention that many great men have thought that even in the letters to the Romans and Galatians the Apostle meant only the abrogation of the ceremonial part.

units.la: Sciendum igitur, duplicem motā esse per Iudæos de lege in primitiua ecclesia disputationem. Prior erat, qua contendebant, quòd etiamsi per Euangelium annunciaretur iustitia per Christum, nihilominus legem adhuc esse obseruandam. Et ad hanc sententiam confirmandam multa habebant valida in speciem argumenta.
units.tr: It must therefore be understood that a twofold dispute about the law was stirred up by the Jews in the primitive Church. The first was that, even if justification through Christ were proclaimed by the Gospel, nevertheless the law was still to be observed. To confirm this opinion they had many arguments that were strong in appearance.

units.la: Primum, quòd tota Lex à Deo ipso erat instituta, & propterea nequaquam contemnenda. Præterea sancta erat, utilis multis nominibus ac necessaria.
units.tr: First, that the whole law had been instituted by God himself, and therefore was by no means to be despised. Moreover it was holy, useful in many respects, and necessary.

units.la: Adhæc Deum non mutare sententiam, ut modò irritum facere velit, quod anteà seue-rissime præceperit.
units.tr: In addition, that God does not change his mind, so as now to wish to make void what he had most strictly commanded before.

units.la: Ac de moralibus præceptis nemo non lubenter consentiebat, quando etiam Gentiles ea semper venerati sunt & studiosè conseruarunt.
units.tr: And nearly everyone gladly agreed about the moral precepts, since even the Gentiles had always revered them and carefully preserved them.

units.la: De iudicialibus insuper non erat admodum magna controuersia. Nam hæc è moralibus fiuunt. Tum quæ Lex docet punienda esse crimina, eadem gentiles quoq; censuerunt, licet non eodem pœnæ genere, vindicanda.
units.tr: Concerning the judicial laws there was not very great controversy, for these flow from the moral ones. Moreover, the Gentiles too judged that the crimes which the law teaches ought to be punished, although not with the same kind of penalty.

units.la: Ceremonialia deinde, pulcherrima legis pars, eò iustius credebantur retinenda, quòd splendida admodum erant, & mouendis animis hominum, in ijs quæ ad cultum pertinent, mirè idonea. Item propriæ notæ, quibus potissimum discreti sunt Iudæi à cæteris nationibus.
units.tr: The ceremonial laws, the most beautiful part of the Law, were believed to be all the more rightly kept because they were very splendid and wonderfully suited to stirring people's minds in matters of worship. They were also distinctive marks by which the Jews were especially set apart from other nations.

units.la: Præterea quasi remedia & medicamenta aduersus quædam peccata constituta. Deniq; eiusmodi, ut eorum omissione Deus videretur grauiter offendendus. Postremò, sine tumultibus hæc non posse omitti vel mutari. Quare, sicut moralia, ita & ceremonialia, vel maximè debere obseruari. Quomodo videmus etiámnum hodie plerosq; sic sentire, quasi nemini hominum traditas ceremonias citra tumultus periculum liceat immutare, earumq; pugnatores varia & probabilia in speciem argumenta producere.
units.tr: Moreover, they were established as remedies and medicines, as it were, against certain sins. Finally, they were of such a kind that God would seem to be gravely offended by their omission. Lastly, they could not be omitted or changed without tumult. Therefore, just as the moral laws, so also the ceremonial laws were especially to be observed. We see even today that many people think in this way, as though no one were permitted to change ceremonies handed down by men without the danger of tumult, and their defenders bring forward various plausible-looking arguments.

units.la: Altera disputatione aliquid amplius contendebant, nimirum non tantum debere simpliciter obseruari legem, & inprimis ceremonias: sed ita quoq;, ut per has iustitia coram Deo pararetur, & sine his iustitia siue salus minimè foret expectanda, sicut licet videre. promissiones insignes propositas esse ijs, qui legem seruarent: nec alios promissionum illarum fore participes, quàm qui legem diligeter fecerint. Difficultas & labor in implen- da lege mercedem amplíssimam promeretur. Legem videri proprie in hoc datam, vt eius obseruatione homines vitam & omnia bona acquirant: & alia, cuiusmodi plura possent ex epistolis ad Romanos, & ad Galatas colligi. Proinde, sicut duæ distinctæ fuerût disputationes pro legis dignitate conseruanda, ita Apostoli coacti sunt duobus modis de legis abrogatione agere. Quantum ergo ad primam disputationem attinet, definierunt Apostoli, Moralia quidem, & partim Iudicialia, quatenus sine eis officia fidei in Deum, & charitatis in proximũ præstari non possunt, esse obseruanda: non quidem prorsus, quia à Mose præscribuntur, vel eo in vniuersum modo, quo sunt præcepta: sed quia tũ natura ipsa approbat, ac facienda dictat, tùm spiritus Sanctus ad perficiendum opera fidei & charitatis ea suggerit. Itaque hic non totam legem abrogatã, sed ceremonialia tantùm: reliquorum magnam partem manere in sua dignitate. Vnde Galat. 3 & Coloss. 2. obseruationem ciborum, dierum, &c. prorsus damnat: & tamen secunda parte principali, vbi agit de doctrina operum, subijcit & vrget præcepta moralia, id est, officia charitatis. Mouebantur autem grauibus rationibus Apostoli, cur ita definirent: è quibus hæc vna erat, Actorum decimoquinto Gentes potius erant reiiciendæ in vniuersum doctrinam euangelicã, quàm vt se circumcidi paterentur, & aliis deinde molestissimis ceremonijs, vt obseruatione ciborum, &c. obstringi. Itaque importabili iugo legis gentes nullo pacto fuisse onerandas. Altera ratio erat, quòd ceremoniæ, vt habetur Colossens 2. tantùm erant vmbræ rerum futurarum: quare præsentibus rebus ipsis, quas illæ præsignabant, debere facesceri. Possunt aliæ rationes addi, veluti diuinum cultum in rebus illis externis nequaquam esse situm, sed Deum velle nunc in spiritu & veritate coli. Debere nos offerre Deo corpora nostra bonasque actiones, non hircos aut vitulos: non coinquinari homines per id, quod intrat in os, &c. Item, prophetas sæpè vaticinatos, sacrificia, & id genus, cessatura. Quas rationes Christus & Apostoli diuersis in locis exponũt. Atq; hoc pacto etiam in hac epistola ad Hebræos de abrogatione legis disputatur, non quidem vniuersę, sed potissimum Ceremonialium. Hinc est, quòd ad probandam abrogationem ceremoniarum, sacrificiorum, & omnium eò pertinentium, asserit sacerdotium Christi, quod per sacerdotium legale fuerit adumbratum, & omnia quæ in lege facta sunt per sacerdotes, nihil aliud quàm typos fuisse eorum, quæ per Christum debebant perfici, & nunc verè perfecta sunt. Huc tendũt omnia, quæ pluribus capitibus hic disputatur: & sæpius inculcatur, vetera omnia typum & vmbram fuisse tan tùm rerum euangelicarum, sicut in sequentibus plenius declarabimus. Et sunt distinguendæ hæ disputationes, sicut Apostolus quoque eas hic distinguit. De iustificatione autem per fidem etiam absq; operibus, seorsum postea disputationem instituit, hic contentus agere contra eos, qui sacerdotium & ceremonias legis retinendas esse pertinacissimè contendebant: qua de re certè acres controuersiæ in primatiua ecclesia sunt habitæ, & Iudæi grauissimè commouebantur hac assertione de abrogato sacerdotio & ceremonijs, in quibus gloriam suam præcipuam sitam esse existimabát & iactabant.
units.tr: In the second dispute they contended for something more: namely, that the Law should not only be observed simply, and especially the ceremonies, but also that righteousness before God should be obtained through them, and that without them righteousness or salvation was by no means to be expected. As can be seen, notable promises are set before those who keep the Law, and none shall share in those promises except those who have carefully done the Law. Difficulty and labour in fulfilling the Law earn the greatest reward. The Law seems to have been given properly for this purpose, that by its observance men may acquire life and all good things; and other such arguments could be gathered from the epistles to the Romans and to the Galatians. Accordingly, just as there were two distinct disputes in defence of the dignity of the Law, so the Apostles were compelled to treat the abrogation of the Law in two ways. As far as the first dispute is concerned, the Apostles determined that the moral laws, and partly the judicial laws, are to be observed insofar as without them the duties of faith toward God and of charity toward neighbour cannot be performed. Not indeed altogether because they are prescribed by Moses, or in the general manner in which they are commanded, but because nature itself approves them and dictates that they be done, and because the Holy Spirit suggests them for the performance of the works of faith and charity. Thus here the whole Law is not abrogated, but only the ceremonial laws; and a great part of the rest remains in its dignity. Hence in Galatians 3 and Colossians 2 he utterly condemns the observance of foods, days, etc.; and yet in the second principal part, where he treats the teaching on works, he also adds and urges the moral precepts, that is, the duties of charity. The Apostles were moved by weighty reasons to define things this way, and one of these was that in Acts 15 the Gentiles were rather to be rejected altogether from the evangelical doctrine than to suffer themselves to be circumcised and then bound by other most burdensome ceremonies, such as the observance of foods, etc. Therefore the Gentiles were in no way to be burdened with the intolerable yoke of the Law. Another reason was that the ceremonies, as is said in Colossians 2, were only shadows of things to come; therefore, now that the realities which they foreshadowed are present, they ought to cease. Other reasons may be added: that divine worship is by no means located in those external things, but God now wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth; that we ought to offer God our bodies and good actions, not goats or calves; that men are not defiled by what enters the mouth, etc.; and likewise that the prophets often prophesied that sacrifices and such things would cease. Christ and the Apostles set out these reasons in various places. And in this way the Epistle to the Hebrews also disputes about the abrogation of the Law, not of the whole Law, but chiefly of the ceremonial part. Hence it is that, to prove the abrogation of the ceremonies, sacrifices, and everything pertaining to them, he asserts the priesthood of Christ, which was foreshadowed through the Levitical priesthood, and that all the things done in the Law through the priests were nothing other than types of those things which were to be accomplished through Christ, and which have now truly been accomplished. All that is argued in many chapters here tends to this end, and it is often impressed that all the ancient things were only types and shadows of evangelical realities, as we shall declare more fully in what follows. And these disputes ought to be distinguished, as the Apostle himself also distinguishes them here. But the disputation concerning justification by faith even apart from works he later undertook separately, here being content to argue against those who most stubbornly contended that the priesthood and the ceremonies of the Law were to be retained. Certainly sharp controversies were held concerning this in the primitive Church, and the Jews were most gravely disturbed by this assertion about the abrogated priesthood and ceremonies, in which they thought and boasted that their chief glory lay.

units.la: Quod ad secundam disputationem attinet, qua contendebatur, ex lege parandam iustitiam coram Deo, hìc definierunt Apostoli, legem in vniuersum abrogatam, id est, non habere locum in caussa iustificationis, quæ contingit per solam fidem absque operibus legis. Neque ceremonialia præcepta, neque moralia, neque alia quæcunq; momentum ullum habere, vt quis iustus reputetur coram Deo: sed tantùm fidem in Christum reputari ad iustitiam, & iustos pronunciari credentes propter Christum, non propter propriã dignitatem, vel obseruationem legis: id quod pluribus & grauibus argumentis docetur Roman 4. & Galat. 3. Non quidem, quòd ita accipiendum sit, legem vniuersam abrogari, quasi non amplius debeant per nos fieri, quæ de officijs fidei in Deum, & charitatis in proximum, in lege præscribuntur: quis hoc velit, cùm Christus apertè dicat, Non veni soluere legem, sed adimplere? Et Apostolus Roman. 3. legem per fidem abolemus? Absit: imò legem stabilimus: sed quòd ea, quando non plenè per nos præstatur, non habeat tamen potestatem condemnandi: nec sumus propter eam obnoxij execrationi: sicut non habet potestatem iustificandi, etiamsi tota seruaretur: (cùm interim seruari totam, vti par est, impossibile sit, quod Romanor. 2. & 3. item 8. docetur, & Actor. 15. Petrus fatetur) ita nec habet potestatem condemnandi, etiamsi fuerit omissa. Huc pertinet illud Roman. 6. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur: Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Roman. 8. Nulla igitur nunc est condemnatio his, qui insiti sunt in Christo Iesu, qui non iuxta carnem versantur, sed secundum spiritum. Nam lex spiritus vitæ per Christum Iesum liberum me reddidit à iure peccati & mortis: & quæ ibi sequuntur. Gallat 3. Christus nos redemit ab execratio-
units.tr: As for the second dispute, in which it was contended that righteousness before God was to be obtained from the Law, here the Apostles determined that the Law was abrogated in general, that is, that it has no place in the cause of justification, which comes through faith alone apart from the works of the Law. Neither the ceremonial precepts, nor the moral, nor any others whatever have any weight in making a man be reckoned righteous before God; but faith alone in Christ is reckoned for righteousness, and believers are pronounced righteous on account of Christ, not on account of their own worth or the observance of the Law. This is taught by many weighty arguments in Romans 4 and Galatians 3. Yet this does not mean that the whole Law is to be taken as abrogated, as if the things which the Law prescribes concerning the duties of faith toward God and charity toward neighbour should no longer be done by us. Who would hold this, since Christ plainly says: "I came not to destroy the Law, but to fulfil it"? And does the Apostle in Romans 3 say: "Do we then make void the Law through faith? God forbid; yea, we establish the Law"? Rather, the Law is confirmed; but insofar as it is not fully performed by us, it nevertheless does not have the power to condemn, nor are we liable to its curse on account of it. Just as it does not have the power to justify even if it were kept in full (since it is impossible for it to be kept entirely, as is taught in Romans 2, 3 and 8, and as Peter confesses in Acts 15), so it does not have the power to condemn even if it has been left undone. To this pertains what is said in Romans 6: "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the Law but under grace." Romans 8: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit; for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death," and what follows there. Galatians 3: "Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us."

units.la: D execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus execratio. Itaq;, ut elegater ait Augustinus,nō,nē fiat, abrogata eit lex,sed ne nos condemnet. Nam magnum & necessarium esse, & manere vsum legis, Apostolus ipse scribens ad Romanos & Galatas explicat.Roman.5. Lex subijt, ut abundaret delictum.Roman.7. Per legem cognitio peccati. Ibidem, Lex sancta & praeceptum sanctum, ac iustum, & bonum. Galat. 3. Lex propter transgresiones additafuit. Ibidem: Lex paedagogus noster fuit ad Christum.Et capite quinto: Vos in libertatem vocati fuistis fratres, tantum ne libertatem in occasionem detis carni, sed per charitatem servite vobis inuicem. Nam tota lex in vno verbo completur, nempe hoc, Diliges proximum tuum ut teipsum: quibus locis, quis sit vsus legis, indicat: & etiamsi non faciat ad iustitiā coram Deo, non tamen frustra datam: praeterea manere legem, & seruanda, quantum ad officia attinet charitatis.
units.tr: Therefore, as Augustine elegantly says, the Law was not abrogated so that it might not happen, but so that it might not condemn us. For that the use of the Law is great and necessary, and remains, the Apostle himself explains when writing to the Romans and Galatians. Romans 5: "The Law entered that the offence might abound." Romans 7: "Through the Law comes the knowledge of sin." In the same place: "The Law is holy, and the commandment holy, just and good." Galatians 3: "The Law was added because of transgressions." In the same place: "The Law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ." And in chapter 5: "You, brethren, have been called to liberty; only do not use liberty as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole Law is fulfilled in one word, namely this: You shall love your neighbour as yourself." These passages show what the use of the Law is; and even if it does not contribute to righteousness before God, it was not given in vain; moreover, the Law remains, and is to be kept as far as the duties of charity are concerned.

units.la: Adhaec dicitur alia ratione tota lex abrogata, quod videlicet ij, qui iam per fidem in Christum iusti sunt, & spiritu Dei aguntur, opera legis faciant, non quia lex praecipit, sed quia spiritus ipsos impellit & incitat: & talia opera potius opera spiritus, quā legis opera sunt dicenda. Huc pertinet illud 1.Timoth. 1. Iustis nō est lex posita. Rom.8. Lex spiritus vitae per Christum Iesum liberum me reddidit à iure peccati & mortis. Ibidem: Quòd si spiritu facta carnis mortificaueritis, viuetis, &c. Ita namque qui habet spiritum Sanctum, habent legem in cordibus suis scriptam, nec amplius respiciunt in tabulas lapideas, siue in literā, quae sine spiritu occidit, non viuificat. Quibus autem spiritus hic non contingit, eos vilegis literae contineri in officio, vtile & necessarium est.
units.tr: Moreover, the whole law is said to be abrogated for another reason: those who are already righteous through faith in Christ and are led by the Spirit of God do the works of the law, not because the law commands them, but because the Spirit impels and urges them. Such works should rather be called works of the Spirit than works of the law. To this belongs 1 Timothy 1: "The law is not laid down for the righteous." Romans 8: "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death." And in the same place: "If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live," etc. For whoever has the Holy Spirit has the law written in his heart and no longer looks to the tables of stone or to the letter, which kills without the Spirit and does not give life. But for those to whom the Spirit does not come, it is useful and necessary that they be held in their duty by the letter of the law.

units.la: Haec opinor satis esse ad explicadum, de qualis legis abrogatione hic disputetur, quòdque distinguenda sit haec disputatio ab illis disputationibus, quę habetur de abrogatione legis in epistolis ad Romanos & Galatas.
units.tr: I think this is enough to explain what kind of abrogation of the law is under discussion here, and that this disputation must be distinguished from those disputations on the abrogation of the law which occur in the Epistles to the Romans and the Galatians.

units.la: Neque enim hic disputatur de iustificatione per legem, sed tantum contra ambitiosos & superstitiosos sacerdotij ac ceremoniarū propugnatores, num post annunciatū enangelium omnia legalia, & in his potissimum ceremonialia sint seruandi: de iustificatione autem, quòd ea per fidem sola contingat, propria disputatio paulò post instituetur. Caeterum causas ob quas debuit Lex hac in parte abrogari, in progressu ostendemus.
units.tr: For here it is not disputed about justification through the law, but only against the ambitious and superstitious defenders of the priesthood and of the ceremonies, namely whether, after the gospel has been proclaimed, all legal things, and among them especially the ceremonial things, are to be kept. Concerning justification, that it comes through faith alone, a separate disputation will be set up shortly. Meanwhile, we will show in the course of the argument the reasons why the Law had to be abrogated in this part.

units.la: Nam is, de quo dicuntur haec, ad aliam tribum pertinet, de qua nullus altari adstitit. Palàm est enim, quòd è tribu Iuda exortus sit Dominus noster. At nihil locutus est de sacerdotio Moses, quod ad hanc tribum pertineat.
units.tr: For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one has attended the altar. For it is plain that our Lord arose from the tribe of Judah. But Moses said nothing about priesthood pertaining to that tribe.

units.la: Confirmat, quod priori consequentia tacitè intulerat, videlicet, translatum esse sacerdotium: idque rectè à se dictū duabus euincit rationibus, non citra occupatione, ut mihi videtur, adiectis.
units.tr: He confirms what he had tacitly inferred in the preceding consequence, namely that the priesthood has been transferred. He proves this, rightly stated by himself, by two reasons, which, as it seems to me, are added not without purpose.

units.la: Credibile est, aduersarios obiecisse. Etsi Christus sit sacerdos, non tamen distinctum erit eius sacerdotium à sacerdotio legali seu Aaronico: sed potius communi atq; vhtato more ad istud referetur, atque ita sacerdotium minimè dicetur translatum.
units.tr: It is likely that the opponents objected: even if Christ is a priest, his priesthood will not be distinguished from the legal or Aaronic priesthood; rather it will be referred to it in the common and customary way, and so the priesthood will not be said to have been transferred at all.

units.la: Respondet Apostolus, id haud posse sic accipi, sed necessariò distinguendum sacerdotium Christi à legali seu Aaronico: quod duplici probat ratione: quarum prior est haec.
units.tr: The Apostle replies that this cannot be understood in that way, but the priesthood of Christ must necessarily be distinguished from the legal or Aaronic priesthood. He proves this by a double reason, of which the first is this:

units.la: Moses siue lex loquitur de sacerdotio, quòd tantùm pertinet ad tribum Leui.
units.tr: Moses, or the law, speaks of a priesthood which pertains only to the tribe of Levi.

units.la: Christus autem non erat de tribu Leui, sed de tribu Iuda, ex qua nulli solent ad sacerdotium admitti. Igitur sacerdotium Christi necessariò distinguedum est à sacerdotio Leuitico: & rectè à nobis dictum est per sacerdotium Christi translatum esse sacerdotium legale. Argumentum sumptum est à diuersitate tribuum sacerdotum legalium & Christi.
units.tr: But Christ was not of the tribe of Levi but of the tribe of Judah, from which no one is accustomed to be admitted to the priesthood. Therefore the priesthood of Christ must necessarily be distinguished from the Levitical priesthood, and it is rightly said by us that the legal priesthood has been transferred through the priesthood of Christ. The argument is taken from the difference between the tribes of the legal priests and of Christ.

units.la: Quod sacerdotium legale tātum ad tribum Leuiticam pertineat, diximus suprà verbis illis, Atque ij quidem, qui, quòd sunt de numero filiorum Leui, &c.
units.tr: That the legal priesthood pertains only to the Levitical tribe we said above in those words: "And those indeed who, because they are of the number of the sons of Levi," etc.

units.la: Hoc solum explicādum est nobis, quomodo Dominus sit ex tribu Iuda, de qua nullus vnquàm alteri ministrauit, seu ad sacerdotium admitti potuit.
units.tr: This only remains for us to explain: how the Lord is from the tribe of Judah, from which no one ever ministered at the altar or could be admitted to the priesthood.

units.la: Primùm verò liquet id ex vaticinijs aliquot de Christo ad patres factis, ut Genef. 49. Non auferetur sceptrum de tribu Iuda, donec veniat qui mittendus est, & ipse erit expectatio gentium, &c. Vbi patriarcha Iacob significauit, ex ea tribu huc Mesiam oriturū. Esaiae 65. Educam de Iacob semen, & de Iuda possidentem montes sanctos meos: & hereditate obtinebunt eam electi mei, & serui mei habitabant ibi. Hieremiae 23. Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, & suscitabo Dauid germen iustum, & regnabit rex, & sapiens erit, & faciet iudicium & iustitiā in terra. In diebus illis saluabitur Iuda, & Israel habitabit confidenter. Et hoc est nomen, quo vocabunt eum, Dominus iustus noster.
units.tr: First, indeed, this is clear from several prophecies about Christ made to the fathers, such as Genesis 49: "The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah until he comes who is to be sent, and he will be the expectation of the nations," etc. Here the patriarch Jacob signified that the Messiah would arise from that tribe. Isaiah 65: "I will bring forth a seed from Jacob, and from Judah one who will possess my holy mountains; my elect shall obtain it as an inheritance, and my servants shall dwell there." Jeremiah 23: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a king shall reign and be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the land. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely. And this is the name by which they will call him: The Lord our righteousness."

units.la: Prorsus similia habētur capite tricesimo tertio. Michaeę quinto. Et tu Bethlehē Ephrata paruulus es in millibus Iuda, ex te mihi egredietur, qui sit dominator in Israel, & egressus eius ab initio, à diebus æternitatis. Quod etiam citatur Matthæi secundo, ut ostendatur verè ex tribu Iuda et in terra Iuda natus. Huc etiam pertinet omnes promissiones, omnes item alij loci in nouo testamento, quibus describitur Christus filius Dauid secundū carnem quem Dauidem esse è tribu Iuda notissimū est. Vide Matthæi 1. Lucæ 1. Et Matthæi 1. item Lucæ 2. Iosephaccensetur domui & familiæ Dauid. Et ad Mariam dictū est Lucę 1. Ecce concipies in vtero, & paries filium: & vocabis nomen eius Iesum: Is erit magnus, & filius altissimi vocabitur: & dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem Dauid patris ipsius, &c. Roman. 1. Genitus fuit ex semine Dauid, secundum carnem. Et Esaiæ vndecimo, Egredietur virga de radice Iesse, & flos de radice eius ascendet, & requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, &c. Qui loci satis aperte euincunt, Beatam virginem, ex cuius semine carnem assumpsit Christus, ex familia Dauid ortam. Neque est, quod obijciatur, eam potius fuisse tribus Leui, & ex familia Aaronis, propterea quòd Lucæ primo, Elizabeth vxor Zachariæ sacerdotis, de filiabus Aaron cognata virginis appellatur.
units.tr: Quite similar things are found in chapter 33, and in Micah 5: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity." This is also cited in Matthew 2, to show that he was truly born of the tribe of Judah and in the land of Judah. To this pertain also all the promises, and all the other passages in the New Testament, in which Christ is described as the son of David according to the flesh; that David was of the tribe of Judah is very well known. See Matthew 1 and Luke 1; and again Matthew 1 and Luke 2: Joseph is reckoned to the house and family of David. And to Mary it was said, Luke 1: "Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father," etc. Romans 1: "He was born of the seed of David according to the flesh." And Isaiah 11: "A shoot will come forth from the stem of Jesse, and a flower will grow from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him," etc. These passages sufficiently clearly prove that the blessed Virgin, from whose seed Christ took flesh, was descended from the family of David. Nor is there any force in the objection that she was rather of the tribe of Levi and of the family of Aaron, because in Luke 1 Elizabeth, the wife of the priest Zechariah, is called a kinswoman of the Virgin, "of the daughters of Aaron."

units.la: Sciendum enim in veteri lege, viros sæpè duxisse vxores ex alia tribu, quàm sua: quomodo Dauid ex tribu Iuda duxit filiam Saul, qui erat ex tribu Beniamin. Et sacerdotes tribus Leuiticæ memorantur duxisse vxores ex tribu Iuda, quæ similiter erat tribus excelletissima: quomodo Exodi sexto, Aaron duxit filiam Aminadab, sororem Naason, qui fuit dux in tribu Iuda. Et 2. Paralipom. 22. Ioiada sacerdos habuit vxorem Iosabeth filiam regis Ioram.
units.tr: For it must be understood that in the old law men often took wives from a tribe other than their own, as David, of the tribe of Judah, took the daughter of Saul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin. And priests of the Levitical tribe are recorded to have taken wives from the tribe of Judah, which was likewise a most distinguished tribe; as in Exodus 6, Aaron took the daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon, who was leader in the tribe of Judah. And 2 Chronicles 22: the priest Jehoiada had as his wife Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram.

units.la: Itaque ut Augustinus habet libro quæstionum, veteris testamenti septimo in librum Iudicum, verosimile est, aliquam ex tribu Leui nupsisse cuipiā in tribu Iuda, vnde cognatio istainter Mariā tribus Iuda, & Elizabeth tribus Leui prouenerit: vel, ut alij opinatur, quampiam è tribu Iuda nupsisse viro Leuiticæ tribus.
units.tr: Therefore, as Augustine has it in his Questions on the Old Testament, book seven, on the Book of Judges, it is likely that some woman of the tribe of Levi married a man of the tribe of Judah, and from this the kinship between Mary of the tribe of Judah and Elizabeth of the tribe of Levi arose; or, as others suppose, that some woman of the tribe of Judah married a man of the Levitical tribe.

units.la: Voluit interea spiritus Sanctus, obiter per euangelistam indicari hanc cognationem Mariæ tribus Dauid cum Elizabeth, quæ erat tribus Leuiticæ, ut, quemadmodum ibidem refert Augustinus, Domini caro non solum de regia, sed etiam de sacerdotali stirpe progeneraretur: quandoquidem ipse & rex & sacerdos agnoscì debuit: sicut Melchisedech quoque typus Christi pariter regia & sacerdotali dignitate fuit insignitus.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Holy Spirit willed, by way of the evangelist, to indicate in passing this kinship of Mary of the tribe of David with Elizabeth, who was of the Levitical tribe, so that, as Augustine there reports, the Lord's flesh would be born not only of the royal but also of the priestly stock; since he ought to be acknowledged both king and priest, just as Melchizedek, a type of Christ, was likewise marked with both royal and priestly dignity.

units.la: Itaq; Christum de tribu Iuda esse, siue matrem respiciamus (quam reuera primo loco respici decet, quandoquidem ex eius semine carnem contraxit, siue putatiuum patrem Iosephum, certum est.
units.tr: Thus it is certain that Christ is of the tribe of Judah, whether we look to his mother (whom indeed it is fitting to look to first, since from her seed he took his flesh) or to his putative father Joseph.

units.la: Vnde eleganter Chrysostomus, Translatum est, inquit, sacerdotium, non ordine tantum, neque præceptis, sed etiam tribu. Oportebat enim & tribum mutari. Et quomodo translatum est sacerdotium ex tribu in tribum? De sacerdotali ad regalem, ut eadem ipsa tribus sit & regalis & sacerdotalis. Intuere mysterium.
units.tr: Hence Chrysostom elegantly says: "The priesthood has been transferred, not only in order and precepts, but also in tribe. For the tribe too had to be changed. And how has the priesthood been transferred from tribe to tribe? From priestly to royal, so that the same tribe is both royal and priestly. Consider the mystery."

units.la: Primò fuit regalis, postea facta est sacerdotalis: sic etiā in Christo, rex quippe erat semper, sacerdos autem factus est, quando carnem suscepit, quando sacrificium obtulit.
units.tr: At first it was royal; afterwards it was made priestly. So also in Christ: he was always king, but became priest when he assumed flesh and when he offered the sacrifice.

units.la: Cæterum ex hac tribu Iuda quòd nunquam aliquis altari astitit, hoc est, in sacris ministra uit (Metonymia est in ea locutione) satis notum est, tum ex eo, quòd sola tribus Leuitica ius & honorem obtinuit: tum, quòd ius illud non legitur violatum: nisi quòd semel contra fas, & cunctis reluctantibus rex Ozias (qui erat è tribu Iuda) tentauit adolere in censum: sed is statim lepra percussus, temeritatis poenas dedit, 1. Paralipom. 26. Adeò in digne fert Deus, si quispiam diuersum à sua vocatione aggrediatur, & alienum ministerium inuadat, seu interturbet. Vtinam hodie hac parte non nimium peccaretur.
units.tr: Moreover, that no one ever stood at the altar from this tribe of Judah, that is, ministered in sacred office (a metonymy in that expression), is well enough known. This is clear both from the fact that the Levitical tribe alone held the right and the honour, and from the fact that this right is not read of as having been violated, except that once, against divine law and with everyone resisting, King Uzziah (who was of the tribe of Judah) tried to offer incense. But he was at once struck with leprosy and paid the penalty of his rashness (1 Chronicles 26). So greatly does God take it amiss if anyone undertakes what is contrary to his calling and invades or disturbs a ministry that is not his own. Would that today there were not so much sinning in this respect.

units.la: Sed est, quod adijciamus, quòd per Iudæos contra argumentum Apostoli posset obijci videlicet, etiamsi Christus factus sit sacerdos, atque etiam ex altera tribu, non propterea sequi, quòd translatum sit sacerdotium.
units.tr: But there is something we should add: the Jews could object against the Apostle's argument that, even if Christ was made a priest and that from another tribe, it does not follow that the priesthood has been transferred.

units.la: Nam 1. Samuel. 3. scribitur, quòd Samuel constitutus sit in locum Heli, simul, ut Augustinus habet libro de ciuitate Dei 18. cap. 4. sacerdotis & Iudicis fungens munere. Aciudi caseeum aperte ibi dicitur.
units.tr: For in 1 Samuel 3 it is written that Samuel was appointed in the place of Eli, and at the same time, as Augustine has it in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 4, he discharged the office of priest and judge. That this is plainly said there.

units.la: Sacerdotio functum, videtur inde colligi, quòd orauerit pro populo, & sacrificium obtulerit, 1. Samuel. 7 Item, quòd reges Saulem & Dauidem vnxerit: & præterea, quod ad Heli dictum fuit de Samuele, Suscitabo mihi sacerdotem fidelem.
units.tr: That he exercised the priesthood seems to be gathered from the fact that he prayed for the people and offered sacrifice (1 Samuel 7); likewise from the fact that he anointed the kings Saul and David; and besides, from what was said to Eli about Samuel: "I will raise up for myself a faithful priest."

units.la: Vnde etiam in psalmo nonagesimo octauo, Moses & Aaron in sacerdotibus eius, & Samuel inter eos, qui inuocant nomen eius. Nec tamen propterea dictum fuit translatum sacerdotium.
units.tr: Hence also in Psalm 99 (98): "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name." Yet it was not said for that reason that the priesthood had been transferred.

units.la: Respondetur: Non esse simile. Nam Samuel non fuit alterius tribus, quàm Leuiticæ, licet verum sit, quòd non fuerit ex familia Aaronis, neque filius sacerdotis. Numeratur enim pater Samuelis 1. Paralipom. 6. in tribu Leui, mater verò de tribu Iuda. Nec pater Samuelis fuerat sacerdos; Mos autem tunc erat, filios succedere patribus. Itaque in hac tantùm parte intelligitur tunc translatum fuisse sacerdotium, videlicet non ad aliam tribum, sed tantùm ad aliam familiam: id quod clarius indicat idem Augustinus libro secundo retractationum. Potest & hoc addi, vaticinum de sacerdotio Christi, quod hic citatur, editum esse per Spiritum sanctū postillam translationem sacerdotij ab Heli ad Samuelem.
units.tr: The answer is that the cases are not alike. For Samuel was not of any tribe other than the Levitical, although it is true that he was not of the family of Aaron nor a son of a priest. For Samuel's father is counted in the tribe of Levi (1 Chronicles 6), but his mother was from the tribe of Judah. Nor was Samuel's father a priest; and the custom then was for sons to succeed their fathers. So the priesthood was then transferred only in this respect, namely not to another tribe but only to another family, which Augustine himself indicates more clearly in book 2 of his Retractations. This may also be added: the prophecy about the priesthood of Christ, which is cited here, was given by the Holy Spirit as a foreshadowing of the transfer of the priesthood from Eli to Samuel.

units.la: Hoc nihilominus obseruandū, ibi verbis prophetæ ad Heli de substitutione Samuelis vaticinium habitum, & typum sacerdotij à Iudæis transferendi: quod Augustinus clarissimè docet lib. de ciuitate Dei 18. cap. 4. sicut & in reiectione Saulis & electione Dauid typus reijciendi regni temporalis, & erigendi spiritualis.
units.tr: Nevertheless this must be observed: in those words of the prophet to Eli about the substitution of Samuel, a prophecy was given, and a type of the priesthood being transferred from the Jews. Augustine teaches this very clearly in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 4, just as in the rejection of Saul and the election of David there was a type of the rejection of the temporal kingdom and the raising up of the spiritual.

units.la: Atq; hinc consolatio non mediocris ad gentiles prouenit, quòd videlicet ipsi eliguntur, & ablatum est regnum à Iudæis, ac datum facienti fructus eius, &c.
units.tr: And from this comes no small comfort to the Gentiles, namely that they themselves are chosen, and that the kingdom has been taken from the Jews and given to a nation bearing its fruits, etc.

units.la: Idq; magis etiam liquet, siquidem ad similitudinem Melchisedech exoritur sacerdos alius, qui non iuxta legem mandati carnalis factus sit, sed iuxta potentiam vitæ indissolubilis. Testificatur enim ad hunc modum: Tu es sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: And this is made clearer still, since after the likeness of Melchizedek another priest arises, who has been made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life. For it is testified in this way: "You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek."

units.la: Secunda ratio, qua probat, sacerdotium Christi distinguendum à Legali seu Leuitico, sumpta à diuersitate ordinis.
units.tr: The second reason, by which he proves that the priesthood of Christ must be distinguished from the legal or Levitical, is taken from the difference of order.

units.la: Christus est sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedec, quemadmodum Spiritus sanctus diserte testificatur.
units.tr: Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek, as the Holy Spirit plainly testifies.

units.la: Sacerdotes legales, sunt sacerdotes secundum ordinem Aaron: Igitur, sicut distinguuntur ordines, ita distingui oportet sacerdotium.
units.tr: The legal priests are priests after the order of Aaron. Therefore, just as the orders are distinguished, so the priesthood must be distinguished.

units.la: Quare recte dicimus, propter sacerdotium Christi nunc exoriens, translatum esse sacerdotium legale. Atque iterum inculcat vocem ἐπεσ, ut discernendi necessitas eò eluidentius conspiciatur.
units.tr: Hence we rightly say that, on account of the priesthood of Christ now arising, the legal priesthood has been transferred. And again he presses the word ἐπεὶ [epei], so that the necessity of distinguishing may be seen more clearly.

units.la: Sed est hic annotandum, consultò dixisse Apostolum, secundum similitudinem Melchisedech: Aliquid enim amplius ea locutionis formula innuit, quàm si simpliciter dixisset, secundum ordinem: nimirum, Christum non ita prorsus per omnia parem ipsi Melchisedech, quasi nihil haberet eminentius, sed reuera multis modis superiorem, ut in sacerdotio Melchisedech tantùm similitudo & typus Christi eluxerit: & Christus longè verius dicatur sacerdos secundum similitudinem Melchisedech, quàm simpliciter secundum ordinem: præsertim quando ipse non tantùm homo, sed etiam natura Deus ad ordinem sacerdotij humani redigi nullo iure posset.
units.tr: But it must be noted here that the Apostle deliberately said "after the likeness of Melchizedek." For that form of expression suggests something more than if he had simply said "after the order": namely, that Christ is not altogether and in every respect equal to Melchizedek himself, as if he had nothing more eminent, but in truth is superior in many ways; so that only a likeness and type of Christ shone forth in the priesthood of Melchizedek. And Christ is said far more truly to be a priest after the likeness of Melchizedek than simply after the order, especially since he is not merely man but also God by nature, and could by no right be reduced to the order of a human priesthood.

units.la: Hac igitur primùm de causa placuit illi dicere, ad similitudinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: For this first reason, then, it pleased him to say "after the likeness of Melchizedek."

units.la: Sed hinc præterea arripit occasionem & materiam alterius argumenti, in quo tacitè prius facta similitudine seu comparatione typici sacerdotij Melchisedech, cum veritate sacerdotij Christi, maximam excellentiam sacerdotij Christi iterum euincit, ob quam à sacerdotio legali maximè veniat distinguendum.
units.tr: But from this he further seizes the occasion and matter of another argument, in which, having tacitly made first the likeness or comparison between the typical priesthood of Melchizedek and the reality of Christ's priesthood, he again proves the great excellence of Christ's priesthood, on account of which it must be distinguished above all from the legal priesthood.

units.la: Apparet autem, ab Apostolo formatam in intellectu similitudinem seu comparatione sacerdotij Melchisedech cum sacerdotio Christi, expenitius considerata particula illa, qua sequitur dictum est, sacerdotium Christi manere æternum, (propter quam etiam initio huius capitis septimi dicebatur, Melchisedech assimilatum filio Dei) in hunc modum: Melchisedech manet sacerdos in æternum, neque initium dierum habens, neque vitæ finem: sequitur, quòd typus hic significat sacerdotium Christi itidem manere æternum.
units.tr: Now it appears that the likeness or comparison between the priesthood of Melchizedek and the priesthood of Christ was formed in the Apostle's mind, when that particle which follows is considered more carefully: it has been said that the priesthood of Christ remains for ever (and on account of this it was said at the beginning of this seventh chapter that Melchizedek was made like the Son of God), in this way: "Melchizedek remains a priest for ever, having neither beginning of days nor end of life." It follows that this type signifies that the priesthood of Christ likewise remains for ever.

units.la: Si autem æternum est, necessariò quoque erit secundum summam potentiam institutum, vitam adferens, spirituale, in rebus internis, inuisibilibus, non crassis & carnalibus occupatum.
units.tr: But if it is eternal, it must necessarily also be instituted according to supreme power, bringing life, spiritual, occupied with inward and invisible things, not gross and carnal.

units.la: Ita namque in re significata quædam multo augustiora accipi debent, quàm in typo significantur, & in corpore plus spectatur, quàm in umbra.
units.tr: For in this way, in the thing signified, certain much greater things ought to be understood than are signified in the type, and more is looked at in the body than in the shadow.

units.la: Et profectò valdè subtiliter, nec minus interim efficaciter istud collectum est.
units.tr: Truly this has been gathered very subtly, and no less effectively for the moment.

units.la: Iam cùm talé ac tantum sit sacerdotium Christi, hinc facilè colligitur, sacerdotium Christi à sacerdotio legali longissimo interuallo esse distinguendum. Quare sic argumentatur.
units.tr: Now since the priesthood of Christ is such and so great, it is easily gathered from this that the priesthood of Christ must be distinguished from the legal priesthood by a very great interval. Therefore he argues thus.

units.la: Sacerdos legalis instituitur iuxta legem mandati carnalis.
units.tr: The legal priest is instituted according to the law of a carnal commandment.

units.la: Sacerdos autem Christus instituitur iuxta potentiam vitæ indissolubilis.
units.tr: But Christ is instituted a priest according to the power of an indissoluble life.

units.la: Sed Lex mandati carnalis longissimè distat à potentia vitę indissolubilis. Igitur pari ratione longisimè distinguendum sacerdotium Christi à legali.
units.tr: But the law of a carnal commandment is very far removed from the power of an indissoluble life. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the priesthood of Christ must be distinguished from the legal by a very great distance.

units.la: Ducitur argumentum istud à diuersitate institutionis et obiectorum seu officiorum: id quod quiuis intelligit, qui modò paulò occulatius in has antitheses, secundum legem mandati carnalis,& secundum potentiam vitæ indissolubilis intuetur.
units.tr: This argument is drawn from the difference of institution and of objects or offices; which anyone understands who looks a little more carefully at these antitheses, "according to the law of a carnal commandment" and "according to the power of an indissoluble life."

units.la: Vbi Lex significat,quàm vulgari more legem Mosaicam nuncupamus.
units.tr: Here "law" means what we commonly call the Mosaic law.

units.la: Potentia verò notat euangelium,quod potentia Dei describitur Roman.1.
units.tr: But "power" denotes the gospel, which is described in Romans 1 as the power of God.

units.la: Mandatum significat literam legis occidentem, ceremonias,& similia.
units.tr: "Commandment" signifies the letter of the law that kills, the ceremonies and similar things.

units.la: Vita autem significat vim viuificandi, quae in euangelio exhibetur.
units.tr: "Life," however, signifies the power of quickening, which is exhibited in the gospel.

units.la: Carnale idem quod vsitato more,carnale,praeterea externum,citò periturum.
units.tr: "Carnal" means the same as in common usage: carnal, moreover external, and soon to perish.

units.la: Indissolubile significat spirituale,internum,& manens æternum.
units.tr: "Indissoluble" signifies spiritual, inward, and remaining for ever.

units.la: Ita ut breuiter ex his omnibus hæc colligatur sententia: Sacerdos Leuiticus constitutus est per legem,ut versetur circa ceremonias,mandata, obseruationes, & quidem carnales, externas tantùm & citò perituras.
units.tr: So that briefly from all these things this sense is gathered: the Levitical priest was constituted through the law, to be occupied with ceremonies, commandments and observances, and indeed carnal, external only, and soon to perish.

units.la: At verò Christus est constitutus sacerdos, per euangelium, ut versetur in rebus vitam adferentibus, spiritualibus, internis,& æternis.
units.tr: But Christ has been constituted priest through the gospel, to be occupied with things that bring life, spiritual, inward and eternal.

units.la: Qua profectò vna ratione pariter summa dignitas sacerdotij Christi præ legali,& summa inter vtrumque diuersitas ostenditur: ut clarissimè intelligi inde queat, legale sacerdotium iam per sacerdotium Christi esse translatum & abrogatum. Quòd si quis plenio-rem velit antithetorum elucidationem, id non adeo difficile factu est.
units.tr: By this one reason, certainly, both the supreme dignity of Christ's priesthood above the legal and the great difference between the two are shown alike; so that it may be most clearly understood from this that the legal priesthood has now been transferred and abrogated through the priesthood of Christ. But if anyone wishes a fuller elucidation of these antitheses, that is not very difficult to do.

units.la: Primò quidem legem accipi pro vniuersa lege Mosaica,secundum quam institutum sit sacerdotium, ceremoniæ & omnia his affinia, vulgo notissimum est, & prima simplicissimaque eius vocis significatio. Atque hoc pacto opponitur euangelio, quemadmodum videre est 2. Corinth. 3. vbi Lex vocatur administratio mortis in literis, euangeliū administratio spiritus, seu potius vitæ in spiritu, &c.
units.tr: First, that "law" is taken for the whole Mosaic law, according to which the priesthood was instituted, with the ceremonies and everything akin to them, is most commonly known, and is the first and simplest meaning of that word. And in this way it is opposed to the gospel, as may be seen in 2 Corinthians 3, where the law is called the ministration of death in letters, the gospel the ministration of the Spirit, or rather of life in the Spirit, etc.

units.la: Quòd autem potentiæ nomine conueniat intelligi euangelium, liquet ex eo, quòd Roman. 1. ita deuinitur, Euangelium potentia est Dei & salutem omni credenti.
units.tr: That the word "power" is rightly understood of the gospel is clear from Romans 1, where it is defined thus: "The gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes."

units.la: Qandoquidem in euangelio potentia Dei mirabiliter elucet,nec non mirabili potentia est propagatum: vnde etiam Christus Lucæ 14. potens opere & sermone appellatur, & ut potestatem habens docuit Matthæi 7. & omne potestatem sibi datam in cœlo & terra (Matth.28) prædicat:& discipulis suis potestatem remittendi peccata,potestatem edendi miracula,contulit, Marci 16.
units.tr: For in the gospel the power of God shines forth wonderfully, and it has been spread by a wonderful power. Hence also Christ in Luke 14 is called powerful in deed and word, and taught as one having authority (Matt. 7), and proclaims that all power is given to him in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28), and he gave his disciples power to forgive sins and power to work miracles (Mark 16).

units.la: Per mandatum diximus significari literam legis occidetem, ceremonias,&c. Id manifestum fit 2. Corinth.3. Vbi lex vocatur administratio literæ & quidè occidentis. Etsi verò sæpè ea vox significet etiam prima præcepta,qualia sunt de dilectione Dei & proximi,ut Matthæi 19. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata: tamen frequenter ad minutiora & ceremonialia,imò traditiones hominum accommodatur. vt Ephes. 2. dicitur per Christū abrogata lex,mandatorum, τὼν cvrολῶν, sita in decretis.Et Colossens.2. Decreta,elementa mundi,ceremonias,præcepta, & doctrinas hominum, quæ etiam Matthæi 15. & ad Titum 1. mandata hominum appellantur.
units.tr: We have said that by "commandment" is signified the letter of the law that kills, the ceremonies, and so on. This is evident from 2 Corinthians 3, where the law is called the ministration of the letter, and indeed of the letter that kills. Although this word often signifies even the first precepts, such as those concerning the love of God and neighbour, as in Matthew 19, "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments," nevertheless it is frequently applied to the lesser and ceremonial matters, and indeed to the traditions of men. Thus in Ephesians 2 the law of commandments is said to have been abrogated by Christ, "the law of commandments in ordinances [τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν]." And in Colossians 2, ordinances, elements of the world, ceremonies, precepts and doctrines of men, which in Matthew 15 and Titus 1 are also called commandments of men.

units.la: Vita autem pulchrè significat contrarium mandati,nempe Spiritum viuificantem, & doctrinam Christi,per quam vita æterna obtinetur, quæ longè excellentior est illa, quæ habebatur in lege.
units.tr: Life, on the other hand, aptly signifies the opposite of commandment, namely the Spirit who quickens, and the doctrine of Christ through which eternal life is obtained, which is far more excellent than what was had in the law.

units.la: Dicendum fuisset,Spiritus:sed maluit effectum exprimere,per Metonymiam. Ioan.12. Qui misit me pater,ipse mihi mandatum dedit, quid dicam, & quid loquar. Et scio, quòd mandatum eius vita æterna est Ioan.6. Verba,quæ ego locutus sum vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt. Ibidem Petrus ad Christum, Domine, ad quem ibimus? Verba vitæ æternæ habes.
units.tr: One should have said "Spirit," but he preferred to express the effect, by metonymy. John 12: "The Father who sent me, he himself gave me a commandment as to what I should say and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is eternal life" (John 12:49–50). John 6: "The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life." In the same place Peter says to Christ, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."

units.la: Carnale, quod vsitato more carnale appellamus, & quod opponitur spirituali, item externum & citò periturum seu temporale.
units.tr: "Carnal," which in common usage we call carnal, is opposed to spiritual; likewise external and soon to perish, or temporal.

units.la: Sic Lex vocatur carnalis,item mandata carnalia,quia circa iustitias carnales,externas, humanas, occupabatur: item quia circa res perituras: item quia habebat promissiones carnales populo carnali propositas. Ioann. 6. Spiritus est, qui viuificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Galat.3. Adeò stulti estis, cum spiritu coeperitis, nunc carne consumamini? Ephes.2. Vos quondam gentes in carne, vocabimini præputium, ab ea,quæ vocatur circumcisio in carne,quæ circumcisio manibus fit. Philippens.3. Nos sumus circumcisio, qui spiritu Deum colimus,& gloriamur in Christo, & non confidimus in carne.
units.tr: So the law is called carnal, and its commandments carnal, because it was concerned with carnal, external, human righteousnesses; also because it dealt with perishable things; and also because it set before a carnal people carnal promises. John 6: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing." Galatians 3: "Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being made perfect by the flesh?" Ephesians 2: "You who were once Gentiles in the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by those called circumcision in the flesh, which is made by hands." Philippians 3: "We are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and glory in Christ, and do not trust in the flesh."

units.la: Atque huius epistolæ capite nono de ceremonijs dicitur,quòd non possint iuxta conscientiam perfectum reddere cultorem,in cibis duntaxat & potionibus,& diuersis ablutionibus, ac iustificationibus carnis,ideoque ad tempus tantùm fuerunt impositæ. Ibidem: Si sanguis taurorum & hircorum aspergens inquinatos sanctificat ad carnis puri-ficationem, ficationem, quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum se ipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus, &c.
units.tr: And in chapter nine of this Epistle it is said of the ceremonies that they cannot make the worshipper perfect as regards the conscience, being only in meats and drinks and various washings and fleshly justifications, and that therefore they were imposed only for a time. In the same place: "If the blood of bulls and goats, sprinkled on the unclean, sanctifies to the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works," and so on.

units.la: Indissolubile: Ratio antitheseos postulasset dici, Spirituale, vel potius sic erant ponenda antitheta, temporale & æternum: sed quia respexit potissimum in vocem æternum, vbi dicitur, sacerdotium Melchisedech & Christi manere æternum: ideo dixit indissolubile, volens innuere, quòd Euangelium & sacerdotium Christi euangelicum versetur non circa ceremonias, sacrificia carnalia, sed circa spiritualia, interna, & æterna, de quibus infra cap. 10. plura: & opponendo ista carnalibus manifesta sunt omnia.
units.tr: Indissoluble: the logic of the antithesis would have required the word "spiritual," or rather the antitheses should have been set out as temporal and eternal. But because he looked chiefly to the word "eternal," where it is said that the priesthood of Melchizedek and of Christ remains for ever, he therefore said indissoluble, wishing to indicate that the gospel and the evangelical priesthood of Christ are concerned not with ceremonies and carnal sacrifices, but with spiritual, inward and eternal things, of which more below in chapter 10. And when these are set against the carnal, all things become plain.

units.la: Cæterùm hoc loco eleganter confertur Euangelium cum lege, & ostenditur, quanta sit Euangelij dignitas præ lege. Vnde reuera consolationem petere debent omnes tempore, qui in Euangelio acquieuerunt. Præterea hac Euangelij dignitate ad verum cultum Dei spiritualem & internum debent omnes magnopere incitari, idq; eo magis, quòd liberati ab onere legis, & externis obseruationibus, edocti sint, iustitiam per vnum Christum parari, cuius nomine omnia sunt & facienda & ferenda.
units.tr: Moreover, in this place the gospel is elegantly compared with the law, and it is shown how great is the dignity of the gospel above the law. Hence indeed all who have rested in the gospel ought to seek consolation in every time. Besides, by this dignity of the gospel everyone ought to be greatly stirred to the true, spiritual and inward worship of God, all the more so since, freed from the burden of the law and from external observances, they have been taught that righteousness is obtained through Christ alone, in whose name all things are both to be done and to be borne.

units.la: Nos suprà de differentia legis & Euangelij copiosius disseruimus capite tertio, vbi de domo Domini egimus, in qua ministrum egit Moses, & in qua ministrum egit Christus.
units.tr: We discussed the difference between law and gospel more fully above, in chapter three, where we treated of the house of the Lord, in which Moses acted as minister, and in which Christ did so.

units.la: Abrogatur enim, quod præcessit præceptum, propter imbecillitatem & inutilitatem. Nam nihil ad perfectionem adduxit lex, verum erat introductio ad spem potiorem, per quam appropinquamus Deo.
units.tr: For the former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, for the law made nothing perfect, but there was a bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.

units.la: Confirmat quod posteriori consequentia aperte intulerat, videlicet, translato sacerdotio simul necessario translatam esse legem. Ac reddit causas, cur lex merito sit abrogata, & quidem, si bene aduertimus, duas potissimum: quarum prior est, quòd lex fuerit imbecillis & inutilis: altera, quòd Euangelium succedens multo sit præstantius. Palàm autem est, vbi præsens habetur, quod efficacius, vtilius, & præstantius est, merito omitti, quod imbecille, inutile, & vile est: Quamobrem iustissimis de causis lex imbecillis, inutilis, vtilis, abrogatur. Vtramq; vero causam succinctè nec non perspicuè probat. Priorem quidem, quando ait: Nam nihil ad perfectionem adduxit lex: ex quibus istud argumentum rite conficitur. Illud imbecille & inutile est, quod ad perfectionem & finem nihil confert.
units.tr: He confirms what he had clearly inferred in the latter consequence, namely that with the priesthood transferred, the law is necessarily transferred too. And he gives the reasons why the law was rightly abrogated, and indeed, if we pay close attention, two chief ones: the first is that the law was weak and useless; the second, that the gospel which succeeds it is much more excellent. It is plain that where what is more effective, more useful and more excellent is present, what is weak, useless and worthless is rightly set aside. Therefore, for the most just reasons, the law, being weak and useless, is abrogated. He proves both causes briefly and clearly. The first he proves when he says, "For the law made nothing perfect," from which the argument is duly constructed: that which contributes nothing to perfection and to its end is weak and useless. But the law is of this kind. Therefore it is weak and useless, and for that reason it is rightly abrogated.

units.la: Atqui lex est huiusmodi.
units.tr: But the law is of this kind.

units.la: Igitur est imbecillis & inutilis. Quamobrem merito abrogatur.
units.tr: Therefore it is weak and useless; wherefore it is rightly abrogated.

units.la: Quòd si iam pergis rogare: Quis igitur vsus legis? An frustra est data? En tibi per occupationem respondet Apostolus, atque vno verbo ostendit, quis proprius fuerit legis vsus. Erat tantum introductio, inquit, ad spem potiorem. Qua ratione satis declarat, nunquam fuisse in hoc institutam, vt perfectio ex ea, vel per eam haberetur, atque aduersarijs clamantibus, legi graue iniuriam fieri, quando dicit, eam abrogari, os obturat. Sunt autem & verba eleganter admodum posita: ἀθέτησις γίνεται, inquit: ἀθετεῖω, reprobo, improbo, reijcio, irritum facio, casso, sperno. Vnde ἀθέτησις, &c. Itaq; vox significat planè annihilationem quandam, & summam abiectionem legis. Et quædam exaggerationis forma opponitur ei, quod prius dixerat modestius, & per μείωσιν, legis factam μετάθεσιν. Sic enim quodibi modestius agi decuerat, nunc conuenit cum maiori vehementia exprimere. Et notandæ sunt hæ formulæ locutionum, vt, quoties de legis abrogatione, vel inefficacia disputandum est, proprijs vtantur verbis, quorum certè delectum semper habuisse Apostolos, extra controuersiam est, potissimumque vbi grauiores controuersias tractarunt.
units.tr: But if you go on to ask, "What then is the use of the law? Was it given in vain?" the Apostle answers you in passing, and shows in a single word what the proper use of the law was: "It was only a bringing in," he says, "of a better hope." By which reasoning he sufficiently declares that it was never instituted so that perfection should be had from it or through it; and when the adversaries cry out that a grave injury is done to the law when he says it is abrogated, he stops their mouths. The words are also elegantly chosen. "ἀθέτησις γίνεται," he says [an annulling takes place]. ἀθετεῖω means to reject, disapprove, reprove, cast off, make void, annul, spurn; hence ἀθέτησις, and so on. So the word plainly signifies a certain annihilation and utter rejection of the law. And a form of exaggeration is set against what he had said earlier more modestly, namely the "transfer" [μετάθεσιν] of the law, which he had put more mildly as a "diminution" [μείωσιν]. For as it was fitting to speak more modestly before, so now it is fitting to express the matter with greater vehemence. And these forms of expression are to be noted, so that whenever we must dispute about the abrogation or ineffectiveness of the law, we use their proper words. That the Apostles always had a careful choice of words is beyond controversy, and especially when they treated of more serious controversies.

units.la: προσχόησις ἀπειρίας: quasi dicas, præcedentis & præeuntis mandati. Et hæc locutio significat, legem seu mandatum iam abiisse, adeoque euanuisse: Sicut quod iam prætergressum est, non amplius est in conspectu, neque eius vis siue effectus amplius sentitur: Ita lex quoque iam prætergressa est, & vix aliquam sui reliquit memoriam.
units.tr: "The preceding commandment [προαγούσης ἐντολῆς]": as if you were to say, of the commandment that went before and preceded. And this expression signifies that the law or commandment has now passed away and so has vanished. As what has already gone by is no longer in sight, nor is its force or effect any longer felt, so the law too has now gone by and has left hardly any memory of itself.

units.la: Διὰ τὸ αὐτὸς ἀδύνατες: id est, propter ipsius imbecillitatem & inutilitatem. Notanda est inprimis particula αὐτῆς, quæ magnam habet Emphasin, quam & oportet obseruare, ne quis accipiat, legem abrogatam esse propter infirmitatem nostram, quem in modum Petrus Actorum decimo quinto videtur huiusmodi causam indicare, vbi ait, non esse imponendum iugum super ceruices discipulorum, gentilium inquam, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus. Sed per gratiam Domini Iesu Christi credimus, nos saluos futuros, quemadmodum & illi (supple patres) salui facti sunt per gratiam Christi, non per opera legis. Non igitur propter infirmitatem nostram Apostolus hic dicit, legem abrogatam, sed propter infirmitatem suiipsius: quemadmodum Roman. 8. dicitur; Quod lex præstare non poterat, ea parte, qua imbecillis erat per carnem, hoc Deus proprio filio misso sub specie carnis peccato obnoxiæ præstitit. Et Galat. 4. At nunc posteaquàm cognouistis Deum, quin potius cogniti estis àDeo, quomodo conuertimini denuò ad infirma & egena elementa, quibus iterum ab integro seruire vultis? Dies obseruatis, & menses, & tempora, & annos: Metuo de vobis, ne frustra laboraueri m erga vos, &c.
units.tr: "Because of its weakness [διὰ τὸ αὐτῆς ἀσθενὲς] and uselessness": that is, on account of its own weakness and uselessness. The particle "its" [αὐτῆς] in particular is to be noted, since it carries great emphasis, and one must take care that no one understands the law to have been abrogated because of our weakness. In this way Peter in Acts 15 seems to indicate such a cause, where he says that a yoke should not be laid on the necks of the disciples, of the Gentiles I mean, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear; but through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we shall be saved, just as they (supply: the fathers) were saved through the grace of Christ, not through the works of the law. Therefore the Apostle here does not say the law was abrogated because of our weakness, but because of its own weakness; as Romans 8 says: "What the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh." And Galatians 4: "But now, after you have known God, or rather are known by God, how do you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, which you wish to serve afresh from the beginning? You observe days, and months, and seasons, and years. I am afraid for you, lest I have laboured over you in vain," and so on.

units.la: Ergo ipsa lex per se infirma & imbecillis est, & propter suiipsius imbecillitatem abrogatur. Interpretatur autem, quid sibi velit nomine imbecillitatis, cùm addit de inutilitate. Reuera enim quod vtilitatem nullam adfert, merito infirmum & imbecille asseritur. Non sine causa tamen hisce verbis vtitur: Quandoquidem suprà quàm dici potest, legem extenuant, & propemodum pessundant. Quid enim vilius dicatur, quàm ad nihil esse vtilem? Vt hæretici quondam hinc arripuerint occasionem sic contemnendi vniuersam legem veterem, quasi ab vno & summo bono Deo nequaquàm esset profecta. Quàmuis aduertendum est, contra hos ita insultantes, non dici legem malam, sed inutilem & imbecillem: quare autem ita merito vocetur, ipse Apostolus mox aperit, quando vtriusque rationem reddit, dicens:
units.tr: Therefore the law itself is weak and feeble, and it is abrogated because of its own feebleness. He explains what he means by weakness when he adds "of unprofitableness." For what brings no benefit is rightly called weak and feeble. Yet he uses these words not without reason: "since they weaken the law beyond what can be said, and nearly destroy it." For what could be called more worthless than being useless for anything? Heretics once seized on this as an occasion to despise the whole Old Testament, as though it had never come from the one and supreme good God. However, it must be noted that against such scoffers the law is not called evil, but unprofitable and feeble. The Apostle himself soon explains why it is rightly so called, when he gives the reason for both, saying:

units.la: Nam nihil ad perfectionem adduxit lex.
units.tr: For the law brought nothing to perfection.

units.la: Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν. Simili modo supra dictum est, per sacerdotium non potuisse contingere consummationem.
units.tr: For the law made nothing perfect [Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν]. In the same way it was said above that perfection could not be attained through the priesthood.

units.la: Neque enim vel lex, vel sacerdotium in hunc finem instituta fuerunt à Deo, vt per eam homines perfectionem, hoc est, salutem & vitam æternam obtinerent: sed tantùm vt adumbrarent res in Euangelio futuras, & ad Christũ quasi manu ducerent, ac pro tempore homines rudes de spiritualibus rebus & euangelicis docerent. Huc pertinet illud Galat 3. Si data fuisset lex, quæ posset viuificare, vere ex lege esset iustitia: Sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccatum, vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus, &c.
units.tr: For neither the law nor the priesthood was instituted by God to this end, that through it men might obtain perfection, that is, salvation and eternal life. They were instituted only to foreshadow things that would be in the Gospel, to lead men by the hand, as it were, to Christ, and to teach rude men, for the time being, about spiritual and evangelical matters. To this belongs what is said in Galatians 3: "If a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be by the law. But Scripture has concluded all things under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe," and so on.

units.la: Sed iam audiens aliquis legem inutilem & imbecillem, quia ad perfectionem non conducit, quæret fortasis, Quare igitur data fuit lex? Quid necessum fuit eam introduci, & sic præscribi?
units.tr: But someone now hearing that the law is unprofitable and feeble, because it does not lead to perfection, will perhaps ask: why then was the law given? Why was it necessary to introduce it and so to prescribe it?

units.la: Respondet: Erat introductio (εἰσαγωγὴ) ad spem meliorem. Hic vsus est legis, & ob hanc causam lata est, vt videlicet introduceret rudes homines ad spem potiorem, id est, ad euangelium, in quo & per quod perfectio erat obtinenda.
units.tr: He answers: it was an introduction (εἰσαγωγὴ) to a better hope. This is the use of the law, and for this reason it was given, namely to introduce rude men to a better hope, that is, to the Gospel, in which and through which perfection was to be obtained.

units.la: Vocat autem legem hic introductionem, quomodo alibi vocat elementa, seu elementalem institutionem, στοιχεῖα. Galat. quarto, Posteaquàm cognouistis Deum, quid denuò conuertimini ad infirma & egena elementa? Colossens. secundo: Videte, ne quis sit, qui vos deprædetur per philosophiam & inanem deceptionem, iuxta constitutionem hominum, iuxta elementa mundi, & non iuxta Christum. Ibidem: Itaque si mortui estis cum Christo ab elementis mundi, quid quasi viuentes in mundo decretis tenemini? Ne tetigeris, ne gustaris, neq; contrectaris, &c. Quibus omnibus locis intelligit per elementa doctrinam legis, atque inprimis eam, quæ est de ceremonialibus: cuius rei argumentum est, quòd ea omitti, negligi, contemni vult, docens nimirum, hac in parte legem abrogatam.
units.tr: Here he calls the law an introduction, just as elsewhere he calls it the elements, or elementary instruction [στοιχεῖα]. Galatians 4: "After you have come to know God, why do you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements?" Colossians 2: "Take heed lest anyone plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ." And again: "If therefore you died with Christ from the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, are you subject to decrees? Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle," and so on. In all these passages he understands by the elements the teaching of the law, and especially that part which concerns the ceremonies. The proof of this is that he wants these things omitted, neglected and despised, clearly teaching that in this respect the law has been abrogated.

units.la: Lex igitur non erat consummatio, sed tantùm introductio. Quò autem introducebat? Ad spem potiorem: Id est, ad Euangelium, in quo potiora bona, nempe vera omnia & spiritualia contingunt, non tantùm vmbratica vel carnalia.
units.tr: The law therefore was not the fulfilment but only an introduction. But to what did it introduce? To a better hope, that is, to the Gospel, in which better goods are attained, namely all things true and spiritual, not merely shadowy or carnal ones.

units.la: Et hic indicatur secunda ratio abrogatarum ceremoniarum, videlicet, quòd euangelium succedens multo sit præstantius.
units.tr: Here is indicated the second reason for the abrogation of the ceremonies, namely that the Gospel, which succeeds the law, is far more excellent.

units.la: Rectè autem Euangelium intelligitur per spem potiorem: quandoquidem ipse sic interpretatur, mox vbi ait, de Euangelio loquens, vt opponitur legi, Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est IESVS: vbi Christum notat secundum multo præstantius testamentum ordinatum esse sacerdotem, quàm fuerint Leuitæ, qui per legem erant constituti. Sed alibi quoq; spes Euangelio propriè tribuitur, propter excellentiam rerum sperandarum, quæ in Euangelio omnibus credentibus proponuntur & offeruntur. Huc pertinent illa Colos.1. Reconciliauit vos Deus in corpore carnis suæ, per mortem, vt exhiberet vos sanctos, & irreprehensibiles, & inculpatos in conspectu suo. Siquidè permanetis in fide fundati ac stabiles, nec dimouemini à spe Euangelij, quod audistis, quod prædicatum est apud vniuersam creaturam, quæ sub cœlo est, cuius factus sum ego Paulus minister. Et spem Euangelij. Roma. 5. Iustificati igitur ex fide, pacem habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem & contigit nobis, vt fide perduceremur in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei.
units.tr: Now the Gospel is rightly understood by "a better hope," since he himself explains it so, soon after, when speaking of the Gospel as opposed to the law: "By so much was Jesus made the surety of a better testament," where he means that Christ was appointed priest of a much more excellent covenant than the Levites, who had been established by the law. But elsewhere too hope is properly ascribed to the Gospel, on account of the excellence of the things to be hoped for, which are set forth and offered in the Gospel to all who believe. To this belong Colossians 1: "God has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy, blameless and unreproachable in his sight, if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast, and are not moved away from the hope of the Gospel which you have heard, which has been preached to every creature under heaven, of which I, Paul, have become a minister." And "the hope of the Gospel."
