Romans 5: "Therefore, justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God."

units.la: E cce quomodo quò lex nō potuit perducimur, eò adducimur per Christū, vbi spem gloriæ Dei apprehendimus. Et de cognitione Euangelij ad Tit. 1. Paulus Seruus Dei, Apostolus autem Iesu Christi, iuxta fidem electorum Dei, & agnitionem veritatis, quæ est secundum pietatem in spe vitæ æternæ, quam promisit is, qui mentiri nescit Deus, ante tempora æterna.
units.tr: Behold how we are brought, through Christ, to where the law could not bring us: there we grasp the hope of the glory of God. And concerning the knowledge of the Gospel, Titus 1: "Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before eternal times."

units.la: Et fides, quæ Euangelij quasi propria est, vocatur rerum sperandarum substantia, infrà capite vndecimo. Et 1. Petri 1. de confessione Euangelij, Sitis parati semper ad responden-dum cuilibet petenti, ut loquamini de ea, quæ in vobis est, spe, cum mansuetudine & reuerentia.
units.tr: And faith, which is as it were the proper possession of the Gospel, is called "the substance of things hoped for," in chapter eleven below. And 1 Peter 1, concerning the confession of the Gospel: Be ready always to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and reverence.

units.la: Denique sicut hic lex dicitur introductio ad spem potiorem: ita Galat. 3. Lex dicitur pædagogus ad Christum prorsus eadem sententia. Sed hæc satis ad ostendendum, quòd per spem potiorem euangelium intelligi conueniat.
units.tr: In short, just as here the law is called an introduction to a better hope, so in Galatians 3 the law is called a schoolmaster to Christ, with exactly the same meaning. But these things are enough to show that it is fitting to understand the better hope as the Gospel.

units.la: Quamuis Apostolus ipse idem non obscure indicat, quando addit: Per quam appro-pinquamus Deo: Per Euangelium proprie appropinquamus Deo, quod vtique per legem fieri non poterat. Cum lex (Exod. 19.) daretur, iussi sunt omnes procul abesse à monte, in quo loquebatur Dominus: id significauit haud dubiè, homines per legem nequaquam Deo propinquos reddi, nequaquam perfectos reddi. Certè per Euangelium nos Deo potissimum propinquos reddi satis indicat Apostolus Ephe. 2. Nunc autem per Christum Iesum vos, qui quondam eratis longinqui, propinqui facti estis per sanguinem Christi.
units.tr: Although the Apostle himself indicates the same not obscurely, when he adds: through whom we draw near to God. We draw near to God properly through the Gospel, which certainly could not be done through the law. When the law was given (Exodus 19), all were commanded to keep away from the mountain on which the Lord was speaking. This clearly signified that men are by no means brought near to God by the law, nor made perfect by it. Certainly the Apostle sufficiently indicates in Ephesians 2 that through the Gospel we are chiefly brought near to God: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ."

units.la: Et licet ibidem subijciatur de Christo, quòd veniens euangelizauit pacem vobis, qui procul aberatis, & his qui prope, ista particula ad Iudæos, illa ad gentiles vtens: tamen sciendum est, Iudæos non fuisse propinquos Deo per legem, nisi quodam respectu & per comparationem ad gentiles. Alias reuera longè adhuc à salute aberant: &, si propinqui esse incipiebant, in Christum serpentem æneum debebant respicere. Facit huc, quod 2. Corinth. 3. Iudæi sub lege non poterant intueri gloriam faciei Mosaicæ: sed velum coactus est Moses faciei obducere. Nos autem in Euangelio, retecta facie, gloriam Domini speculo repræsentamus. Diximus supra, prudenter distinguendam esse hanc disputationem de abrogatione legis, ab alijs disputationibus de eadem caussa in cæteris epistolis, inprimis ad Romanos & Galatas habitis. Hic enim agi potissimum de abrogatione non quidem totius legis, sed eius partis, quæ ceremonialia complectitur. Nunc verò addit etiam caussam eius partis abrogatæ: præterea, quis fuerit eius vsus: Et multa deinceps sequuntur in hanc sententiam, quibus & vsus ceremonialium omnium, & caussa item abrogationis eorundem omnium ostenditur.
units.tr: And although in the same place it is added concerning Christ that coming he preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near, using the one phrase for the Jews and the other for the Gentiles, yet it must be understood that the Jews were not near to God through the law, except in a certain respect and by comparison with the Gentiles. Otherwise, in truth, they were still far from salvation, and if they began to be near, they had to look to the bronze serpent in Christ. To this relates what is said in 2 Corinthians 3: the Jews under the law could not look upon the glory of Moses' face, but Moses was compelled to cover his face with a veil. We, however, in the Gospel, with unveiled face, reflect the glory of the Lord as in a mirror. We said above that this disputation about the abrogation of the law must prudently be distinguished from the other disputations on the same cause, held in the other epistles, especially in Romans and Galatians. For here the chief subject is the abrogation not of the whole law, but of that part which contains the ceremonies. Now, however, he adds also the cause of this abrogated part, and besides, what its use was. And many things follow in this sense, by which both the use of all the ceremonies and the cause of their abrogation are shown.

units.la: Proinde videmur factuři operæ precium, si paulò copiosius de institutione, partibus, vsu ceremonialium, præterea etiam de eorundem abrogatione disseramus: quibus intellectis cætera quę sequuntur, lõge erunt faciliora. Prius tamen quàm ad rem veniamus, commonstrandum est, quare Apostolus has rationes de vsu & abrogatione legis posue-rit, potius quàm alias: & quòd appositissimè redditæ sunt de ceremonialibus, de quibus hic proprie disputatur. Vbi alias de abrogatione legis disputatur, aliquādo dicitur, eam abrogatam propter nostram infirmitatem, sicut supra ex Actor. decimo quinto citauimus: Et Hieremias capite tricesimo primo imbecillitatem hominū notat, dum patres accusat, quòd vetus pactum non seruauerint, ideoq; opus fit aliud pactum seu aliud testamentum condere. Quam rationem etiam Apostolus exponit capite octauo & decimo huius epistolæ. Hæc autem ratio etsi accipi possit vt dicta de ceremonijs, in quibus pleræque erant obseruatu difficiles, tamen potissimum intelligitur de præceptis moralibus, maximèq; quę sunt primæ tabulæ, vbi diligere Deū ex toto corde, ex tota anima, &c. quis non videat, quàm difficile, quàm à nullo, ea, qua par foret, ratione perficiatur? Sed & illud è secunda tabula: Non concupisces, quis est, qui exactè caueat?
units.tr: Therefore we shall seem to be doing worthwhile work if we discuss somewhat more fully the institution, parts and use of the ceremonies, and besides their abrogation; once these are understood, what follows will be far easier. Yet before we come to the matter, it must be shown why the Apostle put forward these reasons about the use and abrogation of the law, rather than others, and that they are very aptly applied to the ceremonies, which are the proper subject of this disputation here. Where elsewhere the abrogation of the law is discussed, it is sometimes said that it was abrogated on account of our weakness, as we cited above from Acts 15. And Jeremiah in chapter 31 notes the weakness of men, while he accuses the fathers of not keeping the old covenant, and therefore a new covenant or new testament had to be made. The Apostle also explains this reason in chapters 8 and 10 of this epistle. Although this reason could be taken as said about the ceremonies, in which most things were difficult to observe, it is chiefly understood of the moral precepts, and especially those of the first table, where we are to love God with our whole heart, with our whole soul, and so on. Who does not see how difficult this is, and how it is never accomplished by anyone in the proper manner? But also that from the second table: "You shall not covet." Who is there who guards against this exactly?

units.la: Alias verò dicitur, legem abrogatam, propter infirmitatem sui ipsius, ac dignitatem potentiamque Christi: quia videlicet, quod lex præstare non poterat, Christus præstit, nimirum iustitiam coram Deo, quæ nobis accommodatur & imputatur, etiamsi legem non impleuerimus. Atque istud quidem de tota lege rectè accipiatur. Nam reuera ipsa non potest, etiamsi tota seruaretur, iustos coram Deo facere.
units.tr: On the other hand, the law is said to be abrogated because of its own weakness and because of the dignity and power of Christ: namely, because what the law could not supply, Christ supplies, that is, righteousness before God, which is applied and imputed to us even though we have not fulfilled the law. And this, indeed, may rightly be understood of the whole law. For in truth the law itself, even if it were kept entire, could not make men righteous before God.

units.la: Sed tamen aptissimè, meo iudicio, hanc rationem vsurpauit Apostolus, loquens hoc loco de ceremonialibus, quæ reuera maximè videbantur instituta, vt, vbi quispiam legis deprehensus fuisset transgressor, & peccasset vel in primam tabulam, vel secundam, per ceremonias, veluti per sacrificia, ritus, lotiones, purificaretur, & quodammodo iustus iterum redderetur, peccatorum obtenta remissione. Hinc sacrificia pro peccatis, item pro certis criminibus certa expiationum genera. Et tamen Apostolus diserte ait, ista omnia non potuisse homines perfectos reddere, neque iustitiam adferre. Atque hæ sunt duæ causæ principales abrogatæ legis, potissimumque spectandæ, quotiescunque de abrogatione legis disputatur.
units.tr: Yet, in my judgment, the Apostle employed this reason most aptly, speaking here of the ceremonial laws, which indeed seemed chiefly instituted so that, when someone was caught as a transgressor of the law and had sinned either against the first table or the second, he might be cleansed through ceremonies, as through sacrifices, rites and washings, and might in some measure be made righteous again once forgiveness of sins was obtained. Hence the sacrifices for sins, and likewise certain kinds of expiation for certain crimes. And yet the Apostle plainly says that all these things could not make men perfect, nor bring righteousness. These are the two principal causes of the abrogation of the law, and they are chiefly to be looked at whenever the abrogation of the law is disputed.

units.la: Nam, quòd aliàs dicitur lex abrogata, quia videlicet non est posita iustis, hæc ratio sumpta est à qualitate personarum, facientium ea, quæ sunt legis: seu potius ab autore impellente, & vires conferente, quibus lex queat perfici, hoc est, à Spiritu sancto. Quibus enim spiritus sanctus dat, vt & possint, & velint præstare ea quę sunt legis, facturi, etiamsi legem nunquam audiuissent, sola charitate in Deum & homines, à Spiritu sancto incensi, profectò talibus lex abrogata dicitur, & faciunt legem, etiam si opera legis omnia nequaquam præstent. Charitas enim diffusa in cordibus est impletio legis, & imputatur pro omnibus operibus legis.
units.tr: For when the law is said in other respects to be abrogated, because it is not laid down for the righteous, this reason is taken from the quality of the persons who do the things of the law; or rather from the author who drives them on and confers the powers by which the law can be fulfilled, that is, from the Holy Spirit. For those to whom the Holy Spirit gives both the ability and the will to perform the things of the law, even though they had never heard the law, kindled by the Holy Spirit with love alone toward God and men, are certainly said to be free from the law, and they do fulfil the law, even if they do not perform all the works of the law. For "love poured out in our hearts is the fulfilling of the law," and it is imputed in place of all the works of the law.

units.la: Quòd denique dicitur, legem abrogatam, quòd videlicet non posset maledictioni obnoxios reddere (Roman. 8.) hæc ratio potius explicatio quædam est, quomodo prudenter intelligi debeant de abrogatione legis disputationes, ne videlicet petulantes homines sic interpretarentur abrogatam legem, quasi non amplius bene agere ex præscripto legis oporteret: &, quasi liceret iam quicquid lubeat impune designare. His dicitur, legem abrogatam esse, non, ne fiat: sed ne, cum facta plenè non est, nos condemnet.
units.tr: Finally, when it is said that the law is abrogated because it could not make men liable to the curse (Rom. 8), this reason is rather a kind of explanation of how the disputations about the abrogation of the law ought to be understood prudently, lest wanton men should interpret the law as abrogated, as if it were no longer necessary to do good according to the law's prescription, and as if it were now lawful to do whatever one pleases with impunity. Of these men it is said that the law is abrogated, not so that it should not be fulfilled, but so that, since it is not fully fulfilled by us, it should not condemn us.

units.la: Cum denique nonnulli dicunt, legem abrogatam, propter promissiones de eius abrogatione & immutatione factas, hæc ratio ex duabus primis rationibus fluit.
units.tr: Lastly, when some say that the law is abrogated on account of the promises made concerning its abrogation and change, this reason flows from the two first reasons.

units.la: Ideo enim Deus vaticinia de abrogatione legis præire voluit, quia & homines videbat infirmiores, quàm qui possent eam præstare: & ipsam præterea infirmiorem, quàm quæ posset perfectos reddere. Quamobrem ordinauit constituitque filium mittere, qui pro omnibus hominibus solus semel vniuersam legem impleret, & sua plena obedientia omnes homines perfectos redderet.
units.tr: For God wished to send prophecies of the abrogation of the law beforehand, because he saw that men were too weak to be able to keep it, and that the law itself was too weak to make men perfect. Therefore he ordained and decreed to send the Son, who alone, on behalf of all men, would once fulfil the whole law, and by his full obedience would make all men perfect.

units.la: En ergo, quibus de causis lex dicatur abrogata, &, quòd multo aptissimè Apostolus de ceremonialibus potissimum disputans dixerit, eam abrogatam, propter suam infirmitatem.
units.tr: Here, then, are the causes for which the law is said to be abrogated; and that the Apostle, disputing chiefly about the ceremonial laws, very aptly said it was abrogated on account of its weakness.

units.la: Sed, nònne Decalogus (dixerit quispiam) est etiam abrogatus? Videtur tamen nihilominus manere.
units.tr: But (someone may say) is the Decalogue also abrogated? Yet it seems nonetheless to remain.

units.la: Respondetur: Cum agitur de Iustificatione, verè est abrogatus, nihil facit ad iustificationem.
units.tr: The answer: when the question concerns justification, it is truly abrogated, since it contributes nothing to justification.

units.la: Quantum verò attinet ad literam, & præceptorum qualitatem, non potest abrogari, quia naturalis est, & in hominum animis perpetuus.
units.tr: But as far as the letter and the nature of the precepts are concerned, it cannot be abrogated, because it is natural and perpetual in the minds of men.

units.la: Et seruatur à pijs, non quia in lege præscriptus, sed quia etiam in Euangelio per Spiritum sanctum suggeritur, & charitatis officia complectitur.
units.tr: And it is observed by the godly, not because it is prescribed in the law, but because it is also suggested in the Gospel through the Holy Spirit, and it embraces the duties of love.

units.la: Quid verò dicendum de iudicialibus? Multa adhuc seruantur, vt, de Coniugijs, de distinctione dominiorum. Respondetur: Si quæ seruantur, non tamen quia legis Mosaicæ sunt, sed quia naturæ consentiunt, & ad tuendam publicam pacem magis vtiles. Alias vbi publica vtilitas suadet, ab illis discedituir, vt in suspendendo fures, in puniendis adulteris, vbi lex non seruatur.
units.tr: What, then, must be said of the judicial laws? Many are still observed, for example those concerning marriage and the distinction of lordships. The answer: if some are observed, they are not observed because they belong to the Mosaic law, but because they agree with nature and are more useful for preserving public peace. Otherwise, where public advantage advises it, men depart from them, as in hanging thieves and punishing adulterers, where the law is not kept.

units.la: Iam cùm dixit, legem fuisse introductionem ad spem potiorem, rectissimè quoque id ab eo dictum esse, ostendamus, & simul quàm varijs de causis lex lata, & quàm multiplex eius vsus.
units.tr: Now, that he said the law was an introduction to a better hope, we shall show that this was also said most rightly, and at the same time how the law was given for various causes, and how manifold its use is.

units.la: Primùm igitur in hoc data erat lex, vt mali homines, quorum iam cognitio naturalis per assiduitatem vitiorum erat penitus obscurata, disciplina legis intra honesti cancellos retinerentur, maximè propter pœnas, quæ in lege præscribuntur, contra eos, qui legem non obseruarint, quos oportet fræno legis in ordinem redigi. Hanc causam expresit Apostolus 1. Tim. 1. vbi ait, legem positam esse, non iustis, sed iniustis, inobsequentibus, impijs, & peccatoribus, irreuerentibus, & profanis, parricidis, & matricidis, homicidis, fornicatoribus, &c. Hæc verò causa potissimum accipienda est de legibus moralibus & iudicialibus, quæ institutæ sunt ad malos homines coercendos. Atq; hodie etiam quæq; bonæ leges politicæ ex hac causa trahunt originem.
units.tr: First, then, the law was given so that evil men, whose natural knowledge had been utterly obscured by the constant practice of vices, might be held within the bounds of honesty by the discipline of the law, chiefly on account of the penalties prescribed in the law against those who have not kept it, whom it is proper to bring into order by the bridle of the law. The Apostle expressed this cause in 1 Tim. 1, where he says that the law was laid down not for the righteous but for the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the irreverent and profane, murderers of fathers and of mothers, manslayers, fornicators, and so on. This cause, however, is chiefly to be understood of the moral and judicial laws, which were instituted to restrain evil men. And even today all good political laws take their origin from this cause.

units.la: Secundò: In hoc data fuit lex, ut omnes in genere homines conuincerentur suæ iniquitatis & infirmitatis, nullisq; operibus superbirent, vel iustos se esse putarent, sed agnoscerent, se damnationi obnoxios.
units.tr: Second: the law was given so that all men in general might be convicted of their iniquity and weakness, and might take no pride in any works, nor think themselves righteous, but acknowledge that they are liable to damnation.

units.la: Huc pertinent illa Rom. 3. vbi, cùm omnes ostendit reos peccati & mortis, per legem inquit, est cognitio peccati Roman. 5. Lex obiter subingressa est, vt abundaret delictum. Roman. 7 Peccatum non cognoui, nisi per legem. Nam & concupiscentia non nouissem, nisi lex diceret, Non concupisces.
units.tr: To this belong those passages in Rom. 3, where, after showing that all are guilty of sin and death, he says "through the law comes the knowledge of sin"; Rom. 5, "the law entered in incidentally, that the offence might abound"; Rom. 7, "I had not known sin except through the law. For I had not known concupiscence unless the law said, 'You shall not covet.'"

units.la: Atque haec causa potissimum de moralibus, in quibus maxima difficultas, est intelligenda: & secundum hunc modum lex dicitur administratio mortis, quae iram operatur & occidit, dum malos irritat, vt irascantur Deo, atque etiam in desperationem prolabantur. Si defit Spiritus gratiae, non potest hoc pacto considerata lex aliud facere, quam reos facere & occidere, sicut Augustinus diserte ait in libro de correptione & gratia.
units.tr: And this cause is to be understood chiefly of the moral laws, in which the greatest difficulty lies; and in this way the law is called "the ministration of death," which works wrath and kills, while it provokes evil men so that they rage against God and even fall into despair. If the Spirit of grace is lacking, the law, considered in this way, can do nothing else than make men guilty and kill them, as Augustine plainly says in his book On Correction and Grace.

units.la: Tertio: In hoc data fuit lex, vt duceret ad Christum: sicut hoc loco & ad Galatas tertio docet Apostolus. Et quamuis haec causa etiam de legibus moralibus non inepte accipiatur, quia videlicet homines earum difficultate & multitudine rei facti & consternati, coguntur cogitare de imploranda ope Dei propter Christum; & sic pulchre dicentur etiam leges morales ad Christum ducere: tamen multo proprijsimè de ceremonialibus legibus causa haec exponetur, praesertim quando ceremonialia omnia ad ea, quae diuini cultus sunt, pertinent, nec non Christum, eaque quae per Christum forent perficienda, vt iustificatio, purificatio, mundatio, satisfactio pro peccatis nostris, plenissimè adumbrabant, sicut paulo post plenius ostendemus: & in omnibus ceremonialibus perficiendis semper animi piorum patrum in Christum promissum defigebantur, cuius nomine accepta Deo omnia iudicari debebant. Itaque Apostolus disputans hic de vsu legis, & praecipue ceremoniarum, rectissime dixit, legem fuisse introductionem ad spem meliorem.
units.tr: Third: the law was given to lead to Christ, as the Apostle teaches here and in Galatians 3. And although this cause may not unfittingly be taken also of the moral laws, since men, made guilty and dismayed by the difficulty and multitude of the precepts, are compelled to think of seeking the help of God on account of Christ, and so the moral laws too can fittingly be said to lead to Christ, nevertheless this cause will be set out far more properly of the ceremonial laws, especially since all the ceremonies pertain to the things of divine worship, and most fully foreshadowed Christ and the things that were to be accomplished through Christ, such as justification, purification, cleansing, and satisfaction for our sins, as we shall show more fully a little later. And in performing all the ceremonies, the minds of the godly fathers were always fixed on the promised Christ, in whose name everything was to be judged acceptable to God. Therefore the Apostle, discussing here the use of the law, and especially of the ceremonies, rightly said that the law was an introduction to a better hope.

units.la: Quaecunque praeterea adferri solent causae datae legis, siue vsus, ad has praecedentes referri merito debent. Veluti, quod quidam solent addere, in hoc datam legem, vt videlicet, qui iam Spiritu sancto donati sunt fideles, in eam tanquam in speculum iugiter intueantur, discantque assidue, quae sit Dei voluntas bona: & quae facere aut omittere in omni vita deceat: Item, vt seipsos contemplatione & calcaribus legis per omnem vitam ad virtutes extimulent: atque ita, quae aliis est administratio mortis, cedatipsis ad salutem: Haec profecto causa fere fluit ex prima, & docet, quatenus lex vtilis sit, etiam bonis, & iam Spiritu sancto illustratis, quibus alias lex non dicitur proprie esse posita, & tamen intelligi conuenit, non debere eos prorsus exleges viuere. Certe tales, licet liberati sint ab execratione legis, tamen adhuc vtilitatem ex lege magnam accipient, & cum spirituales sint, spiritualem legem praestare omni tempore adnitentur. Confirmatur hic vsus legis illis locis 1. Timoth. 1. Lex bona, & sancta est, si quis ea legitime vtatur. Item Romanor. 7. Lex ipsa quidem sancta, & praeceptum sanctum ac iustum & bonum, &c.
units.tr: Whatever other causes of the giving of the law, or uses of it, are usually brought forward, ought rightly to be referred to these preceding ones. For example, what some are accustomed to add: that the law was given so that the faithful, who are now endowed with the Holy Spirit, may continually look into it as into a mirror, and learn diligently what the good will of God is and what it becomes them to do or omit in every part of life; likewise, so that by contemplating it and by the goads of the law they may spur themselves on to virtues throughout their whole life, and so that what is a ministration of death to others may become for them a means of salvation. This cause indeed flows largely from the first, and teaches how far the law is useful even to the good, who are already enlightened by the Holy Spirit, and to whom the law is otherwise not properly said to have been laid down; and yet it is fitting to understand that they should by no means live without law. Certainly such men, although they are freed from the curse of the law, will nonetheless derive great usefulness from the law, and since they are spiritual, they will strive at all times to perform the spiritual law. This use of the law is confirmed by those passages, 1 Tim. 1: "The law is good and holy, if anyone uses it lawfully"; and Rom. 7: "The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good," etc.

units.la: DE CEREMONIIS.
units.tr: On the Ceremonies.

units.la: Hic ita expositis, de ceremonialibus ordine didactico quaedam explicabimus. Primum, si de ratione nominis quispiam certior fieri velit, video apud scriptores nostros haud satis conuenire.
units.tr: Having set these matters out, we will now explain some points about the ceremonial laws in a didactic order. First, if anyone wishes to be better informed about the reason for the name, I see that our writers do not agree very well among themselves.

units.la: Valerius Maximus libro 1. cap. 1. refert, quod vrbe a Gallis capta, cum Flamen Quirinalis, virginesque vestales, sacra, onere partito, ferrent, easque pontem sublicium transgressas, & cliuium, qui ducit ad ianiculum, descendere incipientes, L. Aluanius plaustro coniugem & liberos vehens aspexisset, propior publicae religioni, quam priuatae charitati, suis vt plaustro descenderent imperauit, atq; in id virgines & sacra imposita, omisso coepto itinere, Cerete oppidum prouexit, vbi cum summa veneratione recepta, grata memoria, ad hoc vsque tempus hospitalem humanitatem testantur. Inde enim institutum est, sacra ceremonias vocari, quia Ceretani ea infracto reipublicae statu perinde ac florente coluerunt. Nonnulli suspicantur, à celeberrimis sacris Cereris nomen ceremoniarum deriuatum. Aulus Gellius libro 4. cap. 9. ex sententia Massurij Sabini ait, sicut verbum religionis a relinquendo dictum, ita ceremonias a carendo. Quam rationem ample&ctitur etiam Augustinus in libro de Spiritu & Litera: & Retractationum libro 2. cap. 37. vbi sic ait: Cùm autem agerem de obseruationibus Iudaeorum (videlicet, in libro de Spiritu & Litera) à quibusdam escis secundum veterem legem abstinentium, dixi: Quarundam escarum ceremoniae, quod nomen non est in vsu literarum sanctarum: ideo tamen mihi congruens visum est, quòd à carendo appellatas ceremonias, quasi caremonias, memoria tenebam, eò, quòd obseruantes careant his rebus, à quibus abstinent. Quòd si est alia origo huius nominis, quæ abhorret à vera religione, secundum hanc ego non sum locutus,sed secundum illam, quam suprà memoraui. Certè vetus translatio variè transtulit. Aliquando legimus ceremonias, vbi septuaginta habent Αι-ρεσίματαρ, vt videre est Genes. 26. Deut 4. Rursus vbi habent προστάγματα, vt Exod. 18. Cum tamé Genes. 26. sic habeatur מִשְׁמֶרֶת מִצְוֹת חֻקֹּתַי וְתוֹרֹתָי: id est, græcè, τὰ προστάγματα μου, καὶ τὰς σὺντολάς μου, καὶ τὰ δικαιώματά μου, καὶ νόμιμα μου. Ad Abraham dicta sunt, In semine tuo benedicetur omnes gentes,eò quòd obedierit Abraham voci meæ,& custodierit præcepta, & mandata mea, &ceremonias legesque obseruauerit. Sed hæc de voce sint satis.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 1, reports that when the city had been taken by the Gauls, the Quirinal Flamen and the Vestal Virgins were carrying the sacred objects, dividing the burden between them. When they had crossed the Sublician bridge and begun to go down the slope that leads to the Janiculum, Lucius Albinius saw them from his wagon, in which he was carrying his wife and children. Being more mindful of public religion than of private affection, he ordered his own family to get down from the wagon, and had the virgins and the sacred objects put on it. Abandoning the journey he had begun, he conveyed them to the town of Caere, where they were received with the greatest honour, and the grateful memory of this hospitable kindness is still attested to this day. From this, it is said, the custom arose of calling sacred rites caerimoniae, because the people of Caere kept them up as diligently when the state was broken as when it was flourishing. Some suspect that the name of the ceremonies was derived from the most famous rites of Ceres. Aulus Gellius, book 4, chapter 9, following the opinion of Massurius Sabinus, says that just as religio is named from relinquere (to leave behind), so caerimoniae are named from carere (to abstain). Augustine too follows this explanation in his book On the Spirit and the Letter, and in the second book of his Retractations, chapter 37, where he says: "When I was discussing the observances of the Jews (namely, in the book On the Spirit and the Letter), of those who abstained from certain foods according to the old law, I said: 'the ceremonies of certain foods', a term not in use in the holy letters. Nevertheless it seemed fitting to me, since I held in memory that the ceremonies were called from carere, as it were caremonies, because those who observe them abstain from the things they refrain from. But if there is another origin of this name, one that is alien to true religion, I have not spoken according to that, but according to the one I mentioned above." Certainly the old translation renders it in various ways. Sometimes we read 'ceremonies' where the Seventy have [αἱρέσιματα], as can be seen in Genesis 26 and Deuteronomy 4; and again where they have [προστάγματα], as in Exodus 18. Yet in Genesis 26 the Hebrew reads [משמרת מצות חקותי ותורותי], that is, in Greek [τὰ προστάγματά μου, καὶ τὰς ἐντολάς μου, καὶ τὰ δικαιώματά μου, καὶ νόμιμά μου]. It was said to Abraham: "In your seed all the nations shall be blessed, because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my precepts and my commandments, and observed my ceremonies and laws." But let this suffice concerning the word.

units.la: Iam verò definire licet, ceremonias esse externas quasdam actiones rebus sacris decorè adhibitas, ad animos hominum commouendos ad verum cultum internum, ad confesionem fidei,&c. idoneas,siue aliàs semper spirituale quiddam ad Dei honorem pertinens, significantes. Itaque non sunt ceremoniæ res otiosæ & inutiles, sed suprà, quàm dici potest, necessariæ. Quia enim Deus coli debet ab hominibus toto corde, tota anima, & omnibus viribus, adeoque & anima & corpore debent sese Deo totos dedere: Ideo,partim, vt exterius testarentur, se totos esse Deo deuotos, submissos, obstrictos, ex eo pendentes, partim, vt animi intus magis mouerentur ad veram fidem, humilitatem, gratitudinem pro acceptis beneficijs,&c. Ideo Deus voluit externas quoq; actiones ceu ad cultum pertinentes in vsu haberi. Non satis est, corde credere ad iustitiam, sed oportet etiam ore confiteri ad salutem. Ita non satis est, simpliciter sola mentis apprehensione Deum venerari, sed oportet etiam externis signis & factis eum cultum testatum facere. Maximè autem videtur opus esse ceremonijs, propter hominum rudes animos, qui externis elementis doceri debent, & sine his vix possent in cognitione cultus diuini retineri.
units.tr: Now we may indeed define ceremonies as certain external actions, fittingly employed in sacred matters, suited to moving people's minds to the true inward worship, to the confession of faith, and so on, or otherwise always signifying something spiritual that pertains to the honour of God. Therefore ceremonies are not idle and useless things, but are necessary beyond what can be said. For since God ought to be worshipped by human beings with the whole heart, the whole soul and all their strength, and therefore people ought to give themselves wholly to God both in soul and in body, God willed that external actions also be used, as belonging to worship. Partly this was so that people might outwardly testify that they are wholly devoted, submitted, bound to God and dependent on him; partly so that their minds might be more stirred inwardly to true faith, humility, gratitude for the benefits received, and so on. It is not enough to believe in the heart unto righteousness; it is also necessary to confess with the mouth unto salvation. Thus it is not enough to venerate God by the mind's apprehension alone; one must also bear witness to that worship by external signs and deeds. Ceremonies seem especially necessary because of the dull minds of human beings, who must be taught by external elements, and without these could scarcely be kept in the knowledge of divine worship.

units.la: Itaque hac de causa statim ab initio mundi Deus animis hominum suggesit, vt ritus quosdam externos ceremoniasque instituerent: nec dubium, quin Adam primus minister verbi, ad quem facta fuit promissio de semine benedicto, suis filijs tradiderit quædam huiusmodi, qui mox eadem quasi per manus alijs commendarunt. Sic verò Genesios 4. Cain & Abel fructus & primitias offerunt & incendunt. Genes. 8. Noah erigit altare offertque holocausta. Similiter Genes. 22. Abraham ædificauit altare Domino: item Genes. 14. Melchisedech sacerdos Dei altissimi celebratur. Atque tùm etiam erat institutum, offerri Domino fruges vel animalia, quasi in signum gratitudinis erga Deum, pro eiusmodi bonis ab ipso acceptis: partim etiam ad significandum vnicum sacrificium Christi, quo peccata hominum expiarentur. Atque hac prima simplicique ceremoniarum exercitatione patres contenti fuere, donec post per peccata horrenda excæcati homines cœpere quiduis comminisci, diuersos cultus, diuersa idola, vnde paulatim ita degenarunt, vt verus cultus integer nusquàm retineretur, sed omnia superstitionibus esse ntadimpleta. Itaque tunc Deo placuit certis & electis quibusdam, nempe Abrahamo, & posteris præscribere ceremoniam circumcisionis, quæ signum foret fœderis inter Deum & Abraham, omnesque posteros eius, qui & eo signo discreti sunt à cæteris, qui à vero cultu discesserunt, nec non admoniti, se cooptatos in numerum electi populi Dei, vt in vero legitimoque cultu perseuerarent, quem à sanctis patribus suis acceperant. At verò cum idololatria passim vires auctiores reciperet, & superstitionis ritibus mundus esset plenus: præterea sic quoque maxima pars mortalium degenerarat à primæua simplicitate, vt honestatis externæ & ciuilis vix aliquod cerneretur reliquum vestigium, indiesque pericula crescerent, atque idololatria passim confirmaretur: voluit Deus electo suo populo, posteritati videlicet Abrahæ legem præscribere, in qua cum de ritibus ac ceremonijs ad veram religionem pertinentibus, tum de omnibus communis & ciuilis vitæ officijs, id est, & de his quæ erga Deum, & de illis, quæ erga proximum sunt præstanda, plenissimè edocerentur.
units.tr: Therefore, for this reason, from the very beginning of the world God suggested to the minds of men that they should institute certain external rites and ceremonies. There is no doubt that Adam, the first minister of the Word, to whom the promise concerning the blessed seed was made, handed down such things to his sons, who soon passed the same things on, as it were by hand, to others. Thus in Genesis 4, Cain and Abel offer and burn the fruits and firstfruits. In Genesis 8, Noah erects an altar and offers burnt offerings. Similarly, in Genesis 22, Abraham built an altar to the Lord; and in Genesis 14, Melchizedek is celebrated as the priest of the most high God. And at that time it was also the custom to offer to the Lord fruits or animals, as a sign of gratitude towards God for such goods received from him; partly also to signify the unique sacrifice of Christ, by which the sins of men would be expiated. And the fathers were content with this first and simple exercise of ceremonies, until afterwards, men, blinded by horrible sins, began to invent whatever they pleased, diverse worships and diverse idols. From this they gradually degenerated so far that the true worship was nowhere kept whole, but everything was filled with superstitions. Then God was pleased to prescribe to certain chosen persons, namely Abraham and his posterity, the ceremony of circumcision, which would be a sign of the covenant between God and Abraham, and of all his descendants; and by this sign they would be distinguished from others who had departed from true worship, and also be reminded that they had been adopted into the number of God's chosen people, so that they might persevere in the true and lawful worship which they had received from their holy fathers. But when idolatry recovered its strength more and more everywhere, and the world was full of superstitious rites, and moreover the greatest part of mortals had so degenerated from primitive simplicity that scarcely any remaining trace of outward honesty and civil decency could be seen, and dangers grew daily, and idolatry was confirmed everywhere, God willed to prescribe to his chosen people, namely the posterity of Abraham, a law in which they would be most fully taught both the rites and ceremonies pertaining to true religion, and all the duties of common and civil life, that is, both those duties owed towards God and those owed towards neighbour.

units.la: Legem ergo dedit Deus lectissimis præceptis refertam, quorum alia dicta sunt moralia, plurima sanè & primo loco necessaria, vtpote ad docendos homines,quæ fugere in vita, vel expetere debeant, edita, timorem ac fidem in Deum, nec nō charitatem in proximum præcipientia,imò omnia in vnum hunc finem,videlicet dilectionem Dei & proximi tendentia. Alia autem erant quàmplurima, sed omnia reuera ad hunc quoque finem quasi media quædam ordinata: è quibus ad Deum pertinentia vocata sunt ceremonialia, ad perficiendum videlicet ea, quæ externo cultui Dei conueniebant, idonea. Alia verò iudicialia, quibus continebantur, quomodo qui transgresi essent præcepta illa, quæ moralia diximus, punirentur. Exod. 21. Hæc sunt iudicia, quæ propones eis. Ita nihil in hominum vita ad bene recteque viuendum est necessarium,quod non plenissimè sit in lege Domini traditum & expositum.
units.tr: God therefore gave a law filled with most choice precepts. Some of these are called moral, and indeed they are very many and, in the first place, necessary, since they were issued to teach people what they ought to flee from or seek after in life, enjoining fear and faith in God, and likewise love towards neighbour; indeed all of them tend towards this one end, namely the love of God and neighbour. There were also very many others, but all of them really were ordained as certain means towards this same end. Of these, those that pertained to God were called ceremonial, that is, suited to bringing about those things which were fitting for the external worship of God. Others were judicial, containing how those who transgressed the precepts we called moral should be punished. Exodus 21: "These are the judgments which you shall set before them." Thus nothing necessary for living well and rightly in human life has been left untaught or unexplained in the law of the Lord.

units.la: Nos de ceremonialibus potissimum differemus. Cæterum ipsa ceremonialia etsi omnia in genere eiusmodi sint, quæ ad sacros ritus, & ad religionem pertinent, tamen multiplicia considerari possunt, prout etiam multæ res in ijs concurrunt, & circa sacra diuersæ res considerantur.
units.tr: We shall deal chiefly with the ceremonial matters. However, although the ceremonial things are, all in general, those which pertain to sacred rites and to religion, they can nevertheless be considered in many ways, just as many things come together in them, and various matters are considered concerning sacred things.

units.la: Primùm enim ubi sunt ceremoniæ, oportet tibi esse sacerdotes. Ergo ad ceremonias primum inprimis sacerdotum institutio, & ordinatio, unctio, &c. Atq; ita etiam Leuitici septimo, Hæc est unctio Aaron & filiorum eius in ceremonijs: Secundò, ubi est sacerdos, oportet esse sacrificia, oblationes, expiationes, purificationes, qualia multa Numer. 15. & alibi: quare hæc omnia quoq; inter ceremonialia numerabuntur. Tertiò, ubi offeruntur sacrificia, oportet ibi quoq; haberi locum instrumenta, vasa, certosq; perficiendorum sacrorum ritus. Itaq; huc iam pertinent, tabernaculum, templum, altare, candelabrum, thuribula, mare æneum, vestes, &c. cum suis consecrationibus. Exodi 38. Hęc sunt instrumenta tabernaculi testimonij in ceremonijs Leuitarum.
units.tr: For first, where there are ceremonies, there must be priests for you. Therefore, among the ceremonies, the first place belongs to the institution and ordination of the priests, their anointing, and so on. And thus Leviticus 7 says: "This is the anointing of Aaron and of his sons in the ceremonies." Secondly, where there is a priest, there must be sacrifices, offerings, expiations, purifications, of which there are many in Numbers 15 and elsewhere; wherefore all these will also be counted among the ceremonials. Thirdly, where sacrifices are offered, there must also be a place kept for the instruments, vessels and certain rites for performing the sacred things. Hence there now belong here the tabernacle, the temple, the altar, the candlestick, the censers, the bronze laver, the garments, and so on, together with their consecrations. Exodus 38: "These are the instruments of the tabernacle of testimony, in the ceremonies of the Levites."

units.la: Quartò ubi sacerdotes, & ubi sacrificia, atq; huiusmodi necessum est ibi quoque considerari populum seu congregationem, & quædam etiam circa hanc fieri. Huc ergo pertinent circa populum per sacerdotes fieri solita, cuiusmodi inprimis sacramentum circumcisionis, item benedictiones, item iudicium de lepra: Item feriarum institutio, obseruationes temporum, ciborum, lotionum, & huiusmodi.
units.tr: Fourth, where there are priests and sacrifices and things of that kind, the people or congregation must also be considered, and certain things are also done with regard to them. To this belong the things customarily done by the priests with regard to the people: above all the sacrament of circumcision, likewise blessings, likewise the judgment concerning leprosy; also the appointment of festivals, the observance of times, of foods and washings, and such things.

units.la: Itaq; ut discernatur de ijs, quæ sunt religionis, oportet considerare quædam ex parte colentium, nempe & sacerdotes & populum subditum: quædam verò ex parte cultus: quò pertinent sacrificia & instrumenta, præterea & obseruationes. Multas igitur habebat gens Iudæorum ceremonias, & sicut alios omnes populos religione excellebat, ita etiam legum & inprimis ceremoniarum præstantia. Quod ad amplissimam laudem populi Iudaici cedere vult Moses, ubi ait Deuteron. 4.
units.tr: So, in order to distinguish what belongs to religion, one must consider some things on the part of the worshippers, namely both priests and the subject people, and some on the part of the worship, to which belong the sacrifices and instruments and, besides these, the observances. The Jewish nation therefore had many ceremonies, and just as it surpassed all other peoples in religion, so also in the excellence of its laws and especially of its ceremonies. Moses wishes this to redound to the very great praise of the Jewish people, where he says in Deuteronomy 4.

units.la: Scitis, quod docuerim uos præcepta atq; iustitias, sicut mandauit mihi Dominus Deus meus, sic facietis ea in terra, quam possessuri estis, & obseruabitis, & implebitis opere. Hæc est enim uestra sapientia & intellectus coram populis, ut audientes uniuersi præcepta hæc, dicant: En populus sapiens & intelligens, gens magna. Nec est alia natio tam grandis, quæ habeat Deos appropinquantes sibi, sicut Deus noster adest cunctis obseruationibus nostris.
units.tr: You know that I have taught you precepts and justices, as the Lord my God commanded me, so you shall do them in the land which you are to possess, and you shall observe them and fulfil them in deed. For this is your wisdom and understanding before the peoples, so that all who hear these precepts will say: Behold a wise and intelligent people, a great nation. Nor is there another nation so great that has gods drawing near to it, as our God is present to us in all our observances.

units.la: Quæ enim est alia gens sic inclyta, ut habeat ceremonias iustaq; iudicia, & vniuersam legem, quam ego proponam hodie ante oculos vestros? Sed quare voluit Deus tot & tam multiplices ceremonias populo Iudaico præscribere? præsertim, cum oneri potius fuerint, quam honori? Id quod de obseruationibus manifestissimum est, cum vel propter has semper detrectarint gentiles legem Iudaicam recipere? Respondetur: varias in promptu esse causas.
units.tr: For what other nation is so renowned as to have ceremonies and just judgments and a whole law, which I set before your eyes today? But why did God wish to prescribe so many and such manifold ceremonies to the Jewish people, especially since they were rather a burden than an honour? This is most evident regarding the observances, since the Gentiles have always refused to receive the Jewish law, even on account of these alone. The answer is that there are various causes at hand.

units.la: Primam, quòd per huiusmodi ceremonias (id quod de tota lege dici potest) adeò excellentes, inprimis per circumcisionem Deus voluit electum suum populum à cæteris gentibus discernere, sicut proximè citato testimonio ex Deuteronomij quarto satis ostenditur.
units.tr: The first is that through ceremonies of this kind (which can be said of the whole law), so excellent, and especially through circumcision, God willed to distinguish his chosen people from the other nations, as is sufficiently shown by the testimony just cited from Deuteronomy 4.

units.la: Secunda ratio: Ne ad alias ceremonias idololatris usitatas abducerentur, sed in his præscriptis solis & satis multis occuparentur. Vnde non legimus Iudæis præscriptas ceremonias de ritibus & sacrificijs, nisi postquàm promptitudinem suam ad idololatriam declararunt, erigentes sibi vitulum, Exod. 32. id quod Hieremiæ septimo etiam illis obijcitur. Tertia ratio: quòd nullis alijs modis commodius posset exprimi affectus animorum erga Deum, atque huiusmodi ceremonijs: veluti agnitio proprij peccati & reatus, confessio fidei de misericordia obtinenda, gratiarum actio ob beneficia accepta, laus potentiæ & bonitatis Dei: hæc omnia pulcherrimè in sacrificijs, quorum aliud dicebatur sacrificium pro peccato, aliud hostia pacifica, ad gratiarum actionem, vel pro prosperitate obtinenda aliud, aliud holocautoma, quod totum incendebatur, potétiæ & bonitati Dei celebrandæ accommodum.
units.tr: The second reason: lest they be led away to the other ceremonies used by idolaters, but occupied themselves with these prescribed and quite numerous ones alone. Hence we do not read that rites and sacrifices were prescribed to the Jews until after they had shown their readiness for idolatry by raising up a calf for themselves, Exodus 32, which is also thrown at them in Jeremiah 7. The third reason: because the affections of minds towards God could be expressed in no more fitting way than by ceremonies of this kind, such as acknowledgment of one's own sin and guilt, confession of faith in obtaining mercy, thanksgiving for benefits received, and praise of God's power and goodness. All these are most beautifully expressed in the sacrifices: one was called the sacrifice for sin, another the peace offering, for thanksgiving or for obtaining prosperity, another the holocaust, which was wholly burned, and which was suited to celebrating God's power and goodness.

units.la: Quartò, ideo institutæ sunt plures & mirandæ ceremoniæ, ut Christus per illas præfiguraretur, atq; illarum auspicijs homines paulatim ad Christum introducerentur: sicut Apostolus 1. Corinth. 10. Colos. 2. præsentis epistolæ capite 8.9. & passim Euangelistæ etiam satis docent. Quid autem singulis ceremoniarum generibus significetur, prolixius foret explicatu, & in sequentibus id fiet oportunius, ubi Apostolus ipse multas figuras de Christo explicat.
units.tr: Fourth, many and wonderful ceremonies were therefore instituted so that Christ might be prefigured through them, and men might gradually be led to Christ under their guidance, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Corinthians 10 and Colossians 2, and in chapters 8 and 9 of the present epistle, and as the Evangelists also teach everywhere. But what is signified by each kind of ceremony would be too lengthy to explain here; it will be more opportune to do so in what follows, where the Apostle himself explains many figures of Christ.

units.la: Sed iam quæritur. An ne ea fuerit etiam vis ceremoniarum, ut per eas homines iustificari potuerint? Et certè videtur istud potuisse per eas fieri maximè, quando crebrò in lege præscribitur, hostias offerendas pro peccatis, quarum oblatione peccatorum remissio videtur obtineri.
units.tr: But now the question arises: did the ceremonies also have the power to justify men? Indeed it seems they could have done so, especially since the law often prescribes that victims be offered for sins, and by the offering of these remission of sins seems to be obtained.

units.la: Item Itē multa de expiationibus ac purificationibus traduntur, quæ sanè omnia videntur àdremissionem peccatorum & emundationem conscientiarum facere.
units.tr: Likewise, many things are handed down about expiations and purifications, all of which seem to effect the remission of sins and the cleansing of consciences.

units.la: Respondetur simpliciter, neque ceremonias, neque legem vnquam in hoc fuisse edi- tas, ut per eas homines iustificarentur. Atque ut proprie de ceremonialibus respondea- mus, sciendum est, duplicem considerari immunditiam, alteram corporalem & externa, seu carnalem, quæ quidem contrahebatur, aliquid contra præscriptum legis agendo, ma ximè vbi lex ipsa decernebat, immunditiè inde sequi. Eratq; hæc immundities, tantùm quædam nota, quæ homines à sacris excludebat, & sacrorum vsu. Alia verò est immun-ditiës transiens ad animam, ex transgressione præceptorum, quibus fides in Deum, & charitas in proximum debet exerceri: hæc est spiritualis, interna immundities, per quam homines in totum separantur à Deo, necnon damnationem æternam incurrunt. Iam ergo prima illa immunditiës, carnalis videlicet & externa tantùm, ex ceremonialibus inducta, poterat equidem per ceremonias deleri ac tolli.
units.tr: The answer is simply this: neither the ceremonies nor the law were ever issued so that men might be justified through them. To answer properly about the ceremonial things, one must know that two kinds of uncleanness are considered. The first is bodily and external, or carnal, which was contracted by doing something contrary to the prescription of the law, especially where the law itself decreed that uncleanness would follow. This uncleanness was only a certain mark which excluded men from sacred things and from the use of the sacred rites. The other is uncleanness that passes into the soul, arising from the transgression of the precepts by which faith in God and love toward one's neighbour ought to be exercised. This is spiritual, internal uncleanness, through which men are wholly separated from God and incur eternal damnation. Now therefore that first uncleanness, namely carnal and external only, induced by the ceremonial things, could indeed be removed and taken away by ceremonies.

units.la: At verò secundi generis immunditiës non nisi per Christum, qui proprie in hoc ordi- natus est. Vnde huius epistolæ capite nono, Si sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis iuuencæ, aspergens inquinatos, sanctificat ad carnis purificationem: quanto magis san- guis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus, ad seruiendum Deo viuenti? Et paulò ante: In tabernaculo priore offeruntur dona sacrificiaque, quæ non possunt iuxta conscientiam perfectu m reddere cultorem, in cibis duntaxat & potionibus, & diuersis ablutionibus, & iustificationibus carnis, vsque ad tempus correctionis impositæ. Vides sanctificari ad purificationem carnis, item iustificationes carnis, non autem conscientiarum. Et Hebræorum decimo, Non potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata: quare nō per ceremonias legis, sed per solum Christum iustificari homines potuisse: ideoq; qui verè peccatorum remissionem obtinere volebant, debebant intueri in personam Christi, quæ in sacrificijs adumbrabatur, qui verus agnus, tollens peccata mundi, verus hircus portans peccata in solitudinem. Et sacrificia illa tantùm erant signa externa professionis fidei internæ, de expectatione remissionis peccatorum, propter Christum, ad quem & sacrificia, & mentes offerentium dirigi oportebat. Atq; ita intelligendi veniunt loci, qui videntur remissionem peccatorum propter ceremonias polliceri: veluti cùm Leuitici 4. & 5. sæpius præscribitur, pro qualibus peccatis quales offerri debeât victimæ: & semper ferè subijcitur, post expositas ceremonias, orabitq; pro eo sacerdos, & dimittetur ei. Dimittetur ei, videlicet, primū exteriorimmunditiës, propter externum: secundò verò interior expectabitur remittenda, propter Christum, cuius typum gerunt hostiæ illæ, & simul sacerdotes: quam fidem in Christum oportet omnes offerentes habere, si ab interna immunditie volunt liberari. Ergo non in hunc finem latæ leges ceremoniarum, vt iustificarent, sed tantùm propter fines prius positos.
units.tr: But the second kind of uncleanness cannot be removed except through Christ, who was properly ordained for this. Hence in chapter nine of this epistle: "If the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the unclean, sanctify to the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" And a little before: "In the former tabernacle gifts and sacrifices are offered, which cannot make the worshipper perfect as to conscience, but only concern foods and drinks, diverse washings, and justifications of the flesh, until the time of correction was imposed." You see that they sanctify to the purification of the flesh, and likewise the justifications of the flesh, but not of consciences. And Hebrews 10: "It is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins." Therefore men could be justified not through the ceremonies of the law but through Christ alone. Hence those who truly wished to obtain remission of sins ought to look upon the person of Christ, who was foreshadowed in the sacrifices: the true lamb taking away the sins of the world, the true goat bearing sins into the wilderness. Those sacrifices were only external signs of the professed inner faith, of the expectation of remission of sins on account of Christ, to whom both the sacrifices and the minds of the offerers had to be directed. Thus must be understood those passages which seem to promise remission of sins on account of the ceremonies. For example, in Leviticus 4 and 5 it is often prescribed what kind of victim should be offered for what kind of sins, and almost always it is added, after the ceremonies have been set out, "the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him." "It shall be forgiven him": namely, first the external uncleanness, on account of the external; but secondly the internal is to be expected to be remitted, on account of Christ, whose type those victims bore, and whom the priests also prefigured. This faith in Christ all offerers must have if they wish to be freed from internal uncleanness. Therefore the laws of the ceremonies were not enacted for this end, that they might justify, but only for the ends set before them.

units.la: Iam restat explicandum, quando ceremonialia suas vires suumq; vsum amiserint. Nā hoc quidem constanter ab omnibus asseritur, ea per euangelium abrogata esse, neq; post reuelatum euangelium citra peccatum seruari posse. Quæstio igitur est, quo primùm tempore ceremonialia suas vires amiserint, & obseruari non licuerit? Neque verò de nihilo hæc quæstio mouetur. Nam Apostolus ad Galatas quinto, Ecce, inquit, Ego Paulus dico vobis, quòd si circumcidamini, Christus nihil vobis proderit: contestor omnem hominem, qui circumciditur, quòd debitor est totius legis seruandæ: Christus vobis factus est otiosus, quicunque per legem iustificamini. E diuerso autem Actorum decimo-sexto dicitur, quòd Paulus assumptum Timotheum, patre quidem gentili natum, matre verò Iudæa, circumciderit, propter Iudæos, qui erant in locis illis. Item Actorum vicesi-mo primo, Paulus consilio Iacobi, (quoniam apud Iudæos delatus erat Paulus, quòd alienaret Iudæos sparsos apud gentiles à circumcisione & lege Mosaica) rasisse caput, & purificatum cum alijs quatuor viris: quo signo testaretur, se ceremoniarum diligentem obseruatorem. Atque apparet ibi, eam fuisse communem Apostolorum sententiam, vt saltem legales ceremonias obseruarent: à gentilibus verò conuersis nihil aliud ex omnibus legalibus exigeretur, quàm vt cauerent ab his, quæ immolata erant simulachris, & à sanguine, & suffocato, & scortatione: qua de re extat decretum Apostolorum decimoquinto.
units.tr: It remains to explain when the ceremonial things lost their power and their use. For it is constantly asserted by all that they were abrogated by the gospel, and that after the gospel was revealed they cannot be kept without sin. The question therefore is: at what time did the ceremonial things first lose their power, so that it was no longer lawful to observe them? Nor is this question raised for nothing. For the Apostle says to the Galatians in chapter five: "Behold, I Paul say to you, that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. I testify again to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law. Christ is made of no effect to you, whoever of you are justified by the law." On the other hand, Acts 16 says that Paul, having taken Timothy, born of a Gentile father but a Jewish mother, circumcised him, because of the Jews who were in those places. Likewise Acts 21 says that Paul, on the counsel of James (since it had been reported to the Jews that Paul was turning the Jews scattered among the Gentiles away from circumcision and the Mosaic law), shaved his head and purified himself with four other men, by which sign he would testify that he was a diligent observer of the ceremonies. And it appears there that it was the common opinion of the Apostles that at least the legal ceremonies should be observed; from Gentiles who had been converted nothing else would be required out of all the legal things than that they abstain from what had been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. Concerning this there exists the decree of the Apostles in chapter fifteen.

units.la: Præterea verò Petrus apud Antiochiam, vt habetur Galat. 2. vnà cum gentibus cibum sumebat, vbi verò aduenissent quidam à Iacobo, subduxit ac separavit se à gentibus, metuës eos, qui erat ex circumcisione, ac simulabat vnà cū eo cæteri Iudei. Sed Paulus videns, quòd non recto pede incederet ad veritatem euangelij, grauisimè eum coram omnibus reprehendit. Actorum decimo, Petro per visionem oblata sunt omnis generis animalia,
units.tr: Moreover, Peter at Antioch, as we read in Galatians 2, used to eat with the Gentiles. But when certain men came from James, he drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles, fearing those who were of the circumcision, and the rest of the Jews joined him in this pretence. When Paul saw that they were not walking uprightly toward the truth of the gospel, he rebuked Peter severely before everyone. In Acts 10, all kinds of animals were shown to Peter in a vision,

units.la: E lia,iussusque est vesci:at ipse recusauit,dicens:se nunquam aliquid commune vel immū-dum edisse.
units.tr: and he was commanded to eat. But he refused, saying that he had never eaten anything common or unclean.

units.la: Ex his igitur locis in speciem dissidentibus oritur quæstio, Quo tempore ceremo-nialia legis finem habuerint,neque amplius obseruari potuerint? Et,utrùm Iudæi magis fuerint à conuersione sua obligati ad ea, quàm conuersi gentiles? Respondetur ad quęstionem:abrogata fuisse per mortem Domini Iesu Christi legalia, satis id per se manife-stum est,quando,vt Apostolum audiuimus loquentem,abrogatum est præceptum pro-pter imbecillitatem suam, & præterea propter euangelij succedentis præstantiam: sed quo potissimum tempore citra peccatum non potuerint obseruari,dubia videtur & per-plexa admodum quæstio. Disputarunt autem hac eadem de re Hieronymus & Augustinus valde excellenter.Nos sententiam vtriusque explicabimus,& quænam magis arri-deat amplectendaque videatur,ostendemus. Hieronymus quidem ita distinguit,duo vi-delicet tempora iubens considerari:alterum ante Christi mortem:quo quidem ceremo-nialia nec mortua erant, id est, nequaquam abrogata erant, suaque dignitate spolia-ta,sed adhuc obligabant Iudæos,& in sua dignitate debebant retineri: donec per Chri-stum implerentur.quæ typus ceremonialibus erant præfigurata & adumbrata: neque etiam erant mortifera,id est,mortem non adferebant ijs,qui illa obseruarant,imò pecca-to potius obnoxij futuri erant,qui non obseruarent.
units.tr: From these passages, which seem to disagree, arises the question: at what time did the ceremonial laws of the Law come to an end and cease to be observable? And were the Jews more bound to them after their conversion than the converted Gentiles were? To this question the answer is that the ceremonial laws were abrogated by the death of the Lord Jesus Christ. This is clear enough in itself, since, as we have heard the Apostle say, the commandment was set aside because of its weakness, and also because of the greater excellence of the gospel that succeeded it. But the question of the precise time after which they could no longer be observed without sin seems doubtful and very perplexing. Jerome and Augustine have disputed this very matter most excellently. I shall explain the opinion of each, and show which seems more agreeable and worth embracing. Jerome distinguishes as follows, bidding us consider two periods. The first is before the death of Christ. In that period the ceremonial laws were not yet dead, that is, they had not been abrogated or stripped of their dignity, but still bound the Jews and had to be retained in their force until they were fulfilled through Christ, for they were types and shadows prefigured in them. Nor were they deadly, that is, they did not bring death to those who observed them; rather, those who did not observe them would be liable to sin.

units.la: Alterū tempus à morte Christi,post quam videlicet dixisset,consummatum est:quo tempo-re ceremonialia & mortua erant,& præterea mortifera,id est,eiusmodi,vt citra peccatū obseruari deinceps haudquaquam possent. Atque ita,si quid obseruatum videtur ab A-postolis post istud tempus,non verè fecerunt,sed simulatorie,quadamq; pia simulatio-ne, ne videlicet Iudæi offenderentur,aut à fide propterea auerterentur.Et sic Paulus cir-cumcidens,Petrus abstinens,non propter legem id fecerunt,sed pia quadam simulatio-ne.Sed quia non videtur hic res ludicra: & absurdum,tribuere tantis viris,in tali causa, simulationem:ideò Augustinus paulò aliter distinguit, & acutius, & melius,tria con-stituens tempora.
units.tr: The second period is from the death of Christ, after he had said, "It is finished." In that period the ceremonial laws were both dead and, moreover, deadly, that is, of such a kind that from then on they could in no way be observed without sin. Accordingly, if anything seems to have been observed by the Apostles after that time, they did not really do it but did it in pretence, with a certain pious dissimulation, namely so that the Jews would not be offended or turned away from the faith on that account. Thus Paul circumcising and Peter abstaining did not do so because of the law but by a kind of pious pretence. But since this matter does not seem to be a jest, and since it is absurd to attribute dissimulation to such great men in such a cause, Augustine distinguishes somewhat differently, and more keenly and better, setting up three periods.

units.la: Primùm ante mortem Christi,quo neque mortua erant ceremonialia,neque morti-fera:sed obligabant reuera Iudæos,sicut antea semper fecerant.
units.tr: First, before the death of Christ, when the ceremonial laws were neither dead nor deadly, but in truth bound the Jews, as they had always done before.

units.la: Aliud tempus à morte Christi,quo mortua quidem erant,hoc est, non amplius vires habebant,vel aliquem obligabant,non tamen mortifera:quia saltem à conuersis Iudæis poterant adhuc citra peccatum obseruari, modò tamen iustitiam ex illis non concipe-rent,aut ea non ducerent ad salutem necessaria.
units.tr: The second period is from the death of Christ, when they were indeed dead, that is, they no longer had force or bound anyone, yet were not deadly, because at least by converted Jews they could still be observed without sin, provided, however, that they did not conceive righteousness from them or regard them as necessary for salvation.

units.la: Tertium tempus, videlicet reuelati, & satis propagati passim Euangelij per Apostolorum prædicationem:quo quidem tempore omnibus etiam Iudæis tum mortua,tum mortifera facta sunt,nec amplius ab vllis omnino seruari potuerunt,ea ratione,qua àle-ge præcepta erant.Alias si quis alia ratione aliquid tale faciat,nihil refert: veluti tonde-re caput,edere cibos,&c.Atq; hæc distinctio & sententia Augustini ab omnibus maiori applausu recipitur.Pro ratione igitur secundi temporis factum est, vt Paulus Timotheū matre Iudæa natum circumciderit,quòd item ipse caput raserit: Iudæis enim nondum erant mortifera.(Augustinus:Timotheum circumcidit Paulus,ne Iudæi putarentur à le-galibus tanquam nefarijs arcendi. Titum verò non passus est circumcidi,ne gentiles ad ea , tanquam necessaria crederentur compellendi.)Tametsi gentilibus interea nullo pa-cto erat lex obtrudenda,qui potius videbantur euangelium reiecturi in vniuersum,quà legem vllo modo admisuri.Et præterea Apostolus etiam nullo pacto passus fuit, Titū gentilem natum circumcidi,Galatarum secundo, Hoc solum exigebatur à gentilibus, vt cauerent ab his,quæ immolata erat simulachris,& à sanguine,& à suffocato,&à scor-tatione.
units.tr: The third period is that of the gospel fully revealed and sufficiently spread abroad through the preaching of the Apostles. In that period the ceremonies were made both dead and deadly even for all Jews, and from then on they could in no way be observed by anyone in the way in which they had been prescribed by the Law. Otherwise, if someone does something of that kind for some other reason, it makes no difference, as in shaving the head or eating certain foods, and so on. This distinction and opinion of Augustine is received by all with great approval. Therefore, in accordance with the reason of the second period, it came about that Paul circumcised Timothy, who was born of a Jewish mother, and likewise shaved his head, since for Jews these things were not yet deadly. (Augustine: Paul circumcised Timothy so that the Jews would not be thought to be kept away from the Law as impious men. But he did not permit Titus to be circumcised, lest the Gentiles should be compelled to believe these things were necessary.) Yet by no means was the Law to be forced upon the Gentiles in the meantime, since they seemed rather likely to reject the gospel altogether than in any way to admit the Law. Moreover, the Apostle in no way allowed Titus, a Gentile by birth, to be circumcised, as we read in Galatians 2. Only this was required of the Gentiles: that they abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication.

units.la: Neque verò hæc ideò prohibita illis,ut ea in parte viderentur ceremoniarum legalium obseruatores,sed ut ita conuictus Iudæorum cum gentilibus pacatior induceretur, Iu-dæiq; hoc saltem nomine æquanimiter ferret gentiles recens euangelium amplexatos. Iudæi enim execrabantur sanguinem in cibo,& suffocatum . Et quos vidissent vesci ijs, quæ immolata fuerant idolis,crediderint facilè vel adhuc comprobare idololatria, vel certè breui ad eam rediturōs.Pro tempore conueniebat veteri more illa obseruanda prę-cipi:quando ecclesia pòst robustior facta,etiam illud de sanguine non edendo, non am-plius obseruat,edocta,verum esse,quod habetur Matth.15.nihil,quod intrat in os,homi-nem coinquinare:&1. Tim. 4. nihil reijciendum, quod cum gratiarū actione percipitur, & verbo Dei sanctificatur.Fornicatio autem prohibebatur,quòd Gentiles eam inter pec-cata vix numerarint.Dicunt nonnulli,solitos eadem præscribere Iudæos quibuscunque gentibus,quos sibi ad societatem adiunxerant,vel alias potestate subiugarant.
units.tr: Nor were these things forbidden to them so that they might appear to be observers of the ceremonial laws in that respect, but so that the fellowship of Jews with Gentiles might be brought about more peacefully, and so that the Jews might at least on this account bear patiently with Gentiles newly embracing the gospel. For the Jews abhorred blood in food and what is strangled. And if they saw men who had eaten things offered to idols, they would readily believe that they were either still approving idolatry or would soon return to it. For the time it was fitting that these things be commanded in the old manner. Later, when the Church had grown stronger, it no longer observed that rule about not eating blood, having been taught that what enters the mouth does not defile a man (Matt. 15), and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving and sanctified by the word of God (1 Tim. 4). Fornication, however, was forbidden because the Gentiles hardly counted it among sins. Some say that the Jews customarily prescribed these same things to whatever Gentiles they had admitted into their fellowship or had otherwise brought under their power.

units.la: Sanguine uesci
units.tr: Eating blood.

units.la: Sanctificatio ciborum. Fornicatio per prohibita.
units.tr: Sanctification of foods. Fornication forbidden.

units.la: Quòd si quis roget, quare non eadem ratione gentilibus permissum sit, suos quoque ritus ad tempus seruare, ut Iudæis? Respondetur: Non esse simile: nam ritus gentiles simpliciter erant illiciti: ritus verò Iudaici non ita, vtpote à Deo instituti, & utiliter adhuc ad tempus permissi, vt discrimen inter ritus gentilium & Iudæorum propius diceretur.
units.tr: But if someone asks, why was it not likewise permitted to the Gentiles to keep their own rites for a time, as it was to the Jews? The answer is that the cases are not alike. For the rites of the Gentiles were simply unlawful, whereas the Jewish rites were not so, since they had been instituted by God and were still usefully permitted for a time, so that the difference between the rites of the Gentiles and those of the Jews might be more plainly stated.

units.la: Hinc verò liquet, quid dicendum sit de verbis Apostoli ad Galatas quinto: sunt enim ea dicta ad gentiles, quibus nullo pacto erant imponenda ceremonialia: & præterea eo tempore, quo ipsis abundè erat manifestatum euangelium. Deinde sic dicta contra eos, qui vrgebant circumcisionem, quasi ad salutem foret necessaria. Quod ad factum Petri attinet apud Antiochiam, quocunque tandem tempore accideritt, siue ante visum, quo edoctus fuerat, siue ante editum decretum apostolorum, & ut liberum illi, utpote natura Iudæo fuerit, ceremonialia obseruaret, tamè reprehensionem non euadit, tū quòd sciuerit hauddubiè mortua & mortifera, quando communi cibo cum gentibus vsus est, & rursus sic egerit, quasi vel Iudæis significaret non esse mortua, vel Gentilibus adhuc ad salutem necessaria. Oportebat enim, cùm Petrus ita ageret, vel Iudæos vel Gentiles aliquid tale animis concipere. Dum Petrus adeò curiosè præsentibus Iudæis vult ostendere suum erga legem studium, grauissimè offenderit gentiles necessum est. Satius ergo fuisset illi, ceremonialia, quæ sciebat & mortua & mortifera, omittere, quàm contra conscientiam agendo teneras hominum conscientias ita affligere. Sed ex his satis liquet, quamdiu ceremonialia duraverint, & quo tempore citra peccatum obseruari non potuerint.
units.tr: From this it is clear what must be said about the words of the Apostle to the Galatians in chapter 5. For those words were spoken to Gentiles, on whom the ceremonial laws were in no way to be imposed, and moreover at a time when the gospel had already been abundantly made manifest to them. Next, they were spoken against those who urged circumcision as if it were necessary for salvation. As for Peter's deed at Antioch, whatever time it occurred, whether before the vision by which he had been taught, or before the decree of the Apostles was issued, and even if it was free for him, being a Jew by nature, to observe the ceremonial laws, he does not escape rebuke. This is so both because he doubtless knew that they were dead and deadly when he ate common food with the Gentiles, and because he then acted again as if he were signifying either to the Jews that they were not dead, or to the Gentiles that they were still necessary for salvation. For when Peter acted in this way, it was inevitable that either Jews or Gentiles would conceive something of the kind in their minds. While Peter, in the presence of the Jews, so carefully wished to show his zeal for the Law, he was bound to offend the Gentiles very gravely. It would therefore have been better for him to omit the ceremonial laws, which he knew to be both dead and deadly, than by acting against his conscience to afflict the tender consciences of men in this way. But from these things it is sufficiently clear how long the ceremonial laws lasted, and at what time they could no longer be observed without sin.

units.la: Sequitur alia quæstio, Vtrùm post euangelium iam toto orbe reuelatum expediat, in ecclesia multas ceremonias ad imitationem Iudaicæ gentis, institui? Ac certè apparet, posse retineri eas, quæ ad exprimendos affectus pios erga Deum sunt magis necessariæ.
units.tr: There follows another question: whether, now that the gospel has been revealed throughout the whole world, it is expedient to institute in the Church many ceremonies in imitation of the Jewish nation? And indeed it appears that those may be retained which are more necessary for expressing pious affections toward God.

units.la: Respondetur. Agentibus sub gratia atque euangelio nullo modo imponenda esse ceremonias legales, ne Iudaizare videantur, sicut Colossens. 2. Nemo vos iudicet in cibo aut potu, aut in parte diei festi, aut nouilunij, aut sabbatorum, quæ sunt vmbra futurorū. Vbi etiam ratio adiecta est, quare nunc non liceat legales ceremonias in ecclesiam reuocare. Illæ ceremoniæ, inquit, sunt vmbrę futurorum, id est, præsignant res per Christum perficiendas. In hoc proprie erant institutæ. Quamobrem si quis nunc vellet easdem ceremonias reducere, is videtur negare, ea per Christum esse perfecta, quæ ceremoniæ illę significabant facienda. Nihilominus propter rudes animos, qui sine externis spectaculis actionum ceremonialium, non facile ad perficiendum ea, quæ sunt interni cultus, mouerentur, necessum est, in ecclesia quasdam ceremonias retineri: quales nonnullas à Christo & apostolis, deinde sanctis patribus videmus institutas. Nam Christus instituit loco circumcisionis baptismum, qui significaret mortem Christi, & præterea nostram ipsorum mortificationem, imò & resurrectionem Christi, ac nostram in vitæ nouitatem resuscitationem, Roman. 6. Item loco esus agni paschalis instituit sacramentum cœnæ Dominicæ, itidem in suæ mortis, & sui sacrificij, semel pro peccatis omnium oblati, & liberationis nostræ è seruitute diaboli, commemorationem. Ita aliis signis proditur confessio nostra de rebus per Christum peractis, quàm olim idem confitebantur patres, spe rantes res adhuc peragendas. Similiter, in quem vsum constitutum erat obseruatio diei sabbati, Apostoli, ne viderentur velle cogere ad Iudaizandum, sabbatum abrogarunt; & nihilominus vt usus retineretur, subrogarunt diem dominicum pari in honore, propter Christi resurrectionem habendum. Præterea loco vnctionis sacerdotum veteris testamenti, & omnis illius apparatus, successit simplex manuum impositio, per quam & ecclesiæ commendantur ministri, & spiritus Sancti dona suscipiunt. In locum Iudaici paschatis successit nouum nostrum pascha, quo commemoramus immolationem immaculati agni, videlicet Christi. Atque, ut quosdam dies sacros habebant, in memoriam acceptæ legis apud montem Sina: ita nos quoque sacros dies habemus pentecostes, in memoriam missi ad Apostolos spiritus S. per quę lex vitæ mundo illata est. Ita omnia nostra res peractas significant, quas illorum ceremoniæ præfigurabant, adhuc multis post seculis peragendas.
units.tr: The answer is this. For those living under grace and the gospel, the legal ceremonies must in no way be imposed, lest they seem to Judaize, as Colossians 2 says: "Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of the new moon, or of the sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come." Here a reason is also added why it is not now lawful to bring the legal ceremonies back into the Church. Those ceremonies, it says, are shadows of things to come, that is, they foreshadowed the things to be accomplished through Christ. In this they were properly instituted. Therefore, if anyone now wished to bring back the same ceremonies, he would seem to deny that those things which the ceremonies signified were to be done have been perfected through Christ. Nevertheless, on account of rude minds, which without external displays of ceremonial actions are not easily moved to perform the things of inner worship, it is necessary that certain ceremonies be retained in the Church. We see that some of these were instituted by Christ and the Apostles, and then by the holy Fathers. For Christ instituted baptism in place of circumcision, which signifies the death of Christ, and also our own mortification, and indeed the resurrection of Christ and our own rising again into newness of life (Rom. 6). Likewise, in place of eating the paschal lamb, he instituted the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, which is also a commemoration of his death and of his sacrifice, offered once for the sins of all, and of our liberation from the servitude of the devil. In the same way, by other signs our confession is set forth concerning the things accomplished through Christ, just as the Fathers of old made the same confession while hoping for things still to be accomplished.
