Similarly, the observance of the Sabbath day, which had been established for a certain purpose, the Apostles abrogated so that they might not seem to wish to compel people to Judaize; nevertheless, so that the practice might be retained, they substituted the Lord's day, to be held in equal honour on account of the resurrection of Christ. Moreover, in place of the anointing of the priests of the Old Testament and all its apparatus, there succeeded the simple laying on of hands, by which ministers are commended to the Church and receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In place of the Jewish Passover there succeeded our new Passover, by which we commemorate the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb, namely Christ. And just as they had certain holy days in memory of the law received at Mount Sinai, so we too have the holy day of Pentecost, in memory of the Holy Spirit sent to the Apostles, through whom the law of life was brought to the world. Thus all our observances signify things accomplished, which those ceremonies of theirs prefigured, to be accomplished many centuries later.

units.la: Itaque diuersissima sunt omnia nostra à ceremonijs Iudaicis, neque quicquam à nobis huiusmodi obseruatur, eo, quòd lex præceperit: sed quia vsus rerum nostrarum simi le quiddam postularit. Plura deinde addita in ecclesijs, vt videlicet ordinatè omnia fiant, sicut Apostolus prima Corinthiorum decimoquarto ait, atque alijs locis indicata sunt conuenire. Sæpe nouæ ceremoniæ institutæ, eædem postea abrogatæ, vt licet videre in Scriptis patrum: & aliter multa fiebant apud Orientales ecclesias, aliter apud Occidentales.
units.tr: Therefore all our rites are entirely different from the Jewish ceremonies, and we observe nothing of that kind because the law commanded it. Rather, the practice of our own affairs has demanded something similar. Afterwards, several additions were made in the churches so that everything might be done in an orderly way, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 14, and as other passages indicate is fitting. New ceremonies were often instituted and then abolished again, as can be seen in the writings of the Fathers. And many practices were carried out differently among the churches of the East than among those of the West.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: Sed, quo rectius de huiusmodi ceremonijs, alio atque alio tempore in ecclesia instituti possimus iudicare, annotabimus, quae in ceremonijs, vt admittantur, vel non admittantur, sint consideranda.
units.tr: But so that we may judge more correctly about such ceremonies, which have been introduced in the Church at one time or another, we will note what must be considered in deciding whether ceremonies should be admitted or not.

units.la: Primò illud considerandum est in ceremonijs, ne aduersentur verbo Dei, hoc est, ne quic quâ vel repraesentent, vel suggerant animis, cuius doctrina in sacris literis non sit prius exhibita: vel certè, ne sint eiusmodi, quae videantur aliquam impiam opinionem confirmare, vel contra fidem & bonos mores facere, sicut Augustinus ait, scribens ad Ianuarium, verba eius haec sunt: Ecclesia Dei inter multam paleam multaque zizania constituta multa tolerat, & tamen, quae sunt contra fidem vel bonam vitam, nec approbat, nec tacet, nec facit. Sic Apostolus noluit Christianos vesci idolothytis, quando ipsis constabat idolothyta esse. Simile videtur, quod alibi videmus genuflexiones, thus incensum imaginibus, &c. Iussus Cyprianus sacrificare idolis, cum ductus esset ad locum supplicij, monitusque vt consuleret secum, num vellet facere: Respondit, in re tali nulla opus esse consultatione.
units.tr: First, in ceremonies we must consider that they should not conflict with the Word of God. That is, they must not represent or suggest to minds anything whose teaching has not first been set forth in the Holy Scriptures. Or at least they must not be of a kind that seems to confirm some impious opinion, or that runs against faith and good morals. Augustine says this in writing to Januarius, and his words are these: "The Church of God, established amid much chaff and many tares, tolerates many things; yet what is contrary to faith or good living it neither approves, nor keeps silent about, nor does." Thus the Apostle did not wish Christians to eat meat offered to idols when it was clear that the meat had been so offered. Something similar seems to be the case where we see kneeling, incense burned before images, and so on. When Cyprian was ordered to sacrifice to the idols, and was led to the place of execution and advised to consider with himself whether he would do it, he replied that in such a matter there was no need for deliberation.

units.la: Secundò, utiles sint, non otiosae, semper aliquid doceant, nempe, vel, quid per Christum factum sit, vel quid per nos fieri deceat. Cuiusmodi sunt prostrationes nostrae, de quibus apud Patres etiam legitur, quae significant agnitionem peccati nostri, humiliationem, implorationem vel alia: item luminaria apud veteres in baptismo, repraesionem quorumcunque vitiorum notabant.
units.tr: Second, ceremonies should be useful, not idle, and always teach something: either what has been done through Christ, or what it is fitting for us to do. Such are our prostrations, of which we also read among the Fathers, which signify the acknowledgment of our sin, humiliation, supplication, or other things. Likewise the lights used by the ancients at baptism signified the renunciation of all vices.

units.la: Item ieiunium tempore necessitatis institutum significat mortificationem carnis, sine qua verum ieiunium nullum apud Deum reputatur. Sunt huiusmodi ceremoniae quasi elementarij libelli rudium. Augustinus: Quae vtilis non est, perturbatione infructuosa, consequenter noxia est.
units.tr: Likewise, fasting instituted in a time of necessity signifies the mortification of the flesh, without which true fasting is counted as nothing before God. Ceremonies of this kind are, as it were, the elementary little books for the untaught. Augustine: "What is not useful, being unfruitful in its disturbance, is consequently harmful."

units.la: Tertiò, non introducantur sine necessitate, sed praecipuè propter bonum ordinem, sicut Apostolus ipse praescribit. Hinc discretiones officiorum in ecclesia: & singulis ministris suum officium, legendi, docendi, psallendi, suo tempore praescriptum est.
units.tr: Third, they should not be introduced without necessity, and especially for the sake of good order, as the Apostle himself prescribes. Hence come the distinctions of duties in the Church, and to each minister his own office is assigned at its proper time: reading, teaching, and singing.

units.la: Sic ecclesia ordinauit certa tempora baptizandi, dies aliquot festos, templa item, in quibus homines convenirent ad audiendum verbum, ad percipiendum sacramenta. Haec quia necessaria sunt ad bonum ordinem, merito obseruantur.
units.tr: So the Church has ordained certain times for baptizing, several festival days, and likewise buildings in which people may gather to hear the Word and to receive the sacraments. Because these are necessary for good order, they are rightly observed.

units.la: Quartò, danda opera, ne sint nimis multae, aut nimis difficiles: vnde Augustinus ad Ianuarium secundam epistolam scribens, conqueritur, ceremonias Christianorum immodicè excreuisse sua aetate, ut iam Iudaeorum conditione propemodum grauior esset conditio Christianorum: cum Iudaei tantùm grauarentur ceremonijs institutis ab ipso Deo: Christiani verò iis etiam, quas instituerunt nescio quales homines. Et tales ceremoniae etiamsi non sint contra fidem, tamen resecandae sunt. Vide item Augustinum epistola 59. ad Paulinum, vbi respondet Paulini quaestionibus: & quaestione septima explicat copiosè illud Colossens. secundo, Nemo vos iudicet in cibo aut potu. Item libro quaestionum super numeros, quaestione 59. ait, ceremonias & abstinentias tunc ratas esse, cum fuerint rationabiles.
units.tr: Fourth, care must be taken that they are not too many or too burdensome. Hence Augustine, writing to Januarius in his second letter, complains that the ceremonies of Christians had grown excessively in his own time, so that the condition of Christians was now almost heavier than that of the Jews. For the Jews were burdened only by ceremonies instituted by God himself, whereas Christians were burdened also by those which I know not what men have instituted. And such ceremonies, even if they are not against faith, must nevertheless be cut away. See also Augustine, letter 59 to Paulinus, where he answers Paulinus' questions, and in the seventh question he explains at length that passage of Colossians 2, "Let no one judge you in meat or drink." Also in his Questions on Numbers, question 59, he says that ceremonies and abstinences were then valid only when they were reasonable.

units.la: Quintò, non affigatur ceremonijs persuasio iustitiae vel cultus Dei. Frustra me colùt, inquit Christus Matth. 15. mandatis hominum. Si nō potuit talis potestas tribui ceremonijs ab ipso Deo institutis, quanto minus tribuentur ijs, quas ob causas fortasis non adeò necessarias instituerunt homines, non dico quales plerunque.
units.tr: Fifth, let no persuasion of righteousness or of the worship of God be attached to ceremonies. "In vain do they worship me," says Christ in Matthew 15, "teaching the commandments of men." If such power could not be assigned to ceremonies instituted by God himself, how much less will it be assigned to those which men, for reasons perhaps not so necessary, have instituted, and I do not say what sort of men for the most part.

units.la: Sextò: non ita praescribantur, quasi mutari pro tempore & loco non possint. Namita videmus in ecclesia factum saepius, vt alibi alia sint instituta, eadem postmodum abrogata rursus: quae intercciderant denuò restituta.
units.tr: Sixth, they should not be prescribed in such a way as if they could not be changed according to time and place. For we often see in the Church that in one place different things have been instituted, and afterwards the same things have been abolished, and again what had fallen out of use has been restored.

units.la: Haec de qualitate ceremoniarum, & ad iudicandum de ijs, quae recipi debeant, aut reijci, puto sufficere.
units.tr: This is enough, I think, concerning the nature of ceremonies and for judging which should be received or rejected.

units.la: Obligant ne huiusmodi ceremoniae bene constitutae conscientias? Quod ad ceremonias a Christo institutas attinet, inprimisq; baptismum & eucharistiam, quae sic instituta sunt praecepti forma, Nisi quis ederit, &c. Item, quia sunt initia & professionis nostrae signa primaria, nullo modo debent aut possunt praetermitti. De alijs verò responderi potest, quòd minimè conscientias obligent, quando quidè in hoc nequaquam sunt instituta, nec institui possunt, vt conscientijs laqueu inijciant. Quòd si ramè eas transgrediatur aliquis per contemptum ecclesiae, volès ita vnitate dissoluere, ministros verbi, vel doctri nā eorū sanā in contemptū adducere: vel cū offendiculo fratrū infirmorū, hic profectò graviter peccatur. Quomodo Apostolus dicit alibi, se potius nō comesturū carnes in aeternū, quā fratre offendat: 1. Cor. 8. Rom. 14. vide plura. Quaobrē magna prudetia opus est, vbi episcopus vel alius minister idoneus cupiat receptas ceremonias immutare, etiā iustis de causis. Nec sine periculo, aut tumultu solent abrogari vel mutari, quae bene constitutae sunt. Cuius rei exempla plurima sunt in historijs. Ipsa mutatio consuetudinis, inquit Augustinus, etiam quae adiuuat vtilitate, nouitate perturbat.
units.tr: Do such well-established ceremonies bind consciences? As far as the ceremonies instituted by Christ are concerned, especially baptism and the Eucharist, which have been instituted in the form of a command, "Unless a man eats," and so on, and also because they are the first beginnings and primary signs of our profession, they ought in no way to be omitted, nor can they be. Concerning the others, it can be answered that they do not at all bind consciences, since they were in no way instituted, nor can they be instituted, to cast a snare upon consciences. But if anyone nevertheless transgresses them out of contempt for the Church, wishing thereby to dissolve unity, and to bring the ministers of the Word or their sound teaching into contempt, or does so to the stumbling of weak brothers, then truly he sins gravely. As the Apostle says elsewhere, he would rather not eat meat forever than offend a brother: 1 Corinthians 8; Romans 14. See more passages. Therefore great prudence is needed where a bishop or another suitable minister wishes to change accepted ceremonies, even for just causes. Those that have been well established are not usually abolished or changed without danger or tumult. There are very many examples of this in histories. Augustine says that the very change of custom, even one that helps by its usefulness, disturbs by its novelty.

units.la: Tria sunt ceremoniarum genera, vt habet Augustinus ad Ianuarium. Quaedam institutae ab ipso Christo, vt Baptismus, Coena Domini. Quaedam non scriptae, sed traditae ab Apostolis & concilijs, quae & toto terrarum orbe obseruantur, vt obseruatio festorum Paschatis, Ascensionis Domini, Missionis spiritus Sancti. Aliae vero per loca terrarum regiones que variantur, veluti, quod alij ieiunant sabbato, alij nequaquam. Primum genus reuera obligat. Secundum non temere est infringendum, propter pacem publicam ecclesiarum conseruandam. Tertium liberas habet obseruationes, tantum ne libertatem in his demus occasionem carni. In his pariter contentiosa obstinatio, & superstitiosa timiditas periculosa est. Haec Augustinus.
units.tr: There are three kinds of ceremonies, as Augustine has it in his letter to Januarius. Some were instituted by Christ himself, such as baptism and the Lord's Supper. Some are not written down but were handed down by the Apostles and councils, and these are observed throughout the whole world, such as the observance of the feasts of Easter, the Lord's Ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. Others vary from place to place and region, for example, that some fast on the Sabbath and others not at all. The first kind truly binds. The second is not to be broken rashly, in order to preserve the public peace of the churches. The third has free observances, provided only that we do not give liberty in these matters as an occasion to the flesh. In these matters, likewise, stubborn contentiousness and superstitious timidity are dangerous. So Augustine.

units.la: Deformat ne ecclesiam tanta varietas in ceremonijs, quando alibi alias videmus obseruari? Praeterea vbi quis venerit ad aliam regionem, vtetur ne patrijs ceremonijs, an accommodabit se peregrinis? Respondetur. Cum de hac re Ianuarius consuluerit Augustinum, facile est de vtroque definire. Ad primam quaestionem: Varietas in ceremonijs praesertim quae sunt tertij generis, nihil obest: imo, sicut aliae leges alijs conueniunt ciuitatibus, prout situs, mores hominum, copia vel inopia aliquarum rerum, vsus, contractus, &c. postulant: ita interdum pro ruditate hominum, vel peritia, pro loci qualitate, quaedam ceremoniae proderunt, quaedam nequaquam admittentur. Ita tempore Augustini sabbato ieiunabatur Romae, & in Aphrica, Mediolani vero nequaquam. Alibi quotidie communicabant quidam corpori & sanguini Domini, alibi certis tantum diebus. Liberum ergo in his esse debet, variare ab alijs, modo tamen per dissensionem huius modi non perturbetur publica pax ecclesiarum, vel dissoluatur concordia in fide. Hoc enim incommodum si sequeretur ex variatione ab alijs ecclesijs vel dum introducitur, quod aliae vicinae non obseruant: vel dum omittitur, quod aliae obseruant: indignum est propterea scindi vnitatem: ideoque proderit alijs ecclesijs ea in parte confirmari, ne deformitas scandalum pariat.
units.tr: Does such great variety in ceremonies disfigure the Church, when we see different ones observed elsewhere? Moreover, when someone comes to another region, will he use his native ceremonies, or will he accommodate himself to the strangers' practices? The answer is this. When Januarius consulted Augustine on this matter, it is easy to settle both points. To the first question: variety in ceremonies, especially those of the third kind, does no harm. Indeed, just as different laws suit different cities, according to the situation, the customs of the people, the abundance or scarcity of certain goods, usage, contracts, and so on, so at times, because of the rudeness or skill of people, or the character of a place, some ceremonies will be useful and others will by no means be admitted. Thus in Augustine's time people fasted on the Sabbath at Rome and in Africa, but at Milan not at all. Elsewhere some communicated daily in the body and blood of the Lord, and elsewhere only on certain days. Therefore there ought to be freedom in these matters to differ from others, provided only that the public peace of the churches is not disturbed by such dissension, nor the concord in faith dissolved. For if this inconvenience followed from a variation from other churches, either when something is introduced which neighbouring churches do not observe, or when something is omitted which others observe, it is unworthy for unity to be torn apart on that account. Therefore it will be profitable for other churches to be confirmed in that matter, lest the deformity give rise to scandal.

units.la: Ad secundam quaestionem respondeamus, quomodo Ambrosius respondit Augustino, roganti ad votum matris, num Mediolani agenti matri ieiunandum foret sabbato, sicut consueuerat in Aphrica, vel Romae, cum tamen ecclesia Mediolanensis ieiunium eius diei non habet in vsu? Sic autem respondit Ambrosius, loquens de ceremonijs tertij generis. Cum Romam venio, ieiuno sabbato, cum Mediolani sum, non ieiuno. Sic etiam tu, ad quam forte ecclesiam veneris, eius morem serua, si cuiquam non vis esse scandalo, nec quenquam tibi. Quo responso vsus est & Augustinus in simili causa ad Ianuarium.
units.tr: Let us answer the second question as Ambrose answered Augustine, when Augustine asked, at his mother's wish, whether his mother, staying at Milan, should fast on the Sabbath as she had been accustomed to do in Africa or at Rome, since the Church of Milan did not observe a fast on that day. Ambrose answered, speaking of ceremonies of the third kind: "When I come to Rome, I fast on the Sabbath; when I am at Milan, I do not fast. So you too, into whatever church you happen to come, keep its custom, if you do not want to be a scandal to anyone, nor anyone to you." Augustine also used this answer in a similar case, in his letter to Januarius.

units.la: Atq; hoc potiorem, quod non absque iureiurando res acta fit. Nam illi quidem citra iusiurandum sacerdotes facti sunt: hic vero cum iureiurando, per eum, qui dixit ad illum, iurauit Dominus, & non poenitebit eum, tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinationem Melchisedec. Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus.
units.tr: This is the more weighty point, that the matter was not done without an oath. For those indeed were made priests without an oath; but this one was made so with an oath, by him who said to him: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent, You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedec. By so much was Jesus made the surety of a better testament.

units.la: Probat posteriorem causam abrogatae legis, quod videlicet agamus nunc sub spe potiore: seu, quod euangelium sit lege praestantius, duabus rationibus: quas tamen ducit non simpliciter a dignitate vel effectibus ipsius euangelij, sed a praestantia sacerdotij Christi, prae sacerdotio legali, sentiens nimirum, aequissimum esse, vt a dignitate sacerdotij aestimetur dignitas testamenti. Prior itaque ratio haec est, sumpta a forma institutionis sacerdotij Christi. Christus in euangelio institutus est sacerdos adhibito iureiurando, cum in lege intuerentur sacerdotes citra iusiurandum. Ergo sacerdotium Christi praestantius est sacerdotio legali. Priorem partem antecedentis confirmat testimonio psal mi centesimi noni saepius citato. Alteram partem per se notam existimat ex legis historia.
units.tr: He proves the latter ground for the abrogation of the law, namely that we now live under a better hope, or that the gospel is more excellent than the law, by two reasons. He draws them not simply from the dignity and effects of the gospel itself, but from the excellence of Christ's priesthood over the legal priesthood, plainly judging it most fitting that the dignity of the testament be measured by the dignity of the priesthood. The first reason, then, is taken from the manner of the institution of Christ's priesthood. Christ was instituted in the gospel as priest with an oath, whereas under the law the priests were instituted without an oath. Therefore Christ's priesthood is more excellent than the legal priesthood. He confirms the first part of this premise by the testimony of Psalm 109, cited often already. He regards the second part as self-evident from the history of the law.

units.la: Hinc vero infert Apostolus, Tanto potioris testamenti Christum esse sacerdote, quod perinde valet, ac si dicat.
units.tr: From this the Apostle infers that Christ is the priest of a better testament, which comes to the same as saying:

units.la: Oportet testamentum illud esse praestantius, in quo praestantius & efficacius est sacerdotium.
units.tr: That testament must be the more excellent in which the priesthood is more excellent and more effective.

units.la: Ergo, quanto praestantius est sacerdotium Christi, quam Leuitarum, tanto oportet iu dicari praestantius esse euangelium, quam legem. Hoc inquam pacto, ut supra dixi, vult a dignitate sacerdotij colligi dignitatem testamenti, atque inde postea intelligi, propter dignius testamentum succedens, recte dici, legem abrogatam: id quod significatum fuit in eo, Duae rationes petitae a praestantia sacerdotij Christi. 1. ratio a forma institutionis sacerdotij. Christus iusiutus & confirmatus sacerdos per iusiurandum. Confirmatio prioris partis antecedentis ex psal. 109. Posterior patet ex lege. Testamenti dignitas aestimatur a dignitate sacerdotij. in eo, quòd sacerdotes legis instituti fuerunt citra iusiurandum, quasi Deus declarasset per id sibi in animo fuisse, legem abrogare per sacerdotium Christi, siue per euangelium.
units.tr: Therefore, as the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than that of the Levites, so the gospel must be judged more excellent than the law. In this way, as I said above, he wants the dignity of the testament to be inferred from the dignity of the priesthood, and from this to be understood that the law is rightly said to be abrogated because a more worthy testament succeeds it. This was signified in the fact that the priests of the law were instituted without an oath, as if God had shown by this that it was in his mind to abrogate the law through the priesthood of Christ, that is, through the gospel. Two reasons drawn from the excellence of Christ's priesthood. (1) The reason from the manner of the institution of the priesthood: Christ was installed and confirmed as priest by an oath. The first part of the premise is confirmed from Psalm 109. The second is plain from the law. The dignity of the testament is measured by the dignity of the priesthood.

units.la: Satis autem fuisset simpliciter ita argumentari: Sacerdotium Christi est excellentius sacerdotio legali: Ergo & testamentū, in quo Christus est sacerdos, est excellentius legē: Vt antecedens manifestum intelligeretur, ex variis argumentis, quibus supra excellentia sacerdotij Christi præ sacerdotio legali est comprobata: sed placuit Apostolo nouum argumentum producere, quo eminentiam sacerdotij Christi iterum demonstraret, & quidem ex testimonio psalmi centesimi noni iam sæpius citato, & totius adeò disputationis fundamento: ne videlicet aliquam eius testimonij particulam videretur reliquisse, ex qua non deprompserit argumenta præsenti causæ accommoda.
units.tr: It would indeed have been enough simply to argue thus: Christ's priesthood is more excellent than the legal priesthood; therefore the testament in which Christ is priest is also more excellent than the law. The minor premise would have been evident from the various arguments by which the excellence of Christ's priesthood over the legal priesthood has been proved above. But the Apostle chose to produce a new argument, by which he might demonstrate again the eminence of Christ's priesthood, and this from the testimony of Psalm 109, already cited so often and the foundation of the whole argument. He wanted, that is, to avoid seeming to have left out any part of that testimony from which he had not drawn arguments suited to the present case.

units.la: Excutit igitur nunc particulam illam, qua dicitur: iurauit Dominus, & non pœnitebit eum: indeque excellentiam sacerdotij Christi pro legali clarissimè euincit.
units.tr: He therefore now examines that particle in which it is said: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent, and from it he most clearly proves the excellence of Christ's priesthood over the legal one.

units.la: Neque est, quod cauilletur aliquis, nos haud rectè interpretari hæc verba Apostoli, ad concludendum potius præstantiam euangelij præ lege, quàm sacerdotij Christi, præ sacerdotio legali. Nam hanc esse Apostoli germanam sententiam, quam reddimus, perspicuum euadit ex illa acclamationis instar subiecta particula: Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus: quæ reuera nihil aliud sibi vult, quàm ex dignitate sacerdotij Christi deprehendi posse, quòd reuera nunc agamus sub spe potiore, quàm olim agebant illi sub lege: vel, quòd euangelium tali ornatum sacerdotio sit præstantius testamentum, quàm erat lex. Quòd si de natura Christi tantùm voluisset agere, ita intulisset: Tanto potioris ordinis sacerdos factus est Iesus: sed quia de dignitate euangelij agere constituit, dixit, Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus.
units.tr: Nor should anyone quarrel that we do not interpret these words of the Apostle correctly, as if he were concluding the excellence of the gospel over the law rather than of Christ's priesthood over the legal priesthood. That this is the Apostle's true meaning, as we render it, becomes clear from the phrase added like an acclamation: By so much was Jesus made the surety of a better testament. This in fact means nothing other than that from the dignity of Christ's priesthood it can be perceived that we now truly live under a better hope than those under the law once did; or that the gospel, adorned with such a priesthood, is a more excellent testament than the law was. If he had wished to speak only of the nature of Christ, he would have concluded: Jesus was made priest of a more excellent order. But since he intended to speak of the dignity of the gospel, he said: Jesus was made the surety of a more excellent testament.

units.la: At roget aliquis: Unde valet hæc consequentia: Sacerdotium est præstantius: Ergo ipsum quoque testamentum est præstantius? Vnde hoc, vt à dignitate sacerdotij iudicium petatur de dignitate testamenti? Videbatur potius contrarium faciendum, nempe, ut ex dignitate testamenti spectaretur dignitas sacerdotij. Respondetur: Rectissimè Apostolum ratiocinari.
units.tr: But someone may ask: how does this inference hold, that the priesthood is more excellent, therefore the testament itself is more excellent? How is a judgment about the dignity of the testament sought from the dignity of the priesthood? It would seem rather that the reverse should be done, namely that from the dignity of the testament the dignity of the priesthood should be judged. The answer is that the Apostle reasons most rightly.

units.la: Reuocandum autem in memoriam est, quod supra dixit, populum accepisse legem per sacerdotium: præterea, quòd ibidem sic intulerit. Translato sacerdotio, necessum est legis quoque translationem fieri. Quæ ita ab Apostolo dicta sunt, quòd (quemadmodum & eo loco indicauimus) legis summa dignitas in sacerdotio & adiunctis cerimonijs sita fuerit, atque ob sacerdotium potissimum Iudæi reliquis gentibus (quæ interea perinde atque illi moralia ac iudicialia præcepta valde præclara habebant) eminentiores habiti.
units.tr: We must recall what he said above, that the people received the law through the priesthood, and also what he inferred in the same place: when the priesthood is transferred, the law must of necessity be transferred too. The Apostle says these things because (as we also indicated in that place) the chief dignity of the law lay in the priesthood and the attached ceremonies, and it was chiefly on account of the priesthood that the Jews were regarded as more eminent than the other nations, which in the meantime, like the Jews, had very fine moral and judicial precepts.

units.la: Præterea, quòd lex per sacerdotes inprimis tradita, expósita, administrata, conseruata fuerit, & relatiuorum more secum inuicem lex & sacerdotium conferantur, ita, vt, quo in statu fuerit sacerdotium, in eo fuerit & lex, & bene se habente sacerdotio, simul bene habuerit lex: E diuerso autem, vbi concideret sacerdotium, necessum foret simul concidere ipsam legem.
units.tr: Moreover, since the law was first delivered, expounded, administered and preserved through the priests, and since law and priesthood are compared with one another in the manner of correlatives, so that in whatever state the priesthood was, in that state the law also was; and when the priesthood was flourishing, the law flourished too; conversely, where the priesthood fell, the law of necessity fell with it.

units.la: Hæc inquâ, ibi manifestissimè docentur, atq; à dignitate sacerdotij pendere dignitatem legis, clarissimè euincitur. Igitur nunc quoque ex dignitate sacerdotij Christi æquissimum erit æstimare dignitatem euangelij, præsertim quando istud omnem reuera dignitatem ex sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi obtinet: præterea per vnum Christum plenissimè fidelissimeque traditum atque administratum est: quando item nec euangelium sine Christo, nec Christus sine euangelio relatiuorum more potest intelligi, & non nisi manente dignitate Christi sua euangelio dignitas incolumis maneat. Quamobrem rectè & efficaciter argumentatur Apostolus, quòd, sicut sacerdotium Christi præstantius est sacerdotio Leuitico, ita consentaneum est sentire, euangelium præstantius esse lege.
units.tr: These things, I say, are taught most plainly there, and it is most clearly proved that the dignity of the law depends on the dignity of the priesthood. Therefore now too it will be most fair to measure the dignity of the gospel by the dignity of Christ's priesthood, especially since the gospel in truth obtains all its dignity from the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ; moreover, it has been most fully and faithfully delivered and administered through Christ alone. Likewise, the gospel cannot be understood without Christ, nor Christ without the gospel, in the manner of correlatives, and the dignity of the gospel remains unimpaired only while the dignity of Christ remains. Wherefore the Apostle argues rightly and effectively: just as Christ's priesthood is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood, so it is consistent to think the gospel more excellent than the law.

units.la: Quis autè non uidet, quàm subtiliter ista ab Apostolo sint excogitata? Quis nostrum vel suspicatus fuisset, hac ratione potuisse probari euangelij præ lege excellentiam? Tantum de dispositione.
units.tr: But who does not see how subtly these things were devised by the Apostle? Who among us would have suspected that the excellence of the gospel over the law could be proved by this line of reasoning? So much for the arrangement.

units.la: Habemus autem hic mirabile exemplum diligentiæ & fidei in tractandis Scripturis, & quomodo in explicandis testimonijs, quæ de Christo aliquid præclari docent, vel fidei doctrinam continent, singulæ partes debeant accuratissimè examinari & expendi. Nihil reliquit Apostolus in testimonio illo, quod sæpius diximus sumptum pro fundamento & basi totius disputationis de sacerdotio Christi, quod non ostenderit ad amussim suo instituto conuenire: & præterea sacerdotij Christi excellentiam præ sacerdotio legali mirificè extollere.
units.tr: Here we have a remarkable example of diligence and faithfulness in handling the Scriptures, and of how, in expounding testimonies which teach something excellent about Christ or contain the doctrine of faith, each part must be examined and weighed with the greatest care. In that testimony, which we have often said was taken as the foundation and basis of the whole discussion about Christ's priesthood, the Apostle left nothing out which he did not show to fit his purpose exactly, and besides he wonderfully extols the excellence of Christ's priesthood above the legal priesthood.

units.la: Nunc ergo discutit particulam illam, qua dictum est in Psalmo centesimo nono, Iurauit Dominus, atque inde infert, Spem potiorem, id est, Euangelium, eo reuera esse excellentiorem, quòd in eo institutio sacerdotij Christi haudquaquam citra iusiurandū transacta sit: statim animaduertit hanc circumstantiam de iureiurando, & vidit non parum facere ad negotij cuiuspiam certitudinem atque excellentiam, si iureiurando adhibita sit sancita. Quamobrem putauit sibi grauissimum argumentum inde arripiendum, quod sic praecedentibus annectit. id est, in quantum, vel quatenus non sine iureiurando, vt sic ad verbum cohaereat praecedentibus: Erat introductio spei melioris, per quam appropinquamus Deo, idque quatenus non sine iureiurando. Sed interpres illustrandae sententiae causa ita reddidit: Atque hoc potiorem, quòd non absque iureiurando res acta sit, quasi dicatur: Dixi legem fuisse introductionem ad spem potiorem, id est, euangelium. Nunc probatur, quòd euangelium sit spes potior. Eatenus est potior, quatenus sacerdotium eius confirmatum est iureiurando, quod neque quaquà factum est in lege: id quod Apostolus disertis verbis confirmat, nec quid desideretur, pleniorem addens narrationem.
units.tr: Now therefore he examines that particle in which it is said in Psalm 109: The Lord has sworn, and from it he infers that the better hope, that is, the gospel, is truly more excellent, because in it the institution of Christ's priesthood was by no means carried out without an oath. He at once noticed this circumstance of the oath, and saw that it contributes not a little to the certainty and excellence of any matter if it is ratified with an oath added. Therefore he thought he should seize upon this as a most weighty argument, and he attaches it to what precedes in this way: that is, inasmuch as, or in so far as, not without an oath, so that it coheres word for word with what precedes: there was the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God, and this in so far as it was not without an oath. But the translator, for the sake of clarifying the sense, rendered it: And by so much better, because the matter was not done without an oath, as if it were said: I said that the law was an introduction to a better hope, that is, the gospel. Now it is proved that the gospel is the better hope. It is better to the extent that its priesthood was confirmed with an oath, which was in no way done under the law; the Apostle confirms this in plain words, adding a fuller account, so that nothing that is needed is left out.

units.la: Nam illi quidem citra iusiurandum sacerdotes facti sunt) Id quod verum est, si quis consideret sacerdotij legalis institutionem; Exodi capite vicesimo octauo, & aliis locis de ordinatione ac ritibus ordinandorum. At verò Christus institutus est sacerdos cum iureiurando, per eum qui dixit ad eum, Iurauit Dominus, &c. Illud, per eum, qui dixit Ἀνωτὴς, intelligi potest vel de propheta, per quem spiritus Sanctus vaticinium istud de sacerdotio Christi edidit: vel, de Deo Patre, cuius illa sunt verba ad Christum, Tu es sacerdos in aeternum, &c. habet enim hoc testimonium quaedam verba ipsius prophetae narratoria, nempe haec: Iurauit Dominus, & non poenitebit eum: quaedam verò in persona ipsius Dei, vt: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum. Quae variatio personarum cum in aliis Psal mis, tum in illo ipso centesimo nono crebra est: vt, statim initio verba Prophetae sunt, Dixit Dominus Domino meo: Deinde verba Dei, Sede à dextris meis, &c. Rursus verba Prophetae: Virgam virtutis emittet Dominus ex Zion: Quòd si igitur verba ista, Per eum, qui dixit: accipiamus de Propheta, tùm vbi mox additur, ad eum, particula accipietur pro, vt fit sensus, Prophetam ita locutum, non ad Christum, sed de Christo: Iurauit Dominus, &c. quomodo capite primo illud, Et ad angelos quidè dicit, Qui creat angelos suos spiritus.
units.tr: For those indeed were made priests without an oath. This is true if one considers the institution of the Levitical priesthood, in Exodus chapter 28 and other passages on the ordination and rites of those being ordained. But Christ was instituted priest with an oath, through him who said to him [ὁ λέγων πρὸς αὐτόν], The Lord has sworn, etc. The words through him who said can be understood either of the prophet, through whom the Holy Spirit gave this prophecy about Christ's priesthood, or of God the Father, whose words to Christ are You are a priest forever, etc. For this testimony contains some words of the prophet narrating, namely The Lord has sworn, and will not repent, but some words in the person of God himself, such as You are a priest forever. This change of persons is frequent both in other psalms and in this very hundred-and-tenth psalm. For example, at the very beginning the words are the prophet's, The Lord said to my Lord; then the words of God, Sit at my right hand, etc.; then again the prophet's words, The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength out of Zion. If, then, we take the words through him who said as referring to the prophet, the particle to him will be taken as concerning, so that the sense is that the prophet spoke not to Christ but about Christ: The Lord has sworn, etc. In the same way, in the first chapter, And to the angels indeed he says, who makes his angels spirits.

units.la: Iurauit Dominus) Simplex quidem assertio vel promissio Dei sufficere debet, vt fides ei habeatur, quando ipse natura verax, & neminem potens fallere, & semper praestans, quod semel se praestiturum pronunciarit. Sed nostra infirmitas; & propensio ad incredulitatem, in causa est, cur Deo humano more iuramenti vsus tribuatur. Deus hac in parte se accommodat nostrae infirmitati, & labantes animos vult erigere, iuramentū, vbi alias nō deberet, adhibēdo. Sed de iuramento Dei, deq; omni iuramentorum vsu & abvsu supra fusius disseruimus cap.6.
units.tr: The Lord has sworn. A simple assertion or promise of God ought to be enough for us to give him credence, since he is true by nature, can deceive no one, and always performs what he has once declared he will perform. But our weakness and our propensity to unbelief are the reason why the use of an oath, in the human manner, is attributed to God. In this matter God accommodates himself to our weakness, and wishes to lift up our wavering minds by adding an oath where otherwise he would not need to. But concerning God's oath, and concerning every use and abuse of oaths, we have discussed more fully above, in chapter 6.

units.la: Et non poenitebit eum) Hac particula amplificatur & confirmatur non mediocriter iuramenti diuini immutabilis veritas, & necessaria certitudo, adiectaq;, est ad ostendendum, quantum interfit inter promissiones seu assertiones Dei, & promissiones seu assertiones hominum, qui sanè vt aliquid promittant se facturos, atque etiam iuramento adhibito se obstringant, tamen subinde post paululum temporis ducuntur poenitentia, dispiciunt; si quo modo euadere queant; quo minus quae polliciti sunt, perficiant. At verò Deus si quid semel promiserit, siue iuramentum accesserit, siue non, id ratum habet, & haud dubiè suo tempore, & quo placet modo praestat.
units.tr: And will not repent. By this phrase the unchangeable truth and necessary certainty of God's oath are not a little amplified and confirmed. It is added to show how greatly the promises or assertions of God differ from the promises or assertions of men. Men, when they promise that they will do something, and even bind themselves by an oath, nevertheless after a little time are often led to repentance and look for some way to escape, so that they may not perform what they have pledged. But God, if he has once promised something, whether an oath has been added or not, holds it fixed, and undoubtedly fulfils it at his appointed time and in the manner he pleases.

units.la: Etiamsi differat, & non eo modo perficiat, quo nos speramus, tamen citra dubitationem & fraudem ipse tandem quae semel constituerit, perficit. Est autem ab humano more loquendi formula ad Deum translata, ad significandam facti, non autem consilij mutationem. Vt enim homines, vbi se errasse deprehendunt, & mutant factum, dicuntur duci poenitentia, Ita cùm Deus in operibus suis expectatam nobis mutationem edit, nos pro ruditate nostri intellectus hanc mutationem factorum accipimus, quasi Deum prioris facti poeniteat: cùm tamen, sicut nec errasse in priori facto, ita nec poenitere ex posteriori possit intelligi: Quandoquidem mutatio facti succedit, non ex mutatione affectuum, quorum Deus est prorsus expers: sed ex immutabili ipsius prouidētia & voluntate, qua ab aeterno decreuit, talem mutationem in operibus futuram.
units.tr: Even if he delays, and does not bring it about in the way we hope, yet beyond doubt and without deceit he at last performs what he has once decreed. The phrase is, moreover, transferred to God from human speech, to signify a change of deed, not a change of purpose. For just as men, when they perceive that they have erred, change what they have done and are said to be led to repentance, so when God brings about in his works a change that we did not expect, we, because of the crudeness of our understanding, take this change of deeds as if God repented of his earlier deed. Yet, just as he cannot be understood to have erred in his earlier deed, so neither can he be understood to repent of the later one. For the change of deed follows not from a change of feelings, from which God is wholly free, but from his unchangeable providence and will, by which he decreed from eternity that such a change would occur in his future works.

units.la: Igitur tantùm per similitudinem & Metaphoram Deus poenitentia duci intelligitur.
units.tr: Therefore God is understood to be led to repentance only by way of comparison and metaphor.

units.la: Sed, habemus, inquis, manifestos Scripturae locos, qui poenitentiam Deo tribunt: Genef. capite 6, Videns Deus, quòd multa malitia hominum esset in terra, & omnis cogitatio cordis intenta esset ad malum omni tempore, poenituit eum, quòd hominem fecisset in terra. Et pręcauens in futurum, & tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus, delebo, inquit, hominem, quem creaui, à facie terræ, ab homine vsq; ad animantia, à reptili vsque ad volucres cœli. Poenitet enim me fecisse eos. Item 1. Samuel. 15. Factum est verbum Domini ad Samuel, dicens: Poenitet me quòd constituerim Saul regem, quia dereliquit me. Et hic aperte poenitentia Deo tribuitur.
units.tr: But, you say, we have clear passages of Scripture which attribute repentance to God. Genesis chapter 6: Seeing that the wickedness of men was great on the earth, and every imagination of the thoughts of their heart was only evil continually, it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth. And foreseeing the future, and moved inwardly with grief of heart, he says, I will destroy the man whom I have created from the face of the earth, from man even to the beasts, from the creeping thing even to the birds of the heaven, for it repenteth me that I have made them. Likewise 1 Samuel 15: The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying, It repenteth me that I have set up Saul as king, for he has turned back from me. Here repentance is plainly ascribed to God.

units.la: Respondetur: Vt in Deum neq; error, neque ignorantia, neque mutatio cadit, ita nec poenitentia. Si enim poenitentia ei volumus ascribere, id profecto tale erit, a cši dicamus, aut ignorasse aliquid, quod futurum erat: aut praecipitater & inconsiderate aliquid prius statuisse: aut effugere, vbi velit, nō posse: quae valde absurda sunt. Sicut etiā ipse Samuel 1. Reg. capite decimoquinto, suis verbis testatur: Triumphator in Israel non parcet & poenitudine non flectetur, neque enim homo est, vt agat poenitentiam. Et longè ante hoc idem fassus est impius Balaam, Numeror. cap. vigesimosecundo, Non est Deus quasi homo, vt mentiatur, nec vt filius hominis, vt mutetur. Dixit ergo, & non faciet? Locutus est, & non implebit? Ergo nullo pacto dici potest, poenitentiam in Deum cadere.
units.tr: The answer is this: just as neither error nor ignorance nor change can fall upon God, so neither can repentance. For if we want to ascribe repentance to him, it would clearly be such that we would say either that he was ignorant of something that was going to happen, or that he had rashly and inconsiderately decided something beforehand, or that he could not escape when he wished to. These are very absurd. Samuel himself also testifies in his own words, in 1 Samuel chapter 15: The Triumphant One of Israel will not spare, and will not be turned by regret, for he is not a man, that he should repent. And long before this the impious Balaam confessed the same thing, Numbers chapter 22: God is not as a man, that he should lie, nor as the son of man, that he should be changed. Has he said, and will he not do it? Has he spoken, and will he not fulfil it? Therefore it can in no way be said that repentance falls upon God.

units.la: Proinde hæ formulae loquendi per antropopatheiam Deo attribuuntur, propter intellectus nostri ruditatem, vt ita Dei voluntas clarius nobis explicetur, & intelligamus eum non talem, qualis ipse in se est, sed qualis à nobis ex factis suis sentitur, quas locutiones cùm audimus, non debemus imaginari in Deo talem affectum, mutationem, & perturbationem, qualis cernitur in iratis hominibus: sed potius animo concipere inde, quod velit iudicium in peccantes exercere. Eodem modo si audimus, Deum duci poenitudine, significatur factorum mutatio, quia videlicet solent homines, dum facta sua mutant, testari, quòd poeniteat eos facti alicuius. Mutatio facti apud homines significat, quòd aliquid melius cogitarint, quàm prius: Deinde, quòd doleant de priori: atque ita dicuntur duci poenitentia. At in Deo non est simile. Mutat quidem factum, non tamen propter praeeuntem correctionem, vel poenitentiam, vel alio modo mutatos affectus, sed propter prouidentiam ab æterno, & consilium immutabile, quo quod semel ordinauit, efficit & prosequitur, vtcunque apud homines appareat subita varietas & quasi poenitentia. Breuiter & argutè Augustinus de Ciuitate libro decimoseptimo, capite septimo, vbi legitur, quòd poeniteat eum, mutatio rerum significatur immutabili praescientia diuina manente. Vbi ergo non poenitere dicitur, non mutare intelligitur.
units.tr: Accordingly, these forms of speech are attributed to God through anthropopatheia, on account of the crudeness of our understanding, so that God's will may be explained to us more clearly, and we may understand him not as he is in himself, but as he is perceived by us from his deeds. When we hear such expressions, we ought not to imagine in God such an affection, change, or perturbation as is seen in angry men; rather we should conceive from them that he wishes to exercise judgment upon sinners. In the same way, when we hear that God is led to repentance, a change of deed is signified, because men, when they change their deeds, are accustomed to declare that they repent of some deed. Among men a change of deed signifies that they have thought something better than before, and then that they grieve over the earlier deed, and so they are said to be led to repentance. But in God it is not similar. He does indeed change his deed, yet not because of a preceding correction, or repentance, or affections changed in some other way, but because of his providence from eternity and his unchangeable counsel, by which he brings about and carries through what he has once ordained, however sudden a variation and something like repentance may appear among men. Augustine says this briefly and acutely in the seventeenth book of The City of God, chapter 7, where it is read that it repents him: a change of things is signified while the divine foreknowledge remains unchanged. Therefore where it is said that he does not repent, it is understood that he does not change.

units.la: Sed clarius, vbi enarrat hæc ipsa verba testimonij ab Apostolo citati, Iurauit Dominus & non poenitebit eum: Quid est, inquit, non poenitebit eum? Non mutabit. Non enim dolorem poenitentiae patitur Deus, aut in aliquo fallitur, vt velit corrigere, in quo errauit. Sed, quomodo hominem cùm poenitet, mutare vult, quod fecit: sic vbi audis, quia poenitet Deum mutationem ipsam spera. Aliter illam facit Deus, quamuis nomine poenitentiae appellet, aliter tu. Tu enim facis, quia errareras: illæ autem facit, quia vindicat, quia liberat. Et paulo post: Cùm ergo mutat opera sua per incommutabile consilium suum, propter ipsam non consilij, sed operis mutationem poenitere dicitur. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: But Augustine says it more clearly where he explains these very words of the testimony cited by the Apostle, The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: What is, he says, will not repent? It means he will not change. For God does not suffer the grief of repentance, nor is he deceived in anything, so that he should wish to correct what he has erred in. But as a man, when he repents, wishes to change what he has done, so when you hear that God repents, understand the change itself. God makes that change in one way, although he calls it by the name of repentance, and you make it in another way. For you act because you had erred; he acts because he avenges, because he delivers. And a little later: Therefore, when he changes his works by his unchangeable counsel, he is said to repent, not on account of any change of counsel, but on account of the change of the work itself. Thus far there.

units.la: Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus. Quare hisce verbis acclamationem subiecerit, satis est à nobis comonstratum. Est autem nobis harum vocum reddeda ratio. Aduectendum, vbi interpres ponit testamentum, græcè haberi vocem διαθήκη, quæ vox passim occurrit & apud septuaginta, vt Genesis capite decimoseptimo, Exodi vigesimoquarto, Iosuae vigesimoquarto, Hieremiae trigesimoprimo. Cui tamen respondet in Hebreo vox בְּרִית, quae significat proprie foedus, pactum, pacis certitudinem ac sponsionem, adeoque confirmationem, à verbo כָּרַת pepigit, foedus percusit.
units.tr: Jesus became the surety of a far better covenant. Why he added this acclamation with these words has been sufficiently shown by us. But we must now give an account of these words. It should be noted that where the translator has "testamentum," the Greek has the word διαθήκη [diathēkē], which occurs throughout and also in the Septuagint, for example in Genesis 17, Exodus 24, Joshua 24 and Jeremiah 31. In Hebrew, however, the corresponding word is בְּרִית [berith], which properly means covenant, compact, the assurance and pledge of peace, and so confirmation, from the verb כָּרַת [karath], "he made a covenant, he struck a covenant."

units.la: Verum quidem est, διαθήκη græcis non tantum significare pactum aut foedus, sed etiam testamentum: neque etiam omninò malè rem ipsam, quæ de foedere inter Deum & homines in Scripturis intelligitur nomine testamenti significari, quomodo praesentis epistolae cap. 9. & Galat. 3. dicitur, vbi testamentū est, debere intercedere mortem testatoris, & Christus moriturus instituit testamentum in suo sanguine: tamen plurimis in locis multo significantius redderetur nomine pacti seu foederis, quàm nomine testamenti: id quod citra dubitationem pacti seu foederis, quàm nomine testamenti: id quod citra dubitationem plurimi possunt, potissimumq; in libris veteris instrumenti, obseruare. Et sumpta est etiam foederis appellatio ab humano more. Quemadmodum enim confoederari dicuntur subditi cum principe, quādo inuicē fidem promittunt, subditi quidem quod parebunt ipsius iustis legibus, quòd tributa & alia necessaria praestabunt: princeps verò, quòd eos pro virili tuebitur, publicâ pace domi & foris seruari procurabit, hostes armis propul-
units.tr: It is true that διαθήκη in Greek signifies not only a compact or covenant but also a testament. Nor is it altogether wrong that the thing itself, which in Scripture is understood as the covenant between God and men, is in this way signified by the name of testament, as in chapter 9 of this present epistle and in Galatians 3, where it is said that where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene, and that Christ, about to die, instituted the testament in his own blood. Nevertheless, in very many places it would be rendered much more significantly by the name of pact or covenant than by the name of testament. Very many people can observe this without doubt, and especially in the books of the Old Testament. The term covenant was also taken from human custom. For just as subjects are said to be confederated with a prince when they mutually promise faith, the subjects indeed that they will obey his just laws and furnish tributes and other necessary things, but the prince that he will defend them as far as he can and will take care that public peace is kept at home and abroad, repelling enemies by arms,

units.la: 1. Obligatio inter reges et subditos. propulsando, domesticos legibus coercendo: vel etiā principes cum principibus dicun tur percutere foedus, sicut Abrahā cum regibus, & alij saepius fecisse leguntur. Similiter Deus dicitur inire foedus cum sanctis, quando videlicet Deus promittit, se fore illis vere Deum, id est, protectore, seruatorem, & sancti vicissim promittunt, se fore illius populum, id est, subditos & obreperantes eius praeceptis. Proinde, quia Deus hanc suā voluntate saepius aperuit hominibus, & vicissim ab illis fidem & obedientiā exegit, quoties id fecisse olim legitur apud Patres, toties vetus pactū confirmasse dicitur, & omnia illis temporibus inter Deum & patres acta, ad vetus testamentū referuntur. At vero vbi Deus misit filium suum in mundum, aliud pactū cum hominibus inijt, aliasque conditiones hominibus, qui vellent foederis huius esse participes, praescripsit. Vbi enim olim exegit circumcisionem, & quarundam legum obseruationem, hic quaedam certe signa externa instituit, cuiusmodi est baptismus & coena Domini, sed potissimū fidem in Christū exegit. Et omnia, quae ab hoc tempore facta sunt, ad nouū foedus sunt referenda. Non opus est nunc pluribus de his agamus. Satis est de voce testamenti ista nunc admonuisse: quae in hoc à nobis dicta sunt, quòd foederis vel pacti significatio mihi videretur hic retinenda, idq́; eo magis, quòd Christus vocatur hic huius διαθήκης ἔγγυος, id est, sponsor seu fideiussor. Nam à ratione foederum appellatio isthaec Christo hic tribuitur. Vt enim solent, vbi foedera percutiuntur, praeter conditiones de seruanda pace praescriptas, etiam vtrimque vel pignora deponi, quae amittent, qui primi contra fidem datam foedus ruperint, vel certe obsides ac fideiussores constitui: Ita intelligendus est Christus huius noui foederis, quod pater pepigit cum hominibus, quasi obses seu fideiussor inter vtramque partem constitutus, qui nos quidem certos facit de accipiendis bonis per patrem promissis, dum induit nostram carnem, nec non mortem ex voluntate patris subijt: rursus vero apud patrem pro nobis fideiubens, dum peccata nostra omnia in se recepit, pro nostris transgressionibus satisfacit, & nunc adhuc per omne tempus pro nobis intercedit, preciosum suum sanguinem quasi sigillum, Chirographum, & pignus pro conseruanda pace apud vtramque partem depositū, proprie ad hoc diuinitus ordinatus, vtpote in hoc duplicis naturae dignitate praeditus, per diuinam videlicet partes agens ipsius Dei, per humanam vero partes agens hominum. Singulari igitur consilio ab apostolo factum est, quòd Christum vocauerit Sponsorem noui foederis, euangelici, cùm in foedere legis reuera nequaquam talis sponsor seu mediator extiterit. Huc pertinent omnes illi loci, quibus Christus mediator inter Deum & homines, aduocatus, patronus, pacifi catae, pax, iustificatio, iustitia nostra describitur. Illi vni omnia bona ista spiritualia debent ferri accepta, quando ipse foederis huius sponsor est, efficiens, vt pater ea nobis donet. Ac valde consolatorium est, intueri in hanc descriptionē, qua Christus proponitur nobis sponsor, fideiubens, & certos nos reddens de bonis, quae Deus pater promisit, accipiendis. Si metuis, Deum patrē tibi non daturum promissa bona, en Christum sponsorē, qui pro te intercedit vnā cum spiritu Sancto. Si rursus Deus pater peccatis tuis offensus videtur, pro sua iustitia inflicturos tibi poenas, en Christum iterum, qui pro te fideiubet apud patrem, mitigat iratum, pro peccatis tuis satisfacit.
units.tr: 1. Obligation between kings and subjects. repelling, and restraining domestic offenders by laws. Or again, princes are said to strike a covenant with princes, as Abraham did with kings, and as others are read to have done quite often. Similarly God is said to enter into a covenant with the saints, when God promises that he will truly be their God, that is, their protector and saviour, and the saints in turn promise that they will be his people, that is, his subjects and obedient to his precepts. Therefore, since God has very often revealed this his will to men, and in turn has required faith and obedience from them, as often as this is read to have been done of old among the Fathers, so often the old covenant is said to have been confirmed, and all the things done in those times between God and the fathers are referred to the Old Testament. But when God sent his Son into the world, he entered into another covenant with men and prescribed other conditions for those men who wished to be partakers of this covenant. For where he formerly required circumcision and the observance of certain laws, here he instituted certain external signs, such as baptism and the Lord's Supper, but above all he required faith in Christ. And all the things that have been done since this time are to be referred to the New Covenant. There is no need to say more about these matters now. It is enough to have given this admonition about the word testament; what has been said here by us is that the meaning of covenant or pact seems to me to be retained here, the more so because Christ is here called the ἔγγυος [engyos] of this διαθήκη [diathēkē], that is, surety or guarantor. For this designation is applied to Christ here from the nature of covenants. For, as is customary when covenants are struck, besides the conditions prescribed for keeping the peace, pledges are also deposited on both sides, which will be forfeited by those who first break the covenant against the faith given, or at least hostages and sureties are appointed. In this way Christ must be understood as the surety of this new covenant, which the Father made with men, constituted as a kind of hostage or guarantor between both parties. He indeed makes us certain of receiving the good things promised by the Father, since he put on our flesh and underwent death by the will of the Father; and again, as surety before the Father on our behalf, since he took all our sins upon himself, makes satisfaction for our transgressions, and even now at all times intercedes for us, having deposited his precious blood before both parties as a seal, a handwriting, and a pledge for keeping the peace, being divinely ordained specifically for this purpose, since in this he is endowed with the dignity of a twofold nature, acting through the divine nature as God himself, and through the human nature as man. Therefore it was by a singular counsel that the apostle called Christ the Surety of the New, that is, the Gospel, covenant, since in the covenant of the law there was in truth no such surety or mediator. To this belong all those passages in which Christ is described as mediator between God and men, advocate, patron, our peacemaker, peace, justification and righteousness. All these spiritual goods are to be credited to him alone, since he himself is the surety of this covenant, bringing it about that the Father gives them to us. And it is very comforting to look upon this portrayal, in which Christ is set before us as surety, standing as guarantor and making us certain of receiving the good things that God the Father has promised. If you fear that God the Father will not give you the promised goods, behold Christ the surety, who intercedes for you together with the Holy Spirit. If again God the Father seems offended by your sins and about to inflict punishments upon you in accordance with his justice, behold Christ again, who stands surety for you before the Father, calms the angry One, and makes satisfaction for your sins.

units.la: NON ESSE HIC ALLEGORIAS, AC DE RATIONE tractandarum Allegoriarum:
units.tr: THAT THERE ARE NO ALLEGORIES HERE, AND ON THE METHOD OF TREATING ALLEGORIES:

units.la: Quartò est & hoc adijciendum, argumenta haec, quibus iam probatum est testimonium illud, Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech, conuenire Christo, non esse per Allegoriam seu similitudinem collecta, vt quidam suspicati sunt. Nam hoc pacto parum essent firma, possentque ad aliam causam pari iure petrahi: Sed simpliciter iuxta sensum historicum seu grammaticum esse exposita.
units.tr: Fourthly, this must also be added: the arguments by which it has already been shown that the testimony Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek belongs to Christ were not drawn by allegory or similitude, as some have suspected. For in that case they would be weak, and the same reasoning could be dragged to some other purpose with equal right. They are instead expounded simply according to the historical or grammatical sense.

units.la: Nam reuera totus ille Psalmus simpliciter & sensu grammatico acceptus continet vaticinium de Christo, depingitq́; propriē Christi regnum & sacerdotium, quemadmodum satis expositum est, semel capite primo huius epistolae, & praeterea capite quinto, vt neq; Dauidi, neq; aliis personis accommodari possit. Posteriora autem ista argumenta simplici ter & sensu grammatico collecta sunt, ad confirmandū clarius & certius, proprie de Christo accipiendū illud testimonii, & minutissimas quasq; partes pulcherrimè Christo conuenire, vt recte dicat, sacerdote esse secundū ordine Melchisedech. Quare solida magnūq; podus habetia sunt haec argumenta, nec infringi vel reijci quoquo pacto possūt. Quod & statuendū est de argumētis in tota hac disputatione sequetib.quę fere omnia vel ex causis, vel ex effectibus, vel ex definitionib vel ex contrarijs, aut similibus locis ducta sunt, sicut semp annotabimus, vt nō tantum in specie pbabilia, sed simpliciter certa & evidentia hatia haberi ea deceat. Sed quò clarius istud perspiciatur, lubet de allegorijs earundemque vsu in medium quaedam producere.
units.tr: For indeed that whole Psalm, taken simply and in its grammatical sense, contains a prophecy about Christ, and portrays properly the kingdom and priesthood of Christ, as has been sufficiently explained once in the first chapter of this epistle and again in the fifth, so that it cannot be applied either to David or to other persons. The later arguments, however, are gathered simply and in the grammatical sense, to confirm more clearly and certainly that the testimony is rightly understood of Christ, and that even the smallest parts agree most beautifully with Christ, so that it rightly says he is a priest after the order of Melchizedek. Therefore these arguments have solid and great weight, and they cannot be overturned or rejected in any way. This must be held also of the arguments in the whole of this discussion that follow, nearly all of which are drawn from causes, effects, definitions, contraries, or similar topics. As I shall always note, these are to be regarded not merely as probable in kind, but as simply certain and evident. But so that this may be seen more clearly, it is good to bring forward some points about allegories and their use.

units.la: Sacra Scriptura, sicut & quodcunque ferè scripti genus, varie exponi solet. Primum sensu grammatico hiue historico: vbi videlicet simplex & primaria vocum significatio spectatur, secundū quam certa sententia eligitur, vt id dici & significari intelligatur, quod communi loquendi more verba significant. Haec ratio exponendi primo semper loco inquirenda est, priusquam longius progredi fas sit.
units.tr: Sacred Scripture, like almost every kind of writing, is commonly interpreted in various ways. First, by the grammatical or historical sense, where the simple and primary meaning of the words is considered, and by which a definite sense is chosen, so that what the words signify in common usage is understood to be said and meant. This method of interpretation must always be sought first, before it is right to proceed further.

units.la: Secundò exponitur oratio sensu paulò remotiore, siue spirituali, cùm videlicet praeter praecedentem exponendi rationem excerpitur inde aliquid vel pertinens ad formandam vitam seu mores: vel in rebus diuinis arcanum quiddam significans: vel alia ratione aliud quippiam docens atque innuens, quàm quod primo aspectu verba praese ferunt, quodque sequi inde aliquo modo magis apparet, quàm simpliciter notatur. Istud verò varijs modis fit, ac singuli sua quadam appellatione distinguuntur, & in eis allegoria quoque locum suum obtinet, praesertim in sacrarum literarum enarratione.
units.tr: Secondly, a passage is expounded in a somewhat more remote sense, or spiritual sense, when, besides the preceding method of interpretation, something is drawn from it either pertaining to the forming of life and morals, or signifying some hidden thing in divine matters, or teaching and hinting at something else by some other means than what the words express at first sight, and what appears to follow from them in some way rather than being plainly stated. This is done in various ways, and each is distinguished by its own name, and allegory also has its place among them, especially in the exposition of the sacred letters.

units.la: Quibus igitur, & quot modis istud fit? Duobus potissimum. Postquam enim habita est perspicua sententia iuxta sensum grammaticum, cuius ratio ex artificio grammatico, dialectico, rhetorico, petitur: venitur proximè ad notandum, quae pertinent ad mores, & disciplinam, vt de virtutibus aut vitijs, de expetendis vel fugiendis in communi vita, aliqua doctrina referatur. Hanc rationem vocarunt quidam Tropologiam, licet voce non admodum accommoda: Nam etsi τρόπος graecis significat & Schema, & modum, & vitam seu mores hominis, tamen ea vox vsitatius nobis figuratam locutionem exprimit: vt, vbicunque vox aliqua à natiua significatione deflectitur ad vicinam, Tropologia ibi esse rectè dicatur. Vnde de Tropis Schematibus libellos suos Rhetores inscripserunt: qui hoc discriminis inter Schemata & Tropos ponunt, quòd Tropi potissimum sint in vocibus, Schemata in orationis gestu. Nos interea docendi ergò etiam Tropologiam dicemus: etiamsi rectius Moralem seu Ethicen quis dicere possit, quòd, quae ad vitam moresque formandos pertinent, comprehendat & circa ea versetur. Exemplum, vbi legitur historia inebriationis Loth, adijcitur, quàm detestanda sitebrie tas & crapula, potissimum in Senibus: quàm horrenda deinde flagitia eam comitentur: quales eius effectus, &c. Chrysostomus, & omnes verè recentiores hanc explicandi Scripturas rationem, vt vitae hominum emendandae pernecessariam & vtilissimam diligenter ample stuntur.
units.tr: By what means, and in how many ways, is this done? Chiefly in two. For once the plain sense has been established according to the grammatical sense, whose method is taken from the grammatical, dialectical and rhetorical arts, one comes next to note what pertains to morals and discipline, so that some teaching is drawn out about virtues or vices, or about what is to be sought or avoided in common life. Some have called this method tropology [τρόπος], though the word is not altogether suitable. For although in Greek tropos signifies both a figure and a manner, and also the life or morals of a man, yet that word is more commonly used by us for a figurative mode of speaking. So wherever a word is turned from its natural meaning to a neighbouring one, one may rightly say that tropology is present there. Hence the rhetoricians wrote their books on tropes and figures, and they draw this distinction between figures and tropes: that tropes are chiefly in words, figures in the arrangement of the speech. For our part, for the sake of teaching, we shall also call it tropology, although one might more correctly call it moral or ethical, because it embraces what pertains to forming life and manners and is concerned with them. For example, where the history of Lot's drunkenness is read, there is added how detestable drunkenness and gluttony are, especially in the old; how dreadful the crimes that accompany it are; what its effects are, and so on. Chrysostom, and all truly later writers, carefully enlarge upon this method of expounding the Scriptures as most necessary and most useful for amending the lives of men.

units.la: Alter modus est, cùm facta quaedam, vel sententiae aliter accipiuntur, quàm sonant, accommodantur & conferuntur cum alijs rebus similitudinem cum illis habentibus, maximèque cum his, quae in Christo vel ecclesia eius corpore cernuntur, quaeque alijs in locis Scripturae simpliciter & sine figuris sunt proposita: veluti, cùm quae in lege gesta describuntur à quibusdam sanctis patribus, accommodantur ijs, quae in Euangelio sunt per Christum, vel per ecclesiam peracta, ostenditurque, maximam similitudinem inter se habere. Haec interpretatio confirmatur eo, quod habetur 1. Corinthiorum 10. Haec omnia figurae contingerunt illis, scripta autem sunt propter admonitionem nostri. Et Romanorum 15. Quaecunque scripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam praescripta sunt, vt per patientiam & consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. 2. Timoth. 3. Omnis doctrina diuinitus inspirata, & vtilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quae est in iustitia, vt integer sit Dei homo, ad omne opus bonum apparatus. Exemplum Ephesiorum 5. Coniunctio viri & mulieris magnum sacramentum dicitur Christi & ecclesiae. Item 1. Corinthior. 10. Mare, nubes, baptismum, Manna, coenam dominicam significare ait Apostolus. Allegorica est interpretatio de baptismo Roman. 6. Hanc porrò explicandi rationem vocant allegoriam, in qua Origenes apud Graecos, & Ambrosius apud Latinos, maximè, penè & nimium se exercuerunt.
units.tr: The other method is when certain deeds or sayings are understood otherwise than they sound, and are applied and compared with other things that have a likeness to them, and especially with those things that are seen in Christ or in his body, the Church, and that are set forth simply and without figures in other places of Scripture. For example, when certain holy Fathers apply to the things done under the law what is done in the Gospel through Christ or through the Church, and show that they have the greatest likeness to one another. This interpretation is confirmed by what is found in 1 Corinthians 10: "All these things happened to them as figures, but they were written for our admonition." And Romans 15: "Whatever things were written before were written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope." 2 Timothy 3: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." An example is Ephesians 5: "This is a great sacrament, of Christ and the Church, the union of man and woman." Likewise 1 Corinthians 10: the Apostle says the sea, the cloud, baptism, the manna and the Lord's Supper signify something. The interpretation of baptism in Romans 6 is allegorical. This method of explanation they call allegory, and in it Origen among the Greeks, and Ambrose among the Latins, especially, and almost excessively, exercised themselves.

units.la: Addiderunt nonnulli tertium modum explicandi Scripturam, cùm videlicet sic accipitur Scripturae sententia quaepiam, vt per eam praeter verborum significationem, dicatur significari aliquid pertinens ad coelestem gloriam, post hanc vitam expectandam, & mysteria Trinitatis seu diuinae naturae, & à vihbilibus eatur ad inuisibilia, vt 2. Corinth. 3. à speculo & aenigmatae ad Dei claritatem ascendit Apostolus. Ioannes ab aqua ascendit ad Spiritum. Hanc ratione Dionysius, & qui eum secuti sunt, vocant ἀναγωγὴν, quasi dicas Subduction̄e: Sed reuera ab allegoria non est secernenda, id quod ipse quoq; Dionysius non dissimulat. Huc pertinet, quod Gennadius in catalogo illustriū virorum scripbit de Rufino, quòd benedictionem Iacob super patriarchas, triplici, id est, historico, morali, & mystico sensu exposuerit. Sanè Augustinus libro de Vtilitate credendi ad Honoratum fatum cap.3. & rursus libro imperfecto de Genesi ad literam cap.2. ait, quartam esse sacrarum literarum exponendarum rationem. Priorem secundū historiam,cùm videlicet dicetur,quid scriptum, aut quid gestum sit, quid non gestum, sed tantùmodo scriptum, quasi gestū sit: veluti cùm Christus Matthæi capite duodecimo. citat ex 1. Regum 21. de Dauide,quòd comederit panes propositionis. Nos etiam vocauimus sensum historicum cum seu grammaticum. Altera ratio secundum æticologiam,quàdo ostenditur,quid,qua de causa,vel factum,vel dictum sit. Exemplum Matth.19. Vbi Christs prohibuit repudium vxoris,excepta fornicationis causa, alij rogarunt, quare Moses ergo permisisset libellum repudij,causam huius reddidit Christus,propter duriciam cordis vestri. Non puto distinguendam rationem hanc à præcedenti. Tertia ratio secundum Analogiam, qua vtriusque testamenti congruentia demonstratur. Mihi istud videtur idem,quod paulo post dicturi sumus de typo.
units.tr: Some have added a third way of expounding Scripture, when a certain sentence of Scripture is so taken that, beyond the meaning of the words, something is said to be signified that pertains to heavenly glory to be expected after this life, and to the mysteries of the Trinity or of the divine nature; and one passes from visible things to invisible, as the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 3 rises from the mirror and the enigma to the brightness of God; John rises from the water to the Spirit. Dionysius, and those who followed him, call this method anagogē [ἀναγωγὴν], as if to say "leading up"; but in truth it is not to be separated from allegory, which Dionysius himself does not deny. To this belongs what Gennadius wrote in his catalogue of illustrious men about Rufinus: that he expounded Jacob's blessing over the patriarchs in a threefold sense, that is, historical, moral and mystical. Certainly Augustine, in his book On the Usefulness of Believing, to Honoratus, chapter 3, and again in his unfinished book on Genesis according to the letter, chapter 2, says that there is a fourth method of expounding the sacred letters. The first is according to history, when it is said what was written or what was done, or what was not done but only written, as if it had been done; for example, when Christ in Matthew 12 cites from 1 Samuel 21 concerning David that he ate the showbread. We too have called this the historical or grammatical sense. The second method is according to aetiology, when it is shown what was done or said, and for what cause. Example: Matthew 19, where Christ forbade the divorce of a wife except on account of fornication; when others asked why then Moses permitted a bill of divorce, Christ gave the reason: "because of the hardness of your hearts." I do not think this method should be distinguished from the preceding one. The third method is according to analogy, by which the agreement of the two Testaments is demonstrated. This seems to me the same as what we shall say shortly about the type.

units.la: Quarta ratio secundum Allegoriam, cùm docetur, non ad literam accipienda quaedam, quæ scripta sunt,sed figuratè intelligenda. Exemplum, prima Corinthiorum decimo Apostolus historiam Exodi notat allegoriam fuisse populi Christiani.
units.tr: The fourth method is according to allegory, when it is taught that certain things which are written are not to be taken literally but understood figuratively. Example: in 1 Corinthians 10 the Apostle notes that the history of the Exodus was an allegory of the Christian people.

units.la: Sed paulò plura notat huc pertinentia Augustinus in libro de vera religione,cap.50. Distinguamus,inquit,quam fide debeamus intelligetiq, quid mademus memoriæ,verū esse,nescientes,sed credentes tamē. Et vbi fit verū,quod non venit, & transit,sed semper eodē modo manet. Qui fit modus interpretandæ allegoriæ,quæ per sapientiam dicta credi turin spiritu Sancto: vtrum à visibilibus antiquioribus ad visibilia recentiora facta,mores,eam perducere sufficiat: an vsq; ad animæ affectiones atq; naturā, an vsq; ad incommutabile æternitate. An alia significent gestu visibilia, aliæ motus animorū, aliæ lege æternitatis,an aliquæ inueniātur,in quibus hæc omnia inuestigādæ sint. Et quæ sit stabilis fides siue historica & temporalis, & siue spiritualis & æterna, ad quā omnis interpretatio autoritatis dirigeda sit,& quid ,psit ad intelligeda & obtineda eterna,vbi finis est omnium bonarū actionū, fides rerū temporaliū. Et quid interfit inter allegoriā historiæ, & allegoriam facti, & allegoriā sermonis,& allegoriā Sacramenti. Et quomodo ipsa locutio diui narum Scripturarum secundū cuiusq; linguæ proprietatem accipiēda sit. Hæc ibi. Quibus verbis valde multiplex explicandi scripturas ratio indicatur:Sed ita tamē, vt omnia videamur præcedenti nostra partitione complexi,cùm eadem sæpius ibi,& diuersis modis significentur.
units.tr: But Augustine, in his book On True Religion, chapter 50, notes more that bears on this point. "Let us distinguish," he says, "by what faith we ought to understand, and what we should commit to memory: that it is true, though we do not know it, yet still believe it. And where there is truth that does not come and go, but always remains in the same way. What is the method of interpreting allegory, which is said to be believed through wisdom in the Holy Spirit: whether it is enough to lead it from older visible things to more recent visible deeds and customs, or whether it reaches to the affections and nature of the soul, or to the unchangeable eternity. Whether some visible things signify by gesture, others by the motions of minds, others by the law of eternity, or whether there are some in which all these things must be investigated. And what is the firm faith, whether historical and temporal, or spiritual and eternal, to which all interpretation of authority ought to be directed, and what helps toward understanding and attaining the eternal, where the end of all good actions is, and the faith of temporal things. And what difference there is between the allegory of history, the allegory of deed, the allegory of speech, and the allegory of sacrament. And how the very language of the divine Scriptures is to be taken according to the proper usage of each tongue." So far Augustine.
