By these words a very manifold method of explaining Scripture is indicated; yet in such a way that we seem to have embraced all of it in our previous division, since the same things are signified there more often and in different ways.

units.la: Hieronymus itē sæpè de historico & spirituali sensu Scripturarū loquitur,& per spiritualem modò quam diximus vsitato more Tropologiam,modò Allegoriā, modò Anagogen, (qua voce vtitur generaliter)intelligit,illas rationes vix inter se distinguens. Licet id animadvertere in commentarijs ipsius in Esaiam 1.8.10.54.15. Ezech.16. Debemus, inquit Hieronymus in Amos 4. Scripturā sanctam primum secundum literā intelligere, facientes in Ethica quæcunq; præcepta sunt: Secundò,iuxta Allegoriam,id est,intelligentiam spiritualem. Tertiò,secundum futurorum beatitudinem. Hieronymus ad Hedibiā: Præcipitur nobis,Solomone dicente,Tu autem describe ea tripliciter in consilio & scientia, vt respondeas verbū veritatis,his qui proponunt tibi. Triplex in corde nostro descriptio & regula Scripturarum est. Prima,vt intelligamus eas iuxta historiam: Secunda, iuxta Tropologiam:Tertia,iuxta intelligentiam spirituale. In historia,eorum quę scripta sunt,ordo seruatur. In tropologia de litera ad maiora consurgimus, & quicquid in priori populo carnaliter factū est,iuxta moralē interpretamur locū; & ad animæ nostræ emolumentū cōuertimus. In spirituali theoria ad sublimiora transfimus,terrena dimittimus, de futurorum beatitudine,& cœlestibus disputamus;vt præsentis vitę meditatio vmbra futurae beatitudinis sit.
units.tr: Jerome also often speaks of the historical and spiritual sense of Scripture, and by "spiritual" he understands, in the customary way we have mentioned, sometimes tropology, sometimes allegory, sometimes anagoge (a word he uses in general), hardly distinguishing these methods from one another. This may be observed in his commentaries on Isaiah 1, 8, 10, 54 and 15, and on Ezekiel 16. "We ought," says Jerome on Amos 4, "first to understand Holy Scripture according to the letter, doing in our conduct whatever precepts there are. Second, according to allegory, that is, spiritual understanding. Third, according to the blessedness of things to come." Jerome to Hedibia: "It is commanded us, Solomon saying, 'But you describe them threefold in counsel and knowledge, that you may answer the word of truth to those who propose it to you.' There is a threefold description and rule of the Scriptures in our heart. The first is that we understand them according to history; the second, according to tropology; the third, according to spiritual understanding. In history, the order of what is written is kept. In tropology we rise from the letter to higher things, and whatever was done carnally among the former people we interpret according to a moral sense and turn to the profit of our soul. In spiritual contemplation we pass to higher things, leave earthly things behind, and dispute about the blessedness of the future and heavenly things, so that the meditation of the present life may be a shadow of future blessedness."

units.la: Sed rogat aliquis: Vnde tanta varietas explicādi Scripturam? Hæc videtur potius perturbare,quàm adiuuare. Respondetur:Opus est hanc varietatē adhiberi, tum quòd Scriptura sit veluti ager valde fœcundus,nihil habens,quod non ingentē vtilitatem adferat si rectè accipiatur,adeò vt etiam quæ in speciem absurda sunt,aut non rectè dicta,aut fa&ta,tamen;si commodè explicentur aliquo dictorum modo, magnū fructum pariant ad animarū eruditionē,consolationē,confirmationē,&c. Ergo cùm nihil sine certa causa, et sine fructu sit in penuario illo spiritus sancti repositum,opus est, vt rectè vtamur; varia subinde interpretatione adhibere. Id similitudine melius explicabimus. In poetis enarrādis,qui theologi fuerūt gentiliū,& sub fabulis inuolucris coplexi sunt maximarū rerū cognitione,scitis,quàm multiplex sit etiam fabularū,quæ inanes videtur, vel historiarū explicandi ratio. Præter sententiā grāmaticam colligitur, quod pertinet ad doctrinā vel institutionē morū:veluti, cùm Dij describuntur solliciti pro salute ducū vel populi alicu ius cōmendatur prouidētia diuina.Prẽterea addit,quid per fabulā confictā poetæ signifi carint,
units.tr: But someone asks: whence such variety in explaining Scripture? This seems rather to confuse than to help. The answer is that this variety must be employed, both because Scripture is like a very fertile field, holding nothing that does not bring great benefit if it is rightly understood, so that even those things which seem absurd, or were not rightly said or done, if they are properly explained in one of the ways mentioned, yield great fruit for the instruction, consolation, and confirmation of souls, and so on. Therefore, since nothing has been stored in that storehouse of the Holy Spirit without a certain cause and without fruit, we must use it rightly, applying various interpretations as occasion requires. We will explain this better by a comparison. In expounding the poets, who were the theologians of the gentiles and wrapped knowledge of the greatest things in fables, you know how manifold is the method of explaining even those fables, or histories, which seem empty. Besides the grammatical sense, there is gathered what pertains to doctrine or the instruction of morals: for example, when the gods are described as anxious for the safety of leaders, or the divine providence is commended to some people. Besides this, he adds what the poets meant by the invented fable,

units.la: 1. Secundū historiam. 2. Aetiologia. 3. Analogia. 4. Allegoria. Anagoge. Allegoria. Variae allegoriae. Origenes in epist. ad Gal.5. Homilia 2. et 17. In Genesin. homilia 11. in lib. Numerorum. lib.4.c.2. carint, & quæ fabulæ origo vel occasio: vt videre est apud Pataphatum, qui scripsit de non credendis historijs, & apud Fulgentium. Deque varia hac exponendi ratione fabulas poetarum egit etiam Basilius in libello de ratione legendi Scriptores gentiles. Si ergo tāta varietas requiritur, & vtilis est in explicandis poetis, quid ni multo maiori diligentia varie explicetur Scriptura, quę mysteriorum est per se fœcundissima, & vberrimam materiam spiritualium bonorum ad omnes vitæ & cognitionis spiritualis vsus suppeditat?
units.tr: 1. According to history. 2. Aetiology. 3. Analogy. 4. Allegory. Anagoge. Allegory. Various allegories. Origen, on Galatians, homilies 2 and 17; on Genesis, homily 11; on Numbers, book 4, ch. 2: and what was the origin or occasion of the fable, as may be seen in Pataphatus, who wrote on histories not to be believed, and in Fulgentius. Basil too treated the fables of the poets according to this varied method of explanation, in his little book on how to read the gentile writers. If, then, so great a variety is required, and is useful in explaining the poets, why should Scripture, which is in itself most fruitful in mysteries and supplies a very rich store of spiritual goods for every use of life and spiritual knowledge, not be explained in many ways with far greater diligence?

units.la: Et si sub inuolucris fabularum poeticarum latet subinde grauis doctrina, quare non statuamus, in narrationibus Scripturarum, præsertim veteris Testamenti reposita esse amplissima mysteria? Et non solum vtilitas, sed etiam necessitas exigit, vt tam variis modis exponi debeat: id quod & apostolica Scripta veterumque patrum commentarij satis testantur, & nos paulo post etiam causas indicabimus.
units.tr: And if serious teaching sometimes lies hidden beneath the coverings of poetic fables, why should we not hold that the most ample mysteries are stored up in the narratives of Scripture, especially of the Old Testament? Not only usefulness but necessity demands that it be expounded in such varied ways. The apostolic writings and the commentaries of the ancient fathers bear sufficient witness to this, and we shall indicate the causes a little later.

units.la: Allegoriæ vero magis sitæ sunt in doctrina ac præceptis, quemadmodum, vbi quæ in lege explicantur de sacerdotio, sacrificijs, ritibus, ea spiritualiter nobis ostenduntur obseruanda. Quomodo Augustinus sæpe interpretatus est multa, plurima etiam Origenes, item Eucherius, maximè in libris legalibus, in quibus plus gratiæ habent Allegoriæ. Nam hoc notandum est breuiter: vbi nudæ & perspicuæ sunt historiæ, vt in libris Iosuæ, Iudicum, Ruth, Esther, Regum, commodius morales expositiones adhibentur: sicut & in libris didacticis, quales sunt, Proverbia, Ecclesiasticus, Iob, &c. In legalibus vero potissimum ceremonialibus explicandis allegoriæ gratiam obtinent.
units.tr: Allegories are, however, found more often in doctrine and precepts; just as, where the things explained in the law concerning the priesthood, the sacrifices and the rites are shown to us to be observed spiritually. Thus Augustine interpreted many things often, and Origen very many, likewise Eucherius, especially in the books of the law, in which allegories have the greater grace. For this should be noted briefly: where the histories are bare and plain, as in the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Esther and Kings, moral expositions are more suitably applied; as also in the didactic books, such as Proverbs, Ecclesiasticus, Job, and so on. But in explaining the legal books, and above all the ceremonial ones, allegories obtain their proper place.

units.la: Vbi ergo, & quando Allegorias tractari conueniat, primum explicemus.
units.tr: First we will explain where and when allegories ought to be treated.

units.la: Post expositum sensum grammaticum siue historicum, atque addita, quæ ad vitam formandam pertinent.
units.tr: After the grammatical or historical sense has been set out, and what pertains to forming life has been added.

units.la: Secundo loco conueniet adijcere quædam allegorica. Quem ordinem in tractatione Scripturarum commendant Hieronymus & Augustinus multis in locis.
units.tr: In the second place it will be fitting to add certain allegorical matters. Jerome and Augustine commend this order in handling Scripture in many places.

units.la: Id autem tunc, vbi vel cogit necessitas, vel suadet vtilitas.
units.tr: This, however, is to be done when either necessity compels or usefulness suggests.

units.la: Necessitas quidem varie contingit. Primum, quando Scriptura, ni tropum adhibeas, præ se ferunt falsitatē. Exemplū Psalmus habet de Christo, Super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis, & conculcabis Leonem & draconem. Istud Christus nō legitur fecisse: quare opus est allegorice explicare ea verba, de conculcato & superato mūdo, peccato, morte, diabolo, & sententia euadit perspicua.
units.tr: Necessity arises in various ways. First, when Scripture, unless you apply a trope, presents something false. An example: the Psalm says of Christ, "Upon the asp and the basilisk you shall walk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon." Christ is not read to have done this; therefore the words must be explained allegorically, of the trampled and conquered world, sin, death and the devil, and the sense becomes plain.

units.la: Secundò: quando verba Scripturæ in sensu grammatico accepto pariunt absurditatem. Quò pertinent omnes illæ locutiones de Deo, quibus ei tribuuntur affectus humani, ira, pœnitentia, descensus, ascensus, dubitatio, vel ignoratio, somnus, furor, &c. Item Romanorum cap. 12. Hoc faciens, carbones ignis congeres super caput eius. Vbi cùm de cibado & reficiedo inimico verba præcedunt, ista quidè videntur contra amicitiæ leges esse addita: Verum oportet allegorice interpretari, sicut Augustinus libro secundo de doctrina Christiana, capite decimosexto, vt intelligas, te ad beneficentiam reuocari, & carbones ignis esse vrentes pœnitentiæ gemitus, quibus superbia sanatur eius, quidler, se inimicum fuisse hominis, à quo eius misericordiæ subuenitur.
units.tr: Second, when the words of Scripture, taken in the grammatical sense, produce absurdity. To this belong all those expressions about God by which human affections are attributed to him: anger, repentance, descent, ascent, doubt or ignorance, sleep, fury, and so on. Likewise Romans 12: "In doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head." Here, since the preceding words speak of feeding and refreshing an enemy, these words seem to have been added against the laws of friendship. But they must be interpreted allegorically, as Augustine does in book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 16, so that you understand that you are called to beneficence, and that the coals of fire are the burning groans of repentance, by which the pride of the man who was an enemy is healed, and he is helped by the mercy of the one he has wronged.

units.la: Tertiò: quando sensus grammaticus pugnat cum sana doctrina, siue aduersaturbonis moribus & vitæ sanctimoniæ: vt multa in canticis canticorum, item in Euangelio, de parentibus odiendis, & ferenda cruce: Item, quòd Oseas iubetur scortum ducere: Item Ieremiæ capite vigesimoquinto, Bibite, inebriamini, & vomite: de qualibus Augustinus de doctrina Christiana libro tertio, capite vigesimosecundo. Si quæ facta leguntur à patribus etiam sanctis, quæ tamen abhorrent à consuetudine bonorum, qui post aduentum Domini diuina præcepta custodiunt, figuram ad intelligentiam referat id est, ad mysterium per Allegoriam) factum verò ipsum ad mores non transferat.
units.tr: Third, when the grammatical sense conflicts with sound doctrine, or is opposed to good morals and holiness of life: as with many things in the Song of Songs, likewise in the Gospel, about hating parents and bearing the cross; also that Hosea is commanded to take a harlot; also Jeremiah 25, "Drink, be drunk, and vomit," concerning which Augustine writes in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 22. If any deeds are read of even holy fathers which nevertheless shrink from the custom of good people who, since the coming of the Lord, keep the divine precepts, let the figure refer to understanding, that is, to mystery through allegory, but let the deed itself not be transferred to morals.

units.la: Quandocunque igitur huiusmodi loci occurrunt, necessariò ad allegorias confugiendum est, alias namque simplex & grammatica interpretatio errores non paruos gigneret.
units.tr: Whenever passages of this kind occur, we must of necessity have recourse to allegories. Otherwise a simple, grammatical interpretation would give rise to no small errors.

units.la: Sic enim natus est error Anthropomorphitarum Deo tribuentium humana membra & affectus, quia noluerunt ἀνθρωπομορφίας in scripturis obuias, quemadmodum decet, accipere. Errarunt similiter Euchitæ, semper orandum esse stolidè contendentes, quia in Euangelio dicitur, oportet semper orare, & nunquam cessare. Quidam impru denter seipsos castrarunt, quòd in euangelio dicatur beati, qui seipsos castrauerint propter regnum Dei. Chiliastæ itidem lapsi sunt, dùm locum Apocalypseos capite vigesimo, de regno Christi & sanctorum per mille annos, secundum literam acceperunt: Iudæi etiam num hodie in expositione de requie Sabbati delirant.
units.tr: In this way the error of the Anthropomorphites arose, who attributed human members and affections to God, because they would not understand the anthropomorphisms [ἀνθρωπομορφίας] found in Scripture as they ought to be understood. The Euchites likewise erred, stubbornly insisting that one must always pray, because the Gospel says that we ought always to pray and never cease. Some foolishly castrated themselves, because the Gospel says, "Blessed are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God." The Chiliasts also fell into error when they took literally the passage in Revelation chapter twenty about the reign of Christ and the saints for a thousand years. Even today the Jews rave in their interpretation of the rest of the Sabbath.

units.la: Ergo manifestum est, vbi allegoricas interpretationes adhiberi necessum sit.
units.tr: It is therefore clear where allegorical interpretations must be employed.

units.la: Vtilitas verò suadet adhiberi allegorias, quando in verbis Scripturæ grammaticè accepta
units.tr: Usefulness, moreover, recommends the use of allegories when the words of Scripture, taken grammatically,

units.la: ωσολογία.
units.tr: Osologia [ωσολογία].

units.la: In fabulis doctrinæ graues sæpe latent.
units.tr: Grave doctrines often lie hidden in fables.

units.la: Allegoriæ locus.
units.tr: The place of allegory.

units.la: 1. quādo utēdū sit allegorijs.
units.tr: 1. When allegories should be used.

units.la: 1. Necessitas allegoriarum. Psalmo 91.
units.tr: 1. The necessity of allegories. Psalm 91.

units.la: 2. Absurditas declinanda.
units.tr: 2. Absurdity must be avoided.

units.la: 3. Sensus grammaticus inconueniens. Luc. 14.
units.tr: 3. The grammatical sense is unsuitable. Luke 14.

units.la: Errores ex sensu grammatico Antropomorphitæ. Euchitæ. Origenistæ. Chiliastæ. Iudæorum Sabbatismus. Vtilitas allegoriarum. acceptis modica aut nulla doctrina videtur reposita, aut si aliqua ntula sit, tamen vberi- or conspicietur, si allegorica interpretatio adhibeatur. Exempli causa in libris legalibus vide in historia Iacob, quomodo deceptus fuerit à Laban, quomodo seruierit tot annis pro habenda Rachele, quomodo gregem suum auxerit virgulis positis in aqua: haec per se non habent magnam vtilitatem vel doctrinam: Sed vbi quis ad allegoriam inquirendam veniet, deprehendi mysteria magna poterunt. De his causis recipiendi allegorias eleganter disserit Origenes homilia vndecima in librum Numerorum.
units.tr: Errors arising from the grammatical sense: the Anthropomorphites, the Euchites, the Origenists, the Chiliasts, the Jewish Sabbatism. The usefulness of allegories. From the historical books, which seem to have little or no teaching in their plain sense, yet if an allegorical interpretation is applied they will be seen to yield a richer fruit. For example, in the books of the Law, look at the history of Jacob: how he was deceived by Laban, how he served for so many years to obtain Rachel, how he increased his flock by means of rods set in water. These things in themselves have little usefulness or teaching. But when someone sets out to seek an allegory, great mysteries can be discovered. Origen discusses elegantly the reasons for receiving allegories in his eleventh homily on the Book of Numbers.

units.la: Sed iam roget aliquis: Quando ita dicis, necessitate aliquando adhibendas allegorias, quare Deus voluit in Scripturis tales extare sententias, quæ haberent obscuritatem, & sine allegoria recte non possunt intelligi? Videtur profecto, quod satius fuisset, omnia clare & sine inuolucris exprimi.
units.tr: But someone may now ask: since you say that allegories must sometimes be used of necessity, why did God want such sayings to exist in Scripture, sayings which have obscurity and cannot be rightly understood without allegory? It would surely have been better, it seems, for everything to be stated clearly and without wrappings.

units.la: Respondetur secundum Augustinum ex libro secundo, de doctrina Christiana capite sexto, & aliis locis, prouide & vtiliter à Deo id esse factum.
units.tr: The answer, following Augustine in the second book of On Christian Teaching, chapter six, and in other places, is that God has done this wisely and profitably.

units.la: Primò, quia non conuenit cœlestis philosophiae mysteria tam clare & perspicue semper proponi, ne vilescat. Quæ enim nimis sunt obuia, fere contenuntur, vtpote cuiuis in proptu & communia. Secundò, vt humani ingenij torpor excutiatur, acuaturq; in perscrutandis Scripturis diligentia. Si omnia essent peruia, quis laboraret ad parandam eorum cognitionem, imò quis vel attento animo in illis legendis versaretur? Non conuenit statim omnes omnia intelligere, sed per gradus quosdam decet ad perfectionem contendere. Tertiò, potest haec ratio addi, difficultatem esse inspersam Scripturis, vt homines admoneantur, sine gratia & dona Spiritus se non posse assequi mysteria illic abdita, eoq; opem Dei imploret, semetipsi Deo submittant, cristas non erigat, aliorum piorum interpretationes modeste audiant, alter ab altero discere non grauetur. Quàm multa videmus ab Apostolis expósita esse, quę sanè eum in modum exponi haud potuissent, nisi spiritus Sanctus inspirasset & manifestasset.
units.tr: First, because it is not fitting that the mysteries of heavenly philosophy should always be set forth so clearly and plainly, lest they become cheap. For things that are too obvious are almost despised, being ready to hand and common to everyone. Second, so that the sluggishness of the human mind may be shaken off and diligence in searching the Scriptures may be sharpened. If everything were plain, who would labour to acquire knowledge of them? Indeed, who would even apply an attentive mind to reading them? It is not fitting that everyone should understand everything at once, but one ought to strive toward perfection by certain steps. Third, this reason may be added: difficulty has been sprinkled through the Scriptures so that people may be warned that without grace and the gifts of the Spirit they cannot attain the mysteries hidden there; so that they may implore God's help, submit themselves to God, not raise their crests, listen modestly to the interpretations of other godly people, and not be ashamed to learn from one another. How many things we see expounded by the Apostles which could certainly not have been expounded in that way unless the Holy Spirit had inspired and revealed them.

units.la: Quartò, habet, Inescio quid occultę voluptatis & gratiæ, vbi cognoscitur, quod quasi velamine quodam tectum erat. Quare iucundum inprimis est, ex obscuris locis per allegoriam, claram sententiam eruere, et sub duro cortice dulcem inuenire nucleum. Sed iam quomodo allegoriae sint formandae, explicemus.
units.tr: Fourth, there is a certain hidden pleasure and charm in it: when something that was covered as with a veil is recognised. Therefore it is especially delightful to draw a clear sense out of obscure passages by allegory, and to find a sweet kernel under a hard shell. But now let us explain how allegories are to be framed.

units.la: Non est cuiusuis in hac parte versari, sed tantum summorum artificum, & sobrie. Nos paucis quaedam annotabimus veluti regulas.
units.tr: It is not for just anyone to engage in this, but only for the greatest craftsmen, and then soberly. We shall note a few things briefly, as rules.

units.la: Primum, valde temerarium est, quouis loco adhibere allegorias, sicut Origenes, aliquando etiam Ambrosius ausi sunt: Vide Ambrosium in Lucam in historia passionis Christi. Haec audacia labefactat autoritatem Scripturæ, quasi nihil certi habeat, & quasi ad quamuis rem quæuis verba accommodare liceat. Oportet videre, vbi locus allegoriam postulet, vbi, vt dixi, id exigat necessitas, vbi suadeat vtilitas.
units.tr: First, it is very rash to apply allegories to any passage whatever, as Origen and sometimes Ambrose too have ventured to do. See Ambrose on Luke, on the history of Christ's passion. This boldness undermines the authority of Scripture, as if it had nothing certain and as if any words might be fitted to any matter. One must see where the passage demands an allegory, where, as I said, necessity requires it and usefulness recommends it.

units.la: Secundò, quoties vis allegoriam texere, vide inprimis, vt ea interpretatio, quam adferre vis, in alijs locis Scripturæ, nudè & simpliciter expressa habeatur sine inuolucris, & analogiæ fidei respondens. Hac de causa non satis tutum est, quasuis ab alijs confictas sequi allegorias: sed examinare eas decet, num cum doctrina in sacris literis tradita per omnia conueniant.
units.tr: Second, whenever you wish to weave an allegory, look above all that the interpretation you bring forward is found expressed plainly and simply, without wrappings, in other passages of Scripture, and that it agrees with the analogy of faith. For this reason it is not safe enough to follow whatever allegories have been invented by others; one ought rather to examine whether they agree in every respect with the doctrine handed down in the sacred letters.

units.la: Tertiò, dabitur opera, vt allegoria potissimum versentur in locis communibus Euangelij, & summaria eius doctrina. Extra hos locos deducit, videtur sanè extra oleā currere, & non multum fructum adferet.
units.tr: Third, care should be taken that allegories are chiefly concerned with the common topics of the Gospel and its main doctrine. Drawing them out from outside these places clearly seems to run beyond the olive grove, and will bring little fruit.

units.la: Quartò, ita componenda est allegoria, vt fere per omnia quadret partibus sententiae vel historiae, quàm ἀναγωγὴν enarrandam suscipis, nec prorsus pugnet cum præcedentibus in ea, aut sequentibus. Alias, si longius petita erit interpretatio tua, aut omninò dubior, amittet gratiam. Non quidem, quòd necesse sit excutere, sed saltem explanari debent quæ principales sunt, & causam magis illustrant.
units.tr: Fourth, the allegory must be so constructed that it fits almost entirely the parts of the sense or history which you undertake to explain by the anagoge, and that it does not conflict at all with what comes before or after it. Otherwise, if your interpretation is drawn from too far off, or is altogether doubtful, it will lose its favour. Not indeed that every detail must be unfolded, but at least those points which are principal and which throw more light on the matter must be explained.

units.la: Quintò, ita artificiosè proponenda vestiedaq; erit allegoria, vt pondus habere videatur, & animos non tantùm delectet, verumetiam, quàm fieri potest, vehementissimè afficiat. Quòd si hæc virtus absit, frigida erit interpretatio, parumq́ue in loco adhibita.
units.tr: Fifth, the allegory must be presented and dressed so artfully that it seems to carry weight, and not only delights the minds but also moves them as strongly as possible. If this quality is lacking, the interpretation will be cold and of little use in the passage.

units.la: Sextò, non oportet nimis diu immorari, aut longius, quàm res poscit, persequi. Vnde multis placet satis esse, si paucis verbis, sed tamen argute attingantur verius, quàm pertractentur.
units.tr: Sixth, one should not linger too long, nor pursue the matter further than the subject demands. Hence many think it enough if the point is touched upon briefly, but with wit, rather than worked over at length.

units.la: Quod genus valde vsitatum est, & laudatur in Scripturis. Quomodo tractantur allegoriæ, Ephes.5. de Christo & ecclesia: Item 1. Cor.10. velamen Mosis. Item Ioan. 2. Soluite templū hoc, & in triduo ego reædificabo illud. Item vbi Christus iubet cauere à fermento Pharisæorum: Item, Non alligabis os boui triturânti, &c.
units.tr: This kind is very common and is praised in the Scriptures. Examples of how allegories are treated: Ephesians 5, on Christ and the church; likewise 1 Corinthians 10, the veil of Moses; likewise John 2, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"; likewise where Christ bids us beware of the leaven of the Pharisees; likewise, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn," etc.

units.la: F
units.tr: F

units.la: Septimò, cùm nihil obsit, quo minus idem locus varie exponatur, cauendum, ne vna sententia vel factum nimis multis modis explicetur. Aut, si forte possit explicari, aut inueniatur multipliciter exposita apud doctiores, tamen ea sola veniet vsurpanda, quæ plus gratię habet, magisq; conuenit præsenti argumento, quæque in locis versatur communibus, atque alibi in scripturis delineata reperitur. Etsi vero breues allegoriæ esse debeant, nihilominus perspicuę. Ex ambiguis locis, aut omninò obscuris nihil possis euincere, quales alibi occurrunt: vt Ezechielis 1. vbi de animalibus vndique oculatis, & totis. Et alibi non dissimiles, quæ plane ænigmata videntur: tanta inest eis obscuritas. Itaque magno iudicio opus est prudentia volenti allegorias, quæ gratiam habiturę sint, texere. Augustinus habet hanc regulam, vbi enarrat Psalmum octauum, ad finem.
units.tr: Seventh, since nothing prevents the same passage being explained in various ways, one must take care not to explain a single saying or deed in too many ways. Or if perhaps it can be explained in many ways, or is found explained in several ways by the learned, yet only that interpretation should be taken up which has the most grace, agrees best with the present argument, moves among the common topics, and is found drawn out elsewhere in the Scriptures. Although allegories ought to be brief, they must nonetheless be clear. From ambiguous or altogether obscure passages you can prove nothing, such as those that occur elsewhere: for example, Ezekiel 1, where the living creatures are full of eyes all round and over. And elsewhere there are similar passages which plainly seem to be riddles, so great is the obscurity in them. Therefore great judgment is needed by one who wishes to weave allegories that will have grace. Augustine gives this rule where he expounds Psalm 8, at its end.

units.la: Sed dicat iterum aliquis, Si adeò difficile est formare aptas allegorias, & raro producuntur sine periculo, nec efficaces sunt ad confirmanda religionis dogmata, videntur ergo potius explodendæ esse, quàm vllo pacto admittendæ, imò in totum abstinendum esse ab ijs.
units.tr: But someone may again say: if it is so hard to frame apt allegories, and they are rarely produced without danger, and are not effective for confirming the dogmas of religion, then they seem rather to be driven out than admitted in any way; indeed one should abstain from them altogether.

units.la: Respondetur, Non penitus reijciendas esse, imò magnum esse earum vsum, si tamen sobriè & in loco adhibeantur. Ostendimus autem breuiter, quis earum fit in enarrandis Scripturis vsus.
units.tr: The answer is that they are not to be rejected entirely; their use is great, provided they are employed soberly and in the right place. But we will show briefly what use they have in the explanation of Scripture.

units.la: Primùm supra diximus, necessitatem aliquando exigere, aliquando vtilitatem. Vtilitas verò hæc inde prima cedit ex allegorijs. Ad excitandos animos segnes aut fastidiosos, in oratione præsertim graui & longa, habent gratiam: Si quid subtile vel inopinatum profertur, ea res tollit tædium, & animos irritat incitatque. Vt in ferculis exoticum aliquid admixtum delectat, etiamsi non perinde salubre: ita in oratione voluptatem adfert etiam quod præter causam aliquando profertur. Qua ratione rhetores tradunt, quædam ornamenta orationibus adhibere, quę illustrant causam, & præterea exornant: eadem ratione adhibendæ sunt allegoriæ, vtpote quæ illustrant & exornant, & animos audito rum blandè demulcent.
units.tr: First, I said above that sometimes necessity requires allegories and sometimes usefulness. The usefulness of allegory appears first in this way: it has a welcome effect for rousing sluggish or weary minds, especially in a long and serious discourse. If something subtle or unexpected is brought forward, it removes tedium and stirs and excites the hearers. As an unfamiliar dish mixed into a meal delights, even if it is not equally wholesome, so in a speech even something introduced beside the point gives pleasure. For this reason the rhetoricians teach that certain ornaments should be used in speeches, which both illustrate the cause and adorn it. In the same way allegories should be employed, since they illustrate and adorn and gently soothe the minds of the hearers.

units.la: Tertiò confirmat allegoria. Nā qui dociles sunt, & non refractarij, valde mouetur allegorijs, benignęq; excipiût, quod per doctorę, eruditum & pium in medium producitur. Et confirmantur animi, vbi vident causam, qua de agitur, etiam in veteri testamento aliqua sententia vel historia comprobatam. Nam etiamsi non euincit allegoria, tamen confirmat, & suppeditat argumentationes probabiles, licet non necessarias. At vt dubitare possis, vtrùm spiritus Sancti mes fuerint, vt sententia vel historia significet eas res, quas signi ficare per allegoriam prædicatur: tamen quando interpretatio ea analoga est fidei, non potes eam protinus damnare, quasi spiritui Sancto contrariam, cùm etiam constet, spiritum sanctum id non sensisse.
units.tr: Third, allegory confirms. Those who are teachable and not obstinate are greatly moved by allegories and receive them kindly, when they are brought forward by a learned, erudite and pious teacher. Minds are strengthened when they see that the matter under discussion is supported by some saying or history even in the Old Testament. For although allegory does not compel conviction, it does confirm, and it supplies probable arguments, though not necessary ones. And even if you doubt whether the Holy Spirit intended the saying or history to signify those things which are proclaimed to be signified by the allegory, nevertheless, when that interpretation accords with the faith, you cannot condemn it outright as contrary to the Holy Spirit, since it is also certain that the Holy Spirit did not mean it.

units.la: Quartò, dùm multipliciter exponitur Scriptura, eius fœcunditas commendatur, & multiplex vtilitas aperitur. Nec potest fieri, quin semper aliqui fructū aliquem ex multiplici expositione referant. Quod vnius palato non sapit, tamen sapit id palato alterius. Quomodo manna vnicuiq; sapiebat, quod volebat: ita in cibo Scripturę vnicuiq; id maximè prodest, quo maximè afficitur. Sed hæc de allegorijs satis, nisi fallor, multa.
units.tr: Fourth, while Scripture is expounded in many ways, its fruitfulness is commended and its manifold usefulness is revealed. Nor can it happen that some profit does not always come from a manifold exposition. What does not taste good to one person's palate tastes good to another's. As the manna tasted to each person whatever he desired, so in the food of Scripture each person is most benefited by that which most affects him. But enough, unless I am mistaken, has been said about allegories.

units.la: Et illi quidè plures facti fuerūt sacerdotes, propterea quòd per mortè non sinerētur permanere: At hic, quòd idem maneat in æternum, perpetuum habet sacerdotium.
units.tr: And indeed those were made priests in greater number, because they were prevented by death from continuing; but this one, because he remains forever, has a perpetual priesthood.

units.la: Secunda ratio, siue secundum argumentum, quo iterum à præstantia sacerdotij Christi præ sacerdotio legali probat excellentiam Euangelij præ lege. Apostolus satis aperte expressit argumenti antecedens, tu modò adde illationem: Ergo sacerdotium Christi est præstantius sacerdotio legali. Inde rursus subijciatur, quemadmodum priori argumento, Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus: hoc est, Quanto præeminentibus est sacerdotium Christi præ sacerdotio legali, tanto oportet iudicari Euangelium præstantius esse lege. Ducitur argumentum illud de dignitate sacerdotij Christi, ab eius durati-one: Sacerdotiū Christi perpetuū est, inquit, vbi Leuitarū tātum erat temporale: Vnde vnus Christus pluribus Leuitis opponitur & opponitur. Sed præterea causam siue pbationem vtriusque membri antecedentis interposuit: Christi quidem sacerdotium ideo est perpetuum, quòd ipse sit, qui idem maneat in æternum: Leuitarum verò sacerdotium temporale, quòd ipsi mortales essent, minimeque possent propter mortem permanere. Ita nihil obscurum, nihil non probatum relinquitur. Et quiuis animaduertere facile potest argumenti huius occasionem ex particula vaticinij toties citati, in æternum, quæ sola adhuc expendenda supererat.
units.tr: This is the second reason, or second argument, by which again he proves from the excellence of Christ's priesthood over the Levitical priesthood the excellence of the Gospel over the law. The Apostle has expressed the antecedent of the argument quite clearly; you need only add the conclusion: therefore the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood. Then it may be added again, as in the former argument: Jesus has become the surety of a better covenant; that is, as the priesthood of Christ is far more outstanding than the Levitical priesthood, so the Gospel must be judged more excellent than the law. That argument about the dignity of Christ's priesthood is drawn from its duration: Christ's priesthood is perpetual, he says, whereas the priesthood of the Levites was only temporary. Hence the one Christ is set over against, and opposed to, many Levites. But he also inserted the cause, or proof, of each part of the antecedent: Christ's priesthood is perpetual because he himself is the one who remains forever; but the Levitical priesthood was temporary because those priests were mortal and could not continue on account of death. So nothing obscure is left, nothing unproved. And anyone can easily see that the occasion of this argument arises from the phrase forever in the prophecy so often cited, which alone remained to be examined.

units.la: Verum quidem est, quod supra dixerat, Christum sacerdotem factum iuxta potentiam vitæ indissolubilis: Sed ea ratio quodammodo obliquè & indirectè hinc petita videri poterat, & in alium finem, nempe ad ostendendum simpliciter, discrimen necessariò constitui debere inter sacerdotium Christi & sacerdotium legale.
units.tr: It is true that he had said above that Christ was made priest according to the power of an indissoluble life. But that reasoning could seem to be drawn in a somewhat oblique and indirect way from this, and for another purpose, namely to show simply that a distinction must necessarily be drawn between the priesthood of Christ and the Levitical priesthood.

units.la: Sunt verò hæc argumeta probantia à dignitate sacerdotij dignitate euangelij multò artificiosissimè excogitata, & supra quàm dici queat, illi descriptioni euangelij, qua id prius appellauerat Spem potiorem, conuenientia. Potiore enim esse spem in Euágelio propositam, quomodo aptius confirmemus, quàm si ostendamus, euangelicũ sacerdotiũ iuramento adhibito esse roboratũ & sancitum? Quis diffidat de accipiendis promissis & speratis, vbi Deus etiam sacro iureiurando ad ea præstanda se obstrinxit? Rursus vbi, qui præstare debet, siue qui sponsor est seruandorũ pactorum, manet in æternum, quis metuat, eum morte impediendũ, quo minus promissa posit in tépore adimplere? Ergo simul quomodo euangelium proprie sit Spes potior, simul quomodo id sit lege excellentius, duobus hisce argumentis euidentissimè comprobatum est.
units.tr: These arguments proving the excellence of the Gospel from the dignity of the priesthood are devised with great skill, and they fit exceedingly well that description of the Gospel by which he had earlier called it a better hope. For how can we more aptly prove that the hope set before us in the Gospel is better than by showing that the Gospel priesthood was confirmed and sanctioned with an oath? Who would distrust the promises to be received and hoped for, when God has bound himself to fulfil them even by a sacred oath? Again, where he who must perform, that is, the surety for keeping the covenants, remains forever, who would fear that he might be prevented by death from fulfilling the promises in due time? So by these two arguments it is most clearly proved both how the Gospel is properly a better hope and how it is more excellent than the law.

units.la: Quod ad partes attinet, satis sunt omnia expósita. Animaduertendum autem, quòd non dicit simpliciter, sacerdotium legale fuisse temporale: Sed vtitur verbis tantundem significantibus, ac dicit: Et illi quidem plures facti sunt sacerdotes: vbi verba quidem simpliciter videntur sonare tantundé, ac si vellet per antithesin pluribus vnum Christum opponere, & quasi euincere veller, id ad laudé sacerdotij euangelici facere, quòd istud administretur per vnum: in lege autè succedebant plures: Atqui nulla est de vnitate vel multitudine metio, verum de duratione res agitur. Quamobrè hæc est verborũ sententia, quòd sacerdotiũ in lege erat duntaxat temporaneũ, sacerdotium verò euangelicũ ipsius Christi est æternum. Posterius membrum antecedentis satis arguit, quæ sententia sit membri prioris. Sed placuit Apostolo eo pacto formare priore partem antecedentis, dicendo: At illi quidé plures facti sunt sacerdotes, propterea quòd per mortẽ non sineretur permanere, vt ratione habita antithetorũ, quibus solet Apostolus mirũ in modũ delectari, & in collationibus seu potiùs contentionibus maximã habent gratiã: ita alteram partẽ antecedetis efficeret: At hic quòd idem maneat in æternum, perpetuum habeat sacerdotium: vbi reuera insignis laus ac dignitas Christi ostenditur, cùm non solùm sacerdotium æternum, verum etiam persona Christi manens in æternum prædicatur. Quá sanè ex parte dignitas Christi omnium sacerdotum legalium dignitati non abs re præfertur. Neque fuisset tàm præclarum: tamq; firmum, quod dici potuisset sacerdotium Christi æternum, nisi addi potuisset, ipsum quoque Christum manere æternum. Nam aliàs quidem sacerdotium Aaronicum aliquo modo posset æternum dici, quando videlicet id per multa secula à sacerdotibus inuicem succedentibus administraretur: Quando etiam ipsius Dei verba simile quiddam sonant Exodi capite vigesimo octauo. Vbi post multa dicta de institutione & ordinatione sacerdotum legalium tandem subijcitur: Legitimum sempiternum erit Aaron & semini eius post eum. Atqui id non satis erat, vt sacerdotium legale æternum diceretur. Nam vt per multa secula plures successerint in sacerdotio illo, & sic sacerdotium illud diu fuerit stabile, tamen quia omnes fuerunt mortales, tandem isti defecerunt atque his deficientibus simul necessum fuit deficere sacerdotium, quemadmodum euentus coprobauit. At verò in sacerdotio euangelico lóge aliter res habet. Vnus est sacerdos, sed talis, qui sua natura manet in æternum: & cùm ipse maneat in æternũ, facilè & clarè sequitur, & sacerdotium ipsum manere æternũ. Ex his igitur est videre, quare Apostolus non dixerit simpliciter, sacerdotium legale fuisse duntaxat temporaneum, euangelicum verò sacerdotium esse æternum: Sed aliis verbis tantùdem significari, quorum posteriore parte quæ posita sunt, dignitatẽ Christi magis illustrat, & æternitatem sacerdotij euangelici clarissimè euincunt. Posset quide aliqtio modò sacerdotium euangelicum dici æternum, etiámsi Christus non maneret in æternum, modò perpetuo ordine alij administratores alijs succederent, modò item aliud præstantius sacerdotium ei non succederet: Sed multo splendidius est, & glorię Christi magis conueniens, atq; etiam efficacior ratiocinatio, quòd dicatur sacerdotium euangelicum æternum, eò quòd ipse sacerdos Christus in æternum maneat.
units.tr: As for the parts, everything has been sufficiently set forth. But it should be noted that he does not simply say that the legal priesthood was temporary. Instead he uses words of equivalent meaning when he says: And indeed those were made priests in greater number. Here the words seem simply to sound the same as if he wished, by antithesis, to set the one Christ against many priests, as if he meant to prove that the Gospel priesthood is praiseworthy because it is administered by one, whereas under the law many succeeded one another. Yet there is no mention of unity or multitude; the matter at issue is duration. Therefore the sense of the words is that the priesthood under the law was only temporary, but the evangelical priesthood is eternal, belonging to Christ himself. The second part of the antecedent sufficiently shows what the meaning of the first part is. But it pleased the Apostle to form the first part of the antecedent in this way, saying: And indeed those were made priests in greater number, because they were prevented by death from continuing, so that, given the antitheses, in which the Apostle is accustomed to delight in a remarkable way, and which have great charm in comparisons or rather contests, he might thereby make the other part of the antecedent: But this one, because he remains forever, has a perpetual priesthood. Here indeed the remarkable praise and dignity of Christ is displayed, since not only an eternal priesthood but also the person of Christ, remaining forever, is proclaimed. In this respect the dignity of Christ is rightly preferred to the dignity of all the legal priests. Nor would it have been so glorious and so firm to say that Christ's priesthood is eternal, unless it could also be added that Christ himself remains forever. For otherwise the Aaronic priesthood could in some sense be called eternal, namely when it was administered for many ages by priests succeeding one another; and indeed the words of God in Exodus chapter 28 sound something similar. There, after many things have been said about the institution and ordination of the legal priests, it is finally added: It shall be a statute forever for Aaron and his seed after him. Yet that was not enough for the legal priesthood to be called eternal. For although many successors held that priesthood over many ages, and so the priesthood remained stable for a long time, nevertheless, since they were all mortal, at last they failed; and with their failing the priesthood necessarily failed as well, as the outcome showed. But in the evangelical priesthood the matter stands quite differently. There is one priest, but such a one as by his nature remains forever; and since he himself remains forever, it follows easily and clearly that the priesthood itself remains eternal. From these things, therefore, it can be seen why the Apostle did not simply say that the legal priesthood was only temporary and the evangelical priesthood eternal, but used other words of equivalent meaning, whose latter part illustrates the dignity of Christ more and most clearly proves the eternity of the evangelical priesthood. The evangelical priesthood could indeed in some way be called eternal even if Christ did not remain forever, provided that other ministers succeeded others in a continuous order and no more excellent priesthood succeeded it. But it is far more splendid, more fitting to the glory of Christ, and also a more effective reasoning, to say that the evangelical priesthood is eternal because Christ the priest himself remains forever.

units.la: Cæterùm, quòd Christus maneat in æternum, nequaquam opus est vt probetur, quando id plus satis notum est, ex his, quæ de diuinitate Christi in prima disputatione præsertim primo capite huius epistolæ dicta sunt, veluti ex Psalmo centesimo primo: Ettu in initio Domine terræ fundamenta iecisti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli; ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes: & omnes vt vestimentum veterascent, ac velut amictum circumuolues eos, & mutabuntur: tu autem idem es, & anni tui non deficient.
units.tr: But that Christ remains for ever need not be proved at length, since it is already well enough known from what was said about the divinity of Christ in the first disputation, especially in the first chapter of this epistle, from Psalm 102: "And thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth, and the works of thy hands are the heavens. They shall perish, but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as a garment, and as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed. But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail."

units.la: Secundum diuinam naturam fuit ab æterno, erat in principio, manet verò nunc in æternum, non tantùm secundum diuinam naturam, verumetiam secundum humanam; nam: Semel enim excitatus à mortuis vltrà non moritur, mors illi non amplius dominabitur. Nam quòd mortuus fuit, peccato mortuus fuit semel, quòd autem viuit, viuit Deo: Roman. 6.
units.tr: According to his divine nature he was from eternity, he was in the beginning, and he now remains for ever. He does so not only according to the divine nature but also according to the human; for: "Christ, being raised from the dead, dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him. For in that he died, he died unto sin once; but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God." Romans 6.

units.la: Porrò valdè proprie dixit Apostolus, Christum habere sacerdotium ἀπαραβατον, quod alij quidem verterunt, perpetuum, vel sempiternum. Sed proprie ea vox significat, quod ad alium non demigrat, siue ad alium per successionem non transit, quasi dicat, immigrabile, intransferibile, vt ita clarissimè opponatur sacerdotium Christi lacerdotio legali, in quo cùm sacerdotium ab vno transfibat ad alium, & sic longa serie per homines mortales & miseros administrabatur, in sacerdotio tamen Christi aliter res habet, nec potest transferri ab vno ad alium, sed cùm vnus sit Christus, atque idem manens in æternum, manet etiam sacerdotium ipsius ἀπαραβατον. Vnde Chrysostomus vocens aperire vim huius vocis, Ergo qui saluat, inquit, non moritur, quia semper viuit, & non habet successorem. Valde igitur apposità est hæc vox ad illustrandam sacerdotij Christi dignitatem.
units.tr: The Apostle spoke quite properly when he said that Christ has a priesthood that is ἀπαραβατον [untransferable]. Others have rendered it "perpetual" or "everlasting", but the word properly means what does not pass over to another, what is not handed on to another by succession. It is as if he said "immigrable" or "untransferable", so that the priesthood of Christ is set in the clearest contrast with the Levitical priesthood. In that priesthood the office passed from one man to another and was carried on through a long series of mortal and wretched men. The priesthood of Christ is otherwise: it cannot be transferred from one to another. Since Christ is one and the same, remaining for ever, his priesthood also remains ἀπαραβατον. Hence Chrysostom, seeking to open up the force of this word, says: "Therefore he who saves does not die, because he lives always and has no successor." This word is therefore very aptly chosen to illustrate the dignity of the priesthood of Christ.

units.la: Cæterum, quando ex dignitate sacerdotij colligenda venit dignitas Euangelij, sequitur, vt, quia sacerdotium prædicatur æternum, simul habeatur æternum euangelium, cui nulla lex, nullum nouum fœdus sit successurum. Vbi enim euangelium successit legi, tanquam præstantius imbecilliori, non est, quod in hac vita aliquid aliud expectetur.
units.tr: Moreover, when the dignity of the Gospel is to be inferred from the dignity of the priesthood, it follows that, since the priesthood is declared to be eternal, the Gospel is likewise held to be eternal, and no law and no new covenant is to succeed it. For where the Gospel has succeeded the law, as the more excellent succeeds the weaker, there is nothing else to be expected in this life.

units.la: Omnia ad salute nostram pertinentia plenissimè sunt in euangelio reuelata, vt non opus sit aliquid amplius vel plenius manifestari, donec ad alteram vitam perueniatur: de qua 1. Corinth. 13.
units.tr: All things pertaining to our salvation have been most fully revealed in the Gospel, so that nothing further or fuller needs to be made manifest until we come to the other life. On this see 1 Corinthians 13.

units.la: Ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus, ast vbi venerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Cùm essem puer, vt puer loquebar, vt puer sentiebam, at vbi factus sum vir, aboleui puerilia. Cernimus enim per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc vero cognoscam, quemadmodum & cognitus sum. Vbi non quidè de tempore aliquo, quo præstantior cognitio in terris dabitur, sed de pleniore cognitione post hanc vitā sermo est. Indicio id est, quòd ibi agit de charitate solatùm superfutura, postquàm prophetiæ, linguæ, scientia, & cæteræ cessarint.
units.tr: "We know in part and we prophesy in part, but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face: now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I also am known." Here the apostle is not speaking of some time on earth when a higher knowledge will be given, but of a fuller knowledge after this life. This is clear from the fact that he there speaks of love alone as remaining, after prophecies, tongues and knowledge, and the rest, have ceased.

units.la: Verum est quidem, imaginati sunt plerique, distinguenda esse mundi tempora, ex ratione personarum in diuinitate, ita vt primum tempus videlicet legis naturæ & legis scriptæ, totum assignaretur Deo patri, cuius vnius gloria tunc maximè innotuit: tempus verò reuelati euangelij proprie ascriberetur filio: sed præterea expectandum fore tempus tertium, quod tribuendum foret spiritui Sancto. Sed hi falsi sunt huiusmodi confictis rationibus, quando in primo etiam filius, imò & spiritus Sanctus sanctis patribus & Prophetis abundè innotuit, sicut licet ex vaticinijs & scriptis illorum cognoscere: quando item in secundo tempore spiritus Sanctus non solùm promissus, sed etiam à Christi glorificatione datus est, vt Acta apostolorum testantur: & præterea per eundem Spiritum Apostoli tunc plenissimè edocti sunt omnem veritatem, quæ ad salutem cognitu in hac vita necessaria est: sicut Christus Ioan. 16. promiserat. Quamobrè valde sunt detestandi impostores illi, qui aliud euangelium siue aliud pactum dandum, vel, alium spiritum Sanctum mitti debuisse confingebat, vt Montanus & Priscilla ausi sunt iactare, se primù accepisse illum Spiritū doctorem omnis veritatis promissum, & nouà prophetiam (de qua & apud Tertullianum videre est) comminisci: Item, vt Manichæi suæ sectæ autorem qui Manes apud Persas gaudebat appellari, cùm antea dictus esset Vrbicus, græcis tamen pudore ductis ob tale nomen vocantibus eum Manichæum, quasi Manna fundentem) paracletum promissum prædicare non erubuerunt. Quos omnes vel ex eo vt malè sibi conscios licet iudicare, quòd Acta Apostolorum, quæ plenissimè de spiritu Sancto misso ad Apostolos testantur, exploserint, quo vno libro videbant omnia sua somnia euerti.
units.tr: It is true that many have imagined that the times of the world should be distinguished according to the persons of the Godhead, so that the first time, namely that of the law of nature and of the written law, is assigned wholly to God the Father, whose glory alone was then most clearly known; while the time of the revealed Gospel is properly ascribed to the Son; but that a third time is yet to be expected, which should be attributed to the Holy Spirit. But these men are wrong, with such invented arguments, since in the first time the Son, and indeed the Holy Spirit, was made abundantly known to the holy fathers and prophets, as may be recognised from their prophecies and writings; and likewise in the second time the Holy Spirit was not only promised but was also given after Christ's glorification, as the Acts of the Apostles bear witness; and moreover, by that same Spirit the apostles were then most fully taught all the truth that is necessary to know for salvation in this life, as Christ had promised in John 16. Therefore those impostors are to be utterly detested, who maintained that another gospel or another covenant ought to be given, or that another Holy Spirit ought to have been sent: Montanus and Priscilla dared to boast that they were the first to receive that Spirit, the teacher of all truth, promised, and to devise a new prophecy (which may be seen in Tertullian). Likewise the Manichaeans, whose founder, who delighted to be called Manes among the Persians, had previously been called Urbicus, but the Greeks, out of shame at such a name, called him Manichaeus, as though "manna-pouring", were not ashamed to proclaim the promised Paraclete. All of these one may judge to be conscious of their own wrongdoing from this alone: that they rejected the Acts of the Apostles, which most fully bear witness to the Holy Spirit sent to the apostles; for in that one book they saw that all their dreams would be overthrown.

units.la: Hæc visum est admonere, ad muniendos infirmorum animos, contra quosdam phanaticos, quos non puduit nostra tempestate comminisci, etiam nouum spiritum Sanctum in nouo baptismo dari, & tempus adesse, quo soli isti spirituales homines sint toto orbe corporaliter regnaturi: quomodo Chiliastæ etiam olim nescio quid tale sunt imaginati.
units.tr: I thought it right to remind readers of this in order to strengthen the minds of the weak against certain fanatics, who in our own time were not ashamed to invent that a new Holy Spirit is given in a new baptism, and that the time has come when these spiritual men alone will reign bodily over the whole world. The Chiliasts too once imagined something of this kind.

units.la: Secundò, est & hoc annotandum, quòd sicut ex hisce duobus posterioribus argumentis euangelij excellētia præ lege colligitur ex præstantia sacerdotij Christi præ sacerdotio legali: ita ex omnibus alijs argumentis, quibus supra excellentia sacerdotij Christi demonstrata est, debere & excellentiam euangelij colligi. Potest & huc adduci, quod ad finem capitis octaui adiecimus, de Iudæis opponenti bus, pro conseruatione suæ legis, quædam testimonia, quæ videntur promittere legis æternitatem. Sed de hoc infrà plura.
units.tr: Secondly, it should also be noted that just as the excellence of the Gospel over the law is inferred from these two later arguments, namely from the pre-eminence of the priesthood of Christ over the Levitical priesthood, so the excellence of the Gospel ought to be inferred from all the other arguments by which the excellence of the priesthood of Christ was shown above. What we added at the end of the eighth chapter may also be brought in here, concerning certain testimonies that the Jews opposed in defence of their law, which seem to promise the eternity of the law. But more on this below.

units.la: Vnde et saluos facere ad plenū potest, qui per ipsum adeunt Deū, semper viuēs, ad hoc, vt interpellet pro illis. Talis enim decebat, vt esset pōtifex, pius, innocēs, impollu-tus, segregatus à peccatoribus, & sublimior cœlis factus, cui non sit quotidie necesse, quemadmodum illis pōtificibus, prius pro proprijs peccatis victimas offerre: deinde pro peccatis populi. Nam id fecit semel, cum semetipsum obtulit: Siquidem Lex homines constituit pontifices, habentes infirmitatem. Porrò sermo iurisiurandi, qui supra le-gem fit, filium constituit in æternū consummatum, &c. usque ad, quod nixit Deus, & non homo.
units.tr: "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself. For the law maketh men high priests which have infirmity; but the word of the oath, which was since the law, maketh the Son, who is consecrated for evermore." And so on, to the words "which the Lord sware, and not man."

units.la: Conclusio valde didactica & consolatoria, in qua ex præcedentibus argumentis de dignitate & officio sacerdotis Christi nonnulla valde proprijs verbis infert, ad ingētem conscientiarum doctrinam & consolationem. Nos ordine progrediendi singulas particulas explicabimus, easque in primis, quæ ad consolationem conscientiarum sunt collectæ: quando multa & varia sunt inspersa, quę non facile vno Syllogismo comprehēdi possent. Ac primùm quidem infert, Christo id tribuendū, quòd per ipsum omnes ad plenum salui, id est, perfecti fiunt. Sed vnde istud ex ijs, quæ dicta sunt, sequitur? Legem abrogatam cùm ob imbecillitatem suā, quòd videlicet perfectos non posset reddere, tum quòd euangelium multo excellentius succederet, ostendit. Hinc verò habita ratione an tieseos, qua euangelium opponitur & anteponitur Legi, fuisset inferendum, quòd per euangelium homines perfecti efficiantur, quod & rectissimè dici potuisset. Sed Apostolus vt semper quæres gloriam Christi illustrare, præsertim apud Iudæos, maluit eam potestatem ad Christi personam transferre, idq; eo iustius, quòd ab hoc omnis pendet euangelij dignitas, & si quid præclari habet euangelium, vni Christo acceptum ferri debet. Vide autem, quàm eleganter expressit Apostolus hanc particulam.
units.tr: This conclusion is very instructive and consoling. From the preceding arguments concerning the dignity and office of the priest Christ, it draws some points in very particular words, for the great instruction and comfort of consciences. We shall explain the individual clauses in the order of the text, especially those gathered for the comfort of consciences, since many and varied matters are sprinkled in, which could not easily be comprehended in a single syllogism. First he infers that to Christ must be attributed that through him all are saved to the uttermost, that is, made perfect. But how does this follow from what has been said? He showed that the law has been abrogated, both because of its weakness, namely that it could not make men perfect, and because the Gospel succeeds it far more excellently. From this, taking account of the antithesis by which the Gospel is set against and preferred to the law, it could have been inferred that through the Gospel men are made perfect, which could also have been said quite correctly. But the Apostle, who always seeks to illustrate the glory of Christ, especially before the Jews, preferred to transfer that power to the person of Christ. He did so the more justly because the whole dignity of the Gospel depends on him, and if the Gospel has anything excellent, it must be credited to Christ alone. Note how elegantly the Apostle has expressed this clause.

units.la: Potest, inquit, saluare: Quod reuera præclarum est, sicut Angelus etiam de Christo prædicarat Matthei 1. Vocabis nomen eius Iesum, is enim saluum faciet populū suum à peccatis suis. Nonne hic est pclatus titulo, quo titulo appellatur Saluator & seruator? Et tamen non fuit contentus Apostolus hac præclara Christi appellatione, addidit insu per, εἰς τὸ παντελὲς, ad plenum, in integrum, consummatè, absolutè. Id verò, simul, vt ostenderet, à solo Christo, citra vllius alterius personę vel rei adminiculum, salutem procurare: simul vt non tantùm corporalem & externam coram mundo, qualis ferè à lege præstabatur, verumetiam spiritualem & internam coram Deo iustitiam seu perfectionem ab vno Christo expectandam declararet. Si enim opus foret aliquo alio auxilio, vel si nequaquam animæ salus procuraretur, non rectè diceretur Christus ad plenum saluos facere, sed adhuc magna pars deesset. Nonnulli autē istud εἰς τὸ παντελὲς verterunt, in perpetuum, in hac vita & in altera, (vt Theophylactus) vel hic, & illic (vt Chrysostomus) quasi ad tempus proprie referretur, vt etiam responderet ei, quod ostenditur hîc Christum semper viuere, vt coniungat hæc præcedentibus, qua interpretatione significatur, Christum & hic temporaneâ, & post hanc vitam etiam æternam salutem conferre. Neq; est quod interpretemur, quasi Origeniānum aliquid resipiant illi Patres.
units.tr: He is able, he says, to save. This is indeed a distinguished title, just as the angel also declared of Christ in Matthew 1: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins." Is this not an honour conferred by the title by which he is called Saviour and Preserver? Yet the Apostle was not content with this distinguished appellation of Christ, but added besides to the uttermost [εἰς τὸ παντελὲς], that is, completely, wholly, perfectly. He did this, first, to show that salvation is procured by Christ alone, without the help of any other person or thing; and second, to declare that the righteousness or perfection to be expected from Christ alone is not merely the outward and bodily kind, before the world, which the law for the most part provided, but the spiritual and inward kind, before God. For if some other help were needed, or if the salvation of the soul were not procured at all, it would not rightly be said that Christ saves to the uttermost, since a large part would still be lacking. Some have rendered to the uttermost [εἰς τὸ παντελὲς] as "forever, in this life and in the next" (as Theophylact does), or "here and there" (as Chrysostom does), as if it referred properly to time, so that it would answer to what is shown here, that Christ always lives, and so join it to what precedes. By this interpretation it is meant that Christ confers salvation both temporal here and eternal after this life. Nor need we interpret it as if those Fathers were tasting of something Origenist.

units.la: Itaque aptissimè vsus est loquendi forma, qua consummatam perfectionem, & aliquid plus etiam, quàm voce perfectionis significatur, expressit. Non dubium interim, quin saluū facere ad plenum, pro eo, quod est perfectum facere, vsurpare voluerit: atq; etiam ad id, quod suprà de lege dictum est, eam videlicet non posse perfectos reddere, respexerit.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle has very aptly used a form of speech that expresses complete perfection, and something more besides, than the word "perfection" alone signifies. There is no doubt that he wished to use to save to the uttermost in place of to make perfect, and that he also had in view what was said above about the law, namely that it could not make men perfect.

units.la: Qui per ipsum adeunt Deum) En quales saluos ad plenum faciat, nempe eos, qui Deum adeunt, inuocant, orant, vitam sibi dari petunt, sed per Christum, & propter Christum non per legem vel ἰδικολογησιν, vel quamcunque aliam viam. Ita periphrasis hæc simpliciter significat credentes in Christum. At necessarium fuit particulam hanc interpo-nere, propterea quòd Hebræi pertinacissimè semper contendebant pro dignitate legis, & inprimis ceremoniarum, per quas putabant, se debere Deum adire: aut, etiamsi per Christum, non tamen solum, & citra ceremonias legales fieri id posse arbitrabantur. Solus autem Christus, via, vita, veritas est ad patrem, solus est ostium, per quod in ouile Dei admittamur: Vnde & Ioannes capite sexto ait, Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Roman. 5. Iustificati ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem & contigit nobis, vt fide perduceremur in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus.
units.tr: Who come to God through him. See what sort of people he saves to the uttermost: namely, those who come to God, call upon him, pray, and ask that life be given them, but through Christ and on account of Christ, not through the law, nor through their own devices [ἰδικολογησιν], nor by any other way. So this periphrasis simply means believers in Christ. But it was necessary to insert this phrase, because the Hebrews always contended most stubbornly for the dignity of the law, and especially of the ceremonies, through which they thought they ought to approach God; or, even if they admitted that this could be done through Christ, they did not think it could be done through him alone, apart from the legal ceremonies. Yet Christ alone is the way, the life, and the truth to the Father; he alone is the door through which we are admitted into the sheepfold of God. Hence also John says in chapter 6: "No one comes to the Father except through me." Romans 5: "Justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand."

units.la: Omnes quidem volunt adire Deum, & iactant, se id strenuè facere: sed plurimi in hoc errant, quòd per rectam viam, quæ est Christus, non ingrediuntur. Alij traditiones suorum patrum, alij propria somnia à se excogitata amplectuntur, præ doctrina Christi: alij per sanctos, qui hinc migrarunt, salute quærunt. Sed certi esse debent tales, se eo pacto nunquam ad patrem peruenturos. Proinde valde vtiliter & circumspectè Apostolus ad Hebræos scribens, particulam istam interseruit. Sequitur:
units.tr: All indeed wish to approach God, and boast that they do so zealously; but most are in error in this, that they do not enter by the right way, which is Christ. Some embrace the traditions of their fathers, others their own dreams devised by themselves, in preference to the teaching of Christ; others seek salvation through the saints who have departed from here. But such people ought to be certain that they will never reach the Father in that way. Therefore the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, inserted this phrase very usefully and circumspectly. It follows:

units.la: Semper viuens, ad hoc, ut interpellet pro ipsis) Exponit, quomodo possit saluos facere. Semper interpellando, inquit, Patrem, pro credentibus. Est ratio sumpta ab officio Sacerdotis, quod quidem officium, sicut ipse sacerdos manet in æternum, ita exerceri quoque in æternum debet. Neque enim imaginari licet Christum ita esse sacerdotem, vt interea non præstet, quæ sunt sui officij, aut quasi fessus ad tempus ferietur, aliosue substituat. Quare de perpetua & nunquam intermissa interpellatione Christi agitur. Ac fluit ratio hæc de perpetua interpellatione Christi, ex argumento, quo proximè probatum est, Christum in æternum manere, & sacerdotium similiter æternum habere. Si Christus æternus est, etc. semper manet sacerdos: Ergo & semper interpellat.
units.tr: Living always, to make intercession for them. He explains how he can save them. By always interceding, he says, with the Father, for believers. This is an argument taken from the office of the priest; and just as the priest himself remains forever, so this office too must be exercised forever. For we may not imagine that Christ is a priest in such a way that meanwhile he does not perform the duties of his office, or that he rests for a time as if weary, or appoints substitutes. Therefore we are speaking of a perpetual and never interrupted intercession of Christ. And this argument about the perpetual intercession of Christ follows from the argument just proved, that Christ remains forever and likewise has an everlasting priesthood. If Christ is eternal, etc., he always remains a priest; therefore he also always intercedes.

units.la: Cæterum, officium esse Sacerdotis, interpellare Deum pro credentibus, satis liquet ex descriptione Sacerdotis habita initio capitis quinti: vbi quædam eodem spectantia aliunde citauimus. Christum verò hoc ipsum apud Deum patrem fecisse, & assiduæ fa-cere, ibidem dicitur, hisce verbis: Christus in diebus carnis suæ, cum precationes & supplicationes cum clamore valido & lachrymis obtulisset, exauditus est. Adhuc verò in cœlis idem eum facere, 1. Corinthiorum 2. Ephesiorum 1. prima Ioannis capite secundo, & aliis multis locis, vbi celebratur mediator, reconciliator, aduocatus noster, perspicuum euadit. Porrò non caret Emphasi, quòd maluit dicere, Christum semper viuentem potius, quàm semper manentem, sicut antè appellauerat. Magis enim convenit viuentis appellatio ei, qui alios debeat saluos ad plenum facere, & vitam mortuis impendere. Deus enim Deus est viuentium, non mortuorum. Similiter valde apta est insti-tuto vox ςυντυχανων, quæ similiter, & simili significatione habetur Romanorum capite octauo, vbi dicitur, quòd Spiritus intercedit (græcè est ὑπερεντυγχάνει) pro nobis, gemitibus inenarrabilibus. Item Romanorum capite vndecimo. An nescitis de Elia, quid dicat Scriptura? quomodo interpellat (ἐντυγχάνει) apud Deum aduersus Israel? Cæterum, officium interpellandi Deum patrem Christo tribuitur, secundum humanitate, secundum quam etiam sacerdos constitutus est, vt hic notat Theophylactus: ita tamen vt diuinitas ab humanitate non separetur: secundum quam diuinitatem Christus vna cum patre potestomnia.
units.tr: Moreover, that it is the office of the priest to intercede with God for believers is sufficiently clear from the description of the priest given at the beginning of chapter 5, where we cited some passages bearing on this from elsewhere. That Christ himself has done this before God the Father, and continually does it, is said in the same place in these words: "Christ, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, was heard." That he still does the same in heaven becomes evident from 1 Corinthians 2, Ephesians 1, 1 John 2, and many other places, where he is celebrated as mediator, reconciler, and our advocate. Furthermore, there is emphasis in the fact that he preferred to call Christ "living always" rather than "remaining always," as he had said before. For the title "living" better suits one who must save others to the uttermost and bestow life on the dead: "God is the God of the living, not of the dead." Similarly, the word intercedes [ςυντυχανων] is very fitting here, and it has the same meaning in Romans 8, where it is said that the Spirit intercedes [ὑπερεντυγχάνει] for us with inexpressible groanings. Likewise in Romans 11: "Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah? How he pleads [ἐντυγχάνει] with God against Israel?" Moreover, the office of interceding with God the Father is assigned to Christ according to his humanity, according to which he is also appointed priest, as Theophylact notes here; yet in such a way that the divinity is not separated from the humanity, and according to that divinity Christ together with the Father has all power.

units.la: Talis enim decebat, vt esset nobis pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, sublimior cœlis factus, cui non sit quotidie necesse, quemadmodum illis pontificibus, prius pro proprijs peccatis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi. Nam id fecit semel, cum semetipsum obtulit. Siquidem Lex homines constituit pontifices habentes infirmitatem: Porrò sermo iurisiurandi, qui supra legem fuit, filium constituit in æternum consummatum.
units.tr: For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, made higher than the heavens, who does not need daily, as those high priests did, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. For he did this once for all, when he offered himself. For the law appoints men as high priests who have weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, made perfect forever.

units.la: Confirmat, quòd Christus posset ad plenum saluos siue perfectos reddere: idque potissimum, sumpta ratione ab excellentia & summa perfectione personæ Christi, videlicet, Christum esse per omnia eiusmodi, qualem esse decebat eum, à quo id fieri deberet. Sententiam horum omnium, quæ hoc capite sequuntur, licebit hoc pacto in vnum Syllogismum crassius, nostro more, constringere.
units.tr: He confirms that Christ is able to save or make perfect to the uttermost; and he does this chiefly by an argument taken from the excellence and supreme perfection of the person of Christ, namely that Christ is in every respect such as it was fitting that he should be, by whom this would have to be done. The sense of all that follows in this chapter may, in our manner, be compressed in this way into one rather crude syllogism:

units.la: Vt quis alios ad plenum saluos & perfectos posset facere, decebat inprimis perfectum & consummatum esse.
units.tr: For someone to be able to save and make perfect others to the uttermost, it was fitting above all that he himself be perfect and complete.

units.la: Atqui Christus est huiusmodi, perfectus, inquam, & consummatus:
units.tr: But Christ is such, perfect, I say, and complete.

units.la: Igitur potest & alios perfectos reddere.
units.tr: Therefore he is able also to make others perfect.

units.la: Maior non videtur probationem pleniorem requirere. Minorem declarat haec congerie: Christus, inquit, est pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, sublimior cœlis factus, nullis infirmitatibus obnoxius: igitur est perfectus & consummatus. Interea quę illustrandi amplificandiue causa sunt admixta, nos inter explicandum, quantum opus erit, adnotabimus.
units.tr: The major premise does not seem to require fuller proof. The minor he sets out in this series: Christ, he says, is a high priest, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, made higher than the heavens, subject to no weakness; therefore he is perfect and complete. Meanwhile, whatever has been mixed in for the sake of illustration or amplification, we shall note as we explain, as far as is needed.

units.la: Cæterum non est imaginandum, ita hæc tribui Christo vti solent Rhetores vel Poetæ in Panegyricis magnifica quædam canere de principibus, potius significantes, quales illos esse cupiant, quàm quales sint. Sed iustissimè verissimeq; hæc omnia de Christo prædicantur, nec respondent eius meritis, nec verba dignitatem eius satis exprimunt: id quod nos citra negotium possemus & ex prophetarum de Christo vaticinijs, & ex rebus per ipsum gestis comprobare. Ait ergo: Talis enim decebat, ut esset nobis pontifex, in- primis, pius: Atque ita accipiendæ sunt virtutes, quæ hîc prædicantur in Christo, ut intel- ligantur plerunque opponi, & simul præferri virtutibus illis, quæ esse debebant in sacerdotibus legis veteris, cum quibus Christus contentione rhetorica fere vbique hîc comparonitur. Vnde & de Christo secundum humanam naturam omnia dicta esse oportet intelligi. Quantulum enim id esset, si ei tribuerentur hæc secundum naturam diuinam? Itaque primùm dicitur Christus ὅσιος, id est, pius, sanctus, & res sacras sanctè tractans. Proprie enim hæc vox significat ea, quæ pertinent ad pietatem erga Deum: ita ut ratio- nem habuisse videatur Apostolus in hac congerie huiusmodi diuisionis, qua primùm in Christo ostendat maximam dignitatem, quòd vere pius & religiosus esset in Deum. Secundò, quòd innocens erga proximum. Tertiò, quòd impollutus, quantum ad suam personam, siue erga seipsum. Quibus ita expositis, facilè perspicitur, Christum per om- nia perfectum esse & consummatum. Dicitur verò ὅσιος, quasi ὅσιος, ab ἀ, id est, colo, veneror, & honorem exhibeo. Proinde huiusmodi pij, & religioni sanctimoniæque toti dediti debebant esse sacerdotes ac Leuitæ veteris testamenti, licut multis in locis, præfer tim libri Leuitici, præcipitur. Sed nullus ita proprie ὅσιος dici potest, uti vnus Christus quam Daniel quoque capite nono sanctum sanctorum appellare non dubitauit, & Angelus Lucæ primo ad Mariam dixit, quòd ex ea nasceretur, sanctum vocandum. Secundò prædicatur Christus ἄκακος, interpres vertit innocens: licet non sit, Cicerone teste, apud græcos vox, quæ simpliciter respondeat voci innocentiæ. Significat proprie ἄκακος alienum ob omni malitia, dolo, fraude, vel voluntati nocendi. κακία significat studium nocendi, quæ vox sæpe inuenitur in Scriptis apostolicis. Itaque per contrarium ratione particulæ priuatiuæ, ἀκακος dicitur, qui à studio nocendi quàm longissimè abest. Requirebatur autem & summa ἀκακία in sacerdotibus veteris testamenti: vnde & multa negotia erant illis singulariter interdicta, quæ videlicet ad dolum & fraudem potuissent impellere: atque ita functionem suam debebant instituere, ut è nemine quicquam acce- pisse, vel neminem grauasse viderentur, & nemo de illis posset conqueri. Atqui in nullo vnquam talis innocentia deprehensa est, qualis in Christo emicuit, de quo Esaias capite quinquagesimo tertio, quòd iniquitatem non fecerit, & dolus non fuerit inuentus in ore eius. Vbi & innocentissimo anniculo oui obmutescenti, cùm ducitur ad mortem, comparatur: qui loci 1. Pet. 2. 1. Ioan. 3. & Actor. 8. de Christo proprie exponuntur, qui etiam pro crucifixoribus orauit.
