units.tr: Yet we must not imagine that these things are attributed to Christ in the way that orators or poets are accustomed to sing lofty praises of princes in panegyrics, signifying rather what they wish them to be than what they are. Rather, all these things are declared of Christ most justly and truly, and neither do the words fully express his merit nor do they exhaust his dignity; which we could easily prove from the prophetic utterances about Christ and from the deeds he performed. He says, therefore: For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest: first, holy [ὅσιος]. And the virtues that are proclaimed here in Christ must be understood in such a way that they are generally understood to be set against, and at the same time preferred to, those virtues which ought to have been in the priests of the old law, with whom Christ is almost everywhere compared here by a rhetorical contrast. Hence all the things said of Christ must also be understood as said of him according to human nature. For how small a thing it would be if these were ascribed to him according to the divine nature! Thus first Christ is called holy [ὅσιος], that is, pious, sanctified, and one who handles sacred things sacredly. For this word properly signifies those things which pertain to piety toward God; so the Apostle seems to have had in mind a division of this kind, by which he first shows Christ's supreme dignity, in that he was truly pious and devout toward God. Second, that he was innocent toward his neighbour. Third, that he was undefiled as regards his own person, or toward himself. With these points thus set out, it is easily seen that Christ is perfect and complete in every respect. It is said holy [ὅσιος], as if from holy [ὅσιος], by a privative from ἀ, that is, to honour, to revere, and to pay reverence. Accordingly, such pious men, wholly devoted to religion and holiness, ought to have been the priests and Levites of the Old Testament, as is commanded in many places, especially in the book of Leviticus. But no one can be properly called holy [ὅσιος] as only Christ can be; so Daniel too in chapter 9 did not hesitate to call him the Holy of Holies, and the angel in Luke 1 said to Mary that the child born of her would be called holy. Second, Christ is called innocent [ἄκακος], which the interpreter renders as innocent, although, as Cicero testifies, there is no Greek word that simply corresponds to the word for innocence. Properly ἄκακος [ἄκακος] signifies one who is free from all malice, guile, fraud, or will to harm. Malice [κακία] signifies the zeal to harm, a word often found in the apostolic writings. Thus, by contrast, through the force of the privative particle, one is called innocent [ἀκακος] who is as far as possible from a zeal to harm. Now the highest innocence [ἀκακία] was also required in the priests of the Old Testament; hence many dealings were specially forbidden to them, namely those that might have driven them to deceit and fraud; and so they had to conduct their office in such a way that they seemed to have received nothing from anyone, or to have burdened no one, and no one could complain about them. Yet in no one has such innocence ever been detected as shone forth in Christ, of whom Isaiah in chapter 53 says that he did no iniquity and that no guile was found in his mouth. There he is also compared to an innocent lamb that is dumb when it is led to slaughter; and these passages, 1 Peter 2, 1 John 3, and Acts 8, are properly explained of Christ, who also prayed for his crucifiers.

units.la: Tertiò prædicatur Christus ἀμίαντος, non inquinatus, impollutus. Hæc particula po- sita est propterea, quòd in sacerdotibus veteris legis requirebatur mirabilis mundities, & à certis rebus abstinentia, adeò ut etiam solo contractu quarundam rerum iudicaban-tur polluti & immundi, veluti si quis attigisset mortuum, si tempore sacrificij vsus fuisset vino, iunxisset se vxori, attigisset leprosum, menstruosam. Propter hæc iudicabatur im-mundus, debebatque certis cæremonijs iterum purificari. Similiter qui vitium habebat in corpore, vt gibbum: item cui defuissent testiculi, non poterat admitti ad ministerium: Leuit. 21. Imò & de hostijs quærebatur, num essent mundæ & absque macula. Quando igitur maximopere cauebatur, ne sacerdotes seu Leuitæ his modis polluerentur, iam spectatur, an' ne Christus quoque hac in parte fuerit sacerdotio dignus. Ac dicitur simpli citer Christus impollutus, hoc est, nullam habens in se maculam, nulla re contaminatus, non tantùm corporaliter, sed nec secundum animam. Quamobrem adumbratus fuit in veteri lege peragnum anniculum sine macula, Exodi duodecimo, & in euangelio prædicatur conceptus & natus de spiritu Sancto, præterea omnibus Spiritus Sancti donis exornatus.
units.tr: Thirdly, Christ is proclaimed ἀμίαντος [amiantos], undefiled and unpolluted. This term is used because the priests of the old law were required to be remarkably clean and to abstain from certain things. Merely by contact with certain things they were judged polluted and unclean: for example, if someone had touched a dead body, had drunk wine at the time of sacrifice, had lain with his wife, or had touched a leper or a menstruating woman. For these reasons a man was judged unclean and had to be purified again by certain ceremonies. Likewise one who had a defect in his body, such as a hunchback, or one who lacked testicles, could not be admitted to the ministry: Lev. 21. Indeed even the victims were examined, to see whether they were clean and without blemish. Therefore, since great care was taken that priests or Levites should not be polluted in these ways, it is now considered whether Christ too was worthy of the priesthood in this respect. And Christ is simply called undefiled, that is, having no stain in himself and contaminated by nothing, not only in body but not even in soul. For this reason the year-old lamb without blemish was foreshadowed in the old law, Exod. 12, and in the gospel he is proclaimed conceived and born of the Holy Spirit, and furthermore adorned with all the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quartò, prædicatur Christus segregatus à peccatoribus, hoc est, nihil habens commune cum peccatoribus. Versatus quidem est in mundo, & inter peccatores, & tentatus per omnia iuxta similitudinem nostram, sed, ut supra dictum est capite 4. absque peccato, quod in ipso locum habere nullo modo potuit.
units.tr: Fourthly, Christ is proclaimed separated from sinners, that is, having nothing in common with sinners. He indeed lived in the world and among sinners, and was tempted in all things according to our likeness, but, as said above in chapter 4, without sin, which could in no way have any place in him.

units.la: Fuit verò & hoc in lege cautum, ne sacerdotes palàm flagitiosis hominibus cohabitarent, vel alias consuetudinem cum eis haberent: idque ne vel ipsi paribus vitijs assuescerent, vel viderentur in alijs malefacta comprobare. Hac igitur ratione Christus quoque dicitur segregatus à peccatoribus, quandoquidem neque aliorum vitijs inquinari potuit, neque ea vllo pacto visus est comprobare. Verum quidem est, versatus est etiam cum publicis peccatoribus, quod illi probro vertere ausi sunt tumidi pharisæi, Matthæi nono. Sed id fecit, nō ut approbans eorum facta, sed ut boni & pij medici instar illos in rectam viam reduceret, & à peccatis liberaret.
units.tr: This too was provided for in the law: priests were not to live openly with wicked men, or otherwise have dealings with them, lest they themselves become accustomed to the same vices, or seem to approve the wrongdoing of others. By this reasoning Christ too is said to be separated from sinners, since he could be stained by no one else's vices, nor was he ever seen to approve them. It is true that he also associated with public sinners, which the proud Pharisees dared to turn into a reproach, Matt. 9. But he did this not to approve their deeds, but like a good and godly physician, to bring them back to the right way and free them from sins.

units.la: Conuictus externus non potuit illi esse noxius; in quo esse non poterat, consensus in malo internus. Qui ab hoc consensu immunis est, citra reprehensionem inter impios versatur, cum sanctis etiā semper, quādiu in hoc mundo uiuunt inter impios necessariò sit agendum: aut alias, sicut alibi Apostolus ait, de mundo exeundum. Sed tamen Dominus suos seruat, quomodo seruauit Esaiam, qui capite sexto queritur, se habitare in medio populi polluti labijs: & Ezechielis secundo capite se habitare cum scorpionibus: & Philippensium secundo, Apostolus vult credentes filios Dei irreprehensibiles agere in medio nationis prauæ ac tortuosæ, & inter hos lucere tanquam luminaria in mundo, sermonem vitæ sustinentes.
units.tr: Outward association could not harm him, since inward consent to evil could not exist in him. One who is free from this consent lives among the impious without blame. Saints too must always, as long as they live in this world, necessarily act among the impious; otherwise, as the Apostle says elsewhere, they would have to go out of the world. But the Lord keeps his own, as he kept Isaiah, who in chapter 6 complains that he dwells in the midst of a people of unclean lips; and Ezekiel, in chapter 2, that he dwells with scorpions; and in Philippians 2 the Apostle wishes believers, the sons of God, to be blameless in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, and to shine among them as lights in the world, holding forth the word of life.

units.la: Quintò prædicatur Christus sublimior cœlis factus, id est, planè cœlestis & supramundanus factus, nihil humile vel terrenum sapiens. Ita namque hanc particulam quodammodo ad insinuandum, res maximas, & quibus nihil sublimius cogitari vel dici queat, esse in Christo, apparet esse additam, ut iam nulli amplius sacerdotes legales veniant cum eo comparandi.
units.tr: Fifthly, Christ is proclaimed made higher than the heavens, that is, made wholly heavenly and beyond the world, savouring nothing lowly or earthly. This phrase seems to have been added in order to suggest, in a way, that the greatest things, than which nothing higher can be thought or said, are in Christ, so that no legal priests may now come to be compared with him.

units.la: Sic autem Christus humana carne indutus vere erat spiritualis homo, vtpote de spiritu Sancto conceptus, & spiritu Sancto semper plenus, spiritum Sanctum habens in se manentem: Et prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto, Primus homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo ipse Dominus de cœlo, &c. Etiamsi videri posset Apostolus respexisse ad id, quod supra dixit, Christum penetrasse cœlos, capite quinto: & rursus capite sexto, introisse eum vsque ad ea, quæ sunt intra velum: &, quod mox subijcitur, Christum considere ad dexteram throni maiestatis in cœlis, quæ verba nos mox plenius explicabimus: in quam sententiam & dictum est Ephes. 1. Christum in cœlestibus sedere supra omnem principatum, potestatem, virtutem, & dominium. Cæterum in his verbis:
units.tr: Thus Christ, clothed in human flesh, was truly a spiritual man, since he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, was always full of the Holy Spirit, and had the Spirit abiding in him. So also 1 Cor. 15: "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man, the Lord himself, is from heaven," and so on. Although it might seem that the Apostle had in view what he said above, that Christ penetrated the heavens, chapter 5; and again in chapter 6, that he entered as far as the things within the veil; and what is immediately added, that Christ sits at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens, words which we shall soon explain more fully. To the same effect is what is said in Eph. 1, that Christ sits in the heavenly places above every principality, power, virtue and dominion. But in these words:

units.la: Cui non sit necesse quotidie, quemadmodum illis pontificibus, prius pro propriis peccatis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi. Nam id fecit semel, cum semetipsum obtulit.
units.tr: "Who has no need daily, as those high priests, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people. For he did this once, when he offered himself."

units.la: Præterquam quòd excellentia Christi illustratur præ dignitate sacerdotum legalium, maximè quia dicitur, hos debuisse quotidie offerre, quo de Christo nullo modo dici potest. Latet insuper hic & aliud argumentum, probans, Christum posse perfectos reddere, sumptum ab efficacia sacrificij eius, estque hæc sententia:
units.tr: Besides, the excellence of Christ is set forth in comparison with the dignity of the legal priests, chiefly because it is said that they had to offer daily, which can in no way be said of Christ. Moreover there is a further argument hidden here, proving from the efficacy of his sacrifice that Christ can make men perfect; and the sense is this:

units.la: Olim sacerdotes legales quotidie noua offerebant sacrificia, quia videlicet nullu poterat pro peccatis satisfacere, siue homines perfectos reddere.
units.tr: Formerly the legal priests offered new sacrifices every day, because clearly nothing could satisfy for sins or make men perfect.

units.la: Christus autem non ita quotidie debet offerre, sed obtulit tantum semel.
units.tr: But Christ does not need to offer daily in this way; he offered only once.

units.la: Quare consequens, id est, quòd possit ad plenum saluos facere.
units.tr: Therefore it follows that he is able to save completely.

units.la: Ita namque intelligi vult Apostolus hanc fuisse causam, cur in lege sine intermissione repetebantur sacrificia, quòd videlicet nunquam perfectos redderent homines, siue à peccatis expiarent. Hoc verò vbi sic habet, rectè per contrarium colligitur, Christi sacrificio homines perfectos reddi, quando nequaquam opus fuit illud repeti. Huc pertinet, quod in sequentibus sæpius, & ut acri studio obseruandum, & ut maximè ad gloriam Christi faciens inculcat, Christum semel tantum obtulisse: ut capite nono, per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sancta, æterna redemptione reperta. Rursus eodem capite: Ingressus est Christus in ipsum cœlum, ut appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis, non vt sæpius offerat semetipsum, sed nunc semel sub consummatione seculorum, ad profligationem peccati, per immolationem sui ipsius apparuit. Ibidem statim sequitur: Christus semel oblatus, vt multorum peccata tolleret. Vbi particulæ de profligando peccato, deque tollendis peccatis sunt notandæ. Sed multo adhuc apertius capite decimo, cuius initio dicit, easdem victimas ideò singulis diebus continenter offerri, quia nunquam possunt accedentes perfectos reddere, alioqui offerri desijssent. Et paulum progressus ait de Christo, quòd vnica oblatione perfectos reddidit in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur. Vbi clarè exprimitur, quænam sit præsentis loci germana sententia. Hoc autem argumentum de efficacia sacrificij, non sumitur ex argumentis præcedentibus, quid de sacrificio Christi adhuc nihil dictum est: sed tantum de institutione & præstantia sacerdotij eius præ sacerdotio legali. Dicetur autem de sacrificio Christi plenius in sequentibus, ad quæ videtur sibi viam hic voluisse parare.
units.tr: For the Apostle wishes it understood thus: that this was the reason why sacrifices were repeated without intermission under the law, namely that they never made men perfect or cleansed them from sins. Where this is so stated, it is rightly inferred by contrast that men are made perfect by the sacrifice of Christ, since there was no need at all for it to be repeated. To this belongs what he often impresses in what follows, and what must be observed with keen attention and above all for the glory of Christ: that Christ offered himself only once. So in chapter 9, he entered once into the holy places through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. Again in the same chapter: Christ entered into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us, not that he should offer himself often, but now once at the end of the ages he has appeared, for the putting away of sin by the sacrifice of himself. Immediately afterwards in the same place follows: Christ, once offered, to bear the sins of many. Here the phrases about putting away sin and bearing away sins are to be noted. But much more plainly still in chapter 10, at whose beginning he says that the same victims were offered continually every day because those who come can never be made perfect; otherwise they would have ceased to be offered. Going on a little, he says of Christ that by one offering he has made perfect for ever those who are sanctified. Here the true sense of the present passage is clearly expressed. This argument from the efficacy of the sacrifice is not drawn from the preceding arguments, since nothing has yet been said about the sacrifice of Christ, but only about the institution and the excellence of his priesthood beyond the legal priesthood. The sacrifice of Christ will be discussed more fully in what follows, for which the author seems to have wished to prepare the way here.

units.la: Quis autem non miretur, præsentem conclusionem in tam paucis verbis, tam grauia & multiplicia argumenta continere? Et quis non miretur tam artificiosè constitutam? Sunt autem membra singula diligenter expendenda, & utrinque singula singulis opponenda,
units.tr: Who would not marvel that the present conclusion contains such weighty and manifold arguments in so few words? And who would not marvel that it is so skilfully constructed? Each member must be carefully weighed, and each part set against the corresponding part on the other side.

units.la: Christo, inquit, non est necesse: Non citra Emphasin vsus est voce necessitatis, σαρουσ. Significat enim, sacerdotum legalium maximam fuisse imperfectionem, vt qui necessitate coacti sint semper redire ad nouas oblationes. Ac duplex, si bene animaduertimus, eos ad id cogebat necessitas: altera ex parte ipsorum, quandoquidem ipsi semper infirmi erant, & semper peccabant. Altera ex parte hostiarum, quæ nunquam poterant per se expiare peccata.
units.tr: "There is no need for Christ," he says. It is not without emphasis that he uses the word for necessity, ἀνάγκη [anankē]. For it signifies that the legal priests suffered the greatest imperfection, since they were forced by necessity always to return to new oblations. And, if we observe rightly, two sources compelled them to this necessity: one on their own side, since they were always weak and always sinned; the other on the side of the victims, which could never by themselves expiate sins.

units.la: Porrò, in Christo neutra necessitas habebat locum: quando & ipse immunis erat à peccato, & hostiam multò efficacissimam ad tollenda omnia omnium hominum peccata obtulit. Necessitas autem fuit sacerdotibus, vt offerrent quotidie. Quotidie exorientibus nouis peccatis, & nullo vnquam pro illis sacrificio satisfaciente, necessum erat quotidie noua sacrificia offerri. Nullum autem diem potuisse transigi sine sacrificio, clarè dicitur Numerorum vicesimo octauo, Agnos anniculos immaculatos duos quotidie in holocaustum sempiternum offeretis, vnam mane, & alterum ad vesperam, decimam partem Ephi similæ, quæ conspersa sit oleo purissimo, & habeat quartam partem Ephi Hin: Holocaustum iuge est, quod obtulistis in monte Sina, in odorem suauissimum in conspectu Domini, &c. At Christus obtulit tantum semel. Ex quo necessariò sequitur, longè efficacius esse debere vnum sacrificium Christi, quàm tot & perpetua illa sacrificia pontificum legalium.
units.tr: Furthermore, in Christ neither necessity had any place, since he himself was free from sin and offered a far more efficacious victim for taking away the sins of all men. But the priests were under necessity to offer every day. Since new sins arose daily, and no sacrifice ever satisfied for them once and for all, new sacrifices had to be offered daily. Numbers 28 states plainly that no day could pass without sacrifice: "You shall offer two unblemished yearling lambs daily as a perpetual burnt offering, one in the morning and the other at evening, with a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the purest oil, and a fourth part of a hin. It is the continual burnt offering that was offered at Mount Sinai, a sweet savour before the Lord, etc." But Christ offered only once. From this it necessarily follows that the one sacrifice of Christ must be far more efficacious than those many and perpetual sacrifices of the legal priests.

units.la: Semel autem obtulit, videlicet, quando semel pro omnibus mortuus est, adeò vt non magis potuerit sæpius quàm semel offerre, quàm posset sæpius, quàm semel mori: sicut adhuc capitis noni subijcitur. Esset autem dignus typus ille veteris testamenti de iugi seu quotidiano sacrificio agnorum, in quem oculatius intueremur. Agnorum oblatio quid aliud sibi voluit, quàm admonere homines, quòd deberent intenti esse fide in agnum Christum, qui ad tollenda peccata mundi erat promissus? Duos verò offerri præcipiebatur simul, vt significaretur, neque quamlibet multos potuisse purgare peccata: simul, nondum adfuisse tempus, quo vnus agnus Christus sufficeret. Quotidie illi offerebantur, vt expectaretur tempus, quo vnus semel pro omnibus satisfaceret.
units.tr: He offered once, namely when he died once for all, so that he could no more offer more than once than he could die more than once; as is further explained in the ninth chapter. That Old Testament type of the continual or daily sacrifice of lambs is worthy of closer attention. What did the offering of the lambs intend, except to remind men that they ought to be intent in faith upon the Lamb Christ, who was promised to take away the sins of the world? Two were commanded to be offered together, to signify that no matter how many could not cleanse sins; and at the same time that the time had not yet come when the one Lamb, Christ, would suffice. They were offered daily so that they might await the time when the one sacrifice would satisfy once for all.

units.la: Vesperi & mane offerebantur, quia omni tempore ab initio mundi ad finem vsque salus ab vno agno Christo expectari debuit. Si tempus ferret, possemus de vino, de simila, pleniorem interpretationem adferre. Rursus alia antithesis hic obseruanda est. Pontifices obtulerunt victimas: Christus obtulit semetipsum.
units.tr: They were offered in the evening and the morning, because from the beginning of the world to its end salvation had to be looked for from the one Lamb, Christ. If the occasion allowed, we could bring a fuller interpretation from the wine and the flour. Again, another antithesis is to be observed here: the priests offered victims; Christ offered himself.

units.la: Satis quidem fuisset, argumentū ita expressisse: Pontifices necesse habuerunt sæpius offerre: Christus autem tantum semel obtulit: Ergo signum est, per sacrificium eius perfectos esse redditos.
units.tr: It would have been enough to state the argument thus: the priests had to offer often; Christ offered only once; therefore it is a sign that by his sacrifice they have been made perfect.

units.la: Sed voluit insuper Apostolus speciem oblationis utriusque partis exprimere, vt vel hinc tanto probabilius omnibus fieret, ipsam hostiam, quam Christus obtulit, esse eiusmodi, quæ merito potuerit ad plenum saluos facere. Quid ergo obtulerunt pontifices? Victimas, inquit: nempe brutorum animalium, agnos, &c. Quid obtulit Christus? semetipsum. O, quanta differentia: quomodo posint ista sacrificia inter se conferri? Vt nihil dicamus de modo, quo Christus oblatus est, sponte videlicet, & ad mortem, in ara crucis. Merito ergo, vel ob ipsius hostiæ dignitatem, tribuetur sacerdoti Christo, quòd perfectos posuit reddere. Merito dicemus cum Apostolo nono sequenti, si sanguis taurorum, & hircorum, & cinis iuuencæ aspergens, inquinatos sanctificat ad carnis purificationem, quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram à mortuarijs operibus, ad seruiendum Deo viuenti?
units.tr: But the Apostle wished in addition to set out the nature of the offering on each side, so that from this too it might become all the more plainly evident to everyone that the victim which Christ offered is of such a kind that it could rightly make them fully safe. What then did the priests offer? Victims, he says: namely, the flesh of brute animals, lambs, etc. What did Christ offer? Himself. Oh, what a difference! How can those sacrifices be compared with each other? Not to mention the manner in which Christ was offered, namely willingly and unto death, on the altar of the cross. Rightly, then, on account of the very dignity of the victim, is it attributed to Christ the priest that he was able to make them perfect. Rightly we say with the Apostle in the following ninth chapter: "If the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the unclean, sanctifies them to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?"

units.la: Sed addit adhuc Apostolus, pontifices obtulisse, prius pro peccatis proprijs, deinde pro peccatis populi: Ita quidem debuisse fieri, nempe vt sacerdotes primùm pro se orarent & offerrent, deinde pro populo, habetur Leuitici nono & decimosexto. Sed, quid ista particula ad præsentem causam? Pro peccatis populi obtulisse sacerdotes, pro ijsdem similiter obtulisse Christum satis conuenit. Verum est. Sed quod commemoratur, sacerdotes debuisse offerre pro peccatis proprijs, id tudamplificandæ dignitatis Christi causa insertum est: quando constat, Christum, qui peccatum nullum fecit, sicut antea oportebat dimius, nec potuisse, nec debuisse pro peccatis suis expiandis offerre, vel orare. Est ergo hæc magna excellentia sacerdotis Christi præ sacerdotibus legalibus, quòd, vbi isti debuerunt pro peccatis proprijs offerre, Christus id facere nequaquam debuit. Ac nullus reuera vnquam fuit tam sanctus, tam insignis sacerdos, quin peccatis fuerit obnoxius, acreus coram Deo, etiamsi coram hominibus ad tempus impollutus & sanctus videretur. Quamobrem generaliter præceptum est, sacerdotem quemcunque debere pro se orare, vt nimirum peccatorem se esse semper agnosceret. Similiter ob eandem causam, crassa & grauia etiam amplissimorum sacerdotum, qua-lis Aaron, & quidam alij, peccata in Scripturis memorantur, vt ex illis de aliis iudicium sumeremus. Solus Christus immaculatus sacerdos & immaculata hostia extitit.
units.tr: But the Apostle adds further that the priests offered first for their own sins and then for the sins of the people. Indeed it ought to have been so done, namely that the priests should first pray and offer for themselves and then for the people; this is found in Leviticus 9 and 16. But what does that particle have to do with the present matter? That the priests offered for the sins of the people, and that Christ likewise offered for the same, agrees well enough. True. But that it is recalled that the priests ought to offer for their own sins has been inserted to amplify the dignity of Christ, since it is certain that Christ, who committed no sin, as was formerly required of them, neither could nor ought to offer or pray for the expiation of his own sins. This is therefore the great excellence of the priest Christ above the legal priests: where those had to offer for their own sins, Christ by no means had to do so. Indeed no priest was ever so holy and so distinguished that he was not liable to sin and guilty before God, even if he seemed for a time to be unpolluted and holy before men. Therefore it was commanded in general that any priest whatever ought to pray for himself, so that he would always recognise himself as a sinner. Likewise, for the same reason, the gross and grave sins even of the most eminent priests, such as Aaron and certain others, are recorded in the Scriptures, so that from them we might form a judgment about others. Christ alone was the immaculate priest and the immaculate victim.

units.la: Siquidem lex homines constituit pontifices, habentes infirmitatem. Porro sermo iurisiurandi, qui supra legem fuit, filium constituit in aeternum consummatum.
units.tr: For the law appoints men as high priests, who have weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, made perfect for ever.

units.la: Et ratio redditur, quare necessum fuerit, sacerdotes legales saepius, atque etiam pro seipsis offerre, Christum vero nequaquam: & apte subijcitur, quod ex enumeratis de dignitate Christi, & efficacia sacrificij eius sequitur, nempe Christum esse in aeternum consummatum: ex quo manifestum fit, quod initio conclusionis assumpserat, Christum posse saluos facere ad plenum.
units.tr: And a reason is given why it was necessary for the priests under the law to offer often, and even for themselves, but Christ never; and the conclusion aptly adds what follows from the things enumerated about the dignity of Christ and the efficacy of his sacrifice, namely that Christ is perfected for ever. From this it is clear what he had assumed at the beginning of the argument, that Christ is able to save completely.

units.la: Ac valde eleganter iterum collationis, seu potius contentionis curam habuit, vt sic Christi dignitas amplificaretur, necnon illustrior in conspectu poneretur. Suntque antitheta, quorum Apostolus semper est admodum diligens obseruator, optimo ordine ac magna cum gratia collocata.
units.tr: Very elegantly he has again taken care to set things side by side, or rather to contrast them, so that the dignity of Christ may be enlarged and placed more brightly before our eyes. These are antitheses, of which the Apostle is always a most careful observer, arranged in the best order and with great grace.

units.la: Lex primum opponitur sermoni iurisiurandi. Per sermonem autem iurisiurandi, intellige vaticinium prophetae toties citatum, quod post legem editum, & ita iureiurando confirmatum longe maxime debet esse ponderis, sicut, quae posterioris ordinantur, solet praestantiora duci, imo & abrogare ea, quae constituta fuerunt prius. Vel potius intelligePer sermonem iurisiurandi ipsum euangelium, ut fit sententia. In lege quidem, seu per legem, constitutos esse sacerdotes homines infirmos, peccatis obnoxios: at in euangelio, seu per euangelium, constitutum esse sacerdotem Christum in aeternum consummatu.
units.tr: The law is first set against the word of the oath. By the word of the oath understand the prophecy of the prophet, cited so often, which, being published after the law and so confirmed with an oath, ought to carry far greater weight; just as, in general, what is ordained later is usually considered more excellent, and indeed abrogates what was established earlier. Or rather, one may understand by the word of the oath the gospel itself, as the sense requires. In the law, or through the law, men, weak and liable to sin, were appointed priests; but in the gospel, or through the gospel, Christ, the Son made perfect for ever, was appointed priest.

units.la: Atque haec interpretatio non male conuenit, tum ob id, quod subijcitur, quod sermo iurisiurandi supra legem fuit, quod de euangelio maxime dici conuenit, & euangelij dignitatem non parum illustrat: tum quod euangelium recte sermo iurisiurandi appellet-ur, utpote quod adhibitis iuramentis patribus saepius fit promissum, sicut patet ad Abraham, Genes. 22. & ad Dauid, psalm. 131. sicut etiam Zacharias Lucae primo, vbi de exhibendo reuelando quoque euangelio loqueretur, dicebat: Et erexit cornu salutis nobis in domo Dauid pueri sui, sicut locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a seculo fuerunt, prophetarum suorum, fore ut seruarentur ab inimicis nostris, & de manu omnium, qui oderunt nos: ut vteretur misericordia erga patres nostros, ac memor esset pacti sui sancti, praestaretque iusiurandum, quod iurauit ad Abraham patrem nostrum. En vbi Euangelium iuramento promissum praedicetur, ut sermo iurisiurandi appellari recte debeat.
units.tr: This interpretation fits well, both because of what follows, that the word of the oath came after the law, which is said above all of the gospel and greatly illustrates the dignity of the gospel; and because the gospel is rightly called the word of the oath, since with oaths God often promised it to the fathers, as is plain in the case of Abraham, Genesis 22, and of David, Psalm 131. So too Zechariah, in Luke 1, where he speaks of the gospel being displayed and revealed, said: "And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; to show mercy to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant, and to grant the oath which he swore to Abraham our father." Here the gospel, promised with an oath, is proclaimed, so that it may rightly be called the word of the oath.

units.la: Caeterum, quod attinet ad particulam illam, Qui supra legem fuit, sciendum est, cum praepositio μετὰ cum accusatiuo uariam habeat significationem, varie reddi posse, nempe, vel supra legem, vel post legem.
units.tr: Further, as regards that phrase, "which came after the law," it must be noted that since the preposition μετὰ with the accusative has various meanings, it can be rendered in various ways: either "above the law" or "after the law."

units.la: Quomodocunque autem legas, certum est, eam interpositam esse ad amplificandam sacerdotij Christi dignitatem, nec non ad confirmandum, quod Christus praesacerdotibus legalibus saluos ad plenum posse facere. Quod si enim legas, post legem, sententia erit, sacerdotium Christi per vaticinium illud manifestatum aliquot seculis post latam legem, ideoque maioris esse dignitatis: quando, quae posterius constituuntur, maxime si iuramento sint sancita, derogant, adeoque abrogant, quae constituta erant prius, citra iuramentum.
units.tr: However you read it, it is certain that it has been inserted to enlarge the dignity of the priesthood of Christ, and also to confirm that Christ, in contrast with the legal priests, is able to save completely. For if you read "after the law," the sense will be that the priesthood of Christ, made known through that prophecy some centuries after the law was given, is therefore of greater dignity; since what is established later, especially if it is sanctioned by an oath, sets aside and so abrogates what was established earlier without an oath.

units.la: Si vero legas, supra legem, euangelij praelege excellentia ostendetur, vel certe sacerdotium Christi eo nomine praeferendum sacerdotio legali, quod illud iuramento adhibito fuerit institutum, istud autem citra iuramentum.
units.tr: If, however, you read "above the law," the excellence of the gospel will be shown in advance; or at least the priesthood of Christ is to be preferred to the legal priesthood on this ground, that the one was instituted with an oath, the other without an oath.

units.la: Si denique iubet reddere, ante legem, quomodo nonnulli faciundum putant, sententia erit, sacerdotium Christi multo esse antiquius sacerdotio legali, respiciendumque erit ad id, quod typus sacerdotij Christi iam per iuramentum confirmati, in Melchisedec aliquot seculis ante legem emicuerit. Itaque clare vides, quomodocunque reddatur vox μετὰ, non mediocriter illustrari Christi dignitatem, eamque ob causam esse particulam hanc, qui supra legem, non otiose superadditam.
units.tr: Finally, if one renders it "before the law," as some think should be done, the sense will be that the priesthood of Christ is far older than the legal priesthood, and we must look to the fact that the type of the priesthood of Christ, already confirmed by oath, shone forth in Melchizedek some centuries before the law. Thus you see clearly that, however the word μετὰ is rendered, the dignity of Christ is not slightly illustrated, and for this reason the phrase "which came after the law" has not been added to no purpose.

units.la: Secundo, perquam eleganter opponuntur hae voces, homines, & filius. Supra capite tertio, vbi ostendebatur, Christum excellentiorem esse prophetis, atque ipso adeo Mose, vox filij opponebatur voci ministri, sic enim ibi legimus: Moses quidem fidelis fuit in tota domo illius, veluti minister, in testimonium eorum, quae post dicenda erant: At Christus tanquam filius administrauit domum ipsius.
units.tr: Second, the words "men" and "Son" are set against each other most elegantly. Above, in chapter 3, where it was shown that Christ is superior to the prophets, and indeed to Moses himself, the word "Son" was set against the word "servant"; for there we read: "Moses indeed was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken afterwards; but Christ as a Son over his own house."

units.la: Vbi & recte obseruata est antithesis ratio: Hic autem nequaquam perinde videtur obseruanda, quando homines opponit filio. Sed sciendum est, hic eandem habeti ratio-nem nem oppositionis, quæ habita est capite tertio: hoc est, sacerdotibus, qui tantum erant vt ministri, recte opponi filium: sed præterea vocem filij pro Deo usurpari, ut intelligatur, Deum oppositum esse hominibus. Prudenter autem hac voce filij, ingerit omnium animis diuinitatis Christi memoriam, vt vel hac ratione, quia nimirum Deus est, clarius confirmetur, ipsum posse ad plenum salvos facere. Statim enim, quicunque audit, Christum appellari filium, de diuinitate Christi vocem accipit: perpendens autem Christum esse Deum, facile animaduertit, rectissimè de eo dici, quòd possit ad plenum saluos facere. Quare Apostolus prudenter has voces ita selegit.
units.tr: Here too the antithesis has rightly been observed; yet here it does not seem to be observed in the same way, since he sets men against the Son. But it must be understood that the same kind of opposition is intended here as in chapter 3: that is, the Son is rightly set against priests who were only servants; but further, the word "Son" is used of God, so that God is understood to be set against men. Moreover, by this word "Son" he prudently brings to the minds of all the memory of the divinity of Christ, so that by this very fact, namely that he is God, it may be more clearly confirmed that he is able to save completely. For whoever hears that Christ is called Son at once takes the word as referring to the divinity of Christ; and, weighing that Christ is God, one readily perceives that it is most rightly said of him that he can save completely. Therefore the Apostle has prudently chosen these words.

units.la: Tertiò, opponuntur hæ voces, habentes infirmitatem & consummatus. Supra capite quarto Christus describitur potens affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, vtpote qui tentatus fuerit per omnia, iuxta similitudinem, idque absque peccato. Item capite secundo, Diminutus infra angelos propter cruciatum mortis. Præterea, particeps factus carnis & sanguinis cum fratribus.
units.tr: Third, the words "having weakness" and "perfected" are set against each other. Above, in chapter 4, Christ is described as able to be affected by a sense of our infirmities, since he was tempted in all things according to likeness, and yet without sin. Likewise in chapter 2: "made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death." Moreover, "made a partaker of flesh and blood with the brethren."

units.la: Rursus: Fratribus per omnia similis, & tentatus, vt posset his, qui tentantur, succurre-re. Adhæc capite quinto, vbi dicebatur, sacerdotem debere esse placabilem, quandoquidem & ipse circudatus est infirmitate: statim in altera parte adijciebatur de Christo, quòd ex his, quæ passus fuerat, obedientiam didicisset.
units.tr: Again: "made like to his brethren in all things, and tempted, that he might be able to help those who are tempted." Furthermore, in chapter 5, where it was said that the priest ought to be able to bear gently with others, since he himself is also surrounded by weakness, it is immediately added on the other side concerning Christ, that from the things which he suffered he learned obedience.

units.la: In summa vbicunque describitur Christus propter nos humiliatus, & nostri similis per omnia, tamen nusquam exprimitur, ipsum esse infirmum, vel infirmitate circundatum, sed bene tentatum, aut huiusmodi. Ratio est, quia ἀσθένεια significat infirmitatem illam, quæ ingenita est carni nostræ, & semper etiam in sanctis inhæret, qua ad malum omnitempore proclives ferimur, & malum perpetramus: de qua dictum est, quòd etiam septies in die cadit iustus. Proinde talis ἀσθένεια semper fuit spectabilis etiam in summis sacerdotibus: At in Christo utpote de spiritu Sancto nato, ea locum non habuit. Et propterea etiam non dixit, Christũ ratione antitheseos simpliciter firmum, vel potentem, sed, quod multò illustrius est, τετελειωμένον, id est, perfectum & consummatum: quæ vox commodissima est ad suggerendum, quòd cùm ipse talis sit, possit etiam alios consummatos reddere.
units.tr: In sum, wherever Christ is described as humbled for our sake and in all things like us, yet nowhere is it expressed that he was weak or surrounded by weakness, but rather that he was tempted, or words of that kind. The reason is that ἀσθένεια signifies that infirmity which is innate in our flesh and always clings even to the saints, by which we are carried toward evil at all times and commit evil; of which it has been said that even seven times a day the righteous man falls. Accordingly, such ἀσθένεια was always visible even in the chief priests; but in Christ, who was born of the Holy Spirit, it had no place. And for this reason the Apostle did not say simply that Christ, by way of antithesis, was firm or powerful, but, which is far more striking, τετελειωμένον, that is, perfected and consummated; a word most suitable for suggesting that, since he is such, he is also able to make others perfect.

units.la: Sed & amplificationis causa addidit vocem in æternum, ne videlicet putetur more hominum infirmorum aliquando à summa perfectione sua posse decidere, vel alio tempore in posterum rursus nouum sacrificium oblaturus: quorum alterum si contingeret, æterna consummatio tribui Christo propter vnicum sacrificium haudquaquam posset.
units.tr: But also for the sake of amplification he added the phrase "for ever," lest it be thought, after the manner of weak men, that he could at some time fall from his supreme perfection, or at another time in the future offer a new sacrifice again. If either of these were to happen, the eternal consummation could by no means be ascribed to Christ on account of his one sacrifice.

units.la: Valde igitur artificiosè, atq; aptis amplificationibus omnia hæc esse de Christo sic pèr Apostolum pronunciata manifestum est.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that all these things about Christ, so pronounced by the Apostle, are set forth very skilfully and with apt amplifications.

units.la: CAPVT OCTAVVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHT.

units.la: Caterum eorum, quæ dicimus, illud est caput, quòd talem habemus pontificem, qui consedit ad dexteram throni maiestatis in cœlis, sanctorum administrator, ac veri tabernaculi, quod fixit Deus, & non homo.
units.tr: Now the main point of what we say is this: we have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man.

units.la: Ollectio est, seu breuis omnium comprehensio. Solent enim Rhetores post multa enumerata, ad commendationem seu confirmationem alicuius rei, tandem breuiter argute aliquid subijcere, quo summam totius negotij comprehendant, ibique nonnunquam per hyperbolen aut similes amplificationibus aptas figuras, rem maximopere attollere. Id nunc facit hoc loco noster Apostolus, de Christo verè citraque ullam hyperbolen: imo longè infrà dignitatem, at affectu reuera maximo prædicans, quòd ipse ad dexteram Dei patris consideat, hoc est, instar patris per omnia summus perfectissimusque sit, quo amplius sublimiusue dici cogitariue nihil queat. Estque sententia: Quid verbis opus est? Vt summatim semel complectar omnia, Christus talis tantusque est, sic perfectus & consummatus, vt pari per omnia æqualis ad dexteram throni maiestatis confideat, vbi nihil ad perfectionem deesse aut addi queat. Atque huiusmodi collectio recte κεφαλαίωσις, id est, caput & summa appellatur. Vnde & illæ loquendi formulæ, συνκεφαλαίω, pro quibus nos dicimus, in summa, summatim, ut semel omnia, summa summarum, &c. et κεφαλαιῶ in summam subduco & colligo: hinc & ἀνακεφαλαίωσις apud Rhetores recapitulatio, rerum subductio in vnam summam, qua videlicet breuiter omnia comprehenduntur, & quasi singulorum rerum capita recensentur.
units.tr: This is a summing-up, or a brief comprehension of everything. Rhetoricians are accustomed, after listing many things in order to commend or confirm some point, to add at the end something short and pointed that gathers up the sum of the whole matter. Sometimes they also raise the subject greatly by hyperbole or other figures suited to amplification. Our Apostle does this here, speaking of Christ truly and without any hyperbole. Indeed, he speaks far below his dignity, yet with the greatest feeling, when he says that Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father. That is, he is in every respect the highest and most perfect, like the Father, so that nothing more lofty or sublime can be said or thought. The sense is: Why use more words? To sum up everything once for all, Christ is such and so great, so perfect and complete, that he sits at the right hand of the throne of majesty, equal in all things, where nothing can be lacking to perfection or added to it. Such a collection is rightly called summing-up [κεφαλαίωσις], that is, head and sum. Hence also the expressions to sum up [συνκεφαλαίω], for which we say "in summary," "summarily," "as once for all," "the sum of sums," and so on, and I total up [κεφαλαιῶ], I reckon and collect into a sum. Hence also among the Rhetoricians recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις], the reduction of things into one sum, by which all things are briefly comprehended and, as it were, the heads of the individual things are reviewed.

units.la: Nonnulli vocant enumeratione, vt inquit Fabius lib. 6. Græcanica scholia notant ἀ̓ναφάλαιωσιν rerum multarum summam contractionem appellari, per metaphoram seu simi-litudinem, quòd in animantibus quoque caput & si breue admodum sit, tamen præci-puum & excellentissimum est totius corporis membrum, vtpote in quo præstantissi-morum sensuum sedes sit. Proinde Apostolus summam perfectionem in Christo demo-straturus quasi concipiens res multò maximas, quas tamen haud satis posset verbis ex-primere, magno affectu id in summa de Christo ait vere dici, quòd talis tantusque sit, qui ad dextram maiestatis Dei patris confideat, id est, patri per omnia æqualis, & æque perfectus atque ipse pater sit. τοιοῦτον, tale, inquit, habemus pontificem. Ita iubet intendere in Christi magnitudinem, intueriq; propius, qualis & quantus sit.
units.tr: Some call it enumeration, as Fabius says in book 6. The Greek scholia note that the summary of many things is called [ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν] recapitulation, by metaphor or likeness, because in living creatures the head, though it is very small, is nonetheless the chief and most excellent member of the whole body, as the seat of the most excellent senses. Accordingly, the Apostle, wishing to show the highest perfection in Christ, as if conceiving very great things which he could not sufficiently express in words, says with great feeling, in summary, that this is truly said of Christ: that he is such and so great as to sit at the right hand of the majesty of God the Father, that is, equal to the Father in all things and as perfect as the Father himself. Such, he says, a high priest [τοιοῦτον]. Thus he bids us fix our attention on the greatness of Christ and look more closely at what sort and how great he is.

units.la: Qui consedit ad dextram throni maiestatis in excelsis) Qui convenit, dicet aliquis, vt Christus dicatur iam confidere ad dextram patris, cùm tamen paulò ante descripserit semper vi-uentem, vt semper interpellet pro nobis: non decet interpellatorem sedere. Responde-tur: Nihil hic diuersum vel alienum ab officio Christi dicitur. Secundam humanam na-turam dicitur pro nobis intercedere, & secundum eandem naturam etiam ad dexteram Dei patris sedere. Sed præsenti locutionis formula magis confirmatur id, quod prius de interpellatione Christi dictum est. Significatur enim, Christum per omnia ipsi patri æqualem, ac proinde, quando interpellat, voti sui compotem, quatum ex parte ipsius est fieri, nosque percipere effectus interpellationis eius, nisi ex parte nostra obstet impedi-mentum. Et ad significandum, non absurdè tribui Christo, quòd sedeat, ideò addit, quæ officium sacerdotis luculentius exprimunt, videlicet, quòd ibi sit sanctorum & veri ta-bernaculi administrator. Ergo ad significandum, Christum omnia posse, patrem nihil ei negare, hinc æquè perfectum, consummatum, potentem, & ipsum patrem, aptissimè po-stremo loco particula hæc subijcitur. Cæterum quod ad locutionis formam attinet, quid potissimum significet, quomodo ab humano more sumpta, cùm Deus neque dextera, neque sinistram habeat, neque localis sit Christi sessio, fusius à nobis adhibita etiam sen-tentia Chrysostomi, expositum est capite, & vbi etiā sic habebatur, vt hic, ... ... : reddidimus causas, quare verbis μεγαλωσύνης, item, ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, v-sus sit. Hic additur, illustrandi causa, ad illud, ἐν δεξιᾷ, τῆς θρόνου, vt quadam veluti ὑπερυπάρξα depingatur Deus sublimi regia sede magna maiestate verendus. Non opus esse abitror, pluribus verbis agere.
units.tr: "Who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heights." Someone may object: how is it fitting for Christ to be said now to sit at the right hand of the Father, when a little earlier he described him as always living to make intercession for us? For an intercessor ought not to sit. The answer is that nothing different or foreign to Christ's office is said here. According to his human nature he intercedes for us, and according to the same nature he also sits at the right hand of God the Father. But the present form of expression rather confirms what was said earlier about Christ's intercession. For it signifies that Christ, being equal in all things to the Father himself, and therefore, when he intercedes, obtains his desire so far as it lies in him to do so, and we receive the effects of his intercession, unless an obstacle on our side stands in the way. And to signify that it is not absurd to attribute sitting to Christ, he adds words that express more clearly the office of priest: namely, that he is minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle. Therefore, to signify that Christ can do all things, and that the Father denies him nothing, and so is equally perfect, complete, powerful, and the Father himself, this clause is most fittingly added last. As for the form of the expression, what it chiefly signifies, and how it is taken from human custom, since God has neither right hand nor left and Christ's sitting is not local, I have already explained at length in the chapter, with the opinion of Chrysostom also brought in. There too it was put as here, [μεγαλωσύνης] and likewise [ἐν ὑψηλοῖς]; I gave the reasons why he used the words [μεγαλωσύνης] and [ἐν ὑψηλοῖς]. Here it is added, for the sake of illustration, to the phrase [ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς θρόνου], so that God may be depicted, as it were, by a kind of [ὑπερυπάρξα] exaltation, as one to be revered for great majesty on a lofty royal throne. I think there is no need to say more about this.

units.la: Tantum hoc lubet addere, non esse cur ex eo, quòd dicatur, hac forma loquendi signi-sicari Christum per omnia patri æqualem, & tamen secundum humanam naturam sede-re ad dexteram, ei competat inferre, quòd etiam secundum humanam naturam sit vbiq; sicut quosdam audimus nunc contendere. De ea re breuiter ascribere visum est verba Augustini ex epistola ad Dardanum, quæ numero habetur quinquagesima septima: No-li, inquit, dubitare, ibi nunc esse hominem Christum Iesum, vnde venturus est, memori-terque recole, & fideliter tene Christianam confessionem, quoniam resurrexit à mor-tuis, ascendit in cœlum, sedet ad dexteram patris, nec aliunde quàm inde venturus est, ad iuuos mortuosque iudicandos. Et sic venturus est, illa angelica voce testante, quem-admodum ire visus est in cœlum, id est, in eadem carnis forma atque substantia, cui profectò immortalitatem dedit, naturam non abstulit. Secundum hanc formam non est putandus vbique diffusus. Cauendum est enim, ne ita diuinitatem astruamus hominis, vt veritatem corporis auferamus. Non est autem consequens, vt quod in Deo est, ita sit vbique ut Deus. Nam & de nobis verissimè Scriptura dicit, quòd in illo viuimus, moue-mur, & sumus, nec tamen sicut ille vbique sumus: sed aliter homo ille in Deo, quoniam aliter & Deus ille in homine proprio quodam & singulari modo. Vna enim persona Deus & homo est, & utrumque est vnus Christus Iesus, vbique per id quod Deus est, in cœlo autem per id quod homo. Hæc ibi. Plura qui desiderat, locū consulat. Quæstio erat per Dardanum mota, quomodo Christus credendus foret in cœlo esse, quando pendens in cruce, dixerat latroni, Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso: An forte paradisus in aliqua cœli parte? An, quia Deus vbique, etiam homo ille, qui in Deo, vbique similiter diffusus, ut eodem tempore & in cœlo, & in paradiso extra cœlum fuerit? Respondet Augustinus Christum illo tempore mortis, secundum carnem in sepulchro, secundum animam fuisse in inferno, vbi forte & paradisus sinus Abrahæ, sicut Petrus ait Actor. 2. Secundum diui-nitatem vero vbique, vt & semper est, vide locum. Sequitur.
units.tr: I wish only to add this: from the fact that this form of speech signifies that Christ is equal to the Father in all things, and yet according to his human nature sits at the right hand, it does not follow that he is also everywhere according to his human nature, as some now contend. On this matter I have thought fit to set down briefly the words of Augustine from his letter to Dardanus, which is numbered the 157th: "Do not doubt," he says, "that the man Christ Jesus is now there, whence he will come. Remember this and hold fast faithfully to the Christian confession, that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there alone to judge the living and the dead. And so he will come, as the angelic voice testifies, just as he was seen to go into heaven, that is, in the same form and substance of flesh, to which he indeed gave immortality but did not take away its nature. According to this form he is not to be thought to be diffused everywhere. For we must take care not to assert the divinity of the man in such a way as to take away the truth of his body. But it does not follow that what is in God is everywhere as God is. For Scripture says most truly of us also that in him we live, move, and have our being, and yet we are not everywhere as he is; but that man is in God in a different way, since God too is in the man in a different, proper and singular way. For God and man are one person, and both together are one Christ Jesus, everywhere by what he is as God, but in heaven by what he is as man." So far Augustine. Whoever wants more should consult the passage. The question had been raised by Dardanus: how Christ is to be believed to be in heaven, when hanging on the cross he said to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise." Is paradise perhaps in some part of heaven? Or, since God is everywhere, is that man also, who is in God, diffused everywhere in the same way, so that at the same time he was both in heaven and in paradise outside heaven? Augustine answers that at the time of death Christ was, according to the flesh, in the sepulchre, and according to the soul in hell, where perhaps paradise too is, the bosom of Abraham, as Peter says in Acts 2. But according to his divinity he is everywhere, as he always is; see the passage. It follows.

units.la: Sanctorum administrator ac veri tabernaculi) Pulchrè, ne, cùm sedere ad dexterā dicitur Chri-stus, existimetur, non amplius pro nobis interpellare, quòd tamen perpetuò eum facere paulò ante asserebatur, hæc de officio pontificis attexuntur, ad significandum, eum ab interpellando pro nobis nunquam cessare, sed omni tempore in tanta maiestate consti-tutum, tutum nostri curam adhuc gerere. Quàquàm his vocibus, de quibus nihil adhuc præcef-fit, viam sibi parat Apostolus ad differendum plenius de sacrificio, nec non de ingressu Christi in suum tabernaculum, adeòque de omnibus per Christum verè adimpletis, quæ in ceremoniis veteris legis per eundem adimplenda præfigurabantur. Alludit enim ad id, quòd in veteri lege sacerdotes ingrediebantur tabernaculum: item semel in anno in sancta sanctorum, oblaturi: significatque, id plane per Christum iam esse factum, imò etiā nunc adhuc fieri, quando Christus in uero tabernaculo & sanctis sanctorum versetur: id quod in sequenti parte disputationis fusius explicabitur.
units.tr: "Minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle." Well put. Lest, when Christ is said to sit at the right hand, it should be thought that he no longer intercedes for us, although it was asserted a little before that he does so continually, these words about the priestly office are added, to signify that he never ceases to intercede for us, but being established in such majesty, still cares for our welfare at all times. Although by these words, of which nothing has been said before, the Apostle prepares the way for himself to treat more fully of the sacrifice, and also of Christ's entry into his own tabernacle, and so of all the things truly fulfilled through Christ, which were foreshadowed in the ceremonies of the old law to be fulfilled by him. For he alludes to the fact that in the old law the priests entered the tabernacle, and once a year into the holy of holies, to offer sacrifice. He signifies that this has now plainly been done through Christ, and indeed is still being done, since Christ dwells in the true tabernacle and in the holy of holies. This will be explained more fully in the following part of the discussion.

units.la: Vocatur autem Christus sedens ad dexterā Patris. λειτουργὸς interpres commodisime rededidit administrator, atque etiam admonet scite, λειτουργῶν non esse simpliciter quemuis ministrum, sed plerunque ministrum sacrorum, & pontificem rebus sacris occupatū: ipsum ministerium, quod vulgo officium, dictum esse λειτουργίαν. Quanquam vox hinc deriuata creditur, quod olim λήιτον appellarint prytaneum, id est, locum publicū, in quo versabantur magistratus, & ἔργον, opus: unde commutatis aliquot literis λειτουργοί dicti, qui in his locis inseruiebant magistratibus. Hinc forte translata est vox ad significandū eos, qui ipsi Deo summo magistratui seu principi inseruiunt.
units.tr: Christ is said to be sitting at the right hand of the Father. The Greek word [λειτουργὸς, leitourgos] is best rendered "administrator," and the author also rightly observes that [λειτουργῶν, leitourgōn] does not mean just any servant, but usually a minister of sacred things, one occupied with holy duties. The ministry itself, commonly called an office, is called [λειτουργίαν, leitourgian]. The word is thought to derive from the old term [λήιτον, leiton] for the prytaneum, that is, the public place where the magistrates met, and [ἔργον, ergon], work. With a few letters changed, those who served the magistrates in these places were called [λειτουργοί, leitourgoi]. The word was perhaps then transferred to those who serve God, the supreme Magistrate or Prince, himself.

units.la: Vocem ἁγίων nonnulli de sanctis hominibus credentibus interpretantur, ut sit sententia: Christū esse ministrum sanctorum hominū, quia videlicet illorum causam agit apud Deum, dat illis spiritum Sanctum, & procurat illorum salutem, licet in maxima gloria constitutus. Ac sanctos homines etiā posse nomine tabernaculi intelligi, cum in Scripturis sancti interdum vocetur templum Dei, 1. Corinth. 6. Item domus Dei, praesentis epistolę capite tertio: & Deus dicatur in illis habitare.
units.tr: Some interpret "of the holy things" as referring to holy believing men, so that the sense is: Christ is the minister of holy men, because he pleads their cause before God, gives them the Holy Spirit, and secures their salvation, even though he is set in the greatest glory. They also suggest that holy men may be understood by the word "tabernacle," since in the Scriptures the saints are sometimes called the temple of God (1 Corinthians 6), and the house of God (in the third chapter of this epistle), and God is said to dwell in them.

units.la: Sed rectius per Sancta & tabernaculum coelos ipsos intelligemus, vbi nunc & sedet Christus, & pro nobis assiduè interpellat: quorum sanctorum & cuius tabernaculi vim bram gesserunt sancta sanctorum & tabernaculum legale. Sanè ipse Apostolus passim in sequentibus sancta & tabernaculum ita interpretatur: nec dubium, quin eadem significatione ista accipiat. capite octauo vocat tabernaculum Mofaicum exemplar: & capite 9. idem exprimit plenius, addens, Christum pontificem futurorum bonorum per maius & perfectius tabernaculū nō manu factum ingressum, et semel ingressum in sancta aeterna. Eodem capite, non enim in manu facta sancta ingressus est Christus exemplaria verorum, sed in ipsum coelum. Vbi clare vides Apostolum sui ipsius agere interpretem.
units.tr: But it is more correct to understand by the holy places and the tabernacle the heavens themselves, where Christ now sits and continually intercedes for us. The holy of holies and the legal tabernacle were a shadow of these holy things and this true tabernacle. Certainly the Apostle himself everywhere in what follows interprets "holy places" and "tabernacle" in this way, and there is no doubt that he uses these words with the same meaning. In chapter 8 he calls the Mosaic tabernacle a copy, and in chapter 9 he expresses the same more fully, adding that Christ, the high priest of the good things to come, entered through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, and entered once into the eternal holy places. In the same chapter: for Christ entered not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself. Here you clearly see the Apostle acting as his own interpreter.

units.la: Ait autem veri tabernaculi, ad discrimen legalis seu Mofaici, quod non erat verum tabernaculum, sed tantum typicum & umbraticum. Quantum differt imago vel umbra rei a reipsa, tantum etiam tabernaculum Mofaicum a tabernaculo euangelico siue illo, quod ingressus est pontifex noster Christus. Sed & cùm addit, Quod sitit Deus & non homo: Interpretatur, qualenam sit illud tabernaculum, nimirum coelestę, non terrenum, quod Deus solus sua virtute erexit & constituit. Fuit quidem tabernaculum legale erectum praecepto Dei, sed adhibita opera ac ministerio hominum: At verò tabernaculum, quod semel ingressus est Christus, solus fixit & erexit Deus, quando, referente Mose, in principio coelos creauit.
units.tr: He says "the true tabernacle" in contrast to the legal or Mosaic one, which was not the true tabernacle but only a typical and shadowy one. As much as the image or shadow of a thing differs from the thing itself, so much does the Mosaic tabernacle differ from the gospel tabernacle, that is, the one into which our high priest Christ entered. And when he adds "which the Lord pitched, and not man," he explains what kind of tabernacle this is: namely a heavenly, not an earthly one, which God alone erected and established by his own power. The legal tabernacle was indeed set up by the command of God, but with the work and ministry of men employed. But the tabernacle into which Christ entered once was fixed and erected by God alone, when, as Moses reports, he created the heavens in the beginning.

units.la: Per tabernaculū autem, sicut per Sancta, intelligi coelos, Apostolus ipse in sequentibus interpretatur, quemadmodum alibi quoque in Scripturis, ut Psalmo decimoquarto, Domine, quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo, aut quis requiescet in monte Sancto tuo? Vbi per tabernaculum significari, vitam coelestem & aeternā, satis arguit postremus eiusdem Psalmi versus. Qui facit haec, non commouebitur in aeternum: Item Psalmo 84. Quàm dilecta taber nacula tua Domine exercituū? Cōcupiscit, & deficit anima mea ad atria Domini. Et Lucę decimo sexto, facite amicos de Mammona iniquitatis, ut recipiant vos in aeterna tabernacula. Nequaquam opus est, hic referre, aliàs crebrò per tabernaculū significari ecclesiā ut in Esaia: nonnunquàm & corpus seu carnem, quam anima veluti tabernaculum non diu duraturū incolit, ut 2. Corinth. 5. 2. Petri. 1. Sed & elegantet dixit, fixum esse hoc tabernaculum, quadoquidem palis & clauis ligneis in terram defixis erigitur & confirmatur.
units.tr: The Apostle himself, in what follows, explains that by "tabernacle," as by "holy places," the heavens are meant, as elsewhere in the Scriptures, for example in Psalm 14: "Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy hill?" That the tabernacle here signifies heavenly and eternal life is sufficiently shown by the last verse of the same psalm: "He who does these things shall not be moved forever." Likewise Psalm 84: "How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs, and faints for the courts of the Lord." And Luke 16: "Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles." There is no need here to point out that elsewhere the church is often signified by the tabernacle, as in Isaiah, and sometimes also the body or flesh, which the soul inhabits as a tabernacle that will not last long (2 Corinthians 5; 2 Peter 1). And he elegantly said that this tabernacle is fixed, since it is set up and made firm by poles and wooden pins driven into the ground.

units.la: Simili modo apud septuaginta Genesis 35. Iacob postquàm lepelijset Rachele, egressus inde, ἔπηξε τὴν σκηνὴν, fixit tabernaculum trans turrim gregis. Item Iosue 18. congregati sunt omnes filij Israel in Silo, & ἔπηξαν ἐκεῖ τὴν σκηνὴν, fixerunt ibi tabernaculum testimonij, & fuit eis terra subiecta. De his satis. Tempus est, ut locus cōsolatorios multiplicemque doctrinam in conclusione hac considerandam breuiter exponamus. Neque enim est vlla tàm exigua particula, quae nō doctrinam egregiam, & consolationem praeterea ingentem in se contineat, quamque non decerer iusta & bene longa oratione explicare. Nos, quanta licebit breuitate, tantùm quae praecipua sunt, percurremus.
units.tr: Similarly, in the Septuagint, Genesis 35: after Jacob had lain with Rachel and set out from there, he [ἔπηξε τὴν σκηνὴν, epēxe tēn skēnēn] pitched his tent beyond the tower of the flock. Also Joshua 18: all the children of Israel gathered at Shiloh, and [ἔπηξαν ἐκεῖ τὴν σκηνὴν, epēxan ekei tēn skēnēn] they pitched there the tabernacle of the testimony, and the land was subdued before them. Enough of these points. It is time that we briefly set out the comforting places and the manifold teaching to be considered in this conclusion. For there is no part so small that it does not contain some outstanding teaching and, besides, great consolation, and it would not be fitting to explain it in a fair and rather long discourse. We shall run through, with as much brevity as we can, only the principal points.

units.la: Primùm, quando id praedicatur de Christo, quòd possit ad plenum saluos facere, excelles prædicatur Christi dignitas & potetia, quòd videlicet vnus ita saluos faciat perse, ut nullius alterius adminiculi ratio habeatur, vel desideretur. Vnus Christus per se plenissimè potest & vult saluos facere. Qua de re possent innumeratum ex prophetis, tum ex scriptis apostolicis proferri testimonia. Est autem istud valde cōsolatorium illis anxiis conscientijs, magnitudine peccatorum, & paucitate suorum benefactorum perterrefactis. Si quando enim inspiciunt tantùm peccata sua, rursusq; vident, quàm nihil boni fecerint, quàm nulla opera in se habeant ad iustitiam coram Deo profectura: atque ita coguntur de salute desperare: Hic postquàm fuerint corde contriti & humiliati, se rursus erigant, intuentes in istud verbum, quo dicitur, quòd vnus Christus posset ad plenum saluos facere: Nec dubium, quin mirabilem dulcedinem ex hoc loco sint percepturi.
units.tr: First, when it is said of Christ that he is able to save completely, the excellence of Christ's dignity and power is proclaimed: namely that he alone saves in such a way, by himself, that no account is taken of, or need is felt for, any other help. Christ alone, by himself, is most fully able and willing to save. On this matter countless testimonies could be brought forward, both from the prophets and from the apostolic writings. This is very comforting for those anxious consciences which are terrified by the greatness of their sins and the scarcity of their good works. For when they look only at their sins, and again see how little good they have done, and how they have no works to bring them to righteousness before God, they are thus compelled to despair of salvation. Here, after they have been contrite and humbled in heart, let them raise themselves again, looking to this word, in which it is said that Christ alone is able to save completely. There is no doubt that they will perceive a wonderful sweetness from this passage.

units.la: Secundò, cùm dicitur, eos potissimum saluos fieri, qui per ipsum adeunt Deum, paritèr consolatio ingens & doctrina valde vtilis in his verbis continetur.
units.tr: Second, when it is said that those are especially saved who approach God through him, an equal great consolation and a very useful teaching are contained in these words.

units.la: Primùm, quòd per ipsum solum sit adeundus Deus, non per vires nostras, per opera nostra, multo minus aliorum, siue nunc adhuc in terris viuentium, siue hinc profectorum. Solus Christus est via, vita, & veritas, & hanc gloriam alteri non concedit. Nemo ad patrem venit, nisi per ipsum, sicut ipse Ioannis sexto aperte clamat. Neque patitur gloriam hanc sibi præripi, & ad alium eam transferri. Non est nisi vnum ostium in cœlum, atque id est ipse Christus. Is intercedit, interpellat pro nobis patrem: Quare per hunc debemus patrem adire, si æternæ salutis participes esse volumus. Vnus est Christus, in quo patri bene complacuit, & propter quem vnum pater misericordiam suam gratis impendit. Hinc verò consolationem accipient omnes, quicunq; in solû Christum spem suam defixerint, non nitentes sanctorum inuocationibus, peregrinationibus, emptis indulgentiarum diplomatis, vel huiusmodi humanis inuetis, quæ Deo propinquos nos reddere nequaquâ possunt. Qui præ his negligunt Deum, à recta via quàm longissimè discedunt, & certam consolationem in necessitate extrema non accipiunt.
units.tr: First, that God must be approached through him alone, not through our own strength, our own works, and much less through others, whether those still living on earth or those who have departed from here. Christ alone is the way, the life, and the truth, and he does not grant this glory to another. No one comes to the Father except through him, as he himself plainly cries out in John 6. Nor does he allow this glory to be snatched from him and transferred to another. There is only one door to heaven, and that is Christ himself. He intercedes and pleads with the Father for us. Therefore we must approach the Father through him, if we wish to share in eternal salvation. Christ is the one in whom the Father is well pleased, and because of him alone the Father freely bestows his mercy. Truly all will receive consolation from this who fix their hope on Christ alone, not relying on invocations of the saints, pilgrimages, purchased certificates of indulgences, or such human inventions, which can by no means bring us near to God. Those who neglect God for these things turn very far from the right way, and do not receive a sure consolation in extreme necessity.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd addit, Christum semper viuere, ad hoc, vt interpellet pro nobis, similiter doctrinam & consolationem parit. Si semper viuit, ergo potest vitam nobis donare. Et, si in hoc semper viuit, vt interpellet pro nobis, ergo nunquam cessator est in suo officio, etiamnum hoc tepore idem agit, pro nobis intercedit. Quis iam alios interpellatores valde requirat? Quis poterit imaginari, Christum habere opus vicarijs aut successorib. quasi ipse iam desiisset officium suum facere, aut tædio aliquo frangeretur, aut se indignum id munus duceret? Non ita est. Christus per se suo munere etiamnum hodie perfungitur apud Patrem in cœlis: Et nobiscum ipse adest, videns necessitatem nostram, qua ad interpellandum pro nobis mouetur. Ecclesiam suam nunquam deserit, per spiritum Sanctum eam etiam docens & gubernans: vt nequaquâ opus sit alios imaginari vicarios aut substitutos, qui ne pro seipsis quidem possent apud Deum Patrem pro peccatis ad plenum satisfacere. Hic cocidunt superbi vicariorum Christi & successorum tituli. Oportet solum Christum agnoscamus perpetuò retinentem suam gloriam summi sacerdotij. Habet quidem ipse hic suos ministros, sed nequaquam ut pares successores: Tantùm sunt nunci, legati, & organa, per quæ ipse, quæ vult, ad utilitatem nostram perficit: semper prima actio & vis agendi ad ipsum debet reduci. Est autem & valde consolatorium in omnibus tentationibus, quæ ad desperandum nos possent impellere, ad Christum semper viuentem, & semper pro nobis interpellantem oculos mentis attollere. Atque, vt id semper faciat, est nobis semper interpellandus. Bernhardus alicubi pulcherrimam habet meditationem de Christo apud Patrem interpellante.
units.tr: Third, when he adds that Christ always lives in order to intercede for us, this likewise produces teaching and consolation. If he always lives, then he is able to give us life. And if he always lives in order to intercede for us, then he never ceases in his office; even now, in this age, he does the same thing and intercedes for us. Who, then, would greatly seek other intercessors? Who could imagine that Christ needs deputies or successors, as if he had already ceased to perform his office, or were broken by some weariness, or considered himself unworthy of that duty? It is not so. Christ himself, even today, carries out his office in person before the Father in heaven, and he is present with us, seeing our need, which moves him to intercede for us. He never forsakes his Church, teaching and governing it through the Holy Spirit, so that there is by no means any need to imagine other vicars or substitutes, who could not even fully satisfy God the Father for their own sins, let alone for ours. Here the proud titles of Christ's vicars and successors fall to the ground. We must acknowledge that Christ alone perpetually retains his glory of the high priesthood. He indeed has his ministers here, but by no means as equal successors: they are only messengers, envoys, and instruments through whom he accomplishes, for our benefit, what he wills; the first action and the power of acting must always be referred back to him. It is also very comforting, in all temptations that could drive us to despair, to lift up the eyes of the mind to Christ, who always lives and always intercedes for us. And so that he may always do this, we must always be interceding for him. Bernard somewhere has a most beautiful meditation on Christ interceding before the Father.

units.la: Quartò: sunt hæc quoq; verba, Talis decebat, ut esset nobis pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, & sublimior cœlis factus: ad exemplum seu imitationem, deinde etiam ad amplissimam consolationem propositá. Sunt præclari tituli, dignitatem Christi multo illustrius ponentes ob oculos, quàm sunt illi, qui solent imperatoribus tribui, cùm magis ex more, quàm ex re appellantur Augusti, Fœlices, inuicti, gloriosi. Hi tituli verè in unum Christum proprie competunt, ut nullis alijs accommodari ritè queant. Solus Christus huiusmodi titulos suo iure obtinet. Cæterùm describunt nobis hæ voces, quales etiam omnes ministros Dei, præsertim sacris deditos esse deceat: pios, innocentes, impollutos, segregatos à peccatis & peccatoribus, solisq; rebus cœlestibus intentos esse conuenit. Hanc doctrinam primo loco omnes ministri verbi ad se pertrahât, ut exemplu Christi capitis & summi pontificis strenuè per omne vitam imitentur. Sed quàdo in super omnes Christiani per Christum facti sunt sacerdotes, qui quotidie debent semetipsos totos Deo consecrare, omnium quoq; interest dare operam, ut his virtutibus ducem & ordinatorem Christum sequantur. Pietatem in Deum, innocentiam erga proximum, puritatem in semetipsis, ne vel corporis, vel anima admittant contagium, omni studio conseruabût. Ab omnibus, quæ ad peccatum possent pellicere, quæque peccati speciem præ se ferunt, diligentèr diligenter caueat, ne infirmis fratribus offendiculum præbeant. Denique tantùm cœlesti bus & spiritualibus rebus inhient & incumbant. De his omnium piorum communibus studijs & officijs possent quàmplurima adduci in medium, si tempus ferret.
units.tr: Fourthly, these words also: "Such a high priest became us: holy, harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens." They are set forth both as an example or imitation and for the greatest consolation. They are excellent titles, setting Christ's dignity before our eyes far more brightly than the titles commonly given to emperors, such as Augustus, Fortunate, Invincible, or Glorious, which are used more by custom than by reality. These titles belong truly and properly to Christ alone, so that they cannot rightly be applied to anyone else. Christ alone holds such titles by his own right. Moreover, these words also describe what all ministers of God ought to be, especially those devoted to sacred things: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sins and sinners, and intent on heavenly things alone. All ministers of the Word should first draw this doctrine to themselves, so that they may vigorously imitate the example of Christ, the head and chief priest, throughout their whole life. But since all Christians have also been made priests through Christ, and must consecrate themselves wholly to God every day, it is in the interest of all of them to take pains to follow Christ as their leader and guide in these virtues. They should preserve piety toward God, innocence toward their neighbour, and purity in themselves, so that neither body nor soul admits contagion. They should take the greatest care to avoid everything that could entice them to sin, and whatever bears the appearance of sin, lest they give a stumbling block to weak brothers. Finally, they should long for and devote themselves only to heavenly and spiritual things. Very many examples of these common pursuits and duties of all the godly could be brought forward, if time permitted.

units.la: Sunt insuper collationes multiplices nobis in hisce Christi virtutibus propositæ. Cùm audimus eum pium, statuere pro certo debemus, eum omnia facturum, quæ ad patris gloriam illustrandam possent fieri: atque vbi patri nulla ex re maior accesserit gloria, quàm ex plurimorum salute, accipere debemus, Christum omni tempore apud patrem pro salute nostra esse sollicitū, & nihil omittere, quod saluti nostrę procurandæ sit necessarium.
