Rursus, cum audimus, Christum innocentem, quid est, quod confingamus, nobis illum iratum & crudelem iudicem, aut suspicemur, perdere potius velle, quàm seruare?
units.tr: Moreover, Christ's virtues set before us many comparisons. When we hear that he is godly, we ought to be certain that he will do everything that could be done to advance the glory of the Father; and since no greater glory can come to the Father than from the salvation of many, we ought to understand that Christ at all times before the Father is anxious for our salvation and omits nothing that is necessary for procuring it. Again, when we hear that Christ is innocent, what is there that we could imagine, or suspect, that he is an angry and cruel judge who would rather destroy than save us?

units.la: Cùm audimus illum impollutum, cogitemus, ipsum sua munditie nos quoque posse & velle purgare, ac mundos coram Deo patre statuere.
units.tr: When we hear that he is undefiled, let us reflect that by his own purity he can and will cleanse us also, and make us clean before God the Father.

units.la: Cùm audimus, segregatum à peccatoribus, expectemus, nos quoque olim in iudicio iussu ipsius à peccatoribus segregados, sicut agni ab hœdis separantur: qua de re Matth. 25. expectemus illum inditurum tales animis nostris motus, per quos ad vitandum quæcunque vitia feramur.
units.tr: When we hear that he is separated from sinners, let us expect that we too, separated from sinners at his command in the judgment, as lambs are separated from goats, will one day be so separated; concerning this, see Matthew 25. Let us expect that he will implant in our minds such motions that we are carried toward avoiding every vice.

units.la: Cùm denique audimus, illum sublimiore factum cœlis, accipiamus, id nostri quoque causa ita factum, vt videlicet vnà cùm ipso in cœlos transferamur, & ut habetur Ephes. 2. cum eo inter cœlestes confideamus. En, quàm vberes consolationes ex tàm paucis verbis percipiantur?
units.tr: Finally, when we hear that he has been made higher than the heavens, let us understand that this was done for our sake too, namely that we might be carried up into the heavens together with him, and, as is stated in Ephesians 2, that we might sit with him among the heavenly ones. Look how rich are the consolations that can be drawn from so few words!

units.la: Quintò, quando prædicatur, Christum non debuisse sæpius offerre sacrificiū, sed semel tantùm id obtulisse: præterquam quòd efficacia sacrificij Christi, clarissimè ostenditur, tùm discimus hic falsam & inanem esse illorum iactationem, qui per sacerdotes clamant Christum quotidie offerri. Apostolus clarè dicit, Christum semel obtulisse, semel tantùm oblatum, item quod ipse sese obtulerit: Quamobrem frequentem & iteratam oblatione confingere, est oblationi Christi vires detrahere, quasi non fuerit sufficiens ad satisfaciendum pro peccatis totius mundi.
units.tr: Fifthly, when it is taught that Christ ought not to have offered sacrifice often, but offered it only once, then, besides the fact that the efficacy of Christ's sacrifice is most clearly shown, we learn here that the boasting of those who, through priests, cry out that Christ is offered every day, is false and empty. The Apostle clearly says that Christ offered himself once, and was offered only once, and likewise that he offered himself. Therefore, to invent a frequent and repeated offering is to take away the power of Christ's offering, as if it were not sufficient to make satisfaction for the sins of the whole world.

units.la: Sed ita rectè dicitur, quotidie fieri memoriā sacrificij Christi, & orare patrem, vt propter vnicum sacrificium Christi semel oblatum velit nobis ignoscere. Sicut impossibile est Christum sæpius mori, ita impossibile est, Christum sæpius offerri, id quod clarè dicitur ad finè capitis noni. Instituit autem Christus sui sacrificij frequente fieri memoriā, dicens Hoc quotiescunque feceritis, in mei memoriam facietis. Sed est insuper hic propositā consolatio, ut videlicet sciamus, nos in hoc vno sacrificio Christi posse conquiescere, nec non pro certo statuamus, eius fructum propter Christum nobis impendi & accommodari, si modo fide misericordiam Patris propter Christum apprehendamus. Et, si diligenter intueamur in vnicum Christi sacrificium, non est, quod opera nostra vel iustitias nostras ad calculum reuocemus, quasi propter illas expectanda nobis foret misericordia Dei potius quàm propter Dei patris misericordiam.
units.tr: But it is rightly said that the memorial of Christ's sacrifice is made daily, and that we pray the Father, for the sake of the one sacrifice of Christ offered once, to be willing to forgive us. Just as it is impossible for Christ to die often, so it is impossible for Christ to be offered often, which is clearly stated at the end of chapter nine. Christ, however, instituted the frequent making of a memorial of his sacrifice, saying: "As often as you do this, you will do it in remembrance of me" [Luke 22]. But there is also set before us here a consolation: namely, that we may know we can rest in this one sacrifice of Christ, and be certain that its fruit is bestowed on us and applied to us for Christ's sake, provided we apprehend by faith the mercy of the Father for Christ's sake. And if we look attentively at the one sacrifice of Christ, there is no reason to bring our works or our righteousness into the reckoning, as if the mercy of God were to be expected by us on account of them, rather than on account of the mercy of God the Father.

units.la: Sextò: quando dicitur, lege constitutos esse sacerdotes homines habentes infirmitatē, Christum verò solum esse in æternum consummatum: ijs verbis non solùm sacerdotes seu ministri huius temporis, sed omnes in genere Christiani admonentur, ut agnoscere velint propriam infirmitatem & fragilitatem: cogitent, se nihil aliud, quàm miseros peccatores, se non posse suis viribus ex cœno peccatorum attolli vel subleuari: sed solū esse Christum immunem ab omni peccato, per quem liceat liberari, qui in æternum consummatus, posit & nos in æternum consummatos reddere. Vbi pariter doctrina & consolatio maxima emicat.
units.tr: Sixthly: when it is said that priests are appointed by the law as men having infirmity, but that Christ alone is perfected for ever, by these words not only the priests or ministers of this time, but all Christians in general, are admonished to acknowledge their own infirmity and frailty. Let them consider that they are nothing but wretched sinners, that they cannot by their own strength be lifted or raised up from the mire of sins, but that Christ alone is free from all sin, through whom deliverance may be obtained; and since he has been perfected for ever, he is able to make us also perfect for ever. Here both doctrine and the greatest consolation shine forth together.

units.la: Septimò: quod interseritur, Sermone iurisiurandi esse supra legem, non mediocriter facit ad explicandam Euangelij præstantiam, de qua aliàs sæpius iam dictum est, sicut & plura in hanc partem occurrerunt.
units.tr: Seventhly: what is inserted, that "the word of the oath" is above the law, contributes not a little to explaining the excellence of the Gospel, concerning which much has often been said already, as also many more things in this regard have occurred.

units.la: Octauò: cum omnibus subijcitur, Christum esse eiusmodi potificem, qui confideat ad dexteram Dei Patris in cœlis: admonemur, hoc vnum semper restare, vt, quotiescunque de animarum salute agetur, in solum Christum respiciamus, ab hoc solo, non aliunde, felicitatem æternam expectemus, & speremus, nos per eum & propter eum ad simile gloriam in cœlis perducendos. Rectè igitur à nobis dictum, valde consolatoria ab Apostolo conclusionem esse subiectam.
units.tr: Eighthly: when it is added to everything that Christ is such a high priest, who sits at the right hand of God the Father in heaven, we are admonished that one thing always remains: whenever the salvation of souls is at stake, we should look to Christ alone, expect eternal happiness from this one alone and not from elsewhere, and hope that through him and for his sake we shall be brought to a like glory in heaven. Rightly, therefore, have we said that the Apostle has added a conclusion that is very consoling.

units.la: Postremò: habemus & hoc ad methodum docendi pertinens, quòd, postquam locum aliquem didacticè tractauerimus, subijciemus cōclusiones, in quib. nō tantū summa eorum, quæ dicta sunt, breuiter comprehendamus, quantum requirit communis dictorum ratio: sed adijciamus insuper, quæ usum disputationum declarent, nempe, quæ vel docent aliquid ad vitam formandam, vel certè conducant ad consolationem conscientiarum. rum: Sic enim Apostolu cum alibi, tu hoc loco fecisse cernimus. Et certe adeo istud est ne-cessarium, ut, nisi fiat, nunquam satis intelligere possint auditores, quem proprie in finem tendat disputatio, & quem fructum inde expectare debeat. Quare nec valde intentus erit ad altius expendendum, seu memoriae infigendum ea, quae audierit.
units.tr: Lastly, we have also, pertaining to the method of teaching, this: after we have treated some passage in the manner of doctrine, we will add conclusions, in which we not only briefly comprehend the sum of what has been said, as the common order of the matter requires, but also add what shows the use of the disputation, namely what either teaches something for forming life or certainly tends to the comfort of consciences. For thus we see the Apostle does elsewhere, and in this place he has done so too. And indeed this is so necessary that, unless it is done, the hearers can never sufficiently understand toward what end the disputation tends, and what fruit they ought to expect from it. Wherefore they will not be very attentive to weighing more deeply, or fixing in memory, what they have heard.

units.la: Verum est quidem, solent quidam initio de usu & fructu argumenti, quod tractandum suscepepint, agere, ut videlicet auditorum animos sibi concilient, nec non attentiores ad causam totam reddant: sicut & Apostolus praesentis disputationis initio visus est agere ad finem capitis quarti: sed tamen non minus apte, imo frequentius id fit in conclusione: ubi, quae ad affectus movendos faciunt, breviter congerenda Rhetores non indiligenter praeceperunt.
units.tr: It is true indeed that some are accustomed, at the beginning, to speak about the use and fruit of the subject they have undertaken to treat, so as to win over the minds of their hearers and make them more attentive to the whole cause; just as the Apostle seemed to do at the beginning of the present disputation, at the end of chapter four. Yet this is done no less aptly, indeed more often, in the conclusion, where the Rhetoricians have not carelessly prescribed that things which serve to move the emotions be briefly heaped together.

units.la: Valde igitur prudenter & consulte factum est ab Apostolo, quod conclusioni interserit non pauca, ex quibus & doctrina ingens, & consolationes amplissimae hauriri queat. Sic enim habebunt pij lectores sive auditores, quo se spiritualiter reficiant, & in longa disputatione non solum leuabitur eis taedium, sed multiplex etiam utilitas obueniet, ut non dicam, quod pariter praeparantur ad ea, quae sequentur.
units.tr: Therefore it was very wisely and deliberately done by the Apostle to insert into his conclusion not a few things from which both a great doctrine and the fullest consolations can be drawn. For thus the godly readers or hearers will have something by which they may refresh themselves spiritually, and in a long disputation not only will their weariness be relieved, but also manifold usefulness will come to them, not to mention that they are at the same time prepared for what follows.

units.la: Omnis enim pontifex ad offerendum donaria & victimas constituitur, unde necesse est, ut hic etiam habeat aliquid quod offerat.
units.tr: For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; therefore it is necessary that this one also have something to offer.

units.la: Sequitur secunda pars disputationis huius de Christi sacerdotio, ac legis per id abrogatione, in qua agit de Christi sacrificio. Est autem dispositio partis praecedentis breviter repetenda, ut, quam decenti ordine, & quam necessario ad hanc alteram partem perueniatur, clarius eluceat.
units.tr: There follows the second part of this disputation concerning Christ's priesthood and the abrogation of the law through it, in which he treats of Christ's sacrifice. It is worth briefly recalling the arrangement of the preceding part, so that it may be clearer how fittingly and how necessarily we arrive at this second part.

units.la: Propositio erat (ad finem capitis quarti) Christum esse pontificem maximum, qui coelos penetrarit. Quae sic enunciata sufficiens erat, ad id postea inferendum, quod cupiebat, nimirum, per excellentissimum sacerdotium Christi abrogari sacerdotium legale. Mox (capite quinto) quatuor argumentis perspicuis & efficacibus, Christum esse sacerdotem seu pontificem probauit: in quibus vnum erat profecto validissimum, sumptum ex ipsius spiritus Sancti testimonio Psal. 109. quod proprie de sacerdotio Christi fuerat multis ante seculis editum. Hinc vero capite septimo (nam digressione, quae intercedit reliqua parte capitis quinti, & toto capite sexto, lubenter omittimus) testimonium illud de Christo proprie accipiendum, & in vnum Christum per omnia competere, argumentis aliquot demonstrauit.
units.tr: The proposition at the end of the fourth chapter was that Christ is the great high priest who has passed through the heavens. Stated in this way, it was sufficient for inferring afterwards what he wished to establish, namely that the legal priesthood is abrogated by the most excellent priesthood of Christ. Then, in the fifth chapter, he proved by four clear and effective arguments that Christ is a priest or high priest. Of these, one was certainly the most powerful, taken from the testimony of the Holy Spirit himself in Psalm 109, which had been published many centuries earlier and refers properly to the priesthood of Christ. Then in the seventh chapter (for we gladly pass over the digression that lies between the rest of the fifth chapter and the whole of the sixth) he demonstrated by several arguments that this testimony is rightly understood of Christ, and that it applies entirely and only to Christ.

units.la: Inde conferendo sacerdotium Christi cum sacerdotio legali seu Aaronico euidetissimis rationibus euicit, sacerdotium Christi longe excellentius esse sacerdotio legali: ex quo protinus intulit, per sacerdotium Christi adeo excellens ac praestans, sacerdotium legale, & cum hoc simul ipsam legem, id est, omnia ad sacerdotium pertinentia iam translata esse atque enervata. Ne autem quispiam adhuc morosius contenderet, sacerdotium Christi referendum esse ad sacerdotium legale: atque ita non recte dici, legem per illud abrogatam, iterum ostendit duabus rationibus, sacerdotium Christi necessario distinguendum a sacerdotio Aaronico, & praeterea recte dici, quod translato sacerdotio simul translata fit & lex, utpote cum haec per se sit inutilis, & Euangelium succedens longe ea sit excellentius. Quibus omnibus subiecit conclusionem valde consolatoriam proxime a nobis expositam. Sed iam ut etiam satis luculenter expositu fit (maximeque autoritate testimonij e Psal. 109. atque argumentis ex eo collectis) Christum esse sacerdotem, praeterea multo excellentius esse sacerdotium ipsius, quam fuerit sacerdotium legale: Item admodum diuersum esse sacerdotium Christi a legali, ideoque istud recte dici translatum: Tamen exoritur nouus scrupus, ac probandum adhuc restat, quod Christus sacerdotij munere secundum nouum ordinem sit perfunctus, quod sacrificia obtulerit, & huiusmodi, quae sacerdotes quoscunque decet, fecerit: quod reuera longe difficilimum probatu videbatur, sicut initio capitis quinti rationibus non paucis, & minime obscuris indicauimus.
units.tr: Next, by comparing the priesthood of Christ with the legal or Aaronic priesthood, he proved by the most evident reasons that the priesthood of Christ is far more excellent than the legal priesthood. From this he at once inferred that, through the priesthood of Christ, which is so excellent and outstanding, the legal priesthood, and together with it the law itself, that is, everything pertaining to the priesthood, has already been transferred and made void. Lest anyone should still contend more stubbornly that the priesthood of Christ must be referred to the legal priesthood, and so that it should not be wrongly said that the law has been abrogated through it, he shows again by two reasons that the priesthood of Christ must necessarily be distinguished from the Aaronic priesthood, and further that it is rightly said that when the priesthood is transferred, the law is transferred along with it, since the law is in itself useless and the Gospel that succeeds it is far more excellent. To all these things he added the very consoling conclusion which we have just expounded. But now, so that it may be explained clearly enough (especially by the authority of the testimony from Psalm 109 and the arguments gathered from it) that Christ is a priest, and moreover that his priesthood is far more excellent than the legal priesthood was, and likewise that the priesthood of Christ is very different from the legal one, and therefore that it is rightly said to have been transferred, nevertheless a new doubt arises, and it still remains to be proved that Christ has discharged the office of priest according to the new order, that he offered sacrifices, and did the other things that befit any priests. This indeed seemed by far the most difficult thing to prove, as we indicated at the beginning of the fifth chapter with not a few and not at all obscure reasons.

units.la: Ac verosimile est, peruicaces Hebraeos, auditis omnibus, quae dicta sunt, adhuc plus satis odiose obiecisse, quod etiamsi Christus esset sacerdos, & quidem praestantioris ordinis, quam fuerit Aaronicus, per quam leue tamen abhuc id esse, si tantum gerat nouum titulum, atque interea nunquam fit sacerdotij functus munere, nunquam sacrificium in altari vllo obtulerit. Titulum enim gerere sine re prorsus inanem esse gloriolam. Ad haec ut omnino cocedatur, per nouum sacerdotium Christi abrogatum esse sacerdotium vetus, at non propterea sequi, sacrificia & ceremonias legales omnes esse abrogatas: imo ipsum Christum ijsdem sacrificijs ac ceremonijs, aut certe non admodum disparibus vsurum. Neque quicquam obest, quo minus eaedem retineantur ceremoniae: praesertim quando ipse Melchisedech atque omnes adeo patres ab initio inde orbis primum conditi similiter sacrificiorum ac donariorum genere, pecoribus, inquam, frugib. & caeteris eiusmodi semper vsitatis. litasse legantur, nec temerè vnquam apud vllas gentes hac in parte fit variatum.
units.tr: For these reasons, therefore, the Apostle now undertakes the second part of the disputation, in which he will teach more fully that Christ discharged the office of priesthood, that is, that he offered a sacrifice, and one so outstanding and effective that by it the legal victims and sacrifices can clearly be understood to have been abrogated altogether as well. Yet until now nothing has been treated concerning the priesthood of Christ, but only a way has been prepared, somewhat incidentally, for discussing it in the nearest conclusion, where it was said in one word that Christ offered himself once for all. And here again one will see a wonderful art, by which these parts must be judged not unlike the earlier ones but all mutually answering one another beautifully.

units.la: His igitur de causis Apostolus nunc altera disputationis parte instituit, in qua plenius docebit, quòd Christus sacerdotij munus obierit, hoc est, quòd sacrificium obtulerit, & quidè tàm præstàs atque efficax, ut per id victimas seu sacrificia legalia iam pariter omnia esse abrogata clarè possit intelligi. Neque verò hactenus quicquam de sacerdotio Christi actum est, sed tantùm via ad disseredum de eo in conclusione proxima utcunque obiter parata, vbi vno verbo dicebatur, Christū semel semetipsum obtulisse. Atque hinc rursus cernere erit mirabile artificiū, ut à prioribus non dissimilia, sed omnia sibi inuicè pulchrè respondentia debeant iudicari.
units.tr: For these reasons, therefore, the Apostle now undertakes the second part of the disputation, in which he will teach more fully that Christ discharged the office of priesthood, that is, that he offered a sacrifice, and indeed one so outstanding and effective that through it it can be clearly understood that all the legal victims and sacrifices have likewise been abrogated. Indeed, nothing has so far been said about the priesthood of Christ, but only a way has been prepared, somewhat incidentally, for discussing it in the nearest conclusion, where it was said in a single word that Christ offered himself once. And here again one may see the wonderful skill of the author, in that the parts should be judged not as unlike the earlier ones, but as all answering one another beautifully.

units.la: Cæterum quia hic altera disputationis pars est, orditur ab vniuersali, eodè modo quò confirmationem capite quinto agressus fuerat, dicens: Omnis enim pontifex inquit, &c. vbi & eadem verba habentur, ut studio appareat Apostolū ita repetiuisse, quàdoquidè argumentū, quod inter reliqua, quæ ibi proferebantur, primo loco positū erat, sumptumq; à principali pōtificis officio, adeoq; à propria & usitata pōtificis descriptione, hactenus nondū fuit dilucidè expositū, sed hoc tantùm ibi addebatur, quòd Christus in dieb. carnis suæ, cū & precationes & supplicationes apud illū, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare, cū clamore valido & lachrymis obtulisset, exauditus sit pro reuereētia: nulla deinceps probatione aut declaratione subiuncta, cū tñ cetera fere argumenta in confirmatione sint satis coprobata. Iam ergo vt hæc quoque pars confirmationis vera de Christo intelligatur, Apostolus de sacrificio Christi, quale illud fuerit, quamque efficax, planius loqui constituit. Proinde eā aggrediēs peroportunè repetit verba, quæ ibi in antecedeti erant posita, dicendo: Omnis enim pontifex ad offerendum donaria & uictimas constituitur: Quæ vniuersalis ut per se nota concediturr. Ex qua de Christo recte infert: Vnde necesse est, ut hic etiam habeat aliquid, quod offerat.
units.tr: Moreover, since this is the second part of the disputation, he begins from the universal, in the same way as he had begun the confirmation in the fifth chapter, saying: For every high priest, he says, etc. Here the same words are found, so that it is evident by design that the Apostle repeated them, since the argument which was placed first among the others put forward there, and taken from the principal office of the high priest, and so from the proper and usual description of the high priest, has not yet been clearly explained. There it was only added that Christ, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, was heard because of his reverence; no proof or explanation was then appended, although the other arguments in the confirmation were fairly well supported. Now, therefore, so that this part of the confirmation also may be rightly understood of Christ, the Apostle decides to speak more plainly about the sacrifice of Christ, what sort it was and how effective. Accordingly, taking this up, he very fittingly repeats the words that were set down before in the preceding passage, saying: Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. This universal statement is granted as known in itself. From it he rightly infers concerning Christ: Therefore it is necessary that he also have something to offer.

units.la: Necessaria, & uel pueris conspicua est consequentia ab vniuersali ad particulare, siue ab eo, quòd, cui conuenit definitum, eidem & conuenire debet definitio.
units.tr: The consequence from the universal to the particular is necessary and plain even to children; or, to put it another way, what the definition applies to, the thing defined must also apply to.

units.la: Porrò nihil hic est, quod prolixioři egeat explicatione, quando multò plenissimè omnes hæ voces per nos sunt expositæ initio capitis quinti. Dona & victimæ quomodo differant, ibidem satis diximus.
units.tr: For if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law, who indeed serve as a copy and shadow of heavenly things, as was answered to Moses when he was about to complete the tabernacle: For see, he says, that you make all things according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain. But now he has obtained a more excellent priesthood.

units.la: Nam si esset in terra, ne sacerdos quidem esset, vbi sunt sacerdotes, qui offerūt iuxta legem donaria, qui quidem exēplari & umbrae deseruiunt cœlestium, quemadmodū oraculo responsum est Mosi, cum esset absoluturus tabernaculum: Nam vide, inquit, ut facias omnia secundum exemplar, quod ostensum est tibi in monte: nunc verò hoc excellentius sortitus est sacerdotium.
units.tr: For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law, who serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things, as was answered by oracle to Moses when he was about to complete the tabernacle: For see, he says, that you make all things according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain; but now he has obtained a more excellent priesthood.

units.la: Nostro quidem crasso docendi more, erat hęc loco statim subijciendum, quódnam & quale fuerit Christi sacrificium: Verùm Apostolus paululùm diuersa via progreditur. Prius enim, quàm exprimat dignissimum sacrificium Christi, (etiamsi cùm aliàs, tùm in præcedēti potissimum conclusione obiter illud indicarit, dicendo, quod Christus semetipsum obtulerit) agit iterum nō nihil de præstantia sacerdotij Christi, docēs, istud tanto esse excellentius sacerdotio legali, quanto res seu veritas præstantior est vmbra siue typo: item, quanto nouum testamentum siue euangelium præstantius est veteri testamento siue lege. Eademque opera nouum testamentum eminentius esse veteri confirmat aptissimo Hieremiæ testimonio, inferens postea ex eodem rectissimè constitui, quòd per nouum testamentum sit vetus abrogatum.
units.tr: In our crude manner of teaching, it would have been right to add here immediately what and of what kind the sacrifice of Christ was. But the Apostle proceeds by a somewhat different route. Before he sets forth the most worthy sacrifice of Christ (although he had indicated it incidentally both elsewhere and especially in the preceding conclusion, by saying that Christ offered himself), he again deals somewhat with the excellence of the priesthood of Christ, teaching that it is as much more excellent than the legal priesthood as the reality or truth is more excellent than the shadow or type, and likewise as the new testament or Gospel is more excellent than the old testament or law. At the same time, by the most apt testimony of Jeremiah, he confirms that the new testament is more eminent than the old, and afterwards infers from the same passage, quite rightly, that the old has been abrogated by the new testament.

units.la: In his totum caput octauum expenditur: quæ & ideo hoc ordine videntur per Apostolum proposita, vt viam sibi paret ad caussam principalem, atque omnium animis suggerat cogitandum, quod dignissimo Christi sacerdotio debeat respondere dignissimū aliquod sacrificium, & excellentiori testamento couenire excellentius sacrificium, per quod itidem vetera sacrificia omnia abrogentur. His verò ita expositis, capite nono pluribus verbis disserit de tabernaculo legali, ac sacrificiis in eo iuxta legem offerri solitis, ut inde vsitata collationis forma, qua typi siue vmbrę conferūtur cum rebus atque ipsa veritate, demonstret, multa præstantius debere esse tabernaculum, quòd ingressus sit Christus, ac multò item excellentissimum sacrificium, quòd Christus obtulerit. Hac igitur de caussa quale in primis tabernaculum, tum quale fuerit nouum atque excellentissimum Christi sacrificium, ad dimidium fere capitis noni primùm exprimit: sic enim ibi in altera parte collationis ait,
units.tr: In these verses the whole eighth chapter is examined. The Apostle sets out these matters in this order so that he may prepare his way to the main point and bring it to mind for everyone that, to the most worthy priesthood of Christ, there ought to correspond a most worthy sacrifice, and that to the more excellent covenant there should correspond a more excellent sacrifice, by which all the old sacrifices are likewise abrogated. Having set this out, in the ninth chapter he discusses at greater length the legal tabernacle and the sacrifices customarily offered in it according to the law. In this way, using the usual form of comparison, in which types or shadows are compared with realities and with the truth itself, he shows that the tabernacle had to be far more excellent in many respects, because Christ entered into it, and that the sacrifice Christ offered was far more excellent still. For this reason he first sets out, in roughly the first half of the ninth chapter, what the tabernacle was like and then what Christ's new and most excellent sacrifice was like. For he says this in the second part of the comparison:

units.la: At Christus accedens pontifex futurorū bonorum per maius & perfectius tabernaculū non manu factum, hoc est non huius structura, neq; per sanguinē hircorū ac vitulorū sed per proprium sanguinē ingressus est semel in sancta, æterna redemptione reperta.
units.tr: But Christ, coming as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this building, nor by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption.

units.la: Neque aliena vel inusitata existimari debet hæc docendi ratio. Nam & Rhetores mo-nent nent, prodesse nonnunquam, si auditores expositione alicuius rei, quae modo non sit remota ab instituto, aliquamdiu retineantur, & quasi praeparentur, priusquam id, quod principale est, aperiatur. Conducere enim id subinde non solum ad attentos reddendos, verumetiam ad illustrandam amplificandamque rem, qua de agitur. Itaque dum Apollo lus aliquantum immoratur exponendae dignitati sacerdotij Christi, praestantiae rerum prae umbris, euangelij prae lege, praeterquam quod facit, ut auditor auide sit intentus omnibus quae dicuntur, tum valde mouet eum, ut animo concipiat res ingentes, nec non statuat, vbi tam praeclara sunt, quae praemittuntur, multo procul dubio amplissimum fore, quod ad causam principaliter attinens suo postea loco adferetur. Et sic dignitas sacrificij Christi, supra quam credi potest, ex dignitate eorum, quae prius dicuntur, crescit atque illustratur. Verum a paucis tantum hic esse artificium aduertitur, cum tamen eo maior ars hic veniat obseruanda, quo est minus ostentata. Caeterum, quae insuper in singulis argumentis obseruatu digna occurrent, nos ordine progredientes annotabimus.
units.tr: This method of teaching should not be thought strange or unusual. For the rhetoricians also advise that it is sometimes useful, if the hearers are held for a while by an explanation of some matter not far removed from the subject, and are as it were prepared before the principal matter is laid open. For this helps not only to make the hearers attentive but also to illustrate and amplify the matter under discussion. So while the Apostle lingers for some time in setting out the dignity of Christ's priesthood, the superiority of realities over shadows and of the gospel over the law, he does more than hold the hearer's close attention to everything said; he also strongly moves him to form great ideas in his mind, and to judge that, when the things put forward first are so distinguished, what is brought forward afterwards in its proper place, bearing on the main cause, will undoubtedly be most ample. Thus the dignity of Christ's sacrifice grows and is illuminated beyond what can be believed, from the dignity of the things said earlier. Yet few notice the art here, although a greater art ought to be observed here, the less it is displayed. Meanwhile, we shall note in order the other points worth observing in the individual arguments as they come up.

units.la: Primum itaque sacerdotij Christi excellentiam prae sacerdotio legali pergit docere, sumpta occasione ab eo quod in conclusione praecedeti dixit, Christum sublimiorem factum coelis, ibique ad dexteram patris sedere ac sancta administrare. Sic vero respiciens ad illa argumentatur, non quidem syllogismum integrum iusta structura conficiens: sed si pro nostra consuetudine digeramus omnes partes, farciamusque quod deest, argumentationem, ni fallar, quadripartitam suppeditans, in hunc fere modum.
units.tr: First, then, he goes on to teach the excellence of Christ's priesthood above the legal priesthood, taking his occasion from what he said in the conclusion of the preceding passage, that Christ has been made higher than the heavens and sits there at the right hand of the Father and administers holy things. Looking back to these points, he argues, not indeed by constructing a complete syllogism in proper form, but if, according to our custom, we arrange all the parts and supply what is missing, the argument (unless I am mistaken) comes out in roughly the following four-part form.

units.la: Si Christus sacerdotium haberet tantum in terra, vix esset sacerdotis appellatione dignus, nedum caeteris praestantior.
units.tr: If Christ had a priesthood only on earth, he would hardly be worthy of the name of priest, much less more excellent than the others.

units.la: Ratio propositionis: Nam qui in terra sunt sacerdotes sacrificia iuxta legem offerentes, hi tantum umbram habent sacerdotij cuiusdam dignioris, & quicquid faciunt, seruit id vniuersum ad representandas res coelestes alterius veri & consummati sacerdotij.
units.tr: Reason for the premise: for those who are priests on earth, offering sacrifices according to the law, have only a shadow of a more worthy priesthood, and whatever they do serves entirely to represent the heavenly things of another, true and perfect priesthood.

units.la: Comprobatio rationis: Sic enim oraculo responsum est Mosi Exodi vicesimo sexto, cum esset absoluturus tabernaculum: Nam vide, inquit, ut facias omnia secundum exemplar, quod ostensum est tibi in monte.
units.tr: Confirmation of the reason: for this was the answer given to Moses in Exodus chapter 25, when he was about to finish the tabernacle: "For see," he says, "that you make all things according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mountain."

units.la: Assumptio siue minor: Atqui Christus non est amplius in terra, sed, uti iamiam diximus, sublimior factus est coelis, vbi sedet ad dexteram patris sancta administrans.
units.tr: Assumption, or minor premise: But Christ is no longer on earth, but, as we have just said, has been made higher than the heavens, where he sits at the right hand of the Father and administers holy things.

units.la: Complexio siue conclusio: Igitur nunc sortitus est sacerdotium multo excellentius, & pro vno acsolo vero pontifice agnosci debet, qui non vmbram, sed rem sacerdotij habeat, cuiusque omnia sint plane coelestia, non terrena, perfectissima, non imperfecta. Vel sic reddatur argumentatio succinctius.
units.tr: Conclusion: Therefore he has now obtained a priesthood far more excellent, and he must be acknowledged as the one and only true high priest, who has not a shadow but the reality of the priesthood, whose things are wholly heavenly, not earthly, most perfect, not imperfect. Or the argument may be stated more briefly in this way.

units.la: Si Christus esset in terra sacerdos, esset tantum typicus sacerdos, & solam gerens umbram rerum coelestium.
units.tr: If Christ were a priest on earth, he would be only a typical priest, bearing only the shadow of heavenly things.

units.la: Atqui ipse non est in terra, verum in coelis.
units.tr: But he is not on earth, but in the heavens.

units.la: Igitur non est typicus sacerdos, sed verus & coelestis. Quamobrem manifestum est, sacerdotium Christi praestantius esse sacerdotio legali, seu quocunque terreno. Quod ad maiorem attinet, sacerdotium in terra esse typicum tantum & vmbratile, liquet ex illo Mosi Exod. 25. Minor manifesta est ex ijs, quae saepe alias, & iam in proxima conclusione dicta sunt.
units.tr: Therefore he is not a typical priest, but a true and heavenly one. Wherefore it is plain that the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the legal priesthood, or any earthly priesthood. That the major premise is true, that the priesthood on earth is only typical and shadowy, is clear from that saying of Moses in Exodus 25. The minor premise is plain from what has often been said elsewhere, and just now in the preceding conclusion.

units.la: Argumentum ducitur a collatione typi seu vmbrae cum re seu ipsa veritate, qua clarissime euincitur, Christi sacerdotium multis intervallis excellentius esse sacerdotio legali, cum res ipsa semper typo seu vmbra potior esse debeat. Neque vlla est in tota argumentatione obscuritas. Maior annexam habet statim perspicuam probationem, quae, neinfirmari contemniue possit ceu tantum ab Apostoli cerebro profecta, stabilitur mox amplissimo Scripturae testimonio.
units.tr: The argument is drawn from the comparison of type or shadow with reality or the truth itself, by which it is most clearly proved that the priesthood of Christ is far more excellent than the legal priesthood, since the reality must always be superior to the type or shadow. Nor is there any obscurity in the whole argument. The major premise has at once a clear proof attached, which cannot be weakened or despised as if it had come only from the Apostle's own brain; it is soon established by a very ample testimony of Scripture.

units.la: Minor siue assumptio per se manifesta est, & collecta ex ijs, quae dicta sunt in coniunctione paulo ante posita, ex quibus certum est, sumptam, ut semel diximus, praesentis argumenti occasionem.
units.tr: The minor premise, or assumption, is plain in itself and gathered from what was said in the connection placed a little before, from which it is certain that the occasion of the present argument was taken, as we have said once already.

units.la: Reuera autem valde acute excogitatum est ex illis verbis istud argumentum. Sic enim si accurate omnia perpendimus, secum ratiocinatus est Apostolus. Christus postquam semel obtulit sanguinem suum, iam est in coelis, ibique assiduè adhuc interpellat pro nobis Deum patrem.
units.tr: Indeed, this argument has been devised from those words with great acuteness. For if we weigh everything carefully, this is how the Apostle reasoned with himself: Christ, after he once offered his blood, is now in heaven, and there he still constantly makes intercession for us to God the Father.

units.la: Ergo nunc demum vere prae omnibus meretur sacerdotis appellationem, nunc vere fungitur sacerdotis munere, nunc peragit in coelis & spiritualiter, quae olim in lege per sacerdotium & sacrificia terrena ac corporalia adumbrabantur.
units.tr: Therefore now at last he truly deserves the name of priest above all others; now he truly performs the office of priest; now he carries out in heaven and spiritually those things which in the past were foreshadowed under the law through the earthly and bodily priesthood and sacrifices.

units.la: Hoc iam solum supererat illi inquirendum, quomodo videlicet probare posset, sacerdotium legale cum adiunctis omnibus tantum fuisse vmbram siue typum rerum praestantiorum & coelestium.
units.tr: This was the only thing left for him to inquire: how he could prove that the legal priesthood, with all its accompaniments, was only a shadow or type of higher and heavenly realities.

units.la: Ecce autem, ad hanc rem protinus inuenit testimonium longè aptissimum, quod pro-ductum cernimus, quod profectò quasi fundamentum et basis est multorum, quæ in hac secunda parte disputationis de dignitate Christi sacrificij sequuntur. Ideoque diligenter inspiciendum est, atque animo imprimendum. Nam sæpè posthac vmbræ seu typi fiet mentio, & ab vmbrâ ad veritatem argumenta plerunque ducentur, quæ omnia vires habent, & fluunt ex hoc vno testimonio, sicut in præcedenti parte disputationis huius, basis & fundamentum fere omnium erat illud ex psalmo 109. Tu es sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: But see, he immediately finds for this matter a testimony by far the most apt, which we see he brings forward; this truly is, as it were, the foundation and basis of many things that follow in this second part of the discussion about the dignity of Christ's sacrifice. Therefore it must be examined carefully and fixed in the mind. For often hereafter mention will be made of the shadow or type, and arguments will for the most part be drawn from the shadow to the truth; all of these have their force and flow from this one testimony, just as in the earlier part of this discussion the basis and foundation of almost everything was that passage from Psalm 109: You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Quòd si iam lubet videre, ânne appositè citatum sit testimonium, sanè inuenietur, nihil in eo longius petitum vel durius tortum.
units.tr: If now we wish to see whether the testimony has been aptly cited, it will surely be found that nothing has been sought from afar in it or twisted too harshly.

units.la: Nam, vt uidere est Exodi vigesimo quinto, Dominus cùm instituere vellet, quæ ad externum cultum religionis forent conducibilia, de tabernaculo erigendo, omnique instrumento, necessario pluribus agit verbis, ac præscribit etiam Mosi, quæ materia, quæ forma, in quem vsum singula essent confiticenda: præterea (sicut solent architecti, aut similes artifices) quasi depictam imaginem, adeoque ideam vniuersi operis futuri, in monte agenti visendam exhibuit. Hoc ergo est, quod Dominus sæpius apud Mosen ibi repetit.
units.tr: For, as may be seen in Exodus 25, when the Lord wished to ordain what would be useful for the external worship of religion, he treats at length of erecting the tabernacle and of every instrument, and he also prescribes to Moses what material, what form, and for what use each thing was to be made. Moreover, as architects or similar craftsmen do, he showed him, as it were, a painted image, and so the plan of the whole future work, to be seen by him while he was on the mountain. So this is what the Lord repeats so often there to Moses.

units.la: Primùm initio capitis vicesimi quinti, Facient mihi sanctuarium, & habitabo in medio eorum, iuxta omnem similitudinem tabernaculi, quod ostendam tibi, & omnium vasorum in cultum eius.
units.tr: First, at the beginning of chapter 25: They shall make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them, according to all the likeness of the tabernacle which I shall show you, and of all its vessels for its service.

units.la: Rursus ad finem eiusdem capitis post multa eleganter delineata, Inspice, & fac secundum exemplar, quod tibi in monte monstratum est. Quæ verba proprie hic citantur.
units.tr: Again, at the end of the same chapter, after many things have been elegantly set out: See that you make them according to the pattern shown you on the mountain. These words are cited here in their proper sense.

units.la: Etrursus capite vicesimo sexto, Et eriges tabernaculum iuxta exemplar, quod tibi in monte monstratum est. Tantum videatur significatio exemplaris, & res erit manifesta. Apud Hebræos initio capitis 25. est vox תבנית, vbi septuaginta reddiderunt τὸ ὑπόδειγμα.
units.tr: And again in chapter 26: And you shall raise up the tabernacle according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain. Only let the meaning of "pattern" be considered, and the matter will be plain. Among the Hebrews, at the beginning of chapter 25, the word is תבנית [tabnit], which the Seventy render τὸ ὑπόδειγμα [to hypodeigma].

units.la: Ad finem capitis apud Hebræos eadem vox תבנית posita est, sed septuaginta reddiderunt ibi, τύπος τῶν ἑπτά.
units.tr: At the end of the chapter the Hebrews again use the same word, תבנית [tabnit], but the Seventy render it there τύπος τῶν ἑπτά [typos tōn hepta].

units.la: Capite autem vicesimo sexto Exodi est Hebræis תבנית, vbi septuaginta τύπος ἄδης. Sed vox תבנית alias sæpius occurrit: vt 1. Paralipom. 28. vbi legimus, Dedit autem David filio suo Solomoni descriptionem porticus & templi & cellariorum & cænaculi. Vbi septuaginta iterum τὸ ὑπόδειγμα habent. Et psalmo centesimo sexto, vbi de idololatria Israelitarum in deserto, Fecerunt vitulum in Horeb, & adorauerunt sculptile, & mutauerunt gloriam suam in similitudinem vituli comedentis fœnum: vbi septuaginta ὁμοίωμα μόσχου. Sed Esaiæ quadragesimo quarto, vbi de sculptura idolorum ita legitur, Artifex lignarius extendit normam, effigiat cum creta, & format ipsum in angulis, atque circularem figuram inducit ei, & facit ipsum in similitudinem viri, & iuxta effigiem hominis, vt sedeat in domo. Vbi septuaginta, in similitudinem viri reddiderunt ὡς μορφὴν ἀνθρώπου. Est igitur proprie תבנית, quod græcis ὑπόδειγμα, τύπος, εἶδος, ὁμοίωμα, μορφή, id est, exemplar, demonstratio, species, idæa, similitudo, forma.
units.tr: In chapter 26 of Exodus the Hebrew has תבנית [tabnit], which the Seventy render τύπος ἄδης [typos hades]. The word תבנית [tabnit] occurs elsewhere more often, for example in 1 Chronicles 28, where we read: David gave to his son Solomon the pattern of the porch, of the temple, of the storehouses and of the upper chambers. There too the Seventy have τὸ ὑπόδειγμα [to hypodeigma] again. And in Psalm 106, where it speaks of the idolatry of the Israelites in the wilderness: They made a calf in Horeb, and worshipped the molten image, and changed their glory into the likeness of a calf that eateth grass, the Seventy have ὁμοίωμα μόσχου [homoiōma moschou]. But in Isaiah 44, where the making of idols is described thus: the carpenter stretches out his line, shapes it with chalk, forms it with planes, marks it out with the compass, and makes it in the likeness of a man, according to the beauty of a man, that it may dwell in a house; there the Seventy, for in the likeness of a man, have ὡς μορφὴν ἀνθρώπου [hōs morphēn anthrōpou]. So תבנית [tabnit] properly means what the Greeks call ὑπόδειγμα, τύπος, εἶδος, ὁμοίωμα, μορφή [hypodeigma, typos, eidos, homoiōma, morphē], that is, pattern, representation, appearance, idea, likeness, form.

units.la: Sententia ergo est, Mosen in monte vidisse similitudinem, figuram, typum, speciem, & quasi delineatam imaginem rerum futurarum, atque id ipsum vniuersum, quod erexit seu construxit, tantum iuxta similitudinem & figuram factum fuit: Et rursus aliarum rerum futurarum & præstantiorum typus ac similitudo erat.
units.tr: The sense, then, is that Moses saw on the mountain a likeness, figure, type and appearance, and as it were a drawn picture, of things to come; and the whole structure that he raised or built was made only according to that likeness and figure. Again, it was a type and likeness of other things to come, and of greater excellence.

units.la: Verum est quidem, vbi architectus primùm delinearit futurum ædificium, dicitur terni exemplar, forma, similitudo, ædificij: vbi autem postea congesta & concinnata materia omni erexerit atque absoluerit ædificium, non amplius similitudo seu forma, sed res ipsa adesse dicitur. At de ijs, quæ post demonstratum exemplar in monte, construxit Moses, non potest eadem ratione dici, quòd res vera & consummata ibi adfuerit: In cuius rei argumentum postea etiam templum extructum est, maiori apparatu, quod successit tabernaculo, in signum, quòd nouum testamentum deberet succedere legi. Et ratio est: quia res vera cultus diuini & consummatio consistit in iustificatione hominis, in placatione Dei. Iam per cultum Mosaicum nihil tale est perfectum, sed sicut Apostolus in sequentibus plenius docebit, id tantùm præstitum est per Christum, eiusque vnicum sacrificium. Itaque & tabernaculum Mosi, & quicquid illud erat præclarum ac magnificum, tantùm typus & figura permansit, delineans tantùm & adumbrans res ipsas, quæ per Christum postea debebant perfici, per quem nos veros effectus spiritualis cultus, id est, iustificationem nostram consequeremur.
units.tr: It is true that when an architect first sketches the building to come, we say that the pattern, form and likeness of the building is there. But when the material has afterwards been gathered and put together and the building has been raised and finished, the likeness or form is no longer present, but the thing itself is said to be there. Yet what Moses built after the pattern shown him on the mountain cannot be said, on the same reasoning, to have contained the true and perfected reality. As proof of this, a temple was afterwards built, with greater splendour, to succeed the tabernacle, as a sign that the new covenant was to succeed the law. The reason is this: the true reality and perfection of divine worship consists in the justification of man and the appeasing of God. Now through the Mosaic worship nothing of this kind was accomplished; but, as the Apostle will teach more fully in what follows, this was effected only through Christ and his one sacrifice. Therefore both the tabernacle of Moses, and whatever else was splendid and magnificent in it, remained only a type and figure, sketching and foreshadowing only the realities which were afterwards to be fulfilled through Christ, through whom we would obtain the true effects of spiritual worship, that is, our justification.

units.la: Mosaica omnia tantùm erant externa, temporanea, citò peritura, propterea perfectio illis tribui non poterat: sicut nec depictæ per architectum domui perfectio vel dignitas tribuitur, maximè vbi domus ipsa iam est consummata & perfecta, atque fuccelsit id quod præstantius est. Iam minutiora quaedam in partium dispositione annotemus. Non videtur cohaerere proximis verbis, quod dicitur, Nam si esset in terra: sed, si consideremus respiciendum esse ad id quod prius dictum est, Christum sedere in coelis, nihil scrupi superest. Neque est, quodreferatur ad victimam vel donaria, sicut nonnulli interpretantur, quia agitur de dignitate sacerdotii, sicut liquet ex sequentibus, ubi dicitur illatiue. Nunc vero hoc excellentius sortitus est sacerdotium.
units.tr: All the Mosaic things were merely external, temporary and soon to perish, and so perfection could not be ascribed to them, just as perfection or dignity is not ascribed to a building merely painted by an architect, especially when the house itself is already completed and perfect and what is more excellent has succeeded. Now let us note some smaller points about the arrangement of the parts. The words For if he were on earth do not seem to cohere with what precedes; but if we consider that we must look back to what was said before, that Christ sits in heaven, no difficulty remains. Nor is it to be referred to the victim or the gifts, as some interpret, because the subject is the dignity of the priesthood, as is clear from what follows, where it is introduced with an inferential word: But now he has obtained a more excellent priesthood.

units.la: Necesset sacerdos quidem:) Non sic accipies, quasi detrahatur Christo sacerdotium in terris, quod videlicet non sit natus ex tribu Leui, vel quod non obtulerit pecudes, vel quod alij fuerint in terra sacerdotes, per quos citra tumultum non potuisset ministrare, vel huiusmodi: Sed generaliter ita dicitur, ad significandum quodcunque sacerdotium in terris existens, quale erat sacerdotum legalium offeretium diuersa genera carnalium victimarum, non esse proprie sacerdotium appellandum, ac vix nomine eo dignum, tantum abest, ut ei res tribuatur, praesertim respectu sacerdotij veri, quod est solius Christi agentis in coelis. Est autem artificiosa extenuatio sacerdotij legalis, prudeter collecta, tum ex ijs, quae prius de abrogatione sacerdotij dicta sunt, tum ex eo, quod subijcitur, terrenum & legale sacerdotium non esse quidem verum ac legitimum, sed tantum seruire exemplari atque umbrae. Sine dubio hic valde fremebant aduersarij, sed conueniebat ita in hac causa agere: atque ex hac extenuatione sacerdotij (cuius iam ante probauerat abrogationem) iam amodo tacite suggerit, quid dicturus sit de sacrificijs legalibus, quod videlicet ea etiam nec sacrificia quidem fuerint appellanda, respectu eius sacrificij, quod Christus semel obtulit.
units.tr: Nor would he be a priest at all: do not take this as if the priesthood on earth were being taken away from Christ, as though he had not been born of the tribe of Levi, or had not offered beasts, or as though there were other priests on earth through whom he could not have ministered without disorder, or anything of the kind. Rather, it is said in general terms to signify that any priesthood existing on earth, such as that of the legal priests who offered various kinds of carnal victims, is not properly to be called a priesthood, and is hardly worthy of that name, much less should the thing itself be ascribed to it, especially in comparison with the true priesthood, which belongs to Christ alone acting in heaven. This is a skilful belittling of the legal priesthood, shrewdly drawn both from what was said earlier about the abrogation of the priesthood, and from what follows: that the earthly and legal priesthood is not indeed true and lawful, but serves only as a copy and shadow. Without doubt the adversaries raged loudly at this, but it was fitting to proceed in this way in this cause. And from this belittling of the priesthood (whose abrogation he had already proved earlier), he now tacitly suggests what he is going to say about the legal sacrifices, namely that these too should not even be called sacrifices, when compared with the sacrifice which Christ offered once for all.

units.la: Vbi sunt sacerdotes, qui offerunt iuxta legem donaria, qui quidem exemplari & umbrae deseruiunt.
units.tr: Where are the priests who offer gifts according to the law, who indeed serve as a copy and a shadow?

units.la: De sacerdotum oblationibus supra nonnihil dictum est initio capitis quinti: Sed hoc notandum, quomodo dicantur deseruire exemplari. Quicquid ibi erat, id universum ad exemplar pertinebat, ipsum tabernaculum, victimae, donaria, denique omnia eiusmodi typus erant & figura aliarum rerum, spiritualium, inquam, per Christum gerendarum, sicut ipse Apostolus capite nono utcunque indicat. Et umbrae, inquit: Hac voce adhuc valde extenuans omnia annexa sacerdotio: Non solum exemplar sunt, sed tantum umbra. Quis autem nescit, quantum abfuit umbra a corpore? Ergo tantum abfuit quoque, sacrificia legis a sacrificio Christi. Quin significatur eadem ratione sacerdotes legales, dum ita deseruiebant exemplari atque umbrae, debuisse fide intentos esse in aliquid maius & sublimius, nec non in omnibus, quae agebant, debuisse mentem ad praestantiora conuertere. Vbi enim est exeplar siue umbra, oportet ex natura relationum concipere mete aliquod exeplatu & quoddam corpus, quod & semper est excellentius ipso exemplari. Proinde Apostolus etiam sapienter expresit, cuiusmodi esset exemplarib. significata, siue, quale esset corpus talium umbrarum, quando addidit: Coelestium: Res terrenae & carnales, puta, sacerdotium, sacrificia, tabernaculum, & omnia huius generis, exemplaria sunt rerum coelestium. Ergo sacerdotes illi exiguis rebus erant occupati, & debebant contendere ad sublimiora, nempe coelestia: sicut ipse quoq; Moses in ista respiciebat, ubi ipsi praescribebantur a Deo, & ipse rursus proponebat populo. Quomodo vero adumbrarint coelestia, Apostolus in sequentibus aliquo modo exponit, vbi tabernaculum & sancta sanctorum ait significasse coelum, quod Christus etiam semel ingressus est: sanguinem vitulorum, taurorum, typum fuisse sanguinis Christi: purificationem externam & carnalem, significasse purificationem per Christum faciendam internam & spiritualem.
units.tr: I have said something about the sacrificial offerings of the priests at the beginning of chapter five, but it should be noted here in what sense they are said to serve as a copy. Everything there belonged to the copy: the tabernacle itself, the victims, the gifts, in short all such things were types and figures of other realities, spiritual ones, I mean, to be accomplished through Christ, as the Apostle himself indicates in some measure in chapter nine. And "shadow," he says. By this word he further belittles everything connected with the priesthood: they are not only a copy but only a shadow. Who does not know how far a shadow falls short of the body? So far, then, do the sacrifices of the law fall short of the sacrifice of Christ. Indeed, it is signified by the same reasoning that the legal priests, in serving a copy and a shadow, ought to have kept their faith fixed on something greater and more sublime, and in all that they did ought to have turned their minds to higher things. For where there is a copy or a shadow, one must by the nature of the relation conceive of some archetype and some body, which is always more excellent than the copy itself. Accordingly the Apostle also wisely expressed what kind of things were signified by the copies, or what kind of body such shadows had, when he added: "heavenly." The earthly and carnal things, namely the priesthood, the sacrifices, the tabernacle, and all things of this kind, are copies of heavenly things. Therefore those priests were occupied with trifling matters and ought to have strained toward higher things, namely heavenly ones, just as Moses himself also looked to these things, where they were prescribed to him by God, and he in turn set them before the people. How the heavenly things were foreshadowed the Apostle explains in some measure in what follows, where he says that the tabernacle and the holy of holies signified heaven, into which Christ also entered once; that the blood of calves and bulls was a type of the blood of Christ; and that the external and carnal purification signified the internal and spiritual purification to be effected through Christ.

units.la: Iam hic amodo clare dicit, terrenum sacerdotium legale, esse umbram sacerdotij Christi agentis in coelis: quandoquidem omnia legalia & terrena sunt umbra coelestium. Ergo quanto coelestia sunt excellentiora terrenis, tanto etiam par est sacerdotium Christi intelligi praestantius sacerdotio legali. Valde autem conueniebat, per Apostolum exprimi, quarum rerum essent umbrae seu typi illa legalia. Nam alias aduersarij potuissent interpretari, praesignificasse alias res etiam terrenas, nihilo praestantiores illis prioribus, veluti restaurationem rituum temporibus Esdrae, vel alijs. Quamobrem Apostolus dixit, illa omnia umbras fuisse rerum coelestium. Et cum ante dixisset, Christum agere in coelis, sequebatur hoc, ut illa res Christi adumbrarent. Neq; vero difficile est subinde alias interpretationes in typis, sicut & allegorijs, colligere, quod & videmus a Iudaeis & fanaticis nostri temporis spiritibus fieri: sed cum certum sit, a Deo constituta illa legalia, ad adumbrandum non quaslibet res, sed certas, & potissimum spirituales, quaeq; per Christum forent gerendae, voluit spiritus Sanctus per os Apostoli aperire, quid nam potissimum per sacerdotium & sacrificia legalia fuerit adumbratum, sicut alias saepe multi typi in Euangelijs & epistolis noui testamenti breuiter annotantur.
units.tr: Now here he says plainly that the earthly legal priesthood is a shadow of the priesthood of Christ, who acts in the heavens, since all legal and earthly things are shadows of heavenly ones. Therefore, as the heavenly things are more excellent than the earthly, so the priesthood of Christ must be understood to be far more excellent than the legal priesthood. It was very fitting that the Apostle should state what things those legal institutions were shadows or types of. Otherwise the opponents could have interpreted them as foreshadowing other things, also earthly ones, no more excellent than the former, such as the restoration of the rites in the time of Ezra, or others. For this reason the Apostle said that all those things were shadows of heavenly realities. And since he had said earlier that Christ acts in the heavens, it follows that those things foreshadowed Christ's work. Nor is it difficult to gather other interpretations afterwards in types, as in allegories, which we see being done by the Jews and by the fanatical spirits of our own time; but since it is certain that those legal institutions were established by God to foreshadow not just any things but certain ones, and above all spiritual things, to be accomplished through Christ, the Holy Spirit willed to disclose through the mouth of the Apostle what, above all, was foreshadowed by the legal priesthood and sacrifices, just as elsewhere many types are briefly noted in the Gospels and the epistles of the New Testament.

units.la: Est autem diligenter notandum, quòd, quæ in veteri testamento instituta sunt ceremonialia omnia,imò & illustria facta plurimorum sanctorum patrum, Christi typus,umbra, & exemplar fuerunt, nec non aliquid per Christum gerendum perficiendumque significabant. Adeò nihil per Christum gestum est, quàmdiu in terris egit, nihil præterea vel nunc tempore revelati Euangelij fit in Ecclesia, quod non apud patres fuerit variis modis in lege & factis patrum adumbratum. Qua de re liceret nobis multo plenius disserere, si vacaret, possemusque de singulis, quæ Christus gessit, & vaticinia prophetarum congerere: sicut Chrysostomum fecisse videmus in libro, quo contra Gentiles probat, Christum esse Deum. Item possemus typos & figuras colligere, sed extant libelli prie in hoc scripti: imò alicubi videre est, eadem omnia picturis clarissimè expressa. Pro inde inter cætera habemus istud hoc loco, quòd sacerdotium legale erat tantùm typus sacerdotij Christi: tabernaculum legale erat typus tabernaculi, quod ingressurus esset Christus: item sacrificia legalia typi erant unici sacrificij Christi, sicut Apostolus clarius exponit capite sequenti. Certè passim licet videre in novo testamento typos huiusmodi expositos: 1. Corinth. 10. de Baptismo, de cœna Domini typi exponuntur, atque omnia in figura contigisse patribus ibidem clarè dicitur. Galat. 4. interpretatur ejectionem Ismaelis maioris natu, sed ex serva nati, præfigurasse abrogationem legis. Item, quòd Ismael persecutus sit Isaac, significatum, quòd Iudaicus populus, & quicunque impij persequerentur electos atque pios. Et sic alibi alia explicantur. Christus, Ionam gessisse typum suæ resurrectionis: item serpentem erectum in deserto typum fuisse suæ crucifixionis: item agnum paschalem, &c. Ac notandum interea, patres & prophetas Spiritu sancto afflatos, etiam in his figuris Christum agnouisse, probeque iam tùm animaduertisse, quòd omnia illa adumbrarent aliquid per Christum perficiendum. Quare Moses in monte cernens delineatum tabernaculum, item postea tale materiale erigens, haud dubiè mente respiciebat ad tabernaculum, quod ingressurus esset Christus, & in quod nos vnà cum Christo, & per Christum, perduceremur. Item considerans sacrificia pro certo, apprehendebat animo dignissimum sacrificium, quod per Christum, pro vera expiatione omnium peccatorum, debebat in posterum in ara crucis offerri. Sciebat quippe, se, sicut ipsi à Deo dictum erat, nihil aliud, quàm exemplaria & typos in his omnibus videre, ideoque debebat intellectum & fidem suam ad maiora, sublimiora, & præstabiliora convertere. Ergo sacerdotium, sacramenta, ceremoniæ, & omni deniq; quàmlibet præclara, res futuras illis adumbrabant, maximeque eas, quæ per Christum, & propter Christum debebant perfici. Neque audiendi sunt Iudæi contendentes, nihil quàm nudum exemplar propositum in monte, sicut architecti solent. Hac ratione valde derogatur dignitati ordinationum diuinarum. Deus non adeò humiles res ita curabat, sed sublimiora voluit intelligi. Et Deo, & Mosi sunt iniurij, quando ad tàm humiles & perituras res defigunt consilium Dei, & generosum spiritum Mosis. Ex quo & nos debemus hanc doctrinam colligere, quòd ea, quæ nobis in sacris vsitata sunt, signa atque ceremoniæ, debent etiam aliquid significare: ac primum præterita, videlicet, quæ per Christum hactenus sunt gesta: deinde & quæ propter Christum sunt adhuc in ecclesia olim perficienda, siue quæ iubeant nos ad res cœlestes intueri. Ac ne longiores hic simus, lubet breuiter baptismi & cœnæ Dominicæ signa intueri. Hæc inquam nobis significant aliquid iam factum per Christum, & præterea aliquid adhuc perficiendum. Baptismus siquidem, in quo mergimur aquis, ac rursus erigimur, significat inprimis mortem Christi, eiusque resurrectionem, per quam liberati sumus à peccatis: cuius virtute fit,ut nos quoque spiritualiter moriamur peccato, deinde & in nouitatem vitæ resurgamus. Sed præter hæc etiam resurrectio & noua vita post huius vitæ terrenæ cursum significatur. Quæ omnia declarantur pluribus verbis Roman.6. Sepulti igitur sumus vnà cum illo per Baptismum in mortem, ut, quemadmodu excitatus est Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris, ita & nos in nouitate vitæ ambulemus. Nam si insititij facti sumus illi per similitudinem mortis eius, nimirum & resurrectionis participes erimus. Similiter cœna Domini significat aliquid gestum per Christum, & aliquid in altera vita geredum. Gestum quidem, quia fit iuxta præceptum & verbum ipsius, in commemorationem mortis eius, & effusi sanguinis in remissionem nostrorum peccatorum. Gerendum verò, quia refert nobis resurrectionem, vitam et gloriam in cœlis apud Christum obtinendum. Quò pertinet, quod Christus Matthæi 26. & Marci 14. adiecit, dicens, Non bibà post hac ex hoc fructu vitis vsque in diem illum, cùm illud bibam vobiscum nouum in regno patris mei.
units.tr: It must, however, be carefully noted that all the ceremonial institutions of the Old Testament, and indeed the illustrious deeds of many holy fathers, were types, shadows, and copies of Christ, and signified something to be done and accomplished through Christ. So much so that nothing has been done through Christ while he lived on earth, and nothing further now, in the time of the revealed gospel, is done in the Church, which was not in various ways foreshadowed among the fathers in the law and in the deeds of the fathers. On this matter we might discourse much more fully, if there were time, and we could gather up the prophecies of the prophets concerning each of the things that Christ did, as we see Chrysostom did in the book in which he proves against the Gentiles that Christ is God. Likewise we could collect types and figures, but there are already booklets written on this subject; indeed, somewhere one may see all these things most clearly portrayed in pictures. Therefore, among other things, we have this point here: the legal priesthood was only a type of the priesthood of Christ; the legal tabernacle was a type of the tabernacle which Christ was to enter; likewise the legal sacrifices were types of the one sacrifice of Christ, as the Apostle explains more clearly in the following chapter. Surely such types can be seen set out throughout the New Testament: in 1 Corinthians 10 the types of baptism and of the Lord's Supper are explained, and it is clearly said there that all things happened to the fathers in figure. Galatians 4 interprets the casting out of Ishmael, the elder son born of the bondwoman, as having prefigured the abrogation of the law. Likewise, that Ishmael persecuted Isaac signifies that the Jewish people, and all the ungodly, persecute the elect and the pious. And other things are explained similarly elsewhere. Christ says that Jonah was a type of his resurrection; likewise that the serpent lifted up in the wilderness was a type of his crucifixion; likewise the paschal lamb, and so on. And it should be noted meanwhile that the fathers and prophets, inspired by the Holy Spirit, recognized Christ even in these figures, and had already well perceived that all those things foreshadowed something to be accomplished through Christ. Hence Moses, seeing on the mountain the pattern of the tabernacle, and afterwards erecting such a material tabernacle, undoubtedly looked in his mind to the tabernacle which Christ was to enter, and into which we, together with Christ and through Christ, were to be brought. Likewise, when he considered the sacrifices, he grasped in his mind that most worthy sacrifice which, through Christ, was to be offered in future on the altar of the cross for the true expiation of all sins. For he knew that, as had been said to him by God, in all these things he saw nothing but copies and types, and therefore he ought to turn his understanding and faith to greater, higher, and more excellent things. Thus the priesthood, the sacraments, the ceremonies, and in short all the most splendid things foreshadowed future realities, and especially those which were to be accomplished through Christ and on account of Christ. Nor are the Jews to be heard when they contend that Moses was shown on the mountain nothing but a bare pattern, as architects usually have. By such reasoning the dignity of the divine ordinances is greatly diminished. God did not take such care over such humble things, but willed that higher things be understood. Both God and Moses are wronged when they confine the counsel of God and the noble spirit of Moses to such humble and perishable things. From this we too ought to draw this teaching: that the signs and ceremonies which are in use among us in the sacred things must also signify something, both things already done through Christ up to now, and also things still to be accomplished in the Church on account of Christ, or things which bid us look to heavenly realities. But that we may not be too long here, let us briefly consider the signs of baptism and of the Lord's Supper. These, I say, signify to us something already done through Christ, and besides, something still to be accomplished. For baptism, in which we are immersed in water and raised again, signifies above all the death of Christ and his resurrection, by which we have been freed from sins; by its power it comes about that we too die spiritually to sin, and then rise to newness of life. But besides these things, the resurrection and new life after the course of this earthly life are also signified. All these things are set forth more fully in Romans 6: "Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been grafted into him by the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be partakers of his resurrection." Similarly the Lord's Supper signifies something done through Christ, and something to be done in the other life. Done, indeed, because it is performed according to his command and word, in remembrance of his death and of the blood shed for the remission of our sins. To be done, because it brings before us the resurrection, life, and glory to be obtained in heaven with Christ. To this belongs what Christ added in Matthew 26 and Mark 14, saying: "I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father."

units.la: Hæc in præsens de typis, siue significatione signorum ac cerimoniarum tàm in veteri testamento, quàm novo, sint satis.
units.tr: These things, for the present, about types, or the meaning of signs and ceremonies in both the Old Testament and the New, will be enough.

units.la: Quod
units.tr: That

units.la: Quo praestantioris est testamenti intercessor, quod in praestantioribus promissis sanctum est. Etenim si prius illud tale fuisset, vt nihil in eo posset reprehendi, haud quaquam fuisset secundo quaesitus locus. Nam incusans eos loquitur illis: Ecce dies venient, dicit Dominus, & consummabo super domum Israel, & super domum Iuda testamentum nouum, non iuxta testamentum, quod feci patribus illorum, vt educerem eos ex Aegypto. Quoniam ipsi non perstiterunt in testamento meo, & ego neglectui eos habui, dicit Dominus. Nam hoc est testamentum, quod disponam domui Israel post dies illos, dicit Dominus, dans leges meas in mentem illorum, & in corde illorum inscribam illas, & ero illis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Et non docebunt quisque proximum suum, & vnusquisque fratrem suum, dicentes: Cognosce Dominum, quod omnes cognituri sint me ab eo, qui pusillus fuerit inter eos, vsque ad eum, qui magnus est inter illos, quoniam placatus ero super iniustitiis illorum, & peccatis eorum, & iniquitatum illorum non recordabor amplius. Apparet Apostolum, cum diceret: Nunc vero hoc excellentius sortitus est sacerdotium, voluisse alteram partem, quae ad absoluendam argumentationem ante coeptam desiderabatur, adijcere, ad eum fere modum, quo nos in enarratione pro tenuitate nostra eam complexi sumus. Sed ecce, quasi non cogitanti protinus aliud succurrit argumentum, quo rursus multo clarissime, licet valde breuiter, & quasi vno verbo docet, sacerdotium Christi praestantius esse sacerdotio legali, idque ratione sumpta a praestantia noui testamenti, siue Euangelij, hoc pacto:
units.tr: By so much is he the surety of a better testament, which was established upon better promises. For if that first had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second. For finding fault with them, he saith: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord: I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people. And they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying: Know the Lord; for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest: because I will be merciful to their iniquities, and their sins I will remember no more. It appears that the Apostle, when he said, "But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry," wished to add the other part, which was needed to complete the argument he had begun. He does this in much the same way as we followed it in our exposition, as far as our small ability allowed. But look: as if he had not yet thought of it, another argument immediately comes to mind, by which he teaches again, much more clearly though very briefly, and as it were in a single word, that the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood. He takes this from the excellence of the new testament, or Gospel, in the following way:

units.la: Oportet sacerdotium illud habere praestantius, quod excellentioris est testamenti.
units.tr: That priesthood ought to be more excellent which belongs to the more excellent testament.

units.la: Atqui testamentum nouum praestantius est testamento veteri:
units.tr: But the new testament is more excellent than the old testament.

units.la: Ergo & sacerdotiu Christi, quod est noui testamenti, praestantius est sacerdotio legali.
units.tr: Therefore the priesthood of Christ, which belongs to the new testament, is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood.

units.la: Haec est prima consequentia, ex illis sumpta verbis, Quo praestantioris est testamenti intercessor. Ac potuissemus quidem etiam sequentia interponere, omniaque constringere quodammodo in vnam argumentationem quadripartitam, sicut superius fecimus, sed malumus singula seorsum crasius reddere, vt a quibuslibet clarius tota dispositio perspiciatur. Proinde, quod ad consequentiam iam formatam attinet, Maior est eiusmodi, vt nemo non lubenter sit eam largiturus.
units.tr: This is the first consequence, drawn from the words By so much is he the surety of a better testament. We could indeed have added the following consequences too, and drawn everything together in a single four-part argument, as we did above; but we prefer to set out each part separately and more fully, so that the whole arrangement can be seen more clearly by anyone. Accordingly, as far as this consequence already framed is concerned, the major premise is of such a kind that no one would not gladly grant it.

units.la: Minori autem attexitur statim ratio valde idonea, ideo videlicet Euangelium esse praestantius, quod sanctum sit in praestantioribus promissis. Aequum siquidem esse, vbi praestantiora, efficaciora, magisque salutifera sunt promissa, ibi censeatur excellentius testamentum.
units.tr: The minor premise is at once supported by a very suitable reason, namely that the Gospel is more excellent because it was established upon better promises. For it is fitting that where the promises are better, more effective, and more saving, there the testament should be judged more excellent.

units.la: Iam, quod si quis istud quoq; vellet dissimulare, aut fortasis contenderet, etiam vetus testamentum talibus promissis confirmatum, atque omnia, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, pari modo potuisse in veteri testamento obtineri, opponit aliam probationem Apostolus, cuius haec est sententia:
units.tr: Now if anyone should wish to pass over this point too, or perhaps contend that the old testament also was confirmed by such promises, and that everything necessary for salvation could equally have been obtained under the old testament, the Apostle sets against this another proof, whose sense is this:

units.la: Si prius testamentum tale fuisset, vt nihil in eo posset reprehendi seu desiderari, haud quaquam opus fuisset aliud testamentum ei succedere.
units.tr: If that first testament had been such that nothing in it could be found fault with or lacking, there would by no means have been any need for another testament to succeed it.

units.la: Sed constat, iam olim diuinitus constitutum, vt veteri testamento succedat nouum, atque istud quidem habens promissiones de salute & perfectione spirituali atq; aeterna, quales sane promissiones vetus testamentum non habebat.
units.tr: But it is clear that from of old it was divinely ordained that a new testament should succeed the old, and that this one indeed has promises of salvation, of spiritual and eternal perfection, such as the old testament certainly did not have.

units.la: Igitur testamentum nouum sanctum est praestantioribus promissis, quam vetus: ac merito debet veteri anteponi. Huius vero argumenti minorem (quandoquidem haec sola videtur probatione indigere) manifestam esse vult ex testimonio Hieremiae capite tricesimo primo, cuius priori parte noui testamenti post vetus institutio & successio cum insigni discrimine exprimitur: posteriori promissiones euangelicae de bonis spiritualibus & aeternis, nempe de donatione Spiritus & remissione peccatorum, indicantur. Quibus omnibus, sacerdotium Christi praestantius esse sacerdotio legali, apertissime euincitur, sumpta videlicet ratione a praeeminentia noui testamenti siue Euangelij, vti prius diximus. Sunt autem non pauca hic obseruanda de ratione consequentiarum istarum: Item de propria sententia testimonij, quae non ita possunt statim plene explicari: quamobrem singula sunt per ordinem expendenda.
