units.tr: Therefore the new testament, being established upon better promises than the old, rightly ought to be preferred to it. He wishes the minor premise of this argument, since this alone seems to need proof, to be made plain from the testimony of Jeremiah, chapter thirty-one. In the first part of that passage the institution and succession of the new testament after the old is expressed with a remarkable distinction; in the latter part the evangelical promises of spiritual and eternal goods are indicated, namely the gift of the Spirit and the forgiveness of sins. From all these things it is most clearly proved that the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood, the argument being taken, as we said before, from the pre-eminence of the new testament, or Gospel. There are, however, not a few things to be observed here about the nature of these consequences, and also about the proper meaning of the testimony, which cannot be fully explained at once; therefore each point must be weighed in order.

units.la: Quanto praestantioris est testamenti intercessor) Paulo ante conclusionem praecedentis partis probauit Apostolus dignitatem Euangelij, duobus argumentis ductis a dignitate sacerdotij, nunc autem e contrario probat dignitatem sacerdotij, a dignitate Euangelij. An valeat haec varietas & reciprocatio consequentiarum? Quid ni? Nam ibidem diximus, & ostendimus, quodammodo relationum cum more se habere testamentum siue pactum, & sacerdotium.
units.tr: By so much is he the surety of a better testament. A little before the conclusion of the preceding part, the Apostle proved the dignity of the Gospel by two arguments drawn from the dignity of the priesthood; now, on the contrary, he proves the dignity of the priesthood from the dignity of the Gospel. Can this variation and reversal of the consequences stand? Why not? For we said and showed in the same place that a testament or covenant and a priesthood stand in a certain relation to one another, as is customary.

units.la: Neque enim alterum sine altero subsistere: & quo in statu unum est, in tali esse & alterum: in omni pacto esse debere sacerdotes quasi mediatores inter utramque partem inter se pacisccentium. Sed & multo euidentior ratio est, atque vnicuique magis obuia, vt probetur à dignitate testamenti dignitas sacerdotij, quàm vt fiat diuersum. Quamobrem, sicut supra capite septimo, ita & hic optimè constabit consequentiarum ratio. Eleganter autem vocatur Christus noui testamenti intercessor, <bl>μεσίτης</bl>, id est, mediator. Solent, vbicúq; pacta fiunt inter aliquos, adhiberi mediatores, id est, qui vtrique parti æqui esse velint, & vtrinque procurare, quæ ad concordiam firmandam conseruandamque conducant, necnon conditiones pacti vtrinque diligenter tueri. Sic videmus Paranymphos adhiberi contractibus coniugij, proxenetas contractibus mercatorum, sequestros inter litigantes. Eodem, inquam, pacto Christus est verus mediator inter Deum & homines, inter quas personas pactum constitutum est, quo Deus pollicitus est, se fore hominibus in Deum, id est, protectorem, conseruatorem: atque homines rursus obstringunt se fore obedientes illi, & præcepta eius seruantes: quam rationem pactorum sæpe licet videre expressam in veteri testamento, & item à Christo propositam in Euangelio. Ac duplici ratione vocatur Christus mediator:
units.tr: For neither can exist without the other, and in whatever state the one is, in such the other also must be; in every covenant there must be priests, as it were mediators between the two parties making the agreement. Yet it is a much clearer reason, and one more obvious to everyone, that the dignity of the priesthood should be proved from the dignity of the testament, than the reverse. Therefore, just as above in chapter seven, so here too the force of the consequences will be very well established. Christ is elegantly called the mediator [μεσίτης] of the new testament, that is, the mediator. Wherever agreements are made between parties, mediators are usually called in, that is, persons who wish to be impartial toward both sides, and who on each side take care of what contributes to establishing and preserving concord, and who diligently guard the terms of the agreement on both sides. Thus we see go-betweens employed in marriage contracts, brokers in the dealings of merchants, and arbiters between litigants. In the same way, I say, Christ is the true mediator between God and men, between whom the covenant has been made: as God has promised that he will be to men a God, that is, a protector and preserver, so men in turn bind themselves to be obedient to him and to keep his commands. This manner of covenanting can often be seen expressed in the old testament, and likewise set forth by Christ in the Gospel. Christ is called mediator for a twofold reason:

units.la: Primùm ratione officij. Quia enim pontifex est, oportet illum esse mediatorem inter Deum & homines: vnde & ad finem capitis secundi dicitur, Christum per omnia similem fratribus redditum, vt nimirum misericors esset, & fidelis pontifex, in his, quæ apud Deum forent agenda, ad expiandum peccata populi. Et initio capitis quinti, Omnis pontifex pro hominibus constituitur in his, quæ apud Deum aguntur.
units.tr: First, by reason of his office. For since he is a high priest, he must be the mediator between God and men. Hence at the end of the second chapter Christ is said to have been made like his brethren in all things, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in those matters which were to be transacted before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. And at the beginning of the fifth chapter: Every high priest is appointed for men in those things which are done before God.

units.la: Huc etiam pertinet, quòd Moses Galat. 3. vocatur simili de causa <bl>μεσίτης</bl>: Ordinata est, inquit, lex per angelos in manu intercessoris: Intercessor autem vnius est, Deus autem vnus est
units.tr: To this also belongs the fact that Moses, for a similar reason, is called a mediator [μεσίτης] in Galatians 3: The law, he says, was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one.

units.la: Secundo dicitur Christus mediator ratione vtriusque naturæ, diuinæ inquam & humanæ, per quas optimè nouit, & quæ Dei sunt, & quæ hominum: nec potuisset alia persona vllo modo ad mediatoris officium apta reddi. Sic describitur 1. Timo. 2. Vnus est Deus, vnus etiam conciliator (<bl>μεσίτης</bl>) Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit semetipsum precium redemptionis pro omnibus. Simili modo vocatur Christus capite nono, & duodecimo huius epistolæ <bl>μεσίτης</bl>.
units.tr: Secondly, Christ is called mediator by reason of both natures, the divine and the human, through which he best knows both the things of God and the things of men; and no other person could in any way have been fitted for the office of mediator. So he is described in 1 Timothy 2: There is one God, and one mediator [μεσίτης] between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all. In the same way Christ is called mediator in chapters nine and twelve of this epistle.

units.la: Iam quod ad rationem illam attinet, quod in præstantioribus promissionibus sancitum est, videndum, valeatne consequentia, quòd, vbi promissiones sunt potiores, ibi oporteat, vt sit præstantius testamentum. Deinde, an ne etiam promissiones Euangelicæ sint potiores promissionibus legalibus. Proinde, vt de primo dicamus, quemadmodum à præstantia effectuum solet iudicari de dignitate causarum efficientium: item obiecta solent diligentissimè expendi atque æstimari: item finis solet omnia antecedentia commendare: Ita & in hac parte faciendum est.
units.tr: Now as regards the reason which is set forth in the words, that it was established upon better promises, we must consider whether the consequence holds, namely that where the promises are better, the testament must be more excellent there. Then we must consider whether the evangelical promises are also better than the legal promises. Accordingly, to speak first of the former point: just as the dignity of efficient causes is usually judged from the excellence of their effects, and just as the objects are usually weighed and esteemed most carefully, and the end usually commends all that precedes it, so it must be done in this part too.

units.la: Cùm igitur promissiones euangelicæ longè ampliora & præclariora bona proponant, atque ob oculos constituant fide apprehendenda, quàm legales: Præterea maior etiam fit certitudo accipiendorum bonorum istorum, quam olim fuit in lege, merito propter excellentiam promissionum etiam testamentum ipsum excellentius iudicatur. Cæterum, quomodo promissiones euangelicæ ampliora bona proponant, quàm legales, alias quidem à nobis dictum est capite tertio, vbi de discrimine legis & Euangelij fusius egimus, explicantes locum de domo Dei, quæ constat omnibus credentibus, cuius domus administrator est Christus: Item paulo ante capite septimo dictum est, Euangelium spes, qua appropinquamus Deo. Hoc nihilominus obiter repetemus, promissiones legales fere loqui de bonis temporalibus, sicut Esaiae 1. diserte dicitur, Si volueritis & audieritis me, bona terræ comedetis. Sed multò copiosissimè & apertissimè licet videre Leuit. 26. vbi seruantibus præcepta plurima promittuntur, sed omnia temporale & terrenum quiddam sonantia. Item Deuter. 5. & 28. Euangelium autem promittit spiritualia bona, videlicet de iustificatione conscientiarum coram Deo, de vita æterna, de regno cœlorum. Quòd si patres vlli sub velamine bonorum temporalium, vt possessionis terræ Canaan, & similium intellexerunt, & fide apprehenderunt patriam nostram cœlestem seu regnum cœlorum: Certè tales patres in Christum respexerunt, sicut Christus de Abraham testatur Ioann. 8. & ad Euangelium magis, quàm ad legem pertinere debent iudicari. Potest & hoc addi ad excellentiam promissionum Euangelicarum faciens, quòd, vti, ad accipiendum fructus promissionum legalium requirebatur conditio obseruatæ legis: sub Euangelio nequaquàm talis conditio requiritur: qua ex re magis certæ reddunt conscientiæ. Promissiones enim Euangelij sunt gratuitæ, sicut Apostolus diserte exprimit multis in locis. Roman. quinto, Iustificantur autem gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus reconciliatorem per fidem, interueniente ipsius sanguine. Sed in testimonio Hieremiæ, quod Apostolus lus mox citat, præstantia Euangelicarum promisionum satis aperitur, vbi dicit Deus, quòd dabit legem in mentibus & inscriptam cordibus, significans, se daturum spiritum Sanctum, cuius ductu filij adoptati seu electi ad bene agendum mouerentur, sicut clarius id exponitur Rom.8. Item vbi loquitur de remissione peccatorum, significans haud dubiè gratuitam iustificationem propter Christum. Ex quibus, spiritualia esse bona, quæ in Euangelio promittuntur & conferuntur, non obscurè potest intelligi. Porrò eleganter dicit, Euangelium esse sanctum talibus promissionibus. Sic enim & leges, & testamenta Romano more dicuntur sanciri, id est, confirmari. Græca vox est νομοθετέω, à νομοθέτης, id est, legem constituo, vel lege statuo, sancio: supra habita est eadem vox capite 7. vbi dicebatur, ὁ λαὸς γὰρ ἐπ' αὐτῇ νενομοθέτηται.
units.tr: Since the evangelical promises set before us, and place before the eyes for faith to grasp, far greater and more excellent goods than the legal promises do, and since the certainty of receiving these goods is also greater than it was under the law, the covenant itself is rightly judged more excellent because of the excellence of its promises. How the evangelical promises set forth greater goods than the legal ones we have explained elsewhere, in the third chapter, where we discussed the difference between law and Gospel more fully, expounding the passage about the house of God, which consists of all believers and whose steward is Christ. Also, a little earlier, in the seventh chapter, it was said that the Gospel is the hope by which we draw near to God. Still, we will briefly repeat the point: the legal promises speak mostly of temporal goods, as Isaiah 1 plainly says: "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land." But Leviticus 26 shows this far more fully and clearly, where many things are promised to those who keep the precepts, yet all of them have a temporal and earthly sound. So also Deuteronomy 5 and 28. The Gospel, however, promises spiritual goods: the justification of consciences before God, eternal life, and the kingdom of heaven. And if any of the fathers, under the veil of temporal goods such as possession of the land of Canaan and the like, understood and grasped by faith our heavenly homeland or the kingdom of heaven, then surely such fathers looked to Christ, as Christ testifies of Abraham in John 8, and they must be judged to belong to the Gospel rather than to the law. This also may be added to the excellence of the evangelical promises: to receive the fruits of the legal promises required the condition of keeping the law, whereas under the Gospel no such condition is required, and for this reason consciences are made more certain. For the promises of the Gospel are free, as the Apostle states plainly in many places. Romans 5: "They are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith, through his blood." But in the testimony of Jeremiah, which the Apostle cites immediately after, the excellence of the evangelical promises is made sufficiently clear, where God says that he will give the law in their minds and write it on their hearts, signifying that he will give the Holy Spirit, by whose guidance the adopted or elect sons are moved to act well, as this is explained more clearly in Romans 8. Also, where he speaks of the forgiveness of sins, he undoubtedly signifies justification freely given on account of Christ. From these things it can be clearly understood that the goods promised and conferred in the Gospel are spiritual. Moreover, he elegantly says that the Gospel is ratified by such promises. For laws and testaments are said, in the Roman manner, to be "sanctioned," that is, confirmed. The Greek word is nomotheteō [νομοθετέω], from nomothetēs [νομοθέτης], that is, to establish a law, or to ordain and sanction by law. The same word was used above in chapter 7, where it was said: "for the people has received the law upon it" [ὁ λαὸς γὰρ ἐπ' αὐτῇ νενομοθέτηται].

units.la: Etenim si prius illud tale fuisset, ut nihil in eo posset reprehendi, haudquaquam fuisset secundo quæsitus locus.
units.tr: For if the first covenant had been such that nothing could be found fault with in it, there would by no means have been a place sought for a second.

units.la: Ista est satis commoda probatio, à Signo, ut apparet, petita: quandoquidem vbi aliquid additur veluti ad perfectionem necessarium, manifestum est, id, quod prius erat, fuisse im perfectum, atque aliquid in eo desideratum. Ergo vbi aliquid superadditur, signum est, aliquid defuisse. Certum verò est, Deum non fuisse ordinaturum nouum pactum sine fa dus sine grauibus causis, & si prius illud testamentum fuisset sufficiens ad salutem.
units.tr: This is a fairly sound proof, drawn, as is evident, from a sign. For when something is added as if necessary to perfect what exists, it is clear that what was there before was imperfect and that something was lacking in it. Therefore, where something is added on top, it is a sign that something was wanting. It is certain, however, that God would not have ordained a new covenant without grave causes, if the former covenant had been sufficient for salvation.

units.la: Proinde διαθήκη refert testamentum, διαθήκλυ, non λειτουργίαν siue sacerdotium: ut sermo sit de toto testamento veteri. Etiamsi Chrysostomus videatur intelligere sacerdotium, motus videlicet eo, quòd de sacerdotio potius dici queat, quòd fuerit imperfectum, quàm de lege: item, quòd statim subijcitur, Nam incusans eos, non, incusans illud, quasi sacerdotes notarentur, non testamentum. Sed tum præcedentia, tum sequentia verba satis arguunt, de testamento veteri, cui succedere debeat nouum vt præstantius, sermonem haberi. Sed idem Chrysostomus sic interpretatur vocem ἀμέμπτος, id est, irreprehensibile, inculpabile, in quo nihil desideretur, significetur potens inculpabiles reddere, idque ne videatur legi tribuere, quòd ipsa aliquid culpabile in se habeat. Sed fine causa scrupulum sibi inijcit Chrysostomus. Neque enim Apostolo religio fuit capite præcedenti dicere, quòd Lex nihil adduxit ad perfectionem, & abrogatam eam propter imbecillitatem. Item Roman.8 vocatur Lex infirma. Quod lex, inquit, præstare non poterat, ea parte, qua imbecillis erat per carne, hoc Deus proprio filio misso sub specie carnis peccato obnoxiæ præstitit. Petrus Actor. 15. legem vocat iugum importabile. Sed quid de illis locutionibus dicemus? Roman. 4. Lex iram operatur. Roman.5 Lex subintroijt, ut abundaret delictum. Item Roman. 7. Occasione accepta peccatum, per præceptum, genuit in me omnem concupiscentiam: Siquidem absque lege peccatum erat mortuum. Ego autem viuebam sine lege quondam. Porrò veniente mandato peccatum reuixit, ego verò mortuus sum. Et repertum est mandatum, quod institutum erat ad vitam, mihi cedere ad mortem.
units.tr: Accordingly, diathēkē [διαθήκη] refers to the testament or covenant, not to leitourgia [λειτουργία] or the priesthood, so that the discussion concerns the whole of the old covenant. Although Chrysostom seems to understand the priesthood, being moved by the fact that it could be said more fittingly of the priesthood than of the law that it was imperfect, and also because it is immediately added, "For finding fault with them," not "with it," as if the priests were being censured rather than the covenant. But both the preceding and the following words sufficiently prove that the discussion is about the old covenant, which the new must succeed as more excellent. Yet the same Chrysostom interprets the word amemptos [ἀμέμπτος], that is, blameless or faultless, in which nothing is wanting, as signifying what is able to make people blameless, and he does this so that it may not seem to ascribe to the law that it has something blameworthy in itself. But Chrysostom raises this scruple for himself without cause. For the Apostle had no scruple in the preceding chapter in saying that the law brought nothing to perfection, and that it was abrogated because of its weakness. Likewise, in Romans 8 the law is called weak: "What the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh." Peter in Acts 15 calls the law a yoke that is hard to bear. But what shall we say about those expressions? Romans 4: "The law works wrath." Romans 5: "The law came in besides, that the offence might abound." Also Romans 7: "Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, produced in me all manner of concupiscence, for apart from the law sin was dead. But I was alive without the law once. But when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death for me."

units.la: En certè locutiones, quibus videtur legis dignitas non parum minui, cùm dicitur, ad perfectionem non adducere, imbellicis, inutilis, infirma, iugum importabile, iram operas, faciens abundare delictum, gignere omnem concupiscentiam, cedere ad mortem. Et tamen hæ locutiones non habent talem, qualis putatur primo aspectu, absurditatem: neque potest ex his inferri, legem fuisse per se malam, inutilem, vel noxiam, sicut Apostolus Roman.7 plenius exponit. Habuit ipsa multas utilitates, atque etiam nunc utilitate nō prorsus caret: & habuit in se eam perfectionem, ob quam fuit ordinata, nempe ut inhiberet transgressores, ut humiliaret præsumptuosos, ut cogeret ad agnitionem peccati, & invocationem misericordiæ diuinæ, & sic adduceret ad Christum.
units.tr: Indeed, here are expressions by which the dignity of the law seems not a little diminished: when it is said that it does not bring to perfection, that it is weak, unprofitable, infirm, a yoke hard to bear, that it works wrath, makes the offence abound, begets all concupiscence, and turns to death. And yet these expressions do not have the absurdity that might be thought at first sight, nor can it be inferred from them that the law was evil in itself, useless, or harmful, as the Apostle explains more fully in Romans 7. The law had many uses, and even now it is not entirely without use; and it had in itself the perfection for which it was ordained, namely, to restrain transgressors, to humble the presumptuous, to compel people to acknowledge sin and to call upon the divine mercy, and so to lead them to Christ.

units.la: Ad maiorem autem perfectionem, videlicet, ut iustos nos redderet coram Deo, non fuit ordinata: sed hæc facultas proprie seruata fuit Euangelio. Itaq; respectu suijpsius, fuit lex perfecta, potens, & faciens id, ad quod erat condita. Respectu autem nostri, id est, nostræ imbecillitatis, item respectu Euangelij, fuit valde infirma, imbecillis, & inutilis. Quo pertinet, quòd ibidem Roman.7. dicit, lex Spiritualis, at ego carnalis sum, &c.
units.tr: But it was not ordained for the greater perfection, namely, to make us righteous before God; that power was properly reserved for the Gospel. Therefore, with respect to itself, the law was perfect, powerful, and accomplishing that for which it was made. With respect to us, that is, to our weakness, and likewise with respect to the Gospel, it was very weak, feeble, and unprofitable. To this belongs what he says in the same place, Romans 7: "The law is spiritual, but I am carnal," and so on.

units.la: Itaque nihil prohibet, quo minus dicamus, legem esse culpabilem, reprehensibilem, siue aliquid in ea desiderari, quod quidem verum est, quatenus ipsa non potest quicquam ad perfectionem adducere, utpote quæ nec in hoc vnquam fuit ordinata. Quòd si enim fuisset in hoc ordinata, nequaquam fuisset opus, aliud testamentum, siue Euangelium succedere, per quod omnia perficerentur. Breuiter, non dissimile ab eo, quod hic dicitur, est illud Galat.3. Etenim si data fuisset lex, quæ posset viuificare, verè ex lege esset iustitia. Quibus si addas: sed non est data, ut viuificaret: Ergo per eam nō est iustitia. Syllogismus est perfectus. Ita hoc quoque loco negatiuè: Si prius illud testamentum fuisset tale, ut nihil in eo desideraretur, nequaquam fuisset opus aliud testamentum succedere. Sed debet
units.tr: Thus nothing prevents us from saying that the law is blameworthy and open to criticism, or that something is lacking in it. This is indeed true, insofar as the law cannot bring anything to perfection, since it was never ordained for this. For if it had been ordained for this, there would have been no need for another covenant, or the Gospel, to succeed it, through which all things would be perfected. In brief, the passage in Galatians 3 is not unlike what is said here: "For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be by the law." Add to this: "But it was not given to give life; therefore righteousness is not by it." The syllogism is complete. So in this place too the argument runs negatively: If the former covenant had been such that nothing in it was lacking, there would by no means have been need for another covenant to succeed it. But another ought to succeed it; therefore it is not such.

units.la: Euangelium promittit spiritum Sanctum per gratiam. bet aliud succedere: Ergo non est tale. Non opus est, ut plura hoc loco adijciamus: nam de causis & latæ legis, & abrogatæ, plenius diximus capite septimo. Nunc ad testimonium illud explicandum veniamus:
units.tr: The Gospel promises the Holy Spirit through grace. It is not necessary to add more here, for we spoke more fully in the seventh chapter about the causes both for enacting the law and for its abrogation. Now let us come to the explanation of that testimony.

units.la: Nam incusans eos loquitur illis: Ecce dies venient, dicit Dominus, & consummabo super domum Israel, & super domum Iuda testamentum nouum, non iuxta testamentum, quod feci patribus illorum in die, cum apprehenderem manum illorum, vt educerem eos ex Aegypto, quoniam ipsi non perstiterunt in testamento meo, & ego neglectui eos habui, dicit dominus. Nam hoc est testamentum, quod disponam domui Israel post dies illos, dicit dominus, dans leges meas in mentem illorum, & in corde inscribam illas, & ero illis deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Et non docebunt quisque proximum suum, & vnusquisque fratrem suum, dicentes: Cognosce Dominum, quoniam omnes cognoscent me a paruo eorum vsque ad magnum inter illos: quia placatus ero super iniustitijs illorum, & peccatis eorum, & iniquitatum illorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: For he speaks to them in accusing them: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of Egypt; because they did not abide in my covenant, and I regarded them with neglect, saith the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord: I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their heart, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying: Know the Lord; for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest among them: for I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.

units.la: Hic autem hoc ordine progredi debebimus. Primùm, rectè & appositè citatum esse ab Apostolo, ostendemus. Quod quò euidentius fiat, ea etiam quæ præcedunt & sequuntur apud prophetam, explicabimus. Hinc singulas exponemus partes, in quibus primò varia lectio tam apud Hebræos, quàm septuaginta, tum dispositio, tum plenior expositio, & si quæ alibi plura in eandem sententiam se referant, id omne à nobis examinabitur.
units.tr: Here, however, we must proceed in this order. First, we will show that the Apostle has quoted this passage rightly and to the point. To make this clearer, we will also explain what goes before and what follows in the prophet. Then we will expound the individual parts, and first the variant readings, both among the Hebrews and in the Septuagint, then the arrangement and a fuller explanation, and whatever else elsewhere refers to the same sense. All of this we will examine.

units.la: Rectè igitur citatum esse præsens Hieremiæ testimonium ad causam præsentem, vel ex eo liquet, quòd probare debebat Apostolus id, quod proximè præcedenti consequentia dicebatur, videlicet, quæsitum esse locum alteri testamento, quod priori tanquam ad perfectionem non sufficienti succederet: deinde, hoc ipsum testamentum succedens præstantioribus promissis esse sancitum. Utrumque verò clarissimè vno eodemq; hoc testimonio prophetæ exprimitur. Ac primùm quidem dum ait, Dominum diserte dixisse, se velle nouum testamentum siue pactū constituere, quod plane diuersum foret ab eo, q olim conditum erat, quo tempore patres educti sunt ex Aegypto, hoc est, à lege, quę Moysi erat tradita. Alterum verò, nempe de præstantioribus promissis, satis aperte ibi indicatur, vbi Dominus ait, se in nouo testamento scripturum leges in cordibus, item omnes cognituros Dominum, hauddubiè significans, se daturum spiritum Sanctum, qui vice legis esset credentibus, utpote per quem tanquam legem, & legislatorem pij gubernarentur, nec non ad bene agendum excitarentur aut dirigerentur: per quem præterea omnes in cognitione Dei atque omnis veritatis plenissimè instituerentur. Rursus, vbi ait, quòd placatus esse velit super iniustitijs, & iniquitatum non amplius recordari, annòn euidentissimè aperit totius euangelij summam & caput, nimirum iustificandos homines gratis per fidem in Iesum Christum? Vides igitur & nouum diuersumq; testamentum debere succedere veteri, & noui testamenti præcipuas promissiones, de donatione inquam spiritus Sancti, & gratuita iustificatione per fidem in Christum, (quæ longè superant omnes promissiones legales, quæ tantùm bona temporalia sonabant) citra ambages & inuolucrum in vno hoc testimonio comprehendi ac declarari.
units.tr: That this testimony of Jeremiah was rightly cited for the present case is clear, first, from the fact that the Apostle had to prove what was said in the immediately preceding inference, namely, that room had been sought for a second covenant, which would succeed the first as not sufficient for perfection; and, second, that this very covenant, succeeding the first, was ratified with better promises. Both are most clearly expressed in this one testimony of the prophet. First, indeed, when he says that the Lord expressly declared that he wished to establish a new covenant or pact, which would be plainly different from that which was once made when the fathers were led out of Egypt, that is, from the law which had been given through Moses. The second, namely about the better promises, is indicated quite plainly where the Lord says that he will write his laws in their hearts, and that all will know the Lord; undoubtedly signifying that he will give the Holy Spirit, who would be to believers in place of the law, inasmuch as through him as through a law and a lawgiver the godly are governed, and are stirred up and directed to do well; through whom, moreover, all are most fully instructed in the knowledge of God and of all truth. Again, when he says that he is willing to be merciful towards iniquities and to remember sins no more, does he not most evidently set forth the sum and head of the whole gospel, namely that men are justified freely through faith in Jesus Christ? You see, therefore, that both a new and different covenant ought to succeed the old, and that the chief promises of the new covenant, namely the gift of the Holy Spirit and free justification through faith in Christ (which far surpass all legal promises, which only spoke of temporal goods), are comprehended and declared in this one testimony without ambiguity or veil.

units.la: Propriam interea ac simplicem hanc esse prophetæ sententiam, quam reddidimus, neq; quicquam tortum hic esse aut longius petitum, quiuis intelligit, cui modò vacarit di spicere, quibusnam de rebus toto illo capite tricesimo primo agitur. Plura enim ibi expo nuntur vaticinia, & promissiones, ad euangelium proprie pertinentes: primùm de vniuersali misericordia erga omnes cognationes Israel, id est, erga omnes credentes, tā Iudeos quā Gentiles: tum de reliquijs Israel seu populi Iudaici postremis temporibus ad salutē perducendis: item de persecutione piorum propter Christum, eorundemque consolatione. Vbi habetur de Rachele plorante, filios, quem locum Matthæus cap.2. citat, & historiæ euangelicæ accommodat. Adhæc apertissimum vaticinium de Christi incarnatione, de uocatione gentium seu fructificatione Euangelij: quibus omnibus ibidē subijcitur præsens testimonium. Ea verò omnia ad euangelium proprie referenda, & de euangelio proprie dicta, nemo potest dissimulare. Sed id, quò magis conspicuum fiat, nos breuiter summam eius capitis percurremus. Post multa expositā à cap.25. de abducendis Iudaeis in Babylonem per Nabuchodonosorem, ac seruitute septuaginta annorum, in cit propheta cap.29. consolari, & eos, qui abducti erant, & qui domi in afflictione manserant. Et quemadmodum solent prophetæ semper in consolationibus admiscere promissiones de euangelio, vt de liberatione per Christum, volentes ita animos omnium ad spiritualia & æterna bona paulatim erigere: addit Hieremias cap.30, non pauca, de expetā-da vera & postrema liberatione per Christum Iesum, & vltione in omnes piorum aduersarios,
units.tr: Meanwhile, that this is the prophet's own and plain meaning, which we have rendered, and that nothing here is twisted or sought from afar, anyone will understand who has leisure to consider what matters are treated in that whole thirty-first chapter. For many prophecies and promises there set forth belong properly to the gospel: first, of the universal mercy towards all the families of Israel, that is, towards all believers, both Jews and Gentiles; then of the remnant of Israel or the Jewish people to be brought to salvation in the last times; likewise of the persecution of the godly for Christ's sake, and their consolation. There is the passage about Rachel weeping for her children, which Matthew cites in chapter 2 and applies to the evangelical history. Besides, there is the most manifest prophecy of Christ's incarnation, and of the calling of the Gentiles, or the fruitfulness of the gospel; and to all of these the present testimony is added there. No one can deny that all these things are to be referred properly to the gospel and are spoken properly of the gospel. But so that this may become more evident, we will briefly run through the summary of that chapter. After many things set forth from chapter 25 about the carrying away of the Jews to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and the servitude of seventy years, the prophet in chapter 29 consoles both those who had been carried away and those who had remained at home in affliction. And just as the prophets usually mingle in their consolations promises about the gospel, such as deliverance through Christ, wishing thus gradually to raise the minds of all to spiritual and eternal goods, Jeremiah adds in chapter 30 not a few things about the true and final deliverance to be expected through Christ Jesus, and about vengeance on all the adversaries of the godly.

units.la: H farios. Hinc vero latius prosequitur consolationem vere euangelicam cap.31.cuius initio statim de vniuersali misericordia erga quoscunque credentes ita concionatur.
units.tr: Hence he pursues more widely the truly evangelical consolation in chapter 31, at the beginning of which he at once preaches about universal mercy towards all believers in this way:

units.la: In tempore illo, dicit Dominus. Ero Deus vniuersis cognationibus Israel, & ipsi erunt mihi in populum.
units.tr: In that time, saith the Lord, I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they shall be my people.

units.la: Cognationes Israel vocans in genere omnes credentes, sicut Apostolus Roman. interpretatur. Propheta deinceps plura addit de colleƈtione & restauratione ecclesiæ, & paululum progressus pronunciat, etiam reliquias Israelis extremis temporibus adsalutem perducendas, gentibus valde admirantibus, sic autem ait: Salua Domine populum tuum reliquias Israel. Et paulo post ad gentes: Audite verbum Domini gentes, & annunciate in Infulis, quæ procul sunt, & dicite: Qui dispersit Israel, congregabit eum, &c. Vbi egregiæ promissiones annecti tur prorsus euangelicæ, id est, de salute æterna loquentes: quandoquidem distrte addit, Erit anima eorum, sicut hortus irriguus, & ultra non esurient: siue, vt alia interpretatio habet, & ultra non dolebunt. Et post pauca repetens de persecutione innocentum seu piorum, habet eadem verba, quæ Matthæus cap.2. de temporibus Christi, ac persecutione tunc facta per Herodem exponit, vt vel hinc manifestum sit, prophetam de euangelio in toto hoc capite disserere. Progressus deinde Christi incarnationem verbis non obscuris delineat, dicens: Creauit Dominus rem nouam super terram, fœmina circumdabit virum: Quis hic dissimulare possit, se non videre, de euangelio clarissimè hic disseri? Addit mox etiam de vocatione Gentium: Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, & seminabo domum Israel, & domum Iuda, semine hominum & semine iumentorum: Vbi per homines intelligi Iudæos, per iumenta vero Gentiles, absurdum nequaquam censeri debet. Sic enim & in Psalmo tricesimo sexto, cùm dicitur, Homines & animal seruas Iehoua: quàm pretiosa est misericordia tua Deus, & filij hominum in vmbra alarum tuarum sperant. Iudæos & gentiles intelligi, interpretantur quidam veteres, in quibus est Arnobius. Quamuis non male exponas de fructificatione ecclesiæ, & de euangelij successu. Sequuntur deinde verba, quæ Apostolus hic citat de euangelio, quod succedere debeat testamento veteri: item de euangelij excellentissimis promissionibus, vti nos exposuimus. Postea iterum addit de multiplicatione credentiū, eorundemque atque euangelij æterna duratione, vt neque populus, neque lex alia credatur successura. Si defecerint, inquit, leges istæ coram me, dicit Dominus, tunc & semen Israel deficiet, vt non sit gens coram me cunctis diebus: & cætera quæ sequuntur. Quæ conueniunt planè cum verbis Christi Marci decimoquarto, Amen dico vobis, quòd non præteribit generatio hæc, donec omnia facta fuerint: cœlum & terra præteribunt, sed verba mea non præteribunt. Et Matthæi 5. Amen dico vobis, donec prætereat cœlum & terra, iota vnum aut vnus apex non præterierit ex lege, quoadomnia facta fuerint. Tantum ergo ad demonstrādum, quòd valde appositè adhibitū sit præsenti causæ testimonium Hieremiæ prophetæ. Iam ad testimonij partes explicandas, præmittit autem Apostolus, dicens:
units.tr: By calling the families of Israel, in general, all believers, as the Apostle interprets in Romans. The prophet then adds more about the gathering and restoration of the Church, and, going a little further, declares that even the remnant of Israel is to be brought to salvation in the last times, while the Gentiles marvel greatly; and he says: Save, O Lord, your people, the remnant of Israel. And a little later, to the Gentiles: Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and declare it in the islands that are far off, and say: He who scattered Israel will gather him, etc. Here excellent promises altogether evangelical are attached, that is, speaking of eternal salvation, since he expressly adds: Their soul shall be like a watered garden, and they shall hunger no more; or, as another interpretation has it, and they shall grieve no more. And after a few words, repeating about the persecution of the innocent or godly, he has the same words which Matthew in chapter 2 applies to the times of Christ and the persecution then carried out by Herod, so that from this alone it is clear that the prophet, in this whole chapter, is discoursing about the gospel. Then, advancing, he sketches Christ's incarnation in no obscure words, saying: The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man. Who could pretend that he does not see that the gospel is most clearly discussed here? Soon after he adds also about the calling of the Gentiles: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, and I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of men and the seed of beasts. Here it ought by no means to be thought absurd that by men are understood the Jews, and by beasts the Gentiles. For so also in Psalm 36, when it is said: Men and beasts you save, O Lord; how precious is your mercy, O God, and the sons of men hope in the shadow of your wings, some of the ancients, among whom is Arnobius, interpret it as meaning Jews and Gentiles. Although you might not wrongly explain it of the fruitfulness of the Church and the success of the gospel. Then follow the words which the Apostle here cites about the gospel, which ought to succeed the old covenant; likewise about the most excellent promises of the gospel, as we have expounded. Afterwards he adds again about the multiplication of believers, and about the eternal duration of them and of the gospel, so that neither a people nor another law is believed to be going to succeed. If these laws shall fail, he says, before me, saith the Lord, then also the seed of Israel shall fail, so that it may not be a nation before me all days; and the rest that follows. These agree plainly with the words of Christ in Mark 14: Verily I say unto you, this generation shall not pass away until all these things be done: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. And in Matthew 5: Verily I say unto you, till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all things be fulfilled. So much, therefore, to demonstrate that the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah has been very aptly applied to the present cause. Now, to explain the parts of the testimony, the Apostle first introduces it, saying:

units.la: Nam increpans eos loquitur illis. Hæc de propheta seu potius domino per prophetam loquente. Nam & propheta ita præfatur, Hæc dicit Dominus, suis nimirum verbis, vel sua autoritate nihil pronuncians. Quos autem increpans, & quare increpans? Certè Iudæos eius temporis, atque omnes peruicaces illos Dei mandata audentes transgredi. Si autem quare, rogas: certè propterea, quòd ut exprimitur in testimonio, ipsi non perstiterunt in testamento, siue fœdere, quod cum Deo pepigerunt: quam ob causam iustissimè accusantur. Itaque tametsi totum testimonium complectatur promissiones de manifestando euangelio, tamen interposita est etiam accusatio eorum, qui veteris pacti fuerunt transgressores. Iam prophetæ verba: Ecce dies venient, dicit Dominus: ἰδοὺ ἡμέραι ἔρχονται, λέγει κύριος. Sæpe hac formula utuntur prophetæ de rebus futuris differentes: sed tunc potissimum, vbi & aliquid singulare atque eximium, deinde, vbi pertinens ad Christi tempora siue euangelium quicquam annunciant. Atque hinc fit, quòd hoc ipso capite apud Hieremiam, quandoquidem de euangelio concionatur, aliquoties eadem particula repetitur.
units.tr: For in finding fault with them he speaks to them. This is said of the prophet, or rather of the Lord speaking through the prophet. The prophet himself introduces his words with "Thus says the Lord," declaring nothing on his own authority but speaking in the Lord's words. Whom does he rebuke, and why? Certainly the Jews of that time, and all the stubborn people who dared to break God's commands. If you ask why, the reason is stated in the testimony itself: they did not abide in the testament, or covenant, that they had made with God, and for this they are most justly accused. So although the whole testimony contains promises about the revealing of the gospel, an accusation of those who broke the old covenant is also inserted. Now the prophet's words: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord [ἰδοὺ ἡμέραι ἔρχονται, λέγει κύριος]. The prophets often use this formula when speaking of future things, but especially when they announce something singular and remarkable, or something that pertains to the times of Christ, that is, to the gospel. And so it happens that in this very chapter of Jeremiah, since he is preaching about the gospel, this particle is repeated several times.

units.la: Et consummabo super domum Israel, & super domum Iuda testamentum nouum.
units.tr: And I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah.

units.la: Sciendum in primis, Apostolum potius citasse hoc testimonium, sicut & alia pleraque iuxta septuaginta, quàm iuxta hebraicam veritatem: etiamsi nec septuaginta interpretū verba vbique retinuerit, non adeò solicitus de singulis verbis, modò sententiam, atque ea quoque verba, quæ in præsenti argumento maiorem habent emphasin, retineret. Nam huiusmodi verba proprie sunt obseruanda, in quibus argumentorum præcipua vis sita est, quæque suam in causa, quæ agitur, habent ἀσύνωσις.
units.tr: First of all it must be noted that the Apostle cited this testimony, as he does many others, following the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew truth. Yet he did not keep the Seventy's words everywhere; he was not overly anxious about single words, provided he kept the sense and those words which carry the greater emphasis in the present argument. For those words must be properly observed in which the chief force of the arguments lies, and which have their own cohesion [ἀσύνωσις] in the matter under discussion.

units.la: Aliàs etiam si quis non singula verba ita exacte, & ad numerum syllabas referat, fieri id potest nonnunquam citra periculum: neque propterea statim atrociter inclamã dum, ac cœlum terræ miscendum, quasi sacræ Scripturæ maiestas oppriimeretur. Ipsi septuaginta interpretes quàlibet afflati spiritu Sanƈto, vt creditur, tamen aliquando consulto ab hebraica veritate paululum declinarunt.
units.tr: Otherwise, if someone does not report each word so exactly, even to the number of syllables, this can sometimes be done without danger. Nor should one therefore cry out savagely, as if heaven and earth were being thrown into confusion, as though the majesty of Holy Scripture were being crushed. The Seventy translators themselves, though inspired by the Holy Spirit, as we believe, nevertheless sometimes deliberately departed a little from the Hebrew truth.

units.la: Proinde nos, si quid hîc variatum à septuaginta, aut sicubi hi quoque ab hebraica veritate discesserint, interdum indicauimus. Sic igitur hoc loco Apostolus: νηὶ σωτηλέσω ζνὶ τ̀ ἑαυτ̀ ἰσραὴλ, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον ἰούδα διαθήκην καινὴν. Septuaginta non habent διαθήσομαι διαθήκην, id est, perfi-ciam, consummabo: sed propius ad hebraicam veritatem διαθήσομαι διαθήκην, id est, dispo-nam fœdus: cùm hebraicè sit ברית id est, percutiam fœdus seu pactum. Interim de sententia nihil variatum est. Porrò nomine domus Israel intelliguntur, si tantùm li-teram spectemus, decem illæ tribus, quæ temporibus Roboam filij Solomonis defece-runt (sicut prædictum fuerat à Domino Solomoni, 1. Reg. 11.) ad Hieroboamum, sicut li-cet videre 1. Reg. 12.
units.tr: Accordingly, where something here differs from the Septuagint, or where they too have departed from the Hebrew truth, we have sometimes pointed this out. So the Apostle here reads: I will make [διαθήσομαι] a new covenant with the house of Israel, and upon the house of Judah [καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰούδα διαθήκην καινήν]. The Septuagint does not have I will make a covenant [διαθήσομαι διαθήκην], that is, I will perfect, I will consummate; but the Apostle's wording comes closer to the Hebrew truth, I will dispose a covenant [διαθήσομαι διαθήκην], that is, I will arrange, whereas the Hebrew is ברית, that is, I will strike a covenant or compact. Still, nothing has been changed in the sense. Moreover, by the name house of Israel, if we look only at the letter, are understood those ten tribes which in the days of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, revolted to Jeroboam, as had been foretold to Solomon by the Lord (1 Kings 11), as can be seen in 1 Kings 12.

units.la: Per domum autem Iuda, duas reliquas tribus, videlicet Iuda & Beniamín, quæ regib, ex Iuda & familia Dauid descendentibus constanter adhæserunt. Verùm hoc valde vsi-tatum est, præsertim in prophetis, & maximè cùm hæc duo, Israel & Iuda coniunguntur, quasi ex eis vna fiat congregatio, vt ecclesia credentium significetur, ac sermonem fieri ad ecclesiam Christi, quæ colligitur & ex Iudæis, qui in vero cultu perstiterunt, & ex gē-tilibus, qui instar illorum, qui secuti sunt Hieroboam, falsum cultum obseruarunt, acci-piatur. Sic verò Apostolus Rom. 9 interpretatur, illos esse Israel, qui verè credunt, non qui secundum carnem tantùm sunt Israel. Et 1. Cor. 9. Israel secundum carnem distingui-turab Israele secundum Spiritum. Et Christus ipse longè ante distinctionem hanc indi-cauerat, vbi Ioan. 1 viso Nathanaele, dixit, Ecce verè Israelita: hauddubiè notàs, esse mul-tos falsò Israelitas. Reuera autem Etymologia nominū pulcherrimè quadrat, vt nomi-ne Israelis & Iudæ ecclesia intelligatur: siquidem Israel vincentem Deū significat, Iuda verò confitentem Deum.Consummabo ergo super domum Israel & super domum Iuda: Videtur A-postolus dixisse,consummabo, cum quadam emphasi, ad extollendam etiam dignitate eu-angelij, quasi antea quidem cœptum fuisset pactum istud patribus proponi, nunc autè id consummaretur: vel, quasi vetus testamentum ad perfectionem non profuerit, istud verò ad perfectionem præstaret. Et forte respexit Apostolus ad illud Esaiæ 10. cōsumma-tionem & abbreuiationem faciet Dominus super terra. Quid? Testamentū nouū, vel, secun-dum hebræos, pactum aut fœdus nouum. Hoc admonendum est: Non posse, sicut Iudæi volūt, hanc promissione Dei accipi de restauratione templi & legis facta per Esdram, quasi ibi nouū fuerit pactū siue fœdus constitutū. Falluntur in hoc, tum quia historiæ ipsæ satis testantur, decem tribus in terra promissam nunquā redijsse, nunquā pristinæ gloriæ om-nia fuisse restituta: tū quòd hîc aperte subijcitur de alio prorsus pacto, quā fuerit illud, cp datum fuit in deserto tempore Mosis, cùm Esdras idē pactu, eandē legē restaurarit, quæ data fuerat in deserto. Igitur, constitutum sit, ante omnia propositionem hîc haberi de nouo testamento, tempore Christi manifestando, quod diuersum omnino foret à testa-mento illo veteri tempore Mosi reuelato.
units.tr: By the house of Judah, however, are meant the two remaining tribes, namely Judah and Benjamin, which constantly adhered to the kings descended from Judah and the family of David. But this usage is very common, especially in the prophets, and above all when these two, Israel and Judah, are joined together as if one congregation were to be made out of them, so that the church of believers is signified, and the address is understood to be made to the church of Christ, which is gathered both from the Jews who persevered in the true worship and from the Gentiles, who, like those who followed Jeroboam, observed a false worship. The Apostle interprets it in this way in Romans 9, that those are Israel who truly believe, not those who are Israel only according to the flesh. And in 1 Corinthians 9 Israel according to the flesh is distinguished from Israel according to the Spirit. And Christ himself had indicated this distinction long before, when in John 1, seeing Nathanael, he said, Behold, truly an Israelite, clearly implying that there are many who are falsely Israelites. Indeed, the etymology of the names fits very beautifully, so that by the names Israel and Judah the church is understood: for Israel signifies one who prevails with God, and Judah one who confesses God. I will consummate therefore upon the house of Israel and upon the house of Judah. The Apostle seems to have said I will consummate with a certain emphasis, also to raise up the dignity of the gospel, as if this covenant had indeed been begun before and proposed to the fathers, but now would be brought to completion; or as if the old testament did not lead to perfection, but this one would bring perfection. And perhaps the Apostle had in mind that passage of Isaiah 10: The Lord will make a consummation and an abbreviation upon the earth. What follows? A new testament, or, according to the Hebrews, a new pact or covenant. This must be noted: it cannot be that this promise of God is to be taken, as the Jews wish, of the restoration of the temple and the law made by Ezra, as if a new testament or covenant had been established there. They are mistaken in this, both because the histories themselves bear sufficient witness that the ten tribes never returned to the promised land, and that all things were never restored to their former glory; and also because here it is openly added that the covenant is quite different from that which was given in the wilderness in the time of Moses, since Ezra restored the same covenant and the same law that had been given in the wilderness. Therefore, it must be established that above all here is set forth a promise of a new testament, to be manifested in the time of Christ, which would be altogether different from that old testament revealed in the time of Moses.

units.la: Recte igitur dicit, se consummare velle testamentum nouum. Obseruanda hîc appel-latio noui testamenti. Neq; enim Christus primus ita appellauit, vt suspectū propterea haberi possit, sicut Iudæi volunt nouum testamentum Christi eo nomine reijcere. Sed ipse Deus per prophetam tot ante seculis ita expressè appellauerat & promiserat. Alias quidè sæpe multa de innouatione sub euangelio futura prophetæ sunt locuti, vt Esaias capit. 41. vbi descripsit aduentum Christi electi, in quo patri bene complacuit, subijcit in persona Dei: Priora ecce venerunt, & noua ego annuncio, &, antequam oriantur, audita vobis faciam. Rursus idem cap. 62. vbi sub nomine Zion ecclesiam intelligens, huic pro-mittit Christum, dicens: quod etiam gentes videbunt iustitiam Zion, & omnes reges ter-ræ gloriam eius, & quod nomine nouo ipsa quoque fit vocanda, quod os Domini nomi-nabit. Item cap 65 Vbi post multas promissiones euangelicas etiam de vocatione om-nium gentium disseruisset, dicens: futurum tempus, quo omnes, qui benedicent sibi in terra, benedicent sibi in Deo vero, & qui iurauerint in terra, iuraturos in Deo uero, mox addit: Ecce enim ego creo cœlos nouos, & terram nouam, & non memorabuntur priora, neque ascendent super cor. Similiter apudalios prophetas passim multa extant de conferendo Spiritu nouo, de nouo populo: quęomnia ad euangelij manifestationem pertinent.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, he says that he wishes to consummate a new testament. The name of the new testament is to be observed here. For Christ was not the first to use this name, so that it could be regarded with suspicion on that account, as the Jews wish, who want to reject Christ's new testament under this name. Rather, God himself through the prophet had so many centuries before expressly named and promised it. Certainly the prophets spoke often of many innovations to be expected under the gospel: for example Isaiah, chapter 41, where he describes the coming of Christ the chosen one, in whom the Father was well pleased, adds in the person of God: Behold, the former things have come, and I announce new things; before they spring forth I will make them heard by you. Again the same, chapter 62, where, understanding the church under the name of Zion, he promises her Christ, saying that the nations shall see the righteousness of Zion and all the kings of the earth her glory, and that she shall also be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name. Likewise chapter 65, where after many gospel promises, including the calling of all nations, he had spoken of a future time when all who bless themselves in the land shall bless themselves in the true God, and those who swear in the land shall swear by the true God; then he immediately adds: For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they come into the heart. Similarly, in other prophets many passages occur everywhere about the bestowing of a new Spirit and a new people; all of which pertain to the manifestation of the gospel.

units.la: Sed quia ista omnia, quasi duntaxat de quadam temporanea mutatione rerum dice-rentur, ab aduersarijs possent exponi, singulari consilio spiritus Sancti factum est, quòd hoc loco apud Hieremiam disertè nouum testamentum exprimatur, ne videlicet Christi institutio de nouo testamento reijci posset, & quasi contraria prophetis damnati. Quare istud testimonium plurimum valet aduersus Iudaeos, qui vel hoc solo clarissimè convincuntur, ut euadere nulla via possint.
units.tr: But since all these things could be explained by our adversaries as if they spoke only of some temporary change of things, it was by a singular counsel of the Holy Spirit that the new testament is expressly named here in Jeremiah, so that Christ's institution of the new testament could not be rejected, and so that the prophets would not be made to seem contrary to themselves and condemned. Therefore this testimony is of great weight against the Jews, who are most clearly convicted by this one point alone, so that they cannot escape in any way.

units.la: Non iuxta testamentum, quod feci patribus illorum, in die, cùm apprehenderem manum illorum, ut educerem eos ex Aegypto.
units.tr: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day when I took hold of their hand to lead them out of Egypt.

units.la: Per omnia conueniunt Apostoli uerba cum verbis septuaginta, nisi quòd, vbi hi habent, ὑπ' ἀνθρώπων, quod disposui, Apostolus ait, ὑπ' ἐποίησα, quod feci. Hebraicè autem est לא כברית אשר כרתי : caetera omnia sunt paria. Proinde Apostolus, ut clarius intelligatur, nouum istud testamentum non tantùm fore simplicem quandam renouationem veteris testamenti seu foederis, qualis ante facta legitur temporibus Iosuae, libri eius capite quarto: aut temporibus Iosiae, secundo Regum vicesimo secundo, aut restaurationem quandam legis ac foederis iam diu neglecti, qualis post vaticinium istud editum facta est temporibus Esdrae (1. Esdrae cap. 9.) Sed prorsus diuersum, necessarioque distinctum à lege veteri: ideò apertè subijcit, tale testamentum siue pactum nouum constituendum, quod planè aliud erit ab illo, quod patribus in deserto tempore Mosis fuerat constitutum, à temporis circumstantia legem Mosaicam perapte insinuans. Ac necessarium quidem erat, hanc periphrasin, qua à circumstantia temporis lex Mosaica insinuatur, adijcere, ne quis suspicaretur, etiam pacta seu promissa ad alios patres facta, iam rescissa abrogataue inprimis illa, quae ad Adamum, ad Abrahamum, Dauidem, de semine, in quo benedicentur omnes gentes, facta erant. Haec certè neque immutata, neque abolita sunt, sed plenissimè in Christo, & per Christum consummata.
units.tr: Throughout, the Apostle's words agree with the words of the Seventy, except that where they have "which I arranged" (ὑπ' ἀνθρώπων, quod disposui), the Apostle says "which I made" (ὑπ' ἐποίησα, quod feci). In Hebrew the phrase is "not according to the covenant that I cut" (לא כברית אשר כרתי). All the rest is the same. So, to make the meaning clearer, the Apostle means that this new covenant will not merely be a simple renewal of the old covenant or testament, such as was made in the time of Joshua (Joshua, chapter 4), or in the time of Josiah (2 Kings 22), or a restoration of a law and covenant that had long been neglected, such as was made in the time of Ezra (1 Esdras 9). It will be entirely different from, and necessarily distinct from, the old law. That is why he plainly adds that a new testament or covenant of such a kind is to be established, one that will be quite other than the one made with the fathers in the wilderness at the time of Moses. By this circumlocution he aptly hints at the Mosaic law from the circumstance of time. It was indeed necessary to add this periphrasis, by which the Mosaic law is indicated from the circumstance of time, lest anyone suppose that the covenants or promises made to the other fathers had also been rescinded or abrogated, above all those made to Adam, to Abraham and to David, concerning the seed in whom all the nations will be blessed. These were certainly neither changed nor abolished, but were most fully fulfilled in Christ and through Christ.

units.la: Prudenter autem considerandum est, quomodo diuersa sint testamenta, nouum & vetus, inter se diuersis modis distincta. (Vide de his plenius, vbi egimus initio capitis tertij in illud, cuius domus sumus nos.) Ad Galat. 4. diserte dicitur, Abraham habebat duos filios, alterum ex ancilla, alterum ex libera: verùm is qui ex ancilla natus est, secundum carnem natus est, qui verò ex libera, per repromissionem: quae per Allegoriam dicuntur. Nam haec sunt duo testamenta, vnum quidem à monte Sina, lege videlicet significans, & per contrarium subintelligi volens alterum, videlicet euangelium manifestum Hierosolymis. En ergo duo distincta inter se testamenta, quorum alterum vetus, alterum nouum appellatur.
units.tr: We must carefully consider how the two testaments, the new and the old, are distinguished from one another in different ways. (See more fully on this where we treated, at the beginning of the third chapter, the words "whose house we are".) In Galatians 4 it is plainly said that Abraham had two sons, one by the bondwoman and one by the free woman; but he who was born of the bondwoman was born according to the flesh, while he who was born of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are said allegorically: for these are the two covenants, one from Mount Sinai, signifying the law, and by contrast wishing the other to be understood, namely the gospel made manifest at Jerusalem. Here, then, are two testaments distinct from one another, of which one is called the old and the other the new.

units.la: Et tamen si bene consideramus, tantum vnum testamentum inuenietur: quandoquidem in utroque testamento tam patribus, quàm nobis, idem scopus, eadem spes est proposita bonorum post hanc vitam obtinendorum: item praecepta fidei & charitatis in utroque eminent, & ab omnibus ex aequo requiruntur: praeterea communis fides & cognitio patribus & nobis est proposita, quòd videlicet per vnum Christum, & propter vnum Christum salutem debeamus gratis consequi. Proinde sciendum est, vt breuiter satisfaciamus, vtrumque recte dici, videlicet, quòd vnum tantùm sit testamentum & aeternum: ac rursus, quòd duo sint testamenta. Vnum quidem, quantum ad substantiam attinet, & principales res, fidem & charitatem respicientes: quod verò attinet ad traditionis rationem, ad signa, & huiusmodi, diuersa sunt.
units.tr: Yet if we consider carefully, we will find only one testament. For in both testaments the same aim and the same hope of good things to be obtained after this life are set before the fathers as well as before us. Likewise the precepts of faith and charity stand out in both and are required equally of all. Moreover, a common faith and knowledge is set before the fathers and us: namely, that we ought to obtain salvation freely, through the one Christ and on account of the one Christ. Therefore, to answer briefly, we should know that both statements are rightly made: that there is only one testament, and it is eternal; and again, that there are two testaments. There is one as far as its substance is concerned and its principal matters, which regard faith and charity; but as far as the manner of handing it down is concerned, as to signs and the like, they are different.

units.la: Patribus fides in Christum per figuras & typos tradebatur, sed nobis apertè, & citra figuras. Patres habuerunt signa, circumcisionem, sacrificia, &c. Nos habemus baptismum, & coenam Domini, in memoriam vnici sacrificij Christi. In summa non magis differunt, quàm vnus idemque homo aetate pueruli & virilis: vnus quidem homo: sed tamen aliter se habens, aliter viuens, aliter tractandus dum puer est, aliter verò dum factus est vir. Sic re uera testamentum Dei erga homines semper idem fuit, est, & manebit: sed pro varia hominum & temporum conditione, aliter atque aliter id manifestatum est. Veteris testamenti traditio facta est eo modo, quo doctrina aliqua proponitur pueris: vnde Galat. legem uocat Apostolus paedagogiam: & capite 4. Omnes sub lege agentes similes esse pueris. At noui testamenti traditio facta est, ut conueniens uiris & prouectis, sicut ibidem Apostolus declarat, & praesentis epistolae capite quinto ad finem obiter indicauit. Hinc omnes differentiae, quae occurrunt, ad discernendum nouum testamentum à veteri, nihil aliud, quàm perfectionem quandam ostendunt noui testamenti prae veteri, potius quàm omnimodam diuersitatem. In ueteri testamento bona temporalia, timor, praecepta bene uiuendi, item fidei. Alias autem vetus in nouo continetur, & nouum velatu erat in veteri, sicut nucleus in cortice, quae duo tamen vnam faciunt nucem. Vocatur autem testamentum nouum, ratione noui modi tradendi, & nouorum signorum: item quia in eo euidentius ac plenius renouantur homines ad caeleste haereditatem per manifestiorem donationem spiritus Sancti innouantis corda, quàm vnquam factum fuerat in testamento veteri. Tanta mutatio facta est in euangelio diuina misericordia sese magis in apertum proferente, vt prorsus alia res a lege videatur. Non praetereunda est elegans loquendi forma, cum apprehenderem manum illorum: commendat ea forma mirabilem Dei benevolentiam & curam erga patres illorum, sumpta est a more parentum, qui manu altera apprehensa solent paruulos deducere, necno studiose cauere, ne hi impingat, vel cadant, vel alias quocunq; modo periclitentur. Multae passim occurrunt in Scripturis huiusmodi εἰκόνες siue imagines, quibus tanquam picturis spectanda nobis proponitur & nostra infirmitas, per quam non possumus tuto progredi, aut quicquam boni efficere: & Dei erga nos bonitas atq; cura, qua ille semper solicitus est de nostra salute.
units.tr: To the fathers faith in Christ was handed down through figures and types, but to us openly and without figures. The fathers had signs: circumcision, sacrifices, and so on. We have baptism and the Lord's Supper, in memory of the one sacrifice of Christ. In sum, they differ no more than one and the same man in boyhood and in manhood: he is indeed one man, yet he is otherwise disposed, otherwise living, and otherwise to be treated while he is a boy, but otherwise when he has become a man. So in truth the testament of God toward men has always been, is, and will remain the same; but according to the varying condition of men and times, it has been made manifest now in one way, now in another. The handing down of the old testament was done in the way that some teaching is set before boys; hence the Apostle in Galatians calls the law a schoolmaster (paedagogia), and in chapter 4, "all who live under the law are like children." But the handing down of the new testament was done so as to suit grown men and those advanced in years, as the same Apostle declares in that place and briefly indicated at the end of the fifth chapter of the present epistle. Hence all the differences that occur, which serve to distinguish the new testament from the old, show nothing other than a certain perfection of the new testament over the old, rather than a complete diversity. In the old testament there were temporal goods, fear, precepts for living well, and likewise faith. Moreover, the old is contained in the new, and the new was veiled in the old, as the kernel is in the shell; yet these two make one nut. The testament is called new by reason of the new manner of handing it down and the new signs; also because in it men are renewed more evidently and fully to the heavenly inheritance, through the clearer gift of the Holy Spirit renewing hearts, than ever happened under the old testament. Such a great change has been made in the gospel, the divine mercy showing itself more openly, that it seems an entirely different thing from the law. The elegant form of speech, "when I took hold of their hand," must not be passed over. That form commends God's wonderful goodwill and care toward their fathers. It is taken from the custom of parents, who, grasping a child by one hand, lead it along and carefully take heed lest it stumble, fall, or be endangered in any other way. Many such εἰκόνες [eikones], or images, occur throughout the Scriptures, by which our weakness is set before us to be contemplated as in pictures, a weakness through which we cannot safely advance or accomplish anything good; and likewise God's goodness and care toward us, by which he is always solicitous for our salvation.

units.la: Caeterum de historia educatorum Israelitarum ex Aegypto, nihil opus est proferre in medium, quando satis nota est. Satis fuit hac ratione insinuare, se loqui de abrogatione legis Mosaicae.
units.tr: As for the history of the Israelites being led out of Egypt, there is no need to bring it forward, since it is well known. It was enough to hint in this way that he is speaking of the abrogation of the Mosaic law.

units.la: Quoniam ipsi non perstiterunt in testamento meo, & ego neglectui eos, habui, dicit Dominus.
units.tr: Because they did not abide in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

units.la: Nihil hic diversum habet Apostolus a septuaginta: sed in hebraeo aliter habetur, Quia ipsi dissoluerunt pactum meum בריתי, id est, & ego dominatus sum eis, dicit Dominus: vt sit sententia: Ipsi dissoluerunt pactum meum, tam etiam cum ego ostendi, me illis esse Dominum, & mariti instar: quasi significare velit Dominus, multo iniquissimum esse: quod illi pactis non steterint, cum ipse instar potentis domini semper punierit transgressores: vel potius, cum ipse instar fidelis mariti pacta semper seruauerit. Ita enim gravior erit similitudo, atq; acerbior exprobratio in Iudaeos, quod, cum Dominus tanquam fidelis maritus pacta semper seruarit, ipsi tamen pactis nequaquam steterint. Et propterea Dominus merito eligeret nouum populum, cum quo nouum iniret foedus, sicut si quis deprehensa vxore in adulterio, eam repudiet, & aliam ducat, cui fidem despodeat. Cui similitudini etiam valde quadrant sequentia, quae subiiciuntur de nouis pactis. Et alibi quoque ecclesia comparatur sponsae, Deus marito. Aperit autem hisce verbis accusatorijs quandam abrogandi veteris testamenti & noui instituendi causam, videlicet hominum infirmitatem ac malitiam, per quam factum est, quod pacto veteri ipsi non steterint. Quamobrem diuina bonitas mota est ad instituendum nouum testamentum siue pactum, nempe euangelicum, quod est de gratuita misericordia propter Christum, etiam absq; operibus legis accipienda. Quod sane pactu passim in omnib. scriptis euangelicis primo atq; vltimo loco inculcatur. Nequaquam ipsius testamenti vitio factum est, quod perstare non potuerit. Nam lex quidem & iusta & sancta, & bona: praeterea efficiens, quatum satis est, id ad quod proprie erat instituta, hoc est, cohibens transgressores, inducens ad agnitionem peccati & poenitentiam, deducit quasi paedagogus ad Christum, id est, ad inuocandum Deum, & implorandum misericordiam propter Christum. Haec, inquam, officia probe lex praestitit, & in hunc quoq; diem, qua parte adhuc locum habet, non seg-niter praestat: nam altiora, non est, quod ab ea expectes. In causa enim iustificationis fatendum est, eam esse infirmam & imbecillem, sicut Apostolus ipse dixit praecedenti capite, abrogari eam, propter suam ipsius infirmitatem & inutilitatem. Quam rationem apposit isime produxit disputans de caeremonialibus, quae videbantur ad cultum Dei, ad iustitiam coram Deo parandam vel maxime facere. Praeterea, non est factum Dei mutabilitate aut inconstantia, quod pactu fuerit mutandum: quado quidem Deus per se immutabilis est, neq; deliberando, ut homines faciunt, propositum mutat: & quicquid semel statuit, non potest non esse bonum: & omnia illius decreta semper ad bonum tendunt. Itaq; cum semel lex bona, & ad bonum finem a Deo fit condita, non est, quod Deus eam voluerit mutare sua causa. Infirmitas igitur ipsorum hominum potissimum in causa est, cur decuerit abrogare pactum vetus, & nouum condere.
units.tr: The Apostle here differs in no way from the Seventy, but the Hebrew reads otherwise: "Because they broke my covenant" (בריתי), that is, "and I was lord over them, says the Lord." The sense is: they broke my covenant, although I had shown that I was their Lord and their husband, as it were. The Lord seems to mean that it is most unjust that they did not keep the covenants, since he himself, like a powerful lord, always punished transgressors, or rather, since he, like a faithful husband, always kept the covenants. For in this way the comparison is stronger and the rebuke more bitter against the Jews: although the Lord, like a faithful husband, always kept the covenants, they nevertheless in no way kept them. Therefore the Lord rightly chose a new people with whom he would enter a new covenant, just as a man who catches his wife in adultery divorces her and takes another whom he betroths to himself. The following words about the new covenants fit this comparison very well. Elsewhere too the Church is compared to a bride and God to a husband. By these accusing words, however, the Apostle reveals a certain cause for abrogating the old covenant and instituting the new one, namely the weakness and wickedness of men, through which it came about that they did not keep the old covenant. Therefore divine goodness was moved to institute a new covenant or testament, namely the gospel one, which concerns free mercy on account of Christ, to be received even without the works of the law. This covenant is indeed urged everywhere, first and last, in all the evangelical writings. It was not through any fault of the covenant itself that it could not endure. For the law is indeed just, holy and good; moreover, it effects as much as is enough for that purpose for which it was properly instituted, that is, it restrains transgressors, leads to the knowledge of sin and to repentance, and, like a tutor, brings us to Christ, that is, to calling upon God and imploring mercy on account of Christ. These offices, I say, the law has duly performed, and to this day, in so far as it still has a place, it does not cease to perform them. For you must not expect from it anything higher. In the matter of justification it must be confessed that it is weak and feeble, as the Apostle himself said in the preceding chapter, and that it is abrogated on account of its own weakness and unprofitableness. The Apostle set forth this reason most clearly when he discussed the ceremonial rites, which seemed especially to serve to prepare righteousness before God. Furthermore, it was not by any changeableness or inconstancy of God that the covenant had to be changed, since God is in himself unchangeable and does not alter his purpose by deliberation, as men do; and whatever he has once decreed cannot but be good, and all his decrees always tend toward good. Therefore, since the law was once made good and by God for a good end, there is no reason why God should wish to change it for its own sake. The weakness of men themselves is therefore chiefly the cause why it was fitting to abrogate the old covenant and establish a new one.

units.la: Atq; haec causa alibi quoq; in Scripturis confirmatur. Pet. Actor. 15. legem vocat iugum, quod neq; patres, neq; qui tum viuebant Iudaei, portare potuerint, ideoq; nullo pacto imponendum cerviciibus discipulorum gentilium. Sanctissimi Pharisaei, qui videri ambiebant etiam plus quam lege, opera quaedam praestare (ut nostrorum temporum Pharisei appellarunt) supererogationis, cum minutioribus valde essent intenti, praecipua tamen opera neglexerunt, sicut Christus aperte obiecit eis, Matth.23. Vae vobis Scribae & Pharisaei hypocritae, quia decimatis mentam & anethum & cyminum, & reliquistis, quae grauiora sunt legis, iudicium & misericordiam, ac fidem: haec oportuit facere, & illud non omittere. Et Rom.8. Affectus carnis inimicitia est aduersus Deum: nam legi Dei non subditur: siquidem potest quidem. Vbi loquitur de innata & semper inhaerent ad malum propensione, destituta spiritu Sancto, sine quo illi impossibile est, ea quae legis sunt facere. Atq; ibidem plura habentur, vt quod lex debuerit per Christum impleri, vt iustificatio legis impleretur in tur in nobis. Item Rom. 2. & 3. vbi probatur, omnes ad vnum homines esse peccatores & reos coram Deo: Annon clarissimè ostenditur, legem nō potuisse per homines adimpleri? Itaq; rectè dicitur, imbecillitatem hominum esse vnam quoq; è causis, ob quas sit abrogatam sui ipsius, sicut capite praecedenti locutus est Apostolus: item: quia iustis non est lex posita, ut dicitur prima Timothei primo: item quòd condemna-tioni obnoxios non potest reddere, ut dicitur Roman. 8. Sed hanc vnam multò appositissimè hoc loco propheta expresit, propterea, quòd, licet promissionibus de liberatione à captiuitate babylonica, necnon uaticinijs de euangelico negotio, cuperet animos Iudeorum in certa spe erigere, voluit nihilominus graues obiurgationes subinde intermiscere, quibus ad poenitentiam ipsos commoueret. Ad hanc autem rem sciebat propheta hanc ratione fore aptissimam & efficacissimam, si videlicet obijceret, propter malitiam ipsorum futurum, ut Dominus olim eligat nouum populum sibi in peculium, & cum hoc nouum foedus ineat. Neq; enim quicquam sic premebat Iudaeorum animos, quod prophetae inculcabat, se, nisi resipiscerent, abijciendos, & alios in locum ipsorum pro populo Dei subrogandos: deinde praeclara quaq; maximè gloriabantur, lege abroganda, & successurum huic euangelium.
units.tr: This cause is also confirmed elsewhere in the Scriptures. In Acts 15 Peter calls the law a yoke, which neither the fathers nor the Jews of that time were able to bear, and therefore it must by no means be laid on the necks of the Gentile disciples. The most holy Pharisees, who wished to seem to perform certain works of supererogation beyond the law (as the Pharisees of our own times have called them), though they were very intent on minor matters, neglected the chief works, as Christ plainly charged them in Matt. 23: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law, judgment and mercy and faith; these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others." And Rom. 8: "The mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it does not submit to the law of God, indeed it cannot." There the Apostle speaks of the innate propensity to evil that always clings to us, bereft of the Holy Spirit, without whom it is impossible for us to do the things of the law. And in the same place there are many further passages, such as that what the law ought to have accomplished had to be fulfilled through Christ, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. Likewise in Rom. 2 and 3, where it is proved that all men without exception are sinners and guilty before God: does it not most clearly show that the law could not be fulfilled by men? Thus it is rightly said that the weakness of men is one of the causes for which the old covenant was abrogated, as the Apostle spoke of it in the preceding chapter. Likewise, because the law is not laid down for the righteous, as is said in 1 Tim. 1; and because it cannot make those liable to condemnation free, as is said in Rom. 8. But the prophet expressed this one cause most fittingly in this passage. Although, with promises of deliverance from the Babylonian captivity, and also with prophecies about the gospel business, he wished to raise the minds of the Jews to a sure hope, he nevertheless wanted from time to time to mix in severe rebukes, by which he might move them to repentance. The prophet knew that for this purpose it would be most apt and effective to point out that, on account of their wickedness, the Lord would one day choose a new people for himself as his own possession and enter into a new covenant with them. For nothing so weighed on the minds of the Jews as the prophet's repeated warning that, unless they repented, they would be cast off and others substituted in their place as the people of God; and then they, who boasted most of all of their outstanding privileges, would see the law abrogated and the gospel take its place.

units.la: Nam hoc est testamentum, quod disponam domui Israel post dies illos, dicit Dominus) Consensit cum septuaginta ad verbum Apostolus, neq; ab hebraica veritate quicquam immutatum est, nisi quòd in hebraeo constanter retinetur vocabulum בְּרִית pacti siue foederis. Quod tantum domum Israel repetit, omissa domo Iuda, fieri potest, vel quòd mentione domus Israel satis etiam intelligatur domus Iuda, vel certè ad tacitè indicandum, quòd promissiones hae noui testamenti ad gentes potissimum pertinerent, quas diximus per regnum Israel, in quo idololatria per Hieroboamum primum regem in Samaria introducta & aperte excita est, significatas. Et repetit mentionem dierum, dicens: post dies illos, siue attentionis excitandae causa, siue ad apertius insinuandum tempus manifestandi longè post euangelij, & nequaquam tempus illud, quo fieret renouatio quaedam per Esdram, seu, quo antea factae renouationes fuerant.
