Incipit ergo propheta plenius explicare, quomodo nouum testamentum diuersum fit futurum à veteri, & quae illi erunt propria, quibus maxime discernetur. Vnde subijcit: Dans leges meas in mentem illorum & in corde illorum inscribam illas, & ero illis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus: & non docebunt quisq; proximum suum, & unusquisque fratrem suum, dicentes: cognosce Dominum, quod omnes cognituri sint me, ab eo, qui pusillus fuerit inter eos, usque ad eum, qui magnus inter illos. [Greek text]
units.tr: "For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord." The Apostle agrees word for word with the Seventy, and nothing has been changed from the Hebrew truth, except that in the Hebrew the word בְּרִית, covenant, is consistently retained. The repetition only of "the house of Israel," with "the house of Judah" omitted, may be because the house of Israel sufficiently implies the house of Judah as well, or certainly to indicate silently that these promises of the new covenant pertained chiefly to the Gentiles, whom we said are signified by the kingdom of Israel, in which idolatry was introduced and openly stirred up by Jeroboam, the first king, in Samaria. And he repeats the mention of days, saying "after those days," either to arouse attention or to suggest more clearly that the time of manifesting the gospel was far off, and by no means that time in which a renewal was effected through Ezra, or those earlier renewals had been made. So the prophet begins to explain more fully how the new covenant will be different from the old, and what will be proper to it, by which it will be most clearly distinguished. Hence he adds: "I will put my laws into their mind and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And they will not teach each one his neighbour, and each his brother, saying, 'Know the Lord,' for all will know me, from the least of them to the greatest." [Greek text]

units.la: Omnia conueniunt cum septuaginta, nisi quòd initio, vbi Apostolus tantum habet [Greek], In propheta legitur, [Greek], phrasi hebraica energiae causa, quasi dicas, dans dabo. Et vbi Apostolus, [Greek], &c. Apud septuaginta praemittitur, [Greek]: quasi diceretur, & videbo eis, vel videbor & apparebo eis. Et pro [Greek], id est, ciuem.
units.tr: Everything agrees with the Seventy, except that at the beginning, where the Apostle has only [Greek text], the prophet reads [Greek text], a Hebrew idiom for the sake of emphasis, as if you said "giving I will give." And where the Apostle has [Greek text] and so on, the Seventy put [Greek text] before it, as if it were said "and I will see to them," or "I will seem and appear to them." And for [Greek text], that is, "citizen."

units.la: In hebraeo autem sententia eadem ad verbum manet, vt neque quidquam additum, neque quicquam derogatum vsquam appareat: si quid in vocibus diuersitatis appareat, nos admonere inter explicandum non grauabimur. Duas proinde ponit insignes notas Euangelij proprias, quibus à veteri testamento secernitur: alteram de manifestissima donatione spiritus Sancti, qualis antea nunquam facta est: alteram de gratuita remissione peccatorum, propter Christum, absque operibus legis. Priorem autem, videlicet donationem spiritus Sancti explicat, non quidem simpliciter dicendo, donabo spiritum Sanctum, vel huiusmodi. Sed, quod multò splendidius ac magnificentius est, proprios eius affectus ponendo ob oculos, è quibus clarè cognosci queat: sinprimis verò duos magis prae caeteris (sunt namque adhuc multiplices & uarij) spectabiles in quibus euangelij dignitas potissimum sita est, maximeque elucet. Ait ergo, Dans leges meas in mentem illorum, & in corde illorum inscribam illas: primus effectus spiritum Sanctū clarè delineas: Estq; horum verborum sententia: Dabo leges meas in mentem illorum, id est, dabo eis spiritum Sanctum in corda, per quem ipsi legem facient, sine quo alioqui impossibile esset, eam exactè praestare: quandoquidem Spiritus quibus datus est, & suggerit, quae secundum voluntatem Dei sunt agenda, vel omittenda: & impellit ad sponte alacriterque ea facienda: denique addit etiam uires & facultatem.
units.tr: In the Hebrew, however, the sense remains the same word for word, so that nothing appears to have been added or taken away anywhere. If any difference shows up in the wording, we will not hesitate to point it out in the course of explaining. He therefore sets out two distinctive marks of the gospel by which it is set apart from the Old Testament: the first concerns the most manifest bestowal of the Holy Spirit, such as was never made before; the second concerns the free forgiveness of sins for Christ's sake, apart from the works of the law. He explains the first, the bestowal of the Holy Spirit, not by simply saying "I will give the Holy Spirit" or something of that kind, but, what is far more splendid and magnificent, by setting before our eyes its proper effects, from which it can be clearly known. Of these he picks out two above the rest (for there are many and varied effects) as the most conspicuous, in which the dignity of the gospel chiefly lies and shines most brightly. He says, then: "Putting my laws into their mind, and I will write them on their heart." The first effect clearly depicts the Holy Spirit. The sense of these words is: "I will put my laws into their mind," that is, "I will give them the Holy Spirit in their hearts, through whom they will keep the law, without whom it would otherwise be impossible to fulfil it exactly. For the Spirit, where he is given, both suggests what must be done or left undone according to God's will, and drives men to do it willingly and eagerly; finally, he also adds strength and ability."

units.la: Ita spiritus Sanctus legislator est, & lex in nouo testamento, ipse debet praescribere, gubernare, ut fiant ea, quae Deo accepta esse posint. Ipse in hunc diem gubernat ac dirigit ecclesiam, multò sanctius atque efficacius, quàm olim effecit lex.
units.tr: So the Spirit is the lawgiver, and in the New Testament the law is his: he himself must prescribe and govern, so that those things may be done which can be acceptable to God. To this day he governs and directs the Church, far more holily and effectively than the law once did.

units.la: Multa
units.tr: Many things

units.la: Lex impleri propter homi-num improbi-tatem nequiuit. Plures causae legis abrogatae. Infirmitas legis. Iusto lex non est posita. Iudaeorum malitia fecit, ut nouus populus eligeretur, & legi abrogatae succederet euangelium.
units.tr: The law could not be fulfilled because of human wickedness. Several causes of the abrogation of the law. The weakness of the law. The law was not laid down for the righteous. The malice of the Jews brought it about that a new people should be chosen, and the gospel should succeed the abrogated law.

units.la: Diuersitas noui & ueteris testamenti.
units.tr: The difference between the New and the Old Testament.

units.la: Duae notae euangelij, quibus differt à lege. 1. Donatio S.S. 2. Remissio peccatorum gratuita propter Christum.
units.tr: Two marks of the gospel by which it differs from the law: (1) the bestowal of the Holy Spirit; (2) the free forgiveness of sins for Christ's sake.

units.la: Euangelij effectus spiritus Sancti donatio. Aliud est praestare ea quae sunt legis: & aliud praestare vel facere legem. Spiritus Sancti opus in credentibus. Multa passim occurrunt in hanc sententiam Roman. 5. Dilectio Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per spiritum Sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Roman. 8. plurima habentur: Lex spiritus vitae per Christum Iesum liberum me reddidit a iure peccati & mortis. Item: ut iustificatio legis impleretur in nobis, qui non secundum carnem versamur sed secundum Spiritum. Nam qui carnales sunt, quae carnis sunt, faciunt: at qui spirituales, quae Spiritus sunt. Nam effectus carnis mors est: effectus vero Spiritus vita & pax.
units.tr: The effect of the gospel is the bestowal of the Holy Spirit. It is one thing to perform what belongs to the law, and another to perform or make the law. The work of the Holy Spirit is in believers. Many passages everywhere occur to this effect, Romans 5: "The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us." Romans 8 contains very many: "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death." Likewise: "that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For those who are according to the flesh mind the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the Spirit the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace."

units.la: Iterum: Vos autem non estis in carne, sed in Spiritu: si quidem Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Quod si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est eius. Et paulo post: Quod si spiritu facta corporis mortificetis, viuetis. Etenim quicunque Spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filij Dei. Non enim accepistis Spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus Abba pater: Idem spiritus testatur vnà cum Spiritu nostro, quòd sumus filij Dei. Item, Spiritus auxiliatur infirmitatibus nostris, &c. ad Galatas capite quarto, Quod si Spiritu ducimini, non estis sub lege. Vbi & fructus Spiritus subijciuntur longè speciosiores, quàm sunt fructus legis siue carnis.
units.tr: Again: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. And a little later: But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are the sons of God." Likewise: "The Spirit helps our infirmities," etc. And in Galatians chapter 4: "But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law." Here too the fruits of the Spirit are set out, far more splendid than the fruits of the law or of the flesh.

units.la: Præterea Apostoli Actorum capite decimoquinto, quando scripturi erant gentibus, quid obseruare deberent, visum est, inquiunt, spiritui Sancto & nobis, &c. Sed haec satis ad comprobandum, quòd per collationem legis diuinae in mentes, intelligatur donatio spiritus Sancti, qui omnibus credentibus lex est & regula, & in nouo testamento praescribit, ostendit, & perficit ea omnia, quae Deo accepta esse possint, longe certius & plenius, quam id vnquam fecit lex Mosaica. Caeterum sumpta est haec locutionis formula dabo leges meas in mentem illorum, & in corde illorum inscribam illas: per contrarium ab eo quod olim lex vetus externis tantum signis exhibita fuit & crassis elementis, scripta in tabulis lapideis.
units.tr: Moreover, in Acts chapter 15, when the apostles were about to write to the Gentiles what they ought to observe, they say: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us," etc. But these things are enough to prove that by the writing of the divine law into the minds is meant the bestowal of the Holy Spirit, who is to all believers law and rule, and who in the New Testament prescribes, shows, and accomplishes all those things which can be acceptable to God, far more surely and fully than the Mosaic law ever did. Moreover, this form of expression, I will put my laws into their mind, and I will write them on their heart, is taken by contrast with the fact that the old law was once presented only by external signs and gross elements, written on tables of stone.

units.la: Lex autem Spiritus arcano afflatu Dei ingeritur animis hominum, vbi occultè agit, & longe viuacius, quàm agere poterant vel tabulae scriptae, oculis expositae, vel vocale verbum Mosis, aures quidem feriens, mentem tamen nequaquam penetrans. Itaque valde diuersum est istud nouum testamentum à veteri, & haud dubiè multò praestan-tius, quàm vetus: sicut & omnia quae Euangelij sunt, multò excellentiora sunt iis, quae sunt legis. Et propterea decebat etiam aliter, & in alia materia, legem euangelicam describi. Vtraque quidem lex digito Dei, id est, spiritu Sancto cooperante descripta est: sed illa in tabulis lapideis, posterior autem in cordibus carneis, vt inquit Ezechiel capite trigesimosexto, siue, vt noster propheta ait, in mente & in cordibus. Atque in signum abolitionis illius veteris legis, & quòd noua lex aliter foret describenda, etiam fractae sunt tabulae lapideae per Mosen, & aliae fuerunt describendae. Ex hoc etiam loco propheta Apostolus mutuatus est, quae habet secunda ad Corinthios capite tertio, vbi etiam de efficacia spiritus Sancti agentis in cordibus. Declaratis, inquit, quòd estis epistola Christi subministrata, à nobis inscripta, non atramento, sed spiritu Dei viuentis, non in tabulis lapideis, sed tabulis cordis carneis. Et mox subijcitur: Si ad aliquid idonei sumus, id ex Deo est, qui idoneos fecit nos ministros noui testamenti, non literae, sed spiritus. Vbi etiam nouum testamentum spiritu descriptum, non crassis elementis significatur.
units.tr: But the law of the Spirit is poured into the minds of men by the secret breath of God, where it works in secret, and far more vividly than could work either written tables set before the eyes, or the spoken word of Moses, which strikes the ears but by no means penetrates the mind. Thus this new covenant is very different from the old, and without doubt far more excellent than the old, just as everything that belongs to the gospel is far more excellent than what belongs to the law. For this reason it was also fitting that the gospel law should be described otherwise, and in a different material. Both laws were indeed written by the finger of God, that is, by the cooperating Holy Spirit; but the former on tables of stone, the latter on fleshy hearts, as Ezekiel says in chapter 36, or, as our prophet says, in the mind and in the hearts. And as a sign of the abolition of that old law, and that the new law was to be written differently, the stone tables were also broken by Moses, and others had to be written. From this passage the apostle borrowed what he has in 2 Corinthians chapter 3, where he also speaks of the efficacy of the Holy Spirit working in hearts: "You are manifestly," he says, "a letter of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tables of stone but on tables of fleshy hearts." And soon after it is added: "If we are fit for anything, that is from God, who has made us fit ministers of the new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit." There too the new covenant, written by the Spirit, is signified, not by gross elements.

units.la: Caeterùm, quòd dicitur, Leges meas, apud septuaginta plurali numero, forte fit ad significandum, quòd vna lex spiritus Sancti abundantissimè continet, quicquid omnibus legibus, videlicet, moralibus, iudicialibus, ceremonialibus comprehenditur. Nihil omittit spiritus Sanctus in suo compendio, quod non plenissime suggerat piorum mentibus, vel duobus mandatis omnia constringens, altero de dilectione Dei, altero de dilectione proximi: in quibus verè tota lex pendet & prophetae, testante Christo: & dum charitas diffunditur per spiritum Sanctum in cordibus, verè tota lex adimpletur. Dicit verò, In mentem & in cor, quia lex vt verè impleatur, ista potissimum requirit. Et spiritus Sanctus in his tanquam in proprio domicilio agit & dictat suas leges: & quaecunque Deo accepta erunt, debent ab his proficisci. Mente enim & cor Deus potissimum respicit. Possunt multa praeclarè fieri, possunt externa opera seruari vel ab hypocritis: Sed si non fiant mente & corde, nequaquam lex impletur, neque Deo quicquam eorum placet. Deus Spiritus est, & adorari vult in Spiritu & veritate. Ioan. capite 4. Et Christus mentem requiri copiosè explicat Matthaei 5. 6. Huc etiam pertinent, quae passim in lege & prophetis occurrunt de colendo Deo ex tota mente, ex tota anima ex toto corde, ex omnibus viribus Deut. 6. Etiamsi ibi apud Hebraeos, siue apud Septuaginta non sint eadem voces, quae hoc loco apud prophetas: quod tamen ad sententiam attinet, planè idem sibi volunt. Inscribam) non sine Emphasi dictum videtur: Nam etiamsi respiciat ad inscriptionem tabularum lapidearum, ac notet insuper, agi hic de abrogatione legis scriptæ, non autem de illa, quæ ante tabulas scriptas insita erat patrum cordibus, quæ sane per Euangelium non aboletur: tamen significat aliam infixionem præceptorum diuinorum in corda credentium, quæ altissime radicatur, & insculpitur per spiritum Sanctum, vt charitas vera nunquam excidat. Proinde magna est differentia inter nouum testamentum & vetus, & nouum longe est veteri excellentius.
units.tr: Moreover, that it is said my laws, in the Septuagint in the plural number, perhaps is to signify that the one law of the Holy Spirit contains most abundantly whatever is comprehended in all the laws, namely the moral, judicial, and ceremonial. The Holy Spirit omits nothing in his compendium that he does not most fully suggest to the minds of the pious, binding everything in two commandments, one concerning the love of God, the other concerning the love of neighbour; on these two truly hang the whole law and the prophets, as Christ testifies; and while charity is poured out in hearts through the Holy Spirit, the whole law is truly fulfilled. He says, moreover, "into the mind and into the heart," because for the law to be truly fulfilled it chiefly requires these. And the Holy Spirit acts in these as in his own dwelling and dictates his laws; and whatever will be acceptable to God ought to proceed from them. For God chiefly regards the mind and the heart. Many things can be done excellently, and external works can be kept even by hypocrites; but if they are not done with mind and heart, the law is by no means fulfilled, and none of them pleases God. God is Spirit, and wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth (John chapter 4). And Christ explains at length that the mind is required, in Matthew 5 and 6. To this also belong the passages that occur throughout the law and the prophets about worshipping God with the whole mind, the whole soul, the whole heart, with all strength (Deut. 6), even if the words there, whether in the Hebrew or in the Septuagint, are not the same as the words used here by the prophets; yet as far as the sense goes, they plainly mean the same. I will write seems to be said not without emphasis: for although it looks to the writing on the stone tables, and additionally notes that what is here treated is the abrogation of the written law, and not that law which was implanted in the hearts of the fathers before the written tables, which is certainly not abolished by the gospel; nevertheless it signifies another engraving of the divine precepts in the hearts of believers, which is rooted very deeply and carved in by the Holy Spirit, so that true charity never falls away. Therefore the difference between the New and the Old Testament is great, and the New is far more excellent than the Old.

units.la: Et ero illis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus) Quemadmodum in fœderibus, quæ homines inter se percutiunt, solent conceptis verbis legitimaque forma conditiones pacti, seu potius summa pacti ab vtraque parte exprimi: Ita & hic summa pacti pro vtraque parte, Deo, inquam, & hominibus, quasi verbis conceptis præscribitur, quibus demum seruatis prouenient ad homines bona, quæ hic promittuntur, nempe spiritus Sancti donatio, et peccatorum gratuita remissio. Est autem hæc communis pactorum formula, & in veteri testamento sæpe obuia.
units.tr: And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Just as in covenants that men make with one another, the conditions of the agreement, or rather its main points, are usually stated on each side in set words and in legal form, so here the main terms of the covenant are laid down for both parties, for God and for men, as if in set words. If these are kept, the good things promised here will come to men, namely the gift of the Holy Spirit and the free forgiveness of sins. This is the common formula of covenants, and it often occurs in the Old Testament.

units.la: Quamobrem cum de nouo fœdere percutiendo, cum nouo populo hic agitur, recte per prophetam interseritur, vt nimirum certius atque euidentius ista noui testamenti institutio intelligatur, tanquam si iam coram iunctis dexteris nouum fœdus percuti conceptis istis verbis conspiceretur, ac Deus quidem diceret ad nouum populum. Ego volo fideliter vobis esse in Deum, modo vos mihi fitis in fidelem populum. Ex altera parte item populus: Nos erimus tibi fidelis populus, modo tu quoq; fis nobis fidelis Deus.
units.tr: Therefore, since here the making of the new covenant with the new people is in question, the prophet rightly inserts it, so that this institution of the new covenant may be understood more certainly and clearly, as if one saw the new covenant being struck in these words, face to face, with right hands joined, and God were saying to the new people: "I want to be faithful to you as your God, provided you be a faithful people to me." And on the other side the people likewise: "We will be a faithful people to you, provided you too be a faithful God to us."

units.la: Porrò huiusmodi verbis pactorum, n omine Dei & populi, non pauca significantur. Cum dicit Deus, se fore illis Deum, tantundem sibi vult, ac si dicat, se vellle illis omnibus in rebus esse auxilio, fortunare, prouehere, defendere, & semper seruare: denique nihil non, quod Dei potentiæ & bonitati conuenit, præstare. E diuerso, vbi illi dicunt, se fore ei populū, id sibi volunt, erimus tibi in omnibus morigeri, & te toti pendebimus, te vnum præ omnibus venerabimur.
units.tr: Moreover, by such words of covenants, spoken in the name of God and of the people, not a few things are signified. When God says that he will be their God, he means the same as if he said that he wishes to be a help to them in all things, to prosper, advance, defend and always preserve them; in short, to do everything that befits God's power and goodness. On the other hand, when they say that they will be his people, they mean: "We will be obedient to you in all things, we will depend wholly on you, and we will honour you alone above all."

units.la: Et non docebunt quisq; proximum suum, & vnusquisq; fratrem suum, dicentes: cognosce Dominum: quod omnes cognituri sint me, ab eo, qui pusillus fuerit inter eos, víq; ad eum, qui magnus est inter illos.
units.tr: And they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for all shall know me, from the least of them even to the greatest of them.

units.la: Secundus effectus, ex quo spiritus Sanctus cognoscitur. Ipsius enim proprium munus est, omnes docere immediate, in cordibus timorem & dilectionem Dei, ita vt ipsius solius ductu, impulsu, auxilio, intelligant, aggrediantur, & perficiant ea quæ sunt bonæ voluntatis Dei. Quod & factum esse per spiritum Sanctum multo potentissime, successus ipse initio reuelatio euangelij palàm docuit, vt licet videre Actorum capite secundo, & deinceps. At recte nos ista de docendi hominibus per spiritum Sanctum, explicare, liquet tum ex eo, quod Petrus quoque Actorum capite secundo, in eandem sententiam loquitur, citans testimonium ex Ioelis secundo: Hoc, inquit, nunc impletum cernitis, quod dictum est per Prophetam: Et erit in nouissimis diebus, dicit Deus, effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem, & prophetabunt filij vestri, & filiæ vestræ, & iuuenes vestri visiones videbunt, & seniores vestri somnia somniabunt. Et quidem super seruos meos, & super ancillas meas, in diebus illis effundam de spiritu meo & prophetabunt, &c. tum, quod Christus ipse Ioannis capite sexto diserte ait, Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Est scriptum in prophetis: Et erunt omnes docti à Deo. Omnis ergo, qui audiuit à patre, & didicit, venit ad me.
units.tr: This is the second effect by which the Holy Spirit is recognised. For it is the proper office of the Spirit to teach all men immediately, in their hearts, the fear and love of God, so that by his guidance, impulse and help alone they understand, undertake and carry out the things that are the good will of God. That this has been done by the Holy Spirit, far more powerfully, the very success of the beginning of the revelation of the gospel plainly showed, as may be seen in Acts chapter 2 and what follows. And that we explain these things rightly, about men being taught by the Spirit, is clear both from the fact that Peter too, in Acts chapter 2, speaks to the same effect, quoting the testimony from Joel chapter 2: "This, he says, you now see fulfilled, which was spoken by the prophet: 'And it shall come to pass in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. And indeed upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy,' etc." And also from the fact that Christ himself plainly says in John chapter 6: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." "It is written in the prophets: 'And they shall all be taught of God.' Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me."

units.la: (Intelligendum autem patrem istud efficere per Spiritum, quem ipse ob id missurus est, sicut Christus ipse alibi declarat) Denique quod passim præsertim in nouo testamento de hoc spiritus Sancti proprio officio, quod videlicet docere debeat omnes omnem veritatem, testimonia occurrunt: è quibus nos aliqua etiam recitabimus. Ioannis capite decimosexto, Cum venerit ille, qui est spiritus veritatis, ducet vos in omnem veritatem: non enim loquetur à semetipso, sed quæcunque audierit, loquetur, & quæ futura sunt, annunciabit vobis. Ille me glorificabit, quia de meo accipiet. Ecce vbi ostenditur quod spiritus Sanctus ab alio, videlicet à Patre & filio audiet. Lucę capite duodecimo. Cum adduxerint vos ad synagogam & ad magistratus ac potestates, nolite soliciti esse qualiter aut quid respondeatis, aut quid dicatis: spiritus Sanctus docebit vos in eadem hora, quid oporteat vos dicere. Prima Corinthiorum capite secundo. Porrò sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Et paulo post sequitur: Nobis autem reuelauit Deus per spiritum suum. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Plura in eandem sententiam ibi sequuntur. Prima Corinthiorum capite duodecimo, varia & amplissiamplißima dona spiritus Sanƈti enumerantur, & apostolos, prophetas, doƈtores, per eundem constitui dicuntur Ephef.4. Alia alibi in eandem sententiam dicuntur. Cæte-rum est & in hac locutione antitheseos ratio speƈtanda, quádoquidem in hoc constitui-tur diuersitas noui testamenti à veteri, quòd in veteri quidem Moses ipse edoƈtus est per tabulam scriptam, cæteri verò per hunc Mosen ab illis deinde alij longa temporum serie. At in nouo testamento sine scripto, & citra vocem, aut quamcunque opem huma-nam Apostolis ac discipulis cognitio veritatis infusa est: Sola spiritus Sanƈti inspiratio-ne edoƈti sunt Apostoli omnia mysteria, ipso die, quo missus est ad eos spiritus Sanƈtus: similiter deinceps innumeri alij sanƈti spiritum Sanƈtum postea accipientes nulla tabu-la vel libro, nullius item præceptoris voce adiuti. Verum est quidem postea scripti sunt libri, quos euangeliorum & epistolarum nominibus appellamus: Sed ex his non primùm traditum euangelium apostolis: sed hiid scripserunt, quod per spiritum San-ƈtum prius fuerunt edoƈti, sicut Petrus prioris epistolæ capite primo dicit, Apostolos annunciasse euangelium per spiritum Sanƈtum.
units.tr: (It must be understood that the Father accomplishes this through the Spirit, whom he himself is going to send for this purpose, as Christ himself declares elsewhere.) Finally, testimonies about this proper office of the Holy Spirit, namely that he ought to teach all men all truth, occur everywhere, especially in the New Testament; some of these we shall also recite. In John chapter 16: "When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth; for he will not speak of himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will receive of mine." Here it is shown that the Holy Spirit will hear from another, namely from the Father and the Son. Luke chapter 12: "When they bring you before the synagogues and the magistrates and the powers, do not be anxious how or what you are to answer or what you are to say; the Holy Spirit will teach you in that same hour what you ought to say." First Corinthians chapter 2: "Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect." And a little after it follows: "But God has revealed to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." Many more to the same effect follow there. In First Corinthians chapter 12 the various and most abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit are enumerated, and it is said that apostles, prophets and teachers are appointed by the same Spirit (Eph. 4). Other passages are said to the same effect elsewhere. Yet in this manner of speaking by antithesis the following point must also be considered: the difference between the New Testament and the Old lies in this, that under the Old, Moses himself was taught through a written tablet, and the others were then taught through this Moses, and afterwards by others, over a long succession of times. But under the New Testament, without writing and without any voice or any human aid whatever, knowledge of the truth was poured into the apostles and disciples. The apostles were taught all mysteries solely by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit on the very day on which the Holy Spirit was sent to them; and in the same way countless other saints afterwards, receiving the Holy Spirit, were helped by no tablet or book, and likewise by the voice of no teacher. It is true that books were afterwards written, which we call by the names of Gospels and Epistles; but the gospel was not first handed down to the apostles from these writings. Rather, they wrote what they had previously been taught by the Holy Spirit, as Peter says in the first chapter of his first epistle, that the apostles proclaimed the gospel through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Scripserunt autem partim ad refutandos aduersarios & pseudoapostolos, qui iam tùm incipiebant inficere falsa doƈtrina ecclesias: qualis Ebion, aduersus quem Ioannes scripsit Euangelium: Lucas aduersos alios historiam Christi & ecclesiæ depravantes: & pseudoapostoli, contra quos toties agit Paulus: partim consulere volentes posteritati, vt quando religio in mundo foret per traditiones hominum & alia vitia penitus corru-pta, & propè extinƈta, adminiculo horum librorum vera religio iterum instauraretur. Qua in parte prouidentiæ diuinæ fruƈtum nos nostris temporibus experimur. Si enim non extarent libri sacri ab Apostolis scripti, Deus bone quę nunc foret confusio? Sed de hac re mox iterum.
units.tr: They wrote partly to refute adversaries and false apostles, who already then began to infect the churches with false teaching, such as Ebion, against whom John wrote his Gospel; Luke wrote against others who were corrupting the history of Christ and the Church; and the false apostles, against whom Paul so often contends. Partly they wished to provide for posterity, so that when religion in the world was entirely corrupted by the traditions of men and other vices, and was almost extinguished, true religion might be restored again with the aid of these books. In this respect we experience the fruit of divine providence in our own times. For if the sacred books written by the apostles did not exist, good God, what confusion there would be now! But of this matter again shortly.

units.la: Et non docebunt, inquit, quisq; proximum suum, & vnusquisq; fratrem suum.
units.tr: And they shall not teach, he says, every man his neighbour, and every man his brother.

units.la: Ipsa forma locutionis quoniam geminationem seu repetitionem habet, notat diligē-tiam, ac laborem, qui in discenda lege insumi debebat, & ipsius legis magnitudinem & difficultatem. Cùm ait, proximum suum, item fratrem suum, his vocibus Iudæos potissi-mùm notat, ad quos solos Lex visa est pertinere. Notus in Iudæa Deus: & non nisi proxi-mos ac fratres suos docebat, reliquos auersabantur. At Euangeliũ docendum erat apud omnes gentes.
units.tr: The very form of the expression, since it has a doubling or repetition, marks the diligence and labour that ought to be spent in learning the law, and the greatness and difficulty of the law itself. When he says "his neighbour" and likewise "his brother," by these words he chiefly indicates the Jews, to whom alone the Law seemed to belong. God was known in Judea, and he taught only his neighbours and brothers; the rest turned away. But the gospel had to be taught among all nations.

units.la: Dicens: Cognosce Dominum) Elegans Sermocinatio. Ponuntur enim hæc verba, tanquam si audiatur quispiam docens ad alterum ita dicere. Crebræ sunt in prophetis. Hinc verò sumpta est, quòd passim in lege Dominus præscribit, quomodo Patres & senes & filios ac posteros suos docerent ostendetes, quid hoc vel illud præsertim è ceremonijs sibi vel let: vt deagno paschali: & præcepta de docēdis filijs ac nepotibus passim extát, vt Deut. 4.6.11. Psalmo 78.
units.tr: Saying: "Know the Lord.") An elegant speech-in-character (sermocinatio). For these words are set down as if one were to hear someone teaching another and saying this. They are frequent in the prophets. The origin of this lies in the fact that the Lord everywhere in the Law prescribes how the fathers, elders and their sons and descendants should teach, showing what this or that, especially among the ceremonies, means to them, as in the case of the Passover lamb; and precepts about teaching sons and grandsons are found everywhere, as in Deut. 4, 6, 11; Psalm 78.

units.la: Quòd omnes cogniturí sunt me) Est veluti ratio, quare non erit opus, vt alter ab altero do-ceatur: quia, inquit, omnes per se erunt doƈti. Neq; exprimit, quòd doƈti erunt à spiritu Sanƈto: sed quia satis constat, docendi munus proprie ad Spiritum sanƈtum pertinere, sicut ante ostendimus, ideo facilè intelligitur, per spiritum Sanƈtum edocendos, sicut historia quoque rerum gestarum, Actor. capite 2. satis testatur.
units.tr: "All shall be taught of me." This is, as it were, the reason why there will be no need for one person to teach another, because, he says, all will be taught by themselves. He does not state that they will be taught by the Holy Spirit, but since it is well established that the office of teaching belongs properly to the Holy Spirit, as we showed earlier, it is readily understood that they are taught through the Holy Spirit, as the account of the deeds recorded in Acts chapter 2 also clearly attests.

units.la: Ab eo, qui pusillus fuerit inter eos, vsquè ad eum, qui magnus est in-ter illos.
units.tr: From the least of them even unto the greatest of them.

units.la: Distributio est, qua euidentius explicat vniuersalem notam omnes, ac pulchrè osten-dit, euangelicam gratiam communiter citra personarum acceptionem impendendam, sicut & Petrus Actorum capite decimo, confitetur, & Paulus passim in epistolis incul-cat Romanorum capite secundo, Ephesiorum capite sexto, Colossensium capite ter-tio, Galat.3.
units.tr: This is a distribution, which explains more clearly the universal word all, and shows beautifully that the grace of the gospel is bestowed on all alike, without respect of persons. Peter also confesses this in Acts chapter 10, and Paul repeatedly urges it in his epistles: Romans chapter 2, Ephesians chapter 6, Colossians chapter 3, Galatians 3.

units.la: Cæterum, quando hoc pacto promissitur donatio spiritus Sanƈti in nouo testa-mento, per quem omnes instituerentur, regerentur, gubernarentur, qui esset vi-ce legis & legislatoris in piorum cordibus, qui eosdem doceret omnem veritatem: & ita promittitur spiritus Sanƈtus, tanquam proprie pertinens ad Euangelium: non sic simpliciter accipi hæc debent, quasi Patres etiam non habuerint spiritum San-ƈtum sub lege & in veteri testamento (constat enim & illorum plurimis spiritum Sanƈtum fuisse datum) Sed quòd nunquam tàm aperte, tàm abundè datus sit spiritus Sanƈtus, atque sub Euangelio. Nunquam antea talibus signis inclaruit. efficacia spiritus Sancti in tàm multis hominibus, sicut in Euangelio. Præterea, per Spiritum sanctum reserata sunt omnia & patefacta, quæ ante fuerant clausa & occulta: & clarissimè manifestauit spiritus Sanctus, omnes typos, omnia obscura vaticinia legis esse in Euangelio per Christum adimpleta. Adhæc, nunquam sic manifestatus fuit spiritus Sanctus, vt agnosceretur in diuinitate distincta persona, quomodo in nouo testamento, vbi baptismus institutur conferendus in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti: vbi item spiritus Sanctus datur Apostolis, vt posint soluere à peccatis, atque ligare etiam in cœlis. Propter hanc igitur adeò insignem, inusitatam & largam donationem spiritus Sancti, qualis nunquam antea audita est, propria est hæc euangelij nota, qua discernitur à lege, quòd videlicet sub Euangelio donatus sit spiritus Sanctus.
units.tr: Moreover, when the gift of the Holy Spirit is promised in this way in the New Testament, through whom all are to be instructed, ruled and governed, who would be in the hearts of the godly in place of the law and the lawgiver, and who would teach them all truth, the Holy Spirit is promised as belonging properly to the Gospel. These words should not be taken simply, as if the Fathers did not have the Holy Spirit under the law and in the Old Testament (for it is clear that the Spirit was given to many of them too). Rather, the Holy Spirit was never given so openly and so abundantly as under the Gospel. Never before did the efficacy of the Spirit shine forth with such signs in so many men as in the Gospel. Furthermore, through the Holy Spirit all things have been unlocked and laid open, which before had been closed and hidden, and the Holy Spirit has most clearly made known that all the types and all the obscure prophecies of the law are fulfilled in the Gospel through Christ. In addition, the Holy Spirit was never so manifestly revealed that he was recognised as a distinct person in the Godhead, as he is in the New Testament, where baptism is instituted to be conferred in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and where the Spirit is likewise given to the apostles so that they may forgive sins and also bind in heaven. Therefore, on account of this so remarkable, unusual and generous gift of the Holy Spirit, such as was never heard of before, this is the distinctive mark of the gospel, by which it is distinguished from the law: that under the Gospel the Holy Spirit has been given.

units.la: Porrò patres habuisse spiritum Sanctum, Petrus posterioris epistolæ suæ capite primo de Prophetis loquens, testatur, quòd spiritu Sancto impulsi locuti sint sancti Dei homines.
units.tr: Moreover, Peter, speaking of the prophets in the first chapter of his second epistle, testifies that the holy men of God spoke, moved by the Holy Spirit, which shows that the Fathers had the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quare non est dubium, quin Noe, item Abraham, aliisque innumeri etiam ante legem spiritum Sanctum, & quidem valde largiter acceperint. Genesis quadragesimo primo, Pharao prædicat Iosephum vt spiritu Dei plenum. Exodi vigesimo octauo, Sapientes corde eliguntur Spiritu prudentiæ impleti, qui conficiant vestes Aaron. Exodi capite trigesimo primo describitur Beseleel impletus spiritu Dei, & sapientia, & intelligentia, & scientia, in omni opere fabrili. Numerorum capite vndecimo. Septuaginta seniores electi, & Spiritus eis datus, cumque requieuisset in eis spiritus, prophetauerunt. Item Iosue, Samson, Samuel, Dauid, spiritu Dei afflati & ornati clarè dicuntur, vt non opus sit, plura in medium producere. Habuerunt igitur & Patres spiritum Sanctum, at nunquam tàm aperte, tàm abundè, nûquam tàm apertis signis, nunquam tot homines, nunquam sic omnia per eundem patefacta ac reserata, nunquam tàm euidenter declaratus est distincta persona à patre & filio.
units.tr: Therefore there is no doubt that Noah, likewise Abraham, and countless others even before the law, received the Holy Spirit, and indeed in large measure. In Genesis chapter 41, Pharaoh proclaims Joseph to be a man full of the Spirit of God. In Exodus chapter 28, wise men of heart are chosen, filled with the spirit of wisdom, to make the garments of Aaron. In Exodus chapter 31, Bezalel is described as filled with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding and knowledge in every craft. In Numbers chapter 11, seventy elders are chosen, and the Spirit is given to them, and when the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied. Likewise Joshua, Samson, Samuel and David are clearly said to have been inspired and adorned by the Spirit of God, so there is no need to bring forward more. Thus the Fathers too had the Holy Spirit, but never so openly, never so abundantly, never with such manifest signs, never in so many men, never were all things so unlocked and revealed through the same Spirit, and never was the Spirit so plainly declared to be a distinct person from the Father and the Son.

units.la: Quoniam placatus ero super iniustitijs illorum, & peccatis eorum, et iniquitatum illorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness, and their sins and their iniquities I will remember no more.

units.la: Conuenit per omnia cum Septuaginta, nisi quòd Apostolus addidit veluti interpretationis causla, ὅτι τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν. Certè in Hebraeo non habentur nisi duæ voces ‏עָוֹן‏ iniquitas, peccatum, & ‏חָטָא‏ peccauit, deliquit ‏נָשָׂא‏, quod ferè idem significat. Est autem hæc altera nota propria euangelij, qua & discernitur à lege, & præstantius lege demonstratur, de gratuita remissione peccatorum. Ac prioribus quidè verbis, quando ait, Quoniam placatus ero, aptissimè significat peccatorum remissionem: Quando verò addit, Non recordabor, indicat etiam gratuitam fore, hoc est, remittenda peccata, non ideo quidem, quòd in sanctis nulla erunt, vel, quòd illi pro peccatis suis satisfaciant: sed quòd Deus nolit recordari, tanquam si non essent perpetrata, sed, vt Roman. 4. plenius id exponitur, Deus non imputabit. Ita namq; non recordari, idè, quod non reputare, nec sine magna Emphasi videatur additum.
units.tr: This agrees in every respect with the Septuagint, except that the Apostle added, for the sake of interpretation, ὅτι τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν [that their iniquities]. Certainly in the Hebrew there are only two words: ʿāwōn [עָוֹן], iniquity or sin, and ḥāṭā' [חָטָא], he sinned or transgressed, and nāśā' [נָשָׂא], which means nearly the same. This is the second distinctive mark of the gospel, by which it is also distinguished from the law and shown to be superior to the law: the free forgiveness of sins. In the earlier words, when he says For I will be merciful, he very aptly signifies the remission of sins; and when he adds I will not remember, he indicates that this forgiveness will also be free, that is, that sins are to be pardoned, not indeed because there will be none in the saints, nor because they make satisfaction for their sins, but because God is unwilling to remember them, as if they had never been committed. As Romans 4 explains this more fully, God will not impute them. For "not to remember" is the same as "not to reckon," and it does not seem to have been added without great emphasis.

units.la: Cæterùm pluribus hæc exponere, vel testimonia plura adducere, hanc promissionè illustrantia, non est opus, quando nusquâ non, præsertim in Apostoli scriptis occurrunt, quæ huc faciunt. Iam nonnulla ad doctrinam & consolationem conducentia ex his omnibus colligamus.
units.tr: There is no need to explain these matters at greater length, or to adduce more testimonies illustrating this promise, since passages that bear on it occur everywhere, especially in the writings of the Apostle. Now let us gather from all these things some points that serve for doctrine and consolation.

units.la: Quomodo accipiendum, omnes doceri à Deo.
units.tr: How it is to be understood that all are taught by God.

units.la: Verùm, quia fuerunt etiam nostra tempestate, qui turpissimè abusi sunt hisce verbis Hieremiæ, quibus dicit, quòd omnes cogniturj sint Deum. Item Esaiæ: & similibus:
units.tr: But because in our own time there were also some who have shamefully abused these words of Jeremiah, where he says that they shall all know God, and likewise the words of Isaiah and similar passages,

units.la: Atque alij quidem ad confirmandam suam falsam doctrinam, quam ceu immediatè à Deo acceptam ausi sunt mundo obtrudere: Alij verò adducti sunt ad contemnendum externam prædicationem, & docendi munus in ecclesijs vsitatum.
units.tr: some indeed, to confirm their false doctrine, which they dared to thrust upon the world as if received immediately from God; others were led to despise external preaching and the teaching office customary in the churches.

units.la: Deniq;, quidam hac occasione omnes bonas artes, omnem diligentiam versandi in sacris literis, imò ipsas has sacras literas vilipendere atque auersari: Ideo, priusquam ea, quæ ad doctrinam pertinent, adferamus, visum est, paulò plenius germanù sensum horum verborum excutere, vt deinde talibus impijs opinionibus contraire tantò facilius quiuis possint.
units.tr: Finally, some on this occasion despised and shunned all the liberal arts, all diligence in working through the sacred letters, and even the sacred letters themselves. Therefore, before we bring forward what pertains to doctrine, it seemed good to examine the true sense of these words somewhat more fully, so that anyone may then more easily oppose such impious opinions.

units.la: Sciendum itaque, hæc verba non vno modo à sanctis patribus explicari, nos quidem recitare non grauabimur.
units.tr: It must be known, then, that these words have not been explained in only one way by the holy Fathers; we shall not hesitate to recite the various interpretations.

units.la: Primùm nonnulli exponunt de cognitione, quam electi habere debent post hanc vitam, quæ quidem ibi non tradetur hominibus ab hominibus, sed plenissima erit omnibus ab ipso Deo immediatè. In hanc sententiam interpretatur Augustinus libro de spiritu &
units.tr: First, some explain them of the knowledge which the elect are to have after this life. This knowledge will not be given there by men to men, but will be most full to all, immediately from God himself. Augustine interprets it in this sense in his book On the Spirit and the Letter,

units.la: 1. Enthusiastæ. 2. Contemptus externæ prædicationis. 3. Neglectio bonarum et studiorum. 1. Augustl. li. de spiritu et litera ad Marcellinum. Doctrina post hanc uitam. ritt & litera ad Marcellinum capite vigesimoquarto, atque adducit illud prima Corinthiorum cap. decimotertio, Ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: ast vbi venerit, quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Cùm essem puer vt puer loquebar, vt puer sentiebâ, vt puer cogitabâ: at vbi factus sum vir, aboleui puerilia. Cernimus enim nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc verò cognoscam, quemadmodum & cognitus sum. Eodem referri potest & illud 1. Ioannis capite 3. Charissimi, nunc filij Dei sumus, & nondum apparuit id quod futuri sumus. Scimus autem, quòd si apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum, sicuti est. Itaque plena & perfecta eruditio à Deo continget in patria, ac de ea primum rectè accipiuntur prophetæ verba. Sed quia istud nihil singulare foret, sub euangelio expectandum, quando etiam sub lege agentes talem spem de instructione diuina post hanc vitam habebant, ideo rectius de eruditione piorum facta à Deo etiam in hac vita interpretabimur, quòd videlicet hoc singulare foret expectandum in Euangelio, quòd sub eo non amplius homines ab hominibus, vt olim in lege, sed immediatè ab ipso Deo docerentur, quod reuera ad incomparabilem facit Euangelij gloriam.
units.tr: (1) Enthusiasts. (2) Contempt of external preaching. (3) Neglect of the good arts and studies. (1) Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, to Marcellinus. Teaching after this life. Chapter twenty-four, and he cites that passage of 1 Corinthians 13: "We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect comes, what is in part will be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, just as I also have been fully known." To the same purpose may also be referred that passage of 1 John 3: "Beloved, now we are the children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when it appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is." Therefore full and perfect instruction will come from God in the fatherland, and the words of the prophet are rightly taken of that first of all. But since that would be nothing singular, to be looked for under the gospel, when even those living under the law had such hope of divine instruction after this life, we shall rather interpret it of the instruction of the godly by God, even in this life. The singular thing to be expected in the Gospel is this: that under it people would not be taught by men, as formerly under the law, but immediately by God himself. This truly adds to the incomparable glory of the Gospel.

units.la: Sed, quomodo, inquis, vera erunt hæc verba, quòd omnes cognoscent Deũ, quando palàm cernitur, non omnes nosse Deum, seu edoceri per spiritum Sanctum, veluti gentiles, qui doctrinam etiam summa fide propositam nunquam tamen percipere voluerunt aut potuerunt? Item multi ab initio inde ecclesiæ ad nostra usque tempora rudes & rerum diuinarum ignari, qui à Deo non solùm non doceri, sed planè deseri videntur, ac neilla quidem, quæ per Catechistas traduntur, valent assequi?
units.tr: But, you will say, how will these words be true, that all shall know God, when it is plainly seen that not all know God, or are taught through the Holy Spirit? Thus the Gentiles, who never wished or were able to grasp even the doctrine set forth with the highest faith. Likewise, many from the beginning of the Church down to our own times have been rude and ignorant of divine things, who seem not only not to be taught by God but plainly to be forsaken, and cannot even grasp those things which are handed down through the catechists?

units.la: Respondetur, vocem omnes varie exponi. Primùm, secundum Chrysostomum in Ioannem homilia quadragesimaquinta, vt vox omnes accipiatur per Synedochen pro quamplurimis, vt sit sententia, Si non omnes; at certè quamplurimos à Deo doctos. In quam sententiam etiam Matthæi capite octauo dicitur, Multi ab oriente & occidente venturi sunt, & accumbent cum Abraham, & Isaac, & Iacob in regno cœlorum. Quo loco non dicitur, Omnes, sed multi. Vniuersalem autem omnes subinde accipi pro quamplurimis, liquet ex illo Psalmi decimioctaui, In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum: In omnem, in est, in maximam partem. Etaliàs sæpè omnes pro multis: Roman. 5. Matth. 26. Hebr. cap. 2.
units.tr: The answer is that the word "all" is explained in various ways. First, according to Chrysostom in his forty-fifth homily on John, the word "all" is taken by synecdoche for very many, so that the sense is: "not all, but at any rate very many, are taught by God." To this sense also Matthew 8 is referred: "Many shall come from east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven." Here it does not say "all" but "many." That "all" is sometimes taken universally for very many is clear from that psalm verse (Psalm 18): "Their sound has gone out into all the earth" — "into all," that is, into the greater part. And elsewhere "all" is often used for "many": Romans 5, Matthew 26, Hebrews 2.

units.la: Alio modo hic exponunt omnes, sicut & prioris ad Timotheum vltimo: Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad agnitionē veritatis venire, hoc est, ex parte Dei qui dem, huius voluntas est, omnes homines saluos fieri: verùm quo minus id ita fiat, ipsi homines sibi accerrunt impedimentum. Eodem verò modo omnes cognoscunt Deum, id est, quantum ad Deum quidem attinet, Deus vult omnibus sui plenissimam cognitionem etiam in hac vita elargiri: sed quòd id non fiat, culpa hominum vsuvenire. Et sic etiam Chrysostomus homilia quadragesimaquinta, in Ioannem interpretatur, explicans verbum Esaiæ à Christo citatum, Erunt omnes docibiles Dei. Omnes, inquit, de pluribus dictum est, & addit: Etiam volentes significat. Et ibi in Ioanne Euangelista subijcitur, quod huc videtur quadrare. Augustinus etiam simile quiddam habet libro primo, de prædestinatione Sanctorum capite octauo. Profectò autem vt Sol, quantum in se est, omnes illuminat, quòd tamen omnes non percipiant lucem, aliud est in causa, nempe, vel cæcitas, vel manus, aut aliud quippiam visui oppositum: Ita Deus, inprimis spiritus Sanctus est verè illuminans omnes homines, sed non omnes apprehendunt lucem eius, quia per propriam malitiam vel peccata impediuntur.
units.tr: In another way, some explain "all" here, as also in the last chapter of the first letter to Timothy: "God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." That is, on God's part indeed, this is his will, that all men be saved; but it is men themselves who put up the obstacle so that it does not happen. In the same way, "all know God" means that, as far as God is concerned, God wills to bestow his fullest knowledge on all, even in this life; but that this does not happen comes about through the fault of men. So Chrysostom also interprets it in his forty-fifth homily on John, explaining the saying of Isaiah cited by Christ, "They shall all be taught of God." "All," he says, is said of many, and he adds: "It also signifies those who are willing." And there in the Gospel of John what follows is added, which seems to fit here. Augustine also has something similar in the first book On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter eight: "Indeed, as the sun, so far as it is in itself, illuminates all, yet that all do not perceive the light is due to something else, namely, either blindness or a hand or some other thing opposed to sight. So God, above all the Holy Spirit, truly illuminates all men, but not all apprehend his light, because they are hindered by their own malice or sins."

units.la: Alij restringunt vocem omnes, vt per eam notentur pauci electi, sitque sententia, illos demum plenam habere in hac vita cognitionem rerum diuinarum, quos Deus ad hoc præ cæteris elegerit, quales erant apostoli, & in his electus ille Paulus.
units.tr: Others restrict the word "all," so that by it only a few elect are noted, and the sense is that those alone have full knowledge of divine things in this life whom God has chosen above others for this purpose, such as the apostles, and among them that chosen Paul.

units.la: Quæ interpretatio etiam est Augustini in libro de Spiritu & litera capite vigesimo quarto, Cognoscent Dominum, inquit, omnes, qui sunt domus Israel, domus Iuda, & addit, de veris Israelitis, & de iis qui secundum propositum vocati sunt. Et sic quos docet Deus, docet ex misericordia: quos non docet, non docet ex iustitia: eadē ratione qua quos vult eligit, & quos vult reiicit. Neq; propterea est ei resistendum, vel cum eo expostulandum, Rom. 9.
units.tr: This interpretation is also Augustine's, in his book On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter twenty-four: "They shall all know the Lord," he says, "who are of the house of Israel, the house of Judah," and he adds that these are the true Israelites and those who are called according to purpose. And so, whom God teaches, he teaches out of mercy; whom he does not teach, he does not teach out of justice, by the same reason by which he chooses whom he wills and rejects whom he wills. Nor on that account is one to resist him or dispute with him (Romans 9).

units.la: Quòd si hæc interpretatio minus arridet, quia non electis tantùm, sed omnibus in genere vocatis abundè proposita & infusa est cognitio Dei, ita vt sint inexcusabiles, sicut Romanorum capite primo, & capite tertio, clarius dicitur, & sic nequaquam plaçet, vniuersalem illam restringi ad comprehendendum tàm paucos, in promptu est alia interpretatio eiusdem Augustini libro 1, de prædestinatione sanctorum capite octauo vbi ait,omnes nosse Deum,idem sibi velle,ac si diceretur:Omnes,qui Deum noscunt,à Deo esse instituti:seu,nullos nosse Deum,nisi qui à Deo docentur. Vel,omnes, qui docen⁠tur,à Deo docentur:sicut,inquit,de literarum magistro, qui solus in aliqua ciuitate agit, dicimus:Ecce,hic omnes docet,non quia omnes discunt, sed quia, quicunq; ibi discit, ab illo discit. Atque ita omnes,qui aliquid in ecclesi a Dei assequuntur,vere docetur non ab hominibus,sed ab ipso Deo:quando etiam, quod ab hominibus audimus, & conamur discere,tamen non percipimus : nisi Deo per spiritum suum sanctũ docente,quamlibet alioquin magnam adhibeamus diligentiam. Inter Hebræos Abraham filius Ezræ enarrans illud Ioelis,Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem, ait, particulam omnis,non de vno quoque homine,sed de quacunque hominum conditione accipiendam, quia Deus in conferendo spiritu Sanctum non respicit personam, sed quibuscunq; in genere,siue seruis,siue liberis.
units.tr: But if this interpretation does not please, because the knowledge of God has been set forth and poured out abundantly not only to the elect but to all men in general, so that they are without excuse, as is said more clearly in Romans 1 and Romans 3, and so that universal word is by no means to be restricted to such few persons, another interpretation of the same Augustine lies ready to hand, in his first book On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter eight, where he says that "to know God" means the same thing as if it were said: all who know God have been appointed by God; or, no one knows God except those who are taught by God. Or: all who are taught are taught by God, just as, he says, of a schoolmaster who alone teaches in some city, we say: "Behold, this man teaches all," not because all learn, but because whoever learns there learns from him. And so all who attain anything in the Church are truly taught not by men but by God himself, since even what we hear from men and try to learn, we do not perceive unless God teaches us through his Holy Spirit, however great the diligence we otherwise apply. Among the Hebrews, Abraham son of Ezra, explaining that passage of Joel, "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh," says that the particle "all" is to be taken not of every single man but of every condition of men, because in bestowing the Spirit God does not regard the person, but in general whoever they are, whether slaves or free.

units.la: Quem in modum Augustinus quoq; alibi interpretatur locum illum,Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri. Ergo variis modis,atq; optimo sensu potest vox, omnes, explanari,vt sententia plana & clara habeatur. Sed & hoc quoque addendum, de cognitione seu cognoscendo: Non hic agi de cõsummata ciusmodi cognitione,qua possimus enarrare. Scripturas,eruere mysteria,diuina qualis facultas in apostolis,ac deinde in paucis duntaxat quibusdam emicuit: sed de cognitione dilectionis & timoris Dei, vel charitatis erga Deum & proximum certè præcipuorum capitum doctrinæ, quæ ad salutem omninò est necessaria. Huiusmodi verò cognitione Deus omnibus citra exceptionem personarum benignè impartitur, vt Deum, quantùm satis est, noscant, neque excusari possint,si quòd æquum est,in colendo Deum non fecerint. Aut certè cognitio, quæ spiritualis est, nō prouenit,nisi à Deo. Verbũ Dei auditur & legitur, à carnalibus hominibus carnaliter:sed nihil prodest hoc pacto nosse literam,nisi adiungatur spiritus: Hic verò à Deo est postulandus & accipiendus, 1. Cor. 2. Et sic verba prophetæ multis modis vera esse intelliguntur,& consentaneæ sunt Scripturis interpretationes,quas in medium adduximus.
units.tr: In the same way Augustine also interprets that passage, "God wills all men to be saved." So the word "all" can be explained in various ways, all in a good sense, so that the statement is held to be plain and clear. But this must also be added, concerning knowledge or knowing. Here we are not speaking of the perfect knowledge by which we could expound the Scriptures and bring out their mysteries, such as shone forth in the apostles and afterwards in only a few. We mean the knowledge of the love and fear of God, or of love toward God and neighbour, and certainly of the chief heads of doctrine, which is wholly necessary for salvation. God bestows this kind of knowledge kindly on all, without exception of persons, so that they may know God as far as is enough and cannot be excused for failing to worship God as is right. Or at any rate, spiritual knowledge does not come except from God. The Word of God is heard and read by carnal men in a carnal way, but it profits nothing to know the letter in this way unless the Spirit is added. This must be asked of God and received from him, 1 Cor. 2. And so the words of the prophet are understood to be true in many ways, and the interpretations we have brought forward are consistent with the Scriptures.

units.la: Iam verò non difficile erit respondere ijs, qui verbis prophetæ ad decipiendum imperitos sunt abusi. Ac primùm illis,qui prætextu horum verborum ausi sunt falsam doctrinam suam mundo commendare. Deus,inquiunt,omnes docet, omnibus largitur suum spiritum citra discrimè, quare quæ nos proponimus,accipienda sunt,vt à Deo no bis reuelata. Non est abbreuiata manus Domini: Deus æquè nunc docet nos per somnia & visiones,atque olim Sanctos patres sub lege & ante legem.Et in hanc sententiam protinus congerunt valde multa,vt ex Ioelis secundo. Deinde adhibent alias impostu-ras,& hypocrisin,per quas possint fallere.Sed contra horum venenum primo respondendum est,etiamsi verba prophetæ sonent,omnes edoctos à Deo,tamen prudenter id accipiedum:deinde,non omnem,qui dicit,Domine, Domine, item qui in nomine Dei eiecerit dæmonia,& virtutes multas,esse à Deo missum. Potest spiritus per eos loqui, sed spiritus medax,spiritus vertiginosus,qualis loquebatur 1.Reg.22. per Zedechiã & alios falsos prophetas,Micheæ aduersarios. Deus semper adest suæ ecclesiæ, & reliquit ei inter alia dona etiam discretionē spirituum,de qua 1. Corinth.12. Et 1.Ioan. 4. Charissimi,ne cuiuis spiritui credatis,sed probate spiritus, an ex Deo sint, quoniam multi pseudoprophetæ exierunt in mundum. Atque ibi addit regulam quandam dignoscendorum spirituum. Item. 1.Thessalon.5.Spiritũ ne extinguatis,prophetias ne aspernemini: omnia probate,quod bonum fuerit,tenete. Rationem autem probandi licet adhuc ex aliis locis colligere. Quicquid proponitur,exigatur ad Lydium lapidem Scripturarũ:Si cum hoc non conuenit,si is iudicat diuersum esse à Scripturis, id quod proponitur, certum sit à malo spiritu proficisci.Huc pertinet,quòd Christus,quòd Apostoli semper Scriptu-ras veteris testamenti pro confirmatione suæ doctrinæ citabant, ac iubent omnes, qui dubitant, ad Scripturas recurrere.Ioan.5.Scrutamini Scripturas,& illæ sunt,quæ testifi-cantur de me.Item Actor.17. Thessalonicenses quotidie scrutabantur Scripturas, an hæc ita se haberent 2 Petri 1. commendatur lectio Prophetarum, & iubentur Euangelium conferre cum prophetis.Et propterea voluit Deus extare ad perpetuam memoriam sacros libros incorruptos magno miraculo, vt in arduis controuersijs illi consulerëtur, & oracula inde peterentur.Proinde non credetur thrasonibus illis, qui audent omnia sua iactare,tanquam à spiritu prophetā, nisi quatenus comperientur Scripturis per omnia consentanea. Scire debent,Deum etiam alijs Sanctis hominibus conferre suum spiritum vt examinare possint ac iudicare. 1.Corinthior. 4.Spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur. 1.Corinthiorum 12.Alios quidem posuit Deus in ecclesia, primùm apostolos,deinde prophetas,tertiò doctores, deinde potestates,deinde dona sanationum, subsidia, gubernationes, genera linguarum. Num omnes apostoli? num omnes prophetę? spiritus peculiariter diuidit vnicuiq; sicut vult. Tantum contra spiritus impostores.
units.tr: Now it will not be difficult to answer those who have abused the words of the prophet to deceive the unlearned. First, I answer those who, under the pretext of these words, have dared to commend their false doctrine to the world. "God," they say, "teaches all, and gives his Spirit to all without distinction; therefore what we propose must be accepted as revealed to us by God. The hand of the Lord is not shortened. God now teaches us by dreams and visions just as he did of old to the holy fathers under the law and before the law." And to this effect they at once heap up a great many examples, such as from Joel 2. Then they employ other deceits and hypocrisy, by which they may mislead. But against the poison of these men, I must first reply that, even if the words of the prophet sound as though all are taught by God, yet they must be understood with prudence. Next, not everyone who says "Lord, Lord," or who casts out demons and does many mighty works in the name of God, has been sent by God. A spirit may speak through them, but it is a lying spirit, a giddy spirit, such as spoke through Zedekiah and the other false prophets, adversaries of Micaiah, 1 Kings 22. God is always present to his Church, and among his other gifts he has left it the discernment of spirits, of which 1 Cor. 12. And 1 John 4: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world." And there he adds a certain rule for recognising spirits. Likewise 1 Thess. 5: "Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophesyings; test all things, hold fast what is good." Now the manner of testing can still be gathered from other passages. Whatever is put forward should be brought to the touchstone of the Scriptures. If it does not agree with them, if it judges that what is proposed differs from the Scriptures, it is certain that it comes from an evil spirit. To this belongs the fact that Christ and the apostles always cited the Scriptures of the Old Testament to confirm their doctrine, and they bid all who doubt to have recourse to the Scriptures. John 5: "Search the Scriptures, for they are those which testify of me." Also Acts 17: the Thessalonians examined the Scriptures daily, to see whether these things were so. 2 Pet. 1 commends the reading of the prophets, and the Gospel is bidden to be compared with the prophets. And therefore God willed that the sacred books should stand, uncorrupted by a great miracle, for ever in memory, so that in difficult controversies men might consult them and seek oracles from them. Accordingly, those braggarts who dare to boast of all their own ideas as if from a prophetic spirit are not to be believed, except insofar as they are found to agree with the Scriptures in every respect. They ought to know that God also gives his Spirit to other holy men, so that they may examine and judge. 1 Cor. 14: "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets." 1 Cor. 12: "God has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healing, helps, governments, kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? The Spirit divides to each one individually as he wills." This applies only against the impostors of the Spirit.

units.la: Quando verò nonnulli prætextu horum verborum impedire volunt externam prædicationem, dicentes, Deum omnes satis docere interius. Respondendum est, grauissimè aberrare eos, quando à Christo præcepta, & ab Apostolis multis diligentissimè exercita- ta est externa verbi prædicatio: Ite, inquit, & docete omnes gentes, prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ.
units.tr: But when some, under the pretext of these words, wish to hinder the external preaching, saying that God teaches all sufficiently inwardly, it must be answered that they greatly err, since Christ commanded external preaching of the Word, and the apostles practised it most diligently: "Go," he says, "and teach all nations; preach the Gospel to every creature."

units.la: Non omnes paria dona acceperunt, & ideo doceri per alios debent. Aut, ut etiā norint prima religionis elementa, tamen sunt docendi sublimiora, sicut huius epistolæ capite 5. & alibi sæpius admonentur ad maiora percipienda.
units.tr: Not all have received equal gifts, and so they must be taught by others. Or, even if they know the first elements of religion, they must still be taught higher things, as in chapter 5 of this epistle, and elsewhere they are often admonished to receive greater things.

units.la: Deinde confirmandi sunt infirmi, & fides audita est alenda. Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei: Quomodo credent, si non audierunt. Roman.10. Sæpe etiam inter audiendum verbum, nonnulli spiritum Sanctum acceperunt: ut illi in familia Cornelij, concionante Petro Actor.10. Et sermo Dei vocaliter auditus etiam agit in cordibus audi-torum, & per spiritum Sanctum fit valde efficax, & fructus mirabiles sæpe edit: 1. Thessalon.2. Gratias agimus Deo indesinenter, quòd, cum acceperitis sermonem à nobis, quo Deum discebatis, accepistis nō sermonem hominum, sed, sicut erat vere, sermonem Dei, qui & agit in vobis credentibus. Experimur ipsi tales fructus valde sæpe.
units.tr: Then the weak must be strengthened, and faith that has been heard must be nourished. "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. How will they believe if they have not heard?" Rom. 10. Often too, while the Word is being heard, some have received the Holy Spirit, as those in the household of Cornelius did while Peter was preaching, Acts 10. The Word of God, when heard with the voice, also works in the hearts of the hearers and, through the Holy Spirit, becomes very effective and often produces wonderful fruits. 1 Thess. 2: "We thank God without ceasing, that when you received from us the word of God's message, you accepted it not as the word of men but, as it truly is, the word of God, which also works in you who believe." We ourselves experience such fruits very often.

units.la: Cùm verò tanta imbecillitas sit & cæcitas humanarum mentium, ut etiam, quæ diligentissimè & creberrimè inculcantur, tamen vix percipiant: velle impedire externam prædicationem, quid quæso aliud erit, quàm summam barbariem inducere, & velle efficere, ut homines pecudum more sine omni cognitione boni & æqui veniant?
units.tr: But since human minds are so weak and blind that even things which are inculcated most diligently and most often can scarcely be grasped, what, I ask, would it be to wish to hinder external preaching, other than to introduce the greatest barbarism, and to bring it about that men, like cattle, come to have no knowledge of what is good and just?

units.la: Sed iam multo perniciosissimi sunt illi, qui propter verba prophetę audent suggerere imperitis, non opus esse, dare operā lectioni sacrarum literarum, aut bonas artes addiscere, quibus ad earum perceptionem adiuueris: Deus, inquiunt, omnem cognitionem necessariam suggerit: atque etiamsi legas, audias, congeras omnia scripta, tamen nō propter rea vere eris doctus, nihil assequeris, nisi Deus te suo spiritu afflauerit. Valeant doctorū tituli, & illa, hæc nihil ad veram doctrinam faciunt, frustrà conaris: Ipsa Scriptura est tantum mortua & inanis litera, quæ non tam potest esse vtilis, quin pariter possit esse noxia & occidat. E cœlis expectandum est, vt verè docearis, non ex libris petendum. Talia impudenter isti spirituales homines obganniunt, atque instillant ignarę plebeculæ aut etiam iuuentutis auribus, atque auocant à studijs bonarum artium, adducunt ad contemptum doctorum hominum.
units.tr: But now those are far more pernicious who, appealing to the words of the prophet, dare to suggest to the unlearned that there is no need to devote oneself to reading the sacred letters or to learn the liberal arts, by which one might help oneself to grasp them. "God," they say, "supplies all necessary knowledge; and even if you read, hear, and gather together all the writings, you will not therefore truly be learned; you will gain nothing unless God has breathed upon you by his Spirit. Away with the titles of teachers! These things contribute nothing to true doctrine; you labour in vain. Scripture itself is only a dead and empty letter, which can be not so much useful as equally harmful and kill." One must look for true teaching from heaven, not seek it from books. These spiritual men shamelessly mutter such things and instil them into the ears of the ignorant common people or even of the young, and they turn them away from the study of the liberal arts and lead them to contempt for learned men.

units.la: His quoque respondendum est: Non satis esse, ut expectes doceri te à Deo, sed opus est, ipse quoq; adhibeas quandam diligentiam. Quod in Apostolis & similibus factum est in primitiua ecclesia, quia id tùm expediebat, non habendum est pro regula generali, sed factum non facit legem. Alias certè non abes à tentatione Dei. Perinde enim est, ac si di cas, non esse operandum, quia Deus pascit omnes, etiam aues & minutissima animalcula: quod quàm falsum sit, nemo nescit. Est ergo operandum, & nihilominus quæcunq; obueniunt, fatebimur, solius Dei beneficio prouenire. Similiter est diligenter discedum, atque, vbi profeceris, Deo ages gratias, qui dedit vt proficeres. Tuam requiret diligentiā, item diligentiam præceptorum: sed ipse interea est, qui dat incrementum, iuxta illud 1. Corinth.3. Quis Paulus? Quis autem Apollo? nisi ministri, per quos credidistis, & vt cuique Dominus dedit. Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit, sed Deus dedit incrementum. Et paulò post: Etenim Dei sumus cooperarij. Ergo, sicut opus fuit Paulum plantare, Apollo rigare, vbi Dominus volebat dare incrementum: ita opus est nobis, ut & discamus, & præceptores audiamus, si incrementum à Deo expectamus. Deus quidem omnia in nobis operatur, sed nos propterea non possumus esse cessatores, oportet nos cooperari.
units.tr: To these men also this must be answered: it is not enough that you expect to be taught by God; you must also apply some diligence yourself. This was done by the apostles and their like in the primitive Church, because it was then expedient; but it is not to be taken as a general rule, and an exception does not make a law. Otherwise, you certainly do not escape tempting God. For it is just as if you said that one should not work, because God feeds all, even the birds and the tiniest creatures; and how false this is no one doubts. Therefore we must work, and yet we will acknowledge that whatever comes to us comes by the benefit of God alone. Similarly, one must study diligently, and when you have made progress, give thanks to God, who gave you the ability to progress. He requires your diligence, and the diligence of teachers too; but he himself meanwhile is the one who gives the increase, according to 1 Cor. 3: "What then is Paul? What is Apollos? Only ministers through whom you believed, as the Lord gave to each. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase." And a little later: "For we are God's fellow workers." Therefore, just as it was necessary for Paul to plant and Apollos to water, where the Lord willed to give the increase, so it is necessary for us both to learn and to listen to teachers, if we expect the increase from God. God indeed works all things in us, but we cannot on that account be idle; we must cooperate.

units.la: Porrò tituli & insignia verum est quòd nihil faciunt ad ea, quæ sunt spiritus, & per se non conferunt doctrinam, sed tantùm sunt incitamenta animorum, & quasi temporanea quædam diligentiæ præmia, per quæ alij excitantur: præterea, sunt testimonium ecclesiæ, vel societatis alicuius, nempe scholæ, ad declarandum, personam titulis ornatam esse idoneam ad minus in ecclesia vel republica: hic inquam est titulorum vsus. Proinde cùm Deus ipse velit & in ecclesia, & in omni societate hominum diuersos esse ordines, (alios enim ponit doctores, alios pastores, alios euangelistas, &c.) & vocat ipse ad eiusmodi munera plerunq; per homines, ideo æquum est adniti & laborare, ut tale testimonium, quòd idonei simus, promereamur, ac Domino etiam in ecclesia vel republica cooperemur. Igitur Deus vult esse, qui alios doceat: vult extare Scripturam, per quam doceantur: & qui hæc contemnit media, planè ipsum contemnit Deum: sicut Deus sæpè de ministris suis loquens testatur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is true that titles and insignia contribute nothing to those things which belong to the Spirit, and that of themselves they do not impart doctrine; they are only incentives to minds, and as it were temporary rewards of diligence, by which others are stirred up. Besides, they are a testimony of the Church, or of some society, namely a school, declaring that the person adorned with the titles is fit, at least for the Church or the commonwealth. This, I say, is the use of titles. Therefore, since God himself wills that there be different orders both in the Church and in every human society (for he appoints some teachers, others pastors, others evangelists, etc.), and since he usually calls men to such offices through other men, it is right to strive and labour so that we may earn such a testimony that we are fit, and so cooperate with the Lord in the Church or the commonwealth. Thus God wills that there be those who teach others; he wills that Scripture exist, through which they may be taught; and whoever despises these means plainly despises God himself, as God often testifies when speaking of his ministers.

units.la: Valde vtilis est externa prædicatio: non satis est, quòd domi legas aut mediteris, sed quantū aliàs licet, debes externum verbū audire: quando viua vox alterius plus efficit, quàm priuata meditatio. Vide in vita Augustini, quomodo digressionem fecit inter concionem, licet inuitus fere, & auertit ab errore quendam mercatorem.
units.tr: External preaching is very useful. It is not enough to read or meditate at home; as far as otherwise permitted you ought to hear the external word, since the living voice of another accomplishes more than private meditation. See in the life of Augustine how, almost against his will, he turned aside to listen to a sermon and turned a certain merchant away from error.

units.la: Verum quoque est, ipsam scripturam esse tantùm rem externā, &, si spectemus librorum sacrorum materiā, puta chartam, atramentū, vocabula, syllabas, literas, puncta, hæc omnia nihil sunt: sed tamen Deus voluit talia extare administrcula, & instrumēta, quibus infirmitas nostra, & memoria iuuaretur. Et in illis ipsis voluntas Dei nobis propositā est, vt vbi toto animo, & implorata ope Spiritus sancti inteti fuerimus in res ipsas, & doctrinam ibi propositam, etiam fructum mirabilem interius percipiamus, sicut & de prædicatione vocali, & collocatione seu scrutatione scripturarum supra diximus.
units.tr: It is also true that Scripture itself is only an external thing, and if we consider the matter of the sacred books, such as paper, ink, words, syllables, letters and points, all these are nothing.
