By the word redemption he indicates the very great power of Christ's blood, namely that those who were captives and slaves have through him been restored again to liberty. This figure of speech occurs everywhere in explaining the mystery of human salvation obtained through Christ, and it is taken from those who recover by a price something deposited or lost. Matt. 20 and Mark 10: "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." 1 Cor. 1: "Christ is made unto us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." Since he calls this redemption eternal, it is clear that it is spiritual and retains its force even after this life; so this word too adds emphasis. Finally, when it is said that this redemption was found, whether because Christ discovered it, this beautifully shows that our justification is free, obtained by no merits or powers of ours, but to be ascribed to the good counsel and ordinance of God alone. The form of speech is taken from people who deliberate, and who, among various plans, find one more convenient and choose it. So God too, from the many ways by which he could have freed mankind, judged the most fitting of all to be that it should happen through the death of the Son, as was said in the second chapter of this epistle: For it became him, etc. Thus all these things, set forth together, wonderfully illustrate what was done through Christ in the New Testament, and there is almost no word that does not carry some amplification within it. So much for the explanation of the parts. Now let us briefly show what is to be gathered from these things for doctrine and comfort, and, since it is worth the effort, let us also set out more fully, typologically concerning Christ, those things that were seen in the legal tabernacle. First, when in the Old Testament worship, justifications and the sanctuary are spoken of, and in the second part of the comparison it is added that all these same things are had in the New Testament, but far more excellent, here we have comprehended all that were the chief things of the Old Law. Second, we must note for doctrine that the place of the tabernacle is called the Holy in its first part and the Holy of Holies in its inner part, but these names are not to be understood as if holiness inheres in a place in itself, or as if holiness could be acquired from a place; rather the Holy of Holies is so called from the holy works done there. Otherwise, wherever a man may be, that place is holy insofar as he himself does what is holy. Indeed every place is holy by God, who fills all things and is everywhere; yet where we too act well, namely by confessing sins, calling upon God, hearing the word of God, that place is acknowledged by us as holy in a special way. Therefore Solomon, about to build the temple, said in 1 Kings 8 that that house could not contain him, since the heaven of heavens could not contain him. Meanwhile God wished at last to prescribe to that chosen people a place where he would be worshipped; not indeed because he preferred one place to another, but partly so that there might be an outward testimony of God's will toward that people, namely that he wished above all to be worshipped among them; partly so that the people, being rude and moved by external things that instruct, might be the more stirred to the worship of the one God; partly so that by this means they would be kept from idolatry and from the custom of erecting altars everywhere, or devising scattered forms of worship, as men had begun to do everywhere before the law was given. (For if worship had been prescribed in one place, this would have served to keep all men in unity of religion; something of this can be seen in Joshua 22.) Hence we read in Deut. 12 the commands not to offer anywhere but in the chosen place. Those who were about to pray turned toward the ark of God as the seat of God; afterwards they betook themselves to Jerusalem, the ark of God having been carried thither; those praying in the Babylonian captivity turned their eyes to the same place, as is clear from the history of Daniel.

units.la: Verum in Euangelio Christus Ioan. 4. docet, tempus adesse, quo neq; Hierosolymis, neq; in monte Garizim, neq; simili loco adorabitur Deus, sed vbiq; locorum in Spiritu &veritate. Idem docet alibi ingrediendum in cubiculum (etiamsi hoc proprie contra orantes in plateis dictum, non contra ingredientes templum) cum orare volumus: & Apostolus 1. Tim. 2. vult viros orare in omni loco sustollentes puras manus. Actor. 17. Dominus non habitat in templis manu factis: unde haec mutatio est? Respondetur: Sicut olim ante legem, dum quivis passim sibi erigebat fanum pro arbitrio, multi enati sunt abusus & idololatrici cultus, & propterea opus fuit unum aliquem locum electo populo praescribere: Ita dum rursus abusus enati sunt ex templo & in templo, Deus voluit unà cum sacerdotio & ceremoniis omnibus simul templum & praecepta de uno loco abrogari, & credentibus hanc per Euangelium parare libertatem, ut, vbicunq; essent (praesertim cum iam Euangelium toto orbe annunciaretur) locum orandi oportunum habe-rent, & ex omni loco sciret se exaudiendos. Non convenissent omnibus populis, quod antea uni populo satis conveniebat. Unde Christi extat vaticinium de templo suciten-do. Quamvis autem abrogatum est hoc ius unius templi, tamen ut omnia ordinate fieret in ecclesia, locos aliquos constitui, ad quos orandi et audiendi verbi caussa omnes convenirent, non est ab Euangelio alienum. Sic enim Apostoli ab ascensu Christi in coelos in unum locum convenieban̄t ad orandum: & paulo post adhuc vbi accepissent spiritum Sanctum, ascenderunt Apostoli ad horam orationis nonam (quamvis magis id faciebant, ut ibi opportunius docerent, non quasi approbarent locum vel tempus orandi) & 1. Corinth. 11. de coeuneiendo in unum locum ad edendum coenam dominicam, ad audiendum verbum, tamen citra superstitionem, qualis erat apud Iudaeos. Ac diu etiam fuerunt Christiani sine templis seu congregationibus. Sicut Iudaei quoq; singulis oppidis habuerunt suas synagogas, sed vnicum templum: Christiani autem loco Synagogarum habent ecclesias, templum autem nullum, sicut nec altare, nec sacerdotium, nec sacrificium, habent quippe immensum sacerdotem Christum, qui est hostia. Vide Hieronymum ad Paulinum. Hilarion cum in Palaestina ageret, semel tantum iuit Hierosolymam, ne videretur locum contemnere: & non amplius, ne videretur loco plus, quam par est, tribuere. Tertio loco, veniamus ad explicandum paulo plenius, quid tabernaculum eius q; disposition nobis adumbrarit. Videtur enim Apostolus nos quasi inuitare ad id, quando ipse inserit interpretationem eius, quod non omnes sacerdotes ingrediebantur in sancta. Etiamsi rursus tacite moneat nos ad sobrie agendum hac in parte, & non nimis temere progrediendum, vbi ait, Sibi non fuisse de singulis nunc dicendum. Prius autem quam ad rem ipsam veniamus, iterum inculcandum est, quemadmodum et supra capite septimo fecimus, non ex se hic allegorica argumenta, sed proprie typos e veteri testamento erutos, qui in hoc fuerant tunc editi, ut ea quae per Christum gerenda forent, adumbrarent. Alias non essent satis firma argumenta, facileq; possent reijci. Nam vbi allegorice quaedam per te exponuntur vno modo, alius quispiam eadem interpretabitur allegorice in sensum diversum. Verbi gratia, exponit aliquis, quae Caiphas caeteriq; Sacerdotes & Scribe contra Christum conspirantes faciunt, de pontifice Romano, eius q; auxiliatibus copijs persequentibus pios hoc tempore: At aliquis stans ab eius partibus eadem omnia exponit aliter, puta de haereticis: rursus alius de diabolo insidiante fidelibus: alius denique adhuc aliter: & sic parum firmae argumentationes huiusmodi erunt, atq; alia interpretatio super aliam sine fine adducetur. Itaq; sic accipienda sunt quae proferuntur per Apostolos, ut typos expositos intelligamus, & nequaquam allegoricas interpretationes, vel allegorica argumenta. Atque, ut clarius statuamus discrimen inter typos & allegorias, nos breviter quomodo discernendae sint ostendemus.
units.tr: But in the Gospel Christ teaches, John 4, that the time is coming when God will be worshipped neither at Jerusalem, nor on Mount Gerizim, nor in a similar place, but everywhere in spirit and truth. He teaches elsewhere that we are to enter our chamber when we wish to pray (although this was said properly against those praying in the streets, not against those entering the temple). And the Apostle, 1 Tim. 2, wants men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands. Acts 17: "The Lord does not dwell in temples made with hands." Whence comes this change? The answer is: just as formerly, before the law, when each man everywhere set up a shrine at his own discretion, many abuses and idolatrous forms of worship arose, and therefore it was necessary to prescribe one place to the chosen people; so, when abuses again arose from and in the temple, God willed that together with the priesthood and all the ceremonies, the temple and the precepts about one place should be abrogated at the same time, and that for believers he should obtain this liberty through the Gospel, so that wherever they were (especially since the Gospel was now proclaimed throughout the whole world) they should have a suitable place for prayer, and know that they would be heard from every place. What had suited one people well enough could not suit all peoples. Hence there is the prophecy of Christ concerning the raising up of the temple. Although this right of the one temple has been abrogated, nevertheless it is not foreign to the Gospel that certain places should be appointed, so that all might gather there for prayer and for hearing the word, in order that everything be done in an orderly way in the Church. Thus the Apostles, from the ascension of Christ into heaven, assembled in one place to pray; and shortly afterwards, when they had received the Holy Spirit, the Apostles went up at the ninth hour of prayer (although they did this rather so that they might teach there more conveniently, not as if they approved the place or the time of prayer). And 1 Cor. 11 speaks of coming together into one place to eat the Lord's Supper and to hear the word, yet without superstition such as obtained among the Jews. And for a long time Christians also existed without temples or buildings for assembly. Just as the Jews had their synagogues in each town but one temple, so Christians have churches in place of synagogues, but no temple, and likewise no altar, no priesthood, no sacrifice, since they have Christ, the eternal priest, who is himself the victim. See Jerome to Paulinus. When Hilarion was active in Palestine, he went to Jerusalem only once, so as not to seem to despise the place; and not again, lest he seem to attribute more to the place than is fitting. Third, let us come to explain a little more fully what the tabernacle and its arrangement have foreshadowed for us. For the Apostle seems to invite us to this when he himself adds the interpretation of what it meant that not all priests entered into the holy places; although again he tacitly warns us to proceed soberly in this matter and not too rashly, when he says that he did not wish to speak now of each thing individually. But before we come to the thing itself, it must again be insisted, as we also did above in the seventh chapter, that these are not allegorical arguments of our own invention, but types properly drawn from the Old Testament, which were then set forth precisely in order to foreshadow what was to be accomplished through Christ. Otherwise the arguments would not be firm enough and could easily be rejected. For when someone expounds certain things allegorically in one way, another person will interpret the same things allegorically in a different sense. For example, someone explains what Caiaphas and the other priests and scribes did in conspiring against Christ as referring to the Roman pontiff and his auxiliary forces persecuting the godly at this time; but another, standing on the other side, explains all the same things differently, namely of heretics; again another of the devil lying in wait for the faithful; and another finally in yet another way. And so arguments of this kind will be weak, and one interpretation will be brought forward upon another without end. Therefore those things which the Apostles set forth must be taken in such a way that we understand the types as expounded, and by no means allegorical interpretations or allegorical arguments. And so that we may establish more clearly the difference between types and allegories, we will briefly show how they are to be distinguished.

units.la: Typi, quos vulgo figuras etiam appellant, sunt, cum facta aliqua seu gestae res colliguntur ex veteri testamento, & ostenditur, ibi aliquid significatum, in novo testamento gerendum, sive iam gestum & adimpletum. Vt Ionas tribus diebus in ventre Ceti typus fuit ea in parte sepulturae & resurrectionis Christi. Serpens erectus in deserto typus erat Christi crucifixi, sicut Christus ipse peritissimus interpretatur. Allegoriae magis sitae sunt in doctrina ac praeceptis, nosq; docent aliquid spirituale per nos agendum: sicut passim licet videre tales interpretationes allegoricas apud Scriptores veteres. Typi oriuntur ex nudis narrationibus historicis: Allegoriae ex alijs, ut sententijs, praeceptis, & similibus: sicut, Non alligabis os boui trituranti. Typi non ex quavis parte historiae eruuntur, sed ea tantum, quae proprie ad rem, qua de agitur, pertinet, & ad quam intendebat Spiritus S. Sed allegoriae, item moralis sensus bene ex quavis parte colligitur. Typi proprie exponendi referendaeq; sunt ad personam Christi, & res per ipsum gerendas, vixq; ulterius progrediuntur. Allegoriae latius deducuntur, & plurimum ad personas aliorum.
units.tr: Types, which people commonly also call figures, are those cases where some deed or event is taken from the Old Testament and shown to have signified something that was to be done in the New Testament, or that has already been done and fulfilled there. For example, Jonah's three days in the belly of the whale were a type of the burial and resurrection of Christ in that respect. The serpent lifted up in the desert was a type of the crucified Christ, as Christ himself, the most skilled interpreter, explains. Allegories are rather located in doctrine and precepts, and they teach us that something spiritual is to be done by us. Such allegorical interpretations can be seen everywhere in the ancient writers. Types arise from plain historical narratives; allegories arise from other material, such as sayings, precepts and the like, as in "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain." Types are not drawn from just any part of a history, but only from those things that pertain properly to the matter under discussion and that the Holy Spirit intended. Allegories, and likewise the moral sense, are readily drawn from any part whatever. Types are properly to be explained and referred to the person of Christ and to the things to be done by him, and they do not go much further. Allegories are extended more widely and are applied mostly to the persons of others.

units.la: Typi directe & simpliciter sua narratione respondent rei significatae, ut manifestum sit Spiritum sanctum rem istam voluisse ibi adumbrare, & non aliam (sicut & hic cernimus
units.tr: Types correspond directly and simply to the thing signified by their narration, so that it is plain the Holy Spirit wished that particular thing to be foreshadowed there and no other (as we see here too,

units.la: ab Apostolo dictum, significante hoc Spiritu sancto) Allegoriae non ita proprie convenient, sed plerunq; longius petuntur, & obliquè accommodantur, & non sunt intentæ à Spiritu sancto, sed vt quisq; affectus est, ita aliter atq; aliter possunt eas explicare. Typica sunt & perspicui, neq; verborum mutationem requirunt, vel tropos, sed simpliciter eis narratio cum narratione componitur. In allegoriis semper est quædam obscuritas, unde & mystica intelligentia appellatur. Allegoricæ interpretationes sæpè adhibetur necessitate, quando alias ob verborum obscuritatem seu tropos non constat certa sententiæ ratio: In typis nihil tale fit, nulla necessitate, sed ob claram similitudinem elicitur, & tropos in verbis non habent. In summa, oportet semper prudenter distinguere inter allegoriam & typum: quod ideo sicâ nobis ostenditur, quia plurimos videmus, qui sibi videntur maximi artifices, & mirè sibi placent, in allegoriis tractandis insulse vtinam non etiâ periculosè) ludere. Vereor ne quibusdam contingat, quod Hieronymus sibi vsu- ueniisse dolet, quòd videlicet calore iuuenili provocatus gloriatus fit apud se, quòd posset interpretari Abdiam Prophetam allegoricè, cùm tamen nondum intelligeret nudam & simplicem historiam. Stultum se vocat, qui eo tempore ausus fuerit sibi de se tantum persuadere. Sed hæc satis. Iam simpliciter, clarè, & citra ambages typicè de Christo res tabernaculi explicemus. Neq; verò istud audebimus pro nostro capite, sed ducem sequemur Apostolum, qui nobis fœliciter viam strauit. Proinde cùm ipse interpretatus sit summum pontificem, Christum: Sancta sanctorum, cœlum: ingressum, & unicam oblatione semel in anno, unicum sacrificium Christi semel in morte peractum: prohibitionem cæterorum ab ingressu, quòd via in sancta seu cœlos nondum fuerit sub lege manifestata. Hæc inquam omnia quando Apostolus ita cœpit interpretari, æquum est nos sequentes istud exordium progrediamur, & tali fundamento conuenientem structuram supponamus. Inprimis ve- rò quæ summi pontificis sunt, Christo tribuemus: quæ verò cæterorum sacerdotum, ea reliquis quoq; sanctis, atq; in his potissimum Apostolis tribuemus. Constituamus ergo Christum ingredientem in primum tabernaculum siue tabernaculi atrium. Quid autem primū istud tabernaculum nobis significat? Quemadmodum Apostolus interius tabernaculum dicit esse cœlos, ita conuenit per comparationem exterius seu primum tabernaculum dicere esse typum ecclesiæ hic in terris constitutæ. Quæ & tabernaculum diuersis Scripturæ locis appellatur: vt Psal. 14. Domine, quis habitabit in tabernaculo, aut quis requiescet in monte sancto tuo? Esai. 33. Oculi tui videbut Hierusalem habitationem opulentam, tabernaculum, quod nequaquam transferri poterit, nec auferentur clauì eius in sempiternum, & omnes funiculi eius non rumpentur, quia solummodo ibi magnificatus est Dominus Deus noster. Præterea ecclesiæ conuenit, sanctæ appellatio, vt si cui rei alteri. In sola enim ecclesia sanctitas est, iuxta illud, Domũ tuam Domine decet sanctitas in longitudine dierum. Proinde tabernaculum istud Christus pontifex ingressus est, quando è cœlis in terras descendit, et velum (quod etiam nō absurdè humanā carnem dixerimus) subintrauit: sicut Apostolus ipse & deinde Chrysostomus, & quidā alij interpretati sunt. Hac enim quasi velo diuinitas fuit tecta & abstrusa, donec potentia & virtute palàm cōmonstrata est. Quò pertinet, quòd corpus humanū etiam tabernaculum vocatur. 2. Corint. 5. & indui atq; exui ibidem de carne vsurpatur. Ingressus tabernaculū statim occurrit altare holocausti concauum, in qua bruta animalia Deo offeruntur, & igne exuruntur. Hoc altare concauum significat nobis summam Christi humiliationem & obedientiā, qua semetipsum exinaniuit, forma serui assumpta humilem præbuit semetipsum, factus obediens vsq; ad mortem, mortem autē crucis, Philip. 2. Victimam brutam attulit Christus, nempe suam carnem, secundum quam, vt de ipso ait Propheta, quasi ouis ad occisionem ductus est, & sicut agnus coram tondente se mutus, sic non aperuit os suum. In humilitate ipsius iudicium eius sublatum est. Iterum alibi, Oblatus est, quia ipse voluit. Ignis verò est ingens Christi charitas, qua ad ita se humiliandum pro salute humani generis inflammatus est. Sic enim & charitas in Scripturis frigescens & ardescens describitur, & magna charitate inflammati sancti dicuntur. Esai. 4. Si abluet Dominus, sordes filiarum Sion, & sanguinem Hierusalem lauerit de medio eius, in spiritu iudicij & spiritu ardoris. Cæterùm quòd in hoc altari non tantùm summus sacerdos, sed etiam cæteri cooperabantur, significat, quòd etiam alios sanctos humilitas & obedientia erga Deum deceat, ac parati etiam esse debeant animam suam per charitatem pro fratribus suis ponere.
units.tr: as the Apostle said, the Holy Spirit signifying this). Allegories do not fit so properly; they are usually sought from farther off and applied obliquely, and the Holy Spirit did not intend them. Rather, each interpreter explains them as he is disposed, and they can be explained in one way after another. Types are clear and plain, and they do not require a change of words or tropes; their narrative is simply set alongside the narrative they signify. Allegories always carry some obscurity, which is why they are called mystical understanding. Allegorical interpretations are often resorted to out of necessity, when otherwise the certain sense of a passage is not evident because of the obscurity of the words or the tropes. Nothing of this kind happens with types: they are not drawn out of any necessity, but are elicited from a clear likeness, and they contain no tropes in their words. In sum, one must always distinguish prudently between allegory and type. This is pointed out here because we see many who seem to themselves to be the greatest craftsmen and take great pleasure in toying with allegories, foolishly (I wish it were not also dangerously). I fear that some may experience what Jerome regretted happening to himself: when, stirred by youthful ardour, he boasted to himself that he could interpret the prophet Obadiah allegorically, although he did not yet understand the bare and simple history. He calls foolish the man who dared, at that time, to persuade himself of so much about himself. But enough of this. Now let us explain the things of the tabernacle typically concerning Christ simply, clearly and without circumlocution. We shall not dare to do this on our own authority, but we shall follow the Apostle as our leader, who has happily paved the way for us. Accordingly, since he himself has interpreted the high priest as Christ, the Holy of Holies as heaven, the entrance, and the one offering made once a year as the one sacrifice of Christ, accomplished once in death, and the prohibition of the others from entering because the way into the holy places, or heavens, had not yet been made manifest under the law: when the Apostle began to interpret all these things in this way, it is fitting that we follow this beginning and lay down a structure suited to such a foundation. First of all, we shall ascribe to Christ what belongs to the high priest; what belongs to the other priests we shall ascribe to the rest of the saints, and especially among them to the Apostles. Let us therefore establish Christ entering the first tabernacle, or the court of the tabernacle. What then does this first tabernacle signify to us? As the Apostle calls the inner tabernacle the heavens, so by comparison it is fitting to say that the outer or first tabernacle is a type of the Church established here on earth. The Church is also called a tabernacle in various places of Scripture, as in Psalm 14: "Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy hill?" And in Isaiah 33: "Your eyes shall see Jerusalem, a peaceful habitation, a tabernacle that cannot be moved, nor shall its stakes ever be pulled up, and none of its cords shall be broken, because there the Lord our God will be exalted alone." Moreover, the name holy belongs to the Church, as to nothing else; for holiness is found only in the Church, according to the saying, "Holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days." Therefore Christ the high priest entered this tabernacle when he descended from heaven to earth and passed through the veil (which we may not absurdly call human flesh), as the Apostle himself and afterwards Chrysostom and some others have explained. For the divinity was covered and hidden, as it were, by this veil, until it was openly displayed in power and virtue. To this belongs the fact that the human body is also called a tabernacle, in 2 Corinthians 5, and that being clothed and unclothed is used there of the flesh. Immediately on entering the tabernacle one meets the hollow altar of burnt offering, on which brute animals are offered to God and burned with fire. This hollow altar signifies to us the supreme humiliation and obedience of Christ, by which he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even the death of the cross (Philippians 2). Christ brought the brute victim, namely his own flesh, according to which, as the Prophet says of him, he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is dumb, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Again elsewhere: "He was offered because he himself willed it." The fire, however, is Christ's immense love, by which he was kindled to humble himself so greatly for the salvation of the human race. For thus love in the Scriptures is described as growing cold and growing hot, and saints inflamed with great love are said to be so. Isaiah 4: "If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall cleanse the blood of Jerusalem from her midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." Moreover, that not only the high priest but also the other priests cooperated at this altar signifies that humility and obedience toward God befit other saints too, and that they ought also to be ready to lay down their lives for their brothers through love.

units.la: Sequitur altare incensi. Hic Aaron quotidie mane & vespepi adolebat incensum suaue fragrans, & semel in anno deprecabatur in sanguine, qui oblatus erat pro peccato. Sic vero & Christus suaue incensum obtulit, quando igne charitatis inflammatus pro omnibus, qui in ipsum credituri erant, Deum patrem assiduè orauit. Ioan. 17. Orationem vero rectè comparari incenso, liquet ex illo psal. 141. Oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo.
units.tr: Next comes the altar of incense. Here Aaron every morning and evening burned sweet-smelling incense, and once a year he made atonement with the blood that was offered for sin. So also Christ offered a sweet incense when, kindled with the fire of love, he constantly prayed to God the Father for all who were about to believe in him (John 17). That prayer is rightly compared to incense is clear from Psalm 141: "Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you."

units.la: Pet Per incensum videtur posse accipi studium illustrandi patris gloriam, & perficiendi eius voluntatem. Vel, incensum congregatio credentium, quam Christus patri collegit & obtulit. Christi bonus odor sumus, 2. Corinth. 2. Et cùm Christus semper pro salute hominum orauerit, etiá pendens in cruce, rectè dicitur quotidie incensum obtulisse. Semel deinde deprecatus est in sanguine, quando propter mortem & sanguinem oratio ipsius potissimum exaudita est & accepta: sicut & instante morte potissimùm & ardentissimè orasse legitur. Patri acceptum fuisse incensum Christi, liquet ex eo, quòd pater dixerit: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene còplacitum est: tùm ex eo, quòd, vti dictum est capite quinto, cùm precationes & supplicationes obtulisset cum clamore valido & lachrymis, exauditus est pro reverentia. Iam venitur ad candelabrum aureum & mensam propositionis, quæ vtraq; etiam per summum sacerdotem parabantur, vt habetur Leuit. 24. Mensa aurea, cui imponebantur per singula Sabbatha duodecim panes cum lucido thure, quibus deinde Aaron & filij eius vescebantur, pulchrè significat nobis, purum verbum seu doctrinam, qua nihil excellentius, salutarem, quam Christus in Ecclesia propositi, per ministros, potissimumq; per duodecim Apostolos deinde propagandam, qua omnes sancti vescerentur: sicut & Christus solo verbo sustentatus est, quando adversus diabolum decertauit, vt ipse aiebat, recitans illud Deut. 8. Non solo pane viuit homo, sed omni verbo, quod egreditur per os Dei. Quòd nunquam vacuum sit altare, significat, quòd Deus ecclesiam suam nunquam vult verbo destitutam esse, sed semper per interualla illi Deū prospicere. Thus superadditum, quòd doctrina & officium docendi Deo sit quasi grata victima, & quòd ad gloriam vnius Dei omnis debet tendere. Quòd panes sine fermeto, significatur, puram & sine fermento Pharisaico semper debere proponi. Et panes hi propositionis seu facierum, quòd doctrina Euangelica semper ob oculos constituta esse debeat. Candelabrum aureum cum septem lucernis omni tempore lucens, & quotidie vesperi & mane per pontificem præparatum, significat vitam Christi & exemplum, quod itidem in Ecclesia est per ipsum propositum, vt omnes illud sequantur, & in offenso pede gradiantur. Quod valde bene positum est è regione mensæ, quòd doctrina & vita simul debent ab omnibus considerari, & omnibus ingredientibus in Ecclesiā statim esse conspicua, sicut Christus describitur potens opere sermone. Septem lucernæ impositæ, sunt actiones illæ Christi, in quibus dona spiritus Sancti maximè eminent, de quibus Christus etiam per miraculum Lucæ 4. legebat ex Esaiæ 61. de Spiritu Domini super ipsum: sed de donis Spiritus in operibus Christi relucentibus Esaiæ 11. Egredietur virga de radice Iesse & flos de radice eius ascendet, & requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, Spiritus sapientiæ & intellectus, Spiritus consilij & fortitudinis, Spiritus scientiæ & timoris Iehouæ, & replebit eum Spiritus timoris Domini. Quanquam per septenarium numerum perfectio crebrò notatur, & sic summa perfectio in vita Christi ostendetur. Per lucem autem siue lumen rectè intelligi vitam ac mores siue opera liquet, ex verbis Christi Matth. 5. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant vestra bona opera, glorificentq; patrem vestrum, qui est in cœlis. Et Ioann. 5. Christus vocat Ioannem lucernam ardentem & lucentem. Quod autē Christus propriè lucem hanc accendat, patet Ioan. 1. Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem, &c. Ioan. 8. Ego sum lux mundi, qui sequitur me, nō ambulat in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ. Porrò quòd & mensa & lucerna per pontificem parabantur, ideo id factū, quia doctrina & exemplum nullius nisi Christi debent in Ecclesia proponi. Sancti quidem hac in parte collaborant, sed tamen neque quaquàm vt ipsi audiendi, spectandi, sequendi proponuntur. Immediatè à Christo omnis sana doctrina & exemplum operum debet accipi. Post hæc labrū æneum plenū aqua, in qua pontifex cū filijs lauat, repræsentat Christi passionē ac mortem, de qua ipse alias dixit Luc. 12. Ignem veni mittere in terrā, & quid volo, si iam accensus est? Sed baptismo habeo baptizari, & quomodo coartor donec perficiatur. Item Marci 10. ad filios Zebedæi, Nescitis quid petatis, potestis bibere poculum quod ego bibo, et baptismate, quo ego baptizor, baptizari? & cætera, quæ sequūtur. Itaq; per baptismū passionem Christi rectè intelligemus, ex qua & baptismus nostrer lauacrum regenerationis trahit originem, & in quā baptizamur & cōsepelimur. Rom. 6. Et non solus pontifex, sed & filij lauantur, quia cum Christo oportet etiā alios gestare, cùm alias via in sancta sanctorū, id est, cœlos nō nisi per tribulationes & angustias pateat. Et quotidie lauamur, dum quotidie in mundo premimur, & p omne vitam pœnitentia agimus. Qui non accipit crucē, & sequit me, nō est me dignus. Et nō est discipulo melior præceptore. Si me psecuti sunt, et vos psequent.
units.tr: Per the incense may be understood the zeal for advancing the Father's glory and carrying out his will. Or the incense may be the congregation of believers, which Christ gathered and offered to the Father: "We are the good savour of Christ," 2 Cor. 2. And since Christ always prayed for the salvation of men, even while hanging on the cross, it is rightly said that he offered incense daily. Then he prayed once in the blood, when, because of his death and blood, his prayer was especially heard and accepted, just as he is read to have prayed most earnestly and intensely when death was at hand. That Christ's incense was acceptable to the Father is clear from the fact that the Father said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"; and also from the fact that, as was said in chapter five, when he offered prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, he was heard because of his reverence. Now we come to the golden candlestick and the table of the showbread, which were both prepared by the high priest, as is related in Lev. 24. The golden table, on which twelve loaves were placed every Sabbath with pure frankincense, and of which Aaron and his sons then ate, beautifully signifies to us the pure word, or doctrine, than which nothing is more excellent or saving, set forth in the Church by ministers, and especially by the twelve apostles, to be propagated afterwards, on which all the saints might feed. Just as Christ himself was sustained by the word alone when he struggled against the devil, as he himself said, quoting Deut. 8: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." That the altar is never empty signifies that God never wills his Church to be destitute of the word, but always to look upon her at intervals. The frankincense added signifies that doctrine and the office of teaching are, as it were, an acceptable sacrifice to God, and that everything ought to tend to the glory of the one God. That the loaves are without leaven signifies that they ought always to be set forth pure, without Pharisaic leaven. And these loaves of the setting forth, or of the faces, signify that evangelical doctrine ought always to be placed before the eyes. The golden candlestick with seven lamps, shining at all times and prepared daily by the priest morning and evening, signifies the life and example of Christ, which is likewise set forth in the Church by him, so that all may follow it and walk in its footsteps. It is very well placed opposite the table: doctrine and life ought to be considered together by all, and be conspicuous at once to all who enter the Church, just as Christ is described as mighty in work and in word. The seven lamps set upon it are those actions of Christ in which the gifts of the Holy Spirit especially shine forth. Christ himself, by a miracle, read of these in Luke 4 from Isaiah 61: the Spirit of the Lord is upon him. But concerning the gifts of the Spirit shining in the works of Christ, see Isaiah 11: "A shoot shall come forth from the stem of Jesse, and a flower shall grow up from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Jehovah; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him." Although perfection is often noted by the number seven, so the highest perfection is shown in the life of Christ. That by light or lamp is rightly understood life, manners, or works, is clear from the words of Christ, Matt. 5: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." And in John 5 Christ calls John "a burning and shining lamp." That Christ himself properly kindles this light is plain from John 1: "That was the true light, which enlightens every man," etc. John 8: "I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." Furthermore, that both the table and the lamp were prepared by the priest, that was because doctrine and example ought to be set forth in the Church by no one but Christ. The saints indeed labour in this part, but they are by no means set forth as those to be heard, looked at, or followed. Every sound doctrine and every example of works ought to be received immediately from Christ. After these, the bronze laver full of water, in which the priest and his sons wash, represents the passion and death of Christ, of which he himself spoke elsewhere, Luke 12: "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish, if it is already kindled? But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I constrained until it is accomplished?" Likewise Mark 10, to the sons of Zebedee: "You know not what you ask. Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" and the rest that follows. Thus through baptism we rightly understand the passion of Christ, from which our baptism, the bath of regeneration, also draws its origin, and into which we are baptized and buried with him, Rom. 6. And not only the priest but also the sons are washed, because with Christ it is necessary to bear others as well, since otherwise the way into the holy of holies, that is, heaven, lies open only through tribulations and straits. And we are washed daily, while we are daily pressed in the world, and throughout our life we practise repentance. "Whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me." "The disciple is not above his teacher." "If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also."

units.la: His ita peractis ingreditur pontifex per aliud velum in sancta sanctorum: ita & Christus assumpta iterum, carne sua gloriosa in resurrectione, ascendit in cœlos. Quid autem intra tabernaculum? Arca testimonij & propitiatorium arcę impositum,
units.tr: When these things have been done, the high priest enters through the other veil into the holy of holies; so Christ, having taken up again his glorified flesh in the resurrection, ascends into heaven. What is inside the tabernacle? The ark of the testimony, with the mercy seat placed upon the ark.

units.la: Et coram hoc sacerdos semel in anno ingrediens incensum offert, precatur, & septies aspergit sanguinem expiationis. Arca cum propiciatorio suo situ ac dispositione pulchrè nobis sedem omnipotentis Dei repræsentat, ita ut propitiatorium sit veluti suprema sedes, arca verò se habeat fere instar scabelli: sicut etiam 1. Reg. 4. vbi agebatur de ea perferenda in exercitum, vocatur arca fœderis Domini exercituum sedentis super Cherubim. Iterum 2. Reg. 5. Surrexitque Dauid & abijt, & vniuersus populus qui erat cum eo de viris Iudah, vt adducerent arcam Dei, super quam inuocatum est nomen Domini exercituum sedentis in Cherubim super eam. Sed & Psalm. 79. 98. & alijs locis eodem pacto scriptura loquitur. Coram Deo patre igitur confidente in sede maiestatis Christus incensum offert & precatur, dum nimirum intercedit & interpellat pro nobis, sicut supra capite septimo dictum est, & alibi saepius id faciens describitur. 1. Ioann. 2. aduocatus vocatur, alibi mediator. Aspergit sanguinem, videlicet suum sanguinem, & mortem offerens, pro peccatis, vt pater moueatur ad condonandum peccata. Et quidem septies, id est, plenè & efficaciter, vt ad satisfaciendum pro omnis generis peccatis abunde sufficiat. Et ad orientem, quia ad eam plagam more scripturae Deo suus locus tribuitur, iuxta illud psalm. 67. Psallite Deo, qui ascendit super coelum coeli, ad orientem. Et Christus ipse ex alto oriens demonstratur, Lucae 1. Ad dandam scientiam salutis populo ipsius per remissionem peccatorum: per viscera misericordiae Dei nostri quibus visitauit nos oriens ex alto.
units.tr: Before this, the priest, entering once a year, offers incense, prays, and sprinkles the blood of atonement seven times. The ark with its mercy seat and arrangement beautifully represents to us the throne of almighty God, so that the mercy seat is as it were the supreme seat, while the ark is roughly like a footstool. So also in 1 Sam. 4, where it is spoken of being carried into the army, the ark is called "the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits upon the cherubim." Again, 2 Sam. 6: "David arose and went, and all the people who were with him from the men of Judah, to bring up the ark of God, upon which the name of the Lord of hosts who sits upon the cherubim is invoked." But also Psalm 79 and 98, and other places, Scripture speaks in the same way. Christ therefore offers incense and prays before God the Father, who sits on the throne of majesty, namely while he intercedes and pleads for us, as was said above in chapter seven, and as he is often described as doing elsewhere. In 1 John 2 he is called an advocate, and elsewhere a mediator. He sprinkles the blood, namely his own blood, offering his death for sins, so that the Father may be moved to forgive sins. And indeed seven times, that is, fully and effectively, so that it is abundantly sufficient to make satisfaction for every kind of sin. And toward the east, because according to the manner of Scripture God's place is assigned to that quarter, in accordance with Psalm 67: "Sing to God, who rides over the heaven of heavens, toward the east." And Christ himself is shown as rising from on high, Luke 1: "to give knowledge of salvation to his people by the remission of their sins, through the tender mercy of our God, by which the dayspring from on high has visited us."

units.la: Cherubim obumbrantes propitiatorium, angeli & sancti congaudentes & congratulantes, propter salutem per Christū procuratam: sicut Ezechiel. 10. & 11. describitur. Cherubim gloriam Domini testificantes: & Christus in Euangelio dicit angelos laetari super vno peccatore poenitentiam agente. Iam, quòd tabulae testimonij, virga Aaron, Manna, sunt in sancta sanctorum translata, & quidem in arca, siue prope arcam repositá, quasi sub Dei pedibus significari videtur, quòd lex, sacerdotium legale, & electio populi Israelitici essent abroganda, & non amplius in ecclesia locum habitura. Quamuis aliter etiam rectè interpretabimur tabulas repositas & recoditas in arca, significare, quòd lex in coelis quiescat, nō amplius vires habeat, quia ibi soli sancti sunt, quibus nihil amplius praescribitur, quia omnia obseruant spiritualiter, & Christus omnia in omnibus adimplet.
units.tr: The cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat show the angels and saints rejoicing and congratulating one another over the salvation procured through Christ, as Ezekiel 10 and 11 describe. The cherubim bear witness to the glory of the Lord, and Christ says in the Gospel that the angels rejoice over one sinner who repents. Now, that the tablets of the testimony, Aaron's rod and the manna were placed in the Holy of Holies, and indeed in the ark or stored close beside it, seems to signify, as it were beneath God's feet, that the law, the legal priesthood and the election of the Israelite people were to be abrogated and would no longer have a place in the Church. Yet we may also rightly interpret the tablets placed and hidden in the ark as signifying that the law rests in heaven and no longer has force there, because only the saints are there, to whom nothing more is prescribed, since they observe all things spiritually, and Christ fulfils all things in all.

units.la: Virga Aaron florens, æternū & semper durans Christi sacerdotium adumbrat in coelis, vbi Christus etiam manet semper pro nobis intercedens. Manna verò significat plenam fruitionem gloriae & bonitatis Dei, qua sancti ibi satiantur, longè magis, quàm vlis bonis hic in terris possemus satiari. Atq; haec de Christo sic expolita sufficiant.
units.tr: Aaron's rod in flower signifies the eternal and ever-enduring priesthood of Christ in heaven, where Christ also remains always interceding for us. The manna signifies the full enjoyment of the glory and goodness of God, by which the saints are satisfied there far more than we could be satisfied by any good things here on earth. Let these things about Christ, set out in this way, suffice.

units.la: Iam si quis auet explicare officia caeterorum piorum, quę in atrio ipsi peragant, secundum moralem interpretationem, videat Origenem homilia 9. in Exodum, item Rabanū, item Cyrillum in Leuiticum. Nos verbum non addemus amplius. Iam progredientes doctrinam & consolationes in caeteris ostendere, annotabimus illis verbis, Significante illud Spiritu sancto, nihil frustrà ordinatum esse in veteri testamento: sed omnia mirabili prouidentia Dei, vel ad formandam vitam externam, vel ad instruendas conscientias de mysterijs rerum Euangelicarū esse sic constituta & praescripta. Nec potest Spiritus sanctus aliter, quàm optimè omnia disponere, non potest errare, vel labi in iudicio, et priusquàm aliquid ordinat, praeuidet ac praedefinit finem, & bonum ad quod ordinat. Secundò, discimus ex ijsdem verbis, quanto in honore sint sacra scripta habenda, quando nimirum autore Spiritu sancto sunt edita, qui Scriptores omnes afflauit atq; instituit. Spiritui sancto palàm resistit, quicūq; Scripturas contemnit. Quae ab hominibus scripta vel dicta sunt, qua ratione suscipiuntur, eadem & reijciuntur: at quae à Spiritu S. dicta sunt, reijci sine graui crimine haud possunt. Tertiò, discimus eas quaerendas & recipiendas interpretationes, quae sunt propriae Spiritus sancti: quandoquidem sicut ipse Scripturarum est Autor, ita fidelissimus interpres, & contra ipsius gloriam alia gloria non admittetur. Quamuis interea nō credendū cuiuis iactanti quòd Spiritus S. dicat, aut quòd Spiritus ipsi reuelarit: probādi sunt .n. Spiritus, num ex Deo sint. 1. Ioan. 4. Quartò, habemus hic certū documentū, quòd vetus testamentū non sit conditū à Deo malo vel in clemente, vt Manichaei suspicati sunt, neq; item à quoda Deo medio, vt voluerūt Ptolomaitę, sed à Deo bono omnia quàm ordinatissimè ad docēdos homines de salute sua cōstituente. Non solum lex moralis à sapiente bono & misericorde Domino lata esse declaratur, verūmetiā ceremonialis, in quo omnia plena fuerunt mysteriis, & adumbrarunt res per Christum nostrae salutis causa perficiendas. Quintò, quòd, cum à bono Deo conditam legem cōstet, non ita tamen, vt ad solùm patrem referatur, sed etiā ad filium & ad spiritum Sanctum. Nam ecce Spiritus sanctus ordinator ceremoniarum hic palàm describitur.
units.tr: Now if anyone wishes to explain the duties of the other pious people, which they perform in the court, according to a moral interpretation, let him see Origen, Homily 9 on Exodus; likewise Rabanus; likewise Cyril on Leviticus. We will add no more words. Proceeding now to show the teaching and consolations in the rest, we will note those words: "The Holy Spirit, signifying this, [shows] that nothing in the Old Testament was ordained in vain, but that all things, by the wonderful providence of God, were so established and prescribed either to form external life or to instruct consciences about the mysteries of the Gospel matters." The Holy Spirit cannot arrange things otherwise than most excellently; he cannot err or slip in judgment, and before he ordains anything he foresees and predefines the end and the good to which he ordains it. Secondly, we learn from the same words how greatly the sacred writings are to be held in honour, since they were published with the Holy Spirit as their author, who inspired and instructed all the writers. Whoever despises the Scriptures openly resists the Holy Spirit. Writings or sayings of men are received or rejected on grounds of reason, but what the Holy Spirit has said cannot be rejected without grave crime. Thirdly, we learn that the interpretations to be sought and accepted are those which are proper to the Holy Spirit; for just as he is the author of the Scriptures, so he is their most faithful interpreter, and no other glory will be admitted against his glory. Meanwhile, however, one must not believe any boaster who says that the Holy Spirit says this, or that the Spirit has revealed it to him; for the spirits must be tested, whether they are of God (1 John 4). Fourthly, we have here a certain proof that the Old Testament was not founded by an evil or unmerciful God, as the Manichaeans suspected, nor by some intermediate God, as the Ptolemaeans wished, but by the good God, who arranged all things most orderly to teach men about their salvation. It is declared that not only the moral law but also the ceremonial law was given by the wise, good and merciful Lord, in which everything was full of mysteries and foreshadowed the things to be accomplished through Christ for the cause of our salvation. Fifthly, since it is established that the law was founded by the good God, it is not referred to the Father alone, but also to the Son and to the Holy Spirit; for behold, the Holy Spirit, the orderer of the ceremonies, is openly described here.

units.la: Sextò, quādo dicitur, quòd sacrificia legis nō possunt iuxta conscientiā pfectos reddere,
units.tr: Sixthly, when it is said that the sacrifices of the law cannot make the worshippers perfect in conscience,

units.la: habemus perspicuum argumetum, quòd neq; sacrificia, neq; Sacramenta ex opere operato iustificent. Quę enim instituta sunt ad exercendos rudes, in humilitate, in confessione peccatorum, et ad testandā suam fidem, ea iustificationem ex sese non conferunt: sed quòd quispiam illorum vsu salutem consequatur, id per fidem in Christum (qui in sacrificijs & Sacramentis omnibus adumbratur) contingit, cùm sine fide & quidem propria ad salutem aditus nulli pateat. Septimò: diligėter, est Euangelij obseruanda præ lege dignitas, ex ratione diuersi modi iustificandi, videndum q;, quantum differnt iustificationes carnis, & iustificationes spiritus. Et cum in multis cernantur iustificationes carnis, qui videlicet coram mundo norunt sese gerere tanquàm omnium mortalium sanctissimi, tamen à iustificatione interna et spititus absunt longissimè, sunt sepulchra foris speciosa, at intus scatent vermibus: foris gestant vestitum ouium, intus verò sunt lupi rapaces. Octauò: quando, vbi dicitur, legem fuisse similitudinem pro tempore tùm præsente, vsq; ad tempus correctionis impositam, manifestè ostenditur, tempus illud correctionis esse tempus Euangelij, quo videlicet omnia corriguntur & instauratur: sicut idem quoq; diserte praedicatur Ephes. 1. & alibi: debet descriptio hæc temporis Euangelici non solùm Euangelij præ lege excellentiam ostendere, verùmetiam extimulare nos ad vitam in melius restituendam & corrigendam, ad aspirandum ad maiorem perfectionem, ad laborandum, vt iustitia nostra abundet supra iustitiam Scribarum & Pharisæorum. Nonò: quinetiam, quando omnia sunt in Euangelio correcta, & in locum corporaliū tùm operū, tùm præmiorū, successerunt spiritualia, pariter opera in quam & præmia, æquum est spiritualibus exercitijs, quæ in Euangelio proponuntur, nos assiduè exerceamus, & simus intenti, vt cœlestia & spiritualia bona nobis & in hac vita & in altera obueniant. Decimò: sed & consolatione accipere inde debemus, nosq; fœlices iudicare, quibus omnia meliora & perfectiora sunt proposita, quàm patribus sub lege agentibus. Vndecimò: vbi describitur nobis Christus nouus pontifex futurorum & cœlestium bonorum, & ingrediens p maius & perfectius tabernaculum, per proprium sanguinem: hæc omnia præbent nobis consolationum materiam. Videmus enim non solùm excellentiam Euangelij pro lege, sed quomodo salus nostra sit peracta, per sanguinem videlicet Christi: quomodo item tabernaculum nobis sit per eundem præparatū, quod migrantes hinc ingredi debeamus. Hic deberet vniusquiusq; animus sanctissimis meditationibus occupari, atq; altissimè cōtemplari, qualis thesaurus sanguis Christi, qualia sint futura bona, quale tabernaculum sit nobis paratū: & habere contra omnia pericula, quę in hac vita possunt tàm spiritualia, quàm corporalia obtingere, præsentissima remedia. Quinetiam moueremur talibus bonis propositis ad ita vitam instituendā, similiter ad agendas Deo pro immensa bonitate sua gratias, vt bonorum illorum fructus suo tempore ad nos perueniat. Postremò: quando ita audimus agi de redemptione æterna, cogitemus è contrario, quàm refugienda atq; horrenda sit res, æterna seruitus peccati, mortis et diaboli, atq; æterna damnatio: Ac tùm incipiemus intelligere, quàm expetenda res sit æterna redemptio. Quòd si deinde hanc recte possemus æstimare, non dubium, quin per omnem vitam à peccatis abstineremus.
units.tr: we have a clear argument that neither sacrifices nor sacraments justify ex opere operato. For those things which were instituted to exercise the untaught, in humility and in the confession of sins, and to attest their faith, do not of themselves confer justification; but if anyone obtains salvation by their use, this happens through faith in Christ, who is foreshadowed in all sacrifices and sacraments, since without faith, and indeed one's own faith, no access to salvation lies open. Seventhly, the dignity of the Gospel above the law is to be carefully observed, and from the reason of the different mode of justifying we must also see how far the justifications of the flesh differ from the justifications of the spirit. Although many justifications of the flesh are seen, men who know how to conduct themselves before the world as the holiest of all mortals, yet they are far distant from the inward justification of the spirit: they are sepulchres, fair outwardly, but inwardly full of worms; they wear sheep's clothing outwardly, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. Eighthly, when it is said that the law was imposed as a figure for the present time, until the time of correction, it is clearly shown that this time of correction is the time of the Gospel, in which, namely, all things are corrected and restored, as the same is also expressly preached in Ephesians 1 and elsewhere. This description of the Gospel time ought to show not only the excellence of the Gospel above the law, but also to stir us to restore and correct our life for the better, to aspire to greater perfection, and to labour so that our righteousness may abound above the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. Ninthly, moreover, since all things have been corrected in the Gospel, and spiritual things have succeeded in place of bodily works and rewards, it is equally fitting that we constantly exercise ourselves in the spiritual exercises set forth in the Gospel, and be intent that heavenly and spiritual goods may come to us both in this life and in the next. Tenthly, we ought also to take consolation from this and count ourselves happy, to whom all things are set forth better and more perfectly than to the fathers who lived under the law. Eleventhly, where Christ is described to us as the new high priest of future and heavenly goods, entering through a greater and more perfect tabernacle by his own blood, all these things provide us with matter for consolation. For we see not only the excellence of the Gospel over the law, but how our salvation has been accomplished, namely through the blood of Christ; and likewise how a tabernacle has been prepared for us by the same, which we ought to enter when we depart hence. Here every mind ought to be occupied with the most holy meditations and to contemplate most highly what a treasure the blood of Christ is, what good things are to come, and what tabernacle is prepared for us; and to have at hand the most present remedies against all the dangers which can befall us in this life, whether spiritual or bodily. Moreover, moved by such goods set before us, we would order our life accordingly, and likewise give thanks to God for his immense goodness, so that the fruit of those goods may reach us in its time. Lastly, when we hear the eternal redemption spoken of in this way, let us think on the contrary how dreadful and to be shunned a thing is eternal slavery to sin, death and the devil, and eternal damnation; then we will begin to understand how desirable eternal redemption is. And if we could then estimate this rightly, there would be no doubt that we would abstain from sins throughout all our life.

units.la: Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis iuuencæ aspergens inquinatos, sanctificat ad carnis purificationem: quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam uestram à mortuarijs operibus, ad seruiendum Deo uiuenti? Quòdnam sit sacrificium Christi, audiuimus. Et quàmuis paucis verbis ostenderit, id multò excellentius esse omnibus sacrificijs legalibus, tamen nunc, ne abs re videatur illud fecisse, subijcit probationes nonnullas, quibus præstantiam eius plenius docebit. Ac primùm quidem, quia asseruit hunc effectum sacrificij Christi, æternam videlicet redemptionem, quam opponi vult effectui sacrificiorū legaliū, id est, iustificationibus carnis, euincere vult, verum esse, quòd per oblatū Christi sanguinē redemptio æterna seu iustificatio spiritus habeatur, idq; huiusmodi Enthymemate: Sanguis taurorum & hircorū & cinis iuuencę aspergens inquinatos peccatis, sanctificat ad iustificationē carnis. Ergo multo magis sanguis Christi sanctificabit ad iustificationē Spiritus. Argumētatur à comparatis, siue à minore ad maius. Et maioris lucis caussa extulit per interrogationem. Tametsi quia in consequente non idem praedicatum est, quod in antecedente (in antecedente enim sermo est de iustificatione secundum carnem: in consequete verò infertur de iustificatione secundum spiritum:) potius iudicandum est, Apostolum argumentari à proportione, quasi in hunc modū diceret.
units.tr: "For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctify to the purification of the flesh: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" What the sacrifice of Christ is, we have heard. And although he has shown in few words that it is far more excellent than all the legal sacrifices, nevertheless, lest it seem to have been said without reason, he now adds some proofs by which he will teach its pre-eminence more fully. And first, because he has asserted that this effect of Christ's sacrifice, namely eternal redemption, which he sets against the effect of the legal sacrifices, that is, the justifications of the flesh, he wishes to prove that it is true that through the blood of Christ offered, eternal redemption or justification of the spirit is obtained; and he does so by this enthymeme: the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those unclean with sins sanctify to the justification of the flesh; therefore much more will the blood of Christ sanctify to the justification of the spirit. He argues from comparison, or from the lesser to the greater, and for the sake of greater clarity he brought it out by a question. Yet because the predicate in the consequent is not the same as in the antecedent (for in the antecedent the discussion is of justification according to the flesh, while in the consequent it is inferred of justification according to the spirit), it is rather to be judged that the Apostle argues from proportion, as if he were saying in this way...

units.la: Sicut se habet sanguis porcorum ad sanguinē Christi, ita se habet iustificatio carnis ad iustificationem Spiritus.
units.tr: Just as the blood of pigs stands to the blood of Christ, so the justification of the flesh stands to the justification of the Spirit.

units.la: Sed sanguis porcorum iustificat secundum carnem.
units.tr: But the blood of pigs justifies according to the flesh.

units.la: Ergo & sanguis Christi iustificat secundum spiritum.
units.tr: Therefore the blood of Christ also justifies according to the Spirit.

units.la: Valde autem necessarium erat, huiusmodi argumenta, probantia tàm præclarum effectum ctum sacrificij Christi, exponi, propterea quòd Hebræi legalia sua sacrificia extenuari in dignisimè ferebant, atque ut concesissent fortasis, sacrificium Christi legalibus sacrificijs æquari, tamen nunquàm admissuri erant, quòd aliqua in parte excelleret. Hoc igitur pluribus argumentis erat cōmonstrandum: quando in præstantia sacrificij Christi totius negotij cardo vertitur, & neq; abrogatio sacrificiorum legaliū, neque iustificatio nostra per id fieri posse intelligitur, nisi multò præstabilius atque efficacius omnibus sacrificijs legalibus ostendatur.
units.tr: It was very necessary to set out arguments of this kind, which prove so excellent an effect of the sacrifice of Christ. The Hebrews took their legal sacrifices to be greatly diminished by this. Even if they might have conceded that the sacrifice of Christ was equal to the legal sacrifices, they would never have admitted that it excelled them in any respect. This therefore had to be shown by several arguments, since the whole matter turns on the pre-eminence of the sacrifice of Christ. Neither the abrogation of the legal sacrifices nor our justification by Christ's sacrifice can be understood unless it is shown that his sacrifice is far more excellent and effective than all the legal sacrifices.

units.la: Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum) Præcedenti loco meminit vitulorū & hircorum: Quid est quod nunc de tauris loquitur? Respondendū: Non esse hic curiosè discrimen aliquod ponendum. Nam etiamsi præcepta quidè sonent de vitulis & hircis offerendis, uti ex Leuitici 16. ostendimus, vbi agitur de sacrificijs expiatorijs: tamen sæpe alias etiā tauros oblatos legimus, & coniunctos tauros cum hircis: ut Psal. 49. Nunquid manducabo carnes taurorum, aut sanguinem hircorum potabo? Immola Deo sacrificium laudis & redde altissimo vota tua. Quo loco etiam de abrogatione sacrificiorum agitur. Et 2 Paralipom. 29. Dauid cum omni multitudine immolauit victimas Domino, & obtulerūt holocausta die sequeti tauros mille, arietes mille, agnos mille, cū libaminib. suis, & vniuersò ritu, abundantissimè in omnem Israel: quod factum est, cùm Solomon inunctus esset in regem præsen te patre. Item 2. Paralip. 29. postquàm Ezechias iusiisset aperiri templum, restituisset q; sacerdotes, obtulit vniuersa multitudo hostias & laudes & holocausta mente devota. Porrò numerus holocaustorum, quæ obtulit multitudo, hic fuit, tauri septuaginta, arietes centum, agni ducenti, sanctificaueruntq; boues sexcentos, & oues ter mille. Sic deinceps sæpius factitatum est, & sub Esdra, aliisq;. Atq; apparet, ut maiorem gratitudinem cupiebat declarare, ita eos maiora & præstatiora solitos animalia offerre. Proinde Apostolus sumptuosissima quæq; sacrificia voluit nomine taurorum & hircorum intelligere, ut significaret, nulla quamlibet selecta & magnifica sacrificia aliquid altius potuisse adferre, quàm sanctificationem secundum carnem, & adhuc nullo modo conferenda esse cū sacrificio Christi. Iam addit & de cinere iuuencæ, quo asperguntur inquinati, de quo nulla adhuc facta mentio. Describitur autem purificatio solita fieri cinere iuuencæ, Num. 19. hisce verbis: Locutus est Dominus ad Mosen: præcipe filijs Israel, ut adducant ad te vaccam rufam æatis integræ, in qua nulla sit macula, nec portaueritiugum, tradesq; eam Eleazaro sacerdoti, qui eductam extra castra immolabit in conspectu omnium, & tingens digitum in sanguine eius asperget contra fores tabernaculi septem vicibus, comburetq; eam cunctis videntibus, tàm pelle & carnib. eius, quàm sanguine & fimo flammæ traditis. Lignū quoq; cedrinū & hyssopū, coccumq; bis tinctum sacerdos mittet in flammam, quæ vaccā vorat. Et paulo post: Colliget autem vir mundus cineres vaccæ, & effundet eos extra castra in loco purissimo, ut sint multitudini filiorum Israel in custodiam, & in aquam aspersionis, quia pro peccato vacca combusta est. Atque hoc vocatur ibi Israelitis sancto iure perpetuo. Cinis autem iste admiscebatur aquis, quæ seruabantur, & magnus ad purificationes diuersas erat eius usus: inprimis autem valebat ad emundandos eos, qui tetigissent cadauer hominis mortui: item purgabantur illi, qui erant in tentorio eius, qui obierat: itè omnis suppellex in eodē tentorio. Cùm ergo magna esset cineris huius exi stimata dignitas, voluit Apostolus hoc loco non tantum recensere de expiatione illa, quę fiebat semel in anno in sanctis sanctorum per sanguinem vituli & hirci, sed etiam de expiationibus alio tempore usitatis, eaq; potissimum, quæ fiebat cinere iuuencæ, ut sic generaliter comprehenderet præcipuas expiandi rationes: præ omnibus tamen longè maiorem expiandi vim sanguini Christi inesse euinceret. Erant quidem & alij mundationum ritus, nempe per ablutiones, cuiusmodi plures describuntur Leuitici decimoquinto: tantùm Apostolus hic enumerauit eas, quæ summo loco & quasi maioris efficaciæ habebātur. Atq; eò iustius etiā produxit exemplū, de cinere iuuencæ rufæ, quòd in hoc non minus fuerit typicè adumbratus Christus, quàm in exemplo de sanguine vituli & hirci. Nam vacca rufa seu bos Christū signat propter carnē, propter quam Christus apud proph etam dicitur habere vestes tinctas sanguine. Item absque macula erat vacca, quandoquidem Christus erat, licet per omnia similis fratrib. tamen absq; peccato, quod maculat & inquinat animam. Deniq; inexperta iugo, quòd Christus etiamsi carnem haberet, tamen neq; carnis, neq; peccati seruitute siue iugum gestauit. Merito ergo & ista particula de cinere iuuencæ ꝑ Apostolū est appositā. Ista verò omnia ait sanctificare ad carnis purificationē: Quia hoc tantum cōsequebant ita purgati, quòd in cōmune cœtū admittebant, anima interea manebat peccatis obnoxia. Et sicut maculæ his purgādæ erat potissimū carnales (cōtrahebatur enim cōtactu mortui, vel huiusmodi) ita purgatio non erat nisi carnalis. In summa, sicut externo cōtactu nō inquinatur anima, Christo id asserete, vbi ait, Nō qd' intrat in os, &c. ita externa lotio vel aspersio non purificat animam, sed tantum carnem, vbi facta est inquinatio. Notandum est, has voces, purificationem, sanctificationem, iustificationem, redemptionem, fere pro eodem vsurpari: etiamsi Apostolus, quoties de sacrificio Christi loquitur, semper maluit splendidioribus vti vocabulis: veluti vbi ante dixit, Iustificationes carnis, appositum, perfectum reddere iuxta conscientiam: item aeternam redemptionem. Sic & hoc loco dicit sanctificari ad purificationem carnis, cui opponitur purgatio conscientiarum ab operibus mortuis.
units.tr: "For if the blood of bulls and goats..." He mentioned calves and goats in the previous place. Why does he now speak of bulls? The answer is that no subtle distinction should be drawn here. For although the precepts speak of offering calves and goats, as we showed from Leviticus 16, where expiatory sacrifices are treated, we often read of bulls being offered elsewhere, and of bulls being joined with goats. So Psalm 49: "Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High." In that place the abrogation of sacrifices is also treated. And 2 Chronicles 29: David with all the multitude sacrificed victims to the Lord, and they offered burnt offerings on the following day: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, a thousand lambs, with their libations and every rite, very abundantly for all Israel; this was done when Solomon was anointed king in the presence of his father. Likewise, 2 Chronicles 29: after Hezekiah had ordered the temple to be opened and had restored the priests, the whole multitude offered victims, praises and burnt offerings with devoted minds. Moreover, the number of burnt offerings which the multitude offered was this: seventy bulls, a hundred rams, two hundred lambs; and they consecrated six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep. So it was often done afterwards, and under Ezra and others. And it is clear that, as he wished to show greater thankfulness, so they were accustomed to offer larger and more excellent animals. Therefore the Apostle wished to understand by the names of bulls and goats all the most costly sacrifices, to signify that no sacrifice, however select and splendid, could bring anything higher than sanctification according to the flesh, and that it is in no way to be compared with the sacrifice of Christ. Next he adds also the ashes of the red heifer, with which the unclean were sprinkled, of which no mention has yet been made. The purification customarily performed with the ashes of a red heifer is described in Numbers 19, in these words: "The Lord spoke to Moses: command the sons of Israel to bring to you a red cow of unblemished age, in which there is no spot, and which has not borne a yoke; and give her to Eleazar the priest, who shall lead her outside the camp and slaughter her in the sight of all; and dipping his finger in her blood he shall sprinkle it seven times towards the door of the tabernacle; and they shall burn her before all eyes, both her skin and flesh, with her blood and dung, given to the flame. The priest shall also cast cedar wood and hyssop and twice-dyed scarlet into the fire that consumes the cow." And a little later: "A clean man shall gather the ashes of the cow and pour them outside the camp in a most clean place, that they may be kept for the multitude of the sons of Israel, and for the water of sprinkling, because the cow was burnt for sin." And this is there called a holy and perpetual law for Israel. This ash was mixed with the waters that were kept, and its use for various purifications was great. Especially it served to cleanse those who had touched a dead human body; likewise those were purified who had been in the tent of one who had died, and every piece of furniture in that same tent. Since the esteem for this ash was therefore great, the Apostle in this place wished to recall not only that expiation which was performed once a year in the Holy of Holies by the blood of the calf and the goat, but also the expiations used at other times, and above all that which was performed with the ashes of the red heifer. In this way he would comprehensively take in the principal methods of expiation, while proving that the blood of Christ has a far greater power of expiation than all of them. There were indeed other rites of cleansing, namely by washings, of which several are described in Leviticus 15. The Apostle here has listed only those which were held in the highest place and as of greatest efficacy. And he rightly brought forward the example of the ashes of the red heifer, because Christ was no less typically foreshadowed in this than in the example of the blood of the calf and the goat. For the red cow, or ox, signifies Christ on account of his flesh, on account of which Christ is said by the prophet to have garments dyed with blood. Likewise the cow was without blemish, since Christ was, although in all things like his brothers, yet without sin, which stains and defiles the soul. Finally, she had never been yoked, because Christ, although he had flesh, bore neither the servitude of the flesh nor that of sin, nor any yoke. Therefore that particular reference to the ashes of the red heifer was rightly added by the Apostle. He says that all these things sanctify to the purification of the flesh, because those so cleansed attained only this, that they were admitted into the common assembly, while the soul meanwhile remained subject to sins. And just as the stains to be cleansed by these were chiefly fleshly (for they were contracted by contact with a dead body or the like), so the purification was only fleshly. In sum, just as the soul is not defiled by external contact, as Christ asserts when he says, "What enters the mouth," and so on, so external washing or sprinkling does not purify the soul, but only the flesh where the defilement took place. It should be noted that these words, purification, sanctification, justification, redemption, are used almost interchangeably. Yet the Apostle, whenever he speaks of the sacrifice of Christ, always preferred to use more splendid terms, as where he said above, "justifications of the flesh," that is, to make perfect as to conscience, and likewise "eternal redemption." So here too he says that they sanctify to the purification of the flesh, to which is opposed the purging of consciences from dead works.

units.la: Porro de iustificatione conscientiæ & de iustificatione carnis, supra satis diximus, vt nequaquam opus sit repetere: sicut duplex est inquinatio, corporis inquam seu carnis, & praeterea conscientiae: ita duplex purificatio. Et sanctificare quidem per se praeclarum est, sed quando additur de purificatione carnis tantum, tota dignitas illius legalis sanctificationis deijcitur, & qualis sit existimanda illa sanctificatio, aperitur. In summa, omnes illæ purificationes legales, tantum carnales, externæ, & circa carnem versabatur, nihilque aliud, quàm vmbra erant purificationis spiritualis per vnicum sacrificium Christi peragendæ, ad animum nequaquam pertingebant illæ oblationes.
units.tr: Further, concerning the justification of the conscience and the justification of the flesh, we have said enough above, so that there is no need to repeat it. Just as there is a twofold defilement, namely of the body or flesh, and besides it of the conscience, so there is a twofold purification. To sanctify is indeed excellent in itself; but when it is added that it concerns only the purification of the flesh, the whole dignity of that legal sanctification is cast down, and it is made clear what sort of sanctification it is to be considered. In sum, all those legal purifications were merely fleshly and external, and concerned the flesh; they were nothing but a shadow of the spiritual purification to be accomplished by the one sacrifice of Christ, and those offerings did not reach the mind at all.

units.la: Qui per spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo) Erat quidem sine his perfecta consequentia, sed interposita sunt ad euidentius comprobandum, quòd posisibile sit, imò & valde conueniens, vt sanguini Christi facultas purgandi conscientias tribuatur. Pronuntur enim hic tres circumstantiæ de modo, quo Christus suum sacrificium obtulit, valde ad id persuadendum idoneæ. Prima est, quòd Christus obtulit se per spiritum Sanctum, id est, impellente & cooperante spiritu Sancto. Ex quo recte infertur, quòd quia spiritus Sanctus Christo sanctificanti cooperatur, agnoscendum est, spiritualem quoque effectum nempe purificationem conscientiarum ex sacrificio Christi proueniFre. Secunda est, quòd Christus obtulit semetipsum. Vnde sic licet ratiocinari: Qui offert semetipsum sua sponte, multò excellentius Deo; gratius facit opus, ac merito plus effi ciat, quàm qui duntaxat per alium aut inuitus offertur: quare consentaneum est, vt sanguis Christi, qui sua sponte semetipsum obtulit, maioris cæseatur efficaciæ, quàm sanguis brutorum, quæ non nisi per alios offerebantur. Tertia circumstantia est, quòd Christus sit immaculatus: vnde animis nostris tacitè hoc argumentum suggeritur. Vt homines à peccatorum maculis purgarentur, non poterat id fieri, nisi per hominem, eundemque omni peccati macula prorsus immune. Solus autem Christus talis est inuentus: Quæ solius Christi sanguis potest homines à peccatorum maculis purgare. Bruta animantia quomodo purgent homines, qui sunt omninò diuersi ab ipsis generis? Quomodo item immaculata, id est, pura à peccatis dici queant instar Christi, quando ad contrahendam maculam peccati, non magis quàm ad benè agendum neque iudicium habent, neque potestatem? Solus ergo Christus proprie immaculatus, ac proinde solus Christus purgadis conscientijs à peccatorū sordibus idoneus. Hæc inquam rationes suasoriæ non obscure demonstrantes, per Christi sanguinem purgari conscientias meo iudicio in hisce paucis verbis latent, & nequaquam ofcitanter sunt prætereundæ. Lubet autem propterea, quòd ab aliis vix attinguntur, singulas fusius explicare. Theophylactus & Chrysostomus quidem sic exponunt, vt oblationem Christi per spiritum æternum, intelligamus opponi oblationi animalium per ignem temporaneum, siue alios offerendi modos. Alij Spiritum æternum interpretantur ardentissimam charitatem, quæ à spiritu æterno & sancto profecta est, quæ & tanta fuit in Christo, vt anima voluerit pro alijs ponere, sicut ipse ait Ioan. 15.13. Rursus quidā coniungūt ista, Christū esse immaculatum per spiritum Sanctum, & per Spiritum æternum, accipi volunt veram in Christo diuinitate, per quam factū est, vt Christus immaculatus perstiterit, & grata hostia Deo patri fieri potuerit. Nō quidè quòd secundum diuinā naturā passus sit, aut, quod multo absurdius est, quasi per spiritū, id est, spiritualiter, & non vere, neq; in carne passus: sed quòd diuinitas adiuncta humanitati & patris; effecerit, vt humanæ naturæ opus, id est, sensus & grauitas suppli tij, fuerit Deo multò acceptissimum. Qua de re paulo post plenius dicturi sumus.
units.tr: "Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God." Without these words the consequence would indeed have been complete, but they are inserted to prove more clearly that it is possible, indeed very fitting, that the power of cleansing consciences should be ascribed to the blood of Christ. For three circumstances are stated here about the manner in which Christ offered his sacrifice, very suitable for persuading us of this. The first is that Christ offered himself through the Holy Spirit, that is, with the Holy Spirit urging and cooperating. From this it rightly follows that, since the Holy Spirit cooperates with Christ in sanctifying, we must acknowledge that the spiritual effect, namely the purification of consciences, also comes from the sacrifice of Christ. The second is that Christ offered himself. Hence one may reason thus: he who offers himself of his own accord does a work far more excellent and more acceptable to God, and by merit achieves more, than one who is offered only by another or against his will. Therefore it is fitting that the blood of Christ, who offered himself of his own accord, should be esteemed of greater efficacy than the blood of brute beasts, which were offered only by others. The third circumstance is that Christ is without blemish. Hence this argument is silently suggested to our minds: for men to be cleansed from the stains of sins, this could not be done except by a man, and one entirely free from every stain of sin. Only Christ has been found to be such. Therefore the blood of Christ alone can cleanse men from the stains of sins. How could brute animals cleanse men, who are wholly different from them in kind? Or how could they likewise be called unblemished, that is, pure from sins, like Christ, when they have neither the judgment nor the power to contract the stain of sin, any more than to act well? Christ alone, then, is properly unblemished, and therefore Christ alone is fit to cleanse consciences from the filth of sins. These reasons, I say, which persuasively demonstrate without obscurity that consciences are cleansed by the blood of Christ, lie hidden in these few words in my judgment, and they must not be passed over carelessly. It is worth explaining each of them more fully, since others hardly touch on them. Theophylact and Chrysostom indeed expound it so that we understand the offering of Christ through the eternal Spirit to be set against the offering of animals through temporal fire, or other modes of offering. Others interpret the eternal Spirit as the most ardent charity, which proceeded from the eternal and holy Spirit, and which was so great in Christ that his soul was willing to lay down his life for others, as he himself says in John 15:13. Again, some join these things: that Christ is unblemished through the Holy Spirit and through the eternal Spirit, and want the true divinity in Christ to be understood, through which it came about that Christ remained unblemished and could be made an acceptable sacrifice to God the Father. Not indeed that he suffered according to his divine nature, or, what is far more absurd, as if he suffered through the Spirit, that is, spiritually, and not truly, nor in the flesh; but that the divinity joined to the humanity made the work of the human nature, that is, the sensation and gravity of the punishment, most acceptable to God. We shall speak more fully about this a little later.
