units.la: Vel certè per spiritū Sanctum, distinctam videlicet personam, qua Christus conseruāt is sit ab omni macula, sicut & ab angelo dictū est beatæ virgini, quod ex ea nasceretur, sanctum fore, quia de spiritu Sancto erat. Nos autem accipimus, vt hic sint distinctæ particulæ, videlicet particula de Spiritu Sancto, altera de oblatione spontanea sui ipsius, & tertia de eo, quòd Christus immaculatus, ac singulæ conducant ad ostendendum, quòd Christi sanguis posiit emūdare conscientias. Neq; difficile est, nostram interpretationē hanc coprobare. Primò enim quòd per Spiritū æternum rectè distincta persona spiritus Sancti accipiatur, non est controuersia: quando vox æternitatis aptissima est ad notandū diuinitate, sicut & cap. 1. probatū est Christū esse Deū, ex eo, quòd ab æterno fuisset, & in æternum.
units.tr: Or certainly through the Holy Spirit, meaning the distinct person, by whom Christ was preserved free from every stain, just as the angel said to the blessed Virgin that the child born of her would be holy, because he was of the Holy Spirit. We, however, understand these to be distinct clauses: one about the Holy Spirit, another about his voluntary offering of himself, and a third about his being spotless, and each of them serves to show that the blood of Christ can cleanse consciences. Nor is it difficult to confirm this interpretation of ours. First, that the eternal Spirit is rightly taken to be the distinct person of the Holy Spirit is not in dispute, since the word "eternal" is most fitting for signifying divinity, just as it was shown in chapter 1 that Christ is God, because he existed from eternity and remains to eternity.

units.la: L æternū maneret, citato testimonio Pfalm.101. Et tu in initio Domine terrā fundamenta iecisti, et Quòd verò spiritu Sācto autore, impulsore, cooperante, acta sint omnia, quæ Christus peregit etiā in morte, nō est obscurū. Nam procuratio redēptionis humanæ tribus personis in diuinitate accepta ex æquo ferri debet. Et spiritus Sānctus cooperatus est in Christi natiuitate, spiritus Sācto tulit testimoniū in Christi baptismo: spiritu Sācto inducēte progressus est Iesus in deserto, vt tētaretur à diabolo: sic etiā spiritu Sācto Christus sese ad morte obtulit: Caro quidē erat infirma, & detrectabat bibere calicē, sed Spiritus Christi proptus factus est, haud dubiè per spiritū sanctū cōfirmatus, qui Christo plenissimè & citra mensurā collatus fuerat, imò qui in Christo plenè requiescebat, vt habetur Luc. 4. Esaiæ 11. & fine quo ea quæ verè spiritualia sunt, impossibile est perfici. Esaiæ 59. Cūm venerit quasi fluuius violetus, quem spiritus Domini cogit, & venerit Sion redemptor, & eis, qui redemit ab iniquitate in Iacob, dicit Dominus, Hoc fœdus meum cum eis dicit Dominus, &c. Proinde iam sequitur, quando Christus à spiritu Sancto inductus est, vt seipsum offerret pro peccatis, sequitur, hac ratione spirituales effectus sanguinis Christi potuisse prouenire. Vbi spiritus sanctus cooperatur, ibi spiritualia perficiuntur opera. Iustificatio conscientiarum seu emundatio à peccatis est res spiritualis: quare non nisi per spiritum effici potuit: Vnde & iustificatio spiritui Sancto tribuitur, Roman. 1. vbi dicitur Christum declaratum filium Dei secundum spiritum Sanctificationis: Roman.8. Spiritui Dei tribuitur resuscitatio Christi, & viuificatio nostrorum mortalium corporū: quid nī ergo spiritui tribuetur promptitudo Christi & obedientia ad mortem? Porrò in veteri testamento etiamsi præcepto Domini offerrentur hostiæ, tamen Spiritus, in eis, sicut in Christo, nequaquam operabatur vel cooperabatur, ideoq; nihil spirituale per hostias illas contingebat. Singulare itaque est, & ad conficiendum, quòd per sanguinem Christi contingat iustificatio spiritualis, quòd Christus dicitur per spiritum se obtulisse.
units.tr: Since he remains for ever, as is shown by the testimony cited from Psalm 101: And you, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundations of the earth, and ... That all the things that Christ accomplished, even in his death, were done under the authority, impulse and cooperation of the Holy Spirit, is not obscure. For the work of redeeming mankind must be credited equally to the three persons in the Godhead. The Holy Spirit cooperated in the birth of Christ; the Holy Spirit bore witness at Christ's baptism; by the leading of the Holy Spirit Jesus went into the desert to be tempted by the devil; so too by the Holy Spirit Christ offered himself to death. The flesh was indeed weak and shrank from drinking the cup, but the spirit of Christ was ready, undoubtedly strengthened through the Holy Spirit, who was bestowed upon Christ fully and without measure, indeed who rested fully upon Christ, as is found in Luke 4 and Isaiah 11, and without whom those things that are truly spiritual cannot be accomplished (Isaiah 59): "When he shall come like a rushing river, which the Spirit of the Lord drives, and the Redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those who turn from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord: this is my covenant with them, says the Lord," etc. Therefore it follows that, when Christ was moved by the Holy Spirit to offer himself for sins, the spiritual effects of Christ's blood could arise in this way. Where the Holy Spirit cooperates, there spiritual works are accomplished. Justification of consciences, or cleansing from sins, is a spiritual matter, and so it could not be brought about except through the Spirit. Hence justification too is attributed to the Holy Spirit, in Romans 1, where Christ is said to have been declared the Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification; and in Romans 8 the raising of Christ and the quickening of our mortal bodies is attributed to the Spirit of God. Why then should the readiness and obedience of Christ unto death not be attributed to the Spirit? Moreover, in the Old Testament, although the victims were offered by the command of the Lord, yet the Spirit did not work or cooperate in them as in Christ, and therefore nothing spiritual came to pass through those victims. It is therefore unique, and to be noted, that through the blood of Christ spiritual justification comes about, and that Christ is said to have offered himself through the Spirit.

units.la: Quod ad alterā particulā attinet, videlicet, quòd Christus seipsum obtulit, cōstat eam creberrimè in Scripturis inculcari, ad cōmendandā ipsius amplissimā charitate, quę cū fuerit vsq; adeò excellens, sine dubio debuit & mors ipsius maximas res efficere. Huc pertinent illa Esaiæ 53. Oblatus est, quia voluit. Ephes. 5. Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem ac victimam Deo in odorem bonę fragrantiæ. Philipens. 2. Humilem præbuit semetipsum, factus obediēs vsque ad mortem, morte autem crucis. Ibidē: Semetipsum inaniuit forma serui sumpta. Igitur istud quoq; singulare est de Christo, & qd' nullo pacto potest oblatis brutis animātibus cōsiderari: ac pinde euideter per hoc demōstratur, quòd oblatio sanguinis Christi debeat esse multo efficacior, quàm oblatio sanguinis animaliū. Tertia particula, quòd Christus sit immaculatus, Etistud longè alia ratione de Christo dicitur, quàm de brutis animantibus. Verum enim est quod de brutis quoq; in lege dicitur, Offeres vitulū, taurū, hircū, agnū, sine macula, &c. Sed his intelligit, vt sint sine macula corporali, nēpe sine scabie, morbo, &c. Sed de Christo cum dicitur, cp sit sine macula, intelligit de macula spirituali, id est, peccato quod est macula animæ. Ergo, sicut animal sine macula in corpore faciebat ad purgatione carnalem, ita Christus sine macula in anima facit ad purgationem spiritualem, id est, liberationem à macula peccatorum. Huc pertinet, quod Christus pasim sine peccato fuisse praedicatur, vt suprà cap.2. Nam alias si ipse maculā peccati habuisset, quomodo alios à macula tali absoluerit? Igitur manifestū est & istud, nēpe quòd esse immaculatum, singulariter sit Christo attributū, vt ostendatur, eum idoneum, qui posset etiā à spirituali macula peccati animas liberare. Et sic puto, non abs re à nobis factum, quòd ita singulas particulas distinxerimus, etiamsi id ab alijs nequaquam factum sit.
units.tr: As for the second clause, namely that Christ offered himself, it is clear that this is very often impressed upon us in the Scriptures, to commend his very great love; and since that love was so excellent, his death too must undoubtedly have produced the greatest results. To this belong those words of Isaiah 53: "He was offered because he willed it." Ephesians 5: "Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God as a fragrant aroma." Philippians 2: "He humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, and death on the cross." And in the same place: "He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." Therefore this too is unique about Christ, and cannot in any way be compared with the offering of irrational animals; and accordingly it is plainly shown by this that the offering of Christ's blood must be far more efficacious than the offering of the blood of animals. The third clause, that Christ is spotless, is said of Christ in a quite different sense from what is said of irrational animals. It is true that the law also says of animals: "You shall offer a calf, a bull, a goat, a lamb, without blemish," etc. But these are meant to be without bodily blemish, namely without scab, disease, and the like. But when it is said of Christ that he is without blemish, it is meant of a spiritual blemish, that is, of sin, which is the stain of the soul. Therefore, just as an animal without blemish in its body served for carnal purification, so Christ, without blemish in his soul, serves for spiritual purification, that is, for deliverance from the stain of sins. To this belongs the fact that Christ is everywhere proclaimed to have been without sin, as above in chapter 2. For otherwise, if he had had the stain of sin himself, how could he have freed others from such a stain? Therefore it is also clear that being spotless is uniquely attributed to Christ, so that he may be shown to be fit to free souls from the spiritual stain of sin. And so I think it was not without reason that we distinguished the individual clauses in this way, even though others have by no means done so.

units.la: Purgabit conscientiā uestrā à mortuarijs operibus ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων) Non tantùm ait, purgabit conscientiam vestram, quod alioquin satis erat futurū: sed addit praeterea, à mortuarijs operibus, peccata nimirū per Metonymiam significās, quæ reuera morte adferunt, iuxta illud Rom.6. Autoramenta peccati mors. Et elegans metaphora à lauantibus & purgantibus aliquid liquore sumpta. Significat enim, quòd sanguine Christi lauabuntur atque reputgabuntur conscietiæ, quomodo Apocal.1. dicitur Christus dilexit nos, & lauit nos à peccatis nostris per sanguinē ipsius. Simili modo cap.6. huius epist. de fundamēto pœnitentiæ ab operibus mortuis sermo est. Item Ephes.2. Et vos cùm essetis mortui per delicta ac peccata, in quib. aliquādo ambulastis, iuxta seculū mūdi huius. Quod & habetur Col.1. ἐν ὑμῖς νεκρὸς ὄντας τοῖς παραπτώμασι. Ac prodest hoc pacto peccatis morte attribuere, & peccatores mortuis coparare, simul vt animi à peccato discant magis abhorrere, simul vt beneficiū Christi liberatis à morte, quæ per peccata incurritur, tanto magis illustretur, & interiori mente cōsideretur. Quid? quod eleganter opponitur hic, fieri purgatione aboperibus mortuis, ei quod in lege tantū purgationes fuerint à cōtactu mortuorū corporū vel huiusmodi? Longè plus est purgari ab ipsis operibus mortuis, seu mortem adferentibus, quàm macula illa externa contracta ex contactu corporis mortui.
units.tr: He will cleanse your conscience from dead works [ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων]. He does not merely say "he will cleanse your conscience," which would otherwise have been enough; he adds besides "from dead works," meaning by metonymy the sins which in truth bring death, according to Romans 6: "The wages of sin is death." And it is an elegant metaphor taken from those who wash and cleanse something with liquid. For it signifies that by the blood of Christ consciences are washed and cleansed, just as Revelation 1 says: "Christ loved us and washed us from our sins by his blood." In a similar way, in chapter 6 of this epistle, there is talk of the foundation of repentance from dead works. Likewise Ephesians 2: "And you, when you were dead through trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world." This is also found in Colossians 1: [ἐν ὑμῖν νεκροὺς ὄντας τοῖς παραπτώμασιν]. And it is useful in this way to attribute death to sins and to compare sinners with the dead, so that souls may learn to shrink more from sin, and so that the benefit of Christ, who frees from the death incurred through sins, may be made the more illustrious and be considered with the inner mind. And what of the fact that here there is an elegant contrast: cleansing from dead works, as opposed to the purifications in the law, which were only from contact with dead bodies or things of that kind? It is far more to be cleansed from the dead works themselves, or from those things that bring death, than from that external stain contracted by contact with a dead body.

units.la: Ad seruiendum Deo uiuenti) Et hæc particula omitti poterat, sed Apostolus (qui semper impensè delectatur antithetis) videtur eam adiecisse antithesis perficiedæ causa, permotus eo quod dixit de operibus mortuis seu mortuarijs, ut nimirū liberatio ab operibus mortuis intelligatur ad vitā nostrā cedere & ad Dei viuetis gloriā. Atq; hoc pacto vnūquemq; obiter quidē, sed valde salubriter de vero vsu tāti beneficij, per Christi sanguine parati, admonet. Neq; enim in hoc purgātur conscientiæ à maculis peccatorū, vt, postea-quā semel mundati fuerimus, redeamus denuò ad peccandū, aut pergamus vlterius magna licet nos nouis peccatis conspurcare: sed vt sancti & puri semper maneamus. Qua de re pluribus agit Apostolus Rom. 6. & Petrus 1. epist. cap. 4. Sed breues huiusmodi formulæ de vsu beneficij Christi pasim alibi videtur inspersæ: vt Ephes. 1. Elegit nos ante-quā iaceretur fundamēta mundi, vt essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles coram illo per charitatē. Et 2. cap. ibidem, Gratia estis seruati per fidem, &c. condi ti in Christo Iesu ad bona opera, quæ præparauit Deus, vt in eis ambularemus. Dicitur Deus viues, tum quia, vt ipse dicit Deuteron. 32. viuit in æternum: tum quia vitam confert omnibus, & à morte spirituali, quæ per peccata contrahitur, ad vitam reuocat, & præstat, vt post opera mortuaria perficiatur opera viua. Atq; ita pasim in Scripturis Deus Deus viuens appellatur. Iosuæ 3. 1. Reg. 17. Esaiæ 33. Hierem. 10. Ioan. 6.
units.tr: To serve the living God. This clause could have been omitted, but the Apostle (who always takes great delight in antitheses) seems to have added it for the sake of completing the antithesis, moved by what he said about dead works or works of death, namely so that the deliverance from dead works may be understood as bearing on our life and on the glory of the living God. And in this way he admonishes each of us, in passing but very profitably, about the true use of so great a benefit, provided through the blood of Christ. For we are not cleansed in consciences from the stains of sins so that, once we have been purified, we should return again to sinning, or go on further to defile ourselves with new sins, however great they may be; rather, that we may remain holy and pure always. The Apostle treats this at greater length in Romans 6, and Peter in 1 Peter 4. But short formulas of this kind about the use of Christ's benefit seem to be scattered everywhere else: as in Ephesians 1: "He chose us before the foundation of the world was laid, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love." And in chapter 2 of the same: "By grace you have been saved through faith," etc., "created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." God is called living both because, as he himself says in Deuteronomy 32, he lives for ever, and because he bestows life on all, and calls back and provides from spiritual death, which is incurred through sins, to life, so that after dead works living works may be carried out. And so throughout the Scriptures God is everywhere called the living God: Joshua 3; 1 Kings 17; Isaiah 33; Jeremiah 10; John 6.

units.la: Quod ad doctrinam attinet, ex eo, quod adfert de cinere iuuencę, discimus, omnia reuera sacrificia, omnia item expiandi genera, typos fuisse vnici sacrificij Christi, & verę expiationis per eundem perficiendæ. Expiatione verò hac confecta per Christum in ara crucis, typos illos, externasq; purificationes sublatas siue abrogatas. Corpore enim & reipsa adueniente vmbra tollatur & transeat est necesse.
units.tr: As regards doctrine, from what he says about the ashes of the heifer we learn that all sacrifices, and likewise all kinds of expiation, were types of the one sacrifice of Christ and of the true expiation to be accomplished through him. Once that expiation has been completed through Christ on the altar of the cross, those types and external purifications are taken away or abrogated. For when the body and the reality itself arrive, the shadow must of necessity be removed and pass away.

units.la: Secundò discimus nobis diligeter intuendū esse omni tempore vt vsum beneficiorum Christi rectè intelligamus, vt vbi participes facti fuerimus spiritualiū bonorū, vt remissionis peccatorum, & huiusmodi, non simus Deo ingrati, sed eos producamus fructus, è quibus gloria Dei magis magisq; illustretur, & fratres nostri ad idē faciundum excitentur. Eleganter Chrysostomus ait, eos non posse seruire Deo vero & viuo, qui non habet opera viua. Vide plenius Chrysostomum. Mortua sunt opera, inquit, quæ non spirant, id est, quæ non habent spiritum.
units.tr: Secondly, we learn that we must always pay careful attention so as to understand rightly the use of Christ's benefits. Having become partakers of spiritual goods such as the remission of sins and the like, we must not be ungrateful to God, but must bring forth those fruits by which the glory of God is more and more illustrated, and by which our brothers are stirred to do the same. Chrysostom says elegantly that those cannot serve the true and living God who do not have living works. See Chrysostom at greater length. "Dead," he says, "are the works which do not breathe," that is, which do not have spirit.

units.la: Tertiò, notandum est, quòd ex illis verbis, per Spiritum obtulit semetipsum, non est infe rendum, quòd Christus non verè passus sit, sed tantùm in Spiritu & imaginarie & simulate (sicut Manichæi, item Archontici quidā contendebant: quorum error crassior est, quàm vt multis refelli debeat) neq; item, quòd passus sit secundum diuinitatem. Qua de re cùm audiam scrupos alicubi enatos, & quidam etiam priuatim me ea de re consuluerint, lubet paulò plenius agere.
units.tr: Thirdly, it must be noted that from the words through the Spirit he offered himself it should not be inferred that Christ did not truly suffer, but only in spirit, imaginarily and in pretence (as the Manichaeans and certain Archontics contended, whose error is too gross to need refuting at length), nor likewise that he suffered according to his divinity. Since I hear that doubts about this have arisen in some places, and some have even consulted me about it privately, I am pleased to treat the matter somewhat more fully.

units.la: Quod Christus non sit passus secundum diuinitatem.
units.tr: That Christ did not suffer according to his divinity.

units.la: Hoc simpliciter statuendū, quòd Christus in carne & perfecta humanitate passus sit in veritate, in cruce, præsente quidē ipsius Deitate (quę neq; à corpore, neq; ab anima sepa rata est) sed non ad patiendum conuersa, sicut ipsa à passione & mutabilitate omni aliena est. Ita vt verę sint hæ consequentiæ, Christus Deus passus est pro nobis: ité, Christus Deus non est passus pro nobis: de hypostasi quidem seu persona verę sunt, sed ita, vt opere sit precium, semper distinguere naturas, & vtriusq; proprietatem retinere, hoc est, vt secundum humanam tantum intelligatur Christus passus, secundum diuinam nequaquam. Neq; tamen ita, vt humana natura tempore passionis Christi fuerit separata à diuina, per se videlicet existente humanitate, & per se agente diuinitate: sed simul præsens aderat humanitati Deitas, non tamen patiebatur, propter essentię synceritatē & incōpatibilitatē: ita vt carne quidē morte sentiret in carne; Deitate autem viueret, atq; etiā mortuos suscitaret. Verū est quidē, sunt loci in Scripturis obscuri, & argumenta quędā quę videtur mouere ad sentiendum, etiam diuinitate aliquid simul passam, sed nos eadem haud difficulter diluemus.
units.tr: This must be laid down plainly: Christ suffered in truth, in the flesh and in perfect humanity, on the cross, with his deity indeed present (a deity which was separated neither from the body nor from the soul), but not turned to suffering, just as the deity itself is free from all passion and mutability. So these consequences are true: "Christ God suffered for us," and also "Christ God did not suffer for us." They are true with respect to the hypostasis or person. But it is worth the effort always to distinguish the natures and to keep the property of each, so that Christ is understood to have suffered according to the human nature only, and in no way according to the divine. Yet this does not mean that at the time of Christ's passion the human nature was separated from the divine, so that the humanity existed on its own and the deity acted on its own. Rather, the Godhead was present alongside the humanity, yet did not suffer, on account of the sincerity and incompatibility of the essence. Thus in the flesh he felt death in the flesh, but in the Godhead he lived and even raised the dead. It is true that there are obscure passages in Scripture, and certain arguments that seem to move us to think that the deity too suffered something at the same time. But we shall resolve these without much difficulty.

units.la: Refert Gregorius Nazianzenus 1. epist. ad Clidoniū, item Epiphan. lib. 2. contra hæreses tomo 2. vbi agit cōtra Ariomanitas, Arianos ita sensisse, quòd videlicet Christus passus esset secundū diuinitate, atq; ita inferior patre nō tantùm secundū humana naturā, sed etiā secundum diuinā. Idem Gregorius Nazianzenus in epistola ad Nectarium episcopum Constantinopolitanū, inter alia impia dogmata Apollinarij refert & hoc ex ipsius libro: Hoc omniū grauissimū, inquit, quòd ipsum vnigenitū Deum iudicē omniū, autore vitę, mortis destructore, mortale esse facit, ac propria eius diuinitate passione suscepisse, & in triduana illa mortificatione corporis diuinitate quoq; vnà cùm corpore occubuisse, ac ita se, ac ita à patre rursus à morte resuscitatū. Augustinus itē libro de hæresibus ad Quod vult Deum memorat quosdam damnatos hæreseos, qui idem ausi sunt afferere, sed nomen autoris sectæ non exprimit.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, in his first letter to Clidonius, reports this, and so does Epiphanius in book 2 against the heresies, volume 2, where he argues against the Ariomanites, that the Arians thought thus: namely, that Christ suffered according to divinity, and so was inferior to the Father not only according to human nature but also according to divine nature. The same Gregory Nazianzen, in his letter to Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, reports among the other impious dogmas of Apollinaris this one from his book: "This is the gravest of all, that he makes the only-begotten God, judge of all, author of life, destroyer of death, mortal, and that he underwent suffering by his own divinity, and that in that three-day mortification of the body the divinity too lay down together with the body, and thus was raised again from death by the Father." Augustine too, in his book on heresies addressed to Quodvultdeus, mentions certain condemned heretics who dared to assert the same, but does not name the author of the sect.

units.la: Certè Cyrillus in quadam epistola Synodali, refert ea de re contra hæreticos Synodi sententiam: Si quis, inquit, non confitetur Dei Verbum passum carne, & crucifixum carne, anathema sit. Item in Concilio Ephesino de eadem re actum. Item Athanasius episcopus Alexandrinus in quadam epistola ad Epictetum episcopum Corinthiorum de eadem re pluribus disserit. Sed objiciat aliquis, ex 1. Corinth. 2. Si enim cognouissent, nequaquam Dominū gloriæ crucifixissent. Ergo mortuus est ut dominus gloriæ, id est, ut Deus, Respondetur: Hoc argumentum fuit cuiusdam Vitaliani Semiarriani, ut refert Epiphanius, asserentis, Christum habuisse quidem carnem & animā, sed nequaquam mentem, cuius loco erat ipsi diuinitas. Hæc autē est solutio Epiphanij: Dominum gloriæ cōfitemur etiam ipsum in carne aduentū. Non enim diuisus est à Deitate aduētus in carne, si vnūquoq; propositum rectè intelligatur, & simul omne negotium ad vnam œconomiā ac dispensationem & ad vnam perfectionē à nobis couniatur. Passibilis enim nobis prædicatur Christus & creditur. Faciunt huc Scripturarum loci, qui Christū in carne passum, crucifixum, & mortuum, siue victimam & maledictione factum esse testificantur. 1. Petri 2. Cùm maledictis incesseretur, non regesit maledicta: patiens non minabatur: tradidit autē iudicanti iustè, qui peccata ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, quo peccatis mortui iustitiæ viuemus. Et mox in eadē epist. cap. 3 Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit, iustus pro iniustis, vt nos adduceret Deo mortificatus quidē carne, viuificatus autē spiritu. Quibus locis D. Petrus docet, Christū, qui Deus fuit ab æterno, pati nequiuisse nisi secundū carne: In spiritum enim & diuinitatem cruciatus mortis, crucis, aut alterius passionis nihil cadere potest: soli humanæ naturæ competit crucis & mortis imbecillitas, siue maledictio.
units.tr: Cyril, in a certain synodal letter, reports against the heretics the judgment of the Synod on this matter: "If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh and was crucified in the flesh, let him be anathema." Likewise the matter was debated at the Council of Ephesus. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in a letter to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth, also discusses the same matter at length. But someone may object from 1 Corinthians 2: "For had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." Therefore he died as the Lord of glory, that is, as God. The answer: this argument belonged to a certain Vitalian, a semi-Arian, as Epiphanius reports, who asserted that Christ had flesh and soul, but in no way a mind, the divinity taking the place of the mind. This is Epiphanius's solution: we confess that the Lord of glory also came in the flesh. For the coming in the flesh is not separated from the Godhead, if each statement is rightly understood and the whole matter is referred by us to one economy and dispensation and one perfection. For Christ is preached and believed to be passible. Scripture passages support this, which testify that Christ was crucified, dead, and made a victim and a curse in the flesh. 1 Peter 2: "When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten; but he committed himself to him who judges justly, who himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we, dead to sins, might live to righteousness." And soon after in the same epistle, chapter 3: "Christ once suffered for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the spirit." By these passages St Peter teaches that Christ, who was God from eternity, could not suffer except according to the flesh. For the torments of death, of the cross, or of any other passion cannot fall upon the spirit or the divinity. The weakness of the cross and of death, or the curse, belongs to human nature alone.

units.la: Hinc 2. Cor. 5. Eum, qui peccatū non nouit, pro nobis ait Apostolus peccatū esse factū, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum. Et Galat. 3. Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio, scriptum est enim: Execrabilis omnis, qui pendet in ligno, &c. Hebr. 2. Posteaquam pueri cōmertium habet cum carne & sanguine, & ipse similiter particeps factus est eorūdem, vt per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, diabolū, &c. En execrationem & peccatū fieri, in Deum secundū diuinitatem minimè competere: sed potius homini & humanitati cōuenire, quam Χϝ⊗, siue filius Dei, verus Deus, assumpsit. Peccatum in carne expiari oportuit, quod in carne erat contractū. Huc pertinet totum redemptionis mysterium, quod in morte, crucé, sepultura, ac resurrectione consummatū est. Christo secundū humanitatem in abstracto (vt loquuntur) voces illæ & phrases Prophetarū, & spiritus Sancti congruunt soli: quibus dicitur passus, mortuus, sepultus, resuscitatus, &c. Matth. 26. dicit Filium hominis tradendū vt crucifigatur: in quo naturæ humanæ patibilitatem designat. Psal. 22. Inter varias voces ea insignis est, qua dicit, Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me dereliquisti? Derelinquere seipsam natura diuina, quæ nec pati per se potest, nequaquā dicitur: humanitatis potius ista querela est, quæ dolores mortis & horrores inferni subiens ἀνθρωποπάθως in crucis ara ista effundit. Multa in Psalmis & Esaia de cruce & morte Christi referuntur, quę carnis ac humanitatis affectus, eaq; designat, quę filius hominis erat passurus: cuius modi sunt illa Esai. 50. 53. 64. psal. 8. 22. 40. 110. Et passim in Scripturis loci occurrunt, qui de morte & resurrectione Christi vaticinantur. Ac licet multa in his ipsis talia sint, quæ participationem aliquam & communitatem passionis & cruciatuum, duabus in Christo naturis pro ratione personæ & hypostaticæ vnionis, conuenientium, videantur denotare: vt cùm Deus, Dei filius, Dominus gloriæ passus & crucifixus esse dicitur: in his tamen ipsis diligenter naturarum proprietates & officia debent considerari. Quæ enim Christo crucifixo & mortuo toti & personæ eius, quæ duabus naturis constat, in concreto (vt loquuntur) tribuuntur, & à persona eius, absque blasphemia & errore, diuelli nequeunt: ea plerunque talia sunt, vt singulis naturis seorsim consideratis nequaquam attribui possint, quippè quùm mortis, dolorum, & aliarum id genus infirmitatum diuinitas prorsus sit expers. Ad solam igitur humanitatem crux & mors ista pertinet.
units.tr: Hence 2 Corinthians 5: the Apostle says that he who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God through him. And Galatians 3: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, since he was made a curse for us, for it is written, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," etc. Hebrews 2: "Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil," etc. Behold: to become a curse and sin does not belong to God according to his divinity at all, but rather pertains to the man and to the humanity which the Son of God, the true God, assumed. Sin had to be expiated in the flesh, since it had been contracted in the flesh. To this pertains the whole mystery of redemption, which was accomplished in death, cross, burial, and resurrection. Those voices and phrases of the prophets and of the Holy Spirit suit Christ in the abstract (as they say), according to humanity alone, by which he is said to have suffered, died, been buried, been raised, and so on. Matthew 26 says that the Son of man is to be delivered up to be crucified, and in this he designates the passibility of human nature. Psalm 22: among its various cries, the notable one is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" To forsake oneself is by no means said of the divine nature, which cannot suffer of itself. This is rather the lament of humanity, which, undergoing the pains of death and the horrors of hell, pours forth this cry on the altar of the cross in a human manner [ἀνθρωποπάθως]. Many things in the Psalms and in Isaiah concerning the cross and death of Christ are related, which denote the affections of the flesh and of humanity, and what the Son of man was to suffer. Such are Isaiah 50, 53, 64, and Psalms 8, 22, 40, 110. And throughout the Scriptures passages occur which prophesy about the death and resurrection of Christ. Although many such things in these very passages seem to denote some participation and communion in suffering and torments, belonging to the two natures in Christ according to the unity of the person and the hypostatic union, as when God, the Son of God, the Lord of glory is said to have suffered and been crucified, nevertheless in these very things the properties and offices of the natures must be carefully considered. For what is attributed to Christ crucified and dead, to the whole person who consists of two natures, in the concrete (as they say), and cannot be torn from his person without blasphemy and error, is for the most part of such a kind that it cannot be assigned to either nature considered separately, since the divinity is altogether free of death, pains, and infirmities of that kind. Therefore this cross and death pertain to the humanity alone.

units.la: Patet hoc idem ex homine, qui anima & corpore constat. In quo quidem illa immortalis est, hoc verò corruptioni & putredini est obnoxium. Ac sanè dicitur homo mori, computrescere, si personam spectes. At si animæ proprietates discutias, & seorsim intueris, nihil computrefactionis aut corruptionis huic assignari poterit. Idem distinctionis modus in naturarum Christi proprietatibus discernendis seruandisque tenendus est.
units.tr: This is evident also from man, who consists of soul and body. In him the soul is immortal, while the body is subject to corruption and decay. Indeed, if you look at the person, one says that a man dies, rots and decays. But if you examine the properties of the soul and consider it separately, no decay or corruption can be assigned to it. The same manner of distinction must be kept and observed in distinguishing the properties of Christ's natures.

units.la: Sunt quidem nonnulla, quæ Christo ab aduersarijs & crucifixoribus illata sunt, talia, vt ad vtramq; natura referri possint, cuiusmodi sunt contumeliæ, ludibria, blasphemiæ, sarcasmi, illusiones, scomata, quæ tàm ante mortem, quàm in cruce ei contigerunt. Unde & Marci 3. Matt. 12. blasphemiam illam, qua per Beelzebub principem dæmoniorum eijcere dæmonia dicebatur, in spiritum Sanctum committi, ac propterea nunquam remitti posse, asserit. Sed nos hoc loco de morte, & infirmitatibus illis loquimur, quas Christus non nisi in carne experiri & perferre potuit ac debuit, quæq; carni & corpori Christi proprie conueniunt. Patebunt hæc dilucidius, si diligenter regulæ illæ de communicatione Idiomatum obseruetur, quas nos in huius operis parte prima posuimus, ad quas lectorem remitto.
units.tr: Some of the insults inflicted on Christ by his adversaries and crucifiers can be referred to either nature: such as contumelies, mockeries, blasphemies, sarcasms, illusions and scoffs, which befell him both before death and on the cross. Hence also Mark 3 and Matt. 12 state that the blasphemy by which it was said that he cast out demons through Beelzebub, prince of the demons, is committed against the Holy Spirit and therefore can never be forgiven. But here we are speaking of death and those infirmities which Christ could and ought to experience and endure only in the flesh, and which properly belong to the flesh and body of Christ. These matters will become clearer if the rules on the communication of idioms, which we set out in the first part of this work, are carefully observed; I refer the reader to them.

units.la: Qui plura desiderat, legat Augustinum lib. 1. de trinitate, cap. 13. Item epist. 57. ad Dardanum: lib. 2. ad Simplicianum, quæstione secunda: Damascenum lib. 3. Chrysostomum in Epistolam ad Hebræos: Ambrosf. de fide ad Gratianum: Augustin. lib. 2. cap. 4. Theodoret. dialogo 3. Fulgentium ad Thrasimundum lib. 3. Item Cyrillum in epist. ad Ioannem Antiochenum. Et D. Irenæi illud præclarum est: verbum aderat, & quiescebat: Non vtiq; moriebatur per se, neque patiebatur: quemadmodum anima nostra morienti homini, seu carni adest, cùm tamen ipsa reuera non moriatur, &c.
units.tr: Whoever desires more should read Augustine, On the Trinity, book 1, chapter 13; likewise letter 57 to Dardanus; book 2 to Simplicianus, question 2; Damascene, book 3; Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Ambrose, On Faith, to Gratian; Augustine, book 2, chapter 4; Theodoret, dialogue 3; Fulgentius to Thrasamund, book 3. Also Cyril in his letter to John of Antioch. And the splendid saying of Irenaeus: the Word was present and remained still. It did not die of itself, nor did it suffer, just as our soul is present to a dying man, or to the flesh, although it does not in truth die, etc.

units.la: Et ob id noui testamenti conciliator est, vt morte intercedente ad redemptionem earum prævaricationum, quæ fuerant sub priori testamento, ij qui vocati sunt, promissionem accipiant æterna hæreditatis.
units.tr: And therefore he is the mediator of a new testament, so that, a death having taken place for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the former testament, those who are called may receive the promise of an eternal inheritance.

units.la: Alia ratio confirmans, quòd sacrificium sanguinis Christi debeat multo efficacius esse omnibus sacrificijs legalibus, sumpta ab officio conciliatoris, seu à causa finali, ob quam Christus institutus est conciliator noui testamenti, & perficiendæ conciliationis modo. Est q; sententia: Hac de causa Christus institutus est mediator noui testamenti, vt nimirum credentes per ipsum accipiat salutem seu redemptionem æternam, quam in veteri testamento accipere nulli poterant, & quidem intercedete ipsius morte, siue sanguine. Igitur sacrificium sanguinis ipsius multo maioris efficaciæ est, quàm quæcunq; sacrificia legalia, ac merito dicetur, per illud redemptionem æternam esse paratam. Nulla est in hoc argumento difficultas, modò obseruetur, in antecedente diuersas esse partes, quæ ex ijs, quæ hactenus diuersis locis dicta sunt, notæ esse possunt. Nos propter tyrones eas breuiter per ordinem explicabimus.
units.tr: Another argument confirming that the sacrifice of Christ's blood must be far more effective than all the legal sacrifices is taken from the office of mediator, or from the final cause for which Christ was appointed mediator of the new testament, and from the manner in which the reconciliation is accomplished. The argument runs: For this reason Christ was appointed mediator of the new testament, namely that believers might receive through him salvation or eternal redemption, which none could receive under the old testament, and indeed through the intervention of his death or blood. Therefore the sacrifice of his blood is of far greater efficacy than any legal sacrifices, and it will rightly be said that eternal redemption has been procured through it. There is no difficulty in this argument, provided it is observed that the premise has different parts, which can be known from what has been said hitherto in various places. For the sake of beginners we shall briefly explain them in order.

units.la: Prima pars est, Christum esse conciliatorem noui testamenti. Id assertum est cap. 8. hisce verbis, Nunc verò hoc excellentius sortitus est sacerdotiū, quo prestantioris est testamenti interc̄ssor, quod in præstantioribus promissis situm est. Item cap. 7. Tanto prioris testamenti sponsor factus est. Altera pars est, quòd credentes accipere debeant in nouo testamento salutem & redemptionem, quæ in veteri testamento accipi non poterat. Hæc quoq; manifesta est ex causa abrogationis veteris testameti, & instituendi noui: de qua sic iterum cap. 8. Etenim si prius illud tale fuisset, ut nihil in eo posset reprehendi, haud quaquam fuisset secundo quæsitus locus. Item cap. 7. Abrogatur enim, quod præcessit præceptum, propter imbecillitatem & mutilitatem: Nam nihil ad perfectionem adduxit lex, verùm erat introductio ad spem potiorem, per quam appropinquamus Deo.
units.tr: The first part is that Christ is the mediator of the new testament. This was asserted in chapter 8 in these words: "But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is the mediator of a better covenant, which is established upon better promises." Also in chapter 7: "By so much Jesus has become the surety of a better covenant." The second part is that believers ought to receive salvation and redemption in the new testament, which could not be received under the old. This too is clear from the cause of the abrogation of the old testament and the institution of the new, concerning which again in chapter 8: "For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion sought for a second." Also in chapter 7: "For the former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, for the law made nothing perfect, but was the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God."

units.la: Tertia pars est, quòd redemptio æterna deberet prouenire intercedente Christi morte siue sanguine. Hæc expositæ est cap. 2. vbi agebatur de causis suscepte à Christo humanitatis: atque inter cætera dictum est, Christum ideò debuisse fieri hominem, vt per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, id est, diabolum: et liberos redderet eos, quicunque metu mortis per omnem vitam obnoxij erant seruituti. Quanquam istud declaratur plenius verbis statim sequentibus. Ex his inquam locis partes omnes manifestæ euadunt, nec dubium, quin Apostolus formans hanc consequentiā ad eos respexerit. Vbi igitur hæc ita se habent, videlicet quòd Christus conciliator sit noui testamenti, & quidem ob id, vt credentes accipiant redemptionem æternam, quæ sub veteri testamento accipi non poterat: hanc autè parandā ipsius morte siue sanguine, nemo non clarè vi det, rectissimè sequi, quòd sanguis Christi sit longè efficacior quibuscunq; sacrificijs legalibus, & quòd iure dicatur, redemptionem æternā, siue purgationē conscientiarū ab eo prouenire. In prioribus nihil est, quod plixiore expositione egeat. Ob id, inquit, noui testamenti conciliator est: Quòd Christus sit μεσίτης noui testamenti, & quàm appositè itatum propter officium, tum propter vtraq; naturas, appelletur, diximus cap. 8. super illo verbo, Quanto melioris testamenti intercessor est.
units.tr: The third part is that eternal redemption was to come about through the intervention of Christ's death or blood. This was set out in chapter 2, where the causes of the humanity assumed by Christ were discussed; and among other things it was said that Christ had to become man so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to bondage all their lives. This is declared more fully in the words that immediately follow. From these passages, I say, all the parts become evident, and there is no doubt that the Apostle, in forming this consequence, had them in view. Since these things stand thus, namely that Christ is the mediator [μεσίτης] of the new testament, and indeed for this end, that believers may receive eternal redemption, which could not be received under the old testament, and that this is to be procured by his death or blood, everyone clearly sees that it rightly follows that the blood of Christ is far more efficacious than any legal sacrifices, and that eternal redemption, or the purging of consciences, rightly comes from it. In the former points there is nothing that needs a fuller explanation. Therefore, he says, he is the mediator of the new testament. How aptly Christ is called mediator [μεσίτης], both on account of his office and on account of both natures, we have explained in chapter 8 on the words, "by as much as he is the mediator of a better testament."

units.la: Vt ij, qui uocati sunt, promissione accipiant æternæ hæreditatis) En officiū mediatoris Christi, seu causa finalis, propter quam Christus factus mediator. In veteri lege tātum accipiebatur hæreditas tēporanea promissæ terræ Chanaan, quæ typum gerebat vitæ æternæ accipi-finalis. endæ in nouo testameto, sicut omnia patribus in figura cōtingebāt. Et ad inducedos homines in eam mediator cōstitutus erat Moses, qui hic appellatur Galat.3. atq; ea in parte typū gessit Christi. Porrò in nouo testameto promissa est, & accipitur hæreditas æterna, & quidē mediatore Christo. Eleganter autē Apostolus & qualitate personarū accipientium eam hæreditatē, & ipsius hæreditatis excellētiam expressit. Personarum qualitas notatur, quando dicitur, uocatos, ea voce intelligens per Metonymiam electos. Ad solos enim electos pertinet hæreditas. Quāplurimi quidem vocantur, sed perpauci eligūtur: quia non omnes apprehendunt vocationē, neq; obediunt. Matth.20.&22. Et varios habet Deus vocādi modos. Qua de re plura Rom.8. Ephes 1. & supra huius epist.cap.3. sup illo verbo. Vnde fratres sancti uocationis cœlestis participes: Hæreditatis excellētia exprimitur, quando vocatur æterna: sic enim, quod summū est, & omnibus rebus temporaneis, quæq; cum tempore pereunt, excellentius significatur: quemadmodū paulo ante dixit, per Christum redemptionem æternam esse repertam. Videtur autem studiose voluisse vsurpare locutionē hanc de hæreditate ætherna, propterea quòd verbis sequētibus sic agit de testa mtéo, quomodo more humano, & iure ciuili cōditur testamentū à moriturisin quo & hæredes coscribuntur, sicut ibi plenius ostēdemus. Huc haud dubiē respiciēs maluit hæreditatis vti vocabulo, qp iustificationis, vel redēptionis æternæ, vel huiusmodi, etiāsi aliās crebrò, ppter quod Deus adoptat credētes in filios, & ipse se erga hos gerit instar patris, dicatur pijs hæreditas à Patre proposita, quā cum Christo naturali filio cōmuniter acci-piant: qua de re Rom.8.fusius: Non quòd Deus pater mori possit, aut filij intelligantur mortuo succedere, quod impossibile est: sed quòd per abundante suam misericordiam eligit quasi in filios, & se etiam semper viuo hæreditatem eis distribuit gratis, quam aliās nullo ex paɛto eis debet. Igitur ad amplificandam gratuitam misericordiam Dei erga credentes, qua æquat eos filio suo Christo, & participes facit omnium, quæ is obtinet, in more habet Scriptura, bona æterna & cœlestia appellare credentium hæreditatem. Atq; huc pertinet quod fere semper, cùm de hac hæreditate habetur sermo, simul aliquid adiicitur de promissione, sicut & hic factum videmus, vt videlicet non iure aliquo, sed tantum gratuita collatione & promissione intelligatur ad credentes redire: sicut & adoptatis filijs quæcunque donantur, gratis donari intelligūtur. Porrò de excellentia huius æternæ hæreditatis, plura & clarius Petrus prioris epistolæ capite primo, & Ephesiorum primo.
units.tr: That those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. Here is the office of Christ the mediator, or the final cause for which he became mediator. Under the law only the temporal inheritance of the promised land of Canaan was received, which bore a type of eternal life to be received under the new testament, just as all things happened to the fathers in figure. Moses, who is here called the mediator, was appointed to lead men into it (Gal. 3), and in this respect he bore a type of Christ. Moreover, under the new testament the eternal inheritance is promised and received, and indeed through Christ the mediator. The Apostle has elegantly expressed both the quality of the persons receiving that inheritance and the excellence of the inheritance itself. The quality of the persons is marked when he says "those who are called," using the word by metonymy to mean "the elect." For the inheritance pertains only to the elect. Many indeed are called, but few are chosen, because not all grasp the calling or obey (Matth. 20. & 22.). And God has various modes of calling. More on this in Rom. 8, Eph. 1, and above in chapter 3 of this epistle on the words "holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling." The excellence of the inheritance is expressed when it is called eternal, for thus what is highest, and is signified more excellently than all temporal things which perish with time, is indicated, just as a little earlier he said that eternal redemption has been found through Christ. He seems to have deliberately chosen this language of an eternal inheritance because in the following words he speaks of the testament in the way that a testament is drawn up by men about to die, according to human custom and civil law, in which heirs are also named, as we shall show more fully there. Clearly having this in view, he preferred to use the word inheritance rather than justification, or eternal redemption, or the like, although elsewhere it is often said that, because God adopts believers as sons and himself behaves toward them as a father, the inheritance is set before the godly by the Father, which they receive in common with Christ the natural Son. On this see Rom. 8 more fully: not that God the Father can die, or that the sons are understood to succeed a dead man, which is impossible, but because in his abundant mercy he chooses them as if they were sons, and even while he lives he distributes the inheritance to them freely, which otherwise he owes them by no agreement. Therefore, to magnify the free mercy of God toward believers, by which he makes them equal to his Son Christ and partakers of all that he possesses, Scripture is accustomed to call the good and heavenly things the inheritance of believers. And to this pertains the fact that almost always, when this inheritance is spoken of, something is added about the promise, as we see happening here too, so that it is understood to come back to believers not by any right, but only by free bestowal and promise, just as whatever is given to adopted sons is understood to be given freely. Moreover, about the excellence of this eternal inheritance, Peter in the first chapter of his first epistle, and Ephesians chapter 1, speak more fully and clearly.

units.la: Morte intercedente)Mors Christi est caussa formalis, adeoq; medium principale & instrumentum parandæ nobis hæreditatis æternæ, ideoq; magna Emphasi, imò vt amplificationis causa interposita, debet particula hæc accipi. Ea enim potissimū euincitur excellētia sacrificij Christi præ sacrificijs legalibus, (& quidem duobus modis) quæ non sunt vllius hominis, sed tantùm pecudum morte peracta: & præterea ostenditur, quòd Christus redemptionē pararit, non tantùm fundendo aliquātum sui sanguinis: quatamen re potuisset pater placari, & abundè pro peccatis satisfieri, si ita diuinæ prouidentiæ visum fuisset: sed etiam mortem proferendo, quo nihil maius in gratiam aliorum potest fieri. Estq; eo diligentius hæc particula obseruanda, quòd sequentia argumenta ex ea fluunt deriuanturq;.
units.tr: "Death intervening": the death of Christ is the formal cause, and so the principal means and instrument by which the eternal inheritance is procured for us. For this reason the particle should be taken with great emphasis, even as an intensifier added for the sake of amplification. It mainly proves the excellence of Christ's sacrifice over the legal sacrifices, and it does so in two ways: the legal sacrifices were not of any human being, but were accomplished only by the death of animals. Moreover, it shows that Christ obtained redemption not merely by shedding some of his blood, which would have been enough to appease the Father and make full satisfaction for sins if the divine providence had so willed, but by bearing death itself, than which nothing greater can be done for the benefit of others. This particle is to be observed all the more carefully because the arguments that follow flow from it and depend on it.

units.la: Ad redēptionem earum prævaricationum quæ fuerant sub priori testameto) Effectus mortis Christi necessarius, vt promissio hæreditatis æternę accipiatur: ac talibus quidē verbis expres-sus, quę clarissimè ostendant, sub veteri testamento nihil tale potuisse effici, vnde quiuis cogitur expendere agnoscere q;, sacrificium Christi multo esse excellētius sacrificijs legalibus. Clarè enim dicitur, prǫuaricationes sub veteri testameto māsisse, nec potuisso ibi expiari, sed sub nouo testameto primùm factā earundē redeptionem. Est autē redemptio hic vocabulum forense valde accommodum instituto, quomodo aliquis dicitur crimen seu pœnam redimere multa pecuniaria, atque ita fit liber. Sic autem Christi sanguis depensus est in precium εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν παραβάσεων. Vtroque autem modo inuenitur in Scripturis vocabulum redemptionis, vt & peccata dicantur redempta seu potius pœnę pro peccatis, & nos redempti à peccatis: & ipse sanguis sæpè describitur vt depensum precium: vt 1. Petri 1. Non caducis rebus, veluti argento & auro estis redēpti, sed preciofo sanguine velut agni immaculati & incontaminati Christi.
units.tr: "For the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament": This is the necessary effect of Christ's death, by which the promise of the eternal inheritance is received. It is expressed in such words that they most clearly show that nothing of the kind could be achieved under the Old Testament, so that anyone is compelled to weigh and acknowledge that Christ's sacrifice is far more excellent than the legal sacrifices. For it is plainly said that transgressions remained under the Old Testament and could not be expiated there, but that their redemption was first accomplished under the New Testament. Now "redemption" is a legal term very well suited to the present purpose: just as someone is said to redeem a crime or penalty by paying a fine and so becomes free, so Christ's blood was paid out as the price "for the redemption of the transgressions" [εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν παραβάσεων]. The word redemption is found in Scripture in both senses: sins are said to be redeemed, or rather the penalties for sins, and we are said to be redeemed from sins; and the blood itself is often described as a price paid out. So 1 Peter 1: "You were redeemed not with corruptible things, such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot."

units.la: Proinde vocabulo redemptionis mirificè commendatur incomparabilis efficacia sanguinis Christi: quandoquidem is solus est, quo redemptæ sunt pœnæ æternæ, quas nostris peccatis seu prævaricationibus eramus commeriti. Hoc enim significat redimere prævaricationes, nempe, precio depenso satisfacere pro pœnis, quæ propter peccata erant infligendæ.
units.tr: Therefore by the word redemption the incomparable efficacy of Christ's blood is wonderfully commended, since it alone is that by which the eternal punishments we had deserved by our sins or transgressions were redeemed. For to redeem transgressions means this: by paying a price to make satisfaction for the punishments that were to be inflicted on account of sins.

units.la: Cæterum, hic etiam propter mediatorē Christū multa habetur consolationū materia. Sed hoc peculiater est notandum, quod dicit, prævarications fuisse sub lege, siue sub priori testamento. Non dissimili ratione Roman. 5. per legem dicitur exuberasse peccatum, & alibi peccatum per legem vires accepisse: sed per Christum post exuberasse gratiam. Ita enim multum aberat lex à collatione gratiæ, à purgatione conscientiarum, imò potius augebat peccatum.
units.tr: Moreover, here too there is much material for consolation because of Christ the Mediator. But this must be noted particularly: he says that the transgressions were under the law, or under the first testament. For a similar reason, Romans 5 says the law caused sin to abound, and elsewhere that sin gained strength through the law; but through Christ grace has since abounded. For the law was far removed from bestowing grace and from cleansing consciences; indeed it rather increased sin.

units.la: Siquidem vbi testamentum est, mors intercedat necesse est testatoris. Namtestamentum in mortuis ratum est: quandoquidem nondum valet, cum viuit testator.
units.tr: "For where a testament is, there must of necessity be the death of the testator. For a testament is of force after men are dead, otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth."

units.la: Quia in præcedenti argumento dixit conciliationem noui testamenti debuisse perfici, facta morte, hinc forte aliquis per admirationem rogaturus erat, annón potuerit nouum istud pactum alia ratione ratum fieri ac confirmari, quàm morte Christi: quandoquidem hæc conditio plane dura & iniqua apparet, imò & valde absurdum videtur, Deum velle placari humano sanguine, vtpote quod etiam barbaræ gentes pertinacissimè sint auersatæ: qui verò paulò rectiori iudicio erant prædíti, iudicabant, Deum alia ratione commodius potuisse humanæ saluti consulere. Propterea etiam Apostolus alibi crucem Christi vocat gentium stultitiam & Iudæorum offendiculum.
units.tr: Since in the preceding argument he said that the ratification of the New Testament had to be accomplished through death, someone might wonder, with astonishment, whether this new covenant could not have been ratified and confirmed in some other way than by the death of Christ. For this condition seems plainly harsh and unjust, and it even seems very absurd that God should wish to be appeased with human blood, something that even barbarous nations have most stubbornly rejected; and those who had a somewhat more correct judgment thought that God could have provided for human salvation more fittingly by another means. For this reason the Apostle elsewhere calls the cross of Christ foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Jews.

units.la: Præterea cum sacerdotium ac sacrificium Christi quam plurimis demonstrata ac probata sint typis veteris testamenti, certè alienum hoc esse ac minimè respondens illis typis videtur, vt idem sacerdos sit & hostia simul, & non alieno sanguine, sed proprio, imò & morte sua pro aliis satisfaciat. Respondet Apostolus per occupationem, sed mutata nonnihil vocabuli testamenti significatione: Recte, inquit, dicimus, testamenti noui conciliationem non perfici, nisi morte Christi intercedente. Vocatur enim testamentum.
units.tr: Moreover, since the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ have been shown and proved by very many types of the Old Testament, it certainly seems strange and quite out of keeping with those types that the same person should be both priest and victim at once, and should satisfy for others not with another's blood but with his own, and even by his own death. The Apostle answers by a figure of speech, but with the meaning of the word "testament" somewhat altered: "Rightly," he says, "we say that the ratification of the New Testament is not accomplished unless the death of Christ intervenes. For it is called a testament."

units.la: Scitis autem testamentum (ut hoc secundo loco non simpliciter pactum, quomodo hactenus semper, sed potius extremam voluntatem morientium, qua destinant alios in suam hæreditatem successores, significet) ratum non fieri, nisi mors testatoris intercedat. Quod sanè ab humano more & ciuili iure perspicuum est. Docent namq; leges testamentū tum primum ratum fieri, quando testator moritur, & nequaquā sequi effectus testamenti, hoc est, ab aliis non adiri hæreditatem, quamdiu testator adhuc uiuit. Igitur quando hoc nouum testamentum se prorsus habet instar testamenti, quod à moriturís conditur, & Christus eius sit autor ac mediator, conuenit, morte sua id ratum faciat, quo pij credentes, qui se habent instar hæredum, cœlestem & æternam hæreditatem promissam consequantur.
units.tr: "But you know that a testament" (in this second place it means not simply a pact, as it has so far always meant, but rather the last will of the dying, by which they appoint others as successors to their inheritance) "is not ratified unless the death of the testator intervenes." This is plainly according to human custom and civil law. For the laws teach that a testament is then first ratified when the testator dies, and that the effects of the testament, that is, the taking up of the inheritance by others, do not follow while the testator is still alive. Therefore, since this New Testament altogether resembles a testament made by those about to die, and Christ is its author and mediator, it is fitting that his death should ratify it, so that the faithful believers, who stand in the place of heirs, may obtain the heavenly and eternal inheritance that was promised.

units.la: Atque ita etiamsi hac in parte sacrificium Christi videatur diuersum esse à typicis sacrificijs legis, tamen constat, æquum & necessarium fuisse, ut nouum testamentum morte ipsius Christi pontificis ratum fieret. Hanc equidem puto simplicem & germanam esse Apostoli sententiam, neq; aliud eum velle, quàm docere, quòd necessum fuerit, Christũ mori, vt spirituales effectus, id est, æterna redemptio, purgatio conscientiarum, vita æterna, in nouo testamento omnibus credentibus contingerent. Tametsi verò etiam de morte per Christum subeunda dictum est capite secundo, vbi de causis suscepta ab eo humanitatis agebatur, tamen & hoc loco, vbi disseritur de Christi sacrificio, decet rursus de morte illa agere, propterea, quòd Christus ipse simul sacerdos, & simul hostia extitit. Et quia insuper de sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi multa dicta sunt ac demonstrata, colligendo quæ in typis veteris testamenti sunt de vtroq; adumbrata, nequaquam verò satis respondent typo, quòd, cum in veteri testamento sacerdotes offerrent sanguinem alienum, Christus in nouo testamento offerret sanguinem proprium: deinde, cùm in veteri testamento perficerentur sacrificia morte pecorum, in nouo autem testamento Christus perficeret sacrificium morte propria. Hæc inquam cùm non satis aptè sibi inuicem videantur respondere, necessarium erat adijcere rationem, quare oportuerit Christum in nouo testamento sacrificium offerre intercedēte morte propria. Hanc porrò sumit in præsenti argumento à vocabulo testamenti, quasi diceret: Quia testamentum appellatur, merito dicimus id ratum fieri, intercedente morte Christi, qui est huius testamenti conditor ac mediator: quandoquidem more ac iure humano, tunc ratum fit testamentum, vbi testatoris mors intercesserit.
units.tr: And so, even if in this respect the sacrifice of Christ seems different from the typical sacrifices of the law, nevertheless it is clear that it was right and necessary that the New Testament should be ratified by the death of Christ himself, the high priest. I indeed think this is the simple and genuine meaning of the Apostle, and that he wishes to teach nothing other than that it was necessary for Christ to die, so that the spiritual effects, namely eternal redemption, the cleansing of consciences, and eternal life, might come to all believers under the New Testament. Although indeed it was said in the second chapter that Christ had to undergo death, where the causes of the humanity he had assumed were discussed, nevertheless here too, where the sacrifice of Christ is treated, it is fitting to speak again of that death, because Christ himself was at once priest and victim. And since many things have been said and shown about the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, by gathering what was foreshadowed of both in the types of the Old Testament, it is by no means a sufficiently close correspondence to the type that, whereas in the Old Testament the priests offered another's blood, Christ in the New Testament offered his own blood; and then, whereas in the Old Testament sacrifices were completed by the death of animals, in the New Testament Christ completed the sacrifice by his own death. Since these things do not seem to correspond to one another well enough, it was necessary to add the reason why Christ had to offer the sacrifice in the New Testament through his own death. The Apostle takes this reason in the present argument from the word testament, as if he were saying: because it is called a testament, we rightly say that it is ratified by the intervention of the death of Christ, who is the author and mediator of this testament, since by human custom and law a testament is then ratified when the death of the testator has intervened.

units.la: Quanquam non dissimulanda, nec prorsus explodenda est hic interpretatio Chrysostomi. Nam is quoque per occupationem adiecta esse ista agnoscit, Fortassis, inquit, possent multi, qui infirmiores erant, ex eo, quòd mortuus dicitur Christus, non credere promissionibus eius. Paulus igitur ex abundanti hoc ponit, & exempla ex communi assumens consuetudine. Quale autem hoc est? Propterea igitur oportet vel maximè confidere. Quare? Quia non viuentibus testatoribus, sed mortuis, tunc rata sunt testamenta & vires accipiunt. Ita Chrysostomus.
units.tr: Yet the interpretation of Chrysostom is not to be concealed, nor altogether rejected. For he too acknowledges that these words were added by way of a figure, saying: "Perhaps," he says, "many who were weaker might, because Christ is said to have died, not believe his promises. Paul therefore adds this in abundance, taking examples from common custom. And what is this? Therefore we ought above all to be confident. Why? Because testaments are not ratified and do not gain force while the testators are living, but when they are dead." Thus Chrysostom.

units.la: Sed nostra interpretatio, ni fallor, magis conuenit causæ, quæ agitur, meliusque respondet. spondet & præcedentibus & sequentibus,ac consilium Apostoli videtur proprie explicare.
units.tr: But our interpretation, unless I am mistaken, agrees better with the matter under discussion and answers it more fittingly. It corresponds both to what precedes and to what follows, and it seems properly to explain the Apostle's purpose.

units.la: Restat,ut ostendamus,nihil hic vitij commissum, quando vocabulum testamenti aliter hoc vno loco,quàm vsquam alibi in vniuersa Scriptura vsurpatur : neque esse, cur ob id cauillentur alij,hanc epistolam pro Paulina nequaquam cognoscendam.Primùm fiue vocem hebraeam בריח spectes,siue graecam διαθηκη, non longè disceditur à natiua earum significatione,si pro testamento, id est,extrema voluntate morientium,quain bonis suis successuros hæredes instituunt, accipiantur. Nam בריח cùm proprie significet pactum siue fœdus,testamentum verò à morientibus condi solitum, quodammodo fit pacti quædam species,clarè vides,vbi vox בריח posteriori significatione ponitur,genus pro specie per metonymiam vsurpari:quemadmodum si dicas magistratu pro consule,senatore, vel prætore:aut certè non ita longè petita id fieri metaphora.Vox autè διαθηκη, quæ Græcis valet simul & fœdus ,& quod vulgato more nominamus testamentum,quando hoc loco ponitur pro testamento,supra verò(sicut & aliàs semper) posita erat pro pacto:tantum abest,ut incommodi aliquid accidat,ut etiam non mediocris subsit gratia atq; elegantia,per schema nimirum quod rhetores vocant ἀντανάκλασις, quod fit,cum eadem vox repetitur,sed cum iucunda quadam significationis,aut simul etiam literarum mutatione:quomodo etiam Romanorum oftauo dixit Apostolus, De peccato condemnauit peccatum.Igitur neque in hebraica lingua,qua credunt plerique præsentem epistolam scriptam,neque in græca,cùm voces,quæ alias pactum seu fœdus in Scripturis significant,vsurpantur hoc loco pro testamento seu extrema morientium voluntate,quicquam peccatum est.
units.tr: It remains for us to show that no fault has been committed here, when the word testament is used in this one place in a different sense from anywhere else in the whole of Scripture; nor is there any reason for others to cavil on that account and to deny that this epistle can be recognised as Pauline. First, whether you look at the Hebrew word בריח [berith] or the Greek word διαθηκη [diathēkē], the meaning does not depart far from their natural signification, if they are taken for a testament, that is, the last will of the dying, by which they appoint heirs to succeed to their goods. For בריח [berith], although properly it signifies a pact or covenant, and a testament customarily made by the dying is in some way a kind of pact, you clearly see that when the word בריח [berith] is used in the latter sense, the genus is used for the species by metonymy, just as if you were to say "magistrate" for "consul," "senator," or "praetor"; or at least this is done by a metaphor not far-fetched. The word διαθηκη [diathēkē], which in Greek means both covenant and what we commonly call a testament, when it is used here for testament, whereas above (as also elsewhere always) it was used for pact, is so far from causing any inconvenience that there is also no small grace and elegance in it, namely by the figure which the rhetoricians call ἀντανάκλασις [antanaklasis], which happens when the same word is repeated but with a pleasing shift of meaning, or at the same time a change of letters; just as the Apostle also said in Romans 8: "He condemned sin through sin." Therefore there is no fault either in the Hebrew language, in which many believe the present epistle was written, or in the Greek, when words that elsewhere in Scripture signify pact or covenant are here used for testament or the last will of the dying.

units.la: Secundò,cùm de fœdere euangelico agitur,rectè id significari nomine testamenti vel ex eo liquet, quòd præstantissimum signum huius noui fœderis Christus imminente morte,eo prorsus modo, quo solent morituri testamentum condere, instituerit, in sui perpetuam memoriam seruari obseruariq; voluerit ab omnibus,qui hæreditatem ipsius adire cuperent,idq; insuper testamenti appellatione(simili sensu)honorarit. Sicenim qua nocte suis valedicebat,sciens se tradendum,& præfatus fuerat,quæ vellet per discipulos fieri,quasi rebus omnibus bene compositis tandem instituit,in sui memoriam sacrum corpus & sanguinem suum sæpe sumi,accepto videlicet in manus panem, dicens: Accipite & comedite:Hoc est corpus meum,quod pro vobis frangitur. Ad eundem modum sumpto poculo dixit,Hoc poculum nouum testamentum est in meo sanguine:hoc facite quotiescunque biberitis,in mei commemorationem. Quod signum & cuprimis venerandum sacramentum (corporis inquam & sanguinis sui)ipse seu munusculum relictum seu credentibus omnibus commune & velut hereditarium esse voluit,& æternæ ac cœlestis hæreditatis post hanc vitam accipiendæ certum symbolum.
units.tr: Second, when we speak of the gospel covenant, it is rightly signified by the name of testament, and this is clear from the fact that Christ, at the approach of his death, instituted its most excellent sign in exactly the way those who are about to die usually make a will. He wished it to be observed and kept by all who desired to enter upon his inheritance, in perpetual memory of himself. He also honoured it with the name of testament, in a similar sense. For on the night when he was bidding farewell to his own, knowing that he was about to be handed over, and having first stated what he wished to be done by his disciples, as if all things were now settled, he at last instituted that his sacred body and blood be often taken in remembrance of him. Taking bread in his hands, he said: "Take and eat: this is my body, which is broken for you." In the same way, having taken the cup, he said: "This cup is the new testament in my blood; do this as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me." This sign, and above all this most venerable sacrament of his body and blood, he wished to be left either as a little gift or as something common to all believers and, as it were, an inheritance, and a sure pledge of the eternal and heavenly inheritance to be received after this life.

units.la: Hinc iam factum apparet atque vsu receptum,quòd,quicquid ad euangelium pertinet,ab hoc principali euangelici fœderis signo,noui testamenti nomine appelletur. Valde autem credibile est, Apostolum ad eam Christi institutionem & uerba respexisse,quà do hic significationem seu בריח seu διαθηκης vsurpauit .
units.tr: From this it now becomes apparent, and has become established by usage, that whatever pertains to the gospel is called by the name of the New Testament, from this principal sign of the gospel covenant. It is also highly credible that the Apostle had regard to that institution and those words of Christ when he used here the word meaning either [בריח] in Hebrew or [διαθηκης] in Greek.

units.la: Tertiò,concedendum est,euangelium pactum testamentum nomine non male appellari,quando constat,de eodem rectissimè dici posse omnia, quæ in testamento ad præscriptum consuetudinis ac iuris ciuilis facto considerari solent: quae de re lubet nonnihil adijcere. Traduntiure consulti,quatuor inprimis requiri substantialia, ut loquuntur, per quæ testamentum rite fiat. Primùm, oportet esse testatorem: Secundò hæredes seu legatarios:Tertiò,bona certa, quæ designentur,& quæ testator velit fieri . Quartò, formam siue solennitatnm testamenti conficiendi.Hæc verò omnia in euangelico negotio obseruari possunt. Testator est ipse Christus:quandoquidem Apostolus ita eum præsenti loco nominat,& vbique noui testamenti autor conciliatorq; describitur:ut nequaquam opus sit pluribus verbis eam rem explicare. Bona legata, & quæ velit fieri is testator,passim etiam describuntur in euangelio,vbi vita æterna promittitur,quam passim sacrae literæ ideò vocant hæreditatem cœlestem & æternam,sicut iam quoque proximo loco ab Apostolo factum vidimus.Et quæ Christus velit fieri,in omnibus illis concionibus & factis ob oculos sunt posita,& in summam semel omnia comprehensa in extrema illa ante mortem concione, qua dedit mandatum nouum,vt omnes sese mutuò diligerent. Vide Ioan.14.15.16.17.
units.tr: Third, it must be granted that the gospel is not wrongly called a covenant by the name of testament, since it is agreed that everything which is usually considered in a testament made according to the custom and civil law can be rightly said of it. On this matter it is worth adding something. Jurists teach that four substantial elements, as they call them, are chiefly required for a testament to be validly made. First, there must be a testator; second, heirs or legatees; third, certain goods which are designated and which the testator wishes to pass; fourth, the form or solemnities of making the testament. All these can be observed in the business of the gospel. The testator is Christ himself, since the Apostle names him as such in this passage, and everywhere he is described as the author and mediator of the New Testament, so there is no need to explain the matter at length. The legacies, and what the testator wishes to be done, are also described throughout the gospel, where eternal life is promised, which the Sacred Scriptures everywhere call the heavenly and eternal inheritance, as we have already seen the Apostle do in the immediately preceding place. What Christ wishes to be done is set before our eyes in all those sermons and deeds, and all of it was summed up once for all in that final discourse before his death, in which he gave the new commandment that all should love one another. See John 14, 15, 16, 17.

units.la: Hæredes seu legatarij sunt omnes credentes,quotquot ab initio mundi ad finem vsque fuerunt vel erunt:quos etiâ passim in euangelicis & apostolicis scriptis ita cernimus appellari,præterea & adoptatos filios,vt nequaquam necessum sit,probationes copiosas in medium producere,Iâ q; ad formâ attinet, si qs in primis requirat,sit'ne testamentum Christi
units.tr: The heirs or legatees are all believers, as many as there have been or will be from the beginning of the world to its end. We see them everywhere in the evangelical and apostolic writings called by this name, and also adopted sons, so that there is no need to bring forward copious proofs. As for the form, if anyone first asks whether the testament of Christ is

units.la: Vetus testamentum. Christi sine scriptis traditum, quod alias vocant nuncupatiuum, an scriptis traditum.Respondetur, nequaquam scriptis traditum à Christo, sed præsentibus legitimis testibus, & reliquis rebus ritè peractis,& sic esse nuncupatiuum. Testes legitimi sunt duodecim apostoli, quos etiā testes suos Christus appellauit, Lucæ 24, Act.1.Ioan.15. & qui se tales sæpenumerò profitentur. Actor.2.4.10.13.18.26. 1.Petri 5.
units.tr: the Old Testament, that is, whether it was handed down by Christ without writing, which some call nuncupative, or handed down in writing. The answer is that it was not handed down in writing by Christ, but with lawful witnesses present, and the other formalities duly performed, and so it is nuncupative. The lawful witnesses are the twelve apostles, whom Christ himself called his witnesses (Luke 24; Acts 1; John 15), and who very often profess themselves to be such: Acts 2, 4, 10, 13, 18, 26; 1 Peter 5.

units.la: Pronunciauit Christus his præsentibus bona legata: item quid vellet fieri, quod decerneret hæredes, confirmauit institutione noui signi: deniq; ratum esse voluit in morte semetipsum offerendo, ut morte ipsius intercedente, sicut loquitur Apostolus, credentes, qui vocati & electi sunt, promissionem accipiant æternæ hæreditatis. Tantum ergo de voce testamenti, aliter quàm alibi, hoc loco usurpata. Atq; his intellectis omnia sunt perspicua. Quatenus liceat in comprobatione rerum futurarum ex rebus humanis argumenta ducere, alias à nobis dictum est, cap.6. vbi de iuramento agebatur.
units.tr: Christ, in the presence of these, declared the legacies; likewise he stated what he wished to be done, appointed the heirs, and confirmed it by instituting the new sign. Finally, he wished it to be ratified by offering himself in death, so that, by his death intervening, as the Apostle says, believers who are called and chosen may receive the promise of eternal inheritance. So much for the word testament, used here in a sense different from elsewhere. Once this is understood, everything is clear. How far it is lawful to draw arguments from human affairs in confirming future things, we have said elsewhere, in chapter 6, where the oath was discussed.

units.la: Quod verò ad consuetudinem seu legem humanam attinet, quà probationis loco adfert Apostolus, ea non habet quicquam difficultatis, & extat etiam in iure ciuili, quod à Romanis acceptum hodie in manibus est, lib.1. Pandectarum, vbi in vnum locum digesta sunt omnia, quæ de testamentis scitu sunt necessaria. Cur autem ratum non sit testamentum aliquod, nisi mortuo testatore, duæ possunt adferri causæ: Altera, quòd, quoniā testamentum proprie intelligitur extrema voluntas, nunquam aliquod testamentum sic conditum est, quin testator, quamdiu viuat, possit id mutare(nisi fortasis ipse sibi legem aut conditionem præscripserit aliquando de non mutando) & sic nunquam extrema voluntas plenè cognoscitur, nisi cùm ex hac vita semel migrarit. Altera causa est, quòd, quamdiu testator viuit, bona ipsius ab alijs, quos hæredes conscripsit, non possunt ipso inuito occupari, semperq; manent in ipsius potestate, dum viuit.
units.tr: As for the human custom or law which the Apostle brings forward by way of proof, this presents no difficulty, and it is also found in the civil law, which, received from the Romans, is today in our hands, in book 1 of the Pandects, where everything that needs to be known about testaments is gathered into one place. Two reasons can be given why no testament is ratified unless the testator is dead. The first is that, since a testament is properly understood as a last will, no testament is ever made in such a way that the testator, as long as he lives, cannot change it (unless perhaps he has himself prescribed a law or condition at some time forbidding change).
