Thus the last will is never fully known until he has once departed from this life. The second reason is that, as long as the testator lives, his goods cannot be seized by those whom he has named heirs against his will, and they always remain in his power while he lives.

units.la: Cæterum quòd Christus hic describitur testator, qui morte sua velit ratum facere nouum testamentum, in quo cœlestis hæreditas ab omnibus credentibus, qui sunt veluti legitimi hæredes designati, accipiatur, istud profectò insignem charitatem Dei patris & Christi pariter nobis commendat, & propterea inenarrabilem nostram fœlicitatem, quibus hæreditas illa, modò in Christum credamus, & vere adhibeamus fidem nostro testatori, adeunda proponitur.
units.tr: Moreover, that Christ is here described as a testator who by his death wishes to ratify the New Testament, in which the heavenly inheritance is to be received by all believers, who are as it were the designated lawful heirs, this certainly commends to us the remarkable love of God the Father and of Christ alike, and therefore our inexpressible happiness, since that inheritance is set before us to be entered upon, provided we believe in Christ and truly place our faith in our testator.

units.la: Et cùm constet, mortem ipsius iā intercessisse, debemus hac cognitione in fide confirmari, ac certi esse, propter mortem talis testatoris cœlestem hæreditatem nobis obuenturam, etiamsi nullum ius sit, nulla nostra merita, quæ possimus prætendere. Nam nos adoptati sumus in filios, ut per Christum, & cum Christo filio naturali hæreditatem illā obtineamus. Habemus ergo hic, sicut in omnibus hisce descriptionibus de sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi, ingentem consolationem, qua possumus nos in tentationibus erigere. Ac propterea hauddubiè voluit Apostolus tā prolixè de sacrificio Christi agere, vt beneficiū mortis ipsius propius agnoscerimus, atque vberiores inde acciperemus consolationes.
units.tr: And since it is agreed that his death has already taken place, we ought to be confirmed in faith by this knowledge, and be certain that, on account of the death of such a testator, the heavenly inheritance will come to us, even though we have no right and no merits of our own that we could plead. For we have been adopted as sons, so that through Christ, and together with Christ the natural Son, we may obtain that inheritance. Here, then, as in all these descriptions of the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, we have a great consolation by which we can raise ourselves up in temptations. Therefore the Apostle undoubtedly wished to treat the sacrifice of Christ so fully, so that we might more closely recognise the benefit of his death and receive from it richer consolations.

units.la: Vnde ne prius quidem illud absque sanguine dedicatum fuit.
units.tr: Hence not even the first covenant was dedicated without blood.

units.la: Cùm enim Moses omne præceptum iuxta legem exposuisset omni populo, sumpto sanguine vitulorum et hircorum, cum aqua & lana coccina, & hyssopo, simul & ipsum librum, & totum populū aspersit, dicens: Hic est sanguis testamenti, quod mandauit uobis Deus. Insuper aut & tabernaculum, & omnia vasa ministerij sanguine consimiliter aspergebat. Et omnia fere secundum legem sanguine purificantur, & absq; sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Itaq; necesse est, ut exemplaria quidem eorum, quæ sunt in cœlis, hisce rebus purificentur. Cæterum ipsa cœlestia potioribus, quàm hæsint, victimis mundentur.
units.tr: For when Moses had spoken every precept according to the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you. Moreover he likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry with blood. And almost all things are purified by blood according to the law, and without shedding of blood there is no remission. It is therefore necessary that the copies of heavenly things be purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.

units.la: Aliud argumentū, quo probatur, æquū esse, vt nouū testamentū intercedente morte Christi ratum fiat, à collatione typi ad veritatem: veritas debet respondere typo: quod & apparet non citra occupationem esse adiectum. Præcedenti enim argumento fortasis non satis fiebat morosis ingenijs, quæ occlamabant, non congruere, vt diceretur, eodē pacto debere agi in causa euangelij & spiritualium bonorum, quo agitur in causa testamentorum ciuilium & bonorum terrenorum, ideoque aliud argumentum proferendū è Scripturis, quo illud stabiliretur. Hac igitur de causa aliud argumentum producit Apostolus, è typis ductum, seu potius ab eo, quòd res adumbratæ semper debeant esse præstantiores vmbris siue typis, ex excellentiori modo perfici. Estque hæc argumenti sententia.
units.tr: Another argument, by which it is proved that it is fitting that the new covenant be ratified through the death of Christ, is drawn from the comparison of type and truth: the truth ought to correspond to the type. And this appears to have been added not without reason. For perhaps the preceding argument did not sufficiently satisfy those stubborn minds which cried out that it did not fit that it should be said that in the cause of the gospel and of spiritual goods one should act in the same way as in the cause of civil testaments and earthly goods. Therefore another argument had to be brought forward from the Scriptures, by which that point might be established. For this reason the Apostle produces another argument, drawn from the types, or rather from the fact that the things foreshadowed must always be more excellent than the shadows or types, and be accomplished in a more excellent manner. And this is the substance of the argument.

units.la: Vetus testamentum, vbi tantùm erant exemplaria seu vmbrae rerum futurarum & cœlestium, sancitum est ac ratum factum, adhibito immolatarum pecudum sanguine.
units.tr: The Old Testament, where there were only copies or shadows of future and heavenly things, was sanctioned and made valid by the application of the blood of slain beasts.

units.la: Ergo nouum testamentum, ubi adsunt res ipsæ, & bona cœlestia, multo præstantiori modo, nempe sanguine ac morte ipsius Christi, sanciri ratumque fieri conuenit. Valet consequentia ab eo, quòd semper debent præstantiores esse res adumbratæ, ut dignius, quàm ipsæ umbræ: quod quidem ex iis, quæ supra maximè capite octauo dicta sunt de excellentia rerum euangelicarum præ legibus, abundè est manifestum. Et certè si Christus tantùm obtulisset sanguinem pecorum, & non nisi pecorum mors intercessisset pro confirmatione noui testamenti, qua obsecro in parte iudicari posset nouum testamentum excellentius veteri? Porrò antecedens argumenti Apostolus pluribus exemplis luculenter probat, vbiq; sanguinem & mortem pecudum ostentantibus. Nulla epistola, (id quod supra monendum fuerat) quamlibet sublimibus argumentis referta, habet tot occupationes seu antipophoras, atq; ista. Id verò propterea, quòd Apostolo negotium erat cum hebraeis, qui, quicquid dicebatur de Christi dignitate, facilè poterant eludere, & semper in promptu habebant quod obijcerent. Itaq; ut satisfieret morosis ingenijs, atq; ora illis obstruerentur, opus erat crebras occupationes disputationi admisere. Est autem multò artificiosissimè argumentum istud excogitatum. Nam alias debuisset producere aliquem typum ex veteri testamento, in quo idem fuisset simul sacerdos & hostia, atque vbi morte alicuius eximiæ personæ fuisset testamentum seu pactum roboratum.
units.tr: Therefore the New Testament, where the things themselves and the heavenly goods are present, ought to be sanctioned and made valid in a much more excellent manner, namely by the blood and death of Christ himself. The inference holds from the fact that the things foreshadowed must always be more excellent, as worthier than the shadows themselves; and this is abundantly clear from what was said above, especially in chapter eight, about the excellence of the gospel realities over the law. And certainly, if Christ had offered only the blood of animals, and if only the death of animals had intervened to confirm the new covenant, in what respect, I ask, could the new covenant be judged more excellent than the old? Moreover, the Apostle, as was to be noted above, clearly proves the antecedent of the argument by several examples, everywhere pointing to the blood and death of animals. No epistle, however full of sublime arguments, contains so many objections or antiphorae of this kind. And this is because the Apostle had to deal with the Hebrews, who could easily evade whatever was said about the dignity of Christ and always had something ready to object. Therefore, so that the stubborn minds might be satisfied and their mouths stopped, it was necessary to admit frequent objections into the discussion. Moreover, this argument has been devised with very great skill. For otherwise he would have had to produce some type from the Old Testament in which the same person was at once priest and victim, and in which a covenant or pact had been ratified by the death of some eminent person.

units.la: Hoc verò erat impossibile: neq; enim in Scripturis tale quiddam repetitur. Itaq; huc confugit, ut argumentum duceret ab eo, quòd res adübratæ debeant esse excellentiores ipsis typis: & cum in veteri testamento intercesserit mors pecudum, hoc iam inde sequi debebat, ut, si nouum testamentum præstantiori modo veniret confirmandum, morte alicuius hominis id perficeretur: quando alias nullo modo excellentius aliquid factum consideraretur.
units.tr: But this was impossible: for no such thing is repeated in the Scriptures. Therefore he has taken refuge in this, that he draws the argument from the principle that the things foreshadowed must be more excellent than the types themselves. And since in the Old Testament the death of animals intervened, it must follow from this that, if the new covenant was to be confirmed in a more excellent manner, this would be accomplished by the death of some man; since otherwise nothing could be regarded as done more excellently.

units.la: Vnde ne prius quidem illud absque sanguine dedicatum fuit) Propositio est, siue antecedens Enthymematis. Quòd verò ait, dedicatum est, perinde est, atq; quod supra dixit, ratum factum est & confirmatum: quanquam præsens vox paulò euidentius significat, omnia in veteri testamento facta ad Dei gloriam ἐγκαινίζειν enim est innouare, dedicare, & consecrare, adeoq; rem quampiam certis ceremonijs nuncupare, vt pro sancto deinceps habeatur: quemadmodum vasa tabernaculi, vestes, & id genus leguntur dedicata & consecrata: sic enim & 3. Regum 8. de templo Solomonis, Et dedicauerunt templum Domini Rex & filij Israel: vbi septuaginta habet, ἐνεκαίνισαν τὸν οἶκον. Et Deut.20. Quis est homo, qui ædificat domum, & nō dedicat eam, ἐνκαινίσας αὐτὴν: Ibidem repetitur vox, atq; alibi sæpius. Hinc & τὰ ἐγκαίνια, dedicatio seu festi dies dedicationis alicuius rei: quæ vox habetur 2. Machab. 8. & Ioan. 10.
units.tr: Hence not even the first covenant was dedicated without blood. This is the proposition, or antecedent, of the enthymeme. But when he says "was dedicated," it is the same as what he said above, "was made valid and confirmed," although the present word signifies somewhat more plainly that all the things done in the Old Testament were done for the glory of God. For enkainizein [ἐγκαινίζειν] means to renew, to dedicate and to consecrate, and so to set apart a thing by certain ceremonies so that it is thenceforth regarded as holy; just as the vessels of the tabernacle, the garments and the like are read of as dedicated and consecrated. Thus also in 3 Kings 8 concerning the temple of Solomon: And the king and the sons of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord, where the Seventy have [ἐνεκαίνισαν τὸν οἶκον], they dedicated the house. And Deut. 20: Who is the man who builds a house and does not dedicate it [ἐνκαινίσας αὐτὴν], having dedicated it? The word is repeated in the same place, and more often elsewhere. Hence also ta enkainia [τὰ ἐγκαίνια] means the dedication, or the feast day of the dedication of something; this word occurs in 2 Maccabees 8 and John 10.

units.la: ἐγκαινίζειν quid.
units.tr: What enkainizein means [ἐγκαινίζειν].

units.la: Cùm enim Moses præceptum iuxta legem expositiffet omni populo, sumpto sanguine vitulorum & hircorum, cum aqua, & lana coccina, & hyssopo, simul & ipsum librum, & totum populum aspersit, dicens: Hic est sanguis testamenti, quod mandauit vobis Deus.
units.tr: For when Moses had expounded the precept according to the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded you.

units.la: Instituit probationem propositionis seu antecedentis, idque verbis pluribus, nécnon argumentis petitis ex diuersis locis, hoc fere ordine, vt primo loco commemoret, quomodo tota lex, cùm primùm promulgata esset, & velut pro conditionibus fœderis proposita, etiam sanguinis aspersione sit sancita. Secundo autem loco, quomodo tabernaculum item cum adiunctis omnibus, sanguine sit consecratum. Tertio, summatim volens complecti omnia alia purificationum legalium genera, ait, Nihil in lege solitum put gari citra effusum sanguine n. Hoc inquam ordine probatio hæc est constituta. Nos singula membra explicabimus. Primum autem sumptum est ex Exod.24. vbi sic legitur: Postquam iussu Domini ascendisset Moses solus in montem, Aarone & cæteris procul stantibus & adorantibus iterum descendit Moses, & narrauit plebi omnia verba Domini atq; iudicia: responditq; omnis populus vna voce: Omnia uerba Domini, quæ locutus est, faciemus: & sequitur, Scripsit autè Moses vniuersos sermones Domini (quales quatuor capitibus ibidem exponuntur) & mane consurgens ædificauit altare Domino ad radices montis, & duodecim titulos per duodecim tribus Israel: misitq; iuuenes de filijs Israel, & obtulerunt holocausta immolaueruntque victimas pacificas Domino vitulos duodecim. Tulit itaq; Moses dimidiam partem sanguinis, & misit in crateras, partem autem reliduam fudit super altare. Assumensq; volumen fœderis, legit audiente populo: Qui dixerunt, omnia quæ locutus est Dominus faciemus, & erimus obedientes. Ille verò sumptum sanguinem respersit in populum, & ait: Hic est sanguis fœderis, quod pepigit Dominus vobiscum super cunctis sermonibus. En quod ad præsentem locum pertinet: Moses mediator {a}diator inter Deum & Israelitas, iussu Domini promulgat populo legem, quæ velut conditiones continet pacti propositi: populus recipit legem, atq; etiam viva voce se obstringit Deo: quare confirmatur fœdus aspersione sanguinis. Pulcherrima figura Christi, qui etiam est mediator noui testamenti, qui legem & voluntatem Domini palàm proposuit, & quotquot crediderunt, lubenter etiā doctrinam eius & conditiones pacti (videlicet vt crederent in Deum, & quem is misit Iesum Christum) receperunt. Quamobrem Christus confirmauit, sanciuit, etiam hoc pactum inter Deum & omnes credentes, aspersione sanguinis, verùm non alieni, sed sui: licet interea animantia bruta propter innocentiā & speciem carnis peccati, Christi figura fuerint. Vide quàm omnia quadrent, quæ in vetere testamento acta sunt, ad ea, quæ post adimpleta sunt per Christū in testamento nouo.
units.tr: He sets out the proof of the proposition, or antecedent, in more words, and also with arguments drawn from various passages, in roughly this order: first he recalls how the whole law, when first promulgated and set forth as it were as the conditions of the covenant, was also sanctioned by the sprinkling of blood. Second, how the tabernacle, with all its accessories, was likewise consecrated with blood. Third, wishing to sum up briefly all the other kinds of legal purifications, he says that nothing under the law was ordinarily cleansed without the shedding of blood. In this order, I say, this proof is constructed. We shall explain the individual members. The first is taken from Exod. 24, where it is read thus: After Moses had gone up alone into the mountain at the command of the Lord, while Aaron and the others stood afar off and worshipped, Moses came down again and told the people all the words and judgments of the Lord; and all the people answered with one voice: We will do all the words which the Lord has spoken, and we will be obedient. And it follows: Moses wrote all the words of the Lord (which are set out in four chapters there), and rising early he built an altar to the Lord at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars according to the twelve tribes of Israel; and he sent young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings to the Lord, twelve calves. Moses therefore took half of the blood and put it into basins, and poured the rest upon the altar. And taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people. They said: All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient. Then he sprinkled the blood on the people and said: This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words. Here, as far as the present passage is concerned: Moses, the mediator between God and the Israelites, by the command of the Lord promulgates the law to the people, which contains as it were the conditions of the proposed pact; the people receive the law and also bind themselves by a spoken vow to God; therefore the covenant is confirmed by the sprinkling of blood. A most beautiful figure of Christ, who is also the mediator of the New Testament, who openly set forth the law and the will of the Lord, and as many as believed gladly received his teaching and the conditions of the pact (namely that they should believe in God and in Jesus Christ whom he sent). Wherefore Christ confirmed and sanctioned this pact also between God and all believers by the sprinkling of blood, yet not of others but of his own; although meanwhile the brute animals were figures of Christ on account of their innocence and the appearance of sinful flesh. See how well everything that was done in the Old Testament agrees with those things which have since been fulfilled through Christ in the New Testament.

units.la: Omne præceptum iuxta legem) Id est omnia præcepta, quæ in lege continentur, quæ lex præscribit. Præceptum iuxta legem videtur dici, ad discrimen præceptorum, quæ non iuxta legem, sed iuxta traditiones hominum instituuntur: & ut præceptum latius pateat, quà lex. Vocatur volumen fœderis, quia lex fuit scripta, & necessum fuit eà promulgari, prius quàm populus se stare velle fœderi promitteret: & sic aptissimus est locus ad probandum, confirmationem totius fœderis seu testamenti factam esse sanguine. Christus verò fœdus Dei promulgauit, non scripto, sed viua tantùm voce, per quam illud fœdus inscripsit piorum cordibus: quod quidem fecit Christus toto tempore, quo in terris vixit & docuit. Post verò confirmauit fœdus illud oblato suo sanguine, quo aspersæ sunt omnes tribus, id est, vniuersa multitudo verorum Israelitarum, id est, credetium, qui promissionis sunt filij ex Abraham, non carnis. Et sicut Moses dixit, hic est sanguis fœderis: ita Christus cùm instaret mors, & instituere vellet memoriale signum Matth. 26. sine dubio respiciens ad illa verba Mosaica, Hic est, inquit, sanguis noui testamenti, qui pro vobis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Sed hic obijciat aliquis rursus, non rectè conuenire verba præsentis loci cum historia Mosaica: primùm enim hic addit Apostolus de sanguine hircorum, quorù tamen ibi non fit mentio, sed tantù vitulorū. Responderi potest, Apostolum annumerare hircos, cōmuni quodam numerandi more, quo præcipua in aliqua re solent numerari ad efficacius aliquid significandū. Iam constat, sanguine vitulorū, & præterea hircorū præcipuè solitū in cæteris expiationib. principalibus exhiberi, sicut de illa expiatione, quæ semel in anno in sanctis sanctorū fiebat, dictū est: Leuit. 16. Igitur Apostolus loquens de prima illa confirmatione legis obiter vna voce hircorum adiećta, voluit in memoriā regerere, id quod ad annuas expiationes & confirmationes principales attinebat. Et certè in prima illa confirmatione per sanguinem, etiam cæterę, quæ post institutæ sunt, comprehenduntur, & iam tum in prima ostendebatur, nihil sine sanguine deinceps faciundum. Quòd si secundo obijciatur, nullam in Exodo fieri mentionem aquæ, lanæ coccinæ, & hyssopi. Respondetur, nihil aliud, quàm aspersionum faciendarū modū hic appositum esse. De aspersione sanguinis agni paschalis cum hyssopo, Exod. 12. Sed clarius Leuit. 14. vbi de purificatione domus infećę lepra sic additur: In purificatione eius sumet duos passeres lignum q; cedrinum, & vermiculū atq; hyssopū & coccum, & passerem viuum, & tinget omnia in sanguine passeris immolati atq; in aquis viuentibus, & asperget domū septics, purificabitq; eam tam in sanguine passeris immolati, quàin aquis viuentibus, & in passere viuo, lignoq; cedrino, & hyssopo, atq; vermiculo: alibi quoq; sæpius de aqua lustrationis. Prudenter autē consultoq; videtur Apostolus ista de modo aspergendi interposuisse, ad tacitè significandū, in omnibus adūbrandum aliquid per Christū gerendū foret, vt oēs ryporū haberent rationē. Lana coccina carnem Christi sanguine tinćtā refert: aqua vim purificandi, seu successurum baptismū aquę: Hyssopus pœnitentiam, seu vim purificandi præ se fert, quam propheta in psalmo notat, dicens: Asperge me Domine hyssopo, & mundabor. Si cui vacaret ex Physicorum libris plura congerere, inueniret, nihil esse otiose adhibitum.
units.tr: "Every precept according to the law": that is, all the precepts contained in the law, which the law prescribes. The phrase "according to the law" seems to be used to distinguish these from precepts instituted not according to the law but according to the traditions of men, and so that the precept may extend as widely as the law does. The law is called "the book of the covenant" because it was written, and it had to be published before the people promised that they wished to stand by the covenant. So this is a very apt place to prove that the confirmation of the whole covenant or testament was made by blood. Christ, however, published the covenant of God not in writing but only by the living voice, and through that voice he inscribed the covenant on the hearts of the godly. He did this throughout the whole time he lived and taught on earth. Afterwards he confirmed that covenant by offering his blood, with which all the tribes were sprinkled, that is, the whole multitude of true Israelites, that is, of believers, who are the children of the promise and of Abraham, not of the flesh. And as Moses said, "This is the blood of the covenant," so Christ, when death was near and he wished to institute a memorial sign (Matth. 26.), doubtless had in mind those Mosaic words: "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for you for the remission of sins." But someone may object again that the words of this passage do not agree properly with the Mosaic history. For first, the Apostle adds "of goats" to the blood, yet there is no mention of goats there, only of calves. It can be answered that the Apostle counts in the goats by a common manner of counting, by which the chief items in some matter are usually counted in order to signify something more forcefully. It is well established that the blood of calves, and besides it especially the blood of goats, was customarily offered in the other principal expiations, just as was said of that expiation which was performed once a year in the Holy of Holies (Leviticus 16.). So the Apostle, speaking of that first confirmation of the law, added in passing the single word "goats," wishing to recall to memory what pertained to the yearly expiations and the principal confirmations. And certainly in that first confirmation by blood, all the others that were instituted afterwards are also included, and already then it was shown that nothing was to be done thereafter without blood. But if it is objected a second time that Exodus makes no mention of water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, the answer is that the passage merely sets out the manner of making the sprinklings. On the sprinkling of the blood of the paschal lamb with hyssop, see Exod. 12. But more clearly Leviticus 14., where the purification of a house infected with leprosy is described thus: "In its purification he shall take two sparrows, and cedar wood, and scarlet and hyssop, and the living sparrow, and he shall dip all of them in the blood of the slain sparrow and in living waters, and he shall sprinkle the house seven times, and so purify it, both with the blood of the slain sparrow and with the living waters, and with the living sparrow, the cedar wood, the hyssop, and the scarlet." Elsewhere too, more often, there is mention of the water of lustration. The Apostle seems to have inserted these details about the manner of sprinkling wisely and deliberately, to signify tacitly that something was to be prefigured in all these things to be accomplished through Christ, so that all the types would have their meaning. The scarlet wool represents the flesh of Christ dyed with blood; the water represents the power of cleansing, or the baptism of water that was to follow; the hyssop represents repentance, or the power of cleansing that it carries with it, which the prophet marks in the psalm, saying: "Purge me with hyssop, O Lord, and I shall be clean" (Ps. 51.). If anyone had leisure to gather more examples from the books of the natural philosophers, he would find that nothing was used to no purpose.

units.la: Porrò de libro asperso similiter sanguine non satis expressum apparet, sed tamen, quoniam inter sancta etiam inuentus est, satis est vero consentaneum, quòd ipse quoq; sanguine aspersus credatur, idq; eò magis, quòd Deut. 31. iussus est inter sacra serutari, & in latere arcæ fœderis Domini reponi.
units.tr: Moreover, it does not appear clearly that the book was sprinkled with blood in the same way, but nevertheless, since it too was found among the holy things, it is quite consistent with the truth to believe that it too was sprinkled with blood, all the more because in Deut. 31. it was commanded to be examined among the sacred things and placed at the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord.

units.la: Tametsi rectius dicatur, ab Apostolo additum de libro asperso, propter mysterium, nepe ad significandum, corda credentium aspergi in nouo testamento, in quorum cordibus Dominus legem Spiritus inscripsit: Dabo legem meam in cordibus illorum. Cùm deniq; dicit, aspersum sanguine totum populum, intelligē per Synecdochen maiorem populi partē, & seniores in primis, qui Mosi astabant propinquiores. Alias enim sexies centena millia qui potuissent tantillo sanguine aspergi. De phrafi illa, Hic est sanguis testamenti, quod mandauit vobis Deus, non opus est curiosè disputare.
units.tr: Yet it is more correct to say that the Apostle added the detail about the sprinkled book on account of the mystery, namely to signify that the hearts of believers are sprinkled in the New Testament, in whose hearts the Lord has written the law of the Spirit: "I will put my law in their hearts" (Jer. 31.). Finally, when he says that the whole people was sprinkled with blood, we are to understand by synecdoche the greater part of the people, and above all the elders, who stood nearest to Moses. For otherwise six hundred thousand men, who could have been sprinkled with so little blood? There is no need to dispute curiously about that phrase, "This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded you."

units.la: Proderit obseruare hanc formulam, ad intelligendum verba coenae Domini, quae hoc tempore, proh dolor, quidam foedissime torquent, & ad stolidum suum sensum perra- hunt, magna spiritus Sancti iniuria. Conferantur Scripturarum loci inter se, & ipse spi- ritus Sanctus inuenietur, quod vno loco obscurius est positum, alio loco lucidius expo nere. Recte dictum est, Scripturam esse sui ipsius interpretem. Faceßant inter ea curiosę, & ideo periculosae quaestiones, de quibus aperte in Scriptura nihil pronunciatur. Curio- sitas à gloria opprimitur: & sic Deus sinit curiosos sophistas in foedos errores pro- labi.
units.tr: It will be useful to observe this formula for understanding the words of the Lord's Supper, which in these times, alas, some twist most foully and drag to their own foolish sense, to the great injury of the Holy Spirit. Let the passages of Scripture be compared with one another, and the Holy Spirit himself will be found to explain in a clearer place what is set down more obscurely in another. It has been rightly said that Scripture is its own interpreter. Let them cease, therefore, their curious and for that reason dangerous questions about matters on which Scripture clearly pronounces nothing. Curiosity is crushed by glory, and so God allows curious sophists to fall into foul errors.

units.la: Insuper autem & tabernaculum, & omnia vasa ministerij sanguine consimiliter aspergebat.
units.tr: Moreover, the tabernacle too, and all the vessels of the ministry, he likewise sprinkled with blood.

units.la: Secundum membrum probationis, de consecratione taberuaculi & omnium adiun- ctorum. generale vocabulum, ad significandum quaecunq; instrumenta, apparatu, cultum, suppellectilem, &c. In magna domo diuersa sunt vasa. Caeterum nequaquam expressum est, sanguine aspersum esse tabernaculu cum instrumento, in prima erectione eius & consecratione, quae Exodi 40. describitur facta unctione sacri olei, vbi dicitur, omnia uncta fuisse oleo, quo quidem non facile fit aspersio: sed potius accipiendum est de consecratione & dedicatione facta, quae describitur Leuit. 8. quae durabat per septe dies, vbi & diserte dicitur, & altare, & sacerdotes, & vestimenta aspersa sanguine, ex quibus etiam reliquorum instrumentorum aspersio intelligitur.
units.tr: This is the second member of the proof, concerning the consecration of the tabernacle and of all its accessories. A general term, signifying all the instruments, furnishings, equipment, household goods, etc. In a great house there are diverse vessels. However, it is nowhere expressly stated that the tabernacle with its instruments was sprinkled with blood at its first erection and consecration, which is described in Exodus 40., when the anointing with holy oil was performed, where it is said that everything was anointed with oil, and sprinkling with oil is not easily done. Rather, it must be understood of the consecration and dedication that is described in Leviticus 8., which lasted for seven days, where it is clearly said that the altar, the priests, and the garments were sprinkled with blood, and from these the sprinkling of the remaining instruments is also understood.

units.la: Etiam omnia fere secundum legem sanguine purificantur, & absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio peccatorum.
units.tr: Almost everything according to the law is purified by blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins.

units.la: Purificationes quaedam alio modo, quam sanguine fiebant: at vero expiatio a peccatis non fiebat sine sanguine. Est autem hic tertium membrum probationis, de expiatio- num generibus, quas omnes fere dicit fieri sanguine. Certe principales, & quae iudicabatur efficacissimae, fiebant oblatione animalium, & sanguinis eorundem aspersione: qua de re supra diximus agentes de sanguine taurorum & hircorum, & cinere iuuencae rufae. Significanter autem dicit fere, ἀλόν: nam quaedam expiationes fiebant aqua lustrali & ablutionibus, de quibus Numeror. 19. Et generalis quaedam regula de praedis acceptis ab hostibus purgandis. Numer. 31. Aurum & argentum, & aes, & ferrum, & plumbum, & sta- num, & omne quod potest transire per flammas, igne purgabitur. Quicquid autem igne non potest sustinere, aqua expiationis sanctificabitur. Potest etiam particula ἀλόν referri, ut & Chrysostomus interpretatur, ad purificationem seu remissionem, vt sit sententia, non integre, sed tantum propemodum adeoque imperfecte fieri solitam purgatione, quae tantum externas sordes eluerit, & mundos reddiderit coram hominibus, at nequaquam coram Deo.
units.tr: Some purifications were done in another way than by blood, but expiation from sins was not done without blood. Here is the third member of the proof, concerning the kinds of expiation, which he says nearly all take place by blood. Certainly the principal expiations, which were judged the most effective, were made by the offering of animals and the sprinkling of their blood, concerning which we spoke above when dealing with the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of the red heifer. The author says "almost" with good reason, for some expiations were made with lustral water and ablutions, of which Numbers 19. speaks. There is also a general rule concerning the spoils taken from enemies, which must be purified (Num. 31.): "Gold and silver, bronze, iron, lead, and tin, and everything that can pass through fire, shall be purified by fire. But whatever cannot endure fire shall be sanctified with the water of expiation." The particle "almost" may also be referred, as Chrysostom also interprets it, to purification or remission, so that the sense is that the purging customarily done was not complete but only almost, and therefore imperfect, washing away only external filth and making people clean in the sight of men, but by no means in the sight of God.

units.la: Itaq; necesse est, vt exemplaria quidem (τὰ ὑπόδειγματα τῶν ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς) eorum quae sunt in coelis, hisce rebus purificentur.
units.tr: Therefore it was necessary that the copies of the things in the heavens [τὰ ὑπόδειγματα τῶν ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς] should be purified with these things.

units.la: Illatio est ex trib. membris probationis, seu repetitio propositionis, sed paulo alijs verbis enunciatae. Quasi diceret: Huc in modu ea quae sunt sub lege, quae veteris sunt testamenti, purificata sunt sanguine. Exemplaria eorum, quae in coelis sunt, vocat typica & vmbratica omnia in lege fieri solita, quae adumbrat eas res, quae in coelis, id est, nunc in ecclesia sunt: quandoquidem ecclesia habet res coelestes praesentes, & spiritualia habeo bona, etiamsi in terris sit constituta. Sic vero supra capite octauo dicebat, ea quae fiebant in ueteri testamento, seruijsse exemplari atque vmbrae rerum coelestium. Et sequentia verba satis indicant, ita quoque accipienda haec esse. Subijcitur enim, caeterum ipsa coelestia potioribus, quàm hae sint, uictimis mundantur: ipsa coelestia, id est, quae noui testamenti sunt, non amplius vmbratica, sed vera, spiritualia, & coelestia. Quia enim regnum coelorum clarissime in euangelio propositum est & apertam, mysteria omnia reserata, vita spiritualis & plane coelestis tradita, ostensum, quomodo, postquam resurreximus cum Christo, super- na & coelestia debeamus & posimus quaerere, & animis in coelis versari, propterea re- ctè coelestia omnia appellantur. Et ecclesia collecta ex credentibus, qui etiamnum in terris degunt, rectè dicitur in coelis, quia ibi constitutum est eius caput, quod est Chri- stus. Et sicut angeli dicuntur coelestes, & gaudent in coelis, conspicientes Deum patrem, nihilominus etiam hic in terris apud nos sunt: ita ecclesia est terrena, & nihilominus in coelis versatus, cupiens semper voluntatem Domini fieri, sicut in coelo, ita & in terra.
units.tr: This is an inference drawn from three parts of the argument, or a restatement of the proposition in rather different words. It is as if he said: in this way, the things that are under the law, that is, of the Old Testament, were purified with blood. He calls the copies of those things that are in heaven all the typical and shadowy things customary under the law, which foreshadow the things that are in heaven, that is, now in the Church. The Church has heavenly things present and has spiritual blessings, even though it is set up on earth. Indeed, in the eighth chapter above he said that the things done in the Old Testament served as a copy and shadow of heavenly things. The following words make it clear that these words must be understood in the same way. For it continues: but the heavenly things themselves are purified with better sacrifices than these. The heavenly things themselves, that is, those of the New Testament, are no longer shadowy but true, spiritual and heavenly. For the kingdom of heaven is set forth most clearly in the gospel, all mysteries are unlocked and laid open, and a spiritual and wholly heavenly life is delivered and shown: how, after we have risen with Christ, we ought and are able to seek the things above and heavenly, and to dwell in heart in heaven. Therefore all these things are rightly called heavenly. And the Church, gathered from believers who still live on earth, is rightly said to be in heaven, because its head, which is Christ, is established there. Just as the angels are called heavenly and rejoice in heaven, beholding God the Father, yet nonetheless are here on earth among us, so the Church is earthly, and yet dwells in heaven, always desiring that the will of the Lord be done on earth as it is in heaven.

units.la: Nec dissimili modo Galat. 4. ecclesia vocatur Hierusalem sursum agens, quę est mater omnium credentium.
units.tr: In a similar way, in Galatians 4 the Church is called "Jerusalem above," which is the mother of all believers.

units.la: Huc etiam pertinet, quod supra dixit initio capitis, In ueteri testamento fuisse sanctu mundanum: vbi mundanum coelesti opponitur. Alias vero si coelestia accipiamus deijs, quæ post hanc vitam sunt propositæ de angelis, quomodo obsecro conueniet, vt ibi dicantur, aliqua immunda, aliqua adhuc nouis victimis purganda? Itaque cœlestia sunt, quæ ad euangelium pertinent, & de rebus cœlestibus in hac vita aguntur, cognoscuntur. Ita ut hoc discrimen liceret colligere inter euangelium & legem, quale est inter terrena & cœlestia. Quòd verò dicit, Victimis emundanda esse cœlestia, non accipiendũ, quasi plures sint victimæ in nouo testamento, cũ via tantũ vna sit, quæ est ipse Christus in morte se offerens: sed vt hoc dicit potiores victimas noui testamenti, colligit Chrysostomus, & recte victimas veteris testamenti etiam bonas fuisse, & nequaquam contemnendas. Porrò ex omnibus his iam subijciendum, quòd, si nouũ testamentũ non potuisset præstantiori modo confirmari, quàm intercedente morte ipsius Christi, cũ si tantũ obtulisset pecudes, &c. nequaquam posset præstantiori modo confirmatum: atq; ita opus erat nouum testamentum morte Christi confirmari.
units.tr: To this also belongs what he said above at the beginning of the chapter: that in the Old Testament there was a worldly sanctuary, where the worldly is set against the heavenly. But if we took the heavenly things to mean the things set before us after this life, concerning the angels, how, I ask, would it fit that they are said there to include things unclean, and things still to be cleansed by new sacrifices? Therefore the heavenly things are those that pertain to the gospel, and are dealt with and known in this life as heavenly matters. So from this one may draw the distinction between the gospel and the law, such as there is between earthly and heavenly things. But when he says that the heavenly things are to be cleansed with sacrifices, this must not be taken as if there were many sacrifices in the New Testament, since there is only one way, which is Christ himself offering himself in death. Rather, by saying "better sacrifices of the New Testament," Chrysostom infers that the sacrifices of the Old Testament were also good and by no means to be despised. Moreover, from all this one must now add that if the New Testament could not have been confirmed in a more excellent way than by the intervention of the death of Christ himself, since if he had offered only the flesh of beasts, and so on, it could by no means have been confirmed in a more excellent way; and thus it was necessary for the New Testament to be confirmed by the death of Christ.

units.la: Cæterùm qu od ad doctrinam attinet, illud excerpemus, quòd, quia sub euangelio habentur cœlestia, ita vitam discamus instituere, vt conuersatio nostra in cœlis esse intelligatur magis quàm in terris & rebus terrenis. Si patres, quibus olim terrena potissimũ ob oculos erant posita, adeò sanctè in timore Dei vixisse leguntur, quanto æquius est, nos ita vitâ instituere, quibus cœlestia iâ adsunt? Imò, ut Chrysostomus hic pulchrè docet, studeamus ipsi cœlum fieri, semper animi serenitate per conscientiæ tranquillitate ex fide in Christum conspicui, vt Dominus in nobis habitare dignetur: nullis maculis vel tenebris tentationum seu aduersitatum obfuscemur, etiamsi coram mundo obnubilari & dolere videamur: animus noster semper à terrenis distet quàm longissimè: terrena è sublimi quasi muscas despiciamus & contemnamus: semper apud Deum & cum Deo & rebus diuinis mens nostra occupetur, vt nihil nos à charitate Dei vnquam separet.
units.tr: As for doctrine, however, we shall take this from it: since heavenly things are had under the gospel, we should learn to order our life so that our conversation is understood to be in heaven rather than on earth and among earthly things. If the fathers, to whom earthly things were chiefly set before their eyes, are read to have lived so holily in the fear of God, how much more right is it for us, to whom heavenly things are now present, to order our life in this way? Indeed, as Chrysostom teaches here beautifully, let us strive to become heaven ourselves, shining by faith in Christ with the serenity of the mind and the tranquillity of conscience, so that the Lord may deign to dwell in us. Let us not be clouded by any stains or the darkness of temptations or adversities, even if we seem to be overshadowed and to grieve before the world. Let our mind always stand as far as possible from earthly things. Let us look down upon and despise earthly things from on high, as we would flies. Let our mind always be occupied with God, with God, and with divine things, so that nothing may ever separate us from the love of God.

units.la: Non enim in manufacta sancta ingressus est Christus, exemplaria verorum, sed in ipsum cœlum, vt appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis.
units.tr: For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us.

units.la: Absolutis duabus rationibus probantibus, nouum testamentum non debuisse ratum fieri, nisi intercedete Christi morte: iâ pergit, quemadmodũ ante cœperat, rursus aliquot argumentis ostendere efficaciâ & præstantiâ sacrificij Christi præ sacrificijs legalibus: & quo, quod proximis verbis dixit, cœlestia, seu illa, quæ sub euangelio sunt, potiori victima mũ dentur, quàm vnquam mundata sunt ulla sub lege. Sumit autem primum argumentum à circumstantia, nempe à præstantia tabernaculi, quod Christus cum sua victima est ingressus. Tabernaculum, inquit, quod Christus ingressus est, longè excellentius est tabernaculo legali: ingressus est enim ipsum cœlum. Igitur oportebit & sacrificium Christi multo esse excellentius.
units.tr: Having completed the two arguments proving that the New Testament could not have been ratified unless by the intervention of Christ's death, he goes on, as he had begun before, to show again by several arguments the efficacy and excellence of Christ's sacrifice over the legal sacrifices. By this he means that what he said in the preceding words, namely that heavenly things, or those under the gospel, are cleansed with a better sacrifice than any cleansed under the law. He takes his first argument from the circumstance, namely from the excellence of the tabernacle into which Christ entered with his sacrifice. The tabernacle, he says, which Christ entered, is far more excellent than the legal tabernacle, for he entered heaven itself. Therefore Christ's sacrifice must also be much more excellent.

units.la: Præsupponit autem, spectari debere proportionem tabernaculorum ad inuicem, atq; ex eorum habitudine iudicari de qualitate sacrificiorum, ut excellentissimo tabernaculo excellentissimũ sacrificium accomodetur. Sic autem cohærent ista proximè præcedentibus, ut diuelli non possint, particula γὰρ quodammodo copulante ista præcedentibus: sicut reuera & pulcherrimè respondent ijs, quæ dixerat de cœlestibus purgandis per victimas potiores. Sunt enim illa veluti probantia illud: etiâsi, vt diximus, coniungenda sint illis, quæ de præstantia sacrificij Christi suprà dicere cœperat. Porrò non simpliciter effert, Christum ingressum in cœlum, sed antithesi rem illustrat.
units.tr: He presupposes that the proportion of the tabernacles to one another must be considered, and that from their relation one should judge the quality of the sacrifices, so that the most excellent sacrifice is fitted to the most excellent tabernacle. These things are joined so closely to what immediately precedes that they cannot be separated, the particle "for" (γάρ) linking them in some way to what came before. They correspond beautifully to what he had said about heavenly things being cleansed by better sacrifices. For these things stand as proofs of that point, although, as we have said, they are to be joined with what he had begun to say above about the excellence of Christ's sacrifice. Moreover, he does not simply state that Christ entered into heaven, but illustrates the matter by antithesis.

units.la: Non, inquit, in manufacta sancta ingressus est Christus, exemplaria uerorum, sed in ipsum cœlum.
units.tr: He did not, he says, enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself.

units.la: Suprà quidem simili ferè modo dixerat, Christum ingressum in maius et perfectius tabernaculum, non manufactum, & ingressum item in sancta: sed, qualia sancta, nondum expresserat. Hic igitur clarè & diserte exponit, quænam illa sancta fuerint, ipsũ inquit, cœlum. Iubet autem eleganter respicere iterum in uetus tabernaculum & sancta, quæ dicitur manufacta, utpote ab hominibus extructa, inprimis architecto Beseleel: ut nimirum duorum tabernaculorum collatione huius noui tabernaculi constet dignitas: sicut vulgò dicitur, Contraria iuxta inuicem posita magis elucescunt: ita si bene conferas cœlestia cum terrenis, certè vilitas terrenorum ostendet tibi amplissimam dignitatem cœlestium. Igitur nulla fuerunt sancta illa veteris testamenti, quamlibet specie præclara & magnifica, præ istis sanctis sanctorum noui testamenti. Quò pertinet, quod illa adhuc extenuationis causa appellat exemplaria uerorum, ἀντίτυπα: ut uera intelligantur, quæ noui testamenti sunt, videlicet cœlestia: horum autem ἀντίτυπα fuerunt omnia, quæ fiebant in ueteri testamento.
units.tr: Above he had said, in almost the same way, that Christ entered into a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, and likewise entered into the holy places; but he had not yet expressed what sort of holy places they were. Here, therefore, he clearly and plainly explains what those holy places were: heaven itself, he says. He elegantly bids us look again at the old tabernacle and holy places, which are called made with hands, as being built by men, above all by the craftsman Bezalel, so that the dignity of this new tabernacle may be established by comparing the two tabernacles. As is commonly said, contraries placed side by side shine forth the more; so if you compare heavenly things well with earthly ones, the meanness of the earthly will surely show you the very great dignity of the heavenly. Therefore those holy places of the Old Testament, however splendid and magnificent in appearance, were nothing compared with these holy places of the holies of the New Testament. To this belongs his calling them, still by way of diminishing, copies of the true things (ἀντίτυπα), so that the things of the New Testament, namely the heavenly ones, may be understood as true; and all the things done in the Old Testament were copies of these.

units.la: Superius quidem vbi interpres reddidit exemplaria, dixit; ὑποδείγματα: at hoc loco ἀντίτυπα;
units.tr: Earlier, where the translator rendered "copies," he used the word for pattern (ὑποδείγματα); but in this place, the word ἀντίτυπα.

units.la: M ἀντίτυπα, vsus hoc loco voce accommodatione ad rem, & significatione. ὑπόδειγμα proprie significat alicuius rei demonstrationem euidentem, quasi ratione & exemplis confirmatam, & oculis probe subiectam: mathematicorum demonstrationes ita liceat appellare. ἀντίτυπον, aliquid ab alio, seu contra aliud expressum, quomodo solent artifices quidam artem fusoriam exercentes, vel sculptoriam, nasti imaguncu lam, imprimere eam in argillam, vel, sicut fit in typographica, aliam materiam mollem & tenacem formae, cui potea infundentes plumbum, vel eiusmodi quiddam, eandem imaginem scitissime reddunt. ἀντίτυπον ὑπόδειγμα ἐστὶ ἀντίτυπον: ut simulachrum eius rei simulachrū est, ad cuius similitudinem deformatum est. Ita vt prima demonstratio facta in monte recte ὑπόδειγμα appellari queat: quod vero factum est postea per Beseleel & erectum, magis proprie ἀντίτυπον. Igitur cum quae fiebant in veteri testamento, vocantur ἀντίτυπα, adhuc saepe ditur, tantum simulachra aliquarum rerum ibi utcunque expressa ac delineata: res autem veras ibi nondum habitas, quia eae seruabantur manifestandae per euangelium. In illa autem non est Christus ingressus, sed in ipsum caelum. Ingressus dicitur Christus secundum humanitatem: quandoquidem secundum diuinam naturam vbiq; est, omnia implens, & caelum nunquam deserit. De hoc autem tabernaculo eius q; magnificentia bone Deus quomodo possemus oratione explicare ea, quae merito dici deberent? Ideoq; magna emphasi dixit Apostolus, in ipsum caelum. Neq; hic caelum accipiemus pro caelestibus, vti praecedenti argumento diximus, per caelestia significari ea, quae in ecclesia hic in terris geruntur, sed quod communi more in Scripturis caelum appellatur: sicut Matth. vlt. dicitur, Dominus quidem Iesus assumptus est in caelum. Et Act. 1. Hic Iesus, qui assumptus est a vobis in caelum: in quo capite sequenti describitur perpetuo sedere ad dexteram patris. Neque enim sensus est, Christum ingressum in ecclesia in terris agente, sed eo, unde ex hac ecclesia post emigratur, & ad quae in hac ecclesia paratur via. Nam & eo nomine, quae in ecclesia sunt, dicuntur caelestia, & in ecclesia dicuntur habere caelestia, quod in ea via ad caelos aperitur, via in sancta sancto-rum manifestatur, ita vt, dum Apostolus hic dicit, Christum ingressum in caelum, interpretatio hinc accipi queat, quare quae in ecclesia fiunt, caelestia appellauerit.
units.tr: He uses ἀντίτυπα here with a view to its fitness for the thing and its meaning. ὑπόδειγμα properly signifies a clear demonstration of some thing, as it were confirmed by reason and examples and set plainly before the eyes; one might so call the demonstrations of the mathematicians. ἀντίτυπον is something impressed from another, or formed against another, as certain craftsmen who practise the art of casting or sculpture do: when they press an image into clay, or, as is done in printing, into another soft and tenacious material of a mould, and then pour in lead or something of the kind, they reproduce the same image most skilfully. An ἀντίτυπον is a copy of a pattern, as an image of a thing is an image of that to whose likeness it has been fashioned. So the first demonstration made on the mountain may rightly be called ὑπόδειγμα, while what was afterwards made and set up by Bezalel is more properly ἀντίτυπον. Therefore, since the things done in the Old Testament are called ἀντίτυπα, this still indicates that they were merely images of certain things, somehow expressed and outlined there, while the true things were not yet present there, because they were reserved to be made manifest by the gospel. Christ, however, did not enter into those things, but into heaven itself. Christ is said to have entered according to his humanity, since according to his divine nature he is everywhere, filling all things, and never leaves heaven. Yet who, good God, could explain in speech the magnificence of this tabernacle, as it rightly ought to be described? Therefore the Apostle said with great emphasis "into heaven itself." Nor are we to take "heaven" here for heavenly things, as we said in the preceding argument, where by heavenly things are meant those things done in the Church here on earth; rather, heaven is named in the common manner of the Scriptures, as in Matthew at the end: "the Lord Jesus indeed was taken up into heaven"; and Acts 1: "this Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven," and in the following chapter it is described as sitting perpetually at the right hand of the Father. For the sense is not that Christ entered into the Church acting on earth, but into that place from which he afterwards departs from this Church, and toward which the way is prepared in this Church. For in this sense the things that are in the Church are also called heavenly, and it is said that they have heavenly things in the Church, because in it a way to heaven is opened, and the way into the holy of holies is revealed. Thus, while the Apostle here says that Christ entered into heaven, an explanation may be drawn from this why he called the things done in the Church heavenly.

units.la: Vt apparcat nunc in conspectu Dei) Alludit ad ritum veterum sacerdotum, qui, quando semel in anno ingrediebantur in sancta sanctorum, dicebantur venire in conspectum dei: quanquam ad significandum, quod non vere ibi Deus conspiceretur, iussi sunt incenso illato, fumū excitare, vt propitiatorium penitus obumbraretur, nihil q; ibi viderent ac veti ti praeterea curiosius ibi quicquam inspicere. Significatur autem haec forma verborum officij Christi administratio, & quod ille in caelum ingressus pro nobis apud patrem intercedat, sicut olim summus sacerdos ingressus in sancta orabat: sic & saepius ita faciès Christus describitur, vt, vbi aduocatus, mediator, intercessor appellatur. Neq; vero filius vnquam a patre abfuit, vel a patris aspectu remotus, sed nostrae infirmitatis causa, vt intelligeremus aliquando quid illa nostra causa agat etiamnum nunc postquam terras reliquit, Scriptura ea loquendi forma vtitur.
units.tr: "That he may now appear in the presence of God." This alludes to the rite of the ancient priests, who, when they entered the holy of holies once a year, were said to come into the presence of God. Yet to signify that God was not really seen there, they were ordered to bring in incense and raise a cloud of smoke, so that the mercy seat was completely hidden, and they would see nothing there and would not presume to look at anything more closely. This manner of speaking, however, signifies the administration of Christ's office: that he entered heaven and now intercedes with the Father for us, just as the high priest of old, having entered the holy place, prayed. Christ is often described in this way, when he is called advocate, mediator and intercessor. Nor was the Son ever absent from the Father or removed from the Father's sight, but Scripture uses this form of speech because of our weakness, so that we may understand what he is doing for our cause even now, after he has left the earth.

units.la: Quanquam etiam aliter a resurrectione agit apud patrem, quam antea egerat. Precio enim depesto etiam secundum humanam naturam plenissime caelestì gloria perfruitur, & patrem contemplatur: sicut de nobis quoq; dicitur, quod hinc egressi videbimus eū sicuti est, & cognoscemus ut cogniti sumus. Iam particula illa, pro nobis, magnam habet emphasin, & officium Christi mirifice nobis commendat. Omnia enim nostra causa Christus fecit, pro nobis natus, pro nobis mortuus, pro nobis a morte resurrexit, pro nobis caelum ingressus est, pro nobis patrem ibi interpellat.
units.tr: Yet from his resurrection he also acts before the Father in a different way than he did before. For once the price has been paid, he enjoys the heavenly glory fully, even in his human nature, and beholds the Father. So also of us it is said that when we go hence we shall see him as he is, and shall know as we are known. Now that particle, "for us," has great emphasis and commends Christ's office to us wonderfully. For Christ did all things for our sake: born for us, dead for us, rose from death for us, entered heaven for us, and there pleads for us before the Father.

units.la: Caeterum omnia ista, quod videlicet Christus vt percursor noster (sic enim appellatus cap. 6.) ingressus est in caelum, quodq; ibidem appareat in conspectu Dei, nostra causam agens, valde consolatoria sunt, & fidem nostram debent acuere, ac spem certam facere, quod nobis quoq; via in caelum sit per eundem aperta, quod iuerit locum nobis paraturus, sicut loquitur Ioan 14. quod nos ad se trahet: quod ipsius oratio & intercessio assidua nobis accommodabitur: & quaecunq; tam in hac vita, quam post hanc vitam ad salutem sunt necessaria, obtinebit. Si ipsi oremus patrem, vt nobis propter Christum largiatur, certum est, patrem in nomine Christi omnia liberaliter concessurum, quantoma-gis dabit pater, vbi sic interpellat pro nobis ipse filius?
units.tr: Moreover, all these things, namely that Christ, as our forerunner (for so he is called in chapter 6), entered heaven and there appears in the presence of God, pleading our cause, are very comforting and ought to sharpen our faith and make our hope certain: that the way into heaven is also opened for us through the same Christ, that he has gone to prepare a place for us, as he says in John 14, that he will draw us to himself; that his prayer and continual intercession will be applied to us; and that he will obtain whatever is necessary for salvation, both in this life and after it. If we ourselves pray the Father that he would grant us favours for Christ's sake, it is certain that the Father will grant all things generously in the name of Christ. How much more will the Father give when the Son himself so pleads for us?

units.la: Itaque, quotiescunque conscientiae percellun tur peccatis, couertamus animum ad hūc Christum, qui ingressus est caelum, & agit in conspectu patris, interpellans pro nobis, propter hunc expectemus misericordiam, & vitam aeternam nobis conferendam. 1. Ioan. 2. Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem Iesum Christum iustum, & ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris autem tantum, sed etiam pro totius mundi.
units.tr: Therefore, whenever consciences are struck down by sins, let us turn our mind to this Christ, who entered heaven and acts in the presence of the Father, interceding for us. On account of him let us expect mercy and the eternal life to be bestowed upon us. 1 John 2: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world."

units.la: Non vt saepius offerat semetipsum, quemadmodum pontifex ingreditur in sancta singulis annis, per sanguinem alienum: (alioqui oportuisset illum saepius passum fuisse a condito mundo:) nunc autem semel sub consummatione seculorum, ad profligatio-nem peccati, per immolationem sui ipsius apparuit. Et quatenus illud manet homines, vt semel moriantur, post hoc autem iudicium: ita & Christus semel oblatus, vt multorum peccata tolleret, rursus absque peccato conspicietur iis, qui illum expectant in salutem.
units.tr: Not that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the holy place every year with blood not his own (otherwise he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world); but now once at the end of the ages he has appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. And just as it is appointed for men to die once, and after that the judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, without sin, to those who eagerly wait for him for salvation.

units.la: Aliud argumentum itidem a circumstantia, ab eo videlicet, quòd Christus tantùm semel obtulerit suum sacrificium, idque vnicum suffecerit ad peccatorum expiationem. Sic autem crassius reddi potest.
units.tr: Another argument, likewise drawn from the circumstance, namely that Christ offered his sacrifice only once, and that this single offering was sufficient for the expiation of sins. This can be put more plainly as follows.

units.la: Christus non obtulit sacrificium suum saepius, sed tantùm semel sub consummatione seculorum, atque id vnicum ad profligationem peccati suffecit.
units.tr: Christ did not offer his sacrifice often, but only once, at the end of the ages, and this single offering was sufficient to put away sin.

units.la: At vero sacrificia legalia saepius offerebantur, & adhuc nequaquam sufficiebant ad peccati profligationem.
units.tr: But the legal sacrifices were offered often, and still never sufficed to put away sin.

units.la: Igitur sacrificium Christi est praestantius sacrificijs legalibus.
units.tr: Therefore the sacrifice of Christ is more excellent than the legal sacrifices.

units.la: Vides argumentum istud iterum fieri quadam collatione, qua conferuntur & modus sacrificandi, & sacrificiorum impares effectus. Et quia tam propositionis, quàm assumptionis plures sunt partes, nos eas quoque explicabimus, & quantum opus erit, suas singulis adjiciemus probationes. Est autem haec prior pars propositionis seu maioris, quòd Christus tantùm semel, idque sub consummationem seculorum, obtulerit. Hanc Apostolus vt principaliter in hoc argumento spectandam euidentissime comprobat, quadam temporum distributione, in hunc fere modum:
units.tr: You see that this argument again proceeds by a comparison, in which both the manner of sacrificing and the unequal effects of the sacrifices are compared. And because both the proposition and the assumption have several parts, we shall explain these also and, as far as necessary, add a proof of its own to each. This first part of the proposition, or major premise, is that Christ offered himself only once, and that at the end of the ages. The Apostle proves this most evidently, as the principal point to be considered in this argument, by a certain distribution of times, in this manner:

units.la: Christus neque ante tempus consummationis vnquam obtulit, neque etiam post oblaturus est.
units.tr: Christ neither offered before the time of the consummation, nor is he going to offer afterwards.

units.la: Igitur tantùm semel, & quidem sub illud ipsum tempus consummationis obtulit.
units.tr: Therefore he offered only once, and indeed at that very time of the consummation.

units.la: Quòd autem non ante tempus consummationis, probat ratione petita ab inconuenien tiue ab absurdo.
units.tr: That he did not offer before the time of the consummation, he proves by reasoning drawn from inconvenience, that is, from absurdity.

units.la: Cùm Christus sacrificium suum peragere non potuerit, nisi morte, si saepius obtulisset, oportuisset ipsam iam saepius esse mortuum.
units.tr: Since Christ could not complete his sacrifice except by death, if he had offered often, he would have had to die often already.

units.la: Sed istud non est factum: quandoquidem absurdum est & inconueniens.
units.tr: But this has not happened, since it is absurd and inconvenient.

units.la: Igitur nunquam ante tempus consummationis obtulit.
units.tr: Therefore he never offered before the time of the consummation.

units.la: Rursus autem quòd non sit se oblaturus in posterum, probatur adhibita similitudine, quam sumit a communi lege mortis temporalis tantùm semel obeundae. Quemadmodum, inquit, non potest fieri, vt homines plusquam semel moriantur, sed à morte solù superest expectandum iudicium: ita (quandoquidem Christus non nisi per mortem sacrificium suum peragit) non potest fieri, vt Christus plusquam semel sese offerat, sed hoc tantùm superest, vt veniat ad iudicium. Atque ita manifestum est, quòd Christus tantùm semel, nempe sub consummationem seculorum sese obtulerit, & neque ante id vnquam facere potuerit, neque post fit facturus. Quamobrem & intelligi debet, vnicum eius sacrificium multò excellentius esse sacrificijs legalibus, quae semper repeti erat necessum.
units.tr: Again, that he is not going to offer himself in the future is proved by adding a comparison, which he takes from the common law that temporal death is to be undergone only once. Just as, he says, it cannot happen that men die more than once, but after death only judgment remains to be awaited, so (since Christ completes his sacrifice only through death) it cannot happen that Christ offers himself more than once, but this only remains: that he come to judgment. And so it is clear that Christ offered himself only once, namely at the end of the ages, and that he could neither have done so before, nor will he do so afterwards. Wherefore it must also be understood that his single sacrifice is far more excellent than the legal sacrifices, which had to be repeated always.

units.la: Atque istud est, quod praesenti argumento potissimum agitur, quòdque principaliter spectari hic oportet. Caeterarum partium veritas partim ex praecedentibus nota praesuppo nitur, partim in sequetibus patefiet: quod nos propter rudiores indicare hoc loco haud grauabimur. Siquidem quòd Christi sacrificium sufficiat ad profligationem peccati, cápite sequenti plenius confirmatur, adducto etiam testimonio Hieremiae prophetae. Iam in assumptione seu minore, quòd sacrificia legalia, inprimis verò quae censebantur maxime expiatoria, debebant repeti, notum est ex historia, & saepius auditum. At quòd eadem non suffecerint ad profligationem peccatorum, supra quidem assertum est, vbi debatur, in veteri tabernaculo dona sacrificiaque offerri solita, quae non possint iuxta conscientiam perfectum reddere cultorem: item sanguine taurorum & hircorum sanctificare tantùm ad carnis purificationem: sed multò efficacissime id euincitur initio cap.10. vbi docet Apostolus, vel hoc ipsum argumento esse, quòd sacrificia illa nó profligarint peccata, quòd semper debuerint repeti. Quod argumentum proprie ad probationem praesentis ibidem subiectum est, vt suo loco dicemus plenius.
units.tr: This is what is chiefly at issue in the present argument, and what must principally be considered here. The truth of the other parts is presupposed, partly known from what has gone before, partly will be made clear in what follows; which we shall not hesitate to point out here for the sake of the less learned. For that Christ's sacrifice suffices for the putting away of sin is more fully confirmed in the following chapter, with the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah also adduced. Now in the assumption, or minor premise, that the legal sacrifices had to be repeated, and especially those which were thought to be most expiatory, is known from history and has often been heard. That they did not suffice for the putting away of sins was indeed asserted above, where it was said that gifts and sacrifices were offered in the old tabernacle, which could not make the worshipper perfect as regards conscience, and that with the blood of bulls and goats they sanctified only to the purification of the flesh. But this is proved much more effectively at the beginning of chapter 10, where the Apostle teaches that this very fact is an argument that those sacrifices did not put away sins, because they always had to be repeated. This argument is subjoined precisely for the proof of the present point, as we shall say more fully in its place.

units.la: Est igitur valde appositum argumentu istud ad probandam excellentiam sacrificij Christi praesacrificijs legalibus. Quid enim praeclarius dici posset, quàm vnico sacrificio Christi semel oblati purificari peccata omnia: quod multiplicia & toties repetita sacrificia legalia efficere non poterant. Quamobrem accuratè respiciendum est in praesens argumentum: neque ob id solum, quia tam prudenter est excogitatum, ad causae, quàm Apostolus tractantractandam suscepit, firmamentum: verum etiam quia difficiles & perplexas quasdam nostri temporis controuersias optime dirimit, sicut mox plenius ostendemus. Interea pauca, quae ad partes pertinent, explicabimus.
units.tr: This argument is therefore very apt for proving the excellence of Christ's sacrifice above the legal sacrifices. For what could be said more outstandingly than that all sins are cleansed by the single sacrifice of Christ offered once, which the manifold legal sacrifices, repeated so often, could not accomplish? Wherefore the present argument must be attended to carefully: not only for this reason, that it has been so prudently devised as a support for the cause which the Apostle undertook to treat, but also because it resolves certain difficult and perplexed controversies of our own time very well, as we shall show more fully shortly. Meanwhile we shall explain a few points that pertain to the parts.

units.la: Non ut saepius offerat semetipsum, quemadmodum pontifex ingreditur in sancta singulis annis, per sanguinem alienum.
units.tr: Not that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy places every year with the blood of another.

units.la: Non sine emphasi inculcat particulam semetipsum. Nam potuisset quidem omitti, & perfecta fuisset sententia: verum hoc pacto addita tacite suggerit excellentiam & Christi, (sicut etiam statim initio epistolae, per semetipsum purgatione facta) prae sacerdotibus legalibus, & pariter sacrificij, quod in nouo testamento oblatum est, prae sacrificijs legalibus. Qua de causa etiam mox subijcit, Christum apparuisse per immolationem suipsius, ut opponatur id ei, quod sacerdotes legales ingredi sunt soliti per sanguinem alienum. Supra quidem dictum est, Christu ingressa semel in sancta, non per sanguinem hircorum aut vitulorum, sed per sanguinem proprium: item, mortem illius debuisse intercedere & sanguine debuisse nouum testamentum firmari: neque praeterea quicquam ad vim argumenti praesentis facit, quod exprimatur, qualesacrificium obtulerit, cum hoc solum docebatur, cur tatum semel obtulerit, & quod unica ipsius oblatio praestantior fuerit cunctis oblationibus legalibus, sed hoc pacto tamen mirum in modum commendatur beneficiorum Christi, ipsiusque erga genus humanum insignis charitas: quando ita praedicatur seipsum obtulisse. Et quia haec charitas Christi nunquam satis potest inculcari ac demonstrari, ideo tam frequenter particula ista repetitur.
units.tr: The particle himself is inserted with deliberate emphasis. It could have been omitted and the sentence would still have been complete. But added in this way, it tacitly suggests the excellence of Christ above the legal priests (as also at the very beginning of the epistle, "by himself purging our sins"), and likewise the excellence of the sacrifice offered under the New Testament above the legal sacrifices. For this reason he goes on at once to say that Christ appeared through the sacrifice of himself, so that this is set against what the legal priests were accustomed to enter with, namely the blood of another. It has been said above that Christ entered once into the holy places, not by the blood of goats or calves but by his own blood; likewise that his death had to intervene and the new covenant had to be confirmed by blood. Nothing further adds to the force of the present argument in stating what kind of sacrifice he offered, since what was taught there was only why he offered once, and that his single offering was more excellent than all the legal offerings. Yet in this way the benefits of Christ and his remarkable love toward the human race are wonderfully commended, since it is proclaimed that he offered himself. And because this love of Christ can never be sufficiently impressed and demonstrated, this particle is repeated so often.

units.la: Alioqui oportuisset illum saepius passum fuisse a condito mundo) Si haec vt per parenthesin adhibita legantur, clarius cernetur, quomodo sequentia cohaereant cum praecedentibus: necnon probatio, quod videlicet non potuerit offerre Christus ante tempus consummationis, constabit integra. Oportuisset illum inquit saepius passum fuisse, quasi diceret: Christus non offert nisi per suam mortem: id quod probatum est duobus argumentis praecedentibus, altero de confirmatione testamenti per mortem testatoris, altero de confirmatione totius veteris testamenti per sanguinem. Ergo, si Christus antehac obtulisset, oportuisset illum ante hoc tempus alias fuisse passum & mortuum. Istud vero cum nunquam factum sit ab initio mundi hucusque, clarum est, quod nunquam antehac obtulerit. Liquet autem hinc, quod Christi sacrificium situm est in ipsius morte, non in institutione coenae dominicae, aut aliqua alia re: quandoquidem coena non est instituta, ut, quoties ea peragitur, toties Christus denuo offeratur, & in coena imaginemur, nos nouum habere sacrificium: sed vt mortem Christi & sacrificium eius per mortem commemoremus. Ipse simul sacerdos & hostia, & hostiam obtulit seipsum, ac tunc quidem obtulit, quando seipsum in mortem tradidit, factus obediens patri usque ad mortem. Et sicut neq; ante vnquam mortuus est, neq; post. Ita non nisi semel est oblatus. Igitur & mori & offerre Christo idem sunt.
units.tr: "Otherwise he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world." If this is read as inserted in parentheses, it will be seen more clearly how what follows coheres with what precedes, and the proof, namely that Christ could not have offered before the time of consummation, will stand complete. "He would have had to suffer often," he says, as if to say: Christ offers only through his death. This has been proved by two preceding arguments, one from the confirmation of a testament by the death of the testator, the other from the confirmation of the whole old covenant by blood. Therefore, if Christ had offered before this, he would have had to suffer and die earlier than this time. But since this has never happened from the beginning of the world until now, it is clear that he never offered before. From this it is also evident that Christ's sacrifice lies in his death, not in the institution of the Lord's Supper or in anything else. For the supper was not instituted so that, as often as it is celebrated, Christ should be offered anew, and so that in the supper we imagine we have a new sacrifice; rather, it was instituted so that we might commemorate the death of Christ and his sacrifice accomplished through death. He was at once priest and victim, and he offered himself as the victim; and he offered then, when he gave himself over to death, having become obedient to the Father even unto death. Just as he never died before, nor after, so he was offered only once. Therefore for Christ to die and to offer are the same thing.

units.la: A condito mundo, seu a conditione mundi) Vox καταβολή, ut supra diximus capite quarto, significat fundamentum, molitionem, constitutionem, quomodo etiam redditum est Ephes. 1. Comprehendit autem & intelligit Apostolus vniuersum tempus ab initio mundi conditi, ad istud vsque, quo Christus oblaturus apparuit. Fuit quidem Christi natiuitas & mors statim a condito mundo promissa primis parentibus, ac deinde variis typis adumbrata (in quam sententiam Apocalypseos decimotertio dicitur, adorasse bestiam inhabitatores terrae, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae agni, qui occisus est ab origine mundi) sicut statim in sacrificio Abelis eiusdem morte: deinde in sacerdotio Melchisedec, in oblatione Isaac, tum in sacrificijs legalibus, apparuit: sed tamen res ipsa siue oblatio ipsa non fuit exhibita, quia tempore non fuit natus, neq; mortuus.
units.tr: "From the foundation of the world," or "from the constitution of the world." The word καταβολή [katabolē], as we said above in chapter four, means foundation, construction, establishment, as it is also rendered in Ephesians 1. The Apostle means the whole time from the beginning of the created world until that time in which Christ appeared about to offer. Indeed, Christ's birth and death were promised to the first parents at the very founding of the world, and then foreshadowed by various types (to this sense it is said in Revelation 13 that the inhabitants of the earth adored the beast, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world). Thus he appeared at once in the sacrifice of Abel, in his death; then in the priesthood of Melchizedek, in the offering of Isaac, and then in the legal sacrifices. Yet the thing itself, or the offering itself, was not yet exhibited, because he had not yet been born in time, nor had he died.

units.la: Nunc autem semel, sub consummationem seculorum, ad profligationem peccati, immolationem suipsius apparuit.
units.tr: But now once, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the putting away of sin by the sacrifice of himself.

units.la: Non antehac vnquam obtulit Christus, sed nunc primum. Ita nunc habet magnam emphasin, signatque tempus praesens reuelati euangelij, quo Christus suum peregit sacrificium: quod tempus distinguitur ab illo vniuerso, quod antecessit, & omni ei, quod sequitur. ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ, quasi dicat, instanti consummatione: ea vim habet particula ἐπί, maxime iuncta Datiuo. Itaque significat iam cum instaret mundi finis & consummatio, & ipso, vt ficloquamur, mundi senio. Vt enim homini, ita & mundo suae aetatis partes tribuuntur.
units.tr: Christ did not offer before this, but now for the first time. So "now" carries great emphasis and marks the present time of the revealed gospel, in which Christ accomplished his sacrifice. This time is distinguished from all that preceded it and from everything that follows. ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ [epi synteleia] is as if to say: at the imminent consummation. The particle ἐπί has this force, especially when joined with the dative. Thus it means that already, when the end and consummation of the world was at hand, and, so to speak, in the very old age of the world. For as parts of life are assigned to a man, so also are ages assigned to the world.

units.la: Prima aetas ab Adam ad Noe, seu diluuium, quae se habet instar infantiae. Secunda a Noa ad Abraham, instar pueritiae: Tertia ab Abraham ad Dauid, instar adolescentiae, quae fraeno indiget, ideoque lex data. Quarta a Dauid ad transmigrationem Babylonis, instar iuuentæ. Quinta à transmigratione ad Christum, instar senectæ. Sexta à Christo ad finem: hæc est ætas decrepita, postquam nulla alia, sicut post Christū nulla alia instauratio expectanda. Hoc autem nunc, vocat consummationem seculorum. Oportebat enim certa præire secula à Deo præordinata, post quæ agnus ille ab initio mundi promissus offerretur.
units.tr: The first age runs from Adam to Noah, or the flood, and resembles infancy. The second, from Noah to Abraham, resembles boyhood. The third, from Abraham to David, resembles adolescence, which needs a bridle, and therefore the law was given. The fourth, from David to the Babylonian transmigration, resembles youth. The fifth, from the transmigration to Christ, resembles old age. The sixth, from Christ to the end, is the decrepit age, since no other follows it, just as after Christ no other renewal is to be expected. Now he calls this the consummation of the ages. For it was necessary that certain ages, predetermined by God, should go before, after which that lamb promised from the beginning of the world should be offered.
