units.la: Sic vero Christus ipse, cùm sacrificium suum offerret, dixit, consummatum est: quandoquidem omnia ibi consuummata & perfecta sunt, quæ ad salutem humani generis per Christum debebant fieri. In Christo facta est consummatio legis & prophetarum. Et Apostolus Galat. 4. plenitudinem vocat temporis. Tit. 1. Promisit Deus ante tempora æterna, patefecit autem temporibus suis sermonem suum per prædicationem, &c. Ephes. 3. Mysterium Christi in aliis ætatibus non innotuit filijs hominum, quemadmodum nunc revelatum est sanctis Apostolis eius & prophetis per Spiritum. Ibidem paulò post: Erat ab sconditum à seculis in Deo, qui vniuersa condidit per Iesum Christum, ut nota fiat nunc principatibus & potestatibus in cœlestibus. Quædam in eandem sententiam 1. Cor. 2.
units.tr: When Christ himself offered his sacrifice, he said, "It is finished" (John 19:30), since all the things that were to be done for the salvation of the human race through Christ were then completed and perfected. In Christ the fulfilment of the law and the prophets was accomplished. The Apostle in Galatians 4 calls it "the fullness of time." Titus 1: God promised before eternal times, but in due time revealed his word through preaching, etc. Ephesians 3: The mystery of Christ was not made known to the sons of men in other ages, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. A little after, in the same place: the mystery "had been hidden from the ages in God, who created all things through Jesus Christ, so that it might now be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places." Certain things to the same effect are found in 1 Corinthians 2.

units.la: Ad profligationem peccati) Poterat & hæc particula de sacrificij effectu omitti, sicut necin præcedenti membro aliquid habebatur, cui respondeat: sed in serta est sine vllis probatio nibus ad illustrandum beneficium & bonitatem Christi erga genus humanum, & ad amplificandam dignitatem sacrificij Christi præ sacrificijs legalibus, quorum certè nulla hanc vim habuerunt, sicut iam sæpius dictum est. Et peccati dicitur, vt generaliter vniuersum regnum peccati reiectum & euersum intelligatur. Ita vides Apostolum nunquam omittere, quod facit ad illustrandam dignitatem sacerdotij & sacrificij Christi.
units.tr: "For the putting away of sin." This particle too could have been omitted with respect to the effect of the sacrifice, as nothing in the preceding clause was present to which it would answer. But it is inserted without any proofs, to illustrate the benefit and goodness of Christ toward the human race, and to magnify the dignity of Christ's sacrifice above the legal sacrifices, none of which indeed had this power, as has often been said already. And it is said "of sin" so that the whole kingdom of sin is understood generally as rejected and overthrown. So you see that the Apostle never omits what serves to illustrate the dignity of Christ's priesthood and sacrifice.

units.la: Per immolationem suijpsius) Eadem ratione hæc particula inseritur, quia prius dixit, semetipsum, atq; opponitur illæ particulæ de sacrificio legali, per sanguinem alienum: Quamuis plus gratiæ hic est & virium, quòd dicit, per immolationem suijpsius, quàm foret, si diceret tantùm, per sanguinem ipsius. Significatur enim, quòd non modò aspersione aliqua sui sanguinis procurarit salutem nostram, sed quòd se totum devouerit & obtulerit, quodque ipse factus sit vtua & salutifera hostia. Nò disimili schemate vsus est Apostolus 2. Tim. 4. Nam ipse iam immolor, & tempus meæ resolutionis instat: certamen bonum decertaui, &c. Sed multò aptius 1. Corinth. 5. Etenim pascua nostrum immolatus est Christus. Vbi etiam vsus immolationis, quantum ad nos, ostenditur, nimirum, vt quando talis hostia pro nobis immolata est, omnes simus puri, & ab omni fermento vitiorum alieni.
units.tr: "By the sacrifice of himself." For the same reason this particle is inserted: he had said "himself" before, and it is set against that phrase about the legal sacrifice, "by the blood of another." Yet there is more grace and power in saying "by the sacrifice of himself" than if he had said only "by his own blood." For it signifies that he procured our salvation not merely by some sprinkling of his blood, but that he devoted and offered himself entire, and that he himself became a living and saving victim. The Apostle used a not dissimilar figure in 2 Timothy 4: "For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand; I have fought the good fight," etc. But much more aptly in 1 Corinthians 5: "For Christ our passover has been sacrificed for us." There also the use of the sacrifice, as far as we are concerned, is shown: namely, that when such a victim has been sacrificed for us, we should all be pure and free from every leaven of vice.

units.la: Apparuit) Caue ex hac voce patiaris tibi persuaderi, Christum non veram carnem habuisse, aut non verè passum, sed tantum apparenter & plantasticè, sicut quidam hæretici hac voce abutentes imaginati sunt: cum tot alios locos habeas in Scripturis obuios, qui manifeste ueram carnem, veram passionem & mortem Christi astruant.
units.tr: Apparuit) Beware, from this word, of letting yourself be persuaded that Christ did not have true flesh, or did not truly suffer, but only seemingly and in appearance, as certain heretics, abusing this word, have imagined; when you have so many other passages in the Scriptures before you which clearly affirm the true flesh, the true passion and the death of Christ.

units.la: Et quatenus illud manet homines, & semel moriantur, post hoc autem iudicium: ita & Christus semel oblatus.
units.tr: And inasmuch as it is appointed for men once to die, and after this the judgment; so also Christ, having been offered once.

units.la: Cùm homo sic conditus esset, vt posset non peccare, & non peccando etiam euadere mortem: tamen quando natura præditus fuit tali, quæ fragilitatem posset in se recipere, ipse peccauit, & per peccatum incurrit mortem, vt clarius exponitur Rom. 5. Atq; ita homo sibi pœnam mortis accersiuit, Deusq; illū iuste inflixit, sicut ipse quoq; prædixerat: Quocunq; die comederitis, morte moriemini. Et sic Deus constituit hanc legem, vt omnes morerentur, quia diaboli suggestionibus stultus homo credidit. Atq; hoc pacto conciliantur loci isti, quibus dicitur, Sapientiæ 2. In inuidia diaboli mors introiuit in orbem terrarum. Et Sapient. 1. quòd Deus mortem non condiderit, nec lætetur in interitu viuorum. Rom. 5. per vnum hominem introijt peccatum in mundum. Nam & diabolus & homo & Deus pariter causa mortis dici possunt. Semel autem moriuntur homines communi lege naturæ loquendo. Nam quòd qui à morte resuscitantur, dicuntur bis mori, id à lege naturæ diutesum est.
units.tr: Since man was created in such a way that he could not sin, and by not sinning could also escape death, nevertheless, because he was endowed with a nature capable of receiving frailty into itself, he himself sinned, and through sin incurred death, as is more clearly set out in Rom. 5. And so man brought upon himself the punishment of death, and God justly inflicted it upon him, just as he himself had foretold: "On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Thus God established this law, that all should die, because foolish man believed the suggestions of the devil. And in this way those passages are reconciled which say, Wis. 2: "Through the envy of the devil death entered the world"; and Wis. 1: that God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living; and Rom. 5: "through one man sin entered the world." For the devil, man and God can alike be called the cause of death. Men die once, however, speaking by the common law of nature; for those who are raised from death are said to die twice, and this is an exception to the law of nature.

units.la: Post hoc autem iudicium) Nullum est medium, nullus pœnitentiæ aut emendationis aut sacrificij offerendi locus. Statim ut quis mortuus est, vel transit à morte carnali in vitā æternam, vel à morte secunda absorbetur. Non restat, nisi vt expectet omnipotentis Dei de se iudicium seu particulare, quod statim sequitur, seu vniuersale, quod ad finem mundi palàm omnibus feretur, de quo 2. Cor. 5. Matth. 13. 24. 25. Quare hic concidit purgatorium, & quicquid eiusmodi mediorum inter mortem & iudicium proponitur. De iudicio statim à morte vide Augustinum. Item cōuincuntur hic quidam Origeniani, quibus expro bratur, quòd statuerint, Christum iterum passurum pro dæmonibus angelis malis. Quāuis hic potius de vniuersali iudicio sermo sit. Ita & Christus semel oblatus est) Quia tantùm semel potest communi lege naturæ mori, ipsiusq; offerri est mori, Roman.6. Christus semel pro peccatis nostris mortuus est. Quomodo verò Christo mori conuenerit, etiamsi peccatum non habuerit, cuius poena est mors, dicitur est supra cap.2. cùm non habuerit peccatum originale, videtur quòd mori non debuerit: sed ipse sese obtulit. Oblatus est, quia voluit, Elaiæ 53. Et Ioan.10. Nemo tollet animam meam. Et ideò vbi mors nostra est effectus peccati: stipendia peccati mors, Rom.6. mors Christi est eneruatio peccati.
units.tr: "After this the judgment") There is no middle ground, no place for repentance or amendment or offering a sacrifice. As soon as someone has died, he either passes from bodily death into eternal life, or is swallowed up by the second death. Nothing remains but to await the judgment of almighty God upon him, either the particular judgment, which immediately follows, or the universal judgment, which will be openly declared to all at the end of the world (2 Cor. 5; Matt. 13. 24. 25). Hence purgatory falls here, and whatever such intermediate means between death and judgment is proposed. On judgment immediately after death, see Augustine. Likewise, certain Origenists are refuted here, who are reproached for holding that Christ would suffer again for the wicked angelic demons, although here the discourse is rather about the universal judgment. "So Christ also was once offered") Because by the common law of nature he can die only once, and to be offered is to die (Rom. 6: "Christ died once for our sins"). How it was fitting for Christ to die, even though he had no sin, whose punishment is death, has been explained above in chapter 2. Since he had no original sin, it seems he ought not to have died; but he offered himself. He was offered because he willed it (Isa. 53; John 10: "No one takes my life from me"). And so, where our death is the effect of sin ("the wages of sin is death," Rom. 6), the death of Christ is the undoing of sin.

units.la: Vt multorum peccata tolleret) Iterum commemorat effectum seu fructum sacrificij Christi, vt beneficium seu bonitas Christi erga nos illustretur. Ita autem sustulit Christus peccata, non ne prorsus ulla sint, sed ne nobis amplius dominentur, ne condemnatio propter ea proueniat: qua de re Rom.sexto & octauo. Dicit autem multorum, & non omnium: quia, vt inquit Chrysostomus, non omnes crediderunt. Multi sunt vocati, pauci verò electi. Quatum quidem ad Christum attinet, & voluit omnium peccata tollere, & mors ipsius sufficiebat: sed quo minus id succedat omnibus, in causa est ipsorum incredulitas, quia nimirum nolunt fide apprehendere misericordiam oblatam propter solum Christum. Qua de re & suprà nonnihil à nobis dictum est capite octauo, in enarratione Hieremiæ, vbi dicebatur, omnes cogniturí sunt me.
units.tr: "To take away the sins of many") Again he recalls the effect or fruit of Christ's sacrifice, so that the benefit or goodness of Christ toward us may be made clear. Christ has taken away sins not in the sense that none remain at all, but so that they no longer have dominion over us and condemnation does not follow because of them (on this see Romans 6 and 8). He says "of many," not "of all," because, as Chrysostom says, not all believed: "Many are called, but few are chosen." As far as Christ is concerned, he both willed to take away the sins of all, and his death was sufficient. But the reason it does not succeed for all lies in their own unbelief, since they are unwilling to lay hold by faith on the mercy offered on account of Christ alone. On this matter we have also said something above in chapter 8, in the exposition of Jeremiah, where it was said, "they shall all know me."

units.la: Simili modo dixit Christus, Hic est sanguis noui testamenti, qui pro vobis & pro multis effundetur, pro multis, non pro omnibus.
units.tr: In a similar way Christ said, "This is the blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for you and for many": for many, not for all.

units.la: Rursus absque peccato conspicietur) Si quis roget, Ergo Christus non amplius est ad nos venturus? Respondet, Certè ut patiatur, vt offerat, seu ut offeratur, non est amplius venturus. Est tamen venturus in δευτέρᾳ, secundario venturus, nepe ad iudicium ferendum, quod homines omnes post mortem suam debent expectare. Tunc, inquam, conspicietur, inquit, sicut & Christus, Videbunt filium hominis venientem in nubibus, &c.
units.tr: "Again, without sin, he will be seen) If someone asks: so Christ is not going to come to us any more? He answers: certainly he will not come again to suffer or to offer, or to be offered. Yet he will come a second time [δευτέρᾳ], namely to hold the judgment which all men must await after their death. Then, I say, he will be seen, it says, just as Christ: "they will see the Son of man coming in the clouds," and so on.

units.la: Sed absque peccato) Quid hoc est? Num antea apparuit cum peccato? cum capite secundo huius epistolæ dictum fit, per omnia similem fratribus, sed exclusso peccato.
units.tr: "But without sin) What is this? Did he previously appear with sin? It was said in chapter 2 of this epistle that he was like the brethren in all things, but with sin excluded.

units.la: Secundo suo aduentu Christus apparebit absque peccato, id est, non amplius futurus hostia pro peccato, neque amplius in similitudine peccati. Sic prima Corinthiorum quinto, Eum qui peccatum non nouerat, pro nobis fecit peccatum, id est, hostiam pro peccato, vel, similem habenti peccatum. Item Romanorum octauo, De peccato condemnauit peccatum. Neque enim Christus amplius futurus est hostia: neque item venturus cum humili & fragili nostra carne, in similitudine carnis, peccat, seu portans peccata non stra super lignum: sed gloriosa & splendida, quæque iudicem formidabilem nobis possit reddere, de qua re Matthæi vicesimo quarto & vicesimo quinto. His igitur de causis in secundo aduentu conspicietur absq; peccato.
units.tr: At his second coming Christ will appear without sin: that is, he will no longer be the victim for sin, nor any longer in the likeness of sin. So 1 Corinthians 5: "He who knew no sin he made to be sin for us," that is, a victim for sin, or one like someone having sin. Likewise Romans 8: "God condemned sin in sin." For Christ will no longer be a sacrifice, nor will he come again with our lowly and frail flesh, in the likeness of flesh, or bearing our sins upon the tree; but glorious and splendid, so that he can make himself a formidable judge to us, as Matthew 24 and 25 describe. For these reasons, then, at the second coming he will be seen without sin.

units.la: Iis qui expectant illum, in salutem) Addit, quid futurum sit in illo secundo aduentu, siue, quid per eum faciedum, si nequaquam amplius erit hostia pro peccato. Certè ijs, inquit, qui expectant illum, id est, qui sic se gerunt, vt fide expectent, per illum sibi dandam misericordiam, largietur salutem æternam. Et supplendum est per contrarium, quòd non expectantibus eum, id est, impijs & incredulis venturus erit ad damnationem. Sed maluit istud subticere, atque exprimere, quod conscientijs pauidis iudicabat fore gratius.
units.tr: "Those who wait for him, unto salvation) He adds what will happen at that second coming, or what will be done through him, if he will by no means be any longer a victim for sin. Certainly, he says, to those who wait for him, that is, who so conduct themselves as to wait in faith for the mercy to be given through him, he will grant eternal salvation. It must be supplied by contrast that for those not waiting for him, that is, the impious and unbelieving, he will come to damnation. But he preferred to pass over this and to express the other, judging it more welcome to frightened consciences.

units.la: Sic enim per contrarium quod subticetur, debet intelligi ex altera parte, quæ apertè exprimitur, quod in Scripturis crebrò occurrit faciendum. Et per expectantes Dominum recte intelligi pios, qui recte sese gerunt in fide confessione & charitatis exercitatione, liquet ex eo, quòd pij, quia hic affliguntur, valde cupidè desiderant tempus suæ liberationis, sicut Apostolus idem dicit Romanorum octauo, de vniuersa creatura, quòd expectet liberationem. Et Philippensium tertio, Saluatorem expectamus Dominum Iesum Christū, q reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ, &c. Huc pertinet etiam parabola de seruis expectantibus dominum, & vigilantibus, & de alijs non expectantibus, percutientibusque suos fratres, Luc.12.
units.tr: For what is passed over is to be understood by contrast from the other side, which is plainly stated; this is often to be done in Scripture. That by those waiting for the Lord the godly are rightly understood, who conduct themselves rightly in faith, confession and the exercise of charity, is clear from the fact that the godly, because they are afflicted here, very eagerly long for the time of their deliverance, as the same Apostle says in Romans 8 of the whole creation, that it waits for its deliverance; and Philippians 3: "We wait for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation," and so on. To this belongs also the parable of the servants who wait for their master and keep watch, and of the others who do not wait and beat their fellow servants (Luke 12).

units.la: Cæterùm tota vis argumenti est in eo, quòd Christus tantùm semel oblatus est, & quidem sub consummationem seculorum, ita vt nec ante fuerit oblatus, nec in posterum offerendus. Hæc inquam sunt potissimum in toto argumento spectanda.
units.tr: But the whole force of the argument lies in this: that Christ was offered only once, and that at the close of the ages, so that he was neither offered before nor is to be offered afterwards. These, I say, are the chief points to be considered in the whole argument.

units.la: Sed hic iam quærat aliquis: Quare Christus etiam ante illud tempus non fuit oblatus, nempe breui post mundum conditum: vel, quare non est oblatus tardius, videlicet ad finem mundi? Hæc quæstio non est omnino reijcienda quasi inutilis, sed proderit piis mentibus ad considerandum mirabilem Dei prouiprouidentiā ac bonitate erga genus humanum. Neq; verò inquirimus, vtrū aliter non potuerit Deus facere, sed tantum quatenus decuerit ita fieri, (ne quis putet quæstione istam curiosam, & ad lædendam Dei maiestatem tendere) sicut supra capite secundo quæsitum est, quare decuerit Christum, cùm Deus esset, homine fieri, maximè cùm ratione Deus potuisset hominum saluti prospicere. Itaque sicut tibi ostenditur, non potuisse conuenientiorem modum reperiri, quo genus humanum restitueretur, quàm si Christus homo fieret, & sua morte pro peccatis hominum satisfaceret, & a morte æterna credentes liberaret. Sic & in præsenti respondemus, commodiori tempore Christum non potuisse in mundum venire, & sacrificium suum peragere, quàm, vt Apostolus loquitur, nunc sub consummatione seculorum: idq; rationibus aliquot ex pijs patribus productis ostendemus. Ac primum quidem, quòd non ante illud tempus conuenisset, Christum offerre, suum sacrificium, sic probatur. Fuisset quidem charitatis diuinæ, statim succurrere, postquam homo in peccatum erat prolapsus: nam charitas non differt beneficium, sed potius accelerat: verum diuina prouidentia vidit, ratione lapsus hominis, vt aliter erigeretur expedire. Quia enim homo per superbiam erat lapsus, expediebat eum aliquanto tempore suis viribus relinquere, primum sola lege naturæ: deinde & lege scripta instituere, vt suam infirmitate propius agnosceret, vt sese malitia ipsius apertius proderet, atque ita humiliatus & suam agnoscens miseriam opem medici imploraret, ac tanto acrius suscipéret. Gregorius Nyssenus, referente Theophylacto, hanc rationem eleganti exprimit similitudine: Quemadmodum medicus, inquit, febricitanti non statim propo nit remedia, sed finit morbum ad tempus vires suas exercere, donec prorsus maturuerit, & totum hominem quodammodo occuparit: ita Dominus non statim post lapsum, sed longe post, cùm longius progressa fuit iniquitas, statuit humano generi succurrere.
units.tr: But here someone may now ask: why was Christ not offered even before that time, namely shortly after the world was created; or why was he not offered later, namely at the end of the world? This question is not to be dismissed altogether as useless; it will profit pious minds to consider the wonderful providence and goodness of God toward the human race. Nor do we inquire whether God could have acted otherwise, but only how far it was fitting for it to happen so (lest anyone think this a curious question aimed at impairing the majesty of God). Just as above in chapter 2 it was asked why it became Christ, being God, to be made man, especially since by reason God could have provided for the salvation of men, so, as it has been shown to you, a more fitting way could not have been found by which the human race might be restored than if Christ became man, satisfied by his death for the sins of men, and freed believers from eternal death. So also in the present case we answer that Christ could not have come into the world and accomplished his sacrifice at a more suitable time than now, as the Apostle puts it, at the consummation of the ages; and we will show this by several reasons drawn from the godly Fathers. First, that it would not have been fitting for Christ to offer his sacrifice before that time, is proved thus. It would indeed have been an act of divine charity to help at once after man had fallen into sin, for charity does not delay a benefit but rather hastens it. But divine providence saw, given the manner of man's fall, that it was expedient to raise him in another way. For since man had fallen through pride, it was expedient to leave him for some time to his own strength: first under the law of nature alone, then also to instruct him under the written law, so that he might recognise his weakness more closely, his malice might be more openly revealed, and so, humbled and acknowledging his misery, he might implore the help of the physician and receive it all the more eagerly. Gregory of Nyssa, as reported by Theophylact, expresses this reason in an elegant simile: "As a physician," he says, "does not immediately offer remedies to one with a fever, but lets the disease exercise its strength for a time, until it has fully ripened and has in a manner taken over the whole man, so the Lord did not decide to help the human race immediately after the fall, but long after, when iniquity had advanced much further."

units.la: Huc pertinent illa Romanorum capite quinto, vbi de origine & propagatione peccati per vnum hominem ad multos, disseritur, & subijcitur, Vbi exuberauit peccatum, ibi magis exuberasse gratiam. Ante lapsum non opus fuisset. Non enim bene habentibus opus est medico: Matthæi capite nono, Quamuis, sicut Deus praeuiderat hominem lapsurum, ita prædestinarat, quomodo per Christi mortem repararet.
units.tr: To this belong those words in Romans 5, where the origin and spread of sin from one man to many is discussed, and it is added: "Where sin abounded, grace abounded much more." Before the fall there was no need of it. "Those who are well have no need of a physician" (Matthew 9). Just as God foresaw that man would fall, so he had also predestined how he would repair him through the death of Christ.

units.la: Secunda ratio, cōueniebat differri, vt interea temporis mysteria perficienda per prophetas & sanctos patres vaticinijs & typis varijs prænunciaretur: & per prædicationē venturi in fide exerceri: Sicut docet parabola euangelica Matthæi capite 21. de eo, qui cum misisset plures seruos ad colonos, qui eos male tractarunt, tandem misit & filium suum.
units.tr: The second reason: it was fitting that it be deferred, so that in the meantime the mysteries to be accomplished might be foretold by the prophets and holy fathers through prophecies and various types, and that faith might be exercised through the preaching of the one to come. This is what the parable of the gospel in Matthew 21 teaches, about the man who sent many servants to the tenants, who treated them badly, and at last sent his own son.

units.la: Tertia, quòd si Christus statim ab initio lapsus humani fuisset in carnatus & obla-tus, vbi instaret mundi finis, omnis plane cognitio beneficiorum eius prorsus fuisset extincta, propter tempus adeò longum intercedens. Et si Christus respectu sui temporis dixit Lucæ capite decimoseptimo, Cùm filius hominis veniet (de posteriori aduentu ad iudicum loquitur) putás ne inueniet fidem in terra? Quantula fides restitisset, si passus fuisset à mundi initio? Profectò ne minima quidem scintillula.
units.tr: Third, if Christ had been conceived and offered in the flesh at once from the beginning of the human fall, when the end of the world was at hand, then all knowledge of his benefits would have been utterly extinguished, because of the very long interval of time. And if Christ, with respect to his own time, said in Luke 17, "When the Son of man comes (he is speaking of the later coming, to judge), will he find faith on the earth?", how small a faith would have remained if he had suffered from the beginning of the world? Surely not even the tiniest spark.

units.la: Quarta, addi potest, quòd elegerit tempus, sicut & locum, quod maximè idoneum foret ad propagandum beneficium Christi & sanctum euangelium. Iam, quare non expedierit Christum nasci & mori ad finem mundi, possunt similiter rationes quædam proferri.
units.tr: Fourth, it may be added that he chose the time, as well as the place, that would be most suitable for spreading the benefit of Christ and the holy gospel. Now, similar reasons can be given for why it was not fitting for Christ to be born and die at the end of the world.

units.la: Prima, ante illud adeò longum tempus plane interijsset omnis notitia de Deo, & omnis lux veritatis fuisset penitus extincta. Si enim statim initio mundi multum fuit oppressa cognitio omnis de Deo, ita vt Abraham & alij patres fuerint eligendi & mittendi, qui homines excitarent: & rursus, vbi prolapsi homines, ac denuò magis excæcati, mittendus fuit Moses cum lege scripta: certè non profuisset diutius differri aduentum ipsius Christi, quando nulla reuerentia Dei superesset, & beneficium Christi à nullis agnosceretur.
units.tr: First, before that very long time, all knowledge of God would have perished entirely, and all the light of truth would have been utterly extinguished. For if, at the very beginning of the world, the knowledge of God was so greatly oppressed that Abraham and the other fathers had to be chosen and sent to rouse men, and again, when men had fallen and been blinded still more, Moses had to be sent with the written law, then surely it would not have profited to defer the coming of Christ himself any longer, when no reverence for God remained and the benefit of Christ would be recognised by no one.

units.la: Secunda ratio, conueniebat, vt sicut prioribus temporibus hominibus manifestabatur bonitas Dei prædicatione rerum futurarum: ita post quoq; manifestaretur prædicatione rerum gestarum.
units.tr: The second reason: it was fitting that just as in earlier times the goodness of God was made manifest through the preaching of things to come, so afterwards it should be made manifest through the preaching of things done.

units.la: Quamobrem optimo ordine constitutum, vt Christus medio tempore, id est, neque initio mundi, neq; in fine mundi nasceretur & offerretur. Atq; huc iam pertinet illud Habacuc 3. Domine audiuit auditione, & timui: Domine opus tuum in medio annorū viuifica illud. In medio annorum notū facies, cùm iratus fueris, misericordiæ recordaberis. Hinc item vulgata illa suppututio, 2000. mane, 2000. lex, 2000. Mesiah. Igitur re-tisimè dictum, quòd Christus oblatus est semel, sub consummationem seculorum, &neque ante id tempus, neque post offerri debuerit aut potuerit. Iam verò hic concidit impia quorundam assertio, qui contendunt, Christum quotidie in missis immolari, ac missas propterea audent sacrificij nomine appellare: quo de quoniam homodie controuersiae passim oriuntur, nos aliquanto fusius suo tempore disseremus.
units.tr: For this reason it was arranged in the best order that Christ should be born and offered in the middle time, that is, neither at the beginning nor at the end of the world. And to this belongs that passage in Habakkuk 3: "O Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid. O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years; in the midst of the years make it known; when you are angry, remember mercy." Hence also that common reckoning: 2000 years before (mane), 2000 years of the law, 2000 years of the Messiah. Therefore it was said most rightly that Christ was offered once, at the consummation of the ages, and that he neither ought nor could be offered before that time or after it. Indeed, here falls the impious assertion of certain men, who contend that Christ is immolated daily in the masses, and who therefore dare to call the masses by the name of sacrifice. Since controversies about this arise everywhere today, we shall discuss the matter at somewhat greater length in its proper place.

units.la: CAPVT DECIMVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 10.

units.la: NAm lex vmbram obtinês futurorum bonorum, nō ipsam imaginem rerum,his hostijs quas singulis annis easdem continenter offerunt, nunquam potest accedentes perfectos reddere. Alioqui nõne desissent offerri? Propterea quòd nullam iam habuissent conscientiam peccatorum,qui sacrificassent,ac semel purgati essent. Atqui in istis commemoratio sit mortis quotannis.
units.tr: For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never by those sacrifices, which they offer continually year by year, make the worshippers perfect. Otherwise would they not have ceased to be offered? For the worshippers, once purged, would have had no further consciousness of sins. But in those sacrifices there is a yearly remembrance of sins.

units.la: VIa verò proximo argumento constanter & diuersis uerbis inculcatū est Christi sacrificiū licet semel tantùm oblatum, sufficies nihilominus atq; efficax esse ad satis faciendū pro peccatis: quod interim sacrificijs legalibus nequaquam tribuitur. (ita enim duplici nomine euicit, sacrificium Christi legalibus esse excellentius, & quod tantùm semel, inquâ, oblatum, & quod peccata tollat) Iam subijcit probationem, quòd legalia sacrificia minimè auferant peccata. Ac maximè necessarium erat probationem hanc addere, simul, quòd, etiamsi suprà saepius dictum sit, sacrificia legalia non habuisse vim purgandi conscientias at nullo adhuc argumento euidenti est id demōstratum (nisi forte quis velit tantundem significatum ab Apostolo illis verbis capite octauo: Etenim si prius illud talè fuisset, ut nihil in eo posset reprehendit, &c. Sed ibi potius agitur in genere de imperfectione totius testamenti, seu totius legis) simul quod Hebraei non sine graui offendiculo audierint, suis sacrificijs eam facultatem prorsus adimi. Est autem, si bene intueamur, argumentum Apostoli multò argutissimè excogitatum. Apparet aduersarios voluisse extenuare, imò in totum euertere effectus sacrificij Christi, idque eo potissimum nomine, quòd tantùm semel fuisset oblatum: è diuerso autem in coelum extulisse sua sacrificia legalia, quòd crebra essent & multa, ideoque merito iudicanda efficaciora. Sed apostolus veluti quadam in uersione dialectica utês, hac ipsa ex causa colligit, sacrificia legalia inutilia & inefficacia, quòd saepius repeterentur. Quòd, inquit, ea quotannis debeant repeti idipsum, reuera certissimum est signū, quòd ad tollenda peccata non suffecerint. Si enim aliquando suffecissent, haud fuisset opus denuò repeti. Qui semel obtulissent, abundè fuissent purgati animis, neque ullis nouis sacrificijs, quę pro peccatis offerrent, indiguissent. Quamobrè palàm est, sacrificium Christi etiam tantùm semel oblatū longè omnib. legalibus esse praestantius.
units.tr: In the next argument the Apostle establishes, in constant and varied words, that Christ's sacrifice, though offered only once, is nevertheless sufficient and effective to make satisfaction for sins, which is something that is by no means ascribed to the legal sacrifices. (He proves the point under two heads: that Christ's sacrifice is more excellent than the legal ones, both because it was offered only once and because it takes away sins.) Next he adds the proof that the legal sacrifices by no means take away sins. It was especially necessary to add this proof, because, although it has been said several times above that the legal sacrifices had no power to purge consciences, no clear argument has yet been given for it. (Unless perhaps someone wishes to read the same meaning into the Apostle's words in chapter 8: For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no place sought for a second, etc. But there the Apostle is speaking in general about the imperfection of the whole testament, or the whole law.) At the same time he addresses the fact that the Hebrews heard, not without serious offence, that this power was completely taken away from their sacrifices. If we look at it closely, the Apostle's argument is devised with great subtlety. It is clear that the opponents wanted to diminish, or indeed to overthrow altogether, the effects of Christ's sacrifice, and that they did so chiefly on the ground that it was offered only once. On the other hand, they exalted their own legal sacrifices to the heavens because they were frequent and many, and so were rightly to be judged more effective. But the Apostle, using a kind of dialectical reversal, draws from this very cause the conclusion that the legal sacrifices are useless and ineffective, because they had to be repeated so often. He says: that they must be repeated every year is in truth a most certain sign that they did not suffice to take away sins. For if they had ever sufficed, there would have been no need to repeat them. Those who had offered once would have been fully purged in their souls, and would have had no need of any new sacrifices to offer for sins. Therefore it is plain that Christ's sacrifice, even though offered only once, is far superior to all the legal ones.

units.la: Haec est argumenti summa. Verùm apostolus instructiore apparatu id constituit, quèadmodum inter enarrandum ostendemus. Ait itaque: Nam (cohęret haec particula quo-dammodo praecedenti) lex umbram obtinens futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum, his hostijs, quas singulis annis easdem continenter offerunt, nunquam potest accedentes perfectos reddere.
units.tr: This is the sum of the argument. But the Apostle sets it out with a fuller array, as we shall show in the exposition. He says, then: For the law (this particle is in some way connected with what goes before), having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with these sacrifices, which they offer continually every year, make the comers perfect.

units.la: Primùm propositio argumenti hisce verbis exprimitur. Lex his hostijs, quas singulis annis continenter offerunt, nunquam potest accedentes perfectos reddere. Interpo-nuntur autem nonnulla, sed ea mirè conuenientia instituto, imò aptissimæ comprobationis loco habenda.
units.tr: First, the proposition of the argument is expressed in these words: the law can never make the comers perfect with these sacrifices, which they offer continually year by year. Some things are inserted, but these agree remarkably well with the design and are to be regarded as a most apt confirmation.

units.la: Cùm enim dicit, legem tantùm obtinere vmbram futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum, nónne satis aperte significat, sacrificia legalia nequaquam potuisse veros effectus spirituales producere, tantùm vmbras ac typos fuisse cuiusdam sacrificij excellentioris per Christum longè post offerēdi? Nónne hoc pacto sacrificiorum legalium, profernit vniuersam gloriam? Sunt autem repetita haec verba ex capite octauo, vbi dicebatur, sacerdotium & sacrificia Christi deseruire exemplari atq; vmbrae coelestium, quae quidem nos tùm dicebamus veluti pro fundamento praesentis disputationis fuisse posita, ideoque prudenter eadem in memoriam nunc reuocat. Et cum omnia ferè sint semel dicta, non est quod partibus explicandis diu immoremur.
units.tr: For when he says that the law has only a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, does he not quite clearly signify that the legal sacrifices could never produce true spiritual effects, and were only shadows and types of a more excellent sacrifice, to be offered later through Christ? Does he not in this way strip the legal sacrifices of all their glory? These words are repeated from chapter 8, where it was said that the priesthood and sacrifices of Christ serve as a pattern and shadow of heavenly things. We then said that this was laid down as the foundation of the present discussion, and so he wisely recalls the same words to our memory now. And since almost everything has been said once already, there is no need for us to linger long in explaining the parts.

units.la: Lex nunquam potest accedentes perfectos reddere) Simili modo dictū est cap.7. Lex nihil ad perfectionē adduxit, verùm erat introductio ad spē potiore. Hic autē, sicut in tota hac disputatione, tatione, Lex accipitur pro ea potissimum parte quæ habet ceremonialia, de quorum abrogatione hic disputatur, & quæ proprie vmbra sunt ac typus. Nam etiamsi ad Romanos vel Galatas disputetur etiá de abrogatione decalogi: tamen hic nihil ita, quando nec Decalogus dici potest vmbra vel typus. Atq; habet Emphasin particula Nunquam: adimit enim facultatem perfectionis in omne tempus, sed ab euangelio esse expectandam.
units.tr: The law can never make the comers perfect. In a similar way it was said in chapter 7: the law made nothing perfect, but was the introduction to a better hope. Here, as in the whole of this discussion, the law is taken chiefly for that part which contains the ceremonial laws, whose abrogation is discussed here, and which are properly shadows and types. For although the abrogation of the Decalogue is also discussed in Romans and Galatians, nothing of the kind is discussed here, since the Decalogue cannot be called a shadow or type. The word never carries emphasis: it takes away the power of making perfect at any time, and says that perfection must be looked for from the gospel.

units.la: Et eleganter dicit προσφερομένους: proponitur vtile & inutile, lex & euangelium: tuum est accedere vel retrogredi: sicut multi discipuli accesserunt ad Iesum: quidam vero (vt dies ille, qui volebat prius suos parentes sepelire) retrocedebant.
units.tr: And he says elegantly approaching [προσφερομένους]: the useful and the useless, the law and the gospel, are set before us; it is up to you to draw near or to draw back. Just as many disciples drew near to Jesus, while some (like the man who wished first to bury his parents) drew back.

units.la: Proinde, qui hoc pacto accedunt legem, ei se adiungunt, eam ample ctuntur, se ei submittunt, deducuntur, & veluti manu ducuntur per legem, sed nequaquam ad perfectio nem. Quod si uero accedas euangelium, & pontificem Christum, ibi poteris ad consummationem & perfectionem perduci. Quo sensu dictum est capite quarto, Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ, vt consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam inuenia mus ad oportunum auxilium. Et capite septimo: Vnde & saluos facere ad plenum potest, qui per ipsum adeunt, προσερχομένους, Deum. Et hoc ipso capite decimo, Cum igitur fratres habeamus libertatem adeundi in sancta; per sanguinem Iesu; ea via, quam dedicauit nobis recentem ac viuentem, per velamentum; hoc est, per carnem suam, cumque habeamus sacerdotem magnum, præfectum domui Dei accedamus cum vero corde, in certitudine fidei, &c. prima Petri capite secundo, Si quidem gustastis, quod benignus sit Dominus, ad quem accedentes, qui lapis est viuus, &c. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: Accordingly, those who approach the law in this way attach themselves to it, embrace it, submit to it, are led, and are, as it were, guided by the hand through the law, but never to perfection. But if you approach the gospel and Christ as high priest, there you will be brought to completion and perfection. In this sense it was said in chapter 4: Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. And in chapter 7: Wherefore he is able also to save to the uttermost those who come [προσερχομένους] to God through him. And in this very chapter 10: Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way which he has consecrated for us, through the veil, that is, his flesh; and having an high priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, etc. And in 1 Peter chapter 2: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious; to whom coming, as unto a living stone, etc. But enough on these points.

units.la: His hostijs, quas singulis annis easdem (& quantum ad modum offerendi easdem videlicet ceremonias: & quantum ad substantiam: quia semper hircos & vitulos offerebant) continenter offerunt. Etiamsi viderentur ad hoc instituta, & summa diligentia singulis annis, (loquitur enim de hostijs illis in festo expiationis, de quibus semper disputatum est, quasque semel in anno tantum offerebat sacerdos ingrediens in sancta sanctorum) tamen veram & spiritualem, quæque conscientijs prodest iustitiam non conferebant, sed tantum externam & corporalem, vt haberentur iusti coram ecclesia, & non eij cerentur ab ecclesia ceu prophani. Et ratio est:
units.tr: With these sacrifices, which they offer continually year by year (both as to the manner of offering them, that is, the ceremonies, and as to their substance, since they always offered goats and calves). Even though these sacrifices seemed to have been instituted for this purpose, and were offered every year with the greatest diligence (for he is speaking of those sacrifices on the Day of Atonement, which have always been discussed, and which the priest offered once a year only, when he entered the Holy of Holies), nevertheless they did not confer a true and spiritual righteousness, which benefits consciences, but only an external and bodily one, so that the people might be held righteous before the Church and not be cast out by the Church as profane. And the reason is this:

units.la: Lex vmbram tantum obtinebat futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum.
units.tr: The law held only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things themselves.

units.la: Quomodo lex vmbram tantum habuerit, & quidé futurorum bonorum, id est, cœlestium post hanc vitam expectandorum, seu potius eorum, quæ post per Christum forent in ecclesia (quæ & ipsa cœlestis non male dicitur) peragenda, satis dictum est. Sed est consideranda hic quomodo differant vmbra & imago, εικών. Si in vetere lege vmbra est, in Euangelio autem tantum imago rerum, iam non videtur euangelium valde excellere legem, imo nec euangelium res ipsas habere agnoscetur. Sciendum ergo, vmbra & imaginem in hoc convenire, quod pariter aliquid aliud repræsentat; sed tamen imago omnino plenius & consummatius, quam vmbra: & ita multum adhuc inter se differunt. Licet id clarius videre in vmbra, nihil aliud quam cernis obscurum quiddam & informe; nulla certa magnitudinum aut proportionum ratio habita: & vmbra nunquam membrorum certam exprimit symmetriam. At vero imago, puta statua sculpta, vel pictura in tabula, iam longe efficacius omnia proponit visenda, & clarius, vt singulorum membrorum forma dispositio, proportio cerni possit. Licet contemplari discrimen istud in tabula picta, in qua imago aliqua est expressa, & ad latus alicubi etiá vmbra eiusdem reddita. Eodem igitur modo se habent & lex & euangelium. Res ipsæ promissæ & vere non possunt plenæ obtineri in hac vita, sed tantum post hanc vitam contemplabimur & perfruemur omnibus abundantissimè in Deo. Et tamen Deus earum rerum semper quasi gustum quendam præbere voluit, & certos nos de ijs obtinendis reddere.
units.tr: How the law had only a shadow of good things to come, namely the heavenly things to be awaited after this life, or rather those things which were afterwards to be accomplished in the Church through Christ (which may also fittingly be called heavenly), has been sufficiently explained. But we must consider here how a shadow differs from an image [εἰκών]. If the old law is a shadow, and the Gospel is only an image of things, then it no longer seems that the Gospel greatly surpasses the law; indeed, it will not be recognised that the Gospel has the things themselves. We should therefore understand that a shadow and an image agree in this, that each equally represents something else; but an image is altogether fuller and more complete than a shadow, and so they still differ greatly from one another. This can be seen more clearly in a shadow: you discern nothing but some dark and formless thing, with no fixed ratio of sizes or proportions; and a shadow never expresses the exact symmetry of the limbs. But an image, such as a carved statue or a painting on a panel, sets before the eyes all things far more effectively and more clearly, so that the form, arrangement and proportion of each limb can be discerned. This difference can be observed in a painted panel, in which some image is portrayed and somewhere at the side a shadow of the same is also rendered. In the same way, then, the law and the Gospel stand. The promised things themselves cannot be fully possessed in this life, but only after this life shall we behold and enjoy them in God most abundantly. Yet God has always wished to give us, as it were, a certain foretaste of those things, and to make us certain of obtaining them.

units.la: Igitur agentibus sub lege exhibita est quædam vmbra, crassa inquam & obscura: agentibus sub euangelio exhibita est lucida & bene colorata imago. Ac revera typi & res gestæ patrum se habent instar rudis & crassæ vmbræ: Res vero gestæ in euangelio per Christum, claram & manifestam imaginem nobis ostenderunt, atque earum quidem rerum, quæ post hanc vitam nobis sunt expectandæ. Sic Sacramenta & ceremoniæ legales erant vmbræ. Sacramenta vero euangelica sunt imago: Res vero adhuc à nobis debent expectari.
units.tr: Therefore, to those living under the law was shown a certain shadow, coarse, I say, and dim; to those living under the Gospel is shown a bright and well-coloured image. Indeed, the types and the deeds of the fathers stand in the place of a rough and coarse shadow; but the deeds accomplished in the Gospel through Christ have shown us a clear and manifest image, and indeed of those things which we are to await after this life. Thus the legal sacraments and ceremonies were shadows; but the evangelical sacraments are the image; the things themselves are still to be awaited by us.

units.la: Itaq; recte iste voces sic constituuntur, vt vmbra referatur ad legem, imago ad euangelium. Atq; huc etiá pertinet, quod Christus ipse vocatur imago, εικών, Dei invisibilis, Col. 1.
units.tr: Therefore these terms are rightly set so that the shadow is referred to the law, and the image to the Gospel. To this also pertains the fact that Christ himself is called the image [εἰκών] of the invisible God, Col. 1.

units.la: quæ appellatio ita Christo cõpetit, non quasi ipse patre inferior sit, sed quòd per omnia patri sit similis: &, licet distincta sit persona, tamen natura nihil distinguitur. Atq; ideo etiam apparet, hic ab Apostolo cum maiori quadâ efficacia dictû, ⸀αὐτὸν ⸁τὴν εἰκόνα, ipsam imaginé, vt sic significet, in veteri testamento ne imaginem quidè visam, sed tantum crassam & informem vmbram: in euangelio autem habere ipsissimam imaginem.
units.tr: This title belongs to Christ not as though he were inferior to the Father, but because he is in all things like the Father; and although the persons are distinct, nothing is distinguished in nature. Hence it also appears that the Apostle says here, with a certain greater force, the very image itself [αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα], so as to signify that under the Old Testament there was not even an image seen, but only a coarse and formless shadow; whereas in the Gospel we have the very image itself.

units.la: Alioqui nonne desijssent offerri? Propterea quod nulla tam habuissent conscientiam peccatorum, qui sacrificassent, ac semel purgati essent. Atqui in istis commemoratio fit peccatorum quotannis.
units.tr: Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? For those who offered the sacrifices, having been once purged, would have had no further consciousness of sins. But in these sacrifices there is a remembrance of sins every year.

units.la: Ratio seu probatio propositionis sumpta à signo ex ritu offerendi: postea sequitur secunda ratio à qualitate rerum oblatarum. Sic autem colligit: Si sacrificia illa abstulissent peccata, aut perfectos reddidissent, non opus fuisset ea denuò offerri.
units.tr: This is the reason, or the proof of the proposition, drawn from the sign taken from the manner of offering; afterwards follows a second reason, drawn from the nature of the things offered. He argues thus: If those sacrifices had taken away sins, or had made the worshippers perfect, it would not have been necessary to offer them again.

units.la: Atqui nos videmus ea quotánis, & quidè cum noua commemoratione peccatorū offerrum: Igitur, quòd ita semper repeti debuerint, certũ signũ est, quòd peccata non abstulerint. Addit autem Apostolus quadam probatione Maioris in hunc modum. Ideo desijssent offerri, inquit, quia, qui sacrificassent ac semel purgati essent, iam nullam haberent amplius peccatorum conscietiam, fuissent in totum à peccatis per prius oblatum sacrificiū purgati. Hæc est clara & perspicua Apostoli sententia, nihil habens intricatum.
units.tr: But we see that they were offered every year, and indeed with a fresh remembrance of sins. Therefore, that they had to be repeated in this way is a sure sign that they did not take away sins. The Apostle adds a proof of the major premise in this manner: They would have ceased to be offered, he says, because those who offered sacrifice and were once purged would no longer have any consciousness of sins; they would have been wholly cleansed from sins by the sacrifice offered earlier. This is the clear and plain meaning of the Apostle, containing nothing intricate.

units.la: Sed & verba & schemata sunt elegantissimè depositá. Nonne, inquit, desijssent offerri? Quadâ expostulationis forma quasi cogit fateri, quòd res ita se habeat. Et valde accommoda est hæc ratio. Chrysostomus eam confirmat perelegāti Similitudine, quam breuissimè nos reddemus. Vbi pharmacū adhibetur ægroto, & non tollit morbū, signum est, pharmacū illud esse inefficax: & quòd deinceps oportet nouū pharmacum adhibere, eò plenius ostenditur illius pharmaci impotentia & imbecillitas: Ita, inquit, sacrificia quæ se haberet veluti pharmaca, quia repetuntur, signum est, quòd non sint efficacia: si enim prodesse ent, non deberent repeti. Hæc est medicamenti laus & virtus, si semel impositum statim iuuet. Similiter vbi semel vi bellica depulsi & repressi sunt hostes, tùm pax agnoscitur. At vbi istud non est factum, manet bellum.
units.tr: But both the words and the figures of speech are most elegantly placed. Would they not, he says, have ceased to be offered? By a form of expostulation he, as it were, compels us to admit that the matter stands thus. And this argument is very apt. Chrysostom confirms it with a most elegant comparison, which we shall give as briefly as possible. When a medicine is applied to a sick man and does not remove the disease, it is a sign that the medicine is ineffective; and since another medicine must then be applied, the impotence and weakness of that medicine is shown all the more fully. So, he says, sacrifices, which were like medicines, since they were repeated, are a sign that they were not effective; for if they had been of benefit, they would not need to be repeated. This is the praise and virtue of a medicine, if once applied it immediately helps. Similarly, when enemies have once been driven off and repressed by military force, then peace is recognised; but where this has not happened, war remains.

units.la: Atqui in istis commemoratio fit peccatorum quotannis) Argumenti ratio postulasset ita dicere. Atqui videmus semper offerri: sed maluit Apostolus aliter dicere, videlicet, quotannis fieri commemorationem peccatorum, causam nimirum exprimendo pro effectu, vel id quod prius est, pro posteriori. Conscientia enim peccatorum, causa erat, cur ad iterandā sacrificia confugerent. Si non fuissent conscij peccatorum, non opus fuisset solicitos esse de sacrificijs. Et propterea etiam vocabantur hostiæ pro peccato, & homines peccata sua confitebantur, & orabant pro peccatorum remissione obtinenda. Quapropter multò rectius facit, dicendo, fieri quotannis commemorationem peccatorum, quàm si dixisset, quotannis repeti sacrificium. Et certè etiamsi dixisset, repeti quotannis sacrificium, exigi adhuc poterat causa, respondendum q; fuisset, agnitionem peccati fuisse causam. Interea & illud valde facit ad extenuationem sacrificiorum, ac plane tollitur iustificatio per ea, quando dicitur illis fieri semper nouâ peccatorum commemorationem. Illa enim sacrificiorū oblatio, peccatorum erat constitutio, non oblatio vel solutio. In eo, quòd offerebatur, peccatorum confessio: quòd verò semper iterū offerebantur, peccatorum persistetia, siue quòd peccata semper remanerent & sublata non essent. Item probatio illa Maioris:
units.tr: But in these sacrifices there is a remembrance of sins every year. The logic of the argument would have required him to say: But we see that they were always offered. Yet the Apostle preferred to put it otherwise, namely, that there is a remembrance of sins every year, expressing the cause for the effect, or what is prior for what is posterior. For consciousness of sins was the cause why they had recourse to repeating the sacrifices. If they had not been conscious of sins, there would have been no need to be anxious about sacrifices. And for this reason the sacrifices were also called sin-offerings, and men confessed their sins and prayed to obtain the forgiveness of sins. Therefore he does far better in saying that there is a yearly remembrance of sins, than if he had said that the sacrifice was repeated every year. And indeed, even if he had said that the sacrifice was repeated every year, the cause could still be asked, and the answer would have been that the acknowledgement of sin was the cause. Meanwhile this also greatly serves to diminish the sacrifices, and justification through them is plainly taken away, when it is said that a fresh remembrance of sins is always made by them. For the offering of those sacrifices was a constituting of sins, not an offering or a payment of them. In that they were offered there was a confession of sins; but that they were always offered again shows the persistence of sins, or that sins always remained and were not taken away. Likewise, there is that proof of the major premise:

units.la: Propterea, quòd nulla tam habuisset conscientia peccatorum, qui sacrificasset, ac semel purgati essent) Etiā elegantissimè est reddita, maximè quia dicit, non habuissent conscientiā peccatorum. Conscientia significat internum quiddā & reconditū. Ergo vt etiam tales visi fuissent semel absoluti à peccatis coram ecclesia, tamen non purgabantur animis & coram Deo, quod solùm valde magnum est & necessarium: semper manebat sub lege grauata conscientia: quandoquidem solius proprium est euangelij reddere pacatas conscientias: Roman. 5. & 8. Legales hostiæ purgabat secundùm carnem, vt dictũ est capite præcedenti, at non secundum conscientiam. Atq; ita tollitur, quòd fortasis obij ceretur, nempe sacrificia illa offerri solita pro peccatis anteactis, non pro futuris: vbi autem postea aliqui iterū peccarunt, opus erat tùm iterum offerrent. Respondemus: Non illam fuisse causam, cur repeterentur sacrificia, quia videlicet homines iterum subinde peccarent (alias enim cùm & in nouo testamēto subinde relabamur in peccata, esset opus & Christũ frequenter immolari) sed quia illa sacrificia nunquam purgabant conscientias, & non habebát vim satisfaciendi pro peccatis coram Deo. At Christi sacrificium habuit hanc, vim, deoque nunquam debet repeti. Ergo hac forma locutionis notat vim historiarum legalium, & galium, & earum imbecillitatem, quòd videlicet conscientias non liberabant à peccatis coram Deo: Item q; discrimen legis ab Euangelio, in quo solo pacatæ conscientiæ possunt obtingere, pulchrè delineat. Sunt itaque valdè appositè omnia per Apostolum expressa.
units.tr: Because the one who offered sacrifice, having been once purged, would have had no consciousness of sins. This is also most elegantly expressed, especially because he says they would not have had a consciousness of sins. Conscience signifies something inward and hidden. Therefore, even if such persons had seemed to be once absolved from sins before the Church, yet they were not purged in their souls and before God, which alone is very great and necessary; under the law the conscience always remained burdened, since it belongs solely to the Gospel to render consciences at peace: Romans 5 and 8. The legal sacrifices purged according to the flesh, as was said in the preceding chapter, but not according to conscience. And thus that objection which might perhaps be raised is answered: namely, that those sacrifices were customarily offered for past sins, not for future ones; and when afterwards some sinned again, it was necessary then to offer again. We reply: this was not the reason why the sacrifices were repeated, namely that men sinned again from time to time (for otherwise, since in the New Testament too we fall back into sins from time to time, it would be necessary for Christ to be frequently sacrificed), but because those sacrifices never purged consciences, and did not have the power of satisfying for sins before God. But the sacrifice of Christ has this power, and therefore it ought never to be repeated. Therefore by this form of speech he marks the power of the legal histories, and the weakness of them, namely that they did not free consciences from sins before God; and he also finely outlines the difference between the law and the Gospel, in which alone consciences can attain peace. Therefore everything expressed by the Apostle is very aptly put.

units.la: Sed si hæc ratio Apostoli firma est iudicāda, videlicet, ideo non potuisse purgari conscientias illis sacrificijs, quia ea subinde repetebantur: videtur, quòd idem quoq; dici potest de sacrificio Christi, quod & apud nos subinde repetitur. Hanc obiectionem profert Chrysostomus: Sed eandem ipsius quoq; verbis, & sanè valdè aptis, dissoluem us. Sic enim respondet: Nonne per singulos dies offerimus? Offerimus quidem, sed ad recordationem facientes mortis eius. Et vna est hæc hostia, non multæ. Quomodo vna est & non multæ? Et quia semel oblata est illa, oblata est in sancta sanctorum. Hoc autem sacrificium exemplar est illius, idipsum semper offerimus: Nec nunc quidem alium agnum, crastina alium, sed semper idipsum.
units.tr: But if the Apostle's reasoning is to be judged sound, namely that those sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience because they were repeated from time to time, it seems that the same might be said of the sacrifice of Christ, which among us too is repeated from time to time. Chrysostom raises this objection, and in his own words, which are quite apt, we may answer it. For he replies: "Do we not offer every day? We do offer, but we offer in remembrance of his death. And this sacrifice is one, not many. How is it one and not many? Because it was offered once, it was offered in the Holy of Holies. Moreover, this sacrifice is the copy of that one: we always offer the same thing, not one lamb today and another tomorrow, but always the same."

units.la: Proinde vnum est hoc sacrificium. Alioqui hac ratione, quoniam in multis offertur, multi Christi sunt? Nequaquam, sed vnus vbique est Christus, & his plenus existens & illic plenus, vnum corpus. Sicut enim, qui vbique offertur, vnum corpus est, non multa corpora: ita etiam & vnum sacrificium. Pontifex autem noster ille est, qui hostiam mundantem nos obtulit, ipsam offerimus & nunc, quæ tunc oblata quidem consumi non potest. Hoc autem, quod nos facimus, in commemorationem quidem fit eius, quod factum est: Hoc enim facite, inquit, in meam commemorationem. Non aliud sacrificium, sicut pontifex, sed idipsum semper facimus, magis autem recordationem sacrificij operamur. Hactenus Chrysostomus. Ex quibus verbis clarum fit, sacrificiū Christi per nos nequaquam iterari, sicut olim iterabantur sacrificia legalia, sed tantùm commemorari: & quicquid per nos ea in parte fit, id vniuersum ad recordationem fit vnici sacrificij semel per Christum oblati. Vnde & Cyprianus lib.2. epistola 3. diserte, quotiescunque sacrificium à nobis fieri in vsu Cœnæ Dominicæ dicitur, nihil aliud, quàm fieri mortis & sacrificij Christi memoriam.
units.tr: Therefore this is one sacrifice. Otherwise, by the same reasoning, since it is offered in many places, would there be many Christs? By no means. Christ is one everywhere, and being full here he is full there too, one body. For just as the body that is offered everywhere is one body, not many bodies, so also the sacrifice is one. Yet it is that same High Priest of ours who offered the cleansing victim, and we offer it now, though what was offered then cannot be consumed. What we do, however, is done in commemoration of what was done: "Do this," he says, "in remembrance of me." We do not offer another sacrifice, as the high priest did, but we always do the same thing, or rather we perform the remembrance of the sacrifice. Thus far Chrysostom. From these words it is clear that the sacrifice of Christ is in no way repeated by us, as the legal sacrifices were once repeated, but only commemorated; and whatever is done by us in this matter is done entirely in remembrance of the one sacrifice once offered by Christ. Hence also Cyprian, in book 2, epistle 3, plainly says that whenever a sacrifice is said to be made by us in the use of the Lord's Supper, it is nothing other than the making of a memorial of the death and sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Quod quidem annotandum fuit à nobis, propter illos, qui missam esse sacrificium non verentur stolidissimè, & magna Christi iniuria afficerare. Qua de plenius in libris Rhapsodiarum humanarum dictum est. Atque hæc pro doctrina satis sit breuiter propo suisse, videlicet q; missa nullo modo sit sacrificiū appellāda. Sed & illud pro doctrina est excerpendū hoc loco, maximum videlicet esse discrimen inter legem & euangelium: cum sub lege, etiamsi multa & optima quæque sacrificia offerantur, tamen maneat peccatorum conscientia, nunquam tollantur peccata, nunquam conscientiæ pacem cum Deo habeant. At in euangelio per vnicum sacrificium Christi pacem habemus cum Deo. Romanorum capite quinto, Nulla est nobis condemnatio. Romanorum capite octauo, Qui semel purgati sunt per Christū, non opus est, vt alijs modis purgari queant. Et hæc est illa libertas Christiana, in conscientijs videlicet sita, qua liberati sunt credentes à peccatis, quæ sub lege cōtingere non poterat, vtpote cuius perpetua erat seruitus, sub qua semper timor. At nunc non accepimus Spiritum seruitutis aut timoris, sed spiritum adoptionis, per quem, vtingenui, clamamus Abba pater.
units.tr: This we had to note, on account of those who do not fear, most foolishly, to call the Mass a sacrifice and so do great injury to Christ. This has been treated more fully in the books of the Rhapsodiae humanae. And let it be enough to have briefly set forth this doctrine, namely that the Mass must in no way be called a sacrifice. But there is also a doctrine to be drawn from this passage, namely that there is the greatest difference between law and gospel: under the law, although many and excellent sacrifices were offered, the consciousness of sin nonetheless remained, and sins were never taken away, and consciences never had peace with God. But in the gospel, through the one sacrifice of Christ, we have peace with God. Romans 5: "There is therefore now no condemnation for us." Romans 8: "Those who have once been cleansed through Christ have no need to be cleansed in any other way." And this is that Christian liberty, which lies in the conscience, by which believers are freed from sins, which could not be obtained under the law, since its servitude was perpetual, and under it there was always fear. But now we have not received the spirit of bondage or fear, but the spirit of adoption, through whom, like free-born children, we cry, "Abba, Father."

units.la: Non enim potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata.
units.tr: For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins.

units.la: Altera ratio probans, quòd sacrificia legalia ad tollenda peccata non suffecerint, sumpta à Qualitate rerum ablatarum, quarum sanè quiuis intelligit nullam esse proportionem siue ad Deū, qui erat placadus: siue ad hominē, pro quo offerebatur: siue ad peccata, quæ debebat expiare. Vis argumenti in voce ἀλλὰ, q magnā habet emphasin. Et certè, si quis velit exactius perpendere, quales sint victimæ illæ, qualis Deus, qualis homo qui peccat, qualis sit natura peccati, facilè animaduertet, nullo pacto coeunire posse, vt sentiatur, vt hostias posse pro peccatis satisfacere. Primùm enim quid est Deus? Nonne spiritus? Nonne iustus, qui suo iure potest perdere, non solùm, quia condidit & Dominus est: sed quia etiā per nos grauissimè est offensus? Nonne item omnipotens, vt nihil sit, propter quod ipse moueri aut posset, aut debeat? Quid ergo brutorum animalium carnes oppones spiritui Deo? Quæ nam hic est collatio? Non tàm distat cœlum à terra, quàm brutum à Deo. Deinde, num bruta animantia omnis sensus, omnis boni ac mali expertia opponēs iustitiæ ac bonitati Dei? Sunt ne animantia eiusmodi, vt quando illa offeruntur ab hominibus ad mortem, Deus debeat eorum mortibus magnopere commoueri, quādo eorum casu ne homo quidem moueatur, nec se placari patiatur? Et quæ vtilitas Deo, vel, quid habet commodi, si ei offerantur bruta, & quidem mortua? Quæ nam ei hinc manat gloria? Quem refert ipse fructum? Nunquid manducabo, inquit, Psalmo quadragesimonono, carnes taurorum, aut sanguine hircorum potabo? Ibidem: Non accipiam de domo tua vitulos, neq; de gregibus tuis hircos. Quoniam meæ sunt omnes feræ sylvarum, iumenta in montibus, & boues, &c.
units.tr: The second reason proving that the legal sacrifices did not suffice to take away sins is drawn from the quality of the things removed, of which surely anyone can see there is no proportion either to God, who was to be appeased, or to the man for whom they were offered, or to the sins which they were to expiate. The force of the argument lies in the word "but" (ἀλλὰ), which carries a great emphasis. And indeed, if anyone wishes to weigh more exactly what those victims are, what God is, what man is who sins, and what the nature of sin is, he will easily perceive that they cannot agree in any way, so that the victims could be felt to satisfy for sins. For first, what is God? Is he not spirit? Is he not just, who by his own right can destroy, not only because he made us and is Lord, but because he is also most gravely offended by us? Is he not also almighty, so that there is nothing by which he could, or ought, to be moved? What then will you set the flesh of brute animals over against the Spirit of God? What comparison is there here? Heaven is not so far from earth as a brute beast is from God. Next, are brute animals, which lack all sense and all knowledge of good and evil, to be set against the justice and goodness of God? Are animals of such a kind that when they are offered to death by men, God ought to be greatly moved by their deaths, when a man himself is not moved by their fall, nor allows himself to be placated? What use is it to God, or what advantage does he have, if brute animals, and indeed dead ones, are offered to him? What glory flows to him from this? What fruit does he himself gain? "Shall I eat," he says in Psalm 49, "the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?" And again: "I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. For all the beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the hills, and the oxen," and so on.

units.la: Iam quod ad homines attinet, nónne magnum est discrimen inter homines & bruta animantia? Si autè non est iustitia in homine, si non potest homo, qui creatus est ad imaginem Dei, per se placere Deo: si non potest ipse vllis, qualibet præclaris operibus satis facere pro peccatis proprijs, quanto minus sanguis bruti animatis, quod profecto animans neq; boni quicquā potest agere, vt nec malû, satis faciet pro peccatis alienis? Nun quid homo præstantior est apud Deũ omnibus brutis? Nunquid passeribus istis pluris estis vos, inquit Christus? Quomodo ergo placebit brutū pro homine? Et quid preciosius hominis anima immortali, & ad viuendū æternum formata? pro hac ne ergo satisfaciet brutum animal, cuius anima simul cum corpore interit? Vitam ne dabit, quod vitam in se non habet? Tu es qui peccasti & putas, ςp pro te satisfaciet miserũ pecus? Quo iam te abijcis, infra pecora? Sed videamus, quomodo etiam se habeat bruta animantia ad peccatum. Peccatum est res spiritualis: Quod autē huiusmodi est, tolletur ne rebus corporalibus? Et minimum peccatum eiusmodi est, vt ne omnium quidem hominum bona opera simul collecta possint pro eo apud iustitiā Dei satis facere: quomodo ergo tanta vis tribuitur sanguini, aut carni brutarum pecudum? Nunquid carnes sanctæ auferet à te malitias, in quibus gloriata es, inquit Hieremias propheta cap. 11. Et Esa. 1. Vt quid offertis mihi multitudinem victimarum vestrarum, dicit Dominus? Satur sum: holocausta arietum, & adipem bubulorum, & sanguinem vitulorum, & agnorum, & hircorum nolui. Et paulo post: Lauate vos, mundi estote, remouete malum operum vestrorum à conspectu oculorum meorum, desinite malefacere, discite benefacere, quasi diceret: Putatis, quod vos purgatos faciet sanguis brutorum, quando ipsi vos semper contaminatis nouis peccatis? Et quando bruta per se non sunt pura, quomodo alios puros facient? His igitur ita consideratis, quia videlicet adeò nulla est proportio brutorum animantium, siue ad Deum, siue ad homines, siue ad hominum peccata: rectissimè dixit Apostolus, sacrificia legalia non tollere peccata, quando impossibile id fit, & ab hircorum taurorumque natura alienissimû. Et propterea, quandoquidé nihil poterat inueniri, quod pro peccatis satisfaceret, non angelus, non homo, non brutū, non aliquod opus qualibet eximiū, necessum erat venire eū, qui Deus erat, vt sic diuinæ potentiæ ac iustitiæ opponi propter potentiam & iustitiam posset: & qui homo efficiebatur, vt hominis partes tanto suscipe ret diligetius tuedas, & qui sine omni prorsus peccato esset, vt pro peccatis alienis possef dependere.
units.tr: Now as far as men are concerned, is there not a great difference between men and brute animals? If there is no righteousness in man, if man, who was created in the image of God, cannot by himself please God, if he cannot by any outstanding works, however excellent, make sufficient satisfaction for his own sins, how much less will the blood of a brute animal, which certainly can do neither good nor evil, make satisfaction for the sins of others? Is man not more excellent before God than all brute beasts? "Are you not of more value than the sparrows?" says Christ. How then will a beast be pleasing in place of a man? And what is more precious than the human soul, immortal and formed to live forever? Will a brute animal, whose soul perishes together with its body, make satisfaction for this soul? Will what does not have life in itself give life? You are the one who has sinned, and do you think that a wretched herd will make satisfaction for you? Where are you casting yourself now, below the beasts? But let us see how brute animals stand in relation to sin as well. Sin is a spiritual thing. Will what is of this kind be removed by corporeal things? And the smallest sin is of such a kind that the good works of all men gathered together could not make satisfaction for it before the justice of God; how then is such great power attributed to the blood or flesh of brute cattle? "Will holy flesh take away from you your wickedness, in which you boast?" says the prophet Jeremiah, chapter 11. And Isaiah 1: "What is the point of the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full: I have not desired the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts, and the blood of calves, and of lambs and goats." And a little later: "Wash yourselves, be clean, remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes, cease to do evil, learn to do good." As if he were saying: Do you think that the blood of beasts will make you clean, when you yourselves always defile yourselves with new sins? And since beasts are not clean in themselves, how will they make others clean? Having therefore considered these things, since there is so little proportion between brute animals and God, or men, or the sins of men, the Apostle spoke most rightly that the legal sacrifices did not take away sins, since this was impossible and most alien to the nature of goats and bulls. And therefore, since nothing could be found that would make satisfaction for sins, neither an angel, nor a man, nor a brute, nor any work of whatever excellence, it was necessary that he come who was God, so that he could be set over against the divine power and justice on account of that power and justice; and who was made man, so that he might take up the parts of man with all the more careful protection; and who was entirely without any sin, so that he could pay the price for the sins of others.

units.la: Sacrificia verò legalia tantùm in hoc erant ad tempus instituta, vt per continuam oblationem, homines se esse peccatores profiterentur, sese humiliarent ac submitterét, se item omnia beneficia, & quæcunq; haberent, à Deo accipere testarentur: vt item coram hominibus iuxta carnem aliquo modo purgarentur: denique vt sanguis innoxiorum animalium sanguinem innocentis Christi effundendum pro peccatis hominum adübrarent: atq; homines talibus externis figuris mouerentur ad respiciendum in solum Christum verum seruatorem suo tempore aduenturum. Hic erat finis sacrificiorum legalium & omnium quæ ibi fiebant: non autem vt peccata tollerent, vel purgarent conscientias coram Deo: qua de re iam aliquoties à nobis dictum est. Manifestum ergo est, quòd sanguis taurorum & hircorum ne posset quidem peccata tollere.
units.tr: The legal sacrifices were instituted for a time only, so that through their continual offering people would profess that they are sinners, humble and submit themselves, and also testify that they receive all their blessings and whatever they have from God. They were also meant to purify people to some extent before other people in the flesh, and finally to foreshadow that the blood of innocent animals pointed to the blood of the innocent Christ, which was to be poured out for the sins of men. And by such outward figures people were moved to look to Christ alone, the true Saviour, who would come in his time. This was the purpose of the legal sacrifices and of everything that was done there. They were not meant to take away sins or to cleanse consciences before God, as we have said several times already. It is therefore plain that the blood of bulls and goats could not even take away sins.

units.la: Cæterum discimus hîc, ex nullo opere operato operari posse iustitiâ, nō ex sacrificijs, non ex Sacramentis, non ex vllis alijs. Sacrificia erant præcepta à Deo, & videbanturin hoc instituta, vt à peccatis homines purgarentur per ea: adhibebantur precationes, offerebantur optima quæque: sed non poterant tamen iustificare per se: oportebat fidem accedere in vnicam hostiam, Christum, per quem solum contigit peccatorum remissio. Sic item circumcisio, si per sese spectetur, & opus operatum, nihil est, vt etiam Galat. capite 6 aperte dicitur. Huc pertinet illud: Qui in lege gloriaris, Deum inhonoras per legis iustificationem. Sic item nostra Sacramenta ex opere operato non iustificant, quia Dei virtus non est alligata Elementis vel Sacramentis: alias etiam impij fumentes perciperent effectus spirituales, & valeret impię missarum applicationes. Quòd si verò ex hisce non coparatur spiritualis & vera iustitia, quanto minus ex ijs, quæ homines sibiupsis imaginati sunt, parabitur? vt ex vestibus, rasuris, cibis & similibus?
units.tr: Furthermore, we learn here that righteousness cannot arise from any work done (ex opere operato), not from sacrifices, not from sacraments, not from any other thing. Sacrifices were commanded by God, and they seemed to be instituted for this purpose, that people might be cleansed from sins through them. Prayers were offered, and the best of everything was brought. But they could not justify of themselves. Faith had to be joined to the one sacrifice, Christ, through whom alone forgiveness of sins was obtained. Likewise circumcision, if it is viewed in itself and as a work done, is nothing, as Galatians 6 also plainly says. To this belongs the saying: "You who boast in the law dishonour God through the justification of the law" (Rom. 2). Likewise our sacraments do not justify by the work done, because the power of God is not bound to the elements or the sacraments. Otherwise even the wicked who receive them would obtain spiritual effects, and the wicked application of masses would be effective. But if spiritual and true righteousness is not obtained from these things, how much less will it be obtained from those things which men have imagined for themselves, such as clothes, shavings, foods and the like?

units.la: Quapropter cum ingressurus est mundum, dicit: sacrificium & oblationem noluisti: corpus autem aptasti mihi, holocautomata, & pro peccato non comprobasti. Tunc dixi: Ecce adsum: In capite libri scriptum est de me, vt faciam Deus voluntatem tuam. Superius dicens, sacrificium & oblationem & holocautomata, & propeccato
units.tr: Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says: "Sacrifice and offering you did not want; but you prepared a body for me; burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you did not approve. Then I said: Behold, I am here. In the roll of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God." Speaking above of "sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and for sin

units.la: Doctrina. Ex nullo opere operato proueniri iustitia, &c. Sacrificia non poterant iustificare. Circumcisio. Sacramenta. Dei virtus non est alligata elementis vel Sacramentis. cato noluisti, neque comprobasti, quae iuxta legem offeruntur, tunc dixit: Ecce adsum, ut faciam Deus voluntatem tuam.
