Tollit primus, ut secundum statuat: per quam voluntatem sanctificati sumus, per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel peractam.
units.tr: Doctrine. Righteousness comes from no work done (ex opere operato), etc. Sacrifices could not justify. Circumcision. Sacraments. God's power is not bound to the elements or the sacraments. sacrifice for sin you did not want nor approve, which are offered according to the law; then he said: Behold, I am here, that I may do your will. He takes away the first, that he may establish the second: by which will we have been sanctified, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

units.la: Sacrificia legalia non potuisse iustificare seu tollere peccata, satis est probatum: Nunc peroportunè, & veluti quadam illationis forma subijcit, quare oportuerit Christum alia ratione, quàm in lege solebat fieri, sacrificium suum peragere, videlicet non offerendo vitulos, hircos, aut similia, quae pro peccatis offerri praecipiebantur: sed offerendo proprium suum corpus, ac voluntatem Patris sui ita perficiendo. Estq; sententia: Quapropter (quia nimirum legalibus illis sacrificijs peccata tolli non poterant) Christus vbi venisset in mundum, ut tolleret peccata, & pro peccatis omnium satisfaceret, non debuit sacrificium ex hircis, vitulis, vel huiusmodi, offerre, sed proprium suum corpus, quod illi eum in finem erat aptatum, & quo debebat, quae Deus pater praeordinauerat, pro salute hominum per ficere. Atq; erat reuera admodum necessarium, ut, quare oportuerit Christum ita offerre semetipsum, ratio redderetur. Nam hactenus quidem crebrò auditu est, Christi sacrificiũ eo nomine praestare sacrificijs legalibus, quòd Christus obtulerit semetipsum: at interea absurdum humanae rationi apparuit, quòd Christus omissis sacrificijs vsitatis semetipsum ita immolarit: imò non dubium, quin Iudaei nouum istud sacrificandi genus aut palam deriserint, aut certè vehementer cotempserint: quemadmodum 1.Corinth.1. Christus crucifixus scribitur Iudaeis fuisse offendiculum, gentibus stultitia. Causas igitur offendiculi semouere, necnon omnibus satisfacere cupiens Apostolus, ne quicquam videretur asseruisse citra probationem, reddit nunc rationem, quare oportuerit Christum non vitulos vel hircos, sed proprium suum corpus offerre, adducens etiam è sacris literis testimonium, quoid euidentissimè per prophetam longe ante Christi in carnem aduentum, expressum fuerat. Multò verò appositissimè ipse testimonium illud explicat, suoq; instituto cōuenire oftedit. Primum simpliciter citat testimonium personę Christi (sicut reuera in persona Christi propheta locutus est, quod & paulò post docebimus) illud attribuens: Christus, inquit, ingressurus in mundum, dicit: sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus autem, &c. Deinde breuiter exponit, diuidendo testimonium in duas partes, hoc pacto. Superius (inquit) dicit sacrificium & oblationem & holocautomata, &c. postea subijcit: Ecce adsum, ut faciam Deus, &c. partibus ita seorsim consideratis, En, inquit, tollit seu negat prius, videlicet sacrificium, oblationem, holocautomata, more legali, &c. ut constituat posterius, oblationem inquâ sui corporis & perfectione voluntatis sui patris. Ex quibus deinde sic infert: per hanc voluntatem sanctificati sumus, per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel peractâ. Atq; ita satis demonstratum relinquitur, cur, quando per sacrificia legalia tolli peccata non poterant, oportuerit Christum nouo sacrificandi vti genere, & semetipsum offerre.
units.tr: That the legal sacrifices could not justify or take away sins has been sufficiently proved. Now he appropriately adds, in a kind of logical form, why it was necessary for Christ to complete his sacrifice in a way other than was customary under the law, namely not by offering calves, goats, or the like, which were commanded to be offered for sins, but by offering his own body and so fulfilling his Father's will. The meaning is this: therefore (because indeed sins could not be taken away by those legal sacrifices), when Christ came into the world to take away sins and to make satisfaction for the sins of all, he ought not to offer a sacrifice of goats, calves, or such things, but his own body, which was prepared for this very purpose, and by which he was to accomplish what God the Father had foreordained for the salvation of men. And indeed it was truly very necessary that the reason why Christ had to offer himself in this way be given. For until now it has often been heard that the sacrifice of Christ surpasses the legal sacrifices on this account, that Christ offered himself. But meanwhile it appeared absurd to human reason that Christ, leaving aside the usual sacrifices, should sacrifice himself in this way. Indeed there is no doubt that the Jews either openly mocked this new kind of sacrificing or certainly despised it greatly. Just as it is written in 1 Corinthians 1 that Christ crucified was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles. So the Apostle, desiring to remove the causes of offence and to satisfy everyone, so that nothing might seem to have been asserted without proof, now gives the reason why Christ had to offer not calves or goats but his own body. He also adduces a testimony from the sacred letters, which had been expressed most clearly through the prophet long before Christ's coming in the flesh. He explains that testimony most aptly and shows that it agrees with his purpose. First he cites the testimony simply as the words of Christ's person (as indeed the prophet spoke in the person of Christ, which we will also show shortly), attributing it thus: "Christ, coming into the world, says: Sacrifice and offering you did not want; but a body you prepared for me," etc. Then he briefly explains it, dividing the testimony into two parts in this way. "Above," he says, "he says: sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings," etc.; afterwards he adds: "Behold, I come to do your will," etc. Having considered the parts thus separately, he says: "Behold, he takes away or denies the first, namely sacrifice, offering, burnt offerings, in the legal manner, etc., so that he may establish the second, namely the offering of his body and the perfection of his Father's will." From these things he then infers: "By this will we have been sanctified, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all." And so it is sufficiently shown why, since sins could not be taken away by the legal sacrifices, Christ had to use a new kind of sacrificing and offer himself.

units.la: Supra quidem capite secūdo etiam audiuimus, Christū debuisse morte sua satisfacere pro peccatis, vbi nimirum dicebatur, eum per afflictiones debuisse perfectum reddi, & per mortem debuisse abolere diabolum, nosque ab aeterna morte liberare: verùm hoc ibi dictum est, duntaxat ad ostendendum, quòd propterea opus fuerit, Christum hominem fieri & ad reddendam rationem humanae naturae à Christo susceptae. Verùm ibi nondum satisfactū est quaestioni, quae post moueri poterat, quare videlicet Christus homo factus non alia ratione potuerit, quàm morte sua pro peccatis hominum satisfacere. Huic igitur quaestioni plenissimè respondetur praesenti disputatione de Christi sacerdotio & sacrificio, ubi, posteaquàm declaratum, quomodo Christus sit verus, summus pōtifex, mediator inter Deum & homines, etiam iam exponitur, quare tantum morte sua, & sacrificio suiipsius potuerit Deo patri pro peccatis omnium satisfacere. Atque ad cōfirmationem suae sententiae inuenit apertissimum sacrae Scripturae testimonium, sicut quiuis facilime potest animaduertere.
units.tr: Indeed, in the second chapter we also heard that Christ had to make satisfaction for sins by his death, where it was said that he had to be made perfect through afflictions and had to destroy the devil by death and free us from eternal death. But that was said there only to show that it was therefore necessary for Christ to become man, and to give an account of the human nature that Christ assumed. But the question which could be raised afterwards was not yet answered there: namely, why Christ, having become man, could make satisfaction for the sins of men by his death alone and by no other way. This question is therefore answered most fully in the present disputation concerning the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, where, after it has been declared how Christ is the true and supreme high priest and mediator between God and men, it is now also explained why he could make satisfaction to God the Father for the sins of all by his death and sacrifice of himself alone. And to confirm his view, he finds a most clear testimony of Holy Scripture, as anyone can very easily perceive.

units.la: Sumpta autem sunt uerba haec è psalmo 39. vel iuxta hebraeos 40. Atque, ut perspiciat omnes rectè citata esse ab Apostolo, necnon proprie Christo accommodata: Nos totum illum psalmum de Christo vaticinari, aliquot rationibus (vti alias quoque soliti sumus, quotiescunque, testimonia è veteri testamento producta obueniunt) docebimus. Ante omnia ut etiam concedendū foret, Dauidem de sua persona psalmum istum totum cecinisse, tamen, quando Dauidem caeterosque patres in multis gesisse typum Christi extra controuersiam est, certè hac ratione psalmum Christo non inepte attribui, quiuis intelligit. Dauid afflictus & innocens Dominum inuocans Christi instante morte anxij persona retulit.
units.tr: The words here are taken from Psalm 39, or according to the Hebrews 40. And so that everyone may see that they were rightly cited by the Apostle and properly applied to Christ, we will show, for several reasons (as we have been accustomed to do elsewhere whenever testimonies produced from the Old Testament come up), that the whole psalm prophesies of Christ. First of all, even if it were granted that David sang this whole psalm about his own person, nevertheless, since it is beyond controversy that David and the other fathers in many things bore the type of Christ, anyone can understand that the psalm is not unfittingly attributed to Christ in this way. David, afflicted and innocent, calling upon the Lord, speaks in the person of one anxious at the approaching death of Christ.

units.la: Secundò, est hoc omnino certū, sanctos patres & prophetas potius de rebus maximis, & ad totam ecclesiam pertinentibus, potissimúque de promissionibus diuinis ac beneficijs per Messiam expectandis solitos canere, quàm de priuatis suis negotijs. Quare cum ecclesiæ maximè interesset, cognoscere, quænam per Christū forent pro salute humani generis peragenda, neque in ullo argumento pij homines magis gaudebant occupari, probabilius est, eum psalmū de persona Christi, quàm de Dauide, vel alio quopiá esse decantatum. Sed & nunquam tractant prophetæ aliquid uel de suis negotijs, vel de rebus sui seculi tùm præsentis, quin admisceant semper consolatoria aliqua de persona Christi, quod fecisse & hoc psalmo prophetam dissimulari nequit.
units.tr: Secondly, this is entirely certain: the holy fathers and prophets were accustomed to sing about the greatest matters, which pertain to the whole Church, and above all about the divine promises and blessings to be expected through the Messiah, rather than about their private affairs. Therefore, since it was of the greatest concern to the Church to know what things were to be accomplished through Christ for the salvation of the human race, and since godly men rejoiced more to be occupied with no subject than with this, it is more probable that this psalm was sung about the person of Christ than about David or anyone else. Moreover, the prophets never treat anything, either of their own affairs or of the things of their own age, present as it was, without always mixing in some words of comfort concerning the person of Christ. That the prophet did this also in this psalm cannot be denied.

units.la: Quid? Quòd quædam habentur in hoc psalmo, quæ Dauidi citra molestiorem interpretationem attribuere ægre queas? cuiusmodi inprimis sunt illa: Non abscondi misericordiam tuam, & veritatem tuam à concilio multo. Vbinam Dauid concionatus est publice coram cœcilijs, sicut Christū fecisse nouimus? Item: In capite libri scriptū est de me: quod de Dauide nō potest commodè exponi: quádoquidé de eo nulla fuerant in volumine legis edita vaticinia vel oracula: sed in solum Christum cōpetit, de quo solo statim in capite legis promissiones sunt factæ, quòd ipse esset semen mulieris, à quo caput serpetis deberet cōteri, quòdipse esset illud semen benedictum, in quo benedictionem acciperent omnes gētes. Adhæc, quis dicetur voluntatem Domini perfecisse, uti eam perfecit Christus?
units.tr: What of this: are there things in this psalm that you could hardly attribute to David without a rather forced interpretation? Chief among them are these: I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from the great assembly. Where did David ever preach publicly before a great assembly, as we know Christ did? Likewise: In the head of the book it is written of me, which cannot conveniently be explained of David, since no prophecies or oracles concerning him were set down in the volume of the law. They apply to Christ alone, for promises concerning him were made at once at the beginning of the law: that he would be the seed of the woman, by whom the serpent's head would be crushed, and that he would be the blessed seed in whom all nations would receive blessing. Moreover, who could be said to have performed the will of the Lord as Christ performed it?

units.la: Errant autē fœdisimè, qui illud, In capite libri, interpretantur, in initio libri Psalmorum, vbi pij & beati viri bona voluntas erga legem Dei describitur: ut sic ad Dauidem, aut etiā alium quemuis pium præsentem locum detorqueāt: quasi vero Dauidis ætate psalmi in eum ordinem ac numerum digesti fuerint, quo nunc cernuntur, cùm omnium fere communis sententia sit, psalmos quosdam aliquot retrò seculis etiām à captiuitate Babylonica editos, & per Esdram tandem ita collectos. Postremò, eum psalmū optimo iure de Christo canere asseremus, cuius singulas partes ab initio ad finem personæ Christi optimè congruere ostedi potest. Reuera enim si quis pleraque conferat, ex psalmo vicesimo primo, cuius initium est, Deus, Deus meus respice in me, quare me dereliquisti? vbi omnia per prophetam in persona Christi sunt prolata: item nonnulla ex Ioannis capite decimo septimo: Is citra negotium deprehēdet, omnia quæ in præsenti psalmo sunt posita, Christo pulcherrimè conuenire. Sed nos, quo fides plenior nobis habeatur, breuiter tetigimus psalmū de persona Christi explicare.
units.tr: Those who interpret "In the head of the book" as the beginning of the book of Psalms, where the good will of a pious and blessed man towards the law of God is described, and so twist the words to David or some other pious person of the time, translate very foully. As if the psalms had been arranged in that order and number in which they are now seen in David's day, when almost everyone agrees that some psalms were published many centuries earlier, even after the Babylonian captivity, and were finally collected in this order by Ezra. Lastly, we maintain that this psalm rightly sings of Christ, since its individual parts, from beginning to end, can be shown to fit the person of Christ very well. Indeed, anyone who compares many passages, from Psalm 21, whose opening is "My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?", where everything is spoken by the prophet in the person of Christ, and likewise some things from John chapter 17, will easily see that everything set down in the present psalm agrees most beautifully with Christ. But so that our faith may be held more fully, we have briefly touched on explaining the psalm concerning the person of Christ.

units.la: Constituamus igitur Christum in medio agone illo, quo instante morte periclitabatur hisce verbis loquentem. Psal.40. Expectans expectaui Dominū, et intendit mihi, & exaudiuit preces meas, & eduxit me de lacu miseriæ, & de luto cœni: & statuit super petrā pedes meos & direxit gressus meos; Sunt verba Christi certò statuentes, quòd post mortem pater non daret, eum videre corruptionem, ut alio loco dicit: sed maiore cum gloria se fore à morte suscitandum. Conueniūt autem hæc cum illis Ioannis 17. Pater venit hora, glorifica filium tuum, vt & filius tuus glorificet te. Et cū illis Psal.21. Deus Deus meus respice in me, quare me dereliquisti? Et multa ibidem sequuntur in eandem sententiam. In te sperauerūt, & liberasti eos. Item, Quoniam tu es, qui extraxisti me de ventre, spes mea ab uberibus matris meæ. Rursus, Tu autem Domine ne elongaueris auxilium tuum à me, &c.
units.tr: Let us therefore place Christ in the midst of that struggle in which, with death at hand, he is in peril, speaking in these words: Ps. 40. "I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined to me, and heard my prayers, and brought me up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps." These are words of Christ, certainly affirming that after death the Father would not allow him to see corruption, as he says elsewhere, but that he would be raised from death with greater glory. These agree also with John 17: "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you." And with Ps. 21: "My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?" Many things follow there to the same effect: "In you they hoped, and you delivered them." Again: "For you are he who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother's breasts." And again: "But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me," etc.

units.la: Et immisit in os meum canticum nouum, hymnum Deo nostro. Videbunt multi & timebunt, & sperabunt in Dominum. Beatus vir, cuius est nomen Domini spes eius, & non respexit in vanitates, & in insanias falsas. Multa fecisti tu Domine Deus meus mirabilia tua, & cogitationibus tuis non est qui similis sit tibi. Annunciaui & locutus sum, & multiplicata sunt super numerum, &c.
units.tr: And he put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God. Many will see and fear, and will hope in the Lord. Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, who has not turned to vanities and false follies. Many are the wonders you have done, O Lord my God; and there is none like you in your thoughts. I have announced and spoken, and they have been multiplied beyond number, etc.

units.la: Nonne hæc pulchrè conueniunt Christo, commemoranti se functū suo officio in annunciando & propagando euangelio, ut id fructum attulerit? Similia autem loquitur Ioan. 17.
units.tr: Do not these words agree beautifully with Christ, recounting that he has discharged his office in announcing and spreading the gospel, so that it has borne fruit? He says similar things in John 17.

units.la: Ego te pater glorificaui super terram, opus consummaui, quod dedisti mihi, ut facerem. Et nunc glorifica me tu pater apud temetipsum, gloria, quam habui, priusquam hic mundus esset, apud te. Manifestaui nomē tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi in mundo. Tui erant, & mihi eos dedisti, & sermonem tuum seruauerunt: & cætera, quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: "I have glorified you, Father, on the earth; I have finished the work which you gave me to do. And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was. I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me in the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word," and the rest that follows.

units.la: Sacrificiū & oblationem noluisti, aures autem perforasti mihi. Holocaustum & pro peccato nō postulasti tunc dixi: Ecce venio: in capite libri scriptum est de me, ut facere voluntatem tuam, Deus meus volui, & legem tuam in medio cordis mei.
units.tr: You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you have pierced ears for me. You did not require burnt offering and sin offering. Then I said, Behold, I come; in the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, my God. I have desired it, and your law is in the midst of my heart.

units.la: En Christū lubenter sese offerentē ad mortem pro salute humani generis, & promptu ad voluntā
units.tr: Behold Christ gladly offering himself to death for the salvation of mankind, and ready for the will of the Father.

units.la: Ratio ab incō uenienti.
units.tr: An argument from the absurd.

units.la: De Christo scriptum est in capite voluminis diuini. Genes. 3.
units.tr: Concerning Christ it is written in the head of the divine volume: Gen. 3.

units.la: Falsa interpretatio.
units.tr: A false interpretation.

units.la: 4. psal. 46. de Christi persona vaticinatur, cōgruunt que ei omnes partes. psal. 21. Iann. 17.
units.tr: Psalm 40 prophesies of the person of Christ, and every part of it fits him. Ps. 21. John 17.

units.la: Christus in agone mortis loquatur.
units.tr: Christ speaks in the agony of death.

units.la: Christi fides, psal.16. psal.8. Christi precatio Ioan.17.
units.tr: Christ's faith: Ps. 16, Ps. 8. Christ's prayer: John 17.

units.la: Christus gloriatur de officio probè ad ministrato.
units.tr: Christ glories in having faithfully discharged his office.

units.la: Christi promptitudo ad crucis mortem. ad voluntatem patris perficiendam. Huc pertinent illa Ioan. 12. Nunc anima mea turbata est: & quid dicam? Pater serua me ex hora hac: sed propterea veni in horam hanc. Pater illustra nomen tuum. Et Matth. 26. Pater mi, si posiibile est, transeat à me calix iste: veruntamen non sicut ego volo, sed sicut tu. Ibidem: Si non potest hoc poculum transire à me, nisi bibam illud, fiat voluntas tua, &c.
units.tr: Christ's readiness for death on the cross, to perform the Father's will. To this belong those words of John 12: "Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name." And Matt. 26: "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." And again there: "If this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it, your will be done," etc.

units.la: Annunciaui iustitiam in Ecclesia magna, ecce labia mea non prohibebo Domine, tu scisti. Iustitiam tuam non abscondi in corde meo, veritatem tuam & salutare tuum dixi: Non abscondi veritatem tuam à concilio multo.
units.tr: I have proclaimed righteousness in the great congregation; behold, I will not restrain my lips, O Lord; you know it. I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation. I have not hidden your truth from the great assembly.

units.la: Iterum commemorat Christus, quàm strenuè officium suum peregerit. Sic verò adhuc Ioan. 17. Ego tradidi eis sermonem tuum, &c. Item: Notum feci eis nomen tuum, & notum faciam, vt dilectio, qua dilexisti me, in ipsis sit, & ego in ipsis. Rursus, Ioan. 18. Ego palàm locutus sum mundo, ego semper docui in Synagoga, & in templo, quò omnes Iudaei conueniunt, & in occulto locutus sum nihil. At Psalmo 22. sic legimus: Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in medio ecclesiae laudabo te, &c. Sequitur in praesenti Psalmo:
units.tr: Again Christ recalls how vigorously he has performed his office. So also in John 17: "I have given them your word," etc. Likewise: "I have made known to them your name, and will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them." Again, John 18: "I have spoken openly to the world. I always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and in secret I have said nothing." But in Psalm 22 we read: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you," etc. What follows in the present psalm:

units.la: Tu autem Domine, ne longè facias miserationes tuas à me, misericordia tua & veritas tua semper suscepérunt me. Quoniam circumdederunt me mala, quorum non est numerus: comprehenderunt me iniquitates meae, & non potui vt viderem. Multiplicatae sunt super capillos capitis mei, & cor meum dereliquit me. Complaceat tibi Domine, vt eruas me, Domine ad adiuuandum me respice.
units.tr: But you, O Lord, do not remove your mercies far from me; your mercy and your truth have always upheld me. For evils have surrounded me, which have no number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I could not see. They have been multiplied above the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me. Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me; O Lord, look upon me to help me.

units.la: Et haec mirè conueniunt Christo orânti vt transferatur à se calix. Et in eandem sententiam psalmo 22. Deus meus es tu, ne discesseris à me. Quoniam tribulatio proxima est, & non est qui adiuuet. Circumdederunt me vituli multi, & tauri pingues obsederunt me. Aperuerunt super me os suum, sicut Leo rapiens & rugiens. Et plura ibidem sequuntur: Confundantur & erubescant simul, qui quaerunt animam meam, vt auferant eam. Auertantur retrorsum & reuereantur, qui volunt mihi mala. Ferant confusionem suam, qui dicunt mihi, Euge, Euge. Haec contra impios Scribas, Sacerdotes, Pontifices, qui consilia inibant, quomodo Iesum perderent, Christus: pro quibus idem Ioannis decimo septimo dicit, se non orare: Non pro mundo rogo, inquit: Et mox addit, mundum odisse suos discipulos. Et dicentes, Euge, Euge, nonne irrisores sunt, de quibus alij Euangelistae testantur, & de quibus etiam psalmo 22. Christus, Vidientes me deriserunt me, locuti sunt labiis & mouerunt caput, Speravit in Domino, eripiat eum, saluum faciat eum, quoniam vult eum? Item ibidem: Foderunt manus meas & pedes meos, dinumerauerunt omnia ossa mea. Exultent & laetentur super te omnes quaerentes te: & dicant semper, magnificetur Dominus, qui diligunt salutare tuum. Similiter & psalmo 21. Qui timetis Dominum, laudate eum, vniuersum semen Iacob glorificate eum: timeat eum omne semen Israel; & caetera, quae pluribus ibi tractantur.
units.tr: These words agree wonderfully with Christ praying that the cup be taken from him. To the same effect in Psalm 22: "You are my God; do not depart from me. For trouble is near, and there is none to help. Many bulls have surrounded me, and fat bulls have besieged me. They have opened their mouth against me, like a lion ravening and roaring." Much more follows there: "Let those be confounded and put to shame together who seek my soul to take it away. Let those be turned back and dishonoured who wish me evil. Let those bear their shame who say to me, Euge, euge (Well done, well done!)." These are against the impious scribes, priests and high priests, who plotted how they might destroy Jesus, and for whom Christ, in John chapter 17, says that he does not pray: "I do not pray for the world," he says; and immediately he adds that the world hates his disciples. And those who say "Euge, euge," are they not mockers, of whom the other evangelists testify, and of whom Christ also speaks in Psalm 22: "All who see me have mocked me; they have spoken with their lips and shaken their heads: He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he delights in him"? Likewise there: "They have pierced my hands and my feet; they have counted all my bones." "Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you, and let them always say, Let the Lord be magnified, who love your salvation." Similarly in Psalm 21: "You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him; let all the seed of Israel fear him," and the rest, which are treated at greater length there.

units.la: Ego autem mendicus sum & pauper, Dominus solicitus est mei: Adiutor meus & protector meus tu es, Deus meus ne tardaueris.
units.tr: "But I am poor and needy; the Lord takes thought for me. You are my helper and my deliverer; O my God, do not delay." (Psalm 40:17)

units.la: Conueniunt haec cum illis, Tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. Item: Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me deseruisti? Et psalmo illo 21. Ego sum vermis, & non homo, opprobrium hominum, & abiectio plebis. Rursus: Tu autem Domine ne elongaueris à me, ad defensionem meam respice. Erue à framea Deus animam meam; & de manu canis vnicam meam. In summa, si quis velit exactius & pleniore iudicio ista expendere, nec non copiosius explicare, locos cum locis conferendo, comperiet, omnia mirabili ratione Christo conuenire. Manifestum igitur est, testimonium huius psalmi ab Apostolo recte & oportune citatum, atque optimo iure Christo attributum. Nunc, si quid in partibus explicatione egeat, breuiter percuiramus.
units.tr: These words agree with those other words: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death" (Matt. 26:38). Likewise: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matt. 27:46). And in that same Psalm 21: "I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and the outcast of the people." Again: "But you, O Lord, do not go far from me; look upon my help. Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the power of the dog." In sum, if anyone wishes to weigh these matters more exactly and with fuller judgement, and to explain them more fully by comparing passage with passage, he will find that everything agrees with Christ in a wonderful way. It is therefore plain that the testimony of this Psalm was rightly and fittingly cited by the Apostle and most justly ascribed to Christ. Now let us briefly examine whatever in its parts needs explanation.

units.la: Quapropter cum ingressurus est mundum, dicit: Sunt hic singula verba nobis diligenter expendenda. Ideo habet vim Illationis, ac sequitur reuera huius argumenti ratio ex duobus argumentis praecedentibus.
units.tr: Therefore, when he is about to enter the world, he says: here each single word must be carefully weighed by us. Hence the "therefore" has the force of an inference, and the reasoning of this argument truly follows from the two arguments that precede it.

units.la: Quando enim proximè demonstratum est, sacrificia legalia non potuisse liberare à peccatis, rectè infertur, Christum, qui venit, vt auferret peccata, nequaquàm debuisse eiusmodi sacrificia legalia adhibere, sed alio vti sacrificandi genere.
units.tr: For when it has just been shown that the legal sacrifices could not free from sins, it is rightly inferred that Christ, who came to take away sins, ought by no means to have employed such legal sacrifices, but another kind of sacrifice.

units.la: Sed quare præmittit hæc verba, Cum ingressurus est in mundum: Nonne satis fuisset sim‑pliciter citare Prophetæ testimonium? Respondetur, Testimonium per se quidem sum‑ptum mirè conuenire præsenti negotio, vtpote quo continetur argumentum efficacitér probans, ceremonias legales debuisse finem accipere, nec amplius Deo fore acceptas: sed Deum requirere quendam synceriorem cultum, nempe promptam obedientiam, qua homo se totum ipsi submittat & addicat, voluntatemque ipsius studeat perficere: sed tamen multò magis quadrat, ista verba præmitti, vt sciatur, proprie de persona Christi accipiendum, & sic ratio reddatur, quare oportuerit Christum ad tollenda peccata alio sacrificij vti genere, quàm in lege erat præscriptum: atque ita aduersarijs satisfiat, tàm negantibus, Christi mortem agnoscendam pro sacrificio, quàm nouum sacrificandi ritum contemnentibus. Et propter hanc causam proderat verba ista personæ Christi attribui. Addi potest, & alia de causa hæc verba præmitti, videlicet vt intelligeretur, non nouum aut suspectum existimandum, quòd ita assereretur, per vnicum sacrificium Christi abrogari sacrificia legalia: sed id ita prædictum per Prophetas, longè etiam ante, quàm Christus in mundum veniret.
units.tr: But why does he put in front these words, "When he is about to enter the world"? Would it not have been enough simply to cite the testimony of the Prophet? The answer is this: the testimony, taken by itself, certainly fits the present matter remarkably well, since it contains the argument effectively proving that the ceremonial laws were to come to an end and would no longer be acceptable to God; and that God requires a purer kind of worship, namely prompt obedience, by which a man submits and devotes himself wholly to him and strives to carry out his will. Yet it fits much better to put these words first, so that it may be known that they are to be understood properly of the person of Christ, and thus the reason may be given why it was necessary for Christ, in order to take away sins, to use a different kind of sacrifice from that prescribed in the law. And so satisfaction is given to the opponents, both to those who deny that the death of Christ is to be acknowledged as a sacrifice and to those who despise the new manner of sacrificing. And for this reason it was useful to ascribe these words to the person of Christ. It may be added that these words are put first for another reason too, namely so that it might be understood that it should not be thought new or suspicious that it is asserted in this way that the legal sacrifices are abrogated through the one sacrifice of Christ; rather, this was foretold through the Prophets, long before Christ came into the world.

units.la: Cæterum quòd ad phrasin attinet, Christum ingredi in mundum, idem est, quod carnem humanam induere, & hominem fieri: quemadmodum & capite primo huius epistolæ, vbi dictus est Christus primogenitus inductus in orbem terræ, duplicem Christi in mundum aduentum seu introductionem annotauimus. Ideo autem moneo obseruandas huiusmodi phrases, propterea, quòd quidam turpissimè his nostra tempestate sunt abusi. Anabaptistæ enim huiusmodi formulas plures arripiunt, veluti ex Ephes. 3. & Colossens. 1. vbi Christus vocatur primogenitus omnis creaturæ, per quem condita vniuersa: rursus Ephes. 4. Idem ascendit, qui & descendit. Item Ioan. 3. Christus è cœlo à patre missus. 1. Corinth. 15. Christus nouus homo è cœlo. Item Hebræor. 13. Christus heri, hodie, & in secula. Atque ex his colligere volunt, idem prorsus esse, Christum, quod verbum, & verbum, quod Christum: deinde, carnem Christi non esse nostram carnem è limo deductam, sed cœlestem, hoc est, è cœlo deductam. Sed hisce locis opponi debent alij Scripturæ loci, per quos commoda interpretatio parari possit, & præterea error de carne è cœlo allata euerti. Proderunt autem hi loci, quibus describitur Christus, veniente tempo‑rum plenitudine, conceptus in vtero, natus ex virgine, factus ex muliere, ex semine Abrahæ, Dauidis, ex patribus secundùm carnem, Item filius hominis, &c. Matth. 1. 2. Lucæ 1. Galat. 4. Genes. 3. Roman. 1. &c. Sed hæc de re alias nonnulla diximus capite secundo, vbi dicebatur, Christum participem factum cum pueris carnis & sanguinis. Item, Christum semen Abrahæ assumpsisse, &c. Et plura congessimus in libris Rhapsodiarum. Ve‑niamus ad verba Prophetæ.
units.tr: As for the phrase "Christ enters into the world," it means the same as "to put on human flesh and become man," just as in the first chapter of this epistle, where Christ is called the firstborn brought into the world, we noted a twofold coming or introduction of Christ into the world. I give warning that such phrases ought to be observed with care, because in our own time some have abused them most shamefully. For the Anabaptists seize upon many such formulas, as from Ephesians 3 and Colossians 1, where Christ is called the firstborn of every creature, through whom all things were created; again, Ephesians 4: "He who descended is also the one who ascended"; likewise John 3: Christ sent from heaven by the Father; 1 Corinthians 15: "the second man is from heaven"; and Hebrews 13: "Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever." And from these they wish to conclude that Christ is altogether the same as the Word, and the Word the same as Christ; and then that the flesh of Christ is not our flesh drawn from clay, but heavenly, that is, brought down from heaven. But against these passages other passages of Scripture ought to be set, through which a sound interpretation can be obtained, and besides, the error about flesh brought from heaven be overturned. Those passages will serve, in which Christ is described as, when the fullness of time came, conceived in the womb, born of a virgin, made of a woman, of the seed of Abraham and David, descended from the fathers according to the flesh; also "the Son of man," etc. (Matt. 1; Luke 1; Gal. 4; Gen. 3; Rom. 1, etc.). But we have said some things about this matter elsewhere in the second chapter, where it was said that Christ was made a partaker of flesh and blood like the children, and likewise that Christ took on the seed of Abraham, etc. And we have gathered more in our books of Rhapsodies. Let us now come to the words of the Prophet.

units.la: Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus verò aptasti mihi, holocautomata & pro peccato non comprobasti.
units.tr: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; but a body you have prepared for me; burnt offerings and sacrifice for sin you did not approve."

units.la: Apostolus citat, vt alias solet, testimonia potius ex septuaginta, quàm ex Hebræo. Si quid in terea dissonum occurrat, id indicabimus. Sunt autem verba Christi ad patrem, cui ipse debebat satisfacere pro peccatis humani generis. Porrò pro hoc negotio peragendo dicit, Patrem non velle aliquod genus sacrificiorum legalium vel huiusmodi, sed proprium ipsius corpus. Sic enim præordinatum erat à patre etiam ante constitutionem mundi, vt per Christum restauraret omnia, Ephes. 1. Et statim à lapsu primorum parentum prom‑sio ad illos facta, quòd veniret semen, per quod serpentis caput foret con‑terendum. De modo autem, quo id fieret, nempe quòd per mortem Christi deberet id fieri, succedentibus temporibus semper apertius reuelatum est, & Prophetæ palàm sunt testati. Quare autem oportuerit potius morte Christi perfici negotium, quàm alia ratione, demonstratum est capite secundo. Cæterùm enumerat quatuor sacrificiorum seu oblationum genera, ita comprehendens plane omnia, quæcunq; ad placandum Deum offerri solent, & ita aperte significans, Deum prorsus nullum sacrificium esse amplius acceptu-rum. Primùm vocat sacrificium, hebraicè est זבח, Kimhi, & qui eum sequuntur, solent vertere hostias pacificas, siue sacrificia pacificorum, quæ nimirum pro conciliatione & pace alenda fiebant: quibus videlicet cum Deo, cum sacerdotibus, cum coniunctis, deniq; cum tota Ecclesia, li velle redire in gratiâ significabant: quemadmodū osculū pacis apud quasdam ecclesias videtur institutū. De quo sacrificij genere sæpius fit mētio, plenissimè aüt describitur Leuit. 3. & 7. Secundo loco ponit oblationem: vbi in hebræo est מנחה, à verbo נחם obtulit, alij vertūt libamentum aut victimam cibariam: constabat plerūq; vel farina vel cibis oleo aspersis, & impositio thure, etiā vino. Num. 15. Certè ex rebus fiebat in‑animatis (fuerunt eius quinque species.) Vide descriptionem oblationum pleniorem Leuitici secundo. Tertio loco ponit ὁλοκαύτωμα, quasi dicas, tota incensa: Erant hostiæ, quæ totæ incendebantur, nec quicquam tedebat aut sacerdotibus, aut offerentibus. De lege holocausti Leuitici 6. Quarto loco, ponit victimam pro peccato, περὶ ἁμαρτίας πκνοη, quæ vox & peccatū significat, & oblatione pro peccato: de qua hostia vide Leuitici 4.5.6. Etsi igitur hæc sacrificiorum genera fuerint à Deo instituta, & non abs re magni habita, & propter multas vtiles causas præscripta in lege, tamen ad tollenda peccata nihil possunt efficere, ideoque Christus ad patrem dicit, quod ea non requirat: in ἀνολόκησας, inquit, id est, non comprobasti, in illis non est tibi complacitum. Tametsi septuaginta habeant, ἐν ἐυδοκήσας, id est, non petiuisti, non postulasti: & in Hebraeo eadem significatio est quod videlicet Deus non postulet illa sacrificia. Apparet Apostolum dixisse, non comprobasti, quasi per interpretationem, & ad maiorem euidentiam. Nam præscripsit quidem Deus id genus sacrificia offerri, & sic videtur illa postulasse reuera: sed tamen non erant eiusmodi, quibus ille delectaretur, vel quæ ipsi gratia forent, ut propter ea vellet remittere peccata. Magis instituit illa Deus, ut Iudei retinerentur in disciplina, docerentur confiteri peccata, se gratos in Deum pro bonis acceptis exhibere: ut item auocarentur ab idololatria & imitatione gentium: ut item haberent typos rerum futurarum, quam quod ipse illa lubens accepta-ret. In quam sententiam plura licet videre Esaiae 1. Hieremiae 7. Amos 5. Michaeæ 6. psal. 50. Interponit autem Christus, quid Deus pater voluerit, dicens, corpus autem aptasti mihi: quasi diceret: nō vis tibi offerā holocausta, vel huiusmodi legalia sacrificia pro peccatis: sed uis offeram tibi totum meum corpus. Ac videtur per Synecdochen prius positū pro posteriori, ut videlicet ex aptatione corporis intelligatur eiusdem oblatio, utpote quod in hunc finem datum sit & aptatum.
units.tr: The Apostle quotes, as he usually does, testimonies taken from the Septuagint rather than from the Hebrew. Where there is any discrepancy between them, I will point it out. These are the words of Christ to the Father, for whom he was himself to make satisfaction for the sins of the human race. In carrying out this business, he says that the Father does not want any kind of legal sacrifice or offering of that sort, but his own body. For this had been ordained by the Father even before the foundation of the world, that through Christ he would restore all things (Ephes. 1.). And immediately after the fall of our first parents, a promise was made to them that the seed would come by whom the head of the serpent would be crushed. The manner in which this would be done, namely that it must be accomplished through the death of Christ, was revealed more and more clearly as time went on, and the prophets openly bore witness to it. Why the work had to be completed by the death of Christ rather than by some other means has been shown in the second chapter. Moreover, he lists four kinds of sacrifices or offerings, comprehending clearly all those things that are usually offered to placate God, and thereby plainly signifying that God would never again accept any sacrifice at all. First, he calls it a sacrifice, which in Hebrew is [זבח]. Kimhi and those who follow him are accustomed to render it peace offerings, or sacrifices of peace, which were certainly made to secure reconciliation and to nourish peace: by them, clearly, men signified their wish to be restored to favour with God, with the priests, with their kinsmen, and finally with the whole Church, just as the kiss of peace seems to have been instituted in certain churches. This kind of sacrifice is mentioned often, and it is described most fully in Leviticus 3 and 7. In the second place he sets down the offering, which in Hebrew is [מנחה], from the verb [נחם], to offer; others render it a drink offering or a food victim. It consisted mostly of flour or food sprinkled with oil, with incense laid upon it, and even with wine (Num. 15.). Certainly it was made of inanimate things (it had five kinds). See the fuller description of the offerings in Leviticus 2. In the third place he sets down the [ὁλοκαύτωμα], as if you should say, wholly burnt: these were victims that were burned entirely, and nothing of them was kept back either by the priests or by those who offered them (on the law of the burnt offering, Leviticus 6). In the fourth place he sets down the victim for sin, [περὶ ἁμαρτίας], a word which signifies both sin and the offering for sin; for this victim see Leviticus 4, 5 and 6. Although, therefore, these kinds of sacrifices were instituted by God, and were held in high esteem and prescribed in the law for many useful reasons, nevertheless they can accomplish nothing towards taking away sins. Therefore Christ says to the Father that he does not require them: [οὐκ εὐδόκησας], he says, that is, you did not approve; in them you have not taken pleasure. Although the Seventy have [ἐν ἐυδοκήσας], that is, you did not seek, you did not ask; and in the Hebrew the meaning is the same, namely that God does not demand those sacrifices. It appears that the Apostle wrote "you did not approve" as a kind of interpretation, and for greater clarity. For God indeed prescribed that this kind of sacrifice be offered, and so in truth he seems to have demanded them; but they were not of such a kind as to delight him, or to be acceptable to him, so that for their sake he would be willing to forgive sins. God rather instituted them so that the Jews might be kept under discipline, be taught to confess their sins, and show themselves grateful to God for the good things received; likewise so that they might be drawn away from idolatry and the imitation of the nations; and likewise so that they might have types of things to come, rather than because he gladly accepted them. Many passages to this effect may be seen in Isaiah 1, Jeremiah 7, Amos 5, Micah 6, and Psalm 50. Christ then adds what God the Father willed, saying: but a body you have prepared for me, as if he were saying: you do not want me to offer to you burnt offerings or such legal sacrifices for sins; but you want me to offer to you my whole body. And the earlier is put for the later by synecdoche, so that from the preparing of the body the offering of the same is understood, inasmuch as it was given and prepared for this end.

units.la: Atqui in Hebraeo aliter legitur, אזנים כריית לי, id est, aures perfodisti mihi. Quanquā si bene perpendimus, non est magna diuersitas, quod attinet ad sententiam. Sententia enim ex Hebraeo est, perfodisti, seu aperuisti mihi aures, id est, volusti te vnum audirem, tibi vni semper parerem: sicut etiam interpretatio sequitur: ut faciam voluntatem tuam Deus meus.
units.tr: But in the Hebrew it reads differently, אזנים כריית לי, that is, "you have pierced ears for me." If we weigh this carefully, however, the difference in sense is not great. The meaning of the Hebrew is: you have pierced, or opened, my ears for me, that is, you willed that I should hear you alone and always obey you alone. The translation follows the same sense: "that I may do your will, O my God." [אזנים כריית לי]

units.la: Hanc autem sententiam volentes reddere septuaginta, dixerunt, corpus adaptasti mihi: quod si adiungas sequentibus verbis, vbi item adijcitur, ut faciam voluntate tuam Deus plana est sententia, eadeque prorsus cum Hebraeo: significatur quippe, quod toto corpore, omnibus viribus debeat se mancipare Deo, & laborare, ut voluntatem Domini, quo-quo modo fieri queat, perficiat. Cæterum hinc videtur orta diuersitas in translatione septuaginta. Apparet, perforare aurem, apud Hebraeos prouerbiali quadam figura, aut certè si non prouerbialiter, tamen per Metonymiam, vsitatum pro eo, quod est in seruitutem perpetuam redigere & addicere, occasione inde sumpta, quod Exodi 21 præcipitur, ut seruus Hebraeus anno septimo liber dimittatur cum vxore, liberis, & vestitu, item vti primū aduenit. Quòd si uero seruus ille noluerit abire, dicens: Diligo dominum meum, vxorem, ac liberos, non egrediar liber: offerat eum dominus Dijs (id est, iudicibus) & applicabitur ad ostium & postes, perforabitque aurem eius subula, & erit ei seruus in seculum.
units.tr: The Seventy, wishing to render this sense, wrote "you have prepared a body for me." If you join it to the following words, where it is likewise added, "that I may do your will, O my God," the sense is plain and wholly the same as in the Hebrew. It signifies that with his whole body and all his powers he ought to surrender himself to God and labour to carry out the Lord's will in whatever way it can be done. Moreover, the difference in the Seventy's translation seems to have arisen from the following point. Among the Hebrews, to pierce the ear was a proverbial figure, or at least, if not proverbial, a usual metonymy for reducing a person to perpetual servitude and binding him over to it. This usage took its origin from Exodus 21, where it is commanded that a Hebrew servant be set free in the seventh year, with his wife, children and clothing, as he first came. But if that servant is unwilling to leave, saying, "I love my master, my wife and my children; I will not go out free," then his master shall bring him before God (that is, the judges), and he shall be brought to the door or doorpost, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be his servant for ever.

units.la: Proinde cum adeò elegans esset hæc locutio, quæ parem gratiam in alienalingua, si ad verbum redderetur, non acciperetur, Septuaginta aliter sunt interpretati, sic tamen, ut sententia maneret eadem, imò ut aliquanto significantius videretur expressa: significantius quippe dictum videretur, Aptasti mihi corpus, quàm si dixisset, tantum aurem aptā. Fortasis & spiritus Sanctus suggessit septuaginta interpretibus eam ratione vertendi, propter mysterium, quia nimirum eo loco agitur de oblatione corporis Christi, quod totum debuit pro peccatis nostris immolari.
units.tr: Since this expression was so elegant, yet if rendered word for word into another language would not be understood with the same force, the Seventy translated it differently, but in such a way that the sense remained the same, and indeed was expressed in a rather more forceful way. For it certainly seems more forceful to say, "You have prepared a body for me," than to say only "you have prepared an ear." Perhaps the Holy Spirit also suggested to the Seventy this manner of translating because of the mystery: the passage is clearly about the offering of Christ's body, which had to be sacrificed entirely for our sins.

units.la: Neque verò opus est longius accersere interpretationem, dicendo, Christo datam esse corpus, quia non debuit seruire vmbrae, sed præstare res ipsas & corpus.
units.tr: Nor is it necessary to seek a further explanation of the translation by saying that a body was given to Christ because he was not to serve a shadow, but to present the realities themselves and the body.

units.la: Tunc dixi: Ecce adsum, in capite libri scriptum est de me, ut faciam Deus voluntatem tuam.
units.tr: Then I said: Behold, I am here; in the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God.

units.la: Cum septuaginta prorsus conuenit. Neque etiam discrepat ab Hebraeo, nisi quod, vbi septuaginta habent, ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου, hebraicè legitur, בראש ספר, id est, in volumine libri qua de re mox admonebimus.
units.tr: This agrees entirely with the Seventy. Nor does it differ from the Hebrew, except that where the Seventy have "in the head of the book" [ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου], the Hebrew reads "in the volume of the book" [בראש ספר]. We shall shortly remark on this point.

units.la: Sunt autem hæc verba Christi ad patrem, se totum offerentis, ad faciundum, quicquid patri esset placitum. Quando pater nollet sacrificia vel alia huiusmodi opera pro satisfactione peccatorum humani generis, Christus sponte obtulit semetipsum paratus fieri hostia.
units.tr: These are the words of Christ to the Father, offering himself entirely to do whatever pleased the Father. When the Father did not want sacrifices or other such works for the satisfaction of the sins of the human race, Christ freely offered himself, ready to become the victim.

units.la: Qua ex re mirabilis Christi charitas animaduerti potest. Maiorem enim charitatem nemo habet, quàm ut animam suam ponat quis pro amicis suis.
units.tr: From this fact the wonderful love of Christ can be perceived. For no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends.

units.la: Et oblatus est, quia voluit, &c. Sed hic affectus, & hic ardor charitatis elegantissimè exprimitur verbis testimonij: Tunc dixi, inquit, ecce adsum: Quomodo obsecro posset proptitudo animi aptioribus verbis significari? capite secundo huius epistolæ habemus ex Esaiæ octauo, Christum similimodo ad patrem locutum, Ecce ego, & pueri mei. Promptitudinem autem significari, argumento est, quòd & Samuel ad Heli 1.reg.3. similiformaloquedi vsus fit, Ecce ego, uocasti enim me. Et Lucæ primo, Beata virgo, Ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum. Sed & Christus cùm quæreretur à Iudæis ad mortem, ac interrogati, quem quærerent, responderet se quærere Iesum Nazarenum, Ego sum, inquit, ut verè adimpletum sit in eo, tanquàm ouis ad occisionem ductus est, & sicut agnus coram tondente se, mutus: sic non aperuit os suum. In humilitate ipsius iudicium eius sublatum est.
units.tr: And he was offered because he willed it, etc. But this disposition and this burning of love is expressed most elegantly in the words of the testimony: "Then I said," he says, "Behold, I am here." By what more fitting words, I ask you, could readiness of mind be signified? In the second chapter of this epistle we have, from Isaiah 8, Christ speaking in a similar way to the Father: "Behold I, and the children whom you have given me." That readiness is signified is shown by the fact that Samuel also used a similar form of speech to Eli, "Here I am, for you called me" (1 Sam. 3). And in Luke 1 the blessed Virgin says, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." Moreover, when Christ was sought by the Jews for death, and, when asked whom they sought, answered that they sought Jesus of Nazareth, he said, "I am," so that what was said might be truly fulfilled in him: he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was dumb, so he did not open his mouth. By his humiliation his judgment was taken away (Isa. 53).

units.la: In capite libri scriptum est de me) hebraicè sonat, in uolumine libri: sumpta forma locutionis à more gentis. Soliti enim sunt Iudæi, id quod & hodie cernimus eos facere, legem habere scriptam in membranis, quæ conuoluuntur (& propterea pasim audis volumen legis, Deuter.17.19. Iosuæ 1.8.&c.) non autem ea forma, vt in paginis complicentur chartæ, vti nos nostros libros habemus compactos.
units.tr: "In the head of the book it is written of me" in Hebrew sounds like "in the volume of the book," the form of expression being taken from the custom of the people. For the Jews were accustomed, as we still see them doing today, to have the law written on parchments that are rolled up (and therefore everywhere you hear of the volume of the law, Deut. 17:19; Josh. 1:8, etc.), not in the form in which sheets are folded into pages, as we have our books bound.

units.la: Septuaginta verò habent, in capite libri, fortasis explicandi atque illustrandi caussa: ut, quod in hebraeo generaliter est dictum, videlicet, Scriptum de eo in libro legis, exaltius significetur, etiam in capite eius libri de ipso agi, adeoque caput & summa libri legis de ipso accipiendam, & circa sacrificium eius versari.
units.tr: The Seventy, however, have "in the head of the book," perhaps for the sake of explaining and illustrating the matter: so that what is said in general in the Hebrew, namely, "It is written of him in the book of the law," might be expressed more strongly, namely that in the head, that is the chief part, of that book of the law, it is also treated of him, and that the chief point and summary of the law is to be understood concerning him and is centred on his sacrifice.

units.la: In summa, videtur mihi hic ratio esse posita, quare videlicet Christus debeat paratus esse & obediens patri in negotio restaurationis generis humani, sumpta à diuina praeordinatione, & scriptis vaticinijs de ipso iamdiu editis: vt sit sententia: Ego volo esse paratus ad offerendum me pro salute hominum: quia pater iam ab aeterno ita praeordinauit, & in volumine legis scriptum & praenunciatum est de me: Deus pater consilium & voluntatem suam iam diu patribus manifestauit, & propterea ea, quae praeordinata & scripta sunt, oportet per me adimpleri.
units.tr: In sum, it seems to me that the reason is given here why Christ ought to be ready and obedient to the Father in the business of restoring the human race, drawn from divine predestination and from the prophecies written and published long ago concerning him. The sense is this: "I am willing to be ready to offer myself for the salvation of men, because the Father has predestined it from eternity, and it has been written and foretold of me in the volume of the law. God the Father long ago made known his counsel and will to the fathers, and therefore what has been predestined and written must be fulfilled through me."

units.la: Et conuenit haec interpretatio cum illis verbis, quae Christus pasim inculcat: quòd videlicet oporteret per ipsum impleri ea, quae in lege & prophetis erant de ipso scripta. Lucæ 24. Hæc sunt verba, quæ locutus sum ad vos, cùm adhuc essem vobiscum, quòd necesse foret impleri omnia, quæ scripta sunt in lege Mosi, & prophetis, & psalmis de me. Alibi plura in eandem sententiam sunt obuia.
units.tr: This interpretation agrees with those words which Christ repeatedly insists upon, namely that those things which were written of him in the law and the prophets must be fulfilled through him. Luke 24: "These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written of me in the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms." Elsewhere many passages to the same effect are to be found.

units.la: Et reuera statim initio Geneseos, deinde in omnibus alijs libris, tum manifestis promissionibus, tum etiam actionibus & typis, fuit patribus significatum, quòd per Christum deberet humanum genus à potestate diaboli & mortis redimi.
units.tr: Indeed, from the very beginning of Genesis, and then in all the other books, both by clear promises and also by deeds and types, it was signified to the fathers that the human race was to be redeemed from the power of the devil and of death through Christ.

units.la: His promissionibus ipsi se solabatur, his promissionibus in fide confirmabantur. Huc ergo respiciens Christus ait, in volumine, adeoque in capite libri de se scriptum, & hac ratione ipse sese incitat & instigat, ut ad perficienda ea, quae de ipso scripta erant, accedat promptior.
units.tr: By these promises they comforted themselves; by these promises they were confirmed in faith. Looking to this, therefore, Christ says, "in the volume," and so "in the head of the book," written of himself, and by this reasoning he urges and spurs himself on, so that he may come the more readily to accomplish those things which were written of him.

units.la: Vt faciam Deus uoluntatē tuam)Hoc est, ut fiam hostia pro peccatis. Sic enim Christus orans in horto ante mortem (Lucæ 22.) non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat. Ioann.4. Meus cibus est, ut faciam, quod vult is, qui misit me, & perficiā opus eius. Ioan.5. Non quaero voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem eius, qui misit me, patris. Ioan.6. Descendi de coelo, ut faciam, non quod ego volo, sed quod vult is, qui misit me.
units.tr: That I may do your will: that is, that I may become a victim for sins. For so Christ, praying in the garden before his death (Luke 22), says: not my will, but yours be done. John 4: "My food is that I should do the will of him who sent me, and finish his work." John 5: "I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father." John 6: "I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me."

units.la: Haec est voluntas eius qui misit me patris, ne quid perdā ex omnibus, quae dedit mihi, sed resuscitem illa in nouissimo die.
units.tr: This is the will of him who sent me, the Father, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but should raise them up on the last day.

units.la: Haec est autem volūtas eius qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt filium & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam, & ego suscitabo eum in nouissimo die.
units.tr: And this is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

units.la: En ergo, quomodo Christus etiam semper praedicauit, se in hoc missum, ut voluntatem Dei patris perficeret, sicut & apud prophetam loquens introducitur:
units.tr: Behold, then, how Christ always proclaimed that he was sent for this purpose, to carry out the will of God the Father, just as he is introduced speaking through the prophet:

units.la: Superius cùm dicit: sacrificium & oblationem, & holocautomata, & pro peccato noluisti, neque comprobasti, quæ iuxta legem offeruntur, tunc dixit: Ecce adsum, ut faciam Deus voluntatem tuam: tollit prius, ut posterius statuat.
units.tr: When he says above, "sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and sin offerings you have not desired, nor approved, which are offered according to the law," then he said, "Behold, I come to do your will, O God." He takes away the first, that he may establish the second.

units.la: Iam addit Apostolus interpretationem suam, & accommodat instituto, quemadmodum supra ostendimus: nec opus est per nos plenius explicari.
units.tr: Now the Apostle adds his own interpretation and fits it to his purpose, as we have shown above, and there is no need for us to explain it more fully.

units.la: Per quam voluntatem sanctificati sumus.
units.tr: By which will we have been sanctified.

units.la: Est veluti illatio ex praecedentibus. Christus, inquit, debuit non offerre sacrificium legale aliquod, sed proprium suum corpus, & voluntatem Domini facere: tum verò sic aptae aptat instituto, dicens: Et per hanc voluntatem sumus sanctificati, id est, peccatorum remissionem consecuti, ἡγιασμένοι, simili modo capite secundo ἁγιάζομενοι: & capite nono, ἁγιά- ζα. Atque ita placuit illi, effectum obedientiæ seu mortis Christi rursus exprimere, qui nunquàm satis potest inculcari.
units.tr: This is as it were an inference from what goes before. Christ, he says, had to offer not some legal sacrifice but his own body, and to do the will of the Lord. Then he fits this to his purpose, saying: by this will we have been sanctified, that is, have obtained the forgiveness of sins [ἡγιασμένοι]; in the same way in the second chapter [ἁγιάζομενοι], and in the ninth chapter [ἁγιάζα]. And so he chose to express again the effect of Christ's obedience or death, which can never be inculcated enough.

units.la: Et reuera cùm solus Christus sit ille, qui potest voluntatem Domini plenè facere: nos autem nullo vnquàm modo potuissemus illi reconciliari, neque vllis operibus nostris, neque assiduis sacrificiorum oblationibus, Christus meritò celebratur, qui voluntatem Dei patris ita peregerit.
units.tr: And indeed, since Christ alone is the one who can fully do the will of the Lord, and since we could never in any way have been reconciled to him, neither by any works of ours nor by the continual offering of sacrifices, Christ is rightly praised, for he has so accomplished the will of God the Father.

units.la: Est istud valde consolatorium: si quando enim grauatur conscientia terrore damnationis & inferni, propter peccata, atque iam cogitur desperare, quia videt, se voluntatem Domini non adimplesse, nec adimplere etiamnù posse, tunc confugiat ad Christum, qui pro omnibus nobis satisfecit, & in quo vno patri bene est complacitum.
units.tr: This is very comforting. For if at any time the conscience is weighed down by the terror of damnation and hell on account of sins, and is already driven to despair because it sees that it has not fulfilled the will of the Lord, nor is yet able to fulfil it, then let it flee to Christ, who has made satisfaction for all of us, and in whom alone the Father is well pleased.

units.la: Per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel peractam) Hæc particula valde necessariò est adiecta. Ne enim aduersarij cauillarentur, cùm dicitur Christum debuisse perficere voluntatem Domini, nequaquam intelligendam illam voluntatem de hac oblatione, qua Christus ob tulit semetipsum, sed potius de aliquo alio insigni opere, quod Domino impensè placuit: ideo diserte adiecit, adimpletionem illam voluntatis Dei patris, de qua propheta loquitur, proprie sitam in oblatione corporis Iesu Christi semel peracta. Neque interea negligendum, quòd totiès inculcat particulam semel, quam vult ad dignitatem sacrificij Christi facere, quòd videlicet semel tantùm oblatum, tamen adeò fuerit efficax.
units.tr: By the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. This clause has been added quite necessarily. For lest the adversaries should carp, when it is said that Christ had to accomplish the will of the Lord, that this will is by no means to be understood of this offering by which Christ offered himself, but rather of some other notable work which greatly pleased the Lord, he therefore expressly added that the fulfilment of the will of God the Father, of which the prophet speaks, lies properly in the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once made. Nor meanwhile should it be overlooked that he so often inculcates the word "once," which he wishes to make count for the dignity of Christ's sacrifice, namely that, though offered only once, it was nevertheless so effective.

units.la: Iam vt ad doctrinam veniamus, hoc ante omnia hic discimus, sacrificia legalia per Christi in terras aduentum abrogata, sicut Apostolus hic diserte tribuit Christo apud prophetam ea verba, quibus tantundem clarè significatur: qua de re iam sæpius dictum est, & alias fusius à nobis disputatum.
units.tr: Now let us come to the teaching. First of all we learn here that the legal sacrifices were abrogated by the coming of Christ into the world, as the Apostle here expressly attributes to Christ, speaking through the prophet, those words by which this is equally clearly signified. On this matter we have already spoken often and have disputed it more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Secundò cùm dicitur, sacrificiū & oblationem noluisti, neque comprobasti, clarè nobis proponitur, sacrificia & quæcúque huiusmodi opera, imò & Sacramento ex opere operato apud Deum per se nihil posse. Galat. 4. Nam in Christo Iesu neque circumcisio quicquà valet, neque præputium, sed noua creatura. Quò pertinent omnes illæ sententiæ apud prophetas, quibus ostendunt, Deum sacrificia Iudæorum nolle, & nullius facere. Neque enim per se quicquam prodesse poterant, sicut neque ob id instituta fuerunt, ut per ea ob ūneretur iustitia: sed hoc inprimis displicebat Deo, quòd tantâ in illis sacrificijs & Sacramentis collocarent fiduciam, iudicarique vellent propter illa iusti: interea de sanctis affectibus cordis, de uera pietate, hoc est, de fide in Deum, & charitate in proximum nequaquam erant soliciti. Hoc reuera erat fœdè abuti omnibus illis institutis. Erant quidem plures boni fines, propter quos ceremoniæ instituebantur à Deo, sed neqwaquàm in hoc institutæ vllæ fuerunt, ut freti earum fiducia opera præstantiora omitterent. Huc ergo pertinent illa Esaiæ primo, Quò mihi multitudo victimarum? &c. Et psalmo 50. Non accipiam de domo tua vitulos, neque de gregibus tuis hireos.
units.tr: Secondly, when it is said, "sacrifice and offering you have not desired, nor approved," it is clearly set before us that sacrifices and all such works, indeed even the sacraments, can do nothing by themselves before God through the work done (ex opere operato). Galatians 4: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature." To this belong all those sayings of the prophets by which they show that God did not want the sacrifices of the Jews and accepted none of them. For they could not profit anything by themselves, nor were they instituted for this reason, that righteousness should be obtained by them. But this above all displeased God: that they placed such great trust in those sacrifices and sacraments, and wished to be counted righteous on account of them, while meanwhile they were in no way concerned with holy affections of the heart, with true piety, that is, with faith in God and love towards neighbour. This was indeed to abuse shamefully all those institutions. There were indeed several good ends for which the ceremonies were instituted by God, but they were by no means instituted so that, relying on confidence in them, people should neglect the weightier works. To this belong those words in Isaiah 1: "What to me is the multitude of your victims?" etc., and Psalm 50: "I will not take bullocks out of your house, nor he-goats out of your flocks."

units.la: Non quidem ideo reiecta sacrificia à Deo, quòd offerretur ab impijs; sicuti etiamnum hodie conantur Iudæi obijcere, vt ita tueantur suas ceremonias, quandoquidem & apud Esaiam obijcitur illis statim, Manus vestræ plenæ sunt sanguine: apud psalmographum verò obijcitur: Quare enarras iustitias meas? &c.
units.tr: Nor were sacrifices rejected by God for the reason that they were offered by the wicked, as the Jews even today try to object, in order to defend their ceremonies; since indeed the same objection is made to them at once in Isaiah, "Your hands are full of blood," and in the psalmist it is objected: "Why do you recount my righteousnesses?" etc.

units.la: Sed reuera quòd per se nihil ad iustitiam faciant: id quod testimonio iam citato per apostolum apertissimè comprobatur, cùm eo psalmo nihil de malitia offerentiū adijciatur, ut reuera appareat, hæc de causa potius huius psalmi locum, quàm aliquem alium ab apostolo vsurpatum, cùm hic proprie de ipsis sacrificijs per se consideratis sermo sit.
units.tr: But in truth, they do nothing towards righteousness by themselves. This is most clearly proved by the testimony already cited through the Apostle, since nothing about the wickedness of those who offer is added in that psalm, so that it really appears that for this reason the Apostle chose this passage of the psalm rather than some other, since the discussion here is properly about the sacrifices considered in themselves.

units.la: Sunt verò & alijs locis alia testimonia obuia de abrogatione sacrificiorum, ut Hieremiæ 7. Amos 5. Micheæ 6. psal. 50.
units.tr: There are also other passages elsewhere that testify to the abrogation of sacrifices, as Jeremiah 7, Amos 5, Micah 6, and Psalm 50.

units.la: Cæterum, quemadmodum eo tempore statuebat Deus de sacrificijs, ita statuendum est nunc quoque de nostris ceremonijs, quòd videlicet per se nihil sint coram Deo, neque ex opere operato ad iustitiam conducant.
units.tr: Moreover, just as God then judged concerning sacrifices, so we must judge now also concerning our ceremonies: that they are in themselves nothing before God, and do not contribute to righteousness through the work done.

units.la: Vt animus suscipientis bene est affectus, & egregia fide imbutus, ita spirituales fructus coram Deo percipit.
units.tr: As the mind of the recipient is well disposed and imbued with outstanding faith, so it receives spiritual fruits before God.

units.la: Ex fide est iustitia, non ex externo ceremoniarum usu. Dei virtus non est elementis ullis alligata.
units.tr: Righteousness is from faith, not from the external use of ceremonies. The power of God is not bound to any elements.

units.la: Quid autem dicemus de traditionibus humanis & ἐθελοθρησκείας? Hæc omnium minime iustificabunt.
units.tr: But what shall we say of human traditions and will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία]? These will justify no one at all.

units.la: Tertiò, discimus, præcipuum & gratissimum Deo esse sacrificium, facere ipsius voluntatem.
units.tr: Thirdly, we learn that the chief and most pleasing sacrifice to God is to do his will.

units.la: Quæ autem sit voluntas eius, docemur passim in euangelio.
units.tr: What his will is, we are taught everywhere in the gospel.

units.la: Voluntas eius est, ut credamus, item ut fratres nostros diligamus, atque ita testatu facia mus, nos veros esse ipsius discipulos. Huc pertinet illud 1. reg. 15. Melior est obedientia, quàm victimæ. Item Esaiæ 1. Succurrite egeno, pupillum & viduam defendite. Et Christus Matth. 12. Discite quid est, misericordiam volo & non sacrificium.
units.tr: His will is that we believe, and likewise that we love our brothers, and so show by our deeds that we are truly his disciples. To this belongs 1 Samuel 15: "Obedience is better than sacrifice." Likewise Isaiah 1: "Help the oppressed, defend the fatherless and the widow." And Christ in Matthew 12: "Learn what this means: I desire mercy and not sacrifice."

units.la: Quarto, habemus hic insigne exemplum charitatis in Christo se adeò promptè ad mor tem offerente. Ecce, inquit, adsum, ut faciam voluntatem tuam Deus. Sic ille pro alijs mortem subire paratus.
units.tr: Fourthly, we have here a notable example of love in Christ, who so readily offers himself to death: "Behold, I come," he says, "to do your will, O God." Thus he was ready to undergo death for others.

units.la: Ergo hanc charitatem studeamus imitari, pro fratribus non detrectantes pericula, ubi probabile est, fructum aliquem ex nostra obedientia ad eos rediturum.
units.tr: Therefore let us strive to imitate this love, not shrinking from dangers for our brothers where it is probable that some fruit from our obedience will return to them.

units.la: Quinto, hoc exemplù charitatis & obedientiæ Christi mirè est consolatorium omnib. credentibus, se per mortem ipsius adiuuandos. Quæ enim maior consolatio in vefis pa-uoribus & certaminibus conscientiæ, quàm audire, nos per obedientiam Christi sanctificatos? Nobis peccata esse condonata, propterea quòd Christus obtulit satisfactionem pro peccatis?
units.tr: Fifthly, this example of Christ's love and obedience is wonderfully comforting to all believers, that they will be helped by his death. For what greater consolation is there in the terrors and conflicts of our conscience than to hear that we have been sanctified through the obedience of Christ, that our sins have been forgiven us because Christ offered satisfaction for sins?

units.la: Et omnis quidem sacerdos assistit quotidie, sacra peragens, & easdem sepius offerens hostias quæ nunquam possint auferre peccata: Hic verò vna pro peccatis oblata victi ma, perpetuò sedet ad dexteram Dei, id quod superest, expectans, donec reddantur inimici ipsius scabellum pedum eius. Vnica enim oblatione perfectos effecit in perpetuum, eos qui sanctificantur. Testificatur autem nobis & ipse spiritus Sanctus, nimirum cum prædixerit: Hoc est testamentum, quod condam ergà illos post dies illos, dicit Dominus, dans leges meas in corde illorum & in mentibus illorum inscribam eas, & peccatorum atque iniquitatum illorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: And every priest indeed stands daily, performing sacred rites and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this one, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits perpetually at the right hand of God, waiting from then on until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet. For by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified. And the Holy Spirit himself also bears witness to us, saying: "This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts and write them in their minds, and I will remember their sins and iniquities no more."

units.la: Restat adhuc probandum, quod vnicum sacrificium Christi ad expianda peccata sufficerit: quod quidem iam sæpius dictum est: at nullo adhuc Scripturæ testimonio confirmatum. Istud igitur Apostolus nunc docebit. Primum autem repetit propositionem, quòd videlicet Christus vnica hostia satisfecerit pro peccatis. Verùm hanc non contentus fuit ita simpliciter ac nudè efferre, sed veluti sacrificium Christi eiusque effectus cupiens illustrare, adhibuit, uti sæpè antehac fecit, collationem seu potius contentionem rhetoricam hoc modo.
units.tr: It still remains to be proved that the one sacrifice of Christ was sufficient to expiate sins. This indeed has been said many times already, but it has not yet been confirmed by any testimony of Scripture. The Apostle will now teach this. First he repeats the proposition, namely that Christ satisfied for sins by one sacrifice. But not content to state this so simply and baldly, desiring to illustrate the sacrifice of Christ and its effect, he employed, as he has often done before, a comparison, or rather a rhetorical contrast, in this way.

units.la: Sacerdotes legales quotidie sacrificabant, & easdem semper offerebant hostias, nec tamen omnibus illis hostijs tollebant peccata.
units.tr: The priests under the law offered sacrifices every day, and always offered the same victims, yet none of those victims took away sins.

units.la: At Christus semel duntaxat obtulit, atque vnica hostia pro peccatis satisfecit. Hæc est propositionis sententia, etiamsi ipse nec hoc prorsus modo reddiderit. Nam dum suo more de Christo semper multò maxima prædicat, studeque omnibus modis exornare Christi dignitatem, ipse illi, quod in priori parte collationis dixerat, videlicet sacerdotes legales sæpius offerre eosdem hostias, opponit in posteriori parte, quòd Christus non amplius offerat, sed quòd sedeat ad dexteram patris, id solum expectâs, quod superest, nempe ut reddantur inimici ipsius scabellum pedum eius. Deinde verò tanquam rationem reddes, cur nequaquam denuò offerat, addit, quòd vnica oblatione perfectos reddiderit. Atque ita quasi aliud agens Christi dignitatem mirum in modum amplificat, simulque plenissimè exprimit, quod ad argumenti materiam pertinet.
units.tr: But Christ offered only once, and by that single victim he made satisfaction for sins. This is the sense of the proposition, though he does not state it in exactly this way. For while, as is his custom, he always makes Christ far greater than anything else and labours in every way to adorn Christ's dignity, he sets against what he said in the first part of the comparison, namely that the priests under the law offered the same victims again and again, the point in the second part that Christ no longer offers but sits at the right hand of the Father, waiting only for what remains, that his enemies be made his footstool. Then, as if giving the reason why Christ never offers again, he adds that by one offering he has made them perfect. In this way, as if he were doing something else, he greatly magnifies Christ's dignity and at the same time expresses fully what belongs to the matter in hand.

units.la: Iam propositioni ad eum modum redditæ, attexit mox probationem è sacris literis, nempe ex Hieremiæ 31. dicens: Testificatur autem nobis & ipse spiritus sanctus, nimirum cùm prædixerit, Hoc est testamentum, &c. Ex cuius testimonij posteriori parte vult huiusmodi argumentum colligi:
units.tr: Having stated the proposition in this way, he straightway adds a proof from the sacred writings, namely from Jeremiah 31, saying: "And the Holy Spirit also testifies to us, namely when he has said beforehand, 'This is the covenant,' etc." From the latter part of this testimony he wishes the following argument to be drawn:

units.la: En prædictum est per prophetam, & à Deo promissum, quòd in nouo testamento contingeret peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: Behold, it has been foretold through the prophet, and promised by God, that in the new covenant there would be forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Ergo per vnicum sacrificiû Christi, quod proprie solum est in nouo testamento oblatû, facta est peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: Therefore, through the one sacrifice of Christ, which was properly offered only in the new covenant, forgiveness of sins has been effected.

units.la: Sumpta est, ut vides, hæc ratio à propria nota & effectu euangelij, quo id potissimum à lege discernitur.
units.tr: As you see, this argument is taken from the proper mark and effect of the gospel, by which it is above all distinguished from the law.

units.la: Et omnis quidem sacerdos) omnis inquit sacerdos. Sicut enim suprà enumeratione illa sacrificij, oblationum, holocautomatum, & pro peccato, quasi sufficienti comprehendit omnia sacrificiorum genera: ita nunc quoque dicendo, omnis sacerdos, intelligi vult quæcunque sacrificiorum genera, à quocunque tandem offerantur, siue à summo sacerdote, siue ab alio.
