Constat enim quædam à summo tantùm sacerdote offerri solita, cuiusmodi illud est, Leuitici decimosexto descriptû, in die expiationis semel in anno in sancta sanctorum illatum: alia verò quotidie offerri solita, & ab alijs sacerdotibus. Sed à quocunque tandem sacerdote offerebantur, & quamlibet multa essent, & sæpè repetita, tamen non poterant auferre peccata.
units.tr: And every priest: "every priest," he says. For just as above, in that enumeration of sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings, and sin offerings, he takes in, as if sufficiently, all kinds of sacrifices, so now too, by saying "every priest," he means whatever kinds of sacrifices, by whomever they are offered, whether by the high priest or by another. For it is established that some sacrifices were customarily offered by the high priest alone, such as that described in Leviticus 16, brought once a year into the Holy of Holies on the day of atonement; others were customarily offered every day, and by other priests. But by whatever priest they were offered, and however many they were and however often repeated, they still could not take away sins.

units.la: Quanquam etiam eleganter pluribus sacerdotibus vnus sacerdos Christus opponitur qui solus effecit suo vnico sacrificio, quod omnes simul sacerdotes, nunquam efficere potuissent sacrificijs innumeris.
units.tr: Although, too, it is elegantly contrasted with many priests that the one priest Christ, who alone by his single sacrifice has effected what all the priests together could never have effected with countless sacrifices.

units.la: Hic verò una pro peccatis oblata victima) vna hostia opponitur multis hostijs sæpè repetitis: & hostia pro peccatis opponitur omnibus sacrificiorum generibus, puta hostijs pacificis, oblationibus, holocautomatis, hostijs pro peccato. Vna species opponitur omnibus. Ac dixit victimâ pro peccatis, non pro peccato, ad discrimen euidentius, quòd videlicet vna hæc hostia Christi oblata erat pro omnibus peccatorum generibus, non tantum pro hoc aut illo crimine, pro quo lex præscribebat hostias offerendas. Ita ut veteri testamento suæ tribuantur hostiæ pro peccato, & nouo testamento similiter vna hostia, quæ pro omnibus simul peccatis satisfaceret.
units.tr: But he, having offered one victim for sins: one victim is set against many victims often repeated, and a victim for sins is set against all kinds of sacrifices, namely peace offerings, offerings, burnt offerings, and sin offerings. One kind is set against all. And he said "a victim for sins," not "for sin," to make the distinction more evident: namely that this one victim of Christ was offered for all kinds of sins, not merely for this or that crime for which the law prescribed that victims be offered. Thus under the old covenant sin offerings were assigned, and under the new covenant likewise one victim, which would make satisfaction for all sins at once.

units.la: Perpetuò sedet ad dexteram Dei) Ei, quòd dixerat, sacerdotem assistere quotidie ministrantè, opponit Christum sedentem ad dexteram Dei. Porrò nemo non videt, maximum hîc esse discrimen, inter sedentem ad dexteram Dei, & ministrantem ad altare. Quare mirum in modum crescit hîc Christi dignitas. Quòd autem Christum sedere ad dexteram patris, idem fit, quod patri cum patre præditû esse potestate, gloria, dignitate, sæpius iam à nobis dictum est. Addidit, perpetuò, quia Christus semel mortuus amplius non moritur, Rom. 6. & potestas Christi potestas est æterna: Daniel. 7.
units.tr: He sits perpetually at the right hand of God: to the statement that the priest stands daily ministering, he sets against it Christ sitting at the right hand of God. Now no one fails to see that there is a very great difference between one sitting at the right hand of God and one ministering at the altar. Hence Christ's dignity grows wonderfully here. That Christ sits at the right hand of the Father means the same as that he possesses power, glory and dignity together with the Father, as we have often said already. He added "perpetually" because Christ, having died once, dies no more (Romans 6), and the power of Christ is an eternal power (Daniel 7).

units.la: Id quod super est expectans, donec reddantur inimici scabellum pedum eius.) Ista opponuntur ei, quod dictum est, sacerdotes legales easdem sæpius offerre hostias: ac nihil aliud his significatur quàm, non amplius expectandû, ut Christus denuò offerat. Est enim sententia: Christus sedet ad dexteram Dei, non quidem alio rursus tempore venturus, ut denuò sacrificet, aut simile quiddam pro expiandis peccatis faciat, sed hoc solum expectans, ut reddantur inimici ipsius scabellum pedum eius. Sumptæ autem sunt hæ locutionum formulæ à rebus humanis, ad significandam Christi æternam gloriam, & quòd non amplius sit humiliandus.
units.tr: Waiting for what remains, until his enemies are made his footstool: these words are set against what was said, that the priests under the law offered the same victims again and again; and nothing else is signified by them than that it is not to be expected any longer that Christ should offer again. The sense is this: Christ sits at the right hand of God, not indeed to come again at some other time to offer sacrifice anew, or to do anything similar for the expiation of sins, but waiting only for this, that his enemies be made his footstool. These modes of speech, however, are taken from human affairs, to signify Christ's eternal glory and that he is no longer to be humbled.

units.la: Deinde inimicos reddi scabellum pedum eius) est, omnes vires & potentiam, inimicorum spiritualem inquâ, id est, peccati, mortis, & diaboli, prorsus frangi & euerti: contrà verò solius Christi gloriam, potentiam, dignitatem illustrari. Sed sumpta est loquendi forma à more humano, quo solent, quod valde contemptum volunt innuere, dicere se id pedibus subiecturus: vel certè est descriptio adeoque ἐνωρ insignis victoriæ. Et reuera est admiranda & insignis victoria, qua Christus per mortem superauit mortem, ut Osee 13. eleganter dicitur. Ero mors tua, ô mors. Et Roman. 8. De peccato condemnauit peccatum per carnem, & permittendo, se à diabolo tentari, diabolû superauit. De qua Christi potentia & gloria 1. Corinth. 15. Primitiæ resurgentiû Christus: deinde ij, qui sunt Christi, in aduentu ipsius, mox finis, cùm tradiderit regnum Deo & patri, cùm abolauerit omnem principatum, & omnem potestatem ac virtutem. Nam oportet eum regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. Nouissimus hostis aboletur mors. Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes illius. Rursus eodem capite: Cùm corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatè: tùc fiet sermo, qui scriptus est (Osea) Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Vbi tuus mors aculeus? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Aculeus autè mortis peccatum, potentia verò peccati lex. Sed Deo gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominû nostrû Iesum Christum. Non dissimilia de gloria, potentia, & omnibus subijciendis vni Christo, habentur psal. 8. 109. Et huc adferri possunt, quæ dicuntur alibi de iudicio per Christum futuro, cû gloria & maiestate, & in quo damnabuntur cum diabolis omnes impij ad ignem æternum.
units.tr: Then that his enemies be made his footstool: this means that all the strength and power of his enemies, spiritual enemies that is, sin, death and the devil, are utterly broken and overthrown, while on the contrary the glory, power and dignity of Christ alone are made illustrious. But the form of speech is taken from human custom, by which people who wish to signal great contempt say that they will put something under their feet; or certainly it is a description of a vivid [ἐνάργεια] and remarkable victory. And indeed it is a wonderful and remarkable victory, by which Christ through his death overcame death, as is elegantly said in Hosea 13: "O death, I will be your death." And Romans 8: "God condemned sin in the flesh," and by allowing himself to be tempted by the devil, he overcame the devil. Concerning this power and glory of Christ, 1 Corinthians 15: "Christ the firstfruits of those who rise; then those who are Christ's, at his coming; then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death. For he has put all things under his feet." Again in the same chapter: "When this corruptible has put on incorruptibility, and this mortal has put on immortality, then shall come the saying that is written (in Hosea), 'Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O grave, is your victory?' The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Not dissimilar things about glory, power, and all things being subjected to Christ alone are found in Psalms 8 and 110. And there may be brought here what is said elsewhere about the judgment to come through Christ, with glory and majesty, and in which all the wicked will be condemned with the devils to eternal fire.

units.la: Satis est, quod ad præsens attinet, considerare Christum sedentem ad dexteram patris & subijciendos ei omnes hostes, etiam ut homini: propterea quidam pedes eius interpretantur humanitatem: nequaquam verò eum amplius humiliandum, ut fiat hostia, vel denuò pro ullis offerat sacrificium.
units.tr: For what concerns the present point, it is enough to consider Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father, and all enemies being subjected to him, even as man; for this reason some interpret his feet as his humanity. But by no means is he to be humbled any more, so as to become a victim, or to offer sacrifice again for anyone.

units.la: Vnica enim oblatione perfectos effecit in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur.
units.tr: For by one offering he has made perfect for ever those who are sanctified.

units.la: Ratio, quare Christus non amplius humiliandus, ut denuò offerat: Quia, inquit, eos
units.tr: The reason why Christ is not to be humbled again to offer anew: because, he says, those

units.la: qui sanctificantur, id est, qui eliguntur, ut sancti fiant. Neque enim omnes citra discrimen sanctificantur: sed qui per fidem apprehendunt misericordiam propter Christum: ideoque supra capite nono dixit, quod Christus tolleret multorum (non omnium) peccata, & eos, qui vocati sunt, promissionem accipere aeternae haereditatis. Non quod Deus sit acceptor personarum: vult enim omnes salvos fieri: sed quod homines ipsi obsistat, & per peccata se a participatione salutis excludant.
units.tr: who are sanctified, that is, who are chosen to become holy. For not all are sanctified without distinction, but those who by faith lay hold of mercy on account of Christ; and so above, in chapter nine, he said that Christ would take away the sins of many (not all), and that those who are called would receive the promise of eternal inheritance. Not that God is a respecter of persons, for he wills that all be saved; but that men themselves stand in the way and by their sins shut themselves out from participation in salvation.

units.la: Perfectos effecit in perpetuum, pro eo, quod est, peccata abstulit, seu satisfecit pro peccatis. Vide autem, quam varie exprimat Apostolus effectum unici sacrificij Christi. Capite nono coepit praedicare effectum istum, sed semper aliis atque aliis verbis, ut nimirum dignitatem eius illustraret, & vim maximam ostenderet. Primum ubi tribuisset sacrificijs legalibus, quod sanctificarent ad purificationem carnis, statim subiecit de sanguine Christi, quod purgaret conscientiam a mortuis operibus. Mox adiecit, quod, morte Christi intercedente, redemptio fieret earum praevaricationum, quae fuerant sub priori testamento. Post tribuit ei mundationem, quando ait, caelestia debere mundari potioribus victimis. Tum factam ad profligationem peccati: deinde, ut multum peccata tolleret. Hinc capite praesenti cum dixisset, per sacrificia legalia non reddi perfectos, nec auferri peccata: subiecit, etiam sanctificari per oblationem corporis Christi. Hic vero dicit tandem perfectos reddi, quo nihil maius desiderari potest. Quae observanda sunt, quia explicant effectum sacrificij Christi, ac nos de vero eius usu instituunt.
units.tr: He has made them perfect forever, that is, he has taken away sins, or made satisfaction for sins. Notice how variously the Apostle expresses the effect of Christ's single sacrifice. In chapter nine he began to preach this effect, but always in different words, plainly to illustrate its dignity and show its great power. First, after ascribing to the legal sacrifices that they sanctify to the purification of the flesh, he at once added that the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience from dead works. Soon after he added that, through the mediation of Christ's death, there is a redemption of the transgressions that were under the former testament. Then he ascribed cleansing to it, when he said that heavenly things must be cleansed with better sacrifices. Next he spoke of its effect in abolishing sin, and then that it takes away sins in great measure. Here in this chapter, having said that the legal sacrifices did not make the worshippers perfect nor take away sins, he added that they are sanctified by the offering of the body of Christ. Now he says at last that they are made perfect, and nothing greater can be desired. These things must be noted, because they explain the effect of Christ's sacrifice and teach us about its true use.

units.la: Testificatur autem nobis & ipse Spiritus sanctus, nimirum cum praedixerit: Hoc est testamentum, quod condam erga illos.
units.tr: And the Holy Spirit himself also bears witness to us, namely, when he has said: This is the covenant that I will make with them.

units.la: Confirmatio est ac probatio, quod per unicum sacrificium Christi tollantur peccata. Perspicuum autem est, cum id colligere ex posteriori parte testimonij, qua dicitur, peccatorum atque iniquitatum illorum non recordabor amplius: Quo loco diximus supra capite octavo explicari, propriam esse hanc Evangelij notam, qua discernitur a lege. Nec opus est nos plenius eadem de re nunc agere. Tantum observandum, quomodo ut pondus & robur addat, ita accommodet suo instituto, & praefetur, dicens: Testificatur autem ipse Spiritus Sanctus.
units.tr: This is a confirmation and proof that sins are taken away through the single sacrifice of Christ. It is clear that he draws this conclusion from the latter part of the testimony, where it is said: I will remember their sins and iniquities no more. At that place we said above, in chapter eight, that this is the proper mark of the Gospel, by which it is distinguished from the law. Nor is there need for us now to treat the same matter more fully. It is only to be noted how he adds weight and strength, and so adapts the testimony to his purpose, introducing it with the words: And the Holy Spirit himself bears witness.

units.la: Simili forma citandi testimonia supra usus est capite tertio, item capite nono, significante id Spiritu sancto, inquit. Sic enim conueniebat apud Hebraeos agere, qui cuiusuis hominis testimonium videbantur contemptui. Vide Oecolampadium: Etsi hoc loco μαρτυρεῖ non videatur simpliciter positum pro eo, quod est testimonium ferre, sed potius pro occulta vi & persuasione mentis, de iis, quae salutis nostrae sunt. Nam per Spiritum certae redduntur conscientiae de iis, quae sunt salutis. Romani 8. Idem Spiritus testatur vna cum Spiritu nostro, quod sumus filij Dei.
units.tr: He used a similar way of citing testimonies above, in chapter three, and again in chapter nine, signifying that it is the Holy Spirit who says this. For this was the custom among the Hebrews, who regarded the testimony of any man as worthless. See Oecolampadius. Although here μαρτυρεῖ [martyrei] does not seem to be used simply in the sense of bearing witness, but rather for the hidden power and persuasion of the mind concerning those things that belong to our salvation. For through the Spirit consciences are made certain about the things of salvation. Romans 8: The same Spirit bears witness together with our spirit that we are children of God.

units.la: Caeterum hoc discamus praesenti loco, quod, cum hoc testimonium etiam supra capite octavo sit citatum, licet alia de causa, videlicet ad probandum, quod deberet veteri testamento succedere aliud testamentum nouum, non sit alienum: vnum idemque testimonium saepius & diuersis locis citari, quando id diuersis causis seruire cernitur.
units.tr: Moreover, let us learn from this present passage that, since this testimony was also cited above in chapter eight, though for another reason, namely to prove that the old covenant ought to give way to another, the new covenant, it is not out of place for one and the same testimony to be cited more than once and in different places, when it is seen to serve different purposes.

units.la: Deinde admonemur diligentiae adhibendae, quoties Scripturae sacrae locos tractamus.
units.tr: Next we are reminded that care must be applied whenever we treat passages of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Videre oportet, quam variae res, & quam multiplex doctrina vnoquoque loco confirmetur.
units.tr: We must see how many different things, and how manifold a doctrine, is confirmed by each passage.

units.la: Neq; enim Scriptura sterilis est, sed multo foecundissima quaedam omnis doctrinae parens, & nihil tam angustè in ea dictum, ex quo non multiplex aut exhortatio, aut consolatio, aut mysterium queat excerpi.
units.tr: For Scripture is not barren, but is a most fruitful parent of all doctrine, and nothing is said so narrowly in it that from it there cannot be drawn out manifold exhortation, consolation, or mystery.

units.la: Scriptura se habet instar malogranati, in quo quot grana sunt, tot quasi nuclei: itain Scriptura quot apices, tot mysteria, & propterea Christus dixit, ne apicem quidem fore otiosum.
units.tr: Scripture is like a pomegranate, in which, as there are many seeds, so there are as many kernels; so too in Scripture, as many iota-strokes, so many mysteries. For this reason Christ said that not even an iota would be without purpose.

units.la: Sed hoc nequaquam pretereundum, quod, quia colligitur ex eo, quod hic dicitur de remissione peccatorum, ideo tribui istud sacrificio Christi, videtur istud non satis recte fieri.
units.tr: But this must by no means be passed over: since it is inferred from what is said here about the forgiveness of sins that this is ascribed to the sacrifice of Christ, it seems that this is not done quite rightly.

units.la: Nam alias saepe etiam in lege occurrunt eiusmodi loci, in quibus videtur remissio peccatorum promitti: imo etiam quasi ratione sacrificiorum: sicut licet videre in Leuitico & alibi.
units.tr: For elsewhere, even in the law, passages of this kind often occur in which the forgiveness of sins seems to be promised, even as if by reason of the sacrifices, as may be seen in Leviticus and elsewhere.

units.la: Respondetur, quod in illis locis promittitur remissio peccatorum, sed non quasi ex opere operato sacrificiorum contingeret illa, sed potius propter fidem in Christum in sacrificijs illis adumbratum, sicut alias a nobis dictum est, & ad praefigurandam remissionem peccatorum, quae per Christum debebat obtingere.
units.tr: The answer is that in those places forgiveness of sins is promised, but not as if it came from the sacrifices by their own working, but rather on account of faith in Christ, who was foreshadowed in those sacrifices, as we have said at other times, and in order to prefigure the forgiveness of sins that was to be obtained through Christ.

units.la: 1. Adumbratio remissionis peccatorum in Christo. Deinde, non eodem modo agitur in illis locis de remissione peccatorum, sicut in praesenti testimonio. Hic enim agitur de ea, prout est propria nota, qua discernitur Euangelium a lege, & ut confertur proprie in novo testamento, longe alia ratione, quàm adumbratur in testamento veteri. Plura hic dicenda de hoc effectu sacrificij Christi, quanta item sit remissio peccatorum: quod nunquam in sacrificijs legalibus ea comparari, citra fidem in Christum potuerit: quod item sacrificia legalia eam tantum praefigurarint: & quae generis sunt eiusdem.
units.tr: 1. The foreshadowing of the forgiveness of sins in Christ. Next, the forgiveness of sins is not treated in those places in the same way as in the present testimony. For here it is treated as it is the proper mark by which the Gospel is distinguished from the law, and as it is properly conferred in the new covenant, by a very different manner from that which is foreshadowed in the old covenant. Much more must be said here about this effect of Christ's sacrifice, and also about how great the forgiveness of sins is: that it could never be obtained by the legal sacrifices apart from faith in Christ; that the legal sacrifices likewise only foreshadowed it; and about other matters of the same kind.

units.la: Iam potest & hoc praesenti loco agitari, quando describitur Christus sedens ad dexteram patris, solumque restare, ut subijciantur inimici pedibus eius, manifestum hic fieri, quòd Christus nequaquam iterum sit futurus hostia, ut liberet damnatos seu daemones: sed nec vlla ratione alia hos saluandos, verum subijciendos Christi pedibus. Qua de re Anabaptistae quidam nostro tempore nonnulla moverunt. Dicemus fortasis nonnulla de hac re paulo post.
units.tr: Now this present passage can also raise the question, when Christ is described as sitting at the right hand of the Father, and only remaining that his enemies be put under his feet: it becomes plain here that Christ will by no means be a sacrifice again, to free the damned or the demons; nor will they be saved in any other way, but rather be subjected under Christ's feet. Certain Anabaptists in our time have raised several objections on this matter. Perhaps we shall say something about this matter a little later.

units.la: Porrò, vbi horum est remissio, non est amplius oblatio pro peccato.
units.tr: Moreover, where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.

units.la: Illatio instar Epiphonematis breviter & argutè subiecta, totius disputationis summam complectens, nempe per unicum sacrificium Christi, quod causa est remissionis peccatorum, abrogata esse omnia sacrificia legalia. Etsi autem illatio haec fluere videatur ex proximè praecedenti argumento, atq; ad idem argumentum referenda, ut nimirum significetur, Christi sacrificium nequaquam iterandum, tamen nemo non videt, multò commodissimè ad vniuersam referri disputationem, quam constat in hoc potissimum institutà, ut doceretur contra Iudaeos (qui pertinacissimè contendebant, retinendas esse commiscendasque cum Euangelio legis ceremonias) ipsum adeò sacerdotium, simulque omnia sacrificia legalia esse abrogata. Hic sanè totius disputationis sensus & caput est. Et cur interpretemur de non iterando sacrificio Christi, quando id suprà ad finem capitis noni aliis argumentis propriè in id paratis satis est demonstratum? Ergo pro clausula totius disputationis haec verba accipientur.
units.tr: This conclusion, briefly and skilfully added like an epiphonema, sums up the whole argument: namely, that through the single sacrifice of Christ, which is the cause of the forgiveness of sins, all the legal sacrifices have been abrogated. Although this conclusion may seem to flow from the immediately preceding argument, and to be referred to that same argument, in order to signify that Christ's sacrifice is by no means to be repeated, yet everyone sees that it is much more fittingly referred to the whole discussion, which was undertaken chiefly for this purpose: to teach against the Jews (who most stubbornly contended that the ceremonies of the law were to be retained and mixed with the Gospel) that the priesthood itself, together with all the legal sacrifices, has been abrogated. This is indeed the sense and the heart of the whole discussion. And why should we interpret it of the non-repetition of Christ's sacrifice, when this has already been sufficiently demonstrated at the end of chapter nine by other arguments prepared properly for that purpose? Therefore these words are to be taken as the closing statement of the whole discussion.

units.la: Vide autem, quàm rectè sequatur. Proximo argumento probatum est, vnicum sacrificium Christi efficax fuisse pro obtinenda remissione peccatorum: & initio huius capitis probatum est, sacrificia legalia ideò in usu perpetuo fuisse, & semper eadem repeti solita, quia nunquàm poterant auferre peccata.
units.tr: See how rightly it follows. By the preceding argument it was proved that the single sacrifice of Christ was effective for obtaining the forgiveness of sins; and at the beginning of this chapter it was proved that the legal sacrifices were in perpetual use, and were always accustomed to be repeated, because they could never take away sins.

units.la: Iam igitur rectè infertur, quòd, quando oblatum est illud sacrificium, quo ablata sunt peccata, non amplius requiratur, ut noua sacrificia offerantur: ac finem omnibus sacrificijs, praesertim legalibus esse impositum. Et certè, vbi iam remedium porrectum est effica× ad tollendos morbos nostros, si voluerimus rursus noua remedia superaddere, id peringe erit, ac si primum & principale illud remedium iudicemus inefficax & non sufficiens. Itaque ne hoc pacto sacrificio Christi sua detrahatur dignitas, quasi per id non esset plena peccatorum remissio, non est amplius hostia alia expectanda vel imaginanda.
units.tr: Now it is therefore rightly inferred that, when that sacrifice has been offered by which sins have been taken away, there is no longer any need for new sacrifices to be offered; and that an end has been put to all sacrifices, especially the legal ones. And certainly, when a remedy has already been provided that is effective for removing our diseases, if we wished to add new remedies again, it would amount to judging that first and principal remedy to be ineffective and insufficient. Therefore, so that the dignity of Christ's sacrifice is not diminished, as if through it there were not a full forgiveness of sins, there is no longer any other victim to be expected or imagined.

units.la: Significanter autem ait, pro peccato. Nam ut concedatur, adhuc oblationes seu sacrificia fieri, tamen erunt duntaxat ευχαριστιαι, gratiarum actiones, pro peccatorum remissione obtenta, laudes, petitiones, & commemoratio sacrificij semel peracti: at nequaquam sacrificia pro peccato, quae alias propitiatoria, quasi per ea obtineretur peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: He says significantly for sin. For even if it were granted that offerings or sacrifices are still made, they would be only thank-offerings, that is, acts of thanksgiving for the forgiveness of sins obtained, praises, petitions, and remembrance of the sacrifice once offered; but by no means sacrifices for sin, which were propitiatory, as if the forgiveness of sins were obtained through them.

units.la: Istud sanè nullo modo est concedendum, quòd videlicet aliquod sacrificiū esse posit pro peccato, praeter vnicum sacrificium semel per Christum oblatum.
units.tr: This must certainly by no means be conceded: that there could be any sacrifice for sin apart from the one sacrifice once offered by Christ.

units.la: Atque ideo diserte addidit Apostolus particulã istam, pro peccato, quando alias etiam satis fuisset dicere, nullã amplius restare oblationem, ut sententia intelligeretur de sacrificijs legalibus, quorum prorsus nulla amplius sunt offerenda.
units.tr: And so the Apostle expressly added that phrase, "for sin," when he could otherwise have simply said that no further offering remains; so that the statement would be understood of the legal sacrifices, of which none at all are any longer to be offered.

units.la: Quare palàm fit, non amplius appellanda esse aliqua sacrificia pro peccato, seu propitiatoria: sed, si quae pro sacrificijs habebūtur, ea tantùm proEucharisticis agnoscemus: cùm Apostolus clare dicat, non superesse aliquam oblationem pro peccato.
units.tr: Hence it is plain that no sacrifices are any longer to be called sacrifices for sin, or propitiatory; but if any are still held to be sacrifices, we shall acknowledge them only as Eucharistic ones, since the Apostle clearly says that no offering for sin remains.

units.la: Viderint iam illi, qui missas contendunt esse sacrificium, & quidem pro peccato, quòd videlicet per actionem missae contingat & illis qui faciunt, & qui fieri procurant, peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: Let those now see to it who contend that the Mass is a sacrifice, and indeed a sacrifice for sin, because through the action of the Mass the remission of sins is obtained both for those who perform it and for those who have it performed.

units.la: Hic igitur finis est totius huius disputationis, quae reuera tàm excellenter tractata est, tàm validis conferta argumentis, tanto verborum pondere est conscripta, ut nulli rhetores, quàmlibet aliàs eloquentissimi, possent melius, elegantius, euidentius.
units.tr: Here, then, is the end of this whole discussion, which has in truth been treated so excellently, compiled with such strong arguments, and written with such weight of words, that no orators, however eloquent otherwise, could do it better, more elegantly, or more clearly.

units.la: CONCLVSIQ
units.tr: CONCLUSION

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: CVM igitur, fratres, habeamus libertatem adeundi in sancta per sanguinem Iesu, ea via, quam dedicauit nobis recentem ac viuentem, per velamentum, hoc est, per carnem suam, cumq; habeamus sacerdotem magnum praefectum domui Dei, accedamus cum vero corde, in certitudine fidei, aspersi cordibus, ac depulsa conscientia mala, & abluti corpore aqua pura, teneamus confessionem spei, non vacillantem (fidelis enim qui promisit) & consideremus nos inuicem in hoc, vt prouocemus ad charitatem & bona opera, non deserentes aggregationem nostri mutuam, sicut mos est nonnullis: sed adhortantes inuicem, idq; hoc magis, quod videtis appropinquantem diem. Nam si volentes peccauerimus post acceptam, &c.
units.tr: Since, therefore, brethren, we have boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way which he has consecrated for us, through the veil, that is, through his flesh; and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering (for he is faithful who promised), and let us consider one another, to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as is the custom of some, but exhorting one another, and all the more as you see the day drawing near. For if we sin wilfully after we have received, etc.

units.la: Conclusio totius huius disputationis, & secundae partis epistolae, in qua de abrogatione ceremoniarum legis, id est, tum sacerdotij, tum omnium sacrificiorum hucusque est disputatum. Ac diuiditur conclusio haec in duas partes, nempe in Exhortationem, quae protrahitur eousq;. Nam si volentes peccauerimus, &c. Comminationem, cuius postrema verba haec sunt: Horrendum est, incidere in manus Dei viuentis. Quod ad priorem partem attinet, ea sic constituta est, vt proponat nobis verum sacerdotij ac sacrificij Christi vsum, id est, quomodo nos ex eo utilitatem ac fructum possimus capere, idque hoc quidem ordine: Ante omnia exponitur, quae ad quanta bona nobis per sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi sint parata: Deinde, quomodo nos, qui eorum bonorum effici participes cupimus, tum erga Deum, tum erga proximum gerere debeamus, vt nimirum ex his quasi signis agnosci queat, sacerdotium seu sacrificium Christi vere in nobis esse efficax, beneficiaque spiritualia nobis per id obtingere. Sed nos ista in progressu clarius explicabimus. Cum igitur, fratres, habeamus libertatem adeundi in sancta. Pulchre autem haec conclusio respondet disputationis exordio ad finem capitis quarti posito. Nam statim propositioni ipsi adiuncta erant nonnulla, quemadmodum tum ostendebamus, de sacerdotij Christi vsu: & Christus pontifex magnus penetrans coelum, per quem & nos haberemus aditum ad thronum gratiae pro obtinenda misericordia, describebatur, vt & hic fieri cernimus. Verum praesenti loco ea de re longe fusius, sicuti etiam decet, quandoquidem initio disputationis satis erat gustum aliquem utilitatis ex disputatione capiendae propinare. Quanquam Apostolus non tam multa de vsu sacerdotij & sacrificij Christi dicit, quam merito dici poterant, imo & (prout difficulter capiunt animales homines ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei) debuerant multo plura. Quomodo enim satis praedicari queat & commendari Christi sacerdotium, ex quo pendet vniuersae legis impletio, & nostrae salutis summa? Quid enim per Christum actum est pro nobis, quod non ad sacerdotium ipsius referatur? Quaecunq; in lege erant constituta de sacerdotio, de sacrificijs, de sanctificationibus & purgationibus, haec omnia sacerdotium Christi adumbrabant, & ad sacrificium Christi quasi scopum principalem debebant dirigi: omnia haec in sacerdotio Christi vere sunt adimpleta. Deinde, quod Christus pro nobis humiliatus sit, pro nobis orauerit, pro nobis factus sit obediens vsque ad mortem, pro nobis etiam nunc intercedat apud patrem, haec omnia ad sacerdotium eius pertinent, & abipso vt sacerdote sunt perfecta. In summa, sacerdotio Christi salus nostra vniuersa acceptaferi debet, & citra intellectum sacerdotij Christi nihil de negotio restaurationis humanae possumus assequi. Quare hoc pro certo habeatur, omnem vsum sacerdotij Christi nunquam posse ad plenum explicari. Proinde ita accipiemus, quae hic ea de re ab Apostolo sunt praescripta, tanquam principalia & maximè ad causam facientia, & eodem modo expósita, vt plura ex eis possint intelligi, sicuti revera Apostolus sub paucis verbis multa comprehendit, vultque ex ijs plura colligi. Quamobrem & hac ratione conabimur explicare Apostoli verba, vt summa vsus sacrificij Christi clare ex paucis illis percipiatur.
units.tr: This is the conclusion of the whole of this disputation and of the second part of the Epistle, in which the abrogation of the ceremonies of the law has been discussed up to this point, that is, both of the priesthood and of all the sacrifices. This conclusion is divided into two parts: an exhortation, which extends as far as "For if we sin wilfully, etc.", and a warning, whose last words are: "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God." As for the first part, it is so constructed that it sets before us the true use of Christ's priesthood and sacrifice, that is, how we may draw benefit and fruit from it, and it does so in this order. First, it is set out what great good things have been prepared for us through the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. Then, how we who desire to become partakers of those good things ought to behave, both towards God and towards our neighbour, so that from these, as it were, signs it may be recognised that the priesthood or sacrifice of Christ is truly effective in us and that spiritual benefits come to us through it. But we shall explain these things more clearly as we go on. Since, therefore, brethren, we have boldness to enter into the holy place. This conclusion corresponds beautifully to the opening of the disputation, set down at the end of the fourth chapter. For straight after the proposition itself there were added some remarks, as we then showed, on the use of Christ's priesthood, and Christ as the great high priest who passes into heaven, through whom we too have access to the throne of grace to obtain mercy, was described, as we see is done here too. But in the present place we treat this matter at much greater length, as is also fitting, since at the beginning of the disputation it was enough to offer a taste of the usefulness to be gained from the discussion. Yet the Apostle does not say as much about the use of Christ's priesthood and sacrifice as could rightly be said, or indeed (since "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" with ease) as ought to have been said, and far more. For how can Christ's priesthood be sufficiently preached and commended, when on it depends the whole fulfilment of the law and the sum of our salvation? For what has been done for us through Christ that does not refer to his priesthood? Whatever was laid down in the law concerning the priesthood, the sacrifices, the sanctifications and the purifications, all these foreshadowed Christ's priesthood and ought to have been directed as to their chief aim to Christ's sacrifice; all of them are truly fulfilled in the priesthood of Christ. Next, that Christ was humbled for us, prayed for us, became obedient for us even unto death, and even now intercedes for us with the Father, all these belong to his priesthood and have been perfected by him as priest. In sum, our whole salvation must be received from the priesthood of Christ, and without an understanding of Christ's priesthood we can attain nothing in the business of human restoration. Therefore let this be held for certain: the whole use of Christ's priesthood can never be fully explained. Accordingly we shall take what the Apostle has here prescribed on this matter as principal and most pertinent to the cause, and expound it in such a way that many more things may be understood from it, just as in truth the Apostle comprehends many things in a few words and wishes more to be gathered from them. For this reason too we shall endeavour to explain the Apostle's words in such a way that the sum of the use of Christ's sacrifice may be plainly perceived from those few words.

units.la: Ait ergo: Cum igitur, fratres, habeamus libertatem adeundi in sancta: Graece habetur, ἔχοντες οὖν ἀδελφοί παρρησίαν εἰς τὴν εἴσοδον τῶν ἁγίων: Vallae placuit ita reddere, Habentes igitur fratres fiduciam in introitum: ut sit sententia, nos confidere, quod introituri simus in sancta. Et εἴσοδον ambigue sonat, vt reddi possit haberi fiduciam in introitu, quo Christus ingressus est in sancta: vel, in introitum Sanctorum, vt videlicet nos simus ingressuri. Sed plurimi malunt legere, Libertatem ingrediendi in sancta: Quae lectio etiam magis quadrat cum eo, quod subijcitur, Accedamus cum vero corde.
units.tr: He says, therefore: Since, therefore, brethren, we have boldness to enter into the holy place. The Greek reads: ἔχοντες οὖν ἀδελφοί παρρησίαν εἰς τὴν εἴσοδον τῶν ἁγίων [Having therefore, brethren, boldness for the entrance into the holy places]. Valla preferred to render it: Having therefore, brethren, confidence in the entrance, so that the sense is that we trust that we are about to enter into the holy places. And εἴσοδον is ambiguous, so that it may be rendered either as having confidence in the entrance by which Christ went into the holy places, or as confidence in the entrance of the saints, namely that we are going to enter. But most prefer to read: Liberty of entering into the holy places, and this reading also fits better with what follows, Let us draw near with a true heart.

units.la: Vbi enim liberum factum est ingredi, tum animus adijciendus est, vt ingredi pergamus. Ac reuera multo aptius est institutio, necnon multò alacriores fiunt omnes, vbi audiùt, sibi esse libertatem ingrediendi, quàm si tantùm diceretur, fiduciam, adeoque spem factam ingrediendi. Neque hac ratione vocabulum παρρησίας inepte torquetur. Nam significat quidem fiduciam & libertatem, potissimum in sermone, qua quis intrepide & constanter aliquid loquitur: sed praeterea etiam pro libertate in aliis rebus subinde accipitur: quemadmodum indicauimus & capite tertio, super illo verbo: Cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam tenuerimus. Et capite quarto, ibi, Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae. Nec dubium, quin Apostolus hic respexerit ad illum locum capitis quarti. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: For where entry has been made free, the mind must be added so that we go on entering. And indeed the teaching is far more apt, and all are made much more eager, when they hear that liberty of entering is theirs, than if it were merely said that confidence, and therefore hope, of entering had been given. Nor is the word παρρησίας wrested inappropriately in this way. For it indeed signifies confidence and freedom, chiefly in speech, by which someone speaks boldly and steadily about something; but besides this it is also sometimes taken for liberty in other matters, as we pointed out in the third chapter, on those words: Whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the glorying of hope firm to the end. And in the fourth chapter, there: Let us therefore come with confidence to the throne of grace. There is no doubt that the Apostle here had regard to that place in the fourth chapter. But enough of this.

units.la: En aute valde insignis usus atque fructus ex sacerdotio sacrificioque Christi ad nos redens. Per sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi ait nobis liberum in sancta patere aditum. Per sancta autem tametsi recte possemus intelligere ecclesiam, in quam non datur ingredi, nisi admittamur & introducamur per Christum, in cuius sanguine necessum est omnes ingressuros baptizari: tamen libentius coelos intelligemus, sicut Apostolus ipse supra capite nono interpretatus est, dicens: Christum ingressum non in sancta manu facta, sed in ipsum coelum. Iam vide, quanta res sit, liberè posse ingredi coelos, & intelliges beneficij amplitudinem, quod per sacerdotium Christi es consecutus. Olim quidem aditus tantum patebat in sancta materialia, quae exemplaria quaedam erant, & summo tantum sacerdoti, eidemque prius variis & operosis modis purificato: at nunc libertas tibi facta est ingrediendi coelos, tibi inquam, cuiuscunque sis conditionis, & quamlibet nullis operibus tuis sis purificatus seu mundatus. Sic autem supra capite nono dixit, nondum manifestatam fuisse viam in sancta, priore tabernaculo adhuc consistente. Ergo illud iam per Christi sacerdotium atque unicum sacrificium nobis est collatum, quod olim sublege per nulla sacrificia, quamlibet multa & varia parari poterat.
units.tr: Here, then, is a very remarkable use and fruit of Christ's priesthood and sacrifice reaching us. Through the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, he says, a free access to the holy places lies open to us. By "holy places" we could rightly understand the Church, into which no one may enter unless he is admitted and introduced through Christ, in whose blood all who are to enter must necessarily be baptised. Yet we shall more willingly understand the heavens, as the Apostle himself interpreted it above in the ninth chapter, saying that Christ entered not into holy places made with hands, but into heaven itself. Now see how great a thing it is to be able to enter freely into the heavens, and you will understand the greatness of the benefit which you have obtained through the priesthood of Christ. Formerly access lay open only to the earthly holy places, which were certain copies, and only to the high priest, and to him only after he had first been purified in various and laborious ways; but now liberty of entering heaven has been made yours, yours I say, whatever your condition, and however you are not purified or cleansed by any works of your own. Moreover, above in the ninth chapter he said that the way into the holy places had not yet been made manifest while the first tabernacle still stood. Therefore that which could not be obtained under the law through any sacrifices, however many and various, is now conferred upon us through the priesthood of Christ and his one sacrifice.

units.la: Caeterum commemorat Apostolus hunc sacerdotij Christi usum principalem, ut ex eo plures alij, ex hoc fluentes & huic cognati intelligantur. Ita enim necessarium est, ut, quando audimus, liberum factum nobis aditum in sancta, simul intelligamus, (quam doquidem non poterant iuxta legem, ad quam hic subinde alludit, ingredi in sancta, nisi sacerdotes, & ij quoque purgati ac sanctificati:) nos quoque per sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi factos veros sacerdotes ac Dei ministros, item a peccatis omnibus purgatos & mundos, item sanctificatos, &c. Qua de re etiam Apostolus nonnulla mox subijciet. Nec dubium, quin Apostolus, qui lubeter paucis multa significat, ita velit, nos ex ijs, quae principalia & capitalia sunt, caetera coniuncta affiniaque nostra prudentia eruere & ex cerpere.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Apostle mentions this chief use of Christ's priesthood so that many other things flowing from it and akin to it may be understood. For when we hear that access into the holy places has been made free for us, we must necessarily understand at the same time (since, according to the law, to which he here repeatedly alludes, no one could enter the holy places except priests, and even they only when purged and sanctified) that we too, through the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ, have been made true priests and ministers of God; likewise that we have been cleansed and made clean from all sins, likewise sanctified, and so on. The Apostle will himself add some of these things shortly. And there is no doubt that the Apostle, who in few words signifies much, wishes us, by our own prudence, to draw out and extract from those things which are principal and chief the other things that are joined to them and related to them.

units.la: Per sanguinem Iesu) Causa efficiens nostri in coelos ingressus. Non enim per nostra merita, vel quaecunque opera, sed per solum sanguinem Christi aditus in coelos patefactus est. Ac videtur, sanguinem Christi per Metonymiam posuisse pro sacrificio, ut sit sententia: nos libertatem habere ingrediendi in sancta per & propter unicum sacrificium Christi: sed maluisse vsurpare vocem sanguinis, quod ad recte exponendum verum vsum, hoc est, ad accendendos animos, ut acrius intendant in Christi admirandam charitatem, & beneficij amplitudinem, sit accommodatior. Nescio quid sublimius concipiunt animi, magisque mouentur, vbi audiunt, oblatum pro se Christi sanguinem, quam si simpliciter diceretur, Christum obtulisse pro ipsis sacrificium. Ipsa sacrificij materia considerata plus mouet. Quanquam exiitimo potius hic proponi spectandam causam formalem, atque alludere Apostolum respicereque ad ritum pontificum ingredientium in sancta, sed non absque sanguine, (sicut supra dixit, pontifices ingredi sancta quotannis, per sanguinem alienum) eritque sententia: Nobis apertam viam in sancta caelestia, sed ita, ut adeamus cum sanguine, non hircorum aut vitulorum, sed Christi, qui solus Deo patri acceptus est, ac plene expians peccata. Atque haec interpretatio magis arridet, propter sequentia, in quibus etiam allusio est, seu allegoria, de velamento. Sequitur namq;.
units.tr: Through the blood of Jesus) This is the efficient cause of our entrance into heaven. For access into heaven was opened not through our merits or any works of ours, but through the blood of Christ alone. It seems that by metonymy he has put "blood of Christ" for "sacrifice," so that the sense is: we have freedom to enter into the holy places through and on account of the one sacrifice of Christ. But he preferred to use the word "blood," because it is better suited to expounding the true meaning properly, that is, to kindling minds so that they attend more keenly to Christ's wonderful love and the greatness of his benefit. Minds conceive something more lofty and are more moved when they hear that Christ's blood was offered for them than if it were simply said that Christ offered a sacrifice on their behalf. The very substance of the sacrifice moves more. Yet I think that what is set before us here is rather the formal cause to be considered, and that the Apostle alludes to and looks back at the rite of the high priests entering the holy places, but not without blood (as he said above, that the high priests enter the holy places every year with the blood of another). The sense will be: an open way into the heavenly holy places is given to us, but in such a way that we approach with blood, not of goats or calves, but of Christ, who alone is acceptable to God the Father and fully expiates sins. This interpretation pleases me more, on account of what follows, in which there is also an allusion, or allegory, concerning the veil. For it follows:

units.la: Ea via, quam dedicauit nobis recentem ac viuentem per velamentum, hoc est, per carnem suam.
units.tr: By the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is, through his flesh.

units.la: Pertinet & istud ad causam formalem, seu modum, quo adeunda sunt nobis Sancta. Vbi enim auditum est, potestatem nobis factam libere ingrediundi in Sancta: deinde vero adiectum, quod cum Christi sanguine: hinc statim animus mouetur ad inquirendum etiam, qua via eo contendamus.
units.tr: This too pertains to the formal cause, or the manner in which we must enter the holy places. For when it has been heard that the power has been given to us to enter freely into the holy places, and then it is added, "with the blood of Christ," the mind is immediately moved to inquire also by what way we are to make our approach.

units.la: Docet igitur & hoc Apostolus, dicens, ea via ingrediundum, quam Christus per velamentum, id est, carnem suam, siue humanitatem praemonstrauit. Nam Christus in carne, siue spectetur vt precium depensum pro peccatis, siue vt propositus in exemplum, sane vtroque modo nobis via est, per quam in coelos ingredimur. Etiam præsenti loco potius conueniet, priore modo Christum pro via accipere. Atque iterum alludit ad id, quòd sacerdotes legales introibant in sancta sanctorum per velamentum, vti supra capite nono expositum est.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle teaches this also, saying that we must enter by the way which Christ showed beforehand through the veil, that is, through his flesh or humanity. For Christ in the flesh, whether he is regarded as the price paid for sins or as set forth as an example, is certainly in either way a way for us by which we enter into heaven. In the present passage it will rather fit to take Christ as the way in the former sense. And again he alludes to the fact that the legal priests entered into the holy of holies through the veil, as was explained above in chapter nine.

units.la: Porrò velamentum ipse interpretatur carnem Christi, & recte, quandoquidem eave lata fuit, & quodammodo dissimulata, exinanita & tecta fuit eius diuinitas. Verbum habi tauit in carne nostra, & ea quasi velo fuit circumdatum. Hinc & illæ formulæ loquen di, quibus Christus dicitur induisse carnem nostram, & forma serui indutus. Cumi gitur dicitur, ea via nobis adeundum cœlum, quam dedicauit nobis Christus per car nem suam, sententia est, salutem nobis patere & paratam esse per Christi naturam hu manam, & Christum salutis nostrae vniuersum negotium per carnem peregisse, mor tem videlicet in ea subijisse, & pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, ideoque in eam quasi vi am nobis respiciendum. Quæ interpretatio valde apposita est ad caussam sacrificij, de quo hactenus semper disputatum est. Hostia enim, seu sacrificium fuit Chri sti caro.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle himself interprets the veil as the flesh of Christ, and rightly, since his divinity was in a sense concealed, emptied and covered, as though by a veil. "The Word dwelt in our flesh," and that flesh was, as it were, wrapped around him like a veil. Hence also those forms of speech by which Christ is said to have put on our flesh, and to have taken the form of a servant. So when it is said that we must approach heaven by the way which Christ dedicated for us through his flesh, the sense is that salvation lies open to us and is prepared through Christ's human nature, and that Christ accomplished the whole business of our salvation through the flesh, namely by undergoing death in it and making satisfaction for our sins, and therefore we must look to it as to a way. This interpretation fits very well with the cause of the sacrifice, which has always been the subject of discussion up to now. For the victim, or sacrifice, was the flesh of Christ.

units.la: Sciendum autem, in Scripturis Christi carnem, siue Christum in humana natura du pliciter nobis propositum: vno modo vt precium: quia nimirum Christus in carne sua pro nobis passus est, & pro peccatis nostris dependit. Quo pertinent omnes loci testan tes, nos liberatos & redemptos per sanguinem ac mortem Christi. Alio modo propo nitur nobis vt exemplum: quia Christus doctrina & vita sua ostendit, quomodo sit no bis viuendum, vt Deo patri gratissimus, vt fidem in Deum, & charitatem in proximum testatam faciamus. Huc pertinent omnes ipsius actiones, charitatem ac dilectionem maximam nobis delineantes: item omnes loci, quibus ad imitationem ipsius prouoca mur. Vtroque autem modo dicitur Christus via in cœlos, tàm vbi consideratur vt pre cium, quàm vbi consideratur vt exemplum. Nam sequendo exemplum ipsius, & in se quendo hac in parte vestigia ipsius, per innocentiam, humilitatem, charitatem, patien tiam, &c. eò deducimur, quò ipse ante nos vt præcursor noster ingressus est. Quod au tem ad præsentem locum attinet, ita potius Christum viam in cœlos esse statuemus, vt tanquam precium consideratur. Clarum enim est, morte ipsius, quam in velamento carnis pertulit, viam nobis in cœlos primùm patefactam: & nobis libertatem ingrediun di per hanc, & propter hanc contingere.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that in the Scriptures Christ's flesh, or Christ in the human nature, is set before us in two ways: in one way as the price, because Christ indeed suffered in his flesh for us and hung for our sins. To this pertain all the passages testifying that we are freed and redeemed through the blood and death of Christ. In another way he is set before us as an example, because by his teaching and life Christ shows how we are to live so as to be most pleasing to God the Father, so that we may bear witness of faith in God and love toward our neighbour. To this pertain all his actions, which portray for us his greatest charity and love, and also all the passages by which we are called to imitate him. Yet in either way Christ is called the way into heaven, both when he is considered as the price and when he is considered as the example. For by following his example, and by treading in this part his footsteps, through innocence, humility, charity, patience, and so on, we are led to the place where he himself, as our forerunner, has entered before us. As for the present passage, we shall rather establish that Christ is the way into heaven in the sense that he is considered as the price. For it is clear that the way into heaven was first opened to us by his death, which he endured in the veil of the flesh, and that the freedom to enter comes to us through this and on account of this.

units.la: Si altero quoque modo volumus, Christum in carne hic nobis viam proponere, tùm sententia erit, nos ita demum ingressuros in cœlos, si Christi vitam & virtutes strenuè insequamur. Sed prior interpretatio mihi videtur instituto rectius conuenire. Et quidem eò magis, quòd dicit, Christum eam nobis dedicasse, & primùm innouasse. In gressus est ipse viam vniuersæ carnis, eoque ingressu nobis quoque dedicauit, præpara uit, & innouauit viam in cœlum. Dedicatio dicitur initium vtendi, inquit Chrysosto mus. Nos igitur quotquot verè in Christum credimus, & sacrificium eius Deo patri ac ceptum ad tollenda peccata confidimus, illi sumus, propter quos via per Christu aper ta est, & quos voluit ad gloriam obtinendam insequi. Sic verò & Michææ capite se cundo describit Christum præeuntem in cœlos, vt ipsum credentes sequantur: Ascen det, inquit, pandens iter ante eos. Diuidet, & transibunt portam, & egredientur per eam. Et transibit rex eorum coram eis, & Dominus in capite eorum.
units.tr: If we also wish, in the other way, that Christ in the flesh here sets forth the way for us, then the sense will be that we shall enter into heaven only if we vigorously follow the life and virtues of Christ. But the former interpretation seems to me to fit the purpose more rightly. And all the more so because it says that Christ dedicated this way for us and first renewed it. He himself entered the way of all flesh, and by that entrance he also dedicated, prepared and renewed for us the way into heaven. "Dedication," says Chrysostom, "is the beginning of use." Therefore we, as many as truly believe in Christ and confidently trust that his sacrifice is acceptable to God the Father for the removal of sins, are those for whose sake the way has been opened through Christ, and whom he willed to follow in order to obtain glory. Micah also, in chapter two, describes Christ going before into heaven, so that believers may follow him: "He will go up," it says, "opening the way before them. They will break through, and will pass through the gate and go out through it. And their king will pass before them, and the Lord at their head."

units.la: Cæterum viam hanc per Christum stratam, apertá, recentem, atq; viuentem. Recentem quidem, quia antea ignota fuit, aut certè si patribus quicquam de ea fuit per typos siue vmbras, aut etiam per promissiones prophetarum significatum: tamen ante hac nunquam fuit relata: vt nostram felicitatem præ patribus hic agnoscamus. Veli deo recentem, quòd alia ratione, quàm olim plerique crediderunt: non enim per sacri ficia legalia, vel huiusmodi: non per opera legis, sed per fidem in Christum: vt non pro pter nos, vel nostra opera, sed propter solum Christum aditus sit patefactus.
units.tr: Moreover, this way was made by Christ, open, new and living. New indeed, because it was unknown before, or at least, if anything about it was signified to the fathers through types or shadows, or even through the promises of the prophets, nevertheless it was never before revealed, so that we may here recognise our happiness above that of the fathers. It is also new in that it is by a different reasoning from that which most had believed in former times: not through legal sacrifices or things of that kind, not through the works of the law, but through faith in Christ, so that the access has been opened not on account of us or our works, but on account of Christ alone.

units.la: Viuentem verò, quia recta ad vitam æternam tendit, & eadem exhibetur, quod in lege non eadem ratione fiebat. Hinc vbi in lege promissiones principales pro ponebant temporalia bona, quibus tamen spiritualia adumbrabantur, & patres hu iusmodi fide apprehendebant, in euangelio semper spiritualia proponuntur & reuera exhibentur.
units.tr: And it is living, because it leads straight to eternal life, and that life is exhibited, which in the law did not happen on the same principle. Hence, where in the law the chief promises set forth temporal goods, under which spiritual things were nevertheless foreshadowed, and the fathers laid hold of these by such faith, in the gospel spiritual things are always set forth and in truth exhibited.

units.la: Huc pertinent conciones illæ Christi, Hæc est vita æterna, &c. Ioannis capite sexto & capite decimoseptimo, &c. Vel via per Christum aperta dicitur viens, vtopponatur viæ mortuæ in lege, quæ vitam non adferebat, vtpote in qua omnia mortua erant, quæ offerebantur in signum, quòd vita ex illis pa rari non posset. Christus autem obtulit semetipsum viuum: vnde & vitam adferre potuit. Quanquam & viuens dici potest, quia spiritualis est: quandoquidem viuentia dicuntur, quæ spiritualia sunt, & ex spiritu fiunt. Caro non prodest quicquam, sed spiritus est, qui viuificat. Quapropter Romanorum capite duodecimo, iubemur offerre corpora nostra hostiam viuentem, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem cultum.
units.tr: To this pertain those sermons of Christ, "This is eternal life," etc., in John chapter six and chapter seventeen, etc. Or the way opened through Christ is called living, as opposed to the dead way in the law, which did not bring life, inasmuch as all the things offered in it were dead, and were offered as a sign that life could not be obtained from them. But Christ offered himself living, and therefore was able to bring life. Yet it may also be called living because it is spiritual, since those things are called living which are spiritual and are done by the Spirit. "The flesh profits nothing, but it is the Spirit who gives life." Therefore in Romans chapter twelve we are bidden to offer our bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, a rational worship.

units.la: Igitur propter talem hostiam à Christo oblatam, via, quam Christus per hostiam illam aperuit, viuens quoque appellatur. Debent proinde piæ mentes valde intentæ ese in hanc viæ per Christum nobis patefactæ descriptionem, qua appellatur & noua & viuens. Nam hæ appellationes nos maximarum rerum admonent, si paulò altiori mente considerentur.
units.tr: Therefore, because of such a sacrifice offered by Christ, the way which Christ opened through that sacrifice is also called living. Pious minds ought, accordingly, to be very attentive to this description of the way made known to us through Christ, by which it is called both new and living. For these appellations remind us of very great things, if they are considered with a somewhat higher mind.

units.la: Cum ergo habeamus sacerdotem magnum præfectum domui Dei) En iterum insignis locus de usu sacerdotij Christi paucis verbis multa complectens. Significatur enim hic, non amplius nobis esse sacerdotes legales, qui neque sacrificijs, neque aliis modis possint quicquam efficere: sed unicum sacerdotem verè magnum nobis propositum, qui cùm pecata unica sua oblatione expiarit, tum verò & nunc in cœlis agens apud Patrem pro nobis assiduè intercedere non desinit. Quæ ratio valde profectò consolatoria est, & aliàs crebrò, vt consolationem inde petant credentes, proponitur: clarissimè verò prima Ioannis capite secundo, Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum iustum. Hoc inquam est, quod sibi vult Apostolus, quando ait, nos habere sacerdotem magnum præfectum domui Dei. In certitudine fidei) Interpretatur varijs modis, quomodo Deum vero corde adeamus. Ac primùm ait, opus esse certa, indubitata, inconcussa, in Deum fide: quæ certè primo loco necessaria est ijs, qui Deum adire & beneficiorum spiritualium participes fieri cupiunt. Est autem πληροφορία plena & indubitata, adeoq; iam certis argumentis, autrebus ipsis confirmata fides. Alias à nobis de ea dictum est.
units.tr: "Since then we have a great priest set over the house of God." Here again is a notable passage about the office of Christ's priesthood, comprehending much in a few words. For it signifies that we no longer have legal priests, who could accomplish nothing by sacrifices or by other means; rather, one truly great priest is set before us, who, having expiated sins by his single offering, now also in heaven, acting before the Father, never ceases to intercede for us. This reasoning is indeed very consoling, and it is often set forth elsewhere so that believers may draw comfort from it; most clearly in the first letter of John, chapter two: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." This, I say, is what the Apostle means when he says that we have a great priest set over the house of God. "In the certainty of faith": he explains in various ways how we may draw near to God with a true heart. And first he says that a certain, undoubting, unshaken faith in God is required; this is certainly necessary first of all for those who wish to approach God and become partakers of spiritual benefits. Now "full assurance" [πληροφορία] is a faith that is full and undoubting, and therefore confirmed by sure arguments or by the things themselves. I have spoken of this elsewhere.

units.la: Habemus ergo hic in nomine πληροφορίας insignem commendationem fidei, quæ semper primo loco necessaria est, sicut & capite vndecimo subijcitur: Sine fide heri non potest, vt quis Deo placeat: nam, qui accedit ad Deum, hunc credere oportet, esse Deum, & esse remuneratorem quærentibus se. Non debet mens hæsitare, vel de aliquo dubitare. Et hæc fidei certitudo loco sacrificij apud Deum reputabitur. Elegante verò Chrysostomus: Hic, inquit, nihil visibile est, neque sacerdos iam, neque sacrificium, neque altare, sed omnia fiunt in spiritu & veritate: Id quod etiam adumbratum videtur in summo pontifice semel in anno ingredienti in sancta, qui tùm quoque videri à populo non poterat, imò nec propitiatorium ipse cernebat, thuris incensione nebulam excitans, quæ conspectum propitiatorij intercipiebat. His reuera significabatur, Deum vero corde & spiritu adeundum adorandumq;.
units.tr: Here, then, in the word "full assurance" we have a remarkable commendation of faith, which is always necessary first of all, as is also added in chapter eleven: "Without faith it is impossible to please God; for he who comes to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him." The mind must not waver or doubt anything. And this certainty of faith will be reckoned before God in place of sacrifice. Chrysostom says elegantly: "Here nothing is visible, neither priest now, nor sacrifice, nor altar, but all things are done in spirit and truth." This seems also to have been foreshadowed in the high priest, who once a year entered into the holy places, and at that time could not be seen by the people, nor did he himself even see the mercy seat, since by kindling incense he raised a cloud which blocked the view of the mercy seat. By this it was truly signified that God must be approached and worshipped with a true heart and spirit.

units.la: Aspersi cordibus, ac depulsa conscientia mala) Alludens ad ritum, quo, vt scribitur Leuitici capite decimosexto, qui ingressuri erant in sancta, prius debebant lauari: præterea & sanguinem vituli pro peccatis oblati secum ferre, vt septies aspergerent contra propitiatorium ad orientem: docet nos quoque, si ingredi volumus in sancta, debere similiter lauari ac purificari, sed cordibus potius, quàm corporibus. Cùm tota hac disputatione docuerit, & sacerdotium, & ceremonias legis abrogatas, valde prudenter iam in conclusione præscribit, qualia nobis illarum loco succedant peragenda: & quomodo potiora longè sint, quæ à nobis fieri debeant, quàm quæ fiebant ab illis sub lege. Atq; hac ratione simul satisfacit illis, qui ægrè ferebant, se à ceremonijs legalibus abduci. Certè quando ipsis proponuntur præstantiora & perfectiora, non est quod auidè respirent ad egena & infirma elementa mundi. Ergo corporû aspersioni rectè succedit aspersio cordium.
units.tr: "Sprinkled in our hearts, and our evil conscience removed": alluding to the rite by which, as is written in Leviticus chapter sixteen, those who were about to enter the holy places had first to be washed, and besides had to carry with them the blood of the calf offered for sins, to sprinkle it seven times toward the east before the mercy seat. He teaches us also that, if we wish to enter the holy places, we must likewise be washed and purified, but in our hearts rather than in our bodies. Since in this whole discussion he has taught that both the priesthood and the ceremonies of the law have been abrogated, he now prudently prescribes in the conclusion what must be done in their place, and how the things which we ought to do are far more excellent than those which were done by them under the law. And by this reasoning he at the same time satisfies those who were troubled at being drawn away from legal ceremonies. Certainly, when more excellent and more perfect things are set before them, there is no reason for them to pant greedily after the weak and beggarly elements of the world. Therefore the sprinkling of hearts rightly takes the place of the sprinkling of bodies.

units.la: Porrò exponit, quomodo contingat corda aspergi siue ablui, quando addit, à conscientia mala: Quasi dicat: tùm demùm verè abluta corda, vbi non amplius propter fidem in Christum conscientia mala grauamur, siue non amplius metu damnationis terremur. Sic verò & Petrus Actorum quinto aiebat, fide purificari corda. Suprà quidem initio præsentis capitis dictum est, eos, qui sacrificarunt, adhuc habuisse conscientiam peccatorum: quandoquidem per sacrificia illa non remittebantur peccata.
units.tr: Further, he explains how the hearts are sprinkled or washed, when he adds: "from an evil conscience." As if he said: the hearts are then truly washed when we are no longer burdened by an evil conscience on account of faith in Christ, or no longer terrified by fear of condemnation. So also Peter, in Acts chapter five, said that hearts are purified by faith. Indeed, it was said above at the beginning of this chapter that those who offered sacrifices still had a consciousness of sins, since sins were not forgiven through those sacrifices.

units.la: Proinde hoc loco ait, liberatos nos à conscientia peccatorum: quod quidem fit, vbi per illam πληροφορίαν fidei certò statuimus, nos esse in Christo, id est, Christum pro nobis obtulisse, nostra peccata expiasse: ac tùm quidem verum illud de nobis erit Romanorum capite octauo. Nulla condemnatio hic, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Quanquam videri posset & his respexisse ad id, quòd confitebantur sacerdotes sua & populi peccata, vt vides Leuitici capite decimosexto. Sæpè autem occurrunt in nouo testamento loci, qui docent, nos esse lotos, ablutos, purificatos, mundatos sanguine Christi. Quare valde appositè ait, nos debere aspergi seu ablui cordibus, vt sancta sanctorum, id est, cœlum ingrediamur.
units.tr: Therefore in this place he says that we are freed from the consciousness of sins; and this certainly happens when, by that full assurance of faith, we firmly establish that we are in Christ, that is, that Christ has offered himself for us and expiated our sins; and then that true word of Romans chapter eight will be true of us: "There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." Although it might seem that he also had regard to the fact that the priests and the people confessed their sins, as you see in Leviticus chapter sixteen. Moreover, passages often occur in the New Testament which teach that we have been washed, cleansed, purified, and made clean by the blood of Christ. Hence he very aptly says that we ought to be sprinkled or washed in our hearts, so that we may enter the holy of holies, that is, heaven.

units.la: Et abluti corpore aqua pura) Addit & de vnica externa nostra ablutione corporis, quæ omnibus externis ablutionibus legalibus multo est præstantior, quam cum confessione fidei in ecclesia suscipimus, in internæ aspersionis cordium signum quoddam & certitudinem.
units.tr: "And our bodies washed with pure water": he adds also a word about our single external washing of the body, which is far more excellent than all the external legal washings, and which, when we receive it in the church with confession of faith, is a certain sign and assurance of the inward sprinkling of the heart.

units.la: Loquitur enim de nostro baptismo, in quo externa ablutio significat ablutionem conscientiæ internam, iuxta regulam de Sacramentis, qua dicitur, externa signa symbola esse, & similitudinem habere cum re spirituali & interna, quæ significatur. Atque hac ratione morosis Hebræis molestè ferentibus, omnes illas corporales lotiones deprimi atque excludi, vnum adhuc promittit externam lotionem, baptismi inquam à Christo institui, qui lotionibus omnibus longè est præstantior, & quo reuera non adeò corpora, sed multò magis corda ipsa purificantur: Ideoq; magna Emphasi addidit vocem, Pura: quæ certè, vbi in veteri testamento de lotionibus agitur, non eodem modo inuenitur addita.
units.tr: For he speaks of our baptism, in which the external washing signifies the inward washing of conscience, according to the rule concerning the sacraments, which says that external signs are symbols and have a likeness to the spiritual and inward thing which they signify. And by this reasoning, since the stubborn Hebrews were displeased that all those bodily washings were lowered and excluded, he still promises one external washing, namely baptism instituted by Christ, which is far more excellent than all washings, and by which truly not so much the bodies as much more the hearts themselves are purified. Therefore with great emphasis he added the word "pure," which certainly is not found added in the same way where the washings are spoken of in the Old Testament.

units.la: Nam illa aqua nec verè pura erat, nec purificandi vim habebat: Nostra autem aqua pura est, indeque vim purificandi obtinet: Non quidem per se se, sed propter verbum, cuius causa fit Sacramentum, & vis illa purificandi superuenit. De nit. De hac aqua Ezechielis capite trigesimosexto, Effundam super vos aquam mundam, & mundabimini ab omnibus inquinamentis vestris, & ab vniuersis idolis vestris mundabo vos. Ad Titum capite tertio, vocatur lauacrum regenerationis & renovationis spiritus Sancti. Quàm verò necessarium sit baptisma volentibus ingredi in sanctaSanctorum, siue in coelum, liquet ex illo Christi Ioannis cap. tertio, Nisi quis natus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei.
units.tr: For that water was neither truly pure, nor had the power of purifying; but our water is pure, and therefore obtains the power of purifying: not indeed of itself, but on account of the word, for whose sake the sacrament is made, and that power of purifying comes upon it. Concerning this water, Ezekiel chapter thirty-six: "I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses, and from all your idols I will cleanse you." To Titus chapter three: it is called "the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit." How necessary baptism is to those who wish to enter into the Holy of Holies, or into heaven, is clear from that saying of Christ in John chapter three: "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."

units.la: Vnde nonnullis placuit ianuam salutis & vestibulum appellare. Vtrùm verò non posse quispiam salutem consequi citra externam ablutionem baptismi, hunc non disputamus. Videatur de hac re Augustinus & alij. Certè licet corde credatur ad iustitiam, tamen requiritur etiam ad salutem, vt accedat oris confessio: Romanorum capite decimo. Itaque necessaria est externa confessio, quae tum multis modis fiet, tum nulla ratione rectius aut melius, quàm externo Sacramenti vsu. Vbi ergo fieri potest, & contingit, qui possit Sacramentum conferre, debet credens summa cum devotione animi id petere & accipere.
units.tr: Hence it has pleased some to call baptism the gate of salvation and the vestibule. Whether anyone can obtain salvation without the external washing of baptism, we do not here dispute; let Augustine and others be consulted on this matter. Certainly, although with the heart one believes unto righteousness, yet confession of the mouth is also required for salvation: Romans chapter ten. Therefore external confession is necessary, which indeed will be made in many ways, yet in no way more rightly or better than by the external use of the sacrament. Where, therefore, it can happen, and it is possible, that someone may confer the sacrament, the believer ought with the greatest devotion of mind to seek and receive it.

units.la: Teneamus confessionem spei non vacillantem) Sicut fidem, ita Spem quoque ait necessariam volentibus spirituales fructus sacerdotij Christi percipere. Vtraque enim ex aequo in Deum, & res promissas tendit: imò sic sunt coniunctae, vt altera sine altera esse nequeat. Neque dicit tantùm, teneamus spem, sed confessionem spei. Oportet confiteri coram hominibus, si volumus, vt Christus agnoscat nos coram suo Patre in coelis. Oportet confiteamur nos esse illos, qui confidant & sperent, se propter Christum acipiendos à patre in gratiam, qui constanter omnia propter Christum relinquant & abijciant. Addit, imò vacillantem, seu quae inclinari aut labefactari nulla ratione queat. Qui perseuerauerit vsque in finem, hic saluus erit. Oportet persuasum habere, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, neque principatus, neque potestates, neque instantia, neque futura, neque altitudo, neque profunditas, neq; vlla alia creatura poterit nos separari à dilectione Dei.
units.tr: "Let us hold fast the confession of hope without wavering": just as faith, so he says hope also is necessary for those who wish to receive the spiritual fruits of Christ's priesthood. For both alike tend toward God and the promised things; indeed they are so joined that the one cannot exist without the other. Nor does he say merely "let us hold hope," but "the confession of hope." It is necessary to confess before men, if we wish Christ to acknowledge us before his Father in heaven. We must confess that we are those who trust and hope that, for Christ's sake, they will be received by the Father into favour, who constantly leave and cast off everything for Christ's sake. He adds "without wavering," that is, which cannot be inclined or weakened in any way. "He who perseveres to the end, the same shall be saved." We must be persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God.

units.la: Et certè si spectemus bonorum nobis post hanc vitam promissorum altitudinem, quòd videlicet sint eiusmodi, quae nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec cor hominis apprehendit, magnum erit nobis calcar ad perseuerandum in sancta spe. Sed ipse Apostolus egregiam rationem subijcit dicens:
units.tr: And certainly, if we consider the greatness of the good things promised to us after this life, namely that they are of such a kind that "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has the heart of man conceived," this will be a great spur to us to persevere in holy hope. But the Apostle himself adds an excellent reason, saying:

units.la: Fidelis enim qui promisit) Ratio obiter interposita, quare sit in fide & spe perseuerandum, à certitudine accipiendi res promissas, siue ab eo, quòd Deus credentes nequaquam fallit. Haec laus de Deo passim in Scripturis praedicatur, & deberet semper versari ob oculos, praesertim in tentationibus, & sentiremus haud dubiè, miserias nostras subinde leuari huius bonitatis diuinae contemplatione.
units.tr: For faithful is he who promised) This reason is inserted in passing for why we must persevere in faith and hope: it rests on the certainty of receiving the promised things, or on the fact that God never deceives those who believe. This praise of God is proclaimed throughout the Scriptures, and it ought always to be before our eyes, especially in temptations. Without doubt we would feel that our miseries are from time to time lightened by contemplating this divine goodness.

units.la: Et consideremus nos inuicem) Iam quid nos deceat erga proximum. Generaliter autem dicit, ante omnia consideremus nos inuicem: hoc est, discamus nosse, primùm nos ipsos, deinde nostros fratres, atque vnicuique suum tribuamus honorem, de vnoquoq; quàm o ptimè iudicemus.
units.tr: And let us consider one another) Now he turns to what befits us towards our neighbour. He says in general, before all, let us consider one another: that is, let us learn to know first ourselves, then our brothers, and give each his due honour, judging each one in the best way.
