units.la: Valde necessarium est, vt nos mutuò hoc pacto consideremus. Nos non sumus nobis solis nati, sed alijs. Nec satis est dicere, ego curo & facio, quod mei est officij, mea non refert, quid faciant alij.
units.tr: It is very necessary that we consider one another in this way. We are not born for ourselves alone, but for others. Nor is it enough to say: I take care and do what belongs to my office; what others do is no concern of mine.

units.la: Imò tua interest, vt alios quoque considerates atque obserues, & vel proponas tibi imitandos qui te virtutibus superant, vel admoneas, quos vides inferiores & errantes. In quam sententiam ipse addit:
units.tr: Indeed, it is in your interest to consider and observe others too, either to set before yourself those to imitate who surpass you in virtues, or to admonish those whom you see to be weaker and erring. To this effect he adds:

units.la: In hoc ut prouocemus ad charitatem & bona opera) Consideremus fratres, non quadam cupiditate vel aemulatione, vt eos inuidiose deferamus aut reprehendamus, (vnde proteruia, fastus, odia, discidia, factiones possent oriri) sed vt vel ipsi meliores efficiamur exemplis alienis, vel alios meliores reddamus exemplo nostro: Vt extimulemus, inquit, nos, mutuò ad charitatem.
units.tr: To provoke one another to love and good works) Let us consider one another not with some desire or rivalry, so that we might malign or rebuke them spitefully (from which arrogance, pride, hatred, division and factions could arise), but so that either we ourselves may become better through others' examples, or we may make others better through our example. So that we may stir up one another, he says, to love.

units.la: Pulcherrimè autem fidei ac spei charitas annectitur, subijciturque. Sunt enim haec tria indiuulsè connexa, nec vera est fides, aut vera spes, si desit charitas, prima Corinthiorum capite decimotertio. Haec charitas erit nostrum sacrificium, quo Deus delectatur, sicut in prophetis passim docetur: & Christus iubet nos discere, misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium. Nec dubium, quin Apostolus hoc loco, quando docuit, abrogata sacrificia legalia, atque ostendere vult, quid credentibus agendum, seu offerendum sit sub euangelio: inculcans hic fidem, spem, charitatem, ad eiusmodi concione nes prophetarum respexerit. Et quivis intelligit, ita, demùm optimè satisfieri rixosis Hebraeis, ipsis ostenditur, qualia Deus loco sacrificiorum, ablutionum, & obseruationum legalium à nobis requirat. Nec habent amplius, quod cauillentur, vbi meliora sacrificia ipsis proponuntur. Addit autem non sine causa, de bonis operibus: Quia nec vera fides, nec vera charitas poterit esse otiosa, sed necessario proferūt bonos fructus. Nec bona sunt operā, quamlibet alioquin speciosa, nisi ex fidei radice, ex trunco spei, ex ramis charitatis pullulēt: si ijs non illustretur gloria Dei, nō iuuetur proximus, inter bona opera vix sunt numeranda. Incedas nudis pedibus, viuas mendicatō, &c. ista nihil ad lineam Charitatis. Iactare fidē, iactare spem, charitate, per quàm facile & leue est, & multi istud possunt, at qui bona opera producant, quae testetur veram fidem & veram charitatē, perpaucos videas. Hinc 1.Ioan.3. fratres nō diligamus verbo, neq; lingua, sed opere & veritate. Heu quanta esset nunc querelarū materia, si in temporum nostrorū statum infœlicisimū intuerēmur, in quibus verè refriguit charitas, imō penitus extincta est, dum bona opera externa tatum non irridentur à quibusdam, atq; odiosè exbilantur, statim occlamant, nouus monachismus, aut anabaptismi incurrunt notam.
units.tr: Now love is most beautifully joined to faith and hope and follows them. For these three are inseparably connected, and neither faith nor hope is true if love is lacking (1 Corinthians 13). This love will be our sacrifice, in which God delights, as is taught throughout the prophets; and Christ bids us learn: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. There is no doubt that the Apostle, in this place, when he taught that the legal sacrifices were abrogated and wishes to show what believers must do or offer under the gospel, inculcating here faith, hope and love, had in mind such sermons of the prophets. And anyone can see that the quarrelsome Hebrews are fully satisfied in this way, when it is shown to them what God requires of us in place of sacrifices, ablutions and legal observances. Nor have they anything further to cavil at, when better sacrifices are set before them. He adds, not without reason, of good works: because neither true faith nor true love can be idle, but necessarily bring forth good fruits. Nor are works good, however splendid they may otherwise look, unless they sprout from the root of faith, the trunk of hope and the branches of love; if the glory of God is not illustrated by them and the neighbour is not helped, they are scarcely to be counted among good works. You may walk barefoot, live as a beggar, and so on; these things have nothing to do with the line of love. To boast of faith, to boast of hope, to boast of love: how easy and light that is, and many can do it. But you would see very few who produce good works that bear witness to true faith and true love. Hence 1 John 3: let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed and truth. Alas, how great would be the matter for complaint now, if we looked at the most unhappy state of our times, in which love has truly grown cold, indeed has been utterly extinguished, so that external good works are not merely mocked by some and hatefully derided, but at once they cry out "new monachism!" or incur the mark of Anabaptism.

units.la: Non deferentes aggregationem nostri mutuam, sicuti mos est nonnullis, sed adhortantes inuicem.
units.tr: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as is the custom of some, but exhorting one another.

units.la: Hoc maximè alienum est à vera charitate, sese subducere à fratrum societate, sese abillis alienare, siue cùm sacri coetus habentur, aut de rebus ecclesiæ vtilibus agendum est, siue alias à quotidiana & familiari consuetudine discedere. Maximè verò hac in parte peccant, qui ijs sunt donis ornati, vt prodesse alijs possent vel exhortando, vel docendo. Siue igitur id faciant, metuentes aduersarios atq; hostes doctrinæ euangelicæ (quæ admodum legimus plures fuisse etiam, quo tempore Christus adhuc docebat in terris, Ioannis cap.6. de quibusdam narratur, quòd abierint retrò, & cum illo non ambularint. Lucæ cap.8. ad tempus credunt, & tempore tentationis deficiunt: & ex ijs, quæ post pauca hoc ipso capite commemorantur, quòd plurimi fuerint tales, cùm hæc epistola scribebatur, fit manifestum) quòd videlicet metuerent excludi synagoga, aut ne alias de facultatibus, aut de vita periclitaretur: siue quodam animi fastu contenentes miseros fratres inferiores, & nequaquam paribus donis Spiritus præditos: vtrumque iuxtā reprehensioni est obnoxium, & grauissimè peccant in Dei ecclesiam, & Deum ipsum, quando Dei ecclesiam iuuare & exornare possent, atque etiam tenentur. Qui multum habet, multum ab illo reposcetur. Væ seruo illi, qui talentum domini defodit in terram. Seruus sciens voluntatem domini, & non faciens, afficietur plagis multis. Nequaquam est contemnenda societas fratrum, quamlibet exigua. Christus in medio est credentium, etiamsi duntaxat duo vel tres in nomine ipsius sint congregati.
units.tr: Nothing is more alien to true love than to withdraw oneself from the fellowship of the brothers, to keep aloof from them, whether when sacred assemblies are held or when matters useful to the Church must be dealt with, or otherwise to depart from daily and familiar intercourse. Those who are endowed with gifts by which they could benefit others, by exhorting or teaching, sin most grievously in this respect. Whether they do this out of fear of the adversaries and enemies of evangelical doctrine (for we read that many such existed even when Christ was still teaching on earth: John 6 tells of certain persons who went back and walked with him no more; Luke 8 says that they believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation; and from what is recorded a few verses later in this same chapter it is clear that there were very many such when this epistle was written), namely because they feared exclusion from the synagogue, or lest they be endangered in their property or their lives; or whether, with a certain arrogance of mind, they despise their poorer brothers who are not endowed with equal gifts of the Spirit: both are open to rebuke, and they sin grievously against the Church of God and God himself, when they could help and adorn the Church of God, and indeed are bound to. To whom much is given, of him much will be required. Woe to that servant who buries his master's talent in the earth. The servant who knew his master's will and did not do it will be beaten with many stripes. The fellowship of the brothers, however small, is by no means to be despised: Christ is in the midst of believers, even if only two or three are gathered in his name.

units.la: Vbi plures sunt, plus operis & citius conficitur. Mirum in modum accenditur alterius exemplar, atque pia æmulatio. Sicut ferrum acuitur ferro, sicut lapis ad lapidem concussus elicit ignem: ita frater adiuuat fratrem, & alter alterum ad charitatis officia excitat: Frater à fratre adiutus vt ciuitas firma, Prouerb.cap.18. Primasius ait, notari eos, qui hoc nomine scindebant ecclesiam & congregationem fidelium, quasi propter suam eximiam sanctitatem non possent habitare cum illis, & deserebant congregationem sanctorum, habitantes soli, vt Deo liberius viderentur vacare. Sed hi despiciunt fratres, & charitatem violant. Christus iussit suos vnà esse congregatos, vt expectarent spiritum Sanctum, non sparsim vel separatim agere. Paulus quocunque venerat, statim adibat congregationem fratrum, exhortans & docens, &c. Sed de his satis. Certum est, parenthesi illa, sicuti mos est nonnullis, tacitè perstringi quosdam, qui cum exhortando & consolando prodesse possent ecclesiæ, seu congregationi credentium, tamen sese subducebant, fortasis fastu & contemptu fratrum inferiorum: vel, quod etiam fieri potuit, metu Iudæorum persequentium eos, qui doctrinæ euangelicæ adhærebant. Horum exemplum ponit ob oculos, vt ita deterreat cæteros, ne simile quiddam audeant.
units.tr: Where there are more, more work is done and it is completed more quickly. The example of another and pious emulation is wonderfully kindled. As iron is sharpened by iron, and as a stone struck against a stone draws out fire, so a brother helps a brother, and one stirs up the other to the duties of love: a brother helped by a brother is like a strong city (Proverbs 18). Primasius says that those are noted who, by this name, split the Church and the assembly of the faithful, as if on account of their singular holiness they could not live with them, and who forsook the congregation of the saints, living alone, so that they might seem to be at leisure for God more freely. But these despise the brothers and violate love. Christ commanded his people to be gathered together, so that they might await the Holy Spirit, not act scattered or apart. Paul, wherever he came, at once went to the assembly of the brothers, exhorting and teaching, and so on. But enough of these things. It is certain that by that parenthesis, "as is the custom of some," certain persons are tacitly rebuked who, though they could benefit the Church or the congregation of believers by exhorting and comforting, nevertheless withdrew themselves, perhaps from arrogance and contempt for their inferior brothers, or, which could also have happened, from fear of the Jews persecuting those who adhered to evangelical doctrine. He sets their example before our eyes, so that he may thus deter the others from daring anything similar.

units.la: Idque hoc magis, quòd uidetis appropinquantem diem. Ratio, quare non deferenda aggregatio fratrum, imò quare accedere debeamus cum fide, & vt ad omnia referatur hæc cratio ab expectatione extremi iudicij imminentis. Magnum calcar ad peragendum ea, quæ sunt nostri officij, in memoriam reuocare extremum iudicium, in quo vnicuique erit reddenda ratio, & prout quisque gesserit, ita mercedem accipiet. Si crebrò & diligenter volueremus animo doctrinam de extremo iudicio, peccata studiosius vitaremus, & officium præstaremus ardentius.
units.tr: And so much the more, as you see the day drawing near. This is the reason why the assembly of the brothers must not be forsaken, indeed why we ought to draw near with faith, and he refers all this exhortation to the expectation of the impending last judgment. Calling to mind the last judgment, in which an account will be rendered by each one and each will receive a reward according to what he has done, is a great spur to carrying out the things that belong to our duty. If we were often and diligently to ponder the teaching about the last judgment in our minds, we would avoid sins more earnestly and perform our duty more ardently.

units.la: Vnde aliàs sæpè Apostolus hinc argumenta trahit suasoria. Roman. 13.2. Thessalon. 5. Eleganter autem ait, Videtis: ita enim concinuit illos, quasi iam videant ipsi, & certò sciant, instar illum diem: ac propterea non posse detractare aut refugere.
units.tr: Hence the Apostle often elsewhere draws persuasive arguments from this (Romans 13:2; 1 Thessalonians 5). He says elegantly, "you see": for he speaks as if they themselves already see it and know for certain that the day is at hand, and therefore they cannot shrink from it or flee it.

units.la: Per diem autem etiamsi vniuscuiusque dies extremus aptè posit intellligi, tamen cómodius extremum diem per Antonomasiam accipiemus, qui & vocatur alias dies Domini, propterea, quòd Christus Dominus in illo maiestatem suam sit mundo manifestaturus, & solus triumphaturus: & quia ipse solus tunc omne iudicium, omnem dignitatem & gloriam obtinebit, propterea ipsius dies appellatur.
units.tr: Although the last day of each person may fittingly be called "the day," we shall more conveniently take "the day" by antonomasia to mean the last day. It is also called elsewhere the day of the Lord, because Christ the Lord will then manifest his majesty to the world and alone triumph, and because he alone will then hold all judgment, all dignity and all glory, which is why it is called his day.

units.la: Cæterùm hac ratione propositá Apostolus prudenter sibi viam parat ad sequentem comminationem.
units.tr: Having laid down this principle, the Apostle prudently prepares for himself a way into the warning that follows.

units.la: Hic igitur habemus, quomodo tum erga Deum, tum erga proximum nos geramus, vt spiritualium bonorum ex sacerdotio Christi prouenientiū simus participes, hic quasi signa quædam sunt propositá, ex quibus an etiam in nobis efficax sit sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi, an ad nos pertineat, dignosci posit. Certum est, qui hoc pacto se non gerunt, ab ingressu Sanctorum excludentur.
units.tr: Here, then, we have how we are to conduct ourselves both towards God and towards our neighbour, so that we may share in the spiritual goods that flow from the priesthood of Christ. Here are set out, as it were, certain signs by which we may discern whether the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ is effective in us too, and whether it pertains to us. It is certain that those who do not conduct themselves in this way will be shut out from entering among the saints.

units.la: Iam, si velimus excerpere capita doctrinæ totius huius loci exhortatiui, non est difficile. Neque opus est nos ijs fusius explicandis diu immorari: quandoquidem magna ex parte iam sunt tractati.
units.tr: Now, if we want to pick out the heads of doctrine in this whole hortatory passage, it is not difficult. Nor is there any need for us to linger long in explaining them at length, since for the most part they have already been treated.

units.la: Primùm, vbi describitur vsus sacerdotij Christi, quòd videlicet per id patefactus sit nobis liber ingressus in cælum: item quomodo habeamus Christum magnum pontificem: sunt ea valde consolatoria, & sæpe in tentationibus mente reuoluenda. Sed & eadem nos docent, quomodo à grauamine ceremoniarum legalium, ac proinde & à grauamine traditionum humanarum simus liberati, nec angi propter tales res in conscientia debeamus. Habemus omnia præstantiora in Christo, vt nequaquā opus sit ad infirma elementa mundi respicere, aut iterum aspirare.
units.tr: First, where the use of Christ's priesthood is described, namely that through it a free entrance into heaven has been opened to us, and how we have Christ as our great high priest: these things are very consoling and are often to be turned over in the mind in temptations. But these same things also teach us how we have been freed from the burden of the legal ceremonies, and therefore also from the burden of human traditions, and that we ought not to be troubled in conscience on account of such things. We have all things more excellent in Christ, so that there is no need at all to look back to the weak elements of the world or to long for them again.

units.la: Secundò, vbi venitur ad exhortationem, reuera summa totius doctrinæ ac vitæ Christianæ delineatur. De officijs fidei, spei, charitatis, in quibus consistit summa euangelij & nostræ religionis, clarè & breuiter disseritur. De adeundo Deo propter & per pontificem ac mediatorem Christum, quàm suauiter verba facit? Quàm iucundam habet hic pia mens meditationē? De purificatione conscientiarum per fidem mirè erigit animos hæc doctrina male affectos propter inopiam & raritatem suorum meritorum, quæ prorsus nulla in se inueniunt. De constantia & fortitudine spei doctrina est, non tantum in spiritualibus, sed etiam in externis periculis valde necessaria & consolatoria. Quò pluriè mum facit consideratio Dei fideliter præstantis, quæcunque promiserit. Fides nostra sit intenta potius in bonitatem Dei, quàm in nostram ipsorum qualitatem, & poterimus promissiones cœlestes accipere.
units.tr: Second, where he comes to exhortation, the very summary of the whole Christian doctrine and life is laid out. The duties of faith, hope and love, in which the sum of the gospel and of our religion consists, are discussed clearly and briefly. How sweetly he speaks of drawing near to God through and by the high priest and mediator Christ! How pleasing a meditation this holds for a pious mind! This teaching wonderfully raises up minds troubled by the poverty and scarcity of their merits, which they find altogether absent in themselves, by showing the purification of conscience through faith. It is a teaching on the constancy and strength of hope, very necessary and consoling not only in spiritual matters but also in external dangers. The consideration of God as faithfully performing whatever he has promised helps greatly in this. Let our faith be fixed rather on the goodness of God than on our own qualities, and we shall be able to receive the heavenly promises.

units.la: Postremò, hæc officia charitatis de prouocando atq; excitando inuicem, de non deserendo aggregationem credentium, hoc periculosissimo tempore, sunt vbique summo studio inculcāda. Quæ enim alia causa est, quòd ita labefactatur ecclesiarum autoritas, magistratuum dignitas, atq; vnusquisq; facit, quod suo capiti rectum videtur, nisi quòd omnes, atque illi quoque, quorum maximè intererat curare aliorum salutem, sic agunt, quasi ad ipsos non pertineret, quid alij faciant? quasi sibi solis essent nati, refugiunt conuentus aliorum, contemnunt infirmiores fratres, nequaquam ex animo proferunt sana consilia, tantùm quæ sua sunt, quærunt, non quæ Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Lastly, these duties of love, of provoking and stirring up one another, and of not forsaking the assembly of believers in this most perilous time, must be pressed everywhere with the utmost zeal. For what other cause is there that the authority of churches is so weakened, and the dignity of magistrates, and that everyone does what seems right to his own head, except that all, and especially those whose chief concern should have been to care for the salvation of others, act as if it did not concern them what others do? As if they were born for themselves alone, they shun the gatherings of others, despise the weaker brothers, do not sincerely put forward sound counsels, and seek only what is their own, not what is of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Nam si volentes peccauerimus post acceptam cognitionem veritatis, non vltra pro peccatis reliqua est hostia: sed formidabilis quædam expectatio iudicij, & ignis vehementia, qui deuoraturus aduersarios. Qui aspernatus fuerit Mosi legem, absq; misericordia sub duobus aut tribus testibus moritur: quanto putatis peioribus afficietur supplicijs, qui filium Dei conculcarit, & sanguinem testamenti ceu rem prophanam habuerit, per quem fuerat sanctificatus, & Spiritum gratiæ contumelia affecerit? Nouimus enim eum, qui dixit: Meum est vlcisci, ego reependam, dicit Dominus. Et rursum: Dominus iudicabit populum suum. Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viuentis.
units.tr: For if we sin wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains no longer a sacrifice for sins, but a certain dreadful expectation of judgment and the fury of fire that is about to devour the adversaries. He who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy under two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by him who has trodden underfoot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant, by which he was sanctified, as a profane thing, and has insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said: Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. And again: The Lord will judge his people. It is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. (Hebr. 10.)

units.la: Hæc est comminatio, grauis profectò, & iram Dei atq; extremum iudicium eis, qui sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi nolunt agnoscere, admodum seueriter proponens. Conueniebat autem, apud Hebræos duræ ceruicis homines, & terroribus atque fulminationibus legis assuetos, & ceremonijs eiusdem pertinacissimè addictos, exhortationi comminationem subijcere, vt, qui rei dignitate ad agnitionem non adducebantur, tandem formidine pœnæ ad eam amplectendā permouerentur. Erant Apostolo probè perspecta Hebræorum ingenia, probeq; norat, qua ratione cum ijs agendum foret. Cæterùm instituit hìc Apostolus pleniorem argumentationem: qua eos erudit, qui nolunt agnoscere Christi sacerdotium, atq; vnicum sacrificium pro peccatis efficax & sufficiens: cuius hæc est propositio: nam si volentes peccauerimus, &c. Estque hæc sententia: Si qui sunt, qui post acceptam cognitionem veritatis, de sacerdotio inquam & vnico sacrificio Christi, peccata omnium expiante, nolunt tamen eam pro certa agnoscere, & constanter retinere: sed potius scientes volentesque peccant, aspernando euangelium, & coculcando Christi sanguinem ceu rem prophanam, inutilem, inefficacem, atq; siue leguliibus, siue aliis imitandum sibi putant sacrificijs: sciant illi, nullam amplius restare offerendam pro hominum salute hostiam, verùm hoc vnum superesse, ut mudum Christum iudicet, & quotquot ipsum contemnunt, nolentes credere, æternis supplicijs deuouendos. Hanc esse simplicem & propriam præsentis loci interpretationem, diuersis rationibus possumus comprobare. Primùm quidem ex ipsa caussæ constitutione siue statu. Cùm enim tota disputatione demonstratum sit, Christum esse sacerdotem, atq; vnico sacrificio expiasse peccata, ac iam in conclusione admoniti sint omnes, vt fiducia misericordiæ propter Christum, eiusq; sacrificium, ad sancta sanctorum, id est, cœlos contendere nt, sanè appositissimè iam subijcitur per contrarium, ut quotquot ea via nolunt ingredi, sed imaginantur alia salutis obtinendæ remedia, & sic scientes volentesque ab agnita veritate desiciunt, sciant, nullam aliam hostiam pro peccatis in posterum offerendam, nihil; aliud, quàm formidabile iudicium sibi expectandum. Quis non videt hanc interpretationem per omnia quadrare instituto, & caussæ principali: Et quis insuper dissimulare queat, contra eos, qui sacerdotium Christi aspernabantur, & ceu inefficax contemnebant, comminationem hanc totam institutam?
units.tr: This is a warning, certainly a grave one, which sets forth very severely the wrath of God and the last judgment for those who are unwilling to acknowledge the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. It was fitting, however, to append a warning to the exhortation for the Hebrews, a stiff-necked people accustomed to the terrors and thunderings of the law and most obstinately devoted to its ceremonies, so that those who were not drawn to acknowledgment by the worth of the matter might at last be moved by fear of punishment to embrace it. The Apostle had thoroughly perceived the character of the Hebrews and knew well how he must deal with them. But here the Apostle sets out a fuller argument, by which he instructs those who are unwilling to acknowledge the priesthood of Christ and his unique sacrifice for sins as effective and sufficient. Its proposition is: "For if we sin wilfully," and so on. The sense is this: if there are any who, after receiving the knowledge of the truth (of the priesthood, I mean, and of the unique sacrifice of Christ, which expiates the sins of all), nevertheless are unwilling to acknowledge it as certain and to hold it firmly, but rather sin knowingly and willingly, scorning the gospel and trampling the blood of Christ underfoot as a profane, useless and ineffective thing, and think that they must imitate other sacrifices, whether the legal ones or others, let them know that no further sacrifice remains to be offered for the salvation of men. Only this remains: that the Christ whom they despise will judge them, and that all who despise him, refusing to believe, are to be given over to eternal punishments. That this is the simple and proper interpretation of the present passage we can prove by several reasons. First, from the very state of the case. For since the whole discussion has shown that Christ is priest and has expiated sins by one sacrifice, and now in the conclusion all are admonished to draw near to the holy of holies, that is, to heaven, with confident trust in mercy on account of Christ and his sacrifice, it is very fitting that the contrary now be added: whoever are unwilling to enter by that way, but imagine other remedies for obtaining salvation, and so, knowing and willing, fall away from the truth they have acknowledged, should know that no other sacrifice for sins is to be offered in future, and nothing awaits them but a dreadful judgment. Who does not see that this interpretation fits the purpose and the principal cause in every respect? And who could further deny that this whole warning was framed against those who scorned the priesthood of Christ and despised it as ineffective?

units.la: Secundò si examinemus partes totius huius propositionis, quadam analysi facta, inuenimus, nos nequaquam à recta linea discedere. Quod ad priorem partem attinet, quales Apostolus intelligat per voluntarie peccantes post agnitam veritatem, ex sequentibus licet colligere, vbi ait: Qui aspernatus fuerit legem Mosi, item, qui filium Dei concul carit, & sanguinem testamenti ceu rem prophanam habuerit, per quem fuerat sanctificatus. Quibus verbis non obscurè declarat, quos hic voluntarie peccates significet, eos videlicet, qui euangelium Christi aspernantur, qui sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi conspuunt, quasi nullum esset, aut certè prorsus inefficax. Contra hos ergo sic post agnitam veritatem (quandoquidem eam ex his, quæ hactenus fusè tractata sunt, plenissimè percipere potuerunt) sponte & suapte malitia peccantes, rectè dicitur, nõ vltrà pro peccatis reliquam esse hostiam: vnicam semel per Christum esse oblatam ad expiationem peccatorum, neque aliam deinceps offerendam: hoc solum restare, vt Christus exerceat iudicium, quo aduersarij & increduli omnes malè perdentur.
units.tr: Second, if we examine the parts of this whole proposition by making a certain analysis, we find that we do not depart in any way from the straight line. As to the first part, what sort of people the Apostle means by those who sin wilfully after the truth has been acknowledged may be gathered from what follows, where he says: "He who has set aside the law of Moses," and likewise "he who has trodden underfoot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant, by which he was sanctified, as a profane thing." By these words he declares, not obscurely, whom he means here by the wilful sinners: namely, those who spurn the gospel of Christ, who spit upon the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ as though it were nothing, or at least wholly ineffective. Against these, then, who thus sin of their own accord and by their own malice after the truth has been acknowledged (since they could fully perceive it from what has been treated at length so far), it is rightly said that there is no longer any sacrifice for sins. One sacrifice has been offered once for all through Christ for the expiation of sins, and no other is to be offered henceforth. Only this remains: that Christ should exercise judgment, by which all adversaries and unbelievers will be utterly destroyed.

units.la: Iam quod ad posteriorem partem attinet, præcesserunt diuersis locis non pauca, quæ interpretationem nostram stabiliunt. Nam in eandem sententiam dictum est ad finem capitis noni, nullam amplius hostiam expectandam, sed solum superesse iudicium, in quo Christus sine peccato conspicietur omnibus ipsum expectantibus. Item capite decimo, Christum vna pro peccatis oblata victima sedere ad dexteram patris, expectante, vt subijciat omnes aduersarios. Rursus proximè ante conclusionem, vbi peccatorum est remissio, nulla est amplius oblatio pro peccato. Proinde eodem sensu ista repetit in conclusione, consentaneum est statuamus.
units.tr: As to the second part, not a few things have gone before in various places that confirm our interpretation. For in the same sense it was said at the end of chapter nine that no further sacrifice is to be expected, but only judgment remains, in which Christ will be seen without sin by all who await him. Likewise in chapter ten, that Christ, having been offered as one victim for sins, sits at the right hand of the Father, waiting until he puts all his adversaries under his feet. Again, shortly before the conclusion, where there is remission of sins, there is no longer any offering for sin. Therefore it is fitting that we hold that he repeats these things in the conclusion in the same sense.

units.la: Quanquam possunt hæc verba (sicut illa quoq; capite sexto, Fieri non potest, ut, qui semel fuerint illuminati, gustauerintq; donum cœleste, & participes facti fuerint spiritus Sancti, gustauerintq; bonum Dei verbum ac virtutes futuri seculi, si prolabantur, denuò renouentur per pœnitentiam) non inepte accipi de peccato in spiritum Sanctum, vt iuxta doctrinam Christi (Matth. 12. Marci 3.) sententia sit, eis, qui peccarint in spiritum Sanctum non superesse ullam hostiam, id est, veniam seu remissionem peccatorum expectandam. Et eos qui volentes peccant post agnitam veritatem, rectè dici peccare in spiritum sanctum, ostendi potest, ex vsitata peccati in spiritum Sanctum definitione. Ea autem est huiusmodi. Peccatu in spiritum Sanctu (quod Marcus dicit blasphemare contra spiritum Sanctum, Matthæus vocat spiritum blasphemiæ) est, cùm quis diuinæ veritati, quam tamen sic agnitam habet, vt ignorantiam prætexere non possit, destinata malitia resistit, & in hoc tantùm resistat.
units.tr: Although these words (as also those in chapter 6: "It is impossible that those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, if they fall away, should be renewed again to repentance") can fairly be taken as referring to the sin against the Holy Spirit, so that, according to the teaching of Christ (Matt. 12; Mark 3), the sense is that for those who have sinned against the Holy Spirit no sacrifice remains, that is, no pardon or remission of sins is to be expected. And that those who sin willingly after the truth has been acknowledged are rightly said to sin against the Holy Spirit can be shown from the customary definition of that sin. The definition is of this kind. The sin against the Holy Spirit (which Mark calls blaspheming against the Holy Spirit, and Matthew calls the blasphemy against the Spirit) is when someone resists divine truth, which he has so acknowledged that he cannot plead ignorance, with settled malice, and resists in this alone.

units.la: Sunt, qui peccant in filium, cùm videlicet ignoranter Christo maledicunt, Christum contemnunt, quomodo Paulus fatetur, se persecutum esse ecclesiam Dei, sed per ignorantiam. Qui verò per spiritum Sanctum illuminati sunt, & norunt filium, ac iam post agnitam veritatem adhuc resistunt & impugnant, hi, quandoquidem resistunt spiritui, qui ipsos illuminauit, peccant in spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: There are those who sin against the Son, when they blaspheme Christ or despise him in ignorance, as Paul confesses that he persecuted the Church of God, but through ignorance. But those who have been enlightened by the Holy Spirit and know the Son, and who, even after acknowledging the truth, still resist and assail it, these sin against the Holy Spirit, since they resist the Spirit who enlightened them.

units.la: In contemptores euangelij.
units.tr: Against the despisers of the gospel.

units.la: 1. probatio huius sententiæ.
units.tr: First proof of this opinion.

units.la: Genuina interpretatio huius loci.
units.tr: The genuine interpretation of this passage.

units.la: 2. pars. Voluntarie peccantes post agnitam veritatem.
units.tr: Second part. Those who sin willingly after acknowledging the truth.

units.la: Peccatum agnitam veritatem abnegantium.
units.tr: The sin of those who deny the truth once acknowledged.

units.la: 2. pars. Hebr. 9. Hebr. 10.
units.tr: Second part. Heb. 9; Heb. 10.

units.la: Peccatu in spiritum Sanctu.
units.tr: The sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Definitio peccati in spiritu Sanctum. Marc. 3. Matth. 12. In solium peccare quid. Quomodo etiam Stephanus Actorum septimo aiebat, Iudaeos semper restitisse spiritui Sancto.
units.tr: Definition of the sin against the Holy Spirit. Mark 3; Matt. 12. What it is to sin against the Son. How also Stephen in Acts 7 said that the Jews had always resisted the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Hoc igitur modo peccantibus certè nulla amplius superest hostia, peccatum eorum neque in hoc seculo, neque in futuro remittetur. Atq; ita multò grauissima hic proposita est comminatio aduersus eos, qui agnitam veritatem, de dignitate & praestantia sacer dotij, necnon sacrificij Christi, quae abundè tradita est hactenus praesenti epistola, audet impugnare, ut certò sciant, se, cum adeò aperte omnia sint ipsis exposita, si pergant volen tes contemnere & resistere, iudicium Dei nunquam euasuros. Et institutio haec interpreta tio satis conuenit: imò eo magis conuenit, quòd in sequenti ratio subijcitur, qui Spiritū gratiae contumelia affecerit: quod quid aliud est, quàm spiritum blasphemare, sicut Christus loquitur? Nec desunt, qui exponunt ista verba de non iterando baptismo. Sic enim post Chrysostomum, Theophylactum, Primasius: his verbis non poenitentiam, inquit, excludit, neque propitiationem, quae fit per poenitentiam: neque repellit & deijcit per desperationem delinquentium: sed secundum excludit lauacrum baptismi. Non est ita inimicus salutis nostrae, ut diceret, non esse vltrà poenitentiam, neque remissione peccatorum: sed hostia, inquit, vltrà non est, hoc est, crux ultrà non est, vt iterum Christus crucifigatur, iterumque nos baptizemur. Nam sicut Christus semel mortuus est, & iam non moritur: ita & nos semel baptizari instar mortis eius & sepulturae (sicut Apostolus alibi dicit: Consepulti cum illo per baptismum in morte) iam non possumus rebaptizari. Tantum Primasius. Sed nequaquam video opus esse, ut ad huiusmodi interpretationem confugiatur. Satis quidem mihi videtur cap. 6. quadrare, sicut ibidem ostendimus: sed hic non videtur mihi ulla de baptismo esse cogitatio.
units.tr: In this way, for those who sin thus, no sacrifice certainly remains; their sin will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. So a much more severe threat is set forth here against those who dare to attack the truth, already acknowledged, about the dignity and excellence of the priesthood and also of Christ's sacrifice, which has been abundantly taught so far in the present epistle. They should know for certain that, since all these things have been laid out so openly before them, if they persist willingly in despising and resisting, they will never escape the judgment of God. This interpretation fits well; indeed it fits all the better because in what follows a reason is added: he who has insulted the Spirit of grace. What else is this than blaspheming the Spirit, as Christ speaks? Nor are there lacking those who expound these words as referring to not repeating baptism. Thus after Chrysostom, Theophylact and Primasius: "In these words," he says, "he excludes neither repentance nor the propitiation which is made through repentance, nor does he reject and cast down offenders through despair; but he excludes only the washing of baptism. He is not so hostile to our salvation as to say that there is no longer repentance or remission of sins; but, he says, 'there is no longer a sacrifice,' that is, 'there is no longer a cross, so that Christ is crucified again and we are baptized again.' For as Christ died once and dies no more, so we too, having been baptized once in the likeness of his death and burial (as the Apostle says elsewhere, buried with him through baptism into death), can no longer be rebaptized." Thus far Primasius. But I see no need at all to take refuge in such an interpretation. It seems to me to fit chapter 6 well enough, as we showed there; but here I do not think there is any thought of baptism.

units.la: Proinde manifestum est, nullo modo patrocinari hunc locum Nouatianis, vel nostri temporis Anabaptistis Nouati discipulis & similibus. Perspicuum est, non dici, quòd ijs, qui voluntariè peccarint, non superfit locus poenitentiae: sed nullam amplius supereße hostiam pro peccatis, hoc est, non expectandum, ut alia ratione iustificentur, quàm ea hostia, quae semel per Christum oblata est. Quae interpretatio per omnia seruit constitutioni seu statui totius causae, & verbis illis ipsis clare exprimitur.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that this passage in no way lends support to the Novatians, or to the Anabaptists of our time, the disciples and similar followers of Novatus. It is plain that it is not said that for those who sin willingly there is no room left for repentance; rather, no sacrifice for sins remains, that is, one must not expect to be justified by any means other than that sacrifice which was offered once for all through Christ. This interpretation serves the whole argument and position of the case in every respect, and it is clearly expressed in those very words.

units.la: Caeterum possemus hic pleniorem propter Anabaptistas nostri temporis disputationem de non neganda poenitentia siue venia recusanda instituere: sed praesenti loco non putamus conuenire. Vide Cypriani epistolam ad Antonianum libro quarto epistolarum, epistola secunda. Item tomo secundo ad Nouatianum haereticum. Item Athanasium in epistola ad Serapionem. Augustinum libro quaestionum veteris & noui testamenti, quaestione 102, vbi copiose ea de re agitur.
units.tr: Otherwise we could, on account of the Anabaptists of our time, set out a fuller discussion on not denying repentance or refusing pardon; but we do not think it suits the present place. See Cyprian's letter to Antonianus, in the fourth book of his letters, letter 2; likewise in volume 2, his letter to Novatian the heretic; likewise Athanasius in his letter to Serapion; and Augustine, in the book of Questions on the Old and New Testament, question 102, where the matter is treated at length.

units.la: Quaedam etiam habet Chrysostomus libello de reparatione lapsi. Item Bullingerus contra Anabaptistas libr. 1. tractat. 8.
units.tr: Chrysostom also has some things in his little book On the Restoration of the Fallen. Likewise Bullinger against the Anabaptists, book 1, tractate 8.

units.la: Nam si uolentes peccauerimus post acceptam cognitionem veritatis) Vox ἑκούσιως diligenter est obseruanda. Notum est vel ex philosophia, vt quid pro vitio habeatur, vel pro virtute, spectandum, voluntariè ne fit factum, an inuoluntariè. Quam ob causam philosophi, inprimis autem Aristoteles libro tertio Ethicorum capite primo, de voluntario & inuoluntario differunt, atque inuoluntaria definiunt, quae fiunt vel ignoranita vel coactione.
units.tr: "For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth": the Greek word [ἑκουσίως] must be carefully noted. It is known, even from philosophy, that whether something is regarded as a vice or a virtue depends on whether the deed was done willingly or unwillingly. For this reason the philosophers, above all Aristotle in book 3 of the Ethics, chapter 1, discuss the voluntary and the involuntary, and define as involuntary those things that are done either through ignorance or through compulsion.

units.la: Voluntaria autem ignorantia principium est ipso agente, vel sciente actionem atque praecipuas circumstantias. Plura vide ibidem apud Aristotelem, item libro quinto capite octauo.
units.tr: Voluntary ignorance, however, is a principle lying in the agent himself, who knows the act and its chief circumstances. See more in Aristotle in the same place, and also in book 5, chapter 8.

units.la: Hinc verò natum est illud de ciuilibus delictis, peccatum non esse peccatum, nisi sit voluntarium: & qui per ignorantiam vel coactionem peccarint, humanis legibus absoluuntur, maximè qui peccarint ignorantia facti, modò non affectata sit ignorantia, (qua lis in Iudaeis, quibus Christus ait: Si locutus non fuissem, peccatum non haberetis:) quae siue facti fit, siue iuris, excusationem non meretur.
units.tr: Hence arose the saying about civil offences, that a deed is not a sin unless it is voluntary; and those who sin through ignorance or compulsion are absolved by human laws, especially those who sin through ignorance of fact, provided the ignorance is not feigned. (Such was the case with the Jews, to whom Christ said: "If I had not spoken, you would not have sin.") Ignorance of this kind, whether of fact or of law, does not deserve excuse.

units.la: Ad haec Augustinus libro octuagesimo tertio quaestionum, quaestione vicesima sexta dicit, alia peccata infirmitatis, alia imperitiae siue ignorantiae, alia malitiae. His ergo bre uiter praemiisis facilius intelligi poterit, quod praesenti loco conuenit, nempe, peccata fieri voluntarie, quaedam verò non voluntarie, veluti, quae per ignorantiam facti fiunt siue proprij, siue alieni, vt qui vescitur consecratis.
units.tr: Moreover Augustine, in book 83 of the Questions, question 26, says that some sins come from weakness, some from inexperience or ignorance, and some from malice. With these things briefly premised, what fits the present passage can more easily be understood, namely, that some sins are committed willingly and some not willingly, such as those committed through ignorance of fact, whether one's own or another's, as when one eats of the consecrated things.

units.la: Porrò apud tribunal Christi nullum est peccatum, quod excusationem meretur, siue per ignorantiam aut coactionem fit factum, siue voluntarie animo sciente aut deliberato omnes ex aequo apud Deum sunt rei, & minimum peccatum dignum est morte aeterna: etiam si qui per ignorantiam deliquerint, vel per infirmitatem, mitius plecten tur, iuxta illud Christi, Melius agetur cum Tyro & Sydone, quàm vobiscum:
units.tr: Furthermore, before the judgment seat of Christ no sin deserves excuse, whether it is done through ignorance or compulsion, or willingly, with a knowing and deliberate mind. All are equally guilty before God, and the least sin is worthy of eternal death. Even if some have sinned through ignorance or weakness, they will be punished more mildly, according to that saying of Christ: "It will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for you."

units.la: Apostolus, persecutus sum ecclesiam Dei, sed ignorans feci, quapropter misericordiam consecutus sum. Qui vero voluntarie deliquerint, grauius punientur, iuxta illud, Seruus sciens voluntatem Domini, & non faciens, vapulabit plagis multis. Proinde ad exaggerandum Hebraeis crimen suum, si despicerent vel negligerent adeo clare propositam veritatem de sacerdotio atq; vnico sacrificio Christi, quod sane non potuerunt non intelligere, nec praetexere vllam ignorantiam, ait: si volentes peccauerimus, quasi diceret: Si nequaquam satis fuisset vobis expósita veritas de sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi, atq; ita conte psisset Christum eiusq; euangelium, aliquo modo fuisset veltrum peccatum excusabile: at nunc, quando satis superq; veritas vobis audita est, imo & nota, iam adhuc reiicitis Christum, non possum aliud dicere, quam vos scientes volentesq; peccare, neque excusationem ullam estis habituri. Ergo mirabiliter hic exaggeratur durities & incredulitas Iudaeorum, & valde mouentur hac ratione eorum animi ad dolorem siue ad ad resipiscentiam. Interea non est statuendum, ea quae voluntarie fiunt peccata, nequaquam etiam posse veniam apud Deum obtinere, quasi ea sola veniam obtinerent, quae perignorantiam aut infirmitatem perpetrantur: unde & appellata sunt vulgo quaedam peccata venialia, quaedam vero mortalia. Certum est, cum Dominus in lege instituerit, quaedam sacrificia ad expiandum peccata per ignorantiam admissa, quaedam vero ad expianda, quae sponte ac deliberato animo fuerant perpetrata, vt Leuitici 4. 5. 6. describuntur peccata ἑκούσια, id est, sponte & voluntarie perpetrata: aeque veniam esse paratam voluntarium peccatorum, atque eorum, quae per ignorantiam vel infirmitatem committuntur.
units.tr: The Apostle says: "I persecuted the Church of God, but I did it in ignorance; therefore I obtained mercy." But those who sin willingly will be punished more severely, according to that saying: "The servant who knew the will of the Lord and did not do it shall be beaten with many stripes." Therefore, to heighten the guilt of the Hebrews, if they despised or neglected the truth about the priesthood and the unique sacrifice of Christ, so clearly set before them, which they certainly could not fail to understand nor plead any ignorance of, he says: "if we sin willingly," as if to say: If the truth about Christ's priesthood and sacrifice had not been set out sufficiently for you, and so you had opposed Christ and his gospel, your sin might in some way be excusable. But now, since the truth has been heard by you more than sufficiently, indeed is known to you, and you still reject Christ, I can say nothing else than that you sin knowingly and willingly, and you will have no excuse at all. Thus the hardness and unbelief of the Jews is here wonderfully magnified, and by this reasoning their minds are greatly moved to sorrow or to repentance. Meanwhile it should not be held that sins committed willingly can by no means obtain pardon before God, as if only those committed through ignorance or weakness obtained pardon. Hence certain sins have commonly been called venial, and others mortal. It is certain that, since the Lord in the law ordained certain sacrifices to expiate sins committed through ignorance, and others to expiate those committed of one's own accord and with a deliberate mind (as in Leviticus 4, 5, 6 the sins are described as [ἑκούσια], that is, committed of one's own accord and willingly), so pardon is equally ready for willing sins as for those committed through ignorance or weakness.

units.la: Debet in veritate adimpleri, quod ibi typis est adumbratum. Quid dicemus de Dauid? Annon is sponte deliberatoq; animo commisit adulterium & homicidium? Et tamen veniam potuit, vbi serio paeniteret, obtinuit. Annon & Petrus sponte deliberatoq; animo abnegauit, adhibito iuramento, eoq; iterato, Christum? Et tamen receptus est iterum in gratiam. Innumera sunt eiusmodi exempla. Itaque etiam quae voluntarie admittuntur, tamen, si paeniteat nos, veniae locus superesset. Verum quidem est, apud veteres licet inuenire, ea potissimum condonari, quae ex quotidiana infirmitate designabantur: si quae vero essent magis enormia, diluebantur publica paenitentia per canones constituta. Si quis autem denuo huiusmodi perpetrasset, putabant, non iterandam publicam paenitentiam, non magis, quam iteratur baptismus. Sed sciendum est, ea seueritate voluisse distinguere euidentius graviora crimina a leuioribus: deinde, sic diligentius voluisse deterrere ab id genus publicis criminibus, ex quibus maxima nasci solebant offendicula. Etiamsi tata seueritas moderanda erat lege charitatis erga personam ream, sicut Apostolus ad Corinthios scribens iubet caueri, ne absorbeatur prae tristitia is qui Satanae fuerat traditus. Sed de his satis. Constat ijs, quae voluntarie committuntur, etiam veniae locum superesse: & sic nihil esse, quod patrocinetur Nouationis. Item constat, multa voluntaria peccata esse, nec ea statim appellanda peccata in spiritum Sanctum. Quanquam ex eo, quod hic additur de voluntarie peccando post agnitam veritatem, & paulo post subijcitur, de conculcantibus Christum, habentibusq; sanguinem eius ceu rem prophanam, & contumelia afficientibus Spiritum gratiae: recte etiam de peccato in spiritum Sanctum potest hic locus exponi, sicut supra diximus: ut posteriori parte sententia fit, non esse talibus reliquam hostiam, id est, remissionem peccatorum. Tametsi quam primo loco posuimus interpretationem, existimamus magis simplicem, & menti Apostoli magis consentaneam.
units.tr: What was foreshadowed there by types must be fulfilled in truth. What shall we say of David? Did he not commit adultery and murder deliberately and of set purpose? Yet when he repented in earnest, he obtained pardon. Did not Peter also deny Christ deliberately and of set purpose, even with an oath, and that repeated? Yet he was received back into grace. There are countless examples of this kind. So even sins committed willingly still leave room for pardon, if we repent. It is true that among the ancients one can find that the sins pardoned were chiefly those arising from everyday weakness; if the offences were more serious, they were expiated by public penance laid down by the canons. If anyone had committed such a sin again, they thought public penance should not be repeated, any more than baptism is repeated. But it must be understood that by this severity they wished to distinguish more clearly the graver crimes from the lighter, and secondly, to deter more diligently from public crimes of this kind, from which very great stumbling-blocks were wont to arise. Yet even so great severity had to be tempered by the law of love towards the guilty person, as the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, bids us take care lest he who had been delivered to Satan be swallowed up by sorrow. But enough of these matters. It is agreed that for sins committed willingly there is still room for pardon, and so there is nothing here that supports the Novatian heresy. It is also agreed that there are many willing sins, and that these should not at once be called sins against the Holy Spirit. Although from what is added here, about sinning willingly after the truth has been recognised, and what is said a little later, about those who trample underfoot Christ, and count his blood as a common thing, and insult the Spirit of grace, this passage can rightly also be explained as referring to the sin against the Holy Spirit, as we said above, so that the sense of the latter part is that no other sacrifice remains for such people, that is, forgiveness of sins. Yet we think the interpretation which we put first is simpler and more consonant with the mind of the Apostle.

units.la: Caeterum quam graue peccatum sit, agnitam veritatem non recipere, seu, post agnitam & receptam retrocedere, Dominus in euangelio aperit, dicens Matth. 11. quod melius erit in die iudicio Tyro & Sidoni, quam ijs, qui auditum euangelium noluerunt recipere. Et Matth. 21. longa parabola de interfectis seruis & filio, missis ad agricolas, docet reijci dum populum Iudaicum, quia noluit veritatem recipere: addens & hoc: ideo dico vobis auferetur a vobis regnum Dei, & dabitur genti facienti fructum eius. Et qui ceciderit super lapidem illum, confringetur: super quem vero ceciderit, conteret eum. Actorum decimo tertio, Vobis oportebat primum loqui sermonem Dei: Sed quando repellitis illum, ecce conuertimur ad agentes: sic enim praecepit nobis Dominus. Ecce de illis, qui nolunt recipere verbum, & huiusmodi omnia Apostolus voluit Hebraeorum animis proposita esse, vt sic metu reiectionis Christi sacerdotium eiusq; sacrificium agnoscerent. Porro de illis, qui agnitam veritatem reijciunt, sunt illa de peccato in spiritum Sanctum: item quod Stephanus aiebat, Iudaeos resistere spiritui Sancto: item 2. Pet. 2. Si posteaquam refugerunt ab inquinamentis mundi, per agnitionem Domini, & seruatoris Iesu Christi, tamen his rursum inuoluti superantur, facta sunt illis postrema peiora primis. Satius enim fuisset illis, non cognouisse viam iustitiae, quam, vbi cognouerunt, conuerti ab eo, quod illis traditum
units.tr: Moreover, how grave a sin it is not to receive the truth once known, or to draw back after it has been known and received, the Lord opens in the gospel, saying in Matthew 11 that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgement for Tyre and Sidon than for those who were unwilling to receive the gospel when they heard it. And in Matthew 21, in the long parable of the servants who were killed and the son sent to the husbandmen, he teaches that the Jewish people were rejected because they were unwilling to receive the truth, adding this also: "Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruit. And whoever falls on that stone will be broken; but on whomever it falls, it will crush him." In Acts 13: "It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you thrust it away, behold, we turn to the Gentiles; for so the Lord has commanded us." Concerning those who refuse to receive the word, and all such things, the Apostle wished them set before the minds of the Hebrews, so that by fear of rejecting Christ they might acknowledge his priesthood and his sacrifice. Further, to those who reject the truth once known belong those words about the sin against the Holy Spirit; likewise what Stephen said, that the Jews resist the Holy Spirit; likewise 2 Peter 2: "If, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in these and overcome, their last state has become worse than the first. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them."

units.la: Actor. 7. traditum fuit sancto praecepto. Proinde, qui hoc pacto volentes peccant, reijciendo agnitam veritatem, quae de sacerdotio atque unico sacrificio Christi est clarissime tradita: tales scire debent, non expectandam aliam hostiam pro peccatis per Christum offerendam: neque etiam quamcunque rationem, qua pro peccatis hominum satisfiat. Aut, si placet aliam sequi interpretationem, sciant sibi nequaquam ita facile (si modo non resipiscant) veniam paratam, & hostiam Christi, quam ipsi habent ceu rem profanam, nequaquam profuturam ad remissionem peccatorum. Sed manet ipsos.
units.tr: Acts 7. Therefore, those who sin wilfully in this way, rejecting the truth once known, which has been most clearly taught concerning the priesthood and the unique sacrifice of Christ, ought to know that no other victim is to be expected to be offered for sins through Christ, nor any other means by which satisfaction may be made for the sins of men. Or, if they prefer to follow another interpretation, let them know that pardon is by no means so readily available to them (unless they repent), and that the sacrifice of Christ, which they hold as a profane thing, will by no means avail for the remission of their sins. But there remains for them...

units.la: Formidabilis quaedam expectatio iudicij) Respicit istud ad id, quod iamiam dixerat: quia vide tis appropinquantem diem: quae erat ratio vniuersalis ad totam exhortationem, quae praecesserat: ex qua & aptissime illata est tota haec comminatio. Quo facit causalis particula γὰρ connectens comminationem hanc cum illa ratione suasoria. Appositis autem verbis depingit poenam imminentem, ut tanto magis commoveat. Neque enim simpliciter dicit, expectationem iudicij esse, sed addit, formidabilem, φοβερὰν, qua voce elegans descriptio insinuatur.
units.tr: A certain fearful expectation of judgement This refers to what he had just said: "since you see the day drawing near"; this was the general reason for the whole exhortation that had preceded, and from it this whole threat is most aptly introduced. To this the causal particle [γὰρ] points, connecting this threat with that persuasive reason. By the words added he paints the punishment impending, so that he may move them all the more. For he does not say simply that there is an expectation of judgement, but adds "fearful" [φοβερὰν], by which word an elegant description is suggested.

units.la: Ita namque impijs, potissimum & veritatem agnitam reijcientibus, valde formidandum est iudicium, sicut Dominus Matth. vndecimo plenius docet. Sanctis quidem desiderabile est illud tempus, quia tunc accipient coronam vitae, & liberati ab omnibus malis, quibus hic presi fuerunt, perpetuo suauiter agent in gloria: unde & ad finem capitis noni dicti sunt pij expectare Christum ad salutem. Non quod Sancti habeant huiusmodi fiduciam, propter suam dignitatem: nequaquam ita est: nam omnes se reos fatentur: sed fide sic confirmantur, ut pro certo audeant expectare adimpletionem diuinarum promissionum: & hoc nomine, quia respiciunt in misericordiam & promissiones Dei, auidissime exoptant diem aduentus.
units.tr: For judgement is indeed to be greatly feared by the wicked, especially those who reject the truth once known, as the Lord teaches more fully in Matthew 11. That time is desirable for the saints, because then they will receive the crown of life, and, freed from all the evils with which they were beset here, will live sweetly in glory for ever; whence also at the end of chapter 9 the godly are said to wait for Christ unto salvation. Not that the saints have such confidence on account of their own worth; by no means is it so, for all confess themselves guilty. But they are so confirmed by faith that they dare confidently to expect the fulfilment of God's divine promises; and for this reason, because they look to the mercy and promises of God, they most eagerly long for the day of his coming.

units.la: Et ignis uehementia (ignis furens) Admodum elegans Metaphora, qua, quod est rei animatae, tribuit inanimatae: quasi prosopopoeia quadam ignem describeret, instar vehementissime indignantis & furentis hominis grassantem. Sic enim alibi ... alibi saepius & pro iusta ira, & in malam partem sumitur. Ergo & hic valde elegans est descriptio formidabilis illius iudicij. Saepe vero in Scripturis ignis, & quidem aeternus, ut res valde metuenda, in iudicio Dei describitur, Matthaei 24. & 25: & alibi in prophetis, psalmis, & nusquam non.
units.tr: And the vehemence of fire (raging fire). A very elegant metaphor, by which that which belongs to a living thing is attributed to a lifeless one; as if by a kind of prosopopoeia he were describing fire rampaging like a man most vehemently indignant and raging. For thus it is used elsewhere, and more often both for righteous anger and in a bad sense. So here too the description of that fearful judgement is very elegant. And often in the Scriptures fire, and indeed eternal fire, is described in God's judgement as something to be greatly feared, in Matthew 24 and 25, and elsewhere in the prophets, the psalms, and nearly everywhere.

units.la: Qui devoraturus est aduersarios) Et hic metaphora est, sed valde idonea describendae grauitati supplicij. Et crebro tali modo omnia vorans, absumens ignis in iudicio Dei describitur: quando etiam materialis ignis omnia absumit ac devorat: sicut licet videre in historia Coræ, Dathan & Abyron: item in historia Danielis de illis aduersarijs coniectis in fornacem. In summa, damnatio aeterna, & multo grauissima proposita est omnibus aduersarijs, qui veritatem Dei in iniustitia detinent, qui agnitam veritatem reijciunt, vel semel receptam post impugnant. Istud vero etiam nostris temporibus merito deberet proponi veritatis contemptoribus & impugnatoribus. Reges & principes fouent fallos doctores, & praemia constituunt: sed certum est, talibus contingere, quod olim Coræ, & sacerdotibus Baal. Sed quid de ijs, quibus nunquam fuit annunciata veritas? Num ij quoq; erunt rei iudicii? Vide Pom. 10. in illud, Annon audierunt? Atqui in omnem terram exiit sonus eorum, &c. Vide ibidem commentarios, item in praesentem epistolam Aquinatem. Item disputationem illam de gentilibus saluandis: vide Augustinum.
units.tr: About to devour the adversaries) Here too is a metaphor, but one very fitting to describe the gravity of the punishment. And in such a manner the fire that devours and consumes everything is often described in the judgement of God, since even material fire consumes and devours all things; as may be seen in the history of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and likewise in the history of Daniel concerning those adversaries cast into the furnace. In sum, eternal damnation, and a far more grievous one, is set before all adversaries who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, who reject the truth once known, or after receiving it once, attack it. Indeed this ought rightly to be set before the despisers and assailants of the truth in our own times as well. Kings and princes foster false teachers and grant them rewards; but it is certain that for such people there will befall what befell Korah and the priests of Baal. But what of those to whom the truth was never proclaimed? Will they too be liable to judgement? See Rom. 10 on the words, "Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth," etc. See there the commentaries, and likewise Aquinas on the present epistle. Likewise that disputation on the salvation of the Gentiles: see Augustine.

units.la: Qui aspernatus fuerit Mosi legem, absque misericordia sub duobus aut tribus testibus moritur. Quanto putatis peioribus afficietur supplicijs, qui filium Dei conculcarit, & sanguinem testamenti ceu rem profanam habuerit, per quem fuerat sanctificatus, & spiritum gratiae contumelia affecerit?
units.tr: He who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy under two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant, by which he was sanctified, as a common thing, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?

units.la: Ratio propositionis a minori ad maius. Et certè si quis conferat legem cum euangelio exacteq; perpendat, quanta sit huius pre illa excellentia (quam pasim in hac disputatione Apostolus variis argumentis tradidit, potissimumque toto capite octauo) facile intelligit, æquum esse, ut multo seueri ius puniantur, qui contemnunt euangelium, quàm qui contempserint legem. Vt enim excellentior est res, quæ contemnitur, ita grauius pec catum Excellentius est autem Euangelium, non solùm quia situm est in præstantioribus promissionibus, quod tamen revera valde magnum est: verum etiam quia omnia, quæ ad salutem pertinent, in Euangelio clarius, plenius, certius, sunt manifestata: & propter hanc pleniorem cognitionem etiam maiorem incurrunt contemptores poenam. Ioan. 15. Si locutus eis non fuissem, peccatum non haberent. Et hic comminatio instituitur contra eos, qui clarissime propositam doctrinam de Christo eiusq; sacerdotio ac sacrificio tame adhuc reijciunt atq; contemnunt. Non valde dissimile argumentum habetur Galat.3.vbi Apostolus ait,Hominis licet testamentum, tamen fi fit comprobatum,nemo reijcit,aut addit aliquid.
units.tr: The reasoning of the proposition from the lesser to the greater. And certainly, if anyone compares the law with the gospel and weighs carefully how great is the excellence of the latter over the former (which the Apostle has set out in various arguments throughout this disputation, and especially in the whole eighth chapter), he easily understands that it is only fair that those who despise the gospel should be punished far more severely than those who have despised the law. For the more excellent the thing that is despised, the graver the sin. Now the gospel is more excellent, not only because it rests on the more excellent promises, which in truth is very great, but also because all things that pertain to salvation have been made manifest in the gospel more clearly, more fully and more certainly; and because of this fuller knowledge, those who despise it incur a greater punishment. John 15: "If I had not spoken to them, they would not have sin." Here a threat is directed against those who still reject and despise the doctrine concerning Christ and his priesthood and sacrifice, though it has been set forth most clearly. Not very different is the argument in Galatians 3, where the Apostle says: "Though it is only a man's covenant, yet when it has been confirmed, no one sets it aside or adds anything to it."

units.la: Qui aspernatus fuerit Mosi legem) ἀθετήσας τις,id est, qui aliquid in ea irritum fecit, reprobauit,reiecit,&c.Itaq; late patet hec aspernandi lege ratio:neq; enim istud fit tantum apete conuiciando,vel damnando,sed quacunq; transgressione,potissimumq; spontanea, in qua videri queat quidam legis contemptus. Hoc autem modo peccant, qui faciunt contra id,quod in lege scriptum est,vt,qui collegit ligna die sabbatho : item qui adulterium,vel huiusmodi committit,quibus transgressoribus ipsius legis verbis mors infligitur.Item,qui docent aliquid contra legem, qui falsam doctrinam inducunt (Deut. 13.) item qui idola coluerint,vel alios ad idololatriam induxerint:ibidem & cap.17. tales omnes morte pleƈti iubentur.Plura autem huiusmodi precepta habes Exodi 21.22.In summa,passim extant in lege,quæ docent,contemptum legis morte puniedum,cui rei clarissimum exemplum habemus Actor.6.vbi contra Stephanum dicebant, locutum contumeliosa aduersus legem:similiter Actor.21.contra Paulum.In quibus plurima sunt, quæ mortem infligunt.Accipitur autem vox legis hoc loco non tantum pro iudicialibus preceptis per synechdochen,sed pro vniuersa lege, prout opponitur euangelio, cuius nullæ sunt partes,quas contemnere impune liceat, & singularum contemptus manifestus & testibus comprobatus grauissimè punitus est,quando vbiq; vel pœna temporalis præscribitur,vel certè illud adijcitur:peribit anima eius, aut huiusmodi, quo punitio etiam temporali grauior significatur.
units.tr: He who has set aside the law of Moses) that is, one who has annulled [ἀθετήσας τις], that is, has made something in it void, rejected it, cast it off, and so on. The scope of this despising is therefore wide. It is not only done by reviling or condemning the law, but by any transgression, above all a deliberate one in which a certain contempt for the law may be seen. Those sin in this way who act against what is written in the law, such as the man who gathered wood on the sabbath, or who commits adultery or something similar, which transgressions the very words of the law punish with death. Likewise those who teach something against the law, who introduce false doctrine (Deut. 13.), and those who worship idols or lead others into idolatry; in the same place and in chapter 17 all such are commanded to be put to death. You will find many precepts of this kind in Exodus 21 and 22. In sum, throughout the law there are passages teaching that contempt of the law is to be punished with death. The clearest example of this is in Acts 6, where they said against Stephen that he had spoken reproachfully against the law, and similarly in Acts 21 against Paul. Among these there are many which inflict death. The word "law" in this place is taken not merely for the judicial precepts, by synecdoche, but for the whole law, as it is set over against the gospel. No part of it may be despised with impunity, and the contempt of any single part, when it is manifest and proved by witnesses, is most severely punished. Wherever a temporal penalty is prescribed, or at least this is added: his soul shall perish, or something of the kind, by which a punishment heavier even than a temporal one is signified.

units.la: Sub duobus aut tribus testibus)Sumptū ex Deut.19. Ita quidem passim in lege, generali & ciuili quadam ratione præcipitur,vt in ore duorum vel trium testium stet omne verbum. Deut.19.In ore duorum vel trium testium peribit,qui interficietur. Quod verbū & Christus citat Matth.18.Sic autem ista accipienda sunt de testibus,ad euincendū, propter externa delicta,vt propter interna delicta constituatur testis coram Deo, reos æternæ mortis arguens vnuscuiusq; conscientia.Qui euadunt manus hominum, quando lege Dei contempserint,nequaquam tamen euadunt manus Dei. Ac Deus semper sedet pro tribunali,laturus sententiā in transgressores & contemptores,atq; assiduè apud eum odio sissimè accusant miseros diabolus & conscientia, propter quos duos testes ibi omnes conuincuntur,ut ad supplicia pertrahantur. Ergo quamlibet occultè quid fiat,tamè sem per adsunt obseruatores,semper circumstant, qui accusent, vt impossibile sit diuinam vltionem euadere.
units.tr: under two or three witnesses) Taken from Deut. 19. Indeed, throughout the law, on a general and civil footing, it is commanded that every matter shall stand on the mouth of two or three witnesses. Deut. 19: "At the mouth of two or three witnesses he shall be put to death." Christ also cites this word in Matt. 18. These things about witnesses are to be understood in this way: to prove external offences, whereas for internal offences the witness is set up before God, the conscience of each one accusing the guilty of eternal death. Those who escape the hands of men, when they have despised the law of God, by no means escape the hands of God. God always sits on the judgment seat, about to pronounce sentence on transgressors and despisers, and the devil and the conscience accuse wretched men continually and most bitterly before him. Because of these two witnesses all are convicted there and dragged off to punishment. So, however secretly a thing is done, there are always observers present, always bystanders to accuse, so that it is impossible to escape divine vengeance.

units.la: Absque misericordia)Sumptum est & ex hoc ex Deut.19. Vbi bis id habetur, & de lege talionis ita subijcitur:Non misereberis eius,& auferes noxium sanguinem de Israel, vt bene sit tibi.Et rursus ibidem:Non misereberis eius , sed animam pro anima, oculum pro oculo,dentem pro dente, manum pro manu,pedem pro pede exiges. Atq; hac nota potissimum discernitur euangelium à lege,quòd in euangelio misericordia est parata:in lege autem,quæ lata per ῥαβδόφοροῦ Mosen,misericordiæ non est locus. Atq; hinc assiduæ comminationes & terrores in lege,& accipiebantibi spiritū timoris & seruitutis, Rom.8. In euangelio promissiones blandæ.Beati mites, beati pacifici, &c. Matth.5.Nō audisamplius,Maledictus, Maledictus, &c. (Et propterea euangelij nomen receptum est:) et acceptus est à credētibus spiritus adoptionis,in quo clamamus, Abba pater. Ibi Dominus exercituum, Deus potens,fortis,vlciscens in tertiam & quartam generationem:Hic verò Deus pater misericordiarum.Atq; hoc docuit Christus Ioan.8.vbi,cùm producta esset muliercula,quę secundum legem Mosaicā debuisset lapidari,veluti intercedens,non vt damnans legem,dixit:Qui vestrūm immunis est à peccato , primus in illam lapidem iaciat:& postquam abijssent accusatores,ad mulierem:Nemo te condemnauit?quæ vbi di xisset,Nemo:Nec ego,inquit,te condemno:vade, & posthac ne peccaueris. Ibi egregiè ostendit Christus,gratiorem esse Deo misericordiam,quã legale sacrificium:& euangelij magnum ostendit discrimen à lege.Neq; verò hæc ita accipientur, quasi semper eodē modo conueniret impunè permittere peccata : nequaquā ita sentiendum est.Iustè enim lex Mosaica seueritatem adhibuit: iustè item nunc magistratus grauiter puniunt delinquentes,quandoquidem propter societatem humanam conseruādam opus est legibus, pœnis,mulētis.Et Deus addit promissiones in lege seueritatem illam exigentibus,diset teq; expressit & repetiuit,absque misericordia reos puniendos . Lex quippe propter transgressores posita est,& debent pœnarum metu cōtineri mali in officio. Sed eatenus adhibēda est misericordia, quatenus gloria Dei potest ea illustrari,& utilitati publicę nō ncommodatur.Nam si aliàs misericorditer cum sontibus agatur,metuendum , ne pericula grauia sequantur,ne quidam rursus mala perpetrent: aut alij freti spe misericordiæ similiter obtinendæ paria & atrociora designent:vnde mox damna ad proximum,multa offenoffendiculà: deniq; & nomen Dei apud aduersarios malos audit. Sic delinquentibus condonabitur, ut tamen gloria Dei maneat integra, & bonorum res in tuto sint collocatę.
units.tr: without mercy) This also is taken from Deut. 19, where it occurs twice, and concerning the law of retaliation it is added thus: "You shall not pity him, but you shall take away the guilty blood from Israel, that it may go well with you." And again in the same place: "Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall exact life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." It is chiefly by this mark that the gospel is distinguished from the law: in the gospel mercy is offered, but in the law, which was given through Moses the rod-bearer [ῥαβδόφορου], there is no place for mercy. Hence in the law there are constant threats and terrors, and men received "the spirit of fear and of bondage" (Rom. 8). In the gospel there are gentle promises: "Blessed are the meek, blessed are the peacemakers," etc. (Matt. 5). "Hear no more, Cursed, cursed," etc. (And for this reason the name of gospel has been received.) And among believers the spirit of adoption has been accepted, by which we cry, "Abba, Father." There the Lord of hosts is God, mighty, strong, avenging unto the third and fourth generation; here God is the Father of mercies. Christ also taught this in John 8, where, when a woman was brought forward who according to the Mosaic law ought to have been stoned, he, as one interceding, not as condemning the law, said: "He among you who is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her." And after the accusers had gone away, he said to the woman, "Has no one condemned you?" When she had said, "No one," he said, "Neither do I condemn you. Go, and sin no more." There Christ clearly showed that mercy is more acceptable to God than the sacrifice of the law, and he displayed the great difference between the gospel and the law. Yet these things are not to be taken as if it were always equally proper to permit sins with impunity; by no means is that to be thought. For the Mosaic law justly applied severity, and so now the magistrates justly punish offenders severely, since for the preservation of human society laws, penalties and fines are necessary. God also adds promises in the law that demand that severity, and he expressed and repeated it, that the guilty are to be punished without mercy. For the law was laid down on account of transgressors, and evil men must be restrained within their duty by fear of punishment. But mercy is to be applied only so far as the glory of God can be illustrated by it and public utility is not harmed. For if otherwise the guilty were treated mercifully, it is to be feared that grave dangers would follow, that some would again commit evils, or that others, relying on the hope of obtaining mercy in the same way, would devise equal and more atrocious crimes. Thence would soon come harm to one's neighbour and many stumbling blocks; and finally the name of God would be heard among wicked adversaries. So pardon will be granted to offenders, provided the glory of God remains whole and the interests of good men are kept safe.

units.la: Quanto putatis peioribus afficietur supplicijs) Graue & extremum supplicium in lege erat mors: quid enim ultrà posset inferri? Et tamen hic loquitur de peioribus supplicijs. Loquitur igitur de morte secunda, seu de morte aeterna, quam opponi vult temporali, & agnoscit, sicuti vere est, quanto is morte temporali longè acerbiorem & magis formidabilē.
units.tr: How much worse, do you think, will be the punishment The grave and extreme punishment under the law was death; for what further could be inflicted? And yet here he speaks of worse punishments. He therefore speaks of the second death, or eternal death, which he wishes to be set against temporal death, and he acknowledges, as is truly the case, how much more bitter and more terrible it is than temporal death.

units.la: Qui filium Dei conculcarit) Elegantī metaphora summum contemptum exprimit, exaggerandi criminis caussa. Quid enim odiosius, quàm aliquid conculcare? Conculcare plus est, quàm irritum facere. Non enim solùm negligit, sed etiam afficit iniuria maiore, qui conculcat. Ac diserte dicit, filium Dei. Legi opponendum fuisset euangelium, obseruata ratione antithesis: sed placuit Apostolo hic in secunda parte argumenti nominare filiū Dei, ad declarandum, quòd, cùm euangelium sit ipsius Christi, & de Christo, vbi contemnitur euangelium, ibi contemnatur ipse Christus. Itaq; exaggeratur crimen contemptus Christi. Quinetiam Christus hac ratione praefertur Mosi, quòd, cùm Moses, vt suprà cap. 3. dictum est, administrauerit domum Dei vt seruus, Christus eandem administrarit vt filius. Proinde, qui contemnit euangelium, peccat, non in hominem, qualis Moses, sed in ipsum Deum.
units.tr: who has trampled under foot the Son of God) By an elegant metaphor he expresses the highest contempt, to heighten the seriousness of the crime. For what is more hateful than to trample something underfoot? To trample is more than to make void. For he who tramples not only neglects but also inflicts a greater injury. And he expressly says the Son of God. The gospel should have been set against the law, observing the rule of antithesis; but the Apostle chose here, in the second part of the argument, to name the Son of God, to declare that, since the gospel belongs to Christ himself and is about Christ, where the gospel is despised, there Christ himself is despised. Thus the crime of despising Christ is magnified. Moreover, Christ is preferred to Moses on this ground: whereas Moses, as was said above in chapter 3, administered the house of God as a servant, Christ administers the same as a son. Therefore he who despises the gospel sins not against a man, as Moses was, but against God himself.

units.la: Et sanguinem testamenti) Sanguis is est precium depensum pro nostra salute, est sacrificiū per Christum oblatum Patri: non leue igitur crimen, habere talem sanguinem ceu rem profanam.
