Est res sacra, longeq; excellentior, quàm villus sanguis in lege, quomodo er go eum aestimabimus ceu rem profanam, nullarum virium nullosq; effectus spirituales adferentem: Amplificat autem mirum in modum eum sanguinem, quòd vocat sanguinem testamenti, significans, eum esse eiusmodi, per quem confirmatum sit nouum testamentum, sicut Christus ipse Matth. 26. aiebat, dicens: Hic est sanguis noui testamenti. Vnde, sanguinem istum contemnere, est plane contemnere ipsum testamentum, ipsumq; euangelium: imò est, omnia quae ad salutem nostram pertinent, omnesq; promissiones diuinas euertere. Per hunc sanguinem omnia effecta sunt, diluta sunt nostra peccata, placatus est pater, promissiones sunt confirmatae, sanguis est precium, redemptio, sanctificatio, sigillum & omnia.
units.tr: and the blood of the covenant) This blood is the price paid for our salvation; it is the sacrifice offered to the Father through Christ. It is therefore no slight crime to regard such blood as a profane thing. It is a holy thing, far more excellent than any blood in the law. How then shall we value it as a profane thing, bringing no power and no spiritual effects? He magnifies that blood wonderfully by calling it the blood of the covenant, signifying that it is that through which the new covenant was confirmed, just as Christ himself said in Matt. 26: "This is the blood of the new covenant." Hence to despise this blood is plainly to despise the covenant itself and the gospel; indeed it is to overturn everything that pertains to our salvation and all the divine promises. Through this blood all things have been accomplished: our sins have been washed away, the Father has been appeased, the promises have been confirmed. The blood is the price, the redemption, the sanctification, the seal, and everything.

units.la: Per quem factus est sanctificatus) Haec particula interpositia mire facit ad exaggerandū crimē. Eum sanguinem, per quem fueris sanctificatus, tamen existimare, quasi esset res profana, quis ferendum putet? Elegans ἀντίθεσις in vocibus κοινόν, & ἡγιασμένον, profanū & sanctificatus. Et constat loqui Apostolum contra eos, qui iam semel participes fuerunt doni coelestis, & in baptismo per sanguinem Christi sanctificati. Atq; omnes quidem per sanguinem Christi sanctificantur: quando quidem sanguis ille ad hoc est oblatus, & efficax ad omnia peccata tollenda, & omnibus ex aequo impenditur, quantum attinet ad voluntatem Dei: sed quo minus succedant effectus spirituales, & ab omnibus percipiantur, in causa est ipsorum qui recipere debebant, malitia.
units.tr: by which he was sanctified) This inserted clause greatly serves to heighten the crime. Who could think it bearable to regard as a profane thing the blood by which you were sanctified? There is an elegant antithesis in the words κοινόν [common/profane] and ἡγιασμένον [sanctified]. And it is clear that the Apostle is speaking against those who had already once been partakers of the heavenly gift and had been sanctified in baptism through the blood of Christ. Indeed all are sanctified through the blood of Christ, since that blood was offered for this very purpose and is efficacious for taking away all sins, and is bestowed equally on all, so far as the will of God is concerned. But the reason why the spiritual effects do not follow and are not perceived by all lies in the wickedness of those who ought to have received them.

units.la: Et spiritum gratiae contumelia affecerit) Loquitur ergo de iis, qui iam dona Spiritus aliqua acceperant, atque ideo contemnentes illa, veluti impugnando agnitam veritatem, vel huiusmodi perpetrando peccabant in Spiritum Sanctū. Credentes enim accipiebant Spiritum, eiusq; dona (nam à donis & propter dona vocatur spiritus gratiae, quasi habes & conferens multa charismata: alias satis fuisset simpliciter dicere, Spiritum non addendo gratiae:) plerunq; etiam externis & visibilibus signis: & per Spiritum hunc innotabantur corda, ac prorsus nouae efficiebantur creaturae. Proinde, iam velle redire ad ingenium, relabi in veterem perfidiam, hoc erat plane spiritum gratiae contumelia afficere.
units.tr: And have insulted the Spirit of grace) He is speaking, then, of those who had already received some gifts of the Spirit, and who, by despising them, as if by attacking the truth they had come to know, or by committing acts of this kind, sinned against the Holy Spirit. For believers received the Spirit and his gifts (he is called the Spirit of grace from the gifts and because of the gifts, as one who has and bestows many charismata; otherwise it would have been enough simply to say "the Spirit" without adding "of grace"). They often received these gifts also through external and visible signs, and through this Spirit their hearts were known and they became entirely new creatures. Therefore, to wish to return to their former nature and fall back into their old unbelief was plainly to insult the Spirit of grace.

units.la: Sed & quicunque donis spiritus abutuntur, vel, non sinunt ea florere, suumq; officium peragere, omnes hi se spiritui Sancto opponunt. Huc pertinet, quod Ephes. 4. dicitur, Ne contristetis spiritum Sanctum Dei, per quem obsignati estis in diem redemptionis: Item 1. Thessal. 5. Spiritū ne extinguatis, prophetias ne aspernemini. Proinde mirum in modum amplificatur crimen eorum, qui post agnitam veritatem peccant: quando ita ostenditur, per tales & conculcati filium Dei, & sanguinem Christi vilipendi ceu rē profanam & immundam: deniq; & spiritum gratiae affici contumelia. Caeterùm debemus hic excerpere doctrinam contra eos, qui etiam nostro tempore sanguine Christi ceu rē profanam vilipendunt. Hi sunt qui sacramenta, quae habent efficacia ex sanguine Christi, & quorum vsu efficimur sanguinis Christi participes, contemnunt. Videant tales contemptores, quomodo ira Dei ipsos maneat. Baptismus in sanguine Christi valet: vnde ablui & sanctificari in baptismo sanguine Christi dicimus. Apocal. 1. Dilexit nos, & lauit nos à peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. 1. Cor. 6. Sed abluti estis, sanctificati estis, &c. In coena Domini ibi ipsisimus sanguis Christi nobis offertur: conscientiae de participatione patione sanguinis Christi confirmantur: deniq; sanguis ille noui testamenti nobis ob oculos mentis proponitur. Proinde intendant in verba apostoli, quicunque audent Sacramenta contemnere, vel externum eorum vsum paruifacere. Iam quia mentionem fecimus peccati in spiritum Sanctum, atq; interpretati sumus verba Apostoli, & hoc capite, & cap. 6. de peccato in spiritum Sanctum non male posse accipi, non abs re fecerimus, si locum de peccato in spiritum Sanctum exactius examinauerimus: quo de vide libros nostros Rhapsodiarum diuinarum.
units.tr: But also all who abuse the gifts of the Spirit, or who do not allow them to flourish and to perform their office, set themselves against the Holy Spirit. To this belongs what is said in Ephesians 4: "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." Likewise 1 Thessalonians 5: "Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies." So the crime of those who sin after they have come to know the truth is magnified in a remarkable way, since it is shown that by such acts they trample underfoot the Son of God and count the blood of Christ as a profane and unclean thing, and finally insult the Spirit of grace. Moreover, we must here draw out a teaching against those who, even in our own time, despise the blood of Christ as something profane. These are the people who scorn the sacraments, which have their efficacy from the blood of Christ, and through whose use we become partakers of that blood. Let such despisers consider how the wrath of God remains upon them. Baptism has its power through the blood of Christ; hence we say that in baptism we are washed and sanctified by the blood of Christ. Revelation 1: "He loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood." 1 Corinthians 6: "But you were washed, you were sanctified," etc. In the Lord's Supper the very blood of Christ is offered to us; consciences are confirmed in their participation in the blood of Christ; and finally that blood of the new covenant is set before the eyes of our minds. Therefore let all who dare to despise the sacraments, or to make light of their outward use, take note of the words of the apostle. Now, since we have made mention of sin against the Holy Spirit and have explained the words of the apostle, both in this chapter and in chapter 6, and since the sin against the Holy Spirit can rightly be understood in this way, it will not be out of place if we examine more exactly the passage about sin against the Holy Spirit; on this see our books of Rhapsodiae divinae.

units.la: Nouimus enim eum, qui dixit: Meum est vlcisci, ego retribuam, dicit Dominus. Et rursum: Dominus iudicabit populum suum.
units.tr: For we know him who said: Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. And again: The Lord will judge his people.

units.la: Rationis confirmatio a Scripturae testimonijs, quae ad mouendum terrendum q; contemptores, eosq; qui agnitam veritatem repuunt, multo sunt aptissimę. Habet aute vim atq; acrimoniam quandam ad mouendum, quod praemittit, quasi diceret: Quare non credimus, quod contemptores Christi & sanguinis eius graviter punientur? Nos scimus, qualis sit Deus, quam zelotes, quam seuerus & incorruptus vltor sit ille, vt nunquam sinat impunitum contemptum sui. Ergo tacite reuincit illorum conscientias, & cogit fateri, quod pro certo sciant, sibi vltionem Dei grauissimam, si non in tempore resipiscant, paratam. Sumptum autem est vtrumq; testimonii ex cantico Mosi Deut.32. Atque appositę esse accommodata praesenti causae, perfacile est demonstrare.
units.tr: A confirmation of the argument from testimonies of Scripture, which are most fitting for moving and terrifying despisers, and those who reject the truth they have known. The sentence that precedes it has a certain force and sharpness for moving, as if he said: Why should we not believe that those who despise Christ and his blood will be severely punished? We know what kind of God he is, how jealous, how severe and incorruptible an avenger, so that he never allows contempt of himself to go unpunished. So he tacitly convicts their consciences and compels them to admit what they know for certain, that God's most grievous vengeance is prepared for them if they do not repent in time. Both testimonies are taken from the song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32, and it is very easy to show that they are well suited to the present cause.

units.la: Nam ibi Moses, posteaquam conuocata vniuersa multitudine Israelitarum, praedixisset futurum, vt breui a morte ipsius a vero Dei cultu deficerent, ideoq; grauissime olim a Deo puniendos, idem argumentum plenius iusto cantico est complexus. In quo primum multis verbis commemorat, quanta beneficia populus ille a Deo accepisset, paulo post describit, eum foede relapsum in peccata, atq; neglecto vero Dei cultu conuersum ad idolatriam & superstitiones. Hinc introducit Deum e sublimi contemplantem, necnon comminantem, quod sui neglectum acerrime sit vlturus, quodq;, vt irritarunt ipsum eligendo in Deos, qui Dij non erant, ita vicissim se irritaturum illos reprobando eos, & alium populum, qui non erat populus, eligendo: praeterea innumera mala immittendo. Deinde addit Deus, (hunc enim loquentem & expostulantem magna cantici parte introducit) fuisse sibi in animo statim perdere illos funditus, vt ne memoria quidem ulla foret in terris superstes: sed non expediuisse propter aduersarios gentiles, qui protinus arrogantissime iactassent, sua potius potestate, quam Dei nutu iudicio q; Israelitas deletos.
units.tr: For there Moses, after assembling the whole multitude of the Israelites, had foretold that shortly after his death they would fall away from the true worship of God, and therefore would one day be punished most severely by God; and he treated this same subject more fully in the song. In it he first recounts in many words what great benefits that people had received from God; shortly afterwards he describes them as having shamefully fallen back into sin, and, neglecting the true worship of God, turned to idolatry and superstitions. Here he introduces God looking down from on high, and threatening that he will most bitterly avenge their neglect of him; and that, just as they provoked him by choosing gods that were not gods, so in turn he will provoke them by rejecting them and choosing another people, which was not a people; and besides this he will send countless evils. Then God adds (for he introduces him speaking and complaining at length in a large part of the song) that it had been in his mind at once to destroy them utterly, so that no memory of them would remain on earth; but that it was not expedient, on account of the Gentile adversaries, who would straightway have boasted most arrogantly that the Israelites had been destroyed by their own power rather than by the nod and judgment of God.

units.la: Quare mox subijcit Deus, se sibi seruare vltionem & retributionem, quodq; ipse velit suu populu suo tempore iudicare, ac de eo vindictam sumere. In quo ordine, quaq; occasione haec verba ibi sint posita. Cum aut contra eos ibi dicta sint, qui post agnita veritate, & accepta innumera beneficia, verbu ac veru cultu Dei deseruerunt, manifesta etiam idololatria committentes: quiuis intelligit, eade praesenti loco optime couenire, vbi grauis comminatio illis, qui ab agnita veritate vellet deficere, proponitur. Neq; vero opus est copiosius explicemus, quae ad canticum illud pertinent. Animaduerte interea, paucula quidem selecta & producta ab Apostolo esse verba, sed tamen eiusmodi, quae ut sumpta ex historia & carmine omnibus Hebraeis notissimo ita mirabile habent pondus, & supra quam dici queat, omnium animos excitant & percellunt. Vultq; Apostolus, caetera ibi posita reuocari in memoriam, tanquam proprie de tempore reuelati euangelij Moses ibi fuisset vaticinatus, sicut & reuera fuit, quando ibi agit de reiectione Iudaeorum, & vocatione gentium. Rom.10. Vbi Paulus citat ex hoc cantico. Sunt q; haec duo testimonia sibi, paucis intercedentibus, coiuncta. Sic enim ibi legimus iuxta hebraicam veritatem, Mea est vltio & retributio, tempore oportuno labetur pes eorum: nam propinquus est dies perditionis eorum, & festinant, quae ventura sunt eis. Quoniam iudicabit Dominus populum suum, & super seruos suos se solabitur, cum viderit abijsse potentiam, & quod velut in nihilum conclusus seu redactus sit atq; derelictus. Ita vides prope inuicem posita, & eodem sensu accipienda, pulcherrimeq; inter se conuenire. Caeterum Apostolus prius testimonium potius citat ad veritatem hebraicam, quam ad versionem Septuaginta. Sic enim hic apostolus, ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω: ἐν καιρῷ, id est, in die ultionis retribuam in tempore. In Hebraeo autem sic: לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלּוּם, id est, Mea ultio & retributio.
units.tr: Therefore God immediately adds that he reserves vengeance and retribution to himself, and that he himself will judge his people in his own time and take vengeance on them. Whatever the order and occasion in which these words are placed there, since they were spoken against those who, after they had known the truth and received countless benefits, abandoned the word and the true worship of God, committing even manifest idolatry, anyone can see that they agree very well with the present passage, where a grave threat is set before those who would wish to fall away from the truth they have known. Nor is there need to explain at greater length what pertains to that song. Meanwhile observe that the words the apostle selected and quoted are few, yet they are of such a kind that, taken from history and from a song most well known to all Hebrews, they carry so remarkable a weight and stir and strike the minds of all beyond what can be said. The apostle also wishes the rest of what is written there to be recalled to memory, as if Moses had there prophesied specifically about the time of the revealed gospel, as indeed he did, when in that place he deals with the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. Romans 10, where Paul cites from this song. These two testimonies are also joined together, with only a few words between them. For thus we read there, according to the Hebrew truth: "Mine is vengeance and retribution; in due time their foot will slip, for the day of their destruction is near, and the things that are to come upon them hasten." "For the Lord will judge his people, and will comfort himself over his servants, when he sees that power has departed, and that they have been shut up and reduced to nothing and forsaken." So you see they are placed nearly side by side, are to be understood in the same sense, and agree most beautifully with one another. Moreover, the apostle cites the first testimony as it stands in the Hebrew truth rather than in the Septuagint version. For the apostle here has: ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω: ἐν καιρῷ, that is, "to me vengeance, I will repay, in the time"; that is, "I will repay in the day of vengeance, in due time." In the Hebrew, however, it is: לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלּוּם [li naqam veshillum], that is, "Mine is vengeance and retribution."

units.la: Quod ad alterum testimonium attinet, citat id Apostolus simpliciter ex Septuaginta, ἐκδικήσει ἐκδικήσω τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ: in quam sententiam & hebraice habetur, יָדִין יְהוָה עַמּוֹ, iudicabit Dominus populum suum. Quo loco notandum יָדִין iudicabit, exponi pro vindicabit, quod videlicet ipse ultor sit futurus in populum suu: non permissurus, vt a gentibus deleantur, qui gloriarentur, se suis viribus populum Israelitarum attriuisse: quo sensu prioriloco dicit, ad se pertinere vltionem & retributionem.
units.tr: As for the second testimony, the apostle cites it simply from the Septuagint: ἐκδικήσει ἐκδικήσω τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ, "he will avenge his people." In the Hebrew the same sense is given: יָדִין יְהוָה עַמּוֹ [yadin YHWH ammo], "the Lord will judge his people." Here it should be noted that יָדִין, "will judge," is rendered as "will vindicate," namely that he himself will be the avenger upon his people, and will not permit them to be destroyed by the nations, who would boast that they had worn down the Israelites by their own strength; in this sense he says in the first passage that vengeance and retribution belong to him.

units.la: Quamobrem testimonia haec ita sunt citata, vt proponant ob oculos vindictam ipsius Dei, cuius manus effugere nunquam licet. Atque ut daretur euadere manus hominum, neq; male succederet nobis propter incredulitatem apud homines, tamen Deus puniet populum suum. Itaq; is est metuendus, & propter hunc decet nos in sana doctrina constantes manere. Ac Deus semper multò seuerissimè animaduertit in populum suum. Hinc illud 1.Pet.4. Incipit iudicium à domo Dei. Et 1.Cor.11. Cùm iudicamur, à Domino corripimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Phrasis haec iudicandi in Scripturis familiaris est & frequens, & tam ad praesentis, quàm futurae vitae poenas diuinitus infligendas potest referri. Deut.32. Iudicabit Dominus populum suum: quo tamen loco in meliorem partem sumpta videtur vox, & assertionem diuinam aduersus impias gentes denotat. Quemadmodum & saepe in Scripturis diuinam defensionem & protectionem voce iudicij Dominus designat. Sed nos hoc loco, interprete apostolo, ad poenam & ultionem referimus, quam Dominus improbis & negligentibus infligit. Ezechiel. 7. terrae Israel minatur Deus excidium, his verbis: Nunc finis super te, & mittam furorem meum in te, & iudicabo te iuxta vias tuas, ponamque super te omnes abominationes tuas. Et non parcet oculus meus tibi, neq; miserebor: sed vias tuas super te ponam, & abominationes tuae in medio tui erunt, & scietis, quòd ego Iehouah, &c. Et cap.38. Et iudicio contendam cum eo peste & sanguine: & imbrem inundantem, & lapides grandinis, ignem & sulphur pluere faciam super eum, & super exercitus eius. Ezech.16. Iudicabo te iudicijs adulterarum, & effundentium sanguinem, daboq; te sanguinem irae & zeli, &c. quae isidem sequuntur de ira & poena Dei aduersus Iudaeos & populum Dei. In Scripturis passim Deus minatur populo iudicium & visitationem: qua quidem commination e varia mala comprehendit, quę coelitus in populum ingratum ac perfidum erat missurus. In deserto murmurantem populum serpentibus affligit, igne consumit, ac variis deniq; modis castigat, donec annis quadraginta sexcenta millia eorum delet, qui ex Aegypto fuerant egressi, propterea, quòd ab exploratoribus ad incredulitatem & diffidentiam sese flecti fuissent passi. In Philistaeorum, Moabitarum, Ammonitarum, Midianitarum, caeterorumq; finitimorum hostium manus propter peccata & idololatriam saepe fuerunt traditi. Fame, peste, gladio, quae tres Dei virgae sunt gravissimae, non semel à Deo fuerunt puniti: de quo legere est 1.Reg.17. Amos 3. Agg.1. Oseae 1. Ierem.9. & alibi: In Assyria transportantur decem tribus, quae Deum verum deseruerant, & ad gentium idolomanias desciuerant. Idem Iudaeis & Hierosolymitanis euenit, quos Dominus Babylonem abduci siuit, ut septuaginta annorum captiuitate perfidiam & idololatriam luerent, à qua toties perfidos prophetas Dei admoniti discedere, & ad Deum reuerti recusarant.
units.tr: Wherefore these testimonies are cited so as to set before our eyes the vengeance of God himself, whose hand one can never escape. And even if it were granted to escape the hands of men, and even if things did not go badly for us because of unbelief among men, God would still punish his people. So he is to be feared, and on account of him it is fitting for us to remain steadfast in sound doctrine. And God always punishes his own people much more severely. Hence the saying of 1 Peter 4: "Judgment begins at the house of God." And 1 Corinthians 11: "When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we are not condemned with the world." This manner of speaking about judgment is familiar and frequent in Scripture, and it can refer to punishments divinely inflicted both in the present life and in the life to come. Deuteronomy 32: "The Lord will judge his people," where, however, the word seems to be taken in a better sense and denotes the divine defence against impious nations. Just as also often in Scripture the Lord signifies divine defence and protection by the word judgment. But in this place, with the apostle as our interpreter, we refer it to the punishment and vengeance which the Lord inflicts on the wicked and the negligent. In Ezekiel 7 God threatens the land of Israel with destruction in these words: "Now the end is upon you, and I will send my fury upon you, and I will judge you according to your ways, and I will set upon you all your abominations. My eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity; but I will set your ways upon you, and your abominations will be in your midst, and you will know that I am the LORD," etc. And chapter 38: "And I will contend with him by pestilence and blood; and I will make rain pour down in flood, and hailstones, fire and brimstone, upon him and upon his armies." Ezekiel 16: "I will judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and of those who shed blood, and I will give you the blood of wrath and of jealousy," etc., which follow in the same way concerning the wrath and punishment of God against the Jews and the people of God. Throughout Scripture God threatens his people with judgment and visitation; this threat embraces various evils which he was about to send from heaven upon an ungrateful and faithless people. In the desert he afflicted the murmuring people with serpents, consumed them with fire, and at last chastised them in various ways, until in forty years he destroyed six hundred thousand of those who had come out of Egypt, because they had allowed themselves to be turned to unbelief and distrust by the spies. Because of sin and idolatry they were often delivered into the hands of the Philistines, the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Midianites, and other neighbouring enemies. Famine, pestilence and sword, which are the three most grievous rods of God, were more than once used by God to punish them; on which one may read 1 Kings 17, Amos 3, Haggai 1, Hosea 1, Jeremiah 9, and elsewhere. The ten tribes, which had abandoned the true God and had fallen away to the idolatries of the nations, were carried off into Assyria. The same happened to the Jews and the Jerusalemites, whom the Lord allowed to be led away to Babylon, so that by seventy years of captivity they might pay for their faithlessness and idolatry, from which the prophets of God had so often warned them to depart and return to God, and which they had refused.

units.la: Tandem cum restituti libertati & fortunis pristinis, Christum filium Dei repudiarent, in crucem agerent, prophetas, Apostolos, & sapientes Dei lapidarent, in exilium eiicerent, variisq; ludibrijs & iniurijs afficerent, adeò furor Dei in eos exarsit, ut misso exercitu Romanorum, duce Tito, latrones occideret, templum & urbem excinderet ac solo équaret, & aeternae uastitati devouperet: teste Daniele cap 9. & Matth.21. Luc.19. Pertinet quoq; ad Dei iudicium dissipatio tribuum & caecitas, quae genti durae ceruicis euenit propter euangelij reiectionem: quanquam caecitatem hanc & obdurationem Israeli ex parte contigisse dicit Apostolus, (Roman.11.) vsq; quo plenitudo gentium introierit. Caeterum, quae vniuersaliter de gente Iudaica dicuntur, quemadmodum Deus populũ suũ visitarit & punierit: eadem de pijs & credentibus etiam dici possunt, quòd à Domino vi sitentur, castigentur, probentur, ne videlicet cum mundo poenitere nescio aeternum condemnentur, (sed velut in ordinem & gyrum à Deo patre ducantur, ne rebus ad voluntatem fluentibus, legibus fidei disruptis, ad securitatem & luxuriam declinent. Tu quoq; vtbonis corporalibus desertis ad spiritualia & coelestia animos intendant, fideq; vniuer sa mundi mala vincere, & tandem cum Christo coronam consequi discat. Pertinet huc, quae in Scripturis de aduersis & calamitatibus piorum leguntur: cuiusmodi sunt illa de patriarchis, de prophetis, de Christo, de apostolis, de Iobo, de Dauide, & alijs sanctis, qui Catharmata mundi fuerunt & spectacula. Contra impij in magnis honoribus, opibus, delicijs, & admiratione vulgi florent. Qua de re vide querelas pios, Ierem.12. Psal.75 37. Abac 1. Luc.12.16. &c. Ex quibus omnibus patet quomodo iudicium Domini, à domo domini inchoetur. Non dicam nunc de vniuersali illo iudicio mundi, & excidio impiorum: quod procul dubio Apostolus ex hisce colligere voluit: sic argumentando: Si Deus impios electos iudicij sui sententiam exequitur, utiq; in impios & reprobos animaduertit durius. At pios à Deo iudicari & sententiam eius experiri, ex Scripturis & historijs sacris liquet. Ergo impiorum vltio & retributio erit certa, qua Dominus in eos furorem suum diffundet.
units.tr: At last, when they had been restored to liberty and their former fortunes, they rejected Christ the Son of God, put him to the cross, stoned the prophets, Apostles and wise men of God, drove them into exile, and subjected them to various mockeries and injuries. So the wrath of God blazed up against them: he sent a Roman army under the leadership of Titus, who slaughtered the robbers, tore the temple and city down, levelled them to the ground, and devoted them to eternal desolation. Daniel 9, Matthew 21 and Luke 19 bear witness to this. The scattering of the tribes and the blindness that befell that stubborn-necked nation because it rejected the gospel also belong to God's judgment, although the Apostle says that this blindness and hardening came upon Israel only in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in (Romans 11). Moreover, what is said in general terms about the Jewish nation, how God visited and punished his people, can also be said of the godly and the believers: that they are visited, chastised and tested by the Lord, lest they be condemned eternally along with the world that refuses to repent. Rather, they are led by God the Father back into order and into the right course, lest, with worldly things flowing according to their will and the laws of faith broken, they turn aside to security and luxury. So too, when they have abandoned bodily goods, they are to direct their minds to spiritual and heavenly things, to overcome all the evils of the world by faith, and at last to learn to attain the crown with Christ. To this belong the things that Scripture records about the adversities and calamities of the godly: such as those concerning the patriarchs, the prophets, Christ, the Apostles, Job, David and the other saints, who became the offscouring of the world [καθάρματα] and a spectacle. The wicked, by contrast, flourish in great honours, riches, pleasures and the admiration of the crowd. On this matter see the complaints of the godly in Jeremiah 12, Psalms 73 and 37, Habakkuk 1, Luke 12:16, etc. From all these things it is plain how the judgment of the Lord begins at the house of the Lord. I will not now speak of that universal judgment of the world and the destruction of the wicked, which the Apostle no doubt wished to infer from these things, arguing thus: If God carries out the sentence of his judgment on the elect, then surely he will take vengeance more severely on the wicked and the reprobate. But that the godly are judged by God and experience his sentence is clear from the Scriptures and sacred histories. Therefore the punishment and recompense of the wicked will be certain, and the Lord will pour out his wrath upon them.

units.la: Argumentum fere simile à maiore ad minus Paulus vsurpat ad Rom. cap.11, vbi à Iudaeorum dæorum pœnis ad gentilium iudicium progreditur. Si Deus, inquit, naturalibus ramis non pepercit, vide ne tibi quoq; non parcat.Item 2. Pet.2. Si Deus Angelis, qui peccauerant non pepercit,sed catenis caliginis in tartarum detrusos,tradidit ad damnantionem seruatos.Et prisco mundo non pepercit:& quæ ibi sequuntur.In Esaiæ & Ieremiæ concionibus multa de Iudæo tum castigationibus occurrunt,à quibus prophetæ argumentantur de iudicio Dei aduersus gentes.De iudicio impiorum particulari in hac vita,& vni uersali ad finem mundi,plura passim leguntur. Vide de iudicio vniuersali, Matth.25. Marc.13. Luc.21.17.Ioan.5. 2. Corinth.5. Apocal.20.21.&c.
units.tr: Paul uses a similar argument from the greater to the lesser in Romans 11, where he moves from the punishments of the Jews to the judgment of the Gentiles: If God, he says, did not spare the natural branches, take care lest he also not spare you. Likewise 2 Peter 2: If God did not spare the angels who sinned, but cast them down into hell and delivered them into chains of darkness, reserved for judgment, and did not spare the ancient world, and what follows there. In the sermons of Isaiah and Jeremiah many things occur about the chastisements of the Jews, from which the prophets argue about the judgment of God against the nations. Many passages speak everywhere about the particular judgment of the wicked in this life and the universal judgment at the end of the world. See on the universal judgment Matthew 25, Mark 13, Luke 21:17, John 5, 2 Corinthians 5, Revelation 20 and 21, etc.

units.la: Doctrina autem hinc colligitur duplex: Prima, quòd Deus suam ecclesiam, quæ domus eius est,visitet,castiget,corripiat,instar patris suam familiam corrigentis & visitantis. Deinde, quòd impios etiam iudicet,cum in hac, tum in futura vita: eosq; omnes, qui ecclesiam & verbum eius persequuntur,virga ferrea plectat, & iusta ultione attribuat mala ecclesiæ inflicta.Potest hisce & tertia adiungi, videlicet,Dei iustitiæ & ultioni committenda esse, quæ piis inferuntur per impios:nec animum ad ulciscendum debere inclinari.Imò potius pro inimicis orandum,ijsq;, qui malefaciunt,benefaciendum.
units.tr: Two doctrines are gathered from this. The first is that God visits, chastens and corrects his church, which is his house, as a father corrects and visits his family. The second is that he also judges the wicked, both in this life and in the life to come, and that he will strike with a rod of iron all who persecute the church and his Word, and will repay with just vengeance the evils inflicted on the church. A third may be added to these: that the injuries inflicted on the godly through the wicked must be committed to the justice and vengeance of God, and the mind must not be inclined to take revenge. Rather, we ought to pray for our enemies and do good to those who do evil to us.

units.la: Horrendum est,incidere in manus Dei viuentis) Sunt hæc instar epiphonematis siue amplificationis,qua concludit ea,quæ dixit de Dei vltione in impios,& iudicio in domum suam, ostenditq;,graue ac periculosum esse, Dei iudicium & manum per incredulitatem experiri,hoc enim tale esse,ut nusquam detur effugere aut eripi:id quod Christus Matth.5. 18.22.docet,vbi carceres æternos & cruciatus minatur impijs.
units.tr: It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. These words serve as an epiphonema, or amplification, by which the author concludes what he has said about God's vengeance on the wicked and his judgment on his own house. He shows that it is grave and dangerous to experience the judgment and hand of God through unbelief, for this is of such a kind that there is nowhere to escape or be rescued from it. Christ teaches this in Matthew 5:18–22, where he threatens the wicked with eternal prisons and torments.

units.la: Manus Dei viuentis in Scripturis pro potestate,robore,& iudicio,vsurpatur: eadem fere ratione,qua Deo dextera ascribitur.Per anthropopathiam enim Scriptura Dei virtutem,potestatem,iram,& iudicium exprimit manus siue manuū asignatione.Exod.15.In manu eius forti eduxit eos,&c.psal.31. In manu tua sunt tempora mea, erue me è manu inimicorum meorum.psal.89.Tibi est brachium cum fortitudine,robusta est manus tua, exaltata est dextera tua.Iob.13. Manum tuā longè à me facito, & terror tuus ne exerceat me.Quod verò dicit,horrendum esse,incidere in manus Dei viuentis, id ad incredulorum & improborum pertinet supplicium & comminationem, qui zelo Dei & ira eius ita percelluntur,ut nusquam consistendi locum habeant:sic 1.Samuel.5. Manus Domini fuit contra ciuitatem Gath contritione magna valde. Item ibidem, Manus Domini aggrauata est in Asdodios,& desolauit eos,& percusit eos marisicis, Asdod & fines eius: videntes verò viri Asdod,quòd sic esset,dixerunt: Ne maneat arca Dei Israel apud nos, quia dura est manus eius contra nos,& contra Dagō Deū nostrū. Antiochus Epiphanes, de quo extat 2. Machab.9. à Domino plaga insanabili percutitur. Actor.12. Herodes ab angelo Dei percutitur,& phthiriasi miserè perit.Sic impij in Dei manum incidere dicuntur, quando verbo eius resistentes pœnas iustas exoluunt. Vnde Ecclesiast.2. cap.dicitur, Si pœnitentiam non egerimus,incidemus in manus Domini,non in manus hominum. Sic Saul,Iudas,Cain,alijq; impij in manus Domini incidunt. Incidunt & pij in manus Domini,at spe gratuitæ misericordiæ freti sustentantur,tametsi graviter vapulent:Hinc Dauid 2.Samuel.24.ad prophetam Gad trium malorum optionem Dei iussu offeretem, Incidā obsecro,inquit,in manū Iehouę, quia multæ sunt miserationes eius: & in manu hominum ne incidam.Deligit ibi trium dierum pestem præ fame septemnali, & persecutione trium mensium:non ignorans,quàm sit facilius , cum Deo in gratiā redire,quā cum hominibus.Non tamen idcirco Dei gratia debet contemni & peccatis irritari,àpeccatis potius est recedendum,si Deo placato vti exoptamus. Dei iudicium & manum experiuntur hostes & reprobi,at magna sua cum pernicie & damno.Pij eandem agnoscunt at pœnitudine peccatorum ducti Deum sentiunt clementem & misericordem.
units.tr: In Scripture the hand of the living God is used for power, strength and judgment, in much the same way that the right hand is ascribed to God. For by anthropopathy Scripture expresses God's power, might, anger and judgment by ascribing to him a hand or hands. Exodus 15: "In his strong hand he led them out," etc. Psalm 31: "My times are in your hand; deliver me from the hand of my enemies." Psalm 89: "You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand, high is your right hand." Job 13: "Take your hand far from me, and let your terror not overwhelm me." But when he says that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God, this refers to the punishment and threat for unbelievers and the wicked, who are so struck down by the zeal and anger of God that they have nowhere to stand. So in 1 Samuel 5: "The hand of the Lord was against the city of Gath with a very great destruction." Likewise in the same place: "The hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Ashdodites, and he laid them waste and struck them with tumours, both Ashdod and its territory. When the men of Ashdod saw that it was so, they said: Let not the ark of the God of Israel remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god." Antiochus Epiphanes, of whom we read in 2 Maccabees 9, was struck by the Lord with an incurable plague. Acts 12: Herod was struck by an angel of God and died miserably, eaten by lice. So the wicked are said to fall into the hand of God when, resisting his word, they pay the just penalties. Hence Ecclesiasticus 2 says: "If we do not repent, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, not into the hands of men." So Saul, Judas, Cain and other wicked men fall into the hands of the Lord. The godly also fall into the hands of the Lord, but, relying on the hope of free mercy, they are sustained, although they are severely scourged. Hence David, in 2 Samuel 24, when the prophet Gad offered him by God's command a choice of three evils, said: "Let me fall, I pray, into the hand of Jehovah, for his mercies are many; but let me not fall into the hand of men." There he chose a three-day pestilence over seven years of famine and three months of persecution, not ignorant of how much easier it is to be reconciled to God than to men. Yet the grace of God must not on that account be despised and provoked by sins; rather we must depart from sins, if we desire to have God appeased and to use him as our friend. Enemies and the reprobate experience the judgment and hand of God, but to their great ruin and loss; the godly acknowledge the same hand, but, led by repentance for their sins, they find God merciful and gracious.

units.la: Discimus itaque hinc. Primùm,graue & periculosum esse, temerè Deum peccatis ad vindictam & zelum provocare. Impij enim qui id facere gestiunt, seuerissimum aliquando iudicem experiuntur. Deinde,pios etiam interdum in manus Dei, extra vias eius exorbitando,cadere:at pœnitentiæ studio iterum in viam reduci,& in gratiam recipi. Tertiò,grauis vltio manet hostes ecclesiæ & verbi Dei,qui contra stimulum calcitrantes,iustaq; eius iudicia aspernantes,tandem in extremum discrimen salutis & exitium incurrunt. Quartò,pijs hoc consolationi est in periculis,quòd sciunt, impios suum habituros esse iudicem ac vindicem,coram quo non est acceptio personarum. Quintò,ad Dei timorem nos cohortabimur,quòd scimus,Deum perdere impios ad gehennam, & non solùm corpus,sed etiam animam posse condemnare. Hæc partis secundæ,de abrogatione sacerdotij & sacrificiorum, cæterarumq; ceremoniarum legalium,deq; euangelij præstantia,est absolutio.
units.tr: From this we learn the following. First, it is grave and dangerous to provoke God rashly to vengeance and zeal by sins. For the wicked who eagerly do this sometimes experience a most severe judge. Second, the godly too, sometimes wandering out of God's ways, may fall into his hand; yet by zeal for repentance they are brought back again into the way and received into grace. Third, a grievous vengeance awaits the enemies of the church and of the Word of God, who kick against the goad, spurn his just judgments, and at last incur extreme peril to their salvation and destruction. Fourth, it is a consolation to the godly in dangers that they know the wicked will have a judge and avenger, before whom there is no respect of persons. Fifth, we shall be exhorted to the fear of God because we know that God is able to destroy the wicked in hell, and to condemn not only the body but also the soul. This concludes the second part, concerning the abrogation of the priesthood and sacrifices and the other legal ceremonies, and concerning the excellence of the gospel.

units.la: BREVIS EPITOME PARTIS SECVNDAE, SECVNDA PARS EPISTOLAE AD HEBRAEOS HOC PACTO COMMODISSIME potest inscribi.
units.tr: A brief summary of the second part: the second part of the Epistle to the Hebrews can most conveniently be entitled in this way.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS EPISTOLAE DE ABROGATIONE ceremoniarum legalium, sacerdotij inquam & omnium sacrificiorum.
units.tr: The second part of the Epistle, on the abrogation of the legal ceremonies: namely of the priesthood, I mean, and of all sacrifices.

units.la: Ocet namque tota hac disputatione, Christum esse sacerdotem, & quidem multò præstantiorem, quàm fuerunt sacerdotes legales. Præterea Christum obtulisse sacrificium, & quidem multò præstantius, efficacius q;, quàm fuerunt legalia sacrificia, quæ omnia huc tendunt, ut demonstretur, quòd, vbi præsens est sacerdos, & sacrificium maioris dignitatis, quàm fuerit sacerdotium cum sacrificijs in lege, hæc omnia per sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi abrogentur. Hic inquá totius disputationis scopus est: & propterea titulus recte ita, ut diximus, constituetur.
units.tr: The whole of this discussion is concerned with Christ being a priest, and indeed a far more excellent priest than the priests of the law were. Moreover, Christ offered a sacrifice, and again one far more excellent and effective than the legal sacrifices. All of this points to the conclusion that where a priest is present, and a sacrifice of greater worth than the priesthood with its sacrifices under the law, all those things are abrogated through the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. This, I say, is the whole aim of the discussion, and for that reason the title is rightly set as we have said.

units.la: Quæ fuit occasio tractandi hanc partem de abrogatione ceremoniarum?
units.tr: What was the occasion for treating this part on the abrogation of the ceremonies?

units.la: Oportet nos videre, quo in statu fuerint ecclesiæ Hebræorum, & tum cognoscemus. Sciendum ergo, quòd, cùm primùm spargeretur doctrina euangelica, & per apostolos assiduè inculcaretur, homines iustificari per fidem absq; operibus legis: multi Hebræi hinc grauiter sunt offensi, ac iudicarunt, (id quod res erat) multum detrahi dignitati legis, inprimis autem ceremonijs & sacrificijs, in quibus summa omnis sanctimoniæ & veræ iustitiæ sita videbatur. Huius rei argumenta habemus Actor. 6. 21. vbi Stephanus, & Paulus accusantur, quasi contra legem & locum sanctum locuti: & Actor. 15. Plurimi contendebant, circumcisionem, ac proinde & cæteras ceremonias ad salutem necessarias. Item Ephes. 2. Col. 2. tales passim similia occinere solitos indicatur. Et videbantur habere omnino graues causas, quibus ad ita iudicandum mouerentur. Nam tota lex, & in hac excellentissimo loco habitæ ceremoniæ à Deo erant institutæ. Tota lex vtilis, sancta, bona, & necessaria erat. Nec probabile, Deum immutare velle, aut irritū facere, quòd ipse antea adeò seueriter sanciuerat. Ceremonias verò pulcherrimam esse legis partem: magnum esse earundem vsum ad permouendos animos hominum ad verum Dei cultum. Item in illis quasi remedia & medicamina mortalibus proposita, per quæ salutem & remissionem peccatorum consequerentur. Quò pertinet omnia de sacrificijs pro peccatorum diuersi generis expiatione. Adhæc sic esse præceptas, vt earū omissione Deus grauissimè offendi videatur. Tum maximè illustres esse notas, quibus Iudæi à cæteris gentibus distinguerentur, & excellentiores iudicarentur. In summa, sine magnis motibus & tumultibus nihil videbatur posse immutari. Atq; eò pertinacius etiā pro ceremoniis retinendis Hebræi decertabant, quòd cùm iam spoliati essent regno, constitutis vbiq; per Romanos Tetrarchis & præsidibus, nec de regno recuperando liceret illis aliquid moliri, nihil habebant priscæ gloriæ suæ reliquum, præter pompam sacerdotalem & ceremonias, (etiamsi sacerdotalis dignitas iam multum erat per eos, qui pretio parabant in annos singulos, deformata) quibus semel sublatis, plané de vniuersa gētis gloria actum foret.
units.tr: We must see in what condition the churches of the Hebrews were, and then we shall understand. It must be known, therefore, that when the evangelical doctrine was first spread abroad, and was constantly impressed by the apostles, that men are justified through faith without the works of the law, many Hebrews were gravely offended by this. They judged (as was the case) that much was taken away from the dignity of the law, above all from the ceremonies and sacrifices, in which all the sum of holiness and true righteousness seemed to lie. We have evidence of this in Acts 6:11–14, where Stephen and Paul are accused of speaking against the law and the holy place; and in Acts 15, where many contended that circumcision, and therefore the other ceremonies too, were necessary for salvation. Likewise Ephesians 2 and Colossians 2 indicate that such men were accustomed to sing similar things everywhere. And they seemed to have wholly serious grounds that moved them to judge in this way. For the whole law, and in it the ceremonies held in the highest esteem, had been instituted by God. The whole law was useful, holy, good and necessary. Nor was it likely that God would wish to change, or make void, what he himself had so severely ordained before. The ceremonies were the most beautiful part of the law; their use was great for moving the minds of men to the true worship of God. Moreover, in them remedies and medicines were set before mortals, by which they might obtain salvation and forgiveness of sins; to this belongs everything about sacrifices for the expiation of sins of various kinds. Besides, they had been so prescribed that God seemed grievously offended by their omission. Then, the marks by which the Jews were distinguished from the other nations, and judged more excellent, were most conspicuous. In short, it seemed that nothing could be changed without great upheavals and tumults. And the Hebrews fought all the more stubbornly to retain the ceremonies, because, having already been deprived of their kingdom, with tetrarchs and governors appointed everywhere by the Romans, and with no permission to attempt anything toward recovering the kingdom, they had no remnant of their ancient glory except the priestly pomp and the ceremonies. (Although the priestly dignity was already much debased by those who bought it for a price each year.) Once these were taken away, the whole glory of the nation would clearly be lost.

units.la: Quia ergò adeò acriter pugnabant Iudæi pro gloria sacerdotij & sacrificiorum, & hæc externa reuera abducebant animos à spiritualibus, quæ propriè ad salutem pertinent: Apostolus debuit docere, legem ea in parte prorsus abrogatam: id autem nulla ratione iudicauit commodius posse fieri, quàm si doceret, Christum quoq; esse sacerdotē, præterea & obtulisse sacrificium, quod omnibus sacrificijs legalibus longè sit eminentius.
units.tr: Since, therefore, the Jews fought so fiercely for the glory of the priesthood and the sacrifices, and these external things in truth drew minds away from the spiritual things that properly pertain to salvation, the Apostle had to teach that the law was wholly abrogated in this respect. He judged that this could be done in no more fitting way than by teaching that Christ is also a priest, and moreover has offered a sacrifice which is far more eminent than all the legal sacrifices.

units.la: Erat autem necessarium, per apostolos doceri istam abrogationem legis multis de causis.
units.tr: It was, however, necessary that this abrogation of the law be taught by the apostles, for many reasons.

units.la: Primò, quod falsum erat, ceremonias & sacrificia illa facere ad iustitiam: quod tamen Iudæi audebant spargere ac docere: sicut liquet Actorum decimo quinto, Galat. 1. 2. 3. Colossens. 2.
units.tr: First, because it was false that those ceremonies and sacrifices made men righteous. Yet the Jews dared to spread and teach this, as is clear from Acts 15, Galatians 1, 2 and 3, and Colossians 2.

units.la: Secundò, quia illa omnia erant duntaxat instituta, vt essent vmbræ & typi rerum futurarum, & per Christum gerendarum, ideoq; vbi res adsunt præsentes, æquum est vmbras cessare: qua de re Coloss. 2. præsentis epistolę cap. 9. 10.
units.tr: Second, because all those things were instituted only to be shadows and types of things to come, to be accomplished through Christ. Therefore, when the realities are present, it is fitting that the shadows cease. On this matter see Colossians 2, and chapters 9 and 10 of the present epistle.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd gentes quiduis potius erant factupræ, & renunciatæ potius euangelio, quàm ut paterentur se circumcidi, obligari observationibus ciborum, potuum, dierum: qua de re habes verba Petri Actor. 15.
units.tr: Third, because the Gentiles had been made, and had been proclaimed to the gospel, as it were, for anything whatever, rather than allowing themselves to be circumcised and bound by observances of foods, drinks and days. On this matter you have the words of Peter in Acts 15.

units.la: Quartò, quòd cultus Dei non sit situs in rebus externis & corporalibus, sed potius in spiritu & veritate, & obedientia, misericordia. Qua de re Esaiae 1. Ioan. 4. Oseae 6. Matth. 9.
units.tr: Fourth, because the worship of God does not consist in external and bodily things, but rather in spirit, truth, obedience and mercy. On this see Isaiah 1, John 4, Hosea 6, Matthew 9.

units.la: Nec posse homines inquinari iis, quae intrant in os, docet Christus Matthaei decimo quinto. Item offerre debemus Deo corpora nostra, officia charitatis, spiritum contritum, cor humiliatum: de quibus prophetae passim cecinerunt, sacrificiorum externorum rui, nam praenunciantes.
units.tr: Christ teaches in Matthew 15 that men cannot be defiled by what enters the mouth. Likewise we ought to offer our bodies to God, works of charity, a contrite spirit, a humbled heart. The prophets everywhere sang of these things, foretelling the ruin of external sacrifices.

units.la: Sed, quare, dicis, hic agitur tantum de abrogatione ceremonialium, & non de abrogatione totius legis, quomodo disputatur in epistolis ad Romanos, ad Galatas? Respondetur: Distinguendas esse has disputationes: sicut Apostolus etiam lôge alia ratione hic agit de abrogatione legis, atq; in illis epistolis. Sciendum est, duplicem esse motam per Iudaeos in primitiua ecclesia de lege disputationem: alteram, qua contendebant, quòd etiamsi per euangelium annunciaretur iustitia per Christum, nihilominus legem esse simul cum euangelio observandam, potissimumq; ceremonias, quae praestantissima est legis pars. Atq; hoc Iudaeorum genus erat cordatius & modestius, euangelio non adeò aduersans, licet scrupulosius, quàm par erat: utpote existimantium, non posse omitti legem. Sed erant alij pertinaces & praeduri, qui contendebant, non tantum legem cum euangelio observandam, sed praeterea euangelio praeferendam, & ex lege, ac per opera legis parandam iustitiam coram Deo. Sic docebant, nisi circumcidamini, non poteritis salutem consequi, &c. Actor. 15. Erant igitur duae ac distinctae in primitiua ecclesia de retinenda lege disputationes. Proinde apostoli distinctas quaestiones diuerso modo tractarunt: &, cùm ad primam disputationem respondere vellent, definierunt simpliciter ceremonias omnes abrogatas, non amplius locum aut vires habere. Atq; hoc pacto tractata est disputatio praesentis epistolae, Item Colossensis 2. vbi clarè cernitur, de ceremonijs disputari, & argumenta, & conclusiones de iis agere. Ad secundam autem disputationem cùm vellent respondere, definierunt, non tantum abrogata ceremonialia, sed vniuersam prorsus legem, & neq; moralia, neque iudicialia quicquam ad iustitiam coram Deo facere: non quòd abrogata sic sit in vniuersum, ne amplius fiat, vt exleges quicquid lubet faciamus, sed quòd non sit vtilis aut necessaria ad iustitiam coram Deo: quòd iustitia ista contingat tantùm per fidem in Christum. Habet quidè suas vtilitates lex, ut quòd paedagogum agat, deducendo ad Christum: quòd doceat agnoscere peccatum: quòd cogat humiliari. Sed ad iustificationem coram Deo nulla est in ea particula. Et sic non prorsus damnatur lex, & tamen ex ea iustitiam non esse expectandam ostenditur. Hoc verò pacto disputatur de abrogatione vniuersae legis in epistolis ad Romanos & Galatas.
units.tr: But, you say, why is this only about the abrogation of the ceremonial things, and not about the abrogation of the whole law, as is discussed in the epistles to the Romans and the Galatians? The answer is that these discussions must be distinguished, just as the Apostle here treats the abrogation of the law by a quite different method from that in those epistles. It must be known that there were two debates about the law among the Jews in the primitive Church. One was that they contended that, even though justification through Christ was announced by the gospel, nevertheless the law must be observed together with the gospel, especially the ceremonies, which are the most excellent part of the law. This class of Jews was more sensible and moderate, not greatly opposed to the gospel, although more scrupulous than was right, since they thought the law could not be laid aside. But there were others, obstinate and hard, who contended not only that the law must be observed along with the gospel, but also that the law should be preferred to the gospel, and that righteousness before God must be obtained from the law and by the works of the law. So they taught: unless you are circumcised, you cannot obtain salvation, and so on (Acts 15). There were therefore two distinct debates in the primitive Church about retaining the law. Accordingly the apostles treated the distinct questions in different ways. When they wished to answer the first debate, they defined simply that all the ceremonies were abrogated and no longer had place or force. In this way the discussion of the present epistle was handled, and likewise in Colossians 2, where it is plainly seen that the ceremonies are debated, and the arguments and conclusions deal with them. But when they wished to answer the second debate, they defined that not only the ceremonial things, but the whole law, was abrogated, and that neither the moral nor the judicial precepts contribute anything to righteousness before God. This is not because the law is abrogated in such a way that it should no longer be done, so that we may act as lawless people as we please, but because it is not useful or necessary for righteousness before God, since that righteousness comes only through faith in Christ. The law indeed has its uses: it acts as a schoolmaster, leading us to Christ; it teaches us to recognise sin; it compels us to be humbled. But for justification before God there is no part of it that helps. So the law is not wholly condemned, and yet it is shown that righteousness is not to be expected from it. It is in this way that the abrogation of the whole law is discussed in the epistles to the Romans and the Galatians.

units.la: Habentes igitur pontificem magnum) Propositio & exordium est vniuersę disputationis, cuius haec est sententia, Christus est verus summus pontifex, omnibus pontificibus legalibus excellentior. Quae sententia satis est perspicua, ut post ea inferat, & nunc quia apud se tacitè ratiocinetur, per adeò excellentem sacerdotem vetus sacerdotium dignitate sua deiici abrogariqúe.
units.tr: "Having therefore a great high priest": this is the proposition and opening of the whole discussion, whose sense is this: Christ is the true High Priest, more excellent than all the legal priests. This statement is clear enough that the author may afterwards infer, and now reason tacitly within himself, that through so excellent a priest the old priesthood is deposed and abrogated in its dignity.

units.la: Conuenisset fortasis, respectu principalis causae, quae agitur, propositione aliter instituì, nempe hoc modo: Sacerdotium & sacrificia legalia, manifestato euangelio, sunt abrogata: vel simili ratione: sed quia, si ita locutus fuisset Apostolus, antequam argumenta producta forent causam probantia, potuissent offendi atq; alienari auditores, commodissimè extulit eo modo, quem cernimus.
units.tr: It would perhaps have been fitting, given the main point under discussion, to set out the proposition in a different way, namely: "The priesthood and the legal sacrifices have been abrogated now that the gospel has been made manifest," or something similar. But since, if the Apostle had spoken in that way before the arguments proving the case had been put forward, his hearers might have been offended and alienated, he set it out most conveniently in the manner we see.

units.la: Cæterum apostolus propositionem hanc non nudam extulit, quemadmodum subinde solet fieri, sed quadam forma exhortationis. Id autem non solùm, vt (quod fieri solet in exordijs) attentiores omnes redderet: verumetiam ut altiore mente tum dignitatem Christi, tum beneficia à sacerdotio eius expectanda considerarent. Quare maximo artificio istud per Apostolum factum est. Dicit ergo hortando.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle did not state this proposition bare, as he often does, but in a certain form of exhortation. He did this not only to make all his hearers more attentive, as is customary in exordia, but also so that they would consider with a higher mind both the dignity of Christ and the benefits to be expected from his priesthood. Therefore the Apostle did this with the greatest skill. He speaks, then, by way of exhortation.

units.la: Teneamus confessionem, &c.
units.tr: Let us hold fast the confession, etc.

units.la: Non enim habemus pontificem) Ratio, quare tenenda constans confessio Christi eiusq; sacerdotij, ab vtilitate, quae ex sacerdotio Christi nobis est parata, siue à bonitate & officio Christi erga nos. Proinde videmus propositioni adiuncta esse nonnulla de sacerdotij Christi vsu: quemadmodum solent, qui artem aliquam tradere volunt, de vsu artis quaedam praemittere. Prorsus inquam eodem modo artificiosissimè hic agit Apostolus, vt sciamus, quanta vtilitas nobis ex hac disputatione sit expectanda.
units.tr: "For we have not a high priest..." This is the reason why the steadfast confession of Christ and of his priesthood must be held fast: it arises from the usefulness that Christ's priesthood has prepared for us, that is, from the goodness and office of Christ towards us. Accordingly, we see that some things about the use of Christ's priesthood have been attached to the proposition, just as those who wish to teach some art usually set out some things about its use beforehand. I say that the Apostle proceeds here in exactly the same way, most skilfully, so that we may know how great a benefit is to be expected for us from this discussion.

units.la: Accedà:
units.tr: "Let us draw near:"

units.la: Accedamus igitur cum fiducia) Adhuc plenius per Exhortationem proponit vsum sacerdotij Christi, vt tantò ardentioribus animis omnes sint præsenti disputationi, & cogno scendis beneficijs per Christum paratis intenti.
units.tr: "Let us therefore draw near with confidence..." By this exhortation he sets out still more fully the use of Christ's priesthood, so that all may be the more ardently attentive to the present discussion and intent upon learning the benefits prepared for us through Christ.

units.la: CONFIRMATIO.
units.tr: CONFIRMATION.

units.la: Nam omnis pontifex) Hæc est Confirmatio, quæ sanè longa est, & ad multam partem capitis decimi protrahitur. Diuiditur autem ab Apostolo, vt clariore modo doceat, in duas partes: quarum priore nihil aliud, quàm docet, Christum esse sacerdotem, & quidem multò præstantiorem, quàm fuerint sacerdotes legales. Vnde infert, per sacerdotium Christi abrogatum esse sacerdotium legale: & hæc ad cap. 5 6.7. Altera parte initio capitis octaui, docet Christum quoq; functum publicè officio sacerdotis, & sacrificium obtulisse multò præstantius, quàm fuerint sacrificia legalia. Vnde etiā clarè infert, omnia sacrificia legalia abrogata. Atq; his duobus ita comprobatis, efficitur, omnia simul ceremonialia legis abrogata. Hæc inquam est totius confirmationis summa & perspicua dispositio. Proinde priorem partem sic aggreditur.
units.tr: "For every high priest" (Heb. 5.1). This is the Confirmation, which is indeed long and extends over a large part of the tenth chapter. The Apostle divides it, so that he may teach more clearly, into two parts. In the first he does nothing other than teach that Christ is a priest, and indeed a far more excellent one than the priests of the law were. From this he infers that by the priesthood of Christ the Levitical priesthood has been abrogated; and this is treated in chapters 5, 6 and 7. In the second part, at the beginning of chapter 8, he teaches that Christ also discharged the office of priest publicly and offered a sacrifice far more excellent than the legal sacrifices. From this he also clearly infers that all the legal sacrifices have been abrogated. With these two points thus established, it follows that all the ceremonial parts of the law have been abrogated at once. This, I say, is the sum and the plain arrangement of the whole Confirmation. Accordingly, he takes up the first part in this way.

units.la: Nam omnis pontifex) Ante omnia probat aliquot argumentis, Christum esse verum pontificem. Colligit enim omnia, quæ sunt necessaria, vt quis pro vero pontifice agnoscatur, eademque docet in Christo inueniri, atque ita Christum esse verum pontificem euincit. Sunt autem omnia antecedentia, siue ea, quæ in pontificibus requiruntur, prius vno fasce comprehensa: pòst subijcitur de Christo, quòd eadem omnia in eo conspiciatur, sed non prorsus eodem ordine ponuntur membra respondētia, quo posita erant in antecedere: deinde nō ijsdē verbis repetitis, sed magnificētius & splendidiori orationis figura. Nos singula singulis crasso nostro more exprimemus, & iusta etiā Syllogismorū forma.
units.tr: "For every high priest." First of all he proves by several arguments that Christ is the true high priest. For he gathers together all the things that are necessary for someone to be acknowledged as a true high priest, and he teaches that these same things are found in Christ, and so he demonstrates that Christ is the true high priest. Now all the antecedents, that is, the things that are required in high priests, are first set out together in one bundle; afterwards it is added of Christ that all these same things are seen in him, but the corresponding members are not set down in exactly the same order as they were in the antecedents; and then the same words are not repeated, but with a more magnificent and splendid figure of speech. We shall express each point in turn, in our own plain manner, and also in the proper form of syllogisms.

units.la: Primum igitur argumentum est à principali officio pontificis, adeoq; à propria & vsitata pontificis definitione, hoc pacto.
units.tr: The first argument is taken from the principal office of the high priest, and so from the proper and usual definition of the high priest, in this way:

units.la: Omnis pontifex, qui ex hominibus assumitur, pro hominibus cōstituitur in his, quæ apud Deum aguntur, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis.
units.tr: Every high priest who is taken from among men is appointed for men in those things that are transacted before God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.

units.la: Atqui Christus etiā homo ex hominibus est assumptus, & pro hominibus cōstitutus in his quæ apud Deum sunt agenda, atq; obtulit insuper donaria & victimas.
units.tr: But Christ too was taken from among men, and was appointed for men in those things that are to be transacted before God, and he moreover offered gifts and sacrifices.

units.la: Igitur Christus est verus pontifex.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true high priest.

units.la: Maiore vides verbis Apostoli contextā. Minore vero idē expressit, sed paulò magnificentioribus verbis, quasi studio illustrādi Christi dignitatē, nēpe hisce verbis: Ita & Christus in diebus carnis suę precationes & supplicationes apud illum, qui poterat ipsum à morte seruare, cū clamore valido, & lachrymis obtulit, & pro reuerentia exauditus est.
units.tr: You see the major premise woven into the words of the Apostle. The minor he expressed in the same way, but in somewhat more magnificent words, as if eager to set forth the dignity of Christ, namely in these words: "So also Christ, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with strong crying and tears, and was heard for his reverence" (Heb. 5.7).

units.la: Secundum argumentum à qualitate personæ, quæ ad pontificatum posit assumi, hoc modo.
units.tr: The second argument is taken from the quality of the person who may be taken up into the priesthood, in this way.

units.la: Omnis, qui assumitur in pontificem, debet esse placabilis ignorantibus & errantibus.
units.tr: Everyone who is taken into the high priesthood must be able to deal gently with the ignorant and the erring.

units.la: Atqui Christus est placabilis & misericors erga ignorantes & errantes.
units.tr: But Christ is gentle and merciful towards the ignorant and the erring.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus pontifex.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true high priest.

units.la: Maior apud Apostolum habet annexam rationem. Quandoquidem & ipse circundatus est infirmitate. Præterea eiusdem rationis comprobationem: Et propter hanc debet, &c. Minoris vero sententiam sic extulit: ita Christus, tametsi filius erat, tamē dicit ex his, quæ passus est, obedientiam, ac perfectus redditus, omnibus, qui sibi obedierunt, fuit causa salutis æternæ. Vbi vno verbo dicēs Christū passum, notat, eum infirmitates & miserias humanas expertum, vt ita magis misericors erga homines redderetur. Quæ addita sunt, illustrant Christi dignitatem.
units.tr: The major premise has a reason attached to it in the Apostle: "since he himself also is compassed with infirmity" (Heb. 5.2). Moreover, there is the confirmation of the same reasoning: "and for this reason he ought," etc. The minor he stated thus: "so Christ, although he was a son, nevertheless learned obedience from the things that he suffered, and being made perfect, became to all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation" (Heb. 5.8-9). Here, by the single word "suffered," he indicates that Christ experienced human infirmities and miseries, so that he might be made more merciful towards men. The things that are added illustrate the dignity of Christ.

units.la: Tertium argumentum sumptum est à modo vocationis ad pontificatum.
units.tr: The third argument is taken from the manner of calling to the high priesthood.

units.la: Pontifex non sibijpsi vsurpat honorē, sed vocatur à Deo, quemadmodum & Aaron.
units.tr: A high priest does not assume the honour to himself, but is called by God, just as Aaron was (Heb. 5.4).

units.la: Atqui Christus non sibi vendicauit honorem, vt fieret pontifex: sed vocatus est ab eo, qui dixerat illi: Filius meus es tu, &c. hoc est, à patre suo cœlesti.
units.tr: But Christ did not claim the honour for himself, that he might become high priest; rather he was called by him who said to him: "You are my Son, etc." (Heb. 5.5), that is, by his heavenly Father.

units.la: Igitur Christus est verus pontifex:
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true high priest.

units.la: Omnia expressa sunt apud apostolum. Sed is addidit præterea Scripturæ testimonium, quo confirmantur argumenta reliqua, propter quod etiam apparet factum, quòd consequentia non sunt statim subiecta suis antecedentibus membris, quibus respondent: quia potuisset infirmari consequentia, vbi testimonium istud nondum fuisset auditum.
units.tr: All these things are expressed in the Apostle. But he added besides the testimony of Scripture, by which the remaining arguments are confirmed. For this reason it also appears that the consequents are not placed immediately after the antecedent members to which they correspond: because the consequence might have seemed weak where that testimony had not yet been heard.

units.la: Videtur autem & quartum argumentum repositum esse in illis verbis postremis: Cognominatus à Deo pontifex, &c. ab eo videlicet, quòd pontifices semper secundum certum aliquem ordinem seu ritum constituuntur. Huiusmodi autem videtur eruendum argumentum.
units.tr: But it seems that a fourth argument is also contained in those last words: "named by God a high priest," etc. This is the argument from the fact that high priests are always appointed according to some fixed order or rite. An argument of this kind seems to be drawn out as follows.

units.la: Omnis pontifex secundum aliquem certum ordinem instituitur.
units.tr: Every high priest is instituted according to some fixed order.

units.la: Atqui Christus institutus & cognominatus est pontifex à Deo, secundum certum ordinem, videlicet Melchisedech. Ergo Christus est verus pontifex.
units.tr: But Christ was instituted and named high priest by God according to a fixed order, namely that of Melchizedek. Therefore Christ is the true high priest.

units.la: Maior per se nota est, & ex testimonio perspicua.
units.tr: The major is evident in itself and plain from the testimony.

units.la: Minor exprimitur postremis illis verbis.
units.tr: The minor is expressed in those last words.

units.la: Quod argumentum putauimus eò diligentius expendendum, quia Apostolus postea ab excellentia huius ordinis colligit, Christi sacerdotium esse praestantius sacerdotio Aaronico. Si quis velit, posset omnia argumenta haec in unum Syllogismum redigere, in hunc modum:
units.tr: We have thought this argument worth weighing more carefully, because the Apostle afterwards argues from the excellence of this order that the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the Aaronic priesthood. If anyone wishes, he could reduce all these arguments into one syllogism, in this way:

units.la: Quicunque constituitur in his, quae apud Deum pro hominibus sunt agenda, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis: item qui placabile & misericordē se praebet erga ignorantes & errantes: praeterea, qui non seipsum ambitiosè ingerit, sed diuinitus vocatur: postremo, qui secundum certum ordinem sacerdotio allegitur: talis est verus legitimusq; pontifex.
units.tr: Whoever is appointed in those things that are to be transacted before God for men, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; likewise whoever shows himself gentle and merciful towards the ignorant and the erring; moreover, whoever does not thrust himself forward ambitiously but is called by God; lastly, whoever is chosen to the priesthood according to a fixed order: such a one is a true and lawful high priest.

units.la: At Christus hoc modo constitutus est in his, quae apud Deum pro hominibus sunt agenda, vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis: praeterea placabilis est & misericors erga ignorantes & errantes: item vocatus est ad munus hoc à Deo patre suo caelesti: postremo, secundum certum ordinem, videlicet Melchisedech, institutus est & praefectus: nec denique aliquid illi deest, quod in bono legitimoque pontifice posset desiderari.
units.tr: But Christ has been appointed in this way in those things that are to be transacted before God for men, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; moreover he is gentle and merciful towards the ignorant and the erring; likewise he was called to this office by God his heavenly Father; lastly, according to a fixed order, namely that of Melchizedek, he was instituted and set over it; nor, finally, is anything lacking in him that could be desired in a good and lawful high priest.

units.la: Igitur Christus est verus legitimusque pontifex.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and lawful high priest.

units.la: DIGRESSIO.
units.tr: DIGRESSION.

units.la: De quo nobis multa forent) à capite quinto, vsque ad finem fere capitis sexti durat haec digressio, qua auditorum animos sibi conciliat, & alacriores reddit ad ea percipienda, quae de Christi sacerdotio, legisq; abrogatione erat dicturus.
units.tr: There would be much to say about this. This digression runs from the fifth chapter almost to the end of the sixth chapter; by it he wins over the minds of his hearers and makes them more eager to take in what he was about to say concerning the priesthood of Christ and the abrogation of the law.

units.la: REDITVS.
units.tr: THE RETURN.

units.la: Iuxta ordinē Melchisedech pontifex in aeternum) Redit ad institutū, atq; ij sdē plane verbis, qui bus ante digressionem docendi finem fecerat: quod & valde aptum est volenti ad instituerti: & praeterea vtile, vt nimirum rursus ob oculos ponat testimonium illud è Psalmo 110. desumptū, quod totius disputationis quasi basis est & fundamentum, nec non è quo adhuc plura ducturus est argumenta.
units.tr: According to the order of Melchisedec a priest for ever. He returns to his subject and uses the very words with which he had ended his teaching before the digression. This suits a writer who wants to get back to his argument, and it is also useful, since it again sets before the eyes the testimony from Psalm 110, which is the basis and foundation of the whole disputation and from which he is still going to draw further arguments.

units.la: Caeterum hoc iam constituit probare, nimirum quòd sacerdotium Christi sit praestantius sacerdotio legali, vt inde inferatur, sacerdotium legale per sacerdotium Christi abrogari. Id autē hac via facere aggreditur. Ante omnia docet, Christum rectè dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Hunc vero ordinem postea docebit excellentiorem Aaronico, atq; ita quod cupit, efficiet.
units.tr: Now he has decided to prove this: that the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the Levitical priesthood, so that it may be inferred that the Levitical priesthood is abrogated by the priesthood of Christ. He sets about doing this in the following way. First of all, he teaches that Christ is rightly called a priest according to the order of Melchisedec. Later he will teach that this order is more excellent than the Aaronic, and so he will achieve what he desires.

units.la: Erat autem necessarium ostendere, quòd Christus rectè dicatur sacerdos secundū ordinē Melchisedech, vel ob id, vt ostenderet, testimonium supra citatum Christo proprie conuenire. Sic ergo rem aggreditur.
units.tr: It was necessary to show that Christ is rightly called a priest according to the order of Melchisedec, partly so that he might show that the testimony cited above applies properly to Christ. So he approaches the matter in this way.

units.la: Nam hic erat Melchisedech) Exponit, quis & qualis fuerit ille Melchisedech, ex Geneseos capite 14. ostenditque, eum per omnia assimilatum Christo, & in Christum competere, quę de Melchisedech dicuntur: atq; ita colligit Christum rectè dici sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: For this Melchisedec was... He explains who and what sort of man Melchisedec was, from the fourteenth chapter of Genesis, and shows that he was in all respects made like Christ, and that what is said of Melchisedec applies to Christ. And so he concludes that Christ is rightly called a priest according to the order of Melchisedec.

units.la: Qui primum quidem ex interpretatione) Primum argumentum, quo probat in Christum competere, quę spectantur in Melchisedech, sumptum ab interpretatione nominis siue Etymologia.
units.tr: Who indeed first of all, from the interpretation... The first argument, by which he proves that the things seen in Melchisedec apply to Christ, is taken from the interpretation of the name, or etymology.

units.la: Vocabulum Mechisedech idem significat, quod rex iustitiae.
units.tr: The word Melchisedec means the same as king of righteousness.

units.la: Atqui Christus verè etiam est rex iustitiae.
units.tr: But Christ truly is also king of righteousness.

units.la: Ergo de Christo dicuntur, quę de Melchisedech: & Christus rectè dicitur sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech.
units.tr: Therefore what is said of Melchisedec is said of Christ, and Christ is rightly called a priest according to the order of Melchisedec.

units.la: Deinde uero etiam rex Salem) Secundum argumentum à vitae conditione, seu publica dignitate. Melchisedech erat rex Salem, id est, rex pacis.
units.tr: Then also king of Salem... The second argument, from his condition in life or public dignity. Melchisedec was king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

units.la: Sed Christus etiā est verus rex & collator pacis. Igitur de Christo rectè dicitur, quòd sit sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Ignoti patris, ignotæ matris) Tertiū argumentum sumptum ab vtriusque initio & exitu. Melchisedech erat ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neque initium dierum, neque vitæ finem habens.
units.tr: But Christ is also the true king and bestower of peace. Therefore it is rightly said of Christ that he is a priest according to the order of Melchisedec. Without father, without mother... The third argument, taken from the beginning and end of each. Melchisedec was without father [ἀπάτωρ], without mother [ἀμήτωρ], without genealogy [ἀγενεαλόγητος], having neither beginning of days nor end of life.

units.la: Sed Christus itidem ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neq; initium dierum, neq; vitæ finē habens. Ergo rectè dicitur de Christo, quæ Melchisedech, & Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, rectè colligitur.
units.tr: But Christ likewise is without father [ἀπάτωρ], without mother [ἀμήτωρ], without genealogy [ἀγενεαλόγητος], having neither beginning of days nor end of life. Therefore what is said of Melchisedec is rightly said of Christ, and it is rightly concluded that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchisedec.

units.la: Præsupponit autem, spiritum Sanctum data opera suppresisse initium & finem Melchisedech, vt ita tanto certius typum Christi exprimeret.
units.tr: He presupposes, moreover, that the Holy Spirit deliberately suppressed the beginning and end of Melchisedec, so that he might thereby express the type of Christ all the more certainly.

units.la: Manet sacerdos in perpetuū) Respicit ad particulam in æternum. Quartum argumentum fluens ex præcedenti, imò coniunctum cum præcedenti.
units.tr: Abiding a priest for ever... He looks to the phrase for ever. This is a fourth argument, flowing from the preceding one, indeed joined to it.

units.la: Melchisedech manet sacerdos in æternum.
units.tr: Melchisedec abides a priest for ever.

units.la: Igitur & Christus manet sacerdos in æternum.
units.tr: Therefore Christ also abides a priest for ever.

units.la: Quod adiectū videtur ad plenius ostendendū, Christo quadrare illud testimoniū, Tu es sacerdos in æternum. Ac necessum erat adijci propter aduersarios, qui vt concesissent, Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, tamen propterea nihilo pluris fecissent, sed iudicassent id abrogatum, sicut reuera poterat videri abrogatum, quando ei successit Aaronicum veluti præstantius. Sed Apostolus intuens in testimonium supra citatum, probat & sacerdotium Melchisedech manere in æternum, (quod quidem sumit ex verbis præcedentibus) ac deinde etiam sacerdotium Christi manere æternum. Atq; ita Christus sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech: & Christo verè competit illud testimonium.
units.tr: This seems to have been added to show more fully that the testimony Thou art a priest for ever fits Christ.
