It was necessary to add this on account of the adversaries, who, even if they conceded that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchisedec, would still count it as no more than that, and would judge that order to have been abrogated, as indeed it could seem abrogated, since the Aaronic order succeeded it as if more excellent. But the Apostle, looking to the testimony cited above, proves both that the priesthood of Melchisedec abides for ever (which he takes from the preceding words) and then that the priesthood of Christ abides for ever. And so Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchisedec, and that testimony truly applies to Christ.

units.la: Considerate uero, quantus hic) Incipit iam probare, ordinem Melchisedech præstantiore esse ordine Leuitico seu Aaronico, vt ita post inferre possit, per sacerdotiū Christi Melchisedecicum abrogari sacerdotium Aaronicum. Sumit autem adhuc argumenta ex breui historia Melchisedech supra posita: primumq; argumentum ducit à collatione Leuitarum & Melchisedech: sed tamen prius colligit, ipsum Melchisedech maiorem Abrahamo, vt ita viam sibi argumenta cætera sternat.
units.tr: Consider, moreover, how great this man is... He now begins to prove that the order of Melchisedec is more excellent than the Levitical or Aaronic order, so that afterwards he may infer that the Aaronic priesthood is abrogated by the Melchisedecian priesthood of Christ. He still draws his arguments from the brief history of Melchisedec set out above. His first argument he takes from a comparison of the Levites and Melchisedec; but first he concludes that Melchisedec himself is greater than Abraham, so that he may pave the way for his other arguments.

units.la: Qui decimas accipit, maior est, quàm qui dat.
units.tr: He who receives tithes is greater than he who gives them.

units.la: Atqui Melchisedech est qui accipit, Abraham autem, qui dat: Ergo Melchisedech est maior Abrahamo. Ex hoc iā sequitur, quòd etiam maior Leui. Hinc ita confert ordinem Melchisedech cum Leuitico: Leuitæ decimas accipiebant à sibi paribus, nempe suis fratribus & contribulibus, qui omnes perinde atq; ipsi ex eodem parente orti fuerant.
units.tr: But Melchisedec is he who receives, and Abraham is he who gives. Therefore Melchisedec is greater than Abraham. From this it follows that he is also greater than Levi. Hence he compares the order of Melchisedec with the Levitical order thus: the Levites received tithes from their equals, namely their brothers and fellow tribesmen, who had all sprung from the same parent just as they had.

units.la: At Melchisedech non accepit à talibus, cùm nequaquam eiusdē fuerit generis, sed ab ipso Abraham, qui omnium illorum etiam Leuitarum communis extitit parens.
units.tr: But Melchisedec did not receive from such people, since he was not at all of the same kind, but from Abraham himself, who was the common parent even of all those Levites.

units.la: Igitur ordo Melchisedech Leuitico longè maior est.
units.tr: Therefore the order of Melchisedec is far greater than the Levitical order.

units.la: Sumptum est argumentum ex particula illa historiæ,
units.tr: The argument has been taken from that particular part of the history,

units.la: Cui & decimas impertitus est Abraham. Et habenti promissiones benedixit:
units.tr: To whom also Abraham gave a tenth. And he blessed him who had the promises:

units.la: Tertium argumentum, quo iterum, sicuti primo argumento, confert Melchisedech cum Abrahamo hoc modo:
units.tr: The third argument, by which again, as in the first argument, he compares Melchizedek with Abraham, runs as follows:

units.la: Qui dat benedictionem, maior est eo, qui accipit.
units.tr: He who gives the blessing is greater than he who receives it.

units.la: Atqui Melchisedech est qui dat, Abraham qui accipit.
units.tr: But Melchizedek is the one who gives, and Abraham the one who receives.

units.la: Igitur Melchisedech maior est Abrahamo.
units.tr: Therefore Melchizedek is greater than Abraham.

units.la: Amplificatur autem dignitas Abrahæ nonnihil, quòd describitur habens promissiones: Sed ex ea amplificatione simul crescit dignitas Melchisedech. Et hoc argumentum sumptum est ex illa particula historiæ, & benedixit illi.
units.tr: Abraham's dignity is somewhat magnified by being described as the one having the promises; but from that magnification the dignity of Melchizedek grows at the same time. This argument is drawn from that part of the history: and he blessed him.

units.la: Atq; hic moriuntur homines, qui moriuntur.
units.tr: And here men die, who die.

units.la: Quartum argumentum, quo, quēadmodum argumento secundo egerat, confert ordinem Melchisedech cum Leuitico.
units.tr: The fourth argument, by which, as he had done with the second argument, he compares the order of Melchizedek with the Levitical order.

units.la: Hic nempe in ordine Leuitico decimas accipiunt homines mortales.
units.tr: Here, in the Levitical order, mortal men receive tithes.

units.la: At in ordine Melchisedec accepit decimas homo immortalis, qui manet in æternum.
units.tr: But in the order of Melchizedek a man receives tithes who is immortal, who abides for ever.

units.la: Ergo ordo Melchisedech est præstantior ordine Leuitico. Sumptum est ex illa particula historiæ, neq; initium vitæ, neque finem dierum habens, manet sacerdos in perpetuum.
units.tr: Therefore the order of Melchizedek is more excellent than the Levitical order. This is drawn from that part of the history: having neither beginning of days nor end of life, he remains a priest for ever.

units.la: Et ut ita loquar in Abraham) Quintum argumentum, quadam Amplificationis forma additum. Ipse ordo Leuiticus, dedit decimas Melchisedeco: Igitur ordo Melchisedech est præstantior Leuitico. Valet consequentia ab eo, quòd maior est, qui accipit decimas, quàm qui dat. Ne autē videatur absurdè dictum, quòd Leui dederit decimas Melchisedecho, quando Leui tunc non fuerit,id iam ita confirmat.
units.tr: And, so to speak, in Abraham) The fifth argument, added in a form of amplification. The Levitical order itself gave tithes to Melchizedek; therefore the order of Melchizedek is more excellent than the Levitical. The inference holds from the fact that he who receives tithes is greater than he who gives them. Lest it seem absurd to say that Levi gave tithes to Melchizedek when Levi was not yet born, he now confirms it thus:

units.la: Cùm Abraham dedit decimas Melchisedech,Leui erat in lumbis Abrahæ: siquidé ex hoc debebat ordo Leuiticus nasci ac propagari.
units.tr: When Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek, Levi was in the loins of Abraham, since from him the Levitical order was to be born and propagated.

units.la: Ergo quando Abraham dedit decimas, simul intelligendus est cum eo dedisse decimas,ipse Leui,seu ordo Leuiticus.Probatio videtur duƈta ex consequenti:si pater dedit decimas,ergo & filius.
units.tr: Therefore when Abraham gave tithes, Levi himself, or the Levitical order, must be understood to have given tithes along with him. The proof seems to be drawn from the consequence: if the father gave tithes, then so did the son.

units.la: Proinde si consummatio) Quando satis probatum est, Christum esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech: deinde, ordinem Melchisedech præstantiorem esse ordine Leuitico:iam incipit inferre,quòd ordo Leuiticus, seu sacerdotium Leuiticum per nouum sacerdotium Christi noui ordinis abrogetur. Est hæc istorum verborum sententia.
units.tr: Therefore if consummation) Since it has been sufficiently proved that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and then that the order of Melchizedek is more excellent than the Levitical order, he now begins to infer that the Levitical order, or the Levitical priesthood, is abrogated by the new priesthood of Christ of the new order. This is the sense of these words.

units.la: Quando igitur Christus exoritur nouus sacerdos, alterius & præstantioris ordinis, argumentum est, per sacerdotium Leuiticum non esse habitam consummationem seu perfectionem: (alioqui si habuisset illud perfectionem, quorsum opus fuisset, spiritum Sanƈtum vaticinari de nouo sacerdotio Christi secundum alium & perfectiorem ordinem? ) deinde vt perficiamus consequentiam:Si per illud sacerdotium non habetur consummatio,sed hæc potius expeƈtanda proponitur à sacerdotio nouo Christi. Ergo illud sacerdotium isto adueniente abrogatur. Hæc est plana & simplex illatio apostoli. Sed hac illatione non contentus,pergit aliam attexere consequentiam.
units.tr: Therefore when Christ arises as a new priest of another and more excellent order, it follows that perfection or completion was not attained through the Levitical priesthood (for otherwise, if it had attained perfection, why would there have been any need for the Holy Spirit to prophesy of a new priesthood of Christ according to another and more perfect order?). Then, to complete the inference: if completion is not attained through that priesthood, but is rather proposed as something to be expected from the new priesthood of Christ, then that priesthood is abrogated when this one arrives. This is the plain and simple conclusion of the apostle. But not content with this inference, he goes on to add another consequence.

units.la: Quandoquidem traslato) Quasi dicat:
units.tr: Since the priesthood has been transferred) As if he said:

units.la: Si tranlatum est sacerdotium:
units.tr: If the priesthood has been transferred,

units.la: Ergo simul translata est Lex.
units.tr: then the law has been transferred at the same time.

units.la: Rationem huius consequentiæ notam esse vult ex illis per parenthefin interpositis: (Siquidem per hoc populus legem acceperat.)
units.tr: He wishes the reason for this consequence to be known from those words inserted in parenthesis: (for on the basis of it the people had received the law.)

units.la: Nam is de quo dicuntur hæc)Iam quia duæ præcedentes illationes valde graues erant Hebræis,& magnas apparet inde nasci potuisse tragœdias,ideo Apostolus per occupationem aliquot rationibus eas nunc confirmat. Ac primùm eam priori loco positam,qua dixerat,abrogatum esse sacerdotium.
units.tr: For he of whom these things are said) Now, because the two preceding inferences were very grave for the Hebrews, and it appears that great tragedies could arise from them, the apostle, by anticipating objections, confirms them now with several reasons. And first he confirms the one placed first, in which he had said that the priesthood was abrogated.

units.la: Verosimile autem est,aduersarios obiecisse: Etsi Christus est sacerdos, non tamen ita distinƈtum erit eius sacerdotium à sacerdotio Aaronico seu legali:sed potius communi atque vsitato more ad Aaronicum referetur: atque ita sacerdotium minimè dicetur translatum.
units.tr: It is likely that his opponents objected: even if Christ is a priest, his priesthood will not be so clearly distinguished from the Aaronic or legal priesthood; rather, by the common and customary manner, it will be referred to the Aaronic, and so the priesthood will not be said to have been transferred at all.

units.la: Respondet Apostolus,id haud posse sic fieri,sed necessariò distinguendum esse sacerdotium Christi à Leuitico,ideoque rectè didici translatum sacerdotium Leuiticum.
units.tr: The apostle replies that this cannot be done in that way, but that the priesthood of Christ must necessarily be distinguished from the Levitical, and therefore it was rightly concluded that the Levitical priesthood has been transferred.

units.la: Moses, inquit, siue Lex loquitur de sacerdotio, quod tantùm pertinet ad tribum Leui.
units.tr: Moses, he says, or the Law, speaks of a priesthood that pertains only to the tribe of Levi.

units.la: Christus autem non erat de tribu Leui,sed de tribu Iuda, ex qua nulli solent ad sacerdotium admitti. Igitur sacerdotium Christi distinguendum est à Leuitico,& sacerdotiū legale prorsus translatum est. Argumentum sumptum est à diuersitate tribuum sacerdotium legalium & Christi.
units.tr: But Christ was not of the tribe of Levi, but of the tribe of Judah, from which no one is accustomed to be admitted to the priesthood. Therefore the priesthood of Christ must be distinguished from the Levitical, and the legal priesthood has been wholly transferred. The argument is drawn from the difference of the tribes of the legal priesthood and of Christ.

units.la: Idq; magis etiam liquet) Alia ratio ad idé,à diuersitate ordinis,Christus est sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech,sicut spiritus sanƈtus diserte testificatur.
units.tr: And this is made even clearer) Another reason to the same effect, drawn from the difference of order: Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, as the Holy Spirit expressly testifies.

units.la: Sacerdotes autem legales sunt sacerdotes secundum ordinem Aaronis.
units.tr: But the legal priests are priests according to the order of Aaron.

units.la: Igitur ratione diuersorum ordinum necessariò debet sacerdotium Christi à legali distingui, & rectè dicimus,propter sacerdotium Christi nunc exoriens, translatum esse sacerdotium legale. Quanquam si bene animaduertimus,etiam aliud argumentum hic latet,maximè in illis verbis, iuxta legem mandati carnalis, & iuxta potentiam vitæ indissolubilis:vt sit argumentum à diuersitate institutionis, & obiectorum seu officiorum hoc modo:
units.tr: Therefore, by reason of the different orders, the priesthood of Christ must necessarily be distinguished from the legal, and we rightly say that, because of the priesthood of Christ now arising, the legal priesthood has been transferred. Yet if we attend well, there is also another argument lying hidden here, especially in those words, according to the law of a carnal commandment, and according to the power of an indissoluble life; so that the argument is drawn from the difference of institution and of objects or offices, in this way:

units.la: Sacerdos legalis instituitur iuxta legem mandati carnalis.
units.tr: A legal priest is instituted according to the law of a carnal commandment.

units.la: Sacerdos autem Christus instituitur iuxta potentiam vitæ indissolubilis.
units.tr: But Christ is instituted as priest according to the power of an indissoluble life.

units.la: Sed lex mandati carnalis longissimè distat à potentia vitæ indissolubilis.
units.tr: But the law of a carnal commandment is far removed from the power of an indissoluble life.

units.la: Ergo sacerdotium Christi similiter est à Legali distinguendum.
units.tr: Therefore the priesthood of Christ is likewise to be distinguished from the legal.

units.la: Porrò, quòd dicit, Christi sacerdotium esse iuxta potentiam vitæ indissolubilis, videtur sumpsisse ex illa particula testimonij, in æternum. Tantū ad confirmandū priorem consequetiam.Sequitur ad confirmandam posteriorem, qua dixerat, etiam translatam esse legem.
units.tr: Moreover, when he says that the priesthood of Christ is according to the power of an indissoluble life, he seems to have taken this from that part of the testimony, for ever. This serves only to confirm the former inference. He goes on to confirm the latter, in which he had said that the law too has been transferred.

units.la: Abrogatur enim quod præcessit) Ne vsq; adeò mirarentur, aut ægrè ferret secundam illam consequentiā,qua intulerat, traslato sacerdotio,translatum esse simul legem: Iam confirmat. firmat etiam, quòd Lex fit translata, & quidem duabus, si bene perpendimus, rationibus.
units.tr: For what went before is abrogated) Lest they should wonder too much at, or take ill, that second inference, in which he concluded that, with the priesthood transferred, the law was transferred at the same time, he now confirms it. He also confirms that the law has been transferred, and indeed, if we weigh it well, by two reasons.

units.la: Prior est, quia lex erat imbecillis & inutilis. Altera, (quæ potius latet & fluit ex illa) quòd succedat spes potior, id est, euangelium, quod præstantius est. Manifestum autem est, vbi aduenit, quod præstantius est, & vtilius, merito omitti abrogari, quod vile est & inutile.
units.tr: The first is that the law was weak and useless. The second, which lies rather hidden and flows from the first, is that a better hope succeeds, that is, the gospel, which is more excellent. It is plain that where what is more excellent and more useful has come, what is worthless and useless is rightly set aside and abrogated.

units.la: Quòd autem Lex sit inutilis & imbecillis, breuiter probat, dicens: Nam nihil ad perfectionem adduxit lex: quare merito censetur inutilis.
units.tr: That the law is useless and weak he proves briefly, saying: for the law brought nothing to perfection; wherefore it is rightly judged useless.

units.la: Quòd si interea quis rogaret, Quis igitur vsus Legis? An frustra data? Respondet per occupationem: erat tantum introductio ad spem potiorem. Igitur recte dicitur, eam translatam.
units.tr: But if anyone meanwhile should ask, What then is the use of the law? Was it given in vain? He answers by anticipation: it was only an introduction to a better hope. Therefore it is rightly said to have been transferred.

units.la: Atque hoc potiorem, quod non) Sed iam probandum est, quòd euangelium, ad quod introducebat Lex, sit præstantius siue quòd spes nobis proposita sit potior. Hoc verò iam probat duabus rationibus, quas tamen non ducit simpliciter à dignitate vel effectibus euangelij, sed à præstantia sacerdotij Christi præ sacerdotio legali, sentiens nimirum, æquissimum esse, vt à dignitate sacerdotij æstimetur etiam dignitas testamenti.
units.tr: And this better hope, which is not) But it still has to be proved that the gospel, to which the law led, is more excellent, or that the hope set before us is better. This he now proves by two reasons, which he does not draw simply from the dignity or effects of the gospel, but from the excellence of the priesthood of Christ over the legal priesthood, clearly feeling that it is most fitting that the dignity of the covenant should also be estimated from the dignity of the priesthood.

units.la: Prior itaque ratio sumitur à forma institutionis sacerdotij Christi.
units.tr: The first reason, then, is taken from the form of the institution of the priesthood of Christ.

units.la: Christus in euangelio institutus est sacerdos adhibito iureiurando, cùm in lege instituerentur sacerdotes citra iusiurandum.
units.tr: Christ was instituted in the gospel as priest with the addition of an oath, whereas in the law priests were instituted without an oath.

units.la: Igitur Christi sacerdotium est præstantius sacerdotio legali.
units.tr: Therefore the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the legal priesthood.

units.la: Hinc vltrà infert Apostolus: Tanto præstantioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus. Quasi diceret: Tanto etiam est præstantius testamentum, in quo Christus est sacerdos.
units.tr: Hence the apostle further infers: By so much better a covenant has Jesus become surety. As if he said: by so much also is that covenant more excellent in which Christ is priest.

units.la: Antecedentis autem priorem partem probat Scripturæ testimonio, dicens, iurauit Dominus, &c.
units.tr: He proves the first part of the antecedent by the testimony of Scripture, saying, the Lord swore, etc.

units.la: Vnde sumpta est materia argumenti. Quomodo autem valeat consequentia, quà à dignitate sacerdotij colligitur dignitas testamenti, copiosius ibi expositum.
units.tr: This is the source from which the matter of the argument is taken. How the inference holds, by which the dignity of the covenant is gathered from the dignity of the priesthood, has been set out more fully there.

units.la: Et illi quidem plures facti fuerunt) Secunda ratio, qua iterum probat à præstantia sacerdotij Christi præ legali, præstantius quoque esse euangelium ipsa lege, hoc modo.
units.tr: And indeed, those were made priests many in number) The second reason, by which again, from the excellence of the priesthood of Christ over the legal, he proves that the gospel is also more excellent than the law itself, runs as follows.

units.la: In lege erant plures sacerdotes, idque quia per mortem non poterant manere: sed necesse erat alios alijs succedere.
units.tr: In the law there were many priests, and this because they could not remain through death; but it was necessary for one to succeed another.

units.la: At Christus vnus est, isque, quia manet in æternum. Ergo sacerdotium Christi est præstantius sacerdotio legali. Iam rursus subijciatur: Tanto potioris testamenti sponsor factus est Iesus: hoc est, Quanto præeminentius est sacerdotium Christi præ legali, tanto oportet iudicari euangelium præstantius esse lege.
units.tr: But Christ is one, and he is so because he remains for ever. Therefore the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the legal priesthood. Let it be added again: by so much better a covenant has Jesus become surety; that is, by how much more eminent the priesthood of Christ is than the legal, by so much must the gospel be judged more excellent than the law.

units.la: Argumentum ducitur ab eo, quòd in nouo sit vnus, & ab eius duratione: sumptaque est occasio seu materia argumenti ex particula illa, in æternum.
units.tr: The argument is drawn from the fact that the new covenant has one priest, and from his lasting forever. The occasion, or the material, of the argument is taken from the phrase for ever.

units.la: Vnde & saluos facere ad plenum) Conclusio valde didactica & consolatoria, in qua ex præcedentibus argumentis de dignitate & officio sacerdotis Christi nulla valde proprijs verbis colligit, ad ingentem conscientiarum doctrinam & consolationem.
units.tr: Wherefore he is able also to save to the uttermost. This is a conclusion very instructive and comforting. From the preceding arguments about the dignity and office of Christ as priest, he draws in very apt words an inference of great teaching and comfort for consciences.

units.la: Quàm multiplex verò doctrina lateat, itemque consolationes: quales amplificationes de officio ac dignitate sacerdotis Christi: quomodo item tam perspicuè probetur, quòd posset ad plenum saluos facere, satis fusè ibi à nobis expositum est.
units.tr: How much doctrine lies hidden here, and likewise how much comfort; what amplifications there are about the office and dignity of Christ as priest; and how it is so clearly proved that he is able to save to the uttermost: all this we have set out at sufficient length there.

units.la: Omnis enim pontifex ad offerendum) Sequitur secunda pars totius disputationis, in qua agit de Christi sacrificio, docetque, quòd Christus, cùm sit sacerdos, etiam sacerdotij munere functus sit. Eratque necessarium, hanc partem etiam tractare, tum quòd Christus alias exi-stimatus fuisset sacerdos tantum titulo tenus, qui nunquam fuisset interea sacerdotij functus munere, nunquam sacrificium obtulisset: tum quòd nisi probaretur, Christum vti noui ordinis est sacerdos, ita nouum sacrificiorum genus obtulisse, neque doceri posset, sacrificia legalia esse abrogata.
units.tr: For every high priest is ordained to offer: here begins the second part of the whole disputation, in which he treats of Christ's sacrifice and teaches that Christ, being a priest, also discharged the function of the priesthood. It was necessary to treat this part as well, both because otherwise Christ might have been thought a priest in name only, who never performed the function of the priesthood in the meantime and never offered a sacrifice; and because, unless it were proved that Christ, as priest of the new order, offered a new kind of sacrifice, it could not be taught that the legal sacrifices had been abrogated.

units.la: Vtrumque iuxta debet ostendi, & quòd sit sacerdos, & quòd sacrificium obtulerit, atque ita tam sacerdotiū, quàm sacrificia abrogata, inferri poterit. Hæc igitur est præsentis partis propositio, quadam Enthymematis forma enunciata.
units.tr: Both points must be shown in turn, that he is a priest and that he offered a sacrifice, and so both the priesthood and the sacrifices may be inferred to have been abrogated. This, then, is the proposition of the present part, stated in the form of an enthymeme.

units.la: Omnis, inquit, pontifex ad offerendum donaria & victimas constituitur:
units.tr: Every high priest, he says, is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices.

units.la: Ergo & Christus debet aliquod sacrificiorum genus obtulisse.
units.tr: Therefore Christ too must have offered some kind of sacrifice.

units.la: Ab vniuersali ad particulare, siue ab eo, quòd, cui conuenit definitum, eidem conueniconuenire debet definitio. Quando enim Christus est sacerdos, oportet eū & sacerdotis munus peragere.
units.tr: From the universal to the particular, or from this: the definition must apply to the same person to whom the thing defined applies. For when Christ is a priest, it is necessary that he also perform the office of a priest.

units.la: Nam si esset in terra) Quia admodum difficile erat, imò impossibile videbatur, probare de Christo, quòd sacrificium obtulerit, (vbi enim legitur, Christū vel altare erexisse, vel hostias macta sse, vel huiusmodi aliquid fecisse?) Ideo nō statim subijcit probationes, sed præmittit nonnulla, quibus sibi viam pa ret, & quæ quodammodo pro fundamento disputationis sternat. Quemadmodum enim præcedenti parte arripuit pro fundamento, testimonium illud è Psalmo 110. Tu es sacerdos in æternum: ita hic quoq; arripit pro fundamento, quòd, quæ in lege fiebant, quantum ad sacrificia & huiusmodi, erat tantum typi siue exemplaria. Qua de re vbi nonnulla præmiserit, tùm sacrificium Christi quale fuerit exprimet. Quod quidem fit capite decimo, vbi ait, At Christus accedens pontifex futurorum bonorum, &c.
units.tr: For if he were on earth: because it seemed very difficult, indeed impossible, to prove of Christ that he offered a sacrifice (for where is it read that Christ erected an altar, or slew victims, or did anything of the kind?), he does not at once add proofs, but first sets down some points by which he makes a way for himself and which in some measure lay a foundation for the disputation. For just as in the previous part he took as his foundation the testimony of Psalm 110, Thou art a priest for ever, so here too he takes as his foundation that the things done under the law, as regards sacrifices and the like, were only types or copies. Having premised some points on this, he will then set out what kind of sacrifice Christ offered. This he does in chapter 10, where he says, But Christ, coming as high priest of the good things to come, etc.

units.la: Proinde repetit nonnulla de sacerdotij Christi excellentia præ sacerdotio legali, simul adiungens nouam rationem, quam pro fundamento huius partis est assumptus, & vnde paulatim ad causam principalem oratio deducetur.
units.tr: Accordingly he repeats some points about the excellence of Christ's priesthood above the legal priesthood, at the same time adding a new reason, which he has taken as the foundation of this part, and from which his discourse will gradually be led on to the main matter.

units.la: Sic autem ratiocinatur, sumpta occasione ab eo, quod in conclusione præcedenti dixerit, Christum sublimiorem factum cœlis, & eò respiciens:
units.tr: He reasons thus, taking his occasion from what he had said in the preceding conclusion, that Christ was made higher than the heavens, and looking to that:

units.la: Si Christus, inquit, sacerdotiū haberet tantùm in terra, vix esset sacerdotis appellatione dignus, nedum cæteris præstantior. Hæc est propositio.
units.tr: If Christ, he says, had his priesthood only on earth, he would hardly be worthy of the name of priest, much less more excellent than the others. This is the proposition.

units.la: Ratio propositionis: Nam qui in terra sunt sacerdotes sacrificia iuxta legem offerentes, hi tantùm vmbram habent sacerdotij cuiusdam dignioris, & quicquid faciunt, seruiut id vniuersum ad repræsentandas res cœlestes alterius veri, & consummati sacerdotij.
units.tr: The reason for the proposition: those who are priests on earth, offering sacrifices according to the law, have only the shadow of a more worthy priesthood, and whatever they do serves wholly to represent the heavenly things of another, true and perfected priesthood.

units.la: Rationis comprobatio: Sic enim oraculo responsum est Mosi Exodi 25. cùm esset extructurus tabernaculū. Nam vide, inquit, vt facias omnia secundùm exemplar, quod ostensum est tibi in monte.
units.tr: Proof of the reason: for so an oracle was given to Moses in Exodus 25, when he was about to construct the tabernacle. See, he says, that you make all things according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mountain.

units.la: Assumptio siue Minor: Atqui Christus non est amplius in terra, sed, vt iam iam diximus, sublimior factus est cœlis, vbi sedet ad dextram patris sancta administrans.
units.tr: The assumption, or minor premise: but Christ is no longer on earth, but, as we have just said, has been made higher than the heavens, where he sits at the right hand of the Father, administering holy things.

units.la: Complexio siue conclusio: Igitur nunc sortitus est sacerdotium multò excellentius, & pro vno, ac solo, vero pontifice agnosci debet, vt qui non vmbram, sed rem ipsam sacerdotij habeat, cuiusq; omnia sint cœlestia, non terrena.
units.tr: The conclusion, or summing up: therefore he has now obtained a far more excellent priesthood, and must be acknowledged as the one and only true high priest, since he has not the shadow but the very reality of the priesthood, and all his things are heavenly, not earthly.

units.la: Argumentum ducitur à collatione typi seu vmbræ, cum ipsa veritate: clarisimeque ostenditur excellentia sacerdotij Christi præ sacerdotio legali: vt interea illud quoque quivis non apprehendat, necessum esse, vt sacrificium Christi præstantius sit sacrificijs legalibus: & intererea interpositum est probationis loco, id quod pro fundamento sequentium volebat producere.
units.tr: The argument is drawn from the comparison of the type or shadow with the truth itself, and the excellence of Christ's priesthood above the legal priesthood is most clearly shown. Meanwhile, anyone may also grasp that the sacrifice of Christ must needs be more excellent than the legal sacrifices; and in the meantime he has inserted, by way of proof, what he wished to bring forward as the foundation of what follows.

units.la: Vide obsecro, quàm artificiosè istud fecerit, vt nullam offensionis causam aduersarij possent arripere.
units.tr: Please see how skilfully he has done this, so that the adversaries could seize on no cause of offence.

units.la: Quo præstantioris est testamenti) Aliud argumentum de sacerdotij Christi excellentia. Apparet autem Apostolum cùm diceret: Nunc verò hoc excellentius sortitus est sacerdotium, voluisse alteram partem, quæ ad absoluendam argumentationem ante cœptam desiderabatur, adijcere, ad eum modum, quo nos eam absoluimus: sed ecce quasi præ animi vehementia non cogitanti, priusquam absolueret, aliud ei succurrit argumentum, præcedenti affine, in quo docet itidem, sacerdotium Christi præstantius esse sacerdotio legali, ratione sumpta à præstantia testamenti: quæ reuera & fluit ex præcedentibus, vbi dictum est, ea quæ in veteri testamento fiebant, tantùm deseruisse vmbræ atque exemplari: sed alia ratione probatur: sic autem habet argumentum.
units.tr: By so much is he the mediator of a better covenant: another argument for the excellence of Christ's priesthood. It appears that the Apostle, when he said, But now he has obtained a more excellent priesthood, meant to add the other part, which was required to complete the argument begun earlier, in the way in which we complete it. But see, as if through the vehemence of his spirit, before he could finish, another argument comes to him, akin to the preceding one, in which he likewise teaches that Christ's priesthood is more excellent than the legal priesthood, this time by reason taken from the excellence of the covenant. This indeed flows from what went before, where it was said that the things done in the Old Testament served only as shadow and copy; but it is proved by another reason. The argument runs thus:

units.la: Oportet sacerdotium illud æstimari præstantius, quod excellentioris est testamenti.
units.tr: That priesthood must be judged more excellent which belongs to the more excellent covenant.

units.la: Atqui testamentum nouum, in quo Christus est sacerdos, longè præstantius est testamento veteri.
units.tr: But the new covenant, in which Christ is priest, is far more excellent than the old covenant.

units.la: Igitur sacerdotium Christi est præstantius sacerdotio Legali.
units.tr: Therefore the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the legal priesthood.

units.la: Maiorem nemo non lubenter largitur.
units.tr: No one fails to grant the major premise gladly.

units.la: Minor probatur à dignitate promissionum, quando ait: Quod in præstantioribus promissis sancitum est.
units.tr: The minor is proved from the dignity of the promises, when he says: which was enacted upon better promises.

units.la: Semper autem obserua, ista de dignitate sacerdotij Christi propterea sic inculcari, vt animo concipiatur, multo similiter excellentius esse debere Christi sacrificium, quàm fuerint sacrificia legalia. Etenim si prius illud tale) Iam quia aduersarij fortasis ægrè laturi erant, quòd diceretur, aliud quoddam & præstantius esse testamentum, idque etiam confirmatum præstantioribus promissionibus, debuit Apostolus probationem huius subijcere. Sic ergo probat, & fere à signo:
units.tr: But always observe that these things about the dignity of Christ's priesthood are so pressed in order that it may be taken in that Christ's sacrifice must likewise be far more excellent than the legal sacrifices. For if that first one had been faultless: since perhaps the adversaries were likely to take it ill that it was said that there is another and more excellent covenant, and this also confirmed by better promises, the Apostle had to add a proof of this. So he proves it thus, and almost from a sign:

units.la: Si prius testamentum fuisset consummatum, & promissiones habuisset prorsus perfectas, haud quoque fuisset opus, aliud testamentum succedere, in quo perfectiores promissiones exhiberentur.
units.tr: If the first covenant had been brought to completion, and had possessed promises wholly perfect, there would by no means have been need for another covenant to succeed it, in which more perfect promises were set forth.

units.la: Sed constat, iam olim diuinitus constitutum, ut veteri testamento succedat nouum, atque istud quidem habens promissiones de salute & perfectione spirituali æternaque, quales vetus testamentum non habebat.
units.tr: But it is plain that it was long since ordained by God that the new covenant should succeed the old, and that this indeed has promises of salvation, spiritual and eternal and perfect, such as the old covenant did not have.

units.la: Igitur est quoddam nouum testamentum, quod & sancitum est præstantioribus promissis, quàm vetus: ac merito debet illud huic anteponi.
units.tr: Therefore there is a certain new covenant, which is enacted on better promises than the old; and rightly it ought to be placed before it.

units.la: Minorem Apostolus diserte exprimit in testimonio ex Esaiæ capite tricesimo primo, cuius priori parte noui testamenti institutio & successio cum insigni discrimine describitur: posteriore verò promissiones euangelicæ de bonis spiritualibus & æternis, nempe de donatione spiritus Sancti, & remissione peccatorum, indicantur.
units.tr: The minor premise the Apostle states plainly in the testimony from Isaiah chapter 31, of which the first part describes the institution and succession of the new covenant with a remarkable distinction, while the latter part indicates the gospel promises of spiritual and eternal good things, namely the gift of the Holy Spirit and the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Perspicuum ergo est, sicut nouum testamentum præstantius est: ita sacerdotiû Christi præstantius quoque esse. Atque vlterius progrediendo, sacerdotium Christi est præstantius. Ergo habebit etiam præstantiorem hostiam. Huc enim tendunt ista omnia.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that, just as the new covenant is more excellent, so too the priesthood of Christ is more excellent. And advancing further: the priesthood of Christ is more excellent. Therefore it will have also a more excellent sacrifice. For all these things tend to this.

units.la: Per hoc, quòd dicit nouum) Apostolus ipse suis verbis ex testimonio citato, duobus infert Enthymematibus, & aliud succedere testamentum, quod distinguendum sit à veteri: præterea istud nouum tàm esse efficax & excellens, ut per ipsum abrogetur illud testamentum vetus. Arripit ad suum institutum, præcipuè vocem, Nouum. Et reuera non est alius locus in Scripturis apertior & commodior ad vuincendum, noui testamenti subrogationem, & abrogationem veteris, id quod ne Iudæi quidem ipsi dissimulare possunt.
units.tr: In that he says new: the Apostle himself, from the cited testimony, draws two enthymemes in his own words: first, that another covenant succeeds, which must be distinguished from the old; and further, that this new covenant is so effective and excellent that the old covenant is abrogated by it. He seizes, for his purpose, chiefly on the word New. And indeed there is no clearer and more suitable place in the Scriptures for proving the substitution of the new covenant and the abrogation of the old, a point which not even the Jews themselves can deny.

units.la: Hactenus parauit viam ad agendum de Christi sacrificio, & clarè docuit, quod pro su-turo gerendo tantum typos atque vmbras fuisse rerum futurarum & cœlestium: deinde, Christum esse sacerdotem præstantioris cuiusdam testamenti, quâ fuerit testamentum vetus. Vtrunq; probauit manifestis Scripturæ testimonijs. Etin id ea sunt hoc modo parata, ut iam ostendatur, sacrificium quoq; Christi aliud omninò esse ac diuersum à sacrificijs legalib. præterea multò præstantius esse debere, quàm fuerint illa legalia. Ac necessarium erat hoc modo ista præmitti, propterea quod alias difficulter potuisset ostendi, Christû sacrificasse, qui, ut suprà dixi-mus, neq; aram extruxisse, neque sancta ingressus, neque bruta animantia mactasse, more cæterorum pontificum, legitur.
units.tr: So far he has prepared the way to treat of Christ's sacrifice, and has clearly taught that the sacrifices of the law were only types and shadows of the things to come and of heavenly things. Then he showed that Christ is the priest of a more excellent covenant than the old one. He proved both points by clear testimonies of Scripture. Now these things are laid down in such a way that it can be shown that Christ's sacrifice is also altogether other and different from the legal sacrifices, and that it must be much more excellent than they were. It was necessary to put these points first, because otherwise it could hardly have been shown that Christ offered a sacrifice, since, as I said above, he is not read to have built an altar, entered the holy places, or slaughtered brute animals, in the manner of the other priests.

units.la: Igitur habebat quidem etiam prius) Iam descendit ad exprimendum, quòdnam fuerit excel-lentissimum Christi sacrificium. Suntque omnia hæc coniungenda, ad illum usq; locû, Nam si sanguis taurorum, &c. estque sententia: Igitur (quando videlicet demonstratum est, ea quæ in lege fiebant, typos fuisse atque exemplaria rerum cœlestium seu euangelicarû: item Christû præstantioris testamenti esse pontificem, quàm fuerit testamentum vetus) quemadmodum in priori testamento tabernaculum habebatur magnificentissimè apparatum, & in eo certus locus appellatus Sancta Sanctorû, quem semel quotannis solus pontifex ingrediebatur, atque offerebat ibi sanguine pro populi ignorantijs: ità & Christus accedens pontifex noui testamenti, & futurorum bonorû, etiam ingressus est semel quoddam tabernaculum, & in eo etiam Sancta Sanctorum: præterea non sine sanguine quem pro peccatis populi obtulit. Hæc inquam simplex & perspicua est omnium illorû verborum sententia, in quibus nihil aliud facit Apostolus, quàm simpliciter confert typû siue vmbram cum re ipsa, visitato more collationum primò proponens vmbram: deinde addens rem de Christo & per Christum adimpletam. Atque ita quòdnam sit sacrificium Christi exprimit. Facilius aut crasius mens apostoli non posset exprimi.
units.tr: Therefore the first covenant also had: Here he now goes on to set out what Christ's sacrifice was, the most excellent of all. All these words are to be joined together up to the passage For if the blood of bulls, and the sense is this: Therefore (since it has been shown that the things done under the law were types and copies of heavenly or gospel things, and that Christ is the priest of a more excellent covenant than the old one), just as in the former covenant the tabernacle was furnished with great magnificence, and in it there was a particular place called the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered once a year, offering there blood for the ignorances of the people; so also Christ, coming as high priest of the new covenant and of the good things to come, entered once for all a certain tabernacle, and in it also the Holy of Holies, and moreover not without the blood which he offered for the sins of the people. I say that this is the plain and clear sense of all those words, in which the Apostle does nothing other than simply compare the type or shadow with the reality itself, following the customary method of comparisons, first setting out the shadow, then adding the thing fulfilled concerning Christ and through Christ. And so he sets out what Christ's sacrifice is. The Apostle's meaning could not be expressed more easily or more plainly.

units.la: Sed videtur aliquatulum subesse orationi apostolicæ obscuritatis, propterea quod illi priori collationis parti multa sint inspersa & pluribus verbis expósita: ut, quod tabernaculum in duas partes fuerit diuisum: quæ item eo loco, qui Sancta Sanctorum nominabatur, fuerit asseruata: præterea quòd eundem locum non quouis tempore, nec quiuis soliti sint ingredi. Verùm hæc non sine consilio aut otiosè sunt admixta: partim quidem, ut tabernaculi legalis splendor nonihil amplificaretur: ac deinde ex hac amplificatione intenderetur etiam præstantia tabernaculi noui testamenti, quod Christus est ingressus: partim vt animi auditorum in omnia illa quàmlibet præclara in speciem intuentes cogitarent nihilominus, typica tantùm esse, & leuiter quædam adumbrare per Christû peragenda: sicut ipse tacitè excitat ad talem contemplationem, vbi obiter interpretatur, quid voluerit voluerit spiritus Sanctus, eo quòd non quiuis ingrediebantur in Sancta Sanctorum. Denique potest & hæc addi ratio, ut nimirum ostendatur, non tantum una aliqua re, nempe oblatione sanguinis adumbratû ibi Christi sacrificiû, sed plura ibi facta, quæ singula præfigurarint aliquid per Christum agendum, & sic melius quoque fides fiat de omnibus.
units.tr: But there seems to be some slight obscurity in the Apostle's language, because in the first part of the comparison many details are inserted and explained at greater length: for example, that the tabernacle was divided into two parts; that in the place called the Holy of Holies something was kept; and moreover that this place was not entered at every time, nor by just anyone as they pleased. But these things have not been added without purpose or idly. Partly, indeed, so that the splendour of the legal tabernacle might be somewhat magnified, and so that from this magnification the excellence of the tabernacle of the new covenant, which Christ entered, might be the more emphasised; partly so that the minds of the hearers, looking at all those things, however splendid in appearance, should nevertheless think that they were only typical, and that they hinted faintly at certain things to be accomplished through Christ. Just as the Holy Spirit himself secretly stirs us to such contemplation, when in passing he explains what the Holy Spirit meant, because not just anyone entered into the Holy of Holies. Finally, this reason may also be added: that it might be shown that Christ's sacrifice was foreshadowed not by one thing alone, namely the offering of blood, but by many things done there, each of which prefigured something to be done through Christ, and so that faith might be made stronger concerning all of them.

units.la: Posteriorem autem partem collationis apostolus extulit quadam cõtentionis forma, vt videlicet ita doceret, omnia illustriora esse, quæ per Christum sunt peracta, quàm erant quæ fiebant sub lege.
units.tr: The Apostle, however, set out the latter part of the comparison in a certain form of contrast, so as to teach that all the things accomplished through Christ are more illustrious than those that were done under the law.

units.la: Illudque præcipuè notandum, quòd hostiæ Christi tribuit hanc virtutem, quòd per eâ inuenta sit redemptio æterna, qua profectò parte longè excellentissima asseritur.
units.tr: And it must be especially noted that he ascribes to Christ's sacrifice this power, that through it eternal redemption has been obtained, which is certainly asserted as the most excellent part of all.

units.la: Nam si sanguis taurorum Sacrificium Christi quódnam sit, expressit, & ita expressit, vt id longè præstantius omnibus sacrificijs legalibus descripserit, maximè quando dixit, per id repertam esse redemptionem æternam, cùm per sacrificia legalia non cõtingerent nisi iustificationes carnis. Iam colligit argumenta, quibus hanc excellentiam sacrificij Christi confirmet, & respiciens ad id, quòd dixit, redemptionem per id repertam, sic argumentatur.
units.tr: For if the blood of bulls: He has set out what Christ's sacrifice is, and has set it out in such a way as to describe it as far more excellent than all the legal sacrifices, especially when he said that eternal redemption was obtained through it, since through the legal sacrifices there came only justifications of the flesh. Now he gathers arguments by which he confirms this excellence of Christ's sacrifice, and, looking back at what he said, that redemption was obtained through it, he argues thus.

units.la: Merito dico, per sanguinem Christi oblatum repertam redemptione. Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum & cinis iuuencæ sanctificat ad iustificationem carnis: Ergo multò magis sanguis Christi sanctificabit ad iustificationem spiritus.
units.tr: I rightly say that redemption was obtained through the blood of Christ offered. For if the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer sanctify to the purifying of the flesh, then much more will the blood of Christ sanctify to the purifying of the spirit.

units.la: Argumentatur à comparatis, siue à minore ad maius. Quanquàm, quia in consequente non idem prædicatum est, quod in antecedente, (in antecedente enim sermo est de purificatione carnis, in consequente verò inferrur de purificatione spiritus) rectius iudicabimus, argumentum duci à proportione.
units.tr: He argues from things compared, or from the less to the greater. However, because the predicate in the consequent is not the same as in the antecedent (for in the antecedent the discussion is about purification of the flesh, while in the consequent it is inferred about purification of the spirit), we shall judge it more correct to say the argument is drawn from proportion.

units.la: Sicut se habet sanguis pecorum ad sanguinem Christi: ita se habet iustificatio carnis ad iustificationem spiritus. Sed sanguis pecorum iustificat secundum carnem. Igitur & sanguis Christi iustificat secundum spiritum.
units.tr: As the blood of animals stands to the blood of Christ, so the justification of the flesh stands to the justification of the spirit. But the blood of animals justifies according to the flesh. Therefore the blood of Christ also justifies according to the spirit.

units.la: Et ob id noui testamenti conciliator est) Aliud argumentum, quo probat excellentiam sacrificij sanguinis Christi præsacrificijs legalibus, sumptum ab officio cõciliatoris, & perficiendæ concilationis modo, siue à causa finali, ob quam Christus institutus est conciliator noui testamenti. Quasi dicat:
units.tr: And for this reason he is the mediator of the new covenant: This is another argument by which he proves the excellence of the sacrifice of Christ's blood over the legal sacrifices. It is taken from the office of the mediator and the manner of accomplishing the mediation, or from the final cause for which Christ was appointed mediator of the new covenant. As if he were to say:

units.la: Christus est conciliator noui testamenti.
units.tr: Christ is the mediator of the new covenant.

units.la: Sed cõciliatio debebat fieri ipsius morte, sine sanguine. Ergo sanguis Christi, quo facta est conciliatio, est præstantius sacrificium, quàm fuerint omnia sacrificia legalia: & merito statuitur, per hoc sacrificium Christi repertam æternam redemptionem.
units.tr: But the mediation had to be made by his death, and without blood. Therefore the blood of Christ, by which the mediation was made, is a more excellent sacrifice than all the legal sacrifices were; and it is rightly stated that eternal redemption was obtained through this sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Siquidem ubi testamentum est.) Occupatio est. Quia enim graviter offendi poterat, eo quòd diceretur, conciliationem noui testamenti non perficiendam, nisi morte Christi (valde enim absurdum videtur, Deum voluisse placari humano sanguine, cùm id sacrificiorum genus etiam in barbaris detestemur: præterea, non respondere typis veteris testamenti, ut idem sacerdos sit & hostia, proprio litans sanguine, non alieno: & dura conditio ista videtur, ac filio Dei indigna: multoque hac in parte mitius agi in veteri testamento, quàm in nouo: Denique Deum posse alia ratione, si vellet, placari.)
units.tr: For where there is a testament: This is an occupatio. For because it could be seriously objected that the mediation of the new covenant was not to be accomplished except by the death of Christ (for it seems very absurd that God should have wished to be appeased with human blood, since we detest this kind of sacrifice even among barbarians; moreover, that it does not correspond to the types of the old covenant, that the same priest should also be the victim, offering with his own blood, not another's; and this condition seems harsh and unworthy of the Son of God; and that in the old covenant things were dealt with much more gently in this respect than in the new; and finally, that God could, if he wished, be appeased by some other means), the Apostle replies, but with a slight change in the meaning of the word testament.

units.la: Respondet Apostolus, sed mutata paululum vocis testamenti significatione. Recte, inquit, dicimus, testamenti noui conciliationem debuisse perfici intercedente morte.
units.tr: Rightly, he says, we say that the mediation of the new covenant had to be accomplished through the intervention of death.

units.la: Vbi enim est testamentum (quo videlicet vltima voluntas significatur) id ratû non fit, nisi morte intercedente testatoris.
units.tr: For where there is a testament (by which, clearly, a last will is meant), it is not made valid unless the death of the testator intervenes.

units.la: Sed nouum testamentum est testamentum, & Christus se habet in eo instar testatoris, (est enim autor ac mediator eius testamenti).
units.tr: But the new covenant is a testament, and Christ stands in it in the place of the testator (for he is the author and mediator of that testament).

units.la: Igitur nouum testamentum non potuit fieri ratum, nisi intercedente Christi morte.
units.tr: Therefore the new covenant could not be made valid unless the death of Christ intervened.

units.la: Est argumentum à simili, quod sumitur ab humano more seu iure ciuili.
units.tr: This is an argument from likeness, taken from human custom or civil law.

units.la: Vnde ne prius quidem illud absque sanguine) Secundum argumentû, quo idem probatur. Quia enim morosis ingenijs forte non satis fiebat, ac rursus obijcere ausi sunt, non eode pacto debere agi in causa euangelij, quod spirituale est, & bonorum spiritualium, quo agitur in causa testamentorum ciuilium, & bonorum terrenorum: aliud producit argumentum cum Scriptura conueniens, sumitque id à collatione veritatis cum typis, & ab eo, quòd res adumbratæ debeant præstantiores esse ipsis umbris siue typis, hoc modo.
units.tr: Hence not even the first was dedicated without blood: This is a second argument by which the same thing is proved. Because perhaps it was not sufficiently clear to people of stubborn minds, and they dared to object again that in the cause of the gospel, which is spiritual and concerns spiritual goods, the same procedure should not be followed as in the cause of civil testaments and earthly goods, he produces another argument agreeing with Scripture, taken from the comparison of the truth with the types, and from the fact that the things foreshadowed ought to be more excellent than the shadows or types themselves, in this way.

units.la: Vetus testamentum ubi tantum erant exemplaria seu vmbræ rerum futurarum & cœlestium, & sancitum ac ratum factum est adhibito immolatarum pecudum sanguine.
units.tr: Where the old covenant had only copies or shadows of future and heavenly things, it was also sanctioned and made valid with the blood of slaughtered beasts.

units.la: Ergo nouû testamentû, vbi adsunt res ipsæ & bona cœlestia, multo præstantiori modo, nempe sanguine ac morte ipsius Christi, sanciri ratumque fieri conuenit.
units.tr: Therefore in the new covenant, where the realities themselves and the heavenly goods are present, it is fitting that it should be sanctioned and made valid in a far more excellent manner, namely by the blood and death of Christ himself.

units.la: Antecedens argumenti Apostolus pluribus exemplis luculenter probat, ubique sanguinem & mortem pecudum ostentantibus.
units.tr: The Apostle, by many examples, clearly proves the preceding argument, in every case pointing to the blood and death of the animals.

units.la: Non enim in manu facta sancta.) Absolutis duobus propositis argumentis, per occupationem interpositis, pergit, quod ante coeperat, probare, videlicet excellentia sacrificij Christi praesacrificijs legalib. Proinde hic habemus tertium argumentum istud probans, a circumstantia, nempe a praestantia tabernaculi. Tabernaculum quod Christus ingressus est, longe excellentius est tabernaculo legali. Probatio. Ingressus est enim ipsum coelum. Igitur oportet & sacrificium Christi multo esse excellentius. Praesupponit autem spectari debere proportionem tabernaculorum ad invicem, atque ex eorum habitudine iudicari de qualitate sacrificiorum, ut excellentissimo tabernaculo excellentissimum sacrificium accommodetur.
units.tr: For Christ has not entered into holy places made with hands.) Having completed the two arguments proposed, he interposes an aside and then goes on to prove what he had begun, namely the excellence of Christ's sacrifice over the legal sacrifices that preceded it. Here, then, we have a third argument, drawn from the circumstances, namely from the superiority of the tabernacle. The tabernacle Christ entered is far more excellent than the legal tabernacle. Proof: he entered heaven itself. Therefore Christ's sacrifice must also be much more excellent. The argument presupposes that the proportion of the tabernacles to one another must be considered, and that from their relation the quality of the sacrifices is to be judged, so that the most excellent sacrifice is fitted to the most excellent tabernacle.

units.la: Non ut saepius offerat semetipsum.) Quartum argumentum itidem a circumstantia, ab eo videlicet, quod Christus tantum semel obtulerit, & peccata etiam unico illo sacrificio expiarit. Est, inquit, sententia:
units.tr: Nor that he should offer himself often.) The fourth argument is likewise drawn from the circumstances, namely from the fact that Christ offered himself only once, and atoned for sins by that single sacrifice. The statement runs thus:

units.la: Christus non obtulit sacrificium suum saepius, sed tantum semel sub consummatione seculorum, atque id unicum ad profligationem peccati sufficit.
units.tr: Christ did not offer his sacrifice often, but only once, at the consummation of the ages, and that single offering is sufficient for the abolition of sin.

units.la: At sacrificia legalia saepius offerebantur, & adhuc nequaquam sufficiebant ad peccati profligationem. Igitur sacrificium Christi est praestantius sacrificijs legalibus. Vides argumentum fieri quadam collatione, qua confertur & modus sacrificandi, & sacrificiorum impares effectus. Atque haec inquam est argumenti summa. Verum Apostolus fusius id exponit. Nam maiorem illam, seu propositionem, quae principaliter hic spectanda est, probat quadam distributione temporum, in hunc fere modum.
units.tr: But the legal sacrifices were offered often, and still never sufficed for the abolition of sin. Therefore Christ's sacrifice is more excellent than the legal sacrifices. You see that the argument is made by a comparison, in which both the manner of sacrificing and the unequal effects of the sacrifices are set side by side. This, I say, is the sum of the argument. But the Apostle sets it out more fully. For he proves the major premise, which is the principal point here, by a distribution of times, roughly in this way:

units.la: Christus neque ante tempus consummationis unquam obtulit, neque etiam post oblatus est. Igitur tantum semel, & quidem illo tempore consummationis obtulit.
units.tr: Christ neither offered himself before the time of consummation, nor is he to be offered again after it. Therefore he offered himself only once, and indeed at that time of consummation.

units.la: Quod non ante tempus consummationis, probat ab inconveniente seu absurdo.
units.tr: That he did not offer himself before the time of consummation he proves from an inconvenience, or absurdity:

units.la: Cum Christus peragere suum sacrificium non potuerit, nisi morte, si saepius obtulisset, oportuisset illum iam saepius esse mortuum.
units.tr: Since Christ could not accomplish his sacrifice except by death, if he had offered himself often, he would already have had to die often.

units.la: Sed istud non est factum: absurdum enim est & inconveniens.
units.tr: But this has not happened, for it is absurd and unfitting.

units.la: Igitur nunquam ante tempus consummationis obtulit. Rursus quod non sit oblaturus in posterum, probat adhibita similitudine a communi lege mortis temporalis tantum semel obeundae. Quemadmodum, inquit, non potest fieri, ut homines plus quam semel moriantur, sed a morte solum superest expectandum iudicium: ita non potest fieri, ut Christus plus quam semel se offerat (quandoquidem non nisi per mortem sacrificium suum, ut supra probatum est, peragit) sed hoc tantum superest, ut veniat ad iudicium.
units.tr: Therefore he never offered himself before the time of consummation. Again, that he is not going to offer himself in the future he proves by an added comparison with the common law of temporal death, which is to be undergone only once. Just as, he says, it cannot happen that men die more than once, but after death there remains only judgment to be expected, so it cannot happen that Christ offers himself more than once (since, as has been proved above, he accomplishes his sacrifice only through death), but there remains for him only to come to judgment.

units.la: Itaque Christus tantum semel obtulit, & hoc nomine sacrificium eius praestantius est omnibus sacrificijs legalibus.
units.tr: Thus Christ offered himself only once, and on this account his sacrifice is more excellent than all the legal sacrifices.

units.la: Sed notandum est, quod Paulus etiam admiscuerit particulas illas, ad profligationem peccati &, ut multorum peccata tolleret: quae sane valde illustrant dignitatem unici sacrificij Christi, & alterum argumentum constituunt: sed tamen eas hic non probat, acturus de tanto effectu paulo post.
units.tr: But it should be noted that Paul has also added those particles, for the abolition of sin and that he might bear the sins of many. These certainly greatly illustrate the dignity of Christ's unique sacrifice and constitute a second argument. Yet he does not prove them here, since he is going to treat of so great an effect shortly afterwards.

units.la: Nam Lex umbram habens futurorum.) Quia vero praecedenti loco asseruit dignitatem sacrificij Christi, ex eo, quod tantum semel oblatum fuerit, addens etiam, quod semel sic oblatum fuerit ad tollenda peccata, atque ita ista asseruit, quasi sacrificia legalia minoris essent facienda, quae saepius offerrentur, neque ea etiam ullam haberent vim tollendis peccatis: quibus sane rebus valde offendi poterant Hebraeorum animi. Ideo nunc per occupationem ostendit, sacrificia legalia vere eo nomine esse indigniora, quod toties deberent repeti, simulque ex eo confirmat, quod peccata tollere non potuerint. Sic aut argumentatur.
units.tr: For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come.) But because in the preceding passage he asserted the dignity of Christ's sacrifice from the fact that it was offered only once, adding also that it was so offered to take away sins, and thus asserted these things as though the legal sacrifices were of lesser worth, since they were offered over and over and had no power to take away sins at all, things by which the minds of the Hebrews could be deeply offended, he now shows by an aside that the legal sacrifices were truly the less worthy on this very count, that they had to be repeated so often, and at the same time he confirms it from the fact that they could not take away sins. He argues thus:

units.la: Propositio: Lex his hostijs, quas singulis annis eadem continenter offerunt, nunquam potest accedentes perfectos reddere.
units.tr: Premise: the law, by these victims which they offer continually, year by year, can never make those who approach perfect.

units.la: Ratio propositionis a signo: Alioqui non nonne desiissent offerri? quasi diceret: Si illa sacrificia abstulissent peccata, non opus fuisset denuo offerri.
units.tr: The reason for the premise is drawn from a sign: otherwise would they not have ceased to be offered? As if he said: if those sacrifices had taken away sins, there would have been no need to offer them again.

units.la: Sed videmus, quod semper debuerint denuo offerri, & cum nova commemoratione peccatorum. Igitur signum est, quod nequaquam abstulerint peccata. Additur ratio, quod non oportuisset denuo offerri.
units.tr: But we see that they had always to be offered again, with a fresh remembrance of sins. Therefore this is a sign that they by no means took away sins. The reason is added that they would not have needed to be offered again.

units.la: Nam qui semel sacrificassent, nullam amplius habuissent peccatorum conscientiam, fuissentque omnino purgati.
units.tr: For those who had offered once would have had no further consciousness of sins, and would have been wholly cleansed.

units.la: Igitur sacrificia legalia ex eo, quod toties repetebantur, in efficacia fuisse convincuntur, imo etiam quod non potuerint peccata tollere.
units.tr: Therefore the legal sacrifices, from the fact that they were repeated so often, are convicted of being ineffective, indeed of not having been able to take away sins at all.

units.la: Eleganter autem illud praemittitur repetitum ex capite c. 1. quod lex tantum umbram obtineat futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum. Sunt haec verba quasi probationis & fundamenti vice. Si enim sacrificia tantum umbrae fuerunt: Ergo non potuerunt spirituales effectus producere, sed adumbrarunt id perficiendum per aliud quoddam sacrificium longe excellentius, nempe Christi.
units.tr: He rightly prefaces this with what was repeated from chapter 10:1, that the law holds only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things. These words serve as a kind of proof and foundation. For if the sacrifices were only shadows, then they could not produce spiritual effects, but foreshadowed that this was to be accomplished through another and far more excellent sacrifice, namely Christ's.

units.la: Non enim poterat sanguis taurorum) Aliud argumentum probans, quòd sacrificia legalia non potuerint tollere peccata, sumptum à qualitate rerum oblatarum, quarum sane quiuis intelligit, nullam esse proportionem, siue ad Deum, qui erat placandus: siue ad hominem, pro quo erat sacrificandum: siue ad peccata, quae debebant expiari. Magna Emphasis sunt singula verba accipienda, Sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & ἀδύνατον. Et ista imbecillitas sacrificiorum legalium non fuerat suprà probata.
units.tr: For it is impossible that the blood of bulls) Another argument proving that the legal sacrifices could not take away sins, taken from the nature of the things offered. Anyone can see that there is no proportion between them and God, who was to be appeased, or between them and the man for whom the sacrifice was made, or between them and the sins which were to be atoned for. The individual words, blood of bulls and of goats, and impossible [ἀδύνατον], are to be taken with great emphasis. And this weakness of the legal sacrifices had not been proved above.

units.la: Quapropter cum ingressurus est mundum) Quadam illationis forma subijcit, quare oportuerit Christum alia ratione, quàm in lege solebat fieri, sacrificium suum peragere, videlicet, non offerendo vitulos, hircos, aut similia, quae pro peccatis offerri praecipiebantur: sed offerendo proprium suum corpus, ac voluntatem patris sui ita perficiendo. Estque sententia: Quapropter (quia nimirum legalibus illis sacrificijs peccata tolli non poterant) Christus vbi venisset in mundum, ut tolleret peccata, & pro peccatis omnium satisfaceret, non debuit sacrificium ex hircis, vitulis, vel huiusmodi offerre, sed proprium suum corpus, quod illi in eum finem erat aptatum, & quo debebat, quae Deus pater praeordinauerat, pro salute hominum perficere. Eratque necessarium, hanc rationem reddere aduersarijs, propterea quod nouo isto sacrificij genere, quo vsus est Christus, grauiter offendebantur, sicut 1. Corinth. 1. Christus crucifixus Iudaeis dicitur offendiculum, gentibus autem stultitia: imò pro sacrificio nolebant agnoscere hanc oblationem, qua Christus semetipsum obtulit. Apostolus ergo rationem reddit, & quidem è Scripturis, valdeq; appositè argumentum suum constituit. Primùm enim simpliciter citat testimonium personae Christi (sicuti reuera propheta in persona Christi locutus est) illud attribuens: Christus, inquit, ingressurus in mundum dicit, Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus autem, &c. Deinde breuiter exponit diuidendo testimonium in duas partes, hoc pacto: superius, inquit dicit, sacrificium & oblationem & holocautomata, &c. postea subijcit, Ecce adsum, ut faciam Deus, &c. Partibus ita seorsum consideratis, En, inquit, tollit seu negat prius, videlicet sacrificium, oblationem, holocautomata, more legali, &c. vt constituat posterius oblationem, inquam, sui corporis, & perfectionem voluntatis sui patris. Ex quibus deinde sic infert: Per hanc voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel peractam. Atque ita satis demonstratum relinquitur, cur, quando per sacrificia legalia tolli peccata non poterant, oportuerit Christum nouo sacrificandi vti genere, & semetipsum offerre. Quàm artificiosè omnia ista sunt parata?
units.tr: Therefore, when he comes into the world) He adds, in a form of inference, why it was necessary for Christ to accomplish his sacrifice by a different method from that which was customary under the law, namely not by offering calves, goats, or the like, which were commanded to be offered for sins, but by offering his own body and so fulfilling his Father's will. The sense is: therefore (because, of course, sins could not be taken away by those legal sacrifices), when Christ came into the world to take away sins and make satisfaction for the sins of all, he ought not to have offered a sacrifice of goats, calves, or such things, but his own body, which was fitted to this end and by which he was to accomplish, as God the Father had foreordained, the salvation of men. And it was necessary to give this reason to the adversaries, because they were gravely offended by this new kind of sacrifice which Christ used, as in 1 Corinthians 1: Christ crucified is said to be a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles. Indeed, they refused to acknowledge this offering by which Christ offered himself as a sacrifice. The Apostle therefore gives the reason, and indeed from the Scriptures, and he very aptly constructs his argument. For first he simply cites the testimony as the person of Christ (as indeed the prophet spoke in the person of Christ), attributing it thus: Christ, he says, coming into the world, says, Sacrifice and offering you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me, etc. Then he briefly explains it by dividing the testimony into two parts, thus: above, he says, it says, sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings, etc.; afterwards he adds, Behold, I come, that I may do, O God, etc. Having considered the parts thus separately, behold, he says, he takes away or denies the first, namely sacrifice, offering, and burnt offerings in the legal manner, etc., so that he may establish the second, I mean the offering of his own body and the fulfilment of his Father's will. From these things he then infers thus: by this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once made. And so it is sufficiently shown why, since sins could not be taken away by the legal sacrifices, it was necessary for Christ to use a new kind of sacrificing and to offer himself. How skilfully all these things are arranged!

units.la: Sed restat adhuc probandum, quòd vnicum sacrificium Christi ad expianda peccata suffecerit: quod argumento illo quarto principali, & saepè aliàs, assertum est, at nullo adhuc Scripturae testimonio confirmatum. Istud igitur Apostolus nunc docebit. Primùm repetit propositione quòd videlicet Christus vnica hostia satisfecerit pro peccatis. Sed hanc non nudè effert, verùm illustrandi causa per collationem seu contentionem rhetoricam, hoc modo:
units.tr: But it still remains to be proved that the single sacrifice of Christ sufficed for the expiation of sins, which was asserted by that fourth principal argument, and often elsewhere, but has not yet been confirmed by any testimony of Scripture. This the Apostle will now teach. First he repeats the proposition, namely that Christ by one victim made satisfaction for sins. But he does not state it baldly; rather, for the sake of illustration, he sets it out by a comparison or rhetorical contrast, in this way:

units.la: Sacerdotes legales quotidie sacrificabant, & eadem semper repetebant hostias, nec tamen omnibus illis hostijs tollebant peccata.
units.tr: The priests under the Law offered sacrifices every day, and always repeated the same victims, and yet by none of those victims were sins taken away.

units.la: At Christus semel duntaxat obtulit, atque vnica hostia pro peccatis satisfecit.
units.tr: But Christ offered once only, and by one sacrifice He made satisfaction for sins.

units.la: Haec est propositionis sententia, etiamsi in posteriori parte, uti solet, Christum adhuc magnificentius celebrat, alia orationis forma adhibita.
units.tr: This is the sense of the proposition, although in the latter part, as is usual, he praises Christ still more magnificently, using a different form of expression.

units.la: Iam propositioni sic redditae attexit mox probationem è sacris literis, nempe ex Hieremiae tricesimo primo, dicens, testificatur autem nobis & ipse spiritus Sanctus, nimirum cum praedixerit, Hoc est testamentum, &c. Ex cuius testimonij parte posteriore vult huiusmodi argumentum colligi.
units.tr: Having thus restated the proposition, he next adds a proof from the sacred letters, namely from Jeremiah chapter 31, saying: "The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us," namely when He had foretold, "This is the covenant, etc." From the latter part of this testimony he wishes the following argument to be drawn.

units.la: En praedictum est per prophetā, & à Deo promissum, quòd in nouo testamento contingeret peccatorum remissio. Ergo per unicum sacrificium Christi quod propriè solum est in nouo testamento oblatum, facta est peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: Behold, it has been foretold by the prophet, and promised by God, that in the new covenant there would be forgiveness of sins. Therefore, through the one sacrifice of Christ, which was properly offered only in the new covenant, forgiveness of sins has been effected.

units.la: Sumpta est haec ratio, vt vides, à propria nota & effectu enangelij, quo id potissimum à lege in illo testimonio Hieremiae discernitur.
units.tr: As you see, this reasoning is taken from the proper mark and effect of the gospel, by which, in that testimony of Jeremiah, it is chiefly distinguished from the law.

units.la: Porrò ubi horum est remissio) Illatio instar Epiphonematis breuiter & argutè subiecta totius disputationis summam complectens, nempe per sacerdotium atque vnicum sacrificium Christi, quòd causa est remissionis peccatorum, abrogata esse vnà cum sacerdotio simul omnia sacrificia legalia. Hic siquidem totius disputationis status & caput est.
units.tr: "Now where there is remission of these" (an inference, briefly and pointedly appended like an epiphonema, summing up the whole of the discussion): namely, that through the priesthood and the one sacrifice of Christ, which is the cause of the remission of sins, all the legal sacrifices have been abrogated together with the priesthood. For this is indeed the state and the heart of the whole disputation.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Cum igitur fratres habeamus libertatem) Conclusio totius huius disputationis, & secundae partis epistolae,
units.tr: Since therefore, brothers, we have freedom) This is the conclusion of the whole of this disputation and of the second part of the Epistle.

units.la: De vsu præsentis disputationis.
units.tr: On the use of the present disputation.

units.la: Etsi in ipsa conclusione, præterea in exordio huius disputationis diximus per apostolum ipsum vsum vtilitatemque totius disputationis de sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi indicari: tamen nos quoque putamus, non pœnitendum fore, si tum illa, tum alia quædam repetentes in summam varias vtilitates huius disputationis contrahamus, quæ tum publicè ad ecclesiam, tum priuatim ad vniuscuiusque conscientiam redire inde possunt.
units.tr: Although we said in the conclusion itself, and also at the beginning of this disputation, that the use and profit of the whole disputation about the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ is pointed out by the apostle himself, we also think it will not be wrong, if, repeating both those points and others, we gather into a summary the various benefits of this disputation, which can flow from it both publicly to the Church and privately to the conscience of each person.

units.la: Primò, hæc est insignis utilitas, quam capiet ex hac disputatione ecclesia, quòd ipsa certa sit, se habere vnum, verum, summum pontificem, vnum caput, vnum mediatorem, inter Deum & hominem, qui placat patrem, atque etiam nunc in cœlis agens intercedit pro omnibus credentibus & ecclesiæ membris. Certum est, Christum non gestat inane pontificatus titulum, sed vere etiam pontificis munus indefessè peragit, sicut hic facere describitur, & quod scribitur, clarissimè est comprobatum. Sed præterea vbi Christus ecclesiæ est pontifex, non dubium, quin nunc quoque sua sapientia & bonitate eam regat & gubernet, beneficijs ornet, donis Spiritus Sancti illustret. Dū sacris omnibus ipse præest, hauddubiè sacrorum omnium solicitam curam gerit. Huic pontifici ecclesia se committat, hunc audiat in omnibus, & sequatur, certumque est, salua erunt omnia, & quod turbatum videtur aut deformatum, sedabitur tandem, atque in ordinem redigitur. Hic habet claues ecclesiæ, hic absoluit & ligat, hic docet, hic administrat, & instituit sacramenta, adhuc hodie omnia ista peragit.
units.tr: First, this is the remarkable benefit which the Church will receive from this disputation: that it may be certain that it has one true and supreme high priest, one head, one mediator between God and man, who appeases the Father and, even now in heaven, intercedes for all believers and members of the Church. It is certain that Christ does not bear the empty title of high priest, but truly and tirelessly performs the office of a priest, just as is described here, and what is written is most clearly proven. Moreover, since Christ is the high priest of the Church, there is no doubt that even now by his wisdom and goodness he rules and governs it, adorns it with blessings, and illumines it with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. While he presides over all sacred things, he surely takes anxious care of all of them. The Church should commit itself to this high priest, hear him and follow him in all things, and it is certain that all will be safe, and whatever seems disturbed or deformed will at last be calmed and brought back into order. He holds the keys of the Church; he absolves and binds; he teaches; he administers and institutes the sacraments; he still does all these things today.

units.la: Itaque & ingentem consolationem & certitudinem in rebus dubijs ecclesia ex hac disputatione percipiet. Et hæc utilitas notata est ab apostolo in conclusione & in propositione, vbi dixit, nos pontificem vere magnum habere Iesum Christum: præterea initio capitis quinti & cæteris argumentis, vbi pontificatus Christi comprobatur.
units.tr: Thus the Church will also receive from this disputation both great consolation and certainty in doubtful matters. This benefit was noted by the apostle in the conclusion and in the proposition, where he said that we have a great high priest, Jesus Christ; and also at the beginning of the fifth chapter and in the other arguments, where the priesthood of Christ is proved.

units.la: Secundò, proderit hæc disputatio ecclesiæ, quia in ea clarissimè est expositum, vnde & quomodo peccatorum remissio in ecclesia obtingat, per pontificatum videlicet atque vnicum sacrificiū Christi, quod solum idoneum Deus pater acceptauit, vt per id peccata tollerentur, cuius sacrificij tantùm vmbram habuerunt sancti patres: nos autem rem ac cepimus. Quare ecclesia sibi congratulari debet propter tantum beneficium per Christū acceptum, omnemque curam deponere aliorum sacrificiorum, siue operum, quæ pro peccatis non possunt satisfacere. Respiciat credentes in vnicum verè propitiatorium sacrificiū Christi, propter hoc credant sibi remittenda peccata, & ex animo à Deo patre id postulet, certissimum est, Deus pater lubentissimè condonabit. Hoc solum sacrificium est in quo patri bene est complacitum, nullum aliud cogitari, nullum aliud expectari potest. Et hæc utilitas indicatur ab Apostolo tum in exordio huius disputationis, vbi ait, nos per illum consequi misericordiam, & per illum debere accedere cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ: tum in conclusione, vbi dicit, nos habere per sanguinem Christi liberum aditum in sancta idest, in cœlos: denique omnibus illis argumentis, quibus sacrificium Christi describitur eiusdemque efficacia comprobantur.
