units.tr: Second, this disputation will profit the Church, because it sets out most clearly whence and how the forgiveness of sins is obtained in the Church: namely through the priesthood and the unique sacrifice of Christ, which alone God the Father accepted as fit, so that sins might be taken away by it. The holy fathers had only a shadow of this sacrifice, but we have received the reality. Therefore the Church ought to rejoice in so great a benefit received through Christ, and to lay aside all care for other sacrifices or works, which cannot make satisfaction for sins. Let believers look to the one truly propitiatory sacrifice of Christ; let them believe that their sins are forgiven on account of it, and let them ask this of God the Father from the heart. It is most certain that God the Father will most willingly grant it. This is the only sacrifice in which the Father is well pleased; no other can be imagined, and no other can be expected. This benefit is pointed out by the apostle both at the beginning of this disputation, where he says that through him we obtain mercy, and that through him we ought to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace; and in the conclusion, where he says that we have free access through the blood of Christ into the holy place, that is, into heaven; and finally in all those arguments by which the sacrifice of Christ is described and its efficacy proved.

units.la: Tertiò, certa redditur ecclesia per hac disputationem, deliberatione sua à graui onere legis, quod nec Sancti patres, testante Petro, ferre potuerunt: quod onus omnes deijcie- batin profundissimū desperationis barathrum. Consideremus, quanta molestia fuerit, obseruare dies, menses, annos, cibos, potum, & huiusmodi: quam operosum, ob leuicu- las causas toties debere lauari, toties offerre redemptionis pretium aliquod, & quasi multam: & cum omnia hæc exactissimè essent peracta, tamen nihil inde spiritualis commodi accipere, nullam coram Deo consequi iustitiam: sed tantum coram mundo & paucis hominib. conscijs nostri peccati, haberi excusatum & utcunque purgatum. At quanto fœlicius nobiscum agitur in nouo testamento, vbi non solum fumus ab illis liberati molestijs, verùm etiam gratis & nullis nostris meritis intercedentibus cōsequimur iustitiam coram Deo, dummodo in sacrificium Christi intueamur, & fide statuamus, nos propter illud solum Deo charos redditos, & per illud solum magis purgatos, quàm olim in lege purgare potuissent sacra omnia? Quauis nō hic tantū effectus sacrificij Christi cōsideran- dus est, quod videlicet per id abrogatæ sint ceremoniæ, sed id quoque statuendum per id effectum, ut ne moralis quidem lex, si eius transgressores inueniamur, nos possit coram Deo condemnare, dummodo sacrificio Christi constanter adhæreamus.
units.tr: Third, by this disputation the Church is made certain that it is freed by Christ's deliverance from the heavy burden of the law, which, as Peter bears witness, neither the holy fathers were able to bear, and which would have cast everyone down into the deepest abyss of despair. Let us consider how great a trouble it was to observe days, months, years, foods, drinks and things of that kind; how laborious it was, for trivial causes, to be washed so many times, and to offer again and again some price of redemption, as though a fine; and, when all these things had been done most exactly, yet to receive from them no spiritual advantage and to obtain no righteousness before God, but only to be considered excused and somehow cleansed before the world and a few men who knew of our sin. But how much more happily we are dealt with in the New Testament, where we are not only freed from those troubles, but also, without any of our merits interceding, freely obtain righteousness before God, provided we look to the sacrifice of Christ and by faith hold that we have been made dear to God on account of it alone, and cleansed through it alone more thoroughly than all the sacred offerings of the law could once cleanse us? Yet this effect of Christ's sacrifice is to be considered not only in that the ceremonies have been abolished by it, but this effect must also be affirmed: that even the moral law, if we are found to be its transgressors, cannot condemn us before God, provided we steadfastly cling to the sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Habet hic ecclesia, quo tranquillet pauidas conscientias. Atque hæc vtilitas etiam aperte notatur ab apostolo, tum capite septimo & octauo, vbi aperte de abrogatione legis disserit: tū in conclusione, vbi docet, nos debere deinceps adire Deū cum vero corde, in certitudine fidei, aspersis cordibus, hoc est, in spiritu & veritate, citra ceremonias, resq; externas, Deum adorare.
units.tr: Here the Church has that by which it may calm frightened consciences. This benefit is also plainly noted by the apostle, both in the seventh and eighth chapters, where he speaks openly about the abrogation of the law, and in the conclusion, where he teaches that we ought henceforth to draw near to God with a true heart, in the assurance of faith, with hearts sprinkled, that is, in spirit and truth, apart from ceremonies and external things, worshipping God.

units.la: Quartò, habet ecclesia hic, quomodo reuincat perfidos Iudaeos pro sua lege & ceremoniolis pertinacissimè dimicantes, & salutem in illis constituentes. Hic concidisse eas, nullasque vires habuisse, ostenditur: hic legem tantùm introductionem fuisse ad euangelium demonstratur: hic typos & umbras tantùm habitas in lege. At sub euangelio habeti res ipsas & corpus veritatis euincitur.
units.tr: Fourth, the Church has here how to refute the faithless Jews, who contend most obstinately for their law and little ceremonies and place their salvation in them. Here it is shown that those things have fallen and had no force; here it is demonstrated that the law was only an introduction to the gospel; here that the types and shadows were only held under the law; but under the gospel the realities themselves and the body of truth are possessed.

units.la: Quare perfacile foret, Iudaeos, si modò se ad discendum submitterent, huiusmodi disputatione in viam reducere & ab erroribus auocare. Certè primitiua ecclesia propter tumultuantes Iudaeos magnum fructum, & salutarem doctrinā, & laetam pacem ex hac disputatione est consecuta.
units.tr: Therefore it would be quite easy to lead the Jews back to the right way and call them away from their errors by this kind of disputation, if only they would submit themselves to learn. Certainly the primitive Church, because of the troublesome Jews, gained great fruit, wholesome teaching and peaceful quiet from this disputation.

units.la: Sed & hodie arripit ecclesia ex hac disputatione arma, non tantùm contra Iudaeos, verùm etiam contra Iudaeorum similes nostri temporis, qui pro ceremoniolis nescio qualibus, & traditiunculis, somnolentia hominum, & fraude impostorum introductis, odiosissimè & superbissimè digladiatur: interea in quo salutis prora & puppis consistit, sacrificium inquam Christi, contemnentes, & contumelia afficientes Spiritum Sanctum: Intelligo missatores quaestum facientes ex nundinationibus suarum missarum, qui pecuniis conducti applicant actiones suas, quibus volunt, tum uiuis, tum mortuis, & per suam actionem permittunt peccatorum remissionem: hominum animos a vero atque unico sacrificio Christi abducentes, & in huius locum substituentes inanes ἐθελοθρησκείας, & innumera sacrificiorum nouorum commenta.
units.tr: But today too the Church takes up from this disputation weapons, not only against the Jews, but also against those of our own time who are like the Jews, who fight most bitterly and arrogantly for some kind of little ceremonies and little traditions, introduced by human drowsiness and the deceit of impostors; meanwhile they despise and insult the sacrifice of Christ, in which the prow and stern of salvation rest, and insult the Holy Spirit. I mean the mass-priests who make a profit from the bargaining over their masses, who, hired for money, apply their actions to whomever they wish, both living and dead, and through their action grant the forgiveness of sins; who draw men's minds away from the true and unique sacrifice of Christ and put in its place empty self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκείας] and countless inventions of new sacrifices.

units.la: Quintò, habet vniuersa ecclesia hic propositam sibi admirandam Dei bonitatem, & charitatem erga homines, quòd sic dilexit mundum, ut tali pacto & tali sacrificio voluerit per proprium suum filium sibi satisfieri. Potuisset sine dubio Deus alia ratione placari, potuissent alio modo tolli peccata: sed Deus iudicauit hunc multis de causis commodissimum, vt omnia salutis nostrae media instrumenta illi vni accepta referemus, & ad diligentem gratiarum actionem tota ecclesia eo iustius accenderetur. Ea propter debebat haec doctrina de sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi in ecclesia omni tempore proponi, inculcari, & vrgeri, quandoquidem beneficium redemptionis nostrae nullaratione clarius doceri & explicari potest. Tantum de vtilitate praesentis disputationis, quantum ad vniuersam ecclesiam.
units.tr: Fifth, the whole Church here has set before it the wonderful goodness of God and his love toward men, in that he so loved the world that in this way and by such a sacrifice he willed to be satisfied through his own Son. Without doubt God could have been appeased by another means, and sins could have been taken away in another manner; but God judged this most fitting for many reasons, so that we should refer all the means of our salvation to him alone, and so that the whole Church might be more justly kindled to diligent thanksgiving. For this reason this doctrine of the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ ought to be set forth, impressed and pressed upon the Church at all times, since the benefit of our redemption can be taught and explained in no clearer way. So much for the use of the present disputation as far as the whole Church is concerned.

units.la: Sed iam etiam vnusquisque priuatim maximam vtilitatem ex ea percipiet. Praeterquam enim, quòd quae generatim ad ecclesiam pertinere diximus, etiam vnusquisque priuatim ad se pertrahet: tum verò quilibet in afflictionibus & tentationibus tam externis, quam internis se contemplatione sacerdotij & sacrificij Christi reficiet, eriget, & solabitur.
units.tr: But now each person privately will also receive the greatest benefit from it. For besides the fact that what we have said in general concerns the Church, each one will also draw it to himself privately; and indeed, in afflictions and temptations, both external and internal, each person will be refreshed, raised up and comforted by contemplating the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Intueatur, quicunque affligitur, in Christum sacerdote: cogitet, illum vere talem esse, qualis hic describitur, nempe qui possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum: qui, quod nos non possumus efficere nostris viribus, pensat sua bonitate: qui bonum agens pastoris curā gerit suarū ouicularū, & tam morbidarū, quàm bene habentiū: qui deinde, si quando in peccata prolapsi fuerimus, aduocatum nostrum agit apud patrem, & sua iustitia sarcit nostram iniustitiam: hic inquam intueatur afflicta conscientia in sacerdotem Christum, & sentiet statim mirabiles consolationes, sentiet, de salute non esse desperandum, vbi talis habetur patronus: sentiet perquam leuia esse mala, quae hic obueniunt, quando talis nostri curam recipit, mirum in modum confirmabitur, & salutem propter Christum alacriter expectabit, etiamsi omnia, quae in mundo sunt, deplorata, & ad desperationem adigere videantur.
units.tr: Let everyone who is afflicted look upon Christ as priest. Let him consider that Christ is truly such as he is described here: one who can be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; who makes up by his goodness what we cannot accomplish by our own strength; who, as the good Shepherd, takes care of his sheep, both the sick and those who are doing well; and who, if at any time we have fallen into sin, acts as our advocate before the Father and makes good our unrighteousness with his own righteousness. Let the troubled conscience, I say, look upon Christ the priest, and it will at once feel wonderful consolations; it will feel that salvation is not to be despaired of when such a patron is at hand; it will feel that the evils which befall us here are very light when such a one takes up our cause. It will be strengthened in a remarkable way and will eagerly await salvation on account of Christ, even though all the things in the world seem to be given up for lost and to drive us to despair.

units.la: Septimò: proponet quilibet sibi Christum sacerdotem, & intercedentem pro nobis, in exemplum, cogitabit, se quoq; communi sacerdotio cum Christo donatū, ad se quoq; pertinere, ut omnis generis officia charitatis in fratres exerceat, afficiatur sensu infirmitatum fratrum suorum, placabilis sit & misericors erga ignorantes & errantes, pro fratribus suis Deum patrem assiduè interpellet, prouocetur exemplo Christi, ut egregiè apostolus monet in conclusione, ad charitatem & bona opera, gratus esse laboret erga Deum propter beneficia per sacrificium Christi accepta, & se vere gratum esse testetur, officijs charitatis erga fratres impensis: denique cogitet, per omnem vitam se debere Deo litare spirituales hostias, & sanctas actiones, quas nouit ad veram religionem pertinere, et Deo patri esse acceptas: de qualibus hostijs Roman.12. Hi sunt fructus, qui & communiter ad ecclesiam, & priuatim ad omnes credentes, ex sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi, totaq; hac disputatione redeunt.
units.tr: Seventhly: let each person set before himself Christ the priest, who intercedes for us, as an example. He will reflect that he too, having been endowed with the common priesthood together with Christ, belongs to that priesthood as well, so that he may exercise every kind of duty of love toward the brethren; that he may be moved by the feeling of his brethren's infirmities; that he may be gentle and merciful toward the ignorant and the erring; that he may constantly plead with God the Father on behalf of his brethren; that he may be stirred by the example of Christ, as the apostle admirably admonishes in his conclusion, to love and good works; that he may labour to be thankful to God for the benefits received through the sacrifice of Christ, and may show himself truly thankful by the duties of love performed toward the brethren. Finally, let him reflect that through his whole life he ought to offer to God spiritual sacrifices and holy actions, which he knows pertain to true religion and are acceptable to God the Father; concerning such sacrifices see Romans 12. These are the fruits which, both in common for the Church and privately for all believers, flow back from the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ and from this whole discussion.

units.la: Faxit Deus pater, ut per filium omnes horum fructuum participes effecti in Sancta Sanctorum, id est, coelos ingredi & regno aeterno cum pontifice nostro potiri aliquando valeamus, Amen.
units.tr: May God the Father grant that, through the Son, we all being made partakers of these fruits, we may at last be able to enter into the Holy of Holies, that is, heaven, and to obtain the eternal kingdom with our high priest, Amen.

units.la: TERTIA PARS; SIVE TERTIUS LOCUS EPISTOLÆ, in quo asserit, homines iustificari tantum per fidem: ideoque hortatur, ut constantes in ea permaneant.
units.tr: THE THIRD PART, OR THIRD PLACE OF THE EPISTLE, in which he asserts that men are justified only through faith, and therefore exhorts them to remain steadfast in it.

units.la: EXORDIVM.
units.tr: EXORDIUM.

units.la: REdeant autem vobis in memoriam superiores dies, in quibus illuminati ingens certamen sustinuistis afflictionum, partim quidem, dum & probris, & pressuris affecti spectaculo fuistis omnibus: partim, dum consortes ita conversantium facti estis. Siquidem & afflictionum, quæ ex vinculis meis contigerunt, participes fuistis, & direptionem facultatum vestrarum cum gaudio accepistis, scientes, vos habere in vobis potiorem substantiam in cælis ac manentem. Ne abieceritis igitur fiduciam vestram, quæ magnam habet præmij retributionem. Nam patientia vobis est opus, ut, ubi voluntatem Dei peregeritis, reportetis promissionem. Adhuc enim perpusillum temporis, & qui venturus est, veniet, & non tardabit.
units.tr: Call to mind the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle of afflictions: partly while you were exposed to reproach and distress as a spectacle to all, and partly while you became companions of those who were so treated. For you shared in the sufferings of my chains, and you accepted with joy the plundering of your goods, knowing that you have a better and abiding possession in heaven. Do not, therefore, cast away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need patience, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive the promise. For yet a very little while, and he who is coming will come and will not delay.

units.la: HÆC est tertia pars epistolæ, quæ continetur assertio de iustificatione per solam fidem. Tria autem sunt nobis consideranda, explicandaq; priusquam progrediamur.
units.tr: This is the third part of the epistle, which contains the assertion concerning justification by faith alone. Before we go further, three things must be considered and explained.

units.la: Primum, Quare, seu, qua occasione hæc pars sit addita.
units.tr: First, why, or on what occasion, this part was added.

units.la: Secundum, quare aliter tractata, quam in cæteris epistolis, puta ad Romanos, vel Galatas.
units.tr: Second, why it is treated differently from the other epistles, for example those to the Romans or the Galatians.

units.la: Tertium, quare hoc pacto exordiatur, & quare nos hic exordium huius partis constituamus.
units.tr: Third, why it begins in this way, and why we make this the opening of this part.

units.la: Quod ad primum attinet, qua occasione, & quibus de causis hæc pars sit adiecta, diximus in argumento, ut nequaquam opus sit prolixius repetere.
units.tr: As for the first point, the occasion and the reasons for which this part was added, we have said enough in the argument, so there is no need to repeat it at length.

units.la: Sed multo clarissimè occasio & finis huius partis exprimitur verbis Apostoli capite duodecimo, ubi sic ait: Proinde nos quoque cum tanta septi simus nube testium, deposito onere omni, & tenaciter inhærente peccato, per tolerantiam curramus in propositio nobis certamine, respicientes ad fidei ducem & consummatorem Iesum.
units.tr: But the occasion and purpose of this part are stated much more clearly in the words of the Apostle in chapter twelve, where he says: Therefore we also, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, laying aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the leader and perfecter of faith.

units.la: Ubi duplicem ipse indicat huius partis adiectæ causam: Alteram, ut confirmaret nos in fide, qua respicerent in salutis autorem Iesum Christum. Alteram, ut fide confirmati tanto æquanimius perferrent quæcunque aduersa, quæ propter novam confessionem fidei inferebantur: ut revera hic potius de visu fidei differere agnoscatur, quam de iustificatione per fidem. Et periculum erat, ne propter molestias plerique à fide deficerent: quod licet colligere ex conclusione huius partis: Et propterea opus erat, hoc pacto de fide apud illos agere. Atque hinc factum est, quòd non eodem pacto hic de iustificatione per fidem agat Apostolus, quo in epistolis ad Romanos vel ad Galatas.
units.tr: Here he himself indicates a twofold cause for adding this part. The first is to strengthen us in faith, so that we may look to Jesus Christ as the author of salvation. The second is that, strengthened by faith, they might bear with more equanimity whatever adversities were brought upon them because of their new confession of faith. Thus it is recognised that here he is discussing the vision of faith rather than justification by faith. There was also a danger that many would fall away from the faith because of their troubles, as can be gathered from the conclusion of this part. For this reason it was necessary to deal with them about faith in this way. And this is why the Apostle does not argue about justification by faith here in the same manner as in the epistles to the Romans or the Galatians.

units.la: Nam in illis Apostolus pluribus & validis argumentis, homines fide iustificari, confirmat & euincit: deinde etiam diluit, quæ per aduersarios pseudoapostolos obijci poterat: ut disputationes illæ iustis confirmationibus & confutationibus sint instructæ.
units.tr: For in those epistles the Apostle confirms and proves with many strong arguments that men are justified by faith, and then he also refutes what the false apostles, his opponents, could object. Those discussions are therefore furnished with solid proofs and refutations.

units.la: Hic verò nihil aliud, quam simpliciter asseriti deinde enumeratione quadam & congerie exemplorum sententiam illustrat.
units.tr: Here, however, he does nothing more than simply assert, and then illustrates his statement by a kind of enumeration and accumulation of examples.

units.la: Propterea ne suspicabimur præsentem epistolam non esse ab eodem Apostolo Paulo profectam, à quo ille?
units.tr: Shall we therefore suspect that the present epistle did not proceed from the same Apostle Paul from whom the others came?

units.la: Minimè verò, sed dispiciemus aliquot circumstantias, atque inueniemus iustissimis de caussis diuersitatem hanc in docendo accidere. Ac duae potissimum causae meo iudicio videtur Apostolum mouisse, ut hic aliter, quàm in superioribus epistolis progrederetur.
units.tr: Not at all. If we examine some circumstances, we will find that this difference in teaching arose for very just reasons. In my judgment, two main causes moved the Apostle to proceed here differently from the earlier epistles.

units.la: Prior est, quòd ad eos scribat, qui satis fœlicitèr erant instituti, ac iustitiam coram Deo contingere tantum per fidem in Christum lubenter agnoscebant: sed in hoc nonnihil decepti, quòd existimarunt, euangelio quasi vtilem & decorum appendicem adiungendas esse legis ceremonias, quam in opinione etiam Petrum ipsum ad tempus fuisse legimus.
units.tr: The first is that he writes to those who had been instructed quite happily and who willingly acknowledged that righteousness before God comes only through faith in Christ. But they were somewhat mistaken in thinking that the ceremonies of the law must be added to the gospel as a useful and fitting appendage. We read that Peter himself held this opinion for a time.

units.la: Proinde apud huiusmodi pios fratres satis erat, sanam doctrinā, quam de iustificatione rectè perceperant, & alacriter suscéperant, simpliciter citra scrupulosiorem disputationem afferere, sicque paucis eos confirmare.
units.tr: Therefore, among such pious brothers it was enough simply to assert, without a more careful disputation, the sound doctrine of justification which they had rightly understood and eagerly accepted, and so to strengthen them with a few words.

units.la: Altera caussa haec est. Hactenus in praesenti epistola satis fusè demonstratum esse legem esse abrogatam, & homines nunquam potuisse ullis ceremonijs iustificari: ex quo sanè quiuis statim intelligit, multo minus alijs operibus homines iustificari posse, quàdo nulla quàmlibet praeclara opera sacrificijs fuerint aequanda, & sacrificia proprie videbantur ad expiandā hominum peccata diuinitus instituta. Quamobrem ex huiusmodi disputatione nō obscure sequitur, alia ratione, quà operibus, nempe fide iustificados. Quod ergo ex praecedētibus magna ex parte factum est manifestum, quorsum opus fuisset id denuò operosius repetendo, nimirum eadem vel similia argumenta demonstrare? Perlege disputationes illas ad Romanos & ad Galatas, inueniesque maximam illarum partem, potissimumque confutationes, in declaranda abrogatione legis occupari.
units.tr: The second cause is this. In the present epistle it has already been demonstrated at sufficient length that the law has been abrogated and that men could never be justified by any ceremonies. From this anyone at once understands that men can be justified much less by other works, since no works, however excellent, could be compared with the sacrifices, and sacrifices were plainly appointed by God to expiate men's sins. Hence it follows clearly from such a discussion that men are justified by faith and not by works. Since much of this has already been made plain by what goes before, why would it have been necessary to repeat it again, more laboriously, proving the same or similar arguments? Read those discussions in the epistles to the Romans and the Galatians, and you will find that the greater part of them, and especially the refutations, is occupied with declaring the abrogation of the law.

units.la: De hac igitur cū in praecedenti parte epistolae satis superque fit dictum, quis admodum requirat, de eadem agi denuò, vbi ad locum de iustificatione per fidem ventum est.
units.tr: Since this has been said quite enough, and more than enough, in the earlier part of the epistle, who would think it necessary to treat it again here, when the place has come to justification by faith?

units.la: Addi queat & tertia ratio. Probabile est, aduersarios, cum crebro palàm conuicti essent ab apostolis, nihilque haberent amplius, quo se defenderent, ausos impudenter obstrepere, Patres, Patres, nec non clamitare, omnes hos operibus iustificatos, & licet videre in Iacobi epistola, licet alio sensu.
units.tr: A third reason may also be added. It is probable that the adversaries, since they were often openly refuted by the apostles and had nothing further with which to defend themselves, dared to clamour shamelessly, "The Fathers, the Fathers!", and also to cry out that all these men were justified by works, and that one may see this in the epistle of James, though in another sense.

units.la: Certè tales sciolos, quibus nihil futurum erat satis, satis erat vna aut altera ratione retundere, atque quadam exemplorum enumeratione simpliciter contrà afferere, Patres omnes iustificatos fide. His, ni fallor, de caussis, Apostolus in praesenti epistola alia via, quàm in epistolis ad Romanos vel ad Galatas, ingredi in afferenda iustificatione per fidem debuit: neque quisquam propterea occasionem est arrepturus, ut hanc, quasi Pauli non esset, reijciat. Restat, ut hoc loco sumendum esse exordium nouae disputationis, ostendamus, nec nō, quare hoc pacto exorsus sit Apostolus rationem reddamus.
units.tr: Certainly, for such smatterers, who would never be satisfied with anything, it was enough to repel them with one or another argument and simply to assert against them, by a list of examples, that all the Fathers were justified by faith. For these reasons, I think, the Apostle had to proceed in the present epistle in a different way from the epistles to the Romans or the Galatians when asserting justification by faith. Nor will anyone seize this as an occasion to reject it on the ground that it is not Paul's. It remains for us to show that a new discussion must start at this point, and also to give the reason why the Apostle began in this way.

units.la: Nouum ergo hic sumendum esse exordiū, liquet primò ex eo, quòd prorsus diuersum hic agitur, quàm in proximè praecedentibus actum est. Andiuimus enim exhortationem & comminationem ad eos, qui ceremonijs Iudaicis immodicè addicti, & plus iusto fidētes videbantur sacerdotium & sacrificium Christi neglecturi.
units.tr: That a new opening must be made here is clear, first, from the fact that what is treated here is entirely different from what was dealt with in the immediately preceding part. We heard an exhortation and a warning addressed to those who were excessively devoted to Jewish ceremonies and who, trusting more than was right, seemed likely to neglect the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Hic verò habemus consolationem ad eos, qui propter veritatis confessionem iniurijs affecti fuerant.
units.tr: Here, however, we have a consolation addressed to those who had been wronged because of their confession of the truth.

units.la: Secundò ostendimus, quae proximè constituimus pro conclusione, optimè fuisse collocata, & epiphonemate, quod solet aptissimum esse conclusionibus, terminata. Saepe enim ita solent disputationes arguto & graui epiphonemate finiri.
units.tr: Second, we have shown that what we have just set down as the conclusion was well placed, and that it ends with an epiphonema, which is usually most fitting for conclusions. For disputations are often thus concluded with a clever and weighty epiphonema.

units.la: Tertiò, mirè quadrant omnia quae hic habentur ad consolationem afflictorum propositā, cum ijs, quae post iterum subijciuntur capite duodecimo, eodem prorsus pertinentia, ut omninò statuendum sit, ibi conclusionem haberi eorum, quorum hic cernimus exordium, atque ita vltima primis optimè respondere.
units.tr: Third, everything found here, offered as consolation for the afflicted, fits remarkably well with what is set out again afterwards in chapter twelve, which pertains to exactly the same matter. So it must be concluded that there is the conclusion of those things whose beginning we see here, and thus the last things answer well to the first.

units.la: Propter has igitur caussas sunt ista consolatoria separāda à praecedentibus, & nouae caussae initium hic decet constitui.
units.tr: For these reasons, then, this consolatory matter is to be separated from what precedes, and it is fitting to establish here the beginning of a new subject.

units.la: Caeterum, vt ad exordium ipsum explicandū veniamus, totū hoc exordium constat exhortatione. Quod hac de caussa factum est. Graues mouebantur per aduersarios persecutiones aduersus eos, qui fidem in Christum confitebantur, sicut licet ex Actis cognoscere, adeò vt periculum foret, ne multi ex fratribus victi afflictionum magnitudine ab euangelio deficerent: proinde opus fuit fratres in confessione fidei per Apostolum confirmari, ne se abduci à sana doctrina rectè & alacriter accepta paterentur.
units.tr: Moreover, to come to the opening itself, this whole opening consists of exhortation. This was done for the following reason. Serious persecutions were being stirred up by the adversaries against those who confessed faith in Christ, as can be learned from the Acts. So much so that there was a danger that many of the brothers, overcome by the magnitude of the afflictions, would fall away from the gospel. Therefore it was necessary for the brothers to be strengthened by the Apostle in their confession of faith, so that they would not allow themselves to be drawn away from the sound doctrine they had rightly and eagerly received.

units.la: Hoc igitur ita facit apostolus, ut quae singula seorsum debuisset facere, nimirū & propter Christum iustitiam coram Deo contingere, & ut aduersa aequanimiter ferrent, vno fasce utraque comprehendat, & doctrinam exhortatione permisceat: eadem plane opera paucis reddens eos in doctrina fidei constantes, & tolerantia periculorum fortes.
units.tr: The Apostle therefore does this: he embraces in one bundle two things which he ought to have dealt with separately, namely that righteousness before God comes on account of Christ, and that they should bear adversity with equanimity. He mingles doctrine with exhortation, and by the same effort, in a few words, makes them steadfast in the teaching of faith and strong in enduring dangers.

units.la: Et quiiam aliàs de legis abrogatione, ac per fidem iustificatione abundè erant edocti, qua alia re opus habebant, nisi ut breuiter excitarentur ad constantiam, & consolatione quadam confirmarentur ad perferenda propter confessionem fidei pericula? Imò tota hæc pars ad exhortandum magis, quàm ad docendum est accommodata. Exempla enim maximè adhortandum valent, & ita sunt hic proposita exempla, ut singula habeat quasi inuolutas exhortationes.
units.tr: And since they had already been thoroughly taught about the abrogation of the law and justification by faith, what else did they need than to be briefly stirred up to steadfastness and strengthened by a certain consolation to endure the dangers for the confession of faith? Indeed, this whole part is adapted more to exhorting than to teaching. For examples are especially powerful for exhortation, and the examples here are set forth in such a way that each one has, as it were, exhortations folded up within it.

units.la: Et fuit hæc epistola scripta diu post illam ad Romanos & Galatas, ideoq; non opus erat, hic eadem argumenta repetere. Hunc autem esse Apostoli scopum, liquet ex initio capitis duodecimi, ubi ait: Proinde nos quoq; cùm tanta septimus nube testium, deposito onere omni, & tenaciter inhærente peccato, per tolerantiam curramus in proposito nobis certamine, respicientes ad fidei ducem & consummatorem Iesum. Ex quibus versbis, quæ fuerint causæ & occasiones, cur istam partem de doctrina iustificationis per fidem adiecerit, & cur itá, uti cernimus, tractarit, colligere cuiuis promptum est. Neq; vero potuisset Apostolus aut prudentius, aut artificiosius hanc causam agere, quàm hoc pacto sumendo excitandi consolandiq; materiam ab ipsius fidei dignitate, propter quam periculum omnibus pijs fratribus creabatur. Ipsa enim doctrina fidei probè cognita secum amplissimam utilitatem adfert, ut non solùm in fide confirmet, uerùm etiam ut animos acuat, & consolationem longè vberrimam aduersus tentationes ac pericula quecunq; subministret. Sic enim & in epistola ad Romanos statim initio capitis quinti hic vsus efficaciaq; fidei proponitur, vbi Apostolus ait: Iustificati igitur ex fide pacé habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem & contigit nobis, ut fide perduceremur in gratiam hanc, in quà stamus & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei: nec id solum, verùm etiam gloriamur super afflictionib. scientes, quòd afflictio patientiam pariat, patientia verò probationem, probatio autem spem: porrò spes non pudefacit. Sed multo plenius capite octauo in illa conclusione totius disputationis, Proinde fratres debitores sumus non carni, ut secundum carnem viuamus, &c.
units.tr: This letter was written long after the one to the Romans and the Galatians, and therefore there was no need to repeat the same arguments here. That this is the Apostle's aim is clear from the beginning of the twelfth chapter, where he says: "Therefore we also, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, laying aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the leader and perfecter of faith." From these words it is easy for anyone to gather what the causes and occasions were for his adding this part on the doctrine of justification by faith, and why he treated it as we see he did. Nor could the Apostle have handled this matter more wisely or skilfully than by taking the material for stirring up and consoling from the very dignity of faith, on account of which danger was threatening all the godly brethren. For the doctrine of faith, when properly understood, brings with it the very greatest benefit: it not only confirms in faith but also sharpens the minds and supplies a most abundant consolation against temptations and dangers of every kind. In the same way, at the very beginning of the fifth chapter of the letter to the Romans, the use and power of faith is set forth, where the Apostle says: "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only that, but we also rejoice in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint." But much more fully in the eighth chapter, in that conclusion of the whole disputation: "Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh," and so on.

units.la: Rectè igitur huiusmodi exordio Apostolus de iustificatione fidei acturus vtitur, præser- tim vbi talis erat causa & ecclesiarum status.
units.tr: Rightly, then, the Apostle uses such an introduction when he is about to treat of justification by faith, especially since such was the cause and the condition of the churches.

units.la: Atque hinc licet colligere, maximam vtilitatem ex hac parte ita tractata redituram ad pios nostri temporis, præsertim qui alibi constituti adhuc hodie propter confessionem fidei, maximeq; propter doctrinam de iustificatione per fidem in Christum graviter affliguntur.
units.tr: And from this it may be gathered that this part, treated in this way, will bring the greatest benefit to the godly of our own time, especially those who, living elsewhere, are even today severely afflicted for the confession of faith, and above all for the doctrine of justification by faith in Christ.

units.la: Qualis fuit status primitiuæ ecclesiæ, talis nunc quoq; aliqua ex parte status ecclesiarum cerni potest. Pijs spoliantur bonis & fortunis omnibus, mittuntur in exilium, pertrahuntur ad supplicia, ad furcas, ignes, gladios, nullum sæuitiæ genus praetermittitur. Et si summa causæ consideretur, hæc vna est, quòd profiteantur, se nequaquam posse iustificari ex operibus, sed tantùm fide in Iesum Christum. Propter hanc confessionem, quâ vi- demus primo atque vltimo loco in omnibus scriptis euangelicis urgeri, quam Deus voluit hoc seculo reuocari in lucem, propter impias persuasiones de iustitia operum, ac dignitate traditionum humanarum, quæ solæ oppresså dignitate fidei arcem in ecclesia obtinuerant, tàta tyrannis per Satanà excitatur. Dū hæc scriberem, multa nobis allata sunt de crudelissimis edictis & proscriptionib. in inferiori Germania editis, Deum immortalem: Itá ne dirimuntur controuersiæ? Hoccine est pacem quærere? Hæc'ne sunt media? Siccine coram nobis simulant tyranni, se velle studere in hoc, ut sarciatur concordia? & mox vbi à nobis discesserunt, exercent inauditam crudelitatem? Quid dicam de manifestis signis & miraculis ibi editis, dùm quidam sancti confessores ad supplicia pertrahuntur? Quid item dicam de sectis apud illos excitatis? Omnia sunt in aperto, & in cationes etiam triuiales vulgi relata. Quàdo ergo nos immutare hac in parte nihil possumus, Deum orabimus, ut quandoquidem ipse in manu habet corda regum & principum, corda eorum immutet, & ex hostibus pietatis reddat pietatis patronos, ex persecutoribus professores.
units.tr: The state of the early Church can now be seen in some measure in the condition of the churches. The godly are stripped of all their goods and possessions, they are sent into exile, they are dragged off to punishments, to gallows, fires and swords; no kind of cruelty is left out. And if the chief cause is considered, it is this one alone: that they profess that they cannot be justified by works, but only by faith in Jesus Christ. Because of this confession, which we see urged first and last in all evangelical writings, and which God has willed to be brought back into the light in this age, against the impious persuasions about the righteousness of works and the dignity of human traditions, which alone had obtained the citadel in the Church while the dignity of faith lay crushed, such tyranny is stirred up by Satan. While I was writing these things, many reports were brought to us of the most cruel edicts and proscriptions issued in Lower Germany. Immortal God! Is this how controversies are settled? Is this what it means to seek peace? Are these the means? Do tyrants pretend in our presence that they wish to labour to mend concord, and then, as soon as they have left us, practise unheard-of cruelty? What shall I say of the manifest signs and miracles reported there, while certain holy confessors are dragged to punishment? What shall I say likewise of the sects stirred up among them? All these things are out in the open, and even the trivial chatter of the common people is reported. Since therefore we can do nothing to change matters in this respect, we will pray to God that, since he holds the hearts of kings and princes in his hand, he may change their hearts, and make patrons of piety out of enemies of piety, and confessors out of persecutors.

units.la: Cæterùm fratres illos, qui malis affliguntur, etiam Domino similiter asiduis precibus commendabimus: deinde, ut in fana doctrina confirmetur & perseuerent, proponemus eis primùm pro summa vniuersæ doctrinæ euangelicæ, diligenter versanda ediscendaq; capita aliquot epistolæ ad Romanos & ad Galatas, quibus clarissimè, certissimè, plenissimeq; docetur, hominess iustificari per fidem absque operibus legis.
units.tr: Meanwhile, we will also commend those brothers who are afflicted by evils to the Lord with constant prayers. Then, so that they may be confirmed and persevere in sound doctrine, we will first set before them, for the sum of the whole evangelical doctrine, certain chapters of the letters to the Romans and the Galatians, to be carefully studied and learned by heart, in which it is taught most clearly, most certainly and most fully that men are justified by faith without the works of the law.

units.la: Hanc summam vbi imbiberint, prorsusq; suam fecerint, actùm sentire incipiunt molestias & tentationes, siue internas, quæ immittuntur à Satana & nostrapte infirmitate: siue externas, quas excitant falsi fratres: accipiant in manus hanc partem præsentis epistolæ: & certò scio sentient mirabiles in conscientijs consolationes, nec non ad constantiam in fide vehementer inflammabuntur. Legant & relegant, minutatim singula excutiant, tam quæ in exordio habentur, quàm quæ in conclusione sunt posita: tum in confirmatione oculatè intueantur in exempla Sanctorum patrum pulcherrima, non dubito, quin breui sic afficientur, ut cum magnanimo apostolo dicere possint (Roman. 8.) neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, neque principatus, neque potestates, neque instantia, neque futura, neque altitudo, neque profunditas, neque ulla creatura alia poterit nos separare à dilectione Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Quod illis ad gloriam suam, & ecclesiarum ædificationem concedat Dominus Deus benedictus in secula, Amen.
units.tr: When they have soaked up this summary and made it wholly their own, they will begin to feel the troubles and temptations, whether inward, which are sent by Satan and by our own weakness, or outward, which false brothers stir up. Let them take in hand this part of the present letter, and I know for certain that they will feel wonderful consolations in their consciences, and will be greatly kindled to constancy in the faith. Let them read and re-read, examine each thing minutely, both what is given at the beginning and what is set down in the conclusion; then in the confirmation let them look attentively at the most beautiful examples of the holy fathers. I do not doubt that they will soon be so moved that they can say with the great-hearted Apostle (Rom. 8): "Neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." May the Lord God, blessed for ever, grant this to them for his glory and for the building up of the churches. Amen.

units.la: Iam ad exordium explicandum veniamus.
units.tr: Now let us come to the explanation of the introduction.

units.la: Redeant autem vobis in memoriam superiores dies, in quibus illuminati ingens certamen sustinuistis afflictionum, partim quidem, dum et probris affecti spectaculo fuistis omnibus: partim, dum consortes ita conuersantium facti estis: siquidem & afflictionum, quæ ex vinculis meis contigerunt, participes fuistis, & direptionem facultatum vestrarum cum gaudio accepistis, scientes vos habere in vobis potiorem substantiam in cælis ac manentem. Ne abiceritis igitur fiduciam vestram.
units.tr: "But call to mind the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings: partly, being made a spectacle to all by reproaches and afflictions; partly, becoming partners with those who were so treated. For you both had compassion on me in my chains, and joyfully accepted the plundering of your goods, knowing that you have in yourselves a better possession and an abiding one in heaven. Do not therefore cast away your confidence."

units.la: Hortatur autem hoc exordio pios fratres, qui propter confessionem Christi multa gravia passi fuerant, ad constantiam in fide, à commemoratione fortitudinis & constantiæ ipsorum in malis anteactis. Suntque hæc omnia coniungenda, redeant vobis in memoriam, ad illa usque verba: quæ magnam habet præmij retributionem: quorum hæc est sententia: Vos hactenus fuistis in confessione fidei constantes: quare decet nunc quoque constantes maneatis.
units.tr: The Apostle, however, in this introduction exhorts the godly brothers, who had suffered many grievous things for the confession of Christ, to constancy in the faith, by calling to mind their own courage and steadfastness in the evils of the past. All these things are to be joined together, from "call to mind" down to those words "which has a great reward of recompense." The sense of these words is this: you have hitherto been steadfast in the confession of faith; therefore it is fitting that you remain steadfast now also.

units.la: Estque hæc valde efficax & idonea hortandi ratio, quando ita excitamus ad graviora perferenda, revocado in memoriam pericula, quæ ante experti fuerimus, & superauerimus. Sic videmus subinde in historijs duces exhortari suos milites: ut Annibal apud T. Liuium, Aneas apud Virgilium: O socij, neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum, O passi graviora, dabit Deus his quoque finem.
units.tr: This is a very effective and suitable way of exhorting, when we stir people up to bear heavier things by recalling the dangers which they have already experienced and overcome. Thus we see in histories that leaders often encourage their soldiers: as Hannibal in Titus Livy, and Aeneas in Virgil: "O comrades, for we are not ignorant of evils before now; O you who have suffered greater things, God will give an end to these also."

units.la: Sic etiam rhetores solent præsentia mala conferre cum anteactis, &, quæ adsunt, ita per collationem extenuare, ut perquam leuia ac facilia plane videatur. Ac fit nescio quomodo, ut etiam iucundum sit, meminisse malorum anteactorum. Quare hic non tantum exhortatio, verum etiam admixta quædam consolatio habetur.
units.tr: So too the rhetoricians usually compare present evils with past ones, and by such comparison so lessen those that are at hand that they seem quite light and easy. And somehow it happens that it is even pleasant to remember past evils. Hence here there is not only exhortation but also a certain mingled consolation.

units.la: Forsitan hæc olim meminisse iuuabit, &c. Est autem valde insigne, ubi nos ita gesserimus, ut nobis nostrum ipsorum exemplum proponi possit pro virtutum speculo atque incitamento: si patrum, si propinquorum, aut si aliorum exempla proponantur, habent quidem hæc ad incitandos animos vim non mediocrem: & hac de causa, ad excitandos inquam posteros res magnorum virorum cœperunt mandari literis: item erigi statuæ, non tantum quasi præmia rerum bene actarum: sed magis, inquam, ut incitamenta posterorum. At uero ubi nobis proponitur nostrum ipsorum recte factum, hic reuera multo magis inflamamur, & pudor erit, non progredi ad altiora, degenerésque arguemur, si non semper ad altiora cotendamus. Neque hic possumus aliquid caussari vel prætexere, quasi difficile vel impossibile nobis foret, quod exigitur, quando iam antea non minora perfecerimus. Est igitur hic grauis & efficacissima exhortandi forma, qua ita vult excitare illos ad constantiam in fide, proponedo eis propriam constantiam & fortitudinem, quam antea ediderunt.
units.tr: Perhaps it will one day please you to remember these things, etc. It is very striking when we have behaved in such a way that our own example can be set before us as a mirror and spur to virtue. Examples of our fathers, our kinsfolk, or others certainly have considerable power to stir the mind, and for this reason the deeds of great men began to be committed to writing, and statues were erected, not only as rewards for well-done deeds but, I say, rather as incitements for posterity. But when our own right action is set before us, we are truly inflamed much more, and it will be a shame not to press on to higher things, and we shall be shown to be degenerate if we do not always strive towards the higher things. Nor can we here plead or pretend that what is demanded is difficult or impossible for us, since we have already accomplished no lesser things. This is therefore a serious and most effective form of exhortation, by which he wishes to rouse them to constancy in the faith, setting before them the constancy and courage they showed earlier.

units.la: Redeant uobis in memoriam, inquit, superiores dies, in quibus illuminati, &c.) Dies illos intelligit, quibus primum baptizati fuerunt, & spiritus Sancti donis ornati: quando in baptismo & acceptione donorum illuminatio spiritualis fiebat, sicut supra dictum est capite sexto. Fieri non potest, ut qui semel fuerint illuminati, gustauerintć donum cœleste, & participes facti fuerint spiritus Sancti, gustauerintque bonum Dei uerbum, ac virtutes futuri seculi, &c. Et hic in memoria reuocat hac appellatione illuminationis bona spiritualia, quæ illi in baptismo acceperat, à quibus sane & hæc facultas manauit, ut aduersitates perferre possent.
units.tr: "Call to mind," he says, "the former days, in which you were enlightened," etc. He means the days on which they were first baptized and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, when spiritual illumination took place in baptism and in the reception of the gifts, as was said above in chapter six. "It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come," etc. Here by this term "illumination" he recalls to memory the spiritual good things they had received in baptism, from which indeed that ability flowed by which they were able to endure adversities.

units.la: In baptismo non solum tollebantur peccata, sed dabatur etiam spiritus Sanctus, per quem confirmabantur, ut possent intrepide confiteri, & uim tentationum perferre. Itaq; quod tam fortiter sese gesserint, qui recens illuminati erant, non ipsorum viribus, sed spiritui Sancto erat ascribendum.
units.tr: In baptism not only were sins taken away, but the Holy Spirit was also given, through whom they were strengthened so that they could confess fearlessly and endure the force of temptations. Therefore, that they conducted themselves so bravely, though they had only recently been enlightened, must be ascribed not to their own strength but to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sicut Christus quoque prædixerat apostolis, se daturum spiritum, per quem, quando coram regibus & principibus foret reddenda fidei ratio, ipsi animarentur, & docte intrepideque responderent.
units.tr: Just as Christ also had foretold to the apostles that he would give the Spirit, through whom, when the account of their faith had to be rendered before kings and rulers, they would be encouraged and would answer learnedly and fearlessly.

units.la: Et egregium habemus eius effectus exemplum Actorum 4. in Petro & Ioanne.
units.tr: And we have a notable example of this effect in Acts 4, in Peter and John.

units.la: Ingens certamen sustinuistis afflictionum) Chrysostomus elegantter obseruauit amplificationis formam. Non dixit, inquit, tentationes, sed ἀθλήσεις: & non simpliciter ἀθλησιν, sed insuper πολλην. Egregia ergo virtus animi describitur, & pericula obita amplificantur: sicut reuera semper statim ut aliqui illuminati sunt, sentiunt mirabiles tentationes, statim ingrediun-tur palaestram, in qua debent multa experiri aduersa, quia nemo coronabitur, nisi qui legitime hic certauerit, & per multas angustias & afflictiones oportet nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Ea de causa Dionysius vocauit Christum ἀθλοθέτην, & vitam euangelicam ad Christi praescriptum & exemplum in molestijs & periculis agendam ἀθλοθεσίαν.
units.tr: "You endured a great contest of afflictions." Chrysostom neatly observed the form of amplification. He did not say, he says, "temptations," but "contests" [ἀθλήσεις]; and not simply "a contest" but moreover "a great one" [πολλην]. An excellent courage of mind is therefore described, and the dangers undergone are magnified. Indeed, as soon as anyone has been enlightened, they really do feel marvellous temptations; at once they enter the wrestling ground, in which they must experience many adversities, because no one will be crowned unless he has struggled lawfully here, and we must enter the kingdom of God through many straits and afflictions. For this reason Dionysius called Christ the "judge of contests" [ἀθλοθέτην], and the evangelical life, to be lived according to Christ's pattern and example amid troubles and dangers, "the arrangement of contests" [ἀθλοθεσίαν].

units.la: Et fit, ut in principio mirabiliter feruentes omnes, ac dum dona spiritus adhuc recentia in se sentiunt, accenduntur ad res maximas peragendas.
units.tr: And it happens that at the beginning all are wonderfully fervent, and while they still feel the gifts of the Spirit fresh within them, they are kindled to accomplish very great things.

units.la: Spiritus ille ignis est, & in specie ignis apparuit: quare non potest manere occultus, sed necessario erumpit: & charitas diffusa in cordibus per eum reddit animosos, ut omnia audeant propter dilectionem Dei, ut omnia pericula contemnant propter Deum. Huiusmodi impetus spiritus plus quam heroicos licet videre in omnibus sanctis renatis, cum in primitiua illa ecclesia, tum etiam hodie, vbi qui recens per spiritum sunt renati, ut confiteri Christum eiusque euangelium intrepide audeant.
units.tr: That Spirit is fire, and he appeared in the form of fire; therefore he cannot remain hidden but necessarily breaks out, and charity poured out in hearts through him makes men bold, so that they dare all things for love of God and despise all dangers for God's sake. Such impulses of the Spirit, more than heroic, may be seen in all the holy reborn, both in that primitive Church and today, where those who have recently been reborn through the Spirit boldly confess Christ and his gospel without fear.

units.la: Sed nescio qui fit, paulatim refrigescit ignea illa charitas: tade socordes & pigri efficiuntur, qui antea erant mire alacres itrenuique: imo eo delabuntur degeneres animi, ut ad pessima peccata, veluti canes ad vomitum, redeuntes, postremo etiam penitus excaecentur: & fiunt peiora omnia, ut satius foret, tales nunquam agnouisse veritatem, quam post agnitam sic relabi. Tales perstringit Apostolus in praesenti epistola capite sexto, & proxime praecedenti conclusione.
units.tr: But I do not know how it happens that gradually that fiery charity grows cold; eventually those who were before wonderfully eager and energetic become sluggish and lazy, and indeed their minds sink so far into degeneracy that, like dogs returning to their vomit, they fall back into the worst sins and at last are utterly blinded, and all things become worse, so that it would have been better never to have known the truth than, having known it, to slip back in this way. The Apostle censures such people in the present epistle in chapter six, and in the conclusion immediately preceding.

units.la: Proinde valde vtile ad excitandos animos, reuocare in memoriam primam illuminationem & spiritus feruorem. Quod si nos quoque satis essemus memores primi nostri feruoris & studij, haud dubie etiam hoc die ad maiorem diligentiam incitaremur, & nullo pacto tam torpide & tam frigide in spiritualibus ageremus. In multis nostrum mirabilis ardor & zelus cospiciebatur, videbatur prorsus noui homines, & aperta signa spiritus in illis apparebant, dixisses nouos quosdam apostolos: at nunc, Deum immortalem, vbi fides illa inconcussa? vbi charitas? vbi consolationes & exhortationes fratrum? vbi caeterae euangelicae pietatis testimonia? Omnia refriguerunt, pene dixeraм, prorsus extincta sunt, & vix scintillae in aliquo cinere sunt reliquae. Ni aliter prospiciatur, omnis religio tandem funditus euertetur. Respiciamus ergo ad primum nostrum feruore: cogitemus quomodo tum fuerimus illuminati: & demus operam, ut nunc quoque illi feruori & spiritui respondeamus.
units.tr: Therefore it is very useful for rousing the mind to call to memory the first enlightenment and the fervour of the Spirit. If we too were sufficiently mindful of our first fervour and zeal, we would undoubtedly be stirred even today to greater diligence, and we would by no means act so sluggishly and so coldly in spiritual matters. In many of us a remarkable ardour and zeal was seen; they seemed altogether new men, and clear signs of the Spirit appeared in them; you would have said they were a new kind of apostles. But now, immortal God, where is that unshaken faith? Where is charity? Where are the consolations and exhortations of the brethren? Where are the other testimonies of evangelical piety? Everything has grown cold, I might almost say, has been utterly extinguished, and scarcely a spark remains in any of the ashes. Unless something is done about it, all religion will at last be utterly overthrown. Let us therefore look back to our first fervour: let us consider how we were enlightened then, and let us take care that now also we respond to that fervour and that Spirit.

units.la: Partim quidem, dum & probris affecti spectaculo fuistis omnibus, partim dum confortes ita conuersantium facti estis:
units.tr: Partly, indeed, while you were all exposed to reproach and made a spectacle, and partly while you became partners with those who were so treated:

units.la: Probatio, quod ingens certamen sustinuerint, per distributionem: Vos, inquit, gravia perpessi estis, tum in vobis ipsis, tum in vestris fratribus. Atque ita per distributionem illam non leuiter exaggerat mala. Duplex molestia est, duplicia pericula, pati in se, & pati in fratrib. De vtroque plenius videamus. Probris affecti sunt, & spectaculo fuerunt omnibus. Sic autem Christus praedixerat futurum suis discipulis, ut homines mentirentur contra ipsos, item odio prosequerentur ipsos, & quidem propter confessionem Christi. Atqui ita etiam euenit. Ipso Christo adhuc a gente in terris iam probra debebat audire, qui de illo honorificentius ausi sunt loqui: & e synagoga eiiciebantur: Ioannis 9. de parentibus caeci nati.
units.tr: This is proof that they endured a great struggle, shown by distribution: "You," he says, "have suffered grievous things, both in yourselves and in your brothers." By this distribution he magnifies the evils, and not lightly. There is a double distress and a double danger: to suffer in oneself, and to suffer in one's brothers. Let us look at each more fully. They were exposed to reproaches and made a spectacle for all. Christ had foretold this to his disciples: that men would lie against them, and likewise hate them, and indeed on account of their confession of Christ. And so it came about. Even while Christ was still on earth, he himself had to hear reproaches from his own people, since those who dared to speak more honourably of him were cast out of the synagogue: John 9, concerning the parents of the man born blind.

units.la: Et Nicodemus noctu veniebat ad Iesum propter metu Pharisaeorum, Ioan. 3. Et Iosephab Arimathia occultus discipulus propter metum Iudaeorum describitur Ioan. 19.
units.tr: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night for fear of the Pharisees (John 3). And Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, is described as acting for fear of the Jews (John 19).

units.la: A morte autem Christi statim graues minae & poenae sunt additae. Vt Actor. 5. prohibuerunt, additis minis, ne apostoli amplius loquerentur de Christo. Mox iecerunt manus in apostolos: caedi virgis iusserunt apostolos: qui tamen alacri & laeto animo verbera ista & contumelias exceperunt. Actorum octavo scribitur de publica persecutione, inprimis Hierosolymis, deinde & in aliis ciuitatibus, ut Damasco, missis ad omnia loca explorato-ribus & lictoribus. Iam ergo poenis & probris afficiebant, ac spectaculo fiebant omnibus quicunque Christum ausi sunt confiteri. θεατρίζομενοι, in spectaculo & theatro positi, sicut solent rei, & qui flagitium aliquod designarunt, publice sic proponi omnibus ludibrio, atque etiam irridendi, ut reuera in theatrum produci pro summa contumelia accipi merito videatur, & quodam incremento adiectum. In quam sententiam Apostolus quoq; dixit 1. Corinth. 4. se & reliquos apostolos factos mundo θεατρον, spectaculum. Iam, an leue est, affici probris & contumeliis, & palàm haberi ludibrio? Omnibus hominibus à natura inditû est, appetere laudem & gloriam. Contra naturam ergo videtur quemquam ita affici contumelia. Valde excelsi animi eum esse oportet, qui contumelia se afficí patienter fert, & maximè, si benemeritus fis, si propter Deum, si item à tuis & domesticis malè tracteris, omninò maxima crux est. Sed nulla res magis torquet animum, quàm si patiaris propter pietatem, & quidem publicè si fias spectaculo. Ideo propheta psal. 41. fuerunt mihi lachrymæ meæ panes die ac nocte, dum dicitur mihi quotidie, vbi est Deus tuus? Nec posset aliquis istâ cruce ferre, nisi spiritus Sanctus, qui suggerit ipsam confessionem fidei, simul suggereret constantiam, vires, & auxilium, sicut Christus futurum promiserat.
units.tr: After Christ's death, severe threats and punishments were immediately added. As in Acts 5, they forbade the apostles, with threats, to speak any more about Christ. Soon they laid hands on the apostles and ordered them to be beaten with rods; yet the apostles received those blows and insults with a cheerful and glad mind. Acts 8 records public persecution, especially at Jerusalem and then in other cities, such as Damascus, with informers and officers sent to every place. Thus those who dared to confess Christ were already being punished and reproached, and made a spectacle for all. θεατριζόμενοι: placed in a theatre, as criminals and those who have marked some disgrace usually are, publicly exposed to all for ridicule and mockery. Being led into the theatre is rightly regarded as the highest insult, and as an addition to it. To the same effect the Apostle also said, in 1 Corinthians 4, that he and the other apostles had been made a spectacle (θέατρον) to the world. Now, is it a small thing to be afflicted with reproaches and insults, and to be held publicly in ridicule? Nature has implanted in all men the desire for praise and glory. It seems therefore contrary to nature for anyone to be so afflicted with contumely. A man must have a very lofty spirit who bears insult patiently, especially if he has deserved well, if it is for God's sake, and if he is ill-treated by his own and his household; that is altogether the greatest cross. But nothing torments the mind more than suffering for piety, and suffering publicly, made a spectacle. Therefore the prophet says in Psalm 41: "My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, 'Where is your God?'" No one could bear this cross unless the Holy Spirit, who prompts the very confession of faith, at the same time supplied constancy, strength and help, as Christ had promised would happen.

units.la: Sed iam non minus molestum est, videre mala aliorum. Nam qui vera est charitate præditus, sic afficitur, dum videt aliquem è fratribus duriter affici, quasi ipse in se affligatur, prorsus eo modo, quo in corpore humano dum vnum membrum dolet, simul dolet alia: ita ut, qui testatum facere vult, se esse verum ecclesiæ membrum, idem debeat fratrum suorum malis affici. Ac tunc potissimum, quando frater affligitur caussa religionis. Cogitare enim debet vnusquisque, qui eiusdem syncerae religionis est cultor, idem periculum sibi quouis tempore imminere, quod iam cernit in suo fratre. Nec debet dolorem hunc apud aduersarios dissimulare, quasi sperans, se hac ratione fore tutiorem: sed aperte eum præ se ferat, ne ipsam religionem suam videatur parui facere vel auersari, aut impiorum tyrannidem simulatione & blando vultu comprobare. Hypocrisis cùm in omnibus actionibus, tum verò hic in primis est vitiosa: & non solùm fratres, verumetiâ Deum irridet, qui in his officijs charitatis segnis est. Fratrem periclitâtem si non agnoscis & ipsum, & ipsius dominum videris abnegare: sicut Petrus Christum, cum captus praedicaretur, aiebat, se non nosse & innumeri alij, qui tũ defecerunt. Qui non est mecũ, contra me est, inquit alibi Christus, qui non colligit mecum, dispergit.
units.tr: But it is no less grievous to see the evils of others. For one who is endowed with true charity is so affected when he sees one of his brothers harshly treated, as if he himself were being afflicted. It is just as in the human body: when one member hurts, the others hurt too. So whoever wishes to show that he is a true member of the Church ought to be affected by the evils of his brothers, and especially when a brother is afflicted for the sake of religion. For each person who worships in the same pure religion ought to consider that the same danger may at any time hang over himself, which he now sees in his brother. Nor should he dissemble this grief before the adversaries, as if hoping he would be safer by this means. He should openly display it, lest he seem to make light of his own religion or to turn away from it, or to approve the tyranny of the ungodly by pretence and a smiling face. Hypocrisy is vicious in all actions, but especially here; and it mocks not only the brothers but God as well, when a man is slack in these duties of charity. If you do not acknowledge a brother in danger, you seem to deny both him and his Lord, just as Peter denied Christ when he was being taken captive, saying that he did not know him; and countless others then fell away. "He who is not with me is against me," Christ says elsewhere, "and he who does not gather with me, scatters."

units.la: Siquidem & afflictionum, quæ ex vinculis meis contigerunt, participes fuistis, & direptionem facultatum vestrarum cum gaudio accepistis:
units.tr: Since you also shared in my afflictions, which came upon me from my chains, and accepted with joy the seizure of your goods:

units.la: Exponit praecedetis distributionis singula membra: ac primùm quod in distributione ponebatur posteriori loco, hoc est, quomodo consortes facti aliorum, qui affligebantur. Vos, inquit, participes facti estis afflictionum, quae ex vinculis meis contigerunt.
units.tr: He sets out the individual members of the preceding distribution. First he takes what was placed in the second position in the distribution, that is, how they became partners of others who were suffering. "You," he says, "became sharers in the afflictions which came upon me from my chains."

units.la: Egregium est charitatis documentum, aliorum malis magnopere affici, & maximè dom esticorum. At multo maximæ est charitatis, affici malis etiam alienorum. Proinde tantam quèque charitatem notat in Hebræis apostolus. Nam ut hac ratione amplificet, illustriorem quoque reddat illorum charitatem, ideo Apostolus addit exemplum de suis ipsius vinculis.
units.tr: It is an outstanding proof of charity to be deeply affected by the evils of others, and especially of one's own household. But it is a far greater charity to be affected even by the evils of strangers. Therefore the apostle marks such great charity in the Hebrews. To magnify this and make their charity more illustrious, the Apostle adds the example of his own chains.

units.la: Non erat eorum proprius apostolus, sed gentium: deinde supra modum inuisus omnibus Iudaeis, ut iam illi bene velle aliqua ex parte vel dolere ipsius vicem, periculosum foret. Praeterea semper ab illis aberat. Ergo talis hominis procul positi, absentis, adeò inuisi, & publicè iudicati hostis, & alieni aduersitatibus dolere, quis non videat, rarae cuiusdam & excellentis charitatis opus? Porrò, si sic doluerunt malis alterius & alieni, ut sic loquamur, quàm credamus illos solitos angi malis suorum & domesticorum?
units.tr: He was not their own apostle but the apostle of the Gentiles; moreover, he was excessively hated by all the Jews, so that it would be dangerous for them to wish him well or to grieve on his behalf in any way. Besides, he was always absent from them. Who would not see that to grieve over the troubles of such a man, distant, absent, so hated, publicly judged an enemy and a stranger, is the work of a rare and excellent charity? Furthermore, if they grieved so over the evils of another and a stranger, so to speak, how can we not believe that they were accustomed to be distressed by the evils of their own kin and household?

units.la: Probabile autem est apostolü loqui de captiuitate sua, quàdo Hierosolymis (Act. 21.) captus est, quae Hebraeis toto orbe maximè nota fuit, & per aduersarios, quasi spes ita foret, breui actum iri de vniuerso atque omni Christianismo, odiosissimè vulgabatur. Meminit diuersis in locis suorum vinculorum apostolus, Ephes. 3. Philip. 1. 2. Timoth. 1. 2. quas epistolas & è carcere scripsit. Vero simile est etiam, Apostolum mentionem facere suorum vinculorum, ut tacitè soleturatque erigat eos suum exemplum in perferendis periculis proponendo, quomodo alias quoque solet ad confirmandos fratres suorum vinculorum mentionem facere.
units.tr: It is probable that the apostle is speaking of his captivity, when he was seized at Jerusalem (Acts 21). This was very well known to the Hebrews throughout the world, and the adversaries spread it about most odiously, as if there were hope that soon the whole of Christianity would be finished. The apostle mentions his chains in various places: Ephesians 3, Philippians 1, 2 Timothy 1 and 2, letters which he wrote from prison. It is also likely that the Apostle mentions his chains so that, silently, he might console and encourage them, setting his own example before them of enduring dangers, just as he is accustomed elsewhere to mention his chains in order to strengthen the brothers.

units.la: Videamus nunc nostra tempora, vbi talem inueniamns charitatem? Vbi sunt, qui dolent malis eorum, qui procul sunt positi, & propter euangelium affliguntur? Imò vix videas, qui domesticorum suorum afflictionibus moueantur.
units.tr: Let us now look at our own times: where do we find such charity? Where are those who grieve over the evils of those who are far away and suffer for the gospel? Indeed, you can hardly find anyone moved by the afflictions of his own household.

units.la: Vbi quis iam periclitatur, omnes refugiunt, omnes erubescunt: ut ne pater quidem filium confitentem Christum velit agnoscere: sicut & Christi tempore factum legimus Ioan. 9.
units.tr: Wherever anyone is now in danger, all flee, all are ashamed; so that not even a father will acknowledge a son who confesses Christ. We read that this also happened in Christ's time (John 9).

units.la: Omnes sumus edocti, quicquid vni ex minimis confessoribus impenditur, id à Christo sic accipi, quasi ipsi impensum foret. Et nouissimo die expostulabit cum illis, qui ipsum in carcere constitutum, sitientem & esurientem, non iuuerint iuuerintque, & tamen nullus, ubi hoc tempore tanta est propter afflictiones piorum occasio, ista consideret nemo putat ad se pertinere. O miseranda tempora, in quibus iuxta vaticinium Christi, vere refriguit charitas in multorum cordibus.
units.tr: We have all been taught that whatever is bestowed on one of the least of the confessors is received by Christ as if it had been bestowed on himself. On the last day he will call to account those who did not help him, or who did help him, when he was held in prison, thirsty and hungry. And yet, although at this time there is such great occasion because of the afflictions of the pious, no one considers that these things pertain to himself. O wretched times, in which, according to the prophecy of Christ, charity has truly grown cold in the hearts of many.

units.la: Respiciamus saltem ad pios Hebraeos, qui non tantum domesticorum, verumetiam procul agentium malis plurimum afficiebantur, & Pauli procul positi pericula tanquam propria moleste tulerunt. Sequitur alterius membri expositio.
units.tr: Let us at least look to the pious Hebrews, who were greatly affected not only by the troubles of their own, but also by the evils of those who lived far away. They bore with grief the dangers of Paul, though he was far off, as if they were their own. There follows the exposition of the other member.

units.la: Et direptionem facultatum vestrarum cum gaudio accepistis.
units.tr: And you accepted the plundering of your goods with joy.

units.la: Semper intendebatur tyrannis, crudelitas quotidie vires accipiebat. Gamaliel initio suadebat, remittendam esse omnem saeuitiam, ne viderentur θεομαχ- χεῖν, & placuit omnibus sententia.
units.tr: The tyranny was always aimed at them, and the cruelty grew stronger every day. At first Gamaliel advised that all violence should be held back, so that they would not seem to be fighting against God [θεομαχεῖν], and everyone agreed with his opinion.

units.la: Sed statim graves minae, mox flagella, tum atrociora successerunt: vt Herodes etiam Actorum 12. gratiam promereretur apud Iudaeos ex sua crudelitate, occiso Iacobo fratre Domini, & tentando idem facere in Petrum.
units.tr: But soon came grave threats, then whippings, and then still more atrocious measures. Herod, in Acts 12, won favour with the Jews by his cruelty, having killed James, the brother of the Lord, and he tried to do the same to Peter.

units.la: Tandem etiam facultates credentium direptae, si qui aliquas haberent. Quam ob causam probabile est, eo diligentius contulisse fratres sua in commune, ne videlicet postea per praedones tyrannos diriperentur.
units.tr: At last the goods of the believers were seized, whatever they had. For this reason it is likely that the brothers pooled their possessions all the more carefully, so that they would not afterwards be plundered by tyrannical robbers.

units.la: Haec tyrannis primum in Iudaea, Hierosolymis sancta ciuitate (sicut nunc quoque Romae) excitata est, sed postea etiam ad exteros propagata, quod liquet ex illo 1. Thessalon. 2. Vos imitatores facti estis, fratres, ecclesiarum Dei, quae sunt in Iudaea in Christo Iesu, quod eadem passi sitis & vos a propriis contribulibus, quemadmodum & ipsi nos a Iudaeis, qui & Dominum occiderunt Iesum, & proprios Prophetas: ita & nos persecuti sunt, & Deo non placent, & omnibus hominibus aduersantur.
units.tr: This persecution first broke out in Judea, in the holy city of Jerusalem (as it does now also at Rome), but afterwards it spread to foreigners as well, as is clear from 1 Thessalonians 2: "You, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen, just as they did from the Jews, who both killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and drove us out; and they do not please God and are opposed to all men."

units.la: Proinde vere dicit, illos in se passos grauia, qui direptionem facultatum acceperunt. Facultates sunt, quibus victui necessaria quotidie parantur.
units.tr: Therefore he rightly says that those who had the plundering of their goods accepted had suffered grievous things. Goods are those things by which the necessities of life are provided day by day.

units.la: His ergo spoliari, est vitae praesidijs priuari.
units.tr: To be stripped of these, then, is to be deprived of the means of living.

units.la: Proinde, quanto maior est vsus & necessitas earum facultatum, quae ad moderatum victum requiruntur, tanto grauius fertur earundem amissio.
units.tr: Therefore, the greater the use and need of those goods which are required for a modest livelihood, the more grievous is their loss.

units.la: Ergo grauia passi sunt, quibus ademptae sunt facultates, qui nudi relicti coguntur profugi & mendici agere, sicut Actorum octauo indicatur. Sed qui vere pius est, diuitias omnes, imo propriam animam paratus est profundere, & perdere, vt animam saluam faciat.
units.tr: Those therefore suffered grievously from whom their goods were taken, and who, left naked, were forced to live as fugitives and beggars, as is shown in Acts 8. But he who is truly pious is ready to pour out, and even to lose, all his riches, indeed his very life, so that he may save his soul.

units.la: Alias enim quid proderit homini, si vniuersum mundum lucretur, animae vero suae detrimentum patiatur? Hoc igitur edocti erant pij Hebraei, & sciebant, amittere facultates temporales, esse tantundem atque lucrari facultates aeternas & spirituales. Et sic constanter magnoque animo direptionem facultatum perferebant. Atque ea de causa prudenter ait Apostolus <bl>προσδεξασθε</bl>, accepistis, ea voce, vt notat Chrysostomus, notans vltroneam ad promptam obedientiam.
units.tr: For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? The pious Hebrews were therefore taught this, and they knew that to lose temporal goods was the same as gaining eternal and spiritual goods. And so they bore the plundering of their goods steadfastly and with a great spirit. For this reason the Apostle wisely says "accepted" [προσδέξασθε], a word which, as Chrysostom notes, signifies a willing and ready obedience.

units.la: Sed multo clarius exprimit talem affectum, addendo, μετὰ χαρᾶς. Haec particula magnam habet Emphasin, & valde amplificat illorum fortitudinem.
units.tr: But he expresses such a disposition much more clearly by adding with joy [μετὰ χαρᾶς]. This phrase has great emphasis and greatly enhances the courage of those people.

units.la: Magnum enim est aequanimiter perferre illatam iniuriam: at vero etiam cum gaudio ferre, quis non admiretur? Est ergo valde mirabilis particula, sed multis de causis addita.
units.tr: For it is a great thing to bear a wrong inflicted with equanimity; but who would not marvel at bearing it even with joy? This phrase is therefore very remarkable, and it has been added for many reasons.

units.la: Significat enim incomparabilem vim Spiritus sancti in prima illuminatione acceptam, & fortitudinem Christianam a Philosophica apte distinguit.
units.tr: For it signifies the incomparable power of the Holy Spirit received in the first enlightenment, and it aptly distinguishes Christian fortitude from philosophical fortitude.

units.la: Vim quidem Spiritus sancti, quia, qui posset fieri, vt quis etiam in malis suis laetaretur, nisi Spiritus sanctus illum intus reficeret & recrearet? Certe per naturam illud fieri non potest, sed per Spiritum sanctum diffunditur in corda dilectio Dei, quae tanta est, & tam vehemens, vt prae Deo omnia, quae in mundo sunt, contemnantur. Roman. 5. & 8. Tali Spiritu accensi erant illi Apostoli, qui ibant gaudentes a conspectu concilij, quoniam digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine Iesu contumelia afficerentur.
units.tr: The power of the Holy Spirit, because how could anyone rejoice even in his own afflictions, unless the Holy Spirit refreshed and revived him inwardly?
