Certainly this cannot happen through nature; but through the Holy Spirit the love of God is poured out into our hearts, and it is so great and so vehement that, in comparison with God, all the things that are in the world are despised (Romans 5 and 8). Those apostles were kindled by such a Spirit, who went away from the presence of the council rejoicing, since they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus.

units.la: Tali Spiritu agebatur Stephanus, qui, cum sisteretur in concilio, tamen placido & alacri vultu, planeque angelico semper perstitit.
units.tr: Stephen was moved by such a Spirit, who, when he was brought before the council, nevertheless remained always calm and cheerful of countenance, and altogether angelic.

units.la: Distinguitur autem haec particula fortitudo Christiana a philosophica: quia fortitudo gentilium quamlibet insignis, & stoicis dogmatib. probe confirmata, vt ab homine omne <bl>ἀπάθεια</bl> abstulisse videatur: tamen non poterat cum gaudio aduersa tolerare. Pertulerunt quidem multi magni viri graues molestias, & valde aequanimiter, vt vix signum alicuius doloris aut moestitiae, quasi affectus omnes exuissent: sed, quod propterea gauisi fuissent, & quidem vere talique ratione, qua pij fratres, hoc non potest ostendi.
units.tr: Christian fortitude is distinguished from philosophical fortitude by this phrase, because the fortitude of the Gentiles, however remarkable, and however well supported by Stoic doctrines, so that it seems to have removed all apatheia [ἀπάθεια] from a man, nevertheless could not endure adversities with joy. Indeed many great and serious men bore heavy troubles, and very calmly, so that there was scarcely any sign of grief or sadness in them, as if they had put off all feelings; but that they rejoiced on that account, and truly in the way that the pious brothers did, this cannot be shown.

units.la: Ratio est, quia non habuerunt Spiritum sanctum exhilarantem corda: non item habuerunt buerunt certitudinem vitæ æternæ, vti nos: sed, si quid præ oculis habuerunt, maximè spem celebritatis temporaneæ apud suos, & forte apud posteros.
units.tr: The reason is that they did not have the Holy Spirit gladdening their hearts; nor did they have the certainty of eternal life as we do. But if they had anything before their eyes, it was chiefly the hope of temporary fame among their own people, and perhaps among posterity.

units.la: Hæc inanis gloriæ ipes illos fortes reddidit. At pij non hac de causa fiunt fortes, sed per spiritum sanctum, qui est Spiritus fortitudinis, intus agens in afflictorum pectoribus, qui confirmat afflictos proposita spe bonorum æternorum & cœlestium. Atque ideo addidit Apostolus:
units.tr: This vain desire of glory made those brave men what they were. But the pious are not made brave for this reason; they are made brave through the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of fortitude, working inwardly in the hearts of the afflicted, and who strengthens them with the hope of good things eternal and heavenly. And so the Apostle added:

units.la: Scientes, vos habere in vobis potiorem substantiam in cœlis, ac manentem.
units.tr: Knowing that you have in yourselves a better substance in the heavens, and an abiding one.

units.la: Causa tantæ fortitudinis ac tolerantiæ, ab obiecto, & bonis per promissiones Euangelicas oblatis, quæ duplici nomine prædicat, tum quòd cœlestia, tum quòd æterna. Hic erigendus est animus, & oportet omnes tota mente intendere.
units.tr: The cause of such great fortitude and endurance lies in the object, and in the good things offered through the evangelical promises, which he praises under a double name, both because they are heavenly and because they are eternal. Here the mind must be raised up, and all should direct their whole attention to it.

units.la: Scientes, inquit: Ergo omnino certi erant, nullusque scrupus erat reliquus. Hæc est fidei natura, vt magna certitudine, πληροφορίᾳ, statuat, sibi misericordiam Dei adfuturam. Certa & perfecta fides est plusquàm certa cognitio, adeoque experientia, licet de rebus futuris.
units.tr: Knowing, he says. They were therefore entirely certain, and no doubt remained. It is the nature of faith to establish, with great certainty, full assurance [πληροφορία], that the mercy of God will be present to it. A certain and perfect faith is more than certain knowledge, and so it is an experience, even though it concerns things to come.

units.la: Et unde ista certitudo? Spiritus sanctus (Roman. 8.) testificatur vnà cum Spiritu nostro in cordibus nostris, quòd sumus filij Dei: Quòd si filij, igitur & hæredes. Ergo certò sciunt credentes, sibi dona patris sui cœlestis obuentura.
units.tr: And whence this certainty? The Holy Spirit testifies (Romans 8) together with our spirit in our hearts that we are children of God; and if children, then also heirs. Therefore believers know for certain that the gifts of their heavenly Father will come to them.

units.la: Propter hanc igitur certitudinem, quæ nullis minis posset concuti, recte dixit, Scientes, vos habere in vobis, ἐχαρ οἶ ἐαυτοῖς: Iam ergo quasi in manibus habent, & ipsis sic sunt addita, vt præripi (modò ne ipsi sua sponte abijciant) nullo pacto queant. Et sic est. Deus illa iam nostra facit, iam offert: tantùm requiritur, vt nos fide apprehendamus, constantesque in fide maneamus. Et Deus habitat in nobis, cum quo etiam omnia bona spiritualia in nobis sunt.
units.tr: On account of this certainty, which could not be shaken by any threats, he rightly said, Knowing that you have in yourselves [ἔχοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς]: they now have them, as it were, in their hands, and they have been so added to them that they cannot be snatched away in any way (provided that they do not themselves cast them away of their own accord). And so it is. God now makes those things ours and now offers them; only this is required, that we lay hold of them by faith and remain steadfast in faith. And God dwells in us, and with him all spiritual good things are in us.

units.la: ὑπαρξιν substantiam. Spiritualem substantiam opponit substantiæ temporali, maioremque gratiam habet in græco. Nam suprà dixit, ὑπαρχόντων: hic autem ὑπαρξιν. Sed nulla est huiusmodi substantiarum comparatio. Fluxa & caduca erant, quæ eripiebantur. Sed quæ recipiuntur, cœlestia sunt & æterna.
units.tr: Substance [ὕπαρξιν]. He sets spiritual substance against temporal substance, and the Greek has a greater force. For he said above "of those possessions" [ὑπαρχόντων]; here, however, "substance" [ὕπαρξιν]. But there is no comparison of substances of this kind. Those that were being taken away were fleeting and perishable; but those that are received are heavenly and eternal.

units.la: Quis non ambiat talem commutationem? malitque aurea accipere pro ferreis? Diligenter expendendæ sunt illæ particulæ, in cœlis, & manentem: Et qui in eas quo decet acumine intuebitur, is ad constantiam in fide, & ad pericula adeunda confirmabitur. Ad cœlos debet omnis nostra conuersatio tanquàm ad patriam tendere: &, licet hic hæreamus corpore, tamen mente debemus ibi esse occupati, in rerum diuinarum contemplatione, & ad eas semper auiditissimè ferri. Et sic semper contemplanda sunt cœlestia, vt omnibus terrenis intelligamus longè esse superiora, & omninò eiusmodi, qui ob dignitatem terreno sensu non possint percipi. Præterea ad manentia & æterna bona quis non aspiret? quando vsque adeò laborant plerique pro caducis & periturris, quæ auferri hinc non possunt, sicut nec huc per nos adferuntur, & plerunque sunt nostræ perditionis causa.
units.tr: Who would not desire such an exchange, and prefer to receive gold in place of iron? Those phrases, in the heavens and abiding, must be weighed carefully; and whoever looks into them with the sharpness they deserve will be strengthened in steadfastness of faith and in facing dangers. Our whole conduct ought to tend towards heaven as to our homeland; and, although we cling here in body, yet in mind we ought to be occupied there, in the contemplation of divine things, and always to be carried towards them with the greatest eagerness. And so heavenly things must always be contemplated, so that we understand that they are far superior to all earthly things, and altogether of such a kind that, because of their dignity, they cannot be perceived by earthly sense. Moreover, who would not aspire to good things that remain and are eternal? When most people toil so hard for things that are perishable and fleeting, which cannot be carried from here, just as they cannot be brought here by us, and which for the most part are the cause of our ruin.

units.la: Cæterùm addiscimus hic, pericula & mala quæcunq; ferenda esse in hoc mundo, non quidem propter sese, sed propter aliud; nempe propter Deum, & bona per fidem expectanda, nobisq; à Deo promissa. Ac damnanda prorsus est illa Stoicorum ἀπάθεια. Volunt remouere affectus huiusmodi è natura, qui naturæ sunt ingeniti, & nobis congeniti: cuiusmodi sunt dolere aduersis, &c. Non ita est. Non accersuntur quadam opinione isti affectus (quasi mala per se non essent mala, sed tantùm nostra opinione) verùm naturaliter in hominibus existunt: & mala ferenda, non quia reipsa non sunt mala, sed quia maiora bona patienter ferentibus sunt proposita, cœlestia in quâ & æterna, vti hic videmus. Et hic rursus sese aperit nouum inter fortitudinem Christianam ac Philosophicam discrimen, quod sumitur ex obiecto. Quia Philosophica fortitudo respicit ad temporanea & terrena, vix etiam potens aliquid de futura vita & immortalitate animæ recte iudicare: at fortitudo Christiana respicit in bona cœlestia & æterna, cum Deo, & in Deo accipienda. Et possent hic aliæ quoq; differentiæ inter fortitudinem philosophicam & Christianam explicari, si locus ferret. Nam etiam causis differunt: siquidem vbi fortitudo philosophica versatur circa pericula varijs de caussis ijsque temporaneis obuenientia: fortitudo Christiana circa ea tantùm, quæ obueniunt propter Christum.
units.tr: Furthermore, we learn here that all dangers and evils are to be borne in this world, not indeed for their own sake, but for the sake of something else; namely, for the sake of God, and in expectation of the good things promised to us by God through faith. And that apatheia [ἀπάθεια] of the Stoics is wholly to be condemned. They want to remove such affections from nature, although they are innate in nature and congenital in us: of this kind are grieving at adversities, and so on. It is not so. These affections do not arise from some opinion (as if evils were not evils in themselves, but only by our opinion); rather they exist naturally in men; and evils are to be borne, not because they are not really evils, but because greater goods are set before those who bear them patiently, heavenly and eternal ones, as we see here. And here again there opens up a new difference between Christian and philosophical fortitude, which is drawn from the object. For philosophical fortitude is concerned with temporal and earthly things, and is scarcely able to judge rightly anything about the future life and the immortality of the soul; but Christian fortitude looks to heavenly and eternal good things, to be received with God and in God. And other differences between philosophical and Christian fortitude could also be explained here, if the place allowed. For they differ also in their causes: where philosophical fortitude is concerned with dangers arising for various causes, and those temporary ones, Christian fortitude is concerned only with those that arise on account of Christ.

units.la: Si quis enim patitur vt Christianus, id gloriosum est, inquit Petrus.
units.tr: "If anyone suffers as a Christian, he is to be glorified," says Peter.

units.la: Item fortitudo Christiana à Spiritu sancto est, & Spiritu instruitur.
units.tr: Likewise, Christian courage comes from the Holy Spirit and is taught by the Spirit.

units.la: Philosophica ex carne est, & carnis voluntate, nempe iudicio infirmæ rationis, &c. Sed de his alibi latius.
units.tr: Philosophical courage comes from the flesh and the will of the flesh, that is, from the judgment of weak reason, and so on. But I shall treat these matters at more length elsewhere.

units.la: 1. Petri 2. Ne abiecceritis igitur fiduciam uestram: μὴ ἀποβάλητε οὖν τὴν παῤῥησίαν ὑμῶν, hic significat audaciam liberè & intrepidè confitendi Christum, & non tantùm in discendo libertatem, sed & in confitendo. Qua de re plura à nobis dicta sunt capite tertio, super illis verbis, Cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam tenuerimus. Iterum capite quarto ibi: Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ. Est autem semper opus hac constantia & audacia confitendi fidem, etiam in medijs periculis: quia licet corde creditur ad iustitiam, tamen ore etiam debet fieri confessio ad salutem. Roman. 10. Ideoq; Apostoli Actorum 4. hanc fiduciam liberè intrepidèque confitendi petebant sibi periculosissimo illo tempore dari.
units.tr: 1 Peter 2: "Do not cast away therefore your confidence" [μὴ ἀποβάλητε οὖν τὴν παῤῥησίαν ὑμῶν]. Here it means the boldness of confessing Christ freely and fearlessly, and freedom not only in learning but also in confessing. I have said more about this matter in chapter three, on the words "Whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of hope firm unto the end"; and again in chapter four: "Let us therefore draw near with confidence to the throne of grace." This steadfastness and boldness in confessing the faith is always needed, even in the midst of dangers, for although with the heart one believes unto righteousness, yet confession must also be made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10). Therefore the Apostles in Acts 4 asked that this confidence, to confess freely and fearlessly, be given to them in that most perilous time.

units.la: Et nunc Domine respice in minas eorum, inquiebant, & da seruis tuis, ut cum omni fiducia (μετὰ παῤῥησίας πάσης) loquatur sermonem tuum. Et 1. Thessalon. 2. Ipsi nostis fratres introitum nostrum ad vos, quòd non fuerit inanis, sed quòd antè malis afflicti & contumelijs affecti, quemadmodum scitis, Philippis audacter egerimus (ἐπαῤῥησιασάμεθα) in Deo nostro, ad loquendum apud vos Euangelium Dei in multo certamine. Quæ verba mirè conueniunt præsenti loco. Nam Apostolus ibi ait, se cum multo certamine, & postquam graviter afflictus fuisset, intrepidè se adhuc confessum & docuisse veritatem. Eadem igitur ratione vult Apostolus Hebraeos constantes manere, & ad reddendum suæ fidei rationem, & confitendum Christum, omni tempore paratos.
units.tr: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats," they said, "and grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all boldness" [μετὰ παῤῥησίας πάσης]. And in 1 Thessalonians 2: "You yourselves know, brethren, that our coming to you was not in vain; but though we had suffered before and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we dared [ἐπαῤῥησιασάμεθα] in our God to speak to you the gospel of God amid much conflict." These words agree remarkably with the present place. For the Apostle there says that, after much conflict and after being grievously afflicted, he still boldly confessed and taught the truth. By the same reasoning the Apostle wishes the Hebrews to remain steadfast, and to be ready at all times to give an account of their faith and to confess Christ.

units.la: Qualem se Paulus præbuit, tales sine dubio cupiebat omnes fieri, sicut ipse eam ob causam volebat omnes præire & exemplum fieri. Non quidem quòd intelligendum sit, Apostolum voluisse, quòd eodem modo publicè docerent, uti ipse faciebat: quis hoc sentiat? Et, qua ratione hoc ab eis exegisset? Sed quantum conueniebat vniusque iusque vocationi.
units.tr: Such as Paul showed himself to be, undoubtedly he wished all to become; for this reason he wished all to go before him and become an example. Not, indeed, that we should understand the Apostle to have wanted them to teach publicly in the same way he did. Who would think that? And by what reasoning could he have required this of them? Rather, he wanted each to do so as far as his calling allowed.

units.la: Certum est, quorum non intererat docere ex officio, ab illis non exigebatur tale quid: sed satis erat, ipsos esse paratos ad confitendum, quando tempus foret, & quando rogarentur.
units.tr: It is certain that those whose office did not include teaching were not required to do such a thing. It was enough that they be ready to confess when the time came and when they were asked.

units.la: Quanquam hoc interea illis erat præstandum, ne quid committerent, quo viderentur Christianam religionem improbare, aut ea, quæ huic aduersantur, approbare. Nam qui huiusmodi aliquid facit, aut significationem saltem dat, is reuera Christum negat.
units.tr: Yet in the meantime they had to take care not to do anything by which they might seem to disapprove of the Christian religion, or to approve of those things that oppose it. For whoever does something of this kind, or at least gives a sign of it, in truth denies Christ.

units.la: Abijs verò, quibus incumbit ex officio docere populum, sicut incumbebat Apostolo, requiritur, vt veritatem constanter doceant, intrepidè confiteantur, & non solùm cùm publicè rogantur, sed quotiescunque fert occasio, potissimumque cùm in docendi munere versantur. Sed de his alias. Significanter autem ait: Ne abiecceritis.
units.tr: But those to whom it falls, by office, to teach the people, as it fell to the Apostle, are required to teach the truth constantly and to confess it fearlessly, and not only when they are publicly asked, but whenever occasion offers, and especially when they are engaged in the work of teaching. But of these matters I shall speak elsewhere. He says significantly, "Do not cast away."

units.la: Hoc enim ad laudem calcar quoddam videtur facere, ac significare, quòd hactenus quidem παῤῥησίαν illam retinuerint, hoc tantum superesse, ne posthac eam abijciant: simulque ea voce notat, grauissimum peccarum fore, si velint deficere.
units.tr: For this seems to act as a kind of spur to praise, and to signify that, up to now, they have indeed kept that boldness [παῤῥησίαν], and that only this remains: that they not cast it away from now on. At the same time by that word he marks that it would be a most grievous sin if they were to fall away.

units.la: Nam παῤῥησία illa erat diuinitus collata: neque enim potest nisi à Deo contingere, sicut liquet ex oratione Apostolorum Actorum quarto.
units.tr: For that boldness was bestowed by God; indeed it can come only from God, as is clear from the prayer of the Apostles in Acts 4.

units.la: Iam si illam abiecissent, nonne hoc fuisset dona Dei & bonitatem eius contemnere? Discimus ergo, quibus non datur παῤῥησία, orandum esse assiduè, vt Deus ipsis largiatur: Vbi autem obtigerit, constanter enitendum, vt eam retineant, & nequaquam vilipendant. Pusillanimitatem quorundam & metum quidam mirantur, & valde damnant: certè si illi antea habuerint παῤῥησίαν, & abiecerint, merito damnantur: at si semper fuerunt infirmi, & nunquam magno animo præditi, magis miseratione digni sunt, quàm damnatione.
units.tr: Now if they had cast it away, would this not have been to despise the gifts of God and his goodness? We learn, therefore, that those to whom boldness is not given must pray constantly that God would bestow it on them; and where it has been granted, they must strive steadfastly to keep it and by no means despise it. Some marvel at the timidity and fear of certain people and condemn them strongly. Certainly, if they had possessed boldness earlier and cast it away, they are rightly condemned; but if they have always been weak and never endowed with a great spirit, they are more worthy of pity than of condemnation.

units.la: Qua magnam habet præmij retributionem.
units.tr: Which has a great reward in store.

units.la: Adduntur quædam rationes suasoriæ, quibus piorum animi ad constantiam in fide excitentur: è quibus prima hæc est à certa spe certitudine & magnitudine præmij. Animus hominis ad quascunq; res spe præmij accenditur: quamobrem Deus etiam promissionesmaximarum rerum credentibus semper proposuit. Si tanta esset nostra perfectio, quanta esse deberet, nihil opus foret, proponi præmia, sed propter solum Deum, & Dei amore quàmlibet arduas res adiremus, & subiremus: Vnus Deus esset nobis omnia, idem qui dat vires & facultatem adeundi pericula, idem esset causa nos mouens, idem solus obiectum, idem solus præmium, præ quo omnia alia negligerentur: sicut reuera omnia bona in ipso solo sunt, & ipse solus est omne bonum, atque qui eum habet, habet omnia: sed propter nostram imbecillitatem, qua primum ipsi in nobis subinde fluctuamus: deinde, quia crebris obruimur tentationibus, partim per blanditias, partim per minas, quæ nos à scopo nostro abducunt; debemus erigi quibusdam promissionibus: sibus: sicut pueris, quibus prima elementa discenda proponuntur, vires dant cruula blanst)da, ut in quit ille.
units.tr: Some persuasive reasons are added, by which the minds of the godly may be roused to constancy in the faith. The first of these is the certain hope, the certainty and greatness, of the reward. The human mind is kindled by the hope of reward for whatever undertaking; for this reason God has always set before believers the promises of the greatest things. If our perfection were as great as it ought to be, there would be no need for rewards to be set before us; but for the sake of God alone, and out of love for God, we would undertake and endure whatever difficult things. God alone would be all things to us: the same one who gives the strength and the ability to face dangers, the same would be the moving cause, the same alone the object, the same alone the reward, before which all other things would be disregarded. Indeed, all good things are in him alone, and he alone is every good, and whoever has him has all things. But on account of our weakness, by which we first waver again and again in ourselves, and then because we are overwhelmed by frequent temptations, partly through flatteries and partly through threats, which lead us away from our goal, we ought to be lifted up by certain promises, just as boys, to whom the first rudiments are set to be learned, are given sweet biscuits, as that writer says.

units.la: Ergo propter nostram infirmitatem praemia sunt propositá. Ac Deus illis vult testa-tam facere nobis suam bonitatem, vt certò audeamus ab illo omnia bona semper expe-ctare.
units.tr: Therefore, because of our weakness, rewards have been set before us. God wishes to assure us of his goodness through them, so that we may boldly expect from him all good things at all times.

units.la: Caeterùm alia ratione adhuc excitatur Christianus quàm gentilis. Gentilis enim dire-ctè respicit in praemia, & propter ea ipsa mouetur impelliturque: aut certè, si quo altius progreditur gentilis, dicet, se bene agere, non propter praemium, sed propter ipsam ve-ritatem, illud sibi inculcans: Ipsa sibi merces virtus pulcherrima: Quod sanè magnum est & praeclarum, neque altius licet conscendere. At verò Christianus multo sublimius & excelsius tendit: non respicit immediatè in praemia: neq; haec habet pro causa principali, quae ipsum moueat, neq; etiam respicit tantum ad ipsam virtutem, quatenus praeclara quaedam res est in sese: sed respicit immediatè in ipsum Deum, quiipse est opulentissimum praemium, ditissima merces, virtutis omnis autor & largitor, & omni virtute longè excellentior. Quanto igitur excellentior est Deus quibuscunq; praemijs, vel quacunque virtute, tanto etiam excellentius agit Christianus, quàm Gentilis. Sed videamus etiam praemiorum diuersitatem, & inueniemus hac in parte magnam Christianarum virtutum praé virtutibus Philosophicis excellentiam. Gentilis agit fortiter & constanter spe praemij huiuscemodi, nempe (vt omittam alias rationes, & referam tantùm praecipuas:) quòd proderit suis vel reipublicae: deinde, quòd propter benefacta celebrabitur toti posteritati: vix quicquam altius ille apprehendit, quàm huiusmodi mercedem temporalem & vnà cum hominibus fluxam & perituram.
units.tr: Besides, the Christian is roused by a different reason from the pagan. For the pagan looks directly to rewards, and is moved and driven by them; or certainly, if a pagan advances further, he will say that he acts well not for the sake of reward but for the sake of truth itself, impressing this upon himself: "Virtue itself is its own most beautiful reward." This is surely great and admirable, and one cannot climb higher. But the Christian strives much higher and more sublimely: he does not look immediately to rewards, nor does he hold these as the principal cause that moves him; nor does he look only to virtue itself, insofar as it is some excellent thing in itself. Rather, he looks immediately to God himself, who is the most abundant reward, the richest recompense, the author and giver of all virtue, and far more excellent than every virtue. Therefore, as God is more excellent than any rewards or any virtue whatever, so the Christian acts more excellently than the pagan. But let us also look at the diversity of the rewards, and we shall find in this respect the great excellence of the Christian virtues above the philosophical virtues. The pagan acts bravely and constantly from hope of a reward of this kind, namely (to omit other reasons and mention only the chief ones): that it will benefit his own people or the commonwealth; and then, that on account of his good deeds he will be celebrated by all posterity. Scarcely anything higher does he grasp than such a temporal reward, fleeting and perishing together with men.

units.la: At Christianus respicit ad praemia spiritualia, coelestia & aeterna, sicut suprà dictum est. Haec illi sunt praecipua, & omnia in solo Deo ac fruitione Dei collocata, sicut iam paulò ante diximus.
units.tr: But the Christian looks to spiritual rewards, heavenly and eternal, as was said above. These are his chief rewards, and all are placed in God alone and in the enjoyment of God, as we said a little while ago.

units.la: Verùm quidem est, etiam temporalia praemia promittit Deus etiam in hac vita concedenda, sed, vt diximus, propter crassos & carnales homines, qui possunt ad spiritualia aspirare. Sed spirituales homines, quales nos potissimum pro veris Christianis agnoscimus, non nisi ad coelestia tendunt, & etiam cum carne in terris haerent, animo in coelis versantur. Colossens. 3. Horum igitur proprium, ad spiritualia & coelestia tantum praemia aspirare. Quòd si iam quis roget, qualia praemia spiritualia & coelestia sint propositá illis, qui alacriter & intrepidè Christum confitentur, habemus diserte à Christo expressum Matthaei quinto, Beati estis, cùm insectati vos fuerint homines, & dixerint omne malum aduersùm vos mentientes propter me: Gaudete & exultate, quoniam merces vestra multa est in coelis. Marci octauo: Quisquis perdiderit animam suam mea causa, & Euangelij, hic seruabit eam. Item, Matth. 11. Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor ego eum coram patre meo. 1. Petri 4. Si probris afficimini in nomine Christi, beati estis, quoniam gloria & spiritus Dei super vos requiescit. Alia in eandem sententiam passim occurrunt, quae non opus est omnia nunc congeramus.
units.tr: It is true that God also promises temporal rewards, to be granted even in this life; but, as we have said, these are for gross and carnal men, who can aspire only to spiritual things. But spiritual men, such as we chiefly acknowledge as true Christians, strive only for heavenly things; and even though they cling to the flesh on earth, in spirit they dwell in heaven (Col. 3). It is therefore the mark of these to aspire only to spiritual and heavenly rewards. But if anyone should ask what spiritual and heavenly rewards are set before those who eagerly and fearlessly confess Christ, we have it expressly stated by Christ in Matthew 5: "Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." Mark 8: "Whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it." Likewise Matthew 10: "Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him before my Father." 1 Peter 4: "If you are reproached for the name of Christ, you are blessed, for the glory and the Spirit of God rests upon you." Other passages to the same effect occur everywhere, which there is no need to gather all together now.

units.la: Nam patientia vobis est opus, vt, vbi voluntatem Dei peregeritis, reportetis promissionem.
units.tr: For you need patience, so that when you have done the will of God, you may receive the promise.

units.la: Alia ratio suasoria, ab eo, quòd praemia coelestia non nisi per patientiam & longanimitatem possint accipi.
units.tr: A second persuasive argument: heavenly rewards can be received only through patience and longsuffering.

units.la: Ita comparatum est diuina ordinatione & prouidentia, non molliter & suauiter hic viuentibus, sed aduersa tolerantibus propter Christum: deinde non statim, sed longanimiter expectantibus bona spiritualia promissa obueniunt.
units.tr: By divine ordering and providence it has been so arranged that spiritual goods are not given at once, nor to those who live here softly and pleasantly, but to those who endure adversity for Christ's sake and wait patiently for the promised goods.

units.la: Sic verò vocabulum ὑπομονὴ non simpliciter significat patientiam, qua perferimus aduersa, sed patientem expectationem, qua praemium promissum expectamus.
units.tr: The word ὑπομονή [hypomonē] does not simply mean the patience by which we bear adversity, but the patient expectation by which we wait for the promised reward.

units.la: Eadem significatione Lucae 21. Christus postquàm praedixisset discipulis, quòd multa passuri essent propter Euangelion, ἐν τῇ ὑπομονῇ ὑμῶν, in patientia vestra possidete animas vestras.
units.tr: With the same meaning, in Luke 21, after Christ had told his disciples that they would suffer much for the gospel, he said: "In your patience possess your souls" [ἐν τῇ ὑπομονῇ ὑμῶν].

units.la: Et necessaria est haec ὑπομονὴ, vt perficiatur fortitudo Christiana. Nisi enim duret fortitudo ad finem vsque, nequaquàm pro fortitudine agnoscetur. Vnde Iacob. 1. ἀ δὲ ἔπιστον ὑπομονὴ, patientia, inquit, opus perfectum habeat, vt sitis perfecti & integri, nullaque in parte diminuti. Mitthaei 24. Qui perseuerauerit vsque in finem, hic saluus erit. Et propteres Prouerb. 16. Melior est patiens viro forti.
units.tr: This patience is also necessary if Christian fortitude is to be made complete. For unless fortitude endures to the end, it will by no means be recognised as fortitude. Hence James 1: "But let patience have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and entire, lacking in nothing" [ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ ἔργον τέλειον ἐχέτω]. Matthew 24: "He who endures to the end will be saved." And so Proverbs 16: "The patient man is better than the strong man."

units.la: Igitur opus est longanimitate, vt accipiamus promissionem. Quamobrem etiam multis aliis locis ad patienter ferendum, & ad expectandum longanimiter misericordiam Dei hortatur.
units.tr: Therefore we need longsuffering in order to receive the promise. For this reason, in many other places too, he urges us to bear troubles patiently and to wait longsuffering for the mercy of God.

units.la: Porrò cùm addit, ut, ubi uoluntatem Dei peregeritis: Latet ibi aliud argumentum suasorium à necessitate obediendi diuinæ voluntati. Significat enim, hanc esse diuinam voluntatem, vt & affligantur ad tempus, & longanimiter expectent bona cœlestia promissa. Est autem hæc ratio non tantùm hortatoria, verùmetiàm consolatoria: Hortatoria quidem, quòd pij, quando audiunt, se pati ex voluntate Dei, qui immittit persecutiones, vt suos probet, item vt mirabiliter eos eripiendo exerat suam potentiam, vt ex constantia sanctorum animentur & confirmentur cæteri fratres infirmiores: item expectent, se exemplo aliorum è periculis liberandos: denique propter multas alias vtiles causas, licet nobis non satis cognitas, atque ita bona voluntate Dei omnia geri, excitentur ad se submittendum alacriter diuinæ voluntati, cui resistere nefas est. Propterea Paulus, cùm iam illi prædictum esset Cæsareæ ab Agabo, quòd Hierosolymis foret alligandus & tradendus gentibus, respondit, se paratum etiam mori, & fratres ab ipso victi dixerunt hoc tantùm, Domini voluntas fiat. Et quo animo dicemus quotidie, Fiat voluntas tua, si tamen pati pro nomine eius detrectamus? Scientes igitur, hanc esse voluntatem Domini, vt omnes, qui piè volunt viuere, persecutionem patiantur, animo fortissimus, & pericula quæcunque magno animo adeamus. Sed & cùm scimus, bona voluntate Dei nos affligi, consolationis materiam inde arripiamus, cogitemusque, malum aut noxium esse non posse, quod Deus propter bonum aliquod immittit. Quòd si hanc particulam satis possemus in nostris aduersitatibus expendere, reuera omnia propter Dei voluntatem forent leuiora: &, si inæquanimiter ferendo expectandoque voluntas Dei perficitur, obedientiaque præstatur, & obedientia Deo acceptior est, quàm victimæ: certè nihil maius Deoque acceptius per nos præstari potest, quàm quòd eo modo voluntati ipsius obtemperamus, & omnia boni consulimus.
units.tr: Moreover, when he adds "that when you have done the will of God", there lies hidden another persuasive argument, drawn from the necessity of obeying the divine will. For it signifies that this is the will of God: that they be afflicted for a time, and patiently await the heavenly goods promised. This argument is not only exhortatory but also consolatory. It is exhortatory because the godly, when they hear that they suffer by the will of God, who sends persecutions to prove his own, and also so that by wondrously delivering them he may display his power, and so that the weaker brethren may be encouraged and strengthened by the constancy of the saints, and so that they may expect to be delivered from dangers as others have been; and finally, for many other useful reasons, though not well known to us, and so that all things are done by the good will of God, they are roused to submit cheerfully to the divine will, to which it is wrong to resist. Therefore Paul, when Agabus had already foretold at Caesarea that he would be bound at Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles, replied that he was ready even to die; and the brethren, overcome by him, said only, "The will of the Lord be done." And with what spirit shall we say every day, "Your will be done", if we refuse to suffer for his name? Knowing therefore that it is the will of the Lord that all who wish to live godly suffer persecution, let us be most brave in spirit and face whatever dangers with a great mind. But also, since we know that we are afflicted by the good will of God, let us take from this material for consolation, and reflect that what God sends for some good cannot be evil or harmful. If we could weigh this point well in our adversities, truly all things would be lighter because of God's will; and if, by bearing and waiting with an even mind, the will of God is accomplished and obedience is rendered, and obedience is more acceptable to God than sacrifice, then certainly nothing greater or more acceptable to God can be offered by us than that in this way we obey his will and take everything in good part.

units.la: Sed & hoc notandum est, cùm dicitur, reportetis promissionem, hic explicari quadam correctionis forma, quod de præmio prius dictum est,
units.tr: But this too is to be noted: when it says "that you may receive the promise", here, by a certain form of correction, what was said earlier about the reward is explained.

units.la: Nam postulasset quodammodò ratio sententiæ dici, ut reportetis præmium: sed quia vocabulum præmij quodammodò abusiuè vsurpatur in Scriptura, sicut vocabulum mercedis vel meriti, propter rudicatem videlicet captus nostri: & quia opus est, nos vt pueros præmiolis inuitari, ideo maluit hoc secundo loco dicere promissionem, quæ vox accommodatior est ad significandum gratuitam beneficiorum Dei collationem. Præmium enim, sicut & merces, quodammodò præsupponit aliquid fieri per eum, qui id accipiet, & sic veluti debitum reddi: quod sanè de beneficijs spiritualibus Dei dici non potest.
units.tr: For the logic of the sentence would seem to require "that you may receive the reward"; but since the word reward is used somewhat loosely in Scripture, as are the words wage and merit, on account of the crudeness of our understanding, and since we need to be enticed like children with small prizes, he preferred to say "promise" in the second place, a word better suited to signify the free bestowal of God's benefits. For reward, like wage, presupposes in some sense that something is done by the one who receives it, and so is paid as if it were owed; and this certainly cannot be said of God's spiritual benefits.

units.la: Promissio autem magis significat gratuitum munus ob solam promissionem collatum, quodque promittens magis sua causa, vt videlicet fidem suam liberet, quàm alterius personæ causa, confert. Quare non sine causa secundo loco promissionis nomen positum exisitimabimus.
units.tr: A promise, however, signifies more a free gift bestowed on the strength of the promise alone, and one that the promiser gives more for his own sake, namely to keep his faith, than for the sake of the other person. So we shall not think it without reason that the word promise is placed in the second position.

units.la: Adhuc enim perpusillum temporis, & qui venturus est, veniet, & non tardabit.
units.tr: For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come, and will not delay.

units.la: Alia ratio ab imminente secundo aduentu Domini, qui nos eripiet; siue à breuitate temporis, quo hic pati debemus. Non dissimili modo in præcedenti conclusione adiecit etiam rationem suasoriam, vt excitaret ad amplectendam agnitionem pontificatus Christi, & ad præstanda officia charitatis, dicendo: Idq; eò magis, quòd uidetis appropinquantem diem: Alij autem volunt, hæc ipsa verba ex Abac. 2. desumpta, apud quem ita legitur iuxta hebraicam veritatem. Est adhuc uisio ad certum tempus, quæ disserit (de his, quæ) ad finem sunt, & non mentietur: si moram fecerit, expecta illam, quoniam veniens veniet, & non tardabit: Ecce anima illius, qui in semetipso non est rectus, putat, se satis munitam esse, cum interim iustus in sua fide uiuat. Hæc ibi. Voluntigitur, hæc accipi tanquàm verba Abacuc. Alij propter exiguam vocum varietatem ex Aggæi secundo desumpta volunt, apud quem sic quoq; Spiritus Domini loquitur: Sic dixit Dominus exercituum: adhuc unum modicum est, & ego commouebo cælum & terram, mare & aridam. Et commouebo omnes gentes, venientq; (cū eo, quod) desiderabile est cunctis gentibus, & implebo domum istam gloria.
units.tr: Another argument is drawn from the imminent second coming of the Lord, who will deliver us, or from the shortness of the time we have to suffer here. In a not dissimilar way, in the preceding conclusion he also added a persuasive reason, to stir us to embrace the acknowledgement of Christ's priesthood and to perform the duties of love, saying: "and all the more because you see the day drawing near." Others, however, want these very words to be taken from Habakkuk 2, where, according to the Hebrew truth, it is read thus: "There is still a vision for an appointed time, which speaks of the things that are to the end, and it will not lie; if it delays, wait for it, for it will surely come and will not tarry. Behold, the soul of him who is not upright in himself thinks itself sufficiently fortified, but the righteous lives by his faith." Thus far there. Some therefore wish these words to be taken as the words of Habakkuk. Others, because of the slight variation in wording, want them taken from Haggai 2, where the Spirit of the Lord also speaks thus: "Thus says the Lord of hosts: yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land. And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory."

units.la: Satius est accipiamus, vt ipsius Pauli verba, quando is aliàs quoq; solet talibus rationibus in suadendo vti: & nimiùm etiam distant in prophetia Abacuc, à testimonio, quod mox subijcitur: In Aggæo verò longè aliud agitur, nempe de aduentu Christi in carnem. Præterea, non ijsdem verbis apud Prophetas expressa sunt, quibus hic expressa cernimus. Pauli igitur verba esse statuamus, quibus mox subijcitur noua propositio, prophetæ Abacuc verbis expressa. Est autem hæc ratio mitè consolatoria, & ad suadendam patientiam periculorum efficax. Si enim cogitemus, non diu ferendas esse molestias, vniuersam hanc vitam esse veluti momentum adeoque punctulum temporis ad æternam illam, quæ post hanc sequitur, quæ certe exiguæ nobis videbuntur, quàmtis diuturnæ molestiæ. Aegrotus lubenter permittit medicum exiguo tempore secantem, quia sperat, se post ad multum tempus bene habiturum.
units.tr: It is better to take them as Paul's own words, since he is accustomed to use such arguments in persuading elsewhere as well. Moreover, the passages in question are too far apart: in the prophecy of Habakkuk the words are too remote from the testimony that is immediately subjoined, while in Haggai something quite different is treated, namely the coming of Christ in the flesh. Besides, they are not expressed among the Prophets in the same words in which we see them expressed here. Let us therefore hold them to be Paul's words, after which a new proposition is immediately added, expressed in the words of the prophet Habakkuk. This argument is gently consolatory and effective in urging patience in dangers. For if we reflect that the troubles are not to be borne for long, and that this whole life is like a moment, indeed a tiny point of time, compared with that eternity which follows it, then these troubles, however long they last, will surely seem small to us. A sick man willingly allows the doctor to cut him for a short time, because he hopes that afterwards he will be well for a long time.

units.la: Et, ut turpissimum foret, si athleta, posteaquàm iam multòs multis certaminibus vicisset, nihilque restaret, quàm breue tempus, quo adueniret agonothetes largiturus præmia, tamen nollet paululum temporis adhuc perferre sitim & æstu pulueris: ita turpissimum, si credentes, postquam multa iam perpessi essent aduersa, & superassent omnia, grauarentur adhuc aliquanto tempore affligi, donec aduenirét tempus accipiendæ apud Christū gloriæ.
units.tr: And just as it would be most shameful for an athlete, who had already conquered many opponents in many contests, and had only a short time left until the president of the games came to award the prizes, to be unwilling to endure a little longer the thirst and the heat of the dust; so it is most shameful for believers, who have already suffered many adversities and overcome them all, to grow weary of being afflicted for some further time, until the time comes to receive glory with Christ.

units.la: Eleganter autem expressit Apostolus temporis breuitatem, dicens: ἔτι γὰρ μικρὸν ὅσον, ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἥξει. Vbi conduplicatio illa emphasin habet, ad significandum admodum breue tempus, iuxta hebraismum, quo solent geminationes & accelerationem, & certitudinem, vehementiamque significare: ut Hieremiæ 24. Ficus bonas bonas, & ficus malas malas. Item Esaiæ decimo, Quoniam adhuc parum, plus quam parum furor & indignatio mea finietur. 1. Regum 2. Quacunque die egressus fueris, & transieris torrentem Cidron, sciens scias, quòd morte morieris.
units.tr: The Apostle expressed the brevity of time elegantly, saying: "For yet a very little while, he who comes will come" [ἔτι γὰρ μικρὸν ὅσον, ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἥξει]. Here the doubling carries emphasis, signifying a very brief time, according to the Hebrew idiom, by which repetitions commonly signify speed, certainty and vehemence: as in Jeremiah 24, "good figs, very good, and bad figs, very bad." Likewise Isaiah 10: "For yet a little, a very little, my wrath and indignation will be finished." 1 Kings 2: "On whatever day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall surely die."

units.la: Sunt autem passim alij loci in Scripturis, quibus pij hac ratione consolationem accipiunt, quòd videlicet non diu durabit afflictio. Esaiæ 54. Ad punctum in modico dereliqui te, et in miserationibus magnis congregabo te, in momento indignationis parum per abscondi faciem à te, & misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui. 2. Corinth. 2. Momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostræ mirè supra modum æternæ gloriæ pondus parit nobis, dum non spectamus ea quæ videntur, sed ea quæ non videntur.
units.tr: There are also many other passages in the Scriptures by which the godly receive comfort in this way, namely that the affliction will not last long. Isaiah 54: "For a little moment I have forsaken you, but with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of wrath I hid my face from you for a little while, but with everlasting kindness I will have mercy on you." 2 Corinthians 2: "Our light affliction, which is but for a moment, works for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen."

units.la: Nam quæ videntur, temporaria sunt, at quæ non videntur, æterna. Iacobi vltimo, Patientes estote & vos, & confirmate corda vestra, quoniam aduentus Domini appropinquat. Ibidem: Ecce iudex ante ianuam assistit. 1. Petri 1. Custodimini per fidem ad salutem quæ in hoc parata est, ut patefiat in tempore supremo, in quo exultatis nunc ad breue tempus afflicti variis experimentis.
units.tr: For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal. James, last chapter: "Be patient, you also, and establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand." In the same place: "Behold, the judge stands before the door." 1 Peter 1: "You are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, ready to be revealed in the last time, in which you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials."

units.la: Cæterùm cùm dominus ita venturus citò & expectandus describitur, solet id etiam duplici aduentu explicari, altero particulari, seu speculi, quo unumquemque visitat, quando è mundo & miseriarum valle eripit: altero generali, quando venturus est ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos.
units.tr: Moreover, when the Lord is described as coming soon and to be awaited, this is usually explained as a twofold coming: one particular, or private, by which he visits each person when he snatches them out of the world and the valley of miseries; the other general, when he will come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Vterque verò aduentus omni tempore est expectandus, & pijs valde optabilis, propter immarcessibilem & æternam coronam, quam tum sunt accepturi.
units.tr: Yet both comings are to be expected at all times, and are greatly desired by the godly, on account of the unfading and eternal crown which they will then receive.

units.la: Repetenda autem hoc loco sunt capita doctrinæ in toto exordio traditæ, tractandusque locus de discrimine inter fortitudinem Christianam & philosophicam.
units.tr: The heads of doctrine delivered in the whole introduction must be repeated at this point, and the question must be treated of the difference between Christian and philosophical fortitude.

units.la: PROPOSITIO.
units.tr: PROPOSITION.

units.la: Iustus autem ex fide viuet, & si se subduxerit, non probabitur anima mea. At nos non sumus, qui subducamus nos in perditionem, sed ad fidem pertinemus in acquisitionem animæ.
units.tr: "But the just shall live by faith; and if he draws back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. But we are not of those who draw back to perdition, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul."

units.la: Hactenus exordium costans exhortatione, qua hebræos excitauit, ut in doctrina & confessione fidei constātes permaneant. Iam adijcit nonnulla, quæ dignitatem fidei, aciustificatione per eam plenius docent: quæ omnia ad confirmandos animos mirè conducunt.
units.tr: Up to this point the introduction has consisted of an exhortation by which he stirred up the Hebrews to remain steadfast in the doctrine and confession of faith. Now he adds some points which teach more fully the dignity of faith and justification through it, all of which greatly help to strengthen the minds of his readers.

units.la: Proinde hæc est huius partis propositio, iustificari hominem ex fide, expressa verbis prophetæ Abacuc. Etsi verò hæc ita proposita sint, ut in diuulsè cohærere cum præcedentibus videantur, maximèque quia apud prophetam quædam in eandem sententiam, & pene ad verbum reddita præeunt: nos tamen sic accipimus, ut reuera ab Apostolo ipso eum in modum distincta: quandoquidem & docendi caussa ita fieri multo est commodissimū, & series sermonis, ut separentur, videtur postulare.
units.tr: Accordingly, this is the proposition of this part: that a man is justified by faith, expressed in the words of the prophet Habakkuk. Although these words are set forth in such a way that they seem to be loosely connected with what precedes, and especially since in the prophet certain statements to the same effect, almost word for word, go before, nevertheless we take them as indeed distinguished in this way by the Apostle himself, since both for the sake of teaching it is much more convenient to do so, and the sequence of the discourse seems to require that they be separated.

units.la: Nam apostolum hic aggredi doctrinam de iustificatione, siue, ut nunc loquitur de testimonio accipiendo apud Deum per fidem, quiuis facilè iudicat.
units.tr: For that the Apostle here takes up the doctrine of justification, or, as he now speaks of it, of receiving the testimony before God through faith, anyone can easily judge.

units.la: Atque eo quoque iustius nos ita disiungimus, propositionemque eius doctrinæ, quæ sequitur, constituimus, quod eodem sensu, ad asserendum videlicet, Homines iustificari fide. Apostolus hoc testimonium in propositione epistolæ ad Romanos vsurparit. Ibi enim cum suis verbis dixisset, per euangelium patefieri iustitiam ex fide in fidem, protinus sententiam stabilire cupiens attexuit præsens testimonium.
units.tr: And we separate them all the more justly in this way, and set up the proposition of the doctrine that follows, because it is used by him in the same sense, namely to assert that men are justified by faith. The Apostle used this testimony in the proposition of his Epistle to the Romans. For there, after saying in his own words that righteousness is revealed through the gospel from faith to faith, eager to establish the point at once, he added the present testimony.

units.la: Etrursus Galat. 3. simili in caussa id producit, dicens, Quod in lege nullus iustificeetur apud Deum, palàm est: siquidem iustus ex fide sua uiuet. Et hoc ipsum valde confirmat me, ut hanc epistolam pro Paulina agnoscam. Habemus ergo hic propositionem eorum, quæ mox plenius confirmantur. Atque hæc breuis tractatio de iustificatione per fidem valde oportunè adhibetur apud eos, qui in ea doctrina satis quidem fœliciter erant instituti, sed debebant in ea aliquantum confirmari.
units.tr: Again, in Galatians 3 he produces it in a similar case, saying, "That no one is justified before God by the law is evident, for 'the just shall live by faith.'" And this very thing greatly confirms me in acknowledging this Epistle as Pauline. Here, then, we have the proposition of those things which are soon more fully confirmed. And this brief treatment of justification by faith is very fittingly applied to those who had been fairly well instructed in that doctrine, but who needed to be confirmed in it somewhat further.

units.la: Dum autem proponuntur fructus fidei, quos patres ex fide acceperunt, habebunt hic exempla, in quæ si toto animo intueantur, sentient, ad constantiam in fide se incitatos.
units.tr: While the fruits of faith which the fathers received through faith are set forth, they will have here examples, and if they look upon them with their whole mind, they will feel themselves urged on to constancy in the faith.

units.la: Superest, ut ostendamus, hoc testimonium appositè citari, & de iustificatione per fidem, prout hic de ea disputatur, rectissimè intelligi. Cum in Iudæa passim omnis generis vitia intr'uiffent, atque impij pios indignissimè opprimerent, ut hi se plane à Deo neglectos arbitrarentur: ad consolationem piorum vaticinatus est propheta Abacuc, breui fore turum, ut impiorum tyrannis per Babylonios (quorum monarchia tunc inclaruit) puniretur: captiuos enim omnes Israelitas in Babyloniam abducendos. Sed vbi victores postea insolentiores fierent, iterum futurum, ut populus Israeliticus restituatur, ac de Babylonico tyranno vicissim graues sumantur poenæ. Hæc totius prophetiæ Abacuc summa est. Quo autem loco posterius iflud initio capitis secundi prædicit, sic scribitur:
units.tr: It remains for us to show that this testimony is aptly cited, and that it is most rightly understood concerning justification by faith, as it is discussed here. When every kind of vice had crept into Judea, and the wicked were oppressing the godly most unworthily, so that these latter thought they were plainly neglected by God, the prophet Habakkuk prophesied, for the comfort of the godly, that before long the tyranny of the wicked would be punished by the Babylonians, whose monarchy was then famous; for all the Israelites were to be led away captive into Babylon. But when the victors afterwards became more insolent, it would again come about that the Israelite people would be restored, and in turn severe punishments would be exacted from the Babylonian tyrant. This is the sum of the whole prophecy of Habakkuk. The passage in which the latter point is foretold at the beginning of the second chapter is written thus:

units.la: Respondit Dominus mihi, & ait: Scribe visionem, & explica eam in tabulis, ut percurrat, qui legerit eam. Quia est adhuc visio ad certum tempus, quæ disserit (de his, quæ) ad finem sunt, & non mentietur. Si moram fecerit, expecta illam, quoniam veniens veniet, & non tardabit. Ecce anima illius, qui in semetipso non est rectus, putat se satis munitam esse, cum interim iustus in sua fide viuat. Et utique propter viuum præuaricatur, & fit stupidus, & non firmat sedem, sed dilatauit quasi infernus animam suam, similisq; est morti, & saturari nequit.
units.tr: The Lord answered me and said: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, so that he who reads it may run. For the vision is yet for an appointed time, and it speaks of (those things which are) toward the end, and it will not lie. If it tarries, wait for it, for it will surely come, and will not delay. Behold, the soul of him who is not upright in himself thinks itself well fortified, but the just shall live by his faith. And indeed, because of wine he transgresses, and becomes proud, and does not stay at home, but enlarges his desire like hell, and is like death, and cannot be satisfied.

units.la: His verbis aperte agit de restitutione populi Iudaici, nec non tyranni Chaldæi punitione, atque apta antithesi: Ecce, inquit, anima illius, qui in semetipso non est rectus, putat se satis munitam: cum interim iustus in fide sua viuat.
units.tr: In these words he plainly speaks of the restoration of the Jewish people, and also of the punishment of the Chaldean tyrant, and with a fitting antithesis: "Behold," he says, "the soul of him who is not upright in himself thinks itself well fortified; but the just shall live by his faith."

units.la: Quæ verba sic posita sunt pro generali sententia, ad significandum impios & incredulos Deo displicere: credentes vero iustos esse ac Deo acceptos: ut ex hoc vniuersali colligatur, etiam pios Israeliticos liberandos, & impios Chaldæos similiter puniendos.
units.tr: These words are put forward as a general statement, to signify that the wicked and unbelieving displease God, while believers are just and acceptable to God, so that from this universal truth it is inferred that the godly Israelites too are to be delivered, and the wicked Chaldeans likewise to be punished.

units.la: Cùm ergo ibi generalis sit sententia, qua pios dicit victuros fide, rectissimè Apostolus præsenti instituto, ubi agere decreuit de iustificatione per fidem, ea verba accommodat.
units.tr: Since, then, there the statement is a general one, by which he says that the godly shall live by faith, the Apostle very rightly applies those words to his present purpose, where he has decided to treat of justification by faith.

units.la: Sed neque negari potest, ibi vaticinium haberi de expectando Mesia vero liberatore patribus promisso: quemadmodum rectè interpretatur Hieronymus.
units.tr: But it cannot be denied either that there is a prophecy there concerning the expectation of the true Messiah, the deliverer promised to the fathers, as Jerome rightly interprets.

units.la: Quare perapte locus ille de salute obtinenda per fidem in Christum exponitur, conuenit; tempori euangelico, quo remissio peccatorum per fidem debet apprehendi, sicut multis aliis prophetarum testimonijs id demonstratur. Adhæc etiamsi ibi vaticinium contineretur de liberatione & salute certo quodam tempore exhibenda, tamen nota est regula in omnibus promissionibus etiam de rebus temporalibus & externis, semper respicere solitos patres ad principalem promissionem primis parentibus & Abrahamo factam de misericordia & salute expectanda, propter semen benedictum, id est, Messiam: quæ promissio altissimè semper insidebat omnium piorum pectoribus, & quasi parens ac fons reliquarum promissionum censebatur. Quare adhuc commodè ad causam de salute per Christum, prophetæ verbum accommodatur.
units.tr: Hence that passage fits very aptly as an exposition of salvation to be obtained by faith in Christ, in the gospel time, when the forgiveness of sins ought to be laid hold of by faith, as is shown by many other testimonies of the prophets. Besides, even if a prophecy of deliverance and salvation to be given at a certain time were contained there, it is nonetheless a known rule that in all promises, even those concerning temporal and external things, the fathers always looked back to the principal promise made to our first parents and to Abraham, of mercy and salvation to be expected on account of the blessed Seed, that is, the Messiah. This promise always sat most deeply in the hearts of all the godly, and was regarded as, as it were, the parent and fountain of the other promises. Therefore the word of the prophet is still fittingly applied to the cause of salvation through Christ.

units.la: Interea statuendum est, Apostolum non nisi Spiritus Sancti præceptoris instinctu locutum, ideoque non potuisse nisi recto sensu citare hoc testimonium, cùm tali præceptori erratum, vel Scripturæ ineptam interpretationem impingere nefas sit.
units.tr: Meanwhile it must be established that the Apostle spoke only under the impulse of the Holy Spirit, his teacher, and therefore could not have cited this testimony except in its right sense, since it is wicked to charge such a teacher with error or with an inept interpretation of Scripture.

units.la: Postremò, cùm dicitur, iustum fide sua victurum, clara est sententia, fidem in Deum esse veluti medium, per quod quis iustus fit, ac Deo acceptus, & vitam spiritualem accipit: atque ita quidem fide id fieri, ut nequaquàm simile contingat, quàmlibet diligenti externa obseruatione legis: sicut Apostolus quoque ad Galatas 3. apertè ratiocinatur, dicens: Quòd in lege nullus iustificetur apud Deum, palàm est: Siquidem iustus ex fide sua viuet.
units.tr: Finally, when it is said that the just shall live by his faith, the statement is clear: faith in God is as it were the means by which someone becomes just and acceptable to God, and receives spiritual life; and this comes about by faith in such a way that nothing similar happens through however diligent an outward observance of the law, as the Apostle also plainly reasons in Galatians 3, saying: "That no one is justified before God by the law is evident, for 'the just shall live by faith.'"

units.la: Igitur hoc testimonium prophetæ Abacuc præsenti instituto, quo de iustificatione per fidem agitur, rectè accommodatur: neque alio sensu est præsenti loco vsurpatum, quàm in epistola ad Romanos vel Galatas.
units.tr: This testimony of the prophet Habakkuk is therefore rightly applied to the present subject, which treats of justification through faith. It is used in this place in no other sense than in the epistle to the Romans or to the Galatians.

units.la: Animaduertendum autem, modicè variare in verbis, Apostolum, & Septuaginta, & hebraicam veritatem: cùm enim Apostolus ita efferat, ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται, Septuaginta habent, ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μου, id est, iustus autem meus.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that the Apostle, the Septuagint and the Hebrew text differ slightly in wording. The Apostle writes "ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται" [ho de dikaios ek pisteōs zēsetai], whereas the Septuagint has "ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μου" [ho de dikaios mou], that is, "but my righteous one."

units.la: R In Hebræo autem sic, יעריק באמונתו חי, id est, & iustus in fide sua viuet. Ideoque, Hieronymo teste, significantius reddidit Symmachus, ὁ δίκαιος τῇ ἰσότῃ αὐτοῦ ζήσεται. Idem admonet, quòd in Septuaginta habeatur μου: & quodammodo, ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ μου, id est, ex fide mea factum esse errore quodam, quòd videlicet in hebræo pro ׳ legerint ״ finale. Ergo in versione septuaginta erroris nonnihil subest, & melius reddidit Symmachus: obseruandaque emphasis, cùm dicitur, In fide sua, ne quis alienam fidem tantoperè profuturam arbitretur ei, cui non adest propria. Verum quidem est, Christus videns fidem illorum, qui adferebant paralyticum, Marci 2. Matth. 9. Motus est misericordia, & sanauit paralyticum. Sed id eo pacto accipiendum, quomodo Deus mouetur orationibus, quæ ex fide fiunt pro aliis. Non autem eadem ratione coram tribunali Dei, vt quis ibi iustificetur, fides aliena proderit, sed fides propria requiritur. In astricto illo iudicio Dei vnusquisque pro se respondebit, fides aliena non poterit infidelem quiq: ipse fidem non habeat, liberare, non magis, quàm potest ob doctrinâ alienam aliquis indoctus esse doctus. Doctus fieri aliena scientia quis potest, at esse non nisi sua ipsius potest.
units.tr: In the Hebrew it reads "יעריק באמונתו חי" [yaʿiq be'emunatho ḥai], that is, "and the righteous one in his faith shall live." So, as Jerome testifies, Symmachus rendered it more meaningfully: "ὁ δίκαιος τῇ ἰσότητι αὐτοῦ ζήσεται" [ho dikaios tē isotēti autou zēsetai]. The same writer observes that the Septuagint has "μου" [mou], and that this reading arose from some error, namely because they read the final letter of the Hebrew word differently, so that "my faith" came in place of "his faith." Therefore there is some error in the Septuagint version, and Symmachus rendered it better. The emphasis must be observed in the words "in his own faith," lest anyone think that another's faith will greatly profit a person who does not have his own. It is true that Christ, seeing the faith of those who brought the paralytic (Mark 2; Matt. 9), was moved with compassion and healed him. But this must be understood in the way that God is moved by prayers made in faith on behalf of others. Before the tribunal of God, however, another's faith does not profit anyone for justification; a person's own faith is required. In that strict judgment of God each one will answer for himself. Another's faith cannot free an unbeliever who does not have faith himself, any more than an unlearned person can become learned through another's teaching. One can become learned through another's knowledge, but one can be learned only through one's own.

units.la: Ita saluari quis potest aliena fide, id est, salutis fieri particeps: at saluus esse nemo nisi sua propria fide potest: Salus enim & vita iusti est fides ipsa.
units.tr: Thus a person can be saved by another's faith, that is, become a partaker of salvation. But no one can be saved except by his own proper faith, for the salvation and life of the righteous is faith itself.

units.la: Nec de paralytico dicitur, quòd fidem non habuerit: Vero simile est, eum quoq; credidisse. Atque ea de causa Propheta generaliter dixit, iustus in fide sua viuet. Proinde Apostolus rectius citauit etiam, quàm Septuaginta: & licet non expresserit illud ἰσότῃ, vt Symmachus, tamen satis intelligitur. Hæc obiter pro versione ipsa visum fuit annotare.
units.tr: Nor is it said of the paralytic that he lacked faith; it is likely that he too believed. For this reason the prophet spoke in general terms: the righteous one in his faith shall live. Therefore the Apostle quoted more accurately than the Septuagint, and although he did not express the word "ἰσότης" as Symmachus did, it is nonetheless sufficiently understood. These points about the translation itself seemed worth noting in passing.

units.la: Iam deberemus hic multò copiosissimè explicare, quis hic proprie iustus dicatur, quid item fides. Sed vbi ventum fuerit ad sequentem fidei descriptionem, fiet id oportunius. In præsens satis fuerit notare, id quod & ad confirmandos animos in fide conducet, duos videlicet, imò tres mirabiles effectus fidei hisce verbis, Iustus ex fide viuet, demonstrari, nempe, quòd & iustificet, & vitam conferat, & quidem æternam.
units.tr: We ought here to explain at great length who is properly called righteous, and likewise what faith is. But this will be done more fittingly when we come to the following description of faith. For the present it will be enough to note, which will also serve to strengthen minds in faith, that these words, The righteous one shall live by faith, demonstrate two, indeed three, remarkable effects of faith: namely, that it justifies, that it bestows life, and indeed eternal life.

units.la: Quòd iustificet satis indicat vox iustus. Neque enim ita accipies hæc verba, quasi significaretur, prius debere esse iustum, propter aliquam qualitatem: ac deinde vbi iustus fuerit, tùm debere deinceps fidem habere, & per eam viuere: sed significatur, quòd per ipsam fidem iustus aliquis fiat, nec iustus quisquam sit, nisi quatenus fidem iam habeat. Iustus aliquis est, non quia aliquid egerit, vel iam aliquid agat: sed quia acceptatus est Deo, & pro iusto reputatus. Atque ita non propter aliquod opus, imò ne propter fidem quidem ipsam, quatenus est animi qualitas, iustus aliquis dicitur: sed tantùm imputatione diuina, & propter Christum: quæ imputatio non fit nisi erga illos, qui fide miseri cordiam propter Christum expectant & apprehendunt. Igitur fide iustificantur homines, & quatenus habent fidem, hæc ad iustitiam ipsis à Deo imputatur. Quòd autem viuificet fides, ostendit vox ζήσεται. Vita spiritualis contingit omnibus, qui in Christum credunt. Hæc est vita æterna, vt cognoscât te, & quem misisti Christum Iesum, vt omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam, Ioann. sexto, &c. Atque hæc æternitas vitæ significatur in voce Futuri temporis, tàm in hebræo, quàm in græco expressa. Post hanc vitam futura est, & perpetuò duratura. Proinde hæc tria de effectibus fidei quoniam præclara sunt, & mortalibus omnibus valde expetenda, maximum debent ad excitandos omnium animos habere calcar, & mirè faciunt ad fidem omnibus commendandam.
units.tr: That faith justifies is sufficiently indicated by the word "righteous." You should not take these words as if they meant that a man must first be righteous because of some quality, and only then, once righteous, have faith and live by it. Rather, they mean that a man is made righteous through faith itself, and no one is righteous except insofar as he already has faith. A man is called righteous not because he has done something or is now doing something, but because he has been accepted by God and reckoned as righteous. Thus a man is called righteous not on account of any work, nor even on account of faith itself as a quality of the mind, but only by divine imputation and for Christ's sake. This imputation is made only to those who await and grasp mercy for Christ's sake through faith. Therefore men are justified by faith, and insofar as they have faith, it is imputed to them by God for righteousness. That faith gives life is shown by the word "ζήσεται" [zēsetai]. Spiritual life comes to all who believe in Christ: "This is eternal life, that they know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 6, etc.). This eternity of life is signified in the future tense, expressed both in Hebrew and in Greek. The life that follows this one will be future and will last forever. Therefore, since these three effects of faith are excellent and greatly to be desired by all mortals, they ought to be the strongest spur for arousing the minds of everyone, and they serve wonderfully to commend faith to all.

units.la: Et si se subduxerit, non probabitur animo meo.
units.tr: And if he draws back, my soul will take no pleasure in him.

units.la: Propius respiciens ad locum Prophetæ, verbis indidem petitis, addit per contrarium, quæ à deficiendo à fide deterreat, dicendo, quòd sicut iustus fide sua est victurus, ita è diuerso qui à fide defecerit, Deo displicebit & peribit. Etsi autem hæc verba non eodem ordine apud Prophetam sint posita, nam præeunt ibi & non sequuntur: tamen rectissimè sunt ab Apostolo eo, quem cernimus, modo adiecta. Id autem non solùm, quia contrariorum iuxta inuicem collocatio sententiam illustrat, & clarius intelligitur, iustos Deo placere per fidem, quando additur, eos displicere Deo, qui fidem abiecerint: sed etiam quia ingenijs Hebræorum conueniebat, vt adhortationi ad constantiam in fide breuis quædam comminatio subijceretur, apud eos, de quibus metuebatur, quòd in fide non satis essent confirmati. Porrò cum in propheta ipso occurreret, quod huic instituto seruiret, satius erat prophetica verba adhibere, quàm proprijs tantundem enunciare. Hæc sine dubio causa est, cur Apostolus ista adiecerit, ac verba prophetæ sic transposuerit. Sciendum autem, hæc verba hic citari, vt habentur apud Septuaginta, apud quos sic legitur: ἐὰν ὑποστείλῃται, οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν αὐτῷ: quasi diceret: Si retraxerit se, non complacet animæ meæ in illo.
units.tr: Keeping closer to the prophet's passage, and using words taken from the same place, he adds by way of contrast what deters people from falling away from faith. He says that just as the righteous shall live by his faith, so on the other hand whoever has fallen away from faith will displease God and perish. Although these words are not in the same order in the prophet, for there the clauses come the other way round, the Apostle has added them quite rightly in the way we see. He did this not only because placing contraries side by side clarifies the sense, and makes it clearer that the righteous please God through faith when it is added that those who have cast off faith displease God. He also did it because it suited the Hebrew temper that a brief threat should be attached to the exhortation to constancy in faith, for the sake of those who were feared not to be sufficiently confirmed in faith. Moreover, since the prophet himself contained something that served this purpose, it was better to use the prophetic words than to state the same thing in his own. This is without doubt the reason why the Apostle added these words and so rearranged the prophet's wording. It should be noted, however, that these words are cited here as they are found in the Septuagint, where they read: ean hyposteilētai, ouk eudokei hē psychē mou en autō [ἐὰν ὑποστείλῃται, οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν αὐτῷ], as if he had said: If he draws back, my soul does not take pleasure in him.

units.la: At in
units.tr: But in

units.la: Ait in Hebræo, תגה עפלה לא רשרחבמשי בר, quod perinde est, ac si dicatur, Ecce, qui roboratus seu erectus est corde, non recta est anima illius in semetipso. Verba quidem diuersum quiddam sonant à verbis Septuaginta, tamen nihil diuersi est in sententia. De scribitur enim incredulus & subducens se à fide; per periphrasin, elatus corde & arrogans, quod reuera de incredulis optime dici poterit. Qui enim non fidit Deo, quid aliud, quàm vt sibi fidens, se contra Deum erigit?
units.tr: The Hebrew says [תגה עפלה לא רשרחבמשי בר], which is just as if one said: Behold, he who is strengthened or made upright in heart, his soul is not upright within itself. The words indeed sound somewhat different from the words of the Septuagint, yet there is no difference in sense. For the unbeliever and the one who draws back from faith is described by a periphrasis: proud in heart and arrogant. This can truly be said best of unbelievers. For whoever does not trust God, what else does he do, if not set himself up against God, trusting in himself?

units.la: Summa est arrogantia & fastus, Deo non credere, quasi per te citra illius opem efficere aliquid possis. Et propterea vulgata editio, quæ Hieronymi nomine circumfertur, sensu integerrimè reddidit: Ecce qui incredulus est, non erit recta anima eius in semetipso.
units.tr: Not to trust God is the height of arrogance and pride, as if you could accomplish anything by yourself without his help. For this reason the Vulgate edition, which circulates under the name of Jerome, rendered the sense most faithfully: Ecce qui incredulus est, non erit recta anima eius in semetipso.

units.la: Et Septuaginta ad sensum hauddubiè respexerunt. Itaque dum de sententia constat, ad quam pariter Septuaginta, & Apostolus respexerunt, id satis esse nobis debet. Gravis itaque habetur hic comminatio contra fidei desertores, & apta Hebræorum ingenijs, quæ vt valde procliuia ad deficiendum, & assueta comminationibus ac terroribus legis, conueniebat saltem obiter comminatione quadam iræ Dei admoneri. Neque vero lenis aut parum pungens est comminatio, cùm ita dicitur: Ecce, qui roboratus siue erectus est corde, non recta est anima illius in semetipso: Quid odiosius, quàm describi arrogantem & superbum, qui sese Deo opponat? Nonne hoc vno crimine non solùm incredulitas, sed omnis adeò malitia, superbia, & contumelia in Deum significatur? Quis es homo, qui te opponas Deo? Voluntati eius quis resistet? Frustra contra stimulum calcitrabis.
units.tr: The Septuagint also undoubtedly had regard to the sense. So while the meaning is agreed, to which the Septuagint and the Apostle alike had regard, that should be enough for us. The threat here is therefore a serious one against deserters of faith, and it suits the Hebrew temper: since they were very prone to falling away, and accustomed to the threats and terrors of the law, it was fitting that they be warned, at least in passing, by some threat of God's wrath. Nor is the threat mild or lacking in sting when it is said: Ecce, qui roboratus sive erectus est corde, non recta est anima illius in semetipso. What could be more hateful than to be described as arrogant and proud, one who sets himself against God? Is not unbelief signified by this one fault, but indeed all wickedness, pride and insolence against God? Who are you, a man, to set yourself against God? Who will resist his will? You will kick against the goad in vain.

units.la: Certè tuis subnixus viribus nihil efficies, si Dei promissiones contemnis, si non credis ab illo solo omnia, quæ obtingere possunt, bona expectanda, tu quodammodo eum mendacij arguis, & Deum esse, id est, omnipotentem, beneuolum, iustum, misericordem esse negas.
units.tr: Certainly, if you rely on your own strength you will accomplish nothing, if you despise God's promises, if you do not believe that all the good things that can come to pass are to be expected from him alone. In a sense you accuse him of lying, and deny that God is what he is: almighty, benevolent, just and merciful.

units.la: Ergo non solùm incredulitatem, sed omnia sanè, quæ contra Deum & Dei gloriam fieri possent, hac locutionis formula Propheta complectitur. Deinde verò quòd dicit, Non est recta anima eius in semetipso: tantundem valet, ac si diceretur, anima eius non bene se habebit, nullo pacto poterit Deo placere. Qui verè credit, verè timet, recta est anima in semetipso, quieta agit, non experitur molestas pugnas tentationum, impellentium ipsum ad desperationem.
units.tr: Therefore the prophet, by this form of speech, embraces not only unbelief but indeed all those things which could be done against God and the glory of God. Next, when he says, Non est recta anima eius in semetipso, it amounts to the same as if it were said: his soul will not be well, and in no way will he be able to please God. He who truly believes truly fears; the soul is upright in itself, it acts quietly, and does not undergo the troublesome struggles of temptations driving it to despair.

units.la: E diuerso autem qui non credit, non verè timet, huius cor non est rectum in semetipso, quia iudicat, Deum sibi non esse propitium, Deum incipit odisse, ac tandem in præcipitium desperationis perlabitur.
units.tr: On the other hand, he who does not believe does not truly fear. His heart is not upright in itself, because he judges that God is not favourable to him; he begins to hate God, and at last slides into the precipice of despair.

units.la: Pax interna & læta conscientia per veram fidem in Deum contingit. Et aptisimè describitur verbis Prophetæ perturbatio conscientiæ, quæ omnibus contingit incredulis, & certissimum est irati Dei in nos signum, ita vt per Metonymiam, perturbatio cordis iram Dei pulchrè repræsentet.
units.tr: Inner peace and a joyful conscience come through true faith in God. And the disturbance of conscience, which befalls all unbelievers, and which is the most certain sign of God's wrath upon us, is aptly described by the prophet's words, so that by metonymy the disturbance of the heart beautifully represents the wrath of God.

units.la: Reuera enim qui non verè credit, sentit mirabiles motus & perturbationes in corde, Deo irascitur, Dei iram amodo in se experitur.
units.tr: For indeed, whoever does not truly believe feels strange movements and agitations in his heart, he is angry with God, and from now on he experiences God's wrath within himself.

units.la: Cùm ergo dicitur in Hebræo: Non est recta anima illius in semetipso, id non dissimile est ab illo, quod apud Septuaginta dicitur, Non complacet anima mea in illo. Satis ergo manifestum est, pro grauissima comminatione hæc verba esse appositä, & clarissimè significari, quòd, sicut iustus ex fide sua viuet, ita qui incredulus fuerit, anima eius sit peritura non bene habebit, & habebit Deum sibi iratum.
units.tr: So when it is said in the Hebrew, Non est recta anima illius in semetipso, this is not unlike what is said in the Septuagint, Non complacet anima mea in illo. It is therefore clear enough that these words are added as a most serious threat, and it is very plainly signified that, just as the righteous shall live by his faith, so the one who is unbelieving, whose soul is to perish, will not be well, and will have God angry with him.

units.la: At nos non sumus, qui subducamus nos in perditionem, sed ad fidem pertinemus in acquisitionem animæ. Correctio qua remouet ab illis peccatum incredulitatis, & Dei iram, dicens, se confidere, quòd nulli sint inter ipsos, in quos comminatio illa valere queat. Atq; hæc incredulitatis ac minarum remotio blanda quædam ac vehemens est ad constantiam fidei inflammatio.
