Hoc autem valde prudenter factum, & ad mouendos affectus accommodum, quòd per antithesin sententiam expresserit, & in vtraq; parte effectus, hinc inquâ incredulitatis, in de verò fidei appositione. Subducere sese à fide, siue erigere cor contra Deum, est se deijcere in perditionem, & quidem animæ, sicut liquet ex sequenti. Qui enim non credit, iam iudicatus est. Contrà verò qui in fide constantes manserint, ad fidem pertinent, hoc est, in numero sunt verè credentiū, tales acquirunt animam suam. Quis autem non studeat salvam facere animā suam? Crede ergo, & saluasti. Et valde illustrat ista antithesis, seu contentio sententiam. At nos: Annumerat se illis quadam sua modestia, & illos sibi pares faciendo erigit confirmatq;. Primùm hoc disci mus, quòd plurimum profuerit ad consolationem hoc modo propositä fidei tanta efficacia, vtq; velint in eius cofesione perfistere. Secundò: non minus proderit comminatio perditionis æternæ, ad eos retinendos in officio, qui duriori ingenio minis & terroribus trahi magis, quàm duci volunt.
units.tr: At nos non sumus, qui subducamus nos in perditionem, sed ad fidem pertinemus in acquisitionem animae. This is a correction by which he removes from themselves the sin of unbelief and God's wrath, saying that he is confident there are none among them against whom that threat could hold. And this removal of unbelief and of threats is a kind of gentle yet vehement kindling of constancy in faith. It was done very wisely, and suited to moving the emotions, that he expressed the sentence by antithesis, setting out the effects on both sides: on the one hand of unbelief, on the other of true faith. To draw back from faith, or to raise the heart against God, is to cast oneself into destruction, and indeed the destruction of the soul, as is clear from what follows. For whoever does not believe is already judged. On the contrary, those who remain constant in faith belong to faith; that is, they are counted among true believers, and such people gain their souls. Who, then, would not strive to save his soul? Believe, therefore, and you have saved it. This antithesis, or contrast, illustrates the sense very well. At nos: with a certain modesty he counts himself among them, and by making them equal to himself he raises them up and confirms them. Here we learn first that it is of great benefit for consolation that faith, proposed in this way, has such efficacy that people are willing to persist in its confession. Second, the threat of eternal destruction will be no less useful for keeping in their duty those of a harder disposition, who want to be driven by threats and terrors rather than led.

units.la: Ioan. 3. Credens saluat animam suam. Tertiò: habemus hic, quod facit ad docendi methodum, nimirum, quòd, vbi propo-sitionem, vel aliquid tale didactico more proponimus, commodum adijcimus nonnihil, quod vsum eius, quod proponitur, commonstret, quodque ad rectè vten-dum commonefaciat.
units.tr: John 3. Whoever believes saves his soul. Third, we have here something that bears on the method of teaching: namely, that when we set forth a proposition, or something of that kind in the manner of teaching, it is useful to add something that shows the use of what is proposed, and that reminds us to use it rightly.

units.la: CONFIRMATIO. CAPVT VNDECIMVM.
units.tr: Confirmation. Chapter Eleven.

units.la: EST autem fides earum rerum, quae sperantur, substantia, argumentum eorum, quae non videntur.
units.tr: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

units.la: HIC commodum docendi causa praesentis partis constituetur confir-matio: quandoquidem hic argumenta, quibus probatur, sicut praece-denti propositione dictum est, iustitiam coram Deo contingere per solam fidem, colliguntur. Quamuis ita omnia sunt constituta, vt non tam ad docendum, quàm ad confirmandos animos in fidei constantia, quò potissimum tota hac parte spectat Apostolus, maximè sint idonea. Neq; enim apud eos, qui iam abundè erant de iustificatione per fidem absque operibus legis edocti: quibus item ex praecedenti parte etiam constare satis poterat, ne per sacrificia quidem legis (multo igitur minus per reliqua opera moralia) potuisse homines iustificari: Denique, de quibus tantum metuebatur, ne ob periculorum & afflictionum magnitudinem à fidei confessione abducerentur, opus videbatur alia ratione agere. Est autem primum argumentum sumptum à fidei definitione, quam Apostolus eiusmodi reddidit, quo optimè posset causae inseruire, id est, vt aptissima foret, ad animos in tolerantia aduersitatum propter confessionem fidei, confirmandos. Sic autem habet haec definitio: Fides est earum rerum, quae sperantur, substantia, argumentum eorum, quae non uidentur. Graecè multò sonat significantius πίστις ἐστὶν ὑπόστασις πραγμάτων ἐλπιζομένων, ἐλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων. Solent autem plerique anxiè contendere, num hic sit definitio, an tantum quaedam obscura descriptio, an potius quaedam fidei commendatio. Sed nos rectè dicemus definitionem, & quidem perfectam, multoque aptissimam, in tanta brevitate contineri. Atque id duabus potissimum ostendemus rationibus: Prior est, quòd Apostolus, licet aliam omninò definitionem facile fuisset ei condere, tamen hanc ita condidit, rationem habens eius argumenti, in quo versabatur.
units.tr: Here, for the sake of teaching, a confirmation of the present part is set out, since the arguments by which it is proved, as was said in the preceding proposition, that righteousness before God comes through faith alone, are gathered together here. Although all things are so arranged that they are especially suited not so much to teaching as to strengthening minds in constancy of faith, which is the chief aim of the Apostle throughout this whole part. For these arguments are not addressed to those who had already been sufficiently taught that justification comes through faith without the works of the law, and who could also gather well enough from the previous part that men could not be justified even by the sacrifices of the law, much less by the other moral works. Finally, for those whom they feared might be drawn away from the confession of faith by the magnitude of dangers and afflictions, it seemed necessary to proceed in another way. The first argument is taken from the definition of faith, which the Apostle framed in such a way that it might serve his cause best, that is, that it might be most apt for strengthening minds to endure adversities for the sake of the confession of faith. The definition runs thus: Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. In Greek the sense is much more expressive: πίστις ἐστὶν ὑπόστασις πραγμάτων ἐλπιζομένων, ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων. Many people anxiously dispute whether this is a definition, or merely some obscure description, or rather a commendation of faith. But we shall rightly say that a definition, and indeed a complete and most apt one, is contained in such brevity. We will show this chiefly on two grounds. The first is that the Apostle, although he could easily have framed some quite different definition, nevertheless framed this one with regard to the subject he was treating.

units.la: Erat enim ei in animo, fratres Hebraeos, qui passim per Pseudoapostolos, item per domesticos suos tyrannos solicitabantur, vt à fide deficerent. Ad hos igitur confirman-dos qui potuissent aptiorem rationem adferre, quàm huiusmodi fidei definitionem? Singulae voces, si quis bene perpendat, habent ingentem vim ad animos in constantia fidei confirmandos. Fides, inquit, est ὑπόστασις, id est, subsistentia, basis, firmum & solidum fulcrum & fundamentum, in quod tutò innitimur. Ita vt haec sit sententia: Fides est ὑπόστασις, id est, non leuis & è variis coniecturis collecta opinio, sed firma & indubitata notitia, adeoq; non tantùm notitia, sed quodammodo vehemens & certus affectus & assensus, quo animus apprehendit Dei promissa: Vnde & nonnulli ὑπόστασιν verterunt expectationem, ad sensum videlicet respicientes.
units.tr: For he had in mind the Hebrew brethren, who were on all sides being pressed, through false apostles and likewise through their own domestic tyrants, to fall away from the faith. To strengthen these, what more suitable reason could he have offered than such a definition of faith? If anyone weighs the individual words carefully, they have a great power for confirming minds in constancy of faith. Faith, he says, is substance [ὑπόστασις], that is, subsistence, a foundation, a firm and solid support and ground on which we may safely rest. So the sense is this: faith is substance [ὑπόστασις], that is, not a light opinion gathered from various conjectures, but a firm and indubitable knowledge, and therefore not merely knowledge but, in a certain way, a vehement and certain affection and assent, by which the mind grasps the promises of God. Hence some have also rendered ὑπόστασιν as expectation, looking, of course, to the sense.

units.la: Porrò haec vox non valde accommoda est ad excitandam firmam fidem in omnium animis, qui inter credentes numerari volunt?
units.tr: Moreover, is this word not very well suited to rousing a firm faith in the minds of all who wish to be counted among believers?

units.la: Nónne clare significat, fidem debere esse solidam & inconcussam, aut aliàs nequa-quàm pro fide agnoscendam? Haec enim necessaria est consequentia: Si Fides est: Ergo hypostasis est. Constituta specie, necessariò constituitur eius genus. Quare qui firmi non sunt, certè ij nec fidem, quae proprie sic veniant appellanda, habent.
units.tr: Does it not clearly signify that faith must be solid and unshaken, or else it must by no means be acknowledged as faith? For this is a necessary consequence: if there is faith, then there is substance. When the species is established, its genus is necessarily established. Therefore those who are not firm certainly do not have that faith which properly deserves to be so called.

units.la: Altera particula est, quod fides sit ὑπόστασις πραγμάτων ἐλπιζομένων, rerum sperandarum. Loco differentiae ista particula posset accipi. Significat enim, fidem esse certam notitiam & assensum, non quidem ad res praesentes, quae subiectae sunt rationi, vel sensibus: sed quae in posterum, & proprie post hanc vitam obuenient. Differentia est sumpta ab obiectis, circa quae versatur fides. Caeterùm, cùm obiecta vel maximè moueant, ac semper versari debeant ob oculos eorum, qui seriò cupiunt virtutum actiones perficere, adeoque virtutes potissimum fiant virtutes ratione finis seu obiecti, habent hic omnes pij, quo sese ad fidem amplexandā constanterq; tuendam inflamment. Bona illa promissa, in quae fides intuetur, nempe remissio peccatorum, vita aeterna, sunt eiusmodi, vt spe ea
units.tr: The second part is that faith is the substance of things hoped for [ὑπόστασις πραγμάτων ἐλπιζομένων]. This phrase could serve as a differentia. It means that faith is a certain knowledge and assent not to present things, which fall under reason or the senses, but to things in the future, which properly come after this life. The differentia is taken from the objects with which faith is concerned. Since objects especially move us, and ought always to be before the eyes of those who earnestly desire to perform the actions of the virtues, and since the virtues chiefly become virtues by reason of their end or object, all the godly have this here, by which they are inflamed to embrace faith and steadfastly to maintain it. The good promised things on which faith fixes its gaze, namely the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, are of such a kind that anyone who hopes to receive them ought to be ready to undergo even the harshest dangers. What is added next is added plainly for the sake of interpretation and clarity.

units.la: 1. 2. 3. spe ea percipiendi quilibet paratus esse debeat vel asperrima pericula subire. Iam quae adijciuntur, plane interpretationis causa & euidentiae adiecta sunt.
units.tr: Anyone who hopes to receive them ought to be ready to undergo even the harshest dangers. What is added next is added plainly for the sake of interpretation and clarity.

units.la: ἐλέγχος enim clarius explicat, quid intelligendum per ὑπόστασιν, & cum dicit ὲ βλεπομένων, respondet id ei, quod prius dicebatur, πραγμάτων ἐλπιζομένων.
units.tr: For evidence [ἔλεγχος] explains more clearly what is to be understood by substance [ὑπόστασιν], and when it says of things not seen [οὐ βλεπομένων], this corresponds to what was said before, of things hoped for [πραγμάτων ἐλπιζομένων].

units.la: Significat autem ἐλέγχειν conuincere, & causam aliquam eò deducere, vt obijci aut praetexi nihil amplius queat: Verbum est forense.
units.tr: Now ἐλέγχειν means to convict, and to bring a cause to such a point that nothing more can be objected or pretended against it. It is a forensic word.

units.la: Quo sensu etiam saepius in sacris literis vsurpatur: vt ad Tit. primo. Oportet Episcopum inculpatum esse, &c. & tenacem eius, qui secundum doctrinam est fidelis sermonis, vt potens sit etiam exhortari per doctrinam, sanam, & contradicentes conuincere.
units.tr: It is used in this sense quite often in the sacred letters, as in Titus chapter one: the bishop must be blameless, and must hold fast the faithful word as taught, so that he may be able both to exhort by sound doctrine and to convince those who contradict.

units.la: τὸς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχει. Ioan. decimo sexto, Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum (ἐλέγχει τὸν κόσμον) de peccato, de iustitia, & de iudicio, &c.
units.tr: τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχει. In John chapter sixteen: the Holy Spirit will convict the world [ἐλέγχει τὸν κόσμον] of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment, and so on.

units.la: Ea propter interpres Chrysostomi vertit ἐλέγχειν conuictionem, secutus opinor Augustinum, qui pluribus locis ita transtulit, Homilia in Ioan. 79. & 95.
units.tr: For this reason the translator of Chrysostom rendered ἐλέγχειν as convicting, following, I think, Augustine, who in several places translated it in this way, in his homilies on John 79 and 95.

units.la: Item de peccatorum meritis & remissione libro secundo capite trigesimo primo. Itaque vox ἐλέγχος clarius & euidentius exprimit, qui priori loco per ὑπόστασιν sibi voluerit, & non apaprentium, significat res sperandas, videlicet spirituales, & in hac vita non accipiendas, sed tantum post hanc vitam.
units.tr: Likewise in his book on the merits and remission of sins, book two, chapter thirty-one. Thus the word ἔλεγχος expresses more clearly and evidently what the first word, by ὑπόστασις, was meant to convey, and not what is apparent; it signifies the things to be hoped for, namely spiritual things, which are not to be received in this life but only after this life.

units.la: Et ex his posset colligi haec crassior & plenior definitio: Fides est substantialis cognitio, seu certa & inexpugnabilis fiducia accipiendi eas res, quae nobis sunt a Deo promissae, & post hanc vitam obtinentur.
units.tr: And from these things a fuller and more explicit definition could be drawn: faith is a substantial knowledge, or a certain and unconquerable confidence of receiving those things which have been promised to us by God and are obtained after this life.

units.la: Quae perfecta est, & completitur praecipua fidei insignia, completitur genus, completitur differentiam, & in tanta breuitate nihilominus completitur, quod ad summam fidei pertinet.
units.tr: This is a complete definition, and it embraces the chief marks of faith: it embraces the genus, it embraces the differentia, and yet, in such brevity, it embraces whatever pertains to the sum of faith.

units.la: Quamobrem recte statuitur, hic haberi iustam definitionem, nec non eam optime comparatam ad causam, quae agebatur. Tantum de prima ratione.
units.tr: Wherefore it is rightly maintained that here we have a proper definition, and one most well suited to the cause that was being pursued. So much for the first reason.

units.la: Iam altera ratio, quare asserimus hic propriam & legitimam definitionem, haec est, quod tota natura fidei in illa breui definitione explicatur, & quaecunque possent in alia definitione fidei poni, si vellemus pleniorem texere, eadem omnia in hac Apostoli brevissima definitione insinuantur, & saltem tacite sunt repositia.
units.tr: Now the second reason why we assert here a proper and legitimate definition is this: the whole nature of faith is set forth in that brief definition, and whatever could be put into another definition of faith, if we wished to weave a fuller one, all of these things are hinted at in this very brief definition of the Apostle, and at least are tacitly laid up in it.

units.la: Id nos etiam demonstrabimus, colligentes primum absolutissimam quandam fidei definitionem, atque ostendentes, omnia eius membra latenter etiam in hac, quam Apostolus profert, contineri.
units.tr: We shall also demonstrate this, by first gathering a certain most complete definition of faith, and then showing that all its parts are also latently contained in this one which the Apostle sets forth.

units.la: Porro huiusmodi definitionem colligemus, expendendo, quomodo fides nascatur, & quae ad veram absolutamq; fidem necessaria requiruntur, eademque simul compingendo.
units.tr: Moreover, we shall gather a definition of this kind by considering how faith arises, and what is required for true and complete faith, and by putting these together at the same time.

units.la: Primum ergo vt habeatur fides, necessaria est cognitio Dei ex verbo. Ad verbum enim siue exterius per ministros exhibitum, siue interius diuina virtute reuelatum, fides debet componi, & quasi ad Lydium lapidem probari.
units.tr: First, therefore, in order that faith may exist, the knowledge of God from the word is necessary. For faith must be built upon the word, whether it is set forth outwardly through ministers, or revealed inwardly by divine power, and it must be tested, as it were, by the touchstone of the word.

units.la: Neque enim est vera fides, nisi quatenus verbo innititur. Huc iam pertinet illud Roman. 10. Quomodo credent ei, de quo non audierunt? Et paulo post: Ergo fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei.
units.tr: For there is no true faith except insofar as it rests upon the word. To this belongs that passage in Romans 10: How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And a little later: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.

units.la: Secundo, vt nascatur fides, oportet eiusmodi haberi ex verbo cognitionem, qua doceamur de Dei erga nos voluntate.
units.tr: Second, in order that faith may arise, it is necessary to have from the word such a knowledge by which we are taught about the will of God toward us.

units.la: Nam, si sciamus, ex verbo, Deum esse, & quidem iustum, bonum, potentem, & huiusmodi, atq; id etiam toto animo credamus, tamen haec nondum est absoluta fides.
units.tr: For if we know from the word that God exists, and indeed that he is just, good, powerful, and such like, and even believe this with our whole mind, nevertheless this is not yet complete faith.

units.la: Nam eiusmodi habent etiam gentiles, siue ex reuelatione, siue ex conditione uisibilium (vt habetur Roman. 1.) eam didicerunt: at nunquam potuerunt de voluntate Dei erga se aliquid statuere.
units.tr: For the Gentiles also have such knowledge, whether from revelation or from the condition of visible things (as in Rom. 1.), and they learned it. But they could never settle anything about God's will toward themselves.

units.la: Oportet igitur nos edoctos esse ex verbo de bona Dei erga nos voluntate, sine qua cognitione fides non potest solida subsistere. Huc pertinet, quod Ephes. 1. tantopere praedicat Apostolus arcanum voluntatis diuinae & propositum Dei in Euangelio nobis patefactum. Item Roman. 8. Spiritus testatur vna cum Spiritu nostro, quod sumus filij Dei, videlicet adoptati. Denique, ex multis aliis Scripturae locis id potest comprobari.
units.tr: It is necessary, therefore, that we be taught from the Word about God's good will toward us, without which knowledge faith cannot stand firm. To this belongs what the Apostle so greatly proclaims in Eph. 1., the hidden mystery of the divine will and God's purpose made known to us in the Gospel. Likewise Rom. 8.: "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God," that is, adopted. Finally, this can be confirmed from many other passages of Scripture.

units.la: Tertio, haec cognitio voluntatis Dei debet esse de ipsius erga nos misericordia. Nam cognoscitur voluntas Dei etiam in lege, vtpote quae praescribit, quid Deus velit nos facere aut vitare: Item ex plurimis locis, in quibus iustitia & seueritas, ira Dei & punitio peccatorum describitur.
units.tr: Third, this knowledge of God's will ought to concern his mercy toward us. For the will of God is also known from the law, since it prescribes what God wills us to do or to avoid; and from very many passages in which God's justice and severity, his wrath and the punishment of sins, are described.

units.la: Sed hi loci non solantur, non confirmant conscientiam, sed potius terrent, deijciunt, ac cogunt tandem desperare. Huc pertinet illud Roman. 4. Lex iram operatur. Ergo oportet edoctos esse de voluntate Dei bona erga nos, qua ille offert misericordiam, promittit se velle esse nobis placatum. Hæc cognitio voluntatis Dei potest erigere, potest fidem in nobis excitare. Atque huc conferendæ sunt omnes promissiones de beneficijs Dei erga nos, præsertim spiritualibus, vt de electione nostra ante constitutionem mundi, Ephes. 1. de remissione peccatorum, de vita æterna: quæ passim occurrunt in lege, Prophetis, Euangelio.
units.tr: But these passages do not comfort or confirm the conscience. Rather, they terrify and cast down, and in the end compel despair. To this belongs Rom. 4.: "The law works wrath." Therefore it is necessary to be taught about God's good will toward us, by which he offers mercy and promises that he wishes to be reconciled to us. This knowledge of God's will can lift us up and kindle faith in us. To this must be referred all the promises of God's benefits toward us, especially the spiritual ones: such as our election before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1.), the forgiveness of sins, and eternal life. These occur everywhere in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel.

units.la: Quartò: non latis est intueri in illas promissiones, sed oportet etiam scire, gratuitas esse. Nam etiam si sciremus, multa præclara nobis esse promissa, tamen, si suspicemur, requiri nostra beneficia & merita, vt illa obtineamus, sane hic quando fragilitatem nostram agnoscimus, cogimur iterum diffidere, incipimus dubitare, an etiam ad nos pertineant illæ promissiones. Huc illud pertinet Roman. 3. Iustificantur autem gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, quem propósuit Deus reconciliatorem per fidem, interveniente ipsius sanguine, ad ostensionem iustitiæ suæ. Item Roman. 1. describitur Euangelium potentia Dei in salutem omni credenti. Ita fides in misericordiam, & quidem gratuitam, non propter opera proveniente debet respicere, iuxta illud quoque Roman. 3. Arbitramur hominem iustificari fide absque operibus legis.
units.tr: Fourth, it is not enough to look upon those promises; we must also know that they are free. For even if we knew that many excellent things had been promised to us, yet if we suspected that our benefits and merits were required in order to obtain them, then, when we recognize our frailty, we would be forced to distrust again, and would begin to doubt whether those promises pertain to us at all. To this belongs Rom. 3.: "They are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as the reconciler through faith, by his blood, for the showing of his justice." Likewise Rom. 1. describes the Gospel as "the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes." Thus faith ought to look to mercy, and indeed free mercy, not arising from works, in accordance with Rom. 3. as well: "We hold that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law."

units.la: Quintò: non omittendum est, promissiones, ad quas fides refertur, proprie esse de Christo, propter quem solum, & cuius sanguine nos apud Deum iustificamur. Finis promissionum & causa est Christus. 2. Corinth. 1. Quotquot sunt promissiones, per ipsum sunt etiam, & per ipsum Amen, Deo ad gloriam per nos. Et solus Christus est ille, de quo promissiones principales sunt editæ statim ab initio mundi, ad omnes patres, & propter quem Deus dilectionem suam in homines profert, iuxta illud Matth. 17. Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacet, &c.
units.tr: Fifth, it must not be overlooked that the promises to which faith refers are properly about Christ, on account of whom alone, and by whose blood, we are justified before God. Christ is the end and cause of the promises. 2 Cor. 1.: "However many the promises of God are, in him they are yes, and in him Amen, to God's glory through us." Christ alone is he about whom the chief promises were published from the very beginning of the world, to all the fathers, and on account of whom God pours out his love upon men, according to Matt. 17.: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," etc.

units.la: Sextò: quia maxima est nostra infirmitas, & mirabilis ad dubitationem ac diffidentiam inclinatio, & fides debet esse firma inconcussa, adeoque immobilis ὑπόστασις, ideo opus est Spiritus sancti ope, à quo & fidem accipiamus, & per quem in fide confirmamur, sicut in Roman. 8. dicitur: Accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba pater: Idem Spiritus testatur vna cum Spiritu nostro, quòd sumus filij Dei. Item Christus ad Petrum Matthæi 16. de confessione fidei factâ: Beatus es Simon Bar Iona, quia caro & sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed pater meus, qui est in cœlis. 1. Corinth. 2. Nobis autem Deus revelavit per Spiritum suum.
units.tr: Sixth, because our weakness is very great and our tendency to doubt and distrust is remarkable, and because faith ought to be firm, unshaken, and so an immovable hypostasis, there is need of the help of the Holy Spirit. It is from him that we receive faith, and through him that we are confirmed in faith, as Rom. 8. says: "You have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God." Likewise Christ to Peter, Matt. 16., when Peter had made his confession of faith: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." 1 Cor. 2.: "But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit."

units.la: Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Quis enim hominum novit ea, quæ sunt hominis, nisi Spiritus hominis, qui est in eo? Sic & ea, quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit, nisi Spiritus Dei. Nos verò non Spiritum mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum, qui est ex Deo, vt sciamus, quæ à Christo donata sint nobis. Ergo non nisi per Spiritum possumus firma fide applicare ea, quæ per Christum nobis sunt donata.
units.tr: For "the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." Who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. "But we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things that have been given to us by Christ." Therefore we can apply with firm faith the things given to us through Christ only through the Spirit.

units.la: Septimò: hanc certitudinem mente acceptam oportet postremò & confirmari in corde, quia non vere diligitur Deus, non vere timetur, nisi id fiat toto corde: Istud verò non fit, nisi animus quadam certitudine obfirmetur, & nisi fiat constanter. Et propterea etiam Spiritus sanctus dicitur tanquam arrha obsignare confirmareque corda, vt certi simus de promissionibus accipiendis. 2. Corinth. 1. Porrò qui confirmat nos vnà vobiscum in Christum, & qui vnxit nos, Deus est, qui etiam obsignavit nos, deditque arrham Spiritus in cordibus nostris. Et Ephes. 1. Vt simus nos in laudem gloriæ illius, qui priores speravimus in Christo, in quo speratis & vos auditò verbo veritatis, Euangelio salutis vestræ, in quo etiam postea quàm credidistis, obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ. Pariter à Spiritu sancto est, vt credamus, & vt animus in fide obfirmetur. Atque his modis puto omnibus numeris absolutam fidem habere, ideoque absolutam quoque fidei definitionem, seu malis descriptionem posse colligere.
units.tr: Seventh, this certainty, once received in the mind, must finally also be confirmed in the heart, because God is not truly loved or truly feared unless this is done with the whole heart. But this does not happen unless the soul is fixed by a certain assurance, and unless it is done constantly. For this reason the Holy Spirit is also said to seal and confirm our hearts, as a pledge, so that we may be certain about receiving the promises. 2 Cor. 1.: "Now he who confirms us together with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God, who also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts." And Eph. 1.: "That we who first hoped in Christ might be to the praise of his glory; in whom you also, having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, in whom also, after you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance." Likewise it is by the Holy Spirit that we believe, and that the mind is strengthened in faith. And in these ways I think that faith is complete in every respect, and so one may also gather a complete definition, or if you prefer a description, of faith.

units.la: Colligamus ergo hanc fidei descriptionem: Fides est firma certaque, ex verbo Dei, cognitio, de Dei bona voluntate ac misericordia gratuita, propter Christum, per Spiritum sanctum revelata, & in cordibus obsignata. Hæc, inquam, est eiusmodi definitio, vt nihil amplius in ea, quod ad explicandam naturam fidei attinet, desiderari queat. Plenissima enim est, & leges bonæ definitionis ei conueniunt.
units.tr: Let us therefore gather this description of faith: Faith is a firm and certain knowledge, from the Word of God, of God's good will and free mercy on account of Christ, revealed through the Holy Spirit and sealed in the hearts. This, I say, is such a definition that nothing more could be wanted in it that pertains to explaining the nature of faith. For it is most full, and the rules of a good definition apply to it.

units.la: Porrò nos iam ostendemus, eadem omnia posse deprehendi inclusa in definitione fidei, quam Apostolus hic nobis propositum, dicens: Fides est ὑπόστασις rerum sperandarum, & ἔλεγχος non apparentium. Primum ὑπόστασις & ἔλεγχος nònne clarissimè significat firmam cognitionem, imò longè efficacius euidentiusque, quàm vlla alia vox id posset? Certè substisubsistentia & euictio aliquid latentis energiæ habent, quod alijs vocibus non posset exprimi: & propterea statuendum est, singulari iudicio Apostolum istas voces selegisse. Iam fi adeò certa est cognitio, vnde obsecro habebit certitudinē? Ex verbo hominūne? Atqui omnis homo medax. Igitur ex verbo Dei, quod solum verum est & stabile, & cui foli tutū est credere. Cœlum & terra transibunt, verbum autē Domini manet in æternū. Itaq; palàm fit, nō posse esse ὑπόστασιν aut ἔλεγχον, nisi quatenus verbo innitatur, & ad verbum referatur, & verbis illis, clarè significari certitudinem ex verbo petitam. Et cùm Apostolus protulerit huiusmodi definitionem fidei, apud eos, qui iam non infœliciter erant instituti, quis potuisset intelligere firmam hypoftafin seu elenchū fine Dei verbo? Igitur & hæc particula, Ex verbo Dei, etiam in Paulina definitione inclusa latet. Eadem ratione particulas illas, quòd videlicet fides per spiritum Sanctum reuelerur, quodq; per eundē obsignetur in cordibus, reuera in ijsdem vocibus, ὑπόστασις inquam, & ἔλεγχος, esse repositas, manifestum debet euadere. Cùm enim fides fit donum Dei: deinde tam firma & insuperabilis subsistentia euictioq;, humanis viribus nec parari eam posse, nec retineri, quivis mediocriter in ijs, quę sunt religionis, edoctus per sese videt, & quilibet in vocibus ὑπόστασις ἔλεγχος tantundem animo complectebatur. Esse donum Dei, & idcir co opus spiritus Sancti, non solū oraculis vel doctriua Apostolorum id probabatur, sed etiam ipsa experiētia hoc demonstrabat, cùm viderent, perpaucos ad fidem peruenire: deinde, paucissimos perstare. Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum. Caro & sanguis non reuelat, sed pater meus, qui est in cœlo. Cæteræ verò particulæ illæ, de voluntate Dei bona, ac misericordia gratuita propter Christum, includuntur in illis verbis, de rebus sperandis, & non apparentibus. Quomodo quis speret aliquid, nisi primùm constet ei de bona voluntate promittentis?
units.tr: We will now show that all these same things can be found contained in the definition of faith that the Apostle sets before us here, saying: "Faith is hypostasis of things hoped for, and elenchos of things not seen" [ὑπόστασις ... ἔλεγχος]. First, does not hypostasis and elenchos most clearly signify firm knowledge, indeed far more effectively and evidently than any other word could? Certainly subsistence and conviction have a certain hidden energy that could not be expressed by other words, and therefore it must be held that the Apostle chose these words by singular judgment. Now if knowledge is so certain, whence, I ask, will it have its certainty? From the word of men? But every man is a liar. Therefore from the Word of God, which alone is true and stable, and to which alone it is safe to trust: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but the word of the Lord remains forever." Thus it is plain that there cannot be hypostasis or elenchos unless it rests upon the word and is referred to the word, and those words clearly signify that certainty is sought from the Word. And since the Apostle put forward this definition of faith before those who were already not unhappily instructed, who could have understood firm hypostasis or elenchos without the Word of God? Therefore this phrase, "from the Word of God," is also hidden within the Pauline definition. By the same reasoning, it ought to become evident that those phrases, namely that faith is revealed through the Holy Spirit and sealed by the same Spirit in the hearts, are truly contained in those very words, hypostasis I mean, and elenchos. For since faith is the gift of God, such firm and unconquerable subsistence and conviction can be neither produced nor retained by human powers. Anyone moderately instructed in matters of religion sees this for himself, and whoever heard the words hypostasis and elenchos grasped this equally in mind. That faith is the gift of God, and therefore the work of the Holy Spirit, was proved not only by the oracles and teaching of the Apostles; experience itself demonstrated it, since they saw that very few come to faith, and then that very few persevere. "No one comes to me unless the Father draws him." "Flesh and blood does not reveal, but my Father who is in heaven." The remaining phrases, concerning God's good will and free mercy on account of Christ, are included in those words of things hoped for, and not seen. How could anyone hope for something unless it were first established for him that the one promising is of good will?

units.la: Ergo quando pronuntur res sperandæ, simul voluntas Dei præsupponitur.
units.tr: Therefore, when the things to be hoped for are named, the will of God is presupposed at the same time.

units.la: Deinde, quando spes propriè est de bonis, sicut è contrario metus proprie de malis, palàm fit, fidem esse de voluntate Dei, qua exhibet ipse nobis misericordiam. Iram eṅ nim Dei ac iudiciū quis dicatur sperare? Formidanda hæc est & metuēda, non speranda.
units.tr: Further, since hope properly concerns good things, just as fear properly concerns evils, it is plain that faith concerns the will of God, by which he himself offers us mercy. For who would say that a person hopes for the wrath and judgment of God? That is to be dreaded and feared, not hoped for.

units.la: Sed difficile est ostēdere, aliquid haberi de gratuita misericordia, in definitione Pauli. Imò difficile non est, ex illa voce, rerum sperādarum, gratis contingere misericordiam, demonstrare. Quod enim quis propter opera sua vel laborem expectat, præsertim à bono & æquo homine, non dicitur id sperare, sed potius suo iure reposcere. Et vbi constat, boni & æqui amante virū esse, qui reddere debet, is cui debet, nō dicit, se sperare, sed certò statuet, quòd accipiet id, quæ ipsi debetur. Verum, si improbus esset is, qui debet merce dem, atq; omnia deplorata, adeoq; non esset spes recipiendi, pòst aūt iterum affulgeret aliquid, vnde existimaret, sibi satisfaciendum, tūm diceret is, se sperare adhuc, quòd recepturus sit mercedem: sed de bono viro non ita iudicat. Igitur, quando à Deo optimo maximoq; dicitur aliquis aliquid sperare, id reuera intelligitur non vt mercedem expectare, sed vt gratuitum donum, ex mera contingens liberalitate, nullis meritis vel operibus præeuntibus. Rursus autem quia aliqua caussa videtur requiri, quæ Deū moueat ad conferendum bona spiritualia, & nulla inueniatur caussa ex parte nostra, necessum est intueri Christum, & statuere, quòd propter hunc Deus pater velit misereri, præser-tim cùm sciamus, Christum esse illum, in quo solo patri est complacitum: item hanc esse regulam omnium promissionum, quòd videlicet propter Christum sint factæ, & propter Christum adimplendæ. Quando igitur in definitione, quam Apostolus hic adhibuit, omnia spectantur, quæcunq; in alia pleniore definitione possent explicari, & tota natura fidei satis dilucidè adeò paucis verbis describitur, manifestū est, iustam absolutamq; definitionem hīc esse positam, & non tantùm obscuram descriptionem, aut qualemcunque commendationem.
units.tr: Yet it is hard to show that something is included about free mercy in Paul's definition. Indeed, it is not hard to demonstrate from that phrase, "the things hoped for," that mercy comes freely. For when someone expects something because of his works or labor, especially from a good and just man, he is not said to hope for it, but rather to claim it as his due. And when it is known that the man who ought to repay is a good and just lover of right, the one to whom he owes does not say that he hopes, but firmly concludes that he will receive what is owed to him. But if the man who owed the wages were dishonest, and all things had been given up for lost, so that there was no hope of recovering them, and then something flashed up again by which he thought he must be paid, then the creditor would say that he still hopes to receive his wages. But a good man does not judge in this way. Therefore, when someone is said by God, the best and greatest, to hope for something, this is really understood not as expecting a wage, but as a free gift, given purely by an unforced generosity, with no merits or works going before. Again, since some cause seems to be required that moves God to bestow spiritual goods, and no cause is found on our side, we must look to Christ and hold that God the Father wills to show mercy on account of him, especially since we know that Christ is the one in whom alone the Father is well pleased. Likewise this is the rule for all promises: that they are made on account of Christ and are fulfilled on account of Christ. Therefore, when in the definition the Apostle uses here all the things are taken into account that could be explained in a fuller definition, and the whole nature of faith is described quite clearly in so few words, it is evident that a just and complete definition has been set down here, and not merely an obscure description or some sort of commendation.

units.la: Sed iam vt adhuc clarius perspiciatis naturam fidei, nec non definitionis habitæ integritatem, & quid per ὑπόστασιν seu ἔλεγχον intelligi coueniat, lubet exéplum in medium producere, ex quo omnia manifestiora euadent.
units.tr: But now, so that you may perceive more clearly the nature of faith, and the completeness of the definition given, and what ought to be understood by hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] or elenchos [ἔλεγχον], let us bring forward an example from which all these things will become clearer.

units.la: Quemadmodū autem Abrahæ insignis fides proponitur alibi ab Apostolo, ad comprobandum, quòd homines fide iustificentur, ita eiusdem Abrahæ fidem puro commo difsimè posse & hīc à nobis proponi, ad ostendendam naturā fidei, & quid per ὑπόστασιν seu ἔλεγχον intelligi coueniat. Sic vero Apostolus Abrahæ fidem Romanorum capite quarto, scitissimè depingit suis coloribus, dicens: Qui præter spem sub spe credidit, se fore patrem multarum gentium, iuxta id, quod dictum est: Sic erit semen tuum. Ac non infirmatus fide haud consideraùit suum ipsius corpus iam emortuum, quùm centumferè natus esset annos, nec emortuam vuluam Saræ: verùm ad promissionem fidei non hæsitabat ob incredulitatem, sed robustus factus est fide, tribuens gloriam Deo,
units.tr: Just as the Apostle elsewhere sets forth the remarkable faith of Abraham to prove that men are justified by faith, so we can very fittingly set forth the same faith of Abraham here, to show the nature of faith and what ought to be understood by hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] or elenchos [ἔλεγχον]. Now the Apostle, in Romans chapter four, depicts the faith of Abraham most skilfully in its own colours, saying: "Who, against hope, believed in hope, that he should become the father of many nations, according to what was said: So shall your seed be. And not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body, already dead, since he was about a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sarah. But he did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief; rather, he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God,

units.la: Rom. 2. Verbo Dei nihil solidius. Fides per spiritum Sanctum reuelatur, et in cordibus per eundem obsignatur. 1. fides insuperabilis subsistentia. Fidem Dei donum esse. Ioan. 6. Matth. 16. certa persuasione concepta, quòd is, qui promiserat, idem potens esset & præstare. Quapropter etiam imputatum est illi adiustitiam.
units.tr: Rom. 2. Nothing is more solid than the Word of God. Faith is revealed by the Holy Spirit and is sealed in hearts by the same Spirit. 1. Faith is an unconquerable subsistence. That faith is a gift of God. John 6. Matt. 16. Faith is conceived with a firm persuasion that he who had promised was also able to do what he promised. For this reason it was also reckoned to him for righteousness."

units.la: Hæc ibi. Habemus autem hic valde artificiose descriptam fidei naturam, & propriè ὑπόστασιν seu ἔλεγχον, de quibus nunc differimus. Vt verò clarius assequamur ista, repetenda est nobis breviter Abrahæ historia. Genesis cap. 12. cùm Abraham esset 75. annorum, promissio ad eum facta est, faciam te in gentem magnam, & benedicam tibi, & magnificabo nomen tuum, eris·que benedictus. Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, & maledicam maledicentibus tibi: atque in te benedicentur vniuersæ cognationes terræ. His tamen nihil spei apparebat, sed adhuc multas pertulit molestias, & propter communem famem coactus est ire in Ægyptum.
units.tr: So far the Apostle. We have here a nature of faith described very skilfully, and properly the hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] or elenchos [ἔλεγχον], which we are now discussing. But so that we may grasp these things more clearly, we must briefly recall the history of Abraham. In Genesis chapter 12, when Abraham was seventy-five years old, the promise was made to him: "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." Yet nothing of hope appeared in these words; rather, he still suffered many troubles, and because of a general famine he was forced to go down into Egypt.

units.la: Postea iterum reuersus adiuit adhuc semel similem promissionem Genes. 13. non multo post bellum gesit cum quinque regibus: & obtinuit victoriam: Genes. 4. Iterum Genes. 15. narratur quomodo Abraham deplorarit apud Deum, se sine liberis moriturum, & hæredem fore sibi vernaculum Eliezer, cui Dominus educes eum foras, Suspice, inquit, cœlum & numera stellas, si potes. Sic erit, inquit, Semen tuum: Mox subijcitur: Credidit Abraham Deo, & reputatum est illi ad iustitiam. Sed nulla ne tùm quidem adhuc affulgebat spes, tametsi annis aliquot post repetita denuò esset promissio. Qua de causa Sara de prole desperans, Genes. 16. rogat Abraham: um, vt ancillæ Agar sese commisceat, & ex ea sobolem procreet: quod & fecit Abraham, natusque est ei Ismael, cùm iam annum ageret octoagesimum sextum. Cùm verò Abraham, vt habetur Genesis capite decimo septimo, iam ingressus esset annum nonagesimum nonum, iterum audiuit aliam promissionem, quòd pater foret multarum gentium, cum institutione Signi circumcisionis. Quàm multa ipse Abraham iam admirabundus coactus est secum dicere? Putas' ne centenario nascetur filius, & Sara nonagenaria pariet, cui, (vt additur capite decimo octauo) muliebria fieri desierant? Tandem verò post alia adhuc tolerata pericula sublata fuit Sara per Abimelech, cùm Abraham centum esset annorum, nascitur ei filius Isaac.
units.tr: Afterwards, when he returned, he heard a similar promise once more, in Genesis 13. Not long after, he waged war with five kings and gained the victory (Genesis 14). Again, in Genesis 15, it is told how Abraham complained before God that he would die without children, and that his heir would be Eliezer, his home-born servant. The Lord led him outside and said: "Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you can. So shall your seed be." Immediately it is added: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness." Yet even then no hope yet shone forth, although the promise was repeated again some years later. For this reason Sarah, despairing of offspring, asked Abraham in Genesis 16 to go in to her maidservant Hagar and beget a child by her. Abraham did so, and Ishmael was born to him when he was eighty-six years old. When Abraham, as we read in Genesis chapter 17, had already entered his ninety-ninth year, he heard another promise, that he would be the father of many nations, together with the institution of the sign of circumcision. How many things did Abraham himself, already amazed, feel compelled to say to himself? "Shall a child be born to a man of a hundred years? And shall Sarah, at ninety, bear a child?" She, as is added in chapter 18, had ceased to have the ways of women. At last, after other dangers had been endured, Sarah was taken away by Abimelech, and when Abraham was a hundred years old, Isaac was born to him.

units.la: Proinde, si rectè supputamus à prima promissione facta de multiplicando semine vsque ad natiuitatem Isaac, cum totpericulis, peregrinationibus, bellis & amissa propemodum Sara ipsa, intercesserunt anni vigintiquinque. Possemus adhuc adijcere, quomodo iterum omnis spes posteritatis Abrahæ sublata fuerit, quando iussus est à tentante Deo filium illum vnigenitum charissimum procul abducere, atque immolare. Hic certè iterum spes tot annorum (fere 40.) prorsus intercidisset. Et facta est tùm promissio illa memorabilis, quòd in Semine ipsius benedicendæ forent omnes gentes. In hoc igitur rerum cursu Deus bone quale exercitium fidei licet videre in Abrahamo?
units.tr: Accordingly, if we count correctly from the first promise, made about the multiplying of the seed, down to the birth of Isaac, there passed twenty-five years, with so many dangers, journeys, wars, and Sarah herself nearly lost. We could add how, again, all hope of Abraham's posterity was taken away when he was commanded by God, who was testing him, to lead away his only and most beloved son and offer him in sacrifice. Here, surely, the hope of so many years (about forty) would have utterly perished. And then that memorable promise was made, that in his Seed all the nations would be blessed. In this course of events, good God, what a training of faith can be seen in Abraham!

units.la: Quis enim ibi non plus millies desperasset? Imò quis non quotidie contemptisset tot & toties promissa, de quorum adimpletione nullum vsquam apparebat vestigium? Si homo cum homine sic ageret, planè aut rideri, aut perfidè fraudari alterum omnes iudicarent. Hic, hic planè licet cernere, quid proprie sit ὑπόστασις rerum sperandarum, quid ἔλεγχος non apparentiū, propter huiusmodi hypostasin & elenchum non apparentium, & tantum spiritualium, ita placuit loqui Apostolo Romanorum capite quarto, Præter Spem sub spe credidit. Corpus ipsius iam erat emortuum. Sarae item desierant fieri muliebtria: tot annni iam intercesserant à prima illa promissione, vsque ad præsentem: tot moles-tiæ, tot pericula insuper obuenerunt: periclitatus etiam aliquoties de ipsa vxore amittenda, ex qua nasci debebat promissus filius: imò ipse de sua vita propria creberrimè periclitatus, quomodo hic potuisset manere vlla subsistentia vel elenchus? 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6.
units.tr: For who there would not have despaired a thousand times over? Indeed, who would not every day have scorned so many and such repeated promises, of whose fulfilment no trace anywhere appeared? If a man dealt in this way with another man, everyone would judge that the other was either mocking him or faithlessly cheating him. Here, here indeed one can see what hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] of things hoped for properly is, and what elenchos [ἔλεγχος] of things not seen is; on account of such a hypostasis and elenchos of things not seen, and only spiritual, the Apostle chose to speak in Romans chapter four: "Against hope, he believed in hope." His body was already dead. The ways of women had also ceased in Sarah. So many years had already passed since that first promise, down to the present; so many troubles and dangers had moreover come upon him; he was also more than once in danger of losing his very wife, from whom the promised son was to be born; indeed, he himself was very often in danger of his own life. How, in these circumstances, could any hypostasis or elenchos remain? 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6.

units.la: Humana ratio non poterat assequi, tale quiddam futurum: ipsa naturæ lex vitæ est abhorrere: consilia nulla, nullus modus superesse videbatur, quo spes eius vel leuiter salutem potuisset confirmari: & tamen vt Apostolus subijcit, ad promissionem fidei non hæsitabat, ὃ ἀσθενῶν, inquit, id est, non ambigebat, non disceptabat, non disquirebat, an ne fieri id posset nec ne: sed robustus factus est fide, tribuens gloriam Deo, certa persuasione concepta, quòd is, qui promiserat, idem potens esset præstare.
units.tr: Human reason could not grasp that such a thing would come to pass. The law of nature itself is to shrink from death; no counsel or means appeared, by which her hope could be even slightly strengthened. Yet, as the Apostle adds, she did not waver in the promise of faith: who was weak [ὃ ἀσθενῶν], that is, she did not doubt, did not dispute, did not inquire whether it could happen or not. Rather she was made strong in faith, giving glory to God, with the firm conviction that he who had promised was also able to perform it.

units.la: In hac igitur virtute, cùm videlicet ita, vbi non solùm nihil apparet eorum quæ promissa sunt, verùm etiam plurima occurrunt impedimenta, quæ nos à sperando auocent, tamen adhuc constanter perfistitur, consistit proprie hypostasis.
units.tr: In this virtue, then, when nothing of what is promised appears, but many obstacles present themselves that would draw us away from hoping, and yet one still persists constantly, there properly consists the substance [ὑπόστασις].

units.la: Cùm non inquirimus, quomodo potest istud fieri? quomodo posse-bile est, vt talia bona accipiam? Cùm contemnimus dictamen rationis, suggestiones diaboli, imò totius mundi iudicium, & solas promissiones Dei intuemur, tribuentes Deo hanc gloriam, quòd salutem nostram perficere lubenter & velit, & facilè possit: hic veram esse in nobis ὑπόστασιν rerum sperandarum ostendimus. Huiusmodi πληροφορία certa perfuafio, quæ nunquam possit ex animo dimoueri, aduersus quam, Christo teste Matthæi capite decimo sexto, ne portæ quidem inferorum possunt præualere, est, quæ hic appellatur ὑπόστασις siue ἔλεγχος. Sed hæc sint satis.{a}
units.tr: We do not ask, "How can this come about? How is it possible that I should receive such good things?" When we set aside the verdict of reason, the suggestions of the devil, and even the judgement of the whole world, and look only to the promises of God, ascribing to God this glory, that he both willingly wishes and easily can complete our salvation, then we show that the true substance [ὑπόστασιν] of things hoped for is in us. This kind of full assurance [πληροφορία], a certain persuasion that can never be removed from the mind, and against which, as Christ testifies in Matthew chapter sixteen, the gates of hell cannot prevail, is what is here called hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] or proof [ἔλεγχος]. But let these things suffice.{a}

units.la: Nec video, quomodo crasius possem explicare, quid per has voces intelligi conueniat, quàm proposito hoc exèplo Abrahæ, & de eodem verbis Apostoli, quæ ex Rom. 4. iam citauimus.
units.tr: Nor do I see how I could explain more plainly what these words ought to be understood to mean than by setting forth this example of Abraham, and the Apostle's words about him, which we have already cited from Romans chapter four.

units.la: Constat igitur, per Apostolum hisce vocibus, ὑπόστασις & ἔλεγχος, fidei proprietatem, adeoque totam naturam optimè expressam, & definitionem hanc optimè conditam.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that through these words, hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] and proof [ἔλεγχος], the Apostle has very well expressed the property of faith, and so its whole nature, and that this definition is very well framed.

units.la: Cæterùm, quando hoc pacto fides vocatur ὑπόστασις & ἔλεγχος, duo fœdisimi errores hic reuincuntur scholasticorum & sententiariorum. Alter, quòd statuunt, fidem esse posse sine dilectione seu charitate, talem inde facientes definitionem, qua diuidunt fidem in informem & formatam, informem eam appellantes, quæ consistat sine charitate, quam etiam dæmonibus concedunt: formatam verò eam, quæ per dilectionem operetur. Alter est, quòd docent, neminem posse statuere, an Deo acceptus sit, id est, vt ipsi loquuntur, num sit in gratia Dei. Quin etiam hic simul cadit illa distinctio de fide implicita & explicita. Sed de illis duobus erroribus potissimum est nobis paulò plenius disserendum.
units.tr: Moreover, when faith is called in this way hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] and proof [ἔλεγχος], two most foul errors of the schoolmen and the Sentences writers are refuted here. The first is that they hold that faith can exist without love or charity, making from this such a definition, by which they divide faith into unformed and formed: calling unformed that which subsists without charity, which they even grant to the demons, but formed that which works through love. The second is that they teach that no one can determine whether he is acceptable to God, that is, as they themselves put it, whether he is in the grace of God. Indeed, that distinction between implicit and explicit faith also falls here at the same time. But it is especially about these two errors that we must discuss somewhat more fully.

units.la: Primùm, inquam, quomodo potest vocari fides, cui adiuncta non sit charitas? Vt enim quis assentiatur, & quidem constantissimè, promissioni diuinæ, qua promittitur salus & liberatio, & vita æterna, quomodo possit istud fieri, quin simul Deum promittentem talia ac tanta bona vehementissimè diligat?
units.tr: First, I say, how can that be called faith to which charity is not joined? For how can anyone assent, and indeed most constantly, to the divine promise, by which salvation and deliverance and eternal life are promised, without at the same time loving most intensely God who promises such and so great goods?

units.la: Si vel homo quispiam esset, qui promitteret nobis, se daturum hæreditatem suam, item immunitatem & alia huiusmodi, certè eius promissionibus non credemus, quin simul eum toto animo diligamus, paratique erimus vicissim quævis in eius gratiam facere. Aut, quomodo sperare audeas, te ab illo accepturum bona, quem putas tibi non impensissimè fauere, & erga quem vicissim non sis pari affectus animo? præsertim, quando is tuum potest animum inspicere? Quomodo obsecro Abraham, cuius exemplum supra propositum, potuisset sic in fide perfistere, si non maximè dilexisset? Vera igitur fides non potest intelligi, vbi simul non est ardentissima Dei dilectio.
units.tr: If there were some man who promised us that he would give us his inheritance, and likewise immunity and other such things, surely we would not believe his promises without at the same time loving him with our whole heart, and we would be ready in turn to do whatever for his favour. Or how would you dare to hope that you will receive good things from one whom you think does not very greatly favour you, and towards whom you are not in turn of a like disposition of mind? Especially when he can look into your mind! How, I ask, could Abraham, whose example was set forth above, have persevered thus in faith, if he had not loved most greatly? True faith therefore cannot be understood where at the same time there is not most ardent love of God.

units.la: Per fidem proprie certi reddimur de dilectione Dei erga nos: quomodo ergo huiusmodi fides sit in nobis, si Deum non vicissim diligamus? Hinc illæ ex vera fide ebullientes voces, Romanorum capite octauo; Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? &c.
units.tr: Through faith we are properly made certain of God's love towards us. How then can such faith be in us if we do not in turn love God? Hence those words, bursting forth from true faith, in Romans chapter eight: "Who shall separate us from the love of God?" etc.

units.la: Non charitas format fidem, sed è contrario fides format charitatem, vt charitas nusquam eluceat, nisi vbi simul adsit fides. Fides non est otiosa quædam æqualitas, quæ consistit in corde frigido & segni, sed omninò vitiida est, & necessariò producit aliquos fructus, testatum facientes, ipsam esse veram, & ita erga Deum constitutam, qualem esse oportet. Apparet autem, motos esse sophistas illis locis, quia alibi vident scriptum, Iacobi capite secundo, Dæmones credunt, & contremiscunt: ac de dæmonibus nullo pacto concedendum, quòd charitatem habeant.
units.tr: It is not charity that forms faith, but on the contrary faith forms charity, so that charity shines forth nowhere except where faith is also present at the same time. Faith is not some idle equality that consists in a cold and sluggish heart, but it is wholly living, and necessarily produces some fruits, showing that it is true and that a person stands towards God as he ought. It appears, however, that the sophists were moved by those places, because elsewhere they see it written, in James chapter two, "The demons believe and tremble"; and it must in no way be conceded about the demons that they have charity.

units.la: Igitur quandam esse fidem sine charitate. Rursus verò Galatar. capite quinto, ita legitur: In Christo Iesu neq; circumcisio quicquam valet, neq; præputium, sed fides per dilectionem operans. Hinc ergo aliam finem imaginati sunt, quæ perficeretur accedente charitate. Sed non vident isti, quid vtrobique agatur. Ineptæ & ridiculæ sunt distinctiones.
units.tr: Therefore they say there is a certain faith without charity. Again, however, in Galatians chapter five it is read thus: "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." Hence they have imagined another kind of faith, which is perfected by the addition of charity. But these men do not see what is being done on either side. Their distinctions are silly and ridiculous.

units.la: Respiciamus in præsentem definitionem Apostoli, & inueniemus, vnam tantùm esse fidem fidei appellatione dignam, quæ sit ὑπόστασις & ἔλεγχος rerum sperandarum, apprehendens beneficia propter Christum. Atque hæc est perfecta fides.
units.tr: Let us look at the Apostle's present definition, and we will find that there is only one faith worthy of the name of faith, which is the substance [ὑπόστασις] and proof [ἔλεγχος] of things hoped for, laying hold of the benefits on account of Christ. And this is perfect faith.

units.la: Locus autem ille Iacobi non de fide accipiendus est, de qua nos hic loquimur, sed de cognitione quadam, quæ fidem antecedit, quæque in verbo discenda proponitur. Est tantùm notitia rerum gestarum, qua creditur simpliciter, acta ac gesta esse, quæ nobis in Scripturis gesta proponuntur. Quod liquet ex exemplo, quod ipse ibi proponit, dicens: Tu credis, quòd Deus vnus est? recte facis: Dæmonia credunt ac contremiscunt. Atque hoc pacto verum est, quòd credunt etiam dæmones gesta esse, quæ nobis in Scripturis proponuntur: credunt item, Christum natum de virgine: credunt eundem esse filium Dei, & aliquoties confessi sunt: credunt ascendisse in cœlos: denique nihil non hoc modo credunt. Sed non habent hanc fidem, quæ vocatur fides rerum sperandarum, hoc est, non credunt etc.
units.tr: But that passage of James is not to be understood of the faith of which we are speaking here, but of a certain knowledge that precedes faith, and which is set forth to be learned in the Word. It is only a knowledge of the things done, by which one simply believes that those things which are set before us as done in the Scriptures were in fact done and performed. This is clear from the example that he himself sets forth there, saying: "Do you believe that God is one? You do well: the demons believe and tremble." And in this way it is true that the demons also believe that the things set before us in the Scriptures were done: they likewise believe that Christ was born of a virgin; they believe that he is the Son of God, and have confessed it on several occasions; they believe that he ascended into heaven; in short, they believe nothing that is not believed in this way. But they do not have that faith which is called the faith of things hoped for, that is, they do not believe etc.

units.la: {a} Matth. 16.
units.tr: {a} Matt. 16.

units.la: promissiones spirituales erga nos adimplendas: non credunt, Deum velle nobis esse propter Christum propitium: non credunt, recipi nos in gratiam propter Christum: offerri nobis propter Christum misericordiam. Obiectum fidei illorum est veritas rerum gestarum, nullo habito respectu ad gratuitam misericordiam. Obiectum fidei nostrae est veritas rerum sperandarum, & assensus in promissiones propter Christum erga nos adimplendas. Illius modi fides, fatemur, semper debet praeire: post vero sequitur firmus assensus rerum sperandarum, qui est fides absoluta ab Apostolo hic descripta. Talem fidem temporibus Iacobi iactabant multi, & existimabant eam sufficere: sed Apostolus adhuc requisiuit illam posteriorem. Illa enim tantum introductio quaedam est, & velut accessio, rudibus animis primum ingrediunda, (quomodo enim credent, nisi prius audierint?) sed ista fides rerum sperandarum non nisi prius adiuuante spiritu succedit. Illa fides sine spiritu Sancto habetur, nam daemonibus tribuitur: at haec fides sine spiritu Sancto non habetur.
units.tr: spiritual promises to be fulfilled towards us. They do not believe that God wishes to be merciful to us on account of Christ; they do not believe that we are received into grace on account of Christ; that mercy is offered to us on account of Christ. The object of their faith is the truth of things done, with no regard had to free mercy. The object of our faith is the truth of things hoped for, and assent to the promises to be fulfilled towards us on account of Christ. We confess that this kind of faith must always go before; afterwards there follows the firm assent to things hoped for, which is the complete faith described here by the Apostle. Many in James's time boasted of the former kind of faith and thought it sufficient; but the Apostle still required the latter. For the former is only a certain introduction and, as it were, an approach, to be entered first by untrained minds (for how will they believe, unless they have first heard?); but this faith in things hoped for does not follow except by the prior help of the Spirit. The former faith is had without the Holy Spirit, for it is attributed to the demons; but this faith is not had without the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Itaque improprie fides appellatur, nec fidei nomine digna est, cum tantum sit quoddam veluti illectamentum ad fidem, & rudis praeparatio: ad quam postea requiritur assensus, & quidem in promissiones de misericordia expectanda. Hic vero longe aliares est, & modo obuia, & in promptu. Tolerabile esset, si dicerent, initio fidei, & fidem vel imperfectam vel perfectam: quamvis non hoc satis proprie fieret. Imperfecta enim est, quae vera quidem sit, sed nondum adulta: sicut apostoli petebant, sibi fidem augeri.
units.tr: Therefore it is improperly called faith, and is not worthy of the name of faith, since it is only a kind of enticement to faith and a crude preparation; to which afterwards assent is required, and indeed assent to the promises of mercy to be awaited. Here, however, it is far otherwise, and it is ready to hand and at the surface. It would be tolerable if they spoke of the beginning of faith, and of faith either imperfect or perfect; although this would not be said quite properly. For that is imperfect which is indeed true, but not yet grown up, just as the apostles asked that their faith be increased.

units.la: Iam, quod fidem vocant formatam, cui adiuncta sit charitas: iuxta illud Galat. capite quinto, turpissime & ibi hallucinantur. Neque enim ibi sermo est de perfectione fidei, quasi sine illa charitate non sit perfecta: sed de effectu fidei: quia nimirum fides charitatem necessario producit: id quod nec Sententiarij ipsi prorsus dissimulant, concedentes, fidem proprie dici fundamentum, sic sibi ipsis contradicentes.
units.tr: Now as to what they call "formed" faith, to which charity is joined, appealing to Galatians chapter five: they are shamefully mistaken here too. For the passage is not speaking of the perfection of faith, as if faith without that charity were not perfect. It speaks of the effect of faith, because faith necessarily produces charity. Even the Sententiarii themselves do not entirely deny this, granting that faith is properly called the foundation, and so they contradict themselves.

units.la: Fides, ut hic ab Apostolo describitur, vera & perfecta fides est, quatenus versatur circa res sperandas, non quatenus operatur. Fides per se seorsum consideranda est, eique iustificatio propriae tribuenda. Charitas autem seorsum iterum spectabitur, ut fidei accessorium, & fidei testimonii, (qua ratione etiam Iacobus secundo capite vrget opera, quasi signa, videlicet quae fide sequuntur) & hinc diserte dicit Apostolus ibi Gal. 5. Fides per dilectionem operatur, non dicit, fides per dilectionem operas iustificat, vel gratum facit, vel huiusmodi. Quod si deniq; ita fides non perficeretur, nisi per charitate, non redte fidei tribueretur iustificatio: sed deberet tribui charitati, vtpote perfectiori, quod est absurdum, & contra vniuersam doctrinam euangelij. Adferunt & illud 1. Corinth. 13. Si quis omnem fidem habeat, vt montes transferat, charitate vero non habeat, nihil est. Sed non vident, Apostolum, ibi agere, vt doceat, omnia dona spiritus accommodanda esse ad publicam vtilitatem ecclesiae, & ea maxime sectanda, a quibus maior redit ad alios vtilitas. Vsurpat autem hic fidem pro facultate edendi miracula, quam capite duodecimo ibidem vocat dona virtutum: & hanc vult accommodari vtilitati ecclesiae. Vocabulum fidei ωολόνυμον est, quod si animaduertitur, omnis error discutitur. Sed haec satis sint. Consideremus vnam solam perfectam fidem, quae hic describitur, cuius vnius proprium est, accipere a Deo iustitiae imputationem: non temere confundamus fidem & charitatem in iustificationis causa: sed multo minus imaginemur, fidem aliquam esse perfectam, cui deest item charitas. Si hypostasis est & conuictio rerum spiritualium: igitur charitatem in Deum habet, a quo sperat, se illa bona acceptrurum.
units.tr: Faith, as the Apostle describes it here, is true and perfect faith, insofar as it is concerned with things to be hoped for, not insofar as it works. Faith must be considered by itself, and justification must be assigned to it alone. Charity is to be considered again separately, as an accompaniment of faith and a testimony of faith. (It is for this reason that James in the second chapter also insists on works, as signs, namely those which follow faith.) This is why the Apostle says plainly in Galatians 5: "faith works through love." He does not say that faith works through love justifies, or makes us acceptable, or anything of the kind. But if faith were not perfected in this way without charity, then justification would not rightly be assigned to faith; it would have to be assigned to charity, as the more perfect thing. That is absurd and contrary to the whole doctrine of the gospel. They also bring forward 1 Corinthians 13: "If anyone has all faith, so as to move mountains, but does not have charity, he is nothing." But they do not see that the Apostle is there teaching that all the gifts of the Spirit are to be adapted to the common benefit of the Church, and that those are to be pursued above all which bring the greater benefit to others. He here uses "faith" for the power of working miracles, which in chapter twelve of the same letter he calls "gifts of powers," and he wills that this be directed to the good of the Church. The word "faith" is equivocal [ὁμώνυμον]; if this is noticed, every error is dispelled. But let this be enough. Let us consider only the one perfect faith described here, to which alone it belongs to receive from God the imputation of righteousness. Let us not rashly confuse faith and charity as the cause of justification; and much less let us imagine that any faith is perfect which lacks charity as well. If faith is the substance [ὑπόστασις] and the proof of things spiritual, then it has charity towards God, from whom it hopes to receive those good things.

units.la: Iam quod ad alterum errorem illum attinet, quo docent, neminem posse statuere, num sit in gratia, est profecto istud a fidei natura alienissimum. Quomodo enim poterit ὑπόστασις & conuictio certa indubitataq;, vbi adhuc supererit dubitatio? Quomodo ibi erit vera fides, vbi adhuc manet aliqua diffidentia? Ipsa nuda vocabula satis reuincunt errorem, vt nihil amplius de natura fidei in medium producamus.
units.tr: As for the other error, by which they teach that no one can determine whether he is in grace, this is certainly most alien to the nature of faith. For how can there be assurance and certain, indubitable conviction where doubt still remains? How can there be true faith where some distrust still lingers? The bare words themselves sufficiently refute the error, so that we need not bring forward anything further about the nature of faith.

units.la: Per hanc testimonium meruerunt Seniores) Definitioni fidei iam subijcit principalem effectum. Tali enim fidei, qualem definiuit, iustificationem attribuit. Tantundem autem sibi vult, quod ait, patres per fidem testimonium promeritos, atque si diceret, per fidem iustificatos, & ipsius Dei sententia iustos pronunciatos. Id quod licet colligere ex ijs quae mox sequuntur. Ita namque subijcit: Abel per fidem testimonium meruit, quod esset iustus. Iterum, Enoch priusquam transferretur, testimonii meruerat, quod placuisset Deo. Rursus, Noe eius, quae secundum fidem est, iustitiae factus est haeres, Quibus omnibus locutionum formulis prorsus idem dicitur, quod in epistolis ad Romanos vel Galatas verbo iustificandi.
units.tr: "By this faith the elders obtained testimony." Having defined faith, he now adds its principal effect. To such faith as he has defined he attributes justification. Indeed, what he says, that the fathers obtained testimony through faith, means exactly the same as if he said they were justified through faith, and pronounced righteous by the very judgment of God. This may be gathered from what follows immediately. For he continues: "By faith Abel obtained testimony that he was righteous." Again: "Enoch, before he was taken up, had obtained testimony that he pleased God." And again: "Noah became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith." In all these forms of expression exactly the same thing is said as in the epistles to the Romans and Galatians by the word "justify."

units.la: Sic vero alias quoq; testimonium in Scripturis significat Dei de nobis iudicium, bonamque erga nos voluntatem. Vnde & ipsius oracula itemq; promissiones, in quas fidem nostram decet esse omni tempore intentam, testimonia subinde appellantur. Psalmo 118. Inclina cor meum Deus in testimonia tua.
units.tr: Elsewhere too, Scripture uses "testimony" to mean God's judgment concerning us and his good will towards us. Hence his oracles and also his promises, to which our faith ought always to be directed, are from time to time called "testimonies." Psalm 118: "Incline my heart, O God, to your testimonies."

units.la: Testimonium Domini fidele, sapientiam praestans paruulis, iustitiae Domini rectae, laetificantes corda. Quibus locis proprie oracula illa Dei intelliguntur, quibus Deus suam erga nos beneuolentiam expressit, quorum contemplatione veram sapientiam paruuli & humiles peccatores parant, & apprehenduntin corde iustitiam.
units.tr: "The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones; the righteousness of the Lord is right, rejoicing the hearts." In these passages, those oracles of God are properly meant by which God has expressed his good will towards us, and by contemplating which little ones and humble sinners acquire true wisdom, and grasp righteousness in the heart.

units.la: Ergo, cum dicitur, Seniores per fidem meruisse testimonium, perinde id est, atq; si diceretur Deum edidisse testimonium, quo testatus est suam erga ipsos voluntatem, quòd nimirum eos pro iustis reputarit. Sicut pater testimonium edidit de filio, esse nempe eum, in quo sibi bene erat complacitum: ita edit testimonium similiter de pijs, significans eos esse, qui sibi placeant propter vnicum filium Christum. Quod testimonium patris de pijs licet non eadem ratione proferatur aperta voce de caelis, sicut prolatum est de vnico filio, tamen interea notum fit, tum ex veris fructibus fidei, per quos pij inter dum etiam foris discernuntur ab impijs: tum ex occulto testimonio Spiritus animos nostros de bona Dei voluntate latenter confirmatis, iuxta illud Romanorum capite octauo, Spiritus testificatur vnà cū spiritu nostro, quòd sumus filij Dei. Sanè qui hoc habet testimonium, verè apud Deum iustificatus est. Atque hoc modo Sancti patres omnes testimonium Dei per spiritum apud sese habuerunt. Neque enim Deo satis est, quòd ipse quidem electos suos acceptos habeat, sed vult praeterea hos ipsos certos facere, ideoque largitur spiritum Sanctum, qui de patris voluntate iudicioque certiores faciat & confirmet. Hoc igitur est, quod ait, patres per fidem testimonium consecutos, testimonium, inquam, apud Deum: deinde certitudinem eius testimonij apud sese per spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: Therefore, when it is said that the elders obtained testimony through faith, it is just the same as if it were said that God issued a testimony by which he attested his good will towards them, namely that he counted them as righteous. Just as the Father bore witness concerning the Son, that he is the one in whom he is well pleased, so he likewise bears witness concerning the godly, signifying that they are those who please him for the sake of his only Son Christ. Although this testimony of the Father concerning the godly is not delivered in the same way, with an audible voice from heaven, as it was delivered concerning the only Son, nevertheless it becomes known, partly from the true fruits of faith, by which the godly are at times distinguished even outwardly from the ungodly, and partly from the hidden testimony of the Spirit, which secretly confirms our minds about the good will of God, according to Romans chapter eight: "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God." Surely whoever has this testimony is truly justified before God. And in this way all the holy fathers had the testimony of God within themselves through the Spirit. For it is not enough for God that he himself holds his elect as accepted; he wills besides to make these same persons certain of it, and therefore he bestows the Holy Spirit, who assures and confirms them of the Father's will and judgment. This, then, is what he means when he says that the fathers obtained testimony through faith: testimony, I say, before God, and then the certainty of that testimony within themselves through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ac videtur reuera nostrae iustificationis modus aliquanto euidentius significanti usque exprimi hac locutionis forma, quàm vocabulo iustificandi. Iustificare enim proprie vocabulum forense est, quo aliquis, qui accusatus fuerit, vt reus ac damnatus, pronunciatur postea, innocens, vel certè absoluitur, vt à crimine immunis. At testimonium ferre aliquanto clarius innuit formam & modum iustificationis nostrae, quod vi delicet contingat iustitiam imputatiue: vt testimonium per Deum ferri, quòd ipsi placeamus, idem fit, quod Deum imputare, & sic accipere nos, quasi iusti simus, cum tamen, quod ad nos attinet, tales nequaquam simus. Sed, quod pro nostra qualitate non sumus, id pensat & farcit Dei iudicium ac testimonium. Si ille sic vult de nobis sentire ac testari, quòd placeamus ipsi propter filiū, id satis est: & protinus tales per diuinam eius virtutem efficimur, quales ille nos reputat iudicatq;.
units.tr: And indeed, the manner of our justification seems to be expressed more clearly by this form of speech than by the word "justify." For "to justify" is properly a forensic term, by which someone who has been accused, as a defendant and condemned, is afterwards pronounced innocent, or at least absolved, as free from the charge. But "to bear testimony" hints somewhat more clearly at the form and manner of our justification, namely that righteousness comes to us by imputation. For to have testimony borne by God that we please him is the same as God imputing it to us and so accepting us as if we were righteous, although as far as we ourselves are concerned, we are by no means such. But what we are not by our own quality, God's judgment and testimony make up for and supply. If he is willing to think and testify about us in this way, that we please him for the sake of the Son, that is enough; and immediately we are made, through his divine power, such as he counts and judges us to be.

units.la: Et hinc quoq; liquet, quomodo accipienda vox μαρτυρέω, quasi diceret: testimonio sunt probati: passiuè enim sonat: licet interpres reddit, testimonium meruerunt.
units.tr: And from this it is also clear how the word μαρτυρέω should be understood, as if he said: "they were approved by testimony." For it has a passive sense; although the translator renders it "they obtained testimony."
