units.la: Neque enim intelligi debet, quòd fides sit eiusmodi qualitas in nobis, cui tanquam actui cuidam per se considerato rependi debeat iustificatio, seu qua nos iustificationem promereamur: non ita, inquam, debemus intelligere modum nostrae iustificationis. Sed cum Deus nobis offerat misericordiam propter Christum, in nobis debet esse fides, qua oblatam gratiam apprehendamus. Tantum apprehendamus per fidem: & id ex parte nostra satis est. Non opera nostra non fides, sunt eiusmodi, vt eis misericordia debeatur: sed Deus acceptat nos, qui credimus, & quasi iustos (cum alias & simus, & manemus, quod ad nos attinet, iniusti) reputat. Ipsa fides sic imputatur ad iustitiam, & iustificatio per fidem est illa iustitiae imputatio. Id quod eo clarius intelligitur, quòd ipsa fides quoque Dei donum est, iuxta illud Ephesiorum capite secundo, Gratia estis seruati per fidem, idque non ex vobis, Dei donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur.
units.tr: For it must not be understood that faith is a quality in us of such a kind that justification is owed to it as to some act considered in itself, or that by it we earn justification. We should not understand the manner of our justification in that way, I say. Rather, since God offers us mercy for Christ's sake, there must be faith in us by which we lay hold of the grace offered. It is enough, on our side, that we apprehend it through faith. Neither our works nor our faith are of such a kind that mercy is owed to them; but God accepts us who believe and counts us as righteous (although as far as we ourselves are concerned, we are and remain unrighteous). Faith itself is thus imputed for righteousness, and justification through faith is that imputation of righteousness. This is understood all the more clearly because faith itself is also a gift of God, according to Ephesians chapter two: "By grace you have been saved through faith, and this not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast."

units.la: Quamobrem non est, quòd, quia inter presita reddidit vocem μαρτυρέω, testimonium meruerunt, & similiter aliquot locis sequentibus, de merito hic disputetur: nisi forte velimus dicere, meritum omne nostrum non in operibus, sed in fide esse: quo sensu & Diuus Ambrosius loquitur. In aliud tempus ea disputatio seruabitur.
units.tr: Therefore there is no reason to dispute here about merit, because in the preceding passage he rendered μαρτυρέω as "they obtained testimony," and similarly in several of the following verses. Unless perhaps we wish to say that all our merit lies not in works but in faith, which is the sense in which Blessed Ambrose also speaks. That discussion will be reserved for another time.

units.la: Porrò valde insignis est haec vis fidei, & ad confirmandos animos, in constanti eius confessione supra quàm dici queat, idonea. Qui enim audit per fidem id obtingere, vt Deo probemur, vt ipse testetur, nos sibi placere, quomodo non paratus sit quaevis potius tius atrocissima perferre, quàm pati, se à fide abduci? Ad confirmandos autem animos propositam esse tam definitione fidei, quę præcessit: quàm hunc fidei effectum: manifestum est, tum ex eo, quòd, vt iam aliquoties diximus omnia in eum finem quæ hic habentur, sint parata: tum ex eo, quod ad finem præsentis capitis eadem verba prorsus in eundem vsum repetuntur: Sic enim ibi legitur.
units.tr: Moreover, this power of faith is very remarkable, and it is wonderfully suited to strengthening souls in their steadfast confession. For who, hearing that it comes about through faith that we are approved by God, so that he himself bears witness that we please him, would not be ready to endure the most atrocious things rather than allow himself to be drawn away from faith? That both the definition of faith given earlier and this effect of faith are set forth to strengthen souls is clear: partly because, as we have said several times, everything that is found here is arranged to that end, and partly because the very same words are repeated, in exactly the same use, at the close of this chapter. For there it reads as follows.

units.la: Atq; omnes hi testimonium promeriti per fidem non acceperant promissionem, quòd Deus de nobis melius quiddam prouiderat, ne sine nobis consummati fuissent.
units.tr: And all these, though they had obtained testimony through faith, did not receive the promise, because God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.

units.la: Vbi clarè vsus horum omnium, atque in quem finem ista omnia in medium sint producta, ostenditur, nimirùm ne diffidant in periculis, sed cum patribus sperent, se promissa bona, si constantes in fide permanserint, accepturos. Et si bene animaduertimus, omnia quæ toto hoc capite continentur, vna argumentationis forma, quam vocant Inductionem, comprehendi possunt.
units.tr: Here it is plainly shown what the use of all these examples is, and to what end all these things have been brought forward: namely, that they should not lose heart in dangers, but, with the fathers, should hope that they will receive the promised good things if they remain steadfast in faith. And if we observe well, everything contained in this whole chapter can be comprehended under one form of argument, which they call induction.

units.la: Primum enim hæc verba, Per hanc Seniores testimonium sunt promeriti, loco propositionis aptissimè accipiantur. Deinde, quę nunc sequuntur exempla, probationis vice sunt posita. Postremò, ad fine capitis, verba propositionis pro conclusione repetuntur, vt omnium horum hæc sit summa.
units.tr: First, these words, "By this faith the elders obtained testimony," are most aptly taken in the place of the proposition. Next, the examples that now follow are set in the place of proof. Finally, at the end of the chapter, the words of the proposition are repeated in place of the conclusion, so that the sum of all these is this:

units.la: Per fidem sancti patres testimonio Dei sunt probati.
units.tr: Through faith the holy fathers were approved by the testimony of God.

units.la: Probatio: Fide enim probatus est Abel.
units.tr: Proof: For by faith Abel was approved.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Enoch.
units.tr: By faith Enoch was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Noah.
units.tr: By faith Noah was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Abraham.
units.tr: By faith Abraham was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificata est Sara.
units.tr: By faith Sarah was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Isaac.
units.tr: By faith Isaac was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Iacob.
units.tr: By faith Jacob was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Ioseph.
units.tr: By faith Joseph was justified.

units.la: Fide iustificatus est Moses.
units.tr: By faith Moses was justified.

units.la: Et nemo est præterea, qui alia ratione fit iustificatus.
units.tr: And there is no one besides who was justified in any other way.

units.la: Ergo omnes per fidem iustificantur, seu testimonio Dei probantur.
units.tr: Therefore all are justified through faith, or approved by the testimony of God.

units.la: Hæc, inquam, clara est, & perspicua omnium, quæ toto hoc capite habentur, sententia: & euidentissimè hic docetur, omnes homines fide iustificari. Præterea aptissima habetur ad pios, vt in fide, quamvis grauiter afflicti, constantes maneant, adhortatio consolatioque.
units.tr: This, I say, is the clear and evident meaning of everything contained in this whole chapter, and it is most plainly taught here that all men are justified by faith. Besides, it is most fittingly offered to the godly as exhortation and consolation, so that they may remain steadfast in faith even when grievously afflicted.

units.la: Cæterum hic statim proponetur principalis fidei effectus, videlicet iustificatio, qui omnes alios effectus, quales passim & in aliis Scripturæ locis, & toto præsenti capite commemorantur, in se comprehendit, & omnium aliorum effectuum spiritualium caput est. Quamobrem diligenter debet hic effectus expendi. Ad Romanos capite quinto & capite octauo, insuper capite præsenti alij effectus referuntur: sed hic est præcipuus.
units.tr: But here at once the principal effect of faith is set forth, namely justification, which comprehends in itself all the other effects that are mentioned here and there in other passages of Scripture and throughout this chapter, and is the head of all the other spiritual effects. Therefore this effect must be weighed carefully. In Romans chapters five and eight, and besides in this chapter, other effects are related, but this is the chief one.

units.la: Per fidem intelligimus perfecta fuisse secula verbo Dei, vt ex hiis, quæ non apparebant, ea quæ videntur, fierent.
units.tr: By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen was made from things that do not appear.

units.la: Iam pergit declarare, quòd per fidem Sancti patres sint iustificati, idque, sicuti iamiam diximus, inductione, seu enumeratione exemplorum.
units.tr: He now goes on to declare that the holy fathers were justified through faith, and he does this, as we have just said, by induction, or by enumerating examples.

units.la: Prius tamen, quàm ad ipsa exempla perueniat, hûc fidei effectum seu officium præmittit, quòd videlicet per eam intelligimus inprimis omnia, quę existunt, à Deo esse creata & perfecta, quæ aliàs quomodo condita sint, aut existere coeperint, ratione humana intelligere nullo modo queamus. Neque enim istud ad inductionem, quæ instituitur, pertinet: neque respondet propositioni, qua dicitur, Seniores per fidem promeritos Dei testimonium. Prudenter autem, & non sine iustissimis causis istud est præmissum.
units.tr: Yet before he comes to the examples themselves, he sets down this effect or office of faith in advance: namely, that through faith we understand first of all that everything that exists has been created and perfected by God, and how these things were otherwise framed, or began to exist, we cannot in any way grasp by human reason. For this does not belong to the induction that is undertaken, nor does it correspond to the proposition, which states that the elders obtained the testimony of God through faith. But this has been prefixed prudently, and not without most just causes.

units.la: Prima causa est, quòd cum dictum sit, fidem ἐλεγχον rerum non apparentium, aptissima sane est ad id comprobandum præsens ratio de prima vniuersi creatione.
units.tr: The first cause is that, since it has been said that faith is the proof [ἔλεγχος] of things not seen, the present reasoning about the first creation of the universe is certainly most apt to confirm this.

units.la: Hæc enim quomodo peracta sit, quandoquidem humana mens nullo modo potest assequi, nihilq; minus intellectui nostro apparet, quàm ex nihilo omnia esse condita: rectissimè statuitur, tantùm fide hanc creationem vniuersi apprehendi posse.
units.tr: For since the human mind cannot in any way attain to how this was accomplished, and nothing is more evident to our understanding than that all things were made out of nothing, it is most rightly laid down that this creation of the universe can be apprehended only by faith.

units.la: Adhibe, inquam, lumen tuæ rationis, quantum quantum in te est, consule omnes archiuos reipublicæ sapientum huius mundi, & nihil inuenies, quod de mundi prima conditione pro certo statuerint. Tantùm videbis mirabiles contencontentiones,& opinionum diuersissimas pugnas, monstrosasque philosophorum magnorum sententias.
units.tr: Bring, I say, the light of your reason, as far as it is in you, consult all the archives of the wisdom of this world's sages, and you will find nothing that they have established with certainty about the first condition of the world. You will see only wonderful contentions, most diverse battles of opinions, and monstrous doctrines of great philosophers.

units.la: In quibus tuendis monstrosis quoque vtuntur vocabulis, cuiusmodi sunt ideæ panspermia, atque id genus alia, vbi voces prodigiosæ portentosas quoque pepererunt opiniones. Primùm inter se digladiantur, num mundus sit æternus, an vero in tempore fuerit conditus. Et in neutram sanè partem adhuc conuentum est: alijs putantibus, fuisse ab æterno, & æternum mansurum: alijs putantibus (ut Platone) in tempore quidem fuisse conditum, sed nunquam finiendum: alijs contrà vt (Democrito) ab æterno fuisse, & in tempore finiendum: & sic deinceps, alij alia rationis cæcæ somnia protulerunt.
units.tr: In defending these they also use monstrous words, such as "ideas," "panspermia," and others of that kind, where prodigious words have also given birth to portentous opinions. First they fight among themselves over whether the world is eternal or was created in time. And indeed they have not yet agreed on either side: some think it existed from eternity and will remain eternally; others think (as Plato did) that it was created in time but will never end; others, on the contrary (as Democritus did), that it existed from eternity and will end in time. And so on, one after another, they have put forward the blind dreams of reason.

units.la: Porrò, qui in eo conuenerunt, quòd mundus in tempore fuerit conditus, tamen ex nihilo conditum nunquam potuerunt imaginando assequi, sed rati sunt, necessariò spectandam præiacentem materiam, & quædam rerum omnium creatarum principia: quia ex nihilo nihil fit.
units.tr: Moreover, those who agreed that the world was created in time could never by imagination reach the idea of creation out of nothing, but thought that a pre-existing matter and certain principles of all created things must necessarily be presupposed, because out of nothing nothing comes.

units.la: Itaque quidam suspicati sunt, omnia ex infinitis minutissimis & atomis corporibus constare, quæ per diuinam mentem rediguntur in ordinem, vt certam formam accipiat: si sensit Anaxagoras Clazomenius. Xenophanes dicebat, vnum esse omnia, & ex illo variis omnia generata, idque solum immutabile. Leucippus, Diodorus, Democritus, plenum & vacuum posuerunt principia. Epicurus atomos & inane: Pythagoras Samius numeris omnia constare censuit. Alij quatuor elementis: nonnulli vno aliquo solo. Thales Milesius ex sola aqua: Anaximenes & Diogenes libertus, infinitum aerem dixere rerum principium. Hipparchus & Heraclitus Ephesius ignem: Parmenides calidum & frigidum, tanquam ignem, qui moueat, & terram, quæ formet. Empedocles quatuor elementa, & præterea litem & amicitiam: Plato ac Socrates Deum, Ideas, materiam: Aristoteles materiam & appetitum formæ per priuationem, quæ tertium quoddam est cōmerens. Vides, qualem syluam confusionum, vbi præter rationem nihil adhibetur in consilium.
units.tr: So some suspected that all things consist of infinitely many very small bodies and atoms, which are brought into order by a divine mind so as to receive a definite form; so Anaxagoras of Clazomenae thought. Xenophanes said that all things are one, and that all things were generated from it in various ways, and that this alone is unchangeable. Leucippus, Diodorus, and Democritus posited the full and the void as principles. Epicurus, atoms and empty space. Pythagoras of Samos thought all things consist of numbers. Others held four elements, and some a single one: Thales of Miletus, water alone; Anaximenes and Diogenes the freedman, infinite air as the principle of things; Hipparchus and Heraclitus of Ephesus, fire; Parmenides, the hot and the cold, as fire which moves and earth which shapes. Empedocles, four elements, and besides strife and love; Plato and Socrates, God, ideas, and matter; Aristotle, matter and the appetite for form through privation, which is a third thing that remains. You see what a forest of confusions this is, where, apart from reason, nothing is taken as counsel.

units.la: Sed hic satis erratum non est, nisi etiam postea mouisset ebria ratio quæstiones, an mundus tantum vnus foret (quod statuerunt Thales & Empedocles) num plures an infiniti, sicut Epicurus & Metrodorus. O stultam & ineptam iudicatricem rerum humanam rationem. Quis te prouexit ad istud tribunal, in quo feras de huiusmodi rebus sententiam? Non potes ipsa aliud, quàm errare, & miseris mortalibus perpetuo omne genus fœdissimorum errorum suggeris. Itaque de his rebus non est nisi fide iudicandum: neque potest humana mens assequi, sit ne mundus conditus in tempore, an extiterit ab æterno: item, ex præiacente materia an secus: item, an plures mundi sint, an vnus tantùm: sed tantùm fides id apprehendit.
units.tr: But the error would not be sufficient, had not blind reason afterwards also raised questions: whether the world was only one (as Thales and Empedocles held), or whether there are several or infinite, as Epicurus and Metrodorus held. O foolish and inept judge, human reason! Who has raised you to that tribunal, where you pronounce judgment on such matters? You can do nothing but err, and you constantly pour out for miserable mortals every kind of most foul error. Therefore in these matters judgment belongs only to faith. Human mind cannot attain whether the world was created in time or existed from eternity; likewise whether it came from pre-existing matter or otherwise; likewise whether there are many worlds or only one. Faith alone grasps this.

units.la: Hæc autem fides ex verbo Dei sumitur, quod nobis in scriptis potissimum propositum est. Illi verbo Dei credamus, & habebimus de conditione vniuersi certas rationes: non quæramus probationes ex scriniis nostrarum mentium, sed sacrum verbum nudè asserens innumerarum probationum vice sit. Non dicamus cum infatuato illo sapiente, si legamus vel audiamus narrationes Mosaicas, Hic philosophus multa dicit, sed nihil probat: verum istud tribuamus Scripturæ, quod impudenter & blasphemè quidam accommodare voluit suis dictis, αὐτὸς ἔφα: Fide, hæc tantùm hic opus est.
units.tr: This faith, however, is drawn from the word of God, which has been set before us chiefly in the Scriptures. Let us believe that word, and we shall have certain grounds concerning the condition of the universe. Let us not seek proofs from the storehouses of our own minds, but let the sacred word, simply asserted, stand in place of countless proofs. Let us not say with that infatuated sage, when we read or hear the Mosaic narratives, "This philosopher says many things, but proves nothing." Rather let us ascribe to Scripture what that man impudently and blasphemously wished to apply to his own sayings: [αὐτὸς ἔφα, autos epha] "He himself has spoken." Here, faith alone is needed.

units.la: Hoc ergo est, quod nunc nobis de fide proponit Apostolus, quòd nimirum fides sit non apparentium, & quæcunque existunt, à Deo esse omnia condita, nosque ea non posse nisi fide apprehendere. Hæc igitur vera est causa, ob quam istud de creatione vniuersi est præmissum, vt videlicet declaretur, fidem versari circa res non apparentes. Atque ad hanc causam pertinent innumeri loci de rerum creatione, vbi Deus ostenditur omnia citra præiacentem materiam condidisse, solius verbi sui immensa potentia: quod verbum Dei quando philosophi non agnouerunt, nihil mirum, si, quomodo conditus fuerit mundus, non intellexerint. Qua de causa etiam factum, quòd in Symbolis, quæ vocant, sem per articulus de creatione proponitur. Secunda causa, quare Apostolus istud præmisit, hæc est, Methodica tractatione præmittenda sunt minutiora, vt inde conscendamus ad maiora. Decuit igitur istud præmitti, à quo ad altiora conscenderetur, & sine quo ad astra non posset peruenire. Cùm autem institutum Apostoli sit, docere, omnes per fidem iustificari, necessum erat, prius proponi, fide apprehendendam Dei potentiam ac bonitatem. Quomodo enim credas, Deum te posse & velle seruare ac iustificare, nisi prius dideris, eundem esse omnipotentem & præterea optima erga te uoluntate?
units.tr: Therefore this is what the Apostle now sets before us concerning faith: namely, that faith is of things not seen, that all things which exist were created by God, and that we cannot grasp these things except by faith. This is the true reason why this teaching about the creation of the universe is placed first: to make clear that faith is concerned with things not seen. To this reason belong countless passages about the creation of things, where God is shown to have made all things without any pre-existing matter, by the immense power of his word alone. Since the philosophers did not recognize this word of God, it is no wonder that they did not understand how the world was made. For this reason also the article on creation is always set first in the creeds, as they are called. The second reason why the Apostle put this first is this: in a methodical treatment, lesser matters must be put before greater, so that we may climb from them to higher things. It was fitting, therefore, that this be placed first, since from it one ascends to higher things, and without it one cannot reach the heights. Since the Apostle's purpose is to teach that all are justified through faith, it was necessary first to set forth God's power and goodness, to be apprehended by faith. For how could you believe that God is able and willing to save and justify you, unless you first grasped that he is almighty and, moreover, of the best will toward you?

units.la: Hæc autem potentia & bonitas Dei nusquam clarius perspicitur, quàm in ipsa vniuersi creatione: sicut etiam disertè Apostolus Romanorum primo asserit, dicens: Siquidem quæ sunt inuisibilia illius, ex creatione mundi, dum opera intelliguntur, præuidentur, ipsa q; æterna eius potentia ac diuinitas, in hoc, vt sint inexcusabiles.
units.tr: Now this power and goodness of God is seen nowhere more clearly than in the creation of the universe itself. The Apostle also states this plainly in Romans 1: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse."

units.la: Vt igit certiores fierent animi de Dei potentia, eiusdéq; erga homines voluntate, secundum quam potest & vult omnes saluos facere, necessum fuit, hanc particulam de creatione uniuersi præmitti. Qua cognita, aperitur via ad progrediendum ad altiora. Notum enim est, quosdam esse gradus fidei & pietatis, aliosque se habere, vt paruulos, alios vt adolescentes, alios vt viros, alios vt perfectos. Ephes. 4. Ite, quædam esse religionis elementa paruulis conuenientia: ut supra capite quinto, & prima Corinthiorum tertio, quædam vero conuenire proue ctioribus ac doctioribus: ideoq; in schola Christi, id est, ecclesia, spiritus Sanctus Scholarcha vult singulis pro suo captu doctrinam proponi.
units.tr: So that the minds of believers might be more certainly assured of God's power, and of his will toward human beings, by which he is able and willing to save all, it was necessary that this part about the creation of the universe be placed first. Once this is known, the way is opened to advance to higher things. For it is known that there are degrees of faith and piety, and that some are as little children, some as young people, some as grown men, and some as perfect. Eph. 4. Indeed, certain elements of religion suit little children, as above in chapter 5 and in 1 Corinthians 3, but certain others belong to the more advanced and more learned. Therefore, in the school of Christ, that is the Church, the Holy Spirit as schoolmaster wills that teaching be set forth to each according to his capacity.

units.la: Cum vero doctrina de iustificatione per fidem sit valde sublimis, & teneris animis non conueniens, nec statim proponenda, (liquet hoc tum ex eo, quod olim semper apud Iudæos ad Christi usque tempora fuerunt innumeri, qui doctrinam hanc capere non potuerunt, sed pertinacissime semper impugnarunt, statuentes, se operibus potius, quam fide iustificandos: vt videre est passim apud prophetas, item in sermonibus Christi contra Pharisæos: item in Scriptis Apostolicis omnibus: tum ex eo, quod hodie quoq; totus mundus hanc doctrinam explodit: quia non conuenit puerorum stomacho:) valde prudenter fecit Apostolus, qui istud de creatione fide apprehendeda præmisit. Atq; hac etiam de causa in symbolis semper primo loco inculcatur articulus de creatione, in quo elucet Dei bonitas & potentia: pòst vero secundo loco, vbi de persona Christi agitur, proponitur de nostra redemptione ac iustificatione: postremo de conseruatione.
units.tr: Since the doctrine of justification through faith is very lofty and not suited to tender minds, nor to be put forward at once, the Apostle acted very wisely in placing before it the teaching about creation, to be grasped by faith. This is clear, first, from the fact that among the Jews, from of old right up to the time of Christ, there were countless people who could not grasp this doctrine but always opposed it most stubbornly, insisting that they were to be justified by works rather than by faith. This may be seen everywhere among the prophets, likewise in Christ's sermons against the Pharisees, and in all the apostolic writings. It is clear, second, from the fact that even today the whole world rejects this doctrine, because it does not agree with the stomach of children.

units.la: Tertia causa, ob quam recte istud præmittitur, est, quod fides ita quidé versetur proprie, sicut iam sæpius dictum est, circa res sperandas, ut tamen respiciat etiam in antea-ctas. Hac enim ratione fides alitur, fouetur, & excitatur, quod contemplatur anteacta, quæ proponuntur ei in verbo. Sic enim statuit fides, dum videt, & certa est facta per verbum, quod Deus mundum tam mirabiliter, tamque excellenter de nihilo condidit, in hoc ostendens summam suam potentiam ac bonitatem, statim concepit, maiora in posterum expectanda: ac iudicat, quod, qui ita mundum condidit, etiam eum, propter quem ipse mundum condidit, hominem in quam, velit seruare & beare. Atque ita res sperandas & cœlestes, non apparentes in hac vita expectat longanimius & audacius, quia videt intelligitque, tam magnas & mirabiles res antea per Deum nostra causa peractas. Consideratio rerum anteactarum est maxima certitudo rerum in posterum sperandarum. Et in hunc vsum omnia in sacris literis sunt prodita, & quæcunque præscripta sunt, ad nostram salutem præscripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus.
units.tr: A third reason why this is rightly put first is that faith, while it properly concerns things to be hoped for, as has been said many times already, also looks back to things past. For faith is nourished, cherished and stirred up by contemplating past things, which are set before it in the Word. Faith reasons thus: when it sees, and is made certain through the Word, that God created the world from nothing so wonderfully and so excellently, showing in this his supreme power and goodness, it at once conceives greater things to be expected in the future, and judges that he who created the world in this way is also willing to save and bless man, for whose sake he created the world. And so faith awaits the heavenly things to be hoped for, which are not seen in this life, with more patience and boldness, because it sees and understands that such great and marvelous things have already been done by God for our sake. The consideration of past things is the greatest certainty of the things to be hoped for in the future. And for this purpose all things have been handed down in the sacred letters, and whatever has been written was written for our salvation, so that through the patience and comfort of the Scriptures we may have hope.

units.la: Propterea voluit Deus seruari thesaurum sacræ Scripturæ integrum & inuiolatum, ut nos ibi semper ad manum haberemus, vnde in fide alamur: sic quoque Apostolus, ut docet, homines fide iustificari, proponit Romanorum quarto exemplum Abrahæ: & hoc loco exempla omnium fere patrum ab initio inde mundi ad Christi vsque tempora, non ob aliud inquam, quàm vt fides intuens in res anteactas certior fiat de expectandis in posterum. Sic item Christus instituit in ecclesia sua sacramenta, quæ sunt fidei nostræ pabulum & exercitium, & in hoc instituta, vt eorum vsu certi reddamur de promissis bonis accipiendis post hanc vitam. Sed tamen in his ipsis rerum anteactarum diligens commemoratio proponitur: vt in cœna Domini, commemoratio fit mortis Christi, & propter hanc fides iubetur expectare remissionem peccatorum. Sic etiam in symbolis proponuntur anteacta de creatione mundi: item de Christi morte & resurrectione, ut eò constantius expectemus per fidem spiritum Sanctum & remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: For this reason God willed that the treasury of Holy Scripture be preserved whole and inviolate, so that we might always have it at hand, from which to be nourished in faith. So also the Apostle, teaching that men are justified by faith, sets before us in Romans 4 the example of Abraham. And in this place he sets before us the examples of almost all the Fathers from the beginning of the world up to the time of Christ, for no other purpose, I say, than that faith, looking back on past things, may be made more certain about what is to be expected in the future. Likewise Christ instituted in his Church the sacraments, which are the food and exercise of our faith, and were instituted so that by using them we may be made certain of the good promises to be received after this life. Yet even in these the careful remembrance of past things is set before us: thus in the Lord's Supper a remembrance is made of Christ's death, and on account of this faith is bidden to expect the forgiveness of sins. So too in the creeds, past events are set forth: the creation of the world, and likewise the death and resurrection of Christ, so that we may the more steadfastly await by faith the Holy Spirit and the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Eodé vero modo intelligimus, per fidem secula esse verbo Dei condita, ac deinde ea re per fidem speramus, Deum velle nos seruare, & æternum beare.
units.tr: In the same way we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God through faith, and on this ground we hope by faith that God wills to save us and to bless us eternally.

units.la: Igitur propter hanc quoque causam, ut videlicet fides contemplatione rerum anteactarum confirmaretur, ad expectandas res futuras, profuit, istam particulam de creatione per fidem apprehendenda, præmisit.
units.tr: Therefore, also for this reason, namely that faith might be strengthened by the contemplation of past things for the sake of awaiting the things to come, it was useful to put first this part about creation, to be grasped by faith.

units.la: Neque vero ex hac postrema causa habent maleuoli, quod definiant, fidem esse tantum assensum rerum antecedentium à Deo peractarum. Non hoc dicimus. Semper tribuimus fidei res sperandas vt proprium obiectum: sed tantùm dicimus, eam rerum anteactarum contemplatione ali confirmari que.
units.tr: Nor do the ill-disposed have grounds, from this last reason, for defining faith as merely assent to the things previously done by God. We do not say this. We always attribute to faith the things to be hoped for as its proper object; we only say that it is nourished and strengthened by the contemplation of past things.

units.la: Nequaquam conquiescit fides in rebus anteactis, dum statuit veras esse, sicut verbo Dei proponitur, (huiusmodi autem assensum quo iure appellemus fidem, cùm talem etiam habeant dæmones & contremiscant?) Sed vt uera & perfecta fiat fides, debet ipsa altius assurgere, & respicere ad res futuras sperandasque: atque hic si constans fuerit, tum appellari merebitur talis fides, qualem Apostolus paulò ante descripserat.
units.tr: Faith does not rest at all in past things, in so far as it holds them to be true as they are set forth in the Word of God. (For by what right would we call such assent faith, since the demons also have it, and tremble?) But for faith to be true and perfect, it must rise higher and look to the things to come and to be hoped for. And if it is steadfast in this, then it will deserve to be called such faith as the Apostle described a little earlier.

units.la: Ethæc, quare ista particula de creatione mundi, quæ non est, ut apparet, rerum speradarum, sit præmissa, sufficere in præsens arbitror. Nunc apostoli uerba plenius discutiamus.
units.tr: And why this part about the creation of the world, which, as is evident, is not one of the things to be hoped for, has been placed first, I think is enough to say for the present. Now let us examine the Apostle's words more fully.

units.la: Per fidem intelligimus perfecta fuisse secula) Cur Scriptura passim vsurpet vocem seculorum, pro cœlo & terra, omnibusq; creatis, diximus capite primo super illo verbo, per quem condidit & secula, ostendimusque, significantius dici, condita secula, quàm condita cœlum ac terram.
units.tr: "By faith we understand that the worlds were framed." Why Scripture everywhere uses the word "worlds" (secula) for heaven and earth and all created things, I explained in chapter 1 on the words "by whom he also made the worlds," where I showed that "the worlds were made" is a more expressive way of speaking than "the heaven and the earth were made."

units.la: Neque dicit simpliciter, esse facta secula, sed ἀπαρτισθαι, perfecta esse, absoluta, con-summata, vt nihil in illis siue ad splendorem, siue ad commoditatem desiderari possit.
units.tr: Nor does he say simply that the worlds were made, but that they were ἀπαρτισθαι [ἀπαρτισθῆναι], that is, brought to completion, finished, and perfected, so that nothing in them could be wanted, either for beauty or for convenience.

units.la: Reuera enim summa est orbis conditi, maximeque, ut ante lapsum hominis conditus fuerat, excellentia & perfectio. Certo tempore omnia primùm edita sunt: deinde singulæ partes sunt suis ornamentis insignitæ, ut nihil amplius, quo diuina potentia ac bonitas illustrior fieri posset, adiungendum fuerit iuxta illud Geneseos primo, Vidit Deus cuncta, quæ fecerat, & erant valde bona.
units.tr: Indeed, the sum of the created world, and especially its excellence and perfection as it was before man's fall, is highest. All things were first made at a set time; then each part was adorned with its own ornaments, so that nothing more could be added by which the divine power and goodness might be made more evident, according to that passage in Genesis 1, "God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good."

units.la: Longeque alia specie constituta fuisse omnia initio, quàm post lapsum hominis, constat ex illo Geneseos tertio, vbi Deus Adæ transgressori dixit: Maledicta terra in opere tuo, in laboribus comedes ex ea cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ: spinas & tribulos germinabit tibi, & comedes herbas terræ. Ecce mirabile discrimen, & prorsus nouam faciem, à prima illa mundi recens creati constitutione.
units.tr: That all things were constituted in the beginning in a very different appearance from that after man's fall is clear from Genesis 3, where God said to Adam the transgressor: "Cursed is the ground for your sake; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the field." Behold a remarkable difference, and a wholly new face, from that first constitution of the newly created world.

units.la: Hic plane mutata omnia ac deformata, ex vno illo peccato primi parentis. Quid credemus accessisse corruptionis ex peccatis posterorum ad nostra vsq; tempora? Certum est, ne cœlum quidem mundum ac purum esse, sed à contagio nostrorum scelerum maculas quasdam contraxisse.
units.tr: Here everything was plainly changed and deformed by that one sin of our first parent. What corruption must we believe has been added from the sins of his descendants down to our own time? It is certain that not even the heaven is pure and clean, but has contracted certain stains from the contagion of our wickedness.

units.la: Huc pertinet & illud Romanorum octauo, de creaturæ vniuersæ expectanda restitutione, Vanitati creatura subiacet, non volens, sed propter eum, qui subiecit illam sub spe. Quoniam & ipsa creatura liberabitur à seruitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei, &c.
units.tr: To this belongs also that passage in Romans 8 about the expected restoration of the whole creation: "The creature was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope. For the creature itself also will be set free from its bondage to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God," etc.

units.la: Qua de re etiam secunda epistola Petri capite tertio, Summa igitur mundi, cùm primùm is fuit conditus, extitit perfectio. Sic autem mundum esse factum, & quidem ideò perfectum, non possumus apprehendere, nisi fide. Quæ nunc existunt in tanta mundi corruptione, à nobis percipi non possunt, & intellectus noster ad manifestissima corruptæ naturæ nō aliter sese habet, atque oculus nòctuæ ad solem, confitēte id illo sagacissimo rerum naturalium peruestigatore Aristotele: quid ergo possemus in telligere de illis ea perfectione constitutis, quam habebant initio creationis? Rectè igitur dictum, quòd fide apprehendimus, seculà Deo esse perfecta, & non ab æterno extitisse: vel aliunde, quàm à Deo suam traxisse originem. Sequitur:
units.tr: Hence also 2 Peter 3: "The sum of the world, when it was first created, was perfection." We cannot grasp, however, that the world was made in this way, and indeed perfect for this reason, except by faith. What now exists in such great corruption of the world cannot be perceived by us; our intellect stands towards the most obvious things of corrupted nature no differently than the eye of an owl stands towards the sun, as that most keen investigator of natural things, Aristotle, confesses. What then could we understand of those things established in the perfection they had at the beginning of creation? Rightly, therefore, it is said that by faith we apprehend that the ages were made perfect by God, and did not exist from eternity, or derived their origin from anything other than God. The text follows:

units.la: Verbo Dei: ῥήματι θεοῦ) Causa formalis, siue modus creationis mundi, quo potentia & bona voluntas Dei optimè declaratur, hic exprimitur, & circa hanc particulam fides potissimum versatur, quæ apprehendit, mundum à Deo simpliciter, & quidem solo verbo ac nutu voluntateque Dei. Si enim quis quærat, quomodo mundus sit conditus, num ex præiacente materia, vel aliena ope concurrente? aptissimè respondebitur, solo Dei verbo, ac nutu à Deo esse creatum. Sumpta forma à more regum potentium, quorum iussu res statim perficiuntur. Hoc verbum, & voluntas Dei, pro materia & pro modo, & pro omnibus auxiliis accipiendum est. Ipse dixit & facta sunt, ipse mandauit, & creata sunt.
units.tr: "By the word of God" [ῥήματι θεοῦ]. The formal cause, or manner of the creation of the world, by which the power and good will of God are best displayed, is expressed here, and faith is chiefly occupied with this phrase, which apprehends that the world was made by God simply, and indeed by the mere word, command and will of God. For if someone asks how the world was made, whether out of pre-existing matter or with the help of some outside concurrence, the most apt answer will be that it was created by God by the mere word and command of God. The form is taken from the custom of powerful kings, by whose order things are at once accomplished. This word and the will of God must be taken for matter, for manner, and for all assistance. "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created."

units.la: Hac responsiuncula omnes quæstiones, quas curiosi philosophi solent de pluribus principiis rerum, de mundi initio ac duratione mouere, diluuntur: id quod ipse Apostolus etiam hic disertè exprimit, dicens: verbo Dei factum, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων γεγονέναι, quasi diceret: vt fierent ea, quæ nunc videntur, ex ijs, quæ non apparebant; hoc est, ex nihilo, ex nulla materia: quia, vnde ista fierent, non erat, nusquam aliquid apparebat.
units.tr: By this short reply all the questions that curious philosophers are wont to raise about the plurality of principles of things, and about the beginning and duration of the world, are resolved; and the Apostle himself expresses this clearly here, saying that by the word of God things were made "so that what is seen was not made out of things which appear" [εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων γεγονέναι]. As if he were saying: that those things which are now seen might come to be from things which did not appear; that is, from nothing, from no matter, because there was nothing from which they might come, and nothing appeared anywhere.

units.la: Prorsus absurdum atque alienum videtur, ac nullo modo apparet posse fieri, vt, vbi nulla adest materia, ibi quicquam formetur. Et tamen vbi adeò nihil apparebat, Deus omnia ista, quæ nunc videntur, condidit. Quomodo igitur istud intelligamus, nisi fide?
units.tr: It seems altogether absurd and contrary to reason, and in no way evident, that anything should be formed where no matter is present. And yet where nothing at all appeared, God created all those things which now are seen. How then are we to understand this, except by faith?

units.la: Gertè ratio hic nihil potest cernere, semper requirit præiacentem materiam. Verum quidem est,& philosophos quosdam voluisse afferere aliquo modo ea,quæ videtur,codita esse ex inuisibilibus:vnde nonnulli, vt Anaxagoras, constituerunt occultas quafdã formas latentes, actum quidem,vbi aliquid procreatur,prodeuntes : Plato confingit ideas,& species in mente diuina repositas. Auicenna constituit quandam intelligentiã. Sed hi omnes cùm fine verbo locuti sint,imaginabantur, Deum quasi hominum more, primùm mente concipere:deinde etiam deliberare ratiocinarique,vti solent, qui in animo habent,aliquid conficere seu ædificare. Sed oës hæ imaginationes sunt reijciendæ, non solùm quia fine verbo sunt:sed etiam,quia non ostendunt Dei potentiam, sed potius affinguntimbecillitatem humanæ imbecillitati propemodum similem. Sola Scriptura recte expressit modum creationis rerum, quando passim inculcat, Deum condidisse omnia solo verbo,fecisseque,ut ex inuisibilibus non apparentibus, id est, non existentibus,ea quæ nunc existunt,apparerent.
units.tr: Certainly reason here can discern nothing; it always requires pre-existing matter. It is true that some philosophers wished to assert that what is seen was in some way made from invisible things; thus some, like Anaxagoras, posited hidden forms lying concealed, which come forth as an act when something is produced; Plato devised ideas and species laid up in the divine mind; Avicenna posited a certain intelligence. But all these, since they spoke apart from the word, imagined God, after the manner of men, first conceiving in his mind, then also deliberating and reasoning as those are wont to do who have something in mind to make or build. But all these imaginings are to be rejected, not only because they are apart from the word, but also because they do not show the power of God, but rather invent a weakness almost similar to human feebleness. Scripture alone has correctly expressed the mode of the creation of things, when it repeatedly impresses that God made all things by the word alone, and brought it about that from invisible things, not appearing, that is, not existing, those things which now exist should appear.

units.la: Proinde non est otiosa contemplatio fidei,quando occupatur in consideratione creationis mundi. Hic enim intuetur in Dei immensam potentiam & bonitatem, quarecte animaduersa & vtcunque cognita,via nobis,qua ad Deum peruenimus,aperitur. Facile quidem recipit & agnoscit, mundum ita à Deo conditum solo verbo, vti Scriptura id factum esse testatur. Sed præterea ex modo & ex forma operis diutius inhæret in consideratione tantæ potentiæ ac bonitatis,atque inde paulatim eò deducitur, vt certissimè statuat mens,Deum quoque sibi velle esse propitium,velle beneficijs spiritualibus ornare,& vitam æternam largiri. Hic fides mirabile recipit incrementum,secum ipsa, supra quàm dici potest,lætatur,Deum ardentissimè diligit, & parata est omnia propter Deum tolerare:Laudat Dominum in creaturis, sed non ita inhæret creaturis, quin ad creatorem multò magis anhelet,& fe totam illi foli commendet,ex eo solo pendeat. Sic verò Patres fidem suam subinde solent acuere & refocillare contemplatione creationis mundi. Dauid Psalmo decimonono, Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei,& opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum. Iterum Pfal.103. Omnia in sapientia fecisti,impleta est terra possessione sua.Item totus Psalmus 148. Laudate Dominum de cœlis, laudate eum in excelsis.
units.tr: Therefore the contemplation of faith is not idle when it is occupied in considering the creation of the world. For here it looks upon the immense power and goodness of God; which, rightly noted and in whatever measure known, opens the way by which we come to God. Faith readily receives and acknowledges that the world was thus created by God by the word alone, as Scripture testifies. But further, from the manner and form of the work, it dwells longer on the consideration of so great power and goodness, and from this is gradually led to the point where the mind most certainly determines that God also wishes to be propitious to it, wishes to adorn it with spiritual benefits, and to bestow eternal life. Here faith receives a wondrous increase; it rejoices within itself beyond what can be said, loves God most ardently, and is ready to endure all things for God's sake. It praises the Lord in his creatures, but does not cling to the creatures so as not to long much more for the Creator, and to commit itself wholly to him alone, depending on him alone. Thus the Fathers were wont to sharpen and refresh their faith from time to time by the contemplation of the creation of the world. David in Psalm 19: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands." Again, Psalm 103: "In wisdom you have made them all; the earth is full of your possession." Likewise the whole of Psalm 148: "Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights."

units.la: Per fidem vberiorem hostiam Abel obtulit Deo, quàm Cain, per quam testimonium meruit, quòd effet iustus, testimonium perhibente de donarijs illius Deo, & per hanc mortuus adhuc loquitur.
units.tr: By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts; and by it he being dead yet speaketh.

units.la: Hic habes primum exemplum institutę Inductionis, de Abele per fidem iustificato. Quod pluribus de caussis pri no loco ponitur.Primùm,quia Apostolus in enumeratione hac exemplorum studiosè feriem temporum sequitur, atque ut Sancti patres inuicè successerunt tempore,ita collocat eos ordine. Secundò,quia constat,Abelem primum extitisse iustum,& in confessione fidei iniuste interfectum: quo nomine etiam Christus eum celebrat Matthæi vicefimotertio. Potest addi & tertia ratio, quòd videlicet in hoc exemplo clarissimè ostenditur, veram religionem verumq; Dei cultum à fide trahere initium.
units.tr: Here you have the first example of the instituted induction, of Abel justified by faith. This is placed first for several reasons. First, because the Apostle, in this enumeration of examples, carefully follows the order of times, and as the holy fathers succeeded one another in time, so he arranges them in order. Second, because it is clear that Abel was the first to be righteous and was unjustly slain for his confession of faith; for this reason Christ also honours him in Matthew 23. A third reason may be added, namely that this example most clearly shows that true religion and the true worship of God take their beginning from faith.

units.la: Cùm autem prima religionis cura esse debeat,iuxta illud : Quærite primùm regnum Dei,consentaneum est,istud exemplum primo loco poni ob oculos.Potest addi & quarta ratio,ex Chryfoftomo : Quandoquidem ad eos,qui graui propter iustitiam perpessi erant à suis contribulibus,sermo est, prudenter primo loco is proponitur, qui & àprio fratre propter iustitiam iniurijs & morte affectus est.
units.tr: Since the first care of religion ought to be, according to that saying, "Seek ye first the kingdom of God", it is fitting that this example be set before our eyes first. A fourth reason may be added, from Chrysostom: since the discourse is addressed to those who suffered grievously for righteousness at the hands of their fellow-countrymen, he wisely puts first him who was also wronged and killed by his own brother for righteousness' sake.

units.la: Rationes hç nihil habent obscuritatis.Quod ad primam attinet,conuenientissimum est,non solùm propter ordinem rerum gestarum,verumetiam propter docendi methodum.Facilius enim,imò & iucundius vnusquisque ea accipit,quæ decoro seruato ordine proponuntur,nécnon memoriæ citius commendantur, quæ iuxta feriem temporū, & sacrorum librorum,digesta conspiciuntur.
units.tr: These reasons are not at all obscure. As to the first, it is most fitting, not only on account of the order of events but also on account of the method of teaching. For each person more easily, and even more pleasantly, takes in what is set out in a fitting order, and such things are also committed to memory more quickly when they are arranged according to the sequence of times and of the sacred books.

units.la: Quod ad fecundam causam attinet,ea per fe,maximeque ex verbis Christi manifesta est: sic enim ait Matthæi vicesimo tertio, Vos quoque implete mensuram patrum vestrorum,&c.vt veniat super vos omnis sanguis iustus, qui effusus est super terram,à sanguine Abel iusti,vsque ad sanguinem Zachariæ filij Barachiæ,quem occidistis inter templum & altare.
units.tr: As to the second cause, it is clear in itself, and especially from the words of Christ; for thus he says in Matthew 23: "Fill ye up also the measure of your fathers... that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar."

units.la: Non dubium quidem est,etiam Adamum fuisse iustum, assidueque in suis laboribus & ærumnis egisse pœnitentiam,ac respexisse per fidé in promissionem semel factam de semine benedicto,per quod contereretur caput serpētis:verum,quia ipse autor fuit peccati,& ruinæ totius humani generis:ideò Scriptura illū nō proponit iustū,sed ut peccati & &omnium nostrarum miserarum architectum & autorem. Vnde Oseæ 6.propter hoc dolaui in prophetis, & occidi eos in verbis oris mei, & iudicia tua quasi lux egrediëtur: Quia misericordiam volui, & non sacrificium, & scientiam Dei plus quàm holocaustũ: ipsi autem sicut Adam transgressi sunt paƈtum, vbi præuaricati sunt in me, &c. Rom. 5. Regnauit mors ab Adam vsq; ad Mosen, in eos quoque, qui non peccauerant ad similitudinē transgressionis Adam, prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto, Quemadmodum per Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & per Christum omnes viuificabuntur. Hac igitur de causa ipse Abel potius vt primus iustus celebratur, quàm Adam. Quæ ad tertiam aut quartam causam pertinere videntur, mox explicabuntur latius & oportunius. Iam ad verba Apostoli, ut, quantus sit fidei e ffeƈtus, videamus.
units.tr: There is no doubt that Adam too was righteous, and that in his labours and hardships he constantly practised repentance, and looked by faith to the promise once made concerning the blessed seed, by whom the head of the serpent would be crushed. But because he himself was the author of sin and of the ruin of the whole human race, Scripture does not set him forth as righteous, but as the architect and author of sin and of all our wretchedness. Hence Hosea 6: "Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and thy judgements are as the light that goeth forth. For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. But they like Adam have transgressed the covenant; there have they dealt treacherously against me," etc. Romans 5: "Death reigned from Adam unto Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression." 1 Corinthians 15: "As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive." For this reason Abel himself is celebrated as the first righteous man rather than Adam. What seems to pertain to the third or fourth cause will be explained shortly, more fully and more opportunely. Now let us look at the words of the Apostle, to see how great the effect of faith is.

units.la: Per fidem, inquit, uberiorem hostiam Abel obtulit, quàm Cain) Apostolus demonstraturus, quomodo iustificatio contingat per fidem, duas proponit personas prorsus inter se diuersas, vt ex vnius damnatione tanto manifestior euadat alterius iustificatio: sicut & Christus in euangelio proponit pharifæum & publicanum, Lucæ decimo octauo.
units.tr: "By faith," he says, "Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice than Cain." The Apostle, about to show how justification comes through faith, sets before us two persons entirely different from each other, so that the justification of the one may appear the more clearly from the condemnation of the other; just as Christ in the gospel sets forth the Pharisee and the publican, Luke 18.

units.la: Cùm verò Apostolus omnia exempla ista collegerit ex Scripturis, non poterimus mentem ipsius commodius intelligere, quàm si ipsam Scripturam consulamus. Sicautem de Abele & Caino Geneseos quarto legi ur: Fuit Abel pastor ouium, & Cain agricola. Factum est autem post multos dies, vt offerret Cain de fructibus terræ munera Domino, Abel quoque obtulit de primogenitis gregis sui, & de adipibus eorum. Et respexit Dominus ad Abel & ad munera eius: ad Cain autem, & ad munera illius non respexit: iratusque est Cain vehementer, & concidit vultus eius: dixitque Dominus ad eum: Quare iratus es, & cur concidit facies tua? Nónne si bene egeris, recipies? Sin autem male, statim in foribus peccatum tuum aderit: sed sub te erit appetitus eius, & tu dominaberis illius. Tantum ad præsens.
units.tr: Since the Apostle gathered all these examples from the Scriptures, we cannot understand his mind more conveniently than by consulting the Scripture itself. Thus concerning Abel and Cain we read in Genesis 4: "Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a tiller of the ground. And it came to pass after many days that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord. And Abel also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering; but unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell. And the Lord said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen? If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him." So much for the present.

units.la: Habemus hîc duos fratres nobis propositos, Abelem & Cainum: sed sicut diuersis nominibus ita omnibus in rebus & politicis & spiritualibus, multum diuersis conditionibus. Cain primogenitus est, & à matre appellatus eo nomine, quod significat possessionem: existimabat enim illa, vbi nacta esset filium Cain, se possidere illum virum illudque semen, per quod conterendum foret serpentis caput.
units.tr: Here we have two brothers set before us, Abel and Cain; but as their names differ, so in all things, both civil and spiritual, they differ greatly in their circumstances. Cain is the firstborn, and was called by his mother by a name which signifies possession; for she thought that, having obtained a son, she possessed that man and that seed by which the head of the serpent was to be crushed.

units.la: Contrà Abel minorem natu ita appellauit, voce significante, inane, vanum, superuacaneum: iudicans, hunc nullius spei aut utilitatis fore. Ita iudicium hominum ferè semper fallitur: & Dominus illos eligere solet, quos nos despicimus: stulta mundi eligit, vt confundat fortia: quomodo etiam factum in Esau & Iacob cernimus.
units.tr: On the other hand, she named the younger son Abel, by a word signifying vain, empty, superfluous, judging that he would be of no hope or use. So the judgement of men is almost always mistaken, and the Lord is wont to choose those whom we despise: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise"; as we see also happened in Esau and Jacob.

units.la: Ideò duo illi fratres Cain & Abel, statim significant duo genera hominum: Cain hypocritas & impios, sicut & Ioannes prioris epistolæ suæ capite tertio indicat: Abel verò iustos sicut Christus ipse interpretatur Matthæi vicesimo tertio. Et ipsa diuersa vitæ genera comprobât. Cain enim agricola erat, rebus terrenis vtique intentus, & temporales frvctus colligens. Abel verò pastorem agebat, quod genus vitæ contemplationi rerum diuinarum magis idoneum est, & eum, qui præesse gubernareq; alios, maximeque in rebus spiritualibus, possit, significat.
units.tr: Therefore these two brothers, Cain and Abel, at once signify two kinds of men: Cain the hypocrites and the impious, as John also indicates in the third chapter of his first epistle; Abel the righteous, as Christ himself interprets in Matthew 23. Their different ways of life confirm this too. For Cain was a tiller of the ground, certainly intent on earthly things and gathering temporal fruits. Abel, however, was a keeper of sheep, a way of life better suited to the contemplation of divine things, and it signifies one who can preside over and govern others, especially in spiritual matters.

units.la: Vnde & patriarchæ etiam pastores fuisse leguntur, inprimis Iacob cum suis, referēte itaIosepho ad Pharaonem, itē Moses, Dauid, pastores fuerunt: & pastores vocantur prophetæ, & quos Dominus ecclesijs vult præsici.
units.tr: Hence the patriarchs too are read to have been shepherds, especially Jacob with his family, as Josephus reports in his account to Pharaoh; likewise Moses and David were shepherds; and the prophets are called shepherds, as are those whom the Lord wishes to be set over the churches.

units.la: Nec dissimile est, quod Augustinus quoque alibi de hisce duobus fratribus notat: Cain quandoquidem primus condidit ciuitatem, significare ciues huius seculi, quique sic agunt, quasi perpetuò hic mansuri de alia uita non cogitantes. Abel verò, qui non ædificauit, significare sanctos, qui iudicant, se hîc non habere ciuitatem, sed futuram inquirunt. Veriùm hæc satis. Nunc quomodo sacrificium, & quàm diuerso modo obtulerint.
units.tr: Nor is it unlike what Augustine also notes elsewhere about these two brothers: Cain, since he was the first to found a city, signifies the citizens of this age, who act as if they were to remain here forever, not thinking about another life. Abel, who built no city, signifies the saints, who judge that they have no city here but seek the one to come. But enough of this. Now let us see how they offered sacrifice, and in how different a manner.

units.la: Per fidem, inquit, uberiorem hostiam Abel Deo obtulit, quàm Cain) In Genesi tantùm dicitur, Factum est autem post multos dies, vt offerret Cain de fructibus terræ munera Domino: Abel quoque obtulit de primogenitis gregis sui, & de adipibus eorum. Ex his constabit, quomodo Abel vberiorem hostiam obtulerit.
units.tr: "By faith," he says, "Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain." In Genesis it is only said: "It came to pass after many days that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord; Abel also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof." From these words it will be clear how Abel offered the more excellent sacrifice.

units.la: Prius tamen hoc obseruandum, statim à condito orbe constitutam ecclesiolam: ritus item sacrificiorum, & externa exercitia, quibus homines in ijs, quæ ad confessionem fidei, ad inuocationem, ad gratiarum actionem pertinent, sese occuparent: sicut erant edocti à primo parente, qui & à Deo acceperat.
units.tr: First, however, this must be observed: from the created world there was established a little church, as well as the rite of sacrifices and external exercises by which men occupied themselves in those things that pertain to the confession of faith, to invocation, and to thanksgiving, as they had been taught by the first parent, who had received them from God.

units.la: Ac statim ecclesiola ista habuit malos permixtos bonis, & mali conati sunt opprimere bonos, quod & futurum est semper in ecclesia usque ad finem mundi.
units.tr: And at once this little church had evil men mixed in with the good, and the evil attempted to oppress the good; which will always be the case in the Church until the end of the world.

units.la: Hic tamē omnis generis homines sua offerunt sacrificia, eaq; proferunt, quę habent. Cain quidem fructus terræ, Abel verò pecudes: quæ omnia etiam à Deo accepta sunt, ideoque pro ijs debent Deo per oblationes agi gratiæ. Cernūtur autem adhuc sacrificia paria. Quomodo igitur Abel obtulit vberiorem hostiam?
units.tr: Here, however, men of every kind offer their sacrifices, and they bring forward what they have. Cain indeed offered the fruits of the earth, Abel the flocks; all of which were also accepted by God, and therefore for them thanksgiving ought to be rendered to God through offerings. Yet similar sacrifices are still seen. How, then, did Abel offer a more excellent sacrifice?

units.la: Respondetur: Hoc licet videre ex verbis Scripturæ. De Cain dicitur, quòd simpliciter obtulerit fructus terræ, veluti qualescunq;, nullo delectu, nullaq; cura adhibita. Abel verò obtulit, non qualescunq; pecudes, sed primogenita, quæ proprie debent Deo cedere sicut & in lege postea præceptum est: deinde obtulit primogenita & selecta. Ecce illud diligentiam, ac longè aliam diligentiam. Igitur vel hoc nomine vberiorem hostiam obtulit Abel, quàm Cain: vt non dicamus, ideò etiam posse accipi præstantiorem hostiam Abelis, quòd ad sacrificia legalia proprie accesserit, quæ fiebant item ex pecudibus: & quòd in oblatione pecudis Christus euidentius fit repræsentatus, propter quam hostiam, Christum, in quam peccatorum expiatio erat expectanda. Sed Scriptura non ita exprimit caussam, quæ vtrumq; mouerit ad diuersas hostias ita offerendum.
units.tr: The answer is that this can be seen from the words of Scripture. Of Cain it is said that he simply offered fruits of the earth, of whatever kind, with no choice and no care applied. But Abel offered not just any sheep but firstlings, which properly belong to God, as was afterward commanded in the law; then he offered firstlings and choice ones. See, that is diligence, and a very different diligence. So on this ground alone Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice than Cain. We need not add that Abel's sacrifice may also be taken as the more excellent because it properly approached the legal sacrifices, which were likewise made from flocks, and because Christ was more clearly represented in the offering of a sheep, the Christ in whom the expiation of sins was to be looked for. But Scripture does not express the cause that moved each of them to offer different victims in this way.

units.la: Proinde Apostolus rectè aperit causam: Abel, inquit, habuit fidem, Cain verò nequaquam. Hæc causa non exprimitur in Scriptura, nisi forte in illis verbis accipiamus notam, quæ Dominus locutus est ad Cain, postquam ægrè tulisset, se suumq; sacrificium à Deo non respici: ibi autem sic locutus est Dominus: Nónne, si bene egeris, recipies? Sin autem male, statim in foribus peccatum tuum aderit. Quo loco agere, seu operari est idem quod sacrificare: quod quidam Hebræorum interpretantur, teste Fagio. Notat autem verbis istis Dominus, Cain non syncero animo, non ea, qua decebat, fide obtulisse.
units.tr: Accordingly the Apostle rightly states the cause: Abel, he says, had faith, but Cain certainly did not. This cause is not expressed in Scripture, unless perhaps we take it from the words the Lord spoke to Cain after he was grieved that he and his sacrifice were not regarded by God. There the Lord said: "Shall you not be accepted if you do well? But if you do not, sin is at the door at once." Here to act, or to work, is the same as to sacrifice, as some of the Hebrews interpret, according to Fagius. By these words the Lord indicates that Cain did not offer with a sincere heart, nor with the faith that was fitting.

units.la: Fortasis considebat Cain dignitati suæ ob primogenituram, propter hanc existimabat, se respiciendum præ Abele, & ideò non erat solicitus de præstantioribus victimis offerendis. Hic plane elucet fastus hypocritarum, & propriæ iustitiæ inanis fiducia, Dei contemptus, fratrum despectus: deniq; incredulitas, quæ est omnium malorum fons.
units.tr: Perhaps Cain relied on his dignity as firstborn, and because of this he thought he ought to be regarded before Abel, and therefore he was not anxious about offering the more excellent victims. Here plainly shines out the pride of hypocrites, the empty confidence in one's own righteousness, contempt for God, scorn for one's brothers, and finally unbelief, which is the fountain of all evils.

units.la: At Abel nihil de se præsumebat, nihil sibi arrogabat, sed se submittens, agnoscens priam indignitatem, agit Deo pro acceptis gratias, expectat misericordiam ampliorem in posterum, quam fide apprehendit, atq; ideò ad testandum hunc suum animum seligit optimas & pinguissimas quasq; pecudes, atq; alacri animo eas offert. Hic vides erupere illam fidem, & ex fide summam erga Deum charitatem. Nisi fidem Abel habuisset, nequaquam tam studiosus fuisset in offerendis optimis.
units.tr: But Abel presumed nothing about himself and claimed nothing for himself. Humbling himself and acknowledging his former unworthiness, he gives thanks to God for what he has received and looks for greater mercy in the future, which he grasps by faith. Therefore, to bear witness to this attitude of his, he chooses the best and fattest of the flock and offers them with a willing mind. Here you see faith breaking forth, and from faith the highest love toward God. Unless Abel had had faith, he would certainly not have been so eager in offering the best things.

units.la: Quomodocunq; agas, oportet semper ad fidem quasi ad fontem redire. Etsi egregia fuerint sacrificia, aut alia præclara opera, tamē huiusmodi non possunt intelligi, nisi quatenus ex fide proficiscuntur. Fides mouet, incitat, inflamat ad bene agendum. Atq; hic habemus, quod in secunda ratione supra diximus, veram religionem, verumq; Dei cultum à fide trahere initium. Quicquid vsquam est rituum aut ceremoniarum, imò quicquid præterea bonorum operum, quæ ut pia & religiosa commendanda videantur, certè nisi ex fonte fidei scaturiant, Deus potius irridetur illis, quàm colitur. Manifestissimum id euadit hic in exemplo duorum fratrum offerentium, &c. Sed hęc satis ad explicandum, quomodo Abel vberiorem hostiam obtulerit, quàm Cain, & quomodo Abel talem obtulerit per fidem.
units.tr: However you act, it is necessary always to return to faith as to a fountain. Even if the sacrifices are excellent, or other outstanding works, such things cannot be understood except insofar as they proceed from faith. Faith moves, urges and inflames us to do good. Here we have what we said above in the second reason: true religion and true worship of God take their beginning from faith. Whatever rites or ceremonies there are anywhere, and indeed whatever other good works seem to be commended as pious and religious, unless they spring from the fountain of faith, God is mocked by them rather than worshipped. This becomes most manifest here in the example of the two brothers offering, etc. But these things are enough to explain how Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice than Cain, and how he offered such a sacrifice through faith.

units.la: Per quam testimonium meruit, quòd esset iustus, testimonium perhibente Deo de donarijs illius.
units.tr: Through which he obtained the testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness concerning his gifts.

units.la: Δι' ὧν, per quam, refert fidem potius, quàm hostiam: sicut & in sequenti particula, Δι' ὧν: vbi necessariò de fide, non de hostia intelligitur. Et sententia ipsa postulat ita accipi, Δι' ὧν. Apostolus enim omnia refert ad fidem, non tantùm, quòd iustus à Deo sit pronunciatus, verumetiam quòd hostiam vberiorem obtulerit. Quid igitur est, quòd Abel per fidem meruit testimonium, quòd esset iustus: nisi, quòd Abel à Deo iustus est pronunciatus, & pro iusto acceptus? Sicut suprà testimonium Dei consequi, idem esse ostendimus, quod à Deo iustos reputari. Et primùm quidem Deus habuit Abelem iustum propter fidem: post verò perhibet etiam testimonium de donarijs illius.
units.tr: "Through which" [Δι' ὧν] refers to faith rather than to the sacrifice, as also in the following clause, "through which" [Δι' ὧν], where it must necessarily be understood of faith, not of the sacrifice. The sense itself demands that it be taken so. For the Apostle refers everything to faith: not only that Abel was pronounced righteous by God, but also that he offered a more abundant sacrifice. What, then, is it that Abel through faith obtained the testimony that he was righteous, except that Abel was pronounced righteous by God and accepted as righteous? As we showed above, to obtain God's testimony is the same as to be reckoned righteous by God. First, God held Abel righteous on account of his faith; afterward he also bore witness concerning his gifts.

units.la: Est hic plane idem dictum, quòd & Genes. 4. dicitur, Respexit Dominus ad Abel, & ad munera eius: aduertedusq; est hic iustificationis ordo. Non respicit Deus prius ad munera, ac deinde ad personam, quasi respectu munerum persona foret iustificanda: sed è diuerso, prius ad personam, ac deinde ad opera: vt intelligamus, opera tum demum esse Deo accepta, vbi prius per fidem accepta est persona.
units.tr: This is plainly the same statement as is also made in Genesis 4: "The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts." The order of justification must be noted here. God does not look first at the gifts and then at the person, as if the person were to be justified by regard for the gifts. On the contrary, he looks first at the person and then at the works, so that we understand works to be accepted by God only when the person has first been accepted through faith.

units.la: Discernere oportet personam & actiones siue opera. Opera bona non faciunt iustum: nam hypocritæ & mali etiam norunt opera in speciem bona præstare, sicut Cain quoq; obtulit sacrificium perinde atque Abel: sed qui iam iustus est, is facit opera, & huius opera pera sunt Deo accepta. Sic Christus etiam Matth. 7. Omnis arbor bona bonos fructus facit, & non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere. Ita necessario sunt coniuncta, & sequitur: si persona proba, igitur & opera proba: at non e diverso. Verum quidem est, quod homines non possunt iudicare, nisi a posteriori, hoc est ex fructibus, sicut & Christus Matth. 7. subijcit, Ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos: at Deus primo & statim intuetur personam, hoc est, cor, & fidem, unde opera procedunt.
units.tr: One must distinguish between the person and the actions or works. Good works do not make a man righteous, for hypocrites and wicked men also know how to perform works that are good in appearance, just as Cain too offered a sacrifice in the same way as Abel. But he who is already righteous does works, and his works are acceptable to God. So Christ also says in Matthew 7: "Every good tree bears good fruit, and a good tree cannot bear bad fruit." Thus they are necessarily joined, and it follows: if the person is upright, then the works are upright too; but not conversely. It is true that men cannot judge except a posteriori, that is, from the fruits, as Christ also adds in Matthew 7: "By their fruits you will know them." But God looks first and at once at the person, that is, at the heart and faith from which works proceed.

units.la: Et mirum est, hypocritas non posse intelligere, quod in ordine iustificationis prius respiciatur persona, ac deinde opera, itaque dicuntur iusta sive bona, quia a iusta proveniunt persona. Hoc ipsi ethnici philosophi possunt pro suo quodam modo lo discernere. Nam & Aristoteles 2. Ethicor. cap. 4. palam discernit, aliud esse iusta agere, & iuste agere. Non protinus iuste, inquit, aut temperate aguntur, si sint iusta aut temperata: sed si agens hoc agat modo, primo quidem, sciens: deinde, si eligens propter ipsa: tertio, si animo firmo agat atque immutabili. Sic expendit philosophia, priusquam decernat quenquam iuste agere, etiamsi iusta agat. Eodem igitur propemodum pacto in Theologia debemus iudicare: iusta aliqui faciunt, dum bona in speciem opera peragunt, veluti Cain & Abel dum offerunt: Pharisaeus & publicanus, dum pariter ascendunt templum, ut orent, atque ibi etiam orant. Sed tamen non eodem modo opera illa faciunt Cain & pharisaeus, non iuste agunt illa. Ratio est, quia non faciunt ex fide. Philosophus diceret, quia non faciunt scientes, vel non electione, vel non firmo animo. At Theologus pro his omnibus collocat fidem, quae est aliqua ex parte ex electione, & necessario requirit constantem animum. Sed haec satis de eo, quod Deus primo testimonium perhibuit, Abelem esse iustum: deinde, quod etiam testimonium perhibuit de donariis illius. Caeterum, putant nonnulli, etiam apertum signum a Deo editum, quo notum fieret, hostiam Abel fuisse acceptam, nempe ignem coelitus missum, qui hostiam statim absumpserit: sic ex Hebraeis sentiunt Aben Ezra, & Abraham autor fasciculi mirrhae, & ex graecis Chrysostomus: & Theodotion in hanc sententiam vertit: inflammavit Dominus super Abel, & munera eius: refert ista Primasius. Neque id absurdum, ita factum esse in mundi initio, quando etiam initio manifestati evangelii saepe Deus suum favorem ac donationem spiri tus testatus sit apertis signis: quia nimirum conveniebat, ea ratione erigi & excitari animos ad verae pietatis in Deum officia: Sequitur.
units.tr: It is remarkable that hypocrites cannot understand that in the order of justification the person is looked at first and then the works, so that works are called just or good because they proceed from a just person. The heathen philosophers themselves could perceive this in their own way. For Aristotle in Ethics 2, chapter 4, plainly distinguishes between doing just things and doing justly. Things are not done justly or temperately, he says, simply because they are just or temperate; the agent must act in such a way that, first, he acts knowingly, second, he chooses them for their own sake, and third, he acts with a firm and unchanging disposition. Philosophy thus weighs the matter before it decides that anyone acts justly, even if he does just things. In the same way, then, we ought to judge in theology. Some men do righteous things while performing good works in appearance, as Cain and Abel do when they offer, and the Pharisee and the publican when they go up together to the temple to pray and there indeed pray. But Cain and the Pharisee do not perform those works in the same way, and they do not act righteously in them. The reason is that they do not act from faith. The philosopher would say that they do not act knowingly, or by choice, or with a firm mind. The theologian, in place of all these, sets faith, which is in some measure a matter of choice and necessarily requires a steadfast mind. But these things are enough concerning the fact that God first bore witness that Abel was righteous, and then that he also bore witness concerning his gifts. Moreover, some think that God also gave a clear sign by which it was made known that Abel's sacrifice was accepted, namely fire sent from heaven which at once consumed the victim. So think Aben Ezra and Abraham, the author of the Fasciculus Myrrhae, among the Hebrews, and Chrysostom among the Greeks. Theodotion also translates to this effect: "The Lord kindled fire upon Abel and his gifts." Primasius reports these things. Nor is it absurd that this was done at the beginning of the world, since at the beginning of the manifestation of the gospel too God often attested his favour and his gift of the Spirit by clear signs, because it was fitting that minds be raised and roused by such means to the duties of true piety toward God. It follows:

units.la: Et per hanc mortuus adhuc loquitur) En alius insignis effectus fidei, quod videlicet per eam mortui loquantur, hoc est, viuant & illustres sint, tum apud Deum, tum apud homines: sicut Abraham & alij Patriarchae viuunt: Posterius ponitur pro priori per Synecdochen: Quanquam, quomodo loqui intelligatur Abel mortuus, varie adhuc exponitur. Quidam sic: Abel mortuus loquitur, id est, tametsi interfectus sit, tamen semper manet iucundissima eius memoria, omnium ore praedicatur, & sic adhuc loquitur adeoque inter mortales ipse ut semper viuens & immortalis versatur. Vel, loquitur, dum suo exemplo, quod in studio verae religionis, in confessione fidei, in vitae innocentia, in patientia viuus praebuit, nos iam mortuus ad similes virtutes invitat & hortatur. Tacite enim hoc pacto in omnium animis adhuc hodie loquitur, necnon simili ratione omnes loquuntur Sancti, quorum virtutes Deo sunt probatae, & hominibus ad imitandum propositae. Sed, cum Apostolus nihil temere pronunciet, semperque Scripturis innitatur, probabilius est, eum hic respexisse ad id, quod de Abele mortuo Scriptura Gen. 4. commemorat, Deum vide licet dixisse ad fratricidam Cain, Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra. Quorum verborum sententia haec est: Putasne o Cain, me ignorare, ubi sit frater tuus Abel? Vox sanguinis illius clamat ad me, hoc est, Ego tam certo scio, quomodo cum illo actum sit, atque si sanguis illius iamiam mihi narrasset omnia: ego illius cura adhuc gero, nec mors illius occulta manebit: sed magis magisque illustrabitur. Est autem in verbis Scripturae προσωποποιΐα, dum rei inanimatae sermo tribuitur. Quare aliter, atque verba simpliciter sonant erunda est sententia. Cum ergo & hoc loco Apostolus dicat: Abelem per fidem loqui etiam mortuum, existimo significari, Deo tantopere placuisse fidem Abel, dum viveret, ut iam mortuum etiam maximi faciat, velitque eum gloria & honore coronare, illustremque reddere, qui hic inglorius agere visus fuerat, & cotumeliose est interfectus. Pretiosa est in conspectu Domini mors sanctorum eius, psal. 115. Et sic solet Deus pios, qui hic fuerint oppressi atque infames habiti, (dum videlicet ignominiosis afficiuntur supplicijs) a morte exaltare, ut etiam ab hostibus, hostiumque; posteris praedicentur ac colantur: quomodo Christus etiam obijcit Iudaeis Lucae undecimo, quod prophetarum, quos patres occiderant, monumenta aedificarent, & ornaret: & Herodes Matthaei decimoquarto Ioannem quem obtruncauerat, ut a morte suscitatum, & virtutes multas edentem praedicat. T
units.tr: "And through it he being dead yet speaketh." Here is another notable effect of faith: through it the dead speak, that is, they live and are famous both before God and before men, as Abraham and the other patriarchs live. The later term is put for the earlier by synecdoche. Yet how Abel, being dead, is understood to speak is still explained in various ways. Some say: Abel, dead, speaks, that is, although he was slain, his memory remains most pleasant and is proclaimed on everyone's lips, so that he still speaks and dwells among mortals as one who is always alive and immortal.
