Or he speaks, in that by his example, which he gave while living in zeal for true religion, in confession of faith, in innocence of life and in patience, he now, though dead, invites and urges us to similar virtues. For in this way he still speaks today in the minds of all, and all the saints speak in a similar manner, whose virtues have been approved by God and set before men for imitation. But since the Apostle asserts nothing rashly and always relies on Scripture, it is more probable that he here had in view what Scripture records of dead Abel in Genesis 4, namely that God said to the fratricide Cain: "The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground." The sense of these words is this: "Do you think, O Cain, that I do not know where your brother Abel is? The voice of his blood cries out to me," that is, "I know as surely how things went with him as if his blood had already told me everything. I still take care of him, and his death will not remain hidden but will be made more and more clear." Now in the words of Scripture there is personification, since speech is attributed to an inanimate thing. Therefore the meaning must be drawn in a way other than the words simply sound. So since the Apostle here also says that Abel, though dead, speaks through faith, I think it is signified that the faith of Abel pleased God so greatly while he lived that now, dead, God still values him most highly and wishes to crown him with glory and honour and make him illustrious, though he seemed to live here without glory and was slain shamefully. "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints" (Ps. 115). And so God is accustomed to exalt from death the godly who were oppressed here and regarded as infamous (namely while they undergo ignominious punishments), so that they are proclaimed and honoured even by their enemies and their descendants. Thus Christ also reproached the Jews in Luke 11 for building and adorning the monuments of the prophets whom their fathers had killed; and Herod in Matthew 14 said that John, whom he had beheaded, had been raised from the dead and was performing many mighty works.

units.la: Etin hanc sententiam etiam capite sequenti præsentis epistolæ sanguis Christi, qui est verus sanguis aspersus ad spiritualem nostram purificationem, loqui dicitur, hoc est, illustrior & clarior factus, dum prædicato euangelio eius dignitas & efficacia plenius, quàm antea, cognoscitur. Ac dicitur ibidem loqui meliora, quà loquebatur sanguis Abel: quia nimirum Christum interfectum à fratribus Iudæis, cuius typum gerebat à fratre interfectus Abel, decet longè illustriorem & celebriorem à morte fieri, quàm factus est Abel. Scio autem plerosque interpretari clamorem Abel petitionem vindictæ in fratrem Cain. Sed qua obsecro religione id tribuatur Sanctis à morte, quod ipsi ne in hac fragili quidem vita erant facturi, etiamsi maximè per charitatem licuisset? Deinde, quomodo dicetur Abel id facere per fidem? Deniq;, quomodo intelligemus sanguinem Christi ita loqui, qui ipso supplicij sui tempore pro crucifigentibus ardentissimè orauit? Verum quidem est, Apocal. 6. & 19. sanctorum animas induci petentes, ut Dominus vindicet ipsorum effusum sanguinem. Sed, quod & Augustinus asserit, in lib. quæst. vtriusq; testamenti, quest. 68. ibi non adeò voluntatem seu votum exprimi, quando ipsi etiam num in viuis existentes certo tempore id futurum probè tenebant: sed potius certitudine significari, de persecutoribus suo tempore puniendis. Etq; in Apocalypsi etiam προσωπoποιία & ὑποτύπωσις ad mouendos animos apposita.
units.tr: And in this same sense, in the following chapter of this letter, the blood of Christ, which is the true blood sprinkled for our spiritual purification, is said to speak, that is, to have been made more illustrious and clearer, since by the preaching of the gospel its dignity and efficacy are known more fully than before. And it is said there that it speaks better things than the blood of Abel did, because Christ, slain by his Jewish brethren, whose type was Abel slain by his brother, must necessarily become far more illustrious and celebrated through death than Abel became. I know that most interpreters take the cry of Abel to be a request for vengeance on his brother Cain. But by what religious principle, I ask, is this attributed to the saints after death, when they would not have done it even in this frail life, even if charity had allowed it most of all? Next, how will it be said that Abel did this through faith? Finally, how shall we understand the blood of Christ to speak in this way, when at the very time of his punishment he prayed most fervently for those who crucified him? It is true that in Revelation 6 and 19 the souls of the saints are introduced asking that the Lord avenge their shed blood. But, as Augustine also asserts in his Questions on Both Testaments, question 68, there the will or desire is not so much expressed there, since they themselves, while still living, knew surely that this would happen at a certain time; rather, certainty is signified about the persecutors to be punished in their own time. And in the Apocalypse personification and vivid representation are also employed to move the minds of readers.

units.la: Porrò doctrinam habemus hic huiusmodi. Primò, quomodo omnes actiones nostræ, si eas concupiscimus Deo acceptas esse, & à Deo respici, debeant ex fide nasci. Aliàs peccata potius fore, quam officia siue cultus. Secundò, habemus, quòd Deus nihilominus respiciat bona opera, & testimonium de illis ferat, præsertim si ex fide fuerint perac-ta. Quæ ratio omnes debet ad proferendos fructus fidei, & opera charitatis excitare. Tertiò, habemus hic locum de immortalitate & vita æterna piorum, quodque Deus etiam à morte pios curet & illustret: quod non solùm excitat ad cultum religionis, verumetiam solatur in afflictionibus.
units.tr: Furthermore, we have here the following teaching. First, all our actions, if we desire them to be acceptable to God and regarded by him, ought to spring from faith. Otherwise they will be sins rather than duties or worship. Second, we have that God nonetheless regards good works and bears witness to them, especially if they have been performed out of faith. This reason ought to stir all to bring forth the fruits of faith and the works of love. Third, we have here a passage about the immortality and eternal life of the godly, and that God cares for and makes illustrious the godly even after death; this not only stirs us to the worship of religion but also comforts us in afflictions.

units.la: Per fidem Enoch fuit translatus, ne videret mortem, nec fuit inuentus, propterea quòd transtulerat illum Deus. Priusquam enim transferretur, testimonium meruerat quòd placuisset Deo. Atqui sine fide fieri non potest, ut quis illi placeat. Nam qui accedit ad Deum, hunc credere oportet, esse Deum, & esse remuneratorem quaerentibus se.
units.tr: By faith Enoch was translated, that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had translated him. For before he was translated, he had obtained the testimony that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God. For whoever comes to God must believe that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

units.la: Secundum exemplum institutæ Inductionis de Enoch per fidem iustificato. In quo rursus, quemadmodum in præcedenti, duo sunt insignes fidei fructus obseruandi: Altes quando colligit, eum fide iustificatum: alter, quando ex consequenti adjicit, eundem per fidem esse translatum, & mortem non vidisse. Quod ad priorem illum, & qui præcipuè hic considerandus est, attinet, sic ratiocinatur: Enoch, priusquam transferretur, testimonium meruerat, quòd placuisset Deo, hoc est, iustus à Deo sit habitus. Atqui, ut quis Deo placeat, non potest id fieri, nisi per fidem. Igitur Enoch per fidem Deo placuit, ac iustus pronunciatus est. Partes huius syllogismi decet nos plenius explicare. Primò, Maior manifesta est ex Gen. 5. vbi sic legitur: Henoch vixit 65. annis, & genuit Methuselach: Ambulauit autem Hanoch cum Deo postquà genuit Methuselach, trecentos annos, genuitq; filios & filias. Fuerunt queq; cuncti dies Hanoch quinq; & sexaginta anni atq; trecenti. Ambulauit in quam Hanoch cum Deo: postea esse desijt, quia tulit eum Deus. Quo loco bis prædicatur Enoch, quòd ambulauerit cum Deo. Quæ geminatio hauddubiè per ipsum Spiritum sanctum facta est, ad ostendendum, quàm insigni fide, nec non studio promouendæ religionis ille fuerit præditus. Sancti sua laude & gloria non spoliantur, præsertim qui in fide & promouenda vera religione strenuè laborauerint: quod exemplum, ut obiter admoneam, etiam nos hodie merito deberet animare, ad fortiter decertandum in defendenda illustrandaq; dignitate euangelij: ac certum est, id si faciamus, etiamsi dum viuimus, ingratum, imò hostiliter insidiantem sentiamus totum mundum: tamen spiritus aliquando editurus est testimonium, quòd cum Deo ambulauerimus, sicut de Henoch grauissimum testimonium videmus pronunciatum. Ac talem tantumq; fuisse Enoch, non solùm ex illo Geneseos loco, verumetiam ex epistola Iudæ (quam ne quis existimet contemnendam, ceu nuper primùm receptam ab ecclesijs, Tertullianus Apostolorum temporibus vicinus citat libro de habitu muliebri) constare potest, qui eum non tùm ut sanctimonia vitæ clarum, ac doctorem, verumetiam vt excellentissimū prophetam celebrat. Atq; hæc etiam est causa, cur statim post Abele inter iustos hic numeretur. Nam nemo inter omnes patres ab Abele ad tepora Enoch ita prædicatur, imò nulli laus ulla tribuitur, nisi Enos filio Seth, de quo ad finem cap. 4. additur, Tunc cœptum est inuocari nomen Iehouæ. Quibus verbis significatur, quòd postquam extinctus est iustus Abel, & Cain cum suis conciuibus præualeret, extinctaque propemodum esset omnis vera religio, tandem tempore posteriore Seth cœptam restituì religionem & ecclesiam. Neque verò simpli citer dicitur, ipsum Enos autorem fuisse religionis restituendæ, sed eius tempore tunc cœptum inuocari nomen Domini: quasi propositum foret id pro exemplo ecclesiæ, quæ postquam à tyrannis Cainitis aliquamdiu truculenter oppressa fuerit, tamen incipit itè rum suo tempore respirare. Atq; huc sine dubio respexit Apostolus, hincque factum est, quod Apostolus post Abelem statim subiecerit Henoch, omisso illo Enos.
units.tr: A second example of the method of induction set out: Enoch, justified by faith. Here again, as in the previous case, two notable fruits of faith are to be observed: the first, when he gathers that Enoch was justified by faith; the second, when he adds in consequence that the same man was translated through faith and did not see death. As for the first, which is the one chiefly to be considered here, he reasons thus: Enoch, before he was translated, had obtained the testimony that he pleased God, that is, he was regarded by God as righteous. But no one can please God except through faith. Therefore Enoch pleased God through faith and was pronounced righteous. It is right for us to explain the parts of this syllogism more fully. First, the major premise is plain from Genesis 5, where it is read thus: "Enoch lived sixty-five years and begat Methuselah. And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years, and begat sons and daughters. And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. And Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him." In this place Enoch is twice said to have walked with God. This repetition was undoubtedly made by the Holy Spirit himself, to show with how remarkable a faith, and also with what zeal for advancing religion, he was endowed. The saints are not stripped of their praise and glory, especially those who have laboured vigorously in faith and in advancing true religion. This example, to remind you in passing, ought also today to rightly encourage us to contend bravely in defending and illustrating the dignity of the gospel. And it is certain that if we do this, even if while we live we feel the whole world ungrateful and even plotting hostilely against us, yet the Spirit will at some time give the testimony that we have walked with God, just as we see the most weighty testimony pronounced about Enoch. That Enoch was such and so great a man can be established not only from that passage of Genesis, but also from the Epistle of Jude (which no one should think to be despised, as if only lately received by the churches; Tertullian, who lived close to the times of the Apostles, cites it in his book On the Dress of Women). Jude celebrates Enoch not only as renowned for holiness of life and as a teacher, but also as a most excellent prophet. And this too is the reason why he is numbered here among the righteous immediately after Abel. For among all the fathers from Abel to the times of Enoch, no one is so praised; indeed no praise at all is given, except to Enos, the son of Seth, of whom at the end of chapter 4 it is added: "Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD." By these words it is signified that after the righteous Abel was extinguished, and Cain with his fellow citizens prevailed, and true religion was almost wholly extinguished, at length in a later time under Seth true religion and the Church began to be restored. Nor is it simply said that Enos himself was the author of restoring religion, but that in his time the name of the Lord began to be called upon; as if this were set forth as an example of the Church, which, after being cruelly oppressed for some time by the tyrannical Cainites, nevertheless begins again in its own time to draw breath. And without doubt the Apostle had this in view, and hence it is that the Apostle, after Abel, immediately adds Enoch, passing over Enos.

units.la: Cæterum quod Genes. 5. dicitur de Henoch, Ambulauit cum Deo, hîc autem, εὐαρέστησεν τῷ θεῷ, hoc plane idem sibi volunt, & tantundem significant, atque si diceretur, quod apud Deum iustus sit habitus, seu iustificatus. Qui enim ambulat cũ Deo, id est, verè credit, verè timet Deum, fide & fidei fructibus insignis, certè talis Deo placet, Deoque acceptus est. Hoc ipsum verò quid aliud est, quàm iustum apud Deum reputari? Non est igitur quod quispiam cauilletur, Apostolum aliquid aliud expressisse ab eo, quod habetur libro Genesios.
units.tr: Moreover, what Genesis 5 says of Enoch, that he walked with God, and here (Hebrews 11), εὐαρέστησεν τῷ θεῷ [euarestēsen tō theō, he pleased God], plainly mean the same thing and signify just as much as if it were said that he was held, or justified, as just before God. For whoever walks with God, that is, truly believes and truly fears God, distinguished by faith and the fruits of faith, certainly such a man pleases God and is accepted by him. And what else is this itself than to be reckoned righteous before God? There is therefore no ground for anyone to carp that the Apostle has expressed something other than what is found in the book of Genesis.

units.la: Sed iá hoc fortasis dicturus erat aliquis: Rectè quidem dicitur Enoch placuisse Deo, iuxta illud, quod de ipso dicitur Genes. 5. quòd ambulauerit cum Deo. Atqui ex eo nequaquam videtur euinci posse, quòd placuerit Deo propter fidem: imò potius cùm ambulare cum Deo phrasi hebraica significet, vitam moresque iuxta præceptum ac voluntatem Dei componere, videtur sequi, placuisse eum Deo propter opera.
units.tr: But someone might perhaps already be going to object: It is indeed rightly said that Enoch pleased God, according to what is said of him in Genesis 5, that he walked with God. Yet from this it cannot in any way be shown that he pleased God on account of faith; rather, since to walk with God in the Hebrew idiom means to shape one's life and conduct according to God's precept and will, it seems to follow that he pleased God on account of works.

units.la: Hac de causa Apostolus prudenter adiecit, tollendæ talis dubitationis causa, minore, dicens: Atqui sine fide fieri non potest, ut quis illi placeat: (sicut etiam in præcedenti exemplo dicebat, prius placuisse Abel: deinde munera, respiciens ad verba Genesios: ne videlicet cõtenderet aliquis, placuisse ipsum propter sacrificia:) Quibus verbis clarè significat, non posse intelligi, quenquam ambulare coram Deo, aut quocunque modo bene agere, nisi quatenus id fiat ex fide. Quæcunque enim verè bona opera necessum est ab hoc fonte prodeant. Nemo verè ambulat coram Deo, nisi qui totus ex Deo pendet, totus vni Deo fidit, & omnia sua ad gloriam Dei dirigit.
units.tr: For this reason the Apostle wisely added the minor premise, to remove such doubt, saying: But without faith it is impossible to please him (just as in the preceding example he said that Abel first pleased God, and then his gifts, looking to the words of Genesis, lest anyone should contend that he pleased God on account of the sacrifices). By these words he clearly signifies that no one can be understood to walk before God, or to do well in any way, except insofar as this comes about from faith. For whatever truly good works there are must necessarily proceed from this source. No one truly walks before God except he who depends wholly on God, trusts wholly in God alone, and directs all his things to the glory of God.

units.la: Porrò hic semper initium bonarum actionū fides est: sicut & de Abel supra diximus, eum non fuisse motum ad offerendas pingues hostias, nisi per fidem: & prius fide acceptam fuisse personam, quàm respicerentur munera. Igitur ex eo, quod dicitur Enoch ambulasse cum Deo, clarè infertur, eum egregia fide in Deum fuisse præditum: & ambulare cum Deo nihil aliud esse, quàm Deo verè credere, Deum verè timere, tota fide vni Deo adhærere.
units.tr: Moreover, here faith is always the beginning of good actions; as we also said above about Abel, that he was not moved to offer fat sacrifices except through faith, and that his person was accepted through faith before his gifts were regarded. Therefore from what is said, that Enoch walked with God, it is clearly inferred that he was endowed with an outstanding faith in God, and that to walk with God is nothing other than to believe God truly, to fear God truly, and with the whole of faith to cleave to God alone.

units.la: Proinde sapientissimè Apostolus hanc minorem subiecit, ad comprobandum, quòd Enoch non alia ratione, quàm fide Deo placuerit. Estque hæc minor vniuersaliter enunciata, & tanquam pro communi sententia & κατὰ λήψιν in Theologia debet accipi, cui tanquam basi præsentis argumentationis pondus & structura tota innititur. Et continet reuera hæc minor summam totius doctrinæ euangelicæ, quæ statim ab initio mundi tradita est patribus, & ad nos vsque inuiolata apud piorum exiguam ecclesiam, permansit. Ac de ea nobis forent plurima dicenda: sed quia nonnulla supra à nobis dicta sunt, & sæpe adhuc in sequentibus exemplis erit differendum, ideò prætermittimus. Tantum hoc volumus inculcare, tantì retiera esse fidem, ut nulla actio, quamlibet in speciem præclara & inter uirtutes numeranda, verè talis dici queat, nisi quatenus ex fide nascitur. Adeò, vt Apostolus ausus fuerit definire Romanorum decimoquarto, Quicquid ex fide non est, peccatum esse. Quæ verba tametsi exponiatur à nonnullis, quasi sit sententia: Nõ esse quicquam faciundum contra conscientiam, quæ docet, contra legem esse, quod facere meditaris: quam etiam interpretationem non prorsus reijcimus: tamen proprie significat, opera quæcunque mandata aut concessa à Deo, facienda esse in fide, id est, cũ hac fiducia, quòd Deus propter Christum velit acceptare.
units.tr: Accordingly the Apostle most wisely added this minor premise, to prove that Enoch pleased God by no other means than by faith. And this minor premise is stated universally, and in theology must be taken as a common opinion and by assumption [κατὰ λήψιν], on which the whole weight and structure of the present argument rests as on its foundation. And this minor premise in truth contains the sum of the whole evangelical doctrine, which was handed down to the fathers from the very beginning of the world, and has remained inviolate down to us among the small congregation of the pious. Much could be said to us about it, but since some things have already been said by us above, and it will often have to be deferred in the examples that follow, we pass it over. We wish only to press this point: faith is of such great importance that no action, however brilliant in appearance and to be numbered among the virtues, can rightly be called such unless it arises from faith. So much so that the Apostle dared to define in Romans 14: Whatever is not of faith is sin. Although some expound these words as if the sense were: nothing must be done against conscience, which teaches that what you are planning to do is against the law (an interpretation which we also do not wholly reject), nevertheless it properly signifies that all works commanded or permitted by God are to be done in faith, that is, with this trust, that God will accept them for Christ's sake.

units.la: Prior quidem interpretatio ad legem ducit, & ad legem pertinet, sed posterior ad euangelium, cui Apostolus sententiam suam adeoque totam disputationem Roman. 14. positam accommodat. In summa, commendetur memoriæ, & habeatur pro regula, ad quam examinari debent omnes nostræ actiones, quod Apostolus hîc dicit, sine fide non potest fieri, ut quis Deo placeat.
units.tr: The former interpretation leads to the law and pertains to the law, but the latter to the gospel, to which the Apostle applies his sentence, and indeed his whole discussion, set out in Romans 14. In sum, let what the Apostle says here be commended to memory and held as a rule, by which all our actions ought to be examined: without faith it is not possible for anyone to please God.

units.la: Cæterùm, ne hæc minor ita vniuersaliter expressa durius exciperetur ab aduersarijs, sicut nunc quoque excipitur adhuc à quamplurimis pharisæis & iustitiarijs, Apostolo placuit addere quandam eius probationem sumptam ab officio eius, qui Deo placere cupit, siue à modo, quo quis Deo placere possit: (etiamsi satis constare debuisset de more, ex propositione illa supra cap. 10. habita, Iustus ex fide sua viuet:) Nam qui, in quit, accedit. cedit ad Deum, hunc credere oportet, esse Deum, & esse remuneratorem quaerentibus se: quasi diceret: Si quis velit Deum accedere, illique placere, & esse acceptus, oportet ante omnia credat, esse Deum, & quidem talem, qualem esse naturae eius convenit, hoc est, omnipotentem, optimum, sapientissimum, iustissimum, & praeterea eundem esse remuneratorem, id est, misericorditer & largiter conferre bona, inprimis spiritualia, omnibus, qui ipsum toto corde, & tota mente quaesierint, constanterq; per fidem adhaeserint. Ita namque accipie da sunt posteriora verba, ut ijs officia, & actus fidei plene intelligantur expresi: & tota vim definitionis fidei supra positae oportet in his verbis repositam iudicare. Quod quo facilius ab omnibus fieri queat, nos singula membra exactius discutiemus. πιστεύσω γὰρ ὰ τὸν προσερχόμενον τῷ θεῷ. Qui, inquit, accedere vult Deum. Quare non dicit, Qui placere vult Deo? Ad evidentius exprimendum, quomodo quis placere Deo possit. Prius enim necessum est, ut mens aliquo modo ad Deum feratur, quam credere incipiat.
units.tr: Furthermore, lest this minor premise, so universally expressed, be received too harshly by opponents, as it is still even now received by very many Pharisees and advocates of works-righteousness, the Apostle chose to add a certain proof of it, taken from the duty of one who desires to please God, or from the manner in which anyone can please God (although it ought to have been sufficiently clear from the custom, from that proposition stated above in chapter 10: The just shall live by his faith). For he says: For he who comes to God must believe that God exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. As if he were saying: If anyone wishes to draw near to God, and to please him and be accepted, he must first of all believe that God exists, and indeed such a God as befits his nature, that is, almighty, best, wisest, most just; and besides, that he is the same a rewarder, that is, that he mercifully and bountifully bestows good things, especially spiritual ones, on all who seek him with the whole heart and the whole mind and who have constantly cleaved to him through faith. For the latter words are to be taken in such a way that the duties and acts of faith are fully expressed in them, and the whole force of the definition of faith set out above must be judged to be contained in these words. So that this may be done more easily by all, we shall examine the individual members more exactly. πιστεύσω γὰρ ὰ τὸν προσερχόμενον τῷ θεῷ [pisteusai gar dei ton proserchomenon tō theō, for he who comes to God must believe]. He who, he says, wishes to come to God. Why does he not say, he who wishes to please God? In order to express more clearly how anyone can please God. For it is necessary first that the mind be directed in some way toward God before it begins to believe.

units.la: Huc pertinent omnes illae voces, tum apud prophetas, tu in euangelicis scriptis, quibus homines ad quaerendum, ad audiendum Deum inuitantur. Esaiae 55. Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas, & qui non habetis argentum, properate, emite, & comedite, venite, emite, absque argento, & absque ulla commutatione vinum & lac, &c. Psalm 33. Accedite ad eum, & illuminamini, & facies vestrae non confundentur. Christus Matth. 11. Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos, &c. Et pater, Matt. 3. 17. Hic est filius meus dilectus, ipsum audite, &c.
units.tr: To this pertain all those voices, both in the prophets and in the evangelical writings, by which men are invited to seek and to hear God. Isaiah 55: Come, all you who thirst, to the waters, and you who have no silver, hurry, buy and eat; come, buy without silver and without any exchange wine and milk, etc. Psalm 33: Draw near to him, and you will be enlightened, and your faces will not be ashamed. Christ, Matthew 11: Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you, etc. And the Father, Matthew 3:17: This is my beloved Son; hear him, etc.

units.la: Vbi vero iam mens ad Deum vtcunque conuersa est, proponitur illi in verbo, & per verbum, quod credere oporteat, quae vbi perfecte credit, tum Deo placet. Hac igitur de causa dixit, Accedentem ad Deum oportet credere, &c. Quae autem proponuntur illi credenda? Duo inprimis: Alterum, ut credat, Deum esse. Hic est primus gradus, & cognitio necessaria ad credendum: oportet credere, Deum esse, & quidem talem esse, qualis ipse nobis passim in verbo describitur, hoc est omnipotens, optimus, maximus, iustissimus, &c. Sed haec cognitio perquam exigua est, quam etiam in gentibus, imo & in daemonibus liceat reperire: ideoque per hanc nondum Deo placebimus. Oportet igitur altius progredi, & aliud quiddam credere, nempe, esse remuneratorem quaerentibus se: Hic demum fides absolvitur, vbi potest apprehendere oblatam misericordiam propter semen benedictum. Hic plane habemus, quod ad sensum attinet, totum hoc, quod supra in definitione fidei continebatur. Quid est inprimis quaerere Dominum, nisi firma ὑπόστασις rerum sperandarum, hoc est, tota mente ad vnum Deum dirigi, ex solo Deo pendere, misericordiam & omnia bona ab eo expectare?
units.tr: Where indeed the mind has in whatever way been turned toward God, there is set before it, in the word and through the word, what it ought to believe; and when it believes this perfectly, then it pleases God. For this reason he said: He who comes to God must believe, etc. But what is set before him to be believed? Two things first of all. The first, that he believe that God exists. This is the first step, and the knowledge necessary for believing: one must believe that God exists, and indeed that he is such as he is everywhere described to us in the word, that is, almighty, best, greatest, most just, etc. But this knowledge is quite slight, and it can be found even among the heathen, indeed even among demons; and therefore through this alone we shall not yet please God. It is necessary, then, to advance higher and to believe something further, namely, that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. Here at last faith is complete, where it can grasp the mercy offered for the sake of the blessed seed. Here we plainly have, as far as the sense is concerned, all that was contained above in the definition of faith. For what is it first of all to seek the Lord, other than a firm substance [ὑπόστασις] of things hoped for, that is, to be directed with the whole mind to the one God alone, to depend wholly on God, and to expect mercy and all good things from him?

units.la: Haec est remuneratio Dei, dum, quia tantum credimus, & ipsum solum quaerimus, ipse nobis impendit misericordiam. Neq; enim, quia hic est, μισθαποδότης, sic accipiemus, quasi remuneratio ista sese haberet instar mercedis, quae pro opere aut labore recipitur: quod est aperte contra praedicationem gratuitae misericordiae, quae vsque adeo passim vrgetur ab Apostolo. Sed intelligemus, sumptam esse locutionis formam a communi more loquendi: idque eo magis, quia mire idonea sit ad excitandos animos, ut fide tantorum bonorum participem apprehendant, & ad fidei fructus proferendos omnes sint diligentiores.
units.tr: This is God's reward: while we only believe and seek him alone, he bestows his mercy upon us. Yet we should not take it, because he is μισθαποδότης [rewarder], as though this remuneration were like wages paid for a work or labour. That would plainly contradict the preaching of free mercy, which the Apostle urges so constantly. We should understand rather that this manner of speaking is borrowed from common usage, and all the more so because it is wonderfully suited to rouse minds, so that they may grasp by faith the share in such great goods, and become more diligent in bringing forth the fruits of faith.

units.la: Porro, qui huiusmodi habet fidem, & primum vere credit, Deum esse: deinde, remunerari largiter omnibus ipsum quaerentibus: hic iam Deo placet & acceptus est. Et sic probata est minor illa. Quia sine fide impossibile est, quenquam placere Deo. Cum autem ipse Enoch tali fide fuerit praeditus, sicut liquet ex ipsius verbis, quae citantur in epistola Iudae: clare sequitur, ipsum placuisse Deo, & quidem fide, non autem operibus.
units.tr: Moreover, whoever has this kind of faith first truly believes that God exists, and then that he richly rewards all who seek him. Such a person now pleases God and is accepted by him. And so that minor premise is proved: without faith it is impossible to please God. Since Enoch himself was endowed with such faith, as is clear from his own words cited in the Epistle of Jude, it follows plainly that he pleased God, and indeed by faith, not by works.

units.la: Iam de altero effectu fidei, qui ex praecedenti sequitur, est dicendum. Quia enim Enoch prius per fidem Deo placuit, hinc factum postea, ut translatus fit. Quae de reliquitur Apostolus: per fidem Enoch fuit translatus, ne videret mortem, nec fuit inventus, propterea quod transtulerat illum Deus.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the other effect of faith, which follows from the first. Because Enoch first pleased God through faith, it afterwards came about that he was translated. The Apostle adds this: by faith Enoch was translated, so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had translated him.

units.la: Porro Genesis quinto, vbi fundamentum quaerendum est verborum Apostoli, sicle gitur, בִּי לִקְחוֹ אֱלֹהִים, id est, & non ipse (scilicet inter homines amplius: quasi diceret, subito disparuit) quia tulit ipsum Deus. Vbi etiam Septuaginta sic habent, καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκετο, ὅτι μετέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ θεός: id est, & placuit Enoch Deo, & non inuentus est, quoniam transtulit illum Deus: Haec ibi. Et verum quidem est, Ecclesiastici capite quadragesimo quarto in vulgata editione sic legi. Henoch placuit Deo, & translatus est in paradisum, vt det gentibus poenitentiam. Sed neque ibi reddidit interpres ad fidem Septuaginta, apud hos enim sic legitur, ἀνήρ εὐηρεστημένος, id est, Enoch placuit Domino, & translatus est exemplum resipiscentiae gentibus.
units.tr: Now in Genesis 5, where the foundation for the Apostle's words must be sought, the Hebrew reads בִּי לִקְחוֹ אֱלֹהִים [ki lakhah Elohim], that is, "and he was not" (namely, any longer among men; as if to say, he suddenly disappeared), "because God took him." There the Septuagint also reads καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκετο [kai ouch heurisketo], ὅτι μετέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ θεός [hoti metethēken auton ho theos], that is, "and Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God transferred him." So far the Septuagint. It is true that in Ecclesiasticus 44 the Vulgate reads: "Enoch pleased God and was translated into paradise, that he might give repentance to the nations." But the Vulgate translator did not render this according to the faith of the Septuagint; for in their text it reads ἀνήρ εὐηρεστημένος [anēr euarestēmenos], that is, "Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated as an example of repentance to the nations."

units.la: Iam
units.tr: Now

units.la: Fide Deo accepti reddimur. Quid de Deo credendum. Deus remunerator credetiu. Accedere ad Deum quid. Inuitatio ad Deum. Iam ex his Scripturæ locis æstimandum venit, quid sentire debeamus de translatione Henoch. Atque omnes quidem in hoc conveniunt, quòd translatus sit, sicut clarè Scriptura loquitur. Verùm hic quæstio nascitur, ânne prius mortuus sit? cuius contrarium videtur dicere Apostolus: deinde, quomodo translatus sit. Sed de hac quæstione tota vide in magno volumine, ubi seorsum nonnulla de Henoch fusius sunt expositá. Porrò habemus in hoc exemplo multiplicem & valde salutarem doctrinam nobis propositam. Primò, habemus propositionem illam vniuersaliter dictam, quòd sine fide impossibile est quenquam placere Deo. Quæ propositio tanquam regula quædam à nobis debet ac cipi ad omnium actionum moderationem, utpote per quam scire poterimus, quomodo actiones nostræ instituendæ, ut Deo placeant, vt præstantiores sint, quàm actiones gentilium seu incredulorum. Hæc regula debet omnium animis infixa esse, & perpetuò observari, semper ad opus adhiberi.
units.tr: We are made acceptable to God by faith. What must be believed about God. God rewards those who believe. What it is to draw near to God. An invitation to God. Now from these passages of Scripture we must judge what we ought to think about the translation of Enoch. All agree that he was translated, as Scripture speaks clearly. But here a question arises: did he first die? The Apostle seems to say the opposite. Then, how was he translated? On this question see the whole discussion in the large volume, where several matters concerning Enoch are set out at greater length. Furthermore, in this example we have a manifold and very wholesome teaching set before us. First, we have that proposition stated in general terms: without faith it is impossible to please God. This proposition ought to be received by us as a kind of rule for regulating all our actions, since by it we can know how our actions must be undertaken so that they please God, and so that they are more excellent than the actions of the Gentiles or unbelievers. This rule ought to be fixed in everyone's mind, constantly observed, and always applied to our work.

units.la: Secundò, habemus hic gradus fidei, & modum placendi Deo per fidem propositos, ita vt demonstretur primò, mentem ad Deum conuertendam: deinde ex verbo proponi, vt credamus, Deum esse, & quidem optimum, maximum, sapientissimum, &c. tum, ut omnia bona & misericordiam ab illo expectemus: quibus ita habentibus homo in fide absoluitur, ac Deo placere incipit.
units.tr: Second, we have here the degrees of faith and the way of pleasing God through faith set out, so that it is shown: first, that the mind must be turned to God; then, from the Word, that we are to believe that God exists, and indeed that he is best, greatest, wisest, and so on; then that we should look to him for all good things and for mercy. When these things are so, a man is made complete in faith and begins to please God.

units.la: Tertiò, confutantur hic, qui negant prouidentiam, & casu cuncta regi ferriq; existimant: quando describitur Deus remunerator omnibus quærentibus eum. Si bene egerimus, Dominum toto corde quærentes, largiter ab eo accipiemus; & è diuerso.
units.tr: Third, those are refuted here who deny providence and think that all things are governed and carried along by chance, since God is described as the rewarder of all who seek him. If we act well, seeking the Lord with our whole heart, we shall receive richly from him; and conversely.

units.la: Quartò, particula illa de quærentibus Deum, omnes admonere debet ad summam diligentiam, & laborem, placendi Deo.
units.tr: Fourth, that phrase about those who seek God ought to admonish everyone to the highest diligence and effort in pleasing God.

units.la: Per fidem admonitus oraculo Noe, ea, quæ nondum videbantur, veritus apparauit arcam, ad salutem domus suæ, per quam arcam condemnauit mundum, & eius, quæ secundum fidem est, iustitia factus est hæres.
units.tr: By faith Noah, being warned of God about things not yet seen, moved with fear, prepared an ark for the saving of his house, by which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.

units.la: Tertium exemplum de Noah, in quo nihil aliud, quà breuiter à signis colligit, Noah insigni fide fuisse præditum. Ex quo mox infert, eum per fidem iustificatum. Proinde nos hoc exemplum istud explicabimus. Primò, ipsam illationem, seu assertionem, quòd vide licet Noah fide sit iustificatus, excutiemus: quando quidem ea assertio semper hic spectada principaliter in tota hac inductione. Secundò, explicabimus illa, quæ veluti probatio nis causa præmittuntur: ex quibus videlicet ostenditur, ipsum Noach egregia & heroica fide plane fuisse illustrem, dignissimaque sunt, quæ diligenter expendantur. Illatio siue assertio illa sic habet: Et eius quæ secundum fidem est, iustitiæ factus est hæres: Vide, quàm eleganter Apostolus loquatur: videtur plane rhetoricari, & quasi ornatus causa diuersis vtilocutionum formulis. Sed si penitius intuemur, aliæ rationes & quidem grauissimæ eum mouerunt ad ita mutandum varietate & copia uerborum eandem sententiam. Satis fuisset, simpliciter vbique dicere, & per fidem iustificatus est: Sed aliter loqui visum fuit. Id autem his de causis. Primò, & principaliter, ut nos melius & clarius perciperemus ea, quæ ab ipso dicuntur.
units.tr: This is the third example, that of Noah. In it the Apostle gathers only briefly from the signs that Noah was endowed with remarkable faith, and from this he at once infers that he was justified by faith. Accordingly we shall explain this example as follows. First, we shall examine the inference, or assertion, that Noah was justified by faith, since this assertion is always to be kept chiefly in view throughout this whole argument. Second, we shall explain those things which are set forth first, as it were as proof. From these it is shown that Noah was plainly distinguished by an outstanding and heroic faith, and these things deserve careful consideration. The inference or assertion reads: "and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith." See how elegantly the Apostle speaks: he seems plainly to be writing rhetorically, using varied forms of expression, as it were for the sake of ornament. But if we look more deeply, other reasons, and very weighty ones, moved him to vary the same sentiment in such a wealth of words. It would have sufficed simply to say everywhere, "and he was justified by faith." But it seemed good to speak otherwise. The reasons are these. First, and chiefly, that we might perceive more clearly and distinctly the things that are said by him.

units.la: Secundò, ut semper etiam plenius doceremur de iustificationis nostræ modo atque ordine, quem à nobis rectè cognosci, valde est necessarium. Spiritus Sanctus lubenter utitur formis verborum conuenientibus nostro captui, demittit & attemperat se nobis. Aulici & cancellariistæ habent proprias quasdam & exquisitas loquendi formas, discretas à vulgi more: & gaudent, non à quouis intelligi. At Deus non ita instituit suam curiam, quæ est ecclesia: sed vult, omnes prophetas & doctores in ea loqui crasso more, & homi num more magis, quàm diuino.
units.tr: Second, that we might always be taught more fully about the manner and order of our justification, which it is very necessary for us to know rightly. The Holy Spirit gladly uses forms of words suited to our capacity; he condescends and adapts himself to us. Courtiers and chancery officials have their own peculiar and refined ways of speaking, distinct from the common manner, and they delight in not being understood by just anyone. But God has not so ordered his court, which is the Church. He wills that all prophets and teachers in it speak in a plain manner, and in a human rather than a divine manner.

units.la: Porrò hæc forma verborum, qua nunc vsus est, multò aptissima est intellectui nostro, & magnarum rerum cognitionem pleniorem adfert, ut ostendemus.
units.tr: Moreover, this form of words which he now uses is far best suited to our understanding, and brings a fuller knowledge of great matters, as we shall show.

units.la: Cùm enim ait, Iustitiæ, quæ est secundum fidem, clarissimè connectit fidei iustitiam, euidentissimeque docet, iustitiam quandam propriam esse fidei, quæ distincta sit à iustitia operum. Nam opera quoque inuenimus adiunctam habere suam iustitiam & gloriam: sed, ut Roman. 4. diserte exprimitur, non apud Deum. Mundus quidam iudicat de exteris; & potest iustitiam decernere propter externa opera: sed Deus diuersissima agit ratione, intuetur corda, & contemplatur fidem in cordibus, & huic soli ipse iustitiam tribuit. Hypocritæ pronunciantur iusti coram mundo, quia habent opera, sicut & pij. At coram Deo soli credentes pro iustis ab ipso reputantur.
units.tr: For when he says "the righteousness which is according to faith," he most clearly links the righteousness of faith, and most evidently teaches that there is a certain righteousness proper to faith, which is distinct from the righteousness of works. For we find that works too have their own righteousness and glory attached to them, but, as Romans 4 expressly states, not before God. The world judges by outward appearances, and can decide righteousness on account of outward works; but God acts on a quite different principle: he looks upon the hearts, beholds faith in the hearts, and bestows righteousness on this alone. Hypocrites are pronounced righteous before the world, because they have works, just as the pious do. But before God only believers are reckoned righteous by him.

units.la: Deinde, cùm ait, factum hæredem: certitudinem hic notat gratiæ diuinæ, quæ tanta est, ut in iustitiam ei redundet, qui Deo & verbo eius firmiter credit. Neque iustum solû repureputat Deus credentem: sed bonorum quoque spiritualium & coelestium facit haeredes Filijs parentum bona & haereditates, ijsque in primis, qui fidelem operam obedientiaq; parentibus exhibuerunt, debentur. Pari ratione Deus, quos pro filijs adoptauit, per fidem in Christum filium iustificauit, per spiritum, qui est arrhabo haereditatis futurae, sanctificauit, eosdem aliquando glorificaturus est, & gloriae aeternae vitaeq; coelestis participes redditurus. Id quod Roman. 8. Ephes. 1. & alibi euidenter docetur. Atque hanc remunerationem & haereditatem coelestem spectasse patres olim, ex sequentibus patebit manifestius. Non dican de sacramentis & verbo Dei, vtpote certis documentis gratiae diuinae: quibus ita confirmati fuerunt patres, ut nequaquam de veritate promissionum diuinarum dubitarint, sed potentem Deum crediderint, ad praestandum id, quod veritatis verbo affirmarit. Sed de hoc alibi copiosius.
units.tr: Then, when he says "made an heir," he marks the certainty of divine grace, which is so great that it overflows into righteousness for the one who firmly believes God and his Word. God does not merely count the believer righteous; he also makes him an heir of spiritual and heavenly goods. Goods and inheritances belong to the children of their parents, and above all to those who have shown faithful service and obedience to their parents. By the same reasoning, God, who has adopted as sons those whom he justified through faith in Christ the Son, and sanctified through the Spirit, who is the pledge of the future inheritance, will at some time glorify them and make them partakers of eternal glory and heavenly life. This is clearly taught in Romans 8, Ephesians 1, and elsewhere. And that the Fathers of old looked to this reward and heavenly inheritance will appear more plainly from what follows. I say nothing here of the sacraments and the Word of God, as sure evidences of divine grace, by which the Fathers were so confirmed that they never doubted the truth of God's promises, but believed that God is powerful to perform what he has affirmed by the word of truth. But of this more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Iam ad ea, quae probationis causa diximus praemisi. Est hoc valde laudandum in Apostolo, quod in singulis exemplis non satis putat, simpliciter efferre, hunc vel illum sanctum patrem fide iustificatum: verumetiam semper addit, e quibus fides patrum, qualis, & quanta fuerit, & quibus in rebus maxime emicuerit, potest intelligi. Neq; hoc solum, verumetiam semper visendum praebet aliquem singularem fidei effectum seu officium, vt quilibet possit aliquid singulare ad doctrinam pertinens inde excerpere.
units.tr: Now let us add what we set out in advance for the sake of proof. It deserves high praise in the Apostle that, in individual examples, he does not think it enough simply to state that this or that holy father was justified by faith. He always adds from what things the faith of the fathers can be understood, what kind it was, how great, and in what matters it especially shone forth. He also always presents some singular effect or office of faith, so that anyone may draw from it something singular that pertains to doctrine.

units.la: Per fidem, inquit, admonitus oraculo Noe, quae nondum videntur, veritus, apparauit arcam, ad salutem domus suae.
units.tr: "By faith Noah, being warned by God of things not yet seen, moved with fear, prepared an ark for the saving of his house."

units.la: Ecce mirabile opus fidei, & ex operibus quasi signis & euidentibus testimonijs colligit Apostolus magnitudinem ac dignitatem fidei. Compleditur autem paucissimis versibus summam maximarum rerum, quae copiosius in Scripturis sunt expositae. Quamobrem, ut praesentia verba melius intelligantur, sunt nobis quaedam ex veteri testamento hic recitada. Genesis quinto primum sic scribitur: Noah filius Lamech erat filius quingentorum annorum, & genuit Sem, Ham, & Iaphet. Capite sexto, post pauca: dixit q; Dominus: Non rixabitur spiritus meus cum homine in perpetuum, eo quod ipse est caro: eruntque dies illius centum & viginti anni. Quae praemittimus, quia ibi exprimitur statim, quo Deus manifestauerat pijs, mundum adhuc duraturum, ut interea temporis sese ad poenitentiam pararent. Aliquanto post. Et ait Dominus: Delebo hominem, quem creaui, a superficie terrae, ab homine usque ad iumenta, usq; ad reptile, & usq; ad volatile coeli, quia poenitet me, quod fecerim eos. Noah vero inuenit gratiam in oculis Domini. Iste sunt generationes Noah. Noah vir iustus & integer fuit in generationibus suis, & cum Deo ambulauit Noah ipse. Genuit vero Noah tres filios, Sem, Ham, & Iapheth. Et corrupta est terra coram Deo, & impleta est ipsa terra direptione. Paulo post: Dixitque Deus ad Noah: Finis vniuersae carnis venit coram me: nam repleta est terra violentia a facie illorum, & ecce ego perdo eos cum ipsa terra. Fac tibi arcam de lignis pineis, nidos facies in arca, & bituminabis eam intrinsecus & extrinsecus bitumine. Subijcit ibidem de forma & magnitudine, tum sequitur: Et ecce ego, ego inquam adduco diluuium aquarum super terram, vt perdam vniuersam carnem, in qua est spiritus vitae subter coelum, & omne, quod in terra, expirabit. Et erigam pactum meum tecum, veniesq; in arcam tu & filij tui, vxor tua, & vxores filiorum tuorum tecum.
units.tr: Behold a wonderful work of faith. From its works, as from signs and clear testimonies, the Apostle gathers the greatness and dignity of faith. In very few verses he sums up the chief matters that are set out more fully in the Scriptures. So that the present words may be better understood, some passages of the Old Testament are recited here. In Genesis 5 it is first written: "Noah was the son of Lamech, a son of five hundred years, and he begat Shem, Ham and Japheth." In chapter 6, a little after: "And the Lord said: My spirit shall not remain with man for ever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years." We set this down because there it is immediately stated by what means God had made known to the godly that the world would still endure for a while, so that in the meantime they might prepare themselves for repentance. A little later: "And the Lord said: I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth, from man to beast, to creeping thing, and to the birds of the air, because it repenteth me that I made them. But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God. Noah begat three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence." Shortly after: "And God said to Noah: The end of all flesh is come before me, for the earth is filled with violence through them, and behold, I will destroy them with the earth. Make thee an ark of pine wood; thou shalt make nests in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch." He adds on its form and size, and then follows: "And behold, I, I say, will bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven; everything that is in the earth shall perish. But I will establish my covenant with thee, and thou shalt come into the ark, thou and thy sons, thy wife and the wives of thy sons with thee."

units.la: Vbi adijcit, de animantibus omnis generis quoque in arcam inferendis: post quae sequitur: Fecit igitur Noah iuxta omnia, quae praecepit illi Deus, sic fecit. Hinc capite 7. Et dixit Dominus ad Noah, Veni tu, & omnis domus tua in arcam, quia te vidi iustum coram me in generatione ista. Paulo post: Quia adhuc post septem dies ego pluam super terram quadraginta diebus, & quadraginta noctibus, & delebo omne substantiam, quam feci, de superficie terrae. Fecit itaq; Noah iuxta omnia, quae praecepit illi Deus: paulo post: Et factum est post septem dies, & aquae diluuij fuerunt super terram, in anno sexcentesimo, anno scilicet vitae Noah, in mense secundo, decimaseptima die mensis, in ipsa die rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi, & fenestrae coeli apertae sunt, & fuit pluuia supra terram quadraginta diebus & quadraginta noctibus. Haec in praesens sufficiunt, atque erunt consideratu necessaria. Omnium enim horum summam Apostolus hic est complexus, & his tanquam fundamentis Apostolus innititur.
units.tr: Here he adds that animals of every kind are also to be brought into the ark. After this follows: "Noah therefore did according to all that God commanded him; so he did." Then in chapter 7: "And the Lord said to Noah: Come thou and all thy house into the ark, for I have seen thee just before me in this generation." Shortly after: "For yet after seven days I will rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will destroy every living substance that I have made from the face of the earth. So Noah did according to all that God commanded him." Shortly after: "And it came to pass after seven days that the waters of the flood were upon the earth, in the six hundredth year, that is, of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that very day all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened, and there was rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights." These things are enough for the present and will need to be considered. For the Apostle has here comprehended the sum of all these things, and on these as foundations he rests.

units.la: Proinde sic ait: Per fidem admonitus oraculo Noe. Non est dubium, quin multa alia egregia facinora fuerint ipsius Noe, in quibus fides maxime relucebat, quorum aliqua e Scripturis possent colligi: aliqua vero non sunt prodita sacris Scriptis. Sed istud in sacris literis est pulcherrimum, & ad doctrinam nostrarum conscientiarum vtilissimum. Noe est admonitus oraculo: χρηματισθεὶς, quasi dicat, diuinitus praemonitus, vel, diuinitus responsum accepit.
units.tr: Accordingly he says: "By faith, being warned by the oracle of Noah." There is no doubt that Noah had many other outstanding deeds in which his faith especially shone; some of these could be gathered from the Scriptures, and others are not recorded in the sacred writings. But this is most beautiful in the sacred letters and most useful for the instruction of our consciences. Noah was warned by an oracle: [χρηματισθεὶς], as if to say, divinely forewarned, or, received a divine answer.

units.la: Respicit Apostolus ad id, qd' Deus ante significauit ipsi Noah, quòd mundū vellet perdere, ipsum verò cum suis paucis seruare. Verba cõmemorauimus. Proinde hoc discendū nobis est, amplissimæ esse bonitatis diuinæ, prænunciare hominibus consiliū suæ voluntatis, maximè quotiescūq; vult iudiciū suū exercere. Mittit omni tempore prophetas, & nunquam destituit suam ecclesiam sanctis doctoribus, quibus arcana voluntatis suæ reuelat, per quos sancti sunt patientia & constantia confirmandi, malos verò ad poenitentiā adducendi. Et sic hodie etiamnum facit, quando nunc verè adsunt tempora, qualia erant in diebus Noe: quorū Christus Matth. 24. voluit nos habere diligentē rationē, vt cōsideratione similium temporū & malorū de imminente iudicio certiores efficeremur, & mariteriam inde arriperemus vitam nostram in melius immutandi.
units.tr: The Apostle looks back to what God had earlier signified to Noah himself, namely that he wished to destroy the world but to preserve Noah with a few of his own. We have recalled these words. From this we must learn that it is a sign of the very great goodness of God to announce to men the counsel of his will, especially whenever he wishes to exercise his judgment. He sends prophets at all times, and never leaves his Church without holy teachers, through whom he reveals the secrets of his will, by whom the saints are to be confirmed in patience and constancy, and the wicked are to be brought to repentance. And so he still does today, when truly the times are such as they were in the days of Noah. Christ, in Matth. 24., wished us to take careful account of these, so that by considering the likeness of times and of evils we might be made more certain of the impending judgment, and might take from it a reason for changing our lives for the better.

units.la: Quare valde oculatè intuendum est nunc nobis exemplum Noah, vt fide ipsius imitemur, & promissionibus diuinis inhærentes salutem expectemus.
units.tr: Therefore we must now look very carefully at the example of Noah, so that we may imitate his faith and, clinging to the divine promises, await salvation.

units.la: Porrò ad admonendos homines ad poenitentiam, electus est inprimis à Deo Noah, virnus & quasi solus verbi fidelissimus minister, spiritu Dei afflatus, & propheta insignis toti mundo datus. Huic ergo Deus per suam bonitatem reuelauit, quid de genere humano facere constituisset. Hac de causa ait Apostolus, Noe oraculo admonitum, propter singularem istam reuelationem. Et hic habemus etiam naturam officiumque fidei bona ex parte descriptum. Priusquam enim credatur, proponitur verbum Dei, cui fides inniti debet. Fides enim ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, to admonish men to repentance, Noah was chosen first of all by God: the most faithful, and almost the only, minister of the Word, inspired by the Spirit of God, and given as an outstanding prophet to the whole world. To him therefore God, in his goodness, revealed what he had determined to do with the human race. For this reason the Apostle says that Noah was warned by an oracle, on account of that singular revelation. And here we also have the nature and office of faith largely described. For before anything is believed, the Word of God is set forth, on which faith ought to rest. For faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God.

units.la: Oracula enim & promissiones sunt obiecta fidei, & primæ causæ mouentes animos ad credendum.
units.tr: For oracles and promises are the objects of faith, and the first causes moving minds to believe.

units.la: Ea quæ nondum uidebantur, ueritus) Rectè, quæ nondum videbantur: Nam centum annis, antequam eueniret diluuium, imò centum & viginti annis Deus præsignificauerat. Sed centum annis ante iusit Deus Noe, vt præpararet arcam: ad quæ sine dubio Apostolus hic respexit.
units.tr: "Things not yet seen." Rightly so: for a hundred years before the flood came, indeed a hundred and twenty years, God had foretold it. But a hundred years earlier God had commanded Noah to prepare the ark, and to this the Apostle without doubt looked here.

units.la: Et interim Noah lubeter credens ad fabricandū arcam se parat: constater interea pergens in docendo ecclesiam, & manifestādo Dei voluntate, sicut ipsi ex officio incubebat, & mandatū à Deo acceperat. Sed intra illud spaciū nulli, aut certè paucissimi volebant resipiscere, nulli credebant, ædificabat, contrahebat nuptias, edebat, bibebat, ludebat, & plane irridebat omnes conciones & præmonitiones pij Noah: sicut hodie videmus per impios fieri. Et probabile est, mundū mirabili tum fuisse in dignitate, potētia, opibus, viribus, omnia creuisse, id quod colligi potest ex ijs, quę de gigātibus, & alijs filijs hominū narrantur ibidē. Et sic non apparebat aliquid tale futurū, quale vaticinabatur Noah. At ipse Noah etiāsi multa diuersa cerneret, & fortasis essent pseudoprophetæ, q diuersum prophetabāt: præterea, ipse fortasis patiebatur propter veritatem, grauia odia & persecutiones. Adhæc etiāsi ipse dubitare potuisset, an certus foret de tàm longæua vita, vt vi deret tēpus diluuij, tamē cōstanter credidit. Erat ergo valde insignis fides Noe in rebus adeò nō apparetibus. Et hic habemus iterum officiū & proprietatem fidei, quòd videlicet fides proprie fit ... non apparentiū. Qua de re supra satis multa in definitione fidei. Sed tamē obseruandū hic, quomodo Apostolus selectis verbis vsus fuerit, quibus naturam fidei semper aperiret. Et nos quoque hic admonemur, quotidie expectare Dominum, quando videmus, omnia signa adimpleri, quę Christus prædixit adimplenda. Sed hoc est argumentum nostrę incredulitatis, non curamus, nihil mouemur omnibus hisce signis. Quod verò addit, ueritus ... quasi diceret: cum quadam vene ratione veritus, optimè exprimitur, fidei adiūctum esse timorem, eumq; sanctum & plenum veneratione numinis. Neq; enim fides, etiāsi certos nos reddit de salute, omnem excutit solicitudinem & reuerentiam: non reddit securos & stertentes: sed semper expe ritur tentationes, luctatur cum carne, mundo, Satana, & inter spem metumque assiduè versatur: vt magis excitetur homo ad se committendū vni Deo. Probi filij quo magis suos amant parentes, eo magis etiam metuunt. Ita profsus in fide seu religione est itatuendum. Huc pertinent omnia illa in Scripturis obuia, quæ piis metum & timorem Domini assiduè inculcant. Nunc certè timor Domini nunquam comparet, nec homines, nec Deum timemus.
units.tr: Meanwhile Noah, believing readily, prepares himself to build the ark; meanwhile he continues steadily in teaching the Church and making known the will of God, as his office required and as he had received the command from God. But within that span no one, or very few at most, were willing to repent; no one believed. They built, married, ate, drank and played, and altogether mocked all the sermons and warnings of the godly Noah, as today we see the impious do. And it is probable that the world at that time had grown in remarkable dignity, power, wealth and strength in every way, as can be gathered from what is told there about the giants and the other sons of men. And so it did not appear that anything such as Noah prophesied would come. But Noah himself, although he saw many things differently, and perhaps there were false prophets who prophesied otherwise, and perhaps he himself suffered severe hatred and persecution on account of the truth; besides, even if he could have doubted whether he would be granted so long a life as to see the time of the flood, he nevertheless believed constantly. Therefore the faith of Noah was very remarkable in matters so little apparent. And here again we have the office and property of faith, namely that faith properly concerns things not apparent. On this enough has been said above in the definition of faith. But it is to be observed here how the Apostle, using carefully chosen words, always brings out the nature of faith. We too are here admonished to await the Lord daily, when we see all the signs fulfilled that Christ foretold would be fulfilled. But this is the proof of our unbelief: we do not care, and we are not moved at all by all these signs. As for what he adds, "moved with fear", as if to say, moved by a certain pious reverence, it is very well expressed that fear is joined to faith, and a fear that is holy and full of reverence for the divine majesty. For faith, although it makes us certain of salvation, does not shake off all anxiety and reverence; it does not make men secure and snoring, but always experiences temptations, wrestles with the flesh, the world and Satan, and constantly dwells between hope and fear, so that a man may be more stirred to commit himself to God alone. As good children love their parents the more, the more they also fear them, so must it be established altogether in faith or religion. To this pertain all those things in the Scriptures that constantly impress on the godly fear and the fear of the Lord. Now indeed the fear of the Lord never appears, and we fear neither men nor God.

units.la: Apparauit arcam) Effectum vides fidei & signum præcipuum. Non tantùm mente concipitur, neque ibi hæret sepulta: sed profert viuida exempla, profert fructus & testimonia omnibus conspicua. Bonus & fidelis concionator Noah non tantùm verbo docet, sed etiam operibus doctrinam & fidē suam cōfirmat. Vbi antea potuissent de doctrina ipsius dubitare, certè iam cùm videbāt ædificante, tacitè cogebātur assentire. Nos quoq; habemus doctores, qui nos admonet ac docent: præterea operibus & factis suam doctrinam de imminente die Domini stabiliunt: sed surdi & cæci perstant omnes. Ad salutem) Ecce obiectum fidei, & simul operis ex fide prouenietis. Et respicit Apostolus ad id, quod Noæ erat promissum de nouo foedere, & conseruatione ipsius cum suis, tempore diluuij, ac genere humano deinceps per ipsum propagando. Quinetiam hic exprimitur proprium officium fidei, quòd videlicet ea non tantum respiciat ad non apparentia, sed multo magis ad promissam oblatamque misericordiam ac salutem, iuxta illud, quòd dictum est supra in definitione fidei, esse ὑπόστασιν rerum sperandarum.
units.tr: "He prepared the ark." You see the effect of faith and its chief sign. It is not merely conceived in the mind and buried there; it brings forth living examples and fruits and testimonies visible to all. The good and faithful preacher Noah does not only teach by word but also confirms his doctrine and his faith by his works. Those who might have doubted his teaching would surely have been compelled to assent silently when they saw him building. We too have teachers who admonish and instruct us, and who also confirm their doctrine about the approaching day of the Lord by their works and deeds; yet all remain deaf and blind. "For the saving of his house." Here is the object of faith, and at the same time the work that comes from faith. The Apostle has in view the promise made to Noah of a new covenant, of the preservation of himself and his family in the flood, and of the human race being propagated through him afterwards. Here too is expressed the proper office of faith: it looks not only to things unseen but much more to the promised and offered mercy and salvation, according to what was said above in the definition of faith, that it is the substance of things hoped for.

units.la: Domus suæ) Sicut promissio habebat, numerantur que octo animæ in illa domo, & seruatæ in arca: sicut etiam Petrus prioris epistolæ capite tertio. Hic vero videre licet paruâ ecclesiolam, aut potius reliquias ecclesiolæ, cum tota penè subuersa fuerit factione Cainitica, tamen hanc per fidem, atque vnius potissimùm Noah seruatum. Tota illa ecclesia fidei seruata est, vt deinceps omnis propago eius ecclesiæ ad hoc vsque tempus cum oppressa foret, & ad extremam internecionem redacta, sciret tamen, se adhuc fide seruandam. Et hic habemus, ecclesiam non esse sitam in multitudine aut potentia, sed duntaxat in fide, quæ verbo constanter innititur. Septem, vel octo, imò tres, faciunt ecclesiam, Christo existente in medio eorum. Et in illis paucis fortasis adhuc erant infirmi: qualis fuit Hamm & credi potest tantundem de aliquo alio, & nihilominus erat ecclesia. Sic enim nigra est ecclesia, sed formosa, habet næuos, nihilominus talem sponsam diligit Christus. Valde igitur consolatorium istud est præsentis temporis ecclesiolæ, quæ persecutionem patitur, & certò scit imminere tempus iudicij, auideque expectat, & concionatur, & prouocat ad poenitentiam, sed frustrà omnia: ipsa tamen in fide perstabit & quamlibet despecta exiguaq; numero, tamen salua fiet.
units.tr: "His house." As the promise had it, eight souls were numbered in that household and kept safe in the ark, as Peter also says in the third chapter of his first epistle. Here we may see a small church, or rather the remnants of a small church, which, though almost wholly overthrown by the Cainite faction, was preserved through faith and chiefly through Noah alone. That whole church was kept in faith, so that, although every later offspring of that church was oppressed and brought to utter destruction up to this time, it still knew that it was to be kept in faith. And here we have that the church is not situated in multitude or power, but only in faith, which steadfastly rests upon the Word. Seven or eight, or rather three, make a church, with Christ present in the midst of them. Among those few there were perhaps still weak members, such as Ham; and one may believe the same of some others, yet it was a church nonetheless. For the church is black, yet beautiful; she has blemishes, but Christ loves such a bride nonetheless. This is therefore very consoling for the small church of the present time, which suffers persecution, knows for certain that the time of judgment is at hand, eagerly waits, preaches, and calls to repentance, but all in vain. It will nonetheless persevere in faith, and however despised and small in number, it will be saved.

units.la: Per quam arcam condemnauit mundum) Officium fidelis concionatoris est, non tantum vt bis comprobare ea, quæ dicit vel confirmat, sed etiam rebus & exemplis. Hæc enim plurimum valent ad fidem & autoritatem conciliandam. Hac de causa Noah ædificauit arcam, fidem suam ita declarans, eademq; opera incredulitatem arguens omnium impiorum. Regina Austri & Niniuitæ consurgent in iudicio aduersus eos, qui euangelio manifestato credere noluerunt, & condemnabunt eos.
units.tr: "By which ark he condemned the world." It is the office of a faithful preacher not only to prove by his life what he says and affirms, but also by things and examples. For these count greatly in winning faith and authority. For this reason Noah built the ark, declaring his faith thus, and by the same works condemning the unbelief of all the wicked. "The queen of the south and the men of Nineveh shall rise up in judgment against those who refused to believe the gospel when it was made known, and they shall condemn them."

units.la: At multo magis etiam in terris arguunt & condemnant incredulos, quotquot cognitionem veritatis docent vel ample ctuntur, & præterea etiam rebus ipsis actionibusq; declarant. Quod cum fit, ipsi etiam impij se damnari tacitè agnoscunt, & ad pudore adducuntur. Vides ergo, quàm appositè omnia dicantur ac disponantur. In summa autem hæc omnia opera sic facta sunt euidentissima, & certissima argumenta perfectæ & viuç fidei in Noah.
units.tr: But even more, in this life also they who teach or are instructed in the knowledge of the truth condemn and convict unbelievers, and besides this they also declare it by the things themselves and by their actions. Since this is so, the wicked themselves tacitly acknowledge that they are condemned, and are brought to shame. You see, then, how fittingly all these things are said and arranged. In sum, all these works were so done that they are the most evident and certain arguments of Noah's perfect and living faith.

units.la: Discimus verò ex his omnibus, primò, fide homines iustificari: id quod totius huius loci caput est, valdeq; necessarium est inculcare.
units.tr: From all these things we learn, first, that men are justified by faith. This is the chief point of this whole passage, and it is very necessary to inculcate it.

units.la: Secundò, animaduertimus hic, qualia esse debeant exercitia fidei. Noah non solùm docet alios centum & viginti annos, inuitans ad poenitentiam, iubens implorare misericordiam: verùm etiam solicitus est pro salute domus suæ, fabricat arcam, ita redarguens mundum: denique nihil non facit per plurimos annos, quo fidem suam testatam coram Deo ac toto mundo faciat: vt taceamus, qualia certamina fuerint Noaho in eúda aduersus carnales & potetes, tum aduersus pseudoprophetas, qui diuersum murmurabant suadebant.
units.tr: Second, we notice here what the exercises of faith ought to be like. Noah not only taught others for a hundred and twenty years, inviting them to repentance and bidding them implore mercy; but he was also anxious for the salvation of his household, built the ark, and so condemned the world. Finally, he did nothing for many years that would not attest his faith before God and the whole world. Not to mention what struggles Noah had in that same cause against the carnal and the powerful, and also against the false prophets, who murmured and urged the opposite.

units.la: Tertiò, licet etiam hic obseruare quædam fidei propria, atque effectus insignes veluti cùm dicitur Noah ea, quæ nondum videbantur, veritus: item, quòd prius admonitus oraculo, siue Dei verbo: ostenditur, verbum esse obiectum fidei, siue, quòd fides sit ex auditu. Romanorum cap.10. Nos hæc inter explicandum aliquo modo annotauimus.
units.tr: Third, we may also observe here certain properties of faith and its remarkable effects: as when Noah is said to have feared things not yet seen, and also that he was first warned by an oracle, or the word of God. This shows that the word is the object of faith, or that faith comes by hearing (Romans 10). We have noted these points to some extent in our explanation.

units.la: Per fidem appellatus Abraham obedijt, vt exiret in locum, quem accepturus erat in hæreditatem, & exiuit, nescien s, quò esset venturus: per fidem commigrauit, &c.
units.tr: "By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went. By faith he sojourned," and so on.

units.la: Quartum exemplum de Abraham per fidem iustificato: vbi non vnû aliquod memorabile factû, vti in præcedentibus, refert, in quo fidei coprobatio eluceat: sed plura egregia fidei documenta cogerit, singulisq; explicandis aliquanto diutius immoratur. Id autem Apostolus inconsulto & sine iustis causis non fecit, quarum aliquas indicabimus.
units.tr: This is the fourth example, of Abraham justified by faith. Here the Apostle does not relate one memorable deed, as in the preceding examples, in which the proof of faith shines forth; but he gathers several excellent proofs of faith and dwells somewhat longer on each to be explained. The Apostle did not do this without reason or without just causes, some of which we shall point out.

units.la: Prima est, quòd Abraha vnus sit patriarcha, in quo excellentior fides, quàm in quocunq; alio spectata est: ita vt, quEADmodum Iob, ppositus est in singulare exemplu patientiæ, Moses in exemplum lenitatis: Dauid in exemplum fortitudinis animi: & sic deinceps alij alijs virtutibus heroicis illustres præcæteris extiterunt: ita in vno Abraham plenisimum exemplum consummatæ fidei emicuit, vt etiam pater credentium propterea meruerit appellari.Dignus igitur Abraham,in cuius fide proponeda oratio longior,& diligentia maior impendatur.
units.tr: The first is that Abraham is the only patriarch in whom a more outstanding faith has been seen than in any other. Just as Job is set forth as the unique example of patience, Moses of gentleness, David of courage, and so on, others standing out above the rest for other heroic virtues, so in Abraham alone there shines the most complete example of perfected faith, so that he is rightly called the father of believers. Abraham is worthy, therefore, that a longer discourse be devoted to setting forth his faith, and that greater diligence be expended on it.

units.la: Hacipsa de caussa Apostolus Rom.4.Ité Gal.3,præcipua disputationis suæ argumen ta ab exemplo Abrahæ mutuatus est.
units.tr: For this very reason the Apostle, in Romans 4 and also in Galatians 3, took the chief arguments of his discussion from the example of Abraham.

units.la: Secunda caussa, cùm apostoli propositum sit, in tota hac inductione & exemplo- rum congerie, non solùm afferere, homines fide iustificari, verùm etiam docere varios multiplicesque fidei effectus,nec non officia,vt nimirum omnes tum acrius excitentur ad fidem amplectendam,tum euidentius discant, quomodo ipsos credere deceat, seu quomodo vera fides debeat esse comparata:merito in enarrando exemplo Abrahæ in- hæret diutius,vtpote in quo officia & effectus fidei quàm diuersissimi animaduerti pos- sunt,&longè clariores,quàm in multis multorum aliorum exemplis.
units.tr: The second reason: since the Apostle's purpose, in this whole induction and gathering of examples, is not only to assert that men are justified by faith, but also to teach the various and manifold effects of faith, and likewise its duties, so that all may be more keenly stirred to embrace faith, and may more clearly learn how it becomes them to believe, or how true faith ought to be formed; it is rightly that he dwells longer in recounting the example of Abraham, since in it the duties and effects of faith, very diverse, can be observed, and far clearer than in many examples of many others.

units.la: Tertia caussa est, quòd cùm Apostolus scribat ad Hebræos,qui arrogantissimè semper iactabant & gloriabantur,se filios Abrahæ, æquissimum sanè fuit, fusius ab eo tractari exemplum patris Abrahæ,docerique illum fide inprimis iustificatum, nec non in omnibus actionibus illius fidem potissimum effulsisse: vt hac ratione conuincerentur,si se pro legitimis filijs Abrahæ deinceps vellent venditare, etiam illius exemplum in fide alacriter debere insequi,quod ni facerent,pro nothis & spurijs reijciendos. Neque verò pertinacissimi hostes fidei possent vlla ratione citius fortiusque promoueri, quàm ad hunc modum proposito exemplo patris sui Abrahæ, quando etiam in natura positum est,vt omnes suorum parentum gaudeant laudibus,nec non valde extimulen tur,ad imitandum,quas celebrari maiorum virtutes audiunt. Alias enim magno dede- core se degeneres & supposititios testari videntur.
units.tr: The third reason is that, since the Apostle writes to the Hebrews, who always boasted most arrogantly and gloried that they were sons of Abraham, it was most fitting that the example of their father Abraham be treated more fully by him, and that he be shown to have been justified above all by faith, and that his faith shone forth most in all his actions. By this reasoning they would be convicted: if they wished thereafter to pass themselves off as the legitimate sons of Abraham, they ought also eagerly to follow his example in faith; but if they did not, they would be rejected as bastards and illegitimate. Indeed, the most obstinate enemies of faith could in no way be moved more quickly or more strongly than by setting before them the example of their father Abraham; for it is also in human nature that all rejoice in the praises of their ancestors, and are greatly stirred to imitate the virtues of their forebears which they hear celebrated. Otherwise they appear, by a great disgrace, to show themselves degenerate and spurious.

units.la: Non dissimiliter student mouere Iudæorum animos,Esaias cap.51. & Christus Ioan. 8:exemplum patris Abrahæ vehementer vrgentes.Tantum de caussis, ob quas appa- ret,Apostolum transtando exemplo Abrahæ diutius inhæsisse. Nunc ad explicanda sin gula,quibus fides ipsius cõprobatur,nec non in quibus fidei effectus officiaq; elucent, accedamus.
units.tr: Not dissimilarly, Isaiah in chapter 51 and Christ in John 8 strive to move the minds of the Jews, urging strongly the example of their father Abraham. So much for the reasons why it is evident that the Apostle dwelt longer on the example of Abraham. Now let us proceed to explain the individual points by which his faith is attested, and in which the effects and duties of faith shine forth.

units.la: Per fidem, inquit, appellatus Abraham obedijt, vt exiret in locum, quem acceptururum erat in hereditatem, & exiuit,nesciens,quo esset venturus.
units.tr: By faith, it says, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed and went out to the place he was to receive as an inheritance, and he went out not knowing where he was going.

units.la: Hoc semper repetendum est, fidem non esse otiosam, sed necessaria proferre opera, ex quibus quasi signis cognosci queat:sicut arborem bonam dignoscimus à fructibus.
units.tr: This must always be repeated: faith is not idle, but produces necessary works, by which it can be known as by signs, just as we recognise a good tree by its fruits.

units.la: Hæc igitur prima est comprobatio seu demonstratio insignis fidei Abrahæ, sumptâ ab ipsius obedientia,in suscipienda ex mandato ac iussu Dei peregrinatione in longin- quam & ignotam regionem:nec non ex apprehensione promissæ misericordiæ, ab bo- norum ibidem accipiendorum.
units.tr: This, then, is the first proof or demonstration of Abraham's remarkable faith, taken from his obedience in undertaking, at God's command and bidding, a journey into a distant and unknown region; and also from his grasp of the promised mercy, that is, of the goods he was to receive there.

units.la: Sed dicis,Est ne adeò magnum & singulare opus fidei, proficisci in exteram regionem,vt propterea tantopere sit comendandus Abraham? Plurimi etiam hodie istud faciunt,etiam sine laude aliqua pietatis. Deinde,quanta erit laus,aliò proficisci,vbi speres, te aditurum opulentam hæreditatem? Hoc quiuis paratus esset etiam nunc facere.
units.tr: But you say: is it such a great and singular work of faith to set out for a foreign region that Abraham should be so greatly commended for it?
