Many people do this even today, without any praise for piety. Again, what praise is there in going elsewhere where you hope to reach a rich inheritance? Anyone would be ready to do this even now.

units.la: Respondetur,permagnum esse discrimen inter peregrinationem Abrahæ,& peregri- nationes aliorum.Videamus caussas & fines,quibus alijs mouentur, & quibus motus est Abraham,& intelligemus,quantum intersit. Alij, qui peregrinantur,id faciunt for- tassis necessitatis caussa: sicut aliquando propter famem inualescentem quidam co- guntur mutare solum:quod etiam patres quosdam fecisse legimus,in quibus ipse Abra ham,Iacob:& nostra tempestate multos tales vidimus.
units.tr: It is answered that there is a very great difference between Abraham's journey and the journeys of others. Let us look at the causes and ends that move others and the causes that moved Abraham, and we will understand how much difference there is. Others who travel perhaps do so out of necessity: as sometimes, because of a growing famine, some are compelled to change their land. We read that some of the fathers did this, among them Abraham himself and Jacob; and in our own time we have seen many such people.

units.la: Alij spe quæstus & lucri,vel discendæ exercendæve artis gratia proficiscuntur: sicut passim videmus innumeros facere,qui si contenti essent sua sorte,& non ambirent lu- crum vel commodum, domisuæ possent manere. Hic adhuc pietatem non prætexere. Alij peregrinantur, quia domi perpetrarunt,propter quod non licet manere: atque ita irato Deo incertis oberrant sedibus,foris futuri noxij,sicut antea vixerát apud suos.Sic Cain peregrinatus est: sic Ieroboam manus Solomonis effugit.
units.tr: Others set out in hope of gain and profit, or for the sake of learning or practising a skill. We see countless people doing this everywhere, who, if they were content with their lot and did not seek gain or advantage, could remain at home. Here there is still no pretence of piety. Others travel because they have committed some crime at home, on account of which they may not stay; and so, with God angry, they wander among uncertain dwellings, becoming outlaws abroad just as they had lived among their own people before. So Cain wandered; so Jeroboam escaped the hand of Solomon.

units.la: Alij abeunt, volentes adire hæreditatem, vel honorem consequi, vel aliquâ funćtio- nem,& procurant sibi amicos,vel accipiunt prius literas comendatitias,vel mandatum à principe,seu potentiore quopiam.
units.tr: Others leave wishing to take up an inheritance, or to obtain an honour, or some office; they secure friends for themselves, or first receive letters of recommendation, or a commission from a prince or some more powerful person.

units.la: Alij deniq; animi caussa abeunt,vt hominũ mores videat obseruent;. Hæ ferè sunt caussç,ob quas nonnulli peregrinationes suscipiût.Atqui Abrahã nulla tali de caussa per- motus est:iã habebat vnde viueret,nõ fames,nõ spes quæstus,vel lucri,vel arte discẽdi, vel cuiuscunque similis commodi eum mouebat: sed habebat expressum mandatum Dei: hoc solum mouebat ipsum. Iam bene cum ipso agebatur, aliquamdiu suauiter vixerat in Charran: ac Dominus iubet eum iterum sedem mutare. Quia igitur habebat expressum mandatum, & fides proprie intuetur in mandatum & verbum Dei, ideo ista peregrinatio suscepta, ita in quam obedientia vertitur ei ad laudem fidei.
units.tr: Finally, others leave for the sake of their own mind, that they may see and observe the manners of men. These are nearly the causes for which some undertake journeys. But Abraham was moved by no such cause. He already had what he lived on; neither hunger, nor hope of gain or profit, nor learning a skill, nor any similar advantage moved him. He had an explicit command of God, and this alone moved him. Already things had gone well with him, and he had lived pleasantly for some time in Haran; yet the Lord orders him to change his dwelling again. Because, therefore, he had an explicit command, and faith properly looks to the command and word of God, this journey, undertaken in obedience, is turned to the praise of his faith.

units.la: Nisi enim habuisset egregiam fidem, quod Deus vellet ipsi promissam misericordiam impendere, sane haud potuisset homo septuaginta quinque annorum, qui iam visus fuerat sedem ad senescendum bene fixisse, cum uxore & ampla familia, cum Loth item fratris sui filio, adduci, ut in regionem longinquam, & ignotam, & impijs hominibus habitatam commigraret. Ecce plane mirabilis vis fidei: sed in hoc etiam maxime admiranda, quod iussus peregrinari obedierit, adhuc nescias, quonam foret ipsi eundum. Haec particula, Nescient, quo esset venturus, est in primis observanda. Velle peregrinari, vbi nul la te cogit necessitas, certe ratio vehementer improbaret: sed iam vt habeas mandatu Dei, quod te iubet discedere, tamen nescire, quonam sit tibi cum tota familia abeundum, non nosse certum locum vel regionem, profecto videtur summa esse stultitia, & ratio humana nunquam posset assentiri, vt id faceret. Et tamen pius Abraham statim credit, sibi bene successurum, non quaerit de loco, non petit informari, quales homines ibi sint, quomodo excipietur, quomodo ibi se geret, non deliberat, non procrastinat: sed statim semel admonitus facere, alacri animo peregrinationem, adeoque exilium longe molestissimum suscipit.
units.tr: For unless he had had remarkable faith, believing that God would bestow the promised mercy on him, a man of seventy-five years, who seemed to have settled his dwelling well enough to grow old in it, could hardly have been brought, with his wife and large household, and with Lot, his brother's son, to migrate into a distant and unknown region inhabited by impious men. Behold the truly wonderful power of faith. But it is most admirable in this also: that, being ordered to go abroad, he obeyed without yet knowing where he was to go. This phrase, "not knowing where he was going," is above all to be noted. To wish to travel where no necessity compels you would certainly be strongly condemned by reason. But when you have God's command bidding you depart, yet do not know where you must go with your whole family, do not know a certain place or region, this seems to be the height of folly, and human reason could never assent to doing it. And yet pious Abraham at once believes that things will go well for him. He does not ask about the place, does not seek to be informed what sort of people live there, how he will be received, how he will conduct himself there; he does not deliberate, does not delay. But once he is admonished, he at once undertakes the journey, and this exile, by far the most grievous, with a willing mind.

units.la: Haec, haec est egregia fides, quam omnes magis admirari possumus, quam imitari: & dignissima plane, quae multis laudibus celebretur. Vbi enim obsecro inueniretur, qui ita faceret?
units.tr: This, this is the remarkable faith, which we can admire more than we can imitate, and which is most worthy of being celebrated with many praises. For where, I ask you, would one be found who would do so?

units.la: Sed multo clarius innotescet magnitudo fidem Abrahae, si historiam, ad quam respicit Apostolus, ex Genesis duodecimo repetamus. Sic autem ibi legitur, primum capite vndecimo, Natum esse Abram in Vr Chaldaeorum, ibique diu vixisse: sed tandem patrem ipsius Therah vna cum filio Abram, & nepote Loth egressum de Vr Chaldaeorum, propter malitiam & idololatriam hominum, vt irent in terram Chanaan: sed tamen veniisse in Charan, & ibi habitasse. Ex quo intelligi poterit maior molestia Abrahae, quod iam antea semel migrarit. Iam capite duodecimo sequitur: Et dixit Dominus ad Abram: Egredere de terra tua, & de natione tua, atque de domo patris tui, ad terram, quam ostendam tibi.
units.tr: But the greatness of Abraham's faith will become much clearer if we recall the history to which the Apostle refers, from Genesis 12. There it is read, first in chapter 11, that Abram was born in Ur of the Chaldeans and lived there for a long time; but finally his father Terah, together with his son Abram and his grandson Lot, left Ur of the Chaldeans, on account of the wickedness and idolatry of the men, to go into the land of Canaan; but they came to Haran and lived there. From this it can be understood how great Abraham's trouble was, since he had already migrated once before. Now in chapter 12 it follows: "And the Lord said to Abram: Go out from your land, and from your nation, and from your father's house, to the land which I will show you."

units.la: Ecce praeceptum, in cuius singulis verbis mirabilis videtur latere duritas. Nam, cum dicitur, de terra tua, de natione tua, de domo patris, cuius cor ista non percellant? Nemo nescit, multo grauissimum esse, relinquere solum natale, & subire exilium: quo de etiam Poetae multa quaesti sunt. Naturaliter omnes diligunt patriam, & locum, vbi bene consederint. Deinde, cum dicitur, ad alteram, quam ostendam tibi: Quae hic certitudo? Cuius animus non angeretur? Quae hic apparebat spes?
units.tr: Behold the command, in whose individual words a remarkable hardness seems to lie hidden. For when it is said, "from your land, from your nation, from your father's house," whose heart would not be struck by these words? Everyone knows that it is by far the hardest thing to leave the native soil and undergo exile, a subject on which even the poets have asked many questions. By nature all people love their homeland and the place where they have settled well. Then, when it is said, "to the land which I will show you," what certainty is there here? Whose mind would not be troubled? What hope appeared here?

units.la: Sequitur promissio: Faciamque te in gentem magnam, & benedicam tibi, & magnificabo nomen tuum, vt sis benedictio: Benedicam quoque benedicentibus tibi, & maledicenti tibi maledicam: & benedicentur in te omnes familiae terrae.
units.tr: The promise follows: "And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, so that you may be a blessing. I will also bless those who bless you, and curse him who curses you; and in you all the families of the earth will be blessed."

units.la: Ecce promissionem, sed tamen totam de non apparentibus, & secundum rationem loquedo de impossibilibus. Quomodo enim talia expectari poterant in aliena regione, & iam fere septuagenario? Et tamen vere credidit. Nam sequitur effectus & signum fidei. Abijt itaque Abraham, sicut locutus erat ad eum Dominus. Nulla mora, nulla deliberatione, nulla detrectatione facta statim abijt. Mirabilis fidei promptitudo, & verae magnae fidei documentum. Sed, quo abijt Abraham, quando illi locus non erat designatus? Sine dubio Dominus illi fuit felix Mercurius, dux & autor itineris suscipiendi: vnde sequitur: Et tulit Abram Sarai vxorem suam, & Loth filium fratris sui, & omnem substantiam ipsorum, quam possederunt, & animas, quas sibi acquisierant in Haran, egressique sunt, vt venirent in terram Chanaan, & peruenerunt in terram Chanaan. Transiuit vero Abraham per terram illam, vsq; ad locum Sichem, & vsque ad planiciem Moreh.
units.tr: Behold a promise, but one wholly concerned with things not visible, and, speaking according to reason, with impossibilities. For how could such things be expected in a foreign region, and by a man nearly seventy years old? And yet he truly believed. For the effect and sign of faith follows: "So Abraham departed, just as the Lord had spoken to him." No delay, no deliberation, no hesitation was made; at once he went away. A remarkable readiness of faith, and proof of true and great faith. But where did Abraham go, when no place had been designated for him? Without doubt the Lord was to him a fortunate Mercury, the leader and author of the journey undertaken. Whence it follows: "And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their substance which they had possessed, and the souls which they had acquired in Haran; and they went out to come into the land of Canaan, and they came into the land of Canaan. Abraham passed through that land as far as the place Shechem, and as far as the plain of Moreh."

units.la: Porro Chananaeus tunc erat in terra. Et visus est Iehouah ipsi Abram, dixitque, Semini tuo dabo terram istam: & aedificauit ibi altare Domino, qui apparuerat ei.
units.tr: Moreover, the Canaanite was then in the land. "And Jehovah appeared to Abram and said: To your seed I will give this land." And he built an altar there to the Lord, who had appeared to him.

units.la: Hic audis peregrinationis molestiam, quomodo item paratus fuerit longius progredi, & vbi iussus conquiescere.
units.tr: Here you hear of the trouble of the journey, and how he was ready to go further, and where he was ordered to rest.

units.la: Sed cum huc venisset, adhuc nulla apparebant vestigia occupandae eius terrae, imo plurima secuta sunt impedimenta: oberrauit aliquamdiu, despiciens, vbi sedem deligeret. Exorta famo cogitur proficisci in Ægyptum, & iterum nouum exilium
units.tr: But when he had come here, still no traces appeared of taking possession of that land; indeed, very many hindrances followed. He wandered for some time, looking about for where to choose a dwelling. A famine arising, he is compelled to set out for Egypt, and to undergo a new exile.

units.la: 1. Oberratio. 2. Fames. exilium subire.Ibi rapta est vxor eius deductaque ad Pharaonem, ipse de vitae periculo sibi metuens.
units.tr: 1. Wandering. 2. Famine.

units.la: Post iterum reuersus in terram Chanaan:ibi orta lite inter pastores diuiduntur ab invicem Abram & Loth. Quis hic non desperasset? Sed iterum Dominus erigit illum nova promissione de conferenda terra, & multiplicando Semine. Rursus mouet tabernaculum, & habitat iuxta conuallem Mambre. Paulo post bellum exoritur, in quo capti uus abductus est cognatus ipsius Loth: Abraham cogitur arma induere, & magnis periculis captiuum liberare: itemque pacisci cum rege Sodomorum. Tandem, capite decimoquinto, iterum erigitur consolatione per Dominum, vbi quasi desperans, & sentiens asperrima certamina fidei cum diffidentia, grauiter quaeritur, se sine liberis moriturum: Domi-nus pollicetur sobolem, commemorat, se promisisse innumerabilem posteritatem, praeterea, quod daturus esset terram Chanaan: Ibi Abraham, Domine Deus, unde scire possum, quod sim possessurus eam? &c. Et mox audit etiam, quod semen ipsius futurum sit peregrinum, & seruituum annis quadringentis, & primum generatione quarta occuparet promissam terram. O quales successus & qualis occupatio haereditatis? Quis secundum iudicium rationis loquens non diceret, stultissimum fuisse Abraham, qui ita speraret, vbi non adessent manifestiora signa? Et tamen Abraham statim ini- tio credidit, & in ea fide constans permansit.
units.tr: Afterwards he returned to the land of Canaan. There, a quarrel arising among the herdsmen, Abram and Lot are separated from each other. Who here would not have despaired? But again the Lord raises him up with a new promise of giving the land and multiplying his seed. Again he moves his tent, and dwells near the valley of Mamre. Shortly after, a war breaks out, in which Lot, his kinsman, is taken captive and carried off. Abraham is compelled to take up arms and, with great dangers, to free the captive; and likewise to make a treaty with the king of Sodom. Finally, in chapter 15, he is raised up again by the Lord's consolation. There, as if despairing, and feeling the harshest struggles of faith against distrust, he complains bitterly that he will die without children. The Lord promises offspring, recalls that he had promised an innumerable posterity, and that he would also give the land of Canaan. Then Abraham says: "Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?" etc. And soon he hears also that his seed will be strangers, and in slavery for four hundred years, and that in the fourth generation they will occupy the promised land. O what successes, and what occupation of an inheritance! Who, speaking according to the judgment of reason, would not say that Abraham was most foolish, to hope thus where more evident signs were not present? And yet Abraham from the start believed at once, and remained constant in that faith.

units.la: Merito ergo ista fides Abrahae valde praedicatur, quod audito verbo Dei statim obedie- rit, & peregrinatione illico susceperit. Et hoc exemplum aptissime proponitur Hebraeis, inter quos multi erant, qui propter confessionem veritatis pulsi sedibus cogebantur instar patris sui Abrahami oberrare, & varia subire certamina. Hoc illis restabat faciundum, ut exemplo patris sui Abrahami erecti in fide constantes semper manerent.
units.tr: Rightly, then, Abraham's faith is greatly commended, because, having heard the word of God, he at once obeyed and immediately undertook the journey. This example is also most aptly set before the Hebrews, among whom there were many who, because of their confession of the truth, were driven from their homes and compelled, like their father Abraham, to wander and undergo various struggles. What remained for them to do was to follow the example of their father Abraham, and so, strengthened in faith, always remain steadfast.

units.la: Caeterum & nos hic habemus pariter doctrinam & consolationem. Doctrinam quidem de vocatione & obedientia, quae Deo vocanti maxime accepta est, iuxta illud 1.Samuel.15. Melior est obedientia, quam victima. Et verbum requirit obedientiam: nec fides sine obedientia esse potest. Cum enim fides respiciat in verbum, vult ea se verbo submittere, & ex verbo tota pendere. Hinc Rom.1. Obedientia fidei exigitur. Item Christus Ioan.10. Oues meae vocem meam audiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, we too have here both teaching and consolation. The teaching concerns calling and obedience, which is most acceptable to the God who calls, according to that word in 1 Samuel 15: "Obedience is better than sacrifice." The word requires obedience, and faith cannot exist without obedience. For since faith looks to the word, it wishes to submit itself to the word and to depend wholly on it. Hence Romans 1: "the obedience of faith" is required. Likewise Christ says in John 10: "My sheep hear my voice."

units.la: Consolatio vero hinc ad omnes pios deriuabitur, quicunque exilio aut simili molestia grauatur: illi autem inprimis, qui hoc tempore propter iustitiam & confessionem veritatis pulsi sunt suis sedibus innocentiae suae testimonium circumferentes. Non loquimur de phanaticis quibusdam spiritibus, qui norunt multa cominisci de persecutionibus a se toleratis, & interea vel immodeste se gesserunt domi, offendicula excitates: vel peregrinantur, ut eo praetextu hinc inde corradant, vnde se pascant in otio, vel exploret, quid ab aliis agatur: sed de ijs, qui & innocenter domi vixerunt, & interea significatione data, quod non approbarent impios cultus, coacti sunt, si vitae suae vellent consultum, sedem mutare. His, inquam, volumus propositum esse exemplum Abrahae, vt consolationem inde accipiant. Ego expertus sum, quanta consolatio posit ab exemplo isto capi: praesertim si toto animo accurate expendatur. Neque est, quod obijciatur, pios istos non habere mandatum fugae, sicut habuit Abraham, & sponte ipsos sine necessaria causa exilium subiuisse. Etiamsi non prorsus eodem modo specialiter mandatum habeant, tamen habent etiam expressum mandatum in euangelio, vbi Christus docet, dicens: si vos persecuti fueritis in vna ciuitate, fugite in aliam.
units.tr: The consolation will flow from this to all the godly who are burdened with exile or similar trouble, and especially to those who at this time have been driven from their homes on account of righteousness and the confession of the truth, carrying with them the testimony of their innocence. We are not speaking of certain fanatical spirits, who know how to invent many tales about persecutions they have supposedly endured, and meanwhile have behaved immodestly at home, stirring up offences; or who wander about so that under that pretext they may scrape together, here and there, whatever they live on in idleness, or spy out what others are doing. Rather, we speak of those who lived blamelessly at home, and yet, since they made it clear that they did not approve of impious worship, were compelled, if they wished to look to their lives, to change their dwelling. To these, I say, we want the example of Abraham set forth, so that they may take consolation from it. I have experienced how great a consolation can be drawn from this example, especially if it is weighed carefully and with the whole mind. Nor is there reason to object that these godly people do not have a command to flee, as Abraham had, and that they undertook exile of their own accord, without necessary cause. Even if they do not have a special command in exactly the same way, they nevertheless have an express command in the gospel, where Christ teaches, saying: "If they persecute you in one city, flee into another."

units.la: Deinde, habent hoc mandatum, quod spiritus Sanctus cum spiritu ipsorum loquitur in cordibus, dum suggerit, vt potius fugiant ad salutem suam & aliorum, quam cum de decore & offendiculo aut deficiant aut moriantur.
units.tr: Next, they have this command: the Holy Spirit speaks in their hearts with their spirit, suggesting that they should rather flee for their own salvation and that of others than either fail or die over an offence.

units.la: Postremo habent pro signo mandati & voluntatis diuinae, ipsum successum, quae Deus per suam misericordiam exultatibus largitur, vocans illos, vt alibi doceant, vel in ecclesiasticis scholis: & praeterea concedens patientiam, & vitae necessaria sufficientia.
units.tr: Finally, they have as the sign of the command and the divine will the very success that God, in His mercy, bestows on those who are exiled, calling them so that they may teach elsewhere, or in church schools; and in addition granting them patience and sufficiency of the necessities of life.

units.la: Per fidem commigrauit in terram promissionis, veluti peregrinam, cum in tabernaculis habitasset cum Isaac & Iacob, coheredibus eiusdem promissionis. Expectabat enim habentem fundamenta ciuitatem, cuius opifex & conditor est Deus.
units.tr: By faith he sojourned in the land of promise as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise. For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.

units.la: Secunda comprobatio seu demonstratio fidei Abrahae, similiter a signo, nempe ab eo, quod, posteaquam ad terram promissam venit, sic se gesserit, tanquam paratus alio adhuc proficisci, si ita Domino visum fuisset. Quod ex eo colligit Apostolus, quod Abraham ibi non domum aliquam aedificauerit, sed tantum tabernaculum erexerit. Hoc autem erat reuera promptae & perpetuae obedientiae fidei valde euides argumentum. Nam in tabernaculis habitare, non ædificare, non comparare agros proprios, aut villas, sicut Abraham facile potuisset, plane videtur eius, qui animo habet, dum res postulabit, alio statim migrare.
units.tr: The second proof or demonstration of Abraham's faith is likewise drawn from a sign, namely that after he came to the promised land he so conducted himself as if he were ready to set out elsewhere, should it so seem good to the Lord. The Apostle gathers this from the fact that Abraham built no house there, but only pitched a tent. This was indeed a very clear proof of prompt and lasting obedience of faith. For to dwell in tents, rather than build, or acquire fields and estates of his own, as Abraham could easily have done, clearly seems the mark of one who intends to move on at once elsewhere when circumstances demand it.

units.la: Et propterea fortasis Dominus ita indefinite dixerat, egrediendum in terram, quam ipse erat monstraturus, vt ita fidem Abrahæ clarius probaret. Nec dubium, quin Abraham per incomparabilem suam fidem ita sese composuerit, vt respiciendo semper in illud Dei mandatum, de vertendo solo, subinde cogitarit, sibi adhuc alio migrandum, paratus ea in parte adhuc millies voci Domini obedire: id quod ex eo quoque licet colligere, quod ipse Genes. 15. dixerit, Domine Deus, unde scire possum, quod possessurus sim eam?
units.tr: And so perhaps the Lord had spoken so indefinitely, saying he should go out into the land that He would show him, in order to prove Abraham's faith more clearly. There is no doubt that Abraham, through his incomparable faith, so disposed himself that, always looking to that command of God about leaving the soil, he kept thinking he might have to migrate yet elsewhere, ready in that respect to obey the voice of the Lord a thousand times over. One may also gather this from the fact that he himself said in Genesis 15: "Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?"

units.la: Vbi non quidem vt profusus dubitans sic loquitur Abraham, sed vt paratus etiam alio, si Domino videatur, proficisci.
units.tr: Here Abraham does not speak thus as one doubting without restraint, but as one who is also ready to set out elsewhere, if it should seem good to the Lord.

units.la: Recte igitur dicit Apostolus, quod Abraham commigrarit in terram promissionis, ut peregrinam ut ἀλλότριαν, hoc est, vt talem, in qua ipse tantum hospes & peregrinus foret, quasi alio, cum res postularet, profecturus. Hanc autem fuisse mentem Abrahæ, colligit a Signo, videlicet quod in tabernaculis tantum habitarit, quod est eius, qui paratus sit subinde locum mutare. Atque ita etiam in tabernaculis habitasse describitur Abraham: vt Genesis 11. ad montem, qui erat contra Orientem Bethel, tetendit tabernaculum suum. Item Genesis capite 13. iterum postquam reuersus esset ex Ægypto, eodem loco fixisse tabernaculum commemoratur. Ibidem: mouens tabernaculum suum Abram habitauit iuxta conuallem Mambre. Genes. 18. Apparuit Dominus in conuallem Mambre sedenti in ostio tabernaculi sui.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, the Apostle says that Abraham migrated into the land of promise as a strange [ἀλλότριαν] land, that is, as one in which he was only a guest and a sojourner, as one about to set out elsewhere when the situation required. Now that this was Abraham's disposition, the Apostle gathers from the sign, namely that he dwelt only in tents, which belongs to one who is ready to change his place from time to time. And so Abraham is described as dwelling in tents: as in Genesis 11, he pitched his tent by the mountain which lay east of Bethel. Likewise, in Genesis 13, after he had returned from Egypt, it is recorded that he fixed his tent in the same place. Also there: "Abram, moving his tent, dwelt by the valley of Mamre." Genesis 18: "The Lord appeared in the valley of Mamre to him as he sat at the door of his tent."

units.la: Cum Isaac & Iacob) Hi quoque in tabernaculis vitam egerunt. Ita namque fides & effectus fidei ad eosdem propagati sunt. Filij sicut cohæredes terræ, ita & paternæ fidei, nec vnquam defecerunt etiam tot annis intercedentibus. De Isaac Genes. 24. scribitur, quod inhabitarit tabernaculum matris, & in id induxerit Rebeccam, adductam per seruum patris e Mesopotamia. De Iacob Genes. 25. Iacob vir simplex habitabat in tabernaculis.
units.tr: With Isaac and Jacob. They too lived their life in tents. For thus faith, and the effects of faith, were propagated to these same men. The sons, as heirs of the land, were also heirs of their father's faith, and never failed, even though so many years intervened. Of Isaac it is written in Genesis 24 that he dwelt in his mother's tent, and brought Rebekah into it, who had been brought from Mesopotamia by his father's servant. Of Jacob, Genesis 25: "Jacob, a simple man, dwelt in tents."

units.la: Quod igitur Abraham in tabernaculo tantum vixerit, argumentum euidens est, quod paratus fuerit logius ac diutius peregrinari: quod non nisi per eximiam fidem apud se statuere potuit. Qui enim temporalia ista diligit, & sibi vult prospicere, parat ædes, in quibus tutò & quietè agit: parat item alia, vt hortos, agros, & id genus. At pater Abraham, etiamsi terra illa ipsa promissa foret in hereditatem, tamen nihil huiusmodi curauit, nec fundum, nec agrum accepit, sicut dicitur Actorum 7. ne passum quidem terræ: sed emit agellum Ephronis habentem duas speluncas, in vxoris sepulturam. Et filij sciebant similia, & semen suum adhuc peregrinaturum in Ægypto, ac primum generatione quarta occupaturum totam terram: quare & ipsi in tentoriis semper vixerunt. Mirabile ergo exercitium fidei in Abraham & filijs eius licet cernere: vocantur heredes & possessores terræ, & tamen nihil habent, nec domum quidem, quam inhabitent. Nec mihi probatur, quod quidam exist imant, gentis Chanaan fuisse morem inhabitare tabernacula, præsertim cum ibi memorentur & ciuitates, & reges, & domus: sicut Loth domum inhabitabat in Sodomis. Et quæ fuisset ista singularis laus Abrahæ aliorumque patriarcharum, si in tabernaculis vixissent sicut cæteri omnes? Debuisset & his ad parem commendationem fidei cedere talis habitatio. Magis probaretur mihi, si diceretur inhabitasse tabernaculum, quod exercerent pastoricam, sicut de maioribus suis omnibus prædicat & Ioseph apud Pharaonem: eamque ob causam petiuit illis dari terram Gosen, vbi pastoriciam exercuisse & similiter adhuc tabernaculum inhabitasse verosimile est. Sed neque pastoricia vita, neque inopia lignorum, aut materiæ, neq; quæcunque eiusmodi res in causa erat, cur habitarent in tabernaculis: sed tantum respectus in præceptum Dei, & exercitium fidei, & testatio fidei apud Deum, a quo meliora expectabant.
units.tr: That Abraham lived only in a tent is therefore clear evidence that he was prepared to wander longer and farther, a resolve he could make in himself only through extraordinary faith. For one who loves these temporal things and wishes to provide for himself builds houses in which he can live safely and quietly; he also prepares other things, such as gardens, fields, and the like. But our father Abraham, even though that very land had been promised to him as an inheritance, took no care for such things, and received neither a plot nor a field, as is said in Acts 7: not even a foot's breadth of land. Instead he bought a little field of Ephron, which had two caves, for the burial of his wife. His sons knew similar things: that their seed would still be a sojourner in Egypt, and that it would first possess the whole land in the fourth generation. Therefore they too always lived in tents. In Abraham and his sons, then, one can see a wonderful exercise of faith: they are called heirs and possessors of the land, and yet they have nothing, not even a house to dwell in. Nor am I persuaded by what some think, that it was the custom of the Canaanite people to dwell in tents, especially since cities, kings and houses are mentioned there, as Lot dwelt in a house in Sodom. And what would have been this singular praise of Abraham and the other patriarchs if they had lived in tents just like all the others? Such a dwelling ought to have counted for an equal commendation of faith for them as well. It would seem more convincing to me if it were said that they dwelt in tents because they practised the pastoral life, as Joseph before Pharaoh declares of all their forebears; and for that reason they asked that the land of Goshen be given them, where it is likely they practised herding and likewise still dwelt in tents. But neither the pastoral life, nor a lack of wood or building material, nor any such circumstance was the cause why they lived in tents, but only regard for God's command, the exercise of faith, and the witness of faith before God, from whom they expected better things.

units.la: Expectauerat enim habentem fundamentum ciuitatem) Ratio, quare terram promissam habuerint, tanquam peregrinam, sumpta a spe & expectatione terræ melioris. Non quod Abraham non fuerit contentus ea ipsa terra, quæ contigit, in qua etiam admodum diues auri & argenti, seruorum & pecorum factus est, atque auide exoptarit, aliam sibi dari regionem ditiorem: quod profecto fuisset animi non solum impatientis, verum etiam ambitiosi & auari. Sed quod apostolus aliquid altius voluerit omnium animis suggerere, fidei naturam propius explicare: id quod consulto quoque, imo propemodum necessaria quadam præ occupatione fecisse cum arbitror. Quado enim, quod proxime dictum est, Abraham migrasse in terram promissam, quam accepturus erat in hereditatem, versum est ad amplissimam laude fidei, hic fortasis quidam secum admirati sunt, quomodo tanta fides ibi prædicetur, vbi apparet, eam tantum intentam fuisse in bona temporalia, cum cùm germana illa fides, de qua hic disseritur, respiciat potissimum in bona spiritualia, & in misericordiam oblatam propter semen benedictum, id est, Christum. Hîc igitur Apostolus talibus cogitationibus itobuiam, fideique naturam clarius aperit, ac docet, fidelem patriarcham Abraham non quidem vsque adeò respexisse ad bona temporalia, videlicet ipsam terram promissam: sed potius ad bona spiritualia, quæ per temporalia illa significabantur: & de quibus accipiendis patres certi fiebant, prius accipiendo ista temporalia veluti quandam arrham seu testeram futurorum. Ita namque mens Abrahæ cæterorumque patrum non fuit defixa tota in res terrenas, sed per fidem erigebatur altius & conscendebat insuper ad apprehendendum bona cœlestia & æterna. Quomodo etiam perspicuè cernimus promissioni ad Abraham factæ de terra aliena accipiendâ, & de multiplicanda ipsius posteritate, adiunctam promissionem de benedicto Semine. Sic enim Genes. 12. cùm Dominus illum iuberet peregrinari, promitteretque multiplicandam eius posteritatem, tandem addidit:
units.tr: "For he looked for the city which has foundations." This is the reason why they had the promised land only as strangers, drawn from their hope and expectation of a better land. Not that Abraham was not content with the land itself which fell to him, where he became very rich in gold and silver, slaves and flocks, and eagerly wished that another and richer region had been given him. That would certainly have been the mind of a man not only impatient but also ambitious and greedy. Rather, the apostle wanted to put something higher before the minds of all and to explain more closely the nature of faith. I think he did this deliberately, and almost of necessity, as a matter of prior concern. For when he said a little earlier that Abraham migrated into the promised land, which he was to receive as an inheritance, and this was made the highest praise of faith, some may have wondered to themselves how such great faith could be proclaimed there, where it appears that he was intent only on temporal goods. Yet that true faith, of which we are speaking here, looks chiefly to spiritual goods and to the mercy offered on account of the blessed Seed, that is, Christ. Here, then, the apostle meets such thoughts and reveals more clearly the nature of faith. He teaches that the faithful patriarch Abraham did not look so much to temporal goods, namely the promised land itself, but rather to the spiritual goods which those temporal things signified, and by which the fathers were made certain of their receiving them, since they received these temporal things as a kind of pledge or token of things to come. For the mind of Abraham and of the other fathers was not fixed wholly on earthly things, but through faith was raised higher and rose above them to lay hold of heavenly and eternal goods. We see this plainly in the promise made to Abraham, that he would receive a foreign land and that his posterity would be multiplied, joined with the promise concerning the blessed Seed. For in Genesis 12, when the Lord commanded him to go abroad and promised that his posterity would be multiplied, he finally added:

units.la: Atque in semine tuo benedicentur omnes generationes terræ: quæ promissio etiam postea sæpius repetitur. Hoc ergo est, quod Apostolus hic docet, nimirum fidem Abrahæ non esse accipiendam pro eiusmodi fide, quæ tantùm versata sit circa res temporales recipiendas: sed eam vnà cum temporalibus apprehendisse etiam bona spiritualia: sicut promissiones de vtrisque ferè semper sonabant. Et sic solet Deus beneficijs temporalibus & signis externis, quale fuit Abrahamo circumcisio, & nobis est Baptismus ac cœna Domini, fidem piorum pascere & prouehere. Atque ita etiam soliti sunt patres accipere promissiones temporales, vt sub illis intelligerent res spirituales. Alias enim, quantulum illud fuisset, accipere successus temporales, qui communes erant plerandque impijs iuxta atque pijs? Et vt pijs patribus amplissima temporalia bona fuerint promissa, tamen ista parcius acceperunt: sicut in Abraham, Isaac & Iacob licet videre, qui neque terram Chanaan, neque multas proles se uiuis obtinuerunt. Abraham nè passum quidem terræ Chanaan obtinuit: alij nihilo acceperunt amplius, sed semen eorum adhuc peregrinari debebat, & in aliena regione seruire. Quomodo præterea potuisset animus illorum acquiescere in promissionibus temporalibus? Quæ ibi conscientiæ tranquillitas? Quanta ibi fuisset occasio tantæ patientiæ in tam diuturna mora & dilatione? Adhæc intelligebant sine dubio Sancti patres, se nequaquàm dignos tantis beneficijs, se nihil vnquàm tale perfecisse, propter quod Deus tanta & tàm insignia bona promitteret ipsis præ cæteris hominibus? Necessariò igitur sub tegmine & vmbra temporalium promissionum patres per fidem apprehendebant spiritualia bona, & mens defigebatur magis in bona spiritualia, quàm in temporalia, quorum non admodum erant auidi, quæ etiam illis non ita largiter statim proueniebant præ cæteris mortalibus. Atque eo etiam magis intendebant in spiritualia, quòd promissionibus rerum temporalium adiunctæ fuerunt promissiones rerum spiritualium, sicut supra in promissione ad Abraham facta ostendimus, qua dictum est, in te benedicentur omnes generationes terræ: quæ sine dubio potissimum & semper versabatur illi ob oculos; & quam vnam omnes quoque aliæ promissiones referebant. Estque hoc etiam indubitatò tenendum, patres omnes, cùm plenissimè essent edocti de illa promissione ad primos parentes facta, qua promittebatur Semen, per quod conculcandum foret caput serpentis: & multò ardentissimè expectarent tempus redemptionis, sperantes singuli, in aliquo suorum filiorum adimplendam eam promissionem: præterea cùm scirent, quantum bonum fuisset amissum lapsu primorum parentum, multò melius, quàm nos scire possumus: & rursus certissima fide statuerent, Deum velle esse sibi misericordem, velle genus humanum saluum facere: omni tempore respiciebant ad primam promissionem factam primis parentibus, & quæcunque contingebant illis læta & prospera, ipsi propter primam illam promissionem contingere sunt interpretati, & omnia ad illam ceu fontem bono rum retulerunt. Quare constat, fidem patrum semper intentam fuisse magis in bona spiritualia, quàm in temporalia, & ad promissiones rerum spiritualium omni tempore respexisse. Hoc ergo est, quod Apostolus hic subiecit, dicens: Expectabat enim habentem fundamenta ciuitatem: Hic autem aptissimè exprimitur iterum officium & effectus fidei, cuius proprium est, respicere in futura, id quod per vocem ἐπιδέχεται recte significatur: & deinde in spiritualia: quod delineant illæ voces: ciuitatem fundamenta habentem, cuius opifex & conditor est Deus semper obseruanda est, vt dixi, vocum proprietas, qua Apostolus studiosè voluit effectum & officium fidei vbique exprimere. Porrò opponit ciuitatem tabernaculo, idque valde eleganter, & ad exprimendam bonorum spiritualiū, quæ ille expectabat, præ bonis temporalibus præstantiam. Quantum enim excellit splendida & magnifica ciuitas aliqua exiguum tabernaculum; tantùm excellunt bona spiritualia. tualia quascunque res temporales. Sed exornat praeterea dignitate huius ciuitatis, quae do describit eam habentem fundamenta, qualia in tabernaculis non visuntur. Significat autem haec particula soliditatem & stabilitatem: quare ad significandum res alias, quam temporales, quae non habent soliditatem, nec durare possunt, haec particula est idonea: ideoque regnum coeleste, quod aeternum est, per ciuitatem fundamenta habentem recte intelligitur: vel certe ecclesia, cuius initium est in terris, consummatio vero in coelis: & cui inseri omnes sancti cupiunt, ac debent, solum hoc expetentes, vt in eam recipiantur, ciues & domestici Dei deinceps semper futuri. Et haec fundata est supra firmam petram, quae est Christus: de qua re Ephef. 2. 1. Corinth. 3. Habent & impij suam ciuitatem & ecclesiam, sed non habentem fundamenta, quae super arenam fundata est, non supra petram: sicut licet videre in aduersarijs, qui cum non habeant fundamenta, neque Christum, neque eius verbum, volunt eam firmare stipulis, & arena humanae sapientiae, & potentiae mundanae. Cain talem condiderat ciuitatem, & tempore Abrahae tales multae erant ciuitates: sed ab impijs, vt Sodomitis & similibus occupatae. At pij tantisper habitant in tabernaculis, dum ad ciuitatem perueniant, quae fundamenta habet, & quae a Deo ipso condita est, non a Cain, aut ab vllis hominibus. Ecce autem egregia commendatio eius ciuitatis, ob quam omnes merito exoptamus in ciuitatem illam recipi. Si Deus est conditor, igitur diuina, spiritualis est, bene fundata, perpetuo cum suo conditore duratura. Si Deus est conditor, Ergo optime constituta est, optime administratur, optime in ea viuitur. 2. Corinth. 5. Domum habemus non manu factam, sed aeternam in coelis. Doctrinam vero multiplicem hic habemus.
units.tr: "And in your seed shall all the generations of the earth be blessed." This promise is repeated many times afterwards. So this is what the apostle teaches here: the faith of Abraham is not to be understood as the kind of faith that is concerned only with receiving temporal things, but that he grasped spiritual goods together with temporal ones, just as the promises almost always spoke of both. In this way God is accustomed to nourish and advance the faith of the pious by temporal benefits and external signs, such as circumcision was for Abraham and such as baptism and the Lord's Supper are for us. And so the fathers too were accustomed to receive temporal promises in such a way that they understood spiritual things under them. For otherwise, what a small thing it would have been to receive temporal successes, which were for the most part common to the impious as well as the pious! And even if the pious fathers were promised very great temporal goods, yet they received these more sparingly, as can be seen in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who while alive obtained neither the land of Canaan nor many offspring. Abraham did not obtain even a foot's breadth of the land of Canaan. Others received nothing more, but their seed had still to be strangers and to serve in a foreign country. Moreover, how could their minds have rested in temporal promises? What peace of conscience would there have been? What occasion would there have been for such patience in so long a delay and postponement? Besides, the holy fathers undoubtedly understood that they were in no way worthy of such benefits, that they had never done anything such that God should promise them such great and remarkable goods above other men. Necessarily, then, under the covering and shadow of temporal promises the fathers grasped spiritual goods by faith, and their minds were fixed more on spiritual goods than on temporal ones, for which they were not very eager, and which did not come to them so abundantly at once beyond other mortals. And they attended all the more to spiritual things because promises of spiritual things were joined to promises of temporal things, as we showed above in the promise made to Abraham, where it was said: "In you shall all the generations of the earth be blessed." This undoubtedly lay chiefly and always before his eyes, and all the other promises referred to this one. And this too must be held without doubt: all the fathers, since they had been most fully taught about that promise made to our first parents, in which the Seed was promised who would crush the head of the serpent, and they awaited the time of redemption with far greater ardour, each hoping that this promise would be fulfilled in one of his sons; moreover, since they knew how great a good had been lost through the fall of our first parents, far better than we can know it; and again, they established with the most certain faith that God wished to be merciful to them and to save the human race, they always looked back to the first promise made to our first parents, and whatever happy and prosperous things befell them, they interpreted as befalling them because of that first promise, and they referred everything to it as to a fountain of good things. Therefore it is clear that the faith of the fathers was always intent more on spiritual goods than on temporal ones, and at all times looked to the promises of spiritual things. So this is what the apostle added here, saying: "For he looked for the city which has foundations." Here the office and effect of faith is again expressed most aptly, whose proper task is to look toward things future, which is rightly signified by the Greek word "epidechetai" [ἐπιδέχεται]; and then toward spiritual things, which the words "a city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God" describe. As I have said, the proper meaning of the words must always be observed, by which the apostle wanted carefully to express everywhere the effect and office of faith. Moreover, he sets the city against the tent, and does so very elegantly, to express the excellence of the spiritual goods which he awaited above temporal goods. For as a splendid and magnificent city surpasses a small tent, so spiritual goods surpass all temporal things. He further adorns the city with the dignity of having foundations, which are not seen in tents. This particle signifies solidity and stability; so it is suitable for signifying things other than temporal ones, which lack solidity and cannot endure. Therefore the heavenly kingdom, which is eternal, is rightly understood through the city having foundations; or certainly the Church, whose beginning is on earth and whose completion is in heaven, and into which all the saints desire and ought to be grafted, seeking only this: that they may be received into it, and be citizens and members of God's household for ever. And this city is founded upon the firm rock, which is Christ, concerning which see Ephesians 2 and 1 Corinthians 3. The impious too have their city and church, but it does not have foundations; it is founded upon sand, not upon the rock. This can be seen in our adversaries, who, since they have neither foundations, nor Christ, nor his Word, want to make it firm with straw and the sand of human wisdom and worldly power. Cain had founded such a city, and in Abraham's time there were many such cities, but they were occupied by the impious, such as the Sodomites and the like. But the pious dwell for a while in tents, until they come to the city which has foundations, and which was founded by God himself, not by Cain or by any men. Behold, moreover, the outstanding commendation of that city, for which all of us rightly long to be received into it. If God is the founder, then it is divine and spiritual, well founded, and destined to last for ever with its founder. If God is the founder, then it is excellently constituted, excellently governed, excellently lived in. 2 Corinthians 5: "We have a house not made with hands, but eternal, in the heavens." Here we have a many-sided teaching.

units.la: Primùm, discimus contemptum rerum terrenarum in exemplo patrum. 1. Corinth. 7. iubemur vti praesentibus tanquam si non habeamus. Sic, vtebatur Abraham terra Chanaan. Homines nunc per fas & nefas corradunt, etiam non habentes promissionem: & cum omnia fecerint, tamen adhuc nihil obtinent: solis terrenis rebus inhiant. Mirabilis luxus & abusus rerum vbique conspicitur, vt non mirum foret, mundum suaipsius mole corruere: in patribus summa frugalitas, & propterea etiam omnium rerum sufficientia.
units.tr: First, we learn to despise earthly things from the example of the fathers. In 1 Corinthians 7 we are bidden to use present things as though we did not have them. So Abraham used the land of Canaan. Men now scrape together wealth by fair means and foul, even those who have no promise; and though they have done everything, they still obtain nothing, for they gape only after earthly things. A remarkable luxury and abuse of goods is seen everywhere, so that it would be no wonder if the world collapsed under its own weight. In the fathers, by contrast, there was the greatest frugality, and therefore also sufficiency in all things.

units.la: Secundò, discimus, in his terrenis semper aspirandum nobis ad coelestia: & sicut per creaturas deducimur in cognitionem creatoris: ita per temporalia debemus deduci ad spiritualia: sicut Sanctos patres fecisse videmus. Tertiò, admonemur hic intenti esse in hunc proprium effectum & officium fidei: & fides semper dirigatur ad spiritualia & coelestia potius, quam ad terrena. Quartò discimus, summam curam nobis esse debere de illa ciuitate habente fundamenta, & a Deo condita, id est, vera ecclesia, extra quam non est salus, non magis, quam esse poterat salus extra arcam Noe. Cogitemus crebrò de ciuitatis huius excellentia, amplitudine, potentia, de conditore, de summo magistratu, de legibus seu politia, de ciuibus, de moribus, & vita ciuium, de duratione eius, &c. Certè, si possemus bene considerare, quid interfit inter ciuitatem istam, & exigua tabernacula huius mundi, nos facilè omnia terrena disceremus contemnere.
units.tr: Secondly, we learn that in these earthly things we must always aspire to heavenly things. As we are led through creatures to the knowledge of the Creator, so we ought to be led through temporal things to spiritual things, as we see the holy fathers did. Thirdly, we are admonished here to be intent on this proper effect and office of faith: faith should always be directed to spiritual and heavenly things rather than to earthly ones. Fourthly, we learn that we ought to have the greatest care for that city which has foundations and was founded by God, that is, the true Church, outside which there is no salvation, just as there could be no salvation outside Noah's ark. Let us often think of the excellence, extent and power of this city, of its founder, its supreme magistrate, its laws or polity, its citizens, their morals and way of life, its duration, and so on. Certainly, if we could consider well what lies between that city and the small tents of this world, we would easily learn to despise all earthly things.

units.la: Per fidem & ipsa Sara vim ad concipiendum, ac retinendum semen accepit, ac praeter aetatis rationem peperit, quod fidelem iudicaret eum, qui promiserat. Quapropter & ex vno prognati sunt posteri, eoq; iam annis effoeto, tanto numero, quanio sunt stellae coeli, & velut arena, quae est iuxta marginem maris innumerabilis.
units.tr: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive and to retain seed, and she bore a child beyond the reckoning of her age, since she judged him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and he already worn out with years, descendants were born, as many as the stars of heaven and as the innumerable sand that lies by the shore of the sea.

units.la: Tertia comprobatio seu demonstratio fidei Abrahae, ab admirabili effectu fidei, nempe quod contra atque communi lege naturae fieri solet, iam annis effoetus filium genuerit, a quo deinde innumerabilis secuta est posteritas. Huius autem effectus ratione adidit & praeposuit demonstrationem fidei Sarae, in qua similiter eluxit clarissimum fidei documentum, quando videlicet, cum promissum esset, ipsam fore grauidam, & paritu-ram, quod tamen per aetatis rationem, & naturae ordinariam potentiam fieri haud poterat, lubenter crediderit, & fidei suae effectus admirabilis fit experta. Dicuntur autem haec potissimum ad fidem Abrahae declarandam. In quo perfecte credentis absolutissimam fidem proponitur. Ideoque de Abrahamo potissimum exponimus, & primo loco de eo agimus. Exemplum autem Sarae adjicitur, tum quia coniunctum est, & diuelli non potest ab ea specie facti, & effectu fidei, qui hic proponitur: tum propter alias vtiles causas, quas postea explicabimus. Quamobrem & nos primùm explicabimus id, quod de Abrahamo dicitur: postea agemus de Sara. Hoc autem hic pro fidei effectu praedicatur, quod videlicet ex uno, coq; iam annis effoeto, prognati sunt posteri, & quidem tanto numero: Duo quidem hic dicuntur, fidem Abrahae mirabiliter illustrantia. Primum, quod ex effoeto propter aetatem, quae particula maximè est consideranda hoc loco. Alterum, quod ex vno prognati sint innumeri: quod etiam reuera valde est admirandum, & merito pro insigni fidei effectu accipitur. Videamus, quomodo vtrumque ex Scripturis sit sumptum, & quomodo fides in vtroque emineat. Promissio facta est ad Abraham de multiplicando semine eius, anno aetatis eius septuagesimo quinto: multis tamen annis nihil succesit, quo videretur certa spes affulgere. Tandem cùm Abraham esset annorum octoginta sex, natus est ei filius Ismael ex ancilla Agar. Sed hic nondum promissus ille filius, qui tanto pere expectabatur. Sara iam conclusam se & ineptam ad pariendum fatebatur. Vbi vero Abraham esset annorum nonagintanouem, iterum Dominus promittit illi filium & posteritatem, atque signum foederis, circumcisio inquam, instituitur. Cuius institutioni haec verba adiunguntur: Dixit quoque Deus ad Abraham, Sarai uxorem tuam non uocabis Sarai, sed Saram. Et benedicam ei, & ex illa dabo tibi filium, cui benedicturus sum, erit in nationes, & reges populorum nascentur ex eo. Cecidit Abraham in faciem suam, & risit in corde suo, dicens: Puta' sne centenario nascetur filius, & Sara nonagenaria pariet? Dixitq; ad Deum: utinam Ismael viuat coram te. Et ait Deus ad Abraham: Sara uxor tua pariet tibi filium, uocabisq; nomen eius Isaac: & constituam pactum meum illi in foedus sempiternum, & semini eius post eum. Quae promissio iterum repetitur Genes. 18. per illos, quos excepit hospitio. Et Genes. 21. describitur ipsius Isaac natiuitas, anno aetatis Abrahae centesimo. Vbi & haec habentur verba Sarae: Quis auditurus crederet Abraham, quod Sara lactaret filium, quem peperit & iam senii? Ista sunt nobis consideranda, vt intelligamus verba Apostoli. Nam Apostolus sine dubio ad ista verba respexit. Clare enim dicitur, ipsum Abraham risisse in corde suo. Id autem intelligendum est, fecisse, non per dubitationem, sed per admirationem: cùm Roman. 4. diserte dicatur, At non infirmatus fide haud considerauit suum ipsius corpus iam emortuum, cum centum fere natus esset annos, nec emortuam vuluam Sarae: verùm ad promissionem non haesitabat ob incredulitatem, sed robustus factus est fide, tribuens gloriam Deo, certa persuasione concepta, quod is, qui promiserat, idem potens esset & praestare. Quapropter etiam imputatum est illi ad iustitiam. Cum ergo ipse Abraham tantopere fuerit admiratus, similiter & Sara, id ideo factum, quia nimirum respiciendo naturae communem cursum, & corporum suorum habitudinem, impossibile erat, ex ipsis prolem nasci, nisi Deus sua virtute supra communem & ordinariam legem naturae aliquid faceret, quod quidem facere ipsum & velle, & posse iudicabant, & alacriter expectabant.
units.tr: The third proof or demonstration of Abraham's faith is taken from the wonderful effect of faith: namely, that, contrary to the common law of nature, he who was already worn out with years begot a son, from whom an innumerable posterity then followed. Because of this effect, he has added and placed before it the demonstration of Sarah's faith, in which the clearest proof of faith likewise shone forth. For when it had been promised that she would be pregnant and bear a child, which by reason of age and the ordinary power of nature could by no means happen, she gladly believed and experienced the wonderful effect of her faith. These things are said chiefly to declare Abraham's faith, in which the most perfect faith of the believer is set forth. Therefore we expound chiefly concerning Abraham, and we deal with him first. Sarah's example is added, both because it is joined to, and cannot be separated from, that kind of deed and effect of faith which is set forth here, and for other useful reasons which we will explain later. Wherefore we shall first explain what is said of Abraham, and afterwards deal with Sarah. Now what is proclaimed here as an effect of faith is this: that from one man, already worn out with years, descendants were born, and so many of them. Two things are said here, which wonderfully illustrate Abraham's faith. The first is that the offspring came from one who was worn out by age, a detail that is especially to be considered in this place. The second is that innumerable descendants came from one man; this is indeed greatly to be admired, and is rightly taken as a notable effect of faith. Let us see how each of these is drawn from the Scriptures, and how faith stands out in both. The promise was made to Abraham that his seed would be multiplied in his seventy-fifth year. Yet for many years nothing followed by which a sure hope might seem to shine forth. At last, when Abraham was eighty-six years old, a son, Ishmael, was born to him by the maidservant Hagar. But that son was not yet the promised son, for whom they had waited so long. Sarah already confessed herself shut up and unfit for bearing. But when Abraham was ninety-nine years old, the Lord again promised him a son and posterity, and the sign of the covenant, circumcision I mean, was instituted. To its institution these words are added: "God said also to Abraham: You shall not call your wife Sarai, but Sarah. I will bless her, and from her I will give you a son whom I will bless; he will become nations, and kings of peoples will be born of him. Abraham fell on his face and laughed in his heart, saying: Can a son be born to a man of a hundred years? Will Sarah at ninety bear a child? And he said to God: Would that Ishmael might live before you. And God said to Abraham: Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him." This promise is repeated again in Genesis 18, through those whom he received as guests. And in Genesis 21 the birth of Isaac himself is described, in the hundredth year of Abraham's life. There too these words of Sarah are recorded: "Who would have believed that Abraham would be told that Sarah would nurse a son, whom she bore when already old?" These things must be considered by us, so that we understand the words of the Apostle, for the Apostle without doubt had these words in view. For it is clearly said that Abraham himself laughed in his heart. This, however, must be understood as having happened not through doubt but through wonder. For in Romans 4 it is plainly said: "But not weakened in faith, he did not consider his own body, already dead, since he was about a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sarah. Yet he did not waver at the promise through unbelief, but was made strong in faith, giving glory to God, with a firm persuasion that he who had promised was also able to perform it. Therefore it was also reckoned to him for righteousness." Since, therefore, Abraham himself was so greatly amazed, and Sarah likewise, this happened because, looking at the common course of nature and the condition of their bodies, it was impossible for offspring to be born from them, unless God by his power did something beyond the common and ordinary law of nature. They judged that he was both able and willing to do this, and they eagerly awaited it.

units.la: Igitur fidei ipsorum attribuendum est, quod talis effectus secutus sit, & proles ex foetis parentibus nata. Constat autem vel ex philosophorum, qui naturae historiam diligenter exploratunt, sententiis, homines generationi ad eam aetatem esse ineptos. Aristoteles ad finem libri septimi politicorum censet infirmos esse partus post annum quinquagesimum. Certè Plinius libro septimo, cap. 14. scribit, ex sententia philosophorum, mulierem non gignere post annum quinquagesimum: virum verò raro gignere vltra septuagesimum quintum: etiamsi commemoret, Catonem exacto anno octoagesimo genuisse. Idem Plinius, praeterea Censorinus libro de die Natali, scribunt, compertum esse longa obseruatione Aegyptiorum, hominis cor crescere ad annum vsq; aetatis quinquagesimum: inde verò ad centesimum iterum paribus partibus decrescere, vt centesimo anno ad eandem angustiam contractum sit, qua fuit primo anno natiuitatis: ideoq; secundum naturam non facile posse hominem diutius viuere: saltem raro contingere, vt diuersum conspiciatur. Id verò confirmatur illa quoq; ratione, quod ad illa aetate qui perueniunt, solent repuerascere, debilitate videlicet cordis ita postulante. Iam igitur si secundum communem naturae cursum non poterit quis vltra centesimum annum commodè viuere, quomodo erit alienius, Abrahamum in tali aetate adhuc filium procreare? Perinde reuera erit; atque si dicatur, & puerum, quo tempore primum natus est, statim posse gignere. Ergo quia contra communem naturae legem erat, quod tali aetate talis vir, tot fractus molestijs, generaret, rectè soli potentiae & bonitati diuinae ascribitur, & fide dicitur Abraham promissionem de ea re apprehendisse. Sed hic scrupulus nascitur, quomodo istud tali facto poterit ad tantam commendationem fidei Abrahae referri, quod crediderit, sibi centenario filium nasciturum? Hoc ipsum non videtur supra naturae cursum fieri, ideoque nihil est, quod ad praedicationem fidei tantopere faciat. Neque difficile est, id demonstrare vel e sacris literis. Nam & Genesis 5. legitur Methusalah, cùm uixisset annis centum octoginta septem: genuisse Lamech, ac deinde adhuc vixisse necnon generasse. Lamech verò annis vixit, 182. & genuit Noe, post hunc & alios. Genes. 11. Sem erat centum annorum, quando genuit Arphaxat. Sed et Genes. 25. Abraham scribitur mortua Sara duxisse aliam vxorem nomine Cethuram, & ex ea adhuc sex filios suscepisse. Nihil igitur videtur alienum a communi naturae cursu accidisse, quod Abraham centenarius genuerit, ideoque nullum hic fidei effectum elucere. Ad hanc obiectionem respondetur. Primò, quod ad patres illos attinet primò commemoratos, distinguendum est pro ratione
units.tr: Therefore it must be ascribed to their faith that such an effect followed, and that offspring were born from parents so worn out with years. It is established, indeed, by the opinions of the philosophers who carefully investigated the natural history, that men are unfit for generation at that age. Aristotle, at the end of the seventh book of the Politics, judges that offspring born after the fiftieth year are weak. Certainly Pliny, in book seven, chapter 14, writes that, according to the opinion of the philosophers, a woman does not bear children after her fiftieth year, and a man rarely begets children beyond his seventy-fifth year, although he mentions that Cato begot a child after his eightieth year had passed. The same Pliny, and Censorinus in his book On the Birthday, write that long observation of the Egyptians has found that the human heart grows until the fiftieth year of life, and thence decreases again in equal parts until the hundredth, so that in the hundredth year it is contracted to the same narrowness it had in the first year of birth. Therefore, by nature, a man cannot easily live longer; at least it rarely happens that something different is seen. This is also confirmed by the reason that those who reach that age are wont to become like children again, the weakness of the heart so requiring. Now, if by the common course of nature no one can conveniently live beyond the hundredth year, how much more strange will it be that Abraham, at such an age, should still beget a son? It will be just as if one said that a boy, at the time when he was first born, could immediately beget children. Therefore, because it was against the common law of nature that such a man, so worn down by troubles, should beget at such an age, it is rightly ascribed to the power and goodness of God alone, and it is said that Abraham by faith laid hold of the promise concerning this matter. But here a scruple arises: how can this be referred to so great a commendation of Abraham's faith, that he believed a son would be born to him at a hundred years old? For this itself does not seem to happen beyond the course of nature, and so there is nothing here that contributes so much to the praise of faith. Nor is it difficult to demonstrate this even from the sacred letters. For in Genesis 5 we read that Methuselah, when he had lived one hundred and eighty-seven years, begot Lamech, and afterwards lived on and begot others. Lamech indeed lived 182 years and begot Noah, and after him others. Genesis 11: Shem was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad. And in Genesis 25 it is written that Abraham, after Sarah's death, took another wife named Keturah, and had six more sons by her. Nothing, therefore, seems to have happened contrary to the common course of nature in Abraham's begetting a child at a hundred years old, and so no effect of faith shines forth here. To this objection it is answered: first, as far as those fathers first mentioned are concerned, a distinction must be made according to the reason.

units.la: Respons. i. ratio. Distinctio temporis.
units.tr: Answer, first reason: the distinction of time.

units.la: ratione temporis. Nam ante diluuium longius hominum ætas protrahebatur, quàm post. Tardius etiam illi liberis procreandis dabant operam: id quod licet videre aperte ex eo, quòd patres illi plerique iam centum erant annorum, prius quàm gignerent. At à Diluuio statim inuenis passim homines anno ætatis suæ vicesimoquinto, aut vicesimo octauo, aut tricesimo genuisse. Quamobrem neque ita multis annis postea vixerunt, neque tàm graui ætate genuerunt.
units.tr: The answer is given by the reason of time. Before the Flood people lived much longer than after it. They were also slower to beget children, as is plain from the fact that most of those patriarchs were already a hundred years old before they begot. But from the Flood onward, young men commonly had children at the age of twenty-five, twenty-eight or thirty. So they did not live as many years afterwards, nor did they beget children at so advanced an age.

units.la: De Sem quidem, qui paternam benedictionem acceperat, id refertur: atque haud scio an de aliis post eum humile narretur. Quanquàm in ipso adhuc vestigium originalis mûdi & priscorum patrum supererat. Itaque succedente seculo si quis tali ætate genuisset, id plane pro miraculo habebatur: quod indicium ex verbis ipsius Abrahæ supra citatis licet colligere. Iam, quòd Abraham etiam post centesimum annum genuerit filios ex alia vxore: Respondetur, dicendo, magnum esse discrimen inter Saram & Cethuram: Saram siquidem nonagenariam fuisse, & præterea semper sterilem: de Cethura nihil tales quàm probabile est, & iuuenem fuisse, & natura fœcundam. Itaque etiamsi ex parte Abrahami nihil fuisset novi, quòd ipse gigneret, tamen erat valde novum & incredibile, quòd ex tali gigneret. Deinde, quòd ipse quoque gigneret, cui antea tot annis omnis via augendæ posteritatis præclusa fuerat. Quis credidisset, sicut & Sara recte dicebat, eum generaturum in ea ætate, qui antea in florenti, & viridi ætate neque quaquàm generauerat? Opus igitur hic erat fide, & quidem magna, quòd nulla habita ratione suæ ætatis, vel ætatis Sarae, tamen crediderit, sibi posteritatem nasciturAm.
units.tr: This is recorded of Shem, who had received the father's blessing, and I do not know whether it is told of any of the others after him, though it is a humble account. Yet a trace of the original state and of the early patriarchs still survived in him. So in the following age, if anyone begot a child at such an age, this was regarded as a plain miracle, and we may gather this from Abraham's own words quoted above. As for the fact that Abraham also begot sons by another wife after the hundredth year, the answer is that there is a great difference between Sarah and Keturah. Sarah was ninety years old and had always been barren, whereas Keturah was probably young and naturally fruitful. So even if nothing new had happened on Abraham's side in begetting children, it was still very new and incredible that he should beget them by such a wife. Moreover, he himself was begetting children, when for so many years every way of increasing his posterity had been closed to him. Who would have believed, as Sarah rightly said, that he would beget in that age a child he had not begotten at all in his flourishing and vigorous years? So faith was needed here, and great faith indeed, since without regard to his own age or Sarah's age he nevertheless believed that posterity would be born to him.

units.la: Potest addi & alia ratio, quare fide fuerit hic opus, ex parte filij ex Sara nati. Nam hic erat promissus, sicut & Galat. 4. vocatur filius promissionis: & Roman.9. Filij promissionis pertinent ad semen Abrahæ: de aliis autem non ita fuit edita specialis promissio: sicut nec Ismael fuit filius promissionis. Itaque in expectatione vnius Isaac fides exercebatur: sicut necessario, vbi promissio est, ibi fides requiritur. Tantum ergo de dicta obiectione: & manifestum manet, amplissimum esse documentum fidei, quòd Abraham ex se centenario generandum filium crediderit. Atque hæc de priore particula, eoq; annis effœto. Nunc de altera particula: Et tanto numero, quanto sunt stellæ cœli: Hæc particula etiam valde illustrat effectum fidei. Nam etiamsi vnus tantùm Isaac ex illo fuisset genitus, id vere fuisset maximum, & satisfuisset ad fidei exercitium, necnon ad declarationem bonitatis diuinæ erga Abrahamum. At vero quòd innumeri ex vno illo fuerint prognati, omnes ab illo vno ducentes stemma & originem, istud profecto longè est maximum. Sed quare ita addit Deus similitudinem de multitudine stellarum cœli & arenæ maris? Est comparatio amplificans posteritatis, quæ ex Abraham esset nascitura, frequentiam: vt intenderetur miraculi dignitas, quo ex vno eoque tot annis sterili & effœto nascituri dicebantur homines innumerabiles. Hyperbolicam locutionem nonnulli esse volunt, ad significandum multitudinem, quæ saltem difficulter posset numerari. Nam alias & in deserto, & tempore Dauidis numerati sunt, qui tum viuebant: & angustis finibus Iudæorum terram, si cæteras spectemus latissimas regiones, conclusa fuit. Et tamen multi populi ex Abraham descenderunt, si spectemus eos, qui originem ducunt ex filijs natis ei ex Gethura. Quare apta & vera fuit similitudo, neque adimpleta est. Sed placet quibusdam altius contemplari, & mysterium hic inquirere. Itaque per stellas & arenam significare duo genera filiorum Abrahæ ego existimo: alterum, quod secundum spiritum, & secundum promissionem natum est ex Abraham, siue secundum carnem ex eo natum sit, siue non: hoc est, siue Iudæi fuerint, siue gentiles. Huiusmodi homines sunt vere spirituales, vereq; cœlestes, cœlestem patriam expectantes: sicut mox de patriarchis subijcitur. Quamobrem & stellis recte comparatur: Daniel. 12. 1. Corinth. 15. Alterum est, quod secundum carnem, adeoque secundum solum titulum pro semine Abrahæ agnosci possunt. Huiusmodi sunt omnes, qui neque credunt, vt Abraham: neque operantur, vt Abraham: siue secundum carnem ex eo nati sint, siue non, & tamen iactant se quasi credentes, & quasi filios Abrahæ. Hi verè sunt similes arenæ sterili, & nullo modo cohærenti: sed iactantur fluctibus maris, & turbinibus huius mundi: ne que doctrinam certam sequentes, neq; veram ampleftentes religionem: sed tantum inanes titulos, qui in ventum abeunt, & vento longissimè sparguntur. De vtroque hoc genere filiorum Abrahæ Roman.9. Non omnes, qui sunt ex Israel, sunt Israel, neque quia sunt semen Abrahæ, statim omnes filij: sed per Isaac nominabitur tibi semen: hoc est, non, qui filij carnis, ij filij Dei: sed qui sunt filij repromissionis, recensentur in semen, Galat.4. Qui de libera natus est, filius repromissionis, etc. Nos alibi quoque hac de re egimus. Hæc pro demonstratione fidei Abrahæ in præsens sufficiant. Explicanda sunt nobis etiam, quæ de fide Sarae dicuntur. Primò autem videndum, quare Apostolus interpo-
units.tr: Another reason can be added why faith was required here, on the side of the son born of Sarah. For he was promised, and so he is called the son of promise in Galatians 4, and in Romans 9 the children of promise are reckoned as the seed of Abraham. But no special promise was given concerning the others, just as Ishmael was not a son of promise. So faith was exercised in waiting for Isaac alone, since wherever there is a promise, faith is necessarily required. Enough, then, on the objection mentioned; and it remains plain that the faith of Abraham, in believing that a son would be born to him from himself when he was a hundred years old and his body was dead, is a most ample proof of faith. So much for the first part. Now for the second part, "And in such number as the stars of heaven." This part also greatly sets out the effect of faith. For even if only Isaac had been begotten of him, that would truly have been a very great thing, and it would have been enough for the exercise of faith and for the declaration of God's goodness towards Abraham. But that countless descendants should come from that one man, all tracing their line and origin back to him, is certainly far greater. But why does God add this likeness of the multitude of the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea? It is a comparison that magnifies the abundance of the posterity that was to come from Abraham, so that the dignity of the miracle might be heightened, by which countless men were said to be born from one man, and that a man so barren and worn out by so many years. Some hold that this is a hyperbolical way of speaking, to signify a multitude that could scarcely be counted. For in the wilderness and in the time of David those then living were numbered, and the land of the Jews was confined within narrow limits, if we look at the other very wide regions. Yet many peoples have descended from Abraham, if we consider those who trace their origin from the sons born to him by Keturah. Therefore the likeness was apt and true, and it has not failed of fulfilment. But some are pleased to contemplate this more deeply and to inquire into a mystery here. So I think that by the stars and the sand are signified two kinds of children of Abraham: the first, who were born of Abraham according to the Spirit and according to the promise, whether or not they were born of him according to the flesh, that is, whether they were Jews or Gentiles. Such men are truly spiritual and truly heavenly, looking for a heavenly country, as is added soon afterwards concerning the patriarchs. For this reason they are rightly compared to the stars: Daniel 12; 1 Corinthians 15. The second kind are those who are acknowledged as the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, and so only by the name. Such are all who neither believe as Abraham did nor act as Abraham did, whether or not they were born of him according to the flesh, and yet they boast as if they were believers and as if they were sons of Abraham. These are truly like barren sand, which does not hold together at all, but are tossed by the waves of the sea and the whirlwinds of this world. They follow no sure doctrine and embrace no true religion, but only empty titles, which vanish into the wind and are scattered far and wide by it. Of both these kinds of children of Abraham, Romans 9 says: "Not all who are of Israel are Israel, nor because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children at once; but in Isaac shall your seed be named," that is, those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God, but those who are children of the promise are reckoned as the seed. Galatians 4: "He who was born of the free woman was the son of promise," and so on. We have treated this matter elsewhere too. Let these remarks suffice for the present as a demonstration of the faith of Abraham. We must also explain what is said about the faith of Sarah. But first we must see why the Apostle interposes

units.la: z.particula. Multiplicatio feminis Abrahæ. Maximum fuit ab uno innumeros procreari. Similitudo à stellis & arenæ maris. Multi populi nati ex Abrahamo. Alij dicut signi sicari bonos p stellas: malos p arenà, ac gentiles potissimum. Filij spiritus et promissionis. Filij secundum carnem tantum. Arena sterilis sunt impij & increduli. Quinam vert filij Abrahæ. Fides Sarae. terpofuerit ista de fide Saræ,cùm propriè versetur in explicanda fide Abrahæ, cuius exé- plum principaliter est spectandum, & omnium longè pulcherrimum: præterea de fide Saræ potest aliquantum dubitari, sicut postea dicemus. Respondetur, diuersis de causis, & iustissimis, additum esse exemplum Saræ. Primò, licet in hoc effectu fidei, videlicet nato filio ex centenario, potissimum eluxerit fides ipsius Abrahæ: tamen, quia fortassis iudicari potuisset non adeò magnum, & à naturæ communi cursu alienum, quòd ex cen- tenario nasceretur filius: quando & alij patres leguntur tali ætate & grauiore generasse: conueniebat addi de centenaria, vt miraculi dignitas & fidei exercitium in Abrahamo clarius innotesceret. Nam Abrahamo centenario nasci filium ex Sara sterili, & nonage- naria, hoc certè non poterat nisi per fidem apprehendi. Hac ergo de caussa conueniebat, fieri mentionem ipsius Saræ, pariterque ipsius fidem celebrari. Secundò, cùm demon- stratio hęc fidei Abrahæ sumpta fit ex actu coniugali, qui est procreatio liberorum, reuera nonpoterat prætereiri vxoris eius Sarę mentio, de cuius partu erat facta promissio, & de cuius partu fides Abrahæ erat solicita. Vnde ex ea geniti dicuntur proprie filij promis- sionis, non autem qui geniti sunt ex Agar vel ex Cethura. Propter hanc igitur certitudi- nem & necessariam connexionem opus erat de Sara aliquid exprimere. Tertiò, vt o- stenderetur, etiam in sexu muliebri, fragili, fidei præclara exempla elucere, in omni vitæ genere, & quibuscunque actionibus, puta in coniugalibus, & similibus, fidei exercitia esse proposita, & homines per fidem Deo placere. In Christo Iesu neque seruus, neque liber, neque mas, neque fœmina: Galat.3. 1. Corinth.12. Ephes. 6. Et sic paulo post etiam proponitur fides Rahab meretricis, item mulierum, quæ acceperunt mortuos suos ex resurrectione. Quartò, vt haberetur quoddam exemplum oeconomiæ Christianæ, ac disceremus, mulieres debere, æquè ac viros, esse in iis, quæ sunt pietatis, instituras: fide & pietate maritorum excitari: denique, sicut bona temporalia, & ipsa corpora: ita spiri- tum ac virtutes quascunque esse debere inter coniuges communes: alterum alterius de- bere excitari & confirmari exemplis: sicut hic cernimus fide Abraham illustratam Sa- ram, & in fide confirmatam, ac vicissim fide Saræ illustratam fidem Abrahæ. Non est du- bium, quin Abraham omnes promissiones sibi factas reuelarit vxori suæ, iusseritq; eam similiter credere, perficienda esse, quæ Deus promiserat. Agebat Abraham diligentissi- mum verbi ministrum in sua familia, &c. His inquam de caussis conueniens fuit, de Sara, eiusque fide nonnulla admisceri. Iam audiamus, quomodo & quàm appositis verbis fidei Saræ ab Apostolo prædicetur: Per fidem, inquit, & ipsa Sara uim ad concipiendum ac retinendum semen accepit, ac præter ætatis rationem peperit, quòd fidelem iudicaret eum, qui promiserat. His verbis duo notantur, quę ostenduntur, non potuisse fieri, vt ipsa pareret, ideoque opus fuisse virtute diuina & supernaturali, & fide, qua misericordia Dei apprehenderetur.
