Primum, quòd non habuit vim ad concipiendum ac retinendum semen, εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος τοῦ. Chrysostomus interpretatur, ad suscipiendum & ad retinendum semen. Quidam volunt, ad emittendum semen: sentiunt enim plerique etiam philosophi, etiam mulieres semen emittere, indeque steriles cerni, quòd hac facultate sint destitutæ. Qua de re non est instituti nostri nunc disputare. Quomodocunque res se habeat, significatur, Sarām iam diu natura & corporis affectione fuisse sterilem, & omni spe pariendi destitutam: qua de re Geneseos vedecimo: Erat autem Sarai sterilis, nec habebat liberos. Item Genef.16. Ecce, conclusit me Dominus, ne pārerem, ingredere ad ancillam meam, si forte ex illa suscipiam filios. Alterum dicitur de ætate: quòd videlicet, etiam si antea fuisset fœcunda: tamen nunc per ætatem sterilis erat, quippe nonagenaria. Respicit enim Apostolus ad id, quod Genef.17. commemoratur ab ipso Abrahamo ætas Saræ, & vocatur ibi nonagenaria: item, quòd Saræ, desierant fieri muliebria. Quanto ergo grauiora erant impedimenta ista, tantò maius futurum erat miraculum, ac tantò magis opus erat promissionem fide apprehendi, tantòque latius patebat fidei exercitium. Proinde hæc impedimenta sublata sunt, propter fidem Saræ, quòd fidelem iudicaret eum, qui promiserat. Ecce, quantus hic effectus fidei, & quàm proprijs verbis officium fidei hic describitur. Fides apprehendit promissam misericordiam, non quia nos promeremur eam aliquo modo: non item propter aliquam aliam causam: sed tantùm quia fidelis est ipse Deus, præstat Deus, quæ promittit, propter sui ipsius dignitatem ac gloriam: sicut Roman.3. Deus verax est, sicut scriptum est: vt iustificeris in sermonibus tuis, & vincas cùm iudicaris. Ecce ergo officium fidei, & obiectum fidei principale eleganter expressum. Sed, hic dicis, in scripturis non videtur istud expressum, quòd Sara tanta fide fuerit prædita, imò potius videtur argui incredulitatis. Sic enim legimus Genef.18. Cùmq; comedissent (tres illos viros exceptos hospitio intellige) dixerút ad Abraham: vbi est Sara vxor tua? Ille respondit, Ecce in tabernaculo est: cui dixit: Reuertens veniam ad te tempore isto, secundum tempus
units.tr: Second part. The multiplication of Abraham's offspring. It was a great thing that countless people should be born from one man. The likeness to the stars and to the sand of the sea. Many peoples born from Abraham. Some say the stars signify the good and the sand the wicked, especially the Gentiles. Sons of the Spirit and of promise. Sons according to the flesh only. Sterile sand are the impious and unbelieving. Who, then, are the sons of Abraham? Sarah's faith. The Apostle has inserted these things about Sarah's faith, although his discussion is properly concerned with explaining Abraham's faith, whose example is chiefly to be regarded and is by far the most beautiful of all. Moreover, some doubt may be raised about Sarah's faith, as we shall say later. The answer is that the example of Sarah was added for various reasons, and very just ones. First, although the faith of Abraham itself shone most brightly in this effect of faith, namely the birth of a son from a man of a hundred years, nevertheless, since it might perhaps have been judged not so great, and alien to the common course of nature, that a son should be born from a centenarian (since other fathers are also read to have begotten children at such an age, and even older), it was fitting to add the case of Sarah, who was of the same age, so that the dignity of the miracle and the exercise of faith in Abraham might be more clearly made known. For that Abraham, at a hundred years old, should have a son by Sarah, who was barren and ninety years old, could certainly be grasped only by faith. For this reason, therefore, it was fitting to make mention of Sarah herself and likewise to celebrate her faith. Second, since this demonstration of Abraham's faith is taken from the marital act, which is the procreation of children, Sarah could really not be passed over, she of whom the promise was made and about whose childbearing Abraham's faith was anxious. Hence those born of her are properly called sons of promise, not those born of Hagar or Keturah. On account of this certainty and necessary connection, therefore, it was needful to say something about Sarah. Third, so that it might be shown that even in the female sex, frail as it is, outstanding examples of faith shine forth, and that in every kind of life and in whatever actions (for instance in marital and similar matters) the exercises of faith are set before us, and men please God through faith. "In Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free, neither male nor female" (Gal. 3; 1 Cor. 12; Eph. 6). And so a little later the faith of Rahab the harlot is also set forth, and likewise that of the women who received their dead by resurrection. Fourth, so that there might be an example of Christian household management, and we might learn that women, no less than men, ought to be instructors in the things of piety, and to be roused by the faith and piety of their husbands; and finally, that just as temporal goods and the bodies themselves are held in common between spouses, so the spirit and all virtues ought to be held in common between them, each stirring up and confirming the other by examples. Just as here we see Sarah illumined by Abraham's faith and confirmed in faith, so in turn Abraham's faith is illumined by Sarah's. There is no doubt that Abraham revealed to his wife all the promises made to him, and bade her believe likewise that what God had promised would be accomplished. Abraham was a most diligent minister of the Word in his own household, and so on. For these reasons, I say, it was fitting that something about Sarah and her faith be mixed in. Now let us hear how, and in how apt words, the Apostle describes Sarah's faith: "By faith," he says, "Sarah herself received strength to conceive and to retain seed, and bore a child beyond the reckoning of age, since she judged him faithful who had promised." In these words two things are noted, which show that it could not have happened that she should bear, and that therefore divine and supernatural power was needed, and faith by which the mercy of God was apprehended. The first is that she did not have strength to conceive and retain seed, εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος τοῦ. Chrysostom interprets this as to receive and retain seed. Some want it to mean to emit seed, for most philosophers also think that women emit seed, and that barrenness is seen from their lacking this faculty. This question is not part of our present purpose to dispute. However the matter stands, it is signified that Sarah had long been barren by nature and bodily condition, and destitute of all hope of bearing. Hence Genesis 16: "Now Sarai was barren, and had no children." Likewise Genesis 16: "Behold, the Lord has shut me up so that I cannot bear; go in to my maidservant, that perhaps I may obtain sons from her." The second point concerns age: namely that, even if she had been fruitful before, now through age she was barren, being ninety years old. For the Apostle looks to what is recorded in Genesis 17 by Abraham himself, the age of Sarah, where she is called ninety years old; likewise that it had ceased with Sarah to be after the manner of women. The greater these impediments, therefore, the greater the miracle would be, the more the promise had to be apprehended by faith, and the wider the exercise of faith extended. Accordingly these impediments were removed on account of Sarah's faith, since she judged him faithful who had promised. Behold how great is the effect of faith here, and how in its own words the office of faith is described. Faith apprehends the promised mercy not because we deserve it in any way, nor on any other ground, but only because God himself is faithful, and God performs what he promises for the sake of his own dignity and glory, as in Romans 3: "God is true, as it is written: that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged." Behold, then, the office of faith and the principal object of faith elegantly expressed. But you will say that in the Scriptures this does not seem to be expressed, that Sarah was endowed with such great faith; rather she seems to be charged with unbelief. For thus we read in Genesis 18: "And when they had eaten (understand the three men received as guests), they said to Abraham, 'Where is Sarah your wife?' He answered, 'Behold, she is in the tent.' And he said, 'I will surely return to you at this time, according to the time of life'

units.la: V s tempus vitæ: & habebit filium Sara vxor tua. Quo audito Sara risit post ostium tabernaculi. Erant autem ambo senes proueclæque ętatis, & desierant Saræ fieri muliebria. Quæ risit occultè, dicens: postquàm consenui, & dominus meus vetulus est, voluptati operam dabo? Dixit autem Dominus ad Abraham: Quare risit Sara vxor tua, dicens: Num verè paritura sum anus? Nunquid Deo quicquam difficile est? iuxta condictum reuertar ad te hoc eodem tempore fecundum tempus vitæ, & habebit Sara filium. Negauit Sara, dicens: Non risi, timore perterrita. Dominus autem, non est, inquit, ita: sed risisti.
units.tr: and Sarah your wife shall have a son.' Sarah heard it, laughing behind the door of the tent. Now both were old and advanced in years, and Sarah had ceased to have the manner of women. She laughed secretly, saying, 'After I have grown old, and my lord is an old man, shall I have pleasure?' And the Lord said to Abraham, 'Why did Sarah laugh, saying, "Shall I indeed bear a child, being an old woman?" Is anything too hard for God? At the appointed time I will return to you, at this same time next year, and Sarah shall have a son.' Sarah denied it, saying, 'I did not laugh,' for she was frightened. But he said, 'No, it is not so; you did laugh.'

units.la: Vbi animaduertimus, Saram risisse, ceu rem absurdam audiret: item rationes adiectas, quæ videntur absurditatem vt causam risus approbantes. Deinde risum illum graviter reprehensum, opposita ipsi potentia Dei. Adhæc illam vt conuictam negasse risum. Quæ omnia certè videntur facere ad colligendum, quod non verè crediderit.
units.tr: Here we notice that Sarah laughed as if she heard something absurd; likewise the reasons added, which seem to approve the absurdity as the cause of her laughter. Then that laughter is sharply rebuked, the power of God being set against it. Besides, she is said to have denied the laughter when convicted. All of which certainly seem designed to infer that she did not truly believe.

units.la: Respondemus ad ista: primò, non adeò alienum videri, quòd riserit: nempe præadmiratione: sicut etiam risit Abraham. Et risus præ admiratione non statim tollit fidem, siue contrarius est fidei. Dùm enim mens intuetur in rationem naturalem, & ea, quæ videntur abducere animum, & ostendere, re omnimò esse impossibilem, certè est quod quis moueatur ad admirationem, vel ad risum: præsertim qui ipse deberet expectare in se adimplenda. Deinde sic solent etiam Sancti, vbi proponuntur ipsis inaudita, admirari, & sentiunt statim tentationes: ac diffidentia luctatur cum fide, vt partim credere incipiant, partim à credendo auocentur, donec paulatim exercita fides crescat & augmentum virecque recipiat. Quomodo videmus, sanctos etiam interdum signum aliquod petiuisse, quo confirmarentur ad credendum: sicut Abraham quoque petiuit, vnde sciret, se possessurum terram Chanaan: item Gedeon, & quidam alij signum petiuerunt. Sic autem & fides Saræ etiamsi primò infirma esset, propter rei, quæ proponebatur, magnitudinem: tamen paulatim erecta & confirmata est, maximè quando audijt de Dei omnipotentia. Atque eo quoque probabilius est, eam etiam statim credidisse, post tamen in fide magis confirmatam, vt dubium non fit, eam antea quoque à marito suo edoctam de promissionibus ad ipsum factis, quarum recordationem venisse illi statim in mentem credi par est. Risus igitur ille Sarę non est eiusmodi, vt ex eo colligatur, Saram fuisse incredulam. Sed exemplo & simili fiet tota hæc res illustrior. Cùm annunciaretur beatæ virgini Mariæ de partu, illa certè nemo dixerit incredulam, quandoquidem Elizabeth Spiritus Sancti instinctu diserte ad eam dicit Lucæ 1. Beata, quæ credidit, quoniam perficientur ea, quæ dicta sunt ei à Domino. Et tamen ibidem etiam aperte dicitur, prima statim salutatione turbata esse, & cogitasse, qualis foret illa salutatio? Tùm rogasse etiam, quomodo fieri posset vt ipsa parerct, quæ cum viro non habuisset commercium? Eandem deinde plenius debuisse per Angelum edoceri de virtute altissimi, tum etiam signo addito de grauida facta Elizabeth, ac post omnia confessam, & per fidem professam, se esse promptam ancillam Domini, vt perficeretur in ea, quod à Domino visum erat. En, Mariæ oborta est trepidatio vt tenerę virgini, & pudore quodam affectæ: Neq; trepidatio ea sufficit, vt dicatur fidem non habuisse: cùm sine dubio etiam ante edocta fuerit ex prophetarum oraculis, tale quiddam futurum, quale ipsi iam annunciabatur. Itidem cùm Sara ridet, vt nupta & annis iam, iam non admodum facit contra decorum: & risus talis (quæ alias fortasse suspicari quis posset etiam præ lætitia exortum) non est accusandus vt à fide prorsus alienus, multo minus vt fidei contrarius. Relinquitur ergo, Saram verè credidisse, eiusq; fidem tanti apud Deum fuisse, vt voluerit Dominus pijs votis Sarę aspirare.
units.tr: We reply to these things. First, it does not seem so out of place that she laughed, namely from astonishment, just as Abraham also laughed. And laughter from astonishment does not at once destroy faith, or is not opposed to faith. For while the mind looks to natural reason, and sees things that draw the spirit away and show that the thing is altogether impossible, there is certainly reason for a person to be moved to wonder or to laughter, especially one who himself ought to expect the fulfilment of these things in himself. Next, the saints too are accustomed, when things unheard of are put before them, to marvel, and they at once feel temptations: distrust struggles with faith, so that they partly begin to believe and partly are drawn away from believing, until faith, exercised little by little, grows and receives increase and strength. Thus we see that the saints have sometimes asked for some sign by which they might be confirmed in believing: as Abraham too asked how he might know that he would possess the land of Canaan; and Gideon and certain others sought a sign. So too Sarah's faith, even if at first it was weak because of the greatness of the thing proposed, was nevertheless gradually raised up and confirmed, especially when she heard of God's omnipotence. And it is more probable on this ground that she also believed at once, though afterwards she was more confirmed in faith; so that there is no doubt that she had been taught beforehand by her husband about the promises made to him, and it is fitting to believe that the memory of them came into her mind at once. That laughter of Sarah, therefore, is not of such a kind that from it one may infer that Sarah was unbelieving. But the whole matter will be made clearer by an example and a parallel. When the birth was announced to the blessed Virgin Mary, no one would call her unbelieving, since Elizabeth, moved by the Holy Spirit, plainly says to her (Luke 1): "Blessed is she who believed, for what was spoken to her by the Lord will be fulfilled." And yet in the same place it is also openly said that at the very first greeting she was troubled and pondered what sort of greeting it was; then she asked also how it could come about that she, who had no relations with a man, should bear. Then she ought to have been more fully taught through the angel about the power of the Most High, and also with the sign added of Elizabeth's pregnancy; and after all these things she confessed, and professed by faith, that she was the ready handmaid of the Lord, that what seemed good to the Lord might be accomplished in her. Behold, a trembling arose in Mary, as in a tender virgin affected by a certain modesty. Nor is that trembling enough to say that she did not have faith, since without doubt she had also been taught beforehand from the oracles of the prophets that something of this kind would come, such as was now announced to her. Likewise when Sarah laughs, being a married woman and now no longer young, she does nothing very contrary to propriety; and such laughter (which one might otherwise suspect to have arisen even from joy) is not to be accused as wholly alien to faith, much less as contrary to faith. It remains, therefore, that Sarah truly believed, and that her faith was so great before God that the Lord was willing to breathe his favour upon Sarah's godly wishes.

units.la: Cæterum, quod ad doctrinam attinet, hoc vel primo loco discendum de officio fidei, quòd illa videlicet directè respiciat in potentiam & bonitatem Dei promittentis, statuatque, quòd Deus implere promissa velit, non propter nostra qualitate, sed propter seipsum.
units.tr: As for doctrine, the first lesson to learn here concerns the office of faith: it looks directly to the power and goodness of God who promises, and it holds that God wills to fulfil his promises not because of our qualities but because of himself.

units.la: Secundò, habemus hic commendationem vitę coniugalis, quòd videlicet sint in ea egregia & multa fidei exercitia propositia. Multæ molestiæ, multæ curæ obueniunt, quas nemo posset superare, nisi fidem in Deum coniiceret, expectans, Deum abundè sarturū, quod nos nostra prudentia efficere haud possumus. Falluntur, qui putant, in matrimonio tantùm peccati submimistrari materiam, imò verò nullo in vitæ genere fidei, charitatis, patientiæ, clariora elucent documenta. Tertiò: discimus hic, sobole & posteritate, itè quę his sunt adiuncta, esse dona Dei, per fidem à Deo petenda & expectanda, & credetib. pro benedictione singulari, à bonitate Dei conferri. Qua de re psal. 127. luculeter. Et certissimum est, qui cum timore Dei ineunt coniugiū, & in eo timetes Deū versantur: filios deinde, qui contingunt, in timore Dei instituunt, sentiunt sibi ad benedictionem & ad bonum omnia cōuerti, etia hisce periculosissimis tēporib. quib. præter ira & maledictione nihil videtur superesse.
units.tr: Secondly, we have here a commendation of married life, namely that it offers many outstanding exercises of faith. Many troubles and many cares come upon a married person, which no one could overcome unless he cast his faith upon God, expecting that God will supply abundantly what we cannot bring about by our own prudence. Those are mistaken who think that marriage supplies only material for sin. On the contrary, faith, love and patience shine more brightly in no other walk of life. Thirdly, we learn here that offspring and posterity, and the things joined with them, are gifts of God, to be sought and expected from God through faith, and that they are conferred on believers by the goodness of God as a special blessing. Psalm 127 speaks clearly about this matter. And it is most certain that those who enter marriage with the fear of God, and live in it fearing God, and then bring up the children they have in the fear of God, find that all things turn to their blessing and good, even in these most dangerous times, when nothing seems to remain but wrath and curse.

units.la: Iuxta fidem mortui sunt hi omnes cùm non accepissent promissiones, sed procul eas vidissent & credidissent, salutassentq; et cōfessi fuissent, se hospites atq; aduenas esse in terra. Nam hæc qui dicunt, declarant, se patriam inquirere. Et si illius quidem memores fuissent, unde fuerant profecti, habebant oportunitatem reuertendi. Nunc autem meliorem expetunt, hoc est, cœlestem. Quapropter non erubescit ipse Deus vocari Deus illorum, Parauerat enim illis ciuitatem.
units.tr: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and believed them, and having greeted them, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things declare that they are seeking a homeland. And if indeed they had been mindful of that land from which they had come out, they would have had opportunity to return. But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God; for he had prepared for them a city.

units.la: Quarta comprobatio seu demonstratio fidei Abrahæ ab eo, quòd cùm, ageret in terra illa promissa, & nihil interea eius proprium possideret, constanter tamen promissioni diuinæ ad morte vsq; adhæserit, quasi nulla de re minus, quàm de temporalibus bonis accipiendis foret solicitus, sed ad spiritualia animum magis intenderet. Quæ profecto loga- nimitas, & adeo patiens expectatio certissimum est incomparabilis fidei argumentum, & omnia reliqua opera fidei facile superans. Nam cùm terra aliena primùm promitteretur, certè egredi ad eâ occupandam, atq; ignorare interim, vbinâ sita, & qualis illa foret, præclarum erat opus fidei, vt supra satis est expositum. Deinde, cùm in eâ peruentù esset, habitare tamen adhuc in tabernaculis, quasi quotidie foret iubète Deo, alio proficiscendû: erat sanè & hoc valde euidès excellentis fidei indicium. Rursus autem cùm à multis annis, & sæpius promissa fuisset innumerabilis posteritas, ac nullû tamè toto eo tempore, quo maximè sperandû fuerat, filiû ex vxore suscīperet: sed cētesimo demùm ætatis suæ anno, vxoris verè Saræ nonagesimo, cùm videlicet desperata essent omnia, filiû gigneret, quis non agnoscit, his fide patris Abrahæ mirabiliter fuisse exercitā? At verò, quòd, postquàm tot annis, nempe centum (erat enim Abrahā septuaginta quinq; annorum, cùm egrederetur de Charan, vt scribitur Genes. 12. & mortuus est anno ætatis cētesimo septuagesimo quinto: Genes. 25.) in promissa terra habitasset, ac nihil tamè quicquam eius in propriam possessionem receperit, ne vestigium quidè pedis, vt Actorum 7. dicitur: & nihilominus diuinis promissionib. constanter ad morte vsq; adhæserit, de illis minimè dubitans. istud profecto quicunq; cōsiderant, certū est, qui corruptæ rationis sequūtur iudiciū, inter pre tabuntur, summā Abrahæ fuisse stultitiam: qui verò aliquā Spiritus diuini hauserūt parti culam, incredibilem hic in credendo constantiam admirabuntur & prædicabunt. Quòd si nobiscum ipsi expenderemus, an in simili euctu possemus in fide subsistere, credo equidem inueniremus, nos nihil huiusmodi posse, sed statim intra paucos annos, imò paucos dies, dissideremus, ac Deum existimaremus nunquàm præstiturum promissa. Expendat obsecro quilibet apud se ista altius. Cæterùm etsi institutum Apostoli sit, celebrare inprimis fidem vnius Abrahæ, tamen hoc loco adiungit ei reliquos quoq; patriarchas, filium, inquam, Isaac, & nepotem Iacob, quomodo & supra demonstratione secunda, adiunxit eos, ob hoc, quòd similiter tabernacula inhabitarint, quos ibidem & cohæredes eiusdem promissionis appellauit: & proximè præcedenti demonstratione adiunxit Saram. Nec dubium, quin Apostolus, cùm ista adijceret, diligenter ad ea respexerit, quæ supra in secunda demonstratione fidei Abrahæ dicere cœperat: quandoquidem hic aliqua ex parte propemodum eadè repetuntur, atq; ex ijs, quę ibi dicta sunt, intelligi clarius ple raq; hic poterunt. Quidni aūt adiungeretur hoc loco filij suo patri: Primò, sicut patri erat promissa hæreditas, ita & filijs, quos audimus cohæredes nuncupatos: & sicut pater nihil terræ in peculium acceperat: ita nec filij acceperunt. Atqui in fide non minus, quàm ipse pater, ad mortem vsq; perstiterunt, de promissionum diuinarum adimpletione nullomodo dubitantes. Quos ergo per omnia similes coniungit causa, merito eorùdem fidemodes simul celebratur. Secundò, cōueniebat vel ideo hos hic coniungi, ne postea opus foret, eandem causam bis in vniusquiusq; laudibus seorsim repetere, & longiore oratione non sine molesto tædio explicare, quod pauciorib. explicari posset. Est autē eorū, quę hic dicuntur, hęc propositio: iuxta fidè mortui sunt hi omnes: Intellige, tātum de Abrahā, Isaac & Iacob ista dici, quos & paulo antè coniunxerat, & in quib. proprie cernitur fides de accipienda terra promissa, & eam tamē non acceperunt. Neq; enim vel Abel, vel Enoch, vel Noe, ista satis aptè accommodantur, nisi verba Apostoli torqueamus. Consistere nos oportet adhuc in propositio exemplo Abrahæ, de quo & mox adhuc sequuntur nonnulla: & cùm obiter paulò antè adiunxerit Abrahamo filios, de ijs, quę hic dicūtur, accipiamus. Cæterùm in hac propositione etiam satis clarè explicatur quidda ad perfectā fidē necessarium, nimirū, quòd in fide perfistendū sit vsq; ad morte, & in ea moriendū, edenduq; etiā eius cōstatię aliquod testimonium. Non satis est credere, dùm omnia pro voto succedūt ad tępus, & dùm persecutio venit, deficere: sed oportet ędificatā esse fidē super solidū fundamentum, vt nullis tēpestatibus posit dimoueri: qua de re in parabola Matth. 7. & Luc. 6. itē, Qui perseuerauerit vsq; ad finem, saluus erit, Matth. 4. Et certè si in vllis sanctis visa est fidei cōstantia, at maxima in trib. hisce patriarchis, inprimis in Abrahamo, qui, vt supra semel admonuimus, cētū annis in fide hac de accipiēda terra promissa perstitit, plurimis interea temporis molestijs impetitus, quæ ipsum ad deficiendum merito impulissent. At magna quidem res est, iuxta fidem viuere: at longè maxima, iuxta fidem mori.
units.tr: The fourth proof or demonstration of Abraham's faith is this: although he lived in that promised land and meanwhile possessed nothing of his own, he nevertheless clung constantly to the divine promise until death, as if he were least of all concerned with receiving temporal goods, and rather directed his mind to spiritual things. Such long-suffering and such patient expectation is certainly an incomparable argument of faith, easily surpassing all the other works of faith. For when a foreign land was first promised, to set out to occupy it, not knowing meanwhile where it lay or what it was like, was an excellent work of faith, as has been explained sufficiently above. Next, when he had arrived in it, still to dwell in tents, as if God were commanding him daily to move on elsewhere, was surely also a very clear sign of excellent faith. Again, although the innumerable posterity had been promised for many years and often, yet during all that time, when it was most to be hoped for, he got no son from his wife; but only in the hundredth year of his life, when his wife Sarah was ninety, when all hope was clearly gone, did he beget a son. Who does not recognise that by these things the faith of the father Abraham was wonderfully exercised? Moreover, that after so many years, namely a hundred (for Abraham was seventy-five years old when he went out of Haran, as is written in Genesis 12, and he died in the hundred and seventy-fifth year of his life, Genesis 25), he had lived in the promised land and yet received nothing of it as his own possession, not even a footstep, as Acts 7 says; and nevertheless he clung constantly to the divine promises until death, never doubting about them. Certainly, whoever considers this and follows the judgment of corrupted reason will interpret it as the highest folly in Abraham; but those who have drawn some portion of the divine Spirit will marvel at and proclaim the incredible constancy of his believing. But if we ourselves were to weigh whether we could persist in faith in such a situation, I believe we would find that we could do nothing of the kind, but would soon, within a few years, indeed within a few days, lose heart and think that God would never fulfil his promises. Let anyone, I beg, weigh these things more deeply within himself. Moreover, although it is the Apostle's method to celebrate above all the faith of Abraham alone, yet in this place he joins to him the other patriarchs also: the son, I mean Isaac, and the grandson Jacob, just as he joined them above in the second demonstration, because they likewise dwelt in tents, and there he called them also heirs of the same promise; and in the immediately preceding demonstration he joined Sarah. Nor is there any doubt that the Apostle, when he added these things, looked carefully at what he had begun to say above in the second demonstration of Abraham's faith, since here many things are in some measure almost repeated, and from what was said there many things here can be understood more clearly. Why, indeed, should the sons be joined in this place to their father? First, just as the inheritance was promised to the father, so also to the sons, whom we hear were called fellow heirs; and just as the father had received no land as a possession, so neither did the sons receive any. Yet they persisted in faith no less than the father himself, until death, in no way doubting the fulfilment of the divine promises. Therefore, since they are joined to him by every likeness of cause, their faith is rightly praised together with his. Secondly, it was fitting for these to be joined here, so that afterwards there would be no need to repeat the same cause twice in the praises of each one separately, and to explain at length, not without tiresome tedium, what could be explained in fewer words. The proposition of what is said here is this: "These all died in faith." Understand that these things are said only of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom he had joined a little before, and in whom faith concerning the receiving of the promised land is clearly seen, and yet they did not receive it. For neither Abel, nor Enoch, nor Noah are suitably fitted to these words unless we twist the Apostle's words. We must remain for the time being with the example of Abraham as the proposition, from which some things also follow immediately; and since he has in passing added Abraham's sons a little before, we should take what is said here of them as well. Moreover, in this proposition something necessary for perfect faith is also explained quite clearly, namely that one must persist in faith until death, and die in it, and also give some testimony of its constancy. It is not enough to believe while everything turns out according to our wish for the time being, and to fail when persecution comes; but it is necessary that faith be built upon a solid foundation so that it cannot be moved by any storms. On this matter see the parable in Matthew 7 and Luke 6; likewise, "He who perseveres to the end will be saved" (Matthew 4). And certainly, if constancy of faith has been seen in any of the saints, it has been seen at its greatest in these three patriarchs, and above all in Abraham, who, as we have once already warned above, persisted for a hundred years in this faith concerning the receiving of the promised land, while meanwhile he was assailed by very many troubles, which would have rightly driven him to give up. Indeed, it is a great thing to live in faith; but by far the greatest thing is to die in faith.

units.la: Cùm non accepissent promissiones, sed procul eas uidissent, & credidissent, salutassentq;. Expositio propositionis: Tantundem enim sibi vult, ac si dicat, Mortui sunt in fide, quia, cùm in omni vita sua non accepissent terram & cætera bona promissa, sed tantùm procul vidissent salutassentque, tamen adhuc crediderint, se indubitatò accepturos. Dicit autem, patres non accepisse promissiones, sed procul tantùm eas vidisse salutasseque. Hoc quidem verum est, & quantum ad temporalia, & quantum ad spiritualia bona. Quantum enim ad temporalia attinet, iam antea diximus, quòd Abraham in tota vita sua nihil terræ in peculium acceperat. Vidit quidem terram ipsam, & salutauit, & in ea etiam factus est dives auri, argenti, & pecorum, tamen Dominus terræ factus non est. Imò Genes. 15. audiuit, semen suum adhuc peregrinaturum & seruituru, post quadringentos autem annos primùm reuersurum, addita etiam ratione, quia necdum completæ erant iniquitates Amorrhæorum. Similiter de posteritate innumerabili perpauca adhuc vidit. Nam licet habuerit filios ex Cethura, tamen unum tantùm habuit Isaac ex Sara, filium promissum, ex quo posteritas illa debebat propagari. Itaq; nihil aliud, quàm procul vidit Abraham promissiones illas & salutauit, Genes. 12. cùm primùm vocaretur. Quod ad spiritualia attinet, præter expectationem generalem à patribus acceptam, audiuerat nominatim, Benedicam tibi, & benedicam benedicentibus tibi, & maledicam maledicentibus tibi: item, in Semine suo benedicendas omnes generationes: Quid tùm ille tandem est assecutus? Expertus est multas molestias, & maiores, quàm solent impij: accepit quidem tandem signum fœderis, circumcisionem videlicet: sed vix aliquid præterea. Habuit quidem Spiritum Sanctum, qui subinde confirmabat illius pectus in tentationibus & periculis: sed tamen ipsum Christum, & cõsummata beneficia, quæ postea per Christũ sunt distributa, non habuit. In mirabili natiuitate Isaac præuidit natiuitatem Christi: in oblatione Isaaci sui vidit oblationem Christi: & sic deinde omnia alia mysteria intellexit. Vidit quidem diem Christi, & gauisus est, vt dicitur Ioan. 8. sed tantùm in typis, & in figuris. Omnia figuræ contingebant illis, 1. Corinth 10: & Lucæ 10. Beati oculi, qui vident, quæ vos videtis: Dico enim vobis, quòd multi prophetæ & reges voluerunt videre, quæ vos videtis, & non viderunt, & audire, quæ auditis, & non audierunt. Itaque vidit quidem Abraham promissiones aliquo modo, sed non plenè & perfectè.
units.tr: "Since they had not received the promises, but had seen them from afar, and believed, and greeted them." Explanation of the proposition: this amounts to the same as saying, "They died in faith, because, although in all their life they had not received the land and the other promised goods, but had only seen them from afar and greeted them, yet they still believed that they would undoubtedly receive them." Now he says that the fathers had not received the promises but had only seen them from afar and greeted them. This is indeed true, both as regards temporal and as regards spiritual goods. As far as temporal goods are concerned, we have already said that Abraham in all his life had received no land as his own possession. He did indeed see the land itself and greet it, and he also became rich in it in gold, silver and cattle; yet he did not become lord of the land. Indeed, in Genesis 15 he heard that his seed would still be a sojourner and would be enslaved, and only after four hundred years would it return, with the added reason that the iniquities of the Amorites were not yet complete. Likewise, of his innumerable posterity he saw only a very few as yet. For although he had sons by Keturah, yet he had only one son by Sarah, Isaac, the promised son, from whom that posterity was to be propagated. Therefore Abraham saw those promises only from afar and greeted them, as Genesis 12 says, when he was first called. As for spiritual goods, besides the general expectation received from the fathers, he had heard by name: "I will bless you, and I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you"; likewise, that in his Seed all the nations would be blessed. What then did he finally obtain? He experienced many troubles, and greater ones than the wicked usually suffer; he did indeed at last receive the sign of the covenant, namely circumcision; but scarcely anything beyond that. He indeed had the Holy Spirit, who from time to time strengthened his heart in temptations and dangers; yet he did not have Christ himself, nor the completed benefits which were afterwards distributed through Christ. In the wondrous birth of Isaac he foresaw the birth of Christ; in the offering of his Isaac he saw the offering of Christ; and so afterwards he understood all the other mysteries. He indeed saw the day of Christ and rejoiced, as John 8 says, but only in types and figures. "All these figures happened to them" (1 Corinthians 10). And Luke 10: "Blessed are the eyes which see what you see; for I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." Thus Abraham indeed saw the promises in some way, but not fully and perfectly.

units.la: Quòd autem de Abraham diximus, idem etiam ostendi potest de Isaac & Iacob. Isaac etiam vxorem habuit sterilem: tandem ipsi sexagenario nascuntur gemelli. Postea orta fame peregrinatus est in terra Palæstinorum, atque ibi quidem licet eadem audiret promissiones, quæ factæ fuerant ad patrem, tamen periclitatus est. Vxor rapta est ab Abimelech rege Palæstinorum: tùm coactus d scedere propter inuidiam, quia fœliciter succedebat Isaac in frugibus, gregibus, & seruitijs. Postea migrauit in Berfabe vbi iterum confirmatus est promissione. Sed nihil adhuc Isaac proprium in terra occupabat, nihil adhuc de innumerabili posteritate illa constabat. Mortuus est in Hebron, & sepultus ibidem. Patriarcha Iacob coactus fugere metu fratris sui Esau, ob præreptum ius primogenituræ, & benedictionem paternam, proficisciturin Haràn, & audit in via promissiones de terra posidenda & innumerabili posteritate: interea tamen seruit socero futuro quatuordecim annis in Haràn. Post plures annos cùm reuertitur, muneribus honorat Esau, & semper in metu viuit. Tandem emit partem agri: (sic enim loquitur scriptura Genes. 33.) prope Salem, vbi fixit tentoria. Tandem verò, licet auctus esset filijs duodecim, tamen quanta mala cum his pertulit? Et postremò migrauit in Aegyptum, vbi & moritur, licet vectus in Chanaan, & sepultus in spelunca, quam emerat Abraham Genes. 25. Ecce, quomodo ad impletæ promissiones de terra posidenda, & innumerabili posteritate. Quod verò attinet ad spiritualia, non plura acceperunt, quàm pater Abraham. Itaque verè nihil aliud, quàm procul conspexerunt ac salutarunt bona promissa.
units.tr: What we have said about Abraham can also be shown of Isaac and Jacob. Isaac too had a barren wife, and at last twins were born to him when he was sixty. Later, when a famine arose, he went abroad into the land of the Philistines, and although there he heard the same promises that had been made to his father, he nevertheless came into danger. His wife was taken by Abimelech, king of the Philistines. Then he was forced to depart because of envy, since Isaac was prospering in crops, flocks and servants. Afterwards he moved to Beersheba, where he was again confirmed by a promise. But Isaac still possessed nothing of his own in the land, and nothing of that countless posterity was yet established. He died in Hebron and was buried there. The patriarch Jacob, forced to flee from the fear of his brother Esau, because of the birthright he had snatched and their father's blessing, set out for Haran. On the way he heard the promises concerning the possession of the land and a countless posterity, yet meanwhile he served his future father-in-law in Haran for fourteen years. Many years later, when he returned, he honoured Esau with gifts and lived always in fear. At last he bought a part of a field (for so Scripture speaks, Gen. 33.) near Salem, where he pitched his tents. Yet, although he was blessed with twelve sons, what evils did he endure from them? And finally he migrated to Egypt, where he died, though he was carried back to Canaan and buried in the cave which Abraham had bought (Gen. 25.). Behold how the promises concerning the possession of the land and a countless posterity were fulfilled. As for spiritual things, they received no more than their father Abraham did. Thus, in truth, they saw from afar and greeted the good things promised, and nothing more.

units.la: Et tamen tanta fuit in omnibus illis fidei constantia, vt etiam in fide mortui sint. Est attentem diligenter considerandum, quare Apostolus ita expressè inculcet, patres tàtum procul vidisse promissiones, & salutasse, neque eas accepisse. Hic mirabilis doctrina proponitur de effectu fidei, ex qua & nos quoque consolationem ingentem debemus accipere, & accommodare hæc omnia rebus nostris. Sic solet Deus pijs promittere, & eos interim in fide exercere. Et præstat quidem, quæ promittit, sed non eodem modo, quo pij existimant: etiamsi certi redduntur semper de ipsius bona voluntate, ne occasionem habeant desperandi. Præbet illis quendam gustũ illorum bonorũ, tantũ confert in hac vita, quantum ad salutem est necessarium, cætera pòst largius collaturus. Sic enim videmus, eum cum patribus istis egisse: atque id, vt pij omnibus seculis sic confirmarentur in fide: sicut de:sicut & Apostolus ad finem præsentis capitis ad Hebræos suos dicit: Atque omnes hi testimonium promeriti per fidem, non acceperant promissionem, quòd Deus de nobis melius quiddam prouiderat, ne sine nobis consummarentur.
units.tr: And yet there was such constancy of faith in all of them that they died in faith. Here we must carefully consider why the Apostle so expressly stresses that the fathers only saw the promises from afar and greeted them, and did not receive them. Here a wonderful teaching is set forth about the effect of faith, from which we too ought to draw great consolation and apply all these things to our own circumstances. God is accustomed to promise such things to the godly and in the meantime to exercise them in faith. He does indeed perform what he promises, but not in the way the godly suppose, though they are always made certain of his good will, so that they have no occasion for despair. He gives them a certain taste of those good things, and in this life he bestows only as much as is necessary for salvation, intending to bestow the rest more abundantly afterwards. For we see that he dealt in this way with those fathers, and this so that the godly in all ages might thus be confirmed in faith, just as the Apostle also says to his Hebrews at the end of the present chapter: "And all these, having obtained a good report through faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us" (Heb. 11:39-40).

units.la: Ecce, nos quoque debemus cum illis consummari, & fide exerceri, vt postea omnes simul accipiamus præmia & promissa bona æterna. Sic enim & nobis in euangelio multa sunt proposita, vt Matthæi 19. Vos, qui secuti estis me, in regeneratione, cùm sederit filius hominis in sede maiestatis suæ, sedebitis & vos super sedes duodecim, &c.
units.tr: Behold, we too ought to be made perfect with them, and be exercised in faith, so that afterwards we may all together receive the rewards and the promised eternal good things. For many things are likewise set before us in the gospel, as in Matthew 19: "You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, etc."

units.la: Et omnis, qui reliquerit domos, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut vxorem, aut filios, aut agros, propter nomen meum, centuplum accipiet, & vitæ æternæ sortietur hæreditatem. Item, primùm quærite regnum dei, & hæc omnia adijcientur vobis. Et tamen videmus, pijs non ita contingere, imò sæpè infœlicissimè cum eis agi.
units.tr: "And everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall inherit eternal life." Likewise: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you." And yet we see that this does not happen to the godly, but often they are treated most unhappily.

units.la: Sed tamen Dominus dat, quantum satis est, quantum attinet ad temporalia: Spiritua-lium autem bonorum dat illis gustum quendam in verbo, in Sacramentis, in Spiritu Sancto, quem diffundit in corda cum multis & varijs donis. Item per Christum sumus liberati à peccato, à morte, & Satana, cùm tamen his malis adhuc videamur, & reipsa comperiamur, quàmdiu in mundo agimus, obnoxij.
units.tr: Nevertheless the Lord gives as much as is enough as far as temporal things are concerned; but of spiritual goods he gives them a certain taste in the word, in the sacraments and in the Holy Spirit, whom he pours into their hearts with many and various gifts. Likewise through Christ we are freed from sin, from death and from Satan, although we still seem to be subject to these evils, and in fact find ourselves so long as we live in the world.

units.la: Verùm de his supra diximus capite secundo, super illis verbis: Vt liberos redderet eos, quicunq; metu mortis tenebantur. Quod autem ad præsens attinet, satis est, quòd Deus dat hîc gustum omnium bonorum, tàm temporalium, quàm spiritualium, quantum satis est: sicut patriarchis etiam fame coactis tamen largiter semper prospexit. Et implet Deus verè omnes promissiones, licet non eodem modo, quo humana ratio iudicaret adimplendas.
units.tr: But we have spoken of these matters above in the second chapter, on those words: "that he might free those who through fear of death were held in bondage." As far as the present matter is concerned, it is enough that God here gives a taste of all good things, both temporal and spiritual, as much as is sufficient, just as he always provided generously for the patriarchs even when they were driven by famine. And God truly fulfils all the promises, though not in the way that human reason would judge they ought to be fulfilled.

units.la: Videbantur non adimplendæ in patriarchis illis, & tamen plenissimè Deus omnia præstitit. Terra promissa tradita est posteris eius, vbi per multa secula regnum & sacerdotium totius orbis florentissimum & optimè constitutum extitit. Posteritas item tùm secundum carnem natorum, tum secundum spiritum adhuc durat, & innumerabilis permanet: & in semine illius, Christo inquam omnes gentes terræ sunt benedictæ, & quotidie adhuc benedicuntur.
units.tr: In those patriarchs the promises seemed not to be fulfilled, and yet God performed all things most fully. The promised land was handed over to their posterity, where for many ages there existed a kingdom and a priesthood most flourishing and most excellently established over the whole world. Likewise the posterity, both of those born according to the flesh and according to the Spirit, still endures and remains countless; and in his seed, namely Christ, I say, all the nations of the earth are blessed, and daily are still blessed.

units.la: Itaque omnia adimpleta sunt, licet non prorisus eo modo, quo adimplenda videbantur. Potuisset sine dubio Deus statim efficere, vt Abraham omnia possideret, longè melius, quàm posteà id effecit, educendo Mosen ex Aegypto, qui tot molestijs, & tanta clade suorum multos reges & populos debuit debellare: sed Deo nondum ita visum fuerat, statuitque, alia ratione omnia perficere.
units.tr: Therefore all things have been fulfilled, although not altogether in the way in which they seemed to be fulfilled. Without doubt God could at once have brought it about that Abraham possessed everything, far better than he later did it, by leading Moses out of Egypt, who had to wage war against many kings and peoples with so many troubles and with such great slaughter of his own people. But God had not yet seen fit to do so, and he decided to accomplish everything by another method.

units.la: Et habuit Deus certas caussas, propter quas ita facere voluit, quas nos non possumus dispicere. Sed tamen aliquos licet animaduertere, ob quas vtiliter & salutariter factum, quòd Deus non statim promissa præstiterit.
units.tr: God had certain causes for which he wished to act in this way, and these we cannot discern. Yet we may observe some reasons why it was useful and salutary that God did not immediately perform what he had promised.

units.la: Prima, quòd homines Dei beneficijs sint indigni, nec tenetur Deus illis tale quicquam præsta-re: abundè benefacit, quando largitur omnia necessaria. Secunda, quòd Deus tali pacto, differendo videlicet conferre bona illa, vult exercere pios in fide, & timore, vt semper ab ipso solo pendeant.
units.tr: First, because men are unworthy of God's benefits, and God is not bound to grant them any such thing. He does well enough when he bestows all things necessary. Second, because by such an arrangement, namely by deferring the bestowal of those good things, he wishes to exercise the godly in faith and fear, so that they may always depend on him alone.

units.la: Tertia: nõ expediret, ita conferri, præsertim temporalia, ne accipien-tes ea abducerentur à rebus spiritualibus, sicut solet plerunque fieri: ita vt maiori bono quidam non accipiant, quàm alias acciperent.
units.tr: Third: it would not be expedient for these things to be conferred in such a way, especially temporal things, lest those who receive them be drawn away from spiritual things, as usually happens; so that some would not receive a greater good than they would otherwise have received.

units.la: Quarta: quando saltem gustum accipiunt futurorum bonorum, satis ita confirmantur de accipiendis reliquis.
units.tr: Fourth: when they at least receive a taste of future good things, they are sufficiently strengthened concerning the receiving of the rest.

units.la: Quinta: abundè omnia sarcit Deus, & plus, quàm promissa, præstat, quando quod diminutum videtur in temporalibus, ipse compensat in spiritualibus, & vel externis & visibiliter, vel certè internis: & quæ non profert in hac vita, confert tamen in altera vita.
units.tr: Fifth: God abundantly makes up for everything, and grants more than what was promised, when what seems diminished in temporal things he compensates in spiritual things, either outward and visible, or certainly inward; and what he does not bring forth in this life, he nevertheless bestows in the other life.

units.la: Quibus certè de caussis nos magnam consolationem debemus accipere. Adhærea-mus constanter diuinis promissionibus, & certò adimplendas statuamus: etiamsi nos de modo aut tempore definito certi haud simus. Neque curemus, quid obijciat mundus. Impij putant, pios non recipere promissiones, dùm vident hos affligi: item, putant, Dei promissiones non adimpleri, existimant, nõ esse liberatos per Christum à peccato, mor-te, diabolo, quia vident labi in peccata, mori, affligi à Satana & malis hominibus. Sed sa-tis interea accipiunt pij, dùm peccatum ipsis non imputatur, dùm liberi sunt à morte se-cunda, dùm à diabolo non prorisus perduntur, satis accipiunt, qui gustum habent bonorum spiritualium & æternorum, ex vsu verbi, Sacramentorum, & donis spiritus, & pace conscientiæ: interea expectantes tempus, quo vnà cum patribus nostris tandem consummabimur. Et hoc de eo, quod Apostolus ait, patres non accepisse promissiones, sed tantùm procul eas vidisse & salutasse.
units.tr: For these causes certainly we ought to draw great consolation. Let us hold steadfastly to the divine promises and be sure that they will certainly be fulfilled, even though we are not certain of the definite manner or time. Let us not care what the world objects. The ungodly think that the godly do not receive the promises, since they see them afflicted; likewise they think that God's promises are not fulfilled, and they suppose that they have not been freed through Christ from sin, death and the devil, because they see them fall into sins, die, and be afflicted by Satan and wicked men. But meanwhile the godly receive enough, since sin is not imputed to them, since they are free from the second death, since they are not utterly lost to the devil; they receive enough who have a taste of spiritual and eternal good things, from the use of the word, the sacraments, the gifts of the Spirit and peace of conscience, while meanwhile they await the time when, together with our fathers, we shall at last be made perfect. And this is said concerning what the Apostle says, that the fathers did not receive the promises, but only saw them from afar and greeted them.

units.la: Et confessi fuissent, se hospites atque adœnas esse in terra. Nam hæc qui dicunt, declarant, se patriam inquirere.
units.tr: And they confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth. For those who say such things declare that they seek a country.

units.la: Probat, quòd patres ad mortem vsque in fide perstiterint, idque ratione sumpta ex ipsorum confessione & verbis fidem non obscurè significantibus. Quicunq; inquit, in eo loco, quo habitant, se vocant peregrinos & aduenas, testantur, se illorum non habere pro patria, sed meliorem inquirere. Atqui patres habitantes in terra promissa se nihilo minus vocarunt peregrinos & aduenas. Igitur hac confessione testabantur, se illam pro patria non habere, sed meliorem desiderare. Quòd patres illi se vocarint peregrinos & aduenas etiam in terra Chanaan, nō est difficile commonstrare. De Abraham Genef. 23.ficipse ad filios Heth, Aduena sum & peregrinus apud vos, date mihi ius sepulchri vobiscum. Idem autem a Deo etiam sic vocatus & peregrinari iussus in terra Chanaan, Genef.17. Daboque tibi & semini tuo terram peregrinationis tuæ, & omnem terram Chanaan in possessionem æternam, & ero Deus eorum. Et Genef. 1.Abimelech & Phicol princeps exercitus eius ad Abraham: Deus tecum est in vniuersis quæ agis: Iura ergo per Deum, ne noceas mihi & posteris meis, stirpiquè meæ: sed iuxta misericordiam, quam feci tibi, facies mihi & terræ, in qua versatus es aduena. Et pasim ipse vt peregrinus & aduena describitur: & ipsa terra postea etiam terra peregrinationis, præsertim Abrahæ, appellatur: Exod.6.De Isaac etiam est manifestum: Sic ad eum Dominus, cùm iret propter famen exortam ad Abimelech regem Palæstinorum in Gerara: Ne descendas in Aegyptum, sed quiescè in terra, quam dixero tibi, & peregrinare in ea, eoque tecum & benedicam tibi: tibi enim & semini tuo dabo vniuersas regiones has. Non dubium igitur, quin ipse se quoque peregrinum agnouerit, & vt peregrinum gesserit. De Iacob item patet. Ipse Genef.47.rogatus à Pharaone, quot essent dies annorum vitæ, respondit, Dies peregrinationis vitæ meæ centum triginta annorum sunt, parui & mali, & non peruenerunt ad dies patrum meorum, quibus peregrinati sunt. Et ad eundem Iacob pater eius Isaac Genef. 48. cum prohiberet, ne vxorem duceret de filiabus terræ Chanaan, sed ex Mesopotamia quæreret ex familia Bethuel. Det tibi, inquit, Dominus benedictiones Abrahæ, & semini tuo post te, vt possideas terram peregrinationis tuæ, quam pollicitus est auo tuo. Omnes igitur peregrinos se confessi sunt, etiam in terra illa Chanaan à Deo ipsis promissa. Iam verò, quod, qui se vocant peregrinos, aliam inquirant patriam, id ex communi iudicio per se notum est. Hoc enim in natura positum est, vt quilibet aspiret ad locum, in quo possit quiete agere, & vbi talem locum nactus fuerit, tùm se iudicat nactum esse patriam, tùm non amplius peregrinari intendit. Hinc illud etiam philosophorum gentilium ore iactatum, patria est omnis locus, vbi quis bene agit. Et Socrates ille Apollinis oraculo iudicatus sapientissimus, cùm rogaretur à quopiam, cuias esset, nihil aliud, quàm κοσμόπολίτης se esse respondit, id est, mundanum: significans, vbicunque in mundo bene ageret, ibi se patriam agnoscere. At verò isti patres, de quibus nobis sermo est, nusquàm se ciues esse putarunt, nusquàm hic in terris agnouerunt patriam: sed vniuersaliter siue agerent in Charan, vbi primùm vixerunt: siue in Chanaan, quæ erat illis in hæreditatem promissa: siue alibi, quo propter necessitatem aliquam peruenerunt, semper fasi sunt se aduenas & peregrinos: atq; ita declararunt, se ibi nusquàm sedem perpetuam velle figere, sed aliam adhuc veram & multo excellentiorem patriam inquirere.
units.tr: He proves that the fathers persevered in faith to the end of their lives, and he does so by an argument drawn from their own confession and from words that clearly signal faith. He says: whoever calls themselves strangers and sojourners in the place where they dwell testifies that they do not regard that place as their country, but seek a better one. Yet the fathers, while dwelling in the promised land, nonetheless called themselves strangers and sojourners. Therefore by this confession they testified that they did not regard that land as their country, but desired a better one. That the fathers called themselves strangers and sojourners even in the land of Canaan is not hard to show. Of Abraham, Gen. 23: he spoke to the sons of Heth, "I am a sojourner and a stranger among you; give me a right of burial among you." Likewise God, calling him and bidding him sojourn in the land of Canaan, Gen. 17: "I will give to you and to your seed the land of your sojourning, and all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God." And Gen. 26: Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do. Swear therefore by God that you will not harm me or my posterity and my offspring; but according to the kindness I have shown you, you shall do to me and to the land in which you have sojourned as a stranger." And throughout Scripture he himself is described as a stranger and sojourner, and the land itself was later called the land of sojourning, especially in Abraham's case. Exod. 6. It is also clear of Isaac: when he was going to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar because of a famine that had arisen, the Lord spoke to him thus: "Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land which I shall tell you, and sojourn in it, and I will bless you; for to you and to your seed I will give all these regions." There is therefore no doubt that he too recognised himself as a stranger and conducted himself as one. The same is plain of Jacob. In Gen. 47, when Pharaoh asked him how many days he had lived, he answered, "The days of my sojourning are one hundred and thirty years, few and evil, and they have not reached the days of the sojourning of my fathers." And when his father Isaac, in Gen. 28, forbade the same Jacob to take a wife from the daughters of the land of Canaan, but to seek one from Mesopotamia, from the family of Bethuel, he said: "May the Lord give you the blessings of Abraham, and to your seed after you, that you may possess the land of your sojourning, which he promised to your grandfather." All of them, therefore, confessed themselves strangers, even in that land of Canaan promised to them by God. Now, that those who call themselves strangers seek another country is known in itself from common judgment. For it is implanted in nature that everyone aspires to a place where they can live in quiet; and when they have found such a place, they judge that they have found their country and no longer intend to sojourn. Hence that saying of the Gentile philosophers, repeated on everyone's lips: every place where a man lives well is his country. And Socrates, whom the oracle of Apollo judged the wisest, when someone asked him whence he was, answered only that he was a cosmopolitan, that is, a citizen of the world, meaning that wherever in the world he lived well, there he recognised his country. But those fathers of whom we are speaking never thought themselves citizens anywhere, never recognised a country here on earth; rather, whether they were in Haran, where they first lived, or in Canaan, which was promised to them as an inheritance, or elsewhere, to which some necessity brought them, they always professed themselves strangers and sojourners. And so they declared that they did not wish to fix a lasting seat there, but were seeking another, still true and far more excellent, country.

units.la: Cæterum quemadmodum supra diximus, cùm de inhabitantis tentorijs ageretur: ita & hic admonemur ad rerum terrenarum contemptum, ad agnoscendum, nos omnes, quàmdiu hic viuimus, nihil aliud, quàm peregrinos esse & errones, quomodo pasim videmus patres sanctos fecisse. Apud prophetas multæ sunt huiusmodi meditationes propositæ, Psalm.38. Ad lachrymas meas ne sileas, quoniam aduena ego sum & peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei. Remitte mihi, vt refrigerer, priusquàm abeam, & amplius non ero. 1. Petri 2. Dilecti obsecro vos tanquàm aduenas & peregrinos, abstinete à carnalibus concupiscentijs, quæ militant aduersus animam, & conuersationem vestram honestam intergentes. 2.Corinth.5.de tabernaculo corporis nostri destruendo, i-temque peregrinatione nostra ad Deum plura statim initio capitis, vbi inter alia: Bono animo sumus semper, & scimus, quòd, cùm domi sumus in corpore, peregrinamur à Deo: per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem. Confidimus autem, & probamus magis peregrè abesse à corpore, & præsentes adesse apud Deum. Quapropter contendimus siue domi præsentes, siue foris peregrè agentes, vt illi placeamus. Hic certè clarissime admonemur, non solum quòd deceat nos vt peregrinos agere, verùm etiam quomodo id faciundum, & quomodo in peregrinatione hac nos geramus.
units.tr: Moreover, as we said above when we were treating of those who dwell in tents, so here too we are admonished to despise earthly things, and to acknowledge that all of us, as long as we live here, are nothing but strangers and wanderers, as we see the holy fathers did everywhere. Among the prophets there are many meditations of this kind, Ps. 38: "Do not be silent at my tears, for I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were. Turn away from me, that I may recover strength before I go hence and am no more." 1 Pet. 2: "Beloved, I beg you as sojourners and strangers, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul, and keep your conduct honourable among the Gentiles." 2 Cor. 5, concerning the destroying of the tabernacle of our body, and again concerning our pilgrimage towards God, with much said at the very beginning of the chapter, where among other things: "We are always of good courage, and we know that, while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, and prefer rather to be away from the body and present with the Lord. Therefore we make it our aim, whether at home or away, to be pleasing to him." Here we are most clearly admonished, not only that it becomes us to live as strangers, but also how this is to be done and how we are to conduct ourselves in this pilgrimage.

units.la: Etsi illius quidem memores fuissent, vnde fuerant profecti, habebant opportunitatem reuertendi: nunc autem meliorem expetunt.
units.tr: Indeed, if they had been mindful of that place from which they had set out, they had the opportunity of returning; but now they seek a better one.

units.la: Alia ratio confirmans, ex fide factum, quòd patres se peregrinos appellarint: Sed hæc quasi forma occupationis adijcitur. Dixissent enim aliqui: Quòd patres ita vocarint se peregrinos in terra Chanaan, id factum, quia aspirabant iterum ad patriam suam Charam, vnde primùm exierant. Atque ita confessio illa patrum non iam fidentium & credentium, sed diffidentium, at de terra promissa accipienda desperantium essent. Verum prudenter respondet Apostolus, & ad fidem patrum astrendam confessionem eorundem artificiosissimè conuertit, atque ita ratiocinatur.
units.tr: Another argument confirming that the fathers called themselves strangers from faith: but this is added as a kind of anticipation of an objection. For some might say: the fathers called themselves strangers in the land of Canaan because they aspired to return again to their own country, Haran, from which they had first come out. And so that confession of the fathers would be taken not as the confession of men still trusting and believing, but of men who had lost heart and despaired of the promised land. But the Apostle answers prudently, and to establish the faith of the fathers he most skilfully turns their confession around, and reasons thus.

units.la: Si patres ideo vocassent se peregrinos & aduenas, quòd desiderabant reuerti in ptriam illam, unde prius exierant, potuissent sanè & reuerti. Atqui non sunt ad hanc reuersi. Igitur ad aliam patriam longè excellentiorem, quàm fuerat vel terra Chanaan ipsis promissa, quamquè iam inhabitabant, vel Charam, è qua venerant, spirarunt. Hic nulla est obscuritas, & quilibet clarè videt, Apostolum id unum velle inferre, quòd patres ad mortem usque in fide perstiterint, quòdque fides eorum vel hoc nomine fuerit excellentissima, quia intenta fuerit non usque adeò in promissiones de bonis temporalibus, sed multò maximè in promissa bona spiritualia, in quae fides secundum suam naturam propriè dirigitur ac respicit. Qua de re nonnihil à nobis dictum est, vbi patres humilibus tabernaculis contentos expectasse ciuitatem habentem fundamenta, dicebatur: ad quae verba Apostolum hic respicere certum est. Atque hanc esse mentem Apostoli, confirmatur eo, quòd ipse per interpretationem hic protinus subijcit, dicens:
units.tr: If the fathers had called themselves strangers and sojourners because they longed to return to that country from which they had earlier come out, they could certainly have returned. But they did not return. Therefore they aspired to another country, far more excellent, either than the land of Canaan promised to them, in which they were already living, or than Haran, from which they had come. Here there is no obscurity, and anyone can plainly see that the Apostle wishes only to infer that the fathers persevered in faith to the end of their lives, and that their faith was for this reason most excellent: because it was directed not so much to promises of temporal goods, but far more to the promised spiritual goods, towards which faith by its nature is properly directed and looks. We have said something about this matter already, where it was said that the fathers, content with humble tents, looked for the city which has foundations; it is certain that the Apostle here refers to those words. That this is the Apostle's meaning is confirmed by the fact that he himself immediately adds an explanation, saying:

units.la: Nunc autem meliorem expetunt, id est, caelestem) Caelestem patriam eandem hic intelligit, quam supra dixit ciuitatem habentem fundamenta, & hic etiam mox ciuitatem iterum nominat. Nos autem interpretati sumus ecclesiam, quia reuera ecclesia est sancta ciuitas, vera Hierusalem, ciuitas pacis, extra cuius muros neque pax est, neque salus: quam q; inhabitant soli sancti, fidem in Christum constanter retinentes. Quomodo & Ephes. 2. de ciuitate ista, & ciuibus istiusmodi dicitur, eos, qui non credunt, no pertinere ad rempublicam Israelis, & extraneos à testamentis promissionis, spem non habentes, Deoque carentes in mundo: at per Christum eos, qui longinqui erant, fieri propinquos, per sanguinem videlicet Christi: & paulo post: Iam igitur non estis hospites & incolae, sed conciues sanctorum ac domestici Dei, superstructi super fundamentum Apostolorum ac prophetarum, summo angulari lapide ipso Christo Iesu, in quo quaecunque structura coagmentatur, ea crescit in templum Sanctum in Domino, in quo & vos coaedificamini in habitaculum per spiritum. In hac igitur ciuitate spirituali patres se ciues esse gloriabantur, & gaudebant, non soliciti interim, quòd tentoria tantùm inhabitarent, & in terra Chanaan peregrinos se esse confiterentur, & pro peregrinis haberentur coram Deo & coram hominibus. Et haec ciuitas, ecclesia inquam, etiam in terris existens, & constans piorum verè credentium, vbi vbi sunt, congregatione, rectè caelestis dicitur.
units.tr: But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. By the heavenly country he here means the same thing he called above the city which has foundations, and here too he soon names the city again. We have interpreted this as the Church, because the Church is truly the holy city, the true Jerusalem, the city of peace, outside whose walls there is neither peace nor salvation; and it is inhabited by the saints alone, who steadfastly hold fast to faith in Christ. In the same way, in Eph. 2, it is said of this city and of such citizens that those who do not believe do not belong to the commonwealth of Israel, and are strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and being without God in the world; but through Christ those who were far off are made near, namely through the blood of Christ; and a little later: "So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling place of the Spirit." In this spiritual city the fathers gloried and rejoiced that they were citizens, not troubled meanwhile that they dwelt only in tents and confessed themselves strangers in the land of Canaan, and were regarded as strangers before God and before men. And this city, namely the Church, existing also on earth and consisting of the congregation of the pious who truly believe, wherever they are, is rightly called heavenly.

units.la: Primò, quia, etsi membra haereant in terris, tamen praecipua eius pars & caput est in caelis, vbi Christus sedet ad dexteram patris. Certè à Domino & principe in caelis agente merito caelestis appellabitur. Neque enim opus est distinguere ecclesiam in militantem & triumphantem, sicut quidam faciunt. Vna tantùm est, eaque tota vni Deo addicta, tàm in caelo, quàm in terra, eundem agnoscens dominum & principem.
units.tr: First, although the members cleave to the earth, its principal part and head is in heaven, where Christ sits at the right hand of the Father. Certainly it will rightly be called heavenly, since its Lord and prince acts in heaven. There is no need to distinguish the Church into militant and triumphant, as some do. It is one, and wholly devoted to the one God, both in heaven and on earth, acknowledging the same Lord and prince.

units.la: Secundò: quia eius administratio, politia, & leges, à caelis tota est: Deus eam gubernat, mittit in eam suum Spiritum administratorem, qui eam ornat donis varijs, & in ea omnia in omnibus operatur: sicut Deus eam fundauit & condidit, ita ipse eam adhuc seruat & tuetur, & indies illustriorem reddit. Non humanis viribus aut carnali sapientia, sed tantùm caelesti consilio & doctrina geruntur in ea omnia. Ephes. 1. Qui benedixit nos omni benedictione spirituali in caelestibus per Christum. Non amplius res terrenae offeruntur aut proponuntur, sed spiritualia & caelestia sunt omnia. Item in hac epistola capite octauo dicitur, legis donaria & victimas fuisse vmbras caelestium, id est, spiritualium, quae in ecclesia debebant fieri. Et capite nono, Necessum fuit, exemplaria eorum, quae sunt in caelis, purificari rebus corporalibus, sanguine victimarum, &c.
units.tr: Secondly, its administration, polity and laws come wholly from heaven. God governs it, and sends into it his Spirit as administrator, who adorns it with various gifts and works all in all within it. Just as God founded and established it, so he himself still preserves and protects it, and makes it more illustrious day by day. Everything in it is conducted not by human strength or carnal wisdom, but only by heavenly counsel and teaching. Ephes. 1.: "Who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places through Christ." Earthly things are no longer offered or set forth; all things are spiritual and heavenly. Likewise in this epistle, chapter 8, it is said that the gifts of the law and the sacrifices were shadows of heavenly things, that is, of spiritual things, which were to be done in the Church. And chapter 9: "It was necessary that the copies of those things which are in the heavens be purified with corporeal things, with the blood of victims, etc."

units.la: Tertiò: quòd omnes, qui ecclesiae membra sunt, licet in terris versentur corpore, tamen scopus omnium actionum & finis praecipuus in caelis respicit. Coloss. 3. relictis terrenis ceremonijs iubentur pij respicere ad caelestia & superna. Si resurrexistis vnà cum Christo, superna quaerite, vbi Christus est ad dexteram Dei sedens, superna curate non terrestria: siquidem emortui estis, & vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Et Philip. 3. Nostra conuersatio (πολίτευμα) in caelis est, vnde & seruatorem expectamus. Hinc & credentes vocantur spirituales, quia caelestia tantùm contemplantur, caelestia credunt, ad caelestia semper aspirant. Neque mirum, quòd nos ecclesiam vocamus caelestem ciuitatem: quando Christus saepe eam vocat in Euangelio regnum caelorum: quando parsim proponit parabolas, quibus ecclesiam depingit, etiam eam, quae in terris constituta est, & malos perinde habet admixtos ac bonos: vt Matth. 13. simile ait regnum caelorum verriculo iacto in mare, & ex omni genere piscium congreganti: item cofertur agro habenti zizania admixta tritico: Ibidem plures habentur parabolae in eandem sententiam.
units.tr: Thirdly, all who are members of the Church, although they dwell on earth in body, nevertheless look chiefly to heaven as the aim of all their actions and their chief end. Col. 3.: having left earthly ceremonies, the pious are bidden to look to heavenly and higher things. "If you have risen together with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on earth; for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." And Phil. 3.: "Our citizenship (πολίτευμα) is in heaven, whence we also await the Saviour." Hence believers too are called spiritual, because they contemplate only heavenly things, believe heavenly things, and always aspire to heavenly things. Nor is it strange that we call the Church the heavenly city, since Christ often calls it in the Gospel the kingdom of heaven, and since he sets forth various parables by which he depicts the Church, even that which is established on earth, and in which he likewise has bad mixed with good. In Matth. 13. he says the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind; likewise it is compared to a field in which tares are mixed with the wheat. In the same chapter there are several parables to the same effect.

units.la: Ecclesia ergo est cœlestis patria Abrahæ, Isaac, & Iacob, & omnium denique credentium, qui ab initio mundi fuerunt, sunt, vel erunt, sicut Christus quoque Matth.10. ait: Dico vobis, multi ab oriente & occidente venturi sunt, & accumbent cum Abrahâ, Isaac, & Iacob, in regno cœlorum: filij verò regni eijcientur in tenebras extremas, illic erit ploratus & stridor dentium. Vbi non de eijciendis è cœlo fit sermo, sed de eijciendis ab ecclesia, & quòd inferentur ecclesiæ multi gentiles, futuri concives Abrahæ, Isaac, & Iacob. Et rectè dicitur ecclesia sanctorum patria, quia in ea per Spiritum sanctificantem renascimur, regeneramur, alimur, educamur: deinde dum ad plenam vsque ætatem succrescamus, instituimur: unde Ephes. 4. dicitur Deus dedisse alios apostolos, alios prophetas, alios evangelistas, alios pastores & doctores, ad instaurationem sanctorum in opus administrationis, in ædificationem corporis Christi, donec perveniamus omnes in vnitatem fidei & agnitionis filij Dei, in virum perfectum, in mensuram ætatis plenè adultæ Christi, &c. In summa, quæcunque de patria & ciuitate benè constituta dici possent, eadem omnia, & multò plura, multoque excellentiori modo de ecclesijs dici queunt: &c, non tanta accipit quis in sua patria benè constituta, quin multò præclariora accipiantur à credentibus in ecclesia. Aspiremus igitur & nos pari studio ad ecclesiæ societatem, laboremusque, vt pro membris ecclesiæ agnosci possimus.
units.tr: The Church, therefore, is the heavenly homeland of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and finally of all believers who have been, are, or will be from the beginning of the world. So Christ also says in Matth. 10.: "I tell you, many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the sons of the kingdom will be cast into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Here the talk is not of being cast out of heaven, but of being cast out of the Church, and of many Gentiles being brought into the Church, who will be future fellow citizens of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And the Church is rightly called the homeland of the saints, because in it, through the sanctifying Spirit, we are born again, regenerated, nourished and brought up; then, as we grow to full age, we are instructed. Hence Eph. 4. says that God gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, etc. In sum, whatever could be said of a homeland and a well-ordered city, all these things, and much more, can be said of the churches, and in a far more excellent manner. No one receives so much in his well-ordered homeland that believers do not receive far more splendid things in the Church. Let us therefore aspire with equal zeal to fellowship in the Church, and labour that we may be acknowledged as members of it.

units.la: Quapropter non erubescit ipse Deus, vocari Deus illorum: parauerat enim illis ciuitatem. Alia ratio, probans, patres in fide mortuos, sumpta ab ipsius Dei testimonio, quo declarauit singularem suam ergo illos beneuolentiam & affectum: quem certè nunquam tantum exhibuisset, nisi illi fide admodum excellenti fuissent præditi, constantissimèque in ea perstitissent. Estque hæc argumenti sententia: Deus non dedignatus est, se appellare specialiter illorum Deum, & agnoscere illos pro suis fidelibus subditis & ciuibus.
units.tr: Therefore God himself is not ashamed to be called their God, for he had prepared for them a city. This is another argument, proving that the fathers died in faith, and it is drawn from God's own testimony, by which he declared his singular goodwill and affection towards them. He would certainly never have shown so much, had they not been endowed with a very excellent faith and most constantly persevered in it. The sense of the argument is this: God did not disdain to call himself specially their God, and to acknowledge them as his faithful subjects and citizens.

units.la: Sed hoc non fieret, nisi illi in fide perstitissent: quando constat, sine fide haud posse quenquam placere Deo. Igitur patres in fide ad mortem vsque perstiterunt. Ita Apostolus & ex ipsorum patrum confessione, & ex ipsius Dei testimonio conuincit, eos in fide mortuos. Loci autem, vbi Deus se vocat illorum Deum, plures sunt: vt Genes. 17. vbi dicit, Ero Deus tuus, & seminis tui post te. Genes. 18. ad Iacob: Ego sum Dominus Deus Abraham patris tui, & Deus Isaac. Et seruus Abrahæ missus ad Laban & Bethuel Deum vocat Deum Abraham Domini sui. Genes. 25. Et Iacob Genes. 31. Deum vocat Deum patris sui Isaac, & Abraham. Sed multò clarius Exod. 3. vbi Deus ad Mosen: Locus, in quo stas, terra sancta est: Ego sum Deus patris tui, Deus Abraham, & Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacob. Quo libro passim vocatur Deus Hebræorum. Et deinceps apud prophetas, & in reliquis libris, Deus Abraham, Deus Patrum. Est autem obseruatione inprimis dignum, quòd Apostolus ait, Deum non erubescere propter illos: notat enim mirabilem diuinæ maiestatis submissionem & beneuolentiam ea locutionis forma.
units.tr: But this would not have happened unless they had persevered in faith, since it is certain that without faith no one can please God. Therefore the fathers persevered in faith unto death. Thus the Apostle proves, both from the confession of the fathers themselves and from God's own testimony, that they died in faith. Now there are many passages where God calls himself their God: as Gen. 17., where he says, "I will be your God, and the God of your seed after you."
