Gen. 18., to Jacob: "I am the Lord God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac." Abraham's servant, sent to Laban and Bethuel, calls God the God of Abraham his master. Gen. 25. ... and Jacob, Gen. 31., calls God the God of his father Isaac and of Abraham. But much more clearly Exod. 3., where God says to Moses: "The place on which you stand is holy ground: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." In that book he is everywhere called the God of the Hebrews, and afterwards among the prophets and in the remaining books he is called the God of Abraham, the God of the Fathers. It is especially worth noting that the Apostle says God is not ashamed on their account, for that form of expression denotes the wonderful condescension and goodwill of the divine majesty.

units.la: Quòd enim is, qui alias Dominus cœli & terræ & est, & appellatur, nec non passim amplissimis appellatur epithetis, vt omnipotens, Dominus exercituum, Deus cœli, &c. se ita demittat, vt sibi appellationem imponat à duobus vel tribus suis seruis, istud prosecto contra dignitatem suam videtur facere, & nimium hic se demittere. Ministri quicunque solent dignitatem & gloriam captare, iactando suum dominum, & se præpositos alicuius domini afferendo ministros: at quòd è diuerso dominus appellationem titulumque sumat à suis ministris, hic plane currus bouem trahit, & præpostera fiunt omnia. Propter hanc igitur caussam dixit Apostolus, Deum non erubescere propter illos: mirabilem inquam submissionem diuinæ maiestatis, & incomparabilem beneuolentiam designans. Vocatur igitur Deus, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, Deus Iacob, non quòd ea ratione aliquid decedat ipsius potentiæ, vel, quòd non amplius sit Deus cœli & terræ omniumque hominum: sed quòd peculiari quodammodo Deus illos præ cæteris complectatur, velitque illis singulariter misericordiam suam impendere: sicut rex aliquis quosdam singulariter vult promouere & tueri. Sic enim Deus singulariter quosdam eligit, quos constituit iustificare & glorificare, præ cæteris, & quasi delectatus insignia eorum fide acceptos habet præ omnibus. Alios quidem interea non deserit, multò minus contemnit: sed tamen quosdam præ aliis acceptat. Sic postea Deus gaudebat appellari Deus Hebræorum, quia illos in peculiarem populum elegerat: Exod. 3.5. 6.7. Sic item de Hieremia prædicat Dominus, quòd, antequam formaretur in vtero, noßet eum, & elegisset eum ad mittendum quocunque visum esset. Item Paulus Actor. 9. dicitur vas electum singulariter ad portandum nomen Dei apud gentes. Atque hinc fit, quòd sancti Patres sæpè etiam Deum vocant Deum suum, vt videre est passim in psalmis & prophetis, quòd statuunt, se singulariter à Deo regi ac defendi, maximaque fide apprehendunt eius misericordiam.
units.tr: For he who is otherwise called, and is, Lord of heaven and earth, and who is everywhere also named by the most ample epithets, such as Almighty, Lord of hosts, God of heaven, and so on, seems to act against his own dignity and to humble himself too far when he should so lower himself as to take a title from two or three of his servants. Ministers in general are accustomed to seek dignity and glory by boasting of their lord and asserting that they are the appointed servants of some master; but that, on the contrary, a lord should take his appellation and title from his ministers, here truly the cart draws the ox, and everything is turned backwards. For this reason the Apostle said that God is not ashamed on their account, signifying, I say, the wonderful condescension of the divine majesty and his incomparable goodwill. God is therefore called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, not because by this means anything is taken from his power, or because he is no longer God of heaven and earth and of all men; but because in a certain peculiar way God embraces those men above others and wishes to bestow his mercy on them singularly, just as some king wishes singularly to advance and protect certain persons. For thus God singles out some, whom he has determined to justify and glorify, above others; and as if delighted, he holds their badges, received by faith, above all. Meanwhile he does not desert the others, much less despise them, yet he accepts some before others. So afterwards God was pleased to be called the God of the Hebrews, because he had chosen them as a peculiar people (Exod. 3, 5, 6, 7). So too the Lord declares of Jeremiah that, before he was formed in the womb, he knew him and chose him to be sent wherever it seemed fit. Likewise Paul is called, in Acts 9., a chosen vessel, singled out to bear the name of God among the Gentiles. Hence it comes that the holy fathers often also call God their God, as may be seen everywhere in the Psalms and the prophets, because they hold that they are singularly ruled and defended by God, and with the greatest faith they grasp his mercy.

units.la: Sed hic forte dicis, Deus non est acceptor personarum, atiam, quando se vocat Deum Abraham, Deum Isaac, Deum Iacob, &c. videtur accipere personas. Respondetur, quòd Deus non accipit more hominum: quia non ita accipit aliquos, ut alios negligat.
units.tr: But perhaps you will say here: God is not a respecter of persons, yet when he calls himself the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, he seems to show partiality. The answer is that God does not accept persons in the manner of men, because he does not so favour some that he neglects others.

units.la: Deinde, ista accepto nō contingit propter qualitates aliquas ipsorū hominum, quasi hic vel ille dignior sit ob aliquam rem altero: sed cùm omnes apud ipsum ex æquo sint rei, quosdam tamen accipit ex mera sua & gratuita bonitate, &, ut dicitur Ephes. i. iuxta bene placitum (σὺ δοκίμως) suum, ad ostendendum diuitias gloriæ suæ: id quod eo manifestius est quòd aperte dicatur, Iacob, item Ieremiam, electos, antequàm nascerentur, antequàm boni vel mali quicquam egissent: qua de re Romanorum 9. multò plura.
units.tr: Further, this acceptance does not depend on any qualities in the men themselves, as if one were more worthy than another for some reason. Since all alike are guilty before him, he chooses some out of his mere and free goodness, and, as Ephesians 1 says, according to his good pleasure [εὐδοκίαν] to show the riches of his glory. This is the more evident because it is plainly said that Jacob, and likewise Jeremiah, were chosen before they were born, before they had done anything good or evil. On this matter see Romans 9, which says much more.

units.la: Quòd igitur Deus ita dignatus sit, se peculiariter sanctorum, præterea patriarcharum Deum appellare, euidens documentum est incomprehensibilis bonitatis & gratuitæ misericordiæ, & quòd fidem in sanctis maximè honoret.
units.tr: That God therefore deigned to call himself peculiarly the God of the saints, and moreover of the patriarchs, is clear evidence of his incomprehensible goodness and gratuitous mercy, and that he greatly honours faith in the saints.

units.la: Id quod etiam verbis sequentibus aliquo modo significatur: parauerat enim illis ciuitatem: vbi iterum audis spontaneam beneuolentiam Dei erga illos.
units.tr: This is also signified in some measure by the following words: for he had prepared a city for them. Here again you hear God's spontaneous goodwill toward them.

units.la: Deus enim parat illis ciuitatem, non homines eam sibi parant, aut ius ciuitatis adipiscuntur: sed Deus conditor ciuitatis cœlestis, quos vult, in suam ciuitatem recipit. Huc pertinent illa, Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit illum: Ioan. 6. & Rom. 9. Non volentis est neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei.
units.tr: For God prepares a city for them; men do not prepare it for themselves or obtain the right of citizenship. God, the founder of the heavenly city, receives into his city whom he wills. To this belong the words: No one comes to me unless the Father draws him (John 6), and Romans 9: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.

units.la: Proinde hic admonemur, Deū precari, ut nobis quoque velit esse Deus, & nos in illam suam cœlestem ciuitatem recipere. Non satis est, Deum esse Deum sed expetendum, uti idem sit nobis quoque Deus. Et cùm ille promiserit, se velle Deum esse non tantùm Abrahamo, sed etiam semini eius, det Dominus Deus nobis lumen verae fidei, per quod inter filios promissionis Abrahae conspiciamur, & misericordiae promissae efficiamur participes. Cùm nos simus gentes, & illi promissum sit, quòd foret pater multarum gentium, & in semine ipsius benedicendas omnes gentes, nobis assiduè petendum est, ut benedictionis effectus propter illud semen sentiamus. Dedecus reputant homines, si quis eijciatur, e nobili familia, aut e ciuitate, præsertim propter admissum crimen, quod exilio mulctatur: at non possumus reputare, quantum dedecus sit, propter incredulitatē reijci e familia Abrahę, & e ciuitate, quam parauit illi Dominus.
units.tr: Therefore we are admonished here to pray that God would also be willing to be our God and receive us into that heavenly city of his. It is not enough that God is God; he must be desired, so that he may be our God too. Since he has promised that he wishes to be God not only to Abraham but also to his seed, may the Lord God give us the light of true faith, by which we may be seen among the children of the promise of Abraham and be made partakers of the promised mercy. Since we are Gentiles, and it was promised to Abraham that he would be the father of many nations, and that in his seed all nations would be blessed, we must constantly seek that we may feel the effect of that blessing through that seed. Men count it a disgrace if someone is cast out of a noble family or a city, especially for a crime committed, so that he is punished with exile. But we cannot reckon how great a disgrace it is to be rejected, on account of unbelief, from the family of Abraham and from the city which the Lord has prepared for him.

units.la: Admonemur item, patienter expectare promissa Dei, qui differt interdū, sed nō aufert, & vtiliter etiam nobis non dat, quo de vide supra.
units.tr: We are also admonished to wait patiently for the promises of God, who sometimes delays but does not take away, and who also withholds from us what would not be useful; on this see above.

units.la: Ex reliquis doctrinis prout occurrerunt, quænam doctrina excerpi debeat, satis commonstrauimus, nequaquam opus est pluribus repetere.
units.tr: As to which doctrines should be drawn out from the rest, as they occurred, we have sufficiently shown; there is no need to repeat them at length.

units.la: Est tamen obseruanda doctrina de promissionibus: hic enim habuimus de promissionibus temporalibus, & de promissionib. spiritualibus: item, quomodo patres non acceperint promissiones, & tamen Deus necessariò verax sit: Quomodo ergo istud fiat, copiosius foret explicandum. Vide in maiori volumine, quia disputationem de promissionibus instituimus.
units.tr: Yet the doctrine of the promises must be noted. Here we have dealt with temporal promises and spiritual promises, and also with how the fathers did not receive the promises, and yet God must necessarily be true. How this comes about would need fuller explanation. See the larger volume, since we have set out a disputation on the promises there.

units.la: Per fidem obtulit Abraham Isaac, quum tentaretur: & vnigenitum obtulit, in quo promissiones acceperat, ad quem dictum fuerat: In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen: cum illud secum perpendisset, Deum vel a mortuis excitare posse, vnde illum etiam resurrectionis typo reduxit.
units.tr: By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested; and he offered his only-begotten son, in whom he had received the promises, to whom it had been said: In Isaac shall your seed be called; reckoning that God was able to raise him even from the dead, whence he also received him back as a type of resurrection.

units.la: Quinta demonstratio fidei Abrahae, ab eo, quod, cùm iuberetur vnicum filium, in quo promissa illi erat innumerabilis posteritas, interficere & immolare, paratus fuerit id facere, & constantissimè nihilominus crediderit, promissionem posteritatis, in eo adhuc implendam. Hæc autem est propositio, per fidem obtulit Abraham Isaac (Genes. 22) sequitur probatio, siue expositio: Quum tentaretur.
units.tr: The fifth demonstration of Abraham's faith is this: when he was commanded to kill and sacrifice his only son, in whom the promise of innumerable posterity was made to him, he was ready to do it, and yet most steadfastly believed the promise of posterity, which was still to be fulfilled in him. The proposition is: By faith Abraham offered Isaac (Genesis 22). The proof or explanation follows: when he was tested.

units.la: Quam priusquàm exponamus, repetēda est nobis historia ex Genes. 22. Tentauit Deus Abraham, & dixit ad eum, Abraham, Abraham. At ille respondit: adsum: ait illi: Tolle filium tuum vnigenitum, quem diligis Isaac, & vade in terram visionis, atque ibi offeres eum in holocaustum, super vnum montium, quem monstrauero tibi. Igitur Abraham de nocte consurgens, strauit asinum suum, accepitque duos pueros suos secum, & Isaac filium suum: quumq; concidisset ligna holocausti, surrexit, & perrexit ad locum, quem dixerit ei Deus. Die tertio leuauit Abraham oculos suos, & vidit locum procul: dixitque Abraham pueris suis: manete hic cum asino: ego verò & puer pergemus illuc usq; & adorabimus, ac reuertemus ad vos. Accepit itaq; Abraham ligna holocausti & posuit illa super Isaac filium suum: ipse verò tulit in manu sua ignem, & gladium, & perrexerunt ambo pariter. Dixit autem Isaac ad Abraham patrem suū, dixit inquam, Pater mi, Qui respondit, ecce ego, fili mi. Et dixit: ecce ignis & ligna, sed vbi pecus in holocaustum? Respondit Abraham, Deus prouidebit sibi pecus in holocaustum, fili mi: pergebantq; ambo pariter.
units.tr: Before we explain it, the history in Genesis 22 must be recalled. God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham, Abraham." He answered, "Here I am." God said: "Take your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision, and there offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will show you." So Abraham rose early in the night, saddled his ass, took two of his young men with him and his son Isaac, and when he had split the wood for the burnt offering, he set out for the place God had named to him. On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar. He said to his young men: "Stay here with the ass; I and the boy will go on over there, and we will worship and return to you." So Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac; he himself carried the fire and the knife in his hand, and the two of them went on together. Then Isaac spoke to Abraham his father. He said, "My father." He answered, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Here are the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?" Abraham answered, "God will provide himself a lamb for the burnt offering, my son." And they went on together.

units.la: Quùm autem peruenissent ad locum, quem dixerat ei Deus, aedificauit ibi Abraham altare, ordinauitque ligna, & ligauit Isaac filium suum, & impo̢uit eum altari super ligna: Misitque manum suam, & accepit gladium, ut iugularet filium suum. Tunc clamauit ad eum Angelus Iehouae è coelo, & dixit, Abraham, Abraham: Qui respondit, Ecce ego. Et dixit: Ne extendas manum tuam in puerum, neque facias ei quicquam. Nunc enim cognoui, quòd timens es Dei, quòd non peperceris filio tuo, unico tuo propter me. Quùm autem eleuasset Abraham oculos suos, vidit, & en aries stabat post tergum, detentus in dumo cornibus: perrexitque Abraham, tulitque arietem illum, & obtulit eum in holocaustum pro filio suo. Vocauitque Abraham nomen loci illius, Iehouah videbit. Idcirco dicitur hodie, In monte Iehouah videbitur. Clamauit autem Angelus Iehouae ad Abraham secundo è coelo: & dixit: per memetipsum iuraui, dixit Iehouah: Quandoquidem fecisti rem hanc, quòd non peperceris filio tuo, unico tuo: quòd, inquam, benedicendo benedicam tibi, ac multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum, sicut stellas coeli, & sicut arenam, quae est ad littus maris, possidebitque semen tuum portas inimicorum suorum: & benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terrae, eo quòd obedivisti voci meae.
units.tr: When they came to the place God had named to him, Abraham built an altar there, arranged the wood, bound his son Isaac and laid him on the altar upon the wood. Then he stretched out his hand and took the knife to slay his son. But the Angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham." He answered, "Here I am." He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy, nor do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me." When Abraham lifted up his eyes, he saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket behind him. Abraham went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. Abraham called the name of that place, The LORD will see. Therefore it is said today, On the mount the LORD will be seen. The Angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven and said: "By myself I have sworn, says the LORD, because you have done this thing and have not withheld your son, your only son, that I will bless you by blessing, and multiply your seed by multiplying, as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the shore of the sea; and your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies; and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice."

units.la: Haec ibi ad praesentis probationis fidei Abrahae cognitionem obseruatu necessaria: quae à Spiritu sancto ideò haud dubiè sunt tam clarè, obseruata etiam ratione circumstantiarum, propositta, ut in eam historiam cen valde memorabilem omnes diligentissimè intuerentur. Et certè nihil ab Abrahamo factum in omni vita refertur, ex quo plus laudis fit consecutus, & in quo vis excellentioris fidei clarius eluxerit.
units.tr: These things are there to be observed for knowledge of the present proof of Abraham's faith. The Holy Spirit doubtless set them forth so clearly, and also took account of the circumstances, so that everyone might most diligently consider that very memorable history. Indeed, nothing done by Abraham in his whole life is recorded by which he gained more praise, and in which the force of a more excellent faith shines more clearly.

units.la: Primò autem obseruandum est, quomodo Apostolus conuertat id ad commendationem fidei, & iustitiae ex fide, quod tamen potius videtur nobis ostendere commendationem operum & iustitiae ex operibus. Ipsa Scriptura videtur palàm testari, opus ipsum acceptum Deo, & propter opus deinde personam, sic enim ait: Per memetipsum iuraui, dicit Dominus, quia fecisti hanc rem, & nò pepercisti filio tuo vnico, &c. & paulo post Quia obedisti voci meae. Sed & Iacobus epistolae suae capite secundo aperte videtur contra uertere factum iflud ad laudem operum, & ad probandum, iustificari homines ex operibus: Abraham pater noster nonne ex factis (inquit) iustificatus est, cùm obtulisset Ishac filium suum super altare? Vides, quòd fides adiumento fuerit factis illius, & ex factis fides perfecta fuerit? Et impleta est Scriptura, quae dicit, Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est illi ad iustitiam, & amicus Dei vocatus est. Videtis igitur, quòd ex factis iustificetur homo, & non ex fide tantùm. Facilis est responsio.
units.tr: First, we must observe how the Apostle turns this to the commendation of faith and of righteousness from faith, although it seems rather to show the commendation of works and of righteousness from works. Scripture itself seems plainly to testify that the work itself is accepted by God, and then the person on account of the work: for thus it says, "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son," and a little later, "because you have obeyed my voice." But James too, in the second chapter of his epistle, seems openly to turn that deed to the praise of works, and to prove that men are justified by works: "Was not Abraham our father justified by works," he says, "when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar? Do you see that faith was helped by his works, and that by works faith was made perfect?" And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, "Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness, and he was called the friend of God." You see, then, that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only. The answer is easy.

units.la: Primò, Iacobus non loquitur ibi de fide perfecta, sed tantùm de notitia quadam, quae fidem debet praecedere: sicut semper cognitio quaedam credendorum proponi initio debet. Liquet id ex eo, quòd prius dixit, exemplì caussa, de fide illorum, quos increpabat: Tu credis, quòd Deus vnus est? Rectè facis: Et daemonia credunt, ac cõtremiscunt. Certè daemonia non habent fidem proprie sic dictam, quâ Apostolus passim in Romanis & Galatis docet iustificare, sed bene habent credendorum notitiam.
units.tr: First, James is not speaking there of perfect faith, but only of a certain knowledge, which ought to precede faith: just as some knowledge of the things to be believed should always be set forth at the start. This is clear from the fact that he first said, by way of example, about the faith of those he was rebuking: "You believe that God is one? You do well. The demons also believe and tremble." Certainly the demons do not have faith in the proper sense, by which the Apostle teaches throughout Romans and Galatians that we are justified. They do, however, have knowledge of the things to be believed.

units.la: Secundò: videndum est, contra quales agat Iacobus: contra eos agit, qui, cùm audisset fortasis, bono animo & synceriter tradi, sola fide homines iustificari, ipsi corruptè acceperunt, quasi dictum fuisset, solam notitiam illam rerum credendarum sufficere, intereaut verè per fidem apprehenderent promissiones de oblata propter Christum misericordia, nihil solliciti: deinde nulla re testantes, se fidem veram habere, sed potius omnia temerè & propterueagentes in contrarium. Contra tales igitur solo titulo fidei inaniter gloriantes, ac nullos proferetes fructus fidei, rectè Iacobus loquitur. Ipsius verba in multos etiam nostri temporis iactabundos fidei praecones competunt, doctrinam fidei sua inconsideratà iactantia deformantes.
units.tr: Second, we must consider against whom James is arguing. He argues against those who, having perhaps heard, and having been taught in a good spirit and sincerely, that men are justified by faith alone, received this in a corrupt way, as if it had been said that that bare knowledge of the things to be believed was enough, while they themselves, having no care, did not truly apprehend by faith the promises of the mercy offered for Christ's sake. Moreover, they bore no witness by any deed that they had true faith, but rather acted rashly and wantonly in the opposite direction. So James rightly speaks against such people, who vainly boast in the mere name of faith and produce no fruits of faith. His words also fit many boastful advocates of faith in our own time, who by their thoughtless boasting distort the teaching of faith.

units.la: Tertiò, Iacobus opera commendat, eisque iustitiam tribuit, sed quatenus à fide proficiuntur: ut illa ipsa iustitia ad fonte fidei referenda sit, & opera iusta intelliguntur, quatenus ab eo, qui iam per fidem iustificatus est, fiunt. Intelligit, eam demùm verà fide esse, quae non otiatur, sed fructibus etiam commendabilis est. Huc pertinet, quod ipse citat, Credidit Abraham Deo, & reputatum est illi ad iustitiam: ubi clarè fidei iustitia tribuitur. Sed ea de re alibi quoq; à nobis dictum est: quare supersedemus. Nunc ad Apostoli verba praesentia.
units.tr: Third, James commends good works and ascribes righteousness to them, but insofar as they proceed from faith, so that this very righteousness is to be referred to the source of faith, and good works are understood as being done by one who has already been justified through faith. He understands that faith is true only when it is not idle but is also commendable by its fruits. To this belongs what he himself cites: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness," where righteousness is clearly ascribed to faith. But we have said elsewhere about this matter too, so we will pass it over. Now let us turn to the words of the Apostle before us.

units.la: Cùm tentaretur: πειραζόμενος: Respicit ad id, quod Genef. 22. dicitur, Tentauit Deus Abraham.
units.tr: "When he was tested" [πειραζόμενος]. He refers to what is said in Genesis 22: "God tested Abraham."

units.la: Tentare & Deo tribuitur & diabolo, sed diuersa ratione: sicut etiam diuerso modo tentamur. Diabolus proprie vocatur & per Antonomasiam tentator: ut Matth. 4. & 1. Thess. 3. Ne forte tentauerit vos ille, qui tentat. Et tentat hic ad malum, ut videlicet ad ruinā, vel peccatum quoquo pacto inducat, & ita nobis paret excidium. Hic est ipsius scopus.
units.tr: Testing is ascribed both to God and to the devil, but in different ways, just as we are also tempted in different ways. The devil is properly called, and by antonomasia, the tempter, as in Matthew 4 and 1 Thessalonians 3: "lest perhaps the tempter had tempted you." And he tempts here to evil, that is, so that he may lead us into ruin or sin in whatever way, and so prepare our destruction for us. This is his aim.

units.la: Sed Deus subinde illum fallit & conuertit illius conatus ad eorum, qui fortiter resistunt in tentatione, gloriam. 1. Corinth 10. Tentatio vos non cepit, nisi humana: sed fidelis est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari supra id, quod potestis: imò faciet vnà cum tentatione euentum. {a}quentum, quo possitis sufferre. Et omnes tentationes, quas Satanas Deo permittente inflixerat beato Iob, elusæ sunt, & conuersæ ad Dei & ipsius Iob gloriam. Nec potest ipse Satanas tentare, nisi quatenus Deus permittit, adeò ut omnis tentatio diuinitus quodammodo immittatur: quare & Christus docuit nos orare patrem, Ne nos inducat in tentationem, sed liberet nos à malo. Quamobrem sæpissimè Deus ipse dicitur in Scripturis pios suos ministros tentare: sed alia ratione tentat, quàm diabolus.
units.tr: But God from time to time frustrates him and turns his attempts to the glory of those who resist temptation strongly. 1 Corinthians 10: "No temptation has taken you except what is human; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will even together with the temptation make the outcome by which you may be able to endure it." And all the temptations which Satan, with God's permission, had inflicted on the blessed Job were foiled and turned to the glory of God and of Job himself. Nor can Satan himself tempt except insofar as God permits, so that every temptation is in some sense sent from God. For this reason Christ also taught us to pray to the Father: "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." Therefore God himself is very often said in Scripture to test his godly ministers; but he tests them in a different way from the devil.

units.la: Tentat Deus, ut coronet, certè semper ad eorum, qui tentantur, utilitatem. Vt coronet quidem tentat sanctos suos, dum certamina extrema facit subire, ad illustrandam fidei gloriam: quemadmodum quos martyres celebrat ecclesia, & alij etiam sancti confessores. In eam sententiam dicitur Psal. 26. Proba me Deus, & tenta me, funde renes meos, & cor meum. Vbi offert se ad pericula persecutionum susferenda. Præterea tentat Deus pios, ut ubi illi venerint in tentationem, alij exemplum inde habeant, quomodo & ipsi per fidem debeant tentationes perferre, & liberationem expectare. Quem in modum & tentatio Abrahæ, & tentatio Iob, & tentatio Christi omnibus pijs in exemplum est proposita. Fuerunt enim istorum insignes tentationes in hoc editæ; ut alijs essent exemplo, non tantum propter ipsos, qui tentati sunt. Deniq; tentat Deus interdum, si non ut coronet aut proponat in exemplū, at ut erudiat & doceat homines seipsos nosse, utq; ipsorum virtus vel malitia patefiat. Deut. 8. Recordaberis cuncti itineris, per quod adduxit te Dominus Deus tuus quadraginta annis per desertum, ut affligeret te, atq; tentaret, & nota fierent, quæ in tuo animo versabantur: utrùm custodires mandata illius an non. Affli-xit te penuria, & dedit tibi cibum Manna, quod ignorabas tu & patres tui, ut ostenderet tibi, quòd non in solo pane viuit homo, &c. Ecce tentationem ad prodendum hominis ingenium ad exercitium fidei: qualis nobis perpetua est, dum hic viuimus.
units.tr: God tests in order to crown, and certainly always for the benefit of those who are tested. He tests his holy ones in order to crown them, when he makes them undergo extreme struggles, to display the glory of faith, as the Church celebrates the martyrs and other holy confessors. To this effect it is said in Psalm 26: "Prove me, O God, and test me; refine my reins and my heart," where he offers himself to endure the dangers of persecution. Moreover, God tests the godly so that, when they come into temptation, others may have an example from it of how they too ought to bear temptations through faith and await deliverance. In this way the temptation of Abraham, the temptation of Job, and the temptation of Christ have been set forth as an example to all the godly. For these remarkable temptations of theirs were brought forth so that they might be an example to others, not only for the sake of those who were tested. Finally, God sometimes tests, if not in order to crown or to set forth as an example, then to teach and instruct men to know themselves, and so that the virtue or malice in their hearts may be revealed. Deuteronomy 8: "You shall remember the whole journey by which the Lord your God led you for forty years through the desert, to humble you and test you, and that what was in your heart might be made known, whether you would keep his commandments or not. He afflicted you with want, and gave you manna to eat, which you and your fathers did not know, to show you that man does not live by bread alone," and so on. Here is a test to reveal the character of a man and to exercise faith, such as we have constantly while we live here.

units.la: In summa, quomodocunq; Deus tentat, non nisi ad bonum tentat, & ad utilitatem: ita ut si quis se ad malum solicitari intelligat, sciat vel à diabolo id fieri, vel, ut Iacobus docet, à propria conscientia. Habemus igitur, Abrahám tentatum esse, sed ut coronaretur, ut in exemplum proponi posset cæteris credentibus. Et profecto erat mirabilis hæc tentatio Abrahæ, magnumq; certamen in ea est propositum, præceptum illi erat, offerre filium suum, graue præceptum, sed tamen magni faciendum, quia à Deo editum. Rursus ex alte ratio parte & sensus diuersum iudicabant innitentes primò legi naturæ.
units.tr: In sum, however God tests, he tests only for good and for benefit, so that if anyone perceives himself being urged to evil, let him know that this happens either from the devil or, as James teaches, from his own conscience. We have, then, that Abraham was tested, but so that he might be crowned, and so that he might be set forth as an example to the other believers. And certainly this temptation of Abraham was remarkable, and a great struggle is set before us in it. He was commanded to offer his son, a grievous command, yet one to be obeyed greatly, because it was given by God. On the other side, however, reason and feeling judged otherwise, relying first on the law of nature.

units.la: Hæc autem lex naturæ iubet seruare & tueri liberos. Neq; enim hæ sorì ... à creditibus remouentur, quasi Stoici essent, qui affectus omnes exuissent, ἀπαθεῖαν nescio quam imaginantes. Hac etiam re non parum mouebatur ratio, quòd filius ille esset vnicus, quòd maximè dilectus, quòd seni & post tàm longam expectationem natus: hæ, inquam, circumstantiæ senis animum haud parum mouebant. Sed præterea intueri potest mens in legem Dei, qua præceptum est, Non occidas. Certè innocentem occidi, & à patre occidi filium, istud contra omnes leges, omnemq; æquitatem esse, quiuis intelligit. Succurrebat deniq; ex altera parte promissiones toties repetitæ, quòd videlicet filius ille esset, ex quo expectanda foret posteritas. Promissiones erant Dei, qui mentiri nescit. Præceptum verò prorsus aduersari videbatur illis promissionibus, ut plane dubitare posset Abraham, an præceptum foret à Deo profectum, an verò promissiones forent irritæ. Cogitare potuisset, diaboli esse commentum, in præcepto ita volentes impedire & euertere promissiones de innumerabili posteritate: quandoquidem angelus Satanæ se in angelum lucis callidè potest transformare. Quis obseruo hic non fuisset valde anxius, in tali certamine & animi angustia? Horrendæ & innumeræ cogitationes animum senis discruciabant, & quotidie ad millies negandum, ad millies desperandum sollicitabant.
units.tr: Now this law of nature bids us preserve and protect our children. Nor are these feelings removed from believers, as if they were Stoics who had cast off all emotions, imagining some sort of impassibility. Reason was also moved not a little by the fact that this son was his only one, that he was most dearly loved, and that he was born to an old man after such a long expectation. These circumstances, I say, moved the old man's heart not a little. Moreover, the mind can look to the law of God, by which it is commanded, "You shall not kill." Certainly, that an innocent person should be killed, and a son killed by his father, is, as anyone can see, against all laws and all justice. Finally, there came to mind on the other side the promises so often repeated, namely that this son would be the one from whom posterity was to be expected. The promises were God's, who cannot lie. But the command seemed utterly to contradict those promises, so that Abraham could well doubt whether the command came from God, or whether the promises would come to nothing. He might have thought it was a contrivance of the devil, who wished by such a command to hinder and overturn the promises of innumerable posterity, since Satan's angel can cunningly transform himself into an angel of light. Who, I ask, would not have been very anxious here, in such a struggle and distress of mind? Dreadful and countless thoughts tormented the old man's heart, and every day urged him a thousand times to refuse, and a thousand times to despair.

units.la: Sed his omnibus nihil motus est Abraham, ipse adhuc in fide perstitit, & promissiones nequaquam irritas fore statuebat, & ad offerendum filium est persuasus. Porrò hic habemus, quomodo veræ tentationes fiant, præsertim in magnis viris. Qui prorsus sunt impij, non tentantur, aut certè parum, quia iam manifesta est & plena eorum malitia.
units.tr: But Abraham was not moved at all by all these things; he himself remained steadfast in faith, held that the promises would by no means come to nothing, and was persuaded to offer his son. Here, then, we have how true temptations occur, especially in great men. Those who are utterly wicked are not tempted, or certainly only a little, because their malice is already manifest and complete.

units.la: Sed heroici viri, quales sunt verè credentes, & inprimis Abraham, mirabiliter tentantur, & mirandis modis in varias partes distrahuntur. Occurrunt illis Scripturarum loci, qui diuersum suadent ab eo, quod à Deo iubentur facere, quiq; rationis iudicium videntur in speciem approbare. Rursus alij occurrunt, qui inuitant ad faciendum, quod præceptū est. Exemplū habemus in tentationib. Iob, cui diabolus per amicos diuersa suggerebat, inuitantia ad maledicendum Deo: Rursus ipse alias rationes opponebat: Sed multò clarissimū exemplum in tentatione Christi: vbi diabolus quæ suggerebat, semper colorabat aut commoda ratione, aut Scripturæ testimonio. Sed Christus contrà fortiter perstabat, & rursus Scripturam opponebat, exemplum nobis præbens, quomodo nos quoq; in tentationibus gerere debeamus, ac viuere. Quin etiam nobis hoc loco in Abraham tentato exemplum Ephes. 6. exemplum proponitur, quomodo oporteat nos per omnem vitam tentationibus esse expositos: quandoquidem vita hominis militia perpetua est super terram, teste Iob cap. 7. per tentationes enim fides exercetur & roboratur. Neq; quisquam coronabitur, nisi qui legitime certauerit. Si Abraham non ita certasset in veris tentationibus, haudquaquam ita commendaretur eius fides, haud esset consecutus æternam gloriam. Tantum ergo quomodo Abraham tentatus sit, & quomodo vere dictum sit Genes. 22. & præsenti loco epistolæ, Abraham esse tentatum.
units.tr: But heroic men, such as true believers are, and above all Abraham, are wonderfully tempted and pulled in various directions in wonderful ways. Passages of Scripture come to them that urge something different from what God commands them to do, and that seem to approve the judgment of reason. Other passages in turn come to them that invite them to do what has been commanded. We have an example in the temptations of Job, to whom the devil, through his friends, kept suggesting things that invited him to curse God; and again he himself raised other arguments against Job. But a much clearer example is in the temptation of Christ, where the devil's suggestions were always dressed up either with a plausible argument or with a testimony of Scripture. Christ, however, stood firm and in turn opposed Scripture, giving us an example of how we too ought to conduct ourselves and live in temptations. Indeed, in the tempted Abraham the Ephesians 6 passage also sets before us an example of how we must be exposed to temptations throughout our whole life, since the life of man on earth is a constant warfare, as Job says in chapter 7. For temptations exercise and strengthen faith. And no one is crowned unless he has struggled lawfully. If Abraham had not thus contended in real temptations, his faith would not have been so commended, and he would not have obtained eternal glory. So much, then, for how Abraham was tempted, and how it is rightly said in Genesis 22 and in the present passage of the epistle that Abraham was tempted.

units.la: Et unigenitum obtulit, in quo promissiones acceperat) Respicit ad id, quod & textus habet in Genesi, Tolle filium tuum vnicum, quem diligis Ishac: Ecce vero iam alterum opus & aduersum fidei. Prius quidem credentes tentantur, sed tamen propter tentationes non impediuntur effectus fidei: quin potius opera victoriæ in tentatione proferuntur. Nisi enim in fide sint constantes, qui tentantur, nihil præclari efficiunt: sed veluti segnes sese dedunt & succumbunt. Neq; enim quodlibet opus post tentationes factum accipi debet pro opere fidei. Impij & infirmi etiam edunt opera post tentationes, & quidem difficilia, atq; in speciem præclara: & habent etiam egregias rationes, quibus videantur ea posse commendare & prædicare: sed multum differunt ab opere Abrahæ. Diabolus, angelus Satanæ, ut supra diximus, est mille artifex, & nouit se transformare in angelum lucis: valet & facultate suadendi, nouit Scripturas ad suum institutum torquere: in summa, nihil non potest. Itaq; ad manum est impijs, quo opera sua commendent. Sic enim haud dubie illi, qui immolabant filios suos idolo Moloch, de qualibus sermo habetur Leuit. 20. & Hieremiæ 32. iudicabant, se non minora facere, quam fecerat Abraham: & hodie Monachi, & similes iudicant se Helisæos & quosuis prophetas superare: sed longè falluntur: nequaquam sunt hæc opera fidei. Ratio est: quia non fiunt ex diuino præcepto. Abraham habuit expressum mandatum: quamobrem obedientia illius est vera obedientia fidei. Ergo opus sequens tentationes eatenus est agnoscendum pro opere fidei, quatenus fit ex mandato Dei, & consentit directè præstantiori mandato. Habent Iureconsulti placitum, quòd lex inferior non derogat superiori, veluti quòd lex positiua non tollit legem naturalem: Ita statuendum est in examinandis tentationibus, eas rationes, siue ex Scriptura depromptæ sint, siue aliunde, præferendas esse, quæ directè conueniunt cum verbo Dei, & clara simplicitas, eius sententia. Nostra ratio & diabolus suggerunt multa, & sciunt torquere Scripturam, faciutq;, vt videatur propositò nostro seruire: sed sæpè fallimur. Consulamus simplicem & claram verbi sententiam: & ad eam quasi Lydium lapidem probemus tentationum suggestiones: & factum rectum sequetur. Porrò artificiosè amplificat Apostolus hoc opus fidei Abrahæ, dicendo: unigenitum obtulit: Nam si plures habuisset, haud fuisset itagraue: sed vnigenitum illum, in multa sene ctute natum, hoc profectò longè erat grauissimum. Dicitur autem vnigenitus, quia solus promissus ex Sara: Ismael non erat promissus. Atque ideo adhuc addit: In quo promissiones acceperat: Hic sese attollit fidei dignitas & vehementia. Fides proprie respicit in promissiones, suntq; promissiones diuinæ, ut sæpè à nobis dictum est, principali fidei obiectum: Hic autem iubetur Abraham negligere promissiones, & respicere ad præceptum. Quomodo hic non statim fuisset deiecta fides? Præceptum deterret, & iram operatur: Euangelium seu promissiones erigunt. Pugnant hac in parte lex & Euangelium: & interea Abraham semper in fide perstat. Particula igitur hac valde amplificatur fides Abrahæ. Exponit autem Apostolus, quomodo Abraham in Isaac promissiones acceperit, dicens: Ad quem dictum fuerat, In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen: Id habetur Genes. 21. cùm Sara ab Abraham peteret eijci Ismaelem cum matre, quòd non esset futurus hæres cù filio suo, durè hoc accepit Abraham, & dixit illi Deus: Non tibi videatur asperum super puero, & super ancilla tua, Omnia quæ dixerit tibi Sara, audi vocem eius, quia in Isaac vocabitur tibi semen. Ita nimirum Isaac erat proprie promissionis filius, & de ipso promissiones erat intelligendæ, ex ipso expectanda innumerabilis posteritas, & semen benedictum. Et Roman. 9. Apostolus interpretatur, recenseri in semen, qui sunt filij promissionis. Hac porrò promissione alebatur fides Abrahæ, & tamen contra eam venit nouum præceptum. Sed quomodo Abraham hic sese gesit?
units.tr: And he offered his only-begotten son, in whom he had received the promises. This refers to what the text of Genesis also says: "Take your only son, whom you love, Isaac." Now comes another work, one that is hard for faith. Believers are indeed tempted first, but faith's effects are not hindered by the temptations; rather, works of victory are brought forth in temptation. For unless those who are tempted are steadfast in faith, they accomplish nothing excellent, but like idlers they give themselves up and yield. Nor should every work done after temptations be taken as a work of faith. The wicked and the weak also produce works after temptations, and indeed difficult ones that look splendid, and they have excellent arguments by which they seem able to commend and proclaim them; but they differ greatly from the work of Abraham. The devil, the angel of Satan, as we said above, is a master of a thousand arts, and knows how to transform himself into an angel of light; he has the power of persuasion and knows how to twist Scripture to his purpose; in short, he can do anything. Therefore the wicked have at hand something by which to commend their works. Thus, without doubt, those who sacrificed their sons to the idol Moloch, of whom Leviticus 20 and Jeremiah 32 speak, judged that they were doing no less than Abraham had done; and today monks and the like judge that they surpass Elisha and any prophets you like. But they are greatly mistaken: these are by no means works of faith. The reason is that they are not done by divine command. Abraham had an express command; therefore his obedience is true obedience of faith. Hence a work that follows temptations is to be acknowledged as a work of faith only insofar as it is done by God's command and agrees directly with a higher command. The jurists hold the principle that a lower law does not override a higher, as a positive law does not abolish the natural law. So it must be settled, in examining temptations, that those arguments, whether drawn from Scripture or from elsewhere, are to be preferred which agree directly with the word of God, and its plain and clear sense. Our reason and the devil suggest many things, and they know how to twist Scripture and make it appear to serve their purpose; but we are often deceived. Let us consult the simple and clear sense of the word, and by it, as by a touchstone, let us test the suggestions of temptations; and right action will follow. Moreover, the Apostle elaborately magnifies this work of Abraham's faith by saying "he offered his only-begotten." For if he had had several sons, it would not have been so grave; but to offer up that only son, born in Abraham's very old age, was indeed far the most grievous thing. He is called "only-begotten" because he alone was promised from Sarah; Ishmael had not been promised. And therefore he adds further: "in whom he had received the promises." Here the dignity and vehemence of faith rise up. Faith properly looks to the promises, and divine promises, as we have often said, are the chief object of faith. Yet here Abraham is commanded to disregard the promises and look to a precept. How could faith not have been cast down at once? The precept terrifies and works wrath; the gospel, or the promises, raise up. In this respect law and gospel are at odds; and yet Abraham always persists in faith. This phrase, therefore, greatly magnifies Abraham's faith. The Apostle then explains how Abraham received the promises in Isaac, saying: "To whom it had been said, 'In Isaac shall your seed be called.'" This is found in Genesis 21, when Sarah asked Abraham to have Ishmael cast out with his mother, because he would not be heir with her son. Abraham took this hard, and God said to him: "Let it not seem grievous to you concerning the boy and your maidservant. Whatever Sarah has said to you, hear her voice, for in Isaac shall your seed be called." Thus Isaac was truly the son of the promise, and the promises were to be understood of him; from him was to be expected an innumerable posterity and a blessed seed. And in Romans 9 the Apostle interprets that those who are the children of the promise are reckoned as the seed. Abraham's faith was nourished by this promise, and yet against it came a new command. But how did Abraham conduct himself here?

units.la: Cùm illud secum perpendisset, Deum uel à mortuis excitare posse) En causa Formalis veræ & viuæ fidei. Præceptum quidem videbatur euersurum promissiones: sed Abraham nihil mouebatur nouitate, vel acerbitate præcepti, constanter respiciebat ad promissiones, quæ antecesserant, nec poterat aliter iudicare, quàm Deum fideliter præstiturum, quæ promiserat, eum esse omnipotentem & beneuolum, ideoq; sine dubio successura, quæ promissa fuerant.
units.tr: When he had considered with himself that God was able to raise him even from the dead. Behold the formal cause of true and living faith. The precept indeed seemed to overturn the promises; but Abraham was not moved by the novelty or the harshness of the command. He steadfastly looked to the promises that had gone before, and he could judge in no other way than that God would faithfully perform what he had promised, that he was omnipotent and kind, and therefore that what had been promised would without doubt come to pass.

units.la: Sic enim introducit Apostolus Abrahamum per fidem ratiocinantem, Deus potest etiam mortuum suscitare, & sic promissa adimplere: Igitur faciam quod Deus præcepit, immolabo. molabo filium. Valde proprie hic exprimitur natura fidei: semper respicit in potentiam & bonitatem Dei, ac tamen nullis machinis, imò ne ipsius quidè Dei verbo, quod in speciem videretur contrarium promissionibus, potest dimoueri. Sic verò & Apostolus Roman. 4. pluribus verbis hanc admirabilem vim fidei Abrahæ describit, fideiq; naturâ plenissime aperit, ut nihil opus sit hic repetere.
units.tr: For so the Apostle introduces Abraham reasoning through faith: God is able even to raise the dead, and so to fulfil the promises. Therefore I will do what God has commanded: I will sacrifice my son. Here the nature of faith is expressed very accurately: it always looks to the power and goodness of God, and yet it cannot be moved by any contrivances, nor even by the very word of God, which might seem in appearance to be contrary to the promises. The Apostle too, in Romans 4, describes this admirable power of Abraham's faith in many words and fully reveals the nature of faith, so there is no need to repeat it here.

units.la: Cæterùm non potuisset ille sic perstare, quin de promissionibus dubitaret, & detrecta ret exequi præceptum: nisi spiritus Sanctus pectus illius confirmasset. Contra humanû iudicium est, & supra omnes vires positum, contra spem in spem credere.
units.tr: Moreover, he could not have persisted thus unless he had doubted the promises and shrunk from carrying out the command, had not the Holy Spirit strengthened his heart. It is contrary to human judgment, and placed beyond all powers, to believe in hope against hope.

units.la: Egregium ergo documentum habemus, qualem fidem esse deceat, & qualibus exercitijs fides nostra roboretur, & quomodo promissionibus Dei constanter adhærendum.
units.tr: We therefore have an outstanding lesson of what kind of faith is fitting, by what exercises our faith is strengthened, and how we must cling steadfastly to the promises of God.

units.la: Vnde illum etiam resurrectionis typo reduxit) Hic duo dicuntur obseruatu digna: alterum de effectu fidei: vnde illum inquit, reduxit, quasi diceret: Sicut Abraham credidit, quòd etiâ à morte esset illû recepturus, ita reuera eum recepit. Destinatus erat morti, mors iam impendebat Isaaci ceruicibus, sed statim diuina voce est resuscitatus & à morte seruatus. Sic autem semper contingit pijs, quod per fidem expectant. Deus præstat promissa etiam vbi mille impedimenta videntur obstare: etiam interfectum Isaac potuisset restituere. Et hoc credebat Abraham Deum reuera facturum, ut promissa impleret. Quod verò interserit, Resurrectionis typo, caussam tacitè suggerit, cur omnia sic gesta sint: nimirum propter mysterium, ut typus Christi à morte suscitati in Isaac resplenduisse intellige retur: ac deinde in exemplo, ut videlicet alij quoq; haberent exemplum constanter expectandi promissa. Atq; ita ad sublimiorem contemplationem animos fide præditos erigit. Ac reuera Isaac in quàmplurimis typum Christi gessit, euidentissimeq; expressit.
units.tr: And from there he also received him back in a figure of the resurrection. Two things here are worth noting. The first concerns the effect of faith: "from there," he says, "he received him back," as if to say: just as Abraham believed that he would receive Isaac back even from death, so in truth he did receive him. Isaac had been destined for death; death was already hanging over Isaac's neck; but at once by the divine voice he was raised up and saved from death. And so it always happens to the godly, that they receive through faith what they await. God fulfils his promises even where a thousand obstacles seem to stand in the way; he could even have restored Isaac once slain. And Abraham believed that God would truly do this, to fulfil his promises. As for the phrase he inserts, "in a figure of the resurrection," it tacitly suggests the reason why everything went this way: namely, for the sake of the mystery, so that the type of Christ raised from the dead should be understood to shine forth in Isaac; and then for the sake of the example, so that others also might have an example of steadfastly awaiting promises. And so he lifts minds endowed with faith to a higher contemplation. Indeed, Isaac in very many respects bore the type of Christ and most clearly expressed him.

units.la: Isaac sæpè promissu, antequàm nasceretur, & per multos annos: Christus itidem sæpissimè, & ab initio mundi ad multa secula. Isaac natus ex ea, ex qua neq; per naturam, neq; per alia media videbatur puer nasciturus: Christus natus ex virgine, contra omne rationis iudicium. Cùm Isaac esset ablactatus, pater fecit grande conuiuiû: Christus cùm in mundum venisset, & tempus esset, quo se manifestaret, Deus pater per eum inuitat omnes ad conuiuium cœleste: Venite ad me omnes, & ego reficiam vos: Homo quidam fecit cœnâ magnam: Et ego constituo vobis, ut edatis & bibatis, &c. Quàdo Ismael ludit cum Isaac, & iniuriam huic facit, typus fuit Euangelij per Christum allati, ac legis quę eijci debebat: sicut Paulus interpretatur: item impiorum persequentium Christum & pios: Vide ad Galat 4. Postea vbi Abrahâ iussus est immolare Isaac, hic clarissimè delineatus fuit Christus. Abraham audit vocem & præceptum Dei. Et sic erat Deo patri constitutum, quòd genus humanum vellet per Christi mortem redimere, suamq; voluntatem etiam primis parentibus statim aperuit. Ecce primum nuncium Euangelij. Nocte surgens strauit asinum, & assumit duos iuuenes. Cùm omnis pietas fere esset extincta, & homines in tenebris magnis versarentur, Deus pater eligit asinum, id est, populû Iudaicum, cui lignum siue onus legis imponit. Adiungit duos iuuenes, prophetas videlicet & sanctos, qui itineris sunt comites, & asinum forte deducunt iussu Abrahæ. Tum Isaac assumit, id est, ipsum Christum. Tertio die videt locum procul: possunt per tres dies intelligi tempora illa, quæ nota ntur Matthæi 1. Primum ab Abraham usq; ad Dauid: Secundum à Dauid usque ad demigrationem Babylonicam: Tertium à demigratione Babylonica usq; ad Christum. Ibi iubet pueros expectare cum asino: populus Iudaicus cum sua lege & prophetis nô vlterius progreditur, sed finem hic capiût. Vsq; ad Ioanne lex & prophetę, inquit Christus, Ioan. 1. Pater cũ puero properat ad adorandum in monte. Tempus veræ adorationis Spiritu & veritate constituitur. Ioan. 4. Adueniet hora, & nunc est, quando veri adoratores adorabût patrem in spiritu & veritate. Vera adoratio in Euangelio aperta est, vmbris legalib. subla tis: quia neq; Hierosolymis, neq; in Garizim adoratio ista astricta est. Pollicetur se reditu rum ad eos: quia gratia ab illo populo non ablata est: sed denuò per Euangelium oblata: vnde Christus & Apostoli primû Iudæis annunciarunt Euangelium. Isaac gestat ligna, pater fertignem & gladium. Christus gestat sibi cruce. Ioan. 3. Sic Deus pater dilexit mundum, ut filiû suum vnigenitû daret, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, nô pereat, sed habeat vitâ æter nam. Ecce charitas per ignem significata. Item Rom. 8. Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Qui proprio filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, qui fieri potest, ut non & cum eodem omnia nobis donet? Et cùm pater illum tradidit, etiam in mortem; rectè illi gladius tribuitur. Deus immisit gladium persecutionis in Christû. Ephes. 5. Christus tradidit semetipsum hostiam & oblationem pro peccatis nostris. Et Deus pater per Zachariam, ut citat ipse Christus Matth. 26. percutiam pastorem, & dispergentur oues. Itaque Deo patri gladius conuenit. Sed quid deinceps factû est? Isaac fuit obediens patri usq; ad morte, ac ligatus est, atq; aræ impositus. Idem & Christus plenissimè præstitit. Isaac tamé non moritur, sed verbo Dei prohibetur, aries nihilominus hærens per cornua in veprib. immolatur, atq; Isaac restituitur. Non mihi improbatur, si dicamus, per arietem humanam Christi naturam, secundum quam videbatur peccatorum vepribus obsitus, intelligi, & hanc vere mactatam: secundum vero, quod filius Dei, non moritur. Sed tamen rursus restitutum Christum vitae post triduum: sicut Isaac, qui toto triduo erat morti destinatus, est restitutus. Et pater Abraham reduxit Isaac: sic Christus iterum a resurrectione ad patrem suum in coelos ascendit, ipso sic praedicente. Possent adhuc alia addi de Isaac, ut qui duxit Rebeccam: Christus duxit ecclesiam, quae non est de filijs Chanaa, sed de domo patris eius, quae ecclesia ab initio mundi duravit. Isaac duos habuit ex ea filios (Christus duos populos) Iacob & Esau: quorum hic maior natu reijcitur: licet etiam benedictione non careat. Ita Iudaicus populus vocatur ad ius primogeniturae: sed delectatus carnalibus rebus huius amisit (Roman. 9.) Utriusq; etiam benedictio convenit instituto, sicut paulo post ostendemus.
units.tr: Isaac was promised often, before he was born and over many years; Christ likewise was promised very often, and from the beginning of the world through many ages. Isaac was born of a woman through whom, by nature and by no other means, a child did not seem likely to be born; Christ was born of a virgin, contrary to all the judgement of reason. When Isaac was weaned, his father made a great banquet; when Christ had come into the world and the time had come for him to reveal himself, God the Father, through him, invites all to the heavenly banquet: "Come to me, all of you, and I will refresh you" (Matt. 11.28); "A certain man made a great supper" (Luke 14.16); "And I appoint for you, that you may eat and drink," etc. (Luke 22.29-30). When Ishmael mocks Isaac and does him wrong, this was a type of the Gospel brought by Christ and of the law, which had to be cast out, as Paul explains (Gal. 4.29-30); it is also a type of the wicked who persecute Christ and the godly. See Gal. 4. Afterwards, when Abraham was commanded to sacrifice Isaac, Christ was most clearly portrayed. Abraham hears the voice and command of God. And so it had been determined by God the Father that he would redeem the human race through the death of Christ, and he made his will known at once even to our first parents. Behold the first announcement of the Gospel. "Rising in the night, he saddled his ass and took two young men with him" (Gen. 22.3). When almost all piety had been extinguished and men were living in great darkness, God the Father chose the ass, that is, the Jewish people, on whom he laid the wood, or the burden, of the law. He adds two young men, namely the prophets and the saints, who are the companions of the journey and who, by the command of Abraham, lead the ass along. Then he takes Isaac, that is, Christ himself. "On the third day he saw the place afar off" (Gen. 22.4). The three days can be understood as those periods which are marked in Matthew 1: the first from Abraham to David; the second from David to the Babylonian exile; the third from the Babylonian exile to Christ. There he bids the young men wait with the ass: the Jewish people, with its law and prophets, goes no further, but here comes to an end. "Until John, the law and the prophets," says Christ (John 1.17 [sic, cf. Luke 16.16]). The father, with the boy, hastens to worship on the mountain. The time of true worship is established "in spirit and truth" (John 4.23). "The hour comes, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth" (John 4.23). True worship is revealed in the Gospel, the shadows of the law having been removed; for that worship is bound neither to Jerusalem nor to Gerizim. He promises that he will return to them, because grace was not taken away from that people, but is offered again through the Gospel; hence Christ and the apostles first announced the Gospel to the Jews. Isaac carries the wood, while the father carries the fire and the sword. Christ carries his own cross. "God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3.16). Here is love signified by the fire. Likewise Rom. 8: "If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him freely give us all things?" (Rom. 8.31-32). And since the Father delivered him up, even to death, the sword is rightly attributed to him. God sent the sword of persecution upon Christ. Eph. 5: "Christ gave himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice for our sins" (Eph. 5.2). And God the Father, through Zechariah, as Christ himself cites in Matt. 26: "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (Matt. 26.31; Zech. 13.7). Therefore the sword is fitting for God the Father. But what was done next? Isaac was obedient to his father even unto death, and he was bound and laid upon the altar. Christ also fulfilled this most fully. Yet Isaac is not put to death; rather, by the word of God he is forbidden, and a ram, caught by its horns in the thorns, is nevertheless sacrificed in his place, and Isaac is restored. I do not disapprove if we say that by the ram is understood the human nature of Christ, in which he seemed covered with the thorns of sins, and that this was truly slain; but in respect of the fact that he is the Son of God, he does not die. Yet Christ was again restored to life after three days, just as Isaac, who for three whole days had been destined to death, was restored. And the father Abraham brought Isaac back; so Christ, from the resurrection, ascended again to his Father in the heavens, he himself so foretelling. More could be added about Isaac, such as that he led Rebekah home: Christ led the Church, which is not of the daughters of Canaan but of the house of his Father, and which Church has endured from the beginning of the world. Isaac had two sons by her (Christ, two peoples), Jacob and Esau: of whom the elder is rejected, although he does not lack a blessing. Thus the Jewish people is called to the right of the firstborn, but, delighted by carnal things, lost it (Rom. 9). The blessing of both also fits the design, as we will show a little later.

units.la: Ecce ergo, quomodo in typo, ἐν παραβολῇ, in similitudine, maioris cuiusdam negotij Abraham filium suum reduxerit. Non igitur sine causa Apostolus eam particulam interpositam fuit: sed voluit animos nostros ad sublimiorum rerum contemplationem excitare: sicut revera nihil otiose in veteri testamento contigit, nihilq; per Spiritum Sanctum relatum in sacras literas sine euidenti & necessaria doctrina atq; utilitate. Alioqui quorsum attineret, illa referri in scripturis de ablatione Isaac, & coniunctio facto, de Ismaele peculiariter colludente cum Isaaco? Quanti obscuro momenti ista erunt, si non respiciatur ad mysterium in factis illis latens? Ideoq; Apostolus Galat. 4. valde prudenter historiam de Isaac & Ismaele inter se colludentibus, & hoc illum afficiente iniuria: Item de reiectione Ismaelis interpretatur, significasse abrogationem legis, & vigorem Euangelij. Unde etiam regula tradita est, quod, quando in scripturis occurrit, quod secundum simplicem narrationem, siue secundum sensuum grammaticum leuiculum esse videretur, aut etiam absurdum, aut certe nihil habere in se doctrinae: tum necessitas ipsa suadet, altiorem intellectum spectare, & venari mysterium: Qua de re Augustinus libro 2. de doctrina Christiana cap. 6. Item Origenes homilia undecima in librum Numerorum. Ipsa utilitas interdum suadet, allegoricas interpretationes quaerere, saepe etiam ipsa necessitas: alias vero vix sunt adhibendae. Sed nos alias plenius de hac re egimus supra capite septimo, ubi ostendebatur, Christum esse typo signatum per Melchisedech. Proinde habemus hic doctrinam variam & multiplicem. Primo quidem, quod pij tentantur divina voluntate, sed ad suum inprimis profectum, & aliorum etiam exemplum: quod item in tentationib. oporteat fortes perstare, necullis suggestionibus siue carnis nostrae siue diaboli, frangi. Secundo, habemus, quod fides semper in tentationibus respicit in promissiones, nec non statuere debet, etiam vbi innumera videntur impedimenta concurrere, Deum nihilominus promissa praestitu rum, si modo nos in fide constantes manserimus. Tertio, habemus, quod fides semper debeat respicere in Dei omnipotentiam & misericordiam, iudicareq;, Deum facere, ut ea, quae non sunt, statim sint: & vel ex mortuis viuos faciat: ut promissa praestet, salutemque nostram operetur. Quarto, particula illa ἐν παραβολῇ, admonet nos, interdum mysteria venari, praesertim in historijs veteris instrumenti, & sanctorum patrum, qui plerunq; suis actionibus typum gesserunt rerum per Christum gerendarum. Haec hactenus de fide Abrahae, in qua praedicanda Apostolus non sine causa multus fuit, utpote ex qua multa utilissima possumus addiscere. Per fidem de futuris benedixit Isaac filio Iacob & Esau. Quinto exemplum institutae inductionis de Isaac per fidem iustificato: sumptu a causa & fine benedictionis, quam ille filijs suis impendit est; sententia: Isaac benedixit filijs suis, precas illis omnia bona in futurum. Atqui bona in futurum non petuntur, nisi cum fide, quado fides proprie est ὑπόστασις rerum sperandarum & non apparentium. Igitur quod Isaacita filijs benedixerit, id excellenti quadam fide factum est. Vis argumenti est in particula, de futuris: qua quidem fidei natura proprie notatur. Fides enim semper respicit in futura & non apparentia. Historia autem, quae hic attingitur, scripta est Genes. 27. Priusquam vero eam explicemus, videndum, quare Apostolus expositurus fidem Isaac, hanc potius actionem, quam aliquam aliam elegerit, cum tamen sint & aliae plures, & praeclarae, e quibus fides eius egregie praedicari posset.
units.tr: Behold, then, how Abraham brought back his son in a type, "in a parable" [ἐν παραβολῇ], in a likeness of some greater matter. Therefore the apostle did not insert that passage without cause; he wished to stir our minds to the contemplation of higher things, just as indeed nothing in the Old Testament happened idly, and nothing was recorded by the Holy Spirit in the sacred letters without clear and necessary teaching and usefulness. Otherwise, why would it be worthwhile for those things to be recorded in the Scriptures, the removal of Isaac and the marriage that followed, and Ishmael in particular mocking Isaac? How trivial these would be if one did not look to the mystery lying hidden in those deeds! Therefore the apostle, in Gal. 4, very wisely interprets the history of Isaac and Ishmael, who mock each other and who did this wrong to him, and likewise the rejection of Ishmael, as signifying the abrogation of the law and the power of the Gospel. Hence also a rule has been handed down: that when something occurs in the Scriptures which, according to the simple narrative, or according to the grammatical sense, seems slight, or even absurd, or certainly has nothing of doctrine in it, then necessity itself urges us to look for a higher meaning and to hunt out the mystery. On this matter Augustine, in book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 6, and Origen, in the eleventh homily on the book of Numbers. Usefulness itself sometimes suggests seeking allegorical interpretations, and often necessity itself does so; otherwise they are scarcely to be employed. But we have treated this matter more fully elsewhere, above in chapter seven, where it was shown that Christ was signified by a type in Melchizedek. Accordingly we have here a varied and manifold teaching. First, indeed, that the godly are tested by the divine will, but chiefly for their own progress and also as an example to others; and likewise that in temptations it is needful for the strong to stand firm and not be broken by any suggestions, whether of our flesh or of the devil. Second, we have that faith in temptations always looks to the promises, and ought also to judge, even where countless hindrances seem to concur, that God will nevertheless fulfil his promises, provided that we remain steadfast in faith. Third, we have that faith ought always to look to the omnipotence and mercy of God, and to judge that God makes things that are not to be at once, and even raises the living from the dead, so that he may fulfil his promises and work our salvation. Fourth, that particle "in a parable" [ἐν παραβολῇ] admonishes us that sometimes we should hunt out mysteries, especially in the histories of the Old Testament and of the holy fathers, who for the most part by their actions bore a type of the things to be done through Christ. So far concerning the faith of Abraham, in preaching which the apostle was not without cause lengthy, since from it we can learn very many most useful things. "By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come" (Heb. 11.20). Fifth, the example of the induction established concerning Isaac, justified by faith, is taken from the cause and end of the blessing which he bestowed upon his sons; the sentence is: Isaac blessed his sons, praying for them all good things in the future. But good things in the future are not sought except with faith, since faith is properly "the substance [ὑπόστασις] of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen" (Heb. 11.1). Therefore, that Isaac blessed his sons was done by a certain excellent faith. The force of the argument lies in the phrase "concerning things to come," by which indeed the nature of faith is properly denoted. For faith always looks to things future and not seen. The history touched on here is written in Gen. 27. Before we explain it, we must consider why the apostle, about to expound the faith of Isaac, chose this action rather than some other, since there are indeed several others, and notable ones, from which his faith could be set forth splendidly.

units.la: Nam & Genes. 25. narratur, quod, cū anno aetatis quadragesimo duxisset vxorem Rebeccam, eaq; esset sterilis, orauerit subinde Dominum pro ea, ac non nisi vicesimo anno, id est, aetatis Isaac sexagesimo, genuit gemellos.
units.tr: For in Genesis 25 we read that when Isaac was forty years old and had taken Rebekah as his wife, and she was barren, he prayed to the Lord repeatedly on her behalf, and that she bore twins only in the twentieth year, that is, when Isaac was sixty.

units.la: Nonne autem in precationibus illis, & longa adeo mora egregie exercita est eius fides? Capite vigesimosexto narratur, quomodo voci Domini obedierit, promissionibusque adhaeserit: quod certe fidei praeclarum erat opus: Sic autem ibi legitur: Orta fame abijt Isaac ad Abimelech regem Palaestinorum in Gerara: Apparuitque ei Dominus minus, & ait: ne descendas in Aegyptum, sed quiescE in terra quam dixero tibi.
units.tr: Surely his faith was also admirably exercised in those prayers and in so long a delay? In chapter 26 we are told how he obeyed the voice of the Lord and clung to the promises, which was certainly a notable work of faith. The text reads: "Because of a famine Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines in Gerar. And the Lord appeared to him and said: Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land that I shall tell you."

units.la: Et peregrinare in ea, eroq; tecum, & benedicā tibi: tibi enim & semini tuo dabo universas regiones has, complens iuramentum, quod spopondi Abraham patri tuo. Et multiplicabo semen tuum, sicut stellas caeli, daboq; posteris tuis uniuersas regiones has: & benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terrae: & mox sequitur.
units.tr: "Sojourn in it, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and to your seed I will give all these lands, fulfilling the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. And I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and I will give all these lands to your posterity, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." And soon after it follows:

units.la: Mansit itaq; Isaac in Geraris. Ecce obedientia: & non dubium, quin crediderit, sicut tali promissioni credidit etiam Abraham, imputatumq; est ei ad iustitiam. Rursus eodem capite, cum Isaac abijsset in Berfabe, apparuit ei Dominus in ipsa nocte, dicens: Ego sum Dominus Abraha patris tui, noli timere, quia ego tecum sum: benedicā tibi & multiplicabo semen tuum, propter seruum meum Abraham. Itaq; aedificauit ibi altare Domino, & invocato nomine Domini extedit tabernaculum. Ecce iterum materia & argumentu fidei. Cur abhis nullas sumpsit probationes fidei Isaac apostolus? Respondetur: primo, ideo non respicit ad ista apostolus, quia satis constare potest, fidem in illis egregie exercitam, ex ijs quae prius dicta sunt de Abrahamo. Prorsus enim paria fuerunt: & quiuis intelligit, quae ad praedicandam fidem Abrahae conducunt, eadem conducere ad praedicanda fide Isaac vbi similis est materia. Secundo: in eo quod Isaac benedixerit filijs suis, clarius elucet fides ipsius, quàm in omnibus alijs. Praeterquà enim quod in benedictione facta videatur aperta ipsius de expectatione rerum futurarum confessio tum vero haec ipsa benedictio fundamentū habet in promissionibus omnib. antecedetibus, ad quas respiciebat Isaac, & quibus innitebatur, & propter quas sperabat omnia in posterum perficienda. In benedictione hac continebat tacitè quaedam omnium promissionum, quę praecesserant tā ad Abrahamū, quàm ad Isaac factarū. Quomodo enim ausus fuisset adeo magna precari, & quodámodo pro certo promittere filio Iacob (ita enim dicebat: benedixi ei, & erit benedictus) nisi maximā fidem habuisset in antecedentes promissiones? Rectè igitur factum ab Apostolo, qui hoc factum potiùs, quàm aliquod aliud pro testimonio fidei Isaac proponendū duxit. Nunc videamus, quomodo id se habeat. Genef.27. scribitur, Isaac senem, & iam prae aetate caligantem euocasse filium Esau maiorem natu, iussisseq; vt venando aliquid caperet, atque eo allato, ac bene coćto, benedictionem paternam acciperet. Dum autem Esau foras progreditur, mater Rebecca, quae id audierat, charisimū sibi filium Iacob subornat, ut ipse cito coćto haedo, eoq; ad patrem illato benedictionem accipiat: illaq; fragrantisimis vestibus induit, collū & manus pelliculis texit, ut hirsutus instar Esau videri posset. Quod & factum est. Iacob affert patri cibū coćtum, se Esau esse affirmat: pater contrectatis manibus credidit, licet vox pene prodidisset, esse Iacob: tandē vbi pater bene refectus esset, dixit: accede ad me, & da mihi osculum fili mi, accessit & osculatus est eum: statimq; vt vestimentorum illius fragrantiam sensit, benedicens illi ait: ecce odor filij mei, sicut odor agri pleni, cui benedixit Dominus: det tibi Deus de rore caeli, & de pinguedine terrae, abundantiam frumenti, & vini, & olei. Et seruient tibi populi, & adorét te tribus: esto dominus fratrum tuorum, & incuruentur ante te filij matris tuę: qui maledixerit tibi, sit ille maledictus: & qui benedixerit tibi, benedictionibus repleatur. Vix Isaac sermone impleuerat, & Iacob egressus erat, ecce venit Esau adferens venatione coćtam, & benedictionem poscens: pater admiransdixit, se iam alteri benedixisse, addés: benedixi ei, & erit benedictus: tamen cùm finem precandi & eiulandi Esau non faceret, tandem & ei benedixit pater Isaac, in hunc modum: in pinguedine terrae, & in rore caeli desuper erit benedictio tua. Vives in gladio, & fratri tuo seruies, tępusq; veniet, cum excuties & solues iugum eius de ceruicibus tuis. Ecce igitur, quomodo Isaac benedixerit filijs suis: & quomodo Apostolus obseruet, in hisce benedictionib. fidem Isaac egregie deprehendi. Sed, dicat aliquis: nihil video hic singulare, aut valde praedicandum: primum est simplex comprecatio in vtraq; benedictione: & sic solet quiuis bene precari suo amico Deinde vtraq; uersatur circa bona temporalia in quę fides non usque adeo est intenta: cū per eam potiùs apprehendatur bona spiritualia. Respondendum, ut supra diximus, primū Isaac non potuisse vlla bona suis filijs optare, vel sperare multo minus sic certò polliceri, nisi certus fuisset per fidem de Dei misericordia. Secundo: benedictiones hae totae innite bantur promissionibus, quae antecesserat, quae reuera erat de bonis spiritualibus. Tertiò haec est veluti regula, quod omnes promissiones de rebus temporalibus praesupponunt priùs promissiones de rebus spiritualib. & propter has illae expectantur. Quartò hoc est argumentum, quod & Isaac, & ipse filius Iacob inprimis, respexerunt ad bona spiritualia, quia promissa temporalia non sunt impleta. Neq; enim ipse Isaac acceperat promissa temporaliter: neq; etiam Iacob: quia non seruierunt ei fratres aut populi, sed ipse potiùs seruiuit Esau, & aliis populis.
units.tr: "So Isaac remained in Gerar." See his obedience! And there is no doubt that he believed, just as Abraham believed such a promise, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Again in the same chapter, when Isaac had gone to Beersheba, the Lord appeared to him in the same night, saying: "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father; do not fear, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your seed for the sake of my servant Abraham." So he built an altar there to the Lord, called on the name of the Lord, and pitched his tent. Here again is the material and the proof of faith. Why did the Apostle take no proofs of Isaac's faith from these? The answer is, first, that the Apostle does not look to these because it can readily be seen that his faith was admirably exercised in them, from what was said before about Abraham. For they were entirely alike, and anyone understands that whatever serves to proclaim the faith of Abraham serves equally to proclaim the faith of Isaac where the material is similar. Second: in the fact that Isaac blessed his sons, his faith shines out more clearly than in all the others. Besides the fact that in that blessing there appears an open confession of his expectation of future things, this very blessing rests on all the preceding promises, to which Isaac looked, on which he leaned, and on account of which he hoped that everything would be fulfilled in time to come. In this blessing he tacitly included certain things from all the promises that had gone before, made both to Abraham and to Isaac. For how would he have dared to pray for such great things, and to promise, as it were with certainty, to his son Jacob (for so he said: "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed"), had he not had the greatest faith in the earlier promises? Rightly, then, did the Apostle judge that this deed, rather than any other, should be set forth as the testimony of Isaac's faith. Now let us see how this stands. In Genesis 27 it is written that Isaac, old and already dim-sighted with age, summoned his elder son Esau and bade him go hunting and bring back something, and that, when it was brought and well cooked, he should receive his father's blessing. While Esau was going out, his mother Rebekah, who had heard this, prepared her dearly beloved son Jacob, so that he might quickly cook a kid, bring it to his father and receive the blessing. She dressed him in very fragrant garments and covered his neck and hands with skins, so that he might appear hairy like Esau. And so it was done. Jacob brought his father cooked food and declared that he was Esau. The father, feeling his hands, believed him, although the voice had almost given him away, that it was Jacob. At last, when his father had been well refreshed, he said: "Come near to me, and give me a kiss, my son." He came near and kissed him, and immediately, when he smelled the fragrance of his garments, he blessed him, saying: "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain, wine and oil. Let peoples serve you and tribes bow down to you; be lord over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow before you. Let whoever curses you be cursed, and whoever blesses you be filled with blessings." Scarcely had Isaac finished speaking, and Jacob had gone out, when Esau came bringing game he had cooked and asking for the blessing. The father, astonished, said that he had already blessed another, adding: "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed." Yet since Esau did not cease praying and weeping, at last Isaac his father blessed him too, in this way: "Your blessing will be in the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above.
