You will live by the sword and serve your brother; and the time will come when you shake off his yoke from your neck." See, then, how Isaac blessed his sons, and how the Apostle observes that in these blessings the faith of Isaac is clearly discerned. But someone may say: "I see nothing singular here, nothing to be greatly praised. First, it is a simple prayer in each blessing, and this is how anyone customarily blesses a friend. Second, both concern temporal goods, in which faith is not so much engaged, since by faith spiritual goods are rather laid hold of." The reply is, as we said above: first, Isaac could not have wished any goods for his sons, still less hoped for them or promised them so confidently, unless he had been certain, through faith, of God's mercy. Second, these blessings all rested on the promises that had gone before, which were truly about spiritual goods. Third, this is as it were a rule: all promises about temporal things presuppose earlier promises about spiritual things, and it is on account of these that the former are looked for. Fourth, this is the argument: both Isaac and, above all, Jacob his son looked to spiritual goods, because the temporal promises were not fulfilled. For Isaac himself had not received the promised things in the temporal sense, nor had Jacob, since brothers and peoples did not serve him; rather, he himself served Esau and other peoples.

units.la: Sic enim solet fieri, ut tèporales promissiones non semper impleatur, propterea, quòd Deus vult animos credentium erigere ad expetendum expectandumq; bona spiritualia, &c. Qua de re alias à nobis dictum est: & Augustinus copiosè de ciuitate Dei lib. 17. cap. 10. 11. Hoc verò est, quod apostolus exprimere voluit, quòd Isaac benedixerit filijs, de futuris. Subindicat namq; Isaac respexisse ad omnes promissiones, quę antecesserant, eisq; fidem habuisse, & propterea etiam expectasse bona futura, potissimum spiritualia, æterna, & cœlestia, quæ proprie possunt futura appellari, cùm terrena ista vocetur ut plurimum præsentia. Et sic hac particula, de futuris, natura fidei perapte exprimitur, sicut ex definitione fidei constare satis poterit. Sed & hoc notandum, euidens fidei argumentum esse in eo quod dixit Isaac, Benedixi ei, & erit benedictus. Hoc certè totum à solo Deo prouenire poterat & per gratuitam misericordiam. Et respiciebat procul dubio in verbum Dei, quod ante natiuitatem filiorum dictum erat, Maior seruiet minori. Item quod dixit, seruiat tibi populi, & adorent te tribus, haud dubiè non ad temporale regnum, sed potius ad spirituale regnum Christi, qui ex Iacob erat nasciturus, referri debet, cuius regno subijciendi vere populi & tribus: alias certè nunquàm fuit impleta illa benedictio, si temporaliter illam respiciamus. Item in benedictione Esau, illud, tèpusq; veniet, cum excutias & soluas iugum eius de ceruicibus tuis, significat clarè, quòd Iudaei post lapsum suum aliquando restituerentur atq; iterum populus Dei fierent, & libertatem euangelicam consequeretur. Ita nanq; per duos fratres oportet intelligi duos populos Iudaicu, inquâ, & gentiles: sicut etiam Dominus consultus dixerat, cum Rebecca esset grauida, Genes. 25. Duae gentes sunt in vtero tuo, & duo populi ex ventre tuo diuidentur, populusq; populum superabit, & maior seruiet minori. Esau igitur populum Iudaicum significat, qui maior natu et ius primogenituræ apud Deum habuit: Iacob autem getiles, qui longè post, sunt vocati, & tamen postea ius primogenituræ & benedictione obtinent, dum euangliu amplectuntur. Et quod adeò nullo precio nulloq; labore Iacob simul primogenituram obtinuit, simulque benedictione, aptè gratuita notatur misericordia, quæ per fidem contingit absq; legis operibus. Esau autem benedictionem principalem non obtinet, etiamsi fellus & in venatione laborans: sic & populus Iudaicus etiamsi in lege multum laborarit, tamen iusti tiam & benedictionem nõ est assecutus, sed cogitur seruire iuniori fratri: quado etiã nũc videmus Iudæos amisso regno, sacerdotio debere audire gentes. At nihilominus excutient hoc iugum, quando ad Christum conuersi libertatem euangelicam amplectentur, & fient vnũ ouile, sub uno agentes pastore: & ex duobus populis fiet vnus: qua de re plenius Roman. 9. 10. 11. Non dubium autem, quin ad ista spiritualia Isaac respexerit, & ex promissionib. quæ antecesserat, plenè edoctus fuerit, ita debere omnia perfici. Quod cũ ita se habeat, rectè dicitur, in his benedictionibus fidè Isaac clarè emicuisse: & rectè Apostolus dixit, fidem eius circa res futuras versatam. Ac verum est quidem, quod Iacob etiam aliàs benedictione acceperit ab Isaac, quæ certè præclara erat, & recitatur Geneseos 28. vbi Isaac iubet Iacob proficisci in Mesopotamiam, vt ibi vxorem ducat: sed Apostolus potissimum respexit in eam, quam suprà recensuimus. Cæterum hic discimus, quanti eiusmodi benedictiones, quales solent parentes filijs impendere, sint faciendę. Ego benedixi ei, inquit, & erit benedictus. Ergo Deus respicit comprecationes piorum parentum, & curat efficaces fieri: quando enim sunt testimonia fidei, Deus illas approbat. Quae de re alias à nobis dictum est. Audiant haec pij iuuenes, ac discant obtemperare parentibus, atq; omnibus, qui parentum loco sunt, id est, magistratibus, præceptoribus, & similibus. Dum hi honorantur à te, honoras in his ipsum Deum. Si verò Deum honoras mercedem accipies. Huc pertinet promissio illa præcepto primo posterioris tabulæ annexa, Honora patrem, &c. Per fidem Iacob moriens singulis filijs Ioseph benedixit, & adorauit fastigium virgæ illius: exemplum inductionis de Iacob per fidem iustificato. Proponuntur autem duæ fidei eius probationes seu demonstrationes: prior sumpta est, vti & in præcedeti exemplo factum est, à causa & fine benedictionis, quam Iacob impendit filijs Ioseph. De hac probatione prius dicemus. Sicut suprà diximus de exemplo Isaac: Ita & hic de exemplo Iacob dicere possumus, multa alia potuisse inueniri ad comprobandam fidem Iacob: veluti quod Genes. 27. ausus sit se exponere periculo in peteda benedictione, pro qua reportare potuisset maledictionem: vbi sine dubio mater animabat eum, ex eo quod dictum erat ante natiuitatem ipsius, maior seruiet minori: Item Genes. 28. visio angelorum ascendentiu ac descendentiu per scalam, cui Dominus in cœlo innitebatur, dices: ego sum Dominus Deus Abrahã patris tui & Deus Isaac: terram, in qua dormis, tibi dabo & semini tuo. Eritq; semen tuum quasi puluis terræ, dilataberis ad orientem & occidentem, & septentrionem, & meridiem, & benedicetur in te & in semine tuo cunctæ tribus terræ. Et ero custos tuus quocunq; perrexeris, & reducam te in terram hanc, nec dimittam, nisi compleuero vniuersa, quæ dixi. Huic promissioni dubium non est, quin crediderit: & imputatum est illi ad iustitiam. Item Genes. 31. audit Deum iubentem, ut è Mesopotamia reuerteretur animent
units.tr: For it is usual that temporal promises are not always fulfilled, because God wills to raise the minds of believers to desire and wait for spiritual goods, etc. We have spoken of this matter elsewhere, and Augustine treats it at length in the City of God, book 17, chapters 10 and 11. This is what the apostle wished to express when he says that Isaac blessed his sons concerning things to come. For he indicates that Isaac looked to all the promises that had gone before, trusted in them, and therefore also waited for future goods, chiefly the spiritual, eternal, and heavenly goods, which can properly be called "future," since these earthly things are usually called "present." So this phrase, "concerning things to come," expresses the nature of faith very aptly, as can sufficiently be seen from the definition of faith. But it should also be noted that there is clear evidence of faith in what Isaac said: I have blessed him, and he will be blessed. Certainly all of this could come only from God, and through his free mercy. Without doubt Isaac had in view the word of God spoken before the birth of the sons: "The elder shall serve the younger." Likewise, when he said, "Let peoples serve you, and tribes bow down to you," this without doubt must be referred not to a temporal kingdom but rather to the spiritual kingdom of Christ, who was to be born from Jacob, and to whose rule peoples and tribes truly are to be subjected. Otherwise that blessing was never fulfilled, if we take it in a temporal sense. Likewise in the blessing of Esau, the words "the time will come when you shake off and loose his yoke from your neck" clearly signify that the Jews, after their fall, would at some point be restored and would again become the people of God, and would obtain evangelical liberty. For through the two brothers we must understand the two peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile, just as the Lord, when consulted while Rebekah was pregnant, had said (Genesis 25): "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be separated from your body; one people will overcome the other, and the elder will serve the younger." Esau therefore signifies the Jewish people, who was the elder by birth and had the right of the firstborn before God. Jacob, however, signifies the Gentiles, who were called long afterwards, and yet later obtain the right of the firstborn and the blessing, as they embrace the gospel. And that Jacob obtained at once the birthright and the blessing at no price and with no labour is fittingly a sign of gratuitous mercy, which comes through faith apart from the works of the law. Esau, though he was a hunter and labored in the field, did not obtain the chief blessing; so also the Jewish people, though they labored much under the law, did not attain righteousness and the blessing, but are compelled to serve their younger brother. For even now we see that the Jews, having lost their kingdom and priesthood, must listen to the Gentiles. Nevertheless they will shake off this yoke when, converted to Christ, they embrace evangelical liberty, and they will become one flock, living under one shepherd, and the two peoples will become one (on this matter more fully, Romans 9, 10, and 11). There is no doubt that Isaac looked to these spiritual things, and, being fully taught by the promises that had gone before, understood that all these things must be brought to completion. Since this is so, it is rightly said that faith shone clearly in these blessings of Isaac, and the apostle rightly said that his faith was occupied with things to come. It is indeed true that Jacob also at another time received a blessing from Isaac, which was certainly an excellent one and is recounted in Genesis 28, where Isaac bids Jacob set out for Mesopotamia to take a wife there. But the apostle principally had regard to the blessing we have just recounted. Moreover, here we learn how highly such blessings, such as parents are wont to bestow on their children, are to be esteemed. "I have blessed him," he says, "and he will be blessed." Therefore God regards the prayers of godly parents and takes care that they are effective, for when they are testimonies of faith, God approves them. This too we have spoken of elsewhere. Let godly young people hear this and learn to obey their parents, and all who stand in the place of parents, that is, magistrates, teachers, and the like. While these are honored by you, you honor God himself in them. If you honor God, you will receive a reward. To this belongs the promise attached to the first commandment of the second table, "Honor your father," etc. "By faith Jacob, dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff" (Hebrews 11): an example of the leading of Jacob, who was justified by faith. Two proofs or demonstrations of his faith are set forth: the first is taken, as also in the preceding example, from the cause and the end of the blessing which Jacob bestowed on the sons of Joseph. We shall speak of this proof first. As we said above concerning the example of Isaac, so here too concerning the example of Jacob we may say that many other things could be found to confirm Jacob's faith: for instance, that in Genesis 27 he dared to expose himself to danger in seeking the blessing, for which he might have brought back a curse, where without doubt his mother encouraged him, because of what had been said before his birth, "The elder shall serve the younger." Likewise in Genesis 28 there is the vision of the angels ascending and descending by the ladder on which the Lord was leaning in heaven, saying: "I am the Lord God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your seed. Your seed shall be like the dust of the earth; you shall spread out to the east and the west and the north and the south, and in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. And I will be your keeper wherever you go, and I will bring you back into this land, nor will I leave you until I have accomplished all that I have said." There is no doubt that he believed this promise, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Likewise in Genesis 31 he hears God bidding him return from Mesopotamia, and is encouraged.

units.la: Augustinus. Aliud fidei argumentum. Regnū Christi spirituale. Iudæorum restitutio. Esau primogenitus. Iudæorum libertas. fides Isaac circa res futuras. Magnificicedæ parcum bene dictiones. 6. exemplum in ductionis Iacob. 1. probatio fidei Iacobi à causa & fine benedictionis. 1. periculum Iacobi in peteda paterna benedictione. 2. uisio angelorum in Bethel. 3. Iacob redit Deo iubente ex Mesopotamia in terra Chanaan. in terram Chanaã: quod et fecit, postquam iam vinginti annis seruij sset socero Labano. In qua seruitute tàm diuturna, & migratione ad mandatum Dei fides eius non leuiter exercitata est. Item fidei erat illa precatio, qua Genes. 32. cum rediret ex Mesopotamia, orabat Dominũ, vt propter promissiones factas tueretur ipsum atq; erueret è manibus Esau. Item fidei erat, quod in eodem capite scribitur luctatus cum Angelo, & percussus ab eodem in femore, & tamen noluisse dimittere, nisi benedictione ab eodem acciperet: quo tempore ab angelo immutatum illi est nomen, ut Israel, id est, præualens Deo vocare tur, & non amplius Iacob (supplantans) Item fides elucebat in Iacob, cùm Deus (Genes. 35) iuberet illum ascendere, à Salem, ubi habitarat, in Bethel seu Luzam, & obediuit, ibiq; iterũ accepit benedictionem & promissionem à Deo hisce verbis; Non vocaberis ultra Iacob sed Israel erit in nomen tuum. Et appellauit eum Israel, dixitq; ei, Ego Deus omnipotens, crescè & multiplicare, gentes & populi nationũ ex te erunt, reges de lumbis tuis egredientur. Terraq; quam dedi Abraham & Isaac; dabo tibi & semini tuo post te. Item fidei erat, quod, cum Ioseph narrasset somnium suum de sole & luna, vndecim stellis ipsum adoratibus, Genes. 37. pater rem tacitè cõsiderauit. Item fides eius tum mirabiliter exercita est, quando relicta terra Chanaã, quæ ipsi & semini eius promissa erat profectus est in Aegyptum, Deo sic ad ipsum dicente, Ego sum fortissimus Deus patris tui, noli timere, sed descendere in Aegyptum, quia in gentem magnam faciam te ibi. Ego descendã tecum illuc, & ego inde adducam te reuertentem. Ioseph quoq; ponet manus tuas super oculos tuos: Ex singulis hisce actionibus & plerisque aliis, quas præterimus, potuisset apostolus argumenta colligere ad probandam fidem Abrahæ. Sed maluit illud in primis de benedictione, quam ille impendit filijs Ioseph, seligere, propter eandem causas, quas in præcedentis exempli expositione aperuimus: neque opus esse puto, ut eandem repetamus. Videbimus interim, quod cognitu necessarium est, pertinens ad præsente locũ & benedictione filiorũ Ioseph. Genes. 48. scribitur, quo Ioseph, ægrotãte patre, & morte immi- nente, adierit eũ comitatus duobus filijs Manasse & Ephraim: pater cõmemorãs pauca de promissionib. ad se à Deo factis, duos illos filios petit pro suis numerari, siue eos adoptát, ideoq; etiã benedictione voluit eis impertiri. Ioseph adorato patre illos obtulit, vt benedictione acciperent, Manassem maiorẽ natu cõstituens ad patris dextrã, Ephraim verò minore ad sinistrã. Pater mox manus extendens, & veluti cãcellans, dexterã suam imposuit capiti Ephraim iunioris, sinistram verò capiti Manasse senioris, atq; in hæc verba benè precatus est. Deus, in cuius conspectu ambulauerunt patres mei Abraham & Isaac, Deus, qui pascit me ab adolescentia mea usque in præsentè diem: angelus, qui eruit me de cũctis malis, benedicat pueris istis, & inuocetur super eos nomen meum, nomina quoque patrum meorum, Abraham & Isaac, & crescant in multitudinem super terram. Tum Ioseph admirans, & putans patrem errore (nam caligabant oculi præ senectute) manum dextrã imposuisse Ephraim, sinistram verò Manasse, conabatur manus patris aliter transponere: sed pater, quandoquidem diuino impulsu ita fecerat, renuit, dicens: scio, fili mi, scio, & ipse quippe erit in populos, & multiplicabitur: sed frater eius minor maior erit illo, & semen illius crescet in gentes. Benedixitq; eis in tempore illo, dicens: in te benedicetur Israel, atque dicetur, faciat tibi Deus, sicut Ephraim & Manasse. Et benedictiones hæ non de temporalibus bonis principaliter, sed de spiritualibus debent accipi: ijsdem de causis, quas supra exposuimus agentes de benedictionibus Isaac. Et certè non possunt nisi spiritualiter accipi, mereq; spiritualia sunt illa verba, Inuocetur super eos nomen meum nomina quoq; patrum meorum Abraham & Isaac: quæ verba precantur, omnes posteros perstare in recta inuocatione & cultu vnius Dei: sicut ipse Iacob perstiterat: vt videlicet promissiones spirituales, inprimis de femine benedicto, possent in illis adimpleri. Vnde etiam factum, vt rectè inuocantes Dominum crebrò appellarint Deum, Deum Iacob, sicut & Deum Abraham, & Deũ Isaac. De Deo Iacob psalmo 19. Exaudiat te Dominus, in die tribulationis protegat te nomen Dei Iacob. psalmo 80. Exultate Deo adiutori nostro, iubilate Deo Iacob. Psal. 45. Dominus virtutum nobiscum, susceptor noster Deus Iacob. Psal. 85. Domine Deus virtutum exaudi orationem nostram, auribus percipe Deus Iacob. Psal. 145. Beatus cuius Deus Iacob adiutor eius, spes eius in Domino Deo ipsius. Itè illa verba Iacob, in te benedicet Israel, atq; dicetur, faciat tibi Deus sicut Ephraim & Manasse, quomodo poterunt aliter accipi, quâ de benedictione spirituali? Quæcunque quis posset alteri precari optima, talia precabitur, qualia contigerunt Ephraim & Manasse: quibus constat spiritualem benedictionem: item temporalem, quæ ex spirituali præcedenti fluit, largissimè contigisse. Psalmo 59. & 107. Ephraim celebratur, vt fortitudo capitis, & Psalmo septuagesimonono, primo loco Ephraim numeratur, haud dubio propter benedictionis spiritualis præminentiam, 6 pastor Israel ausculta, qui ducis cis tanquā pecudes Ioseph: qui sedes inter Cherubim, splendē. Coram Ephraim, & Beniamin, & Manasseh suscita fortitudinem tuam, & veni in salutem nobis. Ad spiritualia igitur respexisse Iacob in sua benedictione manifestum est: si autem respexit ad spiritualia, apte ex ea benedictione argumentum fidei ducitur.
units.tr: Augustine. Another argument for faith. The spiritual kingdom of Christ. The restoration of the Jews. Esau the firstborn. The freedom of the Jews. The faith of Isaac concerning future things. The magnificent blessings of the patriarchs. 6. Example of Jacob's leading. 1. Proof of Jacob's faith from the cause and end of the blessing. 1. The danger Jacob faced in seeking his father's blessing. 2. The vision of angels at Bethel. 3. Jacob returns from Mesopotamia to the land of Canaan at God's command. He did so after he had already served his father-in-law Laban for twenty years. In that long servitude and in his migration at God's command, his faith was not lightly tested. Likewise it was an act of faith to make the prayer recorded in Genesis 32, when he was returning from Mesopotamia and asked the Lord to keep him safe, for the sake of the promises made to him, and to rescue him from the hands of Esau. Likewise it was an act of faith, as Genesis records in the same chapter, that he wrestled with the angel and was struck by him in the thigh, and yet was unwilling to let him go unless he received a blessing from him. At that time the angel changed his name, so that he would be called Israel, that is, one who prevails with God, and no longer Jacob (the supplanter). Faith also shone out in Jacob when God (Genesis 35) bade him go up from Salem, where he had been living, to Bethel or Luz, and he obeyed. There again he received the blessing and the promise from God in these words: "You shall no longer be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel." And he called him Israel and said to him: "I am God Almighty; increase and multiply. Nations and peoples of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come out of your loins. And the land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you and to your seed after you." Likewise it was an act of faith, when Joseph had told his dream of the sun and moon and eleven stars bowing down to him, that his father, as Genesis 37 says, quietly pondered the matter. His faith was also wonderfully tested when he left the land of Canaan, which had been promised to him and his seed, and set out for Egypt, God speaking to him thus: "I am the mighty God of your father; do not fear, but go down into Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I will go down with you there, and I will bring you up again from there. Joseph also shall put his hands upon your eyes." From each of these actions, and from many others which we pass over, the apostle could have gathered arguments to prove the faith of Abraham. But he preferred above all to choose the blessing which Jacob bestowed on the sons of Joseph, for the same reasons which we set out in the exposition of the previous example. I think there is no need to repeat them. Meanwhile we shall consider what must be known, and what pertains to the present passage, namely the blessing of Joseph's sons. Genesis 48 records that Joseph, when his father was ill and death was near, went to him accompanied by his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. The father, recalling a few things about the promises made to him by God, asked that these two sons be counted as his own, or adopted them, and so wished to bestow the blessing on them as well. Joseph, having bowed down before his father, presented them so that they might receive the blessing, placing Manasseh, the elder, at his father's right hand and Ephraim, the younger, at his left. The father at once stretched out his hands, as if crossing them, and laid his right hand on the head of the younger, Ephraim, and his left on the head of the elder, Manasseh, and blessed them with these words: "God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, God who has fed me from my youth until this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evils, bless these boys; let my name be named upon them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude upon the earth." Then Joseph, marvelling and thinking that his father had made a mistake (for his eyes were dim with age), placed his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh, and tried to change the position of his father's hands. But his father, since he had done this by divine impulse, refused, saying: "I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he shall be multiplied; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall grow into nations." And he blessed them on that day, saying: "In you shall Israel be blessed, and it shall be said: God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh." These blessings are to be understood principally not of temporal goods but of spiritual ones, for the same reasons which we set out above when treating the blessings of Isaac. Indeed they can only be understood spiritually, and the words "let my name be named upon them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac" are spiritual words. They pray that all posterity may persist in the right invocation and worship of the one God, as Jacob himself had persisted; so that, namely, the spiritual promises, above all concerning the blessed seed, might be fulfilled in them. Hence it also happened that those who rightly invoked the Lord often called him the God of Jacob, just as the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac. Of the God of Jacob, Psalm 20 (19): "May the Lord hear you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you." Psalm 81 (80): "Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob." Psalm 46 (45): "The Lord of hosts is with us; our refuge is the God of Jacob." Psalm 85 (84): "O Lord God of hosts, hear our prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob." Psalm 146 (145): "Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God." Likewise, how could those words of Jacob, "In you shall Israel be blessed, and it shall be said: God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh," be understood otherwise than of spiritual blessing? Whatever good thing one might wish for another, he would pray for things such as came to Ephraim and Manasseh, to whom, it is evident, both the spiritual blessing and also the temporal blessing, which flows from the preceding spiritual one, came most abundantly. In Psalms 59 (60) and 107 (108), Ephraim is praised as the strength of the head; and in Psalm 79 (80) Ephraim is named first, no doubt on account of the pre-eminence of the spiritual blessing. "O shepherd of Israel, give ear, you who lead Joseph like a flock; you who sit between the cherubim, shine forth before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh; stir up your strength and come to save us." It is therefore plain that in his blessing Jacob looked to spiritual things; and if he looked to spiritual things, an argument of faith is fittingly drawn from that blessing.

units.la: Et adorauit fastigium virgae illius) Haec est secunda demonstratio fidei Iacob, sed, ut apparet, longe petita, videlicet a signo: & praeterea cuius verba non porsus veritati hebraicae consentiunt, ut quidam arbitratur. Quare, priusquam declaremus, quomodo fides Iacob hic eluxerit, certa est quaerenda nobis sententia. Proinde apostolus sic habet, Porro prorsus eodem pacto habent Septuaginta, Hoc est, & adorauit ad fastigium virgae illius, scilicet Ioseph. Hebraica autem veritas sic habet, quod vertut plerique omnes, & adorauit Israel ad caput lectuli. Atqui istud non videtur quicquam facere ad institutum praesens, ad probandum videlicet ex eo facto fidem Iacob. Praeterea & Septuaginta & apostolus videntur ab hebraica veritate deviare. Ut igitur scrupum omnem tollamus, prius cognoscenda sunt nonnulla de historia. Proinde sic scribitur Genes. 47. Habitauit ergo Israel in Aegypto, id est, in terra Gosan, & possedit eam, auctus q; est & multiplicatus nimis. Et vixit in ea decem & septem annis, factiq; sunt omnes dies vitae illius centum quadraginta septem annorum: cumq; appropinquare cerneret diem mortis suae, vocavit filium suum Iosephi & dixit ad eum: si inveni gratiam in conspectu tuo, pone manum tuam sub femore meo, & facies mihi misericordiam & veritatem, ut non sepelias me in Aegypto: sed dormiam cum patribus meis, & auferas me de terra hac, codasq; in sepulchro maiorum meorum. Cui respondit Iosephi: ego faciam, quod iusisti. Et ille, Iura ergo, inquit, mihi: quo iurante adorauit Israel Dominum conversus ad lectuli caput. En historiam. Atq; ita vertit Hieronymus, qui & libro quaestionum seu traditionum hebraicarum in Genesin reprehendit eos, qui ita accipiunt verba haec, quasi sententia sit, adorasse Iacob summitatem sceptri Iosephi, sic videlicet potestate Iosephi honorando & adorando: haberi in hebraeo, & adorauit Israel ad caput lectuli, quod scilicet, postquam ei iurauerat filius securus de petitione, quam rogauerat, adoraret Deum contra caput lectuli sui. Et addit, Sanctus quippe, & Deo deditus vir oppressus senectute sic habebat lectulum positum, ut ipse iacetis habitus absq; difficultate ulla adorationem effet paratus. Ita Hieronymus.
units.tr: "And he worshipped on the top of his staff." This is the second demonstration of Jacob's faith, but, as appears, it is far-fetched, namely taken from a sign; and moreover the words do not altogether agree with the Hebrew truth, as some think. Therefore, before we explain how Jacob's faith shone forth here, we must seek out the certain meaning. The apostle thus has it, and the Seventy have it in exactly the same way: "and he worshipped toward the top of his staff," that is, of Joseph. But the Hebrew truth reads, as most translators render it, "and Israel worshipped toward the head of the bed." Yet this does not seem to contribute anything to the present purpose, namely to prove Jacob's faith from that deed. Moreover, both the Seventy and the apostle seem to depart from the Hebrew truth. So, to remove every stumbling block, we must first consider some points of the history. Accordingly Genesis 47 is written thus: "So Israel dwelt in Egypt, that is, in the land of Goshen, and possessed it, and grew and multiplied exceedingly. And he lived there seventeen years, and the days of his life were one hundred and forty-seven years. When he perceived that the day of his death was drawing near, he called his son Joseph and said to him: 'If I have found grace in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and deal kindly and truly with me, that you do not bury me in Egypt; but let me sleep with my fathers, and carry me out of this land, and bury me in their sepulchre.' Joseph answered him: 'I will do as you have commanded.' And he said: 'Swear to me, then.' And when he had sworn, Israel worshipped the Lord, turned toward the head of the bed." Behold the history. And so Jerome translates it; and in his book of Hebrew Questions or Traditions on Genesis he rebukes those who take these words as if the sense were that Jacob worshipped the top of Joseph's sceptre, honouring and worshipping the power of Joseph in that way. In the Hebrew, he says, it reads "and Israel worshipped toward the head of the bed," namely that, after his son had sworn to him concerning the request he had made, he worshipped God facing the head of his own bed. And he adds: "A holy man, devoted to God, weighed down by old age, had his bed so placed that, lying there, he would be ready to worship without any difficulty." So Jerome.

units.la: Augustinus vero sequitur septuaginta, sed non fine moestia. Nam nos habemus in exemplaribus septuaginta, quod retulimus ad Iosephi. Ipse vero legit, mutato spiritu & extrema syllaba, ut tum referatur ad virgam, sive praeposita etiam litera: ut sententia sit, senem adorasse Deum, & quidem innixum suae virgae, quam ipse habebat: vel certe ut quidam volunt, retinendo in manu virgam acceptam a Iosephi. Sed nihil opus est huc confugere. Retinebimus autem nos versionem septuaginta, qua & cernimus in scripto Apostoli, eandemque ostendemus primum non pugnare cum veritate hebraica: deinde etiam optime congruere plenae sententiae: & apostolu amplissime inde collegisse materiam argumenti, quo probaret patriarchae Iacob insignem fidem. Quod ad primum attinet, cum Hebraice habeatur, quod quidem non prorsus male dicitur ad caput lectuli, tamen constat uocem, quae significat lectum, stratum, reclinatorium, significare ite baculum, virgam, sustentaculum. Quare etiam recte vertetur, ad caput virgae. Unde & septuaginta recte verterunt, & Apostolus recte vsurpauit illorum versionem. Neque vero credi debet, septuaginta interpretes sine spiritus afflatu ita reddidisse, ut videlicet in graeco redderent citra ambiguitatem, certa significatione, quae in hebraeo cum ambiguitate accipiuntur: & Spiritus Sanctus procul dubio in eam partem eos movit, quae ad divinam sententiam, & mysteriorum manifestatione foret magis accommoda. Quod ad secundum iam attinet, plena & recta est sententia, cum ita dicitur, Iacob vbi certus esset factus a filio quod vellet ipsum trasferre, adorasse ad caput virgae Iosephi. Principio erat quidā gestus, quo Iacob significaret, se certo credere, quae promisisset filius, & rata habere, adeoq; veluti gratias agere, quod promptum sese exhiberet, quomodo videmus etiamnum hodie, quibusdam gentibus morem esse, ut valedicendo, vel gratias agendo osculentur superioris seu potentioris manu. Secundo, non est absurdum dicere, ita factum a Iacob, quado iam omnia erant adimpleta, quae ille cupiebat, & paratus erat mori, civiliter poterat filium ita pro more gentis honorare, inclinado se ad virgae fiue sceptri, quod dignitatis & magistratus nomine gerebat, summitatem ut videlicet ita declararet, completum vaticinium, quod Iosephi iuuenis praedixerat futurum nempe, ut Pater, & Mater, & Fratres ipsum adorarent. In qua sententia interpretatur verba septuaginta interpretū Chrysostomus, & in enarrationibus huius epistolae, & praeterea libri Genes. homilia 65. vides inquit, senem decrepitum adoratione Iosephi honore declarare, & re ipsa visionis euētū implere. Ac ne cauillus fieret, quod mater
units.tr: Augustine, however, follows the Seventy, but not without misgivings. For in our copies of the Seventy we refer the words to Joseph. He himself reads them differently, changing the spirit and the final syllable so that the words refer to the staff, or with a prefixed letter as well, so that the sense is that the old man worshipped God while leaning on his own staff, which he himself had; or, as some want, while holding in his hand the staff received from Joseph. But there is no need to take refuge in these readings. We will keep the version of the Seventy, which we also see in the writing of the Apostle, and we will show, first, that it does not conflict with the Hebrew truth; second, that it agrees very well with the full sense; and third, that the Apostle has drawn very ample material from it to prove the remarkable faith of the patriarch Jacob. As for the first point, although the Hebrew stands, and it is not altogether wrong to say "at the head of the bed," it is nevertheless certain that the word which means bed, couch or reclining place can also mean a staff, rod or support. Therefore it will rightly be rendered "at the head of the staff." And so the Seventy translated rightly, and the Apostle rightly used their version. Nor should we believe that the Seventy interpreters, without the inspiration of the Spirit, rendered it in such a way that in Greek they expressed, without ambiguity, a definite meaning which in Hebrew is taken ambiguously; the Holy Spirit undoubtedly moved them toward that side which was more suited to the divine sense and to the manifestation of the mysteries. As for the second point, the sense is full and correct when it is said that Jacob, once he was certain from his son that he would be carried away, worshipped at the head of Joseph's staff. In the first place, it was a kind of gesture by which Jacob signified that he firmly believed what his son had promised, and held it as settled, and so in effect gave thanks because he showed himself ready; as we see even today, that among some peoples it is the custom, when taking leave or giving thanks, to kiss the hand of a superior or more powerful man. Second, it is not absurd to say that Jacob did this when all the things he desired had already been accomplished and he was ready to die; he could, in accordance with the custom of the people, honour his son in a civil way, by bowing toward the top of the staff or sceptre which Joseph bore as a sign of his dignity and office, so that he would thereby declare the fulfilment of the prophecy which the young Joseph had foretold, namely that father, mother and brothers would worship him. Chrysostom interprets the words of the Seventy in this sense, in his commentaries on this epistle, and also in homily 65 on the book of Genesis: "You see," he says, "the decrepit old man declaring honour by worshipping Joseph, and in fact fulfilling the outcome of the vision." And lest it be made a quibble that the mother (Reading: "the head of the staff") did not worship Joseph, though Joseph had foretold it, he adds that it is the perpetual manner of Scripture that the whole is signified by the principal part; and so, while it is written plainly that the father worshipped, it should be understood at the same time that the mother would have done the same had she lived. Moreover, wishing to confirm his interpretation, he immediately adds the present passage of Paul to the Hebrews, for there too he makes Paul the author of the epistle. Third, there is nothing absurd in the word "worshipped," as if it had to be supplemented with "the Lord," as is found in the Vulgate edition. It is established that in the manner of Scripture worship is paid to men, especially to those placed in dignity. 2 Sam. 9. "Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and worshipped." 1 Reg. 1. "Bathsheba, with head bowed, worshipped the king," asking that he declare Solomon his successor in the kingdom; likewise, "the king worshipped upon the bed"; and so often. And it is not said that Jacob worshipped the staff or Joseph himself, but "at the head of the staff" [מטה, יתד], so that a gesture of honour toward the staff is understood to be made, in the way it is narrated in Esther 5, where King Ahasuerus, seeing Queen Esther standing in the court, and she pleasing him wonderfully, gaining favour in his eyes, extended toward Esther the golden sceptre which he held in his hand, and Esther, approaching, touched the top of the sceptre. Thus, I say, we should understand that Jacob also worshipped at the top of Joseph's staff.

units.la: Lectio caput virgae. mater non adorauerit Iosephi, de qua tamen Iosephi praedixerat: & sic hunc locum non in telligendum de illa adoratione: addit, scripturae morem esse perpetuum, ut a magis principali totum significetur: & sic dum aperte scribitur patrem adorasse, simul intelligi debere, matrem idem facturam fuisse, si vixisset. Quin etiam confirmare volens, suum interpretationem statim subijcit praesentem locum Pauli ad Hebraeos: nam & ibi Paulum facit autorem epistolae. Tertio: nihil absurdi occurrit propter vocabulum adoradi, quasi propterea esset addendum, sicut in vulgata editione habetur, Dominum. Constat adoratio-nem more Scripturae hominibus, praesertim in dignitate constitutis exhiberi. 2. Sam. 9. Me-phibosth filius Ionathan filij Saulis veniens ad Dauid cecidit super faciem suum & adorauit. 1. reg. 1. vertice inclinato adorauit Bathsheba regem, petitura, ut Solomonem declararet in regno successorem: item, Rex adorauit super lectum: & sic saepius. Et non dicitur, quod Iacob adorauerit virgam aut ipsum Iosephi, sed ad caput virgae, (מטה, יתד) ut intelligatur gestus honoris versus virgam exhibitus, quomodo fere narratur Esther 5. capite, rege Assuerum, cum videret reginam Esther stante in atrio, eaque ei mirifice placeret, gratiam reportans ab oculis eius, extendisse versus Esther sceptrum aureum, quod habebat in manu sua, & accedentem Esther attigisse sceptri summitatem. Sic, inquam, intelligamus, Iacob quoque adorasse ad summitatem virgae Iosephi.
units.tr: The reading is "the head of the staff." Joseph had foretold that his mother too would bow down to him, yet she did not worship him, so this passage is not to be understood of that worship. He adds that it is the constant custom of Scripture for the whole to be signified by its principal part, so that while it is written plainly that the father worshipped, it must at the same time be understood that the mother would have done the same had she lived. Indeed, wishing to confirm his interpretation, he immediately adds the present passage of Paul to the Hebrews, for there too he makes Paul the author of the epistle. Third, nothing absurd arises from the word "worshipped," as if it ought therefore to be supplemented, as in the Vulgate edition, with "the Lord." It is established that in the custom of Scripture worship is paid to men, especially to those placed in dignity. 2 Sam. 9: "Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face and worshipped." 1 Kings 1: "Bathsheba bowed her head and worshipped the king, asking that Solomon be declared successor in the kingdom"; likewise, "the king worshipped upon the bed"; and so often. Nor is it said that Jacob worshipped the staff or Joseph himself, but "at the head of the staff" [מטה, יתד], so that the gesture of honour is understood as directed toward the staff. This is roughly how it is narrated in Esther 5, where King Ahasuerus, seeing Queen Esther standing in the court, and she greatly pleasing him, and obtaining favour from his eyes, extended toward Esther the golden sceptre he held in his hand, and Esther, approaching, touched the tip of the sceptre. So, I say, we should understand that Jacob also worshipped at the tip of Joseph's staff.

units.la: Quarto: sicut statuendum est, a patriarcha Iacob nihil abs re, & citra significationem facti: ita spiritum Sanctum non abs re, & mandasse literis & expresse, sententiam pariter in Hebraeo, & apud Septuaginta, quod Iacob ad caput virgae adorarit. Ibi enim Iacob, postquam mandasset transferri corpus suum in terram promissam Chanaan, cum adoraret ad caput virgae, testatum, se vere credere omnes promissiones, quae de occupanda a se & posteris suis terra, & spiritualibus beneficijs adiunctis factae erant, accipiendas: atq; ita egregiam eo gestu fidei edidisse confessionem. Unde Apostolus suum hic argumentum mutuatur. Et sic solent, uti diximus, vbi quid confirmare volunt veteres, adoratione, vel manuum coniunctione id declarare: sicut & 1. reg. 1. narratur Bathsheba, cum audiuisset a Dauid, Solomonem regnaturum, se inclinasse facie tenus in terram, & incurvasse se ante regem, ac dixisse, viuat Dominus meus rex Dauid in saeculum. Si ibi Dauid habuisset virgam, tum dictum fuisset, quod adorasset ad virgam Dauid. Talis erat sine dubio gestus ipsius Iacob, & ita adorauit ad caput virgae Iosephi. Ergo adoratio Iacob ad caput virgae Iosephi, post manda-tum de se transferendo, signum erat, quo ille declarabat, se credere, quod Iosephi ipsum transferret: deinde, quod adimplendae forent omnes promissiones, quae de terra Chanaa per ipsum & posteros occupanda facta fuerant. Addamus, si lubet, etiam de regno Christi ex semine ipsius expectandi, quod haud dubie patriarcha Iacob vidit in Iosephi filij dignitate adumbratum. Neque enim improbatur mihi, quod Chrysostomus super Genesin scribens scribit, Iacob ita ex fide adorasse, quia praevidebat futurum, ut ex semine ipsius regiu semen exoriretur. Agnouit sine dubio Iacob venturum Christum, cuius regnum in Israel pariter & Aegyptios, id est, in Iudaeos & gentiles extenderetur. Quod eo iustius ita licet accipere, quod agnouerat ille, filium suum Iosephum in valde multis typum Christi gessisse: sicut pater Abraham typum Christi cernebat in filio suo Isaac. Reuera enim Iosephi Christum adumbrauit typice in multis. 1. Quia accusauit fratres suos apud patrem de crimine patrato: Christus proponit humanam miseriam patri, & pro peccatis satisfacit. 2. Iosephi plus amatur prae cunctis fratribus. Christus Dei patris est naturalis & substantialis filius, ideoq; dilectissimus. Tertio: Iosephi proponit somnia de se adorando a suis omnib. Christus proponit doctrinam sanam, testificaturq; suam diuinitatem propter quam adoradus & agnoscendus est seruator omnium. Hinc inuidia magna grauatus est. Quarto: missus est Iosephi in agrum, ut quaereret fratres suos, & nunciaret postea patri, num prospera omnia. Ita Christus missus in mundum, ut quaereret fratres, & salutem apud patrem procuraret.
units.tr: Fourth: just as it must be held that nothing that the patriarch Jacob did was without cause and without meaning, so the Holy Spirit did not without cause and expressly commit to writing, both in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint, the statement that Jacob worshipped at the head of the staff. For there Jacob, after he had commanded that his body be carried into the promised land of Canaan, while he worshipped at the head of the staff, testified that he truly believed all the promises made concerning the land to be occupied by himself and his posterity, together with the spiritual blessings attached to them, were to be received; and thus by that gesture he gave an outstanding confession of faith. Hence the Apostle borrows his argument here. And, as we have said, when the ancients wish to confirm something they declare it by worship or by joining of hands; so too in 1 Kings 1 Bathsheba, when she heard from David that Solomon would reign, is said to have bowed her face to the ground, bent herself before the king, and said, "May my lord King David live for ever." If David had had a staff there, it would have been said that David worshipped at the staff. Such without doubt was Jacob's own gesture, and so he worshipped at the head of Joseph's staff. Therefore Jacob's worship at the head of Joseph's staff, after the command about his own transport, was a sign by which he declared that he believed that Joseph would carry him there, and then that all the promises concerning the land of Canaan, to be occupied through himself and his posterity, would be fulfilled. Let us add, if it please, also the expectation of Christ's kingdom from his seed, which the patriarch Jacob undoubtedly saw foreshadowed in the dignity of his son Joseph. Nor do I object to what Chrysostom, writing on Genesis, says: that Jacob worshipped thus from faith, because he foresaw that a royal seed would arise from his own. Jacob without doubt recognised that Christ would come, whose kingdom would extend over Israel and likewise over the Egyptians, that is, over the Jews and the Gentiles. This may be the more justly taken so, since he had recognised that his son Joseph bore the figure of Christ in very many respects; just as Abraham the father saw a type of Christ in his son Isaac. Indeed Joseph prefigured Christ typologically in many ways. (1) Because he accused his brothers before their father of a crime committed; Christ sets human wretchedness before the Father and makes satisfaction for sins. (2) Joseph is loved above all his brothers; Christ is the natural and substantial Son of God the Father, and therefore most beloved. (3) Joseph related his dreams, in which all his people would worship him; Christ sets forth sound doctrine and testifies to his divinity, on account of which he is to be worshipped and acknowledged as the Saviour of all. Hence he was burdened with great envy. (4) Joseph was sent into the field to seek his brothers and afterwards to report to his father whether all was well; so Christ, sent into the world, sought his brothers and procured salvation with the Father.

units.la: Quinto: veniens ad fratres, destinatus est morti, exutus veste, quae tincta est sanguine, proiectus in cisternam. Sic Christus secundum naturam humanam mortuus & sepultus, non tame penitus interfectus. Sexto: Iosephus venditus mercatoribus, & postea vectus in Aegyptum, vbi iterum venditus Potiphari Eunucho Pharaonis, magistro militum: item ab hoc praefectus toti domui. In hac quoq; parte Christus expressus est, qui venditus a fratribus suis Iudaeis, & traditus deinde getilib. ad crucifigendum. Ille molestatur ab uxore Potipharis, & solicitatur ad inhonesta. Christus a Synagoga, ut cosentiret impiae doctrinae, & hodie adhuc molestatur. Iosephi propter libidinem mulieris improbae falso accusatus, coniectus est in carcerem: Christus insidijs synagogae circumventus est & oppressus. In car-cere Iosephi agens praedicit captiuis alijs suos casus. Christus humiliatus & mortuus patribus praedicabatur, & de liberatione sua multos certos reddebat.
units.tr: Fifth: coming to his brothers, he was condemned to death, stripped of his coat, which was stained with blood, and cast into a pit. So Christ, according to his human nature, died and was buried, yet not wholly destroyed. Sixth: Joseph was sold to merchants, and afterwards carried into Egypt, where he was sold again to Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh and master of the soldiers, and by him was set over the whole household. In this part too Christ is expressed, who was sold by his own Jewish brothers and then handed over to the Gentiles to be crucified. Joseph was harassed by Potiphar's wife and solicited to dishonourable things. Christ is harassed by the synagogue, so that he would consent to impious doctrine, and is harassed even today. Joseph, falsely accused on account of the lust of a wicked woman, was thrown into prison. Christ was surrounded and overwhelmed by the snares of the synagogue. In prison Joseph, speaking to the other captives, foretold their fates. Christ, humbled and dead, was preached to the fathers, and gave many a sure assurance of his deliverance.

units.la: Tandem & ipse Iosephi liberatur, Pharaoni somnium exponens, ac docens, quomodo reipublicæ foret succurrendum. Quam ob caussam etiam per Pharaonem saluator regni est appellatus. Ita verò & Christus à morte & humiliatione resurrexit, parem accipit cū patre dignitatem, gubernatq; ecclesiam suam, ac dedit dona hominibus. Ob quam causf sam pater vulteum ab omnibus saluatorem mundi agnosci & coli. Et seruauit Iosepli, Ægyptios pariter & Israelitas: ita Christus gentium pariter ac Iudæorū est salus. In summa multis varijsque modis Iosephi Christum adumbrauit: possetq; aliquis alius multò fœlicius ac copiosius omnia describere. Sed satis sit, nos commonstrasse ruditer quædam capita, & quodammodo suggesisse occasionem plura cogitandi.
units.tr: At last Joseph himself is set free, when he explains Pharaoh's dream and teaches how the commonwealth should be provided for. For this reason he is also called the saviour of the kingdom by Pharaoh. So too Christ, after his humiliation and death, rose again, received equal dignity with the Father, governs his Church, and gave gifts to men. For this reason the Father wills that the Saviour of the world be acknowledged and worshipped by all. Joseph saved the Egyptians and the Israelites alike; so Christ is the salvation both of the Gentiles and of the Jews. In sum, Joseph foreshadowed Christ in many and various ways, and someone else could describe all of this far more happily and fully. But let it suffice that we have roughly pointed out certain heads and in some measure offered occasion for further thought.

units.la: Penè præterieram, ex benedictione, quam pater Iacob contulerat in filiū Iosephi, præclara posse colligi ad mysterium, & ad manifestationem spiritualium bonorum pertinentia. Cùm igitur hæc ita se habeant, & Iacob per spiritum præuiderit in filio Iosepli tam multa, quæ forent postea perficienda per Christum, nihil mirum, quod pater dicatur ad summitatem virgæ Iosephi adorasse. Cùm verò talia ac tanta Iacob animo apprehenderit, certè non possumus aliter intelligere, quàm in adoratione ad virgam Iosephi insigne confessionem fidei eluxisse. Cæterum, ut aliquam excerpamus ex his omnibus doctrinam, primum animaduertimus hic fidei effectum mirabilem, quòd videlicet semper fixa maneat, nec non certissimè statuat, promissa adimplenda: sicut patriarcha Iacob statuebat ad finem vitæ usque, licet foris habitans.
units.tr: I had almost passed over the fact that from the blessing which the father Jacob bestowed on the son of Joseph, many notable things pertaining to the mystery and to the manifestation of spiritual goods can be gathered. Since these things stand thus, and Jacob by the Spirit foresaw in the son of Joseph so many things that were afterwards to be fulfilled through Christ, it is no wonder that the patriarch is said to have worshipped at the top of Joseph's staff. Since Jacob grasped such great things in his mind, we certainly cannot understand his worship at the staff of Joseph otherwise than as a notable confession of faith. But, to draw some teaching from all of this, we first note the remarkable effect of faith: that it remains fixed and most certainly holds that the promises will be fulfilled, just as the patriarch Jacob held to the end of his life, although he was a sojourner abroad.

units.la: Deinde discimus, honorandos esse eos, qui in dignitate sunt constituti, ratione officij, etiamsi quatenus persona consideratur, videamur non debere. Quod sic intelligo, quia Iacob ratione personæ Iosephi, qui erat filius, non tenebatur adeò magnum honore huic impendere: sed spectans eius officium ac dignitatem, in qua erat constitutus, voluit ad summitatem virgæ eius adorare.
units.tr: Next we learn that those who are set in dignity are to be honoured for the sake of their office, even though, if we consider the person, we might seem not to owe them such honour. I understand this as follows: Jacob, regarded as the person of Joseph, who was his son, was not bound to pay so great an honour to him; but looking to his office and the dignity in which he was set, he chose to worship at the top of his staff.

units.la: Tertiò, discimus & excitamur, quòd diligeter in Scripturarum tractatione oporteat nos versari, & in minutissimis locis inquirere mysteria & doctrinam fidei, sicut videmus Apostolum hic fecisse. Quis autem cogitaret, tā graue argumetum posse erui ex eo, quod Scriptum erat, Et adorauit ad fastigiū virgæ illius? Sed Apostolus spiritu Dei illuminatus videbat, quorsum illud tenderet.
units.tr: Thirdly, we learn and are stirred up that we ought to be diligent in handling the Scriptures, and to inquire into the mysteries and the doctrine of faith even in the smallest passages, as we see the Apostle did here. Who would think that so weighty an argument could be drawn from the words, "And he worshipped at the top of his staff"? But the Apostle, illuminated by the Spirit of God, saw whither this tended.

units.la: Per fidem Iosephi moriens de egressione filiorum Israel meminit, deq; ossibus suis mandauit.
units.tr: "By faith Joseph, when he was dying, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel, and gave commandment concerning his bones."

units.la: Septimum exemplum de Iosepho per fidem iustificato: cuius fidem iterum duabus conprobat rationibus. Prior sumpta est ab aperta fidei in extremo vitæ confessione, quam edidit de adimplendis promissionibus Dei in reductione Israelitarū ex Ægypto in terrā Chanaan. Altera sumpta est à signo adiuncto, adeoq; confirmante rationem præcedentē, quod videlicet iubet, vbi continget migrare in terram Chanaan, eò ossa sua transferri. Qua de re nullo modo fuisset solicitus, nisi indubitato animo credidisset, omnes promissiones Dei ad patres factas adimplendas.
units.tr: This is the seventh example, of Joseph, who was justified by faith. The Apostle confirms his faith again by two reasons. The first is taken from the open confession of faith which Joseph made at the end of his life, concerning the fulfilment of God's promises in the leading of the Israelites out of Egypt into the land of Canaan. The second is taken from the sign attached, which in turn confirms the preceding reason, namely that he commanded that, when they should come to migrate into the land of Canaan, his bones should be carried there. Joseph would in no way have been concerned about this unless he had believed with an undoubting mind that all the promises of God made to the fathers would be fulfilled.

units.la: Historia habetur Genes. 50. hisce verbis: habitauit Iosephi in Ægypto cum omni domo patris sui, vixitq; centum decem annis: & vidit Ephraim filios, usque ad tertiam generationem. Filij quoque Machir, filij Manassē nati sunt in genibus Iosephi. Quibus transfactis locutus est fratribus suis: post mortem meam Deus visitabit vos, & ascendere vos faciet de terra ista: ad terram, quam iurauit Abraham, Isaac, & Iacob: cumq; adiurasset eos, atq; dixisset Deus visitabit vos, asportate ossa mea vobiscum de loco isto: mortuus est explectis centum ac decem vitæ suæ annis. Et conditus aromatibus repositus est in loculo, in Aegypto: hæc de historia, ad quam apostolus respicit.
units.tr: The history is found in Genesis 50, in these words: "Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he and all his father's house, and he lived a hundred and ten years; and he saw Ephraim's sons to the third generation; the children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph's knees. When these things had passed, he spoke to his brothers: after my death God will visit you and make you go up out of this land, to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And when he had made them swear and said, God will visit you, carry my bones with you from this place. He died, having completed a hundred and ten years of his life. And he was embalmed with spices and laid in a coffin in Egypt." This is the history to which the Apostle refers.

units.la: Cæterùm videri posset Iosephi spiritu prophetico prædixisse, quòd à morte ipsius Dominus eos visitaret: sicut constat illum dono prophetiæ fuisse clarum. Sed nos potius accipiemus ista pro simplici confessione fidei, quam habebat in promissiones ad patres, fortasis etiam priuatim ad ipsum factas, quas illi tradiderant quasi per manus suis filijs, & assiduè inculcabant, vt in molestijs & peregrinationibus haberent consolationem, semperq; expectarent promissum illud semen benedictum, in quo omnia bona spiritualia errant accepturi. Abraham manifestarat omnibus, fore, vt semen ipsius per quadringentos annos peregrinaretur, & seruiret: deinde generatione quarta reuerteretur ad occupandā terram, ut ei dictum fuerat à Domino, Genes. 15. Itaq; ad ista omnia Iosephi alijq; respiciebant, & fidem his adhibebant. Eaq; omnia comprehendit Iosephi in voce, vsitabit vos Dominus: visitat Dominus in afflictione, pariter in liberatione. Quodq; Iosephi ossa sua transferri mandarit in profectione illa, fecit id ad confirmandum, se vero credere ita futuru. Habebat exemplū patris Iacob, qui & statim à morte se cupiebat trāsferri. Iosephi petit id saltem fieri in illa generali migratione, quia fortasis fratres eius siue filij haud potuissent ita transferre, sicut ipse transtulerat Iacob. Erat ergo hæc insignis confesso fidei.
units.tr: Yet it might seem that Joseph, by the prophetic Spirit, foretold that the Lord would visit them after his death, just as it is known that he was distinguished by the gift of prophecy. But we shall rather take these words as a simple confession of faith which he had in the promises made to the fathers, perhaps also those made privately to himself, which the fathers had handed down to their sons, as it were by hand, and constantly impressed on them, so that they might have comfort in troubles and wanderings and might always await that promised blessed Seed, in whom they were to receive all spiritual goods. Abraham had made it plain to all that his seed would be a stranger and would serve for four hundred years, and then in the fourth generation would return to take possession of the land, as had been said to him by the Lord, Genesis 15. Therefore Joseph and the others looked to all these things and gave their faith to them. Joseph comprised all of them in the words, "the Lord will visit you": the Lord visits in affliction and likewise in deliverance. And that he commanded his bones to be carried away in that departure, he did so to confirm that he truly believed it would be so. He had the example of his father Jacob, who also wished to be carried away immediately after death. Joseph asked that this at least be done in that general migration, since perhaps his brothers or sons could not carry him as he had carried Jacob. This, then, was a remarkable confession of faith.

units.la: Possent quidem aliæ rationes adferri, quare Iosephmandarit auferri ossa: vt, quam adfert Chrysostomus homilia 66, in Genesin, & Augustinus de mirabilibus sacræ Scripturæ libro primo, capite decimo quinto, ne videlicet Ægyptij à corpore ipsius accipe-rent occasionem idololatriæ, cùm plurima beneficia ab eo accepissent, & ad idololatriam valde essent propensi. Sed tamen præcipua ratio fuit protestatio fidei. Quam ob causam Apostolus hanc actionem obseruauit præ multis alijs actionibus Iosephin quibus fides ipsius singularis potuisset animaduerti: siue quòd in extremo vitæ tepore est edita, & sic docet, Iosephin fide ad finem vsq; vitæ perstitisse: siue quòd per eam etiam alij in eadem fide, & expectanda promissione diuinarum impletione debebant confirmari, & doceri. Propter has, inquam, causas apparet, Apostolum voluisse has potissimum rationes adferre. Alioqui possemus ipsi multa proferre, in quibus fides ipsius Iosephi eluxit: sed revera nullæ sunt aptiores & clariores, quàm hæ duæ, quas Apostolus ipse duobus verbis breuissime attigit.
units.tr: Other reasons, indeed, could be advanced why Joseph commanded his bones to be carried away: such as the one which Chrysostom gives in homily 66 on Genesis, and Augustine in the first book of On the Miracles of Sacred Scripture, chapter fifteen, namely that the Egyptians might not take from his body an occasion of idolatry, since they had received very many benefits from him and were very prone to idolatry. But nevertheless the principal reason was the protestation of faith. For this reason the Apostle chose this action above many other actions of Joseph by which his singular faith could have been noticed: either because it was made at the very end of his life, and thus teaches that Joseph persevered in faith to the end of his life; or because through it others also were to be confirmed and taught in the same faith and in the expectation of the fulfilment of the divine promises. For these reasons, I say, it is clear that the Apostle wished to bring forward these reasons above all. Otherwise we ourselves could set forth many things in which the faith of Joseph shone forth; but in truth none are more fitting and clearer than these two, which the Apostle himself touched on most briefly in two words.

units.la: Et licet hic spectare excellentem effectum fidei, quòd videlicet in ea intendat, quæ post mortem debent contingere: & licet cernat bona promissa non contingere in hac vita, tamen certò statuit, omnia debere obuenire saltem à morte: sicut hic Iosephfaciebat, de egressione loquens, & mandans transferri simul ossa.
units.tr: And although here we may observe an excellent effect of faith, namely that it is directed to those things which ought to happen after death, and although it sees that the promised goods do not come to pass in this life, yet it firmly holds that all things must come to pass at least after death: as Joseph does here, speaking of the departure and commanding that his bones be carried along with them.

units.la: Item, licet hic considerare, aliquid solatij esse sanctis, vel apud piorum sanctam ecclesiam quiescere. Nam Iosephijs patribus gaudebat coniungi, quorum fidem strenuè fuerat æmulatus. Est aliqua fœlicitatis pars in cœtu piorum & viuere, & mori, & sepeliri, maximeque si memoria pij vita functi potest cæteris proponi ad incitamentum virtutum: sicut erat memoria Iosephi & aliorum sanctorum patrum, quorum fides insignis debet nobis per omnem vitam versari ob oculos.
units.tr: Likewise, here we may consider that there is some comfort for the saints, or to rest among the holy Church of the pious. For Joseph rejoiced to be joined to his fathers, whose faith he had earnestly imitated. There is some part of happiness both in living, dying and being buried in the company of the pious, and especially if the memory of a pious person who has departed can be set before the rest as an incitement to virtues: as was the memory of Joseph and the other holy fathers, whose remarkable faith ought to be kept before our eyes throughout our whole life.

units.la: Alias verò frustra hinc arripitur argumentum pompæ & superstitio forum in sepultura rituum. Neque enim Iacob vel Iosephpompæ causa, vel inani quadam opinione adducti fuerunt, vt peterent sepeliri in terra Chanaan: sed id petiuerunt, ad testandam suam fidem, quam habebant in Dei promissiones. Alias enim si quid ad fœlicitatem spiritualem faceret sepultura, infœliciter ageretur cum reliquis sanctis patribus, quorum sepulchra penitus ignorantur, aut qui ne sepulturam quidem, quod sciatur, obtinuerunt: quomodo ipse Moses, Aaron, qui in deserto mortui sunt, & multorum apostolorum sepulchra penitus ignorantur.
units.tr: Otherwise, the argument of pomp and the superstitious rites in burial is taken up here in vain. For neither Jacob nor Joseph were led by a desire for pomp, or by some empty opinion, to seek to be buried in the land of Canaan; they sought it to bear witness to the faith which they held in God's promises. For otherwise, if burial contributed anything to spiritual happiness, it would go ill with the other holy fathers, whose tombs are wholly unknown, or who did not even obtain a burial that is known; as with Moses and Aaron, who died in the wilderness, and the tombs of many apostles are wholly unknown.

units.la: Et credibile est, diuitem epulonem in euangelio honorificè sepultum coram mundo: sed tamen coram Deo sepulchrum habuit infernum: contrà Lazarus, qui forte vix habuit, qui sepeliret, sublatus est per angelos in sinum Abrahæ. Si aliquid prodest impio sepultura pretiosa, inquit Augustinus libro de cura pro mortuis, oberit pio vilis, vel nulla. Et alibi ait, pompam & curam sepulturæ magis esse solatio viuorum, quàm mortuorum: probatq;, philosophos, qui de sepultura nihil fuerunt soliciti, & exercitus pro patria occumbentes, qui insepulti relicti fuerunt: illudque ex Lucæ septimo referens, cœlo tegitur, qui non habet vrnam. Refert etiam ex historia ecclesiastica Eusebij, sanctos martyres multos in Gallia obiectos fuisse feris & canibus, plerosque exultos, quorum cineres etiam in Rhodanum coniecti fuerunt: sed hoc nihil nocere sanctis, qui vt curam non habent vitæ vel mortis, ita multò minus curant sepulturam. Ad summam, sciendum est, eos bene & fœliciter mori & sepeliri, quicunque exemplo patrum in fide discedunt.
units.tr: It is credible that the rich man in the Gospel was honourably buried in the sight of the world, yet before God he had hell as his tomb. Lazarus, on the other hand, perhaps had hardly anyone to bury him, but he was carried by angels into Abraham's bosom. Augustine, in his book on the care of the dead, says: "If an expensive burial benefits the impious, a cheap one, or none at all, will not harm the pious." And elsewhere he says that the pomp and care of burial are more a comfort to the living than to the dead. He proves this by pointing to philosophers who were not at all anxious about their burial, and to armies that fell for their country and were left unburied; and he cites Luke 7 for this: "he who has no urn is covered by the sky." He also reports, from the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius, that many holy martyrs in Gaul were thrown to wild beasts and dogs, and that many were burned, and their ashes were cast into the Rhone; but this did nothing to harm the saints, who, as they have no concern for life or death, care much less for burial. In sum, we must realise that all who depart in the faith after the example of the fathers die and are buried well and happily.

units.la: De constantia in fide ad mortem vsque simus soliciti, non autem de sepultura. Nam si in fide morimur, certum est, etiamsi coram mundo ignibus consumamur, deportabimur tamen per Angelos in sinum Abrahæ.
units.tr: We should be anxious about constancy in the faith unto death, not about burial. For if we die in the faith, it is certain that, even if we are consumed by fire in the sight of the world, we will nonetheless be carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom.

units.la: Hæc ideo adiecta sunt, vt consolatione accipiant pij, ibi agentes, vbi etiamnum hodie talis crudelitas vel in mortuos exercetur, vti nos ipsi vidimus. Londini quidam distus Huni sic fuit interfectus, vidimus & audiuimus historiam rei agi: primùm clàm fuit interfectus in carcere oblongo clauo ferreo candenti per nasum inducto in cerebrum: tùm suspensus in carcere quasi ipse se suspendisset: postea exustus: tùm cineres pernebulonem quendam coniecti in aquas, dicentem, Fuisti, inquit, suspensus & exustus, nunc oportet etiam aquis mergaris, vt omnia elementa, terram, aerem, aquam, ignem, sentias tibi aduersata.
units.tr: These things are added so that the godly may take comfort from them, for such cruelty is still practised today even against the dead, as we ourselves have seen. At London a certain man called Hun was killed in this way. We saw and heard the story being told. First he was secretly done to death in prison: a long iron nail, red-hot, was driven through his nose into his brain. Then he was hanged in the prison as though he had hanged himself. Afterwards he was burned, and his ashes were thrown by a certain scoundrel into the water, who said: "You were hanged and burned; now you must also be drowned in the waters, so that you may feel all the elements, earth, air, water and fire, opposed to you."

units.la: Per fidem, cùm natus esset Moses, occultatus est menses tres à parentibus suis, propterea quòd viderent elegantem puellum, nec veriti sunt edictum regis. Per fidem Moses iam grandis, &c.
units.tr: "By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a goodly child; and they were not afraid of the king's edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown, etc." (Heb. 11.)

units.la: Octauum exemplum de Mose per fidem iustificato. Sed & huius fidem pluribus ar-
units.tr: The eighth example: Moses, justified by faith. But the apostle also confirms the faith of this man by several arguments,

units.la: bus argumentis comprobat:sicut supra etiam egerat copiosius de fide Abrahæ.Quod vi detur Apostolus etiam consultò, sicut & cætera fecisse: qua de re nos aliquot causas probabiles adferemus. Prima est, quòd Moses is est,per quem promissiones diuinæ magna ex parte coeptæ sunt adimpleri:quando ipso Dominus vti voluit ad educendum illum electum populum è seruitute Ægyptiaca, ad libertatem & possesionem Chanaan.
units.tr: just as he had earlier dealt more fully with the faith of Abraham. It seems that the apostle did this deliberately, as he did the rest; for which reason we will offer some probable causes. The first is that Moses is the man through whom the divine promises began, for the most part, to be fulfilled, when the Lord was pleased to use him to lead that chosen people out of Egyptian bondage to liberty and the possession of Canaan.

units.la: Secunda,cùm Moses operum magnitudine fuerit excellens,& constet per eũ traditâ legem ac doctrinam operum,is vnus videri poterat,quem aduersarij dicturi erant iustifi catum propter præclara opera,& à quo accepisset iustitiam ex operibus expectadam: quando in eam sententiam multa passim in lege videntur esse proposita. Istud igitur ne fieret,voluit Apostolus diutius prædicandæ eius fidei immorari,ac pluribus argumen tis docere,eum ipsum sola fide seruatum & iustificatum.
units.tr: Second, since Moses was outstanding for the greatness of his works, and it is well known that through him the law and the teaching of works was handed down, he alone might seem to be the one whom the opponents would say was justified because of his famous works, and from whom they would say justice was to be expected through works, since many things are set forth throughout the law to that effect. Therefore, lest this happen, the apostle wished to linger longer in preaching this faith, and to teach by several arguments that he too was saved and justified by faith alone.

units.la: Tertia,videtur Apostolus in hoc exemplorũ ordine habuisse aliquo modo rationem distinctionis temporum,eamque distinctionem aliqua nota indicare.
units.tr: Third, the apostle seems in this order of examples to have had in some way a regard for the distinction of times, and to indicate that distinction by some mark.

units.la: Primò enim celebrauit fidem pątrum,qui ante diluuium illustres extiterunt.Secundo,à diluuio venit ad Abrahamum,& hunc quoque vehementer extulit,ijsdem de causis,quas suprà commemorauimus. Iam tertiò venit ad tempus legis datę,ac Mosen,per quem ea promulgata est,& à quo sumendum est eius temporis initium, apparet ipsum voluisse plenius commendare,vt vel sic doceret,etiam sub lege operũ iustitiam fidei nõ minus,quàm ante & post legem suam obtinere dignitatem.
units.tr: For first he celebrated the faith of the fathers who were famous before the flood. Second, he came from the flood to Abraham, and extolled him greatly too, for the same reasons we mentioned above. Now, third, he comes to the time of the giving of the law and to Moses, through whom it was promulgated, and from whom the beginning of that time must be taken. It appears that he wished to commend him more fully, so as to teach that, even under the law, the righteousness of works obtains no more dignity than the righteousness of faith does before and after the law.

units.la: Quarta addi potest,quòd,cùm Iudæi non minus gloriaretur ipso Mose,à quo legem acceperant,& rationem bene viuendi,quàm patriarcha Abrahamo,à quo habebant sanguinis originem & vitam:æquum erat & Mosi fidem nõ minus prædicari, quàm antea prædicata est fides Abrahæ.
units.tr: A fourth reason may be added: since the Jews gloried no less in Moses, from whom they had received the law and the rule of living well, than in the patriarch Abraham, from whom they had their blood and life, it was fitting that the faith of Moses also be proclaimed no less than the faith of Abraham was proclaimed before.

units.la: Cæterum hac prima probatione non ipsius Mosi, sed parentum eius fides celebratur, & quidem à signo, estque sententia: Cùm Pharao mandasset submergi omnes masculos,parentes Mosi ausi sunt contra edictum regium eum occultare & seruare.
units.tr: But in this first proof it is not the faith of Moses himself that is celebrated, but that of his parents; and that from the sign, and the argument is this: when Pharaoh had commanded that all the males be drowned, his parents dared, against the royal edict, to hide and preserve him.

units.la: Sed hoc nequaquam ausi fuissent facere,nisi indubitatò credidissent,Deum velle impleri promissiones ad patres factas, de multiplicanda posteritate, & dandæ ipsis terra Chanaan.
units.tr: But they would never have dared to do this unless they had believed without doubt that God wished the promises made to the fathers to be fulfilled, namely that their posterity would be multiplied and the land of Canaan given to them.

units.la: Igitur parentes Mosi eo facto egregiam fidem ostenderunt,& per eam sunt iustificati.
units.tr: Therefore Moses' parents by that deed showed outstanding faith, and by it they were justified.

units.la: Ita vero præsupponit Apostolus,parentes Mosi ea potissimum ratione permotos ad conseruandũ suũ filiũ,quòd respicerent in promissiones ad patres factas de multiplicada posteritate,de expectādo liberatore,qui è seruitute Ægyptiaca eos generatione quarta allevaret,nec non ad possidendũ terrā Chanaan deduceret: deniq; & de expectando semine illo benedicto,in quo omnes gentes benedictione effent accepturæ.Et reuera in has promissiones oportet paretes Mosi intentissima atq; constatissima fide respexisse, priusquàm auderet cum periculo vitæ præceptum tyranni Pharaonis transgredi.
units.tr: Now the apostle presupposes that Moses' parents were moved to preserve their son chiefly for this reason: that they looked to the promises made to the fathers concerning the multiplication of posterity, concerning the expected deliverer who would raise them from Egyptian bondage in the fourth generation and lead them to possess the land of Canaan; and finally concerning the expected seed in whom all nations would receive blessing. And indeed Moses' parents must have looked to these promises with the most intent and steadfast faith before they dared, at peril of their lives, to disobey the tyrant Pharaoh's command.

units.la: Sed quomodo magna fides in parentibus Mosi eluxerit,clarius id euadet, si nonnulla de historia huc adferamus. Exodi primo,Pharao, qui ignorabat Iosephi, videns multiplicari Israelitas, consilium cepit de illis callidè opprimendis, ne forte, si ingrueret bellum, adiungerentur inimicis, & expugnatis ipsis Ægyptijs liberè foràs egederentur.
units.tr: But how great faith shone forth in the parents of Moses will become clearer if we bring forward some points from the history. In the first chapter of Exodus, Pharaoh, who did not know Joseph, seeing the Israelites multiply, took counsel to crush them cunningly, lest perhaps, if war broke out, they should join the enemies and, the Egyptians having been overcome, should go out freely.

units.la: Consilium autem erat, illos seruiliter detineri, & laboribus sordidis luti & lateris prægrauati sub crudelibus præfectis operũ, ita vt vel vitæ posset illos tædere,& sic omnis via ad opes parandas,& ad spem potetiæ illis præcluderetur: extruebant vrbes opitulantes Pharaonis, Pithôm & Raâmses.
units.tr: The plan was to keep them in servile bondage, and to weigh them down with squalid labours of mud and brick under cruel overseers of the works, so that life itself might become wearisome to them, and thus every way of acquiring wealth and every hope of power would be closed to them. They built cities in aid of Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses.

units.la: Vbi verò hoc pacto nihil proficeretur,sed magis multiplicarentur Israelitæ aliud consilium initû est:vocatis obstetricibus Hebræorû,& duabus inprimis celebribus Siphrah, & Puah, mandatumque est feriò, vt omnes masculos occiderent: sed cum hæti merent Deum,ideoq; non auderent id facere,excusauerunt se,dicentes,Hebræos mulieres sic edoctas esse, vt párere possent etiam sine ope ipsorum. Quapropter Deus etiam obstetricibus benefecit.
units.tr: But when this method achieved nothing, and the Israelites rather multiplied, another plan was adopted: the midwives of the Hebrews were summoned, and especially two well-known ones, Shiphrah and Puah, and they were ordered firmly to kill all the males. But since they feared God, and therefore did not dare to do it, they excused themselves, saying that Hebrew women were so skilled that they could give birth even without the help of the midwives. Therefore God also dealt well with the midwives.

units.la: Itaq; tertium consilium repererūt Ægyptij,videlicet vt ex mandato regio proles masculina in toto populo Israelitico raperetur,& in flumen proijceretur,solis fœmellis asseruatis. Quo facto,sequitur statim secundo capite.
units.tr: So the Egyptians devised a third plan, namely that by royal command the male offspring throughout the whole Israelite people should be seized and thrown into the river, with only the females spared. When this had been done, the second chapter follows immediately.

units.la: Egressus est post hæc vir de domo Leui,& accepit vxorem sirpis suæ, quæ concepit,& peperit filium. Et videns eum elegantem, abscondit eum tribus mensibus. Et cum cùm illum amplius abscondere non posset, tulit pro eo arcam arundineam, & liniuit eam bitumine atque pice, & reposuit in eam infantulum illum, exposuitq; in care-ªo, iuxta littus fluminis: & collocauit se soror eius à longè, vt cognosceret, quid illi fie ret. Descendit autè filia Pharaonis, vt lauaret se in flumine, & de ambulabant puel-le eius iuxta ripam fluminis, & videns arculam in medio careªo, misit famulam suam, vt tolleret illam. Cumq; aperuisset, vidit esse infantem, & ecce puer flebat, & miserta illius dicebat, de pueris Hebrœorum est. Dixit autem soror eius ad filiâ Pha-raonis, num vadam, vt vocem ad te mulierem nutricem ex Hebræis, quæ tibi lactet puerum?
units.tr: "After these things a man of the house of Levi went out and took to wife a woman of his own tribe, who conceived and bore a son. And seeing that he was goodly, he hid him three months. And when he could no longer hide him, he took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and pitch, and put the little child in it, and laid it in the flags by the river's brink.
