And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him. And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river, and her maidens walked along by the river's side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it. And when she had opened it, she saw the child; and behold, the boy wept, and she had compassion on him and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children. Then said his sister to Pharaoh's daughter, Shall I go and call to you a nurse of the Hebrew women, to nurse the child for you?"

units.la: Respondit filia Pharaonis, vade: perrexit itaque & vocauit matrem pueri: ad quam ait filia Pharaonis: tolle puerum istum, & lacta eum mihi, & dabo tibi mercedem.
units.tr: Pharaoh's daughter answered, "Go." So the maid went and called the child's mother. And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages."

units.la: Et accepit mulier illa puerum, nutriuitque eum. En historiam, quomodo per parentes absconditus & seruatus Moses. Iam fidem parentum ex his ostendamus. Apparet autem, Apostolum ideo prius fidem parentū voluisse prædicare, vt doceret, non tantum in Mose ipso, qui Deo fuit vnicè charus, fidem excellentè fuisse: sed etiam, in parétibus eius & quasi hæreditariū fuisse omnibus Hebræis, sic in fide viuere. Vel potius, vt ibi discere-mus, ex fide nasci veram obedientiā, & obseruatiam legis, & non nisi per fidem ad eam veniri: nihilq; quod lege præceptum est, rectè fieri, nisi quatenus ex fide fiat. Hoc obiter præmittimus.
units.tr: And the woman took the child and nursed him. Here is the story of how Moses was hidden and preserved by his parents. Now let us show from these things the faith of the parents. It appears that the Apostle wished to speak of the parents' faith first, to teach that excellent faith was present not only in Moses himself, who was uniquely dear to God, but also in his parents, and that living by faith was, as it were, the inheritance of all the Hebrews. Or rather, that we might learn from this passage that true obedience and observance of the law arise from faith, and that no one comes to it except through faith, and that nothing commanded by the law is rightly done unless it is done from faith. We put this forward in passing.

units.la: Cæterum, nonne hæc erat insignis fides parētum? Videbant toties, & tot modis consultatum à Pharaone, quomodo opprimi possent Hebræi. Videbant, publicè mandatū omnibus Ægyptijs, vt pueros Hebræorum raperent, & in flumen conijcerent, videbat summam potentiā & tyrannidem, cui vix Deus ipse videbatur posse resistere. Videbant deniq;, sibi ipsis non tantum fortunarum, quæ iam nullæ propemodum erant, sed capi tis etiam periculum imminere, & reos læsæ maiestatis fore, si quid contra edictum Pharaonis attentarent. At ex altera parte multa succurrebant, quæ inuitabant ad seruādum puerum: Primò naturalis ille affectus parentū erga partum, de eo coseruando, quē & in brutis & feris animatibus licet cōspicere. Secundò, mouebat illos lex naturalis de non occidendo innocente. Quid enim commeruerant paruuli illi, vt sic in fluuiū mergeretur?
units.tr: Moreover, was not this faith of the parents remarkable? They saw how often, and in how many ways, Pharaoh had planned how the Hebrews might be crushed. They saw a public command given to all the Egyptians to snatch the sons of the Hebrews and throw them into the river. They saw a power and tyranny of such size that God himself seemed scarcely able to resist it. Finally, they saw that not only their property, which by now was almost nothing, but their very lives were threatened, and that they would be guilty of treason if they attempted anything against Pharaoh's edict. On the other side, however, many considerations came to mind that urged them to save the child: first, that natural affection of parents for their offspring, to preserve it, which can be seen even in brute beasts and wild animals. Second, the natural law not to kill the innocent moved them. For what had those little children done to deserve being drowned in this way?

units.la: Tertiò, respiciebant haud dubiè ad promissiones, quas sciebant patribus suis factas à Deo de multiplicatione posteritatis: de redimendo ipsos in possessionem terræ Chanaan: item de Semine Benedicto. Hīc certè intelligere quiuis potest, graues tentationes subiuisse parentum animos: mirabiles pugnas experti sunt carnis & spiritus, fidei & desperationis, cùm ita affligeretur omnis populus, & iuxta edictum regis necarentur paruuli, hīc deus videbantur suos penitus neglexisse: videbatur irritæ fieri omnes promissiones de multiplicatione sobolis, de expectanda possessione terræ Chanaā, imò & de expectando semine benedicto.
units.tr: Third, they doubtless looked to the promises which they knew God had made to their fathers: of the multiplication of their posterity, of the redemption of them into possession of the land of Canaan, and likewise of the Blessed Seed. Here anyone can surely understand that the minds of the parents underwent severe temptations; they experienced wonderful struggles of flesh and spirit, of faith and despair. While the whole people was being so afflicted, and the little ones were being killed according to the king's edict, God seemed to have utterly neglected his own people. All the promises about the multiplication of offspring, about expecting the possession of the land of Canaan, and even about expecting the blessed seed, seemed to be made void.

units.la: Rursus verò, qui non parebat edicto regis, hīc periclitabantur simul omnes parētes. Quid igitur facerent? Non dubium, quin multi hisce victi succubuerint, & tyrānidem metuentes omnem spem promissionum diuinarum abiecerint, & sic suas proles ipsi Ægyptijs mergendas tradiderint. At verò parētes Mosi constanter respicientes in solas promissiones Dei (nam affectus naturales erant communiter & in omnibus alijs) quòd necessariò deberent adimpleri, primi & soli ausi sunt præceptum Pharaonis transgredi, seque in vitę discrimen conijcere. In hoc igitur facto egregia fides resplenduit, & fides merito prædicatur, quæ nimirum in grauissimis tentationibus inuicta perstitit.
units.tr: On the other hand, whoever did not obey the king's edict was at once in danger, and all the parents were in peril together. What then were they to do? There is no doubt that many were overcome by these things and, fearing the tyranny, cast away all hope in the divine promises, and so handed their own offspring over to the Egyptians to be drowned. But Moses' parents, looking constantly only to the promises of God (for their natural affections were common to all the others too), because they had to be fulfilled necessarily, alone and first dared to transgress Pharaoh's command and to cast themselves into peril of their lives. In this deed, therefore, an outstanding faith shone forth, and faith is rightly proclaimed, which indeed remained unconquered in the most grievous temptations.

units.la: Sed, dices, potuit fides etiam in alijs elucere; qui filios suos passi sunt mergi. Nam fidei est statuere, Deum præstiturum promissa, etiam vbi minimè apparet posse fieri; quod promissum est: debuissent igitur statuere, quòd etiam occisis omnibus illis infantibus Deus nihilominus liberaret eos suo tempore, & sic ista fides fuisset multo praeclarior.
units.tr: But, you will say, faith could have shone forth also in others, who suffered their sons to be drowned. For it is of faith to hold that God will perform what he has promised, even where it does not appear at all possible that it can be done. They ought therefore to have held that, even with all those infants slain, God would nevertheless free them in his own time, and so that faith would have been far more excellent.

units.la: Respondendum, quòd hoc non erat necessarium, idque primò, quia sciebant omnes illi, factas esse promissiones de liberatore & seminè benedicto, & cùm Deus vtatur ad perficiendum promissa ordinatis medijs, hoc ipsum erat medium, quo perficienda erant promissa, videlicet seruare infantes.
units.tr: The answer is that this was not necessary, and that first because all those men knew that promises had been made about a deliverer and a seed of blessing, and since God uses ordained means to accomplish his promises, this very thing was the means by which the promises were to be accomplished, namely, to save the infants.

units.la: Secundò, cùm promissiones essent factæ in genere de expectando liberatore, & semine benedicto, ex posteris Abrahæ, si decebat vnūquēq; obfirmato animo intueri in promissiones, vt crederet, se illum esse, ex quo liberator ille nasceretur. Quamobrem diffidētium erat, filios suos abijcere, & mergendos tradere. Contrà singularis fides erat parentum Mosi, qui in promissiones Dei adeò constanter intuebātur. Quod verò etiam
units.tr: Secondly, since the promises were given in general terms about awaiting a deliverer and a blessed seed from the posterity of Abraham, each person ought to have fixed his mind on those promises and believed that he himself might be the one from whom that deliverer would be born. It was therefore the mark of those who distrusted God to cast away their sons and hand them over to be drowned. By contrast, the parents of Moses showed a singular faith, since they looked so steadfastly upon God's promises. As for the fact that others were not bound to obey Pharaoh's edict for other reasons, I shall explain that later.

units.la: alija alijs de causis non tenebantur obedire edicto Pharaonis, dicam postea. Nunc verba expendamus: per fidem, inquit, cum natus esset Moses, occultatus est mensibus tres a parentibus suis: Hebraica quidem veritas sonat, quasi mater sola id fecisset: hic vero exprimuntur parentes imo patres, ᾁϑέρων, inquit, quasi etiam auus adhuc superfuerit. Sed nulla verborum hic pugna: pluribus amicis conscijs & consulentibus mater artissime seruabat.
units.tr: Now let us weigh the words: "By faith, when Moses was born, he was hidden three months by his parents" (Heb. 11:23). The Hebrew truth suggests that the mother alone did this, but here the text names the parents, indeed the fathers, and says [πατέρων], as if the grandfather were still alive. But there is no quarrel over the words here: the mother, with many friends knowing and advising her, kept the child hidden very closely.

units.la: Porro spatium trium mensium amplificat fidem parentum. Tanto enim tempore se- se grauissimis periculis exposuerunt, non tantum ad paucos dies.
units.tr: Moreover, the span of three months magnifies the faith of the parents. For they exposed themselves to the gravest dangers for so long a time, not merely for a few days.

units.la: Propterea quod uiderent elegantem puellum) Sic vero & septuaginta habent, ἀστεῖος ἀγαθὸς: in hebraeo vero habetur טוב. Proinde sic adduntur haec verba, quasi ratio hic reddatur, ob quem permoti fuerint parentes ad conseruandum Mosen. Ita scribunt, tum Iosephus antiquitatum lib.2.capite 9. tum Rabini quidam, admodum decora fuisse facie puerum Mosen, etiam cum iam adolesceret, ut nemo eius forma non moueretur.
units.tr: "Because they saw that he was a goodly child." The Seventy also have it thus: [ἀστεῖος ἀγαθὸς]; but in the Hebrew it stands as טוב. Accordingly these words are added as if they gave the reason why the parents were moved to preserve Moses. So write both Josephus (Antiquities, book 2, chapter 9) and certain rabbis, that the boy Moses was of very comely appearance, even when he was growing up, so that no one could look at his beauty without being moved.

units.la: Sed demus hoc ita esse: quantulum vero id, ut vsque adeo mouerentur parentes, ad exponendum se periculo capitis?
units.tr: But grant that this is so: how small a thing it is that the parents should be moved so far as to expose themselves to danger of death!

units.la: Deinde, quantulum hoc, ut ex eo accipiatur fidei occasio seu materia? Non dubium, quin multi alij quoque pueri fuerint formosissimi.
units.tr: And all parents are equally moved by the beauty of their children, since even children who are naturally misshapen wonderfully please their parents, according to the proverb: "Even monkeys think their own young are beautiful, and everyone finds his own beautiful." We must therefore contemplate something a little deeper.

units.la: Et parentes omnes aequè moti sunt puerorum suorum forma, quando vel deformes pueri secundum naturam parentibus mire placeant, iuxta prouerbium, etiam Simiae pulchri sunt fui catuli: & suum cuique pulchrum. Oportet ergo paulò altius quiddam contemplemur.
units.tr: Accordingly, if we look at the words, both the Hebrew טוב [tov] and the Greek "ἀγαθὸς" [agathos], we shall find that they do not simply signify elegance of body, but rather also of mind and morals. For טוב [tov] also means good and is everywhere attributed to God, as in Psalm 107: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good." "ἀγαθὸς" [agathos] signifies elegant indeed, but also courteous and civil.

units.la: Proinde, si intuemur voces tum Hebraeam טוב, tum graecam ἀγαθὸς, inueniemus eas non quidem ita simpliciter significare elegantiam corporis, sed magis etiam animi atque morum. Nam טוב etiam bonum significat, acDeo passim tribuitur: ut Psalmo 107. Confitemini Domino, quoniam bonus. ἀγαθὸς vero significat elegantem quidem, sed urbanum item & ciuilem.
units.tr: Therefore we shall understand Moses to have been called "good and fair" [ἀγαθὸν καὶ καλόν] in such a way that we perceive some outward elegance appeared in him, not the ordinary kind that belongs to nature, but an unusual one, supernaturally and divinely added, which would already bear something great and noble upon it, and would lead the minds of all to contemplate the most excellent good qualities of the mind dwelling in that body, and would draw them on to conceive the spiritual blessings which God wished to work through him.

units.la: Ergo ita accipiemus, Mosen dictum ἀγαθὸν καὶ καλόν, ut intelligamus, externa quandam elegantiam in eo apparuisse, non vulgarem quidem illam, aut naturae: sed inusitatam & super naturalem diuinitus additam, quae iam magni ac generosi quiddam praे se ferret, omniumq; animos perduceret ad contemplandum excellentissima bona animi in eo corpore habitantis, & ad concipienda bona spiritualia, quae Deus per illum operari vellet, pertraheret.
units.tr: Therefore we shall take it thus, that Moses was called [ἀγαθὸν καὶ καλόν], good and fair, so that we understand that some outward elegance appeared in him, not indeed the ordinary kind that belongs to nature, but an unusual one, supernaturally added by God, which already bore something great and noble on its face and drew the minds of all to contemplate the most excellent qualities of soul dwelling in that body, and to conceive the spiritual blessings that God wished to work through him.

units.la: Huiusmodi vero res animo concipere, & credere quod Deus in illo puero, & peril-lum puerum vellet misericordiam suam erga populum Israeliticum ostendere, istud fidei: neque statuere alij potuerant, quam qui diuinis promissionibus constanter adhaerebant.
units.tr: Now to conceive such things in the mind and to believe that God wished to show his mercy toward the people of Israel through that boy, and through that boy in particular, this belonged to faith; nor could others have decided this except those who clung steadfastly to the divine promises.

units.la: Sic vero solet Deus suos electos subinde externis signis ornare, quibus omnes mo-ueantur ad agnoscendum, eos Deo caros, & Deum aliquid magni per eos velle perfi-cere 1. Samuelis capite 9. de Saule, cum eligendus esset in regem, additur a spiritu Sancto, elegantissimum fuisse, qualis non fuerit in vniuerso populo Israelitico. Similiter 1. Samuelis capite 16 de Dauid, cum esset a Samuele vngendus in regem, erat Dauid pulcher aspectu decoraque facie. Et Danielis 1. capite, Daniel cum sociis Anania, Misaele, Azaria, etiam contra naturam pulcherrimi apparuerunt. Et Actorum capite 6. Visa est facies Stephani tanquam facies Angeli: id est, supra communem naturae cursum elegans.
units.tr: Indeed God is accustomed from time to time to adorn his chosen ones with outward signs, by which all are moved to recognise that they are dear to God and that God intends to accomplish something great through them. Of Saul, when he was to be chosen as king, the Holy Spirit adds in 1 Samuel 9 that he was most handsome, such as there was none among the whole people of Israel. Similarly, in 1 Samuel 16, when David was to be anointed king by Samuel, David was beautiful in appearance and of comely face. And in Daniel 1, Daniel with his companions Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah also appeared most handsome, beyond what nature would give. And in Acts 6, the face of Stephen was seen as the face of an angel: that is, elegant beyond the common course of nature.

units.la: Hoc igitur modo Deus apparere facit quandam supernaturalem formam in Mose, per quam mouebantur parentes, ad statuendum, hunc esse illum, qui liberaturus foret populum Israeliticum e seruitute Aegyptiaca: quod illi conceperunt fide in promissiones antea auditas: sicut Simeon accipiens in vlnas Christum, a spiritu Sancto praemonitus, ibi agnouit mundi redemptorem semen benedictum: ita parentes Mosis (haud dubie spiritus Sancti instinctu) agnouerunt illum liberatorem Israelis. Et habet Deus diuersa media, quibus homines ad fidem excitat: crebro enim per verbum externum id facit, crebro per signa: quamobrem signa certa tam in veteri testamento, quam in nouo fuerunt diuinitus instituta, ut per ea fides excitaretur & confirmaretur. Eadem ratione parentes Mosi, qui iam verbum audierunt, promissiones videlicet saepe factas, iam etiam conspecto signo ad fidem sunt permoti.
units.tr: In this way God makes a certain supernatural form appear in Moses, by which his parents were moved to conclude that this was the child who would deliver the people of Israel from Egyptian slavery. They grasped this by faith, in the promises they had heard before, just as Simeon, taking Christ into his arms and forewarned by the Holy Spirit, there recognized the redeemer of the world, the blessed seed. So Moses' parents (undoubtedly by the prompting of the Holy Spirit) recognized him as the deliverer of Israel. God has various means by which he stirs men to faith. He often does so through the external word, and often through signs. For this reason, certain signs were divinely instituted both in the Old Testament and in the New, so that faith might be stirred up and confirmed by them. By the same reasoning, Moses' parents, who had already heard the word, that is, the promises made so often, were now also moved to faith by the sight of a sign.

units.la: Itaque necessario oportet statuere, longe alia ratione parentes Mosi intuitos ipsius formam, quam eam intuebantur ceteri. Filia Pharaonis etiam contemplata est, & mota, sed non ad fidem. Sic multi alij viderunt Christum, itemque Stephanum: non tamen propterea moti sunt ad fidem: quia nimirum nihil praeter externam formam communi more sunt conteplati: at parentes Mosi ad contemplationem spiritualiū sunt perducti. Non igitur adeo exigua aut leuis ratio est haec de forma Mosi, qua fides parentum comprobetur. Nec ueriti sunt edictum regis) Hic eleganter exprimitur officiu & effectus fidei parentu Mosi. Significatur enim, varijs modis illos tetatos,& multas causas habuisse, quare non fuissent seruaturi:sed tamen contra omnia pericula prevaluisse fide. Neq; enim fides est sine tentationibus,& tunc primum perficitur,vbi superatis tentationibus fuerit confirmata.
units.tr: It must therefore be concluded that Moses' parents looked upon his form in a very different way from others. Pharaoh's daughter also gazed at him and was moved, but not to faith. Many others likewise saw Christ, and Stephen too, yet they were not moved to faith by it, because they looked only at the external form in the ordinary manner. But Moses' parents were led to contemplate spiritual things. So this account of Moses' form, by which the faith of the parents is proved, is not a small or trivial matter. "They did not fear the king's edict": here the duty and the effect of the faith of Moses' parents are finely expressed. For it signifies that they were tested in various ways and had many reasons why they might not have kept the child, yet by faith they prevailed against all dangers. Indeed, faith is never without temptations, and it is only then made perfect when, the temptations overcome, it has been confirmed.

units.la: Neq; vero est,quod quisquam obijciat,parētes Mosi,etiamsi fide ostendissent, filium suu ad tres menses conseruando:tamen hic rursus videntur fide excidisse,quando eum in arculam impositu aquis comiserunt. Sed dicendu est, non hoc desperationis argumē tum fuisse,sed potius plenioris fidei. Cum enim curassent,quantum in ipsis erat,ne statim natus raperetur & necaretur,iam emittendo illum aliquamdiu lactatum, & forma etiam magis commendabili conspicuum,testati sunt,se diuinae prouidentiae committere,planeque sperare, Deum etiam mirabili aliquo modo seruaturum,vt foret liberator populi,quem ipsi omni diligentia per trimestre spacium seruauerant.
units.tr: Nor is there any ground for someone to object that Moses' parents, although they had shown their faith by keeping their son for three months, seem to have lost faith again when they committed him to the waters in an ark. It must be said that this was not a sign of despair, but rather of a fuller faith. For when they had taken care, as far as lay in their power, that the newborn child not be snatched away and killed at once, then by sending him out, after he had been nursed for some time and was seen to be of a more commendable form, they bore witness that they were committing themselves to divine providence and hoped with certainty that God would preserve him in some wonderful way, to be the deliverer of the people whom they had kept with all diligence for three months.

units.la: Cuius rei indicium sumi potest ab eo,quod soror pueri (fortasis ita iussa a parentibus) procul secuta sit,vt euentum rei contemplaretur. Nec dubium,quin salutem pueri Deo Iuis precibus assiduè comendarit. Itaq; & in hoc opere fidem suam studiosè & excellenter approbarunt.
units.tr: An indication of this matter can be taken from the fact that the boy's sister (perhaps so instructed by their parents) followed at a distance, so that she might watch the outcome of the affair. And there is no doubt that they commended the boy's safety to God with constant prayers. And so in this work too they earnestly and excellently proved their faith.

units.la: Cæterum habemus hic variam & multiplicem doctrinam. Primò,parentu fidem cæterasq; virtutes plerunq; imitari filios:ex bonis boni procreatur,& ex fidelibus parētibus Deum sine intermissione orātibus pro salute populi, natus est fidelis Moses,postea mediator inter Deum & homines constitutus,& hoc Christi typum gerens. Studeant ergo parentes prēire exemplis suis filijs,& habebunt sui similes filios,ex quibus gloriam accipient,non ignominiam.
units.tr: Moreover, we have here a varied and manifold teaching. First, the faith and other virtues of parents are generally imitated by their children: good comes from good, and from faithful parents who pray to God without ceasing for the salvation of the people was born a faithful Moses, later appointed mediator between God and men, bearing a type of Christ. Let parents therefore strive to go before their children by their examples, and they will have children like themselves, from whom they will receive glory, not shame.

units.la: Secundò,discimus hic effectum fidei,quod videlicet fides non sit sine tentationibus, & omnes tamen tentationes tandem superet:nihil formidat eos, qui possunt occidere corpus,tātum sollicita,vt eum habeat propitium,qui potest post occisum corpus etiam animam mittere in gehennam.
units.tr: Second, we learn here the effect of faith: that faith is not without temptations, yet it finally overcomes all temptations. Those who can kill the body are not to be feared; rather, one should be anxious only to have on one's side him who can cast both body and soul into hell after the body has been killed.

units.la: Tertiò,habemus hic admonitione,quatenus obediendū magistratibus. Edictu Pharaonis,erat contra ius naturæ,quia volebant perdere Israelitas bene meritos:ite quære bat ad opprimendū eos mediū etiam plane crudelissimū & illicitū,nempe interfectionē innocentum puerorum, qui nihil mali fuerant commeriti. Item medium illud erat contrariū promissionibus diuinis de multiplicanda posteritate,& expectando liberatore ac se mine benedicto. Quia ergo huiusmodi erat edictum,pugnans cum natura, pugnans cū voluntate Dei, ideo non tenebantur Israelitæ occidere suos pueros. Hic habebant regulam,quam allegauit Petrus, Deo oportet magis obedire,quàm hominibus. Quàquam hoc pacto attentare aliquid contra edictum, non est cuiuslibet, sed tantum habentium Dei spiritum,& insigni fide præditorum.
units.tr: Third, we have here a warning about the duty of obedience to the magistrates. Pharaoh's edict was contrary to the law of nature, because it intended to destroy the Israelites, who had deserved well; and it sought to oppress them by a means that was utterly cruel and unlawful, namely the slaughter of innocent children who had done no wrong. Moreover, that measure was contrary to the divine promises concerning the multiplication of posterity and the expectation of a deliverer and the blessed seed. Since, therefore, the edict was of such a kind, at odds with nature and at odds with the will of God, the Israelites were not bound to kill their sons. Here they had the rule which Peter cited: we ought to obey God rather than men. Yet to act against an edict in this way is not for just anyone, but only for those who have the Spirit of God and are endowed with remarkable faith.

units.la: Quartò,habemus hic doctrinā,cui admixta est & insignis consolatio,de puerorū videlicet conseruatione. Deus habet multas & varias rationes seruandi suos. Seruauit Mosen in domo parentum,seruauit eundem etiam,aquis expositum. Electis omnia in bonum cedūt. Quos Deus ordinauit,vt sint vasa honoris in domo sua, ij nulla crudelitate, aut malitia hominum possunt conuerti in vasa contumeliae. Quare constantes esse debent in fide etiam hoc tempore omnes pij. Sæuiat licet princeps mundi huius diabolus cū omnibus suis satellitibus,siue principibus,siue pontificibus:tamen Moses & eius pij innumeri seruabuntur. Tota hæc historia plena est consolationis,& nostro tempore,quo ecclesia grauissimè affligitur,mira accommoda. Moses alitur ab ipsa filia Pharaonis:ita impij etiam nescij pietatem promouent hoc tempore, quam maximè conantur extinguere. Habet etiam Dominus suos Abdias,qui furetibus Achabo & Iezabele,prophetas Dei tegunt,& fouent.
units.tr: Fourth, we have here a teaching, mixed with remarkable consolation, concerning the preservation of children. God has many and various ways of preserving his own. He preserved Moses in his parents' house, and he preserved the same Moses when he was exposed on the waters. "All things work together for good for the elect." Those whom God has ordained to be vessels of honour in his house cannot be turned into vessels of dishonour by any cruelty or malice of men. Therefore all the godly ought to be constant in faith even in this time. Let the prince of this world, the devil, rage with all his henchmen, whether princes or priests; yet Moses and his countless godly people will be preserved. This whole history is full of consolation, and in our own time, when the Church is most grievously afflicted, it is wonderfully suitable. Moses is nourished by Pharaoh's own daughter: so the ungodly, even without knowing it, advance piety in this age, though they try most hard to extinguish it. The Lord also has his Obadiahs, who hide and foster the prophets of God while Ahab and Jezebel rage.

units.la: Per fidem Moses iam grandis renuit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis, potius eligēs simul malis affici cū populo Dei, quàm tēporarijs peccati comodis frui, maiores arbitatus diuitias probrū Christi, quam Aegyptiorū thesauros. Respectum enim habebat remuneracionis.
units.tr: By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted together with the people of God than to enjoy the temporary pleasures of sin, and considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians. For he looked to the reward.

units.la: Secunda probatio,quæ pprie agit de fide ipsius Mosi,cuius hic est sensus: Moses grādis peccatus renuit filius filiæ Pharaonis vocari, & maluit se adiungere afflictæ suę genti,quàm in aula Ægyptiaca deliciari & honorari. Atqui istud non potuisset facere,nisi habuisset insignem fide,ac statuisset, Deum velle misereri afflicti populi, quem elegerat.
units.tr: This is the second proof, which deals properly with the faith of Moses himself, and its sense is this: Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, and chose to join his afflicted people rather than to live in delight and honour at the Egyptian court. But he could not have done this unless he had remarkable faith and had determined that God wished to have mercy on the afflicted people whom he had chosen.

units.la: Igitur Moses insigni fide fuit præditus, per quam & iustificatus est. Expressit autē prę sentis argumenti sententiam Apostolus elegantissimis verbis. Nos explicabimus singula membra,prius tamen historia, vnde argumentum sumptum est, debet indicari. Sic autem Exodi capite secundo, legimus: Cùm iam adolescéret Moses, agens sub matre, à qua lactabatur, traditus est filiæ Pharaonis. Et sequitur. Quem illa adoptauit in locum filij, vocauitque nomen eius, Mose, dixitque, Quoniam ex aquis traxi eum: factum verò est in diebus illis, cùm magnus effectus esset Mose, vt egrederetur ad fratres suos, & videret laborem illorum, videretque virum Ægyptium percutientem quendam Hebræum, qui erat ex fratribus suis. Et respiciens huc atq; illuc, & neminem videns, percussit Ægyptium, atq; abscondit in arena.
units.tr: Therefore Moses was endowed with remarkable faith, by which he was also justified. The Apostle expressed the sense of this present argument in most elegant words. We shall explain the individual members, but first the history from which the argument is taken must be indicated. Thus we read in the second chapter of Exodus: "When Moses was grown, while he was living with his mother, who nursed him, he was given to Pharaoh's daughter." And it follows: "She adopted him in place of a son and called his name Moses, and said, Because I drew him out of the waters." Now it happened in those days, when Moses was grown, that he went out to his brothers and saw their burdens, and saw an Egyptian man striking a certain Hebrew, one of his brothers. And looking this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

units.la: Et cùm egressus esset die altera, ecce duo uiri Hebræi rixabantur: dixitque ad reum: quare percutis socium tuum? Qui respondit: quis constituit te in virum principem, vt iudicares nos? Nunquid vt me occidas tu loqueris, sicut interfecisti Ægyptium? Et timuit Moses, dixitque: certè nota facta est hæc res. Et audiens Pharao sermonem istum quærebat occidere Mosen: & fugiens Moses à facie Pharaonis mansit in terra Midian.
units.tr: And when he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrew men were quarrelling; and he said to the one in the wrong, "Why do you strike your fellow?" He answered, "Who made you a prince and judge over us? Do you mean to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?" And Moses was afraid and said, "Surely this matter has become known." And when Pharaoh heard this word he sought to kill Moses; but Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian.

units.la: En hic habemus, quomodo Moses adultus renuerit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis. Adoptatus erat ab ea in filium: quæ profectò non erat contemnenda conditio, præsertim eo tempore, quo populus Israeliticus ita affligebatur: sed tamen adhuc egredi voluit ad fratres suos, seque illis quamlibet afflictis adiungere. Atque vt clarius etiam testaretur, se ex animo malle adiungi suis, quàm suauiter viuere in aula Ægyptiaca, Ægyptium, qui quendam ex Hebræis iniustè cædebat, ille non solùm verbis cohibuit, sed etiam interfecit.
units.tr: Here we have how Moses, when grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. He had been adopted by her as a son, a station which was certainly not to be despised, especially at a time when the people of Israel were so afflicted. Yet he still wished to go out to his brothers and join himself to them, however afflicted they were. And so that he might bear witness more clearly that he preferred from his heart to be joined to his own people rather than to live pleasantly at the Egyptian court, he not only restrained with words the Egyptian who was unjustly beating one of the Hebrews, but also killed him.

units.la: Hic habemus audax facinus, quod nunquam perpetrasset, si illi animus fuisset ad aulam Ægyptiacam. Quanquam, si fortasis ille adhuc laborasset, vt reciperetur denuò in aulam, potuisset viam inuenire: sed hinc potius nata est illi occasio fugiendi etiam aulam Ægyptiacam: quod & ille fortisimo animo fecit.
units.tr: Here we have a bold deed, which he would never have committed if his mind had been set on the Egyptian court. Yet if perhaps he had still been trying to be readmitted to the court, he could have found a way to do it. But this rather gave him the opportunity to leave the Egyptian court altogether, and he did so with the greatest courage.

units.la: Ecce ergo, quomodo renuit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis. Estque hæc propositio: per fidem Moses iam grandus renuit uocari filius filiæ Pharaonis.
units.tr: Behold, then, how he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. The proposition is this: by faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter.

units.la: Et hinc discimus, quantæ virtutis sit, contemnere honores & pompam huius mundi: quod factu est necessarium, si populo Dei coniungi affectamus. Nunc quidam laborant omnibus modis, vt irrepant in aulas regum & principum. At Moses docuit nos aulam fugere, & occasionem etiam oblatam respuere.
units.tr: And hence we learn how great a virtue it is to despise the honours and pomp of this world, which is necessary if we wish to be joined to the people of God. Now some labour by every means to creep into the courts of kings and princes. But Moses taught us to flee the court and to refuse even an opportunity offered.

units.la: Potius eligens simul malis affici cum populo Dei, quàm temporarijs peccati commodis frui.
units.tr: Choosing rather to be afflicted together with the people of God than to enjoy the temporary advantages of sin.

units.la: Quia præcedentia verba non præbebant sufficientem materiam ad explicandam fidem, ideo Apostolus ista adijcit, in quibus verè magnus fidei effectus declaratur. Quomodo enim aliquis sequens rationis & carnis iudicium, non potius eligat præsentibus bonis frui, quàm malis affici? Certè nulli Stoici, quamlibet conarentur persuadere, non esse verè sapientem, qui malis doloribus moueretur, & exilia, orbitates, & id genus incommoda non esse in malis habenda: tamen nunquam potuerunt reipsa quicquam præstare. Quòd igitur Moses sic potuerit facere spiritus tantùm erat, & fidei, non humanæ rationis vel prudentiæ. Aduerte autem, quo modo Apostolus vocet temporaria commoda peccati: non quòd simpliciter bonis temporarijs quis vti nequeat sine peccato, sed quòd peccati materiam subministret. Occasio, inquiunt, facit furem. Ita diuitiæ ad peccatum facilè pertrahunt. Diuitiæ pariunt fastum: fastus contemptum aliorum: contemptus aliorum concipit persuasionem licentiæ: persuasio licentiæ pertrahit ad audendū: audacia malum perpetrat: semel perpetratum erigit animum ad sæpius idem faciundū. Hoc verò vbi contigerit, excæcatus animus ad omne genus malorum prolabitur.
units.tr: Because the preceding words did not provide sufficient material for explaining faith, the Apostle adds these words, in which the truly great effect of faith is declared. For how would someone following the judgement of reason and the flesh not rather choose to enjoy present goods than to be afflicted by evils? Certainly no Stoics, however much they tried to persuade us that one who is moved by painful evils is not truly wise, and that exile, bereavement and that sort of misfortune are not to be counted among evils, could ever actually accomplish anything. That Moses could so act was therefore a matter of the Spirit alone, and of faith, not of human reason or prudence. Note, however, how the Apostle calls temporary advantages "of sin": not because one cannot simply use temporary goods without sin, but because they supply the matter of sin. "Opportunity," they say, "makes the thief." Thus riches easily draw men into sin. Riches produce pride; pride produces contempt for others; contempt for others conceives the persuasion of licence; the persuasion of licence draws one on to dare; boldness perpetrates evil; once perpetrated, it raises the mind to do the same thing more often. When this happens, the blinded mind slides into every kind of evil.

units.la: Omnes, inquit Apostolus, qui volunt diuites fieri, incidunt in laqueos Satanæ. Hi verò, quos commemoraui, laquei sunt diaboli, quos instar plagarum tendit struitq; hominibus.
units.tr: "All who want to become rich," says the Apostle, "fall into the snares of Satan" (1 Tim. 6.9). The snares I have mentioned are the snares of the devil, which he sets and spreads for men like nets.

units.la: Vel ideo commoda peccati vocat Apostolus, quòd commoda aulica vix vnquam a peccato sint immunia: exeat, inquit ille, aula qui vult esse pius: qui tangit picem, inquinabitur ab ea: Malorum consortio etiam pij inficiuntur. Aut certè, quòd Moses, qui erat è numero populi Dei afflicti, citra peccatum haud potuisset se eximere.
units.tr: The Apostle calls them the pleasures of sin perhaps for this reason too: that the pleasures of the court are scarcely ever free from sin. "Let him who wants to be godly," he says, "leave the court; whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it." Even the godly are infected by the company of the wicked. Or certainly, because Moses, who was one of the afflicted people of God, could not have removed himself from them without sin.

units.la: Grauissimè enim peccat, quicunq; subducit se ab ecclesia Dei, & qui cum afflictis fratribus affligi detrectat, cõmunibusq; periculis se studet eximere. Oportet sicut gaudere cum gaudetibus, ita flere cũ flentibus, & cũ infirmatis simul vri. Amos cap. 6. expostulat & perstringit illos grauiter, qui super cõtritione Ioseph nõ mouebantur. Sed & significater vocauit. Notat enim, fruitionē illā bonorū nō esse diuturnā aut durabilē. fabilem: atq; per μείωσιν extenuat bona illa, abducitq; animos, ne illa tam caduca & citò peritura expectant.
units.tr: For he sins most gravely who withdraws himself from the Church of God, who refuses to suffer affliction with his afflicted brothers, and who seeks to escape common dangers. "We must rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, and burn with those who are weakened" (Rom. 12.15; 2 Cor. 11.29). Amos (ch. 6) rebukes and sharply censures those who were not moved over the affliction of Joseph. But he also called them significantly; for he indicates that the enjoyment of those goods is neither lasting nor durable, and by meiosis [μείωσιν] he diminishes those goods and turns men's minds away, so that they do not look for things so fleeting and soon to perish.

units.la: Sed non sine causa etiam vocauit Israelitas populum Dei. Qui enim electi sunt à Deo, talibus nihil deesse potest. In Deo enim habentur omnia. Et qui per fidem respicit in Deũ, is facilè contemnit commoda temporaria, & omnibus modis studet se illi committere, totusq; paratus est, ut ex Deo pendeat. Et hic populus Dei affligitur. Igitur & tu si vis accenseri populo Dei, ab afflictione Dei non abhorrebis.
units.tr: But it was not without reason that he also called the Israelites the people of God. For those who are chosen by God can lack nothing of such things, since in God all things are possessed. And whoever looks by faith to God easily despises temporary advantages, strives in every way to commit himself to God, and is wholly prepared to depend on him. And this people of God is afflicted. Therefore, if you too wish to be counted among the people of God, you will not shrink from the affliction of God.

units.la: Maiores arbitratus diuitias probrum Christi, quàm Aegyptiorum thesauros.
units.tr: Considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians.

units.la: Ratio propositionis, explicans, quare elegerit affligi cum populo Dei, potius quàm commoda temporaria. In qua & vis fidei sese exerit, & certamina conscientiæ Mosi tacite indicantur. Hic enim duo describuntur proposita, ipsi Mosi, thesauri, qui erant in Ægypto, id est, opes, honores, splendor, magnificentia illa aulica: quæ certè cuiusuis animum emollire potuissent, & manendum apud filiam Pharaonis pertrahere: sicut omnes sciunt, & plerique experiuntur. Ex altera parte erant loco diuitiarum proposita probra, & contumeliæ, quales perferre debebat omnis ille electus populus. Hic cogita, quàm anxius esse potuerit Mose animus, & quales tentationes animus eius subierit. Venit in mentem fabula, sed valde salutaris, & minimè fabulosa, de Hercule Prodico, quem Cicero libro 5, epistolarum epist. 2. vocat & Xenophontium, quomodo huic quoque apparuerint virtus & voluptas, illa quidem horrida & inculta, squalida, & proponens labores & ærumnas: hæc verò blanda, iucunda, hilaris, & promittens delicias, splendorem. Et tamen Hercules ille elegit sequi virtutem, ut per eam sibi immortalitatem pararet. Eandem rem licet hic cernere & in Mose, cui propositi sunt thesauri Aegyptij, similiter & probra, & contumeliæ Christi, & tamen elegit ista probra potius, quàm thesauros Aegyptios. Potuisset enim in aulla regia manere, & magnis honoribus frui, hæreditatem & opes hliæ Pharaonis, iure adoptionis & testamenti præscriptione, adire, ac tandem ad regios honores, vel summum aliquem magistratum aspirare, non minus, quàm olim Iosephus, qui ex sordido carcere eductus ad summum honoris fastigium fuerat eueetus. Qua quidem ratione & in delicijs aulicis versari, & in magna populi estimatione omniũ Hebræorum oculos in se conuertere poterat, & quodammodo coram mundo (ut Damocles ille Syracusanus mentiebatur) beatus esse.
units.tr: This is the reasoning of the proposition, explaining why he chose to be afflicted with the people of God rather than to enjoy temporary advantages. In it both the power of faith is displayed and the struggles of conscience are silently indicated in Moses. Two things are set before him here: the treasures that were in Egypt, that is, wealth, honours, splendour and that courtly magnificence, which could certainly soften the mind of anyone and draw him to remain with Pharaoh's daughter, as all know and as most have experienced; and on the other side, in place of riches, the reproaches and insults which that whole chosen people had to endure. Consider here how anxious Moses' mind may have been, and what temptations it underwent. There comes to mind a fable, but a very wholesome one and by no means fabulous, about Hercules and Prodicus, whom Cicero, in book 5 of the Letters, letter 2, calls also Xenophontian: how virtue and pleasure appeared to him as well, the one indeed rough, unkempt and squalid, offering labours and hardships; the other soft, pleasant and cheerful, promising delights and splendour. And yet that Hercules chose to follow virtue, so that through it he might win immortality. The same thing may be seen here in Moses, to whom the treasures of Egypt were set before him, and likewise the reproaches and insults of Christ; and yet he chose those reproaches rather than the Egyptian treasures. For he could have remained in the royal court and enjoyed great honours, by right of adoption and the terms of the will taking up the inheritance and wealth of Pharaoh's daughter, and at last aspired to royal honours or some supreme magistracy, no less than Joseph once, who had been led out of a squalid prison and raised to the highest pinnacle of honour. By this course he could both live in courtly luxury and, enjoying great esteem among the people, turn the eyes of all the Hebrews upon himself, and in a sense be happy in the sight of the world (as that Damocles of Syracuse falsely imagined).

units.la: Sed his omnibus spretis Christi probra, & ecclesiæ consortium deligit, mauultque eũ ecclesia & Christo capite probra, contumelias, persecutionem perferre, ac tandem in cœlis æternæ gloriæ corona potiri, quâ ad tempus deliciari, ac vita hac finita condemnari.
units.tr: But having rejected all these things, he chooses the reproaches of Christ and fellowship with the Church, and prefers to bear, together with the Church and with Christ as head, reproaches, insults and persecution, and at last to obtain in heaven the crown of eternal glory, rather than to take his delight for a time and then be condemned when this life is over.

units.la: Sicq; regnum Christi, quod humile in terris est & abiectum, pluris facit, quàm magnificam illam pompam & splendorem aulicæ vitæ, qui sanè aliquando in summam redit miseriam. Ioannes Baptista, mauult vili cultu & vitu contentus regnum Christi quæ rere, quàm in aula Herodis (cui non ingratus erat) assentando delicias regias & fauore impiorũ sibi demereri. Qui sic? Pluris faciebat regnum Christi, quod vitæ huius probris & miserijs ad tempus agitatum: summam tandem æternamq; fœlicitatem parere potèrat, quàm ad tempus breue deliciari, ac demum à brauio regni illius excludi. Sic pluris fecit regnum Christi Lazarus mendicus, sua forte contentus, & stipem medicans, quippe sciens, in cœlis sibi remunerationem propositam: ad quam sanè diues epulo lachrymis & squalore confectus peruenire nequaquâ poterat. De quo plura vide Luc. 12. & 16.
units.tr: So too he sets more value on the kingdom of Christ, which on earth is lowly and despised, than on that magnificent pomp and splendour of courtly life, which indeed at some point comes to utmost misery. John the Baptist preferred to seek the kingdom of Christ, content with plain clothing and food, rather than to win for himself the royal delights of Herod's court (to whom he was not unfriendly) by flattering him and by the favour of the wicked. Why so? He set more value on the kingdom of Christ, which, though it is for a time troubled by the reproaches and miseries of this life, could in the end bring forth supreme and eternal happiness, than on a brief delight for a time, followed at last by exclusion from the prize of that kingdom. So Lazarus the beggar set more value on the kingdom of Christ, perhaps content with his lot and healing his wounds with alms, knowing that a reward was set before him in heaven, to which the rich man who feasted, worn down by tears and squalor, could by no means attain. On this see more in Luke 12 and 16.

units.la: Sed, cur inquies, Christi ea probra dicuntur, quæ Mosi, Ecclesiæ, & ministris eueniunt? Nondum tum Christus in carnem venerat, quomodo igitur probra in eum conijci poterant, de quo gentes illę idololatræ ne somniare quidem poterant?
units.tr: "But," you may ask, "why are those reproaches of Christ spoken of which befall Moses, the Church and the ministers? At that time Christ had not yet come in the flesh. How, then, could reproaches be cast upon him, of whom those idolatrous nations could not even dream?"

units.la: Respondemus: Rectè ea probra omnia Christi dici, quæcunq; ecclesiæ, prophetis, apostolis, & ministris, imò infimis quibusque & parvulis inferuntur. Quæ enim ecclesię, quæ corpus est filij Dei, imò sponsa (teste Paulo Ephes. 5.) vel benignè siunt, vel aduersa accidunt, ea utique & capiti accidunt, quod est Christus. Sic Matth. 10. 25. ea, quæ in prophetas, apostolos, & pauperes vel minimos conferuntur, tanquam sibi collata acceptat, & æternis præmijs copensat. Qui vos recipit, inquit, me recipit: qui uerò vos spernit, me spernit. Itè, Quicquid uni ex minimis meis fecistis mihi fecistis. Cõtrà, q aspernatur, affligit, & læditmembra, idem & caput affligit: perinde acis, qui principis aut regis alicuius legatum iniuriosè aut tupiter tractat, ipsius regis aut principis maiestatem violat. Ita quì Dei omnipotentis legatos affligit, aut Christi ministros iniuriosius tractat, Deum & filium eius Iesum Christum affligit. Zach. 2. Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Actor. 9. Saulo spiranti cædem & minas aduersus ecclesiam & Christi confessores. Christus fulgore cœlesti & voce diuina sic occurrit, Saule, Saule, quid me persequeris? Erit tibi dura contra stimulum calcitrare. Et ibidem: Ego sum Iesus, quem tu persequeris.
units.tr: We answer: all those reproaches are rightly said to be Christ's, whatever is inflicted on the Church, on the prophets, the apostles and the ministers, indeed on the very humblest and least. For whatever is done to the Church, which is the body of the Son of God, indeed his bride (as Paul witnesses, Eph. 5), whether it is done kindly or adversely befalls her, that surely befalls the head, which is Christ. So in Matthew 10 (vv. 25 and following) he accepts as done to himself whatever is conferred upon the prophets, apostles and the poor or the least, and rewards it with eternal prizes. "He who receives you," he says, "receives me; and he who rejects you rejects me" (Matt. 10.40). Likewise: "Whatever you did to one of these least of mine, you did to me" (Matt. 25.40). On the contrary, whoever despises, afflicts and wounds the members also afflicts the head. Just as one who treats insultingly or cruelly the envoy of a prince or king violates the majesty of the king or prince himself, so one who afflicts the envoys of almighty God, or treats the ministers of Christ more insultingly, afflicts God and his Son Jesus Christ. Zechariah 2: "Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye." Acts 9: Saul, breathing slaughter and threats against the Church and the confessors of Christ, is met by Christ with a heavenly brightness and a divine voice: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It will be hard for you to kick against the goad." And in the same place: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."

units.la: Y
units.tr: Y

units.la: Et Matth.5.Beati,cùm omne genus probri dixerint aduersus vos,propter me:gaudete & exultate,quoniam merces vestra multa est in cœlis.Et 2.Cor.1. Sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis,ita abundat per Christum & consolatio nostra. Quæ verò probra Christi sint,satis notum est ex historia euangelica,& mortis:præterquam enim,quòd filius Dei esse negatur,illuditur,& ludibrijs afficitur,blasphemijs etiam nomen eius pro scinditur,appellatur Beelzebub,habens dæmonium,seductor populi,alijsq; nominibus ignominiosis notatur: quemadmodum videre est, Ioan. octauo, Lucæ vndecimo, Matth.vicesimo septimo.
units.tr: And Matt. 5: "Blessed are you when they revile you and say every kind of evil against you for my sake. Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven." And 2 Cor. 1: "As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." What the reproaches against Christ were is well enough known from the gospel history and his death. Besides being denied to be the Son of God, he was mocked and subjected to ridicule; his name was also torn apart by blasphemies: he was called Beelzebub, said to have a demon, a seducer of the people, and marked with other shameful names. As may be seen in John 8, Luke 11 and Matt. 27.

units.la: A capite igitur Christo deriuata sunt hæc probra ad domesticos & discipulos eius, quòdipse iam pridem ita futurum prædixerat Ioan.16. & Matth.5.10. Imò ab Abele•fq; ad Zachariam probra hæc & afflictiones ecclesiam manserunt,ac manebunt, quamdiu euangelium in mundo(qui semper mundus & immundus manet) prædicatum fuerit. Vnde præclarè admodum D.Paulus (de quo Christus ad Ananiam, Ego ei ostendam, quanta oporteat eum pro nomine meo pati) in suis epistolis de infirmitatibus & afflictionibus propter nomen Christi gloriatur. 2. Corinth.11. multus est in commemorandis aduersitatibus,quæ ppter Christū euenerant: quas tandé sic concludit,dices:Quis infirmatur,& ego non infirmor? Quis offenditur,& ego non uror? Si gloriari oporteat de his,quæ infirmitatis meæ sunt,gloriabor. Sic prima Corint.4. Arbitror, quòd Deus nos, qui sumus apostoli postremi,ostenderit,tanquam morti addictos : quoniam spectaculum facti sumus mundo,& angelis,& hominibus.Nos stulti propter Christum, vos autem prudentes per Christum:nos imbecilles,vos autem validi:vos clari,nos contempti. Ad hoc vsque tempus & esurimus & sitimus,& nudi sumus,& colaphis cædimur:& incertis uagamur sedibus:& laboramus operantes proprijs manibus.Male audientes benedicimus:persecutionem patientes sustinemus.Conuicijs affecti obsecramus. Veluti excrementa mundi facti sumus,omnium reiectamentum ad hunc vsque diem. De apostolorū afflictionibus & probris qui plura legere desiderat,perlegat Acta apostolica, quę cursum & iactationes apostolorum describunt. Id verò hoc loco diligenter notandum est:quantum differt regnum Christi à regno Pharaonis & huius mundi: in tanta etiam differunt præmia,quæ Christus suis fidelibus exoluit,ab ijs, quæ mundus & princeps eius ostendant & largiuntur.Christi regnum spirituale est & æternum,sanctum, & à uitijs remotum:impuri & immundi ab hoc sunt exclusi:spiritu & verbo vitæ administratur:ideoq; ad veritatem eos duci oportet,& spiritu Dei regi,qui ciues & hæredes illius esse expetūt. Atq; hæc regni illius sors est,vt mundi probris,iniurijs,& afflictionibus sit in terris expositum. Tandem vita hac defuncti ciues Christi, & tabernaculo mortali deposito, perfectam illam beatamq; vitam assequuntur in cœlis:hi sunt thesauri, hæ sunt opes Christi, quibus cum angelis in cœlis fruuntur sancti, qui per multas tribulationes βεαβεῖον illud sunt adepti.Atq; hic thesaurus rapi ab hostibus,aut consumi ferrugine,aut labefactari vlla vi non potest. Quemadmodum præclarae promissiones ea de re extant, Luc.12,16. Matth.19.2.Tim.2.4. 2.Cor.4.5. Rom.8. Hebr.11.&c.
units.tr: From Christ as the head, these reproaches have passed down to his household and disciples, as he had long before foretold, John 16 and Matt. 5:10. Indeed, from Abel to Zechariah these reproaches and afflictions have remained in the Church, and they will remain for as long as the gospel is preached in the world, which always remains the world, unclean as it is. Hence the most admirable St Paul (of whom Christ said to Ananias, "I will show him how much he must suffer for my name") glories in his letters in the infirmities and afflictions he endured for the name of Christ. In 2 Cor. 11 he is lengthy in recounting the adversities that befell him for Christ, and at last concludes thus: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I do not burn? If I must glory, I will glory in the things that concern my infirmity." So too in 1 Cor. 4: "I think God has displayed us, the last of the apostles, as men condemned to death, for we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men. We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are honoured, but we are despised. To this day we hunger and thirst, we are naked, we are buffeted, we wander without a fixed home, and we labour, working with our own hands. Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we endure; being slandered, we entreat. We have become as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all things, to this day." Whoever wishes to read more of the apostles' afflictions and reproaches should read through the Acts of the Apostles, which describe the course and tossings of the apostles. But this must be carefully noted here: how greatly the kingdom of Christ differs from the kingdom of Pharaoh and of this world. So too the rewards that Christ pays to his faithful differ greatly from those that the world and its prince display and bestow. The kingdom of Christ is spiritual and eternal, holy and remote from vices; the impure and unclean are excluded from it; it is governed by the Spirit and the word of life. Therefore those who desire to be its citizens and heirs must be led to the truth and ruled by the Spirit of God. And this is the lot of that kingdom: that on earth it is exposed to the reproaches, injuries and afflictions of the world. Finally, those citizens of Christ who have departed this life and laid down the mortal tabernacle, attain that perfect and blessed life in heaven. These are the treasures, these are the riches of Christ, which the saints enjoy with the angels in heaven, having won that prize [βραβεῖον] through many tribulations. And this treasure cannot be seized by enemies, consumed by rust, or shaken by any force. The splendid promises on this matter stand as witnesses: Luke 12:16, Matt. 19:2, 2 Tim. 2:4, 2 Cor. 4:5, Rom. 8, Heb. 11, etc.

units.la: Contrà verò regnum mundi terrenum & caducum tyrannide,voluptatum illecebris, sordibus impiorum,variisq; peccatis pollutum est spiritui Dei & verbo capitali odio infestisq; animis repugnat:splendores,opes,honores,voluptates,& libidines mundi,carnisq; concupiscentias sectatur,in fastu & luxu occupatur, summumq; bonum in rebus carnalibus & caducis collocat. Atq; hinc fit,ut vita hac ciues eius functi à vera vita felicitateq; cœlesti aberrantes pereant æternum,cruciatibusq; inferorū condemnati,magno suo damno experiantur,quàm turpiter à principe mundi huius sint delusi.Vidit hoc Luc.16.diues ille epulo,qui in tartara præcipitatus cruciatus suos deplorat, & frustra ad recreationē guttæ aquæ suspirat.Sciuit hoc Christus, quando,ut est Matth.4. diabolus tentator regna & opes mundi ei falsò pollicetur, quod promissum ut impium & fallax Dominus repudiauit.Plura de incertitudine & fallacia opum terrenarū, Vide Luc.12.16. Matth.19.psal.39.Ierem.17.1.Tim.6.1.Cor.7.
units.tr: On the contrary, the earthly and perishable kingdom of the world, polluted by tyranny, the allurements of pleasure, the filth of the impious and by various sins, is hostile to the Spirit of God and to the word, and it resists with deadly hatred and hostile minds. It pursues the splendours, wealth, honours, pleasures and lusts of the world and the desires of the flesh; it is occupied with pride and luxury, and it places the highest good in carnal and perishable things. And hence it comes that the citizens of that kingdom, when they die in this life, wandering away from true life and heavenly happiness, perish for ever, condemned to the torments of hell, and learn to their great loss how shamefully they have been deceived by the prince of this world. The rich man at the feast, Luke 16, saw this, who, hurled down into hell, laments his torments and vainly sighs for a drop of water to refresh him. Christ knew this, when, as in Matt. 4, the devil the tempter falsely promised him the kingdoms and riches of the world; a promise which the Lord, as impious and deceitful, rejected. On the uncertainty and deceitfulness of earthly riches see Luke 12:16, Matt. 19, Ps. 39, Jer. 17, 1 Tim. 6, 1 Cor. 7.

units.la: Discemus hinc:primū,regni Christi eā esse conditione, vt probris,iniurijs,cruci,persecutioni,& calumnijs,dū hic agunt ciues eius,fit expositū.Deinde, opes,honores,voluptates,mundi splendidas videri & magnificas:quarum irritamentis multi à vera fide ab ducuntur,& ad regnum Satanæ alliciuntur:id quod de Hymenæo & Phileto Paulus,& de pharisæo(Matth.19)Christus queritur. Tertiò,Exitum esse diuersum:ut enim ciues Christi & filij Dei coronam immarcesibilem, & βεαβεῶν veræ beatitudinis in cœlis à iusto iudice accipiunt:ita homines seculares,carni & ventri dediti, Deoq; huius seculi seruientes,spe sua turpiter frustrati in sempiternos ignes & cruciatus incidunt. Hæc illorū merces est,quam Satan mancipijs suis exoluit. Piorum fides hisce firmabitur, animus intentatione erigetur, suffulcieturque spe gloriæ æternæ & diuitiarum Christi: contrà increduli à suis vijs discedant vetri Deo, & prin cipi tenebrarum renuncient: Deumque orent, vt ex potestate illius erepti, in regnum veritatis & filij Dei transferantur: sin minus, temeritatis & apostasiæ graues aliquando pœnas luent.
units.tr: We learn from this: first, that the kingdom of Christ is of such a condition that, while its citizens live here, it is exposed to reproaches, injuries, the cross, persecution and calumnies. Second, that the riches, honours and pleasures of the world seem splendid and magnificent, and by their enticements many are drawn away from true faith and lured into the kingdom of Satan. Paul complains of this in the case of Hymenaeus and Philetus, and Christ in the case of the Pharisee (Matt. 19). Third, the outcome is different. For just as the citizens of Christ and sons of God receive from the just judge the unfading crown and the prize [βραβεῖον] of true blessedness in heaven, so worldly men, given over to the flesh and the belly, serving the god of this age, are shamefully disappointed in their hope and fall into everlasting fires and torments. This is their reward, which Satan pays to his slaves. The faith of the pious will be strengthened by these things; their spirit will be raised up by the warning, and supported by the hope of eternal glory and the riches of Christ. But unbelievers should depart from their own ways, return to God and renounce the prince of darkness, and pray God that, rescued from his power, they may be transferred into the kingdom of truth and of the Son of God; otherwise they will someday pay grievous penalties for their rashness and apostasy.

units.la: Per fidem reliquit Aegyptum, haud veritus ferociam regis. Perinde enim quasi videret eum, qui est invisibilis, ita obdurauit.
units.tr: By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the anger of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.

units.la: Tertia probatio fidei Mosi, ab audacissimo conatu educendi populum Israeliticum ex Aegypto. Quam certè ad rem nunquam potuisset Moses animum adijcere, nisi iam per fidem fuisset aliunde confirmatus, certoque statuisset, diuinam opem sibi non defuturam, sumptumque est hoc argumentum ab ijs, quæ scripta sunt Exod.3.4.5. Nonnulli quidem existimant, hic agi de fuga Mosi post interfectum Aegyptium, cuius supra fecimus mentionem: sed ea fuga non ita poterat commendari pro euidenti testimonio fidei. Quantulû enim illud est, quòd metuens se prodendum, præterea videns, se à Pharaone quæri ad mortem, fugerit? Quis hoc non faciat, præsertim reus criminis, propter quod ciuiliter foret puniendus?
units.tr: This is the third proof of Moses' faith: his most daring attempt to lead the Israelite people out of Egypt. Certainly Moses could never have applied his mind to this task unless he had already been confirmed in faith from elsewhere, and had firmly determined that divine help would not be lacking to him. This argument is drawn from what is written in Exod. 3, 4 and 5. Some indeed think that the flight of Moses after he killed the Egyptian, which we mentioned above, is meant here; but that flight could not be commended as clear evidence of faith. For how small a thing is it that he fled, fearing that he would be betrayed, and seeing that Pharaoh was seeking his death? Who would not do this, especially a man guilty of a crime for which he would be punished by the civil law?

units.la: Verum quidem est, bona diuina ordinatione factum, quòd Moses, postquam interfecisset Aegyptium, qui iniuria afficiebat Hebræum, in signum, quòd ipse futurus esset is, per quem Hebræi omnes postea forent è seruitute Aegyptiaca liberandi: (sicut Stephanus ipse interpretatur Actor. 7.) fugerit in terram Midian, ut ita seruaretur ipse, qui tempore constituto rediret liberaturus populum: verùm hoc non magnoperè facit ad prædicandam fidem Mosi, cùm aperte ibi scribatur Exod.2. eum fugisse præ metu Pharaonis, qui quærebat eum interficere. Est quidem egregium exemplû ibi propositû, quomodo Deus suos seruet in periculis, & quomodo, quos elegit ad res magnas perficiendas in ecclesia sua mirabiliter tueatur, & postea suo tempore ornet præclaris dotibus, vt apti sint ad faciendum, quæ Deus fieri ordinauit. Et habent pij fratres, qui hodie coguntur ire exulatum, & effugere manus tyrannorum, magnam in exemplo Mosi consolationem, iubenturq; statuere, quòd Deus ipsos seruet melioribus rebus, quàm obtingere potuisset, si domi quieti & amici mundi atque impiorum mansissent. Sicut etiam reipsa exprimur in multis, & in nobis ipsis, quos Deus in exilio fouet, & præclaris donis ornat, & fortasis vult alibi præparari, vt postea vtiles sint ecclesijs, vel in patria sua in posterum, vel illis, ad quos diuertunt: sicut Iosephi diuina voluntate fuit venditus, & præmissus in Aegyptum, vt postea & Aegyptum, & suos tempore fa nis seruaret: ita nunc sine dubio Deus ex variis regionibus prospicit, qui se conferunt ad ecclesias reformatas, vt in posterum vel illis ipsis ecclesijs, vel suæ patriæ in suppeditanda doctrina verbi vtiles esse possint. Ergo de illo exitu ab Aegypto agitur, quo Moses secum erat abducturus vniuersum populum Israeliticum, & de quo agitur Exodi 3.4.5. vbi reuera mirabile opus siue effectus fidei describitur. Atqui istud eò magis probabile, quia apostolus probaturus fidei excellentiam in Mose, dicit, sic obdurasse, quasi vidisset Deum inuisibilem. Quibus verbis haud dubiè respicit Apostolus ad id, quod Exod.3. scribitur de apparitione Dei in rubo, vbi aperte hoc dicitur, Abscondit Moses faciem suam, nō enim audebat aspicere contra Deū. Atqui ita illis verbis tantus effectus fidei in Mose clarissimè comprobatur. Sed vt tota res clarius cognoscatur, ex historia illa repetemus. Exod.3. narratur, quomodo Mosi pascenti gregem ad montem Dei Horeb Dominus apparuit in flamma ignis de medio rubi, rubo tamen nequaquam ardente, & manente illæsa. Ex ea Dominus vocat Mosen, significatq;, tempus adesse, quo velit liberare suum populum à seruitute Aegyptiaca: & Mosen emittit ad Pharaonem, designatq; ducem populi, additis signis variis, quibus Moses fidè posset facere Hebræis, se diuinitus ipsorum ducem constitutum. Et præterea præscribit, quali oratione uti debeat apud Pharaonem, dicendo: Dominus Deus Hebræorum vocauit nos: ibimus uiam trium dierum in solitudinem, ut immolemus Domino Deo nostro. Cùm autem Moses adhuc valde anxius, censeretq;, se minus fore idoneum ad tantā legationem feliciter obeundam, causans, se non satis eloquentem seu disertum: Dominus iterum cap.4. pollicetur, se etiam formaturum illi os, & ne quis in mora esset, constituit etiam adiungendum ipsi fratrem Aaronem, qui longè erat facundior, commodeque posset apud Pharaonem legati partes agere. Hac fiducia erectus Mose, ficq; à Deo ipso in structus, petit veniam à Iethro socero abeundi è terra Midian in Aegyptum, ut munus sibi iniunctum à Deo posset peragere. Quo tempore iterum Dominus ipsi apparuit, necnon prædixit, se induraturū cor Pharaonis, nihilominus Mosen semper debere instare, ut populum educeret.
units.tr: It is true that by a good divine ordinance it happened that Moses, after he had killed the Egyptian who was wronging a Hebrew, fled into the land of Midian. This was a sign that he himself would be the one through whom all the Hebrews would afterwards be freed from Egyptian slavery (as Stephen himself explains in Acts 7), and so he was preserved, to return at the appointed time and free the people. But this does not greatly serve to proclaim the faith of Moses, since it is plainly written there in Exod. 2 that he fled for fear of Pharaoh, who sought to kill him. There is indeed a notable example set forth there of how God preserves his own in dangers, and how he wonderfully guards those whom he has chosen to accomplish great things in his Church, and afterwards in due time adorns them with excellent gifts, so that they may be fit to do what God has ordained to be done. And the godly brethren who today are compelled to go into exile and escape the hands of tyrants have great consolation in the example of Moses, and are taught to hold that God preserves them with better things than they could have obtained had they stayed quietly at home, friends of the world and of the impious. As we ourselves experience in many cases, God cherishes in exile those whom he adorns with excellent gifts, and perhaps wishes them to be prepared elsewhere, so that afterwards they may be useful to the churches, either in their own country in the future or to those to whom they turn aside. Just as Joseph was sold by divine will and sent ahead into Egypt, so that afterwards he preserved both Egypt and his own people in due time, so now, without doubt, God from various regions provides for those who betake themselves to the reformed churches, so that in the future they may be useful either to those very churches or to their own country in supplying the teaching of the word. Therefore we are speaking of that departure from Egypt by which Moses was going to lead the whole Israelite people away with him, and of which Exod. 3, 4 and 5 speak, where indeed a truly remarkable work or effect of faith is described. And this is all the more probable because the apostle, wishing to prove the excellence of faith in Moses, says that he endured as seeing the invisible God. By these words the apostle undoubtedly refers to what Exod. 3 writes about the appearance of God in the bush, where it is plainly said: "Moses hid his face, for he did not dare to look upon God." Thus by these words so great an effect of faith in Moses is most clearly proved. But that the whole matter may be better understood, we shall go back over that history. Exod. 3 tells how the Lord appeared to Moses, as he was tending the flock at the mountain of God, Horeb, in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush; yet the bush was by no means burning up, but remained unharmed. From it the Lord calls Moses and signifies that the time has come when he wishes to free his people from Egyptian slavery. He sends Moses to Pharaoh and appoints him leader of the people, adding various signs by which Moses could faithfully convince the Hebrews that he had been appointed their leader by God. Furthermore, he prescribes the form of words Moses should use before Pharaoh: "The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us; we will go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God." When Moses, still very anxious and thinking he would be less fit to carry out so great an embassy successfully, excused himself on the ground that he was not sufficiently eloquent or skilled in speech, the Lord again promises in chapter 4 that he will also form his mouth. And lest anyone be delayed, he also appoints his brother Aaron to be joined with him, who was far more eloquent and could conveniently perform the part of envoy before Pharaoh. Raised up by this confidence, and instructed by God himself, Moses asks leave from his father-in-law Jethro to depart from the land of Midian into Egypt, so that he may carry out the task laid upon him by God. At that time the Lord appeared to him again, and foretold that he would harden the heart of Pharaoh; nevertheless Moses must always press on, so that he might lead the people out.

units.la: Tandem venit in Aegyptum, occurritque ei, sicut Dominus quoque prædixerat, fratter Aaron, cum quo pergit, & conuocat omnes seniores Israel, explicabatque, quomodo Deus ipsum vocasset, & misisset ad liberandum ipsos ex seruitute Aegyptiaca, confirmans id signis, qualia Dominus antea præscripserat: quam ob causam crediderunt ei, & proni Deum adorauerunt. Capite itaque quinto statim exponitur, quomodo Moses & Aaron venerint ad Pharaonem, ac mandatum Dei exposuerint, dicentes: Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Israel, Dimitte populum meum, vt sacrificet mihi in deserto.
units.tr: At length he came into Egypt, and his brother Aaron, as the Lord had also foretold, met him there. He went on with him and gathered together all the elders of Israel. He explained how God had called him and sent him to free them from Egyptian bondage, confirming this by signs of the kind the Lord had earlier prescribed. For this reason they believed him, and bowing low they worshipped God. Then, at the start of the fifth chapter, it is set out how Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and declared God's command, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.

units.la: Hic igitur mirabilis effectus fidei describitur, ingensque fortitudo contra pericula & tyrannidem. Primum hoc cogitetur, annon valde anxius fuerit Moses, cum iuberetur reuerti in terram, ex qua propter perpetratum homicidium fugerat? Nonne hoc iudicare potuisset, si ibi mox pertrahendum ad supplicium? Sed Deus eum hac in parte securum reddidit. Significauit enim, priusquam egrederetur, mortuos fuisse omnes, qui quærebant animam ipsius. At quàm molestum, auelli à socero, apud quem iam vixerat fere annos 40. abducereque ad commune periculum vxorem & paruos liberos? Sed innumera alia occurrebant animo Mosi impedimenta, propter quæ opus fuit animum illius tot modis erigi & confirmari.
units.tr: Here, then, the remarkable effect of faith is described, and the great strength it gives against dangers and tyranny. First, consider whether Moses was not very anxious when he was bidden to return to the land from which he had fled after committing murder. Could he not have judged that he would be dragged straight to punishment there? But God made him secure on this point. For before he set out, God made it known that all those who had sought his life were dead. Yet how painful it was to be torn away from his father-in-law, with whom he had already lived for almost forty years, and to lead his wife and small children into common danger! Still, countless other obstacles presented themselves to Moses' mind, and for these reasons his spirit needed to be raised up and strengthened in so many ways.

units.la: Nunc autem videamus etiam de ferocia Pharaonis. Hic statim indurato animo crudelissime resistit, vt Mosi non videretur, amplius cogitandum de negotio repetendo, quod aggressus fuerat: Quis, inquit, est Dominus, vt audiam vocem eius, & dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, & Israel non dimittam. Ecce blasphemü contra Deum, quasi sola crudelitas & impietas maxima plenissimè describitur. Sed mox etiam ferocit tyrannus in pe- sonas missas. Quare Moses & Aaron solicitatis populum ab operibus suis? Ite ad onera vestra. Hic statim desperare potuisset Moses, & cogitare, vt rediret in Midian: sed nihil adhuc motus est.
units.tr: Now let us also look at the fierceness of Pharaoh. He at once hardened his heart and resisted most cruelly, so that it did not seem to Moses that he should think any more about repeating the business he had undertaken. Who is the Lord, he said, that I should hear his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go. Here is blasphemy against God, and the utmost cruelty and impiety are fully displayed. But soon the tyrant also rages against the men who had been sent. Why, Moses and Aaron, do you distract the people from their work? Go back to your burdens. Here Moses could have despaired immediately and thought of returning to Midian; yet he was not moved at all.

units.la: Iá auĉta iterum tyrannis: nouum init Pharao consilium, & præcipit per præfectos populum grauari maioribus oneribus, & cogi ad quærendum etiam paleas ac stipulas, quæ antea ipsis suppeditabantur per præfectos: & nihilominus tantum operis perficere, quàm antea in singulos dies erant soliti, & cæsi adhuc flagris, qui præstare non poterant. Cū vero conquererentur apud Pharaonem quidam præpositi Israelitarum, hi quoque dura & atrocia audiunt, iubenturq; pergere in opere propositò. Cómoti hi etiam Mosi & Aaroni facefunt negotium, obijcientes, quòd ipsorum causa sic grauerentur. Ad quam rem ipse Mose cómotus nonnihil fuit: vt ipse iterum Dominum consuleret, videns tam infœlicem successum. Et licet Dominus ipsum adhuc multis rationibus in fide confirmaret, tamen iam non amplius ei credebant Israelitæ: ita vt ipse, cùm Dominus iterum iuberet ipsum, vt adiret Pharaonem, dixerit: Ecce, filij Israel non audiunt me, & quomodo audiret Pharao? præsertim cùm incircumcisus sim labijs. Sed & Exodi 8. capite, cum iterum iubetur adire Pharaonem, ac signa etiā edit, Pharao nihilominus perstat, & suos item adhibet magos, qui paria signa edant: vt nulla appareret spes perficiendi, quæ Dominus fieri per Mosen iusserat. Ecce ergo multa ferocia Pharaonis, multa & grauia impedimenta, quæ meritò deterruissent Mosen à propósito. Sed his omnibus ipse nihil mouetur, verùm, sicut dicit Apostolus, perinde quasi uidisset cum, qui est inuisibilis, ita obdurauit. Ethis officium fidei aperitur. Non dicitur, quòd viderit Deum, qui est inuisibilis, sed quasi vidit. Ita enim fides versatur circa res non visas, & non apparetes: nihilominus sic perstat, quasi iá vidisset & accepisset omnia bona spiritualia. Murus aheneus est fides: nullis externis rebus percellitur.
units.tr: Tyranny increased again: Pharaoh devised a new plan, and ordered that the people be burdened with heavier loads through their overseers, and be compelled to gather straw as well, which had previously been supplied to them by the overseers; and yet they were to produce the same amount of work they had been accustomed to produce each day, and those who could not manage it were still beaten with whips. When some of the Israelite foremen complained to Pharaoh, they too heard harsh and savage words, and were ordered to go on with the task set before them. Stirred by this, they also made trouble for Moses and Aaron, objecting that they were being burdened so because of them. Moses himself was somewhat disturbed by this, seeing so unhappy an outcome, and he consulted the Lord again. And although the Lord still confirmed him in faith by many arguments, the Israelites no longer believed him. So when the Lord again bade him go to Pharaoh, he said: Behold, the children of Israel do not listen to me, and how would Pharaoh listen? Especially since I am uncircumcised in my lips. But also in the eighth chapter of Exodus, when he is again bidden to go to Pharaoh and even performs signs, Pharaoh nonetheless persists, and likewise brings in his magicians, who perform equal signs; so that no hope appeared of accomplishing what the Lord had commanded to be done through Moses. Here, then, is the great fierceness of Pharaoh, and the many grave obstacles which might rightly have turned Moses from his purpose. But Moses was moved by none of these things; rather, as the Apostle says, he endured as if he had seen him who is invisible. Here the office of faith is revealed. It is not said that he saw God, who is invisible, but as if he saw him. For faith is occupied with things not seen and not apparent; nevertheless it persists as if it had already seen and received all spiritual goods. Faith is a wall of bronze: it is shaken by no external things.

units.la: Cæterùm hic discimus, primò, quòd in vocatione nostra manere debemus, ac certò statuere, Deum nobis, si modò non simus ipsi cessatores, adfuturum in omnibus. Quomodo Mosen fecisse videmus, qui nō reiecit vocationem, licet initio successus infœlices viderentur. Omnia pulchra & præclara sunt initio difficilia: ac Deus interdum vult videre fidem ac diligentiam suorum, & quodammodo probare eos. Si autem videt constantes, & donis suis recte vti, talenta bene dispensare, auget dona illa, & multiplicat, iuxta promissiones euangelicas, Matth. 25.
