units.tr: They quenched the power of fire) This refers to Aaron in Numbers 16, who ran in and prayed for the people so that the fire which was attacking the murmurers might be put out; fourteen thousand and seven hundred had been consumed by the fire. Likewise it refers to those three cast into the burning furnace, Ananias, Azariah and Mishael, I mean, and Daniel (Daniel 3).

units.la: Effugerunt acies gladij) Phrasis est Scripturis vsitata. γόμφα, id est, os gladij, pro acie gladij: Cadent in ore gladij, &c. passim sic dicūt, quòd ea parte mordeat: γόμφα à τέμνω, id est, incido, seco: & suprà capite quarto verbum Dei dixit penetrare ... id est, duplicem aciem habentem, vtrimque incidentem. Effugerunt autem aciem gladij Israelitae euadentes manus Pharaonis: Dauid declinans iactum hastae Saul 1. Samuelis 19. Item Helias effugit gladium Iezabel, quae decreuerat iam amputandum caput Eliae, primo Regum decimonono.
units.tr: They escaped the edge of the sword. This is a phrase in common use in Scripture. The mouth of the sword [γόμφα], that is, its edge, stands for the blade itself. People speak of falling by the mouth of the sword, and so on, everywhere, because the blade bites with that part. γόμφα comes from temno [τέμνω], meaning I cut or I slice. Above, in chapter four, the word of God is said to penetrate, that is, to have a double edge, cutting on either side. The Israelites escaped the edge of the sword when they got away from Pharaoh's hands. David dodged Saul's thrown spear (1 Sam. 19). Likewise Elijah escaped Jezebel's sword, since she had already decided to cut off Elijah's head (1 Kings 19).

units.la: Validi sunt facti ex imbecillitate) Hoc est, qui omnino depressi erant, vt videretur ipsis despe randum, ij iterum receperunt animum, & vires ac dignitatem.
units.tr: Made strong out of weakness. That is, those who had been utterly cast down, so that they seemed bound to despair, recovered their courage, their strength and their standing.

units.la: Quare de oppressis filijs Israel & postea mirabiliter liberatis:itē de captiuis in Babylo-ne, & rursus restitutis: de Machabæis: & sic de multis alijs rectè potest accipi. Etiáfi nō-nulli de ægritudine corporis, & recuperata illorum sanitate exponant. Sic autem Eze-chias valetudinem per fidem recuperauit. 2. Reg. 20. Et Esaiæ 38. Item Dauid Psal. 6.
units.tr: This may rightly be understood of the sons of Israel when they were oppressed and afterwards wonderfully delivered; of the captives in Babylon who were later restored; of the Maccabees; and of many others in the same way. Some, however, explain it of sickness of the body and the recovery of health. Thus Hezekiah recovered his health through faith (2 Kings 20; Isa. 38). So too David (Ps. 6).

units.la: Efficti sunt robusti in bello) Vt Samson: Iudic. 15. Dauid, Machabæi. Machabæor. 4. 5. è qui-bus sex millia interfecerunt centum millia hostiū, & rursus tria millia misi Antiochiam ad auxiliandum, Demetrio interfecerunt centum & viginti millia.
units.tr: Made strong in war. As Samson (Judg. 15), David, and the Maccabees (Maccabees 4. 5.), of whom they slew six thousand, and a hundred thousand of the enemy; and again I sent three thousand to Antioch to give aid, and they slew a hundred and twenty thousand for Demetrius.

units.la: Incursiones euerterunt exterorum, ut Ionathas) 1. Reg. 14. Assa. 2. Paralipom. 14. Iosaphat 2. Paralipom. 20.
units.tr: They overthrew the invasions of foreigners, as Jonathan (1. Reg. 14), Asa (2. Paralipom. 14), and Jehoshaphat (2. Paralipom. 20).

units.la: Mulieres acceperunt ex resurrectione mortuos suos) Id est, resurgentes à morte; suos, scilicet fi-lios, intelligendum enim de Sarepthana vidua, quæ propter fidem suam & Heliæ recepit filium mortuum, 1. Regum capite 17. Rursus de Sunamitide, cuius filium à morte suscitauit Helisæus. 2. Regum capite 4. Vox γυναῖκες non tantum vxores significat, sed & sexum: propterea non est cauillandum hic, quasi diceretur, vxores quasdam recepisse maritos: vt inde moueantur quæstiones, vtrum mortuus maritus & reuiuiscens sit restituendus vxori? &c.
units.tr: Women received their dead by resurrection. That is, the dead rising again; "their" means their sons. This refers to the widow of Zarephath, who for her faith received back her dead son (1 Kings 17), and to the Shunammite, whose son Elisha raised from the dead (2 Kings 4). The word for women [γυναῖκες] means not only wives but the sex in general. So there is no need to quibble here, as if it said that certain wives received back their husbands, from which questions would arise: whether a dead husband who comes back to life should be restored to his wife, and so on.

units.la: Porrò hi præclari effectus fidei hic propositi ita à nobis debet accipi, vt intelligamus, nobis quoque omnia paria euenta per fidem expectanda. Si bellum, si morbi, si incendium, si periculum à feris, si denique mors ingruat, fidem in Deum defigamus, assiduè implorremus illius opem, & sentiemus auxilium. Et non tantum in temporalibus periculis, sed etiam in spiritualibus, vbi etiamnum hodie multi spirituales viri percipiunt taÏles effectus. Certamina sunt illis cum hostibus multis, cum regno Sathanæ, cum pecato. Et tandem Deus dat per fidem victoriam. Hæc est victoria, quæ vincit mundum, si des nostra. Rivius Atendoriensis ostendit, paria miracula etiam nunc contigisse in libro de admirabili consilio Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, these outstanding effects of faith set out here should be understood by us in such a way that we recognise that similar outcomes are to be expected through faith for ourselves too. If war, if disease, if fire, if danger from wild beasts, or finally death itself presses upon us, let us fix our faith on God, constantly implore his help, and we shall feel his aid. And this holds not only in temporal dangers but also in spiritual ones, where even today many spiritual men experience such effects. They have conflicts with many enemies: with the kingdom of Satan, with sin. And in the end God gives victory through faith. This is the victory that overcomes the world, if you give our part. Rivius of Attendorn shows that similar miracles have happened even in our own time, in his book on the wonderful counsel of God.

units.la: Alij vero distenti sunt, aspernati redemptionem, vt potiorem sortirentur resur-rectionem.
units.tr: Others, however, were tortured, refusing deliverance, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

units.la: Alij, &c. Alios adhuc attexit effectus fidei, sed admodum diuersos à præcedentibus; ac diuersa ratione. In proximis enim commemoratę sunt res, quas patres per fidem fortiter egerunt: hic vero commemorantur è diuerso, quas patres per fidem fortiter sunt passi. Adeò vt duo, si bene consideramus, hic proponantur effectuum fidei ordines: alter quidè explicans, quàm magna & præclara bona per fidem queant effici: alter, quàm ardua & periculosa mala per fidem queant ferri ac superari. Atque ita clarissimè ostendi tur, ad quęcunque magna seu difficilia, quæ pios aut agere, aut pati decet, vnam fide esse certissimam viam, qua omnia fiant possibilia: &, ad summa, solam fidem esse, qua ad ve-ram salutem detur peruenire.
units.tr: Others, etc. The apostle adds yet other effects of faith, but very different from the preceding ones, and in a different manner. In the earlier ones he recorded the things which the fathers accomplished bravely through faith; here, on the other hand, he records the things which the fathers bravely suffered through faith. So that, if we consider well, two orders of the effects of faith are set out here: the one showing how great and glorious the goods are that faith can bring about; the other, how hard and dangerous the evils are that faith can bear and overcome. And so it is most clearly shown that for whatever great or difficult things godly people ought to do or suffer, faith alone is the most certain way by which all things become possible, and that, in the highest matters, faith alone is the means by which one may attain true salvation.

units.la: Prudenter aut Apostolus hoc modo posterioris ordinis effectus adiecit. Mirè enim conueniunt hi effectus fidei ita expensi Hebræis, vtpote quorum res erant propter confessionem veritatis afflictæ: vnde metuendum erat, ne ob periculorum magnitudinem à fide deficerent.
units.tr: The apostle wisely added effects of this second kind. For these effects of faith, thus weighed, fit the Hebrews very well, since their circumstances were that they were afflicted for confessing the truth. Hence there was reason to fear that, because of the greatness of the dangers, they would fall away from faith.

units.la: His autem fidei effectibus ob oculos positis, pariter ad periculorum omnium contemptum adducuntur, & ad constantiam fidei retinendam non mediocriter confirmantur.
units.tr: With these effects of faith set before their eyes, they are likewise led to despise all dangers, and are not a little strengthened in holding fast to the constancy of their faith.

units.la: Quinetiam aptissimè parat sibi hic viam ad conclusionem, in qua mox, sicut & Exordio huius sedundæ partis egerat, hortaturus est eos, vt in fide constantes permaneant, & periculorum frequentia ac magnitudine non frangantur.
units.tr: Indeed, he very aptly prepares for himself here a way to the conclusion, in which he will soon exhort them, as he had also done in the opening of this second part, to remain constant in faith and not be broken by the frequency and magnitude of dangers.

units.la: Et certè dùm propius intueor, valde ad consolationem afflictorum isti effectus conducunt: atque hic Christiana vereque heroica fortitudo clarissimè describitur. Hoc enim est vere fortem esse, circa honestam mortem, & quæcunque pericula ei adiuncta, non commoueri: res terrenas despicere, & difficilima quæque propter summum illud bonum, quod est Deus, aggredi & subire. Cui Christus eius que gloria illustranda, tanquam scopus est propositus, & sic animo est compositus, vt neque mors, neq; vita, neq; Angeli, neq; principatus, neq; potestates, neq; instantia, neq; futura, neque altitudo, neque profunditas, neq; vlla creatura eum possit à dilectione Dei, quæ est in Christo, sepa-rare: hunc vere forte merito appellabimus. Hoc vero pacto animatos Patres hoc loco Apostolus in exemplum proponit, nec non ea animorum vim ad fidē quasi fonte transfert. Nos breuiter singulis membris ostendemus, in quibus tanta animi virtus sit conspecta.
units.tr: And certainly, as I look more closely, these effects contribute greatly to the comfort of the afflicted, and here Christian and truly heroic courage is most clearly described. For to be truly brave is this: not to be moved by an honourable death and whatever dangers attend it; to despise earthly things, and to undertake and endure the most difficult things for the sake of that highest good, which is God. Christ, and the illustration of his glory, is set before such a man as his goal, and he is so disposed in mind that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any creature, can separate him from the love of God which is in Christ. Such a man we shall rightly call truly brave. The apostle sets before us the fathers, who were thus animated, as an example, and he also traces this strength of mind back to faith as to its source. We shall briefly show in each member in what respects such great virtue of mind has been seen.

units.la: Alij vero distenti sunt) Græcè est ιτυμπανισθησαν, id est, detenti sunt, vel pulsati, vt tympanū. Nam tympanum funibus & neruis extenditur, deinde assiduè pulsatur.
units.tr: Others were stretched. In Greek it is ἐτυμπανίσθησαν [ἐτυμπανίσθησαν], that is, they were stretched or beaten, like a drum. For a drum is stretched with cords and sinews and then is constantly struck.

units.la: Sic verò & sancti funibus & neruis distenti leguntur. Quomodo Hieremias prophe ta cap.20. dicitur percussus & missus in neruum per Pashur sacerdotum principem in domo Domini. Significat verò τυμπανίζω etiam verbero: Nam tympanum significat li gnum, quo fontes caedebantur. Quare nonnulli interpretantur: quosdam sanctos patres percussos & contusos fustibus: quomodo etiam probabile est, multos tùm prophe tas, cùm in carceres essent coniecti, sub Saul, Iesabel, Manasse & similibus tyrannis: item temporibus Machabaeorum, fustibus caesos, & plagis affectos. Eleganter verò Apostolus describit insignem animi fortitudinem, quando addit: Aspernati redemptionem: Non est vera fortitudo, inuitū pati, & tùm solùm, quando nō apparet ratio evadendi: sed pati, vbi alias licet effugere.
units.tr: In the same way the saints too are read of as stretched with cords and sinews. Just as the prophet Jeremiah (ch. 20) is said to have been struck and put into the stocks by Pashur, the chief of the priests in the house of the Lord. Moreover, τυμπανίζω [τυμπανίζω] also means to beat with blows, for a drum [τύμπανον] means the wood with which drums were struck. Hence some interpret it as meaning that certain holy fathers were struck and bruised with clubs; and it is also probable that many prophets, when they were cast into prisons under Saul, Jezebel, Manasseh and similar tyrants, and likewise in the times of the Maccabees, were beaten with rods and afflicted with blows. The apostle describes remarkably well the outstanding courage of mind when he adds: refusing deliverance. True courage does not consist in suffering against one's will, and only when no way of escape appears; but in suffering when one could otherwise flee.

units.la: Sic verò Sancti patres pasi sunt, non recipientes liberationem, ne cupientes quidem se à tormentis dimitti, cùm tamen possent euadere, videlicet recantando, aut pro nutu tyrannorū aliud faciendo. Sic Hieremias si voluisset loqui grata: item Michaeas si voluisset loqui, vt caeteri pseudoprophetae loquebantur, non fuissent percusi: atq; ita se à periculis redemisset. Ergo egregiè hîc describitur causa formalis constantiae & fortitudinis Christianae.
units.tr: Thus indeed the holy fathers suffered, not accepting release, not even wishing to be let go from the torments, though they could have escaped by recanting, or by doing something else at the nod of the tyrants. So Jeremiah, if he had wanted to speak pleasing things, and Micaiah, if he had wanted to speak as the other false prophets spoke, would not have been struck, and so would have bought themselves out of dangers. Therefore the formal cause of Christian constancy and courage is here described admirably.

units.la: Vt potiorem surrirentur resurrectionem) Ratio tantae fortitudinis à causa finali: nempe expectatione alterius & praestantioris vitae aeternae. Presisi in hac vita cogitabant de resurrectione ad vitam meliorem: atque ita confirmati sunt, vt tormenta omnia, quae in momentanea hac vita possunt obtingere, pro leuibus ducant, respectu foelicitatis, quae post hanc vitam credentibus succedet 2.Corinthiorum capite 4. Ex resurrectione vitam aeternam oportet intelligere, ex priori posterius: sic Christus Ioan.5. Resurgent in resurrectionem vitae. Quod verò Apostolus addit, potiorem: id dupliciter potest accipi.
units.tr: That they might obtain a better resurrection. This is the reason for such great courage, drawn from the final cause: namely, the expectation of another and more excellent life, eternal life. Those who were established in this life thought about a resurrection to a better life, and were so strengthened that they count all the torments which can befall in this momentary life as light, in view of the happiness which will follow this life for believers (2 Cor. 4). One must understand eternal life from the resurrection, the former from the latter; so Christ says in John 5: they shall rise to the resurrection of life. But as for what the apostle adds, better, this can be taken in two ways.

units.la: Primò, potior resurrectio dicitur respectu liberationis, & quodammodo resurrectionis, quam accipere potuissent recantando, vel se simili ratione liberando.
units.tr: First, the better resurrection is spoken of with respect to deliverance, and in a sense to a resurrection, which they could have obtained by recanting, or by freeing themselves in a similar way.

units.la: Qui enim iam destinati erant morti, & in tormentis positi, vt iam morti essent vicini: si huiusmodi contigisset adhuc liberari, vtsi fuissent quodammodo à morte resurgere.
units.tr: For those who were already destined for death and placed in torments, and so were already close to death, if such a deliverance had come to them, it would have been as though they had in some sense risen again from death.

units.la: Sed huiusmodi resurrectionem liberationemque non curarunt, magis spectantes in aliam, quae posset mortem semel toleratam aeterna debebant succedere. Vel dicitur potior resurrectio, ideo, quòd qui ita pasi sunt multa propter Christum, in vniuersali resurrectione piorum ipsi excellentiorem gloriam sunt accepturi prae caeteris.
units.tr: But they did not care for such a resurrection and deliverance, looking rather to another, which, once death had been endured, was to follow eternally. Or the resurrection is called better because those who suffered many things thus for Christ will receive a more excellent glory than the rest in the general resurrection of the pious.

units.la: Certum enim est, licet pios omnes maneat aeterna gloria, tamen alijs contingeret illustrior, quàm alijs, iuxta illud 1. Corinth.15. Stella differt à stella in gloria, sic & resurrectio mortuorum.
units.tr: For it is certain that although eternal glory awaits all the pious, yet it will be more illustrious for some than for others, according to 1 Corinthians 15: "One star differs from another star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead."

units.la: Proinde huiusmodi rationes explicatas natura tum fidei, tum verae fortitudinis Christianae deberet merito animis omnium insculptae inhaerere, & sic confirmarentur in constantia fidei, nec non consolationem in quotidianis periculis acciperent.
units.tr: Therefore these reasons, explained, ought to cling deservedly to the minds of all, engraved there by the nature both of faith and of true Christian courage, and so they would be confirmed in steadfastness of faith and receive consolation in daily dangers.

units.la: Alij rursus ludibrijs & flagris explorati sunt, insuper & vinculis, & carcere, &c.
units.tr: Others again were tested by mockings and scourgings, moreover by chains and prison, etc.

units.la: Sic Esaiae capite 50. Corpus meum dedi percutientibus, & genas meas vellentibus, faciem meam non verti ab increpantibus & conspuentibus in me, Dominus Deus auxiliator meus. De se loquitur: licet in persona Christi: non tamen dubium, quin ipse quoque Propheta talia passus sit. Hieremiae capite 20. factus est mihi sermo Domini in opprobrium & derisum. Helisaeus item irrisus vel à pueris, & per contemptum appellatus calvus. Sic mundus semper irridet & contemnit verbum, eiusque fidos ministros. Et Christus ipse irrisus, salutatusque est per contemptum rex. Matth.27. Flagella, vincula, carceres, expertus est Michaeas 1.Reg.22. Item Hieremias 37. &38. in lacum coniectus est.
units.tr: So Isaiah 50: "I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked out the hair; I did not turn my face from those who reproached and spat upon me; the Lord God is my helper." He speaks of himself, though in the person of Christ; yet there is no doubt that the prophet himself also suffered such things. Jeremiah 20: "The word of the Lord was made to me a reproach and a derision." Elisha likewise was mocked even by boys and called "bald" with contempt. So the world always mocks and scorns the word and its faithful ministers. Christ himself was mocked and greeted with contempt as king, Matthew 27. Micaiah experienced scourges, chains and prisons, 1 Kings 22. Likewise Jeremiah, in Jeremiah 37 and 38, was thrown into a pit.

units.la: Lapidati sunt) Zacharias filius Ioiadae, quia reprehenderat Iudaeos, quòd dereliquissent Dominum, in atrio domus est lapidatus, secundo Paralypomenon capite vigesimoquarto. Referunt nonnulli, etiam Hieremiam lapidibus obrutum à Iudaeis in Aegypto. Certè saepe solitos Iudaeos lapidationis poena opprimere sanctos, liquet ex eo, quod Christus eis obijcit Matthaei 23. Hierusalé, Hierusalem, quae occidis prophetas, & lapidas eos qui ad te missi sunt, &c.
units.tr: They were stoned: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, because he had rebuked the Jews for forsaking the Lord, was stoned in the court of the house of the Lord, 2 Chronicles 24. Some report that Jeremiah too was stoned by the Jews in Egypt. Certainly it is clear that the Jews often used the punishment of stoning to oppress the saints, from what Christ charges them with in Matthew 23: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you," etc.

units.la: Dissecti sunt: ἐπρίσθησαν) Esaias fuit dissectus ferra lignea, iubente Manasse, eò quòd dixisset, se vidisse Dominum exercituum: scribit Origenes super Matthaeum 25.
units.tr: They were sawn asunder [ἐπρίσθησαν]: Isaiah was sawn asunder with a wooden saw, at the command of Manasseh, because he had said that he had seen the Lord of hosts; Origen writes this on Matthew 25.

units.la: Tentati sunt) Vt Helias, dùm profugit desperans de vita (primo Regum capite decimonono) Quanquam haec particula nec in Chrysostomo, nec in Theophylacto, & quibusdam exemplaribus graecis non invenitur. Apparet ergo, adiectam esse ab aliquo. Occisione gladij occubuerunt) De Manasse aperte dicitur 2. Regum capite vigesimo primo, quòd multum sanguinem innocentem fuderit: item de Iezabele, & aliis tyrannis.
units.tr: They were tempted: as Elijah was when he fled, despairing of his life, 1 Kings 19. Although this phrase is not found in Chrysostom, nor in Theophylact, nor in some Greek copies, it appears therefore to have been added by someone. They died by the slaughter of the sword: it is said plainly of Manasseh, 2 Kings 21, that he shed much innocent blood; and likewise of Jezebel and other tyrants.

units.la: Quare dum ista supplicior um genera enumerantur, intelligi debent etiam multi innocentes & pij propter veritatem talibus supplicijs affecti, quorum nomina in Scriptu ris non exprimuntur. Et nota, pariter fide perferri suppliciū gladij: sicut etiam quidā fide effugerunt acies gladij: sive viuamus, sive moriamur, Domini sumus. Alius per fide moritur, & constanter perfert: alius per fide liberatur: ita fides vbiq; nos fortes reddit, & in vitandis periculis, & in subeundis.
units.tr: Therefore, while these kinds of torture are being listed, we must understand that many innocent and godly people, too, were subjected to such punishments for the sake of the truth, whose names are not expressed in the Scriptures. And note that, likewise, by faith some endured the sword's punishment, while others by faith escaped the edge of the sword: whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. One dies by faith and endures steadfastly; another is delivered by faith. So faith everywhere makes us strong, both in avoiding dangers and in facing them.

units.la: Oberrarunt in ouillis & caprinis pellibus destituti, presi, afflicti, quibus indignus erat mundus.
units.tr: They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy.

units.la: Alia pericula contemnentium mundum & molestias recenseт, qui propter tyrannos coacti sunt fugere, & magnas pati miserias: vt nihil omittat, quod ad piorum calamitates pertinet. Sic autem Helias describitur, de quo, vt est 2. Reg. 1. dicitur, quòd fuerit virpilosus, & cingulo pelliceo accinctus renes suos. De eiusdem fuga & exilio lege 1. Reg. 18.19.20. Vbi trucidatis Baalitis in monte Horeb, in syluis, in latibulis se abdere & obberrare, propter furorem Achab & Iezabel fuit coactus. In spiritu & virtute, imò & cultu hunc Iohannes Baptista repræsentauit, de quo Christus Matth. cap. 11. & cap. 17. Marci capite 9. vaticinium Malachiæ exponit, dicitque eum Heliam. De vestitu Ioannis tenui & horrido extat Matth. 3. quòd videlicet habuerit indumentum è pilis Camelorum, & zonam pelliceam circa lumbos suos, cibusque eius fuerint locustæ, & mel sylvestre. Et Christus Matthæi cap. vndecimo negat molli vestitu eum incedere. Ex quo discimus: Non in cibo & potu, neque in uestitu regnum Dei quærendum esse viris grauibus, inprimisque verbi Dei doctoribus. Facili cultu & victu natura contenta est: Aulicæ deliciæ, & fastus mundi debent declinari. Hæ enim causa fuerunt condemnationis diuitis epulonis Lucæ capite decimosexto, & sæpe viros Dei à veritate & fide auocant, faciuntque assentari eos, qui delicijs aulicis assuefacti pro gratuitate suo muneris in peccata animaduertere nequeunt. In illud: Quibus dignus non erat mundus, vide Chrysostomū, sicut & in sequentia verba: In desertis errantes: Ac sane non absre dicit, mundum illis non fuisse dignum: id quod ad summam reiectionem impiorum pertinet. Sic Iudæi non erant digni Ioanne Baptista, Christo & Apostolis, quorum monita & præcepta repudiabant, & capitali odio persequebantur. Sic Actorum capite decimotertio, Paulus ad Iudæos Antiochenos: vobis oportebat primùm loqui sermonem Dei: sed quoniam repellitis illum, & indignos vos iudicatis æterna vita, ecce conuertimur ad gentes. Matth. 10. 11. Luc. 14. & alibi ingratitudo indignitasq; Iudæorum describitur. Plura vide Esa. 5. Ezechiel. 16. &c. Mundus igitur se indignum facit verbo & regno Dei, quando contemnit id, & ministros contumelijs afficit, à quibus salus annunciatur.
units.tr: Other dangers and hardships are listed for those who despise the world, who were forced to flee because of tyrants and suffered great miseries, so that nothing that pertains to the calamities of the godly is left out. Elijah is described in this way: as 2 Kings 1 says, he was a hairy man, girded with a leather belt about his loins. For his flight and exile, read 1 Kings 18, 19 and 20. After he had slain the prophets of Baal on Mount Horeb, he was forced by the rage of Ahab and Jezebel to hide in woods and caves and wander about. John the Baptist represented him in spirit and power, and indeed in his manner of life, as Christ says in Matthew 11 and Mark 9 (the Gospel passage, not the chapter numbering given here, is at Matthew 17), where he explains the prophecy of Malachi and says that John is Elijah. Matthew 3 records the plain and rough clothing of John: he wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt about his loins, and his food was locusts and wild honey. Christ in Matthew 11 also says that John did not go about in soft clothing. From this we learn that the kingdom of God is not to be sought in food and drink, nor in clothing, by serious men, and above all by the teachers of God's Word. Nature is content with simple dress and food; the luxuries and pomp of the court and of the world ought to be avoided. These were the cause of the condemnation of the rich man and Lazarus's feaster in Luke 16, and they often draw men of God away from truth and faith and make them compliant, since men accustomed to courtly pleasures cannot notice sins in the light of the gratuitous nature of their office. On the words "of whom the world was not worthy", see Chrysostom, and likewise on the words that follow, "wandering in the deserts." Indeed, he does not say without reason that the world was not worthy of them, which pertains to the strong rejection of the wicked. Thus the Jews were not worthy of John the Baptist, of Christ and of the apostles, whose warnings and precepts they rejected and whom they pursued with deadly hatred. So in Acts 13 Paul says to the Jews of Antioch: "It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles." Matthew 10 and 11, Luke 14 and elsewhere describe the ingratitude and unworthiness of the Jews. See more in Isaiah 5 and Ezekiel 16, etc. The world therefore makes itself unworthy of the Word and kingdom of God when it despises them and treats with insults the ministers through whom salvation is announced.

units.la: Cæterum hæc omnia etiam nostri seculi pijs valde conueniunt: quando & nunc propter veritatis confessionem multa à tyrannis debent pati, qualia patres perpessi esse memoratur. Multi etiam coguntur oberrare, exilia subire. Restat hoc, vt in exempla patrum intueantur, à fide non deficiant, & per fidem fient idonei ad perfereda quæcunq; aduersa.
units.tr: Moreover, all these things apply very well also to the pious of our own age, since now too, on account of confession of the truth, many must suffer much at the hands of tyrants, such as the fathers are recorded to have suffered. Many also are compelled to wander and to undergo exile. It remains that they look to the examples of the fathers, do not fail in faith, and through faith become fit to endure whatever adversities come.

units.la: Atq; omnes hi testimonium promeriti per fidem, non acceperant promissionē, quòd Deus de nobis melius quiddam prouiderat, ne sine nobis consummarentur.
units.tr: And all these, having obtained a testimony through faith, did not receive the promise, because God had foreseen something better concerning us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.

units.la: Illatio seu Conclusio institutæ hactenus Inductionis. Omnes hi, inquit, testimonium promeriti seu iustificati sunt per fidem. Vnde intelligi debet generaliter, omnes homines per solam fidem iustificari. Ex quo deinde cupit, Hebræis persuasissimum esse, quòd ipsi quoque per fidem sint iustificandi: dummodo patrum exemplo constantes in confessione fidei perstiterint: nec se vllis terroribus, aut blanditijs abduci inde patiantur. Quam sententiam ipse Apostolus suis verbis non obscure explicat, quando addit: Patres illos nō accepisse promissionem, quòd Deus prouiderit omnes nos vnà cum illis consummari. Quod reuera perinde est, ac si dicatur, patres quidem illos esse fide iustificatos, & Deo acceptos, hoc solum restare, vt pij quoq; patribus in fidei confessione adiungatur, & vnà cum his iustificetur, parem gloriam apud Deū accepturi. Atq; ita habemus absolutā omnibus membris inductionē hucusq; protractā, valde profecto accommodā, tum ad docēdū, quòd per solā fide homines iustificetur: tum ad suadendum Hebræis, vt contemptis omnibus periculis exeplo patrum constantes in fide permaneant: ad quæ duo præcipuè tota hæc disputatio dirigitur.
units.tr: The conclusion, or inference, of the induction set out so far. All these, he says, obtained a testimony, that is, were justified, through faith. From this it must be understood in general that all men are justified through faith alone. From this he then wishes it to be most firmly persuaded to the Hebrews that they too are to be justified through faith, provided they persevere steadfastly in the confession of faith after the example of the fathers, and do not allow themselves to be drawn away from it by any terrors or enticements. The Apostle himself explains this view not obscurely in his own words when he adds: that those fathers did not receive the promise, because God had foreseen that we should be made perfect together with them. This is really the same as saying that those fathers were indeed justified by faith and accepted by God, and that it only remains for the godly to be joined to the fathers in the confession of faith, and to be justified together with them, so as to receive equal glory before God. And so we have a complete induction, carried through all its parts up to this point, very much suited both to teaching that men are justified by faith alone and to persuading the Hebrews that, having despised all dangers, they should remain steadfast in faith after the example of the fathers. It is to these two ends that this whole discussion is chiefly directed.

units.la: Cæterum
units.tr: Moreover,

units.la: Ceterùm quod dicit, patres non acccepisse promissionem, nos quidem supra exposuimus ve rum fuisse in patribus illis, ad quos promissiones erant factae de possessione terrae Chanaan, & de semine benedicto exipsis nascituro: sed nondum liquet, impletas non esse promissiones reliquis patribus, qui post secuti, qui terram Chanaan possederunt: item, quomodo non impletae sunt in illis, qui etiam viderunt semen benedictum.
units.tr: As for his saying that the fathers did not receive the promise, we have indeed explained above that it was true of those fathers to whom promises were made concerning the possession of the land of Canaan and concerning the blessed seed to be born from them. But it is not yet clear that the promises were not fulfilled for the remaining fathers who came later and possessed the land of Canaan; nor how they were not fulfilled in those who even saw the blessed seed.

units.la: Verum nos de hac re attigimus etiam eodem loco. Ac primo quidem ostendimus, sub euangelio proprie & spiritualiter adimpletas omnes promissiones ad Abrahamum & patres factas: vt ij demum beati dicantur præ patribus, præ regibus & prophetis mul tis, quibus datum fuit in luce reuelati per Christum euangelij versari: iuxta illud Lu cæ capite decimo, Beati oculi, qui vident, quæ vos videtis. Dico enim vobis, multi pro phetæ & reges voluerunt videre, quæ vos videtis, & non viderunt: & audire, quæ audi tis, & non audierunt.
units.tr: Indeed we touched on this matter in the same place. And first we showed that all the promises made to Abraham and the fathers have been fulfilled under the gospel, properly and spiritually, so that those are rightly called blessed beyond the fathers, beyond many kings and prophets, to whom it was granted to live in the light of the gospel revealed through Christ, according to that passage of Luke chapter ten: Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you, many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.

units.la: Secundò, ostendimus, quòd Dominus etiam iis, qui sub euangelio constituti sunt, in hoc mundo nondum plane confert omnia bona spiritualia, sed tantum quendam gustum in verbo suo, in sacramentis, in donatione spiritus Sancti, quem in corda abunde cum multis & varijs donis diffundit.
units.tr: Secondly, we showed that the Lord, even for those who live under the gospel, does not yet in this world confer plainly all spiritual goods, but only a certain taste of them in his word, in the sacraments, and in the gift of the Holy Spirit, whom he pours abundantly into hearts with many and various gifts.

units.la: Et hoc pacto etiam adimpletæ sunt spiritualiter in filijs spiritualibus promissiones il læ ad patres factæ, quas ipsi in spiritu videbant adimplendas. Verum restant adhuc sum ma & æterna illa bona cœlestia post hanc vitam expectanda, quæ primùm contingent omnibus communiter post vniuersalem corporum resurrectionem. Intelligi potest, beatitudine animarum, quam statim consequuntur, simulatq; emigrant ex hoc carcere suo fragili corpusculo: illa quoq; beatitudine, quam omnes accipiunt post vniuersale resurrectionem in corporibus. Ibi enim primùm erit vera consummatio, ibi etiam mors finem accipiet, vti Apostolus plenius declarat 1. Corinth. 15. Et propterea disertè notanda vox τελεωθῶσιν. Acceperunt quidè patres illi iam vnà cum Christo ascendete in altum, & captiuam ducente captiuitatem, suam gloriam: sed tamen consummatio, post quam nihil aliud restat, nondum illis contigit: sed obuenit, cùm facta fuerit vniuersalis etiam corporum resurrectio: tunc consummabuntur sancti pariter & anima & corpore, sicque totus homo gloriam accipiet.
units.tr: And in this way those promises made to the fathers, which they saw in the Spirit were to be fulfilled, have also been spiritually fulfilled in their spiritual children. Yet the greatest and eternal heavenly goods still remain to be awaited after this life, which will first come to all in common after the universal resurrection of bodies. It can be understood of the blessedness of souls, which they immediately obtain as soon as they depart from this prison of their frail little body; and also of that blessedness which all receive after the universal resurrection in their bodies. For there will first be the true consummation; there death too will receive its end, as the Apostle declares more fully in 1 Corinthians 15. And therefore the word τελεωθῶσιν [they might be made perfect] is to be noted expressly. Those fathers have indeed already received their glory, together with Christ ascending on high and leading captivity captive; but the consummation, after which nothing else remains, has not yet come to them. It will come when the universal resurrection of bodies has taken place; then the saints will be consummated both in soul and in body alike, and so the whole man will receive glory.

units.la: Neq; vero hic habent aliqui, quod pro se arripiant ad afferendum, animas, cùm hinc emigrant, in cœlum nequaquam peruenire, neque beatitudinem apud Christum accipere, sed vsq; ad vltimum iudicium dormire: sicut audimus, quosdam Anabaptistas nostra tempestate somniare. Contra hos extat elegans liber Ioannis Caluini, hoc titulo, Psychopannychia.
units.tr: Nor do some have here something to seize upon in support of the claim that souls, when they depart hence, do not at all reach heaven or receive blessedness with Christ, but sleep until the last judgment, as we hear some Anabaptists dreaming in our own time. Against these there exists an elegant book of John Calvin under the title Psychopannychia.

units.la: Quanquā ita quoq; accipi possunt hæc verba Apostoli, vt sententia sit: Patres quidem non acciepisse promissionem, non vidisse ea per Christum adimpleta, quæ nos adimplē ta vidimus, & tamē eos perstitisse constantes in fide. Distulisse autem Deum implere pro missiones, vt videlicet nos postremis seculis existētes acciperemus vitam & bona promissa vnà cum ipsis. Atque ita suberit ratio suasoria, à minore ad maius, quasi dicatur: Patres perstiterunt in fide, cùm non accepissent promissiones: igitur multò magis decet nos esse in fide constantes, quibus promissiones iam præoculis sunt positæ, vt accipiantur. Cœuenire videtur sententia cum parabola illa Matth. 20. qua ostéditur, eos, qui tardissimi venerūt in vineā, accepisse parē mercedē, cum iis, qui primi & summo mane aduenerant. Proinde, quomodocūq; accipiamus, debet hæ rationes etiā nos hoc tépore admonere & mouere, vt in fide constantes persistamus. Possent hic nonnulla addi plenius de iustificatione per fidem. Sed hac de re nos alibi copiosius.
units.tr: Although these words of the Apostle can also be taken in such a way that the sense is: the fathers indeed did not receive the promise, that is, did not see those things fulfilled through Christ which we have seen fulfilled, and yet they persevered steadfast in faith. God, however, deferred fulfilling the promises so that we, living in the last ages, might receive life and the good things promised together with them. And thus there will be a persuasive argument from the lesser to the greater, as if it were said: the fathers persevered in faith although they had not received the promises; therefore much more ought we to be steadfast in faith, to whom the promises have already been set before our eyes to be received. The sense seems to agree with that parable of Matthew 20, in which it is shown that those who came last into the vineyard received the same wage as those who came first and early in the morning. Therefore, however we take it, these reasons ought also to admonish and move us at this time to persevere steadfast in faith. Some things could be added here more fully about justification by faith; but we have treated that matter more fully elsewhere.

units.la: CAPVT DVODECIMVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWELVE.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: PRoinde nos quoq; cùm tanta septi simus nube testiū, deposito onere omni, et tenaciter inhærete peccato, per tolerantiā curramus in proposito nobis certamine respicientes ad fidei ducē & consummatorē Iesum, q proposito sibi gaudio pertulit crucē, ignominia contepta, & ad dexteram throni Dei cōsedit. Reputate enim quod iis, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the leader and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him who endured such hostility from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary and lose heart. (Heb. 12.1–3). Reputate enim quod iis, &c.

units.la: HÆC est coclufio tertiæ partis præsentis epistolę: in qua Apostolus, sicut & in exordio huius partis egit, vt in fide constātes esse velint, hortatur, nec non in tolerandis periculis, quæ propter fidei confessionē diuersa & grauia obuenie bant. bat, fortes esse iubet: pluribus rationibus suasorijs hanc ad re optimo ordine congestis. Ita enim sunt collocatę, vt etiā Rhetorū preceptiones studiose obseruasse Apostolus vt deri queat, monentiū, vt in conclusione conferantur praecipue rationes suasorię, quæ exi stimantur ad mouendos affectus magis vtiles, quasq; prodest auditorum animis altius ac diutius inhærere. Estq; hæc præsentis conclusionis propositio. Omnibus rebus mūdi postpositis constanter retineamus fidē in Iesum Christū, nec non aduersa quæcunque fortiter toleremus.
units.tr: This is the conclusion of the third part of the present letter. In it the Apostle, as he did at the beginning of this part, urges his readers to remain steadfast in the faith, and also bids them to be brave in enduring the dangers and grave trials that came upon them because of their confession of the faith. He has set out several persuasive reasons for this, arranged in the best order. They are placed so skilfully that one may see that the Apostle carefully observed the precepts of the rhetoricians, who advise that the persuasive arguments be gathered at the close, since these are thought most useful for moving the emotions, and it is helpful that they cling more deeply and lastingly to the minds of the hearers. The proposition of this conclusion is this: setting aside all the things of the world, let us constantly hold fast to the faith in Jesus Christ, and bear bravely whatever adversities come upon us.

units.la: Aptissimè autem infert ex præcedentibus: Proinde nos quoque cum tanta sepți simus nube testium: Quasi dicat: Cum tot, tam multos, tam densam cohortem sanctorum patrum, martyrum, siue testium habeamus, quorum exemplis edocti sumus, tum per fidem iustificari homines, tum per fidem fortes reddi in tolerandis aduersis: æquum sane est, in nobis quoq; paria efficere posse statuamus: quamobrem & currere in cœpto decet studio & ad solum Christum oculos defigere.
units.tr: The Apostle draws the inference very fitly from what has gone before: Therefore we also, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses, as if he said: since we have so many, so great, so dense a company of holy fathers, martyrs, or witnesses, whose examples have taught us both that men are justified through faith and that through faith they are made brave in bearing adversity, it is only right that we should resolve that we too can produce like results. Therefore it is fitting to run with zeal in the course we have begun, and to fix our eyes on Christ alone.

units.la: Hic enim exemplorum vsus est, vt videlicet, non ad superstitionem & abiectionem, sed ad fidem & animi confirmationem ea seruiant, quæ ab alijs per fidem gesta, dicta & facta sunt.
units.tr: For the purpose of the examples is this: that they serve not for superstition and dejection, but for faith and the strengthening of the mind, namely those things that others have done, said and performed through faith.

units.la: Duplex itaque hic doctrina proposita est: altera, vt exempla patrum & martyrum cum fide & fortitudine imitemur: altera, ut si constantes in fide esse expetamus, omne onus siue impedimentum deponamus. Onera vero, quæ hominum animis incumbunt, faciunt q;, ne alacriter regnum Dei persequi, & in fide progredi possint, sunt varia: non se cus ac currentibus onera sunt impedimento, quo minus alacriter ad metā propositam contendant: & nauigantibus onera sæpe obstant, ne cursu assequi scopum exoptatum, vel interdum etiam tuto nauigare, & pericula euadere queant. Ita & hominibus aliorā quæretibus, & ad metam veræ beatitudinis contendentibus onera sæpe obstant, ne ad expetitum terminum perueniant. Alijs obstant diuitiæ huius mundi, in quibus sum- mum bonum stolidè collocandum esse censent, summamq; se beatitudine perfrui posse persuasum habet, si thesauros & opes, quàm maximas corradat, & ad hæredes suos transmittant. Atq; sic pro Deo habent thesaurum suum terrenum. Quo facto, à regno Dei aberrat. Vt enim impossibile est, duobus dominis inseruire, ita impossibile est, duobus regnis diuersis potiri. Christus non semel in concionibus suis grauissimis idipsum declarat. Matth. 6.19. Luc. 6.12.16. Et D. Apostolus idololatras hunc cupat tales, qui laqueis Satanæ sint astricti. 1.Tim. 6. Ephes. 4. 1.Cor. 5.
units.tr: Here a twofold teaching is therefore set forth: the first, that we should imitate the examples of the fathers and martyrs with faith and courage; the second, that if we desire to be steadfast in the faith, we should lay aside every burden or hindrance. Now the burdens that press upon men's minds, and prevent them from pursuing the kingdom of God eagerly and advancing in the faith, are various. Just as burdens hinder runners from striving eagerly toward the goal set before them, so for sailors burdens often stand in the way, so that they cannot reach the desired destination by their course, or sometimes even sail safely and escape dangers. So too for men who seek other things, and who strive toward the goal of true blessedness, burdens often stand in the way, so that they do not arrive at the longed-for end. For some, the riches of this world stand in the way; foolishly they think the highest good is to be placed in them, and they are persuaded that they can enjoy the highest blessedness if they gather together treasures and wealth as great as possible and pass them on to their heirs. And so they hold their earthly treasure in place of God. By doing so, they wander away from the kingdom of God. For just as it is impossible to serve two masters, so it is impossible to possess two different kingdoms. Christ declares this more than once in his most weighty sermons (Matt. 6.19; Luke 6.12, 16). And the blessed Apostle calls those who are bound by the snares of Satan idolaters (1 Tim. 6; Eph. 4; 1 Cor. 5).

units.la: Ad diuitias accedit solicitudo & auaritia, quæ mali vniuersi radix est: qua quidem qui imbuti sunt, omne studium in terrenarum rerum comparatione consumunt, regnumque Dei penitus deserunt, imò pluris faciunt vitæ huius opes caducas, quam thesauros Christi cœlestes æternos. Lucæ capite 14. In parabola de cœna refert Christus, inuitatos venire recusasse, alterum emisse villam quam exierit, vt videret, alterum quinque boum iuga sibi comparasse, ad quę probanda exeundum prætexeret. Lucæ 8. Matth. 13. Christus de semine refert, quod inter spinas & vepres cadens suffocatum fit: & in expositione parabolæ, eos se dicit notare, qui audientes verbū, & à sollicitudinibus & diuitijs ac voluptatibus vitæ euntes suffocantur, nec ferunt fructū. Hinc præcipit Christus Matthæi capite 6. vt regnum Dei & iustitiam eius inprimis quærant, nec reponant sibi thesauros in terra, vbi erugo & tinea corrumpit, & fures perfodiunt ac furantur: sed in cœlo sibi thesauros recondant: vitæque huius curam Deo committant. Non dicam, quanta mala & iniurię ex auaritia enascatur. Paulus vno nomine omnia complectitur, radicē eam omnis mali appellans. Radix itaq; ista ex animis credetium extirpanda, ne fructus ferat ad interitum.
units.tr: Added to riches are anxiety and avarice, which is the root of all evil. Those who are steeped in these spend all their zeal on acquiring earthly things, and entirely abandon the kingdom of God; indeed they value the fleeting wealth of this life more than the heavenly and eternal treasures of Christ. (Luke, chapter 14.) In the parable of the feast, Christ tells how those invited refused to come: one had bought a field that he had to go out and see, and another had bought five yoke of oxen, and he pretended he must go out to test them (Luke 8; Matt. 13). Christ speaks of the seed that falls among thorns and brambles and is choked, and in explaining the parable he says that he means those who hear the word, but are choked by cares, riches and pleasures of life as they go on, and bear no fruit. Hence Christ, in Matthew chapter 6, commands that men seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and not lay up for themselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth consume and thieves break in and steal, but store up treasures for themselves in heaven, and commit the care of this life to God. I will not speak of how many evils and injuries spring from avarice. Paul embraces all of them in a single word, calling it the root of all evil. This root, then, must be torn out of the hearts of believers, lest it bear fruit to their destruction.

units.la: Pertinet huc quoque voluptatum regnum, in quo qui hærent, ad veritatis & regni Dei lucem difficulter admodum emergere possunt. Paulus 1. Timoth. capite quinto, viduas lasciuientes viuas dicit esse mortuas: ita omnes illi, qui illis dediti sunt mortis æternæ laqueis sunt implicati, & à regno Dei alienati. Hinc Christus diligenter monet ecclesiam & discipulos, vt sibi à crapula & auaritia temperent, nec dies Domini incautos & securius itertentes opprimat. Lucæ capite vigesimoprimo, Cauete ne corda vestra grauentur crapula & ebrietate, & curis huius vitæ, subitusque vobis ingruat dies ille. Luc. capite 17. Matthæi capite 24. Sicut erant dies Noæ, ita erit & aduentus filij hominis. Sicut enim erant in diebus, qui præcesserunt diluuium, edentes & bibentes, contrahentes matrimonium, & nuptum dantes, vsque ad eum diem, &c. 1. Thessal. 5. Idem apostolus hortatur. Diligenter itaque pij, & qui salui in die Domini euadere cupiunt, onus hoc voluptatum & crapulæ declinabunt, ne cum seruo helluone condemnentur. Sunt alia quoque onera quæ homini obsunt, ne ad cœleste regnum aspirare possit, at hæc tria sunt præcipua, quæ & Christus notauit. De vsu diuitiarum & mundi vide 1.Cor.7. Psal.62. Iob.31.
units.tr: To this belongs also the realm of pleasures, in which those who remain are very hard put to emerge into the light of truth and the kingdom of God. Paul in 1 Timothy chapter 5 says that widows who live in pleasure are dead while they live. So all those who are given over to these pleasures are entangled in the snares of eternal death and estranged from the kingdom of God. Hence Christ diligently warns the Church and his disciples to guard themselves against drunkenness and avarice, lest the day of the Lord overtake them unwary and too secure. Luke chapter 21: "Take heed that your hearts are not weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly" (Luke chapter 17; Matthew chapter 24): "As were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as in the days before the flood, they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day..." etc. (1 Thess. 5). The same Apostle exhorts us likewise. Therefore the pious, and those who desire to be saved in the day of the Lord, will diligently avoid this burden of pleasure and drunkenness, lest they be condemned with the wicked servant who was a glutton. There are other burdens too that hinder a man from aspiring to the heavenly kingdom, but these three are the chief ones, and these Christ also noted. On the use of riches and the world, see 1 Cor. 7; Ps. 62; Job 31.

units.la: Discimus itaq; hinc, rerum terrenarum onere deposito ad regnum Dei contendere, thesaurúq; in cælo reponere, eidemq; cor apponere. Qui secus fecerit, ne is ad superna regna peruenire nunquam poterit, sed in sordibus ac luto mundi hærens supprimitur æternum.
units.tr: Thus we learn from this that, laying down the burden of earthly things, we should strive toward the kingdom of God, store up our treasure in heaven, and set our heart upon it. Whoever does otherwise will never be able to reach the heavenly kingdoms, but, remaining stuck in the filth and mire of the world, will be held down for eternity.

units.la: Tenaciter inhærente peccato) Vocat Apostolus peccatum ἀνπερίσπαστον: quasi diceret valde circumstans. Qua voce non modò scite depingitur nostra infirmitas, & naturæ nostræ corruptæ perpetua ad peccandum inclinatio: verùm etiam comprehendi videtur grauissima ratio, docens inprimis, nos nullo pacto posse iustificari nostris operibus: quando nunquam à nobis abest peccatum.
units.tr: Tenaciously clinging to sin: the Apostle calls sin [εὐπερίστατον], that is, as if he said, very encircling. By this word not only is our weakness neatly portrayed, and the constant inclination of our corrupted nature to sin; but also a most weighty argument seems to be comprehended, teaching above all that we can by no means be justified by our works, since sin is never absent from us.

units.la: Deinde necessario impellens ad id, quod subijcitur, nempe ad respiciendum ad fidei ducem.
units.tr: Then, of necessity, it urges us toward what follows, namely that we look to the leader of faith.

units.la: Est quidem homo per spiritum Sanctum renatus, totus est mundus, vt ait Christus, at nihilominus opus habet, vt pedes lauentur. Semper enim peccati fomes in eo ad malum videtur repullulare. Vnde Paulus Roman. cap.7. copiosè luctam carnis, & Spiritus depingens, sub peccatum se venùdatum esse inquit. Et scriptura alibi de sanctis testifica tur, quod septies in die cadant, iterumque resurgant. Et Christus quotidie orare iubet, pater, remitte nobis peccata. Dauid non semel in Psalmis peccata sua & imbecillitatem deplorat. Et quamdiu homo mortalis est, tamdiu corpori corruptibili peccatum inhabitat. Quanquam piorum est, operam dare, ne regnare sinant in se malum. Atq; ita vel sola hæc vox ad constantiam in fide, & ad expectàdam salutem per solam fidem in Christum debet excitare.
units.tr: A man who has been reborn through the Holy Spirit is indeed wholly clean, as Christ says, and yet he still needs his feet washed. For the tinder of sin always seems to sprout up again in him toward evil. Hence Paul, in Romans chapter 7, describing at length the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit, says that he has been sold under sin. And Scripture elsewhere testifies of the saints that they fall seven times a day and rise again. And Christ bids us pray every day, "Father, forgive us our sins." David more than once in the Psalms laments his sins and his weakness. And as long as a man is mortal, sin dwells in his corruptible body. Yet it is the duty of the godly to take care that they do not allow sin to reign in them. And so this one word alone ought to rouse us to steadfastness in the faith, and to await salvation through faith alone in Christ.

units.la: Respicientes ad fidei ducem & consummatorem Iesum: qui proposito sibi gaudio pertulit crucem, ignominia cótempta, & ad dexteram throni Dei consedit. Reputate enim, quod is tale sustinuerit à peccatoribus aduersus se cóprádictionem, ne defatigemini animis desecti.
units.tr: Looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest you be wearied and faint in your minds.

units.la: Sequuntur iam rationes suasoriæ, ad periculorum aduersitatumq; in confessione fidei tolerantiam. Est autem hæc prima ratio sumpta ab exemplo Christi, quo certè nullum grauius vel efficacius proponi posset. Sicut solent, qui ad certamina se præparant, diligenter obseruare excellentissimum aliquem artificem, cuius artem & motus omnes obseruent: ita Apostolus proponit cursuris in stadio fidei & patientiæ ipsum Christum.
units.tr: There follow now the persuasive reasons for enduring dangers and adversities in confessing the faith. The first reason is taken from the example of Christ, than which certainly nothing more weighty or effective could be set before us. Just as those who prepare themselves for contests are accustomed to observe carefully some outstanding master, whose skill and every movement they study, so the Apostle sets Christ himself before those who run the race in the stadium of faith and patience.

units.la: Eleganter autem appellat Christum ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν: quasi diceret, initiatorem & consummatorem. Multum gratiæ inest in græcis verbis. Sunt enim voces oppositæ ἀρχὴν & τέλος. Vtraque ad Christum sese refert. Vt enim is initium & radicem fidei in cordibus piorum figit: ita idem est, qui perficere & cõsummare fidem valet iuxta illud, sine me nihil potestis: & Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per filium. Ioan cap. 15. 16. discipulis promittit spiritum Sanctum, qui in veritatem eos sit ducturus. 1. Corinthior. 3. Deus esse dicitur, qui incrementum dat plantantibus & rigantibus per verbum Dei. Luc.17. Discipuli Christum orant, vt fidem in ipsis augeat. Philip.2. Deus est, qui operatur in vobis, & vt velitis, & vt efficiatis pro bono animo proposito. 2. Thessalon.3. Non omnium est fides: sed fidelis est Dominus, qui stabiliet vos, & custodiet à malo. Item, Dominus dirigat corda vestra in dilectionem Dei, & in expectationem Christi. Ephef.3. Genua flecto ad patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ex quo omnis à communi patre cognatio in cœlis & in terra nominatur, vt det vobis iuxta diuitias gloriæ suæ, vt fortitudine corroboremini per spiritum suum in internum homine, vt inhabitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris, in charitate actis radicibus, & fundamento iacto, vt valeatis assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit latitudo & longitudo, & profunditas & sublimitas, cognoscereq; præeminentem cognitionis dilectionem Christi, vt impleaminii in omnem plenitudinem Dei, &c. Plura de Christi donis vide Ioelis capite 2. Ierem. cap.32. Actor. cap 2.
units.tr: The Apostle elegantly calls Christ the author and perfecter [ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν], as if to say, the initiator and consummator. There is much grace in the Greek words, for the terms opposed are ἀρχὴ and τέλος. Both refer to Christ. For just as he plants the beginning and root of faith in the hearts of the godly, so he is also the one who is able to bring faith to perfection and completion, according to the saying, "Without me you can do nothing," and "No one comes to the Father except through the Son" (John 15 and 14). In John 16 he promises the disciples the Holy Spirit, who will lead them into the truth. In 1 Corinthians 3 God is said to be the one who gives the increase to those who plant and water through the Word of God. In Luke 17 the disciples ask Christ to increase their faith. In Philippians 2 it is God who works in you both to will and to do for his good pleasure. In 2 Thessalonians 3, "Not all have faith, but the Lord is faithful, who will establish you and keep you from evil"; likewise, "may the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the patient waiting for Christ." In Ephesians 3, "I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and earth is named, that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man, that Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith, being rooted and grounded in love, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height, and to know the love of Christ which passes knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God," etc. Read more about the gifts of Christ in Joel chapter 2, Jeremiah chapter 32, and Acts chapter 2.

units.la: Doctrina hinc colligitur vniuersalis omnium credentiū propria, quòd videlicet Christus sit, à quo fides, salus, & confirmatio in fide pendeat, ideoq; neminem habere quod glorietur extra Christum.
units.tr: From this is drawn a universal doctrine, proper to all believers: namely that Christ is the one on whom faith, salvation and confirmation in faith depend, and therefore that no one has anything to glory in apart from Christ.

units.la: Qui proposito sibi gaudio) Quod nam erat istud gaudium Christo propositum? Christo erat hoc gaudium propositum, vt conscenderet in cœlos ad patrem ibique æterna potiretur gloria. Atq; ita respiciens ad huiusmodi gaudium sibi propositum, táto erat animatior ad perferendam nostra de caussa crucem: atque etiam lætus mortem adiuit, quam alias potuisset haud dubie, si voluisset, euadere. Huc pertinet prolixa illa oratio Christi ad patrem Ioann.17. Pater venit hora, glorifica filium tuum, ut & filius tuus glori-ficet te: & cætera quæ ibidem sequuntur. Item ad discipulos in cœcione illa Ioann. 14. & 15. Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique, quod dixerim, vado ad patrem. Et rursus: Desiderio desideraui manducare hoc pascha vobiscum. Et quid mirum si dicamus, Christum cum gaudio pertulisse crucem, quando etiam de apostolis talia legimus? ut Actor.5. Ibant gaudentes a conspectu concilij quod digni habiti essent, vt pro nomine eius contumelia af-ficerentur. Quod vero occurrunt loci, qui videntur de Christo diuersum significare, veluti ille, tristis est anima mea usq; ad mortem: & pater si fieri potest, transfeat a me calix iste. Hoc quidem secundum humanam naturam ei conueniebat, & declaratum est ibi, Christū verum hominem, & tentatum in statu nostri. Neq; hoc simpliciter malum est, metuere videlicet mortem: ita enim conditi sumus, & ingenitus est nobis iste horror. Sed spiritus tamen hunc horrorem superat & mitigat. Vnde ipse etiam Christus, non mea, inquit, sed tua, pater, voluntas fiat. Cernitur certamen hoc in pijs, qui aliquando afflictati doloribus & ærumnis mallet secundum carnem non pati: at spiritus eos iterū subleuat & roborat in anxietatibus, ut ad certamen reddantur alacriores, vnde recte apostolus ait Roman. 8. Spiritus auxiliatur infirmitatibus nostris.
units.tr: "Who for the joy set before him." What joy was this that was set before Christ? It was set before Christ that he should ascend into heaven to the Father and there enjoy eternal glory. Thus, looking to this joy set before him, he was so much the more eager to bear the cross for our sake, and even went gladly to death, which he could undoubtedly have escaped, had he wished. To this belongs that long prayer of Christ to the Father in John 17: "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you," and what follows there. Likewise his words to the disciples in John 14 and 15: "If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I said, I go to the Father." And again: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you" (Luke 22). And why should it be surprising if we say that Christ endured the cross with joy, when we read such things also of the apostles, as in Acts 5: "They went out from the presence of the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name." As for the passages which seem to signify the opposite concerning Christ, such as "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death" and "O my Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me," these indeed belonged to him according to his human nature, and it is shown there that Christ was a true man, and tempted in our condition. Nor is it simply wrong to fear death; for we have been so created, and this dread is implanted in us. But the Spirit nevertheless overcomes and softens this dread. Hence Christ himself also said, "Not my will, but yours, Father, be done." This conflict is seen in the godly, who at times, afflicted by pains and distresses, would prefer according to the flesh not to suffer; but the Spirit again raises them up and strengthens them in their anxieties, so that they are made more eager for the conflict. Hence the Apostle rightly says in Romans 8, "The Spirit helps our infirmities."

units.la: Ac quëadmodum Christus regnum cœlorum & gaudium æternum per morte ingreditur, sicut ipse testatur Lucæ 24. ita credentibus, qui in hoc mundo affliguntur, præmia in cœlis æterna sunt reposita. Vnde item Paulus loco citato ad Roman. Hæredes Dei, cohæredes autem Christi: fiquidé simul cum eo patimur, ut & vnà cum illo glorificemur. Nam reputo, non esse pares afflictiones præsentis temporis, ad gloriam, quæ reuelabitur erga nos. 2. Corinth. 4. Momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostræ, mire supra modum æternum pondus gloriæ parit nobis, dum non spectamus ea quæ videntur, sed ea, quæ non videntur. Nam quæ videntur, temporaria sunt: at quæ non videntur, æterna. Ad sum mam, quicunque in Christo Iesu volunt pie viuere, & aliquando cum eo regnare, hos & afflictiones persecutiones q; vnà cum Christo pati necessum est: qua de re uide 2. Timoth. 2. Actor. 14. Matth. 10. Quæ capiti eueniunt, ea membris quoq; infliguntur, neq; discipulus debet esse supra magistrum. Contrà Christo glorificato, credetes quoq; aliquando ad gloriam cœlestem euchendos esse. sequitur:
units.tr: And just as Christ entered the kingdom of heaven and eternal joy through death, as he himself testifies in Luke 24, so for believers who are afflicted in this world, eternal rewards are laid up in heaven. Hence also Paul in the passage cited in Romans: "heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified together with him. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us" (Rom. 8). In 2 Corinthians 4: "The momentary lightness of our affliction works for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen; for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal." In sum, whoever wishes to live godly in Christ Jesus and at some time reign with him must of necessity suffer afflictions and persecutions together with Christ; on this see 2 Timothy 2, Acts 14, and Matthew 10. What befalls the head is also inflicted on the members, nor is the disciple above the master. On the contrary, since Christ has been glorified, believers too must be brought at some time to heavenly glory. There follows:

units.la: Pertulit crucem, ignominia cōtempta) Genus mortis ignominiosissimū notat, quōd Christus in cruce inter latrones, quasi latro, & sceleratorum princeps pertulit. Fecit hoc ideo, ut nos ad gloriam & regnum cœlorum reduceret, & morte maledicta ire patris satisfaceret, nobisq; æternam benedictionē redderetur. Ioannis 3. Christus ipse ad ἀνάλυσιν patris hoc refert, quod exaltari filium oporteat, instar æneii illius serpentis in deserto (Numeror. 21) ut omnis, qui credit non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Apostolus ad Philippenses cap. 2. humiliationem Christi describens, usq; ad crucis mortem dicit obediente factū. Et ad Galat. 3. Christus nos redemit, inquit, ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio. Scriptū est enim, Execrabilis omnis, qui pendet in ligno, ut ingentes benedictio Abraham veniret per Christum Iesum, &c.
units.tr: "Endured the cross, despising the shame." He denotes the most shameful kind of death, since Christ endured it on the cross among thieves, as if he were a thief and the chief of criminals. He did this so that he might lead us back to glory and the kingdom of heaven, and by dying the accursed death might satisfy the wrath of the Father, and eternal blessing be restored to us. In John 3 Christ himself refers to the purpose of the Father's glorification of the Son, that the Son of man must be lifted up, like that bronze serpent in the wilderness (Num. 21), so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. The Apostle, describing the humiliation of Christ in Philippians 2, says that he became obedient even unto the death of the cross. And in Galatians 3: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us; for it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles through Jesus Christ," etc.

units.la: In cruce Christo probra, verbera, ignominiae, aliæq; coplures iniuriae sunt illatæ, hasce omnes fortiter pertulit, propter peccata nostra. Huc facit illud Esaiae 53. Non erat forma ei neq; decor: aspeximus aute eum, & non erat aspectus, & non desiderauimus eum videre. Despectus fuit & reiectus inter viros vir dolorum, & expertus infirmitate & velut abscessio faciei ab eo, despectus inquam, & non putauimus eum. Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros portauit, &c. Euangelistæ quatuor prolixius historiam hanc describunt: quare operæ precium non esse arbitor hoc loco plura recensere.
units.tr: On the cross Christ suffered reproaches, scourgings, dishonours and many other injuries, and all these he bore bravely, for our sins. To this pertains that passage of Isaiah 53: "He had no form nor comeliness; and when we saw him, there was no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief; and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows," etc. The four evangelists describe this history at greater length, so I judge it not worthwhile to recount more here.

units.la: Cæterum ideo ista sic expressa sunt ab apostolo, ad amplificandum mala, quæ Christus pertulit, ut Hebræi, collatione facta, intelligerent, sua mala nequaquam esse paria ijs quæ Christus passus est. Calicem eius haurire, & baptismate eius baptizari posunt quidē credentes, at nequaquam ea perfectione, fide, robore, & efficacia, sicuti Christus, qui morte sua ἀπολύτρωσις est factus, hoc est, redemptio pro vniuersis hominibus, quique primogenitus est mortuorum & resurgetium, fregit q; potestatem eius, qui potestatem mortis habebat, hoc est, diaboli, & liberos reddidit credentes a iure peccati & seruitute legis (Hebr. 2)
units.tr: Moreover, the apostle expressed these things in this way to magnify the evils that Christ endured, so that the Hebrews, by making the comparison, might understand that their own evils are by no means equal to those Christ suffered. Believers can indeed drink his cup and be baptized with his baptism, but not with the same perfection, faith, strength and efficacy as Christ. Christ, by his death, became redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις], that is, redemption for all men. He is the firstborn from the dead and the resurrection, and he broke the power of him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and made believers free from the right of sin and the slavery of the law (Heb. 2).

units.la: Ad dexteram throni Dei consedit)Sedere ad dexteram est esse æqualem Deo, gloria obtinere Dei, id quod nulli creaturæ, quam soli Christo, potest cōtingere aut asscribi. Diximus hac de re supra capite primo in priori parte huius voluminis. Nam Deus neque dextera habet neque sinistram, sed loquendi forma deducitur a more humano.
units.tr: He sat at the right hand of the throne of God) To sit at the right hand is to be equal to God and to obtain the glory of God, which can belong or be ascribed to no creature but to Christ alone. We spoke of this matter above, in the first chapter, in the first part of this volume. For God has neither right hand nor left, but the form of speech is drawn from human custom.

units.la: Cæterum particula hac explicatur: quale gaudium fuerit Christo propositum, post crucis mortem & resurrectione: pariterq; intelligi datur, quale gaudium etiam Hebræos manet.
units.tr: Moreover, this phrase explains what joy was set before Christ after the death of the cross and his resurrection. At the same time it is made clear what joy also awaits the Hebrews.

units.la: A a neat, omnesque credentes, si Christum ducem strenuè sequantur.
units.tr: And all believers, if they strenuously follow Christ as their leader.

units.la: Reputate enim, quòd is talem sustinuerit) Accommodatio est exempli ad ipsos Hebraeos, & altera pars Enthymematis. Omnia sunt, emphatica.
units.tr: For consider that he endured such things. This is the application of the example to the Hebrews themselves, and the second part of the enthymeme. All these words are emphatic.

units.la: Talem) Emphaticùs magnitudinem declarat , amplificatque: quasi diceret: Vos certè nequaquam paria pertulistis: sicut & postea dicit, Nondum usque ad sanguinem decertastis.
units.tr: Such emphatically declares and amplifies the greatness of the suffering, as if he said: You certainly have not endured equal things, as he also says afterwards: You have not yet resisted unto blood.

units.la: Contradictione: Lucae 2. Simeon Christū signum appellat cui contradiceretur. Actor. 28. De secta hac notum est nobis, quia ubiq; ei contradicitur. Praedicationi Christi & factis contradicitur, passim in evangelica historia, quemadmodum videre est Luc. 11. Ioan. 3. Matth. 9. Morituro contradicunt increduli pontifices, pharisaei, & irrisores crucis (Matth. 27) atque hi impingunt in lapidem offendiculi: de quo Esaiae 8.28. 1. Petri 2. Actor. 7. Stephanus idem illis exprobrat. Resurrectioni Christi contradicunt Turci, Iudaei, & omnes, qui mortis eius efficaciam, ac redemptionem generis humani pernegat. Perierunt olim Iudaei contradicentes Mosi & Deo, Numeror. 16. 20. Ita omnes illi qui contradicunt filio Dei, peribunt aeternum. Vae ei, qui contradicit factori suo. Esia. 45. Oseae 4. Actor. 13, &c.
units.tr: Contradiction: Luke 2. Simeon calls Christ a sign that will be spoken against. Acts 28. Concerning this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against. Christ's preaching and deeds are contradicted throughout the evangelical history, as may be seen in Luke 11, John 3, Matt. 9. Unbelieving high priests, Pharisees and mockers of the cross contradicted him as he was about to die (Matt. 27), and these stumble over the stone of offence, concerning which see Isa. 8.28; 1 Pet. 2; Acts 7. Stephen reproaches them with the same. The Turks, the Jews, and all who deny the efficacy of Christ's death and the redemption of mankind contradict his resurrection. The Jews once perished for contradicting Moses and God (Num. 16, 20). So all who contradict the Son of God will perish eternally. Woe to him who contradicts his Maker (Isa. 45; Hos. 4; Acts 13, etc.).

units.la: A' peccatoribus) & haec particula mirum in modum exaggerat in dignitate supplicij Christi: ipse iustus affligitur ab iniustis. Ne igitur detrectemus nos, qui peccatis plagas fumus commeriti, pro Christi gloria subire ignominiam.
units.tr: By sinners: this phrase also greatly heightens the dignity of Christ's suffering, since the just one is afflicted by the unjust. Therefore let us not shrink from bearing shame for the glory of Christ, we who have deserved blows by our sins.

units.la: Ne defatigemini animis defecti) causa finalis, ob quam Christi mors & passio nobis proponitur. Varius autem est usus passionis Christi: & Christus proponitur nobis duplicater: primò, ut saluator & mediator. Secundò ut exemplum vitae instituendae in terris.
units.tr: That you be not wearied, fainting in your minds: this is the final cause for which Christ's death and passion are set before us. Christ's passion has a varied use, and Christ is set before us in two ways. First, as Saviour and mediator. Second, as the example of the life to be lived on earth.

units.la: Discimus hinc. Primum, quòd Christus ubiq; ut dux fit proponendus, qui est via, vita & veritas, tum quoad doctrinam, tum quoad vitae institutionem. Proponuntur quidem & sancti, sed ut imperfecti, & ipsius Christi imitatores: ergo satius est, perfectum exemplar in ipso Christo sectari. plura vide 1. Petri 2.
units.tr: From this we learn, first, that Christ is to be set forth everywhere as leader, who is the way, the life and the truth, both as to doctrine and as to the ordering of life. Saints too are set forth, but as imperfect imitators of Christ himself. It is therefore better to follow the perfect pattern in Christ himself. See more in 1 Pet. 2.

units.la: Deinde doctrinā hic habemus de usu passionis Christi, de quo passim Christus & apostoli concionantur.
units.tr: Next, here we have teaching on the use of Christ's passion, about which Christ and the apostles preach everywhere.

units.la: Tertiò addi potest consolatio, proponendo gaudium vitae futurae, in hisce malis vitae praesentis. Consideratio futuri gaudij praesentem tristitiam subleuat: vide plura Ioan. 16. & Rom. 8, &c.
units.tr: Thirdly, consolation may be added, by setting before us the joy of the future life amid the evils of the present life. The consideration of future joy lightens present sorrow. See more in John 16 and Rom. 8, etc.

units.la: Nondum usque ad sanguinem resistitis, aduersus peccatum repugnantes.
units.tr: You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.

units.la: Secunda ratio suasoria, ab extenuatione malorum, quae ipsi pertulerunt. Extenuat autem per tacitam comparationem ad maiora mala, quae vel alij viri sancti iam pertulerant, vel ipsi Hebraei adhuc perferre possent. Et latet hic inuitatio seu praeparatio quaedam ad maiora pericula perferenda: imo latet tacita quaedam segniciei exprobratio, qua animum abiectum & parum virilem Hebraeis indignum inesse ostendit. Caeterum inter varia piorum certaminia, quorū vita militia est, teste Iobo cap. 7. haec duo prae caeteris maximè sunt illustria: alterum est cum mundo & hostibus euangelij externis: alterum est cum carnis concupiscentijs, cum peccatis, ac ipso denique diabolo & principe aeris. Primum genus est externum & corporale, fide tamen & fortitudine ad victoriam reportandam opus habens: tale est illud, quod cum mundo impio & poenitere nescio suscipitur, ac tamdiu geritur, quamdiu veritas, siue euangelium Christi in mundo praedicatur. Non enim venit Christus pacem mittere, sed gladium: & si Christi verbum audijsset mundus, audiret etiam apostolus. At quia regnum Christi non est ex hoc mundo, mundus id capitali odio prosequitur & vi, armis, ferro igneque persequitur. Certamen hoc Christus, qui caput est ecclesiae, sustinuit, qui cum Saducaeis, Pharisaeis, & Scribis, vsque ad sanguinem, id est usq; ad mortem (est enim in vocabulo hoc metonymia, vbi signum ponitur pro re signata) luctatus est: in quo quidem certamine victus vicit.
units.tr: This is the second exhortation, drawn from the diminishing of the evils which they themselves have endured. He diminishes them by a tacit comparison with greater evils, which either other holy men had already endured or which the Hebrews themselves might still have to bear. Here lies hidden an invitation, or a certain preparation, to endure greater dangers. Indeed, there is hidden a certain tacit rebuke of sloth, by which he shows that a dejected and not very manly spirit, unworthy of the Hebrews, is present in them. Moreover, among the various struggles of the pious, whose life is a warfare, as Job testifies in chapter 7, two are especially outstanding above the rest. One is with the world and the external enemies of the gospel; the other is with the lusts of the flesh, with sins, and finally with the devil himself and the prince of the air. The first kind is external and bodily, yet it needs faith and fortitude to win the victory.
