Such is the struggle undertaken with the impious world, which knows no repentance, and it is carried on as long as the truth, that is, the gospel of Christ, is preached in the world. For Christ did not come to send peace but a sword; and if the world had heard the word of Christ, it would hear the apostle too. But because the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, the world pursues it with deadly hatred and persecutes it with force, arms, iron and fire. Christ, who is the head of the Church, endured this struggle. He wrestled with the Sadducees, Pharisees and Scribes unto blood, that is, unto death (for in this word there is a metonymy, where the sign is put for the thing signified). In this struggle he was defeated, yet in it he conquered.

units.la: Ab Abele usque ad Zachariae caedem prophetae et pij semper usque ad sanguinem restituerunt impijs & incredulis, ac sanguine suo veritati & Deo testimonium perhibuerunt. Iohannes Baptista vsque ad sanguinem restitit sceleribus Herodis & improbissimorum Iudaeorum. Non dicam de certaminibus Apostolorum, inprimisq; D. Pauli, qui ut est 2. Corinth. 11. & in Actis apostolorū, quam plurima certamina propter Christum fortiter sustinuit, tandem ubi vidit se propediem immolandū, & tempus resolutionis suae instare magna voce ait, certamen bonum decertaui, cursum consummaui, fidem seruaui: quod superest, repositæ est mihi iustitiae corona, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illo die, &c. De Eliae pugna cū pseudoprophetis & Baalitis est in 1. lib.reg.ca.17. 18.19.20, &c. In fide itaq; & vera religione usq; ad mortem viriliter est perfistendum: cuius praeclarum exemplum extat in tribus illis, qui ut est Daniel 3. in fornacem Babyloniorum coniecti a Deo mirabiliter seruati sunt. Huc refer martyres, qui a Turcis, imperatoribus & pontificibus Romanis ensibus
units.tr: From the slaying of Abel to the slaughter of the prophet Zechariah, the prophets and the pious always resisted the impious and unbelieving unto blood, and bore witness to the truth and to God with their blood. John the Baptist resisted unto blood the crimes of Herod and of the most wicked Jews. I will not speak of the struggles of the apostles, especially St Paul, who, as is shown in 2 Cor. 11 and in the Acts of the Apostles, bravely endured very many struggles for Christ. At last, when he saw that he was soon to be sacrificed and that the time of his departure was at hand, he said with a loud voice: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will give me in that day," etc. Elijah's contest with the false prophets and the Baalites is in 1 Kings 17, 18, 19, 20, etc. Therefore one must persevere manfully unto death in faith and true religion. A notable example of this stands in those three men who, as in Daniel 3, were cast into the furnace of the Babylonians and were wonderfully preserved by God. Here refer the martyrs who were torn apart by the swords of the Turks, emperors and Roman pontiffs

units.la: Ioan. 16. Christus exemplar in ipso sectari. aenfibus fuerunt laniati, & aliquando feris obiecti, aliquando exusti, securi percusi, in exlium multati fortunis omnibus relegati, ita tamen constantes ad mortem usq; permaserunt, ut neque ad dextram impiorum pollicitationibus, neque ad sinistram comminationibus suppliciorum grauissimorum sese flecti sint passi.
units.tr: John 16: Christ is to be followed as the pattern in himself. They were torn by swords, and at times were thrown to wild beasts, at times burned, beheaded, and exiled, and stripped of all their fortunes. Yet they remained so steadfast unto death that they were moved neither to the right by the promises of the impious, nor to the left by the threats of the most grievous punishments.

units.la: Alterum genus certaminis spirituale est,et cum peccatis, siue cocupiscentijs prauis fusci pitur: hæ enim quia in renatis manet & inuerteratæ mebris internis, id est,cordi,renibus & cæteris partibus, in quibus affectus praui oriûtur,residet,semper est pijs lucta cum carne vitiosa & prauis eius affectibus. Ea enim parte, qua per spiritum Dei regeneratus est homo,ad bonum fertur,& malo reluctatur: qua vero adhuc parte concupiscentiæ prauæ & affectus vitiosi delitescunt, ad malum rapitur.
units.tr: The other kind of struggle is spiritual, and it is waged with sins, that is, with depraved lusts. These, because they remain in the regenerate and dwell unchanged in the inner members, that is, in the heart, the kidneys and the other parts where evil affections arise, the pious always have a struggle with the sinful flesh and its evil affections. For in that part by which a man is regenerated through the Spirit of God, he is carried toward good and resists evil. But in the part where depraved lusts and vicious affections still lie hidden, he is carried toward evil.

units.la: Pugnam hanc describit Paulus Roman.7. Scimus,inquit,quòd lex spritualis est,at ego carnalis sum,venditus sub peccatum. Quod enim ago,non probo. Non enim quod volo hoc facio, sed quod odi, hoc ago. Si verò quod non volo,hoc facio, consentio legi,quòd bona sit. Nunc autem nō iam perpetro illud, sed inhabitans in me peccatum. Noui enim quòd non habitet in me,hoc est, in carne mea bonû. Nam velle adest mihi:at ut facià bonum,non reperio. Non enim quod volo,facio bonum,sed quod non volo, malû,hoc ago. Si verò quod non volo ego,hoc facio, non iam ego perpetro illud, sed inhabitans in me peccatum. Reperio igitur per legem,volenti mihi facere bonum,quòd mihi malum adiûctum sit. Delectat enim me lex Dei secundum internum hominum,sed video aliam legem in membris meis,rebellantem legi mentis meæ,& captiuum reddentem me legi peccati, quæ est in membris meis.
units.tr: Paul describes this battle in Romans 7: "We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For what I do I do not approve; for I do not do what I want, but what I hate, that I do. But if I do what I do not want, I consent to the law, that it is good. Now, however, it is no longer I who commit it, but sin that dwells in me. For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For the willing is present with me, but I do not find how to do the good. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want, that I do. But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me. I find, therefore, by the law, that when I want to do good, evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, but I see another law in my members, rebelling against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin which is in my members."

units.la: Ad Galat.5. caro concupiscit aduersus spiritû, spiritus aute aduersus carnem. Hæc aute inter se mutuò aduersantur,ut nō quæcunq; volueritis,eade faciatis. Opera carnis & fructus spiritus ibidem copiosè describuntur, ac tandem concluditur,eos qui Christi sunt, carnem crucifixisse cum affectibus & concupiscentijs. Sic 2. Corinth.4. Quamuis externus homo noster corrumpitur,internus tamen renouaturin dies singulos. Ephes.3. Fortudine corroboremini per spiritum in internum homine, ut inhabitet Christus in cordibus vestris,&c. De mortificado veteri homine cum cocupiscentijs,& crucifigendis affectibus malis,plura lege Roman.6.Ephes.4. Coloss 3.&c.
units.tr: Galatians 5: "The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are contrary the one to the other, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would." The works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit are described at length in the same place, and the chapter concludes that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts. So 2 Corinthians 4: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Ephesians 3: "Be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man, that Christ may dwell in your hearts," and so on. On the putting to death of the old man with his lusts, and the crucifying of evil affections, read more in Romans 6, Ephesians 4, Colossians 3, and elsewhere.

units.la: Cæterum quòd in hac pugna negotium nobis facesi dixi à Satana,qui vnà cum carne & per carnem nos oppugnat, ita debet intelligi;nō quòd diabolus carnem nostrâ crearit, aut in manu sua habeat ad impellendû,quò velit: sed quòd carnis affectibus blandiendo, libidines incitando,titillando,ac praua suadendo per externum hominem,id est,concupiscentias,hominem internum conetur turbare,in peccatû ducere,ac de gradu fidei deijcere,atq; ad peccatum propellendo sub iugum suum mittere: atque sic prauis effectibus & vitiositate natiua velut instrumento quodam vtitur ad hominem supprimendû. Nota est historia Matth.4. qua Christû filiû Dei in quem natiua illa carnis vitiositas non cadit, tentat,eumq; varijs artibus aggreditur, ut vel in desperatione, vel temeritatè,vel idololatriam seducat: cui fortissime ex verbo Dei Christus restitit,ac tandem deuicit. Vtinam id ipsum Eua in Paradiso pari telo ac clypeo serpenti,in quo Satan fallebat,resistendo fe-ciffet, nunquam se & posteritate in mortis & irę Dei pericula calamitatesq; coniecissēt. Prudenter itaq; versari in vitæ huius cursu debent fideles, ne à tanto hoste,qui cuniculis & varijs artibus pugnat, incauti opprimantur. Monet hoc D. Petrus 1. Petri 5. vbi leoni rugienti eum confert propter crudelitatem & horrendos conatus:in fide huic resistendū esse monet.Ephes.6. elegans est exhortatio Pauli,qui palum in carne,& Satanam pugnis ipsum cædente expertus fuerat,ubi iubet intentos esse fideles ad conatus principis mundi Satanæ,hic,in quiès:Quod superesset,fratres,sitis fortes perDominum,perque potentiâ roboris illius: induite armaturam Dei,ut posisitis stare aduersus assultus diaboli. Quoniâ non est nobis lucta aduersus sanguinem & carnem, sed aduersus principatus,aduersus potestates,aduersus mûdi dominos,rectores tenebrarum seculi huius,aduersus spiritualies astutias in coelestibus,&c. plures loci & exempla certaminis huius in scripturis occurrunt: imò homines renati singulis fere momentis luctam hanc ingredi coguntur:fortitudinis itaque & prudentiæ sint memores.
units.tr: But when I said above that in this struggle Satan causes us trouble, he attacks us together with the flesh and through the flesh, and this must be understood as follows. It is not that the devil created our flesh, or holds it in his hand to drive it wherever he wishes. Rather, by flattering the affections of the flesh, by stirring up and tickling our lusts, and by persuading us to evil through the outward man, that is, through the concupiscences, he tries to disturb the inward man, to lead him into sin, to throw him down from the step of faith, and to drive him into sin and put him under his yoke. Thus he uses the evil affections and the innate corruption of the flesh as a kind of instrument for subduing man. The story in Matthew 4 is well known, where he tempts Christ the Son of God, in whom that innate corruption of the flesh finds no place, and assails him with various arts, to seduce him into despair, rashness or idolatry. Christ resisted him most bravely with the word of God and in the end overcame him. Would that Eve in Paradise had resisted the serpent, through whom Satan deceived her, with the same weapon and shield, and she would never have cast herself and her posterity into the dangers and calamities of death and the wrath of God. Therefore the faithful ought to conduct themselves prudently in the course of this life, lest they, being careless, be overwhelmed by so great an enemy, who fights by tunnelling and by various arts. Saint Peter warns of this in 1 Peter 5, where he compares him to a roaring lion because of his cruelty and terrible attempts, and advises that we resist him in faith. Ephesians 6 contains a fine exhortation of Paul, who had experienced the thorn in the flesh and Satan buffeting him with blows. There he bids the faithful be alert to the attempts of Satan, the prince of this world. "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places," and so on. Many passages and examples of this conflict occur in the Scriptures; indeed, regenerate men are almost every moment compelled to enter this struggle. Let them therefore remember courage and prudence.

units.la: Doctrinæ duæ hinc excerpi possunt: Prima, pijs in hoc mundo semper certâdum esse cum impijs & incredulis,imò mortem aliquando ipsam, nedum innumera alia mala,eis incumbere. In quibus tamen fide & spe vincunt,ad exemplum Christi ducis & consummatoris fidei.
units.tr: Two teachings can be drawn from this. The first is that the godly in this world must always contend with the wicked and the unbelieving; indeed, death itself, not to mention countless other evils, sometimes falls upon them. Yet in these things they conquer by faith and hope, following the example of Christ, the leader and perfecter of faith.

units.la: Secunda,militandum quoq; hic contra carnem,contra peccata,& ipsum denique diabolum & cohortes eius. In quo certamine spiritus Sanctus per verbum fidei ita nos armat, ut viriliter certare,& victoriam reportare, ac tandem in coelis coronari,posisimus.
units.tr: The second is that we must also wage war here against the flesh, against sins, and finally against the devil himself and his hosts. In this contest the Holy Spirit so arms us through the word of faith that we are able to fight manfully, to win the victory, and at last to be crowned in heaven.

units.la: Aa Et obliti estis exhortationis, quae nobis tanquam filiis loquitur: fili mi, ne neglexeris correptionem Domini, neque deficias, cum ab eo argueris. Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit: flagellat autem omnem filium, quem recipit. Si castigationem sustinetis, veluti filiis vobis offert se Deus. Quis enim est filius quem non castigat pater? Quod si alieni estis a castigatione, cuius participes sunt omnes: igitur spurii estis, non filii. Itaque cum carnis nostrae patres habuerimus castigatores, et reveriti fuimus illos, an non multo magis subiiciemur patri spirituum, et viuemus?
units.tr: "And have you forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children: My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him. For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons. Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?" (Hebrews 12:5–9)

units.la: Tertia ratio a certa exhortatione seu consolatione in Scripturis proposita, quae docet, afflictiones patienter ferendas, tum quod divinitus quidem immittantur: tum quod certum sint signum divinae erga pios benevolentiae: quandoquidem eos pro filiis suis dilectis Deus agnoscit, quos in hoc mundo corripit. Sumpta est autem sententia ipsa ex Prover.capite 3. vbi sic legitur, בִּי יִרְצֶה הָאֵל הָאָב בְּתוֹכְחוֹתָיו ... רָאָה, id est, ad verbum, castigationem Domini fili mi ne abieceris, neque fastidium habeas in correptione eius. Quoniam, quem diligit Dominus, huc corripit, et sicut pater filium gratum habebit. A Solomone conscripta sunt illa pro exhortationib. potius, quam pro consolationibus: bene tamen etiam consolationem dixerimus. Exhortatione vocat, sicut et Theophylactus interpretatur, quasi insinuans, etiam expetendum esse affligi a Domino. Dicit ad eos tanquam ad filios pertinere, quia Solomonis verba habent, fili mi: quae sic vult accipi, tanquam a Deo profecta, et ad omnes pios pertinentia. Apud apostolum autem legimus ad verbum, quemadmodum habent Septuaginta. Sententia est satis perspicua, et apostolus eam suis verbis et explicat, et instituto accommodat: quare non opus est nos multis de ea agamus. Tantum hoc notemus insignem esse sententiam. Primum apertissime docet mala immitti ab ipso Deo: quod sane nulla philosophia, nulla humana ratio nunquam potuit assequi vel credere. Philosophia arbitrata est, causa et fortuito geri omnia: ideo quidam etiam providentia sustulerunt, exististimantes, Deo rerum humanarum nullam esse curam, maxime quia viderunt bonos affligi, optima quaeque cödicere: malos autem et mala obtinere summum locum. Ratio autem interpretatur, mala immitti quidem a Deo, sed irato, ideoque ipsa hominum inducit ad irascendum Deo, ad desperandum de salute. At vero Scriptura, quae sola sequenda est, ut vere sapiens magistra, docet, a Deo tanquam bona parente immitti tam bona, quam mala: et quae pijs mala contingunt, indicia esse benevolentiae divinae, quod Dominus dignatur illos visitare, et punire mauult in hoc saeculo, quam in futuro. Exemplum in Lazaro et divite extat Lucae 16. Atque hinc arripiunt pij occasionem ad invocandum Deum, ad sperandum auxilium, ad desiderandum, ut dissolvantur, et sint cum Christo, deniqueetiam ad gratias agendas. Non quod Dominus etiam non corripiat ut iratus: nam videmus passim apud prophetas comminationes irati Dei proposi tas, et eas etiam postea perduci ad opus: sed hae comminationes pertinent ad impios et malos quos Dominus percutit, ut etiam perdat, tum in hac vita, tum in altera. Deus dum immittit mala, erga impios iram suam, erga pios vero dilectionem declarat. Et si contingat simul affligi, tamen pij interea liberantur a communibus periculis: sic bene cessit Hieremiae, Danieli et similibus, in captivitate Babylonica: Item Apostolis in euersione Hierosolymae sub Tito et Vespasiano. Vel certe ad tempus una cum caeteris affligutur, ut postea meliús habeant, et ad bonum ipsorum. Ita enim Dominus temperat afflictiones, ut etiam fructum faciant pij ex tentationibus, omnia ad bonum ipsis cedant. Exemplum huius diseriminis licet videre etiam in hominibus, qui alio affectu corripiunt suos seruos, alio suos filios, etiamsi pares propemodum infligerent poenas. Item debemus et hoc notare, quod generaliter loquitur de quacunque correptione. Nam varia obueniunt pijs mala: sed omnia ad castigationem diuinae benevolentiae sunt referenda. Dominus ipse est, qui dilectos suos corripit, non refert per quos, aut quomodo. Modo exercet nos fame sicut exercuit Abrahamum, Iacobum, Heliam, qui solum vertere propter inopiam coacti sunt. Modo peste, sicut Dauid correptus est: modo aegritudine, ut idem Dauid et Ezechias: modo etiam bonorum direptione, sicut Iob: modo fuga hostium, sicut Iacob, Dauid, Heliae. Omnia autem haec mala a Domino ita sunt immissa, ad sanctorum correptionem, et sanctis ad bonum versa sunt. Tertio, debemus notare ac discere, quotiescunque huiusmodi mala immittuntur, signa esse non irae Dei, sed benevolentiae et dilectionis: qua de re iam paulo ante coepimus dicere. Atque ista doctrina praecipue est notanda, quia est maxime consolatoria, et ex ea ducit apostolus hic praecipuas suas rationes suasorias, unde sequitur: Si castigationem sustinetis. Praecedentem sententiam exponit, nec non instituto suo accommodat, et primo quidem inferendo ex ea, quando pij immissis malis a Deo castigantur, eu-dens esse hoc argumentum, quod a Deo habeantur pro filiis. Quae certe ratio valde est consolatoria. Quis enim non ambiat recenseri inter filios Dei? Atque ut ea de re certiores essemus. {ss}emus, voluit Deus in filio suo naturali tale exemplum afflictionis edere. Nam & hic afflictus est, ut exemplum omnibus foret patientiæ: 1. Petri 2. Atque huc pertinent illa: Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur: non est discipulus supra magistrum. Ratio: cum Christo glorificabimur: si tamen & cum eo patiamur. Item, oportet Christum pati, & sic introire in gloriam Actor. 14. per afflictiones & angustias oportet intrare in gloriam. 2. Tim. 3. Omnes, qui pie volunt vivere in Christo Iesu persecutionem patientur. Qui omnes loci ad consolationem sunt propositi. Et notandum est, quod castigationem Domini vocat παιδεία: quæ vox significat correptionem, qualis est puerorum, quos instituendos suscepimus: quos oportet nonnunquam severius corripi, ne lasciuiant: quia alias facile errant & seducuntur. Ita vero & castigatio piorum est utilis ac necessario, nihilque aliud est, quam castigatio, qualis parentum est in filios. Et nisi Dominus aliquando immitteret adversa, certè metuendum foret, ne in cæcitatem prolaberentur, Deumque negligerent: atque ita à virtutis tramite exorbitarent, donec tandem ad extrema præcipitarentur. Optium, fœlices successus, securitas, multis alioqui bonis fuerunt causa lapsus. Item ὑπομένει cùm dicitur, clarè significatur, nos nō tantum probari paucis, & ad breue tempus, sed longiore etiam tempore subinde manere & perseuerare debere in tolerantia aduersitatum. Perseuerantia est, quæ perfectos reddit.
units.tr: The third reason is drawn from a sure exhortation or consolation set forth in the Scriptures, which teaches that afflictions are to be borne patiently, both because they are sent by God's providence, and because they are a certain sign of God's benevolence towards the godly, since God acknowledges as his beloved sons those whom he chastens in this world. The saying itself is taken from Proverbs 3, where it is read thus: כִּי יִרְצֶה הָאֵל הָאָב בְּתוֹכְחוֹתָיו ... רָאָה [Hebrew as printed], that is, word for word: "My son, do not reject the chastening of the Lord, nor be weary of his correction. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and as a father delights in a son, so will he." Solomon wrote these words more as exhortations than as consolations, though we may well call them consolation too. Theophylact interprets it as an exhortation, as if to hint that we should even desire to be afflicted by the Lord. He says that these words pertain to them as to sons, because Solomon's words read "my son"; and he wants them taken as coming from God and pertaining to all the godly. In the apostle we read it word for word as the Seventy have it. The sense is quite clear, and the apostle both explains it in his own words and applies it to his purpose; so there is no need for us to say much about it. Let us only note that it is a remarkable saying. First, it most plainly teaches that evils are sent by God himself, something which no philosophy and no human reason has ever been able to grasp or believe. Philosophy has thought that all things happen by chance and by fortune; hence some have even removed providence, supposing that God has no care for human affairs, chiefly because they saw the good afflicted and the best things perishing, while the wicked and evil things held the highest place. Human reason, however, interprets that evils are indeed sent by God, but by an angry God, and therefore it leads men to be angry at God and to despair of salvation. Scripture, on the other hand, which alone is to be followed, as a truly wise teacher, teaches that good things as well as evil things are sent by God as by a good parent, and that the evils which befall the godly are signs of divine benevolence, because the Lord deigns to visit them and prefers to punish them in this age rather than in the future. An example is in Luke 16, in Lazarus and the rich man. From this the godly seize the occasion to call upon God, to hope for help, to desire to be released and to be with Christ, and finally to give thanks. Not that the Lord does not also correct as one who is angry; for we see throughout the prophets threats of an angry God set forth, and these threats afterwards brought to effect. But these threats pertain to the wicked and evil whom the Lord strikes so as to destroy them, both in this life and in the next. While God sends evils, he declares his wrath towards the wicked, but his love towards the godly. And if it happens that they are afflicted at the same time, yet meanwhile the godly are delivered from common dangers. So it went well for Jeremiah, Daniel and the like in the Babylonian captivity; likewise for the apostles at the overthrow of Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian. Or at least they are afflicted together with the others for a time, so that afterwards they may fare better, and it turns to their good. For the Lord so moderates afflictions that the godly reap fruit even from temptations, and all things work together for their good. An example of this distinction can be seen even among men, who correct their servants in one spirit and their sons in another, even when they inflict punishments that are nearly equal. We must also note that this is said generally of any correction whatever. For various evils befall the godly, but all are to be referred to the chastening of divine benevolence. It is the Lord himself who chastens his beloved; it matters not through whom or how. He now exercises us with famine, as he exercised Abraham, Jacob and Elijah, who were compelled to leave their country because of poverty; now with plague, as David was chastened; now with sickness, as the same David and Hezekiah; now also with the plundering of goods, as Job; now with the flight from enemies, as Jacob, David and Elijah. Yet all these evils were so sent by the Lord for the correction of the saints, and they were turned to the good of the saints. Third, we ought to note and learn that whenever evils of this kind are sent, they are signs not of God's anger but of his benevolence and love; this we began to say a little while ago. This teaching is especially to be noted, because it is most consoling, and from it the apostle here draws his chief arguments of persuasion, whence follows: "If ye endure chastening." He explains the preceding saying and applies it to his purpose, and first he infers from it that when the godly are chastened by God through the evils sent, it is evident that they are regarded by God as sons. This reason is truly very consoling. For who would not wish to be counted among the sons of God? And so that we might be more certain of this matter, God willed to display such an example of affliction in his natural Son. For he too was afflicted, so that he might be an example of patience to all (1 Peter 2). To this belong the words: "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; the disciple is not above the master" (John 15:20). The reason: "we shall be glorified with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him" (Romans 8:17). Likewise: "it behoved Christ to suffer, and so to enter into glory" (Acts 14:22), and "through many afflictions and distresses we must enter into glory." "All who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Timothy 3:12). All these passages are set forth for consolation. And it should be noted that he calls the chastening of the Lord παιδεία [chastisement]. This word signifies correction of the kind given to children whom we have undertaken to bring up, and who must sometimes be corrected rather severely, lest they grow wanton, since otherwise they easily go astray and are led into error. Indeed the chastening of the godly is useful and necessary in the same way, and it is nothing other than the chastisement that parents give to their sons. And unless the Lord sometimes sent adversity, there would surely be cause to fear that they would fall into blindness, neglect God, and so go astray from the path of virtue until at last they were hurled into utter ruin. Prosperity, happy successes and security have otherwise been the cause of many falls for many good people. Likewise, when ὑπομένει [endures] is said, it is clearly indicated that we are not only to be tested by a few things and for a short time, but that we must also remain and persevere for a longer time in patient endurance of adversities. "Perseverance is what makes men perfect."

units.la: Veluti filijs offert se Deus: προσφέρεται, id est, offert: etiamsi Augustinus libro de tempore barbarico reddiderit, aggreditur. Et autem hæc sententia, quòd Dominus se visendum offert, atq; ingerit sui memoriam, leniter percutiendo, & quasi aurem vellicando: non aliter, atque qui vult quempiam sui memorem reddere, captat occasionem obuiandi alicubi, ut sit in conspectu, atq; ita se offert illi. Ita prorsus nobiscum agit Deus, mala nonnunquam immittendo. Ea propter etiam Deus dum percutit, dicitur subinde in scripturis visitare: vt, visitabo vos in virga. Visitantur ægroti & dilecti: ita & Deus suos quoq; visitat. Ergo cogitemus, nos quoq; si quando contingat corripi, quòd Dominus tali modo se nobis offerat, ut habeamus occasionem ipsum invocandi, & ipse nos adiuuandi. Veluti filijs: Hæc particula, veluti filijs, præcipuè spectanda est. Nam hæc probanda est: & hac probata sequitur Illatio. Si vti filios corripit: ergo ad salutem, non ad perditionem. Sic enim parentes solent castigare suos filios. Si vti filios: ergo non vt alienos & maleficos, &c.
units.tr: As to sons, God presents himself: offers himself [προσφέρεται], that is, he offers. Although Augustine, in his book on the barbarian age, rendered it approaches. This sentence means that the Lord offers himself to be seen and thrusts his memory upon us by gently striking us and, as it were, tugging at our ear. It is like someone who wants a person to remember him and looks for a chance to meet him somewhere, so that he is in his sight and so presents himself to him. God really deals with us in this way, sometimes by sending evils. For this reason, when God strikes, the Scriptures say he also visits us from time to time: "I will visit you with the rod." The sick and the beloved are visited, and so God also visits his own. Let us therefore think that, if we ever happen to be chastened, the Lord presents himself to us in this way so that we have an opportunity to call upon him, and he may help us. As to sons: this phrase deserves especial attention. For this is what must be proved, and once it is proved the inference follows: if he chastens them as sons, then he does so for their salvation, not their destruction. For this is how parents usually correct their sons. If as sons, then not as strangers and evildoers, and so on.

units.la: Quis enim est filius, quem non castigat pater? Probatio, quòd Deus, quos corripit, habeat pro filijs, à simili, quod sumitur à more humano. Patres enim solent corripere suos filios, non autem alienos. Quare, quàdo corripiuntur à Domino pij, signum est, quòd eos agnoscat pro filijs & nō pro alienis. Ita vero comparatū est, vt parentes, quò studiosiores sunt salutis filiorum, eò acrius ipsos coerceant: qua de re non pauca in prouerbijs, vbi etiam dicitur, quòd qui parcit virgæ, oderit filium. Et nulli etiam prouecti magis diligunt suos parentes, quàm qui seueriore correctione optimè fuerunt ab ipsis instituti. Quòd si alieni estis à castigatione, cuius participes sunt omnes, igitur spurij estis non filij. Iam ex præcedenti probatione infert per contrarium, quòd si immunes forent afflictionum, quarū participes sunt omnes filij Dei, argumentum esset, eos non haberi à Deo pro filijs, sed potius pro spurijs. Quæ sanè Illatio vehementer omnium animos debebat permouere, quando reuera grauissima uociturignominia, (& merito quidem) eos qui filij sunt, excludi tanquam spurios. Magna autem vis inest particulæ vniuersali omnes: Hac enim vera, quòd omnes, qui sunt filij, affliguntur, clarissimè sequitur, eos qui non affliguntur, nequaquam esse filios. Ac vera quidem est iuxta illud. Omnes qui pie volūt viuere in Christo Iesu, afflictione patientur. Ite si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur. Ac valet consequentia: Filius Dei est: igitur persecutio eū manet & affligetur. Nam affliguntur etiam mali, videlicet à Deo irato, & non vt filij. Nō etiam oportet pios semper & citra intermissione affligi: hoc enim modo haud possent perfistere: sed quaudo Dominus iudicat pro tepore expedire. Quanquàm, dū nō affliguntur exterius, habent tamen certamina interna, nec vnquàm sunt prorsus securi, etiamsi in fide cofirmati. Quia securitas periculosa. 2. Petri 2. dicitur Loth afflictus animo etiam propter aliena peccata. Atque ideo non per afflictiones proprie agnoscuntur filij Dei, sed per fide potius. Ioa. 1. Dedit eis, vt possent filij Dei fieri, qui credut in nomē eius. Cæterum quàm graui fit, censeri inter spurios, notum est vel ex iure ciuili, item canonico, vbi varie notantur: priuantur bonis paternis, nec possunt adire hæreditatem: item nō possunt citra dispensatione promoueri ad functione ecclesiastica: item nec fungi magistratu. Vide plura in Iure. Atqui eodem modo agitur cū ijs, qui in spiritualibus declarat, se esse spurios, degenerādo videlicet per omnia à patre cœlesti, nequaquam imitando eū in misericordia, oftédedo deniq;, se potius esse ex patre diabolo: sicut Christ dicebat ad Iudæos, Ioan. 8. Et Esaiæ propheta cap. 57. Iudeos appellat (spurios. Hi aut omnes nō possunt adire hæreditate cœlestè, nullo censentur loco in vera Dei ecclesia. Precemur igitur nos, ne
units.tr: For what son is there whom the father does not chasten? This is the proof that God regards those whom he chastens as sons, argued from a likeness drawn from human custom. For fathers usually correct their own sons, not those of others. Therefore, when the godly are chastened by the Lord, it is a sign that he acknowledges them as sons and not as strangers. Indeed, it is so ordained that the more parents care for the welfare of their children, the more sharply they restrain them; on this point there is no shortage of sayings in Proverbs, where it is also said that he who spares the rod hates his son. And none of those who have grown up love their parents more than those who were brought up by them with stricter correction. But if you are without chastisement, of which all are partakers, then you are bastards and not sons. From the preceding proof he now infers by the contrary: if they were free from afflictions, in which all the sons of God share, this would be an argument that they are not regarded by God as sons but rather as bastards. This inference ought surely to stir the minds of all most powerfully, since bastards are in fact excluded, and rightly so, from the most serious disgrace as not being sons. The universal particle all carries great force. For if it is true that all who are sons are afflicted, it follows very clearly that those who are not afflicted are by no means sons. And this is indeed true according to that saying: "All who want to live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim. 3:12); and again, "If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also" (John 15:20). And the consequence holds: he is a son of God, therefore persecution remains with him and he is afflicted. For the wicked are also afflicted, namely by an angry God, but not as sons. Nor is it necessary that the godly be afflicted always and without interruption, for in that way they could not endure; rather, this happens when the Lord judges it expedient for the time. Yet, while they are not afflicted outwardly, they still have inward struggles, and they are never entirely secure, even when they are confirmed in faith, because security is dangerous. In 2 Peter 2 it is said that Lot was vexed in his soul even by the sins of others. And so the sons of God are recognised not properly by afflictions but rather by faith: "He gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name" (John 1:12). Moreover, how grave it is to be counted among bastards is well known even from civil law, and likewise from canon law, where they are variously marked: they are deprived of their father's goods and cannot take up an inheritance; likewise they cannot be promoted to ecclesiastical office without dispensation, nor hold civil magistracy. See more in the law. Yet in the same way it goes with those who, in spiritual matters, show that they are bastards, namely by degenerating in every way from the heavenly Father, by not at all imitating him in mercy, and finally by showing that they are rather from the father, the devil, just as Christ said to the Jews (John 8). And the prophet Isaiah, chapter 57, calls the Jews "bastards." All such people cannot take up the heavenly inheritance and are counted in no place in the true Church of God. Let us therefore pray that we may not

units.la: Matth. 10. Ioan. 16. 2 Timoth. 2. Luc. 24. nos, ne inter spurios & hircos, sed inter filios & oues inueniamur, praesertim in notiss modie, quando haereditas illa omnibus filijs distribuetur. Itaq; cum carnis nostrae patres habuerimus castigatores, & reueriti simus illos, annon multo magis subijciemur patri spirituum, & uiuemus?
units.tr: Matth. 10. Ioan. 16. 2 Timoth. 2. Luc. 24. be found among the bastards and goats, but among the sons and sheep, especially since that inheritance will be distributed to all the sons. Therefore, since we have had fathers of our flesh as correctors, and we have revered them, shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits, and live?

units.la: Illatio ex tota hac sententiae e prouerbijs citatae expositione, ad institutum maxime accommoda. Cuius haec est sententia: Si castigatores debemus ferre patres carnales, & non solum patientes esse, verum etiam eos reuereri: multo magis decet feramus castigatorem ipsum Deum, & ad ferulae eius manum patienter nos submittamus. Consequentia valet a Minori ad maius affirmatiue: & optime sequitur haec illatio, postquam probatum est, eos corripi a Domino uti filios. Comparat patres carnales cum uno omnium communi & spirituali patre Deo. Quanto autem est huius maior excellentia, quam illorum, (est autem maximum, ut reuera carnales illi respectu huius, ne nomine quidem patrum digni sint, iuxta illud Matthaei 23. Patrem nolite vocare vobis in terra: vnus est enim pater vester, qui in coelis est. Item Ephes. 3. ab eodem dicitur esse omnis paternitas in coelo & in terra) tanto quoque debet esse maior nostra erga Deum obedientia, quam erga patres carnales. Et reueriti sumus illos: Quanta reuerentia & obedientia debeatur parentibus castigantibus, notum est vel ex poetarum & philosophorum scriptis. Sed vrget in terea haec particula, vt Deum quoque flagellantem non solum patienter feramus, verum etiam reuereamur, & omnibus modis honoremus. Non tantum igitur patientia in afflictionibus requiritur, verum etiam dilectio Dei, invocatio, gratiarum actio, &c.
units.tr: This inference, drawn from the whole exposition of the saying cited from Proverbs, is especially suited to the matter in hand. Its sense is this: if we ought to bear with fathers of the flesh who correct us, and not only be patient but also revere them, much more should we bear with God himself, the one who corrects us, and submit ourselves patiently to the rod of his hand. The consequence holds affirmatively from the lesser to the greater, and this inference follows very well, once it has been proved that they are chastened by the Lord as sons. He compares fathers of the flesh with the one common and spiritual Father of all, God. But the excellence of the latter is greater than that of the former (and indeed it is the greatest, since in comparison with him those fleshly fathers are not even worthy of the name of father, according to Matthew 23: "Call no one your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven"; likewise Ephesians 3 says that every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named from him). Therefore our obedience towards God ought to be all the greater than towards fathers of the flesh. "And we have revered them": how great reverence and obedience are owed to parents who correct us is known even from the writings of poets and philosophers. But this particle presses further: that we should not only patiently bear with God when he scourges us, but also revere him and honour him in every way. Therefore not only patience in afflictions is required, but also love of God, invocation, thanksgiving, and so on.

units.la: Patrem uocat spiritum) vt intelligatur generaliter pater omnium secundum spiritum, & omnium denique vere spiritualium. Quod si tantum dixisset patrem spiritus, quidam ita forte rapuisset, quasi Deus quidem esset pater alterius partis hominis, nempe carnis: sicut etiam reuera spiritus siue anima a Deo potissimum infunditur: sed ita etiam malorum & impiorum esset secundum alteram partem pater: & ipsi impij secundum alteram partem essent etiam filij Dei, sed nunc dicitur generaliter pater spirituum, vt intelligatur pater praecipue spiritualium, & quidem omnium talium.
units.tr: He calls him the Father of spirits, so that it is understood generally that he is the Father of all according to the spirit, and of all who are truly spiritual. For if he had only said "Father of spirits," someone might perhaps seize on it as though God were the father of only one part of man, namely the flesh (just as indeed the spirit or soul is chiefly infused by God); but then he would also be a father, in another respect, of evil and impious men, and the impious themselves would in another respect also be sons of God. But now he is named generally the Father of spirits, so that it is understood that he is the Father principally of spiritual beings, and indeed of all such.

units.la: Et uiuemus) Dicturus erat Apostolus, ratione consequentiae suis membris perficiendae, & reuerebimur: sed maluit aliquid sublimius, & quo animi fortius mouerentur, apponere. Est autem hic apposita quaedam ratio suasoria, ab vtili: qua significat, obedientiam erga Deum esse causam vitae & quidem vitae aeternae: quae sane ratio omnes merito ad obedientiam & patientiam permoueat. Atque apparet, Apostolum tacite respexisse ad promissionem annexam praecepto de honorandis parentibus Exodi 20. qua dicitur, longaevos fore, qui patrem & matre honorarint. Ex ea igitur hic infert, multo magis victuros, qui honorarint Deum patrem spiritualem. Atq; vt vita promittitur, praecipue temporalis, honorantibus parentes carnales: ita accipiendum est, vitam successuram spiritualem & aeternam honorantibus patrem spiritualem Deum. Qualis parens est, talis promittitur propter obedientiam erga eum vita. Ergo debet haec ratio altissima mete reposta manere.
units.tr: And live: The Apostle was going to say, for the sake of completing the consequence in its parts, "and we shall revere him," but he preferred to add something more lofty, by which minds would be more strongly moved. Here a certain persuasive reason is added, drawn from usefulness, by which he signifies that obedience towards God is the cause of life, and indeed of eternal life; this reason surely rightly moves everyone to obedience and patience. And it is clear that the Apostle tacitly looked back to the promise annexed to the command about honouring parents in Exodus 20, where it is said that those who honour father and mother will be long-lived. From that he therefore infers here that those who honour God, the spiritual Father, will live much more. And just as temporal life, in particular, is promised to those who honour their fleshly parents, so it must be understood that spiritual and eternal life will follow for those who honour God, the spiritual Father. Life is promised on account of obedience towards such a parent as he is. Therefore this reason ought to remain stored in the highest mind.

units.la: Caeterum hic habemus multiplicem doctrinam: Primo, quod, quae in scripturis proponuntur, ea omnia sic accipienda sunt, tanquam ad nos proprie pertinentia. Sic enim Apostolus exhortationes a Salomone propositas in proverbijs, oftedit ad ipsos Hebraeos putare. Secundo: discimus hic, quomodo sententias scripturae debeamus interdum prouide explicare, & nostro accommodare instituto: ac deinde ex ijs aptas rationes suasorias inferre. Tertio: de obedientia erga Deum, item erga parentes: de patienter ferendis castigationibus quantum praesenti argumento conuenit, satis ostendimus.
units.tr: Moreover, here we have several teachings. First, whatever is set forth in the Scriptures must be taken as pertaining properly to us. Thus the Apostle shows that he thinks the exhortations which Solomon set forth in the Proverbs were addressed to the Hebrews themselves. Second, we learn here how we ought sometimes to explain the sentences of Scripture carefully and adapt them to our purpose, and then from them to draw suitable reasons for persuading. Third, we have sufficiently shown, as far as the present argument requires, what is owed to God and to parents in obedience, and how chastisements are to be borne patiently.

units.la: Atq; illi quidem ad paucos dies pro arbitratu suo nos erudiebant: hic autem ad commodum nostrum, in hoc, vt impartiat nobis sanctimoniam suam.
units.tr: Indeed, those men trained us for a few days at their own discretion, but he does so for our advantage, in order to impart to us his holiness.

units.la: Quarta ratio suasoria ab vtili, fluens ex comparatione praecedenti, qua contulit patres carnales homines cum patre spirituali Deo. Atque ostendit, longe diuerso fine nos corripi a Deo, quam corripimur a parentibus, multoque maiorem fructum ad nos redire ex correptione diuina, quam ex correptione humana: atque ideo aequum est, mala a Deo immissa patienter feramus. Videtur Apostolus motus ad subijciendam hanc rationem, ex proxime subiecta particula, & uiuemus: quae dedit occasionem, alia de vtilitate correptionis diuinae cogitandi. Vide autem, quam eleganter Apostolus sententiam suam expresserit: Illi quidem, inquit, ad paucos dies: Notat tempus, quo liberi solent sub parentibus agere, & quo per illos instituuntur, quod certe breve est, ad illud tempus collatum, quo Dominus nos erudit & instituit. Parentes carnales iam proue&os & adultos filios non amplius curant, a se quodammodo reijciunt. At Deus pater noster spiritualis perpetuo curam nostri gerit, a prima infantia ad extremam vsque senectam: atque ita quidem curat, vt ne capillum capitis sinat nobis citra consilium decidere. Ergo haec particula maiore curam & prouidentiam Dei erga nos commendat, quam esse posset parentum carnalium
units.tr: The fourth reason for persuasion comes from usefulness, and follows from the preceding comparison, in which the Apostle compared earthly fathers with our heavenly Father, God. He shows that we are corrected by God for a far different end than we are corrected by our parents, and that much greater fruit comes back to us from divine correction than from human correction. Therefore it is right that we bear patiently the evils sent by God. The Apostle seems to have been moved to add this reason by the immediately following words, "and we shall live," which gave occasion for thinking further about the usefulness of divine correction. Notice how elegantly the Apostle has expressed his meaning: "Those indeed," he says, "for a few days." He points to the time during which children are usually under their parents and are trained by them, which is certainly brief compared with the time in which the Lord instructs and trains us. Earthly parents no longer care for their children once they have grown up and become adults; they somehow cast them off. But God, our spiritual Father, constantly takes care of us, from earliest infancy to extreme old age, and he so cares for us that he does not allow a single hair of our head to fall without his counsel. Therefore this phrase commends a greater care and providence of God toward us than could be found in earthly parents.

units.la: Tempus eruditionis & castigationis pater in mundo breue est. Pro arbitratu suo) id est, secundum quod ipsis videbitur. Hic præcipuè notatur diuersa ratio corripiendi in parentibus carnalibus. Corripiunt, inquit, & erudiunt, pro arbitratu suo: hoc est, pro suo affectu, nunc iracundi & commoti, nunc spectantes, ut aliquid sibi per nos fiat: & sic magis habetes rationem suorum affectuum, vel sui commodi, quam nostri: aut, ut maximè videantur aliquid facere nostræ vtilitatis gratia, tamen spectant tantum vti- litatem externam & momentaneam, puta honorem, exi-stimationem apud populū, aut denique prouentum & argumentum facultatum terrenarum. Hoc autem perquam exi-guum est ad id, quod spectat Deus in correptione. Ad quid igitur spectat Deus? Hic autem ad nostrum commodum: Hoe est, Deus non corripit nos, ullis affectibus motus, sicut carnales patres, sed solùm respiciens ad nostrā vtilitatem Deus omnia, quæ erga nos agit, propter nos agit & propter nostram vtilitatem: intellige de pijs, quibus omnia ad bonum cedunt. Percutit & vulnerat Deus ut sanet: occidit, ut viuificet. Est igitur ista particula valde no- tanda, & in omnibus afflictionibus intentissima mente consideranda: & per hanc potis-simum discernuntur afflictiones piorum ab afflictionibus impiorum. Impijs cedunt ad perniciem, pijs verò ad salutem. In hoc, ut imparticipat nobis sanctimoniā suā) Exponit, quomodo multo maior vtilitas proueniat à correptione diuina, quàm prouenire posset à correptione parentum carnalem. Si nulla vtilitas venit à carnalibus parentibus, hæc tamen externa tantùm erit, & itidè carnalis, & quæ summa esse potest, hæc est, quod videlicet ciuiliter & mortaliter erimus boni: vera interim sanctimonia, quæ Deo sit accepta, manibus destituti. At verò quando Deus corripit suos filios, hinc consequuntur vtilitatem spiritualem, nempe veram sanctimoniam, hoc est, ut sancti efficiamur, quemadmodum ipse pater sanctus est. Secundum quod & apud prophetam dicit: Sancti estote, quoniam & ego sanctus sum. Et nisi fallor, respicit Apostolus inparticula, suam, ad id, quod filij bene instituti solent imitari mores suorum parentum: omneq; studium bonorum patrum in hoc insumitur, ut filios sibi quàm similimos reddat. Ita plane & Deus facit, corripit suos filios, id autem, ut faciat sibi similes, ut discant ipsius exemplo etiam sancti esse. Sed, dices contingit ne hoc, ut aliqui participes fiant sanctimo- niæ diuinæ per correptiones? Imò, inquam, nam correpti inuocant Deū, mouentur malis suorum fratrum, efficiuntur misericordes, sicut pater cœlestis misericors est: suam volun-tatem in omnibus conformant voluntati patris cœlestis: & sic per omnia accedunt ad di-uinam indolem, suumq; patrum Deum imitatur: atq; ita sancti cum illo & per illum fiunt. Est autem valde salutaris ista doctrina & consolatoria, quòd afflictiones coducunt ad sanctimoniam, & fructum adfert spiritualem: in quem, si quoties immittit Deus aduersa, spe- ctaremus fierent nobis omnia leuia & tolerabilia. Secundi successus alienant à Deo, & ab ducunt à sanctimonia: aduersi verò deducunt ad Deum, & conferunt ad sanctimoniam. Iam ergo eligamus & statuamus, utra magi conducant. Ad summam, afflictionum in hac vita usus est varius. Primùm humiliantur ijs animi hominum, qui alioquin rebus pro sperisq; ferociunt & luxuriant. Deinde abducuntur ab amore rerū temporalium, sectariq; discunt spirituales cœlestes: harum æternitatem & constantiam illarum mobilitati & fra- gilitati longè anteponunt. Tertiò, cogitant de spiritualibus adipiscendis, de salute animæ comparanda, deq; vitæ malæ & peccatricis emendatione, ferijsq; & dulcibus pœnitetiæ fructibus proferendis. Quartò inuocant Deum, in eoq; (dum de rerum humanarū præsi-dijs desperatur) spem fiduciamq; collocare discunt. A qua fide & spe nihil prorsus sese deinceps abduci patiuntur. Quintò, exercetur hisce fides: discitur misericordia & dile- ctio proximi, verbumq; Dei studiosè & assiduè colitur, & cum fructu in animis recondi-tur. Hic præcipuè sunt fines & fructus afflictionum piorum. Omnis autem castigatio in præsens quidem non videtur esse gaudij, sed molestiæ. At postea fructum tranquillum iustitiæ reddit ijs, qui per illam fuerint exercitati. Quinta ratio suasoria iterum ab vtili: sed de ea potisimum agens vtilitate, quæ ex afflictionibus contingit post hanc vitam. Ita autem exposita est hæc ratio, ut inclusam habere videatur occupationem, qua diluitur, quòd delicata & sui amans caro, afflictiones semper refugiens solet obijcere. Castigatio, inquit, in præsens quidem non videtur esse gaudij, sed molestiæ) Ita enim iudicat caro etiam in sanctissimis viris. Quamdiu in carne hærent, fieri non potest, quin sentiant eius impetus, ac molestias omnes, quoad eius fieri potest, refugiant: sicut Christus ipse carnis vires infensiens dixit: Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem: & pauescebat, & tædio afficiebatur, & orabat, pater si fieri potest transeat à me calix iste. Sed spiritus interea adiuuat infirmitatē carnis.
units.tr: The father's time of instruction and chastisement in the world is brief. At their own discretion: that is, as seems good to them. This especially marks the different manner of correcting in earthly parents. They correct and train, he says, at their own discretion, that is, according to their own feelings: sometimes angry and stirred up, sometimes looking to have something done by us for their own benefit. Thus they regard more their own emotions or their own advantage than ours. Or, even when they seem to do something for our good, they look only to external and temporary usefulness, such as honor, reputation among the people, or finally the profit and proof of earthly wealth. But this is very small compared with what God aims at in correction. What, then, does God aim at? But he does so for our advantage: that is, God does not correct us moved by any affections, as earthly fathers do; but God, looking only to our usefulness, does all that he does toward us for our sake and for our advantage. This is to be understood of the godly, for whom all things work together for good. God strikes and wounds in order to heal; he kills in order to make alive. This phrase, therefore, is to be carefully noted, and in all afflictions is to be considered with the most attentive mind; and chiefly by this the afflictions of the godly are distinguished from the afflictions of the wicked. For the wicked they turn to destruction, but for the godly to salvation. In order to impart to us his holiness: he explains how a much greater usefulness comes from divine correction than could come from the correction of earthly parents. If no usefulness comes from earthly parents, that usefulness will nevertheless be only external and merely earthly, and the highest it can be is that we become good in a civil and mortal sense, while true holiness, acceptable to God, is lacking. But when God corrects his sons, they thereby obtain spiritual usefulness, namely true holiness, that is, that we become holy as he himself, the Father, is holy. Accordingly he also says through the prophet: "Be holy, for I also am holy." And unless I am mistaken, the Apostle in the particle his looks to the fact that well-trained children usually imitate the morals of their parents; and all the effort of good fathers is spent on making their sons as like themselves as possible. Clearly God also does so: he corrects his sons, and he does this so that he may make them like himself, that they may learn by his example to be holy too. But you will say: does this happen, that some become partakers of divine holiness through corrections? Indeed, I answer, for those who are corrected call upon God, are moved by the evils of their brothers, become merciful, as their heavenly Father is merciful, conform their will in all things to the will of the heavenly Father; and thus in all respects they draw near to the divine nature, and imitate their Father God; and so they become holy with him and through him. This teaching is very wholesome and comforting, that afflictions lead to holiness and bring spiritual fruit. If we would keep this in view whenever God sends adversity, all things would become light and bearable for us. Prosperous successes estrange us from God and draw us away from holiness; adverse ones, however, lead us to God and contribute to holiness. Let us therefore choose and determine which of the two is more profitable. In sum, afflictions in this life have various uses. First, they humble the minds of men who otherwise grow proud and extravagant in their prosperity. Second, they draw men away from love of temporal things, and teach them to seek spiritual and heavenly things, placing the eternity and constancy of these far above the mobility and fragility of the former. Third, they lead men to think about obtaining spiritual goods, about procuring the salvation of the soul, about amending an evil and sinful life, and about bearing the sweet fruits of repentance. Fourth, they teach men to call upon God, and, when hope in human help has failed, to place their hope and trust in him; and they allow nothing whatever to draw them away from this faith and hope. Fifth, by these things faith is exercised: mercy and love of neighbor are learned, the Word of God is diligently and constantly cultivated, and is stored up in the minds with fruit. These are chiefly the ends and fruits of the afflictions of the godly. Now all chastisement seems at present not to be a matter of joy but of grief; but afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

units.la: Roman. 8. Sicut & Christus dicebat, spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma. Itaque sentiunt pij in sese luctam istam carnis & spiritus: & caro subinde praevalet in nō nullis, ut vel fugiant pericula, vel veritatem abnegent. Hoc ergo est ingenium carnis, iudi care, castigationem esse molestiae, non gaudij. Retinet verò vocabulū πασδείας, respiciens ad institutionem filiorum. Nam & filij subinde horrent castigatione, quae tamen propter utilitatem illorum in posterum secuturam adhibetur. Sed contra eiusmodi iudiciū carnis aliter sentit spiritus, ac facile tollit illas suggestiones carnis, proponendo utilitates, quae post hanc vitam sequuntur ex talibus afflictionibus.
units.tr: This is the fifth reason for persuasion, again from usefulness; but it treats especially of that usefulness which comes from afflictions after this life. This reason is so set out that it seems to contain an answer which removes an objection that the delicate, self-loving flesh, always shunning afflictions, is accustomed to raise. Chastisement, he says, seems at present not to be a matter of joy, but of grief: for the flesh judges so even in the most holy men. As long as they dwell in the flesh, it cannot be that they do not feel its impulses, and that they do not, as far as possible, shun all its discomforts; just as Christ himself, feeling the strength of the flesh, said: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death"; and he was amazed and troubled, and prayed, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." But meanwhile the spirit helps the weakness of the flesh. Rom. 8. As Christ also said: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." Thus the godly feel within themselves this struggle of flesh and spirit; and the flesh at times prevails in some, so that they either flee dangers or deny the truth. This, then, is the nature of the flesh: to judge chastisement a matter of grief, not of joy. But the Scripture retains the word παιδείας [paideias], looking to the training of children. For children too sometimes shrink from correction, which is nonetheless applied for their future advantage. But against this kind of judgment of the flesh, the spirit thinks otherwise, and easily removes those suggestions of the flesh by setting forth the advantages which follow such afflictions after this life.

units.la: At postea, inquit, fructum tranquillū iustitiae reddit ijs, qui per illam fuerint exercitati) Et haec appositissimè sunt reddita. Afflictiones quidem & castigationes sunt molestae, sed sequuntur maximae utilitates. Recte dicebat ille, amaras esse radices virtutis, & scientiae, sed fructus suauissimos. Idem nos de afflictionibus dicere poterimus. Castigatio reddit, inquit, frutum. Certe fructus & utilitatis percipiendae gratia, iniquum fuerit labores aliquantos detrectare. Spe praemij certant athletae: spe recuperandae valetudinis amara pharmaca bibunt aegroti: spe pacis parandae durissima bella suscipiuntur à principibus & nobilibus: spe lucri & commodi per mare, per terras periclitantur cum fortunis suis mercatores: pro commodis accipiendis doctrinae per plures annos in phrontisterijs laboramus. Igitur spe fructus aequum est castigationes perferre. Sed non satis est apostolo, dicere, fructum pro positum afflictis: sed addit etiam, Fructum illum esse tranquillum, εἰρηνικὸν, quasi dicat, patum, hoc est, qui pacem adfert certam & stabilem, & quidem non externam modò, ut in apocalypsi dicitur: sed qua habent etiam pacem apud Deū in conscientijs suis, & certò sciunt, Deum sibi placatum & propitium: de qua Roman. 5. Quae pax & in hac quide vita contingit sanctis, sed praecipuè in altera. Et haec pax praecipuè dicitur fructus iustitiae. Nam addit, hic afflictis dari fructum iustitiae. Ita nam que qui decertarunt pro iustitia, accipiunt iustitiae fructum. Matthaei 5. Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam, quoniam illorum est regnum coelorum. Sicut qui laborarunt & sudarunt pro doctrina paranda, tandem accipiunt doctrinę aliquem fructum, & sic de alijs. Ita quoq; iudicandum, qui certarunt pro iustitia & veritate, pro gloria Dei. Sicut suprà exempla audiuimus eorum patrum, qui pro veritate & gloria Dei passi sunt cruciatus & aduersitates: qui omnes nunc obtinent coronam & fructum iustitiae, veritatis, gloriae apud Deum.
units.tr: But afterwards, he says, it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. This is put very fittingly. Afflictions and chastisements are indeed unpleasant, but the greatest benefits follow them. That man spoke rightly who said that the roots of virtue and of learning are bitter, but their fruits most sweet. We can say the same about afflictions. Chastisement, he says, yields fruit. Surely it would be unfair to shrink from some labours for the sake of gaining fruit and benefit. Athletes strive for the sake of the prize; the sick drink bitter medicines in hope of recovering their health; princes and nobles undertake the harshest wars in hope of establishing peace; merchants risk their fortunes on sea and land in hope of gain and profit; we labour for many years in the schools to acquire the benefits of learning. Therefore it is only fair to endure chastisements in hope of fruit. But it was not enough for the apostle to say that fruit is set before the afflicted; he adds that this fruit is peaceable [εἰρηνικὸν], as if to say that it is calm and brings a certain and stable peace, and not only an outward peace, as is said in the Apocalypse, but that peace which those people also have before God in their consciences, knowing for certain that God is reconciled and propitious to them, as in Romans 5. This peace comes to the saints in this life, but chiefly in the next. And this peace is especially called the fruit of righteousness. For he adds that the afflicted here are given the fruit of righteousness. Thus those who have struggled for righteousness receive the fruit of righteousness. Matthew 5: "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Just as those who have laboured and sweated to acquire learning at last receive some fruit of learning, and so on, so too we must judge that those who have striven for righteousness and truth, for the glory of God, receive it. As we heard above in the examples of those fathers who suffered torments and adversities for the truth and the glory of God, all of them now obtain the crown and the fruit of righteousness, truth and glory with God.

units.la: Sed & notandū est, quòd addit, ijs demum reddi fructum, qui fuerint per castigatione exercitati, τοῖς δὲ αὐτῶς γεγυμνασμένοις, Metaphora ab ijs sumpta est, qui in publicis certaminibus exercetur, vbi, sicut & apostolus alibi notat, nemo coronatur, nisi qui legitimè certauerit: sed interea hic tacitè proponit apostolus considerandum omnibus pij, quòd haec fit diuina ordinatio, ut nō nisi ij percipiant tales fructus iustitiae, qui videlicet afflictiones & molestias pro iustitia subiuerint. Omnes qui piè volunt viuere in Christo Iesu, persecutio nem patientur. Qui vult me sequi, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Non est discipulus supra magistrum. Arcta est via, quae ducit ad salute. Oportet Christum pati, & sic introire in gloriam. Item 1. Thessalon. 3. Nam ipsi nostis, nos in hunc vsum positos esse.
units.tr: But it must also be noted that he adds that the fruit is given only to those who have been trained by chastisement [τοῖς δὲ αὐτῶς γεγυμνασμένοις]. The metaphor is taken from those who train in public contests, where, as the apostle notes elsewhere, no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully. Meanwhile the apostle here silently sets before all the godly that this is the divine ordinance: that only those receive such fruits of righteousness who have undergone afflictions and troubles for righteousness. "All who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." "If anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." "A disciple is not above his teacher." "The way that leads to salvation is narrow." "Christ had to suffer and so enter into glory." Likewise 1 Thessalonians 3: "For you yourselves know that we were appointed to this."

units.la: Secundò, hoc proponit apostolus considerandum, quòd afflictiones nihil aliud sunt quàm vtilia exercita ad parandam perfectionem in vera pietate. Exercitia autem si sunt vtilia, & affectanda etiam in quacunq; arte, in qua perfecti cupimus euadere. Igitur multo magis in perfectione coram Deo. Suprà autem exposuimus, quomodo fidės exercetur afflictionibus: & quanti fructus praeterea inde sequantur.
units.tr: Secondly, the apostle sets this before us to consider: afflictions are nothing other than useful exercises for attaining perfection in true godliness. If exercises are useful, they are also to be pursued in any art in which we wish to become skilled. Much more, then, in perfection before God. We have explained above how faith is exercised by afflictions, and what great fruits follow from this besides.

units.la: Proinde intentis animis cōtemplemur istam vtilitatem verè maximam afflictionum corporalium: & inueniemus regulam certisimam si velimus exempla obseruare in sacris literis: quod, quicunque hic passi sunt aduersa propter iustitiam, ijdem etiam fructu iustitiae acceperint, si non in hac vita, certè in altera, frequenter tamen in vtraq;. Econtrà autem qui hic in mundo pati detrectarunt, pōst luisse, & infoelices habuisse exitus, & prę terea in aeternos incidisse cruciatus. Exempla habes de omnibus tyrannis, &c. vide Chrysostomum. Qui indulgent suo corpori ut mulieres, fiunt infirmiores, otium, ciborum sa-tietas, pariunt aegritudines: & à corporum affectione etiam animus vitia contrahit: sicut sonus in instrumentis musicis aliter atque aliter se habet, dum extenduntur, vel dum remittuntur chordae. Corpus ita curatum reddit procliues ad libidinem, segnes, nihil viris dignum operantes: & cùm corpora male habent, irritabiles efficimur, iracundi, morosi, alijs inuidentes. Sic etiam nobiscum agitur, ubi omnia in mundo pro uotis succedunt.
units.tr: Therefore let us contemplate with attentive minds this truly very great usefulness of bodily afflictions, and we will find a most certain rule if we observe the examples in the sacred letters: whoever has suffered adversity here for righteousness's sake has also received the fruit of righteousness, if not in this life then certainly in the next, and often in both. On the other hand, those who refused to suffer in this world have afterwards paid the penalty, had unhappy ends, and moreover fallen into eternal torments. You have examples of all the tyrants, and so on; see Chrysostom. Those who indulge their body, like women, become weaker; idleness and satiety of food beget sicknesses; and the mind also contracts vices from the disposition of the body, just as the sound of musical instruments varies as the strings are tightened or loosened. A body thus pampered makes us prone to lust, sluggish, doing nothing worthy of men; and when bodies are ill-disposed, we become irritable, angry, peevish, envious of others. So it also goes with us when everything in the world turns out according to our wishes.

units.la: Quapropter manus remissas, & genua soluta surrigite, & facite, ut recti sint gressus pedibus vestris, ne claudicatio aberret à via, imo sanetur potius.
units.tr: Therefore lift up the drooping hands and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be turned out of the way, but rather be healed.

units.la: Expresso
units.tr: Expressed.

units.la: Expositis sat multis rationibus suasoriis, ut finem faciat, breue subiicit exhortationem, inferens ex dictis omnibus, debere eos forti esse animo, & in fide sanaq; doctrina constantes perseuerare, non vacillare, aut dubitare, ut ita salutem possint consequi.
units.tr: Having set out enough persuasive reasons, the apostle, to bring the matter to an end, adds a brief exhortation, drawing from all that has been said that they ought to be strong in spirit and persevere constantly in the faith and sound doctrine, not wavering or doubting, so that they may thus attain salvation.

units.la: Sumpta aute sunt priora aliquot verba ex Esaiae capite tricesimo quinto, id quod valde prudenter facit apostolus, & in conclusione valde oportune. Ita namque & plus ponderis habitura est exhortatio, & altius infixa haerebit omnium animis. רפו ידים ... id est, confortate manus remissas, & genua nutantia roborate. Sed apostolus interpres potius secutus est Septuaginta, apud quos ita legitur, ἰσχύσατε χεῖρας ἀνειμένας καὶ γόνατα παρειλυμένα, quasi dicat: Cofortate manus robustae et genua dissoluta. Apostolus autem habet sententiam fere clariore, ἀνόρθωσατε, id est, sursum erigite.
units.tr: The first few words are taken from the thirty-fifth chapter of Isaiah, which the apostle does very wisely, and very fittingly in his conclusion. For in this way the exhortation will carry more weight and cling more deeply to the minds of all. רפו ידים [Hebrew] ... that is, "Strengthen the weak hands, and confirm the tottering knees." But the apostle, as translator, followed the Septuagint rather, where it reads: "Strengthen the hands that are relaxed and the knees that are loosened" [ἰσχύσατε χεῖρας ἀνειμένας καὶ γόνατα παρειλυμένα], as if to say: "Make strong the robust hands and the loosened knees." The apostle, however, has a rather clearer sense: "Set upright" [ἀνόρθωσατε], that is, "raise up."

units.la: Videtur adhuc metaphora subesse sumpta a certaminib. praesertim a certamine cursus, de quo & initio huius capitis. Sic autem solebant membra sua certaturi extendere, brachia videlicet in altum iactando, genua & pedes erigendo, ut licet videre apud Virgilium li. 5. & Gellium lib. 13. cap. 27.
units.tr: The metaphor seems still to lie beneath, taken from contests, especially from the footrace, which is also mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. Indeed, those about to compete used to stretch their limbs in this way, namely by throwing the arms high and raising the knees and feet, as one may see in Virgil, book 5, and in Gellius, book 13, chapter 27.

units.la: Caeterum valde appositę sunt haec verba ex Esaia in medium producta. Nam propheta ibi vaticinatur de ecclesia, quae post graues afflictiones debet a Christo & propter Christum consolationem praesertim tempore reuelati euangelij accipere: Sicuti quilibet legens totum illud caput facile poterit deprehendere: quādo ad idem caput etiā Christus Matthaei vndecimo, & Lucae septimo, mittens ad Ioannem, & comprobare volens, se esse promissum Messiam, videtur respexisse, & sententiam prophetae suo instituto accommodasse. Proinde aptissime etiam hoc loco citantur haec verba ab apostolo, & mirifice conducunt ad consolandos erigendosque animos.
units.tr: Moreover, these words from Isaiah are very aptly brought forward. For the prophet there prophesies about the Church, which after severe afflictions is to receive consolation from Christ and for Christ's sake, especially at the time of the revealed gospel. As anyone reading that whole chapter will easily perceive; and when Christ, in Matthew 11 and Luke 7, sending to John and wishing to prove that he is the promised Messiah, seems to have had regard to this same chapter and adapted the prophet's words to his purpose. Therefore these words are cited by the apostle in this place most appropriately too, and they serve wonderfully to console and raise up the spirits.

units.la: Quapropter, inquit, manus remissas, & genua soluta surrigite. Quasi diceret: quando igitur res ita se habet, quod videlicet afflictiones sunt signa beneuolentiae Dei, & testimonia, quod fitis Deo chari, item amplissima praemia sunt omnib. afflictis proposita: nefitis amplius pusillanimes, nolite desperare, quasi vos Deus deseruisset: sed potius animos per fidem erigite, & constates etiā in medijs periculis perseuerate. Elegānter autem describit apostolus languorem animi, & pusillanimitatem, qualis solet contingere post toleratas molestias & labores: ad significandum, talibus similitudinibus seu metaphoris a corpore ductis, qua les sint affectis animorum tempore aduersitatum, & post multas & graves tentationes.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "lift up the drooping hands and the feeble knees." As if he were saying: since things stand thus, namely that afflictions are signs of God's goodwill and testimonies that you are dear to God, and since the most ample rewards are set before all the afflicted, do not be fainthearted any longer; do not despair, as though God had forsaken you; but rather raise your spirits through faith, and persevere steadfastly even in the midst of dangers. Now the apostle elegantly describes the languor of spirit and the faintheartedness that usually befall people after they have endured troubles and labours, signifying by such likenesses or metaphors drawn from the body what kind of state the minds of men are in during times of adversity, and after many and grievous temptations.

units.la: Tunc enim solet totus homo propter molestias laguidior effici, animo moeres ac tristis, sicut Christus dicebat de se ipso, sicut item fugens crudeles manus Iezabelis Helias ut etiam mori cupiant. Proinde vbi talis contingit affectio, oportet iterum nos sursum erigere. Apostoli interpres, contra atque in Hebraeo, & apud Septuaginta habetur, dixit, ἀνορθώσατε, quasi diceret, sursum erigite: ea voce, opinor, admonens, respicere debere eos, qui affligūtur, ad bona coelestia omnib. fortiter decertantibus in coelis propositā: necnon e sublimi exspectandum ipsis auxilium. Si eo animus & mens feratur, manus & pedes, hoc est, totus homo, non dubium, quin fortes efficiamur ad satanae & satellitum eius molestias perferendas.
units.tr: For then the whole man is usually made more feeble on account of his troubles, his mind grieving and sad, just as Christ said of himself, and as Elijah, fleeing from the cruel hand of Jezebel, also wished to die. Therefore, when such a state arises, we must again raise ourselves up. The translator of the apostle, contrary to what is found in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint, said ἀνορθώσατε, as if to say: "Raise up," admonishing, I suppose, by this word that those who are afflicted ought to look to the heavenly goods set before all who strive bravely in the heavens, and also to expect help from on high. If the mind and spirit are carried thither, the hands and feet, that is, the whole man, will undoubtedly be made strong enough to bear the assaults of Satan and his minions.

units.la: Et facite, vt recti sint gressus pedibus vestris, ne claudicatio aberret a via.
units.tr: And make straight paths for your feet, lest what is lame be turned out of the way.

units.la: Eos alloquitur qui magnitudine afflictionum permoti, nec non pseudo apostolorum persuasionibus aliquo modo adducti incipiebant apud sese dubitare, vtram viam ingrederentur, hoc est, num iterum relaberentur ad Iudaismū, an in cofessione Christi & euangelicae veritatis pergerent. Quales multos ad id tempus fuisse inter Hebraeos certum est. Et certe in grauibus tentationibus animi modo huc, modo illuc impelluntur: & nisi spiritu Dei informentur, facile ad priorem vitam, cui a teneris & qua diutissime assueuerunt, recidunt. Quantum vero credimus, pseudoapostolos passim emissos a pharisaeis pontificibus, laborasse, ut credentes Hebraeos ab euangelio abducerent. Contra tales pseudoapostolos, nosterPaulus in singulis fere agit epistolis: & ecclesia Galatarum infoeliciter fuit technas eorum experta. Si autem apud Galatas tantum valuerunt, & non minora tentarunt efficere apud Ephesios, Colossenses, Romanos, quid non conati sunt apud Hebraeos? Nihil sine dubio, sive quod ad minas & crudelitatem attinet, sive quod ad blanditias & dolos attinet, omiserunt. Propter has igitur causas multi permoti sunt ad dubitandum, ut nescirent, qua via sibi foret ingrediendum. Atq; huiusmodi anxietas ac dubitatio aptissime exprimitur hisce similitudinibus de no recte incededo, & de claudicado. Fluctua re enim ac dubitare animo, est vere claudicare & dubie incedere. Sic vero ambulare, ingredi, incedere, creberrime in Scripturis ad animum referuntur. Esaiae 30. Haec est via, ambulate in ea, & non declinetis neq; ad dextra neq; ad sinistram. Item psal. 15. Qui ingreditur sine macula. Videtur autem apostolus respexisse ad verba & historiam Eliae, 1. regum 18. vbi Helias ait ad omnem populum, vsquequo claudicatis in duas partes?
units.tr: He addresses those who, moved by the greatness of their afflictions and in some measure drawn in by the persuasions of false apostles, began to doubt among themselves which way they should walk: that is, whether they should fall back again into Judaism, or persevere in the confession of Christ and the truth of the gospel. That many of the Hebrews were of this kind at that time is certain. Indeed, under severe temptations the mind is driven now this way, now that, and unless it is shaped by the Spirit of God, it easily falls back into its former life, to which from childhood and for a very long time it had been accustomed. We may believe that the false apostles, sent out everywhere by the Pharisaic priests, laboured to draw the believing Hebrews away from the gospel. Our Paul deals with such false apostles in nearly every one of his epistles, and the church of the Galatians had unhappily experienced their snares. But if they prevailed so much among the Galatians, and attempted no less among the Ephesians, Colossians and Romans, what did they not try among the Hebrews? Without doubt they left nothing undone, whether by threats and cruelty or by flattery and deceit. For these reasons many were moved to doubt, not knowing which way they ought to go. Such anxiety and doubt are most aptly expressed by these likenesses of not walking straight and of limping. For to waver in mind and to doubt is truly to limp and to walk unsteadily. And walking, going and proceeding are very often used in Scripture of the mind. Isaiah 30: "This is the way, walk in it, and do not turn aside to the right hand or to the left." Likewise Psalm 15: "He who walks without blemish." Moreover, the apostle seems to have had in view the words and history of Elijah, 1 Kings 18, where Elijah says to all the people, "How long will you limp between two opinions?"

units.la: Si Dominus est Deus, sequimini eum: fi autem Baal, fequimi illum. Tunc quoque magnam exercebatin pios tyrannidem Achab & Iezabel, & triumphabant falsi doctores, & sacerdotes Baal, velcentes de mensa Iesabel.
