Prophetę Baal quadringenti quinquaginta, prophetæ item lucorum quadringenti: veri prophetæ erant perpauci, & hi eiecti, profugi hinc inde sparsi: pauca millia vere colentium Deum, respectu eorum, qui Baal colebant. Sic vero prorsus agebatur initio reuelati euangelij: Tyrannis sacerdotum & pontificum grassabatur vehementer: pusillus grex verę ecclesiæ sparsus hinc inde oberrabat. Itaque multi claudicare coeperunt, ac dubitare, utri parti sese adiungerent. Proinde recte monet apostolus Hebræos eo in statu constitutos, ut curent rectos esse gressus pedibus suis, ne claudicatio aberret a via: si adhuc claudicent, periculum est, ne aberret a via: imo sanetur potius ista claudicatio, ἰᾶθῆ ἀπὸ μάσσων. Elegas & hic est similitudo ex re medica, & a corpore ad animam transfertur. Sicut qui vitium contraxerunt in pedibus, possunt, si tepestiuè adhibeas remedium, curari: ita qui in sana doctrina coeperunt fortasis fluctuare, possunt rectius institui, & ad salutem perduci per medicos animarum.
units.tr: If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him. At that time Ahab and Jezebel also exercised a great tyranny over the godly, and the false teachers and the priests of Baal triumphed, eating at Jezebel's table. There were four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and likewise four hundred prophets of the groves; the true prophets were very few, and these were cast out, fled and scattered here and there: a few thousand who truly worshipped God, compared with those who worshipped Baal. Just so, indeed, things went at the beginning of the revealed gospel: the tyranny of priests and high priests raged violently, and the little flock of the true church wandered scattered here and there. Therefore many began to limp and to doubt which party they should join. Accordingly the apostle rightly warns the Hebrews, who were placed in such a condition, to take care that the steps of their feet are straight, so that what is lame be not turned out of the way; if they still limp, there is danger that they wander from the way. Rather, let this limping be healed: ἰαθῇ μᾶλλον [ἰαθῇ μᾶλλον]. This is again a likeness drawn from medicine, transferred from the body to the soul. Just as those who have contracted a defect in their feet can be cured if a remedy is applied in good time, so those who in sound doctrine have perhaps begun to waver can be set right more correctly and brought to salvation through the physicians of souls.

units.la: Atque hæ rationes sunt valde efficaces, ad animos omnium, ut constantes esse velint, permouendos, & aptissime ad finem imponendum toti huic parti.
units.tr: These arguments are very effective for moving the minds of all to wish to be steadfast, and they are most apt for bringing this whole part to its close.

units.la: Posset hic fieri mentio de ijs, quæ nos ipsi vidimus tum in Anglia, cum exueretur Antonius Barus, & Hieronymus a Stepne, & M. Gerardus pastor in Houilau, cū quibusdā alijs, &c. Cæterum & nos accipere debemus hæc verba ad Hebræos facta, imo totā hac partem postremam hortatoriam ad constantiam in fide, ut ad nos maximè pertinentia. Nam nostra tempestate prorsus eadem causa agitur, quę temporibus Apostoli agebatur. Passim multi sunt, qui falsam doctrinam proponendo, item tyrannidem exercendo conantur pios vbique terrarū a confessione veritatis euangelicæ, & fidei, abducere, totus q; mundus in duas partes diuisus est: sicut tempore Eliæ diuisus erat Israel & maior numerus vult seruire Baal: pauci seruati sunt, qui detrectāt flectere genua Baal, multi claudicāt nescientes, vtram viam ingredi debeant. Hocigitur restat, ut pij doctores & prophetæ proponant eis istam doctrinam Apostoli, fortiter inculcent, per fidem iustificari nos apud Deum: qua ratione omnes sancti ab initio inde mundi ad nostra usque tempora salutem consecuti: ac deinde exhortentur, ut fortes perfistant, pericula omnia & tormenta sperēt se per fidem superaturos: postremò nullo modo claudicent, seu abduci se a sana doctrina per hæreticos & falsos doctores patiantur. Quod si fiat, habebimus verum huius doctrinæ apostolicæ vsum nobis accommodatum ad illustrandam Christi gloriam, & nostram salutem accommodandam.
units.tr: Here mention could be made of those things which we ourselves saw in England, when Antonius Barus was burned, and Hieronymus a Stepne, and Master Gerardus, minister at Houilau, together with some others, and so on. Yet we too ought to receive these words spoken to the Hebrews, indeed this whole last hortatory part concerning constancy in the faith, as bearing very much upon ourselves. For in our own time exactly the same cause is being fought that was fought in the apostle's day. Everywhere there are many who, by propounding false doctrine and likewise by exercising tyranny, attempt to draw the godly away from the confession of evangelical truth and from the faith; the whole world is divided into two parts, just as in the time of Elijah Israel was divided, and the greater number wishes to serve Baal. Few are preserved who refuse to bend the knee to Baal; many limp, not knowing which way they ought to go. What remains, therefore, is that godly teachers and prophets set before them this doctrine of the apostle, and strongly inculcate that we are justified before God through faith, by which way all the saints from the beginning of the world until our own times have obtained salvation; and then that they exhort them to persevere bravely, hoping that through faith they will overcome all dangers and torments; and finally that they by no means limp, nor allow themselves to be drawn away from sound doctrine by heretics and false teachers. If this is done, we shall have the true use of this apostolic doctrine, fitted to us for illustrating the glory of Christ and for applying our own salvation.

units.la: Porrò nequaquam opus esse arbitramur, hic repetere dispositione totius huius partis, sicut in duabus antecedentibus partibus huius epistolæ egimus. Nam & hæc pars breuis fuit, suum habens tantùm exordium & conclusionem hortatoriam, & pauca loco confirmationis admixta didactica, quæ ipsa etiam ad exhortationem pertinent: neque quicquam præterea occurrit, quod magnam habeat difficultatem.
units.tr: Moreover, we judge that there is by no means need here to repeat the arrangement of this whole part, as we did in the two preceding parts of this epistle. For this part too was brief, having only an introduction and a hortatory conclusion, with a few didactic elements mixed in place of confirmation, and these too pertain to exhortation. Nor does anything else present itself which has great difficulty.

units.la: QVARTA PARS
units.tr: THE FOURTH PART

units.la: QVARTA PARS; SIVE QVARTVS LOCVS EPISTOLAE, in quo hortatur ad exercitium bonorum operum.
units.tr: FOURTH PART; OR THE FOURTH SECTION OF THE EPISTLE, in which he exhorts to the practice of good works.

units.la: Pacem sectemini cum omnibus, & sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum, curam agentes: ne quis sit, qui deficiat à gratia Dei, ne qua radix amarulentiae suppullulans obturbet, & per hanc inquinentur multi: ne quis scortator, aut profanus, velut Esau, qui vnico edulio permutauit ius primogeniti.
units.tr: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one shall see the Lord; take care that no one fall away from the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and through it many be defiled; lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. (Heb. 12.14–16)

units.la: HAEC est quarta pars huius epistolae, in qua post inculcatam doctrinam de iustificatione per fidem, exhortationesq; ad fidem constanter retinendam, subijcit exhortationes ad exercitia bonorum operum. Quae doctrina quàm sit necessaria iis, qui de fide semel recte sunt instituti: Item qua de causa, quoties de iustificatione per fidem agitur, subijci debeat potius, quàm prius, æquum est ostendamus: Primò igitur nouam hic potissimum accipiendam esse epistolae partem, liquet ex his rationibus. Prima ea omnia, quae proximè dicta sunt, apertissimè demonstrauimus superioribus, quae de constantia in fide sunt eleganter, nec minus grauiter exposita, indiuulsè adhærere, propterea[q;] diuelli inde hactenus nihil potuisse. Secunda, Quiuis perspicuè animaduertit hoc loco, & deinceps alijs de rebus, quàm de fide ac iustificatione per eam agi. Exhortatur namq; Apostolus ad pacem & sanctimoniam, atque alia eius generis praecepta breuibus quasi aphorismis exposita per ordinem sequuntur.
units.tr: THIS is the fourth part of this epistle, in which, after the doctrine of justification by faith has been pressed home, and exhortations to hold fast to faith have been given, he adds exhortations to the practice of good works. It is right that we show how necessary this teaching is for those who have once been rightly instructed in faith, and also why, whenever justification by faith is treated, it ought to be placed after it rather than before. First, then, that this part of the epistle should be taken as a new section is clear for the following reasons. First, everything said just before we have most plainly shown in the earlier chapters, which were set forth with elegance and no less weight on steadfastness in faith, and which hold together without break; for this reason nothing has so far been able to be torn from them. Second, anyone can see clearly that in this place, and in what follows, the subject is other than faith and justification through it. The Apostle exhorts to peace and holiness, and the other precepts of that kind follow in order, set out as brief maxims.

units.la: Tertia, cùm neq; prius, neque post vsquam commodius sectionem facere liceat, tum ut hic quidem fiat, etiam consentaneum est, & valde conuenies cum caeteris apostolicis, atque inprimis Pauli epistolis: in quibus semper videmus post expositam doctrinam de fide, etiam seorsim tradi, quae pertinent ad doctrinam operum. His igitur de causis nouam hoc loco epistolae huius partem instituì, æquum est.
units.tr: Third, since a division cannot be made more fitly either before or after, it is also fitting that it be made here, and it agrees very well with the other apostolic letters, and especially with the letters of Paul. In these we always see that, after the doctrine of faith has been set out, the matters that pertain to the doctrine of works are also treated separately. For these reasons it is right that we make a new section of this epistle at this point.

units.la: Iam quàm necessarium sit, post expositam doctrinam de iustificatione per fidem, addi etiam de exercitijs bonorum operum, paucis declarabimus.
units.tr: Now we shall explain briefly how necessary it is that, after the doctrine of justification by faith has been set out, a teaching about the practice of good works be added as well.

units.la: Primùm, hoc poscit natura verae fidei. Neque enim vera, consummata, & viua fides potest agnosci, quae bonis operibus sit destituta, non magis, quàm agnoscitur arbor bona, quae bonos fructus non profert. Sanè bona opera sunt fidei fructus, & necessariò fidè sequitur charitas, perinde atq; causam sequitur affectus. Quamobrem Apostolo placuit Galat.5. fidem appellare operantem per dilectionem. Coniungi namq; debent fides & bona opera, etiamsi diuersa sint vtriusque officia: ac fides quidem proprie sola iustificat: ex operibus autem, etiamsi omnia quàm exactissimè perficerentur, quę tota lege praecipiuntur, non iustificatur omnis caro. Rom.3. Secundò, operae precium est, eum, qui verè credit corde, etiam exterius suam fidem contestari & notam facere, iuxta illud Rom.10. Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Sed quia ore etiam saepè magna fraus committitur, necessum est, manifestas adiungere actiones, cordi, atq; oris confessioni respondentes: sicut ille ait, 1. Ioan.3. Non diligamus verbo, neq; lingua, sed opere & veritate. Sunt igitur & opera in credentibus necessaria: neq; id quidem propter personam tantùm ipsorum, ut videlicet ex operibus agnoscantur viua membra ecclesiae Dei: sed etiam propter alios, qui bono exemplo eorum debent instrui, excitari, confirmariq;.
units.tr: First, the nature of true faith requires it. For a true, perfect and living faith cannot be recognised if it is destitute of good works, just as a good tree is not recognised if it does not bear good fruit. Good works are indeed the fruit of faith, and love necessarily follows faith, just as affection follows its cause. For this reason the Apostle was pleased to call faith "working through love" (Gal. 5.6). Faith and good works ought indeed to be joined, even though the duties of each are different; and faith alone properly justifies, whereas by works, even if all the things the whole law commands were performed most exactly, no flesh is justified (Rom. 3.20). Second, it is worth while that the one who truly believes in his heart should also bear witness to his faith outwardly and make it known, according to that saying in Romans 10: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom. 10.10). But since great deceit is often practised by the mouth too, it is necessary to add clear actions that correspond to the heart and to the confession of the mouth, as John says: "Let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3.18). Good works are therefore necessary in believers, and not only for their own sake, namely so that living members of the Church of God may be recognised by their works, but also for the sake of others, who ought to be instructed, roused and strengthened by their good example.

units.la: Tertiò, poscit hoc omnium hominum fragilitas & innata segnities. Tametsi enim plerique, sint recte excellenterq; in iis, quae fidei sunt, instituti: praeterea satis sciant, & sentiant, decere, ut bonos fructus bonorum operum proferant: tamen, quae est diaboli, semper im pedimenta quaedam molientis, astutia & potentia, quaeq; est omnibus hominib. ingenita ad bonū tarditas atq; imbecillitas, vix vnquā, aut valde raro, ad bene agendum sese parant, & magna cum difficultate bene operari aggrediuntur. Hac ergo de causa interest piorum doctorum, adhortationes, obsecrationes, increpationes adhibere, quibus pigros animos ad exercitia bonorum operum extimulent. Quartò: Postulat interdum ipse ecclesiarum, ad quas epistolae mittuntur, status, ut post expositam doctrinae euangelicae summa, quae in causa fidei consistit, etiam quaedam de vita seu moribus praecepta inculcetur. Aliquando enim in ecclesijs, qualibet alioqui recte institutis, obrepunt etiā noua & publica offendicula: quidā relabuntur in pristina vitia (neq; enim potest in terris haberi illa ecclesia omnib. numeris absoluta, cuiq; prorsus nulla adlit ruga vel macula) Vbi ergo ista eueniunt, oportet proponendo doctrinam bonorum operum, ecclesiam rectiorem in viam revocare, & aberrantes oues in ouile reducere. Hiā
units.tr: Third, this is required by the frailty of all men and their innate sloth. For although most people have been rightly and excellently instructed in the things that belong to faith, and moreover know and feel well that it is fitting for them to bring forth the good fruit of good works, nevertheless the cunning and power of the devil, who is always contriving some obstacles, and the slowness and weakness towards good that is inborn in all men, scarcely ever, or very rarely, prepare themselves to act well, and they begin to do good works only with great difficulty. For this reason it is the concern of pious teachers to apply exhortations, entreaties and rebukes, by which they may spur sluggish minds to the practice of good works. Fourth, the very condition of the churches to which the letters are sent sometimes requires that, after the sum of the evangelical doctrine, which consists in the cause of faith, some precepts about life and conduct also be pressed upon them. For sometimes in churches otherwise rightly instituted, new and public stumbling-blocks creep in; some slip back into their former vices (for that church cannot be had on earth that is perfect in every respect and has no wrinkle or spot at all). Where these things happen, it is necessary, by setting forth the teaching of good works, to call the church back into the straighter way and to lead the straying sheep back into the fold. [...]

units.la: His igitur de caussis fit, quòd in singulis ferè epistolis videamus semper adijci partem aliquam de exercitijs bonorum operum, eádemq; exhortationibus, obsecrationibus, increpationibus, & eiusmodi, ad emendandos lapsos, salutaribus remedijs refertam.
units.tr: For these reasons it comes about that in almost every letter we always see some part added about the practice of good works, filled with exhortations, entreaties, rebukes and similar salutary remedies for correcting those who have fallen.

units.la: Et reuera opus est ei, qui cæteros cupit in viam reducere, non mediocri prudentia & consilio. In magna multitudine sunt varia ingenia, animi variè afficiuntur. Qui prædagogum agit in Scholis, debet discere, qui pueri duci debeant, & qui velint trahi, qui freno egeant, qui calcaribus. Ita doctor quoq; euangelicus debet omnium habere rationem, provectorum in fide & infirmorum, modestorum & malorum: debet cogitare, alios esse blandè inuitandos, alios duriter increpandos: sicut apostolus ea de re suum Timotheum prudenter admonuit, 2. Tim. 4. prædica Sermone, insta tepestiuè, intempestiuè argue, increpa, exhortare, cum omni lenitate & doctrina. Porrò hoc ipsum Apostolus in suis quoq; epistolis egregiè præstitit in ijs partibus, quas de bonis operibus solitus est adijcere. Quin etiá id quod dico de ecclesiarum diuerso statu, in causa est, cur in epistolarum posteriori parte conspiciatur adeò varia de operib. doctrina, nequaquá etiam eodé ordine in singulis epistolis expolita. Alia enim alium decent locum, & pro auditorum qualitate diuersa via est ingrediundum: sicut etiam pro locorum & ingeniorum diuersitate opus est in rebuspublicis diuersas proponi leges, ac ius municipale constitui.
units.tr: And indeed, the one who desires to lead others back into the way needs no small prudence and counsel. In a large crowd there are various dispositions, and minds are moved in various ways. He who acts as a tutor in schools must learn which boys ought to be led and which want to be dragged, which need the bridle and which the spur. So too the evangelical teacher ought to take account of everyone: of those advanced in faith and of the weak, of the modest and of the wicked. He ought to consider that some are to be invited gently, others to be rebuked sharply; as the Apostle wisely admonished his Timothy on this matter: "Preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching" (2 Tim. 4.2). Moreover, the Apostle himself has done this admirably in his letters too, in those parts which he was accustomed to add about good works. Indeed, what I say about the different condition of the churches is also the reason why in the latter part of the letters there is seen such varied teaching about works, and not always set out in the same order in each letter. For different things suit different places, and a different way must be taken according to the quality of the hearers, just as in commonwealths different laws must be proposed according to the diversity of places and dispositions, and local law established.

units.la: Ita tamen in diuersis epistolis sacris doctrina bonorum operum est tradita, ut si e singulis vniuersa excerpas, eaq; quodammodo in vnum corpus digeras, habiturus fis egregium quoddá opus, seu librum, & in quo, quicquid de pijs & sanctis actionibus præcipi posset, inuenias. Habebis Christianam Ethicen, habebis Christianam oeconomiam, pene dixeram & politiam (neque enim hanc formandá apostolus suscepit) habebis in summa, quic quid ad bene beateq; viuendum apud homines est necessarium. Si vocaret, possemus lo-ga oratione & luculenta id comprobare.
units.tr: Yet the teaching of good works has been handed down in the various sacred letters in such a way that if you were to excerpt from each the whole, and arrange it in a certain way into one body, you would have a remarkable work, or book, in which you would find whatever could be taught about pious and holy actions. You would have Christian ethics, you would have Christian economy, I might almost say politics too (for the Apostle did not undertake to shape this); in short, you would have whatever is necessary for living well and happily among men. If the occasion called for it, we could prove this with a long and lucid discourse.

units.la: In epistola ad Romanos cum de alijs officijs agat capite duodecimo copiosè, tum cap. 13. ualde clarè agit de magistratibus: quid videlicet his debeant subditi: atque è diuerso, quid illi subditis: capite decimo quarto tradit perspicuè, quomodo statuendum de adiaphoris siue medijs actionib. Nequaquam opus est, de singulis longiore oratione dicere.
units.tr: In the letter to the Romans, while he treats the other duties at length in chapter twelve, he also speaks very clearly of the magistrates in chapter thirteen: what subjects owe to them, and conversely what they owe to subjects. In chapter fourteen he clearly teaches how one should judge about adiaphora, or indifferent actions. There is no need to speak of each at greater length.

units.la: Epistola priore ad Corinthios discutiuntur difficiles & sublimes aliquot quæstiones, ecclesiæ eorum ad id tempus conuenientes, longè quidem excellentiori modo, quàm à Philosophis solet fieri in ijs libris, quos de moribus inscriptos edunt.
units.tr: In the first letter to the Corinthians several difficult and lofty questions are discussed, suited to their church at that time, and in a far more excellent manner than philosophers are accustomed to do in those books which they publish under the title of morals.

units.la: In epistola ad Ephesios & Colossenses de officijs mutuis cuiuscunque generis hominum inter se eleganter præcipitur: ut de officijs mariti erga uxorem, & rursus uxoris erga maritum, parentum erga filios, filiorum erga parentes: dominorum erga seruos: similiter seruorum erga dominos: adeoq; quæcunque ad Christianam oeconomiam pertinent, partim ibi, partim alibi, in posteriore parte epistolarum traduntur. Et hoc nomine excellentius commodiusque, quàm in libris philosophorum, quòd non tantum virtutum descriptio species, describitur modus: sed insuper rationes suasoriæ adduntur, quibus ad virtutem exciteris: & præterea quomodo, seu vnde parari possit vera virtus, ostenditur, veluti cum ex fide proficisci bona opera, à spiritu sancto donari, ut verè bona opera exerceas, clarè docetur. Longum foret, per singulas epistolas eundo in certa capita redigere, quæ de bonis operibus sunt in illis expositæ.
units.tr: In the letter to the Ephesians and the Colossians, the mutual duties of every kind of person towards one another are set out elegantly: the duties of husband towards wife and, again, of wife towards husband; of parents towards children, and of children towards parents; of masters towards servants, and likewise of servants towards masters. In short, whatever pertains to Christian household management is handed down, partly there and partly elsewhere, in the latter part of the letters. In this respect it is more excellent and more useful than in the books of the philosophers, because it does not merely describe the outward form of the virtues but also sets out the manner of them. Moreover, reasons of persuasion are added by which you are stirred up to virtue; and besides, it is shown how true virtue may be obtained, or whence it comes. Thus it is plainly taught that good works proceed from faith and are given by the Holy Spirit, so that you may truly perform good works. It would be tedious to go through each letter and reduce to certain heads what is set out in them concerning good works.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur in cæteris epistolis omnibus, ita in hac quoq; ad Hebræos, post expolitam doctrinam fidei, non pauca de doctrina operum subijciuntur: idq; tum, quia natura fidei ita postulat, tum quia opus est, credentes, fidem suam etiam operibus testatá faciant: præterea, quia sic decet excitari tardos & segnes animos: deniq;, quia status ecclesiæ Hebræorum poscebat, eos de quibusdam bonis operibus admoneri.
units.tr: Therefore, just as in all the other letters, so also in this one to the Hebrews, after the doctrine of faith has been laid out, not a few points of the doctrine of works are added. This is done both because the nature of faith requires it, and because it is needful that believers should show their faith by their works as well; further, because it befits the sluggish and slow minds to be roused; and finally, because the condition of the Hebrew church called for them to be admonished about certain good works.

units.la: Et quod videmus hunc in modum distributam esse istam epistolá, ut videlicet post doctrinam fidei tradatur etiam doctrina operum, facit profectò istud, ut tanto lubentius eam pro Paulina agnoscamus. Licet enim hic plane Pauli in docendo morem cernere, quem neque in Iacobi, neque in Petri, neque in Ioannis epistolis inuenies.
units.tr: And the fact that we see this letter arranged in this way, namely that after the doctrine of faith the doctrine of works is also delivered, certainly makes us acknowledge it all the more gladly as Pauline. For here you can plainly discern Paul's manner of teaching, which you will not find in the letters of James, Peter or John.

units.la: Sed quæ est causa, inquis, cur doctrina operum traditur post expositam doctrinâ fidei? Cur non potius crasiori modo præit doctrina operum & postea exponitur, quæ subli-mior est, doctrina fidei?
units.tr: But what is the reason, you will ask, why the doctrine of works is delivered after the doctrine of faith has been set out? Why does the doctrine of works not rather come first in a cruder manner, and afterwards the doctrine of faith, which is the more sublime, be expounded?

units.la: Respondetur: Primò, natura operum id postulat. Quod enim ad opera ipsa attinet, vere bona dici non poterunt, nisi ex fonte fidei emanent. Fides se habet instar fundamenti: bona opera, ut reliquum ædificium. Quemadmodum ergo opus est, prius substerni fundamentum, quàm aliqua superstruas: ita necessario fides præire debet.
units.tr: I answer: first, the nature of works demands it. For as far as the works themselves are concerned, they cannot truly be called good unless they flow from the fountain of faith. Faith stands in the place of a foundation; good works are like the rest of the building. Just as the foundation must be laid before you build anything upon it, so faith must necessarily come first.

units.la: Secundò, necessum est ita fieri ratione personarum bene agentium. Neque enim quis profert verè bona opera iustitiæ titulo honestanda, quæque non tantùm coram mundo, sed etiā coram Deo pro bonis & Christianis operibus æstimetur, nisi qui iam per fidem iustificatus fuerit. Opera, quæ fiūt ante fidem, & citra fidem, quamlibet speciosa, magnifica, rara, difficilia, tamen sunt tantum philosophica & ethnica, non Christiana, imò abeunt etiam interdum in peccata: quando, quicquid non fit ex fide peccatum est, testante Apostolo.
units.tr: Second, it must be so because of the persons who do good. For no one produces truly good works, which deserve to be honoured with the title of righteousness, and which are esteemed as good and Christian works not only before the world but also before God, unless he has already been justified through faith. Works that are done before faith, and apart from faith, however showy, magnificent, rare or difficult they may be, are nonetheless merely philosophical and ethnic, not Christian; indeed they sometimes even turn into sins, since, as the Apostle testifies, whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.

units.la: Tertiò, fidem necessariò sequuntur bona opera, & propterea etiam prius de fide agi conuenit, vt inde ad bona opera veniatur. His igitur de causis optima methodo Apostolus progreditur, qui postquam exposuit doctrinam fidei, de doctrina operum aliam partem subijcit.
units.tr: Third, good works necessarily follow faith, and therefore it is fitting that faith be treated first, so that we may come from it to good works. For these reasons the Apostle proceeds by the best method: after he has set out the doctrine of faith, he adds another part on the doctrine of works.

units.la: Vt vero propius accedamus ad institutum, operæ precium est videamus, de quibus & qualibus potissimum operibus Apostolus in hac postrema præsentis epistolæ parte concionetur, vt inde quoq; discamus, qualia expetēda, & qualia fugienda, quantaq; vti litas sit nobis ex his expectanda.
units.tr: But in order to come closer to our purpose, it is worth our while to see of what kinds and especially which works the Apostle preaches in this last part of the present letter, so that we may also learn which are to be sought after and which are to be avoided, and how great a usefulness we may expect from them.

units.la: Primus locus est de ampletēda pace, & vera sanctimonia, contra dissidia, amarulentiam, & contra immunditiam moresq; Epicureorum.
units.tr: The first topic concerns cultivating peace and true holiness, against dissensions, bitterness, and against the uncleanness and morals of the Epicureans.

units.la: Secundus locus cap. 13. est de charitate, inprimis verò hospitalitate, & misericordia erga vinctos propter confessionem euangelij.
units.tr: The second topic, in chapter 13, concerns charity, above all hospitality, and mercy towards those in chains for the confession of the gospel.

units.la: Tertius est de coniugio sancte colendo, vitandisq; stupris atq; adulterijs.
units.tr: The third concerns holding marriage in holy honour, and avoiding fornication and adulteries.

units.la: Quartus contra auaritiam concionatur.
units.tr: The fourth preaches against avarice.

units.la: Quintus commendat ministros verbi doctores euangelicos, eosq; vult in honore haberi, atq; in exemplum proponi: simulq; docet, pseudoapostolos, & varias peregrinasq; doctrinas eorundem omni studio vitandas.
units.tr: The fifth commends the ministers of the Word, the evangelical teachers, and wishes them to be held in honour and set forth as an example; at the same time it teaches that false apostles and their various strange doctrines are to be avoided with every effort.

units.la: Sextus generaliter ad beneficentiam erga pauperes excitat.
units.tr: The sixth generally stirs up beneficence towards the poor.

units.la: Septimus præcipit, vt superioribus, hoc est, doctoribus seu pastoribus animarum lubenter pareant, & nequaquam sint molesti.
units.tr: The seventh enjoins, as above, that superiors, that is teachers or pastors of souls, be obeyed willingly and not be troubled in any way.

units.la: Octauo loco pro se orari petit, & se commendat. Atque his locis ista pars vltima absoluitur. Nam postea breuem tantum comprecationem, pro generali conclusione totius epistolæ subiectam videmus.
units.tr: In the eighth place he asks to be prayed for, and commends himself. With these topics this last part is finished. For afterwards we see only a brief prayer, appended as the general conclusion of the whole letter.

units.la: Sunt autē per hos locos sparsæ exhortationes, obsecrationes, obiurgationes, deniq; omnia illa, quæ doctorem euangelicum pro qualitate rerum, quibus de agitur, & personarum, ad quas sermo habetur, adhiberi conuenit.
units.tr: Through these topics exhortations, entreaties, rebukes, and finally all those things which an evangelical teacher ought to employ according to the nature of the matters under discussion and the persons to whom he speaks, are scattered.

units.la: Et hoc obseruatu multò est dignissimū, quòd, vbi hic agit cum Hebræis, mirabili prudentia addit rationes suasorias, plerasq; fere ex lege petitas: aut certè ijs aptas, qui antea in lege sunt versati. Quod profectò alia ratione fit, quàm in cæteris epistolis, quæ ad Gentiles sunt perscriptæ. Sed, si bene aduertimus, singulari prudentia id factum est.
units.tr: And this is very much worth observing: where he deals with the Hebrews, with wonderful prudence he adds reasons of persuasion, mostly drawn from the law, or at least suited to those who were previously versed in the law. This is certainly done otherwise than in the other letters, which were written to the Gentiles. But if we pay close attention, it was done with singular prudence.

units.la: Cæterum ex his licet videre, quantam etiam vtilitatem ad nos deriuandam sperare debeamus. Sunt enim omnes fere loci hic expensi nostris aptissimi temporibus, & de quibus nunc doceri admoneriq; ecclesias, valdè est necessarium. Quàm enim rara nunc est beneficetia erga peregrinos, erga eos, qui persecutione & vincula patiūtur propter iustitiam? Coiugium alibi dehonestatur stupris & adulterijs, alibi etiam iniuriā patitur ab immodica prædicatione impuri cœlibatus. Ministris verò vix vsquā suus defertur hominos. Perpauci etiam eorum ita viuunt, vt in exemplum proponi fratribus posint.
units.tr: Moreover, from these things one may see how great a usefulness we ought to hope to derive for ourselves as well. For nearly all the topics treated here are most apt for our own times, and it is very necessary that the churches now be taught and admonished about them. How rare now is beneficence towards strangers, towards those who suffer persecution and chains for righteousness' sake? Marriage is dishonoured in one place by fornication and adultery, and in another it also suffers injury from the immoderate preaching of impure celibacy. Scarcely anywhere is due honour paid to ministers. Very few of them, too, live in such a way that they can be set forth to the brothers as an example.

units.la: Auaritia omnium animos occupauit, & paucos inuenire est, qui non ad quæstum tutpem animum adijciant. De doctrinis varijs & peregrinis heu nimium multa forent nobis hoc tempore dicenda, si vellemus errores, falsa dogmata, traditiones impias omnes perstringere. Proinde admonitos omnes volo, vt hanc partem, in qua tot & tam vtiles loci pertractantur, diligenter legant atq; expedant, non ea quæ vsui fore intelligunt, sic sibi accommodent, vt cum fructu & proposito vitæ in melius corrigendæ ista legisse ab omnibus queant iudicari. Nos bona fide explicare singulos locos aggrediemur.
units.tr: Avarice has taken hold of all minds, and it is hard to find few who do not apply their mind to base gain. Alas, we would have far too many things to say at this time about the various and strange doctrines, if we wished to touch upon all the errors, false dogmas and impious traditions. Therefore I want all of you, having been admonished, to read and study diligently this part, in which so many and such useful topics are handled, and not to accommodate to yourselves for use those things which you understand to be of use in such a way that you may be judged by all to have read them with fruit and with the purpose of correcting your life for the better. We shall undertake to explain the individual topics in good faith.

units.la: PRIMVS LOCVS DE PACE ET vera sanctimonia.
units.tr: THE FIRST PASSAGE, CONCERNING PEACE AND TRUE HOLINESS

units.la: Pacem sectemini cum omnibus, & sanctimoniam.
units.tr: Follow peace with all men, and holiness (Heb. 12:14).

units.la: PRimus locus, in quo hortatur omnes ad colendam pacem, & veram minimeq; simulatam sanctimoniā. Ac de his statim & ante alia agi valde erat necessarium. De pace quidē, primò, quòd ingenia Hebræorū ad rixas & dissidia erant admodum proclivia, sicut nunc quoq; videmus animis esse valde irritabilibus. Tunc verò maximè concitantur animi ad odia, lites, dissidia, vbi iniustè ab aduersarijs lacefsiuntur, aut quovis modo iniurijs afficiuntur. Sic autem cùm lacesserentur pij Hebrei, meritòad pacem colendam primo loco excitabantur.
units.tr: This is the first passage, in which he exhorts everyone to cultivate peace and true holiness, not feigned holiness. It was very necessary to deal with these matters at once and before others. First, on peace: the minds of the Hebrews were very prone to quarrels and dissensions, just as we now see that people's tempers are very easily roused. Minds are most stirred to hatred, strife and dissension when they are unjustly provoked by adversaries or wronged in some way. Since the godly Hebrews were being provoked in this way, they were rightly urged first of all to cultivate peace.

units.la: Secundò, multi erat inter pios Hebræos falsi fratres, subornati haud dubiè à cæteris Iudæis, vel sua sponte huc intenti, vt dissidia inter fratres sererent. Ne quid ergo hinc periculi in ecclesia nasceretur, voluit Apostolus statim de pace studiosè sectanda agere.
units.tr: Second, among the pious Hebrews there were many false brothers, no doubt put up by the other Jews, or intent on this of their own accord, so as to sow dissensions among the brothers. So that no danger might arise from this in the Church, the Apostle wished at once to speak of pursuing peace with diligence.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd pax sit præcipuum stabilimentum ecclesiæ: sicut è contrario discordia est ruina ecclesiæ: Imò non tantùm ecclesiæ, verùm etiam cuiuscunq; reipublicæ.
units.tr: Third, peace is the chief support of the Church, just as on the contrary discord is the ruin of the Church. Indeed it is the ruin not only of the Church but of any commonwealth whatever.

units.la: Et propterea præceptum huiusmodi de colenda pace, est generale quoddam præceptum ad omnes omnium temporum ecclesias ex æquo pertinens.
units.tr: For this reason, this precept about cultivating peace is a general precept that applies equally to the churches of every age.

units.la: Sed & ideo est necessarium, in ecclesia quacunque pacem studiosè coli, quòd ex dissidijs grauissima oriantur offendicula: & aduersarij nulla re magis gaudent, nihilque molestius obijciunt, quàm quòd, qui se pios, & euangelij sectatores profitentur, tamen odijs & dissensionibus perpetuis inter se conflictantur: quemadmodum id hodiè, proh dolor, licet videre. Et fine dubio aduersarij Hebræis valde moleste insultassent, & exprobrassent dissidia.
units.tr: It is also necessary, in any church whatever, that peace be cultivated with diligence, because the most serious stumbling blocks arise from dissensions. Adversaries rejoice in nothing more, and object nothing more troublesome, than that those who profess themselves godly and followers of the gospel nevertheless wrestle with one another in perpetual hatreds and quarrels, as, alas, can be seen today. Without doubt the adversaries would have insulted the Hebrews very bitterly and reproached them for their dissensions.

units.la: De sanctimonia verò opus fuit statim proponere aliqua: Primò, quòd Hebræi omnes valde propensi ad hypocrisin & omnem simulationem fuerint, simulata & ficta sanctimoniæ specie gaudentes: de interna autem & vera sanctimonia patrum foliciti.
units.tr: As for holiness, it was necessary to set out some points at once. First, the Hebrews were all very inclined to hypocrisy and every pretence, delighting in a feigned and fictitious appearance of holiness, while being careless of inward and true holiness.

units.la: Secundò, erat hoc quasi per se notum, quòd crassis illis vitijs, impuritatem redolentibus, vt scortationi, gulæ, non debebat more gentilium inuolui, apud quos ista vix pro peccatis censebantur.
units.tr: Second, it was taken as self-evident that they should not be caught up in those gross vices that smell of impurity, such as fornication and gluttony, in the manner of the Gentiles, among whom such things were scarcely counted as sins.

units.la: Propterea voluit Apostolus statim contra ista agere, & de vera sanctimonia ampleSten differere.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle wished to act at once against these things, and to speak at greater length of true holiness.

units.la: Proinde huius primi loci de colenda pace & vera sanctimonia, hæc est hortatoria propositio, Pacem sectemini cum omnibus, & sanctimoniam.
units.tr: Accordingly, the exhortation of this first passage, about cultivating peace and true holiness, is this: Follow peace with all men, and holiness.

units.la: De pace illa eum agere potissimum, quam homines inter homines seruare debent, notum est ex sequentibus. Appositè verò ait, Sectemini, διώκητε: quasi diceret: magno studio expetite, & vel fugientem conemini apprehendere. Etiam cùm occasiones pacis videntur præcludi vel impediri, tamen omnia sunt nobis tentanda, & potius iniuriam aliquam debemus ferre, quàm vt per nos pax rumpatur. In eundem sensum & in Psalmo dicitur, Inquire pacem & persequere eam.
units.tr: That he is mainly speaking of the peace that men must keep among men is clear from what follows. He says aptly, Follow (διώκετε), as if to say: seek with great eagerness, and try to seize what flees from you. Even when opportunities for peace seem to be shut off or hindered, we must still try everything, and rather bear some wrong than let peace be broken through us. In the same sense it is said in a Psalm: Seek peace and pursue it (Ps. 34:14).

units.la: Cum omnibus) Et hoc ἐμφατικῶς dicitur: Non solùm cum Hebræis & domesticis, sed etiam cum gentilibus & peregrinis: non tàtum cum coniunctis religione, vel erga nos beneficijs, sed etiam cum extraneis atque aduersarijs. Sic & Romanorum capite 12. explicatur huius loci sententia, vbi dicitur:
units.tr: With all men: this is said emphatically. Not only with Hebrews and members of one's household, but also with Gentiles and strangers; not only with those joined to us in religion or bound to us by benefits, but also with outsiders and adversaries. So also the sense of this passage is explained in Romans 12, where it says:

units.la: Proinde parantes honestam in conspectu omnium hominum, si fieri posit, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuentes, non vosmetipsos vlciscentes dilecti, quin potius datæ locum iræ. Et maximè opus est eos hoc pacto pacem colere, qui omnibus sunt inuisi, & ad quos lædendum omnes putant dentes & manus suas impunè acui. Neque aduersarij vllare citius aut vehementius mouentur, quàm si videant eum, quæ ipsi quoq; acrius insectantur, aut alias afficiunt iniuria, placidù tamen adhuc & pacis studiosum. Huc pertinet columbina illa simplicitas, discipulis tantopere commendata.
units.tr: Therefore, providing honest things in the sight of all men, if it be possible, as much as lies in you, live peaceably with all men; dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath (Rom. 12:17-19). And it is especially necessary that those who are hated by all should cultivate peace in this way, those whom everyone thinks they may wound with impunity, sharpening their teeth and hands against them. Nor are adversaries ever moved to rage more quickly or more violently than when they see a man whom they attack more fiercely, or wrong in other ways, still calm and eager for peace. To this belongs that dovelike simplicity so strongly commended to the disciples.

units.la: Et sanctimoniam) Bimembris est propositio: Agit enim non tantùm de pace, sed etiam de sanctimonia. Est autem vox sanctimoniæ latè patens & generalis: & non vno aliquo modo sanctimonia paratur: sed hic vsurato quodam Scripturæ Schemate restringitur vocabulum istud ad significandum puritatem & mundiciem in carne, siue continentiam & sobrietatem in moribus, qualis illos potissimum decet, qui sacra sunt tractaturi.
units.tr: And holiness: the proposition has two members, for he speaks not only of peace but also of holiness. The word holiness is broad and general, and holiness is not attained in only one way. Here, however, by a certain customary figure of Scripture, the word is restricted to signify purity and chastity in the flesh, or continence and sobriety in conduct, such as especially befits those who are to handle holy things.

units.la: Opponitur hæc præcipuè Scortationi, & illis id genus actionibus, ob quas homines censentur profani, & à sacris arcendi. Id quod liquet ex ijs, quæ mox subijciuntur, illis verbis: Ne quis scortator aut profanus, sicut Esau: Apparet Apostolum Hebræorum more respexisse ad veterem ritum sacrificandi, quo videlicet ipsi sese dicebantur sanctificare dum videlicet ieiunando, orando, abstinendo à mulieribus ad res sacras tractandas se præparabant. In quam sententiam Exodi capite 19. Dominus præcepit, vt populus, an tequam legem acciperet, per triduum sanctificaretur. Et apud prophetas crebrò externa istiusmodi sanctificatio requiritur, quæ internæ & spiritualis sanctimoniæ indicium sit & quasi signum.
units.tr: This is opposed chiefly to fornication and to those kinds of actions on account of which men are judged profane and kept away from holy things. This is clear from what follows immediately, in the words: lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau (Heb. 12:16). It appears that the Apostle, after the manner of the Hebrews, had regard to the old rite of sacrifice, by which they were said to sanctify themselves, that is, to prepare themselves for handling sacred things by fasting, praying and abstaining from women. To this effect, in Exodus 19 the Lord commanded that the people be sanctified for three days before they received the law. And among the prophets such outward sanctification is often required, which is a sign and, as it were, a token of inward and spiritual holiness.

units.la: Sine qua nemo videbit Dominum) Potest hæc particula tàm ad pacem, quàm ad sanctisanctimoniam referri. Neque enim Deum videbunt, qui vel pace neglecta dissidiorum sunt autores & amatores: vel sanctimonia neglecta impure agunt, & rerum diuina rum sunt contemptores.
units.tr: Without which no one shall see the Lord: this phrase can be referred both to peace and to holiness. For those will not see God who, neglecting peace, are the authors and lovers of dissensions, or who, neglecting holiness, live impurely and despise divine things.

units.la: Si tamen magis placet referre ad solam sanctimoniam, cui proximè adiungitur, benè erit. Ac potest tùm dupliciter exponi: vno modo, vt addita intelligatur, ad ostendedum discrimen quoddam eius sanctimoniæ, quæ talis agnoscitur coram Deo, ab ea, quæ apparet tantum apud homines. Eritque sententia: Eam sanctimoniam omni studio consectandam, qua peruenitur ad Deum, quæque apud Deum pro vera sanctimonia reputatur. Quam sanctimoniam valde necessarium erat vrgere, præsertim apud Iudæos hypocriticæ tantum & externæ sanctimoniæ deditos. Alio modo, vt sit obiter apposita ratio seaforia à necessario, quasi dicat: colite sanctimoniam, quam quidem necessarium est habere eos, qui Deum videre cupiunt. Certè ipse Christus de huiusmodi sanctimonia Matthæi capite quinto ait, Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt: vbi & de pace, Beati pacifici, quoniam filij Dei vocabūtur. Quamobrem particula hæc magnum pōdus apud omnes habere debet, nec sine graui caussa addita censebitur, quocunq; tandem modo accipiatur.
units.tr: If, however, it is preferred to refer it only to holiness, to which it is immediately joined, that will be good. This may be explained in two ways. In one way, the phrase is understood as added to show a certain difference between that holiness which is recognised as such before God and that which appears only before men. The sense will be: pursue with all zeal that holiness by which one comes to God and which is reckoned before God as true holiness. It was very necessary to press this holiness, especially among the Jews, who were devoted only to hypocritical and external holiness. In the other way, the reason is incidentally added from what is necessary, as if he said: cultivate that holiness which those who desire to see God must indeed have. Certainly Christ himself, in Matthew 5, speaks of this kind of holiness: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God; and, of peace: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God (Matt. 5:8-9). Therefore this particle ought to carry great weight with everyone, and it will not be thought to have been added without serious cause, however it is taken.

units.la: Curam agentes, ne quis sit, qui deficiat à gratia Dei, ne qua radix amarulētiæ supp pullulans obturbet, & per hanc inquinentur multi.
units.tr: Taking care that no one fall short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and through it many be defiled.

units.la: Expositio propositionis, ac primùm eius membri, quod est de pace. Officia enim pacis, & quædam ex contrario euenientia incommoda describit, è quibus clarius, quomodo pax coli debeat, & de quali pace sermonem faciat, intelligi poterit.
units.tr: An explanation of the proposition, and first of that part of it which concerns peace. For he describes the duties of peace and certain inconveniences that arise from the opposite, and from these it will be understood more clearly how peace ought to be cultivated and what kind of peace he is speaking of.

units.la: Eleganter autem ait ἐπισπουδάζοντες, hoc est, accuratè intendentes. Valde prodest in exhortationibus verba adhiberi, quæ ad diligentiam acuunt atque impellunt. Et videtur hæc vox omnes cōpellare, obstringere q;, vt nō solùm ipsi laboret pacem tueri, verum etiam aduigilent, ne per alios quippiam contra pacis dignitatē committatur. Ita namq; ἐπισπουδάζοντες proprie dicuntur, quibus etiam aliorum cura est concredita.
units.tr: He elegantly says ἐπισπουδάζοντες [epispoudazontes], that is, attentively taking care. It is very useful in exhortations to use words that sharpen and urge on diligence. This word seems to address and bind all, so that not only do they themselves labour to keep the peace, but they also keep watch that nothing be committed against the dignity of peace through others. For those are properly called epispoudazontes to whom the care of others has also been entrusted.

units.la: Ne quis sit, qui deficiat à gratia) μὴ τις ὑστέρων: quasi dicat: Ne quis non sit potens assequi gratiam Dei. Suprà initio capitis quarti, μὴ ἀρα τις ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑστερηκέναι. Metaphora est, seu allusio potius ad eos, qui per infirmitatem, vel segnitiem non possunt in via eos assequi, qui præcedunt, & semper posteriores ingrediuntur. Sententia igitur præsentis loci est, eos, qui pacem non coluerint, non posse in gratia Dei proficere, nec posse assequi eos, qui in gratiæ Dei cognitione præeunt, & præ cæteris proficiunt.
units.tr: "Lest anyone fall short of the grace of God": μή τις ὑστέρων [me tis hysteron], as if he said: lest anyone be unable to attain the grace of God. Above, at the beginning of chapter four, μή ἄρα τις ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑστερηκέναι [me ara tis ex hymon hysterekenai]. It is a metaphor, or rather an allusion, to those who through weakness or sloth cannot keep up on the way with those who go before, and always come up behind. The sense of the present passage, therefore, is that those who have not cultivated peace cannot make progress in the grace of God, nor can they attain to those who go before in the knowledge of God's grace and advance beyond the rest.

units.la: Et gratiam Dei rectè intelligemus hic cognitionem misericordiæ Dei in euangelio oblatam. Plurimum autem à profectu in cognitione gratiæ Dei impediuntur animi, vbi dissidijs vel publicis, vel priuatis molestantur & cruciantur. Hoc verò cùm sit malum longè maximum, est profectò quod à dissidijs vehementer abhorreamus. Atque ita per contrarium, quod nam sit officium pacis, seu quomodo feruetur pax, ostendit.
units.tr: And we shall rightly understand by the grace of God here the knowledge of the mercy of God offered in the gospel. Minds are most hindered from advancing in the knowledge of God's grace when they are troubled and tormented by dissensions, whether public or private. Since this is by far the greatest evil, we ought surely to shun dissensions vehemently. And so, by the contrary, he shows what the duty of peace is, or how peace is kept.

units.la: Ne qua radix amarulentiæ suppullulans obturbet) Amarulentia dissidiorum, vt in apertum erumpant, caussa est. In animo hæret & fouetur: vnde omnes oriuntur ecclesiarum perturbationes: atque id vocat amaruleuiam: quæ vox etiam habetur Ephesiorum capite quarto, vbi dicitur, Omnis amarulentia & tumor, & ira, & vociferatio, & maledicentia tollatur à vobis. Et Iacobus capite tertio πικρὸν ζηλον ponit. Sed sunt elegantes metaphoræ in voce πίκρα & φθόνος, quibus notatur, odium seu amarulentiam primùm reconditam latere in corde, non aliter quàm radix latet in terra. Quomodo Christus quoque dixit, peccata omnia ex corde oriri. Et notatur hac metaphora, quodammodo ingenitam esse propensionem ad odia & dissidia, nec facilè reuelli in totum posse: sicut difficile est, malarum herbarum radices penitus eruere.
units.tr: "Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you": the bitterness of dissensions is the cause of their breaking out into the open. It lodges in the mind and is nourished there, and from it all the disturbances of the churches arise; and this he calls amarulentia (bitterness). The word is also found in Ephesians chapter four, where it is said: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking be put away from you." And James in chapter three puts πικρὸν ζῆλον [pikron zelon], bitter envy. But there are elegant metaphors in the words πικρία [pikria] and φθόνος [phthonos], by which it is noted that hatred or bitterness, at first hidden, lies concealed in the heart, just as a root lies hidden in the earth. Christ too said that all sins arise from the heart. And this metaphor indicates that there is, in some measure, an innate propensity to hatreds and dissensions, and that it cannot easily be wholly plucked out, just as it is difficult to dig up the roots of bad herbs entirely.

units.la: Tunc verò radix amarulentiæ suppullulat & enascitur, cùm à peruersis cordis cogitationibus progressus fit ad verba & ad actiones. Ista enim se habent instar caudicis siue trunci, & ramorū atq; fructuū. Vbi ergo radix amarulentię suppullulat, id est, erumpit in apertum, fieri non potest, quin multi obturbentur, imò & inquinentur multi. Vitia ista transeūt ad animam, eaq; nō leuiter inficitur. Et fieri non potest, vbi pax violatur, statim plures sese interponunt: atque hi quidem adiungunt se vni parti, alij adiungunt se alteri.
units.tr: The root of bitterness then springs up and sprouts forth when, from perverse thoughts of the heart, it proceeds to words and deeds. For these stand like the stem or trunk, with the branches and fruits. Where, then, the root of bitterness springs up, that is, breaks out into the open, it cannot be that many are not troubled, indeed that many are not defiled. These vices pass over to the soul, and the soul is not lightly infected. And when peace is violated, it cannot but be that several people straightway interpose themselves: and some indeed join themselves to one side, others to the other.

units.la: Cuius rei consideratio debet omnes valde deterrere à mouendis dissidijs. Neq; enim ipsi rei sunt propter suam tantùm personam, verùm etiam propter omnes illos, quos ipsi labi faciunt: imò ratione redden̄, & peccata illorū suis humeris accumulāt, qui difsi dij excitatis offendūtur. Dominus omniū istorū animas reposcet ab illis, qui dissidio- rum autores extiterint.
units.tr: Consideration of this matter ought greatly to deter everyone from stirring up dissensions. For they are guilty not only on account of their own person, but also on account of all those whom they cause to fall; indeed they render an account and heap the sins of those upon their own shoulders who are offended by the dissensions that have been stirred up. The Lord will require the souls of all these from those who have been the authors of the dissensions.

units.la: Ne quis scortator, aut profanus, velut Esau, qui vnico edulio permutauit ius primogeniti.
units.tr: Lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single morsel of food.

units.la: Expositio alterius membri de sanctimonia. Per contrarium enim declarat, quibus in rebus sanctimonia, de qua ipse loquitur, sita sit, nempe in vitatione scortationis, & omnium adeò eiuscemodi actionum, ob quas quis profanus & à sanctimonia alienissimus, adeoque à sacris arcendus iudicatur. Sicut autem supra diximus, sanctimoniæ vocabulum latè patere: ita intelligi conuenit, multa vitia ei esse opposita: quæ omnia so- rent explicanda ei, qui sanctimoniæ vim vellet exactè reponere.
units.tr: An explanation of the other part, concerning holiness. For by the contrary he declares in what things that holiness of which he speaks consists: namely, in avoiding fornication, and indeed all such actions on account of which someone is judged profane and utterly alien from holiness, and therefore to be kept away from sacred things. But, as we said above, the word holiness extends widely, so it is fitting to understand that many vices are opposed to it, all of which would have to be explained by anyone who wished to set out exactly the force of holiness.

units.la: Verum Apostolo satis est, vno aut altero verbo indicare, vt ex ijs cætera quoq; depre hendantur. Sanctimoniæ igitur opponit primò fornicationem, vt, quemadmodum sanctimonia more legali potissimum constituitur in carnis munditie, vti supra ostendi- mus: ita contrarium situm est in carnis immundicie.
units.tr: But it is enough for the Apostle to indicate them with one or another word, so that the rest may be gathered from these. Therefore he first sets fornication against holiness, so that, just as holiness is established, in the manner of the law, chiefly in purity of the flesh, as we showed above, so the contrary is placed in impurity of the flesh.

units.la: Scortator autem non est is, qui per infirmitatem semel fortassis lapsus est, sed qui iam sæpius recidiuat: & ad scortationis nomen referre decet. quibuscunque vitijs, quæ affinia sunt, deditos, velut adulteros, &c. Ephesiorum capite quinto, & sanctimoniæ, & vitiorum contrariorum ratio aliquo modo ostenditur hisce verbis:
units.tr: A fornicator, however, is not one who has perhaps fallen once through weakness, but one who relapses again and again; and it is fitting to refer to the name of fornication those who are given over to any vices that are akin to it, such as adulterers, and so on. In Ephesians chapter five the reason for holiness and its contrary vices is shown in some way in these words:

units.la: Cæterum scortatio & omnis immundicia aut auaritia ne nominetur quidem inter vos, sicut decet sanctos. Hic generaliter scortationem & omnem immunditiam op- ponit sanctimoniæ. Sed in præsenti epistola Apostolus addit aliud vocabulum, βέβηλος. Generale est vocabulum significans impurum & profanum, inquinatum, atque ijs obnoxium vitijs, ob quæ alienus à sanctimonia iudicari queat. Quapropter hoc loco Chrysostomus interpretatus est γαστρίμαργον, intemperantem, rebus profanis deditū, spi- ritualia negligētem, vel etiam contemnentem. Qui nullo pacto curat vel laborat, vtinter sanctos habeatur, vt ne ea præstet, quæ ad sanctimoniam pertinent, talis inter profanos censendus venit.
units.tr: "But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as becometh saints." Here he generally sets fornication and all impurity against holiness. But in the present epistle the Apostle adds another word, βέβηλος [bebelos]. It is a general word signifying impure and profane, defiled, and liable to those vices on account of which a person can be judged alien from holiness. Hence here Chrysostom interpreted it as γαστρίμαργον [gastrimargon], an intemperate person, given over to profane things and neglecting or even despising spiritual things. Someone who in no way cares or labours to be counted among the holy, so that he does not perform the things that pertain to holiness, is reckoned among the profane.

units.la: Aperte vero Apostolus scortatione sola expressa, adiecit protinus generale nomen profani: quia valde agnata sunt, & vel ex sola scortatione sic inquinatur, & excæcatur homo, vt inde in omnia prolabatur flagitia, ob quæ profanus sit & habeatur. Exemplū habemus Romanorum cap. 1. illos Deus per cupiditatem cordium suorum in immunditiam, vt ignominia afficerent corpora sua. Sed Apostolus ipse sui agit interpretem, quando addit:
units.tr: Clearly, after the Apostle had expressed fornication alone, he at once added the general name of profane, because these vices are very closely related: a man is so defiled and blinded by fornication alone that from it he slides into every kind of shameful deed, on account of which he is profane and is held to be so. We have an example in Romans chapter 1, where God gave those people over, through the lusts of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that they dishonoured their own bodies. But the Apostle himself acts as his own interpreter when he adds:

units.la: Velut Esau, qui vnico edulio permutauit ius primogeniti.
units.tr: Like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.

units.la: En ne quis dubitaret, quales profanos velit intelligi, illustrat sententia, adhibito exemplo satis noto, quo ostedit eos omnes esse profanos, qui vitijs quibuscunque deditispiritualia bona omnia, & quæ ad salutem faciunt, paruipendunt, & carnalia præferunt spiritualibus.
units.tr: Lest anyone doubt what kind of profane people he means, the sentence illustrates it with a well-known example. By this he shows that all are profane who, given over to whatever vices, make light of all spiritual goods and everything that leads to salvation, and prefer the carnal to the spiritual.

units.la: Historia quidem manifesta est Geneseos vigesimoquinto, coxit Iacob coctionem, & veniebat Esau de campo, eratque fessus: Et dixit Esau ad Iacob, ciba me quæso de rufo, de rufo isto, fessus sum. Et hinc vocatum est nomen eius Edom: Dixit autem Iacob, vende iuxta hunc diem mihi primogenituram tuam, dixit Esau: En ego vado, vt moriar, & ad quid mihi primogenitura?
units.tr: The story is plain enough in Genesis 25: "Jacob had cooked a stew, and Esau came in from the field and was faint. And Esau said to Jacob, 'Feed me, I beg you, with that red stuff, this red stuff, for I am faint.' Therefore his name was called Edom. But Jacob said, 'Sell me your birthright today.' Esau said, 'Look, I am about to die; what use is a birthright to me?'"

units.la: Respondit Iacob, Iura mihi iuxta hunc diem: & iurauit ei, vendiditque primogenituram suam ipsi Iacob. Porrò Iacob dedit ei Esau panem & coctionem lentium, & ille comedit atque bibit, & surgens abijt, paruipenditque Esau primogenituram. Tantum ibi.
units.tr: Jacob answered, "Swear to me today." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. Then Jacob gave Esau bread and a stew of lentils, and he ate and drank, rose, and went away. Thus Esau made light of the birthright. So far the text.

units.la: Ecce autem quomodo ibi disertè addit Scriptura, volens nimirum indicare peccatum & temeritatem Esau, paruipendit Esau primogenituram. Possent quidem in hoc facto notari plura vitia, vt gulæ & luxus, sicut Chrysostomus ideo reddidit profanum γαστρίμαργον: item cupiditatis: sed, si bene consideramus, præcipuum est contemptus & neglectus rerum spiritualium, ac beneficiorum Dei: sicut etiam Chrysostomus, vbi explicat hunc locum in Genesi, satis indicat.
units.tr: See how plainly Scripture adds this, clearly intending to point out the sin and rashness of Esau: "Esau made light of the birthright." In this deed several vices could indeed be noted, such as gluttony and luxury, which is why Chrysostom called him a glutton [γαστρίμαργον], and also greed. But if we consider carefully, the chief fault is the contempt and neglect of spiritual things and of the benefits of God. Chrysostom, in his exposition of this passage in Genesis, sufficiently indicates this too.

units.la: Nam à gula & similibus potest vtcunq; excusari: erat enim famelicus: fame autē dum premimur, petere cibum quomodo damnandum? Deinde, quàtula erat voluptas, vesci coctione lentiū. Ergo præcipuū est peccatum cōmissum, quod ipsa Scriptura disertè indicat, ꝗ videlicet pro re tantilla, nēpe pro coctione lenticularū, quā potuerat alia ratione obtinere, vtiderist primogenituram: quòd sic dixerit, Quid mihi primogenitura? & quod Scriptura subijcit, Paruipendit primogenituram.
units.tr: For the gluttony and similar faults can somehow be excused: he was hungry, and who could condemn a man for seeking food when he is pressed by hunger? Besides, how small a pleasure it was to eat a stew of lentils! The chief sin, then, is the one Scripture itself states plainly: that for so trifling a thing, namely a dish of lentils, he gave up the birthright, which he could have obtained by some other means. This is shown by his saying, "What use is the birthright to me?" and by what Scripture adds: "He made light of the birthright."

units.la: Clarius autem constabit peccati huius commissi magnitudo, si quid valuerit primogenitura, aduertamus. Sciendum igitur, quod primogenitura secum ferebat singularem praerogatiuam, & erat quasi certa quaedam diuinae electionis nota. Etenim patriarcha tum habebat adiunctum, ita vt primogenitus constituendus esset patriarcha: quae digni tas vere magna est. Item ius sacerdotij in familia: quale ius in sanctis patribus caeteris licet animaduertere.
units.tr: The greatness of this sin will be clearer if we notice how much the birthright was worth. The birthright carried with it a singular prerogative and was a kind of sure mark of divine election. For at that time the patriarchal office was attached to it, so that the firstborn was to be appointed patriarch. That dignity is truly great. Likewise there was the right of priesthood within the family, a right that can be observed among the other holy fathers.

units.la: Vnde & primogeniti vbique leguntur praelati, tanquam electi prae ceteris omnibus. Eoque etiam populus Israel, vt intelligeretur singulariter dilectus a Deo prae omnibus populis. Exodi capite quarto, a Domino vocatur filius primogenitus: Dicesque ad Pharaonem: sic ait Dominus: Filius meus, primogenitus meus, est Israel. Similitudine inde, ni fallor, ducta, quod parentes eos, quos primos genuerint, solent arctissime diligere. Vnde & Dominus Exodi capite 13. etiam omne primogenitum iubet sibi sancti sicari. Et Christus propter excellentiam Colos. 1. celebratur primogenitus vniuersae creaturae. Inde etiam tractum, quod secundum ius diuinum, item secundum ius ciuile, & consuetudines multarum regionum primogenitis filijs debet cedere in diuidenda hereditate duplex portio: & Deuteronomio cap. vigesimo primo, prohibetur filio dilectae conferri ius primogeniturae in diuisione bonorum, quod debetur filio exosae mulieris.
units.tr: Hence firstborns are everywhere read of as preferred, as chosen above all others. So too the people of Israel, so that it might be understood that it was singularly beloved of God above all peoples: in Exodus 4 the Lord calls it his firstborn son, saying: "You shall say to Pharaoh, thus says the Lord: Israel is my son, my firstborn." This image, unless I am mistaken, is drawn from the fact that parents tend to love most tenderly those whom they bear first. Hence also the Lord, in Exodus 13, commands that every firstborn be consecrated to him. And Christ, because of his excellence, is praised in Colossians 1 as the firstborn of all creation. From this too it follows that, by divine law and likewise by civil law and the customs of many regions, a double portion of the inheritance must go to the firstborn sons when the estate is divided. And in Deuteronomy 21 it is forbidden to confer the right of the firstborn, in the division of goods, on the son of the beloved wife, to the detriment of the son of the hated wife.

units.la: Cum igitur tanta sit dignitas primogenituræ, & non tantum in temporalibus, sed multo maxime in spiritualibus, hinc videre est, quantum fuerit peccatum Esau, qui ob vnicum ferculum exigui pretij se tam insigni praerogatiua priuarit. Hic plane profanus dici poterit, qui ob rem carnale nullius momenti, & quam alia ratione potuisset comparare, iacturam tantam rerum spiritualium voluerit facere. Ergo in genere omnis qui contemnit vel negligit spiritualia, & prae his eligit temporalia & carnalia, profanus censeri debet, & ab omni sanctimonia, quae sita est potissimum in amplexandis rebus spiritualibus, alienissimus est.
units.tr: Since, then, the dignity of the birthright is so great, and not only in temporal things but far more in spiritual things, we can see how great was the sin of Esau, who for a single dish of small value deprived himself of so distinguished a prerogative. He may plainly be called profane who, for a carnal thing of no weight, which he could have obtained by some other means, was willing to incur so great a loss of spiritual things. In general, therefore, everyone who despises or neglects spiritual things, and chooses temporal and carnal things before them, ought to be counted profane and is utterly estranged from that holiness which consists chiefly in embracing spiritual things.

units.la: Atque hoc pacto censendi sunt omnes profani, qui nostro tempore tanquam Epicurei viuunt, & prae corporalibus quibus toti inuoluuntur, tanquam sues in volutabro, negligunt spiritualia, quibuscunque interea vitijs sint dediti. Omnes tales sunt sectatores Esau, & amittunt primogenituram suam, quia deseruunt primam suam vocationem. Et certe magnum erat, quod Esau ita diceret: Quid mihi primogenitura? Sicut si nunc quoque dicerent: Qui mihi profesio religionis, qua non iuuor in necessitate mea, imo ob quam debeo etiam pericula metuere? Quid mihi, vt praeficiar ecclesiae, vt fiam doctor euangelij? Hae voces sunt similes voci Esau, sunt profanae voces, & indicia mentis a rebus spiritualibus alienatae, cui nunquam sit expectandus laetus successus coram Deo, non magis, quam Esau.
units.tr: In this way are to be counted profane all those who in our time live like Epicureans, and who, like swine in the mire, given wholly to the bodily things in which they are immersed, neglect spiritual things, however much they are given over to vices meanwhile. All such men are followers of Esau, and they lose their birthright because they abandon their first calling. Indeed it was a great thing that Esau said, "What use is the birthright to me?" It is as if people now also said: "What use to me is a profession of religion, which does not help me in my need, and on account of which I ought even to fear dangers? What use to me is being set over the Church, or becoming a teacher of the gospel?" Such words are like the words of Esau; they are profane words and signs of a mind alienated from spiritual things, and such a mind can never expect a happy outcome before God, no more than Esau did.

units.la: Proinde aptissime ista ad Hebraeos iam ad religionem Christianam conuersos, & iam factos vere primogenitos, posteaquam crediderunt in primogenitum Iesum Christum, a quo primogenituræ spiritualis itus accipiunt. Quod si relaberentur iam denuo in peccata, & se contaminarent pristinis vitijs, profecto similes Esau agnoscerentur, & se reijciedos deberent intelligere, sicut reiectum sciebant Esau. Estque multo aptissima ad mouendos affectus huiusmodi per exempla demonstratio. Ergo valde eleganter red dita est per Apostolu ista propositio, & nos etiam debemus nobis aliquam doctrinam inde colligere.
units.tr: Therefore this is most aptly applied to the Hebrews who had already been converted to the Christian religion and had now truly become firstborn, since they believed in the firstborn Jesus Christ, from whom they receive the right of spiritual primogeniture. But if they were to fall back again into sins and defile themselves with their former vices, they would surely be recognized as like Esau, and they ought to understand that they would be rejected, just as Esau was known to be rejected. And a demonstration by examples is by far the most fitting way to move such affections. So this proposition was set forth by the Apostle very elegantly, and we too ought to draw some teaching from it for ourselves.

units.la: Primo autem discimus, pacem esse primo loco expetendam, vtpote sine qua ecclesia non possit consistere: pacem autem non tantum in quotidiano conuictu, sed etiam in dogmatibus & opinionibus, & cum hostibus seu alienis perinde atque cum domesticis.
units.tr: First, then, we learn that peace is to be sought above all, since without it the Church cannot stand; and peace is to be kept not only in daily intercourse but also in doctrines and opinions, and with enemies or outsiders just as much as with members of the household.

units.la: Secundo commendatur nobis perpetuum studium sanctimoniae, eiusque potissimum, quae in rebus spiritualibus & internis sita est, & nihilominus debet etiam externis studijs demonstrari, ad fratrum in firmorum aedificationem.
units.tr: Second, a constant zeal for holiness is commended to us, and especially for that holiness which lies in spiritual and inward things; yet it ought also to be shown in outward pursuits, for the building up of weaker brothers.

units.la: Tertio, admonemur fugere fornicationem, gulam, & omnia affinia peccata, quae aduersantur verae sanctimoniae.
units.tr: Third, we are admonished to flee fornication, gluttony, and all related sins that are opposed to true holiness.

units.la: Quarto, admonemur magnifacere dona Dei nobis collata, & tam externa seu corporalia, quam interna & spiritualia, cuiusmodi bona scimus perius primogenituræ carnalis adumbrata. Atque externa solet Deus conferre tanquam adminicula, per quae ad vsum & conseruationem spiritualium promouemur.
units.tr: Fourth, we are admonished to esteem highly the gifts of God bestowed on us, both external or bodily gifts and internal and spiritual ones; we know that such goods were foreshadowed by the carnal birthright. God usually bestows external things as helps by which we are advanced to the use and preservation of spiritual things.

units.la: Scitis enim, quod & postea cum vellet hereditario iure benedictionem assequi, reprobatus fit: Non enim reperit poenitentiae locum, tametsi cum lachrymis quaesiuisset eam.
units.tr: For you know that afterwards, when he wished to obtain the blessing by hereditary right, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance, though he had sought it with tears.

units.la: Sequuntur rationes suasoriae, praecipuè verò prouocantes ad colendam veram sanctimoniam. Nam rationes ad suadendum studium pacis per se abundè notae sunt omnibus, & iam aliquo modo quaedam redditae sunt in expositione prioris membri propositionis, vbi nimirum dicebatur: Sine qua nemo videbit Deum: item, Ne quis deficiat à gratia Dei: ne per amarulentiam atq; dissidia perturbentur inquinenturq; multi. Quę profectò particulę magnū pondus apud omnes habere debent, atq; acriter incitare animos, vt pacem studiosè sectentur actueantur. Ad sanctimoniam igitur excitat hisce rationibus iam sequentibus: quarum prima sumpta est ab exemplo & in infelici successu ipsius Esau, qui iamiam vt profanus & rerum diuinarum negligens, aut potius contemnens est ob oculos propositus. Estque sententia: Vos scitis, quomodo actum sit cum Esau, qui cùm esset primogenitus, & per ius primogenituræ multa bona non tantum temporalia, verùm etiam spiritualia erat acceptturus, tamen contempsit omnia, neque fuit illi curæ, vt acciperet. Vnde factum, vt postea, cùm maximè optaret, nihil prorsus potuerit recuperare, vel denuò obtinere.
units.tr: There follow the arguments of persuasion, chiefly those that urge us to cultivate true holiness. For the arguments for urging zeal for peace are in themselves well known to all, and some have already been given in the explanation of the earlier part of the proposition, where it was said: without which no one will see God; and lest anyone fall short of the grace of God, lest through bitterness and dissensions many be troubled and defiled. These particles surely ought to carry great weight with everyone and sharply stir minds to pursue and cultivate peace eagerly. So with these arguments, which follow, he stirs us to holiness. The first is taken from the example and from the unhappy outcome of Esau himself, who is now set before our eyes as profane and as neglectful, or rather contemptuous, of divine things. The sense is this: You know how it went with Esau, who, though he was firstborn, and was to receive through the birthright many good things, not only temporal but also spiritual, nevertheless despised them all, and did not care to receive them. Hence it came about that afterwards, when he most desired it, he could recover or regain nothing at all.

units.la: Simili igitur ratione vos quoque cauete, ne dona Dei ad sanctimoniam facientia vobis iam partim data, partim adhuc pro benedictione conferenda paruipendatis aut respuatis, ne, cùm ea sitis impensè desideraturi, haud quaquam assequamini. Aptissima ratio & Hebraeis, qui iam non tantum secundum carnem, vti ante habebantius primogeniturae apud Deū, verùm propter fidem in Christū erant primogeniti Dei secundum spiritum, amplissimas benedictiones spirituales debebat recipere, quas contemnere instar Esau grande profectò fuisset piaculum.
units.tr: Therefore, take care in the same way that you do not undervalue or reject the gifts of God that make for holiness, some of which have already been given to you and others of which are still to be conferred as a blessing. Otherwise, although you will desire them eagerly, you will by no means obtain them. The reason fits the Hebrews especially well. They were no longer only firstborn according to the flesh, as they had been before with regard to the privilege of the firstborn before God, but through faith in Christ they were firstborn of God according to the Spirit. They ought to have received the very great spiritual blessings, and to despise them like Esau would certainly have been a grave sin.

units.la: Nota autem est, vt verba Apostoli explicentur, historia, quomodo Esau cupiens iure haereditario benedictionem accipere, reprobatus sit. Genesis capite vigesimoseptimo ita legitur: Factum est, cum Isaac ceßasset benedicere Iacob, atque exeundo exiuisset Iacob à facie patris sui Isaac, venit Esau frater eius de venatione sua. Et fecit quoque ipse cibos, & intulit ad patrem suum, dixitque patri suo: Surgat pater meus, & comedat de venatione filij sui, vt benedicat mihi anima tua. Et dixit illi Isaac pater suus, Quis es tu? Ait ille: Ego filius tuus, primogenitus tuus Esau. Et expauit Isaac pauore magno valde nimis, & ait: Quis ille, & vbi est ille, qui cepit venationem, & attulit mihi, & ego comedi ex omnibus priusquam tu venires, & benedixi ei, eritq; benedictus?
units.tr: To explain the words of the Apostle, we must note the story of how Esau, though he wanted to receive the blessing by right of inheritance, was rejected. Genesis 27 reads as follows: "It came to pass, when Isaac had made an end of blessing Jacob, and Jacob was scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, that Esau his brother came in from his hunting. And he also made savoury meat and brought it to his father, and said to his father: Let my father arise, and eat of his son's venison, that your soul may bless me. And Isaac his father said to him: Who are you? He answered: I am your son, your firstborn Esau. And Isaac was struck with a very great trembling, and said: Who then is he that hunted venison and brought it to me? And I ate of all before you came, and I blessed him, and he shall be blessed."

units.la: Cum audiret Esau verba patris sui, vociferatus est clamore magno, & vehementer amaro, dixitque patri suo: Benedic etiam mihi, mihi inquam mi pater.
