Qui respondit: venit frater tuus cum dolo, & surripuit benedictionem tuam. Et hic rursus ait: Num verè vocatum est nomen eius Iacob? Nam supplantauit me iam duabus vicibus: primogeniturām meam tulit, & ecce nunc quoque accepit benedictionem meam, & ait: Nūquid segregasti & mihi benedictionem? Respondit Isaac & dixit ad Esau: Ecce posui tibi illum in dominum, & omnes fratres eius constitui illi in seruos, frumento & oleo stabilivi eum, & tibi iam quid faciam fili mi? Dixit verò Esau ad patrem suum: Nunquid benedictio vna est tibi pater mi? Benedic etiā mihi, mihi inquam mi pater: & leuans Esau vocem suam fleuit.
units.tr: When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with a great and very bitter cry, and said to his father: "Bless me also, even me, my father. He answered: Your brother came with deceit and took away your blessing. And again Esau said: Is he rightly called Jacob? For he has supplanted me now twice: he took away my birthright, and behold, now he has also taken my blessing. And he said: Have you not kept back a blessing for me? Isaac answered and said to Esau: Behold, I have made him your lord, and I have given all his brothers to him as servants; I have established him with corn and wine. What then shall I do for you, my son? But Esau said to his father: Have you only one blessing, my father? Bless me also, even me, my father. And lifting up his voice, Esau wept."

units.la: Respondit ei Isaac pater suus, & dixit: Ecce vbertates terrae habitatio tua erit, & de rore cœli desuper. In gladio tuo viues, & fratri tuo seruies, eritq;, quādo dominaberis, rupes iugum eius de collo tuo. Inimicatus est itaq; Esau Iacob propter benedictionē, quā benedixit eum pater eius.
units.tr: Isaac his father answered him and said: "Behold, your dwelling shall be in the fatness of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above. You shall live by your sword, and you shall serve your brother; and it shall come to pass, when you shall have dominion, that you shall break his yoke from your neck." So Esau bore a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him.

units.la: Ista igitur pulcherrima est historia, aperiens, quomodo Esau quia antea vididerat primogeniturām, etiam benedictionem amiserit. Debebatur quidem ei benedictio illa, vt constitueretur patriarcha, & dominus fratrum, propter ius primogenituræ: sed quando ipse sua magna culpa vendidit illud ius, merito frustratus est etiam benedictione. Vnde cum diceret, adsum filius tuus primogenitus tuus Esau, hic iam iniuste se ita vocabat, & mentiebatur, quippe qui cesserat iuri suo.
units.tr: This, then, is a most beautiful story, showing how Esau, who had earlier despised the birthright, also lost the blessing. That blessing was indeed owed to him, so that he might be established as the patriarch and lord of his brothers, on account of the right of the firstborn. But since he himself, by his own great fault, had sold that right, he was justly disappointed also of the blessing. Therefore when he said, "Here am I, your firstborn son Esau," he was then wrongly calling himself that, and he was lying, since he had given up his right.

units.la: Neq; potest dici, non valere benedictionem in Iacob collatā, quia is mentitus est patri, & cum dolo accepit. Patris quidem mens eras primogenitum benedicere: Iam verò Iacob obtinuerat primogeniturām, & propterea ei debebatur benedictio. Verum quidē est, pater ipse valde attonitus est, cùm audiret factū Iacob, aduenīete Esau: sed nihilominus, suggerēte haud dubiè spiritu Sancto, ratam habuit benedictionem collatam: dicēs: Benedixi ei, eritq; benedictus: Ita nimirū Deus qui ordinauerat per suā prouidentiā, vt Iacob obtineret ius primogenituræ, idē ordinauerat, vt benedictione quoq; primogeniturae quasi annexā acciperet: sicut egregiè dictū est etiam, antequā nasceretur: Iacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui: Malachiae 1. Roman. 9. Neque interea excusari potest à peccato Esau, quòd primogenita vendiderit. Diuina prouidentia etiamsi faciat, vt necessariò impleatur. pleatur, quod per eam est ordinatum, tamen non facit, vt à peccato excusentur, qui ma- lum perpetrant: qua de re vberius dictum est in libro nostro de prouidentia. Caeterum res poscit, vt de amplitudine huius benedictionis aliquid adijciamus. Diximus quidem de benedictionibus, quas parentes solent in filios conferre, non nihil supra capite 7. v bi Apostoli verba erant. Porrò nemo negat, quin id, quod minus est, ab eo, quod maius est, benedictionem accipiat. Illud praecipuè reuocandum in memoriam, quod ibi quoq; fusè expositum, quomodo videlicet Deus ratam habeat parentum benedictionem, aut etiam maledictionem. Exemplum Genes. 9. in benedictione, qua Noah benedixit Sem & Iaphet, contrà maledixit Cham. Item praesenti loco Isaac dicebat: Benedixi ei, & ipse erit benedictus. Et Iacob Genes. 48. benedixit filijs Iosephi. cap. 49. Benedixit filijs suis omnibus.
units.tr: Nor can it be said that the blessing conferred on Jacob was not valid because he deceived his father and obtained it by fraud. It was indeed his father's intention to bless the firstborn; but Jacob had already obtained the birthright, and therefore the blessing was due to him. It is true that the father himself was greatly astonished when he heard what Jacob had done, Esau having arrived; yet nevertheless, undoubtedly prompted by the Holy Spirit, he regarded the blessing he had conferred as binding, saying: "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed." Thus God, who by his providence had ordained that Jacob should obtain the right of the firstborn, had also ordained that he should receive the blessing of the firstborn as if joined to it. This was well said even before they were born: "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated" (Malachi 1; Romans 9). Nor, meanwhile, can Esau be excused from sin because he sold the birthright. Divine providence, even though it brings it about that what it has ordained must necessarily be fulfilled, does not thereby make excused from sin those who commit the evil. We have treated this more fully in our book on providence. Moreover, the matter requires that we add something about the scope of this blessing. We have indeed said something above, at chapter 7, where the words of the Apostle occur, about the blessings which parents are accustomed to confer on their children. Furthermore, no one denies that what is less receives a blessing from what is greater. What must be especially recalled is what was also set out at length there, namely how God ratifies the blessing, or even the curse, of parents. Genesis 9 is an example: in the blessing with which Noah blessed Shem and Japheth, he cursed Ham on the contrary. Likewise in the present passage Isaac said, "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed." And Jacob in Genesis 48 blessed the sons of Joseph, and in chapter 49 he blessed all his sons.

units.la: Conuenit itaque interpretari, Deum ita velle, vt perficiantur ea in parte vota parentū, primùm, quòd illi patres à spiritu Sancto fuerunt afflati, necnon ad id faciundum addu- ctì: secundò, ut iuniores haberent occasionem venerandi suos maiores, iuxta doctrinam quarti praecepti Decalogi. Sed illud quoq; iâ notandū est, quòd benedictiones illę de reb. corporalibus, erant tantùm vmbrae quaedam & typi nouarum benedictionum spiritualium, quae accipiendae sunt in euangelio propter Christum: in quas spirituales benedictiones sine dubio patres animum & fidem suam praecipuè intendebant: id quod ex eo constare poterit, quòd, nisi istud statuamus, videbuntur benedictione illae non prorsus ef se completae. Nam vbi seruiuit Esau Iacob? Imò Iacob coactus est fugere: deinde per omnem vitam valde metuebat Esau: & studebat muneribus beneuolentiam eius redimere. De spirituali igitur benedictione expectanda ex semine benedicto erat praecipua illorum cura: de qua benedictione passim concionatur euangelium, & praeclarè Ephesiorū primo, Benedictus Deus & pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nos omni benedictione spirituali in coelestibus Christo. Galat. 3. Qui ex fide sunt, benedicuntur cum fideli Abraham. 1. Pet. 3. Scientes, vos in hoc vocatos esse, vt benedictionem haereditate possideatis.
units.tr: It is fitting, therefore, to interpret that God wills the wishes of the parents to be fulfilled in this respect: first, because those fathers were inspired by the Holy Spirit and were led to do it; second, so that the younger sons might have an occasion of honouring their elders, in accordance with the teaching of the fourth commandment of the Decalogue. But this too must be noted, that those blessings concerning bodily things were only certain shadows and types of the new spiritual blessings, which are to be received in the gospel on account of Christ. Undoubtedly the fathers directed their minds and faith chiefly to these spiritual blessings. This can be made clear from the fact that, unless we hold this, those blessings will seem not to have been fully accomplished. For where did Esau serve Jacob? Indeed, Jacob was forced to flee; then all his life Esau was greatly feared by him, and he tried to win Esau's goodwill with gifts. Therefore the chief concern of those men was the spiritual blessing to be expected from the blessed seed. The gospel preaches of this blessing everywhere, and most clearly in Ephesians 1: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ." Galatians 3: "Those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham." 1 Peter 3: "Knowing that you were called to this, that you should inherit a blessing."

units.la: Hoc autem pacto intelligendo benedictionem negandam Esau, de benedictione spirituali, rectissimè accommodatur haec ratio Hebraeis. Iis enim, quando quidem iam primogeniti erant facti, etiam secundum spiritum, benedictio quoq; erat expectanda, & quidem spiritualis, cuius veterum benedictiones de rebus temporalibus erant typi siue vmbrę. Suntq; nomine benedictionis spiritualis intelligenda omnia bona, quae sub euangelio per Christum & propter Christum nobis sunt collata: ne quis putet, simplicem quandam esse benedictionem euangelicam. Hinc verò intelligi poterit, etiam non leue esse hanc rationem, qua proponitur Hebraeis, quòd, vbi sanctimoniam veram colere noluerint, sint in istar Esau benedictionem omnem spiritualem amissuri.
units.tr: Now, if the blessing denied to Esau is understood in this way, as a spiritual blessing, this reasoning is most rightly applied to the Hebrews. For since they had now become firstborn, also according to the Spirit, the blessing too was to be expected, and indeed a spiritual one, of which the blessings of the ancients concerning temporal things were types or shadows. And by the name of spiritual blessing must be understood all the goods which under the gospel are conferred on us through Christ and on account of Christ, lest anyone think the gospel blessing to be some simple thing. From this it can be understood that this reasoning, by which it is set before the Hebrews, is not a slight one: where they were unwilling to cultivate true holiness, they would, like Esau, lose every spiritual blessing.

units.la: Quod additur, non reperisse poenitentiae locum, tametsi cum lachrymis quaesiuisset eam: indicat, ferò desiderari ea bona, quae antea superbè & temerariè contemperimus, praesertim vbi gratis sola Dei spontanea munificentia oblata fuerint: sicut reuera etiam credentibus gratis conferuntur, & quòd credant, (fides enim donum Dei est, ne quis glorietur, Ephes. 2.) & quòd per fidem alia deinceps dona accipiant, omnia à Deo proueniunt, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex gratia: ille enim prior dilexit nos.
units.tr: What is added, that he did not find a place for repentance, although he had sought it with tears, shows that those goods which they had earlier proudly and rashly despised are often sought in vain, especially where they have been offered freely by the sole spontaneous generosity of God. Indeed, these things are truly given freely even to believers, and that they believe (for faith is the gift of God, lest anyone should boast, Ephesians 2), and that through faith they afterwards receive other gifts, all come from God, not from our works but from grace; for he loved us first.

units.la: Quòd verò cum lachrymis quaesierit Esau poenitentia, liquet ex contextu, vbi dicitur eleuata voce fleuisse, & vehementer amaro animo vociferatus. Sed quòd interim non inuenerit poenitentiam, id dicitur, quia non erat vera poenitentia. Neque enim agnoscebat ibi peccatum suum commissum in venditione primogenituræ: neq; etiam de uitae emendatione ulla subibat animum eius cogitatio, sed tantùm indignè ferebat, sibi bona illa, quae expectarat, non conferri, non animaduertens, quòd seipsum indignum reddidisset. Argumentum id est, quòd non verè poenituerit, quòd tantùm inuectus est in fratrem, quòd mox etiam consilium ceperit de fratre occidendo, probabile etiam, quòd tantùm respexerit ad externa & carnalia bona, non ad spiritualia. Ad eundem modum impius Pharao, cùm flagellaretur, clamabat ad Dominum, cupiebatq; vt Moses pro se oraret: sed interea non cogitabat explere Domini voluntatem dimittendo populum, non agnoscebat peccatum suum in contemnendis iussis Dei: atque ita poenitentia eius inutilis fuit. Sic quoque Iudas poenitudine ductus dixit, Peccaui tradens sanguinem iustum: deinde restituit etiam acceptos nummos: sed frustrà, & inutilis imperfectaq; erat ista poenitentia: quia, licet agnosceret peccatum, non tamen habebat fidem de obtinenda venia. Sic denique omnes impij habent quandam poenitentiae speciem, sed veram & absolutam poenitentiam nequaquam: semper aliquid deest, nempe, vel agnitio peccati, vel fides de accipienda misericordia.
units.tr: That Esau sought repentance with tears is clear from the context, where he is said to have wept aloud and cried out with a very bitter spirit. But that he did not find repentance in the meantime is said because his repentance was not true repentance. He did not acknowledge there his sin in selling his birthright, nor did any thought of amending his life come into his mind. He resented only that the good things he had hoped for were not given to him, and he did not notice that he had made himself unworthy of them. The proof that he did not truly repent is that he raged against his brother and soon also planned to kill him. It is also probable that he looked only to external and carnal goods, not to spiritual ones. In the same way the impious Pharaoh, when he was scourged, cried out to the Lord and wanted Moses to pray for him, but meanwhile he did not intend to fulfil the Lord's will by letting the people go, and he did not acknowledge his sin in despising God's commands. So his repentance was useless. Likewise Judas, driven by remorse, said, "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." Then he gave back the money he had received, but in vain. That repentance was useless and incomplete, because, although he recognised his sin, he did not have faith to obtain pardon. Finally, all the impious have a certain appearance of repentance, but never true and complete repentance. Something is always lacking: either the acknowledgement of sin, or faith in receiving mercy.

units.la: Pharaonis clamor. Iudas Iscariotes. Matth. 27. Impij & hypocritae. Ex his verò constare potest, locum hunc non patrocinari Nouatianis, quasi hic dicere tur, Spem veniæ negare ijs, qui semel lapsi fuerint, quantacunq; du cantur pœnitentia. Certè verè pœnitentibus non negatur misericordia, sed tantum hypocritis & impijs, simulantibus se pœnitere, & imperfectè pœnitentibus. De dogmate Nouatianorum, quæque contra id dici debeant, alias diximus, cap.6.
units.tr: The cry of Pharaoh. Judas Iscariot. Matt. 27. The impious and hypocrites. From these things it can be established that this passage does not favour the Novatians, as if it were said here that hope of pardon is denied to those who have fallen once, however great the repentance they show. Certainly mercy is not denied to those who truly repent, but only to hypocrites and the impious, who pretend to repent, and to those who repent imperfectly. Concerning the dogma of the Novatians, and what ought to be said against it, we have spoken elsewhere, in chapter 6.

units.la: Cæterum hîc discimus, dona Dei, quæ nobis adsunt, magnifacere, illisque recte vti. Quòd vbi à nobis fit, tantum abest, ut aliquid decessurum sit, vt etiam certi esse debeamus, augenda potius. Sic Esau si non paruipendisset ius primogenituræ, haudd ubiè accepisset etiam benedictionem. Huc pertinet parabola illa de accipientibus noua talenta à Domino, qui prius habita recte exposuerant, quodq; Dominus alibi ait: Habenti dabitur: non habenti etiam id quod habet auferetur ab eo. Sic quoq; de illis iudicare oportet, qui contemnunt vel negligunt suam vocationem, & ea, quæ vocationis suæ sunt, facere, ij postea reprobantur, sicut Esau & Saul, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, here we learn to value the gifts of God that are ours and to use them rightly. When this is done by us, far from anything being lost, we ought to be certain that they will rather be increased. So Esau, if he had not made light of the right of the firstborn, would certainly not have received the blessing either. To this belongs the parable of those who received new talents from the Lord, who had rightly used what they had before, and the saying of the Lord elsewhere: "To him who has, more will be given; from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away." So too we must judge those who scorn or neglect their calling and do not do the things that belong to their calling: they are afterwards rejected, like Esau and Saul, etc.

units.la: Est etiam cotemplanda admirabilis diuinæ prouidentiæ dispensatio, qua alij contra expectationem & iudicium carnis reprobantur, vt Esau primogenitus: alij, de quibus minimè credebatur, eliguntur, vt Iacob natu minor. Sed hic admonemur, nosmetipsos humiliare, non intumescere propter dona spiritualia: item iubemur intueri in Dei gratiam misericordiam, & ab hac sola constanter omnia bona per fidem expectare. Iudicia Dei abyssus multa.
units.tr: We should also contemplate the admirable dispensation of divine providence, by which some are rejected contrary to expectation and the judgement of the flesh, as Esau the firstborn was, while others, whom no one believed would be chosen, are elected, as Jacob, the younger by birth. But here we are admonished to humble ourselves and not to swell with pride on account of spiritual gifts. We are also commanded to look to the grace and mercy of God, and to expect all good things steadfastly from this alone, through faith. "The judgements of God are a great deep."

units.la: Tertio, discimus hic discrimen inter veram pœnitentiam & falsam, quodq;, cum falsa sit inutilis, vera tamen recipiat veniam.
units.tr: Third, we learn here the difference between true repentance and false, and that, while false repentance is useless, true repentance receives pardon.

units.la: Non enim accessistis ad contactum montem, & incensum ignem ac turbinem & caliginem, & procellam, tubæq; sonitum, & vocem verborum, quam qui audierant, deprecati sunt, ne bis adiungeretur oratio. Non enim ferebant, quod edicebatur: si bestia tetigerit montem, lapidabitur, aut iaculo configetur: & adeo terribile erat visum, quod apparebat. Moses dixit: Expauefactus sum ac tremebundus: sed accessistis ad montem Sion, & ad ciuitatem Dei viuentis, Hierusalem cœlestem, & ad innumerabilium angelorum cœtum, & ad concionem primogenitorum, qui coscripti sunt in cœlis, & ad iudicem vniuersorum Deum, & ad spiritus iustorum perfectorum, & ad noui testamenti conciliatorem Iesum, & ad sanguinem aspersionis meliora loquentem, quam loquebatur sanguis Abel.
units.tr: For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which voice they that heard entreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more: for they could not endure that which was commanded, And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart: and so terrible was the sight, that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake: but ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.

units.la: Secunda ratio suasoria, sumpta à præstantia euangelij præ lege, ob quam par est eos, qui sub euangelio agunt, sanctimonia pollere præ illis, qui adhuc agunt sub lege.
units.tr: The second persuasive reason, taken from the excellence of the gospel above the law, for which those who live under the gospel ought to excel in holiness above those who still live under the law.

units.la: Est autem eleganter admodum, & planè rhetorica contentione tractata hæc euangelij præ lege præstantia, etiamsi in posteriore parte, qua de euangelio agitur, plura membra sint congesta. Quod tamen consultò videtur factum, tum ut dignitas euangelij redderetur illustrior: tum ut ad id ample extendum, quod persuadere cupit, omnium affectus magis moverentur. Et si bene aduertimus, ita se habet præsentis rationis summa, tanquam si à minori ad maius fieret argumentatio in hunc modum:
units.tr: This excellence of the gospel over the law is treated very elegantly and with a truly rhetorical vigour, even though several clauses have been heaped up in the latter part, where the gospel is discussed. This seems to have been done deliberately, both so that the dignity of the gospel might be made more illustrious, and so that, by extending the matter widely, the feelings of all would be moved more strongly towards what he wishes to persuade. And if we pay close attention, the sum of the present argument is as follows, as if the argument proceeded from the less to the greater in this way:

units.la: Decebat vos esse sanctos, etiam agentes sub lege: Igitur multò magis sanctimoniam nunc coletis, quando constituti estis sub euangelio.
units.tr: You ought to have been holy even while living under the law. Therefore you should now cultivate holiness much more, since you have been placed under the gospel.

units.la: Deinde adijcitur aetiologia. Sub lege proponebantur vobis horrendæ minæ, & pœnarum terriculamentis omnia perstrepebant. Sub euangelio autem proponitur vobis gratia & misericordia, omniaque incredibilem fœlicitatem, & innumera bona spirant.
units.tr: Then an explanation of the cause is added. Under the law, dreadful threats were set before you, and everything resounded with the terrors of punishments. But under the gospel, grace and mercy are set before you, and everything breathes incredible happiness and countless blessings.

units.la: Istud verò iam præsupponi debet, quasi per se notum, videlicet Hebræos, si modò non sint degeneri animo, malle duci, quàm trahi: & plus effecturos ob blandas exhortationes, & propositä bona, quàm propter horrendas comminationes poenarum & damnationis. Ita namque spiritu Dei aguntur, qui filij Dei sunt. Filij mouentur promissionibus & blandis monitis: serui excitantur fustibus & plagis: ac planè seruilis degenerisque animi est, bene non facere, nisi metu fustis. Cùm ergo Hebræi iam effecti essent veri filij secundum spiritum, non amplius in carne gloriantes, debent apud illos valere rationes. Passim verò usurpat Apostolus huiusmodi rationem, qua componit statum vitæ anteactæ cum noua uita præsenti. Valde efficax est ad mouendum, ut Rom.13. Nunc propius adest nobis salus, quàm tum cùm credebamus. Nox præterierat est, dies autem appropinquat: Abijciamus igitur opera tenebrarum. Ephes.4. Hocitaque dico & testor per Dominum, ne posthac ambuletis, quemadmodum & reliquae gentes ambulant in vanitate mentis suae, dum mentem habent obtene bratam, &c. Vos autem non sic didicistis Christum: si quidem illum audiftis, & in eo docti fuistis. Sic autem proponit gentibus miseriam & infoelicitatem vitae anteactae in suo paganismo & summa ignorantia omnium rerum diuinarum: ita proponit nunc Hebreis miseriam & infoelicitatem vitae anteactae in suo Iudaismo, cum sub vmbra legis adhuc agerent. Et ostendit nunc, postquam agunt sub euangelio, longe agi cum ipsis foelicius, quam antea. Ne vero quis putet, iniquam fieri a nobis comparationem, quod Iudaismu aequamus paganismo, audiatur ea de re ipse Apostolus Philip. 3. Quo loco, vbi praeclara exposuisset excellentiam, quam vendicare poterat ex lege, tandem subijcit: sed quae mi hi erant lucra, & arbitratus sum propter Christum damnum esse: & quae ibi sequuntur. Item Rom. 2. Ostendit, Iudaeum nihil praestantiorem gentili, vbi vitam nequaquam tran figit sanctius, qua gentilis: Et rursus, gentilem bene operantem parem Iudaeo non operanti melius. Ergo, sicut gentiles solet excitare ad vitae emendationem, proponendo eis infoelicitatem vitae anteactae, & foelicitatem conditionis, quam adepti sunt sub euangelio. Quae ratio debet profecto valde omnium animos mouere. Quis enim, si ei benefiat, & promoueatur ad meliorem conditionem, quam antea habuerit, non lubeter fatetur, se merito debere plura facere? Et quis potius, quam amittat recens acceptam foelicem conditionem, & redeat ad priores miserias, non malit omnia facere, quae iure exiguntur? Et notum est illud, Alia vita, alia dicta: Honores mutant mores. Vbi non sis, qui fueris, non est, cur velis viuere. Valde turpe foret, mutata in melius conditione non etiam melius viuere, aut, postquam iam bene coepisti agere, iterum redire ad pristina praesepia, & ad priores sordes.
units.tr: This must now be presupposed as self-evident: that the Hebrews, unless they are of a degenerate spirit, would rather be led than dragged, and that they will achieve more through kind exhortations and offered goods than through dreadful threats of punishment and damnation. For this is how those who are sons of God are moved by the Spirit of God. Sons are moved by promises and kindly admonitions; slaves are roused by cudgels and blows. It is truly a servile and degenerate spirit to refrain from doing good except out of fear of the cudgel. Since the Hebrews had now become true sons according to the Spirit, no longer boasting in the flesh, reasons ought to carry weight with them. The Apostle uses this kind of argument everywhere, setting the state of the former life over against the new life of the present. It is very effective for moving people, as in Rom. 13: "Now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness." Eph. 4: "This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, etc. But ye have not so learned Christ; if so be that ye have heard him, and have been taught by him." So he sets before the Gentiles the misery and unhappiness of their former life in their paganism and their utter ignorance of all divine things. So now he sets before the Hebrews the misery and unhappiness of their former life in their Judaism, while they still lived under the shadow of the law. And he shows that, now that they live under the gospel, their condition is far happier than before. Lest anyone think the comparison unfair, because we equate Judaism with paganism, let the Apostle himself be heard on this point, Phil. 3. There, after he had set out the excellence he could claim from the law, he finally adds: "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ," and what follows there. Likewise Rom. 2, where he shows that the Jew is in no way superior to the Gentile, where he does not live more holily than the Gentile; and again, that the Gentile who does good is not inferior to the Jew who does not. Therefore, just as he is accustomed to rouse the Gentiles to amendment of life by setting before them the unhappiness of their former life and the happiness of the condition they have obtained under the gospel, so too this argument ought surely to move the minds of all very strongly. For who, if he is benefited and raised to a better condition than he had before, does not willingly admit that he ought rightly to do more? And who, rather than lose a newly acquired happy condition and return to former miseries, would not prefer to do everything that is rightly required? The proverb is well known: "Another life, another speech; honours change manners. Where you are not who you were, there is no reason why you should want to live as before." It would be very shameful, when your condition has changed for the better, not to live better too, or, after you have begun to live well, to return again to the old manger and the former filth.

units.la: Ergo valde apta & solida est ista ratio ad mouendos Hebraeos, ut veram & minime hypocritica sanctimoniam ex animo colant. Nunc videamus, quam appositè Apostolus rationem istam suasoriam expresserit.
units.tr: This argument is therefore very apt and solid for moving the Hebrews to cultivate true and genuinely unfeigned holiness from the heart. Now let us see how fittingly the Apostle has expressed this persuasive argument.

units.la: Non enim accesistis ad contactum montem, & incensum ignem & turbinem.
units.tr: For you have not come to the mountain that may be touched, and to a burning fire, and a whirlwind.

units.la: Illud obseruatu dignum, quod Apostolus agens cum Hebraeis profert rationes suasorias, ex rebus legalibus sumptas, quae apud gentiles non habuissent parem gratiam. Ita Apostolus sapientissime iudicat, quid singulis conueniat: ad gentiles alijs vtitur rationibus: si quando agit de statu prioris vitae, & de meliore succedente, sicut paulo ante indicauimus.
units.tr: It is worth noting that the Apostle, when dealing with the Hebrews, offers persuasive arguments drawn from legal matters, which would not have had the same force among the Gentiles. So the Apostle judges wisely what suits each people. For the Gentiles he uses other arguments, when he speaks of the condition of their former life and of the better life that follows, as we indicated a little earlier.

units.la: Erit autem hic indicandum, ad quam historiam legis Apostolus respiciat: tum quomodo per descriptionem istam ostendatur legis indignitas prae euangelio: & quomodo omnia quae gesta narrantur, aliarum rerum umbra fuerint, ac res magnas minimeq; praetereundas significarint. Dicit ergo Apostolus, Non enim accepistis ad contactum monte, &c. Historia, quae hic paucis perstringitur, descripta habetur Exodi 19. & valde appositè additur hic, vbi de sanctimonia agitur. Nam ibi quoque Dominus praecepit populum sanctificari, & sic praeparari ad audiendum ipsum loquentem. Quare & hic de sanctificatione agens apostolus rectè eorum, quae ibi gesta sunt, recordatur. Sic enim Dominus ad Moysen ibi: Vade ad populum, & sanctifica eos hodie & cras, lauentq; vestimenta sua: sint parati in diem tertium, quoniam in die tertio descendet Dominus in oculis totius populi super montem Sinai. Tantum de sanctificatione, vt intelligatur, ea, quae hic dicuntur, recte ad propositum de sanctimonia accommodari.
units.tr: Here, however, we must point out which history of the law the Apostle has in view, and how this description shows the unworthiness of the law compared with the gospel, and how all the things narrated as done were shadows of other things and signified great matters that must not be passed over. The Apostle therefore says: For you have not come to the mountain that may be touched, etc. The history that is briefly touched on here is related in Exodus 19, and it is added very fittingly here, where the subject is holiness. For there too the Lord commanded the people to be sanctified, and so to be prepared to hear him speaking. Hence the Apostle, treating of sanctification here, rightly recalls what was done there. For so the Lord said to Moses there: Go to the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments; let them be ready for the third day, for on the third day the Lord will come down in the sight of all the people upon Mount Sinai. Let this suffice concerning sanctification, so that it may be understood that what is said here is rightly applied to the subject of holiness.

units.la: Ad contactum montem) Exodi 19. iussus est Moses dicere ad populum: Cauete vobis, ne ascendatis in montem, aut tangatis extremitatem eius: omnis qui tetigerit montem, morte interficiatur. Non tangat eum manus: alioquin lapidando lapidabitur, aut iaculis feriatur, siue iumentum fuerit, siue homo, non uiuet. Quod etiam verbum mox hic citatur. Qua ratione igitur, cum contingi non potuerit, vocatur mons contactus? Quibusdam placet, contactum dici per antiphrasin, quasi minime tangendum. Alijs placet dici contactu, vt postea per contrarium suggeratur animis mons quidam intangibilis, nempe spiritualis, in quo fundata est ecclesia, quem & mox vocat montem Sion, haudquaquam spiritualem Sion, non autem corporalem vel terrenam intelligens. Et hic tangi seu palpari non potest, sicut mons Sina tangi & palpari poterat, cum terrenus esset & corporalis. Et hoc fere pacto Chrysostomus, pluresque eum secuti. Simplicior sententia est, contactum dici, quod de caelo tactus fuerit, vt flammam & fumos & sonos mirabiles ederet. Quo sensu psalmo 144 Domine inclina caelos tuos, & descende, tange montes, & fumigabunt. Eijce fulmen, & dissipa eos, mitte sagittas tuas, & disturba illos.
units.tr: To the mountain that may be touched) In Exodus 19 Moses was commanded to say to the people: Take heed to yourselves, that you do not go up into the mountain or touch its border; whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death. No hand shall touch him; otherwise he shall be stoned or shot through with arrows, whether beast or man, he shall not live. This word is also cited shortly here. By what reasoning, then, since it could not be touched, is the mountain called one that may be touched? Some hold that it is called "that may be touched" by antiphrasis, as if it were by no means to be touched. Others hold that it is called "that may be touched" so that afterwards, by contrast, there may be suggested to the minds a certain intangible mountain, namely a spiritual one, on which the Church is founded; this is the one he calls right afterwards Mount Zion, by no means a spiritual Zion, but understanding it not as a bodily or earthly one. And here it cannot be touched or handled, as Mount Sinai could be touched and handled, since that was earthly and bodily. Chrysostom, and several who followed him, explain it in roughly this way. The simpler sense is that it is called "that may be touched" because it was touched from heaven, so that it produced flame and smoke and wonderful sounds. In this sense Psalm 144: Lord, bow your heavens and come down; touch the mountains and they will smoke. Hurl lightning and scatter them; send out your arrows and trouble them.

units.la: In hunc modum & præsenti loco dicitur mons contactus, quia diuina potentia ac nutu flamma, fumus, turbines, in eo excitati sunt: quod & sequetibus verbis declaratur. Et incensum ignem) Sunt hic singula diligenter obseruanda. Describunt enim nobis conditiones legis, atque ita quidem, ut intelligi inde possit, legem nullo pacto ad eam peruenire excellentiam, ad quam euangelium. Quod igitur ad incensum ignem attinet, liquet id ex capite Exod.19. Factumque est, in quit, die tertio, cum aurora illucesceret, facta sunt tonitrua & fulgura, atque nubes grauis super montem, & vox tubæ vehementissima, vt terreretur vniuersus populus, qui erat in castris. Et eduxit Moses populum in occursum Dei extra castra, steterunt- que iuxta inferiora montis. Mos autem Sinai totus fumigabat, eo quod descendisset super eum Dominus in igne, & ascendit fumus eius, quasi fumus fornacis, & plurimum tremuit vniuersus mons. Et factum est, cum vox tubæ procederet, loquebatur Moses, & Deus respondebat ei per vocem. Et postea capite vicesimo: Omnes itaque populi videbant voces & lampades, & vocem tubæ, & montem fumantem, &c.
units.tr: In this manner the mountain is also called "that may be touched" in the present passage, because by divine power and command flame, smoke and whirlwinds were stirred up on it, which is also declared in the words that follow. And a burning fire) Each of these things must be carefully observed. For they describe to us the conditions of the law, and in such a way that it may be understood from them that the law by no means reaches that excellence which the gospel reaches. As for the burning fire, this is clear from Exodus 19: And it came to pass, it says, on the third day, when morning dawned, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mountain, and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people who were in the camp trembled. And Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. Now Mount Sinai was wholly smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire, and its smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain trembled greatly. And when the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice. And afterwards, in chapter twenty: And all the people saw the voices and the lightnings, and the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking, etc.

units.la: Ex his verbis sumpta sunt, quæ hoc loco habet Apostolus. Quod igitur Dominus in igne apparuit, & mos ardere videbatur, id argumentum erat, quod lex deberet terrere, & commouere hominum animos, & conscientias: sicut igne incendioque homines maxime terrentur, etiam procul tantum conspecto: sic autem lex considerata diligentius a peccatore, eum vehementer commouet, ponitque ob oculos Dei iram, & ignem æternæ damnationis. Præterea terrorem inducit, vt etiam de abstinendo in posterum a peccatis cogitet.
units.tr: From these words the Apostle takes what he says in this place. The fact that the Lord appeared in fire, and the mountain seemed to burn, was a sign that the law ought to terrify and move men's minds and consciences, just as men are especially terrified by fire and conflagration, even when they see it only from afar. So too the law, when considered more carefully by a sinner, deeply disturbs him, and sets before his eyes God's wrath and the fire of eternal damnation. Moreover, it induces terror, so that he also thinks about abstaining from sins in future.

units.la: Huc pertinet, quod Moses capite vicesimo adfert, reddendo causam, quare Dominus tam horrenda forma apparuerit: Ne timueritis, propterea enim, ut tentaret vos, venit Deus, & ut timor illius esset in facie vestra, ne peccaretis.
units.tr: To this belongs what Moses adds in chapter twenty, giving the reason why the Lord appeared in such a dreadful form: Do not fear; for God has come to test you, and so that his fear may be before your faces, lest you sin.

units.la: Ac turbinem) γνόφῳ turbinem & caliginem significat: quæ vox etiam habetur Exod.20. vbi dicitur, apud Septuaginta, Mosen per caliginem ingressum ad Dominum. Turbo igitur & caligo significat legis obscuritatem, quodque in ea non clare videretur diuinæ & spirituales, sicut in euangelio, sed tantum per vmbram & caliginem. Vnde supra capite decimo dicitur lex obtinens vmbram futurorum bonorum, non ipsam rerum imaginem. Quæ imago competit euangelio, res vero tantum post hanc vitam obtinentur.
units.tr: And a whirlwind) [γνόφῳ] signifies a whirlwind and darkness; this word is also found in Exodus 20, where it is said in the Septuagint that Moses entered into the darkness to the Lord. The whirlwind and darkness therefore signify the obscurity of the law, and that in it the divine and spiritual things did not appear clearly, as in the gospel, but only through shadow and darkness. Hence above, in chapter ten, the law is said to have the shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the things. That image belongs to the gospel, but the things themselves are obtained only after this life.

units.la: Et caliginem) In Exodo vicesimonono dicitur, de nube graui. Septuaginta γνοφώδες, quasi diceret, nubes caliginosæ. Tenebræ igitur & caligo in lege, quia ibi nondum vera lux, quæ est Christus, effulsit: adhuc ambulabant in tenebris, & vmbra mortis, qui sub lege agebant: sicut Zacharias pater Ioannis fatebatur: Per viscera misericordiæ Dei nostri, in quibus visitauit nos oriens ex alto, vt illucesceret his, qui in tenebris, & in vmbra mortis sedebant, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis.
units.tr: And darkness) In Exodus 29 it is spoken of a thick cloud. The Septuagint has [γνοφώδες], as if they meant cloudy darkness. Darkness and gloom therefore belonged to the law, because the true light, which is Christ, had not yet shone forth there; those who lived under the law still walked in darkness and in the shadow of death, as Zechariah, the father of John, confessed: Through the tender mercy of our God, by which the dayspring from on high has visited us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

units.la: Et procellam) Numeratur θύελλα inter ventos seu flatus repentinos, a verbo θύω quod est impetum facio, quod maximo impetu & non sine horribili sono proruat. Non est in hebræo aut græco vox respondens, quia Apostolus magis sententiam spectauit, quam verba: sed pariter in Hebræo & græco de tonitru & fulgure fit mentio, quæ appa ret hic per θύελλαν & ignem notari. Significatur autem, legi non adesse spiritum, qui consoletur atque animet, quemadmodum in nouo testamento: sed potius perturbet, & ad desperationem prope deiiciat. Etiamsi Chrysostomus interpretatur, significatum, quod segnities veteris illius populi debebat hoc pacto excuti, animisque commoueri atque erigi ad diligentius audiendum.
units.tr: And a storm) [θύελλα] is counted among the sudden winds or blasts, from the verb [θύω], which means to rush upon, because it bursts forth with the greatest force and not without a dreadful sound. There is no word in the Hebrew or the Greek corresponding to it, because the Apostle regarded the sense rather than the words; but in both the Hebrew and the Greek there is mention of thunder and lightning, which appear here to be indicated by the [storm] and the fire. It is signified, however, that the law has no Spirit present to console and quicken, as in the New Testament, but rather that it disturbs and nearly casts men down into despair. Although Chrysostom explains that what was signified is that the sluggishness of that ancient people ought in this way to be shaken off, and their minds stirred and roused to listen more attentively.

units.la: Tubæq; sonitum & uocē uerborum) Supra ex textu Exodi commemoratum est: Factum est, inquit, cum vox tubæ procederet, loquebatur Moses, & Deus respondebat ei per vocem. Atque hac ratione oportebat certos fieri, quod ipse Deus Mosi præcepta daret, non ipse sibi confingeret, aut mentiretur a Deo data: sicut mentiebatur Numa, dicens se edoceri a Dea Aegeria: alij multi similiter se a Deo doctos confingebant. Hic palam audiebatur ipsius Dei loquentis viua vox.
units.tr: And the sound of the trumpet and the voice of words) It was mentioned above from the text of Exodus: It came to pass, it says, when the sound of the trumpet went on, that Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice. And by this means it was necessary to be certain that God himself gave the precepts to Moses, and that he did not invent them himself or lie about things given by God, as Numa lied, saying he was taught by the goddess Egeria; and many others likewise falsely claimed to have been taught by God. Here the living voice of God himself speaking was plainly heard.

units.la: Quam qui audierant, deprecati sunt, ne his adiungeretur oratio:) Id est: ne diutius cogerentur audire ipsum Dominum loquentem. Græce est, παρῃτήσαντο μὴ προσθῆναι αὐτοῖς λόγον: quasi diceret: deprecati sunt, non addi seu adijci sibi sermonem. Territi antecedentibus cupiebant omitti sequentia, veriti longe graviora fore, quæ sequi debebant. Sic autem Exodi vicesimo: Omnes itaque populi videbant voces & lampades, & vocem tubæ, & montem fumantem, & videntes populi commoti sunt, steterunt-que procul. Atque dixerunt ipsi Mosi, loquere tu nobiscum, & audiemus, & non loquatur nobiscum Deus, ne forte moriamur. Id quod Moses quoq; repetit Deut.5. Item Deut.18. vbi quia non amplius possent audire Dominum loquentem de medio ignis, promittitur illis alius propheta Christus: propheta suscitabo eis de medio fratrum suorum, sicut tu, & pona verba mea in ore eius, & loquetur eis omnia, quæ præcepero illi. Erit autem, quicunq; non audierit verba mea, quæ loquetur in nomine meo, ego requiram ab eo, &c. De hoc paulo pòst, vbi agitur de persona Christi, Videte ne aspernemini eum, qui loquitur. In summa, omnia plena sunt terroribus, vbi lex illa datur.
units.tr: Those who had heard it begged that no further word be added to these things. That is, they begged not to be made to hear the Lord himself speaking any longer. The Greek is "they asked that no word be added to them" [παρῃτήσαντο μὴ προσθῆναι αὐτοῖς λόγον], as if he said: they begged that no speech be added or joined to them. Terrified by what had gone before, they wished the following things to be left out, fearing that what was to follow would be far more grievous. So in Exodus 20: "And all the people saw the voices and the lamps, and the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking; and when the people saw these things, they trembled and stood afar off. And they said to Moses, 'You speak with us, and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest perhaps we die.'" Moses repeats the same in Deut. 5. Likewise in Deut. 18, where, because they could no longer hear the Lord speaking out of the midst of the fire, another prophet, Christ, is promised to them: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And it shall be that whoever does not hear my words, which he speaks in my name, I will require it of him," etc. More on this shortly, where the person of Christ is discussed: "See that you do not refuse him who speaks." In sum, everything is full of terrors where that law is given.

units.la: Non enim ferebant, quod edicebatur: si bestia tetigerit montem, lapidabitur, aut iaculo configetur.
units.tr: For they could not bear what was commanded: if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned or pierced with a dart.

units.la: Exaggeratio metus hominum, ab edicto, quo arcebantur à montis accessu etiam bru-ta animantia. Ac videtur subesse ratiocinatio quædam à minori ad maius. Si periculum erit bruto animanti, vbi accesserit propius, quod tamen ratione non est præditum, quod┬ solet ad radicem montis pastum quærere: quanto maius periculum paratum est nobis, si accesserimus? Edictum autem hac de re habes Exod.19. Præscribes terminum populo per circuitum, dicens: Cauete vobis ne ascendatis in montem, aut tangatis extremitatem eius: omnis qui tetigerit montem, morte interficiatur. Nō tangat eum manus, alioquin lapidando lapidabitur, aut iaculis ferietur, siue iumentum fuerit, siue homo. Cæterū hoc loco Apostolus non meminit hominis, sed tantum iumenti: sed id per se intelligitur, maximè si consideretur, exaggerationis causa exprimi ista de iumentis.
units.tr: This is an exaggeration of the people's fear, drawn from the edict by which even brute animals were kept from approaching the mountain. And there seems to lie beneath it a kind of argument from the lesser to the greater: if a brute animal, which nonetheless lacks reason, will be in danger when it comes nearer (as it is accustomed to do, seeking pasture at the foot of the mountain), how much greater danger is prepared for us if we draw near? The edict on this matter is in Exodus 19: "You shall set bounds for the people all around, saying: Take heed to yourselves that you do not go up into the mountain or touch its border; everyone who touches the mountain shall be put to death. No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot through with darts, whether it be beast or man." However, here the Apostle makes no mention of man, but only of the beast; yet this is understood of itself, especially if one considers that these things about beasts are stated for the sake of exaggeration.

units.la: Significatur autem hoc edicto, quòd hominibus pecuino more viuentibus ad Deum res q; diuinas aditus non pateat. Animales homines, nihil supra hominem sentientes, nō possunt sapere ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei: & non multò præstantiores brutis sunt, si spectetur in quam rerum diuinarum cognitio.
units.tr: By this edict it is signified that the way to divine things toward God was not open to men who live in a brutish manner. Animal men, who perceive nothing above man, cannot understand the things that are of the Spirit of God; and they are not much better than brutes, if one considers their knowledge of divine things.

units.la: Et adeò terribile erat visum, quod apparebat. Moses dixit: Expauefactus sum ac tremebundus.
units.tr: And the sight that appeared was so terrible. Moses said: I am exceedingly afraid and trembling.

units.la: Alia exaggeratio à persona Moseh: quasi dicatur: Ipse Moses, qui erat interpres Dei, & & conscius rerum perficiendarum, fuit perterrefactus, & nullus à terrore immunis fuit: quid mirum igitur, quòd reliqui sunt perterriti, quòd non adeò sciebant, quænam essent gerenda?
units.tr: Another exaggeration, drawn from the person of Moses: as if it were said: Moses himself, who was the interpreter of God and aware of what was to be done, was struck with terror, and no one was free from fear. What wonder, then, that the rest were terrified, since they did not know well what was to be done?

units.la: Cæterum hæc verba ex illorum videntur numero, propter quæ nonnulli aliquando caussati sunt, hanc epistolam non esse Pauli. Neque enim inuenitur in sacris, à Mose hu-iusmodi quicquam esse dictum. Sed dici potest, nihil absurdè fieri hic, si tribuatur ei quasi per ἀδοποιίαν, quod certum est, in ipso considerari debere, atque in ipsius hæsisse animo. Certè Exodi tertio, cùm Moses vocaretur à Deo ex rubo, ibi dicitur: Operuit Moses faciem suā, quoniā timuit aspicere ad Deum. Et hoc ipso cap. Exod.10. ad populū sic ait; Ne timueritis, propterea enim, ut tentaret vos, venit Deus, & ut timor illius esset in facie vestra, ne peccaretis. Si igitur Moses antea quidem valde timuit, cū primum vocaretur, & iam postea significat in populo timorem requiri, certum est ipsum quoq; tunc nequaquam fuisse timore vacuum. Et profectò est religiosi animi, cum timore & tremore ad ies sacras accedere. Non est igitur alienum, tribui Mosi, tanquam si ea dixerit, quæ illi in animo fuisse non est dubium, per ἀδοποιίαν. Proinde hæc omnia faciunt ad ostendendum summatim, quicquid in lege erat, tendere ad timorē nihilq;, ad consolationem in ea positum: & nihilominus debuisse eos in tali timore sanctificari. Ex quo clarissime sequitur, quòd, cùm in euangelio omnia sint diuersissima, & ad bonum parata, æquissimum sit, vt sanctimonium multò quàm antea colant diligentius. Hæc est omnium istorum summa. Sequitur autem nunc altera pars contentionis, de euangelio videlicet.
units.tr: Moreover, these words seem to belong to those on account of which some have at times alleged that this letter is not Paul's. For nothing of this kind is found in the sacred books as said by Moses. But it can be said that nothing absurd happens here if it is attributed to him by way of prosopopoeia, since it is certain that these things ought to be considered in him and lay in his mind. Certainly in Exodus 3, when Moses was called by God out of the bush, it is said there: "Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look upon God." And in Exodus 20 he says to the people: "Do not fear, for God has come in order to test you, and so that his fear may be before your faces, that you may not sin." If therefore Moses earlier greatly feared, when he was first called, and now afterwards indicates that fear is required in the people, it is certain that he himself was not free from fear at that time either. And truly it is the mark of a religious mind to approach holy things with fear and trembling. It is not therefore unfitting to attribute to Moses, as if he had said those things which there is no doubt were in his mind, by prosopopoeia. Accordingly, all these things serve to show, in summary, that whatever was in the law tended to fear, and that nothing was placed in it for consolation; and that nevertheless they ought to have been made holy in such fear. From this it follows most clearly that, since in the gospel all things are most different and prepared for good, it is most fitting that they cultivate holiness far more diligently than before. This is the sum of all those things. Now follows the second part of the contrast, namely concerning the gospel.

units.la: Sed accessistis ad montem Sion) Secunda pars contentionis, in qua omnia diligenter obseruanda, vt intelligatur amplissima euangelij præ lege dignitas atque eminentia. Et singula membra magnum habent pondus ad amplificandam euangelij præstantiam, maxime quia etiam cum ratione quadam incrementi sunt ita, vti vides, collocata, & nullu fere est, ex quo non aliqua apta & grauis ratio suasoria ad colendam veram sanctimoniam posset colligi.
units.tr: But you have come to Mount Zion. This is the second part of the contrast, in which everything must be observed carefully, so that the very great dignity and pre-eminence of the gospel above the law may be understood. And each single member carries great weight for magnifying the excellence of the gospel, especially since they are arranged, as you see, with a certain ratio of increase; and there is scarcely any of them from which some apt and weighty argument for persuading the cultivation of true holiness could not be drawn.

units.la: Recte hic Chrysostomus: Qui comparationes faciunt, alteram partem deprimunt, ut res alterius partis emineant: hic & hic ex comparatione illorum nostra maiora declarantur, & meliora, & manuetiora, & admirationum plenissima.
units.tr: Chrysostom rightly says here: "Those who make comparisons lower the one side so that the things of the other side may stand out. Here, by comparison with those things, our things are declared to be greater, better, and gentler, and full of wonders."

units.la: Neque verò ita est contentionis hic decorum obseruatum, vt membra membris respondeant: sed ad ostendendam excellentiam euangelij, diuersa & longè superiora sunt omnia in hac posteriori parte.
units.tr: Nor indeed is the fitting order of the contrast observed here in such a way that member answers to member; rather, to show the excellence of the gospel, all the things in this latter part are different and far superior.

units.la: Tantùm opponitur mons monti:ille,qui erat Syna,ei,qui dictus est Syon:cætera noncoueniunt.Nam incenso igni,qui perterrefaciebat,debebat rursus aliquid aliud opponi ex euangelio,quod animos placidos & quietos redderet: Turbini & caligini opponendû erat aliquid aliud de charitate & perspicuitate facta in euangelio. Procellæ & tubarum sono debebat opponi vehementia prædicationis euangelij, & sonus Apostolorum, qui exijt in vniuersum orbem.
units.tr: Only mount is set against mount: that which was Sinai against that which is called Zion; the rest do not correspond. For against the fire that kindled terror, something else from the gospel ought to be set, which would render the minds calm and quiet; against the storm and the darkness something else had to be set concerning the charity and clarity made in the gospel. Against the crash of the trumpets ought to be set the vehemence of the gospel's preaching, and the sound of the Apostles, which went out into the whole world.

units.la: Voci verborum opponenda erat vox Dei patris de cœlo audita:vel certè vox ipsiusChristi concionantis.Sed apostolus non curauit omnia tam pueriliter obseruare : sedposuit interea,quæ multis interuallis sunt præstantiora. Et potuisset profectò facile in-uenire in historia euangelica,quæ ijs, quæ gesta sunt, cùm daretur lex, respondentferé per omnia. Nam solent quidam res gestas in Syna accipere, tanquam typum eorum, quæ gesta sunt in misione spiritus Sancti ad Apostolos diepentecostes: & in hac misione Spiritus multa paria esse conspecta.Sic namque Actorum secundo:Factusest repente de cœlo sonitus, tanquam impetu venientis flatus vehementis, & repleuittotam domum, vbi erant sedentes.Et visæ sunt illis differtæ linguæ, velut igneæ, sede-runtque super singulos eorum,& repleti sunt omnes spiritu Sancto,coeperuntque loquialijs linguis,prout Spiritus ille dabat eloquii illis. Et paulò post:Is rumor cùm increbuis-set,conuenit multitudo & confusa est, quòd audiret vnusquisque lingua sua illos lo-quentes . Ecce sonitus tanquam impetuosi flatus & thyellæ,ecce ignis linguarum spe cie dispersus:ecce vox nouis linguis loquentium apostolorum: ecce multitudinem con currentem & confusam.Quò pertinet,quòd in Syna latam legem literæ dicunt,hic ve-rò legem Spiritus. Quid?Quòd in tepore cöeuniunt ? Nã, vt ǵo. die à celebrato pafcate data lex:ita ǵo. die à celebrato pafcate per Christũ,missus est S. S. Potuisset igitur Apostolus facile hoc pacto alia proferre,quib.ratio cötentionís fuisset,vt apparet,exactius red-dita, & quæ euangelij dignitatem non parum illustrassent : sed placuit illi alia via ingre-di, & longè grauiora in medium proferre.Quid ergo facit Apostolus? Vbi in priore parte contentionis constituit illa de monte contacto, & commemorauit,ad omnium horro-rem & consternationem facta, quæ legis naturam arguunt:nùc in posteriori parte etiam ponit de monte,sed longè diuerso, & valde amœno:neq; colligit, aliqua in eo gesta, sed adiungit monti ciuitatem,tum ciues,politiam,magistratum,religionem,in ea,& in sum ma,amplissimam constituit eius ciuitatis dignitatem.
units.tr: To the voice of words ought to be opposed the voice of God the Father heard from heaven, or certainly the voice of Christ himself preaching. But the Apostle did not care to observe everything so childishly; instead he has set forth those things which are far more excellent by many intervals. And he could certainly have easily found in the evangelical history things that correspond almost in every respect to those things which happened when the law was given. For some are accustomed to take the events at Sinai as a type of those things which happened in the mission of the Holy Spirit to the Apostles on the day of Pentecost; and in this mission of the Spirit many parallels have been observed. For thus in Acts 2: "Suddenly there came from heaven a sound, as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them tongues divided, as of fire, and they sat upon each one of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." And a little after: "When this rumor had spread, the multitude came together and was confused, because each one heard them speaking in his own language." Behold a sound as of a rushing and violent wind, and behold fire dispersed in the form of tongues; behold the voice of the apostles speaking in new tongues; behold the multitude coming together and confused. To this pertains what they say, that at Sinai the law was given in letter, but here the law of the Spirit. What of this, that they assemble on the fiftieth day? For as the law was given on the fiftieth day after the celebrated Passover, so on the fiftieth day after the celebrated Passover through Christ, the Holy Spirit was sent. The Apostle could therefore easily have set forth other things in this way, by which the reason of the contrast would have been rendered, as it appears, more exactly, and which would not a little have illustrated the dignity of the gospel; but it pleased him to enter by another path and to bring forward things far weightier. What then does the Apostle do? Where in the first part of the contrast he set down those things about the mountain that was touched, and recalled, to the horror and consternation of all, the things that show the nature of the law; now in the second part he also speaks of a mountain, but a very different one, and very pleasant; nor does he gather any deeds done in it, but he joins to the mountain a city, then its citizens, polity, magistracy, religion in it; and in sum, he sets up the most ample dignity of that city.

units.la: Quibus profectò sic illustratur dignitas Euangelij,ut clarè percipiatur, tanto potius esse,sub euangelio,quàm sub lege,quàtò satius est,esse in ciuitate bene munita, optimis legibus ordinata,in religione probè confirmata,vbi tutò & quietè agas, omniaque habeas ad vitam necessaria:quàm esse in deserto,oberrare perpetuò,vbi vndique imminet pericula:nullam habere rempublicam:non inuenire, quæ ad vitam sustentandam sunt necessaria.Hoc discrimen mihi videtur hic expositum, quod reuera magnum est. Sed clarior euadet discriminis huius magnitudo in singulorum membrorum consideratio-ne,ait ergo:
units.tr: Through these things the dignity of the Gospel is so clearly set forth that it is plainly seen to be far better to live under the Gospel than under the Law. It is as much better as it is to live in a well-fortified city, ordered by the best laws and firmly established in religion, where you can act safely and quietly and have everything necessary for life, than to be in a desert, wandering endlessly where dangers threaten on every side, without any commonwealth and unable to find what is needed to sustain life. This contrast seems to me to be what is set out here, and it is truly a great one. But the greatness of this contrast will become clearer if we consider each of the parts separately. So he says:

units.la: Sed accessistis ad montem Sion:)En mons Sion opponitur monti contacto Sina.De situ etiâ diuerso non est quod multa in præsentiarum adferamus. Hoc verò præcipuè considerandum est,quomodo ab istis corporalibus rebus debeamus hic transitum facere ad spiritualia.Alias quidem perexiguum foret,decere,quod credentes transfissent ad montem Sion terrestrem,& Hierosolymam terrestrem:patres verò tantùm hæsissent prope monte Sina,& in deserto.Et quis erat statua montis Sion & Hierosolymæ terrenæ,cùm ista scriberentur?Ibi erant hostes euangelij,& crudelissimi persecutores omnium credentium euangelio. Ergo necessarium est, de spirituali Hierosolyma, de spirituali monte Sion ista intelligamus.
units.tr: "But you have come to Mount Sion" (Heb. 12:22). Here Mount Sion is set against Mount Sinai, the mount that could be touched. There is no need to say much at present about the different location. What must be considered above all is how we ought to pass from these bodily things to spiritual ones. Otherwise it would be quite pointless to say that the believers had come to the earthly Mount Sion and the earthly Jerusalem, while the fathers had remained only near Mount Sinai, in the desert. And what was the state of the earthly Mount Sion and Jerusalem when these things were written? There were the enemies of the Gospel, the most cruel persecutors of all who believed the Gospel. Therefore we must understand these things of the spiritual Jerusalem and the spiritual Mount Sion.

units.la: Ita namque alijs quoque locis noui testamenti docemur, ea quæ corporaliter gesta sunt olim in veteri testamento,spiritualiter rebus nostris in euangelio accommodare. Hinc Christus serpentem in deserto exaltatum à Mose interpretatur fuisse suæ personæ typum,Ioan.3.1.Corinth.10.ait Apostolus,Patres omnes in nube & mari baptizatos ef-fe:aquam è petra fluetem significasse spiritualem potum sanguinis Christi:omnia deni-que figuras fuisse nostri & rerum nostrarum.Galat.4.Duos filios Abrahæ ait adumbras-se legem & euangelium:& montis Sina meminit,veluti quem opponere vellet monti Sion.
units.tr: For in other places of the New Testament we are also taught in this way: that the things which were done bodily in the Old Testament are to be applied spiritually to our situation in the Gospel. Hence Christ interprets the serpent lifted up in the desert by Moses as a type of his own person (John 3:14). The Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 10 that all the fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea; that the water flowing from the rock signified the spiritual drink of Christ's blood; and, in short, that all these things were types of us and of our affairs. In Galatians 4 he says that the two sons of Abraham foreshadowed the Law and the Gospel, and he mentions Mount Sinai as if he wished to set it against Mount Sion.

units.la: Ephes.2.Carnali circumcisioni,& reipublicæ Israelis opponit credentes,quorum cir-cumcisio est spiritualis,& pertinent ad veram Dei rempublicam. Sic denique alibi alia occurrunt,quæ non obscurè nos docent,quomodo à corporalibus debeamus ad spiri-ritualia transfire. In hac epistola lex dicitur vmbra futurorum bonorum: & Melchisedec typus Christi: Item tabernaculum typus ecclesiae: sancta sanctorum regnum coeleste.
units.tr: In Ephesians 2 he sets believers, whose circumcision is spiritual and who belong to the true commonwealth of God, against fleshly circumcision and the commonwealth of Israel. So too, in other places, other passages occur which teach us plainly how we ought to pass from bodily things to spiritual ones. In this letter the Law is called "a shadow of the good things to come" (Heb. 10:1); Melchizedek is a type of Christ (Heb. 7); likewise the tabernacle is a type of the Church, and the Holy of Holies is the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Simili igitur ratione & hoc loco est faciundum. Monti Sina opponitur mons Sion: sed spiritualiter. Sina quidem legem repraesentat: sicut & Apostolus interpretatur Galat. 4. dicens: Num haec duo sunt testamenta? vnum quidem a monte Sina, in seruitutem generans, quae est Agar. Nam Agar Sina mons est in Arabia, confinis est autem ei, quae nunc vocatur Hierusalem, seruit autem cum filijs suis. Sion vero repraesentat Euangelium. Vterque mons: quia ecclesia saepe in scripturis nomine montis appellatur, vtpote in sublimi posita, bene fundata, immobilis, &c. Psalmo 14. Domine, quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo, aut, quis requiescet in monte Sancto? Item psalm. 47. Mons Dei mons pinguis, mons in quo beneplacitum est Deo habitare in eo. Sed mons Sion maxime proprie significat ecclesiam: quia mons Sion erat habitatio populi Dei. Vbi autem populus Dei, ibi credentes: vbi credentes, ibi ecclesia. Sic de vocatis per gratiam Dei in ecclesiam psalm. 77. Induxit eos in montem sanctificationis suae, quem acquisiuit dextera eius. Et ex Sion egressa est lex, egressum est Euangelium, iuxta illud Esaiae 2. Erit in nouissimo dierum, erit praeparatus mons domus Domini in vertice montium, eleuabiturque supra colles, & fluent ad eum omnes gentes. Et ibidem: Quoniam de Zion exibit lex & verbum Domini de Hierusalem. Eadem habentur Micheae 4. Et vtrobique additur diserte, quod ad illum montem ibunt gentes multae. Quare necessario de ecclesia collecta ex gentibus locus intelligitur. Sententia igitur Apostoli est in hoc primo membro, quia translati erant Hebraei ex seruitute legis in libertatem Euangelij, & iam inhabitabant montem spiritualem Zion, quae est ecclesia, merito eos debere sanctimoniam studiose colere.
units.tr: Therefore in the same way we must proceed in this passage. Mount Sion is set against Mount Sinai, but spiritually. Sinai indeed represents the Law, as the Apostle himself explains in Galatians 4, saying: "Are these two covenants? One indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar. For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she is joined to that Jerusalem which is now called, and she serves with her children." But Sion represents the Gospel. Both are mountains, because the Church is often called by the name of a mountain in the Scriptures, since it is set on high, well founded, immovable, and so on. Psalm 15 (14): "Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? Or who shall rest on your holy mountain?" Likewise Psalm 47 (48): "The mountain of God is a fat mountain, a mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell." But Mount Sion most properly signifies the Church, because Mount Sion was the dwelling place of the people of God. Where the people of God are, there are believers; where believers are, there is the Church. So of those called into the Church by the grace of God, Psalm 78 (77): "He brought them to the mount of his sanctification, which his right hand has acquired." And "the law went out of Sion, and the Gospel went out," according to that saying of Isaiah 2: "In the last of the days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be lifted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it." And in the same place: "For out of Sion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." The same things are found in Micah 4, and in both places it is expressly added that many nations will go to that mountain. Hence the place must necessarily be understood of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. The meaning of the Apostle in this first member, therefore, is this: the Hebrews had been transferred from the bondage of the Law into the freedom of the Gospel, and now they dwelt on the spiritual mountain Sion, which is the Church; and for that reason they ought to cultivate holiness diligently.

units.la: Et ciuitatem Dei viuentis) Non in deserto amplius agentes, sed in ampla & celebri ciuitate: neque ciuitate impiorum, qualis est Hierosolyma coelestis, sed Dei. Sunt quidem omnes ciuitates Dei: quandoquidem Domini est terra & plenitudo eius: sed haec potissimum sic appellatur, quia Domino placet in ea coli, Dominus eam cum suis sanctis inhabitat. Sic quoque dicebatur Hierusalem ciuitas Dei, quod Deus illam prae caeteris delegisset, sed in typo ecclesiae, de qua est illud: Haec requies mea in seculum seculi, hic habitabo, quoniam elegi eam. Et Christus ad discipulos: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem seculi.
units.tr: "And to the city of the living God" (Heb. 12:22). Not dwelling any longer in the desert, but in a great and famous city: not a city of the impious, as the earthly Jerusalem was, but the city of God. All cities are indeed God's, since the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof (Ps. 24:1); but this one is called so above all, because it pleases the Lord to be worshipped in it, and the Lord dwells in it with his saints. So also Jerusalem was called the city of God, because God had chosen it above others; but this was in a type of the Church, of which it is said: "This is my rest for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it" (Ps. 132:14). And Christ said to the disciples: "Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the world" (Matt. 28:20).

units.la: Sed vocatur insuper ciuitas Dei viuentis, quia Deus autor vitae in illa vitam dat, ita vt extra eam non sit salus cuiquam expectanda. Efaiae autem tricesimo tertio etiam Sion vocatur ciuitas. Respice, inquit, Sion ciuitatem solemnitatis nostrae. Proinde ex hoc membro istud sequitur, quod, qui volunt agnoscere tanquam ad ciuitatem istam pertinentes, ita vitam instituant, vt decet bonos ciues. Vbi quis recusat viuere legibus ciuitatis, ad quam peruenerit, iubetur exire: ita plane & hic fiet, qui nolet sanctimoniam colere, non poterit in monte sancto, siue in ecclesiae sancta ciuitate haerere.
units.tr: But it is moreover called the city of the living God, because God, the author of life, gives life in it, so that outside it no one may expect salvation. In Isaiah 33 Sion is also called a city: "Look upon Sion," he says, "the city of our solemnity." Accordingly, from this member the following follows: those who wish to acknowledge that they belong to that city ought to order their lives as good citizens should. If anyone refuses to live by the laws of the city to which he has come, he is ordered to leave; so too here, whoever refuses to cultivate holiness will not be able to remain on the holy mountain, that is, in the holy city of the Church.

units.la: Hierusalem coelestem) Ad discrimen illius terrenae, quae etiam ciuitas Dei gaudebat appellari, sed reuera nullo modo conferenda cum praesenti: & in hac sola datur vera pacis visio, qualis in lege videri non poterat. Sic vero & ad Galat. 4. ecclesia vocatur Hierusalem coelestis & libera, quia in Euangelio libertas: at Hierusalem terrena pertinax cultrix legis seruit cum filijs suis. Porro appellatio ciuitatis coelestis admonet omnes, vt coelestia tantum velint sapere, & licet corporibus haereant in terris, animo tamen versentur in coelis: quemadmodum etiam Colos. 3. dicitur, si resurrexistis vna cum Christo, super na quaerite, vbi Christus est, ad dexteram Dei sedens: superna curate, non terrestria. Ergo habent & hic Hebraei latens argumentum, quoad sanctimoniam colendam excitentur.
units.tr: "To the heavenly Jerusalem" (Heb. 12:22). This is set in contrast with that earthly Jerusalem, which also rejoiced to be called the city of God, but which in truth is in no way to be compared with the present one; and in this one alone is given the true vision of peace, such as could not be seen under the Law. So also in Galatians 4 the Church is called the heavenly and free Jerusalem, because in the Gospel there is liberty; but the earthly Jerusalem, a stubborn worshipper of the Law, serves with her children. Moreover, the name of the heavenly city admonishes everyone to desire to savour only heavenly things, and although they cling to the earth in their bodies, to dwell in their minds in heaven. Just as Colossians 3 says: "If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God; mind the things that are above, not the things that are on the earth." Therefore the Hebrews also have here a hidden argument, by which they are roused to cultivate holiness.

units.la: Et ad innumerabilium angelorum coetum) (id est, cum millenarijs aliquot angelorum: ita enim sonat graecum) Mirabiliter exornat istam ciuitatem, quae est ecclesia, Apostolus: & quicquid in bene constituta ciuitate ad conseruationem eius posset desiderari, Apostolus etiam ecclesiae tribuit. Solent autem in ciuitatibus constitui praesidia, quae eam seruent: item quae prohibeant motus ac tumultus. Ita in ecclesia constituuntur Angeli custodes eius, & omnium piorum, qui inuigilant, ne diabolus damnum inferat. Sic autem Dominus in parabola angelos introducit constitutos ad separandum zizania a tritico. Et angeli alioqui sunt ministratorij spiritus, ad tuitionem etiam bonorum ordinati, semper assistentes coram Deo parati ad omnia. Neque inter creaturas vllae excellentiores, neque puriores cum ita ordinarit Deus, vt semel seruando eos a lapsu impeccabiles deinceps eos reddiderit. Vnde pro summa puritate solet puritas angelica describi. Quamobrem qui in talium angelorum coetu volet viuere, debebit & ipse sanctimoniae dare operam, aliás per sanctos illos angelos expellendus. Et ad concionem primogenitorum, qui conscripti sunt in coelis) Iam audis, quales etiam cives ibi inhabitent: nempe concio & frequentia primogenitorum, id est, electorum, & omni virtute praestantium. Ita enim primogeniti electi & praestantes prae caeteris appellantur: quando primogenitis semper praerogatiua quaedam concessa est: & populus Israel electus vocatus est a Deo primogenitus. Exodi 4. Quanquam primogeniti possunt dici credentes, quadam participatione, qua a Christo vere primogenito vniuersae creaturae, Colof. 1. ius primogenituræ spiritualis ac cipiunt, vt sint dilecti filij patris coelestis.
units.tr: "And to an innumerable company of angels" (that is, with some thousands of angels; for so the Greek sounds). The Apostle wonderfully adorns that city, which is the Church, and whatever could be desired in a well-ordered city for its preservation, the Apostle also attributes to the Church. Garrisons are usually placed in cities to guard them, and likewise to prevent movements and tumults. So in the Church guardian angels are appointed, both for it and for all the godly, who keep watch lest the devil inflict harm. And the Lord in the parable introduces angels appointed to separate the tares from the wheat (Matt. 13:30). Angels are, moreover, ministering spirits, ordained also for the protection of the good, always standing before God and ready for all things. Among creatures there are none more excellent or purer, since God so ordained that, having preserved them once from falling, he made them thenceforth unable to sin. Hence angelic purity is usually described as the highest purity. Therefore whoever wishes to live in the company of such angels must himself also take pains to cultivate holiness, or else he will be driven out by those holy angels. "And to the assembly of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven" (Heb. 12:23). Now you hear what sort of citizens also dwell there: namely the assembly and throng of the firstborn, that is, of the elect and those who excel in every virtue. For the firstborn, the elect and the outstanding, are called so above others, since a certain pre-eminence has always been granted to firstborns; and the people of Israel, being chosen, was called by God his firstborn (Exod. 4:22). Although believers may also be called firstborn, by a certain participation, by which they receive from Christ, the true firstborn of every creature (Col. 1:15), the right of spiritual primogeniture, so that they may be the beloved sons of the heavenly Father.

units.la: Addit: qui conscripti sunt in coelis: forma inde sumpta, quod cives solent in album praetoris conscribi, ac tum gaudere iure municipali, & immunitate aliisque publicis priuilegijs. Sic vero & piorum nomina conscripta sunt in coelis, dicente Christo, Gaudete & exultate, quia nomina vestra conscripta sunt in coelis, Lucae 10. Et hinc quoque liber vitae toties memoratur, qui revera est liber huius ciuitatis, videlicet ecclesiae. Estque haec conscriptio ipsa Dei praedestinatio, qua, quicquid semel constitutum est, non potest mutari vel expungi. Unde certitudo, quam credentes debent de Dei bonitate habere, in libri huius Scriptura denotatur. Proinde qui volunt inter cives talis ciuitatis haberi, & nomina sua manere conscripta in libro vitae, debent sanctimoniam studiose colere.
units.tr: He adds, who are enrolled in heaven: the image is taken from the custom by which citizens are written on the praetor's list, and so enjoy municipal rights, exemption, and other public privileges. So too the names of the godly are enrolled in heaven, as Christ says: "Rejoice and be glad, because your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10). And hence the book of life is also so often mentioned, which is truly the book of this city, namely the church. This enrolment is itself God's predestination, by which whatever has once been decreed cannot be changed or blotted out. Hence the certainty that believers ought to have concerning God's goodness is signified in the Scripture of this book. Therefore those who wish to be counted among the citizens of such a city, and to have their names remain enrolled in the book of life, ought to cultivate holiness diligently.

units.la: Et ad iudicem uniuersorum Deum) hic describitur magistratus ciuitatis: est in ea Iudex, & quidem qui non potest falli, neque ferre iniquam sententiam, nempe Deus.
