Qui est iudex non tantum quorundam, sed vniuersorum, etiam extra ciuitatem illam agentium: vt optio detur iudicari vel in ciuitate illa, vel extra ciuitatem, tamen iudicari ab illo necessum est: siue boni, siue mali debent ab illo audire extremam sententiam ad vitam, vel ad mortem aeternam. Est autem iudicium in ecclesia, quia ecclesia etiam lege vtitur ad commonendum & perterrefaciendum malos, quibus oportet ostendi peccata, & argui, vt adducantur ad poenitentiam. Ergo restat, vt, quando ecclesia habet suum coram illo inueniamur, & nequaquam cum mundo immundo damnemur.
units.tr: And to God the judge of all: here the magistracy of the city is described. In it there is a judge, and indeed one who cannot be deceived or pronounce an unjust sentence, namely God. He is judge not only of some but of all, including those who act outside that city. So although there is the option of being judged either in that city or outside it, one must in any case be judged by him: good and bad alike must hear from him the final sentence, to eternal life or to eternal death. Now there is judgment in the church, because the church also uses the law to warn and terrify the wicked, to whom their sins must be shown and reproved so that they may be brought to repentance. It remains, therefore, that when the church holds its judgment, we be found before him, and by no means be condemned with the unclean world.

units.la: Et ad spiritus iustorum perfectorum) Ecce senatus huius ciuitatis, homines plane spirituales & iam perfecti. Qui certe non possunt intelligi, nisi corpore exuti, & alteram iam adepti vitam in coelis. Tales enim proprie sunt perfecti: nulli autem hic mundo perfecti. Tales etiam sunt spiritus, quando nimirum anima illorum cum Deo, & apud Deum, & per Deum viuit. Sic vero & Christus promisit Apostolis suis, quod cum ipso sessuri esSent super duodecim sedes & iudicaturi duodecim tribus Israel. Et alibi quoque describitur venturus cum multitudine & sanctis innumeris. Iam qui intuetur talem Senatum, & cogitat, se apud talem sisti debere, quomodo non erit solicitus, vt perfectus euadat, vt vitam spiritualem transfigat. Hinc quoque liquet, quod sancti, qui hinc migrarunt, pertinent ad ecclesiam, suntque eius iudices & inspectores: neque opus est distingui ecclesiam in militantem & triumphantem.
units.tr: And to the spirits of just men made perfect: behold the senate of this city, men who are truly spiritual and already perfect. These cannot be understood except as stripped of the body and having already attained another life in heaven. For these are properly the perfect; but no one in this world is perfect. Such too are the spirits, namely when their souls live with God, before God, and through God. So Christ indeed promised his apostles that they would sit with him on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel. And elsewhere he is described as coming with a multitude and countless saints. Now whoever looks upon such a senate and considers that he must stand before such judges, how will he not be anxious to become perfect and to pass his life in the Spirit? Hence it is also clear that the saints who have departed hence belong to the church, and are its judges and overseers; nor is there any need to distinguish the church into militant and triumphant.

units.la: Et ad noui testamenti conciliatorem Iesum) Hic de religione agitur in illa ciuitate. Proponitur conciliator inter Deum & homines summus sacerdos Iesus Christus. Hic etiam intercedit pro nobis coram feuerisimo iudice, & Senatu apostolico. Iuxta illud: Si quis nostrum peccauerit, habemus aduocatum Iesum, qui interpellat pro nobis. Iudex paulo ante propositus aliquid legale & metuendum exhibebat: sed hic additus conciliator Christus, quod euangelij est, refert. Ita enim ecclesia & euangelio regitur, & post legem praedicatam proponit euangelium, in quo gratiam propter Christum promittit. Et propter ea etiam additur hic, quod sit conciliator noui testamenti. Nam in veteri testamento non erat talis conciliator propositus, non erat gratia oblata, quemadmodum in Euangelio offertur. Quamobrem decet, vt propter talem conciliatorem etiam moueamur ad sanctimoniam colendam.
units.tr: And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant: here religion in that city is spoken of. Jesus Christ, the highest priest, is set forth as mediator between God and men. He also intercedes for us before the most severe judge and the apostolic senate, according to that saying: "If anyone of us sins, we have an advocate, Jesus, who intercedes for us." The judge, proposed a little before, presented something legal and fearful; but the mediator Christ, added here, brings what belongs to the gospel. For so the church is governed too: after the law has been preached, it sets forth the gospel, in which for Christ's sake it promises grace. For this reason it is added here that he is mediator of the new covenant. In the Old Testament no such mediator was set forth, and grace was not offered as it is offered in the Gospel. Wherefore it is fitting that, on account of such a mediator, we also be moved to cultivate holiness.

units.la: Et ad sanguinem aspersionis, meliora loquentem, quam loquebatur sanguis Abel) Additur & de sacrificijs in hac ciuitate. In ea valet sanguis aspersus, non quidem taurorum, hircorum, aut vitulorum: sicut solet fieri in Hierusalem terrena: sed sanguis Christi, qui per sanguinem veteris testamenti adumbrabatur, & qui solus inuentus est efficax ad tollendum peccata: qua de re supra saepe & copiose: quamuis videri potest respicere Apostolus ad id, quod populus post acceptam legem aspersus est sanguine. Ergo propter talem sanguinem, ne videaris eum conculcare, debes ad sanctimoniam veram colendam excitari, magis quam mouebatur vnquam vlli propter res vmbraticas in lege, per quas vera sanctificatio non poterat contingere.
units.tr: And to the sprinkling of blood, speaking better things than the blood of Abel: there is also mention of sacrifices in this city. In it the sprinkled blood avails, not indeed that of bulls, goats or calves, as was usual in earthly Jerusalem, but the blood of Christ, which was foreshadowed through the blood of the old covenant, and which alone has been found effective for taking away sins. On this matter we have often and fully spoken above, although it may be seen that the Apostle is looking to the fact that the people, after receiving the law, were sprinkled with blood. Therefore, on account of such blood, lest you seem to trample it underfoot, you ought to be stirred to cultivate true holiness, more than anyone was ever moved by the shadowy things of the law, through which true sanctification could not come about.

units.la: Et ad sanguinem Abel, quam loquebatur sanguis Abel: facit id ad commendationem effectus sanguinis Christi, in quo habemus omnia bona expectare, nempe remissionem missionem peccatorum, &c. Sanguis quidem Abel loquebatur & clamabat vltionem de terra (ita enim per prosopopœiam legimus de sanguine Abel: id quod supra cap.11. à nobis est expositum) at sanguis Christi non clamat vltionem, sed potius misericordiâ. Vnde Christus etiam orauit Patrem, vt ignosceret crucifixoribus. Et priusquam mo- retetur, Matth.26. Hic est sanguis noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Estque elegans typus Christi in Abel. Nam Christus à fratribus quoque interfectus est, vt Abel, & quidem innocenter. Cain propterea reiectus est à Domino, & profugus egit super terram: hoc idem & in Iudæis licet in hunc vsque diem videre. Sed hoc diuersum est in Christo & Abele, quòd Christus filius Dei, & sanguis eius postulat remitti peccata: Abel filius hominis, & sanguis eius postulat vindictam. Ergo sanguis Christi longè meliora loquitur. Porrò de efficacia sanguinis Christi supra dictum est. Porrò dignum esset, agere fusius de huius ciuitatis amplitudine ac dignitate: sed tempus non fert: quare ad doctrinam, quam hinc colligere debemus, properabimus.
units.tr: And to the blood of Abel, which spoke: this serves to commend the effect of Christ's blood, in which we are to expect all good things, namely the remission of sins, and so on. The blood of Abel indeed spoke and cried out for vengeance from the earth (for so, by prosopopoeia, we read of Abel's blood; this we explained above at chapter 11). But the blood of Christ does not cry out for vengeance but rather for mercy. Whence Christ also prayed the Father to forgive his crucifiers, and before he died, Matt. 26: "This is the blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins." And Christ is an elegant type in Abel. For Christ too was killed by brothers, as Abel was, and indeed innocently. Cain was therefore rejected by the Lord and wandered over the earth; the same can be seen in the Jews even to this day. But there is a difference between Christ and Abel: Christ, the Son of God, and his blood asks for sins to be forgiven; Abel, the son of man, and his blood asks for vengeance. Therefore the blood of Christ speaks far better things. Moreover, what the efficacy of Christ's blood is has been said above. It would be worth treating more fully the greatness and dignity of this city, but time does not permit; so we shall hasten to the teaching we ought to gather from this.

units.la: Discimus autem ex his, primò, maximam esse Euangelij præstantiam præ lege: quanta est inter desertum, & ciuitatem benè constitutam.
units.tr: We learn from these things, first, that the excellence of the Gospel over the law is very great: as great as the difference between a desert and a well-founded city.

units.la: Secundò: hoc potissimum differre, quòd lex habet omnia plena timoris, & perterrefacit, incutitque timorem. Contrà, Euangelium solatur, erigit, proponit dilectionem Dei & hominum.
units.tr: Second: this above all differs, that the law is full of fear, terrifies, and instils dread. On the contrary, the Gospel consoles, raises up, and sets forth the love of God and of men.

units.la: Tertiò: Sed & alia legis officia & proprietates ex descriptionibus, quæ hîc habentur, colligi queunt: vt quòd lex tantùm sit in caligine: quòd tantùm habeat vmbram futurorum bonorum: cuiusmodi nonnulla inter explicandum adnotauimus.
units.tr: Third: other offices and properties of the law can also be gathered from the descriptions given here: that the law is only in darkness, and has only the shadow of future good things. Some of these we have noted in the course of the explanation.

units.la: Quartò: discimus, quomodo, quæ in terra promissa contigerunt temporalia, ad fœlicitatem sub lege referenda, ea nos spiritualiter accipere debeamus & interpretari de vera fœlicitate, quæ exhibetur sub Euangelio. Ita mons Sion, ciuitas Hierusalem nobis adumbrant ipsam ecclesiam, in qua verè percipiuntur spiritualiter longè plura bona, quàm vnquàm per cipi poterant in Sion vel Hierosolyma terrestri.
units.tr: Fourth: we learn how the temporal things that happened in the promised land, which were referred to felicity under the law, we ought to take spiritually and interpret of the true felicity that is offered under the Gospel. Thus Mount Sion and the city Jerusalem shadow forth for us the church itself, in which far more good things are truly received spiritually than could ever be received in earthly Sion or Jerusalem.

units.la: Quintò: Et hîc habemus quandam rationem, obseruandi in sacris literis typos & figuras: & quomodo debeamus spiritualiter multa interpretari, vbi sola grammatica expositio integram sententiam non redderet: sicut hîc quantum esset, quod diceretur, Hebræos ingressos in Zion terrestrem.
units.tr: Fifth: here we have a certain method for observing types and figures in the sacred letters, and for seeing how we ought to interpret many things spiritually where the grammatical exposition alone would not give the whole sense; as here, where it would be a great matter to say that the Hebrews had entered earthly Zion.

units.la: Sextò: Habemus hîc dignitatem ecclesiæ longè elegantissimè & grauissimè expressam: vnde plurima possent per nos ad ædificationem colligi, si tempus ferret.
units.tr: Sixth: here we have the dignity of the church expressed most elegantly and weightily, from which very many things could be gathered by us for edification, if time allowed.

units.la: Septimò: admonemur, considerata dignitate ecclesiæ, ita vitam instituere, vt digni in ea ciues inueniamur. Respiciamus assiduè ad tale præsidium, ad tales conciues, ad talem iudicem, & Senatum, ad talem sacerdotem, ad sacrificium: & sentiemus magnam da nobis occasionem sanctè & piè viuendi.
units.tr: Seventh: we are admonished, considering the dignity of the church, to order our life so that we may be found worthy citizens in it. Let us look constantly to such a protection, to such fellow-citizens, to such a judge and senate, to such a priest and to the sacrifice; and we shall feel that it gives us a great opportunity of living holily and piously.

units.la: Videte ne asperneminì eum, qui loquitur. Nam si illi non effugerunt, qui auersabantur eum, qui loquebatur in terra, multò magis nos, si eum, qui de cœlis est, auersemur, cuius vox tùm concussit terram, at nunc denunciauit dicens: Adhuc semel ego concutio, non modò terram, verùm etiam cœlum. Porrò illud quod dixit, adhuc semel, significat eorum, quæ concutiuntur, translationem, vtpote quæ facta sint, vt maneant ea, quæ non concutiuntur.
units.tr: See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those did not escape who turned away from him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who is from heaven, whose voice then shook the earth, but now has declared, saying: Yet once more I shake not only the earth but also the heaven. Now the words yet once more signify the removal of the things that are shaken, as things that have been made so that those that are not shaken may remain.

units.la: Tertia ratio suasoria, ab autoritate & excellentia eius, qui in Euangelio nobis loquitur, siue per quem Euangelium mundo est patefactum.
units.tr: The third persuasive argument, drawn from the authority and excellence of him who speaks to us in the Gospel, or through whom the Gospel has been revealed to the world.

units.la: Norum verò est, quantam vim huiusmodi ratio habere debet ad persuadendum credentibus. Inferiores non possunt citra periculum contemnere verba ac iussa superiorum. Quod iudicium etiam à natura insitum est omnium animis. Proinde primùm simpliciter effert, uidete, ne asperneminì eum, qui loquitur: Graecè est, μὴ παραιτήσησθε, quasi diceret, ne quid prætexatis, quo minus audiatis loquentem. Non solùm oportet audire, sed etiam lubenter, nihil prætexendo ad excusationem. In parabola Euangelica multi vocabantur ad nuptias, sed omnes aliquid prætexebant, sese excusantes. Atqui nos non oportet ita facere. Hæc est perspicua sententia. Cæterùm non exprimit personam, sed paulò pòst licet colligere, quam intelligat, quando ait, loquentem de cœlis. Interea est hîc notandum, quòd hîc agit de loquente: quia tunc etiam, cùm lex daretur in monte Sina, audita est vox loquentis cum Mose, ea occasione inducit & in Euangelio quendam loquentem. Licet de lege agens potissimum intelligat loquentem Mosen, de Euangelio verò ipsum Deum, ipsum Christum. Aliàs enim si ad Deum referimus locutionem in lege data, cùm idem Deus sit autor Euangelij, qui legis: non erit hic apta differentia: Item, nò recte dicetur, quin lege loquebatur, loqui de terra: qui vero in Euangelio, loqui e cœlis. Sed ea de re paulo pòst. Apparet autem, venisse in mentem, ut adijceret istam rationem de loquente, propterea quòd proximè induxerat sanguinem Christi loquentem.
units.tr: It is well known how much force an argument of this kind ought to have in persuading believers. Inferiors cannot despise the words and commands of their superiors without danger, and this judgment is implanted in the minds of all by nature. Accordingly, he first states the point plainly: See that you do not refuse him who speaks [Greek: μὴ παραιτήσησθε]. It is as if he said: do not make any excuse for not listening to the one who speaks. We ought not only to listen, but to listen gladly, making no excuses. In the Gospel parable many were invited to the wedding, but all of them made some pretext, excusing themselves. But we ought not to do so. This is the plain meaning. However, he does not name the person, but a little later we may gather whom he means, when he says, him who speaks from heaven. Meanwhile it should be noted here that he is speaking of the one who speaks, because even when the law was given on Mount Sinai, the voice of the one speaking with Moses was heard, and on that occasion he brings in a certain speaker in the Gospel as well. Although, in speaking of the law, he mainly means Moses as the speaker, in speaking of the Gospel he means God himself, Christ himself. For otherwise, if we refer the speaking in the giving of the law to God, since the same God is the author of the Gospel as of the law, there will be no fitting difference here; likewise it would not be rightly said that the one who spoke in the law spoke from the earth, while the one who speaks in the Gospel speaks from heaven. But more on this matter a little later. It appears, moreover, that the words about the speaker came to his mind so that he might add this reason, because just before he had introduced the blood of Christ as speaking.

units.la: Nam si illi non effugerunt, qui auersabantur eum, qui loquebatur in terra: multò magis nos, si eum, qui de cœlis est, auersemur.
units.tr: For if those did not escape who turned away from him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who is from heaven.

units.la: Ratio, quare potius audiendus, qui loquitur in Euangelio, quàm qui loquebatur in lege, à magnitudine pœnarum, quæ imminent audire detrectantibus. Argumentatur autem à minori ad maius. Grauissimè puniti sunt, qui non audiebant loquentem in lege. Igitur multò grauius punientur, qui non audiunt loquentem in Euangelio. Quem vero intelligat loquentem in lege, satis arguit particula, in terra: nimirum Moses intelligit mediatorem constitutum inter Deum & homines, qui, cùm non possent audire Deum loquentem de cœlis, debebant hunc audire loquentem de terra. Nam & ipsi dicebant, ne loquatur nobis Deus, alioquin moriemur. Vide locum: Terreni homines nō possunt audire, nisi ex terra loquentem. Alias quidem, si ad Deum referimus locutionem, à quo Lex peræque est atque Euangelium, non constabit argumenti ratio, neque erit præstantior is, qui in Euangelio loquitur, quàm qui loquebatur in lege. Est ergo de ministris legis & Euangelij sermo: vt prior pars de Mose accipiatur, posterior de ipso Christo. Et quòd conueniat ita accipere, liquet ex eo, quod habuimus præsentis epistolæ capite decimo, vbi prorsus in eandem sententiam habetur argumentum paratum expressis etiam Mosis & Christi nominibus. Qui aspernatus fuerit Mosi legem, inquit, absque miseri-cordia sub duobus aut tribus testibus moritur: quantò putatis peioribus afficietur supplicijs, qui filium Dei conculcarit, & sanguinem testamenti ceu rem profanam habuerit. Nonnulli quidem interpretantur priorem partem, vbi dicitur loquens in terra, angelum, qui Mosi legem iussu Dei tradiderit: & nituntur illis verbis, quæ habentur præsentis epistolæ capite secundo: Etenim si is, qui per angelos dictus fuerat sermo, fuit firmus, & omnis transgressio & inobedientia iustam præmij repensationem accepit, quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem, quæ per Dominum primùm enarrari coepit? Sed priorratio commodior est: idque vel ob illam quoque causam, quòd Moses Deuteron. 18. dicit, ob id, quòd recusauerunt audire loquentem ipsum Dominum, & suam personam (Mosi inquam) iam diu & sæpè contempserunt, futurum, vt alius propheta suscitetur, quem audire debebunt.
units.tr: This is the reason why the one who speaks in the Gospel ought rather to be heard than the one who spoke in the law: it is drawn from the greatness of the punishments that threaten those who refuse to listen. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater. Those who did not listen to the speaker in the law were most severely punished. Therefore those who do not listen to the speaker in the Gospel will be punished much more severely. Who it is that he understands to be speaking in the law is sufficiently shown by the phrase on earth: clearly Moses is meant, the mediator appointed between God and men, who, since they could not hear God speaking from heaven, had to hear this one speaking from earth. For the people themselves said: Let not God speak to us, otherwise we shall die. See the passage: earthly men cannot hear anyone speaking except from the earth. Otherwise, if we refer the speaking to God, from whom the law comes just as the Gospel does, the force of the argument will not stand, and he who speaks in the Gospel will not be superior to him who spoke in the law. So the discussion concerns the ministers of the law and of the Gospel: the first part is to be taken of Moses, the latter of Christ himself. That it is right to take it this way is clear from what we had in the tenth chapter of this present letter, where the same argument is set out, with the names of Moses and Christ expressly given. He who has set aside the law of Moses, it says, dies without mercy under two or three witnesses: how much worse punishment, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God and has counted the blood of the covenant as a profane thing? Some indeed interpret the first part, where it is said speaking on earth, as the angel who handed the law to Moses at God's command, and they rely on those words found in the second chapter of this letter: For if the word spoken through angels was firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we have neglected so great a salvation, which was first spoken through the Lord? But the first reading is more suitable, and this is so also for the reason that Moses says in Deuteronomy 18 that, because they refused to hear the Lord himself speaking, and had long and often despised his own person (Moses, I mean), another prophet would be raised up whom they would have to hear.

units.la: Sic enim ibi dicitur: Prophetam de medio tui ex fratribus tuis sicut me, suscitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus, illum audietis. Iuxta omnia, quæ petiisti à Domino Deo tuo in Horeb, in die congregationis, quando dicebas: Non adijciam, vt audiam vocem Domini Dei mei, atque ignem illum magnum non videbo amplius, ne moriar. Dixitque Dominus ad me: Bene egerunt in hoc, quod locuti sunt, Prophetam eis suscitabo de medio fratrum suorum, sicut te, ponamque verba mea in ore eius, & loquetur ad eos, quæcunque mandauero illi. Et homo, qui noluerit audire verba mea, quæ loquetur in nomine meo, requiram ego ab eo. Hæc ibi, qui igitur locutus est in terra, Moses debet intelligi, non Deus, quem audire Israelitæ noluerunt: qui vero locutus est de cœlis in Euangelio, Christus est verus homo, & verus Deus, è cœlo ad nos descendens: sicuti multis locis clarè docet, se descendisse à patre cœlesti, & doctrinam suam è cœlo esse, & se cœlestia loqui, non terrena. Est quidem & patris vox de cœlis audita, Matth. 3. 17. sed tantùm confirmans, quæ Christus loquebatur: propterea initio huius epistolæ dicitur locutus nobis Deus in filio.
units.tr: For there it is said: The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from the midst of you, from your brethren, like me; you shall hear him. According to all that you asked of the Lord your God in Horeb, on the day of the assembly, when you said: I will not add to hear the voice of the Lord my God, nor see that great fire any more, lest I die. And the Lord said to me: They have done well in what they have spoken. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brethren, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them whatever I command him. And the man who will not hear my words, which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him. So far that passage. Therefore the one who spoke on earth must be understood to be Moses, not God, whom the Israelites were unwilling to hear; but the one who spoke from heaven in the Gospel is Christ, true man and true God, descending from heaven to us. This he teaches clearly in many places: that he has come down from the heavenly Father, that his teaching is from heaven, and that he speaks heavenly things, not earthly. There was indeed a voice of the Father heard from heaven, Matthew 3:17, but it only confirmed what Christ was saying; therefore at the beginning of this letter it is said that God spoke to us in the Son.

units.la: Iam verò non effugisse iram Dei, qui recusarunt audire Mosen, manifestum est. Nam quotquot sese opposuerunt Mosi, murmurantes aduersus eum, infeliciter ceciderunt. Exodi 16. Numeror. 12. 15. 14. Item 16. vbi interficiuntur 14700. Sed & quotquot præcepta Dei per Mosen prolata transgressi sunt, grauiter puniti sunt omnes 1. Corinth. 10. Quanquàm hic præcipuè agitur de audiendis personis à Deo missis, de Mose videlicet & de Christo. Quòd si igitur sic puniti sunt, qui recusarunt audire Mosen, certum est, multò grauius puniendos, qui detrectant audire ipsum Christum. Et hic rursus obseruandum, quòd Apostolus mirabili prudentia adfert rationes è lege, quando agit cum Hebræis: alias apud gentiles nequaquàm prolaturus tales rationes.
units.tr: Now it is plain that those who refused to hear Moses did not escape the wrath of God. For all who set themselves against Moses, murmuring against him, perished unhappily: Exodus 16; Numbers 12, 15, 14; likewise Numbers 16, where 14,700 are killed. But also all who transgressed the precepts of God delivered through Moses were all grievously punished, 1 Corinthians 10. Although here the chief concern is with hearing the persons sent by God, namely Moses and Christ. If, then, those who refused to hear Moses were so punished, it is certain that those who refuse to hear Christ himself will be punished much more severely. And here again it must be observed that the Apostle, with remarkable prudence, brings forward arguments from the law when he deals with the Hebrews; otherwise he would by no means produce such arguments among the Gentiles.

units.la: Cuius vox tùm concussit terram, nunc verò denunciauit dicens: Adhuc semel ego concutio, non modò terram, verùm etiam cœlum.
units.tr: Whose voice then shook the earth, but now has declared, saying: Yet once more I shake not only the earth but also the heaven.

units.la: Insigni atque ampla periphrasi describit, quis & qualis sit, qui in Euangelio locutus est, nempe qui posit nutu suo non modò terram, verùm etiam cœlum mouere, hoc est, qui natura sit verus Deus. Quare intelligi debet, Christum Deum, qui locutus est in Euangelio, longè quidem superiorem esse Mose, qui locutus est in testamento veteri: & propterea etiam obedientius audiendum.
units.tr: By a remarkable and full periphrasis he describes who and what kind of being it is who spoke in the Gospel: namely one who can, by his nod, move not only the earth but also the heaven, that is, one who is by nature true God. Therefore it must be understood that Christ, God, who spoke in the Gospel, is far superior to Moses, who spoke in the Old Testament, and that for this reason he is to be heard with all the more obedience.

units.la: Est plane eadem hoc loco sententia, quæ est verborum Christi, quibus ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra: Matthæi 28. Maluit autem Apostolus tantundem significare verbis prophetæ, quàm ipsius Christi: idque, tùm, vt ostenderet, etiam prophetas iam diu de eo, qui locuturus erat in Euangelio, multa prænunciasse: tùm vt Christi dignitas atque maiestas ab aliis potius, quàm ab ipso, tantopere prædicata apud omnes amplior haberetur. Proinde videamus, quænam sit propria prophetæ, ex quo citantur hæc verba, mens & sententia, vt inde intelligatur, num appositè in medium sint adducta. Sic verò Aggæi secundo legimus iuxta hebraicam veritatem: hæc dicit Dominus: Verbum quod pepigi vobiscum, cùm exiretis de Aegypto, & spiritus meus perseuerabit in medio vestri: nolite timere, quia sic dixit Dominus exercituum: Adhuc vnum modicum est, & ego commouebo cœlum & terram, mare, & aridam. Et commouebo omnes gentes, & veniet desiderium omnium gentium, ac replebo domum istam gloria, dixit Iehouáh exercituum: meum est argentum, & meum est aurum, dixit Iehouah exercituum: Maior erit gloria Domus huius posterioris, gloria prioris, dixit Iehouah exercituum: & in loco isto dabo pacem, dixit Iehouah exercituum. Hæc ibi: sic repetita per nos, vt clarior sententia colligi inde posit. Apostolus autem citat verba, secutus septuaginta, apud quos sic legitur: ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ τὴν ξηράν· &c. Clarum est autem, prophetam, cùm annunciasset Zerubabel & Iehosua, omnemque populum ad persequendum coeptum opus in ædificando domum Domini, ne quia parum succedebat, & videretur, nunquàm talem domum erigi posse, qualis fuit prior: sicut reuera neque id factum est, testante id omni historia: more prophetico conuerti à rebus temporalibus ad res spirituales, & consolando populum polliceri, futurum, vt Dominus dignetur adhuc habitare in populo suo, & talem domum (spiritualem videlicet, quæ ecclesia est) erigendam, quæ longè superatura sit domum materialem, à Solomone conditam. Vt autem certiores omnes faciat eius rei, dicit, adhuc semel commouendum cœlum & terram, &c.
units.tr: The meaning here is plainly the same as that of Christ's words, "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth" (Matt. 28). The Apostle, however, preferred to express the same thing in the words of the prophet rather than in Christ's own words. He did this partly to show that the prophets had long ago foretold many things about the one who was to speak in the Gospel, and partly so that Christ's dignity and majesty, proclaimed so greatly by others rather than by himself, might be held in higher esteem by all. Let us therefore see what the prophet's own mind and meaning is, from whom these words are cited, so that we may judge whether they have been appositely brought forward. In the second chapter of Haggai we read, according to the Hebrew truth: "Thus says the Lord: the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit will remain in the midst of you; do not fear. For thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet once more, a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says Jehovah of hosts. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says Jehovah of hosts. The glory of this latter house will be greater than the glory of the former, says Jehovah of hosts; and in this place I will give peace, says Jehovah of hosts." So far the prophet; I have repeated it here so that a clearer sense may be drawn from it. The Apostle, however, cites the words as the Seventy translated them, where it is read thus: still once more I will shake the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land [ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ τὴν ξηράν], etc. It is clear that the prophet, having announced to Zerubbabel and Joshua and the whole people that they should go on with the work begun, building the house of the Lord, was doing so lest, because progress was slow, they should think that a house such as the former could never be erected. And indeed this did not happen, as all history attests. In prophetic manner he turns from temporal things to spiritual ones, and to console the people he promises that the Lord will deign to dwell still among his people, and that a house (namely a spiritual one, which is the Church) is to be erected, which will far surpass the material house built by Solomon. To make all certain of this, he says that heaven and earth are to be shaken once more, etc.

units.la: Id est, maximam mutationem futuram. Deinde commouendas etiam gentes: quandoquidem gentes erant vocandæ ad istam domum Domini, quæ est ecclesia. Et ventum desideratum cunctis gentibus, id est, Christum, qui est caput huius ecclesiæ: de quo etiam Genesios 49. ad Iuda dicitur, quòd ex eo veniret Silo & ad ipsum aggregatio gentium: at tùm quidem impleretur domus illa (id est ecclesia) gloria: non quòd Dominus optaret in illa aurum vel argentum, quarum rerum ipse satis diues est: sed alia ratione vellet eam illustrem reddere, dando videlicet in ea pacem, pacem inquàm illam, per quam credentes habent accessum ad Deum, Rom. 5. En clara & perspicua prophetæ sententia. Nec possunt aliter accipi, quando, si secundum literam sumatur vaticinium de magnificentiore ædificio materiali, intelligitur, vanum fuisse vaticinium. Est igitur commotio illa cœli & terræ accipienda de maxima mutatione, quæ facta est in prædicatione Euangelij. Et reuera cœlum terræ miscerì videbatur, statim vt Euangelium annunciari cœpit. Imò statim Christo nato commotus est Herodes & vniuersa Hierosolyma cum illo: commotæ sunt & gentes, quando magi primitiæ gentium venerunt: sed multò maior commotio facta est, & apud Iudæos, & apud gentes, quando à resurrectione Christi Apostoli coeperunt Euangelium publicè primùm Hierosolymis, cum maxima omnium admiratione, deinde toto orbe, annunciare. Actor.2. dicitur, quòd multitudo concurrebat & confusa est, audiens lingua sua loquentes magnalia Dei, &c. Hieronymus quidem ex eo, quod dicitur, Adhuc semel commouendum cœlum & terram, sic interpretatur, vt accipiat, semel quidem motum esse cœlum & terram, quando videlicet in monte Syna data est lex, nec non admiranda signa in cœlo & terra, & in mari (per quod populus eductus fuerat ex Aegypto) fuisse edita: sed postea iterum motum cœlum & terram, in morte videlicet Christi, quando signa similiter diuersa in cœlo & terra sunt edita. Interea tamen cùm succedit locus de gentibus, aperte & rectè interpretatur de vocatione gentium ad Euangelium: & aurum argentumque interpretatur eloquia Domini, quæ sunt speciosiora auro atque argento, & quibus domus Domini ecclesia exornatur. Augustinus de ciuitate Dei lib.18. cap.35. interpretatur motum cœlum, quando angelorum & syderum testimonio incarnatus est Christus: mouit terram ingenti miraculo de ipso virginis partu, mouit mare & aridam, cùm & in insulis, & in toto orbe Christus annunciatur. Iam verò quod sequitur: Et veniet desiderium cunctis gentibus, de nouissimo eius expectatur adoentu. Vt enim desideratus esset expectantibus, prius oportuit eum dilectum esse credentibus. Ità Augustinus. Sed quiuis iudicare potest, nos simplisimplicissimam & certissimam expositionem reddidisse, vt videlicet de maxima muta‑tione facta intelligantur verba prophetæ, tempore euangelij per Christum reuelati, &c.
units.tr: That is, a very great change is coming. Next, the nations too are to be shaken, since the nations were to be called to that house of the Lord, which is the Church. And the desired one will come to all nations, that is, Christ, who is the head of this Church; of whom it is also said in Genesis 49, to Judah, that Shiloh would come from him and the gathering of the nations would be to him. Then that house (that is, the Church) would indeed be filled with glory; not because the Lord wished for gold or silver in it, since he is rich enough in these things himself, but because he wished in another way to make it illustrious, namely by giving peace in it, that peace, I say, through which believers have access to God (Rom. 5). Here is the clear and plain sense of the prophet. Nor can it be taken otherwise: if the prophecy were understood literally, of a more magnificent material building, the prophecy would be shown to have been in vain. That shaking of heaven and earth must therefore be understood as the greatest change, which took place in the preaching of the Gospel. And indeed heaven seemed to be mingled with earth as soon as the Gospel began to be announced. Indeed, immediately at Christ's birth Herod was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him; the nations too were stirred when the Magi, the firstfruits of the nations, came. But a far greater commotion occurred, both among the Jews and among the nations, when after Christ's resurrection the Apostles began to announce the Gospel publicly, first at Jerusalem, with the greatest astonishment of all, and then throughout the world. In Acts 2 it is said that the multitude came together and was confused, hearing them speak in their own tongue the wonderful works of God, etc. Jerome, indeed, from the words "Yet once more the heaven and earth are to be shaken," interprets it so as to understand that heaven and earth were moved once, namely when the law was given on Mount Sinai, and also that wonderful signs were shown in heaven and earth and in the sea (through which the people had been led out of Egypt); but afterwards heaven and earth were moved again, namely at the death of Christ, when signs likewise diverse were shown in heaven and earth. Meanwhile, however, when the passage moves on to the nations, he rightly and plainly interprets it of the calling of the nations to the Gospel; and he interprets the gold and silver as the words of the Lord, which are more precious than gold and silver, and with which the house of the Lord, the Church, is adorned. Augustine, in The City of God, book 18, chapter 35, interprets the moving of heaven as taking place when Christ was made flesh, attested by angels and stars; he says the earth was moved by the great miracle of the virgin birth itself, and the sea and dry land were moved when Christ is proclaimed both on the islands and throughout the whole world. As for what follows, "and the desire of all nations will come," it is looked for at his last coming; for in order that he might be desired by those who wait for him, he had first to be loved by those who believe. So Augustine. But anyone can judge that we have given the simplest and most certain exposition, namely that the words of the prophet are to be understood of the greatest change made in the time of the Gospel, revealed through Christ, etc.

units.la: Cæterum Apostolus ita partitur membra dicti prophetici, vt dignitatem Euangelij præ lege ex eo velit ostendere. Ac videtur hæc e us esse sententia: Cùm daretur lex, & quereturis, qui tantùm erat in terra, videlicet Moses, tùm quidem à Domino concussa est terra: At quando patefactum est Euangelium per loquentem in eo Christum, tùm concussum est etiam cœlum: atque ita euangelium merito iudicabitur præstantius lege. Atque vltrà progrediendo, quandoquidem qui loquitur in Euangelio, is est, cuius nutu & cùm lex daretur, commota est terra, cùm vero Euangelium propalaretur, commotum est etiam cœlum, palàm est, eum audiendum præ illo, qui tantùm loquebatur in terra. In summa, cùm is locutus sit in Euangelio, qui suo nutu mouet & terram & cœlum (id est, cùm sit Deus) æquum est, ipsum audire præ Mose, qui tantùm erat homo de terra terrenus. Clarè autem significatur, vnius eiusdemque nutu atque ordinatione datam legem & Euangelium: eundem Deum vtriusque esse autorem & conditorem, necnon vtriusque populum ad eum pertinere: eandem item vtrobiq; esse ecclesiam, siue domum: sed in qua mutata sit administrationis ratio: qua de re nos supra quoque egimus capite 3.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle divides the members of the prophetic saying in such a way that he wishes to show from it the dignity of the Gospel above the law. And this seems to be his meaning: when the law was given, and he who was then only on earth, namely Moses, was speaking, the earth was shaken by the Lord; but when the Gospel was made known through Christ speaking in it, heaven too was shaken; and so the Gospel will rightly be judged more excellent than the law. Going further: since he who speaks in the Gospel is the one at whose nod the earth was shaken when the law was given, and when the Gospel was made public heaven too was shaken, it is plain that he is to be heard rather than the one who spoke only on earth. In sum: since he has spoken in the Gospel who by his nod moves both earth and heaven (that is, since he is God), it is right that we should hear him rather than Moses, who was only a man, earthly from the earth. Moreover, it is clearly signified that the law and the Gospel were given by the nod and ordinance of one and the same God: that the same God is the author and founder of both, and that the people of both belong to him; likewise that the Church, or house, is the same in both, but that the manner of administration has been changed. We also treated this matter above, in chapter 3.

units.la: Porrò illud quod dicit: adhuc semel: significat eorum, quæ concutiuntur, translatio‑nem, vt pote quæ facta sint, vt maneant ea, quæ non concutiuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, the words "yet once more" signify the transfer of those things which are shaken, inasmuch as they are done so that those things which are not shaken may remain.

units.la: Apostolus ceu delectatus commoditate testimonij iam citati, colligit etiam aliam rationem, qua Euangelij præ lege excellentia demonstratur: sumptum ab eo, quòd, cùm lex debuerit abrogari, sequente noua concussione & immutatione, Euangelium tamen non abrogetur, sed maneat in æternum. Occasionem verò huius rationis capit ex eo, quòd dicit Deus apud prophetam: adhuc semel. Hinc sic argumentatur: cùm dicitur commouendum cœlum & terram, sententia est, antea quidem factam esse quandam commotionem seu mutationem (dùm videlicet lata est lex) & rursus aliam quoque mutationem faciendam, (nempe vbi reuelandum foret Euangelium) post verò nullam aliam mutationem expectandam. Ex quo sequitur, quòd, cùm lex debuerit abrogari, Euangelium verò nequaquàm debeat abrogari, sed maneat in æternum: longè præstantius sit Euangelium ipsa lege.
units.tr: The Apostle, as if delighted by the convenience of the testimony just cited, draws another argument by which the excellence of the Gospel over the law is demonstrated: taken from the fact that, while the law had to be abrogated, with a new shaking and change following, the Gospel is not abrogated but remains forever. He takes the occasion of this argument from God's words through the prophet: "yet once more." He argues thus: when it is said that heaven and earth are to be shaken, the sense is that a certain shaking or change had already taken place (namely when the law was given), and that another change was yet to be made (namely when the Gospel was to be revealed); after that no further change is to be expected. From this it follows that, since the law had to be abrogated but the Gospel ought by no means to be abrogated, but remains forever, the Gospel is far more excellent than the law itself.

units.la: Et certè non est modica dignitas Euangelij, quòd maneat in æternum. Quod enim duntaxat pro tempore floret, neq; alioqui diu potest durare, certè non magni æstimatur.
units.tr: Indeed, the dignity of the Gospel is not small, in that it remains forever. What flourishes only for a time and cannot long endure otherwise is certainly not highly valued.

units.la: Refelluntur autem hoc loco illi, qui existimarunt, ita partienda mundi tempora, vt vniuersum tempus, quod antecessit tempus Christi incarnati, tribueretur Deo patri: quod deinde sequeretur, assignaretur filio Christo: Deinde tertium quoddam expectandum, in quo potissimum audiretur spiritus Sanctus. Quemadmodum Montanus imaginatus est, se illum spiritum Sanctum esse, qui Apostolus promissus fuerat, dicens: Christum de se prædixisse: sicut Christus afferebat, Mosen de se vaticinatum. Et Mahometes simile quiddam conatus est suis persuadere, nempe legem suam esse tertiam & perfectissimam, nec non æternùm duraturam. Est igitur hic locus dignisimus obseruatu, vt certò sciatur, post Euangelium nullam aliam doctrinam expectandam: sicut & Paulus in Galatis dicit, si quis aliud Euangelium prædicarit, anathema sit. Et non est aliud nomen sub cœlo, in quo saluos fieri oporteat. Actor. 4. Est autem mirabile, quòd Apostolus tàm oculatè in singula verba perspexerit, & ex vna quodam modo voce tàm graue argumentum de dignitate Euangelij potuerit colligere. Pudeat nos nostræ ignauiæ & insciriæ.
units.tr: In this passage, those are refuted who thought the times of the world should be divided so that the whole period before the incarnation of Christ would be assigned to God the Father, what followed would be assigned to the Son Christ, and then a third period was still to be expected, in which the Holy Spirit would above all be heard. Montanus imagined that he himself was that Holy Spirit, the Paraclete who had been promised, saying that Christ had foretold this about him, just as Christ asserted that Moses had prophesied about himself. Mahomet also tried to persuade his followers of something similar, namely that his law was the third and most perfect, and that it too would last forever. This passage is therefore most worthy of attention, so that it may be known for certain that after the Gospel no other doctrine is to be expected. Paul also says in Galatians: "If anyone preaches another gospel, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1). And "there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved" (Acts 4). It is remarkable that the Apostle looked so carefully at individual words, and could draw such a weighty argument for the dignity of the Gospel from a single word. We should be ashamed of our laziness and ignorance.

units.la: Et hoc eleganter factum, quod legem & legalia dicit concuti transferriqúe, eaque iam facta, nempe in operibus & obseruationibus lita. (vnde etiam lex videtur dicta lex factorum, Rom.4.) ac propterea citò abeuntia: sicut & omnia carnalia, temporalia, quæ facta sunt, citò abire necessum est. At verò de Euangelio euangelicisque rebus dicit, ea manere & nequaquàm concuti: nimirum quòd spirituale est, & in quo omnia spiritualia, cœlestia, ac propterea durabilia. Huiusmodi autem nota Euangelij mirificè commendat eius dignitatem, atque iterum notat magnam Euangelij præ lege excellentiam. Estque aptissima appellatio, qua euangelium vocatur æternum. Non statim ab initio ante constitutionem mundi Deus prædestinauit euangelium, & elegit suos per euangelium conseruandos: Ephes.1. Et rursus manet in æternum, neque quicquam ei succedet. De lege nihil tale dici potest: coepit in tempore, & finita est in tempore.
units.tr: This is elegantly done: he says that the law and legal things are shaken and transferred, and that they are already things done, consisting in works and observances (whence the law is also called the law of works, Rom. 4), and therefore soon passing away. Just as all carnal and temporal things that have been made must soon pass away, so too the law and its works must pass. But of the Gospel and evangelical things he says that they remain and are by no means shaken, because the Gospel is spiritual, and in it all things are spiritual, heavenly, and therefore durable. This mark of the Gospel wonderfully commends its dignity and again notes its great excellence above the law. "Eternal gospel" is therefore a most apt name. God did not predestine the gospel, and choose his people to be preserved through it, only at the beginning, before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1). It remains forever, and nothing will succeed it. Nothing of this kind can be said of the law: it began in time and is finished in time.

units.la: Discimus autem hic: primò, quòd euangelium debeat magni fieri, propter personam, per quam est ad nos allatum, id est, propter Christum, quem pater de cœlo iussit audiri, Matthæi 17. Matth. 7. Omnis, qui audit ex me sermones hos, & facit eos, assimilabo illum viro prudenti, qui ædificauit domum suam super petrā, &c. Luc.11. Beati, qui audiunt verbum Dei & custodiunt. Regina austri surget in iudicio cum viris nationis huius, &c. Secundò, discimus hic, quæ patribus contigerunt in veteri testamento, figuram fuisse eorum, quæ in nouo testamento sunt peragenda, iuxta illud 1. Corinth. 10. Hæc autem figuræ nostri fuerunt: Et paulo post: Hæc autem omnia figuræ contigeruntillis. Et ideo pœna & præmia, quæ illis contigerunt, sunt nobis quoque proposita.
units.tr: Here we learn, first, that the gospel ought to be held in high regard on account of the person through whom it has been brought to us, that is, on account of Christ, whom the Father from heaven commanded us to hear (Matt. 17). "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken to a wise man who built his house upon the rock," etc. (Matt. 7). "Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it." "The queen of the south will rise up in judgment with the men of this generation," etc. (Luke 11). Second, we learn here that what happened to the fathers in the Old Testament was a figure of what was to be accomplished in the New Testament, according to 1 Cor. 10: "Now these things were our figures." And a little later: "All these things happened to them as figures." Therefore the punishments and rewards that befell them are also set before us.

units.la: Tertiò, discimus, quomodo debeamus accommodare scripturas nostro instituto, & maximè prophetarum, qui de rebus nostris vaticinati sunt. Atq; id quidem maximè est apud eos faciundum, qui & intelligunt eas, & scripturis refelli debent, quales erant Hebræi, ad quos hic scribit Paulus.
units.tr: Third, we learn how we ought to apply the Scriptures to our purpose, and especially the prophets, who prophesied about our affairs. This is to be done chiefly among those who both understand them and ought to be refuted by the Scriptures, such as the Hebrews to whom Paul is writing here.

units.la: Quarto, quinetiam discimus hic rationes nostras accommodare personarum captui, ad quas nobis sermo est. Cuius rei Apostolus fuit diligentissimus obseruator. Quinto, discimus, quomodo in scriptis propheticis debeamus diligenter obseruare, & distinguere, quæ ad legem pertinent, ab iis, quæ pertinent ad Euangelium, & colligere, quæ Euangelij illustrant dignitatem. Sexto, discimus, quàm oculatè debeamus scripturas scrutari, & quomodo interdum ex singulis vocibus grauissima argumenta colligi debeant, quibus res nostras confirmemus.
units.tr: Fourth, we learn here also to adapt our arguments to the capacity of the persons to whom we speak. In this the Apostle was a most diligent observer. Fifth, we learn how carefully we ought to observe, in the prophetic writings, and distinguish what pertains to the law from what pertains to the Gospel, and to gather what illustrates the dignity of the Gospel. Sixth, we learn how carefully we ought to search the Scriptures, and how sometimes the weightiest arguments ought to be drawn from single words, by which to confirm our case.

units.la: Septimò, debemus eo nomine excitari ad colendum Euangelium, quòd sciamus illud manere in æternum & esse situm in rebus spiritualibus.
units.tr: Seventh, we ought on this account to be roused to cherish the Gospel, because we know that it remains forever and is grounded in spiritual things.

units.la: Quapropter regnum assumentes, quod concuti non possit, habeamus gratiam per quam ita colamus Deum, vt illi placeamus, cum reuerentia et religione. Etenim Deus noster ignis consumens est.
units.tr: Therefore, receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us have grace, by which we may worship God acceptably, with reverence and godly fear. For our God is a consuming fire.

units.la: Illatio est ex præcedentibus. Finis namque hic est totius loci, qui pro exhortatione ad colendam pacem veramque sanctimoniam institutus est. Estque conclusio ad tres rationes superiores antecedentes: quàmuis verba præcipuè respiciunt ad eam, quæ proximè antecesit: in qua de translatione eorum, quæ concutiuntur, nonnihil audiuimus. Sed de hac re iterum suo loco.
units.tr: This is an inference from what precedes. For this is the end of the whole passage, which was instituted as an exhortation to cultivate peace and true holiness. It is also the conclusion drawn from the three reasons set out above, although the words chiefly look back to the one immediately before, in which we heard something about the transfer of the things that are shaken. But more on this matter in its own place.

units.la: Est autem sententia: Cùm ita, ô Hebræi, res se habeat, vt videlicet, qui dona Dei nō ea ratione, qua par est, excolunt, ijs tandem exemplo Esau spolientur: cùm item longè præstantior sit facta nostra conditio, vbi iam sub Euangelio agimus, quàm antea, vbi adhuc detinebamur sub lege: Denique, cum non citra ingens periculum posset contemni iis, qui in Euangelio ad nos loquitur, cuiusq; potentia abrogata est lex, & nunc manifestatum Euangelium: Hæc, inquam, cùm ita se habeant, profectò par est, in primis in pace, & concordia: deinde in vera sanctimonia omni studio perfistamus, & qua decet reuerentia ac religione Deum colamus.
units.tr: The sense is this: since matters stand thus, O Hebrews, namely that those who do not cultivate God's gifts in the proper way will at last be stripped of them, as Esau was; since our condition is also far more excellent now that we live under the Gospel than before, when we were still held under the law; and finally, since it cannot be disregarded without great danger by those who speak to us in the Gospel, whose power has abrogated the law, and now that the Gospel has been made manifest: since these things are so, it is surely fitting that we above all persevere, with every effort, in peace and concord, and then in true holiness, and worship God with the reverence and godly fear that befit him.

units.la: Regnum assumentes, quod concuti non possit) De lege & ceremonialibus, earundemque abrogatione pridem dixit, inprimisque per conculsionem & translationem eam est interpretatus: contrà de Euangelio dixit, inconcussum & æternum mansurum usq; ad finem seculi, nec aliud hoc sequi debere. Regnum autem hoc loco dicit eos assumpsisse: partim, quia sacerdotium legale regno confertur, Exod. 19. & 1. Petri 2. vos electum estis, inquit genus, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus peculij ratio: partim verò, quia Christi regnum in Euangelio & eius prædicatione manifestatur in toto orbe terrarum. De hoc regno spirituali quod sacerdotio regali veteris testamenti multis parasangis præfertur, recte dicit, esse inconcussum, nec concuti posse: præterquàm enim, quòd immutabile est & æternum, nulla etiam vi, nullisque machinis Satanæ, aut furoribus mundi subuerti aut concuti potest. Dan. 2. Tempore regum istorum, suscitabit Deus cœli regnum, quod in æternum non corrumpetur, & regnum illud populo alteri non relinquetur (vide immutabilitatem) comminuet & consummabit omnia ista regna, & ipsum stabit in æternum. 1. Sam. 7. statuam semen (verba fuit Dei per Nathan ad Dauidem de Christo) tuum post te, quod egredietur è ventre tuo, & firmabo regnum eius. Ipse ædificabit domum nomini meo, & firmabo solium regni eius usq; in seculum. Psal. 2. Constitui regem meum super Sijon montem sanctum meum: Postula à me, & dabo gentes hæreditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terræ. Psal. 72. Iustitia, pax, & amplitudo regni Christi depingitur. Psal 110. Sacerdotium, regnum, & victoria eius adumbratur. Lucæ 1. Angelus ad Mariam de Christo, hic erit magnus, & filius altissimi vocabitur, dabitque ei Dominus Deus sedem Dauid patris ipsius regnabitque super domum Iacob in æternum, & regni eius non eris finis. Innumerabiles fere loci in scripturis occurrunt, qui regni Christi æternitatem describunt. Regnum autem Christi est ecclesia, in qua spiritus Dei verbum vitæ prædicat, & ad veritatem, iustitiam, fœlicitatem æternam, pacem Dei, vocat electos Dei, imò omnes fere homines: Non enim Deo personarum est respectus. Quòd verò nō omnes salutem assequuntur, id ipsorum fit vitio, quia videlicet, regnum illud Christi nō assumunt. sumunt, non credunt in Deum, non submittunt sese regi gloriæ, nec recipiunt salutem & pacem Dei, gratis & per gratiam sibi oblatam.
units.tr: "Receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken": earlier he spoke of the law and ceremonial matters and their abrogation, and interpreted it especially through shaking and transfer. On the other hand, about the Gospel he said that it will remain unshaken and eternal until the end of the age, and that nothing else should follow from it. He says here that they have received a kingdom, partly because the legal priesthood is conferred on a kingdom: "You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession" (Exod. 19; 1 Pet. 2). Partly, too, because Christ's kingdom is made manifest in the Gospel and its preaching throughout the whole world. Concerning this spiritual kingdom, which is preferred by many parasangs to the royal priesthood of the Old Testament, he rightly says that it is unshaken and cannot be shaken. For besides being unchangeable and eternal, it can be overthrown or shaken by no force, nor by any machinations of Satan or rages of the world. "In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and that kingdom shall not be left to another people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever" (Dan. 2). "I will raise up your seed after you (the words of God through Nathan to David about Christ), which shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever" (2 Sam. 7). "I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion. Ask of me, and I will give the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession" (Ps. 2). The justice, peace and extent of Christ's kingdom are depicted in Ps. 72. His priesthood, kingdom and victory are foreshadowed in Ps. 110. The angel says to Mary about Christ: "He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end" (Luke 1). Almost countless passages in the Scriptures describe the eternity of Christ's kingdom. Christ's kingdom is the Church, in which the Spirit of God preaches the word of life and calls God's elect, indeed almost all men, to truth, righteousness, eternal happiness and the peace of God, for God has no respect of persons. That not all attain salvation is their own fault, namely because they do not receive that kingdom of Christ: they do not believe in God, do not submit themselves to the King of glory, and do not receive the salvation and peace of God, which is offered to them freely and by grace.

units.la: Habeamus gratiam) In regno sacerdotali veteris testamenti legalis requirebatur iustitia, quæ in perfecta consummataque legis obseruatione consistebat. In regno vero Christi, quod in nouo testamento manifestatum est, regnat gratia, qua ij iustificantur & seruantur, qui in Christum credunt. Antitheta hoc loco notanda sunt, Regno & sacerdotio Mosaico commutabili & transferendo oppositum est regnum Christi inconcussum & æternum, cui aliud siue nouum succedere nequit. Operibus item legis opposita est gratia per Iesum Christum, quæ per Euangelium in tota terrarum orbe est prædicata. Pertinent huc omnia illa, quæ in Epistolis D. Pauli ad Romanos, ad Galatas, ad Ephesios copiose hac de re sunt explicata. Et eleganter Ioan. 1. Idipsum exprimitur, vbi Iohannes Baptista præclarè de Christo testificatur, dicens: Et è plenitudine eius omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Quia lex per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum exorta est. Rom. 3. Omnes peccauerunt, ac destituuntur gloria Dei: iustificantur autem gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu: quem propositum Deus reconciliatorem per fidem, interueniente ipsius sanguine, &c. Rom. 4. Idcirco ex fide datur hæreditas, vt secundum gratiam, vt firma sit promissio vniuerso semini, non ei, quod est ex lege tantum, verum etiam ei, quod est ex fide Abraham. Item Rom. 5. Iustificati igitur ex fide, pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem & contigit nobis, vt fide perduceremur in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus, & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Ephes. 2. Gratia estis seruati per fidem (idque non ex vobis, Dei donum est) non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Nam ipsius sumus opus, conditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quæ præparauit Deus, vt in eis ambularemus. Gratia itaque hæc diligenter tenenda & apprehendenda est per fidem: si quidem in ea stamus & certificati de salute æterna gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Qui gratiam hanc regni, Christi inconcusi sperauerit, saluus fieri & particeps regni cœlorum euadere non poterit. Certitudo salutis pedet à gratia Dei per Christum. Certitudo iudicij deriuatur in conceptores gratiæ & hostes fidei.
units.tr: Let us have grace) Under the priestly kingdom of the Old Testament, the law demanded righteousness, which consisted in the perfect and complete observance of the law. In the kingdom of Christ, which has been made manifest in the New Testament, grace reigns, and by it those who believe in Christ are justified and preserved. The antitheses in this passage should be noted. To the Mosaic kingdom and priesthood, which could be changed and transferred, is opposed the unshaken and eternal kingdom of Christ, which no other or new kingdom can succeed. Likewise, to the works of the law is opposed grace through Jesus Christ, which has been preached through the Gospel throughout the whole world. To this belong all the things that St Paul has explained at length on this matter in his Epistles to the Romans, the Galatians and the Ephesians. And John 1 expresses the same thing elegantly, where John the Baptist testifies splendidly about Christ, saying: "And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace. For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ." Romans 3: "All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood," etc. Romans 4: "Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed, not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham." Likewise Romans 5: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God." Ephesians 2: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God; not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." This grace is therefore to be diligently held and grasped by faith, since we stand in it and, assured of eternal salvation, rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Whoever hopes for this grace of the unshaken kingdom of Christ cannot fail to be saved and to become a partaker of the kingdom of heaven. The certainty of salvation depends on the grace of God through Christ. The certainty of judgment falls upon the despisers of grace and the enemies of faith.

units.la: Per quam ita colamus Deum, vt illi placeamus, cum reuerentia & religione) Ne quis Apostolo exprobret, quòd vel legis opera temere aspernetur, vel fenestram peccatis aperiat, dum gratia obtineri regnum Christi doceat: Apostolus hoc loco tacitæ obiectioni occurrit, dicens, eos, qui gratiæ huius vere facti sunt participes, ita colere debere Deum, vt illi placeant, cum reuerentia & religione. In quo quidem fidei obedientia & officium iustificatorum describitur. Cultus diuini & obsequij hi debent meminisse. Non enim ad securitatem & ad libidinem vocantur, sed ad timorem Dei, ad obedientiam, ad castitatem, ad sanctitatem & innocentiam. Rom. 12. Obsecro vos fratres, per miserationes Dei, vt præbeatis corpora vestra hostiam viuentem, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem cultum vestrum. Et ne accommodetis vos ad figuram seculi huius, sed transformemini per renouationem mentis vestræ, vt probetis, quæ sit voluntas Dei, quod bonum est, acceptum & perfectum. Rom. 6. Manebimus in peccato, vt gratia abundet? Absit: qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo posthac viuemus in eodem? An ignoratis, quòd, quicunque baptizati sumus in Christū, in mortem eius baptizati sumus? Sepulti igitur sumus vna cum illo per baptismum in mortem, vt quemadmodum excitatus est Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris, ita & nos in nouitate vitæ ambulemus. Luc. 1. vt sine timore, de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati seruiremus ipsi in sanctitate & iustitia coram ipso, cunctis diebus vitæ nostræ. 1. Thess. 4. Rogamus vos & hortamur per Dominum Iesum, quemadmodum accepistis a nobis, quomodo oporteat vos versari, & placere Deo, vt abundetis magis. Nostis enim, quæ præcepta dederimus vobis per Dominum Iesum. Hęc enim est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, vt abstineatis a fornicatione, & sciat vnusquisque vestrum suum vas possidere cum sanctificatione, & honore, non cum affectu concupiscentiæ, quemadmodum & gentes, quæ non nouerunt Deum. Et paulo post: Non enim vocauit nos Deus immunditiæ causa, sed ad sanctificationem. Et hoc est, quod Apostolus Rom. 1. 16. Et alibi fidei obedientiam inculcat, hortaturque, vt, qui a seruitute legis & peccati sunt exempti, sancte deinceps viuant, nec, instar carnis ad vomitum, ad peccati iugum redeant.
units.tr: Through which we so worship God that we may please him, with reverence and godly fear) Lest anyone reproach the Apostle for either rashly despising the works of the law, or opening a door to sins, while he teaches that the kingdom of Christ is obtained by grace, the Apostle here meets an unspoken objection, saying that those who have truly become partakers of this grace ought so to worship God that they may please him, with reverence and godly fear. In these words the obedience of faith and the duty of the justified are described. They ought to remember this worship and service of God. For they are not called to security or to lust, but to the fear of God, to obedience, to chastity, to holiness and innocence. Romans 12: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." Romans 6: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Luke 1: "That we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life." 1 Thessalonians 4: "Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more. For ye know what commandments we gave you by the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: that every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God." And a little later: "For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness." This is what the Apostle means in Romans 1:16, and elsewhere he presses the obedience of faith and exhorts that those who have been freed from the bondage of the law and of sin should live holily from now on, and not return, like a dog to its vomit, to the yoke of sin.

units.la: Cum reuerentia & religione)Ad timorem non seruile, sed liberale & ingenuum, qualis filiorum est erga parentes, Hebræos inuitat. Qui parentes reueretur pietatis nomen meretur: qui Deum colit, religionis quoque laude adipiscitur. Malach. 1. Filius honorat patrem, & seruus dominum suum timet: quòd si pater ego sum, vbi est honor mei? & si dominus sum, vbi est timor mei? Psal. 2. vbi Christi regiam maiestate & regnum inter gentes describit, tandem tali exhortatione vtitur. Et nunc reges prudenter, erudimini iudices terræ: Seruite Iehoue in timore: & exultate in tremore: osculamini Dominum, ne forte irascatur, & pereatis in via, cum exarserit vel paululum furor eius.
units.tr: With reverence and godly fear) He invites the Hebrews to a fear that is not servile but free and noble, such as that of sons towards their parents. He who reveres his parents earns the name of dutiful; he who worships God also gains the praise of piety. Malachi 1: "A son honoureth his father, and a servant his master: if then I be a father, where is mine honour? and if I be a master, where is my fear?" Psalm 2, where he describes the royal majesty and kingdom of Christ among the nations, finally uses such an exhortation: "Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little."

units.la: Ad Philip. 2. Proinde dilecti mei, sicut semper obedistis, non tanquàm in præsentia mea solùm, sed nunc multò magis in absentia mea, cum timore ac tremore, vestram ipsorum salutem operemini. Luc. 12. Christus hortatur, vt Deum metuant, qui vita hac priuatos, æternùm etiam damnare & animam perdere posit. De timore Dei scriptura passim præcepta tradit: quamobrem locos & exempla commemorare supersedebimus.
units.tr: Philippians 2: "Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." Luke 12: Christ exhorts that God be feared, who after this life is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. Scripture everywhere gives precepts about the fear of God; therefore I shall not trouble to recall passages and examples.

units.la: Etenim Deus noster ignis consumens est) Est obiter adiecta instar Epiphonematis ratio suasoria, à periculo, quod ijs imminet, qui veram sanctimoniam Euangelicam ex animo non coluerint. Estque sumpta ex Deuteronomij quarto, & valde conueniens præsenti loco. Decebat enim, Hebræis qui assueti erant minis legalibus, adhuc aliquod comminatorium inculcare, quod diu & alte animo infixum retinerent, & maximè quod ex scripturis desumptum esset. Locus facilis est, & in scripturis dilucide patefactus, ideoque longiori expositione non habet opus. Discent autem hinc Christi ciues & discipuli.
units.tr: For our God is a consuming fire) This is a persuasive argument, added in passing like an epiphonema, drawn from the danger that threatens those who have not sincerely cultivated true Gospel holiness. It is taken from Deuteronomy 4 and fits this place very well. For it was fitting to press on the Hebrews, who were accustomed to the threats of the law, some further warning that they might retain deeply and firmly fixed in their minds, especially since it was drawn from the Scriptures. The passage is easy and is clearly set out in the Scriptures, so it needs no lengthy exposition. Christ's citizens and disciples will learn from it the following.

units.la: Primùm, regnum Christi & Euangelium æternum esse, & non habiturum esse finem, sicut lex Mosaica, & regale illud sacerdotium Aaronis finem habuit.
units.tr: First, that the kingdom of Christ and the Gospel are eternal and will not have an end, unlike the Mosaic law and the royal priesthood of Aaron, which had an end.

units.la: Secundò, Regnum Christi, in gratia & fide versari. Ex Gratia scilicet offerri, per fidem verò apprehendi & assumi. Ac nisi quis in fide & gratia hac perstiterit vsq; ad finem, saluus fieri nequit.
units.tr: Second, that the kingdom of Christ rests on grace and faith: it is offered from grace, but is grasped and received through faith. And unless someone persists in this faith and grace to the end, he cannot be saved.

units.la: Tertiò: Reuerenter & religiosè Deum colendum esse ijs, qui filij & hæredes eius esse concupiscunt.
units.tr: Third, that God is to be worshipped reverently and with godly fear by those who desire to be his sons and heirs.

units.la: Quartò, proposita est malis & durae ceruicis hominibus ira Dei, quae instar ignis est consumentis. Quae quidem ratio diligenter à peccatis coercebit, & in ordinem ducet eos, qui igni æterno, & consumenti Deo cohabitare cupiunt: (Esaiae 33.)
units.tr: Fourth, the wrath of God, which is like a consuming fire, is set before evil and stiff-necked men. This consideration will indeed restrain diligently from sins and bring into order those who desire to dwell with the eternal fire and the consuming God (Isaiah 33).

units.la: CAPVT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT DECIMVMTERTIVM.
units.tr: Chapter Thirteen.

units.la: Fraterna charitas maneat: hospitalitatis ne sitis immemores: per hanc enim quidam inscientes exceperunt angelos hospitio. Memores estote vinctorum, tanquam unà cum illis vincti. Eorum, qui affliguntur, velut ipsi quoq; versantes in corpore.
units.tr: Let brotherly love continue. Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.

units.la: Ecundus locus huius quartæ partis, in quo hortatur credentes ad exercenda in genere officia charitatis erga fratres, & cum erga omnes quidem, præcipue tamen erga eos, qui propter confessionem suæ veritatis sedibus pulsi hinc inde oberrabant, aut captiui etiamnum alicubi detinebantur: aut denique quocunque ratione in corpore affligebantur, variis presi miserijs.
units.tr: This is the second point in this fourth part, in which he exhorts believers to practise the duties of love in general towards the brethren, and towards all men, but especially towards those who, because of their confession of the truth, had been driven from their homes and wandered here and there, or were still held captive somewhere, or were in any way afflicted in body by various kinds of misery.

units.la: Licet autem colligere tum ex Actis Apostolicis, tum ex ijs, quæ ante, præsertim capite decimo ad confirmandos piorum in fide animos dicta sunt, statim elucescente Euangelio apud Iudæos, per ciuitates singulas & prouincias crudeliter grassatum in omnes, qui Christum, eiusque Euangelium profiteri audebant, & quosdam quidem exutos fortunulis suis omnibus, alios pertractos in carceres: nonnullos raptos ad supplicium diuersa genera: plerosque mulctatos exilio, aliquos sponte exulatum abiisse. Necessum igitur erat, horum omnium in ecclesia haberi rationem: atq; Apostolus putauit ad se pertinere, ut cæteris Iudæis quaqua versum agentibus istos commendaret, & sicut alias solet fieri, quasi publicum testimonium instrumentum q;, in gratiam pauperum, conficeret, miseris quocunque venturi essent, profuturum. Nemo autem credit, nisi expertus, quales tentationes ijs obueniant, qui ita propter iustitiam affliguntur, nécnon coguntur in certis oberrare sedibus. Diabolus mille artifex est, & nullas non admouet machinas, quo tales in suum rete perrahat, atque in desperationem deijciat. Neque verò dubium est, quin, qui ex Hebræis feriò in fide promouerant, lubenter audierint de huiusmodi fructibus fidei siue officijs charitatis verba fieri. Nunc videamus, quanta diligentia Apostolus verus pauperum afflictorumque patronus caussam eorundem egerit. Breuiter quidem, sed in tanta breuitate grauiter magnaque cum gratia, &, quod mireris, non sine aptis rationibus suasorijs, quę aculeos in animos auditorum relinquant, pauperes commendat. Interdum breuitas nescio quid habet acrimonię, suoque modo pungit validius quàm oratio bene longa.
units.tr: We may gather, both from the Acts of the Apostles and from what was said earlier, especially in chapter ten, to strengthen the minds of the godly in faith, that as soon as the Gospel became known among the Jews, a cruel persecution raged through individual cities and provinces against all who dared to profess Christ and his Gospel. Some were stripped of all their meagre possessions, others were dragged into prison, some were seized and put to death in various ways, many were punished with exile, and some went into voluntary exile. It was therefore necessary that the Church take account of all of these, and the Apostle thought it his duty to commend these people, while the other Jews were acting everywhere as they did. As is customary elsewhere, he drew up, as it were, a public testimony and document in favour of the poor, which would be of benefit to the wretched wherever they might go. No one believes, unless he has experienced it, what temptations befall those who are thus afflicted for righteousness' sake, and are also compelled to wander from one settled place to another. The devil is a master of a thousand arts, and he brings to bear every kind of machine to draw such people into his net and cast them into despair. Nor is there any doubt that those of the Hebrews who had recently advanced in faith gladly heard words spoken about such fruits of faith, that is, about the duties of love. Let us now see with what great diligence the Apostle, a true patron of the poor and afflicted, has pleaded their cause. He commends the poor briefly, but in such brevity, gravely and with great grace, and, what is remarkable, not without apt arguments of persuasion which leave stings in the minds of the hearers. Sometimes brevity has a certain sharpness, and it pricks more forcefully in its own way than a well-extended speech.

units.la: Fraterna charitas maneat, inquit. Hæc est veluti propositio, qua generatim omnia Charitatis commendat officia. Et nusquàm non obuia est huiusmodi exhortatio, neque potest satis inculcari. Atqui multum refert, quòd adeò appositis verbis per Apostolum pronatur: φιλαδελφία μενέτω. Est plane exquisitum, piorumque auribus suauissimum vocabulum τῆς φιλαδελφίας, significat quippe amorem fraternum, quoque fratres sese mutuò debent prosequi, neque facile vna voce latina expresseris. Maximè autem ijs conueniit, qui communi eiusdem religionis confessione inuicem sibi sunt obstricti: quo quidem pacto videre est in scriptura statim vbi cœptum est haberi aliquod discrimen Deum ritè colentium, ab impijs, à primis inde sanctorum Patriarcharum temporibus, eos qui in vero cultu Dei perstiterunt, fratres semper appellatos. Et reuera, qui eodem aguntur spiritu, eundem agnoscunt, inuocantque Deum ac patrem in cœlis, omniaque spiritualia, siue ad salutem animarum pertinentia habent inter se communia, ij iustissimè videntur inter sese fratres appellari. Proinde & singularis ista beneuolentia, qua qui huiusmodi sunt, debent sese mutuò præ cæteris ardentissimè complecti, proprie φιλαδελφία nuncupabitur. Sunt profectò omnes ex æquo diligendi homines ratione communis naturæ & conditionis: at interea domesticorum, atq; eundem Dominum Deum profitentium, habendam esse primam rationem, nemo sanus est, qui non intelligat. Ac meo iudicio vox φιλαδελφία non tantùm significat talis beneuolentiæ qualitatem, verùm etiam quantitatem, vtpote quæ, quantam illam esse oporteat, tacitè insinuat. Maximam enim beneuolentiam existere debere declaratur, quæ ab exemplo fratrum proponitur. Quid enim fratribus coniunctius communi iudicio, legitimoque naturæ ordine seruato censetur?
