Atq; inde opinor factum, quòd Apostoli in suis scriptis lubenter ea voce vsi sunt, cùm, an apud alios scriptores extet, vix meminerim. Paulus Roman.10. Dilectio sit non simulata: sitis odio prosequentes, quod malum est: adhærentes ei, quod bonum est, per fraternam charitatem (τῇ φιλαδελφίᾳ) ad mutuò vos diligendos propensi.
units.tr: "Let brotherly love continue," he says. This is, as it were, the proposition by which he commends in general all the duties of love. Such an exhortation is found everywhere, and it cannot be urged enough. And yet it matters greatly that the Apostle urges it in such fitting words: let brotherly love continue [philadelphia menetō]. The word of brotherly love [tēs philadelphias] is indeed exquisite and most sweet to the ears of the godly. It signifies the fraternal affection by which brothers ought to embrace one another, and it can hardly be expressed in a single Latin word. It fits especially those who are bound to one another by the common confession of one religion. In this way one sees in Scripture that, from the earliest times of the holy patriarchs, as soon as some distinction began to be made between those who worshipped God rightly and the impious, those who persevered in the true worship of God were always called brothers. And indeed, those who are moved by the same Spirit acknowledge the same God and Father in heaven, and call upon him, and have all spiritual things, which pertain to the salvation of souls, in common among themselves; such people are most justly seen to be called brothers among themselves. Therefore that peculiar goodwill, by which such persons ought to embrace one another most ardently above all others, will properly be named brotherly love [philadelphia]. All men are indeed to be loved alike on account of their common nature and condition; yet that the first consideration must be given to members of one household and to those who profess the same Lord God, no sane person fails to understand. In my judgement, the word brotherly love [philadelphia] signifies not only the quality of such goodwill but also its quantity, since it tacitly suggests how great it ought to be. For it is declared that the greatest goodwill ought to exist, as it is set forth by the example of brothers. For what is judged, by common opinion and by the lawful order of nature, to be more closely joined than brothers? And I suppose that for this reason the Apostles were glad to use this word in their writings, though I can hardly recall whether it occurs among other writers. Paul, Romans 12: "Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good. Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love [tē philadelphiā], in honour preferring one another."

units.la: Item 1. Thessalon. 4. 1.Petri 1.2. 2 Petri 1. Sed & in hoc ipsum omni adhibito studio subministrate ἐν τῇ ὑπομονῇ τὴν φιλαδελφίαν, ἐν δὲ τῇ φιλαδελφίᾳ τὴν ἀγάπην. Ex quo loco manifestum euadit, ut hoc obiter adnotemus, φιλαδελφία differre ab ἀγάπῃ: atque ἀγάπην quidem esse quodammodo generalius vocabulum, φιλαδελφίαν vero quiddam peculiare, & solis verè credentibus conueniens innuere. Vt igitur dicere coepimus, vox φιλα- δελφία exquisita est, & idonea ad significandum, dilectionem Christianis propriè dignam, in qua Christus ipse asscriptus est communis omnium nostrum frater sub uno constitutus patre caelesti: & ad quam nulli impij vel increduli pertinent: quantumuis etiam non- nulli nouas ἀδελφότητας, vel imitatricem & hypocriticam φιλαδελφίαν confingere introduxereque sunt conati. Loquor de ineptis & ridiculis superstitiosisque fraternitatibus monachorum & similium fanaticorum, inter quos non potest vera charitas coalescere, sed tantùm externa societas quaedam simulari, de qua est & illud tritum, Fratrum quoq; gratia rara. Magnum ergo pondus apud omnes habere, necnon affectus permouere debet tam insignis & accommoda vox, qua Apostolus vti voluit.
units.tr: Likewise, 1 Thessalonians 4; 1 Peter 1:22; 2 Peter 1. Also, in this very thing, "add to your patience, with all diligence, brotherly kindness, and to brotherly kindness, charity" [en tē hypomonē tēn philadelphian, en de tē philadelphia tēn agapēn]. From this passage it becomes clear, as we note in passing, that philadelphia differs from agapē: agapē is in a sense the more general word, while philadelphia points to something peculiar and fitting only for those who truly believe. So, as I began to say, the word philadelphia is exquisite and suitable for signifying the love that properly belongs to Christians, in which Christ himself is counted as the common brother of us all, under one heavenly Father; and to which no impious or unbelieving persons belong, although some have attempted to devise and introduce new brotherhoods, or an imitative and hypocritical brotherly love. I am speaking of the foolish, ridiculous and superstitious fraternities of monks and similar fanatics, among whom true charity cannot grow, but only a certain external fellowship can be feigned, of which the common saying also holds: "Rare is the brotherly favour of the brethren." Therefore so distinguished and fitting a word, which the Apostle chose to use, ought to carry great weight with all men and to stir the affections.

units.la: Non minus insuper valebit apud pios vox μςνέτω. Etenim duo quaedam insinuat, quod Chrysostomus quoque & Vulgarius aduerterunt. Alterum, quòd iam antea fuerint fraterna charitate praediti: quod sanè ad laudem ipsorum pertinet, aculeosque ad constantiam in illa debet addere. Alterum, quòd in posterum quoque debeant in illa persEUerare, adeoque maiori, quàm antè, diligentia illam excolere. In quod profecto non abs re inuigilandum est. Nihil enim proderit, in officijs charitatis foeliciter coepisse versari, nisi detur in ijsdem progredi & perdurare. Hac de causa opinor Christum & Apostolos crebrò tali verborum forma locutos. Ioan. 15. Manete in dilectione. 1. Ioan. 4. Deus charitas est, & qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, & Deus in eo. Proinde adeò necessarium est, φιλαδελφίαν inter credentes conspici, atque etiam permanere, vt, nisi his signis caeteros anteeant, pro legitimis discipulis Christi agnosci aegrè queant: unde Christus Ioan. 13. In hoc cognoscent omnes, quòd discipuli mei estis, si charitatem habueritis inter vos mutuam. Sed & qualis erit fraternitas, in qua postquàm iacta fuerint vtcunque foeliciter fundamenta, postea nihil amplius extruitur? Imò illa ipsa fundamenta dissipantur? Igitur aptissimè haec propositio per Apostolum enunciata est.
units.tr: The word let continue [menetō] will be no less powerful among the godly. For it implies two things, as Chrysostom and Vulgarius have also noticed. The first is that they had already been endowed with brotherly love; this certainly redounds to their praise, and ought to add a spur to constancy in it. The second is that they ought to persevere in it also in the future, and so to cultivate it with greater diligence than before. Surely there is good reason to be watchful on this point. For it will profit nothing to have happily begun to practise the duties of love, unless it is granted to advance and to persevere in them. For this reason I suppose that Christ and the Apostles often spoke in this form of words: John 15: "Abide in my love." 1 John 4: "God is love, and he that abideth in love abideth in God, and God in him." Therefore it is so necessary that brotherly love be seen among believers, and that it also remain, that unless they surpass others in these signs they can hardly be recognised as true disciples of Christ. Hence Christ says, John 13: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." But what kind of brotherhood will it be, in which, after the foundations have been laid somehow happily, nothing further is built up? Nay, rather, are those very foundations not scattered? Therefore this proposition has been most aptly stated by the Apostle.

units.la: Hospitalitatis ne sitis immemores) Subijcit φιλαδελφίας aliquot species siue partes, quadam distributionis forma. Neque enim fraterna charitas otiosa est aut sterilis: neque sita est in verbis tantum, aut inanibus gestibus: sed in veris fructibus, quibus iuuatur proximus, & quibus Deus honorari gaudet: 1. Ioan. 3. Filioli mei, ne diligamus verbo, neque lingua, sed opere & veritate. Porrò species enumerat non omnes quidem, quae sub fraternitate comprehenduntur, (sunt enim huiusmodi propemodum infinitae, & plurima, quae post pauca subijcientur, merito ad hunc referentur ordinem) sed eas, quas maximè exercendas apud Iudaeos per id tempus arbitrabatur: idque propter causas paulo ante à nobis expositas. Prima itaque species hic collocatur, Hospitalitas. Eamque aptissimis verbis commendat: Siquidem non dicit ξενίαν, id est, hospitalitatem: sed φιλοξενίαν, significans nimirum, cum amore & studio multo hospitalitatem exercendam: comprehenditque ea voce omnia simul officia erga pauperes, peregrinos, maximèque qui propter iustitiae confessionem exilium subeunt, impendi solita, quae reuera non pauca sunt. Patres legimus in more habuisse lauare pedes aduentantium: tùm cibum, potum, aliaque id genus solatia suppeditasse: cubiculum impartisse: aegros curasse: vt alia omittamus his affinia. Etsi vnquàm aliàs, at maximè temporibus Apostolorum, quibus innumeri vndique propter Euangelium sedibus pellebantur, hospitalitate opus erat, plurimaque eius exercendae habebatur materia. Vnde etiam factum, quòd Apostoli omnes diligentissimè eam commendarint Romanorum 12. τὴν φιλοξενίαν διώκοντες. 1. Petri 4. φι- λόξενοι erga vos inuicem sine murmuratione. Ab episcopis inprimis hospitalitas requiritur 1. Timoth. 3. Tit. 1. Itaque & hoc loco Apostolus suis Hebraeis vehementer eam praedicat. Rursus, Ne sitis, inquit, immemores: Significat nimirum, illos antea quidem hac virtute fuisse conspicuos, at nunc debere adhuc eidem dare operam, neque de veteri studio quicquam remittendum. Verosimile sanè est, quosdam factis fuisse frigidiores, aut forte praetexuisse, se non perinde, vt antè posse praestare: de facultatibus enim non parum detractum, aut aliquid huiusmodi. Proinde Apostolus iubet, saltem sint memores hospitalitatis, tanquàm si insinuaret, se non velle cuipiam grauius praescribere, sed tantùm postulare, vt pro viribus praestent aliquid. Neq; enim hic sumptuum magnitudo, aut apparatus splendor, sed animi promptitudo respicitur. Etiam solum tectu & calix aquae frigidae suam habet gratiam. Quis verò imperet supra vires posita? Et quis obsecro aduetans peregre atq; pressus inopia, non velit esse contentus vel vili olusculo, atroq; pane, quem sub tecto fratris inuenerit? Ad omnes igitur ex aequo praeceptum istud Apostoli pertinet, cùm nemo sit, qui saltem exiguum quiddam exhibere egenti, non queat.
units.tr: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers." He adds several species, or parts, of brotherly love, in a certain form of division. For fraternal love is neither idle nor barren; nor does it lie in words only, or in empty gestures, but in true fruits, by which the neighbour is helped and with which God delights to be honoured: 1 John 3: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth." Moreover, he does not enumerate all the species that are comprehended under brotherly love (for such are almost infinite, and many which will be set out shortly are rightly referred to this order), but those which he judged most to be practised among the Jews at that time, and this for the reasons which we explained a little earlier. The first species, therefore, is placed here: hospitality. And he commends it in most apt words. For he does not say xenia [ξενίαν], that is, hospitality, but philoxenia [φιλοξενίαν], signifying, that is, that hospitality is to be exercised with love and great eagerness; and by this word he comprehends all the duties usually performed towards the poor and strangers, and above all towards those who go into exile for the confession of righteousness, which in truth are not few. We read that the Fathers were in the custom of washing the feet of arrivals, and then supplying food, drink, and other such comforts; they gave lodging, they cared for the sick, not to mention other things akin to these. Hospitality was needed at other times too, but most of all in the times of the Apostles, when countless people were driven from their homes on every side on account of the Gospel, and there was very much material for exercising it. Hence it is also that all the Apostles commended it most diligently: Romans 12: "pursuing hospitality" [tēn philoxenian diōkontes]; 1 Peter 4: "be hospitable [philoxenoi] one to another without grudging." Hospitality is especially required of bishops, 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1. Accordingly, in this passage also the Apostle strongly urges it upon his Hebrews. Again, "Be not forgetful," he says. This clearly means that they were formerly distinguished by this virtue, but that now they ought still to devote themselves to it, and nothing of their former zeal should be relaxed. It is quite likely that some had grown colder in deeds, or perhaps had pretended that they were no longer able to give as before; for a good deal of their resources had been taken away, or something of that kind. Therefore the Apostle bids them at least to remember hospitality, as if he were suggesting that he does not wish to prescribe anything too heavy for anyone, but only to ask that they give something according to their means. For here what is looked at is not the size of the expense, nor the splendour of display, but readiness of mind. Even a roof alone, and a cup of cold water, have their own worth. Who, indeed, would command what lies beyond his strength? And who, I beg you, when a traveller is pressed by want, would not be content with even a cheap dish of herbs and black bread, if he found it under a brother's roof? This precept of the Apostle therefore applies equally to all, since there is no one who cannot at least provide some small thing for the needy.

units.la: Per hanc enim quidam inscientes exceperunt angelos) Ratio suasoria ab exmeplo, de effectu siue fœlici successu eorum, qui hospitales extiterunt. Quando autem dicit, quidam, notat, plures fuisse, quibus id, quod narrat, euenerit. Commemorat autem Scriptura duos maximè insignes: alterum, inquam, Abrahamum, qui tres excepit hospitio Dei angelos, existimans esse homines peregrè proficiscentes: Genef. 18. Alterum Loth, qui duos recepit angelos, quos etiam ab iniurijs impiorum ciuium, non citra suum suorumque periculum, pro viribus tutatus est. De Angelis apud Loth diuertentibus clara est sententia Genef. 19. At de illis, qui venerunt ad Abraham, num angeli fuerint, posset vtcunque dubitari. Sed enim scriptura exprimit nihilominus, quæ supra hominum fortem fuisse illos, satis arguunt: vt conueniat concedere, aut angelos fuisse: aut, si dici possit, Deum ipsum. Nam rogant de Sara absente, prædicunt futura, vident post ostium ridentem: & diserte de colloquentibus cum Abraham dicitur: Dixitq; Dominus ad Abraham: cur sic risit Sara? Iteñ, Dominus prædicit euersionem Sodomorum, &c. Hæ sanè appellationes non tribuerentur, nisi angeli à Domino missi fuissent. Igitur etiam ad Abraham angeli diuerterunt. Cæterùm cùm sancti patres hoc pacto narrantur recepisse angelos, non adeò magna fœlicitas accessit propter qualitatem personarum: (neque enim valde magnum erat, suscepisse angelos) sed potius propter officium, quod angeli præstiterunt. Abrahamo namque prænunciarunt natiuitatem Isaac: Loth docuerunt ac monuerunt, vt ex periculo Sodomorum eriperetur. Angeli Dei non possunt nisi bona adferre: &, quisquis angelos recipit, intelligitur plura simul bona cum angelis recipere. Ergo hic aliquid amplius innuitur, quàm simpliciter verba sonant: ac palàm fit, longè maximam esse fœlicitatem, angelos hospitio recipere. Quod verò addit, inscientes, aliquo modo fœlicitatem amplificat. Inopinatum enim insperatumque bonum vehementissimè afficit. Porrò huic rationi commodum attexeretur ex sententia Christi, alia promissio, nempe quòd non tantum angelos recipiant, qui hospitalitatem exercent, verùm etiam Christum ipsum: Sic enim Matt. 10 & Lucæ 9. Qui vnum recipit iustum in nomine meo, me recipit: & Matthæi 25. Amen dico vobis, quatenus fecistis vni ex his fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Memores estote uinctorum: Secunda species fraternæ charitatis, beneficientia erga captiuos, maximèque qui ob confessionem veritatis in periculum venerint. Decet quidem illorum, quoque miseremur, qui vel sceleris perpetrati causa poenis subijciuntur, vt nimirum beneficentia, visitatione, auxilio, consilio ue adducantur, si fieri queat, ad refipiscentiam, accipiantque emendandi occasionem: at verò ergà illos præcipuè oportet nos charitatem exercere, qui verè demum fratres sunt, qui propter confessionem communis nostræ fidei ac veritatis, affliguntur: & ad quos proprie φιλαδελφίαν extenditur: idque, ut solatium quale cunque à nobis accipientes in fide constantes permaneant. Atque hanc esse mentem Apostoli, euidens fit exijs, quæ supra capite decimo de certaminibus & pressuris credentium ad id tempus in ecclesia fusius dicta sunt. Eodem pertinent nonnulla dicta à Petro prioris epistolæ capite quarto: vbi inter cætera: Ne quis, inquit, vestrum affligatur, vt homicida, aut fur, aut facinorosus, aut curiosus alienarum rerum. Porrò, si vt christianus affligatur aliquis, ne pudefiat, imò glorificet Deum in parte hac. Et Christus tantundem complexus est, quando ait Matthæi 5. Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Rursus verò aduerte, quàm blandè Apostolus loquatur. Non dicit, oportet vos subuenire vinctis, tanquàm docens, aut præcipiens aliquid, quod illi nescierant: sed simpliciter, Memores estote uinctorum: quasi dicat: Probè noftis, quid facere vos oporteat, vtpote qui iam olim vos sic satis exercuitis in pietatis operibus: tantùm date operam, ne hoc benefaciendi studium animo vestro excidat. Cæterùm multa simul comprehenduntur hic officia erga captiuos præstanda, veluti cibatio, refectio, oratio ad Deum, intercessio apud magistratum, consilium, consolatio. certè impediri non possunt, quo minus pro ipsis orent. Secunda, nulla ratio adiuuandum est efficacior, quàm assidua ecclesiæ pro ipsis oratio, utpote per quam aut mirabiliter exemplo Petri liberantur: aut certè constantes in fide ad mortem usq; redduntur. Tertia, Nullus est adeò pauper, qui saltem hoc officium præstare nequeat. Quamobrem nemo excusatur, quo minus vel hoc modo vinctorum memor sit.
units.tr: For through this some, unawares, have entertained angels. This is an argument of persuasion from example, drawn from the outcome and happy success of those who were hospitable. When he says some, he indicates that there were several to whom what he relates happened. Scripture records two especially notable instances: first, Abraham, who received three angels of God as guests, thinking they were men travelling abroad (Gen. 18); second, Lot, who took in two angels and defended them against the wicked violence of the citizens, not without risk to himself and his family (the clear statement about the angels who lodged with Lot is at Gen. 19). Whether those who came to Abraham were angels might be doubted to some extent. Yet Scripture sets out things which plainly show that they were beyond human strength, so that one must concede either that they were angels or, if it may be said, God himself. For they inquire about Sarah who was absent, they foretell the future, they see her laughing behind the door; and of those conversing with Abraham it is expressly said: The Lord said to Abraham: why did Sarah laugh like that? Again, the Lord foretells the overthrow of Sodom, etc. These titles would not be given unless the angels had been sent by the Lord. Therefore the angels also lodged with Abraham. Moreover, although the holy fathers are described as having received angels in this way, the happiness that came to them was not so very great on account of the quality of the persons (for it was not very remarkable to have received angels), but rather on account of the office which the angels performed. For they announced to Abraham the birth of Isaac, and they taught and warned Lot so that he might be rescued from the danger of Sodom. The angels of God can bring only good things, and whoever receives angels is understood to receive many good things at the same time. Therefore something more is hinted at here than the words simply say, and it is plain that to receive angels as guests is by far the greatest happiness. What he adds, unawares, in some way heightens the happiness, for an unexpected and unhoped-for good affects us very strongly. To this argument may be fittingly added another promise from the words of Christ: that they receive not only angels who practise hospitality but Christ himself. For so Matt. 10 and Luke 9: "Whoever receives one righteous man in my name receives me"; and Matt. 25: "Truly I say to you, inasmuch as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Remember those in bonds: this is the second kind of brotherly love, beneficence towards captives, and especially those who have come into danger for the confession of the truth. Indeed we ought to pity also those who are punished for a crime committed, so that by beneficence, visitation, help or counsel they may, if it can be done, be brought to repentance and given an opportunity of amendment. But towards those above all we ought to exercise love who are truly brothers, who are afflicted on account of the confession of our common faith and truth, and to whom brotherly love [φιλαδελφίαν] properly extends, so that receiving from us whatever comfort, they may remain constant in faith. That this is the mind of the Apostle is evident from what was said more fully in chapter ten about the struggles and sufferings of believers in the church up to that time. To the same purpose pertain some sayings of Peter in chapter four of his first epistle, where among other things he says: "Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or a meddler in others' affairs. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this respect." Christ too embraced the same when he says in Matthew 5: "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Again, note how gently the Apostle speaks. He does not say, "You must help the bound," as if teaching or commanding something they had not known; but simply, Remember those in bonds, as if he said: You know well what you ought to do, since you have long since exercised yourselves sufficiently in works of piety; only take care that this zeal for doing good does not slip from your mind. Many duties towards captives are comprehended here at once: feeding, refreshing, prayer to God, intercession with the magistrate, counsel, consolation. They certainly cannot be prevented from praying for them. Second, no help is more effective than the continual prayer of the church for them, since through it they are either wonderfully delivered, as Peter was, or at least made constant in faith even unto death. Third, no one is so poor that he cannot at least perform this duty. Therefore no one is excused from remembering those in bonds in this way at least.

units.la: Eorum qui affliguntur) Tertia species siue pars fraternæ charitatis, beneficentia videlicet erga τὸς κακουχουμένος, id est, eos, qui male affecti sunt in corpore, siue per ægritudinem, siue per famem, sitim, aliámue necessitatem. Certum est, propter varias molestias, veluti peregrinationes, direptionem facultatum, squalores carceris, aliasq; id genus molestias, multos male affectos fuisse corpore, multos languisse, multos mœrore confectos. Omnium igitur talium Apostolus rationem habere cupit.
units.tr: Those who are afflicted: the third kind or part of brotherly love, namely beneficence towards those who are ill-treated [τοὺς κακουχουμένους], that is, those who are ill in body, whether through sickness, or hunger, thirst, or some other need. It is certain that, because of various troubles, such as journeys, the plundering of goods, the squalor of prison and other troubles of this kind, many have been ill in body, many have languished, and many have been worn down by grief. The Apostle therefore wishes to take account of all such.

units.la: Veluti ipsi quoque uersantes in corpore) Ratio suasoria, quasi diceret: Memineritis, quòd paria vobis quoq; possent in corpore obuenire. Atque ita est: Nulla ratio mouere me debet ad miserendum fratrum nostrorum, quàm consideratio proprię vilitatis, nécnon cogitatio, quòd, quæ cernimus in corpore alieno, eadem in in nostris quoq; corporibus possint obuenire: unde etiam diuina prouidentia ita comparatum, ut frequentissimè, quibus multæ suppetunt opes, ij aliquid incommodi in corpore patiantur, quo videlicet sentire discant interdum, quomodo cum alijs, qui aliqua rerum laborant inopia, agatur. Alij desunt opes, alij deest sanitas, alij aliud: & ad summam, nemo vnus habet omnia, quæ optaret etiam tanquam necessaria, id verò, quo aliorum quoq; aliqua ope se egere intelligant. Christus dicitur factus per omnia similis nostri, & factus infirmitatibus nostris obnoxius, ut sciret, quales nostræ quoq; sint miseriæ, tantoque lubentius nobis succurreret, quanto grauiores in se experiebatur. Sciat igitur ille, sic quoq; ad Christum proximè accedere, qui ex proprij corporis infirmitatibus assuescit iudicare, quomodo cæteri fratres, præsertim ægri in corpore affecti sint. Eaque causa est, cur Deus in oculis & ad fores diuitum riusquam non ingerat pauperum spectacula, quo videlicet habeant quasi specula, in quibus cernant, quid ipsi quoq; esse possint, quantum q; Deo præcæteris debeant, agnoscant, denique, quoad commiserationem inducantur. Quòd si hoc animo versaret diues epulo, cùm audiret & videret ad fores suas Lazarum, nequaquam in pœnas infernales fuisset detrusus.
units.tr: As being yourselves also in the body: an argument of persuasion, as if he said: Remember that similar things might also happen to you in the body. And so it is: no reason ought to move me to pity our brothers more than consideration of my own frailty, and the thought that what we see in another's body can also befall our own bodies. Hence divine providence has so arranged that very often those who have abundant means suffer some inconvenience in body, so that they may learn at times how it goes with others who labour under some lack. Some lack resources, some lack health, others something else; and in sum, no one has everything he would wish, even as necessities, so that each may understand that he too needs the help of others. Christ is said to have been made like us in all things, and made subject to our infirmities, so that he might know what our miseries are, and might help us the more willingly the heavier he experienced them in himself. Let him therefore know that he draws near to Christ in this way too, who by the infirmities of his own body learns to judge how the other brothers, especially those afflicted in body, are. And this is the reason why God does not thrust the sight of the poor before the eyes and at the doors of the rich, that they may have, as it were, mirrors in which they see what they themselves could also be, and how much they owe to God above others, and, finally, that they may be led to compassion. But if the rich man feasting had been disposed in this spirit, when he heard and saw Lazarus at his door, he would by no means have been thrust down into infernal punishments.

units.la: Restat doctrinam aliquam ex his nobis colligamus: primò, discamus hic, quàm necessarium sit, inter credentes, maximeque qui præcæteris sunt cognitione rerum spiritualium illuminati, φιλαδελφίαν eminere, qua sese mutuò tanquam veros fratres complectantur, & quidem longè arctius syn ceriusq;, quàm fratres vlli carnales vnquam possent, cùm spiritualia semper decet carnalibus anteponi. Neque agnoscet Christus in extremo die pro suis discipulis, qui φιλαδελφίαν Christianam hic nō excoluerunt. Valeant interea fraternitates carnales, quæ ex traditionibus humanis suam trahunt originem: ualeat vniuersa carnalis consanguinitas, in qua sunt pater, mater, frater, soror; si nos præpediant, quo minus hanc beneficentiam à Deo commendatam ritè colamus.
units.tr: It remains that we gather some doctrine from these things. First, let us learn here how necessary it is that brotherly love [φιλαδελφία] stand out among believers, and especially among those who are enlightened above others with knowledge of spiritual things, so that they embrace one another as true brothers, and indeed much more closely and purely than any carnal brothers could ever do, since spiritual things ought always to be placed before carnal things. Nor will Christ on the last day acknowledge as his disciples those who did not cultivate Christian brotherly love [φιλαδελφίαν] here. Let carnal fraternities, which draw their origin from human traditions, fare as they may; let all carnal kinship, in which are father, mother, brother and sister, fare as it may, if they hinder us from duly observing this beneficence commended by God.

units.la: Secundo loco, dicere animus est aliquid de hospitalitate, & de redimendis captiuis, & de pauperum in communi subuentione. Ac nunc certè non minus opus est, de his disseri, quàm olim in primitiua ecclesia: quando vbique multi sunt egeni, & supra quàm dici potest, fraterna charitas hac in parte refriguit. Animiaduerti, iam olim à maioribus nostris multa pie excogitata & fancita ad promouendum hospilitatis & beneficentię in captiuos ac pauperes exercitium: sed nunc nescio quomodo pleraq; multis in locis sunt prorsus abolita: aut, si quæ adhuc supersunt, id tamen ita, ut omitti peræquè possent.
units.tr: Secondly, I intend to say something about hospitality, the ransoming of captives, and the common relief of the poor. There is now certainly no less need to discuss these matters than there was formerly in the primitive Church, when the poor are everywhere numerous and brotherly love has cooled in this respect beyond what can be said. I notice that our forebears long ago devised and enacted many pious measures to promote the practice of hospitality and beneficence towards captives and the poor. But now, I know not how, most of these have been utterly abolished in many places, or, where any still survive, they are such that they could just as well be dropped.

units.la: Dicam igitur nonnihil de ueterum diligentia, ut hinc, quid nos quoq; deceat facere, omnes intelligamus. Statim igitur vbi illucere cœpit lux euangelij, apostoli sequentes magistrum Christum, impense commendarunt in omnibus credentibus, tum potissimum ecclesiarum episcopis, hoc munus prouidendi pauperibus, tam peregrinis, quàm domesticis. Credentes interea promptis animis conferebant de suis facultatibus, alibi quidem, ut Hierosolymis, vniuersas: alibi uerò, quantum visum fuerat. Succedente tempore etiam ampli prouentus accreuerunt. Atqui auctis his, cœpit ipsorum episcoporum ac diaconorum, quibus administratio omnis erat demandata, fides, diligentia, syn ceritas, decrefcre, vt alicubi viderentur quidam in suos vsus liberius ecclesiæ opes transferre, veros pauperes negligere, denique alijs modis se in dispensandi officio supfectos redde re. Quid multis? Excogitata est via distribuendi ecclesiæ facultates in certas portiones, ut ita episcopis & ministris ecclesiarum dimensum quoddam redderetur, pauperibus verò cederet, quicquid foret reliquum. Atque, vt fidelius ista gererentur, etiam canones ea de re publicati sunt, quos & ad decretum relatos videre est. Nā 12.q.2. c. concessō vobis. Ex rescripto Gelasij. C. Quatuor autē: eiusdem Gelasij verba sunt. C. de redditibus ex rescripto Simplicij papæ ad Florentium & Equitium episcopos. C. Cognouimus. Gregorius scribit ad Maximianū episcopum Syracusanum. C. Mos est. C. Sancimus. Quorū omnium canonum hæc summa est: Ecclesię redditus in quatuor partes diuidi debere, vnam assignandam episcopo, clericis, siue ecclesiarum ministris, vt inde victum sufficien tem habere queant. Alteram pauperibus ecclesiæ annumeratis: tertiam sacris ædibus, atq; aliis ædificijs farciendis & conseruandis: quartam aduenis extraneisque pauperib.
units.tr: I will therefore say something about the diligence of the ancients, so that from this we may all understand what we too ought to do. As soon as the light of the gospel began to shine, the apostles, following their master Christ, earnestly commended this duty of providing for the poor, strangers as well as members of the household, to all believers, and especially to the bishops of the churches. Meanwhile believers, with ready minds, contributed from their means: in some places, as at Jerusalem, all of their property; elsewhere, as much as seemed fitting. As time went on, the funds also grew large. But with these increased, the faith, diligence and integrity of the bishops and deacons themselves, to whom the whole administration had been entrusted, began to decline, so that in some places certain men seemed to transfer the church's wealth more freely to their own uses, to neglect the truly poor, and in other ways to show themselves unfaithful in the office of stewardship. What more is there to say? A method was devised of dividing the church's resources into fixed portions, so that a certain measure would be set for the bishops and ministers of the churches, and whatever remained would go to the poor. And so that these things might be managed more faithfully, canons were also published on this matter, which can be seen cited in the Decretum: 12 q. 2, c. Concessum vobis; from the rescript of Gelasius, c. Quatuor autem (these are the words of Gelasius); c. De redditibus, from the rescript of Pope Simplicius to the bishops Florentius and Equitius; c. Cognovimus, where Gregory writes to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse; c. Mos est; c. Sancimus. The sum of all these canons is this: the revenues of the church ought to be divided into four parts. One is to be assigned to the bishop, the clergy, or the ministers of the churches, so that they may have sufficient sustenance from it. A second is to be counted out for the poor of the church. The third is for repairing and maintaining the sacred buildings and other structures. The fourth is for strangers and poor travellers.

units.la: Pauperibus igitur primo loco inquilinis seu domesticis: secundo extraneis seu peregrè aduentantibus duplicata cedit portio. Sed enim priscis patribus tanta adhuc fuit ale dorum pauperum cura, vt, si facultates eum in modum distributæ non sufficerent, ante omnia quidem de proprio, mox de parte cedente ædificijs, vel de ipsis vasis, quæ parti huic non abs re annumerantur, detrahebant, vnde pauperum inopiæ succurreretur. Ex quo postea etiam sancitum, ut pro pauperum alimonia, & redemptione captiuorum liceret res sacras, vasa, calices, vestes, distrahere: quemadmodum eadem 12. q. 2. C. Aurum ecclesia palam fit. Id vero sancti patres longè ante viuidis suis actionibus docuerunt. Refertur namque tripartitæ historiæ lib. 5. cap. 37. de Cyrillo Hierosolymorum episcopo, quòd cùm fames prouinciam occupasset, nec posset aliter pauperum egestas subleuari, vasa & vela distraxerit, inque pauperū alimoniam insumpserit. Item lib. 11. cap. 16. Acatius Aundę episcopus, cùm ad septem fere millia Persarum à Romanis militibus captiua detinerentur, & fame propemodum interirent, conuocatis clericis suis, atque habita oratione, quòd Deus noster neque calicibus, neque discis opus habeat, cùm neque bibere neq; edere assueuerit, vasa conflauit, & captiuos peregrinos eorundem pretio redemit, redemptos refectosq; ad regem proprium remisit. Hieronymus scribens ad Nepotianū, vbi in immodicum templorum ornatum inuehitur, inter cætera tandem prædicat Exuperiū Tolosanum episcopum eo seculo superstitē, vertitq; ei maximæ laudi, quòd corpus Domini in canistro vimineo circumferret, & sanguinem in uitro, at verò nullum ex pauperibus esurire pateretur.
units.tr: So the poor receive a double portion: first those who live in the household or at home, and second strangers or those arriving from abroad. But indeed the early fathers still had such great care for feeding the poor that, if the resources so distributed were not enough, they took first from their own property, then from the part assigned to buildings, or even from the vessels themselves, which are not without reason counted in this portion, so that the poverty of the poor might be relieved. Hence it was later also enacted that, for the feeding of the poor and the redemption of captives, it should be lawful to sell sacred things, vessels, chalices and vestments, as 12 q. 2, c. Aurum ecclesiae plainly states. The holy fathers had taught this long before by their own deeds. For the Tripartite History, book 5, chapter 37, relates of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, that when famine had taken hold of the province, and the poverty of the needy could not otherwise be relieved, he sold the vessels and hangings and spent the money on feeding the poor. Likewise, book 11, chapter 16: Acacius, bishop of Amida, when about seven thousand Persians were held captive by Roman soldiers and were nearly dying of hunger, called together his clergy. After a prayer that our God has no need of chalices or dishes, since he has never been accustomed to drink or eat, he melted down the vessels, ransomed the foreign captives with their price, and sent them back, restored and fed, to their own king. Jerome, writing to Nepotianus, where he inveighs against the immoderate adornment of churches, at last among other things praises Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, who was still alive in that age. It redounds to his great credit that he carried the body of the Lord in a wicker basket and the blood in a glass, yet allowed none of the poor to go hungry.

units.la: Posidonius episcopus Calamensis de Augustino scriptum reliquit, quòd, vbi non esset, quod daret pauperibus, & populus publicè admonitus non satis conferret, vasa dominica frangi & conflari iusserit, quo posset in captiuorum redemptionem, & pauperum aliorum vlum erogare. Ambrosius similiter pro captiuis redimendis, quicquid auri vel argentei esset instrumenti in ecclesia, confregit. Quod insigne factum cùm aduersarij Arriani raperent in calumniam, ac probro verterent, accusantes, quasi ecclesiam temere dispoliasset, ipse ita excusauit, vt videre est, de officijs lib. 2. cap. 28. Quæ verba etiam inter canones relata sunt 12. q. 2. C. Aurum ecclesia. Aurum ecclesia, inquit, habet, non vt feruet, sed vt eroget & subueniat in necessitatibus. Quid est opus custodire, quod nihil adiuuat? An ignoramus, quantum auri atque argenti de templo Domini Assyrij sustulerint? Nonne melius conflat sacerdos pro alimonia pauperum, si aliqua subsidia desunt, quàm si sacrilegus contaminat, & asportat hostis? Nonne dicturus est Dominus: Cur pasus es tot inopes fame mori? Certè habebas aurum, vnde ministrasses alimoniam. Cur tot captiui in captiuitatem ducti, nec redempti, ab hoste occisi sunt? Melius fuerat, vt vasa viuentium seruares, quàm metallorum.
units.tr: Posidonius, bishop of Calama, left it written of Augustine that, when there was nothing to give the poor, and the people, publicly admonished, did not contribute enough, he ordered the Lord's vessels to be broken up and melted down, so that the proceeds could be spent on the ransom of captives and the support of other poor. Ambrose likewise broke up whatever gold or silver instruments there were in the church for the redemption of captives. When the Arian adversaries seized upon this remarkable deed, turning it into a slander and a reproach, accusing him of having rashly stripped the church, he himself defended it, as can be seen in On the Duties, book 2, chapter 28. These words too are cited among the canons, 12 q. 2, c. Aurum ecclesiae: "The church has gold not so that it may lie idle, but so that it may give and help in necessity. What is the point of guarding what does nothing to help? Do we not know how much gold and silver the Assyrians carried off from the temple of the Lord? Is it not better that the priest melt down vessels for the feeding of the poor, if some means are lacking, than that the sacrilegious enemy defile and carry them off? Will not the Lord say: Why did you let so many needy ones die of hunger? Surely you had gold from which you could have provided food. Why were so many captives led into captivity, not redeemed, and killed by the enemy? It would have been better for you to keep the vessels of the living than those of metal."

units.la: His non potes respondere. Quid enim dices? Timui, ne templo Dei ornatus deesset? Respondet: aurum sacramenta non quærunt, neque auro placent, quæ auro non emuntur. Ornatus sacrorum redemptio captiuorum est: & vere illa sunt vasa pretiosa, quæ redimunt animas à morte. Hæc ibi: aliaque sequuntur plane lectu dignissima. Quid? quod superiori seculo quidam valde anxiè disputarunt, an clerico, qui addixerit se ecclesiæ ministerio, atque habet interim ex patrimonio satis, vnde viuat, liceret accipere de ecclesiæ redditibus portionem ministro assignatam? Nimirum tanta erat cura alendorū ex bonis ecclesiæ pauperum, vt minister, qui aliquid ex illis acciperet, cui tamen de suo esset, vnde sese posset alere, crederetur pauperibus aliquā portionem præripere: id quod furti culpa haud vacaret.
units.tr: You cannot answer these points. For what will you say? That you feared the temple of God would lack adornment? He answers: the sacraments do not seek gold, nor are they pleased by gold, and things that cannot be bought with gold are not bought with it. The redemption of captives is the adornment of the sacred things, and truly those are precious vessels which redeem souls from death. Thus far he; other passages follow which are well worth reading. And what of this: in the previous century some disputed very anxiously whether a clergyman who had devoted himself to the ministry of the church, and who meanwhile had enough from his patrimony to live on, might lawfully take a portion of the church's revenues assigned to a minister? Certainly so great was the care for feeding the poor from the goods of the church that a minister who received anything from them, even though he had his own means of support, was believed to snatch some portion away from the poor, and this would not be free of the guilt of theft.

units.la: Hæc ideò referre libuit de maiorum nostrorum ad fouendos pauperes diligentia, vt videlicet dispiceretis, quatum à pietate prisca huius seculi homines discesserint, & quā turpiter nunc plerique bonis ecclesiasticis abutantur, ad suum commodum conuerten tes, quæ debita sunt pauperibus.
units.tr: I have thought fit to relate these things about the diligence of our forebears in supporting the poor, so that you may see how far the men of this age have departed from ancient piety, and how shamefully many now abuse ecclesiastical goods, turning to their own advantage what is owed to the poor.

units.la: Vbi obsecro nunc, vt taceam de duplicata portione, pauperibus cedit vel decima pars ecclesiasticarum opum? Audio quidem collegia instituta hospitalariorū, templariorū, & similium, qui redimendis captiuis, excipiendisque peregrinis vacaret: sed ex his quid nunc superest? Fateor quidē, præclara fuisse taliu collegiorum initia, sed progressus atq; exitus
units.tr: Where now, I beg you, to say nothing of the double portion, does even a tenth part of the church's wealth go to the poor? I hear indeed that colleges of hospitallers, Templars and the like were founded, devoted to ransoming captives and receiving strangers; but what of them survives now? I grant that the beginnings of such colleges were splendid, but their progress and outcomes have turned out very differently.

units.la: Distribuio redditum ecclesiasticorum Veterum dilectio et zelus in alendis pauperibus. 1. Cyrillus vasa vela distrahit propter pauperum sustentationem. 2. Acatius vasa conflauit ad redimendos captiuos. 3. Exuperij Tolosani episcopi laus. 4. Augustini diligentia. 5. Ambrosius. Arrianorum scandalū acceptū. 6. Quæstio de clerico diuite, an alendus sit redditibus ecclesiasticis. Vide Angelum de Clan. in summa Clericus §. 3. ubi docet quòd clericus debeat esse bonorum ecclesiasticorum. exitus multum dispares sunt secuti. Ac nunc quidem digladiantur & bella gerunt non- nulli pro bonis ecclesiasticis, sed tamen quis illorum facit mentionem? imo quis vel cogitat de collocandis ecclesiasticis facultatibus in pauperes? Certe si aliquid pro ecclesiarum reformatione est aliquando tentandum, vel primum esse debet illud, ut videlicet de dispensandis aliter, quam nunc, ad morem veteris ecclesiae, bonis ecclesiasticis ratio ineatur. Verum de his alias forte plura. Tantum placuit in praesenti admonere.
units.tr: The distribution of ecclesiastical revenues; the love and zeal of the ancients in feeding the poor. 1. Cyril sells vessels and hangings for the support of the poor. 2. Acacius melts down vessels to ransom captives. 3. The praise of Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse. 4. Augustine's diligence. 5. Ambrose; the offence taken by the Arians. 6. The question about a wealthy clergyman: whether he may be supported from ecclesiastical revenues. See Angelus de Clavasio, Summa, Clericus §3, where he teaches that a clergyman ought to be dependent on ecclesiastical goods.

units.la: Honorabile est inter omnes coniugium, & cubile impollutum. Scortatores autem & adulteros iudicabit Deus.
units.tr: Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled; but God will judge whoremongers and adulterers.

units.la: Tertius locus de sancto & caste colendo coniugio vitandisq; stupris atq; adulterijs. Apparet quoldam ad illud tempus coepisse nuptiarum dignitati detrahere, atq; asseruisse, aut nuptias per se esse detestandas volentibus ad perfectionem euangelicam contendere: aut non convenire quibuslibet: aut certe aliquam ineße ijs pollutionem, atq; sordes, ob quas minoris foret aestimandum coniugium. Aduertens itaq; Apostolus & iniuriam fieri haud leuem coniugio, quod diuinitus erat institutum, & fenestram aperiri hac ratio ne ad scortationem vel adulterium (hoc enim fere sequi solet, ut, qui euangelium detestantur, prolabantur in fornicationem vel adulterium: sicut in hunc usque diem manifesta exempla nos edocent) voluit suam coniugio dignitatem afferere, atque a contrarijs vitijs auocare.
units.tr: The third place concerns holy marriage, which is to be honoured and kept chaste, and concerns avoiding debauchery and adultery. It appears that some at that time began to detract from the dignity of marriage, and asserted either that marriage was in itself to be shunned by those who wished to strive for evangelical perfection, or that it did not suit everyone, or at least that there was some pollution and filth in it, on account of which marriage was to be esteemed less. The Apostle, therefore, perceiving both that no slight injury was being done to marriage, which had been instituted by God, and that a window was being opened by this means to fornication or adultery (for this usually follows, that those who despise the gospel fall into fornication or adultery, as clear examples teach us to this day), wished to vindicate the dignity of marriage and to call men away from the contrary vices.

units.la: Breuiter itaque, sed tamen grauiter exquisitisque verbis de hac re disserit: Honorabile, inquit, est coniugium: τίμιος ὁ γάμος. Certe dum causas coniugij intuemur, multasque circumstantias, honorabile esse vitae genus inueniemus. Si respicis causam efficientem atque autorem is Deus est: si causam finalem, ea est generis humani propagatio conseruatioq;, prolium in timore Dei educatio. Si tempus institutionis eius, inuenies antiquissimum, atq; institutum in ipso paradiso, etiam ante primi parentis lapsum, ut perseuerantibus in iustitia originali conuenire potuerit.
units.tr: Briefly, then, but weightily and with carefully chosen words, he discusses this matter: "Honourable," he says, "is marriage: τίμιος ὁ γάμος." Indeed, when we consider the causes of marriage and its many circumstances, we shall find it an honourable state of life. If you look to the efficient cause and author, it is God; if to the final cause, it is the propagation and preservation of the human race and the upbringing of children in the fear of God. If you consider the time of its institution, you will find it most ancient, and instituted in paradise itself, even before the fall of the first parents, so that it could have befitted those who persevered in original righteousness.

units.la: Inuenies approbatione Dei, & promissionibus praeclaris honestatum. Psalm. 118. Sed neq; causa formalis turpitudine vel indignum in se quicquam continet, sicut mox explicabimus. Honorabile igitur id esse, per se palam est. Neque opus erat huius rei probationes aliquas adijci, quando natura omnibus inseuit hoc iudicium: atque in historijs licet obseruare, etiam gentiles semper in honore habuisse, vehementerque detestatos, immo legibus quoque reprehendisse, si quid contra dignitatem coniugij aut diceretur, aut fieret.
units.tr: You will find it honoured by God's approval and by excellent promises (Psalm. 118.). Nor does its formal cause contain anything foul or unworthy in itself, as we shall explain presently. That it is honourable is therefore plain in itself. Nor was there any need to add proofs of this, since nature has implanted this judgment in all people; and in histories one may observe that even the Gentiles always held marriage in honour, and vehemently detested, indeed even condemned by laws, anything said or done against the dignity of marriage.

units.la: Inter omnes) Non igitur est, quod aliquae personae arceantur, vel aliquibus interdicatur coniugium. Si sunt homines, quemadmodum caeteri: si item ab eodem Deo omnes conditi: neque singulari aliqua nota a caeteris separati: secundum communem Dei ordinationem liceat illis viuere. Alius aetate proiectior est, alius admodum iuuenis, alius pauper, alius diues, alius rex, alius patriarcha, alius propheta, alius sacerdos, atque his omnibus ordinibus coniugium honorabile esse debet. Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, Moses, Aaron, Dauid, Zacharias, Petrus, Paulus, Philippus, diuersorum ordinum eminentissimi viri fuerunt omnesque coniugium coluerunt: quamobrem inter quoscunq; etiam sanctissimos coniugium suo loco honestum manere debet. In summa, vbi caetera paria sunt, vitaque innocenter transfigitur, certe ex parte coniugij dedecus aut culpa non contrahitur. Vnde etiam οὐ πάσι, id est, in omnibus, & per omnia: supple, quae ad coniugium ipsum proprie pertinent.
units.tr: Among all: there is therefore no reason why any persons should be excluded, or marriage forbidden to any. If they are men like the rest, and likewise all created by the same God, and not separated from others by any singular mark, then according to God's common ordinance it is right for them to live in marriage. One is more advanced in years, another very young; one is poor, another rich; one a king, another a patriarch, another a prophet, another a priest. Marriage ought to be honourable for all these orders. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, David, Zacharias, Peter, Paul, Philip, most eminent men of different orders, all cultivated marriage; wherefore marriage must remain honourable in its place among all, even the most holy. In sum, where other things are equal and life is passed innocently, certainly no disgrace or fault attaches to marriage on its own account. Hence also not in all things [οὐ πάσι], that is, in all respects and in every way: supply, those things which properly pertain to marriage itself.

units.la: Et cubile impollutum) Hic perstringit Apostolus ipsum rei caput ac iugulum. Pollutionem aliquam inesse coniugio quidam nitebantur persuadere, fortasis innixi rationibus aliquot in speciem probabilibus: quales etiam num hodie nonnulli adferunt, dum conantur probare, sacerdotibus non esse coniugium permittendum, propterea quod, cum ipsi sacra debeant peragere, coniugalibus amplexibus quasi maculam viderentur contrahere: & alia eiusmodi, quae coelibatus defensores in detestationem coniugij solent congerere. Sed Apostolus hic clare definit coniugij cubile, quatenus videlicet non aliud committitur, quam quod coniugij limitibus continetur, prorsus sine culpa esse, neque maculam ullam adferre. Atque ita etiam causa formalis coniugij honorabilis conuincitur. Sine peccato ibi fit, quod ante omne peccatum, ut fieret, fuerat ordinatum, quodque remedium adferre contra peccatum ostenditur. Non dubium, quin huc respexerit sacer & coelebs ille Paphnutius in synodo Nicaena, qui cum videret hoc ibi agi, ut Clerici cogentur ad coelibatum, ac matrimonio prohiberentur, sapienter in medium prosilijt ac dixit; xit: Honorabiles esse nuptias, & ad castitatem esse concubitum cum propria coniuge. Vide historiam tripartitam lib.2.cap.14. Qua de re mox plenius.
units.tr: And the undefiled bed: Here the Apostle strikes at the very head and throat of the matter. Some tried to persuade that some pollution inheres in marriage, perhaps relying on several reasons that look plausible; such as some even today adduce, when they try to prove that marriage should not be permitted to priests, because, since they must perform sacred duties, they would seem to contract a stain from conjugal embraces; and other arguments of this kind, which the defenders of celibacy are accustomed to heap up to the detestation of marriage. But the Apostle here clearly declares that the bed of marriage, insofar as nothing is committed there other than what is contained within the bounds of marriage, is wholly without fault and brings no stain at all. And thus the formal cause of honourable marriage is also proved: what is done there is without sin, and it was ordained to be done before any sin, and it is shown to be a remedy against sin. There is no doubt that the holy Paphnutius, who was himself celibate, had this in view at the Council of Nicaea. When he saw that there the aim was to compel clerics to celibacy and to forbid them marriage, he wisely stepped forward and said that marriage is honourable and that intercourse with one's own wife is chaste. See the Tripartite History, book 2, chapter 14. More on this matter presently.

units.la: Scortatores autem & adulteros iudicabit Deus)Confirmatio quaedam, & commendatio matrimonii est, ducta a contrario, siue a poenis, quae eos manent, qui, dum coniugium vituperant, concubitum extra coniugium videntur admittere, saltem occasionem audendi diuersum subministrant. Estque clara sententia. Propter coniugium reprehensionem nemo incurret, sed propter concubitum extra coniugium. Duas species peccati extra coniugium enumerat, scortationem, vbi videlicet solutus cum soluta rem habet: adulterium, vbi a tera persona coniunx est. Ex his vero intelligere damnari simul alias quasdam species. Iudicabit, pro eo, quod est condemnabit, quomodo alias saepe ea vox accipitur. Alibi saepe occurrunt conciones contra scortatores & adulteros, maxime in epistolis ad eos, qui ex gentibus erant, scriptis: propterea quod gentilium plerique fornicationem, quam vocant simplicem, inter peccata non numerarunt. Quo factum, quod apostoli in suafy-nodo inter alia hoc quoque constituerunt & scripserunt, vt abstinerent a scortatione: Actor.15. Sed enim, quando, quae hic breuibus ab Apostolo sunt expósita, mire seruiunt praesenti tempori, & statui nostrarum ecclesiarum: sunt enim qui matrimonium simpliciter damnant ceu pollutum & Deo displicens: sunt, qui non omnibus id permittunt, cogentes quosdam pauperes, praesertim sacerdotes atque ecclesiarum ministros, vt, si ecclesiae seruire velint, caelibatum voueant: quo pacto laqueum conscientiis iniiciunt, cum ex viginti ne vnus quidem votum suum feruet. Sunt denique etiam episcopi, qui concubinas pretio permittunt, & palam reque ipsa anteponunt fornicationem coniugio: ideo non possum, quin paulo accuratius hanc quaestionem hoc loco excutiam. Vtrum videlicet sacerdotibus seu ministris ecclesiarum liceat esse maritis: deinde, vtrum hoc tempore in Germania, mariti ut sint, permittere expediat. Sed de his nos proprium alibi libellum conscripsimus, ad huius lectionem remitto expositionem desiderantes.
units.tr: But God will judge whoremongers and adulterers. This is a certain confirmation and commendation of marriage, drawn from the contrary, that is, from the punishments that await those who, while they disparage marriage, seem to admit intercourse outside marriage, or at least provide an occasion for others to dare the same. The meaning is clear: no one will incur condemnation for disparaging marriage, but for intercourse outside marriage. He names two kinds of sin outside marriage: fornication, where an unmarried man has to do with an unmarried woman; and adultery, where one of the persons is married to another. From these, however, one may understand that certain other kinds are condemned at the same time. "Will judge" stands for "will condemn," as that word is often taken elsewhere. Elsewhere, sermons against whoremongers and adulterers often occur, especially in the letters written to those who were from the Gentiles, because most of the Gentiles did not count so-called simple fornication among sins. Hence the apostles, at their council, among other things also decreed and wrote that they should abstain from fornication (Actor.15.). But since what is set out here briefly by the Apostle serves remarkably well the present time and the state of our churches, I cannot but examine this question somewhat more carefully at this point. There are some who simply condemn marriage as polluted and displeasing to God. There are some who do not permit it to all, compelling certain poor men, especially priests and ministers of the churches, to vow celibacy if they wish to serve the church; by this means they cast a snare upon consciences, since out of twenty not even one keeps his vow. Finally, there are also bishops who allow concubines for a price, and openly prefer fornication to marriage in practice. The questions to be examined are these: whether it is lawful for priests or ministers of the churches to be husbands; and then, whether it is expedient at this time in Germany to permit them to marry. But we have written a separate little book on these matters elsewhere, and I refer those who want an exposition to its reading.

units.la: Sint mores alieni ab auaritia, contenti his, quae adsunt, siquidem ipse dixit: Non te defero, neque derelinquo, vt fidetes dicamus: Dominus mihi auxiliator, nec timebo, quid faciat mihi homo.
units.tr: Let your manners be free from covetousness, content with those things which you have; for he himself has said: "I will never leave you, nor forsake you," so that we may confidently say: "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man shall do to me."

units.la: 4. locus de fugienda auaritia
units.tr: 4. Place on fleeing from avarice

units.la: Quartus locus de fugienda auaritia, omnibusque quae auaritiam redolent. Apostolus semper habet rationem personarum, locorum, temporis, & similium circumstantiarum, quantu opus est. Animaduertit Apostolus Hebraeos suos plerunque sordidos, quaestus mire auidos, denique ijs moribus, qui auaritia undique redolebant. Quod ingenium, quos mores licet etiamnum hodie in Hebraeis, quaquauersum dispersi agunt, contemplari, quando vsuram, aliaque ad quaestum sordidum facientia, prae omnibus hominibus exercent.
units.tr: The fourth place concerns fleeing from avarice and from everything that smells of avarice. The Apostle always takes account of persons, places, time and similar circumstances, as far as the matter requires. He noticed that his Hebrews were for the most part grasping and wonderfully greedy for gain, in short, that they lived in customs that reeked of avarice everywhere. One can still observe this same temperament and these same habits today among the Hebrews, who are scattered in every direction, since they practise usury and other sordid money-making more than any other people.

units.la: Fieri insuper potest, ut pro temporis eius ratione quidam visi sint auidius parandis opibus intendere, maxime qui caussari poterant, se antea crudelitate suorum facultatibus spoliatos. Quidam praeterea praetexebant, se debere congerere, vnde non modo sibi suisque necessaria, uerum etiam caeteris inopia laborantibus fratribus aliquid suppeditaret. Quidam deniq;, si quando commendaretur beneficentia in fratres pauperes, excusare se volebant ab eleemosynarum collatione, dicendo: se non habere: seipsos adhuc indigere. Propter has igitur causas, & propter quosdam tales sordide auaros, placuit Apostolo suos de fugienda auaritia admonere, sed breuiter & paucis, veluti sperans, facile & perse istud praestituros.
units.tr: Moreover, it may be that, given the circumstances of that time, some people seemed to strive more eagerly to acquire wealth, especially those who could plead that their property had earlier been stripped from them by the cruelty of their own people. Some, besides, pretended that they had to pile up wealth so that they could supply not only their own needs and those of their families but also something for other brothers suffering want. Finally, some, whenever generosity towards poor brothers was commended, wished to excuse themselves from contributing alms, saying that they had nothing and that they themselves were still in need. For these reasons, then, and because of certain people who were so basely greedy, it pleased the Apostle to admonish his readers to flee from avarice, but briefly and in few words, as if hoping that they would easily and of their own accord carry this out.

units.la: Haec igitur est propositio aptisimis verbis expressa, sint mores alieni ab auaritia: ὁ τρόπος ἀφιλάργυρος. Multum quidem dixisset Apostolus, & omnino grauiter commouisset, dicendo: Fugite auaritiam: & quilibet iudicasset, illis verbis omnes sufficieter admonitos: sed Apostolus exquisita oratione utitur, & omnino multo plus significante. Sint, inquit, mores adeoque omnis vitae consuetudo ab auaritia alieni. Videlicet praecludit omnibus auaris hypocritis suam excusationem, qua solent uti. Probe enim notat, eam esse auarorum indolem, ut suam auaritiam tegere semper studeant, neque patiantur sibi auaritiae crimen impingi: imo etiamsi cernantur palam opibus congerendis seruandisq; valde intenti, tamen prae se ferunt oratione ac verbis, quod animum nequaquam appo nant, neq; corde illis inhient. Sed refelluntur isti ac reuincuntur ab externa sua consuetudine. Mores illorum manifeste arguunt insatiabilem auaritiam. Conuincuntur tota sua vita, & quotidianis actionibus. Itaq; rectissime dixit Apostolus, Mores sint ab auaritia alieni. Atq; ita non tantum praecipit simpliciter fugere auaritia, sed omne illud, quod cum auaritia aliquo modo coniunctum videri queat. Sunt autem huiusmodi valde multa. Ex auaris enim alij omnia sua vendunt carius, quam par est: neq; emunt, nisi vbi qua minimo se putant posse parare, veluti vel res non admodum bonas: uel ab ijs, quos credunt dunt egere,ideoq; minoris daturos:& interea iactant,se cuncta paruo vendere, magno emere.Alij foris affectant videri largi,veste etiam splendida vtuntur, at domi sunt quouis Euclione sordidiores, quantumque in vestibus, aut aliis rebus insumpserint,duplū alibi,nempe in mensa,detrahunt.Alij cum non habent,quaerunt per fas & nefas acquirere:alij etiam cum habent,tamen partis uti neq; sciunt,neq; audent. Et cum sibi suoq; ventri detrahunt,nulli vnquam pauperi elargiuntur.
units.tr: This, then, is the proposition, expressed in the most fitting words: let their manners be alien to avarice [ὁ τρόπος ἀφιλάργυρος]. The Apostle would certainly have said much, and would have moved them strongly, had he said, "Flee avarice," and anyone would have judged that they had been sufficiently warned by those words. But the Apostle uses an exquisite manner of speaking, one that signifies much more. Let, he says, their manners and the whole custom of their life be alien to avarice. Clearly he shuts off from all greedy hypocrites the excuse they are accustomed to use. For he rightly observes that it is the nature of the avaricious always to strive to hide their avarice and not to allow the charge of avarice to be fastened upon them. Indeed, even when they are plainly seen to be intensely busy amassing and guarding wealth, they still profess in their speech and words that they do not set their minds on it and that their hearts do not hanker after it. But such people are refuted and convicted by their outward conduct. Their habits plainly prove an insatiable avarice. They are convicted by their whole life and their daily actions. And so the Apostle rightly said, let their manners be alien to avarice. In this way he commands not merely that we simply flee avarice, but also everything that can be seen to be connected with avarice in any way. There are very many such things. Some avaricious people sell all their goods dearer than is right, and they buy only where they think they can get things for the least, such as goods that are not very good, or from those whom they believe to be in need and therefore willing to give for less. Meanwhile they boast that they sell everything cheap and buy dear. Others want to appear generous in public and wear splendid clothing, yet at home they are meaner than any Euclio, and whatever they have spent on clothes or other things, they take back twice over elsewhere, namely at the table. Some, when they lack money, seek to acquire it by fair means or foul; others, even when they have it, neither know how nor dare to use it. And while they grudge themselves and their bellies, they never give anything to any poor man.

units.la: In summa,cum sint mille modis auari,tamen conantur suam auaritiam mille artibus tegere:verum ea ex certis notis semper deprehenditur. 1. Tim. 6. Qui volunt ditescere, incidunt in tentationem & laqueum,& cupiditates multas, stultas, ac noxias,quae demergunt homines in exitium atque interitum. Siquidem radix omnium malorum est studium pecuniae,quam quidam dum appetunt,aberrarunt a fide, & seipsos implicuerunt doloribus multis.Ecce signa auaritiae aliquot delineata, ex quibus auari dignosci possunt:pariter etiam pericula tam in spiritualibus,quam corporalibus,quae plerunque sunt coniuncta.
units.tr: In sum, although the avaricious are greedy in a thousand ways, they still try to hide their avarice by a thousand devices; yet it is always detected by certain clear marks. 1 Timothy 6: "Those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge men into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all evils, which some, while reaching after it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows." Here are some signs of avarice, by which the avaricious can be recognised, together with the dangers, both spiritual and bodily, that usually go with it.

units.la: Proinde Apostolus vult,credentes,ut tuti sint ab istiusmodi periculis,ita agere,ut nul læ prorsus notæ auaritiae in ipsis resideant: vult omnes mores ab auaritia alienos conspici.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle wants believers, so that they may be safe from such dangers, to conduct themselves so that no mark of avarice at all abides in them. He wants all their manners to be seen as alien to avarice.

units.la: Contenti his,quae adsunt) Exprimit modum seu causam formalem,qua possemus testari, nos ab auaritia esse alienos.Si ijs,q per bonitatem Dei adsunt,contenti vixerimus,euides erit signum,nos auaritiae vitio nequaquam obnoxios. E contrario hoc est praecipuum auaritiae signum,semper appetere plura,quam habes,seu iudicare,tibi non esse satis.Certe natura ipsa paucis contentos esse iubet,eidemq; paucis poterit satisfieri: id quod philosophi testati subinde sunt,qui etiam quae habuerunt,tanquam superflua & naturae ne quaquam necessaria reiecerunt.Sed oportet longe excellentius in eadem sententia confirmatos esse Christianos,quibus Apostolus inculcatillud 1.Tim.6.Est quæstus magnus, pietas cum animo sua sorte contento. Nihil enim intulimus in mundum,videlicet nec efferre quicquam possumus:sed habentes alimenta,& quibus tegamur, his contenti erimus. Itaq; his, quae adsunt,decet esse contentos. Neque dolere vehementer debet,si plura antehac habuerimus:frustra enim de praeteritis,quae vel perierunt, vel alia ratione absumpta sunt,te maceras:neq; solicitos esse decet de futuris,ad quo ut maxime aspires, incertum est tamen,an assequi possis:aut,ut assequaris,incertum,an illis fis usurus: imo incertum,an etiam fis superuiturus. Huc pertinet,quod Christus Matth.6.vetuit,de cra stino esse solicitos:ἀφέντες igitur, τοῖς ωαφῆσιν: item quod Christus docuerit petere tantum panem quotidianum ad praesentem diem:Da nobis hodie,inquit, non addit, cras, vel, perendie,multo minus in annum vel in annos.Etin parabola de diuite sibi placente propter congestas multas opes,Stulte,hac nocte repetent animam tuam:Luc.12. Ergo tantum ea,quae adsunt,& ad praesentem diem,spectare oportet. Nam quicquid illud est, quod adest,a Deo ipso tibi dispensatum est, & ad conseruationem tui in illum diem sufficit.Dulcis prosiliens aqua siue e petra fluens,siue in poculo ministrata, siue ex mandibula asini,ad restinguendam sitim sufficit:sicut Israelitis,Heliae,Samsoni. Panis subcinericiius,locustae,mel syluestre,possunt te confirmare & sustentare, etiam ad plures dies, quod videre licet in Helia,qui ad quadraginta dies habuit satis,Ioanne Baptista,&c. Possunt autem haec te alere:igitur ijs,quae adsunt,contentus esto.
units.tr: Content with what is at hand) He sets out the manner, or formal cause, by which we could testify that we are alien to avarice. If we have lived content with what is present through God's goodness, this will be a clear sign that we are in no way liable to the vice of avarice. On the contrary, the chief sign of avarice is always to desire more than you have, or to judge that what you have is not enough. Certainly nature itself bids us be content with few things, and it can be satisfied with few; the philosophers have often testified to this, and they even cast away what they possessed as superfluous and in no way necessary to nature. But Christians ought to be confirmed in the same opinion far more excellently, and the Apostle impresses on them that saying of 1 Timothy 6: "Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and clearly we can carry nothing out; but having food and clothing, we shall be content with these." Therefore we ought to be content with what is at hand. Nor ought we to grieve greatly if we have had more in the past, for it is vain to waste yourself over the past, which has either perished or been used up in some other way. Nor ought we to be anxious about the future, which you may strive hard to reach, yet it is uncertain whether you can attain it, or, if you do attain it, whether you will be able to use it, indeed whether you will even survive to do so. To this belongs what Christ forbade in Matthew 6, that we should be anxious about tomorrow: "Take no thought, therefore, for tomorrow [μὴ οὖν μεριμνήσητε εἰς τὴν αὔριον]." Likewise, Christ taught us to ask only for daily bread for the present day: "Give us today," he says; he does not add "tomorrow," or "the day after," much less "for a year or for years." And in the parable of the rich man who was pleased with himself because of his great accumulated wealth: "Fool, this night they will demand your soul" (Luke 12). Therefore we ought to look only to what is at hand and to the present day. For whatever it is that is at hand has been dispensed to you by God himself, and it is sufficient for your preservation until that day. Sweet water gushing from a rock, or flowing from a rock, or provided in a cup, or from the jawbone of an ass, was enough to quench thirst, as it was for the Israelites, for Elijah, and for Samson. Bread baked on coals, locusts, and wild honey can strengthen and sustain you, even for many days, as can be seen in Elijah, who had enough for forty days, and in John the Baptist, etc. These things can nourish you; therefore be content with what is at hand.

units.la: Siquidē ipse dixit:Non te deseram, neque derelinquam) Addit breues,tamen magni ponderis rationes suasorias,quibus inducamur,vt ijs,quae adsunt,contenti simus, neq; ad plura anhelemus.Prior hæc sumitur a parte Dei,siue a Dei insigni promissione,qua ipse promisit,se non deserere curā velle habere,ac necessaria velle suppeditare. Certe vbi ipse dixit,vbi Deus promittit,se prospecturum necessaria,necessum est credamus praestare velle.Neq; ille potest fallere.Si princeps aut pater promittit,se benefacturum, fidem adhibemus , atq; in ope promissa conquiescimus:quanto magis acquiescemus promissionibus diuinis.Caeterum haec verba proprie dicta sunt ad Iehosua cap.1.vbi eum Dominus constituit ducem populi a morte Mose,atq; inter caeteras magnificas promissiones de diuidenda terra promissa,addit hoc Deus:Non statuet se quisquam contra faciem tuam, cunctis diebus vitae tuae:nam sicut fui cum Mose,sic ero tecum,non dimittam te,neq; derelinquam te. Respondent hic posita verba hebraicae veritati:quanquam apud Septuaginta ita legitur: οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψω σε, οὐδ' οὐ μὴ ἐπιλήψομαί σε, quasi diceret:Non derelinquam te,neq; despiciam te.No ta autem hic in verbis Apostolis graecisimum,οὐδ' οὐ μή, tres sunt negationes vnam vehementem negationem includentes.Porrò valde appositè citatum est iistud testimonium. Tametsi enim proprie ad Iosue dicta sint haec verba,tamen etiam ad quosquunq; pios pertinent. tinent, recteq; accommodantur. Quàm enim Deo curæ fuit Iehosua, tam etiam illi curæ est quicunq; alius pius. Et quæcunq; ad alios dicta sunt, sic accipi debent à nobis, táquà ad nos quoq; dicta. Quæcunq; enim præscripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam præscripta sunt, Rom.15. Sed ideò commodissimè adferūtur, quæ dicta sunt ad patres, qui ante nos fuerunt, ut mens nostra tantò magis confirmetur, ac certò statuat, ergà se quoq; ea adimplenda, quæ videt, iam diu in alijs quoq; adimpleta. Si enim credimus, quòd erga Iehosua Dominus perfecit, quæ promiserat, sine dubio etiam erga nos perficiet similia. Igitur multò certiores hîc fieri debemus de ope Dei per promissionem factam ad alium, quàm si noua aliqua promissio ad nos alio modo fieret. Præterea est hæc promissio ualde insignis, vtpote, quæ non tantùm promissa sunt Iosuæ ea, quæ ad uictum erant necessaria, verùmetiam multa alia admodum præclara, veluti fœlix successus in administratione & gubernatione populi, insignes victoriæ de aduersarijs, terræ promissæ occupatio, &c. Hinc verò decet nos colligere: si Deus tot tantasque res promisit Iosuæ & præstitit, quantò magis præstabit nobis ad uitam necessaria, & quæ minutiora sunt? Simulq; iubemur animo contemplari innumera bona, quæ Deus ipsi Iosuæ contulit, & similia, quatenus opus erit, à Deo expectare. Itaq; hoc testimonio confirmantur animi nostri, ut cogitemus, nos nunquam à Deo deserendos, quæcunq; etiam necesitas ingruerit. Huc pertinet insignis concio Christi Matt.6. Ne soliciti sitis animę vestræ, quid esuri sitis, aut bibituri: neque corpori vestro, quibus indumentis vsuri, &c. quæ ibi sequuntur.
units.tr: Since he himself has said: I will not leave you nor forsake you) He adds brief yet weighty reasons of persuasion, by which we may be led to be content with what is at hand and not to pant after more. The first is taken from God's side, or from God's remarkable promise, by which he promised that he would not desert those whom he wished to care for and whom he wished to supply with necessities. Certainly when he himself has said it, when God promises that he will provide necessities, we must believe that he is willing to fulfil it. Nor can he deceive. If a prince or a father promises that he will do us good, we give our trust and rest in the help promised; how much more ought we to rest in divine promises? Moreover, these words, properly speaking, were spoken to Joshua in chapter 1, where the Lord appointed him leader of the people after the death of Moses, and among other magnificent promises about dividing the promised land, God adds this: "No man shall stand before you all the days of your life; for as I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will not fail you nor forsake you." These words set out here correspond to the Hebrew truth, although in the Septuagint it reads thus: [οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψω σε, οὐδ' οὐ μὴ ἐπιλήψομαί σε], as if to say: "I will not forsake you, nor will I despise you." Note here in the Apostle's words the Greek [οὐδ' οὐ μή]: there are three negatives that include one emphatic negation. Moreover, this testimony is cited very aptly. Although these words were spoken properly to Joshua, they nevertheless pertain to, and are rightly applied to, all the pious. For as much as Joshua was a concern to God, so is every other pious person. And whatever was said to others ought to be received by us as said to us as well. For whatever has been written beforehand has been written for our instruction (Romans 15). But the words said to the fathers who lived before us are most fittingly brought forward, so that our mind may be all the more confirmed and may firmly determine that the things it sees have long been fulfilled in others will also be fulfilled in our own case. For if we believe that the Lord fulfilled what he had promised to Joshua, then without doubt he will also bring about similar things for us. Therefore we ought to be made much more certain here of God's help through a promise made to another than if some new promise were made to us in a different way. Furthermore, this promise is very remarkable, since not only were those things promised to Joshua that were necessary for sustenance, but also many other very splendid things, such as a happy outcome in the administration and government of the people, remarkable victories over adversaries, the occupation of the promised land, etc. From this we ought to conclude: if God promised and bestowed so many and such great things on Joshua, how much more will he provide for us the things necessary for life, and those that are smaller? At the same time we are commanded to contemplate in our minds the countless good things God bestowed upon Joshua himself, and to expect similar things from God as far as need requires. And so our minds are confirmed by this testimony, so that we may reflect that we shall never be forsaken by God, whatever necessity may press upon us. To this belongs the famous sermon of Christ in Matthew 6: "Do not be anxious for your life, what you will eat or drink; nor for your body, what clothing you will wear," etc., which follows there.

units.la: Vt fidentes dicamus, Dominus mihi auxiliator, nec timebo, quid faciat mihi homo.
units.tr: That confidently we may say: The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me.

units.la: Altera ratio ex parte nostra, seu de fide, qua nos oportet erga Deum esse præditos. Fluitq; hæc ratio ex præcedenti. Nam cùm relatiuè se habeant promissio Dei, & fiducia hominis in promissionem: sanè vbi præcesit ratio de Dei promissione, optimo ordine ista subijcitur de hominis in propositam promissionem fiducia: qua admonentur omnes, de suo officio atq; exercitio fidei, vt, cùm Deum tam benigno audiunt esse animo, omnia sibi de Dei bonitate polliceantur ad vitam & salutem necessaria: atq; itaijs, quæ adsunt, contenti sint, nullum auaritiæ specimen præse ferentes.
