Proinde rectè ait, ut fidentes dicamus: Opponuntur hæc verba relatiuè illis præcedentibus, Ipse dixit: tanquam si dicatur, Deus ipse ita locutus est: igitur par est, nos constanter ei credere. Cæterùm verba hæc sumpta sunt ex psalmo 118. quem Dauid cecinit in publico conuentu, agens Deo gratias, nec non omnes admonens similiter agendum inuitans, postquam semel liberatus fuit è periculis, maximèque à Saulis aduersarij continua persecutione: ac iam sperabat, se quiete posse regnum obtinere. Sic autè post exordium, in quo omnes inuitat, ut secum Dei bonitate celebret, ait: De angustia vocaui Iáh, & exaudiuit me in latitudine Iáh: Iehoua mecum est, non timebo, quid faciat mihi homo. Respondent per omnia veritati hebraicæ verba hic posita. Congruunt autem pijs omnibus fidem suam conijcientibus in bonitatem Dei, licet à Dauid in sua causa dicta, eadem ratione, qua ostendimus ad pios omnes pertinere, quæ dicta fuerant ad Iehosua.
units.tr: The second reason is drawn from our side, namely the faith with which we ought to be endowed toward God. This reason follows from the preceding one. For since God's promise and man's trust in the promise are correlative, then, where the reasoning about God's promise has come first, the right order is to add the matter of man's trust in the promise offered. By this all are admonished about their duty and the exercise of faith: that, since they hear that God is so kindly disposed, they should look to God's goodness for everything necessary for life and salvation, and so be content with what they have, showing no sign of greed. Therefore he rightly says, "that confidently we may say." These words are set against the preceding ones, "He himself has said," as if it were said: God himself has so spoken; therefore it is fitting for us to believe him steadfastly. These words are taken from Psalm 118, which David sang in public assembly, giving thanks to God and inviting all to do likewise, after he had once been freed from dangers, above all from the continual persecution of Saul his adversary, and now hoped he could hold the kingdom in peace. So after the opening, in which he invites all to celebrate God's goodness with him, he says: "Out of distress I called on Jah, and Jah answered me in a wide place. Jehovah is with me; I will not fear what man may do to me." The words placed here agree in every respect with the Hebrew truth. They also fit all the godly who cast their faith upon God's goodness, although David spoke them in his own cause, for the same reason which we have shown applies to all the godly what was said to Joshua.

units.la: Pulcherrimè verò subijcitur ad exprimendum fidem credentium post illa uerba ad Iehosua: idq; propter duas causas: prima, dicendo enim, Nec timebo, quid faciat mihi homo, respicit haud dubiè ad eam partem promissionis, qua dictum erat ad Iehosua, quòd non statueret se quisquam contra faciem eius, hoc est, quòd à nemine mortalium foret ipsi periculum metuendum. Certè ad talem promissionem iustissimè fidelis quilibet verbis Dauidis vtetur.
units.tr: The words are most beautifully added, after those spoken to Joshua, to express the faith of believers, and for two reasons. First, by saying "I will not fear what man may do to me," he surely looks back to that part of the promise by which it was said to Joshua that no one would stand against his face, that is, that no mortal would be a danger to him to be feared. Certainly every faithful person may most justly use David's words for such a promise.

units.la: Secunda ratio, Aptè dicuntur hæc uerba ab ijs, qui per aduersarios antea fuerat facultatibus spoliati, quosq; sic decebat esse fide confirmatos, ut etiam ad perferendum iterum paria, si quando ita necesse foret, parati essent. Quibus enim omnia auferuntur per homines, tamen desperare de ope diuina nequaquam debent: neque cogitabunt homines plus posse in lædendo, quàm Deus potest in benefaciendo. In eandem sententiam occurrunt quædam psal.56. Item sermo Christi est ad discipulos, Matth.10. & Luc.12. Nolite metuere eos, qui possunt occidere corpus: sed eum potius metuite, qui postquam occiderit corpus, potest & animam mittere in gehennam ignis. Dicant ergo pij hæc verba, Dominus mihi adiutor in omnibus, videlicet aduersitatibus, quæ possent obtingere, & non tantùm in quotidianis, veluti cùm cibus aut potus forte deest: verumetiam in quibuscunq; alijs, qualibet raris atque inopinatis. Istud autem si faciant, ijs quę adsunt, erunt contenti: neq; vel nimis auidè appetendo opes in tempus futurum, vel humanis consilijs innitendo, vel fratribus opem poscentibus negando, vel metuendo, ne, quæ habent, auferantur, auaritiæ signa nulla edent. Proinde rationes istas non leue habere pondus ad difuadendam auaritiam, ex his manifestum euadit. Iam doctrinæ spiritualis pauçula capita annotemus. Primò, admonemur fugere auaritiam, & non tantùm eam, quæ passim apud omnes palàm pro tali agnoscitur, verùm etiâ quicquid cum auaritia aliquam habet affinitatē. Idq; eò magis, quòd natura paucis contenta est.
units.tr: The second reason: these words are fittingly spoken by those who had earlier been stripped of their goods by adversaries, and who ought to be so confirmed in faith that they are ready to endure the same again, should it ever be necessary. Those from whom everything is taken by men must by no means despair of divine help, nor think that men can do more in harming than God can do in doing good. Something to the same effect occurs in Psalm 56. Likewise Christ's word to the disciples in Matthew 10 and Luke 12: "Do not fear those who can kill the body; but rather fear him who, after he has killed the body, can also cast soul and body into the fire of hell." Let the godly therefore say these words, "The Lord is my helper in all things," namely in the adversities which might befall them, and not only in daily ones, as when food or drink happens to be lacking, but in whatever other rare and unexpected things. If they do this, they will be content with what they have. Neither by desiring wealth too eagerly for the future, nor by relying on human counsels, nor by refusing help to brethren who ask for it, nor by fearing lest what they have be taken away, will they show any sign of greed. Therefore it is clear from these things that these reasons carry no small weight in dissuading greed. Now let us note a few points of spiritual teaching. First, we are admonished to flee greed, and not only that which is openly recognised everywhere as such, but whatever has any affinity with greed; and all the more so because nature is content with few things.

units.la: Secundò, iubemur omni tempore respicere in promissiones Dei, quæ non tantùm ad quosdam paucos patres, sed & ad omnes, qui verè credunt, pertinent.
units.tr: Second, we are commanded at all times to look to the promises of God, which pertain not only to a few fathers but to all who truly believe.

units.la: Erga paucos quidem manifestatæ sunt apertis & singularibus argumentis, vt cæteri quoq; credentes de ijsdem rebus certi fiant, & per illos paucos annunciatæ sunt cæteris credentibus.
units.tr: Indeed, these promises were made known to a few by open and singular proofs, so that the other believers too might become certain of the same things; and through those few they were announced to the rest of the believing people.

units.la: Tertiò, discimus, quomodo nobis fides semper conijcienda sint in vnum solum Deum, à quo primùm spiritualia, deinde & corporalia beneficia decet nos expectare. Atq; hanc fide de bonitate Dei oportet nos etiam actionibus testatam facere, præsertim non curando tèporalia, & huiusmodi, quibus solent aliqui tanquam idolo suo toti esse mancipati.
units.tr: Third, we learn that our faith must always be cast upon the one God alone, from whom it is fitting for us to expect first spiritual and then also bodily benefits. We ought to attest this faith in God's goodness by our actions as well, especially by not caring for temporal things and the like, to which some are wholly enslaved as if to their idol.

units.la: Quartò, discimus, non metuenda nobis crudelitatem hominū, qui nunquam sic posse nos omnibus spoliare, quin largiturus sit nobis Dominus ea, quæ ad vitam istam corpoream, & ad salutem animarum sunt necessaria.
units.tr: Fourth, we learn that we must not fear the cruelty of men, since they can never so despoil us of everything that the Lord will not grant us what is necessary for this bodily life and for the salvation of our souls.

units.la: Memores estote eorum, qui præsunt vobis, qui locuti sunt vobis sermonem Dei, quorum imitemini fidem, considerantes, qui fuerit exitus conuersationis illorum. Iesus Christus heri & hodie, idem est etiam in secula. Doctrinis varijs & peregrinis ne circumferamini. Bonum est enim, gratia constabiliri cor, non escis, quæ non profuerunt ijs, qui versati sunt in illis. Habemus altare, de quo non est fas edere, ijs, qui tabernaculo deseruiunt. Animalium enim, quorum sanguis infertur pro peccato in sanctaper pontificem, horum corpora cremantur extra castra. Quapropter & Iesus, vt sanctificaret per proprium sanguinem populum, extra portam passus est. Exeamus igitur ad eum extra castra, opprobrium eius portantes. Non enim habemus hic manentem ciuitatem, sed futuram inquirimus. Per ipsum igitur offerimus hostiam laudis semper Deo, hoc est, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius.
units.tr: Remember those who rule over you, who have spoken to you the word of God, whose faith imitate, considering the outcome of their conduct. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever. Be not carried about by various and strange doctrines. For it is good for the heart to be established by grace, not by meats, which did not profit those who were occupied with them. We have an altar, from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us go out therefore to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have no lasting city here, but we seek the one to come. Through him therefore let us always offer the sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.

units.la: Quintus locus, in quo hortatur, & hortando iubet, vt sanæ doctrinæ semel à primis doctoribus euangelij, præsertim Apostolis, acceptæ constanter adhæreant, neque vllo modo admittant nouam aliquam, ab ea, quæ ad id vsq; tempus tradita fuerat, discrepantem.
units.tr: The fifth passage, in which he urges, and by urging commands, that sound teaching, once received from the first teachers of the gospel, especially the Apostles, be steadfastly adhered to, and that no new doctrine differing from what had been handed down up to that time be admitted in any way.

units.la: De vitandis varijs & peregrinis doctrinis, admonitionem hanc necessum erat multis de causis adijcere. Primò, ob eandem cãussam, quia cæterae quoque ecclesiæ tali admonitione egebant: quia videlicet, vbi Deus operatur, ibi etiam non feriatur diabolus: vbi Deus sibi erigit templum, vt vulgò dicunt, satagit diabolus, vt in propinquo habeat sacellum.
units.tr: The admonition to avoid various and strange doctrines had to be added for many reasons. First, for the same cause, because the other churches too needed such an admonition: namely, where God works, there the devil is not idle either; where God erects for himself a temple, as they commonly say, the devil takes pains to have a little chapel nearby.

units.la: Itaq; erat hoc commune periculum omnium ecclesiarum, quamlibet bene essent à sanis Apostolis in sana doctrina institutæ, paulò post irrepebant quidam pseudoapostoli, qui eas perturbabant, atque ita nonnunquam, vt à vera doctrina ad falsam dilaberentur. Exemplo sunt Galatæ. Cùm ergo idem periculum erat metuendum Hebræis, inter quos passim vagabantur animarum seductores, sapienter Apostolus hanc admonitionem inseruit.
units.tr: Therefore this was a common danger of all churches: however well they had been instructed in sound doctrine by the sound Apostles, shortly afterwards certain false apostles crept in who disturbed them, and so sometimes they slipped from true doctrine into false. The Galatians are an example. Since the same danger was to be feared for the Hebrews, among whom seducers of souls wandered everywhere, the Apostle wisely inserted this admonition.

units.la: Secundò, periculum erat, ne seducerentur, ex parte ipsorum Hebræorū. Nam iam per multos annos Hebræi declararant, se rerum nouarum tàm in ijs, quæ religionis erant, quàm in ciuilibus, studiosos: vnde multæ sectæ, item opiniones, dissidia, seditiones extitæ fuerant.
units.tr: Second, there was a danger that they would be seduced from the side of the Hebrews themselves. For already for many years the Hebrews had shown themselves eager for novelties, both in matters of religion and in civil affairs; whence many sects, opinions, dissensions and seditions had arisen.

units.la: Tertiò, à genere doctrinæ, quod per pseudoapostolos adferebatur. Nam plurimi pseudoapostoli laborabant ad inducendum ac retinendum legales obseruationes & ceremonias, inprimis ciborum, dierum, &c. (vnde fit, quòd Apostolus hic diserte attingit de cibis & eiusmodi) ad ista autè recipienda omnes Hebræi erant valde propensi.
units.tr: Third, there was the kind of doctrine which the false apostles brought in. For very many false apostles laboured to introduce and retain the legal observances and ceremonies, above all concerning foods, days, and so on (whence the Apostle here expressly touches on meats and such things); and all the Hebrews were very prone to receive these.

units.la: Quartò, facere aliquid potuissent ad seductionem Hebræorum ipsa pseudoapostolorum conditio. Nam ij plerunque erant Hebræi genere, & titulis sanctimoniæ legalis conspicui: qua ratione facilius potuissent Hebræorum animos permouere. Propterhas igitur causas sapienter fecit Apostolus, quòd de vitandis nouis & peregrinis doctrinis suos tempestiue admonuerit. Nunc ad apostoli verba explicanda.
units.tr: Fourth, the very condition of the false apostles could have helped to seduce the Hebrews. For they were for the most part Hebrews by birth, and conspicuous for the titles of legal holiness, so they could more easily have moved the minds of the Hebrews. For these reasons the Apostle wisely warned his readers in good time to avoid new and foreign doctrines. Now let us turn to the explanation of the Apostle's words.

units.la: Dd
units.tr: Dd

units.la: Memores estote eorum, qui præsunt vobis, qui locuti sunt vobis sermonem, quorum imitemini fidem.
units.tr: Remember those who rule over you, who have spoken the word of God to you, whose faith you should imitate.

units.la: Popositio, qua monet, altissima mente retineant, quæ ab Apostolis audiuerant, atque in eadem doctrina permaneant, imitenturque sanctorum Apostolorum fidem.
units.tr: This is an exhortation in which he urges them, with the highest sincerity, to hold fast what they had heard from the Apostles, to persevere in the same doctrine, and to imitate the faith of the holy Apostles.

units.la: Saluberrimum est ecclesijs, respicere ad prima fundamenta doctrinæ iacta, & ad sta- tum priorum temporum. Ita vt in hunc diem, si quid rectè velimus constituere, si de vlla re dubitamus, non est certius consilium, quàm videre, quid in primitiua eccle- sia simile aut dissimile gestum sit. Neque quicquam potest proponi vtile credenti- bus, cuius non habitum fuerit quoddam exemplum in ipsa ecclesiæ prima ætate. ●
units.tr: It is most healthful for the churches to look back to the first foundations of doctrine that were laid, and to the state of the earlier times. So that to this day, if we wish to decide anything rightly, and if we doubt about any matter, there is no surer counsel than to see what was done in the primitive Church, either similarly or differently. Nor can anything be proposed as useful to believers of which there was not some example in the very first age of the Church.

units.la: Neque quicquam potest proponi noxium, aduersus quod non habeatur etiam in doctrina & praxi primitiuę ecclesiæ aliquod remedium, vel saltem consilium vel exemplum, ad depellendum id, quod malum est.
units.tr: Nor can anything be proposed as harmful for which there is not also, in the doctrine and practice of the primitive Church, some remedy, or at least some counsel or example, for driving away what is evil.

units.la: Atque hæc est caussa, cur Deus extare voluerit sacras epistolas, itemque Acta Apostolorum, vt nimirum in illis haberemus, quis status primitiuæ optimæque ecclesiæ fuerit: atque ex illo disceremus, quomodo in omne æuum ecclesiæ gubernari & conseruari debeant.
units.tr: This is the reason why God willed the holy Epistles, and likewise the Acts of the Apostles, to exist: namely, that we might have in them what the state of the primitive and best Church was, and learn from it how the Church ought to be governed and preserved for all ages.

units.la: Hac igitur ratione Apostolus Hebræos, quos in sana doctrina cupit confirmare, iubet memores esse suorum doctorum, quos antea audierunt.
units.tr: For this reason, then, the Apostle, wishing to confirm the Hebrews in sound doctrine, bids them remember their teachers whom they heard before.

units.la: Qui locuti sunt vobis sermonem Dei) Ostendit, de quibus præpositis sentiat, nempe de iis, qui docuerant Euangelium. Præterquam autem, quòd amplificat talium dignitatem, siue officium, tum tacitè confirmat omnes ad adhærendum eorundem doctrinæ, dicendo, locutos esse sermonem Dei.
units.tr: Who have spoken to you the word of God. He shows what sort of leaders he means, namely those who had taught the Gospel. Besides amplifying the dignity or office of such men, he also tacitly confirms everyone in adhering to their doctrine, by saying that they spoke the word of God.

units.la: Profecto enim si ex illorū ore auditus est sermo Dei, (sicut necessariò verum est, quod Christus dixerat: Luc. cap. 10. & Matth. cap. 10. 16. Quis vos audit, me audit: & vos non estis, qui loquimini, sed Spiritus patris mei loquitur in vobis:) non est, quod quisquam cogitet de tali doctrina semel ex ijs audita recipienda: supra capite 11. dictū est: si illi non effugerunt, qui auersabantur eum, qui loquebatur in terra, multò magis nos, si eum, qui de cœlis est, auersemur.
units.tr: Indeed, if the word of God was heard from their mouths (as it is necessarily true, what Christ had said: Luke 10 and Matthew 10:16, "He who hears you hears me; and it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father speaks in you"), there is no reason why anyone should think that such doctrine, once heard from them, should be received only once. Above, in chapter 11, it was said: if those did not escape who turned away from him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who is from heaven.

units.la: Imitemini fidem) Exprimit, quid potissimum eos velit facere, nempe Sanctorum Apostolorum imitentur fidem. Nomine fidei comprehendit summam religionis, in qua salus nostra consistit, comprehendit, quod præcipuum est, & per quod apud Deum iustificamur. Quod quidem Apostoli tum in doctrina sua semper commendarunt, tum reipsa, totoq; animo sunt pro salute adipiscenda, persecuti.
units.tr: Imitate their faith. He expresses what he most wants them to do, namely to imitate the faith of the holy Apostles. By the name of faith he comprehends the sum of religion, in which our salvation consists; he comprehends what is chief, and that through which we are justified before God. The Apostles indeed always commended this, both in their teaching and in fact, and pursued it with their whole mind in order to obtain salvation.

units.la: Doctrina enim Apostolorum tota in hoc vno consumpta est, quòd videlicet per fidem iustificamur: & ipsi non alia re, quàm fide ad salutem consecuti sunt. Qua de re plenissimè in tota parte tertia præsentis epistolæ, item Romanorum capite 3. & 4. & 6. & 7. Galatarum capite 3. & alibi passim. Itaque hisce verbis breuiter tantundem sibi vult Apostolus, atque si diceret: Persistite in fide ad Deum, sicut nouistis Apostolos in fide perstitisse: similiter adhærete illi doctrinæ de fide, quam ab Apostolis semel accepistis. Neq; potuisset Apostolus aptioribus verbis suam hac in parte sententiam exprimere.
units.tr: For the whole doctrine of the Apostles is spent on this one thing, namely that we are justified through faith; and they themselves attained salvation by no other means than faith. On this matter see most fully the whole third part of the present epistle, likewise Romans chapters 3, 4, 6 and 7, Galatians chapter 3, and everywhere else. Thus in these words the Apostle means briefly just this, as if he were saying: Persevere in faith toward God, as you know the Apostles persevered in faith; likewise cling to that doctrine of faith which you have received once from the Apostles. Nor could the Apostle have expressed his meaning in this part in more fitting words.

units.la: Considerantes, qui fuerit exitus conuersationis illorum) Ratio suasoria, à doctorum siue Apostolorum perpetua in eadem fide ad mortem vsque constantia. Magni ponderis est hæc ratio. Quotiescunq; enim volumus probare doctrinam aliquam, hæc vna est via, si dispiciamus, quomodo se doctores gerant: num videlicet semper constantes maneant, nusquam sibiipsis contradicant, non mutent subinde propositum, non leuiter mo- ueantur, pro caussis ex tempore obuenientibus: si denique vsque ad mortem in ea perseuerent, & non dubitent, eam etiam sua morte confirmare. Quò pertinet, quod Christus iubet cautos esse in eligendis doctoribus, Matthæi capite septimo. Cauete vobis à pseudoprophetis, qui veniunt ad vos in vestitu ouium, sed intrinsecus sunt lupi rapaces. A fructibus ipsorum agnoscetis eos. Item Ioannis capite decimo, de veris pastoribus, qui etiam animam parati sunt ponere pro ouibus. Quòd si è diuerso inueniantur aliqui inconstantes, leues, &c. tùm valde suspecta est eorum doctrina, neque tutum est ei adhærere.
units.tr: Considering what the outcome of their conduct was. This is a persuasive argument, drawn from the constancy of the teachers, or Apostles, in the same faith even unto death. This argument is of great weight. For whenever we want to prove any doctrine, this is the one way: to examine how the teachers conduct themselves, whether they remain always consistent, never contradict themselves, do not change their purpose from time to time, are not lightly moved by causes arising from circumstances, and finally whether they persevere in it even unto death and do not hesitate to confirm it by their death. To this belongs what Christ commands, that we be cautious in choosing teachers, Matthew chapter 7: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you will know them." Likewise John chapter 10, concerning the true ministers, who are ready even to lay down their lives for the sheep. But if, on the contrary, some are found to be inconstant, light, and so on, then their doctrine is greatly suspect, nor is it safe to adhere to it.

units.la: Dicis forte: Nō semper coïenit spectare vitā & mores doctorū: quia diabolus se transformat subinde in angelū lucis, & hypocritę nouerunt mirā sanctimoniam simulare: imò maiorem sæpè, quàm veri sancti doctores:id quod iudicare licet ex pseudoapostolorum moribus, qui obseruabant innumera, vt cibos, dies, &c. ex quibus ignari potuissent iudicare potius sequendos pseudoapostolos, quàm veros Apostolos.
units.tr: Perhaps you will say: it is not always fitting to look at the life and morals of teachers, because the devil often transforms himself into an angel of light, and hypocrites know how to feign a wonderful holiness, indeed often a greater holiness than true holy teachers. This can be judged from the conduct of the false apostles, who observed countless things, such as foods, days, and so on, by which the ignorant might have judged the false apostles, rather than the true Apostles, to be the ones to follow.

units.la: Atque ideo, quando non est tutum iudicare ex vita, oportet consulere sacram Scripturam, ad cuius normam omnis doctrina examinari debet. Et si inuenitur conuenire cum sacra Scriptura, tunc approbetur, etiamsi vita doctoris videatur impia.
units.tr: Therefore, when it is not safe to judge from life, it is necessary to consult Holy Scripture, by whose rule every doctrine ought to be examined. And if it is found to agree with Holy Scripture, then let it be approved, even if the life of the teacher seems impious.

units.la: Respondetur, Verum est, hæc est certissima via, quamq; & primo & vltimo loco ingredi oportet, quotiescunq; examen est habendum: sed tamen hæc quoq; est valde necessaria, vt fides & constantia in doctore consideretur.
units.tr: The answer is: it is true that this is the most certain way, which must be entered both first and last whenever an examination is to be made; but nevertheless this other consideration is also very necessary, namely that faith and constancy in the teacher be taken into account.

units.la: Primò, quia is optimè docet, & efficacissimè mouet omnium animos, ac retinebit etiam sibi consentientes, cuius vita doctrinæ respondet.
units.tr: First, because he teaches best and moves the minds of all most effectively, and will also retain those who agree with him, whose life corresponds to his doctrine.

units.la: Secundò, quia, quicunq; certus est de doctrinæ suæ veritate, is non dubitabit omnia etiam pericula pro ea subire. Alioquin stultorum fuerit, valde afferere, de quo adhuc in animo dubites.
units.tr: Second, because whoever is certain of the truth of his doctrine will not hesitate to undergo every danger for it. Otherwise it would be the mark of fools to assert strongly something about which one is still in doubt in one's own mind.

units.la: Tertiò, oportet intelligere, considerada esse in doctore, non tantùm mores & externam vitam, quæ pro tempore potest in hypocritis optima esse, quæque à Christo signa est per vestitum ouium: sed oportet videre fructus, hoc est, constantiam ad finem vsq; vitæ, item profectum serium in auditoribus.
units.tr: Third, we must understand that what is to be considered in a teacher is not only his morals and external life, which for a time may be most excellent even in hypocrites, and which Christ marked by the sheep's clothing; but we must see his fruits, that is, his constancy to the end of life, and likewise serious progress in his hearers.

units.la: Hæc enim est natura sanæ doctrinæ & verorum doctorum: illa necessario aliquid efficit in auditorum cordibus: iuxta illud Esaiæ, sicut pluuia non cadit in terram, quin aliquem fructum gignat: ita etiam verbum Domini nunquam redit ad ipsum vacuum, quin fructum aliquem adferat: & necessario, quod Christus ait, semen cadens in terram bonam aliud profert centuplum, aliud sexagecuplum. Lucæ capite octauo. Qui ex veris doctoribus sunt, isti etiam tempore persecutionis perseuerant, sicut constat Apostolos omnes fecisse.
units.tr: For this is the nature of sound doctrine and of true teachers: it necessarily produces something in the hearts of the hearers, according to that saying of Isaiah: as the rain does not fall on the earth without producing some fruit, so also the word of the Lord never returns to him empty, but brings forth some fruit; and, as Christ says, the seed falling on good ground produces one part a hundredfold, another sixtyfold (Luke chapter 8). Those who are true teachers also persevere in time of persecution, as it is established that all the Apostles did.

units.la: At verò falsa doctrina non fructificat in auditorum cordibus ad bonum, vt inde sequeretur gloria Dei, aut proximi vtilitas. Similiter falsi doctores adueniente cruce non manent.
units.tr: But false doctrine does not bear fruit in the hearts of the hearers for good, so that the glory of God or the benefit of the neighbour would follow from it. Likewise false teachers do not remain when the cross comes.

units.la: Hæc est certa quædam examinandarum doctrinarum regula: quæ confirmatur verbis Christi supra citatis, de doctoribus in vestitu ouium, de veris & falsis pastoribus: item prima epistola ad Corinthios capite tertio. Cuiusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit. Alibi vocat falsos doctores inimicos crucis Christi: Galatarum capite sexto, ait, quosdam docere falsa, ne ob crucem Christi persecutionem patiantur.
units.tr: This is a certain rule for examining doctrines, which is confirmed by the words of Christ quoted above, about teachers in sheep's clothing, about true and false ministers; likewise by the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 3: "Each one's work will be tested by fire, of what sort it is." Elsewhere he calls false teachers enemies of the cross of Christ; in Galatians chapter 6 he says that some teach false things so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.

units.la: Ioannes prioris epistolæ capite quarto docet, probare spiritus, num ex Deo sint: sed signum ibi tantùm addit de assertione humanitatis Christi: idque propter eos, qui tunc volebant persuadere, Christum non fuisse verum hominem. In ea enim epistola asseritur humanitas Christi: sicut in euangelio Ioannis asseritur potissimum Christi diuinitas.
units.tr: John in the first chapter of his first epistle, chapter four, teaches us to test the spirits whether they are from God. But there he gives only one sign, the confession of the humanity of Christ, and he gives it because of those who at that time were trying to persuade people that Christ was not a true man. In that epistle the humanity of Christ is asserted, just as in John's Gospel the divinity of Christ is chiefly asserted.

units.la: Itaque valde idonea est hæc ratio ab Apostolo addita, sicut vehementer facit ad illustrandam dignitatem doctorum. Est enim præclara res, quando de doctoribus aliquibus potest dici, quòd conuersatio eorum respondet doctrinæ, quòd item non fugiunt crucem, sed perseuerant. Ita magnum habet momentum ad mouendos animos auditorum, vt doctoribus talibus, nec non sanæ doctrinæ eorundem constantes adhæreant.
units.tr: So this reason added by the Apostle is very suitable, and it greatly helps to illustrate the dignity of teachers. For it is a notable thing when it can be said of certain teachers that their conduct matches their doctrine, and that they do not flee the cross but persevere. It has great weight in moving the minds of hearers, so that they cling steadfastly to such teachers and to their sound doctrine.

units.la: Palàmque ex his fit conuersationem sanctorum doctorum opponi conuersationi pseudoapostolorum, atq; vtrasq; partes debere examinari, iustaq; trutina expendi, maximè autem exitum & finem conuersationis.
units.tr: From this it is plain that the conduct of holy teachers is set against the conduct of false apostles, and that both sides must be examined and weighed on a just balance, above all the outcome and end of each way of life.

units.la: Iesus Christus heri & hodie, idem est etiam in secula.
units.tr: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.

units.la: Secunda ratio suasoria ab eo, quòd euangelium semper manet idem, nequò mutari in eo quicquam potest. Qualis doctrina semel tradita est in euangelio per Christum, & deinde Apostolos: talis semper est retinenda. Christus, inquit, semper manet idem. Christum haud dubiè per Enallagen, siue metonymiam, pro Euangelio, seu doctrina euangelica posuit, quomodo alias quoque Moses pro lege ponitur: vt secunda epistola ad Corinthios capite tertio. Vsque ad diem hodiernum idem velamen in lectione veteris testamenti manet, nec tollitur velum, quod per Christū aboletur: sed ad hunc vsque diem, cùm legitur Moses, cordibus illorum impositum est. Hic secundo loco ponitur Moses pro eo, quod priore loco vocabatur vetus testamentum siue lex.
units.tr: The second persuasive argument is drawn from the fact that the gospel always remains the same and nothing in it can be changed. Whatever doctrine was once delivered in the gospel through Christ and then through the apostles, that same doctrine must always be held. Christ, he says, remains the same. Here Christ undoubtedly stands, by enallage or metonymy, for the gospel or evangelical doctrine, just as Moses elsewhere stands for the law, as in 2 Corinthians chapter 3: "To this day the same veil remains when the Old Testament is read, and the veil is not lifted, which is taken away through Christ; but to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts." Here, in the second place, Moses stands for what in the former place was called the Old Testament or the law.

units.la: Rursus Lucæ capite 16. Habent Mosen & prophetas, audiant illos. Hic Moses pro lege posuit: alioqui, cùm Moses quoque propheta fuerit, esset παῤῥησία. Actor. 15. Moses per omne Sabbatū in ciuitatibus prædicatur & legitur. Vbi, quandoquidem disputatio erat de lege, Moses recte pro lege ponitur. Quemadmodū ergo Moses recte pro lege: ita etiam Christus recte pro Euangelio ponitur: sicut Aristoteles pro Philosophia naturali, Homerus pro poësi, aut Bacchus apud poetas pro vino, Mars pro bello, per Enallagen videlicet siue metonymiam.
units.tr: Again, Luke chapter 16: "They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them." Here Moses stands for the law; otherwise, since Moses was also a prophet, it would be a blunt liberty [παῤῥησία]. Acts 15: "Moses is preached and read in the synagogues every Sabbath." Here, since the dispute was about the law, Moses is rightly put for the law. Therefore, just as Moses is rightly put for the law, so Christ is rightly put for the Gospel, as Aristotle is put for natural philosophy, Homer for poetry, or Bacchus among the poets for wine, Mars for war, namely by enallage or metonymy.

units.la: Iam heri, hodie, in secula, pro omnibus temporum differentijs, id est, pro præterito, præsenti, & futuro ponuntur. Estque igitur sententia perspicua, palamque fit, idem planè hoc loco dicere Apostolum, quod alias ait Galatas capite primo. Etiamsi nos aut angelus e cœlo prædicauerit vobis euangelium, præter id quod prædicauimus vobis anathema sit. Christus non mutatur in persona sua, ita etiam nec doctrina eius vlla in parte mutatur.
units.tr: Now "yesterday, today, and forever" stand for all the differences of time, that is, for past, present, and future. The meaning is therefore plain, and it is clear that the Apostle here says the same thing he says elsewhere in Galatians chapter one: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed." Christ is not changed in his person, and so likewise no part of his doctrine is changed.

units.la: Cœlum & terra transfibunt, verba autem Christi non transfibunt, neque peribit vel apex euangelij, donec omnia fiant.
units.tr: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of Christ will not pass away; nor will one jot or one tittle of the Gospel perish until all things are fulfilled."

units.la: Habere autem debet hæc ratio magnam vim apud omnes, ad retinendum ipsos in fide & sana doctrina semel accepta. Respicere oportet in personam Christi, & ex huius dignitate æstimare etiam doctrinam: sicut autem Christus semper manet idem, ita quoque eius doctrina. Non mutat Christus propositum suum, vt hoc tempore illud mandet, alio tempore aliud. Matthæi capite 3. & cap. 17. Hic est filius meus dilectus, inquit pater, ipsum audite. Quare tutum est illi adhærere. Idem Christus semel misit spiritum Sanctum, qui omnem veritatem edocuit, vt nullus alius doctor expectari debeat. Actorum capite secundo, & Ioannis capite decimosexto.
units.tr: This reason ought to have great force with everyone, for keeping them in the faith and in the sound doctrine once received. We must look to the person of Christ, and judge the doctrine also by his dignity. Just as Christ remains the same, so also is his doctrine. Christ does not change his purpose, so as to command one thing at one time and another at another time. Matthew chapters 3 and 17: "This is my beloved Son; hear him," says the Father. It is therefore safe to cling to him. The same Christ once sent the Holy Spirit, who taught all truth, so that no other teacher ought to be awaited. Acts chapter 2, and John chapter 16.

units.la: Cum ergo plena & confirmata & immutabilis sit hæc doctrina Euangelij, æquum est, indiuulsē ei adhærere, neque vllam aliam recipere.
units.tr: Since, therefore, this doctrine of the Gospel is full, confirmed, and unchangeable, it is right to cling to it without wavering and to receive no other.

units.la: Mentitus est Montanus cum sua Maximilla & Prisca, qui suadere conabatur, Apostolus non plenè edoctos à spiritu Sancto, spiritum Sanctum non datum Apostolis ea mensura, qua ipse acceperat. Reipsa, & signis accedentibus, alijsque notis indubitatis innumeris comprobatum est, Apostolus illum Spiritum promissum accepisse, & peccandem Spiritum omnia, quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria, edoctos.
units.tr: Montanus with his Maximilla and Prisca lied when he tried to persuade people that the Apostles had not been taught fully by the Holy Spirit, and that the Holy Spirit had not been given to the Apostles in the measure in which he himself had received it. In fact, by the signs that accompanied it and by countless other undoubted marks, it has been proved that the Apostles received that promised Spirit and were taught by the Spirit all things necessary for salvation.

units.la: Mentiuntur & hodie phanatici Spiritus, qui iactant reuelationes à spiritu Sancto, diuersas ab illa doctrina, quam Christus & Apostoli ecclesijs semel commendarunt.
units.tr: Today also the fanatical spirits lie, who boast of revelations from the Holy Spirit that differ from that doctrine which Christ and the Apostles once commended to the churches.

units.la: Errauit & abbas Ioachim cum suis, qui imaginatus est, quòd, quemadmodum tempore legis manifestata est potestas Dei patris, tempore reuelati euangelij manifestata est potestas Dei filij Christi: ita aliud aliquando seculum successurum, in quo eminebit potestas spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: Abbot Joachim and his followers also erred, who imagined that, just as in the time of the law the power of God the Father was made manifest, and in the time of the revealed Gospel the power of God the Son Christ was made manifest, so at some later age another age would follow, in which the power of the Holy Spirit would stand out.

units.la: Errant Iudei alium Christum, aliud Euangelium expectantes. Oportet fixos in hac sententia manere, Iesus Christus heri & hodie, idem etiam in secula. Et 1. Corinthiorum capite 3. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter hoc, quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Quo etiam videtur pertinere, quod Esaiæ capite 9. promissum est regnum Christi fore æternum, & quod Danielis capite 7. dictum est de regno Christi, potestas eius potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur, & regnum eius nunquam corrumpetur. Ad quem locum respicientes Iudæi Ioannis capite 13. Nos audiuimus ex lege, inquiunt, quòd Christus manet in æternum.
units.tr: The Jews err, expecting another Christ and another Gospel. We must remain fixed in this statement: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever." And 1 Corinthians chapter 3: "No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ." To this also seems to belong what is promised in Isaiah chapter 9, that the kingdom of Christ will be eternal, and what is said in Daniel chapter 7 about the kingdom of Christ: "His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall never be destroyed." Looking to this place the Jews in John chapter 12 say: "We have heard from the law that Christ remains forever."

units.la: Itaque manet idem Christus, manet idem Euangelium: neque vel lex vel legislator, vel Mesias alius debet expectari: neque Euangelium, quod semel traditum est, aliqua in parte mutari: alij quidem explicant hæc, vt accommodentillis verbis suprà positis de fiducia in solum Deum collocanda, atque intelligatur ex his, Christum eundem nunc quoque esse, qui fuerit olim, & posse non minus opitulari suis præsenti tempore, quàm olim fecit, ideoq; nunquam desperandum ijs, qui forte inopia, aut aliqua alia molestia premuntur.
units.tr: Thus the same Christ remains, and the same Gospel remains; neither the law, nor the lawgiver, nor some other Messiah ought to be awaited, nor ought the Gospel, once delivered, be changed in any part. Some explain these words as applying to the trust that must be placed in God alone, and they understand from them that Christ is now the same that he was before, and that he can help his people in the present time no less than he did in former times, and therefore that those who are perhaps pressed by want or by some other distress must never despair.

units.la: Alij exponunt, vt doceant, eandem salutis rationem fuisse ante Christum incarnatum & post incarnatum eundem fuisse salutis autorem tempore legis, perinde ac nunc tempore euangelij. Sed nostra interpretatio pulchrius, meo iudicio, Respondet & cohæret cum antecedentibus & consequentibus.
units.tr: Others explain it as teaching that the same way of salvation existed before Christ was incarnate, and that after the incarnation he was the same author of salvation in the time of the law as he is now in the time of the Gospel. But in my judgment our interpretation fits better, and agrees with what goes before and what follows.

units.la: Doctrinis uarijs ac peregrinis ne circumferamini) Illatio ex præcedentibus rationibus, qua euidenter declarat, in quem finem iusserit eos esse illorum memores, qui Euangelium primi apud eos annunciarant, & quid sibi rationibus proximè expositis voluerit, ita vt non abs re propositionis vice ad totum locum præsentem vsurpari verba ista queant.
units.tr: "Do not be carried about by various and strange doctrines." This is an inference from the preceding reasons, which clearly shows for what purpose he commanded them to remember those who first announced the Gospel among them, and what he meant by the reasons set out just before. So these words can be taken as the proposition for the whole present passage.

units.la: Si enim hoc pacto proponas istam exhortationem: Doctrinis varijs ac peregrinis ne circumferamini: deinde subijcias ea, quæ præcesserunt, videlicet: mementote eorum, qui præsunt vobis, &c. clara & perspicua habebitur sententia. Neq; inusitatum est apud Rhetores hunc in modum, id quod ad propositionem vel sententiam principalem attinet, poştremo loco siue in conclusione argumentationis constitui, præsertim vbi Enthymemata occurrunt. Appellat autem doctrinas varias, illas videlicet, de quibus diuersę & pugnantes circumferuntur sententiæ, & quæ à diuersis diuersó modo euulgantur, per quas homines inducuntur in dubitationes periculosas, & postea in graues errores. Doctrina veritatis simplex est, vbique sui similis, semperque doceri eodem modo gaudet. Doctrina falsiratis nunquam consistit, subinde variat, admiscet, addit, detrahit, transformat aliquid, vt tandem deprehendantur, ne ipsi dogmatistæ quidem intelligere, quid aut de quibus afferant. Quod cùm fit, maxima offendicula atque incommoda & sequi in ecclesijs necessum est. Et quòd huiusmodi doctrinas varias intelligat, liquet ab exemplo, siue specie, quam protinus Apostolus ipse adijcit, nempe de escis, per quas non potest stabiliri cor.
units.tr: For if you put forward this exhortation in this way, "Do not be carried about by various and strange doctrines," and then add what went before, namely, "Remember those who rule over you," and so on, the meaning will be clear and plain. Nor is it unusual among the rhetoricians that what belongs to the main proposition or statement should be placed in the last place, or in the conclusion of an argument, especially where enthymemes occur. Now he calls "various doctrines" those about which differing and conflicting opinions are circulated, and which are spread by different people in different ways, through which men are led into dangerous doubts and afterwards into grave errors. The doctrine of truth is simple, always like itself, and always rejoices to be taught in the same way. The doctrine of falsehood never stays the same; it keeps varying, mixing, adding, subtracting, and transforming something, so that in the end even the dogmatists themselves do not understand what or about what they are asserting. When this happens, the greatest stumbling blocks and troubles must necessarily follow in the churches. And that he means doctrines of this kind of "various" sort is clear from the example, or kind, that the Apostle himself adds straightaway, namely about foods, by which the heart cannot be strengthened.

units.la: De escis enim variæ erant disputationes, atque ex ipsis Iudæis alij quibusvis vescendum, alij non quibusvis vescendum, arbitrati sunt. Qua de re Coloss. cap. 2. & Roman. cap. 14. Et nota est disceptatio Pauli cum Petro apud Antiochiam habita, Galatar. cap. 2. Peregrinas vocat doctrinas Apostolus, quæ antea per Christum & Apostolos non fuerunt propositæ, inter eas, quæ ad salutem sunt necessariæ, quæque in verbo Dei non habent solidum fundamentum.
units.tr: There were indeed various disputes about foods, and among the Jews themselves some held that one may eat anything, others that not just anything may be eaten. On this matter see Colossians chapter 2 and Romans chapter 14. The dispute between Paul and Peter at Antioch, recorded in Galatians chapter 2, is also well known. The Apostle calls doctrines "strange" when they were not set forth earlier through Christ and the Apostles, among those things which are necessary for salvation, and which do not have a solid foundation in the Word of God.

units.la: Talis doctrina pseudoapostolorum, qui ad Galatas penetrarunt, & conabantur contra doctrinam ab Apostolo semel traditam persuadere, necessariam esse legis observatio nem: Ideoq; dixit Apostolus: Si quis vobis prædicauerit Euangelium præter id, quod accepistis, anathema sit. Talis quoque doctrina est, quæ hauritur ex penetralibus irianis philosophiæ, atq; ex sacris literis non potest euidenter comprobari: cuiusmodi doctrinæ per omnes ætates multæ in ecclesiam sunt inuectæ.
units.tr: Such is the doctrine of the false apostles who made their way among the Galatians and tried to persuade them, against the doctrine the Apostle had once delivered, that observance of the law was necessary. Therefore the Apostle said: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be accursed." Such also is the doctrine drawn from the hidden recesses of pagan philosophy, which cannot be clearly proved from the sacred writings. Many doctrines of this kind have been introduced into the Church in every age.

units.la: Origenis doctrina de transmigratione animarum è corporibus in corpora, ex sententia Pythagoræ, Scholastici multas huiusmodi in Sorbonicis suis disputationibus, & e narrationibus sententiarum Petri Lombardi, mundo obtruserunt. Certè Gerson cancellarius Parisiensis multas sua ætate explodendas memorauit. Fortasis eò plures Scholastici congesserunt tales doctrinas, quò ipsi ambiuerunt videri in philosophia doctiores.
units.tr: The Schoolmen, in their Sorbonne disputations and in their narrations of Peter Lombard's Sentences, thrust upon the world Origen's doctrine of the transmigration of souls from bodies into bodies, after the opinion of Pythagoras, and many such doctrines. Certainly Gerson, chancellor of Paris, recorded many that deserved to be exploded in his own day. Perhaps the Schoolmen heaped up so many such doctrines because they were eager to seem more learned in philosophy.

units.la: Nam vt quisq; inter illos erat Aristotelicissimus, ita existimatus est ad explicandā theologiam aptissimus. In summa, ex Iudaismo, ex philosophia carnali, ex stulta persuasio ne spiritualis sapientiæ Christianę, per Iudæos, per Sophistas, per pseudoapostolos & hæreticos, variæ & peregrinæ doctrinæ omnes inducuntur.
units.tr: For the more Aristotelian any one of them was, the more he was thought most fit to explain theology. In sum, from Judaism, from carnal philosophy, and from a foolish persuasion of spiritual Christian wisdom, through Jews, through Sophists, through false apostles and heretics, all sorts of various and strange doctrines are introduced.

units.la: Elegans verò est, quòd ait, huiusmodi doctrinis non debere nos circumferri. Metaphora est apta ad declarandam magnam incertitudinem atque inconstantiam.
units.tr: The statement that we ought not to be carried about by such doctrines is elegant indeed. It is an apt metaphor for showing great uncertainty and inconstancy.

units.la: Si enim modò in hanc, modò in illam partem circumferimur, sicut arundo excitatur vento, successu temporis fit, vt in totum à veritate excidamus, nihilque retineamus solidum seu inconcussum. Huc pertinent hi loci, Galatarum capite primo. Miror, quòd à Christo, qui vocauit vos per gratiam, adeò citò transferamini in aliud Euangelium. Ephesiorum capite quarto. Non amplius simus pueri, qui fluctuemus & circumferimur quovis vento doctrinæ, per versutiam hominum. Secunda epistola ad Thessalonicenses capite secundo, Rogamus vos fratres, ne citò dimoueamini à mente, neque turbemini, neque per Spiritum, neque per sermonem, neque per epistolam, tanquam nobis autoribus. Itaque audire quidem licet & cognoscere doctrinas nouas, sed nequaquam illis circūferri, vt videlicet propterea incipiamus de ijs dubitare, quę antea per Apostolos & sanctos patres iuxta mentem Scripturarum & spiritus Sancti sunt ad nos allatæ.
units.tr: For if we are carried now in this direction, now in that, as a reed is stirred by the wind, in time it comes about that we fall away altogether from the truth and retain nothing solid or unshaken. To this belong these passages: Galatians chapter 1: "I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different gospel." Ephesians chapter 4: "that we be no longer children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by the cunning of men." Second letter to the Thessalonians chapter 2: "We ask you, brethren, not to be quickly shaken in mind or troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter, as if from us." Thus it is indeed lawful to hear and learn new doctrines, but by no means to be carried around by them, so that we begin to doubt on that account those things which were brought to us by the Apostles and holy Fathers, according to the mind of the Scriptures and of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Bonum est enim, gratia confirmari cor: non escis, quæ non profuerunt ijs, qui versati sunt in illis.
units.tr: "It is good that the heart be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not profited those who have been occupied with them."

units.la: Tertia ratio suasoria, quare nō oporteat circūferri varijs & peregrinis doctrinis, sumpta à collatione doctrinarum inter se, earundemq; vtilitate, fructu, effectibus. Est enim horum verborum sententia: alia est doctrina propria euangelij, veluti quòd per gratiā Dei, siue gratuitam misericordiam condonatur nobis peccata propter Christum: alia est doctrina de delectu ciborum & huiusmodi, quæ ab euangelio aliena est, & à pheudoapostolis inuecta. Proinde illa n quidem doctrinam amplecti, hanc verò reijcere, æquum est. Ratio: Quia illa valet ad stabiliendum cor, & ad confirmandum in fide & certa spe salutis internû hominem. Hęc verò nullam secum vtilitatem adfert. Et certè hæc ratio debet habere magnum pondus. Quid enim proponitur hominibus ad amplectendum, & quid recipiant homines, si non certa simul sit vtilitas eius rei proposita? Discunt homines artes illas, quas vocant liberales: quia sperant, sibi per eas aditum aperiendum ad alias artes sublimiores, cuiusmodi est doctrina legum, medicina, &c.
units.tr: The third persuasive reason why one should not be carried about by various and strange doctrines is drawn from comparing doctrines with one another, and from their usefulness, fruit and effects. The sense of these words is this: one doctrine is proper to the gospel, namely that our sins are forgiven us for Christ's sake through the grace of God, that is, his free mercy; another is the doctrine about the distinction of foods and the like, which is foreign to the gospel and was brought in by false apostles. It is right, therefore, to embrace the former doctrine and to reject the latter. The reason is that the former is effective in establishing the heart and in confirming the inner man in faith and in the certain hope of salvation, whereas the latter brings no usefulness with it. And surely this reason ought to carry great weight. For what is offered to men to embrace, and what do men receive, if the thing offered does not at the same time have a certain usefulness? Men learn those arts which they call liberal because they hope that through them a way will be opened to higher arts, such as the study of law, medicine, and so on.

units.la: Et, in summa, quascunque bonas artes ideò discunt, quòd sperent, se per illas paratos qualecunque ad senectutem viaticum. Qua de re boni præceptores solent iuuentuti studiosę magnorum hominū, philosophorum, & poetarum sententias & lepidè dicta inculcare, per quę tanquam stimulos illam ad labores alacriter subeundos excitent. Eadem igitur ratione iudicandum est & de his doctrinis, quæ de religione proponuntur. Quòd si videmus eas adferre insignem vtilitatē, ad salutem præsertim quæ concilicat animarum, statuemus eam nobis amplectendam.
units.tr: In sum, whatever good arts they learn, they learn because they hope that through them they will be furnished with some provision for old age. For this reason good teachers are accustomed to impress upon eager youth the sayings and witty remarks of great men, philosophers and poets, by which, as with goads, they stir them to undertake their labours cheerfully. By the same reasoning, therefore, we must judge also those doctrines which are proposed concerning religion. If we see them bring remarkable usefulness, especially for salvation, which reconciles souls, we shall decide that they are to be embraced by us.

units.la: Quòd si non adferant aliquam vtilitatem, sinamus eas valere, relinquamus stultis sophistis, qui gaudent cerebrum suum fatigare, & bonas horas perdere inutilibus quæstionibus pertractandis. Atque huc pertinent tot loci passim obuij, in quibus sacræ Scripturæ & sanæ doctrinæ vtilitas commendatur: veluti 2. Timotheum capite 3. Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata & vtilis ad doctrinā, ad redargutionē, ad correctionē, ad institutionem, quę est in iustitia, vt integer sit Dei homo ad omne opus bonum apparatus. Item Romanorum cap. 4. 5. 1. Corinthiorum cap. 9. 10. 2. Petri 1. 2. Petri 3. Rursus & illi loci huc pertinet, qui iubent curiosas, inanes, inutiles quæstiones devitare. Vt 1. ad Timotheum capite quarto, Profanas & aniles fabulas reijce, quin potius exerce temetipsum ad pietatē: Item 1. ad Timotheum cap. 6. Si quis diuersam sequitur doctrinam, & non accedit sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & ei, quæ secundum pietatem est, doctrinæ, is inflatus est, nihil sciens, sed insaniens circa quæstiones ac disputationum pugnas, ex quibus nascitur inuidia, contentio, maledicentia, suspiciones malæ, superuacaneæ conflictationes hominum mente corruptorū, & quibus adempta est veritas, qui existimant quęstum esse pietate. Item secunda ad Timotheum capite secundo, Stultas & ineruditas quæstiones respue, sciens, eas parare pugnas. Et ad Titum capite tertio. Stultas autem quæstiones, & genealogias, & contentiones, ac pugnas legales omitte: sunt enim inutiles & superuacaneę. Sunt aliæ multæ huiusmodi sententiæ, sed quis omnes in numerato ponat? Satis igitur constat, quanti momenti ratione istam æstimari oporteat.
units.tr: But if they bring no usefulness, let us allow them to lapse and leave them to foolish sophists, who delight in wearing out their brains and wasting good hours on useless questions. To this belong the many passages met with everywhere in which the usefulness of Holy Scripture and of sound doctrine is commended: for example, 2 Timothy chapter 3: "All Scripture, divinely inspired, is also useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." Likewise Romans chapters 4 and 5; 1 Corinthians chapters 9 and 10; 2 Peter chapters 1 and 3. Again, those passages also belong here which bid us avoid curious, empty and useless questions, such as 1 Timothy chapter 4: "Reject profane and old wives' fables; rather, exercise yourself toward godliness." Likewise 1 Timothy chapter 6: "If anyone teaches a different doctrine, and does not agree to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is puffed up, knowing nothing, but sick with disputes and battles of words, from which arise envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions, and constant wranglings of men of corrupt mind, who have been deprived of the truth and suppose that godliness is a source of gain." Likewise 2 Timothy chapter 2: "Refuse foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they breed quarrels." And Titus chapter 3: "But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions and legal battles; for they are unprofitable and vain." There are many other sayings of this kind, but who could set them all down? It is sufficiently clear, therefore, how great a weight this consideration ought to be given.

units.la: Sed videamus etiamnum, quàm elegantibus verbis Apostolus eam expresit. Bonum est, inquit, gratia consolidari cor: Gratiam videtur posuisse pro capitali & principali doctrina euangelij, videlicet quòd per gratuitam misericordiam, siue gratis, & per gratiam seruamur propter Christum. Quæ doctrina passim in Euangelio, maximeque in epistolis Paulinis, ad Romanos, Galatas, Ephesios, Titum, plenissimè exponitur.
units.tr: But let us look again at how elegantly the Apostle expressed it. "It is good," he says, "for the heart to be strengthened by grace." He seems to have put "grace" for the chief and principal doctrine of the gospel, namely that we are saved through free mercy, or freely, and by grace, for Christ's sake. This doctrine is set out throughout the Gospel, and most fully in the Pauline epistles, to the Romans, Galatians, Ephesians and Titus.

units.la: Quinetiam pro quacunque alia sana doctrina, quæ huic priori est annexa: saltem ex hac vna licet intelligere & reliquas, quæ videlicet in Euangelio clare explicateque traduntur. Et reuera quemadmodum hæc doctrina primaria est in toto Euangelio: ita eam ipsam multiplex adhuc doctrina sequitur, & tanquam ex fonte ex ea prosilit.
units.tr: Moreover, it stands for any other sound doctrine that is joined to this first one. At least from this one teaching it is possible to understand the rest as well, which are plainly and clearly delivered in the Gospel. Indeed, just as this doctrine is primary in the whole Gospel, so many further doctrines follow it and spring forth from it as from a fountain.

units.la: Porrò est hæc insignis commendatio talis doctrinæ, quòd per eam constabilitur cor, id est, conscientia: cor enim posuit pro conscientia, pro interno homine, & principalibus animæ viribus, per quas homo quæ salutis sunt, apprehendit.
units.tr: Further, this is the remarkable commendation of such a doctrine, that through it the heart is established, that is, the conscience. For he put "heart" for conscience, for the inner man, and for the principal powers of the soul, by which man apprehends the things that pertain to salvation.

units.la: Per stabilitionem autem cordis intellige omnes illas præclaras vtilitates, quas in hac vita percipiunt credentes in conscientijs, dum animaduertunt, se gratis propter Christum donari à Deo patre misericordia. De qualibus vtilitatibus Rom. 5.
units.tr: By the establishing of the heart, understand all those excellent benefits which believers perceive in this life in their consciences, while they reflect that they are freely given the mercy of God the Father for Christ's sake. Of such benefits see Romans 5.

units.la: Iustificati igitur ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum) Et Romanorum capite 8. Nulla igitur nunc est condemnatio his, qui insiti sunt Christo Iesu, & cætera, quæ ibi sequuntur. Quæ quidem quantopere stabiliant cor, ij norunt, qui tentationes de ira Dei aliquando in se sentiunt, & contra has tentationes remedij loco vsi sunt doctrina de gratia.
units.tr: Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God. And in Romans 8: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus," and what follows there. Those who have sometimes felt in themselves temptations about the wrath of God know how greatly these words steady the heart, and who have used the doctrine of grace as a remedy against such temptations.

units.la: Reuera enim ita est. Doctrina, quæ impugnat gratiam, terret, deijcit, perdit conscientias: cogit enim de salute in totum desperare: at verò qui doctrinæ de gratia totus innititur, is incredibilem sentit consolationem, atque agnoscendo Dei erga se beneuolentiam, ad omnia officia fidei & charitatis promptus est, neq; vllis aduersitatibus seu corporalibus, seu spiritualibus deijcitur. Sequitur:
units.tr: In truth it is so. The doctrine that opposes grace terrifies, casts down and destroys consciences, for it compels a man to despair of salvation altogether. But he who rests wholly on the doctrine of grace feels an incredible consolation, and, recognising God's goodwill towards him, is ready for all the duties of faith and love, and is not cast down by any adversities, whether bodily or spiritual. It follows:

units.la: Non escis) Doctrina de escis, id est, de delectu ciborum, opponitur doctrinæ de gratia. Atque hic eadem opera videre licet, cuiusmodi doctrinas varias & peregrinas Apostolus hic intelligat. Apertum enim exemplum hic proponit, doctrinam videlicet de escis quæ doctrina ab Euangelio aliena est, & per pseudoapostolos quosdam maximè qui ex Iudæis, ecclesijs obtrudebatur. Ex hac autē specie doctrinæ intelligas oportet alias species consimiles, veluti de delectu dierum, item genealogias Iudaicas, traditiones, & si què huiusmodi in sacris literis, ut reijcienda alibi perstringuntur. Hodie quoq; de multis eius modi doctrinis acerrimè litigatur, quæ ad euangelium proprie non pertinent, sed magis ex traditionibus humanis deriuantur: & de ἀνταξίας rebusq; adiaphoris, non de fide sunt: sed quàm atrocia sint disiidia, nemo credat, nisi qui viderit. Hæc quidem doctrina, quam apostolus commemorat, fundamentum suum quodammodo habebat ex lege: Nam lex certos quosdam cibos præscribit, quosdam prohibet, existimabantq; nonnulli æquum, ut simul cum euangelio retineretur legis obseruatio: & certè non videbatur iniqua ista postulatio. Sed enim quando isti ita urserunt hanc obseruationem, quasi ad salutem esset necessaria, & sine ea à salute homines excluderentur: hic apostolus magno spiritu sese op posuit, & summopere vitandam talem doctrinam definiuit. Quod addedum, ne quis putet, de cibis simpliciter disputatum esse, cùm palàm sit, cibos esse re mediam, & posse pios quibuscunq; bene recteq; uti: posse etiam male uti, cùm videlicet scandalum ex usu eorum sequitur. Proinde de usu ciborum ita Apostolus subijcit.
units.tr: "Not with meats." The doctrine of meats, that is, of the distinction of foods, is opposed to the doctrine of grace. And here we may see at the same time what kinds of varied and strange doctrines the Apostle means. He sets before us a clear example, namely the doctrine concerning meats, a doctrine foreign to the gospel, which was being forced upon the churches especially by certain false apostles who came from the Jews. From this kind of doctrine you must understand other similar kinds, such as the distinction of days, Jewish genealogies, traditions, and whatever of this sort the Scriptures elsewhere condemn for rejection. Today too there is a most bitter dispute over many doctrines of this sort, which do not properly belong to the gospel but derive rather from human traditions; and concerning things of equal value [ἀνταξίας] and adiaphora, which are not matters of faith. But nobody would believe how atrocious these quarrels are, unless he had seen them. This doctrine which the Apostle mentions had, in a way, its foundation in the law. For the law prescribes certain foods and forbids others, and some thought it fair that the observance of the law should be retained alongside the gospel; and indeed that demand did not seem unjust. But when these men pressed this observance as if it were necessary for salvation, and as if men were excluded from salvation without it, the Apostle opposed them with great vigour and defined that such doctrine must be avoided at all costs. It should be added, lest anyone think that the discussion was simply about foods, that it is clear foods are indifferent and that the godly can use them well and rightly; they can also use them badly, namely when offence follows from their use. Accordingly, the Apostle goes on to speak of the use of foods in this way.

units.la: Quæ non profuerunt: Ecce, quare doctrina eiusmodi reijcienda, quia nullam adfert utilitatem. Sic alibi quoque de exercitationibus corporalibus definiuit. 1. Timoth. 4. profanas & aniles fabulas reijce, quin potius exercere temetipsum ad pietatem. Nam corporalis exercitatio paululum habet utilitatis. At pietas ad omnia utilis est, ut quæ promissiones habet vitæ præsentis ac futuræ. Porrò non prodesse escas ad salutem, ipse hic non probat, quàmuis mox confutationem breuem huius doctrinæ subijciet: sed ut per se notum pijs relinquit, maximè quando Christus aperte, & ipse apostolus alibi de hac re egerint. Matth. 15. Non quod ingreditur in os, impurat hominem, sed quod egreditur ex ore, hoc impurum reddit hominem. Roman. 14. Non est regnum Dei esca & potus, 1. Corinth. 6. Escę ventri destinatæ sunt, & venter escis, Deus autem & hunc & illas abolebit. Coloss. 2. Ne quis vos iudicet in cibo aut potu, aut in parte diei festi, aut nouilunij, aut sabbatorum, quæ sunt umbra rerum futurarum, corpus autem Christi. 1. Timoth. 4. Spiritus certò loquitur venturos, qui iubebunt abstinere à cibis, quos Deus creauit ad sumendum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus, & ijs qui cognouerút veritatem, quòd, quicquid creauit Deus, bonum sit, & nihil reijciedum, si cum gratiarum actione sumatur: Sanctificatur enim per sermonem Dei ac precationem. Ecce ergo, quomodo esca nihil prosint. Diserte autem ait non prodesse ijs, qui in illis versati sunt: ci περιπατήσαντες: significat enim, ijs demum esse inutiles tales obseruationes, qui in illis diu inhærent, qui salutis viam in illis constituunt, quasi citra earum obseruationem non foret spes ad vitam perueniendi. Hæc inquam per fuasio & fiducia non solùm est inutilis, verùm etiam noxia. Detrahit namq; vehementer gloriæ Dei, in primis morti Christi tanquam si is sua morte non tantū promeruisset, quin oporteat nos iterum promereri ciborum obseruatione. Regnum Dei non venit cum obseruatione. Regnum Dei non est esca & potus. Alias quidem abstinere certis cibis per se non est damnabile: sed ita abstinere, quasi ad salutem prodesset, aut quasi ad cultum Dei faceret abstinentia, periculo id non vacat.
units.tr: Which have not profited: Here you see why such doctrine is to be rejected, because it brings no benefit. So he also defined elsewhere concerning bodily exercises: "Reject profane and old-wives' fables, but rather exercise yourself unto godliness" (1 Tim. 4). For bodily exercise profits little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having promises of the life that now is and of that which is to come. Moreover, that foods do not profit for salvation the Apostle does not prove here, although he will soon add a brief refutation of this doctrine; he leaves it to the godly as something known in itself, especially since Christ and the Apostle himself have plainly dealt with this matter elsewhere. "Not that which goes into the mouth defiles a man, but that which comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man" (Matt. 15). "The kingdom of God is not meat and drink" (Rom. 14). "Meats are for the belly, and the belly for meats; but God shall destroy both it and them" (1 Cor. 6). "Let no man judge you in meat or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ" (Col. 2). "The Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith... commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer" (1 Tim. 4). Behold, therefore, how foods profit nothing. He says plainly that they do not profit those who have walked in them [οἳ περιπατήσαντες]: for it signifies that such observances are useless to those who cling to them for a long time, who place the way of salvation in them, as if without observing them there were no hope of attaining to life. This persuasion and confidence, I say, is not only useless but also harmful. For it greatly detracts from the glory of God, and above all from the death of Christ, as if by his death he had not merited enough, so that we must merit again by the observance of foods. "The kingdom of God does not come with observance." "The kingdom of God is not food and drink." Otherwise, to abstain from certain foods is not in itself damnable; but to abstain as if the abstinence profited for salvation, or as if abstinence were a worship of God, this is not free from danger.

units.la: Habemus altare, de quo non est fas edere ijs, qui tabernaculo deseruiunt) sequitur breuis confutatio peregrinæ illius doctrinæ de delectu ciborum obiter adiecta. Estque hæc præcipua ratio qua docet, delectum ciborum reijciendum. Ceremoniæ legis & præcepta ceremonialia sunt abrogata, nullasque amplius habent vires ad nos obstringendum. Atqui delectus ciborum inter ceremonialia numeratur: igitur & doctrina de delectu ciborum nunc est super uacanea. & inutilis. Hęc est verborum apostoli simplex ac propria sententia, vti mox clarius ostendemus, & ratio ad euincendum, doctrinam illam esse inutilem, mirè idonea.
units.tr: We have an altar, of which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat: There follows a brief refutation of that strange doctrine about the distinction of foods, added in passing. And this is the chief reason by which he teaches that the distinction of foods is to be rejected. The ceremonies of the law and the ceremonial precepts have been abrogated, and no longer have any force to bind us. But the distinction of foods is counted among the ceremonial matters; therefore the doctrine of the distinction of foods is now also vain and useless. This is the simple and proper meaning of the Apostle's words, as we shall show more clearly below, and the argument for proving that that doctrine is useless is wonderfully apt.

units.la: Inde verò hæc ratio hoc pacto allata est. Aduersarij qui inuehebát in ecclesiam nouam doctrinam de obligandis credentibus, ad delectum ciborum faciendum, fundamentum suum ex media lege, ut ipsi clamitabant, adferebant. Allegabant namque, plurimos cibos expresse à Deo ipso esse prohibitos: id autem, quia procul dubio animam suo quodam modo inficiebant. Huc congerebantilla omnia, quæ Leuitici 11. & Deuteron. 14. de mundis & immundis animantibus, siue quadrupedibus, siue piscibus, siue auibus, siue reptilibus, prolixè commemorantur: atque additur etiam, immundos fore, debereque purificari lotione vestimentorum, quicunque talium animalium cadauera attigissent.
units.tr: Indeed this argument was put forward in the following way. The adversaries who were introducing into the Church the new doctrine of binding believers to make a distinction of foods were bringing forward their foundation from the law itself, as they loudly claimed. For they argued that very many foods had been expressly forbidden by God himself, because without doubt they defiled the soul in a certain way. To this they gathered together everything that is set forth at length in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 about clean and unclean animals, whether quadrupeds, fishes, birds or reptiles; and it is added also that those who had touched the carcasses of such animals would be unclean and must be purified by washing their garments.

units.la: Itaque probabiles admodum in speciem illorum erant rationes: quocunque tandem animo isti hanc caussam agerent, siue studio promouendæ legis diuinæ: siue quadam tantum superstitione: siue pro diu recepta apud Iudæos consuetudine conseruanda: siue vo to grauandi gentiles, alienandiq́ue ab euangelio, quos sciebant hanc doctrinam & iugum nusquam.
units.tr: So their arguments were, in appearance, quite plausible. Whatever purpose these men had in pleading this cause, whether zeal for promoting the divine law, or some superstition alone, or a desire to preserve the custom long received among the Jews, or a wish to burden the Gentiles and alienate them from the gospel, which they knew would never accept this doctrine and this yoke.

units.la: Pontificiorum doctrinæ repu-gnantes cuage-lio sunt falsissi-mæ.
units.tr: The doctrines of the Papists, which conflict with the gospel, are utterly false.

units.la: Lex ceremo-nialis de cibis.
units.tr: The ceremonial law concerning foods.

units.la: Cibus adiapho-rus.
units.tr: Food is indifferent.

units.la: Doctrinæ pe-regrinæ inuti-les & pericu-losæ.
units.tr: Strange doctrines are useless and dangerous.

units.la: Ciborum sanctifi-catio.
units.tr: The sanctification of foods.

units.la: Abstinentia à cibis res indiffe-rens, si absit su-perstitio.
units.tr: Abstinence from foods is an indifferent matter, if superstition is absent.

units.la: Confutatio.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: Aduersariorum argumenta ex lege.
units.tr: The adversaries' arguments from the law.

units.la: Rationes probabiles. nusquam suscepturos. Apud Iudaeos quidem satis erat plausibilis doctrina, vtpote quae altissimè erat infixa omnium animis, adeò, ut etiam Petrus post receptum spiritū sanctū in eadem opinione fuerit, donec viso coelitus facto aliter edoceretur. Qua de re Actor.10 Et iterum de eodem Petro Galat.2. Quòd si autem tantus vir tam facile in hanc adductus est sententiam, quid miremur de ceteris inferioribus? Quia igitur doctrina illa fundamentū suū habere videbatur in lege, ideoque plurimi ea ambabus manibus amplectebantur, non potuisset apostolus ulla ratione commodius eam refellere, quàm docendo, legem, quantum ad ceremonialia attinet, esse abrogatam. Hac una ratione omnis doctrina non tantùm de cibis, verùm etiam de diebus & quibuscunque eius generis observationibus, clarissimè euertitur. Quomodo & in epistola ad Colossenses eandem doctrinam refellit, dicendo, quòd tantùm vmbrae quaedam erant, quae in lege de eiusmodi rebus proponebantur: veritatem autem habere in solo Christo. Et reuera ita erat: ad significationem quandam rerum spiritualium erant omnia eiusmodi instituta, quod miseri Iudaei nec in hunc quidem usque diem volunt intelligere. Omnia quippe aut aliquid perficiendum in Christo, aut de vitae nostrae recta institutione significabant. Qua de re non est praesentis loci fusius agere.
units.tr: Plausible reasons. They would never receive it. Among the Jews this doctrine was indeed plausible enough, since it was deeply fixed in everyone's minds; so much so that even Peter, after receiving the Holy Spirit, remained of the same opinion until, by a vision sent from heaven, he was taught otherwise (Acts 10). And again concerning the same Peter (Gal. 2). But if so great a man was so easily led into this opinion, why should we wonder at the others, who were of lesser standing? Since, therefore, that doctrine seemed to have its foundation in the law, and so very many embraced it with both hands, the Apostle could not have refuted it in any more convenient way than by teaching that the law, so far as the ceremonial matters are concerned, has been abrogated. By this one reasoning every doctrine is most clearly overthrown, not only concerning foods but also concerning days and any observances of that kind. In the same way he refutes this same doctrine in the Epistle to the Colossians, saying that these things were only shadows which the law set forth concerning such matters, and that the truth is in Christ alone. And indeed it was so: all such institutions were for signifying certain spiritual things, which the wretched Jews do not wish to understand even to this day. For all of them either signified something to be accomplished in Christ, or the right ordering of our life. Concerning this it is not the place of the present discussion to treat at greater length.

units.la: Sed iam operae pretium est ostendamus, hunc, quem diximus, esse verborum apostoli sensum. Nonnulli existimarunt, hic esse Allegoriam, ideoque in explicanda allegoria, vehementer sudant. Sed cum non ducantur solida argumenta, praesertim ad confirmandum aliquod dogma, ex allegorijs, & parcissimè alioquin allegoriae in disputationibus graujoribus aspergantur, nos solicitudinem explicandae allegoriae deponemus. Alij alias interpretandi rationes anxiè perquirunt.
units.tr: But now it is worth showing what the sense of the apostle's words is, as I have said. Some have thought that there is an allegory here, and so they sweat hard over explaining the allegory. But since solid arguments are not drawn from allegories, especially for confirming any doctrine, and allegories ought otherwise to be sprinkled very sparingly into weightier disputations, I will set aside the labour of explaining an allegory. Others anxiously search out other ways of interpreting the passage.

units.la: Nos autem statuimus, hic esse simpliciter rationem sumptam à propria dignitate Euangelij, nec non ab exemplo, ut à maiore ad minus fiat argumentatio, quae hunc in modum crassius reddi queat. In euangelio, siue in nouo testamento habemus quidem altare, id est, certum cultū Dei: sed non eiusmodi, ut in eo carnes, vel ulli alij cibi, quibus vescifponsent sacerdotes, offerantur, quemadmodum in veteri testamento fieri solitum est. Ex hoc iam manifeste sequitur: Sine tantilla quidē manet obseruatio de cibis, ut aliqui deinceps ad sacrificium offeratur, multò minus manet integrum, ut extra sacrificia obseruatio, siue delectus ciborum retineatur. Summę & excellentissimę ceremonię de cibis sunt abrogatae, nēpe ceremonię de sacrificijs. Igitur et ceremoniae inferiores de ciborum delectu sunt abrogatae. Non amplius eliguntur certi cibi ad peragenda sacrificia, cur igitur eligatur ad quotidianum esum? Ita meo iudicio proponit euangelij propriam quandam dignitatem, atque exemplum excellentissimae ceremoniae legalis, quam vbi abrogatam esse palàm fit, consequitur plane & inferiorem ceremoniam concidisse. Hanc ego puto claram & minimè intricatam esse interpretationem, eamque parere sententiam, quae ad probandum, inutilem esse doctrinam omnem de ciborum delectu, valde sit idonea. Neq; aliquid quicquam, his verbis significat apostolus, quàm legis ceremonias etiam excellentissimas abrogatas: verte, inuerte, quomodocunq; velis, alium sensum commodiorem nō elicies. Altare per metonymiam potuit pro cultu quocunq; ad nostram religionem pertinente.
