Et respexit hac voce ad ritum legis Mosaicae, quo Iudaei quidem proprie habebant altare, in quo adolebant sua sacrificia: ostenditque, nobis quoq; aliquid in locum eius ritus succesisse, nempe cultum spiritualem, de quo paulo post apertius differet, vbi de spiritualibus nostris hostijs, nempe laudibus Dei, gratiarum actionibus, beneficentia erga proximum. Alias nos altare materiale non agnoscimus, sed mensam, de qua panem & potum mysticū sumimus, nullos verò cibos Deo immolamus, iuxta illud 1 Corinth.10. Non potestis mensae Domini esse participes, & mensae daemoniorum. Actor.6. Non est placitum, ut nos derelicto sermone Dei ministremus mensis. Et coenam agnoscimus Dominicam, non combustionem vel oblationem sacrificiorum. Quòd verò sacerdotes veteris testamenti partem sacrificiorum, siue offerrentur carnes, siue panes, siue placentae, retinuerint sibi ad esum, liquet ex diuersis capitibus Leuitic 2.3.5.6 7. At verò sacerdotib. in euangelio nihil esse, quòd ex sacrificijs edant: quia nimirum nequaquam amplius carnalia sacrificia offerimus, per se palàm est. Magna igitur differetia est inter ea, quae sunt legis, & quae sunt euangelij. Lex quidem de cibis multa constituebat, tum ad ceremonias & ritus sacrorū, tum ad quotidianum vsum. Euangelium verò cibos nullos ad offerendum praescribit, multò minus ad quotidianum vsum. Euangelium habet cultum, habet sacrificia, sed spiritualia. Regnum Dei non est cibus & potus, sed iustitia, & pax, & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto: Roma.14. Apparet autem, ideo voluisse Apostolum huiusmodi ratione adferre, sumptam à ceremonijs sacrorum, potius quàm aliquâ aliam, propterea quòd supra de sacerdotio & ceremonijs multa sint disputata ac declaratum etiam, tàm sacerdotium legale, quàm
units.tr: I hold, however, that the argument here is simply taken from the proper dignity of the Gospel and also from an example, so that the reasoning runs from the greater to the less, which can be put more crudely in this way. In the Gospel, or in the New Testament, we indeed have an altar, that is, a certain worship of God; but it is not of such a kind that flesh or any other food on which the priests might feed is offered on it, as was customary in the Old Testament. From this it follows plainly: if so little as the observance of foods, so that some of them are offered in sacrifice, does not remain, much less does the observance, or distinction of foods, remain intact apart from the sacrifices. The highest and most excellent ceremonies concerning food have been abrogated, namely the ceremonies of sacrifices. Therefore the lesser ceremonies concerning the distinction of foods have also been abrogated. Certain foods are no longer chosen for carrying out sacrifices; why, then, should they be chosen for daily eating? In my judgement the apostle sets forth in this way the proper dignity of the Gospel and the example of the most excellent legal ceremony; and when it is clear that this has been abrogated, it plainly follows that the lesser ceremony has also fallen. I think this interpretation is clear and not at all intricate, and that it yields a sense very well suited to proving that all doctrine about the distinction of foods is useless. The apostle, by these words, signifies nothing other than that the ceremonies of the law, even the most excellent, have been abrogated. Turn it and twist it however you like, you will not elicit a more suitable sense. By metonymy "altar" could stand for any worship pertaining to our religion. He looked, by this word, to the rite of the Mosaic law, in which the Jews properly had an altar on which they burned their sacrifices; and he shows that something has also succeeded in our case in place of that rite, namely spiritual worship, of which he will speak more clearly a little later, where he treats of our spiritual sacrifices, namely praises of God, thanksgivings, and beneficence towards our neighbour. Otherwise we do not acknowledge a material altar, but a table, from which we take the bread and the mystical drink; yet we offer no foods to God as sacrifice, in accordance with that saying of 1 Cor. 10: "You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons." Acts 6: "It is not pleasing that we, having left the word of God, should serve tables." And we acknowledge the Lord's Supper, not the burning or offering of sacrifices. That the priests of the Old Testament kept for themselves a portion of the sacrifices to eat, whether the flesh, or the bread, or the cakes that were offered, is clear from various chapters of Leviticus, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7. But that the priests in the Gospel have nothing from the sacrifices to eat is plain in itself, since of course we no longer offer carnal sacrifices at all. There is therefore a great difference between what belongs to the law and what belongs to the Gospel. The law indeed laid down many things about foods, both for the ceremonies and rites of the sacred things and for daily use. The Gospel, however, prescribes no foods for offering, much less for daily use. The Gospel has worship, it has sacrifices, but spiritual ones: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit," Rom. 14. It appears, moreover, that the apostle wished to bring forward this argument in this way, taken from the ceremonies of the sacred things, rather than some other, because above, much has been disputed and also declared concerning the priesthood and the ceremonies, as much the legal priesthood as

units.la: Euangelium non tradit esum ciborum aut abstinentiam, siue cuiusmodi lex.
units.tr: The Gospel does not hand down the eating of foods or abstinence from them, nor any law of that kind.

units.la: Euangelij cultus et sacrificia spiritualia sunt. quàm ceremonias omnes sacerdotio cõiunctas esse abrogatas. Ex quibus hæc ipsa ratio euadit multo manifestior. Et apud Hebræos quæ ratio potuisset obsecro adferri commodius? Hi enim maximè spectabant ad suas ceremonias & ritus sacrorum, pro his maximè depugnabant.
units.tr: The worship of the Gospel and its sacrifices are spiritual; that all ceremonies joined to the priesthood have been abrogated. From these considerations this very argument becomes much clearer. And among the Hebrews, what argument could, I beg you, have been brought forward more fittingly? For they chiefly looked to their own ceremonies and rites of sacred things, and it was chiefly for these that they fought.

units.la: Iam verò vbi apostolus ostendit istam abrogationem ceremoniarum, maximeq; obseruationem de cibis, in illis ipsis ceremonijs fuisse manifestè adumbratam, quid amplius potuissent tergiuersari? Si agnouerunt illas ad significationem rerum futurarum à Deo fuisse institutas, debebant planè statim obmutescere.
units.tr: Now, where the apostle shows that this abrogation of the ceremonies, and especially the observance concerning foods, was clearly foreshadowed in those very ceremonies, what more could they have offered in evasion? If they acknowledged that those ceremonies had been instituted by God to signify things to come, they ought plainly to have fallen silent at once.

units.la: Animalium enim, quorum sanguis infertur pro peccato, in sancta per pontificem, horum corpora cremantur extra castra. Quapropter & Iesus ut sanctificaret per proprium sanguinem populum, extra portam passus est.
units.tr: For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.

units.la: Confirmatio rationis, quòd videlicet sacerdotes noui testamenti nequaquam vescun tur cibis vllis sacrificium oblatis, ducta à typo, quasi diceret: In veteri lege constitutum erat ut de quibusdam sacrificijs sacerdotes non vescerentur, nempe ijs, quæ tota comburebatur extra castra. Hoc autem non ob aliud constitutum est, quàm ad præsignificandum, quòd in nouo testamento nulla amplius sacrificia, ex quibus sacerdotes vesci possent, offerrentur. Igitur tametsi in nouo testamento habemus altare, id est, certum cultum: nō tamen eiusmodi, qui in cibis vel similibus rebus consistat: sed quicquid ad obseruationem vel delectum ciborum pertinet, id vniuersum abrogatum est. Quod cum ita se habet, palàm fit, doctrinam de ciborum delectu, nunc reuelato euangelio superuacaneam esse & inutilem.
units.tr: A confirmation of the argument, namely that the priests of the New Testament do not at all eat any foods offered in sacrifice, drawn from the type, as if he were saying: In the old law it was ordained that the priests should not eat of certain sacrifices, namely those which were wholly burned outside the camp. This, however, was ordained for no other purpose than to foreshadow that in the New Testament no sacrifices any longer would be offered from which the priests could eat. Therefore, although in the New Testament we have an altar, that is, a certain worship, it is not of such a kind as consists in foods or similar things; rather, whatever pertains to the observance or distinction of foods has been abrogated altogether. Since this is so, it is plain that the doctrine concerning the distinction of foods is now, with the Gospel revealed, superfluous and useless.

units.la: Nihil habet perplexitatis hoc argumentum. Tantum videamus istam historiam, vnde sumptum est, & perspicua fient omnia. Si bene aduertimus, diuersis locis describitur: primum Leuit.4. sacerdos pro peccato suo iubetur offerre iuuecam, quam mactat prius ad ostium tabernaculi, sanguinem infert in tabernaculum testimonij, ac digito aspergit eum septem vicibus ante velum sanctuarij. Quin de eodē sanguine nonnihil ponit ad cornua altaris incensi aromatici: mox reliquum sanguinem ad basin altaris holocausti effundit, in eodem verò altari adipem, duos renes, iecur, incendit: cætera uerò omnia, nempe pelis, carnes, caput, pedes, intestina, fimus, extra castra exuri præcipiùtur. Simili ratione ibidem faciendum mandatur pro peccatis totius coetus Israel. Iterum Leuitici 16. de iumento & hirco offerendis pro peccatis similiter legimus. Denique Numerorum 19. filij Israel adducere iubentur vaccam rufam integram, sine macula, quę iugum non portarit: de cuius sanguine cùm septies fiat aspersio ante faciem tabernaculi testimonij, tota extra castra comburitur, asseruantur̃q; cineres, ut misceatur aquis expiationis. Ecce igitur de diuersis animalibus, quorum sanguis quidem infertur pro peccato in sancta per pontificem, carnes verò exuruntur extra, castra neque cedunt sacerdotib. vtijs vescantur. Proinde euidens est hoc argumentum, ad probandum, verum esse, quod in nouo testamento locum amplius non habeant obseruationes de cibis, idque pluchrè esse in ijs præsignatum. Quantum autem momentum habeant eiusmodi probationes à typijs, supra à nobis diffusè expositum est, ut non sit opus nunc repetere.
units.tr: This argument has no obscurity at all. Let us only look at that passage from which it is taken, and everything will become clear. If we attend carefully, it is described in various places. First, Lev. 4: the priest is commanded to offer for his own sin a young bullock, which he first slaughters at the door of the tabernacle; he carries the blood into the tabernacle of testimony and sprinkles it with his finger seven times before the veil of the sanctuary. Indeed he puts some of the same blood on the horns of the altar of incense; then he pours out the remaining blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering, and on that same altar he burns the fat, the two kidneys, and the liver; but all the rest, namely the hide, the flesh, the head, the feet, the entrails, and the dung, are commanded to be burned outside the camp. In a similar way it is commanded there that the same be done for the sins of the whole congregation of Israel. Again, in Lev. 16, we read similarly about the bullock and the goat to be offered for sins. Finally, in Num. 19, the sons of Israel are commanded to bring a red cow, whole and without blemish, which has not borne a yoke; with its blood sprinkled seven times before the face of the tabernacle of testimony, the whole is burned outside the camp, and the ashes are kept so that they may be mixed with the waters of purification. Behold, then, concerning various animals, whose blood is indeed brought for sin into the holy place by the high priest, while their flesh is burned outside the camp, and which do not fall to the priests so that they might eat of them. Therefore this argument is evident, for proving that it is true that in the New Testament there is no longer a place for observances concerning foods, and that this was beautifully foreshadowed in those rites. How much weight such proofs drawn from types have, we have set out at length above, so there is no need to repeat it now.

units.la: Quapropter & Iesus ut sanctificaret per proprium sanguinem populum, extra portam passus est.
units.tr: Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.

units.la: Alia ratio idem confirmans, videlicet, non amplius in sacrificium offeredos esse cibos, ex quibus sacerdotes vescantur: sumpta à facto Christi in sui ipsius oblatione: quod quidem factum typo siue historiæ iam expositæ pulchrè respondet.
units.tr: Another argument confirming the same point is that foods of which the priests eat are no longer to be offered in sacrifice. It is drawn from Christ's own act in offering himself, and that deed corresponds well to the type and the history already set out.

units.la: Estque sententia: Adurebantur carnes illorum sacrificiorum extra castra, ad præfigurandum, quod oblatio eiusmodi ciborum, quibus sacerdotes soliciti erant vesci, cessare certo tempore deberet. Atqui nunc oblatus est Christus, vnica & cōsummata noui testamēnti hostia, & quidem extra portam siue extra castra, ut in illo & per illū impletum esse, quod ibi typicè adumbrabatur, cuiuis promptum sit intelligere. Igitur nūc tempus illud adest, quocessare debet omnis talis ciborum oblatio. Iam verò ex hoc iterum clare sequitur: per & propter vnicum sacrificium Christi, extra portam passi, abrogatus est delectus ciborum veteris testamenti, in ipsis quoque sacrificijs. Igitur abrogatus est pariter delectus ciborum in vsu quotidiano. Atque hac ratione simul caussam efficientem, siue propter quam, abrogationis ceremoniarum legalium recensetur, nempe vnicum sacrificium Christi. Alias quidem supra multis rationibus demonstratum est, sacrificia legalia, imò & sacerdotiū legale, per postremum sacrificium Christi summi & veri sacerdotis esse penitus abrogata. At vero quando hic memoratur Christus obtulisse suum sacrificium, palàm fit, adimpletum insuper esse, quòd olim per exustionem sacrificiorum extra castra adubrabatur, nimirum tempus adfuturum, quo carnium oblationes, quibus sacerdotes vesci possent, penitus de medio tolleretur. Hoc pacto arbitror clare sententiam apostoli à nobis expressam. Liberum sit interea omnibus, quomodocunque placebit explicare. Video enim alios aliò devolui, ac longum foret, eorundem interpretationes recitare, quarum pleraeq; prorsus sunt allegoricæ, pleréq; duriores, & longius petitæ. Sed hanc nostram existimo antecedentibus & sequentibus proximè congruere. Cæterum quòd adijcit, Vt sanctificaret per pro-prium sanguinem populum: id facit apostolus, tum vt ostédat veritatē in Christo manifestatū typo optimè respondere(nam & illa animalia, quorum carnes cōburebantur extra castra pro expiatione peccatorum tàm sacerdotum, quàm vniuersæ multitudinis offerebātur) tum ut effectum mortis Christi, de quo suprà frequenter actum est, considerandum ceu caussam principalem liberationis nostræ à iugo ceremoniarum, ob oculos poneret. Et quis non delectetur contemplari adeò exactè respondentem typis veritatem? Animalia oblata exurebantur extra castra. Christus verò & extra portam interfectus atque immolatus est. Item animalia illa offerebantur pro peccatis sacerdotum, atque vniuersæ multitudinis Israel, sicut liquet ex locis suprà citatis. Christus similiter oblatus pro peccatis omnium hominum, & ad sanctificandum per proprium sanguinem populum suum.
units.tr: The sense is this: the flesh of those sacrifices was burned outside the camp, to foreshadow that the offering of such foods, which the priests were bound to eat, must cease at a certain time. But now Christ has been offered, the one and perfect sacrifice of the New Testament, and indeed outside the gate or outside the camp, so that anyone can readily see that what was typically foreshadowed there has been fulfilled in him and through him. Therefore that time is now here, when every such offering of foods ought to cease. From this it again follows clearly that, through and on account of the one sacrifice of Christ, who suffered outside the gate, the distinction of foods under the Old Testament has been abrogated, even in the sacrifices themselves. Therefore the distinction of foods in daily use has likewise been abrogated. By this reasoning the apostle also names the efficient cause, or the reason, of the abrogation of the legal ceremonies, namely the one sacrifice of Christ. Elsewhere it has been shown by many arguments that the legal sacrifices, and indeed the legal priesthood too, have been wholly abrogated through the final sacrifice of Christ, the supreme and true priest. But when here it is recalled that Christ offered his sacrifice, it is plain that what was foreshadowed of old by the burning of sacrifices outside the camp is also fulfilled: the time would come when offerings of flesh on which priests might feed would be utterly removed. In this way I think the apostle's sense is clearly expressed by us. Let everyone be free to explain it in whatever way pleases them. For I see others wander off in different directions, and it would be tedious to recite their interpretations, most of which are wholly allegorical, most of them harsher and sought from far away. But I think our interpretation agrees most closely with what goes before and what follows. Moreover, when he adds, "that he might sanctify the people through his own blood," the apostle does this both to show that the truth manifested in Christ corresponds very well to the type (for those animals whose flesh was burned outside the camp were offered in expiation of sins, both of the priests and of the whole multitude), and to set before our eyes the effect of Christ's death, of which we have often spoken above, to be considered as the principal cause of our liberation from the yoke of ceremonies. And who would not delight to contemplate a truth answering so exactly to the types? The animals offered were burned outside the camp; Christ too was slain and sacrificed outside the gate. Likewise those animals were offered for the sins of the priests and of the whole multitude of Israel, as is clear from the passages cited above. Christ was similarly offered for the sins of all men, and to sanctify his people through his own blood.

units.la: Exeamus igitur ad eum extra castra) Conclusio seu illatio ex antecedentibus, quasi diceret: Sequamur igitur Christum, qui patiendo extra portam verè illud perfecit, quod antea in oblationibus, quæ extra castra exurebatur, per typum fuerat adumbratum. Adhæreamus potius veritati in Christo, quàm falsitati, quam obtrudunt pseudoapostoli, qui cum magna iniuria Christi extra portam pasi, adhuc de ciborum delectu otiosè disputant: quasi inanis esset eius mors, aut insufficiens ad liberandum nos à seruitute legis: Galat. liber-tate, qua Christus nos donauit, fruamur. Hac ratione interpretandi cohærent omnia ista cum antecedentibus. Fuerit autem magna ingratitudo, imò magnus contempus ipsius Dei respuere oblatum in Chtisto beneficium. Huc pertinent multa ad Galatas dicta: vt capite secūdo: Non aspernor gratiam Dei. Nam si per legem est iustitia, igitur Christus frustra mortuus est. Galat 5. In libertate, qua Christus nos liberauit, state, & ne rursus iugo seruitutis implicemini. Ecce ego Paulus dico vobis, quòd si circumcidamini, Christus nihil vobis proderit. Exire igitur ad Christum, est se adiungere Christo, sectarique veritatem, quam Christus moriendo extra castra impleuit.
units.tr: Let us go out therefore to him outside the camp: this is the conclusion or inference from what precedes, as if he said: Let us therefore follow Christ, who by suffering outside the gate truly accomplished what had been foreshadowed in type by those offerings burned outside the camp. Let us cleave rather to the truth in Christ than to the falsehood which the false apostles press upon us. To the great injury of Christ, who suffered outside the gate, they still idly dispute about the distinction of foods, as if his death were empty or insufficient to free us from bondage to the law. Let us enjoy the liberty with which Christ has endowed us (Gal. 5.). In this way of interpreting, all these things cohere with what precedes. Moreover, it would be great ingratitude, indeed great contempt of God himself, to reject the benefit offered in Christ. Much said to the Galatians pertains here, as in chapter 2: "I do not reject the grace of God; for if justification is through the law, then Christ died in vain" (Gal. 2.). And in chapter 5: "Stand fast in the liberty with which Christ has set us free, and do not be entangled again in the yoke of bondage. Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing" (Gal. 5.). To go out therefore to Christ is to join oneself to Christ and to follow the truth which Christ fulfilled by dying outside the camp.

units.la: Opprobrium eius portantes) Amplificatio. Oportet nos sequi Christum, etiàsi vnà cum illo nec non ad exemplum illius, & propter illum deberemus probris affici. Christus quidem magno cum opprobrio ac dedecore extra portam crucifixus est, ibique omnes ei sufpefo inter latrones iniuriosissimè insultabant: quemadmodum clarè docet passionis Christi historia: sed prætera quotquot apud Iudæos Christo adhæserūt, cōtumelias atq; iniurias omnis generis ab impijs Iudæis perferre debuerunt. Huc pertinent illa: Matthæi. 5. vbi Christus ita futu rū prædixerat: Beati estis, cùm probra iecerint in vos, & insectati fuerint & dixerint omne malum verbum aduersus vos mentientes, propter me. Actor. 5. Et illi quidē ibant gaudentes à conspectu concilij, quòd digni habiti essent, vt pro nomine eius cōtumelia afficerentur. 1. Thessalon. 2. Ipsi nostis fratres introitū nostrum ad vos, quòd non fuerit inanis, sed quòd antè malis afflicti & contumelijs affecti, quemadmodum scitis, Philippis audaciter egerimus in Domino nostro, ad loquendum apud vos euangelium Dei in multo certamine. Et quid opus est, multa eiusmodi testimonia congerere? Constat in genere omnes, quotquot adhærebant Christo, male apud omnes audiuisse, probra innumera debuisse perferre. Sed illi potissimum afficiebantur probris & contumelijs, qui ex Iudaismo conuersi ita adhærebant Christo, vt confiterentur, non amplius opus esse, obseruare legis ceremonias: abrogata esse sacrificia illa carnalia, non esse faciendum cì borum delectum, & huiusmodi. Hos illi ceu legis diuinæ contemptores & blasphemos capitalibus odijs insectabantur, etiam ad mortem pertrahebant, si ferret occasio. Testatur id historia sacra Actorum 18. vbi Iudei apud Corinthum coram Gallione proconsule Achaiæ, Paulo hoc pro grauissimo crimine impegerunt, quòd contra legem suaderet hominibus colere Deum. Rursus Actorum 21. Iacobus & presbyteri ad Paulum: vides fratres quot millia sunt Iudæorum, qui crediderunt, & omnes studiosi sectatores sunt legis: audierunt autem de te, quòd defectionem doceas à Mose, omnes qui inter gentes sunt, Iudæos, dicens non debere eos circumcidere filios neque secundum instituta viuere (ideo studiosè obseruabant legem, videlicet, quantum ad ea, quæ media erant: Nam sacrificia sine dubio non offerebant: non quòd iudicarent ceremonias esse ad salutem necessarias: sed tantum propter offendiculum in firmorum: qua de re Roman. 14. ne ij qui exilii marent, religionem Christianam esse tantum vitæ licentiam, & excusionem iugi legis)
units.tr: Bearing his reproach: this is an amplification. We ought to follow Christ even though we ought to be afflicted with reproach together with him, and for his sake, and after his example. Christ indeed was crucified outside the gate with great shame and dishonour, and there, as the history of his passion clearly teaches, all who hung with him among the thieves insulted him most abusively. But moreover, all who among the Jews adhered to Christ had to bear insults and injuries of every kind from the impious Jews. To this belong: Matt. 5: where Christ had foretold this: "Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake." Acts 5: "And they indeed departed from the presence of the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for his name." 1 Thess. 2: "You yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain; but though we had previously suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we were bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God in much conflict." Why should I heap up many such testimonies? It is generally agreed that all who adhered to Christ were ill spoken of by everyone and had to bear countless reproaches. But those were especially afflicted with reproaches and insults who, converted from Judaism, so adhered to Christ as to profess that there was no longer any need to observe the ceremonies of the law: that those carnal sacrifices were abrogated, that no distinction of foods was to be made, and suchlike. These the Jews pursued with deadly hatred as despisers and blasphemers of the divine law, even dragging them to death when occasion offered. The sacred history of Acts 18 attests this, where the Jews at Corinth, before Gallio the proconsul of Achaia, charged Paul with the gravest crime, that he persuaded men to worship God contrary to the law. Again, Acts 21: James and the elders said to Paul: "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are who have believed, and all are zealous for the law. But they have heard of you that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to fall away from Moses, saying that they ought not circumcise their children nor live according to the customs." (They therefore diligently observed the law, namely in those matters which were indifferent; for undoubtedly they did not offer sacrifices. This was not because they judged the ceremonies necessary to salvation, but only on account of offence to the weak. On this matter see Rom. 14.) Those who suspected that the Christian religion was merely a licence for living and an excuse for throwing off the law were a danger to them.

units.la: Et paulo post ibidem, Iudæi Asiani contra eum inclamant in templo. Viri Israelitæ succurrite: currite: Hic est ille homo, qui aduersus populum, & legem, & locum hunc omnes ubique docet: insuper & graecos induxit in templum, & profanauit sanctum locum hunc. Sed ipse Apostolus de se Galat. 5. Ego fratres si circumcisionem adhuc praedico, quid adhuc persecutionem patior? Abolitum est igitur offendiculum crucis. Itaque illis inprimis afficiebantur contumelijs & iniurijs, qui videbantur contra legem aliquid sentire, qui iudicabantur ceremonias contemnere, ceu ad salutem nequaquam necessarias. Hac igitur ratione hic dicit: Exeamus ad eum extra castra, opprobrium eius portantes.
units.tr: And a little later in the same chapter: "The Jews of Asia shouted against him in the temple: Men of Israel, help! Hurry! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law, and this place; moreover he has brought Greeks into the temple and profaned this holy place." But the apostle himself says of himself, Gal. 5.: "If I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Then the offence of the cross has been removed." Thus especially those were afflicted with insults and injuries who seemed to think something contrary to the law, who were judged to despise the ceremonies as in no way necessary to salvation. By this reasoning he says here: Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.

units.la: Non enim hic habemus manentem ciuitatem, sed futuram inquirimus.
units.tr: For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one to come.

units.la: Ratio, quare debeamus etiam cum probris Christum sectari, a fine, qui nobis semper debet esse propositus, nempe vt per omne vitā magis intenti simus ad spiritualia, coelestia & aeterna, quam ad corporalia, terrena & momentanea. In quam sententiam multa passim sunt in Scripturis praeclare dicta. Illud in primis occurrit Col. 3. Si resurrexistis vna cum Christo, superna quaerite, vbi Christus est ad dextram Dei sedens: superna curate, non terrestria. Et Christus Matth. 16. Quid prodest homini si vniuersum mundum lucretur, animęque vero suae detrimentum patiatur? Supra capite vndecimo de Abraham: Per fidem commigrauit in terram promissionis, veluti peregrinam, cum in tabernaculis habitasset cum Isaac & Iacob coaeredibus eiusdem promissionis. Expectauerat enim fundamenta habentem ciuitatem, cuius opifex & conditor est Deus. Eodem capite: Hęc qui dicunt, declarant, se patriam inquirere, & quidā meliorē, id est, coelestem. Quapropter nō erubescit ipse Deus uocari Deus illorum: parauerat enim illis ciuitatem. Caeterum est hoc loco obseruandum, valde argute loqui Apostolum, quando ait, non habere nos hic ciuitate manentem. Respicit n. ad id, quod dixerat, nos exire debere ad Christum extra portam. Qui vero egreditur extra portam, praesertim ad locum probrosum & suspectum, statim tenetur iterum desiderio repetendae ciuitatis: ac difficile admodum est vrbanis hominibus seu delicatis, ciuitatem relinquere, & in rus, vbi miserias multas pati debeat, se transferre.
units.tr: The reason why we ought to follow Christ even with reproach is taken from the end that should always be set before us: that throughout our whole life we should be more intent on spiritual, heavenly and eternal things than on bodily, earthly and momentary ones. Scripture says much to this effect in many places. Chiefly this comes to mind from Col. 3: "If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth." And Christ says in Matt. 16: "What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul?" Above, in chapter eleven, concerning Abraham: "By faith he went to live in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God." In the same chapter: "Those who say such things declare that they are seeking a homeland, and a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them." But it must be noted here that the Apostle speaks very cleverly when he says that we do not have here a lasting city. He is looking back to what he had said, that we must go out to Christ outside the gate. Now whoever goes outside the gate, especially to a place of disgrace and suspicion, is at once drawn back by longing for the city he has left; and it is very hard for city people, or for those who are soft and delicate, to leave the city and move to the countryside, where they must suffer many hardships.

units.la: Huc ergo alludens Apostolus ait, non debere nos grauari sequi Christum extra castra. Nam in hoc mundo nulla tam praeclara tamque excellens est ciuitas, quae à Christo nos debeat auocare. Respicere magis decet ad ciuitatem coelestem, quam ad aliquam terrenam. Terrena omnia debent nobis sordere prae spiritualibus bonis & coelestibus. Huc referri aliquo modo potest, quod Apostolus Galat. 4. distinguit inter Hierusalem terrenam & seruientem cum filijs suis, ac Hierusalem supernam, quę libera est cum filijs suis. Significantur praeterea ait Apostolus, non habere nos ciuitatem. Respicit namq; praecipue ad pios, qui propter confessionem veritatis vndiq; e ciuitatibus eiiciuntur & exclu duntur. Tales profecto dicere possunt, se non habere hic ciuitatem: sed quomodocunq; cedat, etiamsi non deturbemur hostium crudelitate: tamen & hoc cogitandum est, nos non habere hic ciuitatem permanentem. Nihil enim sub coelo stabile est. Et nos, & ciuitates cum tempore definimus. Sed ad futuram oportet nos respicere, in qua sola datur beatè viuere. Quod cū ita se habeat, nihil profecto nos debet remorari, quo minus Christum extra castra etiam cum probris sequamur. Estq; haec quasi sententia quaedam perpetuò circumferenda, qua ad contemptum rerum terrenarum inducamur.
units.tr: Alluding to this, therefore, the Apostle says that we ought not to hesitate to follow Christ outside the camp. For in this world there is no city so splendid and so excellent that it should call us away from Christ. We ought rather to look to the heavenly city than to any earthly one. All earthly things should seem worthless to us in comparison with spiritual and heavenly goods. To this one may refer in some way what the Apostle distinguishes in Gal. 4, between the earthly Jerusalem, which is in slavery with her children, and the Jerusalem above, which is free with her children. The Apostle also signifies, besides, that we do not have a city here. For he is looking chiefly at the godly, who on account of confessing the truth are everywhere cast out and shut out of cities. Such people can truly say that they have no city here. But however things turn out, even if we are not driven out by the cruelty of enemies, we must still think on this: we do not have a lasting city here. For nothing under heaven is stable. Both we and cities come to an end with time. We must look rather to the city to come, in which alone it is possible to live blessedly. Since this is so, nothing should keep us back from following Christ outside the camp, even with reproach. This is, as it were, a saying that should be carried about constantly, to lead us to despise earthly things.

units.la: Per ipsum igitur offerimus hostiam laudis semper Deo, hoc est, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius.
units.tr: Through him, then, let us always offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.

units.la: Occupatio obiter adiecta. Quia enim supra dictum est, nos quidem habere altare: sed non amplius in eo offerri sacrificia, quem admodum sub lege fieri solitum est: hinc moueri quispiam poterat ad rogandum: quid ergo? Non amplius offertis hostias? Nulla prorsus sunt apud vos sacrificia? Respondet apostolus: imò, offerimus adhuc hostias, non tamen carnales, mactado videlicet oues aut boues: sed spirituales, ac proinde multo, quàm ueteres fuerunt, praestantiores: nempe, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius, id est, laudes nominis diuini, & gratiarum actiones. Haec sunt nostra & praestantissima sacrificia. Vide prudentiam Apostoli, nihil vult relinquere indissolutum, omnibus, quantū fieri poterit, satisfacit, nec patitur quenquam cum scrupulo aut offendiculo discedere. Supra quidem de sacrificio vnico & aeterno Christi valde copiose egit: hic vero etiā de nostris sacrificijs paucula tribus verbis annotat. Nullas verò addit probationes, tum quia praesens locus non fert: tum quia aliunde loci plures confirmantes hoc genus spiritualium sacrificiorum, quae habitura locum erant post reuelatum euangelium, facile peti possunt. Osee 14. Esa. 57. Psal. 28. 49. 50. & 115. Interea Apostolus valde significanter omnia, quae in sacrificijs nostris spectari debet, expressit. Nos offerimus, inquit, per ipsum: Christus enim solus, per & propter quem orationes nostrae, laudes, gratiarum actiones, & quaecunq; sacrificia θυσίας, Deo patri sunt accepta. Vnde in nomine suo
units.tr: An incidental objection is added. For since it was said above that we indeed have an altar, but that sacrifices are no longer offered on it as was customary under the law, someone might be moved to ask: "What then? Do you no longer offer victims? Do you have no sacrifices at all?" The Apostle answers: On the contrary, we still offer victims, yet not fleshly ones, that is, by slaughtering sheep or oxen, but spiritual ones, and therefore far more excellent than the old ones were: namely, "the fruit of lips that confess his name," that is, praises of the divine name and acts of thanksgiving. These are our sacrifices, and the most excellent ones. Notice the Apostle's prudence: he wishes to leave nothing unresolved; he satisfies everyone as far as possible, and he allows no one to depart with a scruple or a stumbling block. Above, he dealt very fully with the one and eternal sacrifice of Christ; here he touches only briefly, in a few words, on our sacrifices. He adds no proofs, partly because the present place does not allow it, and partly because many passages confirming this kind of spiritual sacrifice, which were to have their place after the gospel was revealed, can easily be sought elsewhere: Hos. 14; Isa. 57; Ps. 28, 49, 50 and 115. Meanwhile the Apostle has expressed very significantly everything that ought to be considered in our sacrifices. "We offer," he says, "through him": for Christ alone is the one through and because of whom our prayers, praises, thanksgivings and all sacrifices [θυσίαι] are acceptable to God the Father. Hence, in his name...

units.la: Ec docuit nos Christus precari, & ecclesia semper illud obseruat. Nam Christus vnicum samel obtulit sacrificium, propter quod Deus pater propitius esse vult, ideoq; ad illud vnum sacrificium oportet nos in omnibus nostris spiritualibus sacrificijs respicere. Offerimus autem hostiam laudis. Nō dixit simpliciter, laudem, sed hostiam laudis, vt omnes intelligant, laudes & gratiarum actiones gratas & esse, & dici hostias posse, nec minus habendas pro sacrificijs, quàm quæcunq; alia sacrificiorum genera, quæ in veteri lege erat celebrata. Cæterū hostia seu sacrificiū laudis legitur psal. 49. 14. Amos 4. &c. Vt palàm fit, Apostolum nihil dicere, nisi quod etiam in Scripturis solidum fundamentum habeat.
units.tr: Christ taught us to pray in this way, and the Church always observes it. For Christ offered one sacrifice once for all, on account of which God the Father wishes to be merciful, and therefore we must look to that one sacrifice in all our spiritual sacrifices. We offer, however, a sacrifice of praise. He did not say simply "praise," but "a sacrifice of praise," so that everyone may understand that praises and thanksgivings are pleasing, and can be called sacrifices, and are to be held as sacrifices no less than any other kind of sacrifice that was performed in the old law. Moreover, a sacrifice or offering of praise is read in Ps. 49:14 and Amos 4, etc., so that it is plain that the Apostle says nothing that does not have a solid foundation in Scripture as well.

units.la: Addidit deinde semper, insinuans, & apud nos esse iuge sacrificium, non minus, quàm olim erat sub lege. Et certè nullum tempus est, quo non deberemus Deo sacrificium laudis offerre, nullum est tempus, quo non aliqui saltem id faciant: sine intermisione dum, & omnes creaturæ sine intermissione Deum laudant, agunt gratias. psal. 33. Benedicam Dominũ omni tempore. Itē, Septies in die laudem dixi tibi, id est, omni tempore.
units.tr: He then added always, hinting that among us too there is a continual sacrifice, no less than there was under the law. And certainly there is no time when we ought not to offer God the sacrifice of praise, and no time when at least some do not do so; and all creatures without interruption praise God and give thanks: Ps. 33, "I will bless the Lord at all times." Likewise, "Seven times a day I have praised you," that is, at all times.

units.la: Nec caret emphasi, quod dicit, Deo: Testatur huiusmodi hostias proprie competere Deo, nec non Deo præ quibuscunq; alijs esse acceptas. Nam hostias cibarias etiam idololatræ offerebant idolis suis, & alicubi dæmones superstitionibus gentilium mire abusi sunt, vt videlicet oblatos cibos crederentur noctu absumere. Sed apud Deum nihil tale potest habere locum, vtpote qui bonorum nostrorum non egeat, & cuius sunt omnes ferae syluarum, iumenta, boues. Esaiae 1. psal. 8. 51. 40. Quanquam videtur Apostolus respexisse ad id, quòd sacrificia veteris testamenti eiusmodi essent, vt pars ex eis cederet sacerdotibus ad esum: verum in novo omnia cedunt soli Deo. Porrò cùm addidit interpretationis causa, Fructus labiorum confitentium nomini eius: multa quidem selectis hisce verbis animaduertenda tacitè suggerit. Vocabulo fructus alludere videtur ad oblationes, quæ fiebant olim ex diuersis fructibus: cuiusmodi erant oblationes primitiarum, decimarum, &c. Quicquid aut ibi tum fiebat, idem notat & in novo testamento verè, imò longè excellentius adimpleri. Labiorum vocabulo suggerit occultè, non tantum labia, verumetiam cor requiri: sed præterea opus esse externa testificatione honoris & cultus erga Deum. Neque enim sola simulatione ea, quæ religionis sunt, præstantur: neq; satis est, solummodo animo religionem circumferre.
units.tr: The phrase "to God" is not without emphasis. It testifies that sacrifices of this kind properly belong to God, and are acceptable to God above all others. For even idolaters offered food sacrifices to their idols, and in some places demons, through the superstitions of the Gentiles, wonderfully deceived people into believing that they consumed the food offered to them at night. But nothing of the sort can have a place with God, who has no need of our goods, and to whom all the beasts of the forest, the cattle and the oxen belong: Isa. 1; Ps. 8, 51, 40. Although the Apostle seems to have looked to the fact that the sacrifices of the Old Testament were of such a kind that part of them went to the priests for food, in the New Testament everything goes to God alone. Furthermore, when he added, for the sake of explanation, the fruit of lips that confess his name, he tacitly suggests many things that ought to be considered in these chosen words. By the word fruit he seems to allude to the offerings that were formerly made from various fruits, such as the offerings of first fruits, tithes, and so on. Whatever was done there at that time is truly fulfilled, indeed far more excellently, in the New Testament. By the word lips he suggests covertly that not only the lips but also the heart is required, and besides, that an outward witness of honour and worship toward God is necessary. For the things that belong to religion are not performed by mere pretence, nor is it enough merely to carry religion in the mind.

units.la: Huc pertinet illud Roman. 10. Corde quidem creditur ad iustitiam: ore autem fit confessio ad salutē. Et Esaiæ 29. Populus hic labijs me honorat, cor autem eorum longè es à me. Ergo & cor, & labia debent in cultu diuino cooperari. Quod contra quosdam est noftrę tempestatis sapientes, qui putant satis esse, si in animo bene sentiant de religione exterius autem liberè posse quæcunq; pro regionum diuersarum consuetudine agere. Qua de re nos nunc non disputamus.
units.tr: To this belongs what is said in Rom. 10: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." And in Isa. 29: "This people honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me." Therefore both heart and lips ought to work together in divine worship. This is against certain wise men of our own time, who think it is enough if they think rightly about religion in their minds, and who believe they may freely do outwardly whatever the customs of different regions prescribe. We do not dispute about this matter now.

units.la: Cùm postremò addit, confitentium nomini eius: latius extendit sacrificiorum nostrorum dignitatem, quàm ante vocabulo laudis expresserat. Neque enim tantùm sacrificamus Deo, vbi illum laudamus: uerùmetiam cùm agimus illi gratias pro beneficijs in nos collatis: aut quacunque ratione confessionem edimus, & contestamur, quòd illum Deum nostrum, seruatorem nostrum agnoscamus. Confiteri enim latè patet, atq;, vbicunque Dei dignitatem, bonitatē, misericordiam, potentiam, iustitiam confitemur, ibi quodammodo nouū sacrificiū spirituale offerimus. Sed hæc satis sint. Nūc paucula & breuiter de multiplici doctrina, quæ ex hisce omnib. toto hoc loco expositis decet elicere, adijciamus.
units.tr: When at last he adds "to those who confess his name," he extends the dignity of our sacrifices more widely than he had expressed with the word "praise." For we do not sacrifice to God only when we praise him, but also when we give him thanks for the benefits bestowed on us, or in any way make confession and bear witness that we acknowledge him as our God and Saviour. For confessing has a wide range, and wherever we confess God's dignity, goodness, mercy, power and justice, there in a certain way we offer a new spiritual sacrifice. But let these things suffice. Now let us add, briefly and in a few words, the manifold teaching that ought to be drawn from all these things expounded in this whole passage.

units.la: Primò quidem & principaliter discimus, atq; admonemur, quotiescunq; variæ & peregrinæ doctrinæ per ecclesias circumferuntur, non temerè eas recipere, sed prudêter prius examinare. Hæc est præcipua doctrina, & summa totius huius loci. Qua de re non abs re hoc tempore plura per nos adferri possent: sed quia iustum libellum de hoc argumento scripsimus, ideò supersedemus. Vide in alio opere.
units.tr: First and chiefly we learn and are admonished that whenever various and foreign doctrines are carried about among the churches, we should not receive them rashly but examine them carefully beforehand. This is the principal teaching and the sum of this whole passage. Much more could be brought forward by us on this matter at this time, but because we have written a full little book on this subject, we shall forbear. See our other work.

units.la: Secundò, discimus hic, quanti sit facienda doctrina ab Apostolis ipsis tradita, ut non temerè recipiamus eam, quæ postea ab hominibus nulla ex parte cum Apostolis conferendis, quamlibet etiam iactarint, se non tantum Apostolorum successores, verumetiam ipsius Christi vicarios, adfertur, & interea dum examinatur ad normam verbi Dei, inuenitur nequaquam conuenire.
units.tr: Second, we learn here how much weight is to be given to the doctrine handed down by the Apostles themselves, so that we do not rashly receive that which is later brought forward by men who, however much they boast that they are not merely successors of the Apostles but the very vicars of Christ himself, cannot in any way be compared with the Apostles; and which, while it is examined by the rule of God's Word, is found not to agree at all.

units.la: Tertiò, discimus etiam respiciendum esse ad constantiam sanctorum, qui non dubitaruntad mortem vsq; pro veritate decertare, suoq; sanguine doctrinam sanā approbare. Quod quidē facit, vt & certissimus de doctrinę veritate, & vbi res poscit, cogitemus, nobis eorundem exemplum imitandum, adeoq; sanguinem pro confessione veritatis fundere simus parati.
units.tr: Third, we learn also that we must look to the constancy of the saints, who did not hesitate to contend for the truth even unto death, and to approve sound doctrine with their own blood. This indeed is done so that, being most certain of the truth of doctrine, we may think, when the matter demands it, that we must imitate their example, and be ready to shed our blood for the confession of the truth.

units.la: Quartò, discimus maximā esse hanc dignitatem euangelij, quòd nunquam mutatur, non magis, quàm ipse Christus. Qua ex re confirmari debemus, ut veritati semel traditæ constanter adhæreamus.
units.tr: Fourth, we learn that this dignity of the gospel is very great: it never changes, no more than Christ himself. From this we ought to be confirmed, so that we constantly cling to the truth once delivered.

units.la: 1. Examen novae doctrinae.
units.tr: 1. The examination of new doctrine.

units.la: Quintò, discimus, quid sentiendū sit de rebus adiaphoris, quodq; de illis non sit scrupulosè & rixosè disputandum. Quia non prosunt res illæ ijs, qui in ipsis versari volunt. Verùm doctrina de gratia & de salute si proponatur, hac audiri & suscipi & retineri à no bis oportet.
units.tr: Fifth, we learn what is to be thought about indifferent matters, and that they should not be disputed over scrupulously and contentiously, since those things do not profit those who wish to be occupied with them. But if the doctrine of grace and of salvation is set before us, we ought to hear it, receive it and hold fast to it.

units.la: Sextò, admonemur in lectione sacrarum historiarum, inprimis ceremoniarū & similium, diligentem habere rationē typorum, vt obseruemus vbiq;, quidnā de Christo vel de euangelio sit adumbratū: sicut videmus hic Apostolū pulcherrimè aduertisse & exposuisse typū de abrogatione obseruationū circa cibos & eiusmodi. Quis nostrū cogitaret, talia argumenta potuisse colligi ex eo, quòd sacerdotes de quibusdam sacrificijs non ederent?
units.tr: Sixth, in reading the sacred histories, and especially the ceremonies and such like, we are admonished to have a diligent regard for types, so that we observe everywhere what has been foreshadowed about Christ or the gospel: just as we see here that the Apostle has most beautifully noticed and expounded the type concerning the abrogation of observances regarding foods and the like. Which of us would have thought that such arguments could be gathered from the fact that the priests did not eat of certain sacrifices?

units.la: Septimò, admonemur, vt, quandoquidē sub præstantiori agimus testamento, quàm patres illi, neq; amplius offerimus carnales hostias: tātò diligētius exerceamus nos in osse rendis hostijs spiritualibus, noui testamēti, atq; euangelij pprijs: quales in primis sunt laus, & gratiarū actio. Libertas nobis parta est ab onere legis, qd patres portare nō potuerūt: eam ob caussā decet nos esse gratos, & in spiritualibus sacrificijs offerendis esse diligētes.
units.tr: Seventh, we are admonished that, since we live under a more excellent covenant than those fathers, and no longer offer carnal victims, we should exercise ourselves all the more diligently in offering the spiritual victims proper to the new covenant and the gospel, of which the chief are praise and thanksgiving. Liberty has been won for us from the burden of the law, which the fathers could not bear; for that reason it becomes us to be grateful and diligent in offering spiritual sacrifices.

units.la: Cæterum beneficentia & communicationis ne obliuiscamini. Talibus enim victimis placetur Deo.
units.tr: But do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.

units.la: Sextus locus, in quo breuiter de beneficentia erga pauperes quoscunq;, & communicatione bonorum, qua decet credentes inter se. Supra quidē semel horratus est ad beneficentiam erga eos, qui propter confessionem euangelij affligebantur, & vel pulsi sedibus oberrabat, vel detinebātur in carceribus, quales certē est multos tunc fuisse. Nunc autē instituit nouū locum, in quo generaliter hortatur ad benefaciedum omnibus operaliena indigētibus, etiam non afflictis propter euangeliū. Sed neq; adiungēda sunt hæc antecedetibus, cùm plane noua exhortatio instituatur, qualis aliàs solet in omnibus epistolis: licet hæc breuis vt sit, ad doctos de hisce rebus.
units.tr: This is the sixth point, in which he briefly speaks of beneficence towards the poor, of whatever kind, and of the sharing of goods, which befits believers among themselves. Above, indeed, he once exhorted them to beneficence towards those who were suffering for the confession of the gospel, and who were either driven from their homes and wandered about or were held in prisons, as there certainly were many at that time. But now he institutes a new section, in which he exhorts in general to doing good to all who need help from others, even those who are not afflicted for the gospel. Nor should these things be joined to what precedes, since a plainly new exhortation is begun, such as is usual in all the epistles; although this one, however brief it may be, is sufficient for the learned in these matters.

units.la: Beneficentia, εὐποιΐα vocabulum latè patet, ac multa in se complectitur. Benefacis fratri, impartiendo de tua substantia, rectum dando consilium, consolando afflictū, præmonendo vt caueat à malis, prohibendo, siue quācūq; ratione impediendo, ne alius ei noceat, remittredo offensam: deniq; innumeris eiusmodi rationibus: vt profectò nullus omninò sit, quem non possis aliqua re iuuare, nullus præterea sis, qui non possis aliquam opem ferre. Qui non eget tua substantia, at eget forte consilio, institutione, consolatione, admonitione. Et si non potes auxiliari suppeditādo pecunias, cibum, potum: at potes iuuare cōsilio, doctrina, consolationibus, & id genus officijs. Itaq; valde accōmodum est instituto istud vocabulum. Sed & multò aptisimū est Christianis vocabulū τὴ κοινωνίας, quod non tantum beneficentiam, sed omnium quodāmodo bonorū communicatione signi ficat: ita vt secundùm hanc vocem cōmunia inter pios esse debeant omnia, siue lœta siue aduersa. Quò pertinet, quòd initio prædicati euangelij apud Hierosolymam, credentes omnia inter se communiter diuidebant, Actor. 4. Et certè si animaduertimus omnes nos esse vnius corporis membra, quotquot in Christum credimus: quæcunque vni ex fratribus accidunt siue bona, siue mala, ita debemus accipere, tanquam si nobis quoque acciderent. Debemus gaudere cum gaudentibus, flere cum flentibus; omnia omnibus fieri. Si etiam mali inter se quandā communionē societatemq; bonorum inter se faciūt, quid nō decet nos facere Christianos? Sed nostra cōmunio debet præstantior esse, quià propter Christū institutitur, quia nititur illo, qui potest omnibus largiter prospicere, nec finit, vt iustus consipiciatur derelictus, aut semen eius quærat panem.
units.tr: The word beneficence [εὐποιΐα] has a wide range and embraces many things. You do good to a brother by sharing of your substance, by giving right counsel, by consoling the afflicted, by warning him beforehand to beware of evils, by forbidding or in any way hindering another from harming him, by forgiving an offence; and finally by countless such means, so that there is certainly no one whom you cannot help in some way, and no one whom you cannot in some way assist. He who does not need your substance perhaps needs counsel, instruction, consolation, admonition. And if you cannot help by supplying money, food and drink, yet you can help by counsel, teaching, consolations and offices of that kind. Therefore this word is very well suited to the present purpose. But the word sharing [τῆς κοινωνίας] is also far more fitting for Christians, since it signifies not only beneficence but a certain sharing of all goods, so that according to this word all things ought to be common among the godly, whether joyful or adverse. To this belongs the fact that at the beginning of the preaching of the gospel at Jerusalem, believers held all things in common and divided them among themselves (Acts 4). And certainly, if we consider that all of us who believe in Christ are members of one body, then whatever befalls one of the brothers, whether good or evil, we ought to take as if it had happened to us too. We ought to rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep; to become all things to all. If even wicked men make among themselves a certain communion and partnership of goods, why should we Christians not do so? But our communion ought to be more excellent, because it is instituted on account of Christ, because it rests on him who can provide abundantly for all, and does not allow the righteous man to be seen forsaken, or his seed to seek bread.

units.la: Ne obliuiscamini) Igitur & ante didicerat, obseruauerātq;. Et certè Hebræi iam adhuc in Iudaismo versantes & sub lege agentes, didicerant ex lege Deuteron. cap. 15. quòd fratrum suorum deberent subleuare inopiā, & si forte mutuò dedissent egeti, ad annum remissionis, gratis debitum remittere: atq; ita benedictione Domini largiter in omnibus bonis prouenturā. Quod ergo probè edocti erat facere antea; nō obliuisci non debebāt in Christianismo, per quem proficere, & gradum ad pietatem facere debebant.
units.tr: "Do not forget." Therefore he had also taught this before and had observed it. And certainly the Hebrews, while still abiding in Judaism and living under the law, had learned from the law (Deut. 15) that they ought to relieve the poverty of their brothers, and if perhaps they had lent to a needy man, to remit the debt gratis in the year of release; and thus they would abound in all good things by the blessing of the Lord. What they had been thoroughly taught to do before, they ought not to forget in Christianity, through which they ought to make progress and advance a step towards godliness.

units.la: Talibus enim uictimis placetur Deo) Ratio suasoria ab vtili. Respicieňs autē Apostolus ad id, quod paulò antè dixerat de sacrificijs spiritualibus noui testamenti, voluit in hac ratione ab vtili declarare, etiam beneficentiam erga fratres suauissimarū victimarum instar apud Deum esse. Atq; ita declarat, nos varia quoq; habere sacrificia, non minus, quàm olim varia erant sub lege. Atque hæc ipsa sacrificia euangelica fuerunt etiam à prophetis prænunciata. Vt Oseæ capite sexto, Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium. Item Micheæ 6. Et Christus repetiuit Matth. 9.
units.tr: "For with such victims God is well pleased." This is an argument of persuasion from usefulness. Looking back at what he had said a little before about the spiritual sacrifices of the new covenant, the Apostle wished in this argument from usefulness to declare that beneficence towards the brothers, too, is before God like the most fragrant victims. And so he shows that we also have various sacrifices, no less than there were various ones under the law. And these very evangelical sacrifices were also foretold by the prophets: as in Hos. 6, "I desire mercy and not sacrifice"; likewise Mic. 6; and Christ repeated it in Matth. 9.

units.la: Præclarum autem est, quodq; omnes mirabiliter excitet ad huiusmodi sacrificia osse-rēda, quòd ait, talibus victimis placere nos Deo. Ita enim Deus acceptat, & gratū habet, tanquam sibi collatum, quicquid in vnum ex pauperibus cōfertur: Matth. 25. Per se qui-dem res, quas damus, non sunt magni momenti: neq; is, cui damus, potest referre: sal-tem ab eo non est expectanda compensatio: sed id præcipuum est, quòd propter Deum alijs benefacimus. Quod igitur propter Deum facimus, id non frustra: quia diues Deus est in omnes, & largiter compensat omnibus. Hinc illa insignis promissio, Date, & dabi-tur vobis: Certumque est, nunquam manet irremuneratum, quicquid in gratiam Dei vn-quam impenditur. Sed, in summa: hæc est amplissima fœlicitas, placere Deo: quod quo-modo fieri queat, hic clarè ostenditur. Græcè est ἀναφιρὰ̇ς θεῷ, quasi diceret conciliatur, placatur, aut delectatur Deus. Sententia satis est perspicua.
units.tr: Moreover it is excellent, and it wonderfully stirs everyone to offer such sacrifices, that he says we are pleasing to God with such victims. For God accepts and regards as done to himself whatever is conferred upon one of the poor (Matth. 25). In themselves the things we give are of no great moment, nor can he to whom we give repay anything; at least no compensation is to be expected from him. But this is the principal thing, that we do good to others on account of God. What we do on account of God is therefore not in vain, because God is rich towards all and abundantly repays all. Hence that famous promise: "Give, and it shall be given to you." And it is certain that whatever is ever spent for the sake of God never remains unrewarded. But in sum: this is the greatest happiness, to please God; how this can be done is clearly shown here. In Greek it is [εὐαρεστεῖται θεῷ], as if he said that God is appeased, pleased or delighted. The meaning is clear enough.

units.la: Cæterum duplicem habemus hic doctrinam. Alteram, qua nobis commendatur benefi-centia in pauperes: quæ non caret magnis præmijs, indubitatasq; secum habet promissiones. Alteram de spiritualibus sacrificijs, quæ nos decent agentes sub gratia, siue sub euangelio.
units.tr: Moreover, we have here a twofold teaching. The first commends to us beneficence towards the poor, which does not lack great rewards and carries with it unquestionable promises. The second concerns the spiritual sacrifices that befit us as those who live under grace, that is, under the gospel.

units.la: Parete ijs, qui præsunt vobis, & concedite: siquidem illi vigilant pro animabus vestris, tanquam ratione reddituri, vt cum gaudio hoc faciant, & non gementes. Nam id est inutile vobis.
units.tr: "Obey those who rule over you, and submit to them, since they keep watch over your souls, as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that is unprofitable for you."

units.la: Septimus locus, de obedientia atq; honore ijs debito, qui præsunt ecclesijs, inuigi-lantq; saluti animarum. Sunt, qui de magistratibus ciuilibus debita obedientia locum accipiat Chrysostomus videtur initio istud facere: sed parum commodè. Primò, quia ad id tempus paucos, vel nullos habuerunt præfectos, qui fidei sese adiunxerant, aut qui aperte euangelium profitentibus fauerent: sed omnes potius tyrannidem exercebant, atq; impia præcipiebant: id quod liquet ex ijs, quæ præcesserunt de pijs propter confes-sionem euangelij afflictis, ita vt alij spoliaretur suis facultatibus: alij pelleretur sedibus, alij in carceribus detinerentur. Aperte cogebant ad negandum Christum eiusq; Euan-gelium: præcipiebant sanCti, ne amplius loquerentur de nomine Iesu: quomodo igitur Apostolus præciperet hic, talibus esse parendum?
units.tr: This is the seventh passage, concerning the obedience and honour owed to those who preside over the churches and watch over the salvation of souls. Chrysostom seems at the start to take this passage as referring to the obedience owed to civil magistrates, but not very aptly. First, because up to that time there were few or no rulers who had joined the faith or who openly favoured those professing the gospel. Rather, they all exercised tyranny and commanded impious things. This is clear from what came before about the godly who were afflicted for confessing the gospel, some being stripped of their possessions, others driven from their homes, others kept in prisons. They openly compelled people to deny Christ and his gospel, and they forbade the saints to speak any more in the name of Jesus. How, then, would the Apostle here command that such men be obeyed?

units.la: Secundò, hic aperte ait, se de illis loqui, qui vigilat pro animabus. Atqui magistratus ciuiles non incumbūt propriè saluti animarū: sed tuētur ea, quæ sunt salutis externæ & corporalis: cauet, ne quis iniuriā patiatur ab altero in corpore vel substantia: curam ani-marum alijs relinquūt, nempe, ijs, qui tractant, quæ ad religionem pertinent, ecclesia-rum videlicet pastoribus.
units.tr: Second, here he plainly says that he is speaking of those who keep watch over souls. But civil magistrates do not properly attend to the salvation of souls. They look after what concerns external and bodily welfare: they take care that no one suffers wrong from another in body or property. They leave the care of souls to others, namely to those who deal with matters pertaining to religion, that is, to the pastors of the churches.

units.la: Proinde huius loci de obedientia erga ecclesiarum pastores, hæc est propositio: Parete ijs, qui præsunt vobis: valde necessarium erat, hunc locū adijcere. Cùm enim inter Hebræos va-riæ subinde sererētur opiniones, quemadmodū ex hac ipsa licet colligere, alijs nimirū negantibus, Christū esse Deū: alijs illum æquatibus tantum Mosi, vel vix etiā æquatibus: alijs ité depugnantibus pro conseruatione ceremoniarū legalium: alijs deniq; peregrinas doctrinas & varias inuehētibus: atq; omnes interea volebant videri rerum sacrarū periti: omnes interpretādi Scripturas facultate sibi arrogabāt: necessarium erat, Hebræos, si quādo, vt solet fieri, dubitaret alicubi vel à vero deflecteret, admonere, vt hic suos adiret atq; audirent doctores legitimè constitutos. Quibus si obedirent, poterant certò scire, quam viam rectè ingrederentur, quomodo viuere & sentire eos oporteret.
units.tr: Therefore, in this passage on obedience towards the pastors of the churches, the proposition is this: "Obey those who rule over you." It was very necessary to add this passage. For among the Hebrews various opinions were sown from time to time, as may be gathered from this very passage: some denied that Christ was God, others made him only equal to Moses, or scarcely even equal; others again fought for the preservation of the legal ceremonies; others finally introduced strange and varied doctrines. And all the while they wished to appear skilled in holy things, and each claimed for himself the ability to interpret the Scriptures. It was necessary to admonish the Hebrews, should they at any time, as usually happens, waver or turn aside from the truth, to go to their own teachers, lawfully appointed, and to hear them. If they obeyed these, they could know for certain which path they were treading aright, and how they ought to live and think.

units.la: Qui nolunt sequi, nisi sua phantasmata, & cerebri sui propè phrenetici sultas imagi-nationes, omnesq; etiam legitimos ecclesiarū ministros, & verbi doctores præ se con-temnūt, non potest fieri, quin ij in absurdos errores labātur. Valde igitur salutariter hæc doctrina, de audiendis ecclesiarū præpositis, ijs, quæ hactenus tradita sunt, attexitur: & multò commodissimè postremo loco, & post locum de non recipiēdis peregrinis doctrinis ampleCtendaque beneficentia. Estque hæc sententia: De omnibus his, de quibus nunc non perscripsi, docebunt vos plenissimè ecclesiarum vestrarum doctores: hos audiatis, his pareatis.
units.tr: Those who refuse to follow anything except their own fancies and the wild imaginings of their nearly frenzied brains, and who despise all the lawful ministers of the churches and teachers of the Word, cannot help slipping into absurd errors. Therefore this teaching, about hearing the leaders of the churches, is very profitably added to what has been delivered so far, and most conveniently at the end, after the passage on not receiving strange doctrines and on extending beneficence. The sense is this: "Your church teachers will instruct you fully about all those matters on which I have now not written. Listen to them and obey them."

units.la: Et concedite) Videtur hoc quadam amplificationis forma additum. Non solum conue-nit illis parēre, verum etiam quędā concedere, permittere. Ita ferè comparatum est, cùm nemo sic ad vnguem factus sit, vt per omnia omnibus queat satisfacere: multi semper aliquid in suis pastoribus desiderāt. Alij causantur, non satis esse doctū eum, qui præest ecclesiæ: ipsorum alij volunt etiam curiosè interdum cum eo disputare: alij accusant aliqua ex parte mores ac vitam: denique quomodocunque ministri se gerant, nunquam sunt sine accusatoribus & calumniatoribus. Propterea Apostolus cupit ali-quid quid illis concedi. Homines enim sunt, & ut omnib. satisfaciant, plane est impossibile. Quod ad doctrinam attinet, si modo synceriter doceant, & praecipua religionis capita tractent fideliter, id pijs & modestis esse satis debet: neque vrgebunt subtiles & acutas disputationes. Doctrina christiana eiusmodi est, ut qua simplicissime tradi gaudeat. Qua ratione apostolus ad Corinthios scribens se sua tractasse omnia gloriatur. Sarciet etiam aliquo modo, cui videtur in eruditione aliquid deesse, si pie sancteque vixerit. Quod ad vitam attinet, etiamsi naevus aliquis in eo appareat, suisque obnoxius sit vitiis: at constat interea iuxta Petri sententiam, parendum etiam discolis. Et Christus iubet audiri doctrinam Pharisaeorum & scribarum in cathedra Mosi sedentium amplecti, facereque omnia quae ipsi secundum Mosis doctrinam praecipiebant, opera vero illorum sectari seu imitari vitam prohibebat. Est igitur ecclesiarum pastoribus non modo obediendum, verum etiam aliquid concedendum. Sequuntur nunc rationes, quae ad faciendum illud impellant.
units.tr: And yield to them) This seems to have been added as a kind of amplification. It is not only right to obey them, but also to make some concessions and allowances to them. This is roughly how things stand, since no one is made so exactly to measure that he can satisfy everyone in every respect; many always find something to miss in their ministers. Some complain that the one who presides over the church is not learned enough; some of them at times want to dispute with him over curious points; others find fault in some respect with his manners and life. In short, however the ministers conduct themselves, they never lack accusers and slanderers. Therefore the Apostle wishes some concession to be made to them. For they are human, and it is quite impossible for them to satisfy everyone. As far as doctrine is concerned, if they teach sincerely and handle the chief heads of religion faithfully, this ought to be enough for the godly and modest, and they will not press subtle and sharp disputations. Christian doctrine is of such a kind that it delights to be delivered most simply. It was in this way that the apostle, writing to the Corinthians, boasted that he had handled all things plainly. Likewise, if someone seems to lack learning, his piety and holiness of life will in some measure make up for it. As for life, even if some blemish appears in a man and he is subject to his own faults, it nevertheless remains, according to the saying of Peter, that one must obey even the froward. And Christ bids that the teaching of the Pharisees and scribes, who sit in Moses' seat, be heard and embraced, and that all the things they prescribed according to the teaching of Moses be done; but he forbade following or imitating their works. Therefore the ministers of the churches must not only be obeyed, but also be granted something. The reasons which impel us to do this now follow.

units.la: Si quidem illi vigilant pro animabus vestris, tanquam ratione reddituri) Prima ratio sua forria, ab amplissima dignitate parique difficultate officij ministrorum ecclesiae. Alibi de magistratib. ciuilib. ita loquitur apostolus, Roma 13. Ministri Dei sunt, in hoc ipsum incumbentes, ut videlicet curent salutem & pacem rerum publicarum, malis existentes terrorem, bonis vero laudem conferentes: at quod ministri ecclesiarum faciunt, longe est excellentius. Vigilat inquit, igitur: labor & multa cura hic notatur: unde & vocabulum vsurpat ἀγρυπνέω, quod proprie est vigilare, ut faciunt pastores in agris. Quod officium suum fuisse etiam Christus ipse testatus est, Ioan. 10. Igitur a diligentia maxima, quam adhibuit Christus pascendis et seruandis iis, quos Dominus ipsi commiserat, licet colligere, quod & quale officium boni pastoris ecclesiae sit. Certe nihil non fecit tum docendo, tum praeeundo exemplis, quo suas oues, praesertim ex ouili Israel ad salutem adduceret: Hierusalem, Hierusalem, inquit, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, sicut gallina congregat pullos suos sub alis, & noluisti. Tandem vero & animam suam in cruce posuit pro salute ouium sibi concreditarum, ne quisquam ex illis periret. Huc pertinet illud 1. Petri 5. Conuersi estis nunc ad pastorem & curatorem animarum vestrarum.
units.tr: For indeed they watch over your souls, as those who must give account) This first reason is taken from the very high dignity and equal difficulty of the office of the ministers of the church. Elsewhere the apostle speaks in this way about the civil magistrates, Rom. 13: they are ministers of God, devoted to this very task, namely to look after the welfare and peace of commonwealths, being a terror to evil men but bringing praise to good men. But what the ministers of the churches do is far more excellent. He says "watch", so labour and great care are noted here; hence he uses the word ἀγρυπνέω [agrypneo], which properly means to keep watch, as shepherds do in the fields. That Christ himself testified this to be his own office, we read in John 10. Therefore from the very great diligence which Christ applied in feeding and keeping those whom the Lord had committed to him, we may gather what and how great the office of a good minister of the church is. Certainly he left nothing undone, both by teaching and by going before them with examples, so that he might bring his sheep, especially those of the house of Israel, to salvation: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem," he says, "how often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!" Finally he even laid down his soul on the cross for the salvation of the sheep committed to him, so that none of them should perish. To this belongs that passage of 1 Peter 5: "You have now turned to the shepherd and overseer of your souls."

units.la: ὡς τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν. Igitur sic quoque debent affecti esse omnes illi, qui sinceri pastores agnosci cupiunt, quibusque Dominus curam suarum ecclesiarum demandauit. Vnde iterum idem Petrus prioris epistolae capite quinto, presbyteros, qui inter vos sunt, obsecro, qui sum & ipse presbyter ac testis afflictionum Christi, atque idem consors gloriae, quae reuelabitur, pascite, quantum in vobis est, gregem Christi, curam illius agentes, non coacte, sed volentes: non turpiter affectantes lucrum, sed propenso animo, neque ceu dominium affectantes adversos cleros, sed sic, ut sitis exemplaria gregis: & cum apsparuerit ille pastorum princeps, reportabitis immarcescibile gloriae coronam. Ex his autem liquet, grauem & difficilem omnino subire eos prouinciam, quicunque hoc munere in ecclesijs perfunguntur. Sed apostolus hic selectis verbis difficultatem tanti muneris optime expresit: vigilat, inquit, pro animabus vestris: non suscipitur cura boum, vel aliorum pecorum quae ipsa tamen non carent arte, sapientia & molestia, sed hominum, quos recte regere vere ars artium dici potest. Neque de facultatibus, aut corporibus est, sed de animis. Quanto vero praestantior anima corporibus atque externis facultatibus, tanto etiam difficilior grauiorque sarcina est curam animorum gerere. O quam pretiosa res est anima una. Quomodo igitur agent in hoc officio, qui multis animabus vel impia doctrina, vel ita corrupta occasionem pereundi praebent? Ideoque diserte addit, Tanquam ratione reddituri: Quid hic dicitur? Et apud quem reddetur ratio? Apud Deum omnium nostrum iudicem, apud Christum, qui est pastorum omnium princeps. Sed quomodo tu, qui non potes reddere rationem pro tua vnius anima, rationem reddes pro animabus aliorum? Sed ita est. Si bene praestiteris, quod tui est officij, reportabis immarcescibilem, vt Petrus ait gloriae coronam: sin secus egeris, requiret Dominus oues suas de manu tua, teste Ezechiele capite 34. Quo loco multa in hanc sententiam contra impios pastores dicitur. Aduertant ergo hic ad muneris sui amplitudinem ac difficultatem, quotquot a Deo ad hoc munus in ecclesia vocati sunt.
units.tr: as the shepherd and overseer of your souls [ὡς τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν]. Therefore all those who wish to be recognised as sincere ministers, and to whom the Lord has entrusted the care of his churches, ought likewise to be disposed in this way. Hence again the same Peter, in chapter five of his first epistle: "I beseech the elders who are among you, I who am also an elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker of the glory that is to be revealed: feed, as far as in you lies, the flock of Christ, taking care of it not under compulsion but willingly, not eagerly seeking gain but with a ready mind, not lording it over the clergy, but so that you are examples to the flock; and when that chief of shepherds appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory." From these words it is clear that those who discharge this office in the churches undertake a task altogether heavy and difficult. But here the apostle has most aptly expressed the difficulty of so great an office in carefully chosen words: "He keeps watch," he says, "over your souls." The care is not of oxen or other cattle, which nevertheless are not without their skill, wisdom and trouble, but of men, whom to rule rightly can truly be called the art of arts. Nor is it concerned with goods or bodies, but with souls. Yet the more excellent the soul is than the body and external goods, the more difficult and heavy a burden it is to take care of souls. O how precious a thing a single soul is! How then will they act in this office who offer occasion of perishing to many souls, either by impious doctrine or by a life so corrupt? And so he adds expressly, "as those who must give account." What is said here? And before whom will the account be rendered? Before God, the judge of us all, before Christ, who is the chief of all shepherds. But how will you, who cannot render an account for your own single soul, render an account for the souls of others? Yet so it is. If you acquit yourself well in what belongs to your office, you will receive the unfading crown of glory, as Peter says; but if you act otherwise, the Lord will require his sheep at your hand, as Ezekiel testifies in chapter 34, where much is said to this effect against impious ministers. Therefore let all who have been called by God to this ministry in the church consider here the greatness and difficulty of their office.

units.la: Proinde cum ta arduu fit istud munus in ecclesia, atq; audis, quisquis es, pastore tuu pro anima tua inuigilare, ita ut etiam redditurus sit Deo pro te rationem: facile intelligis, aequisimum esse, vt illi tanquam fideli pastori & gubernatori obtemperes, nec non, vbi opus fuerit, concedas.
units.tr: Therefore, since this office in the Church is so arduous, and you hear, whoever you are, that the minister must watch over your soul, and will have to render account to God for you, you easily understand that it is most fitting for you to obey him as a faithful shepherd and governor, and, where necessary, to yield to him.

units.la: Vt cum gaudio hoc faciant & non gementes) Secunda ratio a causa formali, requisita ad eius muneris rectam administrationem. Necessarium est in quacunque functione, vt qui recte suum praestet in ea officium, alacri animo omnia aggrediatur. Ne coquus quidem aut calo suum faciat officium, si videat, se semper contemni, si nulli vnquam verbis amicis beneuolis extimuletur. Non studebit diligeter discipulus, si nunquam erigatur laude aliqua per praeceptore: imo si inciderit in eum, qui nihil nouit, qua verba impingere, dicas fulminare, verendu, ne tandem etiam fastidire incipiat literas, quas prius dilexerat. Quid igitur expectandum est ab illis ecclesiarum ministris, qui, cum multos labores subeant, fideliter docendo & multitudini seruiendo exigua accipiunt stipendia, & tamen postea adhuc grauabuntur magnis odijs, a quouis sutore pene dixeram scurra, afficiantur contumelijs, nemine eorum partes tuente, nemine consolante, nemine permittente auxilium? Nonne hic cum gemitu coguntur officium suum facere? Item vbi fidelissime versantur in suo munere, syncerite docent, inculpate, quantum fieri potest, vi- uunt, & tamen non possunt efficere, ut disciplina aliqua introducatur in ecclesiam: magistratus ciuiles nequaquam praebent manum: plebei impune rid" omnia: deniq; nemo respicit ad pij ministri fidem & sedulitatem: Non ne hic cum gemitu ac taedio omnia faciunt?
