Ergo enitendum est auditoribus, ut ab huiusmodi acerbissimis molestijs pij doctores liberentur: non patiantur illos abs quouis affici iniuria & contumelijs: non patiantur frustra sudare: non patiantur perditos homines palam irridere sanctos piorum conatus: praebeant semel occasionem gaudij & laetitia pios defendendo, recte secundum exemplu & doctrinam illorum viuendo: sic enim alibi Apostolus dicit, se maxime gaudere, vbi videt auditores proficere, ac meliores ex doctrina euadere. Philippes. 4. Gaudius sum in Domino magnopere, quod iam tandem reuiguit vestra pro me solicitudo. Philipp. 1. Tantum ut dignum est Euangelio Christi conuersemini: Et paulo post capite secundo, Complete meum gaudium, ut similiter affecti sitis, &c. His inquam modis efficitur, ut alacri animo, sine gemitu ministri ecclesiarum labores omnes subeant.
units.tr: That they may do this with joy and not with groaning) The second reason, from the formal cause, required for the right administration of this office. In every function, whoever performs his duty well must approach it with a willing mind. Not even a cook or a shoemaker will do his work well if he sees that he is always despised and never encouraged by any friendly or kind words. A pupil will not study diligently if his teacher never raises him up with some praise. Indeed, if he falls into the hands of someone who knows nothing and hurls words at him, I was going to say thunders, it is to be feared that he will at last begin to loathe the letters he had once loved. What, then, is to be expected of those ministers of the churches who, though they undergo many labours, teach faithfully and serve the crowd, receive meagre stipends, and yet afterwards are still burdened with great hatreds, are assailed with insults by any cobbler (I almost said buffoon), with no one defending them, no one consoling them, no one offering help? Are they not here forced to do their duty with groaning? Likewise, where they are most faithful in their office, teach sincerely, live blamelessly as far as possible, and yet cannot bring it about that some discipline is introduced into the church, where the civil magistrates by no means lend a hand, the common people mock everything with impunity, and finally no one regards the faith and diligence of the godly minister, do they not do everything with groaning and weariness? Therefore the hearers must strive to free the godly teachers from such bitter troubles. They must not allow them to be affected by injury and insults from anyone; they must not allow them to sweat in vain; they must not allow lost men to mock openly the holy efforts of the pious. Let them once for all give occasion for joy and gladness by defending the pious and by living rightly according to their example and teaching. For the Apostle says elsewhere that he rejoices most when he sees his hearers making progress and becoming better through the teaching. Philippians 4: I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your care for me has flourished again. Philippians 1: Only conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. And a little later in chapter 2: Fulfil my joy, that you may be like-minded, etc. In these ways, I say, it comes about that the ministers of the churches undergo all their labours with a willing mind and without groaning.

units.la: Nam id est inutile vobis) Tertia ratio a damnoso, siue ab incommodo ipsorum subditorum. Putant quidem interdum, se vendicare laudem potentiae, vel exist imationem, si quacunque ratione impediant, vel opprimant ministros ecclesiarum, vel etiam eos, qui sacras literas docent in Scholis: sed profecto faciunt id & suo, & aliorum omnium maximo detrimento, magis quam damno illorum, quos ipsi affligunt. Id quod non est difficile demonstrare.
units.tr: For this is unprofitable for you) The third reason, from the harm or inconvenience to the hearers themselves. Sometimes they think they win praise for power or reputation if in any way they hinder or oppress the ministers of the churches, or even those who teach the sacred letters in the schools. But truly they do this to their own greatest detriment and that of everyone else, far more than to the harm of those whom they afflict. This is not difficult to demonstrate.

units.la: Nam ubi ministri molestantur, fiunt ipsi paulatim negligentiores, tandem incipiunt suos vicissim contemnere auditores, maxime vbi desperant, se profecturos. Hinc vero concidit mox disciplina ecclesiastica, hac subuersa, homines sine timore Dei ruunt in peccata, postremo & obbrutescunt, ac ferinos mores induunt. Necessum est ex his sequi multa & grauia signa irae Dei, bella, famem, pestem. Et post poenas istas temporales deijciuntur impij in gehennam, vbi aeternum cruciantur. Experientia nostri seculi nimium certa dedit nobis eorum, quae dicimus, documenta. Vtinam non vidissemus ita punire contemptum verbi & ministrorum.
units.tr: For when ministers are harassed, they gradually become more negligent; finally they begin in turn to despise their hearers, especially when they despair of making progress. From this, church discipline soon collapses, and with it overthrown, men without the fear of God rush into sins and at last become brutish and adopt savage manners. From these things there must follow many grave signs of God's wrath: wars, famine, plague. And after these temporal punishments the wicked are cast into hell, where they are tormented forever. The experience of our age has given us all too certain proofs of what we are saying. Would that we had not seen the Word and its ministers so punished for contempt.

units.la: Quod ad doctrinam igitur attinet, discimus primo, quid debeamus in genere ijs, qui curam animarum nostrarum suscipiunt.
units.tr: As to doctrine, then, we learn first what we owe in general to those who take up the care of our souls.

units.la: Secundo, discimus etiam non curiose, aut odiose disceptare de pastorum doctrina & vita: non temere in malam partem interpretari, sed aliquid ijs concedere.
units.tr: Second, we also learn not to dispute curiously or spitefully about the teaching and life of pastors, not to interpret them rashly in a bad sense, but to concede something to them.

units.la: Tertio, discunt & illi, qui praesunt ecclesiis, quid ipsos deceat, quomodo videlicet vigilare debeant pro animabus nostris: quam res sit metuenda, ardua, &c.
units.tr: Third, those who preside over churches also learn what becomes them, namely how they ought to watch over our souls, how fearful and arduous a matter it is, and so on.

units.la: Quarto, discimus dignitatem atq; excellentiam muneris ecclesiastici.
units.tr: Fourth, we learn the dignity and excellence of the ecclesiastical office.

units.la: Orate pro nobis: confidimus enim, quod bonam habemus conscientiam, inter omnes cupientes honeste conuersari. Magis autem obsecro vos, ut id faciatis, quo celerius restituat vobis.
units.tr: Pray for us, for we trust that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honourably in all things. But I beg you the more to do this, so that I may be restored to you the sooner.

units.la: Quandoquidem admonuit, ut ijs, qui praesunt ecclesiis, debitum honorem impendarent in omnibus, per occasionem & ceu nactus oportunitatem rogat, ut se quoq;, qui inter ministros ecclesiarum erat no postremus, precibus apud Deum iuuent. Nam & istud inter officia auditorum numerandu est, ut videlicet, qui serio doctores suos cupiunt honorare, pro eorundem quoq; salute Deum orent.
units.tr: Since he has admonished that the honour owed to those who preside over churches should be given in all things, he now, as it were seizing the opportunity, asks that they also help him, who was no small figure among the ministers of the churches, with their prayers to God. For this too is to be counted among the duties of hearers: that those who seriously wish to honour their teachers should also pray to God for their salvation.

units.la: Vnde pro magistratibus ciuilibus, etiam nondum amplectentibus religionem nostram, Paulus orandum praecepit 1. Timoth. 2. Quanto igitur magis orandum est pro salute doctorum Euangelij, quos certum est semper versari in periculis, & nunquam agere sine aduersarijs: & ex quorum salute, ac conseruatione bona pars salutis nostrae, quod inquit attinet ad spiritualia dependet? Propterea Apostolus alias quoque saepius pro se orari petijt, ut Ephes. 6. Colossens. 4. 1. Thessalon. 5. 2. Thessalon. 4. Item ad Philemonem.
units.tr: Hence Paul also commanded that prayers be offered for civil magistrates who do not yet embrace our religion (1 Timothy 2). How much more, then, must prayer be made for the salvation of the teachers of the gospel, who are certainly always in danger and never act without adversaries, and on whose salvation and preservation a good part of our own salvation, as far as spiritual things are concerned, depends? For this reason the Apostle often asked elsewhere to be prayed for himself, as in Ephesians 6, Colossians 4, 1 Thessalonians 5, 2 Thessalonians 4. Likewise in the letter to Philemon.

units.la: Arduum & difficile munus est præesse ecclesijs, animarum curam gerere, cui humanæ vires prorsus sunt impares, & apud mundum hominesq; mundanos contemptum, imò oppressum: ideoq; sine ope, consolatione, auxilio Dei nulli possent in eo munere consiste re: id quod exijs, quæ apostolus crebrò narrat de suis laboribus, patientia, constantia, liberatione expericulis videre est.
units.tr: It is a hard and difficult office to preside over churches and bear the care of souls, for which human powers are altogether unequal, and which is held in contempt, indeed oppressed, by the world and worldly men. Therefore no one could persist in that office without the help, consolation and aid of God. This can be seen from what the apostle often recounts about his labours, his patience, his constancy, and his deliverance from dangers.

units.la: Confidimus enim, quòd bonam habemus conscientiam inter omnes) Addit rationes suasorias, è quibus prior hæc sumpta est ab affectibus Hebræorum erga apostolum. Certò sibi persuadet Apostolus, Hebræos lubenter id factuTo, propterea quòd confidit, omnes illos bene atq; honorificè de ipso sentire, bonoq; esse erga se affectu. Multi ex Iudæis male sentiebât de Paulo, nempe qui euangelium non receperant, aut si receperant, tamen contendebant adhæc vnà cum euangelio obseruari debere legales ceremonias. Plurimi enim semper de his rebus litigabant & Paulum, vbicunque poterant, grauabant inuidia. Atqui tales contentiosos Paulus non alloquit, vtpote quos aperte impugnauit paulo ante, vbi monuit, ne nouis & peregrinis doctrinis talium erronum circumferrentur.
units.tr: For we trust that we have a good conscience among all) He adds persuasive reasons, of which the first is taken from the feelings of the Hebrews towards the apostle. The Apostle is confident that the Hebrews will gladly do this, because he trusts that all of them think well and honourably of him and are well disposed towards him. Many of the Jews thought ill of Paul, namely those who had not received the gospel, or who, though they had received it, still contended that the legal ceremonies must be observed along with the gospel. For many always quarrelled about these matters and burdened Paul with envy wherever they could. Yet Paul does not address such contentious men, since he had openly attacked them shortly before, when he warned that they should not be carried about by new and strange teachings of such errors.

units.la: Sed eos alloquitur, qui euangelium purum agnouerunt quiq; intellexerunt, quanta beneficia per Christum adepti essent. Apud hos omnes confidit, se bonam habere conscie tiam, id est, virum pium, syncerum, serio quærentem gloriam Dei atq; vtilitatem credentium, existimari: atq; ideo illos lubenter pro salute iplorum ipsius Deū oraturos. Sic autè non solemus quicquà petere, nisi speremus nos impetraturos, & confidamus, eos, à quibus aliquid petimus, bene esse erga nos affectos. Igitur de affectu Hebræorum erga apostolum sermo est. Scio quidem, nonnullos sic accipere hæc, quasi apostolus suam purit atem atque integritatem prædicaret, quod videlicet nullius mali sibi esset conscius, nunquam vllo suæ gentis odio laborasset, sicut quidam spargebat, atque eo nomine speraret permouendos, vt lubenter pro se orarent. Sed prior interpretatio magis videtur conuenire instituto. Confirmatur istud etiam verbis adiectis, confidimus, inquit, quòd bonam habemus conscientiam, inter omnes cupientes honestè conuersari: non præfert apostolus se omnibus alijs, sed tantum confidit, se talem æstimari apud bonos, & cupientes recte agere. Nam aliorum iudicia non morabatur, etiamsi ipse quidem his quoque bene cupiebat. Neq; vero quisquam pius curat alijs placere, quam pijs: si mundo placerem, Christi seruus non essem. A laudatis laudari pulchrum est ab improbis laudari, est vituperari. Nota sunt hæc etiam ex philosophorum & poetarum scite dictis. Apud tales ergo cupientes honestè versari confidit apostolus, se bonam habere conscientiam, se æstimari bonæ conscientiæ virum, ideoq; lubenter pro salute ipsius oraturos.
units.tr: But he addresses those who have recognised the pure gospel and understood how great the benefits obtained through Christ are. Among all of these he trusts that he has a good conscience, that is, that he is regarded as a godly and sincere man, earnestly seeking the glory of God and the profit of believers, and therefore that they will gladly pray to God for his salvation. For we do not usually ask for anything unless we hope to obtain it and trust that those from whom we ask are well disposed towards us. So the sense concerns the feelings of the Hebrews towards the apostle. I know that some take these words as if the apostle were proclaiming his own purity and integrity, that he was conscious of no wrong and had never laboured under any hatred of his nation, as some were spreading, and that on this ground he hoped they would be moved to pray gladly for him. But the former interpretation seems to fit the purpose better. This is confirmed also by the added words: "we trust," he says, "that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honourably in all things." The apostle does not prefer himself to all others; he only trusts that he is judged such by good men who desire to act rightly. For he did not wait for the judgments of others, even though he wished well to them too. Nor does any godly man care to please others than the godly: if I still pleased the world, I would not be a servant of Christ. To be praised by the praiseworthy is fine; to be praised by the wicked is to be blamed. These things are also known from the apt sayings of philosophers and poets. Among such men, then, who desire to live honourably, the apostle trusts that he has a good conscience, that he is esteemed a man of good conscience, and therefore that they will gladly pray for his salvation.

units.la: Magis autem obsecro uos, ut id faciatis, quo celerius restituar uobis) Secunda ratio ab vtili siue com modo, quod inde ad ipsos peruenit Hebræos. Aliorum magis caussa, quam sua petit apostolus pro se orari. Multum enim referebat, vt apostolus ecclesijs adesset, easque in sana doctrina confirmaret: ipso periclitante, aut diutius manete foris, metuere debebant, ne Pseudoapostoli Ecclesias inficerent aut penitus subuerterent: sicut Galatas quidam subuerterant. Thessalonicenses multi varijs artibus solicitabant. Colossenses etiam cum Pseudoapostolis concertabant: Corinthij cum Philosophis. Nemo credat, quantum noceat bonorum pastorum etiam ad breue tempus absentia. Hoc Apostolus noster probè nouerat. Itaq; Hebræi, vel suæ vtilitatis caussa merito debebat pro salute Apostoli esse soliciti. Et Apostolus nunquam potuit ecclesiarum solicitudinem deponere: omnibus à Hierusalem vsq; ad Illyricum, imò & Romanis, alijsq; cupiebat semper adesse, vt illis prodesset, vt illos plenius doceret, in fide confirmaret. Verè diligens & syncerus ecclesiarum omnium visitator erat Apostolus: & quamuis proprie esset Apostolus Gentium, tamen Iudæorum suorum curam nunquam deponebat: id quod liquet ex Actis, vbi commemoratur semper primo loco adijsse synagogas, & Christum in ijs prædi casse. Et Roman. 11. ait, se illustrare ministerium suum, quòd gentium esset Apostolus, vt, si quomodo posset, ad æmulandum prouocaret carnem suam, & saluos ex illis nonnullos redderet. Cæterum ex his discimus, primò ac generaliter orandum esse pro salute eorum, qui ecclesiis præsunt, vt Deus eos constanter seruet, nec non pios conatus ipsorum promoveat. Secundò: Discimus, auditores debere de suis doctoribus honorificè tum sentire, tum loqui, ac iudicare bonam esse illorum conscientiam. Hæc est prima via ad lapsum in absurda dogmata, ecclesiæ ministros cótemnere. Si enim vix in humanis artib. proficiūt, qui non amant suos præceptores: quomodo proficient in doctrina pietatis, qui aspernantur pietatis tradendæ magistros? Tertiò: In hoc etiam admitendum doctoribus, vt audito-res de ipsis iudicare ita queant.
units.tr: I beseech you the more earnestly to do this, so that I may be restored to you the sooner. The second reason is drawn from usefulness or advantage, which comes from this to the Hebrews themselves. The apostle asks to be prayed for more for the sake of others than for his own. For it mattered greatly that the apostle be present with the churches and confirm them in sound doctrine. While he was in danger, or remained abroad for longer, they had reason to fear that false apostles would infect the churches or utterly overthrow them, as some had overthrown the Galatians. Many were troubling the Thessalonians by various arts. The Colossians too were contending with false apostles, and the Corinthians with philosophers. No one can believe how much harm even a short absence of good ministers does. Our apostle knew this well. So the Hebrews, even for their own advantage, rightly ought to be anxious for the apostle's safety. And the apostle could never lay aside his concern for the churches. He always wished to be present with all of them, from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and even with the Romans and others, so that he might benefit them, teach them more fully, and confirm them in faith. The apostle was a truly diligent and sincere visitor of all the churches. Although he was properly the apostle of the Gentiles, he never laid aside care for his own Jews. This is clear from the Acts, where it is recorded that he always went first to the synagogues and preached Christ in them. And in Rom. 11 he says that he magnified his ministry because he was the apostle of the Gentiles, so that somehow he might provoke his own flesh to emulation and save some of them. From these things we learn, first and in general, that we must pray for the safety of those who preside over the churches, that God may keep them steadfast and advance their pious endeavours. Secondly, we learn that hearers ought to think and speak of their teachers honourably, and to judge that their conscience is good. This is the first step toward falling into absurd doctrines: despising the ministers of the Church. For if those who do not love their own teachers scarcely make progress in the human arts, how will those make progress in the teaching of piety who scorn the teachers through whom piety is handed on? Thirdly, in this too the teachers must allow that their hearers may judge them in this way.

units.la: Quartò: Discimus ministros verbi nō debere morari iudicia atque obloquia improbo-rum. Satis est, si ijs placeant, quos constat sanctæ & piæ vitæ teneri studio. Id autem, ne propter malorum diuersa iudicia frangatur animo, fiatque remissio in suo munere.
units.tr: Fourthly, we learn that ministers of the Word ought not to dwell on the judgments and complaints of the wicked. It is enough if they please those whom it is clear are held by zeal for a holy and godly life. But this should be done so that the mind is not broken by the differing judgments of the evil, and so that there is no slackening in their office.

units.la: Quintò: discimus ad salutem facere vniuersæ ecclesiæ, si pastor bene habeat. Quinetiam graviter peccare, quicunque præter magnam necessitatem à suis ecclesijs diutius ac longius abesse audent.
units.tr: Fifthly, we learn that it conduces to the salvation of the whole Church if the minister is well. Moreover, whoever dares to be away from his churches for longer and farther than great necessity requires sins grievously.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Deus autem pacis, qui reduxit à mortuis pastorem ouium illum magnum, per sanguinem testamenti æterni, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum absolutos vos reddat in omni opere bono, ad faciendum voluntatem ipsius, efficiens, ut, quod agitur, acceptum sit in conspectu suo per Iesum Christum, cui gloria in sæcula sæculorum Amen.
units.tr: Now the God of peace, who brought again from the dead that great shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: Onclusio quartæ partis, adeoq; totius epistolæ, per comprecationem, quomodo alias quoq; in omnibus epistolis eiusmodi conclusiones additas cernimus. Epistola ad Romanos habet plures huiusmodi conclusiones, propterea quòd magno affectu semper aliquod rursum attexuit. Vide cap.15. & 16. Item ad Philippens.4. Item 1. Thessalon.5. Ipse Deus pacis sanctificet vos totos. Et 2. Thessalon 4. Ipse autem dominus pacis det vobis pacem semper.
units.tr: This is the conclusion of the fourth part, and so of the whole epistle, and it takes the form of a prayer, as we see such added conclusions in all the epistles. The Epistle to the Romans has several conclusions of this kind, because with great feeling he always added something again. See chapters 15 and 16. Likewise Philippians 4. Likewise 1 Thessalonians 5: "May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly." And 2 Thessalonians 4: "May the Lord of peace himself give you peace always."

units.la: Est autem conclusio hæc breuis, sed tamen res maximas & præstantissimas in ea Hebræis comprecatur, ut reuera maius aut præclarius dici nihil posset. Et non tantum ad ea, quæ proximè in hac quarta parte epistolæ dicta sunt, verum etiam ad nonnulla, quæ in antecedentibus partibus seu disputationibus tractabantur, mentem auditorum reuocat: id quod inter explicandum indicabimus.
units.tr: This conclusion is brief, yet in it he prays for the Hebrews for the greatest and most outstanding things, so that truly nothing greater or more splendid could be said. And it recalls the minds of the hearers not only to those things just said in this fourth part of the epistle, but also to some things treated in the preceding parts or disputations. We will point these out as we explain.

units.la: Deus autem pacis) inquit: Sapientissimè quidem huiusmodi comprecationes ad finem subiiciuntur. Vbi enim aut non possunt, aut non expedit, plura & copiosius explicari: vbi item ab omnibus agnoscitur, non posse multiplicis doctrinæ, præceptorum, exhortationum, & similium, quæ præcesserunt, non posse sequi effectum, nisi pater cœlestis auditoribus, siue ijs ad quos scribitur, sua virtute, intellectum, ut percipiant omnia, voluntatem ut cupiant assequi, vires, ut possint exequi, dederit. Hoc vnum certè superest, ut ad Dominum omnes confugiant, huius implorët opem, ab hoc sibi dari has facultates spirituales postulent. Vnde enim habeant miseri aliquid boni, præsertim in rebus spiritualibus, nisi à patre luminum? Iacob.1. Hac igitur de causa prudenter facit apostolus, quòd, quando epistolam vult claudere, comprecationes huiusmodi subiicit.
units.tr: "Now the God of peace," he says. Such prayers are very wisely placed at the end, where more and fuller explanation either cannot be given or is not expedient. Where it is also recognised by all that the effect of the manifold teaching, precepts, exhortations and the like that have gone before cannot follow unless the heavenly Father, by his power, has given to the hearers, or to those to whom he writes, understanding to perceive all things, a will to desire to attain them, and strength to be able to carry them out. Surely this one thing remains: that all flee to the Lord, implore his help, and ask that these spiritual faculties be given to them by him. For where else do wretched people get anything good, especially in spiritual things, unless from the Father of lights? James 1. For this reason the apostle acts prudently when, wishing to close the epistle, he adds prayers of this kind.

units.la: Deus pacis) appellatur Deus, propterea quod largitor est omnis fœlicitatis & successus, quibuscunque in rebus. Ita namque pax sæpenumerò Hebræis fœlicitatem generaliter significat: quomodo psalmo 129. Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam: & alibi frequenter. Vel Deus pacis, quòd nobis spiritualis pacis autor sit, nosq; in gratia receperit, qui antea eramus inimici, nec non pacem à nobis studiosè coli desiderat. Quo sensu Roman.5. dicitur, nos habere pacem cum Deo. Et 1. Corinth.14. dicitur, non esse Deum dissensionis, sed pacis. Item 2 Corinth 13. Vnanimes sitis in pace agite, & Deus charitatis ac pacis erit vobiscum. Ergo hæc ipsa appellatio Dei & animos engit, ut omnis generis ab eo expectent bona, & ad colendam inter nos mutuò pacem invitat. Quare nihil mirandum, si frequenter ab apostolo usurpetur.
units.tr: "The God of peace": God is so called because he is the giver of all happiness and success, in whatever matters. For peace often signifies happiness in general among the Hebrews, as in Psalm 129: "Great peace have those who love your law," and frequently elsewhere. Or he is the God of peace because he is the author of spiritual peace for us, and has received us into grace, who were formerly enemies, and also desires that peace be eagerly cultivated by us. In this sense Romans 5 says that we have peace with God, and 1 Corinthians 14 says that God is not a God of dissension but of peace. Likewise 2 Corinthians 13: "Be of one mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you." So this very title of God both raises minds to expect every kind of good from him, and invites us to cultivate mutual peace among ourselves. Therefore it is no wonder that the apostle uses it so often.

units.la: Qui reduxit à mortuis pastorem ouium illum magnum, per sanguinem testamenti æterni, Dominum nostrum Iesum.
units.tr: Who brought again from the dead that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus.

units.la: Satis quidè fuisset, dicere simpliciter, Deus pacis absolutos vos reddat: sed voluit quædam illustriora adijcere, per quæ animi confirmarentur, ad audacter expectandum ea beneficia, quæ apostolus comprecari Hebræis vult. Huiusmodi sunt hæc: qui reduxit à mortuis pastorem illum magnum.
units.tr: It would have been enough simply to say, "May the God of peace make you perfect." But he chose to add some more illustrious things, by which the minds would be strengthened to expect boldly those benefits which the apostle wishes to pray for the Hebrews. Such are these: "who brought again from the dead that great shepherd."

units.la: Quibus verbis primùm declaratur immensa Dei patris potentia: vt certò simus, nullas res adeò magnas non posse petere, quin pater eas nobis posse elargiri. Nemo facilè expectet sibi conferendum aliquid ab eo, quem existimat non posse illud conferre. Patrem ergo docet longè esse potentissimum, ut quilibet confidat, eum posse res maximas donare. Potentia verò hanc probat, ratione sumpta à resuscitatione Iesu Christi ex morte. Verè enim hoc ingentis potentiæ argumentum est, ut nemo possit diffidere, quin, qui hoc fecit, possit & alia miranda patrare.
units.tr: By these words, first, the immense power of God the Father is declared, so that we may be certain that no matter how great the things we ask, the Father can bestow them upon us. No one readily expects anything to be conferred on him by one whom he thinks unable to confer it. He therefore teaches that the Father is by far the most powerful, so that everyone may trust that he can grant the greatest things. He proves this power by an argument drawn from the raising of Jesus Christ from death. For this is truly a proof of immense power, so that no one can doubt that he who has done this can also accomplish other wonderful things.

units.la: Cæterùm nihil hoc derogat diuinitati aut potentiæ Christi, quòd ipse dicitur per patre suscitatus à morte. Nam aliàs subinde Christus sua quoque virtute diuina seipsum suscitasse ostenditur: quò pertinet illud: Ego potestatem habeo ponendi animam meam, & iterum assumendi eam. Item Ioan.5. Sicut pater suscitat mortuos,& viuificat,sic & filius,quos vult viuificat. Item Ioan.2. Destruite templum hoc,& ego in tribus diebus erigam illud Itaq; communiter ad gloriam patris & filij facit illa resurrectio: sed principaliter patri attribuitur consuetudine Scripturarum, ad declarandum, exijs,quae peregit in filio,summam in patre potentiam.
units.tr: Yet this does not in any way detract from the divinity or power of Christ, that he is said to have been raised from the dead by the Father. For at other times Christ is also shown to have raised himself by his own divine power; to which belongs that saying: "I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again." Likewise John 5: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." Likewise John 2: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Thus this resurrection is commonly to the glory of both the Father and the Son; but it is principally attributed to the Father, by the custom of the Scriptures, to declare from the things he accomplished in the Son the supreme power in the Father.

units.la: Etsi vero mirabiliter praedicarit patrem, tribuendo ei resuscitationem Christi, tamen non minus praedicat Christum, vocando eum pastorem ouium illum magnum: Significat namque ita pastorem esse & conseruatorem, gubernatorem, defensorem omnium animarum. Ita vero tum apud Ezechielem, tum in euangelijs Christus insignis pastor describitur,& a Petro vocatur pastorum princeps: quandoquidem in eum solum vere & proprie appellatio ista competit: in caeteros vero tantum per communicationem seu participationem. Qua ratione etiam supra capite decimo appellatus est Christus sacerdos magnus praefectus domui Dei: Cum habeamus, inquit, sacerdotem magnum, praefectum domum Dei, accedamus cum vero corde in certitudine fidei. Quare hinc liquet, tali appellatione Christi respicere Apostolum non tantum ad ea,quae iam proxime dicta sunt de pastoribus, quos praecepit honore afficere: verum etiam ad illa, quae supra dicta sunt de Christi summo sacerdotio & pontificatu, in prolixa illa disputatione de euangelij praestantia prae lege. Atq; ita haec conclusio tacite reuocat in memoriam pleraq; in antecedentibus disputationibus tractata.
units.tr: Although he has marvellously praised the Father, by ascribing to him the resurrection of Christ, he nonetheless praises Christ no less, by calling him that great shepherd of the sheep. For this signifies that he is shepherd, preserver, governor and defender of all souls. Indeed Christ is described as the outstanding shepherd both in Ezekiel and in the Gospels, and is called by Peter the chief of shepherds; since this title belongs truly and properly to him alone, while to the others it belongs only by communication or participation. For this reason also, above in chapter 10, Christ was called the great priest set over the house of God: "Since we have a great priest set over the house of God," he says, "let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith." Hence it is clear that by this title of Christ the apostle looks not only to those things just said about the ministers, whom he commanded to be honoured, but also to those things said above about Christ's supreme priesthood and high priesthood, in that long disputation on the excellence of the gospel above the law. And so this conclusion tacitly recalls to memory many of the things treated in the preceding disputations.

units.la: Per sanguinem testamenti aeterni) Sicut resurrectionis, ita & mortis Christi mentionem facit: quandoquidem haec duo, resurrectio inquam & mors Christi amplissima sunt salutis nostrae mysteria, semperque habenda prae oculis. Quamvis commemorando sanguinem Christi declarare vult patris erga nos bonitatem ac beneuolentiam: de qua constare debet non minus, quam de eiusdem potentia, vt optata bona ab eo expectemus. Non satis est, vt credamus, Deu patre iuuare nos posse, statuere debemus, eundem etiam id velle facere. Beneuolentia autem patris hic insinuari, ex eo liquet, quod in hoc, quead-modum loquitur Ioannes cap.3.& 1.epistolae cap.4. In hoc apparuit charitas Dei erga nos, quod filium suum vnigenitum misit Deus in mundum, vt viuamus per eum. In hoc est charitas, non quod dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & miserit filium suum propitiatorem pro peccatis nostris. Proinde valere debet haec ratio ad animos commouendos, vt ne dubitent, quin, qui pro salute ipsorum proprium dedit filium, alia quoque pro salute ipsorum sit peracturus. Est autem Metonymia, siue Metalepsis, quado sanguis ponitur pro morte Christi, qui mortem effuso pro nobis sanguine exoluit.
units.tr: "Through the blood of the eternal covenant": as he mentions the resurrection, so also he mentions the death of Christ, since these two, I say, the resurrection and the death of Christ, are the greatest mysteries of our salvation and are always to be kept before our eyes. Yet in recalling the blood of Christ he wishes to declare the Father's goodness and benevolence toward us; of this it ought to be no less certain than of his power, so that we may expect from him the good things we desire. It is not enough that we believe God the Father can help us; we must also be sure that he is willing to do so. Now that the Father's benevolence is hinted at here is clear from what John says in chapter 3 and in chapter 4 of his first epistle: "In this the love of God was made manifest toward us, that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins." Therefore this argument ought to have force in moving the minds, so that they may not doubt that he who gave his own Son for their salvation will also accomplish other things for their salvation. Moreover, this is a metonymy, or metalepsis, when blood is put for the death of Christ, since he paid for death by shedding his blood for us.

units.la: Caeterum sanguis Christi vocatur etiam sanguis testamenti: idque quia veritas, quae per Christum adimpleta est, debet vmbris siue typis respondere. Sicut enim vetus testamentum siue pactum, quod Deus inter se & Iudaeos extare voluit, sanguine effuso sparsoque in populum, fuit publice confirmatum: ita nouum testamentum, siue renouationem pacti voluit pater similiter sanguine cofimari, & quidem sanguine proprij sui filij, non brutorum animalium. Ac de confirmatione veteris testamenti per sanguine, supra quoq; noster Apostolus capite nono, ex libro Exodi cap.24. Ne prius quidem illud testamentum absq; sanguine dedicatum fuit.
units.tr: Furthermore, the blood of Christ is also called the blood of the covenant; and this is because the truth fulfilled through Christ ought to correspond to the shadows or types. For just as the old covenant or agreement, which God willed to exist between himself and the Jews, was publicly confirmed by blood poured out and sprinkled on the people, so the Father willed that the new covenant, or renewal of the agreement, be similarly confirmed by blood, and indeed by the blood of his own Son, not of brute animals. And our apostle, above in chapter 9, spoke of the confirmation of the old covenant by blood, from Exodus chapter 24: "Not even the first covenant was dedicated without blood."

units.la: Cum enim Moses omne praeceptum iuxta legem exposuisset omni populo, sumpto sanguine vitulorum & hircorum cum aqua & lana coccina & hyssopo, simul & ipsum librum,& totum populum aspersit, dicens: Hic est sanguis testamenti, quod mandauit vobis Deus,&c. Et eodem capite nono paulo ante sanguis Christi sanguini vitulorum & hircorum,& efficacior imbecilliori, opponitur. Si sanguis, inquit, taurorum & hircorum sanctificat ad carnis purificationem, quanto magis sanguis Christi? capite vero decimo, Sanguis Christi sanguis testamenti appellatur: Qui aspernatus fuerit legem Mosi, absq; misericordia sub duobus aut tribus testibus moritur: Quanto putatis peioribus afficietur supplicijs, qui filium Dei conculcarit, & sanguinem testamenti ceu rem profanam habuerit? Sed & Christus ipse mysterium legis de approbatione testamenti seu pacti per effusionem sanguinis, in se vere adimpletum interpretatur, quando instante hora mortis, instituens vsum sacrae coenae, ait, porrecto poculo: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum, Matthaei capite vigesimosexto, vel vt Marci capite decimo quarto, hic est sanguis meus noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur.
units.tr: For when Moses had set out every precept of the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and the whole people, saying: "This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you," etc. And in the same ninth chapter, a little earlier, the blood of Christ is set against the blood of calves and goats, and the more effective against the weaker. "If the blood of bulls and goats sanctifies to the purification of the flesh," he says, "how much more the blood of Christ?" In chapter ten the blood of Christ is called the blood of the covenant: "He who has rejected the law of Moses dies without mercy under two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment do you think he will deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God and regarded the blood of the covenant as a profane thing?" But Christ himself also interprets the mystery of the law concerning the ratification of the covenant, or agreement, through the shedding of blood as truly fulfilled in himself. When the hour of his death was at hand, instituting the use of the holy supper, he said, as he handed the cup: "This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26); or as in Mark 14: "this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many."

units.la: Idehabes 1. Corinth.11. Hac igitur ratione & in praesenti sanguis Christi sanguis testamenti appellatur: nec dubium, quin Apostolus hic ad illos locos, & ad figuram veteris testamenti respiciat. Sed dicis, Quid est, quod addit, testamenti aeterni? Et hoc rectissimè factum est, idque duabus de causis: prior, quia nouum testamentum siue Euangelium, quod sanguine Christi confirmatum est, æternum iustissimè dicitur, vtpote quod ab æterno fuit, & æternum manet.
units.tr: You have this in 1 Corinthians 11. For this reason also the blood of Christ is here called the blood of the covenant. There is no doubt that the Apostle here looks back to those passages and to the figure of the old covenant. But you ask: what is meant by the addition of the eternal covenant? This was done quite rightly, and for two reasons. The first is that the new covenant, or gospel, which was confirmed by the blood of Christ, is most justly called eternal, since it has been from eternity and remains eternal.

units.la: Fuit enim ante constitutionem mundi ordinatum (Ephes. cap. 1.) vt electi per sanguinem Christi seruarentur: & Deus pater apud semetipsum ab initio proposuerat, quòd per Christū instauraret omnia, & quæ in cœlis sunt, & quæ in terra. Et Roman. capite 16, euangelium vocatur mysterium reuelatum, temporibus æternis tacitum, nunc verò manifestatum. Et 1. Corinthior. 2. loquimur sapientiam Dei in mysterio, quæ est recondita, quam præfinierat Deus ante secula, in gloriam nostram, quam nemo principum seculi huius cognouit. Quin etiam statim initio mundi promissiones de Christo, & liberatione per sanguinem eius ad primos parentes sunt editæ, Genesis capite tertio, semen mulieris conteret caput tuum. Sed neque expectandum est, vt aliquod testamentum euangelio succedat: Qua de re supra quoque nonnihil diximus, cum alibi, tum capite nono, vbi dicebatur, Christum nunc sub consummationem seculorum semel apparuisse.
units.tr: For it was ordained before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1) that the elect should be saved through the blood of Christ; and God the Father had from the beginning purposed in himself that through Christ he would restore all things, both those in heaven and those on earth. Romans 16 calls the gospel a mystery revealed, kept silent in eternal times but now made manifest. And 1 Corinthians 2: "We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, and which none of the rulers of this age has known." Indeed, at the very beginning of the world, promises about Christ and deliverance through his blood were made known to the first parents (Genesis 3): "the seed of the woman shall bruise your head." Nor is it to be expected that any covenant should succeed the gospel. We have said something about this above, both elsewhere and in chapter 9, where it was said that Christ has now appeared once at the end of the ages.

units.la: Altera causa: Nouum testamentum vocatur æternum, ad illustrandam eius dignitatem atque excellentiam præ testamento veteri, quod non eadem ratione ab initio constitutum dici poterit, sicut de nouo testamento ostendimus: neq; eadem ratione potuit in omne tempus durare: sed tantum vires suas aliquatas ad tempus habuit: manifestato verò euangelio euanuit, ac cessare in æternum debuit.
units.tr: The second reason is this: the new covenant is called eternal to illustrate its dignity and excellence above the old covenant. The old covenant cannot be said to have been established from the beginning in the same way, as we have shown concerning the new; nor could it endure for all time in the same way. It had its strength only for a time, to a certain extent; but when the gospel was made manifest it vanished, and it was bound to cease for ever.

units.la: Absolutos uos reddat) Iam sequuntur petitiones, siue bona illa, quæ Apostolus ipsis compre-catur. Primò igitur precatur, vt Deus nos consummatos & perfectos efficiat, voluntate promptos, viribus sufficientes, ad perficiendum bona opera: non quæcunque, quæ videlicet hominum iudicio talia existimantur: sed quæ talia sunt secundum voluntatem ipsius quàm sanè nos ex sacris literis, quæ propter nos sunt editæ, discere omni tempore possumus. Opera bona ex fide prodeunt, neque hæc potest esse otiosa. Philip pens. 2. de viribus nostris: 1. Thessalon. 4. de voluntate Dei: item Roman. 12.
units.tr: Make you perfect: Now follow the petitions, or the good things which the Apostle asks for them. First, then, he prays that God may make us complete and perfect, ready in will and sufficient in strength to perform good works. These are not just any works that human judgment considers good, but those which are such according to God's will, which we can learn at all times from the sacred letters, given for our sake. Good works proceed from faith, and faith cannot be idle. On our strength, see Philippians 2; on the will of God, see 1 Thessalonians 4; likewise Romans 12.

units.la: Efficiens, vt quod agitis, acceptum sit in conspectu suo per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Working in us what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ.

units.la: Secunda petitio, qua precatur illis à Deo dari, vt quæ bona faciūt, etiam sint accepta. Non abs re petitionem hanc ab antecedenti discernimus. Fiunt subinde bona opera à quibusdam, & quidem secundum voluntatem Dei, quam discunt ex lege: Deus etiam dat, vt illa opera perficiant: sed tamen nondum sunt Deo accepta. Exempla adferre non est difficile. Lucæ capite decimo octauo duo simul ascendunt templum, publicanus & Pharisæus: simul orant: atque hic pro beneficijs acceptis agit gratias, multa bona opera per gratiam Dei à se facta commemorans: & tamen illius tantùm accepta fuit oratio, huius verò nequaquam. Item Marci capite duodecimo, multi mittebant æs etiam multum in gazophylacium: atque ex omnibus donis magis accepta fuerunt duo minuta, id est, quadrans, quam iniecerat pauperacula vidua, quàm ingentes nummi multorum diuitum. Opus quidem, quod ad se attinet, idem erat omnium, voluntas forte similiter eadem: sed tamen non perinde accepta erant munera Domino.
units.tr: The second petition is that it may be granted to them by God that those who do good things may also be acceptable. We do not without reason distinguish this petition from the preceding one. Good works are sometimes done by certain people, and indeed according to the will of God, which they learn from the law; God also gives them the means to perform those works; yet the works are not yet acceptable to God. It is not difficult to adduce examples. In Luke 18 two men go up together to the temple, a tax collector and a Pharisee; they pray together; and the latter, giving thanks for benefits received, recounts many good works done by himself through the grace of God. Yet only the prayer of the former was accepted, and that of the latter by no means. Likewise in Mark 12: many put in much money into the treasury, and of all the gifts the two small coins, that is a quadrans, which the poor little widow had cast in, were more acceptable than the huge sums of the many rich. The work, as far as it concerns itself, was the same for all, and perhaps the will was likewise the same; but nevertheless the gifts were not equally acceptable to the Lord.

units.la: Item Actorum capite decimo, sæpius ac dubiè multa bona opera fecerat. Cornelius Centurio, & bono animo, priusquam semel audiret, ea coram Deo fuisse accepta. Et, in summa, omni tempore faciunt bona opera vere pij: faciunt paria & hypocritæ: Sed illorum sunt accepta coram Deo: hæc nequaquam. Huc pertinent illa Hieremiæ sexto contra contemptores legis: ad quid mihi thus de Seba, atque calamus optimus de terra longinqua? Holocausta vestra non sunt accepta, nec sacrificia vestra sunt grata mihi. Psalmo quinquagesimoprimo. Tunc acceptabis sacrificia iustitiæ, holocaustum, & integram oblationem. Prima Petri capite secundo, Ipsi quoque veluti viui lapides ædificemini, domus spirituales, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias, acceptabiles Deo per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Likewise Acts 10: Cornelius the centurion had often, and with some uncertainty, done many good works, and with a good spirit, before he heard the gospel once; these were accepted before God. In short, truly pious people always do good works; hypocrites too do the same; but the former are accepted before God, the latter by no means. To this pertain the words of Jeremiah 6 against the despisers of the law: "To what purpose is frankincense from Sheba, and the best cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not accepted, nor are your sacrifices pleasing to me." Psalm 51: "Then you will accept sacrifices of righteousness, burnt offering and whole oblation." 1 Peter 2: "You also, like living stones, be built up as spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ."

units.la: Itaque non abs re distinguitur ista petitio à priori. Nam impetrato priore, vt videlicet bona operemur, nisi accedat istud posterius, frustra fiunt omnia. Bonæ voluntatis Dei est, vt rectè aliquid agamus: similiter autem bonæ voluntatis est, vt ipse, quod agimus, acceptet.
units.tr: Therefore this petition is rightly distinguished from the former. For once the former is obtained, that we may do good, unless this latter also follows, all things are done in vain. It is of the good will of God that we do something rightly; and similarly it is of his good will that he himself accepts what we do.

units.la: Cæterùm vt mens certior aliquando fieret, ea, quæ rectè agimus, à Deo acceptari, placuit Apostolo etiam causam formalem, siue causam, propter quam acceptantur bona opera à Deo, addere, quando ait:
units.tr: But so that the mind might at some point be more certain that those things which we do rightly are accepted by God, the Apostle was pleased to add also the formal cause, or the cause on account of which good works are accepted by God, when he says:

units.la: Per Iesum Christum) Per hunc enim, & propter hunc solum, quæcunque nos facimus, mus, Deo accepta sunt, quæ nos ad vtilitatem proximi, & ad gloriam Dei facimus. Christus est ille, in quo patri bene complacitum est, & in quo placent Deo, quæ per alios quoq; fiunt. Christi gloriam obscurant, & bonam voluntatem Dei patris reijci untur, quotquot bona opera sua existimant placitura, vel propter personarum dignitatem vel propter qualitatem ipsorum operum.
units.tr: Through Jesus Christ: For through him, and on account of him alone, whatever we do for the usefulness of our neighbour and for the glory of God is accepted by God. Christ is he in whom the Father is well pleased, and in whom what is done also through others pleases God. All who think their good works will please God, whether on account of the dignity of persons or on account of the quality of the works themselves, obscure the glory of Christ and reject the good will of God the Father.

units.la: Itaque huc decet semper in bonis operibus respicere, vt propter Christum Deus pater velit ea acceptare. Vnde etiam factum, quòd ecclesia etiam in gratiarum actionibus & laudibus, quas Deo offert, semper petit eas acceptari propter Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: Therefore it is always fitting to look to this in good works, that God the Father may be willing to accept them on account of Christ. Hence also it is that the Church, even in thanksgivings and praises which it offers to God, always asks that they be accepted on account of Christ our Lord.

units.la: Et revera non sunt bona opera vere bona censenda, nisi quatenus propter Christum fiunt, sic docente nos Christo: Si quis dederit vel calicem aquæ frigidæ in nomine meo, vel propter me, nequaquam perditurus est mercedem suam. Matth. cap. 10. Marci cap. 9. Si igitur non nisi propter Christum bona sunt, certum est, non nisi propter Christum acceptari. Quæ cum ita se habeant, non otiosè adiecit Apostolus hanc particulam, Per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Indeed, good works are not rightly judged truly good except insofar as they are done on account of Christ, Christ himself teaching us this: "If anyone gives even a cup of cold water in my name, or on account of me, he will by no means lose his reward" (Matthew 10; Mark 9). If, then, they are good only on account of Christ, it is certain that they are accepted only on account of Christ. Since these things are so, the Apostle did not add this particle, "through Jesus Christ," without purpose.

units.la: Cui gloria in secula seculorum) Tertia petitio, qua petit, gloriam Dei semper magis manifestari apud nos illustrari. Huc enim tanquam ad scopum principalem referri omnia, quæ per nos fiunt, debent. Prima Corinthiorum capite decimo, Siue editis, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Et quotidie precari debemus, Sanctificetur nomen tuum, & confiteri: Quia tuum est regnum, potentia, & gloria. Sæpè verò alias solet Apostolus hoc pacto concludere siue sententias, siue disputationes, siue exhortationes, vt videre est Roman. cap. 11. Galat. 1. Ephes. 3. 1. Timoth. 1. Cærerum quòd hic Christo gloriam precatur, facit id ad confirmandam Christi diuinitatem: sicut capite secundo huius epistolæ describebatur nobis quamvis homo, tamen gloria & honore coronatus, iuxta sententiam Psalmi octaui. Nihil præterea derogat patri, cùm gloria filij sit gloria patris, omniaque inter patrem & filium, quæ ad diuinitatem attinent, sint communia. Ego & pater vnum sumus. Pater mihi dedit omnia in manu, &c.
units.tr: To whom be glory for ever and ever. This is the third petition, by which we ask that the glory of God may be ever more clearly manifested and made bright among us. For all that is done by us ought to be referred to this as the chief goal. In 1 Corinthians 10: "Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." And daily we ought to pray, "Hallowed be your name," and to confess: "For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory." Indeed the Apostle often likes to conclude in this way, whether his statements, arguments or exhortations, as may be seen in Romans 11, Galatians 1, Ephesians 3, and 1 Timothy 1. As for the fact that here glory is asked for Christ, this is done to confirm the divinity of Christ: just as in the second chapter of this epistle it was described to us that man, though a man, is nevertheless crowned with glory and honour, according to the sentence of Psalm 8. Nor does this detract at all from the Father, since the glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, and all things between the Father and the Son that pertain to the divinity are common. "I and the Father are one. The Father has given all things into my hand," etc.

units.la: In secula seculorum) Id est, in æternum. Periphrasis est, ad significandam æternitatem, Hebræis familiaris, maximè in comprecationibus.
units.tr: For ever and ever. That is, for eternity. It is a periphrasis, used to signify eternity, familiar to the Hebrews, especially in prayers.

units.la: Amen) אמן dictio omnibus nota, à verbo אמן, probabile fuit: quod tamen in pasiuo tantùm reperitur, vt אמן firmetur, 3. Regum 8.
units.tr: Amen: אמן, a word known to all, probably from the verb אמן; which, however, is found only in the passive, so that אמן is made firm, 1 Kings 8 [Obscura: possibly a misreading; the reference is to 3 Kings 8].

units.la: Hinc autem אמן, quasi אמנה verum fuit, efficiatur, firmum & solidum sit. Atq; ita ea voce vel comprecantis affectus, vel certò statuentis, quòd impleti debeat, quod petitur, perapte exprimitur, ideoq; tàm frequenter vsurpatur.
units.tr: Hence, however, אמן, as if אמנה, was true, let it be made, let it be firm and solid. And thus by this word the affection of one praying, or of one who with certainty declares that what is asked ought to be fulfilled, is very aptly expressed, and so it is used so frequently.

units.la: Cæterum ex his discimus: primò, qualia nobis potissimum à Deo sint petenda, hinc mirum vt ea, quæ salutariter propositæ sunt nobis per verbi ministros, posumus primò intelligere, vt prompti simus & parati ad bene agendum: Secundò vires assequi ad eadem perficienda: Tertiò, vt Deus dignetur, studia, conatus, & labores nostros accepctare.
units.tr: Moreover, from these things we learn: first, what things especially are to be asked of God; hence it is wonderful that we can first understand those things which have been set before us for salvation through the ministers of the Word, so that we may be prompt and ready to act well; secondly, to attain the strength to perform the same; thirdly, that God may deign to accept our zeal, endeavours and labours.

units.la: Secundò, discimus, quibus ex rebus confirmari animus noster debeat, quòd Deus pater & possit & velit nobis benefacere. Resuscitatio Christi à morte, donatio filij in mortem, propter peccata nostra, euidentissima sunt argumenta, quòd & possit, & velit nobis benefacere.
units.tr: Secondly, we learn from what things our mind ought to be strengthened, so that God the Father both can and wills to do us good. The resurrection of Christ from the dead, and the giving up of the Son to death on account of our sins, are most evident arguments that he both can and wills to do us good.

units.la: APPENDIX.
units.tr: Appendix.

units.la: OBSECRO fratres, sufferte sermonem exhortationis. Etenim paucis scripsi vobis, &c.
units.tr: I beg you, brothers, bear with this word of exhortation. For I have written to you in few words, etc.

units.la: Quemadmodum solet fieri in quibuscunque epistolis familiaribus, post expositá ea, quæ fuerant maximè necessaria, subijcit quædam de rebus minutioribus & familiaribus. Ea tamen ipsa haud vacua multiplici & salutari doctrina. Inprimis verò sciens, Hebræorum morosa semper fuisse ingenia atque arrogantia, ciuiliter ac modeste rogat, boni consulant, quicquid hac epistola perscriptum est. Certè capite 4. & 6. ac 10. paulò rigidius visus est cum eis agere, quamvis nihil præter decorum, nihilq; contra doctoris munus.
units.tr: As is customary in any familiar letters, after explaining the matters that were most necessary, he adds some remarks about smaller and more everyday things. Yet these too are not devoid of manifold and salutary teaching. Above all, knowing that the minds of the Hebrews have always been touchy and arrogant, he courteously and modestly asks them to take kindly whatever is written in this letter. Certainly in chapters 4, 6 and 10 he seemed to deal with them rather sharply, although nothing was beyond what was fitting, nor against the office of a teacher.

units.la: Regat igitur, ne offendantur, neue exasperentur. In quàm sententiam etiam Romanorum capite decimoquinto. Audacius scripsi vobis fratres ex parte, veluti commonefaciens vos.
units.tr: Therefore let them read it so that they will not be offended or exasperated. To the same effect is Romans chapter 15: "I have written to you more boldly, brothers, in part, as though reminding you."

units.la: Videntur autem duæ rationes obiter attexi, quæ ipsos ad boni consulendum debebant permouere: altera à genere seu materia epistolæ: altera à forma seu breuitate epistolæ. Quod ad materiam attinet, ait, se scripsisse sermonem exhortationis. Reijcit à se omnem suspicionem arrogantiæ: Neque enim se docere, vel arguere illos voluisse ait, sed tantum amicè exhortari & commonefacere de quibusdam rebus valde vtilibus & ad salutem necessariis.
units.tr: Two reasons seem to be added in passing, which ought to move them to take it kindly: the first from the kind or matter of the letter, the second from the form or brevity of the letter. As to the matter, he says that he has written a word of exhortation. He rejects from himself every suspicion of arrogance: he says that he did not wish to teach or rebuke them, but only to exhort and remind them in a friendly way about certain very useful things, necessary for salvation.

units.la: Quis autem tam impudens, qui, quæ hoc modo & fine fiunt, indignè ferat? Quod ad formam attinet, ait se paucis scripsisse. Nimia prolixitas parit nauseam, certè fastidium gignit, ingrata semper est, præsertim vbi errores & vitia nostra ostenduntur.
units.tr: But who is so shameless that he would take badly what is done in this way and with this purpose? As to the form, he says that he has written in few words. Excessive length breeds nausea and certainly produces weariness; it is always unwelcome, especially when our errors and faults are being pointed out.

units.la: Scripsit autem paucis Apostolus, si materiæ speties dignitatem atque amplitudinem. Late enim patet locus de duabus in Christo naturis. Late patet disputatio de abrogatione legis, & sacerdotij ac sacrificiorum legalium: de sacrificij Christi dignitate & prærogantia. Late item patet locus de iustificatione per fidem. Late patet pars postrema de officijs charitatis, ac de vita instituenda. Et tamen hæc omnia Apostolus quanta fieri potuit breuitate absoluit.
units.tr: Yet the Apostle wrote briefly, if one considers the dignity and breadth of the matter. For the topic of the two natures in Christ extends widely. The discussion of the abrogation of the law, and of the priesthood and legal sacrifices, extends widely; likewise the dignity and pre-eminence of Christ's sacrifice. The topic of justification by faith also extends widely. The final part, concerning the duties of love and the conduct of life, extends widely. And yet the Apostle has completed all these things with as much brevity as could be managed.

units.la: Cæterum hic discimus, primò, quanta humanitate modestiaque opus sit ijs, qui alios, præsertim in ecclesia docere volunt. Cauere debent, quantum fieri potest, ne quid dicant, aut faciant, quo auditores, præsertim pij & dociles exasperarentur. Pios ac dociles dico: nam palam blasphemos, & qui doceri renuunt, oportet etiam palam redarguere, increpare, &c. sicut Apostolus alibi conspicitur & fecisse, & Timotheo ac Tito præcipisse.
units.tr: Moreover, here we learn, first, how much humanity and modesty are needed by those who wish to teach others, especially in the Church. They ought to take care, as far as possible, not to say or do anything by which their hearers, especially the godly and teachable, might be exasperated. I say godly and teachable, for those who are openly blasphemous and refuse to be taught must also be openly refuted and rebuked, etc., as the Apostle is seen elsewhere both to have done and to have instructed Timothy and Titus to do.

units.la: Secundò, discimus, quotiescunque docere volumus breuitatem esse seftandam. Prolixos enim & vix aliqua gratia conditos commentarios quis citra tædium audiat?
units.tr: Second, we learn that whenever we wish to teach, brevity is to be pursued. For who would listen without weariness to lengthy commentaries seasoned with hardly any charm?

units.la: Scitote fratrem nostrum Timotheum solutum esse, cum quo, si celerius venerit, visam vos.
units.tr: Know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom, if he comes more quickly, I shall see you.

units.la: Timotheus eò commendatior esse poterat Hebræis, quòd ipse quoq; circumcisus fuerit, & matre Iudæa natus: Actorum capite decimosexto, solutum verò esse significat haud dubiè à carceribus, in quos alicubi propter confessionem veritatis coniectus fuerat. Neque enim nouum erat etiam sæpè venire in periculum, & sæpè liberari eos, qui euangelium per diuersas prouincias atque vrbes annunciabant.
units.tr: Timothy could be more commendable to the Hebrews because he too had been circumcised and was born of a Jewish mother. "Released" plainly means, without doubt, freed from the prisons into which he had at some point been cast on account of the confession of the truth, as Acts chapter 16 indicates. For it was not new that those who proclaimed the gospel through various provinces and cities should often come into danger and often be set free.

units.la: Id licet de Paulo cognoscere ex Actis Apostolicis: procul dubio quod Paulo euenit, idem etiam Timotheo potuit euenire. Ita verò tunc subinde expediebat, in carceres coniicii iterumque liberari sanctos, vt nimirum gloria euangelij illustrior eo pacto eua-deret, pluresque in agnitione veritatis confirmarentur, videndo nimirum sanctorum mirabilem constantiam, & magis mirabilem liberationem. Sic Apostolus interpretatur vtilem fuisse suam captiuitatem Romæ, Philipp 1.
units.tr: This may be learned about Paul from the Acts of the Apostles. Without doubt what happened to Paul could also have happened to Timothy. At that time it was indeed sometimes expedient that the saints be cast into prison and again set free, so that the glory of the gospel might thereby come forth more illustrious, and more people be confirmed in the knowledge of the truth, seeing, of course, the wonderful constancy of the saints and an even more wonderful deliverance. So the Apostle interprets his own captivity at Rome as having been useful, Philippians 1.

units.la: Quo verò istud facilius credamus de Timotheo, faciunt præclara Pauli de eodem testimonia. Nam integerrimum fuisse, diligentissimumque in subeundis propter euangelium laboribus, passim prædicat, cum in duabus epistolis ad ipsum scriptis, tùm verò & Philipp. 2. 1. Thess 3.
units.tr: To make it easier to believe this about Timothy, Paul's excellent testimonies about him serve well. For he everywhere proclaims that Timothy was most upright and most diligent in undertaking labours for the sake of the gospel, both in the two letters written to him and in Philippians 2 and 1 Thessalonians 3.

units.la: Porrò ideo voluit significare Hebræis, liberaturum esse Timotheum, non tàm, vt spem faceret sui aduentus, posteaquam natus erat fidum suum Achatem, quàm vt indicaret, gaudendum esse Hebræis pro fratre restituto, sicut alias condolendum, quotiescunque frater affligitur. Atqui venturum se promittit, simul vt confirmentur pij, neque patiantur, se vlla noua doctrina moueri, tantisper dùm Paulus ipse adueniat, qui de omnibus poterit sapientissimè respondere: simul & coerceantur aliquo modo pseudoapostoli & falsi doctores: qui audientes de aduentu Apostoli aut non ita audacter sua proponebant, aut in totum se subducebant. Sic ad Corinthios scribens ait, Cætera cùm venero disponam: & alibi similes causas fui aduentus insinuat.
units.tr: Moreover, he wished to signal to the Hebrews that Timothy would be set free, not so much to give hope of his arrival, after he had sent his faithful Achaicus, as to show that the Hebrews should rejoice over a brother restored, just as they should grieve whenever a brother is afflicted. Yet he promises that he himself will come, so that the godly may be strengthened and not allow themselves to be moved by any new teaching while Paul himself is still coming, who will be able to answer most wisely about everything; and at the same time that the false apostles and false teachers may be restrained in some way, who, on hearing of the Apostle's coming, either did not put forward their views so boldly or withdrew altogether. So, writing to the Corinthians, he says, "I will set the rest in order when I come," and elsewhere he hints at similar reasons for his coming.

units.la: Salutate omnes, qui præsunt vobis, & omnes sanctos.
units.tr: Greet all those who rule over you, and all the saints.

units.la: Non sunt præteréunda officia humanitatis. Eleganti verò partitione videtur vti, dùm priore membro salutat eos, qui præsunt, id est, ministros verbi, prophetas doctores, & similes, quos paulò ante commendauit, aciusit in honore haberi: posteriori membro promiscuam multitudinem, quam nomine sanctorum intelligit. Sùt enim omnes illi sancti, qui in sana fide sunt confirmati, & adhærét ecclesiæ, ab ea nequaquam resciliì per ex communicationem. Sancti autem sunt propter Christum, cuius sanguine in baptismo abluti sunt, sanctificati sunt: 1, Corinth. 6. Salutant vos Itali) Fides nunc coniungit Italos Hebraeis, qui antea erant animis maximè disiuncti. Quia in Christo Iesu non est amplius neque Iudaeus, neque Graecus, neque barbarus, neque Scytha, neque mas, neque foemina. Omnes unius corporis membra, sub vno capite Christo. Liquet verò hinc, epistolam hanc scriptam in Italia. Inuenio in graecis exemplaribus subiectum, missam esse hanc epistolam Roma, & quidem per Timotheū. Illud quidem satis vero consentaneum est, maximè quia proximè adscripta est salutatio nomine Italorum. Sed de Timotheo nescio an affirmari quicquam possit: id autem; tum, quia scripsit iamiam, ac renunciauit illis, Timotheum esse solutum. Quorsum opus fuisset in literis renunciare solutum, si coram poterant eum, dū redderet literas, videre? Deinde, qua ratione diceret, quòd cū eo vellet ipsos citò inuisere, si iam reddere literas idem debebat? Magis significatur, aliò fuisse à Paulo amandatum, ac reditum eius breui expectari. Vide alium librum.
units.tr: Courtesies of this kind should not be passed over. The author uses a fine division here: in the first clause he greets those who rule, that is, the ministers of the Word, prophets, teachers and others like them whom he has just commended, and he wants them held in honour. In the second clause he greets the general body of people, whom he calls saints. For all those are saints who have been confirmed in sound faith and who cling to the Church, and who are in no way cut off from it by excommunication. They are saints because of Christ, by whose blood they were washed and sanctified in baptism (1 Cor. 6). Those from Italy greet you. Faith now joins the Italians to the Hebrews, who before were most widely separated in their minds, for in Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither male nor female. All are members of one body, under one head, Christ. It is clear from this that the letter was written in Italy. In the Greek copies I find a subscription saying that this letter was sent from Rome, and indeed through Timothy. That is quite consistent with the truth, especially since the greeting in the name of the Italians is added right after. But I do not know whether anything can be affirmed about Timothy. For the author has just written, and told them, that Timothy has been released. Why would there have been any need to report in a letter that he was released, if they could see him in person when he delivered the letter? Again, on what ground would he say that he wished to visit them soon with Timothy, if Timothy were already to deliver the letter? It is rather implied that Paul had sent Timothy somewhere else, and that his return was expected shortly. See another book.

units.la: SVBSCRIPTIO.
units.tr: SUBSCRIPTION.

units.la: Gratia cum omnibus vobis: Amen. Subscriptio Apostolo usitata. Sic & in aliis epistolis subscribere solet Apostolus, ut ipse testatur 2. Thessal. 4. Nos alibi eam expositimus.
units.tr: Grace be with you all. Amen. This is the subscription the Apostle customarily used. He is accustomed to subscribe in this way in his other letters as well, as he himself attests (2 Thess. 4). We have explained it elsewhere.

units.la: EPISTOLAE AD HEBRAEOS FINIS.
units.tr: THE END OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS.

units.la: LOCI COMMVNES PRAECIPVI IN HOC OPERE VTILITER, PIE, ET orthodoxè explicati.
units.tr: THE PRINCIPAL COMMON PLACES OF THIS WORK, USEFULLY, PIOUSLY AND ORTHODOXLY EXPLAINED.

units.la: Partis primæ.
units.tr: Of the first part.

units.la: Cap.1. 1 | De Euangelij revelatione per filium Dei Iesum Christum, eiusq; autoritate divina.
units.tr: Chap. 1. 1 | On the revelation of the gospel through the Son of God, Jesus Christ, and its divine authority.

units.la: 2 | De Christi divinitate, potentia, & gloria sedentis ad dexteram Dei patris: ubi varij & foedi errores de persona Christi, credentiumq; salute, sunt refutati.
units.tr: 2 | On the divinity, power and glory of Christ, seated at the right hand of God the Father: where various and foul errors concerning the person of Christ and the salvation of believers are refuted.

units.la: 3 | De Communicatione Idiomatum, & proprietatibus naturarum inconfusis in una eademq; persona.
units.tr: 3 | On the communication of idioms, and the unconfused properties of the natures in one and the same person.

units.la: 4 | De angelis, eorundemq; natura, officijs & effectibus: & quòd Christo longè sint inferiores, eidemq; honorem ac cultum summum deferant.
units.tr: 4 | On angels, their nature, offices and effects: and that they are far inferior to Christ, and render him the highest honour and worship.

units.la: 5 | De Christi æternitate, & conditione cœli ac terræ: de creaturarum mutabilitate ex psal.102.
units.tr: 5 | On the eternity of Christ, and the condition of heaven and earth: on the mutability of creatures, from Psalm 102.

units.la: 6 | De mundi excidio & fine seculi: &, an mundus fuerit æternus: an periturus secundum substantiam, an uero secundum qualitates tantum: & qualis rerum status futurus sit post diem extremum siue nouissimum.
units.tr: 6 | On the destruction of the world and the end of the age: and whether the world was eternal; whether it will perish as to substance, or only as to its qualities; and what the state of things will be after the last or final day.

units.la: Cap.2. 7 | An epistola hæc ad Hebræos D. Pauli sit, uel alterius cuiusdam autoris.
units.tr: Chap. 2. 7 | Whether this epistle to the Hebrews is by St. Paul or by some other author.

units.la: 8 | De miraculis veris & falsis, & quatenus ea ad doctrinæ confirmationem seruiant: & an mali mira edere possint.
units.tr: 8 | On true and false miracles, and how far they serve to confirm doctrine; and whether evil men can work miracles.

units.la: 9 | De dignitate & excellentia hominis.
units.tr: 9 | On the dignity and excellence of man.

units.la: 10 | De humiliatione Christi in carne, eiusq; efficacia, & causa mortis.
units.tr: 10 | On the humiliation of Christ in the flesh, its efficacy, and the cause of his death.

units.la: 11 | Cur pij, qui à iure, iugo, & tyrannide peccati & mortis sunt liberati, peccato & morti adhuc dum sint obnoxij.
units.tr: 11 | Why the godly, who have been freed from the right, the yoke and the tyranny of sin and death, are still subject to sin and death.

units.la: 12 | De tentationibus piorum & earundem usu.
units.tr: 12 | On the temptations of the godly and their use.

units.la: 13 | Cur Christus non angelos, sed semen Abrahæ assumpserit. Error Valentini, Apellis, Marcionitarum confutatur.
units.tr: 13 | Why Christ took on the seed of Abraham and not angels. The error of Valentinus, Apelles and the Marcionites is refuted.

units.la: 14. Errores de diuinitate, & humanitate Christi, eorundemq; refutatio. Annexa his est interpretis pia & docta confessio de persona & duabus naturis Christi.
units.tr: 14. Errors concerning the divinity and humanity of Christ, and their refutation. Attached to these is the godly and learned confession of the interpreter concerning the person and the two natures of Christ.

units.la: Cap.3. 15 | Christi & Mosis collatio: ex qua Christi & pontificatus eius excellentia elucet. Vbi veri ac pij ministri Dei virtutes recensentur.
units.tr: Chap. 3. 15 | A comparison of Christ and Moses, from which the excellence of Christ and of his priesthood shines forth. Here the virtues of the true and godly ministers of God are enumerated.

units.la: 17 | Vnam eandemq; esse ecclesiam Christi & Mosis, veteris & noui testamenti: ubi conuenientia atq; discrimen legis & euangelij notatur.
units.tr: 16 | That the church of Christ and that of Moses, of the Old and New Testament, are one and the same: where the agreement and difference of law and gospel are noted.

units.la: 17 | Euangelij authoritas, contemptorum poena.
units.tr: 17 | The authority of the gospel; the punishment of those who despise it.

units.la: 18 | Vsus Scripturæ sacræ.
units.tr: 18 | The use of holy Scripture.

units.la: 19 | De indurations cordis, & libero arbitrio. Et an hominis tantum sit induratio, an uero & Deo ex parte ea ascribenda, &c.
units.tr: 19 | On the hardening of the heart and free will: whether hardening belongs to man alone, or whether it is also in part to be ascribed to God, etc.

units.la: Cap.4. 20 | De requie & sabbatismo spirituali.
units.tr: Chap. 4. 20 | On rest and spiritual sabbatism.

units.la: 21 | De uerbi Dei vi in pijs & impijs.
units.tr: 21 | On the power of God's word in the godly and the ungodly.

units.la: Loci partis secundæ.
units.tr: Common places of the second part.

units.la: 1 | An lex, manifestato euangelio, sit abrogata.
units.tr: 1 | Whether the law has been abrogated now that the gospel has been made manifest.

units.la: 2 | Abrogatio sacerdotij, sacrificiorum, & ceremoniarum veteris testamenti.
units.tr: 2 | The abrogation of the priesthood, sacrifices and ceremonies of the Old Testament.

units.la: 3 | Christus uerus ac summus pontifex, per omnia tentatus, cœlos ingreditur. Eiusdem φιλανθρωπία, συμπάθεια, & misericordia, ad fidei & conscientiæ nostræ confirmationem declaratur: per eundem pontificem thronus gratiæ credentibus est patefactus.
units.tr: 3 | Christ, the true and supreme high priest, tempted in all things, enters the heavens. His philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία], sympathy [συμπάθεια] and mercy are set forth, for the confirmation of our faith and conscience; through this same high priest the throne of grace has been opened to believers.

units.la: Cap.5. 4 | De sacrificio Christi perfecto in ara crucis oblato, per quod sacrificia legalia consummata & abrogata sunt.
units.tr: Chap. 5. 4 | On the perfect sacrifice of Christ offered on the altar of the cross, through which the legal sacrifices were fulfilled and abrogated.

units.la: 5 | De ordine Melchisedecico: ubi & discrimen notandum est veteris & noui testamenti.
units.tr: 5 | On the Melchizedekian order: where the difference between the Old and New Testament is also to be noted.

units.la: 6 | De uocatione uniuersali & particulari: quomodo fiat, & administranda sit.
units.tr: 6 | On the universal and particular calling: how it comes about, and how it is to be administered.

units.la: 7 | De progressu in fide & doctrina euangelij. In ijsdem hærere elementis semper, periculosum ac turpe est.
units.tr: 7 | On progress in faith and in the doctrine of the gospel. It is always dangerous and shameful to remain stuck in the same elementary things.

units.la: Cap.6. 8 | De Catechismo & institutione Christiana, deq; septem fundamentis eiusdem, uidelicet, pœnitentia, fide, baptismate, doctrina, impositione manuum, resurrectione mortuorum, & iudicio æterno.
units.tr: Chap. 6. 8 | On the catechism and Christian instruction, and its seven foundations, namely repentance, faith, baptism, doctrine, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.

units.la: 9 | An homini lapso ad pœnitentiam & gratiam Dei sit reditus. Erroris Catharorum & Nouatianorum refutatio. Cap.6. & 10.
units.tr: 9 | Whether there is a return to repentance and the grace of God for a fallen man. Refutation of the errors of the Cathari and Novatians. Chap. 6 and 10.

units.la: 10 | Verbi Dei fructus, & impiorum sterilitas.
units.tr: 10 | The fruit of God's word, and the barrenness of the ungodly.

units.la: 11 | Fide Abraham assequitur promissiones Dei.
units.tr: 11 | By faith Abraham obtains the promises of God.

units.la: 12 | Promissio Dei iureiurando confirmata certificat credentes.
units.tr: 12 | God's promise, confirmed by an oath, assures believers.

units.la: Cap.7. 13 | De sacerdotio & regno Christi: & collatio Christi cum Melchisedeco, deq; excellentia ordinis Melchisedecici.
units.tr: Chap. 7. 13 | On the priesthood and kingdom of Christ: and a comparison of Christ with Melchizedek, and on the excellence of the Melchizedekian order.

units.la: 14 | De uarijs decimarum generibus, & quatenus unicuiq; pendendæ sint.
units.tr: 14 | On the various kinds of tithes, and to what extent each person is to pay them.

units.la: 15 | De benedictione parentum erga liberos, & maledictione eorundem.
units.tr: 15 | On the blessing of parents towards their children, and the curse of the same.

units.la: 16 Sacerdotio Christi translatum esse sacerdotium Leuiticum, imo hac ipsa translatione abrogatam etiam esse legem, & quatenus lex sit abrogata, quisq; eius sit usus.
units.tr: 16 | That the Levitical priesthood has been transferred to the priesthood of Christ; indeed, by this very transfer the law too has been abrogated; and, insofar as the law is abrogated, what the use of it is for each person.

units.la: 17 De ceremoniis, varietate, usu, abrogatione, & retentione earundem. Vbi & de obligatione conscientiarum sermo fit.
units.tr: 17 | On ceremonies: their variety, use, abrogation and retention. Here also the obligation of consciences is discussed.

units.la: 18 Dignitas sacerdotij Christi & euangelij, qua praefertur legi & sacerdotio Leuitico.
units.tr: 18 | The dignity of the priesthood of Christ and of the gospel, by which it is preferred to the law and the Levitical priesthood.

units.la: 19 De iuramento, veritate & constantia Dei.
units.tr: 19 | On the oath, and the truth and constancy of God.

units.la: 20 De poenitentia Dei.
units.tr: 20 | On the repentance of God.
